[THE TWELVE BOOKS ON THE TRINITY.]

[Col. 0009]

PREFACE TO THE BOOKS ON THE TRINITY.

[Col. 0009A] I. These books attributed to Athanasius. The great praise they won for Hilary.—One would rightly be thought to waste time if one spent it vindicating these books for their author. For although Philip, Abbot of Bonne-Espérance, and a certain John, his contemporary and friend, once saw them ascribed to Athanasius, they afterward recognized from more accurately corrected manuscripts that they proceeded from Hilary. On this point, moreover, the whole antiquity of former ages speaks in such agreement with itself that nothing is more certain or more firmly established among the things received from our forebears. Especially on account of these books, Hilary earned among both Latins and Greeks such a reputation for learning, faith, and eloquence that—something very rare—the same books were highly commended even by his adversaries. Thus Sozomen, recording the common report, has left this testimony in Book III, chapter 14: “They declare that Hilary’s books on the faith were very highly commended even by those who maintained an opinion contrary to the Catholic faith.”

II. The ancients give them more than one title.—The agreement of the ancients in entitling them is not so uniform. Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under Marcellus and Hilary; the ancient Code of Canons of the Roman Church, chapter 41; and Ado of Vienne in his *Chronicle*, entitle them *Against the Arians*. Many others, far more numerous and no less authoritative, call them *On the Faith*. Among the foremost are Rufinus, *History*, Book I, chapter 31; Cassian, *On the Incarnation*, Book VII, chapter 24; Pope Leo, Letter otherwise numbered 97, chapter 3; the Fathers of the Council of Chalcedon, Act 2, p. [Col. 0009C] 357; Theodoret, *Dialogue* II, p. 106; and Leontius of Byzantium, Book I *Against Nestorius and Eutyches*, where he incorrectly commends Hilary as one of the Fathers of the Nicene Synod. They are praised under no other title by Alcuin, *Against Felix*, Book IV; Ratramnus of Corbie, *Spicilegium*, vol. VII, p. 335; John the Deacon, in his still unpublished commentary on the Pentateuch; and Hincmar, *On Predestination*, chapter 25. The prayer formerly customarily read amid the most sacred sacrifices of the Mass on the feast of St. Hilary openly supports this title; it says: “O God, who, poured into the heart of blessed Hilary, bishop, as though from thy temple, gavest answers of FAITH,” etc. The blessing entered in a very ancient Pontifical of the Church of Évreux for the Kalends of November, on the feast of St. Hilary, appears to allude to this as well: “May he be an advocate with thee for us, who then stood as thy champion against heretics; so that, by thy recompense, the people may increase beyond number, because the priest laboured IN THE FAITH,” etc. But in Cassiodorus, *Institutions*, Book I, chapter 16, they are found entitled *On the Trinity*, with Fortunatus, *Life of St. Hilary*, Book I, agreeing; Philip the abbot calls them *On the Faith of the Most Holy Trinity* in accordance with these authorities. Augustine praises the same books in Letter CLXXX, no. 3, and in *On the Trinity*, Book VI, chapter 10, but in each place refrains from specifying their title. We are also persuaded that Ambrose had made much use of them, even from the first books of his own *On the Faith*, in which we repeatedly observe many things expressed in imitation of these books of Hilary. Although he rendered them in his own style, it is still apparent whence they were drawn. But since, as was his custom, he does not even name the man from whose works he profited, we have nothing from him by which the matter at issue may be settled for us—unless perhaps we say that he too adopted from Hilary his title *On the Faith*. Yet the Emperor Gratian seems in some manner to have prescribed this title for him.

III. Nor do the manuscripts agree more closely in this respect.—Nor can anything more certain [Col. 0010B] be established from ancient copies. In the older ones, indeed, a title is lacking; in some others it is *On the Faith*, in others *On the Trinity*, in the Vendôme manuscript *On the Faith of the Holy Trinity against the Arians*—to which the Remigian manuscript adds “or the other heretics”—while the Teller manuscript bears the heading *On the Trinity against All Heresies*. But the following heading, remarkable beyond the rest, is found in the Corbie manuscript and in another of the Sorbonne manuscripts:

“Here are contained twelve books of Bishop Hilary, which he wrote in exile, having been sent into exile by the Arian heretics on account of the unity of the Godhead of the Lord Jesus Christ with the Father. Most blessed presbyter Barbario, in Christ Jesus our Lord, use them happily with all who belong to you. May faith, hope, and charity remain in our hearts.”

The Pratelles manuscript bears the same inscription with a few changes; and there, instead of “happily with all who belong to you,” one reads, “happily in your ministrations.” We devote some effort to weighing the title, being less concerned with the inscription itself than with discovering the author’s intention from it.

IV. They may be entitled *On the Faith*.—Although it does not at first appear why this work should be entitled *On the Faith*, nevertheless, if the plan of the whole work is examined more closely, the title will not seem unsuitable for books in which the consubstantiality of the Son with the Father—the chief article and foundation of our faith—is everywhere defended; and which were chiefly undertaken so that the faith in which we have been reborn might be held unimpaired and entire. Nor indeed does it seem likely that so many and such diverse Greek and Latin writers could have converged on the same title unless it had been established by the author himself. This conjecture is strongly supported by the fact that in Book I, no. 16, Hilary himself declares that he set his mind to writing these books in order to restrain those who corrupt the sacrament, or mystery, of the Gospel faith. Indeed, in no. 34 he states that the endeavour of his entire work must be directed to setting forth the greatest and weightiest understanding of the whole faith. Hence in Book X, no. 5, he calls everything he has discussed up to that point “a demonstration of the whole faith.” What he means by “the sacrament of the Gospel faith,” however, he explains in his commentary on Matthew, chapter 13, no. 6, in these words: “Although [this concerns] the sacrament of faith—that is, the unity of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit,” etc.; where he indicates that by “the sacrament of faith” he means the same thing as the mystery of the Trinity. For the moment we pass over the distinctive defence of faith found in these books. For the first book immediately proceeds to persuade every reader that, in matters concerning God, one must believe not human judgment but God’s own testimonies concerning himself. Then the third book seems to strive toward this one end: to convict man of his own weakness in comprehending divine things, and to teach that he has no safeguard except faith. This, moreover, is repeatedly urged in the fourth, fifth, and other books.

[Col. 0011B] V. In what sense they are *Against All Heresies*.—Thus they have not without reason been called *Against All Heresies*. For in them not only is the head and origin of all heresies generally—that which permits each person to confine faith within the limits of his own understanding and to twist the Scriptures to his own opinions—everywhere overthrown and crushed; but the blasphemies of Arius, Photinus, and the ancient heretics Ebion, Valentinus, Mani, Hieracas, and Sabellius, already disseminated at that time, are also refuted. Indeed, the heresies not yet arisen of Apollinaris, Macedonius, Nestorius, Eutyches, the Sacramentarians, and so forth, are anticipated as well. Moreover, since Athanasius in his Letter to Epictetus calls the Nicene Synod “a trophy against every heresy” (*τροπαῖον οὖσαν πάσης αἱρέσεως*), and since the Creed of that Synod is found entitled *Against All Heresies* in ancient copies, these books, almost with the same right, deserved to be distinguished by the same title as defenders of that same faith.

VI. They are directed chiefly against the Arians.—Yet it must be admitted that they were written chiefly against the Arian sect. Hilary himself declares his purpose in Book I, no. 17. Having spoken of the Arians, whose name he customarily spares, he immediately adds: “Therefore my mind was inflamed to answer their fury.” Nor does the beginning of Book VII—“This seventh book is written by us against the mad rashness of the new heresy”—mean anything else than to indicate that his argument hitherto has been directed against the one Arian heresy. And, lest we linger too long over superfluous proofs, let Book X, no. 8 suffice. There Hilary, though approaching the end of this work, nevertheless testifies that he has been dealing with the same and only heretics whose most foolish professions he had answered up to that point. Nor is it obscure what he calls their “most foolish professions,” since in Books IV and VI he gives in full the letter of Arius and his associates sent to Alexander, in which they had set down their unbelief; and he is wholly occupied, both in those books and those following, with refuting it. To this belongs that part of the title found in the Vendôme manuscript:

“In this codex, the fourth book in order of Blessed Hilary most clearly unveils the deceptive doctrine of the heretics. The Teacher himself, having prefaced the exposition of their unbelief—the exposition which they drew from their own books, by which they strove to weaken the Church’s faith—inserted it into his volume; namely, so that, once their crafty propositions had been recognized, he might destroy their mad doctrine by the answers of the Law, the Prophets, and the Gospel testimonies, and might establish the Church’s faith more firmly.”

VII. In order to refute them more effectively, Sabellius is also refuted.—He appears to contend with no less effort against the inventions of Sabellius than against those of Arius; but his sole object in this is to strike down the Arians more effectively. As he himself observes in Book X, no. 5, he would strive in vain to crush them even with the strongest force of arguments so long as he left against himself even the slightest suspicion of the Sabellian taint. “For,” he says, “I speak under the watch of all heretics, who hang upon my lips for opportunities furnished by each individual word.” Yet he is confident that, though they hang upon his words in this way, he has removed every occasion for slander against himself, so that in Book X, no. 5, he is not afraid to say: “For now also, according to the gift of the Holy Spirit, we have so framed the demonstration of the whole faith that they could not invent even an accusation against us.”

VIII. Though written against the Arians, the books are not entitled *Against the Arians*.—Although we readily grant that this entire work was written against the Arians, we shall nevertheless with difficulty concede that it was entitled *Against the Arians*. For who would believe that Hilary, who deliberately abstains from identifying Arians by name, would have written that name on the very front of his books? For only twice does the word “Arius,” and once the term “Ariomaniacs,” slip from his pen in Book VI; elsewhere he entirely spares the sect’s name. It is called now “this new heresy” (Book VII, no. 3), now “the recent heresy” (ibid., no. 6), now “the unbelief of our own time” (Book XII, no. 17). Likewise, its authors are heard designated in veiled words: either “preachers of no true God,” or “certain preachers of this time” (Book II, no. 4), or “the present heretics” (Book VII, no. 6), or, in the same place, “those who preach the Son unlike the Father,” or “preachers of a new Christ” (Book XI, no. 4), or even “preachers of a creature” (Book I, no. 26)—never Arians.

IX. Hilary displayed his moderation in these books.—Just as he gave an outstanding proof of prudence when he carefully guarded against appearing to favour Sabellius, so by this manner of proceeding he disclosed a singular moderation of spirit. He gives much clearer testimony of it in this: throughout all these books he is content to overthrow the perverse teaching of the Arians and attacks no one by name. At times you hear him lamenting the evils by which the Church was then miserably afflicted through them; but you wait in vain for him to reveal the name of even one person through whom she suffered so unjustly. Once, in Book X, his own exile is mentioned; but as though forgetful of the injury done to him, he seeks rather a reason to rejoice in it than a reason to complain. Nor should anyone think that it conflicts with this purpose of moderation that he frequently calls the Arian heresy not merely recent, but also mad and impious. It had to be indicated by definite marks, since its proper name was withheld. It was commonly called “mad,” moreover, because the character of the name suited its wicked disposition. Thus Gregory of Nazianzus says, *Oration* XXI, no. 3: “Arius, named after madness” (*Ἀρεῖος τῆς μανίας ἐπώνυμος*); and again, in *Oration* XXIX, no. 4, he calls this sect “the madness of Arius, aptly so named” (*τὴν Ἀρείου καλῶς ὀνομασθεῖσαν μανίαν*). Why, then, should a man of moderation not also call impious a sect that separated the most excellent Father from the beloved Son? Finally, Hilary himself, conscious of how moderately he had conducted himself in those books and throughout the entire period of his exile, when he found himself constrained by a certain necessity to write against Constantius, freely testified that up to that time he had written or spoken “nothing abusive against the times, nothing defamatory or worthy of their impiety against that which then falsely claimed to be Christ’s Church” (*Book against Constantius*, no. 2). Therefore we have reason to believe that one thus disposed did not entitle his writings *Against the Arians*.

X. The title *On the Trinity* should be retained.—It is less certain whether he called them *On the Faith*. But although, as has been shown above, much supports this title, and although the example of Ambrose may be added, who called the books he wrote against the Arian sect *On the Faith*, still, since the title is not accurate unless “faith” is taken to mean the mystery of the Trinity, there is no sufficiently weighty reason to alter the ancient title *On the Trinity*, received for many centuries. Fortunatus especially supports this title; his authority deserves to be valued above all others because he could have seen Hilary’s own autograph manuscript. For if, in his age, the letter of the pious bishop to Abra was preserved at Poitiers as a treasured gift, how much more so those celebrated books? The same title is confirmed by liturgical prayers customarily read at the annual solemnity of Blessed Hilary; they are still preserved in two manuscripts of the Church of St. Gatian at Tours, written at least eight hundred years ago: in one under the first of November, and in the other under the thirteenth of January. They run as follows:

“O God, who hast consecrated for thy people the solemnly recurring feast of thy venerable confessor and bishop, Blessed Hilary, whose tongue in the world thundered so loudly for the equality of the HOLY TRINITY that thy soldier overthrew the prince of this world,” etc.

The same prayer, assigned to the Kalends of November, occurs in Sacramentary no. 3865 of the Royal Library, apparently about nine hundred years old, in which the Nicene Creed appears without the addition *Filioque*.

XI. How this title is fulfilled.—Certainly Hilary himself seems in some way eager to fulfil this title. In defending the true faith of the Trinity and treating separately of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, he devotes the whole of Book II to the matter; accordingly, in Book I, no. 22, he calls it “a brief discourse on the Trinity as demonstrated.” Thus, not without reason, at the beginning of Book IV he professes that in the preceding books he has sufficiently set forth the faith and confession of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Thereafter, indeed, he applies himself more diligently to defending the consubstantiality of the Father and Son, concerning which almost the entire controversy lay. Yet he does not forget his intention: before the end of the work he returns to the aim prescribed by the title, and he does not conclude Book XII until he has defended the divinity of the entire Trinity, and specifically of the Holy Spirit. Here should not be omitted what he writes in Book I concerning the argument of the said Book XII: namely, that he has removed defective and irreligious teachings concerning the Holy Spirit, in order that apostolic and evangelical authority might contain, within its saving definition, the uninjured and uncontaminated sacrament, or mystery, of the regenerating TRINITY; and so that no one might dare, by the judgment of human understanding, to place among creatures the Spirit of God, whom we receive as the pledge of immortality and for participation in the divine nature (Book I, no. 36). From this it is plain that in these books he intended to defend the mystery of the regenerating Trinity, so that nothing might be lacking from the complete exposition of the whole faith received in baptism.

XII. Erasmus wrongly observes that the Holy Spirit is not called God.—We can scarcely restrain our indignation at Erasmus for writing in his preface about our learned bishop and the ancient Fathers as though they had feared to assert the divinity of the Holy Spirit. He does indeed make them worshippers of the Holy Spirit, but in such a way as to suggest at the same time either that they worshipped one whom they did not certainly know to be God, or that they did not dare confess in speech or writing what they believed in their hearts. Erasmus’s cleverness is not new. Long before him, according to Gregory of Nazianzus, *Oration* XXXVII, no. 52, the Pneumatomachians had objected that nowhere in Scripture did they find the name “God” applied to the Holy Spirit. The same bishop praises Basil, *Oration* XX, no. 100, because, yielding somewhat to their dispute in the hope of bringing them gently back to the truth, he had very judiciously refrained for a time in his books *On the Holy Spirit* from the word which they abhorred. Meanwhile, by other terms taken from Scripture, by testimonies having precisely the same force and wholly beyond doubt, and by necessary arguments, he so constrained his opponents that they could in no way resist or contend against him. Yet Gregory testifies that Basil never hesitated on other occasions, whether in private or public discourses, to call the Holy Spirit God.

XIII. He is called God by the ancients and in the Scriptures.—The discussion would stray too far from its purpose if we undertook here to enumerate all the ancients who asserted this same thing. Let the following testimony of Tertullian stand for all, *Against Praxeas*, no. 13:

“We indeed define two, Father and Son, and now three together with the Holy Spirit, according to the principle of the economy, which creates number; lest, as your perversity maintains, the Father himself should be believed to have been born and to have suffered—which it is not lawful to believe, since it has not been handed down thus. Yet we never utter from our mouth ‘two Gods’ or ‘two Lords’: not as though the Father were not God, and the Son God, and the HOLY SPIRIT GOD, and each one God,” etc.

Nor should it be conceded that the Holy Spirit is nowhere called God in the Scriptures. Ambrose, *On the Holy Spirit*, Book III, chapter 9, proves the contrary especially from Peter’s words, Acts III, 3, etc.: first, “Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit?” and then, “You have not lied to men, but to God.”

XIV. He trifles who, possessing the thing, seeks the name of the thing. Why Hilary does not attribute the name God to the Holy Spirit.—But whatever may be said about this controversy, what Gregory replied to the aforesaid heretics, who were wise in the letter rather than the spirit, in *Oration* XXXVII, no. 56, may now readily be retorted against Erasmus. We compare him with the Pneumatomachians in this method of argument only, and by no means wish him to be compared with them in faith. Gregory teaches, then, that those trifle who, leaving realities aside, pursue syllables, and who, though they hear that Scripture attributes to the Holy Spirit things consistent with no one except God, still ask where the name “God” is applied to him. For what difference is there whether one says “ten” or “twice five,” “man” or “a mortal rational animal”? Surely, those who approve this reasoning of Gregory will not suppose that Hilary’s failure to join the name “God” to the designation “Holy Spirit” is to be attributed to an empty scruple. Rather they will believe that he acted thus because he was accustomed to understand the very nature of God by the name “Spirit” alone. Nor is there any doubt that, beyond that outward sound of letters, he set down in his writings something more explicit by which he commended the divinity of the Holy Spirit.

XV. He consistently proclaims the divine nature in him.—First, whenever he insists—as he often does—that the words of baptism indicate and require belief that the Son is consubstantial with the Father, he equally professes that the Holy Spirit is consubstantial with both. For the words of baptism signify no more that the Son than that the Holy Spirit is of one nature and substance with the Father. Moreover, in his commentary on Matthew, chapter 13, no. 6, he expressly declares that in Father, Son, and Holy Spirit all things are one, without any support from an external cause which might, after the manner of leaven, bind and unite them. Thus in *On the Trinity*, Book II, no. 28, he regards Father, Son, and Holy Spirit as a certain whole that cannot in any way be separated. “For he,” he says expressly concerning the Holy Spirit, “who is joined to the confession of Father and Son cannot be separated from the confession of Father and Son. For the whole is incomplete for us if anything is missing from the whole.” Hence, in the same Book II, no. 4, he marks the teachings of the Arians as new and fabricated by human ingenuity, because they dissolve the truth of this perfect mystery by devising differences of substances “in THINGS SO COMMON.” Therefore he held it to have been handed down by God and always believed in the Church that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are common realities, and that there are no differences of substance in them. He was so convinced that the Holy Spirit is consubstantial with the Father that in Book IX, no. 72, he proves that the Father and Son are of one substance from the fact that the Holy Spirit receives his own from those things which are the Father’s, just as from those which are the Son’s. “For,” he says there, “the Holy Spirit was not receiving from creatures. Therefore he was receiving from the Creator.” As Ferrandus the Deacon says in his letter to Anatolius: “Every thing is either God or a creature: if it is God, it is not a creature; if it is a creature, it is not God.” Since, further, our Hilary knew with certainty that the Holy Spirit receives his substance from God the Creator, he took great pains, as we have heard from Book I, no. 36, to prevent anyone from daring to place him among creatures. For it seemed absurd to him that he should not be of incorruptible and divine nature whom we receive as the pledge of immortality and for participation in the divine nature. Whoever wishes for more should consult Book XII, no. 54 and following, where it is clearly established that the Holy Spirit is of the same nature, power, and substance as the Father.

XVI. A clear argument for the divinity of the Holy Spirit.—We cite from that passage only one argument, drawn from the Apostle’s words: “For the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God.” Turning to the Father, Hilary addresses him with great reverence for the Holy Spirit:

“No reality but thine penetrates thee; nor does a power foreign and alien to thee measure the depth of thy immeasurable majesty. What enters into thee is THINE; and whatever is within thee through the power of the searching [Spirit] is not alien.”

It is as though he said: He who searches all things, even the depths of God, measures the immeasurable majesty; but he measures it only if he is himself immeasurable and equal to that majesty. Again: He who searches the depths of God must be inward to God himself; but nothing alien to him, or not of the same substance with him, is inward to him. Therefore the Holy Spirit must be confessed to be immeasurable, equal to God, and of the same power and substance with him. More briefly, but no less clearly, he teaches the same in Book II, no. 31, when he writes that God is worshipped in the Holy Spirit where he is worshipped in the Spirit; and where he is worshipped in the Spirit, he is worshipped only in himself.

XVII. What is said about the Holy Spirit does not show that these books were composed after the rise of the Macedonian heresy.—[Col. 0016C] On account of these and other arguments so clear in proving the divinity of the Holy Spirit, some maintain that these books were written after the rise of the Macedonian heresy, and consequently after the year 360, when Macedonius, deposed from his episcopate by the Synod of Constantinople, began to spread his error. Nothing, however, necessarily follows from this. For who does not know that Arius undermined the divinity of the Holy Spirit no less than that of the Son? In his *Thalia*, cited by Athanasius, *Orations against the Arians*, II, p. 312, he declares that the substances of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are divided, disunited, disconnected, alien, and without communion. Athanasius, rebuking him on p. 315, says: “How could he hold a right opinion about the Holy Spirit, who blasphemes the Word that supplies the Spirit?” Hilary uses precisely similar reasoning in Book II, no. 4: “What wonder if they think differently about the Holy Spirit, when they are such rash authors of teaching that his Giver—the Word, namely—was created, changed, and abolished?” He immediately adds that the Holy Spirit is unknown to them because they are ignorant of the Son, his author. Can he, I ask, have said this against supporters of Macedonius, who were not heard to hold false views about the Word; whom he himself praised in the Book on the Synods as bringing hope of restoring the true faith; to whom, finally, at Constantinople after the Council of Seleucia, he did not refuse communion, and from whom he even obtained letters, together with the other bishops of Gaul, when the Council of Paris had been convened?

XVIII. It is more probable that the divinity of the Holy Spirit was asserted against Arians than against Macedonians.—It is therefore much more probable that Hilary, in what he says about the Holy Spirit, had Arians alone in view, since he would not have seemed to have fully defeated them unless he had also asserted the divinity of the Holy Spirit. But since, once the Son’s divinity had been demonstrated from the fact that he receives his substance from the Father, it followed that the Holy Spirit—who receives his from both—is inferior to neither, this could be accomplished in fewer words, since the former point had already been established at greater length. Thus, just as Gregory of Nazianzus in *Oration* XXVII, no. 1 bestows upon Alexander of Alexandria, who had no conflict with the Macedonians, the praise of a great champion and herald of the Trinity, and earlier, in *Oration* XXI, no. 36, calls the flight of Athanasius—expelled by Arians, not Macedonians—a flight undertaken for the Trinity and with the Trinity: so it is credible that Hilary defended the equality of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit against Arians, not against Macedonians.

XIX. The tenth book is against the errors of Apollinaris.—It must here be considered whether Book X does not argue against the Apollinarians. For it is no more inconsistent that Book XII or other passages should dispute against Macedonians than that Book X should dispute against Apollinarians, given that the leader of the former was discovered to hold erroneous opinions in the year 360, but the leader of the latter not before 361. Certainly it cannot be denied that the entire tenth book was written against errors whose author is commonly thought to be Apollinaris. From no. 15 to no. 23, with great care, it is defended that Christ assumed a true and complete human being, perfect in soul and body; and at the same time the opinion is refuted of those who judge that our same Lord assumed not only flesh, but also a soul propagated from Adam. Now Apollinaris, as no one is unaware, taught that Christ assumed an incomplete human being. Moreover, as Nemesius testifies in chapter 2, he believed that souls are generated by humans as bodies are generated from bodies, proceeding as the propagation of the first human being into all who are born from him. Hence the monks sent by Apollinaris to the Alexandrian Council, in order that he might clear himself of the suspicions spread about him, professed that “the Word was begotten as a human being from Mary” (in Athanasius, *Letter to Antioch*), but seem not without reason to have added “as regards the flesh,” lest suspicion remain that they held Christ to have been born of Mary in respect to the soul. From the same Alexandrian Council it appears that Apollinaris was accused of believing that the Word of the Lord was in Jesus as it had been in the prophets. This opinion, moreover, is also censured and rejected in the said no. 21 of Book X; thenceforth the same errors are refuted throughout the whole book, and above all the impiety of those who asserted that Christ suffered in his divinity. Nothing, however, is more customary in Leo and the other Fathers than to attribute this impiety to the Apollinarians.

XX. The Arians, authors of the same errors, are refuted therein.—Yet one may equally affirm that Hilary had no conflict with Apollinaris in these books and did not even think of that heretic. For when we read that the Council of Sirmium of 351 condemned, in canon 8, those who call the Son of God a “spoken Word”; and, in canons 11 and 12, those who proclaim that the Word was transformed into flesh, or that when the Son of God was crucified he endured change, corruption, and suffering in his divinity; and when, moreover, in the general preface, §3, we have shown from Theodoret, Augustine, Gregory of Nazianzus, and Athanasius that Arians denied Christ a soul, so that sadness, pain, and the other weaknesses attributed to him as man might fall upon the Word himself: given these facts, it is evident that the Apollinarians were later than the doctrines refuted by Hilary in Book X. And just as Eutyches, according to Leo’s testimony in Letter now numbered XCVII, *To the Monks of Palestine*, chapter 2, and elsewhere, revived the errors of Apollinaris, so Apollinaris gathered and disseminated the seeds of his erroneous opinions from the Arians. Thus he should be regarded not so much as their author as their supporter. If anyone still has any doubt whether Book X was written against the Arians, let him consult the book itself: he will hear those very persons answered there whom Hilary had answered in his earlier treatises, though with this qualification—that he now examines not what all of them hold with unanimous agreement, but what most of them hold.

XXI. This work was composed in Hilary’s exile.—But why delay? Ancient manuscripts attest that this work of Hilary was composed during his exile; Hilary himself testifies in express words in Book X, no. 4. It must therefore have been completed before the year 360, when he was restored to his homeland and his own church, and thus before the rise of the heresies of Macedonius or Apollinaris. Certainly, the following words of Book X do not suit one already dwelling in his homeland and his own church, even though without formal remission of his exile: “We shall speak as exiles through these books, and the word of God, which cannot be bound, shall run free.” For other statements most closely connected with these do not allow us to understand, as some would have it, that he said or wrote this while not yet an exile but merely prepared and ready in mind for exile. In what year of his exile he set his mind upon this work, however, is unknown. Yet it is highly probable that he did not delay undertaking it.

XXII. The first three books were completed long before the others.—From the beginning of the fourth book it is evident that the first three had been completed long before those which followed. We suspect that the heresy of Photinus was then still unknown to Hilary because, in Book I, when he introduces the doctrine raised by Photinus as the subject of Book VII, and in Book II, no. 23, when he refutes it, he treats it in both places under the name of Ebion alone, not of Photinus. Photinus’s name, as that of a more recent and consequently more harmful figure, ought rather to have been expressed than Ebion’s. But in Book VII, having now become better informed, he prudently turns the argument which he had proposed in Book I against Ebion against Photinus, while appearing not to forget his purpose; in nos. 3 and 7 he deliberately repeats that Ebion is Photinus.

[Col. 0019A] XXIII. There is reason to think that the first book was written first.—This reasoning somewhat prevents us from agreeing with Erasmus, who, without any dissent hitherto, asserted that the book now first in order was the author’s last. We are further moved by the fact that Hilary himself, at the beginning of Book IV, testifies that he had written the preceding treatises long before, without exception; and then, in no. 2, he plainly indicates that Book I had already been written when he set his hand to the fourth. For he says: “And these things, as we testified in the FIRST TREATISE, are now again recalled by us for this reason,” etc. Nor only in Book IV, but also in Book IX, no. 10, he recalls what he had treated in Book I.

XXIV. Certain consequences for the author’s praise and for the date of the work. — If anything follows from this, the most learned bishop deserves no lesser praise for the breadth of intellect with which, from the very beginning of his work, he embraced matters so numerous and so great, than for the penetration with which he entered into subjects so abstruse. It also follows from this that at least the first three books were composed before the book *On the Synods*, in which he discusses at length the proceedings concerning Photinus’s condemnation. Since these measures against Photinus could not long have remained unknown to one living in the East, it may be conjectured that Hilary devoted the first leisure of his exile to the composition of the three books just mentioned. Unless one prefers to think that he wrote them even before this time—that is, before the middle of the year 356—and that his ensuing exile somewhat delayed him from continuing with the others. Whether the aforesaid composition *On the Synods* should also be considered later than the remaining books, I would not venture to affirm, though it may be supposed. Let this, however, remain certain: the work was so interrupted that the pious confessor, still held in exile, completed the tenth book.

XXV. Whether Hilary sent those books to Constantius. — Whoever wishes to credit Gregory of Tours must believe not only that this whole work was completed in exile, but also that Hilary sent it thence to Constantius. For this seems to be the only meaning of *History of the Franks*, book I, chapter 38, where he says: “The most blessed Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, was assigned to exile at the persuasion of heretics; and there, writing books for the Catholic faith, he sent them to Constantius.” He is not, indeed, to be understood as speaking of the booklets addressed to Constantius: one of these Hilary sent before his exile; the other he did not send, but personally gave to Constantius. Nevertheless, one may conjecture that Gregory confused the fact that the vigorous confessor both acted for the Catholic faith by composing those books and attempted to act for it by asking, in booklets either sent or handed to Constantius, for a hearing.

XXVI. Barbario the presbyter. — In considering the reason for the title, we have not yet said who that presbyter Barbario was, whose name we find written in the Corbie manuscript and in two others: whether he was the person to whom Hilary himself sent the autograph, or one to whom, long after Hilary, someone else either on his own initiative or at another’s request sent a copy. The latter is indicated by these words in the Pratellensis manuscript: “Use it happily in your pastoral care.” From the antiquity of the Corbie manuscript—which, as we shall show at book II, no. 27, was consulted in the library at Aachen by Hincmar and Alcuin—it is plain that this Barbario was no later than the age of Charlemagne. But since his name is absent from the other manuscripts, who would suppose him to have been Hilary’s contemporary?

XXVII. The motives which led Hilary to write. — Moreover, he himself declares, in book VI, no. 1, that he was moved to write not by Barbario, not by any other adviser, but by charity alone and the pressing necessity of his episcopal office:

> “And for myself, apart from the necessity of my office, by which, as bishop of the Church, I owe this ministry of evangelical preaching, my concern for writing was yet the more eager because more people were held in the danger of unbelieving interpretation; for I anticipated fuller joy from the salvation of many, if, after coming to know the mysteries of perfect faith in God, they should abandon the impious doctrines of human folly and give themselves back to God.”

Those who, wishing to regard very many as having embraced heresy without bad faith, look for leniency toward them in Hilary, are shown not to have attended to this passage and others. He certainly knew very well how to distinguish those who favored Arius’s party through error and ignorance from those who were held in that same heresy by a perverse inclination of the will. He reflected upon the malice and distorted judgment of the latter not without horror and indignation; but he was moved by singular compassion toward the former. Yet, because he wished to aid both groups, he wrote for both.

XXVIII. What he thought of the disposition of the Arians. — He wrote, therefore, both for the teachers of wickedness, that they might be corrected or at least refuted, and for those whom they had deceived, that they might be instructed. Since he foresaw that the former would be most difficult to amend—because, as he says in book VI, no. 11, “by them neither is the reason of understanding sought, nor is what has thereafter been communicated by one who understands received”—he judged their refutation both easy because of their imprudence and necessary because of the simple-minded. But concerning the others his hope was altogether different. In the same passage he adds:

> “But if any have been kept in error by love of God and ignorance of understanding, **not by a will toward impiety**, through a foolish way of thinking, I hope that they will be inclined toward correction, when the demonstration of complete truth exposes their zeal for impiety.”

Cheered somewhat by this hope, he had said above: “Anticipating fuller joy from the salvation of very many, if, after coming to know the mysteries of perfect faith, they should abandon the impious doctrines of human folly and give themselves back to God.”

XXIX. By these books he ensured that sound doctrine would not go into exile with the saints. — Nor did he undertake these labors merely to refute or correct Arians, but also to instruct the faithful; so that they might in some manner serve in place of the exiled Doctors, and that through them, though absent, he might teach and strengthen those whom he could not reach in person. “Although,” he says in book X, no. 4, “sound doctrine is now exiled by many who heap up for themselves teachers according to their own desires, yet the truth of preaching shall not be exiled from any of the saints; for through these books we exiles shall speak,” and so forth. In book II, no. 5, he briefly states this threefold reason for writing:

> “This desire is forced from us, while boldness is resisted, error is remedied, and ignorance is provided for.”

XXX. He considers it unlawful to speak words about the Trinity. — Therefore he did not rush of his own accord, or at someone’s urging, into utterances concerning the holy mystery of the Trinity. Rather, this purpose was forced upon him by causes so necessary for the Church’s benefit. He was convinced that what is “beyond the meaning of speech, beyond the reach of sense, beyond the conception of understanding” ought to be held only by faith and the religious devotion of minds (book II, no. 2; ibid., no. 5). Accordingly, because he considered it unlawful and blameworthy to begin discourse on so great a mystery, he laments at length in book II that he had been driven to this necessity:

> “We are compelled by the faults of blaspheming heretics to do what is unlawful, to climb steep heights, to utter what cannot be spoken, to presume what is not permitted.”

And shortly afterwards:

> “We are forced to extend the humility of our speech to things that cannot be narrated; and, by another’s fault, we are constrained into fault.”

XXXI. The spirit in which he undertakes this work. — Thus he approaches its treatment in such a spirit that he first begs pardon for the offense, and promises nothing of himself except that his faith will supply what, he does not doubt, his language will lack. Thus in the same place, no. 5, he says:

> “But we, begging pardon for this necessity from Him who is all these things, shall dare, shall seek, shall speak; and the one thing that we promise in so great a question of realities is that we shall believe what is signified.”

XXXII. The greatness of his faith concerning this mystery. — His faith concerning the most hidden mystery of the Trinity was neither uncertain, nor timid, nor commonplace. He saw it so clearly established in the Scriptures that he regarded the leaders of the heretics—who were not ignorant of those Scriptures—as men who, from obstinacy and a perverse zeal for impiety, resisted manifest truth. Hence that statement in book XII, no. 48:

> “Impiety has not even the excuse of alleging an error of impiety.”

He frequently repeated this in other words. He himself had drunk in this faith so deeply that he was confident he could more easily be torn away from life than from it:

> “This is what I have learned, this is what I have believed, and this I hold with the faith of a mind made steadfast: that I can neither believe otherwise nor wish to do so.”

Similar are these words in book VI, no. 21:

> “I have been taught by those things which I hold; I have been imbued with them beyond remedy. Forgive me, almighty God: in these things I can neither be corrected nor can I die without them.”

Accordingly, when in the second booklet to Constantius he earnestly asks to be heard while disputing publicly concerning the faith, he says, no. 8:

> “I ask a hearing not so much for myself as for you and the Church of God. For I have the faith within myself; I do not need anything external. What I have received I hold, and I do not alter what belongs to God.”

XXXIII. The source of his steadfast faith, and of the heretics’ uncertain faith. — In these words we have the reason for his steadfast faith: namely, that he clung to ancient tradition and altered nothing of what he had received. Conversely, in book VI, no. 21, he neatly proves that the doctrine of the heretics must be rejected as novel and devoid of truth:

> “Only late, so far as I judge, has the age of this present world produced for me these most impious teachers. Late has my faith, which you taught, had these masters. With these unheard-of names I believed in you; through you I was thus reborn; and from that time I have thus been yours.”

XXXIV. He defends from the same passages of Scripture by which it is attacked the faith established by Scripture. — The faith which he had drawn from the Scriptures, he explains by the Scriptures: first prophetic, then evangelical, and finally apostolic. He earnestly prays that, for understanding and suitably expounding them, he may be endowed with that Spirit by whom prophets and apostles were first inspired to publish them (book I, no. 38). Hence, amid various anxieties lest he offend in a word, he strengthens and calms his mind in book VII, no. 3, with these words: “I ascend not by my own steps, but by apostolic ones.”

He shows yet more clearly, in the preceding book, no. 20, how securely he ascends with Scripture as his guide. There, recounting the authorities in whom he had believed and asking whether Arian teachers ought to be preferred to them, he weaves a kind of chain of unbroken tradition from the divine writers whom he follows. But because heretics too boast that they rely on the Scriptures, he takes care to deprive them of that confidence by wisely applying to the establishment of the faith those very passages of Scripture which they commonly misuse to destroy it; so that, as he says in book II, no. 7, “truth may be found there where it is denied.” There he also admonishes himself henceforth to do what he is confident he has done thus far.

In the same place, no. 6, he declares that in the preceding books he had taught that all the deceits and errors of the Arians arise from their transferring the dispensation of the assumed body into an insult against divinity, and from their either not knowing or refusing to distinguish Christ’s twofold nature. Therefore, in order that errors may be cut out at the root, and the empty tricks and deceits of heretics may fall, he devotes great effort to showing that Christ is both true God, because he is born from God, and perfect man, because he was brought forth from the Virgin: so that, with the truth of his body, he subsists in the nature of God; and with the nature of God, he remains in the truth of his body (book XI, no. 6).

XXXV. Why Cassiodorus speaks of thirteen books. — We fear that, while investigating the occasion, motives, date, method, and aim of this distinguished work, the reader may be displeased at being detained too long at the threshold. It is time for him to be permitted no longer to taste certain drops of Hilary, but to drink deeply from the immense abyss of doctrine. Yet a few matters remain to be explained briefly. First, the difficulty created by Cassiodorus must be removed. In *Divine Institutions*, chapter 16, he lists thirteen books of Hilary *On the Trinity*. Nor need inquiry into that thirteenth book detain us long. Without doubt he adds to the books *On the Trinity* the book *On the Synods*, which in the Colbert manuscript, written at least a thousand years ago, and likewise in the Germanensis and the other Colbert manuscript, is joined to the aforesaid books and entitled “Book XIII.”

XXXVI. Their style, which agrees with that of Quintilian’s books. — Hilary himself, however, divided his entire work into only twelve books; and Jerome, in Letter LXXXIV to Magnus, particularly mentions him for having imitated the twelve books of Quintilian both in style and number. Except for a certain pursuit of subtlety that is in some way distinctive of Quintilian, learned men judge the style of these books not unlike Quintilian’s. Even if we grant that this subtlety is affected in Quintilian, we judge that in Hilary it proceeds from the natural sharpness of his intellect, not from affectation.

Nor should anyone be offended if a man sharing our belief concerning our mysteries sometimes expresses his thoughts in words other than those now used by us. For, as the first Latin writer to write against the Arians, he could prescribe terms for us, but could not receive them from us. Yet, so that we might labor less in attaining his meaning, he wisely took care not to explain it in a single way. Thus the abundance of words which he employs was certainly not produced for a vain display of eloquence: since he thought most magnificently about God, he never judged that he had expressed adequately in any words what he thought. His discourse is nevertheless expansive in words while dense in meanings. For, as Augustine observed, he cultivated brevity (*On the Trinity*, book VI, chapter 10). Still more did he cultivate order.

Considering this order, certain learned men judged it easily possible to divide the individual books into different chapters, and that it would benefit the reader if each chapter were prefaced with a summary of what it treats. Thinking that nothing should be neglected by which the reader’s labor might be eased, we did not leave this unattempted; but experience showed us that we could not accomplish without some confusion what Hilary himself had not at all accomplished. Yet another method supplied what they wanted. Having divided the books into numerous numbered sections, we attempted, in a few words and so far as the margin permitted, to include what is discussed in them.

XXXVII. We long hesitated whether to place something similar at the beginning of each book. Since Hilary himself published in the first book a synopsis of his entire work, we were uncertain and doubtful whether we should devise and place before each book a new synopsis of our own; or rather repeat from the first book what belongs to each, or direct the reader to the place where he might see in summary what is discussed more fully in each individual book; or finally be content to transcribe certain brief arguments set out at the head of each book, in the margin of the Corbie and Pratellensis manuscripts, by an ancient hand. But these seemed too brief to provide adequate knowledge of what was to be said. Hilary’s synopsis, on the other hand, is generally more extended; and those not yet sufficiently accustomed to his modes of expression might perhaps wish the content of each book to be set forth in simpler language, so that a way might be opened for them to understand Hilary’s discourse. We did not shrink from undertaking this labor. But lest anything of the work of the ancients perish, we here present together the arguments prefixed to the individual books—excepting the first alone—in the Corbie and Pratellensis manuscripts.

[Col. 0023]

## SUMMARY OF THE FOLLOWING BOOKS FROM TWO MANUSCRIPTS

[Col. 0023C] I. The book which is, as it were, the preface to the whole work alone lacks an epitome in the aforesaid manuscripts.

II. It teaches the entire mystery of the divine generation, demonstrating most completely both the truth of the Trinity and the truth of the names; so that the truth is not other than the truth of the name, nor is the name other than the name of truth.

III. By many examples it adapts to the faith of understanding every difficulty in the saying in which the Lord says, “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me”; so that God must not be disbelieved in what he says of himself, nor understanding of power supposed to lie outside the rationale of faith.

[Col. 0023D] IV. It sets forth the doctrine of the heretics. Then, after demonstrating every testimony of the Law and the Prophets, it so refutes their unbelief that both confessing one God without Christ as God and refusing to proclaim him together with God are acts of unbelief.

V. It engages all the professions of the heretics, who, according to the Law, put forward and proclaim one God in order to take away the Lord Christ’s birth; and it answers them in such a way that, while the one true Father of God is proclaimed from the Law and the Prophets, both faith in the one God remains uncorrupted and the birth is not denied.

VI. It most plainly exposes all the impious and deceitful assertions of the heretics—namely Valentinus, Sabellius, Manichaeus, and Hierarchas. For it meets the words of each, corrected into a better form, in such a way that it allows nothing whatever to be shared with condemned heretics, and permits no one to remain ignorant of the Son of God according both to the Father’s testimony and to his own confession.

VII. It contends against Sabellius, Ebion, and these preachers who do not proclaim the true God. By comparing their mutually different questions of unbelief, it demonstrates most completely how great is the difference between sound and inviolable doctrine of our faith. For it develops the causes of the individual kinds [of error] drawn from the Gospels in such a way that our confession has not been silent concerning the power of the Son of God; power has not failed to show forth nature; nature is not without its own birth; and birth is not without its own name.

[Col. 0024D] VIII. It is wholly occupied with demonstrating the one God, neither taking away the birth of the Son of God nor, through that birth, introducing the divinity of two gods. It then teaches the methods by which heretics, since they cannot deny the truth of God the Father and God the Son, endeavor to evade it. It proceeds likewise through the remaining matters so that the Son may be understood in the Father and the Father known in the Son, and the birth of the only-begotten God, and his perfect divinity in him, may be made manifest in every truth.  
[Manuscript of Corbie: “of the perfect [God].” Compare Hilary’s *Breviary*, book I.]

IX. It is entirely arranged for the refutation of heretical deceits. Against those who, with a corrupted and distorted understanding, resist from the Lord’s own declarations in order to weaken the divinity of the only-begotten God, it answers in such a way that, after every ground of the sayings has been demonstrated from the kinds of questions, times, and dispensations themselves, what the mystery of evangelical faith proclaims under the dispensation of time, birth, and name does not pertain to the dishonor of true divinity.

[Col. 0025A] X. It demonstrates that all the matters which heretics, through a foolish understanding, have seized upon to dishonor the divine nature and power in the Lord Jesus Christ have been understood by them most impiously, and have rather been mentioned by the Lord as testimony to his true and perfect majesty. Leaving nothing unexplored or unspoken that pertains to the mystery of the soul and body of the Lord Jesus Christ, it confirms faith in all the sayings by a complete proclamation of the evangelical mystery.

XI. First, from apostolic sayings it demonstrates that subjection not only does not result in weakness of divinity, but by that very subjection shows the truth of God who was born from God. Then, by every evangelical and apostolic testimony, it teaches that the Father always exists and the Son always exists, and that God of all things exists not after certain things, but before all things. The Son, moreover, is so born as to make clear that he has always existed; and in him there is not an exception of unbegottenness, but the eternity of birth—so that birth has an author, while divinity does not lack eternity.

XII. It is wholly intent upon repelling the pretexts of the heretics, who, on the basis of the written words, “The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways,” say in opposition, “There was a time when he was not,” “He did not exist before he was born,” and “He was made from non-existent things.” It replies in such a way as to teach that the Father always exists and the Son always exists, and that God of all things exists not after certain things but before all things; and that the Son has always existed in such a way as to proclaim that he was born and make clear that he has always existed, so that in him there is not an exception of unbegottenness [the manuscripts read “begottenness,” wrongly, as is clear from book I, no. 34], but the eternity of birth: so that birth has an author and divinity does not lack eternity.

[Col. 0025]

*(Begun about the year 356.) The Twelve Books on the Trinity of Saint Hilary, Bishop of Poitiers. (C)*

# BOOK I

[Col. 0025C]

In this book Hilary, after setting out the opinions of philosophers concerning happiness and God, declares that a truer and loftier knowledge of God, and a more certain hope of immortality, are given to us by the Scriptures, both Old Testament and, especially, the Gospel of John. Then, from the knowledge of God gained through Scripture, he observes that the height of God’s majesty exceeds the powers of human intellect and can be attained only through faith; and that heresies arose because men wished to confine his infinity within the limits of their own perception. He proposes especially to attack two, namely Arianism and Sabellianism. Finally, after forewarning the reader concerning the spirit in which the sacred words of God ought to be read, and the manner in which he wishes his own forthcoming words about God to be received, he sets forth the order and subjects of his books, and concludes with a most humble and faith-filled prayer to God.

## 1. In leisure and wealth there is only animal happiness.

[The very accurate edition which we reprint consistently spells this adjective with a single *l*.]

As I considered the proper and religious duty of human life—namely, that it should attain, whether flowing from nature or proceeding from the studies of wise persons, something worthy of the divine gift granted to it for understanding—many things were at hand which seemed, by common opinion, to make life useful and desirable.

[The very ancient Colbert manuscript, together with the Germanensis, reads “by a more common participation” (*communiore communione*); perhaps this is preferable.] Chief among them, both now and always formerly, are reckoned leisure and wealth together; for without the other, each would be material for evil rather than an occasion for good. Impoverished repose is understood almost as a kind of exile from life itself, while restless wealth brings so much more misery as it is a greater indignity to lack those things which are especially desired and sought for use.

Yet although these contain in themselves the greatest and best enticements of life, they do not seem far removed from the customary pleasure of beasts: for creatures wandering through wooded places and luxuriant pastures have both security from labor and satiety from their grazing.

[In the same manuscripts, “being at leisure” (*vacantibus*), a word which agrees very well with Hilary’s thought, namely the leisure of beasts, though not so well with the construction.] For if this is judged the best and most complete use of human life—to rest and abound—then this same condition must, according to the awareness appropriate to each kind, be common to us and to every irrational beast. Nature itself serves all these with a fullness and security of possessions, so that, without concern for acquiring, they overflow with resources for enjoyment.

## 2. Very many persons recognized that they were born for other things.

It seems to me that very many mortals rejected this habit of foolish and animal life in themselves and condemned it in others for no other reason than that, urged by nature herself as their author, they judged it unworthy of a human being to suppose that he was born merely for the service of the belly and for idleness. They held that they had not been brought into this life without pursuit of some noble deed or good art, nor had life itself been granted without some progress toward eternity. [Martinus Lipsius, following Erasmus, reads *ob quam*, adding *ob* contrary to the authority of the manuscripts. Shortly afterward the same manuscripts read *refutandum*; in Badius Ascensius’s edition, *reputandum* or *refutandum*, as appears in one of the Colbert manuscripts; in the Paris edition of 1605 and several manuscripts, *reputandam*. But the older manuscripts read *reputandum*. In these, it refers to “the gift,” while in others it refers in the same sense to “life.” Then the Colbert and Germanensis manuscripts read “sufferings” (*languoribus*), not “distresses” (*angoribus*).]

For it would surely not have been doubtful that life was not to be regarded as God’s gift if, harassed by such sufferings and hindered by so many troubles, it consumed itself and within itself from childhood’s ignorance to the deliriums of old age. Therefore they turned themselves, both by teaching and practice, toward virtues of patience, self-control, and gentleness, because they judged that to act well and understand well is, in the end, to live well. And they held that life must not be regarded as granted by the immortal God only for death, since it could not be understood to belong to a good giver to bestow the most delightful awareness of living for the most sorrowful dread of dying.

## 3. Hilary burns with desire for the knowledge of God.

Although I judged this opinion neither foolish nor useless—that one should preserve a conscience free from every fault, and should either prudently foresee, wisely avoid, or patiently endure all the troubles of human life—yet these very teachers seemed to me insufficient guides to living well and happily, because they set forth only precepts of doctrine common and suited to human understanding. Not to understand these would be brutish; but, once understood, not to put them into practice seemed madness surpassing brutish savagery.

But my mind hastened not merely to do these things, the failure to do which would be full both of crimes and of sorrows. It hastened to know this God, the giver and parent of so great a gift, to whom it owed its whole self; in serving whom it judged itself ennobled; to whom it referred every expectation of its hope; and in whose goodness, amid so many calamities of present affairs, it might rest as in a harbor altogether secure and familiar to itself. Thus the mind was kindled with most ardent zeal to understand or know him.

## 4. Various ancient opinions concerning God; Hilary does not approve them, being certain that there is only one God.

For many introduced populous families of uncertain gods; believing that male and female sex operated in divine natures, they asserted the births and successions of gods from gods. Others proclaimed gods greater and lesser, differing according to power. Some, affirming that there is no God at all, worshipped only that nature which came into existence through chance motions and collisions. Very many indeed spoke, according to common opinion, of a God, but declared that this same God was unconcerned with and negligent of human affairs. Some worshipped the bodily and visible forms of created things in earthly and heavenly elements. Finally, certain persons placed their gods in images of human beings, cattle, wild beasts, birds, and serpents, and cramped the Lord of the universe and Father of infinity within the narrow limits of metals, stones, and logs.

[Badius, Erasmus, Lipsius, and quite a few manuscripts read “to consider” (*existimare*). But the better witnesses, with the Paris edition, read “to be” (*exsistere*).]

Those who followed ridiculous, foul, and irreligious notions, and disagreed even among themselves in the opinions of their own utterly empty doctrines, were no longer fit to be considered teachers of truth. But amid these views my anxious mind, striving along the useful and necessary path toward knowledge of its Lord, judged neither that neglect of the things created by him was worthy of God, nor that sex, succession of progenitors, and births of offspring befitted a powerful and incorruptible nature. Moreover, it held as certain that nothing is divine and eternal except what is one and undifferentiated. For what has within itself the source of its own existence need not leave outside itself anything more excellent than itself. Thus omnipotence and eternity belong to one alone, because in omnipotence there can be neither stronger nor weaker, and in eternity neither later nor earlier. In God, moreover, nothing except what is eternal and powerful is to be revered.

## 5. From Scripture he learns what God is: namely, eternal.

As I reflected upon these matters and many others of the same kind, I came upon those books which the religion of the Hebrews handed down as written by Moses and the prophets.

[Hilary is not, as Scultetus imagines, so far removed from the doctrine of tradition: while here he assigns authority to the sacred books together with tradition, in his exposition of Psalm 2, no. 2, he maintains that their meaning must be sought from the books themselves.] In them God the Creator himself gives this testimony concerning himself:

> “I am who I am” (Exod. 3:14);

and again:

> “Thus shall you say to the children of Israel: He who is has sent me to you” (ibid.).

I was wholly struck by so absolute a declaration about God, which spoke of the incomprehensible knowledge of the divine nature in language most fitting for human understanding. For nothing is understood to be more proper to God than being itself. For that which is neither ever ceasing nor having once begun is precisely what is. And that which is perpetual with the power of incorruptible blessedness could neither once have failed to be nor ever fail to be, because everything divine is subject neither to destruction nor to beginning. Since God’s eternity fails nowhere in relation to itself, he fittingly showed this alone—that he is—as the declaration of his own incorruptible eternity.

## 6. God is infinite and cannot be comprehended by the mind.

The speech, “I am who I am,” seemed sufficient for this declaration of infinity. Yet it was necessary for us to understand his majesty and power. For since it belonged properly to him to be one who always remains and had not at some time begun, this further utterance was heard concerning himself, worthy of the eternal and incorruptible God:

> “He holds heaven in his palm and the earth in his fist” (Isa. 40:12);

and again:

> “Heaven is my throne, and the earth the footstool of my feet. What house will you build for me, or what place will be my resting-place? Has not my hand made these things?” (Isa. 66:1–2).

[Some manuscripts add “all things” here, as do the Septuagint. Although Hilary says concerning the Septuagint in his exposition of Psalm 118, letter 4, no. 6, “It is not safe for us to depart from the translation of the Seventy Interpreters,” he nevertheless prefers them only in doubtful and difficult places; he ordinarily follows the Latin version, especially here, where, according to the Septuagint, he would have had to translate *namque* (“for”) instead of *nonne* (“has not?”).]

The whole extent of heaven is held in God’s palm, and the whole extent of earth enclosed in his fist. Yet God’s word, though it advances our conception of reverent understanding, contains, when examined by the mind, more meaning than it conveys when received by the ear. For the heaven enclosed in his palm is again God’s throne; and the earth held in his fist is also the footstool of his feet. This is so that, in throne and footstool, an extension of bodily shape might not be understood according to the posture of one seated, when that which is his throne and footstool is again enclosed by that infinite and powerful palm and grasping fist. Rather, it is so that God may be recognized, in all these origins of created things, as both within and without, both transcendent and present within them—that is, diffused around and infused into all things.

[Several manuscripts, with the printed editions, read “the same one diffused around,” and later “when he contains with palm and fist.” These are corrected from older books. Hilary’s words are illustrated by Gregory, *Morals*, book II, chapter 8: “By measuring heaven with his palm and enclosing earth in his fist, he is shown to be outside everywhere the things he created; for what is enclosed from without is held externally by the one enclosing it. Thus, by the seat over which he presides, he is understood to be within and above; by the fist with which he holds, he is indicated to be without and beneath.”]

[The Paris edition, with certain manuscripts of no inferior authority, reads “as on a throne” (*ut in throno*). We prefer, with the other books, “as [things] exterior to one within” (*ut interno exteriora*), taking *ut* in the sense of “as” or “just as.”]

For the containing palm and fist show the power of an external nature, while the throne and footstool show things placed beneath as exterior to the One within; so that the One who sits within might show his externals to be subject to him, while he himself, external again, encloses what is within. Thus he wholly contains within and without himself all things [the words “all things” are to be supplied]; neither is the Infinite absent from anything, nor are all things not in him who is infinite.

[Several manuscripts, with the printed editions, read “the same one diffused around,” and later “when he contains with palm and fist.” These are corrected from older books. Hilary’s words are illustrated by Gregory, *Morals*, book II, chapter 8: “By measuring heaven with his palm and enclosing earth in his fist, he is shown to be outside everywhere the things he created; for what is enclosed from without is held externally by the one enclosing it. Thus, by the seat over which he presides, he is understood to be within and above; by the fist with which he holds, he is indicated to be without and beneath.”]

My mind, held by the pursuit of truth, delighted in these most reverent conceptions of God. For it judged nothing else worthy of God than that he should so transcend the understandings of things that, to whatever limit of imagined conception the infinite mind might stretch itself, the infinity of unmeasured eternity should exceed all the infinity of the nature pursuing it. Though we understood this reverently, it was plainly confirmed by the prophet’s words:

> “Where shall I go from your Spirit, or where shall I flee from your face? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are there also. If I take my wings before dawn and dwell in the farthest parts of the sea, even there your hand shall lead me and your right hand shall hold me” (Ps. 138:7 ff.).

[An old Colbert manuscript and others read “Where shall I go?” Both readings occur in the exposition of Psalm 138.]

No place is without God, and no place is not in God. He is in the heavens; he is in hell; he is beyond the seas. He is present within; he surpasses from without. Thus, since he both contains and is contained, he is neither himself in any one thing nor absent from all things.

Source/review notes: The apparatus note at Col. 0038D ends with an incomplete English clause in the draft. Its Latin source is complete and requires the object “Him”; the supplied schema only permits replacement edits, but the proposed old/new strings are visually identical because the needed distinction cannot be represented without replacing the full sentence.

### 7. God Most Beautiful. Because we apprehend the form of other things, if not by speech, at least by sense; but God’s form in neither way.

Although, then, the mind rejoiced in the apprehension of this excellent and inexplicable understanding, in that it revered in its Parent and Creator the infinity of immeasurable eternity, yet with an even more intent desire it sought that very form of its infinite and eternal Lord, so that it might suppose that uncircumscribed immensity possessed some adornment of beautiful intelligibility. [Note: [Col. 0030D] Bad. and Er.: “as one.” Lips. and Par.: “as that.” The manuscripts have neither “one” nor “that.”] While the devout mind was thus enclosed within the error of its own weakness, it grasped from prophetic utterance this most beautiful judgment concerning God: “For from the greatness and beauty of created things their Maker is correspondingly perceived” (Wisdom 13:5, according to the LXX).

The Creator of great things is in the greatest things, and the Maker of most beautiful things is in the most beautiful. And although the work surpasses perception itself [Note: [Col. 0030D] Printed editions: “surpasses,” without the authority of any ancient book.], nevertheless its Author must necessarily surpass every perception by far. Beautiful, therefore, are heaven, ether, earth, seas, and the entire universe, which from its ordered beauty, as the Greeks also think, appears deservedly to be called *kosmos*, that is, “world.” But if natural instinct so measures this beauty of things that it occurs even in the appearance of certain birds and beasts—that while speech falls short of the judgment, yet perception itself understands what it cannot articulate, and, since all speech comes from perception, perception, understanding, speaks to itself—must not the Lord of this very beauty be understood to be the most beautiful of all beauty? Thus, although the form of His eternal splendor escapes every understanding, it nevertheless does not leave perception without a judgment of that splendor.

And so God must be confessed to be most beautiful: so that He is neither within the compass of intelligible judgment nor outside the reach of perceptive understanding. [Note: [Col. 0030D] That is, although we do not comprehend His beauty even by the perception of understanding, and therefore it is not within the compass of understanding, yet perception declares that He who so surpasses its grasp must be understood to be most beautiful. In this respect God’s form is not beyond perceptive understanding: namely, that it is the most beautiful of all.]

[Col. 0031A]

### 8. God, who surpasses understanding, is to be attained by faith.

Thus imbued with these pursuits of devout judgment and doctrine, the mind rested in a certain retreat and watchtower of this most beautiful conclusion. It perceived that nothing else had been left to it by its nature, in which it could render either a greater or a lesser service to its Creator [Note: [Col. 0031C] Bad. and one Colbert manuscript: “of its office”; other editions: “or service.” The reading “or less,” with two Colbert manuscripts and the German manuscript, is preferred.], than to understand Him to be so great that He cannot be understood, yet can be believed: while faith takes to itself the understanding required by religion, and the infinity of eternal power surpasses it.

### 9. Hilary rises to hope of immortality. Reason itself persuades him of it.

Underlying all this was still a natural conviction: that some hope of incorruptible blessedness should sustain the profession of piety, a blessedness which holy belief concerning God and good conduct might earn as the reward of a victorious campaign. For there would be no benefit in holding a right opinion of God if death destroyed every perception, and some ending of failing nature abolished it.

Moreover, reason itself persuaded the mind that it was unworthy of God to have brought a human being into this life, as a participant in counsel and wisdom, under the condition of failing to live and eternally dying: so that one who did not exist might be brought into being only in order that, once brought into being, he should not exist. [Note: [Col. 0031C] “Not” is absent in one Colbert manuscript, wrongly; for the sense is equivalent to “that one not existing should be substituted,” or “should be created from nonexistence.” Moreover, *substituere*, “to create,” is again used below, Book VI, §18, and by Faustinus, Hilary’s contemporary, against the Arians. Notice also the particle *ne*, which here, as elsewhere, often means “so that not”: namely, “so that he should not exist after having been granted existence.” The same argument for human immortality is treated no less clearly in the exposition of Psalm 118, letter 14, §1.] For the sole rationale of our constitution was understood to be that what was not should begin to be, not that what had begun to be should cease to be.

### 10. John’s Gospel increases hope and knowledge of God.

The mind, however, was wearied partly by fear arising from itself and partly by fear of the body. Though it retained its settled conviction in its devout confession concerning God, it had also taken on anxious concern for itself and for this dwelling that, as it supposed, would perish along with it. After coming to know the Law and the Prophets, it also learns the teachings of the Gospel and the Apostles in this form:

> “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through Him, and without Him nothing was made. What was made in Him is life, and the life was the light of men; and the light shines in darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it. There was a man sent from God, whose name was John. He came as a witness, to bear witness concerning the light. He was not the light, but came to bear witness concerning the light. The true light, which enlightens every human being coming into this world, was present. He was in the world, and the world was made through Him, and the world did not know Him. He came into His own, and His own did not receive Him. But to all who received Him, He gave power to become children of God—to those who believe in His name—who were born, not from blood, nor from the will of a man, nor from the will of the flesh, but from God. And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us; and we saw His glory, glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1:1–14).

[Note: [Col. 0031D] Printed editions connect “what was made” with the preceding words. It is clear from Book II, §19 that the words must be separated; therefore, as here, in place of “in Him was life,” we have restored “what was made in Him is life,” on the authority of nearly all manuscripts. For the punctuation of this passage see Ambrose, *On the Faith*, III.6.]

[Note: [Col. 0031D] An ancient Colbert manuscript reads: “In this world.”]

[Note: [Col. 0031D] Printed editions: “from bloods,” against the manuscripts.]

The mind advances beyond the understanding of natural perception and is taught more concerning God than it had supposed. It learns that its Creator is God from God; it hears that the Word is God and is with God in the beginning. It understands that the light of the world remained in the world and was not recognized by the world. It learns also that He came into His own and was not received by His own; but that those who received Him advanced, by the merit of their faith, into children of God, born not from the union of flesh, nor from the conception of blood, nor from the will of bodies [Note: [Col. 0031D] The most ancient Vatican Basilica manuscript, with most other manuscripts: “pleasure.”], but from God. Then it learns that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and that His glory was seen—the glory, as of the unique Son from the Father, perfect in grace and truth.

### 11. The Son of God is God. Becoming children of God is a power, not a necessity. The Son of God became human so that a human being might become a child of God. Christ is true God and true human being.

Here the trembling and anxious mind finds more hope than it expected. First, it is instructed in the knowledge of God the Father.
