What it had formerly judged by natural perception concerning the eternity, infinity, and form of its Creator, it now receives as belonging properly also to the only-begotten God: it does not relax its faith into two gods, because it hears of God from God; it does not lapse into a diversity of nature in passing to God from God, because it learns that God from God is full of grace and truth; nor does it suppose a God from God to be subsequent, because it discovers that God was in the beginning with God.

[Note: [Col. 0031D] Colbert and German manuscripts: “not into two”; and below, §38, “not to be referred to a number of two by a diversity of truth.” Either reading may be confirmed from Book IV, §4, where the Arians invent this reason for rejecting *homoousios*: that, according to the meaning of that word, the Son might be thought to come from a division of the Father’s substance, as though He were a portion cut away, so that one thing had been divided into two. If “not into two” is preferred here, the word “gods” must be silently supplied, as it is expressly stated below in §17: “Taught by God, we neither proclaim two gods nor a solitary God”; and in §24: “We have proclaimed neither two gods nor a solitary true God.” The same occurs in Book VIII, §29.]

[Note: [Col. 0032D] Erasmus, followed by Lipsius: “falling away from God from God,” a reading that would not be displeasing if it had manuscript support. The reading of the very ancient manuscript of St. Peter’s at the Vatican, “falling away into God, God from God,” was also attractive; but the excessive liberties often taken by that ancient scribe in altering texts make us wary where no other manuscript supports it. Most manuscripts, with Bad., read “falling away in God,” or “into God,” from God. Other reputable manuscripts, with Par., read “departing into God from God.” This may conveniently be understood thus: not departing so as to introduce into the Son, who is God from God, a diversity of nature. Those reading “in God from God” may supply “to be believed” before *decedens* or *decidens*.]

Then it recognizes that belief in this saving knowledge is exceedingly rare, but that its reward is exceedingly great: for His own did not receive Him, while those who received Him were made children of God, not by fleshly birth but by faith. To be children of God, moreover, is not a necessity but a power: for the gift of God is set before all, not bestowed by the nature of those who beget, but the will attains the reward.

And lest this very power by which each person becomes a child of God should in anyone obstruct the faith of an anxious mind—because, through its difficulty, what is more desired is with the greatest difficulty hoped for and less readily believed—God the Word became flesh, so that through God the Word made flesh, flesh might advance into God the Word. And lest the Word made flesh should either be something other than God the Word, or the flesh should not be the flesh of our body, “He dwelt among us”: so that while He dwelt, He remained nothing other than God; and while He dwelt among us, He became nothing other than God made flesh of our flesh. By the condescension of assumed flesh, He was not deficient in what was His own: since, as the Only-Begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth, He was both perfect in what was His and true in what was ours.

[Note: [Col. 0033C] For the inhabitant does not become something other than what he previously was merely by dwelling in a house in which he had not formerly dwelt. Accordingly, the word “dwelling” is particularly well suited to express the immutability of the incarnate Word; while “became flesh” is stated beforehand to signify His union with flesh. Further, that Hilary understood “dwelt among us” as “dwelt in what is ours” is clear from the words that follow: “true in what is ours.” Thus Erasmus is refuted, who called into doubt whether Hilary believed that Christ assumed flesh from Mary. Those who think that Hilary was born a pagan and here relates the history of his first conversion to true faith should consider whether reading John’s words alone could of itself have afforded a pagan such knowledge of our mysteries as was already sufficient to refute Apollinaris, Nestorius, and Eutyches.]

### 12. Only faith comprehends divine things.

The joyful mind therefore received this doctrine of the divine mystery. It advanced toward God through flesh; it was called through faith to a new birth; and it was entrusted to its own power for attaining heavenly regeneration. It recognized the care of its Parent and Creator toward itself, judging that it would not be reduced to nothing by Him through whom it had been established from nothing into this very being which it possesses. It measured all these things beyond the reach of human understanding, because the reasoning of common opinions is incapable of heavenly counsel and supposes that only to exist in the nature of things which it either understands within itself or can accomplish from itself.

But it weighed the powers of God in accordance with the magnificence of eternal power, not by perception but by the infinity of faith: so that it did not disbelieve that God was in the beginning with God, and that the Word made flesh dwelt among us, because it did not understand; rather, it remembered that it could understand if it believed.

[Note: [Col. 0033D] For, as Augustine says in Letter 120 to Consentius, §3: “Let faith precede reason, by which the heart is cleansed, so that it may receive and endure the light of great reason”; and again in Letter 137 to Volusianus, §15: “Faith opens an entrance to understanding; unbelief closes it.” Compare Hilary’s preceding words in §8.]

### 15. Christ’s deeds do not yield to the natural perceptions of minds.

And lest it should be delayed in any error of worldly wisdom, it is further instructed by the Apostle’s divine words in the most complete faith of this devout confession:

> “See to it that no one despoils you through philosophy and empty deception, according to human tradition, according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ. For in Him all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily, and you have been made full in Him, who is the head of every principality and power. In Him you were also circumcised, with a circumcision not made by hands, in the stripping off of the body of flesh, but with Christ’s circumcision; buried with Him in baptism, in which you have also risen through faith in the working of God, who raised Him from the dead. And you, when you were dead in the transgressions and uncircumcision of your flesh, He made alive with Him, forgiving you all transgressions, blotting out the handwriting in decrees which stood against us and was contrary to us. He took it from the midst, fastening it to the cross. Having stripped off flesh, He made a public display of the powers, triumphing over them with confidence in Himself” (Colossians 2:8 ff.).

[Note: [Col. 0034C] All manuscripts except one of virtually no authority omit here the word “dead,” though it occurs below in Book IX, §10 and in the exposition of Psalm 67, §23. Hilary, however, is not unusual in repeating the same scriptural passages differently even in the same treatise.]

[Note: [Col. 0034C–D] Vatican Basilica manuscript: “Forgiving us all transgressions, blotting out the handwriting of the decree that was against us, which was hostile to us; and shortly thereafter, stripping Himself of flesh, He publicly displayed the powers, triumphing over them.” This version appears foreign to Hilary. The version printed here is confirmed in Book IX, §10. See the exposition of Psalm 67, §23.]

[Note: [Col. 0034D] Apart from the Vatican Basilica manuscript, only a few and later manuscripts read “the handwriting of the decree.” The explanation that follows is not inconsistent with this reading: namely, that by a new creation of our race in Himself, He abolished the constitution of the former decree. Otherwise in Book IX, §10, where Hilary recalls these apostolic words as already treated here, he interprets this handwriting as “blotting out the handwriting of the law of sin, which by previous judgments was contrary to us.” Hence in Psalm 120, §18 he simply calls it “the handwriting of the law,” but here “the sentence of death.” The reading in one Colbert manuscript, “the handwriting of the decree in judgments,” should not be omitted. It is characteristic of Hilary to combine two versions which he equally approves.]

Steadfast faith rejects the deceptive and useless questions of philosophy. Truth does not yield itself as spoil to falsehood by succumbing to the frauds of human absurdities. It does not retain God according to the perception of common understanding, nor judge concerning Christ according to the elements of the world, in whom the fullness of divinity dwells bodily. Thus, since the infinity of eternal power is in Him, the power of eternal infinity surpasses every embrace of an earthly mind.

Drawing us to the nature of His divinity, He did not bind us still to bodily observance of commandments, nor train us by the shadow of the Law for the rites of cutting the flesh—that is, circumcision. Rather, being circumcised, He purified every natural necessity of the body from vices by the cleansing of the spirit from sins; we were buried with Him in baptism, so that we might return to the life of eternity. For regeneration into life was death from life, and by dying to vices we were reborn to immortality. He Himself died from immortality for us, so that with Him we might be raised from death to immortality.

He received sinful flesh in order that, by assuming our flesh, He might forgive its sins: He became a participant in it by assumption, not by guilt. He abolished through death the sentence of death, so that in a new creation of our race in Himself He might annul the constitution of the former decree. He permitted Himself to be fastened to the cross, in order that, with the curse of earthly condemnation blotted out by the curse of the cross, He might fasten all curses there. Finally, He suffered as a human being in order to shame the powers: while God, who according to the Scriptures was to die, triumphed with the confidence of one conquering them in Himself; while He Himself, immortal and not subject to conquest by death, died for the eternity of mortals.

[Note: [Col. 0035C–D] Only the Victorine codex reads “He made it free from sin,” a reading foolishly embraced by Louis Miraeus. Hilary means only that Christ, in flesh of the same nature as ours, forgave the sins of flesh. As Tertullian teaches in *On Christ’s Flesh*, §16, it would neither suit Christ’s purpose, who was to abolish the sin of flesh, nor contribute to His glory, not to abolish it in that flesh in which lay the nature of sin. When one Alexander objected, “Then, if He put on our flesh, Christ’s flesh was sinful,” Tertullian replied: “By putting on ours He made it His; by making it His, He did not make it sinful.” Hilary here calls it “sinful flesh” because this flesh was propagated through sinners down to Christ; as Tertullian says in the cited place, it is Adam’s by descent, not by fault. Christ, as Hilary says here, became its participant by assumption, not by guilt. Therefore someone’s marginal annotation in one Colbert manuscript, “Read ‘sinful flesh’ cautiously,” is futile. Elsewhere—for example, *On the Trinity*, X.25—Hilary says of the same flesh of Christ: “That flesh was not flesh of sin, but the likeness of sinful flesh.” See the exposition of Psalm 67, §25.]

[Note: [Col. 0035D] Three manuscripts: “the curse of earthly malediction.” In Remigius, Corbie, Pratelles, and others: “of earthly dominion.” We judge that “of earthly condemnation,” found in several others, should be retained, as an allusion to the sentence received by condemned humanity: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go.”]

[Note: [Col. 0035D] Six manuscripts, though not the better ones: “triumphing in Himself with confidence in conquering these.”]

These acts of God, accomplished beyond the capacity of human understanding, do not in turn yield to the natural perceptions of minds. The operation of infinite eternity demands an infinite judgment for measuring it. Thus, when God became human, when the Immortal died, when the Eternal was buried, the matter is not an explanation within understanding but an exception of power. Conversely, it is again not a matter of perception but of power: that God should come from a human being, the Immortal from the dead, and the Eternal from one buried.

We are therefore raised together by God in Christ through His death. But since the fullness of divinity is in Christ, we have both the indication that God the Father raises us together in the One who died and the obligation to confess that Christ Jesus is none other than God in the fullness of divinity.

### 14. Faith in Christ removes both fear of death and weariness of life.

[Col. 0036A]

In this rest, conscious of its security, the mind had rested joyfully in its hopes. It feared the intervention of death so little that it even regarded it as an entrance into eternal life. [Note: [Col. 0035D] Printed editions: “conscious,” against the manuscripts.] [Note: [Col. 0035D] One Remigius manuscript, with Theodorus: “the beginning of eternity.”]

It judged the life of this body neither burdensome nor painful, but believed it to be—as schooling is for childhood, medicine for the sick, swimming for shipwrecked persons, discipline for adolescents, and military service for those who are to command—the endurance of present realities advancing toward the reward of blessed immortality. [Note: [Col. 0035D–0036C] We have restored from the manuscripts the particle *quod*, omitted here in printed editions. The meaning is as though one read: “that it, though afflicted by so many troubles, should be believed to be what schooling is for childhood,” and so forth.]

Indeed, what it believed for itself, it also preached to others through the ministry of the priesthood imposed upon it, extending its office into a service of public salvation.

### 15. The disposition of heretics.

But amid these things there emerged dispositions of impious recklessness—desperate toward themselves and cruel toward all—of persons who measured the mighty nature of God by the weakness of their own nature. They did not rise to the infinity of judging concerning infinite things; rather, they enclosed the unlimited within the boundaries of their own perception. They made themselves judges of religion, although religion’s task was obedience; forgetful of themselves, negligent of divine commandments, correctors of them.

[Note: [Col. 0036C] Thus Par., with the older manuscripts. But Bad., Er., and Lips., with others, read: “was in the office of obedience alone.” Here the obedience of faith is commended; below, §37: “The obedience of faith advances us beyond natural judgment.”]

### 16. The two principal heresies concerning Christ: those of Sabellius and Arius.

To pass over the other utterly foolish pursuits of heretics—though we shall not be silent about them when the course of discussion provides occasion—some corrupt the mystery of evangelical faith in such a way that, under the merely devout confession of one God, they deny the birth of the only-begotten God. They maintain that there was rather an extension into humanity than a descent; and that He who, according to the times of assumed flesh, was the Son of Man was not also always before then, and now, the Son of God. Thus there is no birth of God in Him; rather, He is the same from the same source. So, they think, the inviolable faith of one God is preserved by a line drawn forth from a solid whole into flesh: the Father extended as far as the Virgin and thereby born to Himself as Son.

[Note: [Col. 0036C–D] These remarks concern Noetus, Praxeas, and Hermogenes, but especially Sabellius, who, as Augustine notes in *On Heresies* to Quodvultdeus, became more famous than those with whom he agreed. This heresy is again explained in *On the Synods*, §45: “Some have dared to extend the unbegotten God, by an expansion of substance, as far as the holy Virgin, so that the extension, drawn out in a certain stretching of its nature and assuming a human being, should be called Son; and thus the Son, perfect God, should not have been born before the ages and later also born human.” Both passages are illustrated by Epiphanius. According to him, *Heresies* 62.1, Sabellius asserted that the Son, emitted like a ray, performed in this world everything pertaining to the administration of the Gospel and human salvation, and then returned to heaven as a ray flowing from the sun is afterwards drawn back into that same sun. Just as the sun extends its ray toward earth rather than descends, so he admitted only an extension of God into the Virgin, not a descent. Marcellus thought no differently, according to Theodoret, *Compendium of Heretical Fables*, II: he “entirely thought that the Trinity expands and contracts according to the differing administrations and counsels”; and shortly before: “He said that a certain extension of the Father’s divinity came into Christ, and called this God the Word; but that, once the whole economy had been accomplished, it was drawn back and returned to the God from whom it had been extended.”]

[Note: [Col. 0037C–D] In the Pratelles manuscript the sequence reads “from solid God,” and shortly afterward, “the Father extended as spirit”; the words “God” and “spirit” were doubtless transferred from the margin into the text. This passage too is illustrated by the likeness of the sun: just as a ray is a line drawn from the solid body of the sun down to earth, so the Son is held to be a line drawn from the Father. For just as in the sun there is a threefold power—of illuminating, of warming, and of circular form, or that solid body from which both powers proceed—so the Sabellians imagined in the Trinity a threefold power, of which the Father was the hypostasis and, as Epiphanius says in the cited place, as it were the whole form. From this we gain an understanding of this heresy necessary for grasping Hilary’s books.]

Others, however—because there is no salvation without Christ, who was in the beginning with God as God the Word—denying His birth, professed only His creation. They did this lest birth should admit the truth of God, whereas creation should teach falsehood; for creation, while it falsely intruded upon faith in the one God according to kind, did not exclude Him from the mystery. But by subordinating true birth to the name and faith of creation, they made Him separable from the truth of the one God, so that creation by substitution might not claim for itself the perfection of divinity which birth in truth had not given.

[Note: [Col. 0037D] Bad., Er., and one Vatican Basilica and one Colbert manuscript add: “but creation taught the falsehood of a composite and simulated God.” We suspect this to be a gloss, especially since this mode of expression is foreign to Hilary.]

[Note: [Col. 0037D–0038C] In printed editions and most manuscripts the word “creation” is added here; it is rightly absent from the more correct books. Earlier printed editions read “they falsely intruded,” and later “they excluded,” with scarcely any manuscript support. It would not be objectionable, however, if “which, while” were supplied earlier: “which creation is only falsely introduced into the faith of God, who is one in kind and nature, although He is not excluded from the faith of God in the mystery, insofar as several receive this name by a certain prerogative.” See *Against Auxentius*, §5.]

[Note: [Col. 0038D] Only the Vatican Basilica codex reads “substituting,” less well. The meaning is this: He whom Catholics believe to be true God, since He was born from God by a true birth, those heretics subject to the name and faith of creation.]

[Col. 0037B]

### 17. The true faith against both must be established throughout this whole work.

The mind therefore burned to answer their madness, recalling that this was especially salutary to it: that it had believed not only in God but also in God the Father; hoped not merely in Christ but in Christ the Son of God; and believed not in a creature but in God the Creator, born from God.

Therefore we hasten especially to confound, from prophetic and evangelical proclamations, the madness and ignorance of those who, under the proclamation of one God—a proclamation certainly useful and devout in itself—either deny that Christ, born as God, is God, or contend that He is not true God. They would have the creation of a powerful creature remain within the mystery of faith in one God, because the birth of God draws the religion of those confessing Him outside faith in one God.

[Note: [Col. 0038D] The Paris edition, following ancient books in which changing *t* into *d* is customary, reads “of those confessing.”]

But we, taught by God to proclaim neither two gods nor a solitary God, shall set forth the logic of evangelical and prophetic proclamation in the confession of God the Father and God the Son: so that both are one in our faith, but not one person; neither both the same, nor confessing another between true and false. For in God born from God, birth permits Him to be neither the same nor something other.

[Note: [Col. 0038D] Vatican Basilica manuscript: “we maintain.”]

### 18. Faith is necessary for the reader.

And you whom zeal for faith and the pursuit of truth—unknown to the world and to the wise of the world—have called to read, must remember to cast aside the weak and feeble judgments of earthly minds and to widen every narrowness of imperfect judgment by the devout expectation of learning. For we need to be reborn with new capacities of mind, so that each person may be enlightened by his own conscience according to the gift of heavenly origin.

One must therefore stand beforehand by faith, as holy Jeremiah warns (23:22), “in the substance of God,” so that one who is to hear concerning God’s substance may regulate his understanding toward things worthy of God’s substance. Yet he must regulate it not by some manner of understanding, but by infinity.

[Note: [Col. 0038D] In the LXX: *en hypostasei*, “in [the] subsistence.” Gregory Nazianzen, *Oration* 34, reading *en hypostēmati*, adds for explanation of the term: *kai ousia Kyriou*—“and essence of the Lord.” He denies that this has hitherto been granted to any living person, because none has been given to see the nature or essence of God. Ambrose, *On the Faith*, III.15: “Who has stood in the substance of the Lord and seen His word?”]

Moreover, conscious that he has become a participant in the divine nature, as the blessed apostle Peter says in his Second Epistle (2:14), he must not measure God’s nature by the laws of his own nature, but weigh divine declarations according to the magnificence of God’s testimony concerning Himself.

For the best reader is one who awaits the understanding of what is said from what is said, rather than imposing it; who brings back rather than brings in; and who does not force the words to appear to contain what he had presumed before reading ought to be understood. Therefore, when the subject is divine things, let us grant God knowledge of Himself and serve His utterances with devout reverence. For He is a fitting witness to Himself, since He is not known except through Himself.

### 19. No comparison with divine things is perfect.

If, when discussing the nature and birth of God, we employ illustrative comparisons, let no one suppose that they contain in themselves the perfection of a complete account. For no comparison of earthly things with God exists. Rather, the weakness of our understanding compels us to seek certain forms from lower things as indications of higher things, so that the familiarity of known things may prompt us, from awareness of our own perception, toward a judgment about perception unfamiliar to us. [This is mentioned in Book IV, §2.]

Every comparison, therefore, should be regarded as useful rather to humanity than as appropriate to God, because it indicates understanding more than it fulfils it. Nor should it be considered a presumptuous equation of the natures of flesh and spirit, or of invisible and tangible things. It declares both that it is necessary for the weakness of human understanding and that it is free from the blame of offering an inadequate example. We proceed, therefore, to speak of God in God’s words, yet to instruct our understanding by the forms of our own things.

### 20. The order of the entire work.

First, we have so arranged the plan of the entire work that the sequence of connected little books may be most suitable to the progress of readers. For we thought it right to present nothing unarranged or disordered, lest an unregulated mass of material should produce a kind of uncultivated tumult through confused shouting.

But since no ascent over steep places occurs unless steps are gradually laid down for the feet to be carried upward, we too, arranging certain beginnings for the journey, have made this difficult path of understanding gentler by a sort of milder slope: it is not carved into steps, but descends by a gradually rising plain, so that the ascent may advance almost without the awareness of those climbing.

[Note: [Col. 0039D] This appears to be said in imitation of Pliny, *Letters* VI.5: “Thus it rises gently and gradually, the slope deceiving you, so that when you do not think you are ascending, you realize that you have ascended.”]

[Col. 0039B]

### 21. What the second book contains.

After this little book of the first discourse, the next teaches the mystery of divine generation in such a way that those to be baptized in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit may not be ignorant of the truth of the names, nor confuse understanding with mere words; but may conceive each thing in thought as it is and as it is named. Thus they will recognize with complete certainty in the things that have been said that the reality itself is the truth of the name, and the name is the truth.

### 22. The third book.

After this gentle and brief discourse on the demonstrated Trinity, the third book advances, though gradually, yet now with greater progress. For the third book adapts to faith’s understanding, by as many examples of power as it can, what the Lord has declared concerning Himself beyond the understanding of human perception, saying: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in Me” (John 10:38). Thus what is not grasped by human beings through their dull nature, faith now attains by rational knowledge. For God must be believed concerning Himself, and it must not be supposed that the understanding of power lies outside the rational scope of faith.

[Note: [Col. 0039D] Printed editions, except Paris with one manuscript, read: “yet faith attains by rational knowledge.” The reason is here given why faith is called rational knowledge. It is rational because reason persuades us that God should be believed; it also possesses knowledge because no room is left for opinion when, through effects, we understand that God can do more than human reason can comprehend. Hence the printed editions wrongly read “the power of understanding” for “the understanding of power,” as is clearer from these words in Book III, §5: “There are powers in God of such a kind that, although the reasoning of our understanding cannot comprehend them, faith nevertheless is assured through the truth of their efficacy.”]

23. Fourth Book.—The fourth book, then, takes its beginning from the doctrines of the heretics, cleansing itself of the faults by which the faith of the Church is defamed. It brings forward that exposition of unbelief, published not long ago by many, and proves that they defended the one God from the Law deceitfully and therefore most impiously. It so sets forth all the testimonies of the Law and the Prophets that, without Christ as God, to confess one God is irreligion; and, once Christ the only-begotten God has been confessed, not to proclaim one God is unbelief.

[Note: [Col. 0039D] In the common printed editions, “is weakened,” wrongly; nor is “assailing” later in Bad., Er., and Lips. any better.]

[Note: [Col. 0040D] In place of “not long ago,” Lips. and Par. substituted “already long ago,” against the resistance of the manuscripts and against what is said in Book VI, §3: that the Arian pestilence had only recently arisen. We shall speak of this unbelieving exposition in Book IV.]

24. Fifth Book.—The fifth, however, maintained the order of reply which the heretics had established in their profession. For, having falsely claimed to proclaim one God according to the Law, they further deceived themselves by claiming to bring forward from the same Law one true God; so that, by the exclusion implied in “God,” “one,” and “true,” they might take away birth from the Lord Christ. For where there is birth, there is also an understanding of truth.

[Note: [Col. 0039C] The Verona manuscript reads “maintained,” as a little earlier, “the fourth book takes its beginning,” etc.]

[Note: [Col. 0040D] The Basel Vatican manuscript alone reads, “by the profession of God.” The usage and force of the word *exceptio* may be seen below, §§29, 33, and 34, where it signifies not mere profession, but that from whose fellowship every other being is excluded.]

[Note: [Col. 0040D] That is, there is understood the possession of the true nature of Him from whom the birth is. For Hilary commonly uses *truth* to mean true nature, as we have often seen.]

But we, teaching by the same steps by which this very thing was denied, proclaimed from the Law and the Prophets neither two gods nor one true God in solitary isolation, but the Father as true God—in such a way as neither to corrupt faith in the one God nor to deny the birth. But because, according to them, the title of God was assigned to the Lord Jesus Christ as something created rather than born, rather than inhering in him, the truth of his divinity was demonstrated from prophetic authorities in such a way that, when we proclaim the Lord Jesus Christ to be true God, the truth of the divinity naturally in him is contained within the understanding of the one true God.

[Note: [Col. 0040D] The printed editions read, “or the truth of the one born,” wrongly and against the manuscripts.]

25. Sixth Book.—The sixth book now exposes every deception of heretical assertion. For, in order to make their statements credible, while condemning the sayings and faults of the heretics—Valentinus, namely, Sabellius, Manichaeus, and Hieracas—they stole the Church’s devout proclamations beneath the covering of an impious profession. Thus, by correcting the words of irreligious persons for the better and moderating them by ambiguous meaning, they would extinguish the doctrine of piety under the condemnation of impiety. But we, after setting forth the sayings and professions of each, vindicated the holy proclamations of the Church and allowed them to have nothing in common with the condemned heretics; so that, condemning what must be condemned, we might follow only what must reverently be followed. In this way we taught that the Lord Jesus Christ is the Son of God—a point especially denied by them—while the Father bears witness concerning him, he himself makes profession concerning himself, the Apostles proclaim, the devout believe, demons cry out, Jews confess while denying, and the Gentiles understand while formerly ignorant; so that doubt might no longer be permitted concerning what was not left unknown.

[Note: [Col. 0040C] “Corrupted,” in the same place.]

[Note: [Col. 0040D] We restore “correcting” from the Tellerian and Pratel manuscripts. It had also long ago been adopted in the revised editions of Remigius and Theodore; whereas other books read “corrupting.”]

26. Seventh Book. Sabellius, Ebion, and Arius, by defeating one another, are defeated by the Church.—The seventh book next regulated the course of its argument according to the measure of perfect faith. First, by a sound and incorrupt demonstration of inviolable faith, it engaged in controversy between Sabellius, Ebion, and these preachers of a God who is not true: why Sabellius denied that he subsisted before the ages, whereas the others confessed that he was created. For Sabellius, while he does not doubt that the true God acted in a body, was ignorant of the subsisting Son. These others, however, deny birth and affirm creation, because they do not understand that his works are the works of the true God.

Their controversy is our faith. For while Sabellius denies the Son—and therefore errs—he prevails in this: that the true God acted, as he correctly proves; and the Church defeats those who have denied the true God in Christ. But when these men establish against him that Christ subsisted before the ages and was always active, they triumph for us over Sabellius, whom they condemn along with themselves: Sabellius knowing the true God, but not knowing God’s Son. Ebion, however, is defeated by both: Arius proves that he subsisted before the ages, and Sabellius that the true God acted. All, in defeating one another, are defeated, because the Church bears witness against Sabellius, against the preachers of a creature, and against Ebion, that the Lord Jesus Christ is true God from true God, born before the ages and afterward begotten as man.

[Note: [Col. 0041D] “Knowing,” then “not knowing.”]

[Note: [Col. 0041D] The printed editions and most manuscripts read “knowing,” and then “not knowing”; these are corrected from the very ancient Colbert manuscript, as well as the Germ. and older Remigius manuscripts. For these things are said of Sabellius, not of the Arians. Then a double error in Ebion is noted: first, that he denies Christ before Mary; second, that he wishes him to be a mere human being.]

27. Argument of the Seventh Book.—No one can doubt that it was especially fitting for the doctrine of piety that, since we had first proclaimed from the Law and the Prophets the Son of God, and afterward true God together with the mystery of unity, we should in turn confirm the Law and the Prophets by the Gospels, and from these first teach the Son of God and afterward true God. It was therefore most fitting, after the name “Son,” to show his truth—although, according to the common understanding, the designation “Son” itself secured a conclusive demonstration of truth.

[Note: [Col. 0041D] “Of pious doctrine”: perhaps better.]

[Note: [Col. 0041D] That is, the true designation of the Son manifestly possessed the Father’s true nature. By this Hilary declares that he will show, as it were in addition, that the Son has the Father’s nature, after showing that the name Son properly belongs to him. The word *absolutio*, very familiar to him, should be noted: it means a thing certain and evident.]

But, lest anything should remain to offer an occasion for deception and mockery to those opposing the truth of the only-begotten God, we established through the truth of his divinity the faith of that very propriety by which he is believed to be God’s own Son. We taught in these ways that he is God whose being God’s Son was not denied: by name, birth, nature, power, and profession. Thus he might not be other than he is called; nor might the designation be without birth; nor might birth lose nature; nor might nature fail to retain power; nor might power fail to make itself known by a profession consciously aware of its own truth.

We therefore adduced from the Gospels all the grounds belonging to the several kinds, so that profession might not be silent concerning power, nor power fail to display nature, nor nature fail to be that of its own birth, nor birth fail to be that of its own name. Thus the slander of impiety was left no room, since the Lord Jesus Christ himself, by his declaration of his own natural truth, taught the divinity of true God from true God according to name, birth, nature, and power.

28. Eighth Book.—Now the eighth book, after the two preceding books had greatly advanced believers’ faith concerning the Son of God and true God, was wholly occupied with demonstrating the one God. It did not take birth away from the Son of God, nor yet introduce, by means of that birth, the divinity of two gods. First it taught by what methods the heretics, though unable to deny the truth of God the Father and God the Son, nevertheless attempted to evade it. It refuted their foolish and ridiculous pretexts, by which, on the basis of the saying, “The multitude of believers had one soul and one heart” (Acts 4:32), and again, “He who plants and he who waters are one” (1 Cor. 3:8), and again, “I pray not for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word: that all may be one, as you, Father, are in me and I in you, that they also may be in us” (John 17:20–21), they assert a truth of will and unanimity rather than of divinity.

[Note: [Col. 0042D] The manuscripts consistently give this passage thus. The printed editions, however, read “one heart and one soul.”]

But, considering these very passages according to their proper force—that is, according to the force of their words—we showed that they contain faith in the divine birth in themselves. Reviewing all the professions of the Lord’s sayings, we taught the entire and perfect mystery of both the paternal and only-begotten majesty from the apostolic proclamations and the proper characteristics of the Holy Spirit. For the Son understood to be in the Father and the Father known in the Son showed both the birth of the only-begotten God and the truth of perfect God in him.

[Note: “The force of the Holy Spirit’s utterance”: see Book VIII, §23, for the meaning here.]

[Note: [Col. 0042D] In the earlier edition: “might show.”]

29. Ninth Book. Arguments against Christ’s divinity.—In matters most necessary to salvation, it is not enough to bring forward only those things which are proper to faith’s satisfaction. For assertions of ours that have not been tested often flatter the understanding and deceive it, unless the demonstrated emptiness of opposing propositions also confirms our faith by showing that they themselves are ridiculous. The ninth book, therefore, is wholly devoted to refuting the arguments impiously employed to weaken the birth of the only-begotten God. Those who forget the mystery of the dispensation hidden from the ages do not remember that, according to evangelical faith, God and man are proclaimed.

[Note: [Col. 0042D] “Flattering the understanding.”]

[Note: [Col. 0043D] Some manuscripts read “with an understanding flattered,” and then “in refuting” in place of “in repelling.” Clearly the word “understanding” refers to “deceive,” not to “flattering.”]

[Note: [Col. 0043C] “Refuting.”]

[Note: [Col. 0043C] The reading of our manuscript, “divinity,” appears preferable. For in the ninth book Hilary chiefly defends the true divinity of the Son against the opponents’ efforts, though it belongs to him only from the nature of his birth. All the heretics’ objections which Hilary answers aim at weakening the Son’s divinity.]

For when they deny that our Lord Jesus Christ is God, like God, and equal, as God’s Son, to God the Father; that he is born from God; and that he subsists, according to the property of birth, in the truth of Spirit—that is, divinity—they commonly rely upon these professions in the Lord’s sayings: “Why do you call me good? No one is good except the one God” (Luke 18:19). Thus, since he reproves being called good and testifies that only one God is good, they say that he who is good is outside the goodness of God and that he who is one is not in the truth of God.

[Note: [Col. 0043D] That is, he does not share that goodness by which God is uniquely good, etc.]

They also attach this saying to the arguments of their impiety: “This is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17:3). Thus, since he confesses the Father as the only true God, they say that he himself is neither true nor God, because the exclusion of the only true God does not extend beyond the author of the property signified.

[Note: [Col. 0043D] That is, what is signified as proper to him is wholly contained and enclosed within the Father, and does not proceed from him to be communicated to any other.]

They hold that this was said by him without ambiguity because he also said: “The Son can do nothing from himself, unless he sees the Father doing it” (John 5:19). Thus, since he can act only after the pattern of the work, weakness of nature is understood to be in him; for what is subject to the necessity of another’s action cannot in any way be compared with omnipotence. The logic of understanding itself, they say, indicates that in all things ability and inability to act from oneself differ. They differ, indeed, so far that he declared concerning God the Father: “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28); and in this absolute declaration the slander of opposition must cease, since it is the madness of impiety to refuse to attribute honor and nature to one who disclaims them.

[Note: [Col. 0044C] Our manuscript reads: “the slander of opposition must necessarily appear in an absolute declaration.” This is more correct than the Erasmian and other editions: “and let it cease,” etc.]

In every way, then, they claim that he is so far removed from the proper status of the true God that he also testified: “But of that day and hour no one knows, neither the angels in heaven nor the Son, but the Father alone” (Mark 13:32). Thus, because the Son does not know what the Father alone knows, they claim that one who does not know is far removed from one who knows, since a nature subject to ignorance cannot possess the virtue and power exempt from the dominion of ignorance.

[Note: [Col. 0043D] In the Basel Vatican codex, here and below: “nor the Son of Man.” The word “Man” is absent from the others, not only in this book but also in the ninth. Its removal makes the cited passage, at first sight, more favorable to the Arians.]

[Note: [Col. 0044C] “Exempt.”]

30. The arguments answered.—Showing that these things, through a corrupted and perverted understanding, have been interpreted with extreme impiety, we brought forward all the grounds of these sayings from the very categories of questions, times, and dispensations. We made words subject to their grounds, rather than assigning grounds to words. Thus, although “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28) differs from “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30); although “No one is good except the one God” (Luke 18:19) is not the same as “He who has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9); or although these are so divergent from one another, “Father, all things that are yours are mine, and mine are yours” (John 17:10), and “That they may know you, the only true God” (ibid., 3); or again, “I am in the Father and the Father in me” (John 14:11), and “But of that day and hour no one knows, neither the angels in heaven nor the Son, but the Father alone” (Mark 13:31)—in each case both the declarations of the dispensations and the professions of natural power conscious of itself must be understood.

[Note: [Col. 0044C] Here the Verona codex inserts “again,” as also shortly afterward before the words, “He who has seen me,” and below before “Of that day.”]

[Note: [Col. 0044D] Here and subsequently the printed editions, following the Vulgate, read “he who sees me.” But the better manuscripts consistently read, in accordance with the Greek text and the other Fathers contemporary with Hilary, “He who has seen me has seen.”]

[Note: [Col. 0044D] The printed editions here read “and again,” and a little later “and again, of the day.” In both places the word “again” is absent from the more corrected manuscripts and should be absent; for this is not a collection of testimonies gathered for one point, but four passages opposed to four others.]

[Note: [Col. 0044D] By agreement of the better manuscripts, the word “that,” though found in the preceding section, has here been deleted. Thus in Book IX, §2 it is expressed, but in §57 and in the exposition of Psalm 142, §2, it is omitted.]

Although the author of both sayings is the same, once the powers belonging to the several kinds have been shown—the distinct natures that are in Christ—that which is proclaimed under the dispensation of cause, time, birth, and name does not concern the dishonor of true divinity, but the mystery of evangelical faith.

31. Tenth Book. Certain words of Scripture that superficially favor the heretics.—The rationale of the tenth book is the same as that of the faith. For, from the manner of the Passion and certain professions, they seized, through the understanding of foolish interpretation, some things as dishonoring the divine nature and power in the Lord Jesus Christ. These very things had to be shown both to have been interpreted by them with extreme impiety and to have been spoken by the Lord as a declaration of the true and perfect majesty in himself.

For they flatter themselves with these sayings, that they may be impious under the appearance of piety: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matt. 26:38), so that he in whose soul the ruling fear of impending sorrow had fallen might be far from God’s blessedness and incorruptibility. They say that he was so overwhelmed by the necessity of suffering as to reach this prayer: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (ibid., 39); and that he would undoubtedly appear to fear suffering because he prayed not to suffer it, since fear of suffering supplied the ground for his request. They say further that pain’s force possessed his weakness so greatly that, at the very time of the cross, he said: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matt. 27:46). Stirred by the bitterness of suffering even to a complaint of abandonment, deprived of paternal aid, he breathed out his spirit in the cry: “Father, I commend my spirit into your hands” (Luke 23:46). And, troubled by fear at the exhalation of the spirit, he commended this spirit to God the Father for protection, because despair of safety compelled the need for commendation.

[Note: [Col. 0045C] “Seems.”]

[Note: [Col. 0045D] The printed editions read “seems.” “Would seem” is better in most manuscripts; for these statements, like those preceding and following, are set forth continuously as the opponents’ view.]

[Note: [Col. 0045C] “Then that same.”]

[Note: [Col. 0045D] The older Remigian manuscript: “then that same self.”]

32. Other passages are set against them.—But these most foolish and impious men, not understanding that nothing contrary had been said by the same speaker in these same matters, clung only to words and abandoned the grounds of the sayings. For “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matt. 26:38) is very far different from “From now on you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power” (ibid., 64); and “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (ibid., 39) is not the same as “Shall I not drink the cup which my Father has given me?” (John 18:11). “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matt. 27:46) is very far different from “Amen, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43); and “Father, I commend my spirit into your hands” (ibid., 46) greatly differs from “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (ibid., 34). Incapable of the divine sayings, they lapsed into impiety.

[Note: [Col. 0045C] In the earlier edition, in place of “from that,” which Erasmus also read, stood “or that saying”: incorrectly.]

[Note: [Col. 0045C] “And greatly.”]

[Note: [Col. 0045D] One of the Colbert manuscripts reads “withdrew.”]

Since fear and freedom, haste and excuse, complaint and encouragement, distrust and intercession are incompatible, forgetful of the nature of the divine profession, they treated the acts and sayings of the dispensation as an argument for their impiety. We, therefore, having demonstrated all that belongs to the mystery of both the soul and body of the Lord Jesus Christ, left nothing unexamined and nothing unspoken. Fitting the peaceful understanding of all the sayings to each kind of ground, we showed that confidence does not fear, will does not avoid, safety does not complain, and he who prays in commending himself seeks forgiveness for others. Thus we established faith in all the sayings by the conclusive proclamation of the evangelical mystery.

[Note: [Col. 0045D] We have removed from here the words “for the religious meaning of the mystery,” which we found only in one later Colbert manuscript and which appear superfluous, since Hilary simply declares that he answered every objection of his opponents and concealed none.]

[Note: [Col. 0045D] We retain “left.”]

33. Book XI refutes other heretical arguments.—Accordingly, because even the glory of the resurrection did not restrain within a religious understanding men rendered utterly desperate, but they either took up the weapons of their impiety from the declaration of condescension, or turned the revelation of the mystery into dishonor of God, they argue from the saying: “I ascend to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God” (John 20:17). Since the Father is Father to us and to him alike, and God is God to us and to him alike, they say that he is, in the common profession, outside the exclusion belonging to the true God; and that, just as the necessity of creation subjects us to the Creator God and adoption receives us as sons, so it does him. Thus they conclude that no property of divine nature is any longer to be judged present in him.

[Note: [Col. 0045D] Bad. and Er., with one Colbert manuscript, read “the mystery of revelation”; Lips. and Par., “revelations of the mystery”; the Basel Vatican manuscript, “the religion of the mystery.” Others more truly read “the revelation of the mystery,” namely, the manifestation of the Word in flesh, which according to the Apostle is the mystery hidden from the ages.]

[Note: [Col. 0046C] “And to God.”]

They also rely on the Apostle’s saying: “But when he says, ‘All things are subjected,’ it is except him who subjected all things to him; and when all things have been subjected to him, then the Son himself also will be subjected to him who subjected all things to him, that God may be all in all” (1 Cor. 15:27–28). For subjection, they say, both declares the weakness of the subjected one and signifies the power of the ruler.

[Note: [Col. 0046D] The printed editions here add the pronoun “to him,” which they omit in Book XI. The manuscripts are consistent in both places.]

[Note: [Col. 0046C] The words which P. Coustant here notes as omitted by many manuscripts of excellent quality are also omitted by ours.]

[Note: [Col. 0046D] The words “when all things have been subjected to him” are omitted here by several manuscripts of good quality; in Book XI, §§8 and 22, all omit them.]

The eleventh book is occupied with examining these matters also with the fullest demonstration of piety. It shows from these very apostolic sayings not merely that subjection does not imply weakness of divinity, but that by that very subjection the truth of God is shown, because he is born from God. It also shows that, because the Father is Father and God to him and to us, much is gained for us and nothing taken from him: namely, that the man born and subject to all the sufferings of our flesh ascended to our God and Father, in order that, as our man, he might ascend into God to be glorified.

[Note: [Col. 0046C] “Who is from God.”]

[Note: [Col. 0046D] In the Basel Vatican and other better manuscripts: “because he is born from God,” with no different sense. Hilary maintains that the Son is subjected because he is born; and that, because he is born from God, he possesses the true nature of God.]

[Note: [Col. 0046D] Either the verb “ascended” must here be supplied, by which Hilary proves that much is gained for us: when Christ ascended, our humanity was to ascend into God for glorification. Thus above, §11, he said: “God the Word became flesh, so that through God the Word made flesh, flesh might advance into God the Word.” Or the following *ut* is not causal, but “as our man” means “as one of our nature.” Whoever prefers this should read shortly afterward “he has ascended” in place of “he might ascend”; or certainly, with the Chartres manuscript, “he ascends.”]

34. Book XII attacks the Arian heresy more openly. The Son of God was so born as to have always existed.—We have always remembered that this practice is observed in every kind of instruction: if persons have first been trained for a long time by the limited exercise and long use of a more elementary study, they are then sent on to the actual trials of the things in which they have been instructed. Thus, when they have practiced battles well and are about to become soldiers, they are brought into military service; or when they have tried the lawsuits of academic material, they are then sent into the struggles of the courts; or when a sailor has fearlessly rigged a ship in sheltered domestic waters, he is then entrusted to the storms of the vast and foreign sea.

[Note: [Col. 0047D] “And by long [practice].”]

[Note: [Col. 0047D] “Are sent,” shortly after “are drawn forth.”]

[Note: [Col. 0047D] Thus most manuscripts. Others, with the printed editions, read “academic.”]

We took care to do the same in this greatest and gravest understanding of the whole faith. For when we had previously instructed tender faith, from elementary beginnings, concerning birth, name, divinity, and truth, and by gentle progress had raised the readers’ interest even to uprooting every pretext of the heretics, then we brought them out into the very arena of glorious and great conflict. Thus, insofar as the human mind fails, in common opinion, to comprehend the understanding of eternal birth, they might exert themselves in divine studies to grasp those things which lie beyond the conception of our nature.

[Note: [Col. 0048D] The Basel Vatican manuscript reads “of divinity”: corruptly. Shortly afterward some others read “fails” in place of “is failed,” through the rashness of a pedant. For Cicero likewise says, “A woman abounds in boldness, but is lacking in counsel and reason.”]

This especially resolves the question which, gaining force through the dullness of secular wisdom, imagines that it speaks rationally about the Lord Jesus: “There was when he was not,” “He was not before he was born,” and “He was made from things that did not exist.” Since birth seems to provide the ground that one who was not should come to be, and that one should be born when not existing, they therefore subject the only-begotten God also to the understanding of times—as though faith itself and the logic of birth showed that he at some time did not exist. They consequently say that he was born from that which was not, because birth bestows existence upon what was not.

[Note: [Col. 0048D] The older books read “dullness”; in one Remigius manuscript this was wrongly changed into “condition.”]

But we, proclaiming by apostolic and evangelical testimonies the Father always and the Son always, shall teach that he is God of all things, not after some things but before all things. Nor shall he fall under the rashness of this irreligious interpretation, as though he were born from things that did not exist or did not exist before he was born. Rather, he has so always existed that we proclaim him born; and he is so truly born that we make clear that he has always existed. Thus in him there is not an exemption from being unbegotten, but the eternity of birth: because birth has an author, while divinity does not lack eternity.

35. The words “The Lord created me,” etc., are explained.—Because they are ignorant of the prophetic saying and unlearned in heavenly doctrine, they strive, by a corrupted understanding and a distortion of the sense, to affirm that God is created rather than born on the basis of the saying, “The Lord created me in the beginning of his ways for his works” (Prov. 8:22). Thus they would place him within the common nature of created things, although preeminent in the class of creation; and would assign him not the glory of divine birth but the power of a mighty creature.

[Note: [Col. 0047D] “Are” is absent from the Verona copy.]

[Note: [Col. 0048D] “Me, beginning.”]

[Note: [Col. 0048D] Bad., Er., and Lips. read “beginning,” without “in,” with the agreement of several ancient books and the Septuagint. But the particle “in” must clearly be added both from what follows and from Book XII, §35. Hence the Basel Vatican manuscript and others read “in the beginning.”]

But we, bringing forward nothing new and nothing assumed from outside, shall establish by that very testimony of Wisdom the truth and rationale of the saying. We shall show that what is said to have been created at the beginning of God’s ways and for his works cannot be applied to the understanding of divine and eternal birth, because being created for these things is not the same as being born before all things. Where there is a signification of birth, there is only a profession of birth; but where there is the name of creation, there is an antecedent cause of that creation. And although Wisdom was born before all things, yet because it was also created for certain things, what is before all things is not the same as what began to be after some things.

36. Book XII explains what must be confessed concerning the Holy Spirit.—Next it seemed fitting, once the name of creation had been rejected from the faith which we hold concerning the only-begotten God, to teach also those things which are fitting and devout for confession of the Holy Spirit. Thus, after confirmation by the lengthy and careful treatment of the preceding books, nothing would be lacking for the full exposition of the whole faith. Once the irreligious views of defective proclamations concerning the Holy Spirit had also been removed, apostolic and evangelical authority would preserve, within a saving definition, the unharmed and undefiled mystery of the regenerating Trinity. No one would then dare, by the judgment of human understanding, to place among creatures the Spirit of God, whom we receive as the pledge of immortality and for fellowship in the divine and incorruptible nature.

37. Grace necessary for writing rightly is implored.—For my part, I am conscious that I owe you, almighty God the Father, this as the chief duty of my life: that my every utterance and thought should speak of you. For this very use of speech, granted me by you, can offer me no greater reward than that, by proclaiming you, it may serve you and may show you as what you are: Father, namely Father of the only-begotten God, whether to an age that does not know you or to a heretic who denies you.

[Note: [Col. 0048D] The Verona manuscript does not repeat “Father.”]

In this there is only the profession of my will; but the gift of your help and mercy must be sought in prayer: that you may fill with the breath of your Spirit the sails of our faith and confession, spread out for you, and drive us forward on the course of proclamation we have begun. For you yourself, in saying, “Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened to you” (Luke 11:9), are not the author of an unfaithful promise.

We, indeed, though poor, shall pray for what we need; we shall bring persevering zeal to searching the sayings of your prophets and apostles; and we shall knock at every entrance to an understanding that has been shut up. But it is yours to grant what is asked, to be present to what is sought, and to open to what knocks. For we are sluggish through a certain inert dullness of our nature and, in order to understand your things, are restrained within the necessity of ignorance by our mind’s weakness. Yet the pursuits of your teaching instruct us in the perception of divine knowledge, and obedience to faith carries us beyond natural opinion.

[Note: [Col. 0049D] “Instruct.”]

[Note: [Col. 0049D] The Basel Vatican codex reads “carries obedience onward”: wrongly. How faith advances us to what natural perception does not reach has already been noted above.]

38. Therefore we await your encouragement of the beginnings of this trembling undertaking, your strengthening of it by increasing progress, and your calling us into fellowship with either prophetic or apostolic utterance. Thus we may understand their sayings in no sense other than that in which they themselves spoke, and may follow the proprieties of their words with the same meanings of things.

For we shall speak of what they proclaimed in the mystery: that you are eternal God, Father of the eternal only-begotten God; that you alone are without birth; and that the one Lord Jesus Christ is from you by eternal birth, not to be referred into the number of gods through a diversity of truth. We shall proclaim that he is begotten from you, who are the one God; and we shall confess that he who was born from you, God the true Father, is nothing other than true God.

[Note: [Col. 0049D] The old Colbert manuscript, with the Germ. manuscript as noted above in §11, reads “not into the number of two.”]

[Note: [Col. 0049D] The Basel Vatican manuscript reads “because [he is] God.” Shortly afterward Carn. and some others read “nor into another,” and later, where the text has “from you, God the true Father,” “God” is absent from most manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 0049D] In our manuscript the word “God” is omitted.]

Grant us, then, the meaning of words, the light of understanding, reverence for the sayings, and faith in the truth. Grant that what we believe we may also speak: namely, that, knowing from the Prophets and Apostles you to be the one God the Father and the one Lord Jesus Christ, we may now, against heretics who deny this, so celebrate you as God that we do not believe you solitary, and so proclaim him God that we do not think him false.

[Note: [Col. 0049D] The old Colbert manuscript reads “thus both you and God.” Others better place “God” so that it refers equally to you and to him. Shortly afterward Carn. and others read “neither solitary nor false”: less faithfully. For the sense is this: to celebrate you as God in such a way that we do not believe you solitary, and to proclaim him as God in such a way that we do not think him false. In Corb. the closing word *Amen* is added.]

## BOOK TWO, §§25–26

It discusses in general the truth of the Trinity, and specifically the dignity and office of each person. First, Hilary declares that knowledge of so great a mystery, handed down in baptism, is sufficient. Then, after briefly prefacing some remarks concerning the origin of heresies and the heretics who attack faith in the Trinity, he repeatedly declares that he is brought unwillingly and tremblingly to write on matters so hidden.

After explaining what he thinks concerning the Father, he shows that the matter as it is cannot be adequately explained in words. He then explains what the Son is and is not, and rebukes those who resent being unable to comprehend the mystery of that generation, when in so many other matters, including their own affairs, they calmly endure ignorance. Having first briefly demonstrated the divine nature of this ineffable generation of the Son of God—a generation unknown to the wise of this age, the scribes of the Law, and heretics—he explains it in the words of the Fisherman.

Afterward, commending faith founded upon the Scriptures, he compares it to a medicine suited to cure every disease. He confirms this by bringing forward testimonies of Scripture through which the inventions of Sabellius, Ebion, and the Arians are simultaneously overthrown. He does not pass over certain things recorded in Scripture concerning Christ which seem unworthy of God; but in the very things which he is said to have undergone for the sake of humankind, he shows that there are signs of power and dignity by which we are taught that he is truly God.

Finally, he proves that the Holy Spirit exists as distinct from the Father and the Son, and removes the scruple of those who either do not know or doubt this because they observe that “Spirit” frequently denotes the Father or the Son. Moreover, he demonstrates the divine nature and office of the Holy Spirit, how necessary his gift is for us, and with what zeal it must be merited.

### 1. That the knowledge of the Trinity imparted in baptism is sufficient. [Col. 0050C]

The word of God was sufficient for believers—a word poured into our ears, through the Evangelist’s testimony, together with the very power of its truth—when the Lord says: “Go now, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I command you; and behold, I am with you all days, even unto the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:19–20).

> [Note: Col. 0050D. Printed editions: “I commanded”; the manuscripts oppose this reading.]

For what does it not contain concerning the sacrament of human salvation? Or what remains, or is obscure?

> [Note: Col. 0050D. “In the same sacrament.”]
> [Note: Col. 0050D. Thus the older Colbert, Chartres, German, and other manuscripts read “concerning the sacrament in it.” Others, with the printed editions, read “in the same sacrament.”] All things are full, as proceeding from the Full One, and perfect, as proceeding from the Perfect One.

> [Note: Col. 0050D. “And proceeding from the Perfect One.”]  
> [Note: Col. 0050D. The Basel, Vatican, and Chartres manuscripts, with a few others, read: “and proceeding from the Perfect One.”]

For they embrace the meaning of the words, the efficacy of the realities, the order of the matters concerned, and the understanding of nature. He commanded baptism in the name of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—that is, in confession of the Author, the Only-begotten, and the Gift.

> [Note: Col. 0050D. Two Colbert and German manuscripts: “of the only-begotten God.”]

There is one Author of all things. For there is one God the Father, from whom are all things; and one Only-begotten, our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things; and one Spirit, the gift in all.

> [Note: Col. 0051B. “And one gift of the Spirit.”]

Therefore all things are ordered according to their proper powers and merits: one power from whom are all things, one offspring through whom are all things, one gift of perfect hope.

> [Note: Col. 0051C. In the editions of Badius, Erasmus, and Lipsius, and in a later Colbert manuscript: “one unbegotten power”; a gloss.]  
> [Note: Col. 0051B. “From whom”; then, “through whom.”]

Nor will anything be found lacking within so great a consummation, within which are infinity in the Eternal One, form in the Image, and use in the Gift.

> [Note: Col. 0051C–0052C. Erasmus reads, wrongly: “within which there is not”;  the negative particle has been added contrary to the manuscripts. Shortly afterward, Augustine, *On the Trinity*, VI.10, reads, instead of “infinity in the Eternal One”: “eternity in the Father.” Anyone may conveniently consult the explanation which Augustine there appends, in praise of Hilary, though it would be too long to bring it in here. There is no doubt that “within which” refers to the consummation. This is said either of the consummated and perfect proclamation of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, or also of human hope, for whose blessedness nothing need be desired: inasmuch as in the eternal Father an infinity of blessedness is promised; in the Son, who is the most beautiful image of the Father, complete in every proportion, there is to be bestowed that beyond which nothing more splendid or delightful can fall under sight; and in the Holy Spirit, who is the Father’s and the Son’s gift and bestowal, the enjoyment of both is to be imparted. Although theologians after Augustine distinguished the words *uti* (“to use”) and *frui* (“to enjoy”), referring use to created things and enjoyment to the Creator, Hilary did not know this distinction. Even in reference to God he uses *uti* without distinction; for example, in *On Psalm 2*, §15: “He receives us into an understanding and use of his blessed goodness”; and §16: “He who created us through the benevolence of his blessedness, to be used … through the hope of meriting and using his goodness,” and so forth. Finally, when, in Book I, §36, he teaches that it is impious to reckon among creatures the Holy Spirit whom we receive as a pledge of immortality and for participation in the divine and incorruptible nature, he sufficiently declares what he means here by “use in the Gift”: namely, that the Holy Spirit is the Father’s and the Son’s gift, through whose benefit we receive the pledge of immortality and participation in the divine and incorruptible nature. From this explanation, we think, the opinion of Erasmus falls to the ground. Hilary seemed to Erasmus to have slipped, because, perhaps having read in Greek τὴν χρηστότητα or τὸ χρηστόν, he rendered it *usus in munere* (“use in the Gift”), although those terms signify rather goodness, kindness, and sweetness. But Erasmus merely guesses that Hilary borrowed these words from Greek; and he wrongly wishes the ancients to have spoken of the Holy Spirit’s property in our terminology.]

### 2. The fault of heretics compels him to say more about it

But the faults of heretics and blasphemers compel us to undertake unlawful things, to climb arduous heights, to utter what cannot be uttered, and to presume what has not been permitted. Although what was commanded ought to have been fulfilled by faith alone—

> [Note: Col. 0051B. The words “persons and realities” have been intruded into our text.]  
> [Note: Col. 0052C. In the editions of Badius and Erasmus, and in the Remigius, Corbie, Pratensis, and other manuscripts, “to worship” has been prefixed before “persons and realities”; it is more correctly absent from the older books.]

—namely, to worship the Father, to venerate the Son with him, and to abound in the Holy Spirit—we are compelled to stretch the lowliness of our speech toward things that are ineffable. We are forced into fault by another’s fault, so that what ought to have been contained in the religious devotion of minds is now brought forth into the danger of human speech.

> [Note: Col. 0052C. Two very old Colbert and German manuscripts read “to confess” in place of “to be contained.”]
> [Note: Col. 0051B. “Ought to have been.”]

### 3. Heresy arises from Scripture wrongly understood

For many have arisen who receive the simplicity of heavenly words according to the meaning of their own will, rather than according to the complete truth itself, interpreting otherwise than the force of the sayings requires. For heresy lies in interpretation, not in Scripture; and it is meaning, not wording, that becomes culpable.

> [Note: Col. 0052C. The Basel Vatican manuscript reads “in meaning, not in wording,” corruptly. Ambrose imitates Hilary in *On Faith*, II.1: “The letters are without fault; the meaning is at fault.” A similar passage occurs in *To Constantius*, II.9, where he first says of heretics: “They speak all Scriptures without the sense of Scripture”; then adds: “For Scripture consists not in reading but in understanding, nor in transgression but in charity.” Hence, as is explained in Book VII, §4, that perverse understanding chiefly arises when what is read is fitted to a preconceived meaning rather than when meaning obeys the reading.]

Can truth be corrupted? When the name “Father” is heard, is not the nature of a son contained in that name? Will not the Holy Spirit be what he is called? For in the Father there cannot fail to be what a father is; nor can there be lacking in the Son what a son is; nor can that which is received fail to exist in the Holy Spirit.

But people of perverted minds—

> [Note: Col. 0052D. *Mente* (“in mind”) is absent from the older books. The Basel Vatican manuscript then has *perverse*; the Chartres manuscript, *per se*.]

—confuse and entangle everything; by the perversity of their understanding they strive even for a transformation of nature. Thus they take from the Father what belongs to the Father, while wishing to take from the Son what belongs to the Son. They take it away when they say that he is Son not according to nature.

> [Note: Col. 0052D. We restore the particle *quando* (“when”), erased by Lipsius contrary to the authority of the older books. Shortly afterward Badius, Erasmus, and Paris have *sit filius* (“is Son”); but the better manuscripts have *fit filius* (“becomes Son”), not improperly. Hilary is here speaking from the Arians’ position, since they wished the Son to be made. The particle *cum*, in the sense of “according to,” is especially familiar to him.]

But he is not from nature when the one begotten and the one begetting do not have the same thing in themselves.

> [Note: Col. 0051B. We restore *sit* from our manuscript in place of *fit*: for what follows takes it up as it were by repeating it, “But he is not from nature.”]  
> [Note: Col. 0052B. “The one born and the one begetting.”]

For he is not a son whose substance is other and unlike that of the father. And how will he be Father if he has not begotten in the Son that which belongs to his own substance and nature?

> [Note: Col. 0052B. Thus in our manuscript; the earlier edition has *agnoscat*, “has recognized.”]  
> [Note: Col. 0052D. The Chartres manuscript, corrected by an ancient second hand, reads “has begotten in the Son”; this reading subsequently prevailed in later manuscripts and in Badius, Erasmus, and Lipsius.]

### 4. New teachings of heretics: Sabellius, Ebion, Arians, and Pneumatomachians

Although they are in no way able to alter what these things are, they nevertheless bring forward new teachings and human inventions. Thus Sabellius stretches the Father out into the Son, and thinks that this must be confessed in names rather than realities, since he presents the Son himself as the Father himself. Thus Ebion, conceding every beginning to the Son of God from Mary—

> [Note: Col. 0052B. The words “to the Son of God” are absent.]  
> [Note: Col. 0052D–0053C. The words “to the Son of God” do not occur in the old Basel Vatican, Colbert, Chartres, and other manuscripts. Then, “not man from God, but God from man” means that Ebion does not wish Christ, who had first been God, to have become man, but to have become God after he was made man. For the understanding of many passages, it will be helpful to note this force of the particle *ex* (“from”).]

—puts forward not man from God but God from man. He says that the Virgin did not receive the Word, who previously subsisted and who in the beginning was God with God; rather, that she generated flesh through the word.

> [Note: Col. 0053D. The edition reads “received in the flesh.” *In the flesh* has been removed on the authority of the manuscripts.]

For by “Word,” before Mary generated flesh, he means not the nature of the existent or subsistent Only-begotten God, but an uttered sound of voice.

> [Note: Col. 0053D. Supply: “the flesh which Mary generated.” This is his meaning: by the name “Word,” before Mary generated flesh, Ebion understands an external sound of voice, not the nature of the existing or subsisting only-begotten God. Hence it is more correct to read with the manuscripts *antea non* (“previously not”) than, with the printed editions, *non antea* (“not previously”).]

So too do certain preachers of the present time, who bring forth the form, wisdom, and power of God from nothing and from time, lest, if the Son is from the Father, God should be diminished into the Son—excessively anxious that the Son, born from him, should empty the Father. Therefore they come to God’s assistance in the creation of the Son, constructing him from things that do not exist, so that the Father may remain within the perfection of his own nature, because nothing has been begotten from him.

And what wonder is it if they hold divergent opinions concerning the Holy Spirit—

> [Note: Col. 0053D. The printed editions, from a single later Colbert manuscript, read “now hold divergent opinions.” Shortly afterward Badius, Erasmus, and Lipsius, from the same manuscript, read: “who are such reckless authors in creating his Giver,” and so forth. We shall shortly establish, from the agreement of all manuscript and printed witnesses, with greater certainty that Hilary calls the Son the author of the Holy Spirit. We have shown in the Preface that this is said of Arians, not Macedonians.]

—when they are such reckless authors in creating, changing, and abolishing his Giver? Thus they destroy the truth of this perfect sacrament while they contrive diversities of substances in realities so common—

> [Note: Col. 0053D–0054C. One might prefer “diversities of substances”; but we have already noticed many examples of such figures of speech. This one passage is sufficient to prove how unquestioned the consubstantiality of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit was for Hilary: he expressly rejects diversities of substances in three realities having a substance so common. Hence, below in §5, he describes those who think otherwise as persons “who bring darkness upon light, cut apart what cannot be divided, split what is incorruptible, and partition what is indivisible.”]

—denying the Father, while taking from the Son what it is to be Son; denying the Holy Spirit—

> [Note: Col. 0053C. “By not knowing.”]  
> [Note: Col. 0054D. Thus the older Basel Vatican, Colbert, Chartres, and other manuscripts; but Corbie and later manuscripts, with the printed editions, give “by not knowing” in place of “denying.” It is not obscure that the Son is here called the author of the Holy Spirit, and that those who do not know the Son, from whom the Spirit is and by whom he is given to us, do not know the Spirit’s use—that is, participation in him—and his author.]

—while they do not know both his use and his Author. Thus they destroy the uninstructed while asserting an account of this preaching, and deceive hearers while taking nature away by means of names; for they cannot take names away from nature.

I pass over the remaining names perilous to humankind—the Valentinians, Marcionites, Manichaeans, and other plagues—which sometimes seize the minds of the uninstructed and infect them by the contagion of association. Thus one plague comes to be shared by all, when the disease of the preachers is poured into the minds of their hearers.

### 5. How reluctantly and tremblingly Hilary undertakes speech about divine things [Col. 0053C]

Therefore their unbelief draws us into uncertainty and danger—

> [Note: Col. 0054D. The particle *ac* (“and”) is restored from the manuscripts.]

—so that it is necessary to say something beyond the heavenly prescription concerning matters so great and so hidden. The Lord had said that the nations were to be baptized “in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.” The form of faith is certain; but, with regard to heretics, every understanding is uncertain.

> [Note: Col. 0053C. “All understandings.”]

Therefore nothing is to be added to the commandments; rather, a limit must be set to boldness. Since malice, aroused by the prompting of diabolical deceit, evades the truth of realities through the names of natures, let us set forth the nature of the names.

> [Note: Col. 0053C. “The natures of the names.”]
