Having explained, as we may from the words themselves, the dignity and office of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, let not the names be frustrated of their natural properties; rather, let them be constrained by the names within the meaning of nature.

And I do not know what spirit there is in those who think otherwise concerning these things: who corrupt truth, bring darkness upon light—

> [Note: Col. 0053C. “Upon light.”]

—cut apart what cannot be divided, split what is incorruptible, and partition what is indivisible.

> [Note: Col. 0054D. A later Colbert manuscript, corrupted with a gloss, and from it Badius and Erasmus, reads: “If this were easy for them to do, they would wish to tear perfect things to pieces.” Lipsius and Paris: “For whom it is easy to tear perfect things to pieces.” They are corrected from the other manuscripts. Then, in place of “to impose law,” the Basel Vatican manuscript has “to impose an end.”]

If it is only so easy for them to tear perfect things to pieces, to impose law upon power, and to prescribe a limit to the Infinite—

> [Note: Col. 0054C. *Tantum* (“only”) is absent.]

—then certainly, in answering them, I have agitation amid my cares, wasting away in my mind—perhaps *tabes*, “consumption,” rather than *labes*, “collapse”—stupor in my understanding; and in speech I shall confess not merely weakness but silence. Yet I am compelled to will this, while boldness is resisted, error is remedied, and ignorance is provided for. Immense is what is demanded; incomprehensible is what is dared: that there should be speech about God beyond God’s own definition. He has set forth the names of nature: Father, Son, Holy Spirit. Whatever is sought beyond this lies outside the meaning of speech, outside the reach of sense, outside the conception of understanding: it is neither uttered, attained, nor grasped.

> [Note: Col. 0054C. “Will be sought.”]

The nature of the reality exhausts the significance of words; impenetrable light blinds the contemplation of sense; whatever is bounded by no limit exceeds the capacity of understanding. But, imploring pardon for this necessity from him who is all these things, we shall dare, seek, and speak. And the one thing we promise in so great an inquiry is this: we shall believe those things which shall have been signified.

### 6. The conception of the Father

The Father is he from whom all that exists came to be.

> [Note: Col. 0054C. “Stands.”]  
> [Note: Col. 0054D. Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions have “stands.” Then an old Remigius manuscript reads: “He himself in Christ and through the Spirit.” The Father’s distinctive property, however, is to be the origin of all things—as Augustine says, *Sermon* LXXI, §26: “From him comes the origin of works from whom comes the existence of the cooperating persons.”]

He himself is, in Christ and through Christ, the origin of all things. But his being is in himself—

> [Note: Col. 0055C. Thus two Colbert and two Vatican manuscripts, and also in the extract from this passage transferred to the end of the book *To Constantius*. In the printed editions *ejus* (“his”) is absent; that word alone, without *esse* (“being”), occurs in the older Colbert, Remigius, Corbie, Faurian, Pratensis, and Chartres manuscripts. In this text, in place of *ejus*, a second ancient hand wrote *is* (“he”); that reading was copied into later manuscripts. Shortly afterward the printed editions have *continens* (“containing”) for *obtinens* (“possessing”).]  
> [Note: Col. 0055C. *Esse* (“being”) has fallen out.]

—he does not receive what he is from elsewhere, but possesses what he is from himself and in himself. He is infinite, because he is not contained in anything, but all things are within him; always outside place, because he is not contained—

> [Note: Col. 0055C. The printed editions add “in a place,” from later manuscripts, for greater clarity. Then the Basel Vatican manuscript reads: “always outside time.”]

—always before time, because time is from him. Run in thought, if you suppose that he has any endpoint: you will always find him, because whenever you direct your thought, there is always that toward which you direct it. To keep directing your thought toward his place is, for you, the same as his being without end. Speech will fail concerning him, but his nature will not be enclosed. Turn time back again: you will always find him to be; and when the number of calculations fails in speech, God nevertheless does not cease always to be.

Stir your understanding and embrace the whole with your mind: you grasp nothing. This whole still has a remainder, and that remainder is always in the whole. Therefore that is not a whole which has a remainder; nor is the remainder the all, which is whole.

> [Note: Col. 0055D. The printed editions read: “It is not whole to him to whom …”; we have removed *to him it is*, on the authority of the better manuscripts.]  
> [Note: Col. 0055C. Verona manuscript: “to whom also everything which is whole is.” It is more correct to supply *is* in place of *also*. The Erasmus edition reads: “Therefore neither is it whole to him to whom there is a remainder, nor is there a remainder to whom everything that is is whole.”]  
> [Note: Col. 0055D. Badius: “To whom everything that is is whole.” Erasmus, Lipsius, and Paris: “To whom everything that is is whole.” Later manuscripts: “to whom is everything which is whole.” The corrected books present the true reading.]

For a remainder is a part, whereas “everything” is what is whole. But God is both everywhere and wholly wherever he is. Thus he exceeds the region of understanding—

> [Note: Col. 0055D. Thus most manuscripts with Badius, Erasmus, and Lipsius. Paris, with two Colbert manuscripts and one Sorbonne manuscript, reads “the religion of understanding.” Another Colbert manuscript and the Basel Vatican manuscript read “the reasoning of understanding.”]

—outside him there is nothing, and it belongs to him always to be as he always is. This is the truth of God’s mystery; this is the name of the impenetrable nature in the Father.

> [Note: Col. 0055C. “Impenetrable.”]

God invisible, ineffable, infinite: in speaking him speech must be silent; in investigating him sense must grow dull; in comprehending him understanding must be constrained. Yet, as we have said, he has the name of his nature in “Father”; but he is Father only. For he does not, in the human manner, have from elsewhere that whereby he is Father.

> [Note: Col. 0055D. We have removed from here: “but able in himself to have that whereby he is Father”; it occurs only in a very few and very late manuscripts. If we judge rightly, the eternal Father is here declared not to have from elsewhere either that whereby he is or that whereby he is Father, but to be constituted in his own nature by the very fact that he is Father; and thus to be unlike human beings, who do not become fathers as soon as they become human beings.]

He himself is unbegotten, eternal, always possessing in himself the condition that he always be.

> [Note: Col. 0056C. Printed editions: “that he may always be Father,” contrary to the manuscripts. The Father is now considered not as Father but as eternal.]

He is known to the Son alone: for “no one knows the Father except the Son, and him to whom the Son wills to reveal him”; nor does anyone know the Son except the Father. Their knowledge is mutual; their reciprocal knowledge is perfect. And because no one knows the Father except the Son, let us think concerning the Father with the revealing Son, who alone is the faithful witness.

> [Note: Col. 0055C–0056C. The phrase “with the Son revealing [the Father]” is repeated in the source. Badius, Erasmus, and inferior manuscripts read “with the Son revealing the Son”; this reading was wrongly restored in the final Paris edition. The sense is this: we should think nothing concerning the Father except what the Son has revealed concerning him.]

### 7. The Father is ineffable; knowledge of God is perfect

I would rather have thought these things about the Father than spoken them. For I am not unaware—

> [Note: Col. 0056C. Thus restored with the help of our manuscript. Previously the reading was: “It will have escaped [me].”]

—that every speech is weak for uttering what belongs to him. He must be apprehended as invisible, incomprehensible, eternal.

> [Note: Col. 0056C. In place of “must be apprehended,” the Basel Vatican manuscript has another reading, already mentioned.]

But when one says that he is in himself and from himself, and that he is through himself—

> [Note: Col. 0056C. “In himself and” is absent from our book.]  
> [Note: Col. 0056C. All manuscripts except one omit “in himself.”]

—that he is invisible, incomprehensible, and immortal—

> [Note: Col. 0056C. “Is” is added. Shortly afterward read “eternal,” with the other manuscripts, not “immortal.”]  
> [Note: Col. 0056C. The manuscripts read “eternal.”]

—there is indeed in these terms a confession of honor, an indication for the mind, and a certain circumscription of opinion. Yet speech fails before his nature, and words do not explain the reality as it is. For when you hear that he is in himself, no complete account presents itself to human reason.

> [Note: Col. 0056C. “A complete account occurs to human reason.”]  
> [Note: Col. 0056D. Paris, with the ancient books, reads: “a complete account presents itself to human reason.” Yet in the Chartres and Corbie manuscripts a second hand wrote *ratio* (“reason”) over *rationi* (“to reason”); later manuscripts copied that reading, followed by Badius, Erasmus, and Lipsius. They are corrected from the very ancient Basel Vatican manuscript. Here *absolutio* means a statement free of all ambiguity, clearly and distinctly expressing the nature of the thing.]

For possessing and being possessed are distinguished, and there will be one thing that is, another in which it is. Again, if you receive the statement that he is from himself, no one is both giver and gift to himself.

> [Note: Col. 0056D. That is: it seems contradictory for the same thing both to give itself being and to receive it.]

If he is immortal, then there is something not from him to which another is not subject; and he is not simply that which, by the expression of this word, is vindicated from another.

> [Note: Col. 0056D. The Basel Vatican manuscript has *ante* (“before”) for *alter* (“another”); an older Colbert and German manuscript has *a te* (“from you”). We would prefer *a se* (“from himself”): for by “immortal” death is signified as something to which the Father is not subject by his nature. Thus, if you attend only to the sound of the word, death itself seems to exist apart from the Father, from whom he is protected. In place of that word the Basel Vatican manuscript has *vincatur* (“is conquered”), and the older Remigius manuscript has “it is indicated concerning another.” The received reading is to be retained.]

If he is incomprehensible, then there will nowhere be that which is denied to be reached. If he is invisible, whatever does not present itself to sight lacks itself. Thus confession fails in naming him: whatever collection of words may be applied will not declare God as he is and as great as he is.

> [Note: Col. 0057C. “Will speak.”]

Perfect knowledge is to know God in such a way that, although one knows him not to be unknowable, one nevertheless knows him to be inexpressible. He must be believed, understood, worshipped; and by these offices he must be spoken of.

### 8. What the Son is, and what he is not

We have been carried from harborless places out into the deep upon a stormy sea, and it is dangerous both to retreat and to advance; yet the greater difficulty lies in traversing what remains than in what has already been traversed. The Father is as he is, and must be believed to be as he is. The mind is dismayed at approaching the Son, and every word trembles to betray itself.

For he is the offspring of the Unbegotten: one from one, true from true, living from living, perfect from perfect; power from power, wisdom from wisdom, glory from glory; the image of the invisible God, the form of the unbegotten Father. But what sort of offspring of the Only-begotten from the Unbegotten shall we suppose? For the Father repeatedly cries from heaven: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3:17).

> [Note: Col. 0057D. Printed editions: “in whom I am well …,” contrary to the older books.]

There is no severing or division, for he who begot is impassible, and he who was born is the image of the invisible God; and he testifies: “The Father is in me, and I in the Father” (John 10:38). There is no adoption, for he is truly the Son of God and cries: “He who has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9). Nor was he commanded to exist as the rest of things were: for the Only-begotten is from the One, and has life in himself, as he who begot him has life in himself. For he says: “As the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son also to have life in himself” (John 5:26).

Nor is the Son a part of the Father—

> [Note: Col. 0057D. The Basel Vatican and Chartres manuscripts read: “The Son is a part of the Father”; not badly.]

—for the Son testifies: “All things that are the Father’s are mine” (John 16:15); and again: “All mine are yours, and yours are mine” (John 17:10); and: “Whatever the Father has, he gave to the Son.”

> [Note: Col. 0057C. The words “Whatever the Father has, he gave to the Son” occur in the printed editions but do not appear in our manuscript. Nor do they seem drawn from anywhere except John 3:35, where we now read: “The Father gave all things into his hand,” that is, the Son’s. The Greek text agrees.]  
> [Note: Col. 0057D. These words, “Whatever the Father has, he gave to the Son,” occur only in the printed editions and two manuscripts.]

The Apostle also testifies: “For in him dwells all the fullness of divinity bodily” (Col. 2:9). That which is a part cannot by nature be all things.

> [Note: Col. 0057D. Paris alone has “it is a proportion”; wrongly.]

But he is perfect from the Perfect, because he who has all things gave all things. Nor should he be thought not to have given because he possesses, or not to possess because he has given.

### 9. The generation of the Son of God exceeds human capacity

Therefore each possesses the secret of this birth.

> [Note: Col. 0057D. Lipsius restored “possesses,” contrary to the other books. Here reference is made to Christ’s saying: “No one knows the Father except the Son, nor does anyone know the Son except the Father,” and so forth.]

And if someone perhaps blames his own understanding because he cannot attain the mystery of this generation, although Father and Son are certainly understood—

> [Note: Col. 0057D–0058D. One Colbert manuscript reads “although nevertheless.” The printed editions, with later manuscripts, read “are to be understood.” More correctly, three Colbert manuscripts, together with Chartres, Basel Vatican, German, Sorbonne, and Remigius manuscripts, read “are understood.” For the Gospel clearly proclaims Father and Son, although it veils the manner of generation in silence. Thus we possess the reality; we do not know the manner.]

—he will hear from me that this is unknown with still greater grief. I do not know; I do not inquire; yet I shall console myself. The archangels do not know; angels have not heard; the ages do not contain it; the prophet did not perceive it; the apostle did not ask; the Son himself did not disclose it. Let the grief of complaints cease. I do not call you, whoever you are who inquire into these things—

> [Note: Col. 0058C. “Seek.”]

—to the heights; I do not stretch you out into breadth; I do not lead you down into depth. Will you not calmly remain ignorant of the Creator’s birth, when you are ignorant of the origin of creation?

At least I ask this: do you perceive that you have been begotten, and do you understand what things are begotten from you? I do not ask whence you received reason, whence you obtained life, whence you acquired understanding, or what the faculty of smell, sight, and hearing is in you. Certainly no one is ignorant of what he does. I ask whence you bestow these things upon those whom you beget: how you implant sensation, kindle eyes, establish a heart. If you can, explain these things. Therefore you have things which you do not know—

> [Note: Col. 0058C. “Which you do not know.”]

—and you bestow things which you do not understand. You are calmly ignorant in your own affairs, but arrogantly ignorant in God’s.

### 10. How devoutly, and to what profit, the generation of God may be investigated

Hear, then, the unbegotten Father; hear the Only-begotten Son. Hear: “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28). Hear: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). Hear: “He who has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9). Hear: “The Father is in me, and I in the Father” (John 10:38). Hear: “I came forth from the Father” (John 16:28); and, “He who is in the bosom of the Father”—

> [Note: Col. 0058D. All manuscripts except one omit “and, He who is in the bosom of the Father.” This passage is cited differently in §23.]

—and, “All things which the Father handed over to the Son”—

> [Note: Col. 0058D. Most manuscripts omit “Father.” Then the Basel Vatican and Chartres manuscripts read “to me” for “to the Son.” Hilary cites this passage more than once, but its source is uncertain. It might seem to be Matthew 11:25, “All things have been handed over to me by my Father,” either recalled merely in sense or from a particular translation, unless below, in Book VI, §22, and elsewhere, he agreed with us.]

—and, “The Son has life in himself, just as the Father has life in himself” (John 5:26).

> [Note: Col. 0058C. “Gave.”]

Hear the Son as image, wisdom, power, and glory of God; and understand the Holy Spirit proclaiming through the prophet—

> [Note: Col. 0058C. “The Holy Spirit proclaiming through the prophet.”]  
> [Note: Col. 0058D. Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read “the prophet proclaiming.”]

—“Who shall declare his generation?” (Isa. 53:8). And chide the Lord as he testifies: “No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and him to whom the Son wills to reveal him” (Matt. 11:27). Enter into this secret; immerse yourself in the mystery of unimaginable birth between the one unbegotten God and the one only-begotten God. Begin, advance, persist. Although I know that you will not arrive, I shall nevertheless rejoice that you are advancing. For one who devoutly pursues infinite things, even if he never reaches them, nevertheless advances by going onward. Understanding stands here at the boundary set by the words.

> [Note: Col. 0059D. Paris, with Colbert and German manuscripts, reads “at the boundary of understanding.” This devout bishop seems to give the reason why he says that no one will attain knowledge of the mystery: the end of that investigation will be an understanding of the words—namely, that in God there is a true Father and a true Son of the same nature as the Father; but one will not be allowed to proceed further to the manner of generation.]

### 11. The nature of the Son; the duty of faith

The Son is from that Father who is—

> [Note: Col. 0059D. Erasmus, Lipsius, and Paris read “from him who is Father,” contrary to the other books. This way of speaking will recur more than once and has another force; see Book III, §22.]

—Only-begotten from the Unbegotten, offspring from the Parent, living from the Living. As the Father has life in himself, so life in himself has been given to the Son. Perfect from Perfect, because whole from whole; not division or cutting apart, because one is in the other, and the fullness of divinity is in the Son.

> [Note: Col. 0059D. The Basel Vatican and Chartres manuscripts read “one from the other”; less well.]

Incomprehensible from the Incomprehensible, for neither is known except by the other. Invisible from the Invisible, because he is the image of the invisible God, and because whoever has seen the Son has seen the Father. One distinct from the other, because Father and Son; not one divine nature and another, because both are one. God from God: from the one unbegotten God, one only-begotten God—not two gods, but one from one; not two unbegotten beings, because he is born from the Unbegotten; one distinct from the other, differing in nothing, because the life of the Living One is in the Living One.

We have touched upon these things concerning the nature of divinity—

> [Note: Col. 0059C. “We touch upon.”]

—not comprehending the full measure of understanding, but understanding that the things of which we speak are incomprehensible. “Then,” you say, “there is no duty of faith, if nothing can be comprehended.”

> [Note: Col. 0059C. “You will say”: shortly afterward, “to know itself to be incomprehensible.”]

On the contrary: let faith profess this duty—to know itself to be incapable of comprehending that which it investigates.

### 12. The generation of the Son of God unknown to worldly wise men and scribes of the Law, and not sufficiently proved by miracles

There remains something further concerning the inexpressible generation of the Son—or rather, that “something” still remains the whole. I am agitated, torn apart, dulled—

> [Note: Col. 0059D. Some manuscripts read “I blush,” others “I waste away”; from these our conjecture is confirmed that in §5 one should read “there is wasting away in my mind,” not “there is collapse.”]

—and do not know from where to begin. For I do not know when the Son was born; and it would be impious for me not to know that he was born. Whom shall I invoke? Whom shall I implore? From what books shall I draw words for explaining such great difficulties? Shall I turn over the whole school of Greece? But I have read: “Where is the wise man? Where is the seeker of this age?” (1 Cor. 1:20).

> [Note: Col. 0060D. The printed editions wrongly add here: “Where is the scribe?” It is better absent from the manuscripts, since by “scribe” is meant not a Gentile but a teacher of the Law.]

Therefore in this matter the sophists of the world and the wise men of the age are mute, for they rejected the wisdom of God. Shall I consult the scribe of the Law? But he is ignorant, because the cross of Christ is a stumbling block to him. Perhaps I shall urge you to close your eyes and be silent, because for reverence of him who is preached it should suffice that lepers were cleansed, the deaf heard, the lame ran, paralytics stood, the blind received light—

> [Note: Col. 0059C. “Saw the light.”]

—a man blind from the womb obtained eyes, demons were driven away, the sick recovered strength, and the dead lived. But heretics too confess these things—and perish.

### 13. The Same Things Revealed to a Fisherman. The Word Is Free from Time.

Expect, then, nothing less than the running of the lame, the sight of the blind, the flight of demons, and the life of the dead. [Note: “He stood.”] For there stands with me, in defence of the difficulties set forth above, a needy fisherman, [Note: “Thus we read from the Verona manuscript, not ‘unknown,’ as previously. For shortly afterwards follows: ‘an unlettered, uneducated fisherman.’”] ignorant, [Col. 0060B] uneducated, with his hands occupied in flax, [Note: “His hands occupied in flax; then, his feet covered with mud.”] his clothing wet, his feet covered with mud, altogether fresh from the boat. Seek and understand [Note: “Here the printed editions add ‘look around,’ which is absent from the manuscripts.”] whether it was more wonderful [Note: “The dead.”] to have raised the dead or to have imparted the knowledge of this doctrine to an unskilled man.

For he says: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1). What is this, “was in the beginning”? Times are passed beyond, [Note: “They are transcended.”] ages are crossed, eras are removed. Set down whatever beginning you wish according to your own opinion: you do not grasp it by time, for that of which we are treating “was.” Look at the world; understand what is written concerning it: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Gen. 1:1). Therefore what is created comes to be in the beginning; and [Note: “Containing age.”] [Note: “Bad. has ‘containing age.’ Other editions: ‘contains age.’ From the manuscripts, some read ‘contains ages,’ others ‘ages contain,’ others ‘containing in age.’ More correctly, the three older witnesses read ‘you contain by age’; this is opposed to what was just said of the Word: ‘you do not grasp it by time.’”] what is contained in time is contained in the beginning in order that it may come to be.

But my unlettered, uneducated fisherman is free from time, released from ages, and has overcome every beginning. For that which is [Col. 0060C] was; nor is that which was in the beginning, rather than was made, enclosed within any time so that it should have begun.

### 14. Yet It Is Not Solitary.

But perhaps we shall find that our fisherman has departed from the order of the proposed division. For he has declared the Word free from time, [Note: “(10) The Verona manuscript reads: ‘and it will take to itself that which is free,’ [Col. 0060C] which comes to the same thing. For if the Word is free from time, it seems to follow that it will take to itself that which is free; that is, it will claim for itself that it is its own master, solitary, and dependent upon no one. This objection he removes by the Apostle’s words which follow: ‘And the Word was with God.’ ‘Let us raise our ears,’ he says, etc. For although the Word was before time, it was nevertheless with God; and he who is absent from time is not absent from his Author. Thus indeed we read in the same manuscript. There the reading is *erans* in place of *qui erat*, ‘who was.’”] and that which is free belongs to itself, is solitary, and obeys no one.

Let us raise our ears to what follows. He says: “And the Word was with God” (John 1:1). That which was before the beginning is now without beginning with God. Therefore [Note: “For ‘who was,’ the ancient manuscripts of Colbert, Remigius, and Germany read *erans*. The relative *qui* is also absent from the Chartres manuscript. Then Bad. and Erasmus read: ‘and because he is absent from the condition of time,’ most incorrectly using *quia* for *qui*. Lipsius and Paris, as also several manuscripts, read: ‘and he who is absent from time.’ In the Chartres manuscript: ‘from knowledge of time.’ We read with two Colbert manuscripts, the German manuscript, and the Sorbonne manuscript: ‘from the time of knowledge,’ that is, from whatever time can be conceived; because he is before whatever beginning you choose to posit in your opinion. At one time ‘from the time of creation’ also seemed acceptable, as though from the time appropriate to created things.”] he who was is with God; and he who is absent from the time apprehended by knowledge is not absent from his Author. Our fisherman has escaped; but perhaps he will be caught in what remains.

### 15. Whether, According to Ebion, It Is a Sound of the Voice. “Was” Does Not Suit a Vocal Sound. The Word Is God.

[Note: “You say.”] For you will say: “The Word is the sound of a voice, the expression of matters, and the utterance of thoughts. This was with God and was in the beginning, because the discourse of thought is eternal when the thinker is eternal.”

[Note: “I shall answer. Then, ‘while we see.’”] I answer you briefly for my fisherman’s present defence, while we shall see how he himself defends his rusticity. A discourse has it by nature that it may be; but it follows that it will have been. It exists only while it is heard. And how was that in the beginning which is neither before time nor after time? Indeed, I do not know whether it can even exist in time. For the speech of speakers is not before they speak, and when they have spoken it will not be; and in that very act [Col. 0061B] in which they speak, while they are finishing, that from which they began is already no longer.

These things are from me, as from one among the rest. But the fisherman speaks otherwise for himself, and will first rebuke you for having listened carelessly. For even if, as an untrained hearer, you had missed the first statement, “In the beginning was the Word,” what complaint have you about the next: “And the Word was with God”? Had you heard, “in God,” rather than “with God,” so that you might take it as the discourse of hidden thought? Or had the rustic failed to know the importance [Note: “The significance between *to be*, *to be in*, and *to be with*.”] [Note: “The printed editions read: ‘the importance between *to be*, *to be in*, and *to be with*’; *interesse* is superfluous and is absent from the better manuscripts. Hilary observes that the Word is not merely in the Father, as in a principle, but is also with him, with whom he always was.”] of the difference between being in and being with?

For that which was in the beginning is declared not to be in another, but to be with another. But I draw nothing from what went before; [Note: “The Vatican-Basilica manuscript reads, ‘with the following,’ in two words. [Col. 0062C] The other reading is supported by this passage, Book VII, no. 22: ‘Let the testimony of the divine judgment concerning himself be present to him.’”] let what follows be present to itself; await the status and name of the Word. For he says: “And the Word was God.” The sound of a voice and the utterance of thought cease to be relevant. This Word is a thing, not a sound; a nature, not speech; God, not emptiness.

### 16. Nor Does It Injure the Unity of God.

[Col. 0062A] But I tremble at the saying, and this unfamiliar expression disturbs me. I hear: “And the Word was God,” [Note: “The printed editions read ‘whom . . . they announced.’ More elegantly the manuscripts read ‘to whom,’ etc., as Hilary says this concerning himself.”] to whom the prophets proclaimed one God. Yet lest my fear be able to proceed further, my fisherman, render the economy of so great a mystery, and refer all things back to the one without insult, without abolition, without time. He says: “This was in the beginning with God.” Since this was in the beginning, it is not held within time; since it is God, it is not referred to a voice; since it is with God, [Note: “The printed editions read: ‘nothing is either confused or conferred.’ The word ‘confused’ occurs in only one Colbert manuscript. But the others read: ‘nothing is either injured or taken away,’ [Col. 0062D] two expressions aptly corresponding to the two preceding phrases, ‘without insult, without abolition.’ Moreover, in the expression *nihil nec*, this is not a double negation but a pleonasm familiar to Greeks and to Hilary himself. The Remigius and Theodulf manuscripts avoid it by reading ‘nothing in it.’ If anyone should prefer ‘nothing is either confused or taken away,’ in view of Book VII, no. 21, ‘Thus the nature is neither confused nor abolished,’ he may do so.”] nothing is either injured or taken away. For he is neither abolished into another nor proclaimed alongside the one unbegotten God, from whom he himself is the one only-begotten God.

### 17. Time Is from Him; What Time Is.

We still await from you, fisherman, the fullness concerning the Word. It was indeed [Col. 0062B] in the beginning, but perhaps it was not before the beginning. Here too I offer something for my fisherman: that which was could not not have been; for “was” does not permit “was not” in time. But what does he say for himself? “All things were made through him” (John 1:3). Therefore [Note: “‘If’ is absent from the Verona manuscript.”] [Note: “We add the particle ‘if’ on the authority of the better manuscripts. Soon after, the word ‘and’ is used for ‘also.’”] if nothing exists without him, through whom all things [37] began, then he through whom everything that is came to be is unlimited.

[Note: “The Vatican-Basilica manuscript alone reads: ‘For time is a measured signification of a duration abiding not in place but in age.’ The Chartres manuscript agrees in the final two words.”] For time is the indicated measure of duration abiding not in place but in age. And since all things are from him, no thing is not from him; and therefore time is from him.

### 18. The Word Is Not Solitary.

But someone says to you, my fisherman: “Here you have been excessively facile and indiscriminate: ‘all things were made through him’ admits no limit. There is the Unbegotten, who was made by no one; and he himself is begotten from the Unborn. ‘All things’ are without exception, and ‘nothing’ leaves anything outside.”

But while we dare say nothing further, or perhaps while we attempt to speak, [Note: “Our copyist had first written *occurret*, ‘will meet,’ more aptly and coherently than *occurre*, ‘meet’; a second but ancient hand corrected it to *occurrit plane*, ‘it plainly meets.’”] [Note: “The printed editions read ‘it meets, it plainly meets’; and shortly afterwards, ‘you have rendered the fisherman,’ contrary to the ancient books.”] meet this objection: “And without him was made nothing.” You have rendered him an Author when you have professed him a companion. For when nothing is without him, I understand that he is not alone, because one is he through whom, another [Note: “*Is* is omitted.”] is he without whom. In both, the meaning of the one who intervenes and of the one who acts is distinguished.

### 19. He Was Not Merely Present to the One Making All Things, but Also Made Them.

[Col. 0063A] But [Note: “Anxious—equally good.”] [Note: “Thus the best manuscripts elegantly read: ‘You have relieved my fear by a silent word,’ that is, you have relieved it. But the printed editions have ‘I am made anxious.’”] while I am anxious concerning the Author, who is one and unbegotten, lest in saying “all things” you had excepted nothing, you relieved my fear by saying: “And without him was made nothing.” Yet I am confused and troubled by the phrase, “without him was made nothing.” Is there then something made through another which nevertheless was not made without him? And if something is through another, [Note: “Here *factum*, ‘made,’ is inserted. Later *est*, ‘is,’ is omitted before *intervenisse*, ‘to have intervened.’”] though not without him, then not all things are through him; for it is one thing to have made, another to have intervened with one who makes.

Here, my fisherman, unlike in the other matters, I have nothing to offer from myself. An immediate answer must come from yours: “All things were made through him.” I understand. For the Apostle [Note: “Paul is added.”] taught: “Visible and invisible things, whether Thrones, Dominions, Principalities, or Powers: all things were created through him and in him” (Col. 1:16).

### 20. All Things Were Created in the Word. The Word Exists Perfect Not Successively but by Being Begotten.

[Col. 0063B] Since, then, all things are through him, help us and explain what was made not without him. [Note: “Was made.”] [Note: “Lipsius and Paris, following Erasmus, add here ‘what was made,’ contrary to the authority of the ancient books.”] “What was made in him is life” (John 1:4). Therefore that which was made in him is not without him; for what was made in him was also made through him. “For all things were created through him and in him” (Col. 1:16).

But they were created in him because God the Creator was being born. Yet also, from this, nothing was made without him which was made in him, because the God being born was life. And [Note: “Thus the better manuscripts. The printed editions read: ‘and because he was life.’”] he who was life did not become life after he was born; for in him that which was born is not one thing [Note: “The printed editions read ‘which was born,’ contrary to the manuscripts.”] and that which the one born received another. Birth and development do not have time between them.

But nothing [Note: “Without him.”] was made without himself among the things made in him, [Col. 0063C] because he is life—supply “he”—in whom they were made; and the God born from God did not become God after he was born, [Note: “The Vatican-Basilica manuscript here adds, ‘became God’: a gloss.”] but came forth as God by being born. For, being born living from the Living, true from the True, perfect from the Perfect, he was not born without the power of his own birth; that is, he did not come to experience his birth later, but understood himself to be God in the very fact that God was being born from God.

This is the Only-Begotten from the Unbegotten; this is, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30); this is the one God in the confession of Father and Son; this is the Father in the Son and the Son in the Father. Hence, “He who has seen me has seen the Father also” (John 14:9). Hence, “All things which the Father has, he gave to the Son” (John 16:15). Hence, “As the Father has life in himself, so he gave to the Son also to have life in himself” [Col. 0064A] (John 5:26). Hence, “No one knows the Son except the Father, nor the Father [Note: “Our manuscript adds: ‘who knows,’ but in a second recension. Our Vulgate and the Greek text agree.”] except the Son” (Matt. 11:27). Hence, “In him dwells all the fullness of divinity bodily” (Col. 2:9).

### 21. The Generation of the Word Is Not Comprehended by Human Reason; Therefore It Must Be Held by Faith.

This life is the light of human beings, this light illuminating the darkness. And so that the fisherman might console us concerning the impossibility of recounting his generation, according to the prophet (Isa. 53:8), he added: “And the darkness did not comprehend it” (John 1:4). The discourse of nature has yielded and has nowhere to go; and yet this fisherman, reclining upon the Lord’s breast, received this.

This is not the speech of the age, because the thing under discussion is not a thing of the age. Let something be produced, if anything beyond what has been said can be found in the meaning of the words; and let any other names for the nature we have expounded be brought forward. If they are not—indeed, because they are not—let us marvel at this teaching in the fisherman, and in him recognize [Note: “The Vatican-Basilica manuscript, together with another Vatican manuscript and the Chartres manuscript, reads: ‘the eloquence of God.’”] the utterances of God. Let us hold and adore the ineffable confession of Father and Son, of Unbegotten and Only-Begotten, exceeding every grasp both of speech and understanding; and, in the Lord Jesus, after the example of John, let us recline, that we may be able to think and speak these things (John 13:25).

### 22. The Devices of Heretics against Faith Are Vain. One Faith Conquers All Heresies.

Moreover, the integrity of this faith is commended by evangelical authority, apostolic [39] doctrine, and the idle fraudulence of heretics clamouring on every side. [Note: “Thus we read in our manuscript; *odiosa*, ‘hateful,’ was added on second consideration.”] [Note: “The printed editions read *odiosa*, ‘hateful.’ More suitably, the manuscripts read *otiosa*, ‘idle,’ for it is immediately shown how idle and empty it is.”] For this strong and immovable foundation stands against all [Col. 0064C] winds, rains, and torrents: not to be driven by blasts, not to be penetrated by drippings, not to be undermined by floods [Note: “Four manuscripts read *solvendum*, ‘to be dissolved.’ Corbie, Pratensis, and Faur read *subruendum*, ‘to be overthrown.’ *Subluendum*, ‘to be undermined,’ must be retained, as is clear from the Commentary on Matthew, chapter 6, no. 6, and the Treatise on Psalm 68, no. 3.”] (Matt. 7:25). And it is best that whatever is assailed by many can nevertheless be shaken by none.

For as certain kinds of medicines are so constituted that they are useful not only for individual diseases but cure all ailments in common and possess in themselves the power of general help, so the catholic faith bestows the aid of a common remedy not against individual plagues but against every disease. It is not to be weakened by kind, conquered by number, or deceived by diversity; but one and the same, it stands against each and all. For it is a great thing [Note: “In earlier editions: ‘that there are so many remedies in this one faith.’”] that in this one faith there are as many remedies [Col. 0065A] as there are diseases, and just as many teachings of truth as there will be pursuits of falsehood.

Let the names of heretics be gathered into one, and let all their schools come forth. Let them hear of one unbegotten God the Father and one only-begotten Son of God, the perfect offspring of a perfect Father: begotten not by diminution, not cut off as some portion from a solid mass, but possessing all things and having begotten one who has received all things; not brought forth by derivation or flow, but born from him in and from all things, who does not cease to be in all things in which he is; free from time, released from ages, through whom all things were made. [Note: “Were made.”] For he could not be in those ages which were established by him. This is the catholic and apostolic confession drawn from the Gospels.

### 23. Testimonies against Sabellius, Ebion, and the Arians. Peter’s Confession Is the Rock.

[Col. 0065B] Let Sabellius, if he dares, proclaim the Father and the Son to be the same, and [Note: “The Vatican-Basilica manuscript reads, ‘that he is himself to himself’; it is not pleasing.”] that he is that very one who is called by both names, so that both are one with him, not one thing. He will immediately hear from the Gospels, not once or twice but often: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 17:5). He will hear: “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28). He will hear: “I go to the Father” (ibid., 12); and, “Father, I give you thanks” (John 11:41); and, [Note: “‘Glorify.’ Thus also in the Greek text: δόξασόν με, ‘Glorify me’ (John 17:5).”] “Glorify me, Father” (John 17:5); [40] and, “You are the Son of the living God” (Matt. 16:17).

Let Ebion creep in, [Note: “The printed edition reads ‘every beginning.’ *Every* is absent from the manuscripts, though it occurs in no. 4.”] granting the Son of God his beginning from Mary and understanding the Word as dating from the days of the flesh. [Note: “Let him read again with me.”] Let him read again: “Father, glorify me in your own presence with the glory which I had with you before the world existed” (John 17:5); and, “In the beginning was the Word, [Col. 0065C] and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1); and, “All things were made through him” (ibid., 3); and, “He was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world did not know him” (ibid., 10).

Let there arise [Note: “The printed editions read: ‘but under antichrist.’ The Chartres manuscript, with one Colbert manuscript, reads ‘new apostles under antichrist.’ More correctly the others read, ‘of a new apostleship, but from antichrist’; that is, possessing a new apostleship not from Christ but from antichrist. This is confirmed by Book VI, no. 37: ‘You today, false priesthood of a new apostleship, bring forward to me Christ as a creature made from nothing.’”] preachers of a new apostleship, but from antichrist, mocking the Son of God with every insult; and [Note: “They will hear.”] let them hear: “I came forth from the Father” (John 16:28); “the Son in the Father’s bosom” (John 1:18); “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30); and “I am in the Father and the Father in me” (John 14:11).

Finally, let them be angry together with the Jews [Col. 0066A] because Christ, confessing God as his own Father, made himself equal with God; and together with them let them hear: “Believe at least my works, because the Father is in me and I in the Father” (John 14:28). Therefore this is the one immovable foundation, this the one blessed rock of faith confessed by Peter’s mouth: “You are the Son of the living God” (Matt. 16:17), sustaining within itself as many proofs of truth as there will be questions of perversity and accusations of unbelief raised against it.

### 24. What Christ Undertook for Our Salvation.

In what remains is the dispensation of the Father’s will. Virgin, birth, body, and afterwards cross, death, the underworld: these are our salvation. For the sake of the human race, the Son of God was born from the Virgin and the Holy Spirit—[Note: “That by ‘Holy Spirit’ the Word himself is meant here is clear from what follows. Hence in Commentary on Matthew, chapter 2, no. 5, one expressly reads: ‘Christ, born from a woman, became flesh through the Word.’”] himself serving himself in this operation—and, with his own power, namely that of God, overshadowing, he sowed in himself the beginnings of a body and established the origins of flesh. Thus, having become human from the Virgin, he received in himself the nature of flesh; and through fellowship in this mixture, the whole body of the human race, sanctified in him, [Note: “Here and elsewhere Hilary appears to hold that Christ assumed not an individual but the whole nature of the human race. Yet, as is clear from what follows, he rather held that by assuming one single individual nature he comprehended the whole human nature in it. [Col. 0066D] Pope Leo, Sermon I on the Epiphany, similarly says that Christ assumed the nature of all humanity; and the commonly received text of Titus of Bostra on Luke, chapter 12, says that by the first-fruits of our mass he put on the whole human nature. Hence Gregory of Nyssa, Catechetical Oration, chapter 32, cited by Theodoret, Dialogue III, teaches that we rose with Christ because the man who received God, and who was exalted by resurrection, was from no other source than our mass. ‘Just as if,’ he says there, ‘the whole nature were a single living creature, the resurrection of one part penetrates the whole.’ Likewise Ambrose, On Faith, Book IV, chapter 10, explains that we sit at the Father’s right hand in Christ through the unity of the body. This illustrates how far Hilary, with the other Fathers, asserts that Christ has already made us participants in his nature, holiness, resurrection, and glory. See the Notes on the Commentary on Matthew, chapter 2, no. 5.”] might come into existence; so that, as all might be created in him because he chose to be bodily, so he in turn might be conveyed into all through that which is invisible in him.

Therefore the invisible image of God did not refuse the shame of a human beginning, but passed through every indignity of our nature—conception, birth, crying, and cradle.

### 25. That We Can Render Nothing Worthy in Return.

[41] What worthy return can we make for the affection of such condescension? The one only-begotten God, of inexpressible origin from God, grows into the form of a little human body, having been inserted into the womb of the holy Virgin. He who contains all things, and within whom and through whom all things exist, is brought forth according to the law of human birth. At whose voice archangels and angels tremble, heaven, earth, and all the elements of this world [Note: “They will be dissolved; our manuscript, with other manuscripts.”] [Note: “In most manuscripts: ‘they will be dissolved.’”] will be dissolved—he is heard in the crying of infancy. He who is invisible and incomprehensible, not to be confined by sight, sense, or touch, is wrapped in swaddling clothes.

Whoever considers these things unworthy of God will confess himself indebted for a greater benefit [Col. 0067A] precisely in proportion as these things were less fitting for the majesty of God. He through whom man was made had no need to become man; but we needed God to become flesh and dwell in us—that is, through the assumption of one flesh, to inhabit inwardly the whole of flesh. His humility is our nobility; his dishonour is our honour: that he, God, subsisting in flesh, [Note: “The older Remigius manuscript reads ‘subsisting.’ Then the Chartres and Vatican-Basilica manuscripts read ‘renewed from flesh.’ In Leo, who cites these words of Hilary in Letter 97, now 134, the latest edition restores from a Roman manuscript: ‘renewed in God from flesh.’ Nevertheless *renewed* is preferable. For the discourse concerns our restoration through Christ’s assumption of flesh, and, as it were, a migration into God, not regeneration through baptism. Moreover, the manuscript of the canon-law collection of the Roman Church in Leo, vol. II, p. 142, gives these words again, but with the reading retained here.”] we in return are renewed into God from flesh.

### 26. The Dignity of Conception and Birth Commends Their Humility.

But lest cradles, crying, birth, and conception perhaps detain the scrupulous thoughts of minds, the dignity of God must be rendered to each of them, [Note: “That is, it must be shown how in Christ’s conception, birth, and other things that appear weak in him, divine dignity is displayed. Hilary then calls the weakness of will that which was assumed by a choice of will. ‘The magnificence of power’ likewise means a splendid and glorious display of power.”] so that the humility of his will may be preceded by the splendour of power, and dignity may not abandon condescension.

Let us therefore see what [Note: “Are.”] ministries attended the conception. An angel speaks to Zacharias; a child is granted to a barren woman; the priest comes forth mute from the place of incense; John bursts forth into speech while still confined in his mother’s womb; an angel blesses Mary and promises that the Virgin will be mother of the Son of God. Conscious of her virginity, she is troubled by the difficulty of the event; the angel explains the efficacy of the divine operation. For he says: “The Holy Spirit [Note: “The manuscripts read *superveniet*, ‘will come upon,’ without *de*, ‘from.’”] will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke 1:35).

The Holy Spirit, coming from above, sanctified the Virgin’s inner parts; and, breathing in them—for “the Spirit breathes where he wills” (John 3:8)—[Note: “Bad. and Erasmus read ‘and he did not mingle himself with human flesh’: corruptly. They evidently failed to notice that ‘Holy Spirit’ here does not mean the third but the second person of the Trinity, who formed a body proper to himself. To signify this work Hilary appropriately uses the verb ‘to breathe,’ as Moses used it in Genesis 2:7 in narrating the formation of the first human. We have shown in the first section of our general preface that many Fathers interpreted the descent of the Holy Spirit upon the Virgin in the same way. There we noted that the reading in Cyprian, On the Vanity of Idols, ‘He puts on flesh with the Holy Spirit cooperating,’ is highly suspect of corruption, since the sounder manuscripts instead read: ‘The Holy Spirit puts on flesh.’”] he mingled himself with the nature of human flesh. [Note: “The verb *immiscere*, ‘to mingle,’ here does not signify a confusion of the two natures, but their intimate union. For, as Leporius says in his tract of correction, things may be mingled without corruption and yet be truly mingled. Irenaeus, Book III, chapter 21; Novatian, On the Trinity, chapter 11; Cyprian, On the Vanity of Idols; Augustine, Letter 137, no. 11; Pope Leo, Sermon 3 on the Nativity of Christ; Vigilius, Book I against Eutyches; and others use the same expression for the union of the Word with flesh.”] He took upon himself by his power and might that which was alien to him; [Note: “It has elsewhere been observed that Hilary uses *praesumo*, ‘take upon oneself,’ and *assumo*, ‘assume,’ interchangeably.”] and lest anything should fall away from divine dignity through the weakness of the human body, [Note: “In the Vatican-Basilica manuscript: ‘of the human race.’ Then after ‘fall away,’ supply: ‘from divine dignity.’”] the power of the Most High overshadowed the Virgin, strengthening her weakness as it were by an enveloping shadow, [Note: “Lipsius and Paris read ‘surrounding.’ The Vatican-Basilica manuscript reads ‘shining around.’ Bad. and Erasmus, with nearly all the manuscripts, read ‘enveloping.’”] so that the overshadowing of divine power might temper the bodily substance to the efficacy of the Spirit’s generative entrance. This is the dignity of conception.

### 27. The Dignity of the Birth.

Let us see what dignity follows birth, crying, and cradle. An angel tells Joseph that the Virgin will give birth, and that he who is born shall be called Emmanuel, that is, “God with us.” The Spirit proclaims through the prophet (Isa. 7:14), the angel bears witness: he who is born is God with us. A new light of a star is brought forth from heaven for the Magi, [Note: “The ancient books consistently write *ecfertur* or *haecfertur*, ‘is brought forth.’”] and a heavenly sign attends the Lord of heaven. An angel announces to shepherds that Christ the Lord, the salvation of all, has been born. A multitude of the heavenly host assembles to praise the birth, and the joys of the divine company utter proclamations of so great a work. Then “Glory to God in the highest, and peace on earth to people of good will” [Col. 0068B] is announced.

Then the Magi are present: they adore him wrapped in swaddling clothes; and, after that hidden exercise of their vain learning, they bend the knee before him lying in the cradle. Thus through the Magi the lowliness of the cradle is adored; thus the crying is honoured by the divine joys of angels; [Note: “Is honoured.”] thus the Spirit proclaiming through the prophet concerning the birth, and [Note: “And the angel announcing the same thing.”] [Note: “Thus the manuscripts. But the printed editions add here *idipsum*, ‘the same thing’; and shortly afterwards have ‘coming from above.’”] the angel announcing it, and the star of new light, minister to him. Thus the Holy Spirit coming upon the Virgin and the power of the Most High overshadowing her effect the beginnings of birth.

One thing is understood, another seen; one thing is perceived by the eyes, another by the mind. The Virgin gives birth: the birth is from God. The infant cries: praising angels are heard. The swaddling clothes are soiled: God is adored. Thus the dignity of power [43] is not lost while the humility of flesh [Note: “The humility is assumed. This is the reading required. For the controversy concerning this passage, see what has been prefixed.”] [Note: “Paris reads ‘is admitted’: wrongly. Nor is the Victorinus manuscript better, reading ‘while the humanity of flesh.’ Then Bad. and Erasmus, with certain manuscripts, read ‘is adored.’ This passage once occasioned great controversy when Felix of Urgell cited it in defence of his heresy. Hincmar, at the beginning of his preface to On Predestination, reports that Felix, the unhappy bishop of the city of Urgell, was refuted in a council because, having bribed the younger librarian of the palace at Aachen, he erased a book of blessed Hilary and, where it was written *adoratur*, ‘is adored,’ inserted: ‘the humility of flesh is *adoptatur*, adopted.’ Likewise Alcuin, Against the Same, Book VI: ‘You, most perverse man, entirely say “is adopted,” where blessed Hilary says “is adored”: surely the humility of flesh was adored by the Magi and honoured by the mystical forms of gifts, not adopted.’ We possess a Corbie manuscript written eight hundred years ago which has the final syllables *ptatur* in an erased place; although perhaps the alteration was made in bad faith, *adoptatur* was not incorrectly added. This reading occurs in the Colbert and Chartres manuscripts, written before Felix’s time, and in others at a wholly sound and intact place. Nor does *adoptatur* here mean anything other than ‘is assumed.’ For Hilary shows that even after Christ had assumed the humility of flesh, divine honours were bestowed upon him by angels, Magi, the testimony of the Holy Spirit, and so forth; and he most aptly concludes that the dignity of deity is not lost while the humility of flesh is assumed, or that God does not fall from his power when he begins to be weak as a human being. Thus, as he says in Psalm 55, no. 5, the form of a servant did not take from the self-emptying one the power and nature of God. If, however, you prefer ‘is adored,’ the conclusion will not follow from all the preceding matters assumed, but only from the immediately preceding words, ‘The swaddling clothes are soiled: God is adored.’ Indeed, from this assumption, which includes only that God is adored, there will be no conclusion declaring that the humility of flesh is adored. Therefore Hilary does not say that the humility of flesh was adored by the Magi, but demonstrates from the Magi’s adoration and other arguments the deity hidden beneath the humility of flesh. This is the point of his statement in Psalm 127, no. 8, where he calls the purpose of assuming a body the ‘adoption’ of the body which he was to take from the Virgin. If Felix is in some measure excused by this, who can patiently endure that he sought and cited as patron of his heresy Hilary, who everywhere recoils from the term ‘adoption’ in Christ and, especially throughout Book VI, most vigorously maintains that Christ is not an adoptive but a true and proper Son? Finally, Ambrose seems to have imitated this passage in On Faith, Book I, chapter 4, where, from the Magi’s adoration, the humility of the cradle, the service of angels, and so forth, he concludes: ‘Thus neither is the dignity of natural majesty lost, nor is the reality of assumed flesh disproved.’”] is assumed.

### 28. Christ Acted as God in His Deeds.

[Col. 0068C] The remaining course of his life is likewise of a piece. For all the time that he spent as a human being he fulfilled in the works of God. [Note: “Perhaps more correctly, in our manuscript the preposition *in* is omitted.”] There is no time to speak of each instance. This alone must be considered in every kind of miracle and healing: in the assumption of flesh he existed as a human being, but in the deeds performed as God.

29. That the Holy Spirit exists.—Concerning the Holy Spirit, we ought neither to be silent nor need we speak; yet, on account of those who do not know, it is impossible for us to be silent about him. But it is not necessary to speak about him, who, having the Father and the Son as authors, must be confessed.

[Note: “Who [is] from the Father”: not bad.]

[Note: The printed editions, from a single Colbert manuscript of scarcely any authority, read “because [he is] from the Father.” The manuscripts Corbie, two of Remigius, Theodulf, Pratensis, Vindocinensis, Silvanectensis, etc., read “who [is] from the Father.” We would have preferred “who [is] with the Father.” But from the most ancient manuscripts of all—the Vatican Basilica, Colbert, and Carnotensis—from which it is unsafe to dissent when they agree, and likewise from one German manuscript, another Sorbonne manuscript, and the Colbert manuscript, we restore “who [has] the Father,” that is, if our opinion does not mislead us, “who, having the Father and the Son as authors, must be confessed.” Certainly, we have already heard the Son called the author of the Holy Spirit in §4; and below it is declared that, as the Holy Spirit is through the Father, so also he is through the Son—something which we shall shortly demonstrate in note h.]

And indeed, I think that whether he exists ought not to be debated. For he exists, since he is given, received, and possessed; and he who is joined to the confession of the Father and the Son cannot be separated from the confession of the Father and the Son. For the whole is imperfect for us if anything is lacking from the whole.

If anyone asks the meaning of our understanding on this matter, we read both passages in the Apostle: “Because you are sons of God, God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father’” (Gal. 4:6). And again: “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you have been sealed” (Eph. 4:30). And again: “But we have received not the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God, that we may know what has been given to us by God” (1 Cor. 2:12). And again: “But you are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God is in you. But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he is not his” (Rom. 8:9). And again: “But if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit who dwells in you” (ibid. 8:11).

[Note: The printed editions read “your,” against the manuscripts.]

[Note: The Vatican Basilica and Carnotensis manuscripts add: “unto the day of redemption.”]

[Note: The pronoun “this,” here and below in §35, is absent from the ancient Colbert manuscript and the German manuscript, in agreement with the Greek text.]

[Note: “If indeed.”]

[Note: The Corbie manuscript, with two manuscripts of Remigius and others, reads: “if indeed the Spirit of God [is in you].”]

[Note: Thus, in accordance with the Greek, the better manuscripts read “he who raised Christ”; the printed editions read “he who raised Jesus.” Further on, one Colbert manuscript reads “through his indwelling Spirit in you.”]

Therefore, since he exists, is given, possessed, and belongs to God, let the speech of calumniators cease here. When they ask through whom he exists, for what purpose he exists, or what he is like: if our answer displeases those who say, “Through whom are all things,” and “from whom are all things,” and that the Spirit is God’s Spirit, the gift of believers, then let the Apostles and Prophets also displease them, since they speak only this much concerning what he is; and after them, the Father and the Son will displease them.

[Note: Only the Paris edition has “thus [is] the answer.” Then “of those who say” is referred back to “our,” which has the same force.]

[Note: The printed editions read “in whom”; the manuscripts better read “from whom are all things.” By the former words Hilary commonly indicates the Son, just as by “through whom are all things” he indicates the Father. Thus above, §1: “For there is one God the Father, from whom are all things, and one only-begotten Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things”; and shortly afterward: “One power through whom are all things, one offspring from whom are all things.” Thus, in “through whom are all things” and “from whom are all things” there is an answer to the question posed: through whom is the Holy Spirit? As though he said: He is through him through whom all things are, just as he is through him from whom all things are. The following two questions—why he exists and what he is like—are likewise answered soberly: he is God’s Spirit, the gift of believers, lest anything be asserted which has not been received from the Prophets and Apostles.]

[Note: The Carnotensis manuscript reads: “will displease.”]

30. The Holy Spirit is both Father and Son.—I think, however, that some remain in ignorance and uncertainty because they see that this third term—that is, what is called “Holy Spirit”—is frequently understood as standing for Father and Son. In this there is no difficulty: for whether it is the Father or the Son, he is both Spirit and holy.

[Note: Only the Paris edition reads “rules”: a scribal error. It is superfluous to note those writers among whom the name “Holy Spirit” is customarily understood of the Father and Son. Hermas, Justin, Irenaeus, Tatian, Tertullian, Lactantius, Cyprian, Phoebadius, and Epiphanius use this term indiscriminately; among them, “Spirit” frequently signifies the divine nature common to the three persons.]

[Note: “And the Holy Spirit is.”]

[Note: Most manuscripts with the printed editions read “and the Holy Spirit is.” We prefer, with one Vatican manuscript, “and he is both Spirit and holy,” unless one prefers, with the ancient Colbert and German manuscripts: “or the Son is the Holy Spirit.”]

31. In what sense it is said, “God is Spirit.” The Samaritan woman’s error in confining God to a temple or mountain.—But the statement read in the Gospels, “God is Spirit” (John 4:24), must be carefully considered—how and for what reason it was spoken. For every utterance is spoken for a reason, and the rationale of what is said must be understood from the meaning of the speaking; lest, because the Lord answered, “God is Spirit,” the use and gift of the Holy Spirit should therefore both be denied under the name of the Holy Spirit.

[Note: The printed editions read “of the speaker.” It should be read passively, “of what is spoken,” both on the authority of the better manuscripts and because of the following passage, Book IV, §14: “For the understanding of statements must be taken from the reasons for their being spoken; since speech is not subject to the word, but the word to the thing.”]

The Lord was speaking with the Samaritan woman, for the redemption of all had come. After much discourse about the living water, the five husbands, and the one she then had who was not hers (John 4:20), the woman answered: “Lord, I perceive that you are a prophet. Our fathers worshiped on this mountain, but you say that Jerusalem is the place where one must worship.” The Lord answered: “Believe me, woman, the hour is coming when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem. You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know, because salvation is from the Jews. But the hour is coming—and now is—when true worshipers will worship the Father in Spirit and truth; for the Father seeks such people to worship him. For God is Spirit, and those who worship him must worship in Spirit and truth, because God is Spirit” (ibid. 21 ff.).

[Note: In manuscripts of the best quality: “of the water of life,” and shortly afterward, “who was not hers.”]

The woman, then, mindful of the traditions of the fathers, thought that God must be worshiped either, like Samaria, on a mountain, or, like Jerusalem, in the temple. Samaria had, in transgression of the Law, chosen a mountain site for worshiping God; the Jews, however, considered the temple built by Solomon to be the seat of religion. The presumption of both enclosed God—within whom are all things and outside whom nothing can contain him—either in the height of a hill or in the hollow of a constructed building.

Therefore, because God is invisible, incomprehensible, and immeasurable, the Lord said that the time had come when God was not to be worshiped on a mountain or in a temple: because God is Spirit, and spirit is neither circumscribed nor confined; by the power of his nature he is everywhere and absent nowhere, overflowing as all in all things. Thus those are the true worshipers who will worship in Spirit and truth.

[Note: Some manuscripts with the printed editions read “because.” We follow the better manuscripts. Then the Vatican Basilica and Victorine manuscripts read “surpassing all.” Most others also have “all”; one Sorbonne manuscript, “every”; three others, “all things.” Nothing seems to require alteration. Hilary habitually uses *exubero* (“overflow, abound”) when speaking of the Spirit. Of him he says in Commentary on Matthew 10.2: “However much is taken by all, he nevertheless always overflows in giving himself.” And in 15.10: “The abundance of the Spirit is indicated, since in whatever he gives he overflows.”]

But for those who worship God, who is Spirit, in Spirit, there is one in service, another in office, and another in honor, because that in which each is to be worshiped is distinct. For the name and gift of the Holy Spirit are not removed because it has been said, “God is Spirit.” Rather, the answer was given to the woman who confined God to a temple and mountain: all things are in God; God is in himself; and, invisible and incomprehensible, he is to be worshiped in what is invisible and incomprehensible. Thus the nature both of the gift and of the honor has been made clear, when he taught that God who is Spirit is to be worshiped in the Spirit, showing both the freedom and knowledge of worshipers and the infinity of worship, since God who is Spirit is worshiped in the Spirit.

[Note: In the Vatican Basilica manuscript, “another in service.” Because this was said of the Holy Spirit, it might seem favorable to Arians—who portray the Holy Spirit as minister of Father and Son—to infer that he is different from the Spirit who is to be worshiped. But by this manner of speaking Hilary merely takes account of the relation of procession, or subordination, by which the Holy Spirit is subject to the principle from which he proceeds. Thus, speaking of the Son, who testified that he could do nothing of himself except what he saw the Father doing, Hilary says in Commentary on Psalm 138, §28: “By the honor of reverence he subjected to him, to whom he remembered that all things were to be confessed, the authority which he had affirmed concerning himself; not taking away from himself the ability to do what the Father did, but showing him through whom he could do such things.” Thus, in *On the Synods*, §51, he enumerates various reasons why the Son, even as God, is subject to the Father: “The Son is especially not compared or made equal to the Father in that he is subject through the observance of obedience; in that he sat at God’s right hand only when he was told to sit; in that he is sent; in that he receives; in that he obeys in all things the will of him who sent him. But subjection in piety is not a diminution of essence, nor does the service of religion make the nature degenerate.” Shortly afterward: “Having the name—but the name of him whose Son he is—he becomes subject to the Father both in service and in name.” Finally, in Book IV Hilary regularly distinguishes the God who speaks or commands from the God who accomplishes, though one nature is proclaimed of both. Thus here also, where the Holy Spirit has been shown to be distinct in his manner of subsistence from God—that is, the Father—and from the Lord—that is, the Son—nature is shown by many considerations not to be different. For what else does it mean that the infinite, invisible, incomprehensible, immeasurable God, when worshiped in the Spirit, is worshiped by an infinite manner everywhere, in things invisible and incomprehensible—indeed, in himself—what else, I ask, does this mean but that there is complete correspondence, equality, and perfect unity between the Spirit who honors and the Spirit who is honored?]

[Note: Thus the manuscripts, except that the Carnotensis has “there is the fullest significance.” The printed editions read “is expressed.” The Holy Spirit, who above in §2 was called the gift received from God, now seems to be called the gift offered to God. In fact, we return to God the Spirit whom we have received from him, when, living not by our own spirit but by his, we serve him.]

[Note: Since this infinity of worship derives from that in which God is worshiped, the Spirit must be infinite.]

[Note: The printed editions read “he showed.” The manuscripts read “showing,” referring to “he taught.”]

32. Similar also is the Apostle’s statement: “For the Lord is Spirit; and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Cor. 3:17). For the sake of making the meaning understood, he distinguished the one who is from him whose he is. For to possess and to be possessed are not one thing, nor does the same expression embrace “him” and “his.”

[Note: This use of the distinction recurs in Book IV, §21: “There is a twofold signification in the angel of God: he who is, and he whose he is.” We find a trace of the same in Tertullian, *Against Praxeas*, §26, where he says: “No thing belonging to someone is itself the one to whom it belongs.” The latter member of the distinction is expressed more clearly shortly afterward, when instead of “whose he is” one reads “who is his.”]

Thus when he says, “The Lord is Spirit,” he shows the nature of his infinity; but when he adds, “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom,” he signifies him who is his: because the Spirit is Lord, and where the Spirit is the Lord’s, there is freedom. These things were said not because the argument required them, but lest any obscurity remain in them. For the Holy Spirit is one everywhere: enlightening all the patriarchs, prophets, and the entire company of the Law; inspiring John even in his mother’s womb; and afterward given to the Apostles and the other believers, for the knowledge of the truth granted to them.

[Note: The printed editions read “there is freedom, and he signifies him whose he is,” against the manuscripts.]

[Note: The good manuscripts—Colbert, Remigius, German, and another Colbert manuscript—read “remain,” which may be preferred to “the argument required,” silently supplied. The Victorine manuscript reads “be hidden.” Erasmus once conjectured that the text should read, “lest anyone remain entangled in these difficulties.”]

[Note: “Knowledge.”]

33. What the office of the Holy Spirit is in us.—But let us hear from the Lord’s own words what his office in us is. He says: “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now” (John 16:12). “It is expedient for you that I go; if I go, I will send you the Advocate” (ibid. 7). And again: “I will ask the Father, and he will send you another Advocate, that he may be with you forever—the Spirit of truth” (John 14:16–17). “He will guide you into all truth; for he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak, and he will announce to you the things to come. He will glorify me, because he will take from what is mine” (John 16:13–14).

[Note: The Verona codex inserts: “the Spirit, the Paraclete; he will glorify me.” And again: “I will ask,” he says, “my Father, and he will send you another Advocate.”]

[Note: Most manuscripts, with the printed editions, insert here: “the Spirit, the Paraclete; he will glorify me.” And again: “I will ask,” he says, “my Father, and he will send you another Advocate.” Since these words are wrongly and confusedly repeated, we have removed them on the authority of the Colbert, German, and Victorine codices.]

[Note: “He will take from what is mine.”]

These things were spoken, out of many passages, to open the way to understanding; in them are contained both the will of the giver, and the nature and condition of the gift: so that, because our weakness could not contain either Father or Son, the gift of the Holy Spirit might enlighten our faith, which finds God’s incarnation difficult, by a kind of covenant of his intercession.

[Note: The Holy Spirit is the gift; the giver is he who bestows and sends him. In the passages just cited, this is attributed no less to the Son than to the Father.]

34. It follows now that we should hear the Apostle also explain the power and office of this gift. For he says: “For all who are led by the Spirit of God, these are sons of God. For you did not receive the spirit of slavery again unto fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Rom. 8:14).

[Note: The printed editions read “in fear.” With one Colbert manuscript we prefer “unto fear,” which the ancient books have, with strong agreement, below in Book VI, §44, in accordance with the Greek εἰς φόβον, “unto fear.” After the word “adoption,” the printed editions add “of sons,” with scarcely any manuscript support.]

And again: “No one in the Spirit of God says, ‘Jesus is accursed,’ and no one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (1 Cor. 12:3). And again: “There are distinctions of gifts, but the same Spirit; and distinctions of ministries, but the same Lord; and distinctions of operations, but the same God, who works all things in all. But to each is given the illumination of the Spirit for usefulness. To one, through the Spirit, is given a word of wisdom; to another, a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another, faith in the same Spirit; to another, gifts of healing in one Spirit; to another, the working of miracles; to another, prophecy; to another, discernment of spirits; to another, kinds of tongues; to another, interpretation of tongues. But one and the same Spirit works all these things” (ibid. 4 ff.).

[Note: By the authority of most manuscripts we have removed from here: “And again: But we have received not the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God, that we may know what has been given to us by God.” Since Hilary will cite these words of the Apostle below in §35, prefacing them with “as we have already shown above,” he indicates that they were already cited in §29.]

[Note: “Of God” is absent from the ancient Colbert manuscript; otherwise, Book VIII, §27 reads differently. Further on, the Carnotensis, Colbert, and Victorine manuscripts read “Jesus is accursed,” not “Jesus [as accusative] is accursed.”]

[Note: In earlier editions: “Jesus.”]

[Note: Thus from our manuscript. In the preceding passage: “of gifts.”]

[Note: One Colbert manuscript and a Sorbonne manuscript, with the Carnotensis, read “but the same Spirit,” which they also repeat below, in place of “but the same God.”]

[Note: “Is given.”]

[Note: In the ancient Colbert manuscript: “discernment of spirit.”]

[Note: “Kinds of languages.”]

[Note: Bad., Erasmus, and Lipsius, with several manuscripts, read “interpretation of speech,” against the better manuscripts and the Greek text.]

We therefore have the cause of this gift and its effects; and I do not know what uncertainty there can be about him whose cause, rationale, and power are clearly established.

35. The gift of the Holy Spirit is supremely necessary. Without it, we possess the capacity to understand God, but not its exercise.—Let us therefore make use of such generous gifts and seek the exercise of this most necessary gift. For, as we have already shown above, the Apostle says: “But we have received not the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God, that we may know what has been given to us by God” (1 Cor. 2:12). It is therefore received for knowledge.

For just as the nature of the human body, when the causes of its function cease, will be idle—for the eyes, unless there is light or day, will have no use for their ministry; the ears, unless a voice or sound is produced, will not recognize their function; the nostrils, unless an odor gives fragrance, will not know in what office they are—so also the human mind, unless through faith it has received the gift of the Spirit, does indeed possess the natural capacity to understand God, but does not possess the light of knowledge.

[Note: “Unless there be light or day.”]

[Note: Lipsius and Paris read “unless light comes, no [use],” against the other books.]

[Note: Two Colbert manuscripts, the German, Corbie, Pratensis, etc., read “has increased.”]

But the gift that is in Christ is one and lies open to all; and, though it is nowhere lacking, it is given as much as each person wishes to receive, and remains as much as each wishes to merit. This remains with us until the consummation of the age; this is the consolation of our expectation; this, in the operations of gifts, is the pledge of future hope; this is the light of minds and the splendor of souls. Therefore this Holy Spirit must be sought, must be merited, and thereafter must be retained through faith and observance of the commandments.

[Note: The Silva Major manuscript adds here: “must be worshiped.”]

## BOOK THREE

He establishes the eternal generation of the Word and refutes those who strive against it by human reasoning.
