First, he lucidly explains from Scripture’s teaching about the Father and Son those words of the Son, “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me,” after showing that they surpass the grasp of human understanding. Next, from the wondrous transformation of water into wine and the multiplication of the five loaves, he proves that God can do many things in which the sharpness of the human mind fails. Then he presents the human argument by which they contend that no generation from God can be possible, and refutes it at length: first, because it arises from human wisdom, which God declared in prophetic and apostolic oracles that he would destroy; second, because it is better to hear Christ, who became human in order to be our witness concerning divine things. Here are examined the words by which he explained the work and office of his dispensation and gave much testimony to his true generation from God. Third, because we do not attain understanding even of Christ’s visible deeds—for example, his entrance to the disciples when the doors were shut. Finally, because the nature of the human mind is such that, being created and imperfect, it cannot comprehend the perfect one and its Creator. Lastly, the wise foolishness of believers is praised: they distrust themselves in order to believe God; they do not measure divine things by the weakness of their own reason, but assess them according to the infinity of omnipotent power.

1. Human understanding does not comprehend the Son in the Father and, conversely, the Father in the Son.—The saying of the Lord causes obscurity for many when he says, “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 14:11), and not without reason; for the nature of human understanding does not grasp the rationale of this statement. It seems impossible that what is in another should equally be outside that other; and since the things under discussion must necessarily not be solitary unto themselves, while preserving their number and their own condition in which they exist, they cannot contain one another, so that one who has some other thing within himself, while remaining thus and always remaining external, should in turn remain equally and always internal to that which he has within himself.

[Note: We add “and condition” on the authority of the Tello, Colbert, and Sorbonne manuscripts. By *status* Tertullian means substance in *Against Praxeas*, §2, where, concerning the Trinity, he says: “Three, not in condition, but in rank”; and shortly afterward: “of one substance, one condition, one power.” But here it rather means mode of existence and position. Further on, the verb “contain” is governed by the preceding “it seems.”]

[Note: Three later manuscripts read “and remain outside”: wrongly. For this is the meaning: it seems impossible that one who has another thing within himself, which always remains thus within him and does not change its condition, should be so external to the thing he has within himself that it should, in turn, remain equally and always internal to him.]

Human perception, indeed, will not attain this, nor will human comparison offer any example for divine realities. But what is unintelligible to humanity is possible for God. Let this not be said by me in such a way that the authority of the statement, merely because it was spoken by God, should suffice for the rationale of what is said. We must therefore know and understand what this means: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me,” if indeed we can grasp it as it is, so that the rationale of divine truth may attain what the nature of things is thought unable to admit.

[Note: Two manuscripts read “yet these things.” Other books read “these things only,” which better suits what follows. Hilary states these matters more tersely here; Augustine discusses them more fully in Letter 120. Augustine does not approve of Consentius, who conceded everything to faith and nothing to reason, saying in §4: “The Apostle Peter admonishes us to be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks us a reason for our faith and hope.” And in §3: “Far be it that God should hate in us that by which he created us superior to the other animals.” By these and other considerations he repels Consentius’s error, teaching in §§6 and 8 that faith prepares the mind for the understanding of faith, to which true reason leads. Nevertheless, though it is a reasonable precept that faith should precede reason with respect to certain great things not yet capable of being grasped, he says in §3: “If this precept is reasonable, then undoubtedly some reason, however small, which persuades us of it, itself precedes faith.” For the reason that God—who can neither be deceived nor deceive—must be believed precedes faith. Hilary followed this rule in all things: first believing God’s utterances most firmly, and then not scorning to give an account of his faith. See Book VIII, §1, etc.]

2. Once Father and Son are known according to Scripture, this is more easily perceived. What the Father is.—And so, that we may more easily attain an understanding of this most difficult question, we must first know the Father and the Son according to the teaching of the divine Scriptures, so that our discourse may be clearer from things known and familiar. The eternity of the Father, as we treated in the preceding book, surpasses places, times, form, and whatever can be conceived by human understanding. He is beyond all things and in all things, containing the universe and contained by none; not mutable by approach or withdrawal, but invisible, incomprehensible, full, perfect, eternal, taking nothing from elsewhere, but sufficient to himself in that which remains thus.

[Note: “Place.”]

[Note: The printed editions read “place,” against the manuscripts. So also in Commentary on Psalm 138, §18, the Father’s nature is said to be beyond all places.]

[Note: Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read “taking nothing from elsewhere in what he is.”]

3. What the Son received from the Father in being begotten; what he assumed in being born in the flesh for us.—Therefore the unbegotten Father, before all time, begot from himself a Son: not from some underlying matter, because all things are through the Son; not from nothing, because the Son is from himself; not as a birth-product, because there is nothing mutable or empty in God; not a part of himself, whether divided, severed, or extended, because God is impassible and incorporeal—whereas these are properties of suffering and flesh—and because, according to the Apostle, “in Christ all the fullness of deity dwells bodily” (Col. 2:9).

[Note: Two manuscripts add “begot,” which is properly omitted in the others.]

Rather, incomprehensibly and ineffably, before all times and ages, he brought forth the Only-Begotten from those unbegotten things which were in himself, imparting to his birth, through love and power, all that God is. Thus, from the unbegotten, perfect, and eternal Father, the Son is only-begotten, perfect, and eternal. But those things which belong to him according to the body that he assumed are the purpose of his goodness for our salvation. For though he is invisible, incorporeal, and incomprehensible, being begotten of God, he received into himself only so much matter and humility as there was capacity in us to understand, perceive, and behold him—yielding to our weakness rather than himself failing in those things in which he existed.

[Note: “Which are his”; and shortly afterward, “being begotten from him,” not “begotten from God.”]

[Note: The printed editions read “which are his,” and shortly afterward, “being begotten from him.” “From him, and from God,” with the Vatican Basilica manuscript and another Colbert manuscript, is more pleasing.]

4. In what manner he is in the Father.—Therefore, the perfect Son of the perfect Father and the only-begotten offspring of the unbegotten God—who received all things from him who possesses all things—God from God, Spirit from Spirit, Light from Light, confidently says: “The Father is in me, and I am in the Father” (John 10:38). For as the Father is Spirit, so the Son also is Spirit; as the Father is God, so the Son also is God; as the Father is Light, so the Son also is Light.

Therefore, from the things that are in the Father come those things in which the Son is: that is, the whole Son was born from the whole Father; not from elsewhere, because there was nothing before the Son; not from nothing, because the Son is from God; not in part, because the fullness of deity is in the Son; nor in some things, because it is in all things. But as he who was able willed, so he who begot knew. What is in the Father is also in the Son; what is in the unbegotten is also in the only-begotten. One is from the other, and both are one—not two becoming one, but one existing in the other, because there is not something different in the two. The Father is in the Son because the Son is from him; the Son is in the Father because the Son is not from elsewhere; the only-begotten is in the unbegotten because he is only-begotten from the unbegotten. Thus they are in one another, because, as all things are perfect in the unbegotten Father, so all things are perfect in the only-begotten Son.

[Note: The Paris edition, copied from the Nivellian edition, wrongly reads “so that he may be the one who begot.” Here attention is directed to: “No one knows the Son except the Father,” etc. When Hilary says shortly before, “as he who was able willed,” and similarly in Book VI, §21, and Commentary on Matthew 16.4, he seems to subordinate the Son to the Father’s will both in his existence and in his equality with the Father. Athanasius, however, in *Orations against the Arians* II, p. 335, distinguishes a created thing from the Son in this: the Son is the proper offspring of the Father’s substance, whereas a creature is something external that depends on the Father’s will, to which the Son is not subject: “A thing made need not always exist; for the craftsman works whenever he wishes. But that which is begotten is not subject to will; rather, it is a property of the essence” (Τὸ μὲν ποίημα οὐκ ἀνάγκη ἀεὶ εἶναι· ὅτε γὰρ βούλεται δημιουργὸς ἐργάζεται· τὸ δὲ γέννημα οὐ βουλήσει ὑπόκειται, ἀλλὰ τῆς οὐσίας ἐστὶν ἰδιότης). Cyril likewise says in Book VII of the *Treasury*: “In natural things no will precedes; will has place only in things outside the substance of the one deliberating.” Hilary himself explains his meaning in *On the Synods*, §58. There he first agrees with Athanasius and Cyril: “God’s will brought substance to all creatures; but he gave nature to the Son . . . perfect generation,” etc. Then he indicates that his assertion that the Son was born with the Father willing means only that the Father should not be thought to have begotten him unwillingly or not without suffering. Cyril accordingly says, in Book VII of the *Treasury*: “Although he did not beget the Son from will, he nevertheless does not have him unwillingly; for he wills and loves the Son. So too, although he is good and merciful without antecedent will and choice, he does not possess these unwillingly: he wills to be what he is.” He repeats almost the same in Dialogue 2 on the Trinity.]

This is the unity, power, love, hope, faith, truth, way, and life in the Son and the Father: not to detract from God’s powers, nor, because of the hiddenness and power of the generation, to disparage the Son; to compare nothing with the unbegotten Father; to distinguish the Only-Begotten from him neither in time nor in power; and to confess the Son as God because he is from God.

[Note: In Paris, “this hope” is omitted. Further on, *calumniari* seems to mean diminishing or taking something away from God’s power. We have already read in Commentary on Psalm 137, §16, “in the calumny of a garment,” meaning, “when someone wishes to take away a garment”; and in Book X of *On the Trinity*, §28, “in the very calumny of the mutilated body,” meaning, “in the very cutting off of the ear.”]

[Note: That is, because of the mystery and power of the generation, which the human mind cannot penetrate.]

5. God reveals his power through deeds whose rationale remains hidden. Human beings do not comprehend how water was changed into wine.—There are powers in God of such a kind that, although their rationale is incomprehensible to our understanding, faith nevertheless rests securely in the truth of the effect. Nor do we discover this only in spiritual matters, but also in bodily ones—not as an example of generation, but as a demonstration that an intelligible event may be wondered at.

[Note: That is, our reason certainly apprehends that the effect is from God, although it does not comprehend how it was done, or even by what means it could have been done.]

[Note: The Colbert manuscript with the German manuscript reads “has been shown.” Further on, we restore “in Galilee” from the manuscripts, where the common text had “in Cana of Galilee.”]

On the day of the wedding, wine was made from water in Galilee (John 2:9). Can either our speech or our understanding follow the manner in which nature was changed, so that water’s simplicity vanished and the taste of wine came into being? It was not a mixture but a creation; and a creation not begun from itself, but passing from one thing into another. What is weaker is not acquired by infusion of something stronger; rather, what was is abolished, and what was not begins to be.

The bridegroom is distressed, the household is troubled, the ceremony of the wedding feast is endangered. Jesus is asked. He neither rises nor exerts himself; this work is accomplished while he remains at rest. Water is poured into jars; wine is drawn into cups. The understanding of the one pouring does not accord with that of the one drawing. Those who poured believe that water is being drawn; those who draw suppose that wine was poured in. The time between is insufficient for the nature of the liquid both to arise and to perish. The rationale of the deed defeats both sight and understanding; yet God’s power is perceived in what has been done.

[Note: “Insufficient,” by a second hand.]

[Note: The printed editions, except Paris, and most manuscripts read “is insufficient.” We retain the Paris reading, which belongs to the older manuscripts. Then Erasmus, Lipsius, and Paris read “as in the nature of a liquid.” Better manuscripts omit “in”: here the term “liquid” speaks equally of the wine coming into being and of the water passing away.]

6. Or how the five loaves were multiplied.—The wonder of the event involving the five loaves is similar (Matt. 14:17). By their increase, the hunger of five thousand men and countless women and children is overcome; the understanding of the work escapes the sight of our perception. Five loaves are offered and broken; certain generations of fragments steal into the hands of those breaking them. That from which pieces are broken is not diminished; yet fragments continually fill the hand of the one breaking them. The moments deceive the sight: while you follow one hand full of fragments, you see the other without loss of its portion; meanwhile the heap of fragments grows. Those breaking are engaged in service; those eating are engaged in their task; the hungry are satisfied; the leftovers fill twelve baskets. Neither understanding nor sight grasps the progress of so visible an operation. What was not, exists; what is not understood is seen. Only this remains: that God must be believed able to do all things.

[Note: Bad., Erasmus, and Lipsius read “so inconspicuous.” With Paris and our manuscripts we prefer “so conspicuous,” or with the Vatican Basilica codex, “yet conspicuous.” For the discourse here, as was promised above, concerns a bodily example. Hence in Commentary on Matthew 14.12, concerning the same miracle, one reads: “An invisible operation is performed in a visible work.”]

7. Christ did not do these things for His own sake, but to restrain the human itch for judging matters concerning God. — Therefore the divine things contain no flattery, nor is there in God any pretense intended both to please and to deceive. These works of the Son of God did not arise from a desire for display. For He whom countless thousands upon thousands of angels serve [Col. 0079C] did not flatter humankind. For what of ours did He need, through whom all that is ours exists? Did He demand honor from us—at one time stupefied by sleep, at another exhausted by the dissipation of nights, at another burdened with evil conscience after the quarrels and murders of the day, at another drunk after banquets—He whom Archangels, Dominions, Principalities, and Powers praise in heaven with eternal, tireless voices, without sleep, interruption, or fault? And they praise Him because He, the image of the invisible God, created all things in Himself, made the ages, established heaven, arranged the stars, founded the earth, plunged down the abysses; because He thereafter was born as a human being, conquered death, broke the gates of hell, acquired for Himself a people as co-heirs, and transformed flesh from corruption into the glory of eternity.

[Note: [Col. 0080D] Erasmus, Lipsius, and Paris: “of wakeful nights.” We have deleted the word *wakeful* on the authority of Bad. and the manuscripts; Erasmus appears to have added it on his own initiative.]

[Note: [Col. 0080D] Paris, following Lipsius from Erasmus’s margin: “created through Himself.” Shortly afterward, the Colbert and Carnot manuscripts read *astra distrinxerit*, “arranged the stars,” not *distinxerit*, “distinguished.”]

Therefore He needed nothing from us, such that these ineffable and unintelligible works might adorn Him among us as though He needed praise. But God, foreseeing the error of human wickedness and folly [Col. 0079D] [Col. 0080A] and knowing that unbelief would break out so far as to presume to pass judgment upon matters concerning God, overcame our audacity by examples drawn from those things about which there was doubt.

8. Human reasoning is refuted in opposition to the generation of God. — For there are many who are wise in the world, whose wisdom is folly to God. When they hear that God is born from God, the true from the true, the perfect from the perfect, the one from the one, they object to our preaching as though we were asserting impossibilities, adhering to certain concatenations of propositions as they say:

> “Nothing could be born from one, because every birth is from two. Now if this Son is born from one, He has received a part of Him who begot Him; and if a part, then neither is perfect. For that from which something has departed lacks what has departed; nor will fullness be in that which consists of a portion. Therefore neither is perfect, since both the one who begot loses His fullness and the one who was born fails to obtain it.”

God, foreseeing even through the prophet this wisdom of the world, condemns it thus: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and reject the understanding of the prudent” (Isa. 29:14).

[Note: [Col. 0080D] The Carnot manuscript: “the prudence of the prudent.”]

Likewise, in the Apostle: “Where is the wise person? Where is the scribe? Where is the inquirer of this age? Has not God made foolish the wisdom of this world? For since, in the wisdom of God, the world did not know God through wisdom, it pleased God through the folly of preaching to save those who believe. For Jews seek signs and Greeks seek wisdom; but we preach Christ crucified: to Jews indeed a stumbling-block, to Gentiles folly, but to those who are called, Jews and Greeks alike, Christ [Col. 0080C] the power of God and the wisdom of God; because the foolishness of God is wiser than human beings, and the weakness of God is stronger than human beings” (1 Cor. 1:20 ff.).

9. Christ’s office among us. — Therefore the Son of God, having care for the human race, first became human, so that, being one of ourselves, He might be a witness to us of divine things; and so that through the weakness of flesh He might proclaim God the Father to us who are weak and fleshly, fulfilling in Himself the will of God the Father, as He says: “I have not come to do my own will, but the will of Him who sent me” (John 6:38)—not because He Himself does not will what He does, but because He displays His obedience under the accomplishment of the Father’s will, Himself willing to fulfill the Father’s will.

[Note: [Col. 0080D] In two Remigian manuscripts and one Theodorian manuscript: “not because He did not will”: less correctly. Compare *Treatise on Psalm* 139, §12.]

Now this was the will to be accomplished, of which He Himself is witness when He says: “Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son, [Col. 0080D] so that your Son may glorify you; just as you gave Him authority over all flesh, so that He may give eternal life to all whom [Col. 0081A] you have given Him. And this is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent. I have glorified you upon earth, having completed the work which you gave me to do. And now, Father, glorify me with yourself with the glory which I had with you before the world existed. I have manifested your name to the people whom you gave me” (John 17:1 ff.).

[Note: [Col. 0079D] We read, “so that your Son,” as in the Vulgate and most Greek manuscripts. Thus also Hilary himself below, §10.]

In brief and few words He set forth the whole work of His office and dispensation, at the same time fortifying the truth of faith [Note: [Col. 0081D] The Paris edition alone: “the will of faith.”] against every suggestion of diabolical deceit. Let us therefore run through each force of His discourse.

10. What He asks in saying, “Glorify your Son.” — He says: “Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son, so that your Son may glorify you.” He says not that the day or the time, but the hour has come. An hour is a portion of a day. And what is this hour? Surely that of which, while strengthening the disciples at the time of His passion, He spoke: “Behold, the hour comes for the Son of Man to be glorified” (John 12:23). This, therefore, is the hour in which He prays to be glorified by the Father, in order that He Himself may glorify the Father.

But what is this? He who is to glorify awaits glorification; He who is to render honor asks for it; and does He need that which He in turn will bestow? Let the sophists of the world and the wise men of Greece now come forward and ensnare truth with their syllogisms. Let them inquire how, from what source, and for what reason this is so; and when they are at a loss, let them hear: “God chose the foolish things of the world [Note: [Col. 0081D] Here the Carnot manuscript adds: “to confound the wise.”]” (1 Cor. 1:27). Therefore let us, through our folly, understand what is unintelligible to the wise of the world.

The Lord had said, “Father, the hour has come”; He had indicated the hour of His passion, for at that very [Col. 0081C] moment He was speaking of it. Then He added, “Glorify your Son.” But how was the Son to be glorified? Born of a virgin, He had advanced from cradle and infancy to full manhood; He had lived as a human being through sleep, hunger, thirst, weariness, and tears; and even now He was to be spat upon, scourged, and crucified. What then? These things would testify only that Christ was human. Yet we are not confounded by the cross, not condemned by the scourges, not defiled by the spittle. The Father glorifies the Son. How? At last He is fastened to the cross. What follows? The sun does not set, but withdraws. What do I mean by saying it withdrew? It was not received into a cloud, but failed in the course of its function; and the remaining elements of the world felt their own destruction along with Him. And lest any heavenly operations [Col. 0081D] should participate in this crime, they were deprived, through a certain necessity of this intervention, by their own cessation of activity.

[Note: [Col. 0081D] The printed editions: “those heavenly operations”; corrected from the manuscripts.]

But what did the earth do? It trembled beneath the burden of the Lord hanging upon the wood, [Col. 0082A] testifying that it could not contain within itself Him who was about to die. Did the rocks and stones also yield up their own portion? Rather, shattered, they burst apart and lose their nature, confessing that the tomb hewn from themselves could not contain the body to be laid within it.

11. Christ is the proper Son of God. — Moreover, the centurion of the cohort, the guard of the cross, cried out: “Truly this was the Son of God” (Matt. 27:54). Creation is released through the intervention of this expiatory act; rocks do not retain their firmness and strength. Those who had fastened Him to the cross confess that He is truly the Son of God: the result accords with the proclamation.

The Lord had said, “Glorify your Son.” He testified that He was Son not only by name but also by the property expressed in the word “your.” For many of us are sons of God, but this Son is not such a son. He is both true [Col. 0082B] and proper Son: by origin, not adoption; by truth, not appellation; by birth, not creation. Therefore, after His glorification, confession of the truth followed. For the centurion confesses the true Son of God, lest any believer should doubt what even a human persecutor had not denied.

[Note: [Col. 0081D] Lipsius and Paris, following Erasmus: “which one of the persecutors.” This is supported by no ancient book.]

12. The glory to be given to the Son and rendered by Him to the Father signifies unity of power in both. — But perhaps the Son is thought to have needed the glorification for which He prayed, and will be found weak because He awaits glorification from one greater than Himself.

[Note: [Col. 0081D] “Might be believed.”]

And who will not confess the Father to be greater—as the unbegotten than the begotten, as father than son, as the one who sent than the one who was sent, as the one who wills than the one who obeys? He Himself will be our witness: “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28).

[Note: [Col. 0081D] Hilary here affirms, without injury to faith, that the Father is greater than the Son. Explaining his thought on this in *On Psalm* 138, §17, he says: “For the Father is greater than the Son, but as father to son, by generation and not by kind.” Athanasius agrees, *Oration II against the Arians*, p. 363: “The Father is greater than the Son, not by some magnitude or time, but because of generation from the Father Himself.” Thus may also be excused Origen’s statement, vol. III, *On John*, ed. Huet, p. 70: “Thirdly, this light is called the true light; in this respect the God and Father of truth is more ample and greater than truth, and, being father of wisdom, is superior to wisdom itself; in this respect also He surpasses Him who is the true light, namely Christ.” The same judgment should be made concerning similar statements of other Fathers.]

These things must be understood as they are; but care must be taken lest, among the unlearned, the honor of the Father diminish the glory of the Son. Nor does this very requested glorification permit the Son’s glory to be weakened. For to the words, “Father, glorify your Son,” there follows, “so that the Son may glorify you.” Therefore the Son is not weak, since, though He is to be glorified, He Himself will return the glory in exchange.

[Note: [Col. 0082D] In the printed editions: “allows itself to be weakened.” The reflexive *itself* is absent from the manuscripts; in its place the sense is: “does not allow the glory of the Son to be understood as weakened.”]

[Note: [Col. 0082D] “Itself permits.”]

But if He is not weak, what was He asking? For no one asks except for what he needs. Or is the Father also weak? Or is He so lavish with what He has that glorification must be rendered to Him through the Son? Yet neither does the Father need it nor does the Son lack it; and nevertheless one will bestow it upon the other.

[Note: [Col. 0082D] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions: “will impart it.”]

Therefore the request for glory to be given and in turn rendered neither takes anything from the Father nor weakens the Son; rather, it shows the same power of divinity in both [Col. 0082D]: the Son prays that He may be glorified by the Father, and the Father does not disdain to receive glorification from the Son. But these things show unity of power in Father and Son through the reciprocal giving and repayment of glory.

[Note: [Col. 0083D] In the manuscripts, first *repetendae*, “to be reclaimed,” then, through correction, *referendae*, “to be returned.”]

[Note: [Col. 0083D] The printed editions: “of glory to be given and returned.” In one Sorbonne manuscript: “to be given and received.” In several others: “to be given and reclaimed.” The reading of the ancient Colbert manuscript, “to be given and repaid,” seemed sounder to us.]

13. What is the glory which Father and Son show to one another? — But we must learn what this glorification is and from what it arises.

[Note: Three manuscripts: “must be taught.”]

God, I think, is not subject to change; neither fault nor improvement, progress nor loss, belongs to eternity. Rather, what He is, He always is: this indeed is peculiar to God. What always is cannot at some point have it in its nature not to be. How, then, will that be glorified which has no need of anything of its own and suffers no deficiency from itself—so that there is nothing which it might receive into itself, nor anything lost which it might recover? We hesitate and are delayed.

But the Evangelist does not abandon the weakness of our understanding. He shows what glorification the Son was to render to the Father, saying: “Just as you gave Him authority over all flesh, so that He may give eternal life to all whom you gave Him. And this is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17:2–3). Therefore the Father is glorified through the Son insofar as He is understood by us.

[Note: [Col. 0083D] The printed editions here add “through the Son,” which is absent from the manuscripts. Nor does “through the Son” occur in the Gospel words, “that they may know you,” etc., which are here explained; nor is it relevant to Hilary’s purpose. He intends only that God’s glory adds nothing to Him which He previously lacked, because He is then glorified when He is understood by us, and this knowledge of ours adds nothing to Him.]

This glory, however, consisted in the fact that the Son received from Him authority over all flesh, He Himself having become flesh, in order to give eternal life to those who are frail, bodily, and mortal.

[Note: [Col. 0084D] Thus the ancient Colbert manuscript, supported by the others, which read: “He Himself, having become flesh, [would give] eternal life”; in the Vict. manuscript, “who [would give] eternal life.” The printed editions read: “for He Himself, having become flesh, [would give] eternal life.”]

The eternity of our life was not the result of a work but of power, since the glory of eternity was to be received not through some new operation, but through the knowledge of God alone. Therefore no glory is added to God—for He had not lost it, so that it needed to be added. Rather, through the Son He is glorified among us who are ignorant, apostate, defiled, [Col. 0083C] dead without hope, darkened without law; and He is glorified because the Son received from Him authority over all flesh in order to give it eternal life.

[Note: [Col. 0084D] Bad. and Erasmus: “dead without spirit.” In one Colbert manuscript: “about to die without hope.”]

Thus, through these works of the Son, the Father is glorified. Accordingly, since the Son received all things, He was glorified by the Father; and conversely the Father is glorified when all things come to be through the Son. And the glory received is returned in such a way that whatever glory is in the Son is wholly the Father’s glory: because the Son received all things from the Father; because the honor of the servant is honor to the sender, just as the honor of the begetter is honor to the one born.

[Note: [Col. 0083D] In our manuscript, by correction in an ancient hand: “is thus believed.”]

[Note: [Col. 0084D] Thus one Colbert manuscript. Other books here and shortly afterward read: “into honor.”]

14. The hope of life is not in the Father alone, but also in the Son. Mission distinguishes persons, not nature. — But wherein, finally, consists eternity of life? He Himself says: “That they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent.” [Col. 0083D] What questions of difficulty arise here, and what conflict of words is this? To know the true God is life; but this alone, taken bare, does not constitute life. What, then, is joined to it? “And Jesus Christ whom you sent.”

The honor due from the Son to the Father is rendered when He says, “you, the only true God.” Yet the Son does not separate Himself from the truth of God when He adds, “and Jesus Christ whom you sent.” The confession of believers, whose hope of life is in both, admits no interval between them; nor is the true God lacking to Him who follows in the conjunction.

Therefore, when it is said, “That they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent,” under this signification—namely, of sender and sent—there is no distinction of the truth and divinity of Father and Son by any difference either of meaning or of extension; rather, the faith of religion is instructed toward confession of the begetter and the begotten.

15. Praise of the Son is praise of the Father. — Therefore the Son glorifies the Father unreservedly in what follows: “I have glorified you upon earth, having completed the work which you gave me to do.” All praise of the Father is through the Son, because in whatever the Son is praised, the Father will be praised. For the Son accomplishes all that the Father willed.

The Son of God is born human; but the power of God is present in the virgin’s childbirth. The Son of God is seen as human; but God is present in the works of the human being. The Son of God is fixed to the cross; but in the cross God conquers human death. Christ, the Son of God, dies; but all flesh is made alive in Christ. The Son of God is in hell; but humanity is brought back to heaven. In proportion as these things are praised in Christ, so much greater praise will be gained by Him from whom Christ is God.

By these means, therefore, the Father glorifies the Son upon earth; and again [Col. 0084C] the Son glorifies, through the works of His powers, Him from whom He Himself is, before the ignorance of the Gentiles and the folly of the world.

[Note: [Col. 0084D] The Vatican Basilica manuscript: “through the power of His operations.” The Carnot manuscript: “through the operation of His powers.”]

This reciprocity of glorification does not pertain to an increase in divinity, but to the honor received from the knowledge of those who had been ignorant. For in what did the Father not abound, He from whom all things exist? Or what was lacking to the Son, in whom it pleased all the fullness of divinity to dwell? Therefore the Father is glorified upon earth because the work He commanded is accomplished.

16. What glory the Son awaits from the Father. — Let us see what glorification the Son awaits from the Father; and the matter is clear. For it is contained in the words that follow: “I have glorified you upon earth; I have completed the work which you gave me to do. And now glorify me, Father, [Col. 0084D] with yourself with that glory which I had with you before [Col. 0085A] the world existed. I have manifested your name to human beings” (Job [i.e. John] 17:4).

[Note: [Col. 0084D] “In what follows.”]

[Note: [Col. 0084D] “You, Father,” as in the Greek text and the Vulgate.]

Therefore the Father was glorified by the works of the Son: when He is understood to be God; when He is manifested as the Father of the only-begotten God; when, for our salvation, He willed that His Son, even as one born human from a virgin, should fulfill in His passion all that began with the virgin’s childbirth.

Accordingly, because the Son of God was perfect in every respect, and was born before all time in the fullness of divinity, He was now, from the origin of His flesh, as a human being being brought to completion unto death; He asks to be glorified with God, just as He Himself glorified the Father on earth, because at that time the powers of God were being glorified in flesh before a world ignorant of them.

[Note: [Col. 0085D] One Colbert manuscript: “which is Father”; Carnot: “as is Father.” The common reading should be retained: not because there were parts in the Son of God before His assumption of flesh, but because there was nothing in Him by which He could not be called perfect.]

But what glorification does He now await with the Father? Surely that which He had with Him before the world existed. He had the fullness of divinity, and He has it, for He is the Son of God.

[Note: [Col. 0085D] That is, before the world existed; and He still has it after He Himself became human.]

But He who was the Son of God had also begun to be the son of a human being; for the Word had become flesh. He had not lost what He was, but had begun to be what He was not; He had not ceased to be what was His own, but had taken what is ours. For that which He received—namely, human nature—He asks an advance into that glory which He had not ceased to possess.

Therefore, because the Son is the Word, and the Word became flesh, and the Word is God, and was in the beginning with God, and the Word was Son before the foundation of the world: the Son, now made flesh, prayed that the flesh might begin to be to the Father what the Word is; that what belonged to time might receive the glory of that splendor which is without time; and that the corruption of flesh, transformed into divine power and the incorruption of the Spirit, might be swallowed up.

[Note: [Col. 0085D] Thus in *On the Synods*, §48: “The Word became flesh so that the flesh might rather begin to be what the Word is.” Hilary does not understand this as a change of substance, but of quality: not so that flesh should cease to be what it is, but so that, with corruption swallowed up, it might be transformed into incorruption and the other endowments proper to the divine nature of the Word, as is explained shortly afterward and shown at length in the General Preface, §5. This must be carefully observed, lest, where the ancient Fathers proclaim our flesh to have been deified by Christ after the resurrection, they be rashly judged to have meant the abolition of flesh. Hilary shows himself remote from this error here, when he teaches that Christ will be seen on the day of judgment in that same flesh in which He was transfigured on the mountain.]

This prayer, then, is addressed to God; this is the Son’s confession to the Father; this is the petition of the flesh: the flesh in which all will see Him pierced and recognize Him from the cross on the day of judgment; in which He was prefigured on the mountain; in which He was raised into heaven; in which He sat at the right hand of God; in which Paul saw Him; and in which Stephen honored Him.

[Note: [Col. 0085C] These words, “in which Paul saw Him,” found in the Erasmian and Paris editions and omitted in the edition preceding this one, have been restored on the authority of our manuscript. Paul himself speaks of this vision in 1 Cor. 15:8: “Last of all, as to one untimely born, He appeared also to me.”]

17. Before Christ, God’s name was unknown to human beings. — Having therefore manifested the Father’s name to human beings, He asks this. But by what name? Was God’s name unknown? Moses heard it from the bush; Genesis proclaimed it at the beginning of the created world; the law expounded it; the prophets set it forth; human beings perceived it in these works of the world; even the nations worshiped it while speaking falsely. Therefore God’s name was not unknown.

[Note: [Col. 0086D] The printed editions: “but God plainly.” The word *God* has been deleted on the authority of the manuscripts. Hilary’s thought is more clearly evident from these words in Book V, §27: “And I ask whether He is not true God, who was then both blessed and sworn by according to the opinion of the Jews. For the Jews, not knowing the sacrament of the mystery of God, and through this not knowing the Son of God, worshiped God only, not the Father also. For certainly, in worshiping the Father, they would worship the Son also.”]

Yet it was plainly unknown. For no one knows God unless he confesses both the Father as Father of the only-begotten Son and the Son—not as from a portion, nor by extension, nor by emission, but as born from Him ineffably and incomprehensibly, as Son from Father—possessing the fullness of divinity from which and in which He is born: true, infinite, and perfect God. For this is God’s fullness. If anything of these is lacking, there will no longer be the fullness which it pleased God should dwell in Him (Col. 1:19).

[Note: [Col. 0086D] The printed editions: “or by extension,” wrongly; nor is Erasmus’s and Lipsius’s later “or by remission” any better. The expressions “by extension” or “by emission” guard against the Sabellian heresy, explained in Book I, §16.]

This is proclaimed by the Son; this is manifested to those who are ignorant. Thus the Father is glorified through the Son [Col. 0086B] when He is recognized as the Father of such a Son.

18. Christ established belief in His birth through His deeds. Those who deny divine things because they cannot comprehend them are rebuked. — Therefore, wishing to establish belief in this His birth, the Son set before us examples of His works, so that through the ineffable efficacy of His ineffable deeds we might be instructed concerning the power of His ineffable birth.

[Note: [Col. 0086D] The Vatican Basilica manuscript, together with one Colbert and the Remigian manuscript: “set forth.” Shortly afterward we have restored from the manuscripts the word *ineffable*, formerly omitted.]

Water becomes wine; five loaves, after five thousand men have been fed—apart from all the rest of both sexes and ages—fill twelve baskets with fragments. The event is seen and not known; it happens and is not understood; its reason is not grasped, while its result is forced upon us. It is foolish to bring the charge of inquiry against that which, by its own nature, cannot be comprehended in the very respect in which it is being investigated.

For as the Father is ineffable in that He is unbegotten, so the Son cannot be narrated in that He is only-begotten, because the one who is begotten is the image of the Unbegotten. For when we comprehend an image in thought and words, we must also comprehend Him whose image it is. But we pursue invisible things and attempt incomprehensible things, though our understanding is confined to visible and bodily realities. We are not ashamed of our folly; we do not accuse ourselves of irreligion while we malign the secrets and powers of God. We ask how the Son is Son, from what source He is Son, [Col. 0087A] with what loss to the Father, or from what portion He was born. You had in the example of His works grounds for believing that God can accomplish what you cannot understand how He accomplishes.

[Note: [Col. 0087B] Bad. and Erasmus: *haereas*, “you may be at a loss”; Lipsius and Paris: *haerebas*, “you were at a loss.” Erasmus indeed saw *hebueras* in the manuscripts, and therefore wrote in the margin, “I think *hebueras* should be read, that is, ‘you had been blind’;” Louis de Myraeus wrongly subscribed to this opinion. The manuscript reading is unambiguous: *habueras ut*, “you had grounds whereby,” or “from which,” “you might believe.” Thus in Book VII, §51: “You had, in their confession—those for whom, when the wind raged . . . calm had been restored—grounds for confessing the true Son of God also,” etc.]

19. They are challenged to explain Christ’s entry when the doors were closed. — You ask how the Son was born according to the Spirit; I question you about bodily matters. I do not ask how He was born of a virgin, whether flesh, producing perfect flesh from itself, suffered any loss of itself. And certainly it did not receive [from a man] what it brought forth; rather, flesh brought forth flesh without the shamefulness of our elements, and, itself unimpaired, generated from its own substance one who was perfect.

[Note: [Col. 0087C] The negative particle, which Lipsius had removed in vain, is here restored.]

[Note: [Col. 0087C] That is, from a man. But flesh brought forth perfect flesh—that is, a true and perfect human being—without the shamefulness of our elements, since all of us derive the beginnings of flesh from man and woman. See Book X, §35, and Book XII, §49. We have reconciled this passage with another in the *Treatise on Psalm* 67 in the notes on that same treatise.]

[Note: [Col. 0087C] The phrase *de suis*, “from its own,” is used in Hilary’s manner, so as to refer equally to the preceding phrase “itself unimpaired” and to the following “generated,” as though the text read: “itself generated from its own substance, though not diminished in its own substance.” Thus “unimpaired in its own substance” may mean that she gave birth while her virginity remained whole and inviolate. But some wrongly seize upon what is inferred from this generation of the Blessed Virgin—that the generation of the eternal Father without any loss to Himself may be credible—in order to malign Hilary’s view of Christ’s conception, claiming that he thought Christ received nothing from Mary. As if the point of his comparison were not precisely this: that, just as Christ was born from Mary’s substance while her integrity remained unharmed, so He could be generated from the Father’s substance without loss to the Father. If he denied that Christ was generated from Mary’s substance, his argument would have no force whatever. That he by no means denies it has been shown by most evident arguments in the General Preface, §1.]

And surely it would be lawful to judge not impossible in God what we know to have been possible in a human being through His power.

[Col. 0087B] 20. But you, whoever you are, who pursue things unsearchable and set yourself up as a weighty judge of divine mysteries and powers, I ask you to give to me, an unlearned man who merely believes concerning God all things as they have been spoken by Him, at least an explanation of this event. I hear the Lord, and because I believe what has been written, I know that after the resurrection He frequently made Himself visible in a body to many unbelievers; certainly to Thomas, who would not believe unless he had touched His wounds, as he says: “Unless I see in His hands the mark of the nails, and put my finger into the place of the nails, and put my hand into His side, I will not believe” (John 20:25).

[Note: [Col. 0087D] Most manuscripts read “in His hands.” We retain, with the Paris edition, “the mark of the nails,” supported by the ancient Colbert and Germain manuscripts, in accordance with the Greek, τὸν τύπον τῶν ἥλων, “the mark of the nails.” Other books have “the piercing.” Shortly afterward the Carnotensis manuscript reads “through the places of the nails,” instead of “into the place.”]

[Note: [Col. 0087B] Earlier editions: “the mark.”]

The Lord accommodates Himself to every weakness of our understanding and, intending to satisfy the doubt of unbelievers, performs the secret work of invisible power. You, whoever you may be, investigator of heavenly matters, explain the reason for the event. The disciples were gathered and seated in a closed and secluded place after the Lord’s passion.

[Note: [Col. 0088C] Printed editions read “shut in.” But the manuscripts here read “in a closed place”; and, at the end of the book addressed to Constantius, to which these words were transferred, one Colbert manuscript reads “shut in.” It has already been restored from manuscripts in Commentary on Matthew, ch. 4, §13: “What profit is it for a closed place to contain the expenditure of light?”] The Lord, intending to confirm Thomas’s faith under the conditions laid down, stood among them and offered him the opportunity of feeling His body and touching His wound. And certainly, if He was to be recognized as one who had been pierced, He necessarily brought the body in which He had been pierced.

[Note: [Col. 0088B] “Because [He was] pierced.”] I ask, therefore, through what part of the closed house He entered bodily.

For the Evangelist carefully stated: “Jesus came, the doors having been shut, and stood in the midst” (ibid., 26).

[Note: [Col. 0088C] Printed editions here add “of His disciples,” which occurs neither in the sacred text nor in the manuscripts.]

Did He pass through the constructed walls and the solid timbers, penetrating their impenetrable nature?

[Note: [Col. 0088C] Thus the manuscripts. Printed editions instead read: “and passed through the impenetrable nature of the solid timbers.”]

For He stood there bodily, not in appearance or deception. Let the eyes of your mind follow that penetrating entrance, and let the sight of your understanding enter with Him into the closed house. Everything remains whole and bolted; yet He stands present in the midst, He to whom all things are passable through His power. You cavil at invisible things; I demand from you an explanation of visible things. Nothing yields from its solidity; nor do timbers and stones, by their nature, admit anything as though through an imperceptible slipping. The Lord’s body does not fail away from itself so as to recover itself from nothing. From where, then, is He who stands in the midst? Here both sense and speech yield, and the truth of the event lies beyond human reasoning.

[Note: [Col. 0088C] Printed editions read “we are deceived.” The better manuscripts rightly read “we deceive ourselves”; the Carnotensis manuscript, “we have deceived ourselves.” For these words are introduced in the name of heretics, who reject a truth they do not comprehend. Calvin, an imitator of the feeble reasoning of Arians who trust their own reason too greatly, was even bolder in this respect: on John 20:19 he did not hesitate to deny that Christ passed through closed doors to the disciples. Yet he grants that Christ entered when the doors were “closed” in the sense that, although shut, their entrance was not opened by human hand, as Peter left a locked prison through the ministry of an angel after it had been opened. He then slanders Catholics under the name of “Papists,” alleging that those who think otherwise do so in order to make the glorious body not merely like a spirit, but immense and contained in no place. Yet they think otherwise solely because the words of Scripture are clear and have been understood according to their plain sound by the unanimous agreement of the Fathers.

Certainly Scultetus strives in vain when he tries to persuade himself that Hilary does not differ from his Calvin. For who does not see that Hilary understood the Gospel words so that he believed Christ passed to the disciples through doors that were shut—not opened by an angel’s hand or by some power of divine omnipotence, but remaining shut? Augustine understood them no differently, in Sermon 247, §2, where, as if refuting Calvin and his followers beforehand, he confirms the same event by the example of the nativity: “The Virgin gave birth and remained a virgin: already then the Lord was born through closed doors.” But how did Christ’s true body pass through the impenetrable nature of walls and timbers? Hilary answers: the truth of the event is established by the Gospel words, although its manner wholly escapes human reasoning; yet it is no less certain that God can do more than human reason can grasp.

Nor is Augustine’s answer different, in Sermon 247, §2, and Letter 137, §8, or that of Cyril of Alexandria, Book XII on John. Thus many difficulties could be resolved which Calvin’s followers devise concerning the most holy sacrament of the Eucharist: How can one and the same body of Christ be in heaven and on earth, and matters of that kind? Do not trouble yourself about the manner, since Christ wished you to be certain only of the fact.

Perhaps there will even be persons who explain the manners: philosophers are not now lacking who think they can explain this entrance of the Lord to the disciples through doors that were shut and in no way opened. For, they say, since preservation is continued creation, it was as easy for God to continue the creation of Christ’s body in a distant place, while the intermediate bodies remained unmoved, as in a nearby place. Although according to the common laws of nature He does not continue the creation of any body except in the same or an adjacent place, and only after the body previously occupying that place has been displaced from its position, it was certainly most easy for God that the body which He willed, at one instant of time, to be outside the room, should by the will through which it was created outside the room, at the following instant be willed to be inside the room. By that act it necessarily is inside the room, while the walls and doors remain uninjured and unmoved.

Hilary indeed saw that Christ’s act could be explained in this way. But here the phantasms usually play tricks which prevent them from conceiving a body’s entrance within uninjured walls unless they suppose that the body was first completely abolished outside and then newly created inside. Hence our Hilary says here: “The Lord’s body does not fail away from itself so as to recover itself from nothing.” Yet a body now outside and immediately afterward, through the creating—or rather preserving—will of God, inside the room, does not fail away from itself, since it never ceases to exist for any moment of time. Or it may be said to fail only insofar as it needs, by its nature, to be created at every moment of time; just as by motion it may be said to fail in the place in which it is no longer created, in order to be created in that in which it is preserved.

Whether this entrance of Christ through shut doors occurred in this manner or another, what once seemed contrary to those who placed excessive trust in their weak reasoning no longer appears contrary. So perhaps someone will also dispel the little reasonings—or rather darknesses—by which those same disciples of Calvin think to obscure the truth of Christ’s body and blood in the sacrament of the Eucharist. Meanwhile it will be safer to hold with the whole Church to the truth of the event, although the manner in which it occurs is unknown.]

Therefore, in respect to the nativity we deceive ourselves, and likewise we lie concerning the Lord’s entrance [Col. 0089A] 63. Let us say that the event did not occur because we do not grasp its meaning; and when our understanding fails, let the effect of the event itself cease. But faith in the event overcomes our falsehood. The Lord stood in the midst of the disciples while the house was shut; and the Son was born from the Father. Do not deny that He stood there because, through the weakness of your understanding, you do not comprehend the entrance of Him who stood there. Do not fail to know that from the unbegotten and perfect God the Father the only-begotten and perfect God the Son was born, because the power of generation surpasses the capacity and speech of human nature.

[Note: [Col. 0090B] Thus the Basel and Erasmus editions and the manuscripts; Lipsius had no reason to substitute “the Son, God, was born.”]

21. If they could, they would overthrow all God’s works. — Indeed, all the works of the world could stand before us as witnesses, so that we might not think it permissible to doubt God’s acts and powers. But our unbelief rushes against truth itself, and we violently burst forth toward the destruction of God’s power. If it were permitted, we would raise our bodies and hands against heaven; we would throw the sun and all the other stars out of the bounds of their yearly courses; we would confound the retreat and advance of Ocean; we would stop even the streams of springs, reverse the natures of rivers, shake the foundations of the earth, and rage with utter parricide against these works of God.

[Note: [Col. 0090B] Printed editions read “within the bounds of its yearly course.” The old Colbert manuscript reads “the years of their course within their bounds.” Another Colbert manuscript, with the Sorbonne manuscript, reads “their yearly courses within their bounds.” The reading presented here is that of most manuscripts. Compare Commentary on Psalm 134, §11, where Hilary describes the unchanging stability of heaven, the sun governed by its yearly and tireless courses, and the seasons moderated by fixed bounds, and so forth.]

[Note: [Col. 0090C] Two Colbert manuscripts with the Germain read “the natures of men.” Then printed editions, with two later manuscripts, read “we would restrain”; one has the corrupt reading “we would refer back.” With the others we prefer “we would reverse,” a more Hilarian word, as was observed in the Notes on Psalm 119, note 3.]

But it is well that the nature of our bodies confines us within this necessity of restraint. Certainly we do not deceive ourselves about what we would do if we were permitted.

[Note: [Col. 0089B] “Would do”; shortly afterward “profane” for “of profane.”]

For because we can, with the boldness of profane will we overthrow the nature of truth and wage war against God in our words.

[Note: [Col. 0090C] Printed editions read “because we cannot,” adding a negative particle contrary to the authority of the manuscripts and to Hilary’s meaning. He infers from the heretics’ acts against truth, because they can do this through the freedom of their own judgment, what they would do against the natures of things if they were likewise granted the power.]

22. Christ made the Father known to us as Father, not as Creator. — The Son said: “Father, I have made Your name known to men” (John 17:6). Why do we cavil at this? Why are we agitated? Do you deny the Father?

[Note: [Col. 0090C] We write this word in imitation of the ancient books, as has also been done in Tertullian.]

Yet this was the Son’s greatest work: that we should know the Father. You clearly deny Him when, according to you, the Son was not born from Him.

[Note: [Col. 0090D] Printed editions read “and when the Son is called.” Later Lipsius has “because thus are the rest,” and the Paris edition “because the rest are so”: a corrupt reading followed by faulty punctuation, so that the force of the argument no longer appeared at all. It is restored with the aid of manuscripts. For this is its meaning: one who asserts that the Son was made at will like the rest in fact denies that He is Son; one who denies the Son denies the Father also; and one who denies the Father denies what Christ here was most intent upon teaching. For Christ was not particularly concerned to impress upon us that He was God and the Creator of Christ and of all things, although He could thereby have greatly commended Him to us and awakened our admiration; rather, He wished to show Him to be the true Father who has the true Son. This was Christ’s work and labor.]

And why should He be called Son if He was made according to will like the other things? I can admire God as Creator making the world through Christ; and it is a power worthy of God that He should have made Christ the maker of archangels and angels, of visible and invisible things, of heaven and earth, and of all this creation. But this is not the Lord’s labor: that you should perceive God’s ability in creating all things; rather, that you should know that God is the Father of the Son who speaks.

There are many heavenly powers, both creative and eternal; but there is one only-begotten Son, not differing from the rest merely in power because all things are through Him.

[Note: [Col. 0091C] We have often observed that Hilary customarily understands angels by the name “heavenly powers.” He calls these powers eternal, not because he thinks them eternal from eternity, but because he believes they will not perish. In this sense man according to the soul is called eternal in Psalm 129, §6. Here he notes the Arian view, which wished Christ to differ from those powers only in this: they produce only some things, whereas all things are through Him. Hence it is clear that the earlier printed editions wrongly had “through Him all things were created,” where we restore from the manuscripts, “through Him all things are.”]

But because He is one true Son, let Him not become degenerate, as though born from nothing.

[Note: [Col. 0091D] Lipsius and Paris: “not because He is degenerate,” without authority.]

You hear “Son”: believe that He is Son. You hear “Father”: remember that He is Father. Why do you introduce suspicion, malice, and audacity into these names? Names have been applied to divine things in accordance with the meaning of nature.

[Note: [Col. 0091D] Thus the manuscripts. Printed editions: “are suitable.”]

Why do you bring the force of words against truth? You hear Father and Son: do not doubt that they are what they are called. The sum of the dispensation is this for the Son: that you may know the Father. Why do you render vain the work of the prophets, the incarnation of the Word, the Virgin’s childbirth, the power of His works, Christ’s cross? All these things were expended and granted for you, so that through them both Father and Son might be manifest to you. You now introduce will, creation, adoption: look also to Christ’s service and recompense.

[Note: [Col. 0091D] The Carnotensis manuscript reads “will”; this reading is supported by the fact that at the beginning of this section, according to the heretics’ view, the Son is said to have been made according to will.]

For He cries aloud: “Father, I have made Your name known to men.” You do not hear, “You have created the Creator of heavenly things”; you do not hear, “You have made the maker of earthly things”; but you hear: “Father, I have made Your name known to men.” Use the gift of your Savior.

[Note: [Col. 0091C] “Saving.”]

Know that He who begot is Father, that He who was born is Son; that He was born in the truth of nature from that Father who is.

[Note: [Col. 0091D] Printed editions: “who is from the truth of nature.” The words “from” are absent from the manuscripts. The natural order and meaning of these words are: “born in the truth of nature,” that is, by a true birth with the nature of Him from whom He is born, “from that Father who is”—that is, whose property it is to exist from Himself and not from another, or who is the source of all things. Thus in Book II, §11: “The Son is from that Father who is”; and here, as we shall soon see: “They are one, namely He who is, having nothing that is not also in Him from whom He is,” where “He who is” signifies the Father and “Him from whom He is” the Son. Although in Book II, §32, the Son is called “He who is” in relation to the Holy Spirit, and the Holy Spirit, in relation to Him, “He whose He is,” as it were, He who belongs to Him.]

[Note: [Col. 0091C] “From the truth.”]

Remember: the Father was not made known to you merely as God; rather, God was made known as Father.

23. The Son is distinguished from the Father by subsistence, not nature. As image, He has all that the Father has. — You hear: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). Why do you divide and separate the Son from the Father? They are one: namely, He who is, having nothing which is not also in Him from whom He is.

[Note: [Col. 0092C] In one Remigianus manuscript, and likewise in Theodoret, “He who is, and He from whom He is, having nothing,” etc.; a gloss. For here the reason is given why Father and Son are one: because He who is the source of generation has nothing which is not in Him who is from Him, that is, who derives His origin from Him.]

When you hear the Son saying, “I and the Father are one,” apply the statement to the persons; allow the Begetter and the Begotten the sense of their own confession. Let them be one as are He who begot and He who was begotten. Why do you exclude nature? Why do you destroy truth? You hear: “The Father is in Me, and I in the Father” (ibid., 38); and the Son’s works bear witness to this concerning Father and Son. We do not, in our understanding, put body into body, nor pour water into wine; rather, we confess in both the same likeness of power and fullness of divinity. For the Son received all things from the Father, and is the form of God and the image of His substance.

[Note: [Col. 0092C] “For Him who is from Him who is [is] an image.”]

[Note: [Col. 0092D] Printed editions and some manuscripts: “For Him who is from Him who is [is] an image of substance”; another gloss, corrected with the aid of the Carnotensis, Colbert, Vendôme, Vatican, and Victorius manuscripts. For “Him” refers to the Son, and “from Him who is” is said of the Father. Then “image of substance” is taken materially. Therefore, with most and the better manuscripts, “distinguishes for the understanding” is preferable to the reading in Lipsius and Paris, “understanding distinguishes.”]

For the fact that He is from Him who is, and that He is the image of His substance, distinguishes only for the assurance of subsistence, not for the understanding of any dissimilarity of nature. But the Father’s being in the Son and the Son’s being in the Father is the perfect fullness of divinity in each. For the Son is not a diminution of the Father, nor is the Son imperfect in relation to the Father. An image is not alone—that is, solitary—and likeness does not belong to itself. But nothing can be like God unless it is from Him. For that which is like Him in all things is not from elsewhere; nor does likeness of one to another permit diversity to be mixed into the two. Do not interchange things that are alike, nor divide those inseparable from one another in truth. For He who said, “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26), showed that They are mutually like one another by saying “our likeness.” Do not touch, do not handle, do not corrupt. Hold fast to the names of nature; hold fast to the Son’s confession. I do not want you to flatter, praising the Son from your own resources; it is well that you be content with what has been written.

24. Human wisdom fails in divine matters. It becomes foolish while supposing itself perfectly wise. — Human wisdom is not to be trusted so far that anyone should think himself perfectly wise in what he knows, and judge that the whole sum of complete reason is contained in that which, turning over in his own mind, he thinks established by an opinion of truth evenly balanced on every side. For imperfect things do not comprehend the perfect; nor can that which subsists from another attain an absolute understanding either of its author or of itself.

[Note: [Col. 0092D] That is, from another substance; this manner of expression is contrasted with “from Himself” in the preceding section: “Nothing can be like God unless it is from Him.” Then two Colbert manuscripts with the Carnotensis read “has remained,” and a little later “indeed,” not “itself indeed.”]

It perceives itself only in that wherein it exists; beyond that, it does not extend its sense further than the nature appointed to it. For it does not owe its motion to itself, but to its author; and therefore that which subsists from its author in another is imperfect to itself, since it depends on another.

[Note: [Col. 0093D] “Into another” is absent from the older Colbert and Remigianus manuscripts; it was added in the Corbeiensis by a second hand. Lipsius and Paris, deleting the particle “into,” retained only “another.” From this passage must be understood that statement in the Commentary on Psalm 134, §10: “He who does not owe himself to himself cannot do all things, since he subsists from one more powerful.”]

And it necessarily follows that, where it considers itself perfectly wise, it is foolish. For, not moderating the necessity of its own nature and supposing that all things are bounded by the limits of its own weakness, it now falsely glories in the name of wisdom; because it is not permitted to know beyond the power of its own sense, and it is as limited in perception as it is weak in the power by which it subsists. Therefore the subsistence of an imperfect nature, glorying that it possesses the wisdom of perfect understanding, is reproached with the derision of foolish wisdom, as the Apostle says:

“For Christ did not send me to baptize, but to preach the Gospel, not in wisdom of speech, lest the cross of Christ should be made empty. For the word of the cross is foolishness to those who perish, but to those who are being saved it is the power of God. For it is written: ‘I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and I will reject the understanding of the intelligent.’ Where is the wise person? Where is the scribe? Where is the inquirer of this age? Has not God made foolish the wisdom of this world? For since, in the wisdom of God, the world did not know God through wisdom, God decreed through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe. For Jews ask for signs and Greeks seek wisdom; but we preach Christ Jesus crucified: to Jews indeed a stumbling block, and to Gentiles foolishness; but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God, because what is weak in God is stronger than men, and what is foolish in God is wiser than men” (1 Cor. 1:17 ff.).

[Note: [Col. 0093D] The Carnotensis manuscript reads “this world,” adding “this,” as the old Colbert manuscript also did above in §6. Shortly afterward the Carnotensis and others read “to make [them] saved” for “to save”; and a little later, as also in the old Colbert manuscript, “what is weaker . . . what is more foolish.” We have already noted that passages of Scripture repeated by Hilary are not cited in precisely the same manner.]

Therefore every unbelief is foolishness.

[Note: [Col. 0093D] “Is foolish.”]

For, using the wisdom of its imperfect sense, while it measures everything by the opinion of its own weakness, it judges impossible what it does not understand. The cause of unbelief is a judgment based on weakness: a person does not think something was done because he has decided that it could not be done.

[Note: [Col. 0093D] In the Carnotensis manuscript: “is a judgment of impossibility,” less well. What “a judgment based on weakness” means is explained in the immediately preceding words: “while it measures and regulates everything by the opinion of its own weakness.”]

25. The wise foolishness of believers. — Therefore the Apostle, knowing that the imperfect thought of human nature regards as true only that which it understands, says that he does not preach in wisdom of speech, lest the assertion of his preaching should be empty. And lest he should be thought a preacher of foolishness, he added that the word of the cross is foolishness to those who perish; because unbelievers would think that prudence alone to be wisdom which they understood, and, since they understood nothing except within the bounds of their own weak nature, would think that wisdom—which alone is the perfect wisdom of God—to be foolishness. Thus, through the very opinion of their wisdom, they would be foolish in their weakness.

[Note: [Col. 0094D] Printed editions omit the preposition “through.” Then Erasmus, Lipsius, and Paris add “those same weak persons,” against the Basel edition and the manuscripts.]

Therefore whatever is foolishness to those who perish is the power of God to those who are being saved; because they do not measure anything by the weakness of their own natural sense, but assess the effectiveness of divine power according to the infinity of heavenly might.

[Note: [Col. 0094D] We add “their own” from the manuscripts. It is not far from Hilary’s thought. Gregory, Morals, Book IX, ch. 8: “Therefore he who does not see the reason in God’s acts, by considering his weakness sees why he does not see the reason.”]

And therefore God rejects the wisdom of the wise and the understanding of the intelligent, because through the judgment of human foolishness salvation is given to believers: unbelievers decide that what lies beyond their comprehension is foolish, while believers entrust to God’s power and might the mysteries by which their salvation is to be bestowed.

[Note: [Col. 0094D] The Vatican Basel manuscript and three others read “to be bestowed.” Erasmus and Lipsius, “by bestowing.” The reading “to be bestowed” must certainly be retained with the other books.]

Thus the things that are God’s are not foolish; rather, the foolish wisdom of human nature is that which asks its God either for signs or for wisdom as a condition of faith. It belongs to Jews to demand signs, since, being not wholly unacquainted with God’s name through familiarity with the Law, they are disturbed by the scandal of the cross. It belongs to Greeks to demand wisdom, because in Gentile folly and human prudence they seek an explanation of the God raised upon the cross. Since this is hidden in a mystery from those weak according to the sense of nature, it becomes foolishness to the unbeliever.

[Note: [Col. 0094D] Printed editions: “to unbelievers”; corrected from manuscripts of the best authority, Vatican Basel, Colbert, and others.]

For what the naturally imperfect mind does not conceive, it judges to be without rational ground. But because of this imprudent wisdom of the world, which formerly did not know God through God’s wisdom—that is, did not venerate the wisdom of its Creator through this magnificence of the world and the beauty of a work so wisely ordered—it pleased God to save believers through the preaching of foolishness: that is, that through faith in the cross eternity should come to mortals, so that, when the judgment of human wisdom was confounded, salvation might be found where foolishness was believed to be.

[Note: [Col. 0094D] Printed editions: “the judgment of wisdom,” against the manuscripts.]

For Christ, who is foolishness to Gentiles and a stumbling block to Jews, is the power of God and the wisdom of God; because what is thought weak and foolish in God’s affairs by human judgment surpasses earthly prudence and power in the truth of wisdom and might.

26. In God’s affairs judgment must be made not by one’s own understanding but by faith. — Therefore nothing in divine effects is to be handled by the opinion of the human mind, nor should the material of the work pass judgment on its own Creator. Rather, we must take up foolishness in order that we may receive wisdom—not with a sense of imprudence, but in awareness of our own nature—so that what the reasoning of earthly thought does not comprehend, the reason of divine power may in turn suggest to us. For when, having recognized the understanding of our foolishness, we perceive in ourselves the ignorance of natural imprudence, then through the prudence of divine wisdom we shall be instructed in God’s wisdom: when we measure God’s powers and might without limit; when we do not confine the Lord of nature within natural laws; when we understand that this alone is rightly believed concerning God which He Himself, concerning Himself, stands among us as both witness and author for us to believe.

69–70. BOOK FOUR.

He undertakes to fortify the simplicity of Catholics against the stratagems of Arians. For this purpose he sets forth their opinion concerning Christ. Then he defends the Son’s being *homoousios*—of the same substance—with the Father, and His having always existed; and declares that the Church recoils from the perverse interpretations by which they attempt to suppress those necessary expressions. Next, having brought forward various testimonies of Scripture by which they craftily suggest that the Son is excluded from the possession of the divine nature, he presents in full the profession of faith which Arius, expelled from Alexandria, and others attached to his party sent to Alexander the bishop. He then refutes its first part, chiefly based on the words, “Hear, Israel, the Lord your God is one,” as though Moses had thereby proclaimed God to be one not only in nature but also in person. He does so by many arguments, showing from the creation of the world; from several visions granted to Hagar, Abraham, Jacob, and Moses; and also from the testimonies of the prophets—especially Moses, the Psalmist, Hosea, Isaiah, and Baruch, or, as he calls him, Jeremiah—that although God is one in nature, He is not solitary, but has a Son who possesses with Him both the name and the nature of divinity.

Certain observations on the visions expounded in this book. — Since the arguments of this and the following book rely chiefly on the visions of the patriarchs, it is worthwhile to preface a few remarks concerning them. The opinion seems constant among the ancients that the Son, from the beginning of the world, made Himself visible to human beings in various ways. This is explicitly taught by Justin Martyr, Irenaeus, Origen, Theophilus of Antioch, Clement of Alexandria, Tertullian, Cyprian, the Fathers of the Antiochene council against Paul of Samosata—to omit Faustinus the presbyter, Ambrose, Leo, and very many others. Nor was this denied even by those favorable to Arius. Eusebius frequently proclaims it in the Demonstration of the Gospel; and the Council of Sirmium condemns with anathema, against Photinus, those who thought otherwise.

But since the Arians devised deceit in this doctrine, in order to proclaim the Son—who was visible and seen—dissimilar in nature from the invisible Father, it must firmly be maintained that the holy Fathers asserted that God was seen in such a way that, with Augustine in Book II against Maximinus, ch. 26, §12, they held that the divinity appeared to mortal eyes when it willed, not through its own substance, in which it is invisible and unchangeable, but through a creature subject to itself. And, not to bring in foreign evidence, Hilary himself is an abundant witness on this matter, Book XII, §§45–46: “Certainly He who was formerly an angel is now also a man, lest the diversity of this very assumed creation should permit this to be understood as God’s natural form. Jacob too is present even in the embrace of wrestling in human appearance . . . But afterward the same One is shown to Moses to be fire, so that you might learn that the evidence belongs rather to the appearance of created nature than to the substance of nature.”

Augustine speaks acutely in what was formerly Letter 112, now 147, §20, on Moses’ words: “If I have found favor before You, show me Yourself.” “What then?” he asks. “Was He not Himself? If He were not Himself, Moses would not say to Him, ‘Show me Yourself,’ but, ‘Show me God.’ Yet if Moses saw His nature and substance, he would much less say, ‘Show me Yourself.’ Therefore He Himself was in that appearance in which He had willed to appear; but He Himself did not appear in His proper nature, which Moses wished to see.”

If Augustine rightly maintained from the surrounding words of Scripture that God Himself was seen by Moses, then by the same reasoning it must be granted that God Himself said to Moses in the bush, “I am the God of Abraham,” and so forth; and that the true God addressed Hagar, who cried out, “You are the God who looked upon me.” Nor do those Fathers deny this who think that true angels stood present in those visions.
