For they do not suppose that those angels attributed to themselves the names God and Lord because they spoke as envoys in God’s and the Lord’s name—for what ambassador of a king, emperor, or prince claims for himself the name of the one whose person he represents? Rather, they suppose this because God Himself spoke in them.

Athanasius explicitly teaches this in Oration IV against the Arians, p. 467: “The one perceived by the eyes was indeed an angel, but God spoke in the angel. For just as He spoke words to Moses in the tabernacle from the pillar of cloud, so also God appeared speaking in angels.” Jerome says likewise, in Galatians 3: “When he says, ‘The Law was ordained through angels,’ he wishes this to be understood: in all the Old Testament, wherever an angel is first reported as seen and afterward introduced as speaking like God, whoever among the many ministering angels may truly have been seen, yet in him the Mediator speaks, who says, ‘I am the God of Abraham.’”

Augustine joins them, Book II against Maximinus, ch. 26, §11: “I ask who appeared to Moses in the fire when the bush was burning and was not consumed. Although Scripture itself declares that an angel appeared there . . . Yet who could doubt that God was in the angel?” In agreement with these, Pope Gregory says in the Preface to Job, ch. 2: “The angel who is said to have appeared to Moses is at one time called angel, at another God: angel, clearly, because he served outwardly by speaking; Lord, because inwardly presiding, he supplied the efficacy of speech. Therefore, since one speaking outwardly is directed by one within, he is called angel by reason of service, and Lord by reason of inspiration.”

[Col. 0097A] Augustine further grants, Book II against Maximinus, ch. 26, §9, that those angels were permitted to present themselves under God’s and the Lord’s name because of the prophecy announcing what was to come, since Christ, who is God and Lord, was prefigured in them. So also Irenaeus, Book V, ch. 1: “We have stated beforehand that Abraham and the other prophets saw Him prophetically, prophesying by the vision what was to come.” But however those visions are understood, the force of the arguments which Hilary draws from them remains nearly the same.

1. Three preliminary points against heretics before the assertion of truth. — Although in the earlier books, which we wrote long ago, we consider that we have fully made known that we maintain the faith and confession of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit from evangelical and apostolic teaching, and that we can have nothing in common with heretics, since they deny without measure, reason, or fear the divinity of our Lord Jesus Christ; nevertheless it was necessary to include certain matters in these books also, so that, after all their deceits and impieties had been exposed, knowledge of the truth might become more complete. First, it must be known what rashness belongs to their teaching and what danger to their irreligion; then what opinions they hold contrary to the apostolic faith to which we adhere, what they customarily say in opposition, and by what ambiguity of words they deceive the simplicity of their hearers; finally, by what artifice of their interpretations they corrupt the truth and force of divine utterances.

[Col. 0097C] 2. Divine realities cannot be adequately explained in human words. — We do not fail to recognize that, for explaining divine things, neither human speech nor comparisons drawn from human nature can suffice. For what is beyond narration has no limit or measure of expression; and what is spiritual differs from the form and example of bodily things. Yet, when discourse concerns heavenly natures, those very things which are grasped by the mind must be expressed through the ordinary usage of nature and speech—not indeed in a manner worthy of God’s dignity, but necessary because of the weakness of our understanding; that is, we must speak of what we perceive and understand in terms of our own things and words.

[Note: [Col. 0097D] Thus in the manuscripts. But in the printed editions, “common.”]

And, as we declared in the first book (no. 19), we mention this now for the purpose that, when we set forth something from human comparisons, we may not be thought to conceive of God according to bodily natures, or to compare spiritual things with our passions; rather, we have proposed the appearance of visible things for the understanding of invisible things.

[Note: [Col. 0097D] “We shall set forth.”]

[Col. 0098A] 3. The heretics’ opinions concerning the Son of God. — The heretics say that Christ is not from God; that is, that the Son was not begotten from the Father, and is God not by nature but by appointment. They make his adoption consist in a name: just as there are many sons of God, so this one also is a son of God. Then they make his benefaction consist in dignity: just as there are many gods, so this one also is God. Yet they attribute to him a more generous favour both of adoption and of designation, so that he is adopted before all others, is himself greater than the other adopted sons, and, being created more excellently than all natures, surpasses the remaining creatures.

[Note: [Col. 0097D] The printed editions read, “his adoption is in the name.” *Is* is absent from the manuscripts, some of which add: “because, just as there are many sons of God, so this one also is a son of God.”]

Some of them, moreover, while confessing God’s omnipotence, say that he was created in the likeness of God and, like other things, came into being from nothing in the image of his eternal Creator: namely, that by a word he was commanded to subsist out of non-existent things, God being able to fashion a likeness of himself from nothing.

4. They pretend to reject *homoousion* because of false meanings. What those meanings are. — They even add that, when they hear that Father and Son are of one substance, as preached by earlier bishops, they subtly undermine this under the appearance of a heretical opinion. They say that those bishops use and express the meaning of this term, “of one substance,” which in Greek is called ὁμοούσιον (*homoousion*, “consubstantial”), in the sense that the Father himself is also the Son: that, stretching forth from his infinity into the Virgin, he assumed a body from her and added to himself, in the body which he assumed, the name of Son.

[Note: [Col. 0097D] In the printed editions, “as preached by earlier bishops”: *esse* is redundant and is absent from the manuscripts. That the term *homoousion* was proclaimed by earlier bishops is attested by the letter to Paul of Samosata, in vol. I of the councils, attributed to Dionysius of Alexandria; Eusebius of Caesarea himself acknowledges this in Socrates, book I, chapter 5: “We have learned that certain ancient bishops and writers, men indeed eloquent and illustrious, used this word CONSUBSTANTIAL in expounding the divinity.” Among those who used it Athanasius, *On the Synods*, p. 918, lists the two Dionysii; Tertullian also, *Against Praxeas*, no. 2, declares that the Father and Son are of one substance.]

[Note: [Col. 0097D] In the manuscripts: “concerning *homoousion*.” In writing this term he is inconsistent with himself, sometimes declining it by cases, more often not. That this term was employed in the former sense by Paul of Samosata and rejected by the Fathers at Antioch was indicated by the letter of the Easterners brought to Sirmium; its argument is reported in *On the Synods*, no. 81.]

This is the first falsehood of theirs concerning *homoousion*. The next is that they assert the statement *homoousion* to signify that two persons share a prior and different thing; as though some prior substance or *ousia* were the material of something, shared by two and exhausted in each, testifying that both are of the prior nature and of one thing. For this reason they say that they disapprove the confession of *homoousion*: because its expression neither distinguishes the Son from the Father nor shows the Father to be later than the matter which he shares with the Son.

[Note: [Col. 0098D] One Colbert manuscript with the Victorine and Sorbonne manuscripts reads “greater”: not a bad sense if “matter” then followed, “the Father [is greater than] the matter.” But the others more correctly read “later,” as is clear from *On the Synods*, no. 68. Athanasius relates in *On the Synods*, p. 920, that this second sense, introduced by Paul merely as a quibble, was immediately rejected by the Fathers at Antioch. We shall examine in its place, in connection with *On the Synods*, how this may stand with the judgment of the Easterners mentioned immediately above.]

They invent a third reason also for rejecting *homoousion*: that, according to the meaning of this word, the Son is thought to exist by a division of the Father’s substance; as though he had been cut off from it, so that one thing was divided into two. Thus they are said to be of one substance because a portion cut off from a whole remains in the nature from which it was cut off. Nor, they say, can the suffering of division befall God, because he would be mutable if liable to diminution through division, and would be made imperfect when his substance, falling away into another portion, departed from its perfection.

[Note: [Col. 0099D] Eusebius, in Socrates, book I, chapter 5, testifies to this third sense—which, from no. 12, is evidently Manichaean—and reports that Constantine himself rejected it: “consubstantial” cannot be understood in terms of bodily affections, nor can the Son of God consist by division or, so to speak, severance, etc. Here and thereafter Hilary proclaims the Son consubstantial with the Father with such caution as to remove every suspicion of these false meanings.]

[Note: [Col. 0099C] In two manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 0099C] “Falling away.”]

5. Why they deny that the Son always exists. — They also think that they can cleverly oppose prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic doctrine by declaring the Son’s birth to be within time. Since they wrongly assert that we say the Son always existed, they must, by excluding his eternal existence, confess that his birth was in time. For if he did not always exist, there will be a time when he did not exist. And if there is a time when he did not exist, there will be time before him, because one who is not always does begin to exist in time. But one who is without time cannot lack that which always is.

They affirm that they reject the assertion that the Son always existed for this reason: lest, by saying that he always existed, he be believed to exist without birth; as though the assertion that he always existed proclaimed him unbegotten.

[Note: [Col. 0100C] In the earlier edition: “they think.”]

[Col. 0099B] 6. The Church admits neither *homoousion* nor the Son’s eternal existence in the senses described. — O foolish and impious fears, and irreligious anxiety concerning God! The Church abominates, rejects, and condemns the things alleged concerning the meaning of *homoousion* and concerning the assertion that the Son always exists. For she knows one God, from whom are all things; and she knows also one Lord, our Jesus Christ, through whom are all things: one “from whom,” and one “through whom”; from the one, the origin of all things; through the one, the creation of all things.

[Note: [Col. 0099D] An old Colbert manuscript with Paris reads: “the creation of all things.” The origin of the universe, including that of the Son himself, is from the Father.]

In the one “from whom” she understands the authority of unbegottenness; in the one “through whom” she reveres a power differing in nothing from its Author. For “from whom” and “through whom,” with respect to what is created, are a shared authority in the things that have been created.

[Note: [Col. 0099D] A Vatican-Basilian manuscript reads “to him in these things”; other, later manuscripts, “and in these things.” The sense is that the Father, from whom, and the Son, through whom, are all things, have common authority with respect to creative power and to created things.]

[Note: [Col. 0100C] “Of communion.”]

She knows that God is Spirit, impassible and incapable of being cut apart; for she learned from the Lord that a spirit does not have flesh and bones (Luke 24:39), lest perhaps the losses suffered by bodily passions be thought to befall him. She knows one unbegotten God; she knows also one only-begotten Son of God. She confesses the Father as eternal and free from origin; she confesses also the Son’s origin from eternity: not that he himself is without beginning, but that he is from the One without beginning; born eternally not from himself but from him who eternally is from no one—his birth, that is, deriving from the Father’s eternity.

Therefore our faith is free from the opinion of heretical perversity. For the profession of our meaning has been set forth, though the rationale of that profession has not yet been explained. Yet, lest any suspicion remain in the expression *homoousion*, employed by the Fathers, or in the confession that the Son always existed, these matters have been mentioned: so that the Son might be recognized as subsisting in the substance in which he was begotten from the Father; so that nothing might be understood to have been taken away from the Father’s abiding substance by the Son’s birth; and so that the Son’s *homoousion* with the Father might be recognized as mentioned by holy men learned in the doctrine of God, not for the defects and reasons recounted above. Nor should anyone suppose that the birth of the only-begotten Son is taken away because he is called *homoousios* with the Father.

[Note: [Col. 0100D] Erasmus, Leipzig, and Paris read “men learned in God’s doctrine”: not badly, if supported by some old book.]

7. The necessity which led to the reception of the word HOMOOUSION. — But, in order that we may understand the grounds for receiving these two expressions—namely, that the Son always exists and that he is of the same substance as the Father—and for employing them, against the raging heretics of that time, for the greatest security of faith, I think that the perversity of the heretics must be answered and all their foolish and deadly teachings refuted by evangelical and apostolic testimonies.

[Note: [Col. 0100D] That is, that the Son both always exists and is of the same substance as the Father. See Athanasius, *On the Synods*, p. 921, and Gregory Nazianzen, Oration XXI, no. 25, on the necessity with which the word *homoousion* was devised for the security of the faith.]

[Note: [Col. 0100D] Very ancient Vatican-Basilian and Colbert manuscripts read “ground,” a word familiar to Hilary in the sense of right and merit.]

For they seem to themselves to offer a reason for each particular assertion, because they attach to each of their assertions certain testimonies from the divine books. But, through a corrupted understanding, these flatter only the ignorant and promise an appearance of truth in accordance with the perversity of their interpreters.

[Col. 0100C] 8. Scriptures by which the Arians deceive the simple. — They attempt, after celebrating the divinity of God the Father alone, to take away from the Son what makes him God, because it is written: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one” (Deut. 6:4). The Lord himself says the same to the lawyer who asks what commandment is greatest in the Law: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one” (Mark 12:29). And Paul likewise preaches: “For there is one God, and one mediator between God and human beings” (1 Tim. 2:5).

[Note: [Col. 0100D] Thus the better manuscripts consistently read, sometimes with the agreement of the printed editions, in which the word “God” is repeated here, shortly afterward, and elsewhere.]

[Note: [Col. 0100D] The following words were displaced in the printed editions; we restore them in accordance with the manuscripts.]

Then they say that he alone is wise, so as to leave no wisdom to the Son, according to the Apostle’s statement: “Now to him who is able to strengthen you according to my Gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the mystery kept silent through eternal ages but now made manifest through the prophetic Scriptures according to the command of the eternal God, made known to all nations for the obedience of faith—to the only wise God, through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory for ever and ever” (Rom. 16:25 ff.).

Then they say that he alone is unbegotten and alone is true, because Isaiah said (65:16): “They shall bless you, the true God.”

[Note: [Col. 0101D] The printed editions read “you, the only true God.” Here “only” is absent from the manuscripts, as also in book V, nos. 25 and 26, where this passage is shown to have been corrupted by the heretics.]

And the Lord himself testifies to this in the Gospels, saying: “And this is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17:3). Then they say that he alone is good, so that there may be no goodness in the Son, because he said: “No one is good except one, God” (Mark 10:18). Then that he alone is powerful, because Paul said: “Whom the blessed and only powerful one, the King of kings and Lord of lords, will show us in his own times” (1 Tim. 6:15).

[Col. 0101A] They acknowledge him as unchangeable and immutable, because he said through the prophet: “I am the Lord your God, and I do not change” (Mal. 3:6); and the apostle James said (1:17): “With him there is no change.” They acknowledge him as a righteous judge, because it is written: “God is a righteous judge, strong and patient” (Ps. 7:12). They acknowledge him as caring for all things, because, when speaking of birds, the Lord said: “And your heavenly Father feeds them” (Matt. 6:26); and again: “Are not two sparrows sold for an assarion? Yet not one of them falls to the ground without the will of your Father. But even the hairs of your head are numbered” (Matt. 10:29).

[Note: [Col. 0101D] Thus the Verona manuscript. The earlier edition has “those.”]

[Note: [Col. 0101D] The printed editions read “them.” But the manuscripts read “those,” supplying “flying creatures,” as is found in *Commentary on Matthew*, chapter 5, no. 9.]

[Note: [Col. 0101D] “Does not fall.” In Greek: οὐ πεσεῖται, “will not fall.”]

They acknowledge him as foreknowing all things, as blessed Susanna says: “Eternal God, knower of hidden things, knowing all things before they come to be” (Dan. 13:42). They acknowledge him also as incapable of being contained, according to what was said: “Heaven is my throne and earth the footstool of my feet. What house will you build for me, or what place for my rest? For my hand made these things, and all these things are mine” (Isa. 66:1).

[Note: [Col. 0101D] Vatican-Basilian and Chartres manuscripts read “invisible.” Other books more correctly read “inconceivable,” that is, one whom no place can contain.]

[Note: [Col. 0101D] “Footstool”: a Vitruvian word.]

They acknowledge him also as containing all things, Paul testifying: “For in him we live and move and are” (Acts 17:28); and the Psalmist saying: “Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your face? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present; if I take my wings before dawn and dwell in the farthest parts of the sea, even there your hand will lead me and your right hand will hold me” (Ps. 138 [139]:7 ff.).

[Note: [Col. 0101D] In many manuscripts, “Where shall I go?” In the older ones: “Where shall I depart?”]

[Note: [Col. 0102D] “Into hell.”]

[Note: [Col. 0102D] The earlier edition reads “there.”]

[Col. 0102A] They acknowledge him also as incorporeal, because it has been said: “For God is Spirit, and those who worship him must worship in Spirit and truth” (John 4:24). They acknowledge him as possessing immortality and as invisible, Paul saying: “Who alone has immortality and dwells in inaccessible light, whom no human being has seen or can see” (1 Tim. 6:16); and according to the Gospel: “No one has ever seen God except the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father” (John 1:18). They acknowledge him also as alone abiding, unbegotten, because it has been said: “I am the one who is” (Exod. 3:14); and again: “Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: ‘The One Who Is has sent me to you’” (ibid.); and through Jeremiah: “You who are Lord, O Lord” (Jer. 1:6).

[Note: [Col. 0101D] The word “unbegotten” was wrongly omitted in earlier printed editions. Hilary immediately demonstrates that precisely in it a deception lies hidden among the other Arian assertions. It is restored with the aid of the manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 0102D] Baden, Erasmus, and Leipzig—followed by the final Paris edition—read “You who are, O Lord,” omitting “Lord,” contrary to the manuscripts and the Septuagint: ὁ ὢν δέσποτα Κύριε, “You who are, Master Lord.”]

[Col. 0102B] 9. The deception hidden in the foregoing is exposed. — Who does not understand that these things are full of fraud and deception? Although they are subtly confused and intermixed, they nevertheless plainly display the contrived cunning and absurdity of malice and folly. Among other things, they added that they recognize the Father alone as unbegotten—as though anyone could doubt that he from whom was begotten the one through whom all things are has received from no one what he himself is.

For in the very fact that he is called Father, he is shown to be the author of the one whom he begot; he has a name which indicates both that he is not understood to have proceeded from another and that the one who was begotten subsists from him. Therefore let us leave to God the Father what is his own, peculiar and secret, confessing in him the unbegotten power of eternal might.

[Col. 0102C] But I think no one can doubt that certain things are mentioned in the confession of God the Father as though peculiar and private to him, in order that no one besides him may be left a participant in them. For when they say that he alone is true, alone righteous, alone wise, alone invisible, alone good, alone powerful, alone possesses immortality, by saying that he alone is these things they separate the Son from sharing them.

[Note: [Col. 0102D] The printed editions read “the true God,” against the manuscripts.]

For, as they say, what belongs to one alone is not shared by another. If these things are thought to exist in the Father alone and not also in the Son, it follows that the Son must be believed to be a false god, foolish, bodily according to visible matter, ill-disposed, weak, and outside immortality—excluded from all these things because the Father alone possesses them.

[Note: [Col. 0102D] This is stated in the manner of a philosophical proposition. But if, with the old Colbert manuscript and the German manuscript, you prefer “for they are alone, they say,” “alone” must refer to the Father and “they say” to the Arians.]

[Col. 0102D] 10. The honour of the Son detracts nothing from the Father. — Since we are about to speak of the utterly perfect majesty and full divinity of the only-begotten Son of God, we do not suppose that anyone will think that all this discourse which we shall use pertains to an insult against God the Father, as though something should be taken from his dignity if any of these things are attributed to the Son. On the contrary, the Son’s honour is the Father’s dignity; glorious is the author from whom one worthy of such glory has come forth. For the Son has nothing except what he has by being begotten, and admiration for the honour of the one begotten lies in honouring the one who begets. Therefore any notion of insult ceases, since whatever majesty is shown to exist in the Son will redound to magnify the power of him who begot such a Son.

[Note: [Col. 0103C] We add “God” from the manuscripts. Here Hilary prudently forestalls the standard Arian argument, of which Augustine says (*Sermon* 139, no. 5): “Certainly you say that the Son is not of the same substance in order not to wrong his Father. I shall quickly show you that you wrong both.” See also Augustine, *Against Maximinus*, II.25, and *Sermon* 140, no. 5; similarly Ambrose, *On Faith*, I.6.]

[Note: [Col. 0103B] “Should be taken away”; below likewise, no. 11, *decidere* is used for *decedere*, “to depart/be taken away.”]

[Col. 0103A] 11. The Arian doctrine concerning the Son. — It follows that, now that we have learned what they confess about the Father for the disparagement of the Son, we should hear what they themselves profess about the Son. For, in answering each of their propositions and exposing their irreligious doctrine by testimonies from the divine utterances, we must add to what has been said about the Father what they next recount concerning the Son, so that, by comparing the confession concerning Father and Son, we may maintain one and the same order in resolving each proposition.

[Note: [Col. 0103B] “So that by the confession …”]

[Note: [Col. 0103C] The Chartres manuscript and five others: “so that by the confession …”]

They assert that the Son of God was neither begotten from any underlying matter, because all things were created through him, nor is he from God, because nothing can depart from God; rather, he is from things which did not exist—that is, a perfect creature of God, yet not like the other creatures. They say he is a creature because it is written: “The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways” (Prov. 8:22). They say he is also a perfect product, but not like the other products, on the basis of what Paul said to the Hebrews: “Having become so much better than the angels, as he has inherited a more excellent name than they” (Heb. 1:4). And again: “Therefore, holy brothers, sharers in a heavenly calling, consider Jesus Christ, the apostle and high priest of our confession, who is faithful to him who made him” (Heb. 3:1).

[Note: [Col. 0103B] “Created me as the beginning of his ways.” This reading is likewise preferred by our manuscript in *On the Trinity*, I.35, and by the same work, XII.35.]

[Note: [Col. 0104B] “Said.”]

To weaken the Son’s strength, power, and divinity, they rely especially on his statement: “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28). But they concede that he is not one among all creatures because it is written: “All things were made through him” (John 1:3).

[Note: [Col. 0104B] “They contend.”]

[Note: [Col. 0103C] The heading of the following letter, omitted by Baden, relegated to the margin by Erasmus and Leipzig, and wrongly inserted here by Paris, we restore to its proper place on the authority of the manuscripts. It is clear from *On the Synods*, no. 11, and *Against Auxentius*, no. 12, that Hilary himself customarily gives heretical professions of faith such headings.

Athanasius, *Oration I against the Arians*, p. 313, undoubtedly indicates the following letter in these words: “The devil persuaded Arius to speak as though, under the guise of an opponent, against heresies, in order more effectively to deceive by introducing his own heresy.” This is the same letter so frequently mentioned by the Council of Aquileia, both in the proceedings preserved in Ambrose, vol. II of the new edition, p. 786, and in the letter to the emperors in Ambrose, vol. X. The Fathers of that synod testify that the letter was appended to this letter, and that they had read and recited it in the proceedings; but now only its beginning survives, broken into various interrogations, since Palladius refused to answer the questions put to him.

Ambrose himself, *On Faith*, III.10, no. 132, refers to the same letter when he says: “Arius, the teacher of this impiety, said that the Son of God was a perfect creature, but not like the other creatures.” Athanasius gives it complete in *On the Synods*, p. 885, as does Epiphanius, *Heresy* 69, no. 7, who entitles it Arius’s letter to Alexander, supported by the words of Athanasius and Ambrose just cited. Since it is consistently called simply Arius’s letter by the Council of Aquileia, Arius must be regarded as its chief author, though not its only one. For our Hilary writes not only here but also in book I, no. 23, that it was issued by many.

Nor does the omitted preface of the letter itself say anything else; in Athanasius and Epiphanius it is expressed in the name of several persons as follows: “The faith which we received from our forebears and learned from you, most blessed Pope, is as follows: We know…” The superscription found in those same authors proves this still more certainly: “To the blessed Pope and our bishop Alexander, presbyters and deacons in the Lord, greeting.” Or certainly this letter is Arius’s as its author’s, and belongs to many as those in whose name it was sent and subscribed. We shall give below from Epiphanius the various subscriptions.

It was written before the Council of Nicaea and, as Athanasius testifies in *On the Synods*, p. 883, while Arius, having been removed by Alexander, was staying with Eusebius. Epiphanius says that it was written from Nicomedia to Alexander, as Arius attempted to excuse himself before him. Athanasius’s addition at the end of the letter—“These are, in some measure, the things which the Arians vomited forth from their heretical heart”—indicates that they then vomited forth many others also. It is highly probable that they attempted to confirm by the collection of testimonies mentioned above what they simply asserted in this letter.]

They therefore conclude their entire doctrine of irreligion in words such as these, saying:

## An example of the blasphemy of those who say that the Son of God is a creature

12. “We know one God, alone unoriginated, alone eternal, alone without beginning, alone true, alone possessing immortality, alone best, alone powerful, the unchangeable and immutable creator, ruler, and disposer of all things, righteous and good, of the Law and the Prophets and the New Testament. This God begot an only-begotten Son before all ages, through whom he also made the age and all things. He was born not merely in appearance but in truth, obedient to his will, unchangeable and immutable: a perfect creature of God, but not as one of the creatures; a product, but not like the other products.

[Note: [Col. 0104B] “Alone immense” was added by a second hand. What follows is: “alone possessing immortality,” etc.]

[Note: [Col. 0104D] The printed editions add here “alone immense,” which is nevertheless omitted in book VI; it occurs nowhere in Greek exemplars or in the manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 0105B] It is clear that this is said deceitfully, so that the Son may be believed passible and mortal. Hence, in the proceedings of the Synod of Aquileia, no. 24, Palladius does not assent when Ambrose asserts, “It was not the divinity that died, but the flesh”; instead he evades the matter, saying, “You answer me first.” More plainly, the Fathers of the same synod write to the emperors in their letter preserved in Ambrose, X.7: “Finally, they refer his death not to the sacrament of our salvation, but to a certain weakness of divinity.” This should be noted beforehand, so that the reader may meanwhile learn against whom Hilary, in book X, defends the Son’s impassibility.]

[Note: [Col. 0105C] Athanasius and Epiphanius add here “alone wise.” Likewise, in the proceedings of the Synod of Aquileia, after “alone eternal, alone without beginning, alone true, alone possessing immortality” has been read at no. 17, “alone wise” is read shortly afterward at no. 27. Erasmus inserted these two words above after “alone unoriginated,” against Baden and all our manuscripts. Indeed Erasmus is not consistent with himself in book VI.]

“Nor was he, as Valentinus imagined, a projection—a begotten offspring—of the Father; nor, as Manichaeus declared, a begotten part of the Father’s one substance; nor, as Sabellius divides the union, did he say that the Son himself is also the Father; nor, as Hieracas, a lamp from a lamp, or a lamp divided into two parts; nor was he one who existed before and was afterward born, or created over again as a Son. You yourself, most blessed Pope, frequently rejected in the midst of the church and in the assembly of the brethren those who introduce such things. Rather, as we have said, he was created by God’s will before times and ages, receiving life and being from the Father, with the Father causing glories to subsist in him.

[Note: [Col. 0105C] The printed Athanasius and Epiphanius read “judge of all things.” Hilary’s connection of thought seems stronger, since “creator” is rightly followed by “ruler” and “disposer.” The Greek κτιστὴν, “creator,” could easily have been corrupted to κριτήν, “judge.” Nevertheless, “judge of all things,” not “creator of all things,” also occurs in the proceedings of the Synod of Aquileia, no. 33.]

[Note: [Col. 0105D] The printed editions here and in book VI read “projection.” Paris then reads “begotten.” But the manuscripts read “the projection begotten,” as in Greek προβολὴν γέννημα; hence *natum* must be understood substantivally, “a begotten one,” as though “the Son.”]

[Note: [Col. 0105D] Greek: τὸ μέρος ὁμοούσιον, “the consubstantial part.” Under this name and in this sense the Arians allege a reason for rejecting the word *homoousion* above, no. 4.]

[Note: [Col. 0105D] Erasmus has in the margin “introduces,” a conjecture wrongly adopted by Leipzig and Paris. Sabellius indeed introduces a union in the Trinity, of which there is no discussion here; but in the incarnation, as is explained in book VI, no. 7, he divides the union—that is, he introduces a duality of persons in Christ.]

[Note: [Col. 0105D] Baden and Erasmus add the word “says” here; Leipzig and Paris, following Erasmus’s conjecture, substituted “introduces.” Neither is found in the manuscripts or Greek exemplars. Shortly afterward Baden, Erasmus, and the manuscripts have *lampadam*, not *lampadem*.]

[Note: [Col. 0105B] “Brethren” is absent from our manuscript, as also from the edition at book VI, no. 5.]

[Col. 0106A] [Note: [Col. 0106B] Greek: εἰληφότα, etc., which could more plainly have been translated, “who received both life and being from the Father.”]

[Note: [Col. 0106B] “Causing glories to subsist.”]

[Note: [Col. 0106B] Very few manuscripts read “glory.” The rest, with the printed editions, read “causing glory to subsist.” That *glories* must be read is clear both from the Greek τὰς δόξας and from what follows, where the same word is repeated. The printed editions then add “while the Father subsists”; on the authority of the manuscripts we restore “with the Father causing them to subsist in him,” which more closely corresponds to the Greek συνυποστήσαντος αὐτῷ τοῦ Πατρός. The words τὰς δόξας do not refer to the preceding εἰληφότα, “having received,” but to the following συνυποστήσαντος, which here has active force. The meaning is that the Father granted that the glories, or glorious perfections, which subsist in himself should simultaneously subsist in the Son. Thus Hilary’s *consubsistente* must likewise be taken actively: as though “the Father causing them to subsist together.”]

“For the Father, in giving him the inheritance of all things, did not deprive himself of those things which are held by him as unmade; for he is the fountain of all things.”

[Note: [Col. 0106C] Instead of “not made,” Athanasius and Epiphanius have in Greek ἀγεννήτως, “unbegottenly”; Hilary must necessarily have read ἀγενήτως, “unmade.”]

13. “For this reason there are three substances (*hypostases*): Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. God indeed is the cause of all things, altogether without beginning and alone; but the Son, brought forth by the Father without time and created and founded before the ages, did not exist before he was born. Yet, born without time before all things, he alone subsisted from the Father alone. For he is neither eternal nor co-eternal nor uncreated together with the Father; nor does he have being together with the Father, as some say, introducing two unbegotten principles. Rather, just as unity is the principle of all things, so God is before all things. Therefore he is also before the Son, as you too taught while preaching in the midst of the church.

[Note: [Col. 0106C] The printed editions read “God the Father.” More correctly, “Father” is absent from the manuscripts and the Greek. For since the discourse concerns God when, according to the Arian view, he did not yet have a Son—and therefore is repeatedly called solitary—he should not be called Father. For Arius reasons in Athanasius, *On the Synods*, p. 884: if the Son did not yet exist, it immediately follows that the Father was merely God.]

[Note: [Col. 0106B] “Subsists.”]

[Note: [Col. 0106C] In the Vatican-Basilian manuscript: “or others who introduce …” In Greek, instead of “or some,” there is τὰ πρός τι, which may suitably be translated “things relative to something,” or “relative things.”]

[Note: [Col. 0106D] Erasmus, Leipzig, and Paris read “the Monad is the principle,” contrary to the Greek text, Baden, and the manuscripts. The force of the word “Monad” will be more suitably explained at the end of this book.]

[Note: [Col. 0106D] We have removed the word “Pope” here, since it does not occur in the manuscripts or Greek.]

“Accordingly, because he has being, glories, life, and all things from God, God is his principle. God rules over him as his God, since he is before him. For if the phrases, ‘from him,’ ‘from the womb,’ and ‘I came forth from the Father and have come,’ are understood as though he stretches out a part of one substance, and as though a projection, the Father will be composite, divisible, mutable, bodily according to those people, and—so far as lies in them—a God without a body yet subject to the consequences of bodily existence.”

[Note: [Col. 0106D] Again, most and the better manuscripts read “causing glory to subsist”; as above, we infer *glories*, clearly required by the connection of the sentence and by the Greek τὰς δόξας, whose force is not adequately expressed by the Latin singular *gloriam*, read by a few other manuscripts. Erasmus’s emendation “to glory” is very bad, and is now changed for the first time.]

[Note: [Col. 0107D] Greek: ὡς μέρος τοῦ ὁμοουσίου καὶ ὡς προβολὴ ὑπό τινων νοεῖται, that is, “as some understand it, [he is] a part of one who is of one substance, and as it were a projection.” It is clear, however, that Hilary read from a corrupt manuscript ὡς προβολὴν ἀποτείνων, “stretching out as a projection,” rather than ὡς προβολὴ ὑπό τινων.]

[Note: [Col. 0107D] A second recension inserts: “and mutable.”]

[Note: [Col. 0107D] Epiphanius appends these subscriptions: “We pray that you may fare well in the Lord, most blessed Pope: Arius, Ethales, Achilles, Carpones, Sarmatas, Arius, presbyters; Euzoius, Lucius, Julius, Menas, Helladius, Gaius, deacons; Secundus of Pentapolis, Theonas the African (Greek: Αἴβυς), and Pistus, whom the Arians installed at Alexandria, bishops.”]

14. Because man apprehends divine things only from what God has said of himself, heretical assertions must be refuted from these. God’s sayings are to be weighed not nakedly, but from their own grounds. — This is their error, this their deadly doctrine: in order to confirm it, with their understanding corrupted, they appropriate testimonies from the divine sayings and, under the pretext of human ignorance, lie about them. Yet no one ought to doubt that, for the knowledge of divine things, divine teachings must be employed. For human weakness cannot of itself attain knowledge of heavenly things, nor can bodily sense take upon itself the understanding of invisible things. Neither what has been created and is fleshly in us, nor what has been given by God for the use of our life, discerns by its own judgment the nature and work of its Creator. Our intellects do not rise to heavenly knowledge, nor will our weakness comprehend incomprehensible power by any sense.

God himself must be believed concerning himself; and we must obey those things which he has granted to our knowledge concerning himself. Either, after the manner of the Gentiles, he must be denied if his testimonies are rejected; or, if he is believed to be God as he is, he cannot be understood otherwise concerning himself than as he has testified concerning himself. Let, therefore, the private opinions of men cease, and let human counsels not extend themselves beyond the divine ordinance. Accordingly, against irreligious and impious teachings about God, we follow those very authorities of the divine sayings; and we shall treat each point by the authority of the very one concerning whom inquiry is made, not by fitting together certain verbal expressions, with their grounds withheld, in order to deceive and wrongly instruct the inexperience of hearers. For the meaning of sayings must be derived from the grounds on which they are spoken (see above, Book II, §30), since the thing is not subject to the word, but the word to the thing. We shall, however, set forth everything together with both the occasions of speaking and the force of what is said. Let each point, then, be reconsidered in the order of the proposition.

> [Note: Col. 0108D. “Was born”; shortly afterward, “will discern.”]

> [Note: Col. 0108D. “Custom”; shortly after, “therefore let us follow.”]

> [Note: Col. 0107D. In the Carnotensis manuscript and one Colbert manuscript there is inserted here, “concerning the one God”; this plainly crept from the margin into the text, though it had a suitable place in the margin for indicating what follows.]

15. Moses, in saying “God is one,” did not deny the deity of the Son. — For this is their principal point: “We know,” they say, “one God alone, Moses saying: Hear, Israel, the Lord your God is one” (Deut. 6:4). But has anyone ever dared to doubt this? Or has it ever been known that anyone who believed in God preached otherwise than that there is one God, from whom are all things; one unbegotten power; and that this one power is without beginning? Yet the fact that God is one does not allow the Son of God to be denied that which he is—God.

For Moses—or rather God through Moses—established this as the chief commandment for a people occupied, both in Egypt and in the wilderness, with idols and with cults of supposed gods: that it should believe in one God. And rightly and deservedly did he establish it. For there is one God, from whom are all things. But let us see whether this same Moses also confessed him through whom all things are to be God. For the fact that God is one is not taken away from the Father because the Son too is God. For he is God from God, one from one; therefore there is one God, because God is from himself. Conversely, the Son is no less God because the Father is the one God; for he is the only-begotten Son of God—not unbegotten, lest he take from the Father the fact that God is one, nor himself anything other than God, because he was born from God.

Although there ought to be no doubt that, by being born from God, he is God—and this is why, for our faith, there is one God—yet let us see whether Moses, who said to Israel, “The Lord your God is one,” proclaimed the Son of God to be God. For in confessing the divinity of our Lord Jesus Christ, we must use the testimony of him whose authority the heretics employ when, confessing only one God, they think that the Son must be denied the fact that he is God.

16. In the history of creation he teaches that God is not solitary. One speaks, another acts; both are God. The Son is the God who acts. — Since, then, this is the complete and perfect confession concerning God—to speak, according to the Apostle, thus: “One God, the Father, from whom are all things, and one Lord, our Jesus Christ, through whom are all things” (1 Cor. 8:6)—let us see what Moses says of the origin of the world. For he says: “And God said, Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let it divide water from water. And it was so; and God made the firmament, and God divided the water in the midst” (Gen. 1:6–7).

You therefore have God from whom, and you have God through whom. Or, if you deny this, you must teach through whom that which was made was made; or else demonstrate that the very nature of things to be created was obedient to God, such that, at the words, “Let there be a firmament,” it itself, commanded by God’s word, established itself as a firmament. But the reasoning of divine Scripture does not admit this. For all things, according to the prophet, were made from nothing (2 Macc. 7:28); no existing nature was changed into something else, but that which was not was created and brought to completion.

Through whom? Hear the Evangelist: “All things were made through him” (John 1:3). If you ask through whom, you will hear the same Evangelist say: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. This one was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him” (ibid. 1–3). But if you wish to deny that “Let there be a firmament” (Gen. 1:6) was spoken by the Father, you will again hear the prophet say: “He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Ps. 148:5).

Thus, in the words, “Let there be a firmament,” the Father is shown to have spoken. But in what is added—“And it was so”—and in the statement that God made it, the person of the agent who performs the act is to be understood. For “He spoke, and they were made” does not mean merely that he willed and made; “he commanded, and they were created” does not mean merely that, because it pleased him, they came into being—as though the office of the Mediator between himself and the things to be created had ceased. Therefore God, from whom are all things, says that they are to be made; and God, through whom are all things, makes them: confessed under one and the same equal name, both in the significance of the speaker and in the operation of the agent.

But if you dare to say that “And God made” is not said of the Son, where will be: “All things were made through him”; and the apostolic saying: “One Lord, our Jesus Christ, through whom are all things” (1 Cor. 8:6); and “He spoke, and they were made” (Ps. 148:5)? If these divinely spoken words convict your shamelessness, the Son of God is not denied the fact that he is God because it was said: “Hear, Israel, the Lord your God is one,” since by him who spoke these words the Son was proclaimed to be God in the very establishment of the world. But let us see to what further point this distinction between the commanding God and the acting God is extended.

> [Note: Col. 0108D. From this apostolic passage the heretics used to distinguish the Father from the Son, as is clear from Hilary’s words to the Arian in §19: “For you said, ‘All things are from the Father, but all things are through the Son.’” The Catholics did not dispute this; indeed, nothing was more customary for Hilary than to call the Father God “from whom,” “he from whom,” “from whom are all things,” and the Son God “through whom,” “he through whom,” “through whom are all things.” This should be observed both for understanding these expressions and so that Hilary’s purpose in piercing the Arians with their own weapons may not be missed.]

> [Note: Col. 0109C. “That it might exist as such by the force of obedience,” as you have in Ps. 148, §4. That the reading of this passage has rightly been corrected by us is clear from the present passage, as also from what follows: “nor was any existing nature changed into something else,” etc.; it is evident that we have understood it correctly.]

> [Note: Col. 0109C. “Are” is added.]

> [Note: Col. 0109C. The printed editions read “the confession”; they are corrected from the manuscripts. This conclusion does not concern the immediately preceding passage from the Psalms, but the cited words of Genesis, in which occur: “And God said … and God made.”]

> [Note: Col. 0109C. “Will not convict.”]

> [Note: Col. 0110C. “May be argued.” In the Corbie manuscript: “was argued.” In some copies, including the printed editions: “may be treated.” More correctly in the older Colbert manuscripts, the Carnotensis, and others: “may be extended”: that is, whether this distinction indicates an increase in the number of persons. Tertullian unhesitatingly affirms this in *Against Praxeas*, §12: “Although everywhere I maintain one substance in three who cohere together, yet from the necessity of the meaning I must call distinct the one who commands and the one who acts.” The force of *augere* (“to increase”) may be recalled from Book I, §11, where those receiving Christ as sons of God are said to be increased. This distinction of the commanding God and the acting God was also customary among other Fathers: Irenaeus, Book III, ch. 8, and Book IV, ch. 75; Tertullian, as we have just seen; Origen, vol. II, on John, ed. Huet, p. 61; the Council of Antioch, Letter to Paul of Samosata; Hippolytus, *Against Noetus*; Athanasius, *On the Decrees of the Nicene Synod*; Basil, *On the Holy Spirit*; Cyril, Book XXIX of the *Thesaurus*, p. 255. Augustine, however, in Sermon 140, §6, maintains that the Son himself is the command of the Father—not a command given in time, but a command begotten. “For how,” he says, “is that not the Father’s command which is the Father’s Word?” And in *Against an Arian Sermon*, ch. 3, he rebukes those who fashion for themselves, in the phantasy of their heart, as it were two beings, though placed next to one another, yet established in their own places—one commanding and the other obeying—and do not understand that the Father’s command that all things should be made is nothing other than the Father’s Word, through whom all things were made.]

17. Nor was God solitary in creating man. — Therefore, when the world had been completed and its inhabitant was to be formed, such was the discourse concerning him: “And God said, Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26). [“And again, God made man; in the image of God he made him” (ibid. 27).] I now ask whether you think that God spoke only to himself, or whether you understand this speech to have been addressed not to himself but to another. If you say that he was alone, you are convicted by his own voice saying, “Let us make man in our image and likeness.”

For God, through the lawgiver Moses, spoke according to our understanding: that is, in words which he himself willed us to use, imparting to us knowledge of the things which he did. The indication of the Son of God, through whom all things were made, lay in the statement: “And God said, Let there be a firmament”; and again in the statement: “And God made the firmament.” Yet, lest this be thought an empty and superfluous utterance, if he had himself said to himself that it should be made and then himself made it—for what would be more incongruous for one who was alone than to tell himself that something must be done, when willing alone was needed for it to be done?—he willed this indication to be understood as not referring to himself alone. By saying, “Let us make man in our image and likeness,” he removed the idea of singularity by professing fellowship.

But he cannot himself be a fellowship to one who is solitary. Nor, again, does the solitude of one who is solitary admit “let us make”; nor does anyone speak of “our” to one alien from himself. Both expressions, “let us make” and “our,” no more permit him to be solitary and the same than they signify one different from and alien to himself. Or I ask: when you hear “solitary,” do you not think that he is himself and the same? And when you hear “not himself and not the same,” do you understand merely that he is solitary? In the solitary, therefore, one who is solitary will be found; but in one who is neither the same nor himself, one who is not solitary will be found. Thus “I shall make” and “my” suit one who is solitary; “let us make” and “our” suit one who is not solitary.

> [Note: Col. 0110C. Several manuscripts read, “such is God’s discourse.” What is enclosed in brackets immediately afterward is absent from the old Colbert manuscript and does not seem especially relevant. A similar argument occurs in the Letter of the Council of Antioch to Paul: “But one who commands commands another; and we are persuaded that this other is none other than the only-begotten Son, God, to whom he said, ‘Let us make man,’” etc.]

> [Note: Col. 0110D. We once thought that the particle *cum* (“when”) had been omitted here, so that the indication of the Son might be shown only from the latter passage. But the existence of the Son follows from both: both when he is commanded to make, and when he is indicated to have made what was commanded. For he to whom “Let there be” is spoken, and who is proclaimed to have done what was commanded, is other than he who commanded and said “Let there be.” As the Council of Antioch says in its Letter to Paul of Samosata: “We believe that the Son, who is always with the Father, fulfilled the paternal will in the creation of the universe.”]

> [Note: Col. 0110C. “It was said.”]

> [Note: Col. 0110D. The printed editions read, “here a certain empty …”; they are corrected from the manuscripts.]

18. There is neither solitude nor diversity of deity. — Therefore, when we read, “Let us make man in our image and likeness,” since each expression indicates both that he is not solitary and that he is not different, we too must confess him to be neither solitary only nor diverse, recognizing from his saying “our image,” not “our images,” the property of one nature in both. But it is not enough to have supplied only the verbal argument unless the operation of the things done also follows the meaning of the sayings. For it is written thus: “And God made man; in the image of God he made him” (Gen. 1:27).

I ask what you think must be understood here if the speech was addressed by one solitary being to himself. For I now see a threefold indication: of the maker, of what was made, and of the model. What was made is man; God made; and the one whom he made, he made in the image of God. If Genesis had been speaking of one who was solitary, it would surely have said, “And he made [him] in his own image.” But, proclaiming the evangelical mystery, it spoke not of two gods but of God and God, when it says that man was made through God in the image of God. And so God is found to make man in the image common to himself and God, and in the same likeness: so that the indication of the agent admits no notion of solitude, while the operation, established according to the same image and likeness, permits no diversity of deity.

19. The same point is confirmed elsewhere. — And although, after this, it may seem superfluous to bring forward anything further—for in divine matters, not things more frequently said, but things simply said, suffice—nevertheless we should know what has been said on this same point. For an account must be rendered by us, not of the divine sayings, but of our understanding.

God speaks thus to Noah amid many commands: “Whoever sheds the blood of a man, for his blood his life shall be shed; because I made man in the image of God” (Gen. 9:6). Here too the model, the work, and the worker are distinguished. God testifies that he made man in the image of God. When man was to be made, because he spoke concerning himself but not to himself, he said, “in our image”; but when man had been made, God made man in the image of God. Certainly he did not fail to know the proper use of language, so that, if he had spoken to himself, he would have said, “I made [him] in my image.” For, in order to demonstrate unity of nature, he had said, “Let us make [him] in our [image].” Nor again did he confuse the notion of one who is solitary with that of one who is not solitary, when God, making man, made him in the image of God.

> [Note: Col. 0111D. The printed editions read, incorrectly, “made man.”]

> [Note: Col. 0111D. Erasmus inserted the particle “neither” here without any manuscript authority, and subsequent editions wrongly retained it. For God spoke concerning himself insofar as he said in the first person, “Let us make,” but not to himself insofar as he did not say in the singular, “Let me make.”]

20. The Father did not say “LET US MAKE” to himself as one solitary. — But if you wish to maintain that God the Father, being solitary, spoke these things to himself—as though it could be granted you that one might speak with himself as with another, and that in “I made man in the image of God” he intended this to be understood as “I made man in my image”—you are first refuted by your own testimony. For you said, “All things are from the Father, but all things are through the Son.” For in what is said, “Let us make man,” the origin is from him from whom the speech also began; but in the statement that God made man in the image of God, he through whom the operation is brought to completion is also signified.

> [Note: Col. 0111D. Thus the manuscripts. But the printed editions incorrectly have, “the speech also receives and begins.”]

21. But Wisdom—who, with the heretics’ assent, is Christ—was present with him. — Then, further, lest you have any opportunity here to lie, Wisdom, whom you yourself have confessed to be Christ, rebukes you, saying: “When he set the fountains under heaven in their fixed places, when he made the strong foundations of the earth, I was with him, arranging [them]. I was that in which he delighted. And daily I rejoiced before his face at every time, when he rejoiced in the completed world and rejoiced in the children of men” (Prov. 8:28 ff.).

Every pretext is shut off, and all error is forced into confession of the truth. Wisdom, begotten before the ages, is present with God. Nor is she merely present: she also arranges. Therefore she is with him, arranging. Understand the office of arrangement or ordering. For the Father, in speaking, effects; the Son, in working what has been spoken to be made, arranges. The distinction of persons is so made, however, that the work is referred to both. For in the words, “Let us make,” both the command and the thing made are made equal; while in what is written, “I was with him, arranging” (ibid. 30), Wisdom indicates that God is not solitary to himself in the operation.

She rejoices before him, whom she indicated as rejoicing together with one who rejoices. “And daily I rejoiced before his face at every time, when he rejoiced in the completed world and rejoiced in the children of men” (ibid. 30–31). Wisdom has taught the cause of her joy. She rejoices because of the Father’s joy—of the Father rejoicing in the completion of the world and in the children of men. For it is written: “And God saw that they were good” (Gen. 1). She rejoices that her works, accomplished through herself at his command, please the Father. For she professes that her joy consists in the Father’s being joyful in the completed world and in the children of men—in the children of men, because already in the one Adam the beginning of the whole human race had been established. Therefore the Father does not speak to himself as solitary in making the world, since his Wisdom is with him, cooperating and rejoicing when the cooperation is completed.

> [Note: Col. 0111D. Earlier printed editions read “arranging all things.” The word “all” is consistently absent from the manuscripts here, in Book XII, §37, in Ps. 148, §4, etc., in agreement with the Septuagint.]

> [Note: Col. 0112D. Vatican Basilica manuscript: “do you understand?” Then, in one Colbert manuscript, “of arrangement or dispensation.” More correctly for our sense, in the other manuscript, but not in the Carnotensis, “or ordering” is omitted. For the point here is not Wisdom insofar as she was present while God prepared the heavens, but insofar as she was arranging.]

> [Note: Col. 0112D. That is, the commander and the maker are made equal. Therefore do not read, with Badius, “executes,” or with Erasmus and Paris, “may execute,” still less with the Colbert and German manuscripts, “may carry out.”]

> [Note: Col. 0113C. “He rejoiced.”]

22. Conclusion of what has been proved from §16. — We do not fail to know that much—and of the greatest importance—remains to be said for the full resolution of these statements; but these points have been postponed rather than passed over. For a fuller treatment of them is reserved for other propositions.

For the present, we answer only the assertion made by the impious in their exposition of faith—or rather of unfaith—that Moses proclaimed only one God. We remember that he truly did proclaim this, because there is one God from whom are all things. But for this reason it must not be ignored that the Son is God, since this same Moses throughout the whole body of his work professed God and God. We must therefore see how both election and legislation proclaim God and God in an equal order of confession.

> [Note: Col. 0113D. That is, the matters contained in the same chapter of Proverbs: “The Lord created me,” etc.; in explaining these, almost the whole of Book XII is occupied.]

> [Note: Col. 0113D. In the Leipzig and Paris editions: “both reading and legislation.” More correctly in other books: “both election and legislation,” that is, the New and Old Testaments, in accordance with Paul, Rom. 11:7: “What Israel sought, this it did not obtain; but the election obtained it.” Hence, more clearly in Book V, §2, with regard to this book: “For the Gospels testify rightly that one God was proclaimed by Moses; and Moses, preaching one God, is authority that in the Gospels God and God are faithfully taught.” Thus is easily answered the objection which occurs of itself: if Hilary understands by “election” and “legislation” the Gospel and the Law, why does he afterward show God and God from the Law alone and not from the Gospel? For he treats it as an established fact that God and God are proclaimed in clear words in the Gospel; so that this point will be certain from both Law and Gospel when the Law is shown also to agree with the Gospel in this respect. Hence Genesis, speaking of God and God in §18, is said to proclaim the evangelical mystery.]

> [Note: Col. 0113C. “Legislation.”]

23. The Angel of God who spoke with Hagar is God. The Son is both Angel of God and God. — After God had spoken many times with Abraham, Sarah turned against Hagar, the barren mistress envying the conception of her slave-girl. When Hagar had departed from her presence, Scripture says of her: “And the Angel of the Lord said to Hagar, Return to your mistress and humble yourself under her hands. And the Angel of the Lord said to her, Multiplying I will multiply your seed, and it shall not be numbered for multitude” (Gen. 16:9–10). And again: “And she called the name of the Lord who spoke with her, You are the God who looked upon me” (ibid. 13).

The Angel of God speaks—for the Angel of God has a twofold significance: the one who is, and the one whose Angel he is. He speaks not things appropriate to the designation of his office, for he says: “Multiplying I will multiply your seed, and it shall not be numbered for multitude.” The power to multiply nations exceeds an angel’s ministry. But finally, what did Scripture testify concerning him who, being the Angel of God, spoke what belongs to God alone? “And she called the name of the Lord who spoke with her, You are the God who looked upon me.” First, [he is] the Angel of God; second, the Lord, for “she called the name of the Lord who spoke with her”; then, third, God: “For you are the God who looked upon me.” He who was called the Angel of God is the same as Lord and God.

Now, according to the prophet, the Son of God is “the Angel of great counsel” (Isa. 9:6, according to the Septuagint). In order that the distinction of persons might be complete, he was called the Angel of God; for he who is God from God is himself also the Angel of God. But in order that due honor might be rendered, he is proclaimed both Lord and God.

> [Note: Col. 0114D. Only the Paris edition reads “Angel God”; it is refuted by what follows. The distinction between the one who is [an angel] and the one whose [angel] he is has already been treated in Book II, §32.]

> [Note: Col. 0113C; 0114D. “Which alone.” In most and the better manuscripts: “which alone.”]

24. Why the same speaker is called Angel when speaking to Hagar, but God when speaking to Abraham. — Here, indeed, he is first Angel, then afterward the same one both Lord and God; but to Abraham he is simply God. For once the distinction of persons has safely been set forth, lest the error of solitude should remain, his complete and true name is declared. For it is written: “And God said to Abraham, Behold, Sarah your wife shall bear you a son, and you shall call his name Isaac; and I will establish my covenant with him as an everlasting covenant, and with his seed after him. But concerning Ishmael, behold, I have heard you and blessed him, and I will greatly increase him: he shall beget twelve nations, and I will make him into a great nation” (Gen. 17:19–20).

Can there be any doubt that he who was called the Angel of God is again called God? The discourse about Ishmael is the same, and both now and before he is to be multiplied by the same one. And lest he who had spoken to Hagar should be thought not to be the same one now speaking, the divine speech testifies to the indication of the same person, saying: “And I have blessed him and I will multiply him.” The blessing is from the past, for the speech had already been addressed to Hagar; the increase, however, is future, for now God speaks to Abraham about Ishmael for the first time. God speaks to Abraham, but the Angel of God spoke to Hagar.

Therefore he is God and Angel, because he who is the Angel of God is God born from God. He is called the Angel of God because he is the Angel of great counsel; but afterward he is shown to be God, lest he who is God should be thought to be merely an angel. Let the discourse follow the order of events. The Angel of the Lord spoke to Hagar; the same one speaks to Abraham as God, and the same one addresses them both. Ishmael is blessed, and it is promised that he will be increased into a great nation.

> [Note: Col. 0114C. “Distinction.”]

> [Note: Col. 0114C; 0114D. “Him, and I will increase him.” The Carnotensis manuscript reads *ampliabo*; some others read *amplificabo* (“I will increase”).]

> [Note: Col. 0114D. Colbert manuscript with the German manuscript: *amplicabo*; Vatican Basilica manuscript: *amplificabo*. The latter would not be objectionable if “I have blessed,” rather than “the blessing,” were read first.]

> [Note: Col. 0114D. The words “and God speaks to Abraham,” omitted in earlier printed editions, are restored from the manuscripts.]

> [Note: Col. 0114D. Printed editions: “and he who is the Angel of God, because he who,” etc. More elegantly, the manuscripts read: “who is also angel,” without “of God.” Hilary’s exposition is confirmed by the Letter of the Council of Antioch, which says of Christ: “He who fulfills the Father’s will appears to the patriarchs and speaks with them; in the same clauses and under the same headings he is affirmed at one time as Angel, at another as Lord, and at another as God. For it is impious to suppose that the God of the universe is an angel. But the Son is the Angel of the Father, who is himself Lord and God. For it is written, ‘Angel of great counsel.’” Aptly Tertullian, *On the Flesh of Christ*, §14: “He was called the Angel of great counsel—that is, messenger—by a name of office, not of nature. For he was to announce to the world the Father’s great purpose, namely, concerning the restoration of man. Yet he is not thereby to be understood as an angel in the manner of Gabriel or Raphael. For the Son of the Lord of the vineyard is sent to the cultivators, as are also the servants,” etc. Justin, *Dialogue with Trypho*; Epiphanius, *Heresy* 69, §35, agree. See Augustine, Book II, *On the Trinity*, ch. 13. Nor should Origen be heard, who taught that Christ assumed an angelic nature just as he assumed human nature; these are his words in vol. I on John, p. 32: “Christ became man for men, angel for angels.” For, as Tertullian says, *On the Flesh of Christ*, §14, “that Christ should bear manhood, the salvation of men was the cause … that he should bear angelhood, there is no such reason … For Christ received no command from the Father concerning the salvation of angels.”]

25. Other visions, sayings, and acts are also recounted. — Scripture also shows through Abraham that the one who spoke was God. Isaac is promised as a son to Abraham. Then afterward three men stand by. Abraham, seeing the three, worships one and confesses him as Lord. Scripture states that three men stood by, but the patriarch does not fail to know whom he must worship and confess. Their outward appearance as they stand by is indistinguishable, but he recognized his Lord with the eyes of faith and the sight of the mind.

Then follows: “And he said to him, Returning, I will come to you at this future time, and Sarah your wife shall have a son” (Gen. 18:10). After this the Lord said to him: “I will not hide from Abraham my servant what I am about to do” (ibid. 17). And again: “But the Lord said, The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah is full, and their sins are exceedingly great” (ibid. 20). And again, after much other discourse, which we omit for brevity’s sake, when Abraham was concerned about the destruction of the righteous together with the unrighteous, he said: “Far be it from you, who judge the earth, to do this judgment.” And the Lord said: “If I find in Sodom fifty righteous persons in the city, I will spare the whole place because of them” (ibid. 25–26).

And again, when the discourse to Lot, Abraham’s brother, had ended, Scripture says: “And the Lord rained upon Sodom and Gomorrah sulphur and fire from the Lord out of heaven” (Gen. 19:24). And again: “And the Lord visited Sarah as he had said, and God did to Sarah as he had spoken; and Sarah conceived and bore Abraham a son in her old age, at the time of which the Lord had spoken to him” (Gen. 21:1–2).

Then, after the slave-girl had been expelled from Abraham’s house with her son, and in the wilderness feared the boy’s death for lack of water, the same Scripture says: “And the Lord God heard the voice of the boy where he was; and the Angel of God called Hagar from heaven and said to her, What is the matter, Hagar? Do not fear; for God has heard the voice of the boy from the place where he is. Rise, take the boy, and hold his hand; for I will make him into a great nation” (ibid. 17–18).

> [Note: Col. 0115C. “My servant.”]

> [Note: Col. 0115D. Earlier printed editions add: “that you should destroy the righteous with the ungodly,” against the manuscripts. Since these words are presented at the end of §27 in other language and in another order—namely before, not after, the immediately preceding words—it is evident that they are the work of an interpolator.]

> [Note: Col. 0115C. “If I find in Sodom.”]

> [Note: Col. 0116C. The printed editions read “those righteous”; *righteous* is absent from the manuscripts.]

> [Note: Col. 0115C. “The Lord rained upon Sodom and Gomorrah.”]

> [Note: Col. 0116C. The printed editions read “and behold, he heard.” Three manuscripts read “and he heard”; others, in agreement with the Greek, read “and he heard favorably.”]

26. The several points are examined. The Son is both the Angel of great counsel, and Lord, and God. — What blindness of unfaith is this, what dullness of an unbelieving heart, what rashness of irreligion—to be ignorant of these things, or to disregard them when they are known? Certainly they have been recalled and stated in this way so that no error or obscurity might obstruct the understanding of the truth. If we show that they cannot be unknown, it must necessarily be the crime of impiety to deny them.

The Angel of God began to speak to Hagar, declaring that he would increase Ishmael into a great nation and grant him an innumerable offspring of a people. The confession of the hearer teaches that he is both Lord and God. For the beginning of the speech came from the Angel of God, but it ended in the confession of God. Thus he who, under the ministry of announcing the great counsel, is the Angel of God, is himself God both by nature and by name. For the name belongs to nature; nature is not fitted to a name.

God also speaks to Abraham concerning the same matters: Ishmael is shown already to have been blessed and to be multiplied into a nation. “I have blessed him,” he says (Gen. 17:20). Therefore he did not change the indication of his person, for he shows that he has already blessed him. Scripture surely preserved the order of the mystery and the manner of true proclamation: beginning with the Angel of God, and afterward confessing God as the same one speaking concerning the same matters.

> [Note: Col. 0116C. In the manuscripts, here and elsewhere consistently, “dullness.”]

> [Note: Col. 0116C. Book VI, §15 explains who are guilty of this charge: those whom a will toward impiety, not ignorance, keeps in error. What punishments they deserve he declares in the same book, §3: “For he who will judge all men and, in the mercy proper to his majesty, moderate the penalty due to an error of ignorance, will no longer judge those who deny him, but will deny them.”]

> [Note: Col. 0116C. “Innumerable.”]

> [Note: Col. 0116C; 0116D. Most manuscripts with the printed editions read “under the mystery.” The Carnotensis, Remigiensis, and others more suitably read “under the ministry.” For, as noted above from Tertullian, Christ is called the Angel of great counsel by a title of office, not of nature. Hilary himself says in Book V, §11: “That in ‘angel’ the meaning is of office rather than nature is proved by the fact that angels are called ministers of God.”]

> [Note: Col. 0116D. Thus the best Colbert, Carnotensis, and Remigiensis manuscripts, together with the German manuscript in its first hand. But the printed editions read, “he teaches that Ishmael has already been blessed”; then Paris, after Leipzig, reads “he teaches,” and shortly afterward, with other printed editions, “he blessed,” for “I have blessed.”]

### 27. The Man Whom Abraham Adored among the Three Is Lord, God, and Judge

With a fuller advance in doctrine, the divine discourse proceeds. God there speaks to Abraham and promises that Sarah will bear a child. After this, three men stand near him as he sits; he adores one and confesses him to be Lord. And he who was both adored and confessed by Abraham promises at the same time that he will return in the future; and God, speaking to Abraham, says that Sarah will have a son. Afterwards the same man, seen by Abraham, addresses him concerning these very matters. Only the names are changed; nothing, however, is withdrawn from the confession. For although a man was seen, Abraham nevertheless adored the Lord.

> [Note: [Col. 0117C] The printed editions read, “he adored God,” contrary to the sacred text and the manuscripts. This also conflicts with Hilary’s point: for to him the unqualified word “God” signifies the Father, just as “Lord” signifies the Son; from this he concludes that Abraham recognized Christ’s future assumption of a body. Tertullian speaks similarly of this vision in *On the Flesh of Christ*, §6: “Among those angels the Lord himself appeared to Abraham, without birth, with flesh . . . he who even then was learning, in the guise of flesh not yet born because not yet destined to die, to converse with, deliver, and judge the human race.”]

(Gen. 17:2–3), recognizing, that is, the mystery of the future incarnation. Nor was he without testimony to so great a faith; for the Lord says in the Gospels: “Your father Abraham rejoiced to see my day; and he saw it and rejoiced” (John 8:56).

> [Note: [Col. 0117D] The Carnotensis manuscript and some others read *exsultavit*, “exulted.”]

Therefore the man who was seen promises that he will return at the appointed time. Consider the fulfillment of the promise; nevertheless remember that it is a man who promises. What then does Scripture say? “And the Lord visited Sarah” (Gen. 21:1). Therefore this man is Lord, accomplishing what he had promised. And what follows? “And God did to Sarah as he had spoken” (ibid.). He is called a man when speaking, signified as Lord in the visitation, and proclaimed God in the deed. Certainly you do not fail to recognize the man who was both seen by Abraham and spoke to him. How can you fail to recognize God, when the same Scripture which called him man confesses him to be God? For it itself says: “And Sarah conceived and bore a son to Abraham in his old age, at the time which the Lord had spoken to him” (ibid., v. 2). But it was the man who had said that he would come. Believe him to be merely a man only if he who came is not both God and Lord.

Compare the cause. The man will certainly come in order that Sarah may conceive and bear a child. Learn faith. The Lord and God came in order that Sarah might conceive and bear. As man, he spoke by the power of God; in the accomplishment, God fulfilled it. Thus he signifies himself to be God both by speaking and by acting.

> [Note: [Col. 0117D] The printed editions read, “then, when the three men had been seen”; corrected from the manuscripts.]

Then two of the three men who had been seen depart; but he who remains is both Lord and God. Nor is he only Lord and God: he is also Judge. For Abraham, standing before the Lord, said: “By no means will you do this thing, to kill the righteous with the wicked, so that the righteous should be as the wicked. Far be it from you! Shall he who judges all the earth not do judgment?” (Gen. 18:25). Thus throughout his discourse Abraham displays the faith for which he was justified: he recognizes his Lord among the three, adores him alone, confesses him Lord, and confesses him Judge.

> [Note: [Col. 0117C] “And confessed him God.”]

> [Note: [Col. 0117D] The printed editions read, “and he confessed him God and Judge,” against the manuscripts. Nor does Abraham in Scripture consistently profess God, but Lord.]

### 28. Abraham Adored One of the Three, Not Three as One. The Difference between Lot’s Vision and Abraham’s Vision

And lest perhaps you suppose that, in the confession of one, the honor of all three men who were seen together is included, consider what Lot said when he saw the two who had departed:

> [Note: [Col. 0117D] Thus the more accurate manuscripts. But the printed editions read, “and Lot saw, and rose . . . to the ground”; in Greek, *tō prosōpō epi tēn gēn*, “with his face to the ground.” Then, since Hilary reads “Behold, lords,” both Greek and Latin copies agree with him. Augustine, however, *Sermon* 7, prefers “Behold, lord,” and seems nowhere to have seen “Behold, lords”; for he writes in §6: “When two were sent to Sodom and appeared to Abraham’s brother Lot, he too recognizes divinity in them; and though he sees two, he calls [them] LORD. Abraham [called] the Lord in three, and he [called] the Lord in two.” From this Augustine advances to the opinion that not the Lord himself, but angels in whom the Lord dwelt, appeared to the patriarchs, who gave glory not to the bearers but to the one dwelling in them. See also his *Against Maximinus*, book II, ch. 26, §6.]

“And when Lot saw them, he rose to meet them and bowed with his face to the ground; and he said: ‘Behold, my lords, turn aside into the house of your servant’” (Gen. 19:1–2).
