Here the simple vision of angels retains the plural sense; there the patriarch’s faith confesses singular honor. Here the narrative of divine Scripture signifies that only two of the three were angels; there it proclaims Lord and God. For it says: “And the Lord said to Abraham, ‘Why did Sarah laugh, saying, “Shall I truly bear a child, though I have grown old?”’”

> [Note: [Col. 0118C] “Shall I truly [bear a child]?”]

> [Note: [Col. 0118D] The common editions read, “who have now grown old.” The words “who have now” are absent from the manuscripts and the Greek text.]

“Is any word impossible with God? At this time I shall return to you in the future, and Sarah shall have a son” (Gen. 18:13 ff.).

> [Note: [Col. 0118D] In the Paris edition: “with God,” omitting *a*; in other printed editions: “from the Lord.” More correctly, the manuscripts read “from God,” so that he who spoke in the form of a man in vv. 2–3, and who is called Lord in vv. 1, 3, and 13, may also be shown to be God. This is Hilary’s purpose; he interprets the Greek *para tō Theō* properly as “with God,” as though it were *para tou Theou*, “from God.”]

Scripture therefore preserves the order of truth: it does not mingle plural reference with him who was acknowledged as both God and Lord, nor does it distribute to the two angels the honor which had been rendered to God alone. Lot indeed says “lords,” but Scripture calls them angels. There it is the duty of a man; here it is a confession of truth.

### 29. The Lord from the Lord: the Son

Thereupon the just penalty of judgment comes upon Sodom and Gomorrah. What, then, is the point of significance in this? “The Lord rained sulphur and fire from the Lord” (Gen. 19:24). Thus, Lord from Lord: by the name of nature he did not distinguish those whom he had distinguished by their signification—not as one person. For we read in the Gospel: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22). Therefore the Lord gave what the Lord received from the Lord.

### 30. Jacob Saw Him as God, Yet Not as Solitary

But you who have recognized in “Lord” and “Lord” knowledge of the Judge, recognize also the fellowship denoted by the same name in “God” and “God.” Jacob, leaving because of fear of his brother, saw in a dream a ladder set upon the earth and reaching heaven, with angels of God ascending and descending by it, and the Lord standing above it and bestowing upon him all the blessings which he had given to Abraham and Isaac (Gen. 28). Afterwards the following divine utterance came to him: “And God said to Jacob: Rise, go up to Bethel, dwell there, and make there an altar to God who appeared to you when you fled from the face of your brother” (Gen. 35:1). God demands honor for God, and demands it while indicating another person: “Who,” he says, “appeared to you when you fled,” lest any confusion of the same person arise. Therefore God is the one speaking, and God is he of whom he speaks. The confession of honor does not distinguish by the name of nature those whom the signification distinguishes as subsisting.

### 31. Summary and Aim of the Preceding Discussion, from Section 23

I remember that certain matters are necessary for a fuller treatment of this passage; but the order of the reply must also follow the order of the proposition. Therefore, what remains will be pursued in its proper place in another book. For the present it was necessary only to demonstrate this: in the God who demands honor for God, that the angel of God who spoke with Hagar is both God and Lord, since he himself later spoke to Abraham on the same matters; and that the man who appeared to Abraham is both God and Lord; while the two angels, seen with the Lord and sent by him to Lot, are proclaimed by the prophet as nothing other than angels.

God was present to Abraham in a man; God also came to Jacob in a man. Nor did he merely come: he is shown wrestling (Gen. 32:24); nor merely wrestling, but weak against him with whom he wrestled. It is neither the place nor the time to discuss anything concerning the mystery of the wrestling.

> [Note: [Col. 0119D] The printed editions read, “and it is not the time,” contrary to the manuscripts. This is a pleonasm, examples of which we have already seen.]

He is certainly God, because Jacob prevailed against God, and Israel saw God.

### 32. He Who Appeared to Moses in the Bush Is Lord and God

Let us see whether this angel of God was recognized as God anywhere else besides in his appearance to Hagar. He certainly was recognized. Nor was he found merely to be God, but also God of Abraham, God of Isaac, and God of Jacob. For the angel of the Lord appeared to Moses from the bush, and the Lord speaks from the bush. Whose voice do you judge is to be understood: his who was seen, or someone else’s? There is no room here for falsehood. For Scripture says: “And the angel of the Lord appeared to him in a flame of fire from the bush” (Exod. 3:2). And again: “The Lord called to him from the bush, ‘Moses, Moses.’ And he answered, ‘What is it?’ And the Lord said: ‘Do not approach here; remove the sandal from your feet, for the place on which you stand is holy ground.’ And he said to him: ‘I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’” (ibid., vv. 4 ff.).

He who appeared in the bush speaks from the bush: the place of the vision and of the voice is one; and no one other than he who was seen is heard. He who, when seen, is the angel of God is again, when heard, Lord; and the Lord who is heard is afterwards recognized as God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

> [Note: [Col. 0119D] The common editions read: “and he who is heard, the Lord, is God. Then he is recognized as the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.” This confused reading is restored with the help of the manuscripts.]

When he is called angel of God, he is shown not to belong to himself and to be solitary; for he is the angel of God.

> [Note: [Col. 0119D] The printed editions read, “For the angel of God when . . .,” disrupting the sense and removing the proof that God is not solitary. Corrected from the manuscripts.]

When he is called Lord and God, he is proclaimed in the honor and name of his nature. You have, then, the angel who appeared from the bush as both Lord and God.

### 33. Moses Repeatedly Proclaims God and Lord. Yet Both Are One God. Honor Is Required for the Son as God by Nature. The Son Is Both Angel of God and God

Continue through the testimonies of Moses, and see whether he neglects any opportunity to proclaim God and Lord. From his words you hold, of course: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one” (Deut. 6:4). Now attend to the words of that divine song. For he says: “See, see that I am the Lord, and there is no God besides me” (Deut. 32:39). And although the whole discourse down to the end of the song was from the person of God—

> [Note: [Col. 0119D] Namely, of the Only-Begotten, as is more openly declared in book V, §36.]

—he says: “Rejoice, O heavens, with him, and let all the sons of God worship him. Rejoice, O nations, with his people, and let all the angels of God honor him” (ibid., v. 43).

> [Note: [Col. 0120D] This passage of Deuteronomy is expressed in different words and a different order in the exposition of Psalm 67, §4. There “angels of God” occurs first, not “sons of God”; afterwards “sons of God” occurs in place of “angels of God.” This reading is supported by Justin near the end of the *Dialogue with Trypho*, and favored by Paul in Heb. 1:6. The order which Hilary follows here is also followed by Epiphanius, *Heresies* 69, §60, where he has: “Let all the sons of God worship him, and let all the angels of God strengthen him.”]

God, who says, “I am the Lord, and there is no God besides me,” is to be honored by the angels of God. For the Only-Begotten is God; nor does the name “only-begotten” admit a companion—just as “unbegotten,” in precisely so far as it means unbegotten, admits no participant. For he is one from one. There is no other unbegotten God besides the unbegotten God, nor is there any only-begotten God besides the only-begotten God. Each, therefore, is one and alone, by reason of the proper character in each respectively of unbegottenness and origin. And so each is one God, since between one and one—that is, one from one—there is not a second nature of eternal divinity.

Therefore he is to be worshipped by the sons of God and honored by the angels of God. Thus honor and veneration are demanded for God from God’s sons and angels. Understand the significance of honoring, and of him through whom, and of those through whom God is to be honored—namely, through angels and sons of God.

> [Note: [Col. 0121C] “And of him through whom.”]

> [Note: [Col. 0121C–D] Erasmus, Lipsius, and the Paris edition read, “and of those through whom he is to be honored”; this reading is highly suspect, since it neither sufficiently agrees with what follows nor occurs except in later manuscripts. In the three better manuscripts—Colbertinus, Carnotensis, Corbeiensis, Germanensis, Remigiensis, and others—the reading is: “and of him through whom [the verb ‘honor,’ understood, may be supplied] he is to be honored.” In the Corbeiensis manuscript, corrected in a second hand, is written: “and of him through whom he is to be honored.” But the Vendôme manuscript has: “and of those through whom he is to be honored.” In the older Remigiensis, corruptly: “understand, namely, angel and Son of God.” From these readings one might reasonably infer: “Understand the indication of honor from those through whom God is to be honored, namely, as angel and Son of God.”]

And lest perhaps you suppose that honor is not demanded for God by nature, and think that Moses here meant the Father God to be honored—although the Father is to be honored in the Son—nevertheless consider the blessing which, in the same discourse, he bestows upon Joseph. He says: “And let the things acceptable to him who appeared in the bush come upon the head and crown of Joseph” (Deut. 33:16).

> [Note: [Col. 0121D] In one Vatican manuscript: “under the same name.” Then, in a later Remigiensis manuscript: “Jacob appoints to Joseph for Theodore.” The reading of the other manuscripts is sounder. The words which follow are from Deuteronomy, although they allude to Jacob’s blessing in Gen. 49:26.]

Therefore God is to be worshipped by God’s sons—but God who is also the Son of God. God is to be honored by God’s angels—but God who is the angel of God: for the angel of God, who appeared from the bush, is God; and when Joseph is blessed, the things pleasing to him are wished for Joseph.

> [Note: [Col. 0121D] Thus the manuscripts. But the printed editions read, “The angel is he who [appeared] from the bush.” Ambrose likewise declares in his exposition of Psalm 43, §15, that the Son was seen in the bush: “Who was seen by Moses in the bush except the firstborn Son of God, who said: ‘I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob’? Therefore he showed himself to human sight because he was to come so as to be seen by all.”]

He is not therefore not God because he is the angel of God; nor, conversely, is he not the angel of God because he is God. Rather, with the understanding of the persons indicated, with the meaning of unbegottenness and birth distinguished, and with the dispensation of the heavenly mysteries made manifest, Moses teaches that God is not to be thought solitary, since God, who is angel and Son of God, will be worshipped by God’s angels and sons.

> [Note: [Col. 0122C–D] The printed editions read *distinctio*, “distinction”; this is an error corrected by the manuscripts.]

### 34

Let these answers from the books of Moses suffice for us—or rather, let Moses himself have answered. For heretics, using him as their authority, think that by the confession of one God they can persuade us that the Son of God is not to be proclaimed God. Yet they are impious against the testimony of their own authority, since he, while confessing one God, did not cease to teach that the Son of God is God. But it remains to bring forward many statements of the prophets on the same subject.

### 35. The Prophet Teaches That the Son Is God and Distinguishes Him from the Father. Why the Father Is the Son’s God

You hold the saying: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one”; and would that you held it rightly. But according to your own interpretation of the prophetic saying, I ask for its rationale. For he says in the Psalms: “God, your God, has anointed you” (Ps. 44:8 [45:7]).

> [Note: [Col. 0122D] Lipsius and the Paris edition read, “Let the reader’s understanding distinguish,” against the other books. Thus Tertullian, *Against Praxeas*, §13; Ambrose, *On Faith*, book I, ch. 3; and other Fathers observe that two are plainly distinguished in this passage of the Psalmist. More striking than the others is Irenaeus, book III, ch. 6: “The Holy Spirit indicated both by the appellation ‘God’: both the Son who is anointed and the Father who anoints.”]

Let the reader’s understanding distinguish the anointed from the anointer; distinguish “you” from “your”: show to whom and concerning whom the discourse is addressed. For this order of confession follows the preceding statements. He had said: “Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever; a rod of uprightness is the rod of your kingdom. You loved righteousness and hated iniquity” (ibid., v. 7 [45:6]). He now adds: “Therefore God, your God, has anointed you.” Thus the God of the eternal kingdom, because of the merit of righteousness loved and iniquity hated, is anointed by his God.

Do even the separation of the names confuse our understanding at all? For the distinction of person alone is expressed in “you” and “your,” while the confession of nature is in no respect distinguished. “Your” refers to the source; “you” to the one who is from the source. For he is God from God, as the prophet confesses in the same order: “God, your God, has anointed you.” But there is no God before the unbegotten God, as he himself says: “Be witnesses to me, and I am witness, says the Lord God, and my servant whom I chose, that you may know and believe and understand that I am; and before me there was no other God, nor shall there be after me” (Isa. 43:10).

> [Note: [Col. 0121C–122C] The person of him who is without birth is therefore shown; then, for what he says is equivalent to what follows, and shortly thereafter, because he is read to have been born from God, [it is equivalent to] “born from him.”]

The dignity of him who is without beginning is therefore shown; and the honor of him who is from the unbegotten is preserved: “God, your God, has anointed you.” For “your” refers to birth, but does not destroy nature (see book XI, §18, etc.). And therefore the Father is his God because he was born from him as God. Yet because the Father is God, the Son is not thereby not God: for “God, your God, has anointed you.” Thus, by the indication of both the source and the one begotten from him, the one and same statement places them both under the designation of the same nature and dignity.

> [Note: [Col. 0122D] All editions except the Paris edition read, “who is without birth”; but below, §37, concerning the Father, they read, “who is eternal without beginning.”]

> [Note: [Col. 0122D] The Vatican Basilica manuscript reads, “in the designation of the same nature and dignity and of Lord”; less accurately. This passage especially makes clear the force which *dignitas* has in Hilary: it is here plainly used in place of “divinity.”]

### 36. The Son as Isaiah Proclaims Him to Be

But lest perhaps an occasion for an impious assertion be seized from the statement, “For I am, and before me there is no other God, nor shall there be after me” (Isa. 43:10), as though the Son also were not God because, after God before whom no God exists, no God would thereafter exist: the whole meaning of the statement must therefore be examined.

God himself is witness of his own discourse; but his chosen servant is also, together with him, witness that there was no God before him and that none would be after him. God is indeed a sufficient witness for himself; but to his own witness about himself he joins the testimony of the servant whom he chose. Therefore the testimony of the two is one: that there is no God before him—for all things are from him—and that there will be no God after him; certainly not because he had not already been from him. For the servant was already speaking these things in the Father’s testimony: the servant chosen in the tribe from which he was to be born. He demonstrates the same in the Gospels: “Behold my servant whom I chose, my beloved, in whom my soul was well pleased” (Matt. 12:18).

> [Note: [Col. 0123C] “My soul.”]

Thus: “There is no other God before me, nor shall there be after me,” displaying the infinity of eternal and immutable power in this, that no God exists before or after him—yet placing his servant both in his testimony and in the divine name.

### 37. Hosea’s Passage for the Son’s Divinity. No One Is God to the Father; the Father Is God to the Son; to Us Both Father and Son Are God

It is also easy to learn this from his own person. For he says to the prophet Hosea: “I will no longer continue to show mercy to the house of Israel, but I will oppose them in opposition; yet I will have mercy upon the children of Judah and will save them in the Lord their God” (Hos. 1:6–7). Therefore the Father plainly calls the Son God, in whom he chose us before the ages of the world (Eph. 1:4).

> [Note: [Col. 0123C] *Absolute*, “plainly,” is entirely absent from the Verona manuscript.]

> [Note: [Col. 0123D] In the Paris edition and some manuscripts, *absolute* is omitted; it means “plainly and without any ambiguity.”]

He says “their” because the unbegotten God is from no one, while we are given to the Son as an inheritance by God the Father. For we read: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance” (Ps. 2:8).

> [Note: [Col. 0123D] “As an inheritance.”]

> [Note: [Col. 0123D] The printed editions read, “as your inheritance,” contrary to the manuscripts and *Tractate 2 on the Psalms*.]

For God, from whom all things are and who is eternal without beginning, has no God. But the Father is God to the Son, for God was born from him. To us, however, both the Father is God and the Son is God: the Father confesses of the Son that he is our God; the Son teaches concerning the Father that he is God to us. Yet the Son is called God by the Father—that is, by the very name of the Father’s unbegotten power. And these things are said with reference to Hosea.

### 38. A Splendid Testimony from Isaiah. The Adoration of the Magi Foretold. Who the Magi Were

But how unequivocal is the confession of God the Father concerning our Lord through Isaiah. For he says:

> “For thus says the Lord God, the Holy One of Israel, who made the things which are to come: Ask me concerning your sons and daughters, and command me concerning the works of my hands. I made the earth and man upon it; I commanded all the stars; I raised up a king in righteousness, and all his ways are straight. He shall build my city and restore the captivity of my people, not for a reward nor for gifts, says the Lord Sabaoth. Egypt shall labor, and the merchandise of the Ethiopians, and the Sabaeans. Men of lofty stature shall pass over to you, and they shall be your servants; they shall follow after you, bound in chains; they shall worship you and pray to you, because God is in you, and there is no God besides you. For you are God, and we did not know it, God the Savior of Israel. All who oppose him shall be ashamed and confounded, and shall go away in confusion” (Isa. 45:11 ff.).

> [Note: [Col. 0123D] Although the Greek text, *kai hoi Sabaeim andres* (“and Sabaeans, men”), plainly shows that “Sabaeans” belongs with what follows rather than what precedes, Hilary undoubtedly relates it to “merchandise,” as appears from the following discussion. Tertullian, *Against Praxeas*, §13, agrees with Hilary in using this passage of Isaiah to prove that two possess the one divine name; but differs in reading “and Sabaean men.”]

Is there still any room for rashness, or any remaining occasion of ignorance—unless only this remains, that professed impiety should betray itself? God, from whom all things are, who made all things by commanding them—

> [Note: [Col. 0123D] Lipsius and the Paris edition insert from Erasmus’s margin, “by commanding.”]

—appropriating to himself the work of what was made, which would assuredly not have been made unless he had said that it should be made, testifies that he raised up through himself a righteous king, who builds a city for God and turns away the captivity of his people, not for reward or gifts; for we are all saved by grace.

Then he speaks thus, when, after the labor of Egypt—that is, the affliction of the age—

> [Note: [Col. 0124C] “Captivity.”]

> [Note: [Col. 0123D] Thus the older books. Others read, “the captivity of the age.”]

—and the merchandise of the Ethiopians and the Sabaean men, men of lofty stature shall come over to him. And what kind of labor of Egypt, merchandise of Ethiopia, and Sabaeans should be understood? Let us recall the Magi of the East, worshipping the Lord and presenting gifts, and measure the toil of their journey all the way to Bethlehem of Judaea.

> [Note: [Col. 0123D–124D] The Vatican Basilica manuscript reads, corruptly, “at the beginning, the labor of all Egypt.” Here Hilary gives two statements concerning the Magi: namely, that they were rulers and that they practiced the magical art. It has already been observed in the notes on ch. 1 of the commentary on Matthew, §5, that many ancient writers taught the latter point with him. Tertullian also writes that they were kings, *Against Marcion*, book III, §13, where, about to expound the Psalmic words “Kings of Arabia,” etc., he adds: “For the East commonly had the Magi as kings.” Jerome agrees in his commentary on Daniel, ch. 2. Likewise Caesarius of Arles, in the appendix to Augustine’s *Sermons*, Sermon 139, §3: “Those Magi are said to have been three kings.” Hence Paschasius Radbertus, on Matthew 2: “No one who has read the histories of the Gentiles is ignorant that the Magi were kings.” This explains how all from Saba came to Christ: because, as Hilary explains in his commentary on Matthew, ch. 14, §7, the leader of a people embraces in his name and office the whole community subject to him.]

For in the labor of the rulers, the labor of all Egypt is represented. For to the Magi—who falsely imitated the operations of divine power under an appearance of things—the chief honor of impious religion had from every age been paid. By those same Magi, bringing gifts of gold, frankincense, and myrrh, is shown the merchandise of Ethiopia and Saba. The same thing another prophet also foretold, saying: “The Ethiopians shall fall down before him, and his enemies shall lick the dust. The kings of Tarshish shall offer gifts; the kings of Arabia and Saba shall bring gifts; and to him shall be given gold of Arabia” (Ps. 71:9–10 [72:9–10]).

> [Note: [Col. 0125D] The Vatican Basilica manuscript alone reads, “therefore, in the gifts.”]

Therefore in the Magi and their gifts are displayed the labor of Egypt and the merchandise of Ethiopia and Saba: that is, the error of the world in the Magi who worshipped, and the chosen gifts of the nations offered by them to the Lord whom they adored.

### 39. The Apostles Are Men of Lofty Stature

Who then are the men of lofty stature who are to pass over to him and follow him bound? This is not obscure. Look to the Gospels: Peter, about to follow his Lord, girds himself (John 21:7). Look upon the Apostles: Paul, servant of Christ, glories in chains (Philem. 1). And let us see whether one bound for Christ Jesus fulfilled the things which God had spoken concerning his Son as God. “They shall pray,” he says, “because God is in you” (Isa. 45:14). Recognize then the Apostle’s statement and, having recognized it, understand it: “God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself” (2 Cor. 5:19).

Then follows: “And there is no God besides you.” To this the same Apostle immediately says: “For there is one Lord, our Jesus Christ, through whom are all things” (1 Cor. 8:6); and no other besides him is seen to exist, because he is one. Thirdly he says: “You are God, and we did not know it.” But, as a former persecutor—

> [Note: [Col. 0125D] That is, one who had been a persecutor. We have already observed elsewhere that Hilary commonly uses *ex* to signify a past state and time. Thus he frequently speaks of Christ as emptied into the form of a servant, “man from God,” meaning “when he was God, he became man.” Here, however, the common editions and one later Colbertinus manuscript insert “made a teacher.”]

—of the Church, he said: “Of whom are the fathers, from whom is Christ, who is God over all” (Rom. 9:5). These, therefore, though bound, shall preach these things: lofty indeed, and destined to judge the tribes of Israel upon twelve thrones, and following their Lord by the martyrdom of their teaching and passion.

> [Note: [Col. 0125D] The printed editions read, “the twelve tribes,” contrary to the manuscripts.]

### 40. The Father Says of Himself, “There Is No God Besides Me,” and of the Son, “There Is No God Besides You.” The Son Is Distinguished from the Father by Person, Not by Kind

Therefore God is in God; and he in whom God is, is God. And how is there no God besides you, when God is in the same one? You, heretic, appropriate “There is no God besides me” to confess the solitary Father God. How will you interpret the statement proclaimed by God the Father, “There is no God besides you,” if by “There is no God besides me” (Deut. 32:39) you contend that the Son of God is not God? And to whom, then, did God the Father say, “There is no God besides you”? For here you will not be able to introduce the person of a solitary one.

> [Note: [Col. 0125D] Here, as Tertullian says concerning the same passage, *Against Praxeas*, §13, by saying “God is in you” and “You are God,” he sets forth two: him who was, and him in whom he was—Christ and the Spirit; by “Spirit” he understands the Father.]

For the Lord spoke to the king whom he raised up, in the person of the lofty men who worship and pray: “Because God is in you.” This reality does not admit of a solitary God. “In you” signifies one present, as though the discourse were addressed to him. And what follows—“God is in you”—shows not only him who is present, but also him who remains in the one present, distinguishing the indweller from him in whom he dwells, yet only by distinction of person, not of kind. For God is in him, and he in whom God is, is God. God is not in a dwelling-place of a nature different and alien from himself; rather, he remains in one begotten from himself and of himself.

> [Note: [Col. 0125C] “Remains.”]

> [Note: [Col. 0125D–126D] The Carnotensis manuscript reads, “and remains in one begotten from himself”; incorrectly. Why he remains in him is explained thus in the exposition of Psalm 122, §2: “For God begotten from God is not absent by nature from him from whom he is confessed to be begotten, whereas other things are absent through difference of nature.” The Son, therefore, is in himself a worthy and sufficient dwelling-place for the Father; and the Father also dwells in others, insofar as, joined to the Son, they are in a certain way contained in him, as is elegantly explained in the same place.]

God is in God because God is from God. “For you are God, and we did not know it, God the Savior of Israel” (Isa. 45:15).

### 41. Those Who Oppose the Son Shall Be Ashamed. Whoever Denies the Son Dishonors the Father

The following discourse refutes you when you deny God in God. For it says: “All who oppose him shall be ashamed and confounded, and shall go away in confusion” (ibid., v. 16).

> [Note: [Col. 0126D] The Vatican Basilica manuscript reads, “this saying”; less well.]

This is God’s decree against your impiety. For you oppose Christ, concerning whom the confession of the Father’s voice rebukes you. For he is God whom you deny to be God. But you deny him under the appearance of honoring God the Father, who says: “There is no other God besides me” (ibid., v. 18). But be confounded and ashamed. The unbegotten God does not need the honor you offer him; he does not demand from you this glory of his supposed solitariness, nor does he desire this interpretation of your opinion: that, because he said, “There is no God besides me,” you should deny as God him whom he begot from himself.

And lest you might claim this as peculiarly your own, to overthrow the divinity of the Son, he endowed the glory of his Only-Begotten with the honor of perfect divinity, saying: “And there is no God besides you.”

> [Note: [Col. 0126D] The same manuscript reads “defended”; nor should it be followed here.]

Why do you distinguish what is made equal? Why separate what is compared? It belongs properly to the Son of God that there be no God besides him; it belongs properly to God the Father that there be no God apart from him. Use the words of God concerning God. Confess thus, and pray to the King: “Because God is in you, and there is no God besides you. For you are God, and we did not know it, God the Savior of Israel.” The duty of honor contains no insult, nor does the example of confession contain offense—especially since opposition to him entails complete confusion and shame.

> [Note: [Col. 0126D] The aforementioned manuscript again seems less sound, reading “slander” instead of “insult,” and then “the punishment of confusion” instead of “full confusion.”]

Dwell upon God’s words; confess in God’s utterances; and flee the threatened confusion. For by denying that the Son of God is God, you do not so much revere God as solitary with the honor due to his glory, as you despise the Father by dishonoring the Son.

> [Note: [Col. 0126C] “Solitary.”]

> [Note: [Col. 0126D] The printed editions with some manuscripts read *solitario*, “to the solitary [God].” We prefer with the others *solitarium*, “as solitary,” after restoring the particle *tamquam*, “as,” which Lipsius had deleted without authority. The Father is dishonored when he is proclaimed father of a degenerate Son, as Hilary often suggests; Augustine, *Sermon* 139, §5, and Ambrose, *On Faith*, book I, ch. 6, establish this. He is likewise dishonored when it is asserted that he was at some time without Word and Wisdom, and therefore borrowed reason from elsewhere, as Athanasius shows, *Orations against the Arians*, II, p. 331.]

Confess in faith to the unbegotten God that there is no God besides him; proclaim of the only-begotten God that no God exists apart from him.

[Col. 0127A] 101 42. Jeremiah bears witness to the divinity of the Son. He was seen upon earth. The Son is the one Mediator both in the giving of the Law and in the assumption of flesh. The Father and Son are one. — For hear, besides Moses and Isaiah, Jeremiah also teaching the same thing in a third testimony, when he says: “This is our God, and no other shall be reckoned beside him. He found the whole way of knowledge, and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel his beloved. After this he was seen upon earth and lived among men” (Baruch 3:36 ff.). [Note: He who prepared the latest Paris edition here substituted “Baruch” for the word “Jeremiah,” but neglected to alter the same name when it is repeated shortly afterward.]

For he had already said above: “And he is a man—who shall know him?” You therefore have God seen on earth and dwelling among human beings; and I ask how you think the saying is to be understood, “No one has ever seen God, except the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father” (John 1:18), when Jeremiah proclaims [Col. 0127B] a God who was both seen on earth and lived among human beings. Surely the Father is visible only to the Son. [Note: Here we add “only” on the authority of all the manuscripts. Tertullian supports Hilary’s teaching on the Father’s invisibility, *Against Marcion*, II.27: “The Gospel itself will testify in common that the Father has been seen by no one, Christ saying, ‘No one has known the Father except the Son.’ For he himself had also declared in the Old Testament, ‘No one shall see God and live,’ defining the Father as invisible; by whose authority and in whose name he who was seen—God the Son—was God.” See also the same author, *Against Praxeas*, 14. Thus Ambrose, *On Luke*: “One must therefore necessarily grant that, if no one has ever seen God the Father, the Son was seen in the Old Testament.” So too Prudentius, *Apotheosis*, v. 79, says among other things: “He who is born can be seen; but he who is unborn cannot be seen.” Justin, *Dialogue with Trypho*, agrees with these, and Clement, *Stromata*, IV, p. 537, supports them.

Their view rests especially on John’s words: “No one has ever seen God.” For the Fathers of the earlier centuries customarily interpret the word “God,” whenever it stands without qualification, as referring to God the Father. Hence they concluded that the Son, who was seen, is other than the Father, who was never seen. But what they observed for the distinction of persons, the Arians afterwards distorted—as we have already noted—into a diversity of natures. “The Son,” they say in Augustine, *Sermon* VII.4, “was seen by the Fathers; the Father was not seen: invisible and visible are different natures,” and so forth. As though the Son, according to his divine nature, were not equally invisible with the Father. Augustine therefore rightly calls those men mad in *On the Trinity*, II.14, who maintain that the Son was seen in his own substance. In order to bar every avenue to such madness, Augustine began to explain the appearances to the patriarchs somewhat differently from other Fathers, denying as far as he could that the Son rather than other persons had appeared to them.

Yet, when pressing the Scriptural passage now before us against Maximinus, II.26.13, he teaches that it must be interpreted of the Son. For, as Gregory Nazianzen observes, *Oration* XXXVI, the addition, “he was seen on earth,” plainly declares that the discourse concerns not the Father but the Son: “For this is he who had bodily intercourse with us.” Thus our Hilary shortly calls him God “visible in the man [whom he assumed] and capable of being touched.” Here the Paris edition, following the Nivellian edition, erroneously printed “invisible in the man.”]

Who then is this, who was seen and lived among human beings? Certainly he is our God: God visible in the man and capable of being touched. Understand, too, the prophet as speaking: “No other shall be reckoned beside him.” If you ask, “How?” hear what follows, lest on account of this saying you suppose that the statement is not also proper to the Father: “Hear, O Israel, the Lord your God is one” (Deut. 6:4). For these statements hang together: “No other shall be reckoned beside him; he found the whole way of knowledge and gave it to Jacob [Col. 0128A] his servant and to Israel his beloved; after this he was seen upon earth and lived among men.”

For there is one Mediator between God and human beings, God and man; and he is Mediator both in the giving of the Law and in the assumption of the body. Therefore no other is reckoned beside him. For this one was born into God from God, through whom all things in heaven and on earth were created, through whom times and ages were made. For everything whatsoever exists subsists through his activity. [Note: The rescript to Liberius in Athanasius, p. 244, says nearly the same.] This one, therefore, is he who made dispositions to Abraham, spoke to Moses, bore witness to Israel, remained in the prophets, was born through the Virgin by the Holy Spirit, [Note: Our manuscript has only “from the Spirit.”] [Note: Several good manuscripts read “by the Spirit” and do not add “Holy.”] fastened to the wood of his Passion the hostile powers that opposed and were enemies to us, destroyed death in hell, confirmed by his resurrection the assurance of our hope, and destroyed the corruption of human flesh by the glory of his own body.

[Col. 0128B] Therefore no other shall be reckoned beside him. For these things belong properly to the only-begotten God alone; and this one, born from God, is one in this distinctive blessedness of his powers. No other God is reckoned beside him: for he is God not from another substance, but from God. Nothing in him, therefore, is new, foreign, or recent. For when Israel hears that God is one for it, and that no other God is reckoned beside God the Son, so that he may be God, [Note: In some more recent manuscripts, “so that he may be redeeming God”: a gloss.] Father-God and Son-God are absolutely one—not by a union of persons, but by unity of substance. [Note: Since the word *unio* (“union”) occurs repeatedly, its force must be clearly understood. It answers to the Greek μονὰς (*monas*), and signifies solitude or singleness. It differs from *unitas* (“unity”) in that Hilary always refers unity to nature, but union to persons; thus, while defending unity in God, he vehemently rejects union.

Sabellius appears to have introduced this term and expressed his heresy by it. Hence in *On the Synods*, 26, the heresy is simply called “the heresy of union”; and those attached to it are called *unionitae* (“unionists”) by Prudentius, *Apotheosis*, before v. 178. Thus Sulpicius, p. 255, testifies that the Easterners suspected the Gauls of believing, in accordance with Sabellius, in a three-named union of a solitary God. But the Gauls reply in the Council of Paris, Fragment XI.2, that they detest union itself according to Sabellius’s blasphemies. Again, Sulpicius, p. 242, writes that Photinus differed from Sabellius concerning union, because, namely, he did not proclaim a single person in the Trinity.

In the same sense Maximus of Turin, *Homily* I on St. Eusebius, employs the word “union.” Gelasius, *On the Two Natures*, and Vigilius of Tapsus, *Against Eutyches*, II, likewise employed it to express the singularity of Christ’s person. Because Sabellius rejected this, the Arians accuse him, in their letter to Alexander of Alexandria, of “dividing the union”—that is, as Hilary interprets it, *On the Trinity*, VI.7, of dividing Christ himself in the Virgin.

Jerome, *Letter* XXII to Eustochium, adds to these: Christ’s mother is proclaimed fruitful by a union comparable to that of God, because, as the Father alone without a mother begot the Word, so she alone without a father brought forth Christ. Tertullian, however, in *Against Praxeas*, 13, and *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, 2, refers the term not to persons but to nature itself, treating *unio* and *unitas* as synonyms.

What Hilary calls *unio*, Ambrose calls “singularity,” *On the Faith*, V.1: “It is evident, therefore, that what is of one substance cannot be separated, even if it is not of singularity but of unity. I mean that singularity which in Greek is called μονότης (*monotēs*).” Singularity pertains to persons; unity, to nature.] For the prophet does not allow what the Son of God, who is God, is to be reckoned as belonging to another God. [Note: Thus Badius, with the manuscripts, except that the Chartres manuscript has “the prophet, which is present.” But Erasmus, Lipsius, and Paris read, “the prophet saying that God is one,” changing Hilary’s sense, since by “the prophet” he means Jeremiah or Baruch, not Moses: that is, because the prophet Baruch does not permit that the Son of God, who is God, should be reckoned, insofar as he is God, as belonging to another God.]

## 103–104. BOOK FIVE

It is also called the second, because it is the second book against the perfidy of the Arian party, whose refutation was first undertaken in the preceding book. Hilary recognizes that this perfidy is so cunningly woven together that one who agrees with it seems to deny that the Son is God, whereas one who opposes it seems to proclaim either the Father and Son as two Gods or, in Sabellius’s manner, as one and the same. Accordingly, in the preceding book he fortified believers, from the testimonies of the Law and the Prophets, against the fraud prepared in the first words of the heretics, “We know one God.” Now, in their subsequent words, “the only true [God],” he repels the hidden poison, defending the Son’s status as true God by almost the same testimonies [Col. 0129B] by which, in the fourth book, he showed that God is God—that is, not a solitary and singular God. Then, near the end of the book, he proves that the Father and the Son are one God in distinct persons.

In all this, without yet proceeding to evangelical testimonies, he confines himself entirely within the limits of the Law, in which he demonstrates that the name, power, reality, and nature of God—and hence truth—are attributed to the Son. By “Law” he means everything contained in the sacred writings composed before Christ’s birth.

### 1. It is dangerous either to agree with or to oppose heretics who proclaim one God.

In replying in the preceding books to the impious and mad teachings of the heretics, we were not unaware that we had been brought into such a necessity of contradiction that our answer would stir up no less danger in its hearers than silence would. For when the irreverent assertion of unbelief urged one God, [Note: The editions read, “the assertion of profane unbelief.” The better manuscripts more suitably read, “the profane assertion of an unbeliever.” There is an antithesis: “profane” and “religiously”; “an unbelieving assertion” and “sound faith.”] and, on the other hand, sound faith could not religiously deny one God, discussion of that subject could occur only with awareness of a twofold danger: it might be affirmed no less impiously than it might be denied.

Indeed, to human judgment this will perhaps seem absurd and contrary to reason: that what it is irreligious to deny should itself be irreligious to confess. For the piety of confession condemns the impiety of denial; nor [Col. 0130A] does it accord with reason that what is profitably affirmed should be profitably overthrown. But human understanding, imprudent in its approach to the understanding of divine wisdom and foolish according to heavenly wisdom, judges according to its own weaknesses and reasons according to the frailty of its own nature. It must become foolish to itself in order to be wise toward God: that is, recognizing the poverty of its own understanding and pursuing God’s wisdom, it must not be wise according to human wisdom, but must reason according to that by which it advances toward God, passing into God’s wisdom through its recognition of the world’s folly.

The subtlety of heresy, adapting the understanding of this foolish wisdom as an occasion for deceit, professed one God, using the authority of the Law and Gospels, in which it is said: “Hear, O Israel, the Lord your God is one” (Deut. 6:4; Mark 12:29). It was not ignorant how much danger there was in either answer [Col. 0130B] or silence; and it awaited from both an opportunity for impiety. Thus, if a conniving silence confirmed the holiness of the saying which the heretics had used unbelievingly, [Note: Vatican Basilica manuscript: “the security of the saying.” Shortly after *infideliter* (“unbelievingly”), supply “by the heretics.”] [Note: Paris has *convenientis*. But the manuscripts read *coniventis* or *conibentis*, with *u* changed into *b*, as often happens. From this the Chartres and Vatican Basilica manuscripts have corruptly produced *cohibentis*.] then, because God is one, the Son of God would nevertheless not be God, while God alone remained one. But if contradiction arose against this presumptuous and impious profession, an answer which did not confess one God [Note: The negative particle, wrongly deleted by Lipsius, is restored on the authority of Badius, Erasmus, and the manuscripts.] would not preserve the truth of evangelical faith, since our faith’s confession is of one God; and the confession which professed one God—the Father and the Son—would fall back into the impiety of another heresy. [Note: Badius and Erasmus, following a more recent Colbert manuscript, read “would not profess”: wrongly, and contrary to the other books. Hilary’s entire argument may briefly be stated thus: just as those who do not oppose heretics proclaiming one God run the danger of seeming to deny that the Son is God, so those who oppose them face a double danger: they may seem either to deny one God, or at least to proclaim the Father and the Son as one God in Sabellius’s manner. In fact, the heretics commonly defamed Catholics under this charge. Accordingly, instead of *recideretque* (“and would fall back”), we would much prefer *recideretve* (“or would fall back”).]

Thus worldly wisdom, which is folly with God, would deceive under the appearance of pleasant and deadly simplicity, [Note: The Vatican Basilica manuscript, with the Chartres manuscript and several others, reads “subtlety.”] since it established as the beginning of its creed a proposition with which we must either impiously agree [Col. 0130C] or oppose. By the danger in either course it would secure that the Son of God is not God because God is one; or it would force upon us the necessity of heresy, if, while confessing both Father-God and Son-God, we were deemed to proclaim one God according to Sabellius’s impious opinion. Thus, by this method of its preaching, one God would either exclude another, or would not be one through another [supply: “one”], or would be one only in names: because unity would know no other, another would permit no union, and two could not be one. [Note: Vatican Basilica manuscript: “union.”] [Note: Lipsius supplied from himself “could not.” The sense is: one could not be two, except merely in names.]

[Col. 0131A] ### 2. By what moderation Hilary guarded against every danger. The aim of the preceding book.

But we, having attained the wisdom of God, which is folly to the world, and intending through the wholesome and sincere confession of the Lord’s faith to expose the fraudulence of viperish doctrine, began our answer in an order which would both gain access for demonstrating the truth and not entangle itself in the danger of an impious confession. We held a mean between the two: not denying one God, but proclaiming God and God on the authority of him through whom one God was proclaimed; [Note: “Through whom” does not refer to God but to Moses, on whose authority the preceding book demonstrated God and God, when the heretics were abusing Moses’s authority to preach one God as solitary.] and teaching one God not by union, nor again cutting it down into a number of diverse beings, nor confessing against this that he is one merely in names. Rather, while the question of unity was still deferred for fuller treatment, we showed God and God.

For the Gospels rightly attest that Moses proclaimed one God; and Moses, while proclaiming one God, is authority that God and God are faithfully taught in the Gospels. Thus no contrary answer was made to authority, but an answer was made from authority, lest it should be permissible to deny that the Son of God is God because God is one to Israel, [Note: Five more recent manuscripts read, “because ‘Hear, O Israel.’” One Colbert manuscript reads, “because he says, ‘Hear, O Israel.’”] when the same authority who authorizes the preaching of one God also authorizes the confession that the Son of God is God.

### 3. The aim of this second book. The source of the truth of a thing.

The order of the connected treatise accordingly follows the order of the question. For since the following proposition of impious flattery is set forth—“We know one true God”—the entire argument of this second book concerns whether the Son of God is true God. [Note: The Vatican Basilica manuscript reads, “of this fifth book.” Yet with the others we retain “second,” and thus this book is called not with reference to the whole work, but either because in it Hilary again attacks the heretics’ perfidy, first opposed in the preceding book, as we have said; or because it is the second book from his return to the interrupted work, whose first three books may be regarded as certain preliminaries that could easily be detached from the rest.]

[Col. 0131C] For without doubt the subtlety of heretical ingenuity arranged itself in this order: first saying one God, then confessing one true God, so that it might thereby turn the Son of God away from God’s nature and truth. For if truth remained in the nature of the one God, it would not exceed the natural truth of that one. Therefore, because there is no room for doubt that Moses, when preaching one God, is understood to have indicated concerning the Son of God that he is God, let us return to those same authorities of his indication and ask whether, in indicating him as God, Moses also teaches that he is to be understood as true God.

No one doubts, moreover, that truth arises from nature and power. For example, true wheat is that which, formed into an ear, fenced about with awns, stripped from its husks, [Col. 0132A] ground into meal, [Note: “Ground into *far* [meal].”] [Note: Most manuscripts: “ground into *far*.”] made into bread, and consumed as food, has supplied from itself both the nature and the service of bread. Therefore, since the power of nature supplies truth, let us see whether he whom Moses signifies to be God is true God. We shall speak later of the one God and of that same true God, lest, without first giving assurance concerning the one and true God subsisting in Father and Son, [Note: The editions read: “of the one true God subsisting in Father and Son.” They are corrected from the manuscripts. By “subsisting,” moreover, he calls the Father and Son distinct in persons, in order to avert from himself suspicion of Sabellian error.] the dangerous suspicion of an expectation held in suspense exhaust the reader with anxiety.

### 4. The Son is proved true God from his power of creating.

The creation of the world, therefore, after it has conveyed knowledge of God and signified that the Son of God is God, I ask: in what respect does it deny that he is true God? For there is no doubt that all things are through the Son. For, according to the Apostle, all things are through him and in him (Col. [Col. 0132B] 1:16). If all things are through him, all things are from nothing, and nothing is not through him, I ask in what respect the truth of God is lacking to him, who lacks neither God’s nature nor God’s power. For he employed the power of his own nature so that things which were not might exist and things which pleased him might be made. “And God saw that they were good.”

### 5. In “God who speaks” and “God who makes,” the Law distinguishes only persons. The speaker and maker possess one nature. The Son of God is neither a false nor an adoptive God.

For the Law introduced no distinction other than that of person when it said, “And God said, ‘Let there be a firmament’” (Gen. 1:6), and then added, “And God made the firmament” (ibid., 7). [Note: Chartres manuscripts: “another.” Old Colbert: “another of person,” omitting “than.” Worse still: “some other of person.” Nothing should be changed. Tertullian aptly says, *Against Praxeas*, 12: “You have two: one commanding that it be made, the other making it. But how you should understand ‘other,’ I have already stated: in the name of person, not substance; for distinction, not division.”]

But it distinguished neither power, separated no nature, and changed no name in him in whom it supplied only the understanding of the speaker, in order [Col. 0132C] to convey the indication of the maker. The designation of one who speaks does not take away the truth of nature and power; indeed, it commends that truth itself with the greatest precision. For to bring about in deed what is spoken belongs to the nature which, as an efficient cause, can supply what it speaks. In what respect, then, will he who accomplishes not be true, when he who speaks is true, seeing that the truth of the act follows the truth of the saying?

God is he who said; God is he who made. If truth is in the saying—that is, in the one who said it—I ask why it is denied in the act—that is, in the one who made it. Unless perhaps this one is true in speaking, while that one is not true in making. We have, therefore, in the Son of God, who is God, truth of nature. He is God, he is Creator, he is Son of God, he can do all things.

[Col. 0133A] It is too little to say that he can do what he wills, since will is always a matter of power. Indeed, he can do what is said to him. For perfect power belongs to this: that the nature of the maker can do what the word of the speaker can signify. Thus, since whatever can be said can also be accomplished, the operation which corresponds to the sayings possesses the nature of truth. [Note: Earlier edition: “can be accomplished.”]

Therefore the Son of God is not a false God, not an adoptive God, not a God jointly styled as such, [Note: The editions read “a merely denominative God,” against the manuscripts.] but true God. And there is no need to demonstrate anything from the contrary, by which he would not be true God. [Note: The reviser of the Chartres manuscript seven hundred years ago here deleted the negative particle, though not with bad sense. Shortly afterward, in the same manuscript and in the older Colbert, Remigius, and other manuscripts, the reading is “to be demonstrated,” not “to demonstrate.” As far as can be gathered from what follows, the meaning is: it is not now necessary to expound what the opponents allege, by which they are led to suppose that he is not true God.] For the name and nature of God in him are enough for me. For he is God through whom all things were made. [Note: Vatican Basilica manuscript alone: “Genesis has spoken this to me concerning the Creator of the world.”] The creation of the world has told me this concerning him. God is matched with God in name; truth is matched with truth in work. As the saying signifies God as powerful, so the act gives the understanding of God as powerful.

[Col. 0133B] And after these things I ask: by what authority is truth of nature denied in the confession of Father and Son, when both the power of the name and the name of the power have fulfilled it? [Note: In a more recent Colbert manuscript an interpolator added here, “or divinity,” which subsequently passed into the editions of Badius and Erasmus. Later Lipsius substituted “or of divinity,” and Paris retained it.]

### 6. Objections drawn from the Gospels will be answered elsewhere. Why. Truth is not understood unless the objections are proved false.

The reader, however, should remember that I am not now silent concerning questions usually raised because I have forgotten them or distrust the answers. For such sayings as, “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28), and similar expressions, are neither unknown nor misunderstood, so as not to teach through themselves the nature of true God in the Son. But the order of our answer ought to follow that of the opposing proposition. The progress of pious preaching must tread down the tracks of that impious system, blotting out the very first signs of the deceitful doctrine that turns aside into this profane and irreligious path.

Therefore, setting aside and reserving until the end the proclamations of the Gospels and Apostles, let our present whole struggle against the impious rest upon the Law and the Prophets, refuting their fabricated and deceptive perversity, for the present, by the very sayings by which they attempt to deceive. [Note: Thus the Verona manuscript. The earlier edition has “refuting.”] [Note: The editions, except Paris, have “refuting,” with no old manuscript supporting them, but more scrupulously observing grammatical rules.]

For truth cannot otherwise be understood except by exposing as false those things advanced against it; and this disgraces liars all the more fully if their very lies promote the truth. Indeed, in the judgment common to human opinion, false things are by no means associated with true things, nor are these kinds of realities maintained by mutual agreement. For, owing to the difference of kind and nature’s opposition, discordant things never coalesce, diverse things do not agree, and things alien to one another are not mutually common.

[Col. 0134A] ### 7. The Father, by saying “Let us make,” signifies that the one to whom he speaks is equal to himself.

Since this is so, I ask how, between true God and false God, the following saying is to be understood: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26). Words express a meaning; meaning is the movement of reason; truth impels the movement of reason. Let us therefore follow meaning from the words, understand reason from the meaning, and apprehend truth from reason.

For I ask: he to whom it is said, “Let us make man in our image and likeness”—in what respect is he not true after the likeness of the one who speaks to him? [Note: That is, in what respect is he not true after the manner of the one who says this to him? We have already observed the similar force of the preposition *secundum* (“according to,” “after the likeness of”) in the notes on the *Treatise on Psalm* 139, 10.] For undoubtedly this saying proceeds from the intention and understanding of the speaker. Therefore he who says, “Let us make,” signifies one who does not disagree with him in making, is not alien or weak, but is capable of making the thing about which the speech is made. Without doubt, therefore, the speaker is to be understood to have thought this, because he spoke it.

### 8. By saying “in our image,” the speaker indicates one nature shared with the Son.

Moreover, in order that a fuller truth of nature and operation might be taught, he who expressed his understanding through words also joined to the reasoning of that understanding truth derived from nature, saying, “in our image and likeness.” Where is the false God here, to whom true God says, “in our image and likeness”? “Our” admits neither union, nor diversity, nor separation. For humanity is made, according to the truth of the words, in a common image. But fellowship does not belong to false and true. God who speaks speaks to God; humanity is created in the image of Father and Son. The name does not differ; the nature [Col. 0134C] does not differ.

For the form of the image in which humanity was created is one. [Note: Vatican Basilica manuscript: “the likeness of the image,” omitting the subsequent word “form.”] Amid these things, where does truth disappear, when both fellowship in the act and the truth of the common image remain between the two? This question is not yet to be completed; later we shall show in what image of God the Father and God the Son humanity was created. For the present, we hold this: is not he true God to whom true God said, “Let us make man in our image and likeness”? Distinguish, if you can, true from false in this fellowship of image; and in heretical madness sever these inseparables. For they are one, whose image and likeness have one humanity made as their exemplar. [Note: The editions read “in whose,” against the manuscripts. Shortly after, the Vatican Basilica manuscript with Chartres reads, “humanity is one”: this is not satisfactory.]

### 9. Humanity, to be made in the image of Father and Son, is made [Col. 0135A] in the image of God.

But let us follow the sequence of the reading, so that truth, always consistent with itself, is not altered by the stumbling-block of falsehood: “And God made man; in the image of God he made him” (Gen. 1:27). The image is common: God made humanity in the image of God. I ask him who denies that the Son of God is true God: in the image of which God does he understand humanity to have been made by God?

Yet he must always remember that all things are through the Son, lest perhaps a heretical interpretation assign to itself the working of God the Father. If, therefore, humanity is formed in the image of God the Father through God the Son, it is also formed in the image of the Son; for no one denies to the Son the saying, “in our image and likeness.” Therefore the divine word maintained in its sayings the principle of truth which the work accomplished in deeds: God formed humanity in the image of God, [Col. 0135B] in order to signify God without taking truth away from God, since the true God, who was understood in accomplishing the work, was God the Son in the fellowship of the image.

### 10. The heretics are rebuked from the words spoken.

O ruinous madness of a desperate mind! O foolish recklessness of blind impiety! You hear “God and God”; you hear “our image”: why do you add “true and not true”? Why introduce natural and false? Why overthrow religion under religion’s name? Why, by “one God” and “one true God,” do you attempt to prevent the true God from being one?

I do not yet choke your mad spirits with Gospel and apostolic sayings, in which Father and Son are each one and true God, not by person but by nature. For the present, the Law alone kills you. Did it say “true God and not true God”? Did it employ the term “God” differently in the two except as a name of nature? It said “God and God,” though it said “one God.” But why do I say that it merely said this? Through the truth of the image it proclaimed true God and true God.

First it employed, in naming, the name of nature; next it uses, in kind, the truth of nature. For when the one who is made is created according to the image of both, it cannot fail that both are true God. [Note: “From both.”] [Note: Erasmus, Lipsius, and Paris read “in both”; Badius, with most manuscripts, “from both.” We prefer “from true [God]” with the older Colbert, Remigius, German, and other manuscripts.]

### 11. The Son, as a person other than the Father, is called the Angel of God; as sharing the same nature, he is called God. Why he is called God’s angel.

But let us continue even now along that course of proclamation by which the holy Law has taught concerning God. The Angel of God speaks to Hagar, and that same Angel is God. Yet perhaps he is not true God because he is the Angel of God. For this name appears to denote an inferior nature; and where there is a designation of another kind, truth belonging to the same kind is judged not to be present.

Indeed, the preceding book has already shown the emptiness of this question. In “angel” the understanding concerns office rather than nature. For the prophet is my witness, saying: “He makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a burning fire” (Ps. 103:4). Therefore that burning fire is one of [Col. 0136A] his ministers, [Note: “Those ministers.”] [Note: In the printed editions: “those ministers,” etc., then “his spirits.” In the Corbie manuscripts, one Vatican manuscript, and the Pratensis manuscript: “and making spirits”; in the others, “and coming spirit,” that is, a spirit who comes, sent to announce something.] and the coming spirit is one of his angels. By these words the nature or power of messengers, who are called angels, and of ministers is shown.

Thus this spirit becomes an angel, or this burning fire becomes God’s minister; and their nature receives the office of messenger and minister. [Note: “The office of ministry.”] [Note: Two Colbert manuscripts read, “that it may announce, the office of ministry.” The other manuscripts support this, since almost all have “the office of ministry.” From Hilary’s interpretation it is clear that the Psalmist’s passage must be understood thus: “He makes spirits and burning fire his angels and ministers.” Hence he infers that spirits are not by nature what they become, or what is added to them after their original establishment.]

Therefore, wishing to reveal the person bearing the paternal name—or rather, God through the Law wishing to do so—the Law called God the Son the Angel of God, [Note: The editions read “the Son of God.” The manuscripts more suitably read “God the Son.”] [Col. 0136B] that is, God’s messenger. For in “messenger” it attests the designation of an office; but in calling him God it confirms the truth of nature. This, however, is now an order of dispensation, not of kind. For we preach no other than Father and Son; and we make the natures signified by the names equal, so that the birth of the only-begotten God from the unbegotten God possesses the truth of God.

The designation of sender and sent here teaches nothing other than Father and Son. It does not, however, take away the truth of nature or destroy in the Son the proper character of innate divinity. For no one doubts that in a son’s birth the nature of the begetter is born with him, [Note: The Chartres copy reads “from one.”] so that what exists from one exists as one, since through one it is not distinguished from one. Thus they are one because one is from one.

[Col. 0136C] ### 12. Hilary’s ardor of faith exceeds his intended scope.

O impatient fervor of faith, and silence unable to restrain the discourse for which it longs! For already in the preceding book we exceeded the limit of the proposed argument. When, criticizing the heretics’ impious assertion of one God and teaching that Moses proclaimed God and God, we descended, with pious though unconsidered haste, to the true and religious confession of one God. And now also, while lingering over the business of another question, we have not maintained the order we set; and while speaking of God the Son as true God, we have burst forth, in the ardor of a fervent spirit, as far as the confession of true God in Father and Son.

But let the truth of our faith be reserved for its own treatment. Though it has been introduced for the reader’s assurance, it must nevertheless be treated and completed more fully [Col. 0136D] for the despair of the opponent.

[Col. 0137A] **13. The Angel showed Himself to Hagar as God, in words and deeds.**—The name of an office, therefore, does not bring about a change of nature: for He who is the Angel of God is God. He would certainly not be true God unless He both spoke and acted the things of God. For He increases Ishmael into a great nation and promises him, through his name, the multiplication of nations. And I ask whether this is the work of an Angel. But if it is the power of God, why do you take away the truth of the nature from Him whose power of truth you do not take away? The power of the nature, therefore, retains the certainty of truth; and amid the saving mysteries of His dispensation for the world, He who is true God does not know how ever not to be true God.

> [Note: That is: He who is true God, when, for the sake of our salvation, accommodated Himself to our weakness, made Himself visible to human beings, and was called an Angel.]

> [Note: [Col. 0137D] In the earlier printed editions the word *true* is omitted, and it does indeed seem redundant. Yet the manuscripts have it with unanimous agreement. We therefore judge that the first occurrence of “true God” is to be referred to the Father. Arius is expressly refuted here. In the *Thalia*, as Athanasius testifies (*Oration 2 against the Arians*, p. 311), he dared to say: “For the Word is not even true God; and, even if He is called God, He is not true God, but is so by participation in grace, just as all the others; thus He too is called God by name.”]

**14. He who is God is true God.**—And first I ask what distinction of meaning there can be between “true God” and “not true God.” For I do not grasp the rationale of this expression if someone says to me, “It is fire, but it is not true fire,” or, “It is water, but it is not true water.” I ask in what respect the truth of something of the same kind differs from the truth of its kind. For that which is fire cannot fail to be true fire; nor can a nature, remaining what it is, lack being true.

> [Note: One Vatican manuscript, with Corbie and Saint-Prat, reads *manens in eo* (“remaining in it”), less well.]

> [Note: *In eo*: “in it.”]

Destroy from water that by which it is water, and thereby you may abolish its being true water. But if water remains, it must also persist in being true water. A nature can perish only if it does not exist; but, while it remains, it cannot be untrue. Either the Son of God is true God, in order that He may be God; or, if He is not true God, neither can He be that which God is. For if the nature is not present, the name of the nature does not belong to Him; but if the name of the nature belongs to Him, the truth of the nature cannot be absent from Him.

> [Note: A Vatican manuscript reads, “who, if by nature…” The reading *cui si* would not be objectionable. Yet the other manuscripts more correctly have *quia si*, supplying “in Him.”]

[Col. 0137C] **15. The God whom Hagar named in the appearance of an angel, Abraham worshipped in the form of a man. By worshipping, he was justified. He worshipped true God.**—But perhaps, when the Angel of God is called God, the name is granted by adoption, and in Him there is a designation of God rather than truth. If, when He was called the Angel of God, He insufficiently manifested God’s nature in Himself, then understand, under the name of an Angel, that He was still of an inferior nature; and ask whether He displayed from Himself the truth of God.

> [Note: “Still of an inferior form.”]

> [Note: In many manuscripts, “still of an inferior form”; the word *form* is superfluous as synonymous with *nature*, and is absent from the older Colbert, Carnotensis, and German manuscripts. Hilary presses the point against Arius’s recently mentioned blasphemy, according to which the Word is called God merely by name and through participation in grace—*metochē charitos kai onomati* (“by participation in grace and by name”).]

For a man spoke to Abraham, but Abraham worshipped God. But, O pestilential heretic, Abraham confessed as God Him whom you deny to be God. What blessings promised to Abraham do you impiously expect? He is not, for you, the father of nations that he is; nor, reborn through the blessings of his faith, do you enter into the family of his seed.

> [Note: *Suae* (“his own”) is absent from the old Colbert manuscript.]

You are not raised up from stones as a son of Abraham; rather, you stand forth as a brood of vipers, hostile to his confession. You are not the Israel of God; you are not Abraham’s posterity; you are not justified by faith, for you have not believed God. For by that faith Abraham was justified and made father of nations—the faith by which he worshipped the God in whom he had believed. For that blessed and faithful patriarch worshipped God (Gen. 18:14); and understand what true God he worshipped: Him to whom, as He Himself says of Himself, no word is impossible. Or is not every word possible to God alone? Or, I ask, what is lacking to true God in Him for whom every word is possible?

[Col. 0138B] **16. He recognized the righteous Judge. Even according to the heretics themselves, God alone is the righteous Judge.**—And I ask: who is this God, the destroyer of Sodom and Gomorrah? “The Lord rained from the Lord”: was not the true Lord from the true Lord? Or what else is the Lord from the Lord? Or what, apart from the indication of distinct persons, will you attach to “Lord” and “Lord”?

> [Note: The more recent manuscripts with the printed editions read, “or anything else.” Others read, “or what else?” The point is that the One born is not something other than the Father, nor distinguished from Him except as Lord from Lord—that is, by reason of origin.]

And remember that you have professed Him whom you know as the only true God to be this same only righteous Judge.

> [Note: Arius, in his letter to Alexander, as preserved by Athanasius, Epiphanius, and the acts of the Council of Aquileia, professes God to be Judge of all, as noted above (col. 106, note l of this edition). But Hilary did not there read “Judge,” but “Creator”; indeed, neither Athanasius nor the others have “righteous,” but “Judge of all.” Consequently, the words of the aforementioned letter are not indicated here, but Arian propositions reported in Book IV, §8.]

And understand that the Lord who rained from the Lord, who does not destroy the righteous with the wicked, who judges all the earth, is both Lord and righteous Judge, and rains from the Lord. And amid all this, ask whom you call the only righteous Judge. For Lord rains from Lord, and you will not deny that He who rains from the Lord is the righteous Judge.

For Abraham, the father of nations—and certainly not of unbelievers—said: “By no means will You do this thing, to destroy the righteous with the wicked, so that the righteous shall be as the wicked. By no means will You, who judge the earth, perform this judgment” (Gen. 18:25).

> [Note: Several sound manuscripts read “will You do.”]

Therefore this God, the righteous Judge, must also be true God. I hold you fast, impious man, by your own falsehood. I do not yet produce from the Gospels God as Judge: the Law has spoken to me of God as Judge. Take away from the Son His being Judge, if you would take away His being true God. For you have professed as the only true God Him whom you profess as the only righteous Judge; and Him whom you declare righteous Judge, you cannot, by your own principles, deny to be true God.

He who is Judge is Lord; He is mighty for every word; He is the guarantor of everlasting blessings; He is Judge of the godly and the ungodly; He is Abraham’s God; He was worshipped by Abraham. By the impious and foolish audacity of your assertion, invent at least one point from which He is not true God.

> [Note: Here are briefly gathered the grounds on which it was established that He who was seen by Abraham as a man is true God. He is Judge and Lord (Gen. 18:20; 19:24; 21:1); mighty for every word (Gen. 18:14); guarantor of eternal blessings (Gen. 17:19); Judge of godly and ungodly (Gen. 18:25); Abraham’s God (Exod. 3:2); and worshipped by Abraham (Gen. 18:2).]

**17. The Son was seen by the Fathers as that which He was born to be, without injury to His nature.**—The mysteries of heavenly mercy do not destroy the truth of nature; nor do the appearances adapted for the vision of faith deceive the faith of the saints. For the mysteries of the Law prefigure the mystery of the Gospel dispensation, so that the patriarch may see and believe what the Apostle contemplates and proclaims.

> [Note: “Contemplates and proclaims.”]

> [Note: Thus the old Colbert manuscript, with the German manuscript. Others read, “may contemplate and proclaim.” Since the period of the Law is here compared with the Gospel era, it is clear that “the mysteries of heavenly mercy” above denotes what the Son of God accomplished for us in the flesh; while “appearances” denotes everything in which He made Himself visible to the ancients in order to awaken their faith, and in which He represented what He was to do.]

For, since the Law is a shadow of things to come, the appearance of the shadow expressed the truth of the body. God is both seen, believed, and worshipped in a man—He who, in the fullness of time, was to be born in a man. For an appearance of prefigured truth is assumed for sight. At that time, under the Law, God was only seen in a man; He was not born. Soon, however, that which was seen was also born. The habitual acquaintance with the form of the appearance assumed for contemplation advances toward the truth of His birth.

> [Note: “If the appearance of the form…”]

> [Note: In the editions of Badius, Erasmus, and Lipsius, *formae* (“of form”) occurs, with *speciei* (“of appearance”) omitted. Many manuscripts read *formae speciei*; Corbie and Carnotensis, *formae species*; one Sorbonne manuscript, *formae specie*. With the Paris edition and certain manuscripts one should retain *formam speciei* (“the form of the appearance”). Hilary means what Tertullian says: the Son learned in flesh not yet born what He would afterward be. “He was learning,” says Tertullian, *Against Praxeas*, §16, “in order to prepare faith for us, that we might more readily believe that the Son of God descended into the world if we knew that something such had been done even formerly.” Thus the appearance, repeatedly assumed, in which as in a mirror the form of the One to be born was represented, served to make the truth of His birth credible.]

There a man, according to the weakness of our nature, is assumed so as to be seen through God; here, because of the weakness of our nature, that which had been seen is born. The shadow receives its body in Gospel times; the appearance receives truth; and the vision receives nature. Yet God is not changed from Himself when He is either seen or born for us in a man, since birth and vision have a mutual and familiar correspondence: what was born had been seen, and what had been seen was to be born.

And because this is not yet the place for our comparison of Gospel and prophecy, let us for the present follow the order appointed from the Law.

> [Note: The printed editions read “appointed”; then, “we shall later prove,” without *for*; and shortly afterward, “let us show from the Law … that God is worshipped and proclaimed Judge.” We follow the manuscripts.]

For later we shall prove from the Gospels that the true Son of God was born in a man; now, from the Law, we show that the Son of God, true God, was meanwhile seen by the patriarchs in the appearance of a man.

> [Note: “Let us show.”]

For when a man was seen by Abraham, yet God was worshipped and proclaimed Judge; and when “the Lord rained from the Lord,” there is no doubt that the Law speaks of Father and Son by the statement that the Lord rained from the Lord. Nor, again, should it be imagined that the patriarch did not know that he was worshipping true God when, knowing Him as God, he worshipped Him.

> [Note: A Vatican manuscript reads, “whom God…”—less well.]

**18. Heretics do not comprehend faith in the incarnate Word. Why the Gospels are from the Law.**—The impiety of unbelief entails no small difficulty in understanding true faith. Instruction in religious doctrine does not enter a mind narrowed by irreligion.

> [Note: The printed editions, with more recent manuscripts, read “the sense of irreligion.” Others more aptly read “by irreligion.” As perception is enlarged by piety and charity, so it is contracted into narrowness by irreligion.]

Hence it comes about that the irreligious mind cannot comprehend the things which God accomplished by being born in a man for the mystery of human salvation, because it does not understand that the work of its salvation is God’s power.

> [Note: Thus the manuscripts, as in Book IX, §4 and elsewhere. The printed editions read, “into a man.”]

> [Note: Paris reads “of a salvation not its own,” through a scribal error. Then Lipsius reads, “does not understand [this] to be truth,” with Badius and Erasmus agreeing, except that they add “of God” before “truth.” The manuscripts more correctly read “to be God’s power.” Paul’s statement in 1 Corinthians 1 is plainly intended: Jesus crucified is, for those being saved, God’s power.]

And, observing the birth of nativity, the weakness of infancy, the growth of childhood, the age of youth, the sufferings of the body, the cross of the sufferings, and the death of the cross, through these things they do not perceive true God.
