Yet He brought these things forth in Himself into nature, though they had not previously belonged to Him in the truth of His nature; so that He did not lose the truth of His nature, nor did God cease to be God when made man, since He who is God began to be man. They do not understand that it is possible only through the power of true God that what was not should come to be, and yet that what was should not cease to be.

> [Note: For greater clarity, something must here be supplied. In *On Psalm 2*, §25, this is expressed thus: “The accession of humility does not occur through a departure of divinity.” As Augustine says, man drew near to God; God did not withdraw from Himself. See Augustine, *Sermon* 186, §1. Hilary expresses it again in other words in *On Psalm 67*, §9: “The weaknesses which were in Him from us are not natural, but assumed.”]

For the assumption of weak natures could not occur except through the power of a mighty nature, which, while remaining what it was, could nevertheless become what it was not.

> [Note: The printed editions read “weak”; the manuscripts resist this. To grasp the force of the argument, recall that Hilary understands the Holy Spirit coming upon Mary in her conception to be the Word Himself, who by His own power formed for Himself a body from her.]

O heretical folly and foolish wisdom of the world, which does not understand the reproach of Christ to be God’s power, nor perceive the foolishness of faith to be God’s wisdom! Therefore Christ is not God to you because He who was is born; because He who is unchangeable grows in age; because He who is impassible suffers; because He who lives dies; because He who was dead lives; because everything in Him is contrary to nature? I ask: what else is this than to be omnipotent—which is to be God?

I do not yet appeal to the sacred and venerable Gospels in dealing with you, in order that Christ Jesus may be God in these sufferings on your authority.

> [Note: In the Vatican manuscript: “that Christ Jesus in these sufferings is true God.” The reason why “for you are from the Law” is then added concerning the Gospels is to be sought in Matthew 27, §10: “For both His coming and His passion are from the Law.” Thus, Saint Leo says, *Sermon I on Pentecost*, ch. 1: “Let the diligent Christian recognize that the beginnings of the Old Testament served the principles of the Gospel.” This is what Augustine says in *On Catechizing the Uninstructed*, ch. 4: “In the Old Testament is the concealment of the New; in the New Testament is the manifestation of the Old”; and in *Questions on Numbers* 33, on Num. 11:1: “For the same things are in the Old and New: there shadowed, here revealed; there prefigured, here made manifest.” In no other sense does Hilary say shortly afterward: “The mystery of your faith has borne witness by the power of its mysteries.” This also bears upon the beginning of §20. The Law teaches that the Son, through assumed weakness, does not lose what He was, since it recognizes and professes Him as God even when He appears in an alien and weak form.]

For you are from the Law, and it must teach that God, who is God, does not cease to be through assumed weakness. For the mystery of your faith has borne witness through the power of its mysteries.

[Col. 0141B] **19. Jacob saw God in the wrestling match—not with bodily eyes, but with the eyes of faith.**—Come now, holy and blessed patriarch Jacob; come, with the spirit of your faith, against the venomous hissings of unbelief. Though stronger than the man in wrestling, beg to be blessed by Him who is stronger than you (Gen. 32:26). What is this, that you entreat one who is weak, that you expect from one who is infirm? You overpower in your stronger embrace Him whose blessings you ask.

> [Note: Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “you ask His blessing,” and then “you hold in the deeds.”]

The action of your body differs from the work of your mind: for you perceive something other than what you do. In the gesture of your wrestling you hold a weak man; yet this man is true God to you, not by designation but by nature. For you do not ask, patriarch, to be blessed with adoptive blessings, but with true blessings. You wrestle with a man, but you see God face to face (ibid., v. 30). What you perceive with the sight of your faith is not what the eyes of your body behold. In your judgment He is a weak man; but your soul is saved according to the sight of God.

You are Jacob in the wrestling; after faith in the blessing sought, you are Israel (ibid., v. 28; see *On Psalm 52*, §21). A man is subjected to you according to the flesh, for the mystery of the Passion in the flesh; you do not fail to know God in the weakness of the flesh, for the mystery of blessing in the Spirit.

> [Note: As “flesh” above denotes human nature, so “Spirit” here denotes the divine nature. Thus Jacob, in asking a blessing, disclosed the divine nature of Him whom he saw weak in a man. Compare this passage with *On Psalm 52*, §21.]

Neither the appearance prevents faith from remaining, nor weakness deters the asking of blessing. Nor does His being man make it impossible that He who is man should be God; nor does He who is God fail to be true God, because He who is God cannot fail to be true God, and blesses, translates, and names.

> [Note: A Vatican manuscript reads, “nor does a weak man prevent Him who is man from being God.” The word “prevent” is not objectionable.]

> [Note: A Vatican manuscript, one Colbert manuscript, and Carnotensis read, “true God.” With the others, retain “true God is.”]

> [Note: “And blesses by naming.”]

> [Note: The best Colbert manuscript and the German manuscript omit the words “and by blessing and translating and naming.” Most other witnesses vary considerably. Badius, with the Vienna and Remigius manuscripts, has “and blesses by naming.” The Silva Major manuscript has “and blesses by translating and naming.” Corbie, Saint-Prat, Faur, Colbert, with Erasmus and Lipsius, have “and blesses, translating by naming.” Another Colbert manuscript and one Sorbonne manuscript agree, except that they add “you” after “blesses.” In Carnotensis, the first hand reads corruptly, “and blesses translating naming”; a second hand corrected it to the text, as read in Paris, in the Vatican manuscript, the other Colbert manuscript, and several others. “And blesses by naming Israel” would not be objectionable. Whatever the reading, the blessing is placed in the transfer and change of name by which Jacob is called Israel, because Israel means “one seeing God,” as is said in *On Psalm 52*, §21.]

**20. From another vision granted to Jacob, the Son is shown to be true God. God is understood only through God.**—The shadow of the Law still preserves the order of the Gospel mystery and, as a true rival of apostolic teaching, prefigures its truth in its mysteries.

> [Note: Only the Badius edition reads “in the use of sleep”; the others read “in the vision of a dream.” The text is corrected from the manuscripts.]

In a dream-vision the blessed Jacob had seen God (Gen. 28:13). In the dream there is revelation of the mystery, not bodily contemplation. For the descent and ascent of angels to heaven by a ladder is shown; God resting upon the ladder is shown; and the interpretation of the vision prophesied the revelation of the dream. For, by the patriarch’s words, the place of this vision is shown to be both the house of God and the gate of heaven (ibid., v. 17).

And after a lengthy narration of his deeds, the following occurs: “God said to Jacob, Rise and go up to Bethel, dwell there, and make there a sacrifice to the God who appeared to you when you fled from the face of Esau” (Gen. 35:1).

> [Note: “Go down.”]

> [Note: Badius, Erasmus, and Lipsius, as well as the Vatican, Carnotensis, Corbie, and other manuscripts, read “go down.” With Paris and the excellent Colbert manuscript, we retain “go up.” Thus in Book IV, §28: “Rising, go up.”]

> [Note: Thus the manuscripts, except that the Vatican exemplar and one Colbert manuscript read, “make there a sanctuary.” The printed editions read, “offer sacrifice.” This passage is cited somewhat differently in Book IV, §28: “make there an altar to the God who appeared to you.” This indicates that Hilary often cites Scripture from memory.]

If evangelical faith has access through God the Son to God the Father, and God cannot be understood except through God, then tell us how the God who seeks honour for the God standing above the ladder to heaven is not true God. Or what diversity of nature is there in the two, where one and the same name belongs to the same nature? God was seen; God speaks concerning the God who was seen. God cannot be understood except through God, just as God receives honour from us only through God. For God will not be understood to be worthy of honour unless this One has taught that He must be honoured; nor will God be known unless this God has been known.

> [Note: The printed editions read “He has therefore.” The word “therefore” is better absent from the manuscripts. Before “He has,” Erasmus inserted: “He is the door, as He testified of Himself in the Gospels; David therefore declares Him the gate of heaven in the Psalm.” Erasmus says that he found these words added in one exemplar and considers them sewn on. They do indeed illustrate the passage, which we have just explained from John and Matthew.]

The dispensation of the mysteries has its own order. Through God we are taught to render honour to God.

> [Note: The printed editions read, “has the order of its mysteries”; Lipsius here deleted the particle *ad*. The Paris edition alone then reads “we are led” for “we are taught.” Erasmus reads, “we are taught through God, who is also life and the gate, to honour God,” from a gloss. There are many examples in Hilary’s Psalms commentaries of *doceo* with *ad*: thus, in *On Psalm 130*, §1, the Psalm is said to teach us to humility and gentleness.]

Nature retains its name: neither is anything other than God. And where the one name of one nature belongs to Father and Son, I ask how God the Son can degenerate from Himself so as not to be true.

> [Note: A Vatican manuscript reads, “the Son from God could…” Then a Vienna manuscript, one Vatican manuscript, and Badius read “deny.” In Corbie, by a second hand, “lest He should not be true”; in Vienna, “because He is true.” Nothing should be altered, but *ne verus sit* should be understood as “so as not to be true,” a construction familiar to Hilary. After *ne verus sit*, Erasmus adds a confused interpolation concerning the presumption of divine honour, nature, Jacob, the assumption of flesh, and the Son being seen and worshipped. The interpolator’s composition is altogether badly arranged.]

**21. Secular learning or innocence of life does not suffice for this.**—We must not form our thought about God according to human judgments. For we do not possess a nature capable of raising itself by its own powers to heavenly knowledge. We must learn from God what is to be understood concerning God, because He is known only with Himself as author.

Even if the painstaking discipline of secular learning is present, even if innocence of life is present: these may indeed advance one toward the joy of a good conscience, but they will not attain the knowledge of God. Moses, adopted as the son of the queen and instructed in all the learning of the Egyptians (Acts 7:22), although from natural affection he had avenged by the death of an Egyptian the wrong done to a Hebrew (Exod. 2:12), nevertheless did not know the God of his fathers’ blessings.

> [Note: The ancient Colbert and Carnotensis books read, “all the doctrines of the Egyptians”; this differs from Acts, “all wisdom”—Greek: *pasē sophia*.]

Then, fleeing Egypt through fear of the disclosed killing, while he was shepherding sheep in the land of Midian, he beheld fire in a bush without the bush being consumed; he heard God, asked His name, and learned His nature (Exod. 3:1 ff.). For these things concerning God could not have become known except through God. Therefore we must speak of God in no other way than as He Himself has spoken of Himself for our understanding.

[Col. 0143C] **22. The Son spoke from the bush, and He is true God.**—The Angel of God is He who appeared in fire from the bush; and God speaks from the bush in the fire. You have the dispensation in “Angel,” because in “Angel” there is an office, not a nature; you have God in the name of nature, because the Angel of God is God. But perhaps He is not true God. Is the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob not true God? For the Angel who speaks from the bush is their God forever. And lest you frantically seize an occasion for an adoptive name, that God speaks to Moses who is: for thus it is written:

> “And the Lord said to Moses, ‘I am He who am.’ And He said, ‘Thus shall you say to the children of Israel: He Who Is has sent me to you’” (Exod. 3:14).

The discourse began from the Angel of God, so that the mystery of human salvation in the Son might be understood. He is the same God of Abraham, God of Isaac, and God of Jacob, so that the name belongs to His own nature. Then God who is sends to Israel, so that it might truly be understood that He is what God is.

**23. Nor is He who gave the Law false.**—What falsehoods, with the frenzied spirit of ineffective heretical impiety, do you utter against these things? You, the nocturnal sower, sowing among the wheat of noble seed the tares destined for burning, against the knowledge of so great patriarchs? But if you believed Moses, you would believe also God, God’s Son—unless perhaps you will deny that Moses spoke of Him. When you seek to deny this, you will hear the words of God: “For if you believed Moses, perhaps you would believe Me also; for he wrote of Me” (John 5:46).

> [Note: *Forsitan* (“perhaps”) is absent from the older Colbert manuscript.]

Certainly He will refute you—He whom Moses received in the whole volume of the Law, arranged through angels by the hand of a Mediator. Ask whether He who gave the Law is true God, since undoubtedly He who gave it is the Mediator. Or did not Moses lead the people out to meet God at the mountain (Exod. 19:17)? Or did not God descend upon the mountain (ibid., v. 20)? Or perhaps is this a false and adoptive name rather than the name of His nature?

> [Note: One manuscript omits *quam* (“rather than”).]

> [Note: Here we add *quam* on the authority of the old manuscript of Saint Peter’s in the Vatican. The reader who collated the Carnotensis exemplar seven hundred years ago wrote the same particle above the line; from this it entered one Colbert manuscript. It is omitted in other witnesses.]

Consider the sounding trumpets, the flames of lamps, the smoke from the mountain, burning like furnaces, the trembling of human weakness conscious of the coming of God, and the death acknowledged by the people under God’s voice, when Moses had been asked to speak for them (Exod. 20:19).

> [Note: The printed editions read “Moses”; the manuscripts more correctly read “with Moses having been asked,” that is, Moses was asked by the Israelites to speak to God for them, lest they perish in terror at God’s voice.]

Is He not true God to you, heretic—He whose voice Israel feared to hear, lest it die merely because He spoke, and whose voice human weakness could not endure? Is He therefore not God to you because, in order that you might hear and see Him, He spoke through the weakness of a man?

> [Note: In Corbie and a few other manuscripts: “and live”; a reading not to be despised. The sense is: Is He whom the people of the Law feared to hear speaking in majesty, lest they die, not God to you because now, accommodating Himself to your weakness, He speaks to you in the humility of flesh, so that you may now hear and see Him without fear—or so that, hearing Him, you need not fear for your life?]

Moses ascended the mountain (ibid., v. 24); for forty days and nights he received knowledge of divine and heavenly mysteries; he ordered all things according to the likeness of the truth shown to him on the mountain; through familiarity with God speaking to him he received the glory of unseeable brightness; and the intolerable light of the nearby majesty filled the perishable appearance of his face. He bears witness to God; he speaks concerning God; he summons the angels of God to worship this One with the rejoicing of the nations; he invokes His pleasing blessings upon Joseph’s head (Deut. 33:16). And after these things, when only the name has been granted Him, does anyone dare deny that He is true?

**24. Summary of what has thus far been proved in this book.**—Now, since we consider that throughout this whole discourse we have shown that no rationale can intervene in human thought so as to make “true God” and “false God” conceivable, when the Law has spoken of God and God, of Lord and Lord; and that no diversity has been indicated in names and natures, so that nature might be understood only according to the name of nature, and the name according to nature—since God’s power, God’s authority, God’s works, and God’s name were present in Him whom the Law proclaimed as God—

> [Note: Lipsius and Paris read “whom”; other books read “which,” namely, the Law.]

—these things, according to the arrangement of the Gospel mystery, indicated the distinct persons: God, obedient to God’s words in creating the world; God the Creator, sharing with Him the common image and the image of God in the fashioning of man; the Lord who is Judge, from the Lord, in judging the Sodomites; and the Angel of God who is God, in bestowing blessings and determining the mysteries of the Law.

> [Note: The printed editions read “Lord”; some manuscripts more correctly read “God.” This single sentence shows how compressed Hilary’s style is elsewhere. He calls the Son “God the Creator,” because of Genesis 1:27: “And God made man.” He adds “sharing with Him the common image,” because the Father said to Him, “Let Us make man in Our image.” He then adds “and the image of God,” because what was first described as a common image is afterward said to be the image of the one God: “He made him in the image of God.” Therefore do not delete the particle *and* before “image of God,” although it does not occur in the Vatican manuscript.]

Thus God, always shown in God the Father and God the Son, taught the truth of nature by the very name of nature, since the Law, signifying both as God, left no ambiguity concerning the truth.

**25. The heretics who deny that the Son is true God are answered. The Son is truly what He was born to be.**—Now is the time not to permit what the Law has taught piously and religiously to be proclaimed impiously through the theft of heretical folly. This folly, intending to deny that the Son of God is God, began thus: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one” (Deut. 6:4).

> [Note: Erasmus, Lipsius, and Paris read “intending to deny God.” *God* is absent from Badius and one manuscript.]

And because its impiety was endangered by the name, since the Law had spoken of God and God, it added, in order to deny through the authority of prophetic speech the nature signified by the name: “They shall bless you as true God” (Isa. 65:16). Thus, the Law’s declaration of one God was made to mean that in God the Son there was a name rather than truth, since only one true God was to be understood.

> [Note: That is, only one true God is to be understood.]

And perhaps, foolish man, you suppose that we contradict your statements by denying one true God. Certainly we do not deny it, while confessing it in your sense—that is, in the manner in which you do. For this is our faith, this our conviction, this our declaration. But we understand God as one, and the same God as true God. Nor is our confession endangered in the name, for it proclaims one and true God in the nature of the Son.

> [Note: The Carnotensis manuscript, with one Colbert manuscript, reads “the Son,” less accurately. “In the nature of the Son” means in the affirmation that the Son is God’s Son not merely by designation and adoption, but by nature.]

Learn the meaning of your confession, and recognize the one and true God so that you may piously proclaim the one and true God. For you seize our profession of religion for your own impiety: you deny what is, while not denying what is. Thus you deceive foolish wisdom, so as to destroy truth under the appearance of truth.

> [Note: Thus Paris with the manuscripts: that is, you deceive those who trust more in petty human reasonings than in God’s words. Badius, Erasmus, and Lipsius read “the foolish wisdom of the world,” which can also be suitably understood in the fifth and sixth cases.]

You confess one true God in order to deny one true God. For your profession is thought pious precisely where it is more impious; true precisely where it is false. Thus one and true God is proclaimed by you in such a way that He does not exist. For you deny that the Son of God is true God, though you do not deny that He is God; yet you confess Him as God not by nature, but by name.

If His birth is a matter of name rather than truth, you can take truth away from the name. But if He was truly born God, I ask how He can fail truly to be what He was born to be. Either deny that He is, so that He may not be; or, if He is, how will that which is fail to be, when that which is cannot be so as not to be?

> [Note: In the preceding passage: “How can that which is fail to be, when that which is cannot be so as not to be?” The Erasmus edition agrees with our book.]

> [Note: The printed editions read *ut non*; we prefer the manuscript reading, understood as though it read: “when it cannot come about that something should not be what it is.”]

There will shortly be discussion concerning His birth. For the present, however, I shall refute the impiety of your lie regarding the truth of God’s nature by the prophetic confession—yet in such a way that, while we proclaim one and true God, neither may Sabellius’s heresy arrogate to itself a confession that Father and Son are the same, nor may you, while proclaiming only one true God, falsely deny the truth concerning the Son of God.

### 26. Heretics are refuted for craftily citing Scripture in an interpolated form.

Impiety plainly possesses no wisdom within itself; and where the fear of God, which is the beginning of wisdom, is absent, it carries away with it every beginning of prudence. For the prophetic saying is brought forward to weaken faith in the true God in the Son: “And they shall bless thee, the true God.” First, this was the folly of impiety: that what had been said above (supply: by the same prophet) was either not understood, or, though understood, was suppressed. Then, moreover, by what fraud it equipped itself through the addition of a syllable—an addition which does not occur in the books! It employed this lie for its folly, as though its statements were to be trusted so far that it did not think the authority of the prophetic words themselves ought to be consulted.

[Note: [Col. 0147D] In the manuscripts: “addition.” That this fault was customary among the Arians we learn from Ambrose, who, *On Faith*, II.15.355, denounces them as falsifiers of the Scriptures, and V.16.193 as interpolators of those same Scriptures. In the acts of the Synod of Aquileia, II, p. 795, he says to Palladius, convicted of this charge: “Today we prove that the divine Scriptures are falsified by you.” Hence the Fathers of that synod, in their letter, Ambrose X.6–7, complain to the emperors that they had been so refuted concerning falsification that they confessed it.]

For it is not written thus: “They shall bless thee, the true God” (Isa. 65:16); but, “They shall bless the true God.” For there is no slight force of ambiguity between “thee, the true God” and “the true God.” Where “thee” occurs, the pronoun appears to refer to another person; but where the syllable of the pronoun is absent, there the name is referred to the author of the saying.

[Note: [Col. 0147D] “To the authority of the saying.”]

[Note: [Col. 0147D] Nearly all manuscripts read, “to the authority of the saying.” Hilary sometimes uses an abstract term in place of a concrete one, and specifically *authority* in place of *author*, as in *On the Synods*, no. 33. What is here said of the author of the saying is said below, no. 31, to rest with the speaker.]

### 27. The Son is shown to be the true God precisely from the passage by which they suggested that He was false. Here Scripture, in calling the Son God, adds “true,” contrary to its usual manner, because there would be persons to whom this would be hidden.

And that the complete basis for understanding the truth may be available, the prophet’s very words in their entirety shall be set forth:

> Therefore thus says the Lord: Behold, those who serve me shall eat, but you shall hunger; behold, those who serve me shall drink, but you shall thirst; behold, those who serve me shall rejoice in gladness, but you shall cry out because of the pain of your heart, and you shall howl because of the affliction of your spirit. For you shall leave your name as a joy to my chosen ones, but the Lord shall slay you. But to those who serve me a new name shall be given, which shall be blessed upon the earth; and they shall bless the true God, and those who swear upon the earth shall swear by the true God.  
> (Isa. 65:13 ff.)

[Note: [Col. 0147D] “From affliction.”]

[Note: [Col. 0148D] The Chartres manuscript and certain others, as shortly in all instances, read “from affliction.”]

It is never without cause when the customary manner of proclamation is exceeded; and the basis for this novelty is a basis of falsity.

[Note: [Col. 0148D] “A basis of truth.”]

[Note: [Col. 0148D] The printed editions, with not a few manuscripts, read “a basis of truth.” More pleasing is the reading, with the very ancient Colbert manuscript, the German manuscript, and the Corbie manuscript in a second ancient hand: “a basis of falsity,” that is, where some ground for deception and error underlies the matter. Thus, for example, in Christ the mystery of the assumed body can furnish a reason why someone might be deceived into not believing Him to be true God. This reading is confirmed by the final words of this number.]

For although so great prophecies concerning God had previously existed, and the simple name of God alone had been mentioned to show God’s dignity and nature, we must ask for what reason the Spirit of prophecy now declares through Isaiah that the true God is to be blessed, and that men are to swear upon the earth by the true God. And first, it must be recognized that this saying announces events of a future time. And I ask whether He whom, according to the Jewish understanding, men then blessed and swore by was not the true God.

For the Jews, ignorant of the sacrament—that is, the mystery—of God, and thereby ignorant of the Son of God, worshiped God only, not the Father also [Col. 0147D–0148A] (*See* Book III, no. 17). For surely, if they worshiped the Father, they would worship the Son also. They therefore blessed God and swore by Him. But the prophet declares that the true God is to be blessed. He calls Him true God because, through the mystery of the assumed body, the reality of God in Him would not be understood by all. And confirmation of “true” was necessary where the assertion of “false” was about to break forth. Let us review each statement in turn.

### 28. This prophecy signifies one thing present and another future. What is present concerns carnal Israel; what is future, spiritual Israel.

> Therefore thus says the Lord: Behold, those who serve me shall eat, but you shall hunger; behold, those who serve me shall drink, but you shall thirst.  
> (Isa. 65:13)

Recognize, under this single statement [Col. 0148B], the signification of both times, that you may attain the mystery of the age. “Those who serve me shall eat.” Present religion, certainly, is rewarded with future recompense, so that the punishment of future thirst and hunger may be brought to completion upon present impiety.

Then He added:

> Behold, those who serve me shall rejoice in gladness; but you shall cry out because of the pain of your heart, and you shall howl because of the affliction of spirit.  
> (ibid., v. 14)

According to the preceding meaning, this too is a disclosure of future and present time: those who serve will rejoice in gladness; but those who do not serve will remain in crying and howling because of pain of heart and affliction of spirit.

Thereafter He added:

> For you shall leave your name as a joy to my chosen ones, but the Lord shall slay you.  
> (ibid., v. 15)

The saying is directed to carnal Israel with a signification of the future, reproaching it because it will leave its name to God’s chosen ones. I ask: what is this name? Surely, Israel, to whom the saying was then addressed. Next I ask: who is Israel today? Indeed, the Apostle testifies that those who are so in spirit, not in letter—those who walk according to the rule of Christ—are the Israel of God (Rom. 2:29).

### 29. Isaiah shows the Son to be true God by three titles. The Christian name is the new name.

Moreover, since above it was said, “Therefore thus says the Lord,” we must understand why this is followed by, “But the Lord shall slay you”; and then, after this, what this saying means: “But to those who serve me a new name shall be given, which shall be blessed upon the earth” (ibid., v. 16).

Can there be any doubt that in the words, “Therefore thus says the Lord,” and in what follows, “But the Lord shall slay you,” this was shown: that He who spoke and He who would slay were to be understood as nothing other than the Lord—the One who afterward would reward those serving Him with a new name, who was known also to have spoken in the prophets, and who would be judge of the godly and ungodly?

[Note: [Col. 0149C] The printed editions read “not another [person].” The manuscripts more correctly read “not another [thing],” for the question concerns nature, not person. Hence above, no. 16: “The Lord rained from the Lord. Is not the true Lord from the true Lord? Or what else than Lord?” Hilary’s subsequent statement, as elsewhere, that the Son spoke in the prophets is not so peculiar to him that he does not also attribute this very thing to the Holy Spirit. Seeking to prove the Spirit’s divinity, he says in Book II, no. 32: “For the Holy Spirit is one everywhere, enlightening all patriarchs, prophets, and the whole choir of the Law.”]

The rest of the saying therefore explained the mystery of the evangelical sacrament, so that there might be no doubt about the Lord speaking and the Lord slaying: “But to those who serve me a new name shall be given, which shall be blessed upon the earth.” The entire saying concerns a future time. And what is this new name of religion which will be blessed upon the earth? If the blessedness of the Christian designation had ever existed from the ages before, it is not now new.

[Note: [Col. 0149D] The Vatican-Basilica manuscript reads: “If the name had ever been blessed before, it is now not a new name.” The Chartres manuscript, with one Colbert manuscript: “If there had ever before been a blessing, it is now not a new name.” Bade and Erasmus: “If blessedness had ever been before, it is now not a new name.” Other books are better: “it is now not new” (supply, *a designation*). For “name” has easily been made from “not.”]

But if this name, sanctified by our devotion toward God, is new [Col. 0149B], then this newness of profession is surely the reward of heavenly blessings upon earth.

[Note: [Col. 0149C] “Now it is a new name.”]

[Note: [Col. 0149D] The editions, except Paris, read “is sanctified”; then Erasmus and Lipsius, “our devotion toward God,” against the manuscripts.]

### 30. The words, “They shall bless the true God,” must be understood of Christ.

Now the following saying confirms the consciousness of our entire faith:

> And they shall bless the true God, and those who swear upon the earth shall swear by the true God.

Certainly, those whose new name consists in service to God will bless the true God; and then, the God by whom they will swear is true God. Can there be doubt whom they swear by, whom they bless, through whom those serving Him have their new and blessed name?

Against your impious proclamation, heretic, the fully certain faith of the Church’s saying stands with me: it swears that You, Christ, are true God, through the new name that is through You, and through the profession of service, through the designation blessed from You upon earth.

[Note: [Col. 0150C] The Vatican-Basilica manuscript here adds “your.”]

For every mouth of believers declares that You, Christ, are God. Every faith of believers swears that You are God, confessing that You are true God, proclaiming that You are true God, knowing that You are true God.

### 31. The same point is illustrated from the preceding sayings of the prophet.

Although, therefore, this whole prophetic discourse has left no difficulty in understanding that it signifies God [Col. 0150A]: the One who is served under the new name, the One through whom the newness of that same name is blessed upon earth, the One who is blessed as true God, and the One who is sworn by as true God—all of which the devout faith of the Church, in accordance with the fullness of times, professes in religious devotion toward the Lord Christ; and although the prophetic discourse so fitted itself to Him that it did not alter the signification of another person by adding a pronoun—for if it had added “thee, true God,” the saying could have been referred to someone other than the speaker, but when it says “the true God,” it left the understanding of the reference with the speaker—yet, though there is no doubt whom the present saying signifies, the words connected above show whose profession this must be understood to be.

For He says:

> I openly appeared to those who did not ask for me, and I was found by those who did not seek me. I said, “Behold, I am for a nation that did not invoke my name. I stretched out my hands all day to a distrustful and contradicting people.”  
> (Isa. 65:1–2)

[Note: [Col. 0150C] Erasmus first inserted from himself here, “Behold, I am present,” which Lipsius, retaining it, subsequently published on his own authority: “to nations which did not invoke.” Neither is corrected in the Paris edition; though all manuscripts read, “Behold, I am for a nation which,” etc., agreeing with the Greek, ἰδοὺ εἰμὶ τῷ ἔθνει, οἵ· nor does Hilary’s interpretation permit anything else, for he explains “Behold, I am for a nation” just as “I now belong to a nation.”]

Is the impious falsity of a stealthy proclamation obscure, and will the true God who says these things be unknown? I ask: who appeared to those who did not ask, and who was found by those who did not seek? Who belongs to the nations that had not formerly invoked His name? And who stretched out His hands all day to a distrustful and contradicting people?

Compare with this that sacred and divine Song of Deuteronomy (Deut. 32:21), in which God, provoked by non-gods, stirs the unbelieving to jealousy through a non-nation and a foolish nation; and understand who becomes manifest to the ignorant, who is claimed as one’s own by those formerly alien, and who, stretching out His hands before the distrustful and contradicting people, nailed to the cross the bond of the former decree and spread it out.

[Note: [Col. 0150D] The Vatican-Basilica exemplar reads: “stirred up, you unbeliever, see and understand”; the Chartres manuscript has the same in a second hand. Its first reading, which other books also have and which the sacred text confirms, was preferable: “stirs up the unbelieving.”]

[Note: [Col. 0150D] The editions read “becomes manifest.” Later Erasmus places in the margin, for “who is his own”: “Perhaps, who is his own.” He fails to perceive that Hilary understands the passage of Isaiah, “Behold, I am for a nation which did not invoke,” itself somewhat corrupted as noted above, as though it meant: “I am now God proper to those to whom I was previously alien,” or “to those who did not invoke me.” Nor does he more successfully conjecture that “spread out” should be read as “expunged,” as though the word referred to the bond rather than to the hands which Christ stretched out on the cross.]

For the Spirit of the prophet said, by a discourse continuous and joined together in sequence:

> But to those who serve me a new name shall be given, which shall be blessed upon the earth; and they shall bless the true God, and those who swear upon the earth shall swear by the true God.  
> (Isa. 65:16)

### 32. Paul interprets Isaiah’s words as spoken of the Son.

If heretical folly and impiety, in order to deceive the ignorant and the simpler-minded [Col. 0151A], falsely claims that these things were said in the person of God the Father, so that their meaning may not be received as applying to God the Son, let it hear from the Apostle and teacher of the nations the indictment of its lie. For he proclaims all these things to concern the mystery of the Lord’s Passion and the times of evangelical faith, when he reproaches the unbelief of Israel for not understanding the Lord’s coming in the flesh. Thus he says:

> For everyone who invokes the name of the Lord shall be saved. How then shall they invoke Him in whom they have not believed? But how shall they believe Him whom they have not heard? And how shall they hear without a preacher? And how shall they preach unless they are sent? As it is written: “How beautiful are the feet of those who announce peace, of those who announce good things!” But not all obey the Gospel. For Isaiah says, “Lord, who has believed our report?” Therefore faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word. But I say, have they not heard? Yes indeed: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.” But I say, did Israel not know? First Moses says, “I will provoke you to jealousy by a non-nation; by a senseless nation I will provoke you.” But Isaiah boldly says, “I appeared to those who did not seek me; I was found by those who did not ask for me.” But what does he say to Israel? “All day I stretched out my hands to a people who would not hear.”  
> (Rom. 10:13 ff.; Isa. 52:7; 53:1; 65:1)

[Note: [Col. 0151C] In the Chartres manuscript, in the first hand: “How swift are the feet.”]

[Note: [Col. 0151C] We have removed “of God” after “word,” on the authority of the ancient books.]

[Note: [Col. 0151C] The printed editions add “earth” here, which is absent from the manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 0151C] The editions read “who sought,” against the manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 0151C] “I stretched out,” according to the force of the Greek word ἐξεπέτασα.]

Who are you, that, having passed beyond the spheres of heaven—whether incorporeal or corporeal is uncertain—you have become a more trustworthy interpreter of prophetic sayings than Paul (2 Cor. 12:2)?

[Note: [Col. 0151C–D] Bade and Erasmus, with a single Colbert manuscript of very slight authority, read: “Who entered the third heaven, incorporeal or corporeal.” Other editions retain “entered.” The Chartres manuscript also had this in its first hand; but in a second hand, agreeing with the other manuscripts, it has “went out.” Clearly Paul’s rapture up to the third heaven is intended here—expressed in Ps. 135, no. 10 as “when he was caught up to the heavens.” Then, where “Who, reserved for the cross for the fullness of the Lord’s Passion” follows, there is an allusion to Col. 1:24: “I fill up what is lacking of the sufferings of Christ.” Thus Hilary compares his adversary with the Apostle, as though he transferred to the former what belongs to Paul.]

Who, having heard and kept silent about the ineffable mysteries of heavenly sacraments [Col. 0151C], have proclaimed these things with greater confidence as knowledge revealed to you by God? Who, while reserved for the cross unto the fullness of the Lord’s Passion, escaped by being previously caught up into paradise, have taught more rightly concerning the divine Scriptures than the chosen vessel, while ignorant that these things were said and done by the true God and proclaimed by His true and chosen Apostle for the understanding of the true God?

### 33. The Apostle interprets Isaiah from Isaiah’s own words. Isaiah saw God, and saw none other than the Son.

Unless perhaps the Apostle is a rash interpreter of another’s saying when he uses prophetic words not drawn from the Spirit of prophecy.

[Note: [Col. 0151D] Certain manuscripts read, “from the prophet’s Spirit.”]

The Apostle indeed says everything through Christ’s revelation; but he knows Isaiah’s sayings from Isaiah’s own sayings. For at the beginning of the discourse in which the true God is to be blessed and sworn by those who serve Him, this utterance of the prophet is read:

> From eternity we have not heard, nor have our eyes seen God apart from thee, and the works which thou wilt do for those awaiting thy mercy.  
> (Isa. 64:4)

[Note: [Col. 0151D] The editions read, “which you do,” against the manuscripts and the Greek, ἃ ποιήσεις, “which you will do.”]

Isaiah says that he saw no one as God except this One. For he saw the glory of God, whose mystery of embodiment from a virgin he had foretold.

[Note: [Col. 0151D] Bade and Erasmus read “had proclaimed”: wrongly. The Vatican-Basilica codex reads “was foretelling”; other books, more correctly, “had foretold.” The printed editions read “the mystery of incorporation”; the manuscripts more elegantly, “the mystery of embodiment.” To make Hilary’s argument clearer, it may be stated in a single syllogism: Isaiah saw God, Isa. 6:1, “I saw the Lord sitting,” etc.; but he saw no other person of God than the Son, Isa. 64:4, “Nor have our eyes seen God apart from thee”; therefore the Son is God.]

And if you, heretic, do not know [Col. 0152B] that in that glory he saw the only-begotten God, hear John the Evangelist saying: “Isaiah said these things when he saw His honor and spoke concerning Him” (John 12:41; Isa. 6:1).

[Note: [Col. 0152D] The printed editions read “glory,” a word not inconsistent with Hilary. Yet we restore “honor” on the authority of the manuscripts.]

By apostolic, evangelical, and prophetic sayings, therefore, impious heretic, you are enclosed. For Isaiah saw God; and although it is written, “No one has ever seen God, except the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father—He has declared Him” (John 1:18), the prophet nevertheless saw God and beheld His glory even to the envy aroused by his prophetic dignity. For on this account he was brought by the Jews to judgment of death.

[Note: [Col. 0151C] “Ever” is absent from the Verona manuscript.]

[Note: [Col. 0152D] “Ever” is absent here from nearly all manuscripts, though not so in Book V, no. 42, and Book VI, no. 39. The observation made at col. 127, note b of this edition—that the ancients commonly understood “God,” where the term occurs simply, to mean the Father—has particular force in these Johannine words. Hilary’s reasoning is thus: according to John’s testimony, Isaiah saw God; but John also testifies that no one has seen God the Father; therefore Isaiah saw God the Son.]

### 34. It is shown more closely that Isaiah proclaimed the Son to be true God. The deceit of heretics who deny this.

The only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, has declared God to be seen by no one. Either undo the declaration of the Only-Begotten, or believe Him who was seen; Him who appeared to those who did not understand Him;

[Note: [Col. 0152C] “Or believe God.”]

[Note: [Col. 0152C] “And was made manifest to a nation that did not invoke Him.”]

who became the God proper to nations that had not invoked Him, and who stretched out His hands before a contradicting people—yet so that a new name is given to those serving Him, and that true God is blessed and sworn by upon earth.

[Note: [Col. 0152D] The printed editions, with most manuscripts, read: “and was made manifest to a nation that did not invoke Him.” The Chartres exemplar reads: “was made in the midst of the nations,” etc. More correctly, the older Colbert, Remigius, and German manuscripts read: “was made [the God] of nations not invoking Him”; supply, “God proper to them.”]

Prophecy speaks, the Gospel testifies, the Apostle interprets [Col. 0153A], the Church confesses that He who was seen is true God; yet no one confesses that God the Father was seen. And the madness of heretical fury has broken forth to such a degree that, while it pretends to confess, it denies. For it denies by a new, impious design of confession;

[Note: [Col. 0152D] The manuscripts read “Prophecy.” Note that here faith is established not only from prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic testimonies, but also from the confession of the Church.]

[Note: [Col. 0153C] The Vatican-Basilica manuscript adds “its own.” An allusion is made here to the Arian letter to Alexander.]

and by subtle art, while it feigns faith, it evades it. For when, after the confession of one God—the same true, alone just, alone wise, alone unchangeable, alone immortal, alone powerful—the Son is introduced as differing in substance, not born from God into God but received as Son through creation, possessing not the name of nature but an appellation obtained by adoption, it necessarily follows that the Son lacks all those things which are proclaimed as privileges of majesty existing solely in the Father.

### 35. Arians do not know the one true God: why. What the preceding two books have accomplished, and what must now be accomplished.

Heretical perversity does not know how to know and confess the one true God; and both the faith and the understanding of this confession lie outside its sense of impiety. Father and Son must first be confessed, so that the one true God may be understood.

[Note: [Col. 0153C–D] The Vatican-Basilica exemplar reads “the true Father.” Since it contains additions of this kind elsewhere, it may be suspected that this has been corrupted by an interpolator’s hand. Why knowledge of the true God cannot enter the heretics’ understanding is explained in Book VIII, no. 6: “Since Christ is Wisdom, it follows that whoever either does not know or hates Christ is outside wisdom.”]

And once the mysteries of human salvation, which are completed in us unto life through the power of regeneration in Father and Son, have been known, the mysteries of the Law and the prophets must be pursued.

[Note: [Col. 0153D] The Holy Spirit ought to have been named here, unless the controversy were entirely concerned at this point with the Father and the Son. But the opening of Book II leaves no room for suspicion.]

Impiety, ignorant of evangelical and apostolic proclamation, does not grasp the one true God. Although we shall demonstrate its meaning from the teachings of those very preachers, even to the most complete profession of true piety, so that the Only-Begotten, subsisting from the Father indivisible and inseparable—not in person but in nature—may be understood [Col. 0153C], and so that He may be one God because He is God from God’s nature, nevertheless faith in this perfect unity must be constructed from prophetic sayings.

[Note: [Col. 0153D] “Their” refers to evangelical and apostolic proclamation, as if it had said “the evangelical and apostolic preachers.” Nor should the Son be understood as divided and separable from the Father even in person, except insofar as this signifies only the distinction of the two persons.]

[Note: [Col. 0153D] The printed editions read “must be established.” The Chartres manuscript in its first hand reads “built”; in its second, “instructed,” whence the same reading passed into one Colbert manuscript. The other manuscripts more suitably read “must be constructed.”]

And the foundations of the evangelical house must be laid from this point: that, through the same nature of the one divinity, one God may be understood because the only-begotten God is not referred to another God. For throughout this whole small book of our discourse we have maintained the order that, in the very passages in which we taught in the preceding book that the Son is God, we should now show Him to be true God. And, I hope, the conclusion of all these sayings has been such that He who was not denied to be God is understood as true God.

[Note: [Col. 0154C] The Vatican-Basilica manuscript omits “I hope.” Augustine uses it in the same sense for *to suppose*, in Epistle 157.22: “There are more followers of Caelestius,” he says, “than we can suppose.”]

But the whole remaining argument will now proceed to show that He who is understood to be true God is not counted as another God; and that what does not tend toward another is to be understood as tending toward one. Yet that “one” must not destroy the subsisting nature in the Son, but preserve in God and God the nature of the one God.

[Note: [Col. 0154C–D] The editions, with a single later Colbert manuscript, read: “does not proceed into another, that one.” After “toward another,” supply “for being constituted” or “for being understood”; and after “toward one,” understand “to refer the mind” or “to pertain.”]

[Note: [Col. 0154D] One Colbert manuscript reads “complete,” which the Chartres manuscript also has after revision; this is less consonant with Hilary’s meaning.]

### 36. From Moses: the Son with the Father is one God.

The reasoning of truth demands that this understanding take its beginning from him through whom God began to be manifested to the world—namely Moses, by whose mouth the only-begotten God made this declaration concerning Himself:

> See, see, that I am God, and there is no God besides me.  
> (Deut. 32:39)

[Note: [Col. 0154D] The printed editions here prefer “Moses,” and add “he says” after “declared,” against the manuscripts and with the context made somewhat abrupt. We prefer, with the ancient books, “for Moses,” without “he says”: that is, “namely, from Moses.” For, as has already been observed, Hilary elsewhere uses *namque* in the sense of *nempe*, “namely.”]

And lest perhaps heretical impiety should refer the force of this saying to the unbegotten God the Father, both the argument of the saying itself and the Apostle as authority intervene. As we showed above (Book IV, no. 33), he is the interpreter, speaking in the person of the only-begotten God, of the entire meaning of this discourse. He showed that the words, “Rejoice, nations, with His people” (Deut. 32:43; Rom. 15:10), belong properly to Him, adding, in confirmation of the saying:

> There shall be a root of Jesse, and He who rises to rule the nations; in Him the nations shall hope.  
> (Rom. 15:12)

Since, therefore, Moses has shown that He who said, “There is no God besides me,” is the One of whom he says, “Rejoice, nations, together with Him”; and since the Apostle understands this to refer to our Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten God—in whom, as the ruler of the nations arising according to the flesh from the root of Jesse, hope exists [Col. 0154C]—the argument of the saying itself must now be considered, so that, since there is no doubt that it was spoken, the extent of its meaning may be understood.

[Note: [Col. 0154D] Bade, Erasmus, and Lipsius read “in the Lord.” The preposition *in* was deleted in the Paris edition. The manuscripts read “to the Lord”; supply “to refer” or “to pertain.”]

### 37. He is God from God and in the same nature.

The true, complete, and perfect mystery of our faith is to confess God from God and God in God: not by bodily modes, but by divine powers; not by a transfusion of nature into nature, but by the mystery and power of nature.

[Note: [Col. 0154D–0155C] This “but” may be illuminated by Ambrose, *On Faith*, IV.9.103: “Generation does not lie in the possibility of will, but appears to lie in a certain right and property of the Father’s secret,” etc. What is here called “the mystery of nature” is called in Book VI, no. 19, “the sacrament of substance.”]

For God is not God from God by severance, extension, or derivation [Col. 0155A]; but He subsists by birth, from the power of nature, in the same nature. The book which follows, the clearer interpreter of evangelical and apostolic sayings, will speak of these matters more fully; meanwhile, however, what we speak and believe must be shown from the Law and the prophets.

The birth of God, then, cannot fail to retain the nature from which it came forth. For what subsists from no other source than God does not subsist as anything other than God.

[Note: [Col. 0155C–D] The printed editions read “God from God”; the word “God” is superfluous and does not occur in the manuscripts, in most of which the following word, as also shortly before, is “subsists.”]

And He possesses that same nature in such a way that He who was born is not Himself the One who begot Him—for how will He be Himself, if He has been begotten?—but that He who was begotten subsists in those very things in which the One who begot is wholly present, because what is begotten is not from elsewhere.

[Note: [Col. 0155D] Thus the very ancient Colbert, Corbie, two Remigius, three Vatican, Theodulf, German, and other manuscripts. Some other manuscripts, with the printed editions, read: “in whom the One who begot is wholly present, because He was not begotten from another. Nor is He anything other than God, because He is not from elsewhere,” etc.]

Thus what subsists in one from one is not referred to another; what lives from the living One is not new in itself; nor is what the Living One begot alive into the Living One absent from Himself.

[Note: [Col. 0155D] We have added the preposition *in* on the authority of the manuscripts. So also Book VII, no. 27: “For what is begotten alive from the Living One into the Living One is not new.”]

And so, in the generation of the Son, the incorporeal and unchangeable God follows, as it were, His own nature:

[Note: [Col. 0155C] “And, so to speak, follows His own nature.”]

begetting the incorporeal and unchangeable God. The perfect birth of the incorporeal and unchangeable God from the incorporeal and unchangeable God does not abandon its own nature, by virtue of that mystery that God subsisting from God is God.

[Note: [Col. 0156C] Here the Corbie manuscript has “so to speak” written above the line. This was inserted in the printed editions and later manuscripts, but is absent from the older ones.]

The only-begotten God testifies thus through holy Moses:

> See, see, that I am the Lord, and there is no God besides me.  
> (Deut. 32:39)

For there is no other nature of divinity such that any God exists besides Him.

[Note: [Col. 0156D] Bade, Erasmus, and Lipsius read: “so that another God may exist besides it.”]

For while He Himself is God, nevertheless God is also in Him through the power of nature. And because He Himself is God and God is in Him, there is no God besides Him: since that which is God does not exist from elsewhere, and God is in Him [Col. 0155C], possessing in Himself both what He Himself is and that from which He Himself subsists.

[Note: [Col. 0156D] That is, the Father is in Him in such a manner that He possesses both that which He is and that from which the Son Himself subsists.]

### 38. The indivisible divinity of Father and Son from Isaiah.

The same and one Spirit of prophecy confirms the true and saving confession of our faith, not altering, through succession and intervals of times, the proclamation of reverent doctrine. For in order that the words spoken through Moses in the person of the only-begotten God might be confirmed by fuller progress toward understanding, the same Spirit of prophecy speaks again through Isaiah, in a discourse concerning God the Father and in the person of exalted men:

> Because God is in thee, and there is no God besides thee. For thou art God, and we did not know it—the God, the Savior of Israel.  
> (Isa. 45:14–15)

Let the desperate frenzy of heretical impiety thrust itself into this inseparable confession both of nature and of name, and, if it can, tear apart these sayings and realities joined together with the rabid mouth of its madness.

[Note: [Col. 0155C] “Let it insert itself.”]

[Note: [Col. 0156D] The Chartres manuscript, with several others, and also Bade, Erasmus, and Lipsius, read “let it insert itself.”]

God is in God, and there is no God besides Him. Let it separate Him who is in from Him in whom He is; and let it divide the understanding of this mystery by diversity of kinds.

[Note: [Col. 0155C] “By the truth of kinds” is absent from our exemplar.]

[Note: [Col. 0156D] “By diversity of kinds” is absent from the ancient Colbert, Corbie, Remigius, Vindobonensis, and other books. Did it creep into the text from the margin?]

For in saying, “God is in thee,” Isaiah taught the reality of God the Father’s nature in God the Son, since God was understood to be in Him who is God. But in adding, “And there is no God besides thee,” he showed that there is no God besides Him because God is in Him as God. The third statement, “Thou art God, and we did not know it,” testifies to the devout and faithful confession of human understanding [Col. 0156B]: that, once the mysteries of the birth were known and the name Emmanuel had been announced to Joseph through the angel, men would confess, “For thou art God, and we did not know it—the God, the Savior of Israel.”

They understand that God’s nature subsists in Him, since God is in God and there is no other God besides Him who is God. For He Himself being God, and God being in Him, leaves us no error concerning any other God.

[Note: [Col. 0156D] The printed editions read “understanding.” But the manuscripts read “understanding [plural],” which must be referred to those who shortly before say, “we did not know.”]

And Isaiah, bearing witness to the indivisible and inseparable divinity of Father and Son, thus prophesied.

39. The same point is proved from Jeremiah. — Jeremiah likewise, with no less prophetic power, taught that the Only-begotten is God of a nature undivided from God the Father, saying: “This is our God, and no other shall be reckoned beside him. He found every way of knowledge, and gave it to Jacob his servant, and to Israel his beloved. After these things he appeared upon earth and lived among men” (Baruch 3:36).

[Note: The word “who” is not read in the manuscript, any more than in the Greek.]

Why do you heretically posit another God in the God who is the Son of God? Learn to understand and confess the one true God. No other God is reckoned beside Christ, so that he may be God. He is God by nature, by birth, from God. For the fact that he is God is from God; yet he is not another God. For no other is reckoned beside him, because in him there is no truth other than that which is God’s. Why, beneath the falsely assumed religion of one God, do you combine what is true and not true, degenerate and noble, different and different?

[Note: Thus most manuscripts. But the editor of the Chartres manuscript, whom I indicated at the end of this and the preceding book by the words “I have amended,” failing to notice that this reading creates a stronger antithesis between the clauses, inserted here the particle “not” [Col. 0157D]. The Vatican-Basilian manuscript and three other more recent manuscripts also display it. Yet only the printed editions read “and not different.” Moreover, as Athanasius testifies, *Oration II against the Arians*, p. 311, the Arians with their leader maintained in the *Thalia* that the Word was other, different, and wholly unlike the Father’s substance.]

God is Father, and God is also Son. God is in God; apart from him there is no God, nor is another reckoned beside him so that he may be God. If in these words you understand one God rather than a solitary God, you will profess the religion of the Church, which confesses the Father in the Son. But if, ignorant of the heavenly mystery, you put forward one God in the sense of a solitary God, you are outside the knowledge of God, since you do not confess that God is in God.

[Note: In the Colbert and German manuscripts, “also” stands in place of “are.” He is here called ignorant of the heavenly mystery who does not know God to be the true Father of the true Son; and it is repeatedly affirmed that one who does not know this does not yet know the name of God.]

131–132  
## BOOK SIX

At its very beginning, Hilary portrays the Arian plague as spreading through almost all the provinces of the Roman Empire. Its cure is exceedingly difficult, because error had acquired public authority for itself through the assent of very many people. Yet, moved by his episcopal office and by the hope of bringing many back to the truth [Col. 0157B], Hilary undertakes the defence of the faith. Although in the fourth book he copied out the letter of the Arian party in order to refute it from the Law and the Prophets, in this book he copies it again so that he may refute it more fully from the Gospels and Apostles. Going through it in turn, he unties its knots and lays bare its poison: namely, how, under the pretext of condemning heretics, they attempt to suppress the Church’s devout expressions—“the Son brought forth from God,” *homoousion*, “light from light,” and “begotten without beginning”—and, once faith is extinguished, to introduce heresy. Accordingly, he exposes what is corrupt among heretics and declares that it is condemned by the Church, while confirming what is devoutly proclaimed within her.

Then, prompted by the human reasoning by which they would make God composite or corporeal if the Son is said in Scripture to be begotten from God himself or from his womb—if we understand the Son to be from the Father’s substance [Col. 0157C]—he first observes that heresy is indeed audacious, but lacks wisdom. Next, he observes that it cannot be denied that Christ said, “I am from him”; and that, in saying this, Christ testified that he was neither from nothing, nor from any substance other than the Father’s, nor identical with him from whom he is. Finally, he maintains that it is wicked not to believe God, and therefore that no place is to be given to human reasoning that opposes Christ’s testimony; though it might say much, nothing else ought nevertheless to be set against it. Having recalled the heretics’ view, by which they interpret Christ as Son by adoption, God by designation, Only-begotten by privilege, and Firstborn by the rank which he holds among created things, he turns to God in a tone of complaint [Col. 0157D]: that God had deceived him through Moses and the Prophets, and that, when he had been incurably imbued with evangelical and apostolic teachings [Col. 0158A], God had produced for him these new teachers so late.

At last he comes to the establishment of the true faith. Since, if Christ is the true Son of God, it follows that the nature of God is present in him, in the final and most important part of this book he demonstrates that Christ is the true and natural, not adopted, Son of God. He does so by the united testimony of the Father, the Son himself, and the Apostles; and separately by that of Peter, Paul, and John; as well as by the confession of Martha, the man born blind, demons, Jews, certain persons endangered at sea, and finally the Gentiles.

### 1. The widely spreading Arian heresy can scarcely be driven out.

I am not unaware that I have undertaken to write against the mad heresy of the impious—which asserts that the Son of God is a creature—at a time most difficult and harsh. For already almost all the churches throughout the provinces of the Roman Empire have been infected by the disease of this pestilential preaching; and, as though in a wrongly usurped conviction of this devout faith, they have been imbued by long practice of the teaching and by the counterfeit name of true religion. Nor am I unaware how difficult is the willingness to advance toward correction, when devotion to its own error is held fast by the authority which the agreement of very many persons has already given to a public judgment.

For error among very many is grave and dangerous. The fall of many people, even if it recognizes itself, nevertheless arrogates to itself authority through shame at rising again; it derives from its number this insolence—that it wishes what is erroneous to be thought prudent, and asserts that what errs together with many is an understanding of truth, because error is thought less blameworthy when it is shared by many.

[Note: The Vatican-Basilian manuscript reads “of imprudence.” Lest anyone perhaps conclude from the beginning of this book that at that time the true faith had been almost extinguished throughout the whole world, one should recall what Socrates says, Book II, chapter 27: “The cities of Achaia and Illyricum, and the remaining churches of the western regions, were still calm and unshaken” [Col. 0158D], both because they agreed among themselves and because they held most steadfastly to the rule of faith handed down by the Council of Nicaea. Thus too Lucifer of Cagliari, in *One Must Die for the Son of God*, addresses the Emperor: “If you could traverse all nations in a moment, most foolish Emperor, you would find Christians everywhere believing as we do . . . But your novel preaching and recent religion—blasphemy advanced by you under the pretext of faith, to the destruction of your salvation—has not yet been able to traverse even the Roman frontier,” etc. Indeed Hilary himself, in the preceding book, section 30, challenges the heretics by the faith of the universal Church, “in which every mouth of believers speaks Christ as God.”]

133  
### 2. What moves Hilary to refute it.

And, beyond the obligation of my devotion and office, by which, as bishop of the Church, I owe this ministry of evangelical preaching, my concern for writing was all the more earnest because more persons were held in the danger of faithless understanding. I sought a fuller joy from the salvation of many, if, once they had learned the mysteries of perfect faith in God, they abandoned the impious doctrines of human folly, gave themselves back to God after rejecting the heretics, and rose from the food of death—by which birds are usually enticed into a snare—to the flight of free security. May they follow Christ as leader, the Prophets as messengers, the Apostles as forerunners, a faith brought to perfection, and salvation made perfect in the confession of Father and Son. And, remembering the Lord’s saying: “He who does not honour the Son does not honour the Father who sent him” (John 5:23), may they turn to honouring the Father through honour of the Son.

[Note: In some manuscripts the particle “that” is expressed here; its omission in others is not improper.]

### 3. The plague of the Arian heresy.

For a pestilential and deadly plague for peoples has recently emerged, and, raging with immense contagion, has brought the ruin of a pitiable death. Not even the sudden devastation of cities collapsing—or perhaps, “falling”—into chaos together with their peoples, nor the frequent deaths and funerals of wars, nor the widespread contagions of incurable disease have raged to such an extent as this fatal heresy has raged for the destruction of humankind.

[Note: The printed editions read “nearest.” But the manuscripts read “recently,” referring to “has emerged.” So in Book I, section 23, Arius’s letter to Alexander is said to have been issued “not long ago.”]

For with God, to whom all things live even in death, that alone perishes which perishes from him. Since he himself will judge all, and in the mercy of his majesty will temper the deserved punishment for error due to ignorance, he will certainly no longer judge those who deny him, but will deny them [Col. 0159B] (Matt. 10:33; see *Tractate on Psalm* 140, section 8).

### 4. How craftily it pours out its poison.

For the raging heresy denies—denies—the mystery of the true faith, employing the principles of religion in the service of its impious teaching. As has been set out in the preceding books, it began its exposition of unbelief thus:

> “We know one God alone, alone unbegotten, alone eternal, alone without beginning, alone true, alone possessing immortality, alone good, alone powerful.”

For it advances toward its intended end by this opening of devout confession—“one God, alone unbegotten and alone without beginning”—so that, after those points which were religiously displayed in words, the remaining assertions might be added impiously. For after many other statements about the Son, which it likewise uttered under the guise of a counterfeit profession of religion, it added:

> “A perfect creature of God, yet not like one of the creatures; a product, yet not like the other products.”

[Note: As though one creature among creatures.]

And, after many other things by which the intention of heretical impiety was veiled under interposed confessions of truth, it says, defending with the subtlety of ingenious interpretation the claim that he subsists from things that do not exist:

> “Created and established before the ages, he was not before he was begotten.”

[Note: The printed editions read “of this heretical impiety.” More correctly, “this” is absent from the manuscripts.]

Finally, as though all matters had now been most strongly fortified for the defence of impiety, so that he might be understood as neither Son nor God, it added:

> “For if ‘from him,’ and ‘from the womb,’ and ‘I came forth from the Father and have come’ are understood as though extending a part of his one substance and a kind of emanation, then the Father will be composite, divisible, changeable, and corporeal according to them; and, so far as lies in them, God, though without a body, will undergo the consequences of a body.”

[Note: The manuscripts read “profession”; the printed editions, “defence.”]

[Note: The printed editions here read “corporeal,” and below “body.” The manuscripts are more consistent.]

And because we are now to oppose this exposition of most impious doctrine completely by evangelical discourse, we thought it fitting to insert in this sixth book also the written statement of this heresy, even though it was set down in the first book. Thus a fresh reading and a comparison of the response to each individual assertion may, through evangelical and apostolic teaching, extract the meaning of truth even from unwilling and resistant persons. Therefore they say:

[Note: Our manuscript reads “in the fourth book,” but an ancient hand has corrected it to “in the first.”]

[Note: The more recent manuscripts, together with the printed editions, read “even though in the fourth book.” Two Vatican manuscripts read “even though in the first or fourth book.” But the older manuscripts, which are more numerous, read “even though in the first book.” This reading seemed to us more genuine, since it is less likely to have occurred to those who amend the ancients by conjecture. It is supported by the fact that the preceding book, section 3, is called not the fifth but the second; and this, as we said, because it is the second book against the faithless Arian profession of faith [Col. 0160D]. Although from another standpoint this same book is shortly called the sixth, Erasmus wrote in the margin here: “For my part, I do not doubt that it should be read ‘in four books,’” and Ludovicus Miraeus later agreed with him. They evidently did not notice that the discourse here concerns the faithless Arian letter, which up to this point has been published in one book, not four.]

[Note: This heading is absent from our manuscript.]

[Note: We have restored this heading, omitted in the earlier printed editions, from the better manuscripts.]

### An example of blasphemy.

### 5. Letter of Arius and his followers to Alexander.

> “We know one God, alone unbegotten, alone eternal, alone without beginning, alone possessing immortality, alone good, alone powerful, the unchangeable, immutable, just, and good creator, arranger, and disposer of all things: the God of the Law, the Prophets, and the New Testament. This God begot a Son, only-begotten before all ages, through whom he made both the age and all things. He was begotten not merely in appearance but truly, obedient to the Father’s will, immutable and unchangeable: a perfect creature of God, yet not like one of the creatures; a product, yet not like the other products. Nor was he, as Valentinus imagined, an emanation of the Father’s offspring; nor, as Manichaeus represented, a part of the Father’s one substance; nor, as Sabellius, who divides the union, called the same one both Son and Father; nor like Hieracas, a lamp from a lamp, or a torch divided into two parts; nor was he who previously existed afterwards born or super-created into sonship—as you yourself also, most blessed Pope, have often repudiated in the midst of the church and in the assembly those who introduce such things. Rather, as we have said, he was created by God’s will before times and ages, receiving life and being from the Father, and glorying while the Father coexists with him. For when the Father gave him the inheritance of all things, he did not deprive himself of those things which are held as unmade by himself; for he is the source of all things.”

[Note: Here it repeats: “like one creature among creatures.”]

[Note: The printed editions of Book IV had “who brings in union”; here they have “who divides union,” contrary to the manuscripts in both places.]

[Note: “Glorying.”]

[Note: The printed editions of Book IV read “to glory,” but here, with all the manuscripts, “glorying.” We have already noted that the letter *n* was added through scribal error (col. 106, note j of our edition).]

### 6.

> “Therefore there are three substances: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. God indeed is the cause of all things, wholly without beginning and solitary. But the Son, brought forth by the Father outside time, created and established before the ages, was not before he was begotten; but, born outside time before all things, he alone subsisted from the Father alone. For he is neither eternal nor coeternal, nor unmade together with the Father, nor does he possess being together with the Father, as some say, introducing two unbegotten principles. Rather, as God is the unity and principle of all things, so he is before all things. Therefore he is also before the Son, as we too have learned from you preaching in the midst of the church. Accordingly, since he has from God his being, his glorying, his life, and all things have been given to him, God is his principle in this respect. And God rules over him as his God, because he is before him. For if ‘from him,’ and ‘from the womb,’ and ‘I came forth from the Father and have come’ are understood as though extending a part of his one substance and a kind of emanation, the Father will be composite, divisible, and changeable, and corporeal according to them; and, so far as lies in them, God, though without a body, will undergo the consequences of a body.”

[Note: In the oldest manuscripts of St Martin of Tours, the Vatican-Basilian manuscript, and the Colbert manuscript, “he subsisted from the Father alone” reads “he subsisted from the Father.” This is not bad, if they were consistent with Book IV. But the Greek has: “he subsisted from the Father” (*hypo tou Patros hypestē*), omitting “alone.”]

[Note: “Subsists.”]

[Note: The printed editions add here “he always was,” which the manuscripts, agreeing here and in Book IV, more correctly omit.]

[Note: The printed editions read “and to glory.” The Vatican-Basilian manuscript has “and glorying and living”; others, “and glorying and to live”: the same corruption as above.]

[Note: “And mutable,” as above in Book IV; it has also been added here in our copy by an ancient hand.]

[Note: In one manuscript, after the word “God,” “Truth” is added: an addition in another hand, intended to distinguish the holy Doctor’s words from the heretics’ assertions.]

### 7. The poison hidden in this letter.

Who does not perceive in these words the slippery turns of a serpentine path, or fail to understand the viper’s knots in tortuous coils, by which the dominant power of a venomous mouth is enclosed within the gathered circle of its coiled body? But when everything is stretched out and uncoiled, the entire poison of the hidden head will be laid open.

[Note: The printed editions read “of the twisting spirit”; they are corrected from the manuscripts. Athanasius similarly portrays the deceptive contrivances of Arian heresy, *Oration II against the Arians*, p. 316: “What heresy is not worthy of hatred when it is concealed even from its own followers through distrust, and cherished like a serpent?”]

First, names of truth are pressed upon us so that the poison of falsehood may enter. There is good upon the lips so that evil may come in from the heart. And amid all this I nowhere hear them call the Son of God “God from God”; nowhere do I find the Son proclaimed as Son in such a way that he is Son. The name “Son” is introduced so that the nature may be silenced; the nature is taken away so that the name may be foreign. Other heresies are put forward so that heresy may lie concerning itself.

[Note: “So that the forces of falsehood may enter.”]

[Note: Thus very few recent manuscripts and the printed editions. The rest have, “so that the forces of falsehood may enter.” The latter reading is supported by “the dominant power of a venomous mouth”; the former by “the entire poison of the hidden head.” Since the former prevailed, we have not altered it.]

[Athanasius makes the same observation, *Oration I*, p. 313.]

“One God alone” and “alone true” are introduced so that the Son of God may not be left with that true and proper being which belongs to God.

### 8. What Hilary now proposes to discuss.

Although, therefore, in the preceding books—that is, Books IV and V—we have taught from the preaching of the Law and the Prophets how God and God, true God and true God, and one true God in true God the Father and true God the Son are to be understood according to unity of nature, not union of person; nevertheless, the full exposition of this faith must be supplied from evangelical and apostolic teaching, so that the true Son of God, as God, may be understood to be not of a nature alien from and different from the Father, but of the same divinity, existing through the truth of his birth.

[Note: “The completion of this faith must be proclaimed through evangelical and apostolic teachings.”]

And certainly I do not think that anyone can be so mad as either not to understand God’s declarations about himself when they are known, or, having understood them, not to wish them to be understood by others, or to suppose that they need correction by the prudence of human opinion.

[Note: The printed editions read “not to wish them to be understood,” and shortly afterwards, “by the prudence of human opinion.” The excellent Colbert manuscript, with the Corbie manuscript and others, reads more aptly “would not wish,” and thereafter, with the support of the St Martin and Chartres manuscripts, “by the opinion of human prudence.” Hilary constantly insists that human prudence, uncertain and tossed by various opinions, must never be preferred to the certainty of faith.]
