But before we begin to speak of the matters themselves, the saving mysteries, we must expose every covering of this ingenious malice, lest, once the heretics’ names have been published, the profession of heresy flatter itself in any respect. Thus, by the very means through which the hidden poison conceals itself, it may be betrayed and revealed, and the perception of public conscience may enter into an understanding of its seductive venom.

[Note: “We begin.”]

[Note: “Betrayed and revealed,” referring to “of the seductive [venom],” etc.]

[Note: The manuscripts read “betrayed and revealed,” referring to “of the seductive [venom],” etc.]

### 9. Valentinus’s inventions. The Church is alien to them. By the name “emanation,” heretics seek to abolish birth.

Therefore, wishing to deny that the Son of God is from God, and that God, born from God, is from the nature of God and within that nature, after they had earlier mentioned one God alone, true, without adding “Father”—so as to deny that Father and Son possess one truth, while excluding the distinctive property of birth—they said:

> “Nor was he, as Valentinus imagined, an emanation of the Father’s offspring.”

[Note: “That is, from the nature, namely the substance.”]

Thus, under the appearance of condemning the heresy of Valentinus, they condemned the name “emanation” in order to condemn God’s birth from God.

[Note: The printed editions read “Valentinian,” against the manuscripts. Thus in Book II, section 4, even with the agreement of the printed editions, one reads “Valentinians,” not “Valentinianists.” Likewise, in the book *On the Synods*, Arius’s followers are called Arius’s adherents, not “Arians”; and above, Book V, section 25, several good manuscripts read “the Sabellian heresy.”]

For Valentinus, inventing certain ridiculous and foul notions, introduced, besides the chief God, a family of gods and the powers of numerous aeons, or eternities; and then he maintained that our Lord Jesus Christ was brought forth through the mystery of a hidden will.

[Note: “Ages.”]

[Note: Some manuscripts read “ages”; some others “vanities.” More correctly the remaining books read “eternities,” the Latin rendering of the Greek word *aiōn*, from which the Aeons derive their name.]

[Note: “Then brought forth.”]

The evangelical and apostolic faith of the Church knows nothing of this empty emanation, devised by the madness of a rash and foolish author. For it knows nothing of Valentinus’s Bythos (*bython*), “Depth,” and Silence, and thirty Aeons; it knows only one God the Father, from whom are all things, and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things: God born from God.

[Note: “Bython.”]

[Note: Thus with the Corbie manuscript. Others read “bythonam”; earlier printed editions read “bythonas,” incorrectly. For Valentinus admitted one Bythos, that is, “Depth”—which, according to Epiphanius, *Heresy* XXXI.2, was Hesiod’s Chaos—not several, as may be seen in Irenaeus, Book I, chapter 1; Tertullian, *On Prescription*, chapter 49; Epiphanius, *Heresy* XXXI; Philastrius; and others. Tertullian briefly summarizes his fables in the cited passage: “He says that first there are Bythos and Silence; from them proceeded Seed, Mind, and Truth; from these burst forth Word and Life; from these in turn were created Man and Church—behold the first Ogdoad of Aeons; and from these also proceeded twelve Aeons, and from Word and Life another ten: this is the thirtyfold company of Aeons,” etc. Hilary seems to have treated *bython* among the ancients in the accusative case as though it were nominative, like *bythōn, bythōnos*; hence he could form *bythonam*, just as in *Commentary on Matthew*, chapter 16, section 4, and chapter 26, section 5, he formed *theothetam*.]

[Note: Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read, “For it knows no other [thing].”]

But because God born from God neither took from God, by his birth, the being which belongs to God, nor is himself, in being born, not God; and because he did not begin to be what he is as God, but is born from God; and because that which is born seems, according to human understanding, to have been brought forth in such a way that emanation itself is considered birth—therefore an attempt was made, through Valentinus’s heresy, to exclude the name “emanation,” lest the truth of the birth remain. For the concept of emanation, owing to an earthly conception, would not be far removed from the character of earthly birth.

[Note: The word “born” omitted in the earlier printed editions is restored from the manuscripts.]

[Note: The earlier printed editions read “God is from God”; the word “God” is superfluous and absent from the manuscripts. The Son is denied to have begun, because, being born from God and not made, he possesses the substance and nature of God, which has no beginning.]

The slow and difficult human understanding of divine matters requires that we be reminded more often of what has already been said by us (Book I, section 10, and Book IV, section 2), lest examples drawn from human comparison be thought sufficient for the mysteries of divine power. Such examples present merely an image of an earthly kind, in order spiritually to train the mind concerning heavenly things, so that by this step belonging to our nature we may be advanced to an understanding of divine majesty.

God’s birth is not to be judged by the processes of human births. Where one is from one, and God born from God is concerned, earthly birth provides only an understanding of the signification; the origin of those who are born does not otherwise suffice as an example of comparison, since it includes intercourse, conception, time, and delivery. God born from God must be understood as nothing other than begotten. In its proper place we shall discuss the truth of divine birth according to evangelical and apostolic faith. Meanwhile, however, the ingenuity of heretical craft needed to be shown: it would extinguish the word “emanation” in order to abolish the truth of birth.

### 10. They condemn Manichaeus in order to remove *homoousion*. The Church knows no portion of God in the Son, but fullness.

The same malicious fraudulence of their craft persists in the rest of their statement when it says:

> “Nor, as Manichaeus represented, [was he] a part of the Father’s one substance.”

Emanation was denied above in order that birth might be denied. Now, under Manichaeus’s name, they introduce the denial of a portion of one substance, in order that God from God may not be believed.

[Note: The Paris edition alone reads “by denying,” wrongly. The phrase “portion of one substance” is rendered in the Greek language, in which this letter was first published, as *meros homoousion*, “a portion consubstantial.” This makes clear that the Arians feared the term *homoousion* greatly not only after the Nicene synod, but also before it. They seek to reject it again where they say: “For if ‘from him’ is understood as a part of his one substance,” in Greek, *tou homoousiou*.]

For Manichaeus, in his unrestrained frenzy of condemning the Law and the Prophets, a professed advocate of the devil so far as in him lay, and an ignorant worshipper of his own sun, proclaimed that which was in the Virgin to be a portion of one substance; and he wished that to be understood as the Son which appeared in flesh as extracted by some division from God’s substance.

[Note: “Of his own sun.”]

[Note: The printed editions read “of himself alone”; one Remigius manuscript reads “alone of himself.” Better, the others read “of his own sun.” For the Manichaeans, as Augustine relates in *On Heresies*, XLVI, pray toward the sun as it journeys around them throughout the day, wherever they may be; and he says above that they call this corporeal light the nature of God. Here “an ignorant worshipper” means an unlearned worshipper. Hilary, I think, adds “his own” to “sun” because the sun exists for the sake of man, not man for the sake of the sun.]

Thus, in order that the birth of the Only-begotten Son and the name “one substance” might be removed, “a portion of one substance” is put forward in connection with the Son’s birth. Since that which is asserted concerning the birth from a portion of one substance is preached profanely, first, birth itself would cease to exist, because in Manichaeus it has been condemned under the profession of a portion; then the name and faith of one substance would be removed, because among heretics it would apply to a portion. By this means God would not be from God, because the distinctive property of the divine nature would not be present in him.

[Note: The Vatican-Basilian manuscript reads: “nor would the distinctive property of the divine nature be present in him. Why [do they feign] mad comparisons,” etc. The other books prefer that reading to the one here.]

What mad anxieties does impious frenzy counterfeit under the appearance of invented religion? According to the preachers of heretical madness, the devout faith of the Church condemns Manichaeus.

[Note: The printed editions read “devout”; the manuscripts, “devout [faith].” That is, the faith which, in a devout and sound sense, proclaims *homoousion* condemns Manichaeus no less than the Arians themselves do. This seems to be Hilary’s meaning in the phrase “according to the preachers of heretical madness.” For Hilary commonly uses *secundum* in the sense of “after the manner of” or “equally with.”]

For it knows no portion in the Son; but it knows whole God from whole God, one from one—not cut off, but born. It knows that God’s birth is neither a diminution of the begetter nor a weakness in the one begotten. If God knows this from himself, bring your charge against his rashly claimed knowledge; but if you have learned it from your Lord, allow the one begotten to possess knowledge of his own birth. For these things are thus known to him from the only-begotten God: that Father and Son are one, and that the fullness of deity is in the Son. Therefore it hates the notion of a portion of one substance as applied to the Son, and through the truth of birth it reveres in the Son the distinctive property of true divinity.

[Note: “Rashly.”]

[Note: Thus the Colbert and German manuscripts. Most others read “rashly”; the Chartres and St Martin manuscripts, “through rashness”; the printed editions, “to rashness.”]

[Note: The Basel, Erasmus, Leipzig, and Paris editions add “he.” The manuscripts correct this. For the Church hates the notion of a portion, which loves and proclaims the fullness of deity in the Son.]

But postponing the fuller resolution of each response, let us proceed through the remainder.

[Note: The printed editions read “having set aside”; the Chartres manuscript, “having put down.” With the Colbert, Silvester, and German manuscripts, “having postponed” is preferable—that is, deferred.]

### 11. They reject Sabellius in order to take away the unity of nature in Father and Son.

For this follows:

> “Nor, as Sabellius, who divides the union, called the same one both Son and Father.”

Sabellius, holding this belief, is ignorant of the evangelical and apostolic mysteries. But the heretics do not condemn this simply as an error belonging to a heretic.

[Note: The Paris edition lacks “in the heretic.” Sabellius’s particular and universally known heresy was that he preached union in God; but that he divided the union in Christ was less well known. The heretics deceitfully emphasize the latter, not the former, so that they may condemn Catholics together with Sabellius, as those who detest union in God and profess equality of distinct persons in nature.]

For, wishing there to be nothing one between Father and Son, they cast reproach upon the division of the union by Sabellius. This division of union did not introduce birth, but divided the same one in the Virgin.

[Note: “In the Virgin.”]

[Note: The manuscripts read “in the Virgin.” Since “union” is usually referred to persons, this in itself means that the person in Christ was not singular, as we explained at col. 106, note j of this edition. Yet it seems preferable to understand it thus: Sabellius divided the union in the Virgin, insofar as, after assuming flesh in her, he began to assign the names Father and Son to the same God—multiplying names, not persons.]

But for us, birth belongs to the confession. And while detesting union, we maintain the unity of divinity: namely, that God from God are one in kind of nature, since that which came to exist from God into God through the truth of birth came to subsist from no source other than God. What remains from no source other than God must necessarily remain in that truth which God is; and therefore they are one, since he who is God from God is neither something else nor what he is as God from another source.

[Note: The Paris edition reads “is one.” The other books more correctly read “are one”: so that “God from God” signifies both the Father, the source of divinity, and the Son, who derives his origin from him. Hence the conclusion immediately follows: “and therefore they are one.”]

The impiety of union is therefore imputed to Sabellius in order that the Church’s religion of unity may be taken away. I shall then pursue the remaining artifices of heretical ingenuity, lest I be thought, through suspicions rather than genuine grounds, a malicious interpreter of another’s simplicity. I shall show, by the conclusion of the entire profession, to what end the preface of so deceitful a discourse was directed.

[Note: Three Vatican manuscripts and the Silvester manuscript read “the Church’s faith.” Here the Church is set in opposition to heresy. The religion of its faith is one of unity, because it both believes and reveres unity in the Trinity.]

[Note: The printed editions read “conclusion”; they are corrected from the manuscripts.]

### 12. Hieracas falsely understands the Son as light from light. How the Church understands it.

For this follows:

> “Nor, as Hieracas, [did he exist as] a lamp from a lamp or a torch divided into two parts; nor was he who existed earlier later born or super-created into sonship.”

Hieracas, ignorant of the Only-begotten’s birth and not possessing the power of the evangelical mysteries, proclaimed two lights from one lamp, so that a twofold division of lamp-wicks might imitate the substance of Father and Son, kindled into light from the oil of one vessel. Thus there would be some external substance—like oil in a lamp—containing the nature of both lights; or perhaps like a lamp with papyrus—

[Note: The printed editions read “like oil”; the manuscripts, “like that of oil,” with the word “substance” tacitly supplied. In this view, a substance prior to both Father and Son is posited, shared by both; in this sense *homoousion* is rejected in Book IV, section 4.]

[Note: The Paris edition alone reads “with the same papyrus wick.” Papyrus, or *papyrum*, is a Nile plant with many uses. It was made into paper, sails, mats, ship’s ropes, and so forth. Gregory the Pope also mentions its use in candles and lamps, *Dialogues*, Book I, chapter 5: “He filled all the lamps of the church with water and, as customary, put papyrus in the middle.” Gregory of Tours, *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 8, mentions a little lamp in which neither papyrus was added nor a drop of dripping oil supplied. Finally Paulinus of Nola, 3:

> The bright altars are crowned with densely gathered lamps,
“Bright lights are kindled with fragrant waxed papyri.” Hence, in John of Genoa, *papyrus* is said to mean, as it were, “preparing fire” (*parans pyr*): perhaps more subtly than truly.] woven into the same lamp, so that it might shine at both ends, and the material in the middle might itself extend each light from itself. This error was introduced by human folly, when people derive their wisdom from themselves rather than from God.

But because the confession of the true faith is that God is born from God as light from light—light which, without loss to itself, imparts its own nature from itself, so as to give what it has, and still possess what it has given, and so that what it is may be born; since that which is born is not other than what it is; birth has received what it already was, and has not taken away what it received; and both are one, because it is born from what is, and what is born is neither from elsewhere nor other—since it is light from light: therefore, in order that the understanding of this faith might be diverted, the lamp or lantern of Hieracas has been brought forward as an accusation against confessing light from light, lest that be thought religiously said which has been spoken impiously and has been condemned both now and formerly.

Away, away, most empty fear of heretics! Do not falsely pretend, under the appearance of an anxious assertion, to be the defender of ecclesiastical faith. According to us, there is nothing bodily, nothing inanimate, in the things of God.

[Note: [Col. 0166C] In the earlier edition, “of inanimate things.”]

[Note: [Col. 0166D] The printed editions read “inanimate.” The Corbie manuscript, in the first hand, has *inanimum*; in the second hand, with the rest, *inanium* (“of inanimate things”). By this word it is denied that God undergoes the consequences of bodyhood, just as it was previously proved that He is not a body, in whom nothing bodily is asserted.]

Whatever God is, He is wholly God. Nothing is in Him except power, life, light, blessedness, and spirit. That nature admits no dull material, nor does it consist of diverse elements in order to endure. God, as He is God, remains what He is; and God remaining begot God. They are not contained by an external nature, as lamp and lamp, or lantern and lantern. The birth of the Only-begotten God from God is not a succession but an offspring, not an extension but light from light.

[Note: [Col. 0167C] “Light” is absent.]

[Note: [Col. 0167C] In the common printed texts: “the nature of light from the light. Unity.” We add “light” from the Colbert manuscript and two others, with which the remaining manuscripts agree in other respects.]

It is unity of the nature of light, not an extension produced by connection.

### 13. The birth of God from God, though attacked, is affirmed.

Now consider how much heretical craft and how cunning a profession is contained in this: “Nor was He who existed before afterwards born or super-created into a Son.” God, who was born from God, certainly was not born from nothing, nor was He born from things that did not exist; rather, He possessed the living nature of His birth. Nor was the same God who was already there born; rather, God from God who already was, was born; and the birth possessed, in its very birth, the nature of its source.

[Note: [Col. 0168C] “For if we speak from our own resources.”]

If we speak from ourselves, we are presumptuous. But if we shall teach that we have been taught by God for speaking, then the birth of God must be confessed according to God’s teaching. Therefore, in attempting to exclude this unity of nature in Father and Son, and this indescribable mystery of a living birth, heretical madness says: “Not Him who existed before, afterwards born or super-created into a Son.”

For who could be so mad as to suppose that the Father ceased to be Himself, so that He who had been would later be born or super-created into a Son? Then there would be an abolition of God, in order that birth might succeed from abolition—although birth bears witness to a remaining Author. Or who is so senseless as not to confess that the Son exists through birth? Further, who is so foolish as to dare proclaim, from the fact that God is born, that God did not exist? For it was not the God who remained who was born, but God was born from the remaining God, holding within Himself in His natural birth the nature of the Begetter.

But the birth of God, which came to be from God into God, does not possess things which were not, but, by the truth of being born, possesses the things of God which remained and remain.

[Note: [Col. 0167C] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions, however, read: “which remained in God.” Just as the word *God* is customary in Hilary for “the Father,” so *to remain* means “to be without an initial beginning of existence.” Hence what is here called “the things which remained in God” is shortly afterwards called “the things which were God’s.”]

Therefore, it was not He who was that was born; but God came to be born from and in those things which were God’s.

[Note: [Col. 0167D] In the Chartres manuscript the particle *non* (“not”) was added above this word by a second hand; it thereafter wrongly prevailed in one Colbert manuscript and in the editions of Erasmus, Lipsius, and Paris, against the testimony of the other books. The Arians said, “Nor was He who existed before afterwards born,” directly against Sabellius, who asserted that He who was Father, when subsequently born, acquired the title of Son; but indirectly against the Catholic faith, since they sought to insinuate that the Son came from non-existent things. Hilary replies in such a way as both to reject their devices and to show that the Catholic faith has nothing in common with Sabellius. Above, indeed, against Sabellius, he first states: “Nor was the same God who was born.” When he has proved this, he repeats it by way of conclusion in other words: “Therefore, it was not He who was”—that is, not the Father—“who was born; but God,” the Son, “came to be born from those things which were God’s.”]

Thus all the foregoing language of heretical deceit prepared the way for this most impious doctrine: that, intending to deny the Only-begotten God, it might, as though truth had previously supplied the rationale, proclaim Him born from nothing rather than from God, referring His birth to a creative act out of non-existent things.

### 14. By what artifice they suggest that the Son is from nothing.

Finally, after much preparation, it burst out through this entrance, as though it had been prepared for it, saying: “But the Son, brought forth without time and created and founded before the ages, was not before He was born.” The heretical argument, as it thinks, restrained itself as far as it could, both to confirm impiety and to provide an excuse for slander should the question be pressed, when it said: “He was not before He was born.” By declaring that He was not before being born, it denied Him the nature of a subsisting origin, and made Him begin to be from nothing, since no existing authority was granted to Him before His birth.

[Note: [Col. 0168C] The printed editions read, “before He was born.” We follow the manuscripts. Further, “subsisting origin” means nothing else than what is shortly called “existing authority.” Theologians today would say “an existing principle.”]

Then, if this statement should be judged irreligious, it had a ready defense: because He who was could not be born, nor could one who already existed have had a cause of being born by which He might come to be, since birth advances to this end, that the one who is born may subsist in being.

[Note: [Col. 0168D] The Chartres exemplar, after correction, together with the Vatican-Basilica manuscript, reads: “because none could be born except one who was not, nor,” etc.]

O foolish and impious man, who expects birth in one who subsists without birth? Or how can one who is be supposed to be born, when birth is the nature of being born? But, while craftily striving to deny the birth of the Only-begotten God from God the Father, you wished to escape by saying, “He was not before He was born”; although God, from whom the Son of God was born, was, and the nature of God, from which the Son, God, subsists by birth, remained.

[Note: [Col. 0168D] The Vatican-Basilica manuscript reads “lest God,” and shortly afterwards “might remain,” without the particle *-que*. Here, as above and below, the text has evidently been rashly corrupted.]

If, therefore, He was born from God, a birth from a remaining nature must be confessed: not in such a way that God who was should be born, but so that the birth of God from God who was might be understood.

[Note: [Col. 0168D] In the Vatican-Basilica manuscript, “who was” is lacking. What is said immediately before, “a birth from a remaining nature must be confessed,” can be understood either as being born from a remaining or existing nature, or as the one born possessing a remaining nature, or indeed both.]

### 15. The heresy is bold, but imprudent. In what cases it is difficult, and in what cases easier, to cure.

But heretical passion does not restrain its irreligious heats. By saying, “He was not before He was born,” it labors to make Him be born from non-existent things—that is, not born from God the Father into God the Son by a true and perfect birth. And in the final conclusion of its entire exposition, it burst forth at last into the most profane heat of its irreligious madness, saying:

“For if ‘from Him,’ and ‘from the womb,’ and ‘I came forth from the Father and came’ are understood as though extending a part of His one substance, and as a kind of emission, then the Father will be composite, divisible, and changeable, and, according to them, a body; and, so far as they are concerned, God without a body will undergo the consequences of bodyhood.”

[Note: [Col. 0168D] The common printed texts read “of His one substance,” incorrectly, since *His* refers to the Father and *one* to the word “substance.” We have already noted that the Greek exemplars read *καὶ ὡς προβολὴ ὑπό τινων* (“and as though an emission, according to some”), not *καὶ ὡς προβολὴν ἀποτείνων* (“and as though extending an emission”), as Hilary’s reading is clear from his exposition.]

It would be a grave and very difficult labor to defend the truth of religion against the impiety of falsehood, if impiety took counsel as wisely as it dares greatly.

[Note: [Col. 0169D] The printed editions read “prudence”; corrected from the manuscripts.]

But it is well that the will to irreligion proceeds from a lack of prudence. Thus, although the answer to folly is easy, the correction of fools is difficult: first, because they do not seek the reasoning of understanding; then, because what is communicated by one who understands is not received. Yet if any are held in error through foolish understanding by fear of God and ignorance of understanding, rather than by a will to impiety, I hope that they may be inclined toward correction, since a straightforward demonstration of truth will expose the folly of impiety.

[Note: [Col. 0169D] The Chartres manuscript reads “I believe that”; others, “I hope that.” The printed editions read “I hope that.” Here Hilary reveals his disposition toward those who favored Arius through ignorance and simplicity, as has already been observed against Erasmus’s subtleties in Preface 27. Athanasius was no different, in *Oration II against the Arians*, p. 321, concerning those who deny that the offspring is proper to the Father’s substance, on the ground that this cannot be so unless parts are understood. They think bodily thoughts about the incorporeal, and because of the weakness of their own nature deprive the Son of the propriety of the paternal substance, measuring the Father’s offspring foolishly by themselves. “But,” he says, “those who are disposed in this manner and persuaded that there cannot be a Son of God ought indeed to be treated with mercy; nevertheless, it is fitting to question them and convict them by arguments. Perhaps in this way they may be led to some understanding.”]

### 16. Since the Son is from God Himself, He is neither the Father Himself, nor something else, nor from nothing.

You have said, O fools—and you who say the same even today, not knowing how to think concerning God—“if ‘from Him,’ and ‘from the womb,’ and ‘I came forth from the Father and came.’” I ask you: was this entire statement spoken by God, or not? It certainly was spoken; and since it was spoken by God concerning Himself, it must be understood exactly as it was spoken. We shall deal with these sayings in their proper place, having shown the force of each one. Meanwhile, I appeal to each person’s understanding: what does he suppose is meant when it is said “from Him”? Is it to be understood as from another, or from no one, or is He Himself to be believed to be that one?

It is not from another, because it is from Him—that is, so that God may not be from anywhere else except God. It is not from nothing, because it is from Him; for the nature from which the birth is derived is shown. He is not Himself, because where it is “from Him,” the birth of the Son is referred to the Father.

Then, when “from the womb” is signified, I ask whether it can be believed that He was born from nothing, when the truth of the birth is disclosed through names drawn from bodily processes. For God, though He does not consist of bodily members, when He referred to the generation of the Son, said: “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot You” (Ps. 109:3). Rather, confirming from the truth of His divinity that indescribable birth of His Only-begotten Son from Himself, He spoke so as to lead faith to understanding, in order that, concerning His divine realities, He might instruct human understanding, according to human nature, toward knowledge of faith. Thus, when He says “from the womb,” He teaches that it was not a creation from nothing which came into being, but the natural birth of His Only-begotten from Himself.

Finally, when He said, “I came forth from the Father and came” (John 16:27), did He leave any ambiguity as to whether what God is came to be from no other source than the Father? For in coming forth from the Father, He had neither another nature of birth nor none at all; rather, He declares that He has as His Author Him from whom He professes that He came forth. But I shall speak later about demonstrating and understanding these matters.

### 17. It is impious not to believe God concerning Himself.

Meanwhile, let us consider with what confidence of man the understanding of those things concerning God is forbidden which are not denied to have been spoken by God concerning Himself. O most grievous disgrace of human folly and presumption: not merely to accuse God, by refusing belief, concerning His own profession about Himself, but to condemn Him by correcting Him; to contaminate and assail that ineffable secret of His nature and power with human teachings; and to dare say this: “If the Son is from God, God is changeable and bodily, since He has put forth or extended from Himself that which would be a Son to Him!”

Why are you anxious lest God be changeable? We confess a birth; taught by God, we proclaim the Only-begotten from God. You, lest the birth remain and lest the Only-begotten God stand in the Church’s faith, oppose the nature of the unchangeable God, which cannot be extended or stretched forth.

[Note: [Col. 0170D] The Vatican-Basilica manuscript reads “you explain,” less satisfactorily.]

I might bring before you, unhappy error, even examples from worldly realities of certain natures which beget, so that you would not think birth an extension, or believe the natures of those born to be losses to those begetting; so that you might also see many living souls generated from living beings without bodily intercourse. But it would be impious not to believe God concerning Himself; and it would be madness of the utmost fury to take away the authority for faith from Him to whom you profess reverence for life.

[Note: [Col. 0170D] Lipsius here added “testifying,” which is absent from Badius, Erasmus, and most manuscripts.]

For if life is only through Him, how is faith unto life not likewise through Him? And how can faith unto life be in Him, if He is judged an untrustworthy witness concerning Himself?

### 18. How heretics understand the titles of the Son.

For, most impious heretic, you appropriate the Son’s birth to a creative act of will, so that He may not be born from God, but may subsist through creation, because He who created willed it. Consequently, according to you, the Son is not God, because, while the one God remains, the Son does not hold in His birth the nature of His source; rather, He is a created thing of another substance.

[Note: [Col. 0170D] The printed editions read “is created,” against all manuscripts. The sense is: “According to you—that is, in your view—the Son is not God but a creature”; observe that *cum* here, as elsewhere, means “according to.”]

Though as the Only-begotten He may be more excellent than the other created things and works, nevertheless He is made to subsist so as to have in Himself a granted creation, not to have brought the nature of God through generation. You call that born which subsisted from nothing; and you give Him the title Son, not because He was born from God, but because He was created through God—because you remember that devout men also have been judged worthy by God of this name. Then, moreover, you grant Him the name of God on no other condition than that in which it was said: “I said, You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High” (Ps. 81:6), so that He has favor through the word of one naming Him, not truth of nature through the name; and, according to you, He is Son by adoption, God by designation, Only-begotten by privilege, Firstborn by rank, wholly a creature, God from nothing, because His generation is not a natural birth from God but the substance of a created thing.

[Note: [Col. 0170D] “To make subsist” was a term used by Arians, as we gather from Faustinus, chapter 1, where he explains Arian professions thus: “Thus he also says that all things were made through Him, in order to assert that He was made to subsist from no existing things … since He was not truly born from the Father but made to subsist from nothing.” Its meaning differs little from “to create.” Hence, just as here Hilary uses “creation” for “being made to subsist,” so conversely in Book I, section 16, he uses “being made to subsist” for “creation.”]

[Note: [Col. 0171C] “And all sons of the Most High.” Thereafter, in the expression “by designation.”]

[Note: [Col. 0171C] The Paris edition alone reads “and rather let him be,” rather than “and according to you”; the meaning is the same.]

[Note: [Col. 0171C] Badius and Erasmus read “the whole creation,” from which Erasmus thought it should read, “firstborn by the rank of the whole creation.” The other books more correctly read, “wholly a creature,” as is immediately explained in other words: namely, God from nothing. For *creatio* here, as Erasmus himself observed, means the created thing. The heretics’ reason for calling Him Son by adoption is immediately added: namely, because His generation, etc.—what the schools would barbarously call “because His filiation,” or sonship. Therefore the Vatican-Basilica manuscript, which reads “because His creation,” should not be followed.]

### 19. What Hilary has learned from Scripture concerning God.

First, I ask pardon of You for my most impatient grief; allow me, almighty God, to speak in Your presence, and permit me—earth and ashes though I am, yet bound by the devotion of Your love—to speak these words freely.

I, unhappy man, formerly was nothing; lacking the consciousness of life and without understanding of myself, I lacked that which I am.

[Note: [Col. 0171D] Thus the better manuscripts. Three Vatican manuscripts with the Vindobonensis read “the sense of life,” incorrectly; while the printed editions read “the sense of life.”]

But Your mercy is to me the cause of living; and I do not doubt that You who are good ordained good for me in causing me to be born.

[Note: [Col. 0171D] The Vatican-Basilica manuscript reads “You established.” In these words Hilary does not deny original sin, which elsewhere he frequently and expressly affirms. Most especially clear is the statement cited in his name by Augustine, *Against Julian*, Book II, chapter 8: “In Adam’s offense we lost the nobility of that first and blessed creation.” Hilary means only that everything granted to us by God is good, and that it cannot accord with His goodness that, when we use the reason granted by Him to understand the prophets, He should deceive us through them.]

For You, who have no need of me, would not have begun me unto the origin of evil. But when You had granted me life, endowed with soul and with the understanding of reason, You also instructed me in the knowledge of Yourself through the sacred books of Your servants Moses and the prophets, as I suppose. From them I learned that You are not to be worshiped in Your solitude.

I learned that there is God with You: not another in nature, but one in the mystery of Your substance.

[Note: [Col. 0171C] The Vatican-Basilica manuscript reads, “Lord, not another,” incorrectly. Compare Book V, section 36, where he teaches that God from God and God in God must be confessed, not in bodily ways but by divine powers, nor by transfusion of nature into nature, but by the mystery and power of nature.]

I learned that in God there is God, not confused by mingling, but present through the power of nature: so that, because You are God, You are present in Him who is from You—not in such a way that You Yourself are the same one and are present, but so that the truth of perfect birth teaches that You are present in Him who is from You.

[Note: [Col. 0172C] Nor is the aforementioned manuscript more correct here in reading “from the truth of nature.” For, as we have just heard from Book V, God is in God by divine powers and the power of nature. More expressly, in the following words of the same book: “From the power of nature He subsists by birth in the same nature.” But, as is stated and proved in section 3, the power of nature produces truth. This refers to the passage of Isaiah: “God is in You, and there is none besides You,” discussed in Book V, section 38.]

Again, the voices of the Gospels and apostles speak this to me, and words uttered by the very mouth of Your Only-begotten Son and committed to books bear witness: that Your Son is God, the Only-begotten from You, the unbegotten God; and that He was born man from the Virgin for the mystery of my salvation. In Him the truth of generation from You resides, and Him the nature of birth from You, remaining in You, retains.

[Note: [Col. 0172D] The common texts read “God and man.” We delete “and” on the authority of the manuscripts. What follows contains an exposition of the words, “The Father is in Me, and I in the Father.”]

### 20. A commendation of those whom he has believed.

Into what abyss of hopeless return have You plunged me? For this is what I learned, this I believed, and this I hold with the faith of a mind made steadfast, so that I can neither believe otherwise nor wish to do so. Why have You deceived me, miserable as I am, concerning Yourself, and destroyed my unhappy flesh and soul through teaching them a knowledge alien to You?

The glory of Moses descending from the mountain after the division of the Red Sea deceived me—Moses who beheld with You all the hidden secrets of heaven (Exod. 34:29). I believed him concerning You, upon Your own words. David, found according to Your heart, ruined me (Acts 13:22); Solomon, worthy of the gift of divine wisdom (3 Kings 3:12); Isaiah, preaching after seeing the Lord of hosts (Isa. 6:1); Jeremiah, sanctified in the womb before his formation, prophet for uprooting and planting nations (Jer. 1:5); Ezekiel, witness of the mystery of resurrection (Ezek. 37); Daniel, man of desires and knower of times (Dan. 9:23); the consecrated choir of prophets; and the whole mystery of evangelical preaching: Matthew, chosen from a tax collector into an apostle; John, worthy through friendship with the Lord of the revelation of heavenly mysteries (Matt. 16:18); and, after confessing the mystery, blessed Simon, set as the foundation for the building of the Church and receiving the keys of the kingdom of heaven; all the others preaching by the Holy Spirit; and Paul, Your apostle and vessel of election from being a persecutor (Acts 9:15), living in the depth of the sea (2 Cor. 11:25), a man in the third heaven (ibid. 12:2), in paradise before martyrdom, and in martyrdom a libation completed in the consummation of perfect faith (2 Tim. 4:6–7).

[Note: [Col. 0172D] Thus Tertullian too, in *Scorpiace*, section 12, commends Paul because God made him a partaker of paradise before martyrdom. Yet there is no reason to approve the notion that Hilary agrees with Tertullian in this, especially since in *On the Soul*, section 55, Hilary maintains that paradise is open to none except martyrs.]

### 21. How firm was his faith in the Son’s equality with the Father, and whence it was firm.

From these persons I learned what I hold; by these I have been imbued beyond remedy. Forgive me, almighty God, because in these matters I can neither be corrected nor die with them. Too late, as I judge, has the age of this present world produced for me these most impious teachers. Too late has my faith, which You instructed, acquired these masters. I believed in You without having heard these names; through You I was thus reborn; and thus I have been Yours ever since.

[Note: [Col. 0173D] The printed editions read “by all these persons.” The manuscripts read “by these names”—that is, the names of the new teachers, which are neither ancient nor famous by any title, whereas the names of Moses, Solomon, Isaiah, and the rest are commended by many testimonies and centuries.]

I know that You are almighty, and I await from You alone and from Your Only-begotten alone the explanation of the indescribable birth, known only to You.

[Note: [Col. 0173D] The reading of the Vatican-Basilica and Martin manuscripts is clearer: “known only to You,” etc. But the sense is the same without “only”: “the birth known only to You and Your Only-begotten,” etc. This rests upon the Gospel words: “No one knows the Son except the Father,” etc. As with Hilary, so with Augustine, the eternal generation of the Son is commonly demonstrated from the Father’s omnipotence. “God,” Augustine says in Sermon 139, section 4, “gave to His creatures the power to generate what they are; and do you think that He who is before the ages could not reserve this for Himself?” Likewise, in section 5, he proves the same from the Father’s goodness, wholly free from envy: “The Father rejoices when He has an equal only Son; He rejoices because He does not envy.” And because God does not envy His only Son, He begot what He Himself is.]

For nothing is impossible to You, and I do not doubt that the Son begotten by You exists through the power of Your omnipotence. For if I doubted, I should already be denying that You are almighty. I learned that You are good even from my own birth; and therefore I trust that You do not begrudge Your good things in the birth of Your Only-begotten. For I believe that what is Yours is His, and what is His is Yours. The very creation of the world has also shown me that You are wise; I know that You begot Your Wisdom from Yourself, not unlike Yourself.

[Note: [Col. 0174C] The Silvæ Majores exemplar reads “not unlike Yourself.”]

You are truly and uniquely God to me; but I will not believe that there is in Him who is God from You anything other than what is Yours.

[Note: [Col. 0173C] “True and one,” shortly afterwards, “who is God from You.”]

[Note: [Col. 0174C] Thus the better manuscripts—Chartres, three Colbert manuscripts, Germanicus, one Sorbonne manuscript, etc. Other books read: “True and one … who is God from You.”]

[Note: [Col. 0174D] The printed editions read “than You are”; and in the margin of Erasmus, Lipsius, and Paris, “than that which is Yours,” against the manuscripts.]

Judge me in this, if it is a fault in me to have believed too greatly through Your Son, and the Law, and the prophets, and the apostles.

### 22. If Christ is truly the Son of God, He is also true God. It is known in many ways that He is truly the Son of God.

But let presumptuous speech cease, and let it pass from those matters into which it had burst under the necessity of exposing heretical folly to the service of rendering an account, so that any who can still be saved may hold to the path of evangelical and apostolic doctrine, and understand the true Son of God not by adoption but by nature.

[Note: [Col. 0173C] “If any who can still be saved unto faith may hold,” etc.]

[Note: [Col. 0174D] The Paris edition, with the older Colbert manuscript, reads: “if any of these can still be saved unto faith, [let them hold] evangelical,” etc.]

For this must be the order of our answer: first, that we demonstrate Him to be the Son of God, so that the nature of divinity in Him may be established by His being Son.

[Note: [Col. 0174D] In the Vatican-Basilica and Martin manuscripts “God” is wrongly added here, since Hilary proposes simply to demonstrate that Christ is the Son of God; once this has been demonstrated, the divine nature in Him will be evident.]

For this heresy, with which we are now dealing, labors most earnestly to prevent our Lord Jesus Christ, true Son of God, from being true God. That our Lord Jesus Christ is and is taught to be the true Son of God, the Only-begotten God, is known in many ways: while the Father bears witness concerning Him; while He Himself professes concerning Himself; while the apostles preach; while believers believe; while demons confess; while the Jews deny; and while the Gentiles recognize Him in His Passion.

For what is said with faith in His proper identity does not arise from a shared designation. And since all that Christ the Lord either did or taught surpasses all things belonging to those who are called sons, and since among all those things which are Christ’s preeminent attributes, this is taught to be especially so—that He is the Son of God—His title “Son” is not a name drawn from general kinship.

[Note: [Col. 0174D] That is, among all those names. Shortly afterwards, the Vatican-Basilica manuscript reads “may be called” in place of “may be taught,” omitting thereafter “to be.”]

### 23. The Father testifies that He is not adopted, but proper to Him.

I do not corrupt the faith of truth by establishing this with my own words. Let the Father speak, as He has often done, concerning His Only-begotten, lest Jesus Christ, in the mystery of completing baptism, be unknowable on account of the body: “This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3:17).

[Note: [Col. 0174D] The printed editions here and below, in section 24, read “in whom I am well pleased.” In both places “well” is absent from the manuscripts.]

I ask: in what respect does truth fail, and in what respect is the faith of this declaration weak? The conception from the Holy Spirit announced by an angel, the star revealing Him to the Magi, the honor shown by worship at the cradle, and the power displayed in submitting to baptism under the Baptist’s testimony are not judged sufficient to reveal His majesty. The Father speaks from heaven, and speaks thus: “This is My Son.”

[Note: [Col. 0174D] The Vatican-Basilica manuscript reads “baptized,” which is not to be accepted. For it is John’s reverence that is noted: before baptizing Christ, he recognized Him as superior to himself in dignity.]

What is the force of the faith expressed not by a surname but by a pronoun? Surnames are added to names, but pronouns possess within themselves the force of names. It is a sign of proprietorship where one hears both “this is” and “My.” Understand, then, the truth and reasoning of the words. You had read: “I begot sons and exalted them” (Isa. 1:2), but you had not read, “My sons”; for He had begotten them for Himself as sons through the division of the nations and through making the people of inheritance into sons.

Therefore, lest the title Son should be added to the Only-begotten God through a sharing in adoptive inheritance, the truth of nature was shown by the indication of proprietorship. Let this shared name be granted to Christ, that He is Son, if it can be found said of anyone else, “This is My Son.” But if “This is My Son” is proper and unique to Him, why do we bring a charge against God the Father’s avowed proprietorship concerning the Son?

Or does it not seem to you that this is signified in the words “this is”: “Others indeed have been given the title of sons by Him, but this one is My Son; I have granted to very many the name of adoption, but this one is Son to Me. Do not seek another; do not believe that it is not this one. This one I touch, as it were, with a pointing finger and with the force of the word, when I say both ‘Mine,’ and ‘this,’ and ‘Son’”? After this, what understanding could remain by which He should not be believed to be Son?

And this was the purpose of the Father’s utterance: that He who was to be baptized in order to fulfill all righteousness might not be unknown in what He was, but that He who was seen as man for the mystery of our salvation might be known by the voice of God as the Son of God.

[Note: [Col. 0175C] The printed editions read “this was its purpose,” against the manuscripts. Shortly afterwards Paris, with the Colbert and German manuscripts, reads “so that” instead of “but that.” This argument is illustrated and more fully explained by Faustinus, *To Flaccilla, Against the Arians*, Book I, chapter 2. Since he sets out the same Scriptural testimonies which Hilary adduces here, in the same order and for the same purpose, it may be conjectured that he received some assistance from Hilary himself. He says there: “No one doubted His flesh, or rather, I should say, His manhood, because it could not be doubted; but that which was in the man and born with the man, since it could not be seen by nature, was shown lest it be uncertain by the voice and, as it were, finger of the Father saying, ‘This is My Son,’” etc. And a little earlier: “See that He says this for the first time when Jesus, as man, approached baptism; and I think for no other reason than that He who appeared bodily, and who among other human beings came Himself as man to baptism as though a sinner—although He had no sins of His own—might have been believed not to be the Son of God.”]

24. He declares the same thing again. He gives authority to the Son’s words. — And because life belonged to believers in this confession of faith (for there is no other life of eternity [Note: [Col. 0175D] Paris, with the Vatican Basilica, St. Martin, and Colbert manuscripts, reads “way is” (*via est*). The reading “life is” (*vita est*) with the other books is preferable, so that reference may be made to John 17:3: “And this is eternal life,” etc. Then Erasmus, Leipzig, and Paris read, “unless that Jesus.” It is absent from Badius and the manuscripts.], unless we know Jesus Christ, the only-begotten God, to be the Son of God), a voice from heaven was again heard by the Apostles, repeating this declaration, so that what would be life to believe might be believed more firmly, since not to believe it would be death. For when the Lord stood upon the mountain in the appearance of His majesty, with Moses and Elijah standing by, and with three witnesses—the pillars of the Churches—taken up for confirmation of the vision and the voice, this paternal voice came from heaven: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him” (Matt. 17:5). The splendor beheld was not sufficient confirmation of His honor; He is designated by the voice: “This is my Son.” The Apostles cannot bear the glory of God; mortal eyes are dimmed by the sight, and the faith of Peter, James, and John, dismayed by fear, collapses [Col. 0176A]: yet the Father’s declaration of authority is present, and this Son is shown through the distinct property [Note: [Col. 0175D] Leipzig and Paris read “of the designation,” contrary to the evidence of the other books and with some corruption of the author’s meaning. For distinct property is opposed to adoption, and refers both to the Father who signifies and to the Son signified. Faustinus treats the same argument in the passage cited [Col. 0176C]: “Certainly Moses and Elijah were seen speaking with Him, and you cannot deny that they were made sons of God by adoption. How, then, does the divine voice testify concerning Christ alone, saying, ‘This is my Son,’ etc.? For if Christ too is a son by adoption, when He stood between two adopted sons, He would surely have said, ‘And this too is my Son,’ lest Christ alone be believed to be Son. But when He says, ‘This is my beloved Son,’ He separated the sons of adoption, so that the property of true birth might be believed to belong to Christ alone as Son.”] of the One who signifies Him. Nor is the truth of the Son merely made known by the words “this” and “my”; “Hear him” is added. The Father’s testimony indeed comes from heaven, but the testimony of the Son is confirmed on earth, for He is shown to be one who must be heard. And although no ambiguity remains through the Father’s declaration, nevertheless the Son’s own declaration concerning Himself is also decreed to be believed; and the truth of His sonship in Him is taught to such an extent that the confirmation of the paternal voice [Note: [Col. 0175C] In the Verona codex: “requires that the Son be heard by us,” etc.; but “the Son’s voice” has been added in a later revision.] [Note: [Col. 0176C] The Paris edition alone, with the St. Martin manuscript, reads “to be heard.” The others, with several manuscripts, read “that the Son be heard by us.” *Filii* (“the Son”) is absent from the better witnesses [Col. 0176D].] requires our obedience in hearing Him. Therefore, since this is the voice of the Father’s will—that the Son should be heard—let us hear the Son declaring what He Himself is.

25. Christ rightly calls God His Father and Himself His Son. — Now I do not think anyone is so estranged from common sense as, while understanding from the Son’s declarations throughout all the books of the Gospels His assumption of bodily lowliness—when He says, “Father, glorify me” (John 17:5); and again, very frequently, “You shall see the Son of Man” (Matt. 26:64); and, “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28); but also, “Now my soul is deeply troubled” (John 12:27); or even, “God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matt. 27:46), and many other sayings of this kind, of which there will be discussion in their proper order—yet should accuse Him of arrogance in this continual avowal of lowliness because He calls God His Father, when He says: “Every plant which my Father has not planted shall be uprooted” (Matt. 15:13); or: “You have made my Father’s house a house of trade” (John 2:16) [Note: [Col. 0176D] The printed editions here add “heavenly,” which is absent from the manuscripts and from Faustinus, Hilary’s contemporary and, in our view, his imitator. Shortly afterward the St. Martin manuscript has *mercationis* (“trafficking”) in place of *negotiationis* (“trade”).]; [Col. 0176C] [Note: [Col. 0176D] Instead of “and,” it would be more convenient to read “thus that.”] and wherever He always names God as His Father—as though it were a matter of rash presumption rather than of confident nature, conscious of its own birth, to retain in speaking of the Father the name belonging to a true and natural father [Note: [Col. 0176D] That is, in calling Him Father, He retains the name which belongs to a true and natural father.].

Thus His frequent profession of lowliness does not incur the fault of arrogance, as though He claimed what belongs to another [Note: [Col. 0177C] “Claims.”], rather than defending what is His own, and presumed to equate Himself properly with God. Nor does He, with the same rashness with which He calls Him Father, declare Himself also to be Son, saying: “For God did not send his Son into this world to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him” (John 3:17); or again: “Do you believe in the Son of God?” (John 9:35). What are we doing now, in granting Jesus Christ only the name of adoption [Note: [Col. 0177D] Paris, with the older Colbert, Remigius, and German manuscripts, reads “Jesus Christ.”]? By this we also accuse Him of rash presumption when He calls God His Father.

The Father’s voice from heaven is: “Hear him” (Matt. 17:5). I hear: “Father, I thank you” (John 11:41); I hear: “You say that I blasphemed because I said, ‘I am the Son of God’” (John 10:36). If I do not believe the names, if I do not understand that nature is signified by the terms [Note: [Col. 0177D] The printed editions read “the nature of the term.” The manuscripts more correctly read “by the terms”; supply “to be signified.” Thus in Book I, §21: “Nor should they confuse understanding by means of terms.”] [Col. 0177B], I ask what I am to believe and understand. No other conclusion is left to me. The Father’s authority comes from heaven: “This is my Son.” The Son’s own declaration concerning Himself is [Note: [Col. 0177C] “It is a trustworthy declaration.”] [Note: [Col. 0177D] In the Colbert, St. Martin, Corbie, and other manuscripts: “it is a trustworthy declaration.” In the Carnotensis: “the declaration is faith.” In three others: “it is the declaration of the Son.”]: “My Father’s house,” and “My Father.” The declaration of the name is salvation when the question demands faith, saying: “Do you believe in the Son of God?” (John 9:14). [Note: [Col. 0177D] “Distinctive properties.”] Terms of distinct ownership follow where “my” occurs. I ask you, heretic: whence comes another presumption? You take faith from the Father, declaration from the Son, and nature from the names. You do violence to God’s words, lest they should be what they proclaim. The sole basis of your impiety is your shamelessness in charging God with lying about Himself.

26. Distinctive properties are added to the name of Son. His works attest that He is Son. — Although, therefore, the simple confession alone displays names of nature, so that He of whom it was said, “This is my Son,” and He to whom it was said, “My Father,” are what they are called: nevertheless, lest “Son” in the Son should be a name of adoption, or “Father” in the Father merely a title of honor, let us see what distinctive properties have been added by the Son to the name “Son” [Note: [Col. 0177D] The Vatican Basilica manuscript reads “declarations,” and shortly before likewise has “the names of declarations follow,” rather than “the terms of distinct property follow.”].

He says: “All things have been delivered to me by my Father; and no one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and he to whom the Son wills to reveal him” (Matt. 11:27). Does this accord with what was said, “This is my Son,” and “My Father”: “No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son”? For neither Son through the Father nor Father through the Son could be known except through reciprocal attestation [Note: [Col. 0177D] In the same codex and in St. Martin, “declaration”; a less precise expression.]. The voice is from heaven; the Son’s utterance is also present [Col. 0178A]. The Son is as unknowable as the Father. All things have been delivered to Him, and in “all things” nothing is understood to be excluded. If their power is equal, if the secret of knowing is equal, if nature is in the names, I ask how those who are so called can fail to be what they are called, when neither their force in power nor their difficulty in being known differs [Note: [Col. 0178C] “Right” is clearly written in our manuscript.] [Note: [Col. 0177D] In the manuscripts this word is written so that “right” (*ius*) may be admitted no less than “force” (*vis*).]. Therefore God does not deceive in the terms; neither Father nor Son lies about Himself. And receive [Note: [Col. 0177D] Printed editions read, “what faith is in these things”; corrected from the manuscripts.] how faith in these names is grounded.

27. His works attest that He is Son. The Father’s testimony asserts nothing else. Christ is separated from adopted sons. — For He says: “For the works which the Father has given me to accomplish—those very works which I do—bear witness concerning me, that the Father has sent me. And the Father who sent me has himself borne witness concerning me” (John 5:36–37) [Note: [Col. 0178D] The Vatican Basilica exemplar reads “that I may do [them],” then omitting “which I do”; this is likewise omitted in St. Martin.]. The only-begotten God teaches that He is Son not merely by testimony of name, but also by testimony of power [Note: [Col. 0178D] Badius and Erasmus, as in a later Colbert manuscript, read “of truth.” The Vatican Basilica and St. Martin manuscripts read “by powers.” The reading “of power,” with the other books, is preferable; supply “by testimony.”]: for the works which He does testify that He has been sent by the Father.

I ask: what fact do the works attest? That He has been sent. [Note: [Col. 0178D] We restore the particle “therefore,” wrongly deleted by Leipzig, from Badius, Erasmus, and the manuscripts.] Therefore both the Son’s obedience and the Father’s authority are taught in the One sent, since the works He does cannot belong to another than the One sent by the Father. But works do not suffice for unbelieving persons [Note: [Col. 0178C] “Unbelievers.”] [Note: [Col. 0178D] Leipzig, with several manuscripts, reads “unbelievers.” But Badius, Erasmus, and Paris, with the better witnesses, read “incredulous persons”; this is more genuine, though not in a different sense. Thus in the Commentary on Matthew, chapter 17, §6, the Apostolic generation is called “incredulous and perverse.” The same word is used in the same sense in our Vulgate, as may be seen in Sirach 1:36; 2:18; Baruch 1:19; etc.] as testimony that the Father sent Him. For it follows: “And the Father who sent me has himself borne witness concerning me; you have neither heard his voice nor seen his form” (John 5:37). I ask what the Father’s testimony concerning Him was [Note: [Col. 0178D] In the St. Martin manuscript there occurs here, “other than that which has been heard,” which seems to be supplied from what follows.]. Unroll the Gospel books and review all their content. Give the Father’s testimony other than that which was heard: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3:17), and: “You are my Son” (Mark 1:11).

John heard this, though he was not ignorant of it; nevertheless, the testimony of the paternal voice was sent for our instruction—and even this was not enough. John indeed in the wilderness was worthy of this voice, but the Apostles too were not to be deprived of the authority of this testimony [Note: [Col. 0178D] “They had not been.”]. The same voice from heaven comes to them, but they receive more than John. For John, already prophesying from the womb, did not need the words: “Hear him.” I shall surely hear; nor shall I hear anyone besides Him, unless it be one who has heard in order to teach. If no other testimony of the Father concerning the Son exists in the books than that He is His Son, the truth of this testimony is that the very works of the Father which He performs affirm the truth of this testimony [Col. 0179A]. What pretext for slander remains today—that the name is adoption, that God is false, that the names are empty? The Father has testified concerning the Son; by His works the Son bears witness that He is equal to the Father. Why should what is said and proved not be seen to be in Him—that is, the truth of Sonship [Note: [Col. 0179C] The printed editions read “which is,” and shortly afterward, “which is worthy of God.” In both places we prefer the manuscript reading.]?

The name “Son” in Christ is not from an adoption of favor by God the Father; nor did He earn this name by holiness, as many are sons of God after their confession of faith. For in them there is no indication of distinctive property; the gracious grant is merely one of name, as is worthy of God. “This is,” “this is mine,” and “hear him” are something different: herein are truth, nature, and faith.

28. The Son’s birth from God and His coming to us are shown. He who alone knows the Father because He is from Him is not created. — Certainly the Son bears no less explicit testimony concerning Himself by this distinctive quality of the Father’s declaration [Note: [Col. 0179C] The Vatican Basilica manuscript reads “than a paternal [declaration].” This is to be understood thus: the Son signifies Himself to be God’s own Son in words no less explicit than the Father does.]. For just as, when the Father says, “This is my Son,” there is a manifestation of nature, and when He adds, “Hear him,” there is a hearing of the mystery and faith for which He came from heaven—when we are instructed to hear Him for the saving doctrine of confession—so also the Son taught both the truth of His birth and of His coming, saying: [Note: [Col. 0179C] The Latin and Greek copies now read quite differently, namely: “You know me, and you know where I am from,” a reading also used by Origen in his nineteenth tome on John. There he endeavors to reconcile Christ’s different saying in John 8:19, “You know neither me,” with this, “You know me”; he first answers that they were spoken not to the same but to different persons: “You know me” to the Jerusalemites, but “You know neither me” to the Pharisees. But observing thereafter that even those to whom “You know me” was said were immediately reproached for not knowing the Father, and thus likewise for not knowing the Son, in accordance with John 8:19, “If you knew me, you would know my Father also,” he prefers to reconcile the two passages thus: “‘You know me, and you know where I am from,’” he says, “is spoken of Himself as man; but ‘You know neither me nor my Father’ is spoken of His divinity.” Here, therefore, because of the following words, “He who sent me is true, whom you do not know,” Hilary could legitimately read, “You know neither me,” etc. Indeed, this too is sufficiently suggested implicitly, so that the full and complete sense may be rendered thus: “You know me and know where I am from according to the flesh; but there is something else in me, and in respect of this you know neither me nor where I am from; for I did not come from myself.” Thus the argument Hilary draws from this passage stands: Christ in John 8 expressly declares Himself wholly unknown, whereas in chapter 7 He only implies it silently.] “You know neither me nor where I am from; for I did not come from myself, but he who sent me is true, whom you do not know. But I know him, because I am from him, and he sent me” (John 7:28–29).

No one knows the Father, and the Son frequently makes this declaration (Matt. 11:27). He says, therefore, that He alone knows Him because He is from Him. But I ask whether this being from Him displays in Him the work of creation or the nature of generation. If it is the work of creation, all things that are created are likewise from God. How, then, do not all things know the Father, when the Son does not fail to know Him precisely because He is from Him [Col. 0180A]? But if, in being from God, He is regarded as created rather than begotten, then, since all things are from God, how does He not, along with the rest, fail to know the Father—He who is from Him? [Note: [Col. 0179D] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read “from him.” Arius attempted in vain to evade the force of this argument when, as Athanasius testifies, *Oration II against the Arians*, p. 311, he wrote in his *Thalia* that the Father is hidden from the Son and cannot be fully and exactly seen or known by Him; but that what He knows and sees, He understands according to the measure and capacity of His powers, just as we too understand according to the measure of our capacities. Yet by Christ’s own testimony, although no one knows the Father, He Himself knows Him and knows Him because He is from Him.]

But if knowing is proper to Him precisely because He is from Him, how is not that whereby He is from Him proper to Him? Clearly, that He may be true Son by God’s nature: since He alone knows God precisely because He alone is from Him. You have, therefore, the distinctive property of knowledge from the distinctive property of generation; and that He is from Him does not indicate a created being’s power in Him—for all things exist from Him by the power of creation—but the truth of birth (supply, “you have”), through which He alone knows the Father, while the other things that are from Him do not know Him.

29. “I am from him” cannot be referred to the flesh. Nor is He created whose origin is unknown. — Yet lest heresy perhaps seize upon what He is from Him and refer it to the time of His coming, He immediately added: “Because I am from him, and he sent me” [Note: [Col. 0180C] In Erasmus, Leipzig, and Paris, the particle “to” was omitted. Here, by “coming” is understood the assumption of flesh.]. He preserved the order of the Gospel mystery, declaring Himself begotten and sent, so that, according to the preceding statement, both what He was and whence He was might be understood from His birth. For “I am from him” and “he sent me” are not identical, just as “You know neither me” and “you do not know where I am from” are not identical [Note: [Col. 0180C] The Vatican Basilica manuscript reads “just as this is the same”; this conflicts with what is said in §§30 and 31.].

Is not every human being, though born in the flesh, from God according to the understanding of common opinion? How then does He deny that they know either Himself or whence He is, unless “whence He is” refers to the author of His nature [Note: [Col. 0180C] The Vatican Basilica manuscript reads “refers [it] to authority”; the following word “who,” which must refer to the Father, does not suit this reading. Its meaning is this: since the Jews did not fail to know whence He was according to the flesh, “whence I am” must refer to the author of His eternal generation—as though He said, “You know neither me nor my eternal Father.” For, as is shown in Book III, §17, and Book V, §27, the Jews did not know God’s name so long as they did not know Him to be Father and to have a Son. Incidentally, it should be observed that Hilary simply calls the author of eternal generation the author of Christ’s nature, because he evidently held Christ to be God by nature, but man only according to the dispensation. Hence he usually refers the term “nature” to His divinity. See Book X, §§22, 64, and 65.]—who was unknowable precisely because He was unknown to be the Son of God?

Examine, unhappy man, in your folly, what this means: “You know neither me nor where I am from.” All things, certainly, are from nothing—and so fully from nothing that you have dared to lie that even the only-begotten God arose from nothing [Note: [Col. 0180D] In the Carnotensis manuscript, “dared.” Arius dared this in his *Thalia*, according to Athanasius, *Oration II*, p. 310, saying: “The Son was not always; and the very Word of God was made from nothing.”] [Col. 0180C]. What, then, is this—that the impious do not know Christ, and do not know whence He is? For the fact that His origin is unknown shows, by their not knowing whence He is, the nature from which He is [Col. 0181A]. [Note: [Col. 0181D] That is, His statement that whence He is is unknown.] For one who arose from nothing cannot have it unknown whence He is, because precisely this—being known to be from nothing—does not leave ignorance of whence He is.

But He who came is not from Himself; rather, He who sent Him is true, and Him the impious do not know. Thus, then, He who sent is Himself He whose sending is unknown. Therefore He who was sent is from Him who sent Him; and He is from Him whence His being is unknown; and for this reason He Himself is unknown, because it is unknown from whom He is. He does not know Christ who does not know whence Christ is; nor does he confess the Son who denies that He was begotten; nor does he understand that He was begotten who supposes that He came from nothing. Yet He is so far from being from nothing that the impious do not know whence He is.

30. God is Father only to those who worship the Son, not as an adopted son. What it means to go forth from God. The reason for loving the Son, and the reason for His birth. — They plainly do not know—those who take nature away from the name—[Note: [Col. 0181D] The printed editions read “because, not knowing.” The manuscripts more correctly read “who, not knowing”: those, namely, who neither seek the reason of understanding nor accept it when made known by others, as was said above in §15.] who, not knowing, do not love to know. Let them hear the Son reproaching the impious with ignorance of this knowledge when the Jews called God their Father. For He says: “If God were your Father, you would certainly love me; for I went forth from God and came: nor did I come from myself, but he sent me” (John 8:42).

The Son of God did not disapprove the claiming of this religious name among those who, confessing Him to be God’s Son, called God their Father [Note: [Col. 0181D] Erasmus, Leipzig, and Paris read “who called themselves sons of God,” corruptly and in a way that removes the force of the entire argument. For there, and shortly afterward in “because they did not love him,” the word “him” refers to Christ; and Hilary observes that those were not reproved who, while confessing and loving Christ as God’s Son, called God their Father. But the Vatican Basilica manuscript is still worse here in also having “sons,” and later reading “did not merely disapprove” instead of “did not disapprove”: an error arising from an error.]; but He rebukes the Jews’ rash usurpation in presuming that God was their Father, because they did not love Him: “If God were your Father, you would certainly love me; for I went forth from God” [Col. 0181C].

To all for whom God is Father through faith, He is Father through that faith by which we confess Jesus Christ to be God’s Son. But what faith is there in confessing the Son according to the general designation of the saints, so that we may say, “He is one among the sons”? Are not the rest too sons in this weakness of their created condition? In what, then, does faith’s confession of Jesus Christ as Son of God excel, if, in relation to sons, He is a son not by nature but only by name [Note: [Col. 0182D] Erasmus in the margin reads “according to them,” which Leipzig then adopted and Paris retained. We restore from Badius and the manuscripts, “according to sons,” that is, in the manner of the other sons.]? This faithlessness does not love Christ, and this impious profession does not piously claim God as Father [Note: [Col. 0181D] “Nor does an impious profession piously claim God as Father.”], because, if God were their Father, they would love Christ for this reason: that He had gone forth from God.

I ask what “to go forth from God” means. Certainly it cannot be said that going forth from God is identical with coming, for both are signified: “Because I went forth from God and came” [Note: [Col. 0182D] “To go forth.”] [Note: [Col. 0182D] Three Colbert manuscripts with the Carnotensis and German manuscript read “to go forth.”]. And showing what “I went forth from God” meant and what “and came” meant, He immediately added: “For I did not come from myself, but he sent me” [Col. 0182A]. [Note: [Col. 0182D] Leipzig and Paris read “not from himself,” contrary to the other books. Moreover, for Hilary the word *origo* (“origin”) often means what “beginning” means for us.]

He taught that He was not His own origin when He said, “For I did not come from myself,” and when He again testified that He had gone forth from God and had been sent by Him. But when He says to those who called God their Father that they ought for this reason to love Him because He had gone forth from God, He teaches that the cause of love derives from the cause of birth. For He referred the expression “to go forth” to incorporeal birth, because the religion of confessing God to be one’s Father is to be attained through love of Christ who was begotten from Him.

For when He says, “He who hates me hates my Father also” (John 15:23), by saying “my,” He excluded communion of the name with others through the meaning of distinctive property. Moreover, He condemns one who professes that God is his Father but does not love Him, in that person’s usurpation of the paternal name [Col. 0182B]: [Note: [Col. 0182D] An old codex of St. Martin of Tours reads: “because if he hates the Son, he hates the Father also.”] because he who hates Him hates the Father also. Nor is one devout toward God as Father who does not love the Son, since there is no other reason for loving the Son than that He is from God. The Son, therefore, is from God not by coming, but by birth; and all love for the Father [Note: [Col. 0182D] “All love for the Father will be from this.”] [Note: [Col. 0182D] Thus the better books. Others read “will be from this.”] will rest here: if the Son is believed to be from Him.

31. The reward of perfect faith concerning the Son: distinguishing both His birth from the Father and His coming to us. — The Lord bears witness to this, saying: “I shall not say to you that I will ask the Father for you; for the Father himself loves you, because you love me and believe that I went forth from God and came from the Father into this world” (John 16:27–28). Perfect faith concerning the Son needs no intercession with the Father: faith which believes and loves that He went forth from God [Col. 0182C]. Through itself it already merits both to be heard and to be loved, having confessed the Son as born from God and sent.

Thus His birth and His coming are shown with the most complete truth of the distinctive property signified. “I went forth from God,” He says, lest He be thought to have any nature other than that of birth; for to go forth from God—that is, to subsist by birth—what else could it be than to be God [Note: [Col. 0182D] In the St. Martin manuscript: “than that He was God.”]? And He says, “I came from the Father into this world.” So that this birth from God might be understood as signified to be from the Father, He declares that He came from the Father into this world. The one, therefore, belongs to the dispensation; the other to nature. Nor does He allow “going forth” to be thought “coming,” since after going forth from God He mentions coming from the Father.

For “to come from the Father” and “to go forth from God” are not expressions with the same meaning; and as great as the difference between being born and being present [Note: [Col. 0182D] The printed editions read “between being born,” and shortly afterward, “to go forth into the substance of birth is one thing,” etc. We follow the manuscripts.], so great is the distinction between the two statements [Col. 0183A]. For it is one thing to go forth from God into the substance of birth; it is another to come from the Father into this world to accomplish the mysteries of our salvation.

32. The Apostles believed Christ to be Son by nature, not by adoption. — Indeed, according to the order of the answer we have proposed, this is a most suitable place for us now to teach for the third time that our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, was believed by the Apostles to be Son not by appellation but by nature, not by adoption but by birth [Note: [Col. 0183C] Paris, following Leipzig, reads “handed down,” incorrectly and contrary to the evidence of the other books. For the Apostles’ teaching is not yet being examined, but their faith.].
