Although many and most illustrious [Note: [Col. 0183C] The earlier printed editions have *maxime*, an adverb. Here *maximae* means “most illustrious.” Then in the very ancient Colbert and Carnotensis exemplars, *adhunc* is written, with no other sense.]—declarations of the only-begotten God concerning Himself remain, by which He testifies to the truth of His generation without even a slight opportunity for a slanderous charge of falsehood: nevertheless, the reader’s mind ought not to be burdened by an abundance of accumulated sayings; and since some things concerning the distinctive property of birth have already been shown, all the rest must be reserved for other questions.

But now, since this order of our discourse has been established—that after the Father’s attestation, after the Son’s declaration, we should also be taught the Apostles’ faith in confessing the true Son of God, Son according to birth [Note: [Col. 0183D] Thus in the manuscripts. In the printed editions, “faith.”]—we must see whether, when the Lord said, “I went forth from God,” they understood anything in Him other than the nature of birth.

33. What it means that they first believe that He went forth from God. — For after the many obscurities of the proverbial sayings in which He had spoken in parables—He whom they had already known to have been announced by Moses and the prophets, whom Nathanael had also confessed both Son of God and King of Israel (John 1:49), and after Philip had been rebuked when he asked about the Father, because he did not know that the Father was in Him through the power of His works and that He was in the Father [Note: [Col. 0183C] “To be” is omitted in our manuscript.] [Note: [Col. 0183D] The printed editions, omitting “to be,” read “they added,” and “did not know that He was in the Father,” instead of “that He was in [the Father].” The manuscript reading is more coherent.], and although He had previously taught them by frequent sayings that He was sent by the Father (John 14:9–12)—nevertheless, when they heard Him declare that He had gone forth from God, this was their reply (for the discourse is connected in this way): “His disciples say to him, ‘Now you speak plainly and say no proverb. Now therefore we know that you know all things and do not need anyone to question you; by this we believe that you went forth from God’” (John 16:29).

What, I ask, is this astonishment at these words—that He declared Himself to have gone forth from God? You, holy and blessed men, who had seen so many things, so great and so proper to God, performed by our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, and who by the merit of your faith were granted the keys [Note: [Col. 0183D] In the older manuscripts, “the key” occurs here. Below, however, this word appears in the plural by the unanimous agreement of all the books.] of the kingdom of heaven and received the right to bind and loose in heaven and on earth: do you now first declare that you have attained the understanding of truth at His saying, “I went forth from the Father”?

You had indeed seen wedding water and that same water made into wedding wine, and either a transformation, an advancement, or a creation of one nature into another (John 2). You had also broken five loaves for the food of so great a multitude; and when all had been filled, the fragments of the loaves increased to the full measure of twelve baskets [Note: [Col. 0183D] The older manuscripts read “of loaves.” Erasmus thinks that “the smallness of the material,” rather than “of nature,” should be read. This is supported by what Hilary says of the same work of Christ in his Commentary on Matthew, chapter 14, §12: “Then the material increases”; and shortly afterward: “For so great an increase of loaves shows the author of this universe, through whom the measure of the material handled was enlarged by such an increase.” We should therefore more readily agree with him, if the word “nature,” repeated immediately afterward, were not preceded by the same word. This sentence differs from the preceding one only in vocabulary. Then the Vatican Basilica manuscript reads “the withered hand became green again,” which conflicts with what follows, where Christ’s other deeds are stated in the plural.] [Note: [Col. 0183C] “Fragments of loaves.”]; and the smallness of nature, driving away hunger, increased into an abundance of the same nature [Col. 0184B] (Matt. 14).

You had seen withered hands restored to life, the tongues of the mute loosened for speech, the feet of the lame made swift for running, the eyes of the blind made to see, and the lives of the dead return. Lazarus, stinking in decay, stood at the voice; called out of the tomb, with no interval between the voice and life, he came forth swiftly [Note: [Col. 0184D] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read “quickly.”], and while the odor of death still affected the sense of smell, he himself already stood there alive (John 11:44). I pass over the other works of great power and divine operations.

Do you now first understand who this One sent from heaven is, after hearing, “I went forth from the Father”? Is this now first said to you without a proverb? And do you understand through the power of nature that it is true that He went forth from God, when He silently beholds the thoughts of your wills [Note: [Col. 0184C] “Our.”] [Note: [Col. 0184D] Most and the better manuscripts read “our.” Shortly afterward all read “silently,” whereas the printed editions read “silent.”] [Col. 0184C], when, as though ignorant, He asks about nothing [Note: [Col. 0184D] The printed editions read “concerning some.” The better manuscripts correctly read “concerning none”; for the reference is to, “You have no need that anyone question you.” Later the Vatican Basilica manuscript reads, “when He is the knower of all hidden things”; St. Martin, “when He is the maker of all hidden things”: less genuine readings, since the sacred text to which this refers simply has, “because you know all things.”], though He knows all things? For through all these things, which He does by the power and nature of God, He must be believed to have gone forth from God.

34. They had previously known that he had been sent by God, but had not received the account of his birth. — The holy apostles did not here understand that he had gone forth from God, that is, that he had been sent by God; for throughout all the preceding discourse they had often heard him confess that he had been sent. But, hearing that he had gone forth from God and perceiving in him, from his works, the nature of God [Col. 0185A], they recognize the truth of his nature through the fact that he went forth from God, when they say: “Now therefore we know that you know all things, and have no need that anyone should question you; by this we believe that you went forth from God” (John 16:29). For they believe that he went forth from God through that by which he is able to do, and does, the things that are God’s.

[Note: In the manuscript of St Martin and the Vatican Basilica manuscript: “the power of nature,” less suitably. For the conclusion is that the Apostles were led by Christ’s power and works to believe the hidden truth of the divine nature in him, which he himself preached to them.]

For he does not affirm that God’s nature came from the Father, but that it went forth from God. Finally, this which they now hear for the first time is confirmed for their faith. For when the Lord had said both, “I went forth from God, and I came from the Father into this world” (ibid., 28), they found nothing astonishing in what they had often heard: “I came from the Father into this world.” 159 But their answer bore witness to their faith and understanding of this statement: “I went forth from God.” For they answer only to this when they say, “By this we believe that you went forth from God” [Col. 0185B]; nor do they add, “And you came from the Father into this world.” And whereas one statement is in their confession and the other in their silence, the novelty of the saying required the reason for confession, while understanding of the truth elicited the testimony of professing it. They knew indeed that he could do all things as God, but had not yet received the account of his birth; and though they knew that he was sent by God, they did not yet know that he had gone forth from God. Understanding through the force of this saying that ineffable and perfect birth of the Son, they now confess among themselves that he has spoken without figures of speech.

[Note: Leipzig and Paris manuscripts: “are confirmed.” Badianus, Erasmus, and the manuscripts more correctly: “is confirmed,” namely Christ’s own testimony that he had gone forth from God, by the Apostles.]

[Note: Paris manuscript, with an ancient Colbert and the German manuscript: “the account of novelty.”]

[Note: Certain manuscripts, found to be less reliable, together with Badianus and Erasmus: “now for the first time began to notice, when they profess him to have spoken without figures.”]

35. How aptly “going forth” expresses the Son’s birth. — For God is not born from God according to the ordinary manner of human birth, nor is he brought forth as man from man through the elements of our origin. That birth is whole, perfect, and undefiled [Col. 0185C], whose mode is rather a going forth from God than a birth. For he is one from one. He is not a portion, not a falling away, not a diminution, not an emanation, not an extension, not a suffering; rather, he is the birth of a living nature from the Living One. God going forth from God is not a creature chosen to bear God’s name; he did not begin to be out of nothing, but went forth from One who remains. And “having gone forth” signifies birth, not beginning. For to have begun substance from God is not the same as for God to have gone forth from God. Though awareness of this birth is not subject to words, because it is ineffable, it nevertheless possesses the security of faith in the teaching about the Son: that he manifests himself as having gone forth from God.

[Note: Vatican Basilica and St Martin manuscripts: “to have begun from God”; and afterwards, “in the doctrine of faith concerning the Son of God,” etc.]

[Col. 0186A]

36. Peter, in confessing the Son of God, believed the reality of things. Then for the first time he acknowledged him as God. Where he learned this. — It is neither evangelical nor apostolic faith to have believed in the Son of God by name rather than by nature. For if this designation is one of adoption, and if he is not Son because he went forth from God, I ask: whence did blessed Simon Bar-Jonah confess, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. 16:16)? Was it because all have the power, through the sacrament of regeneration, to be born as sons of God? If Christ is Son of God according to this designation, I ask what that was which flesh and blood did not reveal to Peter, but the Father who is in heaven did reveal (ibid., 17). What merit belongs to a general confession? Or what glory of revelation lies in public knowledge?

[Note: Omitted in a Vatican Basilica manuscript. See Book I, §§10 and 11.]

[Note: The editions, except Paris, and certain recent manuscripts read “public knowledge.” Other books more truly read “public awareness,” that is, awareness shared even by the common people. Thus in Book II to Constantius, §10, Hilary asks permission to discuss the faith under public awareness; and in *Against Constantius*, §2, the heretics at the Council of Béziers refuse to hear what he proposed, fearing public awareness.]

If he is Son by adoption, whence comes Peter’s blessed confession, assigning to the Son what is common to the saints? But apostolic faith reaches beyond human understanding. He had certainly often heard: “He who receives you receives me; and he who receives me receives him who sent me” (Matt. 10:40). Thus he was already not ignorant that he was sent; 160 and of him whom he knew to have been sent, he had heard the confession: “All things have been delivered to me by my Father, and no one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son” (Matt. 11:25). What then is this which the Father now reveals to Peter, and from which he receives the glory of blessed confession? Did he not know the name of Father and Son? On the contrary, he had often heard it. But he speaks what no human voice had yet uttered: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” For although Christ, remaining in the body, had professed himself God’s Son, apostolic faith now for the first time acknowledged in him the nature of divinity [Col. 0186C].

Nor was praise given to Peter merely from confessed honor, but from recognition of the mystery: because he confessed not merely Christ, but Christ to be the Son of God. To confess honor, it would indeed have been enough to say, “You are the Christ.” But it would have been empty that Christ had been confessed by him, unless he confessed the Son of God. For in saying, “You are,” he expounded the power and proper character of natural truth. And the Father, in saying, “This is my Son” (Matt. 17:5), revealed to Peter that he should say, “You are the Son of God”; because in the words “This is” lies the indication of the revealer, while in the answer “You are” lies the acknowledgment of the confessor. Therefore upon this rock of confession is the building of the Church [Col. 0187A] (see Book II, §23, and *Commentary on Matthew*, ch. 16, §7). But the understanding of flesh and blood does not reveal the meaning of this confession. This is the sacrament of divine revelation: not merely to call Christ the Son of God, but to believe it. Or was designation rather than nature revealed to Peter? If designation, he had already often heard it from the Lord, who confessed himself to be God’s Son. Where, then, is the glory of revelation? It was the nature, plainly, not the name; since the name had already repeatedly been professed.

[Note: In the Vatican Basilica manuscript: “bestowing what at first pleased [him].” But there is no reason to depart from the agreement of the others. Still less satisfactory later, with the same manuscript, is “what is common.” We understand *Filio* in the dative and the following word *deferenti* in the ablative, as though: “in Peter, when he ascribes to the Son.”]

[Note: Vienna and Silvius manuscripts: “namely in the nature, because the repeated profession of the name,” etc.—incorrect. This should rather be rendered: “namely, in the fact that a revelation was made to him of the nature, not of the name,” etc.]

37. Peter’s faith is commended. — This faith is the foundation of the Church; by this faith the gates of hell are powerless (variant: weak) against it. This faith possesses the keys of the kingdom of heaven. This faith—whatever it looses or binds on earth is bound and loosed in heaven [Col. 0187B] (Matt. 16:18–19)—is the gift of paternal revelation: it confesses Christ not to be a creature lying falsely out of nothing, but to be the Son of God according to the nature proper to him.

[Note: Earlier printed editions: “knows not a creature.” *Knows* is absent from the manuscripts.]

O impious frenzy of miserable folly, not understanding Peter, martyr of blessed old age and faith—Peter, too, a martyr, for whom the Father was asked 161 that his faith might not fail in temptation; who, after his repeatedly demanded profession of love toward God, groaned that he was still being tested as doubtful and uncertain by the third question (John 21:17); who also deserved to hear three times from the Lord, after the third purification of the weakness of temptations: “Feed my sheep”—he who, amid the silence of all the apostles, understanding by the Father’s revelation the Son of God, merited, beyond the measure of human weakness, the surpassing glory of blessed faith by his confession!

[Note: In certain manuscripts, “and martyr” is not repeated through scribal carelessness; by this word a witness is meant.]

[Note: “After the third purification of the weakness of temptations.”]

[Note: Thus from the Corbie manuscript, supported by others. Nearly the same sense appears in two Vatican manuscripts: “after the third purification of the weakness of temptation”; but the word *temptation*, referred to Peter’s twofold testing, is thereby restricted to one. In the older Colbert and German manuscripts: “after the third purification of the weaknesses of temptation.” Another Colbert manuscript, as well as the Pratensis, Vienna, and Silvius manuscripts with the editions of Badianus and Paris, agree, except that they have “weakness.” To these is added the older Remigius manuscript: “after the third purification of the weakness of temptation.” But in the Chartres, Tell, Theodulf, and another Remigius manuscript: “after the third purification of temptation”; for which Badianus, Erasmus, the St Martin manuscript, one Sorbonne manuscript, and another Colbert manuscript read: “after the third weakness of temptation.” From these various readings let each choose whichever seems preferable. The reading we have preferred means this: that Peter, after the third questioning, as it were a temptation by which his love was tested, was cleansed from the threefold denial in which his weakness had been tested and proved. This is illustrated by these words of Ambrose, *On Faith*, Book V, §2: “Peter was chosen by the Lord’s own judgment to feed the flock; he deserved to hear ‘Feed,’ etc., for the third time. By feeding it well with the food of faith, he wiped away the fault of his earlier fall. And therefore he is admonished to feed for the third time and asked for the third time whether he loves the Lord, so that he who had denied him three times before the cross might confess him three times.”]

To what necessity are we now driven in interpreting your words? He confessed Christ the Son of God; but you today, false priesthood of a novel apostolate, thrust upon me Christ as a creature from nothing. What violence do you inflict upon glorious words? He is blessed because he confessed the Son of God [Col. 0188A]. This is the Father’s revelation; this is the foundation of the Church; this is the security of eternity. From this he has the keys of the kingdom of heaven; from this his judgments on earth are judgments in heaven. He learned by revelation the hidden mystery, concealed from the ages; he spoke faith, he declared nature, he confessed the Son of God. Whoever, confessing him instead as a creature, denies this, must first deny Peter’s apostleship, faith, blessedness, priesthood, and martyrdom; and then understand himself to be alien from Christ, because Peter, by confessing him as Son, merited these things.

[Note: Vatican Basilica manuscript: “for in glory [he confesses] the Son,” etc.; St Martin: “for glorious [he confesses] the Son.”]

[Note: Earlier printed editions had *judgments* only once; the manuscripts repeat it more elegantly.]

[Note: Vatican Basilica manuscript: “by the revelation of God.”]

38. The heretics’ doctrine was unknown to Peter. No faith other than Peter’s. — Or do you, miserable heretic, whoever you are today, suppose that Peter would have been more blessed had he said: “You are the Christ, the perfect creature of God, and a creature surpassing all things made; you who began to exist from nothing, and by the goodness of God—who alone is good—merited by adoption the name of Son, and who were not born from God”? And I ask you what he would have heard 162 for saying this—he who, when he heard of the Passion, answered, “May it be gracious to you, Lord; this shall not be” (Matt. 16:22), and heard it said to him, “Get behind me, Satan; you are a stumbling block to me” (ibid., 23).

[Note: “May the Lord be gracious to you.”]

[Note: Thus the Vatican Basilica manuscript, according to the Greek, ἵλεώς σοι, κύριε, supported by the St Martin, Remigius, and Theodulf manuscripts: “Be gracious to you, Lord.” In other books appears “May the Lord be gracious to you,” except that in the Chartres manuscript *God* stands in place of *Lord*. But in the *Commentary on Matthew*, ch. 16, §9, following the Vulgate, it reads: “Far be it from you, Lord.”]

[Note: In the St Martin manuscript, “behind me” is lacking. See the notes on §10, ch. 16 of the *Commentary on Matthew*.]

Yet Peter’s human ignorance did not bring him to condemnation; for the Father had not yet revealed to him the whole mystery of the Passion. But a small error incurred the sentence of rebuke. Why, then, did the Father not reveal to Peter this faith of confession—namely, creaturehood and adoption? God, I suppose, begrudged Peter this, concealing it until later times, in order to reserve it now for you, new preachers [Col. 0188C].

[Note: The manuscripts of Chartres, Remigius, and Tell: *prava* (“wrong”); corruptly. For, as was just said, it was free from guilt.]

Let another faith exist, if there are other keys of the kingdom of heaven. Let another faith exist, if another Church is to exist against which the gates of hell shall not prevail. Let another faith exist, if there is to be another apostleship, binding and loosing on earth by its own authority, and binding and loosing in heaven. Let another faith exist, if another Christ, another Son of God than the one who is, is to be preached [Col. 0189A]. But if this faith alone, confessing Christ as the Son of God, obtained in Peter the glory of every blessedness, then it is necessary that the faith which confesses him instead as a creature from nothing, having not obtained the keys of the kingdom of heaven and being set outside apostolic faith and power, should neither be Church nor belong to Christ.

[Note: Vatican Basilica manuscript: “has obtained [them], and [is] outside faith and truth.” The reading “and power” with the others is preferable, namely the power especially displayed in authority to bind and loose.]

[Note: The editions, except Badianus, read: “nor is there any Church.” Badianus also reads: “nor Christ.” Three manuscripts: “nor Churches.” More truly, the others by strong agreement: “nor is that a Church”—namely, the body that professes such things—“nor [is it] Christ’s,” that is, it does not belong to Christ, the head of the Church.]

39. John, professing the only-begotten Son, denied that he was adoptive. — Let us therefore set forth all the professions of apostolic faith in which, while confessing the Son of God, they confess not in him a name of adoption but the proper character of nature; and testify not to the lowliness of creation but to the glory of birth. Let John speak—he who remained thus until the Lord’s coming and was left and designated under the mystery of the divine will, while it is said neither that he will not die nor that he will remain.

[Note: Badianus and Erasmus: “having been left, designated.” Leipzig and Paris: “left, designated,” without *and*; and then, with the Vatican Basilica manuscript, “while he is said not to die.” Where Badianus and Erasmus have “while neither [he is said] not to die,” and some manuscripts “while neither not [he is said] to die.” The more correct manuscripts read: “left and designated, while it is said neither that he will not die nor that he will remain”; that is, it is neither said that he will die—for Christ did not wish to disclose his will concerning John’s end—nor [certainly] that he will remain, and thus this remains hidden, or under a mystery. Ambrose, however, in Sermon XX on Psalm 118, says that some doubted St John’s death. Whether Hilary should be counted among them cannot be established with sufficient certainty from this passage, since he adheres as closely as possible to the words of John 21:22–23.]

Let him therefore speak in his customary voice: “No one has ever seen God, 163 except the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father” (John 1:18). Faith concerning the nature did not seem sufficiently explained by the name *Son* unless the force of proper identity were added from without through the significance of the exception. For by naming him both Son and only-begotten, he entirely cut off the suspicion of adoption, since the nature of the only-begotten secured the truth of the name.

[Note: The word *Son* is absent from our manuscript.]

[Note: The word *Son* does not occur in the manuscripts known to us except in the manuscript of St Martin of Tours.]

[Note: In Paris the particle *and*, here equivalent to “also,” is missing. Then, in Badianus, Erasmus, and three Vatican manuscripts, *nothing* is added after *only-begotten*: an interpolator’s fault. For this is its meaning: when the title *only-begotten* is added to the word *Son*, it signifies that he is not from the company of adopted sons, who are many in number, but is proper [to the Father]. For, as Augustine says in the *Conference with Maximinus*, §14: “If he is Son, he is true Son, because he is only-begotten.” From the same Johannine passage Faustinus, following in the footsteps of our Hilary, concludes three things in ch. 2, Book [*Against*] Flacilla: “Therefore the only-begotten Son is not a creature, because he sees God, whom no creature sees. And lest perhaps one should think him one among adopted sons, he removed the opportunity for an impious thought by calling him not merely Son but also only-begotten Son: this name admits no companions.” These are Hilary’s words clearly expressed. He adds: “Adopted sons are in Abraham’s bosom; but the true and only-begotten Son is in the Father’s bosom.”]

40. John’s only-begotten Son is not a perfect creature. — I do not yet ask what he is who is in the Father’s bosom; that question has its own order. I ask what the designation *only-begotten* requires. And let us see whether it means what you profess it to mean: namely, a perfect creature of God—so that *perfect* belongs to *only-begotten*, but *creature* refers to *Son*. But John called him God’s only-begotten Son [Col. 0190A], not a perfect creature. He was not ignorant of these names of blasphemy, saying, “who is in the bosom of the Father,” and hearing from his Lord: “For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life” (John 3:16).

[Note: Though the particle “so” may seem superfluous, it is added on the authority of the ancient books. Next, the Vatican Basilica and St Martin manuscripts have “might give,” in place of “that … might.”]

[Note: “Only.”]

God, loving the world, supplied this testimony of his love for it: that he gave his only-begotten Son. If the proof of love is that he bestowed a creature upon creatures, gave for the world what belongs to the world, and, to redeem beings established out of nothing, supplied one who himself came to be out of nothing, faith in a cheap and contemptible outlay does not make the proof of great merit. But the things that commend love are precious, and great things are valued by great things. God, loving the world, gave not an adoptive Son [Col. 0190B], but his own Son, his only-begotten Son. Here are proper identity, birth, and truth; there are not creation, adoption, or falsehood. From this comes the proof of love and charity: that for the world’s salvation he bestowed both his Son, his own Son, and his only-begotten Son.

[Note: This Son is shown to be proper by two arguments, of which one is not expressed quite clearly. Both are illustrated by Faustinus’s words in the place cited: “If Christ too is a creature, what did he confer on the world by giving creature for creature?” This is the first argument; the other is: “If Christ is a creature, he is a servant; and how does he redeem to freedom, when no servant can by right bestow freedom?” Further, from the words “that everyone who believes in him,” etc., he concludes that Christ is not a creature, since believing in a creature is an offense against divinity.]

[Note: In some manuscripts: “from this, proper identity,” wrongly; still worse, in Badianus and Erasmus: “from this, piety.” For proper identity is opposed to adoption, and is here—that is, in these words of John—plainly declared. From that declaration follows the obligation of our faith and love toward him. This makes clear why *from this* must be read at this point and later.]

164

41. Faith in Christ as God’s Son is necessary for salvation. — I pass over all the designations of the Son. There is no harmful omission where selection may be made from abundance. The benefit of a matter always follows from its cause, and every work plainly shows the necessity of the undertaking it has assumed. In writing the Gospels, surely, John ought to have supplied the reason for writing; and let us see what he declares when he says: “But these things have been written that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God” (John 20:31). He therefore assigned no other reason for writing the Gospel than that all should believe [Col. 0191A] Jesus to be Christ, the Son of God.

[Note: The editions read “the Evangelist”; then Paris: “that we may see.” They are corrected from the manuscripts. Faustinus, pursuing the same argument, says: “If he truly were God’s Son by adoption and not by nature … nowhere would John have explained this more fully than at the end of his writing, lest faith, left in ambiguity, should lose life through the uncertainty of ambiguity.”]

If it is sufficient for salvation to believe Christ, why did he add “the Son of God”? But if believing Christ is only then faith—when one believes not merely Christ, but Christ the Son of God—then the name *Son* in Christ, the only-begotten God, is not from the customary terminology of adoption, but is proper to salvation. If salvation therefore lies in confession of the name, I ask why truth should not lie in the name. But if truth lies in the name, by what authority will creation be asserted, when not confession of creation, but confession of the Son, confers salvation?

[Note: Seven manuscripts: “to believe is not sufficient.” *Not sufficient* is absent from the more authoritative manuscripts.]

[Note: What follows rests upon John’s words, cited immediately before and joined with “and that, believing, you may have life in his name.” Faustinus rightly saw this and elegantly explained it: “Is there even here suspicion of creaturehood, where one who believes that Christ is the Son of God possesses eternal life, and possesses it only in his name? … For in the name of a creature no one can obtain even temporal life.”]

42. The Son is born from the Father. Those who deny the Son are antichrists. — This, therefore, is true salvation; this is the merit of perfect faith: to believe Jesus Christ to be the Son of God. For there is no love in us toward God the Father except through faith in the Son. And let us hear him speaking in the Epistle: “Everyone who loves the Father loves him who has been born from him” (1 John 5:1). What, I ask, is it to be born from him? Is it the same thing as to be created through him? Or why does the Evangelist speak falsely in calling one born from him whom the heretic teaches rather to have been created through him? And let us hear what this teacher says.

[Note: If it is the same, the world too must by equal right be said to have been born from God; nor is Faustinus’s inference unsound: “Therefore the world too must be loved by us, if the Father is to be loved.” But John cries out, “Do not love the world.”]

For it has been said: “This is the antichrist, who denies the Father and the Son” (1 John 2:22). 165 (1 John 2:22). What are you doing, champion of a creature and novel creator of a Christ who does not exist? If you retain the profession, recognize the name of the one professing it. Or do you suppose that, when you proclaim Creator and creature as Father and Son, you can by simulated sounds of names prevent yourself from being understood to be antichrist? If in your faith he is Father by nature and Son by nature, I am a slanderer, fastening upon you the reproach of an alien name. But if all is simulated, and the names are assigned rather than proper, learn from the Apostle the byname of your faith, and hear what faith in the Son is to be believed.

[Note: Printed editions read “who it is”; the manuscripts read more aptly “what it is.” Erasmus wrongly reproached Hilary for calling the Arian an antichrist, when Hilary does not so much say it himself as hear John say it. Hence Ambrose, *On Faith*, Book II, ch. 15: “John says that heretics are antichrists, plainly indicating the Arians.” And Faustinus, so often cited: “You are rightly called antichrist, because by an impious interpretation you deny the Father and the Son.”]

[Note: Some manuscripts: “through assimilated [names],” incorrectly. The hypocrisy of the Arians is here attacked, concerning which Faustinus says at the beginning of his work: “Arian impiety indeed asserts many things with us under the same names, but not in the same senses. For with the same words as we, it voices God the Father and God the Son,” etc. Thus our Hilary immediately says, “all is simulated.” Accordingly, in the following word *proclaim*, not merely the sound of the terms but above all the understanding and judgment of the mind is signified.]

For it follows: “Whoever denies the Son does not have the Father; whoever confesses the Son has both the Son and the Father” (ibid., 23). He who denies the Son lacks the Father; he who confesses and possesses the Son possesses the Father. I ask here what place adoptive names have. Is not this whole matter one of nature? And learn how much it is one of nature.

[Note: “Lacks the Father.”]

43. John and the heretics compared together. — For he says: “Because we know that the Son of God has come and been made flesh for our sake, and suffered, and rising from the dead has taken us up, and has given us the best understanding, that we may know the True One and be in his true Son Jesus Christ: this is the True One, and eternal life, and our resurrection” (1 John 5:20–21).

[Note: “And we are in the true Son Jesus Christ: this is the true God”; Greek: οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ ἀληθινὸς θεός, “this is the true God.”]

[Note: The word *his*, omitted in the printed editions, is restored from the manuscripts.]

[Note: On the authority of the older manuscripts we have removed the word *God* from this place; it is absent likewise from the early editions of Faustinus and was added in later ones only within parentheses—that is, conjecturally. Whether Hilary read “this is the true God” is indeed uncertain; Basil, *Against Eunomius*, Book IV, p. 106; Augustine, *Conference with Maximinus*, §14; and Cyril of Alexandria at the end of Dialogue VIII read it. But it is apparent that Hilary referred the word *true* to the Son; thus he read “this is the True One” and understood “Son.”]

[Note: After *our*, Faustinus adds “in him”; with him the same passage is reproduced in precisely the same words, although the clauses “has been made flesh for our sake,” “suffered,” “and rising from the dead has taken us up,” and “our resurrection,” like the foregoing, are no longer present in either the Greek or Latin sacred text, nor in Cyril at the place just cited.]

O unhappy understanding, devoid of God’s Spirit, advancing into the spirit and name of antichrist, and not knowing that the Son of God came for the sacrament of our salvation—therefore unworthy of the meaning of this best understanding—you confess rather the adoptive name of a creature than that Jesus Christ is the true Son of God. By what secret mysteries have you been instructed in this? Or who today is the new author of this knowledge of yours? Did the Lord perhaps reveal it to you secretly because, through intimate love, you reclined upon his breast (John 13:23)? Or, following him alone to the cross, did you learn this too among the commands entrusting Mary to you as mother, in that testimony of his special love for you (John 19:27)? Or did you gain it by running before Peter also to the tomb (John 20:4)? Or was this doctrine so lovingly revealed to you by the Lamb as guide amid the assemblies of angels 166 [Col. 0192C], the unloosenable bonds of sealed books, the manifold powers of heavenly signs, and the eternal hymns of new and incomprehensible songs, that Father might not be Father, Son not Son, nature not nature, truth not truth (Rev. 5)? For with you all these things are changed into falsehood.

[Note: From these facts, and from what was said in §20, it is clear that Hilary did not regard the John of the Gospel and the author of the Apocalypse as different persons.]

The Apostle, by the excellent understanding granted to him, calls him the true Son of God; you assert creation, you preach adoption, you deny birth. And since he is for us the true Son of God, eternal life, and resurrection, neither eternal life nor resurrection belongs to one for whom he is not true. And this, indeed, is John, the disciple beloved by the Lord.

[Note: Incorrectly in some manuscripts: “the Word of God.” Here again it is helpful to hear Faustinus, Hilary’s excellent interpreter: “For how is he not true God who is true Son? For true God is shown not only from the title of true Son, but also because he is eternal life. Eternal life has neither beginning nor end; therefore Christ is true God, having neither beginning nor end,” etc.]

44. Paul everywhere proclaims Christ the true Son of God. — But the Apostle and chosen vessel, once a persecutor, preached nothing different from these things. What saying of his is not under the confession of the Son? What epistle does not begin with the sacrament of this truth? In what name is there not an indication of proper identity? For when it is said: “We have been reconciled to God through the death of his Son” (Rom. 5:10); and again, “God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh” (Rom. 8:3); and again, “God is faithful, through whom you were called into the communion of his Son” (1 Cor. 1:9)—what room has been left here for the theft of heretics? He is his own Son; he is his Son: he is not his adoption, he is not his creature. The name speaks nature, proper identity declares truth, confession attests faith: I do not understand what can be added to the nature of the Son.

[Note: “For when he says.”]

[Note: The editions read “his Son is,” contrary to the authority of the manuscripts. The Apostle’s preceding passages are meant, in two of which stands *his own*, and in the last *his*.]

[Note: Badianus, Erasmus, Leipzig, and many manuscripts: “than that.” Paris, if its faulty punctuation is corrected, reads better with the older manuscripts: “For that.” The holy Doctor means that nothing can be added for signifying the nature of the true Son where there is not only the name *Son*, but also proper identity marked by the pronouns *his own* and *his*, and finally the Apostle’s confession testifying to both.]

For he who is called Son of the one believed to be Father was not spoken of uncertainly or weakly by him who is the chosen vessel; nor did the Teacher of the Gentiles and Apostle of Christ leave his doctrine in the error of ambiguity. He knows who are sons by adoption and who have merited to be and to be called this through faith. For he says: “For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are sons of God. For you have not received the spirit of slavery again unto fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption, in which we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Rom. 8:14–15).

[Note: “Unto fear.” The editions read “in fear,” against the manuscripts and the Greek.]

167

This name belongs to our faith through the sacrament of regeneration, and our profession bestows adoption upon us. For works performed according to the Spirit of God jointly designate us sons of God; and “Abba, Father” is cried by us as an office of speech rather than as remaining from a proper identity of nature, because outside the proper identity of nature there is the function of utterance, and saying and being are not the same.

### 45. The Proper Son Explicitly Affirmed. The Epistle to the Romans Was Written in Greek.

But let us understand what the Apostle’s faith concerning the Son of God is. For although, throughout all the discourse he employed in teaching the Church, he never spoke of the Father without confessing the Son, nevertheless, in order to show the truth of this name with whatever force human speech could convey, he says: “What then shall we say to these things? If God is for us, who is against us? He who did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us” (Rom. 8:31–32).

Can there still be, then, an appellation of adoption in him in whom there is the name of propriety? For the Apostle, wishing to display God’s love toward us, so that the greatness of God’s affection might be known by comparison, taught that God did not spare his own proper Son: certainly not an adopted one for those to be adopted, nor a creature for creatures, but his own for those who were strangers, his proper Son for those who were to be called sons. Consider the force of the expression, that you may understand the greatness of the love. Consider what “proper” means, lest you fail to recognize the truth.

For the Apostle now calls him the proper Son, although in many other places he had often said either “his” or “his own” [Col. 0194B]. And although many manuscripts, through the simple understanding of translators, have at this place written “his Son” in place of “his proper Son”:

> [Note: In the manuscript of Martin, “of the Latin translators,” in place of “of translators.”]

> [Note: Paris edition: “for his proper Son,” insufficiently distinct. Some manuscripts: “his Son” for “his proper Son.” Faustinus observes that Paul here alludes to Genesis 22:12: “Now I know that you fear God, and have not spared your beloved son”; and that Isaac was a figure of the Son of God. Yet the figure would have been fuller and more perfect in the truth itself if Isaac, a true son, had been offered by his father Abraham, and a son not true [i.e. not a Son by nature] had been offered by God the Father.]

Nevertheless, the Greek language, in which the Apostle spoke, here calls him “proper” rather than merely “his own.” And although, in ordinary usage, the distinction between “proper” and “one’s own” may not be sufficiently evident, the Apostle, while in his other sayings he had referred to “his own Son”—in Greek, *ton heautou huion* (τὸν ἑαυτοῦ υἱὸν)—nevertheless in this passage, where he says, *hos ge tou idiou huiou ouk epheisato* (ὅς γε τοῦ ἰδίου υἱοῦ οὐκ ἐφείσατο), “who did not spare his proper Son,” significantly expressed the truth of nature: so that, having above shown many sons through the Spirit of adoption, he might now show the only-begotten Son, God, by the designation of propriety.

> [Note: Supply “by the designation.” Although the term “propriety” is so arranged that “the Son of propriety” is opposed to sons of adoption.]

### 46. One Who Denies That Christ Is the Son of God Is Inexcusable. He Will Receive Antichrist in Place of Christ.

This is no human error; nor, in denying the Son of God, is there the fault of ignorance where what is denied cannot lawfully be unknown. A creature subsisting from nothing is called the Son of God. Even if neither the Father had spoken this, nor the Son testified to it, nor the Apostle preached it, still to dare to utter it is not merely not to know Christ, but to hate him.

For when the Father says of his Son, “This is he” (Matt. 3:17); and the Son says of himself, “He who speaks with you is he” (John 9:37); and Peter confesses, “You are” (Matt. 16:16); and John testifies, “This is the true one” (1 John 5:20–21); and Paul does not cease to preach concerning the proper Son—I understand nothing else than that there is hatred in denial, where an error of ignorance is not excused from guilt.

Meanwhile, he who will later speak in Antichrist is himself speaking these things plainly through the prophets and forerunners of his coming:

> [Note: An old Colbert manuscript reads “Antichrist,” omitting “in.”]

He unsettles the saving confession of faith by these novel temptations, so that he may first tear away from our conscience, because we so believe, the understanding of the natural Son; and afterward exclude even the remaining name, that which will have become merely adoptive.

> [Note: “Because we so believe.”]

> [Note: The Basel Vatican manuscript, together with some others, reads “because we so believe.” The Paris edition, following older manuscripts, reads “because.” For it gives the reason why the devil does not immediately attempt to take from Christ the name of Son: namely, because it is so firmly fixed in our faith that he is Son that he despairs of being able at once to tear us away from this conviction.]

> [Note: That is, he causes even that condition of adoption itself to make us readily concede that he is not even a son.]

For among those—or according to whose opinion—Christ is a creature, Antichrist himself must be Christ; because a creature does not possess the propriety of Sonship, whereas that one falsely claims to be the Son of God. Therefore, among those by whom this Son of God is now denied, that Antichrist will then be believed to be Christ.

> [Note: The Carcassonne exemplar reads, “because here”; then the Basel Vatican manuscript, “God the Son.” Shortly afterward several others read, “that Christ will be believed.” “Will be believed” is to be retained with the older witnesses, with “must” understood.]

> [Note: “Then that Christ will be believed.”]

### 47. Faith in the Son of God Is Required Before Healing unto Salvation.

What hope, I ask, do you seek, empty madness? And with what confidence in your salvation do you contend with blasphemous speech that Christ is a creature rather than the Son [Col. 0195B]? You ought to have known and retained from the Gospels this mystery of faith. For although the Lord can do all things, yet in each of those who prayed for the effect of his work he willed there to be the merit of confession. The confession of the petitioner did not add power to him who is the Power of God; rather, it was the reward of faith to merit this.

For when he questioned Martha, who was pleading for Lazarus, whether she believed that those who had believed in him would never die, she declared the faith of her conscience, saying: “Certainly, Lord, I have believed that you are the Christ, the Son of God, who has come into this world” (John 11:17). This confession is eternal life, and this faith does not die.

> [Note: Thus from the Colbert and German manuscripts. Other books read, “but she.”]

Martha, pleading for her brother’s life, when asked whether she believed thus, believed thus. From whom, I ask, or what life does one who denies this expect, when to believe thus is the only life? For great is the mystery of this faith, and perfect is the blessedness of this confession.

### 48. The Same Faith Is Required for the Salvation of the Soul from the Man Who Had Received Sight.

The Lord granted sight to a man blind from birth, and the Lord of nature removed the defect of nature. And because this blind man had been born for the glory of God, so that in Christ’s work the work of God might be understood, faith in confession was not required of him beforehand. But he who, upon receiving his eyes, did not know the author of so great a gift afterward merited to learn faith. For the removal of blindness did not bring eternal life.

Therefore the Lord questioned him, now healed and cast out of the synagogue, saying: “Do you believe in the Son of God?” (John 9:35). This was lest he should regard it as a loss that he lacked the synagogue, when this confessed faith would restore immortality to him [Col. 0196A].

> [Note: “That he lacked the synagogue.” In this manuscript occur, similarly, “he lacks the Father” above, no. 42; “nor may he lack power,” Book VII, no. 37; and elsewhere. Thus Greek *ti hysterō?* (τί ὑστερῶ;), and likewise Latin Plautus in the *Curculio*: “I lack what I love.”]

And when he, still uncertain, replied: “Who is he, Lord, that I may believe in him?” (John 9:36), the Lord, unwilling that his ignorance should remain—the one who, after the recovery of his eyes, was bestowing on him understanding for so great a faith—said: “You have both seen him, and he who speaks with you is he” (John 9:37).

> [Note: “Recovery.”]

Does the Lord here, as with the others who prayed for healings, demand a confession of faith in order to obtain salvation?

> [Note: “Demanded.”]

Certainly not. For he spoke these words to one who was already blind no longer, but seeing; and for this purpose alone, that the man might answer: “I believe, Lord” (John 9:38). The faith of that answer would bring, not healing from blindness, but life.

> [Note: The Leipzig and Paris editions read, “but life.”]

Let us carefully reconsider the force of this saying. The Lord asks, “Do you believe in the Son of God?” If any sort of confession of Christ alone were the completion of faith, he would have said: “Do you believe in Christ?” But because nearly all heretics would be about to have this name on their lips—so as to confess Christ while nevertheless denying the Son—that which is proper to Christ is required for faith: namely, belief in the Son of God. But what profit is there in believing in the Son of God if one believes him to be a creature, when faith in Christ is demanded from us, not faith in God’s creature, but in his Son?

### 49. The Demons Did Not Fail to Know the Son of God.

Or did demons not know the propriety of this name? It is fitting that heretics should be refuted now, not by apostolic teachings, but by the mouth of demons. For they cry out, and cry out often: “What have I to do with you, Jesus, Son of the Most High God?” (Luke 8:28).

> [Note: Thus the manuscripts, perhaps through scribal error, read “custom.” The printed editions read “cry.” Shortly afterward, the Basel Vatican manuscript reads, “What is there between us and you?”]

Truth extorted confession from unwilling beings, and the pain of obedience testifies to the power of the nature [Col. 0196C]. They are overcome by power when they abandon bodies long possessed; they render honor while confessing the nature.

> [Note: In the Basel Vatican and Martin manuscripts: “the nature of God.”]

Amid these things Christ testifies that he is the Son of God both by work and by name. Whence, amid these voices of confessing demons, O heretic, do you derive the name of creature and the indulgence of adoption?

> [Note: Printed editions: “Do you presume the name of creature and the indulgence of adoption?” contrary to the manuscripts.]

### 50. The Jews Knew Christ to Be the Son of God, Though They Did Not Know Who Christ Was. The Arians Are More Insulting toward Christ Than the Jews.

Learn, at least from those who do not know, what Christ is, so that the necessary confession of those very ignorant persons may convict your impiety. For although the Jews did not know Christ in the flesh, they nevertheless knew that he who was Christ was the Son of God. When they employed false witnesses against him without any assertion of truth, the high priest questioned him thus: “Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed One?” (Mark 14:61).

> [Note: Earlier printed editions read, “the Son of God, the Blessed One.” The word “God” is absent from the manuscripts and from the Greek. The Jews’ error is here noted as being in fact, not in principle.]

Though ignorant of the mystery, they were not ignorant of the nature. They do not ask whether Christ is the Son of God, but whether this man is Christ, the Son of God. The error lies in the man, not in the Son of God. For there is no doubt that Christ is the Son of God; and thus, while they ask whether this man is he, they nevertheless do not deny that Christ is the Son of God.

And with what faith, I ask, do you deny what even those who do not know do not deny? For perfect knowledge is to know both that Christ is the Son of God abiding before the ages and that he was born of a virgin; yet even those who do not know that he was born of Mary do not fail to know that he is the Son of God.

See, then, into what fellowship with Jewish impiety you have entered by denying the Son of God. For the charge on which they brought condemnation against him is testified by their words: “According to the law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God” (John 19:7). Is not this also the reproach of your impious utterance: Why does he call himself Son, whom you assert to be a creature?

> [Note: “Why does he call himself the Son of God?”]

> [Note: Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “when he calls himself the Son of God, whom you assert to be a creature.”]

He, by confessing himself the Son of God, is judged guilty of death by them. You, by denying that he is the Son of God—what, I ask, do you judge? For his confession displeases the Jews just as it displeases you. I ask whether you maintain a judgment different from theirs when your will is not different. For by the same impiety you deny that he is the Son of God. Yet they are less guilty in this respect, because they do not know. They do not know Christ as born of Mary, but they do not doubt that Christ is the Son of God. You, because you cannot fail to know Christ as born of Mary, nevertheless do not proclaim Christ to be the Son of God.

For them, in what they do not know, salvation may still be secure if they believe. For you, all paths to salvation are now closed, because you deny what you can no longer be ignorant of [Col. 0197C].

> [Note: The reason for this saying should be sought in the exposition of Psalm 135, no. 3, where among other things occurs: “He who has known sin and does not confess what he has known is beyond pardon; and this is so because confession of error is a profession of ceasing from it. Nor does he deserve pardon who refuses to cease from sin.” See the notes on no. 8, exposition of Psalm 140.]

For you do not fail to know that he is the Son of God: indeed, you even grant him the name of adoption, so that you falsely call a creature a son. But by taking away the nature, so far as lies in you, you would take away even the name if you could. But because this is not permitted, you leave no nature to the name, lest he who is called Son should be the true Son of God.

> [Note: Thus the manuscripts, as above, no. 25: “If I do not believe the names, if I do not understand nature from the terms.” The printed editions read, “the nature of the name.”]

### 51. The Apostles Confess Christ to Be Truly the Son of God.

In the confession of those for whom, while the wind raged and the sea was troubled, calm was restored at the command of his word, you had an example by which you too might confess the true Son of God and use their words: “Truly he is the Son of God” (Matt. 14:33). But a raging spirit carries you into the shipwreck of life, and a storm, pressing upon the movements of your mind as upon a wave-tossed sea, exercises dominion.

### 52. The Centurion Who Had Crucified Him Also Confesses Him.

If this faith of the sailors seems uncertain to you because they are thought to have been apostles, it may indeed give me less cause for amazement, but it gives greater authority. Yet receive also the faith of the Gentiles in him. Hear, for amid the savage guard-duty of the cross, a soldier of the Roman cohort subdued to faith [Col. 0198A]. For after seeing the works of such great power, the centurion says: “Truly this man was the Son of God” (Matt. 27:54).

The centurion testifies to this after the spirit had been yielded up, the veil of the temple torn, the earth shaken, rocks split, tombs opened, and the dead raised; and the Gentile man confesses despite unbelief. He recognizes, in the deeds, the nature of the power; in the name he professes the truth of the nature. So great is the reason of truth, and so great the force of faith, that the necessity of truth conquers the will, and not even he who had crucified him denied that Christ, the Lord of eternal glory, is truly the Son of God.

## BOOK VII

At the outset, the excellence of this book is set forth; its reasons for being written; the craftiness of the Arians, which has so far been exposed and repelled; and the difficulty of opposing them without seeming, while refuting Arius, to favor Sabellius, or again, while attacking Sabellius, to favor Photinus. It is also explained how Arius, Sabellius, and Photinus overcome or are overcome by one another for the Church’s advantage. Once these matters have briefly been explained, it is proved that he who is truly the Son of God from nature is also truly God by nature, while preserving faith in one God who is not solitary: for he possesses God’s name, birth from God, divine nature and power, and finally professes himself to be God. Hilary nevertheless admits that the remaining points are so connected with the argument drawn from birth that they cannot be treated separately.

First, he lays down that a thing’s nature is always signified by its name, unless the meaning of accompanying qualifications indicates that it is accidental and not proper. He shows that John says of the Son, “and the Word was God,” and Thomas says, “My Lord and my God,” in such a way that these appellations, even from their accompanying words, express in him the true nature of God. He who possesses, no less than the Father, the name proper to divine nature is of one nature with him; consequently, he and the Father are not two Gods, but one. He briefly touches upon the titles Word, Wisdom, and Power, and declares that they are applied to the Son in order to show that he subsists in the Father without any division or change in the Father himself.

He next adds that it is no less self-evident that one who is born has the nature from which he subsists. Nor can it be doubted that Christ was born from God, since this was the chief reason why the Jews wished to kill him: he called God his own Father, making himself equal to God. Birth, moreover, like equality, admits neither solitude nor difference.

From the very discourse which Christ then addressed to the Jews, he establishes at length both Christ’s birth from God and the unity of his nature with the Father’s. The unity of nature is established because he does what the Father does; because he does all the same things; because both possess one power in raising the dead, one honor, one affront; and because, finally, he possesses all judgment. His birth is established because he never ceases to call himself Son; because he acts as the Father acts, yet not from himself; because he does the same things, yet in like manner; and because he has all judgment, yet has received it from the Father. This is confirmed both by the Jews’ understanding—for they understood Christ in these words to proclaim himself truly the Son of God and truly God—and by Christ’s own replies, by which he did not claim to have been misunderstood, but reproved them for unjust unbelief, since his works made his sayings credible.

Finally, from what Christ said at length when Philip asked that he show him the Father, it is demonstrated that he expressly teaches that he was born from the Father and is of one and the same nature with him.

### 1. This Book Excels the Earlier Ones. Reasons for Writing. The Subtlety of Heretics.

This seventh book is written by us against the insane rashness of the new heresy. It is later in number than the preceding books, but for understanding the mystery of perfect faith it is either the first or the greatest. In it we do not fail to know how difficult and arduous is the path of evangelical teaching which we tread. Although we are held back by the trembling of a conscience aware of our weakness, still, stirred by zeal for faith, moved by the madness of heretics, and disturbed by the danger threatening the ignorant, we cannot remain silent concerning what we do not dare to say. We are subject to fear of danger on both sides: lest either our silence or our preaching should make us guilty of abandoning the truth [Col. 0199C].

> [Note: Some manuscripts read, “by the weakness and trembling of our conscience”; the printed editions also preferred “conscience.” More correctly, the more carefully corrected manuscripts read *consciae*, with “to itself” understood—that is, conscious of what we are conscious of. This manner of speaking occurs in the exposition of Psalm 68, no. 15: “the confidence of salvation conscious in itself.” The reading *conscii*, “being conscious,” from the first hand of the Corbie manuscript, is also not unacceptable.]

> [Note: Printed editions read, “subjected to fear”; against the manuscripts. Then one Vatican manuscript reads, “lest, concerning the abandonment of truth …”]

For heretical subtlety has deployed itself by incredible arts of corrupted ingenuity: first, to feign religion; then, to deceive the security of all simple ears by words; further, to adapt itself to worldly wisdom; and finally, under the appearance of a reasoned argument, to turn people away from the understanding of truth.

> [Note: The Basel Vatican manuscript reads, “to introduce.”]

For after professing one God—in the letter cited in Books IV and VI—it has feigned piety; after again professing the Son of God, it has deceived its hearers in the name; by saying that he did not exist before he was born, it has satisfied worldly wisdom; and by confessing God to be unchangeable and incorporeal, it has excluded the birth of God from God by the display of a subtle argument. It has used our doctrines against us and has fought the Church’s faith against the Church’s faith, creating for us the gravest danger whether in reply or in silence, while by means of what it does not deny it proclaims what it does deny.

### 2. What They Tried to Introduce in Their Letter. How Hilary Met Them. The Earlier Book Showed the True Son; This One Shows the True God.

Indeed, we remember that in the preceding books we warned our readers, while examining the whole publication of their blasphemy, to observe that they strive for nothing other than that our Lord Jesus Christ should be believed neither to be the Son of God nor God. While granting him names only from some kind of adoption, they deny both the nature of God and that of the Son. God is declared unchangeable and incorporeal—as he indeed is—only in order that the Son may not be born from God; and God the Father is confessed as the one God only in order that Christ may not be God in our faith. For an incorporeal nature does not admit the understanding of birth, and the confession of God from God is destroyed for us if there is only one God.

> [Note: The Basel Vatican manuscript adds here “of theirs”; and shortly after “God is believed” adds “from God.”]

But in the preceding little books, teaching from the Law and the Prophets against this deceitful and useless proclamation, we maintained such a form of reply that, in preaching God from God and confessing one true God, we neither failed in the unity of the one true God nor went beyond it into faith in another God. For God is neither solitary for us in confession, nor are there two Gods. And amid these points the perfection of faith is preserved by neither denying nor confessing “one” in isolation: because what they are one in is referred to both, and yet neither of them is the one person.

> [Note: The Basel Vatican exemplar with the Martin manuscript reads “completed,” which is less to the point. As we noted on p. 127 of the Verona edition, the word “complete” occurs in place of “preserve” in the Carcassonne manuscript, later corrected.]

Therefore, in undertaking to establish this indissoluble mystery of perfect faith by evangelical and apostolic teachings, our first duty was to make known to the understanding of our hearers the nature of the Son of God, subsisting by true birth; and to show that the Son is not from elsewhere or from nothing, but from God.

> [Note: Printed editions read “subsisting nature,” against the manuscripts.]

Since, according to the matters set forth in the previous book, it cannot be doubted that, once the name of adoption has ceased, the true Son is such from the truth of his birth, we now also bring forward passages from the Gospels, so that, because he is the true Son, he may be known also to be true God. For he will not be a true Son unless he is also true God; nor true God unless he is also true Son.

> [Note: Printed editions read “it”; they are corrected from the manuscripts. The Martin manuscript reads “we bring forward,” not “we have brought forward.” Later, from the Colbert manuscript we restore “so that because he is Son,” where previously was read “so that he who is Son.”]

### 3. In Refuting One Heresy, One Hardly Escapes Suspicion of Another. Sabellius, Arius, Ebion, Photinus.

Nothing is more grievous to human nature than awareness of danger. For things unknown or sudden possess a pitiable security, but they do not bring fear of what is to come. I do not now launch a ship from harbor unaware of shipwreck; I do not enter a journey ignorant of mountain passes infested with robbers; nor do I cross the sands of Libya uncertain whether scorpions, asps, and basilisks are everywhere present.

> [Note: Only the printed editions read “unknowing.”]

Nothing is free from anxiety or from conscious awareness for me. For I speak under the watchful eyes of all heretics, hanging upon every opportunity afforded by individual words from my mouth [Col. 0201A]; and every course of my speech is either narrowed by straits, cut through by pits, or stretched over with snares. I complain less that the way is steep and difficult, for I climb not my own steps but apostolic ones. Yet to turn aside into straits, to fall into an excavated pit, or to be ensnared in traps is always danger and always fear for me.

> [Note: The Baden, Erasmus, and some manuscripts read “to fall from the straits”; the Leipzig and Paris editions, “to fall in the straits.” They are corrected from the Basel Vatican, Carcassonne, Martin, Corbie, and other manuscripts.]

For when I am about to preach, according to the Law, the Prophets, and the Apostles, one God, Sabellius stands by, swallowing me whole beneath the confession of this word as a desired food with most savage bite. Again, when I deny one God against Sabellius and confess the true God, the Son of God, the new heresy waits to accuse me of preaching two gods. And when I am about to say that the Son of God was born from Mary, Ebion—that is, Photinus—stands beside me, intending to draw authority for his falsehood from the truth of my confession [Col. 0201B].

> [Note: Lipsius, following the later Erasmus edition, reads “who is”; more recent manuscripts, “who also is.” But the older witnesses, together with the Baden edition, read “which is,” as though “that is.” He calls Photinus “Ebion” not only because he revived Ebion’s heresy, but also because in Book I, in the argument of this book, he had proposed to discuss Ebion. Thus we have already observed that the first book was composed before this one and that Photinus’s heresy then seemed unknown to Hilary. A little later, the printed editions read “from the profession of truth,” where “from the truth of the confession” has been restored from manuscripts.]

I say nothing of the rest, whom all know to be outside the Church.

> [Note: “Because they are known by all [to be outside the Church].”]

But this evil, though often condemned and cast out, remains an internal evil even today.

> [Note: Only the Basel Vatican manuscript reads, “that internal evil still …”]

Galatia has impiously nourished many toward the confession of one God.

> [Note: Namely through Marcellus, bishop of Ancyra in Galatia, his instructor and teacher. Jerome’s words in *On Ecclesiastical Writers* concerning Marcellus can refer to nothing else: “Hilary also, in the seventh book against the Arians, mentions his name as that of a heretic.” Jerome undoubtedly understood Marcellus here, so much so that he even wrote his name, perhaps prompted by memory.]

Alexandria has wickedly produced throughout almost the whole world those who deny two gods.

> [Note: Arius, as everyone sees, was their author. He introduced two gods into the world, since, while calling and worshiping the Father God and the Son God, he asserted them to be of different substance; yet he boasted that he wished altogether to maintain one God and denied two. Hence Augustine, against Maximinus, supporter of the Arian sect, Book I, chapter 1: “Where you say that one God is worshiped by you, it follows, I say, either that you do not worship Christ, or that you worship not one God but two.”]

Pannonia has perniciously defended Jesus Christ as born from Mary.

> [Note: That is, through Photinus, bishop of Sirmium. His error is not here stated to be that he defended Christ as born from Mary, but that he proclaimed that temporal birth alone.]

Meanwhile the Church is endangered by not holding the truth through true things, while things are pressed upon it for irreligion by which religion itself is both confirmed and destroyed. For we cannot devoutly proclaim one God if we proclaim him alone, because in the faith of a solitary God the Son will not be God. But when we proclaim the Son of God, as he is, to be God, we risk—in human estimation—being thought not to maintain faith in the one God. And it is the same danger to deny “one” as it is to confess him solitary.

> [Note: Thus our book read in earlier editions; the later reading, “not to deny one,” would involve no danger.]

> [Note: The printed editions, except the Paris edition, read “to deny one God.” More correctly the Paris edition, with the better manuscripts, reads “not to deny one”: that is, one who does not deny the “one” preached by Arians immediately seems to side with them and to take divinity away from the Son.]

And these foolish people of the world do not perceive that “one” is signified in “not solitary,” nor that “not solitary” is understood in “one.”

### 4. The Power of Truth. The Church Earnestly Desires to Hold All in Her Bosom. She Is Known from the Heresies Themselves. She Is One. She Triumphs Because the Heresies Defeat One Another.

But, as I hope, the Church will bring the light of her teaching even to worldly ignorance, so that, although it does not receive the mystery of faith, it may nevertheless understand that we preach the truth of that mystery against heretics. For great is the power of truth: although it can be understood through itself, it nevertheless shines forth through those very things which oppose it, so that, remaining unmoved in its own nature, it acquires daily confirmation of its nature while it is attacked.

> [Note: Erasmus, Lipsius, and Paris read “cannot be understood,” wrongly and contrary to the authority of the manuscripts. What is here affirmed concerning truth is stated more clearly shortly afterward concerning the Church: it is to be understood not only through her own teachings, but through those of her opponents.]

For this is proper to the Church: that she conquers when she is wounded; that she is understood when she is accused; that she prevails when she is abandoned. She would indeed have all remain with her and within herself, and would neither cast out nor lose any from her most tranquil bosom, until they render themselves unworthy of the dwelling-place of so great a mother. Yet, as heretics depart from her or are cast out, by as much as she loses the opportunity to bestow salvation from herself, by so much she gains the faith by which blessedness from her is to be sought.

> [Note: The Basel Vatican manuscript reads “wishes to remain.” Shortly afterward only the printed editions read “cast out some,” against the manuscripts.]

> [Note: The Martin manuscript reads “attains”; the Paris edition, with the Colbert and German manuscripts, “follows from.” Then the Corbie manuscript reads “to be weighed,” not “to be sought.”]

For this is most readily known from the very pursuits of the heretics. Since the Church, founded by the Lord and confirmed by the Apostles, is the one Church of all, from which the raging error of diverse impieties has cut itself off, and since it cannot be denied that division in faith has arisen from the fault of bad interpretation—because what is read is adapted to one’s own sense rather than the sense obeying the reading—yet, because the individual parties oppose one another, she must be understood not only from her own teachings but from those of her opponents. Thus, while all are against her alone, she refutes the most impious error of all precisely by being alone and one [Col. 0202C].

> [Note: In the Basel Vatican and Martin manuscripts, incorrectly, “of faith misunderstood.” See Book II, no. 3, and Book I, no. 18.]

All heretics therefore come against the Church; but while all heretics defeat one another, they gain no victory for themselves. Their victory is, in every respect, the Church’s triumph, because one heresy fights another precisely on the point in which the faith of the Church condemns the other heresy. For there is nothing common to heretics; and while they oppose one another, they affirm our faith.

> [Note: “Because in that respect …”]

### 5. Sabellius’s Error and Its Refutation.

Sabellius proclaims one God while taking away the Son’s birth, yet he does not doubt that the Power of the nature which worked in the man is God.

> [Note: The Baden, Erasmus, the Corbie manuscript, and a few others read, “while by the power of nature.” Shortly afterward, the Leipzig and Paris editions read, “he does not doubt that [Christ] is God,” supported only by the Martin manuscript. Faustinus, often praised above, imitates this passage in chapter 1: “Sabellius, from admiration of the powers which Christ performed, believes Christ to be God”; then, after the manner of the preceding argument, adding: “Let Sabellius defeat Arius in that Christ is true God; let Arius defeat Sabellius in that, under confession of true God, Christ is also true Son; and both have defeated me, a Catholic,” etc. As Vigilius of Tapsus elegantly says in accordance with our Hilary’s thought, Book II against Eutyches: “The discordant opinions of the faithless sound together in the one measure of right faith, and their futile conflicts produce the trophy of our victory. For Sabellius’s unbelief condemns Arius’s error,” etc.]

For, ignorant of the mystery of the Son, he lost faith in true generation through admiration of the deeds. And when he hears, “He who has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9), he impiously seized upon a union of undistinguished and undissimilar nature in Father and Son, not understanding that natural unity is shown under the signification of birth. For the fact that the Father is seen in the Son confirms divinity; it does not abolish birth.

> [Note: In the Basel Vatican and Martin manuscripts, “and indivisible,” wrongly. Faustinus expresses this passage thus in chapter 1: “When he says, ‘He who has seen me has seen the Father,’ just as he does not show the Father and the Son to be one person, so he shows the Godhead to be one, since there is no diversity of substance between Father and Son.”]

Knowledge of one, therefore, is in the other, because one does not differ from the other in nature [Col. 0203B]. And where they differ in nothing, contemplation is undifferentiated by reason of the propriety of nature.

> [Note: Printed editions read “differing”; they are corrected from the manuscripts.]

Nor indeed can it be doubted that he who remained in the form of God showed from himself the image of God’s form. This saying of the Lord also lends support to the foolish madness of this perverse opinion: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). For the unity of undissimilar nature advanced irreligiously into the error of union, and, understanding power alone, did not retain the meaning of the saying.

> [Note: “Toward the union of one [person].”]

For “I and the Father are one” does not signify a solitary being. The conjunction “and,” which signifies both Father and Son, does not permit the understanding of one person; and the word “are” does not allow singularity. But the phrase “we are one” does not remove birth; rather, it does not distinguish the nature according to kind, since “one” does not indicate difference, and “we are” does not indicate one person.

> [Note: The Leipzig and Paris editions omit the particle “that,” which expresses the Greek article *to*. In accordance with these words of Hilary, Maximus of Turin, Homily 1 on St. Eusebius, says: “He says both ‘one’ and ‘we are’; he neither divides himself by separation nor confuses himself by union.”

6. How Sabellius and Arius, while opposing one another, promote the Church’s cause.---Set against the madness of this man [Sabellius] the madness of the present heretics [the Arians], so that they may support themselves against Sabellius. They will claim to have read, “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28); and, understanding nothing either of the mystery of the birth or of the mystery of the God who emptied himself and assumed flesh, they will make a diminution of nature out of the confession that he is greater. For against Sabellius they will maintain that the Son exists to such an extent that he is also less than the Father, that he asks for the restoration of his former glory, fears death, and has died. But Sabellius, on the contrary, defends the nature of God in the deeds performed; and while this new heresy will now not deny that there is one God, lest it believe the Son to be God, Sabellius nevertheless will retain in his confession one God, lest there be a Son at all. The one [Arius] will introduce an acting Son; the other [Sabellius] will contend that God is present in the works. The one will say “one”; the other will deny one God.

Sabellius will defend himself thus, saying: “The works which have been done cannot be effected except by the nature of God: forgiveness of sins, healing of infirmities, the running of the lame, sight for the blind, life for the dead—these come from God alone. No nature other than one conscious of itself could say, ‘I and the Father are one’ (John 10:30). Why do you drag me into another substance? Why do you trouble me with another God? The deeds which are proper to God, the one God performed.”

But those who proclaim the Son unlike God the Father will cry out against this in no less venomous speech: “You do not know the mystery of your salvation. One must believe in the Son through whom the ages were made, through whom humanity was formed, who gave the Law through angels, who was born of Mary, who was sent by the Father, who was crucified, died, and was buried, who, rising from the dead, is at the right hand of God, and who is judge of the living and the dead. Into him one must be born again; him one must confess; his kingdom must be obtained.”

Each enemy of the Church advances the Church’s cause: while Sabellius proclaims God from the nature shown in the works, these others confess from the mystery of faith the Son of God.

[Col. 0205A]

7. Photinus, in his disagreement with Arius and Sabellius, produces the same result. The Church’s faith against the aforementioned heretics.---Now by what victory of our faith does Ebion, who is Photinus, either conquer or suffer defeat? While he reproves Sabellius for denying that the man is the Son of God, he is refuted by the Ariomaniacs for failing to recognize in the man the Son of God. Against Sabellius he defends the Gospels for himself from the Son of Mary; Arius does not leave the Gospels to him as belonging to the Son of Mary alone.
