Against this man [Sabellius], who denies the Son, the man is appropriated by him [Photinus] as the Son. By the other [Arius], who does not recognize the Son before the ages, the Son of God is denied to him as being only from man.

Let them conquer as they wish, since in conquering one another they are conquered: for both these present men—that is, the Arians—are refuted concerning the nature of God; Sabellius is refuted concerning the mystery of the Son; and Photinus is proved either ignorant of, or a denier of, the Son of God born before the ages. But amid these things the Church’s faith, founded on evangelical and apostolic doctrines, both maintains the confession of the Son against Sabellius, the nature of God against Arius, and the Creator of the world against Photinus. And this is truer because these things are not mutually denied by them. For Sabellius proclaims the nature of God in the works, but does not recognize the acting Son. These others name the Son, but do not confess in him the truth of God’s nature. Photinus, however, appropriates the man, but in the man whom he appropriates for himself does not recognize the birth of God before the ages. Thus, while each one defends or condemns these matters, they display the truth of our faith, as it is religiously defended and condemned.

[Col. 0205C]

8. The rationale of the foregoing. The subject of what follows.---These matters, then, had to be demonstrated by me briefly—not from a desire for abundance, but as a precaution of reason: first, that all things among the heretics might be recognized as uncertain and wandering, since at times they disagree among themselves on our behalf; and then, that no one might charge me, when I oppose the blasphemous professions of those now present—that is, the Arians—and proclaim God the Father and the Son of God to be God, and profess Father and Son to be one in name and in an undissimilar kind of divinity, with the error either of two gods or, conversely, of one unique and solitary God. For neither could union be found in the proclaimed God the Father and God the Son, nor could a plurality of gods accord with the demonstration of an indistinguishable nature.

Now, since in the preceding book an answer according to the Gospels was given to those who deny that the Son of God subsists from God in the truth of birth, it must be shown that he who is truly Son of God by nature is also truly God by nature—yet in such a way that our faith does not fall away either into a solitary God or into another God. For it will neither proclaim one God as though he were alone, nor confess him as though he were not one.

9. The ways in which we know Christ to be God. The name “God,” simply given to him, indicates nature.---Therefore we know our Lord Jesus Christ to be God in these ways: by name, birth, nature, power, and confession. And concerning the name I think no ambiguity remains. For we read: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1). What ground is there for cavilling that he is not what he is called? Or is a name not an indication of nature? And since every contradiction has a cause, I now ask the reason for denying that he is God.

For the designation is simple and lacks the offence of an extraneous addition. The Word which became flesh is nothing other than God. No suspicion is left here of an attributed or assumed designation, such that the name “God” should not belong to him by nature.

10. The name of God given additionally to Moses. Other gods are so called by the will of the one who names them.---Consider the other designations, whether attributed or assumed. It was said to Moses: “I have made you a god to Pharaoh” (Exod. 7:1). But was not the reason for the name added when it says, “to Pharaoh”? Or did it confer upon him the nature of God, rather than strike terror into the one who feared him—when Moses’ serpent, though remaining a rod, immediately devoured the magical serpents; when he removed the swarm of flies he had sent; when by the power with which he had summoned it he turned away the hail; when by the strength with which he had brought them he drove back the locusts; when the magicians confessed that the finger of God was in his works (Exod. 7:12; 8:31; 9:33; 10:19; 8:19)?

Thus Moses was made a god to Pharaoh, while he was feared, prayed to, punished, and healed. But it is one thing to be made a god and another to be God. He was made a god with respect to Pharaoh; but he does not have both nature and name so as to be God. I recall also another designation where it is said, “I said, you are gods” (Ps. 81 [82]:6); but there the meaning is of a name granted. And where it is reported, “I said,” the wording belongs rather to the speaker than the name to the thing; for the name of a thing conveys the understanding of the thing, whereas the will behind an appellation comes from another. Where someone shows himself the author of the designation, there the designation derives from the speech of its author, not from a natural name within the class itself.

11. Why the Son is called Word, Wisdom, and Power. The Son is God as he is called.---But here the Word is God: the reality exists in the Word, and the reality of the Word is declared in the name. For the designation “Word,” when applied to the Son of God, belongs to the mystery of his birth, just as do the names Wisdom and Power. Although these exist in God the Son with the substance of true birth, yet, as his own, though born from him into God, they are not absent from God.

For, as we have often said, we proclaim not division in the Son but the mystery of birth. The separation was not an imperfect one, but the offspring was perfect; for birth entails no loss to the begetter, since it retains the advance of being born. Accordingly, those names of things are fitted to the Only-begotten God which, while they establish him as subsisting from birth, nevertheless exist in the Father by the power of his unchangeable nature. For the Only-begotten God is Word, but the unbegotten Father is never at all without the Word. This does not mean that the Son’s nature consists in an utterance of voice; rather, God from God, subsisting with the truth of birth, is signified as Word so that he may be understood to be proper to the Father and inseparable from him through identity of nature.

Likewise Christ is the Wisdom and Power of God, not that effective movement of inward power or thought which is commonly understood, but a nature which, by birth, possesses the truth of substance and is signified by these names of inward realities. For that which subsists by being born cannot itself appear to be that which is perpetually inward to any one thing. But the Only-begotten Son, born from the eternal God the Father into subsisting God, was shown as subsisting through these names of properties—properties of which he from whom he subsisted was not deprived—so that he might be understood not to be alien to the nature of the Father’s divinity.

Therefore the God who is is nothing other than God. For when I hear, “And the Word was God,” I do not hear merely that the Word was called God; I understand that what God is has been shown. For, just as above, in the case of Moses made a god and of the gods so named, the name was added through designation, here, when it is said, “was God,” the reality of substance is signified. For “to be” is not an accidental name, but subsisting truth, abiding cause, and the property of a natural kind.

12. Thomas confesses him as God without injury to faith in the one God. Thomas professes God by nature. Christ does not reject this name.---Let us see whether the Evangelist’s proclamation is followed by the confession of the Apostle Thomas, when he says, “My Lord and my God” (John 20:28). Therefore he is Thomas’s God, whom Thomas confesses to be God. And certainly Thomas did not ignore the saying of the Lord: “Hear, Israel, the Lord your God is one” (Deut. 6:4). How then did the chief apostolic faith become forgetful of the commandment, so as to confess Christ as God, when it must live in the confession of one God?

But the Apostle, understanding through the power of the resurrection the faith of the entire mystery, and having often heard, “I and the Father are one,” “All things that are the Father’s are mine,” and “I am in the Father and the Father in me” (John 10:30; 16:15; 14:11), now without peril to faith confessed the name of nature. For piety did not fall away from the confession of the one God the Father when it confessed God the Son of God, since in the Son of God only the truth of the Father’s nature was believed; nor was the faith of one nature endangered by the impious confession of another God, because the perfect birth of God had not brought in the nature of another God.

Thomas, therefore, understanding the truth of the evangelical mystery, confessed him to be his Lord and his God. This is not a name of honour, but a confession of nature: for he believed him to be God by the very realities and powers themselves. And the Lord taught that the piety of this confession was one of faith, not honour, saying, “Because you have seen, you have believed; blessed are those who have not seen and have believed” (John 20:29). Thomas saw and believed. But what, you ask, did he believe? What else did he believe than what he confessed: “My Lord and my God”? For to rise by his own power from the dead into life was possible only to the nature of God; and the faith of the piety he had believed confessed this: that he is God.

Then shall the name of God not be regarded as a reality of nature, when the confession of the name follows faith in the nature believed? Certainly the devout Son—the one who did not do his own will but the will of him who sent him, and who sought not his own honour but that of him from whom he came—would have rejected the honour of this name in himself, lest what he himself had proclaimed, namely one God, should be dissolved. But truly, confirming the mystery of apostolic faith and acknowledging in himself the name of the Father’s nature, he taught that those are blessed who, though they had not seen him risen from the dead, nevertheless believed him to be God through understanding the resurrection.

[Col. 0210A]

13. Father and Son are one God only.---Therefore the name of nature does not abandon the confession of our faith. For the name that signifies each thing also shows a thing of the same kind; and there are now not two realities, but a reality of the same kind. For the Son of God is God: this is signified by the name. The one name “God” does not count two gods, because “God” is the one name of one and indistinguishable nature. For since both the Father is God and the Son is God, and the proper name of the divine nature belongs to each, the two are one. For although the Son subsists from the natural birth, he nevertheless preserves unity in the name. Nor does the birth of the Son compel the faith of believers to profess two gods, since it confesses Father and Son as one both in nature and in name.

The Son of God, therefore, has the name from birth. This is the second stage of our demonstration: that he is God by birth. Although apostolic authority still remains for me concerning the proper character of the name, for the present it is pleasing to examine the Gospel’s statement.

14. The Son, as born from God, has the nature of God. Being born and beginning to exist are not the same.---First I ask what novelty of nature the Son’s birth could introduce, so that he should not be God. Human understanding excludes the thought that something born can differ from the nature of its origin—unless perhaps something conceived from a diversity of natures, some new thing in itself, belonging to both kinds but being neither, comes into life; and this occurs commonly among cattle and beasts. Yet even that novelty is not present except from connate properties under a diversity of nature; and birth did not introduce their diversity but received it, while retaining what is one for itself from both.

And if this is so in these bodily causes and affections, what madness, I ask, is it to refer the birth of the Only-begotten God to a degenerate nature from God? For birth exists only from the property of nature; and there will no longer be birth if the property of nature is absent in the birth. Hence comes all that heat and madness: that in the Son of God there should not be birth but creation; that, existing, he should not possess an origin from his own nature, but should receive from non-existent things a nature alien to God.

For according to what he says, “What is born of flesh is flesh, and what is born of spirit is spirit” (John 3:6), since God is spirit, it is beyond doubt that nothing diverse from, and alien to, him from whom it is born can be present in the one born. Therefore the birth of God establishes God, so that God is understood not to have begun to exist but to have been born. For to have begun may be other than to be born, since everything that begins either comes to exist from nothing into something, or advances and changes from one thing into another: as gold from earth, liquid things from solid, hot things from cold, crimson from white, living creatures from water, living things from inanimate things. But the Son of God did not begin to be God from nothing, but was born; nor was he anything other before he was God. Thus he who was born into God neither began nor progressed in being what God is. Birth, therefore, retains the nature from which it subsisted; and the Son of God subsists as nothing other than what God is.

15. He who has God as Father and equality with God is truly born from God. Equality belongs neither to one alone nor to things that differ.---Does anyone doubt this? Let him learn the understanding of nature from the Jews, or rather recognize from the Gospel the truth of birth, in which it is written: “For this reason the Jews sought all the more to kill him, because he not only broke the Sabbath, but also called God his own Father, making himself equal with God” (John 5:18). Here, as is often the case elsewhere, the Jews’ words are not reported as spoken by them; rather, this is the Evangelist’s exposition, showing why the Jews wished to kill the Lord.

Therefore let the excuse of defective understanding cease through the impiety of blasphemers, since by the Apostle’s authority natural property has been shown under the signification of birth: “He called God his own Father, making himself equal with God.” Is there not natural birth where equality of nature is demonstrated by the name of one’s own Father? For it is beyond dispute that equality entails no difference. Who then will doubt that birth follows an indistinguishable nature? For this alone is the equality which can truly exist, because birth alone can provide equality of nature.

But equality will never be believed to exist where there is union; nor will it be found where there is difference. Thus the equality of likeness has neither solitude nor diversity, because all equality is neither diverse nor solitary.

16. The Son’s birth and equality with the Father from his own sayings. Several arguments for Christ’s divinity considered together.---Although the judgments of this understanding of ours are shared with human reason—that birth has equality of nature, and that where equality exists there can be neither anything alien from itself nor anything solitary—nevertheless the faith of our argument must also be confirmed from the Lord’s own sayings, lest the rashness of contradiction, under the liberty of differing interpretations of the words, dare to oppose the professions of divine testimony concerning himself.

For the Lord answered: “The Son cannot do anything from himself, except what he sees the Father doing; for whatever things he does, the Son also does these likewise. For the Father loves the Son and shows him all that he himself does; and he will show him greater works than these, so that you may marvel. For as the Father raises the dead and gives life, so also the Son gives life to whom he wills. For neither does the Father judge anyone, but has given all judgment to the Son, so that all may honour the Son as they honour the Father. Whoever does not honour the Son does not honour the Father who sent him” (John 5:19 ff.).

The order of the proposed subject certainly required that the individual classes of the various causes should each be treated separately: so that, having learned that our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, is God by name, birth, nature, power, and confession, our demonstration might proceed through every stage of the proposed arrangement. But the nature of birth does not allow this, since it alone includes within itself name, nature, power, and confession. For without these there will be no birth, because in being born it contains them all. Therefore, as we treat it, we encounter the necessity that the matters mentioned above cannot be postponed to the order of their own treatment.

17. Christ, accused by the Jews, expounds both his nature and his birth. Christ’s power consists in knowledge. What that knowledge is.---For the Lord, answering the Jews because they wished all the more to kill him on the ground that, by calling God his Father, he had made himself equal with God, set forth the whole mystery of our faith while opposing their impious agitation. Earlier, after healing the paralytic, when he had been charged even with a capital offence for violating the Sabbath, he had said: “My Father works until now, and I work” (John 5:17). And from this all hostility was inflamed, because by appropriating the Father’s name he had made himself equal with God.

Accordingly, wishing both to confirm his birth and to profess the power of his nature, he said: “The Son cannot do anything from himself, except what he sees the Father doing” (John 5:19). The opening of the reply was fitted to answer the Jews’ impious agitation, by which they were driven even to the intention of inflicting death. For to the charge of violating the Sabbath he had said, “My Father works until now, and I work,” so that he might be understood to have claimed this on the authority of the Father’s example, while nevertheless indicating that what he himself did was to be understood as the Father’s work, because the Father worked in him as he worked.

And again, against the hostility by which he had made himself equal to God through the paternal name, he added: “Amen, amen, I say to you: the Son cannot do anything from himself, except what he sees the Father doing.” Therefore, lest that equality through name and nature should take away faith in the Son’s birth, he said that the Son could do nothing from himself except what he saw the Father doing. And so that the saving order of our confession concerning Father and Son might remain, he showed the nature of birth: a nature which receives the power of acting not through progressive additions of powers granted for each particular work, but presumes from knowledge.

Yet it presumes not from some example of bodily work, as though the Father first did something which the Son would afterward do; rather, since the nature of God had subsisted into the nature of God—that is, since the Son had been born from the Father—the Son testified that through consciousness of the Father’s power and nature in himself he could do nothing from himself except what he saw the Father doing. And since the Only-begotten God worked by the operations of the Father’s power, he presumed for action only so much as he had in his own consciousness: the power of the God the Father, inseparable from himself, which he possessed through legitimate birth. For God does not see in bodily modes; all his seeing is in the power of his nature.

Notes on readings and editorial matter

6. [Col. 0203D] The Vatican-Basilica manuscript prefers *demutationem*. With the other witnesses we prefer *deminutionem* (“diminution”), since it answers more aptly to the words “greater than I,” from which the Arians proclaimed Christ God as lesser and, as it were, diminished. Immediately before, the printed editions have *faciunt*, above *asserunt*, and afterwards *contendunt*, contrary to the manuscripts’ future forms *asserent*, *facient*, *contendent*.

[Col. 0204C] The manuscript of St Martin has *ingeniti* (“of the unbegotten [God]”). The other books more correctly read *in gestis* (“in the deeds performed”): that is, Sabellius maintains from what Christ did that God’s nature was in him.

[Col. 0203C] The Verona manuscript reads: “the other will deny one.”

[Col. 0204C–D] This is the manuscript reading; printed editions have *hic* rather than *iste*. The St Martin manuscript then reads “will deny one,” whereas the Vatican-Basilica exemplar has “will not deny one.” Since these words plainly concern Arius, just as the preceding “will say one” concerns Sabellius, that reading is supported by the preceding statement that this new heresy will not deny one God. Nevertheless, “will deny one God” should be retained. For the double-faced heresy did not deny one God in order to remove the Son from divinity; yet it denied one God when, compelled to profess God the Father and God the Son, it preached them not as one but as two gods, as has already been observed in §3.

[Col. 0204D] Only the St Martin codex reads “born through Mary”; it has the flavour of an unfaithful hand. Hilary consistently proclaims that Christ was born of Mary.

[Col. 0204C] “God” is not present.

[Col. 0204C–0205C] The word “God” is absent from the St Martin manuscript and also from the Vatican-Basilica manuscript, which shortly before reads “to the mystery of faith”; this reading is no more successful than the preceding readings noted from those same books. Hilary calls “the mystery of faith” all that by which the Arians were presently contending against Sabellius that the Son was not the same as the Father: that is, the mystery of our salvation, or, if preferred, the Apostles’ Creed.

7. [Col. 0205C–D] Thus the Arians are commonly called by Athanasius, Phoebadius of Agen, Gregory Nazianzen, and others, chiefly because the Greek word Ἄρης, “Ares” or “Mars,” whose characteristic quality is frenzy, has the closest affinity with Arius’s name and disposition. Hence Constantine’s letter, vol. II of the Councils, p. 270: “Come then, Mars-Arius, shields must be used”; and later in the speech, *apodeixō tēn Areiou manian* (ἀποδείξω τὴν Ἀρείου μανίαν), “I shall expose the madness of Arius.” This is the point of Vincent of Lérins, ch. 6: “When the profane novelty of the Arians, like a certain Bellona, had first captured the emperor of all, it thereafter ceased not to throw all the heights of the palace into confusion and disturbance.” Since *Ariomanites* has the same sense as “one seized by Martian frenzy,” it is clear what our Hilary means when he calls the heresy frenzied.

[Col. 0205D] That is, the evangelical dispensation and the mystery of our salvation. Arius does not leave this work to the Son of Mary alone when he proves that the ages were made by the Son, that the law was given, and so forth.

[Col. 0205C] In our manuscript *Arrius*, with a double r, is written consistently.

[Col. 0206C] Printed editions read “for this”; the manuscripts more correctly read “by this,” that is, Arius denies to Photinus that the Son is only from man, or only from the time when Christ was man. Then the old Colbert manuscript and others read “because before,” not “who before.”

[Col. 0205C] “Because before.”

[Col. 0206C] Printed editions have “thus, while each one”; no manuscripts support this.

[Col. 0206D] The printed text, with most manuscripts, has “defending and condemning.” We prefer, with the St Martin, Corbie, and Faur manuscripts, “of the one defending and condemning,” because of the attached adverb “religiously,” which suits the Catholic faith, not heresy.

8. [Col. 0206D] Printed editions read “then because”; they are corrected from the manuscripts. Shortly afterwards the old Colbert manuscript reads “professions of blasphemy.”

[Col. 0205C] “In undissimilar [divinity].”

[Col. 0206D] In the Paris edition, “in dissimilar,” as two words; in several manuscripts, “in undissimilar.” The whole phrase is to be understood thus: “lest anyone should charge me, after I have proclaimed the Son God just as the Father is God, and professed Father and Son to be one both in name and—in the sense of ‘and’—in the undissimilar kind of divinity, with the error …”

[Col. 0206C–D] “Lest [he be] alone.” Printed editions read “lest alone,” corruptly. The natural order is: “neither will it proclaim one God as though alone, nor, as though not one, will it confess [him] not alone.”

9. [Col. 0206D] Printed editions add: “But I think that no ambiguity concerning the name remains”; this is a gloss. In place of *remansisse* (“remains”), it is more suitably understood that the words were omitted.

[Col. 0206C] “Nothing other.”

10. [Col. 0207C–D] Printed editions read, here and just above, “God of Pharaoh.” The word “God” is not repeated here in the manuscripts, whose older witnesses have *Pharao*, the name being indeclinable through the cases, in accordance with the Greek Θεὸν Φαραώ; the remaining witnesses have *Pharaoni*, with which the editions below agree, supported by Ambrose, Epistle now XXVIII, §8, who reads, “I shall make you God to King Pharaoh,” and who elsewhere commonly uses *Pharao* even in oblique cases. The argument Hilary here draws from the name God being given simply and absolutely is developed at length by Irenaeus, book III, ch. 6, who says among other things: “Therefore neither the Lord, nor the Holy Spirit, nor the Apostles would ever have named, definitively and absolutely, as God one who was not God, unless he were true God.” And shortly afterwards: “But when Scripture calls those gods who are not gods, it does not altogether show them to be gods, as I said before, but does so with some addition and indication through which they are shown not to be gods.”

[Col. 0207D] One of the Colbert manuscripts reads “while he is honoured,” erroneously.

[Col. 0207C–D] The manuscripts read “in/against Pharaoh.” Irenaeus, book III, ch. 6, translates “before Pharaoh.” “Against Pharaoh” can be explained from the preceding words: “Did it confer on him the nature of God, but rather [strike terror] into him …?”

11. [Col. 0207D] The St Martin manuscript has “and reality.” Here “reality” is opposed to an accident, which is signified by an added name.

[Col. 0207D] Erasmus, Lipsius, and Paris read “into the Son of God”; the old books correct this.

[Col. 0207D] That is, they are not absent from the Father, to whom Word, Power, and Wisdom are not lacking, although they were born from him into God.

[Col. 0207C–0208C] The Corbie manuscript reads “the nature of division”; one Vatican and the St Martin manuscript, “concerning the nature of division”; Baduel and Erasmus, “we assert that God’s nature is divided in the Son”: these are varying glosses. The point excluded is the proposition which the Arians seek to cast as an odium upon Catholics—namely, that the Son is thought to derive from a division of the Father’s substance; see above, book IV, §4. Athanasius makes the same point: in Oration II against the Arians, p. 334, he teaches that the titles Word and Wisdom are applied to the Son in Scripture because they most fittingly signify a true, natural, and coeternal offspring without any passion or division of the Father’s substance.

[Col. 0208C] Thus the St Athanasius manuscript; the printed text has “are not absent from the Father,” and shortly afterwards, “God and Word is.”

[Col. 0208C–D] “Is the Son.” The Corbie manuscripts read “is the Son,” incorrectly. Hilary means that the Son’s nature is not located in an utterance of voice, insofar as that utterance is an accident.

[Col. 0208D] Two manuscripts read “is eternal”; the St Martin manuscript, “is always unto eternity,” corruptly. “Always inward” means always inherent and never emerging into a proper subsistence, as power or wisdom is in us.

[Col. 0208D] Supply “he,” namely the Father, who has never lacked the properties of Power and Wisdom.

[Col. 0208D] The manuscripts restore “God” here, and shortly below “God.”

[Col. 0208D] Erasmus, Lipsius, and Paris read “because not as”; no old book supports this.

[Col. 0208D] One Colbert manuscript reads “the reality signified is substance”; Corbie, “the substance of the reality is signified”; Vienna and the editions of Baduel and Erasmus, “the reality is signified by substance.” We retain the other books’ reading, which can conveniently be understood as “the reality of substance is signified”; thus it is nearly the same as the opening statement of §11, “the reality of the Word is declared in the name,” or “it belongs to substance.”

12. [Col. 0209D] Here “me” has been deleted on the authority of the old books.

[Col. 0209D] The older books omit the particle “in.”

[Col. 0209D] The oldest Colbert codex, with the German manuscript, reads “You are my God.”

13. [Col. 0209D] The St Martin and Corbie manuscripts read “one name of God,” incorrectly. Here “God” is taken materially, as they say.

[Col. 0209D–0210D] In earlier printed editions the word “nature” is separated by punctuation from the preceding word and joined to what follows. The punctuation is changed because otherwise *tamen* (“nevertheless”) would stand too remotely, and because Hilary often uses *nativitas naturae* for “natural birth”; see §22 below: “But although in nature [there may be] God, nevertheless the birth must be understood to be of nature from God”; and book VIII, §18: “they are one not through the mystery of the dispensation, but through nature’s birth.” In the St Martin manuscript *naturae* is repeated after *unitatem tamen*.

[Col. 0209C] “Yet the unity of nature.”

[Col. 0209D] Only the more recent manuscripts have “the true name.”

14. [Col. 0210D] Erasmus preferred *insit* to *in se*. Lipsius then read “and that so,” adding *quod*. The older Remigius manuscript omits *aliquid in se*. The Vatican-Basilica manuscript has “that something beyond these things may be of the kind,” and so forth. For “and so,” “so that” would be preferable.

[Col. 0210D] The Vatican-Basilica manuscript reads “their habits,” an interpolation; in its place one must understand “of those animals,” from which, namely, the birth arises.

[Col. 0210D] Only the Vatican-Basilica codex, with the St Martin manuscript, adds “the Lord.”

[Col. 0211D] Printed editions read “may have been born”; the manuscripts more correctly read “has been born,” for this is said of the Son. Faustinus, ch. 2, argues on the same ground: “How,” he asks, “is he not true God who is true Son?” Augustine, *Conference with Maximinus*, §14: “He is not a true son if the Son is not what the Father is.” Hilary rightly observes here that this is especially true in spiritual realities. Yet the Arians sometimes confessed Christ as the true Son of God while denying him to be true God, as is clear from *Against Auxentius*, §§7 and 13, and Augustine, book I *Against Maximinus*, ch. 6.

[Col. 0211D–0212D] “Nor did he progress in being what God is.” This is the reading of the better manuscripts. Baduel, Erasmus, and Lipsius read “nor does that which is God progress”; this was restored in the final Paris edition.

15. [Col. 0211D] “Or anyone.”

[Col. 0212D] “In men.”

[Col. 0212D] Some manuscripts read “may rejoice.”

[Col. 0212D] The Vatican-Basilica manuscript lacks *tamen* (“nevertheless”). Shortly afterwards, with the manuscripts, read “where there is difference,” that is, where there is discrepancy, not with the printed editions “where it may differ.”

16. [Col. 0212D] Printed editions read, “He who does not honour the Son does not honour …,” agreeing neither with the sacred text nor with the manuscripts nor with themselves below.

[Col. 0212D] Thus Paris with the superior Vatican-Basilica, St Martin, Colbert, Carnot, and other manuscripts; Baduel and Erasmus, with some others, read “we had taught”; Lipsius, “we have taught.”

17. [Col. 0213D–0214D] Christ shows that he has from the authority of the Father’s example the capacity to do what the Father does when he says, “The Son cannot do anything from himself except what he sees [the Father doing].” This signifies that the Father and Son have one common power of acting, as he adds, “My Father works until now, and I work.” By the first manner of speaking he teaches that he is born; by the second, that he is of the same nature as the Father.

[Col. 0213D–0214D] We have added the word “this” from the manuscripts. Augustine’s words in *Against the Arian Sermon*, ch. 14, illuminate Hilary’s meaning: the Son does nothing except what he sees because he sees that he has from the Father the power to act, from whom he sees that he has the nature to exist. This is precisely what follows here: “through consciousness of the Father’s power and nature in himself”; see *On the Synods*, §75.

[Col. 0214D] The word “God,” absent from the printed editions, is restored from the manuscripts.

18. While He does all the same things, He is not another; while He does them likewise, He is another.---Accordingly, He added: “For whatever things the Father does, these the Son also does likewise” (ibid.). He added “likewise” to signify the birth; but He spoke the words “all,” “whatever,” and “the same” in order to show the truth of the nature. For among things which are “all,” “whatever,” and “the same,” there can be neither diversity nor remainder.

[Note: That is, nor anything not imparted but still, as it were, withheld and reserved.]

And so that nature is the same whose natural capacity is to do all the same things. But where all the same things are done likewise through the Son, the likeness of the works excludes the solitary character of the worker: so that all things which the Father does, the Son also does all the same things likewise. This is the understanding of true birth; and it is the most complete mystery of our faith, which, from the unity of the divine nature, confesses in Father and Son the truth of one and undiffering divinity: namely, that, by doing the same things, the Son does them likewise; and, by doing them likewise, the very things which He does are the same things.

[Note: Manuscript of Chartres: “which they do”; wrongly.]

For under this one expression, the things done “likewise” testify to birth, and the same things done testify to nature.

19. The showing of the works establishes birth, not ignorance. It is instruction for our faith. What “to will” means.---Thus the order of the Lord’s answer preserves the entire order of the Church’s faith: it neither separates the nature nor fails to signify the birth. For this follows: “For the Father loves the Son, and shows Him all things which He Himself does; and He will show Him greater works than these, that you may marvel. For as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom He wills” (ibid., 20–21).

Does the showing of the works here convey to us anything other than faith in the birth—that we should believe the subsisting Son to be from the subsisting God the Father? Unless, perhaps, the only-begotten God must be thought to have required instruction by demonstration because of ignorance. But the rashness of this impious opinion cannot be admitted. For one who knows whatever he is to be taught has no need of being taught.

[Note: “Who what.”]

[Note: Basel edition: “whatever anyone”; Erasmus: “who what anyone.” Lipsius subsequently removed “anyone.” The manuscripts more correctly read: “who knows whatever.”]

For after saying, “The Father loves the Son, and shows Him all things which He Himself does,” He immediately added, in order to show that this whole showing by the Father is instruction for our faith—so that both Father and Son may be present to us in confession, and so that no ignorance might here be understood in the Son, to whom the Father shows all the works which He Himself does—“And He will show Him greater works than these, that you may marvel. For as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom He wills.”

The demonstration of the future work, therefore, is not unknown to the Son, to whom it is to be shown, so that by the example of the Father’s nature He may give life to the dead. For He says that the Father will show the Son those things at which they may marvel; and He immediately taught what those same things were: “For as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom He wills” (ibid., 21). The power is equal through the unity of an undissimilar nature. And the showing of the works is not instruction arising from ignorance, but instruction for our faith: it introduced, not into the Son knowledge of things unknown, but into us the confession of His birth, confirming it by the fact that all things which He could do had been shown to Him.

[Note: That is, the showing of the works. For “which does not,” the Vatican-Basel manuscript has “nor.”]

For heavenly speech did not fail to take precautions, lest perhaps the indication of a different nature should creep in under cover of an ambiguous statement. It says rather that the Father’s works were shown to Him than that, for performing them, a nature of power was added to Him.

[Note: In some manuscripts “by the Lord” is wrongly added here, since the verb “says” refers to the heavenly utterance.]

Thus the demonstration itself might be taught to be the substance of birth, to which, through the Father’s love, there belongs by birth a knowledge of the Father’s works which He willed to be accomplished through Him. Moreover, lest through the assertion of demonstration a diversity of nature, as though ignorant, should be believed in Him, He does not fail to know those very things which He declares are to be shown.

[Note: In the manuscripts of Chartres, Corbie, and several others: “which He does not declare.” Shortly afterward the older Colbert manuscript reads “about to perform,” not “performs.” What is said here—“So far is He from performing it by the authority of an example”—seems to conflict with what was said in §17, where the Son is asserted to have appropriated the power of acting by the authority of an example. Yet the two passages are easily reconciled: in §17 “authority” signifies only the origin of the begotten from the begetter; here it signifies the service rendered by a subordinate to his lord. Augustine, Against the Arian Sermon, ch. 23, explaining both senses in relation to the same passage, says: “Nor can the Son do anything of Himself, because He is not Himself from Himself”—not because in all things He waits for the Father’s nod.]

So far is He from being about to act by the authority of an example that He gives life to whom He wills. For willing is the freedom of nature, which subsists, together with the will of choice, in the blessedness of perfect power.

20. The whole judgment given proves both nature and birth. Judgment is given so that honor may be equal.---And lest thereafter the statement, “He gives life to whom He wills,” should seem to contain in Him not the nature of birth but rather to subsist by the right of unbegotten power, He immediately added: “For neither does the Father judge anyone, but He has given all judgment to the Son” (ibid., 22). And in the fact that all judgment has been given, both nature and birth are shown: for only an undiffering nature can possess all things, and birth can possess nothing unless it is given.

But all judgment has been given because He gives life to whom He wills. Nor can judgment seem to have been taken away from the Father when He Himself does not judge, because the Son’s judgment is from the Father’s judgment; for all judgment has been given by Him. Yet the reason why judgment was given is not left unstated. For it follows: “But He has given all judgment to the Son, that all may honor the Son as they honor the Father. He who does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent Him” (ibid., 23).

[Note: “Therefore is lacking.” Shortly afterward: “or what is left?” and then, “The Father does not judge, and has given all judgment to the Son.”]

What room, I ask, is therefore left for suspicion, or what occasion for impiety remains? The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son. The reason for the judgment given is that the Son may be equal to the Father in honor, and that whoever dishonors the Son also dishonors the Father. And after this, how can the nature of the birth be understood to differ, when not only operation, power, and honor, but even the insult of honor withheld, makes Him equal?

[Note: The Martinian manuscript: “operation of power.” Vatican-Basel: “honor of power exercised”—confusedly. The Son is equal to the Father in operation, while He does the same things as the Father; in power, while He gives life to whom He wills as the Father does; and in honor, while He is to be honored by all.]

Therefore the word of the divine answer now shows nothing other than the mystery of birth. Nor could or should the Son have been distinguished from the Father otherwise than by being taught both to be born and yet not to differ.

[Note: Printed editions: “was born.” But most manuscripts: “to be born.” Then all have “and yet not undiffering,” perhaps more genuinely through a Hellenism not unusual in Hilary. Indeed, in On the Synods, §73, we read “through the likeness of an essence not undiffering,” for “through the likeness of an essence not differing.” Other such examples may be found in that work and elsewhere.]

21. The entire faith concerning the Son is drawn from Christ’s foregoing words.---Therefore the Father works until now, and the Son works. You have the names of the natures, since both the Father works and the Son. Understand also the nature of God, through which God works, to be at work.

[Note: “Of God” is missing in the Vatican-Basel manuscript. The proof of this proposition depends upon the appended passage of Scripture.]

And lest you should perhaps think that two operations of dissimilar natures are meant, remember what was said of the blind man: “But that the works of God may be manifested in him, I must work the works of Him who sent Me” (John 9:3). Therefore, in what the Son works, there is the Father’s work; and the Son’s work is God’s work. And the discourse is still concerned with works. Meanwhile, the answer has thus far aimed at nothing other than referring every work to both, so that the nature of both might not differ in working.

[Note: Martinian manuscript: “for the nature of each did not differ in works.” Lipsius and Paris: “for the nature of each does not differ in working.” The verb *differret* is governed by the words “nothing other than … than that.”]

For in the fact that the Father works until now, the Son also works, lest He who is Lord of the Sabbath—for “the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath” (Luke 6:5)—should impiously be thought to work on the Sabbath, when, by the nature of His birth, the authority of the Father’s work was in Him.

Nature, then, is neither confused nor abolished, lest He be Son; yet neither, on the other hand, is nature taken away, lest He be God. They are not separated by difference, lest They be one; nor can Their being one bring it about that each is not.

[Note: That is, lest each should have a proper mode of existence distinct from the other.]

First recognize the Son when it is said: “The Son can do nothing of Himself, except what He sees the Father doing” (John 5:19). You have the Son’s birth, which can do nothing of itself except what it sees. In the fact that He can do nothing of Himself, the error of unbegottenness is removed; for birth cannot have power from itself. But what He sees signifies the recognition, present in Him, of a nature conscious of itself.

[Note: In Badius: “conscience”; in Lipsius and Paris: “conscious”; in the Chartres manuscript: “of consciousness.” Erasmus, with most manuscripts, more correctly reads “conscious.” Thus shortly below: “this is the word of a power conscious of itself”; and at the beginning of this book, “of weakness conscious of itself”; finally, in Psalm 68, §15, “of salvation conscious in itself.”]

And now recognize the true nature of God in this: “For whatever things He does, these the Son also does likewise” (ibid.).

[Note: Printed editions: “through the nature.” The manuscripts more correctly read “after”; supply “now recognized,” from the immediately preceding passage: “Whatever things He does,” etc.]

After the power of the nature, understand through this the unity of an undissimilar nature: “That all may honor the Son as they honor the Father who sent Him” (ibid., 23). And lest the unity of nature should confine you to the union of a solitary being, learn in this the mystery of faith: “He who does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent Him” (ibid.). All arguments against the devices of heretical madness are closed off. He is Son, because He can do nothing of Himself; He is God, because whatever the Father does, He Himself does the same; They are one, because He is equal in honor and does the same things, not different things; He is not the Father Himself, because He was sent.

Therefore birth alone possesses this force of the mystery: that it includes within itself name, nature, power, and confession. For every birth cannot fail to be in the nature from which it is born. It does not bring in the substance of an external kind, because from one source something alien does not subsist. But what is not alien from itself is one in kind of nature; and whatever is one through birth has no solitude, because solitude belongs to a single being, whereas the unity of birth belongs to both.

22. The faith of the Arians opposes their own knowledge. Christ’s power, birth from God, divine nature, and existence in the Father; the hand.---And let the testimony of the divine declaration concerning Himself be added to this.

[Note: Printed editions: “is assumed.” The manuscripts more correctly read “be present.” Thus, in Book II, §15, after certain words of John have been set forth, the transition to the rest is made thus: “let the connected matters be present.”]

For He says: “Those who are of My sheep hear My voice, and I know them, and they follow Me; and I give them eternal life, and they shall not perish forever, nor shall anyone snatch them from My hand. What the Father has given Me is greater than all; no one shall be able to snatch them from the hand of My Father. I and the Father are one” (John 10:27 ff.).

[Note: On the authority of the manuscripts we restore “shall perish” for “shall perish [future form],” and have removed the conjunction *and* prefixed to “no one shall be able,” as well as repeated before “I and the Father.”]

What dullness of sluggish mind, I ask, blunts our understanding, so that sayings thus absolutely stated do not enter our minds? Or what swelling of insolent spirit mocks human weakness, so that, having acquired knowledge of God from these words, people think that God is not to be understood from the things through which He has been made known? Either other Gospels must be produced to teach us, or, if these Gospels alone have taught us concerning God, why do we not believe as we are taught? And if knowledge has been derived only from these, why should faith not arise from the same source as knowledge? But when faith is discovered to oppose knowledge, that faith is no longer faith of knowledge but of guilt: it adopts for itself an irreligious faith against the religion of acknowledged knowledge.

Therefore the only-begotten God, conscious of His own nature, signifies the ineffable mystery of His own birth, yet with the fullest explicitness of words possible for the confession of our faith: so that He may be understood to be born, believed to be in the nature of God, be one with the Father, and, while professing Himself one with the Father, nevertheless not lose what He is as Son by being understood as merely solitary and the Father Himself.

[Note: Paris edition: “professing Himself one”; wrongly.]

[Note: “As one alone.”]

[Note: Printed editions and most manuscripts: “as one alone.” The word “one” has been removed on the authority of the better manuscripts. The suspicion of Sabellian error is avoided: the Son, while professing Himself one with the Father, does not cease to be Son, nor should He be regarded as Himself the Father.]

For He first bears witness to the power of His nature when He says of His sheep: “No one shall snatch them from My hand” (ibid., 28).

[Note: “Snatches.”]

This is the utterance of power conscious of itself, confessing the freedom of untroubled power by the fact that no one snatches the sheep from His hand. But, so that His birth may be understood to be from God in the nature of God, He added: “What the Father has given Me is greater than all” (ibid., 29). He does not conceal that He was born from the Father; for what He has received from the Father is greater than all.

[Note: “And he who receives.” Thus below, “while he receives”; then, “but he who receives from another”; and afterward, “from whom he receives.”]

[Note: Printed editions: “and because He received”; then, “yet afterward He is not from another.” The manuscripts restore the following sense: He who received by being born is not afterward—that is, not after His birth has been constituted—in what He received, as though it were something from which His nature derives its constitution; and yet He is from another insofar as He received. This is illustrated by Book II, §20: “He who was life did not become life after He was born; for in Him what was born is not one thing and what the One born received another”; and shortly afterward: “God, who was born from God, did not become God after He was born, but existed as God by being born.” Here, for “received,” almost all manuscripts have “receives”; nor is that a bad reading.]

And He who receives is, by being born, in that which He receives—not afterward; and yet He is from another, in that He receives. But lest He who receives from another should be understood to exist as something other than, and not in the nature of, Him from whom He receives, He said: “No one shall be able to snatch them from the hand of My Father.” No one snatches them from His own hand, because He has received from the Father that which is greater than all. What does this apparently so different declaration mean—namely, that again no one snatches them from the hand of His Father? The Son’s hand is that which He received from the Father; the Father’s hand is that which gave to the Son. And how is it that what is not snatched from the Son’s hand is not snatched from the Father’s hand? Understand it, if you ask how, from this: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). The Son’s hand is the Father’s hand. For nature does not degenerate through birth, so as not to be the same; nor, again, because it is the same, does it obstruct the understanding of birth, because birth admits nothing alien into itself.

But, so that by this bodily expression you might know the power of the same nature, the Son’s hand was identified with the Father’s hand, because the nature and power of the Father were in the Son.

[Note: Thus the manuscripts. But printed editions read, “are also in the Son.” Then the Vatican-Basel manuscript has “finally, that after the mystery.” From this passage of Hilary one may aptly understand what Irenaeus says, Book IV, ch. 37, where he first states that God, in creating the world, did not need the external ministry of angels: “as though,” he says, “He did not have His own hands”; and then adds: “For His Word and Wisdom, the Son and the Spirit, are always present with Him, through whom and in whom He freely and willingly made all things, to whom also He speaks, saying, ‘Let Us make,’” and so forth. Thus he called the Son and the Holy Spirit God’s hands, because they possess God’s very power and nature.]

Finally, that through the mystery of birth you might recognize the truth of an undiffering nature, it was said: “I and the Father are one,” so that what They are one might be believed neither different nor solitary, since there is not a different nature in the two by reason of the property of birth and generation.

23. The Arians are more unjust toward Christ than the Jews.---So far as it can be understood, the will of diseased minds remains, although the effect of their will has ceased; and the zeal of malevolence does not abandon its malicious mind, though the opportunity for an evil deed is absent. For now the fury of heretics, while the Lord sits in heaven, because they cannot, after the example of the Jews, put Him on the cross, nevertheless with equal unbelief deny Him that which He is—namely, that He exists. And though they cannot deny what was said, they disobey the words, practice hatred of impiety, hurl the stones of words, and, if they could, would drag Him from His throne back to the cross.

[Note: Printed editions: “the Lord sitting in heaven,” against the manuscripts.]

[Note: The Vatican-Basel codex with the Martinian manuscript reads, “not only, disobeying, do they practice hatred of impiety, but also [they hurl] the stones of words,” etc.; these show the work of an interpolator. From this it is evident, as has already been observed, that Hilary regarded consubstantiality as so expressly set forth in Scripture that he thought it could not be denied in good faith by persons learned in the Scriptures.]

And concerning the Jews, stirred by the novelty of this saying, it is written thus (John 10:31 ff.):

[Note: In the Martinian manuscript: “truth.”]

“Therefore the Jews took up stones to stone Him. Jesus answered them, ‘I have shown you many good works from the Father; for which of these works do you stone Me?’ The Jews answered Him, ‘We do not stone You for a good work, but for blasphemy, and because You, being a man, make Yourself God.’”

But you, heretic, recognize what you do and profess; understand that you share the company of those whose example of unbelief you reproduce in yourself. For at the statement, “I and the Father are one,” the Jews raised stones, and their impious grief, unable to endure the mystery of saving faith, broke forth even into an attack intended to inflict death. What do you accomplish less by denying Him, since you have no one to stone? The will does not differ; but the heavenly throne makes your will ineffective. How much more irreligious are you than the Jew! He raises stones against a body; you against the Spirit. He against a man, as he supposed; you against God. He against One dwelling on earth; you against One seated upon the throne of power. He against One unknown; you against One confessed. He against One about to die; you against the Judge of the ages. He says, “Though You are a man” (ibid., 33); you say, “Though You are a creature.” Yet both of you say, “You make Yourself God”: this is the common reproach of your impious mouth against Him.

For you deny God from the generation of God; you deny the Son from the truth of birth; you deny that “I and the Father are one” is a confession of one and like nature in both.

[Note: The Vatican-Basel and Martinian manuscripts add here, “from the truth of nature”; this is absent from the other books and seems superfluous.]

You place God under a new, external, and alien substance, so that He is either a God of another kind, or no God at all, because He does not subsist by birth from God.

[Note: “From the birth of God.”]

[Note: Printed editions with several manuscripts: “from the birth of God.” The Martinian codex: “from God, from the birth of God.” With the Chartres manuscript, two Colbert manuscripts, the German manuscript, and others, we prefer “by birth from God.”]

24. Christ’s answer to the Jews is fitting also for the Arians. The reason and aim of the answer.---But because you are stirred by the mystery of this saying, “I and the Father are one,” so that, as the Jew says, “Though You are a man, You make Yourself God,” you with equal impiety say, “Though You are a creature, You make Yourself God”—for you say: “You are not Son by birth; You are not God in truth; You are a creature surpassing all things, but You are not born into God, because I do not admit that a nature can be born from incorporeal God. Not only are You and the Father not one, but You are not even Son, nor like, nor God”—the Lord indeed answered the Jews, but this entire answer is more particularly fitted to your impiety:

[Note: Here the final words of the Arians’ letter to Alexander, reported in Book IV, §13 and Book VI, §6, are being considered.]

“Is it not written in the Law, ‘I said, You are gods’? If He called those gods to whom the word of God came—and Scripture cannot be broken—do you say of Him whom the Father sanctified and sent into this world, ‘You blaspheme,’ because I said, ‘I am the Son of God’? If I do not do the works of My Father, do not believe Me; but if I do them, even though you will not believe Me, believe the works, that you may know and recognize that the Father is in Me and I in Him” (ibid., 34 ff.).

[Note: Verona codex: “the Father in Me, and I into Him”; and it reads “is reckoned” for “was reckoned” at §26 and §27 shortly below.]

[Note: Thus the manuscripts, according to the Greek. Printed editions, however, according to the Vulgate, read: “The Father is in Me, and I in the Father.” Moreover, this passage is repeated three times in this book. In its first occurrence the manuscripts again agree with the Greek and the printed editions with the Vulgate; in the second, both agree with the Greek; and in the last, both with the Vulgate.]

He brought forward the reason for His answer from the cause of the charge of blasphemy brought against Him. For this was counted as a crime against Him: that, though He was a man, He made Himself God. And He was accused of making Himself God because He had said, “I and the Father are one.” Therefore, intending to show that His being one with the Father arose from the nature of birth, He first refutes the absurdity of the ridiculous reproach: why He should be charged when, though a man, He made Himself God.

For since the Law assigned this title to holy human beings, and the indissoluble word of God confirmed their profession of the name bestowed upon them, how could He whom the Father had sanctified and sent into this world be blasphemous in confessing Himself the Son of God, when the indissoluble word of God had established as gods those who were so named by the Law? Thus it is no longer a crime, though He is a man, that He makes Himself God, since the Law called men gods. And if the appropriation of this name is not irreligious among other human beings, then He—the man whom the Father sanctified, for this entire answer concerns the man, because the Son of God is also Son of Man—does not seem shamelessly to appropriate it when He says that He is the Son of God. For He surpasses those who can without irreligion call themselves gods, by the fact that He was sanctified as Son. Blessed Paul makes known to us the meaning of this sanctification when he says:

[Note: Lipsius and Paris: “not religiously”; corrupt.]

[Note: Badius, Erasmus, and Lipsius: “who before”; the other books disagree. Then Paris with an old Colbert manuscript: “promised,” not “promised beforehand.”]

“Which He promised beforehand through His prophets in the holy Scriptures concerning His Son, who was made from the seed of David according to the flesh, who was appointed Son of God in power according to the Spirit of sanctification” (Romans 1:2 ff.).

[Note: Printed editions: “who was made to Him.” We have removed “to Him” on the authority of the Colbert, German, and Martinian manuscripts, in agreement with the Greek, as well as Irenaeus, Book III, ch. 32, and Tertullian, Against Praxeas, §27. Further, on the evidence of the manuscripts and the Chartres copy, we restore “who was appointed,” supported by the Greek *tou horisthentos*, where previously “who was predestined” was read. The Corbie codex, written at least a thousand years ago and containing Paul’s letters in Greek and Latin, has in Latin “was made to Him” and “was predestined,” but differs in Greek, agreeing there with the commonly printed Greek copies.]

Therefore the charge of blasphemy ceases—that, although He is a man, He makes Himself God—since God’s word has bestowed this name upon many, and He who was sanctified and sent by the Father has professed Himself to be nothing other than the Son of God.

25. “I AND THE FATHER ARE ONE” shows the nature of birth.---No room for doubt remains, I think, that “I and the Father are one” was said concerning the nature of birth. For when the Jews had accused Him of making Himself God, though He was Himself a man, by this saying, His answer confirms that by “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30) He showed Himself to be the Son of God: first by the name, then by the nature, and finally by the birth.

[Note: “Shows.”]

For “I” and “Father” are names of things; but “one” is a confession of nature, because in what each is, neither differs; while “are” does not permit a union. And where there is no union in the words “we are one,” birth makes Them one.

[Note: We supply the word “one,” missing from printed editions, from the manuscripts.]

For all this follows from His profession, as sanctified by the Father, that He is the Son of God; and the profession of the Son of God confirms the statement, “I and the Father are one,” because birth cannot bring a nature other than that from which it subsists.

26. God’s nature in the Son is demonstrated by His deeds. What is outside God cannot be made equal to Him.---The word of the only-begotten God has completed the whole mystery of our faith. For after He had answered why, though He was a man, He made Himself God, He then added the following, so that the saying, “I and the Father are one,” might receive its full and perfect intelligibility:

“You say, ‘You blaspheme,’ because I said, ‘I am the Son of God.’ If I do not do the works of My Father, do not believe Me; but if I do them, even though you will not believe Me, believe the works, that you may know and recognize that the Father is in Me and I in Him” (John 10:36 ff.).

All hope is already desperate through consciousness of unrestrained audacity, and all professed impiety is beyond shame. For no one now blushes at folly once he has lost religion; to contradict these things is madness rather than ignorance.

[Note: Printed editions: “now whoever.” The manuscripts more correctly read “now someone,” that is, “now any person.” Then: “to contradict these things,” that is, “for their contradicting the faith.”]

The Lord had said, “I and the Father are one”: this is the mystery of birth, that Father and Son are in unity of nature. And because the assertion of this nature was being charged as a crime, the basis for asserting it is taught from its cause. For He says: “If I do not do the works of My Father, do not believe Me” (ibid., 37). If He does not do the Father’s works, He is not to be believed when He professes Himself to be the Son of God. Therefore birth does not possess a new and external nature, because He is to be believed to be Son by the fact that He accomplishes the Father’s works. What place does adoption or an indulgent grant of the name find here, so that He might not be Son from the nature of God, when He is to be believed to be Son of God from works belonging to the Father’s nature?

A creature is neither made equal nor like to God, nor is a power of alien nature compared with Him; only the birth of the Son is believed, without impiety, to be equal to Him through likeness.

[Note: Erasmus preferred “not improperly,” which Lipsius and Paris afterwards adopted, against Badius and the manuscripts. Hilary carefully predicates likeness here and below together with equality, as he says that he has always done in his apologetic replies to the work On the Synods.]

For whatever is outside Him, if it is made equal to Him, dishonors His honored power. If anything not from Him can be found like Him and of the same power, He has lost God’s prerogative through association with an equal; and He will no longer be the one God, from whom another god is undiffering. But equality belonging to what is proper to Him brings no dishonor.

[Note: That is, the equality of a thing which is not alien or external, but proper to Him.]

For what is like Him is His own; what is compared with Him in likeness is from Him; what can do His own things is not outside Him; and it is an increase of dignity to have begotten power without alienating nature. The Son accomplishes the Father’s works, and by this asks to be believed to be the Son of God. It is no arrogant claim which asks to be proved only by what it performs. Yet He testifies that He performs not His own works, but those which are the Father’s, lest His birth in nature should be removed because of the greatness of His deeds.

And because, under the mystery of the assumed body and of the man born from Mary, the Son of God was not understood, faith in the name is imparted through the deeds, when He says: “But if I do them, even though you will not believe Me, believe the works” (ibid., 38).

[Note: “Faith for us.”]

[Note: Nearly all books read “faith for us.” The reading “faith in the name” pleased us more, with the best Colbert manuscript and the German manuscript. For Christ, proclaiming His own name and saying, “I am the Son of God,” when He was not believed, sought to establish faith in what He had said through His deeds.]

He does not first wish to be believed to be the Son of God except from the Father’s works which He Himself accomplishes. But if He does the works, and because of the humility of the body is unworthy of faith in His profession, He asks faith in the works. Why indeed should the mystery of the man born impede the understanding of the divine birth, when the divine birth performs all its work through the ministry of the assumed man?

[Note: Printed editions: “under the mystery,” and subsequently “is made equal,” for “performs.” They are corrected with the help of the manuscripts.]

If, then, the man is not believed through the works to be the Son of God, let the works be believed to be those of the Son of God, because they cannot be denied to be God’s. For by being born the Son of God has within Himself all that God has.

[Note: In the Chartres manuscript: “which God is”; the sense is the same.]

And therefore the Son’s work is the Father’s work, because birth is not outside the nature from which it exists, and has within itself the nature from which it subsists.

[Note: Printed editions read “flows,” without manuscript authority. The verb *manere* is familiar to Hilary in the sense “to exist,” as is clear from Book IV, §§6 and 16; Book VI, §13; and On the Synods, §§35 and 41. He frequently uses it to signify the Son’s birth as free from beginning or division. Thus below, §31: “God remaining from God is not from elsewhere”; and Book VIII, §53: “Christ does not remain from non-existent things.” So too Book VI, §19: “whom the nature of birth, remaining from you in you, retained”; and §35: “not as though He began to exist from nothing, but came forth from One remaining.” Finally, in sound manuscripts *manare* (“to flow”) is nowhere found where reference is made to the Son’s eternal generation.]

Source/review notes: The draft omitted inline page markers 198–206 and occasionally rendered the source’s distinction between unus (“one/alone”) and unum (“one”) as the theological term “person.”

[Col. 0223A] **27. The Son in the Father, and conversely. Whatever is in God is one. The Son is life from life, and therefore not from nothing.**—Accordingly, in performing the works of the Father and asking that, if he himself were not believed, the works [198] themselves at least should be believed, he had to show what was to be believed on the testimony of the works—namely, what follows: “But if I do them, and you are unwilling to believe me, believe the works, that you may know and recognize that the Father is in me, and I in him” (John 10:38). This is what “I am the Son of God” means; this is what “I and the Father are one” means. This is the nature of the birth; this is the mystery of saving faith: not to divide those who are one, [Note: [Col. 0223D] The printed editions read “nor of the birth.” The manuscripts more correctly read “nor from the one born,” that is, nor to take away nature from the one born.] nor to take nature away from the one born, and to confess, from the living God, the truth of the living God.

For God, who is life, does not subsist from compounded [Note: [Col. 0223C] Nor from inanimate things.] [Note: [Col. 0223D] The Martigny manuscript, as below, has *inania*, “empty things,” for *inanima*, “inanimate things”; so also here, with the Vatican-Basel manuscript, “and from empty things.” The Corbie manuscript, in its first hand, has “nor from empty things.” Then all witnesses have “from weak things,” where the common editions have “from weaker things.” Hilary appears to use *continetur* (“is contained”) for *constat* (“consists”): lest the Son be thought to have proceeded from the Father in such a way as not always to be contained within him and remain in him. Thus in Book VI, §19, addressing the Father, he confesses one born “in whom the truth of your generation from yourself contained you,” and “whom the nature of birth from yourself, remaining in you, retained in you.] and inanimate elements; nor is he who is power contained by weak things; nor is he who is light fashioned out of darkness; nor is he who is spirit formable from unlike things. Everything in him, in that which he is, is one: so that what is spirit is also light, power, and life; and what is life is also light, power, and spirit. For he who says, “I am, and I do not change” (Mal. 3:6), is not changed out of parts, nor made different by category. For these things indicated above are not in him as parts; rather, this whole, one and perfect reality in him is the living God in all things.

Therefore the living God is the eternal power of living nature; and that which is born from him with the mystery of his own knowledge could not have been born other than living. For when he says, “As the living Father sent me, and I live through the Father” (John 6:58), [Note: [Col. 0223D] The editions here read “because of the Father,” but Book VIII, §16 has “through the Father,” a reading consistently supplied by the manuscripts and confirmed by the immediately following phrase, “through the living Father.”] he taught that life is in him through the living Father. Then, when he says, “For as the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son also to have life in himself” (John 5:26), he testified that all his living reality is from the Living One. But what has been born living from the Living has the advance of birth without novelty of nature. For that which is generated from the living into the living is not new, since life was not sought from nothing for the birth; and life which receives birth from life must, through the unity of nature and the mystery of perfect and ineffable birth, both live in the Living One and have within itself [Note: [Col. 0223C] Life, the Living One.] [Note: [Col. 0224D] The Colbert and German manuscripts read “life, the Living One.”] life, the Living One.

[Col. 0224A] **28. How the Son is in the Father. A comparison from human birth. The difference between the two births.**—We remember that at the beginning of this discourse (Book I, §19; Book IV, §2; and Book VI, §9) we [199] warned that human comparisons do not adequately match divine realities, though our understanding is nevertheless instructed, in some measure, by bodily forms. I appeal to our awareness of human birth: does not the origin of those born remain within their fathers? For although those inanimate and base elements through which the causes of generation begin flow out into another human being, they nevertheless remain mutually within one another by the power of nature. Both through [Note: [Col. 0223C] The nature given by himself.] [Note: [Col. 0224D] The editions read “given by himself”; *by himself* is absent from the better manuscripts. Here it is acutely explained how the Son is in the Father and the Father in the Son. The Father is in the Son because the begetter accompanies the one being born, while his nature is in some manner transmitted into the offspring. But that nature, received by the Son, because it is not lost by the Father but remains in him, grants the Son also to remain in the begetter himself.] the origin of the same nature which he has given, the begetter accompanies the one being born; and through the received birth—whose power, although derived, is nevertheless not [Note: [Col. 0224C] Taken away.] [Note: [Col. 0224D] The Corbie, Pratensis, Vindobonensis, and other manuscripts read “is taken away.” The older Colbert manuscript reads “will be taken away.”] taken away—the one who is born remains in his begetter.

This has been recalled by us only for understanding human birth, not as a complete illustration of birth in the only-begotten God. For the weakness of human nature is composed from unlike things and is sustained from inanimate things unto life. Nor does what is generated in it immediately live, nor does its whole live from life; since in it there are many things which, having grown, are cut away without awareness of their own nature. But in God everything that is, lives. For God is life, and from life [Note: [Col. 0224D] The Chartres manuscript: “anything else.”] nothing can be except living. Nor is this birth by derivation, but by power. Thus, since all that he is lives and all that is born from him is power, he has birth but does not undergo change; he imparts increase without losing nature. For he accompanies the birth which he has given through the likeness of undivided nature, [Col. 0224C] and the birth, living from the Living One, does not abandon in being born that nature.

**29. A second comparison from fire.**—For, to some extent, fire offers an indication of this faith: fire having fire within itself, and fire remaining in fire. For though it has brightness of light, the heat of its nature, the power of burning, and the movement of glowing, yet it is wholly fire, and all these things are one nature. Indeed, owing to weakness, it subsists and lives through material, and fails together with that through which it lived. But that which is [200] [Note: [Col. 0224D] In Badius and Erasmus, *incomparabile*, “incomparable,” is lacking. Then Lipsius, Paris, and most manuscripts have “we know from the part of comparisons.” Martin’s text, “from a comparison we know a part,” is less bad. We restore “by comparison,” etc., on the authority of the Basel-Vatican manuscript and two other Vatican manuscripts, with which Badius and Erasmus agree. Next, the manuscripts have “is in God,” not “is in God” [the latter perhaps a textual distinction no longer recoverable in English].] incomparable in God we know in part by comparison, [Col. 0225A] so that what is found in some measure among earthly elements may not be thought incredible in God.

I ask, then, whether there is division and separation when fire comes from fire. Or is nature cut off so that it does not remain? Or does nature not follow so that it is not present, when, with a light kindled from a light, there is through a certain advance, as it were, of birth no [Note: [Col. 0225C] The printed editions read “defect,” and then “without defect”; they are corrected from the manuscripts. This is relevant to Tatian, *Oration against the Greeks*, who says: “He was born by participation, not by severance. For what is severed is separated from the first; but what is communicated, endowed with its own function, in no way diminishes the one from whom it received its power. Just as many other torches are kindled from one torch, yet the light of the first torch is not diminished because many are kindled from it, so also the Word, proceeding from the power of the Father, did not leave the begetter of the Word without the Word.” Tatian had been preceded by Justin in his *Dialogue with Trypho*, teaching that the Son was generated from the Father not by severance, as though the Father’s substance had been apportioned, in the way that all other things, when divided and cut, are not the same as they were before they were split. “And as an illustration,” he says, “I took what we see when other fires are kindled from a fire: the original fire is diminished in no respect but remains the same, although many fires can be kindled from it.” There he indicates what he had stated much earlier in the same dialogue: “Just as we see another fire made from a fire, without the diminution of that from which the kindling of the other is made, but with it remaining in the same state; and the fire kindled from it likewise appears to exist, without diminishing that from which it was kindled.” From this it is clear why Catholics called the Son “light from light,” and why the Arians undertook to take this conception away from us.] cutting-off, and yet light from light? Or does that which subsists from itself without cutting-off not remain in the source? Or is that not in the source from which it has not been cut, but from which it has gone forth with unity of natural substance? And I ask whether they are not one, since light from light is separable neither by division nor by kind of nature.

**30. The use of comparisons.**—And these comparisons, as I have said, are made only for the understanding of faith, not for the dignity of God: that we might derive our understanding of invisible things [Note: [Col. 0226C] The printed editions read “from comparable things”; corrected with the aid of the manuscripts.] from bodily things, not indeed that any example of comparison should adequately correspond to God’s nature. For it would have been fitting and right to believe God testifying concerning himself. But because heretical frenzy disturbed the faith of simpler people, so that they held that one ought not believe of God what could scarcely be understood without a bodily comparison, therefore, in accordance with that saying of the Lord already mentioned above, “What is born of flesh is flesh, but what is born of Spirit is spirit” (John 3:6), and because God is spirit, we judged it useful to insert these illustrative comparisons in part, lest he should be thought to lie in his declaration about himself when examples from the nature of [Note: [Col. 0225C] Creatures in some manner.] created things provided us with an understanding of the divine declaration.

[Col. 0225C] **31. The Son possesses the divine nature by the power of birth. Through it he himself is in the Father and the Father in him. In naming the Father one also names the Son.**—Therefore, the living Son of God from the Living One, God from God, displaying the unity of inseparable and unlike-less nature and the mystery of birth, says: “I and the Father are one.” And because malicious accusation might arise against this saying as presumptuous, he added, in order to show in the statement the consciousness of nature: “You say that I have blasphemed, because I said, [201] ‘I am the Son of God,’” [John 10:36] attesting that unity of nature comes from birth.
