But in order that this unqualified confession might establish faith in the birth, while the confessed birth should not introduce a division of nature, he maintained this as the conclusion of his whole reply: “Believe the works, because the Father is in me and I in the Father.” What natural and proper thing has not here been shown under the mystery of birth? They are in one another, since birth is only from the Father; since in the other God no [Note: [Col. 0225C] In the editions: “of nature or exterior.”] [Note: [Col. 0226D] Thus the best Colbert manuscript together with the German manuscript. Others read, “a nature or exterior.”] nature, whether external or unlike, subsists; since God remaining from God is not God from any other source.

Bring forward two gods, if occasion allows, belonging to the faith of the Church; or at least falsely call God solitary. If you can, distinguish the Son from the Father while confessing only the truth of birth. The Son is in the Father and the Father in the Son, not by a reciprocal transfusion and reflux, [Note: [Col. 0226D] Or, as Faustinus, often cited already, explains in chapter 1, not indeed through some passive confusion, but because it follows that where the Father is, the Son is known also to be there; and where the Son is, there also you recognize the Father to be present.] but through the perfect birth of living nature. Thus in God the Father and God the Son you will neither count two gods, [Note: [Col. 0226C] “You will call them gods together.”] [Note: [Col. 0226D] The Martigny manuscript reads “countable together.” The others have *connominabis* or *cognominabis*, “you will name together.” We retain *connumerabis*, “you will count,” because of §13: “The one name does not count two gods.”] because both are one; nor will you proclaim a solitary God, because neither is alone.

Therefore apostolic faith has not two gods, because it has neither two Fathers nor two Sons. In confessing the Father, it confesses the Son; in believing in the Son, it believes also in the Father, because the name Father contains within itself the name Son. For he is Father only through the Son; and the designation of Son is the manifestation of Father, because the Son exists only from the Father. Therefore, in confessing the one, he is not alone: for the Son completes the Father, and the Son’s birth is from the Father. Nature is not changed through birth, lest, according to the likeness of its kind, it should be the same. Yet it is the same in such a way that through birth and generation both must rather be confessed to be one, not one person.

[Col. 0226C] **32. Summary. The Father and Son, one God and not solitary, are mutually in one another.**—Let him, then, proclaim two gods who can proclaim one without the other; or let him teach a solitary God who can deny that one [202] is present in the other through the power of nature and through the mystery of generation and birth. Let him also attribute a [Note: [Col. 0227C] And different.] [Note: [Col. 0227C] Lipsius and Paris read “unlike and different,” contrary to the witness of the other books. Augustine, *On the Trinity*, VI.3, argues that the same Scriptural passage excludes a different nature: “I do not know,” he says, “whether in the Scriptures we find ‘they are one’ of things whose nature is different.” Hence in his debate with Maximinus, §14, he addresses him thus: “When you have produced for me that things of different substances are one, then I shall consider what answer I ought to make.”] different nature to each, who does not know that Father and Son are proclaimed to be one.

Let heretics erase the Gospel confession which the Son makes concerning himself: “I in the Father, and the Father in me,” [Note: [Col. 0227D] We have removed from here “I and the Father are one,” which Lipsius wrongly inserted, since what follows in no way refers to this passage, but only to the preceding “I in the Father,” etc.] so that they may proclaim either two gods or one solitary God. In the property of one nature there are not indications of different natures. The truth of God from God does not produce two gods; the birth of God does not permit a solitary God; nor are they not one who [Note: [Col. 0227C] “They are in one another.” “But they are in one another.”] [Note: [Col. 0227D] Badius, Erasmus, and Lipsius with the Corbie manuscript read “they are in one another. But they are in one another.” In is absent from Paris and most manuscripts. Thus in §31: “They are mutually in one another.” They are mutually in one another because, as was just said, they are in the property of one nature—that is, each has as his own one and the same nature.] are mutually in one another. They are mutually in one another because one is from the other: for neither has the one given to the other through generation anything other than what is his own, nor does the one receive from the other through birth anything other than what belongs to the one. [Note: [Col. 0227D] Badius and Erasmus read “than one.” The other books more correctly read “than what belongs to one,” with *what* understood: that is, than what belongs to the one. Thus below one from one is proclaimed to remain in the nature and name of the one.]

Therefore apostolic faith, whether it proclaims the Father, proclaims one God; or whether it confesses the Son, confesses one God, because the same and entirely unlike-less nature of God is in both, [Note: [Col. 0227D] The editions omit the conjunction *and* here, and then read “of both” in place of “of each,” although this word appears before and after in the singular, not the plural. The manuscript reading is restored. The sense may be expressed thus: “and because, while both the Father is God and the Son is God, and while each has one name of nature,” etc.] and because, while both the Father is God and the Son is God, and the name of nature is one for each, “one” signifies both. For God from God, or God in God, does not make two gods, since one from one remains in the nature and name of the one; [Note: [Col. 0228C] Erasmus: “in nature and name.” Then Lipsius and Paris, with the Martigny manuscript: “may remain in the name of one nature”—confusedly. For there *of one* seems equivalent to “of him who is one.”] nor does it lapse into a solitary God, since one and one, in their signification, are not solitary.

**33. The way to the Father through the Son: how this is to be understood.**—The Lord did not leave uncertain or doubtful the teaching of so great a mystery, nor did he abandon us to the error of ambiguous understanding. Let us hear him revealing the whole knowledge of this faith to the Apostles. For he says (John 14:6 ff.): “I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me. If you know me, you know my Father also; and from now on you will know him, and you have seen him.” Philip says to him: “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us.” Jesus says to him: “Have I been with you so long, [Note: [Col. 0228C] “And you have not known me,” from the Greek: καὶ οὐκ ἐγνώκας με, “and you have not known me.”] and you do not know me? Philip, whoever has seen me has seen the Father also. How can you say, ‘Show us the Father’? Do you not believe [Note: [Col. 0228D] Just as *me* is absent from the Greek text, so it is also absent here from two Colbert manuscripts, though it appears below.] me that I am in the Father and the Father [203] is in me? The words which I speak to you I do not speak from myself; but the Father who remains in me himself does his works. Believe me that I am in the Father and the Father in me; but if not, believe because of the works themselves.”

He who is the way does not lead us into wandering and trackless paths; he who is truth does not deceive by falsehood; he who is life does not leave us in the error of death. Since he himself established these names of his gracious dispensation for our salvation, so that, as way, he might lead us into truth and, as truth, establish us in life, we must recognize what mystery of attaining life he declares. “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14:6). The way to the Father is through the Son. And we must ask whether this is through the instruction of teaching or through faith in nature; for it may seem that we come to the Father through the Son’s teaching rather than through confession of the Father’s divinity in him. Let us, therefore, seek the meaning of this understanding in what follows. For faith is not to be adopted according to our own choice, but according to the force of the sayings.

[Col. 0228B] **34. Whoever knows the Son knows also the Father.**—For what follows is: “If you know me, you know my Father also” (ibid., v. 7). Jesus Christ is seen as a human being; and how, if he himself is known, will the Father be known, when the Apostles recognize in him the condition of his own nature—that is, humanity—and God, free from bodily flesh, is not to be known in this weakness of bodily flesh? But in the mystery of the assumed body, the Lord, confirming within himself the divine nature of the Father, maintained this sequence: “If you know me, you know my Father also; and from now on you will know him, and you have seen him.” He separated the time of seeing from the time of knowing. For the one whom he says is to be known he also says has already been seen, [Note: [Col. 0228C] “And in nature.”] [Note: [Col. 0228D] Paris, with an old Colbert manuscript and the German manuscript, reads “and in nature”; the Corbie manuscript also had it in its first hand. We have repeatedly observed that *and* has the same force as *so that*. It is declared below that the divine nature in Christ was seen through miracles.] so that they might now receive, from the time of this revelation, knowledge of the nature already long seen in him.

**35. Why Philip does not grasp this. How, without loss of faith, he asks that the Father be shown to him.**—But the novelty of these words moved the apostle Philip. A man is seen; he confesses himself to be God’s Son; he declares that, when he is known, the Father will be known. He says that the Father has been seen, and that precisely because he has been seen he is to be known. The weakness of the human mind does not grasp this, [204] [Col. 0229A] nor does this declaration of such different things receive human faith: that he who has then been seen is now to be known; that seeing should be knowledge; and that if the Son is known, the Father also is known. For he himself had presented knowledge of the Son according to his human nature through bodily sight and touch; yet knowledge of the Father from him is not supplied by the nature, different from the human being seen, and the Son had often testified that no one had seen the Father.

Therefore Philip, questioning the Lord with apostolic [Note: [Col. 0229D] Some more recent manuscripts: “familiarity and consciousness.”] familiarity and confidence, broke out: “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us.” Faith is not now in danger; rather, this is an error of ignorance. For the Lord had said that the Father had already been seen and would from then on be known; but the Apostle had not understood that he had been seen. Finally, he did not deny that he had been seen, but asked that he be shown to him. Nor did he desire the showing as though it were bodily sight; rather, he asked for an intelligible demonstration of him who had been seen. He had seen the Son in the appearance of a human being, but did not know how he had seen the Father through this. Thus, after saying, “Lord, show us the Father” (ibid., v. 8), he added, “and it is enough for us,” to indicate that the showing was a demonstration for understanding rather than for seeing. Faith was not taken away by his words; rather, he sought a demonstration of knowledge which [Note: [Col. 0229D] That is, which would be sufficient to persuade by some rational ground concerning that which was already held certain and unquestioned because of the speaker’s authority, so that faith might become knowledge furnished with reason, as it is called in Book I, §22.] would suffice for faith in the saying, because the Lord’s declaration gave an unquestionable authority for believing. This request to show the Father arose because he had been said [Note: [Col. 0230C] Thus the manuscripts. The editions: “because it had been said that he had been seen, and was thereby to be known.” Next, some manuscripts: “nor was he imprudent.”] to have been seen, and thereby to be known, because he had been seen. Nor was it presumptuous to ask for a showing of him who had been seen.

[Col. 0229C] **36. He is reproved because he had not yet known the nature of God in Christ.**—The Lord therefore replied to Philip’s words: “Have I been with you so long, and you do not know me, Philip?” (ibid., v. 9). He rebukes the Apostle’s ignorance in knowing him, because above he had said that, when he was known, the Father too would be known. But what is it of which he complains—that he had not been known for so long a time? Surely it is that, when he was known, the divinity of the Father’s nature in him ought to have been understood.

For the things which he did were proper to God: walking on the waves, commanding the winds, [Note: [Col. 0230C] Badius and Paris read *intellecta*; Erasmus reads *in intellecta* as two words. Ludovicus Miraeus, after Erasmus, conjectures that one should read: “in the incomprehensible transformation of wine and the increase of the loaves collected together.” The word *inintellecta* must be referred solely to the verb *gerere*, “to perform,” as though “to perform things not understood”; for in changing the wine and multiplying the loaves Christ performed what human understanding cannot attain. Yet the reality of the deeds stands firm, of which so many were eyewitnesses. Of these same deeds, Book III, §18: “The thing is seen and not known; it occurs and is not understood; the reason is not grasped, yet the effect is presented.” And §20: “Shall we say that it was not done because we do not grasp the understanding of the deed? … But the reality of the deed overcomes our falsehood.”] performing, with the factual reality of his deeds, the incomprehensible transformation of wine [205] and increase of loaves; driving out demons, expelling diseases, restoring bodily losses, correcting defects of birth, forgiving sins, restoring life to the dead; and while doing these things in the flesh, confessing himself amid them to be the Son of God. Hence arose the whole ground of his complaint: that in the mystery of human birth, [Note: [Col. 0230D] Thus the more numerous and better manuscripts. The editions read: “that he had performed these things in a human being, with God’s nature not understood”—incorrectly. For Christ’s complaint was not that he had done these things, but that Philip had not understood his divine nature in the deeds. Yet “when, in the mystery of human birth, he had performed these things,” would not be unacceptable. The Basel-Vatican manuscript reads *gesserit*, “he may have done.”] the nature of God had not been understood in the human being whom he had assumed while doing these things.

**37. He presents the Father as his living image.**—And therefore, rebuking them because, though he had done these things for so long, he had not been recognized, he says to those asking him to show them the Father: “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (ibid.). Here he does not mean bodily contemplation and the sight of fleshly eyes, but the sight of which he had spoken when he said: “Do you not say, ‘There are still four months, and harvest comes’? Behold, I say to you, lift up your eyes and look upon the fields, for they are white for harvest” (John 4:35). Neither the time nor the meaning of fields whitening for harvest permits anything earthly and bodily to be understood here. Rather, he commanded the eyes of understanding to be raised for beholding the blessedness of perfect fruits; and now, in saying, “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father,” he speaks in the same manner.

For what is fleshly from the virgin’s childbirth does not assist in contemplating in him God’s form and image; nor is the appearance of the assumed human being an illustration by which the nature of the incorporeal God is seen. But God is recognized in him—if, indeed, he is recognized by those to whom he has made himself known—through the power of nature; and the understood God the Son makes it possible that the Father also be understood. For he is image in such a way that he does not differ in kind, but signifies his source. Other images, indeed, reproduce the forms of those whose images they are made from diverse metals, [Note: [Col. 0230C] Or pigments.] pigments, materials, or arts. But, in order to be true images, can inanimate things be made equal to living things, or painted, sculpted, or cast things to things naturally born?

But the Son is the Father’s image not in this fashion—not after their likeness—because he is the living image of the Living One; and, born from him, he has no diversity of nature and in no respect possesses differently the power of that nature [Note: [Col. 0231D] Paris has “in which.” The other books better have “from which,” namely, from which he is or subsists, not different.] from which he is not different. Therefore his being image has this effect: the birth of the only-begotten God signifies God the Father; and it signifies him in such a way that he himself is the form and image of the invisible God, and thereby [Note: [Col. 0231C] “Does not lose.” Shortly afterward: “does not lack the power of nature.”] does not lose the united likeness of nature [206], because he does not lack the power of nature.

**38. In God’s words, neither is God solitary nor is the Son unlike.**—Accordingly, this is the meaning of: “Have I been with you so long, and you do not know me, Philip? Whoever has seen me has seen [Col. 0231B] the Father also. How can you say, ‘Show us the Father’? Do you not believe me that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?” (John 14:9–10). No speech about divine things has been left to human utterance other than the word of God; all else is narrow, confined, hampered, and obscure. If anyone wishes to show this in words other than those in which God has spoken it, either he himself does not understand or he leaves those who read him without understanding.

When asked to show the Father, the Lord said: “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father.” To alter this is the work of antichrist; to deny it is the work of a Jew; not to know it is the work of a pagan. But perhaps the sense of understanding is at fault. [Note: [Col. 0231D] The editions read: “is at fault, if in faith”; corrected from the manuscripts.] Let there be fault in our faith if obscurity remains in God’s sayings. For the saying neither signifies one who is solitary, yet the declaration teaches an undifferentiated nature.

For when the Father is seen [Col. 0231C] [Note: [Col. 0232C] The Father in the Son.] in the Son, [Note: [Col. 0231D] The conjunction *and*, upon which the force of the argument against the Sabellians especially depends, omitted in the common editions, is restored from the manuscripts.] he can be neither solitary nor unlike; because through this one that one is seen; because, in the profession of the mystery, they are not not one, nor is either one alone. And I ask what the Lord is thought to have signified when he says: “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father.” You do not grasp the union where the addition of the Father’s name is marked by the conjunction itself. For when “the Father also” is said, the notion of one solitary and unique person is excluded. What remains, then, except that through the united likeness of nature the Father is seen through the Son? And lest this be left uncertain for our faith, the Lord added: “How can you say, ‘Show us the Father’?” [Col. 0232A] For what need remained either to be ignorant of the Father or to show him to those ignorant, when the Father had been seen in the Son?

### 39. The Father Is Seen in the Son through the Property of Nature. Against Sabellius. Against Arius. The Father and the Son Are in Each Other.

But he is seen so truly through the property of nature—since the Begotten and the Begetter are one by indistinguishableness and in the kind of truth—that this saying of the Lord follows: “Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father in me?” (ibid., 10). We cannot teach in any words other than those of the Son that the Father and the Son are inseparable through natural likeness.

For here the Son, who is the way and the truth and the life, does not play theatrical mimes by changing names and forms: calling himself the Son of God in the assumed man, but God the Father in his nature; nor does he, one and alone, falsely represent himself now as someone else by a personal change. Therefore he is not himself solitary, now a son to himself, now professing himself to be his own father, and introducing the names of natures while nature has ceased.

The simplicity of the words here is otherwise: the Father is Father, and the Son is Son. But in these names and realities there is nothing new in itself, nothing different, and nothing alien.

[Note: The phrase “in itself,” referring to nature, has been added on the authority of the manuscripts. Shortly before, the Corbie codex reads “but in all these realities,” incorrectly.]

For the truth of nature retains its proper character: that what is from God is God, and that birth is neither diminution nor diversity.

[Note: The editions of Badius and Erasmus read, “nor is birth a diminution, nor diversity”; the Lyons and Paris editions, “nor is change birth, nor diversity.” The manuscripts correct the text. By these words Arius is refuted, since he proclaimed Christ either of a different substance or at least of an inferior and diminished divinity. See above, section 6.]

For the Son does not subsist in a nature external to and unlike God the Father; nor does the Father, by the birth of the Only-Begotten, acquire something alien to himself, but rather has generously bestowed all that is his without loss.

[Note: One Colbert manuscript reads “through birth”; another Sorbonne manuscript, “by birth.”]

Thus the nature of God does not lack anything, since God is God from no other source than God; nor does he differ from God, since he himself is nothing other than God. For the birth of God consists in the Son; and through birth the nature of God has not lost from itself what it is as God.

[Note: The Badius and Erasmus editions read “the nature of God is”; more correctly the Lyons and Paris editions, with the manuscripts, read “from itself.” That is: the Father, communicating his own nature to the Son, did not lose what he is from himself. The Father, as unbegotten and the source of all divinity, is the nature of God from himself; the Son, obtaining it from the Father, may be called the nature of God from another. In this manner of speaking, see above, section 17: “When the nature of God had been established in the nature of God,” that is, when the Son had been born from the Father.]

Therefore the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father: God in God. This is not by a conjunction of two corresponding kinds, nor by an implanted nature of a more capacious substance. For, by bodily necessity, things outside cannot become internal to the things that contain them. Rather, it is through the birth of the living nature from the living: the reality does not differ; birth does not degenerate from the nature of God; God is born from God into God, not as something other than God. Nothing in them is new, nothing alien, nothing separable. It is impious to believe in two gods in the Father and the Son; it is sacrilegious to proclaim the Father and the Son a solitary God; it is blasphemous to deny that God from God is one in likeness of kind.

### 40. They Are Neither Different Nor One Person: the Son Speaks, Yet Not from Himself; the Father Works, Yet through the Son in Whom He Abides.

And lest evangelical faith should receive this mystery as doubtful and ambiguous, the Lord followed this order in his teaching: “Do you not believe me, that I am in the Father and the Father in me? The words which I speak to you, I do not speak from myself; but the Father, who abides in me, himself does his works” (John 14:10).

By what other words, I ask, could the property of nature in the Father and the Son be demonstrated, or can it be demonstrated, than by these very words—while in all things the meaning of birth takes precedence? For when he says, “The words which I speak to you, I do not speak from myself,” he did not remove his person, deny that he was the Son, or conceal within himself the nature of the Father’s power. For while he himself speaks—designated by the pronoun “I”—he speaks while remaining in his substance; but while he does not speak from himself, he testifies within himself to his birth as God from God the Father.

He himself is in an inseparable and not-dissimilar unity of nature with him. Though he speaks from the Father, he nevertheless himself speaks. For he who does not speak from himself and yet speaks cannot fail to exist while he speaks; and, in not speaking from himself, he shows that what he speaks is not his alone.

For he added: “But the Father, who abides in me, himself does his works.” That the Father abides in the Son does not belong to one solitary and single person; that the Father works through the Son does not belong to one different or external. Just as it does not belong to one person that he does not speak from himself what he speaks, so neither does speaking through the speaker belong to one alien and separable. Rather, this is the mystery of those who are one.

[Note: “Who are both.”]

[Note: Thus the better Colbert manuscript, with the German manuscript. Others read: “who are one, who are both not different, except that in the Martigny manuscript [the text reads] ‘and who are both,’ etc.”]

And the two are not different, since through the property of nature they are in each other. Their unity is this: the one who speaks does not speak from himself; nor does the one who does not speak from himself fail to speak. And because he had taught that the Father in himself both speaks and works, he established faith in this perfect unity by saying: “But the Father, who abides in me, himself does his works. Believe me, that I am in the Father and the Father in me; or else believe because of the works themselves” (ibid., 11). The Father works in the Son; but the Son too performs the Father’s work.

[Col. 0233D]

### 41. Christ Demands Faith in His Divine Birth and Nature. It Is Proper to the Only-Begotten Both to Inhere and to Subsist Simultaneously.

Therefore, lest the Father should be believed to be in the Son and to work merely through the efficacy of power, rather than through the property of nature according to birth, he says: “Believe me, that I am in the Father and the Father in me” (ibid., 11).

What, I ask, is this: “Believe me”? Certainly it refers to what had been said: “Show us the Father.” Faith is confirmed by the command to believe—namely, that faith which had asked for the Father to be shown to it.

[Note: Erasmus, Lyons, and Paris read “by which”; “which,” with Badius and the manuscripts, seemed preferable. In the older manuscripts “had asked” occurs immediately afterward, not “had demanded.”]

For it was not enough to have said, “He who has seen me has seen the Father,” unless he extended our understanding so far that, while we recognize the Father in the Son, we nevertheless remember that the Son is in the Father. Otherwise one might suppose a transfusion of one into the other, rather than the unity of the same nature in each through generation and birth.

Therefore the Lord wills that he be believed, lest perhaps the consciousness of faith be endangered through the economy of the assumed man. Certainly, if flesh, body, and suffering bring any ambiguity, let the works at least be believed: that God is in God, God is from God, and they are one—since by the power of nature each is in the other, and neither is without the other; since the Father loses none of his own things in the Son, and the Son receives wholly from the Father what he is as Son.

This is not the condition of bodily natures: that they should be in each other, that they should possess the perfect unity of a subsisting nature, that the abiding birth of the Only-Begotten should be inseparable from the truth of the Father’s divinity. This belongs properly to God the Only-Begotten alone; this faith belongs to the mystery of true birth; and this is the work of spiritual power: that to be and to be in are not different.

[Note: Badius and Erasmus read “special,” less well, since these statements are contrasted with the words immediately preceding: “This is not the condition of bodily natures.”]

But this “being in” is not one thing in another, as a body in a body. Rather, it is to be and subsist in such a manner that one is in that which subsists; and to be in in such a manner that he himself also subsists. For each subsists, and thereby neither is without the other, since the nature of the subsisting one according to generation and birth is not different.

[Note: In the Paris edition the particle *dum* (“since”) is absent. Shortly afterward, Badius and Erasmus read “subsisting.” Other books better read “of the subsisting [one],” supply “of both”: that is, since the nature of the one who subsists according to generation, or as begetter, is not different from that of the one who subsists according to birth, or as begotten.]

Hence come the sayings: “I and the Father are one”; “He who has seen me has seen the Father”; and “I am in the Father and the Father in me” (John 10:29; 14:9, 11). For birth neither differs nor degenerates; the nature of birth completes the mystery of one divinity in Father and Son, since the Son of God is nothing other than God. Therefore the generation of the Only-Begotten is not reckoned as two gods: because, being born as the Son of God into God, he has displayed in himself the nature of God who begot him.

## BOOK EIGHTH

**211–212**

He defends the natural unity of the Son and the Father. The prologue argues that neither innocence without knowledge nor knowledge without innocence suffices for a bishop. Then the bishop, equally devout and learned, exposes the various stratagems and deceptive questions of the Arians for deceiving the simple.

Because they distort Christ’s words, “I and the Father are one,” into a mere agreement of will, they commonly support that interpretation by these other texts: “The soul and heart of the believers were one”; “He who plants and he who waters are one”; and “That they all may be one, as you, Father, are in me and I in you.” He contends that believers are one indeed through the one nature of one faith; that the planter and the waterer, insofar as through one baptism they become one reality, are also ministers of one regeneration; and finally, that Christ would have spoken altogether ineptly had he prayed “that they may be one” when he meant merely “that they may will one thing.”

He then explains how, through Christ as mediator, we are naturally one with the Father. He maintains that this is granted to us both through eternal glory, by which we receive the honor given to Christ by the Father; through the mystery of the Incarnation, by which he keeps the nature of our flesh most closely united to himself; and especially through the sacrament of the Eucharist, by which we receive his true flesh and blood. Nor is the incredible calumny of the heretics left unmentioned: they commonly allege that those who reject this bare agreement of will affirm that the Father and the Son are at variance.

He next demonstrates their natural unity by several arguments. First, because the Holy Spirit, though proceeding from the Father, is nevertheless sent by and receives from the Son; and this because all things belonging to the Father are his. Second, because the Spirit of Father and Son is so one that the Spirit of Christ dwells in us when the Spirit of God is in us. Third, because those who offer worship to Christ are free from anathema, whereas worship of a creature is under a curse. Fourth, because one speaks in the Spirit of God who confesses Jesus truly to be Lord. Fifth, because the Apostle believed him to be Lord not in name only but in nature, since, owing to the unity of the Spirit, he ascribes the Church’s spiritual gifts now to the Father and now to the Lord. Sixth, because he who is one is truly Lord; or, if Christ, who is one Lord, is not God because God is one, then by the same reasoning the Father too must be denied to be Lord. Seventh, because he is called not only Lord but also God over all. Eighth, because although “God from whom are all things” and “Lord through whom are all things” indicate a distinction of persons, they nevertheless signify unity of efficient operation, power, and nature—so much so that elsewhere the Apostle also says of Christ that all things are from him, through him, and in him. Ninth, because, since he gives eternal life because the Father has sealed him, he must be the living and complete seal of him whose whole form he expresses in himself and whose whole power he contains. Tenth, he so fully expresses the Father’s entire form that the Apostle proclaims him to be in the form of God, in which he is equal to God. Eleventh, because he is the image of the invisible God and therefore neither visible, corporeal, nor finite.

Nor can it be said that this character of image consists in some invisible quality rather than in nature. Paul confirms that it must be placed in power and unity of nature when he adds that all things were created and reconciled through Christ and in Christ, and that the Father reconciles in Christ who reconciles. Finally, he in whom the fullness of divinity dwells bodily—that is, truly and substantially—cannot fail to possess what God is and consequently is one God with him. Thus throughout these arguments he demonstrates the natural unity of the Son with the Father while at the same time maintaining the distinction of persons.

### 1. A Bishop Must Be Both Devout and Learned. Why a Bishop Must Be Good and Learned. Paul Foresees Those Whom a Bishop Must Refute.

The blessed apostle Paul, laying down the pattern for appointing a bishop—

[Note: “Establishing.”]

[Note: Badius and Erasmus, with the Basel-Vatican manuscript and a later Colbert manuscript, read *figens*, “establishing,” which at first seemed preferable.]

—and shaping by his precepts a new kind of man for the Church, taught that this was, as it were, the sum of the virtues perfected in him, saying: “Holding fast the word according to the doctrine of faith, that he may be able to exhort in sound doctrine and refute those who contradict. For there are many unruly, vain talkers and deceivers” (Titus 1:9).

[Note: Erasmus deleted the particle “and” here and below, although it is found in Badius and in all manuscripts, as in the Greek text.]

For he indicates that the things proper to discipline and morals are useful for the worthiness of the priesthood, provided that these other things necessary for the knowledge required to teach and defend the faith are not lacking among the rest. For it is not immediately the mark of a good and useful priest either merely to act innocently or merely to preach knowingly. The innocent man benefits only himself unless he is learned; and the learned man has no authority for his teaching unless he is innocent.

The apostolic discourse does not merely form a man for worldly life through precepts of uprightness and virtue, nor again does it make him, by knowledge of doctrine, a scribe of the synagogue for the Law. Rather, it fashions a perfect leader of the Church by the complete benefits of the greatest virtues, so that his life may be adorned by teaching and his teaching by life.

Finally, he instructed Titus himself, to whom this discourse was addressed, by such a decree for the perfecting of religion: “In all things showing yourself an example of good works, teaching the sound word with reverence, irreproachable; that the adversary may be ashamed, having nothing shameful or evil to say of us” (Titus 2:7–8).

[Note: The Basel-Vatican manuscript reads, “by a saying of this sort.”]

This teacher of the Gentiles, the chosen teacher of the Church, speaking from the consciousness of Christ dwelling and speaking within him, did not fail to know that contagious diseased speech would spread and that the corruption of pestilential doctrine would rage against the health of faithful words. Plunging the plague of its impious understanding down to the very seat of the soul, it would creep onward in a deep evil.

[Note: The Lyons and Paris editions read “light.” The manuscripts more correctly read *luem*, “plague”; Badius and Erasmus had printed *virus*, “poison,” in its place.]

For of such people he says: “Their word spreads like a cancer” (2 Timothy 2:17), infecting the health of a mind pervaded by the ever-secret and creeping contagion.

[Note: “Pervaded.”]

[Note: The Vatican, Basel, and Carnot manuscripts read *perversae*, “perverse”; the Martigny, Corbie, and other manuscripts, with Badius, read *persuasae*, “persuaded.” *Pervasae*, “pervaded,” found in the Colbert manuscript and very many other reliable manuscripts, must certainly be retained.]

For this reason he wished sound doctrine, consciousness of faith, and skill in exhortation to be present in a bishop, prevailing against impious, deceitful, and insane contradictions.

[Note: The printed editions read “resisting.” From the very ancient Vatican, Basel, Colbert, and Carnot manuscripts, and from the Corbie manuscript in an old hand—whose agreement must carry the greatest authority—we prefer “prevailing,” supply “the victory”: that is, doctrine which conquers and overcomes opponents. This reading is supported by Book XII, section 19, where Hilary requires in a pastor that knowledge which surpasses the knowledge of the world’s wise: “as great as is the distinction between divine and human things, so greatly should heavenly reason in Christ’s pastors surpass earthly pursuits.”]

For there are many who, while pretending faith, are not subject to faith. They establish faith for themselves rather than receive it, puffed up by the emptiness of human thought, because they think what they wish and refuse to think what is true. Yet this is the truth of wisdom: sometimes to think what one does not wish. This wisdom of the will is followed by foolish speech, because what is foolishly thought must also be foolishly preached. And how great an evil is foolish preaching for its hearers, when they are seduced into an opinion of folly under the appearance of wisdom!

Therefore the Apostle set out this order concerning them: “For there are many unruly, vain talkers and deceivers.” Thus one must oppose insolent impiety, empty-talking insolence, and seducing empty talk; and one must oppose them through sound doctrine, truth of faith, and sincerity of words, so that there may be sincerity of truth and truth of soundness.

### 2. Hilary Feels That This Time Has Come upon Him. What He Has Already Accomplished. The Method He Follows against Heretics.

The reason, then, why I now recall this apostolic sentence is that men perverted in mind, deceptive in profession, empty in hope, and venomous in speech impose upon us the necessity of opposition. Under an appearance of religion they insinuate deadly doctrines, diseased understandings, and corrupt wills into the simplicity of their hearers. They do this by setting aside the sincerity of apostolic preaching, so that Father may not be Father, Son may not be Son, God may not be God, and faith may not be faith.

Resisting their insane lies, we have now extended the argument of our reply so far that, after demonstrating from the Law that God is God and God is from God (Book IV), then showing from evangelical and apostolic teaching the perfect and true birth of God the Only-Begotten (Book VI), we finally taught in the same course of our exposition (Book VII) that the Son of God is true God and of a nature indistinguishable from the Father. Thus the faith of the Church confesses neither a solitary God nor two gods: for neither does God’s birth permit a solitary God, nor does perfect birth allow the names of diverse natures in two gods.

In refuting their vain talk, we have a twofold concern. First, we must teach what is holy, perfect, and sound, so that our discourse may not wander through turns and windings and emerge from devious, wandering passages, seeking truth rather than displaying it. Next, we must show that the very sophistries by which they adapt empty and deceptive opinions to an attractive appearance of truth are ridiculous and inept to every conscience. For it is not enough for us to have taught what is devout, unless, through the refutation of what is impious, it is understood that these things are supremely devout.

### 3. Heretics Spend More Care in Introducing Falsehood than Catholics Do in Teaching Truth. Questions by Which They Entrap the Faith of the Simple.

Just as it is the nature and earnestness of good and prudent persons to prepare themselves wholly, whether in resources or in time, for attaining some blessed hope, lest their readiness prove in any respect less than expectation, so it is the greatest concern of those made mad by heretical frenzy to labor with all the ingenuity of their impiety against the truth of devout faith: so that, in opposition to the religious, they may prevail in being irreligious; that by the despair of their own life they may be more powerful than our hope of life; and that they may devote more thought to falsehood than we devote teaching to truth.

[Note: An old Colbert manuscript and one Sorbonne manuscript have in the margin, “that they may vindicate themselves as irreligious.” More correctly other manuscripts read, “that they may prevail in being irreligious,” that is, prevail through zeal for impiety. Describing the Arians’ anxious cunning in spreading their heresy, Athanasius, *Oration 2 against the Arians*, p. 329, says that they run about the marketplace, now asking a young girl: “Did he who is make that which did not exist from what did not exist, or that which existed?” and now questioning little women: “Did you have a son before you gave birth? But just as you did not have him, so the Son of God was not before he was begotten.”]

Against the devout confessions of our faith they have elaborated these objections of their impious unbelief. First they ask whether God is one for us in faith; then they add whether Christ too is God; finally, whether the Father is greater than the Son. Thus, when they hear that one God is confessed, they use this to maintain that Christ is not God. For they do not ask of the Son whether he is God; rather, by questioning about Christ, they seek only that he may not be Son. They entrap the person of simple faith in order to drive him, through faith in one God, from confessing Christ as God, since God will no longer be one if Christ also must be confessed as God.

[Note: The Basel-Vatican manuscript reads “to question.” The whole phrase should thus be rendered: “but in questioning about Christ they seek only that he may not be Son.” The Arians feared openly denying Christ’s divinity even in Augustine’s time. Speaking of them in *Against Maximinus*, I.16, Augustine says: “God is also Son, which you too wish; God is also the Holy Spirit, although you do not wish it.” Since the discourse which he undertook to refute began: “Our Lord Jesus Christ, God Only-Begotten,” etc., he begins its refutation: “I answer in this discourse the preceding argument of those who indeed confess our Lord Jesus Christ to be God,” etc. Thus they assailed Christ’s divinity only indirectly. Faith in him had been so implanted in the minds of all believers.]

Then, with how great a subtlety of worldly ingenuity they argue when they say: “If he is one, whoever else may appear to exist will no longer be. But if another exists, this one will no longer be one; for nature does not allow that, where another is, there should be one—or that where one is, another should be.”

[Note: In the Martigny manuscripts: “Or if one is, another is.” Then: “and afterward, when they have obtained this as though by an easier way.”]

[Note: The manuscripts read: “or if one is, another is.”]

After they have deceived the ease with which the believer and hearer accepts this artful assertion, they adapt this point—which they think they have now obtained by an easier path—that Christ is God by name rather than by nature. Thus the general name “God,” when applied to him, does not destroy the faith in the one God, which alone is true. And therefore the Father is greater than the Son: since their natures differ, and since there is only one God, the Father is greater by the property of nature. The Son is here called Son, a creation subsisting through God’s will, because he is less than the Father; and he is not God, because the one God does not allow another God to exist. Whoever is less must necessarily be alien in nature from him who is greater than he.

[Note: The printed editions and many manuscripts omit the verb “adapt” together with the following relative “which.” It is found, however, in the Basel-Vatican manuscript, two Colbert manuscripts, and one Sorbonne manuscript. Yet we would prefer “seek to entrap,” in the sense in which Ambrose, in Letter 25, section 4, to Studius wrote: “When the Jews had found the adulterous woman, they presented her to the Savior, seeking to entrap him, so that if he acquitted her he might seem to be dissolving the Law.”]

How ridiculous they are in this when they prescribe limits to God by asserting that nothing can be born from one, because the birth of all things comes from the union of two; and that God, being unchangeable, cannot grant any birth from himself to one being born, because that which does not change cannot be subject to increase, nor can the nature of one who is solitary and single possess in itself the condition of generating.

[Note: Their own words on this point are found in Book III, section 8. What Eudoxius expressed far more crudely on the matter is found in the book *On the Councils*, section 13.]

### 4. The Catholic Faith Thus Far Maintained Is Confirmed Both by Common Understanding and by the Sayings of the Lord.

But we, having attained evangelical and apostolic faith through spiritual teachings, and pursuing the hope of blessed eternity in the confession of Father and Son, have demonstrated from the Law the mystery of God and God. Without exceeding faith in one God, yet without failing to proclaim Christ also as God, we adopted from the Gospels this order in our answer: that we might teach the true birth of God the Only-Begotten from God the Father. Through this birth he would be true God and not alien from the nature of the one true God. Thus he could neither be denied to be God nor called another God: birth would establish that he is God, while the nature in him of the one God from God would not separate him into another God.

Although common understanding itself urged us to this conclusion—that those whose being does not differ in kind cannot have the same name of nature and yet not be one—we nevertheless chose to show it by the Lord’s own declarations.

[Note: The printed editions read “our” in place of “the Lord’s.”]

For when he had often indicated the one God of our faith and hope, he said, to confirm the mystery of one God by professing and proving himself also God: “I and the Father are one”; “If you know me, you know my Father also”; “He who has seen me has seen the Father”; “The Father who abides in me himself does his works”; and “Believe me, that the Father is in me and I in the Father; but if not, believe at least because of the works themselves” (John 10:30; 14:7, 9–12).

He expressed his birth in the name “Father”; he teaches that the Father is known when he himself is known. He confesses unity of nature when the Father is seen in seeing him. He testifies that he is inseparable from the Father when the Father abides in him. He possesses the confidence of consciousness when he asks that his sayings be believed because of the working of power.

[Note: We initially conjectured that the particle “when,” supported by two Colbert manuscripts, should be added here, so that this sentence might be joined with the preceding one. Yet both may reasonably be understood as independent: the first corresponds to the words, “I and the Father are one”; the other to the following: “If you know me, you know the Father,” etc.]

Thus, in this most blessed faith of perfect birth, every error both of two gods and of a solitary God is extinguished. For he who is one [with another] is not one person; and he who is not one person does not differ from him who is in such a way as to make the two not one.

### 5. “I AND THE FATHER ARE ONE”: They Explain It as Unity of Agreement; Their Arguments.

Although heretics cannot deny these things, since they are stated and understood so absolutely, they corrupt them—things that must be denied, according to their absurd lie of impiety.

[Note: The printed editions read “by denying,” which conflicts with the immediately preceding words, “they cannot deny.” The manuscripts more correctly read “to be denied,” that is, things which they may subsequently deny.]

They attempt to refer the saying, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), to a harmonious agreement, so that their unity may be one of will rather than nature. That is, they are one not through what they are, but through willing the same thing.

[Note: The printed editions read “the same”; it is absent from the manuscripts.]

They apply to this defense the text in the Acts of the Apostles: “Now the multitude of believers were one soul and heart” (Acts 4:32), so that the diversity of souls and hearts might be united into one heart and one soul by agreement of the same will.

[Note: The editions, except Paris, read “to this their definition.”]

[Note: The better manuscripts consistently read, in accordance with the Greek, “one soul”; the printed editions read “one soul,” and afterward, “one soul through agreement.”]

Or they appeal to what is written to the Corinthians: “He who plants and he who waters are one” (1 Corinthians 3:8), so that, because their ministry does not differ with respect to salvation and the advancement of the same sacrament, the two possess unity of will. Or they use the Lord’s words when, asking the Father for the salvation of the nations which would believe in him, he said: “I pray not for these only, but also for those who shall believe in me through their word, that all may be one, as you, Father, are in me and I in you, that they also may be in us” (John 17:20–21). Since human beings cannot be poured back into God, nor can they come together into one undifferentiated heap, they say that their oneness consists in unity of will: all do what pleases God, and they join together through dispositions of mind not at variance with one another. Thus they are one not by nature, but by will.

[Note: The Basel-Vatican manuscript reads “that they may be one in me.” Shortly afterward Badius and Erasmus read “that they too may be one.” Although “one” is not found in the manuscripts, Hilary understood it as though it were, as is clear from section 11.]

### 6. The Folly of the Arians.

Whoever does not know God plainly does not know how to be wise. Since Christ is wisdom, whoever either does not know Christ or hears him must necessarily be outside wisdom. Such are these people: they wish the Lord of majesty, the King of the ages, and God the Only-Begotten to be a creature of God rather than Son. Though they lie foolishly, they reason still more foolishly in defense of their lie. For, extending for a little while further the consideration of the property of unity which is in God the Father and God the Son, they must be refuted from the very texts they themselves use.

### 7. The Unity of Believers Is Natural through the Nature of One Faith. Believers Are One through the Unity of the Sacraments.

For those whose soul and heart were one—I ask whether they were one through faith in God. Certainly through faith; for by faith the soul and heart of all were one. And I ask whether faith is one or another. It is certainly one, since the Apostle himself proclaims one faith, just as one Lord, one baptism, one hope, and one God (Ephesians 4:4–5).

[Note: The Corbie manuscript and certain others here add, “and one Spirit.”]

If, then, all were one through faith—that is, through the nature of one faith—how do you fail to understand in them a natural unity, when they are one through the nature of one faith? For all had been reborn to innocence, immortality, knowledge of God, and faith in hope.

[Note: An ancient Colbert manuscript reads “born.”]

[Note: Thus the older manuscripts. The printed editions read “to the hope of faith.” They then added, “and these things cannot,” omitting the “if” found in all manuscripts.]

If these things cannot be different among themselves—because hope is one, God is one, Lord is one, and the baptism of regeneration is one—then, if these are one by agreement rather than by nature, attribute unity of will also to those reborn into them. But if the regenerate are in the nature of one life and eternity, through which their soul and heart are one, then unity of agreement ceases in those who are one in the nature of the same regeneration.

[Note: The Vatican, Basel, and Martigny manuscripts add here, “as we have said.”]

### 8. Paul’s Statement on This Matter.

We do not speak our own ideas, nor do we construct invented claims from these passages by corrupting their sense in order to mock the ears of our hearers. Rather, holding to the pattern of sound doctrine, we think and preach what is sincere. For the Apostle teaches that this unity of believers arises from the nature of the sacraments, writing to the Galatians: “For as many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ. There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is neither male nor female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus” (Galatians 3:27–28).

[Note: The Vatican-Basel manuscript reads “invented.” Shortly afterward the printed editions read “of the faithful God”; “God” is absent from the manuscripts.]

When they are one amid so great a diversity of nations, social conditions, and sexes, is this through agreement of will, or through unity of sacrament—because their baptism is one and all have put on the one Christ? What place, then, has harmony of minds here, when they are one through putting on the one Christ by the nature of the one baptism?

### 9. He Who Plants and He Who Waters Are One by Nature

Or, since he who plants and he who waters are one, are they not one for this reason: that, being themselves reborn in the one baptism, they are one administration of the one baptism that regenerates? Are they not doing the same thing? Are they not one in the one thing? Therefore, those who are one through the same reality are also one by nature, not merely by will: for they themselves have become the same thing, and are ministers of the same thing and operation.

[Note: The printed editions read: “because they, reborn in the one baptism, are… one administration.” The reading is restored from the agreement of the manuscripts: “they themselves… reborn”; and from the Colbert and German manuscripts, “are an administration,” not “is an administration.” Hence he who plants and he who waters possess a twofold unity: that of the sacrament, because they are reborn in one baptism; and, in addition, that of instrumentality in administering the same sacrament. Thus theirs is not mere unanimity of will. Augustine, *Conference with Maximinus*, no. 14, where he takes this as certain: “When it is said, ‘they are one,’ even if it is not said in what respect they are one, one substance is understood,” offers this sole answer to the passage cited: “We read, ‘He who plants and he who waters are one’; but both were men, of the same substance, not of different substances.”]

[Note: In the Carthusian manuscript, “as of the same,” less well; although it subsequently has “and are also ministers in the others.” For it is customary with Hilary, when two clauses are joined by “and,” not to maintain the same verbal construction. The printed editions nevertheless preferred “they are ministers.”]

### 10. Folly Betrays Itself While Opposing Truth. No Hope for Perverted Faith. The Merit of Simplicity

The contradiction of fools always serves to demonstrate their folly: for, while the truth is firm and immovable, it is necessary that the things which are contrived against it by the ingenuity of the foolish or by perverted interpretation should be understood to be both false and foolish.

For heretics, striving to deceive by the saying, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), lest unity of nature and an undifferentiated substance of divinity should be believed in them, but rather that they were one through mutual love and harmony of wills, brought forward, as we have shown above, an example of this unity even from the Lord’s words: “That they may all be one, as You, Father, are in Me and I in You, that they also may be in Us” (John 17:21).

Whoever is outside faith in the Gospel promises is outside those promises; and the sin of impious interpretation has destroyed simple hope. For there is more reward than pardon in not knowing what one believes: because the greatest recompense of faith is to hope for what one does not know. But it is madness of the utmost impiety either not to believe what has been understood or to have corrupted one’s understanding of what ought to be believed.

[Note: The Leipzig and Paris editions read “by sin,” against the authority of the Baden, Erasmus, and manuscript witnesses. This is the sin of those who corrupt the simple understanding of the thing to be believed, wickedly substituting a false one. Then “simple hope,” that is, the hope of simple faith lacking knowledge, concerning which we have written in Psalm 113, letter 10, no. 12: “There is, however, some greater advantage of knowledge in action than of faith, because faith has the merit of obedience but does not possess the confidence of known truth… He who believes may not know what he believes; but he who has already known cannot, after attaining knowledge, fail to believe what he has known.”]

### 11. Christ Would Have Spoken Improperly of Unanimity If He Had Said “That They May Be One”

Although impiety may distort the sense of its own interpretation, the meaning of the words cannot fail to be evident. The Lord prays to the Father that those who will believe in Him may be one; and that, just as He is in the Father and the Father in Him, so all may be one in Them.

What equanimity, what unity of soul and heart through agreement of wills, do you introduce here? For the abundance and propriety of language were available, so that, if will made them one, the Lord might have prayed thus: “Father, as We will to be one, so may they also will to be one, that we may all be one through harmony.” Or perhaps He who is the Word did not know the meaning of a word? He who is Truth did not know how to speak truth? He who is Wisdom erred in foolish speech? He who is Power was subject to such weakness that He could not express what He wished to be understood?

Certainly He spoke the true and uncorrupted mysteries of evangelical faith. Nor did He merely speak in order to signify something; He also taught for faith, saying: “That they may all be one, as You, Father, are in Me and I in You, that they also may be in Us.” The prayer is first for those concerning whom it is said, “That they may all be one”; then the advance of unity is shown by the example of unity, when He says: “As You, Father, are in Me and I in You, that they also may be in Us,” so that, as the Father is in the Son and the Son is in the Father, so through the form of this unity all might be one in the Father and the Son.

[Note: The printed editions read “and,” not “that.” Faustinus, adapting this argument of Hilary to Christ’s words, “I and the Father are one,” develops it copiously and subtly in chapter 1: “Did He who gave speech to the tongue not know how to speak? Did He fail to explain your meaning in fitting and proper words? Was He unable to say, ‘The Father and I will one thing’?—if, indeed, in this place He intended unity of will and not of divinity and substance.” And shortly afterward: “You, as grammarians, as though supplying for the inadequacy of the Lord’s utterance by changing the implied word, correct it and say that the word ‘are’ which He used must be understood as ‘will.’” He then observes that heretics speak inconsistently, since elsewhere they deny harmony of will to Christ because He said: “I came down from heaven, not to do My own will, but the will of the Father who sent Me” [John 6:38]. From this he adds: “How do you interpret the Father and Son as one in will, when, according to you, the Father’s and Son’s wills are different?” etc.]

[Note: In the printed editions here and shortly below: “that they themselves may be one.” “One” is consistently absent from the manuscripts.]

[Note: In the manuscripts, “that,” not “thus”: perhaps in imitation of the sacred text, in which first occurs “that they may all be one,” and again afterwards “that they also may be,” not “thus.” Augustine, *Conference with Maximinus*, no. 14, on this very form of unity: “He did not say, ‘That they and We may be one,’ but ‘That they may be one,’ united and fused, as it were, in their own nature and substance by harmonious equality, just as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one because of one and the same indivisible nature.” And in book I *Against Maximinus*, chapter 12: “Although He so often said, ‘That they may be one,’ nowhere did He say, ‘That they and We may be one,’ that is, that they may be one with Us; but He said either ‘in Us’ or ‘as We,’ that is, they according to their nature and We according to Ours. For He wished those who were one by nature to be perfected in that very fact in which they were one… unless we are in Him, we cannot exist at all.” Hilary goes on to explain how we may thereafter be one in God.]

### 12. The Glory Received from the Father and Given by the Son to Believers Enables Them to Be One

But because it belongs properly to the Father and Son alone by nature to be one—because God from God, and the Only-Begotten from the Unbegotten, cannot but be in the nature of His own origin, so that He who has been begotten subsists in the substance of His birth, and the birth of divinity does not possess a truth other or different from that from which it proceeded—the Lord, leaving us nothing ambiguous for faith, taught the nature of this complete unity throughout the whole ensuing discourse.

For what follows is this: “That the world may believe that You sent Me” (John 17:21). Therefore the world will believe that the Son was sent by the Father because all who will believe in Him will be one in the Father and the Son. And we are immediately taught how they shall be so: “And the glory which You gave Me I have given them” (ibid., 22).

And now I ask whether glory is the same thing as will, since will is a movement of the mind, while glory is either a nature, a form, or a dignity. Therefore the Son gave to all who would believe in Him the glory received from the Father—not, surely, will. For if will were given, faith would have no reward, since necessity imposed by a fixed will would compel faith in us. But He showed what the giving of the received glory accomplishes: “That they may be one, as We are one” (ibid.). For this reason, therefore, the received glory was given: that all might be one.

Thus all are one in glory, because no glory other than that which was received was given, nor was it given for any other reason than that all might be one. And since through the glory given to the Son and bestowed by the Son upon believers all are one, I ask how the Son can possess a glory different from the Father’s, when the Son’s glory draws all believers into unity with the Father’s glory.

This discourse may perhaps appear strange to human hope, but it will not be faithless. For although it is presumptuous to hope for this, it is irreligious not to have believed it, since the same One and the same is for us both the author of hope and of faith. We shall treat this more fully and extensively in its proper place. Meanwhile, even from the present discourse, we understand that this hope of ours is neither empty nor presumptuous. Therefore, through the glory received and given, all are one. I hold the faith and understand the cause of unity; but I do not yet grasp how the glory given accomplishes that all are one.

[Note: In one Vatican manuscript, “which, if it were so”: corrupt. One may ask why Hilary here denies that faith is given. But since below, no. 30, he lists faith among God’s gifts, it is probable that here he means only that faith is not imposed upon us by the necessity of a fixed will, but that we believe by free will. For, as he states more plainly in Psalm 65, no. 24, faith is the work of soul and heart, a matter of inward will. Augustine agrees: although in Letter 194 to Sixtus, no. 9, he demonstrates at length that faith is God’s gratuitous gift and reproves Vitalis for thinking otherwise in Letter 217, no. 29, yet in the same letter to Vitalis, no. 16, he willingly admits: “We know that those who believe in the Lord from their own heart do so by their own will and free choice.” In *On the Spirit and the Letter*, chapter 31, he says that faith is within one’s power, but that this power exists only from God; accordingly, in *Retractions*, book I, no. 3, he teaches that the will is from God, because He prepares the will, but from us because it does not occur unless we will. “Why one believes and another does not,” he asks in Letter 194, no. 10, “when both hear the same thing and, if a miracle happens before them, both see the same thing, is the depth of the riches of God’s wisdom and knowledge.” Although Hilary does not distinguish so explicitly what is from God and what from us, and considers only freedom of will, he denies that will is given insofar as this implies the necessity of a fixed will. His argument, then, is this: believers are one in the Father and Son through something given; but will, or agreement of will, is not given; therefore they are not one through agreement of will.]

[Note: The Leipzig and Paris editions read “that same one,” incorrectly and contrary to the authority of the manuscripts. Here we note in passing that above the word “to hope” is used of human and natural hope or expectation; but elsewhere the term “hope,” even where there is reference to “a discourse of human hope,” signifies indeed the hope of human beings, but one sustained by God’s promises rather than by human reasoning. Hence first it is called presumptuous to hope; afterwards the hope is not presumptuous.]

[Note: Thus the manuscripts with the Baden and Erasmus editions. Other editions read “more fully.”]

### 13. The Natural Unity of Believers in God Is Bestowed Through the Incarnation of the Word and the Sacrament of the Eucharist

But the Lord, leaving nothing uncertain to the consciousness of believers, taught the very result of this natural operation, saying: “That they may be one, as We are one: I in them and You in Me, that they may be perfected into one” (John 17:22–23).

I now ask those who insert a unity of will between Father and Son whether Christ is in us today through the truth of nature or through harmony of will. For if the Word truly became flesh, and we truly receive the flesh of the Word as the Lord’s food, how are we not to think that He remains in us naturally—He who, born as man, has assumed to Himself the nature of our flesh, now inseparable from Himself; and who has mingled the nature of His own flesh with the nature of eternity, under the sacrament of flesh to be communicated to us? For thus we are all one: because the Father is in Christ, and Christ is in us.

Therefore whoever denies that the Father is naturally in Christ must first deny either that he is naturally in Christ or that Christ naturally is in him; because the Father in Christ and Christ in us make us one in Them. Therefore, if Christ truly assumed the flesh of our body, and if that man who was born of Mary is truly Christ, and if we truly receive, under a mystery, the flesh of His body—then, because the Father is in Him and He is in us, we shall be one—how is a unity of will maintained, when the natural property, through the sacrament, is the sacrament of perfect unity?

[Note: Here a twofold argument is fused into one: first, from Christ’s incorporation with us, by which He truly assumed our nature; secondly, from the sacrament of the Eucharist, by which we truly receive His true flesh.]

[Note: That is, with the nature of divinity. Thus in Fragment 11, no. 32, where Hilary says that the Son is so immutable that, in assuming man, He brought glory to corruption rather than corruption to eternity. What is “corruption” except human nature, and what is “eternity” except divine nature? The force of this word is evident in chapter 31 on Matthew, no. 1, where he argues against heretics who wished Christ’s divinity itself to have suffered: “as though eternity had assumed the nature of frailty.” Why he uses the word “eternity” to signify divinity is clear from chapter 23, no. 5. Scultetus vainly attempts to evade by these words Hilary’s eminent testimony concerning the Eucharist. Nor is he consistent with himself: first he wishes this to be merely a repetition of the preceding argument, namely, that only the unity which we obtain through sharing Christ’s glory is being demonstrated; but eventually, as though Hilary had said elsewhere, “We truly receive the flesh of the Word as the Lord’s food,” he interprets these words of the sacred Supper. Certainly the preceding and following context makes it perfectly clear that the discourse is no longer about Christ’s glory communicated to us, but about the sacrament of the Eucharist. By this twofold argument Christ is shown truly and naturally to be in us: first, because in the mystery of the Incarnation our flesh is in Him; secondly, because in the sacrament of the Eucharist His flesh is in us. And just as the proposition, “He who, born as man, assumed to Himself the nature of our flesh, now inseparable from Himself,” answers the first clause, “If the Word truly became flesh,” so the following proposition, “and mingled the nature of His own flesh with the nature of eternity, under the sacrament of flesh to be communicated to us,” answers the second clause, “and we truly receive the flesh of the Word as the Lord’s food.” This latter part clearly cannot refer to the mystery of assumed flesh; for, in assuming flesh, Christ did not mingle the nature of His flesh with the divine nature, but rather mingled the divine nature with the nature of our flesh, which He then began also to make His own. Does He, in the sacrament of the Eucharist, mingle the nature of His flesh with the divine nature, so that, receiving that flesh joined with divinity, through the mediation of that flesh we may be united with Christ’s divine substance, which is one and the same with the Father’s? This is what Hilary undertakes to prove. He takes it as certain and indubitable that in this sacrament we receive the nature and reality, not a figure, of Christ’s flesh. He calls Christ’s flesh in the Eucharist joined to divinity not only because reason makes this clear—for since that flesh is now inseparable from the Word, it cannot be given to us apart from Him—but also because he is moved by the authority of the divine Word, for it is written: “The flesh profits nothing; the Spirit is what gives life” [John 6:63]. It has already often been observed that by “Spirit” he customarily understands divinity. See Cyril of Alexandria, *Dialogue I on the Trinity*, p. 407, where he likewise shows from the sacrament of the Eucharist that we are one with Christ not merely by harmony of wills but by nature.]

[Note: We are naturally in Christ insofar as He assumed our flesh, just as He is naturally in us when we receive His flesh.]

[Note: The Paris text very incorrectly reads “because He was born of Mary”; for immediately afterward, “Christ is” has the same meaning as “God is,” as is clear from the following: “If that man who was born of Mary is truly God,” it follows that the Father is in Him.]

[Note: That is, veiled beneath mystical species. I do not know how Scultetus thinks that these words have evaded the force of the preceding phrase, “we truly receive the flesh of the Word as the Lord’s food.” For how does “under a mystery” conflict with the Church, which has never believed Christ’s flesh to be manifest in this sacrament? And what benefit is it to Scultetus that it is preached as being under a mystery, while nevertheless we truly receive the flesh of Christ’s body? Why does Hilary so insistently emphasize “truly” above, here, and below?]

[Note: This somewhat compressed statement may be explained thus: the natural property of the flesh, both received by us through the sacrament of the Incarnation and communicated to us through the sacrament of the Eucharist, is the sacrament and bond of our perfect unity, first and in itself with Christ and, through Him, with the Father.]

### 14. In This Sacrament We Receive Christ’s True Body

One must not speak of the things of God by human or worldly reasoning (see book IV, no. 14); nor should an alien and impious perversity of interpretation be forced upon the soundness of heavenly sayings by violent, shameless, and imprudent preaching. Let us read what has been written, and understand what we have read; then we shall perform the duty of perfect faith.

For unless we have learned from Him what we say concerning the natural reality of Christ in us, we speak foolishly and impiously. For He Himself says: “My flesh is truly food, and My blood is truly drink. He who eats My flesh and drinks My blood remains in Me, and I in him” (John 6:56–57). No room for doubt has been left concerning the reality of flesh and blood. For now, by the Lord’s own declaration and by our faith, it is truly flesh and truly blood. Received and drunk, these accomplish that we are in Christ and Christ is in us.

Is this not truth? Let it certainly not be true for those who deny that Christ Jesus is true God. Therefore He Himself is in us through the flesh, and we are in Him, while, together with Him, that which we are is in God.

[Note: Some manuscripts read “by violence,” and subsequently “and shameless”: these readings are also preferred by the printed editions, with the following words expressed so confusedly that “alien” is referred to “soundness.” Here the heretics are reproved who attempt to defend their errors either by human reasonings or by twisting Scripture to suit their opinions.]

[Note: “And shameless.”]

[Note: The Vatican Basel manuscript alone reads “difference”: wrongly. “Perversity” is opposed to “soundness.” The corrector of the Chartres manuscript wrote in the margin: “Throughout this entire chapter he expounds the reality of the Lord’s body and blood.” That manuscript, however, had been corrected more than seven hundred years ago, as is readily proved both from the handwriting of the second hand and from the ancient manuscript formerly of Fleury, now in the Colbert Library, no. 1194. In its first seven books this codex reproduces the Chartres manuscript so faithfully that it presents all and only the readings added there in the second revision.]

[Note: What does “by the Lord’s own declaration” mean except by Christ’s own words? And what does “by our faith” mean except by the faith of the Church, understanding the Lord’s words as they sound? From this it is clear that Hilary thought our faith should rest upon God’s words, and that God’s words should be explained by the faith of the Church; and that from both principles it is confirmed that in the Eucharist we receive Christ’s true flesh and true blood. He warns that any other interpretation of the words, “My flesh is truly food,” etc., is violent and imprudent.]

[Note: The Vatican Basel, Martin, Chartres, one Sorbonne, and two Colbert manuscripts—though not the older Colbert manuscript—read “while according to this”; they do not appear preferable to the other books. The phrase should be understood thus: while, together with Christ to whom we are joined, that which we are is in God the Father, with whom He is one.]

### 15. Our Perfect Unity with God Through Christ the Mediator

But He Himself testifies how we are in Him through the sacrament of the flesh and blood communicated to us, saying: “And this world no longer sees Me; but you shall see Me, because I live and you shall live; because I am in My Father, and you in Me, and I in you” (John 14:19, etc.).

If He had wished only unity of will to be understood, why did He set forth a certain order and progression for the completion of unity? Was it not so that, since He was in the Father through the nature of divinity, we, on the other hand, might be believed to be in Him through His bodily birth, and He again to be in us through the mystery of the sacraments; and thus perfect unity through the Mediator might be taught? For while we remain in Him, He remains in the Father; and while remaining in the Father, He remains in us. Thus we advance to unity with the Father, since we too are naturally in Him in whom He naturally is through birth, while He Himself naturally remains in us.

[Note: That is, through the body which, by being born of Mary, He took from us. Then, by “the mystery of the sacraments,” the Eucharist is plainly indicated, as Hilary consistently pursues his twofold argument.]

[Note: His meaning is this: since we were in Christ, who is naturally in the Father according to His eternal birth, through the flesh of ours which He assumed, and since that same Christ again naturally remains in us through the sacraments of His flesh and blood bestowed upon us, we advance to unity with the Father.]

### 16. How Natural This Unity Is. The Son’s Unity with the Father

How natural this unity in us is, He Himself testified thus: “He who eats My flesh and drinks My blood remains in Me, and I in him” (John 6:57). For no one will be in Him unless He Himself is in that person, having assumed into Himself only the flesh of the one who has received His own flesh.

But He had already taught above the sacrament of this perfect unity, saying: “As the living Father sent Me, and I live through the Father, so he who eats My flesh shall himself live through Me” (ibid., 58). Therefore He lives through the Father; and in the same manner in which He lives through the Father, we live through His flesh. For every comparison is made in order to provide a form for understanding, so that according to the proposed example we may attain the point under discussion.

Therefore this is the cause of our life: that we have Christ dwelling in us who are fleshly, through the flesh; and we shall live through Him under the same condition in which He lives through the Father.
