Therefore, if we live naturally through Him according to the flesh—that is, having received the nature of His flesh—how does He not naturally have the Father in Himself according to the Spirit, when He Himself lives through the Father?

Now He lives through the Father because birth did not bring Him an alien and different nature; because what He is, He is from the Father, yet He is not separated from the Father by any incidental dissimilarity of nature; because through birth He has the Father in Himself in the power of nature.

[Note: Since the Gospel passage cited below is later than the one just quoted from John 6, it is called “above” not in relation to that passage but in relation to the other passage from John 14:19. Next, the manuscripts restore “the living Father” instead of “the living [one].” The Vatican Basel manuscript then reads: “and I live because of the Father.” In Greek and Latin copies of John now in circulation, the reading is “and he who eats Me,” not “and he who eats My flesh.” The Martin manuscript adds: “and he himself lives in Me,” not “and he himself shall live through Me.” I would ask defenders of the Sacrament to weigh carefully what Hilary concludes from this Gospel passage. For he argues thus: Christ lives through the Father by receiving the Father’s nature, just as we live through Christ by receiving His flesh. Then he takes as a more familiar point, concerning which Arians would not dispute: we live through Christ by acquiring the nature of His flesh, so that through eating that flesh we have Christ, dwelling carnally in us who are fleshly, remaining carnally. Finally, against the Arians, he concludes the disputed point: therefore Christ too lives through the Father by receiving the Father’s very divine nature, so that the Father, according to the Spirit—that is, according to the divine nature given to Him—naturally remains in Him. Those who try to twist arguments so clear into another sense show either that they act in bad faith or at least how much the opinions of a prejudiced mind can prevail among men.]

[Note: “We shall live.”]

[Note: Previously the reading was “may attain.” The Verona manuscript more correctly has “may attain.”]

### 17. Summary

We have recalled these things because heretics, falsely claiming that there is only unity of will between Father and Son, used the example of our unity with God as though we were united to the Son, and through the Son to the Father, only by religious obedience and will, and as though no natural communion were granted through the sacrament of flesh and blood. Yet the mystery of true and natural unity must be proclaimed: both through the glory of the Son given to us; through the Son remaining carnally in us; and through our bodily and inseparable union in Him.

[Note: What was said in the preceding section—that through the benefit of the Eucharist we have Christ dwelling in us who are fleshly, through the flesh—is now stated more expressly: the Son remains carnally in us.]

### 18. The Unity of Son and Father Clearly Asserted in Scripture

Thus we have answered the madness of those raging only to expose the emptiness of their falsehood, lest they should deceive the unlearned through the error of a vain and ridiculous assertion. Besides, evangelical faith had no need of our answer. The Lord prayed for our unity with God; but He possesses His own unity and remains in it.

They are not one through the sacrament of an economy, but through the birth of nature, since God, in begetting Him from Himself, does not degrade Him in any respect. They are one: because what is not snatched from His hand is not snatched from the Father’s hand (John 10:28); because when He is known, the Father is known; because when He is seen, the Father is seen; because the Father dwelling in Him speaks what He speaks; because the Father works in Him who works; because He is in the Father and the Father is in Him (John 14:7, 9, 10, 12).

This is not granted by creation but by birth; not accomplished by will but by power; not spoken by unanimity but by nature. For to be created is not the same as to be born; to will is not the same as to be able; and to agree is not the same as to remain.

[Note: The Martin manuscript reads “these things,” which expresses more explicitly what was just said. Later, as in other older manuscripts, it has “unanimity” and “unanimity.”]

[Note: The Vatican Basel manuscript reads, “but birth,” a reading we do not approve.]

### 19. Unanimity Is Not Denied When Unity Is Affirmed. Plain Testimony to the Unity of Father and Son

Therefore we do not deny unanimity between the Father and the Son. For heretics commonly make this false accusation: because we do not admit mere agreement as sufficient for unity, they say that we affirm Father and Son to be discordant. But let them hear in what sense we do not deny unanimity. Father and Son are one in nature, glory, and power; and one and the same nature cannot will different things.

And let them hear further the Son Himself testifying to His unity of nature with the Father. For He says: “When that Advocate comes, whom I shall send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from My Father, He shall testify concerning Me” (John 15:26).

The Advocate will come; the Son will send Him from the Father; and He is the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father. Let every school of heretics sharpen the points of its ingenuity, and let it now seek what it can even falsely assert to the ignorant, and teach what it means that the Son sends from the Father. He who sends manifests His power in what He sends. But when He sends from the Father, what are we to understand: whether it is received, sent forth, or begotten? For one of these must necessarily be signified by what He is to send from the Father.

And He is to send from the Father that Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father. Therefore it is no longer a receiving where a procession has been shown. It remains for us to confirm our judgment: whether in this we should understand the going forth of one who subsists, or the procession of one begotten.

[Note: The Paris edition after Lipsius reads “to unanimity,” incorrectly and contrary to manuscript authority. For “to unity” means: for explaining the passages in which unity is commended.]

[Note: The printed editions read “among the ignorant”; the manuscripts more correctly have “for the ignorant,” that is, among the uninstructed and simple.]

[Note: “The going forth of one who subsists in Him.”]

[Note: Since the word “going forth” signifies a distinction between the one who goes out and that from which he goes out, the word “subsisting” is cautiously added in order that unity of nature may be affirmed of Him. This is illustrated by Cyril’s words, book II on John, chapter 3: “For the Son went forth from the Father into His own existence, although He is in Him according to nature.” What Cyril there calls “going forth,” he here signifies by “being sent.” Thus, for Cyril, to go forth and to be sent are not different. Moreover, it is characteristic of this going forth that it signifies no beginning of the one proceeding. Hence Hilary, book IV, no. 31, had said that the Son’s birth is fittingly expressed by this word: because He did not begin to exist from nothing, but went forth from One who remains; and “went forth” signifies birth—or procession distinguished from that from which one goes forth—not a beginning. Hilary does not state here whether we should regard the procession as that of one begotten. But since in book II, no. 1, he calls the Holy Spirit a gift, Augustine’s answer in book V of *On the Trinity*, chapter 14, may be used: “He went forth, not as one born, but as one given; and therefore He is not called Son.” Yet Hilary’s own judgment is clear in book XII, no. 54: “Knowing that the Only-Begotten was born from You, I shall nevertheless not call the Holy Spirit begotten.”]

20. It is not uncertain from whom the Holy Spirit is. What He receives from the Son, He also receives from the Father. Hence the Father and the Son are one in nature. — Nor on this point do I now impugn freedom of interpretation as to whether they think the Paraclete Spirit to be from the Father or from the Son. For the Lord has not left this uncertain; for in the same discourse He spoke as follows: “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. When that Spirit of truth comes, He will guide you into all truth. For He will not speak from Himself, but whatever He hears He will speak, and He will announce to you the things to come. He will glorify Me, because He will receive from what is Mine and announce it to you. All things whatever the Father has are Mine; therefore I said, ‘He will receive from what is Mine and announce it to you’” (John 16:12 ff.).

[Note: [Col. 0250D] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have “freedom.” From these and the following sayings of Hilary it might seem that a controversy concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit had already arisen at that time. For he plainly indicates that it is by no means uncertain to him that the Spirit is from the Father and the Son, although he is unwilling to dispute too much about the manner of speaking. It has already been observed, Book II, no. 4, note, that he calls the Son both giver and author of the Holy Spirit.]

[Note: [Col. 0250C] “The Holy Spirit.”]

Therefore He receives from the Son, who is also sent by Him and proceeds from the Father. And I ask whether receiving from the Son is the same thing as proceeding from the Father. But if a distinction is thought to exist between receiving from the Son and proceeding from the Father, surely receiving from the Son will be judged to be the same and one thing as receiving from the Father.

[Note: [Col. 0251D] The printed editions read “to differ in no respect.” More correctly, *in no respect* is absent from the manuscripts. The opponents are granted whatever they may wish, so that they may be refuted all the more invincibly.]

For the Lord Himself says: “Because He will receive from what is Mine and announce it to you. All things whatever the Father has are Mine; therefore I said, ‘He will receive from what is Mine and announce it to you’” (ibid., vv. 14–15). This which He will receive—whether it be power, strength, or teaching—the Son said would be received from Himself; and again He signifies that this same thing is to be received from the Father. For when He says that all things whatever the Father has are His, and that therefore He said that the Spirit would receive from what is His, He teaches that the Spirit receives from the Father, yet receives from Himself, because all things of the Father are His. This unity admits no diversity; nor does it differ from whom that is received which, given by the Father, is referred to as given by the Son.

[Col. 0251A] [Note: [Col. 0251C] “Into all truth.” Shortly after: “He speaks.” Later: “He will announce without you.”]

[Note: [Col. 0251D] Thus, in accordance with the Greek, the Vatican Basilica manuscript and the Martinian manuscript read, as do the others in Book II, no. 33; yet here they contain “into all truth.”]

Will unity of will be introduced here also? All things which the Father has are the Son’s, and all things which the Son has are the Father’s. For He Himself says: “All Mine are Yours, and Yours are Mine” (John 17:10). The place has not yet come for me to show why He said, “He will receive from what is Mine”; for this is an expression in the future tense, in which He is shown as about to receive. Certainly, for the present, He says that He will receive from Himself because all the Father’s things were His. Divide, if you can, the unity of this nature, and introduce some necessity of dissimilarity through which the Son may not be in unity of nature.

For the Spirit of truth proceeds from the Father; but He is sent from the Father by the Son.

[Note: [Col. 0251D] The printed editions read: “He is sent by the Son and from the Father.” In the Vatican Basilica manuscript, one Sorbonne manuscript, and another Colbert manuscript: “He will receive from the Son; He is sent from the Father.” In the Martinian manuscript: “He receives from the Son and is sent from the Father.” More correctly in many others: “He is sent from the Father by the Son,” undoubtedly referring to: “whom I shall send to you from the Father.” Hilary thus scrupulously derives all his statements concerning the Holy Spirit from Scripture.]

All things which are the Father’s are the Son’s; and therefore whatever He will receive, that Spirit who is to be sent will receive from the Son, because all things which are the Father’s are the Son’s.

[Note: [Col. 0251C] “He receives.”]

[Note: [Col. 0252D] The manuscripts read: “He receives.”]

Nature therefore retains its own law in all things; and the fact that the two are one is, in each, the signification of the same divinity through generation and birth, since the Son acknowledges that what the Spirit of truth will receive from the Father is to be given by Himself. Therefore heretical perversity must not be allowed liberty for an impious interpretation: namely, to refuse to confess that this saying of the Lord—that, because all things which are the Father’s are His, the Spirit of truth will therefore receive from Himself—must be referred to unity of nature.

21. The Spirit of God and of Christ is one. — Let him speak who is the vessel of election and teacher of the Gentiles, according to the understanding of truth already commended by the faith of the Roman people. For, wishing to teach unity of nature in the Father and the Son, he says (Rom. 8:9 ff.): “But you are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God is in you. But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to Him. But if Christ is in you, the body indeed is dead through sin, but the spirit is life through righteousness. But if the Spirit of Him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, He who raised Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies because of His Spirit who dwells in you.”

[Note: [Col. 0252C] “If indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you,” according to the Greek text.]

[Note: [Col. 0252D] In Book II, no. 29, along with several manuscripts and all editions, the reading is “if nevertheless.”]

[Col. 0252B] [Note: [Col. 0252D] The Carnotensis manuscript has “through sin”; and shortly after, “through righteousness.”]

[Note: [Col. 0252C] “Through justification.”]

[Note: [Col. 0252D] The printed editions read “raised Jesus,” against the manuscripts and the Greek text, as was already noted in Book II, no. 29. Shortly after, the old Colbert manuscript reads “His Spirit,” not “His own.”]

We are all spiritual, if the Spirit of God is in us. But this Spirit of God is also the Spirit of Christ. And although the Spirit of Christ is in us, nevertheless the Spirit in us is the Spirit of Him who raised Christ from the dead; and He who raised Christ from the dead will also make our mortal bodies alive because of His Spirit dwelling in us. Therefore we are made alive, because the Spirit of Christ dwells in us, through Him who raised Christ from the dead.

And though the Spirit of Him who raised Christ from the dead is in us, yet the Spirit in us is Christ’s; nor is the Spirit who is in us thereby not God’s Spirit.

[Col. 0252C] [Note: [Col. 0252D] Again, in the printed copies *then* was substituted for *nevertheless*.]

Distinguish, then, O heretic, the Spirit of Christ from the Spirit of God, and the Spirit of Christ raised from the dead from the Spirit of God who raises Christ from the dead—although the Spirit of Christ dwelling in us is the Spirit of God, and although the Spirit of Christ raised from the dead is nevertheless the Spirit of God who raises Christ from the dead.

22. Whether the Spirit of God is nature or a thing of nature. — And now I ask whether, in “the Spirit of God,” you think that nature or a thing of nature is signified. Nature is not the same as a thing of nature, just as a human being is not the same as what belongs to a human being, nor fire the same as what belongs to fire itself; and according to this distinction God is not the same as what belongs to God.

[Note: [Col. 0252D] For *indeed* is absent from the older manuscripts. The question here is whether by the name “Spirit of God” they wish to signify the Father’s own nature, or rather something indeed proper to Him but nevertheless distinct from Him. Thus in Book II, no. 32, the Holy Spirit is taught to be distinct from the Lord, because the Spirit is one thing and He whose Spirit it is another. But whichever they choose, Father and Son are shown to be of one nature, since the Spirit of Christ and of the Father is one and the same, and therefore is nature; and the Holy Spirit is as much Christ’s as the Father’s, and thus is a thing of one nature—that is, of those whose nature is one.]

[Col. 0253A]

23. At one time He signifies the Father, at another the Son. — For I remember that in “the Spirit of God” the Son of God is so signified that God the Father is understood to be shown in it, and that the designated Spirit of God can pertain to the manifestation of either; and that this is shown not only by prophetic but also by evangelical authority. For it is said: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon Me; therefore He anointed Me” (Luke 4:18); and again: “Behold My servant whom I chose, My beloved in whom My soul was well pleased; I shall put My Spirit upon Him” (Matt. 12:18). And the Lord Himself testifies concerning Himself: “But if I cast out demons in the Spirit of God, then indeed the kingdom of God has come upon you” (ibid., v. 28). These things appear unambiguously to signify either the Father or the Son, yet to manifest the power of nature.

[Note: [Col. 0253C] Namely, by the expression “Spirit of God.”]

[Col. 0253B] [Note: [Col. 0253C] In the Vatican Basilica manuscript, *to us* stands for *not*, and later, together with the Martinian manuscript, “they manifest” for “manifesting”: incorrectly. Here is first given the answer to the question raised: namely, that by the term *Spirit* the power, and consequently the nature, of Father and Son is signified; for the power of nature establishes truth, as we read in Book V, no. 3. Then it is immediately taught that God’s nature is called Spirit because it is supremely simple, and lest we think of God in bodily terms.]

[Note: [Col. 0253C] “They manifest.”]

24. Why both are called Spirit. — For I think that “Spirit of God” is said of each for this reason: lest we believe, according to bodily modes, that the Son is in the Father or the Father in the Son in such a way that God, remaining in one place, would seem to exist nowhere else than in Himself. For a human being, or anything else like him, when he is somewhere, is not elsewhere, because what is there is confined to where it is.

[Note: [Col. 0253D] That is, his nature is incapable of being everywhere. Nor should the more recent manuscripts be followed, in which it reads: “so that he may not be everywhere.”]

His nature is too weak for him, while standing in one place, to be everywhere. But God is living power of immeasurable might, present nowhere not at all and absent nowhere; through what belongs to Him He teaches that He is wholly present, and signifies that what belongs to Him is nothing other than Himself, so that where what belongs to Him is present, He Himself may be understood to be present.

[Note: [Col. 0254C] “And where.” Shortly after, “is understood.”]

[Col. 0253C] Nor is He to be thought, in a bodily manner, to be present somewhere without also being everywhere; since through what belongs to Him He does not cease to be in all things, and what belongs to Him is not other than what He Himself is. And these things have been said for the understanding of nature.

[Col. 0254A]

25. In the Spirit of God the Father is signified; the Son is signified; and the Holy Spirit also is signified. — But I think that God the Father is to be understood as signified in “the Spirit of God” in this way: the Lord Jesus Christ professed that the Spirit of the Lord was upon Himself, by which He anoints Him and sends Him to preach the Gospel. For the power of the Father’s nature is manifested in Him, showing even in the Son born in flesh communion with His own nature through the mystery of this spiritual anointing (Matt. 3:17), when, after the birth associated with His baptism was completed, there was also heard the declaration of His proper sonship, a voice testifying from heaven: “You are My Son; today I have begotten You” (Ps. 2:7).

[Note: [Col. 0253D] That is, in the words of Isaiah 61:1, reported in Luke, by which the Lord says that the Spirit of God is upon Him and that He is therefore anointed and sent to preach the Gospel, I think that God the Father is signified by the name “Spirit of God.”]

[Note: [Col. 0253D] Thus the better manuscripts. Other books read “in the incarnate [Son].” Shortly before, the Vatican Basilica manuscript has “seems to be manifested,” not “is manifested”; and shortly after, “completed” instead of “completed [in the genitive].” A similar passage in Book XI, no. 18 sheds light on this passage, where almost the same point is expressed in other words: “How He was anointed with the Spirit of God and with power is not uncertain, when, as He came up from the Jordan, the voice of God the Father was heard: ‘You are My Son; today I have begotten You’; so that through this testimony concerning the flesh sanctified in Him, the anointing of spiritual power might be recognized.” In that passage, “anointing of spiritual power” is what is here called “communion with His own nature.”]

[Col. 0254B] [Note: [Col. 0254C] Bad., Er., and Lips. omit *also* and the preceding conjunction *when*; in the Paris edition *when* stood in its place. Then the expression “proper sonship” is opposed to adoption. Whether, however, at Christ’s baptism the Father said, “This is My Son,” etc., as Hilary reads in Book VI, no. 23, or said, “You are My Son; today I have begotten You,” as he reads here, in Book VI, no. 23, Book XI, no. 18, on Matthew, ch. II, no. 6, and on Psalm II, no. 29, the force of the argument is the same, which rests upon the words “My Son.”]

For He is not to be understood either as Himself being upon Himself, or as Himself being present to Himself from heaven, or as Himself calling Himself Son. Rather, all this was a demonstration for our faith, so that under the mystery of perfect and true birth we might recognize the unity of nature abiding in the Son, who had also begun to be human.

[Note: [Col. 0254D] The printed editions read “of the Father’s nature.” *Of the Father* is absent from the manuscripts. From this passage it is evident that Hilary interprets Matthew 3:16—“And he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming upon Him”—so as to understand the Spirit of God as the Father. Against the Sabellians, the Father is thereby defended as other than the Son, because He is upon Him, present to Him, and calls Him Son. Yet Hilary must not be thought to have understood the Father by that name in such a way as to deny that the Holy Spirit could also be understood; for immediately afterward he declares that he is showing these things concerning the differing force of the phrase “Spirit of God,” so that whichever way the heretics turn, they cannot evade the force of truth by which we believe the Son to be one with the Father.]

And this is how the Father is found to be signified in the Spirit of God. But we understand the Son to be shown in this manner when He says: “If I cast out demons in the Spirit of God, then indeed the kingdom of God has come upon you”: thereby showing that He Himself—that is, by the power of His own nature—casts out demons, which cannot be cast out except by the Spirit of God.

There is also, in “the Spirit of God,” a signification of the Paraclete Spirit, not by prophetic authority alone but also by apostolic authority. For it is said: “But this is what was spoken through the prophet: ‘And it shall be in the last days, says the Lord, I shall pour out from My Spirit upon all flesh, and their sons and their daughters shall prophesy’” (Acts 2:16 ff.). And this whole prophecy is taught to have been fulfilled in the Apostles when, after the Holy Spirit had been sent, they all spoke in the languages of the nations.

[Col. 0254C] [Col. 0255A] [Note: [Col. 0255C] “But also apostolic.”]

[Note: [Col. 0255D] The printed editions, except the Paris edition, read “all languages.”]

26. God is in us when Christ is in us; when the Spirit of Christ is in us, the Spirit of God is in us. The nature of Son and Father is one. — These matters have necessarily been demonstrated so that, to whatever quarter heretical falsehood might retreat, it might nevertheless be enclosed within the boundaries and prescription of evangelical truth. For Christ dwells in us; and when Christ dwells in us, God dwells in us. And when the Spirit of Christ dwells in us, no Spirit other than the Spirit of God dwells in us. If Christ is understood to be in us through the Holy Spirit, we must nevertheless recognize that Spirit of God as being the Spirit of Christ.

And since, through the nature of the thing, nature itself dwells in us, the Son’s nature will be regarded as indistinguishable from the Father’s, since the Holy Spirit, who is both Spirit of Christ and Spirit of God, is shown to be a thing of one nature.

[Note: [Col. 0255C] “Through the nature of God.”]

[Note: [Col. 0255D] With the old Colbert manuscript and the German manuscript, we prefer “through the nature of the thing,” though the words have been transposed, as often happens in use, namely instead of “through the thing of nature.” In other books it reads “through the nature of God.” From here onward, the answer is directed against those who wish the Spirit of God to be a thing of nature.]

I now ask, then, how are they not one by nature? The Spirit of truth proceeds from the Father; He is sent by the Son from the Father, and receives from the Son. But all things which the Father has are the Son’s; and therefore He who receives from Him is the Spirit of God, yet He is also the Spirit of Christ. He is a thing of the Son’s nature—supply, “the Spirit”—but the same thing is also of the Father’s nature. He is the Spirit of Him who raises Christ from the dead, yet the same Spirit is the Spirit of Christ who was raised from the dead. Let the nature of Christ and of God differ in some respect, lest it be the same, if it can be brought about that the Spirit who is God’s should not also be Christ’s.

27. The Son and Father dwell together in us. — But you, heretic, raging and swept about by the spirit of death-dealing doctrine, are held and constrained by the Apostle, who lays Christ before us as the foundation of faith (1 Cor. 3:11), not ignorant also of this saying of the Lord: “If anyone loves Me, he will keep My word; and My Father will love him, and We shall come to him and make Our dwelling with him” (John 14:23). For by this, while the Spirit of Christ dwells in us, he testifies that the Spirit of God dwells in us, and that the Spirit of Christ raised from the dead is not different from the Spirit of Him who raises from the dead.

[Col. 0255B] [Note: [Col. 0255C] “Of Jesus raised.” Shortly after: “raising Jesus.”]

[Note: [Col. 0255D] On the authority of the better manuscripts we have removed the word “Jesus,” and likewise “Jesus” after “raising.”]

For They come and dwell in us; and I ask whether They will come and make Their dwelling in a companionship of diversities, or in unity of nature.

[Col. 0256A] [Note: [Col. 0255C] “A companionship of distinct beings.”]

[Note: [Col. 0255D] The Martinian manuscript reads “a companionship of distinct beings.” It contains, I know not what further phrase, “a companionship of diversities”; namely, whether the reason for Their coming together lies in some aggregation of diversities or in unity of nature.]

But the teacher of the Gentiles maintains that believers do not have two spirits—God’s, that is, and Christ’s—but the Spirit of Christ, who is also the Spirit of God. It is not a co-dwelling, but a dwelling; yet the dwelling is under the mystery of co-dwelling, because neither do two Spirits dwell, nor is the indweller different from the other.

[Note: [Col. 0255D] Supply “Spirits”; otherwise there will be no mystery of co-dwelling unless two, distinct in persons, dwell. Then the Vatican Basilica manuscript reads: “nor an indweller distinct from another”; the reading “a distinct co-indweller,” found in the Martinian manuscript, could be accepted.]

For the Spirit of God is in us, but the Spirit of Christ is also in us; and when the Spirit of Christ is in us, the Spirit of God is in us. Thus, since what is God’s is also Christ’s, and what is Christ’s is also God’s, Christ cannot be anything different from what God is.

[Col. 0256B] [Note: [Col. 0255D] The Vatican Basilica manuscript and the Martinian manuscript read: “Christ is anything other than what God is”; this reading is not to be accepted.]

Therefore Christ is God: one Spirit with God.

[Note: [Col. 0256C] “One” in place of “the same.”]

[Note: [Col. 0256D] In the Martinian, Carnotensis, Corbie, Pratensis, and several other manuscripts: “one.”]

28. The Arians, alienated from the Holy Spirit, deny that Christ is God and yet worship Him. — And the Apostle teaches that the evangelical statement, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), means unity of nature, not the solitude of an isolated union, writing to the Corinthians: “Therefore I make known to you that no one in the Spirit of God says, ‘Jesus is accursed.’” Do you now know, heretic, in what spirit you say that Christ is a creature (1 Cor. 12:3)? For since those who served the creature rather than the Creator are under a curse (Rom. 1:25), understand what you are when you confess Christ to be a creature, since you do not ignore that worship of the creature is under a curse.

[Col. 0256C] [Note: [Col. 0256D] The printed editions add here the word “speaking,” which they do not have in Book II, no. 34, nor do we find it here except in one more recent Colbert manuscript. Shortly after, the Martinian manuscript and several others have “Jesus,” not “Jesum.”]

[Note: [Col. 0256C] “Jesus,” not “Jesum,” in our manuscript. Shortly after, “you say,” not “you may say.”]

[Note: [Col. 0256D] Ambrose argues similarly, *On Faith*, Book I, ch. 16, no. 104: “Paul himself forbids us to serve a creature; how, then, would he himself serve Christ if he thought Christ a creature?” From this he concludes: “Therefore let them either cease to worship Him whom they call a creature, or cease … to call Him a creature.” And in ch. 11, no. 69: “If they think Him a foreign God, why do they worship Him? For it is written: ‘You shall not worship a foreign god.’” Athanasius, Basil, Gregory of Nyssa, and others construct the same argument against the Arians as worshippers of a creature.]

And observe what follows: “And no one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (1 Cor. 12:3). Do you perceive what you lack by denying Christ what is His own? If Christ is Lord to you by the nature of God, you have the Holy Spirit. But if He is lord by an adoptive title, then, lacking the Holy Spirit, you are animated by the spirit of error; for no one can call Jesus Lord except in the Holy Spirit. And though you call Him lord while declaring Him creature rather than God, you do not say that He is Lord, because to you He is lord from a common genus and familiar name rather than from nature. But learn His nature from Paul.

[Col. 0257A] [Note: [Col. 0257C] The best manuscripts, the Carnotensis and German, with three Colbert manuscripts, read “from a common genus and familiar name.” One Sorbonne manuscript has “from a common, more general [genus],” etc. The Vatican Basilica and Martinian manuscripts have “from community of genus and familiar name.”]

[Note: [Col. 0257C] In Erasmus and one Vatican manuscript: “from Paul and the Spirit of God learn His nature.” In Lipsius and Paris, and in the Corbie manuscript and several others: “from Paul, and learn the nature of God and of the Spirit in Him.” In three Colbert manuscripts and one Sorbonne manuscript: “from Paul [learn] the Spirit of God in Him, and learn the nature of God.” More simply and, we think, more genuinely, Bad., the best Colbert manuscript, with the Carnotensis, Martinian, German, Vindobonensis, Silvanectensis, and two Vatican manuscripts: “learn His nature from Paul”—that is, what His nature is, and how He is Lord not merely by title but truly and by nature. This is proved at length. For from here through no. 35 Hilary demonstrates that God the Father is one and the Lord Jesus Christ another, yet that Their Spirit is one, that Their divinity is one, and that its power and nature are made manifest by its gifts. Afterward he shows more clearly that Christ is Lord by nature.]

29. Distinctions of graces. — For it follows: “Now there are distinctions of gifts, but the same Spirit; and there are distinctions of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are distinctions of operations, but the same God who works all things in all. But to each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for what is useful” (1 Cor. 12:4 ff.). In the present passage a fourfold signification is understood: in the distinction of gifts, the same Spirit; in the distinction of ministries, the same Lord; in the distinction of operations, the same God; and, in the giving of what is useful, the manifestation of the Spirit.

[Note: [Col. 0257D] The Carnotensis manuscript reads, “illumination of the Spirit for what is useful.” This is indeed the reading in Book II, no. 34, with both manuscripts and printed editions agreeing; but here it is clear from what follows that the text must be read differently.]

And so that the giving of what is useful might be recognized in the manifestation of the Spirit, there immediately follows: “To one indeed through the Spirit is given the word of wisdom; to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another faith in the same Spirit; to another gifts of healings in the same Spirit; to another working of miracles; to another prophecy; to another discernment of spirits; to another kinds of tongues; to another interpretation of tongues” (ibid., vv. 8 ff.).

[Col. 0257B] [Note: [Col. 0257D] Thus, with the Greek text supporting it, the reading is found in Book II, no. 34, and here in the Carnotensis exemplar; the Martinian manuscript has “in one Spirit,” while others have “into the same Spirit.” Shortly afterward the printed editions again offer “interpretation of speech,” not “of tongues”; they are refuted by the manuscripts, the Greek text, and the following explanation.]

30. Manifestation of the Spirit. — And indeed that which we said was fourth, namely the manifestation of the Spirit in the giving of what is useful, has a complete meaning. For it was stated through what useful gifts this manifestation of the Spirit occurs. In these powers of division there is no uncertain showing of this gift, concerning which the Lord spoke to the Apostles, commanding them not to depart from Jerusalem: “But wait,” He said, “for the promise of the Father, which you heard from My mouth: for John baptized with water, but you shall be baptized with the Holy Spirit, whom you will receive not many days from now.” And again: “But you shall receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, and you shall be My witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judaea and Samaria and even to the furthest part of the earth” (Acts 1:4 ff.). He commands them to await the Father’s promise, heard from His mouth. Certainly even now it is the utterance of that paternal promise.

[Col. 0257C] [Note: [Col. 0258C] In the Paris edition, “manifestations of the spirit”: incorrectly. “Manifestation” would be more pleasing; but one may refer *manifestation* to the preceding word.]

[Note: [Col. 0258C] The printed editions read “but wait.” Then Lipsius and Paris read “which you heard, He says.” But in all manuscripts it is “wait,” to which only three immediately append “He says,” while neither here nor later does it appear in the others. Shortly after, Colbert, Carnotensis, Martinian, and German manuscripts have “you shall be baptized,” not “you shall be dipped.”]

[Col. 0258A]

Therefore, through these effects of powers, there is a manifestation of the Spirit. For the Spirit’s gift is not hidden where there is a word of wisdom and words of life are heard; or where there is knowledge of divine understanding, lest, like cattle, through ignorance of God we fail to know the Author of our life; or through faith in God, lest, by not believing the Gospel of God, we be outside the Gospel of God; or through gifts of healings, that by the healing of infirmities we may bear witness to the grace of Him who grants these things; or through working of miracles, so that what we do may be understood to be God’s power; or through prophecy, so that through understanding doctrine we may be recognized as taught by God; or through discernment of spirits, lest we be ignorant whether someone speaks by a holy or a perverse spirit; or through kinds of tongues, so that discourse in tongues may be given as a sign of the Holy Spirit bestowed (1 Cor. 14:6); or through interpretation of tongues, lest the faith of hearers be endangered by ignorance when an interpreter of tongues explains a language to those who do not know it.

[Col. 0258B] [Note: [Col. 0258D] The printed editions read “we may understand the power.” Then in Bad. and Erasmus: “or through prophecy, that we may understand through doctrine.”]

[Note: [Col. 0258D] In the Colbert, Martinian, and German manuscripts, *in* is absent. Then the printed editions read “of the Spirit given,” without *Holy*.]

[Note: [Col. 0257C] “Or through interpretation,” as he had previously said “through faith,” “through gift,” “through operation,” etc.; a little later he will complete the construction. Then below, “useful marvels.”]

Thus in all these things, divided to each for usefulness, there is the manifestation of the Spirit, through these marvels useful to each, bestowed while the Spirit’s gift is not hidden.

[Note: [Col. 0258D] The printed editions read “administrations of usefulness.” More correctly, the manuscripts with unanimous agreement read “useful marvels,” or “marvels of usefulness”: for usefulness provided in a manner beyond human power excites wonder and openly declares the divine power of the Spirit by whose aid it is conferred. Thus in Book VII, no. 5, Sabellius is said to have recognized God’s nature in Christ through wonder at His deeds; and in the book addressed to Constantius, no. 8, works of wonder seen before the venerable bones of the Martyrs are proclaimed. Finally, in the exposition of Psalm 91, no. 4, the words “that the Creator’s power might be understood through wonder at the creature” are treated as synonymous with the statement that through the magnitude of these visible works the power of Him who wrought them might be known. See Book III, nos. 5 and 6.]

[Col. 0258C]

31. These gifts are bestowed by one and another, and yet by one Spirit. — In this mystery of heavenly sacraments, most difficult for human understanding, the blessed Apostle Paul maintained both a complete demonstration and careful caution, so as to show that these gifts of distinctions are given through the Spirit and in the Spirit—for it is not the same thing for something to be given through the Spirit and in the Spirit—because the giving of a gift which is received in the Spirit is nevertheless granted through the Spirit.

[Col. 0259A] [Note: [Col. 0259C] In the Carnotensis manuscript: “the mystery of heavenly sacraments.”]

[Note: [Col. 0259C] The person who collated the Vatican Basilica exemplar in the sixth century added opposite the word “show” the words: “lest perhaps all things should not be believed to be through Christ and in Christ.” This addition then prevailed in the Martinian and many other manuscripts—in three of which *were created* was substituted for *were believed*—as also in the printed editions, although it plainly conflicts with what follows, where “through the Spirit” and “in the Spirit” are referred not to the one Christ but to two distinct persons. Hence it appears that the Colbert, Carnotensis, and German manuscripts, in which the preceding words are absent, are more genuine. Then Bad. and Erasmus omit what we have enclosed in parentheses.]

[Note: [Col. 0259B] In place of the words enclosed in parentheses, the Verona manuscript substitutes: “lest perhaps all things should not be believed to be through Christ and in Christ.”]

He completes these distinctions of gifts as follows: “But one and the same Spirit works all these things, dividing to each one as He wills” (1 Cor. 12:11). I now ask which Spirit works these things, dividing to each as He wills: whether the Spirit through whom, or the Spirit in whom, is the division of gifts.

[Note: [Col. 0259C] The Carnotensis exemplar reads “dividing His own things to each,” with the Greek text supporting it: *diairoun idia hekasto* (διαιροῦν ἴδια, or ἰδία, ἑκάστῳ), “dividing His own things to each.” From this Augustine, Letter 187, no. 10, translated: *dividens propria unicuique*, “dividing what is proper to each.” Erasmus indicated that he had not grasped Hilary’s thought when he wrote in the margin here: “Note here many things concerning the Holy Spirit,” failing to see that by the term *Spirit* Hilary most often signifies the Father and the Son. Yet he was not corrected in the subsequent editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0259B] In place of “as He wills”; shortly after: “whether Jesus Christ [is] God Spirit”; a little later: “if not the same thing.”]

[Note: [Col. 0259D] We owe this reading, free from interpolation, to the Colbert, Carnotensis, and German manuscripts mentioned above. In others, and also in Bad. and Erasmus, there occurs here: “whether Jesus Christ [is] God Spirit.” Lipsius, followed by Paris, adding *or*, gives: “whether Jesus Christ is God, or Spirit.” Later all printed editions have “through whom and in whom.” More correctly, the manuscripts have “through whom or in whom.” The holy Doctor asks which Spirit works all things: whether it is the Spirit through whom, or the Spirit in whom, the division of gifts exists.]

If anyone dares to say that the same thing is signified, the Apostle will contradict him, so that he may understand himself to have read wrongly. For he says above: “There are distinctions of operations, but the same God who works all things in all.” Therefore one is He who divides, and another is He in whom the division granted exists. And understand that God always works all these things, yet that Christ works, so that the Son acts with the Father’s work.

[Note: [Col. 0259D] The printed editions and many manuscripts read “if it is not the same thing”; they speak contrary to the preceding: “For it is not the same thing for something to be given through the Spirit and in the Spirit,” and to what follows: “Therefore one is He who divides, another He in whom,” etc. They are corrected from the Vatican Basilica, Colbert, Carnotensis, and German manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 0259D] *Reader* is absent from the old Colbert manuscript. Indeed the preceding word *someone* is sufficient. The Apostle’s contradiction is not sufficiently apparent in the immediately following words; but the connected words must be joined to them: “There are distinctions of ministries, but the same Lord,” so that God is one and Lord another; and God signifies the Father, while Lord signifies the Son. Though They are not one and the same, Their Spirit is one, of one divinity. The opening words of the following section confirm this interpretation.]

[Col. 0259B] [Note: [Col. 0260C] The old Colbert manuscript reads “that the Spirit may work.” With the others, “that Christ may work” is preferable. Here is the answer to the foregoing question: which Spirit works.]

And if you confess Jesus as Lord in the Holy Spirit, understand the force of the Apostle’s threefold signification: in distinctions of gifts there is the same Spirit; in distinctions of ministries there is the same Lord; in distinctions of operations there is the same God; and again one Spirit works all things, dividing to each as He wills. And grasp, if you can, that the Lord in the distinction of ministries and God in the distinction of operations are this same one Spirit, both working and dividing as He wills; because in distinctions of gifts there is one Spirit, and that same Spirit works and divides.

[Col. 0260A] [Note: [Col. 0260C] The printed editions read “and these things”; *these things* is absent from the manuscripts.]

32. Christ distributes charisms.—But if you dislike there being in God and Lord one and the same Spirit of divinity, through the mystery of the birth, show who that Spirit is, and in what Spirit he both effects and distributes these divisions among us. [Note: In the Verona manuscript: “and the Spirit of divinity, the Spirit of division.” Printed editions: “and of divinity.” The Vatican Basilica and Martin manuscripts: “and the Spirit of divinity [Martin: Spirit], of division.” Two others: “and the Spirit of divinity and of division.” In Corbie, three Vatican manuscripts, and many others: “and the Spirit of divinity, the Spirit of division.” The reading of the most excellent Colbert, Carnot, and German manuscripts, which we follow, appeared more polished: “God the Father and the Lord the Son are one Spirit, one God, but through the mystery of the birth”; and accordingly they are distinct in their mode of subsisting. If anyone wishes to add the word “division” after “Spirit,” this may be allowed in the sense that “Spirit of division” means Spirit who is the author of gifts, ministries, and operations.] But you will show nothing other than what belongs to our faith; for the Apostle has shown who is to be understood, saying: “For just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the one body, though many, are one body, so also is Christ” (1 Cor. 12:12). Thus he indicates that the divisions of charisms come from the one Lord Jesus Christ, who is the body of all; because, having shown the Lord in ministry and God in operations, he nevertheless demonstrates that the one Spirit both effects and distributes all these things, distributing these members of graces for the perfection [or: perfection] of the one body.

[Note: Three Colbert manuscripts with the German manuscript read “in which Spirit.” Then, in the Vatican Basilica codex: “these divisions among us in the Lord and God”; in Martin: “these divisions among us in God and Lord,” etc.; in certain others: “these divisions among us in the same God and Lord”: a gloss. Hence only in the printed editions occurs “and operates,” rather than “and effects.” Here Hilary challenges his opponents: if they dislike his own answer to the preceding question, let them offer another. He then establishes that it is not another.]

[Note: Supply “Spirit”: as though he said, “Since the term Spirit has a wider scope and is applied indiscriminately to Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, the Apostle declared which Spirit was to be understood as the giver of spiritual gifts.”]

[Note: “Indicating.”]

[Note: In the manuscripts, “indicating.”]

[Note: “Operates” for “effects”; likewise above, §§13 and 14, “operating” and “operates” for “effecting” and “effects.”]

33. God established operations and ministries; Christ also established them.—Unless perhaps the Apostle is thought not to have preserved the principle of unity in saying: “There are divisions of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are divisions of operations, but the same God” (1 Cor. 12:5–6), so that, because he referred ministries to the Lord and operations to God, one and the same thing may not seem to be understood in ministries and operations. Observe how these members of ministries are members of operations, when he says: “You are the body of Christ and members. And God has appointed some in the Church: first apostles” (ibid. 12:27–28), in whom is the word of wisdom; “second prophets,” in whom is the gift of knowledge; “third teachers,” in whom is teaching in faith; “then powers,” in whom are healings of infirmities, powers of assistance, governments, prophetic gifts, and gifts—varieties of tongues, whether for speaking or interpreting.

[Note: Vatican Basilica manuscript: “gifts of nations.” Certain others, as also Leipzig and Paris: “gifts of kinds.” Prefer, with Baden, Erasmus, and several manuscripts of good authority: “gifts—varieties of tongues,” namely, whether of speaking or interpreting.]

Certainly these are both ministries and operations of the Church, in which is the body of Christ; and God established them. Or confess that they were not established through Christ, because God established them. But you will hear him himself say: “To each one of us grace has been given according to the measure of Christ’s gift.” And again: “He who descended is himself also he who ascended above all the heavens, that he might fill all things. And he himself gave some as apostles, some as prophets, some as evangelists, some as pastors and teachers, for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of ministry” (Eph. 4:7, 10 ff.). Are not the gifts of ministries Christ’s, although they are also God’s gifts?

[Note: “Evangelists.” Shortly afterwards: “both of the effecting One and of God.” Then: “but that,” with the particle “if” omitted.]

[Note: The Carnot codex and Martin manuscript, as in the Greek text, read “evangelists.”]

[Note: Printed editions and many manuscripts: “and of the effecting God.” More correctly, “effecting” is absent from the excellent Colbert, Carnot, and German manuscripts, since the reference is to the Apostle’s passage cited above, 1 Corinthians 12:27: “And God appointed some,” where the word “effecting” is not added. By comparison of that passage with the other passage of the same Apostle, Eph. 4:11, just mentioned, in which the same ministerial gifts are declared to have been bestowed by Christ, it is now at last established more clearly that Christ is the giver of gifts, and therefore one God and one Spirit with the Father. Hilary establishes this step by step and, as it seems to us, not so much from his own position as from the position of his opponents, to whom he concedes something in order to close every avenue of escape. First, he freely grants them that the term “Holy Spirit” sometimes signifies the Father, at other times the Son or the Holy Spirit. Then he allows certain passages of Paul—which in Book II, §§33 and 34, he had referred to the Holy Spirit—to be referred also to Father and Son. He then asks them from which Spirit they wish spiritual gifts to proceed. Finally, he brings them to the point where they cannot deny that ministries in the Church are so appointed by God that they are also said to have been established by Christ; and therefore that Christ is neither of a different power nor of a different nature from the Father. Thus the argument begun at §29 aims to teach that gifts commonly called those of the Holy Spirit belong to the whole Trinity, and specifically to Christ himself; so that, however heretics interpret Paul’s words, the natural unity in Father and Son is nevertheless confirmed for them. We thought it necessary to demonstrate this more laboriously, since we observed that Hilary has not been sufficiently understood.]

34. In calling the Father GOD and the Son LORD, Paul did not distinguish them by nature.—But if impiety has claimed this for itself, that because he says “the same Lord” and “the same God” (1 Cor. 12:5–6), they are not one in nature, I shall add to this understanding of yours defenses which you suppose to be stronger. For the Apostle himself says: “For us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things, and we in him; and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we through him” (1 Cor. 8:6). And again: “One Lord, one faith, one baptism; one God and Father of all, through all and in all of us” (Eph. 4:5–6).

[Note: “And we unto him,” in accordance with the Greek; shortly afterwards the name “Christ” is omitted. A little later: “one baptism.”]

[Note: Printed editions add here, “who is above all.” These words are not present below, at the beginning of Book XI, nor are they found here in the manuscripts; in some of them “and through all” is read as “and above all,” while the Carnot manuscript reads “who is above all.”]

By the expression “one God” and “one Lord,” it seems that being God is assigned to God alone as though proper to the one God; since the property of one does not admit fellowship with another.

O truly rare and difficult gifts of charisms, and truly the manifestation of the Spirit established in this bestowal for benefit! And deservedly was the order of graces to be distributed preserved here, so that the word of wisdom should be first. For it is indeed true: “No one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (1 Cor. 12:3), because unless Christ the Lord could be understood through this word of wisdom, the word of knowledge would then follow, so that we might speak knowingly what we know, and thus know the word of wisdom. The third gift would be faith, because those primary and higher gifts would lose the benefit of the gift unless God were believed. Thus, in the mystery of this greatest and most beautiful apostolic saying, heretics possess neither a word of wisdom, nor a word of knowledge, nor the faith of religion; because impiety, which does not grasp understanding, lies outside the knowledge of speech and outside the simplicity of faith. For no one speaks what he does not know; nor can anyone believe what he cannot speak.

[Note: In Paris, “unless” is lacking. Shortly thereafter certain printed editions also read “can,” rather than “could.”]

[Note: The older of the Colbert manuscripts reads: “unless the Lord were believed.”]

Therefore the Apostle, preaching one God, coming from the Law and called into Christ’s Gospel, maintained the confession of perfect faith. And lest the simplicity of an incautious statement give heretics some occasion to deny the Son’s birth through the proclamation of one God, he confessed one God under the designation of property, saying: “One God, the Father, from whom are all things, and we in him” (1 Cor. 8:6), so that he who is God might also be believed to be Father. Then, because merely believing in one God the Father would not suffice for salvation, he added: “And one Lord, our Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we through him”; showing the purity of saving faith in the proclamation of one God and one Lord, so that for us there might be one God the Father and one Lord Jesus Christ in faith.

[Note: Leipzig and Paris read “might be,” against the other books.]

For he did not ignore what the Lord had said: “For this is the will of my Father, that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him may have eternal life” (John 6:40). But, setting forth the order of ecclesiastical faith and establishing our faith in Father and Son, he spoke of the mystery of that inseparable and indissoluble unity and faith, saying: “One God and one Lord.”

35. If Christ is denied to be God because the Father is one God, then the Father is not Lord because Christ is one Lord.—First, heretic, living outside the apostolic Spirit, understand your folly. For if you employ the confession of one God to ensure that Christ is not God, because where there is one he must be understood as solitary, and what is one is proper and singular to him who is one: what will you confess about the fact that Jesus Christ alone is Lord? For if, according to you, the fact that the Father alone is God has not left Christ free to be God, then, according to you, the one Lord Christ must likewise not leave God free to be Lord, because you wish what is one to be proper to him who is one. Therefore, if you deny that the one Lord Christ is also God, you will likewise deny that the one God the Father is Lord. And what will there be in God’s power if he is not Lord, and in the Lord’s authority if he is not God, since what makes God to be God is that he is Lord, and what establishes the Lord as Lord is that he is God?

[Note: One Vatican codex reads “what is one.” Another, Sorbonne: “what is one,” here and below. More correctly, in the others: “one,” as though, “because someone is one.”]

[Note: “Leaves.”]

[Note: “Because what is one.”]

[Note: “Property.”]

[Note: Printed editions and many manuscripts read “property.” We prefer, with the Carnot and Martin manuscripts and several others, “authority,” since the issue here is not so much property as nature.]

36. Both are one in spirit, not in person.—But the Apostle, holding the mystery of the Lord’s saying, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), while confessing both as one, thereby signifies that both are one not in the solitude of a single person but in unity of Spirit. For one is God the Father and one is Christ the Lord; though each is both Lord and God, they nevertheless do not permit two gods or two lords to exist in our faith. Therefore each is one; and although each is one, he is not alone. Nor can we speak the mystery of faith except in apostolic language. For there is one God and one Lord; and by the fact that God is one and the Lord is one, the Lord is shown in God, just as God is shown in the Lord. You do not maintain union so that God may be solitary; yet neither do you divide the Spirit so that the Spirit is not one.

[Note: “Thus” is absent from our manuscript. Shortly afterwards, “permits” for “permit.”]

[Note: Thus the better manuscripts; in the printed editions and some manuscripts, “permits.”]

[Note: The particle “and,” which here, as often elsewhere, means “also,” has been restored from the manuscripts. Here “is shown” means “is signified,” and this is frequently the force of the word below.]

[Note: The Verona codex reads: “is shown in the Lord, and in the one God the Father would signify both one and Lord; not maintaining union so that God may be a single person, yet not dividing the Spirit so that both are not one.” Shortly afterwards: “will be able” for “you will be able.”]

[Note: Printed editions, except Baden, and the Vatican Basilica manuscript, along with most others, add here: “so that in the one God the Father he might signify both one and Lord.” These words, wrongly inserted here, are absent from the more reliable Colbert, Carnot, and German manuscripts and properly occur below.]

[Note: In the printed editions and many manuscripts: “so that both are not one.” In Martin: “so that both are one,” with the negative particle omitted. More correctly, other manuscripts of no lesser authority read “so that the Spirit is not one.”]

Nor, in the one God and the one Lord, can you distinguish authority, so that he who is Lord is not also God, or he who is God is not also Lord. For by the wording of the names the Apostle guarded against proclaiming either two gods or two lords. Accordingly he employed this mode of instruction: in the one Lord Christ he signified also the one God, and in the one God the Father he signified also the one Lord; yet he did not introduce upon us an impious union which would destroy the birth of the only-begotten God, while confessing both Father and Christ.

[Note: “Jesus Christ.”]

[Note: Printed editions read “yet not,” and shortly after “confessed” add the substantive verb “is.” From this passage or another in §55, where the Baden edition and older manuscripts read *impium* (“impious,” masculine) rather than *impiam* (“impious,” feminine), we suspect that Hilary treated *union* as masculine.]

[Note: “Impious”; shortly afterward, “confessed.”]

37. Paul taught that Christ is not only Lord but also God.—Unless perhaps the frenzy of utter desperation will dare break out so far as to say that because the Apostle called Christ Lord, no one ought to confess him as anything other than Lord, and that, having the property of Lordship, he does not have the reality of God. But Paul does not fail to know Christ as God, saying: “Whose are the fathers, and from whom is Christ, who is God over all” (Rom. 9:5). Here no creature is reckoned as God; rather, he who is God over all is the God of creatures.

[Note: In the ancient Colbert codex: “the reality of Lordship.” Immediately before: “having the property of Lordship,” that is, since it is proper to him to be Lord because he is one. Perhaps from this passage, above at §35, “property” stood in place of “authority”; but the reasoning is not the same.]

[Note: In the Vatican Basilica and Martin codices, “according to the flesh” is added here.]

38. He distinguished him from the Father, but did not divide him.—Learn also, from this very saying of the Apostle now under discussion, how he who is God over all is inseparable in Spirit from the Father. For, having confessed one God the Father, from whom are all things, and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, I ask what difference he introduced by saying “all things from God” and “all things through Christ” (1 Cor. 8:6). Can he from whom, and he through whom, are all things be understood as separable from one another in nature and Spirit? For all things came into being out of nothing through the Son, and the Apostle referred “from whom are all things” to God and “through whom are all things” to the Son. I find no difference, since through each the work is of the same power. For if, with respect to the substance of the universe, it were proper to creatures and sufficient that they are from God, what necessity was there to mention that what is from God is through Christ, unless being through Christ and being from God are one and the same?

[Note: “And is inseparable in Spirit from the Father.”]

[Note: Thus manuscripts of better authority; but Baden and Erasmus: “in the Spirit from the Father”; Leipzig and Paris: “in the Spirit of the Father.”]

[Note: A Corbie manuscript, corrected by a second ancient hand, reads “can.” Then in printed editions: “separable from himself in nature and Spirit.” In almost all manuscripts: “separable from one another in nature and Spirit”; the Carnot manuscript prefixes the preposition *in* to these words. We follow the Vatican Basilica exemplar, although we do not reject the reading of the others, which conveys no different sense.]

[Note: “Separable from one another in nature and Spirit.”]

[Note: Printed editions read “referred.” The manuscripts better read “referred,” describing how the Apostle referred the words “from whom are all things” to the Father and “through whom are all things” to the Son. Shortly afterwards, Baden and Erasmus read “when he attributed both, of the same power” [two manuscripts: “when through both he set forth”]: corruptly.]

But just as Lord and God are ascribed to both, so as to be mutual, so “from whom” and “through whom” are referred to both, for a demonstration of the unity of both and not for the conception of a solitary one. The Apostle’s own statement provides no opening for impiety, and apostolic faith is not careless in its proclamation. For he tempered himself with these precise terms, by which he would be understood neither to signify two gods nor one solitary God: while he rejects a union [of persons] yet does not separate unity. For “from whom are all things” and “through whom are all things,” although they did not establish a single one in the power of efficacy, nevertheless did not show a different one in efficacy; since “from whom are all things” and “through whom are all things” showed an author of the same nature for this purpose. Both, moreover, he declares to be proper to the same nature.

[Note: Vatican Basilica manuscript: “through the Lord.” We prefer simply “the Lord,” with the verb “is” left unexpressed.]

[Note: Printed editions except Paris, with several manuscripts: “pious.” We retain, with the older witnesses, “his,” that is, the Apostle’s; where the Vatican Basilica manuscripts wrongly read “his own.”]

[Note: “A pious statement.” Shortly afterwards, “so that he might neither [preach] two” for “so that he might not [preach] two.”]

[Note: In the power of efficacy.]

[Note: Thus the more corrected manuscripts. Printed editions read “in the power of efficacy.” The Martin manuscript: “into the power of efficacy.”]

For after he had proclaimed that depth of God’s riches, wisdom, and knowledge, confessed the incomprehensibility of his judgments and demonstrated the unsearchableness of his ways (Rom. 11:33), he nevertheless, in the exercise of the duty of human faith, rendered to the depth of the unsearchable and inscrutable heavenly mysteries this honor, saying: “For from him, and through him, and in him are all things. To him be glory for ever. Amen” (ibid. 11:36). Here he refers this to the signification of one nature, because it can be the work only of one nature.

[Note: “And unsearchable.” Shortly afterward, “and uninvestigable,” which we preferred to the earlier reading, “investigable.” Then: “inscrutable.”]

[Note: Baden, Paris, and many manuscripts read “understanding”; corrected from Erasmus, Leipzig, and Corbie manuscripts. Erasmus subsequently restored “uninvestigable,” whereas manuscripts and Baden have “investigable.” Yet one Colbert manuscript supports Erasmus, at Book X, §69. In usage or misuse, moreover, we find that the term *investigabilis* has a negative force, even though the verb *investigare* has an affirmative force.]

[Note: Thus the most ancient Vatican Basilica, Colbert, Martin, etc. manuscripts, in agreement with the sacred Greek and Latin text. Printed editions have “for ever and ever,” omitting “Amen.”]

39. Summary: what has been established from the foregoing passages of Paul.—Since he has specifically ascribed to God that all things are from him, and assigned as Christ’s own that all things are through him; and since now God’s honor is that all things are from him, through him, and in him; and since the Spirit of God is the same as the Spirit of Christ; or since, in the ministry of the Lord and in the operation of God, the one Spirit operates and distributes: they cannot but be one, whose proper attributes belong to one. For in the same Lord the Son and the same God the Father, the one and same Spirit, distributing in the same Holy Spirit, accomplishes all things.

[Note: In two Colbert manuscripts, one Remigius manuscript, and Theodulf: “or since, in the ministry of the Lord’s Spirit and in the operation of God’s Spirit, one Spirit,” etc. This reading, also written in the margin of the Corbie manuscript by an ancient hand, is not displeasing in this sense: although in the dividing of ministries the Spirit is the Lord’s, and in bestowing operation the Spirit is God’s, nevertheless the one Spirit both operates and distributes. In the older Colbert manuscript, and also Martin, Carnot, German, Vindobonensis, Corbie, and one Vatican manuscript: “since in the ministry of the Lord and in the Spirit of God there is one Spirit.” From these Paris has: “since in the ministry of the Lord, and in the operation of God, and in the Spirit of God there is one Spirit.” The reading we restore from other printed editions and certain manuscripts is confirmed by §31: “Grasp, if you can, that the Lord in the division of ministries and God in the division of operations are this one and same Spirit, both effecting and distributing as he wills.”]

[Note: “In the Spirit of God.”]

[Note: Baden, Erasmus, and Leipzig read “in the same Spirit,” without “Holy.” The Carnot codex: “in the Holy Spirit,” without “same”; in the ancient Colbert manuscript the last three letters of that word were deleted in the ancient manner, that is, marked as superfluous by dots beneath them. Hence Martin and almost all other manuscripts read “in that Holy Spirit.”]

O man worthy of the knowledge of great and heavenly mysteries, admitted to divine secrets and chosen as a participant in them: necessarily silent, in silence concerning those things which may not be uttered, and truly an Apostle of Christ! By the proclamation in his unequivocal language of one God the Father and one Lord Jesus Christ, how he has shut up the minds of human perversity! Thus no one can proclaim either two [gods or lords] or one solitary God. Yet he who is not solitary does not thereby become two; nor can he who is not two be understood as solitary. And amid these things the Father showed forth the perfect birth of Christ.

[Note: That is, concerning things of forbidden utterance, or things which it is not permitted to utter. Do not read with the Vatican Basilica codex “uttering forbidden things,” nor afterwards prefer with Vindobonensis, Baden, and Erasmus “establishing,” or with one Colbert manuscript “obeying,” in place of “silent.”]

[Note: “Nor could anyone [preach] two gods.”]

[Note: In the Vatican Basilica codex, Martin, and two other Vatican manuscripts: “two gods.” In the others “gods” is absent, but “lords” is to be understood as suppressed: “neither two gods nor two lords.”]

40. Heretics possess neither faith, hope, nor baptism.—Now stretch out your tongues sharpened with hissing, you serpentine heretics: whether Sabellians, or Photinians, or you who now proclaim the only-begotten God to be a creature. Whoever denies the Son will hear “one God the Father”; for since the Father is Father only through the Son, the Son is signified by the Father. But whoever deprives the Son of unity of undifferentiated nature, let him recognize one Lord Jesus Christ. For unless the Lord is one through unity of Spirit, it will not remain possible for God the Father to be Lord. And whoever regards the Son as temporal and from flesh, let him recognize that all things are through him, and we through him; and that the immeasurable One, who creates all things outside time, is timeless.

[Note: After “times,” the Vatican Basilica codex unnecessarily adds “temporal.”]

Meanwhile let him reread that there is one hope of calling, one baptism, and one faith. And after this, opposing the Apostle’s proclamation, he stands under anathema: since he thinks differently according to his own opinion, he is neither called, nor baptized, nor faithful; because in one God the Father and one Lord Jesus Christ there is one faith of one hope and baptism. Nor can diversity of doctrines boast that it exists in things which belong to one God, one Lord, one hope, one baptism, and one faith.

41. Faith concerning Father and Son.—There is therefore one faith: to confess the Father in the Son and the Son in the Father through unity of inseparable nature—not confused, but undivided; not blended, but undifferentiated; not merely conjoined, but subsisting; not incomplete, but perfect. For it is birth, not division; Sonship, not adoption; God, not creation. Nor is he God of another kind, but Father and Son are one. For nature was not altered by birth, so as to be alien from the property of its origin.

[Note: Thus the manuscripts. Printed editions read here “maintaining,” and later “proclaims.”]

The Apostle therefore maintains this faith of the Son abiding in the Father and the Father in the Son, when he proclaims one God the Father and one Lord Christ to be his God and Lord. For in the Lord Christ there was also God, and in God the Father there was also Lord; and each was one in that which is God, and each was one in that which is Lord. For God would be incomplete unless he is Lord, and the Lord would be understood not to exist unless he is God. Thus, since each is one and the one is signified in each, and neither exists without the one, the Apostle does not go beyond evangelical proclamation in teaching; nor is Christ speaking in Paul different from him who, remaining bodily in the world, spoke before his ascension into heaven.

42. The Son of Man gives eternal life because he was sealed by the Father.—For in the Gospels the Lord had said: “Work not for the food which perishes, but for the food which endures unto eternal life, which the Son of Man will give you. For him God the Father has sealed.” Therefore they said to him: “What shall we do, that we may work the works of God?” And he said to them: “This is the work of God: that you believe in him whom he has sent” (John 6:27 ff.).

[Note: In most ancient books, “signified”: a scribal error arising from similarity of words, also repeatedly found below in the earlier printed editions. The Greek has ἐσφράγισεν, “sealed.”]

[Note: “Him.”]

[Note: Thus the Carnot codex, supported by the Greek, εἰς ὅν, “in whom.” But Martin has *ut credatis eum* (“that you believe him”); others, *ut credatis ei* (“that you believe him”); below, however, all read “to believe in him.”]

In explaining the mystery of both his embodied existence and his divinity, the Lord also taught the doctrine of our faith and hope: that we should work for food which does not perish but endures for eternity; that we should remember that this food of eternity is given us by the Son of Man; that we should know the Son of Man to have been sealed by God the Father; and that we should recognize this to be the work of God, to believe in him whom he sent. And who is he whom the Father sent? Surely he whom God sealed. And who is he whom God sealed? Certainly the Son of Man, who provides the food of eternal life. And who, then, are those to whom he provides it? Those, indeed, who work for food which does not perish. Thus the work that is the working for food is the same as the work of God—namely, believing in him whom he sent. But the Son of Man speaks these things. And how will the Son of Man give the food of life eternal? But he who does not know the Son of Man, sealed by God the Father, as the giver of food unto eternal life, does not know the mystery of his salvation. Here I now ask what meaning of understanding there can be in the Son of Man’s having been sealed by God the Father.

[Note: Leipzig and Paris: “to them indeed”; and shortly afterward, with Baden and Erasmus, “what work of food is this?” against the manuscripts.]

[Note: “Eternal” is absent from the Verona manuscript.]

[Note: “Eternal” is absent from most manuscripts.]

43. God accommodates his speech to our understanding. The Son is equal to the Father. God is uncompounded.—First, it must be recognized that God spoke not for himself but for us, and so moderated the expression of his discourse to our understanding as the weakness of our nature can comprehend in thought. For when above he had been reproached by the Jews for making himself equal to God by professing himself the Son of God (John 5:18), he answered that he did all that the Father did (ibid. 5:19 ff.); that all judgment had been given to him by the Father; and that he himself was to be honored as the Father is honored. In all these things, having first professed himself Son, he made himself equal to the Father in honor, power, and nature. Then he said that, as the Father has life in himself, so he had given the Son to have life in himself (ibid. 5:26); in which he signified unity of the same nature through the mystery of birth. For by what the Father has, he signified that the Father himself is that very thing in having it: because God is not, in the human way, composed of parts, so that one thing in him is what he has and another is he who has it. Rather, all that he is is life—namely, perfect, absolute, and infinite nature, not constituted from unlike elements but itself living throughout. Since what is possessed is of such a kind, what is given is also of such a kind. Even though the birth of him to whom it is given is understood to be signified, it does not introduce diversity of kind, since what is given is such as what is possessed.

[Note: “Could.” Shortly afterwards, “rebuked.”]

[Note: “Himself Son of the Father,” etc.]

[Note: Printed editions: “himself Son of the Father”; corrected from the manuscripts.]

[Note: Printed editions: “he signified that very thing itself.” But the older books read “he signified that very one himself.” Then, from the Vatican Basilica, Martin, two Colbert, and one Sorbonne manuscript, we add “in having,” with the preposition *in*, absent from the other books. This appears to mean: Christ signified that he—the Father—is himself in having, that is, that in the thing possessed he is not other than what he is in himself. Thus Hilary expounds “As the Father has life in himself” as though it meant: “Just as he has life situated in himself, and life which he himself is”; for what is his is not other than what he himself is, as seen above at §24. Since the Son is likewise said to have life in himself, it follows fittingly that he is one God with the Father. Yet to some the holy Doctor may seem to contradict himself here, since in Book II, §32, wishing to prove that the Spirit who is Lord and the Spirit of the Lord are not one, he says: “For to have and to be had are not one.” But the reply is ready: in Book II he speaks of persons, whereas here he speaks of nature, whose supreme simplicity he expressly defended above at §24.]

44. In what sense the Son of Man was sealed by the Father.—After, then, this manifold and particular declaration that the Father’s nature was in himself, he used this saying: “For him God the Father has sealed” (John 6:27).

[Note: In printed editions “to the Apostles” is inserted here; we have removed it on the authority of the best Colbert and German codices, as well as the Gospel text, which reports that Christ addressed this discourse to the crowd. Indeed, Hilary himself affirms in the final words of this section that these things were said to the Jews.]

[Note: “To the Apostles, having used.”]

The nature of seals is such that they fully display the form of the image impressed upon them and have in themselves nothing less than that from which they are sealed; and, while receiving the whole of what is impressed, they present wholly from themselves whatever has been impressed. But this example does not suffice for the illustration of the divine birth, because in seals there are material, difference, and impression, by means of which the forms of stronger kinds are impressed upon more yielding natures. But the only-begotten God, and through the mystery of our salvation the Son of Man, wishing to signify to us in himself the image of the Father’s property, says that he was sealed by God. He says this because the Son of Man was to give the food of eternal life, so that through this the power in him of giving food unto eternity might be understood: because he contains in himself the whole fullness of the Father’s form—of God who seals him—so that what God had sealed would bring forth from itself nothing other than the form of the sealing God. These things, indeed, the Lord spoke to the Jews, who by their unbelief were incapable of this saying.

[Note: “Through which.” Printed editions with the Corbie manuscript read “through which”; the Vatican Basilica codex, “through whom.” From this we judged that “through which” should be read, unless one prefers with most others “through which [feminine].”]

45. Paul explains “sealed by God” by saying “in the form of God.” — But the preacher of the Gospel gives us understanding of this property through the Spirit of Christ speaking in him, when he says: “Though he was in the form of God, he did not regard being equal to God as a thing to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2:6–7).
