[Note: The word “to be” is absent from our manuscript, as also below, where this Pauline passage is repeated.] For he whom God had sealed could be nothing other than the form of God; [Note: Printed editions read “and therefore,” against the better manuscripts.] and that which is sealed in the form of God must necessarily have wholly co-imaged within itself whatever belongs to God. Therefore the Apostle proclaimed that he whom God sealed remained God in the form of God.

For, intending to speak of the mystery of the body assumed and made connatural in him, he says: “He did not regard being equal to God as a thing to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.” What was in the form of God remained God through God who sealed him. But because the form of a servant had to be assumed, and he was to become obedient unto death, he did not seize for himself equality with God; rather, by obedience, he emptied himself into the form of a servant. [Note: “Unto the assumption.” In earlier printed editions, *himself* is missing. Further, in the Paris edition the word *emptied* is not repeated; in other editions it is repeated, but with a negative particle prefixed, on the authority of only one rather recent Colbert manuscript and contrary to Hilary’s meaning. For, as he says on Psalm 68, no. 25: “Coming in the form of a servant, Christ emptied himself of the form of God”; and no. 4: “The heavenly, that is divine, nature had to be drawn out, so that, emptying himself from the form of God, he might descend into the form of a servant and a human being,” etc.] He emptied himself from the form of God, that is, from that in which he was equal to God; yet he did not suppose himself equal to God by seizure, although he stood forth in the form of God and equal to God, God sealed by God.

46. Christ is true God even after assuming humanity; how much more before it. — I now ask [Note: Printed editions read, “Here I do not now ask”; corrected from the manuscripts.] whether the God who remains God in the form of God is of another kind, as we observe among seals, where the sealed and sealing forms are different in kind: when iron impressed upon lead and a gem upon wax either fashions the likeness of an image hollowed into itself or expresses from itself the shape that projects outward. [Note: “In seals.” Thus the Vatican-Basil manuscript and Martin, supported by other older witnesses, in which *in individual things* appears erroneously. Others read *in seals*. This usage occurs above, no. 44, where Hilary has already warned that seals are not comparable in this respect with the divine birth, because between sealed and sealing forms there is a difference of nature.]

But if anyone is so foolish and senseless as to think that God forms from himself into God something other than God, and that he who is in the form of God is himself, in his entirety, something other than God, then, after the mystery of assumed humanity and the humility completed through obedience even to death on the cross (see the exposition on Psalm 2, no. 27, in the notes), he will hear Jesus confessed “in the glory of God the Father” by heavenly, earthly, and infernal beings and by every tongue (Phil. 2:10–11). Therefore, if he will remain in this glory when he has already been in the form of a servant [Note: Several manuscripts read “servile form”; no alteration is needed.], what, I ask, did he remain when he was in the form of God? Was it Christ Spirit, in the nature of God signified by glory, when Christ Jesus—that is, the human being born—will stand forth in the glory of God the Father?

[Note: In the Verona manuscript, *Christ* is written by the first hand; but a second, ancient scribe corrected it to *Christ’s*. Printed editions read “Christ Spirit,” against the better manuscripts. Moreover, “Christ Spirit,” that is, Christ as he was before assuming humanity, is contrasted with Christ who had now become human. Thus, in Book III, no. 19: “You ask how the Son was born according to Spirit,” is explicitly opposed to: “You ask how he was born according to humanity.” So Pope Clement, Epistle II, ch. 9, vol. I of the Councils, p. 186: “Jesus Christ our Lord, who saved us, when he was first Spirit, became flesh.”]

47. God is one, not solitary. — The blessed Apostle maintains everywhere the unchangeable proclamation of evangelical faith, preaching the Lord Jesus Christ as God in such a way that apostolic faith neither degenerates into two gods through a God of another kind, nor gives an impious occasion for proclaiming the Son, inseparable from the Father, as the God of a solitary and singular God. [Note: The Carnotensis witness reads “and of a solitary God,” with no different meaning.]

For in saying “in the form of God” and “in the glory of God the Father,” he taught neither difference nor permitted us to think that the Son does not exist. For one who is in the form of God neither becomes another God nor is himself not God: he cannot be separated from God’s form, since he is in it; nor can one who is in the form of God fail to be God. Likewise, one who is in the glory of God cannot be anything other than God is; and while he is God in the glory of God, he is not proclaimed as another God, distinct from God. For by being in God’s glory, he possesses in himself, from him in whose glory he is, that natural reality which God is.

48. Christ, as God’s image, is not of another nature. — The one faith is not endangered by the many proclamations, lest it cease to be one. For the Evangelist had taught that the Lord said: “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9). But did Paul, teacher of the Gentiles, either fail to know or pass over the force of this saying of the Lord when he said: “He is the image of the invisible God” (Col. 1:15)?

I ask whether a visible image can be the image of the invisible God; and whether infinite God can be co-imaged into a likeness through the image of a circumscribed form. [Note: In Bad., “whether visible God, and whether,” etc.; the passage is mutilated. Other editions read: “whether visible image is the invisible God’s image.” The word *God* is superfluous and absent from the manuscripts. This question challenges the Arians, who argued that the Son was unequal to the Father because they imagined the Son visible and the Father invisible. Augustine specifically marks their madness on this point in *On the Trinity*, II.14, and Sermon VII, no. 4. Hilary’s point here is: “You who wish the Father to be invisible and the Son visible, I ask whether one who is visible can be the image of the invisible God.”]

For an image must reproduce the form of that of which it is the image. Let those who wish the Son’s nature to be of another kind determine what sort of image of the invisible God they want the Son to be: bodily, visible to contemplation, and wandering from place to place by movement and walking? Yet let them remember, according to the Gospels and prophets, that Christ is Spirit and God is Spirit. [Note: After *yet*, the Carnotensis manuscript alone adds “through the Son all things,” which is beside the point. The answer to the preceding question is that Christ is not a bodily image, since he is Spirit, just as God the Father is Spirit.]

If they confine this Spirit, Christ, in a formable and bodily manner, he will not be the bodily image of the invisible God, nor will a defined limitation be the likeness of the unlimited. [Note: Printed editions except Paris omit *Christ*. Then Leipzig and Paris substitute *formal* for *formable*. The better manuscripts are confirmed by Book II, no. 5: “The Father is incorporeal. If the Son according to Spirit is circumscribed by body, then the bodily is no longer the form of the incorporeal.” Printed editions read “bodily image,” and thereafter: “nor an undefined species, a defined limitation.”]

49. He is God’s image insofar as the power of divine nature is in him. — But neither did the Lord leave uncertain the words, “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9), nor did the Apostle leave unspoken what sort of one he was who “is the image of the invisible God” (Col. 1:15). For the Lord had said: “If I do not do the works of my Father, do not believe me” (John 10:37), teaching that the Father is seen in him because he performs the Father’s works; so that the understood power of nature might disclose the nature of the power understood.

Accordingly, the Apostle, indicating that this is the image of God, says: “He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation; because in him all things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, were established, whether thrones or principalities or powers or dominions. All things were created through him and in him; and he is before all things, and all things subsist in him. And he is the head of the body, the Church; he is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, so that he might hold first place in all things; because in him all fullness was well pleased to dwell, and through him to reconcile all things to him” (Col. 1:15ff.).

[Note: In the Carnotensis manuscript, *created* occurs here in place of *were established*, and again in place of *were created*.]

[Note: Printed editions read “in him they subsist,” supported by the Greek ἐν αὐτῷ συνέστηκε, but against the manuscripts.]

[Note: The ancient Colbert and Germaniensis manuscripts, which lack the initial words “who is the image of the invisible God,” may perhaps be more genuine. Yet this addition does no harm.]

Therefore he is the image of God by the power of these works. For surely the Creator of invisible things is not subject to such a necessity of nature that the image of the invisible God should be visible. And lest he be understood to be the image of form rather than of nature, he is the image of the invisible God: God’s nature is to be understood in him through the power of his own nature, not by an invisible quality. [Note: Understand: “rather than the image of nature”; shortly afterward, “not by a visible quality.” Compare Book XI, no. 5, concerning one who “would not reproduce the image of invisible nature in visible substance.” The Vatican-Basil manuscript reads “not by invisible quality”; Bad. reads “but not by visible quality”; Erasmus, Leipzig, and several manuscripts read “not by visible quality.” Paris, with the better manuscripts, reads “not by invisible quality”: that is, that invisible image should not be understood as located in an invisible quality, but in God’s own substance and nature. For, as Book V, no. 3 says, the power of nature establishes and proves truth. There is no doubt that divine power belongs to the image to which the Apostle attributes power to create all things. Thus, to supplement the expression from Ambrose, *On Faith*, I.7: “That image is not a bodily countenance, not fashioned with paints or waxes; but simple, proceeding from God, coming forth from the Father, expressed from the fountain.” And shortly afterward: “This image is truth; this image is justice; this image is the power of God—not mute, because it is Word; not insensible, because it is Wisdom; not empty, because it is Power; not void, because it is Life,” etc.]

50. Who is firstborn and who holds first place in all things. — Therefore he is the firstborn of all creation because all things were created in him. And lest anyone dare to refer the fact that all things were created in him to someone other than him, the Apostle says: “All things were created through him and in him; and he is before all things, and all things subsist for him” (Col. 1:17). Thus all things subsist in him who is before all things and in whom all things are. These matters belong to the beginnings of created things.

But with reference to the dispensation of our body he says: “And he is the head of the body, the Church; he is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, so that he might hold first place in all things; because in him all fullness was well pleased to dwell, and through him to reconcile all things to him” (ibid., 18ff.). [Note: In an old Colbert manuscript and the Germaniensis, “for the dispensation.”]

The Apostle joined bodily operations to spiritual mysteries. For he who is the image of the invisible God is also the head of the body of the Church; and he who is the firstborn of all creation is likewise the beginning, the firstborn from the dead. Thus he holds first place in all things: because he who is the image of God is a body for us; and because he who is the firstborn of creation is likewise firstborn unto eternity, so that spiritual beings, created in the Firstborn, may owe to him their continuance, and human beings may owe to him their rebirth into eternal life in the Firstborn from the dead.

[Note: Printed editions except Paris read “the spiritual mystery of incorporation” (Leipzig, “corporation”). The manuscripts more correctly read “to spiritual mysteries,” that is, operations concerning Christ’s spiritual and divine nature; these are joined with those concerning his bodily and human nature. Nearly all manuscripts read *body*, as above, no. 32, where Christ is proclaimed the body of all; the Vatican-Basil manuscript and Martin read *bodily*, Paris *corporeal*, and other editions *concorporate*. Three Colbert manuscripts read “in the firstborn” incorrectly. Some later witnesses, Erasmus, and Bad. read “may be reborn into eternal life,” less genuinely. “Spiritual beings” means angels, or human beings according to the soul; “human beings” means at least human bodies. Angels owe Christ their continuance, that they may not perish. As Ambrose teaches, *On Faith*, III.3: “Not even an angel is naturally immortal; his immortality depends on the will of the Creator.”]

For he is the beginning, who, though Son, is image; and, because he is image, he is God’s image. He is also the firstborn of all creation, containing in himself the beginning of the universe. Again, he is the head of the body of the Church and the firstborn from the dead, that he himself may hold first place in all things. Since all things subsist in him, the fullness that was well pleased subsists in him, while in him all things are reconciled through him to him, in whom all things were created through him in him.

[Note: The manuscripts, except that in most the first *is* is absent, read: “though he is Son, he is image”; printed editions further omit “when he is image.” The phrase “firstborn of all creation” is explained more clearly in Fragment II, no. 30: “Therefore firstborn of all creation, because in him from the beginning all the origins of the generations of all things which he was to make were established.” Bad. and Erasmus read “the primacy of the head”; one Vatican manuscript reads “the primacy of charity,” a gloss. Colbert and Germaniensis read “may hold the primacies.” Printed editions read “and to him”; *and* is absent from all manuscripts. In many manuscripts *to him* is absent. The reading of Colbert and Germaniensis, “through him, him,” is not entirely displeasing. Later the same manuscripts read “in him” for “in whom.” Printed editions read “through him and in him,” where *and* is absent from the manuscripts.]

51. He is God’s image insofar as all things are created in him. Creation, like reconciliation, belongs to both Father and Son. — Do you now perceive what it is to be the image of God? It is that all things are created in him through him. [Note: “In him and through him.” Printed editions read “in him and through him.” The Colbert manuscript reads “when they are recreated to him,” and shortly afterward, “the things which are created to him.” Martin likewise has *to him* in both places.]

When all things are created in him, understand that he whose image he is also creates all things in him. But when the things created in him are created through him, recognize also in him who is the image the nature of him whose image he is. [Note: The word *to be present in*, absent from earlier printed editions, occurs in all the manuscripts, though corruptly as *to be in itself*.] For he creates through himself the things that are created in him, just as all things are reconciled through him in him.

When they are reconciled in him, apprehend the nature of paternal unity, reconciling all things to itself in him. When all things are reconciled through him, understand him himself as reconciling to the Father in himself all things which he reconciled through himself. For the same Apostle says: “But all things are from God, who reconciled us to himself through Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation, because God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself” (2 Cor. 5:18–19). [Note: Bad., with the Vatican-Basil manuscript, reads *mystery*, incorrectly.]

Compare with these statements the entire mystery of evangelical faith. He who is seen in the one seen, who works in the one working, who speaks in the one speaking, likewise reconciles in the one reconciling (John 14:9–10). Therefore reconciliation is in him and through him because, by an undifferentiated nature, the Father remaining in him restored the world to himself through him and in him by reconciliation. [Note: Erasmus conjectured that *reconciled* should be read; Leipzig adopted this, and it prevailed in other editions, against the manuscripts.]

52. Christ declared his unity with the Father as aptly as possible. — God, therefore, making provision for human weakness, did not teach faith by the bare ambiguity of words. Although the authority of the Lord’s saying alone imposed the necessity of belief, he nevertheless instructed our understanding through the intelligibility of the explanation given, so that we might know, by the very cause of the unity expounded, what he had said: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30).

For when he says that he speaks through the one speaking, works through the one working, judges through the one judging, is seen through the one seen, reconciles through the one reconciling, and remains in him who remains in himself [Note: The lemma reads “to be reconciled”; then, “to remain.” Printed editions read *to be reconciled*, incorrectly. The Vatican-Basil manuscript and Martin read “who himself remained in himself,” adding *himself*.], I ask by what more suitable language of exposition he could have led our understanding to perceive that they are one than by saying that, through the truth of birth and unity of nature, whatever the Son did or said, the Father also spoke and did in the Son.

This, therefore, does not belong to a nature alien from itself, nor to one made into God through creation, nor to one born into God from a portion of God; but to divinity begotten by perfect birth into perfect God. Its confidence in natural self-knowledge is such that it says: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 14:11), and again: “All things that are the Father’s are mine” (John 16:15). [Note: Bad. and Erasmus, with recent manuscripts, read “a nature alien in kind from itself,” and then, with Leipzig, omit *nor*. A nature made comparable to God through creation is one which, though created, nevertheless claims and attains the name of God from a certain prerogative.]

For nothing from God is lacking to him in whom God works, speaks, and is seen, while he works, speaks, and is seen. They are not two—supplying, “distinct in nature”—in one operation, speech, or sight. Nor is God solitary when, in God who works, speaks, and is seen, God also has worked, spoken, and been seen. This the Church understands; this the Synagogue does not believe; this philosophy does not perceive: God and Son, one from one and whole from whole, neither depriving the Father through birth of what he wholly is, nor failing to possess in birth that very whole along with himself. [Note: Printed editions read “which he wholly is,” against the old witnesses. Since the Father is a certain whole, after the Son’s birth that entire reality remains what it was, since no part has been torn away from him.] Whoever remains entangled in this folly of unbelief is either a follower of the Jews or of the Gentiles.

53. Human wisdom; the distinction between the elements of the world and Christ. — To understand the Lord’s saying, “All things that are the Father’s are mine,” learn both the Apostle’s teaching and faith when he says: “See that no one deceives you through philosophy and empty deception, according to human tradition, according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ; because all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily in him” (Col. 2:8–9). [Note: This is the reading of the Verona manuscript; previously, “the fullness of divinity.” Greek: πᾶν τὸ πλήρωμα τῆς θεότητος, “all the fullness of deity.” Thus below Hilary says, “all the fullness of divinity is bodily in Christ.” So also Book I, no. 8, and Book XII, no. 20.]

Whoever does not know Christ as true God, whoever does not recognize in him the fullness of divinity, belongs to the world, savors human teachings, and is philosophy’s spoil. [Note: Erasmus after Bad. reads “who savors human teaching”; Paris after Leipzig reads “and savors human teaching”; the manuscripts correct these. The following phrase, “and is philosophy’s spoil,” shows that Hilary knew the reading followed by Cyprian, Epistle LII and *On the Good of Patience*, Ambrose, *On Faith*, I.5, and Jerome on Galatians 4: namely, “See that no one despoils you,” supported by Greek συλαγωγῶν, “carrying off as spoil.” Indeed, in Book I, no. 13, Hilary himself reads with them: “See that no one plunders you.” The antiquity of the other reading is nevertheless evident from Tertullian, *Prescription against Heretics*, no. 7, where “See that no one deceives you” occurs.]

The human mind knows only what it understands, and the world believes only what it can do, judging possible, according to the natures of the elements, only what it sees or does. For the elements of the world came to exist from nothing; but Christ does not remain from non-existent things, nor did he begin from an origin, but received an eternal origin from Origin. [Note: Bad. reads “not from subsisting things”; other editions, “not from existing things,” an error corrected by the manuscripts. Leipzig substituted *flows* for *remains*, retained by Paris contrary to the manuscripts. See the note at the end of p. 197 (note h, col. 222 of our edition). The better manuscripts read: “nor did he begin from an origin.”]

The elements of the world are either lifeless or have advanced to life; but Christ is life, born from the living God into living God. The elements of the world were established by God; they are not God. Christ, God from God, is himself entirely that which God is. Since the elements of the world are within, they cannot stand forth from themselves so as not to be within; Christ, having God in himself under the mystery, is in God. [Note: That is, they cannot simultaneously be within and outside; whereas Christ, existing in God and simultaneously possessing God in himself, exists both within and outside the Father. See the beginning of Book III.]

When the elements of the world generate from themselves others of their own kind for life, they indeed provide from themselves beginnings of birth through bodily processes; yet they themselves do not exist living in those who are born. But all the fullness of divinity is bodily in Christ.

54. How the fullness of divinity dwells bodily in Christ. — And I ask: whose fullness of divinity is in him? If it is not the Father’s, what other God, preacher of one God though deceitful, do you impose upon me, whose fullness of divinity dwells in Christ? But if it is the Father’s, teach me how this fullness dwells bodily in him.

For if you believe that the Father is in the Son in a bodily way, the Father dwelling in the Son will not exist in himself. [Note: Bad. and Erasmus read *confine*; Leipzig and Paris, with more recent manuscripts, *shut in*. But the better manuscripts read *believe* or *will believe*. Thus above, no. 24, it is observed that both Father and Son are called Spirit, lest we should believe that the Son is in the Father or the Father in the Son according to bodily modes.]

But if, as is truer, divinity remaining bodily in him signifies the truth of God’s nature from God in him, then God is in him not by condescension or will, but true and whole by generation, remaining in bodily fullness according to himself. [Note: The Vatican-Basil manuscript reads *divinity*, incorrectly. Bad., Erasmus, and Leipzig read “signifies unity.” Paris and the manuscripts more rightly read “truth”: Hilary thus interprets divinity dwelling bodily in Christ as God’s nature dwelling there truly and substantially. Tertullian, *Against Praxeas*, no. 7, after saying, “Who will deny that God is body, although God is Spirit?”, immediately indicates that he calls body that which is not without substance: “Even those invisible things, whatever they are, have with God their own body and form, through which they are visible to God alone; how much more will that which has been sent from his own substance not be without substance!” In this sense, in *On the Flesh of Christ*, no. 11, he says: “Everything which exists is a body of its own kind. Nothing is incorporeal except that which does not exist.” Nor is it obscure that Hilary here calls *body* what is full, true, and substantial. So he says on Psalm 131, no. 26: “Now, however, rejoicing with perfect exultation—not in hope but in truth; not in image but in body.”]

For what he himself is, that also is born through God’s birth into God [Note: The lemma reads *was born*.]; and there is nothing diverse or differing in God from that which dwells bodily in Christ. Whatever dwells bodily [Note: The lemma reads *dwells in*.] is that very thing according to the fullness of divinity. Why do you pursue human things? Why cling to the teachings of empty deceptions? Why bring me unanimity, concord, or creaturehood? The fullness of divinity is bodily in Christ.

55. One is the indweller, another the dwelling; each is perfect God. — In this also the Apostle preserved the rule of his faith, teaching that the fullness of divinity dwells bodily in Christ, lest the language of faith fall into impious union or irreligious madness break out into the notion of another nature. [Note: “Lest [it fall] into impious union.” The Vatican-Basil manuscript, Martin, and several others read *impious*; the old Colbert manuscript and Germaniensis, as above in no. 36, read *impious [union]*. Later, most manuscripts have *fall*, not *depart*.]

For the fullness of divinity dwelling bodily in Christ is neither solitary nor separable: bodily fullness does not permit itself to be distinguished from bodily fullness, nor can the indwelling divinity itself be understood as the dwelling of divinity. [Note: Martin and the Vatican-Basil manuscripts read “nor is it separated,” and below “nor is it distinguished,” instead of “to be distinguished,” less correctly.]

Christ is thus such that the fullness of divinity is bodily in Christ; and the fullness of divinity is bodily in Christ in such a way that the indwelling fullness is understood to be nothing other than Christ. [Note: In Bad., Erasmus, and Leipzig, *fullness* is missing; it is here declared to be nothing other than Christ. Shortly afterward, the best Colbert manuscript has *sharpen* rather than the reading *stir up*.]

Steal whatever occasions for verbal quibbling you wish, and sharpen the barbs of an irreligious intellect. At least falsely state whose fullness of divinity dwells bodily in Christ. For Christ exists, and there also exists in him the bodily fullness of divinity dwelling in him.

56. What the bodily dwelling is; whose it is. — And if you ask what the bodily dwelling is, understand what it means to speak in the one speaking, to be seen in the one seen, to work in the one working, God in God, whole from whole, and one from one; and thus recognize the bodily fullness of divinity.

And remember that the Apostle does not leave unspoken whose this fullness of divinity dwelling bodily is, when he says: “For his invisible things, from the foundation of the world, are perceived through the things that have been made, even his eternal power and divinity” (Rom. 1:20). [Note: The Carnotensis manuscript reads “from the creation of the world,” and one Vatican manuscript “from the formation of the world,” with no different meaning. *Foundation* has the same meaning in Book XI, no. 16.]

Therefore his divinity is bodily in Christ, not partially but wholly; it is not a portion but fullness. It remains bodily in such a way that they are one; they are one in such a way that God does not differ from God; God is undifferentiated from God in such a way that perfect birth has produced a perfect God subsisting [Note: That is, it has caused him to subsist.]; and perfect birth subsists because the fullness of divinity dwells bodily in God born from God.

255, 256. BOOK NINE.

Having established in the preceding book the undifferentiated nature of Father and Son, Hilary defends and confirms it against the objections of heretics. From the Scriptures which they cite for this purpose, he first lays down certain seeds of response: namely, that the genuine meanings of Scripture must be sought not from the sound of bare words detached from the rest, but from what precedes and follows and from the occasions of speaking; next, that Christ is one and the same reality from natures united into one, yet not confused, for he always so regulated his sayings and deeds as to declare himself both Son of God and son of man; finally, that one must distinguish what he said or did before becoming human, what he said or did when already human and about to die, and what he said or did as immortal. From this, the reality of the two natures in the one Christ is broadly established.

Having made these points, he answers the first heretical objection, “Why do you call me good? No one is good except the one God,” by saying that Christ does not reject the name “good” or “teacher,” but rebukes the faith of one who called him so while not believing him to be God. Indeed, he testifies that he is God and teacher when he promises a heavenly treasure to the one who follows him. He then demonstrates at length that wherever Christ proclaims one God, he signifies himself as other than the Father, but not of another nature.

He refutes the second objection, “that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent,” from the preceding and connected words of that passage. For when Christ, in John 14, taught that the Father is in him, speaks in him speaking, works in him working, and is seen in him seen (John 16), he commends the faith of the Apostles, who by the term “going forth” believe that he was truly born from God. Finally, in John 17, he asks honor from the Father in such a way that he in turn will honor the one honoring him; he receives power in such a way that he can give eternal life to all flesh and has nothing less than the Father. By all this he indicates that he is born from the Father and one with him in nature. Then, from the very words objected, he concludes that Christ must not be separated from the Father in nature, since he must not be separated from him in faith; nor can the Father properly be called true God without insult if he is believed to have begotten a degenerate Son. Finally, from the words connected with the disputed passage, he expounds copiously and subtly the one glory of Father and Son.

Afterward, prompted by the occasion which gave rise to Christ’s saying, “The Son can do nothing of himself,” he proves that the Son’s equality with the Father, not weakness, is displayed. For, answering Jews who charged him with violating the Sabbath, he first says immediately before: “My Father works until now, and I work.” He thereby declares that his operation and the Father’s are one and common. Likewise, he confirms himself equal to the Father when, as they resent that he makes himself equal to God, he immediately adds: “Whatever he does, these things the Son also does in like manner.” The one will of both is also repeatedly demonstrated.

To their fourth objection, “The Father is greater than I,” he grants that this is truly said because the Father is the Son’s source, and because the Son is not equal to the Father according to the form of a servant. But if the Father is greater than the Son because he gives him what he is, the Son is not less than the Father because he receives everything that the Father is.

[Col. 0279D] Finally, he refutes by several arguments the ignorance which the heretics ascribe to Christ. For the creator of all things, expressly the author and Lord of this day, could not be ignorant of the day of judgment; the Father hides nothing from him, and in him are all the treasures of knowledge. Yet because they are hidden, he rightly says that he does not know what is not to be spoken. Therefore the Father alone knows the day of judgment, because he alone does not keep it silent from the Son; but the Son does not know it because he reveals it to no one.

257  
### 1. What was accomplished in the preceding book; what was refuted

In the preceding book, treating of the undifferentiated nature of God the Father and God the Son, and demonstrating that the saying, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:38), does not lead to a solitary God but to the unity of an undifferentiated nature according to the generation of the Godhead—for God was born from none other than God, and God from God cannot fail to be what God is—and having surveyed testimonies from divine and apostolic utterances, if not all of them, yet sufficient for understanding, by which the inseparable nature and power of Father and Son were taught, we came as far as this passage of the apostolic faith, where he says: “See that no one deceives you through philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ; for in him all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Col. 2:8–9).

[Note: [Col. 0279D] “To the divinity of an undifferentiated nature.”]

In this passage we taught that, through the fullness of divinity dwelling bodily in him, he is shown to be true and perfect God, and God of the Father’s nature: so that the indwelling fullness is understood neither to signify something different nor something singular. For both the bodily indwelling of the incorporeal God teaches the property of natural unity in the God who subsists from God; and God dwelling in Christ shows the birth of the subsisting Christ, because he is Christ’s indweller.

[Note: [Col. 0279D] In the printed editions and in some manuscripts: “of an undifferentiated nature.” In the Basel Vatican codex alone, “of a differentiated nature”; on the authority of this manuscript, and also of the Chartres manuscript, three Colbert manuscripts, one Sorbonne manuscript, and the Martin and German manuscripts, we have subsequently removed the word “nature.”]

[Note: [Col. 0279D] That is, of a distinct subsistence. Nor is the birth itself here shown directly; but since one is he who is dwelt in and another he who dwells, the subsistence of the indwelling Father and of the Son in whom he dwells is not signified as one. Consequently the birth is shown, by which alone the Son subsists as other than the Father.]

By this, I think, a more than adequate answer has been given to the impiety of those who refer the words spoken by the Lord—“He who has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9); “The Father is in me, and I in the Father” (John 10:38); “I and the Father are one” (ibid. 30); and “All things that are the Father’s are mine” (John 16:15)—to unity and harmony of will. Thus, while the authority of the saying remains, their counterfeit religion of deceptive teaching corrupts its meaning; and though agreement of wills cannot be denied in those passages in which unity of nature is proclaimed, they nevertheless suppose that only a partnership of concord exists, in order to abolish the unity which is according to birth.

[Note: [Col. 0280D] The Leipzig and Paris editions: “to unanimity.”]

[Note: [Col. 0280D] In the Martin manuscript: “of will.”]

But after the blessed Apostle’s many unambiguous proclamations of natural truth, when he teaches the fullness of divinity dwelling bodily in Christ, every assertion of impious rashness is cut off, because the bodily indwelling of incorporeal divinity establishes natural unity. Thus the statements that the Son is not alone, but that the Father remains in him; that he not only remains, but also works and speaks; and that he not only works and speaks, but also is seen, are not merely titular but true. For through the mystery of birth he has in himself power from power, authority from authority, and nature from nature; through birth he holds in himself that which is his own, and through the image refers from himself what is in himself, since he is both the image and the truth of the Author. For perfect birth supplies a perfect image, and the fullness of divinity dwelling bodily possesses natural truth.

[Note: [Col. 0280D] After Lipsius, the Paris edition here inserts a full stop and then adds “They are not,” as though these matters were complete in themselves; whereas they plainly refer to the words “that which,” which, although not repeated further, are nevertheless readily understood as requiring repeated supply: for example, “that which not only remains in him, but also works in him”; and “that which not only works and speaks in him, but also is seen in him.”]

[Col. 0281A]

[Note: [Col. 0281C] In one Vatican manuscript: “power from power, authority from authority, and nature from nature.” The Son, who is Power, has in himself the Power who is the Father; for, as is said in the preceding book, no. 24, in God those things which are his are not other than what he himself is; and no. 26: the reality belongs to the Son’s nature, but the same reality also belongs to the Father’s nature.]

[Note: [Col. 0281C] In the editions of Badius and Erasmus, and in the Basel Vatican manuscript: “through his own image.” This should be understood thus: through birth, that is, as the Father’s offspring, he holds in himself that which belongs to him—namely, to the Father—and through the image, that is, insofar as he is the image, which is from himself, that is, from the very substance of the Father, he refers what is in himself, namely in the Father himself.]

### 2. The Scriptures abused by the Arians; why they do not grasp their meaning

And although these things are such as they are, because God, naturally from God, cannot exist except in that nature of his birth in which God is God, and because the undifferentiated unity of living nature is inseparable from itself in the birth of living nature, nevertheless heretics creep in under the saving confession of evangelical faith in order to destroy the truth, by taking sayings spoken otherwise and for another purpose, and arranging them as though they were to be understood otherwise and for another purpose.

[Note: [Col. 0281D] The Paris edition: “so that they have this in themselves.”]

[Note: [Col. 0281D] Two manuscripts: “which God is.” Then the Basel Vatican codex: “as of a living being,” rather than “and.” Here two reasons are indicated by which we are taught that Christ is God: first, because he is born from God and consequently is either God or degenerate; second, because, like the Father, he also has life in himself. See the preceding book, no. 43.]

[Note: [Col. 0281D] In one Vatican manuscript: “for the diversity of truth”; in the other, “for diversity,” which Erasmus suspected should be read, while he himself together with Badius printed “for adversity.” With the other books, “for the destruction of truth” must be retained—that is, so that they may take away the Son’s true nature.]

Thus, denying the Son of God, they employ the authority by which he said: “Why do you call me good? No one is good except the one God” (Mark 10:18). They argue that because his confession spoke of one God, whatever thereafter bears the name of God no longer remains in God’s nature, because God is one. And, in order that he who is called God may be so called by title rather than in truth, they endeavor to establish this from his saying: “This is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God” (John 17:3). To show that he is outside the property of the true God, they add: “The Son cannot do anything from himself, except what he sees the Father doing” (John 5:19). They also attempt to use the statement: “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28). Finally, as though by an indissoluble confession repudiating divinity they had overthrown the Church’s faith, they boast when they read: “But concerning that day and hour no one knows—not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but the Father alone” (Mark 13:32).

[Note: [Col. 0281D] The particles “thereafter” and “now,” omitted in the printed editions, are restored by the aid of the manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 0282C] In the printed editions: “the only and true.” The word “and” is absent from the Greek and the manuscripts; in most of them “hold” follows shortly afterward, not “attempt.”]

For a nature which is necessarily different through ignorance does not seem capable of equality by birth; and the Father’s knowing and the Son’s not knowing would reveal a dissimilarity of divinity, since God ought to be ignorant of nothing, and one who is ignorant cannot be compared with one who knows. But, understanding none of these things by reason, distinguishing neither the times nor the evangelical mysteries, and perceiving neither the force of the sayings, they speak with foolish and unskilled madness against the nature of divinity. To fill the ears of the ignorant, they cite these words alone and bare, while passing over their explanations or their causes in silence; though the understanding of sayings must be sought either from what precedes or from what follows.

[Note: [Col. 0282C] The Basel Vatican manuscript reads “the evangelical mysteries.” This suggests a not sufficiently careful corrector, who did not notice that after “understanding” one must supply “all these things,” namely the Scriptural testimonies just cited in the name of the Arians. They are accused of failing to weigh them according to the evangelical mysteries—that is, according to what the Gospel has revealed to us, among which Christ’s eternal and temporal birth occupies the chief place.]

[Note: [Col. 0282C] The Basel Vatican codex: “knowing.” Bandinus, after Latinius, conjectures “agreeing.” “Perceiving” must certainly be retained, that is, not having sufficiently established and clearly grasped the force of the evangelical sayings just cited.]

[Note: [Col. 0282D] Thus the older books, most of which earlier read “things set forth” rather than “things placed before.” Others read “let it be expected.”]

### 3. Christ is both God and man. Let Nestorius and Eutyches take heed

Since we are about to give an account of these matters just mentioned from the evangelical or apostolic confessions themselves, we consider that all who share the faith must be admonished: that in the confession in which is the eternity of life, there may also be understanding of eternity. He plainly does not know his own life—he does not know it—who does not know Christ Jesus to be true God and likewise true man. And it is a matter of the same danger to deny of Christ Jesus either God the Spirit or the flesh of our body.

[Note: [Col. 0282D] Erasmus, Lipsius, and Paris: “being about to give”; but Badius and the better manuscripts oppose this, although in Book IV, no. 7, and elsewhere, the verb is used in this sense in such expressions.]

[Note: [Col. 0282D] That is, just as the Father, so also the Son is to be understood to be in eternal, that is divine, nature, since confession of the latter as of the former grants us eternal life. This is explained more clearly below, no. 33.]

[Note: [Col. 0282D] These words are cited by Leo to Leo, Augustine, Letter 134, ch. 3, and Theodoret, Dialogue II, p. 106.]

[Note: [Col. 0281C] The scribe added in the margin: “concerning true flesh.”]

Therefore, “Everyone who confesses me before men, I also will confess him before my Father who is in heaven. But whoever denies me before men, I also will deny him before my Father who is in heaven.” These things were spoken by the Word made flesh, and taught by Jesus Christ, the man and Lord of majesty: he himself established in himself as Mediator for the salvation of the Church, and in that very mystery of mediation between God and human beings existing as one who is both. For, from the natures united into one and the same, he is the same reality of each nature; yet in such a way that he lacked neither in either, lest perhaps God should cease to be God by being born as man, and man in turn should fail to be man by remaining God.

[Note: [Col. 0282D] The word “he says,” added here in the printed editions without manuscript authority, is plainly superfluous from what follows.]

[Note: [Col. 0283C] “One.”]

This, then, is the true faith of human blessedness: to proclaim God and man, to confess Word and flesh; neither to have God fail to know that he is man, nor flesh fail to know that it is Word.

### 4. That God, born as man, remains God no longer escapes our understanding

But since God remains God while being born as man, contrary to the nature of our understanding, it is no longer contrary to the nature of our hope that man, having been born, should remain God. For the higher nature, born into the lower, gives assurance that the lower can be born into the higher nature. Indeed, according to the law and custom of the world, the fulfillment of our hope is more readily accepted than the effect of the divine mystery. For the world has, in those things which are born, the capacity for growth; it does not have the power of diminution.

[Note: [Col. 0283C] That is, we grasp more readily that a human being will become God—which is our hope—than that God has become human—which is the divine mystery. Saint Leo agrees, Sermon 4 on the Nativity of the Lord, ch. 2: “It is less marvelous,” he says, “for a human being to advance to divine things than for God to descend to human things.” Augustine, Letter 140, no. 11, likewise says: “Nor should we now despair that human beings can become children of God through participation in the Word, when the Son of God became the Son of Man through participation in flesh.” Lest anyone be suspicious of what our Hilary subsequently discusses on this matter, we should note beforehand that he intends human beings to become God through the closest union with him in such a way that human nature is by no means abolished, as he expressly proves in On Psalm 2, no. 41, where he finally concludes: “Therefore a transformation occurs, but abolition is not brought about.”]

[Note: [Col. 0283D] In the Basel Vatican manuscript: “certainly.” In the printed editions, “grass” stands in place of the word “behold.”]

Behold trees, crops, and animals. Consider also man himself, endowed with reason: he always advances by growth and is never contracted by diminution; nor does that which has grown cease to be itself in itself. For although he may wither through age or be destroyed by death, he has either alteration in time or an end in the condition of life. Yet what he is does not have the power not to be, so as to make himself new through diminution from the same self—that is, so as to decline from an old man into a little child.

[Note: [Col. 0283D] The printed editions read “from himself.”]

[Note: [Col. 0283D] An old Colbert manuscript together with the German manuscript: “in the practice of living.”]

[Note: [Col. 0283D] Badius and Erasmus: “in truth.” The other books rightly read “in power,” that is, in capacity. The purpose of this argument is that we can indeed advance to what we do not have, but cannot cease to be what we already are; for example, an old man can increase the number of years already completed, but cannot similarly reduce it.]

Therefore the necessity of our nature, carried by the law of the world always toward increase, not unreasonably expects the advance of the higher nature: for increase is according to its nature, and diminution is contrary to its nature. It was therefore proper to God to be other than what he remained, and yet not to cease to be what he had remained: to be born as God in man, yet not to cease to be God; to contract himself as far as conception, cradle, and infancy, yet not to depart from the power of God. This is a mystery not for himself but for us. Nor is our assumption an advancement for God; but his willing acceptance of dishonor is our advancement, since he does not lose what he is as God, and acquires for humanity that it may be God.

[Note: [Col. 0283D] In manuscripts of good quality: “rashly.” Shortly afterward Badius and Erasmus, with the Basel Vatican manuscript, read “of the former” in place of “of the higher.”]

[Note: [Col. 0284C] Thus the manuscripts, as below, no. 8, we read “born in man,” and Book V, no. 18, “God being born in man.” But the printed editions read “in humanity.”]

[Note: [Col. 0284C] That is, this mystery of our assumed flesh is the cause of our salvation, but adds or takes away nothing from God. Compare Book XI, nos. 48 and 49.]

### 5. By his words and deeds Christ showed himself Son of God and Son of Man; whence the occasion of heresy

Therefore the only-begotten God, born as man from the Virgin and, in the fullness of time, about to advance humanity in himself into God, maintained throughout the whole manner of evangelical discourse that he should be believed to be the Son of God and should be proclaimed the Son of Man. As man he spoke and did everything that belongs to God; then as God he spoke and did everything that belongs to man. Yet even in that very discourse of both kinds, he never spoke except with an indication both of man and of God. He always showed the one God the Father, and confessed himself to be in the nature of the one God through the truth of his birth; yet he did not fail to show himself subject to God the Father both in the honor of Sonship and in the condition of man. For every birth refers itself to its author, and all flesh confesses itself weak in relation to God.

[Note: [Col. 0284C] The ambiguity will be removed if you read: “about to advance man into God.”]

[Note: [Col. 0284C] “In that very [discourse].”]

[Note: [Col. 0284C] Thus the manuscripts. But the printed editions read, “and yet,” omitting “not” afterward. Christ signified that he was subject to the Father both according to divine nature, insofar as he is Son, and according to human nature, insofar as he is weak.]

[Note: [Col. 0284D] The Basel Vatican codex adds “of God” here, which is rightly absent from the others, since the statement is general.]

Hence the heretics find their opportunity to deceive the simple and ignorant: they falsely assert that things said by him according to his humanity were said according to weakness of divine nature. And because one and the same person speaks all that he speaks, they maintain that he spoke everything concerning himself.

[Note: [Col. 0284D] The printed editions read “concerning himself.” The phrase “concerning himself” should be noted. Though Hilary believes God and man in Christ to be most closely united in one person, he nevertheless considers the man as though distinct from God himself, so that he argues against heretics because they wish him to have spoken concerning himself—that is, concerning his own divinity—what he spoke concerning the assumed man. In this manner of speaking Ambrose says, Book X on Luke, no. 61: “But he is sorrowful—not he himself, but the soul.” The same applies to the statement of the ancient author of *On the Orthodox Faith*, ch. 8, among the appendices to Ambrose, vol. II: “That man suffered, whom the Son of God assumed, clothed himself with, and bore; but because everything that man suffered was referred to the Author, death and passion are therefore judged to be those of the Lord.”]

262  
### 6. Some sayings of Christ belong to the time before he was born, others to the time when he was born and was to die, others to his eternal state

Nor indeed do we deny that the whole discourse which belongs to his nature is his own. But if Jesus Christ is both man and God; if he did not first become God when he became man; if, when he was both man and God, he was not then also not God; and if, after man has been brought into God, the whole man is wholly God—the mystery of his sayings must necessarily be one appropriate to the respective kind.

[Note: [Col. 0285B] That is, the discourse which is his, or which he utters in his own name. Moreover, by “nature” one may understand “person,” just as Hilary more than once uses “person” to denote nature. Or this should be understood thus: the entire discourse belongs to the nature proper and peculiar to Christ. But his own nature is not only that which he received by being born, but also that which he assumed in time.]

[Note: [Col. 0285B] “Then when [he became] man.”]

[Note: [Col. 0285C] The printed editions read “nor when man.” Immediately following “man in God,” that is, after man has been glorified in God. In Christ one must distinguish the time when he had not yet assumed man, the time when he assumed man who was to die, and the time when man was no longer to die. In the first state he is God alone; in the second, God and man; in the last, wholly God, in the sense explained below.]

[Note: [Col. 0285C] The word “mystery” is lacking in the oldest Colbert manuscript. Here it is urged that Christ’s sayings must be understood in accordance with his different natures considered under a threefold state.]

When, according to time, you distinguish man in him from God, distinguish the discourse of God at that time from that of man. And when you confess God and man in time, judge sayings according to God and man in time. But when, from the time of man and God, you again understand the time of the whole man, now wholly God, then whatever was said for the manifestation of that time, fit what has been said to the time.

[Note: [Col. 0285C] In the old Remigius manuscript: “spoken by God and man,” erroneously. If we understand Hilary’s intention rightly, it means this: when, according to the time preceding Christ’s embodiment, you regard God the Son as distinct from man and not yet united to him, do not then attribute to him a discourse appropriate to man; that is, assign to him, when he is God, a discourse distinct and different from that which you would assign to man. Or perhaps the state is also indicated in which the only-begotten God appeared as man for a time in an assumed form; and we are warned to distinguish what belongs to the assumed form and what belongs to him who assumes it.]

[Note: [Col. 0285D] The printed editions read “of the whole God also,” and then “if anything else,” instead of “if that thing,” thereby corrupting Hilary’s meaning. “But when from man and God,” etc., means: when you understand that Christ has passed from his mortal state, in which he was God and man, to the immortal state, in which he is now wholly God even according to man, because, as is explained below, no. 13, he lives wholly to God, the fellowship of our nature having been united to the communion of divine immortality. This manner of speaking, modeled expressly on Paul’s words that God may be all in all, must be understood with the reality of man preserved, as has often already been shown.]

Thus, since God before man is one thing, man and God another, and after man and God the whole man wholly God another, do not confuse the mystery of the dispensation by times and kinds. For according to the quality of the kinds and natures, he must necessarily have had one kind of discourse, in the mystery of man, when not yet born; another while still subject to death; another when now eternal.

### 7. In what respect Christ acted as man and in what respect as God; why he willed to be born, suffer, and die

Jesus Christ, therefore, remaining all these things for our sake, and born as man with our body, spoke according to the condition of our nature, yet without omitting that what he is as God belongs to his own nature. For although in birth, passion, and death he performed the realities of our nature, he nevertheless carried out all these realities by the power of his own nature: since he himself is the source of his birth; since he wills to suffer what it is not permitted for him to suffer; and since he dies who lives.

[Note: [Col. 0285B] “Condition.”]

[Note: [Col. 0286B] In the Colbert and German codices: “not his own nature”—a reading not to be despised, in the sense that Christ, speaking as man things belonging to human weakness, did not omit to indicate that these did not belong to his own nature; for by his own nature he is God, while he is man by dispensation, as is suggested in Book X, nos. 22, 64, and 65. Hence, in On Psalm 139, no. 2: “For what he is as God belongs to his own nature; but that he was man is an assumption of our nature.” Indeed, in this very book, no. 9: “But after the mystery both of his own nature and of our assumption has been shown.”]

[Note: [Col. 0286B] “Performed the reality.”]

[Note: [Col. 0286C] The printed editions read “performed the reality.” If Christ performed the realities of our nature in passion and death, he necessarily truly feared, grieved, and so forth. This should meanwhile be noted.]

[Note: [Col. 0286C] Here Paul’s words in no. 13, to be expounded, are in view: “Though he was crucified from weakness, yet he lives from the power of God.” This also removes the suspicion of those who think that Hilary believed Christ the man to have been abandoned and deserted by the Word before he died. For if he who lives died, God died; and therefore God did not withdraw from Christ before he died. Hence shortly afterward the immortal God is proclaimed to have placed himself under the law of death, God dying through flesh—a point pressed many times in this section.]

Yet when God does these things through man, having been born from himself, having suffered through himself, and having died from himself, he nevertheless did not fail to act as man, since he was born, suffered, and died. These mysteries of heavenly things were established before the creation of the world: that the only-begotten God might will to be born as man, so that man might remain eternally in God; that God might will to suffer, so that the devil, raging through the sufferings of human weakness, might not retain in us the law of sin when God assumed our weakness; and that God might will to die, so that no arrogant power might exist against God, nor might it usurp the nature of created power in itself, since the immortal God had placed himself under the law of death.

[Note: [Col. 0286D] The Son was born from himself because, by his own strength and power, he undertook that which was alien to himself, as is explained in Book II, no. 26. There we showed that Hilary understood by the Holy Spirit coming upon the Virgin the Son himself, who is accordingly here said to be himself the source of his own birth.]

[Note: [Col. 0286D] That is, so that man might remain eternally in God. Similar are Book XI, no. 42: “with all things remaining in God’s glory, that is, in God all in all, through the dispensation of subjection”; and shortly before: “with the whole [humanity] now remaining in God through the dispensation by which he is man.”]

[Note: [Col. 0286D] An allusion to Paul’s words, “blotting out the handwriting against us,” which are treated below, no. 10, and Book I, no. 13.]

[Note: [Col. 0286D] The Basel Vatican manuscript reads “had dwelt,” omitting the preceding “himself.”]

Thus God is born for our assumption, suffers for innocence, and finally dies for vengeance: since our humanity remains in God, the sufferings of our weaknesses are shared by God, and the powers of spiritual wickedness and maliciousness are subjected through the triumph of the flesh, God dying through flesh.

[Note: [Col. 0287C] Corruptly: “and spiritual wickedness and the power of malice.”]

[Note: [Col. 0287C] The Leipzig and Paris editions read “spiritual wickedness,” against the other books. Shortly afterward the Chartres codex reads “in flesh,” not “through flesh.”]

### 8. The faithful are full of God in Christ

The Apostle, therefore, aware of this mystery and having received the knowledge of faith through the Lord himself, since he knew that the world, human beings, and philosophy were incapable of it, says: “See that no one deceives you through philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elements of the world, and not according to Jesus Christ; for in him all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily, and you have been filled in him, which is the head and principle of all rule and authority” (Col. 2:8 ff.).

[Note: [Col. 0287C] “Traditions”; shortly afterward, “and not according to Jesus,” omitting “Christ.”]

[Note: [Col. 0287C] Nearly all manuscripts read “traditions,” although above, no. 1, in the preceding book, no. 53, and in Book I, no. 13, they read “tradition.”]

[Note: [Col. 0287D] Thus most and the better manuscripts, supported by the following words: “That we are filled in him is the head and principle of all authority.” But the printed editions read “who is the head,” as occurs in Book I, no. 13.]

Having set forth the fullness of divinity dwelling bodily in him, he immediately added the mystery of our assumption, saying: “You have been filled in him.” For as fullness of divinity is in him, so we are filled in him. He certainly did not say, “You have been filled,” but “You have been filled in him,” because all who have been regenerated and are to be regenerated unto eternal life through the hope of faith now remain in Christ’s body; later, when they themselves are filled—not now in him, but in themselves—according to that time of which the Apostle says: “He will transform the body of our humiliation to be conformed to the body of his glory” (Phil. 3:21).

[Note: [Col. 0287D] The Basel Vatican codex, the Martin manuscript, two Colbert manuscripts, and one Sorbonne manuscript wrongly add “filled” here. The reason given here why believers are filled with God in Christ is that they remain in his body, which, having already become a participant in glory, is consequently full of God. They remain in his body because, as is said in On Psalm 51, no. 16, “Christ assumed in himself the nature of all flesh.” Hence, in Commentary on Matthew, ch. 4, no. 12, Christ’s flesh is called a city in which a certain gathering of the entire human race is contained. Thus Ambrose says, Letter 76, to Irenaeus, no. 8: “In that flesh of Christ, through participation in the same nature, all flesh of the human race was honored.” They will be filled in themselves when, in their own bodies, they share in the same glory.]

[Note: [Col. 0287C] “Will transform”; then “of the body,” not “to the body.”]

[Note: [Col. 0288C] Several manuscripts read “has transformed.” The Martin manuscript reads “will transform,” as does the Basel Vatican codex, which, with some others, later adds “making [it] conformed to the body,” or “of the body.”]

Now, therefore, we have been filled in him—that is, through the assumption of his flesh, in whom the fullness of divinity dwells bodily. And the power of this hope of ours in him is not slight. For that we are filled in him is the head and principle of all authority, according to the saying: “That at his name every knee may bend, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth; and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. 2:10–11).

[Note: [Col. 0288C] Thus Badius and most manuscripts. But Erasmus, Lipsius, and Paris read “may bend.” In the Basel Vatican manuscript and another Vatican manuscript: “that at the name of Jesus every knee may bend”; from which “heavenly beings,” not “of heavenly beings,” should follow. Greek: ἵνα ἐν τῷ ὀνόματι Ἰησοῦ πᾶν γόνυ κάμψῃ, “that at the name of Jesus every knee may bend.”]

[Note: [Col. 0288C] The Verona manuscript: “is in the glory of God the Father”; Greek: εἰς δόξαν θεοῦ πατρός, “to the glory of God the Father.” Shortly afterward, we have substituted “Jesum” from our manuscript; previously the text read “Jesus.”]

This, then, will be the confession: that Jesus, born as man, remains in the glory of God the Father, no longer in the weakness of our body but in God’s glory. And every tongue will confess this. And when heavenly and earthly beings bend the knee, this is the head of all rule and authority: that all things are subjected to him by bending the knee, in whom we have been filled and who, through the fullness of divinity dwelling bodily in him, must be confessed to be in the glory of God the Father.

[Note: [Col. 0288D] The Martin manuscript adds here: “and infernal beings.”]

[Note: [Col. 0288D] The printed editions add “God” here, a word absent from the better manuscripts.]

### 9. The same God is the author of our regeneration and of Christ’s resurrection

After showing both the mystery of his own nature and that of our assumption—since, while the fullness of divinity remains in him, we are filled in him through the fact that he was born as man—the Apostle proceeds to the remaining dispensation of human salvation, saying: “In whom you were also circumcised with a circumcision not made by hand, in the stripping off of the body of flesh, but in the circumcision of Christ, having been buried with him in baptism, in which you also rose with him through faith in the working of God, who raised him from the dead” (Col. 2:11–12).

Therefore we are circumcised not by fleshly circumcision but by Christ’s circumcision—that is, by being reborn into the new man. For when we are buried in his baptism, we must die to the old man, because the regeneration of baptism is the power of resurrection. And this is Christ’s circumcision: not to strip off the flesh of the foreskin, but to die wholly with him and thereafter to live wholly with him through this. For in him we rise through faith in that God who raised him from the dead. Therefore he must be believed to be God by whose working Christ was raised from the dead, because this faith rises with Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0288C] The Verona exemplar prefers “his baptism.”]

[Note: [Col. 0288D] The ancient Martin, Vatican, Basel, Colbert, and other books read “his baptism.” The Remigius manuscript reads “in baptism with him,” which was quite pleasing. But just as above it is said “Christ’s circumcision,” so now “his baptism,” that is, reception of the baptism instituted by him.]

[Note: [Col. 0288D] The Martin manuscript reads “we rose,” and afterward, “rose with Christ,” not “rises with Christ.”]

### 10. The Same Christ Dies as Man and Raises Himself as God

Then the whole mystery of the assumed man is thus brought to completion:

> And you, when you were dead in sins and in the uncircumcision of your flesh, he made alive together with him, forgiving you all sins, blotting out the handwriting which was against us in the decrees, which was contrary to us; and he took it out of the way, fastening it to the cross; stripping off the flesh, he made principalities and powers a public spectacle, triumphing over them in himself. (Col. 2:13 ff.)

[Note: Thus the manuscripts. Printed editions, however, prefix the particle *cum* (“when”) to *mortui* (“dead”). We noted that it is absent from the manuscripts in Book I, §13. Shortly afterwards the Martinian manuscript has “forgiving you all sins,” as it is read in Book X, §47, but differently in Book I, §13.]

[Note: “Having stripped off flesh.” In the Carnotensis manuscript *with boldness* is added here; this also occurs in Book I, §13, and Book X, §47, where the same passage is not presented in exactly the same way. In the Vatican-Basilican and Martinian manuscripts: “having stripped off flesh, and dishonoring principalities and powers, and triumphing with boldness.” Here, however, it must be carefully observed that *exutus carnem* (“having stripped off flesh”) is to be taken actively, not passively: as though stripping himself of flesh, as is read below in Book X, §47, and indeed here also, where these same words are explained. The whole force of the following argument rests upon this active sense. Although, instead of *exutus carnem et potestates*, Latin codices now read *exspolians principatus* (“despoiling principalities”); and the Greek copies agree, including the Germanensis, which contains Paul’s Epistles in Greek and Latin and was written at least a thousand years ago, in which, as in the others, occurs ἀπεκδυσάμενος τὰς ἀρχάς (“having stripped off the principalities”). Yet from the expression τὰς ἀρχάς (“the principalities”) τὴν σάρκα (“the flesh”) could easily have been produced. Certainly Augustine, *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, ch. 27; Book XVI *Against Faustus*, ch. 29; and *On the Christian Conflict*, ch. 2, reads with our Hilary, “stripping himself of flesh.” So too Ambrose, Book V *On Luke*, §107: “Stripping himself of flesh, he exposed all principalities and powers”; and Book III *On Faith*, ch. 2: “He who fastened it [the handwriting] to the cross stripped himself of flesh; but the Father did not strip himself of flesh,” etc. Finally, in Ambrose himself, the author of the *Treatise on the Apostles’ Creed* says: “Therefore he was not stripped of flesh by anyone’s right or power, but he stripped himself. For he who could avoid dying had he not wished, undoubtedly died because he wished. Proving this, the Apostle says: ‘stripping himself of flesh, he exposed principalities and powers.’” Yet these differ from Hilary in adding *principalities* after “stripping himself of flesh,” a word which Hilary customarily omits, although that same reading was not unknown to him, as is clear from §11.]

The man of this world does not grasp the apostolic faith; nor does any speech other than Paul’s own explain the meaning of his words.

[Note: In the Vatican-Basilican manuscript: “his meaning.” Erasmus should not be heard, who conjectures that *excessus* should be read in place of *sensus*. The sense is this: a person equipped only with the wisdom of the world does not attain Paul’s faith, nor should the interpretation of his sayings be sought from anywhere other than his other sayings.]

God raises Christ from the dead—Christ in whom the fullness of divinity dwells bodily. Yet he made us alive together with him, forgiving us sins and blotting out the handwriting of the law of sin, which, through the preceding decrees, was contrary to us; removing this from the midst and fastening it to the cross; stripping himself of flesh by the law of death; making the powers a public spectacle; and triumphing over them in himself.

[Note: What Hilary here calls “the handwriting of the law of sin,” and above, in §7, simply “the law of sin,” he calls in Book I, §13, “the sentence of death,” with Tertullian’s support, *On Modesty* §19, where he reads: “the handwriting of death having been forgiven.”]

We have already discussed above (Book I, §13) the powers triumphed over in himself and made a public spectacle, the handwriting blotted out, and ourselves made alive. But who can either comprehend or express this mystery? The operation of God raises Christ from the dead; this same operation of God makes us alive with Christ; and this same operation forgives sins, blots out the handwriting, and fastens it to the cross: it strips off flesh, makes the powers a public spectacle, and triumphs over them in himself.

[Note: Again here Erasmus, Lipsius, and the Paris edition read “the operation of God”; the Badius edition and the manuscript disagree.]

You have the operation of God raising Christ from the dead; you have also Christ himself performing in himself these very things which God performs.

[Note: The Vatican-Basilican codex alone reads “performed.”]

For Christ died, stripping himself of flesh. Therefore hold fast that Christ as man was raised from the dead by God; hold fast that Christ as God, when about to die, was performing the operation of our salvation.

[Note: “Operation.”]

Thus, while God performs these things in Christ—God indeed performing—Christ nevertheless, stripping himself of flesh, is about to die; and when Christ has died, God, working before his death, nevertheless raises the dead Christ by his operation. For he who raises Christ from the dead is himself the one who worked as Christ before death, and who, stripping himself of flesh, was about to die.

[Note: Printed editions read “may perform,” contrary to the authority of the manuscripts.]

[Note: The printed editions, except the Paris edition, read “Christ raised from the dead,” against the manuscripts.]

### 11. The Flesh Stripped Off and He Who Strips Himself of Flesh Are One Christ

Do you now understand the mystery of the apostolic faith? Do you now know Christ? For I ask you: who is he that strips himself of flesh, and what is that flesh which was stripped off? For I recognize in the Apostle a twofold meaning: flesh stripped off, and one stripping himself of flesh; and amid these I hear that Christ was raised from the dead by the operation of God.

And since God is the one who raises Christ from the dead, and Christ is also raised from the dead, I ask: who is he that strips himself of flesh, and who is he that raises Christ from the dead and makes us alive with Christ? For if the Christ who died is not the same as the flesh stripped off, show the identity of the flesh stripped off; and again, explain the nature of him who stripped himself of flesh.

For I find that the God-Christ raised from the dead is the same one who stripped himself of flesh; and again, that the flesh stripped off, raised from the dead, is Christ. Further, I find him making principalities and powers a public spectacle and triumphing in himself. Do you understand this one triumphing over the powers in himself? Do you perceive that the flesh stripped off and he who strips himself of flesh are not different from one another? For he triumphs in himself—that is, in that flesh by which he stripped himself of flesh.

Do you see how God and man are thus proclaimed: death being attributed to the man, but the raising of the flesh to God—yet not so that the one who died is another than the one through whom the dead man rises? For the flesh stripped off is Christ who died; and again, Christ who raises Christ from the dead is the same Christ who strips himself of flesh.

[Note: In Leo, Epistle 134 of the new edition, addressed to Emperor Leo, ch. 3, where these and other sayings of Hilary are cited, the text reads “for flesh stripped off,” incorrectly. Everything argued in this book so far, and especially this statement, does not suit one who thought that the Word was separated from Christ’s dead flesh. Hence Hilary is rightly believed to have been remote from that opinion. For since the one and same Christ is he who strips himself of flesh, the flesh stripped off, and he who raises the stripped flesh—and he is one, not by unity of nature but of person—it follows that Hilary believed the person of the Word united to the stripped flesh.]

Understand the nature of God in the power of the resurrection; recognize the dispensation of man in death. And although both belong to their respective natures, remember nevertheless that the one Christ Jesus is he who is both.

### 12. Christ Is Raised by His Own Power: Why Paul Attributes This Work to the Father

Although I remember that the Apostle frequently refers Christ’s resurrection from the dead to God the Father, yet the Apostle is not, in his own statements, contrary to evangelical faith—especially since the Lord says:

> For this reason the Father loves me: because I lay down my life, that I may take it again. No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of myself. I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it again. This command I received from my Father. (John 10:17–18)

[Note: In most manuscripts: “his own statements.” A little earlier the Carnotensis manuscript has “you remember,” not “I remember.”]

[Note: Printed editions read “and take it again,” against the manuscripts.]

[Note: Greek also has αἴρει, “takes away.” *Tollit* is likewise read in Book X, §57.]

Or again, when he was asked to show a sign concerning himself for faith’s sake, he said concerning the temple of his body:

> Destroy this temple, and I will raise it in three days. (John 2:19; see the exposition of Ps. 141, §6.)

For, by both the authority to take up his life and the power to raise the temple, he teaches that he himself is God to himself in his own resurrection. Yet referring all this to the authority of the Father’s command, the Apostle is not to be understood as speaking contrarily when he proclaims Christ to be the power of God and the wisdom of God, and refers all the magnificence of Christ’s work to the Father’s glory; because whatever Christ does, the power and wisdom of God do, and whatever the power and wisdom of God do, God undoubtedly does, whose wisdom and power Christ is.

[Note: Badius, Erasmus, and Lipsius read “refers,” without manuscript authority. Then, for *contrarie*, Latinius and Baudinus conjectured *contraire*; there is no need to alter anything.]

[Note: Lipsius and Paris read “proclaimed,” and then, with the other printed editions, “and all the magnificence of the work,” etc. Corrected from the manuscripts.]

[Note: The Vatican-Basilican manuscript reads: “by this, because he had referred it to the Father’s glory,” corruptly; for the sense is: the Apostle is not understood to have referred all the magnificence of Christ’s work to the Father’s glory in a sense contrary to Christ’s preceding words.]

Finally, Christ is now raised from the dead by the operation of God, because he himself acted by a nature not different from God.

[Note: Thus the Vatican-Basilican and Martinian manuscripts, supported by others. Printed editions read: “he worked by a nature not different from God”; and in that passage omit “God.” We have already heard above that Christ is God of his own resurrection.]

And faith in God as regards the resurrection is faith in him who raised Christ from the dead.

### 13. Two Natures in Christ According to Paul

Therefore the blessed Apostle maintained this proclamation of a twofold signification in Christ, so as to teach both the weakness of man in him and the power and nature of God, according to what was said to the Corinthians:

> For though he was crucified through weakness, yet he lives by the power of God. (2 Cor. 13:4)

[Note: “From our weakness.”]

[Note: In the printed editions: “through our weakness.” *Our* is absent from the more accurate manuscripts and from the Greek, as also in Book X, §65. Shortly afterward *human* is absent from the Colbertine and German manuscripts.]

Thus he shows death to be of human weakness, but life to be of God’s power. And likewise in the Epistle to the Romans:

> For in that he died to sin, he died once; but in that he lives, he lives to God. So also reckon yourselves indeed dead to sin, but living to God in Christ Jesus. (Rom. 6:10–11)

[Note: The printed editions, except Paris, read “what died to sin, died.” Later the Martinian manuscript has “reckon,” not “attribute.”]

He attributes death to sin—that is, to our body—but life to God, to whom belongs by nature that which lives.
