Therefore we must die to our body in order that we may live to God in Christ Jesus, who, having assumed the body of our sin, now lives wholly to God, united through fellowship with our nature to the communion of divine immortality.

[Note: Thus Book I, §15: “For he received the flesh of sin,” since indeed he assumed true flesh from the Virgin, propagated from sinful Adam. Yet, as is clearly stated in Book X, §25, that flesh was not flesh of sin, but the likeness of sinful flesh.]

[Note: “In the communion of immortal substance.”]

[Note: The Vatican-Basilican, Corbie, Pratensis, and other manuscripts: “in the communion of immortal substance.”]

### 14. One Form of God, Another of a Servant: Yet the Same Christ. The Form of God Was Hidden, Not Lost

I had to demonstrate these matters briefly, so that we might remember that the person of both natures is to be considered in the Lord Jesus Christ: because he who remained in the form of God received the form of a servant, through which he became obedient unto death.

[Note: This may be understood thus: although Christ consists of a twofold nature, we are nevertheless admonished that there is one person; the following words favor this interpretation. Yet the immediately preceding statements require that by the term *person* we understand not so much subsistence as the condition and properties of each nature. In this sense Ambrose, *On Faith* II.8.61, says: “Do you wonder if, in the person of man, he said that the Father was greater, who in the person of man called himself a worm?” And in Epistle 48.4: “who in the person of man took the form of a servant”—as though he said, “who, as man, had the form of a servant.” See Hilary himself on Ps. 63, §3.]

For obedience unto death is not in the form of God, just as the form of God is not present in the form of a servant. Yet, by the mystery of the evangelical dispensation, he who is in the form of a servant is not other than he who is in the form of God. Nevertheless, receiving the form of a servant and remaining in the form of God are not the same; and receiving the form of a servant could not occur, unless he who remained in the form of God emptied himself, since the concurrence of the two forms is not compatible.

[Note: In the very ancient Carnotensis, Colbertine, and German manuscripts, “is not”: not inappropriately, if afterwards “of himself” is tacitly understood. This relates to Augustine, Epistle 11.4, who, confirming the necessity of the Incarnation, says: “No one raises another to the state in which he himself is, unless he descends in some measure to the state in which the other is.” Similar is this saying of our Hilary, Book XII, §6: “God could not depart from God into man unless God emptied himself from the form of God,” etc. In what follows here, that the conjunction of the two forms is incompatible, it is evident that the term *form* designates only the outward condition of each nature. Hence one may understand why Hilary calls Christ wholly God after the resurrection, but wholly in the form of a servant before it. Compare this passage with the exposition of Ps. 68, §25.]

But he who emptied himself is not other or different from him who received the form of a servant.

[Note: That is: he who emptied himself is not other than he who received the form of a servant; or, after his emptying, he is not other than he was before.]

For receiving cannot belong to one who does not exist; it belongs to one who subsists to receive. Therefore the emptying of form is not the abolition of nature: for he who empties himself does not lack himself; and he who receives remains.

[Note: “And he who received.”]

And since he himself is both the one emptying and the one receiving, there is indeed in him a mystery—that he empties himself and receives—yet there is no destruction, lest the one emptying cease to exist and the one receiving not exist. Thus the emptying has this result: that the form of a servant may come to be, not that Christ, who was in the form of God, may cease to remain Christ.

[Note: Printed editions read, “that Christ may not remain from himself”; corrected from the manuscripts. Thus below, §39: “that the form of God might remain as being.” The mystery of Christ’s self-emptying is excellently explained in Book XI, §48, and on Ps. 143, §7. Observe incidentally that the term *Christ* is more than once used to signify the divine nature.]

For none but Christ received the form of a servant. And when he emptied himself, so that Christ, remaining Spirit, might be the same Christ as man, the change of condition in the body and the assumption of nature did not destroy the nature of the divinity that remained; because one and the same Christ is both the one changing condition and the one assuming.

[Note: In the Corbie manuscript and several others: “remaining in the body”; a gloss.]

### 15. The Objections of the Heretics Examined. Christ Does Not Rebuke Being Called Good

Having therefore set forth the dispensation of the mysteries, through ignorance of which the heretics deceive some, so that they attribute to the weakness of divinity and assign to the form of God all that was said and done through the nature of the assumed man, whatever is properly suited to the form of a servant, we must now answer their very propositions.

[Note: Thus most manuscripts. Printed editions read “adapted.” Shortly afterward, in the Vatican-Basilican codex: “for by every kind . . .,” not “for safely . . . kinds.”]

For the kinds of each of the things already stated will now be safely judged, when faith alone confesses Word and flesh—that is, God and the man Jesus Christ.

The heretics therefore think that our Lord Jesus Christ must be denied to be God by nature because he said:

> Why do you call me good? No one is good except the one God. (Mark 10:18)

Every method of answering must proceed from the grounds of the questions. For an answer will be given to that from which the question arises. And first I ask the slanderer of this saying whether he thinks that the Lord rebukes being called good, and preferred to be called evil. For this seems to be signified by the saying, “Why do you call me good?”

I do not think anyone will be so foolish as to wish to ascribe a profession of wickedness to him who said:

> Come to me, all who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is pleasant and my burden light. (Matt. 11:28 ff.)

He professes himself gentle and humble, and is he to be believed angry because he was called good?

[Note: The old Colbertine codex has “with good.”]

These professions are inconsistent, if the witness of his goodness should accuse in himself the name of goodness. Therefore he is not understood to be angry at being called good. We must ask what other profession concerning himself he rebukes, since he cannot be believed to rebuke in himself the name of goodness.

### 16. He Rebukes the Questioner’s Faith, Not His Words

Let us therefore see what the questioner said besides “good.” For he said:

> Good Master, what good thing shall I do? (Mark 10:17)

He therefore named two things together: good and master. And because Christ does not rebuke being called good, he must rebuke this: that he was called a good master. Yet he rebukes being called a good master in such a manner as rather to rebuke the faith of the questioner than either the title of master or the name of good in himself.

For the presumptuous young man, through observance of the law, did not know Christ, the end of the law; thought himself justified by works; and did not understand that he had come to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, and that it was impossible for the law to save believers through the faith of justification. He therefore questions the Lord of the law and the only-begotten God as though he were a teacher of the ordinary precepts written in the law.

[Note: Yet he did not obey this from any motive, as is said and shown in *On Matthew*, ch. 19, §5. Augustine says, in what is now Epistle 157, §25: “I think he replied more arrogantly than truthfully that he had kept them.”]

Therefore the Lord, detesting this profession of irreligious faith concerning himself—because he was questioned as though he were a teacher of the law—answered: “Why do you call me good?” And to signify in what sense he ought to be understood and confessed as good, he added: “No one is good except the one God”; not rejecting the name of goodness, if it were attributed to him as God.

### 17. He Shows Himself Both Good and Master

Finally, showing that through the faith of one who questioned him as merely a man, he rebuked the title “good master” in himself, after the young man’s boast and glory in having fulfilled the law he answered:

> One thing is lacking to you: go, sell whatever you have and give to the poor, and you shall have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me. (Mark 10:21)

He who promises a heavenly treasure does not refuse the name of goodness concerning himself; nor does he wish not to be seen as master, who presents himself as guide to this perfect blessedness. Rather, he rebukes faith’s earthly opinion concerning himself, teaching that goodness is in God alone. And in order to signify himself as both God and good, he exercised the offices of goodness, opening heavenly treasures and offering himself as the forerunner to them.

Thus he rejects those things that were rendered to him as merely a man; nor does he profess himself alien from those things which he attributed to God, since, while confessing the one God as good, he himself spoke and did those things which belong to the power, goodness, and nature of the one God.

### 18. He Received the Name of Master When It Was Given with Faith

That he neither refused the name of goodness nor declined the honor of master, but rebuked the faith of one who had conceived in him nothing but what was bodily and fleshly, is understood from this: he spoke differently to the Apostles, who confessed him as master, saying:

> You call me Master and Lord, and you speak rightly, for I am. (John 13:13)

And elsewhere he said:

> Do not be called masters, for your master is Christ. (Matt. 23:10)

Where “master” is used with faith, he praises it so highly that he even professes the name. But here he does not acknowledge the name “good master,” where he is understood to be neither Lord nor Christ. While proclaiming the one God as good, he certainly does not separate himself from God: he who has professed himself both Lord and Christ, and shows himself the guide to heavenly treasure.

[Note: “Separates.”]

### 19. Everywhere the Lord Professes Himself Neither the Same as the Father nor Different from Him. In the Honor of Faith, and Therefore in Nature, He Made Himself Equal to the Father

The Lord always maintained this rule of ecclesiastical faith: while proclaiming the Father to be one God, he did not separate himself from the mystery of the one God; yet through the nature of his birth he professed himself to be neither another God nor God himself. For the nature of the one God does not permit him to be a God of a different kind, nor does his birth allow that what he is as Son should be imperfect in relation to the Father.

Thus he can neither be separated from God nor be God himself. By this means he so qualifies all the meaning of his speech that whatever honor he declares for God the Father, he also shows, by a most restrained confession, to belong to himself.

For when he says:

> Believe in God, and believe in me. (John 14:1)

I ask in what respect he distinguished himself in nature when he made no distinction in honor.

[Note: Some later manuscripts read “in which he [distinguished] himself by nature.” The Vatican-Basilican codex alone: “in which he [distinguished] himself by nature.” With the others, *in quo* is to be retained—that is, “in what respect.”]

For when he says, “Believe also in me,” after saying, “Believe in God,” is he not understood, by saying “in me,” also to have indicated his own nature? Separate the nature altogether if you separate the faith. If believing in God without Christ is life, tear Christ away from both God’s name and his property. But if believing in Christ brings to completion those who believe in God, let the careful reader weigh the force of the words: “Believe in God, and believe in me.”

[Note: We would prefer “in Christ,” if the manuscripts supported it. Shortly afterwards the Vatican-Basilican manuscript has “the force of the words.”]

For when he says, “Believe in God, and believe in me,” joining himself to faith in God, he joined himself also to God’s nature; since, after naming God in whom one must believe, he taught that one must believe also in himself—thereby teaching himself to be God, since those who believe in God must believe in him.

[Note: “In him is.” Thus Hilary had earlier said, “to believe in Christ.” Afterwards, “of irreligious union,” so that even from this may be confirmed the conjecture of the most learned Benedictine editor, who suspects that *unionis* is masculine in Hilary. The noun was of the same gender among all when used for “pearl.”]

Yet he excluded the occasion for an irreligious union: for, though he professed that one must believe both in God and in himself, he did not leave faith concerning himself as directed toward one who is solitary.

[Note: The earlier reading was “solitary.”]

### 20. In What Sense the Father Bore Witness to the Son and Was Not Heard. The Father’s Testimony among the Jews; Christ’s Works

Although in very many, indeed almost all, of his sayings he has provided an explanation of this mystery—lest whenever he confessed God the Father, he should separate himself from unity with him, or, while placing himself in his unity, nevertheless profess him to be one and solitary—yet the mystery of both unity and birth is especially understood from this saying:

> But I have a testimony greater than John’s. For the works which the Father has given me to complete, the very works which I do, bear witness of me, that the Father has sent me. And the Father who sent me has himself borne witness of me. You have neither ever heard his voice nor seen his form, and you do not have his word abiding in you; because you do not believe him whom he sent. (John 5:36 ff.)

How is it truly understood that the Father bore witness to the Son, when he himself was neither seen nor his voice heard? I remember, indeed, that a voice was heard from heaven, saying:

> This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him. (Matt. 3:17)

[Note: “I was well pleased.”]

[Note: The Colbertine codex reads “I was well pleased.” There is no difficulty here in the fact that the words “listen to him” were spoken not to John in the wilderness but to the Apostles on the mountain, since the force of the argument rests in the words “This is my Son.” Yet it is remarkable that the holy Doctor cites in Book VI, §19 words heard by John as we have them in the Vulgate of Matt. 3:17, but in Book VIII, §25, and elsewhere, gives them in the form found in Ps. 2:7, and finally here in the form of Matt. 17:5. Then he teaches that the meaning of the Father’s voice is contained in the voice heard, which pointed out the Son, because the Son cannot be signified without the Father also being signified.]

How then was God’s voice not heard, when the voice heard contains in itself the meaning of the Father’s voice?

[Note: “In itself.” Later: “they had heard.”]

But perhaps those dwelling in Jerusalem did not hear it, because John alone heard it in the wilderness. We must therefore ask how the Father bore witness in Jerusalem. For Christ is no longer using John’s testimony, who heard the voice from heaven; rather, he has a testimony greater than John’s, and he immediately added what it was:

> For the works which the Father gave me to complete, the very works which I do, bear witness of me that the Father has sent me.

I recognize the authority of the testimony: for no one except a Son sent by the Father would do these things. Therefore his work is his testimony. But what follows at last?

> And the Father who sent me has himself borne witness of me. You have neither ever heard his voice nor seen his form, and you do not have his word abiding in you.

Are those who do not know the Father’s testimony free from blame, because he has never been heard or seen among them and his word does not abide in them? But they are not excused by a testimony unknown to them, because he professes that the Father’s testimony concerning him is the testimony of his own works. Therefore the works bear witness concerning him that he was sent by the Father; but this testimony of the works is the Father’s testimony.

And since the Son’s operation is the Father’s testimony, we must understand that the nature by which the Father is witness operates in Christ.

[Note: In the *Treatise on the Unity of the Father and the Son*, in which nearly the whole of this book is transcribed, one should read “is to be understood.” In the Vatican-Basilican manuscript: “we must understand that that nature operates in Christ.” This may be read without obscurity as follows: “we must understand that the nature operates in Christ.”]

Thus Christ working, and the Father bearing witness in his work, are shown to be inseparable in accordance with birth; since God’s testimony concerning Christ is signified to be Christ’s own operation.

[Note: The older Colbertine manuscript: “and in his work.” Three others: “and his work.” Shortly afterwards most manuscripts have “show,” instead of “are shown”; in the *On Unity* treatise the word *se*, “themselves,” follows it.]

[Note: “They show.”]

### 21. The Jews Neither Saw nor Heard the Father Because They Did Not Believe Christ. Hence the Nature of Both Is One

Therefore they are not free from guilt on the ground that the testimony was unknown to them, since Christ’s work is the Father’s testimony. Nor are they without awareness of the testimony because they did not hear the witness’s voice, see his form, or possess his abiding word.

For to what was said:

> You have neither heard his voice nor seen his form, and you do not have his word abiding in you, (John 5:37–38)

[Note: The printed editions read: “And when the Father had borne witness concerning him, yet the reason…” Thus Hilary’s sentence is entirely broken and confused. The whole phrase could be arranged thus: “So that, although the Father had borne witness concerning him, the reason for neither the voice being heard…” might be understood. To what was said, “You have neither heard his voice,” etc., he immediately added: “Because you do not believe him whom he sent.”]

so that the reason why they had neither heard the voice, nor seen the form, nor had the word abiding in them might be understood, he immediately added:

> Because you do not believe him whom he sent. (John 5:38)

He thus shows that, if they believed in him, they would hear the voice of God, see the form of God, and possess his word; since, through the unity of nature, the Father both spoke in him, was seen in him, and was possessed in him.

[Note: In the Colbertine manuscript, *et haberetur* (“and was possessed”) is absent; in its place the Vatican-Basilican and Martinian manuscripts wrongly prefer “and was heard.” For just as “spoke” corresponds to “you have heard his voice,” and “was seen” to “you have seen his form,” so “was possessed” more rightly corresponds to “you do not have his word.” Shortly afterwards in the same Vatican-Basilican codex: “whether separable by any difference of nature”; in the Martinian manuscript: “whether by any separable nature,” etc.]

Does he not also signify the Father when he says that he has been sent by him? Does he distinguish himself from the Father by any difference of nature, when the Father bearing witness concerning him was neither heard, seen, nor understood precisely because they did not believe in the one sent by the Father?

[Note: This would cohere more fittingly with the words “neither heard”: namely, when the Father bore witness concerning him, he was therefore neither heard, seen, nor understood because, etc.]

Therefore the only-begotten God does not separate himself from God while confessing God the Father. Rather, by the designation of Father, having shown God the Father, he also places himself in the honor of God.

### 22. Honor Must Be Sought from God. Those Who Do Not Receive Christ in God’s Name Lack the Love of God

For in this same discourse, in which he teaches that his works testify that he himself was sent by the Father and signifies that the Father bears witness that he was sent by him, he says:

> And you do not seek the honor of him who alone is God. (John 5:44)

[Note: The Vatican-Basilican manuscript reads, corruptly: “yet it must not be unknown, this saying, and not…”]

Yet he did not leave this saying bare or unprepared beforehand for faith in unity. For above he said:

> You are unwilling to come to me, that you may have life. I do not receive honor from men; but I have known you, that you do not have the love of God in you. I have come in the name of my Father, and you have not received me. If another comes in his own name, him you will receive. How can you believe, you who receive honor from one another and do not seek the honor of him who alone is God? (John 5:40 ff.)

He rejects honor from men, because honor should rather be sought from God, and it belongs to unbelievers to receive honor from one another. For what honor can one human being confer upon another?

Therefore he says that he knows that the love of God is not in them; and he teaches that the reason why the love of God does not abide in them is that they do not receive him when he comes in the name of his Father. What, I ask, is it to come in the name of the Father? Is it anything other than to come in the name of God? Or is the love of God not in them precisely because the one coming in God’s name was not received? Or had he not also indicated in himself the nature of God when he said, “You are unwilling to come to me, that you may have life”?

For in the same discourse he had already said:

> Amen, amen, I say to you: the hour is coming, and now is, in which the dead shall hear the voice of the Son of God; and those who hear shall live. (John 5:25)

When he comes in the name of the Father, he is not the Father himself; yet neither is he outside that nature of divinity which the Father possesses. For it belongs properly to both Son and God to come in the name of God the Father.

Then another is to be received, coming in the same name. But he is a man, from whom people will hope for honor and to whom they will return honor in exchange, though he falsely claims that he too has come in the name of the Father.

[Note: Lipsius and Paris read “honor of man.”]

And it is not obscure that the Antichrist is signified here, glorying in the lie of the Father’s name.

[Note: In ancient books it is consistently written *antechristum*.]

When they honor him and are honored by him in turn—for they will receive this spirit of error—they will not seek the honor of him who alone is God.

### 23. The Honour of God and Christ Is Inseparable

Can Christ be understood to separate himself from the honour of the one God, when they lack the love of God for this reason: that they did not receive him when he came in the Father’s name, yet will receive another who comes in that same name; and, receiving honour from one another, do not seek the honour of him who alone is God? Since, by receiving Antichrist, they have not received him, whose rejection means the neglect of the honour of the one God, the honour of the one God must necessarily be contained in his honour. For had they remained in his reception, they would have sought the honour of the one God.

[Note: Five reliable manuscripts, although here [the reading is] the same.]

This same discourse itself bears witness for us, at whose beginning it is written: “That all may honour the Son as they honour the Father. He who does not honour the Son does not honour the Father who sent him” (John 5:23).

[Note: The printed editions: “for a nature is never other.” Then Badius and Erasmus: “is made equal.” They are corrected from the manuscripts. The same point is stated differently in Book XII, §7: “There is never diversity of things except also in diversity of honour: for the same things receive the same veneration,” etc.]

Only things belonging to the same nature are equal in honour; nor does equal honour separate those who are to be honoured. Yet equality of honour is required by the mystery of the birth.

[Note: This sentence, beginning “When the Son,” may be regarded as proof of the preceding statement, and accordingly ought not to be separated from it. Nevertheless, we judged that the customary punctuation—which joined it to what precedes and separated it from what follows—should be altered, so that Hilary’s argument, acutely drawn from two passages of Scripture, may be more clearly perceived. From one he concludes that the honour of Father and Son is inseparable; from the other, that honour given or denied to either is given or denied to the one God. Hence it follows that Father and Son are one and the only God, though not solitary.]

When the Son is to be honoured as the Father is, and when the honour of him who alone is God is not sought, then he whose honour is the same and one with God’s honour is not outside the honour of the one God. For just as one who does not honour the Son does not honour the Father also (ibid.), so one who does not seek the honour of the one God does not seek Christ’s honour either. Therefore Christ’s honour is inseparable from God’s honour.

That the honour of both is one and the same he also teaches in what he said when Lazarus’s illness was reported to him: “This illness is not unto death, but is for the glory of God, that the Son of God may be glorified through it” (John 11:4). Lazarus dies for the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified through Lazarus. Can there be any doubt that the glory of God is in the glory of the Son of God, when Lazarus’s death—which is glorious to God—is to produce glory for the Son of God?

[Note: “To produce.” In the work *On the Unity of the Father and the Son*: “to effect.” In Colbertinus, Germanicus, Martinianus, Corbiensis, etc.: *paratura*, “to produce.”]

Thus both the natural unity of God the Father in Christ through birth is taught, since Lazarus’s illness is for God’s glory; and the mystery of faith is preserved, since the Son of God is to be glorified through Lazarus: God is to be understood in the Son of God through this, yet not understood as God in such a way that the Son of God is not also confessed; for when God is glorified through Lazarus, the Son of God is glorious.

[Note: The Verona manuscript gives the passage thus: “God is to be understood in the Son of God through this, yet not understood as God in such a way that the Son of God is not also confessed.”]

[Note: The printed editions read “likewise”; the manuscripts, “through this,” which is more characteristic of Hilary. Some manuscripts read “in the Son of God.” But the Basel Vatican manuscript has: “God is to be understood in the Son of God through this, yet not understood as God in such a way that the Son of God is not also confessed.” Though difficult, this is nevertheless the true reading and is retained. It becomes clearer thus: Hence the Son of God is to be understood as God, yet not so understood as God that he is not also to be confessed as the Son of God.]

### 24. Christ Declares Himself God Where He Professes That There Is Only One God. The One God. The Scribe Assents

The birth of one living being from another living being is inseparable from the mystery of the divine nature; nor does the Son of God undergo a change of kind, lest the truth of the Father’s nature fail to remain in him. For even by those very expressions in which, by confessing one God alone, he seems under the assertion of divine singularity to have denied the divine nature in himself, he nevertheless placed himself within the unity of the paternal nature, without overthrowing the faith of the one God.

For when asked by the scribe what was the chief commandment in the Law, he answered: “Hear, Israel: the Lord our God, the Lord is one; and you shall love the Lord your God with your whole heart, and with your whole soul, and with all your inward powers, and with all your strength. This is the first commandment. The second is like it: You shall love your neighbour as yourself. There is no commandment greater than these” (Mark 12:29 ff.).

[Note: “Your God,” and likewise below. Then “with strengths,” not “with inward powers.” The printed editions here and below, with most manuscripts, read “your God”; they are corrected on the authority of the Germanicus and Colbertinus manuscripts, in agreement with the Greek text of Mark. Accordingly we restore “the Lord is one,” as it is read below in most manuscripts, whereas the printed editions have “God is one” in both places, and the Martin manuscript has only “one.”]

He is thought to have alienated himself from the nature and worship of the one God, because the confession of the chief commandment is this: “Hear, Israel: the Lord our God, the Lord is one”; and then, as though he did not even place himself within the worship required by the following commandment, when the Law summoned us to love our neighbour just as it summoned us to faith in the one Lord.

[Note: The printed editions read “to faith in the one God,” against the manuscripts.]

The scribe’s answer too is not to be overlooked. He says: “You have spoken well, Teacher, in truth, that God is one and there is no other besides him; and that he is to be loved with the whole heart, with all one’s strength, and with the whole soul; and that one must love one’s neighbour as oneself. This is greater than all burnt offerings and sacrifices” (Mark 12:32–33).

[Note: “God is one”; later, “with all one’s powers”; and he reads likewise below in §25.]

The scribe’s response appears to agree with the Lord’s words: it professes an intimate and inward love of the one God, promises love of neighbour according to the reality of self-love, and understands love toward God and humanity to stand above sacrificial burnt offerings. But we must see what follows.

### 25. He Is Not Far from the Kingdom of God Because He Is Moving toward Love

When Jesus saw that he had answered wisely, he said to him: “You are not far from the kingdom of God” (ibid., 34). What does the declaration of so restrained an answer mean? If this faith brings a person to the kingdom of heaven in its fullness—to believe in one God, to love him with the whole soul, all one’s strength, and the whole heart, and likewise to love one’s neighbour as oneself—why is this scribe not already in God’s kingdom, but merely not far from God’s kingdom?

By another declaration, the kingdom is given to those who clothe the naked, feed the hungry, give drink to the thirsty, visit the sick, and attend those shut up in prison: “Come, blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25:34). Or it is given to those for whom poverty of spirit is the reward: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5:3).

[Note: “It is the reward of one poor in spirit.”]

[Note: In several manuscripts: “poverty of spirit.” In certain others: “the poor in spirit.”]

This is a perfect fruit, a complete possession, and a certain bestowal of the kingdom prepared beforehand (Mark 10:20). Or did the young man confess any less than these things? For, having made love of neighbour equal to his love of himself, what had he not done toward the completion of good work? To be yielding and dutiful on occasion is not perfect love; but perfect love has fulfilled every duty of every kind of generosity, when one who renders to another as much as to himself leaves nothing which he owes to another.

[Note: The printed editions read, “will fulfil the office of generosity of this kind”; they are corrected from the manuscripts.]

Yet the Lord, commending the scribe’s profession of faith while he was held in ignorance of the completed mystery, and answering that he was not far from God’s kingdom, did not nevertheless place him already in possession of the blessed hope itself. For he was advancing on a fortunate course, though in ignorance, with love of God set above all things and love of neighbour made equal to his own self-love. Yet, since he had set the love of God above even this love of neighbour, he was no longer confined by the prescriptions of burnt offerings and sacrifices. This was not far from the evangelical mystery.

[Note: The printed editions read “through profession”; we have deleted “through” on the authority of the manuscripts.

The Paris edition alone: “by a faithful course.” Then the Vatican Basel and Martin manuscripts: “although ignorant.” “Although ignorant” would be preferable with Colbertinus if these two words occurred after “with the love of God set above all things.” But that course is ignorant because it belongs to one ignorant of God, according to Book III, §17: “No one knows God unless he confesses both the Father as Father of the only-begotten Son, and the Son,” etc. For that knowledge of Father and Son is the completed mystery, in ignorance of which the scribe was just said to be held.]

### 26. He Is Not Yet in the Kingdom of God Because He Is Not Yet in Faith in Christ as God

Why he is said to be not far from God’s kingdom, rather than destined to be in God’s kingdom, must be understood from the Lord’s own words. For it follows: “And no one dared any longer to question him. And Jesus answered and taught in the temple: How do the scribes say that Christ is David’s son? For David himself says in the Holy Spirit: ‘The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet’” (Psalm 109 [110]:1). “David himself calls him Lord; how then is he his son?” (Mark 12:34).

[Note: In the printed editions, “who will be,” incorrectly. The sense is: why is he said rather to be not far from the kingdom than destined to be in the kingdom?]

Therefore the scribe who confesses one God, to be loved above all things, is not far from God’s kingdom. Yet by his own confession he is warned why he does not understand the mystery of the Law and does not know that Christ, the Lord and Son of God, is to be confessed through the nature of his birth within faith in the one Lord.

And because, through the Law’s confession of the one Lord, the Son of God did not appear to be left within the mystery of the one Lord, he reminds the scribe how he could call Christ David’s son when David professed him to be his own Lord; nor would nature permit one who was son to so great a patriarch to be also his Lord. This was done so that the scribe, who understood him only according to flesh and the birth from Mary, who was descended from David, might remember that according to the Spirit he was David’s Lord rather than his son; and might not separate Christ from the mystery of the one Lord in the saying: “Hear, Israel: the Lord our God, the Lord is one” (Mark 12:29). For so great a patriarch and prophet professed as his Lord the one who had been begotten from the Lord’s womb before the morning star: certainly not forgetful of the Law, nor ignorant that another Lord was not to be confessed, but understanding that he who had arisen from the womb of the incorporeal God through the mystery of natural birth was to be understood as Lord without violation of the faith of the Law; since, being one from one, through the nature of the one Lord he had in himself naturally what the Lord is.

[Note: The Vatican Basel manuscript with Martin reads “the one God,” less aptly.]

[Note: The word *se*, omitted in the printed editions, is restored from the manuscripts.]

### 27. Epilogue

What place for doubt now remains? The Lord himself, teaching that the chief commandment of the Law consists in confession and love of the one Lord, did not use his own testimony before the scribe but the Prophet’s testimony to show that he is Lord—yet always signifying himself to be Lord through the fact that he is the Son of God.

For through this he remains, by birth, within the mystery of the one God: the divine birth, possessing God’s nature in itself, does not exceed into another God by diversity of nature; and the truth of generation neither deprives the Father of being Lord nor fails to perfect the Son so that he too may be Lord. Thus the Father does not lose authority, nor does the Son fail to possess nature. Therefore neither is God the Father not the one Lord, nor is the only-begotten God the Lord separated from the one; for, from the one Lord, he himself subsists as one Lord. Thus the Law teaches one Lord, while the Prophet’s testimony confirms that he too is Lord (David, Psalm 109 [110]).

[Note: “Even now.”]

[Note: The printed editions read “lest he not be God”: against the manuscripts. The Vatican Basel manuscript reads: “nor does he fail to benefit the Son.”]

[Note: The Colbertinus and Germanicus manuscripts read “the only-begotten Lord,” omitting “God.” The Vatican Basel manuscript: “the only-begotten God to the Lord.”]

[Note: “With testimony.”]

### 28. Christ’s Divine Nature Is Confirmed from the Very Objections of the Heretics. The Heretics’ Objection

Let the evangelical answer proceed through the remaining propositions of impious madness, and oppose them with the very arguments by which it is attacked; conquering with the weapons intended for its destruction, let it demonstrate that the utterances of the one Spirit are also the teaching of the one faith.

For Christ is no other than he who has been preached: namely, true God, remaining in the glory of the one true God. And just as he professed himself Lord from the Law while seeming to deny it, so also in the Gospels he shows himself to be true God while he is thought not to confess it.

The heretics excuse themselves from confessing that he is true God by this saying of his: “This is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17:3). For in saying, “you, the only true God,” he is thought, by the exception of solitary uniqueness, to separate himself from the truth of God, since “the only true God” allows no understanding except that he alone is solitary God.

And indeed the apostolic faith does not permit two true Gods to be believed, because nothing alien to the nature of the one God can be made equal in truth to that same nature. For God will not be one in the truth of the one God if, outside the nature of the one true God, there exists another true God of a different kind and not naturally so by birth.

### 29. The Words Joined to It Refute the Objection. The Apostles Recognize Christ as God from God by Nature

But in order that it may be understood without ambiguity that by this very saying he professed himself to be true God within the nature of the one true God, let our discussion descend from the declarations preceding this saying, though continuous and joined with it; so that, through the successive stages of demonstrated faith, our confidence in freedom may now rest at the summit itself: Christ, true God.

After the mystery of his discourse in which he had said, “He who has seen me has seen the Father,” and, “Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father in me? The words which I speak to you I do not speak from myself; but the Father who remains in me himself does his works. Believe me, that I am in the Father and the Father in me; or else believe because of the works themselves” (John 14:9 ff.), after this manifold discourse of mighty mysteries, the disciples’ response follows: “Now we know that you know all things and have no need that anyone should question you. By this we believe that you came forth from God” (John 16:30–31).

[Note: “And words.” Shortly afterward, “and the Father in me” is without the word “is,” in accordance with the Greek: *καὶ ὁ πατὴρ ἐν ἐμοί*.]

They understood in him not merely the powers of God but God’s nature as well. For to know all things and to know the thoughts of hearts could belong not merely to one sent from God, but rather to one born from God. Therefore they profess that they believe this—that he came forth from God—because the power of God’s nature was in him.

### 30. By the Name “Coming Forth” They Aptly Indicate This. That Coming Forth Signifies Birth, Not Alienation from the Father

The Lord commends their understanding, not indeed that he had been sent, but that he had come forth from God; under the signification of coming forth, he attests the process of birth from the incorporeal God (see Book VI, §30). For he himself had expressed his birth by the representation of coming forth, saying: “You love me and believe that I came forth from God and came from the Father into this world” (John 16:27–28). For he came from the Father into this world because he came forth from God.

[Note: That is, the Lord commends and confirms their understanding, situated in that faith by which they profess belief that he came forth from God, when he immediately answers: “Now you believe.” Therefore the words, “not indeed that he had been sent, but that he had come forth from God,” should be referred not to “he answered,” but to the understanding which he commends.]

In order that it might be understood that he had signified his birth in his coming forth, he added that he had come from the Father. Since he came from the Father because he came forth from God, his coming forth from God is completed birth, followed by confession of the Father’s name.

Therefore, when the apostles understood this mystery of coming forth, he said: “Now you believe. Behold, the hour comes—and now has come—when each of you will be scattered to his own home and will leave me alone; yet I am not alone, because the Father is with me” (ibid., 32–33).

[Note: The word “now” is absent from our manuscript. Shortly afterward, “will be scattered.” Lipsius and Paris read “the hour will come,” against the other books and the Greek, *ἔρχεται ὥρα, καὶ νῦν ἐλήλυθεν*. Therefore we restore “now” from Badius, Erasmus, and the Basel Vatican manuscript.]

Thus he taught that this coming forth was not alienation from God the Father, but birth retaining in himself, by being born, the nature of God the Father. He added that he was not alone, but that the Father was with him—namely by power and unity of nature—since the Father was with him by remaining in him, both acting and speaking in the one who spoke and acted.

Then, in order to reveal the purpose of all this discourse, he added: “I have spoken these things to you, that you may have peace in me. In this world you will have tribulation; but be of good courage, for I have conquered the world” (ibid., 33).

[Note: Thus Lipsius with the manuscripts. Erasmus after Badius: “be of tranquil spirit”; Paris: “be more tranquil in spirit.”]

He spoke these things, therefore, so that they might remain at peace in him and not disagree through contentiousness in disputes over faith: because he who was to be left alone was not alone; and he who had come forth from God had God, from whom he had come forth, within himself. Then, afflicted in the world, they were to endure patiently in reliance on his promises, since he had conquered the world by coming forth from God and having God with him.

### 31. The Request for Glory Does Not Prove the Son Weak, Nor Does His Reception of Power. All Power Is Co-Born with the Son

Finally, when about to speak the faith of the whole mystery, lifting his eyes to heaven he said: “Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son, that your Son may glorify you. As you gave him authority over all flesh, that he may give eternal life to all whom you have given him” (John 17:1–2).

[Note: “Your” is absent.]

Does he seem weak to you because he asks to be glorified? Let him certainly be weak, unless he asks to be glorified precisely in order that he himself may glorify the one who glorifies him. We have discussed receiving and returning honour in another book (Book III, §12), and it would be exceedingly idle to go over the same matters again. Certainly there is no doubt that glory is requested so that the one who grants it may be glorified.

But perhaps he is weak in that he received authority over all flesh. Let this reception of authority likewise be weakness—unless he has power to give eternal life to those whom he received. Yet even in the very fact that he received, some weakness of nature is alleged. Let reception indeed be weakness, unless Christ is true God by birth rather than by unbegottenness.

But if reception of power is merely the signification of birth, in which he received what he is, that bestowal must not be attributed to weakness which completes, in the one being born, his entire existence as God. For, when unbegotten God is author to the only-begotten God of the birth into the perfection of divine blessedness, it belongs to the paternal mystery to be author of birth.

[Note: That is, it is the distinctive property by which the Father alone is distinguished from the Son.]

But that reception, which completes itself as the image of its author by genuine birth, involves no dishonour.

[Note: Paris reads “who.” We prefer, with the manuscripts, “which,” namely reception. Some then omit “itself,” which refers to the only-begotten God. In three Vatican manuscripts: “which is the image of its author.” Badius, Erasmus, and Lipsius: “which expresses the image of its author”: the Father’s giving power meant his begetting the Son; the Son’s receiving it completes the birth. This is a gloss.]

For that he gave authority over all flesh, and gave it for this end, that he might give eternal life, contains in the giver what belongs to the Father and in the receiver what belongs to God. For the Father is signified in having given; and the Son remains God in having received authority to give eternal life.

Therefore all power is natural and co-born with the Son of God. Although it has been given, it does not thereby alienate him from the author because it was given; for what belongs to the author has been given—namely, to give eternal life and to change corruption into incorruption.

[Note: In some good manuscripts, “into incorruption” is omitted.]

The Father therefore gave all things and the Son received all things. Nor is there doubt, since he said: “All things that are the Father’s are mine” (John 16:15). Here, however, the present discourse does not signify the kinds of created things or the various establishments of the elements (see below, §72); rather, opening to us the glory of blessed and complete divinity, it shows that God is to be understood in those things which are his: in power, eternity, providence, and authority. This is not because God has these things as though he were something else outside them; but because in these things, as an accommodation to the limited conception of our understanding, he himself is signified by what he possesses.

[Note: Paris with an old Colbert manuscript: “must be believed.” The same edition, following Erasmus and Lipsius, subsequently reads “he himself who possesses.” We prefer, with Badius and the manuscripts: “which,” namely, “but that in the things he possesses he himself is signified.” Here God is taught to be so simple that in him, unlike among us, possessor and possessions are by no means different. Hence Book VIII, §24 says: “He teaches himself wholly through his own things, and signifies that his own things are nothing other than himself, so that where his things are present, he himself may be understood to be present.”]

Therefore the only-begotten Son, teaching that he subsists in those things which are the Father’s, after saying that the Holy Spirit would receive from himself, added: “All things that are the Father’s are mine; therefore I said, He will receive from what is mine” (ibid.). All things that are the Father’s are his own, having been given and received. Yet things given do not weaken the divinity which establishes him in those things in which the Father is.

[Note: Badius and Erasmus with one Vatican manuscript read “birth,” less well.]

### 32. He Is Inseparable from the Father

Having therefore employed these preceding stages of understanding concerning himself—having taught that he came forth from God, professed that the Father was with him, testified that he had conquered the world (John 16:28, 32, 33), and said that, being glorified by the Father, he would glorify the Father, and that he would use the power received by giving eternal life to all flesh—he finally concluded all this with this statement: “This is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17:1–3).

Heretic, learn either to speak of the faith of eternal life or to believe it. Separate Christ from God, if you can: the Son from the Father, God from God who is true above all, the one from the sole God—for “there is one Lord, Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 8:6)—if eternal life consists in believing in the only true God without Christ. But if, with Christ separated from the sole true God, eternal life is not attained in the confession of the sole true God, I do not understand how he is to be separated from the true God for faith when he is inseparable for salvation.

[Note: The printed editions read, “but not without Christ separated from the true God,” etc., with a less genuine reading and faulty punctuation. They are corrected with the aid of the manuscripts.]

### 33. In the Passage Objected, Christ Is Indicated as True God

Although I know that lengthy resolutions of difficult questions are burdensome to readers’ wishes, nevertheless, having delayed for a little the demonstration of the whole truth, I think that I may be allowed, not without some advancement of faith, to wrestle with you, heretic, using these very evangelical words.

You hear the Lord’s declaration: “This is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent.” I ask what there is here that disturbs your mind lest Christ be true God. For no further description here shows what you believed about Christ. You have nothing except “Jesus Christ”: not “Son of Man,” as he customarily calls himself; not “Son of God,” as he commonly professes himself; not “the living bread descending from heaven,” which he frequently asserts concerning himself, to the scandal of many (John 6:61).

[Note: Badius and Erasmus with the later Colbert manuscript read “frequently asserts”; the other books oppose it.]

But in saying, “you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17:3), he omitted his customary names and additional titles, whether natural or assumed, so that, since confession of the only true God and of Christ Jesus bestows eternity, Jesus Christ undoubtedly appears in that signification in which he is God.

[Note: Badius and Erasmus with the Remigius manuscript read “you had believed.” Lipsius and Paris, with Corbiensis and several others, read “you ought to believe.” We restore the more genuine reading: “you believed.”]

### 34. Nor Is It an Objection That the Father Is Called the Only True God

But perhaps, because he says “you alone,” he separates his communion and unity from God. Let him indeed separate it, if he did not immediately add to the words, “you, the only true God,” “and Jesus Christ whom you sent.” I ask the understanding of the hearer: what is Jesus Christ to be believed to be, when Christ also is to be believed in connection with the Father’s being believed the only true God?

But perhaps the Father, being the only true God, does not leave room for Christ to be God. Let him indeed leave none, if the one God, the Father, did not leave Christ to be one Lord (1 Corinthians 8:6).

[Note: “Certainly”; shortly afterward, “does not leave.”]

[Note: The Paris edition alone reads “the one Lord, the Father,” wrongly. The Apostle’s passage, 1 Corinthians 8:6, is intended here; it was discussed at length in the preceding book, §35.]

But if the one God, the Father, does not deprive Christ of being one Lord, so the Father, being the only true God, does not take from Christ Jesus the fact that he is true God; since this advances toward the attainment of eternal life: that, when the only true God is believed, Christ also is believed.

### 35. There Is No Ground for Believing Christ to Be Something Other Than God

[Note: “Therefore.”]

What nature, then, I ask, do you in the judgment of your folly assign to Christ, heretic—Christ, who is to be believed, and who gives eternal life; who, being glorified by the Father, glorified the Father; who conquered the world; who, though to be left alone, is not alone but has the Father with him; who came forth from God and came from the Father?

[Note: Badius with several manuscripts reads “that when Christ also is believed.” Erasmus, forgetting how strongly he had denounced interpolators in his preface, substituted: “that when God the Father is believed, Christ also is believed.” Lipsius at last restored from himself: “when Christ too is believed to exist,” which later prevailed. We restore the passage according to the manuscripts, in three of which “and Christ” is absent. This repetition has a certain emphasis: You who do not wish us to believe Christ to be God, what nature do you assign to him? To him, I say, who gives eternal life, who, etc.]

What nature and truth do you grant to one born amid such great divine powers? For we believe in vain in the Father as the only true God unless we also believe in Jesus Christ whom he sent. What are you hesitating over? Teach what Christ is to be confessed to be. For you who deny what is written, what remains except that you believe what is not written?

O unhappy will, and falsehood resisting truth! When Christ is united in the faith and confession of the Father as true God, by what faith will one who is denied to be true God be called a creature, when there is no faith in having believed in the only true God without Christ? But your narrow mind, heretic, incapable of the divine Spirit, does not receive the meaning of heavenly utterances; and inspired by serpentine error, you do not know that Christ, true God, must be confessed within faith in the only true God unto eternal life.

[Note: “We shall believe.” Later: “What do you hesitate over? What do you delay?”]

### 36. Because the Father Alone Is True God, Christ Also Is True God. To Say That He Is Something Other Than the Father Is an Injury to the Father

But the Church’s faith, confessing the Father as the only true God, also confesses Christ. Nor, in confessing Christ as true God, does it fail to confess the Father also as the only true God; nor again, when it confesses the Father as the only true God, does it fail to confess Christ also. For it confesses Christ as true God precisely because it has confessed the Father as the only true God. Thus the fact that God the Father alone is true God confirms that Christ also is true God.

For natural birth did not bring a change of nature upon the only-begotten God; nor is he who subsists as God from subsistent God according to the nature of divine generation separable in truth of nature from him who alone is true God.

[Note: The printed editions have “and” instead of “nor,” and below “inseparable” instead of “separable.” The manuscript reading is more coherent.]

[Note: In our manuscript, “subsisted.” Shortly afterward: “inseparable.”]

But the nature of truth retained its order: natural truth brought in the truth of birth, and the one God did not bring forth from himself a God of another kind.

[Note: “Bring forth.” This verb is often written in this form in the same manuscript.]

Thus the mystery of God consists neither in solitude nor in diversity: for neither is he reckoned another God who has subsisted from God with the distinctive property of his own nature, nor does he remain merely in union when the truth of birth teaches that he must be confessed as Father.

Therefore God who is born has not abandoned the distinctive property of his nature. By natural power he is that whose nature he possesses in himself by natural birth. For God in him is neither changed nor degenerate. If birth had introduced any defect, it would rather have brought dishonour upon that nature through which the birth subsisted, since what comes from itself would cease to be what is its own. Thus change would not corrupt him who had come to subsist by birth in a new substance; rather, it would corrupt him who, unable in the birth of the Son to preserve the constancy of his own nature, had begotten something external and alien to himself.

[Note: The printed editions read “would bring”; but Corbiensis, Martinianus, Vatican Basel, and most other manuscripts read “would bring in.” Five older manuscripts read “would adhere,” and before this have “that rather,” not “to that rather.” Hence the reading of Carnotensis is not displeasing: “that dishonour would rather adhere to the nature …” The Father is here called the nature through which the birth subsists, because the discourse is against heretics who assigned to the Son a nature different from his. Augustine, *Sermon* 139, §§3–4, shows how injurious this is to the Father. See above, col. 103, note a, and col. 126, note i, in this edition.]

[Note: Paris reads “had corrupted”; the other printed editions, “would corrupt.” They are corrected from the Colbertinus and Germanicus manuscripts.]

37. The unity of Father and Son must not be conceived in a human fashion. The Son’s birth. — But, as we have often already recalled, in the unity of God the Father and God the Son there is no defect of human notions: as though it were extension, sequence, or flowing forth; as though a spring poured out a stream from its source, a tree held a branch in its trunk, or fire sent heat out into space. For these remain, through an inseparable stretching-out from themselves, as things rather held fast than existing in themselves:

> [Note: Col. 0308C. “It is in the fire.”]

for heat is in the fire, the branch in the tree, and the stream in the spring. And this whole thing is rather one thing existing in itself than a thing established from another thing, because the tree cannot be other than the branch, nor fire other than heat, nor spring other than stream.

> [Note: Col. 0308D. Bad., Er., and one Vatican manuscript omit *ab se* (“from themselves”); another Vatican codex has *in se* (“in themselves”). Either may be admitted. For a branch is extended from a tree and a stream from a spring, and yet in them they remain no less undivided.]

> [Note: Col. 0309B. The Martin manuscript has *sibi insunt* (“they exist in themselves”); Erasmus wrote this in the margin, and afterward the Lyons and Paris editions wrongly transferred it into the text. For *sibi sunt* means that they are not independent nor subsist through themselves; so that branch and trunk are not two complete and perfect things, one established from the other, but only one substance, receiving its subsistence from two parts joined together.]

But the only-begotten God, subsisting by perfect and ineffable birth, is God; he is the true offspring of the unbegotten God; the incorporeal generation of an incorporeal nature; living and true God from living and true God; and God inseparable in nature from God. For the subsisting birth did not produce a God of another nature, nor did the generation which brought forth the substance alter, in begetting, the nature of that substance.

> [Note: Col. 0309B. *Perficit*: “produced.”]

38. Unity with the Father’s nature denied to Christ as man. It is restored to him through glory. — Yet by the economy of the assumed flesh, and by the obedience whereby he emptied himself from the form of God, Christ, born as man, had brought in a newness of nature—not through loss of power or nature, but through a change of condition. Therefore, emptying himself from the form of God, he was born and received the form of a servant. But the Father’s nature, with which he possessed natural unity, did not experience this assumption of flesh; and temporal newness, although remaining in the power of nature, nevertheless lost, together with the form of God, unity with God’s nature according to the assumed man.

> [Note: Col. 0309C. The manuscripts read *exinaniendi* (“of emptying himself”); printed editions, *exinamiendi*.]

> [Note: Col. 0309B. *Novitatem* (“newness”); a second hand reads *nativitatem* (“birth”).]

> [Note: Col. 0309D. The Remigian, German, Martin, and old Colbert manuscripts read *nativitatem*. With the other books we prefer *novitatem*, that is, a new human nature. This may be confirmed from §14: “Having emptied himself, so that Christ, remaining Spirit, might be the same Christ as man, the change of condition in the body and the assumption of nature”—behold the newness of nature—“did not destroy the nature of the abiding divinity”: behold the meaning of “not through loss of power and nature.” At the beginning of §53 it is also stated clearly that the birth of man introduced a new nature.]

> [Note: Col. 0309C. Bad. and Er., with a later Colbert manuscript, read *non sineret* (“did not permit”). What is meant here is clear from §50: “Do you think it unknown that the Father remained outside this assumption of human sufferings … without receiving flesh?”]

> [Note: Col. 0310B. So also the first hand of our codex; but after correction it reads *non amiserat* (“had not lost”).]

> [Note: Cols. 0309C–0310C. In the Corbie manuscript in an old hand, in the second Cistercian manuscript, and in several later manuscripts, *non amiserat*; and subsequently in Paris, *nativitatem* rather than *unitatem*: corruptly. The person who corrected the aforesaid Corbie codex about eight hundred years ago wrote in the margin, “Note a new doctrine,” not understanding what Hilary meant by the loss or recovery of God’s natural unity; for his manner of speaking is new and unfamiliar to us rather than his doctrine. He does not deny that Christ, from the time he assumed flesh, possesses a natural unity between the human and divine natures—a unity which he defended so constantly that above, §11, he would not allow the Christ despoiled of flesh and the Christ despoiling himself of flesh to be denied as one and the same. Much less does he mean that Christ fell away from unity with the Father’s nature, with which he had natural unity even after assuming man, as we have just heard from him and as is abundantly proved throughout the preceding book and elsewhere. What, then, is that natural unity which Christ lost according to man? Surely no other than glory itself. Since his human nature had not yet become a participant in it, it somehow differed from the divine: being passible from the impassible, mortal from the immortal, weak from the almighty. But when through glory it is made incorruptible, immortal, eternal, and so forth, then, insofar as created substance may, it enjoys perfect concord with God’s nature. As will become clearer from what follows, Hilary calls this concord natural unity. Nor should anyone ask why Christ is said to have lost what, according to the assumed man, he had never possessed before the glorious resurrection. For by the same reasoning he is truly said to have lost it as his flesh is truly said to have descended from heaven: “This is the bread which came down from heaven.” For, as St. Leo teaches in what is now Epistle 24, chapter 5, borrowing Augustine’s words from *Against the Arian Sermon*, chapter 8: “Because of this unity of person to be understood in both natures, the Son of Man is also read to have descended from heaven, although the Son of God assumed flesh from the Virgin from whom he was born,” etc. Indeed Christ, before receiving flesh, had possessed that unity simply and absolutely; afterward, according to the assumed man, he did not possess it. But what is it to have possessed something simply, and afterward not to have it in the same way, except to have lost it? This passage might create difficulty because he is also declared here to have made a loss of the form of God, unless it had already been shown above, §14, that by “form” an external condition is meant.]

But this was the consummation of the economy: that the whole Son, namely man and God, might now, through the gracious will of the Father, exist in the unity of the Father’s nature; and that he who remained in the power of nature might also remain in the kind of nature. For this was acquired for man: that he might be God. Yet the assumed man could in no way remain in God’s unity unless, through the unity of God, he attained to a natural unity with God.

> [Note: Col. 0310D. Thus the manuscripts. But the printed editions read *naturalem*, by this alteration utterly obscuring Hilary’s aim and subtle argument. For, wishing to demonstrate that Christ is God by nature, he establishes this from the fact that his flesh, united to the glory and nature of God the Word, is in the unity of the Father’s nature. This cannot occur unless the Father and God the Word have one and the same nature, by means of which the flesh, united with the nature of God the Word, is also united with the Father’s nature, and consequently unless Christ is God by nature.]

Thus, because the Word was God in God’s nature, the Word made flesh might likewise be in God’s nature; and thus the man Jesus Christ might remain in the glory of God the Father, if the flesh were united to the glory of the Word. Then the Word made flesh would return, even according to man, into unity with the Father’s nature, when the assumed flesh had received the glory of the Word.

> [Note: Cols. 0310C–D. That is, consummation and perfection. As explained in the exposition of Psalm II, §27, this consisted in the fact that what was then Son of Man should, by the power of resurrection, be begotten into the perfect Son of God—that is, into the resumption and bestowal upon the body of the glory of his eternity. There, to be begotten into the perfect Son of God means precisely the same as “the whole Son now” here, or “whole man, whole God” above, §6. Accordingly, what is said here—namely, that through the graciousness of the Father’s will he exists in unity with the Father’s nature—must mean the same as bestowing upon the body, through resurrection, the glory of eternity. Compare the two passages.]

Therefore his own unity had to be restored to the Father in himself, so that the birth of his nature might again rest in him and be glorified; because the newness of the economy had introduced an impairment of unity, and unity, perfect as it had formerly been, could now exist only if the assumed flesh had been glorified in him.

> [Note: Col. 0311D. Or: “to the Father,” with “the Son” silently understood; the Son is afterward called the birth of his nature.]

39. The Father’s glory is the Son’s glory; this is the force of “with you.” What was not granted to the assumed man is requested after the economy has been completed. — Therefore, after so long preparing our minds for the understanding of this faith, when he had said, “And this is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17:3), he added, in accordance with the obedience of his economy: “I have glorified you upon earth; I have completed the work which you gave me to do” (John 17:4). Then, that we might understand both the merit of obedience and the mystery of the whole economy, he added: “And now, glorify me, you Father, with yourself, with the glory which I had with you before the world existed” (John 17:5).

> [Note: Col. 0311D. The Chartres codex reads, “Glorify me … with the glory which I had.” Then the Vatican-Basilican manuscript: “before the world was with you.”]

Whoever denies that Christ remains in God’s nature and does not believe him inseparable from and identical in nature with the only true God, let him answer what is the reason for this petition: “And now, glorify me, you Father, with yourself.” For why should the Father glorify him with himself? What is the meaning of this expression, and what is its effect? The Father does not need glory, nor had he emptied himself of the form of his glory.

> [Note: Col. 0311C. “How, then?”]

How, then, will he glorify the Son with himself and with that glory which the Son had with him before the foundation of the world?

But what is the meaning of having with you? He does not say, “the glory which I had before the world existed, when I was with you”; but, “the glory which I had with you.” For “being with you” signifies subsisting with you, whereas “having with you” teaches the mystery of nature.

> [Note: Col. 0311D. The words “when I was with you” are omitted by the Vatican-Basilican codex, but ought not to be omitted.]

Moreover, “Glorify me with yourself” is not the same as “Glorify me.” He does not merely ask to be glorified in such a way as to receive some glory proper and peculiar to himself; rather, he asks the Father to glorify him with the Father himself. For in order that he might remain in his unity as he had remained, the Father was to glorify him with himself, because through the obedience of the economy the unity of his glory had been exceeded: namely, that through glorification he might again be in that nature in which, by the mystery of divine birth, he was united; and that, glorified with the Father himself, he might be with the Father; so that what he formerly had with him might remain, and the assumption of the form of a servant might not estrange the nature of the form of God from him. Rather, the Father glorifies with himself the form of a servant, so that the form of God may remain what it is, because he who remained in the form of God was the same one who was in the form of a servant. And since the form of a servant was to be glorified in the form of God, it had to be glorified with him whose form was to confer honor upon the condition of the servant-form.

> [Note: Col. 0311C. The word *vero* (“moreover”) is absent.]

> [Note: Col. 0311D. We add *me* from the Vatican-Basilican manuscript and another manuscript of the Vatican Library.]

> [Note: Col. 0312C. “Unity.”]

> [Note: Col. 0311D. The better manuscripts read *unitas* (“unity”); printed editions, *unitatem*.]

> [Note: Col. 0311D. The Vatican-Basilican codex together with the Martin manuscript reads, “and the Father might be”; this is not satisfactory.]

> [Note: Cols. 0311D–0312D. The vulgate editions lack *esse* (“to be”), supplied from the manuscripts. So above, §14: “not that Christ, who was in the form of God, might cease to be Christ.” But Bad. and Er. wrongly read, “that the form of God might remain,” because he who remained in the form of a servant was the same as he who was in the form of God.]

40. The character of God’s words. Christ sought glory for the flesh, not for the Word. — This utterance of the Lord is not new, nor is it now for the first time confirmed by Gospel teaching. He had also testified to this very mystery of the Son’s being glorified with the Father by that beautiful exultation of hope, when Judas had gone out to betray him and he rejoiced at the completion of his economy:

> “Now the Son of Man has been glorified, and God has been glorified in him. If God has been glorified in him, God has also glorified him in himself, and God will glorify him immediately” (John 13:31–32).

> [Note: Col. 0312D. Paris, with the old Colbert manuscript, reads *confirmata* (“confirmed”).]

> [Note: Col. 0312D. The Vatican-Basilican and Martin manuscripts read *glorificari* (“being glorified”); then the Vatican-Basilican manuscript alone reads, corruptly, “the Son with himself by the mystery of the Father.” Here *sacramentum* must be understood as though repeated thus: “the mystery of glorifying the Son with himself, which is the mystery of God the Father,” that is, his own proper rationale. In this sense §31 said: “To be the author of the birth is the Father’s mystery.”]

How long, you souls weighed down by muddy bodies, you minds foul and filthy with a conscience stained by sins, shall we swell with pride even to the judgment of a divine declaration concerning us? Why, setting ourselves up as judges of the heavenly—that is, divine—nature, do we rebel against God by the impious arguments of our slander? With what simplicity of words, after all, did the Lord speak the evangelical faith! And he adapted his utterances to our understanding as far as the weakness of our nature could bear, yet not so as to say anything unworthy of the majesty of his nature.

> [Note: Col. 0312D. We add *mentes* (“minds”) from the manuscripts.]

> [Note: Col. 0312D. Bad. and Er., with one Vatican manuscript, read *fallimus* (“we deceive”), which the Corbie manuscript also had in its first hand. Paris, with the Colbert and German manuscripts, reads *repugnamus* (“we resist”). With Lyons and other manuscripts we prefer *rebellamus* (“we rebel”). Thus in Book II to Constantius, §6: “while rejecting novel innovations, we ourselves rebel against God with novel utterances.”]

I consider the first meaning of his saying unambiguous when he says, “Now the Son of Man has been glorified.” For all glory was acquired not for the Word but for the flesh; that is, not for God’s birth, but for the economy of the man who was born. But I ask what the next words mean: “And God has been glorified in him.” For I hear that God has been glorified in him; and, heretic, I do not know what you understand this to be. God has been glorified in him—in the Son of Man, certainly. And I ask whether the Son of Man is the same as the Son of God. Since the Son of Man is not one person and the Son of God another—for “the Word became flesh”—and since he who is Son of God is himself also Son of Man, I ask which God has been glorified in this Son of Man, who is also Son of God.

> [Note: Col. 0313C. In the most ancient Vatican-Basilican, Colbert, and German codices, and likewise in Bad. and Er., here and below, *aliud* rather than *alius*. Although this way of speaking is less exact for us, there can scarcely be doubt that Hilary used it, unobjectionably for his time, to signify unity of person in Christ.]

> [Note: Col. 0313C. The question remains pending, because the answer seems superfluous: the Father, by conferring honor upon the Son and then receiving it from him, has already more than once thereby been shown to be one with him in nature. Or rather, the deferred solution is contained in the following section: “If the glorified God is Christ, Christ certainly is God, who is glorified in the flesh; if it is the Father, it is a mystery of unity when the Father is glorified in the Son.”]

41. How mutual is the glory of Father and Son. What it means that God is glorified in the Son of Man. Which God glorifies in himself the God glorified in the Son of Man. — Since God has been glorified in the Son of Man, who is also Son of God, let us see what this third clause means: “If God has been glorified in him, God has also glorified him in himself.” What, I ask, is this mystery’s meaning? God, glorified in the Son of Man, glorifies in himself the God who has been glorified. God’s glory is in the Son of Man, and God’s glory is in the glory of the Son of Man. God glorifies in himself. Man, certainly, is not glorified through himself. Nor, again, is God who is glorified in man, although he receives glory, anything other than God.

> [Note: Col. 0313C. The manuscripts read “this third [clause]”; printed editions, “what third.” Understanding of the following words, which will seem highly intricate to some, depends especially upon grasping the preceding passages, in which Christ, after the economy has been completed, is proclaimed as received into the glory of God—and therefore into the Father’s nature and unity.]

> [Note: Col. 0313D. Printed editions read “glorifies him”; *him* is absent from the manuscripts and should be absent. The following *neque rursum* must be understood as “and again,” a Hellenism familiar to Hilary.]

But when, after the Son of Man has been glorified, God who glorifies God glorifies in himself, I find the glory of the nature being glorified received into the glory of the glorifying nature. For God does not glorify himself; rather, he glorifies in himself God glorified in man. And what he glorifies in himself, though he does not glorify himself, he nevertheless receives, as glorifying, into the glory of his own nature. And when God, glorifying God because he has been glorified in man, glorifies in himself, he shows that the God whom he has glorified exists in him, because he glorifies him in himself.

> [Note: Col. 0313D. That is, the glory of the Father’s nature is received into the glory of that nature which, insofar as he is man, is glorified, but which, insofar as he is God, glorifies that same nature. Thus, because of the closest union of Son of God and Son of Man, when the Son of Man is glorified, the Son of God is glorified; and again, because of the natural unity of God the Father and the only-begotten Son, when the Son of God is glorified, God the Father is glorified.]

> [Note: Cols. 0313D–0314C. Printed editions read *glorificantis* (“of the glorifying [nature]”), against the better Vatican-Basilican, Colbert, Martin, Chartres, and other manuscripts. From these the sense is supplied: although the Father glorifies another than himself, what he glorifies in himself redounds to the glory of his nature.]

> [Note: Col. 0314C. We add *Deum* (“God”) from most and the best manuscripts, including the Colbert, German, Vienna, and Remigian. They then add: “in himself, he shows [him] to be in himself.” Hence, with another Colbert manuscript and one Sorbonne manuscript, “he shows [him] to be in himself” is acceptable.]

Bring forward now, whoever you are, heretic, the inextricable questions of your tangled doctrine. Though they bind themselves with their own knots, they will contain no difficulty of entanglement in any array. For the Son of Man is glorified, and God is glorified in him; and God glorifies in himself the one glorified in man. For the Son of Man’s being glorified is not the same thing as God’s being glorified in the Son of Man, nor as God’s glorifying in himself the God glorified in man.

> [Note: Col. 0314C. Erasmus reads *glorificari* (“to be glorified”), followed wrongly by other editors. The Colbert and German manuscripts read *glorificans* (“glorifying”).]

Say, according to the meaning of your impiety, in your own words what you mean by God’s being glorified in the Son of Man. Either Christ must be the one glorified in the flesh, or the Father must be the one glorified in Christ. If it is Christ, Christ certainly is God, who is glorified in the flesh. If it is the Father, it is a mystery of unity, since the Father is glorified in the Son. By confessing Christ, you speak, though unwillingly, of God also; or, by understanding God the Father, you will not deny the nature of God the Father in Christ.

> [Note: Col. 0314C. Lyons and Paris read “the Father and God”: wrongly.
