The meaning is this: if you confess that the words, “And God has been glorified in him,” are spoken of Christ glorified in the flesh, you confess Christ to be God; but if you refer them to God the Father, you will no longer deny Christ the Father’s nature, on account of which the Father is glorified in Christ who has been glorified.]

These things have been said concerning the glorified Son of Man and God glorified in the same. But concerning the fact that God glorifies in himself the God glorified in the Son of Man: in what respect, finally, do you think you retain the possibility of putting forth your impiety, so that Christ may not be true God according to the truth of nature? For God glorifies in himself Christ born as man. Is what he glorifies in himself outside himself? He restores to Christ in himself the glory which Christ had with him. When the assumption of the form of a servant is received into the form of God, God, glorified in man, is glorified in himself—he who, before the economy of emptying, was in himself, and is united through the form of a servant and through the nature of his birth. For birth had not made God a God of a new or alien nature; rather, the natural Son subsisted from the natural Father by natural generation. And when, after the birth of man, he who was glorified in man shines again in the glory of his own nature, God glorifies him in himself, when he is received into the glory of the Father’s nature, from which he had been emptied by the economy.

> [Note: Col. 0314C. Printed editions read *in forma Dei* (“in the form of God”). The manuscripts more correctly read *in formam Dei* (“into the form of God”): that is, when the man too is received, united, and transformed into God’s glory, then God who is glorified in man is glorified, etc.]

> [Note: Col. 0314D. Printed editions read *nativitatis* (“of birth”), but the manuscripts restore *vacuitatis* (“of emptying”). Above, §14, this is expressed by the verb “to empty” and the noun “emptying”; and in Book XI, §48, by the verb “to make empty.”]

> [Note: Col. 0314D. Printed editions, with three Colbert manuscripts, two Remigian manuscripts, the Vienna manuscript, and others, read *per formam sui* (“through his own form”). With the Corbie, Vatican-Basilican, Pratellian, Martin, and others, *per formam servi* (“through the form of a servant”) is preferable: that is, he is united in God not only according to the nature which he receives by eternal birth, but also according to the human nature, since man and God are now wholly God, as he says in Book XI, §41. The servant-form advances into the glory of him in whose form it formerly remained, the nature of corruption being swallowed up through the advance of incorruption, as he explains more plainly in the exposition of Psalm 138, §19. Thus *unitus* (“united”) is to be referred not to “was in himself” but to “is glorified.”]

42. The Father and Son do not have different glory. There is no life in knowing God without Christ, who is also true God. — Apostolic faith closes off the most audacious frenzy of your impiety, lest you wander wherever the license of free interpretation takes you, when it says: “And every tongue shall confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father” (Philippians 2:11). For he whom the Father glorified in himself must be confessed in his glory. And he who must be confessed in the Father’s glory, and whom the Father glorified in himself, must doubtless be understood to be in those realities in which the Father is, since the Father glorified him in himself and he is to be confessed in the Father’s glory.

> [Note: Col. 0315C. “Is in the glory of God the Father.”]

> [Note: Col. 0315D. In earlier printed editions the particle *et* (“and”) was lacking.]

For he is not merely now in the glory of God, but in the glory of God the Father. Nor did glory glorify him externally; rather, it glorified him in itself. By restoring him into the glory which is its own, and the glory which he had with it, it glorifies him both with itself and in itself. Thus he is understood to be inseparable from the conjunction of this faith even beneath the humiliation of man, when he says: “And this is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17:3). For without Christ, even though God the Father alone is known, there is no eternal life; and Christ has been glorified in the Father.

> [Note: Col. 0315C. “But glorified glory in himself.” A little later: “and into that glory,” not “and that glory.”]

> [Note: Col. 0315D. On the authority of the manuscripts we have removed the word *gloria* (“glory”) here. For greater clarity, the following should be arranged thus: “By restoring him into the glory which is his own, and the glory which he had with him, it glorifies him both with itself and in itself.” This is noted because the earlier faulty punctuation had obscured the passage.]

But if eternal life consists precisely in knowing the only true God and Jesus Christ whom he sent, Christ should not be regarded as plainly true God if life consisted in having believed in God without Christ. And the fact that God the Father alone is true God does not fail to apply to Christ God, since all Christ’s glory is in the only true God the Father. For if the Father glorifies Christ in himself, and the Father alone is true God, Christ is not outside the only true God, because the Father, the only true God, glorifies in himself Christ glorified into God. And what is glorified in himself by the only true God is not estranged from the only true God, because it is glorified in the true one himself alone.

> [Note: Col. 0315D. Printed editions read “God the Father”; the final word is redundant and absent from the manuscripts.]

> [Note: Col. 0315D. Lyons and Paris, from Erasmus’s margin, read “of Christ as man,” against the other books. Indeed Christ’s glory was always in the one God not only as man, but chiefly as God; and because all was always from and in God the Father, Christ and the Father did not have different glory or different divinity. Consequently, where the Father alone is proclaimed true God, Christ is not excluded.]

> [Note: Cols. 0315D–0316D. The Vatican-Basilican codex here adds *Deo* (“God”) without necessity. Then Paris reads, corruptly: “is not estranged from the only true [God], because in himself alone he is glorified in the true [God].” The meaning is: he is not estranged from him who alone is true, because by him who is true he is glorified in himself alone.]

43. Third objection against the Son’s deity. — But perhaps the assertion of your impious unbelief confronts this our devout faith, so that this necessary confession may appear foreign to the understanding of the true God: “Amen, amen, I say to you, the Son can do nothing of himself, except what he sees the Father doing” (John 5:19). Unless the twofold indignation of the Jews requires a twofold answer, let this plainly be a confession of weakness: that the Son can do nothing of himself except what he sees the Father doing.

> [Note: Col. 0316C. *Exigit*: “requires.”]

But if, under the same statement, an answer was given to the Jews both accusing him of violating the Sabbath and unable to bear equality with God in Christ, which he had attributed to himself by professing God as his Father, do you think that the truth of the sayings can be forced through the confession of the answer? And although we have treated this passage in another book (*Book VII*, §7), yet, because reconsidering faith not only does no harm but also profits religion, let us revisit it, since the subject requires it.

> [Note: Col. 0316D. Three Vatican manuscripts read, “having professed God for himself.” The sense is clearer thus: they could not bear in Christ the equality of God which he had attributed to himself by professing God the Father.]

44. The accusation of Sabbath violation: how it is removed. The Father’s and Son’s work is not different. The second accusation, concerning presumed equality with God. — The necessity of the answer first arose from this: “For this reason the Jews persecuted Jesus and sought to kill him, because he did these things on the Sabbath” (John 5:16). Their anger, then, was inflamed even to the desire to kill because of works performed on the Sabbath. But let us see what the Lord answered: “My Father works until now, and I work” (John 5:17). What, I ask, is this work of the Father, heretic? Show it. For all things, visible and invisible, exist through the Son and in the Son. And you, who are wiser than the Gospels, must have obtained knowledge of the Father’s work from certain other secret doctrines, so that you may show us the Father at work.

> [Note: Col. 0316D. In printed editions *aliis* (“other”) is missing, as are the words *sis cum* with the following *ut*, after *adeptus* (“having obtained”).]

> [Note: Col. 0316D. Two Colbert manuscripts read “show the Father to us” at the end.]

But if the Father works in the Son, according as he himself says: “The words which I speak to you, I do not speak; but the Father who abides in me, he does his works” (John 14:10), do you see what this means: “My Father works until now”? He said this in order that the power of the Father’s nature in himself might be understood as a nature exercising its power in Sabbath work. For when he works with the Father working in him, he himself must work while the Father works; and therefore he says, “My Father works until now” (John 5:17), so that this present work itself—of words and deeds—might be regarded as the operation in him of the Father’s nature.

> [Note: Col. 0316C. “I do not speak from myself.”]

> [Note: Col. 0316D. Printed editions read *intelligeretur majestas* (“the majesty might be understood”), against the manuscripts.]

> [Note: Col. 0316C. “He works while the Father works in him.”]

For the “until now” in “he works until now” is one and the same moment of speech and time, so that no work of the Father other than this work which the Son performs might be believed: since, by the statement that the Father works until now, these very acts were the Father’s operation at the same time as the utterance. And lest faith, left only with knowledge of the Father, should lack the hope of eternal life, he immediately added, “And I work”: so that the Son also works that which the Father is working until now. Thus he taught perfect faith: since that which is “now” is a work of the same time, and that which the Father works the Son also works is beyond the union of mere singularity.

> [Note: Col. 0317D. The Vatican-Basilican and Martin manuscripts read, “the Father works until now.”]

But the hearers’ pain was doubled, for it follows: “For this reason the Jews sought all the more to kill him, because he not only broke the Sabbath, but also called God his own Father, making himself equal with God” (John 5:18). Here again I remind you that, by the Evangelist’s judgment and the common assent of humankind, a son is equal in the nature of his father; and equality can arise only from the same nature, because birth has nowhere else from which it may continue, and every generation is not alien from that which generates it, since it subsists from the same source as that to which it remains.

> [Note: Col. 0317D. The Martin manuscript alone reads *sub eodem* (“under the same [thing]”).]

Let us therefore see what the Lord answered to this doubled indignation: “Amen, amen, I say to you: the Son can do nothing of himself, except what he sees the Father doing. For whatever he does, these things the Son also does in like manner” (John 5:19).

### 45. Reply to the charge of violating the Sabbath. The phrase “cannot” indicates authority, not weakness. What “unless he sees” signifies. Reply to the second charge.

Unless these sayings are proper to the proposition in question [Note: [Col. 0317D] The editions read *propositionis*, “of the proposition”; the manuscripts, *propositioni*, “to the proposition,” namely that of the Jews, to which Christ’s sayings are adapted. Shortly afterward one Vatican manuscript reads “and of a faithful interpretation”; this is not to be approved.], we do violence to the sayings through the presumption of a private and faithless interpretation. But if the reply is directed to the causes of their anger, then our faith speaks what it is taught rather than irreligious perversity defends the error of its impiety. Let us therefore ask whether this is the proper reply to Sabbath-work [Note: [Col. 0317D] Thus the manuscripts; the editions read “concerning Sabbath-work.”]: “The Son cannot do anything of himself, unless he sees the Father doing it.”

For he had said above: “My Father works until now, and I work” (John 5:17). If, by the authority of the paternal nature within himself, he does what he does while the Father does it—he who works until now on the Sabbath—the Son is outside the charge concerning work, since in him the authority of the Father’s operation is set forth. For he referred “cannot” not to weakness but to authority: for he cannot act of himself [Note: [Col. 0317D] “Unless he sees.”] unless he sees. [Note: [Col. 0317D] The printed editions alone here have “unless he sees.” The Vatican-Basilian manuscript reads, corruptly: “For because he cannot of himself unless he has seen; for what advantage does it confer,” etc. Augustine, following Hilary’s thought, writes in *Against the Arian Sermon*, ch. 14: “What he says that he cannot do belongs not to one who fails, but to one who remains in that in which he was born of the Father”; and, a little earlier, says that he says this because he sees that he has from him the power of acting from whom he sees that he has the nature of existing. Hence Augustine concludes: “He cannot, not through deficiency, but through power.”]

For seeing does not confer power; and since sight does not confer power, inability to act without seeing does not weaken the nature, but indicates authority by seeing. For what he says, “unless he sees,” signifies consciousness in the seeing, just as he says to the Apostles: “Behold, I say to you, lift up your eyes and see the fields, because they are white for harvest” (John 4:35).

Therefore, conscious within himself of the paternal nature which operates in him as it operates, lest the Lord of the Sabbath be thought to have violated the Sabbath, he says: “The Son cannot do anything of himself, unless he sees the Father doing it” (John 5:19), so that he might show that what he did was done from consciousness of the nature operating within him, since, while he worked on the Sabbath, the Father also worked on the Sabbath until now.

But to the pain arising from the other indignity [Note: [Col. 0317D] “Indignation.” Thus he had said in the preceding section: “To this twofold indignation, therefore.”] [Note: [Col. 0318D] The editions read “indignation,” against the great consensus of the manuscripts, which read “indignity.”], he gave the reason in the following saying: “For whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does the same” (ibid.). Reproach the Son of God with weakness; take away also equality of nature, if the Son does not likewise do whatever the Father does; if some distinction between the Father’s power and operation is admitted; if equality of honour is not demanded—that which properly belongs to equality of power and nature [Note: [Col. 0318D] The printed texts read “to equality”; most manuscripts, “by equality.” With the Vatican-Basilian codex, “to equality” is preferable.].

For he himself says immediately afterward: “That all may honour the Son as they honour the Father. He who does not honour the Son does not honour the Father who sent him” (ibid., 23). Distinguish equality in an undivided honour; weaken the nature where the operation of power is the same.

### 46. Summary.

Why do you turn the ground of the reply into an insult against divinity? In reply to Sabbath-work he said that he could do nothing unless he saw the Father doing it; but to demonstrate equality he professed that whatever the Father did, he himself did. Take (supply: “the reply”) what pertains to the Sabbath as a reproach of weakness, if the Son does not likewise do whatever the Father does. But if all things whatsoever are without exception [Note: [Col. 0318D] We restore *are* from the manuscripts.], where at last will weakness be found, when there is nothing [Note: [Col. 0318D] The editions read “none”; the manuscripts, “in nothing,” with their word tacitly understood.] which the Father can do that the Son cannot also do? Or how is equality denied through the interposition of weakness when one and the same honour is required for both? And if the power of working is the same, and the worship of honouring is the same, I do not understand in what respect a reproach of weakness can remain for the nature, when in Father and Son alike there are both the power of strength and equality of honour.

### 47. What it means that “the Son can do nothing of himself” is confirmed elsewhere. Merit.

Although these matters have been treated with the very resolution of the facts themselves, still, lest the Lord’s saying, “The Son cannot do anything of himself, unless he sees the Father doing it” (John 5:19), should serve the impiety which weakens his nature rather than demonstrate consciousness of the paternal nature within him, through which he worked on the Sabbath by authority, the meaning of another saying of the Lord relevant to this point must also be shown. He says: “And I do nothing of myself; but as the Father taught me, these things I speak. And he who sent me is with me, and has not left me alone [Note: [Col. 0319D] “Does not leave”; and so twice below.], because I always do the things pleasing to him” (John 8:28–29).

Do you perceive what it is for the Son to be unable to do anything unless he sees the Father doing it? And under what mystery it was said, “I do nothing of myself”; and again, “He has not left me alone, because I always do the things pleasing to him” (ibid., 29)? For if he does nothing of himself because the Father remains in him, how again has the Father not left him alone because he does what pleases him?

According to your interpretation, heretic, the diversity of these sayings does not cohere: he does nothing of himself unless taught by the Father remaining in him; and again, the Father remains in him because he does what pleases him. For if he does nothing of himself because the Father remains in him, how has he merited, by doing what pleases the Father, that the Father should remain in him? It is no merit to do, not of oneself [Note: [Col. 0319D] “To do.”] [Note: [Col. 0319D] Bad. and several manuscripts read “whatever he does”; other editions, “whatever anyone does.” The better manuscripts read simply “what he does,” as below, “not to have done of himself what he did”; this refers to the Son.], what one does. Conversely, how are the things which the Son does pleasing to the Father, when it is the Father remaining in the Son who does those very things?

You are in a narrow place, impiety, and the most strongly fortified piety of our faith shuts you in. Either the Son does something or he does not. If he does not, how is he pleasing in the things which he does? But if he does, how does he act in things which he does not do of himself? For it is proper to have done what is pleasing, and it is without merit not to have done of oneself what one has done.

### 48. In what sense the Son acts through himself, and in what sense not of himself.

This is the unity of the nature which you oppose: that he so acts through himself as not to act of himself, and so does not act of himself as to act through himself. Understand the Son as acting, and the Father as acting through him. He does not act of himself when the Father’s abiding in him must be shown [Note: [Col. 0319D] Thus the older books; others read “must be demonstrated.”]. He acts through himself when, in accordance with the Son’s birth, he himself does the things pleasing to the Father.

Let there be weakness in not acting of himself only if he does not himself act in such a way that the things he does are pleasing. But let there be no unity of nature if the things which he himself does, and in which he is pleasing, are not done through himself, but the Father abiding in him teaches him in order to act. Thus the Father teaches by abiding, and the Son, in acting, does not act of himself; and the Son who does not act of himself, when he does the things pleasing to the Father, himself acts. Thus unity of nature is maintained in acting: he who operates does not operate of himself, and he who has not operated of himself nevertheless operates.

[Note: [Col. 0319D] “Whom you oppose.” Shortly afterward, “and that he act of himself.” Repeated below as “by acting of himself.” There, too, the manuscripts have *weak*, not *weakness*. A little later *commanding* occurs for *remaining*: corruptly.]

### 49. He says that he does not do his own will, but the Father’s—not because of a necessity of acting, but because of unity.

Add also the passage which you employ as a reproach of weakness: “Everything which the Father gives me comes to me, and I do not cast out the one who comes to me; because I came down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 6:37–38). But perhaps the Son lacks freedom of will, so that weakness of nature imposes necessity upon him. Thus perhaps he is subject to necessity rather than will, so that he does not cast out those given to him by the Father who come to him.

But the Lord, signifying in these words the mystery of unity—while he does not reject those given to him and does not do his own will but that of him who sent him—after repeating this same saying to the murmuring Jews, confirms the meaning which we must understand, saying: “Everyone who hears from the Father and learns comes to me; not that anyone has seen the Father, except he who is from God: he has seen the Father. Amen, amen, I say to you: he who believes in me has eternal life” (ibid., 45 ff.).

And I ask first: where has the Father been heard? Where has he taught those who hear? But no one has seen the Father except he who is from God. How then has anyone heard him whom no one has seen?

Therefore, the one who hears from the Father comes to the Son. And since the Son is heard and teaches [Note: [Col. 0320D] “And is heard and teaches.”], the distinctive property of the paternal nature in him is shown, both as heard and as teaching [Note: [Col. 0319D] One Vatican manuscript reads “and of the hearer”: wrongly. Hilary maintains that the Father is never heard or teaches except insofar as the Son speaks and teaches—who, as Augustine writes in *Against the Arian Sermon*, ch. 24, is the Father’s teaching. Hence he reasonably concludes that the distinctive property of the paternal nature is in the Son; that is, the Father and Son have the same nature.]; so that the hearing of what the Son teaches and is heard teaching may be understood as hearing the Father’s teaching.

For since no one has seen the Father, and yet the one coming to the Son hears and learns from the Father in order to come, we are admonished to understand both that in the speaking Son the Father teaches, and that in the visible Son the Father—whom no one has seen—is heard, because the Son’s birth perfectly contains within itself the distinctive property of the paternal nature.

Therefore the only-begotten God, wishing to bear witness to paternal authority while preserving in himself unity of nature, both does not cast out those given to him by the Father and performs not his own will but that of him who sent him. This is not because he does not will the things he does, or because he himself, who teaches, is not heard; but in order that, while showing both him who sends and himself who is sent under the distinctive property of an undifferentiated nature, he might signify that the will, works, and words which he does and speaks are the Father’s.

### 50. Christ has free will, yet does not dissent from the Father’s will.

That he has free will he shows without ambiguity when he says: “For as the Father raises the dead and gives life, so also the Son gives life to whom he wills” (John 5:21). When equality of power and dignity of honour in Father and Son is made manifest, freedom of will is also shown; but when unity is demonstrated, there is signified the disposition of the paternal will. [Note: [Col. 0320D] The Vatican-Basilian and Martin manuscripts read “unity of authority.” The word “authority” has wrongly been added: with Hilary it usually signifies the distinction of Father and Son, not their unity. One might prefer simply “but when authority,” or “but when birth”; nevertheless, the reading received by the great consensus of the other manuscripts should be retained in this sense: while unity is signified together with conformity to the Father’s will, the reverence due to the Father is preserved and singularity of persons excluded. This clause looks rather to the preceding biblical passages than to the immediately preceding one.]

For the things which the Father wills, the Son does. To do, however, is more than to obey a will: for obeying a will has the necessity of something external [Note: [Col. 0321C] This is stated more clearly in the final words of this section, unless one prefers this understanding: doing another’s will belongs to unity when the deed is also the will of the one who does it.]; whereas doing a will belongs to unity, when what is done is also the will of the one doing it.

And when the Son does the Father’s will, he teaches, through the undifferentiated character of the nature, that he has a will natural to himself with the Father, since his will is everything that he does. Certainly the Son wills all that the Father wills, and their natural will does not dissent. For when this is the Father’s will, as he shows in saying, “For this is the will of my Father, that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him should have eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day” (John 6:39), hear now whether the Son’s will dissents from the Father’s when he says: “Father, those whom you have given me, I will that they also may be with me where I am” (John 17:24).

Therefore it is not doubtful that the Son wills. For while the Father wills that believers in the Son should have eternal life, the Son wills that believers should be where he himself is. Unless perhaps dwelling with Christ is not eternal life; or unless Christ does not grant believers a perfect and blessed life in himself when he says: “No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and he to whom the Son wills to reveal him” (Matthew 11:25). Is he not free in will when he wills to grant us consciousness of that paternal mystery? And is his will not free to such an extent that he imparts knowledge of himself and of the Father to whom he wills? Thus both the nature of birth and of unity between Father and Son is demonstrated: the Son is so free in will that what he does willingly is the accomplishment of the Father’s will.

### 51. There is no hope without faith. How Father and Son are in one another. The Father, as author, is greater than the Son, who is also lesser as man. In Christ the nature of God remained, though the form was emptied.

One who plainly does not know the dispensation of faith is outside the understanding of the mysteries; and, without acquiring the teaching of the Gospel, is estranged from the hope of the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0321C] “From hope.”]. The Father must be believed to be in the Son and the Son in the Father: through unity of nature, through power of strength, through equality of honour, through the generation of birth.

But perhaps the Lord’s declaration [Note: [Col. 0321C] Lipsius and Paris: “attestation.”] is contrary to this profession of ours, when he says: “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28). Is this, heretic, the weapon of your impiety? Are these the arms of your madness? Have you forgotten that the Church knows not two unbegotten beings and does not confess two Fathers? Have you forgotten the dispensation of the Mediator, and in it birth, cradle, age, passion, cross, and death? And, reborn, have you not confessed in the Creed that the Son of God was born from Mary?

If the Son, remaining in all these things, says, “The Father is greater than I,” do you think that this dispensation of your salvation—the emptying of the form of God—must be ignored? And that the Father remained outside this assumption of human sufferings, in the blessed eternity of his uncontaminated nature, without assuming our flesh?

For we confess that the only-begotten God remained in the nature of God [Note: [Col. 0321C] Bad. and Erasmus read “remained in human nature.” Lipsius then introduced a further corruption, substituting “into the state of divine unity of nature” for “into the nature of divine unity”; Paris did not correct it. Hilary professes that Christ, according to the form of God, always remained in God’s nature, unity, and glory, although according to the form of a servant he did not immediately, from the assumption of human nature itself, attain the unity of the divine nature, but only through resurrection glory, as explained above.], and we do not immediately transfer the unity of the servant-form into the nature of divine unity. Nor again do we preach the Father as being in the Son by bodily indwelling; rather, we preach that the begotten nature [Note: [Col. 0322C] “The nature begotten in himself.” The editions read this fuller phrase, but *in himself* is rightly absent from the better manuscripts. Hilary calls the Son “begotten nature,” and the Father “begetting nature”; from this he concludes that both natures are of the same kind and are mutually in one another, though in the differing respects of begetting and begotten. Fulgentius similarly says in his reply to Ferrandus, no. 2: “The Father begot from himself the nature of the Son”; and in *On the Incarnation and Grace of Christ*, ch. 3: “For that spiritual nature of the Word of God, begotten from God the Father without beginning, could not in the womb of that holy mother and virgin be conceived temporally without flesh.”], being of the same kind, has in itself naturally the nature which begets it—a nature which, remaining in the form of the nature that begets it, received the form of nature and bodily weakness.

For the distinctive property of the [divine] nature was present [Note: [Col. 0322C] The editions here prefix “human.” They might more tolerably have prefixed “divine”; although the word is not expressed, it must nevertheless be understood.]; but it was now not the form of God [Note: [Col. 0322C] The commonly printed texts read “but not the form of God,” adding the negative particle contrary to the authority of the manuscripts and to Hilary’s meaning. As is his custom, Hilary declares that during the dispensation God’s nature remained entire in Christ, but that the form had been emptied. It is therefore clear that by “form” he understood something different from the nature itself. Nor is it obscure what he understood: by “form” he meant the outward condition which Christ displayed. The Apostle declares that he was found in condition not as God but as man (Phil. 2:7). Thus, when above in no. 38 Hilary teaches that Christ, in being born as man, introduced a new condition in himself—not through loss of power or nature, but through a change of outward condition—and when below in no. 54 he grants that human birth introduced a new nature and humility changed the form under the assumption of a servant, he sufficiently indicates that “form” and “condition” are interchangeable terms for him. By them he understood the glory indeed connatural with the Only-begotten, but withheld for a time from the assumed flesh and to that extent lost, since the conjunction of both forms was not fitting, as he says in no. 14. More explicitly, in no. 40, “The Father has no need of glory, nor had he emptied himself of the form of his glory”: what is there called “glory” and “the form of glory” is here called “the form of God.”], because through its emptying the form of a servant had been assumed.

The nature had not failed so as not to exist; rather, the nature of God, remaining itself amid the lowliness of earthly birth [Note: [Col. 0322D] Here “earthly birth” denotes human nature, just as above, in no. 40, “All glory was acquired not for the Word but for the flesh, that is, not for the birth of God,” the word “birth” signifies the divine nature. Next, “the nature of God remaining itself” means that the person of the Word remained its own master, with its divine nature preserved, which it made manifest by the deeds proper to its kind, and exercised the power of its own nature—as though Hilary had said that it remained entire, true, and proper to itself. Or “it remained itself” may mean that it lay hidden within itself. This is illustrated by the similar passage in book XI, no. 48: “For God, remaining in the form, assumed the form of a servant, not changed but emptying himself, hidden within himself and emptied within his own power”; and, a few words later: “What he contained by emptying himself within himself brought no loss to his power, since . . . he employed in power all the power emptied within himself.”], exercised the power of its own kind in the condition of assumed lowliness.

And God born from God, found as man in the form of a servant [Note: [Col. 0323D] Bad. and Erasmus, following a Vienna manuscript and one Vatican manuscript, read “in the form of God”; another Vatican manuscript, “in the form of God’s servant”: wrongly. Christ was found as man because of the form of a servant, not because of the form of God.], showed himself to be God by his mighty works; nor was he not God, as his deeds taught [Note: [Col. 0323D] The printed texts add “for”; it is absent from the manuscripts.]; nor did he cease to remain man, in whose condition he was found.

### 52. The Father is seen in the Son.

Therefore, in that same preceding discourse, having testified to unity of nature with the Father, he said: “He who has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9), and: “The Father is in me, and I in the Father” (John 10:38). These certainly admit no difference in equality of nature [Note: [Col. 0323D] Thus the manuscripts; the editions read “from quality.” Bad. and Erasmus read *complevisset*, “had fulfilled,” for *compenset*, “makes good”: the latter means that seeing the Son supplies the place of seeing the Father.], since contemplation of the Son makes good the seeing of the Father, and one abiding in one does not distinguish one from one.

And lest it be thought that, through bodily contemplation, he provided from himself the sight of the Father’s contemplation, he added: “Believe me, that I am in the Father and the Father in me; but if not, believe because of the works” (John 14:11–12). Thus, since power belongs to nature and the operation of power itself is might, unity of the paternal nature within him might be known through the power of might: when, insofar as anyone recognized him as God [Note: [Col. 0323D] Erasmus, Lipsius, and Paris read “insofar as anyone,” omitting *himself*, on which the sense of the whole sentence depends.] through the power of his nature, so far he would recognize God the Father through the might of that nature; and when the Son, being as great as the Father is, provided through his deeds that the Father should be seen in himself, the Father would be known as undifferentiated from the Son [Note: [Col. 0323D] The printed texts read “in the Son.” The manuscripts rightly read “from the Son,” namely, undifferentiated from him.] through understanding of this undifferentiatedness in the power of nature.

### 53. Why and in what sense Christ said, while preserving equality of nature: “The Father is greater than I.”

Therefore the only-begotten God, about to fulfil the dispensation of the flesh and consummate the mystery of the assumed servant-form, used a declaration fitted to demonstrate our faith [Note: [Col. 0324C] The Vatican-Basilian and Martin manuscripts here add, “and you were grieved”; it occurs neither in the other manuscripts nor in the Greek or Latin biblical text.], saying: “You heard that I said to you: I go, and I come to you. If you loved me, you would rejoice because I go to the Father, because the Father is greater than I” (John 14:28).

Since, then, in this same preceding discourse he had set forth those matters which concern the nature of divinity [Note: [Col. 0323C] The old books read “await,” but in no different sense.], does this declaration take from the Son the equality of nature which genuine birth completes? Or is it an insult to the only-begotten God that the unbegotten God is his Father, when only-begotten birth subsists from the unbegotten God into an only-begotten nature? [Note: [Col. 0324D] That is: the Son is not his own source.]

For the Son is not the origin of himself, nor did he, who did not exist, procure from nothing a birth for himself. Rather, living nature existing from living nature holds in itself the power of nature, having acknowledged the authority of that nature, in order both to testify to honour and to acknowledge in honour the grace of the birth received. [Note: [Col. 0324D] That is, by these words, “The Father is greater than I,” he confesses the author and source of his nature, and with honour and reverence testifies to the honour and grace of his received birth. As Cyril observes, *Thesaurus*, p. 91, the Son accords greater honour to the Father solely for the sake of reverence.]

And while he renders to the Father what is due, in that he attributes his obedience to the will of him who sent him, he does not thereby weaken unity of nature by the obedience of humility. He became obedient unto death, yet after death he is not without the name above every name.

### 54. The Father is greater as the author of the gift; the Son, to whom he gives all that he is, is not lesser.

But if perhaps he seems unequal on this ground, that after the emptying of the form of God this name is given to him, such calumny is ignorant of the mystery of assumed humility. For if human birth introduced a new nature and humility changed the form under the assumption of a servant, now the gift of the name restores equality of form [Note: [Col. 0324D] The Vatican-Basilian manuscript reads corruptly, “returns into equality of form”; Martin, “returns into the eternity of form.” As Hilary said the form of God was lost through the humility of assumed flesh, so he now says it was restored through the glory and exaltation of that flesh. He means, as no. 56 makes clear, that the Father is greater when asked to restore glory to the assumed man, but the Son is not lesser when he resumes glory with the Father.].

Ask what was given. If what belongs to God was given, the gift of this nature does not bring inferiority upon that divine nature. Accordingly, this name now given to him, although it has the mystery of a gift, nevertheless does not give, in the gift of the name, an alien name. For it is given to Jesus that the heavenly, earthly, and infernal beings should bend the knee [Note: [Col. 0324C] “Bend the knee.”] to him, and that every tongue should confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father (Philippians 2:10). Therefore the honour of this confession is given: that he should be confessed to be in the glory of God the Father.

Do you hear, then: “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28)? Know him of whom it was said on account of the merit of obedience: “And he gave him the name which is above every name” (Philippians 2:9). Hear again: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30); “He who has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9); and “I am in the Father and the Father in me” (ibid., 11). Understand the honour of the given confession: that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father [Note: [Col. 0325C] “Is in the glory of God the Father.”].

When, then, is it that “the Father is greater than I”? Surely when the name above every name is given to him. Conversely, when is it that “I and the Father are one”? Surely [Note: [Col. 0325C] The manuscripts have *namque*, “for indeed.”] when every tongue confesses that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father. If, therefore, the Father is greater by the authority of the giver, is the Son lesser through the confession of the gift? [Note: [Col. 0325C] That is, through the given confession, or the gift of the name, which every tongue is bound to confess.] The giver is indeed greater; but he to whom it is given to be one is no longer lesser. If this is not given to Jesus—that he should be confessed in the glory of God the Father—then he is lesser than the Father. But if it is given to him to be in that glory in which the Father is, then you have both that he is greater in the authority of the giver [Note: [Col. 0325C] The printed texts read “because the Father is greater.” *Father* is absent from the manuscripts, and “greater” rightly refers to the giver.] and that they are one in the confession of the gift.

Therefore the Father is greater than the Son—and certainly greater, who gives him to be as great as he himself is; who imparts to him the image of unbegotten being through the mystery of birth; who begets him from himself into his own form; who again renews him from the form of a servant into the form of God [Note: [Col. 0325D] The editions read “in his own form,” and shortly afterward “in the form of God”; both readings are corrected from the manuscripts. Moreover, the Father generates him in eternity by bestowing a glorious nature, but renews him in time by granting divine glory to the assumed man.]; who grants that Christ, God born according to the Spirit [Note: [Col. 0325C] “Christ, God born according to the Spirit.” The Martin, Corbie, and several other manuscripts read “according to the flesh”: wrongly. Colbert, Carnot, and German manuscripts read “according to Christ,” omitting *Spirit*. It would be preferable to omit *Christ*.], should again be in his glory according to the flesh as Jesus Christ, God dead [Note: [Col. 0326C] “Born—dead.”] [Note: [Col. 0325D] The editions, from inferior manuscripts, added “born” here. There is a play on words between “God born” and “God dead”: born in glory according to the Spirit, that is, as the Word, and granted again to be in glory according to the flesh after he died. Thus the glory of Christ as God is from birth, but that of the man from death.].

He therefore showed the reason why, if they loved him, they should rejoice that he was going to the Father: because the Father was greater.

### 55. The sense in which the Father was called greater is established from what precedes and follows.

He teaches, therefore, that this joy comes from love, because love would rejoice that Jesus is to be confessed in the glory of God the Father; and immediately he adds the merit by which this glory was to be resumed: “For the ruler of this world comes, and has nothing in me” (John 14:30). [Note: [Col. 0326C] “Has nothing”: a Greek idiom corresponding to John’s Greek, *ouk echei ouden* (οὐκ ἔχει οὐδέν).]

The ruler of this world has nothing in him, because, though found as man in outward condition, he remained beyond fleshly sin in the likeness of sinful flesh, condemning sin in the flesh through sin (Romans 8:3). Referring all this to obedience to the Father’s command, he added: “But that the world may know that I love the Father, and as the Father gave me commandment, so I do. Rise, let us go from here” (John 14:31). [Note: [Col. 0326C] *Father* does not occur in the Verona codex.]

He rises hastily [Note: [Col. 0325D] The Colbert and German manuscripts read “to confirm,” probably corruptly.] to fulfil the mystery of bodily passion by love in carrying out the Father’s command; yet immediately unfolds the mystery of bodily assumption, by which we are in him as branches in a vine, and would not yield useful fruit as branches unless he had become the vine (John 15:1 ff.).

For this reason he exhorts us to remain in himself through faith in his assumed body: so that, because the Word became flesh, we might be in the nature of his flesh as branches in a vine. Alienating the form of the Father’s majesty from this assumption of bodily humility at the time when he professed himself the vine for the unity of the branches [Note: [Col. 0325D–0326D] The Tellerian codex reads “for usefulness.” One Colbert manuscript, with another from the Sorbonne, reads “for humility.” “For unity” must be retained with the other manuscripts. For, as Hilary says in *On Psalm 51*, no. 16: “He assumed in himself the nature of all flesh, through which, having become the true vine, he holds within himself the race of every offshoot.” The immediately preceding words, “alienating the form of the Father’s majesty from this assumption of bodily humility,” may refer to Christ himself: wishing to be conjoined with the branches, he withheld the Father’s glory from his own flesh and thus alienated himself from unity with that form. More truly, however, this should be interpreted of Christ’s members, namely the whole human race: although assumed by Christ and existing in him as branches in a vine, they are nevertheless shown to be alienated from participation in the Father’s glory when they are shown to be uprooted by the Father, whether because of unbelief or because of the uselessness of fruits withheld, as is again explained in the passage from *On Psalm 51* cited above.], he showed the Father as the diligent cultivator [Note: [Col. 0326D] An older Colbert manuscript reads “glorious.” “Diligent,” that is, one who takes care, is preferable.] of this vine, assigning its useless and fruitless branches, when cut off [Note: [Col. 0326D] The Vatican-Basilian manuscript reads “to be cut off.” In the commonly printed texts the words are disordered: “he would assign them to be burned, saying thus, ‘He who sees me,’” etc.], to be burned.

Thus, saying, “He who has seen me has seen the Father”; “The words which I speak, I do not speak of myself; but the Father who remains in me does his works” (John 14:9–10); and “Believe me, that I am in the Father and the Father in me” (ibid., 11), he came, in the coherence of his sayings, to say: “Because the Father is greater than I” (ibid., 28), in order to make manifest both the mystery of birth and the mystery of the assumed body.

And immediately, so that the complete rationale of the saying might follow, he added the example of cultivator, vine, and branch, thereby showing the assumption of bodily humility. From this he taught both the reason for his going to the Father and why love ought to rejoice when he went to the Father: namely, because the Father was greater than he, from whom he was to resume glory, with whom and in whom he was to be glorified—not with a new honour, but with the former one; not an alien honour, but that which he had with him.

Therefore, if he is not to be glorified in him [Note: [Col. 0326D] The editions read “in himself”; at the end of the following section, “is glorified in the Father.” The manuscripts support “in him” and “into the Father.”]—that is, so as to be in the glory of God the Father—impute dishonour to the nature. But if being glorified by him is authority, recognize the Father as greater in the authority of glorifying.

### 56. The Father is greater, yet the Son is not lesser.

Why do you seize upon the dispensation for impiety? Why do you attack the mystery of our salvation unto death? The Father, who is to glorify the Son, is greater; the Son glorified in the Father is not lesser. Or how is he lesser who is in the glory of God the Father? Or is the Father not greater?

The Father, therefore, is greater inasmuch as he is Father; but the Son, inasmuch as he is Son, is not lesser. The birth of the Son establishes the Father as greater; but the nature of that birth does not allow the Son to be lesser. The Father is greater when he is asked to restore glory to the assumed man; the Son is not lesser when he resumes glory with the Father.

Thus both the mystery of birth and the dispensation of embodiment are fulfilled. For the Father, inasmuch as he is Father and now glorifies the Son of Man, is greater; and Father and Son are one, inasmuch as the Son born from the Father, after assuming an earthly body, is glorified into the Father.

57. The Unbegotten and the Begotten Are Not of Different Natures. The Begotten Son Did Not Begin to Exist.---Birth, therefore, has no lowliness of nature: for He is in the form of God, and is born from God. And although unbegottenness differs from birth in its very signification, birth is nevertheless not outside the nature of unbegottenness, because it did not derive from elsewhere that by which it subsists. For, although it did not attain to be made co-unbegotten, it nevertheless received from the unbegotten God [Col. 0327C] what God is. Therefore our faith, although it does not grasp the beginning of this birth, nevertheless confesses that the only-begotten God always is; because nature does not permit us to confess that He ever began, whose birth transcends every period of beginning. Yet Him whom it confesses always to be and to be before times, it does not doubt to have been born in timeless infinity; and it confesses Him to have been born by a birth belonging to the understanding of the Beginningless.

> [Note: Bad. reads “in temporal”; the other editions, “in timeless.” Shortly afterwards Erasmus, following Bad., has “from the unbeginning”; Paris, following [Col. 0327D] Lipsius, “from the beginning.” We follow the manuscripts. Faith does not doubt that He was born by a timeless birth, whom it knows to have been born from eternity—His birth, namely, drawing from the Father’s eternity, as is said in Book IV, §6. It also confesses Him to be born by a birth belonging to the understanding of the Beginningless, since it does not grasp the beginning of His birth, as was said immediately before; more clearly in Book XII, §31: whatever the mind, turning backward, investigates concerning the Son, nothing other will occur to the inquirer’s thought than that He is born and always is.]  
>
> [Note: “From the Beginningless.”]

58. The Ignorance of the Day Is Objected against Him.---But the heretics employ this [Col. 0328A] to dishonor His nature, because it was said, “The Father is greater than I”; or again, “But of that day and hour no one knows, neither the angels in heaven nor the Son, but the Father alone” (Mark 13:32). Thus ignorance of the day and hour is charged against the only-begotten God, so that God born from God may not be in that perfection of nature in which God is God: since, if the necessity of not knowing prevails, some external power is already stronger than He, holding Him in the weakness of ignorance as one feeble against itself.

Indeed, the madness of the heretics rightly compels us to the impiety of this interpretation by a kind of necessary confession: namely, that this is to be believed because the Lord Himself so spoke, and because it may seem most irreligious to corrupt, by an opinion of an interpretation other than ours, His own declaration concerning Himself.

[Col. 0328B]

59. The Author of All Things Can Be Ignorant of Nothing. He Who Knows Things Neither in Himself nor through Himself Knows Much More Those Which Are in and through Himself. The Day of the Lord Is Established through and in Him.---First, before considering the meaning and cause of the saying, common judgment must decide whether it can be credible that He should be ignorant of anything among all things, who is the author to all things of what they are and will be. For if all things are through Christ and in Christ—and so through Him that all things are in Him—how can that which is neither outside Him nor not through Him fail also to be within His knowledge, when His knowledge commonly apprehends by the power of His unignorant nature even those things which are neither in Him nor through Him?

> [Note: A Vatican manuscript has, “I ask what is to be thought by the judgment common to all”; this appears to be a gloss, as also in the Martin manuscript, which reads, “I ask whether it is to be thought.”]  
>
> [Note: The printed editions read “His knowledge, that also,” omitting “His,” which the manuscripts correctly preserve. Christ was asserted just above as the universal cause, the author to all things of what they are and will be; here He is said, as a particular cause, to apprehend things neither in Himself nor through Himself—for example, the thoughts of others. Again, the word *commonly* may raise a question: does He not apprehend all things? He does indeed apprehend all things, but made His knowledge concerning certain things only manifest. Here *commonly* signifies not the greater part but an indeterminate part; this usage is familiar to other Fathers also, but especially to Pope Gregory.]  
>
> [Note: In Bad. and Erasmus, “not ignorant.” One Vatican manuscript and one Sorbonne manuscript read, “may He not know and apprehend?”]

But how can that which takes its cause from none but Him, and does not contain within itself motion toward that which is and will be, be outside the knowledge of His nature, through which and in which what is to be made is contained?

> [Note: Two Colbert manuscripts with the German manuscript read, “and not the movement.” Then Bad. has “toward that which is external and will be”; one Vatican manuscript, the Tellier manuscript, and the Vienna manuscript have “toward that which is external”; the Sorbonne manuscript, “toward that which is external-and”: corruptly. Cyril briefly states and explains this same argument in *Treasury*, p. 218: “It belongs to the Word, precisely as Word, to know the beginnings and ends of those things which were created by Him. Time is one of the things created by Him; and He who created time knows how long it will last.”]  
>
> [Note: The Verona manuscript first read “which is and will be,” but was corrected by a second hand to “which is external.”]

For the Lord Christ is not ignorant of human thoughts—not merely as stirred by present impulse, but as to be agitated also by the prompting of a future will—as the Evangelist testifies: “For Jesus knew from the beginning who they were that did not believe, and who it was that would betray Him” (John 6:65).

> [Note: “And who it was.”]

Will then the power of His nature, which comprehends knowledge of things not existing and does not fail to know the future disturbances of minds still at rest, be thought ignorant of that [Col. 0329A] which exists through and within itself? Is He powerful concerning what belongs to another, yet powerless concerning Himself—He of whom we remember it said: “All things were created through Him and in Him, and He is before all” (Col. 1:16); or, “For in Him it pleased all [the] fullness to dwell, and through Him to reconcile all things to Him” (ibid., 19)?

> [Note: “The fullness of divinity.”]  
>
> [Note: Thus the manuscripts, as also in Book VIII, §5, agreeing with the Greek εἰς αὐτόν, “unto Him.” The printed texts have “in Him.”]

Since, therefore, all fullness is in Him, all things are reconciled through Him and in Him, and that day is the expectation of our reconciliation, does He not know that day whose time is in Himself and which comes through His dispensation? For this is the day of His coming, of which the Apostle says: “When Christ, your life, shall appear, then you also shall appear with Him [in glory]” (Col. 3:4).

> [Note: “In glory.”]  
>
> [Note: Namely, through the dispensation and assumed flesh in which He will come to judge the living and the dead. Accordingly, that day belongs to Christ as man, since the Father gave all judgment to the Son because He is Son of Man, as is written in John 5:22, 27. The time of the day is also in Him as the Word, the maker of times.]

No one is ignorant of what is through and within himself. Christ will be present, and does He not know [Col. 0329B] the day of His coming? It is His day, according to the same Apostle: “The day of the Lord will come as a thief in the night” (1 Thess. 5:2). Is He then to be understood as held in ignorance of it? Human beings know, so far as lies within them, what they determine to do; and knowledge of what is to be done follows the will to act. But does God who is born not know what is in and through Himself? For times are through Him, and the day is in Him, since the ordering of things to come is through Him and the dispensation of His coming is in Him. Shall He be in such dullness that, by a torpid natural perception, He does not know that which pertains to Himself—like wild animals and beasts, animated apart from the reasoning of provident counsel, which do not know what they do but, impelled by a certain motion of stupid desire, proceed toward something by a chance and uncertain course?

[Col. 0329C]

60. It Is an Injury to the Father to Ascribe Ignorance to the Son, as Though He Had Envied Him.---How, moreover, can the Lord of glory, whose day of coming is unknown, be believed to have a disordered and imperfect nature—a nature which must come, yet has not obtained knowledge of its own coming? In that case ignorance would be stronger than God, since it would take from Him the power of possessing knowledge.

> [Note: In two manuscripts “God” is absent. By this word the Father is understood: He must be denied the power of knowing all things and must rather be assigned ignorance than that stain of envy by which He might be believed to withhold some knowledge from His beloved Son.]

Further, how greatly is occasion for impiety doubled if, in addition to Christ’s weakness, a fault is also charged against God the Father—if He deprived the only-begotten God, the Son of His love, of the knowledge of this day, and through malicious feeling begrudged Him knowledge of the future consummation. Although He willed that neither the day nor the hour of His Passion should be unknowable to Him, He denied Him the day of His power and the hour of His glorification in His saints; and He removed knowledge of blessedness from Him to whom He granted foreknowledge of death?

> [Note: Bad. and Erasmus read, “an occasion is generated through Christ’s weakness.” In other printed editions the following particle *if* is likewise missing.]  
>
> [Note: Two manuscripts read “by effect.”]

Human conscience cannot endure to make such a judgment concerning God, or to ascribe to Him the faults of human changeableness: that either the Father should deny something to the Son or God born should be ignorant of something.

[Col. 0329D–0330A]

61. As God, He Is Free from Envy; as Father, He Gives All That He Has, Especially Since He Is Simple. As It Is Proper to God, So It Is Proper to God’s Son, to Foreknow Things to Come.---But God is never anything other than love, nor anything other than Father. He who loves does not envy; and He who is Father is not, in any respect, not Father. For this name admits no division, such that He should be Father in one respect and not Father in another. For He is Father of the whole of that which is in Himself, possessing all of Himself in Him to whom what He is as Father does not belong by a part: not because the Father is Himself the father of those things which are His, but because in those things by which He Himself is, He is wholly Father to Him who is from Himself.

> [Note: That is, in begetting the Son the Father gives Him all things which are in Himself.]

And since, according to the nature of human bodies, which come together from unlike elements and consist of composite parts, no father can be father except of all that is his—because perfect birth preserves in sons whatever belongs in each case to kinds and parts—every father is father of all that is his, because birth is from all these and remains in all of them.

> [Note: In the common printed texts *father* is not repeated here or below; shortly afterwards they read “in the son,” not “in the sons.”]

But in God there are not bodily things but absolute realities; not partial things but whole and universal realities; not things made alive but living realities. God is wholly living and wholly one, because He is not composed from portions but perfect in simplicity.

> [Note: “Whole.”]  
>
> [Note: Thus the best Colbert manuscript, with the Martin and German manuscripts. Others read “wholly.”]

It follows that, insofar as He is Father, He is wholly Father, with all that is His, to Him whom He begot from Himself, because the perfect birth of the Son fully establishes Him as Father from all that is His. If, then, the Father belongs properly to the Son, the Son must remain in that property in which the Father is. But how shall He be thought to remain in it if He is outside the nature of foreknowledge, and something belonging to His birth is lacking from its source? For nearly everything will be lacking if He does not possess what is proper to God. And what is proper to God except knowledge of future things: so that a nature capable of invisible and not-yet-existing kinds contains realities which do not yet endure but will endure hereafter?

> [Note: One Vatican and the Carnot manuscript read “from authority”; a reading not to be despised, for *authority* means for Hilary what *source* means for us.]

62. Nothing Is Hidden from Him in Whom Are All Treasures of Knowledge, Though They Are Hidden.---The Apostle of the Gentiles, Paul, does not permit us to profess this impious error, as though the only-begotten God were ignorant of anything. [Col. 0331A] For he says: “Being established in love, unto all riches of the full assurance of understanding, unto the knowledge of the mystery of God Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col. 2:2–3). Christ is the mystery of God, and all treasures of wisdom and knowledge lie hidden in Him.

> [Note: Lipsius and Paris read “of God the Father and Christ,” agreeing with our copies of the sacred text; but Bad., Erasmus, and the manuscripts oppose this reading, as does the exposition of these words below.]  
>
> [Note: “Hidden.” Moreover, *thensauri*, with an inserted *n*, is consistently written in the Verona manuscript.]

This cannot apply to a part and the whole, because a part cannot be understood as all things, and all things do not allow themselves to be understood as a part. For if the Son does not know the day, then not all treasures of knowledge are in Him. He does not fail to know the day, since He contains in Himself all treasures of knowledge. But we should remember that these treasures of knowledge are hidden in Him; and they are not absent because they are hidden. They are in Him by that whereby He is God, but are hidden by that whereby He is mystery.

> [Note: Before the words “does not fail to know the day,” the manuscript has: “If all treasures of knowledge are in Him.” Shortly afterwards it has “all treasure” and then “are” for “are in.”]  
>
> [Note: We have removed “If all treasures of knowledge are in Him,” on the authority of the better manuscripts.]

The mystery of God Christ, in whom all treasures of knowledge are hidden, is not unknown or hidden from us. And because He Himself is mystery, let us see whether He is ignorant in those things which He does not know. For if, in other cases, His profession of not knowing does not signify that He is ignorant, neither does He now truly lack knowledge of what He does not know. For since His ignorance—according to the fact that all treasures of knowledge are hidden in Him—is dispensation rather than ignorance, you have a reason for His saying that He does not know without an implication that He is ignorant.

> [Note: Two manuscripts read “is in Himself,” which is unacceptable. For above Christ is repeatedly proclaimed as mystery—that is, hidden God, whose form was emptied through the assumption of bodily humility. Later the Martin manuscripts read “which are from Himself” for “which He does not know.”]  
>
> [Note: That is, it does not signify that He is to be understood as ignorant. Thus below: “You have a reason for His saying that He does not know without an implication that He is ignorant”: you have a reason why He behaves as if ignorant, without being understood actually not to know.]

63. What It Means When God Is Said Not to Know, or to Know Only Now.---In every case in which God says that He does not know, He indeed professes ignorance, yet is not held by ignorance. For with respect to what He does not know, there is no weakness of not knowing, but either a time for not speaking or a dispensation for not acting.

> [Note: The German manuscript reads, “yet ignorance is not assigned.” Then Lipsius and Paris have “while that,” deleting “but” without authority.]

God speaks to Abraham, saying: “The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah is full, and their sins are exceedingly great. Therefore I will go down and see whether they are consummated according to their cry; and if not, that I may know” (Gen. 18:20–21). Thus we have God as not knowing, though He does not actually lack knowledge. For, although He knows that their sins are exceedingly great, He nevertheless goes down to see whether they are consummated, and, if they are not yet consummated, that He may know. We understand that He does not fail to know because He does not know, but that He then knows because it is time to act.

> [Note: One Vatican manuscript, with Remigius and Theodotion, adds here: “coming to Me.” Then only the Martin and Vatican-Basil manuscripts read “shall be consummated.”]  
>
> [Note: The better manuscripts read “whether they have been consummated, and if they have not yet been consummated.” The Martin manuscript reads, “whether they are to be consummated, and if they are not to be consummated.”]  
>
> [Note: Thus the manuscripts, except one Vienna manuscript, which reads “that He does not know these things because He does not know.” The printed editions read, “that He does not then know these things because He previously did not know.” In place of “because He does not know,” the sense appears to require “because He now knows.” Since old books give *nunc* (“now”) in the two letters *nc*, without separating words in any way, *nesciat* could readily have arisen from *nunc sciat*. The Martin manuscript then has, “but then knows when it is time to act.”]  
>
> [Note: Erasmus preferred *not know* in place of *know*, followed by Lipsius and those who worked on correcting the last Paris edition, though almost all manuscripts oppose it. The meaning is this: when God is said to know, there is no change in Him from ignorance to knowledge, but the fullness of time is indicated.]

Therefore God’s knowing is not a change from ignorance, but the fullness of time. He is still awaited as one who may know; and although we cannot understand that He does not know, yet, since He still awaits the time to know, it follows that what He knows while not knowing, and does not know while knowing, is nothing other than a dispensation either of speaking or of acting.

> [Note: In most manuscripts and in Paris the particle *that* is repeated here.]

64. God Is Said to Know Now What He Now Declares.---Therefore there can be no doubt that God’s knowledge concerns time rather than change, since when God knows, it is the time for professing knowledge rather than for acquiring it. We are taught this also by the words said to Abraham: “Do not lay your hand upon the child, and do not do anything to him; for now I know that you fear God and have not spared your beloved son for My sake” (Gen. 22:12).

> [Note: “The Lord your God.”]  
>
> [Note: The common printed texts read “the Lord your God.” *Lord* is absent from the manuscripts. Moreover *your* is absent from the Greek and Latin text of Scripture.]

God, then, knows now; and to know now is a profession of prior ignorance. Since this cannot apply to God—and since He could not previously have been ignorant that Abraham was faithful to Him, of whom it had been said, “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him for righteousness” (Gen. 15:6; Rom. 4:3)—this “now I know” denotes the time when Abraham received testimony, not the time when God began to know.

> [Note: After *nor* the word *apply* is omitted; accordingly we restore the following particle *that*, wrongly deleted by Lipsius, from Bad., Erasmus, and the manuscripts.]

For Abraham had shown, by offering his son as a burnt offering, the love which he had for God. God knew then when He spoke. Since He must not be understood to have been ignorant before, He is accordingly understood to have known then because He spoke. These examples alone have been set out by us from the many passages concerning God’s knowledge contained in the Old Testament, so that what God does not know might be understood to concern not ignorance but time.

[Col. 0332C–0333A]

65. He Is Said Not to Know Those Unworthy of His Knowledge: Workers of Iniquity and Foolish Virgins.---In the Gospels, however, we find the Lord not knowing many things which He knows. He does not know workers of iniquity who boast in many mighty works and in His name, saying: “And then I will swear, ‘I never knew you. Depart from Me, all you who work iniquity’” (Matt. 7:23). Even with an oath He does not know those whom nevertheless He does not fail to know as workers of iniquity. He does not know them, then, not because He lacks knowledge, but because through their works of iniquity they are unworthy of His knowledge. He confirms the truth of His saying by the sacredness of an oath: having, by the power of His nature, no incapacity to know, and retaining, by the mystery of His will, a refusal to know.

> [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads “through the working of iniquity.” Shortly afterwards the better manuscripts read *of swearing*, not *of an oath*.]

The only-begotten God also does not know the foolish virgins; entering the bridal chamber of His glorious coming, He does not know those who neglected to procure oil for themselves. For they approach and entreat Him, and they are so far from being unknown that He answers them: “Amen I say to you, I do not know you” (Matt. 25:12).

> [Note: “And even so far.”]  
>
> [Note: Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read “even to that point.”]

For their meeting Him and their plea do not permit them to be unknowable. But the reply that He does not know is a matter of will rather than nature, since those who are unworthy to be known are judged so by Him who is ignorant of absolutely nothing.

> [Note: The particle *not* is absent from the common printed texts but present in all manuscripts. Here it has, in Hilary’s Greek-like usage, not a negating but a strengthening force: “who knows absolutely nothing not at all.”]

Finally, lest He be thought ignorant through weakness, He immediately spoke thus to the Apostles: “Watch, therefore, because you do not know the day or the hour” (ibid., 13). As He warns them to watch because they do not know the day and hour, it may thereby be understood that the virgins were not known by Him because, being asleep and negligent, they had remained unworthy of entry into His bridal chamber through their want of oil.

> [Note: “Oil.”]

66. Christ, Knowing Nothing Ignorantly, Speaks as Though Ignorant for the Sake of Dispensation. The Knowledge of the Day Is Hidden and Thus Treated as Unknown.---Therefore the Lord Jesus Christ, God who searches hearts and inward parts, is not in such weakness of nature that He should fail to know; for that very thing which He does not know is understood from His natural knowledge to be what it is. If anyone, however, ascribes ignorance to Him, let him fear to hear from Him who knows their thoughts: “Why do you think evil in your hearts?” (Matt. 9:4).

> [Note: The printed editions read “that He does not know.” But the manuscripts read “what He does not know”—for example, the foolish virgins, workers of iniquity, and so forth. This does not arise from ignorance, but from knowledge by which He knows the former wicked and the latter foolish.]

For when the Knower, who is not ignorant of thoughts and actions, sometimes questions as though He did not know concerning thoughts and actions—such as the woman concerning the touch of the hem of His garment, the Apostles concerning the disagreement of their sayings, or those weeping concerning Lazarus’s tomb—He is not to be understood as not knowing because He is ignorant, but as speaking. Nature does not allow that He who, while absent, knew Lazarus to be dead and buried should not know the place of the tomb; or that He who sees thoughts should not have known the woman’s faith; or that He who has no need to ask anyone anything (John 16:30) should have been ignorant of the Apostles’ disagreement.

> [Note: An old Colbert manuscript reads “knowledges.”]

But for Him who knows all things, it is sometimes a dispensation to speak as though He did not know the very things which He does not fail to know: [Col. 0334B] whether knowledge is concealed for a time in Abraham’s case; or knowledge is denied to the unworthy in the case of the foolish virgins and workers of iniquity; or, in the mystery of the Son of Man, the question of one who appears ignorant arises from His humanity. In all these things He adapts Himself to the truth of bodily birth, in which our natural weakness is held—not such that He who is God should be weak by nature, but such that God, being born man, should assume human weaknesses.

> [Note: Most manuscripts read “in Abraham’s case.”]  
>
> [Note: The printed texts read *truth*; the manuscripts correctly read *to truth*. Hilary’s meaning is this: the question of Him who seems ignorant comes from His humanity, as He accommodates Himself to the truth of bodily nature in all those respects in which our nature is held by weakness. Cyril makes the same point repeatedly in *Treasury*. Thus p. 220: “He says that He does not know insofar as He was made like men, in whom ignorance can occur”; and shortly before: “Not because the Word, as Word and Wisdom of the Father, is ignorant does He say that He does not know; rather, He displays in Himself human nature, to which ignorance especially belongs.”]  
>
> [Note: “Weak.”]

Yet He assumed them in such a manner not that His unchangeable nature was reduced to a weak nature, but that the mystery of the assumption existed in an unchangeable nature. For He who was God is man, and He who is man did not cease to remain God.

> [Note: Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read “in the assumption of a changeable nature,” corrupting Hilary’s meaning: he intends that the mystery of assumed flesh took place while the nature of the Word remained safe and unchangeable.]

Thus, acting and establishing Himself as one born man, while remaining God the Word, He very often makes the profession proper to man, although often the declaration of God accommodating Himself to our capacity is also that of men: He does not know those things which either are not to be declared at that time or are not acknowledged as worthy through merit.

> [Note: The printed texts read “conforming”; the manuscripts more correctly, “establishing.”]  
>
> [Note: That is, although the speech of God Himself, accommodating Himself to our capacity, is often that of men.]  
>
> [Note: That is, because they lack merit, as, for example, workers of iniquity and foolish virgins are not known because of their lack of merit.]

67. How Wisely It Was Hidden.---We must therefore understand why He professed that He did not know the day. If He were believed altogether not to know it, the Apostle would contradict this when he says: “In Him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col. 2:5). There is, therefore, knowledge hidden; and because it must be hidden, He sometimes professes not to know, so that it may be hidden. For if it is openly declared, it will no longer remain secret. He therefore denies that He knows, so that the knowledge may remain hidden. If He does not know for the purpose that the knowledge may remain hidden, then He who knows all things does not fail to know through nature what He does not know solely in order that it may be hidden.

> [Note: Paris omits “is believed.” Then many manuscripts have “the Apostle, therefore,” rather than “the Apostle thus.” Augustine praises Hilary’s interpretation in Letter 180 to Oceanus, §3: “Blessed Hilary opened an obscure question by this obscure form of tropical expression, so that we might understand that He said Himself not to know in the sense in which, by concealing, He makes others not know. He did not excuse a lie, but showed that there was none.” Augustine follows the same view in *On the Trinity*, I.12.23, as does Pope Gregory, Book VIII, Letter 42. Cyril likewise does not dissent, explaining in *Treasury*, p. 222, that Christ moderated His speech because knowledge of the matter exceeded the disciples’ capacity. Eustathius of Antioch, in Facundus, Book XI, comes still more closely to the same view, showing that Christ devised this for human benefit.]

Why knowledge of the day is hidden is not obscure. In warning us to remain always attentive with unremitting faith, He took away the security of a fixed knowledge, so that the mind, anxious in the uncertainty of suspended expectation, might hasten, always expect the day of His coming, and, by always expecting, always hope; and so that uncertainty itself, though not uncertainty as to whether the time will come, might hold it in watchful concern. For the Lord says: “Therefore you also be ready, because you do not know at what hour the Son of Man will come” (Matt. 24:44). And again: “Blessed is that servant whom his lord, when he comes, shall find so doing” (ibid., 46).

> [Note: The word *fixed*, absent from earlier printed editions, is restored from manuscripts.]  
>
> [Note: The printed editions read “shall find watching,” contrary to the manuscripts and the sacred text.]

Ignorance was necessary not for error, but for perseverance. What was denied was not denied to their harm: ignorance brought increase, lest security from knowledge should foster negligence in concealed faith, but undefined expectation should preserve unremitting readiness—an expectation which would always beware the feared coming of the thief, who chooses the time of sleep for theft, while the master of the house remains awake through continual fear of loss.

> [Note: The printed editions, except Paris, read “would not exercise.” Other books read “would arouse,” that is, would produce and foster.]  
>
> [Note: This reading rests upon one Vatican and one Remigius manuscript, with support from others, though the word “coming” is omitted in them and can be omitted without loss of sense. The printed editions read: “which, always guarding through fear of the thief, would choose every time,” etc.]  
>
> [Note: The word “coming” is absent from our manuscript. Then: “every time,” not “the time of sleep.”]

68. Though They Admit That Christ, as the Greater, Penetrates Human Things, They Refuse That He Penetrates the Father’s Things, Calling Him Inferior.---Although it is not obscure that God’s ignorance is not ignorance but mystery—since through a dispensation of acting, declaring, or showing, He so does not know that He knows, and so does not fail to know that He does not know—we must nevertheless consider whether perhaps He is weak in this way: unable to know what the Father knows.
