He may indeed be able to know the thoughts of human hearts, because a stronger nature intermingles with the motions of an inferior nature and, as it were, passes through it in its force as through something weak; yet He may be powerless to penetrate a nature stronger than His own, because the weaker cannot penetrate the stronger.

For just as light things are permeable to heavy, rare things to dense, and liquid things to solid, while conversely heavy things do not yield to light, dense to rare, nor solid to liquid, because strong things are not open to weak things whereas weak things are penetrated by strong things—so the impious say that the Son is ignorant of the thoughts of God the Father because, being weak Himself, He cannot enter into the stronger; and because, being without strength, He cannot pass through what is powerful.

> [Note: The printed editions read “Himself,” against the manuscripts.]  
>
> [Note: “Do not yield.”]

69. Scripture Does Not Permit Christ to Be Called Inferior to the Father. Father and Son Are Mutual Mirror.---If anyone should dare not merely to utter, with reckless mouth, but even to think, with impious heart, such things concerning the only-begotten God, let him recognize that the Apostle believed as follows when writing to the Corinthians concerning the Holy Spirit: “But God revealed it to us through His Spirit. For the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God. For who among men knows the things of a man except the spirit which is in him? So also no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. 2:10–11).

> [Note: The common printed texts add “are” here, which is absent from the manuscripts. Of these, one Colbert and one Sorbonne manuscript omit “which are in him,” as do the common Greek and Latin copies of the sacred text.]

But rejecting these empty analogies of bodily things, let us judge God from God and Spirit from Spirit by Their powers rather than by earthly conditions.

> [Note: Two manuscripts read “earthly thoughts”: wrongly.]

Let us judge, however, not by our own perception but by the divine declaration; and let us believe Him who said: “He who has seen Me has seen the Father” (John 14:9). Nor let us disregard Him who said: “Believe, at least, My works: that the Father is in Me and I in the Father” (John 10:38). Nor let us disregard Him who said: “I and the Father are one” (ibid., 30).

> [Note: The word “My” is absent from the Verona manuscript, does not occur in the Greek text, and is omitted in Book VII, §§24 and 26, where this passage is quoted three times.]

For if the names of things, recalled according to human understanding, establish our understanding, then He has no difference of nature from Him in whom one is seen through understanding; nor does He differ in kind, who, having the abiding One in Himself, abides in the abiding One; nor are They different who are one.

> [Note: The printed editions read “each one.” More correctly, most manuscripts read “one”: that is, He in whom one is seen and understood, when seen and understood, has no difference of nature from Him. Then Lipsius and Paris read “and does not differ in kind”; corrected from Bad., Erasmus, and the manuscripts.]

Understand Their unity, since Their nature is not divisible. Then apprehend the mystery of Their indivisible nature, since each is, as it were, the mirror of the other. But They are mirror in such a way that not an imagined appearance of an external nature emits splendor; rather, living nature is undifferentiated from living nature, since the whole is from the whole. Thus, while He is only-begotten, He has the Father in Himself; and while He is God, He remains in the Father.

70. Heretics wrongly twist statements about unity of nature into unity of will.—Accordingly, since heretics cannot deny these sayings, proclaimed by the Lord to signify the mystery of the birth, they try to evade them by referring them to harmony of will; so that in God the Father and God the Son there may be unity not of divinity but of will. As though the language of divine teaching were deficient, and the Lord could not have said, “The Father and I will one thing”; or as though “The Father and I are one” had the same meaning; or as though, being unskilled in speaking, he had not said, “Whoever has seen my will has seen the will of my Father,” and this were identical with “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father”; or, certainly, as though it were not customary in divine speech to say, “The will of my Father is in me, and my will is in my Father,” but the saying “I am in the Father and the Father is in me” (John 14:11) were appropriate to this meaning.

Though all these things are ugly, foolish, and impious, and though human understanding cannot concede this conclusion of a stupid opinion—namely, that either the Lord could not say what he wished, or said something other than what he said—yet, although he is found to have employed parabolic and allegorical sayings, it is one thing to establish what is said by examples, another to satisfy the dignity of matters by the meanings of proverbs, and another to adapt oneself to the conditions of times. But this passage concerning the unity under discussion does not permit us to believe that the sayings mean anything other than what the words sound like.

> [Note: Erasmus, Lipsius, and Paris read “and although.”]

> [Note: In the earlier edition, “to undermine” (*infirmare*).]

For if they are one because they will one thing, yet natures separable by a difference of kind, disagreeing in diverse wills through that difference of discordant kind, cannot will one thing, how can those will one thing for whom knowing is not one thing? For knowledge and ignorance hinder the unity of a single will. Therefore, since ignorance is contrary to knowledge, things contrary to one another cannot will one thing.

> [Note: In the printed editions, “difference of kind”; corrected from the manuscripts.]

> [Note: In several manuscripts, “ignorance.” In the Martin manuscript, “knowledge,” wrongly.]

71. The Father alone knows the day because he does not keep it silent from the Son alone; the Son does not know because he reveals it to no one.—But perhaps the fact that the Son says that the Father alone knows may establish that the Son, who said that he did not know, does not know. Unless, indeed, he had said that the Father alone knows, a matter of the greatest danger would have been left to our understanding, lest perhaps he himself be thought not to know. For when, in what he does not know, there is in him rather an economy of hidden knowledge than a nature of ignorance, then also from the fact that the Father alone knows he must be believed not to have been ignorant. For, as we taught above, knowledge in God is not an understanding of coming to know what he did not know, but of speaking.

And from the fact that the Father alone knows, the Son is not understood not to know; since the Son says that he does not know for this reason, lest others too should know, and says that the Father alone knows for this reason, lest he himself too should be understood not to be ignorant. For if God is said then to have known that Abraham loved him, when he did not conceal this from Abraham (Gen. 22:12), the Father must likewise be said to know the day for this reason, because he did not conceal it from the Son—not because God’s knowledge arises from a sudden acquisition of knowledge, but because it is declared in time. Therefore, if the Son does not know the day according to the mystery, in order that he may keep silent, conversely the Father alone is necessarily shown to know the day because he does not keep silent.

> [Note: In the printed editions, “of understanding.” More correctly in the manuscripts, “understanding”: that is, when God is said to know, this is not understood or signified as coming to know what he did not know, but as speaking what he had not spoken, as we have already touched on in §62 and explain in §64.]

> [Note: We restore the particle *ob* [“for this reason”], wrongly deleted by Lipsius, from Bad., Erasmus, and the manuscripts. Then, “lest he himself should not not know,” that is, so that he too may be understood not not to know. This is expressed more plainly in §73: “Therefore the Son does not know the day because he keeps silent; and he says that the Father alone knows because he alone does not keep it silent from himself alone. But the Father does not keep it silent from the Son; otherwise, how would he be understood to know it? The Son, however, keeps silent, because he had so learned from the Father that he learned at the same time to keep silent about what it was expedient to be unknown.” This bears upon Augustine, Sermon 97, §1: “Let us not suppose, in a carnal way, that the Father knows something which the Son does not know. For when he said, ‘The Father knows,’ he said this because the Son too knows in the Father. For what is there in the day that was not made in the Word through whom the day was made?”]

72. God is simple and must by no means be conceived after the human manner. He does not change. He can do all things.—Far be it that novelties of bodily change should be imagined in Father and Son, as though at one time the Father speaks to the Son and at another keeps silent. We do indeed remember that a voice was sometimes sent from heaven, in order that the signification of the Father’s utterance might establish among us the mystery of the Son, as the Lord says: “This voice came from heaven not for my sake, but for yours” (John 12:30).

But the nature of God does not need the composite necessities of human operation: the movement of tongue, the adjustment of mouth, the exertion of breath, the striking of air. God is simple: he is to be understood by our religious faith and confessed by our devotion; he is not to be pursued by reasoning but adored, lest a finite and weak understanding presume to comprehend by opinion the mystery of an infinite and powerful nature.

> [Note: That is, a nature constricted within a finite measure. Erasmus’s somewhat unfair marginal note against Hilary had hitherto prevailed: “Why, then, did he define so many things?” Yet what are these many things that he defined, when he scarcely departs from this single aim: to demonstrate that God is neither solitary nor that the Son is something other, or of another substance, than the Father? Did he himself define these matters? Or did he not rather learn each openly transmitted by Scripture from the Church? The Church had long before defined the first, by proscribing the teaching of Sabellius, Noetus, Praxeas, and similar heretics. The Nicene Fathers had recently confirmed the second; the Synod of Antioch had long before declared it against Paul of Samosata, indeed apostolic men had steadfastly defended it against Artemas and others, as Eusebius testifies when, in *History*, book 5, chapter 28, he records writings older than the age of Victor and Artemas, written by brethren both against pagans and against the heretics of their own time in defence of Christ’s divinity. But let each judge on whom the reproach of inconsistency falls: on Hilary, or on Erasmus, who, having admired in book 2 Hilary’s supreme modesty in writing, proposed that it should be imitated in these words: “Listen, you rash definer.” To us, however, the devout bishop nowhere appears forgetful of how weak human reason is. He constantly sets its weakness before our eyes, so that a human being may learn to believe not his own thoughts but God’s utterances.]

> [Note: “Therefore it is not composed of diverse parts of a composite substance.”]

> [Note: Several manuscripts, with Bad.: “Therefore divinity is not composed of diverse parts of a composite substance.” The Martin manuscript reads: “of diverse parts of a composite substance.”]

Therefore, he is not diverse through parts composing divinity, so that in him there is either will after numbness, speech after silence, or action after inactivity; so that he may be thought unable to will anything unless moved to will, unable to say something unless words sound after silence, or not understood to act anything unless he proceeds to a work.

He is not subject to the laws of nature, since every nature receives its law from him; nor is he held back in anything by weakness or change in accomplishing, who is beyond every measure of power, according to the Lord’s saying: “Father, all things are possible for you” (Mark 14:36). As much as human understanding does not grasp, so much can God do. Yet he did not even deprive himself of the power of omnipotence when he said: “Whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does the same” (John 5:19). There is no difficulty where there is no weakness, because the power unable to accomplish is subject to difficulty. For the nature of difficulty lies in weakness of power; and power which has no limit is not constrained by the law of weakness.

> [Note: That is, difficulty is situated in a deficiency of power. Since this power, however, etc. Hence the reading in three Vatican and other later manuscripts, “it is in weakness of power,” should be attributed to an interpolator: “But the nature of God, which has no limit,” etc.]

73. He could never at any time not know the day. The Son’s nature is one with the Father’s.—We have demonstrated this in order that God may not be thought to have spoken to the Son after silence, or the Son to have come to know after ignorance; rather, that our understanding may be instructed by the expressions belonging to our own nature, which would not understand that anything is shown except through one speaking, nor think that anything is not unknown except by knowing.

> [Note: In later manuscripts: “unless by knowing he thought,” wrongly. That “unless by knowing,” that is, unless by learning and, after the manner of human beings, passing from ignorance to knowledge.]

Therefore the Son does not know the day because he keeps silent; and he says that the Father alone knows because he alone does not keep it silent from himself alone. But, as I have said, he does not wait upon these difficulties of nature, so as then to know when he ceases to be ignorant, or then to hear when the Father begins to speak. He taught unambiguously that he possesses with the Father, as the Only-begotten, unity of nature, saying: “All things that are the Father’s are mine.”

For he was not now speaking of acquiring; for it is one thing for external things to be one’s possession, and another to be in one’s own things and to be oneself those things which are one’s own. It is one thing to possess heaven, lands, and the whole world; another to signify oneself in those things which are one’s own—one’s own, not as external things subject to one, but because he himself subsists from what is his own.

> [Note: The printed editions read “and that very thing”; the manuscripts read “and himself,” in the same sense. The meaning becomes clearer if after “and” one supplies “those things which are his own.”]

> [Note: That is, he was not speaking of those goods which are not held by nature, but are afterward obtained by grace or labour.]

> [Note: The Martin manuscript reads “of his substance.” The Colbert manuscript with the German manuscript reads “subsistent,” which may be referred to the Son. One Vatican manuscript and a few others read “of the subsisting one,” which may suitably be interpreted of the Father also. Others, however, read more truly, as is clear from §31, “external subsistence,” that is, external things, such as heaven, earth, and the world; or, as above in §31, the elements and the various kinds of created things. Hilary maintains that Christ does not say merely that the Father’s external and created goods are his own. He proves this from the subsequent statement that the Spirit will receive from what is his. Since it is certain that the Spirit of God receives nothing from creatures, it follows that he calls all the Father’s inward goods—namely power, eternity, providence, and so forth—his own. These indeed are not something other than God himself, although in our imperfect manner of speaking we call them the Father’s, as though the Father who possesses and what he possesses were different things. From this it readily follows that the Son and Father have one nature.]

Now, therefore, when all things that are the Father’s are his, he signifies the nature of divinity, not a sharing in acquired possessions. For, while speaking of the Holy Spirit’s receiving from what is his, he said: “All things that are the Father’s are mine; therefore I said, ‘He will receive from what is mine,’” so that, when he receives from what is his, he might not be thought not also to receive from what is the Father’s; or, when he receives from the Father’s, he might not be understood not also to receive from what is his.

For the Holy Spirit, who is the Spirit of God, did not receive from creatures, so as to appear to receive from them because all these things are God’s. But all things that are the Father’s are not his in such a way that, when the Spirit receives from the Son, he might appear not also to receive from the Father’s, since all that belonged to the Father was understood to belong also to the Son.

> [Note: Erasmus, again applying a censorious stroke to Hilary, says: “Why do you avoid the term ‘communion’?” Hilary might rightly answer: “Why do you lay a false charge against me? I do not avoid communion simply, but communion in acquired possessions: communion in certain external goods that come by accident and are added to an already constituted nature; in short, communion lacking unity of nature. Remember my words in book 9, §34.”]

> [Note: Thus the manuscripts. But the printed editions read, “because he is the Spirit of God.” Shortly afterward it would be more fitting to read, “because all these things are God’s,” rather than “because all this is God’s,” for this refers to creatures. Here the Holy Spirit is plainly shown to be consubstantial with Father and Son.]

> [Note: The printed editions, except Paris, read “but therefore,” deleting the *non* found in the manuscripts. On the authority of the manuscripts we likewise restore “lest he might not also receive from the Father’s” for “lest he might not also receive from the Father.” Their meaning is: The Father’s things are not the Son’s as though the Father had poured all that was his into the Son in such a way as not to retain it himself; and thus what the Spirit receives from the Son he does not also receive from the Father.]

74. His will, and therefore his knowledge, is the same as the Father’s.—This nature, therefore, did not require change, questioning, or address, so as to know after ignorance, ask after silence, or hear after questioning. Rather, remaining perfect in the mystery of its unity, as it had birth from God, so it had universality. And possessing universality, it did not fail to possess what belongs to universality, namely knowledge and will, so that the Son might know through questioning what the Father knows, or might will through indication what the Father wills.

But since all things that are the Father’s were his, it belonged to the property of his nature that he should neither will nor know anything other than the Father.

> [Note: In the Vatican Basilica and Martin manuscripts: “namely, that he may know or will.”]

> [Note: The printed editions read “was in it”; corrected from the better manuscripts.]

Yet, to demonstrate the birth, a demonstration of person is often employed when it is said: “I came not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 6:38). He does the Father’s will, not his own, while through the will of him who sent him he signifies the Father also.

That he himself wills this same thing he shows unambiguously by saying: “Father, those whom you have given me, I will that, where I am, they also may be with me” (John 17:24). Therefore, since the Father wills us to be with Christ—in whom, according to the Apostle, he chose us before the foundation of the world—and the Son himself wills the same thing, namely that we should be with him (Eph. 1:4), the will is the same in respect of nature, though it is distinguished in will for the signification of the birth.

> [Note: “In the one willing.”]

> [Note: Thus, most correctly, the noted manuscripts—two Colbert, Carnotensis, German, Sorbonne, and Victorius—supported by six others, though in them there wrongly stands, “it is not distinguished in will.” But the Corbie manuscript and a few others, with the printed editions, read “in the one willing.” Although, with the sense safe and intact, either “in will” or “in the one willing” could be removed.]

75. The Apostles understood him not as ignorant, but as keeping silence by dispensation.—Therefore the Son does not fail to know what the Father does not fail to know; nor, because the Father alone knows, does the Son therefore not know. For Father and Son remain in unity of nature; and the Son’s not knowing—that Son in whom all treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden—is an economy of keeping silence. The Lord himself testified to this when, asked by the Apostles about the times, he answered: “It is not yours to know the times or moments which the Father has placed in his own power” (Acts 1:7).

Knowledge is denied; and not merely denied, but concern for such knowledge is forbidden, since it does not belong to them to know these times. Certainly, after the resurrection they ask about the times—those to whom, when they asked before, it had been said that not even the Son knew. Nor can they seem to have understood “the Son does not know” according to the mere sound of the words, since they again ask him as one who knows. But understanding the mystery of not knowing to be an economy of silence, and now after the resurrection judging that the time for speaking had come, they ask.

And the Son no longer tells them that he does not know; rather, he says that it is not theirs to know, because the Father has placed it in his own power. Therefore, if the Apostles understand the Son’s not knowing the day as an economy, not a weakness, do we say that the Son does not know the day only so that he may not be God? Since God the Father placed the day in his own power in order that it might not come within the knowledge of human understanding; and the Son, having earlier said when asked that he did not know, now answers again not that he does not know, but that it belongs to them not to know; while the Father has placed the times not in his knowledge but in his power?

For since day and moment fall within the name of times, he who will restore the kingdom to Israel cannot appear to be ignorant of the day and moment of restoring it. But teaching us the understanding of his birth through the reservation of the Father’s power, he did not answer that he did not know; and, showing that the capacity for knowledge had not been granted to them, he professed that this very matter rests in the mystery of the Father’s power.

> [Note: “Or moments” does not occur in our manuscript.]

> [Note: “Or seasons” is consistently absent from the manuscripts, as also in Augustine, Letters 197 and 199 to Hesychius. In Letter 197, §2, Augustine observes that the Greek reads *chronous ē kairous* [χρόνους ἢ καιρούς]: “Our translators,” he says, “call both these words *tempora* [times], although they have a difference between them which should not be neglected. For they call *kairoi* [καιρούς] times perceived in things as opportune or inopportune for some purpose, such as harvest, peace, or war; but *chronoi* [χρόνους] the intervals of time themselves.” Hesychius, however, in the letter placed between those two by Augustine, reads “times or moments”; and it is evident from what follows that Hilary was not unaware of this reading.]

> [Note: Thus the manuscripts. But the printed editions read, “which the Father.”]

> [Note: What follows to the end is plainly supplied by the most ancient codex of the Church of Verona.]

> [Note: That “therefore” fits badly, since a wholly different conclusion is reached than was established above. Indeed, this conclusion appears to conflict with §58, where Hilary denies that Christ can be ignorant of that day, not only because as the Word he is the author of times, but because, according to the mystery of assumed flesh, it pertains to him and is his own day, on which he will come to judge the living and the dead. For this reason we judged that what follows should be printed in smaller type, especially since it is absent from the best manuscripts—the three Colbert manuscripts, the Carnotensis, German, and Sorbonne. Yet we did not remove it altogether from its place, because it occurs in the very ancient Vatican Basilica manuscript, in the Martin, Corbie, and other manuscripts, and is sufficiently distinct in itself from Hilary’s other words. If it had something similar to book 10, §8, we might suspect that the copyist, who is known to have exercised great freedom in transcribing the aforesaid manuscript of Saint Peter, had added these words after the Greek manner. Certainly, the following words of Cyril, *Treasury*, p. 221, are not far from them: “Just as Christ took this upon himself, that, having become human, he should hunger, thirst, and suffer the other things said of him together with human beings, so likewise there is no reason for anyone to be offended if, as human, he is said to have been ignorant together with human beings.” Although this teaching seems to have been asserted by Athanasius, *Oration 4 against the Arians*, pp. 494–495, and not to have displeased Gregory Nazianzen, *Oration 36*, §62, and other great men, Leporius nevertheless retracted and condemned it with an anathema in the booklet to which Augustine subscribed with others, *Councils*, vol. 2; for it may not be said that the Lord of the prophets was ignorant, even according to his humanity. Indeed, Cyril, Athanasius, and the other Fathers, if their opinion is considered more closely, do not so much assert that Christ as a human being was truly ignorant of the day of judgment as that, as a human being, he was permitted by a certain singular design to say that he did not know; and that ignorance is not alien to human nature, whose weaknesses he assumed, an ignorance which he in some manner represented in order to be conformed to us. Thus they seem rather to agree with our Hilary in §66 than with those who, under Justinian’s reign, maintained that Christ as man was ignorant and were called Agnoetae, from their founder Themistius’s error. Against them Pope Gregory I approves Saint Eulogius’s commentary, book 8, letter 42. There is also Agobard’s work against Felix, who thought that the day of judgment, Lazarus’s tomb, the conversations of those going to Emmaus, and so forth, had been unknown to Christ. See the notes on book 10, §8.]

Therefore, because the Son says that he does not know the day and the moment, he is not to be believed ignorant; just as, when according to his humanity he weeps, sleeps, or is sorrowful, God is not to be confessed as subject to tears, fear, or sleep. Rather, while the truth of the Only-begotten remains unimpaired in himself, he must be understood, according to the weakness of flesh and in the same respect according to his humanity, to have professed ignorance of the day and hour along with weeping, sleep, hunger, thirst, weariness, and fear.

> [Note: In the Vatican Basilica and Martin manuscripts, “or death,” not “or fear.”]

## BOOK TEN

The whole book is directed against those who, wishing there to be in Christ no substance that did not suffer in the Passion, none untouched by hunger, thirst, sorrow, or fear, forgetful of the confession and nature of divinity, seized upon deeds and sayings of the economy as arguments for their impiety (Book 1, §32). Some of them asserted that Christ was a mere human being, into whose soul—not a simple fear, but a DOMINATING fear of the approaching sorrow—had entered; that he was overwhelmed by the NECESSITY of the Passion and mastered by the force of pain (ibid., §33). Others, confusing the Word with the flesh, declared that it performed the office of a soul. Nor were there lacking those who, separating the Word entirely from the human being, admitted no presence of it in Christ except that which we recognize in the prophets. Again, they embraced divergent views when, believing both Christ’s flesh and soul to have been propagated from Adam, they interpreted the descent signified in Scripture as being from heaven not of the person of the Word assuming flesh, but of the flesh itself brought down from heaven, in order to evade the Scriptures.

Against these heretics Hilary generally uses that kind of argument which leaves them no answer within their own opinions. What he requests at the beginning of his other works must especially be granted him in this book: namely, that he not be judged before the end. For if the beginnings produce any cause of offence, the end will remove it. Still, once the adversaries’ view is set out, it is easy to judge whether it exempts only Christ’s divinity from pain, fear, and sorrow, or protects his human nature only from dominating and compelled affections of this kind. This too should be noted: Gregory of Nyssa, quoted by Theodoret, *Dialogue* 3, says in *Oration 5 against Eunomius*: “Since the opinion is twofold and ambiguous—whether divinity or humanity suffered—the rejection of one will be the complete confirmation of the other.”

Accordingly, Hilary, beginning in §9 both to expose and refute the mad opinions of heretics against Christ’s divinity, discusses until §36 his wondrous conception, showing thereby that the Word assumed the truth of our nature without abolishing himself and without our vices. From this he concludes that Christ, one and the same, though not conceived according to human law, was nevertheless both true human and true God: as true human, he was exposed to the natures of sufferings; as conceived without the vices of our origin, he was not consumed by the injuries of our sufferings; as true God, he was wholly exempt from them.

Then, through §43, considering the causes of Christ’s sorrow, prayer, and angelic ministry, he maintains that he was sorrowful, prayed, and was strengthened by the angel not for himself but for the Apostles. In the following five sections he explains the signs of divine omnipotence which Christ displayed in the Passion. From them it may readily appear that the necessity, force, and disgrace of pain do not apply to one who could do such things; and that he indeed suffered all weaknesses for us according to his humanity, but triumphed in them all according to God (§47).

At this point the opponents raise Christ’s cry that he was forsaken. What their faith concerning Christ is, §49 declares. Soon afterward, through many opposed questions concerning Christ’s temporal birth, weeping, authority to lay down and take up his soul, commendation and handing over of his spirit—matters which cannot be reconciled with the heretics’ doctrine—§61 unties their knot from the faith of the Church. This Church neither confuses Christ’s natures nor divides his persons, and in the one and same Christ has one complaining that he has been abandoned unto death, because he is human, and one who, while dying, declares that he reigns in paradise, because he is God.

Meanwhile Hilary, in his customary manner, commends the necessity of faith, in order to check the arrogance of heretics who boasted that they comprehended Christ’s mysteries. For, as Athanasius teaches at the end of his work *On the Saving Advent of Jesus Christ*, those who attribute suffering to his divinity, or have no faith in his humanity, or separate the one into two, make a measurement of his flesh and dare to define, apart from the sacred Scriptures, “how much” and “in what manner” (*to poson ē pōs para tas graphas legein tolmountes*, τὸ πόσον ἢ πῶς παρὰ τὰς γραφὰς λέγειν τολμῶντες).

1. Causes of differing opinions. They follow the doctrine of preference, not reason.—It is beyond doubt that every discourse of human speech has always been subject to contradiction. For, since the impulses of wills differ, the understanding of minds differs too; and, with the disposition of opposing judgments fighting against an assertion, it contradicts those assertions by which it is offended.

For although every utterance perfected by the rationality of truth is true, nevertheless, while one thing appears or pleases some persons and another others, the discourse of truth lies open to the answer of opponents. For against truth either not understood or offensive, the error of a foolish or vicious will contends. Every obstinacy of adopted wills is excessive; and the zeal for opposition persists with unbending movement where the will is not subjected to reason and effort is not given to doctrine, but we seek reasons for what we wish and adapt doctrine to what we pursue.

Thus what is fabricated will now be doctrine of a name rather than of a nature; and the principle will no longer be that of truth but of preference—a principle which the will has adapted more for the defence of things pleasing to it than one which, through an understanding of truth, might reasonably move the impulse of the will. Through these vices of partisan wills arise all contradictions of opposing purposes; and between the assertion of truth and the defence of preference there is a stubborn struggle, while truth holds its own ground and will defends itself.

But if will did not run ahead of reason, and instead were moved through understanding of truth to will what is true, doctrine would never be sought for will’s sake; rather, the rationality of doctrine would move every will. Every discourse of truth would be without contradiction, since each person would defend as true not what he wished, but would begin to wish what is true.

> [Note: Martin manuscript and certain others: “assertion.”]

> [Note: Vatican Basilica, Martin, and a few other manuscripts: “the zeal for opposing.”]

> [Note: “For will.”]

> [Note: In the printed editions, “would be sought for will.” Then in most manuscripts, “if will.”]

2. What teachers they seek.—The Apostle, therefore, not ignorant of these vicious wills, among many instructions for attesting the faith and preaching the word, writes to Timothy: “There will be a time when they will not endure sound doctrine, but according to their own desires will heap up teachers for themselves, with itching ears; and they will indeed turn their hearing away from the truth, but will turn aside to fables” (2 Tim. 4:3).

For when, through devotion to impiety, they are beyond the endurance of sound doctrine, then they will heap up for themselves teachers of what they desire, accumulating systems of teaching suited to their own cravings. They do not desire to be taught, but gather teachers for what they desire, so that the very heap of teachers sought out and amassed may satisfy their burning desires with doctrines.

And if anyone does not know by what spirit this great frenzy of foolish irreligion, refusing to endure sound doctrine, will at length seek corrupt doctrine, let him learn from the same Apostle writing to this same Timothy: “But the Spirit plainly says that in the last times some will depart from the faith, giving heed to seducing spirits and doctrines of demons, in the hypocrisy of lying speakers” (1 Tim. 4:1).

For what progress in doctrine is it to seek preferences rather than matters to be taught? Or what devotion to doctrine is it not to desire what ought to be taught, but to amass doctrine for what one has desired? Such incentives are supplied by seducing spirits, and the false speech of simulated religion confirms them. For lying hypocrisy follows the falling away from faith, so that devotion may be in the words while conscience has lost it.

They make even this simulated devotion impious by every falsehood of speech, corrupting the holiness of faith by the institutions of false doctrine, while doctrine is amassed according to the desires of partisan pursuits rather than according to evangelical faith. For, when ears stirred by itching are tickled by the impatient pleasure of listening under the novel preaching of their own desire, they themselves, utterly estranged from hearing truth, devote themselves wholly to fables, so that what they say may acquire an appearance of truth, while they cannot either speak or hear what is true.

> [Note: Thus most manuscripts, supported by the Greek *knēthomenoi tēn akoēn* [κνηθόμενοι τὴν ἀκοήν]. The Vatican Basilica codex alone, with the Martin manuscript, reads “scratching their ears,” as in *Against Constantius*, §1. The printed editions read “itching in their ears.”]

> [Note: Printed editions: “of foolish religiosity”; corrected from the manuscripts.]

> [Note: “Speakers of falsehood.” Greek: *pseudologōn* [ψευδολόγων].]

> [Note: Some manuscripts, with the Vulgate, read “speaking falsehood.” Others, with Bad., Erasmus, and Lipsius, read “lying speakers.” We prefer this reading, with Paris and the ancient Colbert and German manuscripts; what follows confirms it.]

> [Note: “Soundness.”]

3. These predictions suit the Arians.—We have plainly fallen into this most grievous time of apostolic prophecy. For now teachers have been sought to preach creation rather than God; doctrines satisfying human desires are studied rather than those of sound faith. The itching of their ears has stirred them so far toward hearing what they desire that, teachers having been amassed, this preaching alone now prevails for the moment: that the only-begotten God is in our faith either alien from the power and truth of God the Father, or God of another kind, or not God at all.

Either profession of impiety is deadly: either they speak of two gods under a diversity of divinity, or altogether deny God to him whose nature is from God by birth. This pleases ears estranged from hearing truth and turned toward fables. The hearing of sound doctrine is not endured, and sound doctrine itself goes into exile with all its preachers.

> [Note: “Of sound faith.”]

> [Note: “Speaking.”]

4. Hilary is free and joyful in exile.—But although sound doctrine now goes into exile for many who heap up teachers for themselves according to their own desires, the truth of preaching will not go into exile from all holy persons. For we shall speak as exiles through these books, and the word of God, which cannot be bound, will run free, warning of this same time of apostolic prophecy. Thus, when a hearing impatient of truth is found and teachers amassed according to human desires, there may no longer be uncertainty about the time; rather, truth may be understood to be in exile in it, together with the preachers of sound faith, who exult.

And we shall not complain about the times; indeed, we shall rejoice, because iniquity has revealed itself through this time of our exile. Impatient of truth, it banishes the preachers of sound doctrine in order to heap up teachers for itself according to its desires; while we rejoice and exult in the Lord in our exile, it has brought about in us the fulfilment of apostolic prophecy.

> [Note: The manuscripts read “although together with,” not “although now.”]

> [Note: The printed editions read “has gone into exile.” To this word Hilary would have added, not very modestly, “For we shall speak,” remembering himself as one among all the holy. The manuscript reading, “will go into exile,” clears his language of this fault of boastfulness, so that “holy persons” refers to believers who love truth, to whom he promises that true doctrine will by no means go into exile through the help of his books.]

> [Note: “May heap up.”]

### 5. How cautiously he proceeded in the preceding books. The Arians’ customary slanders against Catholics.

Accordingly, in the preceding treatises, while maintaining, as I think, a profession of sincere faith and untainted truth, although, according to the condition of human nature, no discourse is not liable to contradiction, we have nevertheless, I think, so ordered the whole plan of our reply that no one can contradict it except by professing impiety. For the truth of those statements which heretics, according to the artifice of their false-speaking, presume to draw from the Gospels has been so demonstrated that ignorance can no longer be excused in contradiction, but irreligion must necessarily be confessed.

We have also now, according to the gift of the Holy Spirit, so tempered the demonstration of the whole faith that they could not even fabricate any charge against us.

> **Note [Col. 0347C].** Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions instead read: “so that they could not even lie … [and bring] any charge.”

For they are accustomed to fill the ears of the ignorant with such claims about us as to assert that we deny the birth when we preach the unity of the Godhead; and to say that by the words, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), we signify a solitary God.

> **Note [Col. 0347C].** In the printed editions there is added here: “which is written”; the manuscripts oppose this addition.

They say that the unbegotten God descended into the Virgin and was born as a man; that, with reference to the dispensation of the flesh, He began by saying, “I,” but, to demonstrate His divinity, added, “and the Father,” as though He were the father of this man of His; and that, consisting of two things, namely man and God, He spoke of Himself when He said, “we are one.”

> **Note [Col. 0347C–D].** This reading, found in most and the more trustworthy manuscripts, will be complete if “he refers” is supplied here. Three manuscripts read: “because that which is thus said pertains to the dispensation of the flesh.” But the printed editions, without any authority, have: “because that which is thus said pertains to the dispensation of the flesh.” Sabellius’ teaching is indicated here; the Arians transferred its odium to Catholics.

### 6. What has thus far been said about the Son’s eternal generation.

But we, confessing a subsistent birth without time, have proclaimed God the Son to be God, not of a nature alien from God the Father; neither equal to the Unbegotten by unbegottenness, but not unequal by the generation of the Only-begotten.

> **Note [Col. 0347D].** The printed editions, except the Paris edition, read “only-begotten”: wrongly. For the term “unequal” refers to the subsistent birth, that is, to a subsistence distinct from the begetter; this is proclaimed equal to the Father by reason of generation, not by reason of unbegottenness.

Nor have we proclaimed Them one through the union of duplicated names, but through the birth of nature; nor that there are two gods in the faith through diversity of kind; nor, again, a solitary God merely because God alone is to be confessed where the mystery of God the Only-begotten must be confessed.

> **Note [Col. 0347D].** That is, neither are They one by reason of the singularity of a person to whom duplicate names belong. This confirms our observation (col. 165, note c of our edition) that Sabellius so divides the union in the Virgin as to begin to duplicate the names of the same God.

> **Note [Col. 0347C].** The words “merely because” are absent from the Verona codex.

> **Note [Col. 0347D–0348C].** We restore “merely because” from the better manuscripts—Colbert, Carnotensis, Remigiensis, Germanensis, etc.—where *solum* means not “solitary” but “one.” That is: neither because we have proclaimed one God alone have we therefore proclaimed a singular and solitary God; since confession of the only-begotten God admits neither two gods diverse in kind nor a solitary God.

Rather, the Son is signified and exists in the Father, since in Him are both the Father’s nature and name—namely, the name of the nature; and the Father is understood and remains in the Son, since the Son can neither be called Son except from the Father nor exist except from Him. He is the living image of the living nature, and the form of God in God, naturally impressed, of a power and kind so wholly indistinguishable that in Him neither work nor word nor sight is alien from the Father. But because the image naturally has in itself the nature of its Author, the Author, through His natural image, both works, speaks, and is seen.

### 7. What has been said about the temporal birth.

And while proclaiming this timeless, ineffable generation of the Only-begotten, surpassing every apprehension of human understanding, we have also taught the mystery of God born into man from the Virgin’s delivery.

> **Note [Col. 0348D].** Several excellent manuscripts read, “and into this.”

We showed that, according to the dispensation of the assumed flesh, when He emptied Himself from the form of God and took the form of a servant, the weakness of human condition did not weaken the nature of God, but, with the power of divinity preserved in man, God acquired authority for man. For when God was born into man, He was not born so as no longer to remain God, but so that, while God remained, man might be born into God.

> **Note [Col. 0348D].** The printed editions read “in man”; and Hilary elsewhere reads it thus, for instance in Book V, §18 and Book IX, §4. Here, however, on manuscript authority, we restore “into man,” which the printed editions also have shortly before and which agrees better with the following words: “that man may be born into God.”

For His name is Emmanuel—rather, Immanuel—“God with us” (Matthew 1:23): so that there is not a falling-away of God toward man, but an advancement of man toward God (John 17:5).

> **Note [Col. 0348C].** *Immanuel* in place of *Emmanuel*.

Or, when He asks to be glorified, this benefits not the nature of God, but the assumption of humility. For He asks for that glory which He had with God before the foundation of the world.

### 8. What has been said about the unknown hour.

In answering their most foolish assertions, we have gone so far as to demonstrate the matter of the unknown hour. Even if, according to them, it had not been apprehended—that is, perceived—by the Son, this would nevertheless not pertain to the dishonour of the Only-begotten divinity. For nature would not allow His birth to carry Him back to the unoriginated state of unbegottenness, the Father reserving to His own power the determination of the day’s moment as a demonstration of unbegotten authority.

> **Note [Col. 0348D].** Several manuscripts read “an initiable condition”: incorrectly. He calls “uninitiable condition” that mode of subsistence which is without every beginning. It cannot be granted that the Father reserved anything to His own power unless the Son is conceded to be unequal to Him. But Hilary here speaks not so much from his own view as from that of the Arians, according to whom the Son is not simply denied knowledge, but is said not to know insofar as He is understood not to be unbegotten.

Nor can a weak nature be understood in Him in whom there is, from the birth of nature, as much as a perfect birth could contain. Nor should ignorance of the day and hour be imputed to the Only-begotten God as a distinction of divinity, since, in order to demonstrate against the Sabellian heretics the unbegotten and unoriginated authority in the Father, this exception belongs in Him to unbegotten authority.

> **Note [Col. 0348D–0349D].** Erasmus inserted here: “Through this it became evident that the Word’s confession belonged to the fulfilment of the mystery of man: so that He who bore our weaknesses might also assume for Himself the weakness of human ignorance; and thus might say that He did not know the day, as He did not know Lazarus’ tomb and did not know the woman touching the fringe of His garment—being as weak in knowing as in weeping, under the condition of weariness, thirst, and hunger, and not disdaining even the error of ignorance. Especially since, when He had risen from the dead and was about to enter and pass beyond the heavens, the Apostles questioned Him no longer as ignorant but as having power over and knowledge of this very day of His, asking nothing other than what was being concealed under the dispensation of man; so that, when they questioned Him again after He had said that He did not know, they might appear to understand an assumption rather than a necessity of ignorance.”

> He states that he found these words sewn into one manuscript. We found them only in one Remigius manuscript, about the year 700, in which much is elsewhere mutilated or disordered; there they are sewn in at the beginning of this section, immediately after the words, “we have gone so far as to demonstrate the unknown hour.” In the other manuscripts there is no trace of this addition. As in the appendix placed at the end of Book IX, so here too Christ’s ignorance is explained differently from the way it is expounded throughout Book IX. There, moreover, ignorance of the day is attributed to a dispensation of silence; and by “dispensation” is meant not, as here, the mystery of assumed flesh, but God’s hidden counsel, by which He wisely judged that this day was not to be revealed by Christ to human beings. It can scarcely be doubted that this is a mere interpolation. This is confirmed even by the fact that, insofar as we know, it occurs in only two manuscripts, one placing it in one location and the other elsewhere. It is also probable that it belongs to the same person as the addition to Book IX, although that occurs in far more manuscripts. Hilary can be supposed the author of both only on the ground that, after completing his work, he noted a new interpretation of the aforesaid ignorance, sufficiently common among other Fathers.

But because we have taught that this declaration concerning the day not known is not the weakness of ignorance but a dispensation of silence, every occasion for impious assertion must now also be cleared away, and every proclamation of heretical blasphemy must be examined, so that the truth of the Gospel may shine forth through the very things by which it seems to be obscured.

> **Note [Col. 0350B].** The Leipzig edition, from Erasmus’ margin, reads “must be refuted”; less suitably.

> **Note [Col. 0349B].** “By which it seemed obscure.”

### 9. Fear and pain in the Passion are alleged against the Son’s equality.

For many of them maintain, from the fear of the Passion and from the weakness of suffering, that He was not in the nature of the impassible God: that He who feared and grieved was neither in that security of power which does not fear nor in that incorruption of Spirit which does not grieve; but that, being of a nature inferior to God the Father, He trembled with fear of human suffering and groaned at the severity of bodily punishment.

> **Note [Col. 0350B–D].** The point proposed for refutation is not what all Arians, but what many of them, think. They hold, as is made sufficiently clear here, that Christ—whom Hilary acknowledges to have feared and suffered in His humanity—was wholly without the impassible nature of another kind. But Leontius must be heard on this. “Immediately under Constantine’s reign arose the heresy of Arius, which erred both concerning divinity and concerning human nature: concerning divinity, because it declared the Son to be a creature of God, and likewise the Holy Spirit; concerning the incarnation, because it said that Christ’s body was without a soul, the Word holding primacy in it in place of the soul. It said this because it contributed to establishing its doctrine concerning the Trinity.” After some further remarks he explains how it did so: “For this reason the Arian doctrine taught that Christ’s body was without a soul: so that we might attribute such lowly utterances not to Christ as man, but to the Son of God, and so, by the tenor of those utterances, the Son might be found inferior to the Father.” Athanasius confirms this in *On the Incarnation of Christ*, p. 628: “Therefore the Arians frivolously quibble when, positing flesh alone, they impiously refer what is understood of the Passion to the impassible divinity.” Once this opinion has been explained and Hilary’s purpose recognized, what follows will be understood more easily, or at least will not so readily provoke suspicion.

They support this impious assertion because it is written: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matthew 26:38); and again, “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (ibid., 39); and also, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46).

> **Note [Col. 0350B].** “God, my God.”

They add this also: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke 23:46). For they seize all these declarations of our devout faith for the service of their impiety: that He feared because He was sorrowful and prayed that the cup might be removed from Him; that He suffered because He complained in His Passion that He had been forsaken by God; and that He was weak because He commended His spirit to the Father. Thus, they say, anxiety does not permit the likeness of a nature equal to God in the birth of the Only-begotten—of a nature which testifies to its weakness and difference by its prayer concerning the cup, its complaint of abandonment, and its confession in commending the spirit.

> **Note [Col. 0350D].** Vatican Basilica manuscripts: “of the commending of the spirit.”

### 10. He cannot rightly be said to have feared the death which He taught ought not to be feared.

First, before we demonstrate from these very sayings that no weakness either of fearing or of grieving befell Him, we must ask what He could have seemed to fear, so that dread of intolerable suffering came upon Him. And I think no other cause for fear is alleged here than Passion and death.

I ask those who think this: can it be maintained consistently that He feared to die—He who removed from the Apostles every terror of death and urged them to the glory of martyrdom, saying: “He who does not take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me; and he who finds his life shall lose it, and he who loses it for my sake shall find it” (Matthew 10:38–39)?

For if dying for Him is life, what is He to be thought to have suffered in the mystery of death, He who repays life to those dying for Him? And when He teaches that those who kill the body are not to be feared (ibid., 28), did death itself terrify Him with fear of bodily Passion?

> **Note [Col. 0350D].** Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read “from fear.” Fear is excluded from Him for whom dying is life; accordingly Christ is vindicated from this affection of the mind insofar as He is God, not insofar as He is man.

### 11. He voluntarily encountered death, with power to rise again.

Then again, what pain of death would He fear, when He was about to die by the freedom of His own power? Death comes upon the human race either through some external force—fever, wound, accident, or collapse—assailing the body and hastening it onward; or through the very nature of our body, conquered by old age and yielding to that same death.

> **Note [Col. 0350D–0351C].** In the printed editions: “finally.” Here again it is shown that there is in Christ a nature free from fear; and this is proclaimed only of the divine nature, which alone has the power of laying down and taking up again the soul. This is illustrated by Athanasius’ longer discourse on the faith, in Theodoret, *Dialogue* III: “But the Lord’s man was neither overcome by the force of disease nor did he die unwillingly; rather, he came voluntarily to the dispensation of death, strengthened by the God the Word dwelling in him, who said: ‘No one takes my soul from me,’ etc. Therefore it is the Son’s divinity which both lays down and takes up again the soul of the man whom He bore.”

But the Only-begotten God, having power to lay down His soul and to take it up again, in order to accomplish in Himself the mystery of death, after He had testified that He had completed the whole work of human sufferings by drinking vinegar, bowed His head and gave up His spirit (John 19:30).

> **Note [Col. 0351C].** Or: “to take it up again.”

> **Note [Col. 0351C].** Several good manuscripts read “testified.”

If this right has been left to human nature—that a person, exhaling the spirit by himself, rests in death, and that the soul does not depart after the body has been dissolved and shaken, or that, when limbs are torn, pierced, or crushed, the spirit does not break forth or flow away as though violated in its own seat—then let fear of death come upon the Lord of life, if, because He died when He gave up His spirit, He did not exercise the power of His freedom to die.

> **Note [Col. 0351C–D].** An old Colbert manuscript reads “into the God of life.” “The Lord” is preferable, although by this word the divine nature is signified. It is demonstrated in Christ from this fact: by dying of Himself, by a right granted to no human nature, He openly showed Himself to rejoice.

But if He died of Himself and surrendered His spirit through Himself, there is no terror of death in the power to die.

### 12. Death was terrible neither to His body nor to His Spirit.

But perhaps, through the timidity of human ignorance, He feared this very power to die which was in Himself: so that, although He died of Himself, He nevertheless feared the fact that He was to die. If there are perhaps those who think thus, let them determine to which thing they suppose death was terrible—to the Spirit or to the body.

> **Note [Col. 0351C].** The Verona manuscript adds here: “his own.”

> **Note [Col. 0351D].** The printed editions add “his own.” The word is absent from the better manuscripts and is sufficiently expressed by the words “in Himself”: namely, He feared the power of dying which resided in Him.

If to the body, are they ignorant that He, the Holy One who was not to see corruption (Psalm 15:10), was to raise up the temple of His body within three days? If death was terrible to the Spirit, did Christ fear the abyss of hell while Lazarus rejoiced in Abraham’s bosom?

> **Note [Col. 0351C–0352C].** The older manuscripts read “Eleazar,” not “Lazarus.” It is clear from §34 that by “Spirit” he means the divine nature. Christ is divided here exhaustively into body and Spirit—that is, man and God—and this division is adapted to the Arians’ view, which acknowledges in Christ only a body and the Word supplying the function of the soul. Hilary shows them that neither nature is subject to fear, and that there is no reason why Christ should fear in either. Thus Augustine, on Psalm 193, §19: “The Lord prefigured you in His weakness, not Himself; for He who was to rise on the third day did not fear.” Moreover, fear is not rejected here without qualification, but only fear arising from human ignorance. Finally, this argument may be counted among those which appeal to humanity and are established from the opponents’ own position.

These things are foolish and ridiculous: that, having power to lay down His soul and to take it up again, He should fear to die, though He was to die, under the freedom of His will, for the mystery of human life. There is no fear of death in one who dies voluntarily and has the power not to remain dead long, because both the will to die and the power to live again lie outside the nature of fear: death cannot be feared where there is both the will to die and the power to live.

> **Note [Col. 0352C].** “Death of one dying.”

> **Note [Col. 0352C–D].** Vatican Basilica manuscript: “in the will of death.” The printed editions read “death of one dying”: corruptly. Erasmus and later editions have, “and fear of not remaining long in death in the power.” Two Colbert manuscripts and one Sorbonne manuscript read, “and of one able not to die long,” etc. An older Colbert manuscript has: “There is no fear of death in the power to die of one dying and able not to be dead long, and able not to die long.” We follow the other manuscripts, whose reading can be rendered more clearly thus: “There is no fear of death in one who dies willingly and voluntarily and is able not to die long—that is, to return swiftly to life.”

### 13. Did He fear punishment?

But perhaps the punishment of His body hanging upon the cross, the violent bonds of the binding ropes, and the wounds of legs pierced by driven nails were causes of fear? Let us see what sort of body the man Christ had, so that pain might remain in flesh suspended, bound, and pierced.

> **Note [Col. 0352C].** “Punishment”; shortly below, “legs,” not “raw [wounds].”

> **Note [Col. 0352D].** The Pratellensis codex reads “hard wounds.”

> **Note [Col. 0352D].** The Corbie manuscripts and some others read “stripped,” wrongly. This statement and the preceding one teach that Christ’s body was bound to the cross not by nails only, but by the violent bonds of ropes. Erasmus’ margin reads “pain assailed”: this was adopted by Lipsius without other authority and subsequently prevailed. We have already read in Psalm 58, §7: “which would continue unto the people’s impiety.” Therefore the reading in one Vatican manuscript does not please us: “so that pain might remain in flesh suspended, knotted, and pierced.”

### 14. The source of sensation in bodies.

For the nature of bodies is such that, through fellowship with the soul, being animated into a certain sensation by the sentient soul, bodily matter is not dull and lifeless. Rather, when touched it feels; when pricked it suffers pain; when cold it stiffens; when warmed it delights; when deprived of food it wastes away; and it grows fat by food.

> **Note [Col. 0352D].** The Vatican Basilica codex alone reads “unless through fellowship”; shortly after, “they do not feel dull” in place of “it is not dull”; and later, “from someone” in place of “from a certain.”

For, through a kind of pervading movement of the soul which possesses and penetrates it, the body is either pleased or harmed according to the condition in which it is found. Therefore, when bodies are punctured or cut open, the sense of pain receives the sensation of the soul poured into them. Thus the wound of the body hurts as far as this; and the cuttings of nails severed from the flesh do not know [pain].

But if, when disease has advanced, some corrupted part of the limbs loses the sensation of living flesh, then, when it is cut away or burned, it does not feel whatever pain might otherwise have occurred, because the soul’s intermingling no longer remains in it. Or, when the grave necessity of cutting into the body is imminent, the vigour of the soul is put to sleep by a medicinal drink, and the mind, overwhelmed by stronger juices, is brought into the dead forgetfulness of its sensation.

> **Note [Col. 0352C].** “You know.”

> **Note [Col. 0352D–0353B].** The older manuscripts read *sucis* (“juices”), with a single exception. In the best Colbert manuscript a quire has here been torn out; consequently what intervenes from this point until §31 is missing.

Then limbs ignorant of pain are cut, and the deadened sensation of the flesh escapes every blow of the deep wound, while the sensation of the soul has become numb within it.

> **Note [Col. 0353B].** Three manuscripts read “driven”; and shortly after, the Pratellensis manuscript reads “dead,” not “having died.”

Therefore an animated body brings pain upon its weakened sense through the intermingling of the soul with its weakness.

### 15. The source of Christ’s body and soul.

If therefore the man Jesus Christ lived in the body through the beginnings of our body and soul, and if God was not ruler of His own soul in the same way as He was of His own body; if, having been established in the likeness of man and found in condition as a man, He was born—then He would have felt the pain of our body, being animated in the body by our soul and body alike in conception and in origin.

> **Note [Col. 0353B].** “In likeness”: Greek, *en homoiōmati* (ἐν ὁμοιώματι). Thus below, §25: “established in the likeness of man.”

> **Note [Col. 0353B–D].** The printed editions read “equal pain”; *equal* is absent from the manuscripts. Three assertions against the Arian forebears of the Apollinarians are made here: first, that Christ’s human nature was conceived from the Virgin not in the ordinary human fashion but by the Word alone as its author; second, that the Word did not supply the soul’s function, but assumed a soul together with the body; finally, that the Son of God so assumed the whole man that He in no respect failed in His own divine power and nature. Hence Christ, even as man, is rightly denied to have felt the pain of our body, because the pain of our body is the punishment of sin, and we are subject to it. But Christ, conceived under another law, was neither guilty of sin nor liable to punishment, to which He submitted only voluntarily. Yet if His conception is considered here in order that, from its singular mode, He may be shown to possess divine nature beyond human nature, according to which He did not feel the pain of our body, there will be no difficulty in the matters discussed here. For this refutes those who think pain can fall upon the Word as performing the office of the soul. Nor is it apparent why, amid these statements—“In the birth of man He retained what belongs to the mother, while in the power of His origin He possessed what belongs to God”—the truth and distinction of Christ’s human and divine natures are so carefully expounded, unless in order to show that the divine nature alone is free from pain.

But if, after assuming for Himself flesh from the Virgin by His own agency, He also fitted to that body, conceived by His own agency, a soul from Himself and by Himself, then, according to the nature of soul and body, there must also have been a nature of passions.

> **Note [Col. 0353B].** The Verona codex reads “by Himself,” without the particle “also.”

> **Note [Col. 0353D].** We have added the particle “also,” equivalent to “even,” from two Colbert manuscripts and one Sorbonne manuscript. Along with the printed editions these read “from Himself,” where other manuscripts have “by Himself,” but with no other sense. For “from Himself” does not denote a material cause but an efficient one; in the same sense §22 says: “As He assumed a body for Himself by Himself, so He assumed a soul for Himself from Himself.”

For, emptying Himself from the form of God, taking the form of a servant, and being born the Son of Man while also the Son of God, without failing in Himself or in His own power, God the Word perfected a living man.

> **Note [Col. 0353D].** That is, He created and assumed a man who, consisting of body and soul, was a living, perfect, and complete man. There is nothing here of Apollinaris, who held that the Word, joined to flesh, completed a living man insofar as He gave it life and supplied the function of the soul.

For how would the Son of God have been born the son of man, or, while remaining in the form of God, have taken the form of a servant, unless God the Word had power from Himself both to assume flesh within the Virgin and to give a soul to the flesh, so that the man Christ Jesus was born perfect for the redemption of our soul and body?

> **Note [Col. 0353D–0354B].** Several manuscripts read “the Word of God … might assume … might give.” It was just proved that the Word assumed a perfect man because Christ is the Son of Man. The same point is now confirmed from the fact that He is Redeemer not of flesh alone but also of the soul. Gregory Nazianzen employs both arguments against the Apollinarians in *Oration* 51, §13: “What has not been assumed is without healing. … If Adam fell only in part, then what was assumed was only in part.” And shortly afterward: “If He Himself is without a soul, how can He bear the name of man?”

And He assumed the body in such a way that, being conceived from the Virgin, it made Him the form of a servant. For the Virgin generated what she generated only from His own Holy Spirit.

> **Note [Col. 0354B–C].** From two Colbert manuscripts and one Sorbonne manuscript we add here “her own,” that is, from Christ’s Spirit, or: she generated only from the Word. This is declared in clear terms at the end of the following section: “The flesh derived its origin from no other source than the Word.” These matters concern more the explanation of the preceding propositions—which deny that Christ was born through our beginnings—than the confirmation of the immediately preceding statements.

And although she contributed from herself to the birth of the flesh only as much as women contribute from themselves through the received origins of bodies to be brought forth, Jesus Christ nevertheless did not coalesce through the nature of human conception. Rather, every cause of birth having been introduced through the Spirit, He retained in the birth of man what belongs to the mother, while He possessed, in the power of His origin, what God is.

> **Note [Col. 0354B].** “In the birth of origin.”

> **Note [Col. 0354D].** The printed editions read “in the birth of origin.” Three manuscripts read “in origin.” The Remigius manuscript reads “the power in the birth of origin.” The reading preferred, with the Vatican Basilica codex, is “in the power of origin,” that is, insofar as He is ruler and author of His own soul and body. The same manner of speaking occurs in §25: “the defects of our origin, proceeding from itself through power, are not in Him.”

> **Note [Col. 0354D].** The printed editions read “which is God’s.” Almost all manuscripts better read “which is God”: that is, by the power through which He formed His body from the Virgin, He revealed Himself to be God.

[Col. 0354B] **16. Christ: both from heaven, and Son of Man, and in heaven.**—Accordingly, the Lord himself reveals that greatest and most beautiful mystery of the humanity he assumed, saying: “No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3:13).

[Note: [Col. 0354D] To confirm what Hilary has demonstrated above—that Christ is at once perfect God and perfect man, conceived by the power of the Word rather than according to a human law, yet born from Mary’s flesh—he gives these and the next two passages of Scripture their sound meaning, passages abused by heretics. For the disciples of the Arians, the Apollinarians, interpret them thus in Gregory Nazianzen, Oration 46: as though, before he descended, the Son of Man already existed and, in descending, had brought with him the flesh which he possessed in heaven—“something pre-eternal and consubstantial” (*proaiōnion tina kai synousiōmenēn*), implanted in his essence before the ages. This opinion occasioned Athanasius’s Letter to Epictetus and is condemned by Gregory Nazianzen, Oration 51, §12, in these words: “If anyone says that the flesh descended from heaven and is not from here and from us, let him be anathema.” For the saying, “the second man [is] from heaven,” and “No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven,” etc., must be understood with reference to the heavenly union. To this belongs the statement of Eusebius of Emesa in Theodoret, near the end of Dialogue III: “Because the Power that assumed [the flesh] descended from heaven, what belongs to the Power is attributed to the flesh.” Although this Eusebius has been somewhat discredited by the contagion of Arian error, he was nevertheless not among those ruined Arians whose errors are here refuted.]

That he descended from heaven is due to an origin conceived from the Spirit. For Mary did not give the body its origin, although she contributed everything natural to her sex toward the body’s growth and birth.

[Note: [Col. 0355C] Here Erasmus inserted “from herself,” which was afterwards retained, although it is found neither in Bad. nor in the manuscripts. He seems to note in the preface to Hilary’s Works that he himself interpolated the passage; there he says: “In Book III, and still more in Book X, he speaks of Christ’s body in such a way that he seems to think that the Virgin Mary, apart from the service of conceiving, carrying, and giving birth, contributed nothing of her own.” We have rejected this criticism at length in the general preface, §1. It is sufficiently refuted by what was said immediately above in §15: namely, that the Virgin gave from herself as much as women contribute from themselves when they receive the beginnings of bodies to be brought forth; and likewise by the statement in §35: “For she bore a body from herself.” Nor should what follows immediately be suspect: “But that he is the Son of Man is the birth of flesh assumed in—not from—the Virgin.” For, as Tertullian observes, *On the Flesh of Christ*, §20, the Gospel permits both modes of expression. It says not only: “Joseph, husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born”; but also: “You shall conceive in the womb,” not “from the womb”; and: “What is born in her is from the Holy Spirit.” Hence Pope Leo, Sermon V on the Nativity of the Lord, writes that the Son of God came into this world through the womb of the Virgin, “in whom and from whom Wisdom built a house for itself.” Erasmus does not realize that he casts upon this holy man the suspicion of precisely the error which Hilary here deliberately seeks to correct in heretics. They wished Christ’s flesh to have been brought from heaven; he maintains that it was from Mary, so that for this reason Christ is called Son of Man. They objected the Scriptures in which he is proclaimed to have descended from heaven. He replies that this descent must be referred, not to the flesh, but to the Word. The Word is said to have descended because, entering the Virgin, it formed from her a body, and because it assumed to itself the body which it had formed. Mary did not give the body its origin; that is, being a virgin, she conceived his body not by her own power but by that of the Holy Spirit. “The power of the Most High and the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit caused Mary to bear the Saviour,” says Pope Leo, Sermon V on the Nativity of the Lord, ch. 5. Only this must be noted in Hilary’s thought: in those passages, by “Spirit” he understands the Word itself.]

But that he is the Son of Man is the birth of flesh assumed in the Virgin. That he is in heaven is the power of an ever-abiding nature (see *Treatise on Psalm II*, §11), which, having itself initiated and created the flesh, did not constrain itself, by the power of its infinity, within the region of a bounded body. Remaining in the form of a servant by the power of the Spirit and the might of the Word of God, he who is Lord of heaven and world was absent from no place within or beyond the circuit of heaven and world.

Therefore, in this respect he both descended from heaven, is the Son of Man, and is in heaven: because the Word made flesh had not lost its abiding as the Word. For insofar as he is Word, he is also in heaven; insofar as he is flesh, he is also Son of Man; insofar as the Word became flesh, he is from heaven, is the Son of Man, and is in heaven. For the power of the Word, abiding in no bodily manner, was not absent from the place whence it had descended; the flesh derived its origin from no source other than the Word; and the Word made flesh, although it was flesh, nevertheless did not cease also to be Word.

[Note: [Col. 0356C] That is, when the flesh was assumed by the Word into unity of person, it was then from heaven, etc. This is the point of Augustine, *Sermon against the Arians*, ch. 8: “Because of this unity of person, which must be understood in both natures, the Son of Man is said to have descended from heaven, although he was assumed from the Virgin who was on earth; and the Son of God is said to have been crucified and buried,” etc. Pope Leo transcribes these words in Letter X, now XXIV, to Flavian, ch. 5.]

[Col. 0356A] **17. He is from earth as from the Virgin; from heaven as from the Word.**—Moreover, the blessed Apostle spoke plainly also of the mystery of this ineffable bodily birth: “The first man [was] from the dust of the earth; the second man [is] from heaven” (1 Cor. 15:47).

[Note: [Col. 0356C] The Chartres manuscript reads: “from earth, earthly.” It is not irrelevant to observe here that it is not properly this part of the testimony which is explained below, but the other: concerning which the question is considered why Christ, who is the second Adam, is called both man and from heaven. The answer is that he is called man because he is from Mary, but from heaven because he is from the Holy Spirit. Thus in *Psalm* CXXII, §3: “Therefore the second Adam is heavenly, and heavenly for this reason: because the Word was made flesh, man born from Spirit and God.” Here “man born from Spirit and God” means what is stated in this book, §22: “God before man, and, assuming man, man and God.”]

By calling him man, he taught his birth from the Virgin. She exercised the office of a mother and fulfilled the nature of her sex in the conception and birth of the man. And when he says that the second man is from heaven, he bears witness that his origin lay in the coming of the Holy Spirit upon the Virgin. Thus, because he is both man and from heaven, this man’s birth is from the Virgin and his conception is from the Spirit. Such, indeed, are the Apostle’s words.

**18. Since the flesh of the Son of Man is from the Virgin, he is bread from heaven because he is from the Holy Spirit.**—The Lord himself, disclosing the mystery of his birth, spoke thus: “I am the living bread which descended from heaven; if anyone eats of my bread, he shall live for ever” (John 6:51–52). He calls himself bread, for he himself is the origin of his body. And, lest the power and nature of the Word be thought to have failed in becoming flesh, he again called his body his bread; so that, because the bread descending from heaven is shown to be a heavenly body, the origin of the body might not be thought to arise from human conception.

[Note: [Col. 0356D] The printed editions, with several manuscripts, read “in flesh.” The Corbie manuscript and certain others more correctly read “into flesh.” Here he continues to refute the Arians, forerunners of Apollinaris and Eutyches, in language somewhat intricate but highly illuminating for confirming our faith concerning the sacrament of the Eucharist; clarity is supplied by what precedes. He says, therefore, that the Word calls itself bread, plainly on account of the body which it fashioned for itself and assumed. That body is called the Word’s own, so that the thing assumed and the person assuming may be distinguished, and thus the Word may not be thought to have failed by becoming flesh. Finally, that body is called heavenly because of the heavenly and divine person who formed and assumed it; and, conversely, it is called the flesh and blood of the Son of Man because the assumed flesh was truly born from the Virgin’s flesh. Since the holy Doctor says these things concerning the Johannine passage which, as is clear from Book VIII, §§14 and 16, he interpreted concerning the sacrament of the Eucharist—where he refers to that venerable sacrament the things connected with the same passage—it follows that he held the flesh of Christ born from the Virgin and received by us in the Eucharist to be one and the same flesh. Eusebius of Emesa in Theodoret, at the end of Dialogue III, confirms and illustrates all this: “The Lord says that the bread of God descended from heaven; and, explaining it—although I cannot speak more openly because of the mysteries of the Eucharist—he says: ‘It is my flesh.’ Did the flesh of the Son descend from heaven?
