How then does he say that the bread of God lives and descended from heaven, and explain this of his flesh? Because the Power which assumed [it] descended from heaven, what belongs to the Power is attributed to the flesh.” Here you see that Eusebius too considers the flesh received in the mysteries to be no other than that assumed by the Word in the Virgin.]

Yet, since it is his own bread, this is a declaration concerning the body assumed by the Word. For he added: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves” (ibid., 54), so that, because that which is the Son of Man is also the bread descending from heaven, by his bread descending from heaven and by the flesh and blood of the Son of Man we may understand the assumption both of flesh conceived from the Holy Spirit and of flesh born from the Virgin.

[Note: [Col. 0357D] That is, also bread. For this is the meaning: since that which is called the Son of Man in the words, “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man,” is also called bread descending from heaven in the words, “I am the living bread which descended from heaven.”]

[Col. 0357A] **19. Christ perfect God, perfect man.**—Therefore Jesus Christ, as man of this body, is both Son of God and Son of Man; and, emptying himself from the form of God, he took the form of a servant. The Son of Man is no other than he who is the Son of God; nor is he who is in the form of God other than he who was born perfect man in the form of a servant. Thus, as man is born with body and soul through the nature established for us by God, the founder of our origin, so Jesus Christ, through his own power, was man of flesh and soul and God, possessing in himself everything entire and true that man is, and everything entire and true that God is.

[Note: [Col. 0357B] “Founder.”]

[Note: [Col. 0357D] Some manuscripts read *principem* (“founder”); three read *princeps* (“founder/prince”). Nothing should be altered.]

[Note: [Col. 0357D] The printed editions add here “by mixture,” a word absent from the manuscripts. Just as every human being was said immediately above to be man of flesh and soul, so Christ is now called man of flesh and soul against the Arians, who thought that he assumed flesh without a soul.]

**20. Those who teach that Christ assumed Adam’s flesh and soul. The soul is God’s work.**—Although many, by the skill of their heresy, are accustomed to deceive the ears of the uninstructed in this way: because both Adam’s body and soul were in sin, the Lord also took Adam’s flesh and soul from the Virgin, and the Virgin did not conceive the whole man from the Holy Spirit.

[Note: [Col. 0357D] According to Jerome, Letter LXXXII to Marcellus, and *Anaps.* [apparently *Anacephalaeosis*], Apollinaris, after Tertullian, held that just as body is born from body, so soul is born from soul. Nemesius, ch. 2, says of the same man: “Apollinaris thinks that souls are begotten from souls, as bodies from bodies; for he considers that the propagation of the first man advances into all who are generated from him.” Athanasius lends them support in *On the Saving Advent of Jesus Christ*, commonly entitled *Against Apollinaris*. There he refutes heretics who think the soul corporeal: “If, as your opinion maintains, the soul is fleshly, why does it not die and perish together with the body?”]

If they understood the mystery of the assumed flesh, they would also understand the mystery that he is both Son of Man and Son of God. As though, if he had assumed only so much from the Virgin, he had also assumed a soul from her! Whereas every soul is the work of God, but the generation of flesh is always from flesh.

[Note: [Col. 0358C] The printed editions read “the human soul.” The manuscripts more correctly read “every soul,” from which the conclusion now properly follows: if every soul, then Christ’s also. Everyone sees that Hilary had no doubt concerning the soul’s origin—a question which long troubled Augustine.]

[Col. 0358A] **21. Those who wish Christ to be a sound of speech, and, while charging Catholics with denying the manhood, themselves deny it.**—But those who wish the only-begotten God—the God Word who in the beginning was with God—not to be a subsistent God, but the utterance of an emitted voice, so that the Son is to God the Father what one’s own word is to a speaker, subtly insinuate themselves in order to prevent belief that the subsisting Word, God, abiding in the form of God, was born Christ the man.

[Note: [Col. 0358C] The Vatican Basilica manuscript reads “but a sound of speech.” Shortly thereafter the same manuscript has *argute serpere* (“to creep in subtly”) instead of *argute subrepere*. In other manuscripts appears the older spelling *subripere*. Here the heretics are identified who attempt to prevent belief in the embodiment of the subsisting Word of God. It is useful to compare this passage with *On the Synods*, §46.]

They do this so that, when that man is animated rather by the cause of human origin than by the mystery of spiritual conception—the cause of which is the Spirit, God the Word—the God Word may not be shown to have made himself man by the Virgin’s birth; but that, as the Spirit of prophecy was in the prophets, so the Word of God may have been in Jesus. They are accustomed to accuse us of saying that Christ was born not a man with our body and soul.

[Note: [Col. 0358C] That is, rather than by conception, whose cause is the Spirit, God the Word. It may repeatedly be observed that the entire effort of the heretics is directed to suggesting that Christ lacked divinity; while Hilary’s whole endeavour is to demonstrate, from the very fact of his conception, that he whom he proves to be true and perfect man is also true God.]

[Note: [Col. 0358D] Athanasius complains in his Letter to Epictetus that this opinion had gained currency among the Corinthians, and near the end briefly attacks it. Gregory Nazianzen condemns the same doctrine in Apollinaris, Oration 51, §8, by this anathema: “If anyone says that the divinity operated in him by grace as in the prophets, rather than having been united and being united according to essence, let him be bereft of the higher inspiration,” etc.; and in the poem *On His Own Life*: “The nature of man became participant in the whole God—not as a prophet or another of those inspired by God, who was not so much participant in God as in the things of God, but so substantially as the sun [by its rays].”]

But we proclaim that the Word was made flesh; that Christ emptied himself from the form of God and took the form of a servant; and that he was born perfect man according to the condition of human conformity and of our likeness—so that the true Son of God may truly be true Son of Man: neither not man born from God, nor, because man born from God, thereby ceasing to be God.

[Note: [Col. 0359C] The negative particle is absent from two Colbert manuscripts and one Sorbonne manuscript. It must certainly be retained. In order to repel this calumny, Hilary insists here with such earnestness that Christ is perfect man, by nature like us, although he wishes especially to prove his divinity from the uniqueness of his conception. So throughout this whole book, while he directs his attention upon the Arians alone, he fights with nearly equal earnestness against Sabellius, so as to leave no place for their customary calumny.]

[Note: [Col. 0359C] The Vatican Basilica manuscript alone reads “and emptying the form of God”: less faithful. Incidentally, observe that the designation Christ is referred to the divine nature. Thus, just above, “the subsisting Word, God” and “Christ abiding in the form of God” are synonymous.]

[Note: [Col. 0359C] The printed editions read “so that [he is] true.” The manuscripts more forcefully read “so that [he is] truly,” namely, born—he who is truly Son of God. The whole progression may be explained more clearly thus: the Son of God, truly born from the Virgin, is true Son of Man; but he is born Son of Man from the Virgin in such a way that he is man only from God; and finally, being man from God—that is, though he was God—he was so born man as not to cease to be God.]

[Col. 0359A] **22. Christ’s soul is from God. One person in two perfect natures.**—But as he assumed a body from the Virgin for himself, so from himself he assumed a soul for himself—a soul which is certainly never supplied by the origins of human begetters. For if the Virgin did not have conception of the flesh except from God, much more necessarily the soul of the body could not be from anywhere other than God.

And since the Son of Man himself is also the Son of God, because the whole Son of Man is the whole Son of God, how ridiculously, apart from the Son of God who was made flesh, shall we proclaim some other person, as though a prophet animated by the Word of God, when the Lord Jesus Christ is both Son of Man and Son of God?

[Note: [Col. 0359D] That is, so that through the same one who is whole man and whole God, whole man fallen into sin may be re-formed and restored, as Gregory Nazianzen says against Apollinaris, Oration 51, §5. On the word “whole,” see the notes on Psalm I, §27.]

But because his soul is sorrowful unto death and because he has power to lay down and take up his soul, they wish to attribute to him a soul external to him, not one from the Holy Spirit as the body was conceived from it; whereas the God Word, abiding in the mystery of his own nature, was born man.

[Note: [Col. 0359D] That is, a soul neither formed by the Word nor propagated from an alien, external cause, as stated in §20; and neither internally united to the same Word in unity of person. For, as the aforementioned Gregory Nazianzen bears witness, especially near the end of Oration 52, these heretics divided the persons in Christ, assigning Christ’s humble sayings to the human [person], but splendid titles to the divine.]

He was born, however, not in such a way that he might be one person and another; but so that God before becoming man, by assuming man, might be understood to be man and God.

[Note: [Col. 0359B] “Man and God may be.”]

[Note: [Col. 0359D] The manuscripts more correctly retain the particle “and,” omitted in the printed editions, lest a confusion of natures be understood. In agreement with this, Gregory Nazianzen says against Apollinaris, Oration 51, §5: “For we do not separate the man from the divinity; but we confess one and the same—first, indeed, not man but God,” etc., and finally also man.]

For how is Jesus Christ, the Son of God, born from Mary, except because the Word was made flesh—that is, because the Son of God, though in the form of God, took the form of a servant? That he who was in the form of God took the form of a servant is established from opposites, so that the truth of his abiding in the form of God is as great as the truth of his taking the form of a servant.

[Note: [Col. 0360C] And thus those two contrary natures remain unconfused after their union. Gregory Nazianzen likewise, Oration 42, calling human nature “flesh” and divine nature “Spirit,” says: “God advanced with assumed humanity, one [person]—as we would now say, one individual—from two contraries, namely flesh and Spirit; of these, the latter deified (*etheōsen*), and the former was deified (*etheōthē*).”]

For we are compelled to understand the property of nature by a term common to both. For he who is in the form of God is also in the form of a servant. Although the former belongs to nature and the latter to the dispensation, nevertheless both belong to the property of the same truth, so that he is as truly in the form of God as he is truly in the form of a servant.

[Note: [Col. 0360B] “Natural.”]

[Note: [Col. 0360C] The Vatican Basilica manuscript, with some others, reads “natural”: less aptly. From this passage, as well as §§64, 65, and others, it is plain, as we have already observed, that whenever Hilary speaks of Christ he refers the term “nature” to divinity. “What he is as God,” he says in Psalm CXXXIX, §2, “belongs to his own nature; what he is as man is an assumption of our nature.” He gives the reason in Psalm LXVIII, §25: “The assumption of the servant’s form is not nature in the sense of native origin, since what is assumed is not an inward property but an outward addition.” Thus Cyril, Book XI on John, teaches that human nature ascended to union with the Word relationally (*schetikōs*), not naturally (*physikōs*), because it does not possess from itself and by its own condition the capacity to be one with God. Yet Hilary carefully and repeatedly demonstrates that the assumed servant’s form is no less Christ’s own than the form of God itself.]

As taking the form of a servant means nothing other than being born man, so being in the form of God means nothing other than being God. Yet we confess one and the same person—not by a failure of God, but by an assumption of man—to have been found both in the form of God through divine nature and in the form of a servant through the conception of the Holy Spirit, according to the condition of man.

Therefore, since Jesus Christ was born, suffered, died, and was buried—and rose again—he cannot, amid these diverse mysteries, be so divided from himself that he is not Christ. For no one other than he who was in the form of God took the form of a servant; no one other than he who was born died; no one other than he who died rose again; no one other than he who rose again is in heaven; and he who is in heaven is no other than he who formerly descended from heaven.

[Note: [Col. 0360D] The printed editions read: “and rose again, and ascended into heaven; he cannot,” etc. The manuscripts read more simply and truly: “and rose again,” with *et* (“and”) in place of “also.” That is: if you object to Christ’s weakness in birth, suffering, and so forth, I shall set against it the same Christ’s glory in resurrection. Hilary continues to bar the way to the heretics’ error. Their Apollinarian imitators, who introduced two Christs, maintain in Gregory Nazianzen, Oration 52, that the words “He was distressed, was fastened to the cross, and was buried” belong to the outward covering, whereas “He was confident, rose again, and ascended” belong to the inward treasure.]

[Note: [Col. 0361B] Thus the manuscripts. But the printed editions read: “he who rose again ascended into heaven; but in heaven.” From this passage and similar ones, we showed in the general preface, §4, that Hilary was far from holding that Christ’s divinity was ever separated from his body. For if it departed before death, one must say that one was born, another died, and another was in heaven.]

[Col. 0361A] **23. Christ subject to suffering: was he also subject to pain? Prerogatives of Christ in the flesh.**—Therefore Jesus Christ, man and only-begotten God, is both Son of Man through flesh and Word, and Son of God. He assumed true man according to the likeness of our man, without God failing in himself.

[Note: [Col. 0361B] Erasmus, Lips., and Par. read “in whom”; Bad. and the manuscripts differ, among which the Corbie manuscript has in the margin, in an ancient hand: “Read cautiously.” As a precaution, one must recall against whom the Catholic Doctor has disputed thus far. All his words must be interpreted in light of what Gregory Nazianzen reports Apollinaris to have asserted in Oration 46 to Nectarius: “He teaches that the only-begotten God himself, judge of all, author of life, destroyer of death, was mortal and suffered in his own divinity; that in that three-day death of the body the divinity also died together with the body, and was then restored from death to life again by the work of the Father.” This is especially so because Hilary above, §9, declares that the purpose of this entire book is to proceed against proponents of such an error.]

In him, although a blow might strike, a wound penetrate, knots tighten, or suspension lift him up, these things indeed brought the onset of suffering, but did not inflict the pain of suffering. It was as with some missile piercing water, puncturing fire, or wounding air: it inflicts all these sufferings according to its own nature—to pierce, puncture, and wound—but the suffering inflicted does not remain in these things according to its own nature, since it is not in their nature for water to be pierced, fire punctured, or air wounded, although it belongs to the nature of the missile to wound, puncture, and pierce.

The Lord Jesus Christ truly suffered when he was struck, suspended, crucified, and died. But the suffering that rushed upon the Lord’s body was suffering indeed, yet it did not exert the nature of suffering: while it raged in a penal service, the Power of the body received, without perception of punishment, the force of punishment raging upon it.

[Note: [Col. 0361A] The word “Lord” is absent.]

[Note: [Col. 0361C] “Lord” is absent from Bad., Erasmus, and most manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 0361C] The printed editions read *exercuit* (“exercised”), but the manuscripts read *exseruit* (“exerted”). After this verb it is right to understand this with reference to divinity. For immediately above, “the Power of the body” is the same as the Word subsisting in the assumed body—so to speak, embodied Power. In this sense Eusebius of Emesa, in Theodoret, Dialogue III, maintains that Christ, according to his divinity, did not know our sufferings, and consistently calls the Word “Power.” “For,” he says, “Power did not receive the nail so as to fear,” although, as he explains after a few intervening words, it received the sufferings of the body. Thus, whenever Hilary speaks of Christ, he always refers the word “power” to the Word. The Word is here rightly called “Power of the body,” just as above at the end of §15 it was called “Power of origin,” because Hilary held that it gave origin to its body by its own power, as has often been noted. Perhaps he also calls the Word “the body’s Power” by adapting his way of speaking to his opponents’ position. For below, §49, the opponents are said to have held that God the Word, as though some part of God’s powers, extending itself by a kind of continuous line, inhabited the man who began from Mary and endowed him with powers of divine operation. Here, therefore, the perception of punishment is rejected from the nature of the Word alone, to whose person it is attributed. Lest we seem to have devised this convenient interpretation concerning our author, another passage of Hilary should be produced, in which, explaining Christ’s passion in the same way, he calls what is here “the Power of the body” plainly “the nature of divinity.” It is found in Psalm LIII, §12: “Although that passion was not of condition and kind, because no force of injurious disturbance could assail the unchangeable nature of God, it was nevertheless voluntarily assumed, being itself to satisfy a penal office, but not to injure the sufferer by the perception of punishment. This was not because the passion did not possess, by reason of its own character as passion, the capacity to injure; but because THE NATURE OF DIVINITY does not perceive pain. Therefore God suffered, because he voluntarily subjected himself to suffering; but, although he received the natural forces of sufferings assailing him—which must necessarily inflict pain upon those who suffer—he nevertheless did not fall away from the power of his own nature so as to feel pain.” From this one may readily understand the meaning of the analogy just offered, of a missile entering water, fire, or air.]

Certainly the Lord’s body might have had the nature of our pain, if our body had it in its nature to tread the waves and walk upon the billows without being weighed down by its motion, if water did not yield beneath its footsteps, if it penetrated solid things, and if it were not excluded by the obstacles of a closed house.

[Note: [Col. 0362B] Erasmus testifies that in one copy he found inserted here, “from sin,” and again, after the words “to tread the waves,” “by its own nature without the miraculous aid of God.” Hilary seems by this single argument both to deny Christ’s body the nature of pain and to attribute to it a power of working miracles by itself. Yet he is far from attributing the power of working miracles to Christ’s body, since below, §55, he firmly declares that such power does not belong even to Christ’s soul: “It is not fitting,” he says, “that the soul call Lazarus from the tomb, and that, at the soul’s command and power joined to the body, the soul already separated from his dead body should be recalled to it.” Likewise, in *On the Synods*, §48, he proves from miracles that the Word was not transformed into flesh: “Otherwise, whence came to flesh power in works, glory on the mountain, assurance in suffering, life in death? But God, knowing no change, lost none of the goods of his substance by becoming flesh.” Therefore the power of miracles is a proper good not of the flesh but of the divine substance. He teaches this no less clearly in *On the Trinity*, Book VII, §36: “Since the things which he did were proper to God—to walk on the waters, command the winds,” etc.—“from this arose every ground of complaint: that the nature of God acting in the assumed man was not understood.” He confirms the same point in Psalm LV, §5. First he states that divine nature remained in him: “For God made flesh remained God even in the assumption of flesh, using the power of his might in fellowship with our body.” He then proves his statement from miracles: “For he was not weighed down by flesh so as not to walk upon the waters,” etc. Finally he concludes: “Therefore God, performing divine works under the assumption of flesh, does not fear from the flesh.” Thus he attributes neither the power of miracles to Christ’s flesh nor denies it the capacity for pain. Rather, he tacitly leads those who allow no nature in Christ exempt from pain to reflect, from what he did miraculously in the body, that a singular nature existed in him and that it was divine. Nor does he wrongly direct their minds to consider whether, from the punishments inflicted on Christ’s body, they rightly suppose that the Word and the assuming Spirit experienced the nature of our pain. It may even be denied that the Lord’s body possessed the nature of our pain, because our pain pricks and bites even unwilling persons. Or at least this argument is one which so presses the opponents that they have no reply available within their own position.]

But if the sole nature of the Lord’s body is this—that by its own power and its own soul it is carried upon the wet, stands upon the liquid, and passes through structures—what do we judge concerning flesh conceived from the Spirit through the nature of a human body? That flesh—that is, that bread—is from heaven; and that man is from God. Though he possessed a body capable of suffering and did suffer, he did not possess a nature capable of pain.

[Note: [Col. 0363C] Does he first say “by its own power,” as though by the divine power which is the primary cause of the miracle mentioned, and then “by its own soul,” as that which receives this power most immediately from divine nature and communicates it to the body? For, as Gregory Nazianzen says near the end of Oration 35: “God was united with flesh through an intervening mind”; and Rufinus, in his exposition of the Creed: “Therefore the Son of God is born, not joined principally to flesh alone, but generated with the soul as mediator between flesh and God.”]

[Note: [Col. 0363C] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read instead: “the flesh conceived from the Holy Spirit is judged.” That flesh is called from heaven because the person assuming it is from heaven.]

[Note: [Col. 0363C] Erasmus found inserted in one copy here: “weak as ours is from sin.” Since the Word is the subject of “possessing,” and the Word’s nature cannot suffer pain, the difficulty arising from this passage is easily resolved. This may be illustrated from *Treatise on Psalm* LIII, §8. There Hilary rebukes the Jews for regarding this soul—Christ’s—as of human nature and weakness, and he might seem to proclaim that Christ’s soul was not of a nature like ours, unless he defended the contrary view before and after. It is clear that he means only that Christ’s soul belongs to the person of the Son of God, who is God by nature and free from every weakness; and that this was unknown to the Jews.]

For that body belongs to its own and proper nature which is conformed on the mountain to heavenly glory, which drives away fevers by its touch, and which makes eyes from its own spittle.

[Note: [Col. 0363D] “For that body belongs to its own and proper nature,” etc., is the same as the statement at the beginning of §25: “For he had a body, but one proper to its origin,” etc. This signifies that Christ’s body possessed a singular and proper nature, suited to the Son of God; for he himself is the origin of his body, as stated in §18. In this sense Christ’s body must be understood as belonging to its own nature: it was free from the defects of our nature, not that it was not a body of our flesh. For in Book I, §11, God is proclaimed to have become flesh of our flesh, so that he may be perfect in what is his own and true in what is ours; and nothing is sounded more strongly by this book, above and below. In this nature, free from our defects, pain can only be voluntary; from the perception of which nothing follows against Christ’s divinity and power, any more than from his thirst or hunger, as is explained immediately below. The phrase may also be explained thus: the body was proper to its nature and origin because it was proper to the Word and intimately joined to it, rather than, as the heretics above will have it, dwelling in him as in the prophets. This interpretation is favoured by what follows immediately concerning the glory and power of this body. Hilary uses this proof in *On the Synods*, §48, and in Psalm LV, §5, in order to demonstrate that the Word did not fail in itself after assuming flesh. In this sense, it is not the body or man, but the Word possessing the body, that is defended against pain. Compare what follows below in §26.]

[Note: [Col. 0364C] The printed editions read “is transformed,” but the manuscripts almost unanimously read “is conformed”; Gregory Nazianzen, Oration 51, explains that this occurred because divinity overcame the flesh (*hypernikōsēs to sarkion tēs theotētos*).]

[Col. 0363B] **24. Whether Human Passions Were Present in Christ.**—But perhaps, since the affection of weeping, thirsting, and hungering remained in Him, the nature of the other human passions must likewise have been present in Him. Let whoever does not know the mystery of His weeping, thirst, and hunger know also that He gives life while weeping, and does not weep Lazarus’s death (John 11:15), at which He rejoices; that, while thirsting, He supplies rivers of living water from Himself (John 7:38), and does not suffer thirst to wither Him, who is able to give drink to the thirsty; and that, while hungry, He condemns the tree which has not supplied its fruits to one who is hungry (Matt. 21:19), nor is that nature overcome by hunger which, by its command, changes the nature of greenness into dryness (ibid.).

[Note: [Col. 0364C] We have removed the preposition *ob* here on the authority of the manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 0364C] The printed editions read, “to be without thirst”; they are corrected from the manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 0364C] Bad. and Er.: “and the hungry”; Lips. and Par.: “and while He Himself was hungry.” More correctly the manuscripts: “and one who is hungry,” that is: let him know that, even while hungry, He had authority to condemn the tree. In these matters it is evident that Hilary intends only this: that in Christ there existed a nature free from the affection of weeping, thirsting, and hungering, even when He suffered these same affections according to the flesh. He must be understood to have spoken in the same way concerning the sense of pain.]

And if, apart from the mystery of weeping, thirst, and hunger, the assumed flesh—that is, the whole human being—was surrendered to the natures of passions, yet not so that it should be worn out by the injuries of passions: so that, while weeping, He did not weep for Himself; while thirsting, He did not dispel a thirst which He would not drink away; and, while hungry, He did not satisfy Himself with the food of any meal. For when the Lord thirsted, hungered, or wept, He is not shown to have drunk, eaten, or suffered pain. Rather, the customary condition of a body was assumed in order to demonstrate the reality of the body, so that by the customary condition of our nature the body’s customary condition might be satisfied. Or, when He received drink and food, He did not yield Himself to bodily necessity, but to customary usage.

[Note: [Col. 0363B] Read “of passion,” shortly below, not “of drinking.”]

[Note: [Col. 0364D] Supply “was surrendered.” Then the printed texts read “of passion,” and shortly afterward, “and while thirsty, not about to drink away thirst”; these are corrected from the manuscripts. It should not be passed over carelessly here that Hilary himself explains “assumed flesh” as “the whole human being.” He then grants that this was surrendered to the natures of passions, not to the injuries of passions. From this it is clear that he thought Christ, according to the whole human being—that is, both according to soul and flesh—was surrendered to passions; not, indeed, insofar as these are injurious and dishonouring to the Word, but insofar as they are natural to a human being.]

[Note: [Col. 0364D] In the Vatican Basilica manuscript: “let satisfaction be made to the body,” wrongly omitting the earlier word *consuetudini*, “customary condition.”]

**25. In Christ, the Reality of a Human Body, Not Its Defects. Not Flesh of Sin, but Likeness.**—For He had a body, but one proper to its own origin: not existing from the defects of human conception, but subsisting in the form of our body by the power of His own virtue. He bore us indeed in the form of a servant, yet was free from the sins and defects of the human body; so that we were indeed in Him through the Virgin’s generation, but the defects of our origin, proceeding from itself by its own power, were not in Him. For He was born a human being, but not born with the defects of human conception.

For the Apostle maintained the mystery of this birth when he said: “But He humbled Himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of a human being, and found in appearance as a human being” (Phil. 2:7). Thus, by taking the form of a servant, He is understood to have been born in the form of a human being; but by being made in the likeness of a human being and found in appearance as a human being, the appearance and reality of His body bear witness that He was human, while one who knows that He was found in appearance as a human being does not attribute to Him the natures of defects. For generation is in the likeness of nature, not in the property of defects.

[Note: [Col. 0365C] Thus consistently in the manuscripts. But the printed editions, likewise consistently: “in the likeness of human beings.”]

[Note: [Col. 0365C] The printed editions read “nature.” With the manuscripts, “natures” is preferable. By the “natures of defects” are meant disturbances opposed and contrary to reason, which in §24 we heard called “the injuries of passions.”]

[Note: [Col. 0365C] In Er., Lips., and Par., “his generation is.” *His* is absent from Bad. and the manuscripts; thus there is an absolute proposition concerning every generation, for whose reality it is unnecessary that defects be transmitted.]

For since in the words “He took the form of a servant” the nature of His birth seemed to have been indicated, the Apostle added, “made in the likeness of a human being, and found in appearance as a human being,” lest the reality of birth should be believed to be also a property of nature weakened through defects. For there was a true birth in the form of a servant, and in His being found in appearance as a human being there was likeness of nature.

[Note: [Col. 0365C] Bad. omits the particle *in*. Thus the passage seems to be understood: “and in that which the Apostle says, that He was found in appearance as a human being.”]

He Himself, a human being born through the Virgin from Himself, was found in the likeness of sinful, defective flesh. The Apostle testified to this very point in writing to the Romans: “For what was impossible to the law, in that it was weak through the flesh, God sent His own Son in the likeness of flesh of sin, and concerning sin condemned sin” (Rom. 8:3).

[Note: [Col. 0365C] “And into likeness” is corruptly read “and into sinful likeness.”]

[Note: [Col. 0365D] Bad. with several manuscripts: “of defective sins”; wrongly.]

[Note: [Col. 0365C] “Into likeness.”]

[Note: [Col. 0365D] Here Er. and Lips. add “in the flesh”; Par. adds “on the cross.” Neither is found in Bad. or the manuscripts.]

That appearance was not merely *as though* of a human being, but truly that of a human being; nor was that flesh flesh of sin, but the likeness of flesh of sin. For both the bodily appearance belongs to the reality of birth, and the likeness of flesh of sin is free from the defects of human passion. Thus Christ Jesus is human in the reality of birth, insofar as He is human; and He is not in the property of sin, insofar as He is Christ. For He who is human could not fail to be human, being born as He was; and He who is Christ could not have lost what He is as Christ. Therefore, since Christ Jesus is human, He has the birth of a human being, because He is human; yet He is not in the defective weakness of human nature, because He is Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0366C] “Merely of a human being, but also as of a human being.”]

[Note: [Col. 0365D] Thus the Vatican Basilica manuscript and the better manuscripts. Others, with the printed texts, read: “merely of a human being, but also as of a human being.” Hilary makes this distinction between *ut* (“as”) and *tamquam* (“as though”): *tamquam* signifies only an external appearance of a thing, whereas the conjunction *ut* signifies reality.]

[Note: [Col. 0365D] The printed editions read, “because He is human,” and shortly afterward, “because He is Christ,” against the better manuscripts. Everyone sees that Christ is here distinguished from Jesus and from human being. But the following section will make it clearer that “Christ” and “Word” are synonymous, and that both names refer to the divine nature as distinct from the human.]

**26. Christ Remained True God, Though a True Human Being Without Human Defects. The Events of the Passion Examined.**—Although, therefore, apostolic faith instructs us in understanding this mystery, testifying that Christ Jesus was found in appearance as a human being and sent in the likeness of flesh of sin: so that, when He is as a human being in appearance, He is in the form of a servant and not in the defects of nature; and when He is in the likeness of flesh of sin, the Word is indeed flesh, but is rather in the likeness of flesh of sin than itself flesh of sin; and when He is the human being Christ Jesus, He is indeed human, but there cannot be in the human being anything other than what Christ is: therefore He was born human by the birth of the body, yet is not in the defects of humanity, because He is not in its origin.

For the Word, having become flesh, could not fail to be flesh, which it became; and though the Word became flesh, it did not lose being what it is as Word. And since the Word, having become flesh, cannot lack the nature of its own origin, it could only remain what the Word is in the origin of its nature; nor can it be understood other than truly that the Word became flesh. Yet this must be understood in such a way that, because He dwelt among us, that flesh is not the Word, but is the flesh of the Word dwelling in flesh.

[Note: [Col. 0365D] Thus the manuscripts. But the printed editions read, “than itself flesh of sin.” Relevant here are the words cited from Hilary by Augustine, *Against Julian*, I.3: “Therefore, when He was sent in the likeness of flesh of sin, He did not have sin in the same way as He had flesh. But because all flesh comes from sin, that is, is derived from Adam, the first parent, He was sent in the likeness of flesh of sin, since in Him there was not sin but the likeness of flesh of sin.”]

[Note: [Col. 0366C] In very ancient copies, Vatican Basilica and Carnotensis: “it was not necessary.” In this section we have the sum of what has been demonstrated thus far: namely, that in assuming flesh the Word did not lose what it was, and that it assumed the reality of human nature, not its defects. Nor does it appear why Hilary so zealously maintained in Christ the distinction of divine and human natures, unless to prove that our weaknesses, wrongly ascribed by heretics to the divine nature, belong solely to the human. But because it was unfitting that a human being united to God should be subject to the domination of passions, he fittingly shows that Christ did not know the shameful beginnings of our conception and therefore was not subject to our passions insofar as they are injurious and defective and rule over us.]

[Note: [Col. 0366D] The printed editions read “who.” The manuscripts better read “because.” For a reason is given why the Word, though made flesh, cannot be said to have been changed into flesh: namely, because it became flesh in such a way as to be proclaimed as dwelling in flesh; so that, while it dwelt, it remained nothing other than God, says Hilary, Book I, §11. See *Tractate on Psalm 138*, §3.]

Since these things are so, let us nevertheless see whether that entire course of the Passion, once completed, allows bodily pain in the Lord to be understood as weakness. For, postponing briefly the grounds of those sayings from which heresy attributes fear to the Lord, let us compare the events themselves as they occurred. For fear cannot be signified in the words of one whose confidence is displayed in deeds.

**27. Whether There Was Fear of the Passion in Christ.**—Does the Lord of glory appear to you, heretic, to have feared the Passion? Yet because of this error of ignorance, Peter is both Satan and a stumbling-block to Him (Matt. 16:23). Peter, indeed, through love for Christ—whom not flesh and blood, but the Father who is in heaven, had revealed to him—rejected the mystery of the Passion; and, strengthened by so severe a sentence, he was confirmed in faith. What hope will you pursue, denying that Christ is God and adding fear of the Passion to Him? Did He fear, who went out to meet those armed to seize Him (John 18:6)? Was there weakness in His body, at whose approach the ranks of His persecutors were thrown down in terror and, unable to endure the majesty of One offering Himself for bonds, fell backward with their bodies cast to the ground? What weakness, then, do you believe ruled in His body, whose nature possessed such power?

[Note: [Col. 0367C] The printed editions read “in this body.” He does not deny that weakness came upon Him, but that it ruled Him. In fact our weaknesses came upon Christ in such a way that He was always their master.]

**28. Whether There Was Pain.**—But perhaps He feared the pain of wounds. Tell me: what horror did He feel at nails piercing the flesh, He who restored the flesh of a severed ear by touch alone (Luke 22:51)? Explain to us, you defender of the Lord’s weakness, this work of the flesh made weak at the very time of the Passion. For when Peter drew and struck with the sword, the servant of the priest stood there with his ear cut off. How, when Christ touched the wound of the severed ear, was the flesh of the ear restored? From where, amid flowing blood and after the very marks of the cutting sword, in the very penalty inflicted upon the mutilated body, did that which was absent come forth, that which did not exist follow, and that which was lacking be restored? Does the hand which brings forth this ear, then, feel the nail? Does He feel a wound in Himself who leaves no pain of the wound in another? Is He sorrowful from fear of flesh that is to be pierced, whose touch can grant flesh again after slaughter?

[Note: [Col. 0367C] “Terror” in the Verona manuscript.]

[Note: [Col. 0367C] The printed editions read “terror”; corrected from the older manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 0367C] “Severed.” Shortly afterward, “of the cutting,” not “of the descending.”]

[Note: [Col. 0367C] In several manuscripts, “the wound of the severed ear.”]

[Note: [Col. 0367C] Most manuscripts, with the printed editions, read “of the descending [sword].” The Tellerian manuscript reads “of the cutting [sword].” With the Remigian manuscript, “of the cutting” is preferable. Then: “in the very penalty of the mutilated body,” that is, at the very moment when the body was made mutilated by the loss of the ear. Among writers of Middle or later Latin, *calumnia* sometimes means an action by which someone seeks through legal forms to take something away; sometimes a punishment or fine imposed on one who has unjustly brought an action. In the first sense it is understood in Psalm 137, §13; here, however, it is used simply for punishment—unless one prefers to call it the just punishment of Christ, unjustly attacked through calumny.]

[Note: [Col. 0368C] “Came forth.” Then, “that which is lacking.”]

[Note: [Col. 0367D] The printed editions read “that which is lacking”; against the older manuscripts.]

If this power was in Christ’s body, by what faith, I ask, is He defended as naturally weak, to whom it was natural to suppress every kind of human weakness?

[Note: [Col. 0367D] Hilary admits below, §65, that Christ, though human by dispensation, nevertheless remained God by nature; He was the same One who was crucified from weakness and who lived by the power of God. Thus, while weakness was from the form of a servant, nature remained from the form of God; and it was not doubtful in what mystery He both suffered and lived. Since in the same One there was weakness for suffering and God’s power for life, He who suffered and lived was not other than, or divided from, Himself. From this passage it follows: (1) that the power in Christ’s body must be understood as His divinity, as already observed above in §23; (2) that Christ is rightly denied here to have been naturally weak, since He was weak only as human, and since for Hilary He is not human by nature but God, as we also observed in §22; (3) that the natural power to perform miracles is here attributed, not to Christ’s body, but to the Word remaining in the body; this confirms what was proved in §23; and (4) that Hilary’s denial here that Christ is weak by nature and according to the form of God does not prevent him from believing and proclaiming the same Christ weak according to the dispensation and the form of a servant. Nor should one be troubled by his saying above, “Does the hand which brings forth this ear feel the nail?” For “hand” is used figuratively for the Word, whose hand it is—as though he said: “Does He feel pain from an injured hand, who by that same hand could restore the severed ear?”]

**29. Whether He Was Therefore Sorrowful.**—But perhaps, by foolish and impious perversity, an assertion of weak nature in Him will be inferred from this: that His soul is sorrowful unto death (Matt. 26:38). I do not yet charge you, heretic, with failing to understand the force of the saying. But meanwhile I ask you why, when Judas went out to betray Him, you do not remember that it was said: “Now the Son of Man has been glorified” (John 13:31). For if the Passion was to glorify Him, how did fear of the Passion make Him sorrowful? Unless one is so irrational as to suppose that He feared to suffer that which would glorify Him in suffering.

**30. Whether He Prayed That the Cup Might Pass from Him.**—But perhaps He will be thought to have feared so greatly that He prayed for the cup to pass from Him, saying: “Abba, Father, all things are possible for You; remove this cup from Me” (Mark 14:36). Without raising accusations from other matters, could you not from this alone have convicted the dullness of your impiety, since you had read: “Put your sword back into its sheath. Shall I not drink the cup which the Father has given Me?” (John 18:11)? For how could He pray that what He hastened to accomplish through the purpose of the dispensation should pass from Him through fear of suffering? It is not consistent that He should be unwilling to suffer who was willing to suffer. And when you knew that He was willing to suffer, it would have been more reverent to confess that you did not understand the saying than to rush, in the frenzy of impious folly, to assert that He prayed not to suffer, though you knew that He was willing to suffer.

[Note: [Col. 0368C] One Sorbonne manuscript and another Colbert manuscript read: “if all things,” etc. The Carnotensis manuscript: “if it is possible, remove this cup from Me.” Chrysostom, disputing against the Arians concerning these same words, *Homily* 32, vol. I, says: “They indeed say that it is a prayer of divinity; but we say it is of the dispensation.” He then proves that Christ did not will the cup to be removed from Him, since He desired it so zealously that He called Peter Satan when Peter prayed that it might be removed from Him; nor was the Father’s will concerning it uncertain to Him, since it had been foreknown even long before by the prophets.]

[Note: [Col. 0368D] In the Vatican Basilica manuscript and several others, “He prayed for the cup”: a gloss. Shortly afterward, the printed editions read “to be fulfilled.” More suitably, the manuscripts read “to fulfil.” He hastened toward this with the utmost zeal of love, when there was consummated in Him what He Himself had willed to suffer for our salvation; as is found in *Tractate on Psalm 54*, §13, and shortly above: “When He bestowed salvation on the human race by assuming the death of the cross, this mystery of great compassion cannot appear to accuse or refuse [the Passion].”]

[Note: [Col. 0369C] Earlier printed editions: “that He should be unwilling to suffer what He was willing to suffer”; this is changed on the authority of the better manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 0369C] “What He was willing to suffer.”]

[Note: [Col. 0369C] Thus the Corbie manuscript, as Erasmus suspected the passage should be read; he, together with Bad. and most manuscripts, retained *intelligentiam*, “understanding,” in place of which Lipsius afterward inserted *ignorantiam*, “ignorance.”]

[Note: [Col. 0369C] Thus the manuscripts. But the printed editions read “to the frenzy of impious folly”; and shortly afterward, “when you knew,” not “when you had known.”]

**31. Whether He Complained That He Was Forsaken.**—But, I suppose, you will arm yourself also for the battle of your impiety with the saying of the Lord’s voice: “My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?” (Mark 15:34). After the humiliation of the cross, perhaps you think the favour of paternal aid withdrew from Him, and that from this there arose His complaint of forsaken weakness. If, therefore, contempt, weakness, and the cross are humiliation to you in Christ, you ought not to have forgotten this saying: “Truly I say to you, henceforth you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power and coming with the clouds of heaven” (Matt. 26:64).

**32. Recapitulation.**—Where, I ask, in the Passion is fear? Where weakness? Where pain? Where humiliation? Is He said by the wicked to fear? Yet He Himself declares that He wishes to suffer. Is He alleged to be weak? Yet He shows Himself powerful, when He confronts the terrified persecutors and cannot be withstood. Is He accused of feeling the wounds of flesh? Yet in restoring the flesh of the ear from a wound, though He Himself is flesh, He is found outside the fleshly nature of feeling pain from a wound. For while He touches the severed ear with His hand, that hand is from the body; but while the hand brings forth the ear from the wound, that hand is shown not to be a hand of a body subject to weakness.

**33. Whether the Cross Was Dishonouring to Him.**—But the cross is said to be dishonouring to Him. Yet through it the Son of Man is to be seen sitting at the right hand of Power; and the human being born from the Virgin’s childbirth has returned in His majesty with the clouds of heaven. Irreligious man, you do not grasp the causes of natural things; and, filled with the spirit of impiety and error, because you do not understand the mystery of faith, you fall away from even worldly understanding through heretical dullness. For everything feared must necessarily be avoided while it is feared; whatever is weak draws terror from its feebleness; whatever feels pain has within itself an unchangeable nature of feeling pain; and whatever is dishonouring is always dishonourable. But by what rational judgment do you understand our Lord Jesus Christ to fear that toward which He hastens; to tremble in weakness while He overthrows the strong; to feel pain when wounded, though He does not permit wounds to be painful; and to be dishonoured by the shame of the cross, when the cross is His enthronement with God and His return to the kingdom?

[Note: [Col. 0369C] In one Vatican manuscript, “you advance”: wrongly, as Louis Miraeus has already observed. Following Erasmus, he notes that Hilary elsewhere used *disproficere* in the sense “to degenerate.” Both undoubtedly refer to Book XI, §11; yet there the word does not have that force without the accompanying phrase *in genere*. Here, with its modifiers, *disproficit* means a departure from human wisdom: those who first withdrew from faith on account of human reason finally, through heretical dullness and a preconceived opinion, fail even in human reason.]

[Note: [Col. 0369D] Two of the later manuscripts read “changeable.” With the others, “unchangeable” must be retained: namely, a nature which cannot be changed or turned aside by the will. For as Augustine defines it, *City of God*, XIV.15: bodily pain is only the soul’s offence arising from the body, and a certain discord arising from its suffering; just as the soul’s pain is a discord from things that happen against our will. For this reason some philosophers explain why innocent Adam was free from pain: namely, because he was able to alter whatever had arisen from himself so as to produce pain.]

[Note: [Col. 0370C] The printed editions read “to be painful.”]

[Note: [Col. 0370C] Thus the more carefully corrected manuscripts, supported by the opening words of this section and the final words of §2 of the *Tractate on Psalm 61*. In several others, as in the printed editions, “agreement”; a reading not to be despised.]

**34. In Descending to Hell He Did Not Depart from Heaven. The Faith of the Thief Is One Thing, That of Heretics Another.**—But perhaps you think that this too affords an occasion for impiety: that He feared both descent into hell and death’s necessity, since He appears to testify to this very thing in the saying, “Father, into Your hands I commend My spirit” (Luke 23:46). Reading this and not understanding it, you ought either to have been piously silent or reverently to have prayed for understanding; not to wander, incapable of truth, in the foolish frenzy of a shameless assertion. Do you believe that He feared hell’s chaos, torrents of flame, and every avenging abyss of punishments, though He said to the thief on the cross: “Truly I say to you, today you will be with Me in paradise” (Luke 23:43)?

I no longer say that you confine the power of this nature by fear; nor do you even confine it within the region of the infernal seat: for, descending to hell, it is not absent from paradise, just as the Son of Man speaking on earth remains in heaven. It promises paradise to His martyr and pledges the delights of consummate blessedness. This is not the property of bodily fear: to penetrate hell indeed, yet to be extended everywhere by the power of its own nature. Nor does hell’s chaos vindicate for itself, by the terror of death, this nature—the mistress of the world, immeasurable by the freedom of spiritual power, and incapable of lacking paradise’s delights. For the Lord, who is to be in hell, is also to be in paradise.

[Note: [Col. 0370D] “This spirit,” says Theodoret in his *Demonstration that Divinity Is Impassible*, “the Arians and Eunomians say is the divinity of the Only-begotten. For they suppose that He assumed an inanimate body.”]

[Note: [Col. 0370D] The printed editions read “fear,” and afterward, “the region is confining.” Here too it is clear that the power of nature exempt from fear means the divinity.]

[Note: [Col. 0370D] Not insofar as He is the Son of Man, but insofar as He is personally united to the Son of God. Christ’s words in John 3:13 are intended. By this manner of speaking Hilary, while defending divinity alone from human affections, can sometimes seem to exempt even the flesh itself.]

Sever off, for fear of punishment, a portion of the indivisible nature; concerning Christ, place in hell that which suffers pain, and leave in paradise that which reigns. For the thief asks Him to remember him in His kingdom. And, I suppose, the sound of the nails passing through the palms, as he heard it, inflamed him to this faith of blessed confession; and through bodily weakness in Christ he learned Christ’s kingdom through pain. He asks for the favour of One remembering him in His kingdom; you impute the death of the cross to fear. The Lord immediately promises him fellowship in paradise; you confine Christ in hell beneath penal terror. This faith belongs to a different hope. The thief deserved paradise beneath the cross because he confessed the hanging Christ in His kingdom; but if you reckon Christ to be in the pain of punishment and fear of death, you must necessarily be deprived both of paradise and of the kingdom.

[Note: [Col. 0370D] Vatican Basilica manuscript: “and give to Christ.” More correctly others: “and concerning Christ,” that is, “place.” In many ways the defender of Catholic faith here declares what nature he wishes to be immune from human affections: namely, the nature which is mistress of the world, immeasurable, incapable of lacking paradise’s delights, and which, as indivisible nature, is simultaneously in hell and paradise.]

[Note: [Col. 0371C] “Weakness,” wrongly.]

[Note: [Col. 0371C] Thus the principal manuscripts—Vatican Basilica, Colbert, and others. The printed editions read: “of weakness in Christ’s body.” These words are ironic.]

[Note: [Col. 0371D] The printed editions read, “therefore in the pain of punishment,” and shortly afterward, “you will be deprived.” The manuscript reading is more elegant.]

[Note: [Col. 0371C] “You will be deprived.”]

**35. Epilogue: What Sort of Body Christ Had.**—Therefore, when the powers of His words and deeds have been compared, it is unquestionably shown that in the nature of His body there was no weakness of bodily nature, since in the power of His nature He could drive away every weakness of bodies; and that Passion, though inflicted upon the body, did not introduce into the body a nature of feeling pain. For although the form of our body was in the Lord, He was not in the body of our defective weakness, since He was not in the origin which the Virgin brought forth from conception by the Holy Spirit. Though she gave birth by the office of her sex, she did not receive the elements of earthly conception.

For she brought forth from herself a body, but one conceived from the Spirit. It had in itself the reality of a body, but did not have weakness of nature. Thus the body generated from the Virgin is the reality of a body; yet that which took its beginning from spiritual conception is outside the weakness of our body.

[Note: [Col. 0371D] The printed texts omit “in” here and shortly afterward add “the form was in the body which was not,” etc.; they are corrected from the better manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 0371D] Vatican Basilica manuscript: “having received the elements.” In the same sense above in §15 is found “having received origins.” Hilary proclaims cautiously that Christ was not conceived by the common law, while immediately affirming the reality of the Virgin’s maternal honour. For she brought forth a body from herself.]

**36. What It Means That He Was Sorrowful Unto Death.**—But the heretics seem to contend against the demonstration of apostolic faith with this saying: “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matt. 26:38), in order that the declaration of Him who calls Himself sorrowful may testify to a weakness of nature through the awareness of which He began to be sorrowful. First, I ask ordinary human understanding what it means to be sorrowful unto death.

For “to be sorrowful because of death” and “to be sorrowful unto death” do not have the same meaning. Where sorrow is because of death, death itself is the cause of sorrow; but where sorrow is unto death, death is no longer the cause of sorrow, but its end. Therefore, since He is sorrowful not because of death but unto death, we must ask why He is sorrowful. Yet He is sorrowful not for a time uncertain or indefinite to human ignorance, but unto death. So far is sorrow from having been assumed because of death that it is put away through death.

[Note: [Col. 0371D] Lips. and Par., following Erasmus’s marginal note, read “evangelical,” against the manuscripts. Above, at the beginning of §26, apostolic faith, not evangelical, is proclaimed. Clearly the reference is to the Apostle’s words, “made in the likeness of a human being,” etc., which have been discussed to this point.]

[Note: [Col. 0371D] At last here you have him openly confessing that Christ assumed sorrow, and disputing only concerning its cause. He says the same in *Commentary on Matthew*, ch. 13, §4, and *On Psalm 141*, §8, where he explains more clearly in what respect he denies that Christ assumed sorrow: “For He did not say, ‘because of death,’ because, although He gave Himself to the Passion, eternal Power did not receive the pain of the Passion.” Whoever is not unfamiliar with Hilary’s writings knows that his expression “eternal Power” denotes divinity.]

[Note: [Col. 0372C] “Nor indefinite.”]

[Note: [Col. 0372D] Manuscript: “nor indefinite,” or “nor into indefiniteness.”]

**37. The Cause of Christ’s Sorrow. For Whom He Prays That the Cup May Pass. Christ’s Two Wills.**—And so that we may understand the cause of this sorrow, let us see what preceded or followed this declaration of sorrow. For the whole mystery of the Passion and faith had been fulfilled by the Lord in the Paschal supper. After teaching that all would be scandalized in Him (Matt. 26:31–32), He promises that He will go before them into Galilee (ibid. 33). Peter promised with steadfast faith that, although the rest would be scandalized, he himself would not be scandalized. But the Lord, not ignorant by His divine nature of what was to occur, answered that Peter would deny Him three times, so that the scandal of the others might be understood from Peter, when Peter, by denying Him three times, fell into so grave a danger of faith.

Then, taking Peter, James, and John with Him (ibid. 37)—two chosen for martyrdom, and John to be strengthened for the preaching of the Gospel—He declared Himself sorrowful unto death. Then, going forward, He prayed, saying: “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from Me; yet not as I will, but as You will” (ibid. 39). He asks for the cup to pass from Him—certainly a cup already remaining with Him, since it was then being completed in the blood of the New Testament, to be poured out for the sins of many. For He does not ask that it not be with Him, but that it pass from Him. Then He asks that His own will not be done; and He does not wish granted to Himself the very thing which He wills to be done. For He says, “Yet not as I will, but as You will,” signifying by His will to pray for the cup’s removal His sharing in human solicitude, yet not separating from Himself the judgment of the will united to Him and common with the Father.

[Note: [Col. 0372D] Lips. and Par. read “after,” against the older books. Shortly afterward the same editions, following Erasmus, read “to be scandalized,” and below, “those to be scandalized,” without manuscript authority. From the overwhelming agreement of the manuscripts it is clear that *scandalizaturum* was passive for Hilary.]

[Note: [Col. 0372D] Most manuscripts with the printed editions read “was being completed, to be poured out.” We prefer the reading of the excellent Colbert manuscript and the German manuscript, by which Hilary more aptly expresses his thought: he intends to signify an affair already begun and being brought to completion—what in French we would say, *qui achevait de se répandre* (“which was finishing being poured out”).]

But lest He should be understood to pray for Himself, and lest the reason for the will thus signified and the prayer that it should not be granted should remain unexplained, He began this entire petition in this manner: “My Father, if it is possible.” Is something, then, left to the Father which it is uncertain whether He can do? And if nothing is impossible to the Father, it must be understood with reference to whose condition this phrase, “if it is possible,” was left.

[Note: [Col. 0373C] The Vatican Basilica manuscript alone reads “of the prayer.” More correctly the others read “the prayer that [the will] should not be obtained”—supply “will”; that is, the prayer that what He willed and asked as human should not be granted.]

[Note: [Col. 0373C] Bad. and Er., with the Carnotensis manuscript, read “which, if it is impossible.” Then Lipsius substituted *sibi* (“to himself”) for *si* (“if”), and that reading subsequently prevailed. Several later manuscripts read “which is possible”; certain others, “which is impossible.” The reading preferred with the Colbert, Corbie, German, Pratensis, and other manuscripts is: “that which [He says], ‘if it is possible’”—that is, it must be considered to whose condition this conditional petition, “if it is possible,” refers. For here *id quod* has the force of Greek τό.]

For after this prayer comes: “And He came to His disciples and found them sleeping, and said to Peter, ‘Could you not watch with Me one hour? Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak’” (Matt. 26:40–41). Is the cause of His sorrow, and His prayer for the cup to pass, still obscure? For this is why He commands them to watch with Him and pray: lest they enter into temptation, with a willing spirit indeed but weak flesh. For those who promised that they would not be scandalized by the steadfastness of faithful conscience were to be scandalized through the weakness of the flesh. Therefore He is not sorrowful for Himself, nor does He pray for Himself; but for those whom He warns to pray vigilantly, lest the cup of the Passion fall upon them. He asks that it pass from Him so that it may not, that is, remain in them.

### 38. Why He Says, “If It Is Possible”

He prayed that it might pass from Him, if it were possible, because, although nothing is impossible for God, as He Himself says: “Father, all things are possible for You” (Mark 14:36), it is nevertheless impossible for a human being not to be overcome by the terror of suffering, nor can faith be known except through testing. Therefore, as man He wills the cup to pass for the sake of men; but as God from God He is united to the Father’s will for its fulfillment. [Note: Erasmus, Lipsius, and Paris: “may be united.” Better, Badius with the manuscripts: “is united”; that is, as man He wills the cup to pass, but as God from God He is united to the Father’s will. Thus there are two wills in Christ; nor have the Arians any means of escape. Since they admit only one will, they maintain that this prayer is that of His divinity itself. For, as Chrysostom argues at length, Homily XXXII, vol. I, if Christ’s divinity prayed this, the will of Father and Christ would be not one but contrary; and thus they interpret in vain the saying, “I and the Father are one,” as spoken because of unity of will. Faustinus constructs a similar argument against them from other words of Christ, chapter 2.]

What He says, “if it is possible,” He plainly taught in what He said to Peter: “Behold, Satan has demanded to sift you like wheat; but I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail” (Luke 22:31–32). [Note: The older Colbert manuscript and others of no inferior standing read “sift” (*ventilet*). Some later manuscripts read “may sift” (*cribraret*). You will find the word *cerneret* again below, §40, where in some manuscripts *cribraret* was mistakenly added by a second hand.] For through this cup of the Lord’s passion all were to be tested. And the Father is prayed to for Peter, that his faith may not fail: so that, in the weakness which would make him deny, at least the sorrow of repentance might not be absent; [Note: Thus the more numerous and better manuscripts. The printed editions read, “because faith.” When Scultetus rebukes Hilary for trying to excuse Peter as though he had not denied Christ, he undoubtedly has not attended to these words, nor to those above in §37.] so that his faith might not fail in this: that he should repent.

### 39. He Who Is Sorrowful unto Death

Therefore the Lord’s sorrow is unto death, because at His death the faith of the apostles would be confirmed by the earthquake, the darkness of day, the rending of the veil, the opening of the tombs, and the resurrection of the dead—faith which would be shaken both by the terror of the night watch [Note: Carnotensis manuscript: “night watch.”] and by scourges, blows, spitting, the crown of thorns, the burden of the cross, the mockery of the whole passion, and finally the condemnation of the accursed cross.

Knowing, therefore, that all these things would cease after His passion, [Note: Lipsius and Paris, from Erasmus’s margin: “would cease.” Badius, Erasmus, the Vatican Basilica manuscript, and some others: “would fail.” Others more correctly: “would be removed,” passively; as above, “would be scandalized.” Our reading is confirmed by §36: “So far is the sorrow from having been assumed because of death that it is removed by death.”] He is sorrowful even unto death; and He knows that this cup cannot pass unless He drinks it, saying: “My Father, this cup cannot pass from me unless I drink it; Your will be done” (Matthew 26:42). That is, when the passion had been completed in Himself, the fear of the cup would pass—a cup which could not pass unless He drank it. The end of its terror follows only upon the terror of the passion completed in Himself; for after His death, through the glory of His mighty works, [Note: “Through the glory of His power.”] the stumbling of apostolic weakness would be driven away.

### 40. Why He Now Permits the Apostles to Sleep

And although, in saying, “Your will be done,” He surrendered the apostles, amid the scandal of the cup—that is, of His passion—to the decision of the Father’s will, nevertheless He also employed the prayer of repeated petition a third time, after saying: “Sleep now, and rest” (Matthew 26:45).

For He who had previously rebuked them for sleeping does not now command them to sleep and rest apart from awareness of some inward reason. But Luke seems to have given us an understanding of this exhortation. After saying that Satan had demanded to sift the apostles as wheat, and that the Lord had prayed for Peter’s faith not to fail, he adds that, after much prayer by the Lord, an angel stood by strengthening Him; [Note: Most manuscripts: “had stood by.”] and, with the angel standing by, He began to pray more earnestly, so that sweat flowed from His body in drops of blood (Luke 22:43–44).

For, once the angel had been sent to protect the apostles, and the Lord had been strengthened through him so that He need not be sorrowful for them, He said, now without fear of sorrow: “Sleep now, and rest.” [Note: Thus the better Vatican Basilica, Colbert, and other manuscripts. Another Colbert manuscript with the Sorbonne manuscript reads: “He said, now without sorrow and without fear.” Corbie and a few others: “He said that they were now without fear of sorrow.” The printed editions: “Being now without fear of sorrow, He said.” What follows, “Sleep now,” does not occur in Luke; indeed, Luke says something wholly different: “Why are you sleeping? Rise and pray,” etc.]

Matthew and Mark say nothing either of the angel or of the devil’s demand. Yet, after the sorrow of His soul, after the rebuke of those sleeping, after the prayer that the cup might pass, the exhortation to those sleeping did not follow without cause. Rather, because He was about to be absent from them and had been strengthened by the granted help of an angel, He allowed those whom the security of this guardianship was to guard to sleep. [Note: Vatican Basilica manuscript: “of a guardian.”]

### 41. In Many Books Nothing Is Found about the Sweat of Blood or the Angel’s Coming. Christ’s Weakness Is Wrongly Inferred from It

Nor should we be unaware that in very many Greek and Latin codices nothing is found written either about the angel’s coming or about the sweat of blood. Thus, since it is doubtful whether this is absent from various books or superfluous in them—for the diversity of the books leaves this uncertain for us—certainly, if heresy draws any comfort from this in order to assert weakness in Him who required the help of an angel to strengthen Him, [Note: The Verona codex has *confortiantis*, “of one strengthening,” for *confortantis*, just as later it has *confortiari* for *confortatum*.] it should remember that the Creator of angels did not need the protection of His own creation. Then, further, He was necessarily strengthened in the same manner in which He was sorrowful.

[Note: The printed editions read, “for He who is sorrowful for us,” and then, “because therefore He who is sorrowful concerning us,” etc.; they are corrected on the authority of the manuscripts. Two points should be noted here in passing. First, it is not the man but the Creator of angels who is defended against weakness. Second, no controversy is raised concerning the reality of Christ’s sorrow according to His humanity, because no one doubted it; rather, granting it as it were, the discussion immediately concerns its cause and condition, in order to show that it was such as did not dishonor the man united to God.]

For if He is sorrowful for us—that is, sorrowful on our account—it follows that He was strengthened for us and on our account. For He who is sorrowful on our account is also strengthened on our account; and He is strengthened under the same condition under which He is sorrowful.

No one, moreover, will dare attribute the sweat to weakness, because to sweat blood is contrary to nature. Nor is it weakness that He acted contrary to the usual course of nature; nor can that which, through the sweat of blood, serves against the heresy which falsely asserts a phantom contribute in any way to the heresy of weakness, but rather serves to establish the reality of the body. [Note: Hippolytus, cited by Theodoret at the end of Dialogue III, constructs a similar argument from the water and blood which flowed from Christ’s side after His death: “Although dead in the human manner, the body had in itself great power of life. For blood and water, which do not flow from dead bodies, flowed from it, so that we might know how great is the power for life which dwelt in the body.”]

[Note: The heresy of weakness means Arianism, because it referred Christ’s weaknesses according to His human nature to His divine nature; as is explained in the argument of this book, Book I, §32, and Book II, §6.]

[Note: Namely, the heresy of Valentinus, Manichaeus, and similar persons. Theodoret gives the same reason in *Demonstration that the Union Is Unconfused*, §8: this took place so that later persons who believed in the assumption of soul and body might be confirmed by demonstrations, while those who denied it might be refuted by evident testimonies. He prefaces this by saying: “Although the divinity and the Spirit were present as an anointing, neither the united divinity nor the Spirit then sustained the body or soul; rather, they entrusted this service to the angel, in order that they might show the weakness both of soul and body, and that through this weakness the natures of those that were weak might be shown.” Chrysostom says, Homily XXXII, vol. I: “For if, after He Himself had said so many and such great things, some dared to assert that He had not assumed flesh, what would they not have said if none of these things had been spoken?”]

Therefore, since both His sorrow is on our account and His prayer is on our account, everything must be understood to have been done on our account, since all that was feared for us was prayed about on our behalf.

### 42. The Sorrow, the Prayer That the Cup Might Pass, and So Forth Concern the Apostles

The Gospels, moreover, supply one another with mutual fullness, since they are understood from one another, because all are the preaching of one Spirit. John, the foremost preacher of spiritual realities, shows that this unspoken prayer of the Lord for the apostles was such when he reports Him praying: “Holy Father, keep them in Your name. While I was with them, I kept them in Your name; those whom You gave me, I guarded” (John 17:11–12).

That prayer, therefore, was not for Himself but for the apostles. Nor is He sorrowful for Himself, who warns them to pray lest they be tempted. Nor is an angel sent for Himself, who, if He wished, could bring down twelve thousand legions of angels from heaven. [Note: The older Colbert manuscript, with Germaniensis and Remigiensis, reads “ten thousand legions.” Another Colbert manuscript and the Sorbonne manuscript read “twelve legions”; then, with the Vatican Basilica manuscript, “would bring angels down from heaven.” See the notes on Psalm 54, §6.]

Nor does He fear because of death, who is anxious unto death; nor does He ask that the cup pass over Himself, but asks that the cup pass from Him—a cup which cannot pass unless He drinks it. [Note: The printed editions read “could not” instead of “cannot.”] To pass, however, is not to depart from a place, but to cease to exist altogether. This is precisely what both evangelical and apostolic language signifies when it is said: “Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away” (Mark 13:31). And the Apostle says: “Behold, the old things have passed away, and new things have come into being” (2 Corinthians 5:17). [Note: Erasmus, Lipsius, and Paris read “all things new.” “All things” is absent from Badius and the manuscripts. Then only the Carnotensis codex reads: “and when he says, ‘For the form of this world has passed away.’” In some other manuscripts *transivit*, “has passed,” occurs instead of *transibit*, “will pass.”] And again: “The form of this world is passing away” (1 Corinthians 7:31).

Therefore the cup concerning which He prays to the Father that it may pass cannot pass unless it is drunk. And what the Lord prays, He certainly prays for those whom He Himself saved while remaining with them, and whom He left to be saved by the Father. Now, about to accomplish the sacrament of death, He prays that the Father may guard them. And the presence of the angel sent for this purpose—if indeed it is so—is unambiguous; [Note: In some later manuscripts: “is foreknowledge.”] and the manifest security of the prayer granted is shown when, the prayer completed, He exhorts them to sleep.

The Evangelist then shows in the very event of the passion both the effect of the prayer obtained and the security of the sleep He permitted, when he says of all the apostles, who were to escape from the hands of their persecutors: “That the word which He had spoken might be fulfilled: ‘Of those whom You gave me I lost none of them’” (John 18:9). [Note: This is a Greek idiom rendered word for word: *ouk apōlesa ex autōn ouden*, “I lost none of them.” In the printed editions the negative particle *non* had been deleted contrary to the testimony of the manuscripts, in some of which *aliquem*, “anyone,” was substituted for *neminem*, “no one.”] For the prayer’s petition is fulfilled through Him, and all are safe. Yet the Father is prayed to, that He may now save in His own name those whom Christ had saved through Himself. And He so saves them that Peter’s faith does not fail when repentance follows, although it has been terrified.

### 43. Epilogue

Therefore, the Lord’s prayer shown by John, the devil’s demand shown by Luke, and those matters found in Matthew and Mark—the sorrow unto death, the rebuke for sleeping, and again the exhortation—leave no ambiguity. For by the prayer in John, [Note: “Through the prayer of John.”] in which He commends the apostles to the Father, both the cause of the sorrow and the prayer for the cup to pass are made clear: the Lord does not pray that the passion be removed from Himself, but prays that the Father may protect the apostles while He undergoes suffering. And, once the prayer against the devil has been shown through Luke, the previously forbidden sleep is now safely permitted in confidence.

[Note: Paris reads “through the prayer of John”; other editions, “through a prayer by John.” The manuscripts more correctly read “in John,” that is, the prayer found in the Gospel of John. A similar manner of speaking occurs in Fragment I, §2.]

### 44. Christ Is Free from Human Defects. The Source of His Sensibility

Therefore, in that nature which is above humanity there is no anxiety of human trembling. And the body which was not begun from earthly elements is outside the evils of an earthly body, although the Holy Spirit, through the sacrament of conception, brought in the origin of the Son of Man.

[Note: The printed editions, with one Remigiensis manuscript, two Colbert manuscripts, and one Sorbonne manuscript, read “of the Son of Man.” Better are the older Colbert, Corbie, Vindobonensis, another Remigiensis, Germaniensis, Pratellensis, and others: “of the Son of Man.” That is: although Christ possesses a body not begun from earthly elements, since the Holy Spirit is its author, nevertheless He was truly born as Son of Man, the true Son of the Virgin. Compare the final words of §15.]

For the power of the Most High joined to the body the bodily power [Note: “Power to the body.”] which the virgin brought forth from the conception of the Spirit.

[Note: On the authority of the manuscripts named above, we restore “the power of the body,” especially since in §23 we have already read: “The power of the body, without a sensation of pain, received in itself the force of pain raging against it”; and again in §46 we shall hear that the sufferings of our body were undertaken by Christ through the power of His body. The printed editions and most manuscripts read “joined power to the body,” which is not ill-sounding because of the added word. For this seems to have been said of the union of the Word with our nature, which is more fully explained in Book II, §26: “The Holy Spirit, coming down from above, sanctified the virgin’s inward parts and, breathing in them, mingled Himself with the nature of human flesh; and what was alien to Him He took upon Himself by His power and authority.
