And lest anything should fail through the weakness of the human body, the power of the Most High overshadowed the virgin, strengthening her weakness—that is, that of the body—by being poured round it as by a shadow, so that the overshadowing of divine power might temper the bodily substance, weak in itself, for the effective sowing of the entering Spirit.” More precisely, §27: “The Holy Spirit coming upon her, and the overshadowing power of the Most High, accomplish the beginnings of birth.” In these statements the Holy Spirit—that is, the Word—is considered both as the one who assumes the body and as the effective cause of what is assumed. In both senses He is the power of the body: whether creating it or working divinely through it.]

For, through the fellowship of the soul infused into the body, the sensation of the living body lives; and the soul, mingled with the body, gives life to the body itself in relation to the pain inflicted upon it. Yet when, by the blessed ardor of heavenly hope and faith, it despises the earthly origin in its body, it makes the body also the body of its own perception and spirit in pain, so that it ceases to perceive that it suffers what it suffers. Why then should we still speak of the nature of the Lord’s body and of the Son of Man who descended from heaven? Earthly bodies themselves sometimes do not know fear or pain, although they must be capable of pain and fear.

### 45. The Three Children Do Not Fear the Flames. How Much More Christ

For I ask whether the Israelite children feared the flames fed to intensify the heat of the Babylonian furnace, or whether dread of such a great fire assailed that body of our conception [Note: The Vatican Basilica codex reads “our flesh.” Better in the others: “our conception.” Otherwise no distinction appears between the bodies of the Israelites and Christ; Hilary customarily teaches that Christ differs from us not in flesh but in conception. Thus in Psalm 53, §8: “The Son of God, abiding before the ages, was born as man from the Virgin’s childbirth in the form of human nature—that is, with our body and soul.”] (Daniel 3:23). I ask also whether they suffered when surrounded by flames. [Note: The Vatican Basilica codex has “to be burned around” (*circumamburi*). Badius and Erasmus: “to be burned all around” (*circumaduri*). Corbie, Pratellensis, and other manuscripts: *circumamburi*. Three Vatican manuscripts with Remigiensis and Theodotianus: *circumburi*. Vindobonensis ad Silvanum: *circumcomburi*. Colbert and Germaniensis: *amburi*. Carnotensis: *amburi*. It matters little which reading is preferred. The same is expressed in Psalm 144, §13: “For them the fire is tempered in the moisture of dew; these are burned by blazing fire. The flames are both within and without; according to the difference of merits, nature both fails and does not fail them. For what exists remains fire toward those whom it burns; and what does not exist must be present in those for whom there is dew.”]

But perhaps they suffered nothing because they were not burned, and one will then suppose that the flames lacked the nature of burning. Certainly the nature of the body was such that it could fear burning and could be burned. But if earthly bodies, that is, bodies initiated according to the elements of common causes, could neither be burned nor fear through the spirit of faith, then those things which are contrary to nature through faith in God within a human being are not to be judged natural in God, in whom they are initiated according to the origin of nature by the power of the Spirit. [Note: Erasmus, Lipsius, and Paris read “in God-man.” “Man” is absent from Badius and the manuscripts.]

The bound children are in the midst of the fire. They do not fear the fire as they ascend it; [Note: The printed editions read “as they are burned.” Carnotensis and Remigiensis manuscripts read “as they walk”; Corbie and some others, “as they go,” supported by the sacred text, which brings the children forward walking amid the flames. The older Colbert manuscript: “they split the fire, not to be feared.” We prefer, with another Colbert manuscript, one Sorbonne manuscript, and the Vatican Basilica codex, “they ascend,” especially because below we again read of the martyrs: “they ascend, singing, the fires built up for them with piles of wood.”] they do not feel the flames while they pray; they cannot be burned while they are in the fire. In them both their bodies and the fire lose their nature: the bodies are not burned, nor does the fire burn. Yet in others both fire and body retain their nature: those standing around burn, and the instruments of punishment themselves undergo punishment.

Do you refuse, impious heretic, to allow that when the nail passed through Christ’s palms He did not feel pain, or that the wound caused no sharp pain from the piercing weapon? I ask why the children neither feared nor suffered from the fires, or what there was in their bodies by nature that surpassed the nature of fire. If they, by the ardor of faith and the glory of blessed martyrdom, do not know how to fear things that are feared, would Christ—even if He had been conceived from the source of our sins—yet, as the God who would abide through the cross, judge the world, and become King of eternal ages, be sorrowful from fear of the cross? Would He, forgetful of such great rewards, tremble in the anxiety of shameful fear?

### 46. Faith’s Power to Repel Pain

Daniel, to be fed by the prophet’s meal, does not fear the lions’ den. The apostles rejoice that they are beaten and suffer for Christ’s name. Paul’s poured-out offering is his crown of righteousness. The martyrs stretch out their necks to executioners to be cut off, with hymns; and they ascend, with songs, the fires built up for them with piles of wood.

So far does the perception of faith, having destroyed in bodies the fear of natural weakness, transform the bodies themselves into a condition in which pain is not felt, that through the soul’s purpose strength is conveyed into the body, [Note: “To the body.”] and the living body perceives itself only in that toward which it is moved by the soul’s endeavor. Thus what the mind, in desire for glory, despises suffering, [Note: Vatican Basilica manuscript, three Vatican manuscripts, and some others: “strives.” Then the older Colbert manuscript: “assents,” for “does not feel.”] the body, as the soul animates it, does not perceive itself to suffer.

If these things are natural in human beings through the ardor of a soul burning for glory—so that they do not know their sufferings, ignore their wounds, and do not comprehend their deaths—then will the Lord Jesus Christ of true glory, [Note: Erasmus, Lipsius, and Paris: “of true glory”; and later, “whose fringe,” which Badius also has, against the manuscripts. Afterwards His spittle and word are called the nature of His body because they restore to it a body deprived of the integrity of its own nature.] whose very fringe is power, whose spittle and word are the nature of the body—when the maimed man who was maimed is commanded to stretch out his hand, the man born blind does not perceive the defects of his birth, and the one whose ear was cut off is no longer mutilated—be reckoned to have the weakness of a body pierced and in pain, a weakness in which the Spirit of His faith did not leave even glorious and blessed men?

### 47. How Christ Undertook Our Sufferings. He Who Bears Sins

Therefore the only-begotten God suffered all the weaknesses of our sufferings that came upon Him; but He suffered by the power of His own nature, just as He was born by the power of His own nature. For, though He was born, He did not fail to retain in His birth the nature of His omnipotence.

For although He was born under the law of human beings, He was not conceived according to the law of human beings: possessing in Himself, in His birth, the constitution of the human condition, yet Himself outside the constitution of the human condition in His origin. [Note: He was, of course, produced from the Virgin’s flesh and brought forth after nine months had run their course, He who, beyond the law of human beings, was conceived from the Holy Spirit without a man’s agency. To this applies what the bishops assembled at Ancyra say in Epiphanius, *Heresy* 73, §9: “Having been made like human beings, He was human and was not human in every respect: human, indeed, insofar as He assumed human flesh, since the Word became flesh; but He was not human insofar as He was not born in the manner of others—that is, from a man’s seed and the union of the two sexes.”]

Accordingly, He suffered in the body from the weakness of our body in such a way that He undertook the sufferings of our body by the power of His own body. [Note: We have already said that “the power of the body” must be understood as divinity, and we are strongly confirmed in this opinion by comparing these words with those above: “But He suffered by the power of His own nature.” What there is “by the power of His own nature” is plainly signified here by “through the power of His own body.” When He is said to have suffered by the power of His own nature, just as He was born by the power of His own nature, it is no less evident that the power of His nature means the divinity of the Word, by whose power Christ’s birth is constantly affirmed throughout this very book. This is especially illuminated by the exposition of Psalm 138, §§2–3. Hilary first says: “Nor did the body that was assumed abolish the power of the nature that previously existed, since in the body that was assumed the power of the previously existing nature works.” Then in §3 he adds: “Therefore, if anything weak is found said from His person, it must be referred to the man.” Why? “It must be referred,” he says, “for this reason: because He did not assume a human being of alien or simulated nature.” But if He did not assume a human being of alien or simulated nature, neither did He assume fictitious weaknesses. He later explains how these do not fall upon Christ: “For the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, not failing through the power of the Word into the vices and weaknesses of flesh, but, born as man, assuming the weaknesses of our nature. But assumption of weakness did not make Him weak, because it is one thing to be a nature and another to have assumed a nature; and beyond the necessity of kind, assumption is an addition of will. For He was not a sinner, but assumed sins. Nor was He weak, but bore weaknesses. For He Himself, according to the prophet, assumed our sins and bore our weaknesses.” And lest anyone suppose that anything befell the impassible and immutable divinity, he added: “And we thought Him to be in pains.” Therefore He assumed weaknesses because He was born human; and He is thought to suffer pain because He suffers. Yet He Himself is free from pains because He is God. See also what follows, where it is plainly evident that only Christ’s divinity is exempted from pains, while His human nature is subject to all those things to which the human race is liable in itself. Thus, by comparing both passages, the danger is avoided against which earlier editors warned here.]

The prophetic word also bears witness to this faith of ours when it says: “This one bears our sins and suffers for us; and we considered Him to be in pains, and in a blow, and in affliction. But He was wounded because of our iniquities, and was weakened because of our sins” (Isaiah 53:4–5).

Human judgment, therefore, is mistaken when it supposes that He suffers pain in what He undergoes. For though He bears our sins—assuming, that is, the body of our sin—He Himself does not sin. He was sent in the likeness of sinful flesh, bearing sins in the flesh, but ours. And He suffers for us, but not with the sensation of our pain; because, though found in appearance as a man and possessing in Himself a body capable of pain, He does not possess the nature of suffering pain, since He has both the appearance of a human being and an origin not of a human being, having been born from the conception of the Holy Spirit. [Note: In earlier printed editions the particle *ut* was lacking; for its force see above, col. 365, note g.]

Hence He was judged to be in pains, in a blow, and in affliction. For He took the form of a servant, and, born human from a virgin, introduced for us the supposition that He naturally suffered pain in His passion. Yet He was wounded—but because of our iniquities. For although He was wounded, the wound was not from His own iniquity; and whatever He suffers, He does not suffer for Himself. For He was not born human for Himself, nor is He iniquitous from Himself.

The Apostle testifies to the purpose of this dispensation when he says: “We pray through Christ to be reconciled to God; Him who knew no sin He made sin for us” (2 Corinthians 5:20). [Note: The printed editions read “for Christ”; they are corrected from the manuscripts.] For, intending to condemn sin in the flesh through sin, though free from sin He Himself became sin—that is, condemning sin in the flesh through flesh. He was indeed ignorant of flesh, but for us He became flesh; and therefore He was wounded because of our iniquities.

[Note: Erasmus reads: “Though indeed ignorant of the sin of flesh, yet for us, having become flesh, He is the likeness of sinful flesh”—a mere gloss, nevertheless adopted by subsequent editions. Christ is declared free from sin and ignorant of flesh by His own nature and prior to the assumed humanity; but through the assumption He became both sin and flesh.]

### 48. Christ’s Power Shines Forth in the Passion. Christ’s Passion Is Triumph

The Apostle, however, knows no trembling from pain in Christ. Speaking of the dispensation of the passion, he proclaimed it in the sacrament of divinity, saying: “Forgiving you all sins, blotting out the handwriting against us in decrees, which was contrary to us, taking it out of the way and fastening it to the cross, stripping Himself of flesh, and making a public display of principalities and powers with confidence, triumphing over them in Himself” (Colossians 2:13 ff.).

[Note: Erasmus, Lipsius, and Paris read “this dispensation.” Better: *this* is absent from Badius and the better manuscripts. Here Hilary shows his aim more clearly: namely, that he proclaims Christ’s passion as accomplished in the sacrament of divinity. He later adds concerning it: “This Power seems to you to yield to the nail’s wound.” From the human nature, however, he excludes only the disgrace of necessity: “If in His passion there is necessity,” etc. He sometimes calls this necessity “nature”: “If there is necessity and nature there, if there is force there,” etc.]

Does this Power, then, seem to you to yield to the nail’s wound, and, terrified by the blow of the piercing weapon, to have changed itself into the nature of suffering pain? On the contrary, the Apostle, speaking with Christ speaking in him and recalling the work of our salvation through the Lord, describes Christ’s death in such a way that He strips Himself of flesh, disgraces the powers with confidence, and triumphs over them in Himself (2 Corinthians 13:3).

If there is necessity in His passion, and it is not the gift of your salvation; if on the cross there is the pain of piercing rather than the fastening of the decree [Note: Vatican Basilica codex: “by which [decree] death is written against you.”] in which death is written against you; if in death there is the force of death rather than, through God’s power, the stripping off of flesh; if, finally, death itself is something other than the disgrace of the powers, confidence, and triumph—then attribute weakness, if necessity and nature are there, if force, distrust, and disgrace are there.

But if, on the contrary, these things are proclaimed in the sacrament of the passion, what madness, I ask, is it to reject the faith of apostolic teaching, alter the meaning of religion, and drag all this into the disgrace of a weak nature [Note: The printed editions, except Paris, read: “drag into the weakness and disgrace of nature.”]—all that is will and sacrament, power and confidence and triumph?

It is indeed triumph: to be sought for the cross and yet not be restrained when offering oneself; to stand before the sentence of death, yet from there to sit at the right hand of Power; to be fixed with nails, yet to pray for persecutors; to drink vinegar, yet to consummate the sacrament; to be counted among the wicked, yet to bestow paradise; to be raised upon the wood, yet to make the earth tremble; to hang upon the cross, yet to make the sun and day flee; [Note: Erasmus and Lipsius read “to drive away”; and then, in place of “to rise God,” they substituted “to rise.” Finally, the latter reading was preferred in the last Paris edition, against the other books. Hilary says that God rises in the manner in which above he teaches that Christ, even according to His humanity, is God after the resurrection.] to leave the body, yet to summon souls back into bodies; to be buried dead, yet to rise as God; according to humanity to suffer all things weak for us, yet according to God to triumph in all these things.

### 49. They Object That He Was Forsaken. What They Accomplish by It: Nothing

There remains for us still, as the heretics suppose, a great and weighty declaration of admitted weakness, especially uttered in the Lord’s own words, when He says: “My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46). Is it understood as the protest of a most grievous complaint: that He complains of having been forsaken and surrendered to weakness?

But this is the violent presumption of an impious interpretation, which it forces upon itself throughout every kind of the Lord’s sayings: that He who hastens to death, who is to be glorified through it, who after it is to sit at the right hand of Power, should in these many causes of blessedness have feared to die, and for that reason complain that He was deserted by His God to the necessity of dying—when, by undergoing death, He was to abide among those blessed realities!

50. Their various inventions concerning the union of the Word and the man.—Indeed, as though along a road prepared for them toward this irreligion, heretical minds press on by arguing either that God the Word wholly failed into the soul of the body, so that Jesus Christ, the Son of Man, was not also the Son of God; or that God the Word failed from himself while he gives life to the body by performing the soul’s function; or that Christ was not at all born a man, because the Word of God dwelt in him only in the manner of a prophetic spirit. But the error of this ridiculous perversity extends itself into a bolder impiety: namely, that Jesus Christ was not Christ before he was born of Mary; since he was not born as what he already was, but only then began to be what he was born as.

[Note: The author of this erroneous opinion is, as we have already said, not Eutyches or Apollinarius, but Arius; Theodoret testifies to this, *Haereticarum fabularum*, book V, chapter 11. It was condemned by the Roman council convened against Apollinarius through the agency of Pope Damasus, in Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, book V, chapters 10–11; and earlier by the Alexandrian council of A.D. 362, in Athanasius, *Letter to the Antiochenes*.]

[Note: Although this view conflicts with the preceding one, it is nevertheless defended by the same persons. Gregory Nazianzen observes of the Apollinarians, *Oration* LII, that they contradict themselves and dare to discuss the divinity only among trusted disciples.]

[Note: In the printed editions: “began to exist.” *To exist* is absent from the manuscripts. Book VII, no. 7, teaches that this was the invention of Ebion and later of Photinus; no one doubts it.]

Thus there is also added the further fault that God the Word, like some part of God’s powers, extending himself by a certain continuous stretching, dwelt in that man who began from Mary, and endowed him with the powers of divine operation, though he lived by the movement and nature of his own soul.

[Note: It is clear from *On the Synods*, no. 45, that Photinus held this view; and from book I, *On the Trinity*, no. 16, that he borrowed this doctrine from Sabellius. Pope Damasus pronounces an anathema upon it in Theodoret, book V, chapter 11, in these words: “We anathematize those who maintain that the Word of God is separated from the Father by extension and contraction, is without subsistence, and will have an end.”]

51. Consequent errors.—By this subtle and deadly doctrine, then, they are led into error: either that God the Word became the soul of the body by a transformation of his nature into weakness, and that the Word who is God ceased to be; or again, that that man was animated merely by the life-giving motion of a soul, through an external and bare union of nature, while the Word of God—that is, a kind of power of an extended utterance—dwelt in him. Thus in every way an entrance is opened to an utterly impious understanding: either God the Word failed into a soul and did not remain God the Word; or Christ did not exist at all before Mary’s childbirth, because Jesus Christ, a man only in the common sense of possessing soul and body, has his beginning of being man from the point at which he began to be man, while the power of an outwardly extended word strengthened him for mighty works. Now, abandoned again when the extension has been contracted by God the Word, he cries: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” Or else, when he was transformed from the nature of God the Word into the soul of the body, he had used the Father’s help in all things but now, destitute of it and surrendered to death, laments his loneliness and accuses him of abandoning him. In every way, therefore, there arises the deadly danger of a deceived faith, if either weakness of nature is thought to be signified in God the Word by this complaint, or if God the Word did not exist at all, since Mary’s childbirth alone is the beginning of Jesus Christ.

[Note: “Therefore” is absent from Bad., Er., and the Colbert and German manuscripts. Some others read: “These things, therefore, by this …”]

[Note: Bad.: “into the nature of his weakness.” Er. and Lips.: “by transformation of his nature into the nature of weakness.”]

[Note: Only the printed editions add “God.” Above, no. 49, we read: “or God the Word failed from himself,” not “the Word of God”; the same wording occurs below.]

[Note: Supply “dwelt.” The Word dwelt in the man through a bare nature—that is, one not joined to him or substantially united with him, and therefore merely external—if he was in Christ only as he was in the prophets.]

[Note: Bad.: “that he might be man.” Other editions: “that he might become man.” Corrected from the manuscripts.]

52. The true faith opposed to heresy.—But amid these impious and feeble opinions, the faith of the Church, instructed by apostolic teaching, knows a birth in Christ but does not know a beginning. It knows an economy or dispensation, but does not know division. It does not allow Jesus Christ to be such that Jesus is not himself Christ; nor does it separate the Son of Man from the Son of God, lest perhaps the Son of God not also be understood as the Son of Man. It does not absorb the Son of God into the Son of Man. Nor does it divide Christ by a threefold faith, whose woven garment was not torn apart (John 19:23), so as to cut Jesus Christ into Word, soul, and body; nor, conversely, does it absorb God the Word into soul and body. The Word is wholly God to him; Christ is wholly man to him. It preserves this one thing in the mystery of its confession: it believes Christ to be nothing other than Jesus, and proclaims Jesus to be nothing other than Christ.

[Note: We should prefer “divides.” I would ask those to note this passage who suppose that Hilary thought the divinity of the Word withdrew from Christ when he cried, “My God, my God,” etc. For since he says these things, on the occasion of those very words, against those who either confuse or separate Christ’s two natures, he would be wholly unjust if he himself understood them to be separated from those same words.]

[Note: Here *discern* signifies separation; but in book IX, no. 6, only a distinction of natures.]

[Note: In the old Colbert manuscript: “God.”]

[Note: That is, the Church believes the natures of God the Word and of man to be so united in Christ that the Word is wholly in him and he is wholly man. Pope Leo explains this thus, in Letter now numbered XCVII, to the monks of Palestine: “It makes no difference from which substance Christ is named, since, with the unity of person remaining inseparably, he is both wholly Son of Man on account of the flesh and wholly Son of God on account of the divinity one with the Father.” Although theologians later preferred to apply *whole* (*totum*) to natures and *wholly* (*totus*) to the person—as Hilary himself does above, no. 22, because he is wholly Son of Man and wholly Son of God—this rule had plainly not yet been established in his age, even from this passage. Nor does this conflict with book IX, no. 6, where, considering not the unity of person but the distinction of natures, he rightly teaches that man must be distinguished from God. Likewise, when distinguishing Christ’s lowly condition from his glorious one, he rightly says that only in the latter does he obtain to be wholly man and wholly God.]

[Note: Printed editions after Erasmus insert here: “and God the Word”—a gloss absent from Bad. and the manuscripts. Hilary understands Christ as the Word and Jesus as the man assumed by the Word; just as above he refers *whole* to the person, so now he refers *other* to the person.]

[Col. 0385A]

53. In divine matters the human mind fails. It is dulled when it seeks to see more than is granted.—I do not fail to recognize how greatly the majesty of the heavenly mystery obstructs the weakness of human understanding, so that we cannot readily utter these things in words, judge them by perception, or even encompass them in mind. But the Apostle, knowing this to be arduous and exceedingly difficult for earthly nature, writes thus to his lawful son in the faith, one nourished from childhood on the sacred writings, lest we conceive the effectiveness of divine things by our judgment—as though it were keener for understanding than God is mighty for accomplishing:

“As I urged you to remain at Ephesus when I was going into Macedonia, so that you might charge certain persons not to teach differently, nor to give heed to myths and endless genealogies, which furnish questions rather than God’s edification which is in faith” (1 Tim. 1:3–4).

[Note: We restore *our* from Bad. and the manuscripts. Then, in place of *as though*, the Remigian and Theodorian manuscripts incorrectly have *so much*. The meaning is this: as though our judgment were proportionately keener for understanding as God is greater for accomplishing. Here and thereafter Eunomius’ boast seems to be restrained: according to Theodoret, *Haereticarum fabularum*, book IV, chapter 3, he boasted that he was ignorant of nothing in divine matters.]

[Note: The ancient Colbert manuscript reads: “when you were going into Macedonia.”]

He forbids the handling of genealogical discourse and the pursuit of myths of endless inquiry. But he teaches that God’s edification is in faith, so that reverence for God’s faithful omnipotence may set bounds to human modesty, and our weakness may not stretch itself out to behold those things which blunt the very faculty of beholding.

For if the power of concentrated light overwhelms those who merely gaze upon its brightness, so that whenever the keen gaze of curious contemplation investigates too intently the source of shining light, the nature of the eyes is driven back until the faculty of sight is deadened—and it happens that, by straining to see more, one does not see—what ought we to expect in the things of God and in the Sun of righteousness? Will not folly overtake those who wish to be overwise (*ὑπερφρονεῖν*)? Will not that very sharp light of understanding be occupied by the stupor of dull foolishness? For an inferior nature will not understand the cause of a superior nature; nor is the heavenly—that is, divine—reason subject to human comprehension. Whatever is subjected to a weak consciousness will remain within the condition of weakness.

Therefore God’s power surpasses the human mind. If weakness stretches itself toward it, it becomes weaker still, because it loses even what it possesses; for the higher nature of heavenly things has power to blunt it, since that very higher nature weakens, by its own encompassing greatness, all the stubborn striving that pursues it. Therefore, just as the sun must be seen only as it can be seen, and only so much light received as can be admitted, lest, if we desire to seek more, we obtain even less than we can; so heavenly reason must be understood only insofar as it permits itself to be understood, and sought only insofar as it has given itself to be apprehended, lest, if we are not content with the moderation of what is granted, we lose what has been granted. There is, then, in God something that can be perceived—indeed there is, if only you are willing to perceive what is possible. For just as there is in the sun something for you to see, if you are willing to see what you can, while you lose what you can see by straining after what you cannot; so in the things of God you have something to understand, if you are willing to understand what you can. But if you hope beyond your capacity, you will not be able even to do what you had been able to do.

[Note: Some manuscripts with Bad. and Er.: “do not have the nature [for seeing].”]

[Note: Martin manuscript: “to comprehend beyond.” Greek: *ὑπερφρονεῖν*, “to think beyond measure; to be overwise.”]

[Note: Sopor.]

[Note: One Colbert manuscript, another Sorbonne manuscript, and Martin: “of the superior nature.” Another Colbert manuscript and the German manuscript: “of the latter nature.”]

[Note: Martin’s exemplar: “as much as it admits; for if we desire more …” Then Paris, with the Vatican basic manuscript: “to seek.” Other editions: “to look upon.” In some manuscripts: “to await.” In most, with no different meaning, “to expect”; and shortly afterward all have “to be expected,” where printed editions have “to be sought.”]

[Note: “To be sought.”]

[Note: Vatican basic manuscript with the Colbert and Sorbonne manuscripts: “to perceive.” Martin: “to regard”; and shortly after, with the Vatican basic and Remigian manuscripts: “if only you are willing [to perceive] what you can.”]

54. In Christ’s own temporal birth man is blind.—I shall not yet take up the mystery of his timeless birth; that discussion belongs in its proper place. For the present, my subject is the mystery of the assumed flesh. I ask these searchers into heavenly secrets to explain, according to their own nature, the mystery of Christ born from a virgin. Whence, they will say, did conception come to the virgin? Whence childbirth to the virgin? What cause of generative origins will they argue this to be? What grew together within the recesses of the maternal womb? Whence the body? Whence the man?

And further, after these matters, what does it mean that the Son of Man descended from heaven while remaining in heaven? For according to bodily causes, descending and remaining are not the same: the former is a change of departure, the latter the undisturbed state of remaining. The infant cries, yet he is in heaven; the boy grows, yet he remains God in fullness. Again, when he ascends where he was before, and he descends who remains, by what faculty of human understanding can this be contained? For the Lord says: “What if you see the Son of Man ascending where he was before?” (John 6:63). The Son of Man ascends where he was before: what mind can comprehend this? The Son of Man who is in heaven descends from heaven: what reasoning can accomplish this? “The Word became flesh”: what words can speak this? Flesh becomes the Word—that is, man becomes God; and he who is man is in heaven, while he who is God is from heaven. He ascends while descending; yet he descends without descending. He is what he was, and what he is, he was not. We run through causes, and reason fails us; we discern the reason, yet do not understand the causes. But if we understand Jesus Christ thus, we shall know; if we think ourselves wiser than this, we shall not know.

[Note: Printed editions: “of descent.” With the better manuscripts, “of departure” is preferable.]

[Note: Gregory Nazianzen develops this same argument more fully in *Oration* XXXV, no. 88 and following.]

[Note: In an ancient Colbert manuscript: “he does not ascend.” This kind of argument is especially forceful against those who deny that the Word of God is substantially joined to the flesh, or who confuse the Word with it.]

[Note: “We fail.”]

[Note: Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “Jesus, thus understanding, we know … we do not know.” Hilary’s meaning seems to be this: Catholics who understand Christ to be Jesus—that is, both God and man—do not struggle with the questions set forth, just as Hilary himself does not struggle above, no. 16, with the question of the ascent and descent of the Son of Man. But heretics, who think more highly than they ought, cannot extricate themselves from them.]

55. The mystery of Christ’s tears.—Again, how great is the mystery of this saying and deed: that Christ weeps and, through anguish of mind, lets tears flow from his eyes (Luke 19:41)! Whence came these infirmities of his soul, so that sorrow’s grief draws weeping from the body? What bitterness of circumstances, what unbearable pain, dissolved into tears the Son of Man who descended from heaven? Next, who was it that wept in him? God the Word, or the soul of his body? For although the function of tears belongs to the body, yet some grief of the mind, in the body’s service, as it were sweats them out. Then what reason did he have for weeping? Did he follow impious and parricidal Jerusalem with the due honour of tears, because it was about to suffer nothing worthy of the slaughter of so many prophets and apostles and of the death of its own Lord? And, as the calamities of human deaths are mourned, was he grieved by the fall of this ruined and desperate people? What, I ask, is this mystery of weeping? The soul that is sorrowful weeps. But did this soul send the prophets? Did it so often wish to gather Jerusalem’s children beneath the covering of its wings as a hen does her chicks (Matt. 23:37)? Yet grief does not belong to God the Word, nor tears to the Spirit. Nor can it belong to the soul to have done anything before the body. And yet there is no doubt that Jesus Christ truly wept.

[Note: Not “anguish,” as above.]

[Note: The word *his own*, omitted in printed editions, is restored from the manuscripts. It is added both lest the soul be thought a part of the Word—an opinion touched on in no. 57—and to maintain that Christ’s body belonged to God.]

[Note: Lips. and Paris: “yet the soul.” Most manuscripts more correctly: “yet the mind,” namely, grief. Nor is the reading of the Vatican basic and Martin manuscripts pleasing: “yet the soul … as though it sweated them out by a certain grief.”]

[Note: He seems to say: He wept who sent the prophets, who wished to gather Jerusalem’s children beneath his wings as a hen does. But Christ’s soul did not send the prophets, for it did not yet exist; as he says below: “Nor can it belong to the soul to have done anything before the body,” that is, before it was united with the body. Therefore the soul itself did not weep. Yet the Word did not weep, and tears do not come forth from the body unless sorrow has first arisen in the soul. And nevertheless Christ truly wept. These tears are therefore wondrous. The same argument can be drawn from Christ’s sufferings; it is especially effective against those who divided Christ. Against them Gregory Nazianzen says, *Oration* LI, no. 7: “If anyone introduces two sons, one from God and the Father and the other from a mother, rather than one and the same Son, let him fall from adoption as sons,” etc. It presses no less strongly those who confused Christ. That Hilary is concerned with both parties is sufficiently clear from nos. 48–49.]

[Note: Thus with great agreement among the manuscripts. But Bad. and Er.: “covering”; Lips. and Paris: “coverlet.”]

56. What he wept for in Lazarus: whether that weeping was God’s, the soul’s, or the body’s.—Lazarus too was wept for with the same reality of tears (John 11:35). And I ask first: what was wept for in Lazarus? Certainly not his death, which was not unto death and was for God’s glory. For the Lord says: “This sickness is not unto death, but for the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it” (John 11:5). Therefore a death which was the occasion for glorifying God did not bring sadness for weeping.

Nor was there any necessity for weeping because he had been absent when Lazarus died. For he himself plainly says: “Lazarus has died, and for your sake I am glad that I was not there, so that you may believe” (John 11:14–15). His absence, then, had no cause for tears, since it contributed to the apostles’ faith; for though absent, by divine knowledge he had declared the sick man’s death. Thus no necessity for weeping remains; and yet he wept. Yet I ask: to whom will that weeping be attributed—to God, to the soul, or to the body? The body by itself does not have tears which it pours forth in response to the sorrow of a grieving soul. Still less can it be that God wept, he who was to be glorified in Lazarus. Nor can it belong to the soul to call Lazarus from the tomb, and, by the soul’s command and power joined to the body, to recall into its dead body the soul now released from it. Does he who is to be glorified grieve? Does he who is about to give life weep? It does not belong to the giver of life to weep, nor to the one to be glorified to grieve; and yet he who wept gave life, and grieved.

[Note: “Had foretold.”]

[Note: Thus the manuscripts. Printed editions: “pour forth,” less well. The body indeed possesses tears that it may pour forth, but it does not pour them forth unless the soul is in pain. “For what does flesh by itself, without the soul, either suffer or desire?” says Augustine, *City of God*, book XIV, chapter 15. Again, our Hilary, on Psalm LXVIII, no. 12, affirms the reality of Christ’s tears and explains that they were shed because of the unbelief of the human race.]

[Note: Why does it not belong to the soul, except because this is the work of divine omnipotence? Similar is Gregory of Nyssa, *Oration* IV against Eunomius, p. 589, quoted by Theodoret, *Dialogue* III: “Human nature does not give Lazarus life, nor does the impassible power weep for him lying dead; rather, the tear belongs properly to the man, but life belongs to him who is truly Life. Human poverty does not feed many thousands; omnipotent power does not run to the fig tree. Who is wearied by the labour of the journey, and who sustains the whole world effortlessly by a word? What is the splendour of glory, and what is nailed to the cross? What form is struck by blows in the Passion, and what form has been glorified from eternity?”]

[Note: At last sorrow is affirmed of Christ. Thus, where it was denied, it is clear that this was only an attempt to demonstrate, by assuming the adversaries’ position, that sorrow did not befit Christ.]

57. Who in Christ lays down and takes up the soul: the body or the Word?—We do not mention a few things out of many because of any necessity arising from lack of material or ignorance of the sayings, but so that a concise argument may commend a complete exposition. The Lord performs and does what is not known according to conscious understanding—what is neither unknown nor knowable—because there is truth in the facts and mystery in the power by which they are done. As we shall show plainly from what he says:

“For this reason the Father loves me, because I lay down my soul, that I may take it again. No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of myself. I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it again. This command I received from the Father” (John 10:17–18).

He lays down his soul of himself; and I ask, who lays it down? For we do not doubt that Christ is God the Word; nor again are we ignorant that the Son of Man consists of soul and body, as the angel confirms to Joseph: “Rise, take the child and his mother, and go into the land of Israel; for those who sought the child’s life [soul] are dead” (Matt. 2:20). Whose soul, then, is this? The body’s or God’s? If it is the body’s, what power has the body, which is animated into life by the soul’s movement? Then did the body receive any command, when without a soul it is dull and dead? But if someone thinks that God the Word lays down his own soul in order to take it up again, let him show God the Word to have died—that is, to have remained without perception and life, like a dead body—so that he might again take up his own soul in order to live again and be given life again by it.

[Note: Printed editions: “said.” The manuscripts more correctly read “does.” For he now passes from deeds to sayings and proves the former from the latter.]

[Note: Vatican basic manuscript: “again, and in the truth.” This is not satisfactory. Hilary means that the reality of things done by Christ is apparent, but the power by which they were done is concealed. Thus above, “what is not known according to conscious understanding”: it is known as to the deed done, but unknown as to the rationale of the deed.]

[Note: Printed editions: “from my Father.” *My* is absent from the manuscripts here, as in book IX, no. 12.]

58. God does not possess a soul.—Nor will anyone attribute to God a rational soul, although it is frequently written that God’s soul hates sabbaths and new moons, and that it is pleased in certain things (Isa. 1:14; 42:1). But this is customarily mentioned with the same figurative meaning by which hands, eyes, fingers, arm, and heart are numbered among the features of the incorporeal God. For since, according to the Lord’s saying, a spirit does not have flesh and bones (Luke 24:39), no members of bodily parts suited to solidity belong to him who is and does not change (Mal. 3:6); rather, his simple and blessed nature remains one whole, which is all that he is. Therefore God is not animated into life, in bodily fashion, by the function of an inward soul; rather, he himself lives as life to himself.

[Note: Thus the manuscripts. Lips. and Paris read: “the soul of God … is written”; and other printed editions later read: “are mentioned in the incorporeal God.”]

[Note: In the Verona codex: *numinias*. Greek is sometimes written *νουμηνίας*, “new moons,” as in Colossians 2:16.]

[Col. 0390A]

59. God neither lays down a soul nor takes it up, and the body does not take itself up.—And how does he lay down his soul, or take it up once laid down? Or what is the rationale of this command? God, then, neither lays down a soul to death nor takes it up to life. Nor does the body have a command to take itself up, because neither does it take itself up by its own power. For it was said concerning the temple of his body: “Destroy this temple, and after three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19). Therefore God raises the temple of his body. And who lays down the soul in order to take it up again? The body does not take itself up, but is raised by God. Now that which is raised is dead, and that which lives does not lay down its soul. Therefore God neither died nor was buried; and yet it was said by him: “For in pouring this ointment upon my body, she did it for my burial” (Matt. 26:12). What was poured upon his body was done for burying him; and it is not the same thing for him to be himself and for a body to be his own. Nor is it one and the same thing for something to be done for burying him and for his body to be anointed; nor does it accord for the body to be his own and for him himself to be buried.

[Note: Lips. and Paris add here “a soul.”]

[Note: “I will raise [it].”]

[Note: Martin manuscript: “I will build it.” Some others: “I will raise it.”]

[Note: Our manuscript consistently reads “to be anointed.”]

[Note: In the older Colbert, Martin, Corbie, German, and other manuscripts: “to be anointed.” Others also read elsewhere “may anoint” or “may be anointed.”]

60. On what the solution of the proposed question depends.—But the understanding of this divine mystery consists in this: not to be ignorant of God whom you know to be man, and not to fail to know the man whom you recognize as God; not to divide Jesus Christ because “the Word became flesh”; not to think buried him whom you understand to have raised, nor to doubt that he has raised him whom you do not dare deny was not buried. For Jesus Christ was buried because he also died. But he died who spoke as one about to die: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Mark 15:34). Yet the one who said this also said: “Truly I say to you, today you will be with me in Paradise” (Luke 23:43); and while promising Paradise, he cried in a loud voice: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit.” And having said this, he expired (ibid., v. 46).

[Note: Printed editions: “But this is the mystery of divine understanding.” It is corrected from the manuscripts, as though Hilary, now beginning to set out his own meaning, said: The understanding of the whole mystery, inexplicable under the adversaries’ view, lies in recognizing two natures in Christ in one person, to whom the properties of both united natures are attributed.]

[Note: “Whom you understand to have raised, do not doubt to have raised.”]

[Note: Bad. with the Martin, Corbie, Vatican, and several other manuscripts reads: “not not to think buried.” Then the same edition with Er. and Lips. reads: “whom you understand to have raised,” to which most manuscripts add “to have been”; Martin manuscript: “whom you understand to have risen,” and then, “do not doubt to have risen,” etc., where again all printed editions have “do not doubt to have raised.” Later Er., Lips., and Paris omit the negative particle before *buried*. If the manuscripts supported them, one could read: “not not to think buried him whom you understand to have raised; not to doubt he has raised him whom you do not dare deny was not buried,” so that two natures in one person would be indicated. But because all manuscripts have *buried* without a negative particle in the final position, the older Remigian, Colbert, Vienna, German, and other manuscripts are more consistent in the remaining words. From them it follows, so far as we understand, that Christ, as God, was not buried, since he raised his own body—something not fitting for one who was buried; and beyond doubt he was the author of the resurrection of his body, he who cannot be denied to have been unburied. For Jesus was buried, not according to the nature which raised the body, but according to that in which he died. As was said in the preceding section, God neither died nor was buried. How far, moreover, was he from thinking that the Word’s divinity was separated from Christ’s dead body, when even here, where his death and burial are discussed, he teaches so plainly and consistently that Christ is not to be divided?]

61. Against those who divide Christ into three, or reduce him to one.—Various questions about Christ’s death.—You, then, who either divide Christ into Word, soul, and body, or reduce the whole Christ, God the Word, to a mere man of common nature, reveal to us this great mystery of godliness, which was manifested in flesh (1 Tim. 3:16): what spirit Christ gave up; who commended his own spirit into the Father’s hands; who was in Paradise on that same day; and who complained that he was abandoned by God. For the complaint of one abandoned is the weakness of one dying; but the promise of Paradise is the kingdom of the living God. The commending of the spirit is the confidence of one commending it; the giving up of the spirit is the departure of one dying.

I ask, therefore: who dies? Surely the one who gives up the spirit. Then who gives up the spirit? Certainly the one who commended his own spirit to the Father. And if the same one who commended it died in giving up the spirit, I ask whether the body commends the soul, or whether God commends the soul of the body. For *spirit* frequently signifies the soul, as is not doubtful even from this very fact that Jesus, about to die, gave up the spirit. If, then, anyone thinks that the soul is commended by the body—to one that is being dissolved yet lives, to one that is perishable yet eternal, to one that is to be raised yet remains—and if it is unquestionable that the same one who commended the spirit to the Father was on that same day in Paradise with the thief, I ask whether he, having been received in the tomb, remained in Paradise, or whether, while remaining in Paradise, he complained that he was abandoned by God.

[Note: Bad. and Er.: “whether the body [commends] the soul?”—a pointless repetition. Lipsius then, restoring from Erasmus’ margin “or God [commends] the body,” omitted *soul*, and it was not restored in Paris. Here and in no. 55 Hilary says not simply “the soul” but “the soul of the body,” to avoid the absurd opinion he notes in no. 57, namely that the soul might be thought to belong to the Word. Then printed editions and most manuscripts read: “For by spirit.” With Corbie and Remigian manuscripts, “For *spirit*” is preferable. Since Hilary commonly understands Christ’s spirit to mean his divinity, if he had thought that the Word was separated from the dead body, he could easily have explained the giving up of the spirit as the departure of divinity. But what has already been said and what immediately follows allow no room whatever for suspicion of this view. Athanasius likewise, *On the Incarnation of Christ*, p. 630, explains the giving up of the spirit as the departure of the soul; and then rejects the view which some rather unwisely attribute to Hilary: no one, he says, has called expiration a transfer or migration of divinity, but rather the soul’s departure. “For if death came upon him after the departure of divinity, … then he obviously underwent his own death, not ours.”]

[Note: He calls it liable to corruption as well as dissolvable because it was soon to lack life. Yet above, no. 12, he maintains that the Holy One of the Lord would not see corruption.]

62. Solution.—For one and the same Lord Jesus Christ, the Word made flesh, signifies himself throughout all these things: when he signifies himself as abandoned unto death, he is man; but while he is man, he reigns in Paradise as God; reigning in Paradise, as the Son of God he commends his spirit to the Father; but as the Son of Man he gives up to death the spirit commended to the Father. What insult, then, do we now offer to the mystery? In the one complaining, you have one who is abandoned to death because he is man; in the one who dies, you have one who declares that he reigns in Paradise because he is God. Why do we retain only for impiety what he spoke to make us understand his death, while we keep silent about what the same one professed to show his immortality? If this is the voice and utterance of the same one who complains that he is abandoned and declares that he reigns, by what reasoning of unbelief do we divide our faith so that he who died at the same time may not also reign, when he himself testified both things concerning himself, both commending the spirit and expiring? But if the same one who commends the spirit and gives it up both reigns while dying and reigns while dead, then in the mystery of the Son of Man and the Son of God we have the reigning one dying and the dying one reigning.

[Note: Paris with an old Colbert manuscript: “For one …”]

[Note: Thus most manuscripts. Some with the printed editions: “You have [him] complaining …”]

63. Epilogue.—Let every irreligious unbelief, incapable of the divine mystery, cease (compare Ambrose, book X, *On Luke*, no. 56): unbelief which does not know that Christ wept not for himself but for us, so that, by assuming the emotions of ordinary human experience, he himself might testify to the reality of the man he assumed; which does not know that Christ died not for himself but for our life, so that through the death of the immortal God the life of mortals might be renewed; which does not understand both the complaint of one abandoned and the confidence of one reigning, so that our understanding may recognize both the man who died and God who reigns. For the one dying and reigning is not another; nor is the one commending the spirit and expiring another; nor is the one buried and rising another; nor is the descending and ascending one anything other than one.

36664. **Christ Is Undivided. This Escapes the Wise of the World.**—Hear faith instructed in apostolic teaching, not by the perception of the flesh but by the gift of the Spirit, when it speaks to Greeks seeking wisdom and Jews demanding signs: “But we preach Christ Jesus crucified: to the Jews indeed a stumbling-block, and to the Gentiles foolishness; but to those who are called, Jews and Greeks, Christ Jesus the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1:23–24). Is Christ divided, so that one is Jesus crucified and another Christ, the power and wisdom of God? Yet this is both a stumbling-block to the Jews and foolishness to the Gentiles; whereas for us Christ Jesus is God’s power and God’s wisdom—but a wisdom not known by the world or understood by the wise of this age. And learn how little it was understood from the same blessed Apostle, who says: “But we speak the wisdom of God, hidden in a mystery, which God ordained before the ages for our glory, which none of the rulers of this age knew; for had they known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:7–8).

> **[Note: Col. 0392D]** The Chartres manuscript has “none of the rulers,” and shortly afterward, “the Lord of majesty,” rather than “of glory.”

[Col. 0393A] Does the Apostle not know that this wisdom of God is hidden in a mystery and unknowable by the rulers of this age? Does he divide Christ, so that one is the Lord of majesty and another Jesus crucified? Rather, he contradicts this utterly foolish and impious opinion, saying: “For I judged that I should know nothing among you except Christ Jesus, and him crucified” (ibid., v. 2).

65. **Against Those Who Divide Christ: Things Apparently Opposed in Him Are Reconciled.**—The Apostle knows nothing else, nor judges that he knows anything else; but we, weak both in understanding and still weaker in faith, cut up, divide, and duplicate Christ Jesus—presumptuous arbiters of mysteries and slanderers of the hidden sacrament. For to us one is Christ crucified, another the wisdom of God; one is buried, another descends;

> **[Note: Col. 0393D]** One Colbert manuscript and another Sorbonne manuscript here add, “and another ascends.” Three Vatican manuscripts and most later ones read, “another descends to the underworld.” The words “to the underworld” are absent from the older manuscripts, although the discussion here concerns Christ’s descent to the dead. The heretics discussed here could especially be said above to divide Christ into three parts with respect to Christ’s death, since they placed the flesh in the tomb, the soul in hell, and the Word in paradise.

and another is Son of Man, [Col. 0393B] another Son of God. We presume to teach those who do not understand, rebuke those who do not know, and correct the sayings of God; and we do not deign to believe as the Apostle does: “Who shall bring a charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies; who is he that condemns? Christ Jesus who died—indeed rather, who also rose again—who is at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us” (Rom. 8:33–34).

> **[Note: Col. 0393D]** In the Chartres manuscript: “Who, he says, shall accuse God’s elect?” and shortly afterward, “intercedes,” in place of “makes request.”

Is another interceding for us than he who is at God’s right hand?

> **[Note: Col. 0393C]** Earlier editions read, “or who is the right hand in God.”

Or is he who is at God’s right hand not himself the one who rose again? Or is the one who rose again not the same one who died? Or is the one who died not the same one who condemns? Or is the one who condemns not the same God who justifies? Let us then, if we may, separate from the justifying God the condemning Christ; from the condemning Christ, the dead Christ; from the dead [Col. 0393C] Christ, the Christ seated at the right hand, praying for us. If, therefore, Christ is one in all these things, neither is the dead Christ one and the buried Christ another, nor is the one descending to the underworld another and the one ascending to heaven another, according to that saying of the Apostle: “Now, what does ‘he ascended’ mean, except that he also descended into the lower regions of the earth? He who descended is the one who also ascended above all the heavens, that he might fill all things” (Eph. 4:9–10).

> **[Note: Col. 0393C]** “He is the one who also ascended”; so also below.

How far will we extend the babbling ignorance of our impiety, so as to profess that what is hidden in the mystery of God can be explained by us? He who descended is himself also he who ascended. Is there any doubt [Col. 0394A] that Jesus Christ, the man who rose from the dead and ascended above all the heavens, is at God’s right hand? Will it be said that the body which lay in the tomb descended into hell?

> **[Note: Col. 0393D]** The same manuscript has “could,” not “will be said.” In the same way Athanasius, in his Letter to Epictetus, refutes those who confused the Word with the flesh.

If, therefore, he who descended

> **[Note: Col. 0393C]** “He also ascended.”

is himself also he who ascended, and it is neither believed that the body descended into hell nor doubted that the body, rising from the dead, ascended into heaven: what remains here except faith in the hidden sacrament, unknown to the world and to the rulers of this age? Thus, since the descending and ascending one is one and the same, Jesus Christ too is one for us: both Son of God and Son of Man, both God the Word and man as flesh, both suffering and dying and buried and rising again and received into heaven and seated

> **[Note: Col. 0394C]** At the right hand of God.

at God’s right hand—having in himself, one and the same, by the dispensation [Col. 0394B] and by nature, in the form of God and in the form of a servant, without any

67. **The Rule for Apprehending Christ’s Mysteries.**—The only-begotten God indeed suffered what human beings can suffer; but let us use the Apostle’s faith and statement: “For I delivered to you first of all that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, and that he was buried, and that he rose again on the third day according to the Scriptures” (1 Cor. 15:3–4). He did not employ bare definitions of words, providing an occasion for error; rather, in speaking of death and resurrection he admonished us to confess their manner, not only by the names of the events but also by the force of the Scriptures. Thus our understanding of his death was to be that which was contained in the signification of the Scriptures.

For, not leaving weak thoughts and scrupulous slanders against faith unchecked, he added this single qualification to the proclamation of death and resurrection: *according to the Scriptures*. This was so that, tossed about by the wind of empty disputations or hindered by the futile subtleties of deceptive questions, we might not become weak; but that unimpaired faith might always return to this harbor of its religion: believing and confessing the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ, Son of Man and Son of God, according to the Scriptures. # BOOK ELEVEN

At its beginning Hilary explains that among the Arians faith is not one; and that, although Christ can no longer be unknown as true God and Son of God, they nevertheless maintain that he was created and is God in name alone, while they seize upon the dispensation of his assumed body to dishonor [Col. 0398D] his divinity. He then refutes objections drawn from [Col. 0399A] words which apply to Christ after the glory of the resurrection. For when he then says, “I ascend to my Father and your Father, to my God,” and so forth, he will show that he spoke of the nature according to which he has brothers; just as the Prophet spoke of the nature according to which they are his partners: “God, your God, has anointed you above your partners.”

Next he explains the Apostle’s words from which they think they can prove that Christ, as a servant, is to be subjected to the Father, that he will surrender the authority of his kingdom, and that he will undergo an abolition of nature. Yet with the Apostle *end* denotes perfection and an immutable state, not abolition; nor does the handing over of the kingdom deprive the Son of the power to reign any more than the Father is deprived of the ownership of those things which he handed over to the Son; and finally, that subjection belongs to dispensation, not servitude. He then explains the manner and causes [Col. 0399B] of this subjection and declares that it benefits neither God, to whom nothing is lacking and nothing accrues, nor the only-begotten Son, who is equally immutable, but us alone.

It should not be passed over that Jerome, when the presbyter Amandus asked him what Paul meant by the words, “For he must reign until he has put all his enemies,” and so forth, replied in Letter 147: “I am surprised that you wished to ask me this, since Saint Hilary, Bishop of Poitiers, completed his eleventh book against the Arians with this question and its solution.”

1. **As There Is One Lord, So There Is One Faith in the One God. Father and Son Are One God.**—The Apostle, treating in many ways the whole and complete mystery of evangelical faith, spoke also among his other precepts of divine knowledge to the Ephesians: “As you also were called in one hope of your calling. One Lord, one faith,

> **[Note: Col. 0399C]** One baptism.

one baptism, one God and Father of all,

> **[Note: Col. 0399D]** We have removed from here, as also from Book VIII, §34, “who is above all,” since those words occur in only one later Colbert manuscript.

and through all and in us all” (Eph. 4:4 ff.). For he did not abandon us to ambiguous and wandering pursuits of indefinite doctrine, nor did he allow human minds to be committed to uncertain opinions,

> **[Note: Col. 0399D]** The Vatican Basel manuscript reads “committed.” Shortly afterward, the Leipzig and Paris editions incorrectly add *in* to “freedom.”

but, by barriers established and set in opposition by himself, he enclosed the freedom of understanding and will; so that he would not permit us to think except what he himself had preached, since, by the determinate ordinance of immutable faith, it was not permitted to believe in one way and then another.

Therefore, in preaching to us one Lord, [Col. 0400A] he mentions one faith; then, in mentioning one faith of the one Lord, he also shows one

> **[Note: Col. 0399C]** *Baptism* occurs here and consistently throughout this book in our manuscript.

> **[Note: Col. 0399D]** Thus the manuscripts, more elegantly than the printed editions: “in the Lord there should also be one baptism.”

And because the entire mystery both of baptism and of faith lies, as in one Lord, so also in one God, he concluded the consummation of our hope with the confession of one God: so that one baptism and one faith might belong to one God just as they belong to one Lord. For each is one, not by union but by property: since it is proper to each to be one—proper to the Father to be what he is as Father, and proper to the Son to be what he is as Son. And the fact that each is one in his own property is a mystery of unity applying to both: for Christ, the one Lord, cannot take away from God the Father that he is Lord; and God the Father, the one God, is not understood to deny to the one Lord Christ that he is God. For if, by reason of God’s being one, it does not appear also proper to Christ to be God, then it must likewise be understood, by reason of Christ’s being the one Lord, that it does not belong to God [Col. 0400B] to be Lord—if what is one is not the signification of a mystery, but an exception that excludes union.

Therefore, as there are one Lord and one God the Father, so there are one baptism and one faith.

bears witness to him; the tombs of Apostles and Martyrs speak of him through the working of powers; the power of his name proves him; unclean spirits

confess him; the groans of punished demons resound with him. Yet in all these things there is a dispensation of his power. ### 5. Everything that belongs to the Father belongs to the Son as Image

Untaught by apostolic or evangelical preaching, they exalt the majesty of God the Father for the purposes of appropriating it to their impious profession—not with the reverence of faith, but by the artifice of impiety. While they declare that all things belonging to his nature are incomparable, they affirm, by excluding comparison, that the only-begotten God is of a degenerate and infirm nature: God, that is to say, the living Image of the living God, the most complete Form of the blessed nature, and the only-begotten Birth of the unbegotten substance. Unless this Birth possesses the perfect glory of the Father’s blessedness and represents the full form of the whole nature, it is not true Image.

> [Note: Col. 0402D] Thus the manuscript. But the printed editions read: “has birth and … represents the form.”

But if the only-begotten God is the Image of the unbegotten God, the truth of a perfect and complete nature is present in him; and by this he is made to be the Image of the Truth. The Father is powerful; but if the Son is weak, he is no longer the Image of the Powerful One. The Father is good; but if the Son belongs to a divinity of another kind, the nature of evil does not render the Image of the Good. The Father is incorporeal; if the Son, according to the Spirit, is bodily circumscribed, then one who is bodily is no longer the Form of the incorporeal one. See Book VIII, §48. The Father is ineffable; if speech comprehends the Son, the narrable nature lies outside the Image of the unutterable nature. The Father is true God; if the Son exists in false godhood, then the false one is no longer the Image of the True One.

The Apostle does not proclaim him to be an Image in part or a Form by portion; rather, he says that he is the Image of the invisible God and the Form of God (Col. 1:15).

> [Note: Col. 0403D] Only the Paris edition reads “of the invisible God.” This refers either to the celebrated passage in Philippians 2:6, “who, being in the form of God,” or to Hebrews 1:3, where Christ is proclaimed the figure of God’s substance. Shortly afterwards, manuscript Martin has “birth” in place of “divinity.”

The Apostle could not proclaim the nature of divinity in the Son of God more expressly than by saying that Christ is the Image of the invisible God with respect to that which is invisible in God: certainly, in a visible substance, he would not represent the Image of the invisible nature.

> [Note: Col. 0403D] Three sound manuscripts read “than this,” omitting *to*. The Vatican-Basilican manuscript, together with one Colbert and another Sorbonne manuscript, reads “than to that which is invisible.”

> [Note: Col. 0403D] “In an inconspicuous image.”

> [Note: Col. 0403D] In the Vatican-Basilican, Corbie, one Colbert, Sorbonne, and other manuscripts: “inconspicuous,” wrongly, unless with Martin, Colbert, and Sorbonne one subsequently reads, “he would not represent another image than that of the invisible nature”; in Martin alone, “represents.” But the sounder reading is that retained with the older Colbert manuscript, as well as the German, Carnot, and others. Here the familiar Arian argument is refuted: they proclaimed the Son visible, and therefore visible in nature, but the Father invisible, and thus declared the two to differ in nature on that ground.

### 6. They Turn What Belongs to Man into an Insult against the Word

The objections thus far raised have been answered by distinguishing the two natures.

But, as we have taught in the preceding books, they seize upon the dispensation of the assumed body in order to insult the divinity, and derive grounds for impiety from the sacrament of our salvation. If they held fast to apostolic faith, they would understand that he who was in the form of God assumed the form of a servant; nor would they use the form of the servant to dishonor the form of God, since the form of God contained within itself the fullness of God. They would treat with reverent reason what belongs to times and to the mystery, so that neither might divinity receive insult nor the dispensation introduce error.

> [Note: Col. 0404D] Erasmus, Lipsius, and Paris read “for dishonoring the form of God.” Bad. and the manuscript resist this reading.

But since, as I think, all matters have now been demonstrated by us with the fullest completeness, and since beneath the birth of the assumed body the power of the divine nature has been shown, no room remains for doubt that the only-begotten God, both God and man, performed all things by the powers of God, and accomplished all things in the complete truth of man by the powers of God. For in his deeds he possessed the nature of the powerful God, because he was born from God; and he possessed the complete perfection of a perfect man, because he had birth from the Virgin. He subsisted in the nature of God with the reality of a body, and remained in the reality of a body with the nature of God.

> [Note: Col. 0404D] The correct reading of the Colbert manuscript is “reverently and rationally.”

### 7. What Remains, and How It Must Be Answered

Although the whole course of our reply has proceeded as far as the very glory of death, and every proposition of their impious profession has been contradicted from evangelical and apostolic teaching, nevertheless the impious have dared, even after the glory of the resurrection, to allege certain matters in order to demonstrate a degenerate nature’s weakness. These must now be answered.

And, as we have observed in other cases, the explanation of their own statements must be drawn from those statements themselves, so that truth may be found there where it is denied. For things that have been spoken simply and divinely for the instruction of faith must necessarily have been spoken in such a way that they are established with reference to that for which they were spoken, not by examples drawn from statements foreign and external to them.

### 8. They Claim That He Is Weak Because God Is Both His God and Father as He Is Ours, and Because He Is Subject

Among their other impieties, heretics are accustomed to use this saying of the Lord: “I ascend to my Father and your Father, and to my God and your God” (John 20:17). They argue that, because his Father is their Father and his God their God, he is not in the nature of God: since he confesses God the Father to be to the others what he is to himself, the privilege of both nature and birth is eliminated by this commonality—by which he is born God and is Son.

Let them also hold that saying of the Apostle: “But when he shall say, ‘All things are subjected,’ [it is] except him who subjected all things to him. But when all things have been subjected to him, then the Son himself also shall be subjected to him who subjected all things to him, that God may be all in all” (1 Cor. 15:26 ff.).

> [Note: Col. 0403D] The words, “But when all things have been subjected to him,” are absent from our manuscript.

> [Note: Col. 0404D] The verse, “But when all things have been subjected to him,” is absent from the manuscripts except one Colbert manuscript of doubtful authority.

They suppose that this subjection testifies to a weak nature, and therefore that he does not possess the power of the Father’s nature, since natural weakness has subjected him to the power of a superior nature.

> [Note: Col. 0404D] “Is supposed.”

Let them take this as the most strongly fortified and impregnable defense of all their impiety, to abolish the truth of his birth: because by subjection he is not God, and because, through the God and Father common to him and us, he shares the status of a creature. Thus, they say, he too is creation from God rather than generation, since creation subsists from nothing, whereas generation has the natural author of its birth.

> [Note: Col. 0404D] Lipsius and Paris read “may exist.” Shortly afterwards manuscript Martin reads “authority,” not “author.”

### 9. The Mystery of Our Salvation Is a Sacrament of Godliness, Not an Offense against Divinity

Every slander is indeed wicked, because falsehood, once shame has been cast off without restraint, contradicts truth. Yet it sometimes puts forward some veil of equivocal excuse, so that what is shameless in intention may appear modest in defense. But in the matters now impiously alleged to weaken the divinity of our Lord, even the place for modesty or false excuse has been excluded. For, when even the pardon available for ignorance has ceased, the will of irreligious interpretation alone is exposed.

To postpone briefly the demonstration of the evangelical saying itself: could the Apostle’s proclamation have been unknown when he said: “And confessedly great is the sacrament of godliness: which was manifested in flesh, justified in spirit, seen by angels, preached among the nations, believed in this world, taken up in glory” (1 Tim. 3:16)?

> [Note: Col. 0405C] The printed editions read “made alive,” contrary to the manuscripts and to what follows, in which “spirit” is set in opposition to “flesh” and referred to the nature of the Word.

Is anyone still so dull of understanding as to suppose that the dispensation of flesh assumed by the Lord is anything other than a sacrament of godliness?

> [Note: Col. 0405C] In the Vatican-Basilican manuscript, Martin, and two others: “place of understanding”; *place* is superfluous.

First, whoever is outside this confession is outside the faith of God. For the Apostle does not doubt that all must confess that the mystery of our salvation is not an insult to divinity but the sacrament of great godliness: a sacrament no longer hidden in mystery, but manifested in flesh; not still weak through the nature of flesh, but justified in spirit. Thus, through the justification of the Spirit, the weakness of flesh is absent from our faith; through its manifestation in flesh, the mystery is not hidden; and through the unknowable ground of the mystery, confession alone is contained in the sacrament of great godliness.

> [Note: Col. 0405C] The word “in” is absent from our manuscript.

> [Note: Col. 0405C] Colbert, German, and Martin manuscripts read “now in the mystery.”

Thus the Apostle maintained the whole order of faith: because, while it is godliness, it is a sacrament; while it is a sacrament, there is knowledge in flesh; while there is knowledge in flesh, there is justification in spirit. For the sacrament of godliness that is manifested in flesh, in order truly to be a sacrament, is manifested in flesh through justification in spirit.

And lest the nature of that manifestation in flesh—namely, justification in spirit—should be unknown, the sacrament which was manifested in flesh and justified in spirit, which was seen by angels, preached among the nations, and believed in this world, was itself taken up in glory. Thus, in all these things there is the sacrament of great godliness: while it is manifested in flesh, justified in spirit, seen by angels, preached among the nations, believed in this world, and taken up in glory.

> [Note: Col. 0405D] The older Colbert manuscript reads “justification of spirit.” Martin reads “and justification,” etc.

> [Note: Col. 0405C] “While it is justified in spirit, while it is taken up in glory,” omitting the intermediate clauses.

> [Note: Col. 0405D] After “in spirit,” the manuscripts add, “while it is taken up in glory,” omitting the other clauses.

For sight is followed by preaching, preaching by faith, and all things are completed by the assumption into glory. For the assumption into glory is also a sacrament of great godliness; and through faith in this dispensation we are prepared to be taken up in conformity with the Lord’s glory.

> [Note: Col. 0405D] In the Vatican-Basilican manuscripts, one Colbert, and another Sorbonne manuscript: “to the assumption.” In Remigius: “of the assumed one.” The former reading was quite appealing, but the one retained is fuller.

Therefore, the assumption of flesh is a sacrament of great godliness, because through the assumption of flesh the manifestation of the sacrament is in flesh. Yet the manifestation in flesh must be confessed to be nothing other than a sacrament of great godliness, because its manifestation in flesh is also justification of spirit and assumption into glory.

And by what hope in our faith is the mystery of the godly dispensation the weakness of divinity, when through the assumption into glory it must be confessed to be a sacrament of great godliness? Since it is no longer weakness but sacrament, no longer necessity but godliness, the meaning of the evangelical saying must now be sought, lest what is the mystery of our salvation and glory be left as an occasion for impious preaching.

> [Note: Col. 0405D] In the aforementioned Vatican-Basilican, Colbert, Sorbonne, and Martin manuscripts: “And what hope finally remains in our faith, if the mystery of the godly dispensation is weakness of divinity?” This reading is clearer and therefore more suspect than the other, in which a somewhat more hidden meaning is indicated: namely, that divinity was not weakened by the mystery of the dispensation, through which flesh was granted assumption into the glory of brightness; and that those believers fall away from the hope promised to them who believe otherwise.

### 10. They Claim That Christ Is a Creature and Servant Because God and Father Are Common to Him and Us

Weighty and unanswerable for you, heretic, is the Lord’s declaration concerning himself when he says: “I ascend to my Father and your Father, and to my God and your God.” You infer that, because one Father is Father both to us and to him, and one God is God both to us and to him (John 20:17), he is in the same weakness as we are: because through the same Father we are made equal as sons, and through the same God we are compared as servants. Though we are creation by origin and servants by nature, nevertheless, since Father and God are common to us, he shares with us both created nature and servitude.

> [Note: Col. 0405C] “Creation” refers to nature.

> [Note: Col. 0406C] The Vatican-Basilican manuscript alone reads “creation of nature.” The rest read “creation according to nature” or “from nature.” The printed editions read “creation and nature.”

And the frenzy of impious preaching employs even this prophetic saying: “God, your God, has anointed you” (Ps. 44:8), so that he may not possess the power of that nature by which he is God, since God who anoints him is set before him as his God.
