### 11. God Is Both God and Father to Him Because He Is Begotten; and Because He Is Begotten, He Is God

He who does not know God begotten does not know Christ, God. But for God to be begotten is nothing other than to be in that nature in which God is. For since “to be begotten” shows the cause of birth, he nevertheless does not fall away in kind from the author.

> [Note: Col. 0406C] Manuscript Martin reads “cause,” wrongly. The meaning is that the word *to be begotten* is relative and therefore signifies the Father together with the begotten one. Theology now rejects the word “cause” for explaining the Son’s eternal generation, preferring “principle”; but Hilary understood it properly, as he did also the word “author,” concerning which Augustine says, *Against Maximinus*, II.14.6: “If you call God the Father the author of God the Son because the former begot and the latter was begotten, because the latter is from the former and not the former from the latter, I admit and grant it. But if by the name ‘author’ you wish to make the Son lesser,” etc., “I shall detest and reject it.”

But that which does not fall away in kind must indeed owe to its author the cause of its birth; nevertheless, it has not lost in itself the nature of its author. For the birth of God is neither from elsewhere nor something other. If it is from elsewhere, it is not birth; if it is something other, it is not God. But since God is from God, God the Father is both the God of God the Son in respect of his birth and the Father in respect of his nature; because the birth of God is both from God and exists in that nature of kind in which God is.

> [Note: Col. 0406D] From this passage Ludovicus Miraeus, commenting on Book X, §33 according to Erasmus, argues that for Hilary *not to fall away* (*non disproficere*) means the same as “to degenerate.” But if one removes the addition “in kind,” the word by itself certainly does not have this meaning.

> [Note: Col. 0406D] Vatican-Basilican manuscript: “God is both by birth and equally by nature, because Christ’s birth is from God”—the careless work of a second hand is apparent. Yet Martin supports it, differing only in reading “Father,” not “equally.”

### 12. Christ So Moderated His Words as to Reveal Himself Both Begotten and God

Therefore, in all that he spoke the Lord so moderated the manner of this godly and fitting confession that acknowledgment of his birth might not bring insult upon his divinity, nor the reverence of obedience offend the nature of majesty. Rather, his birth confessed the honor owed to it, since it ought to subsist from its author; and the confidence of natural awareness showed the consciousness of nature, since by being born it subsisted in God.

> [Note: Col. 0407C] Formerly “birth” was read.

> [Note: Col. 0407C] For “to subsist from its author”—that is, “to subsist”—Erasmus, Lipsius, and Paris wrongly substituted “to subject itself.”

Hence comes: “He who has seen me has seen the Father”; but also: “The words which I speak, I do not speak from myself” (John 14:9–10). In saying that he does not speak from himself, he necessarily owes to his author what he speaks; but when the Father is seen upon seeing him, this is the consciousness of nature which, for the manifestation in itself of God, subsists as born from God into God and is not alien from God.

> [Note: Col. 0407D] Vatican-Basilican manuscript: “because God does not estrange from Christ in God the manifestation of himself that subsisted as born”—an ancient and evident bold corruption. Here: “which, for the manifestation in itself of God,” that is, which, in being seen, demonstrated God.

Or again: “What the Father has given me is greater than all”; and: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:29–30). The Father’s giving is a confession of received birth; and their being one is the property of nature from birth.

> [Note: Col. 0407C] “Has given.”

> [Note: Col. 0407D] Colbert, Martin, Corbie, German, Vindocinian, Silvanectan, Pratensis manuscripts read “what you have given.” But in Book VII, §22, they agree with the others.

Or: “He has given all judgment to the Son, that all may honor the Son as they honor the Father” (John 5:22–23). In the giving of judgment, birth is not left unspoken; while in the equality of honor, nature is retained.

> [Note: Col. 0407D] Vatican-Basilican manuscript: “is not denied.”

Or: “I am in the Father and the Father in me”; and again, “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:11, 28). In their being in one another, recognize the divinity of God from God; but in the Father’s being greater, understand the confession of paternal authority.

So too: “The Son cannot do anything from himself, except what he sees the Father doing; for whatever he does, the Son likewise does the same” (John 5:19). Because he does not act from himself, the Father is his author according to birth in what he does. Yet because whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does the same, he subsists not as something other than God, possessing within himself the nature of paternal omnipotence for doing everything that God the Father does.

These things have thus been shown according to the unity of the Spirit and the property of nature that belongs to birth: so that birth may confess God as the God of its own establishment, and establishment may not leave unspoken the consciousness of nature. God the Son confesses God as his Father because he is born from him; yet, with regard to that which he is born, he possesses in fullness all that naturally belongs to God.

> [Note: Col. 0407D] Erasmus, Lipsius, and Paris read “of birth,” refuted even by the preceding words: “Their being one is the property of nature from birth.” Lipsius, solely on Erasmus’s conjecture, substituted *subsistence* and *subsistence* for *establishment* (*substitutio*) and *establishment*; this later prevailed. Yet *substitutio* has a somewhat different meaning from *subsistentia*, just as *substituere* differs from *subsistere* in Book VIII, §56: “perfect birth established a perfect God; but perfect birth thus subsists.” There *established* means “made subsistent.”

### 13. Because He Had a Father by Being Begotten, He Began to Have a Lord When He Was Made a Servant

The dispensation, therefore, of the great and godly sacrament made him who was Father by divine birth to be also Lord by reason of the assumed condition: since he who was in the form of God was found in the form of a servant.

> [Note: Col. 0407C] “Made God.”

> [Note: Col. 0408C] Thus manuscript Martin. Other books read “made God.” The dispensation did not make the Father; rather, it constituted as Lord of the assumed man him who was Father by reason of eternal generation.

For he was not a servant when, according to the Spirit, he was God, the Son of God.

> [Note: Col. 0408C] “God the Son,” not “God, God’s Son.”

> [Note: Col. 0408D] Thus the Vatican-Basilican, Martin, one Colbert, and another Sorbonne manuscript. In others the word “God” is omitted without affecting the sense. Yet the preceding word “God” is more important, since it was absent from earlier printed editions.

By common judgment, where there is no servant, neither is there a lord. God is indeed the Father of the only-begotten God by birth; but with respect to that in which he is servant, we cannot reckon him to have a lord except when he is servant. For if previously he was not a servant by nature, and afterwards began according to nature to be what he had not been, no other ground of lordship can be understood than that which arose from servitude. Thus he has a lord by the dispensation of nature when, through the assumption of man, he presented himself as servant.

> [Note: Col. 0408D] Thus all manuscripts, through a Hellenism. But the printed editions read, “we cannot except,” omitting *not*.

### 14. In the Form of a Servant He Said, “I Ascend,” etc.

Remaining, therefore, in the form of a servant—he who had previously remained in the form of God—the man Christ Jesus said: “I ascend to my Father and your Father, and to my God and your God” (John 20:17).

> [Note: Col. 0408D] The Arians, as we learn from Augustine, *Against Maximinus*, II.16.1, maintained that these words of Christ could not belong to the form of a servant. “For,” they said, “he spoke them after the resurrection; but then the form of a servant was no longer present, having altogether been consumed and vanished.” As though, Augustine replies, he had consumed the form of a servant by the resurrection, rather than changed it for the better; as though the form which was killed had not itself risen again.

If, then, a servant spoke these things to servants, how can this declaration fail to be that of a servant? How can it be transferred rather to that nature which is not in the nature of a servant? For he who remained in the form of God and assumed the form of a servant can have community with servants as a servant only in respect of that alone by which he is servant.

Therefore, the Father is his Father as he is Father of men; and God is his God as he is God of servants.

> [Note: Col. 0408C] “His Father as also [he is Father] of servants.”

And since the man Jesus Christ in the form of a servant speaks these words to men who are servants, it is beyond doubt that the Father is his Father as he is that of others in respect of the part by which he is man, and that God is his God as he is that of all in respect of the nature by which he is servant.

### 15. He Spoke in That Form in Which He Calls Us Brothers. Why Christ Is a Worm

Finally, he began this same declaration with the following introduction: “But go to my brothers and say to them, ‘I ascend to my Father and your Father, and to my God and your God’” (John 20:17). I now ask whether they are to be understood as his brothers according to the form of God or according to the form of a servant. Does our bodily constitution have some fellowship with him in respect of the fullness of divinity dwelling in him, so that we may be reckoned brothers to him in respect of that which he is as God?

> [Note: Col. 0409C] “Corruption.”

> [Note: Col. 0409D] The printed editions, with most manuscripts, read “corruption.” On the authority of excellent manuscripts—Martin, Colbert, Remigius, and German—we prefer *corporatio* (“bodily constitution”), a word contrasted with *spirit*, by which Hilary regularly signifies the divine nature.

But the prophetic Spirit also knows in what respect they are brothers to the only-begotten God. For these words were spoken not so much by man as by a worm: “I will declare your name to my brothers” (Ps. 21:23). This worm—whether living not from the conception belonging to ordinary origins, or emerging alive from the depths of the earth—declared, in signification of the assumed flesh, also vivified by itself from hell.

> [Note: Col. 0409D] The phrase “from hell” is to be referred not to the word *flesh* but to “by itself,” so that it was not the flesh but he himself who was in hell. For as we read in Book X, §65: “Will the body which lay in the tomb be said to have descended to hell?” Earlier, the words “by itself” belong no less to *assumed* than to *vivified*. Christ is called a worm because his flesh was conceived from the Virgin by its own power, and, when he himself emerged from hell, was also vivified by its own power.

Having prophetically spoken beforehand throughout the entire psalm the sacraments of his passion, he necessarily has brothers by that dispensation through which he suffered. The Apostle also knows the sacrament of brothers in him (Rom. 8:29), proclaiming him the firstborn from the dead and likewise firstborn among many brothers. Therefore, he is firstborn among many brothers according to that by which he is firstborn from the dead; and since the sacrament of death is in the body, the sacrament of brotherhood is also in flesh. Therefore, men are brothers to God through flesh, because “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us”; but the only-begotten God, in the exception belonging to the Only-begotten, is without brothers.

### 16. God Is Christ’s Father Both in a Proper and a Common Sense

He himself, containing in himself through the assumption of flesh the nature of us all, was what we are and had not ceased to be what he had remained. He had, then, the Father by birth; and now, by bodily constitution, God the Father.

> [Note: Col. 0409D] The printed editions except Bad. read, “then only Father by constitution”; then Erasmus, “now God and Father only by constitution; now God, because all things are from God the Father.” Lipsius, omitting the earlier words, retained only: “now God, because all things are from God the Father.” Paris: “now God according to constitution, because all things are from God the Father”—very disordered and confused. The manuscripts correct the passage. Hilary means that Christ had then, namely before becoming flesh, the Father by birth; but now, having become flesh, he has God the Father by the new and common ground of bodily constitution. The Vatican-Basilican manuscript reads somewhat differently: “having then the Father alone by birth, now God and Father by constitution; God alone now by constitution, because,” etc. The final clause conflicts somewhat with the preceding, as the first also conflicts with §13, where we have already heard that the only-begotten God had God and Father before the flesh by reason of his birth.

Now according to constitution, because all things are from God the Father. For God is Father of all, since all things are from him and in him. But for the only-begotten God, because the Word became flesh, he is not Father only in this respect. He is Father in relation to the God the Word who in the beginning was with God.

But when the Word became flesh, his being Father remains both in the birth of God the Word and in the constitution of flesh. For God is Father of all flesh, but not in the same way as he is Father to God the Word. And God the Word neither ceased to be Word nor ceased to be flesh. For the Word which became flesh and dwelt among us is not, while dwelling, not truly Word; nor, while the Word is flesh, is God as man not truly God. For dwelling necessarily belongs to him who remains, and becoming flesh must be understood of him who is born.

And his dwelling in us is the assumption of our flesh, because by the Word’s dwelling in us after becoming flesh, God is in the reality of our body.

> [Note: Col. 0410D] Thus the manuscript. But the printed editions read “through that by which [he dwells] in us”; shortly afterwards they prefix *while* before “God is.”

If, therefore, Christ Jesus the man according to flesh deprives God the Word of nature, or if Christ Jesus the man who is God the Word is not God the Word according to the sacrament of godliness, then let it be an insult to nature that the Father is his Father and God his God according to us. But if Christ Jesus, God the Word, did not cease to be God the Word, our common relation with him to Father and God belongs only to that nature by which he is brother. For “I ascend to my Father and your Father, and to my God and your God” was announced to brothers not in respect of his being the only-begotten God the Word, but in respect of the Word’s becoming flesh.

> [Note: Col. 0410D] Vatican-Basilican and several other manuscripts: “by which he is man.”

### 17. Christ as Word Has the Father; as Jesus and Servant, God

Apostolic discourse does not speak incautiously, nor in expressions uncertain enough to offer an occasion for impiety. Since the Evangelist begins the Lord’s saying with the declaration of brothers, he teaches that the entire declaration belongs to participation in that nature by which he is brother, because the message was sent to brothers. Thus, what was preached concerning the sacrament of godliness might not be reckoned an insult against divinity: our common relation with him, in which the Father is Father to us and to him and God is God to us and to him, arose according to the dispensation of flesh, since we are counted brothers to him by birth of body.

> [Note: Col. 0410D] The printed editions read “from which”; the manuscripts more correctly read “from which [nature],” namely, the nature.

Therefore no one doubts that God the Father is also the God of our Lord Jesus Christ; but this godly confession of ours affords no occasion for impiety. He is his God—not, however, so that God is of a different kind of nature from him. Rather, because he is God born from the Father and, by the dispensation, is servant, he has the Father because he is God from him, and has his God because he is flesh from the Virgin.

> [Note: Col. 0411C] The Vatican-Basilican manuscript alone reads “from God the Father.”

> [Note: Col. 0411C] Lipsius and Paris, with manuscript Martin, read “God the Father.” Then that manuscript and another Vatican-Basilican manuscript read, “while he is wholly God from him.” In some others: “while he is God from God.”

The Apostle confirms this in a brief and complete statement: “Making mention in my prayers, that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give you a spirit of wisdom and revelation” (Eph. 1:16–17). Where Jesus Christ is, there is his God; but where glory is, there is the Father. Thus, he who is Father to Christ according to glory is the same one who is God to Christ according to Jesus. For the angel gives the name Jesus to the Christ the Lord whom Mary was to bear (Matt. 1:21); but prophecy speaks of Christ the Lord as Spirit.

> [Note: Col. 0411C] Thus the manuscripts. But Bad. reads “the Spirit of prophecy.” That Christ is Spirit—that is, God—has been proved from prophecy throughout Book IV, and specifically from David’s words, in which God is called not only the anointer but also the anointed.

This expression appears more obscure to many in Latin because Latin does not employ the pronouns which Greek regularly uses in honorable and necessary usage. For it is written thus:

> ὁ θεὸς τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ, ὁ πατὴρ τῆς δόξης.

“The God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory.”

If our own language always employed this customary use of pronouns, it would be pronounced thus: “That God of that our Lord Jesus Christ, that Father of that glory.” For by saying “that God of that Jesus Christ” and “that Father of that glory,” a certain proper distinction is expressed according to the capacity of our understanding: where Christ is in glory, there God is his Father; but where Christ is Jesus, there the Father is his God. He has his God in the dispensation when he is servant, and the Father in glory when he is God.

[Col. 0411C] **18. “He anointed you,” etc., is said of Christ as man.** [Col. 0412A] —Times and ages do not, however, introduce a diversity in the Spirit, such that Christ, who remained in the Spirit in the prophets, should not be one and the same when in the body. [Note: The printed editions read “spirit,” contrary to the manuscripts. That he remained in the Spirit is immediately made clear when he is said to have spoken through the mouth of David. To this belongs Tertullian’s statement, *Against Marcion*, III.6: “We for our part are certain that Christ always spoke in the prophets—namely, the Spirit of the Creator.” Yet Hilary, *On the Trinity*, II.3, declares that the Spirit speaking in the prophets is the third person of the Trinity.]

For, speaking through the mouth of the holy patriarch David: “God, your God, anointed you with the oil of gladness above [Note: The phrase is “above your companions,” and henceforth the particle *prae* is construed with the accusative; shortly below, “for he who now …”] [Note: The manuscripts, by strong consensus, read “above your companions.” Thus thereafter too the particle *prae* is consistently joined with the accusative. The observation already made that Hilary read not *ungo* but *ungueo* is confirmed by this passage: in the older manuscripts *unguetur* is written for *ungitur*, and *ungueatur* for *ungatur*. From Augustine, *Against Maximinus*, II.16.3, we incidentally observe that heretics refused to allow this prophetic passage to be applied to Christ in the form of a servant because “God, your God, anointed you,” was written long before Christ came in the flesh. He replies that prophecy foretold as though already done what was future, because in predestination what was to occur in its own time was already done.] your companions” (Ps. 44:8), he spoke according to no mystery other than the dispensation of the assumed body. [Note: In the printed editions, with several manuscripts: “for now indeed.” The reading preferred, with the Vatican Basilica manuscript and some others, is “for he who now.” Earlier, by the words “according to the mystery” is denoted that time which preceded and foreshadowed Christ’s embodiment—for example, when Abraham worshipped the Lord, recognizing the mystery of the future embodiment, as is said in Book IV, no. 27.]

For he who now commands his brethren that their Father is his Father and their God his God, then also spoke of himself as anointed by his God above his companions. Thus, while the only-begotten Christ, God the Word, is not a participant, he is nevertheless known to be a participant in him through that assumption whereby he is flesh. For that anointing did not benefit that blessed, incorruptible birth which remains in the nature of God; rather, it belonged to the mystery of the body and to the sanctification of the assumed man. The apostle Peter bears witness when he says: “They gathered together in truth in this city against your holy Son Jesus, whom you anointed” (Acts 4:27). [Note: Bad. and Erasmus read “men”; Lipsius and Paris, “truly.” The better manuscripts read “in truth,” in accordance with the Greek, ἐπ’ ἀληθείας, “in truth.”]

And again: “You know what occurred throughout all Judaea, beginning from Galilee after the baptism which John preached: Jesus [Note: “the Nazarene.”] the Nazarene, how God anointed him with the Holy Spirit and with power” (Acts 10:37–38). Therefore Jesus is anointed for the mystery of the regenerate flesh. [Note: This appears to be explained by the words in *On Matthew*, ch. II, no. 5: “He himself indeed had no need of the washing; but because he had assumed both the body and the name of our created nature, he therefore fulfilled in himself every mystery of our salvation.” This is repeated there: “Thus, by the prophet’s testimony he has no need of the washing, yet by the authority of his example he completes the mysteries of human salvation, sanctifying man both by assumption and by the washing.”]

And how he was anointed with the Spirit of God and with power is not doubtful: when he came up from the Jordan, the voice of God the Father was heard: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Ps. 2:6). Thus, through this testimony to the flesh sanctified in him, the anointing of spiritual power was made known. [Note: That is: the sanctification bestowed upon the assumed man by the spiritual Power—the assuming Word—might be known. In the baptismal washing there is testimony to the sanctified flesh; but knowledge of this spiritual anointing is supplied by the Father’s own declaration. Thus, as is said in *On Matthew*, ch. II, no. 6, testimony concerning the Lord is sent both by sight and voice, since the Son of God is shown to hearing and sight—namely, sanctifying man both by assumption and by washing. Augustine likewise applies the Psalmist’s prophecy to Christ’s baptism, *Against Maximinus*, II.16.3: “The Son was anointed by God the Father, who became man in such a way as to remain God; and he was full of that anointing, that is, of the Holy Spirit.” Hence it is written of him: “Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan.” See *Tractates on Psalm 2*, no. 29, and Book VIII, no. 25.]

[Col. 0413A] **19. The same statement cannot be understood of the Word, since there is no ground for it in him, who is God by nature and is anointed.** —But since in the beginning God the Word was with God, the anointing of his nature has neither cause nor explanation, for nothing else is proclaimed of him except that he is in the beginning. [Note: In the Vatican Basilica manuscript the word “nature” is omitted. It must certainly be retained with the other books. It is opposed to the term “dispensation” and refers to God the Word. Above, no. 11, Hilary admitted a generating and coeternal cause of the Word; here he rejects only a pre-existent and meritorious cause. When he adds “or explanation,” he refers to Isaiah: “Who shall declare his generation?”]

[Note: “Of being anointed” (*unguendi*). So elsewhere too, *ungueo* is used for *ungo*.]

Nor did God need to be anointed through the Spirit and power of God, since he himself was both God’s Spirit and God’s Power. Therefore God is anointed by his God above his companions. And if, before the dispensation of the flesh, there are many Christs under the Law, then Christ, who is anointed above his companions, is later in time, since he is placed above companions who had already been anointed.

Finally, that prophetic utterance shows that this anointing, which occurs in time, is later, saying: “You loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. 44:8). A consequent and later cause is never represented as though it were prior, because to have deserved something is later than to be one who can deserve. For deserving belongs to one who is himself the originator of acquiring merit. If, then, we attribute to the birth of the only-begotten God an anointing granted on account of the merit of loving righteousness and hating iniquity, the only-begotten God will be understood to have advanced by anointing rather than to have been begotten. God will then be perfected through growth and advancement: he will not have been born God, but, through merit, anointed into God. Christ will then be God by a cause, and not every cause through Christ God.

And where then will be the Apostle’s words: “All things are through him and in him; he is before all things, and all things subsist in him” (Col. 1:16–17)? For the Lord Jesus Christ is God not on account of anything, nor through anything, but he was born God. And he who is God by generation did not, after birth, advance into God through a cause; rather, in being born he is nothing other than what God is. [Note: The word “is,” omitted in the common editions, is restored from the manuscripts. Then: “than God is,” that is, than what God the Father is—unless one prefers to understand the whole thus: “but in his very birth he receives that he may be God, and nothing else.”]

But when he is anointed for a cause, the benefit of anointing does not concern that which needs no increase; [Note: Ancient books read *exspectat*, in the old manner, but with no different sense.] it concerns that which needed the advancement of anointing through the increase of the mystery—namely, that our Christ might become a man sanctified by anointing. If, therefore, even now the prophet displays the dispensation of the servant, [Col. 0414A] on account of which he is anointed by his God above his companions, and is anointed because he loved righteousness and hated iniquity, why should the prophet’s utterance not concern that nature of Christ in which, through the assumption of flesh, he has companions? Especially since the Spirit of prophecy has so moderated its language that, while God is anointed by his God, he has in the dispensation of anointing one who is his God, and in nature is himself God.

God, therefore, is anointed. But I ask: was that Word which was God in the beginning anointed? Certainly not; for anointing is later than God. And because the birth of the Word—which was God with God in the beginning—was not anointed, [Note: Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “was anointed into God; it is necessary,” etc.] that must be anointed in God which is later in the dispensation in which he is God. And when God is anointed by his God, whatever was assumed from him in the mystery of the flesh [Col. 0414B] in servile form is anointed.

**20. In what respect we have communion with Christ.** —Therefore let no one violate with impious thought the mystery of great godliness, which was manifested in the flesh; and let no one equate himself with the Only-Begotten in the substance of divinity. Let him be our brother and companion insofar as the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, insofar as the mediator between God and human beings is the man Jesus Christ. Let him, in relation to us as servants, be both our common Father and our common God; and let him be anointed above his companions in that nature in which companions are anointed, though anointed with a special privilege. In the mystery of the Mediator, let him be true man and likewise true God—God himself from God—having a Father and God in common with us in that communion in which he is our brother.

[Col. 0414C] **21. Objections are raised concerning subjection, the handing over of the kingdom, and the end.** —But perhaps that subjection, the handing over of the kingdom, and then the end are to be understood as abolition of nature, loss of power, or weakness of divinity. For many so choose: either that, when all things have been subjected and he is subjected to God, he is not God because of the condition of subjection; or that, when he hands over the kingdom, he is no longer in the kingdom; or that, when there is an end, his end results in failure. [Note: From the Apostle’s ensuing words Marcellus of Ancyra taught that both Christ’s kingdom and flesh would have an end, if Eusebius may be trusted in his report against him, II.4: “If the man received the beginning of the kingdom not yet four hundred years ago, there is nothing absurd if the Apostle declares that he who received the kingdom only so few years ago will again return the kingdom to God.” And shortly afterwards: “For, since after the judgment all things are to be subjected to Christ, as the Apostle asserts, then he will be subjected to him who subjected all things to him. Therefore, since we have learned that the human flesh which the Word assumed for our sake was not assumed four hundred whole years ago, we know that he will retain it no longer than the future time of judgment.” Marcellus adds there: “As the flesh had a beginning, so the divine Paul declared that it will have an end. Then comes the end, when he has handed over his kingdom to God and the Father.” Yet, by Eusebius’s own admission in that passage, Marcellus maintained this opinion not without hesitation.]

**22. The method of answering.** —It is fitting, therefore, to examine the entire meaning of the apostolic discourse concerning these matters, [Note: The Vatican Basilica manuscript, with Martin’s manuscript, reads “concerning these matters,” not “concerning the foregoing.”] [Note: The Verona manuscript reads *retractare*; below likewise occurs, “let us reconsider the mystery of the present sayings.”] so that, when the rationale of each individual statement has been set forth and explained, we may become capable of the whole mystery through an understanding of the entire discourse. [Note: The common editions read “truth”; the manuscripts more correctly read “entirety,” that is, the whole apostolic discourse.]

He says, then: “For since death is through a man, resurrection of the dead is also through a man. For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all are made alive. But each in his own order: Christ the firstfruits; then those who belong to Christ at his coming; then comes the end, when he hands over the kingdom to God and the Father, when he has abolished every rule and every authority. For he must reign until he has put all enemies under his feet. God indeed subjected all things under his feet. The last enemy conquered by him is death. But when he says, ‘All things have been subjected,’ this excludes him who subjected all things to him. But when all things have been subjected to him, then he himself will be subjected [Col. 0415B] to him who subjected all things to him, that God may be all in all” (1 Cor. 15:21 ff.). [Notes: “of the dead” is absent. Erasmus and Lipsius read “death will be destroyed.” Most and best manuscripts read “are made alive”; the editions read “will be made alive.” “But each” is absent in some. Martin’s and Vatican Basilica manuscripts read “Christ the beginning,” supported by a German copy containing Paul’s Epistles in Greek and Latin, written about a thousand years ago. Bad. reads “at his coming,” without “those who”; Greek likewise has ἐν τῇ παρουσίᾳ, “at the coming.” Erasmus, Lipsius, and Paris read “those who believed in his coming,” also found in the Corbie manuscript in a second hand, against the sounder manuscripts and Greek. “This again is absent in our manuscript.” Again the manuscripts, by broad consensus, omit: “But when all things have been subjected to him.”]

**23. Some things are not immediately grasped by a human being.** —The Apostle, chosen as teacher of the Gentiles not from human beings nor through a human being, but through Jesus Christ, sets forth the mysteries of heavenly dispensations with all the force that complete language can provide. [Note: In Martin’s manuscript and several others: “the secrets of the mysteries.” Shortly after “through Jesus Christ,” the Vatican Basilica manuscript adds “and God the Father”; these words occur in no other manuscript, though they appear at the beginning of the Epistle to the Galatians, to which this refers.]

And he who, caught up to the third heaven, had heard things beyond expression, revealed to human understanding only those things of which human nature is capable. Yet he did not fail to know that some things cannot be understood immediately upon being heard, because our weakness receives more slowly into the true and complete judgment of the mind those things which are poured into the ears. [Notes: Some read “otherwise, into the true.” Corbie and later manuscripts, with Bad., Erasmus, and Lipsius, read “otherwise”; Vatican Basilica, Colbert, Martin, and other ancient copies, with Paris, read “more often”; Remigius reads “more slowly.” We judge that *serius*, “more slowly,” must be read, even though this corrects the text conjecturally beyond our usual practice. The Carnotensis manuscript supports it with *seius*, for those impeded in speech pronounce *serius* in that way. It is confirmed below, no. 30, where we read “late obedience.”]

They are left by a longer delay to the mind rather than to hearing: for hearing is the function of the voice, but understanding of reason—although God reveals understanding to those who desire understanding. For when writing many things to Timothy, who had been trained from infancy in the sacred writings through the glorious faith of his grandmother and mother, he added this too: “Understand what I say, for God will give you understanding in all things” (2 Tim. 2:7).

The exhortation to understand arises from the difficulty of understanding. But the gift of understanding from God is the reward of faith, through which the weakness of the mind deserves the grace of revelation. Therefore, if Timothy—called by apostolic testimony “a man of God” (1 Tim. 6:11) and Paul’s true son according to faith—is exhorted to understand because the Lord will give him understanding in all things, let us also remember that through the Apostle we are exhorted to understanding, knowing that the Lord will grant us understanding of all things.

**24. One should not be ashamed, once truth has been grasped, to alter a mistaken judgment.** —And if perhaps, through the error of our human condition, we hold some presumption in our minds, let us not reject advancement in understanding through the grace of revelation: [Col. 0416B] lest having once thought that we understood something should so prevail in our own judgment that we are ashamed to think more rightly by changing it. [Note: That is, lest the things we have devised and suppose that we understand adhere so closely to our minds that we are ashamed to shake them off. Augustine rebukes this most pernicious shame in Vincentius the Rogatist, Epistle 93.51: “Why, then, do you still hesitate to hold what you think, unless because you are ashamed that what you now think you either once did not think, or defended otherwise? And while you blush to correct error, you do not blush to remain in error—though that is surely what ought rather to cause shame.”]

For this reason the same blessed Apostle wisely and judiciously writes also to the Philippians: “As many of us, therefore, as are perfect, let us think this; and if you think anything otherwise, God will reveal this also to you. Yet, in that to which we have hastened, let us walk in the same” (Phil. 3:15–16). [Notes: Several sound manuscripts read “if any think otherwise,” a reading supported by the first words of this section, whereas the closing words support the common reading. The editions and some manuscripts read “knows”; the more accurate manuscripts read “warned.”]

A prior judgment does not prejudice God’s revelation. For the Apostle instructed those who think perfectly what they ought to think; and for those who think otherwise, he awaits God’s revelation, that they may think what is perfect. Therefore, if any have understood this profound dispensation of hidden knowledge otherwise, and something right and plausible should be offered through us, let them not be ashamed, in accordance with the Apostle, to think perfectly through God’s revelation. Nor should they love having failed to know the truth more than they hate having remained in what is untrue. [Notes: Vatican Basilica, Martin, and Remigius manuscripts read “rather than they should not hate”—incorrectly. Then *permansisse*, “to have remained,” means to have adhered for so long. We have removed, on manuscript authority, the preposition *in* before *non veris*, added by Erasmus.]

For he exhorts those who think otherwise, and to whom God has revealed this, [Note: “Has revealed”—better, so that it refers to the Apostle’s preceding words: “God will reveal this also to you.”] to hasten toward that in which they have begun to walk, so that, abandoning the judgment of their former ignorance, they may attain, through the course of the proposed hastening, [Col. 0417A] the revelation of perfect understanding. [Note: The Vatican Basilica manuscript alone reads “the understanding of perfect revelation.” Then most manuscripts read “that we may attain.”]

Let us therefore walk in that toward which we have hastened. And if perhaps an error of a wandering path delays our hastening, nevertheless, having by God’s revelation again entered into that toward which we hastened, let us not change the course of our hastening. For we have hastened toward Christ Jesus, Lord of glory and King of eternal ages, in whom all things in heaven and on earth have been restored, for whom all things subsist, and in whom and with whom we shall always remain. Having entered into these things, therefore, we think perfectly; and if we think anything otherwise, God will reveal to us what is thought perfectly.

Accordingly, in conformity with the apostolic faith, let us reconsider the mystery of the present sayings; and let us do so in the manner in which all things above have been treated by us, so that [Col. 0417B] from the very truth of the apostolic faith we may expose every preconceived judgment of impious will beneath the apostolic statements. [Note: Bad. and Erasmus read “deceived”; Lipsius and Paris, “pre-empted,” not without merit. Vatican Basilica and Martin manuscripts read “precepts.” The others read “precepted,” that is, preconceived. Compare no. 7.]

**25. Three matters are called into question.** —According to the order of the statements, then, three matters are called into question: first, the end; then, the handing over; then, the subjection. By these, it is alleged either that Christ ceases at the end, or that by handing over the kingdom he does not retain it, or that, subjected to God, he exists outside God’s nature.

**26. The connection of Paul’s words raised in objection.** —And first it must be recognized that this is not the order of the Apostle’s teaching. For first comes the handing over of the kingdom, then subjection, and lastly the end. But to each separate cause are assigned the proper kinds of their respective causes, so that, while individual matters terminate in other matters, the preceding cause always has a cause underlying it.

There will be an end, [Col. 0417C] but when he has handed over the kingdom to God. He will hand over the kingdom, but when he has abolished every rule and every authority. He will abolish every rule and authority because he must reign. He will reign until he has put all enemies under his feet. He will put enemies under his feet because God subjected all things under his feet. God subjected them in such a manner that death, the last enemy, is conquered by him. Then, when all things have been subjected to him, except him who subjected all things to him, he himself will then be subjected to the one subjecting all things to him. The sole purpose of the subjection is that God may be all in all. The end, therefore, is that God be all in all.

[Col. 0417D] **27. What the heretics allege.** —And now, before all else, it must be asked whether an end is failure, whether handing over is loss, and whether subjection is weakness. If these do not entail those contrary meanings, they will stand in the true meaning in which they were spoken. [Note: Martin’s manuscript reads “the things that have been said.”]

[Col. 0418A] **28. They are deprived of the claim that the end is abolition. What the end is.** —Christ, therefore, is the end of the Law. And I ask whether Christ is the abolition of the Law or its perfection. But if Christ, who is its end, does not dissolve the Law but fulfills it, according to his words, “I came not to dissolve the Law, but to fulfill it” (Matt. 5:17), then the end is not failure but consummated perfection.

For all things tend toward an end, not in order that they may cease to be, but in order that they may remain in that toward which they have tended. And all things exist for the end; but the end is not referred to something else. Since the end is all things, [Note: The editions read “is of all things.” The manuscripts read more elegantly “is all things”; in the Corbie manuscript a second hand wrongly attempted to corrupt it.] it remains entire in itself. And because, not proceeding beyond itself, it advances toward no other time or thing rather than toward itself, the aim of every hope is always stretched toward the end itself.

Accordingly the Lord exhorts the patience of devout faith, reserving it for the end: “Blessed is he who has remained to the end” (Matt. 10:22)—certainly not so that failure may be blessed, non-being the fruit, and the abolition of each person the reward of faith; [Note: The common editions read “his own”; the manuscripts more correctly read “of itself,” namely, abolition. This cannot be blessed, since failure is not capable of blessedness. Shortly after, *inexcessus* means a limit beyond which it cannot extend.] but because the end is the unsurpassable limit of proposed blessedness. Blessed, therefore, are those who have remained to the end of the blessedness to be consummated, their faithful hope’s expectation extending no farther.

The end, then, is the immovable state toward which one tends and in which one remains. Finally, the Apostle, warning beforehand of the end of impiety as something to be feared, says: “Whose end is destruction, but our expectation is in heaven” (Phil. 3:19–20). If, then, both the blessed and the impious have an end, and the end is understood as failure, the end makes religion and impiety equal, [Col. 0418C] because through the appointed end both alike have in common non-being. [Note: Bad. reads “each”; sound, if manuscripts supported it. The remaining editions read “on either side.” But the manuscripts, by broad consensus, read “both,” which, said of religion and impiety, must refer to non-being.]

And where is our expectation in heaven if, at the end, we cease to be as the impious do? But if an expectation is said to be due to the saints and an end to the impious, even so the end must not be thought failure. For if the penalty of impiety were to be absolutely not to be, how would there be in them, through their own cessation, any basis for suffering the conscious retribution of punishments? The end, therefore, is the enduring perfection of an unchangeable condition, reserved both for blessedness and prepared for impiety.

**29. The handing over of the kingdom is not a cessation of reigning.** —Since, therefore, it can no longer be doubted that at the end we must understand not failure but an enduring condition that will not pass away—although some matters remain to be considered in the full exposition of the saying—yet, with these points alone having been shown for the meaning, let us see whether the handing over of the kingdom should be understood as a failure of reigning, so that what the Son hands over to the Father he does not retain by handing it over.

If anyone in the frenzy of foolish impiety contends for this, he must admit that the Father, when he handed all things [Col. 0419A] to the Son, lost them by handing them over, if handing them over signifies lack of what has been handed over. For the Lord says: “All things have been handed over to me by my Father” (Luke 10:22), and again: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. 28:18). If, therefore, to hand over is to be without, the Father too was without what he gave. But if the Father was not deprived by handing it over, neither can the Son be understood to lack what he hands over.

Therefore, if the Father, having handed over all things, is not seen to lack the very things he handed over, it remains that in the handing over we should recognize the reason of the dispensation—[Note: Lipsius, Paris, and some manuscripts read “when”; Bad., Erasmus, and more numerous and better manuscripts read “why,” that is, for what dispensational reason.] why both the Father is not deprived by handing over and the Son does not lack by giving.

**30. Christ’s subjection does not signify humiliation, but dispensation.** —With regard to subjection, lest anything dishonoring be attributed to the Son through it, although several other elements support our faith, this very passage especially will help us. First I ask common understanding whether we now suppose subjection is to be understood in this way: as though we set servitude beneath lordship, weakness beneath strength, or dishonor beneath honor, as opposite qualities, so that the Son is subjected to God the Father by a diversity of discordant natures.

If this is thought, the careful wording of the apostolic discourse will forbid this error of human opinion. For he says that, when all things have been subjected to him, he is then to be subjected to the one who subjected all things to him; [Note: Thus the manuscripts; the editions read “is to be subjected,” and shortly after “will be” in place of “he says.”] and by saying that he will then be subjected, he indicated a dispensation in time. For if we understand subjection otherwise, then although he will be subjected then, certainly he is not subjected now. We shall thus make him discordant, arrogant, and impious—one whom the necessity of time will subject to late obedience as though the swelling pride of tyrannical impiety had been broken and crushed.

And where then will be: “I came not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 6:38)? And again: “Therefore the Father loves me, because I always do all things pleasing to him” (John 8:29). [Note: Martin’s manuscript: “I always do.”] Or: “Father, let your will be done” (Matt. 26:40); or the Apostle’s statement: “He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death” (Phil. 2:8)?

He who humbles himself has it in his nature not to be humble; and he who becomes obedient voluntarily assumes that which he obeys, since by humbling himself he becomes obedient. The only-begotten God, then, humbling himself and obeying the Father unto the death of the cross, [Note: Vatican Basilica and Martin manuscripts here add the word “becomes.” Then after “in what kind,” supply “of subjection.”] in what kind of subjection is he to be understood as himself thereafter to be subjected to the Father when all things have been subjected to him? Unless this subjection is not a matter of new obedience but of the mystery being dispensed; [Note: Bad. and Erasmus: “the dispensation of the mystery.”] because obedience already remains, while the subjection is to be entered upon in time. Therefore the meaning of subjection now signifies nothing other than the manifestation of the mystery.

[Col. 0420A] **31. Things said to be subjected are already subjected to Christ.** —And this is to be understood in accordance with this same hope of our faith. [Note: Lipsius and Paris, after Erasmus: “what that may be”; Bad.: “what it is”; Vatican Basilica manuscript: “that it is so”; others: “what it is,” namely the mystery.] For it is not unknown that the Lord Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, sits at the right hand of God, as the Apostle too testifies when he says: “According to the working of the might of his strength, which he worked in Christ when he raised him from the dead and seated him at his right hand in the heavenly places, above every rule and authority and power and dominion and every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the age to come; and he subjected all things under his feet” (Eph. 1:19 ff.).

For apostolic speech, according to God’s power, speaks of things still future as already accomplished. For the things to be done through the fulfillment of the times already subsist in Christ, [Col. 0420B] in whom is all fullness; [Note: Lipsius and Paris read “the fullness of divinity,” against the other books. Then the editions, except Paris, read “has established”; the future events will be an order of dispensation, etc.] and whatever is future is in them rather an order of dispensation than a novelty. For God has subjected all things under his feet, though they are still to be subjected: so that, in their having been subjected, Christ’s power is unchangeable; but in their being subjected, there is advancement toward the end according to the fullness of the times that follow.

**32. What abolition is; how it differs from subjection.** —It is not obscure that every opposing power is to be abolished, and that this prince of the air and power of spiritual wickedness is to be handed over to eternal destruction, according to the saying: “Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire which my Father prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41). [Note: The editions read “to be handed over,” without manuscript authority.]

But abolition is not the same thing as subjection. To abolish an opposing power means to remove its right of power so that it may not remain, and by the abolition of its power to destroy the dominion of its kingdom. Of this the Lord too testified when he said, “My kingdom is not of this world” (John 18:36); he had previously testified concerning this same mighty ruler of the world, [Col. 0420C] whose authority will cease when the dominion of his kingdom has been abolished (John 16:21). [Note: Namely, John 16:11: “The ruler of this world has now been judged.” Shortly after, from the better manuscripts we restore “with its dominion abolished,” in place of “with its dominion abolished [masculine].” On the devil’s authority over the kingdoms of the world, see *Tractates on Psalm 2*, no. 42.]

Subjection, however, which belongs both to obedience and to faith, is likewise a manifestation either of concession or of transformation.

### 33. In What Sense What Christ Subjects to Himself Is Subjected to Him by the Father

Therefore, when the powers have been abolished, His enemies will be subjected. But they will be subjected in such a way that He Himself subjects them to Himself. And He will subject them in such a way that God subjects them to Him. [Col. 0420D] Did the Apostle fail to understand the force of the Gospel saying when he says: “No one comes to me unless my Father draws him to me” (John 6:41)? [Note: The words “to me” are absent from the Verona codex.] [Note: We add the words “to me” from the manuscripts, with which, shortly afterward, “now He Himself” seemed preferable to “and now He Himself” in the printed editions.] Yet it is written: “No one goes to the Father except through me” (John [Col. 0421A] 14:6). Thus He Himself now subjects enemies to Himself, and yet God has subjected them to Him, testifying that every work of His is God's work in Him. Although no one may go to the Father except through Him, nevertheless no one comes to Him unless the Father has drawn him.

For, while the Son of God is understood, the truth of the Father’s nature in Him is learned. And thus, when the Son is known, God the Father calls; and when the Son is believed, the Father receives: because the signification and knowledge of the Father are in the Son, through the signification in Himself of God the Father, who, by His fatherly religion, bears us on into Him as religious persons. [Note: In the Vatican-Basilica codex: “with the Son [known as] God, the Father calls.”] [Note: We restore the word “is,” deleted by Erasmus against the authority of the manuscripts. Then, in an older manuscript and the German manuscript: “through His signification.” This may appear to have been phrased in the manner of the Greeks, who commonly say in similar places *tou en heautō* [τοῦ ἐν ἑαυτῷ], “the one who is in himself,” for “he who is in himself.”] [Note: “Perfected.”] [Note: Thus the manuscripts, with Remigius and Theodulf supporting the Colbert, Corbie, and most other manuscripts, in which stands *perferentes*, “bearing on”; for interchange of *i* and *e* is easy and frequent in ancient books. [Col. 0421D] The sense is therefore that the Father bears us onward in faith and worship toward faith and worship of the Son, while bearing us, religious toward Himself, into the Son. If anyone prefers *perferente* to *perferentis*, we shall not strongly object. In place of *perferentis*, two manuscripts have *perfectos*, “perfected.” One Vatican manuscript, together with the Vindobonensis and Silvianus, has: “bearing [us] perfected in the fatherly religion.” But Bad. has: “in the fatherly religion bearing [us].” In the remaining printed editions: “by fatherly religion He draws [us] perfected.” Thus “He draws” is repeated here without any authority.]

The Father therefore draws in this manner: when the Father, who is the principal reality, is believed. [Note: Printed editions: “while the Father is the principal [reality].” More correctly the manuscripts: “while that which is principal is [believed],” etc. Thus above, no. 2, concerning the Son: “if he should deny that even that which is principal has been born.” In both places “principal” refers to proper nature.] But no one goes to the Father except through the Son, because, when faith in the Son has ceased in us, the Father is unknowable, and we cannot approach the fatherly religion unless we have first embraced reverence for the Son. And thus, once the Son has been known, the Father draws us and receives us unto eternal life; and both are through the Son: for through the Father’s proclamation by Him, the Father leads us to Him, and He Himself leads us to the Father.

Accordingly, for a fuller understanding of the present saying, it was necessary to recall this mystery: that through the Son the Father both draws and receives us, and that through this we might understand [396] in what sense what He Himself has subjected to Himself, God has subjected to Him. That is, the nature of God remains in Him by birth, and performs the things which He Himself performs: He acts in such a way that God acts those things, and yet He Himself performs the things God has performed; yet in such a way [Note: The particle “that” is absent.] [Note: The particle *ut*, “that,” is absent from three Colbert manuscripts, one Sorbonne manuscript, the German manuscript, and Martin’s manuscript.] that, in what He Himself acts, the Son of God is understood to act; but in what God acts, the property of the Father’s nature is perceived to exist in Him as Son.

### 34. Who Are the Enemies to Be Subjected to Christ

Therefore, when the authorities and powers have been abolished, His enemies will be subjected beneath His feet. And the Apostle himself has taught whom we should understand as enemies, saying: “According to the Gospel indeed they are enemies for your sake, but according to election beloved for the fathers’ sake” (Rom. 11:28). These, then, we remember as enemies of Christ’s cross; but because they are beloved for the fathers’ sake, we know that they are reserved for subjection, according to what was said: “For I do not want you, brothers, to be ignorant of this mystery, lest you be wise in yourselves: that hardness has come upon Israel in part, until the fullness of the nations enters; and thus all Israel [Note: In Martin’s manuscript: “will be saved”; and shortly afterward, “their sins,” not “their iniquities.”] will be delivered, as it is written (Isa. 59:20 ff.): ‘There will come from Zion one who delivers, and turns away ungodliness from Jacob; and this is my covenant with them, when I shall take away their iniquities’” (Rom. 11:25 ff.). [Note: “And will turn away,” in accordance with the Greek, *apostrepsei* [ἀποστρέψει].] Therefore the enemies will be subjected beneath His feet.

### 35. They Are Subjected in Becoming Conformed to Christ’s Glory

But we must understand what follows that subjection: namely, this: “Finally death has been conquered by Him” (1 Cor. 15:26). [Note: The printed editions have “last.” Indeed, above at no. 22 there is “the last enemy.” But here the manuscripts, with great agreement, have “finally.”] The conquest of death is nothing other than resurrection from the dead; for, when destruction has ceased through the cessation of corruption, the eternity of a living and now heavenly nature is established, according to what was said: “For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality. But when this mortal has put on immortality, then the saying written shall come to pass: ‘Death has been swallowed up in contention. Where, O death, is your sting? Where, O death, is your contention?’” (1 Cor. 15:53). [Note: For the Greek *eis nikos* [εἰς νῖκος], “unto victory,” Hilary, or the interpreter whom he follows, read *eis neikos* [εἰς νεῖκος], “unto contention.” Indeed, in his exposition of Psalm 59, no. 14, he admits both readings together and combines them into one.]

Therefore in the subjection of enemies death is conquered; and when death has been conquered, the life of immortality succeeds. The Apostle himself has testified what that perfect character of subjection is after the subjection of faith, when he says: “He will transform the body of our lowliness, making it conformable [397] to the body of His glory, according to the working of His power, whereby He is able to subject all things to Himself” (Phil. 3:24). [Note: One Vatican manuscript, another Colbert manuscript, and the Sorbonne manuscript have “making [it] conformable,” as, above, book IX, no. 8, it was observed that some manuscripts read.] Thus this subjection is also a yielding from nature into nature: [Note: The Corbie codex bears in its margin, in an ancient hand, “Cautiously.” But the passage itself supplies its own caution, since it immediately adds: “He ceases, not in order that He may not be,” etc. Nor would I suppose that Hilary is being criticized by Augustine in *Sermon against the Arians*, ch. 37, where he says: “Although there were not lacking persons who thought that that future subjection of the Son should be understood as the transformation of His human form into the divine substance, as though a thing is subjected to that into which it is turned and changed.” We have already indicated at no. 14, from Augustine, *Against Maximinus*, book II, ch. 16, that this opinion belonged to the Arians themselves. Ambrose likewise attributes it to Sabellians and Marcionites in *On Faith*, book V, ch. 13, no. 162: “The Sabellians and Marcionites say that this future subjection of Christ to God the Father will be such that the Son is poured back into the Father.” But here Hilary’s word *natura*, “nature,” does not signify the substance of the bodies themselves, but their quality. This is plainly declared in his exposition of Psalm 2, no. 41: “He will repair the broken bodies, not by giving them some other matter, but by imparting to the old and original matter itself the appearance of beauty pleasing to Him; so that the resurrection of corruptible bodies into the glory of incorruption does not destroy nature by annihilation, but changes it by a condition of quality. For not one body, though it rises into another [condition], rises as another body,” etc. No less clear is the passage in the exposition of Psalm 55, no. 12. I think the holy Doctor said that nature is changed, though he meant only newness of qualities, because glorious endowments are not natural qualities of bodies, but rather certain prerogatives of the divine condition. Thus in all these passages he understands by “nature” a natural condition.]

In yielding to the form of that to which it is subjected, it ceases to be what it is in itself. But it ceases, not in order that it may not be, but in order that it may advance; and by the change it becomes subject, passing into the appearance of another kind which it has received.

### 36. The Son’s Subjection Is Participation in the Father’s Glory

Finally, so that the meaning of this mystery might be complete, after saying that death is finally conquered, he then says: “But when He says, ‘All things are subjected,’ it is plain that He is excepted who subjected all things to Him. Then the Son Himself will be subjected to Him who subjected all things to Him, that God may be all in all” (1 Cor. 15:26 ff.).

The first stage of the mystery, therefore, is that all things are subjected to Him; and then that He Himself becomes subject to the One subjecting all things to Him. Thus, just as we are subjected to the glory of His reigning body, by the same mystery [Note: Vatican-Basilica manuscript, one Colbert manuscript, another Sorbonne manuscript, and Martin’s manuscript: “He Himself reigning unto Himself.”] He Himself, reigning in the glory of His body, is subjected to the One who subjects the universe to Him. We are subjected to the glory of His body so that we may be in that brightness in which He reigns in the body, because we shall be conformed to His body. [Note: Printed editions: “the brightness of the body.” The word “body” is absent from the manuscripts. Here Hilary briefly explains his view of the entire mystery of subjection: just as we are subjected to Christ insofar as we are conformed to His glory, so Christ is subjected to God insofar as, according to His humanity, He becomes a participant in divine brightness. Compare, if you please, the exposition of Psalm 67, no. 37.]

### 37. The Glory of Christ’s Body

The Gospels indeed do not keep silent concerning the glory of His body now reigning. For it is written that the Lord said: “Amen, I say to you, there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in His kingdom” (Matt. 16:28). “And after six days Jesus took Peter, James, and John his brother, and led them apart up a high mountain. Jesus was transfigured before them; His face shone like the sun, and His garments became like snow” (Matt. 17:1–2).

Therefore the Apostles were shown the glory of the body coming into its kingdom. For the Lord stood in the appearance of His glorious [Note: Martin’s and Vatican-Basilica manuscripts: “transfiguration.” But at the end of the following section they agree with the others.] transformation, the brightness of His reigning body having been disclosed.

### 38. Participation in That Glory Is Promised Us

Promising the Apostles participation in this His glory, He says: “Thus it shall be at the consummation of the age. The Son of Man will send His angels, [398] and they will gather out of His kingdom all scandals and those who commit iniquity, and will cast them into the furnace of fire. There shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth. Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father. He who has ears [Note: The word “to hear” is absent in our codex.] [Note: The word “to hear” is lacking in almost all manuscripts, although it appears in the older Colbert manuscript.] to hear, let him hear” (Matt. 13:40 ff.).

Do not all persons have natural, bodily ears open for hearing the words, so that the Lord’s admonition would need to say, “Let him hear”? [Note: In Erasmus and Lipsius: “would have been necessary”; other books resist this reading, in which “would be necessary” has the same force.] But the Lord, intimating knowledge of the mystery, required the hearing of faithful teaching. Therefore at the consummation of the age scandals are removed from His kingdom. We thus have the Lord reigning according to the brightness of His body, until scandals are removed. Again, we have ourselves conformed to the glory of His body in the Father’s kingdom, shining as in the brightness of the sun—[Note: Vatican-Basilica manuscript and Martin’s manuscript: “in which appearance of His kingdom.” The Colbert manuscript omits “kingdom”; alter nothing. Relevant is the statement in Matthew, ch. 17, no. 2: “After six days the appearance of the Lord’s glory is shown . . . the honor of the heavenly kingdom is prefigured.”] the appearance of His kingdom which, transfigured on the mountain, He showed to the Apostles.

### 39. In Imparting Glory, He Delivers Us as a Kingdom to God Without Loss to His Own Kingdom. The Kingdom Delivered Is Ours. Christ Delivers It Also Insofar as He Is Man

He will therefore deliver the kingdom to God the Father, not as though by delivering it He surrenders power, but because we, made conformed to the glory of His body, shall be God’s kingdom. For He does not say, “He will deliver His own kingdom,” but, “He will deliver the kingdom” (1 Cor. 15:24): He will deliver us, made a kingdom to God by the glorification of His body. Therefore He will deliver us into the kingdom, in accordance with the Gospel saying: “Come, blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25:34).

Thus the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father. For the Son will deliver as a kingdom to God those whom He has called into the kingdom, to whom He has also promised the blessedness of this mystery, saying: [Note: “Blessed are the pure in heart,” with the Greek, *makarioi hoi katharoi tē kardia* [μακάριοι οἱ καθαροὶ τῇ καρδίᾳ].] “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8). Therefore, reigning, He will remove scandals, and then the righteous will shine like the sun in the Father’s kingdom. But He will deliver the kingdom to God the Father, and then those whom He has delivered as a kingdom to God will see God. [Note: We add the particle “and” from the manuscripts. Then after “what kingdom,” the verb “will deliver” is understood.] And what kingdom it is, He Himself testified in saying to the Apostles: “For the kingdom of God is within you” (Luke 17:21). Therefore, reigning, He will deliver the kingdom.

And if anyone asks who this is who delivers the kingdom, he will hear: “Christ rose from the dead, the firstfruits of those who sleep; for through man came death, and through man the resurrection of the dead” (1 Cor. 15:21). For the entire present discussion concerns the mystery of the body, because Christ is the firstfruits from the dead. But by what mystery Christ rose from the dead, let us learn from the Apostle, who says: “Remember [Note: “Jesus Christ,” with the Greek.] Christ risen from the dead, from the seed of David” (2 Tim. 2:8), thereby teaching that death and resurrection from it belong only to that dispensation in which there is flesh.

### 40. The Cause of Christ’s Subjection: That God May Be All in All; How This Occurs

But in this same body, now glorious, He reigns until, when the authorities have been abolished and death conquered, He subjects His enemies to Himself. The Apostle has indeed maintained this distinction: abolition is assigned to authorities and powers, but subjection to enemies. When these have been subjected, the Lord Himself will be subjected to the One subjecting all things to Him—namely God—[Note: “Namely God.”] [Note: Some manuscripts, together with the printed editions, have “namely God.” More correctly, the two sounder Colbert manuscripts, the German, Remigius, Sorbonne, and others have “namely the Lord.”] so that God may be all in all (1 Cor. 15:28): our assumed body’s nature will be brought into the nature of the Father’s divinity. [Note: The Remigius codex has: “the nature of our assumed body,” etc. Opposite this passage an ancient hand in the Corbie codex again wrote: “Read cautiously.” One need only guard against understanding the word “nature” otherwise than our Doctor understood it, who called the Father’s nature certain natural endowments of the Father’s divinity: incorruption, immortality, and so forth.]

For God will thereby be all in all because, according to the dispensation, the mediator of God and human beings, having in Himself, from the dispensation, what belongs to flesh, will obtain in all things through subjection what belongs to God; so that He may not be God in part, but wholly God. [Note: Vatican-Basilica codex with Martin’s: “what God is.” This would be less objectionable if we had not just had “what belongs to flesh.” The same doctrine of the Mediator is explained in different words in Psalm 67, no. 37.] Therefore there is no other cause for subjection than that God may be all in all, with no nature of the earthly body remaining in Him in any respect, [Note: Printed editions: “so that He contains two within Himself,” contrary to the authority of the manuscripts and Hilary’s meaning, who refers “two” not to persons but to natures, or rather to qualities of natures. [Col. 0425D] His meaning is this: before the glory of resurrection Christ contained in Himself two—namely man and God, mortal and immortal—and thus two because differing by contrary condition, in one person (the Vatican-Basilica and Martin manuscripts: “constituting [them]”); but now, enjoying the glory of resurrection, He is God alone, because through granted endowments of the divine nature—immortality, eternity, and so forth—the human has in a certain way been absorbed. Thus no nature of an earthly body remains in Him in any respect, insofar as it is earthly and corruptible. But lest this be twisted into an unsound meaning, he carefully adds: “not with the body cast off,” etc.]

Thus, whereas previously He contained two in Himself, He is now God alone—not by casting off the body, but by its transformation through subjection; not by its abolition through failure, but by its change through glorification. He rather acquires man for God than loses God through man. But He is subjected for this reason: not in order that He may not be, but in order that God may be all in all; possessing and retaining, in the mystery of subjection, what He is not, rather than, through failure, being so deprived of Himself that He is not. [Col. 0426A]

### 41. The Foregoing Is Confirmed from the Gospels

And although apostolic authority suffices for the reverent assurance of this understanding—that the Lord Jesus Christ, the firstfruits of those who sleep, must be subjected in time and according to the dispensation, so that God may be all in all—[Note: The Vatican-Basilica codex has: “the Lord in the time of the dispensation,” etc., which produces a sense foreign to Hilary’s thought. For he does not interpret Christ’s subjection of the time when He lives in mortal flesh, which is properly the time of the dispensation; rather, he teaches that Christ is to be subjected *in time*, and consequently insofar as He is subject to time, not insofar as He is eternal, and therefore through dispensation and not by natural necessity. From this he concludes that weakness in the divinity is wrongly inferred from that subjection. Ambrose says nearly the same in *On Faith*, book V, ch. 13, no. 164: “We see that Scripture records Him as not yet subjected, but as to be subjected . . . Therefore there is no servile subjection in Christ’s divinity.”] and that this is not weakness of divinity but the advancement of the assumption, since He who is man and God is now wholly God—[Note: The same manuscript has “He is wholly God.” Something has already been said above concerning the difference between *totus*, “whole,” and *totum*, “wholly.” The observation there that Hilary uses them indifferently is confirmed by this very book, in which we now read “He is wholly God,” while in the preceding section we read “He is whole God.”—] still, lest we be thought to have accepted that He is glorified in the body while He reigns in it, and is later to be subjected so that God may be all in all, without support also from the Gospels, the testimony of our faith must be established by the confession not only of apostolic sayings but also of the Lord’s sayings: so that what Christ spoke through Paul, Christ Himself had already spoken before Paul.

### 42. On the Glory of the Son of Man

Therefore, declaring to His Apostles the dispensation of this glory by the complete significance of His words, He says: “Now the Son of Man has been glorified, and God has been glorified in Him. If God has been glorified in Him, then God has glorified Him in Himself, and God immediately [Note: “Will glorify.”] glorified Him” (John 13:31–32). [Note: Bad., Erasmus, Lipsius, and a later Colbert manuscript have here and below “will glorify,” supported by the Greek verb *doxasei* [δοξάσει]; but immediately before, although the Greek likewise has *doxasei*, they nevertheless have “has glorified,” as it appears here in Par. and the other manuscripts—indeed in book IX, no. 40, in both manuscripts and printed editions.]

We have first the glory of the Son of Man, then the glory of God in the Son of Man, [Note: In the printed editions: “for in what was said”; a disordered and meaningless reading.] in the saying: “Now the Son of Man has been honored, and God has been honored in Him.” This first pertains to the glory of the body, [Note: We would prefer “which,” so that it might refer to the body; nor is “which then” in the Vatican-Basilica and Martin manuscripts—“from the association of the divine nature”—entirely pleasing. Here there is a subtle exposition of the cited Johannine words: they signify (1) the less complete glory of the Son of Man through association with the divine nature, which disclosed itself in divine works; (2) the glory of God the Father, which those same works of the Son secure for Him; and (3) the fuller glory of the Son of Man, granted after He has rendered honor to God through the resurrection, by which human nature passes into the divine in the manner already explained. When, finally, we shall be conformed to this, God will be all in all.] which borrows glory from association with the divine nature. Then follows the advance toward fuller glory, to be obtained through the increase of glory already granted to the body: “If God has been honored in Him, then God has glorified Him in Himself, and God immediately has glorified Him” (John 13:32).

For God has glorified Him in Himself because God has already been glorified in Him. For the fact that God has been glorified in Him pertains to the glory of the body, through which the glory of God has been understood through the body: the glory of God is to be understood through the glory of the Son [Note: In Bad., Erasmus, and Lipsius the word “Man” is absent. Then in three manuscripts the verb “is” is wrongly added after “to be understood.” The sense is this: since God’s glory must be understood through the glorious deeds of the Son of Man, through whose power those deeds were done.] of Man. But because God has been glorified in Him, [Note: We restore the particle “and” from the Colbert and German manuscripts.] God therefore glorified Him in Himself. Through the increase of the God glorified in Him, God glorified Him in Himself, so that, because He already reigns in glory, which is from God’s glory, He may thereafter pass into God’s glory.

For God glorified Him in Himself, that is, [Note: “In” is lacking.] [Note: The preposition “in,” absent from almost all manuscripts; when expressed, it removes ambiguity.] in the nature in which God is what He is, so that God may be all in all, [Note: Bad. and Erasmus: “all.” Then Lipsius: “now in God,” not badly, according to the statement in book IX, no. 7: “That the only-begotten God willed to be born, with the man abiding eternally in God.” Yet the received reading is confirmed by what follows. Thus “abiding transformed into God” means abiding forever in that state in which He was transformed into God, that is, never losing those divine endowments which He obtained through the advance of fuller glory.] abiding now wholly transformed into God through the dispensation by which He is man.

Nor indeed did He keep silent concerning the time, saying: “And God glorified Him in Himself, and God immediately glorified Him” (ibid.); so that, because Judas was going forth to betrayal, He signified in the present the glory which would follow Him after His passion [Note: Remigius’ manuscript has “going forth unto Judas’ betrayal,” against the other books, the sacred text, and the words above in book IX, no. 40, where this passage is discussed.] and resurrection, while reserving for the future the glory by which God would glorify Him in Himself. [Note: The printed editions, except Par., have “the resurrection that was to follow”; restored from the other books. This passage seems to support the reading noted above, “God will immediately glorify Him.” We think, however, that both the immediately preceding Johannine passage and the earlier apostolic passage are considered here, for the elucidation of which John’s words were introduced: from the two passages it is taught that one glory is bestowed on Christ in His own body, another in His members. The first, according to John, was given immediately after the resurrection; the other, according to Paul, is reserved for the future. Since Christ, as stated in book II, no. 25, and elsewhere, assumed the nature of the whole human race, it follows that He is not yet fully and perfectly glorious so long as the glory of anyone from the human race remains outstanding. When this has been given to all through Christ the mediator, God will be all in all, because all things will be subjected to Christ.]

God’s glory was shown in Him through the power of the resurrection, while He Himself will abide in God’s glory—that is, in God, all in all—through the dispensation of subjection.

### 43. Those Who Misunderstand the Subjection Are Rebuked
