And in this matter, how great is the folly of heretical madness: to deny God [Note: Three Vatican manuscripts, Martin’s, Remigius’, and others: “to despair of this concerning God.” Colbert and German manuscripts, with Erasmus, Lipsius, and Par.: “to despair in God.” The Vatican-Basilica codex alone: “to hope this of God.” With Bad. and the Corbie, Chartres, and other manuscripts, we prefer “to despair this of God,” that is, to deny that what they hope for themselves can belong to Christ as God.] what flatters their human hopes! [Note: “And that.”] That God, who is powerful to effect in man what man hopes, should be weak to effect this in Himself? [Note: In Bad., Erasmus, and the manuscripts: “and,” not “that.” Shortly afterward Lipsius and Erasmus, after Bad., omitted the verb “effecting.” The same thought is repeated shortly below in these words: “Should He be unable to confer upon Himself the whole of what God is?”]

Neither speech nor a rationally capable mind can say this: that God, bound by some natural necessity to provide for us, can confer no blessedness upon Himself—not because He requires advancement, who possesses the power of an untroubled nature, but because through the dispensation and mystery of great godliness, He who is God is also man, [Note: Printed editions: “who is God and man.” More aptly in the manuscripts: “who is God,” namely by nature, and through the dispensation is also man. Then “should be unable to confer this upon Himself” refers to the preceding statement: “Neither speech nor a rationally capable mind can say that.”] and should be unable to confer upon Himself the whole of what God is, when He will unquestionably grant even to us that we may be what we are not.

For the end of human life and death is resurrection, and the most certain reward of our warfare is incorruptible eternity: it does not remain for the continuance of punishment, but unceasingly endures for the fruit and delight of perpetual glory. Therefore, when this origin of our earthly bodies passes into the condition of a higher nature and is made conformable to the glory [Col. 0428B] of the Lord’s body, shall God, found in the form of a servant, though already glorified in the body according to that in which He is in the form of a servant, nevertheless not be conformed to God? Shall He who grants us the form of His glorified body be unable to bestow anything further upon His own body than upon us and Himself in common? [Note: We add “in” from the Vatican-Basilica manuscript, one Colbert manuscript, and another Sorbonne manuscript. By a similar manner of speaking above at no. 28: “because both, through an appointed end, have it in common not to be.”] [Note: “Have it in common with Himself.”]

For most heretics affirm the saying, “Then He will be subjected to Him who subjected all things to Him, that God may be all in all” (1 Cor. 15:28), in this manner: that the Son must therefore be subjected to God the Father in order that, through the Son’s subjection, the Father may be all in all—[Note: Thus the older Vatican-Basilica, Colbert, German, Martin, Corbie, and other manuscripts, though some omit the particle “and.” But the printed editions with Remigius have: “as though perfection of God is still lacking to Him”; and some other manuscripts have this too, omitting “to Him.”] as though God Himself still lacks perfection [Note: “Of God”; shortly afterward, “is to be understood, if God.”] which He must obtain through the Son’s subjection. Thus they understand Him as deprived of complete and blessed divinity, if, by the progress of time, He is to attain to being all in all.

### 44. Nothing Is Lacking to the Full God; Nothing Accrues to Him

For my own part, as one who understands God only through reverence, it seems no less impious to answer such persons than to side with them; and it is presumptuous to trust that one can speak, with words whose meaning is still narrower than understanding, about a nature that exceeds the grasp of the human mind—and first to question whether anything is lacking to God, whether He Himself is full, or whether anything remains for One already full to become fuller. [Note: “Remains to Him.”]

But if God, whose being always God is not from another, has an advance by which He may sometime be more, He can never reach the point at which nothing is lacking to Him. For a nature to which advancement remains is never understood to have advanced without some remaining increase; since a nature directed toward advancement, although always advancing, is always open to advancement. But what remains in perfect fullness and always is does not leave it open to itself to become fuller, because perfect fullness cannot admit an addition of fuller [Col. 0429B] fullness. [Note: In Bad., Erasmus, and Lipsius the words “of fuller, perfect fullness” are absent.] And this is the form of a pious understanding concerning God: that nothing is lacking to God, and that He is full.

### 45. The Apostle’s Example in Considering the Things of God

Moreover, the Apostle knows the kind of confession by which one must bear witness concerning God, saying: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are His judgments and unsearchable His ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been His counselor? Or who first [Note: In the Corbie manuscript, one Colbert manuscript, and a few others, here, in accordance with the Greek and the Vulgate: “gave to Him.” But below, no. 47, “to Him” occurs in none. Shortly above and below Erasmus, as usual, substituted “unsearchable” for “searchable.”] gave, and it shall be repaid to him? For from Him, and through Him, and in Him are all things. To Him be glory unto ages of ages.” [Note: The Verona codex adds “Amen” here, as it also appears in the Greek text.] (Rom. 11:33 ff.)

God is not circumscribed by an earthly mind (see book IV, no. 14); nor is this depth of His wisdom reached by the perception of understanding that penetrates it; nor are the judgments of His ordinances grasped by the intellect of those who investigate them; nor do the unsearchable paths of His knowledge abandon themselves to the pursuits of those who follow them. [Note: The preposition “in,” first deleted by Lipsius, is restored here from Bad., Erasmus, and the manuscripts.] All His things are plunged into an incomprehensible depth, and nothing concerning His things will be found or traced out. For no one has known His mind, and He did not need an external counselor.

But all this discourse is now about us, not also about Him through whom all things are, who is the Angel of Great Counsel [Col. 0430A] (Isa. 9:6), and who also says: “No one knows the Son except the Father; neither does anyone know the Father except the Son, and he to whom the Son wills to reveal Him” (Matt. 11:25). But against our weak minds, which plunge themselves into the depth of defining and circumscribing the divine nature, we must use the confession of apostolic declaration, lest rash [Note: “Opinion.”] opinion [Note: The manuscripts have “opinion.” Later the Vatican-Basilica codex and two others have “beyond what is fitting,” not “beyond what is taught.” Then Corbie, with several others, has “may appropriate.” “Opinion … beyond what is taught … may appropriate” would be quite satisfactory.] appropriate to itself something concerning God beyond what is taught.

46. What falls within human understanding. — [Textual notes: The manuscripts read “unless that which”; the Vatican manuscript, after “set before,” also has “opposite.” The printed editions read, “whether an object set before the eyes.” Almost all manuscripts and the printed editions read “one what”; “which” must certainly be read, with the Tellerian manuscript. The printed editions prefixed “while” to “yields,” against the manuscripts. The manuscripts read “which exists” (*quod sit*) for “which comes to be” (*quod fit*). The Veronese manuscript omits “to it.” The words “only” and “to it,” omitted in the printed editions, are supplied from the manuscripts; on their authority “of which its own” is restored as “of which he himself”—that is, the origin—is [the elder]. The Martin and Vatican manuscripts read: “not even merely of those things which are guarded by an eternal principle,” which is less apposite. Other manuscripts more correctly read: “much less merely of those [supply: causes], which are before it by an eternal principle”: if the mind does not comprehend what is before it by any principle, indeed it often fluctuates uncertainly over what is later than itself, and far less will it reach what precedes it by an eternal principle.] This is the common understanding of natural causes: nothing enters perception unless it is subject to perception—whether some object is set before the eyes, or some work is later than our very sense and mind. Of these, the one which is touched or seen yields itself to the judgment of our opinion, to be regulated by touch and sight; while the other, which occurs in time and is produced or established from some beginning later than ourselves, because it does not precede the perception of the understanding, is likewise subject to the judgment of the judging sense.

For neither does our sight judge invisible things, since it distinguishes only what is seen; nor will our mind extend itself into a time in which it did not exist and investigate things earlier than its own origin, since an opinion is left to it only concerning those things of which it is itself the elder. And this opinion, often uncertain through the necessity of its own natural weakness, does not hold absolute knowledge in the understanding of causes—much less can it, by a perception returning beyond its own birth, apprehend those causes which precede it by an eternal principle.

[Col. 0430C] 47. God is an unsearchable depth. He needs nothing. — [Textual note: Lipsius reads “ignorance”; the other editions with the manuscripts read “understanding.” We restore “incomprehensibility” (*inintelligentia*), as Erasmus conjectured it should be read; with manuscript support it is also read in Book X, §30.] Therefore the Apostle, since only those things which came after perception could ever fall within knowledge, having recalled the depth of God’s wisdom, the infinity of His unsearchable judgments, the hiddenness of His untraceable ways, the ignorance of His unknown mind, and the incomprehensibility of His uncommunicated counsel, added: “For who has first given to Him, and it shall be repaid to him? For from Him and through Him and in Him are all things. To Him be glory for ages of ages” (Rom. XI, 35–36).

God, who always is, is not subject to a mode or measure; nor is He anticipated by any motion of mind or understanding prior to Himself. And therefore He, wholly, is a depth that cannot be searched out or explored. He is wholly so, not as though thereby bounded within a mode, but as understood in immensity; for He received what He is from no one, nor did anyone first give to Him, so that a duty of repayment ought to be rendered to the giver. [Textual note: The manuscripts read “within a mode” (*in modum*), but the printed editions read “in a mode” (*in modo*).] For from Him and through Him and in Him are all things. He does not need things which remain from Him, through Him, and within Him—neither as their source, nor as their maker, nor as their container, nor as one external to things made and their creator; and He is never in need of His own things. [Textual notes: The word “and” is absent; shortly afterwards the Martin manuscript reads “external to internal things, a knower among things made,” which is wrong. “Creator of things made” is to be understood as saying that God does not need what He created, or that created things have God as their creator. The manuscripts supply “Himself,” omitted in the printed editions: “nothing is outside Himself.”] Nothing is before Him, nothing is from elsewhere, nothing is outside Him.

What increase in fullness, then, does He lack, so that God might still become all in all through time? Or whence will He receive, outside whom there is nothing? And this “nothing” is such that He Himself always is. [Textual note: An old Colbertine manuscript reads “He Himself is.”] He who Himself always is, and outside whom nothing exists—by what addition is He to be filled, or by what increase changed, when He says, “I am, and I do not change” (Mal. III, 6)? No room remains either for change, no cause for progress, nothing earlier than eternity, nor anything other than God in relation to God except God Himself. Therefore God will not become all in all through the subjection of the Son; nor will He be completed through some cause, when every cause subsists from, through, and within Him. God therefore remains as He always is; He does not require progress, for in order to be what He is, He is always from Himself and for Himself.

48. The Son is unchangeable. In emptying Himself He was not changed. God’s being all in all is our progress. — [Textual note: The printed editions read “because this”; the manuscripts more aptly read “who is for that end,” declaring that God is His own principle.] But neither does any necessity of a nature subject to change belong to the only-begotten God. For He is God, a name denoting full and perfect divinity. As we have taught above, both the signification of restored glory and the reason for subjection are that God may be all in all; but God’s being all in all is a mystery, not a necessity.

For, remaining in the form of God, He took the form of a servant—not changed, but emptying Himself, hiding Himself within Himself, and becoming empty within His own power. He moderated Himself down to the form of the human condition, so that the weakness of the humility He had assumed might bear His mighty and immeasurable nature; the unbounded power moderated itself to the extent necessary for it to submit to the capacity for suffering of the body joined to itself. But in containing Himself while emptying Himself within Himself, He did not inflict loss upon His power; for, within the humility of this self-emptying, He nevertheless exercised every power that He had emptied within Himself.

49. Therefore, God’s becoming all in all is the progress of our assumption. For He who, though in the form of God, was found in the form of a servant, must again be confessed in the glory of God the Father; so that He may without ambiguity be understood to remain in the form of Him in whose glory He will be confessed. Thus there is an economy only, not a change: for He is in that which He was.

But since the intermediate reality is that which began to be—namely, the man who was born—the whole is acquired for that nature which previously was not God, when, after the mystery of the economy, God is shown to be all in all. [Textual note: The Martin manuscript alone reads “through the mystery,” less correctly. Christ’s three states are considered here: in the form of God, in the form of a servant, and in the glory of God the Father. The middle state is called the mystery of the economy, which received fellowship in the Father’s glory.] These, therefore, are our gains and our advancement: namely, that we are to be made conformed to the glory of God’s body. But the only-begotten God, although He was also born a man, is nevertheless nothing other than God all in all.

For that subjection of the body, through which what is fleshly in Him is swallowed up into the nature of the Spirit, will establish Him—who besides being God is also man—as God all in all; whereas that man of ours advances into this. [Textual notes: “In Him” (*ei*), absent in the printed editions, is restored from the manuscripts. This rests on the Apostle’s words, “A spiritual body shall rise.” Explaining them, Augustine, *Against Adimantus* 12.4, says that a body called spiritual in the resurrection is not thereby thought not to be a body but spirit; it is called spiritual because it is wholly subject to spirit without corruption or death. As already seen, Hilary agrees, except that Augustine understands the spiritual body as subject to our spirit, Hilary to the divine Spirit. Thus in *On Psalm IX* 4 he says that, through the subjection of obedience to God, the weakness of the assumed humanity is absorbed into the divine nature. What obeys remains, but the natural condition of flesh—or, as §40 calls it, of the earthly body, to which corruption is due of itself—does not remain, so that it may pass into God’s natural condition, wholly free from corruption. The Vatican manuscript reads “in God”; one Colbertine and another Sorbonne manuscript, “advanced in Him.” It is noteworthy that “our man” is distinguished from “us”: Hilary calls “our man” the nature assumed by Christ.]

But we shall advance into conformity with the glory of our man, and, renewed in the knowledge of God, shall be refashioned according to the image of the Creator, according to the Apostle’s saying: “Having put off the old man with his deeds and put on the new, who is renewed in the knowledge of God according to the image of Him who created him” (Col. III, 9–10). [Textual note: A variant reads “in the knowledge” (*in agnitione*). The older manuscripts omit “him” after “created”; the Martin manuscript previously reads, “Put off the old man … and put on.”]

Thus man, the image of God, is brought to perfection. For, made conformed to the glory of God’s body, he rises into the image of the Creator, according to the appointed pattern of the first man. And after sin and the old man, the new man, made in the knowledge of God, receives the perfection of his constitution: acknowledging his God, and thereby His image; advancing through religion unto eternity, and through eternity destined to remain the image of his Creator.

407–408. BOOK TWELVE

Against the customary assertions of the heretics—“He was not before He was born,” and “He was made from non-existent things”—Hilary maintains the eternal and divine birth of Christ. Against those who wish Him to be a creature because, speaking in the person of Wisdom, He said of Himself, “The Lord created me,” Hilary argues:

1. Christ is worshipped, whereas worship of a creature is forbidden.

2. All things were created through Him, and “Creator” is His proper name.

3. It cannot apply to Him that He should hope, serve, be subjected unwillingly, or need to be liberated—conditions to which, according to the Apostle, every creature is subject.

4. Since the form of God is the nature of God, if Christ, remaining in the form of God, is a creature, the Father also will be a creature.

5. Equal honour is to be rendered to the Father and the Son.

6. By the name “womb,” the Father signifies that He begot Him from His own substance.

Finally, the Father nowhere calls Him anything but His own Son, nor does He call God anything but His own Father. By contrast, other sons are described as made, not born; nor are they anywhere granted the designation of possession. For when God says, “I have begotten sons,” He does not add “my”; but when He says, “Israel is my firstborn son,” “my” applies to “firstborn,” not to “son.”

He then treats the eternity of Christ’s birth, differing from the origin of other things in that they come to be through a cause arising from nothing, after a time in which they did not exist; while He, since He is from Him who is, has never been subject either to not existing at some time or to a cause from nothing.

When they object, “If He was born, there was some time when He was not; for He was not before He was born,” he answers that the Son, born of the eternal Father, is equally eternal.

To their reply, “Everything born did not exist, because it was born in order to exist,” he concedes this concerning human things, but denies it concerning divine things. For as the Father always is, so too the Son always is; and His birth, being before eternal times, is subject neither to time nor to our perception.

They press: “If one does not perceive that He was not before He was born, one must perceive that He who was, was born.” The answer is that one who is proclaimed born is not perceived as having existed beforehand, just as one who is understood always to be born is not understood to have at some time not existed.

Nor do they more effectively invent that God was not always Father; for from the words of Solomon, David, and Paul the Son’s eternity is unambiguous. Wisdom demonstrates it so clearly by declaring not merely that she was founded before the ages, but also that she was present at the eternal preparation of things and therefore coeternal with eternal things, that a Jew may readily be convicted from this that Christ existed before Mary.

The fact that Wisdom calls herself created might perhaps trouble us, had she not also taught that she was begotten. Nor should she be thought to have expressed the same thing in two words: she professes that she was created for a cause, but begotten before the cause.

Likewise, while she teaches that the Father is the maker of the world, she destroys the impious interpretation by which they construe her as created for works, so that Christ was first made in order to make the world. For Christ was called created for works with reference, not to His birth, but to His economy—an economy which He carried out from the beginning of the world, when, in the assumed appearance of diverse creatures, He made Himself visible to Adam, Cain, Abel, Noah, Hagar, Abraham, Moses, Jacob, and the other patriarchs.

Here is touched upon, though not rejected as impious but as uninstructed, the interpretation of some who think that even the eternal birth is called “created” there in approximately the same way that Paul may proclaim Christ truly born from Mary yet nevertheless “made”—namely, so that every notion of suffering in His generation may be removed. At last Hilary concludes this book, and the whole work, with a confession of his faith concerning the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

1. The very objections of the heretics lead to the truth. — [Textual note: The very ancient Vatican manuscript, together with the Tellerian, Remigian, Theodorian, and Cistercian manuscripts, gives this opening: “Read, brother in Christ, and apply your understanding.” Then, with the others, it has “We make for,” etc.] We are at last making for the safe and tranquil harbour of secure faith, with the Holy Spirit now accompanying us. And it happens as it often happens to those who have been tossed about by much sea and wind: when burdensome and heavy waves sometimes delay them around the shores of harbours, at last the very surge of the great and terrible swell drives them into a familiar and trustworthy anchorage.

This, I hope, will happen to us as we labour in this twelfth book against the heretical storm: while we expose our fortified vessel to the wave of most grievous impiety, that very wave may carry us into the haven of the desired peace. For all who are driven about by the uncertain wind of doctrine find here fear, here danger, and here often shipwreck, because under prophetic authority the only-begotten God is defended as a creature; so that in Him there is not birth but creation, because it is said in the person of Wisdom: “The Lord created me, the beginning of His ways” (Prov. VIII, 22). [Textual note: The same manuscripts, with the Martin manuscript, add here, “in His work.”] This is the greatest wave of their winter; this is the heavy billow of the twisting tempest. Once we have met it and broken it with a secure vessel, it will carry us onward even to the utterly safe harbour of the desired shore.

2. The certain truth of faith concerning the Son. — [Textual notes: The printed editions read “unconquerable,” against the great consensus of manuscripts. There is an antithesis between the spirits of the winds, which often desert sailors, and the Spirit of faith, who never departs from believers. True faith is likewise opposed to the perversity of the heretics, who are shortly convicted of dividing the prophetic and evangelical Spirit. Perhaps Christ’s words are also intended: “Behold, I am with you unto the consummation of the age.” The Badius edition with all manuscripts reads: “because He Himself is not [a creature]”; other editions have the gloss, “because He Himself is He who created all things; nor a thing made,” etc.] Yet we do not rely, like sailors, upon uncertain and idle hopes. Those who sail sometimes more by wishes than by confidence are abandoned or driven away by wandering and unstable winds. But the inseparable Spirit of faith is present with us, abiding through the gift of the only-begotten God and leading us by an unchanging course into calm waters.

For we know that the Lord Christ is neither a creature—because He Himself is not one—nor a thing made, because He is Lord of all things made; but God, the proper generation of God the Father. All of us indeed, according to the gracious condescension of His goodness, are called and adopted sons of God; but He is the one true Son of God the Father, and the true and absolute birth, abiding only in the knowledge of the two.

This alone is our religion: to confess the Son not as adopted but as born, not as chosen but as begotten. For we do not proclaim Him either made or not born, because we neither compare the Creator with creatures nor falsely assert a birth without generation. He who exists through birth does not exist through Himself. Nor is He unbegotten who is Son. And He who is Son cannot be what He is as Son except by being born.

3. Among the Arians, the prophetic and evangelical Spirit is at war with itself. — [Textual notes: The printed editions read, with “or” omitted, “that these now,” and later, “divide and partition into quarrels, that these otherwise,” etc.; the manuscripts are followed. The printed editions read “according to an understanding of God’s piety”; the Paris edition omits “God.” The manuscripts read “according to the understanding of impiety”: that is, although these things do not agree with one another, they must nevertheless be conceded if the understanding of the impious Arians is sound. Hilary frequently uses an abstract noun for a concrete one, for example “impiety” for “the impious.”] No one can doubt that the grounds of impiety are always contrary and opposed to the grounds of religion, nor that something cannot be piously undertaken when it is decided that it has been impiously undertaken. Accordingly, either these new reformers of apostolic faith now divide the evangelical and prophetic Spirit into disputes and partition Him into quarrels, or the prophets prophesied one way and the Apostles preached another: because Solomon calls us to venerate a creature, while Paul rebukes those who serve a creature.

These things, according to the understanding of impiety, do not appear consistent with one another: that the Apostle—taught through the Law and set apart by foreordination (Gal. I, 15), and speaking through Christ who spoke in him (II Cor. XIII, 3)—either did not know prophecy or annulled what he knew; that he did not know Christ to be a creature, though he called Him Creator; and that he forbade the worship of a creature, though he taught that the Creator alone must be served, saying: “They changed the truth of God into a lie, and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed for ages of ages” (Rom. I, 25).

[Col. 0436A] 4. Christ is properly called Creator. — [Textual notes: An older Colbertine manuscript with the German manuscript reads “that He may be a creature.” The Vatican manuscript with the Martin manuscript reads “Lord,” not “God.” Gillot substituted Isaiah for Hosea because he did not find this in Hosea in the Vulgate, though similar words occur at Isaiah 45:12. Yet in the Septuagint the same words occur verbatim; the Vulgate has only, “But I am the Lord your God.” Gillot’s correction, retained in the Paris edition, is therefore pointless. Badius, Erasmus, and Lipsius subsequently read “forming heaven,” not “establishing.” Erasmus, contrary to the authority of the old books, added “surnames” here; subsequent editions retained it.] Does Christ God, speaking in Paul, insufficiently expose this impiety of false speech? Does He insufficiently condemn the lie of truth altered? For all things were created through the Lord Christ; and therefore “Creator” is His proper name. Neither the nature nor the designation of what He Himself brings into being can apply to Him.

Melchizedek is a witness for us, proclaiming God as Creator of heaven and earth: “Blessed be Abraham by God Most High, who created heaven and earth” (Gen. XIV, 19). The prophet Hosea also bears witness, saying: “I, the Lord your God, establish heaven and create earth, whose hands created all the host of heaven” (Hos. XIII, 4). Peter too writes: “Entrusting your souls as to a faithful Creator” (I Pet. IV, 19). Why do we impose the name of the work upon its maker? Why do we name God from ourselves? He is our Creator; He is the Creator of all the heavenly host.

5. Christ cannot be called a creature. — [Textual notes: Erasmus again inserted on his own authority “which were made”; it was not subsequently corrected. On “who subjected it in hope,” the Greek reads *ton hypotaxanta ep’ elpidi* (τὸν ὑποτάξαντα ἐπ᾽ ἐλπίδι), “the one who subjected [it] in hope.” The Vatican and Martin manuscripts read “who subjected all things”; the Chartres manuscript, “who subjected them.” A Vatican manuscript with the Martin manuscript reads “may rather await our revelation.” A reading closer to Hilary’s meaning would be “may rather await our glory,” which he indicates is impossible because Christ already enjoys His own glory, which He will communicate to us, and does not await a glory common to us. The words “that He may be known,” preserved only by Miraeus’ edition though supported by the manuscripts, should undoubtedly be restored as “that He may be corrupted,” in view of Paul’s “the creation itself shall be liberated from the bondage of corruption” and Hilary’s “if He is a slave, He remains in the corruption of nature.”] Since these things are to be understood of the Son, through whom all things were made, according to apostolic and evangelical faith, how can He be equated with those very things which He made, and bear the natural designation under which all things are? First, human reason rejects this: that the Creator should be a creature, because creation is through the Creator. If He is a creature, then He is subject to corruption, bound to expectation, and subjected to slavery.

For the same blessed Apostle Paul says: “For the eager expectation of the creature awaits the revelation of the sons of God. For the creature was subjected to vanity, not willingly, but because of Him who subjected it in hope. For the creature itself also will be delivered from the slavery of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the sons of God” (Rom. VIII, 19 ff.).

If, then, Christ is a creature, He must be uncertain under the hope of a distant expectation; His long expectation must wait rather for our revelation; and, while waiting, He must be subject to vanity and, through the subjection of necessity, not voluntarily subject. But if subjected unwillingly, He must also be a slave; and if a slave, He must remain in the corruption of nature. For the Apostle teaches that all these are proper to a creature, which, to be liberated through long expectation, will shine according to human glory.

O imprudent and impious confession concerning God—to assign Him, through the insult of calling Him a creature, to these indignities: that He should hope, serve, be compelled, be corrupted, and be liberated in our condition rather than in His own, though we are advanced from His own things to something higher.

6. If the Son is a creature, the Father also is a creature, because the Son possesses the Father’s nature. The emptying of the Word is abolition. — [Textual notes: The printed editions read “so that He should not be”; some manuscripts, “lest He should not be”; the older manuscripts, “lest He be.” Hilary very commonly uses *ne* for “so that not.” In Miraeus’ edition, as in the Vatican and Martin manuscripts, “His own” is added here. That power remained in Christ in such a way that He sometimes used it has been proved in the preceding book, §48.] But our impiety proceeds with a vast increase of faithlessness through the audacity of this unlawful word: if the Son is a creature, then the Father too does not differ from a creature. For Christ, remaining in the form of God, took the form of a servant. If He who is in the form of God is a creature, then God cannot be apart from creature, because a creature is in the form of God.

But to be in the form of God means nothing other than to remain in God’s nature; and thus God also is a creature, because a creature is in His nature. He who was in the form of God did not seize equality with God, because from equality with God—that is, from His form—He was to descend into the form of a servant. But He could not descend from God into man unless God emptied Himself from the form of God.

Yet in emptying Himself He was not abolished, so as not to be, though He had become other than He had been. For He who emptied Himself into Himself did not fail from Himself, since the power of His might remains even in the power of emptying Himself. And to have passed into the form of a servant is not to have lost the nature of God, since emptying the form of God is nothing other than the power of divine might.

7. The Son is owed honour equal to the Father. — [Textual notes: The same manuscripts read “there is diversity in honour”; see Book IX, §23. The manuscripts read: “for either the highest honour will be unworthily rendered to inferior things, or inferior things will be equated with them in honour to the dishonour of superior things.” Erasmus and Miraeus with several later manuscripts read “if co-creation”; Lipsius and Paris, with an old Colbertine manuscript, “if creation”; the Vendôme manuscript, “as creation.” “If, as creation rather than birth, [He] is equated with the Father by veneration” is acceptable: restoring “if as creation” from Badius and the Vatican, Corbie, Remigius, Martin, and other manuscripts, one understands the unspoken “so” before “as.” The printed editions read “by which He will be equated”; “by which” occurs only in one very suspect Colbertine manuscript.] Indeed, to be in the form of God means nothing other than to be equal to God, so that equality of honour is due to the Lord Jesus Christ, who is in the form of God, as He Himself says: “That all may honour the Son as they honour the Father. He who does not honour the Son does not honour the Father who sent Him” (John V, 23).

A diversity of things is never present unless there is also diversity of honour. For things that are the same receive the same veneration; otherwise either the highest honour will be unworthily rendered to inferior things, or inferior things will be equated in honour with superior ones, to the dishonour of the latter. But if the Son, as a creature rather than a birth, is equated with the Father by veneration, then we have no religion of honour toward the Father, since such veneration of Him is imposed upon us as belongs to a creature. But because He is equal to God the Father in that He was born God from Him, He is equal also in honour. For He is Son, not creature.

8. God, who has no parts, is said to have begotten from the womb because He begot from Himself. Those who make the Son from nothing cannot account for this expression. — [Textual notes: Lipsius substituted “perfect and unchangeable substance,” which Erasmus had entered in the margin, apparently indicating Hilary’s meaning rather than his words. Lipsius and Paris, from Erasmus’ margin, read “of human births,” against all the manuscripts. “Necessities” here are the things necessarily required, according to natural laws, for a given result. Thus after “the property of human necessities,” one may appropriately supply, with reference to generation, “is contained within the causes of the womb.” The Martin manuscript reads “certainly” (*profecto*). Erasmus preferred “our generations,” which Lipsius fruitlessly took from his margin and which was not corrected in Paris; here the subject is not so much the act of generation as its material cause. Miraeus adds “from the womb” after “displays”; it occurs in many manuscripts but not the more carefully corrected ones.] This, moreover, is the Father’s glorious utterance concerning Him: “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot You.”

As we have often said, God is not prejudiced by the weakness of our understanding, as if, because He said that He begot from the womb (Ps. CIX, 5), He consisted of internal and external parts joined through limbs, as though upon the origins of bodily causes. Rather, free and absolute beyond the causality of natural necessities, remaining Lord of all nature, He indicates through the power of His unchangeable nature the proper character of the birth of His only-begotten Son.

For spirit born from spirit, although born from the property of spirit through which it too is spirit, has no cause other than perfect and unchangeable causes for that which is born. And although born from a perfect and unchangeable cause, it must be born from that cause in the property of the cause itself. The property of human necessities lies within the causes of the womb.

But for God, who is perfect not by parts but unchangeable through Spirit—for “God is Spirit” (John IV, 24)—there is no natural necessity of internal causes. Yet because He preached to us a birth of spirit from Spirit, He instructed our understanding by the example of our own causes—not as an example of birth, but for an understanding of generation; so that the example may serve not necessity but understanding. If, then, the only-begotten God is a creation, what is the meaning of the intelligible signification which, through the customary character of human birth, displays an understanding of divine generation?

9. Through the members of our body God’s operations are signified. — [Textual notes: The source citation reads, “Jesse’s son, a man after my heart”; “man” was added from the Vatican, Martin, and several other manuscripts, supported by the Greek text. The difficult sentence on the birth from the womb is corrupt in the witnesses. Lipsius and Paris, with the Corbie manuscript and a few others, read: “the effect must be understood not through a bodily cause of human origin, [but] an understanding of an intelligible birth is supplied”; although this reading is certainly interpolated, it cannot confidently be corrected, since all other readings are faulty. Badius, Erasmus, and the Martin manuscript read: “an understanding of a birth to be understood not through a bodily cause is supplied”; Miraeus: “an understanding of an intelligible birth, to be understood not through a bodily cause of human origin, is supplied”; one Vatican manuscript and one manuscript of the Minims near Tours: “the birth is to be understood not through the cause of bodily things, without effect”; older Colbertine, Remigius, Vatican, Chartres, German, and Vendôme manuscripts: “not through a bodily cause of birth to be understood without affection/effect.” From these the editors propose: “the effect is not to be understood through a bodily cause of birth, since through the other …” Some manuscripts read “of bodily members,” and shortly afterwards “of spiritual efficacies”; this is a gloss.]

For often, through these members of our bodies, God signifies to us the functions of His operations and instructs our understanding through the use of common understanding. Thus He says: “Whose hands created all the host of heaven” (Hos. XIII, 4); or again, “The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous” (Ps. XXXIII, 16); or again, “I have found David, son of Jesse, a man after my heart” (Acts XIII, 22).

For will is signified in the heart, by which David pleased God through excellence of character; knowledge of all things—such that nothing is beyond God’s knowledge—is expressed under the designation of eyes; and the effective power of works, because nothing exists except from God, is understood through the name of hands. Thus God, who wills, foresees, and accomplishes all things, must be understood under the signification of bodily causes, yet without bodily ministry. So too, in saying that He begot from the womb, He supplies an understanding of a spiritual birth, not through a bodily cause of human origin. [The transmitted wording is corrupt and materially uncertain; see the preceding textual note.] Since through the other significations of bodily members the effect of His other operations is likewise demonstrated in God—
10. “From the womb” is said to demonstrate true birth. — Since, then, the heart is put forward for will, the eyes for sight, the hand for action—although God both wills, foresees, and accomplishes beyond the unformed comparison of bodily parts, and these same things are expressed through heart, eyes, and hand—is not the expression by which He “begot from the womb” a demonstration of true birth? Not that He begot from a womb, just as He neither acts through a hand nor sees through eyes nor wills through a heart; but because, through the signification of these things, He truly acts, sees, and wills in all things, so through the signification of the womb He truly begot from Himself Him whom He begot—not because of a womb, but for the confession of the truth. Thus He neither wills, sees, nor acts by bodily causes, but uses these names of parts so that, through bodily ministrations, the power of incorporeal operations may be understood.

> [Note: Col. 0439D] In Erasmus only, and in Miraeus, “beyond”; then in the Leipzig and Paris editions, “the imperfect comparison of parts.” Since this occurs only in a second hand in the Corbie manuscript, we restore “the unformed comparison” on the authority of Bad., Erasmus, and the other manuscripts. Yet we scarcely doubt that *inceptam* (“begun”) should be preferred, especially since we read in Psalm 129, no. 4: “Whatever is composite cannot have been eternal, because composition has a beginning by which it is embodied (or compared; perhaps even more correctly, ‘is joined together’) so as to remain.”

> [Note: Col. 0440D] Thus Bad. with most and the better manuscripts. Other books: “God begot God from the womb.”

> [Note: Col. 0440D] There is nothing hitherto or subsequently about ears, so that, as in the Vatican base manuscript and Miraeus, “nor hears through ears” should be inserted here.

> [Note: Col. 0440D] In Erasmus, Leipzig, and Paris, *genuinae* (“genuine”) is added here; it is absent from Bad. and the older manuscripts and is not preferable to Martin’s reading, “for the truth of confession,” since “truth” here has the same force as true generation, true birth.

11. The Prophet does not call Him a work whom God testifies to be Son. — The nature of ordinary human relations does not allow, nor does the tenor of the Lord’s teaching permit, a teacher to be subject to a disciple or a servant to command a master: that one should be subject to another through ignorance, as the ignorant to the knowing, or should be weaker by condition, as slavery to lordship. Since this is the common judgment of all, by what example of rashness shall we say or think that God is a creature and the Son a work, when neither Teacher nor Lord has anywhere spoken this concerning Himself to His servants and disciples, nor taught His birth, creation, or making? Rather, the Father has never testified to anything other than “Son,” and the Son has professed nothing other than God as His own Father. Declaring Himself born—not made or created—as He says: “Everyone who loves the Father also loves the Son who has been born from Him” (John 5:1).

> [Note: Col. 0440D] In two Colbert manuscripts, “concerning the law,” not “concerning Himself”; this is absent from the older manuscript and from Remigius. In Martin, “this Himself,” without *concerning*.

> [Note: Col. 0440C] The words “declaring Himself” are absent from our manuscript.

> [Note: Col. 0440D] We add “declaring Himself” on the authority of the Vatican base, Colbert, Sorbonne, Faur., and other manuscripts. In place of these, one Remigius manuscript with Theodorus has: “Therefore, born—not made or created—as He says.”

12. The name “Son” does not suit a work. — Things made are works of creatures, not the birth of generation. The heaven is not a son, nor the earth a son, nor the world a birth—concerning which it is said, “All things were made through Him” (John 1:3); and through the Prophet, “The heavens are works of Your hands” (Psalm 101:26); and again through him, “Do not forsake the works of Your hands” (Psalm 137:8). Is a painting the painter’s son, a sword the smith’s son, or a house the architect’s son? These are works of those who produce them; but for a father, only he who is born from him is a son.

13. We were made, not born, sons of God, and therefore are not His own. — We too are sons to God, but sons through making. For we were once “sons of wrath” (Ephesians 2:3); but we have been made sons to God through the Spirit of adoption, and we deserve to be called this rather than are born so. And because everything which is made was not before it was made, we, who were not sons, are made into that which we are. For formerly we were not sons; but after we received this gift, we are sons. We are not born, but made; not generated, but acquired. For God acquired a people for Himself (1 Peter 2:9), and through this He begot them. Yet we never recognize that God has begotten sons with the implication of proper possession. For He does not say, “I begot and exalted My sons,” but only, “I begot and exalted sons” (Isaiah 1:2).

14. Objection: Israel too is called both “His own” and “made.” — Unless perhaps, when He says, “Israel is My firstborn son” (Exodus 4:22), someone will understand His saying “My firstborn” as detracting from the Son’s proper character of generation: so that, because He also said “My” concerning Israel, the designation of sons made by adoption is employed in place of the proper character of birth. And thus what was said of Him—“This is My beloved Son” (Matthew 17:5)—would not be proper to God’s birth, since “My” is also said to be proper to those who are plainly not born. That they are not born, though they are called born, is taught also when it is said: “For the people that shall be born, whom the Lord made” (Psalm 21:32).

15. Israel is not a proper son, but a proper firstborn. He is not properly a son who came to be though formerly he was not. — Therefore the people Israel is born so as to be made; and by the fact that it is said to be born, it is not thereby understood not also to be made. For it is sonship by adoption, not by generation; and it possesses not the reality but the name. For although “My firstborn” is written concerning it, “My beloved Son” and “My firstborn son” differ widely and greatly. Where there is birth, there is “My beloved Son”; but where there is election from among the nations and adoption by will, there is “My firstborn son.” Here, His being “His own” belongs to “firstborn”; there, His being “His own” belongs to “Son.”

And in birth, He is first Son in His own right and then beloved; in election, he is first son as firstborn and then afterward His own. Thus, for Israel, adopted as a son from among all peoples, it is proper that he is firstborn; but for God alone, who is born, it is manifestly proper that He is Son. For there is no true and perfect birth where one is assigned rather than generated; since it is beyond doubt that a people which is born into sonship is also made. But what comes to be though it formerly was not, and is said to be born through that by which it was made, does not possess true birth, because before it was born it was something other than that which was born. Therefore it was not a son before it was born—that is, before it was made—because one who is a son from among the nations is a nation before being a son; and for this reason is not truly a son, because he is not always a son.

But the only-begotten God neither ever was not Son, nor was anything before being Son, nor was He Himself anything but Son. And thus He who is always Son has left no room for the thought that He was ever not so.

> [Note: Col. 0441C–D] “Shall be born,” then: “and by the fact that it is born, it shall not be understood...” The Vatican base exemplar here reads thus; this is what must be tacitly understood. Soon afterward, in several manuscripts of good quality: “and by the fact that it is born.”

> [Note: Col. 0441D] “And in the birth of the Son”; shortly thereafter, “and in the election of the Son.”

> [Note: Col. 0441D] In the older Colbert, Remigius, and other manuscripts, the word *son* is lacking; in its place Bad., Erasmus, Leipzig, and many manuscripts read *of the Son*. This is preferable if, later, with the same editions and nearly all manuscripts, “and in the election of the Son” is prefixed. The reading retained is that of Paris, the Martin manuscript, and some others.

> [Note: Col. 0441D] The Vatican base manuscript reads “but in birth”; this is less satisfactory. Then the printed editions, except Paris, read “the only-begotten God”; they present Hilary’s thought in a weakened form, since he means that being Son is proper to one God alone—that is, to God alone who is born.

> [Note: Col. 0441D] The negative particle omitted in the printed editions is supplied from the manuscripts, whose older copies repeatedly, as elsewhere, read “before he is born.” Immediately after *was made*, as earlier after *was not*, *son* is left unspoken.

> [Note: Col. 0442C] “Before he is born.”

> [Note: Col. 0442D] Vatican base, supported by Martin: “and by that fact, because He is not truly Son, He is a nation”—the work of an unwise interpolator.

> [Note: Col. 0442D] We restore the word *not*, first deleted by Erasmus against the resistance of the manuscripts. It is a pleonasm common both among Greeks and in Hilary; it does not remove the force of the first negation but increases it, as though saying, “nor indeed was He ever not Son.”

> [Note: Col. 0442D] Printed editions: “anything else Himself.” But manuscripts read: “anything Himself,” except that the old Colbert and German manuscripts have “anything to Him.”

16. In human affairs, it is common both to have once not existed and to be from nothing. — Human births have a temporal “not having been”: first, because all are born from those who themselves formerly were not. For although each person born has his origin from one who existed, that very person from whom he is born did not exist before he was born. Then the one who has been born is born after not having existed, while the time before his birth remains. For one born today did not exist in what was yesterday; and he began to be what he is from what he was not. It lies within our understanding that what is born today did not exist yesterday. Thus his birth, by which he exists, remains after what he was not, because it is necessary that today should first exist after yesterday’s time, so that he may have had a temporal nonexistence.

These things are common in the origin of human beings: all receive a beginning of themselves after previously not existing—first, as we have shown, by time; then by cause. By time, it is unquestionable that things which have now begun did not exist earlier. By cause, it is so because they have no subsisting existence from a cause. Review every cause of origins and turn your thought back toward what preceded: you will find that nothing began by cause, while all things are created by God’s power into what they are, not born from something. Hence it is natural even to every kind through succession itself both not to have been and to have begun, since it exists in time after time. And since all things are always after time, they also take their cause from things that did not previously exist, while they are born from things that had not existed: Adam himself, the first parent of the human race, was formed from earth—which is from nothing—and after time, that is, after heaven, earth, day, sun, moon, and stars; he had no origin by birth and began though he had not been.

> [Note: Col. 0442D] That is, not from the substance of a first cause; therefore they have their beginning from nothing. Our attention is here called back even to our first parents, so that we may be shown to derive our origin from those made from nothing.

> [Note: Col. 0443C] When Scultetus charges Hilary with thinking, against Moses, that God created all things simultaneously and at once, and adduces as proof of this judgment only Book XII *On the Trinity*, he thereby shows that even elsewhere he was not a sufficiently fair judge of the opinions defended by the Fathers. Certainly, if man was formed after time because after heaven, earth, and so forth, it does not follow that all things were not created simultaneously and at once.

> [Note: Col. 0443C] That is, his first origin is not birth from a parent’s substance, but creation from nothing.

17. The only-begotten neither ever was not, nor is He from nothing. — But for the only-begotten God, over whom no earlier time rules, no possibility remains that He ever was not; because the very expression “at some time” already implies a prior time, and then “not having been” is already a matter of time. Nor will time begin after Him; rather, He Himself would be after time, if, in the fact that He was not before He was born, that very state in which He was not were set before Him. Further, He who is born from Him who is cannot be understood to have been born from that which was not; because He who is is His cause toward being what He is, whereas that which is not is not an origin of birth. Therefore, for Him, neither in time is there the possibility that He ever was not, nor in the Father—that is, in the Author—the possibility that He subsists from nothing. He has left no occasion for thinking either that He was born from nothing or that He was not before He was born.

> [Note: Col. 0443D] The very oldest manuscripts read *ipsud illud* (“that very thing”). Then the printed editions, except Paris, read, “at some time is already a matter of time,” and “and time will begin,” etc.; these are restored from other books. This contains a very weighty argument against the Arians, who in their formulae—the Antiochene, both Sirmian formulae, the pseudo-Sardican, and others—professed the Son to be before ages and times.

> [Note: Col. 0443C] “May be set before.”

> [Note: Col. 0443C] “Because He who is.”

> [Note: Col. 0443D] Printed editions read: “because His who is”; Leipzig and Paris then have, “the Father is the cause toward being what He is.” They are corrected from the manuscripts. Above it was shown that our origin is from nothing and not from a cause; now the Son’s origin is shown to be from a cause, not from nothing.

> [Note: Col. 0443D] In the old Colbert and German manuscripts, and also in Martin: “so that He was not ever not.” The better reading in other manuscripts does not double the negative particle. The sense is this: that neither with respect to time—ever not having been—nor with respect to an author—subsisting from nothing—applies to Him. For the term “Father” here signifies any cause.

18. Arian subtleties against the Son’s eternity. — I am not unaware that many of those whose minds, whether through impiety, are too dull to grasp God’s mystery, or whose rage, under the appearance of religion, is inclined to disparage God through the domination of an adverse spirit, are accustomed to assert to simpler hearers this: since we say that the Son always existed and was never anything which He was not, we preach Him, by saying that He has always existed, as existing without birth. For, in human opinion, what always was does not permit that it was born; “but the reason for being born is that what was not may be; and, in the common understanding, to be what one was not is nothing other than to be born.”

They add arguments sufficiently subtle and pleasing to the ear: “If He was born,” they say, “He began; and when He began, He was not; and when He was not, it cannot be that He was.” Therefore they contend that this is the language of pious understanding: “He was not before He was born, because, in order that He who was not might be, it was not He who was that was born.” Nor did He who was require birth, since He would be born in order that He who was not might come to be.

> [Note: Col. 0443C] “Which He was not.”

> [Note: Col. 0444C] The same manuscripts read “which He was not,” and are not satisfactory here. It is denied that the Son was ever anything which He had not always been, or that He acquired anything which He once lacked.

> [Note: Col. 0444C] Printed editions: “opinion,” against the manuscripts. The verb *patiatur* must be referred to *that*, as though: “that does not allow that it was born.”

> [Note: Col. 0444C] “Does not allow.”

> [Note: Col. 0444C] Several manuscripts of good quality: “so that He was not.” Perhaps for “so that He was not not”?

> [Note: Col. 0444C] “Not because He was,” then “because He was not.”

> [Note: Col. 0444D] Bad. and many manuscripts: “not because He was, and...” and shortly afterward, “because He who was not might be born.”

19. The poison of deceptive questions; faith is to be preferred to them. — First, those who preferred reverent knowledge of divine things ought, where the truth of evangelical and apostolic proclamation held precedence, to cast aside the winding questions of cunning philosophy and instead pursue faith in God. For weak understanding can easily be stripped of its safeguard of faith by the sophism of a syllogistic question: a deceptive proposition, having elicited a simple answer compliant with the terms of its own question, would finally strip the mind by the question of its own reasoning, so that what it had lost by profession it would no longer retain in conscience.

For what could answer a question more necessarily than this: when we are asked, “Is anything before it is born?” that our confession should be that what is born was not before it was born? For it is neither natural nor necessary that what exists should be born, since something must be born only in order to be, not because it already was. When we have conceded this—which we rightly concede—we are stripped of the consciousness of faith and have already yielded to impious and alien pursuits.

> [Note: Col. 0444D] Erasmus and subsequent editions read “held precedence”; Bad. and the manuscripts read “gave precedence,” namely, to knowledge of divine matters. This is an excellent warning: where the teaching of faith shines forth, we should not lend an ear to the deceptive questions of philosophers or permit ourselves by any argument to be torn away from it. Therefore the Pratelles manuscript’s “was given precedence” is not satisfactory.

> [Note: Col. 0444D] Thus Paris with the better manuscripts. Other books: “before it is born.”

> [Note: Col. 0444D] The older Colbert manuscript with Martin and German reads, “not He who was,” omitting the preceding word *what*. This is not altogether bad.

> [Note: Col. 0444C] “The knowledge of faith.”

> [Note: Col. 0444D] Printed editions read “knowledge of faith.” More correctly, the better manuscripts read “consciousness of faith,” so that it corresponds to what is said above: “what it had lost by profession it would no longer retain in conscience.”

20. These arguments must not merely be avoided but refuted. What instructed faith provides beyond uninstructed faith. — Foreseeing this, the blessed Apostle Paul, as we have frequently shown, warned us to beware, saying: “See that no one despoils you through philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ, in whom all the fullness of deity dwells bodily” (Colossians 2:8–9).

Therefore philosophy must be guarded against, and the pursuits of human traditions are not so much to be avoided as refuted. For we must not yield to them as though they conquer rather than deceive. Since we preach Christ as the power of God and the wisdom of God, it is fitting that we should not so much flee human teachings as refute them; and that we should both block and instruct simpler people, lest they be despoiled by them. For since God can do all things wisely in that very Wisdom, and neither reason is absent from His power nor power from His reason, those who preach Christ to the world must oppose the irreligious and defective teachings of the world with knowledge of wise omnipotence, according to the saying of the blessed Apostle: “For our weapons are not fleshly, but powerful through God for the destruction of fortresses, destroying reasonings and every height raised against the knowledge of God” (2 Corinthians 10:4–5).

The Apostle did not leave faith bare and destitute of reason. Although it is supreme for salvation, unless instructed through teaching it will indeed have a secure retreat for flight amid adversities, but not the steadfast confidence to resist; it will resemble fortifications possessed by the weak after flight, not the fearless courage present among those who hold the fortifications. Therefore insolent disputations against God must be crushed, the strongholds of deceitful reasonings destroyed, and minds exalted toward impiety broken down—not with fleshly weapons but spiritual ones; not with earthly teaching but heavenly wisdom—so that, as great as the distinction between divine and human things is, so much may heavenly reason surpass earthly pursuits.

> [Note: Col. 0445D] Vatican base: “the understanding of simpler persons.” One Colbert manuscript with Martin, Sorbonne, and Miraeus’s edition: “with simpler understanding.”

> [Note: Col. 0445C] “And those very things”; shortly afterward, “will oppose.”

> [Note: Col. 0445D] Bad. and Erasmus read “and all those things.” Miraeus, restoring “in that,” omitted *very*. In many manuscripts, *in* is lacking. With the better manuscripts, “in that very Wisdom” should be retained—namely, Wisdom itself. From the example of God, who in Wisdom, which is Christ, both can do all things and can do all things wisely, defenders of the faith are warned not to seek power and wisdom elsewhere.

> [Note: Col. 0445D] Printed editions: “will oppose.” More correctly the manuscripts read *absistat*, that is, neither is power devoid of reason nor reason of power.

> [Note: Col. 0445C] “Of fleeing.”

> [Note: Col. 0445D] In the Vatican base, Chartres, and some other manuscripts: “of fleeing.” Shortly afterward one Vatican manuscript has “will obtain,” not “will retain.”

> [Note: Col. 0445D] Leipzig and Paris: “of obtaining,” against Bad., Erasmus, and the manuscripts.

> [Note: Col. 0445D] Printed editions, except Bad., read “are”; later, “is present,” not “is not present”; and between these, “those having weapons” for “those having fortifications.” This reading prevailed from Erasmus’s margin.

> [Note: Col. 0446D] Thus the better manuscripts. Printed editions read “so much.” Shortly afterward, the Pratelles manuscript: “may heavenly reason extend itself.”

> [Note: Col. 0445C] “May surpass.”

21. Though born, the Son nevertheless always is, because He is from the Father who always is. — Let the anxiety of unbelief therefore cease. It should not think that we deny, because it does not itself understand, what alone is both rightly understood and believed by us. For when in the very statement of our words we confess Him born, we nevertheless do not proclaim Him unbegotten. For “unbegotten” and “to be born” are not the same: the former is from no one, but the latter is from another. It is one thing to be eternally without an author, another to be coeternal with the Father—that is, with an author.

Where there is a father as author, there is birth; but where the author is eternal, there is also eternity of birth. For as birth is from an author, so birth from an eternal author is eternal birth. Everything which always is, moreover, is eternal. Yet not everything which is eternal is also unbegotten. For what is born from the Eternal possesses eternal being as something born. But what is not born is unbegotten together with its eternity. And if what is born from the Eternal was not born eternally, then the Father, author of the generation, will no longer be eternal.

Therefore, if anything of eternity were lacking to Him who was born from the eternal Father, it is beyond doubt that the same thing was lacking to the Author. For what is limitless to the Begetter is limitless also to the One born. Reason and understanding admit no middle term between the birth of God the Son and the generation of God the Father, because generation includes birth and birth includes generation. These two are without interval from one another, because neither exists without the other. Therefore, what cannot subsist except through both does not remain in all respects unless both remain, because one cannot be left in any respect in which that other itself cannot exist without the first.

> [Note: Col. 0446C] “We confess.”

> [Note: Col. 0446D] Two Vatican manuscripts, with Bad., Erasmus, and Miraeus: “birth is eternal.” The older Colbert manuscript with German: “birth is eternity.”

> [Note: Col. 0446D] Two manuscripts and Miraeus’s edition add, “who is Father”; but Corbie and other more recent manuscripts read, “that is, to the Father, in that He is Father”: a gloss.

> [Note: Col. 0446D] We have added *nor* on the authority of the more reliable Colbert, Remigius, and German manuscripts. We have often already observed such Hellenisms.

> [Note: Col. 0446C] The negative particle is omitted in the Verona manuscript.

> [Note: Col. 0446D] *Not* is absent from the older manuscripts. In the Vatican manuscripts: “therefore, what subsists without both”—corruptly. This passage acutely shows that birth could lack nothing which generation possessed, because neither can subsist without the other.

22. Objection: What has been born was not. — But someone incapable of this divine mystery will object: “Everything that has been born was not, because it was born in order to be.”

23. “Not having been” does not apply to the Son who is always born. — And who indeed doubts that things born in human affairs once were not? But it is one thing to be born from one who was not, another to have been born from Him who always is. Every infancy, because it had not existed earlier, began in time. Growing into childhood, it later drove adolescence on into fatherhood. Nor is one always a father who had earlier advanced into adolescence through childhood, and into childhood through infancy once begun. Therefore, one who is not always a father has not always begotten. But where one is always Father, there also the Son always is.

If, then, in your thought or understanding you have a God in whose mystery of knowledge it is proper that He is Father, but not always Father of a Son begotten by Him, then you also have in understanding and knowledge a Son who was begotten but is not always Son. But if it is proper to the Father, because He is always Father, always to be Father, it must be proper to the Son, because He is always Son, always to be Son. And how can it enter our speech or understanding that He was not before He was born, when it is proper to Him who was born always to be what He was born?

> [Note: Col. 0446C] *Esse* (“to be”) is missing in the earlier edition.

> [Note: Col. 0446D] Erasmus and later editions: “to be born.” But Bad. and the better manuscripts: “to have been born”; Martin and some other manuscripts add *to be*. We have already read in no. 21: “Nor is ‘unbegotten’ the same thing as ‘to be born.’”

> [Note: Col. 0447C] Thus the Vatican base, Colbert, Martin, German, Remigius, and other manuscripts. Some others read “of a Son begotten by Himself”; printed editions, “of the only-begotten Son.”

> [Note: Col. 0447C] Colbert, Martin, and German manuscripts: “what has been born.”

24. As the Son has all things in common with the Father, so too He has always existed. To the Father, being is proper; to the Son, being also is proper. — The only-begotten God, containing in Himself the form and image of the invisible God, is equal in all those things which are proper to God the Father through the fullness of true deity in Himself. For, as we have taught in previous books, by power and reverence He is, like the Father, both worthy of honor and powerful. Thus, since the Father always is, it is also common to the Son, because He is Son, always to be.

For according to what was said to Moses, “He who is sent me to you” (Exodus 3:14), it is beyond doubt to the mind that being is proper to God, because what is cannot be understood or said not to be. For being and not-being are contraries, and these diverse meanings do not meet in one and the same thing: while one remains, the other will not be. Therefore, where there is being, not-being cannot enter either thought or speech.

For our thought, as it is turned back and continually recalled to the understanding of Him who is, only this—what is—is always prior to it in regard to Him. For what is infinite in God always withdraws itself from the returning movement of our infinite thought, so that a thought turned backward cannot grasp anything else before that which is proper to God—namely, always to be—because, beyond proceeding toward the understanding of God by eternity, nothing other than God’s always being continually presents itself.

Therefore, what is signified concerning God through Moses and what common understanding permits us to understand in no other way, the Gospels testify to be proper also to the only-begotten God: “In the beginning was the Word,” and “the Word was with God” (John 1:1); He “was the true light” (John 1:18); “the only-begotten God is in the bosom of the Father”; and “Jesus Christ is God over all” (Romans 9:5).

> [Note: Col. 0447C] Vatican base: “in Himself through true birth.”

> [Note: Col. 0447C] “Generation.”

> [Note: Col. 0447C] Vatican base, three other Vatican manuscripts, Martin, Corbie, and others read “generation”—corruptly.

> [Note: Col. 0447C] Printed editions read “where there is being,” adding *being* without authority from the old books.

> [Note: Col. 0447C–D] Only the Remigius manuscript with Theodorus has “to thought.” The Hebraism should be recognized here, in which the following pronoun *ei* is redundant.

> [Note: Col. 0447C] “God”; shortly afterward, “what is God’s”; a little later, “withdraws”; then, “something else.”

> [Note: Col. 0447D] Some more recent manuscripts: “while that very thing.” Other books: “God Himself.” Let the reader judge whether we rightly substituted “concerning Him”—namely, Him who is—for “God,” especially by comparison with what is said in no. 31 concerning the Son’s infinity.

> [Note: Col. 0447D] Printed editions with most manuscripts: “what is God’s.” Vatican base: “what is God.” More pleasing with Remigius and Theodorus is “what is,” to him, namely to the thought turned back.

> [Note: Col. 0447D] Bad. wrongly reads, “the thought is always itself infinite”; nor is “the thought is always its own infinity” better in the other editions. Erasmus wrongly conjectured that it should read, “if through infinity it withdraws from the return of our thought.” The manuscripts with strong agreement give the true reading. The thought is called infinite whose return has no limit.

> [Note: Col. 0448C] In some manuscripts of good quality, *to* is prefixed here; it seems to have been added because of the nearby word “turned back.” The natural sense of this sentence is: however far thought is turned back, it does not grasp anything else before that which is proper to God, namely always to be. What is said generally here of God is said specifically of the Son below, no. 32: “If thought turned back investigates anything concerning the Son, nothing other than His being born and always being will always meet the investigating mind.”

> [Note: Col. 0448C–D] Printed editions: “proceeds to understand God’s eternity”; then Bad.: “than God”; Erasmus, Leipzig, and Paris: “with God.” They are corrected with the aid of the manuscripts. Here, moreover, proceeding by eternity means what they call progress to infinity.

> [Note: Col. 0448D] Printed editions: “the Evangelist testifies.” More correctly manuscripts read “the Gospels,” under which name the words of the apostles are also included, and thus everything pertaining to the New Testament is signified; just as previously, by the name of Moses, the authority of the entire Old Law was indicated.

25. He is eternal from the Eternal; therefore He is neither from nothing nor was He ever not. — Therefore He was and is, because He is from Him who always is what He is. To be from Him—that is, to be from the Father—is birth. But always to be from Him who always is, is eternity; eternity, moreover, is not from oneself but from the Eternal. From the Eternal comes nothing other than the eternal. If He is not eternal, then neither is the Father, who is the author of generation, eternal.

Since it is proper to Him that the Father always is and that He is always Son, and since eternity is signified in what He is, then what is proper to Him whose being is proper is also eternal. But no one doubts that generation signifies birth, and that birth teaches the continuing existence of the One from whom the born One derives His origin, not non-continuing existence. Moreover, it cannot be doubted that no one who already was comes to be born. For the cause of birth does not advance toward one who remains eternal through Himself.

But the only-begotten God, who is also God’s Wisdom, God’s Power, and the Word, since He is born, testifies to the Father as Author. Since He was born from One who continues, He was not born from nothing. Since He was born before eternal times, He must by His birth precede every understanding. He has left no opening in His words for the statement that He was not before He was born. For if it lies within our thought that He was not before He was born, then our thought and time are prior to His birth, because everything which was not is already subject to thought and time precisely in that meaning in which it was not; for “not having been” is a part of time. But He who is from the Eternal and always was is neither without birth nor ever was not; since both always having been is above time and being born is birth.

> [Note: Col. 0448D] Printed editions read: “If it is proper to Him that the Father always is and proper to this One that the Son always is, and in this...” against the strong consensus of manuscripts. In the words “since it is proper to Him,” the pronoun *Him* seems also to refer to the Son born from eternity, approximately in this sense: since it is proper to the Son, in that He always has the Father whose Son He always is, to exist, and so forth.

> [Note: Col. 0448D] In Paris and many old books, *is proper* occurs only once; it is repeated in earlier editions and in the Vindobonensis, Remigius, Theodorus, and other manuscripts.

> [Note: Col. 0449C] Vatican base: “who always continues”; Martin: “who continues”—a serious error. For the Son always remains eternal, though He does not remain through Himself or from Himself, but from the Father; and for this reason the rationale of birth applies to Him.

> [Note: Col. 0449C] “Remains.”

> [Note: Col. 0449C] He acutely teaches that, if the Son ever had not been, our thought would for that very reason be prior to Him, because in thinking it would in some way precede His birth. It follows that this birth would not be ineffable but subject to our thought, in accordance with what was affirmed in Book XI, nos. 46 and 47.

> [Note: Col. 0449C–D] Here *is* does not mean existence but origin—namely, He who is from the eternal Author. Shortly afterward the printed editions, except Paris, omit “nor is He without birth, nor was He not.” Erasmus notes that he found these words in a certain manuscript. He would certainly have found them in several, had he read more. Nor can we refrain from faulting his negligence: having found them, he did not take even a little care to assess whether they were necessary to the integrity of the sense.

### 26. Human reason impiously strains against the eternal birth.

We therefore confess the only-begotten God to be begotten, yet begotten before eternal times; for we must confess within the bounds prescribed for us by the utterances of apostolic and prophetic preaching. [Note: The editions read “that which”; the manuscripts, “in which” or “into which”: that is, our confession must be contained within the limits established for us by the Apostles and Prophets.] Yet human understanding does not grasp the meaning of a birth beyond time, because it is not possible in earthly natures for anything to be born before times. [Note: The Martin and Vatican Basilica manuscripts read: “in the natures of earthly things.”]

Since this is what we preach, how can we again say, within the compass of the same understanding, that he was not before he is born, when, according to the Apostle, the only-begotten God is before eternal times (2 Tim. 1:9; Titus 1:2)? If, then, his being begotten before eternal times is a profession not of human understanding but of faithful wisdom—because birth has an author, whatever exceeds times is eternal, and what is born before eternal times lies beyond earthly comprehension—then surely it is by an impious will that we exalt the judgment of human reason, in order to say, through an understanding of the world, that he was not before he is born, though the Eternal is born beyond human understanding and worldly intelligence. For whatever exceeds time is eternal.

[Note: In Corbie and a few other manuscripts, “with an impious will of understanding”; this is less sound. Hilary commonly charges with an “impious will” those who openly resist the truth and cannot plead ignorance before fair judges of things. Such are those who seek, through an understanding of the world—that is, from knowledge of worldly things—to measure the knowledge of him who was begotten before eternal times.]

### 27. Of one begotten before times one cannot say, “Before he was born,” nor, “There was a time when he was not.”

For we comprehend all times either by inference or by knowledge. [Note: “By knowledge, indeed” must here be supplied.] By knowledge, we know that what now is did not also exist yesterday, because what was yesterday is not now; and that what now is, is now only, and was not also yesterday. [Note: The word “now,” omitted in the printed editions, is restored from the manuscripts.] By inference, however, we measure the past in this way: before a certain city was founded, there undoubtedly was a time in which that city had not been founded.

Since times are subject either to our knowledge or to our inference, we judge by the understanding of human intelligence, so that we may be thought to have said reasonably of some thing: “It was not before it came to be,” because times always precede the origin of every individual thing. [Note: The editions read “concerning some reason”; the manuscripts more correctly, “concerning some thing, reasonably”: that is, concerning a thing subject to times, we may rightly say, “It was not before it came to be.”]

But in matters concerning God—that is, in God’s birth—nothing is not before eternal time.
