Therefore neither “Before he was born” nor “he at some time was not” applies to one to whom what is eternal was promised before eternal times, according to the saying of the blessed Apostle: “in hope of eternal life, which God, who does not lie, promised before eternal times” (Titus 1:2). [Note: That is, it does not apply to the birth of the only-begotten God that one should say, “Before he was born.”] [Note: “What is eternal was promised before eternal times.” The Basel, Erasmus, and Leipzig editions, with several inferior manuscripts, read “the eternal promise,” omitting “is.” Their sense is: one who possesses the eternal promise before eternal times—not merely by participation in the divine nature, but in fullness—cannot still be under hope of that promise; created things are subject to that condition, as was shown above, no. 5: “If Christ is a creature, he must necessarily be uncertain under hope of a distant expectation.”] For one who must be confessed to exist before eternal times cannot be understood to have begun after something else.

[Note: The connective is also lacking here. The following phrase, “who must be,” is to be understood as though it read, “who must be confessed to be.”]

### 28. Concerning the Son’s birth we are bound to believe otherwise than concerning our own. When we hear “always begotten,” we understand “never not existing.”

If, therefore, for anything to be born before eternal times belongs neither to human natures nor to understanding, and yet this is believed of God in professions concerning himself, how does the unbelief of our present age, through the reasoning of human intelligence, again declare, after apostolic faith has spoken of him as always begotten—that is, as born before eternal times without falling within the apprehension of eternal intelligence—“He was not before he is born”?

[Note: The Vatican Basilica manuscript reads “of human intelligence”; the other manuscripts, more soundly, “of eternal intelligence.” Created intelligence, if we are not mistaken, is called eternal because, by the eternity of its progress, it can strive toward the intelligence of God, though it cannot comprehend him; for what is infinite in God always withdraws itself from the recurrent advance of our finite understanding, as was said above, no. 24.] [Note: In the Paris edition, “him,” not “with him.” Neither occurs in other editions. Some manuscripts read “having conversed” or “having spoken together.” From the better witnesses we restore “having spoken.” Here the rashness of heretics is attacked: after receiving the Apostle’s words declaring the Son begotten before eternal times and thus beyond the grasp of human thought, they nevertheless reason concerning his birth according to human understanding and the law of human nature.] [Note: Erasmus wrongly inserted “estimation” here; subsequent editions retained it against the manuscripts. The unbelief of the Arians—whose name Hilary often spares, calling them “the new heresy” in Book VII, nos. 3 and 6—is here called “the unbelief of our present age.”]

For what is born before time is always begotten, because that which is before eternal time is always. What is always begotten does not allow that it was ever not; for to have been non-existent at some time is no longer to be always. Always being excludes not always having been. And once “not always having been” is excluded by the assertion that he is always begotten, it cannot enter the mind that he was not before he was born. For he who was begotten before eternal times is, in our understanding, always begotten, although his being born before times does not itself fall within understanding.

[Note: That is, when “not always having been” is excluded by the assertion “always begotten.” The phrase corresponds to the Greek article τοῦ (*tou*).] [Note: Erasmus reads “not to be begotten,” adding *not* against both sense and manuscript authority; though corrected later, it was not removed. The Vatican Basilica and Martin manuscripts read, “that it should not enter the mind that he was not,” an interpolation. The meaning is: although it does not enter, but exceeds, our understanding that he was born before eternal times, nevertheless we understand him to be always begotten, since faith has taught us that he was begotten before eternal times.]

For if—as certainly must be confessed—he was begotten before every creature, whether invisible or bodily, before all ages and eternal times, and before every act of understanding; and if, by virtue of having been so begotten, he always is; then it cannot be conceived in any way that he was not before he is born. For he who was born before eternal times is before all understanding; and it can never enter the mind that he, who must be confessed always to be, was not.

### 29. Their reply: “Then he who already was, was born.”

But the malicious sophistry of this question is cleverly advanced: “If,” they say, “it cannot enter the mind that he was not before he is born, then the remaining conclusion for the mind is that he who already was, was born.”

### 30. It is one thing always to be begotten; another to exist before being born.

To the calumniator I shall reply: Does he remember that I have said anything other than “begotten”? Or is the assertion that he is begotten before eternal times the same as saying that he who already existed is born? [Note: The Martin manuscript reads “to be begotten.”] For for that which already was to be born is no longer to be born, but to alter itself by being born. [Note: The Paris edition lacks “itself.” Thus the Word, in being born as man, in some sense changed himself insofar as he assumed what he was not; yet the birth properly belonged not to the Word but to the assumed man, although, because of the unity of person, it is also attributed to the Word.]

But always to be begotten means to outrun, by being begotten, every conception of times, and not to allow understanding to suppose that he was at some time unbegotten. Therefore, to be always begotten before eternal times is not the same as to exist before being born. But always to be begotten before eternal times excludes the assertion that he was not before he is born.

### 31. The Son neither existed nor did not exist before he was born.

Moreover, it does not leave room for existing before being born, because what lies beyond understanding is subject to no understanding. For if “always to be begotten” lies beyond understanding, it is no longer permissible, after the limits of understanding, to say that he was not before he is born. Since, therefore, “always to be begotten” means nothing other than that he must be confessed begotten, the question whether he was or was not before he is born is not subject to understanding. For he always precedes understanding by nothing other than being born before eternal times.

[Note: “It must be confessed.”]

Therefore he is begotten, and always is: for nothing else may be understood or said of him except that he is begotten. Since he is prior to the very time of acts of understanding—for eternal time is before understanding—he does not admit an understanding that judges concerning him that he either was or was not before he is born. [Note: The Basel edition and the Vindobonensis and Silvanus manuscripts read “is understanding”; other editions, “is not understanding”; the Vatican Basilica and Martin manuscripts, “is understanding”; the rest, “is of understandings.” Perhaps one might prefer “is understanding.” The understanding of what is argued here depends especially upon the principles laid down in Book XI, no. 46.] [Note: “Or was.”] [Note: *Not* is lacking in the Basel and Paris editions, as in many manuscripts of no inferior authority; it is restored from Erasmus, Leipzig, and the Corbie, Pratellensis, Remigius, Faurius, and other manuscripts, as both what precedes and what follows require.]

For existing before one is born does not belong to birth; and not having existed belongs already to time. Thus the infinity of eternal times consumes that which belongs to time, namely “not having been”; and birth does not allow what is not its own, namely existing before one is born. But if either existing or not having existed were subject to understanding, birth itself would be after time; for whoever is not always necessarily began after something.

[Note: The Vatican Basilica manuscript alone reads “is after understanding”; although this can be tolerated, the other witnesses more truly read “is after time.” If it is apprehended that he was not before he was born, his birth is later than the time in which he was not; if he existed but was not yet born, birth admits before itself all the time in which he previously existed.]

### 32. “Always begotten” is apprehended in the mind as “always existing.”

The end, therefore, of faith, speech, and understanding is this: that the Lord Jesus is both begotten and always is. For if the mind, turning backward, searches concerning the Son, it will encounter nothing for its searching understanding except that he is begotten and always exists. [Note: Our manuscript lacks the words “and always exists.”] [Note: The manuscripts lack “and always exists.” Such words readily fall out through scribal omission when nearly the same words occur twice. Therefore, the one whom faith teaches to have been begotten before eternal times, and whom speech calls the Son of the eternal Father, understanding apprehends only as always existing and always begotten; thus faith, understanding, and speech terminate in this knowledge.]

Therefore, as it is proper to God the Father to be without birth, so it is due to the Son through birth always to be. Birth will declare nothing other than Father, nor Father anything other than birth. These names and this nature allow no middle term. [Note: The sound manuscripts read “name, these things as nature”; see no. 21.] For either the Father is not always Father if the Son is not always Son; or, if the Father is always Father, the Son also is always Son. For whatever amount of time is denied to the Son, so that he may not always have been Son, is lacking to the Father, so that he may not always have been Father; with the result that, though he may always have been God, he was not Father throughout the infinity in which he is God.

### 33. According to the Arians, God is not always Father.

The confession of impiety extends even to this point: it assigns not periods of birth to the Son, but generation to the Father, because the mode of generation is placed within the times of birth.

[Note: The Vatican Basilica manuscript with Martin reads “so that not only to the Son”; another Vatican witness, “but also to the Father.” The Basel, Erasmus, and Leipzig editions read “assigns generation.” In these we suspect later editorial hands. The phrase “not to the Son,” etc., means that, without mentioning the Son at all, they write that generation came to the Father as an adventitious attribute. To “assign” properly means to add to something already written, and so is used simply for “add.” The Arians are rebuked for attaching generation, as an adventitious mode, to the Father already established in his own nature. Hilary refutes Arius’s statement in the *Thalia*, cited by Athanasius, *Oration II against the Arians*, pp. 310, 314: “God was not always Father; there was when God alone was, and Father was not yet.” And concerning the Word: “There was when he was not; nor was he before he came to be, but he too had a beginning in being created. For God was alone, and Word and Wisdom were not yet; afterwards, when God wished to create us, he made one being and called him Word and Wisdom.” These statements show the opponents with whom Hilary is here dealing.]

### 34. They are refuted. Times according to the Arians.

Do you, heretic, think it pious and religious to confess God as always God, but not always Father? If you think such a belief pious, then you must condemn Paul for impiety when he says that the Son is before eternal times (Titus 1:2); you must also accuse Wisdom itself, which testifies of itself that it was founded before the ages and was present with the Father when he prepared heaven.

But you, in order to assign God a beginning in respect of his being Father, must first determine a beginning for times—when they began. [Note: “When they began.”] If they began, the Apostle lies in professing them eternal. For you customarily reckon times from the creation of the sun and moon, because it is written concerning them: “Let them be for signs and for times and for years” (Gen. 1:14). But he who is before heaven—which, according to you, is itself before time—is also before the age. Nor is he merely before the age, but before the generations of generations that precede the ages.

Why do you confine divine and infinite things within transient, earthly, and narrow limits? Paul knows in Christ nothing except the eternity of times. Wisdom says not that it exists after something, but before all things. [Note: “Itself” is omitted in the Verona manuscript.]

For you, times were instituted from the sun and moon; but David signifies that Christ endures before the sun, saying: “His name is before the sun” (Ps. 71[72]:17). [Note: The Martin manuscript reads “and with the sun,” wrongly. The phrase is the same as above: “You customarily reckon times from the creation of the sun and moon.” “With you,” “according to you,” and “in your judgment” do not differ.] [Note: On manuscript authority, “endures” is removed here, “David” added above, and below the conjunction “and before the generations” deleted.] And lest you suppose that the things of God began with the origin of this world, he says likewise: “and before the moon, generations of generations” (ibid. 5).

Here times are despised by such great men, worthy of the spirit of prophecy; and nothing remains for human understanding in which it may extend itself before the birth that exceeds eternal times. Faith must keep only this measure of religious judgment: it must remember that the Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten God, is begotten in the confession of a perfect birth, and must not fail, in reverence for his divinity, to recognize him as eternal. [Note: “And in the confession of a perfect birth.”]

### 35. An objection: Wisdom testifies that it was created.

But we are accused of falsehood, and with us the teaching of apostolic preaching is charged: it confesses birth, yet professes the eternity of that birth, so that birth testifies to an author, while eternity in the mystery of divine birth exceeds the understanding of human opinion. [Note: The Vatican Basilica and Martin manuscripts add “natural,” an evident interpolation.]

For Wisdom’s declaration concerning itself is brought forward against us, where it teaches that it was created in these words: “The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways” (Prov. 8:22). [Note: “Created me [as] the beginning.”] [Note: The printed texts omit *in* here and below, agreeing indeed with the Septuagint but differing from sounder manuscripts and from Hilary’s following words. Gregory Nazianzen, *Oration 36*, no. 4, attests how familiar this passage was to the Arians: “This one thing, nearly, is always on their lips: ‘The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways.’”]

### 36. What was created from the age was also founded before the age.

O wretched heretic: you turn against the faith of ecclesiastical preaching the weapons granted to the Church against the Synagogue; and you seize the most strongly fortified understanding of saving doctrine against the salvation of all, contending from these words that Christ is a creature. Why do you not rather use these words of Wisdom, subsisting before the ages, to destroy the Jew who denies Christ’s divinity before eternal ages and the efficacy of God in all his works and teachings?

[Note: “God’s efficacy.”] [Note: The editions read “God’s efficacy”; these words destroy the sense of Wisdom subsisting before the ages. A little earlier, the Basel edition reads, “For the Jews rather deny”; Erasmus and Leipzig, “For the Jew,” etc. The manuscripts correct these. The sense is: why do you not rather use these words of Wisdom subsisting before the ages to destroy the Jew, etc.? Hilary treated at length in Books IV and V the efficacy and power, in works and teaching, of Wisdom existing before Mary.]

Wisdom has now said of itself that it was created as the beginning of God’s ways and for his works from the age, lest anyone suppose that it did not remain before Mary. Yet it did not refer its being created to the meaning of its birth, because it was created as the beginning of the ways and for the works. But lest anyone assign this beginning of the ways—which is certainly the beginning of human knowledge concerning divine things—to subjecting its infinite birth to time, it professed that it was founded before the ages (Prov. 8:22, according to the Septuagint).

Thus, since being created as the beginning of the ways and for the works is one thing, and being founded before the ages another, its foundation was understood to be prior to its creation. And the very fact that it was founded for the works before the age showed that its creation belonged to the sacrament or mystery: for its foundation is before the age, while its creation as the beginning of the ways and for the works is after the age. [Note: That is, it showed that its testimony that it was created pertains to the sacrament or mystery—namely, of the economy or dispensation.]

### 37. The age is preceded not in time but in eternity.

Further, lest creation and foundation should offend against faith in the divine birth, there follows: “Before he made the earth, before he established the mountains, before all the hills he begot me” (Prov. 8:25–26). He who was founded before the age is now begotten before the earth; and not only before the earth, but also before the mountains and hills. [Note: “Who was before the ages.”]

Yet here Wisdom, because it speaks of itself, says more than is heard. For everything signified for the understanding of infinity must be of such a kind that it is not second in time to any thing or class of things. Otherwise, temporal things cannot at all be fitted to demonstrate eternity. [Note: The editions read “temporary”; the Vatican Basilica manuscript, “times”; the other manuscripts, with the Basel edition, “temporal.”] For by being later than other things, they do not of themselves disclose the beginninglessness of infinity, since they themselves have received a temporal beginning.

What great thing would it be if God begot the Lord Christ before the earth, when the origin of angels is found to be earlier than the creation of the earth? [Note: Nothing in these words appears contrary to the Fourth Lateran Council, chapter 1, which defines that God “from the beginning of time created both creatures from nothing,” namely spiritual or angelic and corporeal or worldly. The words of Genesis, “In the beginning God created heaven and earth,” were plainly understood by the Council as referring “heaven” to angelic nature and “earth” to worldly nature. Moses, however, mentions heaven before earth; hence Hilary does not disagree with the Council when he says that angels precede the earth.

Nor does Hilary’s statement in *Against Auxentius*, no. 10, that the devil existed before times and ages, conflict more strongly. For here he argues against an Arian, and Arians, as was heard above in no. 34, customarily reckon times from the creation of sun and moon. It follows only that angels, and therefore the devil, existed before sun and moon. Epiphanius, *Heresy* 65, no. 3, does not deny this because of Job 38:7: “When the stars were made, all my angels praised me”;“ although he does not approve those who thought the angels created a certain interval before the world, and in no. 8 argues sharply that it is a certain and unchangeable doctrine that before heaven and earth no created thing whatever existed, because “in the beginning God created heaven and earth”; this beginning is the beginning of creation, before which there was absolutely no created thing.

Ambrose’s view, however, is clear: *Hexaemeron* I.1.19, “Angels, dominions, and powers, although they began at some point, nevertheless already existed when this world was made”; and Preface to Psalm 1, no. 2, “Before the very beginning of the world, Cherubim and Seraphim say with the sweetness of melodious voice, ‘Holy,’ etc.” Erasmus here ascribed the same opinion to Hilary, and all subsequent editors followed him. Yet we see no reason why it should certainly be attributed to Hilary. Indeed, on Psalm 135, no. 8, he appears to teach that the abodes of angels were established before the angels themselves. Augustine, *City of God* XI.32, finds no difference in this opinion, where he says that the opening words of Genesis, “In the beginning,” may be interpreted not of the beginning of time but of the Word, whom Scripture also calls “Beginning”; he declares himself greatly pleased by that interpretation. He teaches only that one must take care not to regard angels as coeternal with God.]

Or why, if he were said to be begotten before the earth, should he also be declared born before the mountains—and not merely before the mountains, but before the hills—when hills follow mountains in significance, and mountains follow the earth in conception? Hence one cannot suppose that these things were said merely in order that he might be understood to exist before hills, mountains, and earth, when by the eternity of his infinity he surpasses those things which are before hills, mountains, and earth. [Note: The Basel, Erasmus, and Leipzig editions and most manuscripts read thus. Several good manuscripts, with the Paris edition, read “because these things”; the Vatican Basilica manuscript, “because he is before earth, mountains, and hills.”]

### 38. He explained his infinity as far as possible; it could not be comprehended through created things.

But the divine word has not left our understanding devoid of reason; for in what follows it reveals the ground of the statement: “God made regions, and uninhabitable places, and the inhabited heights under heaven. When he was preparing heaven, I was with him; and when he was separating his own seat. When he made the strong clouds above the winds on high, and when he set fixed fountains under heaven, and when he made the strong foundations of the earth, I was with him, ordering” (Prov. 8:26, according to the Septuagint).

[Note: The Martin manuscript reads: “I was present with him, and when he separated his seat.”] [Note: “He was separating.”] [Note: The manuscripts read “mountains,” not “fountains.”]

What place for times is there here? Or how far beyond the infinite birth of the only-begotten God is human intelligence permitted to extend itself? [Note: We think one should read “into the infinite,” the preposition *in* having fallen out because of the similar following syllable.] His generation cannot be comprehended through those things whose creation we conceive in the mind. The claim is that, although he is prior to them all and surpasses them, he is nevertheless in time and not infinite, and that this alone is granted him: that he was born before temporal things.

[Note: The best Colbert manuscript, with the Remigius and German manuscripts, reads “although he surpasses”; the Silvanus manuscript, “although he presides over them”: not badly. The sentence is elliptical and marks the heretical position, which grants Christ the first place in the order of temporal things, so that, though he surpasses or presides over them, he is nevertheless in time and not infinite.]

For, although those things are subject to time in their constitution, he, despite being prior to them all, would not be free from time, because their temporal constitution would reveal the time of the birth of him who was born before them: the very fact that he precedes temporal things would then be his time.

[Note: The Remigius and Theodorus manuscripts read “those times”; several others, “those temporal things”; the Vatican Basilica and Martin manuscripts, “those temporary things.” These words again express the heretical view; it becomes clearer if one adds: “For this is what they mean: that, since those things …”]

### 39. He taught that he is coeternal with eternal things.

But the word of God and the teaching of true Wisdom speak perfectly and signify absolutely: they teach that he is not prior to temporal things, but coeternal with eternal things. [Note: The printed editions read “the teaching which speaks”; *which* is lacking in the better manuscripts.]

For when heaven was being prepared, Wisdom was present with God. Was the preparation of heaven temporal for God, as though a sudden movement of thought had unexpectedly entered a mind formerly sluggish and stupefied, and as though, in a human fashion, he had sought out the expenditure and instruments for constructing heaven? [Note: The Basel and Erasmus editions read “and a thing of thought by sudden movement”; one Vatican manuscript with Martin reads “as a movement of reconsideration.” The older Colbert, German, Corbie, and most other manuscripts support “a thing of thought.”]

On the contrary, another is the prophet’s understanding of God’s works, when he says: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the spirit of his mouth all their power” (Ps. 32[33]:6). Yet the heavens required God’s command in order to be established; for their arrangement and power consist in the firmness of this undisturbed constitution, not in the adjustment and mixture of some material, but arise from the spirit of the divine mouth. [Note: “Of its customary condition.”] [Note: These words concern an error often refuted by Hilary: some dared to suppose that the present order of the world came together through chance collisions, and so passed from disorder into order, as he says on Psalm 148, no. 3.]

What, then, does it mean that Wisdom, begotten by God, was present with him while he prepared heaven, when the creation of heaven does not consist in preparation, nor does it belong to God’s nature to linger over devising a work through an apparatus of thought? [Note: The older Colbert manuscript with Martin reads “to be mentioned.”]

For nothing whatsoever that exists in things was not always with God. Although created things began with respect to their own creation, they did not begin with respect to God’s knowledge or power. [Note: Lipsius, uncorrected in the Paris edition, wrongly restored “from God’s foreknowledge or power”; the Basel and Erasmus editions read “unto God’s foreknowledge,” etc. We follow the manuscripts. Here created things are denied a beginning insofar as God’s knowledge and power are concerned, though not insofar as they are considered in themselves. The laws of syntax seem to require “having begun” and “having been initiated.”]

The prophet bears witness for us when he says: “God, who made all things that shall be” (Isa. 45:11, according to the Septuagint). For things that are to be, though they are still to come into being inasmuch as they are to be created, are already made for God, to whom nothing in the creation of things is new or sudden. [Note: Thus the manuscripts; the editions read “recent.”] The dispensation of times provides that they should be created, but in the foreknowing efficacy of divine power they are already created. [Note: “The efficacy of foreknowledge.”] [Note: The editions read “and foreknowledge: efficacy”; the manuscripts correct this.]

Therefore Wisdom, now teaching that it was begotten before the ages, teaches itself to be prior not only to things that have been created, but coeternal with eternal things: namely, with the preparation of heaven and the distinguishing of God’s seat. For the seat was not then distinguished when it was made; distinguishing a seat is one thing, constructing it another. Nor was heaven then made ready when it was prepared beforehand: Wisdom was with the one preparing it beforehand and distinguishing it. [Note: “And determining.”]

Later it ordered together with the one making it ready, showing its eternity by being present with the one who prepares beforehand, and its ministry when it orders together with the one who makes ready. [Note: In the Martin exemplar, here and below, “preparing” occurs instead of “making ready.” The words are confused, though Hilary assigns them different force: here *praeparare* means the eternal disposition of things, while *parare* means their temporal production.]

Therefore it also said that it was begotten before the earth, mountains, and hills, in order to teach that it was present at the preparation of heaven: so that it might be shown that these things were already accomplished with God when heaven was being prepared, because nothing is new to God.

40. God prepared the world from eternity, together with himself. [Col. 0458B]—For the preparation of the things to be created is perpetual and eternal. The body of this universe was not produced by piecemeal thoughts, as though heaven had first been thought of, and then God had subsequently entered upon care and consideration of the earth, and deliberated item by item: so that it would first be spread out into a plain, then later raised into mountains by a better plan, again varied with hills, then fourthly made habitable even upon the heights; and so that heaven, once prepared, and the seat of God might be set apart, while the strong exhalations of winds might hold the clouds aloft; then that definite springs might flow beneath heaven, and finally that the earth might be secured by strong foundations. For Wisdom declares herself prior to each of all these things.

But [Col. 0458C] since all things beneath heaven have been made through God, and Christ was present when heaven was being fashioned, and even precedes the eternity of the prepared heaven itself, this does not permit us to suppose that God had fragmentary thoughts about minute matters. For the whole preparation of these things is coeternal with God. For although, according to Moses (Gen. 1), the firmament’s consolidation, the uncovering of dry land, the gathering of the sea, the establishment of the stars, and the generation by waters and earth of living creatures brought forth from themselves have their own ordered dispensation, yet the creation of heaven, earth, and the other elements is not distinguished even by the slightest instant of operation; because their preparation rested with God in the equal infinitude of eternity.

> [Note: [Col. 0458D] The editions, except Bad., read *consultatumque* (“and deliberated”), against the manuscripts.]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0458D] Lipsius and Paris, without any authority: “and heaven might be prepared”; and shortly after, “might be contained”; and a little later, on Erasmus’s conjecture alone, “springs might flow,” for *mearent* (“might pass/flow”).]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0458C] “Living creatures.”]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0459B] Thus the manuscripts. But the printed editions read “yet not heaven,” subsequently omitting the particle *ne*. We have not yet seen where in this book Hilary, as Scultetus wishes, proclaimed that God created all things simultaneously and at once against Moses. We have already shown repeatedly that he thought otherwise. But if Scultetus supposed himself founded on this passage, its foundation is easily overthrown. For here the consolidation of the firmament, the uncovering of dry land, and so on are expressly affirmed according to Moses, not against Moses. Does he suppose the passage favors him because the creation of heaven, earth, and the other elements is not distinguished even by the slightest moment of operation? But who does not see that this too is expressed by Moses’ words: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth”? Nor is it less rightly denied above that the body of this universe was produced by piecemeal thoughts, where the discussion concerns the eternal preparation of the world, not its temporal establishment. Moreover, what is the point of contrasting the creation of heaven and earth, which is not distinguished by even the slightest instant of operation, with the consolidation of the firmament, the uncovering of dry land, and so forth, which have their ordered dispensation? This may also be clarified from Ambrose, Letter now XLIV, §2, where he says: “Moses sets forth that the world was made in six days, not because God required time for its establishment—for he has within a moment the power to make whatever he wills; for he spoke, and they were made—but because the things that are made require order, and order commonly requires both time and number.” What Ambrose calls “order,” our Hilary seems to call “dispensation.” From the establishment of heaven and earth he rightly suggests that God could have created all things at once; or rather, he confirms what he had previously said concerning the eternal preparation of all things, although above, §16, he expressly maintains that man was formed after heaven, earth, day, and so forth.]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0459B] “The eternity of infinitude.”]

41. Epilogue.—Therefore, although Christ was present with these infinite and eternal realities in God, he allowed us awareness only of his birth: so that, as the birth understood of God advances faith, so the known eternity of that birth may avail for the religion we have embraced. For reason and understanding alike do not permit an eternal Father to be proclaimed except as having an eternal Son.

> [Note: [Col. 0459D] Bad. and Erasmus: “the understanding of God.” Martin manuscript: “the nature of God understood.” Then in the common editions, “unless coeternal,” where the manuscripts read “unless eternal.”]

42. The term “creation” is objected against Christ in vain.—But the term “creation,” together with the declaration itself, troubles us. Let the name of creation indeed trouble us, if there is not also proclaimed a birth before the ages and a creation for the beginning of God’s ways and for his works. For birth cannot be understood as creation, since birth is prior to a cause, whereas creation is through a cause. For he was founded before heaven was prepared and before the age—the one who was created for the beginning of God’s ways and for his works. Or are “to be created for the beginning of God’s ways and for his works” and “to be born before all things” of the same meaning? The former has time in its acts; the latter contains an understanding beyond time.

> [Note: [Col. 0460C] This passage is illuminated by Gregory Nazianzen, Oration XXXVI, §6: “What among all things is without cause? The Divinity; for there is no one who can state a cause of God, since otherwise that would be prior to God. … Therefore, since we find here plainly both ‘He created’ and ‘He begets me,’ I judge simply that what is found joined with a cause must be assigned to the humanity, but what is simple and without cause must be ascribed to the divinity. Come then: does not that ‘HE CREATED’ have a cause attached? For, he says, ‘He created me as the beginning of his ways for his works.’ … But ‘HE BEGETS ME’ was spoken without a cause,” etc.]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0460C] The editions read “before the ages.” Then Bad. and Erasmus: “founded, which is the beginning … is created”; Lipsius and Paris: “founded, who is the beginning,” etc. Later the Martin and Vatican Basilica manuscripts read “is blessed before all works,” corruptly.]

43. It is wrongly alleged that he was created as a kind of minister for making the world.—Or perhaps you wish what is created “for the works” to be understood thus: that he was created on account of the works—that is, that Christ was created as the cause for accomplishing the works, so that he might remain merely the servant and worker of the world, rather than be the Lord of glory by birth; and might be created for the ministry of making the age, rather than also be forever the Son of love and King of the ages?

Yet, although common understanding itself extinguishes this most impious meaning of yours—because it is one thing to be created for the beginning of God’s ways and for his works, another to be born before the ages—nevertheless this same passage refutes you, lest you falsely assert that the Lord Christ was created for the operation of the world: for it shows God the Father to be the maker and worker of the universe. This is safe indeed, because he himself was present, fashioning with the one who prepared all things. But although all Scripture was going to speak of the Lord Jesus Christ as creator of the world, Wisdom nevertheless, to destroy the occasion for impiety, declared God the Father to be the world’s maker; nor did she teach that she was absent from the maker, since she was present even with the one preparing. And when the Father prepared, and Wisdom fashioned with the one fashioning, and was also present with the one preparing, she thereby embraced both points: lest she should be understood to have been created for the works, since she had been present at the eternal preparation of future works; and lest Scripture be made false in saying that she fashioned with the one fashioning.

> [Note: [Col. 0460C] Athanasius, *Oration III against the Arians*, p. 395, testifies that Arius, Eusebius, and Asterius not only said but also wrote that, when God wished to bring forth the created nature and saw that it could not share in his purity and craftsmanship, he first alone made and created one only being, whom he called his Son and Word, so that, once he had been made, the remaining things could then be made through him. Athanasius subsequently demonstrates the absurdity of this opinion by many arguments. See Hilary, Fragment II, §26.]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0460D] Erasmus added “for us” here, and subsequent editions retained it without authority. Earlier, in place of “this indeed is safe,” the Vatican Basilica and Martin manuscripts read “the whole of this indeed,” referring to the security of faith in the Son’s eternity.]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0460D] The printed editions read “for denying”; corrected from the manuscripts.]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0460D] We think *ut* (“that”) should be read for *et* (“and”), having often observed in manuscripts that one is written for the other. We restore the subsequent *et* before “Wisdom” on manuscript authority, after Lipsius had deleted it.]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0460D] In the common editions: “thereby she embraced both points, lest [she be thought created] for the works,” etc.—an interpolated reading supported only by the Corbie manuscript and a few copies derived from it, which read “thereby he embraced both points,” etc. But in the older Colbert, Vatican Basilica, Chartres, Martin, Germain, Remigius, and other manuscripts: “thereby in those things which [were] for the works”—corruptly indeed, but readily restored to Hilary’s thought if corrected thus: “thereby neither [was she] for the works.” For Hilary here clearly establishes three points at once: first, that Wisdom is eternal, present with the Father eternally preparing the world; second, that she was not created for the temporal establishment of the world, since she was eternal and the Father himself is said to have fashioned the world; finally, that the world was so fashioned by the Father that Wisdom fashioned with the one fashioning, lest Scripture be found false when it records that all things were made in Wisdom.]

44. Wisdom says that she was created, with reference to what she accomplished after the age. [Col. 0461A]—But at last, by the revelation of Catholic teaching, learn at the outset, heretic, what it means that Christ was created for the beginning of God’s ways and for his works; and from Wisdom’s own words learn the folly of your impious dullness. For she begins thus: “If I declare to you the things which occur daily, I shall remember to recount the things which are from the age” (Prov. 8:21, LXX). For after she had said, “I call upon you, O men, and send forth my voice to the sons of men. Understand cunning, you simple ones; and you unlearned, apply your heart” (ibid., 4–5); and again, “By me kings reign, and the mighty write righteousness. By me princes are magnified, and tyrants hold the earth through me” (ibid., 15–16); and again, “I walk in the ways of equity, and move in the midst of the paths of righteousness, that I may distribute substance to those who love me and fill their treasuries with good things” (ibid., 20–21)—Wisdom does not conceal her daily work.

First, exhorting all, she instructs both the simple to understand shrewdness and the unlearned to apply their heart, so that the earnest and careful reader may weigh the distinct and discriminated force of the words. Accordingly, she teaches that all things are done, understood, praised, and possessed—or held—by her own ways and ordinances. She shows that the kingdoms of kings, the prudence of the powerful, the celebrated deeds of rulers, and the law of tyrants who hold the earth are contained within her. She also shows that she does not mingle with wickedness or participate in injustice, and that this is so that, by intervening in all works of equity and righteousness, she may furnish those who love her with the abundance of eternal goods and incorruptible treasures.

Therefore, after professing that she will declare the things done daily, she promises also to recall and recount the things which are from the age. And now what understanding of dullness could suppose that the things recalled as being “from the age” were done before the age? For in the things which are from the age every work is after the age; but the things before the age precede the establishment of the age which comes after them. Therefore Wisdom, professing that she remembers to declare the things which are from the age, says: “The Lord created me for the beginning of his ways, for his works” (ibid., 22). This, therefore, is the meaning of things accomplished from the age: it is not an assertion of the birth proclaimed before the ages, but a teaching concerning the dispensation entered upon from the age.

> [Note: [Col. 0461D] This entire sentence is lacking in our Vulgate; but in the Septuagint it occurs after the words contained in verse 24. Then *namque cum* means approximately “for when” or “indeed when.”]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0461C] “Into instruction.”]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0461D] The editions read “in instruction,” subsequently omitting *autem* (“but”); they are corrected from the better Colbert, Chartres, Remigius, and other manuscripts, agreeing with the Greek, ἀπαίδευτοι δή, “and you unlearned indeed.” So also below: “She instructs both the simple to understand and the unlearned to apply their heart.” Then Bad. and Erasmus read “know” for “write.”]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0461C] “All.”]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0461D] The Remigius manuscript reads “in all.” Most others read “all.” Hence perhaps more correctly Martin and several others read “of all.”]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0462C] Read continuously in this manuscript: “He created me as the beginning.”]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0462C] “The teaching has been undertaken.”]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0461D] In the older Vatican Basilica, Colbert, and other manuscripts: “undertaken”; in Martin: “initiated.”]

45. What it means that he was born before the ages and created from the age; he who is the beginning of the way of God’s works; when and why he was created.—[Col. 0462B] We must ask what it means that God was born before the ages and again created for the beginning of God’s ways and for his works. For where birth is before the age, there is the eternity of infinite generation; but where the same one is created from the age for God’s ways and works, the cause of creation is fitted to the works and ways.

And first, because Christ is Wisdom, we must consider whether he himself is the beginning of the way of God’s works. There is, I think, no doubt of it. For he says: “I am the way” (John 14:6), and “No one comes to the Father except through me” (ibid.). The way is the guide of those who travel, the course of those who hasten, the security of the ignorant, and in a sense the teacher of things unknown and desired. Therefore he is created as the beginning of the ways for God’s works, because he both is the way and leads to the Father.

But the reason for this creation, which is from the age, must be sought. For it is the mystery of the final dispensation, in which, created also in a body, he declared himself to be the way of God’s works. But he was created for God’s ways from the age, when, subjected to visible form as a creature, he assumed the appearance of creation.

> [Note: [Col. 0461D] The editions read “there is infinite [eternity]”; and shortly after, “and the same [one] is shown in God’s ways and works.” The preferable manuscripts correct this to: “there are works and ways,” etc. Here is the answer to the question proposed: why the same Wisdom is said both to have been born before the ages and to have been created from the age. For, that is, where she is before the age, etc.; but where the same birth which is before the age is creation from the age for God’s ways, etc. Hilary understands “God’s ways” as the time in which God lives in the age through visible appearance. Thus just above he says: “This is the meaning of things accomplished from the age”; and in his commentary on Matthew, ch. 22, §6: “We have very often warned that ‘way’ must be understood as the time of the age.”]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0462C] Lipsius and Paris here prefix the pronoun “this,” in whose place Christ is understood. Then Erasmus alone reads “therefore, the beginning of the ways”; and thereafter, with Bad. and two manuscripts, “and for God’s works.”]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0462D] The common editions read “which also.” The manuscripts more fittingly read “in which.” Here a twofold dispensation of the Word is distinguished: the final one, in which in the last times he became man and lived among men; and the other from the beginning of the age, from which time, assuming various forms of diverse created things, he appeared in many ways and modes to the fathers. “From that time,” Eusebius says, *Demonstration of the Gospel* V.19, “he began his saving advent to humankind.” The same Eusebius explains, ibid., chs. 9–19, that the Son of God appeared now in the form of an angel, now in a human form, now in an assumed appearance of fire or cloud, as suited each person’s condition. Augustine agrees, Letter CLXIV to Evodius, §17: “From the beginning of the human race, whether to rebuke the wicked—as to Cain, and earlier to Adam himself and his wife—or to console the good, or to admonish both, so that some might believe for their salvation and others might not believe for their punishment, he himself, certainly Christ, came not in flesh but in spirit, addressing whom he wished by suitable visions, as he wished.” You have an elegant comparison of these two dispensations in Book V, §17.]

46. God’s ways from the age: created forms assumed by the Word; why he assumed various forms.—Let us therefore see for what ways of God and for what works Wisdom, born of God before the ages, was created from the ages. Adam heard the voice of God walking in Paradise (Gen. 3:8). Do you suppose that the sound of one walking could have been heard apart from the form of assumed creation, so that he who was heard walking might stand in some created form?

I do not ask in what form he spoke to Cain and Abel and Noah, or in what form he was present when blessing Enoch. An angel speaks to Hagar (Gen. 16:9, 13), and he is certainly the same God. Is he of the same form when he is seen as an angel as he is in that nature in which he is God? Certainly the form of an angel is displayed where God’s nature is afterwards mentioned. But why speak of an angel? A man comes to Abraham (Gen. 18:2). Is Christ present in this appearance of creation according to man, such as he is also as God?

Yet a man speaks, stands present in a body, and is fed with food; nevertheless, God is worshipped. Certainly he who before was an angel is now also a man, lest the diversity of this very assumed creation permit this to be understood as God’s natural form. He is also present to Jacob even to the clasp of wrestling in human appearance: he joins hands, exerts his limbs, bends his side, and stands in every movement and gait of ours (Gen. 32:24). But afterwards he is shown to Moses as fire (Exod. 3:2), so that you might learn to direct faith toward the appearance of created nature rather than the substance of nature. He then possessed in himself the power to burn, yet did not assume the natural necessity of consuming; for the blazing appearance of fire was present without injury to the bush.

> [Note: [Col. 0463D] In two manuscripts: “of God walking.”]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0463D] “Walking in.”]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0463D] The older Colbert manuscript, with Martin and Germain and supported by Remigius, reads *in ambulantis*, “of one walking in.” The two words are not displeasing, so that the voice may be understood as silent in form.]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0463D] The same Colbert manuscript: “what form he was.”]

47. Without loss to eternity he assumed these forms; by the power by which he assumed them, he removed them.—Run through the times and understand in what form he was seen by Joshua, the prophet bearing his own name Jesus; by Isaiah also, who with evangelical testimony declares that he saw him (John 12:41); by Ezekiel, in the assumption reaching even to awareness of resurrection (Ezek. 37); by Daniel, confessing the Son of Man in the eternal kingdom of the ages (Dan. 7:13–14); and by all the others to whom he presented himself in the appearance of diverse creation, for God’s ways and God’s works—for the knowledge of God, that is, and the advancement of our eternity.

What, then, does this dispensation of human salvation now contrive as so impious an insult against the eternal birth? This creation is from the ages; but before the ages is infinite birth. Go on, indeed: endeavor to bring against us a Prophet, a Lord, an Apostle, or any statement whatever that has applied the name “creature” to the eternal birth of divinity. For in all these instances God, who is a consuming fire, is present as created in such a way that he abolishes the creation by the very power by which he assumed it—able again to remove what had existed only for the purpose of being contemplated.

> [Note: [Col. 0464D] The Verona manuscript reads “by Ezekiel”; later, “by Daniel.”]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0463D] Most manuscripts read “Ezekiel,” and shortly afterwards “Daniel.”]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0464D] The word *ingessit* (“presented himself”) is repeated here in the Remigius manuscript; in place of this repetition, the Vatican Basilica, Martin, Colbert, and Sorbonne manuscripts read *incessit* (“entered/walked in”). Later, Lipsius and Paris incorrectly read “and knowledge” for “for knowledge.”]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0464D] Paris had omitted “us”; the old Colbert manuscript together with Germain supports its inclusion.]

48. Paul called Christ “made” as man; he also called him “created.”—But the blessed and true birth of flesh conceived in the Virgin—because then the nature and form of our creaturehood was born—the Apostle called both a creature and a thing made. And certainly this name belongs to him according to the true birth as man when he says: “But when the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the law, that he might redeem those under the law, that we might receive the adoption of sons” (Gal. 4:4).

Therefore he is his own Son who, in man and from man, is a making; and not merely a making, but also a creature, as it is said: “As truth is in Jesus, put off, according to your former manner of life, the old man who is corrupted according to the desires of deception; but be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who has been created according to God” (Eph. 4:21 ff.). Therefore that new man who has been created according to God is to be put on. For he who was the Son of God was also born the Son of Man. Because this was not a birth of divinity but a creation of flesh, the new man received the designation of his kind: created according to God who was born before the ages.

And why the new man was created according to God, he shows by adding: “in righteousness and holiness and truth” (ibid., v. 24). For there was no deceit in him; he was made for us righteousness and sanctification, and he himself is truth. Therefore we put on this Christ, who as the new man is created according to God. He is created according to God because the man who knows no sin was created according to God’s righteousness, sanctification, and truth.

> [Note: [Col. 0464D] In one Colbert and another Sorbonne manuscript: “that we might receive through faith,” contrary to the other books and to the Greek and Latin biblical text.]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0464D] Our manuscript also omits what is enclosed in brackets.]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0464D] What is enclosed in brackets is omitted, together with the Bad. edition, by all manuscripts except one Colbert and another Sorbonne manuscript.]

49. Creation cannot be attributed to eternal birth.—Therefore, if Wisdom, saying that she remembers the things done from the age, said that she was created for God’s works and God’s ways; and was created in such a manner that she taught herself to have been founded before the ages, lest the mystery of that creation, variously and frequently assumed, should appear to have altered her nature—since the firmness of her foundation could not admit the disturbance of an unstable condition; while, lest “foundation” should appear to indicate anything other than birth, she professed herself to have been begotten before all things—why now is creation attributed to birth? For she who was begotten before all things is herself founded before the ages; and she who was founded before the age is herself created from the ages for the beginning of God’s ways and for his works, so that creation from the ages may be understood to differ from the birth which is before the ages and before all things. Impiety has not even this excuse, by which it might allege an error of impiety.

> [Note: [Col. 0465C] Our manuscript elsewhere also has *saltim* for *saltem*, “at least.”]

50. In what sense creation could, though unlearnedly, be attributed to eternal birth without impiety.—[Col. 0465B] For even if weakness of understanding prevented a person of religious conviction from grasping at present what the particular meaning of “creation” was, nevertheless, following the Apostle’s expression that attributes “making” to a true birth, he ought to have thought that “creation” too, though unlearnedly, might nevertheless without impiety contribute to faith in the generation.

For the Apostle, intending to proclaim the birth of one from one—that is, of the Lord from a Virgin without the conception involved in human passions—did not without reason speak of him, whom he knew to have been born and frequently called so, as “made of a woman.” Thus birth might show the truth of generation, while the making might declare the birth of one from one; since the term “making” excluded conception through human intercourse when he was known to have been made from a Virgin, though it was beyond doubt that he was more properly born.

But see, heretic, how impious you are. No prophetic, evangelical, or apostolic statement has said that Jesus Christ was created from God rather than born. But you deny birth and affirm creaturehood—not in the Apostle’s sense, who says “made” so that no one might doubt that one was born from one, but in the most impious sense, lest God should subsist by natural birth, since instead he might subsist as a creature from nothing. This is the first poison of your unhappy mind: not to call the birth a creature, but to assign to creation the faith which belongs to birth. Although it would indeed be a mark of poor intelligence, yet not of extreme irreligion, to have called him created for this reason: that his impassible birth from God, as one from one, might be known.

> [Note: [Col. 0465C] The editions read “irreligious”; corrected from the manuscripts.]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0465C] The old Colbert and Germain manuscripts read “to be attributed.” We would prefer “of the one attributing,” namely, the Apostle. By the example of the Apostle, who said that Christ was both born and made, so that, though his birth was true, the term “making” might indicate that it was from one Virgin and not according to the common law, Hilary teaches that both terms by which Wisdom first testified that she was begotten and then created could, though unlearnedly, nonetheless be referred to her eternal generation—provided that the name “creation” did not exclude the truth of birth, but only showed the unique manner in which one was born from one without any passion. Basil of Ancyra and George of Laodicea are recorded by Epiphanius, *Heresies* LXXIII.20 to have understood the same words of Wisdom in this unlearned but not impious manner. They say: “When the Son said, ‘The Lord created me,’ lest we should suppose his nature to be common with the rest of created things, he necessarily added, ‘He begot me before all hills.’ By these words he expressed for us his own proper relation to the Father, devout and free from every passion.”]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0465D] The printed editions read “that is, God from the Virgin”; corrected from the manuscripts.]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0465C] “Divinity.”]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0466C] The ancient Vatican Basilica, Martin, Chartres, and several other manuscripts read “divinity.” More correctly the old Colbert, Corbie, and others read “birth,” since the discussion concerns Christ’s temporal birth from the Virgin.]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0466C] In place of the word “faith,” Lipsius and Paris vainly substituted “insult” from Erasmus’s margin. The heretics are reproached not because they unlearnedly call the uncreated and eternal generation of Wisdom “creation,” but because they also believe it impiously. Throughout this section, but especially in the following words, Basil’s and George’s interpretation, whose words we cited above, seems to be criticized. Since they wrote these words while assembled at Ancyra before Easter of 358, it may be inferred that this book is later than that synod.]

51. Firm faith concerning the eternal birth of the Son.—But steadfast and apostolic faith permits none of these things. For it knows in what temporal dispensation Christ was created and in what eternity of times he was born. Born from God, he is God; and in him divinity is unambiguous, possessing true birth and perfect generation. [Col. 0466B] For in matters concerning God we confess nothing except what is born and eternal. But he was born not after something, but before all things, so that birth may testify only to its author and not signify within itself something posterior to its author.

Indeed, in the common confession, his birth is second from the author because it is from God; yet it is not separable from the author, because in proportion as our mind attempts to extend its understanding beyond birth, it necessarily also passes beyond generation. This alone, therefore, is pious speech concerning God: to know the Father, and to know with him the Son who is from him. Nor are we taught anything else concerning God except that he is the Father of the only-begotten God and Creator. Therefore human weakness must not stretch itself further; it must say only this, in which alone is its salvation: that before the mystery of the flesh, it has always known in the Lord Jesus Christ that he was born.

> [Note: [Col. 0466D] The editions, except Paris, read “generation,” having shortly before omitted the word “birth.” After “generation,” the unexpressed word “understanding” is sufficiently understood; it is expressly present also in the Pratelli manuscript.]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0466C] Thus ends the sole pious discourse concerning God. The manuscript book proceeds no further, its final leaf being lost.]

52. Hilary professes adherence to this faith, which he does not define by his own understanding.—[Col. 0466C] As for me, so far as I shall be strengthened by this Spirit granted me from you, holy Father, almighty God, I shall confess you to be eternal God and likewise eternal Father. I shall never break out into such folly and impiety as to set myself up as judge of your omnipotence and mysteries, raising the understanding of my weakness beyond reverent belief in your infinity and the faith in eternity made known to me, so as to determine that you were at some time without your Wisdom, Power, and Word—my Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten God.

For the weak and imperfect speech of our nature does not prejudge you for my understanding’s sake, so as to strangle faith in silence through poverty of expression. For although word, wisdom, and power in us are works of our inward activity, in you, perfect God, whose Word, Wisdom, and Power he is, there is a complete generation. Thus he who is shown to be born from you in these names of your eternal properties is always inseparable from you; born, indeed, so that he signifies no author for himself other than you, yet does not lose the faith of infinity because he is said to have been born before eternal times.

> [Note: [Col. 0466D] In the Chartres manuscript the heading is prefixed in the manner of a title: “Prayer”; in other later manuscripts: “Prayer of Saint Hilary.”]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0467C] In the old Colbert and Germain manuscripts: “yet rather,” not “yet with you.”]

53. In many natural things whose cause is hidden, faith comes to our aid; how much more in divine things.—For you have bestowed many things of this sort in human affairs: though their cause is unknown, their effect is nevertheless known. Faith is devout where natural ignorance is also present. For when I lifted these weak eyes of mine to your heaven, I believed it to be nothing other than your heaven. Beholding in it the star-bearing circles, their annual courses, the Pleiades (*Vergiliae*), the *septemtrio*, and the morning star, each assigned its different offices of service, I understand that you are God in things whose nature I do not comprehend.

And when I saw the wonderful risings of your sea, I did not grasp either the source of its waters or the movement of this immeasurable alternation; nevertheless, apprehending faith in its reason, though inaccessible to me, I do not fail to know you also in the things I do not know. Again, when in mind I turn toward the lands, which by the force of hidden causes receive all seeds, dissolve what they have received, give life to what has been dissolved, multiply what has been given life, and strengthen what has been multiplied, I find nothing in them that I can understand by my own mind. Yet my ignorance advances toward understanding you, while, unskilled in the service rendered me by nature, I understand you only through its usefulness to me.

Even without knowing myself, I yet perceive myself, so that I admire you all the more because I am ignorant of myself. For I perceive, though I do not understand, the movement, reason, and life of my discriminating mind; and in perceiving them I owe them to you, who grant me, beyond my understanding of natural origin, the awareness of a nature that delights me. And since, ignorant, I understand you in my own things, and understanding, worship you, neither shall I relax faith in your omnipotence in your things because I do not know them; lest my mind should seize upon and subject to itself the origin of your Only-begotten, and there be something in me by which I might reach beyond both my Creator and my God.

> [Note: [Col. 0467C] The editions read “ignorance.” The very old Vatican Basilica and Colbert manuscripts read “knowledge.” The Chartres reading, “ignorance,” is truer.]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0467C] That is: I believed you alone to be its maker and governor, because no one looking upon heaven fails to sense God’s existence, as Hilary says in his commentary on Psalm 65, §10; but I did not attain the reason by which you govern it.]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0467C] Bad. reads, like the manuscripts, *virgilias*. This is awkward if the *Vergiliae* are named from their rising in springtime. Then the printed editions read “the Seven Oxen,” omitting “and.” Moreover, *septemtrio* is the same as Boötes; for the *triones* were anciently ploughing oxen.]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0467D] The common editions read “and diverse,” incorrectly adding the conjunction. The old Colbert manuscript does not read “morning star,” but “the many.” The Germain manuscript has this reading in the text and “or the Pleiades” in the margin; we do not approve it, since the *Vergiliae*, the Latin name of the Greek Πλειάδες (“Pleiades”), were mentioned above.]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0467D] The Vatican Basilica manuscript with Martin reads “of this immense vastness.” The reading of the other manuscripts, which describes the tide of the sea, is preferable.]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0467D] In the same manuscripts: “the use bestowed by you alone,” corruptly.]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0467D] Thus the preferable manuscripts, whereas Corbie in a second hand and other later manuscripts read “in my things,” with the same sense. The editions read “me.”]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0467D] Several of the older manuscripts read “of your first-born.” Shortly after, the common editions read “where I,” whereas from the manuscripts we restore “that I.”]

54. The Son is born from the Father’s substance, and is therefore second after Him, yet eternal and indivisible from Him. — His birth is before eternal times. If there is anything among things which precedes eternity, there will surely be something which exceeds the comprehension of eternity. For He is your reality, and is your Only-begotten: not a portion, not an extension, not an empty name according to some theory of emanations; but Son, Son from you, God the Father, true God, and [Note: [Col. 0468C] The exemplar of the Vatican basilica has: “and to be confessed by you as born of your nature,” omitting the rest. Bad. and Er., from one very recent Colbert manuscript of highly doubtful authority: “and born from you in the truth of your nature,” etc. Another Colbert manuscript, with one Sorbonne manuscript: “and from you, only-begotten in your nature, begotten,” etc. Martin., Remig., and Theod.: “and begotten from you in the power of your unbegotten nature; thus to be confessed from you,” etc.; a reading adopted by Lips. and Par. But *power* is highly suspect as a corruption of *after you* (*post te*), with the addition of the words *from you*. In an older Colbert manuscript, as also in Corb., [Col. 0468D] Carn., Pratell., and others: “and begotten from you, only-begotten in your unbegotten nature,” etc. The most attractive reading would be: “and begotten from you, congenitally with the nature which is yours,” in accordance with the passage in *On the Synods*, no. 48: “I understand God from God—not of dissimilar essence, not divided, but born; and, from the substance of the unbegotten God, a birth CONGENITAL in the Son, according to likeness, only-begotten.” Nor would the preceding reading be unacceptable if the particle *in* were absent, thus: “and begotten from you, of your unbegotten nature,” so that the unity of Son and Father might be indicated by the words “your nature,” to which “unbegotten” would be added in order to declare the Son’s proper characteristic. Thus in Book IX, no. 68, we read that the Son’s nature does not differ from the Father’s, since it is wholly from the Whole and, while it is only-begotten, has the Father within itself. But the reading of the manuscript of the monastery of Silvac Major was judged more elegant; before that manuscript had been seen, we had conjectured that it should be preferred.] begotten from you in the unity of your nature; to be confessed after you, yet together with you: because you, the author of His eternal origin, are eternal. For insofar as He is from you, He is second after you; but insofar as He is yours, you are not [Note: [Col. 0468D] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions instead read: “He is not to be separated from you.”] to be separated from Him [Col. 0468C]: since you must not be confessed ever to have existed without what is yours, lest you be charged either with imperfection without generation or with superfluity after generation. Thus eternal birth accomplishes this alone: that we may know you to be the eternal Father of your Only-begotten Son, who is from you before eternal times.

[Col. 0468C] 55. The Holy Spirit is not a creature. — And for my part, [Col. 0469A] it is too little for the duty of my faith and speech merely to deny that my Lord and God, your Only-begotten Jesus Christ, is a creature. I shall not permit participation in this designation even to your Holy Spirit, who is assuredly from you and sent through Him. For my reverence toward the things that are yours is great. Nor, because I know you alone to be [Note: [Col. 0469B] Erasmus marked this passage with a censor’s stroke, as though, he says, the Holy Spirit Himself were born from the Father. But since Hilary immediately declares that the Holy Spirit is not to be called begotten, he is plainly affirming that the Father alone is unbegotten—not because He alone is exempt from birth, but because He alone is without beginning, alone without an author, and alone possesses His essence as received from no other, or, as they say, uncommunicated. This manner of speaking is still so accepted among theologians that unbegottenness is considered by them the distinctive notion of the Father. The Council of Sirmium in 351, anathema 19, uses the term in no other sense: “If anyone, calling the Holy Spirit the Paraclete, says that He is unbegotten God, let him be anathema.”] unbegotten, and that the Only-begotten born from you is begotten, [Note: [Col. 0469C] This passage must not be passed over lightly. Here Hilary expressly acknowledges that the Holy Spirit is not begotten, although in Book VII, no. 15, he maintains that only birth can establish equality of nature, and in no. 26: “Only the birth of the Son is believed, without impiety, to be equal to Him through likeness.” Indeed, in this very book we have just heard, in no. 51: “For we confess nothing in the things of God except what is born and eternal.” It follows that the Holy Spirit is not equal to God. Yet here he so clearly asserts both the Spirit’s unity with God and equality with the Father that he must undoubtedly be understood, in the earlier passages, to contrast birth with a condition either from nothing or from an alien substance. Hence, after the words quoted from Book VII, no. 26, “Only birth,” etc., he immediately adds: “For whatever is outside Him will be made equal to Him with insult to His honoured power.” Nor does he deny less clearly that the Holy Spirit is from nothing or from an alien substance than he denies this concerning the Son Himself. For as he says of the Son, “He is your reality,” so he says of the Holy Spirit: “Nothing but what is yours penetrates you . . . Whatever enters into you is yours.” Just as he professes elsewhere, in Book VI, no. 35 and elsewhere, that the Son did not begin to exist from nothing but came forth from One who remains, so here he professes the Holy Spirit to be the power of the nature of the God who remains. Hence he declares that insults to the Holy Spirit recoil upon the Father Himself, just as he is accustomed to teach that the Father is dishonoured by those very persons who dishonour the Son.] I shall nevertheless never call the Holy Spirit begotten, nor shall I ever call Him created. I fear the insults which creep also toward you through this assertion, which is common to me with all the other things established by you. [Note: [Col. 0469D] Thus two Colbert manuscripts, one Sorbonne manuscript, etc. Most others, together with Lips. and Par., have: “I fear the insult creeping also toward you”; in place of which Bad. and Er. have, very badly: “you have exposed an insult to my understanding.” At first sight the reading of the Vatican-basilica manuscripts and Mart. is attractive: “I fear the insult of one proceeding from you also”; Carn. and Vind. favour this, because in them “from you,” not “toward you,” is preferred. Yet this reading is all the more suspect because it occurs more readily to the mind than the other, especially as it appears only in manuscripts in which scribes have permitted themselves certain liberties. Further, the rules of syntax require *procedentem* or *procedenti*, not *procedentis*. Finally, the particle *also* indicates that the insult involved in calling the Holy Spirit created falls not upon Him alone but also upon Him whose Spirit He is. This can be demonstrated much as it was shown above, no. 6, that the Father would be a creature if the Son were a creature.] Your Holy Spirit, according to the Apostle, searches and knows your depths (1 Cor. 2:10), and, as your intercessor for me, speaks to you on my behalf things which I cannot utter. Yet shall I call, or even slander with the name of creation, the power of His nature, remaining from you through your Only-begotten? [Note: [Col. 0470C] Bad. perversely reads: “through your united one who remains.” Erasmus did not alter this, but merely noted in the margin: “with your Only-begotten.” From this Lipsius afterwards fashioned: “with your Only-begotten who remains.” The reading is corrected from Par. and the manuscripts. Here we are taught that the Holy Spirit is the power of His own nature; that is, a power which is His own, subsists through itself, and does not adhere to another. Yet He is not so much “of His own nature” as not to have His origin from the Father through His Only-begotten; rather, He is so from both that He is of a remaining nature—that is, a nature whose own property is to be and not to know a beginning. To this pertains the intimation in Book VIII, no. 19, that the procession of the Holy Spirit should be regarded as the going-forth of One who remains: a going-forth because His subsistence is distinct from that of the One from whom He proceeds, but of One who remains because He does not depart from Him from whom He subsists.] Nothing but what is yours penetrates you; nor does an alien power, foreign to you, measure the depth of your immeasurable majesty. Whatever enters into you is yours; nor is anything alien from you which is present by the power [Note: [Col. 0470D] The older Colbert manuscript with Germ. reads: “is of the one searching.” [Col. 0470D] Another, with one Sorbonne manuscript: “is of the one searching within you.”] of one who searches.

56. He is ineffable. — But He is ineffable to me, whose utterances on my behalf are ineffable to me. [Col. 0470A] For just as, concerning the fact that your Only-begotten was born from you before eternal times, [Note: [Col. 0470D] From the manuscripts we restore “born from you,” which was lacking in the earlier printed editions.] when every ambiguity of language and difficulty of understanding has ceased, only the fact that He was born remains; so also your Holy Spirit is from you through Him: although I do not grasp this by understanding, nevertheless I hold it in consciousness. For I am dull in matters of your Spirit, while your Only-begotten says: “Do not marvel that I said to you, You must be born again. [443] The Spirit breathes where He wills, and you hear His voice; but you do not know whence He comes or whither He goes. So is everyone who is born [Note: [Col. 0470D] Erasmus reads: “born from the Holy Spirit,” I suppose in order to conform to our copies of Scripture. But all editions and manuscripts of Hilary read: “born from water and the Holy Spirit.” Although *holy* does not occur in the manuscripts except in Martin., one Colbert manuscript, and the other Sorbonne manuscript.] from water and the Holy Spirit” (John 3:7–8). I possess the faith of my regeneration without knowing it; and what I do not know I now nevertheless hold. For I am reborn without my own understanding, though with the effective power of rebirth. But the Spirit is subject to no limitation in speaking what He wills, when He wills, and where He wills. [Note: [Col. 0470D] The manuscripts read “speaking.” On this same passage of Scripture Gregory Nazianzen likewise observes, *Oration* XXIV, no. 22, that it bears witness to the divinity of the Holy Spirit, since He approaches in a lordly rather than servile manner—δεσποτικῶς, οὐ δουλικῶς, “as master, not as slave.”] And shall I place among creatures, and confine by a definition of His origin, the nature of Him whose reason for coming and going is unknown, even though it is perceived by the consciousness of His presence? [Col. 0470B] John, who is yours, declares that all things were made through the Son, who was in the beginning with you, God, the Word, God (John 1:1, 3). But Paul enumerates all created things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible (Col. 1:16). [Note: [Col. 0470D] The Martinian manuscript reads “sets forth.”] And when he recalled that all things were created in Christ and [Col. 0471A] through Christ, he considered it sufficient indication concerning the Holy Spirit that he called Him your Spirit. With these men, specially chosen by you, I hold these things in such a manner that, as I say nothing further concerning your Only-begotten, according to them, beyond the reach of my understanding except that He is born, so likewise, according to them, I say nothing else concerning your Holy Spirit beyond the judgment of human intellect except that He is your Spirit. Let there be for me not a useless battle of words, but the steadfast confession of an unhesitating faith.

57. Prayer. — Preserve, I beseech you, this undefiled devotion of my faith, and grant me, until the departure of [Col. 0472A] my spirit, this utterance of my conscience: that I may always maintain what I professed in the creed of my regeneration, when baptized in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—namely, that I may worship you as our Father, and worship your Son together with you; [Note: [Col. 0471A] The words “together with you I worship: holy” are absent from the Colbert and German manuscripts.] that I may be worthy of your Holy Spirit, who is from you through your Only-begotten. For my Lord Jesus Christ, who says, “Father, all that is mine is yours, and all that is yours is mine” (John 17:10), is a fitting witness for my faith: He remains in you, from you, and with you, ever God; He is blessed for ages of ages. Amen. [Note: [Col. 0471A] The Corbie manuscript appends: “The twelfth book ends. Read happily in the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ.” One Sorbonne manuscript: “The twelfth book of Hilary, bishop, on the Trinity, ends happily.” In Silv.: “The twelfth book of Hilary, bishop, on faith in the most holy Trinity against heretics ends.” In Vindocin.: “The twelve books of the holy and incomparable man Hilary on faith in Father, Son, and Holy Spirit end.”]

[THE BOOK ON THE SYNODS.]

[Col. 0471]

445–446 PREFACE TO THE BOOK ON THE SYNODS.

I. Where and when this treatise was written. — This treatise must not be separated from the books *On the Trinity*. Nearly all the manuscripts join it to them so closely that in two Colbert manuscripts and the German manuscript, indeed even by Cassiodorus, it is called the thirteenth book. Nor is it distant from them in time or subject matter. For it too was undertaken to illuminate the faith, and, like the others, was the fruit of exile.
