Hilary had already spent a full three years in exile, as he himself states in no. 2 and no. 63, and was still remaining within the ten provinces of Asia when he published it. Accordingly, in the final words of this book he asks his brethren to remember his exile in their holy prayers. Yet if one listens to Scultetus (*Analysis*, p. 393), this book was written either at Seleucia during the synod, or at Constantinople, or during the very restoration of the Italian churches, after he had already returned from the regions of the East where he had lived in exile. So completely does the ingrained habit of judging matters not according to themselves but according to one’s own preconceived opinions dominate minds! Entangled in the same fault, Erasmus gave little thought to what he was saying when he declared that the book of Hilary mentioned by Jerome, containing the history of the Councils of Rimini and Seleucia, was perhaps combined with this treatise. What, indeed, did he find in it which occurred after those councils already mentioned, or which in itself pertains to their history (Erasmus, Preface to Hilary)?

But from Hilary’s own words in no. 8 it is clear that this book was written after the plan to convene a council at Nicomedia, or even at Nicaea in Bithynia, had been changed because of the earthquake which occurred on 24 August 358; but before it had been decreed that all who could should be summoned to Rimini and Seleucia. At that point it had merely been decreed that two, or one, from each province should assemble at Ancyra and Rimini. [Col. 0472A] Since this was determined toward the end of 358, everyone will readily concede that this treatise was published at the beginning of 359, or even at the end of 358. At least this is certain: its date must be fixed after August 358 and before May 359.

II. On what occasion; for what purpose. — A letter from the Gallican bishops, received shortly after they had condemned the second Sirmian formula and not long before the celebration of the Synod of Ancyra—thus about March 358—provided the occasion for this reply. Its aims were: first, to return the due response of communion in the Lord; second, to satisfy the wishes of certain persons who desired to know what the Eastern bishops were doing or had done in their professions of faith, and what Hilary himself thought of all their statements; third, to work toward the union, in the synods soon to be held, of the Easterners and Gauls. They had joined in opposition to the recently emerging heresy of the Anomoeans, but remained burdened with mutual suspicions and, if perhaps not greatly divided in their opinions, were certainly still divided in their language. The aim was that, after laying aside every suspicion, they might embrace one faith.

[Col. 0472D] III. Summary of the book. — For this purpose, after congratulating the Gauls in most friendly words upon their uninjured and steadfast faith, he first recounts the Sirmian blasphemy and opposes to it the definitions of faith published by the Easterners at Ancyra against the Anomoeans—except for those which their delegates, upon coming to Sirmium, had kept silent. He then sets forth all the creeds composed at various times and places after the holy Synod of Nicaea: namely, the Antiochene of 341, the pseudo-Sardican of 347, and the Sirmian against Photinus of 351. The bishops assembled at Ancyra repeatedly testify in their synodal letter, preserved in Epiphanius, *Heresy* LXXIII, no. 2, that they embrace all these. [Col. 0473A] It is these chiefly whom Hilary means by the name “Easterners.”

Seeking to recall them gently to the truth, he praises those who, content with the ancestral and apostolic faith, do not know written creeds; yet he excuses the plurality of professions and kindly interprets and defends whatever can be defended in them. Indeed, he does not suppress the usual objections against ὁμοούσιον (*homoousion*, “of one substance”); nor does he conceal what may be advanced in favour of the term ὁμοιούσιον (*homoiousion*, “of like substance”). Later, however, after setting forth the Nicene Creed, he establishes and concludes by the strongest arguments that ὁμοούσιον must be retained.

IV. It was not translated from Greek, except for the Eastern creeds. He translated those creeds literally. — I do not know whether, because the aforementioned confessions of faith are rendered in Latin, Scultetus, following Gillot (Preface to Hilary), says that this book was translated from Latin into Greek, not by attaching itself to the words but by rendering the sense. Still less is it established whether Erasmus, perhaps for the same reason, asserts as though certain: “This book, as Hilary himself testifies, he translated from Greek, but with such freedom that, everywhere neglecting the words, he renders only the sense and, where the occasion invites, mixes in something of his own. He allows himself the same freedom when writing on the Psalms.” Common usage does not permit a Latin work to be called a translation from Greek because it contains certain documents translated from Greek.

Yet, although Erasmus’s words in particular have an altogether different meaning, let us grant that they had in view the Eastern formulae incorporated in this book. On what basis do they say that Hilary everywhere neglected the words and rendered only the meaning? They do indeed cite his statement in no. 9 that he will set forth the decrees of Ancyra in language as clear as possible—not because they had not already been published by others, but because a translation from Greek into Latin expressed word for word generally produces obscurity, while the preserved correspondence of the words cannot maintain the same fluency for simplicity of understanding. But first, he speaks here only of the definitions of the Synod of Ancyra. Secondly, he indicates that an exact word-for-word translation is generally obscure, not insofar as it renders words, but insofar as it over-scrupulously preserves the same number, order, and arrangement of words. This he expressly declares in *On Psalm* LXVII, no. 21: he had, he says, already warned that interpreters generally make the force of utterances less clear when they do not dare to alter and adapt the arrangement and order of words. Finally, anyone who compares the Greek texts with Hilary’s Latin version will readily agree that scarcely any translation could have been produced that adheres more closely to the letter; and that Erasmus, Gillot, and Scultetus alike wished to speak concerning a matter they had not established.

V. Title. — Had they also looked more closely into the purpose of the whole work, the commonly received title would have displeased them: *On the Synods of the Catholic Faith against the Arians and the Prevaricators Who Acquiesce in the Arians*. As though the synods whose expositions it includes had been held by Catholics against Arians, rather than, for the most part, by Arians themselves or at least Semi-Arians. [Col. 0474A] At a minimum, it cannot be denied that the Council of Sirmium, which occupies the principal place in this book, met not against Arians but against Photinus; that the Antiochene council met against Athanasius; and finally that the pseudo-Sardican met against that same man and other Catholics.

The oldest manuscript of the Vatican basilica bears a less faulty title: *Book of the Catholic [Faith] against Arians and Prevaricators Acquiescing in Arians*. This is especially so because that manuscript contains only the first part of this book, with the definitions of the Ancyrene faith by which the authors of the Sirmian blasphemy and those acquiescing in it are refuted. Nor does the title *On the Synods*, which has prevailed in manuscripts for five hundred years, give an adequate account of this book. We conjecture that Jerome was its author; having no name by which to indicate this work briefly, he called it *On the Synods*, presumably in imitation of Athanasius’s book so entitled, to which this work appears to bear some affinity.

At Athanasius, however, the specific title is *On the Synods of Rimini and Seleucia*. He deals first expressly with these councils and then, as occasion arises, recounts several confessions of faith—not, as Hilary does, to excuse them kindly, but to demonstrate the Arians’ inconsistency in faith. Hence, even though the two works are alike in this respect, that both present several Eastern definitions of faith, their purpose is very different; and Athanasius’s prefixed title does not properly pertain to that part which appears similar to this work of Hilary. Therefore, the inscription of one should not be the standard for the other. [Col. 0474C] Accordingly, we think that this work bore no title bestowed by Hilary himself other than the names of those to whom he sent it. In all manuscripts of good authority it is simply called a letter; and it is cited no differently by Facundus of Hermiane, Book X, chapter 6: “Blessed Hilary,” he says, “the most powerful and vigorous assailant of the Arians and the most steadfast defender of the Christian faith, in the letter which he wrote from exile to the bishops of First and Second Germany,” etc.

But, in order to avoid the inconvenience of novelty, we do not change the received title *On the Synods*. We nevertheless add, “or On the Faith of the Easterners,” so that the reader may have on the title-page a brief indication of the matters to be treated.

VI. This treatise is commended by its authority. — This treatise, which may be called the fruit of prayer, the seed of peace, and the germ of charity, was plainly seen by Vigilius of Thapsus, from his Book V against Eutyches, no. 3, although he did not adequately observe its purpose. Facundus praised it not only in Book X, chapter 6, but also in Book XII, chapter 3; and Augustine defended it against Vincentius the Rogatist in Letter XCIII, nos. 31 and 32. Jerome esteemed it so highly that he copied it with his own hand: “I ask you likewise to transcribe for me the very long book *On the Synods* by Saint Hilary, which I myself had copied out by hand for him at Trier” (*Letter* VI, to Florentius).

VII. It is a mirror of Hilary’s virtues, especially his gentleness. — It deserves commendation not only because it contains many events that illuminate history, [Col. 0475A] but also because it presents a true and living likeness of that most holy bishop. In this single treatise, as in a mirror, almost all Hilary’s virtues shine forth: prudence, steadfastness, greatness of spirit joined with lowliness or Christian humility, chaste love of country, the highest devotion to peace, sincerity and integrity of faith, and so forth. But especially that outstanding gentleness and modesty, suited to winning the hearts of all, which Rufinus testifies that he possessed (*History*, Book I, chapter 31), shines everywhere so brightly that, even without having heard Rufinus’s testimony, we should immediately reject as false and unfair the prevalent opinion that he was of a somewhat impetuous and vehement temper.

We are confirmed in this judgment no little by the calm and honeyed replies to those criticisms which certain persons made improperly against this treatise. [Col. 0475B] In these replies clearly appears that invincible tranquillity of mind by which, even when injured, he was able to soothe his critics through the peaceful tenor of his language: in a matter concerning himself, he knew absolutely nothing of anger. But something must first be said here concerning those replies, which are now for the first time being brought out of obscurity.

VIII. From where the apologetic replies to this book have been recovered. — In the manuscript of Chartres, written in Roman letters about nine hundred years ago, it appears, and likewise in the Michaelinian manuscript, we find this book enlarged in various places. The passages by which it is enlarged do not sufficiently cohere with the remaining discourse, nor do they belong altogether to it; yet they entirely breathe Hilary and present him answering in his own name on his own behalf. The Tellerian manuscript and a more recent Chartres manuscript exhibit the same additions in the same places, but only written in the margin. The Remigian manuscript has some in the text itself and others in the margin, preceded by the notice that they occur in certain exemplars. Finally, in the very ancient exemplar of the Vatican basilica, which, as we have said, contains only the first part of this book, two additions of this kind are likewise inserted into the text itself.

IX. Their usefulness. — That all these additions are Hilary’s is so clear that it seems superfluous to attempt to prove it. Yet, just as their being mixed into the words of the book confuses its order, so, when placed separately in their proper locations, they provide great help in resolving certain questions which are still debated. [Col. 0475D] They also teach us certain highly noteworthy actions of Hilary which had hitherto remained hidden: namely, that this most devout bishop was spoken of unfavourably by some because of this treatise, and that he was specifically censured by Lucifer—undoubtedly Lucifer of Cagliari, whom everyone knows to have been somewhat harsh and austere in disposition—as an approver of the term ὁμοιούσιον (*homoiousion*) and as an excessively flattering admirer and praiser of the Easterners. By dealing too leniently with them, he was said to have celebrated them as heralds of the true faith. Nor had it been known from earlier authorities that he undertook an apologetic work. This is at least partly represented for us by the aforementioned supplements, which we may suitably call apologetic replies to the critics of the book *On the Synods*.

[Col. 0476A] X. Whether they are fragments or notes; whether any further material is to be sought. — It may be questioned whether these are fragments of a more extensive apology, fitted into their places by some diligent person, or merely notes and appendices attached by Hilary himself to elucidate passages in this book which had given occasion for criticism, and sent with the book thus annotated to his critics. We nevertheless consider it probable that, after Lucifer had warned him concerning what displeased both himself and others in this treatise, Hilary sent Lucifer the same treatise enlarged with those brief replies, by which he made all men more certain of the sincerity of his faith.

But I would not venture to assert that no further replies remain to be sought. For even among those now published for the first time, different manuscripts contain different ones, and none contains them all. Many contain none. In most, the first is found without the others; the second, however, we owe to one manuscript of St Peter’s in Rome; finally, in the Chartres manuscript and others in which the rest occur, the first two are absent.

XI. The points on which Hilary clears himself. — The individual replies are all the more suited to removing suspicions because Hilary clears himself precisely at the passages in which he had been criticized. This scandal was certainly necessary, so that with a kind of glad admiration we might hear from him how great was the prudence he used in moderating every word of his book. Who would not now admire and love him when he shows that he praised the Easterners without the fault of flattery, since he did not fail to rebuke them in their proper place; and that, although he addressed them in conciliatory language, he did so especially in order to avoid insolent insults and subsequently disclose more effectively the concealed dangers in their expositions? He did not remove every suspicion from them, since he said that they brought not the true faith but only hope that the true faith might be restored. Finally, he shows that he accepted *homoiousion* reluctantly and solely for the sake of peace, so as not to dissent from Lucifer, who proclaimed it, and that he did so with the greatest possible caution.

XII. It is falsely believed that he regarded the Easterners as orthodox. — From this the common opinion is now manifestly refuted: namely, that Hilary regarded the Easterners, commonly called Semi-Arians, as orthodox, and approved their formulae as Catholic. He did indeed see them advancing toward the true faith; he saw that their formulae could in some manner be tolerated when understood in a Catholic sense; he praised and, so far as he could, promoted those who were drawing near; he arranged for them the true meaning, so to speak, of their confessions and gently offered it to them as something clarified. But he never regarded them as entirely Catholic, nor did he wish to remove suspicion from them.

453–454 XIII. It is falsely believed that he differed from Athanasius concerning their formulae. The differing manner of speech of each is reconciled by their differing purposes. — Hence also vanishes the notion lodged in almost everyone’s mind: that Hilary in this treatise thought differently about the Eastern formulae from Athanasius in his work likewise entitled *On the Synods*, and praised what Athanasius openly condemns. For if Hilary considered that those assembled at Ancyra—who sharply opposed the Anomoeans and confirmed by so many decrees the likeness in substance of the Son with the Father—had not brought the true faith, he would still less have thought that those brought it who at Antioch, Philippopolis, or Sirmium had not yet come so near to the true faith.

But if anyone asks why, without holding different views, they speak so differently, the answer is ready. Let him attend to the purpose of each, and he will easily reconcile their language. For who does not know that a different mode of speech must be adopted concerning the same matters according to a difference of purpose? Athanasius had set himself the task in this book of convicting the Arians, from faith-formulae so often issued and so often changed, of an inconsistent and therefore perverse faith. Thus he had to disapprove openly and expressly such a great variety of formulae. [Col. 0477B] Hilary, however, had chiefly proposed to himself that, by winning the goodwill of the Easterners and inclining the Westerners somewhat in their favour, he might prepare both sides to enter into concord and peace in the synods already summoned. Accordingly, he had to pass over much in silence, devise reasons for repeatedly composing formulae, and kindly interpret the language in which they were expressed.

XIV. They are reconciled by difference of time. The books to Constantius contain nothing inconsistent with this work. — Moreover, different language was necessary for those who wrote at different times. Hilary wrote before the Synod of Rimini, when he hoped that, just as the Easterners had been received by Constantius against the Anomoeans, so he himself—what he had always wished—would be favourably heard against Valens and Ursacius. If this should ever be granted him, he trusted that those two leaders of the Arian party, who were unsettling the whole East and West, could readily be overcome, and that the Emperor himself could at last be recalled to the true faith. Thinking thus, he ought not to condemn the faith of the Easterners, whom Constantius then extraordinarily favoured, but to praise and approve it as far as was permissible.

Athanasius, however, wrote after the aforementioned synod, when the Church’s welfare required that what was defective in so many confessions of faith should not be concealed. At that time Hilary himself neither concealed it nor spared it. For then, in the pamphlet addressed to Constantius and again in the second book against that Emperor, he openly and expressly disapproved the multitude of formulae. Therefore, after the state of affairs had changed, he changed his style in these books; he did not, as some suppose, make statements contrary to what he had said in the book *On the Synods*.

XV. How many passages in this book indicate that the Easterners’ faith did not meet with his approval. — This is plain not only from the words of the apology but also from the treatise itself: the Eastern confessions were not then approved by him in themselves and without qualification. Why, in no. 6 and again in no. 65, did he so earnestly entreat his readers not to judge him before he had completed his discourse, unless he foresaw that his kindly interpretations could lead to an unfavourable judgment of him? Why, in no. 7, does he say of the formulae he is to set forth: “If anything is understood to be defective in them, no one can charge me with the defect of the statements; for, as you wished, I am their messenger, not their composer”—unless he thought they were not free from every defect? What does he mean when immediately afterwards he adds, “I have faithfully transmitted what was done; you must determine by the judgment of your faith whether these things are Catholic or heretical,” unless he judges them not even free from suspicion of heresy?

But after setting forth all the Eastern formulae, he clearly indicates in no. 63 that none of them meets with his approval, when, lamenting the miserable condition of the East, he says: “So great is the danger to the Eastern churches that it is rare to find either clergy or people of this faith”—a faith whose character, he adds, “you must judge.” This is especially so because he repeats the very point, with a certain emphasis, in no. 66. Finally, what does his statement in no. 3 mean—that the renown of the Gallic faith moved certain Eastern bishops, now at last, to some shame for the heresy nourished and increased among them—unless the same Easterners had nourished and increased heresy up to the Synod of Ancyra, and therefore at Antioch, Philippopolis, and Sirmium as well? Indeed, in no. 9 he declares, not without expressing his grief, that what they dared to do at the Synod of Ancyra itself was impious.

455–456 XVI. He did not regard the false Synod of Sardica as genuine. — Since this is so, we cannot see on what grounds those rely who maintain that the holy confessor, when writing this book, regarded the false Synod of Sardica as genuine. Is it because he did not call its creed Philippopolitan? But this was prudent, lest he alienate the Easterners whom he was most eager to reconcile. Yet [Col. 0478C] neither did he call it Sardican, lest he deceive the Westerners. He gave it the carefully moderated title, “Faith according to the Synod of the East,” so that, without offending the Easterners, he might sufficiently indicate that it was the faith of those who had withdrawn from the Westerners gathered at Sardica. This is equivalent to calling it Philippopolitan.

He did indeed call it Sardican in the book addressed to Constantius, but not so much according to his own judgment as according to that of Constantius himself, whom he was addressing. And certainly he was then better informed about Eastern affairs than to be ignorant of the distinction between the true and false Synods of Sardica.

XVII. Even if he held the Easterners’ faith somewhat in suspicion, yet the goodwill which he displayed toward them in this book he preserved afterward also at Seleucia and Constantinople. Nor did Athanasius act otherwise toward them. Even after the year 360, in his *On the Synods*, p. 916, he writes that Basil of Ancyra and those like him ought to be treated as persons who are not far from accepting the term *consubstantial*. “For,” he says a little earlier, “we do not oppose them as we do Ariomaniacs or enemies of the Fathers; rather, we dispute with brothers as brothers, since we agree with them in doctrine, and the controversy is over words.” In this respect he seems to have thought more favorably of the Easterners than did our Hilary. For although Hilary says certain similar things near the end of section 8, many other statements show that he spoke not so much with firm assurance as from a devout inclination of mind that was not yet free from apprehension. Thus these two most distinguished men have taught us by their example that admirable saying of Gregory Nazianzen, *Oration* XXI, §19: “For I think that in doubtful and uncertain matters we ought to be more inclined toward kindness and humanity, and should acquit rather than condemn those who are at fault.” But as regards our Hilary, his apologetic replies will, as we have said, leave no doubt about his real attitude toward the Easterners; we shall present them both separately in the notes and collected together after this book.

[Col. 0479]

*(WRITTEN ABOUT THE END OF THE YEAR 358.)*  
457–458 **THE BOOK OF SAINT HILARY ON THE SYNODS, OR ON THE FAITH OF THE EASTERNERS.** (C)

[Col. 0479B] To the most beloved [Note: [Col. 0479C] Thus all manuscripts except one of the Vatican Basilica and the later Carnotensis, which, together with the printed editions, prefer “Lords” rather than “most beloved.” But the letter against Auxentius is entitled “to the most beloved brethren” with the strong agreement of the manuscripts.] and most blessed brethren and [Note: [Col. 0479C] Several manuscripts, though not the better ones, read “and fellow bishops,” subsequently omitting the designation of the provinces. But in the later Carnotensis the whole title is interpolated thus: “To the fellow bishops of First Germany, in which Mainz holds first place; and of Second Germany, in which Agrippina—that is, Cologne—holds first place; and of First Belgica, in which Trier holds first place; and of Second Belgica, in which Reims holds first place; and of First Lugdunensis, in which Lyons holds first place; and of Second Lugdunensis, in which Rouen holds first place; and to the people of Narbonensis, in which Narbonne holds first place; and to the clergy of Toulouse,” etc. This appears to have been drawn from what is prefixed at the beginning of the entire treatise in manuscripts of the monasteries of Sylva Major and St Remigius of Reims: “In First Germany Mainz holds first place; in Second, Agrippina, that is Cologne; in First Belgica, Trier; in Second Belgica, Reims; in First Lugdunensis, Lyons; in Second Lugdunensis, Rouen; in Novempopulana, Toulouse”—incorrectly with regard to this final metropolis. For in the sixth-century Corbie manuscript, Elusa is recorded as the chief city of Novempopulana; Toulouse, however, is placed in First Narbonensis after Narbonne.] fellow bishops of the provinces of First Germany, Second Germany, First Belgica, Second Belgica, [Note: [Col. 0479D] The printed editions here and below read “Lugdunensis”; the better manuscripts oppose this.] First Lugdunensis, Second Lugdunensis, and the province [Note: [Col. 0479D] Nine manuscripts omit “and the province of Aquitania.” The ancient Colbertinus and Germanensis read “and the province of Aquitane”; two others, “and the province of Aquitania”; the Carnotensis, “and the province of First Aquitania.” Certainly, in the division of the Gallic provinces supplied by the aforementioned Corbie manuscript written in the middle of the sixth century, two Aquitanias are listed: the metropolis of the first is the city of the Bituriges, and of the second, that of the Bordelais. Likewise four Lugdunenses and two Narbonenses are mentioned. Did Hilary deliberately refrain from naming these provinces distinctly?] of Aquitania, the province of Novempopulana, and [Note: [Col. 0480C] The Corbie manuscript and many others read “and to the people of Narbonensis.” The received reading, supported by the older Colbertinus, Carnotensis, and others, should be retained: as if Hilary were saying, “and from the whole province of Narbonensis”—whose metropolis was Narbonne and under which Toulouse is listed—“especially to the people and clergy of Toulouse.” He had a special concern for them because their bishop Rhodanus, who, according to Sulpicius Severus, was mild by nature and had resisted the Arians not so much through his own strength as through his association with Hilary, had been involved in the same condition of exile.] to the people and clergy of Toulouse from Narbonensis; and to the bishops of the provinces [Note: [Col. 0480C] Tertullian testifies in *Against the Jews*, §4, that Britain was already Christian in his own time, when he mentions regions of the Britons inaccessible to the Romans but subject to the true Christ. Bede writes, *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*, I.4, that they received the faith in the middle of the second century, in the time of King Lucius and Pope Eleutherius. Hilary seems to have no others in view in his exposition of Psalm XIV, §3, where he relates that the Apostles prepared many dwellings for God even on the islands of the Ocean. Now, however, he indicates that the bishops of Britain had joined with those of Gaul in combating the Arian plague, which, according to Bede himself, in the work cited, I.8, spread the poison of its unbelief not only through the churches of the whole world but also through those of the islands.] of Britain: Hilary, servant of Christ, eternal salvation in God and our Lord.

1. **Hilary’s purpose, concerned for the faith of the bishops of Gaul.**—My dearest brethren, during this long period of your silence I had resolved to send you no letter of ecclesiastical discourse. For I had repeatedly informed you, from many cities of the Roman provinces, what faith and zeal our devout brethren, the Eastern bishops, possessed, and how greatly, under the pretext of political disturbances, the devil, with venomous mouth and a tongue of deadly doctrine, had uttered his hisses. I feared that, amid the danger of so grievous an impiety or error shared by so many bishops, your silence had arisen from despair over a conscience polluted and made impious [Note: [Col. 0480D] The printed editions read “suspect”; corrected from the better manuscripts.]; for, having been repeatedly warned, you were not permitted to plead ignorance. I therefore believed that I too ought to keep silence before you, very mindful of the Lord’s judgment, by which, after a first and repeated admonition, he commanded that those who remained disobedient even before the testimony of the Church should be regarded as heathen and tax collectors (Matt. 18:15 ff.).

[Col. 0481A] 2. **He congratulates the bishops of Gaul on refusing communion with Saturninus and condemning the Sirmian creed.**—But upon receiving the letters of your blessed faith [Note: [Col. 0481B] Since through these letters he learned that the Gauls had not merely refused but had condemned the Sirmian confession issued in 357—or, as the manuscripts consistently read, the “Sirmian” confession—it is clear that he received them either at the end of 357 or at the beginning of 358. Since the Gauls’ unwavering constancy in condemning that confession became known to the Easterners before Easter 358, that is, before they met at Ancyra, Hilary must have received the same letters no later than March 358. It is highly probable that the Easterners learned through Hilary himself what had occurred in Gaul. At any rate, he did not first learn it from the Easterners, since before these letters he had been uncertain and anxious about the Gauls’ faith.], whose delay and infrequency I understand to have resulted from both the length and secrecy of my exile, I rejoiced in the Lord that you had remained untainted and unharmed by every infection of the detestable heresy; that, by refusing Saturninus communion even to the present time, now for a full three years, you remained united with me in faith and spirit as sharers in my exile—the exile into which Saturninus, fearing his own conscience, had cast me after deceiving [Note: [Col. 0481C] That is, Constantius, who was then residing at Milan. See *To Constantius*, II.2.] the emperor; and that you had not merely refused to receive, but had also condemned when announced and made known to you, the impiety of the faithless creed recently sent to you from the town of Sirmium.

I understood it to be necessary and religiously incumbent upon me now, as bishop writing to bishops who share communion with me in Christ, to send you communications of salutary and faithful discourse. Formerly, amid fear of uncertainties, I rejoiced only in my own conscience that I was free from all these persons; now I rejoice in the integrity of our common faith. O the unshaken stability of your glorious conscience! O house founded upon the firm foundation of the faithful rock! [Note: [Col. 0481C] Hilary seems here to praise the Gauls for confessing the Son of God, evidently alluding to Peter’s confession, concerning which he says in *On the Trinity*, II.23: “This therefore is the one immovable foundation, this the one blessed rock of faith confessed by Peter’s mouth: You are the Son of the living God”; and VI.36: “Upon this rock of confession, therefore, the Church’s building stands.”] O the uninjured and untroubled constancy of an unstained will! For after the declaration of the Synod of Béziers—in which, before certain of you as witnesses, I had denounced the patrons [Note: [Col. 0481D] Six manuscripts read the singular “patron,” which could conveniently be understood as Saturninus of Arles, leader of the Arian party, as Sulpicius calls him, p. 263. But since the older manuscripts read the plural “patrons,” Ursacius and Valens seem to be indicated along with Saturninus. Sulpicius, p. 247, recounts their attempts and devices at the Council of Milan in 355 to introduce heresy. This is supported by Hilary’s statement in *To Constantius*, §2, that shortly after the Council of Milan he and the Gallic bishops withdrew from communion with Saturninus, Ursacius, and Valens, while granting their other associates the opportunity to repent.] of introducing this heresy—there remained, and still remains, innocent, [Note: [Col. 0481D] Six manuscripts read the singular “patron,” which could conveniently be understood as Saturninus of Arles, leader of the Arian party, as Sulpicius calls him, p. 263. But since the older manuscripts read the plural “patrons,” Ursacius and Valens seem to be indicated along with Saturninus. Sulpicius, p. 247, recounts their attempts and devices at the Council of Milan in 355 to introduce heresy. This is supported by Hilary’s statement in *To Constantius*, §2, that shortly after the Council of Milan he and the Gallic bishops withdrew from communion with Saturninus, Ursacius, and Valens, while granting their other associates the opportunity to repent.] inviolate, devout. [Note: [Col. 0481D] The printed editions, except Bad., read “and inviolate religion,” which is also found in two manuscripts without *-que*. The others, with Bad., read “inviolate, devout”—supply “constancy.”]

3. **They do not yield to a heresy about to break forth, but crush it when it breaks forth. By their example they move the Easterners toward repentance.**—For you awaited the glorious triumph of holy and unchangeable perseverance, refusing to yield to Saturninus’ threats, powers, and warfare. While every assault was being stirred up to inaugurate blasphemy against God, you remained faithful with me in Christ until now: neither previously did you give way to the opportunity for the heresy’s outbreak, nor now, when it broke forth, did you fail to crush all its insolence in combat. You have conquered, brethren, to the great joy of our common faith; and the honour of your unimpaired [Note: [Col. 0481D] Thus the chief manuscripts. The printed editions read “conscience.”] constancy has had a twofold glory: that of the integrity of your conscience, and that of the authority of your example.

For the report of your undisturbed and unshaken faith moved certain Eastern bishops, though late, to some shame concerning the heresy that had been fostered and increased among them. When they heard what had been written at Sirmium with the utmost impiety, they opposed the audacity of irreligious men with certain decrees expressing their own judgments. [Note: [Col. 0482B] The decrees of the Synod of Ancyra are indicated here. After the word “opposed,” earlier printed editions added: “And if this judgment had been carefully weighed, perhaps the purpose of my whole treatise would not have been suspect. For I would not there have kept silent about what could be heard only with scandal.” These words do not cohere with the rest of the discourse and are absent from the sound manuscripts—the two Colbert manuscripts, Germanensis, and Carnotensis. They are found, however, in the very ancient manuscript of the Vatican Church, in Corbie, and in many others. Who does not see that this is one of the apologetic notes mentioned in the preface, referring to the words, “And although not without some scandal to the ears,” etc.? For if this one judgment had indeed been carefully weighed, no place remained for the suspicion into which Hilary fell on account of this treatise: namely, that he considered the Easterners wholly in agreement with Catholic truth. In explicit terms he warns that certain decrees of the aforesaid synod offended devout ears. Here he not obscurely indicates the last two decrees reported by Epiphanius, *Heresies*, LXXIII.11: in one they declared that the Father was Father not only by substance but also by authority; in the other they condemned *homoousion*. Hilary prudently suppresses these in this treatise, because the Easterners themselves, on coming to Sirmium, had been the first to keep silent about them. Yet he indicates here and elsewhere that he was aware of them. Therefore in the apologetic note, instead of “For I would not there have kept silent,” one should undoubtedly read, “For I did not keep silent that they were there.” Likewise, in the opening words, “And if carefully,” the particle “and” is superfluous and absent from the manuscripts.]

And although they resisted not without some scandal to the ears and offense to devout concern, yet they resisted so effectively that they compelled those very persons who at that time had agreed with and confirmed the opinion of Potamius and [Note: [Col. 0482D] In ancient books the name of Osius is consistently written with a double *s*: *Ossius*. The printed editions then read “so that they themselves agreed.” From the better manuscripts we restore: “and so they themselves,” and from all, “thinking and confirming.” Hilary here touches upon what he discusses more fully in §§78–79, where he explains that some, forced to confess their ignorance and make a new subscription, though suspicious of it, condemned what they had done. He then attacks Ursacius and Valens by name, because they could not plausibly plead ignorance. There seems no reason to doubt that this forced subscription occurred shortly after the Synod of Ancyra, when Basil and other delegates brought its decrees to the emperor. There is also strong reason to suppose that this refers to what Germinius says in Fragment XV.3: namely, that in the presence of Basil, Eleusius, Valens, and others, a debate on the faith was conducted before the emperor until nightfall—if the conjecture is correct, the former defending the Ancyran decrees and the latter the appended blasphemy of Osius—and then Marcus of Arethusa was elected by the vote of all to compose a formula, to which each afterward subscribed. It might also be thought that Germinius quoted the words of this formula composed by Marcus in Fragment XIII, where he confesses the true Son of God, begotten before all things, to be like the Father in all things in divinity, love, majesty, power, glory, life, wisdom, and knowledge. These statements seem deliberately opposed to the Osiac blasphemy, by which they declared the Father greater than the Son in honour, glory, majesty, and even in the name “Father.” Yet one thing causes difficulty: why Hilary, in this work in which he promises all the Eastern formulas, should have passed over this final one, which especially served his own purpose to publish. It may, however, be answered that only this one report of that conference was then circulated: that Ursacius, Valens, and the others had confessed themselves to have sinned through ignorance and subscribed to the decisions of Basil and his associates, while each kept the formula there published secret to himself.] Osius—though they themselves had thought and confirmed the same—to confess their ignorance and error, so that by subscribing once more they might condemn what they had done. They certainly did this [Note: [Col. 0483D] The printed editions read “had done.” But the manuscripts read “did,” which seems said of the Easterners and is a partial repetition of the preceding thought: namely, they compelled them to subscribe so that by that subscription they might condemn what they had previously done at Sirmium.] in order first to condemn something else.

4. **Whose communion they avoid.**—But even now your unconquered faith retains the admirable glory of its conscience [Note: [Col. 0484C] The Carnotensis manuscript, with a few others, reads “of constancy,” incorrectly. Hilary first stated that the Gauls’ constancy was adorned with a twofold glory: that of example and that of integrity of conscience. He then explained what their example had accomplished. Now he recounts what constitutes the glory of their own unimpaired conscience.]. Content to do nothing deceitful, ambiguous, or fearful, it perseveres securely in Christ in the confession of its freedom [Note: [Col. 0484C] Seven manuscripts read “secure.”], by abstaining from communion with those who keep in exile bishops who oppose their blasphemies, and by not joining itself, through assent to deceptive dissimulation, to the guilt of an unjust judgment.

For after the great and grievous sorrow of us all over those matters which the impious were carrying on irreligiously, communion in the Lord is confined to ourselves alone [Note: [Col. 0484C] Whom he means by “ourselves” is made clear in §8, where those summoned to the synod in Bithynia are praised for abstaining from others outside Gaul. The communion refused seems to have been only that of letters and sacred mysteries, not conversation. For Hilary himself testifies in *To Constantius*, §2, that he never considered speaking with heretics a crime.], since the Church began to be harassed by these disturbances: bishops are exiled, priests displaced, congregations terrified, faith endangered, and the decrees of the Lord’s teaching established by human decision and power. Your uninjured faith neither pretends not to know this nor declares itself able to endure it, understanding that even assent by dissimulation would not leave it free from the guilt of conscience.

5. **The occasion of this letter; the difficulty of the work.**—And although in all that you have done and are doing you bear witness to the steadfast freedom and security of your faith, yet you also prove the ardour of your fervent spirit in this: some among you, whose writings could be conveyed to me, have desired that the letters of my lowliness should inform you what the Easterners are doing and have done in their confessions of faith. In addition, out of charitable affection, you lay even this burden upon me, the most unskilled and unlearned of all: that I should declare what I myself think concerning all their statements. Yet it is most difficult to set forth in speech even the sense of my own faith, according to the disposition of my inward understanding [Note: [Col. 0484D] The term “inward,” found in only one edition of Miraeus, occurs in all manuscripts. For Hilary’s lack of confidence in expounding his own faith, see *On the Trinity*, II.5 ff. and XI.44.], much less easily to expound the meaning of what is said by others.

6. **On the condition under which it ought to be read; the usefulness of the work.**—But I beg you, by the Lord’s mercy: since, as you wished, I shall in this letter speak to you of divine matters [Note: [Col. 0484D] The Leipzig and Paris editions read “because nothing [is written] to you”; other manuscripts correct this.] and of the unstained conscience of our faith, let no one suppose that judgment should be made about me from the opening parts of the letter before the discourse has been completed. For it is unjust, before the meaning of statements has been ascertained to the end, to render a prejudged verdict from beginnings whose purpose is still unknown; since judgment for understanding must be formed not from things begun but from things completed.

For I fear—not concerning you, as the Lord who knows my mind is witness, but concerning certain persons excessively cautious and wise in their own eyes [Note: [Col. 0484D] The manuscripts read “not understanding.” The Carnotensis then reads “lest they should think proudly”; the Corbie manuscript, in a second hand, “lest they should think proud things,” which subsequently prevailed in many others. The reading of the other manuscripts is confirmed by the Greek expression μὴ ὑπερφρονεῖν, “not to think too highly,” and by *On the Trinity*, X.53: “Will not folly come upon those who wish to be overwise?”]—who do not understand that through the blessed Apostle they have been commanded not to think beyond what is fitting (Rom. 12:3). I fear that they may be unwilling to know all that I shall be obliged to furnish in its completed form, because they avoid understanding the truth from what will be set forth. But whoever undertakes to read and consider these things should grant both himself and me the measure of faithful patience, and should review everything through to its completion [Note: [Col. 0484D] The ancient Colbert manuscript, with the Germanensis, reads “go on continually.” Hilary so little believes those whose confessions he expounds to be Catholics that he repeatedly suggests they might even be thought covert heretics.]. For perhaps this entire discussion of my faith will accomplish this: that neither covert heretics may deceive in the way they desire, nor perfect Catholics fail to attain what they seek.

[Col. 0484C] 7. **What it comprises.**—I therefore comply with the most earnest desire of Your Charity, and I have sent all the creeds published after the holy Synod of Nicaea at different times and places, adding my own explanations of all their propositions [Col. 0485A] and even their words. If anything in them is understood to be erroneous [Note: [Col. 0485C] The printed editions read “erroneous,” against the manuscripts. The words “if anything erroneous is present,” as well as “I am only a messenger, not an author; but if anything is right,” apply to the Eastern formulas themselves, not to their interpretations; they are the words of one who fears that he may seem to approve the formulas he leniently excuses.], no one can charge me with the fault of what has been said, for I am, as you wished, merely its messenger, not its author. But if anything right and prescribed by apostolic teachings [Note: [Col. 0485C] We add from the manuscripts and Miraeus “prescribed,” which was omitted in the other printed editions. As already observed, Hilary prudently refrains from stating what he himself thinks of the Eastern faith, and does not deny that it can also be judged heretical.] is discovered, no one doubts that the glory lies not with the interpreter but with the author. Yet I have faithfully transmitted what has been done; determine by the judgment of your faith whether it is Catholic or heretical.

8. **Its aim; the mutual suspicions of Easterners and Gauls.**—For although it was necessary to answer your letters, by which you had sent me in writing the communion of your faith in the Lord; although some of you, summoned to the synod that seemed likely to be held in Bithynia [Note: [Col. 0485C] That is, at Nicomedia, where it could not be held because that city was destroyed by an earthquake on 24 August 358, as Socrates, II.37, and Sozomen, IV.16, relate.], maintained yourselves within my communion by the firmest constancy of faith [Note: [Col. 0485D] Several manuscripts, though not the better ones, read “conscience.” From what Hilary writes here, some conclude that the Gallic bishops summoned to the Synod of Nicomedia had already reached Hilary himself in Phrygia when he began this work. But that conclusion is not necessary. Nothing prevents him from saying that they kept themselves within his communion in the same sense in which he said above, §2, that the bishops of Gaul adhered to him in faith and spirit, and in which he praised them in §4 for persisting in their resolve to abstain from communion with those who kept bishops opposing heresy in exile. They could certainly do this even without leaving Gaul. Whatever the case, they abstained from bishops who were not Gauls in obedience to the decree mentioned above in §4.], and abstained from others outside Gaul; and although in such a fury of heretics it was certainly worthy of episcopal ministry and speech to confer with you by letter on certain counsels of devout faith—for the word of God, though I was exiled in body, could not be bound and detained so as to prevent its being communicated with you wherever you were (see *On the Trinity*, X.4)—yet especially, when I learned that synods were to be assembled at Ancyra and Ariminum [Note: [Col. 0486C] It is absent from one manuscript. Hilary alone mentions that Ancyra was designated for a synod to be convened after the disaster at Nicomedia. Sozomen, IV.16, does not conflict with this when he reports that different places had been proposed by different persons. Nor would it have been alien to Basil’s character, since he had been entrusted with the matter, to select the city over which he presided. It is also distinctive that Hilary says only one or two men from each province would come to Ariminum and Ancyra. For although Sozomen, IV.16, says that selected bishops from every nation had been summoned to Nicomedia to sit in the council and take part in its decision on behalf of all the bishops of their province, he also testifies there that when the emperor learned that the council’s location had to be changed, he ordered that no longer one bishop from each province, but every bishop able to come, should be summoned.], and that one or two men from every Gallic province would come there, I judged that the matters in which we and the Eastern bishops are held apart by mutual suspicions ought to be explained and published for you—though you already knew them—through me, who was residing in the East. Thus, although you had condemned this heresy which broke out from Sirmium, and they had likewise judged it with anathema, you might know in what confession of faith the Eastern bishops had accomplished the very thing which you had done. And I would not allow you, whom above all I wished to appear commendable at the coming synods, while holding one and the same Catholic understanding of the apostolic faith [Note: [Col. 0486D] Some manuscripts read “Catholically.”], to differ, even to some extent, from the sincerity of Catholic faith through ignorance of the meaning of words.

9. **Why the Eastern decrees against the Sirmian formula are set forth here.**—I indeed judge it right and appropriate, before I begin speaking of the suspicions and disagreements concerning words, to demonstrate in terms as clear as I can the things said and decreed by the Eastern bishops against the heresy written at Sirmium. This is not because all these things have not been published very plainly by others, but because translation from Greek into Latin, rendered word for word, commonly introduces obscurity [Note: [Col. 0486D] Baronius, under the year 357, §11, incorrectly supposes that this refers to the blasphemous Sirmian confession, and from it wrongly concludes in §13 that Hilary did not encounter the genuine edition of that confession, which was written in Latin, but only a Greek version. For who does not see that these words refer to what the Easterners decreed at Ancyra? Still more astonishing is how Erasmus, Scultetus, and Gillotius could have been misled by this passage into thinking that the entire work was published in Greek and merely rendered into Latin by Hilary. Here one is struck by the scrupulousness of the ancients in translating writings from Greek into Latin. As we have observed, Hilary’s translations that follow could scarcely be rendered more literally.], because the preservation of a correspondence of words cannot retain the same clarity in simple intelligibility.

10. **What was attempted in the formula of Sirmium.**—For you remember that in the blasphemy itself lately written at Sirmium this was attempted and laboured for: that, while the Father was proclaimed the one and sole God of all, the Son’s being God might be denied; that, while it was decreed that *homoousion* and *homoiousion* should not be mentioned, it might thereby be established that God the Son was born either from nothing, as a creature, or from another essence, as a consequence of creatures, and not God from God the Father. Further, in the assertion that the Father is greater in honour, dignity, glory, and majesty, this was sought: that the Son should lack all those things in which the Father is said to be greater. Finally, when his birth was declared unknowable, we were commanded by this decree of ignorance not to know that he is from God—as though it could be ordered and decreed either that someone should know what he is going to be ignorant of, or be ignorant of what he has known.

[Col. 0487A] Yet I have reluctantly appended the whole pestilence of this most impious blasphemy, so that the strength and rationale of the responses which the Easterners have set in opposition might be more clearly known. [Note: [Col. 0487B] The responses of the Ancyrene Fathers were not originally set forth specifically against the appended Sirmian formula, but against the views and words of Eudoxius, Acacius, and other supporters of Aetius who had assembled at Antioch; these are described by Epiphanius, *Heresies*, LXXIII.21. Nevertheless, because Eudoxius and his associates agreed with the Sirmian formula in these matters, and encouraged by the example of its authors had ventured to put such things into public, there is no doubt that the same decrees, directed in themselves against the views of Eudoxius and his followers, were directed against the Sirmian blasphemy.] Their concern was to oppose all the devices of the heretics in accordance with the meaning they understood.

[Note: [Col. 0487B] There is no reason to seek this heading, prefixed by Hilary himself, in Athanasius or Socrates. [Col. 0487C] Osius should be considered not so much the writer of the appended formula as one who ratified it by his subscription. And this, as Socrates, II.31, and Sozomen, IV.6 and 12, attest, he did under compulsion of torture, and, as Sulpicius Severus reports in II from Hilary’s lost letters, when he was more than a hundred years old. Hilary may nevertheless have called it Osius’s because the Arians circulated it under his name. On this matter Phoebadius of Agen says: “I am not unaware . . . that the name of Osius, a most ancient bishop and one ever prompt in faith, is being fashioned like a battering ram against us.” He prudently turns back the battering ram sent against him with these words: “If he believed wrongly for nearly ninety years, I shall not believe that after ninety years he thought rightly.” Epiphanius, *Heresies*, LXXIII.14, also seems to have seen it as ascribed to Osius, when he says: “They thought they could condemn the Church by the letter which they fraudulently took from the venerable bishop Osius, in which ‘unlike in essence’ is read.” Sozomen, IV.12, supports this. Vigilius of Thapsus also lists Osius among those who composed this formula, *Against Eutyches*, V. Yet Phoebadius clearly indicates that its principal authors were Ursacius, Valens, and Potamius. This is the point of Sozomen, IV.12: when Osius, at the prompting of Ursacius, Valens, and Germinius, agreed that neither *homoousion* nor *homoiousion* should be used, etc., Eudoxius sent a letter to them, since they had extracted from Osius a letter on this matter, thanking Valens, Ursacius, and Germinius and attributing to their agency the fact that the Westerners held right opinions. Finally, when Hilary himself, in *To Constantius*, §24, calls the utterances of the same formula “the ravings of Osius and the additions of Ursacius and Valens,” what else does he mean than that it was written in part by Osius and enlarged by Ursacius and Valens?]

**A Copy of the Blasphemy Written at Sirmium by Osius and Potamius (in the year 357).**
11. God is one. The term “substance” is to be left unspoken. The Father is greater than the Son.—“Since some discussion concerning the faith was thought necessary, everything was carefully handled and examined at Sirmium, in the presence of our most holy brothers and fellow bishops Valens, Ursacius, and Germinius [Note: [Col. 0488B] Athanasius and Socrates add here, “and others.” Eudoxius names no others in the passage of Sozomen mentioned shortly below. Whether Constantius attended this assembly is uncertain. But if he had attended, would it not have been in the interest of Ursacius and Valens to declare it, thereby adding the strength of authority to their formula? Or did they keep silent so that the name of Hosius alone might have greater effect upon Catholics? Certainly he could have attended, since he is recorded to have come to Sirmium twice in the year 357. Ammianus, indeed, writes in book XVI that Constantius left Rome on the fourth day before the Kalends of June, hastened through Tridentum into Illyricum, and came to Sirmium. That he was again at Sirmium in December is confirmed by the law issued by him, Law 27 of the Theodosian Code, On Appeals; while various subscriptions to laws make clear that he stayed at Milan in the intervening period. The date of this synod is also debated: whether it was held in the middle or at the end of that year. From Hilary’s words there must have been sufficient time between this council and the Synod of Ancyra for its formula to be carried into Gaul; then for a synod of Gallican bishops to be convened; for this synod’s decrees to be conveyed to Hilary in Asia and by Hilary to the Eastern bishops; and for them, stirred by the example of the Gauls, to convene the Synod of Ancyra. Therefore the opinion of those who place this Sirmian gathering about the middle of 357 is more probable.]. It is agreed [Note: [Col. 0488C] In the Greek copies of Athanasius and Socrates, συνέστηκεν: “it was established.” Phoebadius, however, reads with our Hilary, constat: “it is agreed.”] that God the Almighty is one and Father, as is believed throughout the whole world [Note: [Col. 0488C] Athanasius and Socrates do not express the word “one.”]; and that his only Son, Jesus Christ our Lord and Savior, was begotten from him before the ages. But that two gods can neither be nor ought to be proclaimed; for the Lord himself said: “I go to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God” (John 20:17). Therefore the God of all is one [Note: [Col. 0488C] Athanasius and Socrates do not express the word *one*.], as the Apostle taught: “Is he the God of the Jews only? Is he not also of the Gentiles? Yes, of the Gentiles also. For God is one, who will justify [Note: [Col. 0488C] In the better manuscripts, *will justify*. Since the Greek has δικαιώσει, “will justify,” and nothing is more common in ancient books than for *b* to be changed into *u*, we readily judge that *will justify* is to be read.] circumcision by faith and uncircumcision through faith” (Rom. 3:29–30). The remaining matters too were agreed, and could admit of no disagreement.

“But as for the term substance, which in Greek is called *ousia*, that is, more expressly, *homoousion* [Note: [Col. 0488D] Thus the best Colbert manuscript, together with the German manuscript; and the Greek copies establish that this is the reading. The printed editions have: “*homoousion*, or what is called *homoiousion*.” But “or what is called *homoiousion*” is absent from the Carnotensis, Corbiensis, and many other manuscripts.], or what is called *homoiousion*, which troubled some or many persons [Note: [Col. 0488D] Leipzig and Paris: “some, not many.” Other books: “some or many,” which the Greeks rendered πολλούς τινας, “some many persons.”], no mention of it whatsoever ought to be made, nor should anyone preach it, for this cause and reason [Note: [Col. 0488D] Baden, Erasmus, and Migne: “to be the same in reason”; Leipzig and Paris: “for that cause of reason.” They are corrected from the manuscripts and the Greek version: διὰ ταύτην τὴν αἰτίαν καὶ διὰ τοῦτον τὸν λογισμόν, “for this cause and this reasoning.”]: because it is not contained in the divine Scriptures; because it is beyond human knowledge; and because no one can recount the Son’s generation, concerning which it is written: ‘Who shall recount his generation?’ (Isa. 53:8). It is plainly known that the Father alone knows how he begot his Son, and the Son how he was begotten by the Father.

“There is no ambiguity that the Father is greater. No one can doubt that the Father is greater than the Son in honor, dignity, splendor, majesty [Note: [Col. 0489C] Phoebadius expresses this in precisely the same words. But these two terms, “splendor” and “majesty,” are rendered by the one Greek word θεότητι, “divinity,” in Athanasius and Socrates.], and by the very name of Father; as he himself testifies: ‘He who sent me is greater than I’ (John 14:28). And no one is ignorant that this is Catholic doctrine: that there are two persons, Father and Son; that the Father is greater; and that the Son is subject [Note: [Col. 0489C] In Athanasius: “the Son subject to the Father,” as Phoebadius too seems to have read.] together with all things which the Father subjected to him. The Father has no beginning, is invisible, immortal, and impassible [Note: [Col. 0489C] Phoebadius prudently comments on these words: “They set these things forward in order to ascribe their opposites to the Son . . . for if he is proved to have a beginning, he will rightly be believed mortal and passible.” Our Hilary observed and pointed out, in *On the Trinity*, books IV and VI, that the first confession of the heretics was woven together by a similar artifice. But the highly praised Phoebadius is especially displeased by the words below, *through whom he suffered*, as though there had been two sufferers: the assumed man and the assuming Son. Thus Athanasius, *On the Saving Advent of Jesus Christ*, p. 643, accuses those who say that God suffered and rose through the flesh of blaspheming together with the Arians, since Scripture teaches that suffering occurred in his flesh through God, not that God suffered through the flesh.]. But the Son was born from the Father: God from God, light from light. No one knows this Son’s generation, as was said before, except his Father. The Son of God himself, our Lord and God, as it is written, assumed flesh or a body—that is, a human being—from the womb of the Virgin Mary, as the Angel proclaimed (Luke 1:31). And, as all the Scriptures teach, and especially the Apostle, the teacher of the Gentiles, he assumed a human being from the Virgin Mary, through whom he suffered.

“But this is the summary [Note: [Col. 0489D] The printed editions read *clavis*, “key.” More correctly the manuscripts read *clausula*, that is, the summary; rendered in Greek κεφάλαιον.] and confirmation of the whole faith: that the Trinity must always be preserved, as we read in the Gospel: ‘Go and baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit’ (Matt. 28:19). The number of the Trinity is whole and perfect. But the Paraclete Spirit [Note: [Col. 0489D] In the manuscripts consistently *Paraclitus* or *Paraclytus*.] is through the Son; he came when sent according to the promise, in order to instruct, teach, and sanctify the Apostles and all believers.”

12. What essence and substance are. The Synod of Ancyra, A.D. 358. As image, the Son is other than the Father not in name alone.—After, therefore, these many and great professions of impiety had been issued, the Eastern bishops, gathered together, in turn set forth contrary definitions of doctrine. But since frequent use of the terms *essence* and *substance* is now necessary to us, it must be understood what *essence* signifies, lest, while intending to speak about things, we fail to understand the matter of the words.

Essence is the thing which is, or the things from which it is, and which subsists in that which remains. The essence, nature, genus, and substance of any given thing may be spoken of. But it is properly called *essence* because it always is. It is likewise substance because a thing which is must necessarily subsist in itself; and whatever subsists undoubtedly remains in genus, nature, or substance. Therefore, when we say that essence signifies nature, genus, or substance, we understand that which subsists always in all these respects.

Let us now review the definitions of faith set down by the Easterners [Note: [Col. 0489D] Namely, those which they drafted at Ancyra in A.D. 358, gathered shortly before Easter, in order to repress the impiety of the Anomoeans. For when Eudoxius heard what Ursacius, Valens, and their associates had done at Sirmium, he congratulated them warmly and himself undertook, so far as he could, to advance the heresy of Aetius. Those who had come together at Ancyra for the dedication of a church, warned by letters from George of Laodicea, summoned and joined to themselves as many as they conveniently could, in order to check Eudoxius’ efforts. Basil, Epistle 74, mentions this council and calls it a σύλλογος, “assembly”; the word does not mean “conference,” as a scholar otherwise learned supposes, but a gathering, plainly from συλλέγω, “I call together.” Sozomen, book IV, chapter 13, narrates its proceedings. Epiphanius, *Heresies* 73.2 ff., should be consulted on this matter. There, indeed, in sections 10 and 11, he reports more decrees of this synod than our Hilary, because he records those issued at Ancyra, whereas Hilary, as will become evident from the following note, records those carried to and published at Sirmium by the delegates of the synod.].

I. “If anyone, hearing that the Son is the image of the invisible God, says that the image of God is the same thing as the invisible God, as though he did not confess him to be truly Son, let him be anathema.” [Note: [Col. 0490D] Immediately after “let him be anathema,” the editions of Baden, Erasmus, and Migne, and a very ancient manuscript of St. Peter’s at the Vatican, continue in one and the same context: “All expositions, if they contain anything blameworthy, contain it within themselves; otherwise they are not considered to contain it on their outward face. But I knew that these alone had been carried to Sirmium.” In this second apologetic note Hilary declares that none of the definitions which alone, as he knew, had been brought to Sirmium by the delegates of the Synod of Ancyra contains anything apparently blameworthy on its outward face or according to the sound of its words, although he does not deny fraud hidden beneath plausible words. This note wrongly took its place in the text after the preceding words in the said editions; yet Lipsius was also wrong to suppress it altogether. Since it applies equally to all the Ancyran definitions reported below, it ought not to have followed this first one, but rather to have preceded it. “Those alone . . . carried” would be still more pleasing.]

13. Again, he is other, as receiving life from the Father.—The assertion of those wishing Father and Son to be proclaimed by names only is excluded, since every image must be an undifferentiated likeness in species to that of which it is the co-image. No one is his own image; rather, the image must necessarily display the one whose image it is. An image, therefore, is an imagined and undivided likeness of one thing corresponding to another. Thus there is a Father, and there is also a Son, because the Son is the Father’s image; and one who is an image, in order to be the image of a thing [Note: [Col. 0490D] The printed editions read, “in order that he may truly be an image.” The manuscripts state more expressly, “in order that he may be the image of a thing,” that is, not merely of outward appearance and form, but of the inward reality and nature. Other images, as is said in *On the Trinity*, book VII, section 37, reproduce the appearances of the things of which they are fashioned as images, using different metals, pigments, materials, or arts; but they do not impart the things themselves. Hence it is readily apparent that, in the preceding decree, where the person is condemned who says that the image of God is the same as God, the image is not denied to be the same in nature, but in subsistence and person.], must have in himself the form, nature, and essence of his originator, according to what he is as image.

II. “And if anyone, hearing the Son say, ‘For as the Father has life in himself, so he gave also to the Son to have life in himself’ (John 5:26), says that he who received life from the Father and who likewise confesses, ‘I live because of the Father’ (John 6:57), is the same as the one who gave it, let him be anathema.” [Note: [Col. 0491C] We add the conjunction *and* from one Colbert manuscript and another Sorbonne manuscript. Then, in most copies, “this same thing,” not “this same.” Shortly afterward the printed editions alone read “whom also that one,” for “that also that one.” The Greek reads: ταὐτὸν λέγει τὸν εἰληφότα παρὰ τοῦ Πατρὸς τὴν ζωὴν, καὶ ὁμολογοῦντα τὸ, κἀγὼ ζῶ διὰ τὸν Πατέρα, τῷ δεδωκότι, ἀνάθεμα ἔστω: “If he says that the one who received life from the Father, and confesses, ‘I too live because of the Father,’ is the same as the giver, let him be anathema.”]

14. The Son is not unlike the Father in essence because he is his image.—The person of the receiver is distinguished from that of the giver, lest he be one and the same individual. For since one who believes the recipient and giver to be solitary and unique is anathematized, it cannot be understood that the one who gave received from himself. He is not himself alone who lives and through whom he lives, because one lives in himself, while another confesses that he lives through his originator; and no one will profess to be one and the same both the one who enjoys life and the one through whom there is cause for living.

III. “And if anyone, hearing that the only-begotten Son is the image of the invisible God, does not call the Son, who is the image of the invisible God—and whose image is understood also according to essence—similar to the Father in essence, as though not truly calling him Son, let him be anathema.” [Note: [Col. 0491C] In Greek, in Epiphanius, this definition is preceded by the preceding one, whose beginning reads: εἴ τις εἰκόνα ἀκούων τὸν μονογενῆ Υἱὸν τοῦ ἀοράτου Θεοῦ, ἀνόμοιον λέγοι καὶ κατ᾽ οὐσίαν τὸν Υἱόν: “If anyone, hearing that the only-begotten Son is the image of the invisible God, calls the Son unlike also according to essence.”]

15. Again, because, like the Father, he himself has life in himself. The life of Father and Son is the essence of each.—An undivided and not-unlike nature is affirmed. Since the only-begotten Son of God is the image of the invisible God, he must be similar in essence [Note: [Col. 0491D] Thus the manuscripts, except two, with which the printed editions read: “he is essence.”] through form and nature. Or how can the nature of an undifferentiated genus be distinguished between Son and Father, when the Son, subsisting in those things which are proper to the Father, stands by the nature begotten in himself—namely glory, power, authority, invisibility, essence [Note: [Col. 0491D] More manuscripts read *essence*. With the better manuscripts, *of essence* must be retained, with the word “goods” or “similar” understood: that is, “when he subsists in these goods—namely glory, power, etc.—of essence.”]?

Thus in these equal excellences of divinity it is understood that the one is not lesser because he is Son, nor the other superior because he is Father. For the Son is co-imaged to the Father in form and is not unlike in genus, because the Son’s likeness, begotten from the Father’s substance, does not permit diversity of substance. The Son and image of the invisible God comprehends in himself every form of the Father’s divinity, such as it is and as great as it is [Note: [Col. 0491D] The printed editions: “the form, such and so great as it is.” The reading which we give from the manuscripts is to be understood in the same sense.]. And this is truly to be Son: to have reflected, in the perfect likeness of a co-imaged nature within himself, the reality of the Father’s form.

IV. “And if anyone, hearing this: ‘For as the Father has life in himself, so he gave also to the Son to have life in himself’ (John 5:26), does not call the Son similar to the Father also according to essence [Note: [Col. 0491D] For “does not call similar,” the Greek has ἀνόμοιον λέγοι, “calls unlike.”], although he testifies [Note: [Col. 0491D] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read “he himself testifying.” Greek: διαμαρτυρόμενος.] that he has it as he said, let him be anathema.

“For it is manifest that, when the life understood in the Father signifies substance, and the life of the Only-Begotten, which was begotten from the Father, is understood as essence, the word ‘so’ signifies likeness of essence to essence.” [Note: [Col. 0492C] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “that life in the Father is here understood . . . and life also in the Only-Begotten . . . is connected with being signified.” Hilary, adhering too scrupulously to the Greek wording, rendered it somewhat obscurely in Latin. The Greek reads: φανερὸν γὰρ ὅτι τῆς ζωῆς ἐν τῷ Πατρὶ νοουμένης οὐσίας σημαινομένης, καὶ τῆς ζωῆς τῆς τοῦ μονογενοῦς τῆς ἐκ τοῦ Πατρὸς γεγεννημένης οὐσίας νοουμένης, τὸ οὕτως τὴν ὁμοιότητα τῆς οὐσίας πρὸς οὐσίαν σημαίνει: “For it is manifest that, since the life understood in the Father signifies essence, and the life of the Only-Begotten, begotten from the Father, is understood as essence, the word ‘so’—in ‘so he gave also to the Son,’ etc.—signifies likeness of essence to essence.” The Easterners explain their meaning in the preceding letter in Epiphanius, section 8, particularly in these words: “For the Father is not one thing and the life in him another; rather, without any composition, the Father himself is life.” Moreover, “as he has, so he gave also to the Son,” plainly without composition. That is, as the Father has life in himself—life without composition, life not different from himself or from his essence, so that he is his own life and his life is himself—so the Son, receiving life in himself, has life free from composition; and, because he has it as the Father has it, he has an essence similar to the Father’s essence. Hence below Hilary explains their words approximately as follows: “The Father has nothing other than what he gave; but he gave life which does not differ from his own essence. Therefore the Son is similar to the Father according to essence.”]

16. By such a confession of his origin, the perfect birth of an undivided nature is joined together. For what is life in each is in each signified as essence. And in the life generated from life—that is, in essence born from essence—while it is not born unlike, because it is life from life, it retains in itself the not-unlike nature of its origin. For the likeness of the essence which is born and that which begets—that is, of the life possessed and given, namely possessed by the Father and given to the Son—does not differ.

For what God begot from himself, in the likeness of his own nature, did not abandon the property proper to natural substance, in which the likeness is inborn [Note: [Col. 0493C] The printed editions read: “the likeness begotten in him by the natural property of substance,” against all manuscripts, which vary considerably here. Nine read: “in the congenitally born likeness,” etc. The older Colbert and Carnotensis manuscripts read *incongenita similitudo*, “an inborn likeness”; another Colbert manuscript and one Sorbonne manuscript read “in which [there is] an inborn likeness”; and the latter, together with two others, has “the property of natural substance.” We judge this reading preferable, supplying the word *likeness* from the manuscripts cited above. The meaning is this: that in which the likeness is born within, or inborn—not externally sketched—did not abandon or lose the property due to its natural substance. Hilary uses *abandon* similarly in *On the Trinity*, book IX, section 36: “The God who was born, therefore, did not abandon the property of his nature”; and in book V, section 37: “Nor does the perfect birth of incorporeal and immutable God from incorporeal and immutable God abandon its nature.” Nor is the force of the term *ingenita*, “inborn,” doubtful, since in Commentary on Matthew 10.24 it is used of the corruption which we bring by birth: “It is necessary that we hate the habit of the inborn and old work”; and shortly afterward: “Those things which are inborn and derived from some antiquity of lineage,” etc.]. For he has nothing other than what he gave; and, having life, he gave life to be possessed in the same manner. Thus that which is born from essence—as life from life—similar to itself according to essence, admits no diversity or unlikeness between the essence of the one being born and of the one begetting [Note: [Col. 0493D] The printed editions read “of the begotten one.” All manuscripts read “of the one being born.” In some later manuscripts: “and of the one begetting.”].

V. “If anyone, hearing from the same one, ‘He made or created me’ (Prov. 8:22), and ‘He begot me’ (ibid. 8:25), does not understand ‘He begot me’ so much in terms of likeness of essence [Note: [Col. 0493D] Erasmus, Migne, Leipzig, and Paris: “not nevertheless”; Baden and all manuscripts: “not so much.” Greek: μὴ ἐπὶ τοῦ αὐτοῦ καὶ κατ᾽ οὐσίαν ἐννοεῖ, “does not understand [them] of the same [one] and according to essence.”], but says that ‘he begot me’ and ‘he created me’ are identical [Note: [Col. 0494C] The Greek wording, ταὐτὸν λέγοι τὸ γεννᾷ με τῷ ἔκτισέ με, makes it clearer that those are censured who say that “he created me” and “he begot me” are the same in such a way as to explain “he begot me” from the expression “he created me.”], as though he were not speaking of the Son as perfect Son from God [Note: [Col. 0494C] Hilary seems here to have read ἀπὸ Θεοῦ τέλειον, “perfect [Son] from God,” whereas Epiphanius better reads ἀπαθῶς τέλειον, “perfectly without suffering.” Yet the following words make clear that the latter reading was not unknown to him.] signified by two names, but by the two names—namely ‘he created me’ and ‘he begot [me]’—were saying only a created thing and in no way a Son [Note: [Col. 0494C] In Epiphanius, in both Greek and Latin, “the Son signified by two names” is absent; moreover, the Latin version of this decree is wholly contrary to the Easterners’ intention. They condemn those who, upon hearing Wisdom, who is Christ, declare herself both created and begotten, maintain that by these words she signifies an origin not from God’s essence but from nothing—so that Christ is not Son but only a creature. Wisdom uses the expression “he created me” in such a way that, when she adds “he begot me,” she indicates both that he is Son and that he was begotten without suffering.
