Hilary, in *On the Trinity*, book XII, section 50, does not approve this Eastern interpretation as learned, though he acknowledges that it is not impious; here, however, suppressing his own view, he accommodates himself to their position.], although Wisdom conveyed a pious understanding through the two names: let him be anathema.”

17. The phrase “he created me” must be understood from the following “he begot me.” The distinction between birth and creation.—Those who call the Son of God a creature or creation are refuted by the reasoning set forth. For this is the impious presumption of the heretics: they say that they have read, “The Lord made or created me”; and this very phrase seems to mean a creation or creature. But, withholding the following sentence, from which the prior statement receives its meaning, they seize from the first sentence the authority for their impiety, so that they may call him a creature because Wisdom said she was created.

But if she was created, how could she also be born? For every birth, whatever it may be, has its existence in its own nature from the nature which begets; while creation takes its beginning from the power of the creator, since the Creator has power to make a creature from nothing. Wisdom, therefore, who said that she was created, said in the next words that she was also begotten. She referred creation to the immutable nature of the Parent, which, beyond the manner and custom of human childbirth, without any diminution or change in itself, created from itself that which it begot. For the work of creating involves neither suffering, nor mingling, nor childbirth. What is created from nothing begins at some point to exist. And the one who creates makes, by his power, what he establishes; creation is a work of power, not a birth in which nature is begotten from a begetting nature.

Birth, on the other hand, is the perfect advance of lawful origin and genuine nature [Note: [Col. 0494D] The word *perfect*, earlier omitted, is restored from the manuscripts.]: the born nature received its nature from the begetting nature. But because the Son of God was not begotten after the example of bodily parturition, but perfect God was born from perfect God, Wisdom therefore says that she was created, excluding every bodily condition of suffering from her generation [Note: [Col. 0494D] Thus all manuscripts. The printed editions read: “excluding all bodily sufferings in her generation.”].

18. How aptly, in saying that she was both created and begotten, she explains the nature of her origin. Those who attribute only likeness of power to the Son are condemned.—But, in order to show that the nature in her was not creation but birth, she added that she was begotten. Thus, when she confesses herself both created and begotten, she provides a complete understanding of her birth: in creation she signifies the immutable nature of the Father, and she shows that the substance of her own nature, begotten from God the Father, is lawful and proper. Thus the language of creation and generation conveys the understanding of perfect birth: the former is without change, the latter in the property of nature.

Both become one, and each is one perfect reality: the Son, born from God and without change in God, is born from the Father in such a way as to be created; and the Father, immutable in himself and natural to the Son, establishes the Son in such a way as to beget him [Note: [Col. 0494D] Baden: “was born and is born from the Father.” Migne: “was born, and thus from the Father,” etc. Other editions: “was born and from the Father,” etc. The manuscripts correct them.]. Therefore the heresy which dared to profess the Son of God to be a creature is condemned, because the subsequent confession of natural generation extinguishes the impious opinion of a creature from nothing, once the impassible perfection of divinity is shown through the profession by which that opinion relies [Note: [Col. 0495D] Supply “profession” or “expression,” by which the foregoing impious opinion relies—namely, “he created me.”].

VI. “And if anyone, while admitting in the Son the Father’s likeness according to essence [Note: [Col. 0495D] Here, after “the Father’s likeness” (Greek: πρὸς τὸν ἑαυτοῦ πατέρα ὁμοιότητα), “according to essence” must be supplied.], revealed by the Son himself in these words: ‘For as the Father has life in himself, so he gave also to the Son to have life in himself’ (John 5:26), and according to power in what he teaches: ‘For whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does’ (ibid. 19), grants likeness only according to power but deprives the Son of likeness according to essence—which is the chief point of our faith [Note: [Col. 0495D] This would be stated more clearly thus: “but, as for likeness according to essence, which is the chief point . . .”]—as though depriving himself of the knowledge of eternal life [Note: [Col. 0495D] Erasmus, Migne, Leipzig, and Paris read “relationship,” incorrectly, as is clear from the Greek: ὡς ἑαυτὸν ἀποστερῶν τῆς ἐν γνώσει Πατρὸς καὶ Υἱοῦ αἰωνίου ζωῆς, which might be rendered less confusedly: “as though depriving himself of eternal life, which consists in knowledge of the Father and the Son,” in accordance with John 17:3.] which is in the Father and the Son: let him be anathema.”

19. Likeness of power exists only from likeness of nature. Life signifies essence.—Confined by the authorities of Scripture, the heretics commonly grant the Son only this: that he is similar to the Father merely in power; but they take away likeness of nature. They are foolish and impious, not understanding that likeness of power cannot exist except from likeness of nature. An inferior nature never attains the power of a nature superior and stronger than itself. Or what will those who assert this profess concerning God the Almighty Father, if a power of inferior nature is made equal to his power [Note: [Col. 0495D] The printed editions read “his power,” incorrectly.]?

It cannot be denied that the Son can do the same things, since he said: “Whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does” (John 5:19). But likeness of nature follows likeness of power when he says: “As the Father has life in himself, so he gave also to the Son to have life in himself” (ibid. 26). In life there is a signification of nature and essence; and it is taught that it was given to be possessed just as it is possessed. Thus likeness of life entails likeness of power; for likeness of power cannot be unlike in nature. It is therefore necessary that likeness of essence entail likeness of power: for as the things which the Father does, the Son also does, so, as the Father has life, he gave life to the Son to have in the same manner.

Therefore the rashness of this impious profession is condemned: it confesses likeness of power, yet dared to proclaim unlikeness of nature, whereas the principal faith of our hope is to confess an undifferentiated substance of divinity in Father and Son.

VII. “And if anyone, while promising to believe in Father and Son, calls the Father father not of an essence similar to himself [Note: [Col. 0495D] The editions do not repeat “father” here, and Leipzig and Paris earlier suppress *himself*. They are restored from the manuscripts and Greek: τὸν Πατέρα μὴ οὐσίας ὁμοίας αὐτοῦ λέγοι πατέρα, ἀλλὰ ἐνεργείας: “if he does not call the Father father of an essence similar to himself, but [father] of power.” These words condemn those who would have the Father beget and bring forth an essence unlike himself.], but of similar efficacy; as though uttering profane and novel expressions against the Son’s essence and destroying his being truly the Son of God [Note: [Col. 0496D] Thus the manuscripts, in agreement with the Greek, καὶ ἀναίρων τὸ εἶναι ἀληθῶς Υἱόν. The printed editions: “the true Son of God.”]: let him be anathema.”

20. Heretics deceitfully confess Father and Son. They are refuted when they deny that the Son is other than the Father because of likeness of nature.—Very frequently heretics evade truth through confused and mixed-up language, catching unwary ears by the sound of shared terms. They proclaim Father and Son by names alone, not also by the reality of a natural and genuine essence, because they know that God is called father of all creatures and remember that all saints are called sons of God. By this example they confess Father and Son according to the common names of all things, so that they may be called Father and Son rather than actually be so.

For they are called, but are not so, if there is in them a distinct nature of different essence; since the truth of the paternal name cannot be obtained except from offspring of one’s own nature. Therefore a father cannot be called father of a substance alien and unlike to himself, because a perfect birth does not have a discordant diversity of originating substance. Thus every such impiety is rejected which speaks of the Father as father not according to the nature of a Son begotten from himself [Note: [Col. 0496D] Erasmus, Leipzig, and Paris read “and begotten from himself”; corrected from Baden and the better manuscripts. Shortly afterward, with the words *God* and *Father* exchanged, the sentence would be clearer: “For God will not be called Father merely because . . .”].

For God will not be called Father merely because he has a creation similar to his power and efficacy; rather, because he has begotten a nature of essence neither unlike nor alien to himself. Natural birth does not admit diversity from the Father’s nature. Therefore those are anathema who assert that the Father is father of a nature unlike himself: so that something other than God might have been born from God, and they suppose that the Father’s essence has degenerated from itself in the Son through begetting. So far as lies in them, they destroy that very unbegotten and immutable essence of the Father, since they have dared, in the birth of his Only-Begotten, to introduce an unlikeness belonging to a degenerate natural essence [Note: [Col. 0496D] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “because they dared [to introduce it] into the birth of their Only-Begotten.”].

VIII. “And if anyone, understanding the Son to be similar in essence to him whose Son he is understood to be, calls the Son either the same as the Father, or a part of the Father, or a Son subsisting from the incorporeal Father through an emanation or some suffering, as bodily sons do: let him be anathema.” [Note: [Col. 0496D] These words are less obscure if arranged thus: “And if anyone, understanding the Son to be similar according to essence to him whose Son he is understood to be, calls him the same [Greek: λέγοι, “calls”], or a part of the Father”; where the printed editions wrongly have “or the Father’s Father.” Then the Colbert and German manuscripts read “or by an enunciation,” not “or by an emanation.”]

21. In every respect precautions are taken against the errors of individual perversities, and no opportunity for deception is allowed. For many heretics say that the Son is similar to the Father in divinity precisely in order to maintain, by the property of likeness, that the Father and Son are the same; because undivided likeness seems to admit the possibility of a single and solitary being. For what does not differ in kind seems to remain in unity of nature.

22. Because he is begotten, the Son is neither the same as the Father nor other than the Father. They wish the Son to be other than the Father on account of the distinction of person.—But begetting does not allow this fiction, because unity does not admit begetting. For what is begotten has the father of its begetting. Nor, because the divinity of the one born and of the begetter is undifferentiated, is he both begetter and begotten; since the begetter and the one born can only be other and other, nor again can the one born and the begetter be dissimilar. [Note: In the manuscripts, *indissimilis* (“not dissimilar”); and then, in the Vatican manuscript alone, *esse non possit* (“cannot be”). Above, §20, in place of “but if he begets one not dissimilar,” nearly all manuscripts read “not *indissimilis*.” Although this reading may perhaps be more genuine—so that *indissimilis* means, as it were, “inwardly dissimilar”—we have not restored it, lest it occasion error.]

Therefore let him be anathema who, in the Father and Son, proclaims a similarity of nature in order to abolish the Son’s personal distinctness. For although, through reciprocal similarity, one thing differs from another in nothing, that very similarity—because it does not admit unity—confesses Father and Son by this fact: that the Son is the unchangeable similarity of the Father. For the Son is not a part of the Father, so that one might be called both begotten and begetter. Nor is he an emanation, so that, by a continuous flow through a bodily and undivided course, the same flow retained in its source might itself be, by a connected sequence and course, both its own source and its flow. [Note: The older Colbert manuscript has *ipsud*; the same form is again written in it below, §25, and elsewhere.] Rather, he is a perfect begetting, abiding with similarity of nature: not bodily begun by bodily conception and birth, but the incorporeal Son subsisting from the incorporeal Father according to the similarity of the same nature.

IX. “And if anyone, because the Father is never understood to be the Son, and the Son is never understood to be the Father, says that the Son is other than the Father—because the Father is one and the Son another—according to what was said, ‘Another is he who bears witness concerning me: the Father who sent me’ (John 5:32); [Note: In one Colbert manuscript and another Sorbonne manuscript: “bears witness concerning me,” with the Greek also agreeing: ὁ μαρτυρῶν περὶ ἐμοῦ. Thereafter, in place of the words “the Father who sent me,” is added: καὶ, Μαρτυρεῖ γὰρ, φησὶ, ὁ πέμψας με Πατήρ, “and, he says, ‘For the Father who sent me bears witness’”—a different statement, cited from John 5:37 to confirm the same saying.] and, through this pious distinction of the person of Father and Son to be understood in the Church, fears lest at any time Son and Father should be understood to be the same, and therefore does not say that the Son is similar to the Father even according to essence: let him be anathema.” [Note: In Epiphanius’ Latin translation, for greater clarity, “if anyone, I say,” is rightly added here, though it is absent from the Greek, which has only: διὰ ταύτην τὴν εὐσεβῆ ἐν τῇ Ἐκκλησίᾳ νοουμένην ἰδιότητα τῶν προσώπων, Πατρὸς μὲν καὶ Υἱοῦ—“because of this pious distinction, understood in the Church, of the persons of Father and Son.” Hence it is clear that “in the Church” is wrongly omitted in the Paris and Leipzig editions.] [Note: Greek: ἀνόμοιον λέγοι, “should call [him] dissimilar.”]

[Col. 0498A] 23. How carefully the two heresies opposed to the Son of God are destroyed.—The Lord said to the Apostles: “Be prudent as serpents and simple as doves” (Matt. 10:16). By this he willed that the nature of creatures differing from one another should be in us; yet so that the prudence of the serpent might be moderated by the simplicity of the dove, and the simplicity of the dove instructed by the prudence of the serpent. Thus wisdom would be simple and simplicity wise. This precept has been observed in the exposition of this faith.

For the preceding proposition, of which we have spoken, had guarded against the proclamation, through similarity of essence, of personal unity, and against the abolition of the Son’s begetting through sameness of nature—lest he should be, in our understanding, one and solitary, because one did not differ from the other in kind. But in the following proposition, that prudence of the serpent—which we are commanded to combine with the dove’s simplicity—is in turn met by simple and apostolic prudence: lest, perhaps, because personal unity was not admitted, and because the Father is one and the Son another, the assertion of a dissimilar nature might again creep in. Thus, since one is he who sent and another he who was sent—for the sender and the sent are not one—it might be supposed that sender and sent possess distinct and dissimilar natures, although the one born and the begetter cannot be of different essences.

Accordingly, in Father and Son the similarity of an undifferentiated nature is retained through the begetting of essence; yet similarity of nature does not damage personal distinction, so that sender and sent should be one. Nor again, in the distinction of persons—since one cannot be called both Son and Father in relation to himself—is similarity of nature removed. Thus the truth of begetting advances to similarity of essence, and similarity of essence does not lose the personal truth of begetting. [Note: The Corbie manuscript and several others read, “does not remove.”] Nor does the confession of begetter and begotten exclude similarity of essence; for although begetter and begotten cannot be one, the one born and the begetter are not therefore of different natures.

X. “And if anyone understands God to have become Father of his only-begotten Son at some time, and does not believe that the only-begotten Son subsisted from the Father without suffering, beyond times and beyond every human estimation—as though passing beyond the Gospel proclamation, which rejected any interval of times between Father and Son, and faithfully taught us that ‘In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God’ (John 1:1)—let him be anathema.” [Note: In the Greek phrasing, the word “Father” is repeated in place of “God.” Here the teaching of Arius is attacked: he maintained that God is eternal in himself but became Father only in time.] [Note: Greek: πιστεύει τὸν μονογενῆ υἱὸν ἐκ τοῦ Πατρὸς ἀπαθῶς ὑφεστάναι, “believes that the only-begotten Son subsisted from the Father without suffering.”] [Note: The manuscripts unanimously read “an interval of times,” expressed in Greek by the single phrase τοὺς μὲν χρόνους. Further, since Hilary renders παρωσάμενον, “rejected,” by *adspernata est*, he seems to have read καθορασάμενον, or another compound of ὁράω (“to see”), not of ὠθέω (“to push away”).]

24. The Father is not within time. The Gospel teaches that the Son already is, more than that he comes to be born.—It is a pious confession that the Father is not contained within time; for the timeless truth of the paternal name surpasses every capacity of understanding. Although the confession of the paternal name itself—by which he is the impassible source of the one born—is religious, nevertheless it is not held within time. For eternal and infinite God cannot be understood as a temporal Father; and, according to the Gospel proclamation, the only-begotten God the Word is known to be already with God in the beginning rather than to be born.

XI. “And if anyone calls the Father older in time than the only-begotten Son begotten from him, and the Son younger than the Father: let him be anathema.” [Note: In several manuscripts *tempore* (“in time”) is missing; the Greek contains it, not only here but also below after “younger.”] [Note: The manuscripts read “younger from/by the Father.”]

25. As the Father’s image, the Son is not younger than he. Since God is Father once for all, he has always been Father, and the Son has always been Son.—Similarity of essence, conformed in kind, is also shown to be undifferentiated in time, lest he who is the image of God, the Word, God with God in the beginning, and similar to the Father, should, by an interval between himself and the Father, lack within himself the perfection proper both to image, Word, and God.

For if he is proclaimed younger in time, he has lost the truth both of image and of similarity; for that can no longer be similarity which is found dissimilar in time. The very fact that God is Father cannot admit any time in which he is not Father; therefore there can be no time in the Son in which he is not Son. Accordingly, neither should the Father be called older than the Son nor the Son younger than the Father, because the truth of either name cannot exist without the other.

XII. “And if anyone refers the timeless substance of the only-begotten Son from the Father to the unbegotten essence of God, as though calling the Son the Father: let him be anathema.” [Note: Hilary translates the Greek ὑπόστασις as *substantia* (“substance”), as in Book IV, §13, where the Greek reads: τρεῖς εἰσὶν ὑποστάσεις, Πατήρ, Υἱός, καὶ ἅγιον Πνεῦμα—“there are three hypostases: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit”—and he renders it in Latin: “there are three substances: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.” But where he finds οὐσία, he consistently translates it *essentia* (“essence”).] [Note: Greek, in one word: υἱοπάτορα, “Son-Father.”]

26. Though timeless, the Son is not unbegotten.—The preceding definition seemed to give heretics an opening when it denied a time for the Son’s begetting—for it would be impious if the Father were in time, and he would be in time if the Son were subject to time. They might exploit this denial of time to proclaim, under the name of the Son, the Father who is unbegotten as solitary and unique, both Father and Son to himself. For where the time of being born is excluded, the notion of unbegottenness seems to be admitted, so that one whose begetting is not in time may be thought not to be begotten.

Therefore, lest through this denial of time the heresy of unity—that is, Sabellianism—should creep in, this impiety is condemned: the impiety which dares to refer timeless begetting to the one and solitary substance of unbegotten essence. For it is one thing to be timeless and another not to be born: the former has begetting, though outside time; the latter is itself alone and the same eternal source of what it is. [Note: Or, certainly, it does not exclude begetting. Shortly afterwards, the Colbert manuscript reads *aliud ipsud*. We note this in order that *ipsum* may be understood as neuter.]

27. The rationale of these definitions. The character of Hilary’s exposition. Those whose subscription was compelled. A synopsis of them.—We have gone through, dearest brothers, all the definitions of faith issued by the Eastern bishops, [Note: Namely, as we have noted, those which they published at Sirmium, not those which they issued at Ancyra. Epiphanius prefixes five other definitions to these and adds two, in the latter of which those who defend the Son as *tautousios* or *homoousios* with the Father are condemned. Basil of Caesarea appears to identify Eustathius of Sebaste as the author of this latter definition in Epistle 74, where he recalls that Eustathius wrote the anathema against *homoousion* at the council held at Ancyra—unless one thinks that γράψαι, “to write,” should be understood as “to subscribe.”] which, against the heresy recently arising, they framed in a synod assembled among themselves. [Note: Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read “assembled within the synod.” Just as Hilary says here “recently arising,” so the bishops gathered at Ancyra, in Epiphanius, *Panarion* 73.13 and 19, call the Anomoeans’ teaching a new heresy and its advocates new heretics.]

And we, insofar as we could, adapted the language of our exposition to the sense in which they are to be understood, serving their statements rather than seeking to be regarded as authors of the statements of others. [Note: Most manuscripts: “to the sense of their understanding.” Hilary carefully avoids being judged the author of the words he interprets, aware, of course, that the faith he defends is not altogether pure.] Against a new and profane impiety they enact these provisions from the conviction of their conscience and from doctrine long since received. [Note: The printed editions read “their own doctrine.” The manuscripts omit “their own.” Hilary contrasts the antiquity of the Easterners’ doctrine with the novelty of the Anomoeans’ doctrine, because the latter, in Epiphanius, *Panarion* 73.2, after professing adherence to the faith of the Council of Antioch of 341, add this: “Let them learn that we preserve and defend, as an inheritance, that faith which we received by an uninterrupted succession from apostolic times down to our fathers.”]

They compelled those who had composed this heresy at Sirmium, or had adopted it after its composition, to confess their ignorance and to subscribe to such decrees: decrees in which the Son is the Father’s perfect image; in which, under the property of an undifferentiated image, the Son is not abolished by profane fraud so that he may be the Father; in which the Son, proclaimed the Father’s image through the truth of similarity, does not differ in substance from the Father’s substance, whose image he is, by a diversity of substance; in which, through the life possessed by the Father and received by the Son, the Father has nothing differing in the substance signified by life from that which the Son received to possess; in which the begotten Son is not a creature, but is a substance undifferentiated from the Father’s nature; in which, just as power is undifferentiated between Father and Son, so essence admits no diversity between them; [Note: The printed editions read *essentiae* (“of essence”); the manuscripts more correctly read *essentia* (“essence”). Decree 6 is meant, in which the Son is asserted to be similar to the Father both in power and in essence.] in which the Father, in begetting the Son, does not degenerate into a different nature within him; [Note: The Basel edition, with nearly all manuscripts: *in eodem generat* (“begets in him”), supported by Decree 7, here summarized, which condemns one who calls the Father the father of a nature dissimilar to himself. Other printed editions read *in eodem degenerat* (“degenerates in him”). We retain, with the Carnotensis manuscript, one Colbert manuscript, and another Sorbonne manuscript, *in eo degenerat* (“degenerates in him”), especially since above, §20, in explaining the said decree, Hilary approves the rightful condemnation of those who suppose that the Father’s essence has degenerated from itself in the Son.] in which, because similarity of nature differs in nothing in either, the distinctiveness of similarity in the personal names nevertheless rejects unity, lest one subsisting being be called both Father and Son; [Note: The printed editions perversely read “the distinctiveness of nature,” omitting “similarity.” The latter must be restored from the Silva Major and Queen of Sweden manuscripts; unless one perhaps prefers *natura* in place of *naturae*. Shortly afterward the Carnotensis manuscript has “refutes,” not “rejects.”] in which, because Father as sender and Son as sent are piously affirmed, nevertheless the essence is distinguished in nothing between Father and Son—that is, between sent and sender; in which the truth of the paternal name is not contained within time; in which the Son is not later than the Father in time; and in which perfect begetting beyond all time does not admit within itself the error of unbegottenness.

[Col. 0501B] 28. When these decrees were issued; on what occasion and why. The succession of other creeds.—And this whole doctrine of faith which was issued, dearest brothers, arose among the Easterners, assembled in a small number according to the scale of the whole body, at almost the very days on which you rejected the heresy brought forward. [Note: That is, all who, after receiving the letters of George of Laodicea, could quickly be summoned together with those who had already assembled at Ancyra for the dedication of the church, as Sozomen recounts, Book IV, ch. 13. In Epiphanius, *Panarion* 73.12, only twelve subscribers are listed. But Eleusius of Cyzicus and Leontius the presbyter, whom Sozomen in the passage cited says were sent by this synod as envoys to the emperor along with Basil and Eustathius, are not mentioned among them; this indicates that Epiphanius did not list them all. Vigilius of Tapsus wrongly believed, *Against Eutyches*, Book V, §3, that those twelve propositions had been issued by all the Eastern bishops gathered together in one body. He was, I think, misled because Hilary commonly praises the Easterners simply and collectively as their authors.]

The reason why it had to be set forth was that silence concerning “one substance” was being decreed. [Note: One might understand this to mean that Hilary thought the Easterners’ faith needed explanation because in their final definition they had condemned the phrase “one substance.” But he means only to excuse the Easterners generously for setting out their faith again, since they were led to do so by the occasion of a heresy which decreed silence about substance—arising at Sirmium through Valens and Ursacius, and at Antioch through Eudoxius. Hence the following is especially clear: “But at earlier and various times it was necessary for other creeds to be written.” On reading this, Vigilius, not discerning Hilary’s purpose prudently enough, regarded as Catholic the synods which Hilary here attempts to excuse; and in *Against Eutyches*, Book V, §2, looking at the same synods, declares that those who do not know that bishops assembled in different places, after the Nicene synod, issued many statements of faith against the insane outbreaks of new heretics are exceedingly ignorant and rash.]

But at earlier and various times, many such causes requiring it, it had been necessary for other statements of faith to be composed. Their character will be understood from the statements themselves. For once all that they did is known, we shall more easily and more fully provide a devout and unity-consonant resolution of the matters disputed among us.

**Exposition of the ecclesiastical faith, issued in the year 341, which was set forth at the synod held for the dedication of the completed church of Antioch.** [Note: This synod was held, as Athanasius relates in *On the Synods*, in the presence of Constantius, in the consulship of Marcellinus and Probinus, in the fourteenth indiction, the fifth year after Constantine’s death; thus in the fifth year of Pope Julius of Rome, A.D. 341. Its occasion was the dedication of a church whose foundations Constantine had laid ten years earlier. Athanasius and Socrates, Book II, ch. 8, say that ninety bishops attended it. Sozomen, Book V, ch. 5, in Valesius’ edition, agrees with our Hilary.] [Note: If Sozomen, Book III, ch. 5, is to be believed, they said that they had found this faith written in the hand of Lucian himself, the man who suffered martyrdom at Nicomedia. But, as we shall shortly show, Athanasius attributes some portions of it to Acacius and Eusebius as having been delivered at the Dedication; Acacius, moreover, attributes several of its words to Asterius. Hilary indicates plainly enough that those who attended the synod itself were the authors of this formula. We note in passing that this is quite different from the creed of the church of Antioch which Cassian sets forth in *On the Incarnation*, Book VI, ch. 3.]

The ninety-seven bishops who were present set it forth when one of the bishops had come under suspicion of holding erroneous beliefs. [Note: Baronius, under the year 341, §22, thinks that this one was Gregory, accused of holding unsound views when he was first appointed bishop of Alexandria at this assembly. Athanasius gives another reason for drafting this formula in *On the Synods*, p. 891: namely, that since not one but most—especially those leading this synod—were everywhere accused of heresy, they tried at least to cast dust in others’ eyes by issuing ambiguous confessions.]

29. “Following the evangelical and apostolic tradition, we believe in one God, Father almighty, builder, maker, and providential governor of all things that are, from whom are all things; [Note: No Greek equivalent for “providential governor” appears in Socrates, but it will be restored in Athanasius’ final edition from the manuscripts: καὶ προνοητήν, “and providential governor.”] and in one Lord Jesus Christ, his only-begotten Son, God through whom are all things, who was begotten from the Father, God from God, whole from whole, one from one, perfect from perfect, King from King, Lord from Lord, Word, Wisdom, Life, true Light, true Way, Resurrection, Shepherd, Door, unchangeable and immutable, the unchangeable image of the Father’s divinity, essence, power, and glory; [Note: Greek: λόγον ζῶντα, σοφίαν ζῶσαν, “living Word, living Wisdom”; and later in Athanasius, ὁδὸν ἀλήθειαν, and in Socrates ὁδὸν ἀληθείας, “way of truth,” for “true way.”] [Note: The Corbie manuscript, with several others, reads “unchangeable and immutable.” The better manuscripts—Carnotensis, two Colbert manuscripts, Germaniensis, and Sorbonne—following the Greek, read the accusative “unchangeable and immutable.” Athanasius reports the entire sentence as put forward by Acacius and Eusebius at the Dedication in *On the Synods*, p. 911. Acacius, in Epiphanius, *Panarion* 72.6, attributes these and most preceding words to Asterius.] who was always in the beginning with God, God the Word, as the Gospel says: ‘And the Word was God’ (John 1:1); [Note: “Always” is absent from Athanasius and Socrates. Because of this word, from which Hilary indicates in *On the Trinity*, Book IV, §5, that the Arians strongly recoiled, he himself states below, §33, that this formula was less suspect to him.] through whom all things were made and in whom all things consist; who in the last days came down from above, was born of the Virgin according to the Scriptures, became the Lamb, [Note: From the Greek wording one must read “became man”; and shortly afterward, “apostle of faith,” not “predestined for faith.”] the Lamb, mediator between God and men, predestined for our faith, and leader of life.

For he said: ‘I have not come down from heaven to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me’ (John 6:38). He suffered for us and rose for us on the third day, [Note: In Socrates: τὸν παθόντα ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν, καὶ ἀναστάντα ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν, “who suffered for us and rose for us.” This second “for us” is absent from Athanasius.] ascended into heaven, sits at the Father’s right hand, and will come again with glory to judge the living and the dead.

“And [we believe] in the Holy Spirit, given to believers for consolation, sanctification, and perfection, as the Lord Jesus Christ also instructed the disciples, saying: ‘Go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit’ (Matt. 28:19); [Note: The Basel edition, with the manuscripts, reads “instructed disciples”; other editions read simply “disciples.”] plainly, indeed, [the name] of the Father who is truly Father, certainly [the name] of the Son who is truly Son, and of the Holy Spirit who is truly Holy Spirit. [Note: The printed editions read: “Manifestly the Father’s [here Basel adds ‘person’], truly Father’s; and certainly the Son’s, truly Son’s; and knownly the Holy Spirit’s.” They are corrected from the Greek and the better manuscripts.] These names are not set forth simply or idly, but carefully signify the proper substance, rank, and glory of each of those named, so that they are three in substance but one in concord.” [Note: Greek: ὡς εἶναι τῇ μὲν ὑποστάσει τρία, τῇ δὲ συμφωνίᾳ ἕν, “so that they are three in hypostasis/substance, but one in concord.” Huet conjectures, *Origen*, Book II, question 2, §3, that these words were drawn from Origen, *Against Celsus*, Book VIII, where he says that Father and Son are “two things in hypostasis, but one in unanimity, concord, and identity of will”: ὄντα δύο τῇ ὑποστάσει πράγματα, ἓν δὲ τῇ ὁμονόᾳ καὶ τῇ συμφωνίᾳ καὶ τῇ ταυτότητι τοῦ βουλήματος.]

30. “Having, therefore, this faith, and intending to have it from beginning to end before God and Christ, we anathematize every heretical and depraved sect. And if anyone, contrary to the sound and right faith of the Scriptures, teaches that there was or had been a time, interval, or age before the Son of God was begotten: let him be anathema. [Note: Leipzig and Paris read “was begotten.” Erasmus, with the older Colbert manuscript and the Germaniensis manuscript, reads “is begotten”; Basel, with the others, “begotten.” Greek: πρὸ τοῦ τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ, “before the Son of God …”]

“And if anyone calls the Son a creature, as one of created things; or a product of birth, as births are; or a thing made, as made things are—not as the divine Scriptures have delivered each of the things stated above; or if anyone teaches or proclaims another gospel beyond what we have received: let him be anathema. For we truly believe and follow, with fear, all things delivered in the divine Scriptures by the prophets and apostles.”

31. In what respect this faith is suspect.—Perhaps this faith seems to have spoken less explicitly concerning the undifferentiated similarity of Father and Son, especially since it declares that the proper substance, rank, and glory of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are signified in their names in such a way that they are three in substance but one in concord.

32. It is defended from the council’s purpose. A new heresy after the Nicene synod. In what sense three substances are rightly spoken of among the Easterners.—First, it must be understood that the council at Antioch met not against the heresy which dared to proclaim Father and Son of dissimilar substance, [Note: Earlier printed editions add “and the Holy Spirit” here, without authority.] but against that which, after the holy Nicene synod, had broken out so far as to wish to attribute three names to the Father; this we shall discuss in its proper place. [Note: This at least was alleged by the Eusebians, who used to defame their opponents as adherents of the Sabellian heresy.]

For I remember that at the beginning of this discourse I asked readers and hearers for patience and fairness until the completion of all that I had to say, lest anyone rashly become my judge before hearing the whole argument. Therefore the holy synod, gathered with the purpose of destroying that impiety which evaded the reality of the names Father, Son, and Holy Spirit by their number—so that, without the subsisting reality corresponding to each name, a threefold naming might, under the falsity of names, preserve unity, and the Father alone and one might himself have both the name of Holy Spirit and that of Son—therefore said that there are three substances, teaching through substances the subsisting persons, [Note: What our translator renders “three substances,” they said as τρεῖς ὑποστάσεις, “three hypostases.” But Epiphanius warns, *Panarion* 73.17, lest anyone be troubled by the term *hypostases*: the Easterners employ “hypostases” in order to indicate the proper characteristics of persons that subsist and exist. A little later he says: “The Easterners rightly call the proper characteristics of the subsisting and existing Father, Son, and Holy Spirit ‘hypostases’ of subsisting persons,” not in order to call the three hypostases three principles or three gods; for they condemn with an anathema those who say there are three gods. Nor at that time did those who proclaimed three in the Godhead lie under suspicion of heresy. Gregory of Nazianzus later proclaimed the same teaching Catholicly, *Oration* 29.3 and elsewhere; so too did Westerners, for example Consentius in the letter preserved in Augustine, Epistle 119.4: “One power exists, possessed by a threefold power; one substance exists, in which three subsist.” Augustine himself, Epistle 170, to Maximus, §5: “All these are neither confusedly one nor separately three; but though they are one, they are three, and though they are three, they are one.”] while not separating the substance of Father and Son by the diversity of a dissimilar essence. [Note: Again we have removed here the words “and of the Holy Spirit,” added without manuscript authority.]

But the phrase, “that they are three in substance but one in concord,” affords no ground for calumny, because, with the Spirit named together with them—that is, the Paraclete—it is fitting that unity be proclaimed rather in concord than in essence through similarity of substance. [Note: The printed editions read “surnamed”; the manuscripts more aptly read “named together.” Does Hilary understand this to mean that the Holy Spirit, as is said in the schools, does not proceed from the Father formally as similar by virtue of his procession? Certainly, in Book XII, §55, he solemnly declares that he will never call the Holy Spirit either begotten or created. How brilliantly he establishes the divinity of the Holy Spirit has already been shown in the preface to *On the Trinity*, §15; hence this passage should now seem suspect to no one.]

33. This formula proclaims the same essence of Father and Son. The distinction between begetting and unbegottenness. The Son is immutable.—Moreover, the whole preceding statement distinguishes Father and Son in no diversity of essence or nature. For where it says, “God from God, whole from whole,” there is no doubt that whole God is born from whole God. The nature of God from God does not differ; and “whole from whole” means that he is the same whole reality in those respects in which he is Father.

“One from one” excludes the sufferings of human conception and childbirth: so that, while one is from one, he is not from elsewhere, nor is he diverse or another—he who is one from one, perfect from perfect. [Note: Thus the better manuscripts—two Colbert manuscripts, Carnotensis, Germaniensis, and Sorbonne. Other books read *aliud sit*, “be another thing.” As Hilary often uses *aliud* to distinguish person, so here he uses *alius* to distinguish nature.] Begetting differs from unbegottenness only in the cause of origin, since the perfection of both does not differ.

“King from King”: power, called by one and the same name, does not admit dissimilarity of power. “Lord from Lord”: lordship also is equal in Lord; confessed in both, lordship does not admit difference without diversity. And the further statement, after many others—“unchangeable and immutable, the unchangeable image of divinity, essence, power, and glory”—is decisive.

For, being God from God, whole from whole, one from one, perfect from perfect, King from King, and Lord from Lord, the Son both subsists in all that glory and nature of divinity in which the Father abides, and also receives from the Father’s substance that he may not be changeable. For in his being born the nature from which he was born was not changed; rather, he received immutable essence from the authority of immutable nature. [Note: Here *auctoritas* means nothing other than “source” or “author”: that is, born from a source whose nature is immutable.] For although he is an image, he is an unchangeable image—not, that is, with the nature from which he was begotten changed in him through dissimilarity from the Father’s essence—because the image of the Father’s essence was born in him.

Further, when he is taught to be the first brought forth of all creation, and is also called God the Word, who was always in the beginning with God, his being brought forth shows that he was born, while his having always been shows that he is not separated from the Father by time. [Note: The printed editions read: “when he is taught to be the first brought forth of all creation, he himself is also said always to have been in the beginning with God, God the Word. While he is first brought forth, he is shown to have been born,” etc.]

Therefore this synod cannot be thought to have introduced a division of substances—that is, a division intended to separate a different substance in the Son from that in the Father—when it strove only, by the term “three substances,” to exclude a unity of the three names. [Note: One Colbert manuscript, with Carnotensis, Mic., and the printed editions, reads “subsisting”; the other Colbert manuscript, with Germaniensis, “substances.” With the others, we prefer “of substances,” since the Easterners are here defended for introducing the threefold *hypostasis*, and Hilary translates the Greek ὑπόστασις by the Latin word *substantia*.] For the entire exposition of faith distinguishes not Father and Son, unbegotten and only-begotten, in time, name, essence, dignity, or lordship. It is fitting, moreover, that with a shared purpose we should also know the other statements of faith, composed by the same Eastern bishops at different places and times, so that the sincerity of their conviction may be understood through several confessions.

[Note: We have taken care to restore this title in its proper place according to the manuscripts; it was omitted by the Basel edition and added only in the margin in other editions. In its place one Colbert manuscript has: “Exposition of faith according to the Eastern synod,” which has the same sense. But the recent Remigius, in whose text appears “faith composed at Sardica,” is not to be followed.]

## FAITH ACCORDING TO THE EASTERN SYNOD (A.D. 347)

The holy synod assembled at [Note: [Col. 0506C] The manuscripts consistently, and with strong agreement, read “Serdica.” This false heading has misled many, and the Donatists attempted to deceive Augustine by means of it, as he himself attests in Epistle formerly CLXIII, now XLIV, §6. Vigilius was less cautious, in Book V Against Eutyches, §3. Yet our Hilary was not unaware from whom the following formula proceeded, though he did not state it openly. Moreover, it was issued not at Sardica but at Philippopolis in Thrace by those who, conscious of wrongdoing, feared the judgment of the Synod of Sardica. Nevertheless, except for these final words, “Likewise those who say that there are three gods,” etc., it was first published by certain Eusebians some months after the Council of Antioch at the Dedication; and Narcissus, Maris, Theodorus, and Marcus conveyed it into Gaul to Constans as though from a synod, as Athanasius testifies, *On the Synods*, p. 895. Indeed, as he adds there, when the same men met three years later, they sent it into Italy through Eudoxius, Martyrius, and others, enlarged with the aforesaid appendices, “Likewise those,” etc., and others. Finally, the formula immediately appended here against Photinus differs from this one only by the addition of the anathemas.] Sardica, from the various provinces of the Eastern regions—Thebaid, Egypt, [Col. 0506C] Palestine, Arabia, Phoenicia, Coele Syria, Mesopotamia, Cilicia, Cappadocia, Pontus, Paphlagonia, Galatia, Bithynia, the Hellespont, [Note: [Col. 0506D] Several manuscripts of good quality read “Asia, the Phrygias.” Thus below in Bad., and also in an old Colbert manuscript and others, “Europe, Thrace,” which is also read in Vigilius, Book V *Against Eutyches*. Neither reading is confirmed by Fragment III, where one reads: Asia, Europe, Hellespont, Thrace.] Asia, [Col. 0507A] the two Phrygias, Pisidia, the Cycladic islands, Pamphylia, Caria, Lydia, Europe, Thrace, Haemimontus, [Note: [Col. 0507C] The printed editions read “Massilia with Mysia.” The manuscripts have only “Mysia,” or, as it is written in the Colbert and German manuscripts, “Moesia.” The same provinces, in the same order, are listed in Vigilius. But below, in Fragment CXI, there is some discrepancy in the order.] Mysia, the two Pannonias—has set forth this faith.

34. “We believe in one God, the Father almighty, creator and maker of all things, from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named. We believe also in his only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, who was begotten from the Father before all ages: God from God, light from light, through whom all things were made, those in heaven and those on earth, visible and invisible; who is Word, and Wisdom, and Power, and Life, and true Light; and who in the last days for our sake was made incarnate and born from the holy Virgin; who [Col. 0507B] was crucified, and died, and was buried, and rose from the dead on the third day, and was received into heaven, and sits at the right hand of the Father, and [483] will come [Note: [Col. 0507D] Fragment CXI adds here “at the end of the world”; and the Greek formulas which, as noted above, were sent into Gaul and Italy after the Council of Antioch have ἐπὶ συντελείᾳ τοῦ αἰῶνος, “at the consummation of the age.”] to judge the living and the dead and to render to each according to his works; whose kingdom remains without cessation through boundless ages. For he sits at the right hand of the Father not only in this age but also in the age to come. We believe also in the Holy Spirit, that is, the Paraclete, whom, after promising him to the Apostles, he sent after his return to heaven to teach them and remind them of all things; and through him the souls of those who sincerely believe in him are also sanctified. [Note: [Col. 0507D] The letter of the pseudo-synod of Sardica, in Fragment CXI, supplies here: “We believe in the holy catholic Church, in the remission of sins, in the resurrection of the flesh, in eternal life.” These words, omitting “in the resurrection of the flesh,” were transferred from there to this place in the Paris edition, although they occur neither in the other editions, nor in the manuscripts, nor in the Greek formulas.] But those who say that the Son of God is from things that do not exist, or from another substance and not from God, or that there was once a time or age when he was not, the holy and catholic Church knows to be alien from her. Likewise [Col. 0507C] the holy and catholic Church anathematizes those who say that there are three gods; or that Christ is not God before the ages, nor Christ, nor the Son of God; or that he himself is Father and Son and Holy Spirit; or that the Son is unbegotten; or that the Father begot the Son neither by counsel nor by will.” [Note: [Col. 0507D] The older Colbert and German manuscripts add here, “thus saying”; where Bad. has “thus saying” in the singular, while the other editions have “Hilary.”]

35. This faith establishes the eternal origin of the Son, and that origin from God’s substance. — This exposition of faith employs brief but wholly decisive definitions. For, in condemning those who say that the Son is from things that do not exist, it assigns to him an origin not begun but abiding [Col. 0508A]. And lest this abiding origin from which he was born should be understood to be a substance other than God’s, [Note: [Col. 0507D] The Silv. manuscript reads, “from another rather than from God’s [substance],” etc. That the preceding word *manens* (“abiding”) means the same as *exstans* (“existing”) is clear both from several passages and from §40, where one reads in the same sense: “He is not from things that do not exist, so that he may have an existing origin.”] it also pronounces blasphemers those who declare that the Son was born from some other substance and not from God. Thus, [Note: [Col. 0508D] Lips. and Par. read, “does not subsist from nothing”; they are corrected from the other books.] since he did not subsist from nothing and what he is did not come to be from any source other than God, there can be no doubt that he is born from what belongs to God; for the essence of the only-begotten Son is generated neither from things that do not exist nor from any substance other than the unbegotten and eternal substance of the Father. [Note: [Col. 0508D] The printed editions read “of the only-begotten.” The manuscripts more correctly read “only-begotten”: thus earlier “unbegotten” and “eternal” refer to the Father’s substance, not to the designation of the Father himself.] It also rejects intervals of times and ages, so that he who does not differ by nature may not be separable by time.

36. There is only one God; in what sense several may be called gods. The foregoing faith proclaims one substance of Father and Son. — From every direction through which anxious heretics might seek to turn, access is barred to their ingenuity, lest any diversity in the Son be proclaimed. For it anathematizes those who say that there are three gods. According to the truth of nature, this substance admits no plurality of names, except as is usual among human beings and angels, when a name is granted on account of the honor of merits while their substance differs in nature from God’s; and therefore there are several gods. But in the nature of God, God is one; yet the Son too is God, because in him the nature is not different. Since God is from God, both cannot fail to be God, whose essence is not distinguished by any difference of kind. The numerical plurality of the name is rejected in appellation, because there is no diversity in the quality of nature. Therefore, when it is [Col. 0508C] anathema to call them gods, [Note: [Col. 0508D] Erasmus, Miraeus, Lipsius, and Paris wrongly add “two” here. From the definite Eastern proposition, which condemns not those who say “two gods” but those who say “three gods,” Hilary draws an indefinite conclusion.] and anathema to deny that the Son is God, it is conclusively shown that the unity of the one name applied to both belongs to the property of an undiffering substance. For in confessing God the Father unbegotten and God the Son only-begotten—neither differing from the other by dissimilarity of essence—[Note: [Col. 0508D] The printed editions add, “it is said that both”; this is the work of an interpolator and lacks manuscript authority.] although each is God, one God must nevertheless be believed and proclaimed. Thus, with much care and diligent caution, the bishops’ faith safeguards the undifference of the begotten and begetting nature, confirming it by the union of the name. [Note: [Col. 0508D] The printed editions, except Bad., read “union.” The other books more correctly read “by union”: that is, faith safeguards in the begotten and begetting the undifference of nature, which it confirms by the union and singleness of the name.]

37. Yet the faith does not teach a solitary God, and rightly denies that the Son is unbegotten. He is born by will. — Yet lest again the proclamation of one God should be taken to affirm the one and solitary substance of a God without his offspring, it immediately condemns the rashness which, because God is one, would confess one and solitary God the Father, possessing in himself both the name of Father and of Son. God is one, however, to be proclaimed in the begetting Father and the born Son because of the substance of their mutually undiffering nature. The faith of the saints likewise knows no unbegotten Son, since the nature of the Son does not exist except from birth. And in him the nature of birth is so perfect that he who was born from God’s substance is also born from his counsel and will. For the complete perfection of the essence of God, begotten from the essence of God, is from will and counsel, not from a passion of bodily nature. It follows that we should now review the faith [Col. 0509B] which was composed not long ago, [Note: [Col. 0509C] Namely, as Socrates notes, Book II, chapter 29, after the consulship of Sergius and Nigrinianus; in that year, because of military disturbances, no one held the regular consulship—that is, in A.D. 351, when Constantius, after the overthrow of Vetranio, was staying at Sirmium.] when Photinus was deposed from the episcopate.

[485] Example of the faith written at Sirmium by the Eastern bishops against Photinus (A.D. 351). [Note: [Col. 0509C] Socrates, Book II, chapter 30, confusing formulas composed at Sirmium at different times and their authors, states that this one was written in Greek by Mark of Arethusa. Our Hilary more correctly attributes it to the Easterners, that is, to the whole synod. Vigilius, Book V *Against Eutyches*, §3, calls that council catholic and assembled from the whole East. No Westerners, except perhaps certain men from Illyricum, were then able to attend, because the tyrant Magnentius held the transalpine regions and Italy.]

38. “We believe in one God, the Father almighty, creator and founder, from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named; and in his only Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, who was born from the Father before all ages, God from God, light from light, through whom all things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, were made. He is Word, and Wisdom, [Note: [Col. 0509D] From one Colbert manuscript and another Sorbonne manuscript we add here, “and Power,” which occurs in the preceding Sardican formula, from which this one does not differ.] and Power, and Life, and true Light; who in the last days for our sake was made incarnate and born from the holy Virgin, and was crucified, [Col. 0509C] and died, and was buried; who also rose from the dead on the third day, ascended into heaven, sits at the right hand of the Father, and will come at the consummation of the age to judge the living and the dead and to render to each according to his works; whose kingdom, enduring without end, remains through perpetual ages. For he will sit at the right hand of the Father not only in this age but also in the age to come. And [we believe] in the Holy Spirit, that is, the Paraclete, whom, having promised him to the Apostles, after he ascended into heaven he sent to teach them and remind them of all things, through whom the souls of those who sincerely believe in him are also sanctified. [Note: [Col. 0509D] Louis Miraeus reported that he found in one manuscript the following title prefixed to the decrees that follow: “Twenty-six definitions of catholic propositions against Photinus the heretic and against every opinion of heretical unbelief.”]

I. “But those who say: ‘The Son is from no existing things,’ or ‘from another substance and not from God,’ or ‘there was a time or age when he was not’—the holy and catholic Church knows them to be alien from her.

II. “But if anyone calls the Father and the Son two gods, let him be anathema.

III. [Note: [Col. 0509D] In Athanasius and Socrates: καὶ εἴ τις λέγων Θεὸν τὸν Χριστὸν πρὸ αἰώνων υἱὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ, ὑπουργηκότα τῷ Πατρί, “And if anyone, calling Christ God, the Son of God before the ages, who ministered to the Father…” Hilary’s reading seems preferable, since the other does not suit Photinus, who, confessing one God, denied that Christ existed before Mary. This decree has a double meaning: namely, that one who calls God one and nevertheless denies that Christ is God is anathema; Hilary interprets it thus below. The other sense, which seems to us the chief one, is that one who does not confess that Christ was present at the creation of the world and accordingly existed before Mary is anathema.] “And if anyone, while saying that God is one, does not confess that Christ, God and Son of God before the ages, served the Father in the creation of all things, let him be anathema.

IV. “And if anyone dares to say that unbegotten God, or a part of him, was born from Mary: let him be anathema.

[Col. 0510B] V. “And if anyone says that the Son exists from Mary according to foreknowledge or predestination, and not that he was born from the Father before the ages and was with God, and that all things were made through him: let him be anathema. [Note: [Col. 0510D] The words “foreknowledge or predestination” are expressed by the single Greek term πρόγνωσιν, “foreknowledge.” Further, where Hilary translates “from Mary,” he seems to have read, with Socrates, ἐκ Μαρίας, rather than, with Athanasius, πρὸ Μαρίας, “before Mary”; yet below, §45, he reads the latter, and it would fit better here also: “Let him be anathema who grants that Christ existed before Mary only according to foreknowledge.”]

VI. “If anyone says that the substance of God is expanded and contracted: let him be anathema.

VII. “If anyone says that the expanded substance of God makes the Son, or calls the breadth of his substance the Son, [Note: [Col. 0510D] The Greek manuscripts contain nothing corresponding to the words “as it seems to him,” which are accordingly omitted below, in §43.] as it seems to him: let him be anathema.

VIII. “If anyone calls the Son the inherent or uttered Word of God: let him be anathema.

IX. “If anyone says that the Son from Mary is merely a human being: let him be anathema.

X. “If anyone, while saying that God and man were born from Mary, understands this to mean unbegotten God: let him be anathema.

XI. “If anyone, hearing ‘The Word became flesh’ (John 1:14), supposes that the Word was changed into flesh, or says that in assuming flesh he underwent change: let him be anathema. [Note: [Col. 0510D] Greek: ὑπομεμενηκότα, that is, “to have undergone change when he assumed flesh.”]

XII. “If anyone, hearing that the only Son of God was crucified, says that his deity (*theotēs*, θεότης) underwent corruption, passibility (*pathos*, πάθος), change, diminution, or death: let him be anathema.

XIII. “If anyone says that ‘Let us make man’ (Gen. 1:26) was spoken not by the Father to the Son but by God himself to himself: let him be anathema.

XIV. “If anyone says that it was not the Son who appeared to Abraham (Gen. 18), but unbegotten God, or [Note: [Col. 0511C] The printed editions here, in the following article, and in 21 read “the Father,” against the manuscripts and the Greek word μέρος, “part.”] a part of him: let him be anathema.

XV. “If anyone says that it was not the Son, in the form of a man, who wrestled with Jacob (Gen. 32:24), but unbegotten God, or a part of him: let him be anathema.

XVI. “If anyone does not understand ‘The Lord rained from the Lord’ (Gen. 19:24) of the Son and the Father, but says that he himself rained from himself: let him be anathema. For the Lord the Son rained from the Lord the Father. [Note: [Col. 0511C] The ancient books consistently read *pluit*, “rained,” or *pluisse*, “to have rained.”]

XVII. [Note: [Col. 0511C] Bad. reads: “If anyone does not understand the Lord and God as the Father and Son, because he calls Lord and God two gods: let him be anathema.” Erasmus and Miraeus: “If anyone does not understand the Lord and God as the Father and Son, as Lord from Lord,” etc., as Bad. But Lipsius and Paris: “If anyone understands the Lord and Lord, Father and Son, as Lord from Lord, because he calls Lord and Lord two gods: let him be anathema.” In the old Colbert manuscript: “If anyone calls God and Lord, Father and Son, as Lord from Lord, two gods: let him be anathema”; a reading not to be despised and supported by Facundus, Book X, chapter 6, where Hilary’s translation is presented corruptly. But the more genuine reading is that which we give from the other manuscripts, supported by the Greek text of Athanasius; Socrates’s text also teems with errors. The person condemned here is one who, hearing ‘The Lord rained from the Lord,’ understands the Father as Lord and the Son as Lord in such a way as to call them two gods because of the terms “Lord” and “Lord.” The Greek reads: Εἴ τις ἀκούων κύριον τὸν Πατέρα καὶ τὸν Υἱὸν κύριον, καὶ κύριον τὸν Πατέρα καὶ τὸν Υἱὸν (ἐπεὶ κύριος ἐκ κυρίου), δύο λέγοι θεούς· ἀνάθεμα — “If anyone, hearing the Father called Lord and the Son Lord, and the Father and Son called Lord (since Lord is from Lord), should call them two gods: let him be anathema.”] “If anyone calls the Father and Son, Lord and Lord—for the Lord [supply: rained] from the Lord—two gods: let him be anathema. For we do not [487] equate or [Note: [Col. 0511D] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read “we equate or compare.” These two words render the one Greek word συντάσσομεν. It has already been observed above that in the same way the one word πρόγνωσιν was rendered by two words, as though Hilary, uncertain which was more fitting, proposed that both be chosen.] compare the Son with the Father, but understand him to be subject. For he did not descend to Sodom without the Father’s will; nor did he rain from himself, but from the Lord—that is, by the Father’s authority; nor does he sit at the right hand by his own authority, but hears the Father saying, ‘Sit at my right hand’ [Note: [Col. 0511D] Athanasius and Socrates append here ἀνάθεμα ἔστω, “let him be anathema,” and the Latin translation of the councils has the same. This is entirely superfluous, for it is not a new anathema but an explanation of the one just given.] (Ps. 109:1).

XVIII. “If anyone says that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one person: let him be anathema.

XIX. “If anyone, calling the Holy Spirit the Paraclete, calls him unbegotten God: let him be anathema.

XX. “If anyone, as the Lord taught us, does not say that the Paraclete is other than the Son—for he said, ‘The Father will send you another Paraclete, whom I shall ask’ [Note: [Col. 0512C] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read “whom I shall ask him.”] (John 14:16)—let him be anathema.

XXI. “If anyone calls the Holy Spirit a part of the Father [Col. 0511C] or of the Son: let him be anathema.

XXII. “If anyone calls the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit three gods: let him be anathema.

[Col. 0512A] XXIII. “If anyone understands in a Jewish manner the saying, ‘I am God, the first, and I am God, the last, and besides me there is no God’ (Isa. 44:6), which was spoken to destroy idols and those who are not gods, as a destruction of the only-begotten God before the ages: let him be anathema. [Note: [Col. 0512C] The printed and manuscript texts read “only”; but from the Greek word μονογενοῦς, “only-begotten,” and Hilary’s interpretation it is clear that “only-begotten” must be read. Then, from three manuscripts, we restore “understands in a Jewish manner,” in agreement with the Greek Ἰουδαϊκῶς ἐκλαμβάνοι. The Colbert and German manuscripts have “as though understanding in a Jewish manner”; the printed editions have “understands that it was said in a Jewish manner.” The latter reading is found below, §57, in all books.]

XXIV. “If anyone says that the Son was made by God’s will, as though he were one thing among creatures: let him be anathema.

XXV. “If anyone says that the Son was born while the Father was unwilling: let him be anathema. For [Note: [Col. 0512C] Erasmus removed “while the Father was unwilling.” Although it may appear superfluous and is not required by the Greek wording, we restore it on the authority of Bad. and all the manuscripts.] the Father did not, unwilling and compelled, or led by natural necessity, beget the Son when he did not wish to do so; rather, [Note: [Col. 0512C] Miraeus, Lipsius, and Paris, following Erasmus, read “as soon as he willed.” Here and below *ut*, “as soon as,” is absent from Bad. and the manuscripts. Greek: ἀλλ᾽ ἅμα τε ἐβουλήθη, καὶ ἀχρόνως καὶ ἀπαθῶς ἐξ ἑαυτοῦ αὐτὸν γεννήσας ἀπέδειξεν, “but as soon as he willed, he showed him begotten from himself without time and without passion.”] as soon as he willed, he showed him to be begotten from himself without time and without passion.

XXVI. “If anyone calls the Son unbegotten and [Note: [Col. 0512D] Here only Hilary translates the Greek ἄναρχον as “without beginning”; below he translates it “without principle.” Where the Greek reads ὡς δύο ἄναρχα, he translates “as though two without principle”; and shortly afterward εἰς μίαν ἄναρχον τῶν ὅλων ἀρχήν he renders: “to the one who is without principle, the principle of all things, through the Son we refer all things.” The Greek here adds εὐσεβῶς, “piously.”] without beginning, thereby asserting two without principle, two unbegotten, and two unborn, and so making two gods: let him be anathema. For the head—that is, the principle—of all things is the Son; but the head—that is, the principle—of Christ is God. [488] Thus we refer all things through the Son to the one who is without principle, the principle of all things.

XXVII. “And again, confirming the understanding of Christianity, we say that if anyone does not say that Christ, God the Son of God, existed before the ages and ministered to the Father for the completion of all things, but says that from the time when he was born from Mary he was both called Christ and Son and received a beginning so as to be God: let him be anathema [Note: [Col. 0512D] Socrates adds here ὡς ὁ Σαμοσατεύς, “as the Samosatene.” If one wishes to retain it, it should not be understood as “as Paul of Samosata asserted,” as was customary in Latin editions of Socrates before Valesius; rather: “let him be anathema, as is the Samosatene.”].”

39. The manifold deceit of Photinus is repelled. The Son differs from the Father neither in substance nor in time. — Necessity and the time admonished those who then met to arrange the exposition of faith more broadly and diffusely by means of many questions, because the heresy revived by Photinus was attempting to creep into the catholic [Col. 0513A] house through many hidden tunnels. Thus each form of heretical and stealthy fraud was to be met by a corresponding form of uncorrupted and uninjured faith; and there were to be as many solutions of faith as there were occasions of the impiety sought. [Note: [Col. 0513D] The printed editions read “as many.” The manuscripts read “so many”; and shortly thereafter “as many,” for “the same number.” We have the same manner of speaking in *Commentary on Matthew*, chapter 15, §10: “The crowd is counted and satisfied in so many thousands of portions as …”] First, after that general and unquestionable exposition of the mysteries, the beginning of the exposition of faith against heretics is taken from this point:

I. “But those who say: ‘The Son is from no existing things,’ or ‘from another substance and not from God,’ or ‘there was a time or age when he was not’—the holy and catholic Church knows them to be alien from her.”

40. What room for ambiguity is here? Or what remains, from the consciousness of sincere faith? He is not from things that do not exist, so that he may have an existing origin. There is no existing substance other than God’s for him as an origin [Col. 0513B], so that nothing else can be born in him except everything that belongs to God. [Note: [Col. 0513D] The printed editions except Miraeus omit “everything,” which rightly appears in all manuscripts. The error of heretics who asserted that the Son was a part of the Father must be excluded.] Since he does not exist from nothing, he does not subsist from elsewhere. He does not differ in time, so that the Son too is timeless with the Father. Therefore all things are inseparable between the unbegotten Father and the only-begotten Son; equal in time, they are distinguished in no respect of essence by that very sameness with the sole paternal subsistence from which birth is derived. [Note: [Col. 0513D] The printed editions read “the eternity of paternal unbegottenness, from which birth is derived”; then Bad. has “undifference in no respect,” and Erasmus, Miraeus, Lipsius, and Paris “undiffering in no respect.” They are corrected from the manuscripts.]

[489] II. “But if anyone calls the Father and the Son two gods, let him be anathema.

III. And if anyone, while saying that God is one, does not confess that Christ, God and Son of God before the ages, served the Father in the creation of all things, let him be anathema.”

41. As they are one in the name “essence,” so they are one in kind of essence. [Col. 0513C] — The reverent profession of that name itself grants us a complete understanding of the matter. For since it is condemned to call the Father and Son two gods, and again it is anathema to deny that the Son is God, the opinion that their substances are different, one from the other, is excluded in the proclamation of two gods. There is no essence other than that of God the Father, from which God the Son, God timelessly born, was born. Since, necessarily, we confess God the Father and absolutely proclaim Christ, the Son of God, to be God, while the confession of two gods is irreligious between these affirmations, they cannot fail to be one in kind of essence according to the undifference of nature and name; for the name of their essence may be only one.

IV. “If anyone dares to say that unbegotten God, or a part of him, was born from Mary: let him be anathema.”

[Col. 0513D] 42. The Son and Father are not one person. Against those who maintain that the Son existed before Mary only by predestination. — Lest the one name of essence ascribed to Father and Son through their undissimilar nature should give heretics occasion to proclaim that unbegotten God, or a part of him, was born from Mary, this was met by the salutary definition of the judgment that anyone confessing it should be anathema. The reverent unity of name, established from the essence of an undiffering nature, has not taken away the person of the generated essence, so that the substance of a unique and solitary God may be understood through the union of the name. [Note: [Col. 0514D] The printed editions and most manuscripts read “unique.” The Colbert and German manuscripts more correctly read “of the one,” that is, “solitary”: for God’s nature is one, but God is not singular and solitary.] Rather, the name of both essences is one—that is, one God—because the substance of the nature in both is undissimilar and indistinguishable.

V. “If anyone says that the Son existed before Mary according to foreknowledge [Note: [Col. 0514D] In the Corbie manuscript and most others, “and predestination” is absent. Then, by the agreement of nearly all manuscripts, we restore “before Mary,” although above, as here in the printed editions, “from Mary” occurs. Athanasius expressly attributes this opinion to Paul of Samosata near the end of *On the Incarnation of Christ*.] and predestination, but not that he was born from the Father before the ages and was with God, and that all things were made through him: let him be anathema.”

43. Those who are nevertheless going to deny that the Son of God, the God of us all, existed before he was born bodily, maintain that he existed according to foreknowledge and predestination, not according to the essential reality of a subsisting nature. That is, through the Father’s foreknowledge—because he predestined him someday to exist, namely to be begotten from a virgin—he was announced to us rather than having existed as born from the substance of the divine nature before the ages. Thus everything which he himself spoke in the prophets concerning the mysteries of his incarnation and passion is said by them to have been spoken by the Father concerning him through that foreknowledge. The perversity of this teaching is therefore condemned, so that the only-begotten Son of God, known to us, may be understood rather as born from the Father before the ages and creating the ages themselves with all creatures, than as predestined to be begotten.

VI. “If anyone says that the substance of God is expanded and contracted: let him be anathema.”

44. Expansion and contraction do not apply to God; nor is the Son an expansion of the divine substance. — To be contracted and expanded is a bodily affection. But God, who is spirit and blows where he wills, does not expand or contract himself by a change of substance. Remaining free from the necessity of bodily nature, he accomplishes from himself what he wills, when he wills, and where he wills. It is therefore impious to ascribe a change of substance to the freedom of such great power.

VII. “If anyone says that the expanded substance of God makes the Son, or calls the breadth of his substance the Son: let him be anathema.”

45. Although the preceding proposition intended to teach that God is immutable, it nevertheless prepared the way for the following heresy. For some dared to extend unbegotten God as far as the holy Virgin by an expansion of substance (see *On the Trinity*, Book I, §16, and Book X, §50), so that the breadth stretched out by some extension of its nature and assuming a human being might be called Son; [Col. 0515A] and so that the Son might not be perfect God born before the ages and thereafter also born as man. Catholic faith therefore condemns this whole teaching, in which the Father is said to be mutable and the born Son is denied.

VIII. “If anyone calls the Son the inherent and uttered Word of God: let him be anathema.”

46. In what sense heretics proclaim the Son of God to be Word. The Son from Mary is God and man. — Heretics, destroying the Son of God insofar as lies in them, confess that he is merely a word: namely, a discourse proceeding from the mouth of one speaking, and the incorporeal sound of an unsubstantial voice. [Note: [Col. 0515C] That this word was wrongly divided into two in earlier printed editions is clear from *On the Trinity*, Book X, §21, where the same heretics are attacked for wishing the only-begotten God not to be a subsistent God but the utterance of a spoken voice, etc. See there §50, and Tertullian, *Against Praxeas*, §§7–8.] They make the Son Word to God the Father in the same way that, by the inborn nature of our speech, every word is uttered in a voice. This whole fraud, therefore, is under condemnation: it affirms that God the Word, who in [Col. 0515B] the beginning was with God, is like a word of inherent and uttered speech.

IX. “If anyone says that the Son from Mary is merely a human being: let him be anathema.”

We do not proclaim the Son of God from Mary unless we proclaim him both human and God. [Note: [Col. 0515C] The following two sentences, displaced in earlier printed editions and corrupted by interpolations, we restore and correct with the aid of the manuscripts.] But lest our proclamation of God and man provide an occasion for fraud, it immediately added:

X. “If anyone, while saying that God and man were born from Mary, understands this to mean unbegotten God: let him be anathema.”

47. The Son is distinguished from the Father solely by birth. In assuming flesh, he was not changed. — Both the name and the power of substance are preserved. Since it is anathema for anyone to call the Son of God from Mary a human being without God [Col. 0515C], and the same judgment applies to anyone who calls the unbegotten God the one present in the human being, the God who is in the human being is not said not to be God. Rather, unbegotten God is denied, the Father being distinguished from the Son not by the name of nature—since not even [Note: [Col. 0515C] Bad. reads, “since not even by diversity [is he distinguished], solely…” Worse still are the other editions: “since there would not even be diversity, solely…”] by diversity of substance—but solely by the prerogative of unbegottenness.

[Col. 0516A] XI. “If anyone, hearing ‘The Word became flesh,’ supposes that the Word was changed into flesh, or says that in assuming flesh he underwent change: let him be anathema.”

48. When the Son of God was crucified, deity did not undergo corruption. — The dignity [Note: [Col. 0515C] That is, the substance of divinity.] of divinity is preserved, so that in the Word’s becoming flesh, the Word did not lose through flesh what it was as Word, nor was it changed [Note: [Col. 0515D] For the sense in which certain heretics at that time maintained that the Word, in assuming flesh, was changed into flesh, one must consult *On the Trinity*, Book X, §50. There he attacks those who wished God the Word wholly to have passed away into the soul of the body, so that Jesus Christ, Son of Man, would not also be the Son of God, and God the Word would have passed away from himself while animating the body in the function of a soul. They are consequently understood to have said that the Word was changed into flesh insofar as they believed that the Word passed into the body’s soul, or supplied the function of a soul. It is evident from Phoebadius of Agen that Potamius in particular held this view.] into flesh so as to cease to be Word.
