Instead, the Word became flesh so that flesh might rather begin to be what the Word is. [Note: [Col. 0515D] Not so that flesh might cease to be flesh, but so that, having become a participant in the Word’s power, glory, and other gifts, it might express within itself the nature of divinity whose powers it displayed. Nor do the following words leave room for error. See p. 59, note c [note d, col. 85 in our edition].] Otherwise, whence would flesh have power in works, glory on the mountain, [Note: [Col. 0516C] Nearly all manuscripts read “in death.” With one Colbert manuscript and another Sorbonne manuscript, “on the mountain” must be retained, namely that on which Christ was transfigured. Thus *On the Trinity*, Book X, §23: “That body is of its own and proper nature which is conformed to heavenly glory on the mountain,” etc.] knowledge of the thoughts of human hearts, assurance in suffering, and life in death? But God, knowing no change, lost none of the goods of his substance in becoming flesh.

XII. “If anyone, hearing that the only Son of God was crucified, says that his deity underwent corruption, passibility, change, diminution, or death: let him be anathema.”

49. What passibility and passion are. The Son was seen by the patriarchs.—It is fully shown why the Word, although made flesh, was nevertheless not transformed into flesh. For although these kinds of sufferings affect the weakness of flesh, God the Word made flesh could not, by suffering, become changeable in himself.

[Note: Col. 0516C: In Bad., “changeable from himself.” Afterwards, after *from himself* was deleted, *changeable* alone was retained. From the manuscripts and Mir. we restore *from himself*, that is, as regards his own nature, although he is not denied to be changeable with respect to the flesh assumed.]

For suffering and being changed are not the same thing, because every kind of suffering changes all flesh in sensation, pain,

[Note: Col. 0516B: In the editions, *endurance* is added here; it is absent from all manuscripts.]

and endurance. But the Word, which was made flesh, although he submitted himself to suffering, nevertheless was not changed by the passibility of suffering.

[Col. 0516C] For

[Note: Col. 0516D: Thus the manuscripts. But the printed editions: “He could indeed suffer suffering, but he could not be passible in respect of passibility.”]

he could suffer, yet could not be passible; because passibility is the indication of a weak nature, whereas passion is the undergoing of things inflicted:

[Note: Col. 0516D: In the common editions, “and therefore because,” and shortly afterward “sufferings have matter,” in place of “passion.” The manuscripts are better: that is, the things inflicted, because God the Word was made flesh, had in him material for passion, from the affection of which he might be said to have suffered; yet they had it without the weakness of passibility, because he is the same unchangeable God. Nor does Hilary here mean anything other than what he says in Psalm LXVIII, §9, though in other words: “There was not in the only-begotten God a natural weakness, but an assumed one”; and again in §18: “All our weaknesses which were in him are not natural but assumed.” This is as though he said: Weaknesses fall upon the person of the Word by reason of the assumed flesh substantially united to him, yet they do not affect the nature of that same Word. For he calls *passibility* that which affects nature, but *passion* that which is attributed to the person. Yet passion is not attributed to the Word except because it affects the flesh which he assumed; and, as he has just taught, every kind of passion changes all flesh—he does not even except Christ’s—in sensation, pain, and endurance. Therefore he does not consider Christ, according to the flesh, exempt from pain. Certainly it is clear here that he claims this privilege for the Word alone.]

because he is unchangeable God, although the Word was made flesh, they had in him material for passion without the weakness of passibility. [Col. 0517A] Therefore his nature remains unchangeable even in suffering, because the substance born from an impassible essence is indistinguishable from its author.

[Note: Col. 0517C: The printed editions read, “and impassible,” omitting the particle *because* before and *is* after the word. They are restored from the manuscripts.]

XIII. “If anyone says that when it was said, ‘Let us make man’ (Gen. 1:26), it was not the Father speaking to the Son, but God himself speaking to himself: let him be anathema.”

XIV. “If anyone says that it was not the Son who was seen by Abraham (Gen. 17:1), but the unbegotten God or a part of him: let him be anathema.”

XV. “If anyone says that it was not the Son, appearing as a man, who wrestled with Jacob (Gen. 32:26), but the unbegotten God or a part of him: let him be anathema.”

XVI. “If anyone does not understand, ‘The Lord rained from the Lord’ (Gen. 19:4), of the Son and the Father, but says that he rained from himself: let him be anathema. For the Lord the Son [Col. 0517B] rained from the Lord the Father.”

50. Photinus’ opinion.—Because Photinus, against whom the council had then assembled, denied these things, they had to be inserted into the creed: lest anyone should dare to proclaim him the Son of the Virgin without first proclaiming him the Son of God, and should perversely adapt to the unbegotten God, in the most foolish frenzy of heretical madness, all the foregoing things which belong properly to the Son of God; and, while referring these things to the Father, should deny substance to the Son. Since these matters are settled, they leave us no need of interpretation.

XVII. “If anyone says that the Lord and the Lord

[Note: Col. 0517C: Erasmus and Mir. now read with Bad.: “If anyone does not understand the Lord and God as Father and Son, because he calls Lord and God two gods: anathema.” Lips. and Par.: “If anyone does not understand the Lord and the Lord as Father and Son, since he calls the Lord and the Lord two gods: anathema.” The manuscripts are more consistent.]

are the Father and the Son—because ‘the Lord [is] from the Lord’—and calls them two gods: let him be anathema. For we do not make the Son equal to or compare him with the Father, but understand him as subject. Nor indeed did he descend into Sodom without the Father’s will; [Col. 0517C] nor did he rain from himself, but from the Lord, namely by the Father’s authority; nor does he sit at the right hand by his own command, but hears the Father saying, ‘Sit at my right hand’ (Ps. 109:1).”

[Col. 0518A] 51. This definition cleared of suspicion. In what respect the Son is not to be equated with the Father, while equality of nature remains.—Both what precedes and what follows entirely exclude any suspicion that may seem to arise from these statements, lest a diversity of unlike divinities be proclaimed in “the Lord and the Lord.” The Son is not compared in this respect: that it would be impious to call them two gods. Yet he is not therefore not compared or equated with the Father so that he himself might be believed not to be God. For, since it is anathema to deny that Christ is God, it cannot therefore be regarded as profane not to call them two gods, lest Christ too be proclaimed God; since, by the genuine property of natural essence, God is one precisely because the only-begotten Son, God born from the unbegotten God the Father, who is the one God, has from no source other than God that whereby he is God. And the essence of him who is begotten from him who begot cannot fail to bear the one name of an indistinguishable nature.

[Note: Col. 0517D: Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “and he who is begotten cannot be unlike him who begot him; for one is the name of an indistinguishable nature.” What Hilary adds, to explain in what respect he understands the Son not to be coequal with the Father, is illustrated by his exposition of Psalm CXXXVIII, §17: “For the Father is greater than the Son in generation, not in kind. For the Son is Son and came forth from him; and although the property of the designation ‘Father’ differs, nature does not differ. For God born from God is not unlike the substance that begets him. Therefore he cannot be made equal to him from whom he is.” In these words he acknowledges the Son as subject to the Father insofar as he is from him, and as not comparable to him insofar as he is not from himself, while firmly asserting unity of essence, nature, and substance. Therefore a certain anonymous Calvinist is convicted of unjust and evil faith, because on the basis of this canon and the third he removes Hilary from the roll of Catholics. He is the more unjust because the devout bishop immediately warns that the Council’s own words contain a certain appearance of suspicion, but that this is excluded by what precedes and follows; moreover, the books of the ancients are full of such modes of speaking, for which reason they have undeservedly been accused by some of holding unsound views on the mystery of the Trinity. We offer one example from Justin’s *Dialogue with Trypho*, speaking on this same passage of Genesis: “The prophetic word indicates that there are two in number: one on earth, who says that he descended to inspect the outcry of the Sodomites; the other in heaven, who is also Lord of the Lord appearing on earth, as Father and God and author to him, so that he may be mighty and Lord and God.”]

[Col. 0518B] And especially in this respect the Son is not compared or equated with the Father: while he is subject through the service of obedience; while the Lord rains from the Lord, lest he himself should have rained from himself according to Photinus or Sabellius, rather than being Lord from Lord; while he then sat at the right hand of God when he was told to sit there; while he is sent, receives, and in all things obeys the will of him who sent him. But submission in reverence is not diminution of essence, nor does the duty of religion make nature degenerate. For by this—that both the unbegotten Father is God and the only-begotten Son of God is God, yet God is one—both the Son’s submission and his dignity are taught,

[Note: Col. 0518C: In the common editions: “while that very name is subjected to him, to whom none other than Son is to be called [Col. 0518D] subject. Although this belongs to God the Father, it is nevertheless his by nature, having an alien name, but that of him whose Son he is, so that he may be subject to the Father also in obedience,” etc. (Bad. also reads *and may be*.) We follow the manuscripts. They contain the Catholic explanation of the entire preceding canon. When they call Father and Son “Lord and Lord,” they assign the one name of nature to both. But, as is said in *On the Trinity*, V.14: “If nature is not in the Son, the name of nature does not belong to him; but if the name of nature is in him, the truth of nature cannot be absent from him.” When, however, they call them “Lord and Lord” in such a way as not to wish them to be two gods, it follows that the Father and Son are one God—yet one in such a manner that they call one Father and the other Son. Thus, by the name Son, he is shown to be subject, while by that same name he testifies that the Father’s very substance is proper to himself.]

while even that very name, “Son,” is subjected, [Col. 0518C] which, although it belongs to God the Father, is nevertheless his own name by nature. Having the name, yet the name of him whose Son he is, he becomes subject to the Father both in obedience and in name; [Col. 0519A] yet in such a manner that the subjection of the name testifies to the property of a natural and indistinguishable essence.

XVIII. “If anyone says that the Father and the Son are one person: let him be anathema.”

52. Father and Son are not one person.—Utter perversity has no need to contradict itself; yet the foolish madness of certain persons has broken out to such a point that it has dared to proclaim one person under two names.

XIX. “If anyone, calling the Holy Spirit the Paraclete, says that he is the unbegotten God: let him be anathema.”

53. The Holy Spirit is not the unbegotten God. He is other than the Son.—The addition now of “Paraclete” makes the assertion that he is the unbegotten God liable to anathema. For it is utterly impious for him to be called the unbegotten God who was sent by the Son for our consolation.

[Col. 0519B] XX. “If anyone, as the Lord taught us, does not say that the Paraclete is other than the Son—for he said, ‘The Father will send you another Paraclete, whom I shall ask for’: let him be anathema.”

54. Why he is said to be sent by the Father.—We remember that the Paraclete was sent by the Son, and the faith itself stated this at the beginning. But because the Son frequently said, through the power of an indistinguishable nature, that his works were the Father’s works, saying, “I do the works of my Father” (John 10:37), although he repeatedly promised that he himself would send the Paraclete, he sometimes also said that the Paraclete would be sent by the Father, since he was accustomed reverently to refer to the Father all that he did.

[Note: Col. 0519D: This he does while preserving equality of his nature. For, as is stated in Psalm CXXXVIII, §28: “By the honor of reverence he subjected to him, to whom he remembered that all things were to be confessed, the authority which he had attested concerning himself—not taking away from himself the fact that he could do things like the Father, but showing him through whom he could do things like the Father.” See exposition of Psalm CXLI, §6.]

From this heretics frequently seize an occasion to say that the Son himself is the Paraclete; whereas, in saying that he would ask the Father to send another Paraclete, [Col. 0519C] he indicates the distinction between the one sent and the one asking.

XXI. “If anyone says that the Holy Spirit is a part of the Father or of the Son: let him be anathema.”

55. He is not a part of the Father or the Son.—Not a question, but the stupidity of heretical madness compelled these things to be recorded in writing. For since the name Holy Spirit has its own meaning, and the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, has both the office and order proper to his own substance, and since Father and Son are everywhere proclaimed unchangeable, how can the Holy Spirit be asserted to be a part either of the Father or of the Son? But because, among the other forms of madness, even this is commonly advanced by the impious, it had to be condemned by the holy.

XXII. “If anyone says that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are three gods: let him be anathema.”

[Col. 0519D] 56. Three gods denied.—Since the profession of two gods is irreligious, because we remember and proclaim that nowhere is more than one God proclaimed, how much more condemnable is the designation of three gods in the Father, Son, and [Col. 0520A] Holy Spirit? Yet because heretics say this, Catholics rightly condemn it.

XXIII. “If anyone understands what was said, ‘I am the first God, and I am the last God, and besides me there is no God’ (Isa. 44:6), as said for the destruction of idols and of those who are not gods, but Jewishly understands it as spoken for the destruction of the only-begotten God before the ages: let him be anathema.”

57. “There is no God besides me” does not deny that the Son is God.—After the plurality of gods has been condemned and only one God proclaimed, God the Son of God cannot be denied. The genuine property of nature, however, accomplishes this: the name denied as to number is due to essence; and the saying, “There is no God besides me,” cannot take away from the Son that whereby he is God, because no God other than he who is from God exists. And by this utterance of God the Father, he cannot fail to be God who is born from an essence indistinguishable from himself with respect to his nature.

[Note: Col. 0519D: We add the word *itself* here on the authority of the Colbert and German manuscripts.]

The Jews refer this to the unity of God because they do not know the only-begotten God. But when we deny two gods, we reject a diversity of natural essence in the Father and the Son; for “there is no God besides me” destroys the impious belief in false gods. Yet when, confessing one God, we also call the Son God, under the one name we proclaim no diversity of substance in the two.

XXIV. “If anyone says that the Son was made by the will of God as though he were one of the creatures: let him be anathema.”

58. The Son is from God’s substance, not from will as creatures are.—God’s will bestowed substance upon all creatures; but perfect generation gave the Son nature from an impassible and unbegotten substance. For all created things were made such as God willed them to be; but the Son, born from God, subsists such as God is. Nature did not produce a nature unlike itself; rather, begotten from the substance of God, he received an essence of nature according to origin, not an essence of will according to creatures.

XXV. “If anyone says that the Son was born while the Father was unwilling: let him be anathema. For the Father did not, unwilling and compelled, or led by natural necessity, beget the Son when he did not will; but, as soon as he willed, timelessly and impassibly he manifested him from himself as the only-begotten.”

59. Yet the Son is not from an unwilling Father.—When it was taught that the Son does not subsist from will, as other things do, [Col. 0520D] lest he should have his essence according to will only and not also according to nature, an opportunity seemed to be given to heretics to ascribe to God the Father a necessity of begetting the Son from himself, as though, compelled by a law of nature, he had produced him unwillingly.

[Note: Col. 0519D: Thus the manuscripts. But the editions read: “compelled by natural law against his will,” etc. Hilary permits the Son to be called born by will in the sense in which, in *On the Trinity*, XII.50, and above, §17, he allows his generation to be called creation—namely, to remove every suffering or reluctance of the Father in the generation of the Son. For, as Gregory Nazianzen aptly says, *Oration* XXXV.2, one would have to fear lest we introduce some compelled generation, “as though it were a kind of natural excrement” (*perittōma*, περίττωμα), “and an emission difficult to restrain,” something wholly unsuited to divinity. The theologians sometimes spoke somewhat differently, among them the author of *On the Trinity and the Unity of God*, in Augustine, ch. 2: “The Father begot the Son neither by will nor by necessity: not by necessity, because necessity is not in God; not by will, because will cannot precede wisdom, which is the Son. Therefore, to be wisely knowing is rationally prior to willing wisely. Hence the Father begot neither by will nor by necessity, but naturally, by wisdom alone.”]

But this is not the condition of sufferings in God the Father; for in the ineffable and perfect generation of the Son, neither did will alone generate the Son, nor was the essence changed or compelled by the command of a natural law.

[Note: Col. 0521C: In the Colbert and German manuscripts, *to whom*, not *when*.]

No substance was sought for begetting; the nature of the begetter is not different in the one begotten; nor was there, in time, a solitude of the Father’s name. Rather, before all times, the Father, impassibly willing, gave to the Son from the essence of his own nature the essence of a natural generation.

[Note: Col. 0521C: The editions read, “the generation of essence.”]

XXVI. “If anyone says that the Son is unbegotten and without beginning—thus saying that there are two without principle, two unbegotten, and two unborn, and making two gods—let him be anathema. For the Son is the head, which is the beginning of all things; but God is the head, which is the beginning of Christ. Thus through the Son we refer all things to the one unoriginated beginning, [Col. 0521B] the beginning of all.”

[Note: Col. 0521C: The common editions have *without origin*, which may be referred to “beginning”; as observed above, the Greek wording requires this. But since the same word, ἄναρχον, in §39 was translated “that which is without beginning,” rather than “that which is,” we retain with the manuscripts *unoriginated*.]

60. The unity of God does not permit the Son to be called unbegotten.—To confess the Son as unbegotten is utterly impious. For then God will no longer be one, since the proclamation of one God requires the nature of one unbegotten God. Since, therefore, God is one, there cannot be two unbegotten beings; for God is one precisely because unbegottenness belongs to one alone—although both the Father is God and the Son of God is God. The Son, however, is God because he exists as born from an unbegotten essence. Therefore the holy faith rejects the proclamation of the Son as unbegotten, in order that through the one unbegotten God it may proclaim one God; and that, in the one name of the unbegotten God, it may embrace the only-begotten nature, begotten from an unbegotten essence.

[Note: Col. 0521D: In the manuscripts, *essence*. Holy faith embraces in the one name of the unbegotten God the only-begotten nature, to which it assigns the name God in such a way that it nevertheless rejects two gods.]

For the Son is the head of all, but God is the head of the Son. [Col. 0521C] And by this order and confession all things are referred to the one God, since all things receive their beginning from him who himself is their beginning, namely God the Father.

XXVII. “And again, confirming the incomprehensibility of Christianity, we say: If anyone does not say that Christ God, the Son of God, subsisting before the ages and ministering to the Father for the completion of all things, but says that, only from the time when he was born from Mary, he was named both Christ and Son, and received a beginning so as to be God: let him be anathema.”

61. The heresy of Photinus. The chief point of our faith.—The condemnation of the heresy for whose sake [Col. 0522A] the council had assembled had to be concluded by an exposition of the entire faith which it opposed. For it falsely assigned the beginning of the Son of God to the Virgin’s childbirth. This is the chief point of our faith according to evangelical and apostolic teaching: that our Lord Jesus Christ, God and Son of God, is not separated from the Father by confession of honor, by power of might, by diversity of substance, or by interval of time.

62. The difficulty of speaking briefly about God.—Truth has been sought in many ways, as it is understood, through the counsels and judgments of bishops; and the rationale of understanding has been set forth in the several written professions of faith, every form of impious proclamation having been extinguished. For the infinite and immeasurable God could neither be understood nor displayed in the brief utterances of human speech. [Col. 0522B] For brevity of words often misleads both hearers and teachers: through compression of expression, either what is required cannot be understood, or what is signified is corrupted because it is suggested rather than expounded through a full rational explanation. Therefore the bishops, speaking with understanding,

[Note: Col. 0521D: The common editions read, “with their own understanding.” *Their own* is absent from the manuscripts.]

because of the difficulty of natural understanding, employed many definitions and fuller words in teaching, so that by distinctions set forth at length they might imbue the understanding of hearers with truth, and might say nothing else concerning divine things that was dangerous or obscure in this manifold resolution of many pronouncements.

[Note: Col. 0521D: Thus the better manuscripts. But the editions read, “nothing dangerous.”]

63. Faith in the East. Frequently formulated; sound in a few. Hosius. Forced subscriptions to faith. Westerners do not know written creeds.—Nothing should seem surprising to you, dearest brothers, in the fact that professions of faith began to be set forth so frequently:

[Note: Col. 0521D: Hincmar, *On the Non-Trine Deity*, ch. 10, after quoting these words adds: “Hilary used *faiths* in the plural because of the several forms of expression and the plurality of writings, not because faith itself was divided.”]

heretical madness imposed this necessity. For the peril among the Eastern churches is so great that it is rare to find either clergy or people holding this faith—judge for yourselves what sort of faith it is. [Col. 0522C]

[Note: Col. 0522C: The Corbie, Pratensis, Remensis, Faurensis manuscripts: “For many.”]

For through certain persons authority has wrongly been granted to impiety, and through the exiles of bishops—whose cause you know—the strength of the profane has increased. I speak neither of foreign matters nor of unknown things: I have heard and seen the faults of the present time, not of laypersons but of bishops. For apart from Bishop Eleusius and a few with him, the ten provinces of Asia, [Col. 0523A] among which I live, truly do not know God.

[Note: Col. 0522C: Nevertheless Epiphanius counts Eleusius among the Semi-Arians, *Heresies* LXXIII.23. Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History* II.40, sharply rebukes him because he took extreme offense at the alteration of the Creed of the Dedication, although he himself preferred it to the Nicene Creed. Sozomen, *Ecclesiastical History* IV.15, testifies that, together with others, he was the instigator of Liberius’ rejection of *homoousion*; and he writes, with Socrates, II.38, that Eleusius was allied with Macedonius and imitated his cruelty. Indeed, if Sozomen, IV.20, is to be believed, he persecuted defenders of consubstantiality. Yet it is very probable that both Socrates and Sozomen marked him with the stigma of cruelty because of what he did to suppress the Novatians. Sozomen himself admits, IV.20, that Eleusius was gentler than Macedonius and a man of good and upright life. Thus Hilary, while receiving as one who did not know God a man recommended by integrity of life, did not regard him as one professing the Nicene faith, but as one who came very near it and fought most vigorously against the Anomoeans. For when Aetius in Syria and Photinus in Illyricum and other provinces had utterly rejected the Son’s divinity, bishops who strongly resisted them began to be regarded by our people as Catholics and defenders of Christ’s divinity; and then, as Gregory Nazianzen says, *Oration* XXI.43, “the lighter impiety bore the reputation of piety.”]

And would that they did not know him at all; for they would be ignorant with a more ready pardon than they now malign him. But the grief of these bishops, unable to contain itself in silence, seeks the unity of this faith which it long ago lost through others. For the faith of the first assembled exposition had this necessity: because at Sirmium, through Hosius—forgetful of his own deeds and words—a doctrine of impiety, new indeed, yet long festering,

[Note: Col. 0523D: The later manuscripts read, “long dormant.”]

had broken forth. But of him I say nothing,

[Note: Col. 0523D: The printed editions read, “I make no complaint.” Since Hilary was persuaded that perversity of faith springs from moral perversity—so much so that in Fragment II.19 he says, “And it often happens thus: when the growth of vices has brought losses in the love of God, the mad pursuit of corrupted knowledge increases”—he readily believed Hosius’ unbelief had not been sudden but had revealed a long-hidden perversity of mind. Perhaps, however, he calls the impiety long festering not Hosius’ but the doctrine’s.]

because he was preserved for this purpose: that it might not be unknown to human judgment what manner of life he had previously lived. But everywhere there are scandals, everywhere schisms, everywhere faithlessness. Hence it has come about that some of those who had previously written something different were compelled to subscribe to a profession of faith. Nor do I complain of the most patient Eastern bishops, for whom, after a willing blasphemy, even a compelled profession of faith was enough. Indeed, amid the obstinate heresy of so many blaspheming bishops, it seems a matter for rejoicing that one of them is received as repentant. But amid these things, blessed and glorious in the Lord are you who, retaining the perfect and apostolic faith by the profession of conscience,

[Note: Col. 0524C: In the common editions and some manuscripts: “by conscience and profession.” Better in the principal Colbert, Carnotensis, German manuscripts, etc.: “by profession of conscience.” Hilary alludes to the Church’s devout custom of entrusting the faith of the Creed to the hearts, not parchment, of the candidates for baptism. He again refers to the same custom in *Against Constantius*, §6. Augustine’s *Sermon* CCXII.2 is relevant: “You ought by no means to write down the very words of the Creed, but to learn them by hearing; nor, once you have learned them, to write them down, but always retain and rehearse them in memory. What may not be written is made a remembrance of God’s promise, where, foretelling through the prophet, he said of the New Testament: ‘This is the covenant which I shall establish after those days, putting my law in their mind, and I shall write it in their heart.’ For the purpose of signifying this, the Creed is learned by hearing and written not on tablets or any material but in the heart.”]

have until now known no written creeds! [Col. 0523B] For you had no need of the letter, who abounded in the Spirit. You did not require the service of the hand for writing, who confessed with the mouth unto salvation what you believed in the heart. You did not need to read the bishop’s creed, which you held as regenerated neophytes. But necessity introduced the practice that creeds should be set forth and that men should subscribe to those set forth. For where the conviction of conscience is endangered, there a written document is demanded. Yet there is certainly no bar to writing what it is salutary to confess.

64. Hilary’s faith concerning Father and Son.—We indeed confess, always innocent in the gift of the Holy Spirit, and we write willingly: not two gods, but one God; yet not thereby denying that the Son of God is God, for he is God from God. Not two unbegotten beings, because God is one by the authority of unbegottenness; yet not thereby denying that the Only-begotten [Col. 0524A] is God, for his source is unbegotten substance. Not one subsisting being, but a substance not different.

[Note: Col. 0524D: The editions read, “but one substance.” *One* is absent from the manuscripts.]

Not the one name of God in unlike natures, but an essence indistinguishable in name and nature. Not either one superior to the other in kind of substance, but one subject to the other by the birth of nature. The Father greater in that he is Father; the Son not lesser in that he is Son. A difference of designation, not a difference of nature. The Father not confessed as within time, but the Son as coeternal with the Father not denied. The Father proclaimed in the Son, because the Son has nothing in himself unlike the Father; the Son confessed in the Father, because that whereby he is Son is not from elsewhere. We do not fail to recognize that their nature is mutual and alike because it is equal; yet we do not judge them to be one person because they are one. We proclaim them one through the indistinguishability of their not-dissimilar nature, lest they be one person.

65. Hilary lacks words, not understanding.—I have explained, dearest brethren, as far as the customary capacity of human speech allowed, and as the Lord, whom I have always—as he knows—asked, granted me, the conviction of our common faith.

[Note: Col. 0524D: The Roman manuscript, formerly Queen Christina’s, reads frequently, not always; Silv. also has this in a second hand.]

And if something is insufficient—indeed, because little and almost nothing has been said—remember that I lack not understanding but words. Perhaps in this I shall fault my nature, but I shall not fault my will. I pardon nature if it cannot say concerning God what it wills, since for salvation it is enough to have believed the things of God.

66. He proceeds to the second part of the treatise. He asks not to be judged before the end.—Now, because my faith and yours,

[Note: Col. 0524D: In an ancient Colbert manuscript: “my faith.”]

as far as I am conscious, [Col. 0524C] is not endangered before God; because I have shown you, as you wished, what creeds had previously been set forth by Eastern bishops—but by few, for I shall repeat it: in proportion to the number of Eastern churches, this is the faith of few bishops—and because I too have declared what I think concerning divine matters according to apostolic teaching, it remains that you should understand, without any suspicion, those things which, through the security of simplicity, expose us to error; for no occasion for mishearing remains.

[Note: Col. 0524D: Bad., Erasmus, and Mir.: “that the profession which appears from its simple wording to cast error upon us may be heard without any suspicion, because it has now not even been reported.” Lips. and Par.: “that you may know without any investigation those things which bring you error from the security of simplicity, because no hearing has now been left.” They are corrected from the manuscripts. Hilary fears that he may perhaps be ill-regarded when he appears at first sight to approve *homoiousion*, although after such an explicit declaration of his faith no occasion for mishearing remains; by these words he tries to remove every suspicion from himself.]

And although I no longer fear to be judged according to the exposition of the whole faith, yet bear with me: I wish not to be judged until all has been completed.

[Note: Col. 0525D: Thus the manuscripts, except that the later Carnotensis has, “that I may not wish.” The editions read, “that I may not wish.”]

67. When *homoousion* may rightly be proclaimed.—Many among us, dearest brethren, proclaim one substance of Father and Son in such a way that they seem to proclaim it no more piously than impiously; for this word contains both the conviction of faith and a prepared deception. For if, according to the property and likeness of nature—such that likeness conveys not appearance alone but kind—we proclaim one substance piously, provided we understand one substance as likeness in property, so that their being one signifies not a single individual [Col. 0525B] but equals. By equality I mean the indistinguishability of likeness: likeness is equality; equality is called one because it is equal; but the one in which equality is signified must not be claimed for a sole individual.

[Note: Col. 0526D: The common editions read, “is called.” The manuscripts more correctly read, “may be called,” as required by the preceding *so that*.]

Therefore one substance will be proclaimed religiously if it neither destroys the subsisting person nor divides one substance, partitioned into two, provided that, by the property of generation and the likeness of nature, it is so indistinguishable that it is called one.

68. Three erroneous meanings of the same term.—But if Father and Son are said to be of one substance for this reason—that this subsisting being, under the designation, indeed, of two names, is one and sole—we do not hold the Son, confessed in name, in our conviction, if, while confessing one substance, we say that he himself is a unique and solitary being, both Father and Son. Moreover, the occasion for this error at once arises: that the Father may be understood as divided from himself and as having cut off a part which became his Son.

[Note: Col. 0526D: Thus the manuscripts. But the editions read, “of this great error.” Shortly after, the Roman codex reads, “cut off from himself.” Compare, if you please, *On the Trinity*, IV.4.]

For this is what heretics maintain when they proclaim one substance; and the language of our thoroughly pious confession greatly flatters them, so that, while this word is doubtful through its undefined brevity, it advances error. There is, besides, this third error: when Father and Son are said to be of one substance, it may be supposed that there is a substance prior to them, which the two equals share between themselves; and thus the expression may signify three things: one substance and two, as it were, co-heirs of the one substance. For just as there are two co-heirs and the inheritance is prior, of which the two are co-heirs, so two equals may seem to be participants in one prior substance.

[Note: Col. 0526D: The word *equals*, together with the following verb *are*, is missing in the earlier common editions.]

Yet one substance of Father and Son so proclaimed either signifies one subsisting being having two designations; or one divided substance, made into two imperfect substances; or a third, prior substance, which has been both appropriated and assumed by the two, and is called one because one has been cut into two. And where, after this, is generation? Where are Father and Son understood, if Father and Son are proclaimed by either division or participation in a prior substance, rather than by the generation of nature?

69. The context in which *homoousion* may safely be used.—Amid so many and such grave dangers to the faith, then, brevity of expression must be restrained, lest what is understood piously be thought spoken impiously; lest language, though uttered with a clear and innocent conscience, become culpable through a heretical occasion. [Col. 0526B] When a Catholic is about to speak of the one substance of Father and Son, he should not begin from this point; nor should he treat it as though it were the supreme matter, as though without it no true faith existed. He may safely say “one substance” when he has first said: The Father is unbegotten; the Son is begotten; he subsists from the Father; he is like the Father in power, honour, and nature. He is subject to the Father as to his author; nor did he make himself equal, by seizure, to God, in whose form he remained; he was obedient even unto death. He is not from nothing, but [Note: [Col. 0526D] Lipsius, followed by the Paris edition, reads “but was begotten”: not without sense, but without manuscript authority. Yet the later reading, “coeval,” shared by the remaining editions, is very bad.] is a birth. He is not unbegotten, but coeval. He is not the Father, but is Son from him. He is not some portion, but is whole. He is not the author himself, but is the image: the image of God, born from God unto God. He is not a creature, but is God. He is not another God in kind of substance, but one God through the undifferentiated essence of substance. [Col. 0526C] God is one not in person, but in nature, because the Begotten and the Begetter have nothing diverse or unlike in themselves. After these things, in saying that Father and Son are of one substance, he does not err; but, in denying one substance, he now sins.

70. It must not be proclaimed nakedly and before the rest.—Let no one therefore suppose that the one substance is denied by us; its rationale is shown precisely in order that it may not be denied. Let no one suppose that one substance should be proclaimed in a brief and bare formulation, if it is to be said religiously that there is one substance. For I do not hear, “Christ was born from Mary,” unless I also hear, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was God” (John 1:1). I do not hear, “Christ [Note: [Col. 0526D] It is worth observing in passing that Hilary does not deny that Christ hungered, thirsted, and suffered according to his humanity; rather, he wishes these matters to be considered in such a way that one also attends to that in him which was wholly untouched by such affections.] hungered,” unless, after the fast of forty days, I hear, “Man shall not live by bread alone” (Matt. 4:4). I do not hear, “He thirsted,” [Col. 0527A] unless I hear, “Whoever drinks of the water which I shall give him shall never thirst” (John 4:13). I do not hear, “Christ suffered,” unless I hear, “Now is the hour when the Son of Man is glorified” (John 12:23). I do not hear, “He died,” unless I hear, “He rose again.” Let us not bring forward anything isolated from the divine mysteries, to arouse suspicion in hearers and furnish an opportunity to blasphemers. Beforehand the Son’s birth, beforehand his subjection, beforehand the likeness of nature must be proclaimed, so that Father and Son may be declared, not impiously, to be of one substance. And I do not understand why that which cannot piously be proclaimed before the rest, and must thereafter necessarily be denied impiously, should before all else be proclaimed as the greatest, chief, and isolated truth.

71. It may be spoken piously, and piously left unspoken.—The one substance of Father and Son, [Col. 0527B] dearest brethren, is not to be denied; [Note: [Col. 0527D] Lipsius and the Paris edition read “but not,” and, joining what follows with the other editions—“one substance should not be proclaimed irrationally,” etc.—produce a meaning alien to Hilary.] but neither is it to be proclaimed irrationally. Let there be one substance through the property of the begotten nature; let it not arise from portion, union, or communion. One substance [Note: [Col. 0527D] So the manuscripts, except that the Chartres manuscript reads, as in the printed editions, “can be said impiously.”] may be spoken piously and left unspoken piously. You have the birth; you have the likeness. Why do we anxiously cling to the verbal occasion for calumny when we do not disagree in our understanding of the reality? Let us believe and say that there is one substance, but through the property of nature, not as signifying an impious union. Let it be one through likeness, not through solitude.

72. Is the term *homoiousion* less proper?—But perhaps likeness seems to contain too little definiteness. If so, I ask: in what way can I make one equal to another except through likeness? Or is not being alike the same thing as being equal? If I say “one,” it carries the suspicion of singularity; if I say “like,” it carries a comparison of things without difference. Between “like” and “one,” I ask what place “equal” has; and I ask whether it belongs rather to likeness or to solitude. There is no equality among unlike things, nor is there likeness within a single thing. Or how do like and equal differ, so that “equal” may again be distinguished from “one”? Equal things, therefore, are not unlike. And what else can like things be but equal, when there is no equality among unlike things?

73. Likeness of nature signifies perfect equality. What is “likeness” in Moses is “equality” in John.—[Col. 0528A] Therefore, dearest brethren, when we proclaim the Son like the Father in all things, we proclaim nothing other than that he is equal. Likeness contains the meaning of perfect equality; and this must be understood from the holy Scriptures. For we read: [Note: [Col. 0527D] Origen, *On First Principles*, I.2, confirms from these same Scriptures that “image” is sometimes said of that which possesses the nature of the one whose image it is, and that for this reason the Son is called the Father’s image: “Just as, according to the historical account, we say that Adam’s son Seth is Adam’s image; for it is written, ‘And Adam begot Seth according to his form.’” This image also contains the unity of the nature and substance of Father and Son.] “Adam lived two hundred and thirty years, and begot a son according to his own image and according to his own likeness, and called his name Seth” (Gen. 5:3). I ask what sort of likeness and image of himself Adam begot in Seth. Remove the frailties of bodies, the beginning of conception, the pains [Note: [Col. 0527D] Most manuscripts read *paritudinis*; the word *partitudinis* has already occurred in §17.] of childbirth, and every human necessity. I ask whether this likeness which is in Seth differs in nature from its author, or whether there was in the two an essence of another kind, such that Seth, being born, did not possess Adam’s natural essence. But [Col. 0528B] it is Adam’s likeness, [Note: [Col. 0528D] Lipsius and the Paris edition read “even without kind,” contrary to the manuscripts and Hilary’s meaning. The old Chartres manuscript, together with the editions of Michaelinus, Tilius, Badius, Erasmus, and Miraeus, reads “even if [he has] kind,” which readily supplies this sense: namely, although Seth possesses Adam’s kind, he is nevertheless called his likeness. Yet we prefer, with Corbie, Pratel, Silvaniac, Remiremont, Theodulf, Roman, and the other Chartres manuscript, “even if we deny it,” especially since §75 again has “it is plainly equal even if we deny it,” where Lipsius once more introduced on his own initiative “even without kind.”] even if we deny it, because the nature is not unlike. Yet likeness of nature did not give Seth a nature of another kind, because Seth was not born from elsewhere. Thus likeness makes the natural realities themselves equal, through likeness of an essence not without difference. [Note: [Col. 0528D] The printed editions read “natural”; the manuscripts more elegantly and accurately read “natural realities.” In the words “through likeness of an essence not without difference,” the negative particle is superfluous; it is not wrongly omitted in the Roman manuscript, although we have already seen more than once examples of this sort of expression. See *On the Trinity* VII.73.] Every son, therefore, according to natural birth, is his father’s equality, because he is also a likeness of nature. And blessed John teaches that in the nature of Father and Son, what Moses calls likeness in Seth and Adam is this same equality of nature. For he says: “For this reason the Jews sought all the more to kill him, because he not only broke the Sabbath, but also called God his own Father, making himself equal to God” (John 5:18). Why do we bring our minds, sluggish through grave sins, and our dull and reckless senses, [Col. 0528C] into the teachings and words of such great men, and impiously weary them against proclamations that cannot be dissolved? [Note: [Col. 0528D] So the manuscripts. The printed editions read “against the authority of an indissoluble proclamation”; and shortly afterward, “is the Father’s equality,” not “is equal to the Father.”] Through Moses, Seth is Adam’s likeness; through John, the Son is equal to the Father; and we seek some third thing, I know not what, between Father and Son, which nature does not admit. He is like the Father; he is the Father’s Son; he is born from him. By this alone it can piously be proclaimed that they are one.

74. Those who confess likeness without equality are refuted.—Nor am I unaware, dearest brethren, that there are some who, while confessing likeness, deny equality. But let them speak as they wish and inject the poison of their blasphemy into the ignorant. If they say that likeness [Col. 0529A] differs from equality, I ask whence equality is established. For if the Son is like the Father in essence, power, glory, and time, I ask in what respect he is not seen to be [Note: [Col. 0529C] Here again the printed editions read “is equality.” The following words commend the seventh definition of the Synod of Ancyra.] equal. Indeed, this too is a condemnation established in the preceding confession: let him be anathema who says that the Father is father of an essence unlike his own. Therefore, if he gave to the one whom he begot without suffering a nature neither other than nor unlike his own, he could not have given any other than his own. Thus likeness is propriety; propriety is equality; and equality differs in nothing. But things that differ in nothing are one—not by a union of person, but by equality of nature.

75. The Son and Father have the same power.—Although both common sense and divine authorities make it clear that there is no difference between [Col. 0529B] likeness and equality, since according to Moses and John the Son is both like and equal to the Father, let us nevertheless see whether the Lord, when the Jews were angered that in calling God his Father he had made himself equal to God, taught that he is equal to God. For he says: “The Son can do nothing of himself, except what he sees the Father doing” (John 5:19). He distinguished the author when he said, “He can do nothing of himself”; [Note: [Col. 0529C] Gregory of Nazianzus, *Oration* XXXVI, simply rejects the name of obedience, which Hilary here admits in a sound sense to signify the Son’s origin from the Father: “For as Word, he was neither obedient nor disobedient,” ὡς μὲν γὰρ λόγος οὔτε ὑπήκοος, οὔτε ἀνήκοος.] he signifies obedience when he adds, “except what he sees the Father doing.” For an inability to act unless one sees is not a difference of power, since nature supplies power more than sight does; but being able only when one sees is obedience. And so, in that he can act when he sees, he signifies that he does not receive power from sight, but takes authority to act from the authority of what he sees. [Col. 0529C] Therefore the power of nature does not differ in Father and Son. His ability to do what the Father can do is not granted by some advance or increase of nature, but by [Note: [Col. 0529D] The Michaelinus manuscript, together with the Tilius manuscript, reads “an example of authority,” which is not alien to Hilary’s language. Here “the example of the author” or “of authority” comes to the same thing, just as above there is “the authority of sight,” and in *On the Trinity* VII.18, “an awareness in himself of paternal power and nature.”] the example of his author. Finally, the honour preserved by subjection was matched by the power of nature. For he added: “Whatever he does, the Son likewise does in the same way” (ibid.). Is likeness [Note: [Col. 0529D] Lipsius and the Paris edition corruptly read: “Is it not plainly equal even without kind?”] not equal? It is plainly equal, even if we deny it: for he does the same things in the same way. Are things done in the same way not the same? Or do the same things not admit equality? [Col. 0530A] Or does some other thing differ between what is like and what is equal, when things done alike are understood to be the same? Unless perhaps someone will deny that things which are the same are equal, so that things which are alike may not be called equal—although things done in the same way are proclaimed not merely equal in their doing, but the same.

76. *Homoiousion* may rightly be said.—Therefore, brethren, likeness of nature is free from suspicion of insult; nor can the Son be thought not to possess the propriety of the Father’s nature because he is like him, since there is no likeness except from equality of nature, and equality of nature cannot exist unless it is one; yet this oneness is not unity of person, but of kind. This is the pious faith; this is the religious conviction; this is the saving language: not to deny one substance of Father and Son because he is like him, but to proclaim him like him because they are one. [Col. 0530B]

77. Dearest brethren, having expounded with faithful and pious understanding one substance, which in Greek is called *homoousion*, and like substance, which is called *homoiousion*, [Note: [Col. 0529D] In the older Chartres manuscript, what follows is woven into the text here in one sequence; in the other Chartres manuscript and the Tilius manuscript it has been relegated to the margin: “I do not think anyone needs to be advised here to consider why I called the understanding of like substance pious, unless because I understood that there was also an impious understanding. Accordingly I called ‘like’ not only ‘equal’ but also ‘the same’: so that I might neither reject the likeness which you, brother Lucifer, had wished to be proclaimed, [Col. 0530C] nor fail to warn that the only pious understanding of likeness is that which proclaims unity of substance. Yet in the matter that, because I praise them—that is, the Eastern defenders of *homoiousion*—I am represented by some as odious, I have been little understood. For I did not say that they had brought the true faith, [Col. 0530D] but THE HOPE OF RESTORING THE TRUE FAITH: so that, just as they were heard, we too might through this be heard against Valens and Ursacius, and that the conciliatory language of the address—[in the Michaelinus manuscript, *coaptandus*; in the Chartres and Tilius manuscripts, *coapta ea Deus*: perhaps for ‘fitted to them,’ or ‘begun toward them’]—might avoid nothing but the ugliness of insolent reproaches, since in what followed I was to disclose more bitterly, and even more reproachfully, the hidden scandals of their expositions. Now begins the third apologetic answer of this book. Its first part falls under the words ‘pious understanding’; the other extends to the beginning of the next section. From this it is clear: first, that this book displeased Lucifer; second, that because of the same book Hilary also came under suspicion among some; third, that he did not consider the Easterners’ faith true; fourth, with what purpose he lavishes so much praise upon them, and finally why he says so much in favour of likeness of essence.”] and having demonstrated most fully the defects that may arise from either the treacherous brevity or the dangerous nakedness of expressions, I must now address the holy Eastern bishops. Since no suspicion concerning our faith now remains between us, those things which still bring suspicion through words must be cleared away; and they will pardon one who, on the basis of a common conviction, speaks with them more freely.

78. Praise of the Easterners for restraining heresy.—O men at last devoted to apostolic and evangelical teaching, whom zeal for the faith has kindled amid such darkness of heretical night! What hope of restoring the true faith you have brought by steadfastly beating back the assault of audacious unbelief! Previously, secretly and in corners, the Lord Christ was denied to be by nature the Son of God, and, lacking the Father’s essence, was proclaimed to have received an origin from non-existent things along with creatures. But now heresy, breaking forth under the profession of public authority, utters openly what before [Col. 0531A] it muttered secretly, and now [Note: [Col. 0531B] The printed editions read “now victorious”; Miraeus, “will glory”; Lipsius and the Paris edition, “glories.” The old manuscripts of Colbert, Chartres, and St. Germain read, “now already victorious, it gloried.” We prefer, with Corbie, Pratel, Faur, Roman, Remiremont, Silvaniac, etc., “now victoriously it gloried no longer secretly”: namely, after the Council of Sirmium in 357. For previously, to use the words of Sulpicius Severus, II, p. 243: “The Arians concealed their unbelief; not daring openly to proclaim the doctrine of their error, they acted as Catholics.” This is the point of Lucifer’s statement near the end of Book I *For Athanasius*, where he reproaches Constantius for acting like prostitutes, who first practice prostitution secretly, but afterwards become so shameless as to wish to do so in public places.] victoriously glories no longer secretly. For by what tunnels did it not attempt to creep into the Catholic Church? What powers of the world did it not [Note: [Col. 0531C] So the manuscripts. The printed editions read “exercised.”] deploy under the allure of false religion? For these perverse men had proceeded so far that, although they did not dare publicly to proclaim this themselves, they nevertheless deceived the Emperor into [Note: [Col. 0531C] We would greatly prefer “to dare.” Certainly this fits excellently with what Sulpicius Severus, Book II, relates as having occurred at the Synod of Milan in 355: Valens, Ursacius, and the rest, not daring through fear of the people to profess their impieties, sent a letter under the Emperor’s name, full of every perversity, intending that, if the people received it favourably, they might publish what they desired with public authority. But if it were received otherwise, all odium would fall upon the emperor—and would be excusable—for, being still a catechumen, he might reasonably be thought not to have known the sacrament of faith. From this synod Lucifer of Cagliari, as he himself relates at the beginning of his book entitled *That One Must Die for the Son of God*, was driven into exile after he contradicted Constantius standing behind the curtain. Eusebius of Vercelli and Dionysius of Milan were also banished for the same reason, and later Liberius.] give them a hearing. They deceived the ignorant king, so that, while occupied with wars, he might set forth a faith of this kind and, though not yet regenerated, impose a rule of belief upon the churches. They compelled bishops who opposed them into exile. Indeed, they compelled us to choose exile by imposing upon us the necessity of impiety. But let us always be exiled, provided only that truth begins to be proclaimed. For thanks be to the Lord: the Emperor, admonished by you, recognized his ignorance, and recognized through these judgments of your faith that the error was not his own but that of [Note: [Col. 0531D] The printed editions read “those standing by.” The manuscripts more suitably read “those exhorting”: namely, Eudoxius, Acacius, Uranius, Valens, and others, whose heresy was exposed by Basil, Eustathius, Eleusius, and Leontius, ambassadors of the Synod of Ancyra, and immediately condemned by the Emperor, as Sozomen relates, IV.12–13.] those exhorting him. And, by honourably receiving your embassy, he freed himself from the odium of an impious purpose before God and men, when he learned their falsehood—those by whose authority he was being brought into odium—through the confession of his ignorance compelled [Note: [Col. 0531D] The printed editions read “compelled by us,” incorrectly. The address is to the Ancyrene delegates, who compelled Valens and Ursacius to confess their ignorance, as has already been indicated in §§3 and 63.] by you.

79. The authors of the Sirmian formula are always deceitful. They are wittily criticized and refuted. Christ is one, not two. The subscription of Valens and Ursacius is suspect.—For they deceive, dearest brethren [Col. 0532A]—as much as I fear and as it seems to me, they deceive—because they have always deceived; and even that present subscription of theirs is not without falsehood. They excuse themselves for wishing *homoousion* and *homoiousion* to be omitted on the ground that they considered both words to signify one and the same thing. No doubt they are unlearned bishops, ignorant of the meaning of *homoousion*, as though there had never been either a synod or disputes about it! But let us grant that they did not know *homoousion*, [Note: [Col. 0531D] Some manuscripts add here: “Did they not know [Col. 0532B] *homoiousion*? Among the delegates of the Synod of Ancyra, who rejected *homoousion*, the excuse carried force that they had considered *homoousion* and *homoiousion* to have one and the same meaning.”] or did not know that *homoiousion* means being of like essence. If they did not know this, why did they wish the Son’s generation to be unknowable? [Note: [Col. 0532B] The Africans, assembled by order of Huneric, answered similarly under the cited passage of Isaiah in Victor of Vita, *On the African Persecution* III: “For the divine generation is inexpressible, not unknowable. Indeed, it is so far from unknowable—that is, from being unknown whence it is—that both the Father very often declares that he begot from himself and the Son that he was born from the Father.” Phoebadius rebukes the authors of the Sirmian formula on another ground: “Who could endure their holding the birth of one whom they confidently assert to have a beginning as uncertain?” To the same effect is Victorinus, at the beginning of Book I *Against Arius*: “Eusebius adds that the Son’s beginning cannot be known either by a human being or by any higher power or conception; and yet he dares to say that the Son is a creature, subsisting by the Father’s will and determination.” Aptly, Leontius calls this profession of ignorance in divine mysteries, by which heretics wish such things to be ineffable, a reverence truly alien from reverence; for, in order to abuse impiety freely, they flee to honourable names as to a strong and impregnable bulwark. Christian piety, on the contrary, knows how to draw a great distinction in divine mysteries between the thing itself and its mode; it does not make the thing doubtful under the pretext that it does not know the mode, but judges about the other matters as Hilary teaches one must judge about God, *On the Trinity* II.7: “Perfect knowledge is to know God in such a way that you know him not to be unknowable, yet to be inexpressible.”] If the manner in which he was born is unknown, can even this be unknown: that the Son God, born not from another substance but from God, does not have an essence different from his? Had they not read that, as the Father, so also the Son is to be honoured (John 5:25), that they might prefer the Father in honour? Did they not know that the Father is seen in the Son (John 14:9), that the Son might differ from the Father in dignity, splendour, or majesty? Or did this too arise from ignorance: that the Son is subject to the Father together with the rest, so that in being subjected with the rest he is not distinguished from the rest? Yet the Son’s subjection is the piety of his nature, [Note: [Col. 0532D] This passage is wholly corrupted in the editions of Badius, Erasmus, and Miraeus. Other editions read “the property of nature,” not “the piety of nature”; but we prefer the manuscripts. Thus above, §51: “The subjection of piety is not diminution of essence.”] whereas the subjection of the rest is the weakness of creaturehood. They knew, indeed, that he suffered; but let them say, I ask, when they learned that he suffered-with [Note: [Col. 0532D] The printed editions read “how they knew.” Phoebadius also recognizes the same words of the Sirmian blasphemy as full of fraud and poison, and overturns them on nearly the same reasoning. “First,” he says, “I do not see why they preferred to say ‘capable of suffering-with’ rather than freely confess ‘capable of suffering.’ For what is suffering-with other than suffering? Moreover, if God is incapable of suffering, he is certainly incapable of suffering-with. Thus he did not suffer-with any more than he suffered, according to the condition in which he is God.” From this—as is also evident from Hilary—those heretics who say that the Son of God assumed a human being from Mary, through whom he suffered-with, assert two in Christ: one assuming and one assumed, both capable of suffering. For had they said “through whom he suffered,” it would follow only that Christ suffered according to the nature of humanity; but when they write “through whom he suffered-with,” they signify that the nature of the Word was likewise affected by the passion of the human being.]? They avoid *homoousion* and *homoiousion* because neither is written anywhere; I ask: from where did they presume “suffered-with”? Or do they wish there to be two who suffered? For “suffering-with” testifies to this. Where, then, is that “Jesus Christ, Son of God”? Or is Jesus Christ one and the Son of God another? If the Son of God is not the same and one inwardly and outwardly, believe [Col. 0533A] in ignorance concerning *homoousion*, if these things may be unknown. [Note: [Col. 0533C] All manuscripts read “concerning *homoousion*.”] But if, in these very matters, that ignorance itself is impious—and cannot be excused, even falsely—I fear that the profession of ignorance concerning [Note: [Col. 0533C] Some manuscripts, with the printed editions, read *homoousion*. More correctly Colbert, Corbie, Pratel, Faur, etc., read *homoiousion*. Here Hilary returns to what he had already begun: “Even that present subscription is not without falsehood.” They had been compelled to subscribe to the profession of *homoiousion*, not *homoousion*. That Hilary rightly suspected Valens and Ursacius of not sincerely accepting *homoiousion* is attested by Germinius, Fragment XV.3: “I wonder,” he says expressly about Valens, “whether the aforesaid Valens has forgotten, or certainly deceitfully conceals, what was done in the past … when we subscribed with our own hand that the Son is like the Father in all things.” For, as Socrates notes, II.37, these two “always passed over to the side of those whom they saw to be more powerful.”] *homoiousion* is lying. I do not complain much about the pardon which you gave. It is religious to reserve to God what belongs to God, and error through ignorance is human. But may the two bishops, Valens and Ursacius, now pardon me for not believing that, given their age and experience, [Note: [Col. 0533D] Since they had attended the Council of Tyre in 335, and for the preceding twenty-three years almost innumerable gatherings in which disputes over the aforementioned terms were customary.] they were ignorant. And it is exceedingly difficult not to regard as liars persons who can clear themselves in another matter only by lying. [Col. 0533B] [Note: [Col. 0533D] The discerning readily observe that the reference here is to the letter written by Valens and Ursacius to Julius after the Council of Sardica, in which they expressly confessed that everything they had circulated against Athanasius was false.] But may the Lord grant rather that we judge wrongly than that they were not ignorant. For I would rather be judged to think wrongly than have your faith violated by fellowship with a heretical conscience.

80. Yet I ask you, most holy men, to weigh my anxieties with gracious pardon. [Note: [Col. 0534C] Erasmus observes that he found added here in a certain later manuscript: “In your prudence consider what it means to ask most holy men to listen graciously to one who speaks, and whether it belongs to the same person to flatter and to rebuke. This was said because I was about to disclose matters which they had hitherto kept silent, yet I did not wish to seem to bring a calumnious charge in matters that could be defended as excusable.” Miraeus retained Erasmus’s note and its words, which later editions entirely suppressed. The same words were copied in the margin by the scribe who produced the Remiremont manuscript more than four hundred years ago, with the warning that they occur in some exemplars. They survive in the margins of the later Chartres and Tilius manuscripts; in the other Chartres manuscript, written more than nine hundred years ago, and in the Michaelinus manuscript, they also stand in the text. Here Hilary makes his fourth defence: he shows that he called the Easterners “most holy men,” not from a fault of flattery, but as charity dictated, so that the correction he was about to apply might benefit them.] For the Lord is witness to my conscience that in none of these expositions which you brought to Sirmium do I wish to overthrow your faith. But pardon me if there are some things which I cannot understand, and I shall console myself, because I have read: “The spirits of prophets are subject to prophets” (1 Cor. 14:32). From this perhaps I may not presumptuously infer that I too understand what another does not know. [Col. 0533C] Not that I have dared to say that you are ignorant of anything according to the measure of knowledge; but concerning the unity of the Catholic faith, bear with us if our anxieties are no less than yours.

[Col. 0534A] 81. A letter brought to Sirmium on the exposition of *homoousion* and *homoiousion*. *Homoousion* is wrongly rejected on account of birth.—I understand that the letter which Valens, Ursacius, and Germinius asked to have read at Sirmium, concerning your exposition of *homoousion* and *homoiousion*, is in some respects no less cautious than free. And its demonstration of *homoousion* and *homoiousion* left no difficulty remaining. Concerning *homoiousion*, indeed—that is, “like essence”—there is a shared judgment. But in treating *homoousion*, “one essence,” you declared first that it must be rejected because the utterance of this word would suggest a prior substance which two persons had divided between themselves. I understand the fault in this understanding. This meaning is profane and must be rejected by the Church in common judgment. [Col. 0534B] Second, you added that our fathers, when Paul [Note: [Col. 0534D] In the old Colbert and St. Germain manuscripts: “Noetean.” Does Hilary call Paul so after Noetus, whose heresy he in some way renewed? For Epiphanius reports, *Heresies* LXV.1, that Paul held that the Son of God had no subsistence of his own, but subsisted in God; this was also pleasing to Sabellius, Novatus, and Noetus.] of Samosata was pronounced a heretic, also rejected *homoousion*, because by this designation of one essence he proclaimed Father and Son to be solitary and singular in themselves. And the Church now also recognizes this as utterly profane: to reduce Father and Son, under professions of these names and with the property of persons denied, to a unity and singular solitude. You also mentioned a third reason for disapproving *homoousion*: that at the Synod of Nicaea our fathers had been compelled, because of those who called the Son a creature, to introduce the name *homoousion*; and that it should therefore not be accepted because it is found nowhere written. I am much surprised at your saying this. For if *homoousion* must be rejected because of novelty, I fear that *homoiousion* too is imperilled, since it too is nowhere [Col. 0534C] found written. [Note: [Col. 0534D] Athanasius, *Orations* II, pp. 316 and 336, and Epiphanius, *Heresies* LXXIII.14, 19, turn the argument from novelty of expression back equally against the heretics, who called the Father “unbegotten,” the Son “from non-being,” and said “he was not before he was born,” inventing other expressions wholly unknown to Scripture. But as Athanasius teaches, *On the Synods*, p. 913—with our Hilary here concurring—it does not matter if someone uses expressions not found in Scripture, so long as they encompass pious meanings. By contrast, even if a heretic derives his expressions from sacred writings, he will nonetheless hear from the Spirit, as one suspected and corrupt in mind: “Why do you recount my righteous ordinances?”]

82. In what sense it is condemned by common judgment.—But I do not make a charge from this point. For I would rather that you had mentioned something new than rejected it impiously. Setting aside, therefore, the question of novelty, there is no question even in those matters which are condemned by the common judgment of us all. For who of sound mind would proclaim a third substance common to both Father and Son? Or who, reborn in Christ and confessing Son and Father, would, according to Samosata, confess that Christ is himself Father and Son to himself? Our judgment, therefore, is alike in condemning the impieties of heretics; and the understanding of *homoousion* rejects and indeed hates this interpretation. [Col. 0535A] Thus no question of a defective understanding remains where there is common agreement in condemning the defect.

83. What was piously adopted by the Nicene synod ought not to be disapproved.—As I am at last about to speak of the third question, I ask you: where there is peace of conscience, let there not be conflict of suspicions; and do not suppose that I bring anything forward except for the advancement of unity. For it is vain to fear calumny over a word when the reality denoted by the word itself presents no difficulty. Does anyone dislike that *homoousion* was adopted at the Synod of Nicaea? If this displeases anyone, then necessarily what [Col. 0535B] the Arians denied must please him. [Note: [Col. 0535D] The printed editions here read “what was denied by the Arians,” and below “of the Arians,” against the manuscripts. Phoebadius likewise calls them “Arius’s,” not “Arian.” As Hilary does here, Athanasius, *On the Synods*, p. 920, approves the same term *homoousion* as rightly rejected by the Synod of Antioch against Samosata and adopted by Nicaea against the Arians, according to the aim of each council.] For *homoousion* was denied so that the Son, God born from the substance of God the Father, might not be proclaimed, but rather that he was created from nothing like the creatures. We say nothing new: the unbelief of the Arians itself bears witness to this in letters published in abundance. If, because of the impiety of those who denied it, the understanding of those who confessed it was then pious, I ask why today what was then piously adopted is overthrown because it was impiously denied. If it was piously adopted, why is the establishment of piety charged with guilt, when it piously extinguished impiety by the very means through which [Col. 0535C] impiety was being committed? [Note: [Col. 0535D] So the manuscripts. The printed editions instead read “was being impiously treated.” Plautus uses the verb *impiari*, apparently coined after the pattern of Greek ἀσεβεῖν, “to commit impiety.” Moreover, *impiabatur* may suitably be referred to the heresy of Samosata: the term which he, by using it nakedly, employed to express his impiety, when itself explained by other preceding terms extinguished the impiety of Arius at Nicaea. Unless one prefers to see an allusion here to the account in which Ambrose says that *homoousion* was adopted at Nicaea against Eusebius’s subtleties, *On Faith* III.15.125; this is less probable.]

### 84. The purpose of the Nicene Synod. The Nicene Creed.

Let us therefore consider what the Nicene Synod [Note: In the printed editions: “decreed.” The manuscripts more correctly read: “endeavoured,” since the question is not so much whether *homoousion* was decreed as with what purpose.] endeavoured by confessing *homoousion*, that is, “of one substance”: certainly not to bring forth the heresy which is conceived from a faulty understanding of *homoousion*. They will not, I think, say that the Father and the Son divided one prior substance between them into their own substance. And we shall now insert into this discussion of ours the faith then set down in a religious manner, not irreligiously now.

> “We believe in one God, the Father Almighty, maker of all things visible and invisible. And in one Lord, our Jesus Christ, the Son of God, begotten of the Father, only-begotten—that is, from the substance of the Father—God from God, light from light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, of one substance with the Father, [Note: Several manuscripts, as in Fragment II, no. 27: “which the Greeks call *homoousion*.” These words, however, are absent from the sixth-century Corbie manuscript, which contains this Creed together with other ancient records.] which the Greeks call *homoousion*, through whom all things were made, things in heaven and things on earth; who for our salvation descended, [Note: The printed editions add “from heaven,” which occurs neither here in the manuscripts nor in Fragment II nor in Lucifer’s book *On Not Sparing*, etc.] was incarnate and became man, and suffered, and rose again on the third day, and ascended into heaven, and is to come to judge the living and the dead. And in the Holy Spirit. But those who say, ‘There was when he was not,’ and, ‘Before he was begotten he was not,’ and that he was made from things that did not exist; or who say that God is of another substance or essence, or is changeable and mutable—these the Catholic Church anathematizes.”

Here the most holy synod of devout men does not introduce some prior substance divided into two, but declares the Son begotten from the substance of the Father. Do we too deny this? Or what else do we confess? And after the other statements of the common faith it says: “Begotten, not made, of one substance with the Father, which the Greeks call *homoousion*.” What occasion for a faulty interpretation is there here? The Son, having been born from the substance of the Father, is proclaimed not made, lest the birth of divinity be regarded as a work of creation. And he is of one substance, not so that one alone exists or exists solitary, but so that, being born from the substance of God, he does not exist from elsewhere [Col. 0536C], nor exist in some diversity of discordant substance. Or is not this our faith: that he does not exist from elsewhere, and that he exists not as dissimilar? Does *homoousion* attest anything here except that, according to the offspring of nature, the essence of the two is one and dissimilarity-free [Note: Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read “propagation.”], because the Son’s essence is not from elsewhere? Since it is not from elsewhere, both are rightly believed to be of one essence, because the Son has no substance of birth except from the authority of the Father’s nature.

### 85. Must *homoousion* be rejected because it is commonly understood wrongly?

But perhaps, conversely, it will be said that it ought therefore to be rejected because it is commonly understood wrongly [Col. 0537A]. If this is what we fear, let us remove from the Apostle what has been said: “The mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Tim. 2:5), because Photinus uses it to support his heresy; and let it not be read by us because he understands it badly. Let the Epistle written to the Philippians likewise perish, whether by fire or sponge, lest Marcion read there, “And being found in appearance as a man” (Phil. 2:7), confessing that the body was a phantom and not a body. Let the Gospel of John not exist, lest Sabellius learn, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). Nor let these present preachers of a creature possess the text, “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28). Nor let those who wish to assert that the Son is unlike the Father read, “But of that day and hour no one knows, neither the angels in heaven, nor [Col. 0537B] the Son, but the Father alone” (Mark 13:32).

Let the books of Moses likewise not exist, lest darkness be coeternal with God, who dwells in unbegotten light, since in Genesis (1:2) day began after night; lest Methuselah’s years [Note: Concerning Methuselah’s years, Augustine testifies in *City of God*, XV.13, that there was once a very celebrated question, although, as he teaches in *On Original Sin*, II.23, it must be numbered among matters which may be unknown without injury to the Christian faith. Jerome also says in his *Hebrew Questions* that it was debated throughout all the churches. The dispute arose because, according to the edition of the Seventy translators, Methuselah was calculated to have lived fourteen years after the Flood, and thus more than eight souls would have been preserved. According to the Hebrew text, however, with which our Vulgate agrees, there is no difficulty, since he is found to have died in the very year of the Flood. Where manuscripts disagree, Augustine says in the already cited passage of *City of God*, greater credence should be given to the language from which the translation into another language was made by interpreters.
