Although, as he adds in the same place, in certain Greek manuscripts—three agreeing with one Latin and one Syriac—Methuselah was found to have died six years before the Flood.] exceed the age of the Flood (Gen. 5:26), and lest not merely eight souls be preserved (1 Pet. 3:20); lest God, hearing the outcry of Sodom after its sins had already reached their fullness, descend as though ignorant in order to see whether the sins are full in accordance with the outcry, and God be found not to know what he knew (Gen. 18:21); lest anyone who buries Moses know the grave of the buried man [Note: Hilary does not deny Moses’ death, as Scultetus says, against the explicit words of Scripture; rather, he teaches that it is expressed in the sacred writings in such a way as to indicate that the greatest difficulty lies beneath those words. See what has been noted on this matter at no. 10, chapter 20, commentary on Matthew.] (Deut. 34:6); lest, through these matters, as heretics suppose, the Law itself be at variance with itself and hostile to itself. And because these things are not understood by such people, let them not be read by us.

[Col. 0538A] Let all those divine and holy Gospels of human salvation likewise perish, if you please—I do not say this of myself, but the necessity of replying requires it—lest they conflict with one another in the supposed contradiction of their sayings: lest the Lord who is to send the Holy Spirit himself be read as born from the Holy Spirit; lest he who is to threaten death by the sword permit a sword to be bought on credit [Note: The printed editions read “lest death and the sword.” The manuscripts more correctly read “lest death by the sword,” namely, by usurers.] (Matt. 26:52); lest he who is to descend to the lower regions be in Paradise with the thief (Luke 22:36); lest finally the apostles be found guilty, who, though commanded to baptize in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit (Matt. 28:19), baptized only in the name of Jesus [Note: That is, they are said in Acts to have baptized in this way; their expression must therefore be reconciled with the Lord’s command to baptize in the name of the Father, etc. Hilary acknowledges that this was commanded to the apostles by Christ; yet he is far from thinking them transgressors of Christ’s command. It follows, then, that he at least doubted whether the apostles baptized in Christ’s name alone, whatever Scultetus may protest against Bellarmine. Baptism could be called baptism “in the name of Jesus,” because it was instituted not, as John’s had been, but by the authority of Jesus Christ, although it was to be administered in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.] (Acts 10:48).

For I speak to you, brothers, who are no longer nourished with milk but are strong enough for solid food (Heb. 5:12): because the wise of the world do not understand these things [Col. 0538B], and they are foolishness to them, shall we be wise with the world and believe them foolish? And because they are darkness to the impious, shall we fail to shine with the understood truth of doctrine? Sacred things are prejudged wrongly if, because some people do not regard them as sacred, they ought not to exist. Therefore let us not glory in the cross of Christ because it is a scandal to the world; nor let us proclaim death in the living God, lest impious persons charge God with having died.

### 86. Is it to be rejected because eighty bishops rejected it?

*Homoousion* is understood badly: what is that to me, who understand it rightly? Paul of Samosata confessed *homoousion* badly [Note: Athanasius, *On the Synods*, p. 919, seems to suggest that Paul of Samosata did not express his heresy by the word *homoousion*, but that, when seeking to evade condemnation, he raised it sophistically in this way: “If Christ was not made God from a human being, then he is consubstantial with the Father; and it necessarily follows that there are three substances—one prior as their source, and the other two deriving from it.” Thus he did not confess *homoousion* with a sincere mind, although our Hilary here maintains otherwise. Hilary’s opinion is nevertheless confirmed by the letter of the Ancyrene delegates summarized above, which testifies that the Fathers at Antioch rejected the term *homoousion* because Samosatenus, by this designation of one essence, declared the Father and Son to be solitary and unique for himself. Indeed, Athanasius, warning that the letter of the Antiochene synod convened against Paul was unavailable to him when he wrote this, sufficiently indicates that an exact account of the matter should not be demanded from him. Yet with Hilary he defends the term *homoousion*, on the same faith, as rejected by the Antiochene council and received by the Nicene.]—but did the Arians deny it better? Eighty [Note: Athanasius, *On the Synods*, pp. 918–919, mentions only seventy. By contrast, Basil the deacon and other monks, in the petition presented at the Council of Ephesus, enumerate one hundred and eighty: vol. III of the Councils, p. 425. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, VII.29, writes that almost innumerable persons assembled at that synod.] bishops formerly rejected it, but three hundred and eighteen later received it.

[Note: Thus Liberius, writing back to the Easterners in Socrates, IV.12: “Not by chance,” he says, “but by divine direction was so great a number of bishops gathered against the madness of Arius, corresponding to the number by which blessed Abraham through faith put to flight so many thousands of enemies.” The prologue of Ambrose’s *On the Faith*, I.5, and the preface to *On the Holy Spirit*, I—commonly attributed to the deacon Paschasius—agree with this. Since this work has been mentioned, the reader will not object if we provide here certain considerations proving that the two books *On the Holy Spirit* have been falsely ascribed to him. Some have already observed that in a Vatican manuscript these books are attributed to Faustus of Riez. Gennadius’ authority supports this inscription, for he lists two books *On the Holy Spirit* among Faustus’ works; and the remarkable agreement of these books with Faustus’ other works strongly favors it. For example, in Book I, chapter 5, the objection against the Son’s eternity is answered by the same reasoning as in Faustus’ sixteenth letter. Likewise, Book II, chapter 1, just as in that letter, maintains that God alone, not the human soul or angels, is incorporeal. More arguments of this kind are available, but the matter does not belong here. Yet let the reader pardon us once more if we point out that this may greatly assist him in identifying and recognizing the author of most of the homilies falsely attributed to Eusebius of Gaul. Let him compare the preface of the first of these books with one of the said Eusebius’s homilies *On the Creed*, then that homily with another likewise entitled *On the Creed*, and afterwards both with the two homilies *On the Nativity* and most of those *On Easter*, *On the Ascension*, and so forth: he will find so great an agreement in them that he will no longer doubt their parentage. Moreover, whoever compares the Eusebian homily for the feast of the Holy Trinity with chapters 9 and 12 of the said Book I *On the Holy Spirit*, and also with Book II, chapter 4, will readily discover that both works belong to the same author.]

For my own part, that very number is holy to me—the number in which Abraham, conqueror of impious kings (Gen. 14:14), was blessed by him who is the type of the eternal priesthood [Col. 0539A]. Those men rejected it against a heretic; did these men not also approve it against a heretic? The authority of the ancients is weighty; is the holiness of these men weightless? If they thought contrary things, we ought, as judges, to approve the better; but if, both in approving and in rejecting, they established one and the same thing [Note: Thus the manuscripts with Bad.; except that Remigius and Michael read “each.” Erasmus, Lipsius, and Paris read “to each.” Both acts—the approval and rejection of *homoousion*—are one, because of the unity of the end at which they jointly aimed: the confirmation of the one divinity and eternity of the Son.], why do we overthrow what has been rightly established?

### 87. Is it because Hosius, who was present at Nicaea, decreed that it should be kept silent?

But perhaps someone will say to me: “Some alive today among those who were then present at the Synod decreed that *homoousion* should be kept silent.” [Note: The manuscripts read “concerning *homoousion*,” and later “concerning *homoiousion*.” Anyone can easily see that this objection is drawn from Hosius, who, though present at the Nicene Synod, decreed—or at least agreed—at the Council of Sirmium that *homoousion* should be kept silent. When Hilary repeatedly says that he loved his tomb too much, Baronius, under the year 357, no. 16, interprets it as loving his body too much. Yet it seems better understood thus: being near death, he feared that he would end his life in exile and lack the grave of his birthplace. Marcellinus and Faustinus state this more openly in their petition: “Hosius, fearing that, old and wealthy as he was, he might suffer exile or proscription, gave his hand to impiety.” Ambrose confirms this interpretation in Letter LXXXII to the Vercellians, no. 69, where, concerning the holy Eusebius and Dionysius driven into exile, he says: “They did not long for their native tomb, for a heavenly dwelling was reserved for them.”]

And, though unwillingly, I shall reply to him: Do not these very men also decree that *homoiousion* should be kept silent? I beg you, let no one other than old Hosius—he too, that man excessively fond of his tomb—be found who thinks that both should be kept silent. And in such raging storms of heretics, where at last shall we come down if, while we receive neither term, we retain neither? For it cannot seem an impious statement that, because neither is found written, either neither ought to be confessed or both ought to be confessed [Col. 0540A].

### 88. What Hilary understands by *homoousion*. Scruples against *homoousion* removed.

By *homoousion*, most holy men, I understand God from God: not of a dissimilar essence, not divided, but begotten; and, in the Son, a co-begotten, only-begotten birth from the substance of the unbegotten God, according to likeness [Note: Paris, following Lipsius, reads “co-innate,” wrongly and against the testimony of the other books. For it is contradictory that the birth should be both begotten and unbegotten. “Co-begotten” would not be objectionable. Hilary calls the birth co-begotten because it was begotten as soon as the unbegotten essence existed. He adds “according to likeness,” lest it be thought degenerate.]. This was my understanding already, and *homoousion* has strongly confirmed me in it. Why do you condemn my faith in *homoousion*, which you cannot fail to approve through my confession of *homoiousion*? [Note: The manuscripts read “of *homoousion*,” which is not satisfactory. Here the Easterners are pressed: whether they profess *homoiousion* sincerely or not, if sincerely, they understand by this word what Hilary understands by *homoousion*; and consequently, in condemning and proscribing *homoousion*, they are proved either to condemn their own faith or not to profess *homoiousion* sincerely.] For you condemn my faith—or rather your own—when you condemn the meaning expressed by its name. But does another understand it badly? Let us condemn together the faulty understanding [Col. 0540B]; let us not take away the security of faith.

You think the Samosatene Synod should be subscribed to, lest anyone claim *homoousion* for himself according to Samosatenus’s interpretation? [Note: The older books, with Bad., read “the Samosatene [Synod].” One Colbert manuscript reads “of Samosata”; the Teller manuscript, “of the Samosatenes.” Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, VII.27, 20, and 30, indicates that several synods were convened against Paul, but makes no mention of a Samosatene one. He expressly states in chapters 27 and 29 that the first and last were held at Antioch. And although he says in chapter 28 that Firmilian attended one of them, the letter of the final Antiochene synod reports that he had already twice come to Antioch.] Let us subscribe also to the Nicene Synod, lest Arians reject *homoousion* [Note: The Teller manuscript reads, “lest the Arians reproach [it].” Then, with two Chartres manuscripts, one Remigius manuscript, and Michael, it adds: “Did I not here too warn one choosing *homoiousion* that it should not be received otherwise than with reference to unity of substance?” By these words Hilary continues to clear himself of unjust suspicions. At the beginning we would prefer: “Did I not here also choose—or select—*homoiousion*?” From Miraeus’s margin one might restore: “Did I not here warn lest *homoiousion* be received carelessly?” Hilary employs this precaution not only in this book but also in Book VII *On the Trinity*: while preaching likeness, in no. 26 he joins it with equality, and in nos. 37 and 39 with unity.].

But must it be feared that *homoousion* may not signify *homoiousion* according to the faith? Let it be determined that “of one substance” and “of like substance” do not differ, that they are of one substance [Col. 0541A]. [Note: Bad. reads “of essence and substance.” Some manuscripts read “essence substance,” others “the essence of substance,” and others “the substance of essence.” With Chartres, one Colbert, and the second Sorbonne manuscript, “of substance” must be retained.] But can *homoousion* be understood badly? Let it be determined how it can be understood rightly. [Note: The printed editions read: “We think one and the same thing, piously among ourselves,” etc. The fuller reading of the ancient Chartres manuscript appears preferable, and is supported by the others, especially the Colbert and German manuscripts, which have: “We piously think one and the same thing; I ask that we should wish what we think, one and the same thing, to be pious among ourselves.”] We piously think one and the same thing; I ask that we should wish what we think, one and the same thing, to be pious among ourselves. Grant the pardon, brothers, which I have requested so often: you are not Arians; why, then, are you judged Arians by denying *homoiousion*?

### 89. *Homoiousion* is not free from a stumbling-block. True likeness.

But you say: “The ambiguity of *homoiousion* troubles me with scandal.” Hear again, I beg you, without scandal: the bareness of *homoiousion* troubles me also. [Note: Here too the often-mentioned manuscripts add: “Can anyone think that I wish to accept *homoiousion*, when I have discussed these matters?” This belongs with the apologetic passages.] Many things that are alike often deceive. I fear gold leaf, because it may deceive me within, though what is seen resembles gold. I fear the likeness of milk, lest milk offered to me not be sheep’s milk, because cows’ milk too appears like it [Col. 0541B]. For sheep’s milk to be like sheep’s milk, it cannot be alike unless it is from a sheep. True likeness lies in truth of nature. But where the truth of nature is in both, *homoousion* is not denied of both. [Note: This is the reading supported by the manuscripts in great agreement: that is, when the truth of nature is in both, *homoousion* is not denied of either. The printed editions read “*homoiousion* is not denied.” What follows is a proof of the earlier proposition, “True likeness,” not of this immediately preceding one, “But truth, etc.”]

This is likeness according to essence: when a mass like a mass does not deceive by being gold leaf, when milk that has the same colour is not different in taste [Col. 0542A]. Nothing can be like gold unless it is gold; nothing can be like milk unless it is of the same kind. The colour of wine has often deceived me, and yet by taste I recognized a liquid of another kind. [Note: Lipsius and Paris read “by taste.” The Chartres manuscript reads “having tasted a liquid of another kind,” wrongly. For Hilary says that by tasting he recognized that what appeared to be wine was not wine.] I have seen meats like meats, but afterwards taste disclosed to me their dissimilarity of nature. [Note: The Teller, Michael, and Chartres manuscripts read “their likeness of nature”; “dissimilarity” is preferable. The same manuscripts, with another Chartres manuscript and Remigius, add: “Was I careless here too about likeness?” The words belong to the Apology and fit the following sentence better.] For I fear those likenesses which do not arise from unity of nature. [Note: Lipsius wrongly inserted “do not,” a negative particle of his own, without which he had himself previously read: “I fear gold leaf.” Nor was this corrected in later editions.]

### 90. The Ancyrene faith brought to Sirmium with some matters suppressed.

For I fear, brothers, the heresies of the East, springing up in successive periods; and what I fear, I have already said and read. [Note: Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “and I shall say what I fear. I have now also read.” He has already read what he says he fears. He fears, indeed, lest the faith of the Easterners be insincere, because at Ancyra they condemned *homoousion*. He had already reproached them for this in no. 81: “Why do you condemn my faith in *homoousion*?” etc.] Certainly, in those things which you ministers of the mission, undertaken with the agreement of certain Easterners, brought to Sirmium for subscription, no cause for suspicion remained; [Note: Namely, in the twelve definitions set out and explained at the beginning of this treatise. According to the reply of the Apology, quoted above at no. 13 after the first definition of the Ancyrene Synod, only these were brought to Sirmium. Hilary here first expressly indicates that they were brought to be subscribed; but he has already more than once related that certain persons at Sirmium were compelled to subscribe them. Further, when he says that this was done with the agreement of certain Easterners, he should not be understood to mean that certain Easterners judged that only the twelve definitions of the Synod, with the rest suppressed, should be taken to Sirmium. For below he ascribes this suppression to Basil, Eustathius, and Eleusius alone, and that only conjecturally. Rather, the entire Ancyrene Synod determined that its decisions should be brought to Sirmium and subscribed by those defending contrary opinions. This Synod is called one “of certain persons” because neither all the Easterners nor a very great number assembled there.] but from the outset they contained no small ground of offence—matters which I believe you, most holy men Basil, Eustathius, and Eleusius [Note: The Colbert and German manuscripts read “Eustachius.” The Chartres, Corbie, and certain others read “Eustasius.” Erasmus, Lipsius, and Paris most wrongly put “Basil, Eustathius, and Eleusius” in the genitive, when the syntax requires the vocative. Hilary is here addressing Basil, Eustathius, and Eleusius, who were prominent among the Eastern organizers at Ancyra and were delegates from there to the Emperor.] suppressed, lest any scandal should be caused [Note: The older Colbert manuscript, supported by the German and others, reads “be caused.”]. If these matters were rightly written, they ought not to have been kept silent. But if they are now kept silent because they were not rightly written [Note: The printed editions read “are still kept silent”; this is corrected from the manuscripts.], care must be taken lest they someday be spoken.

[Note: After “be spoken,” the Remigius manuscript adds material which the Chartres and Michael manuscripts prefix less aptly to the preceding sentence, “But if they are now kept silent because they were not rightly written,” etc.; it occurs in the margin of another Chartres manuscript and of the Teller manuscript: “Am I thought to remove suspicion from these men, or to praise what I spare? For to spare, and to spare toward this end after delay, is no mark of wickedness or laxity. Do I here allow a like substance to be anything but one? If it is not first confessed as one, it is afterwards impiously proclaimed like.” By this reply Hilary aptly shows that he does not remove suspicion from the Easterners. For one who fears and takes care lest what has been kept silent be someday said is not without suspicion. Still less does he praise one whom he thinks should be spared. Yet he spares only temporarily the person whose mind he will presently disclose: “Grant pardon, brothers, to my grief: what you dare is impious.” The second part of the preceding reply would be better restored at this point, beginning with “Do I here allow a like substance,” etc. There he does not so rejoice in the Easterners’ progress as not to notice in them certain trifles of impiety over which he has reason to grieve.]

For the present I say nothing about these matters, while sparing you; nevertheless, you acknowledge with me that not the whole faith written at Ancyra was in the form in which it appeared at Sirmium [Col. 0543A]. [Note: The printed editions read “written . . . was”; and shortly afterward Bad. and Miraeus read “received from readers” for “received not from laymen.” Hilary here indicates that the faith drawn up at Ancyra was not in the same form as that published at Sirmium; and that he learned this not from popular rumour but from the Synod’s own letters, letters issued and signed not in the name of laymen but bishops. He seems to say this because, at the Council of Milan in 355, they had issued a certain formula of faith in Constantius’s name, so that if Catholics rejected it they would have something with which to excuse themselves, as has already been observed at no. 78. Epiphanius gives those letters in *Heresies*, LXXIII.2. Yet neither he nor anyone else has transmitted to us the letter concerning the exposition of *homoousion* and *homoiousion* summarized above at no. 81.] I do not speak a tale of rumour; I hold the testimony of letters—not received from laymen, but issued by bishops.

### 91. Exhortation to Accept *homoousion*. He Heard the Nicene Faith Only When About to Go into Exile.

I beseech you, brothers: remove suspicion; exclude the occasion [of thinking ill of yourselves]. In order that *homoiousion* may be approved, let us not condemn *homoousion*. Let us consider so many holy bishops now at rest: what will the Lord judge concerning us if they are now anathematized by us? What will become of us, who carry the matter so far that, because they were not bishops, neither have we begun to be bishops? For we were ordained by them and are their successors. Let us renounce the episcopate, because we received its office from men under anathema. Forgive, brothers, my grief: what you dare is impious. I cannot tolerate this declaration: that one who confesses *homoousion* in a devout sense should be under anathema. A term has no guilt when it does not disturb the sense of religion.

[Note: Supply: “of thinking ill of yourselves.”]

[Note: Mir., Lips., and Par.: “nor have we received”; other books read more correctly, “nor have we begun to be,” with “to be” understood. Later, all manuscripts except one read “we are their succession,” not “their successors.” Athanasius presses the Arians with the same argument in *On the Synods*, p. 882: “By what right can they themselves be bishops, if they were appointed by bishops whom they themselves accuse?” Socrates gives the reasoning of this statement in II.40: “How did they accept as sound and lawful the ordination of those Nicene Fathers whose faith they rejected as false and reprobate? For if those men did not have the Holy Spirit, which is imparted through ordination, they did not receive the priesthood. How, indeed, could they receive it from those who had nothing to give?” Hence, in Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History* IV.23, Moses vigorously refused to receive episcopal ordination from Lucius, the Arian patriarch of Alexandria, saying: “Far be it from me to be ordained by your hand; for when you invoke [God], the grace of the Holy Spirit does not come.” To this may be added Innocent I, *Letter to the Macedonians*, ch. 3: “It is maintained that one who has lost his rank cannot confer rank; nor has the recipient received anything, because there was nothing in the giver that he could receive.” We agree, and it is true. Certainly, because he could not give what he did not have, he gave through the laying on of hands the condemnation which he did have. How one made a participant in a condemned man ought to receive rank, I cannot discover. On account of these and other statements of the Fathers, especially in connection with Ebbo of Rheims, there has been debate whether a bishop’s consecration performed by those condemned under anathema was valid. Yet Innocent’s words make clear that he denied not so much the ordination conferred as the honor of the order and the authority to exercise it, since, he says, “the law of our Church is that persons coming from heretics are to be admitted, through the laying on of hands, only to lay communion,” etc. Hence he does not deny that Anysius’ ruling—that those ordained by Bonosus should be received—was duly enacted, though contrary to previous custom, for the Church’s advantage. He also acknowledges that the Nicene synod allowed Novatians returning to the Church to remain among the clergy. In maintaining that this was denied to others, he sufficiently indicates both that it could have been granted and that its denial resulted from disciplinary custom—not from his considering heretics’ ordination invalid. Augustine is an ample witness to the Roman Church’s judgment on this matter, *Letter* 185 (formerly 50), no. 47: “From the beginning African Catholicism maintained, following the judgment of bishops who decided in the Roman Church between Caecilian and Donatus’ party, that, after one Donatus had been condemned … the rest, when corrected, should be received in their ranks, even if they had been ordained outside the Church.” Thus our Hilary also can and should be understood: those who received the episcopal office from persons under anathema, with the strictness of discipline relaxed for them by no synod, are not bishops—or are not reckoned as bishops—in the same sense in which he declares that bishops, although lawfully ordained, are not bishops when they are established in anathema. For Augustine’s reasoning is valid, *Against Parmenian’s Letter* II.13: “The defect lies in the severance itself, not in the sacraments; wherever the sacraments themselves are, they are true.” Accordingly Jerome, defending in his *Dialogue against the Luciferians* the Church’s practice of receiving bishops who came from the Arians, answers the objection that they cannot confer the Holy Spirit: “If an Arian cannot give the Spirit, neither can he baptize; for the Church’s baptism is nothing without the Holy Spirit.” Yet Augustine readily grants, *Letter* 185, no. 47, that the Holy Spirit cannot be possessed outside the unity of Christ’s body. We do not here examine in what sense Jerome denies that the Spirit can be given by an Arian; for this too can be said truly, but it is another question.]

[Note: Because, as Innocent I says in his *Letter to the Macedonians*, ch. 3, it is the Roman Church’s law to grant to those coming from heretics, through laying on of hands, lay communion only, etc.]

[Note: Bad. and Er., with several more recent manuscripts, read “what you hear”: wrongly. Then only the printed editions read “I cannot tolerate.” Here Hilary at last states what he has hitherto concealed: namely, the final decree of the Synod of Ancyra, which, together with the rest of the letter, appears in Epiphanius, *Heresies* LXXIII, and is given in no. 11 in these words: “If anyone, affirming that the Father is Father of the Son in power and substance, says that the Son is consubstantial or of the same substance as the Father, let him be anathema.”]

I do not know or understand *homoiousion*, except in the confession of similar essence.

[Note: Thus, along with the three aforementioned manuscripts, two others. But Er., Lips., and Par. read “the confession of similar essence”; Bad., with more manuscripts, “the confession of dissimilar essence.” Instead of “dissimilar,” “or similar” would not be unacceptable, or, with the German manuscript, corrected by an ancient second hand, “to similar.” After these words the frequently cited manuscripts contain this final part of the Apology: “Can I seem to have been able to approve what I did not know? Certainly not. But because the Catholic faith ought to believe similarity only through unity—so that it mentions similarity solely to exclude union, not for the division of unity—I said that, although I did not know the names *homoousion* and *homoiousion* (the manuscripts, except one recent Carnotensis manuscript, wrongly read ‘did not know,’ and afterward ‘received’), nevertheless I had received similarity through unity. The sentence immediately following establishes this very point: ‘I call God of heaven to witness,’ etc.”]

I call the God of heaven and earth to witness that, although I had heard neither term, I nevertheless always held both senses which ought to be understood through *homoousion* and *homoiousion*: that is, nothing can be similar to itself by nature unless it is from the same nature. Long ago regenerated, and having remained for some time in the episcopate, I never heard the Nicene faith except when I was about to be exiled; but the Gospels and the Apostles taught me the meaning of *homoousion* and *homoiousion*. What we desire is devout. Let us not condemn the Fathers; let us not encourage heretics; lest, while we call out heresy, we nourish heresy. After the Synod of Nicaea our Fathers devoutly interpreted the proper sense of *homoousion*; books survive, conscience remains. If anything must be added to the interpretation, let us consult together. Between us the best condition of faith can be established: that what has been rightly determined may not be disturbed, and what has been wrongly understood may be cut away.

[Note: The printed editions read “through *homoiousion*, *homoousion*.” The manuscript reading better agrees with Hilary’s words just cited—that he received similarity through unity.]

[Note: The printed copies have “religious books”; the manuscripts, “devoutly,” referring to “interpreted,” and illustrated by these words in no. 27 of *Against Constantius*: “For letters survive which teach that what you regard as blameworthy was then devoutly received.” Moreover, Eusebius Pamphilus’ letter still survives in Socrates I.8, near the end, in which he writes that this term was expounded to him devoutly and religiously and was accepted by him.]

### 92.

I have gone beyond, dearest brothers, the modest reserve of human awareness; and, forgetful of my own humility, compelled by love for you, I have written these things concerning matters so great and so hidden, unattempted and unspoken of down to our own age, and have spoken what I myself believed. I am conscious that I owe this as the service of my warfare for the Church: that through this letter I might set forth the voice of my episcopate in Christ according to evangelical teaching. It is yours to deliberate, provide, and act in common, so that you may preserve with religious conscience what you have until now maintained with inviolate faith, and hold what you hold. Remember my exile in your holy prayers. After setting forth this faith, I do not know whether it is as pleasant to return to you in the Lord Jesus Christ as it is safe to die. May God and our Lord preserve you undefiled and unharmed for the day of revelation, I pray, dearest brothers.

[Note: The printed editions read “and” for “that,” and shortly afterward “destinare” for “destinarem”; they are corrected from the manuscripts. Yet with the Colbert and German manuscripts one may prefer: “I owe it to set forth, through this letter …”]

[Note: Er., Mir., Lips., and Par. read “to return to the house of Christ”; Bad. and all manuscripts resist this reading.]

[Note: In more recent manuscripts this book ends thus: “*Homoousion* is Greek. The interpretation of *homoousion* is ‘of one substance’; and *homoiousion* is interpreted ‘of similar substance.’ But through *homoousion* one ought to understand …” This seems rather the note of some student than of the author.]

## 521–522. Saint Hilary’s Apologetic Reply to the Censures of the Books *On the Synods*. (C)

[Note: First printed in the Veronese edition, which we have reprinted.]

### I. On no. 3: “And although not without some offense to the ears … the Easterners resisted the Anomoeans.”

If this statement had been carefully weighed, perhaps the purpose of my whole treatise would not have been regarded with suspicion. For I did not keep silent there that there was something which could not be heard without offense.

[Note: The sense requires this so plainly that we judged it preferable, although the manuscripts read “I had kept silent there.”]

### II. At the beginning of no. 13, after the recitation of the first decree of the Synod of Ancyra.

All the expositions of the Synod of Ancyra described in this book, if they contain anything blameworthy, contain it within themselves; otherwise they are considered not to possess it in their public appearance. But because I knew that these alone had been brought to Sirmium [perhaps: “that they alone had been brought”].

### III. This refers to no. 77: “Having set forth the similar substance which is called *homoiousion*, in a faithful and devout understanding.”

I do not think anyone needs to be reminded to consider in this place why I said “THE DEVOUT UNDERSTANDING OF SIMILAR SUBSTANCE,” unless it was because I understood that there was also an impious one. Therefore I said “similar,” not only “equal” but also “the same,” so that I might neither disapprove the similarity which you, brother Lucifer, had wished proclaimed, nor fail to warn that the only devout understanding of similarity is that which proclaims unity of substance.

### IV. In the manuscripts, continuously joined to the preceding passage, this belongs to no. 78: “O men at last zealous for apostolic and evangelical teaching … what great hope you have brought of restoring the true faith!”

Yet in being accused by some of bringing them into disrepute while praising them, I have been little understood. For I did not say that they brought the true faith, but “THE HOPE OF RESTORING THE TRUE FAITH”: so that, as they were heard, we also might be heard through this against Valens and Ursacius; and so that the conciliatory, gentle language of an address adapted to them might have no other purpose than to avoid the ugliness of insolent reproaches, since later—especially in no. 91—I was going to expose the concealed scandals of their expositions more bitterly and even more reproachfully.

[Note: Thus the manuscript of St. Michael; but Carnotensis and Tellianus read “God adapted them.” Perhaps: “which were adapted to them,” or “an address begun to them.”]

### V. This is suited to no. 80: “But I ask you, most holy men, to assess my anxieties with kindly indulgence.”

In your prudence consider what it means to ask most holy men to hear the speaker with kindly indulgence, and whether flattering and rebuking belong to the same person. This was said for this reason: because I was going to disclose what had hitherto been kept silent by them, the legates sent to Sirmium (nos. 90 and 91); yet I was not to appear slanderous in matters that could be defended as excusable.

[Note: The particle *ut* appears to be missing here.]

### VI. This applies to no. 87: “And I too, unwilling though I am, shall reply,” etc.

Brother Lucifer, it could be known quite plainly that I was unwilling to mention *homoiousion*. But because you proclaimed the Son’s similarity to the Father, I had to expound its demonstration without fault.

### VII. To this is attached no. 88: “You think that the Synod of Samosata must be subscribed. Let us subscribe to the Synod of Nicaea also.”

Did I not here also warn the reader concerning *homoiousion*, showing that it ought to be accepted only if referred to unity of substance?

[Note: From the margin of Erasmus and Miraeus, where this apologetic note lies, it may be restored: “Did I not warn that *homoiousion* should not be received carelessly?”]

### VIII. He sets before the eyes of his critics no. 89: “And the bare term *homoiousion* moves me—with offense,” etc.

Can anyone think that I wish to accept *homoiousion*, after what I have said about it?

### IX. Related to this is the statement after the examples of things that deceive by outward resemblance.

Was I negligent of similarity here also?

### X. Nos. 90 agree with this: “For still sparing them, I say nothing about the things decreed at Ancyra with offense.”

Am I thought to remove suspicion from them, or to praise what I spare? For to spare, and to spare with a postponement to this end, contains nothing improper or lax.

### XI. In the manuscripts, continued with the tenth section, this falls under no. 91: “In order that *homoiousion* may be approved, let us not condemn *homoousion*”; and likewise under these words in the same number: “What you dare is impious,” etc.

Do I here allow similar substance to be anything other than one substance? If it is not first confessed as one, then afterward it is impiously proclaimed as similar.

### XII. The following is added after no. 91: “I do not know or understand *homoiousion*, except in the confession of similar essence,” etc.

Can I seem able to approve what I did not know—by taking *homoiousion* for non-substantial similarity? Certainly not. But because the Catholic faith ought to believe similarity only through unity, so that it mentions similarity solely to exclude union, not for the division of unity, I said that, although I did not know the names *homoousion* and *homoiousion*, I nevertheless received similarity through unity. The sentence immediately following establishes this very point.

## [Letter Sent to Abra and Hymn Sent to Abra.]

## Prefatory Notice on the Following Letter and the Hymn Appended to It

Erasmus calls this letter “the trifling work of an idle and unlearned man.” Gillotius writes that Fortunatus considered it fabricated; and Scultetus, p. 321, maintains that he wrote this with complete truth. Yet fairer judges of the matter rightly think that credibility should not be denied to Fortunatus himself, who presents himself not as its author but as its witness. For they do not believe that the holy bishop of the Church of Poitiers lied when he testified that in his own day the letter, subscribed in Hilary’s own hand, was kept at Poitiers as a treasure. It is far less consistent with truth that, when he had a genuine letter of Hilary in his hands, he suppressed it and substituted a forged one. If, moreover, he expresses its substance somewhat differently from what the letter itself contains, he thereby plainly shows that it was not fabricated by him.

Further, they observe in it nothing unworthy of a devout and prudent father, who calls his most beloved daughter, a very tender girl, away from the vain pomp and pleasures of the world by words adapted to her understanding, so that he may prepare her for her heavenly bridegroom and better blessings. Since obscurities and riddles of expression are very suited to stimulate intellectual powers, a concerned father—already separated from his home for many years—does not unwisely use them in order to test his daughter’s ability and application from her replies. For he had not seen Abra for at least three years when he wrote this letter to her. In it he mentions that he is sending her a morning and an evening hymn alike. The evening hymn has been lost; but the morning hymn, together with the letter, is found in very many manuscripts at the end of Fortunatus’ account of Hilary’s deeds. Both works are appropriately appended to the book *On the Synods* in the ancient editions of Hilary. For just as it is most probable that he received Abra’s letter together with the letters of the Gauls, so it is most probable that her reply was sent together with the book *On the Synods*.

## (Sent About the End of the Year 358.) 525–526. Letter of Saint Hilary to His Daughter Abra. (C,S)*

To his most beloved daughter Abra [in most manuscripts, “Apra”], Hilary sends greeting in the Lord.

### 1. Abra Grieves at Her Father’s Absence.

I received your letter, in which I understand that you long for me; and I hold this certainly to be so. For I know how desirable the presence of those whom we love is. And because I knew that my absence was burdensome to you, lest perhaps you should think me unloving toward you because I have been away from you so long, I wished to explain both my journey and its delays, that you might understand that I am absent from you not unlovingly but for your benefit. For, daughter, as I have you as my only child, so, so far as I am concerned, I have you as one in heart with me; and I should wish you to live more beautiful and healthier than all others.

### 2. Hilary Is Away to Seek a Precious Garment and Pearl for His Daughter.

It was reported to me, then, that there was a certain young man who possessed a pearl and a garment of inestimable value. If anyone could obtain them from him, he would become wealthy and safe beyond human riches and well-being. Having heard this, I set out for him. When I had come to him by many long and difficult roads, I immediately fell down on seeing him. For the young man is so beautiful that no one dares remain standing before his presence. When he saw that I had fallen down, he ordered that I be asked what I wanted and requested. I answered that I had heard of his garment and pearl, and had come for that reason; and that, if he would deign to grant them to me, I had a daughter whom I loved exceedingly, for whom I was seeking this garment and pearl. Meanwhile, prostrate on my face, I wept greatly; groaning night and day, I begged that he would deign to hear my prayer.

[Note: One Colbert manuscript reads “I set out to see him,” without “having heard this.”]

[Note: Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read “prostrate on the ground, face downward.”]

### 3. The Value to Be Set upon This Garment and Pearl.

After this, because the young man is good and nothing is better than he, he said to me: “Do you know this garment and this pearl, which you ask me with tears to grant to your daughter?” I answered him: “Lord, I have learned of them by hearing and believed by faith; and I know that they are excellent, that it is true salvation to wear this garment and to be adorned with this pearl.” At once he commanded his servants to show me both this garment and pearl, and it was immediately done.

First I saw the garment. I saw, daughter, I saw what I cannot express. Was silk not coarse hempen rope in comparison with its fineness? Did snow, compared with its brightness, not become black? Did gold, beside its radiance, not grow pale? For it was itself multicolored, and nothing that could be compared with it could equal it. Afterward I saw the pearl; when I saw it, I immediately collapsed. My eyes could not bear such splendor. Neither heaven, nor light, nor sea, nor earth could be compared with its beauty.

[Note: Bad., Er., and Mir. read “had taken its part”; Lips., from Erasmus’ margin, “was equal”; the latest Paris edition, “was scattered.” The Beccensis manuscript reads “was not prepared”; Ottobonianus, “was in parts.” Hilary means that silk, compared with the fineness of the garment shown to him, was wholly like coarse hemp, from which in ancient times sailors’ ropes and baskets were made.]

### 4. The Benefits and Endowments of Both.

As I lay prostrate, one of those standing by said to me: “I see that you are an anxious and good father and desire this garment and pearl for your daughter. But, that you may desire them more, I shall show you what further good this garment and pearl possess. This garment is never eaten by moths, worn away by use, stained by dirt, torn by force, or lost through misfortune; but it always remains such as it is. This pearl has the power that whoever puts it on does not become ill, grow old, or die. It contains absolutely nothing harmful to the body; but nothing happens to its wearer which brings death, changes age, or impairs health.”

When I heard this, daughter, I began to be consumed still more by longing for that pearl and garment. As I lay prostrate, I began with unceasing weeping and earnest prayer to entreat the young man, saying: “Holy Lord, have mercy on my prayer, and have mercy on my anxiety and my life. For unless you grant me this garment and pearl, I shall be miserable and shall lose my daughter while she lives. I am willing to live as a stranger for the sake of this garment and pearl. You know, Lord, that I do not lie to you.”

[Note: The printed editions read “liable”; they are corrected from the manuscripts.]

[Note: One Colbert manuscript reads “the young man,” not “living.”]

### 5. These Are Promised to Hilary’s Daughter, If She Casts Away Vain Ornaments.

After he heard my words, he ordered me to rise and said to me: “Your prayers and tears have moved me, and it is good that you have believed this. Since you said that you were willing to spend your very life for this pearl, I cannot deny it to you. But you must know my purpose and will. The garment which I shall give is such that anyone wishing to wear another garment—colored, silken, or gilded—cannot receive my garment. I shall give it only to her who is content to be clothed, not in silken attire, but in natural colors and inexpensive fabric; so that, for customary distinction, she may have a very narrow purple stripe on her garment, but the purple itself may not spread over the garment. The pearl for which you ask me has this nature: no one who possesses another pearl can possess it. For other pearls are of earth or sea; but mine, as you yourself see, is beautiful, precious, incomparable, and heavenly, and it does not deign to be where other pearls are. My possessions do not suit human possessions. For whoever wears my garment and pearl is healthy forever: he does not burn with fever, is not exposed to a wound, is not changed by years, is not destroyed by death; for he is always alike and eternal. Yet I will give this garment and this pearl of mine to you who ask, so that you may carry them to your daughter. But first you must know what your daughter wishes. If she makes herself worthy of this garment and pearl of mine—that is, if she is unwilling to possess silken, gilded, and dyed garments, and hates every other pearl—then I shall grant you what you ask.”

[Note: Another of the Colbert manuscripts, together with the Boherian, Ottobonian, and Cenomannian manuscripts, reads “if any girl”; and shortly thereafter only Ottobonianus reads “cannot receive my garment.” This relates to Cyprian, *On the Discipline and Dress of Virgins*: “Those clothed in silk and purple cannot put on Christ.” Likewise Jerome, *Letter* VII to Laeta, after recounting the punishment suffered by the most noble Praetextata because, at her husband Hymetius’ command, she altered the habit and dress of a daughter consecrated to God, concludes: “Thus Christ punishes violators of his temple; thus he defends gems and most precious ornaments.” What he says there about virgins’ dress—especially, “Let others have pearls, which afterward, when sold, will buy the pearl of greatest price”—strongly confirms that this letter bears the stamp of Hilary’s age and is not unworthy of his style. See *Tractate on Psalm* 118, letter 16, no. 16.]

[Note: Other Fathers also commend the natural colors of clothing and condemn artificially obtained ones. “For,” Cyprian says in *On the Discipline and Dress of Virgins*, “God did not make scarlet or purple sheep, nor did he teach people to dye and color wool with the juices of herbs and shellfish.” Cyprian adapted this from Tertullian, *On Women’s Dress* II.10.]

[Note: Par. reads “purple through the august garment”; other editions, “purple through august garments”; two manuscripts, “purple through narrow garments.” Better manuscripts read “a very narrow purple stripe of the garment,” in distinction, evidently, from the broader purple stripe mentioned by Tertullian, *On the Pallium*, no. 4, whence comes the broad stripe mentioned by him in *On the Crown*, no. 13. Jerome, *Letter* 22 to Eustochium, depicting and reproving certain virgins conspicuous in public, says among other things: “only a thin purple stripe in the garment.” Hilary’s passage contributes somewhat to establishing the nobility of this family.]

[Note: The printed editions read “is poured over the garment”; they are corrected from the written copies.]

[Note: Almost all manuscripts read thus. The printed editions, however, read “equal to eternal things.” The Ottobonian manuscript reads: “For my garment is ever the same and eternal”; and shortly before, “does not suffer wounds,” for “is not exposed to a wound.”]

### 6. He Urges His Daughter to Use Modest Clothes.

After these words, daughter, I rise joyful; and, keeping this secret, I have written this letter to you, begging you through my many tears to keep yourself for this garment and pearl and not make an unhappy old man suffer such loss through you, if you do not have this garment and pearl. I call the God of heaven and earth to witness, daughter, that nothing is more precious than this garment and pearl, and that it is yours by right to have them.

Therefore, whenever another garment—silken, dyed, or gilded—is brought to you, say to the person offering it: “I await another garment, for which my father has lived so long as a stranger away from me; he seeks it for me, and I cannot have it if I possess this. The wool of my sheep is enough for me; the color supplied by nature is enough for me; inexpensive cloth is enough for me. But I desire that garment which is said not to be consumed, worn out, or torn.” If, however, a pearl is offered to you to hang around your neck or fit upon your finger, say this: “Let these useless and filthy pearls not hinder me; I await that pearl most precious, most beautiful, and most beneficial. I believe my father, because he too believed the one who promised it to him, for whose sake he told me that he was even willing to die. I await it; I desire it, which will grant me health and eternity.”

[Note: The Beccensis manuscript reads “make”; Cenomannianus, “destroy”; Boherianus and several others, “do not cause such loss to an unhappy old man.” One Colbert manuscript reads “do not make yourself an unhappy seed through such loss.” The German manuscript agrees, except that it omits “yourself.”]

[Note: An example of such an adjuration occurs in *On the Synods*, no. 91: “I call the God of heaven and earth to witness that, although I had heard neither term,” etc.]

[Note: Thus the Ottobonian manuscript; the printed editions read “therefore, whenever another garment is brought to you.”]

[Note: The printed copies read “he who promised believed him”; corrected from the Boherian manuscript.]

### 7. He Awaits His Daughter’s Reply. Morning and Evening Hymn. Abra’s Mother.

Therefore, daughter, relieve my anxiety. Always read this letter of mine, and reserve yourself for this garment and pearl. You yourself, without asking anyone, write back to me in whatever letters you can, whether you will reserve yourself for this garment and pearl, so that I may know what to answer that young man. And if you desire and await it, I may joyfully think of returning to you. When you have written back to me, I too shall tell you who this young man is, what he is like, what he wishes, what he promises, and what he is able to do.

Meanwhile I have sent you a morning and an evening hymn, so that you may always remember me. But if, because of your age, you do not understand the hymn and letter, ask your mother, who desires that by her manner of life she may have begotten you for God. May God, who begot you, guard you now and forever, I pray, most beloved daughter.

## 529–530. Hymn of Saint Hilary Sent to His Daughter Abra. (C,G,S)*

Giver of light, splendid  
[alternative: most excellent],  

by whose serene  
[alternative: spoken] light,  

after the passing times of night,  
the returning [alternative: shining again] day is opened:

you are the true light-bearer of the world,  
not he who, herald of the coming light,  
shines with the narrow radiance  
of a small star;

but brighter than the whole sun,  
yourself wholly light and day,  
illuminating the inmost recesses  
of our heart.

Be present, Creator of all things,  
glory of the Father’s light,  
by whose grace drawn near  
our bodies lie open;

and, filled with your Spirit,  
bearing God within themselves,  
may they not lie open  
to the dreadful deceits of the ravaging enemy;

so that amid the acts of this world  
which the needs of life require,  
free from every fault,  
we may live by your laws.

May the chastity of the mind conquer  
the shameful lusts of the flesh,  
and may the Spirit preserve  
the holy shrine of the pure body.

This is the hope of the praying soul;  
these are its vowed offerings:  
that morning light may be ours  
for watchfulness in the night.

Glory to you, Lord;  
glory to the Only-begotten;  
with the Paraclete Spirit,  
now and through every age. Amen.

[Note: Thus the German manuscript. The Ottobonian manuscript, two Colbert manuscripts, and another from St. Peter of Couture read: “when grace is removed, our bodies tremble”: wrongly. The printed editions read: “at the nod of grace our bodies lie open.” Then another German manuscript adds:

> And may your holy right hand  
> protect us through the ages.  
> After the end of this life,  
> grant everlasting life.

After this, “filled with your Spirit” follows, in place of the printed text: “you also, by your full Spirit.”]

[Note: The German manuscript reads: “May nothing of the creeping traitor’s hidden deceits lie open.”]

[Note: The printed editions read “may we strive by your laws,” against the manuscripts.]

## [A Hymn Incorrectly Attributed to Hilary.]

## Critique of Another Hymn Incorrectly Attributed to Hilary

In a manuscript formerly belonging to Cardinal Sirleto, then to the Altemps library, and now to Cardinal Ottoboni, this hymn is followed by another, longer hymn, which might be thought to be the evening hymn mentioned in the preceding letter to Abra. It is certainly highly suitable for evening. For it begins with the stars and is a general confession of a soul which, lamenting that it is attacked by the vices of lust, pride, envy, discord, vain glory, gluttony, and exuberant joy, asks forgiveness, relying solely on God’s mercy and Christ’s merits.

Moreover, it has the flavor of the age of the Arian heresy, in that, after professing a faithful mind, it expressly detests Arius and Sabellius and adds no heretic except perhaps Simon Magus, merely to complete the verses. Yet its diction does not seem worthy of Hilary. Everywhere the measure of its verses is determined by the number of syllables rather than feet. And although, if this hymn were to be sung by a daughter, its language ought to be feminine, it is masculine throughout. From the beginning and end let the reader judge what should be thought about the rest of the hymn.

## [Hymn Incorrectly Attributed to Hilary. (C,S)]

### Beginning

I am not worthy to raise  
my unhappy eyes to the bright stars of heaven,  
pressed down by the heavy weight of sins.

Spare the redeemed.

I neglected to do the good that I ought;  
I committed shameful crimes without end;  
I perpetrated wickedness bounded by no limit.

Help, Christ.

[Note: “Help, Christ” would fit better here; and afterward, “Spare the redeemed.”]

### End

Singing a hymn with faithful voice,  
I despise Arius and barking Sabellius;  
never did I assent with a whispering ear  
to grunting Simon.

I have been zealous with zeal for Christ’s name;  
for holy Mother Church nourished me  
with Catholic milk throughout all time,  
at her sacred breast.

## [Books Addressed to Constantius.]

## Notice on the Following Book. Some Preliminary Remarks on the Other Books Addressed to Constantius

### I. Order of the Books Addressed to Constantius.

We do not separate from one another the following three books, so that everyone may have them at hand, although chronological order would require that the first of them be placed before the book *On the Synods*. In arranging them among themselves, however, the chronological sequence has been observed, which had previously been neglected.

II. Whether any books addressed to Constantius have been lost.—It may be questioned [Col. 0554D] whether Hilary wrote more works under these same titles than those now extant. For, after Sulpicius Severus, Fortunatus testifies that, while waiting at Constantinople for the emperor’s decision, Hilary sought an imperial hearing in three little books; yet only one work composed at Constantinople remains to us, in which such a hearing is requested. Furthermore, in none of the following books is there to be found the passage which Pope Celestine I commended as written by Hilary to the Emperor Constantius in a council, and which Arnobius inserted in Book II of *Against Serapion*. Finally, Jerome mentions a book by Hilary against Constantius after the latter’s death, whereas it is quite certain that these three were written while Constantius was alive.

III. Yet, though this is so, we judge that no other works besides these are to be sought. Fortunatus, indeed, was deceived by Sulpicius; and Sulpicius, through excessive devotion to brevity, either included the three books which we possess under a title properly applicable to only one of them, or rather, as in many other matters, confused them. There is scarcely any doubt, moreover, that Jerome called the book presented third in order one written against Constantius after his death. As for the passage mentioned by Celestine and Arnobius, we readily accept it as wholly consonant with Hilary’s pen and genius, and do not regard its attribution as false; nevertheless, we readily judge that it belongs to that part of the first little book which is manifestly mutilated and truncated.

IV. Something is missing in the first book. Whether something has been stitched into it from elsewhere.—Learned men have already observed that some things are missing in this first book; and this is evident even from section 7: “For his acquittal would weigh upon them,” etc. Since this must refer to Athanasius, it leads one to suppose that an earlier discussion of that holy man is missing. Again, in section 8, reference is made to the Nicene faith as having already been mentioned, although no word concerning it occurs above. Some have also doubted whether the material remaining from section 4 onward may not have been stitched into this little book from elsewhere. For it seems neither sufficiently connected with what precedes nor internally coherent: from that point onward the discourse nowhere turns to the emperor; and its method of treatment has a close affinity with the discussions in the *Fragments of the History of the Council of Rimini*. Hence they judge Baronius’s opinion insufficiently certain: he proves only from the fact that Hilary, in section 8, announces that he is about to take up an event recently accomplished, namely the exile of Eusebius of Vercelli, that this book was written in 355. But they also oppose to him the words of Fragment I, section 6, where Hilary, intending to recount the proceedings of the Synod of Arles six or seven years later, nevertheless calls them recent events.

V. When it was written.—The gap in this little book is not recent, since it could not be repaired even from the manuscript of St. Peter’s at Rome, copied at the beginning of the fifth century. Yet since [Col. 0555D] that ancient exemplar bears not only at its head, “Here begins another work of the same author addressed to Constantius,” but also at its end, “Here ends Book I of Saint Hilary addressed to Constantius. Here begins Book II of the same author addressed to the same man, which he himself also delivered at Constantinople,” it does not seem easy to concede that anything was stitched in from elsewhere. Certainly, in both parts, 533–534, the same calamities are lamented and the violence of the Arians is denounced in the same manner. It is clear that neither part was written before 355: not the latter, in which not only Paulinus, after the Synod of Arles in 354, but also Eusebius and Dionysius, after that of Milan in 355, are said to have been driven into exile; nor the former, in which the return from exile of distinguished bishops is humbly requested. For before the aforesaid synods the West did not know the exiles of its bishops; and who would not agree that it is especially the evils of the West which move Hilary here? It is no less certain that he wrote this little book before his own exile. For, besides the fact that in works written during exile he is not accustomed to omit mention of his exile, an exile would surely not be a suitable petitioner for the return of others from exile. Since, however, he was banished about the beginning of 356, one must return to Baronius’s opinion.

VI. On what occasion.—Moreover, the occasion for writing this little book appears to have arisen from letters of Constantius. For in 355, as Ammianus testifies in Book XVI, barbarian incursions into Gaul were frequent; to suppress them Julian was created Caesar at the end of that same year. It is likely that Constantius, fearing divisions and disturbances among the Gauls, wrote to them in order to keep them in their duty. Indeed, the following words in section 2 suggest that he had already informed the Gauls that malicious whisperers had raised in him the suspicion of an impending disturbance: “Let no perverse or envious person utter malicious words: there is no suspicion, not merely of sedition, but not even of harsh murmuring.” Everything is quiet and orderly. Taking this opportunity, therefore, Hilary writes back that the Arians are more to be feared, since they disturb everything; and he earnestly petitions against the evils which they have inflicted upon the Churches.

VII. Why it is called the first book. Hilary’s view concerning freedom of faith.—Jerome makes no mention of this little book. It is entitled the first, not because it is connected with the second, but because it was published earlier. We should gladly call it a letter, if authority permitted it. But what this most wise bishop sets forth in it in commending freedom of faith must not be understood as though he had thought that heretics might never lawfully be compelled to profess the true faith. For in the *Book on the Synods* he praises the Easterners, for whom, after a willingness to blaspheme, even subscription to the faith under compulsion was enough. Though such a subscription rightly seemed suspect to him in many cases, he nevertheless considers it a matter for rejoicing that at least some one among them is received as repentant. But he condemns the licence by which heretics compel Catholics, [Col. 0556D] abandoning the ancestral and apostolic faith, to embrace recently devised inventions. “They compel,” he says in section 6, “not that all should be Christians, but that they should be Arians.” Yet, considering the episcopal disposition, which ought always to incline toward mercy and seek a true rather than a feigned faith among the peoples, he declares it especially fitting for the emperor not to permit even the force which the Arians employed against Catholics through various tortures to be used on behalf of the true faith.

[Col. 0557]

(Written in 355 or 356.) 535–536 **BOOK ONE OF SAINT HILARY ADDRESSED TO THE EMPEROR CONSTANTIUS AUGUSTUS.** (C, S)

[Note: [Col. 0557B] *Augustus* is lacking in the manuscript of the Vatican Basilica. In that manuscript alone, and then in the printed editions, *benignifica* is added below; whereas the other manuscripts read *benigna*.]

[Col. 0557A]

1. The Churches must not be afflicted by their brethren. Secular judges must not hear clerical cases.—Your beneficent nature, most blessed lord Augustus, accords with your gracious will. And since mercy flows abundantly from the fountain of your fatherly piety, we trust that we can easily obtain what we ask. We entreat you not only with words but also with tears that the Catholic Churches may no longer be afflicted by most grievous injuries, or endure intolerable persecutions and insults—and, what is impious, at the hands of our brethren.

[Note: [Col. 0557B] In six manuscripts, *sufferings*. Even while Arians cruelly rage against Catholics, Hilary does not deny them the sweet name of brethren. By the same reasoning Gregory Nazianzen, Oration XXXIII, section 17, says: “Brethren, I still call you, although your disposition toward us is scarcely brotherly.” Sozomen, Book IV, chapter 26, likewise recalling a similar persecution, reports that, because of its ignominy, prudent men considered it so much more bitter than that which raged under pagan emperors, because both the persecutor and the sufferer of persecution belonged to the Church . . . although the divine law forbids us to be thus minded even toward outsiders. Therefore Hilary here added the words, “what is impious.”]

May your clemency provide and decree that all judges everywhere—those to whom the administration of provinces has been entrusted, and to whom alone the care and concern of public affairs ought to belong—refrain from religious observances; and that henceforth they neither presume nor usurp the right, nor imagine themselves competent, to hear the cases of clerics or to break and harass innocent persons by varied afflictions, threats, violence, and terrors.

[Note: [Col. 0557C] The Tellerian manuscript reads, “to whom alone.” This can be accepted in the sense that, just as secular judges alone hear secular cases, so bishops alone should hear ecclesiastical cases. There survives a law of Constantius, Theodosian Code XII, *On Bishops and Clerics*, forbidding the cases of bishops to be judged by any except bishops. Baronius, under the year 355, section 78, judges that it was issued in this year in response to these petitions of Hilary.]

[Note: [Col. 0557D] The Vatican Basilica exemplar reads *innocently*, which might be understood thus: “nor suppose that they harass persons innocently,” etc. But the other reading is preferable.]

2. Let the unwilling not be forcibly subjected to the heterodox. The voice of oppressed Catholics, asking that provincial governors not show favour to heretics. Liturgical celebrations and prayers for the emperor.—Your singular and admirable wisdom understands that it is neither fitting nor proper that unwilling and resisting persons should be forced and compelled, oppressed by force, to submit and surrender themselves to those who do not cease to scatter the corrupted seeds of adulterous doctrine. For this reason you labour and govern the commonwealth by wholesome counsels; you also keep watch and remain vigilant, so that all whom you rule may enjoy the sweetest liberty. There is no other way by which what has been disturbed can be restored to order and what has been torn apart can be restrained, unless each person, bound by no necessity of servitude, retains an unimpaired freedom of choice in living.

[Note: [Col. 0557D] In the same manuscript: “for no other reason than that what has been disturbed may be restored to order, what has been torn apart may hold together, and that each person,” etc. This reading was at first attractive. But since the purpose of the emperor’s watchfulness has already been given—namely, that all may enjoy the sweetest liberty—it is awkward to join “for no other reason” to what precedes.]

Certainly the cry of those who exclaim ought to be heard by your gentleness: “I am a Catholic; I do not wish to be a heretic. I am a Christian, not an Arian; and it is better for me to die in this world than, under the prevailing power of some private individual, to corrupt the chaste virginity of truth.” And it ought to seem fair to your holiness, most glorious Augustus, that those who fear the Lord God and the divine judgment should not be defiled or contaminated by accursed blasphemies, but should have authority to follow those bishops and rulers who preserve inviolate the bonds of charity and desire to maintain a lasting and sincere peace. It cannot happen, nor does reason permit, that opposites should agree, things unlike should be glued together, truth and falsehood should be mixed, light and darkness confused, or day and night have any union.

If, therefore—as beyond doubt we both hope and believe—these considerations move your goodness, not acquired but inborn, command that provincial governors show no zeal, favour, or patronage toward grievous heretics. Let your leniency permit the peoples to hear whichever teachers they wish, judge worthy, and choose, to celebrate together the sacred solemnities of the mysteries, and to offer prayers for your safety and blessedness.

[Note: [Col. 0558C] The printed editions read *voices*, and shortly afterward *it is fitting* instead of *it ought*. The Tellerian and Michon manuscripts read *of those crying aloud*. Lucifer likewise mentions and praises this cry of the faithful in *On Dying for the Son of God*: “We see,” he says, “that by this one devout cry, ‘I AM A CHRISTIAN; I do not wish to be as you are, Constantius, apostate,’ every crime is excluded; by this one cry is bestowed the protection of salvation, the bond of liberty,” etc. Victor of Vita similarly recounts this of the Africans when, under Huneric, they were being drawn toward the Arian heresy: they cried out and said with loud clamour, “WE ARE CHRISTIANS; we are Catholics.” The faithful learned this custom of exclaiming from the martyrs. For, as is read in the acts of the martyrs of Lyons in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book V, chapter 1, Blandina’s refreshment and rest, and the removal of every sense of present pain, was the utterance of these words: “I AM A CHRISTIAN.” In the same acts Sanctus is said to have answered every interrogation, “I AM A CHRISTIAN”; that this name was for him country, race, and indeed everything. Chrysostom approves the wisdom of this response near the end of Homily XLVI, where he praises Saint Lucian for likewise answering every question with nothing else, striking the devil’s head with this one simple word. Countless other examples of the same matter are supplied by the acts of the martyrs.]

[Note: [Col. 0559B] This is also missing in the manuscripts.]

3. The suspicion of sedition is removed. The craftiness of the Arians.—Let no perverse or envious person utter malicious words: there is no suspicion, not merely of sedition, but not even of harsh murmuring. Everything is quiet and orderly. And yet those who have been contaminated by the Arian and pestilential infection do not cease, with impious speech and sacrilegious mind, to corrupt the sincerity of the Gospels and to pervert the straight rule of the apostles. They do not understand the divine prophets. Being clever and crafty, they employ a certain artifice in order to conceal the enclosed pernicious corruption beneath a covering of carefully chosen words; and they do not pour forth their poisonous venom until they have seized and ensnared the simple and innocent under the pretext of the Christian name, and have made them, lest they perish alone, liable as partners in their dreadful crime.

[Note: [Col. 0559B] The printed editions read “will be,” and shortly afterward, “Let all things be quiet and orderly.” But now we restore *are* on the authority of the Vatican Basilica manuscript, by whose agreement with the others the subsequent wording is corrected. By these words, as we have noted, Hilary calms the mind of Constantius, who feared that the Gauls might be plotting revolution.]

[Note: [Col. 0559C] Here Hilary calls the apostolic rule—which in Book II addressed to Constantius, section 6, and in the *Book on the Synods*, section 63, he calls the apostolic faith—that which must be confessed in the sacrament of regeneration, as in the said Book II, section 4. To this belongs the statement in Book XII *On the Trinity*, section 56: “Holding fast the faith of my regeneration, I do not know . . .” It is clear that these modes of expression signify the Apostles’ Creed.]

[Note: [Col. 0559C] The printed editions here omit *in order that*, and then read: “they conceal it beneath a covering of carefully chosen words; they do not first pour out their poisoned venom.”]

[Note: [Col. 0559C] The printed editions read, “ensnared, they involve, lest they perish alone, but as partners.” We remove the word *involve* with all the manuscripts, and the particle *but* with the Chartres manuscript.]

4. Let devout bishops return to their sees.—We also entreat your piety to command those who are still held either in exile or in deserted places—that is, the distinguished bishops who excel in the dignity of so great a name—to return to their sees, so that welcome liberty and joyful gladness may be everywhere.

[Col. 0560A]

5. The novelty of the Arian heresy.—Who does not see? Who does not understand? Nearly four hundred years after God’s only-begotten Son deigned to come to the aid of the perishing human race—as though there had been no apostles before, no Christians after their martyrdoms and deaths—a new and most foul pestilence has now been poured out: not a pestilence of corrupted air, but of accursed blasphemers, namely the Arian pestilence. Thus those who believed before had an empty hope of immortality? We have only recently learned that these inventions were devised by two Eusebii, Narcissus, Theodore, Stephen, Acacius, Menophantus, and the two unlearned and wicked young men Ursacius and Valens. Their letters are produced, and reliable witnesses also convict them—witnesses who heard them barking rather than disputing. Those who imprudently and incautiously mingle their communion with theirs, because they are accomplices in wicked deeds, must necessarily be partners in their crimes; and when the day of judgment comes, even those who have already been cast out and rejected in this world will suffer everlasting punishments.

[Note: [Col. 0559C] The Vatican Basilica manuscript, together with the Chartres manuscript, reads “of blasphemers.”]

[Note: [Col. 0559C–0560A] Namely, the bishop of Nicomedia and the bishop of Caesarea, concerning whom Athanasius says in the *Book on the Synods*, p. 886: “Eusebius of Nicomedia praised Arius in magnificent words in a letter, saying, ‘Since you think rightly, pray that all may think so,’” etc. Eusebius of Caesarea in Palestine likewise was not afraid to state openly in his letter to Bishop Euphration that Christ is not true God. Thus Jerome too, in Letter LXV to Pammachius and Oceanus, calls Eusebius of Caesarea “the most open defender of Arius’s impiety.” Hilary here indicates those two Eusebii, following the letter of the Synod of Sardica.]

[Note: [Col. 0559D–0560B] The manuscripts unanimously read *Theodotus*. Athanasius, indeed, in *On the Synods*, p. 886, names Theodotus among Arius’s principal followers. Arius himself, in his letter to Eusebius of Nicomedia, preserved by Theodoret, Book I, chapter 4, includes Theodotus of Laodicea among his own party. Nevertheless we change nothing, since Hilary seems to have drawn this from the Sardican letter, where *Theodore*, not *Theodotus*, is read. Thus Fragment II, section 7, says: “After the two Eusebii, the authors of this party are also THEODORE of Heraclea, Narcissus of Neroniada in Cilicia, Stephen of Antioch, George of Laodicea . . . Acacius of Caesarea in Palestine, Menophantus of Ephesus in Asia, Ursacius of Singidunum in Moesia, and Valens of Mursa.” Nor is it otherwise in Sulpicius Severus, who, closely following Hilary’s wording in Book II, p. 244, writes: “The leaders of this evil were held to be Ursacius of Singidunum, Valens of Mursa, Theodore of Heraclea, Stephen of Antioch, Acacius of Caesarea, Menophanes of Ephesus, George of Laodicea, and Narcissus of Nerophi.” For the same reason, below we retain *Acacius*, rather than *Archaicus*, as in Bad., Erasmus, and all the manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 0560C] The Alexandrian Council identifies the same persons in this way, in Athanasius, p. 733: after mentioning the delegates sent to Mareotis in 335, it says: “To these they add two younger in age and character, Ursacius and Valens.” Again, twelve years later, the Synod of Sardica writes to Julius concerning them, Fragment II, section 13: “Learn what was decreed concerning the impious and ignorant young men Ursacius and Valens.” Hilary imitates these words, taking account of the time when the Arian inventions were devised and confirmed, not the time when he himself composed this little book; for in the *Book on the Synods*, section 79, he already regards them as old men and highly experienced in affairs.]

[Note: [Col. 0560C–D] Scultetus refers the word “whose” to Valens and Ursacius alone; others, more plausibly, to the other persons named as well. What Hilary here declares to be characteristic of those just named, he indicates in Fragment II, section 25, to be characteristic of all heretics: namely, to bark against the Catholic faith.]

[Note: [Col. 0560D] The printed editions read “those who mingle communion with them,” and shortly afterward, “because they become partners.” The manuscripts correct these readings. The word “already” is also absent from the manuscripts, from which we later restore it. “They must necessarily suffer with those who have already,” etc., would be especially attractive. The bishops named above—Narcissus, Theodore, and the others—were condemned by the judgment of the Synod of Sardica: Fragment II, sections 7 and 13.]

6. Letters and embassy after Athanasius’s acquittal. The cruelty of the Arians.—Now no one doubts what kind of concern they undertook for the acquittal of Athanasius, that holy man: so that, after the decisions of the synod—which, out of reverence for priestly judgment, ought to have been kept within priestly or ecclesiastical conscience—it became necessary to write to the emperor and to dispatch an embassy. But what else do they seek in these letters except liberty of faith and the removal of the contagion of the Arian name? They pray that chains, prisons, tribunals, all that deadly apparatus, and even new examinations of the accused may be prohibited.

God taught the knowledge of himself rather than exacted it; and, winning authority for his precepts by the wonder of heavenly works, he rejected a compelled will to confess him. If force of this kind were applied to the true faith, episcopal teaching would come forward in opposition and say: “God is Lord of the universe; he has no need of compulsory obedience; he does not require a forced confession. He is not to be deceived, but won. He is to be revered for our sake, not for his own. I can receive no one unless willing, hear no one unless praying, seal no one unless confessing. He must be sought in simplicity, learned in confession, loved in charity, revered in fear, and retained by the integrity of the will.”

But what is this: that bishops are compelled by chains and ordered by punishments to fear God?
