Bishops are confined in prisons; the people are arranged in custody, bound in an order of chains; virgins are stripped for punishment; and bodies consecrated to God, exposed to public view, are made fit for the profit of a spectacle and an inquisition. For they compel, not that all should be Christians, but that they should be Arians; and they force a faith confessed in God, by wickedness, into partnership with their own sacrilege. They even lead the emperor into error by the authority of his own name, asserting that it is right, under the appearance of the fear of God, to hand over their subjects to this perversity. They demand examinations, seek the aid of judicial proceedings, invoke imperial authority; and even thus they are not ashamed of the perversity of their crime, since they could not extort the connivance of the people even by a right of compulsion.

[Note: [Col. 0560D–0561D] The Vatican Basilica exemplar reads, “a concern of this sort for an acquittal.” The words “of this sort” also occur in three others; the Michon manuscript has “indeed, a concern of this sort.” Silvius reads, “for the acquittal of Saint Athanasius, that man.” This concern was undertaken by the bishops assembled at Sardica, who immediately informed the emperors by letter of what they had done; later, as Theodoret testifies, Book II, chapter 8, Constans sent two selected delegates among them to his brother Constantius with letters. Is this what is being referred to here? Yet there is also some suspicion that these words about actions and letters of the Arians, alien to ecclesiastical character and episcopal clemency, are spoken ironically.]

[Note: [Col. 0561D] The printed editions read *continence*; the manuscripts correct this to *conscience*.]

[Note: [Col. 0561D] This pitiable spectacle was displayed by Sebastian when George invaded the see of Alexandria: after a pyre had been kindled, as Theodoret recounts in Book II, chapter 14, he brought the virgins to it and, having shamefully stripped them, scourged them. But the letter of the Synod of Sardica, Fragment II, section 3, notes that the Arians had earlier committed a like outrage.]

[Note: [Col. 0561D] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “their own crime.”]

[Note: [Col. 0561D–0562C] Several manuscripts read, “the compliance of the people.” Then the printed editions read, “nor could they compel by right”; but all manuscripts read, “nor by a right of compelling,” preceded by a word found only in the Chartres manuscript. We understand the sentence as though it read: “nor even thus are they ashamed . . . that they were unable to extort the connivance of the people even by a right of compulsion.” Here the “right of compelling” denotes force applied, in approximately the sense in which Book IX *On the Trinity*, section 58, says: “The fury of heretics compels us, by a certain right of necessary confession, toward the impiety of this interpretation.” Hilary also praises, in Fragment II, section 24, the proceedings of the Synod of Sardica, where it is shown that every accusation against Athanasius had been fabricated by Arian persecution, and that force had been applied to God’s people to make them pass into connivance with the pestilence of deadly doctrine.]

7. Judicial procedure was not observed in the case of Athanasius.—If these matters, produced from old documents, were instructing the age in which we live, one would, I think, have to hesitate over affairs of such importance. And when the accused man was demanded to be condemned by any others whatsoever, inquiry would be made into the trustworthiness of the letters, the lives of the judges, the credibility of the accusers, and the character and actions of the man himself. For his acquittal, joined to the condemnation of the Arians, would carry weight; and it would be exceedingly dangerous to overthrow a judgment concerning both guilt and innocence without undertaking a fresh inquiry. The whole authority of antiquity, together with the doctrine of faith, would stand by him in his defence.

But when those very persons who were then condemned as Arian heretics agitate the matter, throw everything into confusion, corrupt all by power and ambition, and Athanasius, if he was guilty, can still be guilty: let witnesses speak; let judges see; let the doctrine of faith shine forth through evangelical and apostolic precepts. What dullness of understanding is this? What sluggishness of heart? What forgetfulness of hope? What love of crimes? What hatred of truth? They turn the love of God into favour for the condemned.

[Note: [Col. 0562D] The manuscripts, except the Chartres manuscript, read “not suspect.” Just before, we would prefer, “both of guilt and of innocence.” Athanasius was judged guilty before the Council of Sardica; at that council he was declared innocent, and the condemnation of the Arians was joined to his acquittal.]

[Note: [Col. 0562D] Thus the Vatican Basilica manuscript. Others read, “what death of crimes?” Earlier the manuscripts read *obtunsio*, not *obtusio*—“dullness.”]

8. The unjust condemnation of Eusebius of Vercelli.—I now come to what has recently been done, in which even the profession of crime disdained to keep itself concealed in the secrecy of its own artifice. Eusebius, bishop of Vercelli, is a man who has served God throughout his whole life. After the Synod of Arles, when Bishop Paulinus had opposed so great crimes of these men at Arles in 353, Eusebius was ordered to come to Milan in 355. The synagogue of malicious men having already assembled there, he was forbidden for ten days to enter the church while their perverse malice spent itself against so holy a man. Then, after all plans had festered, he was summoned when they pleased.

He came with the Roman clerics, Hilary the deacon and Pancratius, and with Lucifer, bishop of Sardinia. Summoned to subscribe against Athanasius, he said that the priestly faith ought first to be established, since he knew that some of those present were polluted by heretical taint. He placed before them the faith set forth at Nicaea, which we have mentioned above, promising that he would do everything they required if they would put their profession of faith in writing. Dionysius, bishop of Milan, first took the document. When he began to write his profession, Valens violently snatched pen and paper from his hands, crying that it could not be allowed for anything of that kind to be done. After much outcry, the affair was brought before the awareness of the people. A heavy grief arose among all: the faith was assailed by bishops. Therefore, fearing the judgment of the people, they passed from the Lord’s house to the palace. The sentence which they wrote against Eusebius long before they entered the church speaks for itself concerning them.

[Note: [Col. 0562D] The manuscripts read “and in secrecy.”]

[Note: [Col. 0562D] The manuscripts read, “their perversely malicious malice consumes itself.” The printed editions read “lulled,” whereas we restore “festering” from the Vatican Basilica manuscript. Thus, in the *Book on the Synods*, section 63, where older manuscripts read “the doctrine of festering impiety,” more recent ones read “of lulled impiety.”]

[Note: [Col. 0562D] The manuscript of St. Peter’s, together with other manuscripts, reads, “summoned to subscribe against Athanasius.”]

[Note: [Col. 0562D] The portion in which this mention occurred is missing.]

[Note: [Col. 0562D] The printed editions read “if, for a profession of faith”; corrected from the manuscripts, in which “they should write” amounts to “they should subscribe.”]

[Note: [Col. 0563A] The manuscripts unanimously read “before they entered.” Then only the Vatican Basilica manuscript reads “the sentence itself speaks concerning them,” omitting *of himself*.]

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 0563]

541–542 **NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING LITTLE BOOK ADDRESSED TO CONSTANTIUS**

As Jerome testifies, while Hilary was staying at Constantinople, he himself delivered a little book to Constantius. For he had followed the delegates of the Synod of Seleucia there and, to use the words of Sulpicius Severus, when he perceived the faith to be in its utmost peril, he sought an audience with the emperor in order to dispute concerning the faith in his presence. That this applies most especially to the present little book is evident even from the title prefixed in all the manuscripts. It was offered during the famous controversy, while some contended that the term *substance* (*substantia*) should be retained and others that it should be rejected; during the divided synod—that is, the Council of Constantinople—which was torn into various parties no less by questions of faith than by private quarrels. It was therefore offered at the beginning of 360, when that synod was held.

Accordingly, both Ferrandus the deacon, in his letter to Pelagius and Anatolius, section 2, and the very ancient exemplar of the Vatican Basilica call it the second book addressed to Constantius, not because it is connected with the preceding work, but because it is later in time. We leave others to admire the incredible vigilance, courage, prudence, and faith of this most holy bishop: though an exile and alone, with the heretics armed by imperial power, he did not fear to oppose them in the imperial city itself, indeed he was able to strike fear into them. For he did not oppose the heretics in a futile endeavour. Although he did not obtain what he sought in this little book, he certainly convicted them of their weakness. Thus, even by this manifestation of his spirit, he gained credit with all men, so that when shortly afterward he was to write more severe things against Constantius and declare that he was impelled thereto by no impatience and by no human passions, he would be believed. Though this book seemed slight to Erasmus, nothing whatever is to be desired in it. For the laborious and thorough work which Erasmus observes Hilary to promise but not perform does not concern this little book, but the public disputation on the faith, authority for which is sought in this book.

**Synopsis.**—At its beginning Hilary confesses that he is in exile and asks that Saturninus, being present, be brought to confess the false acts which he committed in that affair. Then, forgetting his own concerns, he lays before the emperor, desirous of knowing the faith, the corruption of evangelical faith which has arisen from its frequent alteration; and accordingly urges a return to the baptismal faith. He next praises the emperor’s zeal in desiring faith only according to what is written. Yet he warns him that there is no heretic who does not confirm his inventions from the Scriptures. Finally, promising to say nothing except from the Scriptures, nothing except for peace between East and West, and nothing except with honour due to the empire and the emperor’s faith, he offers in advance a kind of pledge of his forthcoming discourse.

[Col. 0563]

(Written in 360.) 543–544 **BOOK TWO OF SAINT HILARY ADDRESSED TO THE EMPEROR CONSTANTIUS AUGUSTUS, WHICH HE HIMSELF DELIVERED TO HIM AT CONSTANTINOPLE.** (C)

[Col. 0563D]

1. Hilary in the emperor’s presence.—I am not unaware, most pious emperor, that matters which are brought before the public hearing of conscience concerning certain affairs are accustomed, according to the rank of those who speak, to be thought either weighty or slight: because, amid divergent opinions, contempt for or favour toward a man sways an uncertain judgment toward a particular understanding. But in speaking before you about a divine matter in a devout manner, I have no fear arising from ordinary custom. For since you are good and religious, your religious judgment will not, in the opinion of prudent persons, judge what it hears by the defect of the speaker, but whether the things it hears are religious. And because God has granted me this opportunity of appearing before you, the duty of my conscience has not failed even in this matter: namely, lest some unworthiness in the one speaking with you should offend you in the discourse concerning religion which I hold before you.

[Note: [Col. 0563D] The Vatican Basilica manuscript reads, “concerning most matters, concerning certain ones.” Perhaps: “by most persons, concerning certain matters.”]

[Note: [Col. 0563D–0564D] The manuscripts read, “while, amid such great opinions”; then “moves,” not “promotes”; and later, in two manuscripts, “glory” instead of “favour.”]

2. He remains in communion with the Churches of Gaul. He is exiled through faction. He is confident of his innocence.—I am a bishop remaining in communion with all the Gallican churches and bishops, though in exile, and I still distribute the Church’s communion through my presbyters. But I am in exile not because of crime, but because of faction; and I was denounced to you, pious emperor, by impious men through false reports of a synod—not because I was conscious of any crimes. Nor do I lack an unimportant witness to my complaint: my lord, your religious Caesar Julian, who endured in my exile more insult from wicked men than I endured injury. For the letters of your piety are available, and all the falsehoods by which my exile was procured are not hidden.

Saturninus himself—whether the agent or the author of all these proceedings—is within this city. Confident in the condition of my conscience, I shall make clear that you, Augustus, were deceived and that your Caesar was mocked; so that, if I am proved to have done anything unworthy not only of episcopal holiness but even of lay integrity, I shall no longer expect to retain the priesthood by indulgence, but shall grow old as a layman in penitence.

[Note: [Col. 0564D] The manuscripts read “of all the Churches of Gaul.”]

[Note: [Col. 0565C] The Vatican Basilica manuscript reads “reported.” From what follows it is inferred that Julian either was present at Béziers, or was not far away, when Hilary was sent into exile from there. Moreover, as is clear from Ammianus, Book XVI, Julian, created Caesar at the end of 355, immediately withdrew to Vienne in Gaul and remained there until he moved to Autun, which he reached on 24 June.]

[Note: [Col. 0565C–D] Thus three manuscripts. Others, with the printed editions, read “truly, who.” Here Hilary indicates that, though punished with exile because of hatred for his faith, he was nevertheless exiled under another pretext—as if, that is, he had done what he himself acknowledges to be unworthy not merely of a bishop’s holiness but even of a layman’s integrity. It was easy for enemies of truth to accuse before the emperor of restlessness and readiness for sedition a man against whom such a suspicion had already been raised in 355, as we saw in the preceding book, section 3.]

### 3. He asks to be heard with the author of his exile present. The purpose of this tract.

But now, most gracious Emperor, I leave these matters to your decision: to determine how far and in what manner you command me to speak, while I proceed with those things which at this time must especially be addressed with you. For the present, you will grant this instruction concerning the case: that I may bring into open acknowledgment of the falsehoods which he has committed the man through whose agency I am in exile, when he is present. But I shall say nothing concerning him unless you command it.

[Note: Col. 0565D. Supply, “I speak.” In the printed editions, “because I fear,” with *mihi* omitted; and shortly afterward, instead of “but I have concern because of hope,” the corrupt reading was, “but why is there cause for despair?”]

But now I speak because I fear for the peril of the world, for the guilt of my silence, and for the judgment of God; while I have concern for hope, for life, for immortality—not so much my own as yours and that of all men. [Col. 0565C] Since this is a concern common to me with very many, this expectation of a common hope proceeds from me.

### 4. Constantius desires to hear the faith from bishops, yet does not hear it. The faith sworn in baptism. A faith repeatedly made new, and therefore no faith.

Recall the faith which long ago, excellent and most religious Emperor, you desire to hear from bishops, yet do not hear. For while those from whom it is demanded write their own doctrines, [Note: Col. 0565D. In all manuscripts: “and do not preach those things which are God’s.”] and do not preach what belongs to God, [Col. 0566A] they have carried round the world an everlasting cycle of error and of contention forever returning upon itself.

For it was fitting, in the modesty proper to human weakness, that the whole mystery of divine knowledge should be confined within those limits of one’s own conscience by which one has believed; and that, after the faith confessed and sworn in baptism in the name of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, one should neither doubt nor innovate anything else. But the presumption, [Note: Col. 0565D. Vatican Basilica manuscript: “or capability.” Perhaps, “or foolishness.”] facility, or error of certain persons has in part deceitfully professed, and in part boldly departed from, the unchangeable constitution of apostolic doctrine; while, in the confession of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, it evades the truth of the natural meaning, [Note: Col. 0565D. Vatican Basilica manuscript: “and not that it might remain.” Others: “lest anything should remain.”] lest that which must be confessed in the sacrament of regeneration should remain in the understanding.

For this reason, in the consciences of some, [Col. 0566B] neither is the Father Father, nor the Son Son, nor the Holy Spirit Holy Spirit. Under the seemingly plausible pretext of this necessity, [Note: Col. 0565D. The words “of necessity, as it were,” are lacking in six manuscripts. It seems one should read, “under the not implausible pretext of this necessity,” or, with the Remigian manuscript, “under the plausible pretext of this necessity.”] the practice thereafter arose of writing and revising the faith. Once it had begun to frame new formulations rather than retain what it had received, it neither defended what had grown old nor established what it had innovated. Thus faith became a matter of times rather than of Gospels: it is drafted according to the years, and is not held according to the confession of baptism.

It is exceedingly dangerous and indeed pitiable for us that there should now be as many faiths as wills, as many doctrines as dispositions, and as many causes of blasphemy springing up as there are faults: while faiths are either written as we wish, or understood as we do not wish. [Note: Col. 0566C. Thus the manuscripts. But the printed editions have, “as we wish.” Thus, as Jerome reports in his *Dialogue against the Luciferians*, after the Council of Rimini the whole world groaned and was astonished to find itself Arian: while, although holding the right view, it was understood in a sense it did not intend.] And though, according to one God [Col. 0566C] and one Lord and one baptism, faith also is one, [Note: Col. 0566C. Five manuscripts add here, “and one faith,” which is superfluous. For this is the point: just as the Apostle, Eph. 4:5, proclaims one God, one Lord, and one baptism, so one faith is also proclaimed. Hilary presses the same point from this apostolic passage at the beginning of Book XI of *On the Trinity* and in *To Constantius*, §24: among heretics, faith does not exist.

Col. 0566D. Leipzig and Paris editions: “we fall away.” Other books more suitably read, “we go beyond,” namely, from the one faith to many.] we go beyond that faith which alone exists; and, as they become many, they have begun to be such that none exists.

### 5. Whence so many faiths are written. The faith altered four times.

For we are mutually conscious that, since the synodical assembly at Nicaea, nothing else is being done but the writing of faiths. While there is conflict over words, while there is debate about novelties, while ambiguous expressions give occasion [Note: Col. 0566D. Supply, “for disputing, contradicting, and suspecting one another maliciously.”] for dispute; while there is complaint about authors, [Note: Col. 0566D. Ferrandus the deacon, having transferred these words into his letter to Pelagius and Anatolius, later warns that they are not his own but belong to blessed Hilary in the second book which he wrote to Constantius. In that letter of Ferrandus, Peter Francis Chifflet, on the evidence of the Jura and Auvergne manuscripts, printed “while there is complaint about hearers” in place of “while there is complaint about authors.” He thinks that this reading makes Hilary’s meaning plain, as though he were saying: while there are no lack of people who complain that they have sung to the deaf, and therefore claim for themselves things which were not even rightly heard by their opponents, much less understood. Yet, since all our manuscripts agree with the editions of Hilary, it is not safe to depart from the source itself for a streamlet. Immediately before Hilary wrote this, there had been a complaint about the author of blasphemies which the delegates of the Synod of Seleucia attributed to Eudoxius, while Eudoxius shifted them onto Aetius.] while there is contention over factions, while [Note: Col. 0567C. In Ferrandus, “about agreement.” In the Vatican Basilica manuscript, “about the assembly.”] there is difficulty in agreement, while one has begun to anathematize another, then scarcely anyone belongs to Christ. For we are tossed about by the uncertain wind of doctrines: either, while we teach, we disturb; or, while we are taught, we err.

And what change in itself does the faith of the past year already contain? First, the faith which decrees that *homoousion* be kept silent; then another, which decrees and proclaims *homoousion*; [Note: Col. 0567C. There is no confession of the Arian faith which decrees and proclaims *homoousion*. This seems foreign to Hilary’s purpose, as though he said that *homoousion* was first rejected at the Council of Rimini by those who stood with Valens and Ursacius, and then approved and proclaimed by the Catholics. Therefore here, and perhaps earlier as well, *homoiousion* seems to require substitution for *homoousion*.

Col. 0567D. Nor is it sufficiently clear which confessions of faith Hilary here notes. Some think that the first means the Sirmian confession issued 11 days before the Kalends of June in 358; then the Antiochene confession of 341, subscribed at Seleucia; next the Riminian; and finally that published at Seleucia by the Acacians. But the faith issued at Sirmium does not seem different from that issued at Rimini. Moreover, it is scarcely credible that Hilary would offer the creed of the Dedication, subscribed again, as an instance of a new alteration. Nor is *homoousion* or *homoiousion* proclaimed in it. But if the words “of the past year” are taken not as strictly as they sound, but somewhat more broadly, the first may be understood as the Sirmian creed issued under the names of Hosius and Potamius, which decrees silence not only about *homoousion* but also about *homoiousion*; the second as the creed of Ancyra, which decrees and proclaims *homoiousion* in Definitions 3, 4, 5, and so forth; the third as that read at Rimini and afterward at Nicaea in Thrace, in which the Fathers’ use of *ousia* is excused by indulgence (Athanasius, *On the Synods*, p. 875); and, lastly, as that published at Seleucia by Acacius (Athanasius, p. 904), which no longer excuses the term “substance,” but simply and absolutely condemns it.] then a third, which excuses, by indulgence, the Fathers’ simple use of *ousia*; and a fourth and final one, which does not excuse but condemns it.

And to what point, finally, have we come? To this: that neither among us nor among any before us does anything holy and inviolable henceforth remain. As for the likeness of God the Son [Col. 0567B] to God the Father: if this is the wretched faith of our time—that he is not like either wholly or only in part—then, as distinguished judges of heavenly mysteries and investigators of invisible secrets, we malign God by our professions of faith. [Note: Col. 0568C. If the particle *si* is restored here from the Vatican Basilica codex, the sense becomes: if we now think and believe concerning the likeness of the Son to the Father that the Son is like the Father not wholly but only in part, we malign God by professions concerning the faith—or concerning God himself. Admirable judges, indeed, etc.]

We determine annual and monthly faiths concerning God; we repent of our decrees; having repented, we defend them; having defended them, we anathematize them. We condemn what is another’s in our own formularies, or what is ours in those of others; and, biting one another, we are now consumed by one another (Gal. 5:15). [Note: Col. 0568C. The Basel, Erasmus, and Migne editions read, “dying by a change of manners.” The manuscripts read, “dying, to die mutually.” Perhaps, “biting one another.”]

### 6. The evangelical faith is corrupted.

Then faith is sought—as though there were no faith. Faith must be written (see *On the Synods*, §63)—as though it were not in the heart. Having been regenerated through faith, we are now instructed in faith—as though that regeneration were without faith. After baptism we learn Christ, [Col. 0567C] as though any baptism could exist without [Col. 0568A] faith in Christ. We correct matters, as though forgiveness lay open for having sinned against the Holy Spirit. [Note: Col. 0568C. Vatican Basilica exemplar: “in the Holy Spirit”; such a change of case is frequent in ancient books. For understanding this passage, it will help to recall from *On Matthew*, ch. XII, §17, that for Hilary the sin against the Holy Spirit is to deny that Christ is God and to take away from him the substance of the Father’s Spirit dwelling in him. He says similar things in ch. V, §15. In agreement with these are the words of Athanasius, vol. I, p. 237: “Therefore Christ himself calls the divinity of the Word the Holy Spirit”; and, shortly afterward: “Just as others, who stumble against the Holy Spirit and so utter blasphemies against Christ’s divinity,” etc.]

But this is the chief and enduring cause of that very impiety: [Note: Col. 0568D. Hilary calls the Apostles’ Creed the apostolic faith. The Arians issued confessions of faith much more extensive than it, yet did not retain the evangelical faith—that is, the faith stated in the words of baptism. That this is the intended meaning is made clearer by the final words of this book.] although we set forth the apostolic faith sevenfold, we ourselves refuse to confess the evangelical faith. We defend our impieties before the people with a flood of words, and by the vanity of grandiloquence we deceive the ears of the simple with misleading language. We avoid believing concerning the Lord Christ what he taught concerning himself should be believed; under the attractive name of peace we steal into unity of unbelief; under the pretext of rejecting novelties we ourselves again rebel against God by novel words; under the title of Scripture we falsely assert things not written. We are wandering, prodigal, impious: changing what endures, losing what we received, and presumptuously undertaking irreligious things.

### 7. One must return to the faith confessed in baptism.

Just as, in winter upon a stormy sea, the safest course for sailors is, when shipwreck rages, to return to the harbor from which they put out; or as it is fitting for heedless young men, when, in maintaining their own household, they have transgressed the morals of their father’s discipline and used their liberty extravagantly, that under the very fear of losing their inheritance their sole necessary and safe recourse should be to their father’s way of life: so, amid these shipwrecks of faith, now that the inheritance of our heavenly patrimony has almost been ruined, it is safest for us to retain and understand the first and only evangelical faith, confessed in baptism, and not alter that which alone I have received and heard to be rightly believed.

[Note: Col. 0568D. Four manuscripts read, “their own soil.” Vatican Basilica manuscript: “in maintaining the house of their fatherly affection, transgressors of their own discipline, lavish,” etc.; corruptly.]

This is not to say that what is contained in the synod of our fathers must be condemned as written irreligiously [Col. 0568C] and impiously; but because, [Col. 0569A] through human rashness, it is appropriated for contradiction, so that under the name of novelty the Gospel might be denied, [Note: Col. 0569C. The printed editions read, “without danger”; on the authority of the Vatican Basilica manuscript we restore, “so that it may dangerously be renewed, as though by correction.”] and so that it may dangerously be renewed as though by correction. Whatever is corrected always advances, so that, while every correction displeases, correction following correction condemns every correction—as though, whatever it may be, it were no longer a correction of correction, but had begun to be a condemnation.

### 8. Hilary asks for a hearing and will show the faith from the Scriptures.

How greatly I now truly admire, Lord Constantius Augustus, [Note: Col. 0569C. In the manuscripts: “but you.”] your blessed and religious purpose in desiring only a faith according to what is written; and rightly indeed in hastening to the very words of the only-begotten God, so that a heart capable of imperial care may also be filled with awareness of divine utterances. Whoever rejects this is antichrist, and whoever feigns it is anathema.

But through this sincere hearing granted by your condescension I ask one thing: that, in the presence of the synod [at Constantinople] now disputing about the faith, you may deign to hear from me a few words from the evangelical Scriptures, and that I may speak with you in the words of my Lord Jesus Christ, whose exile or priest I am.

For earthen vessels possess treasures that are not ignoble; the weaker members of the body are more worthy of reverence; and among us unlearned fishermen have now spoken concerning God. God, according to the prophet, looks upon the humble man who trembles at his words (Isa. 66:2). You seek faith, Emperor: hear it, not from new little sheets, but from the books of God. Know that it can be bestowed even in the West, from which those who come will recline in the kingdom of God with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (Matt. 8:11). Remember that it is not a matter for philosophical inquiry, but the teaching of the Gospel. [Note: Col. 0569C. The printed editions read, “not to be a matter for philosophical inquiry, but of evangelical teaching”; corrected from the Vatican Basilica manuscript. In the following words Hilary’s faith is no less apparent than his charity—a charity such as Augustine observes in the martyrs, *On Psalm 65*, §21: “For those who then preached Christ preached him not for themselves, to whom he was then known, but for us who were yet to come, or for those to whom he was then unknown,” etc.]

I ask a hearing not so much for myself as for you and for the churches of God. For I possess the faith within myself; I have no need of anything external. What I received I hold, and I do not alter what belongs to God.

### 9. Heretics draw the Scriptures to their own side.

Yet remember that there is no heretic who does not now falsely claim to preach according to the Scriptures those things by which he blasphemes. [Col. 0570A] Thus Marcellus, when he reads “the Word of God,” does not know it. Thus Photinus, when he speaks of “the man Jesus Christ,” does not know him. Thus Sabellius, because he does not understand “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), is without God the Father and without God the Son. Thus Montanus, through his mad women, [Note: Col. 0569D. That is, Prisca and Maximilla, whom Jerome, *Epistle* 54 to Marcella, in imitation of Hilary, calls mad women. See Tertullian, *On Monogamy*, §2, and *Against Praxeas*, §1.] maintains another Paraclete. Thus Manichaeus and Marcion hate the law, because “the letter kills” (2 Cor. 3:6) and the prince of this world is the devil.

All speak without the understanding of Scripture, [Note: Col. 0569D. The word “Scripture,” omitted in the printed editions, is restored with the help of the manuscripts. Jerome imitates and elucidates Hilary’s following statement at the end of his *Dialogue against the Luciferians*, saying that the Scriptures consist not in reading but in understanding; otherwise, if we follow the letter, we too can devise a new doctrine for ourselves. “For all heretics,” Augustine says, *Epistle* 120 to Consentiu​​s, §13, “who receive them as authoritative, seem to themselves to follow the Scriptures, while in fact they follow their own errors; and thus they are heretics not because they despise them, but because they do not understand them.” And, as Athanasius observes, *Oration II against the Arians*, p. 313, the deviser and inventor of heresies, the devil, uses the words of Scripture out of fear of his own foul odor, so that, concealed under them and having sprinkled in his poison, he may deceive the simple.] and make a pretense of faith without faith. For Scripture does not consist in reading but in understanding, nor in transgression but in charity.

### 10. The manner of the discourse for which he asks leave.

Hear, I beseech you, what has been written concerning Christ, lest under those writings things that have not been written [Col. 0570B] be preached. Lend your ears to what I am about to say from the books; lift your faith toward God. Hear what tends to faith, unity, and eternity. I shall speak with you with honor for your imperial rank and your faith, all things tending to the peace of East and West, [Note: Col. 0570D. Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read, “profitable.” Then “under public awareness,” that is, publicly and openly. Ambrose indicates that it was the Church’s custom for a bishop to dispute concerning the faith in church and before the people. When commanded to come to the emperor’s consistory, he writes (*Epistle* 21, §17): “I would have come, Emperor, to the consistory of your clemency, to present these things there, if bishops or people had allowed me, saying that matters of faith ought to be treated in church before the people.” And in the *Sermon on the Surrender of the Basilicas*, §3, vol. II, p. 864: “I would willingly go to the emperor’s palace, if that were fitting to a priest’s office—if I ought to contend in the palace rather than in the church…. Who would deny that a case concerning faith should be handled in the church?”] before the public, before a divided synod, amid notorious controversy.

### 11. A pledge of his future discourse.

[Note: Col. 0570D. The ancient editions and the manuscripts read “I omit,” which Lipsius has not badly corrected.] Meanwhile, I offer you a pledge of my future discourse. I shall defend nothing that gives scandal or lies outside the Gospel. Rather, you shall understand that, in the mystery of the one true God and Jesus Christ whom he sent (John 17:3), I preach one God the Father, from whom are all things, and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things (1 Cor. 8:6): born from God, who is before eternal ages (2 Tim. 1:9), and who in the beginning was the Word, God with God (John 1:1); who is the image of the invisible God (Col. 1:15), in whom all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily (Col. 2:9); who, though he was in the form of God, humbled himself for our salvation and took the form of a servant, conceived of the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin; becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross (Phil. 2:6); and who, after his resurrection from death, now sits in the heavenly places (Eph. 1:20), will come as judge of the living and the dead (Acts 10:42), and [Col. 0571A] as king of all eternal ages.

For he is the only-begotten God (John 1:18), true God, great God, and God over all (Rom. 9:5); and every tongue shall confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father (Phil. 2:11). This I have so believed in the Holy Spirit [Col. 0572A] that I cannot be taught anything beyond this faith concerning the Lord Jesus Christ—not thereby taking away the religious character of the faith of the fathers, but, in accordance with the creed of my regeneration and the knowledge of evangelical doctrine, not dissenting from it in these respects.

# [BOOK AGAINST CONSTANTIUS]

[Col. 0571]

# PRELIMINARY DISSERTATION ON THE BOOK AGAINST CONSTANTIUS

### I. This book seems to conflict with others.

The glory for steadfast and moderate character which this most holy confessor of Christ gained for himself in his other books, he has, in the judgment of many, almost wholly lost by this one. So deeply rooted in all minds is reverence for kings that they think no reasonable cause existed for his attacking Constantius so vehemently. Some have said that he was driven to it by impatience under his prolonged exile; very many others, by the innate disposition of a more ardent and severe temperament.

Others have even thought that in this little work he is inconsistent with himself, and speaks differently concerning the Orientals, their confessions of faith, and the term *homoiousion* than he had written in the book *On the Synods*—as though here he openly rejects and condemns what there he either praised or excused. Perhaps there will one day be someone who, having asserted that the two works differ not only in manner—for all the words of the book *On the Synods* breathe the utmost humanity—but also in opinion, will seek for another author of this work than Hilary. [Col. 0571C] He may think he can confirm this opinion because, in his earlier treatises to Constantius, Hilary bears himself very differently toward the same Emperor.

For in them he conforms to the pious convention which, as he himself teaches in *On Psalm* 13, §1, requires one who interprets a king’s words and conveys his commands to the ears of the people diligently and cautiously to satisfy the king’s dignity through reverence for his office, so that everything may be both reread and heard with honor and religious regard. And since he approves, not only by custom but also because every kingdom is from God, that the highest reverence is owed to a king (*Fragment* I, §5), and since his discourse accords everywhere with this doctrine, one will be reluctant to persuade oneself that he was then suddenly changed.

### II. It is reconciled with the book *On the Synods*.

Yet no one will ever succeed in taking from Hilary a tract which Jerome enumerates among his works, which Facundus of Hermiane in his book *Against Mocianus*, the Vatican Basilica codex written nearly twelve centuries ago, and all the manuscripts unanimously attribute to him. Nor is there any conflict between it and the book *On the Synods*: what in one is declared less explicitly and in fewer words is set out more fully and clearly in the other.

Certainly, in both works Hilary, unchanged in mind and judgment though circumstances had changed, adopts a different method of argument. When he hoped to bring the Orientals back to the true faith and to the bosom of the Catholic Church, he both passed over and excused their errors, as far as truth could remain unharmed. [Col. 0572A] But when his hope had been disappointed, and he feared that errors he had passed over would grow to the ruin of faith, he openly exposed and condemned those same errors.

Yet, just as in the book *On the Synods* his desire to reconcile the Eastern churches did not carry him so far that he passed over what in them deserved rebuke, so in this tract he restrains himself in such a way that, although he rejects all their professions of faith, he nevertheless does not deny that they may have lacked faults. Clear evidence is found in §24: “Even if it should be affirmed that no faults lie hidden in all these confessions, yet there would be no cause for religious purpose in them, because the devising of evil consists in changing what is good.” Again, although in §23 he affirms that those grounded in the Nicene faith have no need of the Antiochene, Sardican, or Sirmian creed, he nevertheless freely grants that these contain certain expressions most hostile to Arians, by professing which Constantius falsely represented himself to the Westerners as pious.

Nor does he utterly reject *homoiousion*, even though in §25 he calls it superfluous for faith; rather, he does so on precisely the same principle on which he approves it in the book *On the Synods*, §22, where he says: “For my part, likeness is holy, lest occasion be given to unity.” Finally, who would think his attitude toward the Orientals who defended *homoiousion* was otherwise, when one hears him more than once reproaching Constantius for using force upon them to abandon their former faith? In §12 he certainly indicates, not obscurely, that their faith did not wholly meet with his approval; yet he testifies there that some of them put forward certain points reverently in words—moderate in rebuke no less than in praise.

### III. Hilary’s native gentleness is defended by ancient testimony.

We do not judge that more needs to be said to overthrow the common opinion that Hilary in this book retracted and reversed what he had argued in the book *On the Synods* for the sake of the Orientals. Perhaps it will be harder to satisfy those who infer from this book that he had a harsh disposition, or at least that in it he forgot his inborn goodness and gentleness.

Against them we first set Rufinus (*Ecclesiastical History*, I.31), who testifies in express terms not only that Hilary was gentle and calm by nature, but confirms his words by Hilary’s deeds. Certainly there will rarely be a person with whom so notable a testimony has little force; but there ought to be no one unmoved by the ancient custom of the Church, which once sang of Hilary’s gentleness of character in the very heart of its most sacred sacrifice—namely, in the Preface [Col. 0573A] before the Canon.

### IV. Constantius’s disguised impiety and wicked persecution.

Those whom this book has led to another opinion of him should first consider when it was written. They will find that it was written after the Council of Seleucia, at the very time when, as Sozomen testifies (*Ecclesiastical History*, IV.25), a kind of persecution seized all churches everywhere, like that which had formerly raged under pagan emperors. Then, once they see that Constantius was the principal author of this persecution, let them consider its nature.

Certainly, by trying to extinguish the faith more through deceit than open force, he slew so many more souls as he spared bodies more sparingly. Though a wolf, he wished to be called and seen as a sheep. Nor did he lack means to deceive, using words that falsely wore the appearance of truth, putting forward peace and unity, and amid threats and punishments boasting that he was upholding the decrees of councils. This persecution was all the more dangerous because Constantius used bishops themselves as his agents, in order to draw all people into the heresy that he embraced. Thus Sozomen, continuing his discussion of this very persecution, truly said: “And though this persecution seemed milder in respect of tortures, wise men considered it harsher because of its disgrace. For both he who persecuted and he who endured persecution were of the Church.”

### V. Praise produced by the flattery of pseudo-bishops.

[Col. 0573C] These pseudo-bishops, as is the way with those who attempt to win assent to an unjust cause, endeavored by every means possible to create a false impression through Constantius’s name, authority, virtues—whether real or invented—and every other resource. One, therefore, so far as may be inferred from this book, extolled Constantius’s magnificence in building and adorning churches; another praised his reverence for bishops. One set before all his zeal in suppressing heresies; another, his diligence in convening synods.

Constantius himself also—as Lucifer relates more fully—claimed for himself glory not only for piety but for doctrine. He composed a creed for bishops to subscribe, eagerly listening to flatterers who, when they wrote in response to the bishops who had fallen at Rimini, said: “Illuminated by the writings of your piety, we have rendered and render the greatest thanks to God because you have blessed us, making known to us those things which, after consideration by your piety, we ought to do” (*Fragment* IX, §1).

Finally, after commending Constantius’s kindness, religion, and piety, very many inferred that God would not have allowed so pious and religious a king to uphold an incorrect faith; and that the incredible prosperity of his reign was in fact no slight mark and fruit of that excellent faith. We pass over many other things which at that time prevented peoples, terrified by edicts, threats, and punishments, from discerning Constantius’s disguised unbelief.

### VI. Whether a pastor ought to have concealed it.

Here the question arises whether Hilary was permitted to remove the cloak—that is, whether it was permissible for a pastor to expose the hidden wolf, for a bishop to make known to Christians an enemy lying in wait against the faith. Certainly, since Constantius, as has been shown, displayed a sheep’s skin while having a wolf’s mind, a bishop devoted to the Church seemed necessarily bound to do one of two things: either persuade Constantius himself to lay aside his wolfish mind, or warn the people not to let themselves be deceived by his sheep’s skin.

Hilary first attempted the former, which was more fitting for a moderate man. In a petition he most respectfully requested an audience from the emperor, and promised that, if he were granted an opportunity to dispute concerning the faith in his presence, he would speak with equal reverence. But he did not obtain what he most wished: to provide for the wavering Church without injury to the imperial name. [Col. 0574B] The other course therefore remained: since he could neither repel nor change the wolf, he should at least try to fortify the sheep against his snares. This is the entire purpose of the present book. For, as we shall show below, it was directed not against Constantius in order to assail him, but for the instruction and exhortation of Catholics.

### VII. The reason for the forceful discourse.

“But the language is too vehement?” Perhaps language without warmth would have achieved nothing when persecution was heating up; nor would it have been heard without a cry by those whose minds had already been disturbed by the immense noise of Constantius’s edicts.

### VIII. In what sense Hilary calls Constantius antichrist.

If, however, it is vehement, it certainly ought not to be abusive. Nor do they think it consistent with a moderate temperament that they read Constantius more than once called antichrist in it. Pious ears recoil from this name, thinking of everything that can be called detestable or imagined in the mind. But Hilary neither called nor regarded Constantius as antichrist in that common sense. He did so only in the sense in which John wrote: “Antichrist has already come, and now many antichrists have arisen” (1 John 2:18). Explaining this shortly afterward, he says: “He is antichrist who denies the Father and the Son” (ibid., 2:22).

For, as noted in *Against Auxentius*, §2, the defining quality of the name “antichrist” is opposition to Christ. And who could deny that Constantius was opposed to Christ? Hilary also indicates clearly enough that he calls him antichrist in no other sense in these words of §7: “You falsely claim to be Christian; you are a new enemy of Christ; you precede antichrist and perform the mysteries of his hidden counsels.” Certainly, he who precedes antichrist must be someone other than antichrist.

### IX. He seeks not so much to attack Constantius as to protect the Church.

Thus, viewing Constantius as an enemy and himself as a soldier of Christ, Hilary thought it unworthy not to aid his fellow soldiers when he foresaw that Constantius could harm more people by remaining concealed. Yet he did so in such a way that he restrained himself from censuring Constantius’s other faults. For, wishing as far as he could to take nothing from the majesty of Caesar, while he strove above all to preserve whole and inviolate Christ’s right and honor in his divinity, he was indignant only at what he saw taken away from Christ’s right.

Finally, since he regarded Constantius as no less hostile to Christ’s Church than Decius, Maximian, and other tyrants of old, it seemed worthy of his courage, inflamed with hope of martyrdom, to provide for the Church in every way he could.

### X. No conclusion contrary to his native gentleness may be drawn from his forceful language.

If anyone should again maintain that he did this by excessively forceful language, he will indeed recall what Gregory Nazianzen said concerning holy men living in that age (*Oration* XXI, §33): “Although otherwise peaceful and moderate, they cannot endure to be mild and yielding in this matter when God’s cause is betrayed by silence and quiet; rather, they are exceedingly warlike, keen and fierce in conflict.” But no fair judge of matters will ever conclude that a man whom both the testimony of antiquity and the actions of his whole life show to have excelled in gentleness of character was incapable of self-control through excessive severity of disposition.

They will believe instead that he was brought to this work by the impulse of the Holy Spirit rather than by a more excited outburst of anger. His spirit, far from being weakened by five years of exile, was thereby proved better and made stronger, as is shown by the rich fruits which shortly afterward flowed into the Church through his work. For who does not know that we owe the reconciliation of nearly the entire West to his wisdom, seasoned by exceptional gentleness of character? He undertook it immediately after this book and at length brought it to a successful conclusion.

For if we listen to Sulpicius: “It was agreed by all that our Gauls were freed from the stain of heresy through the benefit of Hilary alone” (Sulpicius, Book II). And what Sulpicius says of our Gauls, Rufinus (*Ecclesiastical History*, I.31) testifies that Hilary accomplished for Rufinus’s own Italy and for Illyricum, no less by gentleness of character than by doctrine. By the same means he checked the advance of the Luciferian schism, which had arisen from excessive severity and ought not to be restrained except by the contrary disposition of mind.

### XI. Further examples of Hilary’s moderation drawn from this book.

Indeed, Facundus in *Against Mocianus* directs us to look to Hilary as a model of moderation, and proposes for imitation by his opponents—whom he judges to err through excessively ardent zeal—the examples of this virtue which Hilary supplies in this very book. Certainly, Facundus can rightly approve him from that book as a moderate and prudent governor of the Church: because, communion having been denied to two or three supporters of heresy, he determines that the rest should be allowed an opportunity to repent; because he submits this determination to the judgment and approval of the confessors; because he rejects no honorable condition for making peace; because, though exiled by an unjust faction, throughout all his exile he writes nothing notorious or abusive against heretics; because at Seleucia and Constantinople he bears himself so courteously toward all that he grants even the Anomoeans—whom he greatly abhorred—easy access to himself, and listens calmly and quietly to their blasphemies; and finally, because, when he is to employ more forceful language, he takes such care and pains beforehand to show that he is driven to it not by his own cause but by Christ’s.

XII. Conclusion of the Apology.—Such being the case, it is safer devoutly to venerate the exceptional deed of an exceptional man than rashly to criticize it. For if Hilary may be charged with harshness of spirit because of his severe language, then perhaps Stephen too may be accused of excessive bitterness when he inveighs so sharply against the Jews; the prophets likewise will be charged with lack of self-control, since they rebuked the vices of rulers with such freedom; nor will even our Lord himself, the exemplar of gentleness, be spared, and he will seem to have fallen away from the inborn mildness of his heart when he reproved the Pharisees so bitterly and so severely. Rather, what Augustine thought and said concerning Stephen (On Psalm 132, §8)—“Stephen seemed to rage; he raged with his mouth, but in his heart he loved”—let us think and say concerning our Hilary: “Hilary seemed to rage; he raged with his pen, but in his heart he loved.”

[Col. 0576B] XIII. The letter is addressed to Catholics, not to Constantius.—In the Colbert and Martin manuscripts this work is not improperly called a letter, although it is not pleasing that in those same manuscripts it is repeatedly marked as sent to the Emperor Constantius. For the letter must be considered sent to those whom its writer addresses at the beginning, not to those toward whom he later turns his discourse by a figurative mode of speech. Throughout the opening of this work Hilary addresses “Brethren,” to whom he returns also in §12 and following. His address to Constantius, therefore, is only figurative. By that figure he addresses the Easterners at length and copiously in the Book on the Synods, although that work was directed not to them but to the Gallic bishops. We must therefore not agree with Chifflet, who, in his notes on Ferrandus, maintained that this book could indifferently be entitled either *Against Constantius* or *To Constantius*.

XIV. This book was written while Constantius was alive.—In a very ancient codex of the basilica of St. Peter, as also in the Teller manuscript, it bears the title *Book to the Emperor Constantius*; in other manuscripts, *Book against Constantius Augustus*. Erasmus rashly added to the latter title, “now dead,” and yet this was not corrected in subsequent editions. The occasion of his error arose from the words of Jerome, who, in listing Hilary’s works, mentions a book *Against Constantius* written after the latter’s death. Since Jerome mentions only one book of Hilary against Constantius, and since in his twenty-seventh letter to Eustochium he reproduces certain words from the present book, as we have already noted, there is scarcely any doubt that he believed this very work to have been written after Constantius’s death.

[Col. 0576D] Hilary himself, however, expressly testifies in §2 that he wrote it in the fifth year after the exiles of Eusebius, Lucifer, and Dionysius—that is, five years after the Council of Milan of 355, and consequently in 360, one year before Constantius’s death. Nor does there seem to be any doubt that he wrote it while residing at Constantinople, after he had urgently requested, but had failed to obtain, permission publicly to debate the faith; indeed, after he had there already begun the history of the Councils of Seleucia and Rimini. Nevertheless, because of Jerome’s words, we readily agree with those who hold that, though written before Constantius’s death, it was published only after his death—especially since, shortly afterward, when Hilary was permitted to return to the West, he was given a much easier and freer opportunity to accomplish among his own people what he had intended to do through this book.

[Col. 0577A] XV. It is not incomplete, but enlarged by a foreign hand.—Again, all who edited Hilary’s works after Erasmus adopted Erasmus’s opinion that this book was incomplete. On the contrary, it appears to us not only whole and finished, but also considerably enlarged by another hand with extracts from the books *On the Trinity*—perhaps through the agency of those who pieced together the books *On the Unity of the Father and the Son* and *On the Essence of the Father and the Son* from various centos of those same books. This addition is indeed ancient, since it occurs even in the Colbert manuscript, written about six hundred years ago, and in the Martin manuscript, which surpasses it in antiquity, as well as in seven others. Yet it is easily judged not to have come from the author himself, both because it consists of fragments wholly disconnected from one another [Col. 0578A] and because it is entirely absent from the aforementioned codex of St. Peter, by far the oldest of all.

XVI. Synopsis.—This entire work may conveniently be divided into six parts. The first sets forth the reasons for so vehement a discourse. The second sketches the persecution which Constantius stirred up from the Council of Arles to that of Rimini, whether by flatteries and pretence, falsely representing himself as a sheep, or by threats and punishments, acting as a wolf. The third touches upon the proceedings of the Synod of Seleucia. The fourth marks out and refutes the faith of that council, which had defined the Son as like the Father according to the Scriptures, and the saying of Constantius, “I do not wish things not written to be spoken,” demonstrating the equality of the Son and the Father. The fifth portrays the inconsistency in faith of the Arians and of Constantius himself. Finally, the last part—if indeed it may be called a part of this book—which, though composed of Hilary’s words, has nevertheless been attached by a foreign hand, declares that the nature of the Father and the eternal generation of the Son surpass the powers of human understanding.

[Col. 0577]

*(WRITTEN IN THE YEAR 360.)*  
**561–562. ONE BOOK OF SAINT HILARY AGAINST THE EMPEROR CONSTANTIUS. (C, S)**

1. Exhortation to contend for the faith.—It is time to speak, because the time for silence has now passed. Let Christ be awaited, because [Note: [Col. 0577D] In three manuscripts, “has fallen silent” (*obticuit*). More correctly in others, “has gained possession” (*obtinuit*), supply “the empire,” or something similar. The legates of the Roman Church did not shrink from calling Constantius, to his face, the forerunner of Antichrist. “When we, the legates of the blessed Church, pressed you,” Lucifer says to him in Book I *For Athanasius*, “you said that the sect of Arius, which ought to be condemned, was more Catholic; we foretold that you had been the forerunner of Antichrist.”] Antichrist has gained possession. Let shepherds cry aloud, because the hirelings have fled. Let us lay down [Col. 0577C] our lives for the sheep, because thieves have entered and the raging lion prowls about. Let us go forth to martyrdom at these words, because the angel of Satan has transformed himself into an angel of light. Let us enter through the door, because no one goes to the Father except through the Son (John 14:6). Let false prophets be made manifest in their own peace, because those who have been approved will be made manifest amid heresy and schism. Let tribulation be endured, such as has not been from the foundation of the world; but let it be understood that the days are to be shortened for the sake of God’s elect (Matt. 24:22). The prophecy has been fulfilled which says: “The time will come when they will not endure sound teaching, but according to their own desires will heap up teachers for themselves, tickling their ears; and indeed they will turn their hearing away from the truth, but will turn aside to fables” (2 Tim. 4:3). Yet let the promise of him who declares be awaited: “Blessed are you when they revile you and persecute you and say every evil thing against you on account of righteousness. Rejoice and exult, [Col. 0577D] [Col. 0578B] because your reward is abundant in heaven. For thus they persecuted the prophets who were before you” (Matt. 5:11–12). Let us stand before judges and authorities for Christ’s name, because blessed is the one who endures [Col. 0578C] to the end (Matt. 10:22). Let us not fear one who can kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather, let us fear him who can destroy both body and soul in Gehenna (ibid., 28). Nor let us be anxious about ourselves, because the hairs of our head are numbered (ibid., 30). And through the Holy Spirit let us follow truth, lest through the spirit of error we believe a lie. Let us also die with Christ, that with Christ we may reign. For to remain silent longer is a sign of distrust, not a principle of modesty, since there is no less danger in having always kept silent than in never having done so.

2. How Hilary always sought peace in defending the faith; how he maintained moderation toward his opponents.—I, brethren—as all who either hear me or know me through personal acquaintance are witnesses—foreseeing the gravest danger to the faith long beforehand, five years ago, after the exiles of the holy men [Col. 0578D] Paulinus, Eusebius, Lucifer, and Dionysius, [Note: [Col. 0577D] It is established, both from Book I *To Constantius*, §8, and especially from Fragment I, [Col. 0578D] §6, that Paulinus was expelled from his see by the Council of Arles, which ended in 353; Lucifer, Eusebius, and Dionysius, however, were exiled by the Council of Milan in 355. Nor was Athanasius unaware of what had occurred at those two synods. He writes *To the Solitaries*, p. 829: “When the Emperor was at Arles and Milan, he did everything at the exhortation and suggestion of the heretics; or rather, they themselves acted and assailed everyone, equipped with Caesar’s power.” Yet because Athanasius, in his *Apology*, p. 692, like our Hilary here, mentions the exile of Paulinus together with those of Eusebius, Lucifer, and Dionysius, Socrates, Book II, ch. 36, and Rufinus, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book I, ch. 19, came to think that Paulinus had been driven into exile with the others by the single Synod of Milan. Indeed Rufinus adds Hilary and Rodanus to them, and Sulpicius Severus likewise joins them with the preceding men. Thus Blondel writes that Hilary was exiled in 354. But it was not the time, but one and the same cause—the defence of Athanasius and of the Nicene faith—that joined all these men in exile.] I separated myself, together with the Gallic bishops, from communion with Saturninus, Ursacius, and Valens, while granting their other associates an opportunity to repent: so that the will for peace might not be absent, while the foul limbs of the principal diseases—limbs advancing [Note: [Col. 0579C] In Paris, “that were to advance” (*proficienda*). In the Vatican-Basilica codex, “advancing” (*proficiscentia*). In Colbert and Martin, “professing” (*profitentia*). We prefer, with the others, “advancing” (*proficientia*). For Hilary commonly uses *proficere* both in a good and in a bad sense. This passage shows how well he knew how to distinguish leprosy from leprosy, and Arians who had been led astray from those who led others astray, although Erasmus preferred a different reading.] toward the corruption of the whole body—might be cut off, if only this decree, issued by us, had seemed fit to remain with the most blessed confessors of Christ. [Note: [Col. 0579C] Seven manuscripts read “the decrees then issued” (*edita decreta tum*). Two others read “the decree issued” (*editum decretum*), without *then*. It is highly probable that Hilary was the chief author of framing this decree. Facundus of Hermiane undoubtedly refers to this passage in his Letter to Mocianus. Maintaining that communion must not be entered into with those who attacked the Council of Chalcedon, he says: “Hilary did this with his colleagues. When no decree prejudicial to the Council of Nicaea had yet been issued, and the first schemes of the opponents had begun, they hastened to separate themselves from their communion.” Yet he attributes somewhat too much to Hilary. For Hilary did not cut off all diseased limbs, but only those advancing toward the corruption of the whole body—namely, only three bishops; nor did he do this immediately after their first schemes, but after they had carried through at the Council of Milan what they had first attempted at Arles. Although it is unknown whether the holy confessors confirmed this decree, they certainly followed no other rule when, gathered at Alexandria in 362, they decreed, as Rufinus relates, Book I, ch. 28, that, after only the authors of perfidy had been cut off, the remaining priests should be given the option, if perhaps they wished, after abjuring the error of perfidy, to return to the faith and ordinances of the Fathers. Then, as Jerome says in his *Dialogue against the Luciferians*, the West assented to this judgment, and by so necessary a counsel the world was snatched from Satan’s jaws. Pope Innocent likewise confirmed the Fathers of the Council of Milevis, adhering to the same rule, in these words: “As I judge it harsh to show indulgence to sinners, so I judge it impious to deny a hand to the converted.” Leo also testifies, in Letter 125 to Leo, ch. 1, that at the Council of Chalcedon moderation was observed in this way: only the rebellious and obstinate were rejected from the Church’s unity, while pardon was denied to none who had been corrected. Leo himself approves this in Letter 39, now 59: because both are duties of Christian devotion, that just truth should restrain the obstinate and charity should not repel the converted.] 563 [Note: [Col. 0580C] The printed editions read, “whom later”; then Bade, Erasmus, Miraeus, and Lipsius, “when compelled to the Council of Bourges”; Paris, “when compelled to the Council of Bethers.” They are corrected from the manuscripts, of which only Martin and Colbert have, “when compelled by the Synod of Béziers”: less accurately. Hilary briefly sketches here who came to the Synod of Béziers in 356, what he did there, and finally why he was driven from it into exile.] Later, compelled by the faction of those pseudo-apostles to attend the Synod of Béziers, I offered an examination [Note: [Col. 0580C] We restore the word “for demonstrating” (*demonstrandae*), first deleted by Erasmus, from Bade and the manuscripts.] for demonstrating this heresy. [Note: [Col. 0580C] The Martin manuscript with Colbert reads, “I offered [it] to the hearers.” But these men, fearing the burden of their own conscience, would not hear, etc. We prefer with the others, “fearing public awareness”—that is, fearing being publicly exposed. They had already revealed this fear in the preceding year; for, fearing the people’s judgment, they moved from the church to the palace, as we read in Book I *To Constantius*, §8, whereas Hilary desired nothing more strongly. This he urgently requested at Béziers before his exile, and again at Constantinople while in exile: that he might be allowed to debate the faith under public scrutiny. The Arians, steadily dreading this, sent him into exile after his first request, and back to his homeland after the second.] But they, fearing public awareness, refused to hear what I laid before them, believing that they could lie to Christ about their innocence if they deliberately did not know what they would later do knowingly.

And thereafter, having been held in exile throughout this whole period, I resolved neither to depart from the confession of Christ nor to reject any honourable and plausible basis for establishing unity. Finally, since then I have written or spoken nothing [Note: [Col. 0580D] Bade, Erasmus, and Miraeus, with the manuscripts, read “in times” (*in tempora*). Then two of these have “slanderous” (*maledicum*). By these words he indicates that he fulfilled what he had proposed in Book X *On the Trinity*, §4, where he says: “We shall not complain of the times,” etc.] slanderous against the times, nothing abusive or worthy of their impiety against that body which then falsely claimed to be Christ’s Church, but is now Antichrist’s synagogue. Nor meanwhile did I regard it as a crime for anyone either to converse with them, or, even with the fellowship of communion suspended, to enter a house of prayer, or to hope for the peace that ought to be desired, while we prepared, through repentance, pardon for error and a return from Antichrist to Christ [Col. 0580A] (see *On the Synods*, §§4 and 8). [Note: [Col. 0580D] The printed editions read “of those returning”; against all the manuscripts, supported by *On Matthew*, ch. 2, §2, where through repentance there is said to be a return from error and a recourse from sin. Then four manuscripts read “we may prepare” (*praeparemus*); two others, “we prepare” (*praeparamus*).]

3. What he is now about to say arises not from impatience, but from Christian freedom.—Therefore, if anyone of sound judgment understands the reason for my silence, he will certainly judge that I have restrained the bitterness of a recent wrong until now, and that only now, with freedom in Christ [Note: [Col. 0580D] In the Colbert and Martin manuscripts, “standing in freedom” (*libertate stantem*), which Bandinus and Latinius conjectured ought to be read.] bearing witness, I am moved to write these things not by some fault of human agitation. For I do not speak prematurely, since I have long been silent; nor did I remain silent without moderation, since I now at last speak; nor do I complain of an injury, since I overlooked it when recent, and, lest I should be thought to speak from my own cause, [Col. 0580B] [Note: [Col. 0580D] In the Lipsius and Paris editions: “yet I devoted time to silence.” More correctly, other books have “so much … time”—namely, the four years which he had already spent in exile.] devoted so much time to silence. Now I have no reason for speaking other than Christ’s cause. To him I owed even this, that I remained silent until now; and henceforth I understand that I owe it to him not to be silent.

4. He desires the times of the persecutors.—And would that, almighty God and Creator of all, and also Father of our one Lord Jesus Christ, you had instead granted to my lifetime and my age that I might have fulfilled this ministry of my confession of you and of your only-begotten Son amid the times of Nero or Decius! [Col. 0581A] Nor would I, burning through the mercy of the Lord and God, your Son Jesus Christ, with the Holy Spirit, [Note: [Col. 0581C] On the authority of the Martin manuscript, we have added “with the Holy Spirit.” This passage of Hilary should be compared with Chrysostom’s similar Letter 125 to Cyriacus.] have feared the rack, knowing that Isaiah was sawn asunder; nor would I have feared the fires, remembering that the Hebrew boys sang amid them; nor would I have shrunk from the cross and the breaking of my legs, [Note: [Col. 0581C] The Martin and Colbert manuscripts read “the legs of mine” (*crurium meorum*) and below “a stream” (*undam*) for *rheumam*. Hilary here clearly signifies that what was granted to the thief is granted to martyrs immediately after death. Yet in Psalm 141, §6, he calls it Paradise, the lot and kingdom of his inheritance—that is, Christ’s—and in Book X *On the Trinity*, §34, the delights of consummate blessedness. Accordingly, he does not seem to have doubted that heavenly blessedness is not deferred for martyrs.] after recalling the thief translated into Paradise. Nor would I have trembled before the depths of the sea or the surging torrent of the Black Sea swallowing me, since through Jonah and Paul you had taught the faithful that there is life in the sea. For against your open enemies that contest would have been blessed for me, because there would remain no doubt that those were persecutors who compelled us by punishments, sword, and fire to deny you; nor could we offer you more testimony than our deaths. [Col. 0581B] For we would fight openly and confidently against those who deny, torture, and slaughter; and your people would follow us as their leaders into the sacred confession, instructed by the manifest fact of public persecution.

5. What sort of persecution was Constantius’s.—But now we fight against a deceiving persecutor, against a flattering enemy, against Constantius the Antichrist, [Note: [Col. 0581C] Lucifer likewise condemns those false blandishments of Constantius in *One Must Die for the Son of God*: “In this you are judged most wicked: that, under the appearance of love and professing a wish to give counsel, you flatter us in order to cast us down.” Likewise Athanasius, *To the Solitaries*, p. 838, relates that Hosius was overcome by Constantius, now flattering him and calling him father, now threatening and enumerating the exiled, etc.] who does not strike backs, but strokes bellies; who does not proscribe unto life, but [Note: [Col. 0581D] Liberius testifies in Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book II, ch. 16, that many were deceived by this device: “All who do not love the glory of God, preferring your gifts, condemned one whom they had neither seen nor judged.” Among them was Potamius, who, as Faustinus and Marcellinus say in their Book to the Emperor, at first defended the Catholic faith, but afterward betrayed the faith for the reward of an imperial estate which he had desired to possess. Gregory Nazianzen calls such people, Oration 21, “lovers of gold rather than lovers of Christ,” *philochrysous mallon ē philochristous* (φιλοχρύσους μᾶλλον ἢ φιλοχρίστους), and adds that Constantius expended the property of the poor for those evil purposes. Although the words “does not proscribe unto life, but enriches unto death” are absent in the Colbert and Martin manuscripts, this would not be truly said if proscription signified only exile and not also confiscation of property and a capital penalty; for he had already punished very many by exile. Or certainly Constantius is here portrayed as he wished to appear. For though Lucifer writes of him in *One Must Die for the Son of God*, “You despoil, proscribe, slaughter with the sword,” etc., he nevertheless adds afterward: “You who rage so madly against the innocent think that you can appear Christian, pious, prudent, and just.”] enriches unto death; 565 does not thrust into prison for freedom, but honours within the palace [Col. 0582C] for slavery; does not torment the sides, but seizes the heart; does not sever the head with the sword, but kills the soul with gold; does not publicly threaten fires, but privately kindles Gehenna. He does not contend lest he be defeated, but flatters in order to rule. He confesses Christ in order to deny him; [Note: [Col. 0582C] At least this was the pretext he displayed. Lucifer reports Constantius’s own words at the Council of Milan in 355, in *On Not Meeting with Heretics*: “You said, ‘I wish peace to be established in my Empire,’ while desiring to violate the Lord’s peace among us and to divide God’s people,” etc. Again, shortly afterward: “You said to us, ‘I wish peace to be made’;” and near the beginning: “You said that we had been and were enemies of peace, foes of unity, and adversaries even of brotherly love.”] promotes unity in order that there may be no peace; suppresses heresies [Note: [Col. 0582C] Namely, that of Photinus, as is explained below in §23: “Again you arouse at Sirmium every concern of your Catholic doctrine against Photinus.”] in order that there may be no Christians; honours priests in order that they may not be bishops; [Note: [Col. 0582C] Thus Lucifer, in Book I *For Athanasius*, addresses the emperor: “Though you restore the memorials of martyrs, nevertheless you shed the blood of the servants of the one Son of God.” And Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book III, ch. 12, testifies that Constantius enriched churches with splendid and magnificent vessels.] builds church buildings in order to destroy the faith. He carries you about in his words, in his mouth; and does absolutely everything to prevent your being believed to be God in the manner in which [Col. 0582A] the Father is God. [Note: [Col. 0582D] In the printed editions and several manuscripts: “lest you, as God, [be] so the Father.” With the Vatican-Basilica, Martin, Colbert, and Chartres manuscripts we prefer: “lest you be believed to be God as the Father [is God]”—supply “is God.” Thus “you in his mouth,” etc., refers to Christ, whose divinity Constantius is reproved for wishing to represent as unequal to the Father’s.]

6. Hilary clears himself of the suspicion of abusive speech.—Let, then, the opinion that these are insults, and the suspicion of falsehood, cease. For ministers of truth ought to set forth what is true. If we speak falsely, let the abusive utterance be infamous; [Note: [Col. 0582D] The Vatican-Basilica exemplar has “abusing” (*maledicens*).] but if we show that all these things are manifest, then, after this long silence, we are not outside apostolic freedom and moderation in bringing these charges. Yet perhaps someone will think me rash because I say that Constantius is Antichrist. Whoever judges this to be insolence rather than constancy, let him first read that John said to Herod, “It is not lawful for you to do this” (Mark 6:18); let him know that a martyr said to King Antiochus, “You indeed, wicked man, destroy us from this present life, but the King of the world will raise us, who have died for his laws, to an everlasting resurrection of life” [Col. 0582B] (2 Macc. 7:9); [Note: [Col. 0582D] The Colbert codex with Martin reads, “will raise us to the resurrection of eternal life.” In Greek: *eis aiōnion anabiōsin zōēs hēmas anastēsei* (εἰς αἰώνιον ἀναβίωσιν ζωῆς ἡμᾶς ἀναστήσει).] and again that another rebuked him in a blessed and faithful voice: “Having authority among men, though you are mortal, you do what you will; but do not suppose that our race has been abandoned by God. Endure patiently, and see how his great power will torment you and your seed” (ibid., 16–17). So spoke the boys. But a woman spoke to men no less perfect and blessed, saying: “But you, who have become the inventor of every wickedness against the Hebrews, shall not escape the hand of God. For if the Lord has been a little angry with us while we live [Col. 0583A] for rebuke and correction, he will again be reconciled with his servants” (ibid., 31 ff.). [Note: [Col. 0583B] The Silva Major manuscript reads “one”; Colbert, “now.” “While living” or “alive” would be more pleasing, in accordance with the Greek verb *zōn* (ζῶν). In the printed editions, “will remember.” More correctly, the Colbert and Martin manuscripts read “will be reconciled” (*reconciliabitur*), in agreement with the Greek *katallagēsetai* (καταλλαγήσεται).] This is not rashness, but faith; not thoughtlessness, but reason; not madness, but confidence.

7. Constantius compared with Nero, Decius, and others.—I cry out to you, Constantius, what I would have said to Nero, what Decius and Maximian would hear from me: You fight against God; you rage against the Church; you persecute the saints; you hate Christ’s preachers; you abolish religion; you are a tyrant not now of human but of divine things. [Note: [Col. 0583B] That is, you are now a tyrant not of human but of divine things. What I have said is shared and common to you and them. Thus the things hitherto said are not meant here—for what appears before this §7 is especially characteristic of Constantius—but rather those which Hilary has just testified that he would have cried out to Nero and Decius.] These things are shared and common between you and them, as spoken by me. But now receive what is peculiarly yours. You falsely profess yourself a Christian; you are a new enemy of Christ. You go before Antichrist and work his secret mysteries. You devise creeds while living against the faith.
