[Note: [Col. 0583B] The printed editions read, “You devise a creed.” More suitably, the Vatican-Basilica manuscript with several others reads, “You devise creeds,” in the plural, and hence false ones: living against the faith—that is, neither holding in mind nor in conduct the one true faith. By “creeds” he means the frequent formulae of faith written in Constantius’s presence or with his support, or even those documents of which Lucifer says in *On Not Sparing Those Who Sin against God*: “So far as lay in your power, you handed over him—Christ—of whom you gave written books, and you established preachers of your gracious intention everywhere.” And near the beginning of the same book: “The memorials recited by you and given to even Catholic bishops at Rome will convict you, namely so that your blasphemy might be strengthened everywhere.” Hence, when in Book II *For Athanasius* he recalls that Constantius wished to seem a jurist, and in *One Must Die for the Son of God* that he considered himself learned and had a designated number of dictations, he nevertheless does not deny that his speech was polished and ornate, such as might even be called eloquent and sweet through studied art. These matters illuminate Hilary’s following words, “You are a teacher of the profane.”] You are a teacher of the profane, [Col. 0584A] unlearned in things holy. You bestow bishoprics upon your own [appointees], [Note: [Col. 0583C] All the manuscripts have “your bishoprics.” Then most have “bestowing.” Here too Lucifer should be heard, *On Not Sparing Those Who Sin against God*: “You have transformed yourself into apostles of Christ, as though truly all care for the Church belonged to you; being concerned, forsooth, that no Catholic bishop should preside anywhere in the Church … You remove Catholic bishops; you ordain heretics.” He says to him in *One Must Die for the Son of God*: “The Arian bishops of your doctrine repeatedly acclaim to you, ‘You are bishop of bishops.’” On this replacement of good bishops with evil ones, see also Athanasius, *To the Solitaries*, p. 858, to which refers his remark on p. 860: “With a military escort you send bishops to fifty sees among unwilling peoples,” etc. Perhaps Hilary also here has in view the recent replacement of bishops at the Council of Constantinople, concerning which see below, §15.] and replace good men with bad. You commit priests to custody; you station your armies [Note: [Col. 0583D] The Colbert manuscript reads “for error” (*ad errorem*).] to terrorize the Church; you convene synods and compel the faith of the West toward impiety; you terrify those shut up in one city, Rimini, with threats, weaken them by hunger, wear them down by winter, and corrupt them by dissimulation. But in the East you, the artificer of dissensions, foster divisions; you entice the pliant, incite your supporters; [Note: [Col. 0583D] The Martin manuscript reads “you bind by flatteries.” Then the Colbert manuscript, “you incite a supporter.” The reading “you attract gently; you incite supporters” would not be displeasing. The divisions stirred up at Seleucia and afterward nourished at Constantinople are touched on here.] you are the disturber of the old and the profaner of the new. You accomplish every savage thing without [Col. 0584B] the envy aroused by glorious deaths. [Note: [Col. 0584B] In the Colbert manuscript, “without injury.” Lucifer too did not pass this over in *One Must Die for the Son of God*: “Thus you desire that we, whom you persecute so fiercely, should be tortured in various ways and at every moment; yet you have decided that we should not be killed, as though death alone makes Christ’s soldiers blessed,” etc. Hilary then elegantly declares that Constantius surpasses the devil in ingenuity and skill at torturing Christians.] By a new and unheard-of triumph of ingenuity you conquer the devil and persecute without martyrdom.

8. The relics of martyrs are to be venerated; their power.—Nero, Decius, Maximian, we owe more to your cruelty. For through you we conquered the devil. Everywhere the holy blood of the blessed martyrs has been received, [Col. 0584B] and their venerable bones daily bear witness, [Note: [Col. 0584B] The words, “and their venerable bones daily bear witness,” were perhaps first suppressed in the ancient Vatican-Basilica codex by some disciple of Eunomius or Vigilantius, and afterward were absent from transcripts and printed editions. They have been preserved in the Colbert and Martin manuscripts, by whose aid is restored what was lacking to the integrity of the discourse. For the words, “While demons bellow in them,” etc., could not be referred to the preceding “the blood of martyrs has been received,” but now cohere very suitably with “their venerable bones bear witness.” These miracles plainly attest the glory and power both of those who were slain and of him for whom they were slain. This is illustrated by Book XI *On the Trinity*, §3: “The tombs of apostles and martyrs speak of him—Christ … the bellows of punished demons resound with him.” Jerome follows Hilary’s words in *Against Vigilantius*, where he calls the sacred relics of the apostles “bones to be venerated according to us,” whereas Vigilantius with Eunomius called them worthless dust.] while demons [Note: [Col. 0584C] Five manuscripts read “roar” (*rugiunt*). The better witnesses, with the printed editions, read “bellow” (*mugiunt*), as in Book XI *On the Trinity*, §3 we read “the bellowing of demons,” not “roaring.” Jerome nevertheless supports the former in Letter 27 to Eustochium, ch. 6, where, relating similar things, he says: “Paula saw demons roaring under diverse tortures; and before the tombs of the saints men howling in the manner of wolves, barking with the voices of dogs, growling like lions, bellowing like bulls; others rolling their heads and touching the ground behind them with the crown of the head; and, though women were suspended by the feet, their garments did not fall over their faces.” The latter words, expressed in imitation of Hilary, indicate that this book was not unknown to Jerome. Sulpicius also imitates this passage when he describes Martin’s power in expelling demons in Dialogue III: “You could see the wretches grievously tormented in different ways: some hanging with feet raised aloft as though from a cloud, yet their garments did not fall over their faces, lest the part of the body laid bare should violate modesty.” Likewise Paulinus, in Nativity Poem 7 on St. Felix, portrays a man possessed by a demon at the saint’s threshold:

> With body turned,  
> Hanging by his feet, he gazes up at the roof.  
> Yet as though his garments were stiff, or sewn to his feet,  
> Every sacred part of his body is veiled in chaste covering,  
> So that reverence for the divine work may remain through covered  
> Bodies, and the demon, in the very punishment  
> By which he is tormented, may not delight by exposing naked shame—
Tormented in their limbs, he is the more grievously racked with his modesty left unharmed. Lorraine saw such a prodigy in our own age, as the French-written *Commentaries of the Marquis de Beauvau*, p. 6, attest.] They bellow while illnesses are expelled; bodies are raised without ropes; and, when women are suspended by their feet, their garments do not fall over their faces; spirits are burned without fires; they confess without interrogation while being tormented, doing everything with no less effect than an examiner’s inquiry and an increase of faith. [Note: We restore this passage from the Colbert and Martin manuscripts, though these read *age* for *agere* (“to do”) and *profecto* for *profectu* (“effect”). Other books read: “they confess without an interrogator’s increase of faith.” “But you, most cruel of all cruelties.” Here Hilary shows that unclean spirits are driven and tormented by a certain hidden power, while their wound is hidden and their punishment manifest, as Cyprian says in Epistle II to Donatus, where one may also see torments inflicted on them through exorcists. In those torments some confessed Christ’s divinity, as we heard from Hilary, Book XI, no. 3; others, the faith of the whole Trinity [Col. 0585D], of which Ambrose, Epistle now XXII, no. 21, offers an illustrious example. Others, as Cyprian testifies in his work *To Demetrian*, crying and groaning in a human voice and feeling scourges and blows by divine power, confess the coming judgment. Sometimes also, he says in *On the Vanity of Idols*: “You may see them beaten with lashes by our voice and by the operation of hidden majesty, scorched by fire, stretched by the intensification of their growing punishment, howling, groaning, pleading; confessing, even in the hearing of those who worship them, whence they come and when they depart.” But above all Sulpicius Severus, while borrowing Hilary’s words in Dialogue III, elucidates them thus: “In another part you might see persons tormented without questioning and confessing their own crimes. With no one questioning them, they even disclosed their names: one admitted that he was Jupiter, another Mercury.] But you, most cruel of all cruel men, rage against us with greater harm and less pardon. You creep in under a name; you kill by flattery; under the appearance of religion you carry out impiety; as a lying preacher of Christ, you extinguish Christ’s faith. [Note: The printed editions read, “by the name of one flattering.” Six manuscripts: “by the enticement of the name.” More correctly in the Vatican Basilica, Martin, and Colbert manuscripts: “you creep in under the name”—supply, the name by which you pretend to be a Christian, as no. 9 explains—“you kill by flattery,” etc.] You do not even leave the wretched any excuses, so that before their eternal Judge they might bring forward punishments and some scars on their torn bodies, and weakness might defend necessity. [Note: The printed editions read, “might offer.” Here Hilary approaches Cyprian’s judgment, who in *On the Lapsed* thinks that those who fell under torture should be treated more leniently: “One who has been overcome through torments may be questioned; one conquered in pain may offer an excuse,” etc.] Most wicked of mortals, you so arrange every evil of persecution as to exclude pardon even in sin and martyrdom even in confession. But this is what that father of yours [Note: That is, the enemy of mankind, the father of all heretics, while he oversows tares in the householder’s field.]—the craftsman of human deaths—taught you: to conquer without defiance, slaughter without a sword, persecute without infamy, [Note: In the Colbert and Martin manuscripts: “kill without suspicion.”] plot without suspicion, lie without being understood, profess without faith, flatter without goodness, do [Note: Vatican Basilica manuscript with Colbert and Martin: “what you may will.” Others: “what you might will.”] whatever you will, and not disclose what you will.

### 9. The Lord’s name is in Constantius’ words, not in his deeds. He makes God a liar.

But the only-begotten God himself, whom you persecute in me, warned me not to trust you and not to let this deceitful and counterfeit name in you deceive me, saying: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ shall enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father [Note: The three aforesaid manuscripts omit “who is in heaven.”] who is in heaven—he shall enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 7:21). Do you now recognize the truth of the divine prophecy directed against you and the reliability of the Lord’s sentence, [Note: The Vatican Basilica codex alone reads: “which does not admit …”] by which not profession of the name but obedience to the Father’s will [Col. 0585C] admits one into the heavenly kingdom? But see whether you, though putting forward the Lord’s name in words, accomplish the will of God the Father in deeds. He cries out: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3:17); yet you decree that he is not Son and that there is no Father. You introduce names of adoption, external designations, and a God who feigns everything concerning himself—a new persecutor today of the divine religion. Before this, your fathers—Nero, Decius, and the rest—were enemies only of Christ; but you contend against God the Father, that he may be a liar, that he may have deceived, that he may have professed something of himself which he was not, as though he could not be what he professed. The Son cries: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30); “Believe my works, because the Father is in me and I in the Father” (ibid., 38); and “All things which are the Father’s are mine” (John 16:15). Yet you rebuke Christ for truth; [Note: In the Michaelinus manuscripts: “for piety of truth.” “For injured truth,” as though truth had been harmed, would be less displeasing. Although in compressed wording, with nothing lacking, this is meant: you rebuke Christ as though he were not speaking truth, and you accuse the Father as one professing falsehood.] you accuse the Father for his profession. You, a human being, correct God; you, corruption, regulate life; you, night, illuminate light; you, an unbeliever, promulgate faith; you, impious, counterfeit piety; and you embroil the world by profane pretence, [Note: Six manuscripts: “against piety,” and shortly afterward, “you mingle,” in place of “you commit.” A little later the printed editions lacked “concerning himself.”] denying concerning God what he himself has professed concerning himself.

### 10. Constantius’ sheep’s clothing.

But besides this correction of falsehood, the Lord taught me another saying by which to understand you: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, [Note: In the Colbert manuscript: “within”; in Martin: “inside,” with *from* omitted in both.] but inwardly are ravening wolves. By their fruits you shall know them” (Matt. 7:15–16). For something is in the heart that is concealed in the face and veiled in the mind; and those who thought it a sheep experienced it as a wolf. If they do what belongs to sheep, let them be believed to be sheep; but if they perform the work of ravening wolves, [Note: Thus the two manuscripts mentioned above. Others read: “sheep perform the rapacity of wolves.” As above, *do*, so here *perform* seems to refer to the false prophets.] they are understood to be wolves by their work, and the likeness of their clothing is exposed by the fruit of their deeds. We see your sheep’s clothing, ravening wolf. You burden God’s holy Spirit with the gold of the state, [Note: The printed editions read “you honor”; corrected from manuscripts, including Colbert and Martin: “you burden God’s Spirit,” and “whether wealth taken from temples, or made public by edicts, or exacted by penalties, you offer to God.” Perhaps: “whether published by edicts … wealth you offer to God.” This censures Constantius because, as Lucifer implies at the end of Book I *For Athanasius*, he used to give alms from others’ tears and from the possessions of those who preferred deportation, death, or proscription to denying Christ. Well known is Liberius’ statement in Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book II, ch. 16: “You have despoiled the churches of the world, and you bring me alms as to a condemned man.”] offering to God wealth either taken from temples, made public by edicts, or exacted by penalties. You welcome priests with the kiss by which Christ too was betrayed; you bow your head for blessing so as to trample the faith; you grant a banquet from which Judas went out to betrayal; [Note: Colbert manuscript: “the head-tax.” Josephus mentions this levy in *The Jewish War*, Book II, ch. 16, where Agrippa explains to the people that the magnitude of the revenues Egypt paid to the Romans could be estimated from the census of individual heads. Again, in *Antiquities of the Jews*, Book XII, Antiochus writes: “The tribute paid per head is remitted to senators, priests, temple scribes, and singers.” A law in favor of clerics appears in the Theodosian Code, Book I, under *The Lustral Tax*, issued in December 356: “All merchants must furnish gold and silver; clerics alone are exempt.” Another, Book XIV, *On Bishops and Clerics*, issued in the same month in 357: “Let all bitterness of unjust summons and inequitable exaction be repelled from clerics,” etc. Other immunities are granted them by laws issued in 353 and mentioned in the same Code, Book X, *On Bishops.*] you remit the head-tax which Christ paid so as not to give offense (Matt. 17:26); you give away Caesar’s revenues in order to invite Christians to denial; you relax what is yours so that what belongs to God may be lost. Such are your garments, false sheep.

### 11. The wolf’s deeds. What Alexandria, Trier, Milan, Rome, and Toulouse suffered.

But now, ravening wolf, hear the fruits of your works. Nor do I recount anything other than what has been done in the Church, [Note: Printed editions: “that I might report another tyranny besides that of God.” The six manuscripts: “nor do I seek to report another tyranny besides that of God’s” (Michaelinus: “I am able”): “not because …” The Colbert and Martin manuscripts: “or that I might bring forth another tyranny besides that against God. I do not complain because,” etc. “Against God” would please, had Hilary not already said in no. 7, “you are no longer merely a tyrant over human affairs.” We follow the Vatican Basilica exemplar, supported by others. It is noteworthy, first, how scrupulously Hilary reports matters which, though confirmed by public testimony, he did not himself know with sufficient certainty; then how modestly, speaking for the Church, he abstains from reporting things not done against it. Above, “against the Church” would read better than “in the Church.”] nor do I bring forth any tyranny other than that against God. I do not complain because I am ignorant of the cause; yet the complaint is widely known: bishops whom no one dared condemn were ordered by you to be enrolled even now with the mark of condemnation to the mines inscribed on their ecclesiastical foreheads. [Note: Martin and Colbert manuscripts: “on ecclesiastical foreheads.” Athanasius attributes this to the Arians in *To the Solitaries*, p. 859: “They consigned some to quarries and pursued others to death.” Lucifer ascribes the same, together with our Hilary, to Constantius, by whose authority it was done: “You have filled with the number of those resisting your cunning all mines, all places thought fit to be called places of exile; you do not cease to harass the innocent by banishment, hunger, thirst, and nakedness.” From this passage it is understood that Constantius restored a practice abolished by his father in Theodosian Code, Book II, *On Punishments*, which provides that if anyone is condemned to the games or the mines, no mark shall be written on his face … so that the face, fashioned in the likeness of heavenly beauty, may not be defiled.] Alexandria stands with me, shaken by so many wars and fearing the uproar of so many stirred-up expeditions. [Note: The Vatican Basilica codex adds “more,” which Martin also has; in it, as in Colbert, “lighter,” not “shorter,” occurs earlier. The war against Persia, in which Julian later perished after it had already continued long, was neither slight nor brief.] For the war against Persia was shorter than the one waged against Alexandria with arms. Governors were changed, commanders chosen, peoples corrupted, legions stirred, lest Christ should be preached by Athanasius. I pass over smaller peoples and cities throughout the East, where there is either terror or war. [Note: The Colbert exemplar with Martin: “I pass over the report concerning smaller peoples,” and shortly afterward, “after all these things.”] After you had gathered all arms against the faith of the West and turned your armies against Christ’s sheep, it was permitted me to flee under Nero. Or you banished Paulinus, a man of blessed confession, [Note: Martin manuscript: “a man of blessed confession.”] after trying to entice him by flattery, in 353, and stripped the holy Church of Trier of such a priest. You terrified faith by edicts. You harassed him to death by changing his places of exile, and banished him even outside the Christian name, [Note: The Colbert codex reads “that he might take bread,” an apparent truth but a false one. As Baronius observes under the year 355, no. 29, Hilary says this of Paulinus because he was first banished to Phrygia, where the Cataphrygian heretics, followers of Montanus and Maximilla, lived, and then sent among barbarians: as if to say, it was not enough for Constantius to send Paulinus among the Cataphrygians; he expelled him even outside the Christian name. “Montana” here is judged a scribal error, particularly since in Book II *To Constantius* one finds “Montanus,” not “Montana.”] so that he might take neither bread from your granary nor wait for bread defiled from the cave of Montanus and Maximilla.

How you disturbed the most devout people of Milan by the madness of your terror! [Note: What seemed formerly to be lacking here is restored by changing the punctuation. Otherwise the reading of the Colbert and Martin manuscripts would be preferable: “By how great a terror of your madness you disturbed [them]!” The Milanese people were especially devout because of the constancy of faith they displayed in 355. Since the false synod did not dare spread its corrupt faith among them, though it attempted this in the Emperor’s name, it provoked such popular horror that it judged it unsafe to meet in the church and withdrew to the palace, as has already been noted in Book I *To Constantius*, no. 8. They seem to have suffered these evils in the same year, when, after Dionysius had been expelled, Auxentius of impious unbelief occupied the Church of Milan with arms and an army, as Ambrose says in *On the Holy Spirit*, Book III, ch. 10.] Your tribunes entered the Holy of Holies and, making a way for themselves through the people by every cruelty, dragged priests from the altar. Do you think, wicked man, that you have sinned less grievously than the impiety of the Jews? They indeed shed Zechariah’s blood; but, so far as lies in you, you tore from Christ those made one body with Christ. [Note: The Martin codex alone reads, corruptly, “having become one body … you departed.” Hilary calls priests “made one body” because they receive Christ’s body from the altar; when they are torn away from it, they are in some manner torn away from Christ. “The altar,” says Optatus, Book VI, “is the seat of Christ’s body and blood.” Hence, speaking against breakers of altars, he adds: “What had Christ offended you, whose body and blood dwelt there at appointed moments?” Then, comparing them after the manner of our Hilary with the Jews, he says: “In this way you have imitated the Jews. They laid hands upon Christ on the cross; by you he was struck at the altar.” Nor would both have rightly compared the crime of Arians or Donatists with the Jews’ crime unless they believed that Christ’s true body was received from the altar.] You next extended your war as far as Rome and snatched its bishop, Liberius, from there. And unhappy you! I do not know whether you banished him with greater impiety than you recalled him. What furies you then unleashed upon the Church of Toulouse! Clerics were beaten with clubs, deacons crushed with lead, and hands were laid upon Christ himself—as those holy persons who understand with me [Note: In the Martin and Colbert manuscripts: “the hands of Gentiles were laid upon Christ.” In the other manuscripts “upon himself” is not repeated. There is scarcely any doubt that these things were committed after the Synod of Béziers. But who is this Christ upon whom hands were laid? Certainly not Rhodanus, who had been sent into exile from Béziers and was not permitted to return to his church. There is strong reason to suspect that Christ denotes the venerable sacraments of Christ’s body and blood, and that “as holy persons understand with me” here means what the Fathers elsewhere commonly say, when speaking more guardedly of these same sacraments: “The faithful know.”] understand it. These things, Constantius: if I lie, you are a sheep; but if you do them, you are Antichrist.

### 12. On the Synod of Seleucia.

Now, since these things, which are held in the public conscience, are no more malicious accusations from me than they are true: if anyone has any remaining hope in Christ, if anyone fears the day of judgment, if anyone has renounced the devil, if anyone remembers having been reborn into life, let him receive what I say and judge these matters by the judgment by which he is to be judged. [Note: The word “said,” omitted in Erasmus, Lipsius, and Paris, is restored from Bade and seven manuscripts. Hence earlier we would prefer “malicious” in accordance with no. 6: “If we speak falsely, let the malicious speech be infamous.”] For I did not learn what I am about to say from elsewhere: I myself heard it and was present when it was done. Thus I do not lie in Christ, because, as a disciple of truth, I am now also a witness to truth. [Note: Printed editions: “because I stand by as a disciple of truth”; the passage is mutilated. It is restored from the Vatican Basilica, Martin, and Colbert manuscripts in this sense: “because, as a disciple of truth, so now also I am a witness to truth.” Or, if someone prefers to connect *I stand by* with what precedes—because *where I found*, rather than *where I find*, follows—then with the latter two manuscripts the reading should be: “I found [at] the synod of the Eastern bishops at Seleucia, where there are as many blasphemers as,” etc. Yet in Book III *On the Trinity*, no. 20, we already read: “The Lord, standing by to confirm faith, offered the opportunity of touching his body and handling his wound”; there the present *standing by* is followed in the same narrative sequence by the past *offered.*] I was present, on 27 September 359, at the Easterners’ synod in Seleucia, where I found as many blasphemers as pleased Constantius. For at the first withdrawal in that assembly, [Note: Printed editions: “after my withdrawal.” All manuscripts have *prima* (“first”) for *post* (“after”); then Tellius has “my succession,” Silvius “my session in it,” and the others “my withdrawal.” If the letter *m*, which very frequently is superfluous at the end of words in old books, is removed, there remains “at my first withdrawal,” or “in it”; for the manuscripts write both alike. This yields a sense entirely consistent with the history. On the first day the Acacians withdrew from the council, as Socrates narrates, Book II, ch. 39. After this withdrawal, people began to be separated and counted according to the side to which they adhered; Athanasius likewise notes this in *On the Synods*, p. 881: “After the withdrawal they were divided: some adhered to Acacius, but they were few and suspect; the others, who had left him, were numerous.” Hilary calls this withdrawal the first because, when the same people met together again through Leonas’ intervention on the third day, they were again divided by one party’s withdrawal. He does not refer here, as some think, to the second withdrawal, since he later relates what happened on the third day, when that second withdrawal occurred. Misled by the false reading of earlier editions, they think that Hilary left the council before everyone was gathered together by Leonas. They support this from Socrates, Book II, ch. 40, where the Acacians are reported unwilling to attend the council unless those already deposed and those presently accused were first expelled, and only after they had left to have entered. Yet Socrates does not say there that those formerly deposed had left: “Those who had been accused,” he says, “went out; but the Acacians entered.” No accusation had been brought against Hilary. Moreover, who would believe that he was expelled from the council when, as Sulpicius testifies, Book II, after he had set forth his faith he was received into fellowship and admitted to the council from the very beginning? Indeed, he had won everyone’s goodwill to such an extent that even the Anomoeans confidently disclosed their opinions to him. Nothing, therefore, compels us to think he departed from the council. Nor should one therefore suppose that he or Egyptian bishops attended the meeting at which the formula issued at Antioch in Encaeniis was ratified by subscriptions; that was a private meeting and consisted only of defenders of the *homoiousion.*] I found that one hundred and five bishops proclaimed the *homoiousion*, that is, “of similar essence”; nineteen professed the *anomoiousion*, that is, “of dissimilar essence”; and the Egyptians alone, apart from the Alexandrian heretic George, held most steadfastly to the *homoousion*. When, therefore, on the third day of the council Count Leonas compelled all to gather together, [Note: Printed editions: “they were gathered from those who proclaimed the *homoiousion*—some of them.” By faulty punctuation, this gives the false sense that Leonas gathered only those who proclaimed the *homoiousion*. The final word “of them” is also superfluous and is removed on the authority of the Colbert and Martin manuscripts.] some of those who proclaimed the *homoiousion* stated certain things piously in words: that the Son was from God—that is, from God’s substance—and had always existed. But those defending the *anomoiousion* asserted nothing but the most profane things: that nothing could be similar to God’s substance, that a generation could not come forth from God, and that Christ was a creature; [Note: By supplying “thus” after “that,” the complete reading we present is obtained from the manuscripts; the earlier reading was: “Thus, that he was created.” Then the Colbert and Martin manuscripts read: “in God’s birth.” Theodoret, *Haeretical Fables*, Book IV, ch. 4, reports that heretics who said, “God the Father, and the Son also always created,” maintaining that in God to create and to beget are the same thing, were called Psathyrians by the Antiochenes.] thus, that the fact he was created was counted as his birth; that he was from nothing; and consequently that he was neither Son nor like God.

### 13. Blasphemies publicly recited.

I speak to you of what I myself heard recited publicly in the assembly—what had been recorded when the bishop preached it at Antioch. [Note: We owe this excellent reading to the often commended Colbert and Martin manuscripts. Baronius reproduced it under the year 359, no. 67. Other books read: “what was retained when it was preached at Antioch … was recalled by him.” First, there is no name to which “by him” can refer; next, it is unknown who the man is whose effrontery Hilary later marvels at; finally, there is no antecedent for the words which follow shortly, “when he had compared,” he says. The sentence is now complete and suits Eudoxius, leader of the Anomoeans, excellently. Nor is this contradicted by Theodoret, *Haeretical Fables*, Book IV, ch. 2, who writes that Eudoxius, ordered to go to the Synod of Seleucia, did go but did not dare enter the sitting. Hilary does not say that Eudoxius preached this at Seleucia; rather, what he had preached elsewhere—undoubtedly in the assembly he convened at Antioch as soon as he seized that see—was publicly read at Seleucia, before the Acacians fashioned a new formula of faith, and therefore in the first sitting. This is supported by Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book II, ch. 27, who says that Eustathius and other delegates of the Seleucian synod accused Eudoxius before the Emperor of vomiting forth dreadful blasphemies against God’s Son, and that Constantius, however favorably inclined toward him for his own sake, could temper his anger only by asserting that not Eudoxius but Aetius was their author.] The following statements were therefore recalled as having been made by him:

> “God was what he is. There was no Father, because neither was there a Son. For if there is a son, there must also be a woman, intercourse, [Note: Printed editions: “the intercourse of speech and pricking.” We restore “intercourse and conversation” from the Colbert and Martin manuscripts, and then “and conjugal union” from the Chartres manuscript.] conversation, the conjugal union of a word, caressing, and finally the natural little mechanism for begetting.”

O my miserable ears, that heard the sound of such a deadly utterance—such things spoken about God by a human being and preached about Christ in the Church! After many impieties of this kind, when he had compared Father and Son according to names rather than nature, he said:

> “To the extent that the Son extends himself to know the Father, to that extent the Father extends himself beyond the Son so that he may not be known by the Son.” [Note: Three manuscripts read: “so that the Son may not be known”; wrongly. Eudoxius’ effrontery is astonishing: while uttering these blasphemies concerning God’s Son, he championed Aetius and Eunomius. The latter, Theodoret testifying in *Haeretical Fables*, Book IV, ch. 3, boasted that he was ignorant of nothing concerning divine matters, but knew even God’s essence exactly and possessed the same knowledge of God that God himself possesses of himself. The former, in Epiphanius, *Heresies*, LXXVI, no. 4, dared to say: “I know God, and know him so completely that I do not even know myself better than I know God.” Athanasius has already observed in *On the Synods*, p. 871, that Arians did not hesitate to attribute to human beings what they denied to God’s Son.]

When these were read, an uproar arose.

### 14. In what sense those who deny similarity condemn dissimilarity.

But when even those who call God dissimilar understood that human ears would not accept words of such great impiety, they again—deceivers rather than bishops of the Church—drew up a creed and condemned the *homoousion*, the *homoiousion*, and dissimilarity. [Note: The printed editions with the Vatican Basilica, Michaelinus, and Silvius manuscripts read thus, except that they lack “and” before “dissimilarity.” We restore it from the Colbert and Martin manuscripts, though these have the further error of reading *anomoiousion* for *homoiousion*. Miræus, Lipsius, and Paris, following Erasmus, read most wrongly: “they drew up a creed of the *homoousion* and condemned the dissimilarity of the *homoiousion*.” Plainly Hilary refers here to the formula Acacius handed to Leonas and which, through Leonas, was read in the third session of the Synod of Seleucia. In Athanasius, *On the Synods*, p. 904, and Socrates, Book II, ch. 40, it reads: “We reject the *homoousion* and the *homoiousion* as foreign to the Scriptures, but we anathematize the *anomoion* [‘dissimilar’].” In Epiphanius, *Heresies*, LXXIII, no. 25, the word *homoiousion* is absent; it is clear that it must be restored from Athanasius and Socrates and from our Hilary.] Although this was contrary to their own meaning as hearers—that is, to the judgment of the ears and to the sound of the words—I myself questioned one of them, who happened to approach in order to test me. Pretending ignorance of the proceedings, I asked what they meant in condemning the Son’s being of one substance with the Father, denying that he was of similar substance, and yet condemning dissimilarity. Then he told me: “Christ is not like God, but he is like the Father.” This seemed still more obscure to me. When I questioned him again about it, he spoke as follows:

> “I say that he is unlike God, but that he can be understood to be like the Father, because the Father had wished to create a creature of such a kind as would wish things like himself. And therefore he is like the Father because he is a son of will rather than of divinity; but he is unlike God because he is neither God nor from God—that is, born from God’s substance.”

Hearing this, I was astonished and did not believe it until [Note: We have added “until” on the authority of the manuscripts. This became publicly manifest when, after Acacius’ formula had been read, it was asked in what respect the Son was like the Father. “The Acacians,” says Socrates, Book II, ch. 40, “said that he was like by will alone, not by substance.” This reply caused fresh uproar and the dissolution of the whole council.] the rationale of this utterly profane similarity was publicly proclaimed by the consent of them all.

### 15. Those condemned rule again.

But those who proclaimed the *homoiousion* condemned all who, with the most shameless lack of any shame for impiety, spoke these things. [Note: That is, they deposed them; the rest they excluded from communion. We have already noted that Socrates lists nine bishops as deposed and another nine as excluded from communion. He says this occurred on the fourth day of the council, when Leonas and the Acacian faction refused to attend the session. What follows thereafter belongs to the Council of Constantinople.] The condemned men rushed to their king; received honorably, they confirmed their impieties with all the ambition they could muster, denying that the Son was like God, born from God, or Son by nature. The few ruled over the many. [Note: Printed editions read “the condemned.” More correctly the manuscripts read “the ruling”—namely, the Acacians, few in number against a far greater number of opponents, whose leading men they soon afterward drove from their sees at Constantinople. Thus Sulpicius, p. 261, as though commenting on this passage: “When the best priests had either been terrified by fear or led away into exile, all yielded to the perfidy of a few.” See Sozomen, Book IV, ch. 24.] Constantius extorted acceptance of his blasphemy by the fear of exile. Boasting that he had now conquered the Easterners because he had subjected ten delegates to his will, [Note: The Colbert codex with the Martin manuscript reads “to violence,” not “to will.” Both terms are joined below in no. 26, where the same matter is discussed again. The delegates suffered this violence on 31 December. As Sozomen relates, Book IV, ch. 23, Constantius spent that whole day and most of the ensuing night with the bishops, debating until the delegates who had arrived from the Seleucian council subscribed to the formula of faith brought from the town of Rimini. Sulpicius explains the same thing: “There they find the delegates of the Synod of Seleucia and compel them by royal force, following the example of the Westerners, to accept that corrupt faith. Most refused, but, harassed by an abusive confinement and hunger, surrendered their captive consciences.”] and having threatened both the people through the prefect and the bishops within the palace, he strengthened by heretical communion the heretical bishops appointed throughout the great cities of the East. [Note: The Vatican Basilica manuscript here adds “himself.” Therefore we nearly preferred, with Colbert and Martin, “that he would appoint heretical bishops throughout the great cities of the East and strengthen the heretical communion.” But he soon carried out what he had threatened. For other bishops were soon appointed in place of Macedonius, Cyril, Basil, Eleusius, and others.] He did absolutely nothing else than give over to the devil the world for which Christ suffered.

16. Constantius wrongly forbids words not written. He himself admits unwritten words.—Even now, as before in other matters, he employs the habitual technique of his craft: under the appearance of right he confirms what is perverse, and under the name of reason he establishes madness. “I do not wish,” he says, “words which are not written to be spoken.” I ask at last: who is to command bishops? And who is to forbid the form of apostolic preaching?

[Note: In the manuscripts of Mich. and Colb.: “who is to command a bishop?” With other books, “who is to command bishops?” is preferable; for it belongs to Christian rulers to seek the form of belief from bishops, not to prescribe it to them. Thus Athanasius, *To the Solitaries*, p. 845: “When since the creation of the world has this been heard? When did the judgment of the Church receive its authority from the emperor?” etc. Likewise, when Valentinian wished to sit as arbiter of disputes concerning the faith, Ambrose replied to him, Epistle now XXI, no. 4: “When, most gracious Emperor, have you heard that laymen judged bishops in a matter of faith?” Therefore what Constantius arrogated to himself, Hilary rightly declares to be contrary to the pattern of apostolic preaching: since it was handed down by the Apostles not only that laymen have no right over bishops in matters of faith, but also that new remedies must be devised against new heresies.]

First say whether you think it right to say: “I do not wish new preparations of medicines against new poisons; I do not wish new wars against new enemies; I do not wish fresh counsels against new plots.” For if the Arian heretics now avoid *homoiousion* because they formerly denied it, do you not now avoid it precisely so that they may still deny it?

[Note: In some manuscripts, *homoousion*, which may also rightly be read. For this is the sense: if the heretics have hitherto avoided the word *homoiousion*—how much more *homoousion*!—because they denied the thing signified by that word, namely that the Son is like the Father in substance, do you not, by ordering that this word be avoided, grant them the right to deny the thing denoted by it? Hilary argues similarly in *On the Synods*, no. 83: “Does anyone dislike that *homoousion* was accepted at the Synod of Nicaea? Whoever dislikes this must necessarily approve what was denied by the Arians.”]

The Apostle commands us to avoid novelties of words, but profane ones (1 Tim. 6:20); why do you exclude pious ones? Especially since he has said: “All Scripture, divinely inspired, is profitable” (2 Tim. 3:16). You nowhere read “unbegotten” (*innascibilis*): must it therefore be denied because it is new?

[Note: Lips. and Par.: “and this.” Other books more aptly: “from this.” Moreover, Athanasius, *Oration II against the Arians*, p. 337, shows at length that the term *innascibilis*, or “unbegotten,” is not only unknown to Scripture but also very ambiguous among pagans.]

You decree that the Son is like the Father. The Gospels do not proclaim this: why do you not avoid this word? In one case novelty is chosen; in another it is removed. Where an opening for impiety lies, novelty is admitted; but where lies the greatest and sole safeguard of religion, it is excluded.

17. Scripture hands down that the Son is equal to the Father.—But I shall not keep silent about the deceptive subtlety of your devilish mind. You decree that the Son is to be proclaimed like the Father—something not written—so that you may be silent that Christ is God equal to God, which is written. For this was the cause of the Lord’s death: “For this reason the Jews sought all the more to kill him, because he not only broke the Sabbath, but also said that God was his own Father, making himself equal to God” (John 5:18). John, speaking this, proclaimed it with a loud voice: that the Son, having professed God as his own Father, may be understood to have professed himself equal to God.

[Note: The printed editions have “having professed,” and shortly afterward omit “God.”]

But if perhaps you say that Christ denied equality between himself and God because he said, “The Son cannot do anything of himself, unless he sees the Father doing it” (ibid., 19), remember that Christ also answered regarding the Sabbath, which he was accused of violating, so that in this very matter he set forth the authority of the Father working in him and assumed for himself equality of power and honor: “Whatever things the Father does, the Son likewise does the same things” (ibid.); and again, “That they may honor the Son as they honor the Father” (ibid., 23); and, “He who does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him” (ibid.). If the power is the same, if the honor is the same, I ask: in what is equality lacking?

[Note: Most manuscripts read “assumed.” It is better understood thus: remember that Christ “assumed” equality; the editions add “saying,” against the manuscripts, although grammatical rules would require “saying.”]

18. One in nature.—But likeness pleases you: do you not hear, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30)? Did the Lord deny even this statement, “we are one”—in which neither union nor diversity was left—when the Jews again maliciously accused him of making himself God by that saying? Did he not say: “If I do not do the works of my Father, do not believe me; but if I do them, and you are unwilling to believe me, believe my works, because the Father is in me and I am in the Father” (ibid., 37–38)? I ask, what does equality with God lack? Work? Nature? Profession? For “the Father is in me and I am in the Father” (ibid., 38) is equality: it expresses the reciprocity of equality, since indwelling and being are common to both. But to do the works of his Father is nothing other than to exercise within himself the power of the Father’s divinity. And their being one does not deny equality, but, by an advance in understanding, establishes faith in equality.

19. In the same form and glory.—Therefore you forbid unwritten words to be spoken, yet you yourself use words not written and do not speak those which are written. You want the Son to be proclaimed like the Father, lest you hear the Apostle: “Though he was in the form of God, he did not consider being equal to God a thing to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2:6–7). Christ does not seize what he was—that is, being in the form of God. Being in the form of God is not equality with God, unless being in the form of a servant is not equality with humanity. But if Christ is human in the form of a servant, what else is he in the form of God but Christ God? You therefore want him proclaimed like the Father so that this may not be in your faith: “And every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father” (ibid., 11).

20. “Like according to the Scriptures” is a deceitful profession.—O your deceptive flattery! You cover waters with straw, conceal pits with turf, and place snares beneath bait. You think that you satisfy the ignorant because you say that the Son is like the Father according to the Scriptures.

[Note: Aptly Gregory Nazianzen, Oration XXI, no. 26: “These words, ‘LIKE ACCORDING TO THE SCRIPTURES,’ were a bait for the simpler sort, with the hook of impiety cast around it—a statue turning itself toward all passers-by,” etc.; and immediately before: “By the ambiguity of the written formula he opened a window to impiety: under the pretext, indeed, of revering Scripture and embracing the use of terms most thoroughly approved; but in reality substituting Arianism, disclosed in no place of Scripture, in its stead.” On Constantius’s edict and the violence used to compel subscription to this faith, see the same place, no. 30.]

Hear again the art of your impiety. Do we not rightly say that a human being is like God according to the Scriptures, because it is said: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26)? Therefore man is in the image and likeness of God the Father and God the Son.

[Note: The printed texts read “was made.” *Made* is absent from all manuscripts.]

Catholics, if asked what kind of image this is, will explain.

[Note: Thus the better manuscripts. Others, together with the printed text: “if they ask, they will be taught.” What kind of image the Son is, Hilary teaches in *On the Trinity*, book IX, no. 52.]

But now man is created in the likeness and image of God; likeness is not also proclaimed between Father and Son.

[Note: The editions alone read “between the Father.” After the foregoing words, “likeness is not also…,” supply: “but unity and equality are proclaimed.” For, as we have already read on this same passage of Genesis in *On the Trinity*, book V, no. 8: “‘Our’ has neither union nor diversity nor distinction.” For man is made, according to the truth of the expression, in the common image; and immediately afterward: “For there is one form of the image according to which man was created.”]

For the word “our” is a demonstration of equality, since there is no difference in him whose image and likeness are in the sacrament.

[Note: This passage is again illuminated by these words from book V, no. 8: “Decide what is indivisible. For those are one of whose image and likeness man was made one example.”]

21. Mere likeness is nowhere proclaimed of the Son.—But of the Son you will nowhere find mere likeness. The Apostle does indeed call him the image of God, but with an addition establishing the faith, lest you understand “image” as bodily conformation.

[Note: Codex Colb. with Martin.: “lest [you understand] a bodily image”; then “by confirmation.” Vat. bas.: “conformation.” This is stated in *On the Trinity*, book VIII, no. 49: “lest he be understood to be an image of form rather than of nature.” Earlier, instead of *faith*, “invisible” might please more. But since, according to Pope Gregory, Homily XXVI on the Gospels, faith is “the proof of things not apparent,” what is not visible pertains to faith. Moreover, that addition by which our faith in Christ’s divinity is confirmed is placed, in *On the Trinity*, book VIII, no. 48 and following, not in the word *invisible* alone but also in the accompanying words of the Apostle.]

For he says: “Who is the image of the invisible God” (Col. 1:15), so that the image of the invisible God might be invisible also by virtue of the fact that he himself is invisible.

[Note: Some manuscripts: “by which he himself is invisible.” Then Mich.: “the invisible God was image.” Hilary dwells deliberately on explaining this apostolic passage because the Acacians, proclaiming the Son like the Father, boasted that Paul had preceded them in this. He also insists that Christ, insofar as he is invisible, is the image of the invisible God, so that no place may be given to those who asserted that Father and Son differ in nature because the Father is invisible while the Son is visible.]

But God assigned likeness together with image to man, lest it be thought that the property of truth belonged to one for whom likeness was added to image.

[Note: Lips. and Par.: “with image.” Other books more rightly: “together with image,” as though with the word *image*: namely, where God said that man was made in God’s image, he also added “according to likeness.”]

Finally, where equality of power is indicated, likeness is also shown in the Son’s working; but where an advance in understanding is proclaimed, it is then said: “Whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does the same things” (John 5:19).

[Note: The printed editions read “is made equal.” Codex Colb. has “may be made equal,” from which we adopted “is made equal.” The particle *and*, equivalent to “also,” was wrongly removed by Lipsius. Later, instead of “when, however, the advance… then,” one should read: “when an advance in understanding is proclaimed, it is then said.” This is the sense: likeness is nowhere proclaimed of God’s Son except with additions through which his equality with the Father is understood; but this is more clearly signified by the following passage of John, in which equality of power is demonstrated not merely by similarity of operation but, so to speak, by identity of works. This is illustrated by the final words of no. 18: “Their being one does not deny equality, but by an advance in understanding establishes faith in equality.” There “advance in understanding” is what is here meant by “progress of understanding.”]

“To do likewise” was thought insufficient unless the same things were done which were done alike.

[Note: The editions read “likewise,” against the manuscripts.]

Thus likeness in doing is piously demonstrated in the proper identity of the things done. There is also in the Lord the likeness of sinful flesh (Rom. 8:2); but he does not have likeness of flesh: rather, he has likeness of sinful flesh.

[Note: Supply: because he has the reality of flesh.]

Thus what is in the form of God is God; but what is in the likeness of sinful flesh is a likeness of humanity, since it is in human appearance and outside human sin.

[Note: Erasmus, Miraeus, Lipsius, and Paris: “what is in the form of man is.” I do not know whether this has authority. Then the manuscripts Colb. and Martin. read “is God.”]

[Note: More recent manuscripts: “is in human stature or nature”; Lipsius and Paris: “is in human nature”—wrongly. For here *statura* is synonymous with the Apostle’s *habitus*, indicating in Christ a likeness but not the reality of sinful flesh. As Augustine fittingly says, Epistle now CLXIV, no. 19: “From the Virgin he took a true substance of flesh indeed, yet not flesh of sin, because [it was] not from a substance of flesh either sown or conceived; nevertheless mortal and changeable through the ages, as most like sinful flesh without sin.” See Hilary himself, *On the Trinity*, book X, no. 25.]

What, then, is this crafty profession of your religion: to say that the Son is like the Father according to the Scriptures, when only man was made in the image and likeness of God? Why, then, do you deceive by words? Why evade by artifice? Why do you not piously say that he is equal to God—for this is according to the Scriptures?

22. Once the Son’s equality has been affirmed, likeness may be proclaimed.—But do you fear that by calling him equal you signify him to be unbegotten? Understand the truth: he is understood to be equal to God because he professed God to be his own Father; and to declare that God is his own Father is a demonstration of birth.

[Note: It seems that one should read here: “because he professed God as his own Father.” For John’s words, “making himself equal to God,” are immediately joined to “because he said that God was his own Father”; and Hilary interprets “his own Father” as “a Father proper to himself.”]

For my part, likeness is holy, lest occasion be given to union; but I must not grant it to you, because I shall first piously confess him equal and the same, and afterward like. I shall religiously proclaim him like the Father and also like God; but I shall proclaim him like in such a way that I always place before likeness this saying: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). But you contradict all these things, because you defend likeness as an excuse.

[Note: Bad.: “of excuse”; other editions: “for excuse”; manuscripts: “by excuse.” We think that “by agreement” should certainly be read.]

You deny the Son in respect of birth; you deny God in respect of nature; you deny likeness in respect of equality; you deny the true in respect of unity. And now I ask what likeness you leave him, when you grant him no property of that by which he is Son.

23. Constantius’s inconsistency in faith.—I now ask you, Constantius, in what faith, finally, do you believe? For I proceed through the periods of your alterations, in which, descending to the lowest depth of your blasphemy, you have run down steep stages.

[Note: Printed texts: “For I now do not know your faith through the periods of your alterations, in which each one has run into one abyss of his blasphemy…”—a confused and interpolated passage, into which “I do not know your faith” was added contrary to the evidence of all manuscripts, by whose aid it is now corrected. Although where these exhibit *ego* or *ergo*, we judged that *pergo* should be restored; nor would we shrink from that. In the Martin manuscript it reads: “Therefore until now, through the periods of your alteration, down to the bottom,” etc.]

For after the first true faith of the Synod of Nicaea, when another council was gathered at Antioch in 341, you renew your faith. But what commonly happens to unskilled builders happened to you, who are always dissatisfied with their own work: you continually destroy what you continually build. And lest you accuse me of being an unfair judge of your intention, I shall state what displeases you in that same faith of the Dedication.

[Note: Codex Colb.: “in the same faith of the Dedication”; others: “of the true faith.” The editions alone read *synodicen*, where the Mich. manuscript has “of the Synod of Nicaea,” the Carn. manuscript “in place of the synod,” and the rest “of the Nicene synod.”]

[Note: Thus Vat. bas. One may also approve with Colb. and Martin: “namely that.” Others, less well, with the editions: “that does not deceive me at all.” Hilary calls it “yours” because the Antiochene faith was set forth in Constantius’s presence and with his approval. Its words follow; in previous printed texts they had been interpolated against manuscript authority: “The Fathers said that the Son was begotten of the Father, God from God,” etc. Since Hilary promises Constantius that he will state what is his, he ought not to state it under another name. Who could believe that Hilary would have honored with the glorious name of Fathers those who assembled at Antioch? But whoever previously read “Nicene” in place of “Dedication” attempted here to make the passage fit his reading.]

Unless I am mistaken, this is yours: “He who was begotten from the Father: God from God, whole from whole, one from one, perfect from perfect, king from king, unchangeable image of divinity and essence, power and glory.”

[Note: The editions read “unchangeable.” The manuscripts more correctly read “unchangeable [accusative],” referring to the word *Son*, which appears in the preceding words of the Antiochene formula, rather than to “image,” as is clear from *On the Synods*, no. 29.]

I, indeed, remaining grounded within the faith written by the Fathers at Nicaea, have no need of this; yet by correcting these things you annul them, and, without damage to my faith, you seek from yourself an occasion for faithlessness.

[Note: First Paris edition: “and remaining, not I but…” Others: “I remain, which not I but…” All manuscripts: “and remaining, not I but…” Yet it is evident that *egeo* (“I need”) should be read for *ego* (“I”), so that the text may no longer be deprived of sense. This is confirmed by *To Constantius*, book II, no. 8: “For I possess the faith within myself; I HAVE NO NEED of what is external. What I have received I hold, nor do I alter what belongs to God.” By the same reasoning below, no. 25, where Hilary reproaches Constantius for ordering *homoiousion* to be anathematized by those who had employed it, he shortly afterward explains in what sense he reproaches him: “although the term is idle and superfluous for our faith,” etc.]

Then, after the Synod of Sardica in 347, you again stir up at Sirmium in 351 all the concern of your Catholic doctrine against Photinus. But you are immediately horrified by what was contained in both those confessions: “But the holy and Catholic Church recognizes as alien those who say that the Son of God is from things not existing, or from another substance and not from God, and that there was once a time or age when he was not.”

[Note: Two manuscripts read “true.” The others, “both.” With the printed texts “both” is preferable—namely, both the pseudo-Sardican and the Sirmian confession against Photinus. For the words following belong to both confessions. Although Hilary calls the Philippopolitan assembly Sardican, since he observes that it consisted of the faction favored by Constantius, he should not be thought to have confused it with the Catholic Synod of Sardica.]

You disagree with your own statements and fight as an enemy against your own party.

[Note: Erasmus, Miraeus, Lipsius, and Paris: “you with these very [statements].” Concinnius and Bad., with the manuscripts: “your own [statements].”]

You overthrow old things by new ones; you in turn annul the new things by a further novel correction; and you again condemn what has been corrected by correcting it once more. You also adopt, against the ravings of Hosius and the additions of Ursacius and Valens, condemnations of your corrections; but shortly thereafter you decide that all your own formulations must be corrected—or rather condemned.

[Note: Two manuscripts read “corrected.” Hilary calls the formula issued at Sirmium in 357 “the ravings of Hosius,” because Hosius ratified it by his subscription and perhaps was even author of some of its words; “the additions of Ursacius and Valens,” because, as was their custom, they enlarged it with certain ambiguous propositions; and “the corrections of Constantius,” because, by approving it, he corrected what he had approved at Antioch, Philippopolis, and Sirmium against Photinus. The “condemnations” of that formula mean the definitions of the Eastern bishops assembled at Ancyra in 358; these were shortly afterward corrected by the third Sirmian formula, which was also somewhat altered before being brought to Ariminum. The words quoted below are from canon 11 of the Ancyran assembly.]

For you are offended by these few words most hostile to you: “And if anyone says that the Father is older in time than the only-begotten Son, and that the Son is younger than the Father, let him be anathema.”

24. There is no faith where there is not one faith.—We do not make false accusations about doctrines which, after the Nicene Synod, were annulled, and concerning which we have undertaken to complain.

[Note: In the Martin and Colb. manuscripts: “I have undertaken to complain.” The word “undertaken” also appears in the others.]

For even if it were affirmed that no defects lie hidden in all these, nevertheless no ground of religious intention would exist in them. For devising evil lies in changing good things, and unnecessary correction is an opportunity for perversity. I pass over why you annul what was accomplished by our Fathers at Nicaea; for you do not agree with them. This alone I ask: why do you condemn your own statements?

[Note: Thus Codex Colb. Others read “I complain”; the editions, “I shall complain.”]

For the Apostle proclaims one faith and one baptism (Eph. 4:5). Therefore whatever you have besides the one faith is faithlessness, not faith. For when, by correcting a faith, you condemn it, you establish a condemnation of faith: among you, one faith is abolished by another, which in turn must be abolished by yet another.

25. According to the Arians, no one now remains guiltless.—Whose episcopal hand have you henceforth left innocent? What tongue have you not compelled to false speech? What heart have you not changed so that it condemns its earlier opinion? You decree the condemnation of *homoousion*, the faith of antiquity and safeguard of piety.

[Note: That is, by the confession of faith composed under Acacius and read at the Synod of Seleucia, in which *homoousion* and *homoiousion* are rejected. These words of Gregory Nazianzen, Oration XXI, are not discordant: “Having cast up a rampart and battered it with engines, he overthrew the word *consubstantial*, a pious and ancient doctrine and champion of the Trinity.”]

You ordained that *homoiousion* be anathematized by the very persons who had used it.

[Note: Theodoret, *Compendium of Heretical Fables*, book IV, chapter 5, relates that this term was devised by Macedonius. Yet it is certain that it was employed by those who adhered to him. It is no less certain that those same persons were later compelled at Constantinople to condemn the term.]

Although this term is idle for our faith, it is nevertheless a condemnation of faith for those who revoke it.

[Note: Thus Codex Colb. with Martin. In other books it is corrupt; this not only conflicts with *On the Synods*, no. 72, but also with no. 22 of this work: “For my part, likeness is holy, lest occasion be given to union”; and no. 24: “Even if it were affirmed that no faults lie hidden in all these [formulas maintaining *homoiousion*].”]

You also condemn the term *substance*.

[Note: Namely, by accepting the exposition of faith which Athanasius, *On the Synods*, reports as read at Ariminum; Theodoret, book II, chapter 21, as subscribed at Nicaea in Thrace; and Socrates, book II, chapter 41, as approved at Constantinople.]

By this term you had falsely represented yourself to Westerners as pious both at the Synod of Sardica and at Sirmium; yet the term, accepted on prophetic authority, contained the understanding of faith.

[Note: That is, when you approved and professed what had been defined at the pseudo-Sardican and Sirmian synods: “Those who say that the Son of God is from things not existing, or from another substance,” etc. Thus Baronius, under the year 347, no. 42, wrongly invented from this passage of Hilary certain letters of Constantius to the Synod of Sardica in which he professed the Son to be of one substance with the Father. Even after the Ancyran assembly, letters of the same emperor written to the Antiochenes against Eudoxius and reported by Sozomen, book IV, chapter 14, maintain the term *substance*. There one reads: “Recall, I ask you, those first statements, when we were investigating the faith, by which it was demonstrated that our Savior is the Son of God and like the Father according to substance.” Here Constantius seems to recall the faith set forth among the Antiochenes at the Dedication—regarded as the first confession by those who rejected Nicaea—and to refer to his own words: “an unchangeable image of divinity and essence [καὶ οὐσίας], power and glory.”]

[Note: Bad. and Erasmus: “accepted”; Miraeus, Lipsius, and Paris: “having accepted.” The manuscripts more correctly read “accepted,” namely the term *substance*. Phoebadius of Agen proves that it is used in Scripture and that it applies to the Son’s generation when the Prophet says, “From the womb before the morning star I begot you.”]

Therefore you order everything previously approved to be condemned, and compel what has always been disapproved to be sanctified. O criminal man, who make the Church a mockery!

[Note: Colb. manuscript with Martin: “who make a shrine”; the others: “who make a mockery,” where the printed texts have “that mockery.”]

Only dogs return to their vomit; you have compelled Christ’s priests to swallow again what they had spat out. You order them, by their confessions, to approve against themselves what they had previously condemned.

[Note: The printed texts omit “themselves,” restored on the authority of Vat. bas., Martin, and Colb. manuscripts. Moreover, “in themselves” here means “against themselves,” that is, “in opposition to themselves.”]

By denying, they acquit those whom they had held guilty, and make themselves guilty. You have driven all things into impiety and guilt, since everyone either establishes himself to be guilty and impious from his present statements, or confesses it from his former ones. Truth does not admit falsehood, nor does religion endure impiety.

26. Constantius’s violence against Easterners and Africans.—You call yourself a Christian, but by your own testimony you are not; nor do your deeds correspond to your profession.

[Note: Two manuscripts: “you say and proclaim, but you are not.” Shortly afterward, only the editions have “nor to your confession.”]

For you have subjected Eastern bishops to your will—not only to your will, but to violence.

[Note: This line, “Eastern bishops to your will,” was absent from the earlier printed texts and is restored from the manuscripts. It marks the violence inflicted upon Easterners who defended *homoiousion*, so that they might accept the blasphemy of Ariminum.]

You demand that the subscriptions of Africans be returned to you—subscriptions by which they had condemned the blasphemy of Ursacius and Valens.

[Note: Colb. and Martin manuscripts: “they condemned the blasphemies.” Scholars interpret this blasphemy as the second Sirmian formula described in *On the Synods*. They think the Africans did what the Gauls did, of whom Hilary testifies in *On the Synods*, no. 2, that they condemned the impiety of an unbelieving confession sent from Sirmium. They distinguish, however, that the Gauls received it immediately after its publication from its authors themselves, while it was sent to the Africans through Basil, a most vigorous adversary of its authors, when they were already ashamed of it. Hence they think that Basil is accused by the Acacians in Sozomen, book IV, chapter 24, of having written that he was in communion with Germinius, Ursacius, and Valens while nevertheless accusing them before the African bishops; and shortly afterward, of having become a cause of discord and disturbance to Illyrians, Italians, and Africans. They also therefore judge confirmed the view of those who understand the Sirmian formula—extorted from its holders by the emperor’s edict and by threats and penalties—not as Athanasius, *On the Synods*, p. 914, the third, but as Socrates, book II, chapter 30, and Sozomen, book IV, chapter 6, the second. Yet Hilary does not here say that copies of the blasphemy of Ursacius and Valens were extorted, but only the subscriptions by which it had been condemned. And that Athanasius’s view appears preferable will be shown in the notes on the final Fragment.]

You threaten those who resist and finally send men to plunder them. What? Do you suppose that Christ judges only by a written document, and that God needs a little sheet of paper in order to convict the will? Or that what has been written once and violently torn away by you can be erased from the conscience by the power of divine authority? The sheets of paper will indeed follow you into ashes, but the condemnations of the guilty will live before God.

[Note: The word “into” is absent from the Martin and Colb. manuscripts.]

You accomplish one thing only: by fearing, posterity will be instructed what it ought to decree against them.

27. Arians declare war on the dead.—And to what great advances in impiety you proceed! Other mortals, indeed, have always waged wars against the living, since beyond death one human being has no cause against another. But for you there is no end to enmity. You attack our Fathers, already received into eternal rest, and perversely invade their decrees. The Apostle teaches us to share in the remembrances of the saints (Rom. 12:13); you have compelled those remembrances to be condemned.

[Note: The Latin text currently has *necessitatibus* (“needs”), while the Greek has ταῖς χρείαις (“needs”). Curcellaeus, however, reads ταῖς μνείαις (“remembrances”). Out of reverence for the Fathers, the Catholic bishops write to Constantius from Ariminum, Fragment VIII, no. 2, that it would be unlawful for them to depart from the Nicene faith, which so many saints, confessors, and successors of martyrs had composed.]

Is there anyone today, living or dead, whose words you have not annulled? You have utterly abolished even the episcopates now existing.

[Note: We add *utterly* with all manuscripts. Constantius utterly abolishes episcopates when, by embracing a new faith, he condemns all bishops of former times, and likewise those who, though they agree with him, nevertheless received their episcopate from persons whom they now condemn by anathema. See *On the Synods*, no. 91.]

For no one has not now been condemned in himself, and has not himself also condemned the person from whom he received the priesthood. With whose memory among the saints will anyone now share communion? The three hundred and eighteen bishops assembled at Nicaea are anathema to you; then all who afterward were involved in the various confessions are anathema. Even your own father, long dead, is anathema to you: he who took care for the Nicene Synod, which you disturb by defaming it with false opinions, and which you attack, against human and divine judgment, with your few profane satellites.

[Note: Jerome writes in the *Chronicle* that Constantine fell from baptism into heresy. Lucifer of Cagliari likewise relates in *On Apostate Kings* that he went over to the Arians, and in book I *For Athanasius* that he hated Athanasius because he refused to be an Arian. Tillus comments: “Hence it appears that the Emperor Constantine the Great was an Arian in old age, as many historians also relate.” Yet not only Hilary, but Athanasius, *To the Solitaries*; Epiphanius, *Heresies* 69.12; Ambrose, *On the Death of Theodosius*, no. 40; and others, transmitted something different in their writings. Indeed, the Catholic Fathers of the Council of Ariminum, Fragment VIII, no. 2, testify that Constantine, holding the Nicene faith, was baptized and departed to God’s rest.]

[Note: Martin and Colb. manuscripts read “profane,” and shortly afterward, “now, by powerful sovereignty, even in the future,” where Bandinus and Latinius preferred “by a ruler possessing the kingdom.”]

But you are not permitted, even by a powerful present sovereignty, to prejudge the future. For letters survive which teach that what you consider criminal was then piously accepted.

[Note: The same manuscripts read “is taught.” The principal reference is to the term *homoousion*, whose ambiguity heretics customarily objected to, as appears from these words in *On the Synods*, no. 91: “Our Fathers after the Synod of Nicaea interpreted the proper meaning of *homoousion* religiously. Books survive; conscience remains.”]

Hear the holy understanding of the words; hear the undisturbed constitution of the Church; hear your father’s professed faith; hear the confident assurance of human hope; hear the public judgment condemning heresy; and understand that you are an enemy of divine religion, an enemy of the memories of the saints, and a rebellious heir of paternal piety.

[Note: Bad. and Erasmus read “authors”; Ludovicus Miraeus and Latinius, “forefathers.” The preceding words explain the command to share in the memories of the saints.]

[Note: In the Vatican Basilica manuscript the book ends here. Everything which follows has been transferred here from the books *On the Trinity* and has not been very suitably stitched on. It almost came to be suppressed altogether.]

Addendum from the books *On the Trinity*.

28. From Book II on the Trinity, §6. The Father is he from whom [Col. 0603B] all that exists has its subsistence. He himself is, in Christ and through Christ, the origin of all things. But [Note: [Col. 0604D] The word *esse* (“to be”) is absent from the manuscripts.] his being is in himself: not deriving what he is from elsewhere, but possessing from himself and in himself that which he is; infinite, because he is not contained in anything, but all things are within him; always beyond place, because he is not contained in a place; always before age, because time comes from him. Run with your mind: if you suppose that there is anything ultimate to him, you will always find him; for whenever you direct your thought, there is always something upon which to direct it. But your always directing thought toward his place [584] is to you what his being without end is to him. Speech will fail in him; nature will not be enclosed. Turn time over again: you will always find being; and when the number of reckonings fails in speech, God’s perpetual being nonetheless does not fail. Stir up understanding and embrace the whole with your mind: [Col. 0603C] you grasp nothing. This whole has something remaining; and what remains is always within the whole. Therefore it is neither a whole, if something remains beyond it; nor is it something remaining, if it contains all that is whole. For what remains is a portion, whereas “all” is that which is whole. But God is both everywhere and wholly everywhere. Thus [Note: [Col. 0604D] Thus Bad. and Er., as in *On the Trinity*. Other books have “religion.”] he surpasses the region of understanding: outside him there is nothing, and it belongs to him always to be. This is the truth of God’s mystery; this is the name, in the Father, of an inscrutable nature: God invisible, ineffable, infinite—before whom speech must fall silent when it would speak, sense must grow dull when it would investigate, and understanding must be constrained when it would comprehend.

29. From Book III on the Trinity, §18. Therefore, wishing to establish for us faith in this his birth, the Son set before us examples in his works, so that by the efficacy of his [Col. 0603D] ineffable deeds we might be taught concerning the power of his ineffable birth. Water becomes wine; five loaves, after five thousand men have been fed, apart from the rest distinguished by sex and age, fill twelve baskets with fragments. The thing is seen and not known; it happens and is not understood; its rationale is not apprehended, its result is forced upon us. It is foolish, however, to press the accusation of inquiry in a matter in which that from which inquiry proceeds cannot by its nature be comprehended. For as the Father is ineffable in that he is unbegotten, so the Son cannot be described in that he is only-begotten; because he who is begotten is the image of the Unbegotten. For when we apprehend an image with mind and words, it is necessary [Note: [Col. 0604D] Manuscripts: “it is necessary that he follow along with him whose image he is”: wrongly. Still worse are the printed editions: “Then it is necessary that we apprehend the image with mind and words when we attain him whose image it is.”] that we also attain him whose image it is. But we pursue invisible things and attempt incomprehensible ones, though understanding is confined to visible [Col. 0604B] and bodily things. We do not blush for our folly; we do not accuse ourselves of irreligion, while we malign God’s mysteries and powers. We ask how the Son is Son, whence he is Son, with what loss to the Father, or from what portion he was born. You had examples in these works, so that you might believe God able to effect things whose manner of effecting you cannot understand.

30. From §19 of the same book. You ask how the Son was born according to the Spirit; I question you about bodily matters. I do not ask how he was born of a virgin—whether flesh, generating perfect flesh from itself, suffered a loss of itself. And assuredly it did not receive back what it brought forth; but flesh produced flesh without the shamefulness of our elements, and, itself undiminished, generated a perfect being from its own substance. Indeed, it would be lawful [Col. 0604C] to judge not impossible in God what we know to have been possible in a human being through his power.

31. From §20. But you, whoever you are, who pursue matters that cannot be investigated and set yourself up as a weighty judge of divine secrets and powers, I ask you to furnish me, an unlearned man who only believes all things concerning God as they have been spoken by him, at least an explanation of this event. I hear of the Lord, and because I believe what is written, I know that after the resurrection he often presented himself to be seen bodily by many who did not believe—[Note: [Col. 0604D] Printed editions: “I believe Thomas,” etc. Manuscripts: “Certainly Thomas says that he will not believe unless he touches his wounds.”] certainly by Thomas, who would not believe unless he had touched his wounds, as he says: “Unless I see in his hands [Note: [Col. 0604D] In the manuscripts, “the mark.”] the mark of the nails, and put my finger into the place of the nails, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe” (John 20:25). The Lord accommodates himself to every weakness of [Col. 0604D] our understanding, and, intending to satisfy the doubt [Col. 0605A] of unbelievers, performs a secret work of invisible power.
