You, whoever [Note: [Col. 0605C] Manuscripts: “whoever you are, a heretic.”] you may be, investigator of heavenly things, explain the rationale of this event.

The disciples were shut in and, after the Lord’s passion, had gathered and sat together in secret. The Lord, intending to confirm Thomas’s faith on the conditions proposed, stood among them and offered him the opportunity to touch his body and handle his wound. Certainly, if he was to be recognized as pierced, he necessarily brought the body in which he had been pierced. I ask, then, through what part of the closed house he brought himself in bodily form. For the Evangelist carefully stated: “Jesus came, the doors being shut, and stood in the midst of his disciples” [Note: [Col. 0605C] Here the manuscripts lack only the word “his.”] (ibid., 26). Did he penetrate the construction of the walls and pass through the impenetrable solidity of wood? For he stood bodily, not as an appearance [Col. 0605B] or deception.

Let the eyes of your mind, then, follow the entrance of him who penetrates; and let the sight of your understanding enter the shut house with him. Everything is intact and barred; but behold, he stands in the middle, he for whom all things are passable through his own power. You malign invisible things; I demand from you an explanation of visible ones. Nothing yields from its solidity, nor do wood and stones, by their nature, admit anything as by an imperceptible slipping through. The Lord’s body does not cease to be itself so as to reconstitute itself from nothing. From where, then, is he who stands in the middle? Here both sense and speech yield; the truth of the event lies beyond human reason. Must we therefore lie about the birth [Note: [Col. 0605C] Here again the printed editions read “we are deceived”; they are again corrected from the manuscripts.] as we do about the Lord’s entrance? Shall we say that it did not occur because we do not grasp its rationale, and, because our understanding ceases, let the effect of the event itself also cease? But the faithfulness of the event overcomes our lie. The Lord stood in the midst of the disciples while the house was shut, and the Son was born from the Father. Do not deny that he stood there because, through the weakness of your understanding, you do not [Note: [Col. 0605C] In the manuscripts, “follow.”] comprehend the entrance of him who stood. Do not fail to know that from the unbegotten and [Col. 0606A] perfect God the Father, the only-begotten and perfect God the Son was born, because the power of generation surpasses the sense and speech of human nature.

32. From §21. Moreover, all the works of the world might be present to us as testimony, so that we should not think it permissible to doubt God’s deeds and powers. But our unbelief rushes against truth itself, and we violently break in to destroy God’s power. If it were permitted, we would raise both bodies and hands to heaven; we would drive the sun and the other stars from the limits of their yearly courses; we would mingle the retreat and advance of Ocean; we would restrain even the streams of springs and turn back the courses of rivers; we would shake the foundations of the earth, and in all these works of God rage with parricidal fury. But it is well that the nature of our bodies restrains us within [Col. 0606B] this necessary moderation. Certainly, we do not deceive ourselves about what we would do if it were permitted: for, because [Note: [Col. 0606C] Here too the printed editions prefix a negative particle, against the manuscripts.] we can, with the profane audacity of our will we tear apart the nature of truth and wage war against God with our words.

33. From Book II on the Trinity, §9. Let the pain of complaints cease. For you, whoever you are who seek these things, I do not summon back to heights, nor stretch out into breadth, nor lead down into depth. Will you not calmly remain ignorant of the Creator’s birth, while ignorant of the origin of creation? I ask only this: do you perceive that you have been begotten, and do you understand what things are generated from you? I do not ask whence you have drawn sensation, whence you have received life, whence you have attained understanding, what the thing in you is—smell, sensation, sight, hearing. Surely no one is ignorant of what he does. [Col. 0606C] I ask whence you bestow these things upon those [Note: [Col. 0606C] Several manuscripts: “by which you are held.” Then Mich.: “afflict the heart,” not “fasten the heart.”] whom you beget; how you implant sensation, kindle eyes, fasten the heart. If you can, explain these things. Thus you possess what you do not know and bestow what you do not understand: calmly unlearned in your own affairs, you are arrogantly ignorant in God’s.

[BOOK AGAINST AUXENTIUS.]

[Col. 0605]

## PREFACE TO THE BOOK AGAINST AUXENTIUS

[Col. 0605D] I. In this elegant book, to speak with Jerome (*On Ecclesiastical Writers*), Hilary informs Catholics about his dealings with Auxentius at Milan. It cannot have been published in the time of Constantius, and therefore before the year 361, although the words of Facundus of Hermiane, to be considered in their place, seem to imply this (Facundus, vol. III of the *Spicilegium*, p. 118). Nor is the view of Baronius and Blondel any more consistent with the truth: they would have it written in the year 569, although Jerome, Sulpicius Severus, and Gregory of Tours establish that Hilary had by then departed this life.

Both were misled by an erroneous reading in earlier editions, in which Auxentius wrote in §12: “that the unity of six hundred bishops ought not, after so many labours, to be reopened through the contention of a few men, THE DECREES HAVING BEEN REJECTED ten years before”; this made him appear to complain of contempt for the decrees of Rimini, issued ten years earlier. But from this same reading, now corrected, the date of the work may be discerned more truly. For, instead of *abjectis decretis ante annos decem* (“the decrees having been rejected ten years before”), one must read *ab abjectis ante annos decem* (“by those who were rejected ten years before”); and Auxentius shortly afterwards declares whom he understands to be those rejected, in these final words of his letter: “For thus Your Serenity will know that those who were long ago deposed—that is, Hilary and Eusebius—strive everywhere to create schisms.” It follows only that Auxentius’s letter, and therefore the remainder of the work, was written ten years after these two very courageous bishops had been rejected. Now no one is unaware that Eusebius was driven into exile by the Council of Milan in 355, and Hilary by the Council of Béziers in 356.

II. Furthermore, in order to establish the date of this work more certainly, it will be useful to ascertain when Valentinian was staying at Milan. For it is clear that Hilary’s encounter with Auxentius took place while he was there. Rescripts issued at Milan in that very year—on the Kalends of June, the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July, the fourteenth day before the Kalends of September, the day before the Nones of November, and likewise the fifteenth and seventh days before the Kalends of December—demonstrate that Valentinian was repeatedly there in 364. Various rescripts likewise make clear that he spent the greater part of the following year in the same city. Moreover, Ammianus’s testimony (*Book XXVI*, ch. 6), together with several other records, establishes that Valentinian came to Paris in November 365 and did not subsequently leave Gaul. Since it is therefore clear that the aforementioned encounter occurred before November 365, it remains only to ask whether it took place in 365 or in 364. Neither can be determined with certainty; but the latter will appear far more probable when the occasion of this encounter and the sequence of events in it have been considered.

III. Eusebius of Vercelli, according to Rufinus, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book I, [Col. 0607C] ch. 30, was returning to Italy after the Alexandrian Council of 362 when he found our Hilary there diligently labouring to restore the churches of that region, and he joined him in the same work. Now, just as there is no doubt that these two men then made it their chief endeavour to free Italy from Auxentius as from a most deadly plague, so it must not be doubted that this heretic, who knew how to feign faith when expedient, tried, as soon as the opportunity afforded by the new emperor arose, to anticipate them before him—men from whom he foresaw his own destruction impending.

Thus he came about to slander Hilary and Eusebius before the emperor (§14) as authors of schisms and disturbers of the Milanese church, while they unjustly branded him (§5) before the people with the mark of heresy, although he professed, together with the Emperor, that Christ is God and truly the Son of God, begotten before times (§12). Then (§6) the king, devoted to peace, perhaps judged that, just as it would be foreign to his clemency forcibly to take from Auxentius by his own arrival the churches which Auxentius had occupied, so it was unworthy of royal majesty for him personally to practise the worship of his religion in corners. He rejoiced that, as it seemed to him, catholic faith was maintained by Auxentius, and that by his arrival he could restore to one communion the people who until then had recoiled from their bishop. Therefore, without delay, he issued a stern edict (ibid.) forbidding anyone henceforth to disturb the Milanese church.

Hilary, judging that this edict ought not to be obeyed, even by urgent petition [Col. 0608A] represented that Auxentius believed otherwise than the Emperor himself or all others supposed. Hence, by the king’s order, came the encounter whose proceedings are related in this book. All these matters which can be gathered—or at least inferred—from Hilary’s own words agree much better with the time when Valentinian first came to Milan, and therefore with the year 364, than with the following year.

IV. Nor should it trouble us that Auxentius calls Eusebius and Hilary rejected or deposed ten years before. Those are the words of a heretic in the heat of controversy, speaking hyperbolically in order to make his case appear better; just as shortly before he is not ashamed to boast of the unity of six hundred bishops (§12) at the Council of Rimini, where, according to Sulpicius, with whom Athanasius agrees (*Sulpicius*, p. 252; Athanasius, *On the Synods*, p. 874 and *Letter to the Africans*), not much more than four hundred assembled—or, according to the Arian Maximinus (in Augustine’s debate with that same Maximinus, §2), only three hundred and thirty. And perhaps this man, so eager to feign faith, would scarcely have dared so confidently to praise in 365 a synod which was soon repudiated by all.

V. For the completion of this treatise, the booklet is lacking which Hilary testifies that he presented to the king and attached to his letter (§6); and the creed of Rimini is also lacking, which Auxentius recalls at the end of that booklet that he delivered to Valentinian together with his own booklet.

VI. Nor were there lacking those who doubted whether we possessed a genuine copy of that exposition of Auxentius’s faith, a copy of which is promised in §9. For although the booklet appended at the end of this letter of Auxentius bears that title, the ambiguous words “the true God, the Son born,” do not occur in it—the words which Hilary, in §7, exposes and censures as fraudulently constructed by Auxentius in order to deceive. Further, in the same booklet there appears to them a profound silence concerning the proceedings at Nicaea in Thrace, although, as is clear from §7, Auxentius declares them holy from the very beginning of his discourse.

VII. But the first and principal reason for doubt disappears when the ambiguity of the words is revealed by the restored text of the very ancient codex of St Peter in the Vatican. The second, arising from the different names given to one and the same synod, is easily resolved. For those things which Auxentius falsely boasts as having been done at Rimini by six hundred men, in order to exalt the character of his faith, Hilary declares to have been done at Nicaea in Thrace by very few, in order to diminish it. In fact, the creed of the Council of Rimini was no other than that issued at Nicaea in Bithynia; nor were there properly any proceedings other than those by which Arius’s followers were struck with an anathema. But because the formula coined at Nicaea in Thrace and subscribed by a few was finally imposed at Rimini by force, Hilary permits that formula—which he had previously called Nicene in Thrace—to be called also the creed of the Council of Rimini, saying, “But let us say nothing about the synod of Rimini.” Since he immediately adds that it “has been religiously dissolved by all,” he sufficiently shows that Auxentius’s cause receives no help from it on that account either.

VIII. Thus, from both grounds which had made Auxentius’s booklet doubtful, it is now more certainly established as his. The other points also agree. For in it this crafty heretic professes in §13 what Hilary notes that he had asserted: that he had never known Arius. In §14 he likewise testifies that Hilary, once deposed, ought to assume neither the role of accuser nor that of judge; this, the vigorous confessor of Christ relates in §6, was objected to him by Auxentius. Although Hilary refutes certain things as asserted by Auxentius which do not occur in his booklet, they undoubtedly concern the proceedings themselves at Nicaea in Thrace or at Rimini, proceedings which Auxentius embraced wholeheartedly and took care to append to his booklet.

IX. In an ancient codex of the church of Chartres, this whole work bears the title: “Letter to Catholics concerning Auxentius”; in five others: “Treatise,” or “Book against Auxentius, the Arian Bishop of Milan.” Jerome supports these titles, calling it an elegant booklet against Auxentius. The received title, “Book against the Arians, or Auxentius of Milan,” has been copied from a very ancient manuscript of St Peter’s at Rome. In fact, it is a letter to Catholics against the Arians, whom the opening concerns, but specifically against Auxentius, concerning Hilary’s dealings with whom he informs the Catholics. In all these matters he conducts himself toward the Emperor, from whom he had suffered injustice, with a calm and respectful spirit. He makes it clear that he does not know how to be angry on his own account; and by his example confirms that the highest reverence must be shown to rulers—especially that they must be forgiven when they have sinned through ignorance or error.

[Col. 0609]

*(WRITTEN IN THE YEAR 364.)* 593–594  
**ONE BOOK OF SAINT HILARY AGAINST THE ARIANS, OR AUXENTIUS OF MILAN. (C)**

To the most beloved brethren—bishops remaining in the faith of the Fathers and detesting the Arian heresy—and [Col. 0609C] to all the congregations: Hilary, your fellow-servant, eternal greeting in the Lord. [Note: [Col. 0609D] We restore from the manuscripts the words “eternal in the Lord.”]

1. Hilary vainly attempts to establish true peace.—The name of peace is indeed attractive, and the idea of unity is beautiful; but who can doubt that the only unity which is peace for the Church and the Gospels is that of Christ? This is the peace which he spoke to the Apostles after the glory of his passion (John 20:19), which, when about to depart, he commended to them as the pledge of his eternal command [Note: [Col. 0609D] The manuscripts unanimously read *habituris* (“to those who were to have it”), a phrase admittedly rather singular but not without all meaning.]. This peace, beloved brethren, we have taken care both to seek when lost, to restore when disturbed, and to preserve when found. [Note: [Col. 0609D] Hilary modestly intimates this about himself. Throughout his exile he did not cease seeking lost peace; after the Council of Rimini he restored disturbed peace; and with the utmost zeal he preserved it when it had in large measure been recovered. Yet, forgetting what lay behind, as though he had accomplished nothing, because he had vainly attempted to secure it for the city of Milan, he adds what follows.] But neither the sins of our time have deserved that we should become either participants in or authors of this peace, nor have the forerunners and ministers of the approaching Antichrist allowed it: those who boast in their own peace—that is, in the unity of their impiety—conducting themselves not as bishops of Christ [Col. 0609D] but as priests of Antichrist.

2. Many antichrists.—And lest we be accused of employing abusive and malicious words against them, we do not conceal the cause of public ruin, so that it may be unknown to no one. We have learned, with the Apostle John himself proclaiming it, that there are many antichrists (1 John 2:18). For whoever denies Christ as he was preached by the Apostles is an antichrist. It belongs to the very meaning of the name “antichrist” to be opposed to Christ. This is now being accomplished under the appearance of false piety; this is being pursued under the pretext of evangelical preaching: that the Lord Jesus Christ, while thought to be preached, may be denied.

3. The Church was not founded upon human support.—First, one may pity the travail of our age and mourn the foolish opinions of the present times, by which human resources are thought to lend patronage to God, and by which men labour to defend Christ’s Church through worldly ambition [Note: [Col. 0609D] Facundus of Hermiane, *Spicilegium*, vol. III, p. 118, appears to have erred through ignorance of facts and times when he commends these words as follows: “Saint Hilary, bishop, confessor, and distinguished doctor, said to certain bishops during the time of Emperor Constantius, when the Arians, under the name of peace and king, had overrun almost all the local churches throughout the whole world,” etc. For Hilary wrote this not under Constantius but under Valentinian, when Eusebius, Lucifer, Hilary himself, and others had returned to their churches. Therefore, at least in the West, the Arians did not hold nearly all local churches. Yet, because Hilary’s following declamation bears more upon what the Arians had done under Constantius than upon what they were doing under Valentinian, Facundus’s words may suitably be understood. Since Valentinian, through excessive devotion to peace and love for the local church occupied by Auxentius, feared to examine the faith of this crafty heretic too closely and, content with a profession catholic in the sound of its words, admitted him to communion, Hilary afterwards inveighs against that excessive attachment to the walls of a church. No doubt he feared that the bishops numerous in the Emperor’s retinue would lapse into the same dissimulation and be defiled by heretical communion.].

I ask you, bishops who suppose that you are truly bishops: by what patronage did the Apostles preach the Gospel? By what powers were they aided when they preached Christ and converted almost every nation from idols to God? Did they assume for themselves some dignity from the palace while singing a hymn to God in prison, among chains and after scourging? Did Paul, by royal edicts, gather the Church to Christ while he himself was a spectacle in the theatre? Was he, I suppose, protected by Nero, Vespasian, or [Note: [Col. 0611C] In the older Vatican, Basilica, Chartres, and Colbert manuscripts: “the Decii.”] Decius? Yet through their hatred for us the confession of divine preaching flourished. Supporting themselves by their own hands and labour, assembling in upper rooms and secluded places, traversing by land and sea against decrees of the senate and edicts of kings villages, towns, and almost every nation—did they, I suppose, lack the keys of the kingdom of heaven? Or did not God’s power then manifestly extend itself against human hatreds, when [Col. 0611B] Christ was preached all the more as preaching him was more forbidden?

4. The use of force against faith is condemned.—But now, alas! earthly patronage commends divine faith, and Christ, as though lacking his own power, is demeaned while worldly ambition is enlisted for his name. The Church terrifies by exile and prisons; she compels herself to be believed, though she herself was believed through exile and prisons. She depends [Note: [Col. 0611C] Lipsius and Paris: “upon favour,” against the other books.] on the favour of communicants, though she was consecrated by the terror of persecutors. She drives priests away, though she was propagated by priests driven away. She glories in being loved by the world, though she could not be Christ’s unless the world hated her. This [Note: [Col. 0611C] The manuscripts read “And concerning,” not “This concerning.” Further, Bad., Erasmus, Miraeus, and five manuscripts read “never lost.” In the Michaelinus manuscript, however, the same hand adds in the same context, “or, now lost,” which Erasmus asserted in the margin ought to be read, and after him Lipsius and Paris read it. The Vatican Basilica manuscript has “now greatly lost”; here we restore from the Chartres manuscript “and now lost.”] comparison of the Church handed down to us long ago with that now lost has been proclaimed by the very fact, which is before the eyes and on the lips of all.

[Col. 0611C] 5. The time of Antichrist has already arrived.—I shall briefly explain what this is, which should no longer be unknown. The times have been restricted according to the fullness pleasing to God. [Note: [Col. 0611D] Printed editions read “unrestricted”; they are corrected from the manuscripts.] For their measured order is taught in the heavenly books; and it is necessary that we have fallen into the very age of Antichrist, in which, according to the Apostle (2 Cor. 11:14), his ministers [Col. 0612A] transform themselves into an angel of light, and Christ himself is removed from almost every mind and conscience. For, in order that the affirmation of error may be certain, an uncertain [Note: [Col. 0611D] Miraeus preferred “true,” against all ancient books, and was never afterward corrected. Yet Hilary’s meaning here is not that uncertain opinion is preferred to truth, but that what is true and certain is put forward by Arians as uncertain opinion. Because the Son’s generation was ineffable, they wished nothing to be defined concerning it. Phoebadius of Agen condemns them: “Who could calmly endure that they should hold as certain that he has a beginning, but hold his birth uncertain?” Against this same tactic at the Synod of Rimini, Catholics cried out, according to Athanasius, *On the Synods*, p. 876: “We have not assembled here because we needed faith,” etc.] opinion concerning the truth is preferred; and the way is now open for Antichrist to deceive men that he is Christ, concerning whom there has been disagreement until now. Hence those various opinions; hence, under the one [Note: [Col. 0612C] Paris, with the Colbert manuscript corrected by a later hand: “name of Christ.”] faith of Christ, the preaching of many Christs; hence lately the spirit of Arius, transformed from an angel of the devil into an angel of light [Note: [Col. 0612C] Manuscripts: “fashioned.” It is read differently a little above and at the beginning of the book against Constantius.], whose inheritance [Note: [Col. 0612C] Thus the manuscripts. Printed editions read “inheritance of the name”; and after Lipsius, Paris reads “and the succession flowed down.” These words, as also the preceding, refer to the proceedings of the Council of Rimini. [Col. 0612D] Hilary omits only Demophilus, whom Athanasius adds to those named, *On the Synods*, p. 874: “Germinius, Auxentius, Valens, Demophilus, and Gaius came to the same place. When the other bishops framed their words from the sacred Scriptures, these men presented a little document,” etc. All these are recorded as excommunicated from the synod for that reason.] passed and flowed down in its entirety to Valens, Ursacius, Auxentius, Germinius, and Gaius. For they have now introduced a new Christ, through whom Antichrist might creep in.

6. The opinions of Auxentius, Valens, and others concerning Christ. The concealed heresy does not yet harm the people.—For they wish their [Col. 0612B] Christ not to be of the same divinity as the Father, but [Note: [Col. 0612D] Printed editions read “to be eminent,” omitting “powerful,” which all manuscripts retain.] to be a creature, powerful and more eminent than all other creatures; and to have come into existence out of nothing by God’s will. They confess that before all ages and before absolutely all time he was born God from God; but they deny that he is from God’s substance, and deny that in him must be understood the truth of divine birth and of that majesty [Note: [Col. 0612D] In the Colbert manuscript: “which God is.”] which belongs to God—lest the Son be as truly God as God the Father is truly God. Thus they maintain that the Father and the Son, proclaimed in the Gospels as one (John 10:30), are one only in fellowship of will and love, not in the truth of divinity.

If that divinity in the Son is not the same divinity that belongs to God, so that in the confession of faith there may be one God, why do they confess God the Son, why do they confess him before times and ages, except because the name of God [Col. 0612C] has by the gift of [Note: [Col. 0612D] The word “eternity,” and shortly afterward the negative particle “not,” were lacking in earlier printed editions. On the creation of angels before time, see p. 429, note b (note c in col. 455 of our edition).] eternity been assigned to every holy person? Or are not all who have been reborn truly sons of God? Or were not all angels—surely created through Christ—created before all times and before absolutely all ages? [Note: [Col. 0612D] Printed editions read: “But I think Antichrist is introduced with less odium,” omitting *ad* and adding *arbitror* contrary to manuscript evidence and Hilary’s meaning. To reconcile this, George Bull thought that *perfidia* should be read for *invidia*. But the manuscripts make the sense plain.] But in order that Antichrist may be introduced with less hostility and be believed by miserable people, they grant Christ the name of God, because it has been granted to human beings also; they confess him truly to be God’s Son, because in the sacrament of baptism every person is truly made a son of God; they confess him to be before times and ages, because this cannot be denied of angels and the devil. Thus to the Lord Christ are attributed only those things that belong either especially to angels or to ourselves.

But what is lawful and true for God Christ—that Christ is true God, that is, that the Son has the same divinity as the Father—they deny. And the deceit of this impiety has until now been carried out in such a way [Note: [Col. 0613C] Printed editions read “the occasion of impiety is accomplished through deceit”; by a corrupt interpolation they make Hilary’s thought more obscure. He observes that heretics cloak their impiety under pious words so that, while the people understand their words as they sound, they are not yet corrupted by the heretics’ perversity. Aptly Athanasius, *Letter to Epictetus*, p. 582: “These fugitives from the light, who still conceal themselves and think the thoughts of Arius—I mean Auxentius of Milan, Ursacius, Valens, and Gaius of Pannonia, stirred by one spirit—were struck with anathema by the united judgment of councils gathered in Gaul, Spain, and great Rome.” Forestalling such deceits, he says in *First Oration against the Arians*, p. 291: “If they write phrases from the sacred Scriptures, do not tolerate this kind of writer; even if they speak the words of orthodox faith, do not therefore heed them when they speak. For they do not speak with a right mind, but display these words as sheep’s clothing, while inwardly thinking the thoughts of Arius, just as the devil, founder of heresies, does.”] that, even under the priests of Antichrist, Christ’s people are not yet slain, because they suppose those men to hold the faith which their words express. [Note: [Col. 0613D] Bad., Erasmus, Miraeus, and the Colbert manuscript read: “to be sons of God.” The sense is unchanged whether one understands, “they suppose that these men believe what their words express,” or “they suppose these men think themselves to be sons of God because they proclaim themselves to be such.”] They hear “God, Christ,” and suppose that he is what he is called. They hear “Son of God,” and suppose that the truth of God is present in God’s birth. They hear “before times,” and suppose that the one before times is precisely the one who [Col. 0613B] always is. The ears of the people are holier than the hearts of their priests. If Arians proclaim Christ as true God, they have confessed God without deceit; but if they call him God and deny that he is true, they grant the name and take away the reality.

### 7. Hilary’s dealings with Auxentius at Milan. Auxentius confesses consubstantiality.

Although all the documents of the churches are full of their most impious blasphemies, and books are now full of them as well [Note: Col. 0613D. Jerome likewise, in his *Dialogue against the Luciferians*, says concerning the proceedings of the Council of Rimini: “If anyone thinks that this has been fabricated by us, let him search the public archives; certainly the church chests are full of them.”], nevertheless what happened most recently must not be left unspoken.

When the holy king (Carnotensis manuscript: “most holy”) had ordered the church at Milan—which confesses Christ as true God and as being of one divinity and substance with the Father—to be disturbed by a severe edict, under the pretext and will of unity, I urgently petitioned him that Auxentius was a blasphemer and was altogether to be regarded as an enemy of Christ. I added that he believed otherwise than the emperor himself and all the others believed.

Moved by these matters [Note: Col. 0614C. Thus the manuscripts. But the printed editions read, “moved by which matters.” After hearing Hilary’s representations, the emperor must be understood to have ordered nothing other than what Hilary requested. Thus there can be no doubt that the bishops sat in that meeting as judges, while the Quaestor and the Master were merely witnesses—especially since Valentinian himself, as Ambrose testifies in Epistle XXI.2 and Sozomen confirms, *Ecclesiastical History* VI.7, declared that judgment in ecclesiastical affairs did not belong to him at all.], the emperor ordered us to be heard by the Quaestor and the Master, with nearly ten bishops sitting together with us.

First, as is customary in a court, he made a personal accusation: that I had formerly been condemned by Saturninus [Note: Col. 0614C. Six manuscripts, together with the editions of Bad., Er., and Mir., read “by a certain Saturninus.” Better manuscripts, with Lips. and Par., read “formerly by Saturninus.”], and therefore ought not to be heard as a bishop. This is not the time to relate what answer was made to these charges. But those hearing the case then decided that the matter of faith ought rather to be discussed, as the emperor had wished.

And when there was now imminent danger that he would deny it [Note: Col. 0614D. Mir., Lips., and Par. read “danger,” against other books, which read “with others objecting.”], Auxentius professed that he believed Christ to be true God and to be of one divinity and substance with God the Father. It was therefore agreed that this should be put in writing; and, lest what had been said should slip from the memories of the hearers, I immediately presented to the emperor through the Quaestor a document containing what had been agreed. So that I might not be accused of lying, I appended copies of it.

All were pleased that Auxentius should frequently profess these very things [Col. 0614B]; and he was compelled to write it himself [Note: Col. 0614D. The printed editions read “himself.” The older Vatican, Basel, and Chartres manuscripts read *ipsud*, a form which they use elsewhere too. The others read *ipsum*, that is, “the same thing.” Hence in §9 he is charged with having written not the same thing but something else than he professed. The immediately preceding *frequenter* means “in the presence of a multitude.”]. After long turning over his schemes, he most cunningly evaded the emperor’s faith: he produced a document composed in the style of Antichrist.

### 8. By his written statement he evades the faith he had confessed.

For first he testifies that the things which the impiety of all at Nicaea in Thrace had dissolved were holy [Note: Col. 0614D. In the Chartres manuscript: “Nicaea and Thrace,” perhaps for “at Nicaea in Thrace,” with the word “held” tacitly understood. Then the printed editions read, “the impiety of all would have dissolved itself.” We follow the manuscripts, although we would prefer, “the piety of all had now dissolved [it].” For what else can this mean than what is soon stated in these words: “But let us say nothing about the Council of Rimini, which has been religiously dissolved by all”? That it was dissolved by various councils is affirmed by Sulpicius, Book II, p. 262, and Jerome, *Dialogue against the Luciferians.]. That is, he affirms that violence inflicted upon bishops was the faith of a true confession.

He also denies that he knows Arius, although he had begun to be a presbyter in Alexandria in the Arian church [Note: Col. 0614D. The older books read “in Aria.”] over which Gregory presided. But let us say nothing about the Council of Rimini, which has been religiously dissolved by all. We need only expose the devil’s contrivances.

Accordingly, when it had been agreed that Christ should be written to be true God and of one divinity and substance with the Father, he inserts—as though prompted by a most crafty devil [Col. 0614C]—a statement signifying that Christ, born before all times, is the true God, the Son, so that, according to the Arians, “true” might be referred to the Son rather than to God.

To make the difference in this meaning much greater [Col. 0615A], he adds, “from the true God, the Father,” so that in the Father there might be the truth of God, while in Christ only the truth of the Son might be written. Then, as his statement proceeds, Auxentius proclaims one divinity, but does not confess that the Son is included in it [Note: Col. 0615D. Carnotensis and Colbertinus manuscripts read “the Son.” Here are noted Auxentius’s words in §15: “For this reason we proclaim one deity,” by which he craftily excludes the Son from divinity.], so that one sole divinity might be in the Father alone and not also in the Son.

### 9. He is publicly represented as holding right belief. Hilary uncovers the fraud and is ordered to depart.

It was spread abroad among the people that Auxentius had written that Christ is true God and of one divinity and substance with the Father, and that his statement did not differ from the faith I had set forth. After this, the emperor entered into communion with him, because of the supposed purity of his faith.

But when this mystery of impiety, long concealed, could no longer be kept silent, and when I said that everything was pretended, that the faith was being denied, and that God and men were being mocked [Note: Col. 0615D. Two manuscripts read “names”; then the Chartres codex reads, “God and men were being mocked”; and then, with the Basel Vatican manuscript, “from Mediolanium,” not “from Mediolanum.”], I was ordered to depart from Milan [Col. 0615B], since I had no freedom to remain there against the emperor’s will.

### 10.

Therefore, brothers who fear the judgment of God, I declare that these things occurred in this manner. What Auxentius was afraid to deny, he was unwilling to confess; for I have appended copies of his own exposition. If he wrote the same thing, expose him as a deceiver. But if he wrote something else (Carnotensis manuscript: “otherwise”) than he professed, understand that Christ is now being preached through him as another—that is, as Antichrist.

He has indeed played with words by which he might deceive even the elect; but such a profession of impiety stands exposed.

### 11. Auxentius’s perfidy is set forth.

He denies that he preaches two gods because there are not two fathers. Who does not see from this that the confession of one God is attributed to the Father alone merely because he is alone? [Col. 0615C] Hence that satanic formulation also appeared [Note: Col. 0615D. Five manuscripts read “offspring.” Satan, since he is the author of falsehood and father of deceivers, is presently declared to be Auxentius’s father; but here the word “offspring” does not fit sufficiently with what follows. The printed editions then read, “I know one.” More correctly, the older manuscripts read, “We know one”; for these words, as also the following “the Son like his begetting Father according to the Scriptures,” belong to the formula issued at Rimini or Nicaea in Thrace, of which Auxentius professes himself a defender.]: “We know one sole true God, the Father.”

Then, after his malicious formulations, he says: “The Son is like his begetting Father according to the Scriptures.” If this is written anywhere in the sacred books, he has a profession of innocence. But if the Son and the Father are one in the truth of divinity, why is an imperfect notion of likeness put forward? [Note: Col. 0615D. From the manuscripts the particle *vero*—“but” or “indeed”—is restored, making Hilary’s meaning clearer: namely, if, on the contrary, Father and Son are said in Scripture to be one by truth of nature and not by some mere likeness.]

Christ is indeed the image of God (see *Against Constantius*, §20); but there is no doubt that man also is the image of God, since Adam was made in God’s image and likeness. Why, heir of Arius, do you grant Christ only what belongs to us? Why do you deceive the emperor, the imperial attendants, and God’s Church by the craft of your father—that is, of Satan [Col. 0616A]?

You call Christ God: why do you deceive by the name? Deny that Moses was called a god to Pharaoh (Exod. 7:1). You speak of Christ as the Son and firstborn of God: deny that Israel is God’s firstborn son (Isa. 1:2). You assert that Christ was born before times (see *On the Trinity* XII.35): deny that the devil, created before times and ages, existed. You mention that Christ is like the Father: deny that man began to exist in the image and likeness of God.

You deny to Christ alone what belongs to him, lest he be true God and of one divinity and substance with the Father. You are accustomed, together with your masters, to accuse me of heresy. Set forth, in whatever writings you can, the charge of my impiety, and produce the heading of my blasphemies.

But for me, Antichrist is the one who does not confess that the Son is of one divinity with the Father, and who does not so proclaim the Father as the one true God that the truth of divinity is also understood in the Son. If Christ and God are of one divinity, why did you not write this plainly? If they are not so for you, why did you not deny it plainly?

### 12. Let there not be excessive love for the walls of churches.

I would have wished, brothers, to reveal in person rather than by letter the secret of so deadly a mystery, and to explain every one of Auxentius’s blasphemies word by word. But since this is not permitted, let each person at least understand what is permitted to him.

Shame restrains me from bringing forward many other things concerning the Church; and I fear to commit to a letter the shameful blasphemies of the Arians. I give one warning: beware of Antichrist [600]. For love of walls has possessed you wrongly [Col. 0616C]; wrongly do you reverence the Church of God in roofs and buildings; wrongly under these do you introduce the name of peace. (Facundus cites these words, *Spicilegium*, vol. III, p. 118.) Is it doubtful that Antichrist will sit in these places?

Mountains, forests, lakes, prisons, and chasms are safer for me. For in them the prophets, whether dwelling there or plunged beneath them, prophesied by the Spirit of God [Note: Col. 0616D. The manuscripts unanimously read *lucus*, “grove.” This reading might have been preferred, if *luci*, not *lucus*, were the established nominative plural: as though Hilary had wished to compare, or even prefer, pagan groves to churches polluted by the entry of heretics. Yet, if this is compared with his statement in *Commentary on Matthew* V.1—“We are taught to pour forth prayer in every place; and the prayer of saints has been accepted among wild beasts, in prisons, in flames, from the depths of the sea, and from the belly of a beast”—it is clear that the term *lacus*, “lakes” or “pools,” should be retained. It may allude either to the depths of the sea into which Jonah was cast, or to the lions’ den into which Daniel was thrown and, placed among beasts, deserved to be regarded by God. Compare Dionysius of Alexandria, in Eusebius, Valesius edition, *Ecclesiastical History* I.22: “When we alone were driven out and oppressed by all, nevertheless even then we celebrated festival days. Every place in which we endured our various afflictions one by one—the field, the desert, the ship, the stable, the prison—served as a temple for celebrating sacred assemblies.”].

Therefore withdraw from Auxentius, the angel of Satan, the enemy of Christ, the doomed destroyer, the denier of the faith. He professed it to the emperor in such a way as to deceive; he deceived in such a way as to blaspheme.

Let him now convene against me whatever synods he wishes; let him proscribe me as a heretic under a public heading, as he has often already done; and let him stir up against me whatever wrath of the powerful he wishes. [Col. 0617A] For me he will certainly never be anything but a devil, because he is an Arian. Nor shall the peace of any persons ever be desired, except that of those who, according to the decision of our fathers at Nicaea, after anathematizing the Arians, proclaim Christ to be true God. [Note: Col. 0617C. The Carnotensis manuscript adds the closing word “Amen.”]

[Note: Col. 0617C. Thus the manuscripts; nor does Hilary otherwise customarily entitle heretical writings. But the printed editions read, “Letter of Auxentius of Milan.”]

## A Copy of Auxentius’s Blasphemy

To the most blessed and most glorious emperors Valentinian and Valens Augustus, from Auxentius, bishop of the catholic church of Milan [Note: Col. 0617C. *Catholic* is absent from the Mich. manuscript.].

### 13. Auxentius is called a heretic.

“I, most pious Emperors, judge that the unity of six hundred bishops, after such great labors, ought not to be rubbed raw again through the contention of a few men who were cast out ten years ago [Note: Col. 0617C. The printed editions read, “rubbed raw again after the decrees had been cast aside.” The word *decrees* occurs in no manuscript at all; it was doubtless added by the first editors to round out the sentence. But the preposition *ab*, “after/by,” before *abjectis*, “cast out,” could more easily have dropped out because of the following syllable of the same sound than could the word *decretis*, “decrees.” Once restored, the sense becomes as consistent with the facts as it had been made false by adding *decretis*. As already noted, Hilary’s and Eusebius’s exiles are indicated here; this is clear from the conclusion of the present blasphemy, where the same point is stated more openly.]—as the writings also make clear.

“But if certain persons from the people, who had never been in communion even with the bishops who were before me, have now been further incited by Hilary and Eusebius and, while disturbing some persons, have called me a heretic: your Piety ordered distinguished men, the Quaestor and the Master, to investigate these matters. And, as I said before, those who have once been deposed—by whom I mean Hilary and those who agree with him—are not to act as accusers or judges. Yet, in obedience to your Serenity, I came forward to expose those who speak falsehood [Note: Col. 0617D. Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read “those who teach falsehood.”], who blaspheme, who call me an Arian, and who allege that I do not confess Christ, the Son of God, to be God.

### 14. He sets forth his faith.

“I set forth to the friends of your Piety my confession [Note: Col. 0617D. The manuscripts do not contain the words, “I set forth to the friends of your Piety my confession.”], first making satisfaction on the point that I have never known Arius, have not seen him with my eyes, and have not known his teaching [Note: Col. 0617D. Palladius likewise, in the proceedings of the Council of Aquileia, §14, in Ambrose, vol. II, p. 790 of the new edition, when asked to condemn Arius’s teaching, replies: “I have neither seen Arius nor know who he is.”]. But from childhood, as I was taught and as I received from the holy Scriptures, I believed and believe [Col. 0617C] in one sole true God, the Father almighty, invisible, impassible, immortal; and in his only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, born from the Father before all ages and before every beginning: GOD, TRUE SON, from the true God the Father [Note: Col. 0618C. The words “TRUE SON,” restored here for the first time from a very ancient codex of St. Peter’s Basilica, were precisely those with which Auxentius could play and deceive more easily because punctuation distinctions were then unknown. Although, if he is true God who is true Son of God, as Hilary demonstrates in *On the Trinity* VII.14, it might seem to make little difference whether “true” were referred to God or to Son. Yet this artifice and manner of speaking was used not only by him but also by other Arians, of whom Augustine says in *Against Maximinus* I.6: “You deny that the Son is God of the same nature as the Father, although you do not deny that he is a true Son.” But now that this passage has been restored, every ground is removed for learned persons to doubt the authenticity of this letter.], according as it is written in the Gospel: ‘And this is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent’ (John 17:3).

“For through him all things were made, visible and invisible. He descended from heaven by the will of the Father for our salvation; he was born according to the flesh from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, as it is written; he was crucified under Pontius Pilate, buried, rose on the third day, ascended into heaven, sits at the right hand of the Father, and will come to judge the living and the dead.

“And [I believe] in the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, whom the Lord and God, our Savior Jesus Christ, sent to the disciples: the Spirit of truth. Thus I have believed and believe, just as the only Son of God, when ascending into heaven, handed down to his disciples, saying: ‘Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit’ (Matt. 28:19).” [Note: Col. 0618D. The Mich. manuscript adds “Amen.”]

### 15. He adheres to the faith of Rimini.

“But I have never preached two gods. For there are not two fathers, so that two gods may be spoken of, nor two sons; but one Son from one Father, alone from the Alone, God from God, as it is written: ‘One God, the Father, from whom are all things, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things’ (1 Cor. 8:6). For this reason we proclaim one deity.

“Therefore all heresies that arise against the catholic faith have always been condemned and anathematized by catholic bishops gathered together; and, when meeting particularly at Rimini, we also condemned them there. We have faithfully preserved the catholic faith of the Gospels, which the Apostles handed down.

“But so that your Piety might more truly know the matters transacted at the Council of Rimini [Col. 0618C], I have sent them, and request that you order them to be read willingly. For thus your Serenity will know that those who have long since been deposed [Note: Col. 0618D. The printed editions read, “those who have long since been condemned and deposed,” etc.; corrected from the manuscripts.]—that is, Hilary and Eusebius—are striving everywhere to create schisms. For your Piety sees that those things which have been well expounded from the holy Scriptures for the catholic faith ought not to be reconsidered.”

## Fragments

[Col. 0619]

## Preface to the Fragments of St. Hilary

[Col. 0619A]

### I. Whether this work is Hilary’s. Certain grounds for doubt.

This outstanding monument of antiquity was published in 1598 under the title *Fragments*, through the efforts of Nicolas Faber, from the library of P. Pithou, and was received with universal acclaim. So far as we know, no one has openly rejected the whole work as wrongly attributed to Hilary. Yet some seem to entertain doubts about its authority and to murmur objections against it.

At first we ourselves were somewhat troubled: first, because the letter of the Council of Sardica to all the churches, contained in Fragment II, and the letter of the Council of Rimini to Constantius, which forms the first part of Fragment VIII, though written in Latin, are nevertheless found more correct, fuller, and more elegant in their connected sequence of thought in Greek copies than [Col. 0619B] in these Fragments. Secondly, the translation of the pseudo-Sardican creed differs in *On the Synods*, §34, from that in Fragment III, §29.

Thirdly, since this work must have been written at the time when Liberius, restored to his see, was nobly defending the faith of the Church, it seemed incredible that Hilary should pronounce so many anathemas against him in Fragment VI, §6, now that he had been corrected and had even become a most vigorous defender of the faith. Hilary had spared the Easterners in *On the Synods*, although they did not yet hold right belief, because they were nevertheless approaching the truth more closely; he did not even withhold praise from them.

Furthermore, a certain monstrous appearance of events, and the disorderly and confused heap of diverse letters, discouraged us—something unworthy of Hilary, who elsewhere relates each matter in such orderly fashion. Finally, we were troubled because all these Fragments do not occur in the Pithou manuscripts in the form in which Nicolas Faber published them, under one title and Hilary’s name. Rather, they are divided as if into two parts. The first consists of Fragments XI, XIII, III, VIII, IX, V, and VII, and has no inscription bearing Hilary’s name or that of any other author. Hilary’s name, however, is written both at the beginning and at the end of the other part, which contains Fragments I, II, IV, XII, XIV, XV, VI, and X. Therefore the authority of at least the first part—which comes last in the earlier editions—seemed questionable and weak.

### II. The work is assigned to Hilary on the authority of the manuscripts.

Moved by all these considerations, we applied ourselves to a more careful investigation of the truth. First, we judged that the authority of manuscripts which assign this work to St. Hilary not once but twice and three times ought not to be despised. They do so, namely, at the beginning of the first Fragment: “Here begins the book of St. Hilary of Poitiers, of the province of Aquitaine,” etc.; again in the middle of Fragment VI: “Saint Hilary pronounces an anathema upon him”; and finally at the end of Fragment X: “Here ends the book of St. Hilary, from the Historical Work.”

If anyone thinks that insufficiently secure trust can be placed in Pithou’s paper codex, because it is more recent and was copied only about three hundred years ago, he will not deny that credence should be given to the exemplar of St. Remigius of Rheims. Sirmond, who had it in his possession, calls it very ancient in his notes on the Council of Paris [Col. 0620A]. It had the same arrangement of materials and the same inscriptions.

We sought this exemplar in vain; but Stephen Baluze, born to assist letters, to some extent repaired our loss by supplying Sirmond’s variant readings. Added to this is the fact that Baronius, under the year 357, transcribes from the Cresconian Collection and two manuscripts the letters of Liberius inserted in Fragment VI; and in the latest edition he acknowledges that he found in his manuscripts the same interpolations, likewise attributed to Hilary, as are found in these Fragments.

### III. By the testimony of Jerome.

Jerome supports the manuscripts. For among Hilary’s works listed by him in *On Ecclesiastical Writers* is “a book against Valens and Ursacius, containing the history of the Councils of Rimini and Seleucia.” This is quite plainly promised by the title prefixed to Fragment I: “Here begins the book of St. Hilary of Poitiers, of the province of Aquitaine, in which are all the materials showing how, for what reasons, and at whose instigation the Council of Rimini took place under the emperor Constantius,” etc.

Jerome only states more expressly “against Ursacius and Valens,” whereas this title expresses the matter more generally in the words “how, for what reasons, and at whose instigation.” That these Fragments belong to the work written against Valens and Ursacius is clear from other fragments, and especially from the second, the tenth, and the final two.

Our title indeed promises nothing about the Council of Seleucia, the history of which Hilary’s book ought to contain according to Jerome. But Jerome, who—as has been observed concerning the books *On the Trinity* [Col. 0620C] and *On the Synods*—was accustomed, after examining the works of others, to impose titles of his own, could have referred to the Council of Seleucia the documents in Fragment X which are indicated as forthcoming. For the events there related, which took place at Constantinople among the delegates of the Councils of Seleucia and Rimini, pertain indifferently to both Seleucia and Rimini: to Seleucia, because the synod at Constantinople seemed its continuation; to Rimini, because the Council of Seleucia in some manner went over to its position when its delegates were compelled at Constantinople to accept the creed issued by that council.

### IV. Fragment I bears Hilary’s own stamp. The other Fragments are akin to the first.

The truth of the titles is strongly confirmed by Fragment I. It presents a Gallican bishop, about to begin from events transacted in Gaul (§6); one who preferred to suffer exile rather than enjoy domestic ease after betraying the Church’s faith (§4); one who, in order to persuade the emperor of the true faith, sought a hearing with special earnestness (§5), yet was unable to obtain it; one who has already briefly introduced the corruption of the faith and of the Gospels; and finally one who warns the reader in what spirit he wishes to be read (§7).

Thus Hilary painted himself in his own colors at the very beginning [Col. 0621A], so that he cannot possibly remain hidden from those to whom he is otherwise known. Since the first Fragment announces a work to follow, consisting of various letters and synods and tracing the history of the Council of Rimini farther back from the proceedings of the Council of Arles and other earlier councils, recognition of the author of this Fragment gives great authority to the rest as well.

### V. The agreement of the two parts.

There seems certainly to be no reason why the first part of this collection should not be attributed to Hilary equally with the second. Each consists of various letters and synods. Each, as Nicolas Faber observed, intermingles in several places the author’s own words with the official acts; and these words display the style of that most holy confessor. The documents in each alike demonstrate the wickedness and inconsistency of Ursacius and Valens. Finally, each contains nothing that does not breathe antiquity, agree with the history of the times, or in some way concern the history of the Council of Rimini.

Indeed, if the second part is separated from the first, there is no basis for judging that it belongs to the history of the aforesaid synod, since the first part alone presents that council’s proceedings. In this, too, the first agrees with the second: it includes both what preceded the Council of Rimini and what followed it.

### VI. Its division into two parts arose from corruption.

No one, however, will deny that the entire collection is wrongly divided into two parts in the Pithou and Remigius manuscripts, and that the first part is still more wrongly placed after the second [Col. 0621C], since the beginning of the first part is clearly a continuation of the second. For the letter of the Council of Paris, from which the first part begins in the manuscripts, is a reply to the letters of the Easterners that close the latter part in those same manuscripts.

It follows that the title applies not to one part alone but to the entire collection. Therefore Nicolas Faber did not hesitate to invert the order of those parts and place the latter before the former.

### VII. Other difficulties are removed.

Once this more serious difficulty has been resolved, the scruples which troubled us at first are easily dismissed. For who would be surprised that a man banished to Phrygia encountered not genuine and complete copies of Latin letters, but corrupt ones? Who would deny that a change of places could have caused the translation of the pseudo-Sardican creed in these Fragments to differ from that in *On the Synods* [Col. 0621D]?

Certainly it is not surprising that, in a different work, time, and place, he did not adhere to one translation—he who, in the same book *On the Synods*, translated in different ways the aforesaid pseudo-Sardican creed and the Sirmian creed against Photinus, although both were stated in Greek in the same words.

As for the anathemas pronounced against Liberius, some have answered that perhaps they were written in the margin by another hand and subsequently crept into the text. Others maintain that they were uttered by Hilary when he first received that pontiff’s thoroughly cowardly letter. They think that Hilary’s notes are presented here, copied without order, which he had initially assembled for composing a more finished work.

At that point the Apostle’s words in Galatians 1:8 could have occurred to him: “Even if we, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you a gospel contrary to that which we preach to you, let him be anathema.” Thus he could have judged that against Liberius, deserter of Christ’s cause, he was permitted to do what the Apostle not only allowed but commanded concerning himself and an angel of God.

Nothing is more natural for those who love intensely than to try to compensate with some mark of indignation against one whom they hear has shamefully deserted a friend, because he has departed from the number of those who love. But if one grants that disordered notes for a work never completed have come down to us, one must likewise grant that the documents repeatedly indicated as forthcoming, but which do not follow, were only assigned by Hilary to places where he would have them at hand [Col. 0622B].

Those, however, who prefer to regard these as fragments of a completed work must nevertheless conclude from what is absent that Hilary arranged them differently from their present form. Whichever view one prefers, the confusion of these Fragments does nothing to impair their truth.

### VIII. The source of this book’s confusion.

By Rufinus’s testimony, the corruption of this book must be considered ancient and attributed to heretics—if, indeed, the following statement of his is to be referred to this work. In his *Treatise on the Falsification of Origen’s Books* (in Jerome, vol. IX), he says that Hilary wrote a book of most complete instruction for the correction of those who had subscribed to the perfidy of Rimini, and that it was subsequently so defiled by heretics that Hilary himself did not recognize it.

But since Rufinus intermingles with these words many things plainly false and wholly fabulous in character [Col. 0622C], scarcely anything can be inferred from them—unless perhaps one says that the corruption of this book gave occasion for inventing these tales. Certainly the malice of the Arians was equal to begrudging us the integrity of this book. Its confusion may also have occurred by chance.

### IX. How it has now been restored in a new order.

But it is now less important to know whence the confusion arose than to restore it in whatever way possible. In the sequence in which it appears in the manuscripts, it can scarcely be read without weariness and without some danger of straying from the truth. But what order should be followed?

Some have already desired that the various documents it contains be arranged according to chronology. Yet Hilary indicates that he did not always adhere to this arrangement (Fragment I, §6), when he warns that he will begin with the proceedings at Arles, although the order of events calls for something else. Although he gives there the reason why he follows another order, he indicates quite plainly that in arranging the rest he did not disregard chronology.

He immediately adds: “I will also not uselessly advise that careful attention be given to this whole volume. For all things must both be separated by times and distinguished by judgments,” etc. We therefore judged that the best arrangement would be one which so adjusted everything as to preserve the order of times without altering the plan of matters arranged by Hilary.

For this reason we observed whenever something was missing in the whole work which the author indicated that he had appended, or whenever something followed that did not cohere with what preceded [Col. 0623A]. Then we divided it into as many fragments as we found places where it was disjointed or mutilated in some part, and placed the individual fragments in chronological order.

### X. The usefulness of this new arrangement.

This new order first confirms the truth of the titles supplied by Nicolas Faber; then provides assistance to those who wish either to cite the work or to recognize it when cited; and finally gives the reader a means to read it with greater pleasure and advantage.

For if a confused narrative of events is unpleasant and leads into error, a distinct and orderly narrative ought to be pleasant and lead back to truth. We ourselves have experienced how much light the individual Fragments, placed in their proper locations, shed upon one another. Certainly, even if they do not show what is missing from this book, they generally at least indicate it. Sometimes, too, while they set forth the connected series of events in order, they reveal the meaning hidden beneath corrupt words. Finally, they enable the mind to perceive more clearly the author’s entire design in this work.

### XI. The summary and purpose of this book.

It is immediately evident from Fragment I that Hilary began this book with the Council of Arles, the proceedings of which are missing. It is therefore not unreasonable to suppose that the material concerning the Council of Sardica and the formal retraction of Valens and Ursacius, appended in Fragment II, pertains to elucidating the aforesaid Council of Arles.

For those proceedings openly demonstrate the injustice of the judgment by which Athanasius was condemned at Arles and later at Milan, at the instigation of Valens, Ursacius, and Saturninus. Hence, in the same Fragment, §18, Hilary compares those who secured Athanasius’s acquittal at Sardica with those who conspired for his condemnation at Arles, and says: “Will you deny that you knew that communion had been restored to Athanasius, whose condemnation Valens, Ursacius, and Saturninus demand from you, by Hosius, Maximinus, and Julius?”

Accordingly, the exiles of Lucifer, Eusebius, and the other confessors; the fall of Vincentius and Fortunatianus; and, among these things, Liberius’s first courageous words and deeds, and finally his shameful agreement with the Arians, may rightly be regarded as consequences of the Council of Arles, or at least as beginnings of Rimini. The proceedings of that council then follow in their proper sequence, along with measures taken in various places by Catholics to annul it and attempts made by Ursacius and Valens to defend it.

Thus it is clear that Hilary wished in this one book to include whatever the Arian heresy had done in the West.

### XII. It contains proceedings of several councils, but all relate to the history of the single Council of Rimini.

For when the defenders of the faith began to be expelled in these regions at the Council of Arles, the widespread persuasion was that they had been exiled not for the faith but for the sake of Athanasius alone. This error had so taken hold of almost everyone’s minds that so many bishops were thought to be exiled merely because they would not pronounce sentence against him, a cause allegedly not sufficiently worthy of the exile they had undertaken.

Hilary takes care to correct that error (Fragment I, §4). By explaining the progress of the deceitful heresy, he demonstrates from the outcome itself that it had undertaken the expulsion not of one man but of the entire faith. Therefore whatever he sets forth from various councils he directs toward Rimini as to one end, because there the heresy openly disclosed what it had been plotting in the preceding councils.

Thus, if one considers the events contained in this book, it embraces the history of several synods; if one considers its aim, it embraces the history of the single Council of Rimini. Since that council had so disastrous an outcome principally through the efforts of Ursacius and Valens, the book is fittingly entitled *Against Those Two Leaders of the Arian Sect*. Their perfidy is demonstrated not only by what they plotted at and after the Council of Rimini, but also by their former conduct. Thus again the title of the book recorded in our manuscripts is reconciled with Jerome.

XIII. When This Book Was Written.—Thus Hilary, who never ceased to provide for the welfare of the Church, just as he published the books On the Trinity so that sound doctrine might not go into exile together with the preachers of the true faith who were being banished (On the Trinity, book X, §4), likewise undertook this work so that perversity might not do harm while most of the pastors were absent; and so that thereafter each person, standing by his own judgment, might recognize its falsehood for himself and not follow another’s opinion (Fragment I, §7). This was especially appropriate at the time when all were compelled by the edict of the Emperor Constantius to accept the creed of Rimini, and when Hilary, without offending the emperor’s name, was attempting to show that it ought to be condemned by all, until it became permissible publicly to condemn and abolish it in 611–612 [Col. 0624C] councils. But that he began this book while Constantius was still alive and while Hilary had not yet returned from the East is established with far greater certainty from Fragment I. For to what else but the time of Constantius can one suitably refer these words in §4: “In the affairs of the Roman Empire repose is disturbed, the king is troubled, the palace is seething, bishops are running about,” etc.? And what, moreover, does he mean when shortly before he says: “I undertake a work grave . . . foreign through despair of the places in which the matter occurred and in which we ourselves are acting”? What was that place in which Ursacius and Valens brought it about that the perfidy of the faith of Rimini should prevail, if not the imperial city and the emperor’s court? And what were those places despaired of, if not the East, whose ten Asiatic provinces, apart from a few with Eleusius, we have heard in On the Synods, §63, to be truly ignorant of God? Therefore the work is “foreign” because, since Hilary despaired of being able to accomplish anything in Constantinople, where he was residing, and in the surrounding regions, he addressed it to the West, from which he was absent. For this is clearly the force of the word *foreign* from these words in On the Synods, §63: “I do not speak of foreign matters, nor do I write of things unknown; I have heard and seen the faults of the present time”—where “foreign” matters are plainly contrasted with present ones. He therefore began this in the year 360, while still residing at Constantinople and before writing against Constantius; afterward he enlarged it from day to day, as Fragments II, XII, and others attest.

XIV. We have judged that what Nicholas Faber learnedly and copiously prefaced to the individual items should not be suppressed, lest a work praised by many should perish; but, lest it should be separated by too long an interval from Hilary’s writings, it is to be placed only in the Appendix. Likewise, lest the ancient order in which the individual records of this work were published by him should be lost to anyone, we append its index, so that each reader may compare it with the new one at a glance.

[Col. 0625]
