617–618. FRAGMENTS FROM THE BOOK OF SAINT HILARY OF POITIERS, OF THE PROVINCE OF AQUITAINE, IN WHICH ARE ALL THE MATERIALS SHOWING BOTH HOW, FOR WHAT CAUSES, AND AT WHOSE URGING, UNDER THE EMPEROR CONSTAN­TIUS, THE COUNCIL OF RIMINI WAS HELD AGAINST THE FORMULA OF THE NICENE TREATISE, BY WHICH ALL HERESIES HAD BEEN RESTRAINED. (C, S)

[Note: It is clear from Fragment II, §27 that “restrained” is to be preferred: “Accordingly, in order to repress this evil, three hundred bishops, or more, assembled at Nicaea.” And shortly afterward it is headed, “The Creed composed at Nicaea against all heresies.” We have reproduced this title in full from the manuscripts, except that at the beginning, where they read “Here begins the book,” we have substituted “Fragments from the book.”]

[Col. 0627]

FRAGMENT I  
(Otherwise, I of Part I)

[Col. 0627A]

1. The Excellence of Faith, Hope, and Charity.—Paul the Apostle, filled with the Holy Spirit, speaks thus to the Corinthians: “But faith, hope, charity remain” (1 Cor. 13:13). In this threefold affection of the human mind he comprehends the great mystery of consummate truth; but he declares that the services and gifts of all other things, in which we now engage only in part, are to be abolished (ibid., vv. 8 ff.), when, at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, the perfection of the heavenly assembly is found.

[Note: The manuscript reads “the threefold affection of the human mind,” from which Faber made “a threefold affection.” We prefer to retain the manuscript reading, with the final letter *m* removed, since in the same manuscript it very frequently appears superfluously.]

For when our corruptibility has been transformed into the glory of eternity, that which is now believed to be something will not exist, when that is bestowed which, because it exists, is eternally enduring. But faith, hope, and charity possess this merit: that, when bodies have been dissolved by the debt of death, they always remain and never cease; and although all things in man are partial, these alone are perfect. For whether prophecies shall be abolished, tongues cease, or knowledge be destroyed, those three things mentioned above attain unchangeable perfection; and they will neither be changed from without nor acquire more abundantly than they possess.

[Note: In the archetype, “has obtained.” Faith, hope, and charity are directed to God as their end; when they attain him, they possess perfection, and that perfection is the enjoyment of the immutable God. In that sense faith and hope are not changed from without. Augustine spoke in another sense in Letter 140, §63: “But in the age to come perfect and full charity, without any endurance of evils, neither believes by faith what it does not see nor desires by hope what it does not possess, but contemplates forever the appearance of truth.”]

For while complete truth removes prophecies, tongues, and knowledge, it will embrace faith, hope, and charity—the guides and advocates for attaining eternity—as eternity itself. The blessed Apostle also distinguished the merits of each of these things according to its due, or something similar, of its modest honor, so that it might readily be understood that, when the other things are abolished through the progress of heavenly increase, these three alone remain, not with a scant fruit of their own honor indeed, but abiding permanently.

[Note: Faber, following the Pithoean and Colbert manuscripts, reads “prophecy.” Sirmond, more correctly following the Remigian manuscript, reads “progress.” Soon after, in place of “may indeed remain,” perhaps one should read “may remain the same.”]

[Col. 0628A]

2. The Merit of Faith; the Nature of Hope; the Affection of Charity.—God, the forerunner of righteousness, is reckoned when he is believed by one ignorant that God exists.

[Note: Faber, following the authority of his archetype, printed “is first reckoned,” himself thinking “is rewarded with gifts” preferable—a conjecture not to be despised. We restore from Sirmond “forerunner,” a word better followed by “is mentioned” than by “is reckoned.” Here it is indicated that faith ought to precede God’s righteousness, since no one is justified without faith.]

Therefore Abraham’s faith first justifies him (Heb. 2:6 [apparently Hab. 2:4] and Rom. 4:9); the faith of the Canaanitish mother, testing the Lord in silence, saves her daughter (Matt. 15:28); and in John authority is granted to those believing in his name, that they may be born of God (John 1:12).

[Note: The actions of two faithful women are here blended into one: one, in Matthew 9:20, silently touched the Lord so as to be healed of a flow of blood; the other, in Matthew 15:28, with loud cries entreated healing for her daughter.]

[Note: That is, in the Gospel of John. By a similar mode of speech in On the Trinity, book X, §42, it is said, “through the prayer in John.”]

Great is the merit of faith, and perfect is the blessedness of those who believe God: through it, for those born in a body, amid sin and sickness, there are righteousness, health, and birth from God. Hope, resting in trust in those things which God has ordained, surpasses the attractiveness of worldly life and the goods of this age, winning gains of things to come by loss of things present. The Lord rewards it with this prize: “Everyone who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or mother, or children, or land for my name’s sake shall receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life” (Matt. 19:29).

A noble witness to God’s virtues is the confident assurance of its expectation: despising all present things as nothing and uncertain, but grasping future things as eternal and present. Yet although the same Apostle assigns equal glory to enduring faith, hope, and charity, and signifies that they are equally inviolable, he nevertheless declares charity superior to the other two. For through it we are bound to God by a kind of bond of received love; and, once charity of piety has been infused for his name’s sake, our will becomes indivisible from him—a charity from which neither sword, famine, nor nakedness shall separate us (Rom. 8:35). Through it anger, jealousy, ambition, wickedness, luxury, and greed are restrained. Therefore, though faith, hope, and charity remain, “the greatest of these is charity” (1 Cor. 13:13): through it, mingled together in an inseverable affection in God’s name, no force of worldly upheavals either dissolves or divides us.

3. Charity Urges Hilary Not to Keep Silent about the Perversity of the Heretics.—To this authority of the Apostle, so great and weighty, I also, among the rest, if any place remains for me after them, bear witness through this charity laid up for us before worldly times, we who have been taken up into the hope of heaven. I cleave to the name of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, rejecting fellowship with the wicked and association with unbelievers. With them I could flourish, enjoy domestic leisure in worldly ease, abound in every advantage, glory in familiarity with the court, and, under the false title of bishop, be burdensome to individuals and to all alike, publicly and privately, in lordship over the Church—an authority equal to that of the rest being granted to me—if only I corrupted evangelical truth by falsehood, consoled the guilt of conscience by the blandishment of ignorance, defended judicial corruption by the excuse of another’s judgment, were held bound by the crime of heresy not through my own faith, which would surely be liable, but through the simplicity of the ignorant, and falsely claimed uprightness under the difficulty of public understanding.

[Note: The word “world” would fit the sentence more suitably thus: “enjoy domestic leisure, abound in all worldly advantages.” Or perhaps one should rather read, “flourish in the goods of the world,” since what follows requires “I,” not “we.”]

But charity, abiding in simplicity, in the heart through the faith and hope of Christ, did not permit these things. And since I had received from the Apostle: “For we have not received the spirit of fear” (2 Tim. 1:7), and had learned from the Lord’s saying: “Everyone who confesses me before men, I too will confess him before my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 10:32); and since by that same Lord it had been said: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are you when they revile you and persecute you and say every evil thing against you for righteousness’ sake; rejoice and exult, for your reward is abundant in heaven” (Matt. 5:10 ff.); I could not prefer an ambitious conscience in guilt-laden silence to endurance of injuries for the confession of God.

[Note: The manuscripts read “to prefer ambitious,” from which Faber made “to endure in an ambitious silence of guilt.” We restore the sentence in a fuller and truer form, especially since Sirmond read from the Remigian manuscript “in the silence of guilt,” that is, in silence liable to guilt. To escape this guilt, Hilary says that he preferred to suffer indignities for Christ’s confession rather than to wink at them from an ambitious conscience.]

[Col. 0630A]

4. The Nature of the Work He Undertakes.—I therefore undertake to bring before the public conscience a work grave and manifold, entangled by devilish fraud, subtle in the party of heretics, prejudged by the dissimulation and fear of many, foreign through despair of the places in which the matter occurred and in which we ourselves are acting; ancient in time, new in silence, long ago passed over under a feigned peace of affairs, but recently renewed by the impious cunning of most deceitful men. And in this affair, even in the business of the Roman Empire, repose is disturbed, the king is troubled, the palace seethes, bishops run about, official masters flit to and fro, and against apostolic men there is turmoil through the hurried activity of every office. Thus everywhere there is action, agitation, urgency, so that the labor and concern to prevail have clearly disclosed the iniquity of this assertion.

[Note: It is “ancient in time” because what the Arians finally brought to completion at Rimini, Seleucia, and Constantinople they had attempted much earlier in innumerable councils. Yet because they had previously been eager to hide this design by silence, but had now for the first time openly disclosed it, it is called “new in silence.” Indeed, as is related in On the Synods, §78, in the year 357 the heresy broke forth at Sirmium and gloried as victorious, not secretly but by a public profession of authority, in what it had previously murmured furtively. Yet it was immediately suppressed through the efforts of the Eastern bishops assembled at Ancyra, Valens, Ursacius, and their associates being compelled to subscribe to the Ancyran definitions. That subscription is indicated by the following words: “long ago passed over under a feigned peace of affairs,” unless perhaps they denote the celebrated retraction of Ursacius and Valens after the Council of Sardica.]

For I remember that it has long been current in men’s talk that certain priests of God are exiled for this reason: that they do not pronounce judgment against Athanasius. This error has seized the minds of almost all, so that under his name they judge the cause for which each of them has undertaken exile not sufficiently worthy.

5. What He Omits in It.—I pass over, although the highest reverence ought to be paid to the sovereign—for all sovereignty is from God—yet the fact that his judgment is not admitted with equanimity into episcopal decisions, because what belongs to Caesar must be rendered to Caesar, and what belongs to God to God (Luke 20:25). I am silent about the emperor’s judgment when examination of the case has been removed. I do not complain that a sentence is extorted against one who is absent, although, as the Apostle says, “Where faith is, there also is freedom” (2 Cor. 3:17), and priestly simplicity ought not to suffer such a thing.

[Note: Here he briefly touches upon the various ways in which, in Athanasius’s case, the proper form of judicial proceedings was violated, above all because he was condemned while absent. For, as Ammianus Marcellinus, book XV, chapter 7, himself testifies together with Theodoret, Ecclesiastical History, book II, chapter 16, Liberius, when Constantius ordered him to subscribe against Athanasius, replied that it had never been heard of that sentence was passed against an accused person in his absence. The same is the response of Lucifer and his companions in Athanasius, To the Solitaries, p. 862: “Granted,” they say to Constantius, “that you are the accuser; nevertheless the absence of the accused makes it impossible for him to be judged.” Hilary further indicates that the sentence was extorted and therefore void; nor does Liberius omit this argument in the passage of Theodoret just mentioned.]

But I pass over these things, not because they should be despised, but because matters more serious are involved in them. For although from whatever has been done in the various lands it could be recognized that something very different was being done from what was supposed, nevertheless I have resolved to set forth the whole matter in this volume with more earnest care. At that time these matters were pressed forward hurriedly by us: the corruption of the Gospels, the perversion of the faith, and a simulated, blasphemous confession of Christ’s name. And it was necessary that everything in that discourse should be too hasty, unarranged, confused; because the more earnestly we sought a hearing, the more stubbornly they opposed our obtaining one.

[Note: Either at Béziers, from which he was driven into exile, or even at Constantinople after the dissolution of the Council of Seleucia. Yet he did not fail to do this whenever an opportunity offered. For in the First Book to Constantius, §3, he complains that the Arians do not cease with impious mouth and sacrilegious mind to corrupt the sincerity of the Gospels and pervert the straight rule of the apostles; and shortly afterward that they ensnare the simple and innocent under the pretext of the Christian name. Again, in the Second Book to the same emperor, he steadfastly expounds the perversion of the faith and earnestly demands a hearing.]

[Col. 0631A]

6. Where He Begins.—I shall therefore begin with the events which occurred most recently: namely, at the time when, in the town of Arles, my brother and fellow-minister Paulinus, bishop of the Church of Trier, in the year 353, did not join himself to their destruction and pretence. I shall explain what that judgment was, from which, because he withdrew his consent, he was adjudged unworthy of the Church by bishops and worthy of exile by the emperor. That this should be done is demonstrated not by the sequence of events but by a reason drawn from the present facts: so that, from the circumstances in which injury came upon one who did not assent to them, confession of faith rather than fear in a man may first be understood.

[Note: The printed editions read “their judgment.” The manuscripts more correctly read “that judgment,” namely, the judgment of Arius’s supporters, to which Paulinus refused to consent.]

[Note: Faber, with his manuscript, reads: “and by whom against him who assented, who did not incur injury?” [uncertain] Restoring the word “from” for “and,” since both have one form in ancient books, we correct the rest from Sirmond’s readings. If, moreover, instead of “rather than fear in a man,” one reads “rather than favor toward a man,” both the sense will be sound and Hilary’s reason evident for beginning from the proceedings of the Council of Arles: namely, so that first, from the circumstances in which he who did not consent to them—that is, Athanasius—incurred injury, namely exile, it may be understood that confession of faith rather than favor toward a man was the cause why priests undergo exile. In agreement with this are the words of Sulpicius Severus, book II, p. 246: “They demanded that, before they were compelled to subscribe against Athanasius, the question of faith should rather be debated; and that inquiry into the matter should not then first begin when judgment concerning the person had already been determined.” But Valens and his associates, not daring to contend concerning the faith, wished first to extort Athanasius’s condemnation. Paulinus was driven into exile by this conflict of parties, not merely because he defended Athanasius, but because he defended the faith. Athanasius himself, cited with praise by Theodoret, Ecclesiastical History, book II, chapter 15, testifies that those who were carried into exile from the Council of Milan suffered this for no other reason than that they refused to consent to the Arian heresy and to subscribe to the false calumnies against himself. Theodoret prefaces this by saying that the purpose of the Council of Milan was that Constantius might compel the bishops, after Athanasius had been expelled from the churches, to compose another formula of faith.]

7. How It Should Be Read.—I shall also give this not useless warning: careful attention should be applied to this whole volume. For everything must be separated according to times, distinguished according to judgments, divided according to persons, and weighed according to the force of words, lest perhaps, amid so many letters and so many councils frequently introduced, the reader be filled with a harmful weariness before the end. These matters concern what knowledge of God ought to be sought, what hope of eternity, and in what settled position perfect truth abides. And since the business at hand is so grave, each person ought to devote his care solely to knowing these matters, so that thereafter, standing by his own judgment, he may not follow another’s opinion.

[Col. 0631C] Here ends.

FRAGMENT II  
(Otherwise, I of Part I)

HERE BEGINS A COPY OF THE LETTER

[Col. 0632A]

Of the Council of Sardica to All the Churches.  
(Written in the year 347.)

1. The Cause of the Council.—The Arian heretics have indeed often and repeatedly dared much against the servants of God who preserve the right and catholic faith. For, introducing adulterated doctrine, they have attempted to persecute the orthodox. They have now risen against the faith to such an extent that not even the devout piety of the most merciful emperors escaped notice.

[Note: In Theodoret: “so that not even the hearing of the God-beloved emperors escaped notice.” Athanasius agrees more closely with Hilary: “so that not even the piety of the most reverent [emperors escaped notice].”]

Accordingly, with God’s grace assisting, the most merciful emperors themselves gathered us from various provinces and cities and permitted this holy council to be held in the city of Sardica, so that every dissension might be cut off, unjust doctrine entirely expelled, and piety alone, which is in Christ, preserved by all.

[Note: From the Greek copies one should read: “gathered us from various provinces and cities and [permitted] this holy council [to be held] in . . .”]

For bishops came from the East, stirred by the exhortation of the most pious emperors, especially because of the matter that had repeatedly been the subject of complaint: that is, concerning our most beloved brothers and fellow-bishops, Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, and Marcellus, bishop of Ancyra in Galatia. We suppose that their slanders have reached even yourselves and that they have tried to move your ears, so that you might believe what they say against the innocent while they conceal suspicion of their criminal heresy. But they have not been permitted to do this any longer. For the Lord is the governor of the Churches, he who endured death for the Churches and for all of us, and who, on account of those Churches, granted to all of us ascent into heaven.

[Note: Athanasius likewise omits here Asclepas of Gaza, whom Theodoret includes.]

[Note: The Greek text of Theodoret agrees: “he who [died] for them and all of us.” Yet Athanasius’s reading, “and through himself,” seems truer, because nothing is more customary among the Fathers of that age than to say that, as Christ ascended into heaven, we too ascended with him. See vol. I, p. 217, note f (col. 446, note j in our edition).]

2. The Eusebians Fear to Attend the Council.—Long ago Eusebius, Marius, Theodorus, Diognetus, Ursacius, and Valens wrote to Julius, our fellow-priest, bishop of the Roman Church, against our aforesaid fellow-bishops—by whom we mean Athanasius and Marcellus; and bishops from other places likewise wrote, attesting the innocence of our fellow-bishop Athanasius, whereas what had been done by Eusebius was nothing but full of falsehood and lies.

[Note: From Theodoret, “Menophantus and Stephen” should be added here. Athanasius, however, has only “those around Eusebius,” without naming the other bishops.]

[Note: Again Theodoret adds here Asclepas, in agreement with Athanasius. Then, in place of “as they wrote,” read “and they wrote,” as though: “they wrote together.”]

[Note: What slipped from the copyist because of repetition of the word “bishops” may easily be supplied thus: “bishops from other places wrote, testifying—or so as to testify—to the innocence of our fellow-bishop Athanasius; whereas, etc.”]

For, although from the fact that, when summoned by our most beloved brother Bishop Julius, they were unwilling to come—something made plain by the letters in which their lies were exposed (for they would have come if they had confidence in what they had done against our fellow-bishops)—nevertheless, even from the things which they did in this holy and great council, they made the fabrications of their falsehood more manifest.

[Note: In Theodoret: “And although it was plainly evident from the fact that they were summoned by our beloved colleague Julius and did not appear, and from what was written by Bishop Julius himself, that their calumny was exposed—for they would have come, etc.” In Athanasius several things are lacking here.]

[Note: By the letter extant in Athanasius, vol. I, p. 739.]

For they came even to the city of Sardica; yet, seeing Athanasius, Marcellus, Asclepas, and the others, they were afraid to come to judgment. Called not once or twice but repeatedly, they despised the invitation of the council of all of us bishops who had assembled, and especially of the venerable elder Hosius. On account of both his age, his confession, and his faith tested over so long a time, he undertook such labor at that age for the Church’s benefit that he was to be considered most worthy of every reverence.

[Note: To make the sentence complete, one should read “because of which,” not “who”; and afterward delete “that” before “every.” In the Greek copies there is nothing corresponding to the preceding words, “and his faith tested over so long a time.”]

While all waited and urged them to come to judgment, so that they might, being present, prove all that they had said or written against our fellow-bishops who were absent, they did not come when summoned, as we have said. In this also they showed their falsehood, revealing not merely the invented fraud or contrived cunning which they had perpetrated by their excuse. For those who have confidence to prove what they say against persons absent are ready to prove it when those persons are present. But because they did not dare to come, we suppose that henceforth no one can be unaware that, even if they should again wish to exercise their malice, they are able to prove nothing against our fellow-bishops, whom they accuse when absent but flee when present.

3. They Flee: How Great and How Numerous Their Crimes Are.—For they fled, beloved brothers, not only because of those whom they had falsely attacked, but also because of those who had gathered from various places to accuse them of many crimes. Men returning from exile displayed iron and chains. Again, relatives and kinsmen, friends and brothers sent by those still held in exile brought complaints either of those who survived or of those who had died in those very exiles, prosecuting the shameful wrong done to them.

[Note: The whole passage may be rendered more briefly from the Greek thus: “Fellow-ministers were present as envoys. Relatives and friends of those whom they had killed also came. And what is greatest, etc.”]

And, what is greatest, bishops were present: one displayed the iron and chains which he had borne upon his neck because of them; others testified that death had been threatened against them on their accusation.

[Note: In Athanasius and Theodoret the words “upon his neck” are lacking; their truth is confirmed by the letter to Julius below, §11.]

[Note: To those three words, “death threatened against them,” the Greek answers with the single word *thanaton* (θάνατον, “death”), which is rendered insufficiently aptly in Theodoret and Athanasius as “death inflicted.” For the complaint here is not that the Arians inflicted death, but that they attempted to inflict it.]

They went so far in desperation that they would even have killed bishops, had those bishops not fled their bloody hands.

[Note: The Greek reading requires the addition here: “they attempted to kill [them],” etc. Earlier Athanasius, like our Hilary, reads “bishops” in the plural, whereas Theodoret has “bishop” in the singular. That these things apply to more than one is indicated by Athanasius as quoted by Theodoret, Ecclesiastical History, book II, chapter 15, where he says: “They caused even Theodulus and Olympius, bishops of Thrace, and also us and our presbyters, to be sought out in such a way that, if we were found, we should suffer capital punishment”; and in Letter to the Solitaries, p. 821: “They attacked Olympius of Aenus and Theodulus of Trajanopolis, both good bishops of Thrace, with calumnies.” Constantius orders the same men to be put to death in Socrates, book II, chapter 26.]

For our most blessed fellow-bishop Theodulus died fleeing their assault. He had been ordered to die on their accusation. Others displayed the marks, wounds, and scars of swords. Others complained that they had been tortured by them with hunger. These testimonies were not brought by obscure men, but by men chosen from all the churches, who had gathered here on their behalf and recounted what had happened: armed soldiers, crowds with clubs, threats of judges, and forged letters.

[Note: Faber, following the Pithoean manuscript, reads “Theodorus”; Sirmond reads “Theodosus.” From what is noted immediately below, it is clear that *Theodulus* is to be preferred.]

[Note: Thus Sirmond’s various readings agree with Athanasius and Theodoret. But Faber, with the Pithoean and Colbert manuscripts, reads “suspicions.”]

For letters forged by Theognitus against our fellow-bishops Athanasius and Marcellus were read out, so that the emperor too might be stirred against them. Those who had then been Theognitus’s deacons proved these things. Besides these were the stripping of virgins, the burning of churches, and prisons directed against the ministers of God; and all these things were done because of the unjust and accursed heresy of the Ariomaniacs. For those who renounced communion with them were compelled to endure these things.

[Note: In the Greek copies Asclepas is joined with Marcellus and Athanasius; afterward they read “so that the emperors,” in the plural.]

[Col. 0635A]

4. Having Entered Sardica, the Opponents Dread Their Adversaries’ Presence.—Considering these things, they saw that they were hemmed in. Ashamed to confess what they had committed, because they could no longer conceal it, they finally came to the city of Sardica, in order that by their presence they might seem to dispel suspicion of evil conduct.

[Note: Greek: *hyponoian hōs mē plēmmelēsantes doxōsi apopheresthai* (ὑπόνοιαν ὡς μὴ πλημμελήσαντες δόξωσιν ἀποφέρεσθαι), “suspicion, so that they might not seem to depart as having done wrong.”]

For, seeing those whom they had oppressed by false testimony, and also those whom they had most violently attacked, and having before their eyes, on the one hand, accusers of their conscience and, on the other, betrayers of their own crimes, they could not—or, in Greek, would not—come when summoned, especially because their conscience was troubled by Athanasius, Marcellus, and Asclepas, our fellow-bishops. These men both implored a judgment and challenged their accusers, that they might prove them guilty not only of the false charges which they had invented against them, but might also disclose what impious and wicked acts they had committed against the Churches. But the others were seized by such terror that they fled; and by that flight they exposed and laid bare their falsehood.

[Note: The Greek expression here requires the addition of “their own,” and shortly afterward “of conscience” after the word “terror.”]

### 5. Athanasius’s Innocence Established

Although their malice and falsehood were shown not only by the preceding facts but also by these, so that they could not find in their supposed flight any occasion for another evil device (read: *yet so that not even from that flight*); we demonstrated, in accordance with truth and reason—the rationale of truth—that the acts committed by them ought to be investigated. We found that they had lied even about these matters and had pursued nothing but an attack against our fellow bishops.

For the man whom they said had been murdered by Athanasius, named Arsenius, is numbered among the living. Hence it also became apparent from this that all the other charges advanced by them were full of lies and falsehood. As for their assertions concerning the broken cup [Col. 0635C]—read: assertions as though it had been broken—by Macharius, Athanasius’s presbyter: those who were present, having come from Alexandria, Mareotis, and other places, testified that nothing of the sort had occurred.

> [Note: This passage should be corrected from Athanasius and Theodoret as follows: “those who came from Alexandria, Mareotis, and other places testified that nothing of the sort had occurred.”]

Moreover, bishops writing from Egypt to our fellow bishop Julius emphatically affirmed that no such suspicion had even existed there. (This letter is extant in Athanasius, vol. I, p. 722.) They say that they also possess proceedings against him; but it is clear that whatever proceedings they have were drawn up while the other party was absent.

> [Note: Julius, writing to the Eusebians in Athanasius, p. 742, replies concerning those proceedings: “You know that records of proceedings in which only one party has been present have no force whatever,” etc.]

Yet, in those very proceedings pagans and catechumens were questioned. One catechumen, when questioned, said that he had been inside when Macharius made his incursion; and another, when questioned, said that the notorious Ischyras was lying ill in the church, *in a cell* (ἐν κελλίῳ). Thus it is clear that the mystery was not celebrated at all, because catechumens were inside, while Ischyras was lying sick.

> [Note: What is lacking here may be supplied from Athanasius and Theodoret as follows: “Yet in those very proceedings pagans and catechumens were questioned. One catechumen, when questioned, said that he had been inside when Macharius made his incursion; and another, when questioned,” etc.]

> [Note: Greek: καὶ Ἰσχύραν μὴ παρεῖναι, ἀλλὰ νοσοῦντα κατακεῖσθαι: “and that Ischyras was not present, but lay sick.”]

For Ischyras himself, the contriver of the whole malicious scheme, said that Athanasius had burned a certain book of the divine Scriptures. When convicted on this point, he began to admit that he himself had been ill when Macharius was present; so that it was apparent from this too that he was a false witness.

> [Note: We add “that he was” from Sirmond’s variant readings.]

Finally, as the reward of his falsehood, they gave the same Ischyras the dignity—or, in Greek, the “name” (ὄνομα)—of the episcopate, though he was not even a presbyter. For two presbyters came now to the council—men who had at that time been with Meletius, but later were received by Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, a man of blessed memory, and now were with Athanasius. They testified that this man had nowhere at all been a presbyter of Meletius, and that Meletius had no church or minister at all in that place in Mareotis. Yet they have now brought him with them as though he were a bishop, though formerly he was not even a presbyter, in order that they may seem, by the title of episcopate, to conceal their falsehood from their hearers.

> [Note: The Greek lacks “in the same place”; accordingly it signifies that Meletius possessed neither a church nor a minister, not only in Ischyras’s native place but anywhere at all in Mareotis. It follows that Ischyras was not a presbyter, since he was ordained neither by Meletius nor by the Alexandrian patriarch.]

### 6. Marcellus and Asclepas Blameless

The book composed by our brother and fellow bishop Marcellus was also read; and the carefully contrived malice of Eusebius and those who were with him was discovered.

> [Note: Thus Sirmond. Elsewhere: “of Eusebius and those who were with them.” Greek: οἱ περὶ Εὐσέβιον, “those around Eusebius.” Five books of Eusebius of Caesarea against Marcellus still survive. Julius, in Athanasius, p. 750, judges Marcellus—after he had been heard at the Roman council—to be free from every error.]

For the things which Marcellus stated merely as propositions they represented as though he had advanced them as already proven. Therefore the passages that followed were read, as were also those prefixed to the question; and his faith was found to be sound. For he did not assign to God the Word a beginning from the holy Virgin Mary, as they falsely alleged; nor did he write that his kingdom would have an end, but that his kingdom is without beginning and without end.

> [Note: Elsewhere, “he assigned”; and shortly afterward, “but his kingdom” was missing—a simple scribal slip. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical Theology*, I.18, accuses Marcellus of affirming that before Mary Christ was nothing other than a word very similar to ours. Hilary, if Jerome understood him correctly, supports him in *On the Trinity*, VII.3. Hence Gennadius, *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, ch. 3, associates him with Beryllus and Artemon, who considered Christ a mere man.]

But our fellow bishop Asclepas produced the proceedings drawn up at Antioch in the presence of his adversaries and Eusebius of Caesarea, and showed, from the judgments of the bishops who had decided the case, that he had been judged an irreproachable bishop.

> [Note: Greek: τῶν δικασάντων ἐπισκόπων ἔδειξεν, “he showed [from the judgments] of the bishops who had judged.” They suppose that the proceedings of the Antiochene conventicle of the year 330, by which Eustathius was driven from his see, are mentioned here. Sozomen, *Ecclesiastical History*, III.12, undoubtedly refers to this passage when he says that Asclepas was pronounced innocent at Sardica because he had recovered his episcopate by the judgment of Eusebius Pamphili and many other judges, and had proved these things true by judicial records.]

### 7. Crimes, Names, and Devices of the Eusebians

Rightly, therefore, though repeatedly summoned, they did not dare to come; rightly they fled, driven headlong by the prompting of their own conscience. By their flight they confirmed their falsehoods and caused belief to be given to what their accusers had said and proved in their presence.

What then? Beyond all this, men formerly deposed and expelled from the Church because of the heresy of Arius were not only received, but even promoted to a higher rank: deacons to the presbyterate, and from the presbyterate to the episcopate. This was for no other reason than that they might spread and disseminate their impious doctrine and corrupt the pious faith.

> [Note: Valesius rendered the Greek words ἀπὸ δὲ πρεσβυτέρων as “but presbyters who had been deposed.” Both the Hilarian reading and the preceding words make clear that ἀπό denotes the former rank, not the rank from which someone had fallen but that from which he rose to a higher one.]

After Eusebius, the chief leaders among them are Theodore of Heraclea, Narcissus of Neroniada in Cilicia, Stephen of Antioch, George of Laodicea—though, out of fear, he was not present from the East—Acacius of Caesarea in Palestine, Menophantus of Ephesus in Asia, Ursacius of Singidunum in Moesia, and Valens of Mursa in Pannonia.

> [Note: In the Greek copies: μετὰ τοὺς περὶ Εὐσέβιον νῦν ἔξαρχοι, “the present leaders after those around Eusebius.” Thus the word “two” seems superfluous here; or one should read “after the two Eusebii.” This reading is supported by *To Constantius*, I.5: “We have recently learned that these inventions were devised by the two Eusebii,” etc., especially since, George excepted, the same bishops who are joined here with the two Eusebii are joined there also.]

> [Note: Nothing occurs in Athanasius and Theodoret corresponding to the words, “though, out of fear, he was not present from the East.”]

For the men just named, together with those who came with them from the East, did not allow anyone to enter the holy council or even approach the holy Church of God. Coming to Sardica, they held assemblies among themselves in every place and made agreements under threats, that, when they came to Sardica, they should by no means appear for judgment or meet together with the holy and great synod. They came only for this: that, having come and, for appearance’s sake (ἐπὶ ἀφοσιώσει), shown themselves present, they should immediately flee.

> [Note: This passage may be restored from Theodoret as follows: “but only so that, when they had come and shown their presence for appearance’s sake (ἐπὶ ἀφοσιώσει), they might immediately flee.”]

We were able to learn these things from our fellow bishops Arius of Palestine and Stephen of Arabia, who did indeed come with them but withdrew from their treachery.

> [Note: In the Greek manuscripts these two bishops are named Macarius and Asterius. Yet in Athanasius’s subscriptions of the Palestinians, Arius, not Macarius, is found; and in the *Letter to the Solitaries*, p. 820, it is said that Arius and Asterius—one at Petra in Palestine, the other at Petra in Arabia—were mistreated by the Arians because they had withdrawn from them. There is scarcely any doubt that Asterius should be restored here in place of Stephen; below he signs as Asturus.]

When these men came to the holy synod, they complained indeed of the violence they had suffered, but asserted that nothing was being rightly done by the others. They added that there were very many persons there of sound faith who were prevented from coming to us by threats made against them. For this reason they laboured to remain all together in one house and did not allow them even a little time or freedom to act privately.

> [Note: The word *nec* (“nor”) is redundant. Then, instead of “allow them freedom,” the Greek has one word, ἰδιάζειν, meaning “to act privately.”]

### 8. Judgment of the Synod

Therefore, because it was not right to keep silence or let falsehoods, imprisonments, murders, assaults, forged letters, beatings, the stripping of virgins, exiles, the destruction of churches, burnings, transfers from smaller cities to larger churches, and, above all, the teachings of the Arian heresy rising against the true faith, remain unpunished: for this reason we pronounce our most beloved brothers and fellow bishops Athanasius of Alexandria, Marcellus of Ancyra in Galatia, Asclepas of Gaza, and those who with them minister to God, innocent and pure. We write to each of their provinces so that the people of the individual churches may know the integrity of their bishop and know that they retain their own bishop.

> [Note: Perhaps read “let” or “permit,” as the Greek has; shortly afterward it has τὰς πληγάς, “blows,” in place of “assaults.”]

> [Note: We add “burnings” from Sirmond and the Greek text, which subsequently adds “transfers from smaller cities to larger churches.”]

But those who have forced themselves into their churches like wolves—namely, Gregory in Alexandria, Basil in Ancyra, and Quintianus in Gaza—are neither to bear the name of bishop nor to share at all in communion. No one is to receive letters from them or write to them.

> [Note: The reading of Theodoret, τούτους μηδὲ ἐπισκόπους ὀνομάζειν μηδὲ χριστιανούς, “not even to call these men bishops or Christians,” is confirmed by Athanasius, *To the Solitaries*, p. 820, where he says that Gregory was judged by the synod unworthy to be called either bishop or Christian at all.]

The holy synod has likewise deposed from the rank of the episcopate Theodore, Narcissus, Acacius, Stephen, Ursacius, Valens, Menophantus, and George—although George, as stated, was not present out of fear, yet because he had formerly been deposed by Alexander, bishop of Alexandria of blessed memory—as well as all the others seized by the same Arian madness and implicated in the charges brought against them. We have judged that they are not only not bishops, but ought not even to possess communion with the faithful.

> [Note: Thus Sirmond. Faber has “the others seized,” omitting the word “are,” which occurs in the manuscripts.]

For those who separate the Son and estrange the Word from the Father must be separated from the Catholic Church and be strangers to the Christian name. Let them therefore be anathema to you, because they dared to corrupt the word of truth. For it is the apostle’s command: “If anyone proclaims to you a gospel contrary to what you received, let him be anathema” (Gal. 1:9). Announce that no one is to communicate with them, for there is no fellowship of light with darkness. Keep all these men far away, for Christ has no share with Belial.

Take care, beloved brethren, neither to write to them nor to receive their letters. Moreover, beloved brethren and fellow bishops, as though you had been present in spirit at this synod, see that all which we have established is confirmed by your letters, so that the agreement of the letters may make it plain that all bishops hold the same judgment and that the will of all is one.

> [Note: In place of these words Athanasius has, “May divine providence preserve you holy and joyful, beloved brethren,” and then appends the bishops’ subscriptions. In Theodoret, after these words are omitted, there follows an exposition of the faith—undoubtedly that which Athanasius, *Letter to the Antiochenes*, p. 576, warns is falsely circulated as belonging to the Synod of Sardica, and which both he and Eusebius of Vercelli, in the same author, p. 580, judge should be entirely suppressed, lest it be thought that the Nicene faith is insufficient.]

We pray, brethren, that you may be well in the Lord. End.

629. Here begins a copy of the letter made in the year 347 to Julius, bishop of the city of Rome, sent by the synod to Bishop Julius.

> [Note: Baronius published this same letter from a very ancient Cassinese manuscript of the Cresconian collection, under the year 347, no. 23. In it the following, more correct heading appears: “Here begins a copy of the Synod of Sardica made to Julius, bishop of the city of Rome.”]

### 9. Why Julius Was Not Present at the Synod; the Prerogative of Peter’s See

What we have always believed, we also now hold; for experience proves and confirms what each person has heard by report. For what the most blessed apostle Paul, teacher of the nations, said of himself is true: “Are you seeking proof of Christ who speaks in me?” (2 Cor. 13).

> [Note: We restore the apostle’s words from Baronius’s edition.]

Although, certainly, since the Lord Christ dwelt in him, there can be no doubt that the Holy Spirit spoke through his soul and gave utterance through the instrument of his body.

> [Note: In Baronius: “the Spirit also spoke through his soul.”]

Thus you also, most beloved brother, though separated in body, were present in agreement of mind and will. The excuse for your absence was honorable and necessary, lest schismatic wolves commit theft and seize their prey by stealth, or heretical dogs, stirred to madness by rabid frenzy, bark insanely, or indeed lest the devilish serpent pour out the poison of blasphemers.

> [Note: Baronius has “of blasphemies.” We have repeatedly found “of blasphemies” in manuscripts in place of “of blasphemers.”]

For this would seem the best and most fitting course: that the bishops of the Lord from every province should report matters concerning each one to the head, that is, to the See of the apostle Peter.

### 10. Julius’s Legates

Since the written records and the living testimony of our most beloved brothers and fellow presbyters Archydamus and Philoxenus, and of our most beloved son Leo the deacon, will be able to give a most truthful and faithful account of all that was done, transacted, and decreed, it seems almost superfluous to insert the same matters in this letter.

> [Note: In the Pithoean and Colbertine manuscripts: “Arcydamus and Philoxenus”; and shortly afterward, “were able,” not “will be able.” We correct these readings from Baronius.]

It became clear to all who had assembled from the eastern regions that those who call themselves bishops—although among them there are certain leaders, named in the preceding letter, section 7, whose sacrilegious minds the Arian heresy has stained with its deadly poison—had long delayed and, because of distrust, refused to come to judgment. They criticized both your communion and ours, though it bore no fault, because we had believed alike in Athanasius’s innocence, not merely upon the testimony of eighty bishops at the Council of Alexandria, whose letter is indicated in section 5, but also because, when summoned through your presbyters and by letter, they refused to come to the synod which was to be held in the city of Rome.

> [Note: Faber had substituted “from the synod,” having found “and the synod” in the Pithoean manuscript. Baronius’s “to the synod” is more accurate: namely, the synod held at Rome in 341, from which Julius wrote his letter to the Eusebians, copied by Athanasius in *Apology* II, p. 739.]

And it was sufficiently unjust, when they disregarded this, to deny fellowship to Marcellus and Athanasius although so many bishops bore witness.

> [Note: Baronius has “when they confessed,” a reading not to be despised: for by their flight they betrayed the guilt of their conscience, confessed that the accusations they had fabricated against the bishops were false, and that the testimony offered for them by so many bishops was true. The preceding letter frequently repeats this.]

### 11. Three Matters to Be Considered in the Synod

There were three matters requiring consideration. The most religious emperors themselves permitted a fresh and complete discussion of all matters: first and foremost, of the holy faith and the integrity of truth which they had violated; secondly, of the persons whom they said had been deposed, so that the confirmation of an unjust judgment might become just, if they could prove their allegations; and thirdly, a question truly deserving the name of question: that they had committed grave and bitter injuries, intolerable and even impious outrages, against the churches.

> [Note: Baronius has “chosen persons,” which Faber also found in his manuscript; later Faber himself inserted “as if” in place of “or if.” But an unexpressed particle *ut* is easily understood before “from the unjust [judgment].” Athanasius’s condemnation by the Eusebians was unjust for this reason alone: he was judged while absent. It would have become just if, being present, he could have been convicted of the charges brought against him.]

They seized bishops, presbyters, deacons, and all clerics; sent them into exile; transported them to desert places; killed them by hunger, thirst, nakedness, and every kind of deprivation; shut others in prison and consumed them by filth and stench; bound some with iron chains so tightly—supply “they constricted”—that their necks were strangled by the closest iron collars. Indeed, some of those bound died under that same unjust punishment; there can be no doubt that their death was glorious through martyrdom. Even now they dare to keep some persons confined. There was no cause for accusation except that they resisted, cried out that they abhorred the Arian and Eusebian heresy, refused communion with such persons, and chose not to assist those who agreed with them. Those who had previously been deposed were not only received, but promoted to clerical dignity, and received the reward of falsehood.

> [Note: From the reading of the Pithoean and Colbertine manuscripts, “who preferred to serve the age,” Faber produced “who, however, did not wish to serve the age.” We restore Baronius’s reading.]

### 12. The Perversity of Ursacius and Valens

Learn, most blessed brother, what was decreed concerning the impious and ignorant young men Ursacius and Valens. It was evident that they did not cease to sow the deadly seeds of adulterated doctrine, and that Valens, having abandoned his church, had wished to invade another church.

> [Note: In Baronius, “in Italy,” not “deadly.”]

At the time when he stirred up sedition, one of our brethren who could not escape, Viator, was struck down and trampled; on the third day he died in that same city of Aquileia. Valens, who disturbed and incited the people, was certainly the cause of his death. When you have read the matters which we communicated to the most blessed Augusti, you will readily see that we omitted nothing so far as reason permitted. And, lest the long account be burdensome, we have indicated who committed the acts and what they committed.

> [Note: We add “what” from Sirmond. Baronius, preferring “what they had previously done,” omits “and what they committed.”]

### 13. The Synod’s Decrees to Be Made Known through Julius in Sicily, Sardinia, and Italy

Your excellent prudence should arrange, by means of your letters, that our brethren in Sicily, Sardinia, and Italy learn what has been done and decreed. They must not, through ignorance, receive the letters of communion—that is, letters—from those whom a just judgment has deposed. Marcellus, Athanasius, and Asclepas, however, are to remain in our communion, because an unjust judgment could not harm them, nor could the flight and evasion of those who refused to come for judgment before all the bishops assembled by us delay their acquittal.

> [Note: In the Pithoean and Colbertine manuscripts: “that is, letters”; Sirmond: “that is, episcopal [letters].” These words are lacking in Baronius, who subsequently reads, “whom the judgment of the synod declared outside the episcopate.”]

> [Note: Baronius has “because of their flight and evasion.” “Because of their flight” would not be objectionable: that is, their acquittal ought not to have been delayed longer because their adversaries fled.]

> [Note: In Baronius: “to which we came,” less suitably, as is clear from section 2: “of the synod of all of us bishops who assembled.”]

The complete report of the brethren whom your sincere charity sent will, as we have mentioned above, fully instruct your unanimity concerning the rest. We have taken care to append the names of those who were deposed for their crimes, so that your distinguished Gravity may know who have been deprived of communion. As we have already stated, deign to admonish by your letters all our brethren and fellow bishops not to receive the letters of communion—that is, the letters—of these men.

> [Note: In the Pithoean manuscript: “not [their] letters,” which Baronius also has, reading later “letters brought thence” in place of “that is, letters.”]

## Names of the Heretics

### 14.

Ursacius of Singidunum; Valens of Mursa; Narcissus of Hieropolis; Stephen of Antioch; Acacius of Caesarea; Menophantus of Ephesus; George of Laodicea.

> [Note: In Baronius: “of Neronopolis,” supported by Athanasius at the beginning of *Apology* II, τῆς πόλεως Νέρωνος, “of the city of Nero.” Above, section 7, Hilary reads “of Neroniada.” Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, I.7, says: “Neronias is a city of Cilicia Secunda, which we now call Irenopolis.”]

## Likewise, the Names Below of the Bishops Who Were Present at the Synod of Sardica, Subscribed, and Also Took Part in the Judgment

### 15.

Osius of Spain, bishop of Cordoba; Annianus of Spain, of Castulo; Florentius of Spain, of Emerita; Dominianus of Spain, of Asturica; Castus of Spain, of Caesaraugusta; Praetextatus of Spain, of Barcelona; Maximus of Tuscany, of Lucca; Bassus of Macedonia, of Diocletianopolis; Porphyrius of Macedonia, of Philippi; Marcellus of Ancyra in Galatia; Euterius of Procia, of Caindus; Asclepius of Palestine, of Gaza; Moysius of Thessaly, of Thebes; Vincentius of Campania, of Capua; Januarius of Campania, of Beneventum; Protogenes of Dacia, of Serdica; Dioscorus of Thrace; Hymenius of Thessaly, of Pearata; Lucius of Thrace, of Caynopolis—perhaps Hadrianopolis?—Lucius of Italy, of Verona; ### 16. Athanasius’s Innocence Manifest; the Offering Is the Work of a Presbyter Alone

“The matter,” says Hilary, “as I think, needs no explanation in another discourse. For all things have been so declared and set forth that they have been brought into the light of knowledge: witnesses assembled from Egypt; Athanasius himself present; the nocturnal and shameful flight of the false judges through the testimony of their conscience; the grievous odium of so many crimes, laid before the eyes of all.

“Add the origin of the case, from which an occasion for condemnation was sought against Athanasius. He is accused, through the violence of his presbyter, of an altar being disturbed at the very time of the sacrifices, where Ischyras, a presbyter, was present. Ischyras is denied to have been a presbyter, and the falsehood of the charge is condemned together with its author. Moreover, the work of sacrifice could not have been performed without a presbyter. When the inquiry concerns a man, there is no place at all for so grave an act; in Mareotis there is no church. Did religion itself perhaps fail in that place alone? Or did the place where the sacrifice was violated collapse in some chasm, as usually happens? Ischyras is alleged to have been ordained bishop from being a deacon, so that the authority of the lying bishop may be greater than that of the presbyter who suffered the outrage. But if there was a church, it is there; if there is none, neither was there one. And what is doubtful: whether these informers of false charges asserted that an act had occurred which could have remained unperformed (perhaps: “which was shown to be unperformed”); or whether those who later reported it asserted that it had not been established—though, if it occurred, it cannot not have occurred?”

> [Note: Thus from Sirmond. Elsewhere: “But concerning the origin.”]

> [Note: Namely, in the village inhabited by Ischyras. Elsewhere, there were many churches in Mareotis, though Hilary’s words imply otherwise.]

> [Note: Nicephorus, *Ecclesiastical History*, IX.12, calls Ischyras a self-appointed presbyter. He himself boasted that he was a presbyter of Colluthus. But the presbyters and deacons of Mareotis testify in Athanasius, p. 792, that he was never even regarded as a cleric, except perhaps by his relatives and by those who lived far from his village.]

> [Note: We add “if,” which the completeness of the sentence plainly requires.]

> [Note: Sirmond, from the Remigian manuscript, reads “it was established.” From both readings one may readily form: “it is evident that they lied—[they asserted] that what was shown never to have occurred had occurred; but it is evident that those who later reported it did not lie.” The discussion is certainly both of Athanasius’s accusers, who falsely imputed to him the charge of breaking the cup, and of the Mareotic presbyters and deacons, who later reported the falsehood of this charge in Athanasius, p. 792.]

### 17. Athanasius’s Crimes Are Not Established

“If anyone has been educated by human institutions for the use of common understanding, if anyone follows the precepts of prudence along the path of seeking truth, let him attend carefully and consider what judgment he thinks ought to be maintained in matters of this kind. Meanwhile, let an examination be made of the authorities for the allegations.

“These are the two reports: one affirms a crime, names a place of the crime, and identifies a man who suffered the injury; the other denies the crime, the place, and the man. I ask: toward which judgment would it seem fair for you to incline? Surely, I think, anyone consulted by both parties and placed between their two judgments would say this: If there is a crime, it must be proven; if there is a place, it must be shown; if there is a man, he must be produced. But when there is neither proof of the deed, nor a sacred place, nor a person injured, it will be judged insane to pass judgment when the things upon which one judges do not exist.”

> [Note: In earlier editions and in the manuscript, “communion,” a scribal error very common in manuscripts, as we have found elsewhere; we do not hesitate to correct it here.]

### 18. No Ground for Condemning Athanasius

“Look to heaven and the stars, you priests; and fix your attention, in the freedom of faith and hope which you have received, upon him who made them from nothing, remembering that the pattern of the judgment to come upon you has been set before you: ‘With the judgment with which you judge, you shall be judged’ (Matt. 7:2).

“Answer me as I ask this: by what judgment did you condemn Athanasius? You will doubtless say: ‘By that of bishops’; and this will be the excuse of your confession. ‘We followed,’ you will say, ‘the holy reverence due to judicial decisions in episcopal communion.’ But will you deny that you knew Athanasius—whose condemnation Valens, Ursacius, and Saturninus demand from you—to have been restored to communion by Hosius, Maximinus, and Julius?

“I do not make comparisons. I ask: what was your judgment concerning Athanasius’s alleged crime? His presbyter Macharius is said to have burst into a Mareotic church, disturbed Ischyras the presbyter, and cast down the sacraments of our salvation; catechumen and pagan were questioned as witnesses to this matter. But do you not know that the holy men assembled at Sardica afterward judged that there was no church in Mareotis and that Ischyras was not a presbyter?

“What is it that you followed? You grant authority to false bishops and deny it to others. You decree that things exist which do not exist; and you judge things which are not. But if you believed this allegation—or perhaps this prompting—I suppose prison compelled you, a guard pressed upon you, a torturer bore down on you, a sword hung over you, fire scorched you. In judging things that do not exist, wickedness prevailed among you over episcopal authority; in establishing the truth, did holiness lose its credit? O true disciples of Christ! O worthy successors of Peter and Paul! O pious fathers of the Church! O ambitious intermediaries between God and the people—you have sold Christ’s truth to human falsehood!

“We have therefore satisfied the first proposition, in which we promised to show that Athanasius can be held guilty of none of the crimes alleged against him. It remains for me to say, very briefly, what was done concerning Marcellus and Photinus.”

> [Note: Thus Sirmond from the Remigian manuscript. Elsewhere: “the end of the proposition.”]

[Col. 0645B] 19. Condemnation of Photinus, and the repentance of Ursacius and Valens. — “Photinus was bishop of Sirmium, instructed by Marcellus; for he was also a deacon under him for some time. This man, after corrupting the habits and discipline of innocence, persisted in disturbing evangelical truth by novel preaching. And this happens frequently: when the growth of vices has brought losses in the love of God, the mad pursuit of corrupted knowledge increases.

“Therefore, to remove Photinus from the episcopate—he had already been condemned as a heretic two years earlier at the Synod of Milan (A.D. 347)—bishops from very many provinces assembled (A.D. 349), all the more anxious and troubled because everything was again being disturbed and thrown into confusion, since it had long been necessary for the Church to cut off several bishops as guilty either of false judgments against Athanasius or of communion with the Arian heresy.

[Note: [Col. 0645B] All agree that some celebrated and catholic council is mentioned here. There can be no doubt concerning its date. For, since Hilary says that Valens and Ursacius requested pardon upon the occasion of this council, and since, according to Socrates, book II, chapter 24, they did not turn their minds to this until after Athanasius’s return to Alexandria, it is clear that it was held in A.D. 349, two years after Sardica.

There is greater controversy among scholars concerning its place. We shall not recount what Sirmond, Petavius, and Pierre de Marca thought in their individual dissertations on this location. The name of Sirmium, occurring below at the beginning of §21, has misled many. But that it was held at Milan, not at Sirmium, is indicated quite plainly by the Synod of Rimini, Fragment VIII, §2, which speaks thus of the recantation of Ursacius and Valens: “They requested pardon, as their writings contain, which they then deserved from the council at Milan, with the legates of the Roman Church also in attendance.” More plainly, the Greek words of the same synod, in Athanasius, *On the Synods*, p. 877, declare that they requested and obtained pardon when the council was being held at Milan: “And the time when these things were transacted was when the council was convened at Milan.”

But they obtained pardon only in A.D. 349. From this it follows that the words of the Synod of Rimini refer to the Council of Milan not of A.D. 347 but of A.D. 349. The same must be said of the words of Ursacius and Valens, who below in §20 profess before Julius that, in the petition which they presented at Milan, they had anathematized Arius. For Socrates, book II, chapter 24, does not allow us to understand that this petition was offered in A.D. 347: he writes that Valens and Ursacius burned with a very great zeal for the doctrine of Arius until they learned that Athanasius had been restored, by the Council of Jerusalem in A.D. 349, to his see and ecclesiastical communion. Athanasius assigns their repentance to the same time, *Apology* II, p. 775.

And certainly, in A.D. 347 the affairs of Valens and Ursacius were not so desperate that they would immediately have thought the favor of the Catholics necessary. Their spirits, though somewhat cast down by the judgment of the Synod of Sardica, were revived by the decisions at Philippopolis. At that time the Eusebians were also raging with impunity in many places. Athanasius himself did not dare return to his church until two years later.

Those who think that the petition of Ursacius and Valens was submitted at Milan in A.D. 347 object that they cannot see why, after requesting pardon from the synod, they approached Julius; or at least, if we say that they did so by the synod’s command, then what Hosius says in Athanasius, p. 839—that they came to Rome of their own accord—is already false. But who does not see that “of their own accord” is opposed to violence inflicted by soldiers or punishments, not to the kindly exhortation of a synod? Moreover, it was equitable that those who before the Council of Sardica had scorned to come to Rome when summoned by Julius’s letters—as they themselves confess—should now, penitent, comply with the request of the Roman bishop.

Furthermore, Hilary’s whole narrative says this: Valens and Ursacius first approached Julius; having obtained pardon from him, they presented at Milan a petition in which they condemned Arius and Arius’s inventions; and finally, by letters sent to Julius, they recanted and withdrew whatever they had disseminated against Athanasius.]

“Having seized this opportunity, Ursacius and Valens approached the bishop of the Roman people (A.D. 349), begged that they might be received into the Church, and asked to be admitted by pardon into communion. Julius, acting on counsel, granted the pardon for which they asked, so that, to the advantage of the catholic Church, he might also weaken the Arians by admitting into the communion of reconciled peace those who had formerly disturbed unity but now repented of this policy and audacity.

[Note: [Col. 0646C] Pierre de Marca, in his dissertation on the date of the Synod of Sirmium, here reads *ex concilio* (“by decision of the council”). For he thinks that the synod which we have shown to have met at Milan was held at Rome, and that this is proved both by these words of Hilary and by the words of Hosius, as well as by the letters of Ursacius and Valens. The distinguished scholar Stephen Baluzius agrees with him in the new Collection of Councils, which he undertook with great labor and diligence.

But Hosius’s words in Athanasius, *To the Solitaries*, p. 839, are these: “They [Ursacius and Valens] came voluntarily to Rome and issued a written profession before the bishop and the presbyters there present.” The letter of Ursacius and Valens reads: “We profess before Your Holiness, with all our brother presbyters present.” These words certainly signify not some celebrated council assembled from very many provinces, but only the presence of Julius and his presbyters.

Hence, if anything is to be altered in Hilary’s words, instead of *ex consilio* (“on counsel”), one would most approve *eo consilio* (“with this purpose”), that is, with the purpose of weakening the Arians, etc. Since by this reasoning Hilary excuses a certain readiness of Julius in granting pardon, it confirms what we consider established: the petition of Ursacius and Valens, by which they condemned Arius, was presented at Milan not in A.D. 347 but in A.D. 349. For Julius would not need to be excused for granting pardon rather readily if he had granted it only two years after their public testimony of repentance.]

20. “And because confession is possible only concerning truth, repentance only concerning fault, and pardon only concerning an offense committed, Valens and Ursacius, before being admitted—as they requested—to communion, first professed in letters of this kind concerning Athanasius’s innocence, the falsity of the judgment, and the guilt of the Arian heresy.”

[Col. 0647A] Copy of the letter which, after the declaration of the Easterners, Valens wrote out in his own hand in the city of Rome, affirming that Athanasius was not guilty (A.D. 349), and which Ursacius signed.

[Note: [Col. 0647B] That is, the Easterners who assembled at Jerusalem in A.D. 349, as we infer from Socrates, book II, chapter 24. There Maximus first, after convening the council, restored Athanasius to communion and his former dignity; then the synod informed the bishops at Alexandria and throughout Libya and Egypt by letter of the decisions and judgments concerning Athanasius; and finally, when these things became known, Ursacius and Valens—who had previously clung stubbornly to the Arian doctrine—condemned their former zeal and went to Rome. Athanasius supports this, *Apology* II, p. 775, where, after setting out the letter of the Council of Jerusalem, he adds: “When they saw these things, Ursacius and Valens, despairing of their own case, went to Rome and confessed their sins with repentance,” etc.]

To the most blessed lord Pope Julius, Valens and Ursacius, greetings.

Since it is established that we formerly conveyed in our letters many serious accusations against Bishop Athanasius, and, though summoned by the letters of Your Holiness, did not give an account concerning the matter which we had reported, we profess before Your Holiness, with all our brother presbyters present, that everything formerly brought to your ears concerning the aforesaid man was falsely reported by us and is wholly without force. Therefore we most willingly embrace communion with the aforesaid Athanasius, especially since Your Holiness, in accordance with its innate benevolence, has deigned to grant pardon to our error.

[Note: [Col. 0647C] Were these other letters than those which the Council of Sardica, writing to Julius above in §10, mentions in these words: “Though summoned by your presbyters and by letter, they refused to come to the synod that was to be held in the city of Rome”?

We restore the particle *a* (“by us”), omitted in the printed editions, from the Pithoean manuscript. The reading thus agrees more fully with the beginning: “Since it is established that we formerly conveyed many serious accusations . . .” Athanasius, however, does not render in Greek the words “by us.” With his support we previously restored “to your ears,” whereas the former reading was “to our ears.”]

We also profess that, if at any time the Easterners or Athanasius himself should wish maliciously to summon us to a case, we shall not appear without your knowledge. And we profess, by this hand with which we write, that we have now and always anathematized Arius the heretic and his adherents—who say, “There was a time when the Son was not,” who say that the Son is from nothing, and who deny that the Son of God [add: God] existed before the ages—as we did in our former petition which we presented at Milan; and we say again that we have condemned forever the Arian heresy, as stated above, and its authors.

[Note: [Col. 0647C] In the printed edition of Athanasius, “Eusebius” occurs in place of “the Easterners”; this pleased some, who understood “Eusebians” by that name, since the three well-known Eusebii—of Caesarea, Emesa, and Nicomedia—had died. But our reading is confirmed by an ancient Greek copy of the works of St Athanasius preserved in the royal library.]

And in the hand of Ursacius: “I, Bishop Ursacius, have subscribed to this our profession.”

[Note: [Col. 0647D] In Athanasius, in place of these words: “I, Ursacius, being present, subscribed to this my confession; Valens likewise.”]

[Col. 0648B] “This letter,” says Hilary, “was sent two years after the heresy of Photinus was condemned by the Romans.”

[Note: [Col. 0647B] This letter, which we have shown should be dated A.D. 349, was plainly written while Constans was still alive, from the words of Hosius in Athanasius, *To the Solitaries*, p. 839. Athanasius also presents it in Greek translation in *Apology* II, addressed to Constantius, p. 776.

Those who maintain, first, that Ursacius and Valens presented their petition at Milan and, second, that the Synod of Rimini, Fragment VIII, §2, testifies that they requested pardon at the Milanese council, refer both claims to the Synod of Milan of A.D. 347, and think that they are called “Romans” here because legates of the Roman Church were in attendance. But it has already been shown that the aforesaid petition and the pardon requested belong to A.D. 349; nor is there any record establishing that legates of the Roman Church attended the Milanese synod of A.D. 347.

The words immediately preceding are also very inconvenient for Pierre de Marca, who confirms from this passage his opinion concerning a Roman council of A.D. 349. Stephen Baluzius tries to meet the difficulty by saying that there is an error here and that *quum haeresis* (“when the heresy”) should be read in place of *quam haeresis* (“after the heresy”); but even thus he does not explain the meaning of “was sent two years after,” to which *quam*, not *quum*, then correctly belongs.

But in the words “was sent two years after the heresy of Photinus was condemned by the Romans,” exactly the same time is indicated as in §19: “who had already been condemned as a heretic two years earlier in the Synod of Milan.” Whoever compares the two passages will not deny that the letter of Ursacius and Valens is here said to have been sent in the very year when bishops assembled from very many provinces to remove Photinus from the episcopate, and two years after that heretic had been condemned—not in a Roman but in a Milanese synod.

What, then, does “by the Romans” mean? It is highly probable that Hilary added this expression in order to forewarn that he was not dealing at all with what the Easterners had done against Photinus; accordingly, “Romans” here are set in contrast to “Easterners.” For that Photinus had been condemned by the Easterners before A.D. 347 is attested by their lengthy creed in Athanasius, *On the Synods*, sent into Italy around A.D. 344 or 345 by Eudoxius, Martyrius, and Macedonius; in it the heresy of Photinus is expressly noted. Finally, on its account, he was deposed from the episcopate in A.D. 351 by the Eastern Synod of Sirmium.

Here, therefore, the actions of the Romans against Photinus are distinguished from those of the Sirmians and other Easterners. Indeed, calling the Latin language “Roman” and those who used Latin “Romans” was customary not only among Greeks but also among Latins. Hence Jerome says in Letter LXII to Theophilus: “I think that through constant conversation and daily association with Latins he does not fail to know the Roman language.” In Letter LXIII, Rufinus testifies that many had asked Jerome to make Origen Roman; shortly afterward Jerome promises that he will bestow the books of the *Song of Songs* themselves and very many others upon Roman ears. But why say more? In our Hilary, *On Psalm* II, §35, “into the Roman language” is the same as “into the Latin language.” It follows that “by the Romans” is equivalent to “by the Latins,” by which Italians or also other Westerners are to be understood. Hence, when Epiphanius wrote, *Heresies* LXXI, §1, that Photinus was condemned in the Western Synod of Sardica, he reached the date, if not the name, of the synod.]

638. Likewise, a copy of another letter of Valens and Ursacius (written A.D. 349), which they sent from Aquileia to Athanasius and the bishops some time later, after issuing the preceding letter from Rome.

[Note: [Col. 0649B] Sirmond: “they issued it from Rome.” Pithoean manuscript: “they had sent it from Rome.” What Hosius says in Athanasius, p. 839—that they issued the preceding confession after first sending Athanasius peaceful and friendly letters—conflicts with Hilary’s statement. Athanasius, *To the Solitaries*, p. 826, supports Hosius. It is nevertheless probable that in their letter to Julius, in which they mention the petition they had presented at Milan, they would have mentioned this letter sent to Athanasius if they had written it earlier.

Others think Hilary was deceived because, after Ursacius and Valens had sent Athanasius peaceful letters and delivered their petition to Julius, they again signed other conciliatory letters, which Peter and Irenaeus, presbyters of Athanasius, were collecting from every quarter, as Athanasius relates, *To the Solitaries*, p. 826.]

[Col. 0649A]

To the lord brother Athanasius, Ursacius and Valens.

The arrival of our brother and fellow-presbyter Moysetes, who is coming to your beloved self, has provided an opportunity, dearest brother, through whom we send you our most abundant greetings from the city of Aquileia and pray that you may read our letter in health. For you will give us confidence if you likewise repay us in your reply. Know, indeed, from this letter that we have a place with you and ecclesiastical communion. May divine mercy preserve you, brother.

“Therefore, after the preceding letters had been sent, pardon was granted to those who asked for it, and their return to the catholic faith, together with communion, was bestowed; especially because the very letters of those seeking pardon contained the truth of the Synod of Sardica.

[Note: [Col. 0649B] The preceding letters contain the truth of the Synod of Sardica insofar as they confirm that all the accusations brought against Athanasius are false.]

21. Athanasius separates Marcellus from his communion. — “But meanwhile there was an assembly at Sirmium. Photinus, a heretic who had formerly been declared guilty and long since cut off from the communion of unity, could not even then be removed because of the faction of the people.

[Note: [Col. 0649C] Many distinguished scholars think that the place is here identified where, above in §19, bishops assembled from very many provinces; accordingly, they count this Synod of Sirmium of A.D. 349, against Photinus, among the catholic councils. But it has already been proved that it was different from that indicated in §19. It will shortly be shown to have been Arian, not catholic.

No less far from the truth are the fewer persons who interpret these words as referring to the Synod of Sirmium of A.D. 351. More correctly, “Meanwhile there was an assembly at Sirmium” may be understood either of those who brought the decision of the Milanese synod against Photinus to Sirmium, or of those who at the same time assembled in that same city of Sirmium—as the subsequent material plainly shows—and confirmed the condemnation of Photinus in such a way that they craftily inserted a mention of Marcellus, as Photinus’s teacher, from whom Athanasius himself had withdrawn, in order to overthrow the acts of the Synod of Sardica and revive the question of Athanasius, which had been laid to rest.

The acts of this Sirmian assembly, which are explained hereafter, are illuminated by Sulpicius Severus, who entitles it the Arian Synod of Sirmium. Thus he writes on p. 241, under the heading “Council of Sardica”: “After an interval, Athanasius, having fully discovered that Marcellus’s faith was not sound, suspended him from communion; and Marcellus had the modesty, when censured by the judgment of so great a man, to withdraw voluntarily. Yet, though innocent before, he could seem guilty after becoming corrupted, and to have already been guilty at the time when judgment had been rendered concerning him.”

Then, after placing the heading “Arian Synod of Sirmium,” he adds: “Having therefore found such an opportunity, the Arians conspired altogether to overthrow the decrees of the Synod of Sardica. For they seemed to have some pretext available: the judgment for Athanasius had been as unjust as the acquittal of Marcellus, who was now proved, even by Athanasius’s judgment, to be a heretic. For Marcellus had become a defender of the Sabellian heresy; while Photinus had previously introduced a new heresy, differing indeed from Sabellius in respect of unity, but preaching that Christ’s beginning was from Mary. The Arians, therefore, by a crafty plan, mix the innocent with the guilty and embrace in one judgment the condemnation of Photinus, Marcellus, and Athanasius; thus preparing the minds of the emperors not to think that they had judged Athanasius wrongly, since they had held true opinions concerning Marcellus and Photinus.”

We are convinced that this Sirmian assembly was Arian: first, by Sulpicius’s testimony; second, by its own proceedings, in which it attempted to overthrow the Sardican decrees; and finally, by the creed whose poison Hilary exposes below in §24. It is equally certain that it was different from the council held in the same city in A.D. 351. For, since it craftily tried, in Sulpicius’s words, to prejudice the emperors’ minds against the Sardican decrees, Constans must still have been alive; he died in A.D. 350.
