In demonstrating the Milanese and Sirmian synods of A.D. 349, we have exceeded the proper length of notes; but it was necessary to show at some length what escaped the notice of so many and such great men, otherwise far more acute than ourselves.]

[Note: [Col. 0650C] This statement can formerly be referred to the Synod of Milan of A.D. 347. But it will be useful here briefly to survey whatever was done against Photinus in different places and at different times. First, he was pronounced guilty around A.D. 344 at an assembly of Easterners, from which issued a creed enlarged with many appendices, presented by Athanasius in *On the Synods*. If Sulpicius referred to this, he could say on p. 240 that the judgment by which Photinus was proved a heretic had not been annulled by the Synod of Sardica.

Then, in A.D. 347, he was cut off from communion of unity by the Western Synod of Milan. Epiphanius was mistaken about the date of this synod when he wrote, *Heresies* LXXI, §1, that Photinus was condemned at the Western Synod of Sardica. Two years later, he was again deposed by the judgment of Westerners at Milan, with legates of the Roman Church present; the judgment of deposition was immediately sent to the Easterners and confirmed by them when they assembled at Sirmium, though he could not yet be removed because of the faction of the people. Finally, in A.D. 351, after the Easterners again assembled at Sirmium, he was expelled from the episcopate and Germinius was appointed in his place.]

“But Athanasius separated from his own communion Marcellus, who, after the reading of the book that he had published in writing—for we too possess it—had been restored to the episcopate by the decision of the Synod of Sardica. Athanasius did this when he perceived that Marcellus was introducing certain other novelties and, by ambiguous preaching, was seeking the path to that teaching into which Photinus broke forth. By anticipating it with judgment, Athanasius showed Marcellus’s design of corrupt intention, and did not condemn him on the basis of the publication of the book. But since evil is readily produced from good, he gave authority not to the proceedings formerly taken against Marcellus but to the proceedings to be taken against Photinus.

[Note: [Col. 0650D] This passage causes difficulty, especially because Athanasius everywhere defends Marcellus, expressly so in the Letter to the Solitaries, written no earlier than A.D. 357. In addition, Epiphanius, *Heresies* LXXII, §4, relates that, when he once asked Athanasius what he thought of Marcellus, Athanasius gave no answer but merely smiled slightly, thus displaying only some suspicion concerning him.

Nevertheless, Sulpicius agrees with Hilary, writing the same thing upon his authority; and this very point was also contained, as is explained below at the beginning of §23, in the letter of the Easterners replying from the Sirmian synod to the Milanese synod. Could this have been nothing but a calumny of those Easterners, too readily believed by Hilary? And when he says that Marcellus was excluded by Athanasius at an earlier time than Photinus is charged, he does not mean the period before the Synod of Milan in A.D. 347, but only that before the Milanese synod of A.D. 349, at which Photinus was condemned in a more formal manner.]

[Note: [Col. 0651D] Namely, by the Synod of Constantinople of A.D. 336, whose proceedings were annulled by Sardica.]

22. The Easterners who attempt to nullify the Sardican proceedings undertaken in Athanasius’s favor. — “But all ought to know this: after the judgment against Marcellus which was annulled by the judgments of Sardica, no synod was ever subsequently assembled against him; nor, when a decree concerning Photinus was made by the Westerners and communicated to the Easterners, was any judgment against Marcellus expressly included in it.

[Note: [Col. 0652D] We restore this passage from Sirmond’s readings; formerly the text was: “nor then, whence [the decree] against Photinus.” Here the complaint is that the Easterners assembled at Sirmium wrote craftily concerning Marcellus, although the Westerners had written nothing to them concerning him from the Milanese synod.]

“But men cunning in mind, subtle in intellect, and persistent in malice sought an opportunity to reopen the judgment annulled by Athanasius’s acquittal at Sardica; and, while writing back concerning Photinus, added mention of Marcellus as the teacher of such doctrines, so that the newness of the case might arouse into public recollection the question concerning Athanasius himself, long dead and buried by the judgment of truth, and that the name of Marcellus might be smuggled in through Photinus’s condemnation.

“Moreover, the body of the preceding letter states that Marcellus, upon the pretext of the book which he had published concerning the subjection of the Lord Christ, was condemned by the Arians together with Athanasius. It also teaches that he was found innocent upon the reading of that same book. The reliability of the book, still extant, also proves the falsity of the Arian judgment at the Synod of Constantinople in A.D. 336.

[Note: [Col. 0652D] The printed editions read “preceding”; the manuscript’s “of the preceding [letter]” is better: namely, the Sardican letter in §6.]

“Concerning Photinus alone, as custom required, letters are sent to the Easterners—not, as is now being done, in order wrongfully to extort their assent, but according to the established practice of informing all.

[Note: [Col. 0652D] We add only *tantum* (“alone”) from Sirmond’s readings. The discussion consistently concerns Western proceedings at the Synod of Milan in A.D. 349 and the Eastern reply from the city of Sirmium.

[Col. 0651C] That is, after the Synod of Rimini.]

23. “But why is Athanasius accused, in the reply sent from the Eastern Synod of Sirmium, of having denied communion to Marcellus? Was Marcellus excluded because of an error in his book? They themselves are witnesses that Photinus derived the beginnings of that perversity from Marcellus’s teachings. For, when Athanasius denied him communion, Marcellus kept himself from entering the church. Thus communion with him in that faith [perhaps: ‘in the rightly established faith’] teaches concerning the subjection and the handing over of the kingdom; while its denial, because of the perversity [read: ‘the perversity’] of another doctrine, shows this again.

“Thus each judgment of this man is free from blame: in granting communion, he followed the assent of the Synod of Sardica; in denying it, he acted with Marcellus alone withdrawing himself, without any synodal authority at all. But all this question belongs to another case and another grievance. And although their long-conceived hatreds against Athanasius may thus be satisfied, nevertheless such a great undertaking advances to a greater degree of wickedness.

24. The Sirmian reply, though displaying an orthodox creed, is full of fraud and poison. — “For a third point permits me to show that the creed which they set down at the beginning of the letter is fraudulent, heretical, and suffused beneath flattering words with inward poison. For they make this profession: ‘There is one unbegotten God the Father, and one only-begotten Son of his, God from God, light from light, firstborn of every creature; and,’ adding third, ‘the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete.’ Thus, when the security of readers or the simplicity of the unlearned has been caught by such gentle beginnings, by one and the same agreement of an extorted subscription they proceed to the condemnation of Photinus, the accusation of Athanasius, and the condemnation of the catholic faith.

“And I hope that the Synod of Sardica has supplied no small part of this knowledge—namely, knowledge of Athanasius’s innocence—where it is shown that, through Arian persecution, all the charges against Athanasius were fabricated and that force was applied to God’s people, so that they might pass into a ruinous connivance at deadly doctrine. Yet I shall state the matter briefly, because the case requires it.

25. Apostolic men always labored to defend faith in the Trinity; from this they incurred the hatred of the Church’s enemies. — “It was always the care and task of apostolic men, by steadfast and public preaching of the perfect faith, to suppress every attempt of the barking heresy and, by setting forth the truth of the Gospels, to extinguish the perversity of erring doctrine, lest the contagion of clinging vice, polluting the minds of hearers with a kind of stain, infect them.

“Accordingly, in various letters they carefully, repeatedly, and copiously embraced what belief concerning God the Father, what knowledge concerning the Son of God, and what sanctification in the Holy Spirit ought to be held; so that the Son, God, might be known from God the Father, and God the Father might be in God the Son, and the Son, God, might be in God the Father. And thus, according to his own declaration, ‘I and the Father are one’ (John 10:30), and again, ‘As you, Father, are in me, and I in you’ (John 17:21), our faith is contained in the names and persons of Father and Son: one God.

“For neither Jewish envy, nor Gentile hatred, nor heretical fury has been aroused against us for causes other than that, in confessing the Father as everlasting, we confess in him the power of eternity in the name of the Son: the Son coeternal with him in the substance of eternity, Son not merely in name but in reality, power, and truth.

[Note: [Col. 0652D] The printed editions read “the power of eternity.” The manuscripts’ reading, “the power of eternity,” is preferred in the accusative: that is, by confessing the Father everlasting, we confess the Son coeternal with him in the substance of eternity, who is Son not merely in name but also in reality, power, and truth. This is more clearly explained below in §28.]

“But the perversity of heretics has always arisen from impious belief. For while, occupied with vices and turned away from works of innocence, they entangle themselves in the difficulties of useless questions, having become disapproved in life, will, and judgment, they seek to please by novelty of doctrine after losing the knowledge of truth.

[Note: [Col. 0653C] Up to this point the received text was: ‘they seek to please by life, will, judgment, novelty of doctrine.’ By removing the final letter *m*, which, as we have observed, frequently occurs redundantly in manuscripts, the reading becomes clear.]

26. The occasion of the Council of Nicaea; Arian doctrine. — “Therefore, when it had become known to our fathers that two Arians had arisen as preachers of a most profane creed, and that not mere opinion but the judicial determination of this corruption had extended itself too far, they flew together from every region of the world and assembled at Nicaea, in order that, after the faith had been set forth to the peoples and the path made straight in the light of understanding and divine knowledge, the seedbeds of the emerging evil might be destroyed within its very authors.

[Note: [Col. 0653C] It is unclear which two Ariuses Hilary means. Sulpicius appears to have understood that two men bearing the proper name Arius are designated here, when he says on p. 237: “The Emperor also is corrupted by two Ariuses, most violent authors of this perfidy.” There is no doubt that he wrote this in imitation of Hilary, from his following words, which we think should be copied here in order that the antiquity and authenticity of these Fragments may be increasingly confirmed: “What the Arians preached was of this kind: that the Father of the Lord begot the Son for the purpose of establishing the world; that he made him, by his own power, from nothing, into a new and other substance—a new and other Lord; and that there was a time when the Son had not existed. Therefore, because of this evil, a synod is assembled at Nicaea from the whole world,” etc.

Hence the ancient author of the prologue to Athanasius’s disputation against Arius, both in Athanasius, vol. II, and in Vigilius of Thapsus, cites Sulpicius in the *Chronicles* as witness that two Ariuses hissed like two serpents from one mouth. And indeed two Ariuses subscribe to the first confession of the Arian party in Epiphanius, *Heresies* LXIX, §8. Likewise Alexander, in the encyclical in Socrates, book I, chapter 6, lists among those who had fallen away from the Church Arius, Achillas, Aethales, another Arius, and so on.

Yet this other Arius is scarcely of sufficient importance to be compared and joined with the first, and I would not readily believe that Hilary refers to him here. It is more probable that Hilary marks out the two leaders of the Arian sect: Arius and Eusebius of Nicomedia. For it is clear that, for Hilary, the term “Arians” was not proper to one or two men but common to the whole sect, from these words in *On the Synods*, §83: “Let that which has been denied by the Arians be pleasing”; and shortly after: “The very perfidy of the Arians.”]

“But the Arians taught such things: that God the Father begot the Son for the purpose of establishing the world, and that, by his own power, he made him from nothing into a new and other substance, a new and other God. They were profane toward the Father, thinking that something like him could be begotten from nothing; blasphemous toward Christ, stripping him of the inheritance of paternal infinity.

[Note: [Col. 0654C] Elsewhere the text reads: “or from nothing, into a new and other substance.” With Sirmond from the Remigian manuscript, we prefer “by his own power, from nothing”; the recently cited passage of Sulpicius supports this, and we correct the rest from it. See *On the Trinity*, book VI, §18.]

“Thus, though they had learned from the person of the Father, ‘There is no God besides me’ (Isaiah 45:18), and from the Son, ‘I am in the Father and the Father in me’ (John 14:11), and ‘I and the Father are one’ (John 10:30), they broke the bond of holy unity in both, assigning to our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, a temporal beginning from a non-existent created substance, an origin from nothing, not from another [substance].

[Note: [Col. 0654C] The Pithoean manuscript reads “substance.” Perhaps: “from a non-existent substance of creation,” or “the substance of a non-existent creation.” Then, instead of “not from another,” we would prefer “or from another.” For by “from another” Hilary means “from another substance.” Hence in *On the Trinity*, book VI, §16, he says: “I appeal to every person’s understanding: when it is said ‘FROM HIM,’ what does he think is to be understood? ‘From another,’ or from no one, or must that very one be believed? It is not ‘from another,’ because it is from him,” etc.]

27. “Therefore, in order to suppress this evil, three hundred bishops or more assembled at Nicaea; with the assent of all, a heretical condemnation was decreed against all Arians; and, when the evangelical and apostolic doctrines had been unfolded, the perfect light of catholic unity was brought forth. What, then, was expressed is commended by the creed itself as it was set forth.

[Note: [Col. 0654C] Since Constantine, in Socrates, book I, chapter 9, and Marius Victorinus, book I, write that more than three hundred bishops assembled at Nicaea, they should not be thought to disagree with the common consensus of other Fathers, but rather, along with our Hilary, to have used an indefinite number in place of the certain and definite number. For Hilary himself states not only in *On the Synods*, §86, but also below, that the Nicene Creed was composed by 318 bishops.]

The creed composed at Nicaea (A.D. 325) by the three hundred and eighteen bishops against all heresies begins.

We believe in one God, the Father almighty, maker of all things visible and invisible; and in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, begotten of the Father—that is, of the substance of the Father—God from God, light from light, true God from true God; begotten, not made; of one substance with the Father, which the Greeks call *homoousion* (ὁμοούσιον); through whom all things were made, whether in heaven or on earth; who for us human beings and for our salvation came down, was incarnate, became human, suffered, and rose again on the third day; ascended into heaven; and will come to judge the living and the dead. And in the Holy Spirit. But those who say, “There was when he was not,” and, “Before he was begotten he was not,” and that he was made from things that did not exist—which the Greeks call *ex ouk ontōn* (ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων)—or who say that the Son of God is of another substance or essence, or mutable and changeable: these the catholic and apostolic Church anathematizes.

[Note: In the Colbert manuscript, “only-begotten” is absent. In *On the Synods* this word is placed, not here, but after the following words, “begotten of the Father.”]

[Note: The manuscripts wrongly read *exucuton*. In *On the Synods* the words “which the Greeks call *ex ouk ontōn*” do not occur; earlier it has “from non-existent things”; after “God” it has not “Son of God”; and shortly afterward the words “and apostolic” are omitted.]

### 28. By comparison with the sincere faith, the falsity of the adulterated faith becomes clear.

“Faith compared with faith exposes the falsity of the declaration. For that which was established at Nicaea is full and perfect; and, with every entrance through which heretics are accustomed to creep in barred from every side, it is joined together by the inviolable firmness of eternal unity between Father and Son. But this other faith flatters by simplicity, first asserting that we believe in such a manner—which may be far from anyone.

“But the faith of the Westerners, founded on evangelical teachings, confesses the Father in the Son and the Son in the Father; the Father as unbegotten, the Son as eternal with the substance of eternity: that is, as the Father is always, so also the Son is always in the Father, and, begotten from God, is God—not, of course, conceived, and always existing in the one from whom he is.”

[Note: Thus Sirmond, from the Remigius manuscript; nor did Faber find otherwise in the Pithoean manuscript, though he nevertheless printed *inventionis* (“of invention”). If anything is to be altered, *intentionis* (“of intention”), namely that of the Easterners, would be more attractive; for, in replying from Sirmium, they appended an altogether bare and meagre confession of faith to the condemnation of Photinus.]

### 29.

“But this perfidy—not faith—of the Easterners replying from Sirmium, while calling him God from God, commending him as firstborn, and introducing the name of Trinity, conceals its poison beneath the restraint of religious moderation. It says, ‘God from God, light from light,’ so that, under cover of this confession ‘from God and light,’ God and light may be understood as made by God, not begotten from God—that is, not existing from the substance of paternal eternity. Thus the insult to the Father is diminished, and the Son is made cheap, if God arose from nothing.

“And in the confession of ‘firstborn’ they assign him a certain order among the created things of the world arising from him [perhaps: “the world’s created things”]. Thus, because the world is temporal, Christ too, though prior to the world, is nevertheless temporal; and there is not eternity in him before the times, but an order within created time. Accordingly something prior to him is left over—he who began to exist in time—and everything that belongs to God is dissolved in Christ, since in him the birth from Mary, who at one time did not exist, is temporal.”

### 30. In what sense Christ is the firstborn of every creature.

“Indeed, men empty of every good hope appeal, on the occasion of so great a danger, to apostolic authority, because it was said of him: ‘the firstborn of every creature.’ But, removing the preceding and following statement, they construct a falsehood suited to their doctrines under the Apostle’s name. For the order of the words is as follows: ‘Who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature; because in him all things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, were established, whether thrones, dominions, principalities, or powers: all things were created through him and in him, and he is before all’ (Col. 1:15–16).

“Is, then, the image of the invisible God an order from nothing and something that began in time? Or, because he is the firstborn of every creature, is the order of an unknown creation, joined together in him, expressed thereby—yet does it not follow that he is firstborn as one belonging to the order of every creature? For in him all things in heaven and on earth were established: that is, in him lies the created and established material of all visible and invisible elements of the universe. And for this reason all things are through him and in him; for this reason he is the firstborn of every creature: because in that same one, already from the beginning, all the beginnings of the generations of all things which he was to make were established.

“And he is not first in number among the creatures which have been set in order; rather, he himself, the image of the invisible God, remaining always in himself through the power of effecting, has himself as the firstborn of those things which were to be created as existent through him, visible and invisible, in heaven and on earth.”

[Note: The manuscripts read *incognitae* (“unknown”). *Congenitae* (“co-born”) or *in eo genitae* (“begotten in him”) would not be objectionable. But, while he himself was being born, all things created were joined together and in some fashion begotten in him, because God the Creator was being born, as is explained in *On the Trinity*, II.20: “He is firstborn of every creature,” he says in VIII.50, “because all things were created in him”; and a little later: “He is also firstborn of every creature, containing in himself the beginning of the universe.” From these passages Hilary’s meaning here may be explained thus: Is he who is the image of the invisible God to be thought to be from nothing, and an order—or in the order—of created things, and to have begun in time? Or rather, when he is called firstborn of every creature, is the order of all creation joined together in him as in its cause expressed; yet it does not follow that he is firstborn in such a way as to belong to the order of created things. What follows confirms this explanation.]

[Note: In the printed editions: *constituerat* (“he had established”). In the manuscripts: *constituerunt* (“they established”); and a little earlier, “which **he** was to make,” not “which **things** he was to make.” We do not think we have corrected these two words rashly.]

### 31. How an unequal Trinity is introduced.

“Moreover, the thread of their falsity in their naming of the Trinity is not unlike this. For when, with impious and accursed mouth, they have severed the Son from the Father as belonging to different substances, and authority resides in two separate beings, a third [substance] is counted in the Spirit. And although the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father, and the Holy Spirit receives from both, nevertheless, in that the Spirit is expressed, the unity of this holy and inviolable Trinity gives birth, on the heretical side, to a proclaimed division.”

[Note: The printed text had *distenderent*; the manuscripts have *discederent*. The sense requires *disciderint* (“they have torn apart”); interchange of *i* and *e* is frequent in manuscripts, just as *et* is often found in place of *ut*. Therefore we think the immediately following text should read, “that authority may reside in two separate beings.” This can be understood to mean that the authority from which the Holy Spirit proceeds is not one, but exists in two separate beings. Then a third [sc. substance] is counted in the Spirit.]

[Note: From Sirmond’s readings we add *cum* (“although”); and earlier we would gladly accept *ut* in place of *et*. For the passage seems to require restoration as follows: “so that, although the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father, and the Spirit receives from both, in the fact that the Spirit is expressed the unity of this holy and inviolable Trinity [according to Catholics], the proclaimed Trinity may bring forth division on the heretical side.”]

### 32. How exact the Nicene exposition is.

“But the careful exposition of Nicaea and its perfect language, by the strictest rule of truth, shut up every device of the heretics.

[Note: The printed editions have *inclusit* (“enclosed”). The manuscripts more aptly have *conclusit*, that is, “so shut in that no opportunity for escape was left.” A little earlier we restored *praescripto*, where *perscripto* had prevailed.]

It declares thus: ‘We believe in one God, the Father, and in one Jesus Christ his Son.’ Both are one, and each is one, and [one] in the personal name of Father. And [we believe] in one Son, because he is one from the one [Father]. ‘True God from true God’ teaches that power and designation are common to both in equal truth; nor is one to be thought other than the other, since each is God from God and true from true, and both are one.

“But, while in both there is [one name, power, and so forth], ‘begotten, not made’ refers to the distinctive character of birth and origin; for to be made is subject to being from nothing, whereas to be born is proper to being from the Father, and those who are born possess no form or power other than that of their origin. What is made exists from an act in order that it may be made. Thus, in him, a fabrication did not begin from nothing; rather, there is a birth from the parent. ‘Of one substance with the Father,’ which the Greeks call *homoousion* (ὁμοούσιον): so it is. Eternity alone is like itself, and that which always is, is in God.

“Therefore, lest any stain of heretical perversity should fall upon the Lord Jesus Christ, the truth of essence is explained in him. For essence is named from that which always is; and because it has never needed external aid to sustain itself, it is also called substance, because that which always is subsists within itself and in the power of its own eternity. Thus, in the words, ‘I and the Father are one’ (John 10:30); ‘He who has seen me has seen the Father’ (John 14:9); again, ‘I am in the Father and the Father is in me’ (ibid. 14:11); and, ‘I went forth from the Father’ (John 16:28), one and the same substance of eternity is fulfilled equally in both: that is, in God who is unbegotten and in God [who is begotten].

“But that he came down, was incarnate, became human, rose on the third day, ascended into heaven, and will come to judge the living and the dead: in these are contained the mysteries of our salvation. Yet the Son of God is called immutable and unchangeable, so that, in assuming humanity, he may have brought glory rather than corruption to it, and not a stain upon eternity. But the anathema against those who say that he was made from nothing—what the Greeks call *ex ouk ontōn* (ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων)—and who say, ‘There was when he was not,’ and, ‘Before he was begotten he was not,’ designates, under a curse, the condemnation in Christ of violated eternity, that is, of paternal deity.”

[Note: What is absent here is easily understood: namely, that Father and Son are one by nature, though each is one God under a personal name and property. This was already explained in no. 25: “This is our faith: God is one in the names and persons of Father and Son.” Hence we conjecture that the text should read: “Both are one, and each is one: and [we believe] in one Father, because he is one under the personal name of Father; and in one Son, because he is one from the one [Father]”—or again, “because he is one under the personal name of Son”; and afterward, “and in one God, because he is one from both.”]

[Note: We correct the text thus, where it formerly read “common to the Father . . . .”]

[Note: We supply the particle *a* (“from”) from Sirmond, who subsequently reads: “of one and the same equal substance”; where Faber, from the Pithoean manuscript, retained “but of equal substance.” There is no doubt that the reading we prefer is sound. For here the very words of the Nicene Creed are repeated and explained together.]

[Note: We have already heard in *On the Synods*, no. 12: “Essence is properly so called because it always is.” Hilary discusses essence here because *ousia* (οὐσία), from which *homoousion* is formed, means “essence,” and he customarily renders it in Latin by this name, as is clear from his translation of the decrees of Ancyra in *On the Synods*, no. 14, etc.]

[Note: Supply: “is proclaimed in the Nicene Creed.” The following words closely resemble those of Ambrose, *Treatise on the Orthodox Faith*, ch. 8, in the Appendix to vol. II: “When he deigned to put on humanity, he did not bring a stain upon eternity, so as to change Spirit into flesh; but, having assumed humanity, he bestowed upon it the immortality and eternity of heavenly life.”]

[Note: Again, here the manuscripts have *exucuton*, a corrupt form of *ex ouk ontōn*.]

### 33.

“Accordingly, Athanasius, then a deacon at the Synod of Nicaea and afterward bishop of Alexandria, had been a vigorous advocate for making this faith known to all; and, holding fast to the truth, he had overcome the Arian plague throughout all Egypt. For that reason a conspiracy of testimonies against him fabricated false accusations. The case was afterward decided by the judgment of faithful judges. But it will contribute much to understanding if the address of the Synod of Sardica to Emperor Constantius, after Athanasius’s acquittal, is made known.”

[Note: Not indeed in composing it—for Athanasius himself, *To the Solitaries*, p. 837, attributes to Hosius the credit of having drafted the formula of faith at the Nicene Synod—but in making it known to all.]

[Note: Hilary, *Against Constantius*, no. 12, had already testified that the Egyptians at the Synod of Seleucia most steadfastly maintained the *homoousion*, excepting none among them but George, who had invaded the Alexandrian see. Yet the Meletians must be excepted, for the Arians had attached them to themselves.]

[Note: That is, at the Synod of Sardica.]

[Note: To the great loss of history, this letter has perished. The Fathers of Sardica indicate above, no. 12, that it contained much worthy of knowledge. In that place they also indicate that the synod wrote to Constans; unless perhaps one and the same letter was sent to both emperors. In any case, it is clear that something is missing here for the completeness of this work.]

## FRAGMENT III (formerly Part II)

## THE DECREE OF THE EASTERN BISHOPS AT SARDICA, FROM THE ARIAN PARTY, WHICH THEY SENT TO AFRICA (issued A.D. 347)

[Note: This synod is mentioned by Socrates, book II, ch. 20, and Augustine, book III *Against Cresconius*, and Letter 44. Moreover, Sozomen, book III, ch. 11, and Nicephorus, book IX, give a summary account of its decree.]

[Note: The title is deceptive. When the Arians fled Sardica, they held this pseudo-synod at Philippi in Thrace, at the same time as the true Synod of Sardica was being held. Its proceedings were so unknown to Augustine and Alypius that they took this one alone for the Sardican synod. Faber and many others believe that Hilary too was deceived in the same way in *On the Synods*; but they establish this by no argument. Indeed, he expressly indicates that the confession of faith issued there was that not of an ecumenical synod but of the Easterners alone. And whereas he labels their other formulas by the places in which they were written, he labels this one simply, suppressing the invidious place-name: “The Faith according to the Synod of the East.” In *Against Constantius*, no. 23, he does indeed call it Sardican; but who would suppose that, when he wrote this book, he was ignorant of Eastern affairs? Certainly he does not speak there as one ignorant of them.]

[Note: Evidently with the purpose of attaching the Donatists to themselves. For Augustine, in book III *Against Cresconius*, ch. 34, says as an inference that the African heresy attempted to associate itself with the Eastern heresy; but in Letter 163 in the old numbering, now 44, no. 6, he confirms it by public report: “Since we had heard at some time, I know not when, that the Arians, after separating from catholic communion, had attempted to associate the Donatists in Africa with themselves, brother Alypius whispered this same thing in my ear.” This was certainly fitting for their heretical temper, by which they had already sought alliance with the Meletians. Therefore “which they sent to Africa” should not be understood to mean that this decree was sent to the Church of Africa, but only to the Donatist party existing in Africa. Augustine is himself witness that Africa is not mentioned in it; thus the Donatist Fortunius could not even prove whether those letters were sent specifically to bishops of African churches. He adds that no day or consul is found in them by which their date may be determined.]

To Gregory, bishop of Alexandria; [to] the bishop of Nicomedia; [to] the bishop of Carthage; [to] the bishop of Campania; [to] the bishop of Neapolis in Campania; [to] the bishop of Ariminum in Campania; [to] the bishop of Salonae in Dalmatia; to Amphion, Donatus, Desiderius, Fortunatus, Euthychius, Maximus, Sinfruntius, and to all our fellow-priests throughout the world, presbyters and deacons, and all who are under heaven in the holy catholic Church: the bishops who have assembled and held a council in the city of Sardica from diverse provinces of the Eastern regions—that is, from the province of Thebaid, the province of Palestine, Arabia, Phoenicia, Syria Coele, Mesopotamia, Cilicia, Isauria, Cappadocia, Galatia, Pontus, Bithynia, Pamphylia, Paphlagonia, Caria, Phrygia, Pisidia, the Cycladic islands, Lydia, Asia, Europe, the Hellespont, Thrace, and Haemimontus—in the Lord, eternal greeting.

[Note: For greater clarity Faber had placed the name of each bishop’s see after him in this manner: “To Amphion, bishop of Nicomedia; to Fortunatus, bishop of Neapolis in Campania; to Maximus, bishop of Salonae in Dalmatia; to Sinfruntius,” etc. Yet we judged it preferable to restore the order of words given in the manuscripts, especially since Augustine, book III *Against Cresconius*, ch. 34, book IV, ch. 44, and Letter 44 establish that only the names of the bishops to whom these letters were sent—not the cities over which they presided—were prefixed. Thus it could not in any way be proved whether they were addressed to Donatus of Carthage or another Donatus. These are Augustine’s words, book IV *Against Cresconius*, ch. 44: “It is not customary to read [letters] with the names of cities added, because it is not ecclesiastical custom when bishops write a letter to bishops.” Yet in the same book and in book III he speaks as though by that time the Donatists had added “of Carthage” to Donatus’s name.]

[Note: This word plainly refers to those sending the letter, not to those to whom it is sent. For, after naming all fellow-priests—that is, bishops—and then presbyters and deacons, the designation of all catholics throughout the world rightly follows. This is now conveyed by our reading, in which we restore *episcopi* (“bishops”), where formerly *episcopis* (“to bishops”) prevailed, awkwardly joined to the preceding *omnibus* (“all”) in a needless repetition.]

[Note: *On the Synods* here adds “Egypt.” Although the Egyptians adhered to the Nicene faith and Athanasius, some Meletians nevertheless attended this conventicle.]

[Note: The manuscripts read *Pisauria*. But in *On the Synods* there is neither Isauria nor Pisauria.]

[Note: *On the Synods* also contains Mysia together with the two Pannonias. But the order in which provinces are listed is not the same here as there.]

### 1. A pretended love of unity and of preserving traditions.

“Indeed, beloved brothers, we all have an unceasing prayer: first, that the holy and catholic Church of the Lord, being free from every dissension and schism, may everywhere preserve through right faith the unity of the Spirit and the bond of charity. It is also just that all who call upon the Lord should hold, embrace, guard, and preserve an unstained life—especially bishops, who preside over the most holy churches.

“Second, [we pray] that the rule of the Church, the holy tradition of the Fathers, and [their] judgments may remain forever firm and secure; and that we may never, amid peoples, sects [that is, newly arising sects], and perverse traditions—especially in appointing bishops or expelling them—be disturbed in such a way as to be prevented from maintaining the evangelical and holy precepts, the things commanded to the holy and most blessed Apostles and our elders, and those which have been preserved and are preserved by ourselves down to the present day.”

### 2. The doctrine of Marcellus.

“For in our times there has arisen a certain Marcellus of Galatia, a plague more detestable than all heretics. With sacrilegious mind, profane speech, and corrupt reasoning, he wishes to bring to an end the kingdom of Christ the Lord, which is perpetual, eternal, and without time. He says that the Lord received the beginning of his reign four hundred years ago, and that its end will come at the same time as the world’s end.

“With the rashness of one who has begun to assert it, he also tries to maintain that, at the conception of his body, he then became the image of the invisible God, and then became bread, door, and life. He confirms these things not only in words and in a garrulous assertion, but has also set down in a book full of blasphemies and execrations everything conceived in his sacrilegious mind and uttered by his blasphemous mouth, striving with eager desire [reading uncertain], and many other much worse things. He brings a charge against the divine Scriptures themselves by his own interpretation and wicked mind, applying to them from his pernicious sense things contrary to them; and from these matters he has plainly and openly proved to be a heretic.

“Mixing his assertions with certain foulnesses, now openly blending in the falsehoods of Sabellius, now the malice of Paul of Samosata, now the blasphemies of Montanus, leader of all heretics, and making one confusion from the things mentioned above, this foolish Galatian has turned aside to another gospel—which is not another—according to which the blessed Paul, condemning such persons, says: ‘Even if an angel from heaven should proclaim to you otherwise than what you received, let him be anathema’ (Gal. 1:8).”

[Note: In the archetype manuscript: *concupiscentiam intenti*. Perhaps “with shameless license,” or “with great audacity”?]

[Note: In Labbe: *in ipsis* (“in them”). We would prefer *in ipso* (“in it”), namely, the book.]

[Note: Perhaps read, “which things were against them,” or “which were contrary to them,” with the verb understood. Here is explained what it is to bring an accusation against the Scriptures: namely, to twist them toward alien and contrary meanings. The pseudo-synod speaks in accordance with Eusebius of Caesarea. Having affirmed, in book I *Against Marcellus*, ch. 2, that Marcellus was insufficiently versed in the Scriptures, Eusebius, in book II, ch. 1, after citing Scriptures against his opinion, attacks him thus: “You may learn from Marcellus’s own writings with what audacity he wrote things contrary and opposed to these testimonies, writings in which he denied both the divinity and the humanity of the Son.” Just above he expounds Marcellus’s opinion in these words: “By some means or other he asserts that the Word, not subsisting, assumed flesh and operated in it; and that Jesus first then came to exist as Christ, king, image of God, beloved Son, glorified one, firstborn of every creature—whereas he did not previously exist and had no subsistence at all before.”

“Foremost among the paradoxes is this: that this Word began not four hundred years ago, and is to be turned back after the time of judgment into the same nonexistence, God the Word having finally been united [to God], so that nothing at all may exist besides God; while the flesh which he assumed is left and forsaken by the Word, so that neither the Son of God subsists nor the Son of Man whom he assumed. Marcellus’s words are admittedly ambiguous; yet they can be cleared of every impiety. For Eusebius admits, book I, ch. 1, p. 4, that Marcellus was accustomed to say: ‘The Word existed only inwardly, while he remained in the Father at rest; but the same Word acted when he fashioned created things’: ὡς οὐδὲν ἕτερον ἦν ὁ λόγος ἐνδὸν μένων ἐν ἠσυχάζοντι τῷ Πατρί, etc.—‘as the Word was nothing else, remaining within the Father who was at rest,’ etc. By these words he denies not so much that the Word existed as that he performed an external work. Thus, in the manner of other Fathers, he may also have maintained that Christ’s human nature would pass through glory into God by a certain special union with God, but without the abolition of that nature itself.”]

### 3. His first condemnation. The censure of his doctrine is preserved in the Church’s archive.

“Our fathers and predecessors displayed great concern regarding the aforementioned sacrilegious preaching. Accordingly, in the city of Constantinople, in the presence of the emperor Constantine of most blessed memory, a council of bishops was convened [A.D. 336]. They had come from many Eastern provinces, in order to correct by salutary counsel a man steeped in evil, so that, rebuked by their most holy admonition, he might withdraw from sacrilegious preaching.

“They reproved and rebuked him and, with an affection of charity, appealed to him for a long time, but achieved nothing. For after one, a second, and many rebukes, when they had been able to achieve nothing—for he persisted, contradicted the right faith, and with malign contention resisted the catholic Church—they all began thereafter to abhor and avoid him. Seeing that he was overturned by sin and condemned by himself, they condemned him in the ecclesiastical proceedings, lest he should further defile Christ’s sheep by his more pestilential contacts.

“At that time, moreover, for the remembrance and warning of posterity, they recorded in their most holy writings and deposited in the Church’s archive certain of his most perverse opinions against the right faith and the most holy Church. These, indeed, were the first events in accordance with the impiety of Marcellus the heretic; worse things afterward followed. For what believer could credit or endure those things evilly done and written by him, and rightly anathematized?”

[Note: Unless the words in brackets are superfluous, something is missing here. Or perhaps it should be read: “Were they anathematized together with Marcellus himself by our fathers in the city of Constantinople?”]

[“For [they were anathematized] together with Marcellus himself by our fathers in the city of Constantinople.”]

“For there exists a book of opinions written against him by the bishops. In that book those who are now with Marcellus and support him—namely Protogenes, bishop of the city of Sardica, and Syracusanus—wrote out the very judgment in their own hand. Their handwriting gives powerful testimony that the most holy faith must in no respect be changed, nor the holy Church overturned by false preaching, lest in this way the most grievous plague and pestilence of souls be brought upon all. Paul says: ‘Whether we or an angel from heaven should proclaim to you otherwise than what you received, let him be anathema’ (Gal. 1:8).”

[Note: The archetype manuscript has *Siriacusanais*. If anyone wishes to make from this “Cyriacus of Ariminum,” whose successor Gaudentius is condemned below because he receives Marcellus—against whom Cyriacus had rendered judgment—he must necessarily substitute the name of Cyriacus, then dead, for the church which he had governed. It would be as if it said: the bishops of Sardica and Ariminum, who now support Marcellus, formerly wrote out a judgment against him—thus the text apparently should read, not “in the judgment”—the Sardican in his own name, but the Ariminensian in [the person of] his predecessor Cyriacus.]

### 4. Marcellus, condemned by many bishops, is received into communion.

“We were greatly astonished that certain persons who wish to be regarded as churchmen readily receive into communion one who dares to preach a gospel other than the true one. They neither examine his blasphemies, recorded in his own book, nor are willing to agree with those who carefully investigated everything and, having found [the truth], justly condemned him.

“For, since Marcellus was regarded as a heretic among his own people, he sought the assistance of travel abroad—obviously in order to deceive those who did not know either him or his pestilential writings. But whatever he does among them, he hides his impious writings and profane opinions, presenting falsehoods as truths; and he has made gain for himself from the simple and innocent. Under the pretext of ecclesiastical rule he has drawn many shepherds of the Church [perhaps: “led them astray”] and, bringing them under his own power, has deceived them by cunning fraud, introducing the sect of the heretic Sabellius and restoring both the arts and deceits of Paul of Samosata. For Marcellus’s alien tradition is compounded from the sects of all heretics, as was mentioned above.

“Therefore it was fitting that all rulers of the holy Church, mindful of the words of the Lord Christ, who says, ‘Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravening wolves; by their fruits you shall know them’ (Matt. 7:15–16), should avoid and abhor such persons, should not readily communicate with them, should recognize them from their deeds, and should condemn them beforehand from their sacrilegious writings.

“But now we greatly fear that in our times what is written may be fulfilled: ‘While people sleep, the enemy comes and sows weeds among the wheat’ (Matt. 13:25). For when those who ought to keep watch in guarding the Church do not keep watch, false words imitating [the truth] utterly overthrow what is right.”

[Note: The printed editions read *nutantia* (“wavering”). From the manuscripts we restore *imitantia* (“imitating”); and, if permitted, would add *veritatem* (“the truth”). Immediately afterward, “overthrow” would be preferable to “turn.”]

### 5. Communion is declared to be denied to Marcellus.

“Therefore we, who have fully learned from Marcellus’s book his sect and crimes, have written to you, beloved brothers, that you must admit neither Marcellus nor those joined to him to communion in the holy Church. Remember also the prophet David saying: ‘I said to those who commit iniquity, Do not commit iniquity; and to sinners, Do not lift up the horn. Do not raise your horn on high; do not speak iniquity against the Lord’ (Ps. 74:5–6). And believe Solomon saying: ‘Do not move the ancient boundaries which your fathers established’ (Prov. 22:28).

“Since these things are so, do not follow the errors of the aforementioned most perverse Marcellus. Condemn beforehand those things devised and handed down by him in unjust preaching against the Lord Christ, lest you too become participants in his blasphemies and crimes. But this is enough concerning Marcellus, for brevity’s sake.”

### 6. Fabricated accusations against Athanasius.

“But concerning Athanasius, formerly bishop of Alexandria, hear what occurred. He was seriously accused: as sacrilegious toward God, profane toward the mysteries of the holy Church, and as one who with his own hands smashed the cup consecrated to God and Christ, broke the venerable altar itself, overturned the episcopal seat, and himself demolished to the ground the very basilica, God’s house, the Church of Christ. He also handed over to military custody a presbyter himself, a serious and just man, named Narchen [Ischyras].

“Moreover, he was accused of injuries, violence, murder, and even the slaughter of bishops. During the most sacred days of Easter he allegedly raged in tyrannical fashion, joined with commanders and counts. For his sake, they allegedly shut some persons in custody, harassed others with beatings and scourges, and compelled the rest, by various tortures, into his sacrilegious communion. (The innocent had never committed the deeds alleged.) He hoped in this way that his own faction and party could prevail: through commanders and judges, prisons, beatings, and various tortures, to force unwilling persons into his communion, to drive those unwilling, and tyrannically to frighten those who opposed and resisted him. These were indeed grave and bitter charges raised by his accusers.”

[Note: They did not accuse him of having committed this crime with his own hands, but of having perpetrated it by the hands of his presbyter Macarius; or rather, they alleged now this and now that.]

[Note: Faber printed “of a bishop,” rightly enough if the enemies of truth had stood by the calumnies invented by themselves; for this refers to the fabricated killing of Arsenius. But since everywhere they magnify their earlier falsehoods, we think the archetype manuscript’s “of bishops” should be retained here.]

7. Proceedings at Tyre against Athanasius. — For these reasons, a council at Caesarea in Palestine appears necessarily first to have been convened [Col. 0664A] (in 334, but not held); and since he did not appear at the aforesaid council either personally or through his agents, after another year (in 335) it was necessarily held again at Tyre because of his crimes. Bishops came from Macedonia and Pannonia, Bithynia, and every region of the East, compelled by the emperor’s command. Having learned from the proceedings the disgraceful acts and crimes of Athanasius, they did not rashly or indiscriminately believe the accusers, but chose distinguished and praiseworthy bishops from their own council and sent them to the actual place where the acts of which Athanasius was accused had occurred. Having inspected everything by eyewitness testimony and learned the truth, they returned to the council and confirmed by their own testimony that the charges brought against him by the accusers were true [Col. 0664B]. Accordingly, they pronounced upon Athanasius, who was present, a sentence appropriate to his crimes.

> [Note: Liberius, before Constantius, asserted to this effect in Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, book II, ch. 16, that this was false; neither Constantius himself nor those with him dared dispute him on that point.]

For this reason, fleeing from Tyre, he appealed to the emperor. The emperor also heard him; and, after conducting an examination and recognizing all his offenses, banished him by his own judgment to exile at Trier. Since matters had thus turned out, and Athanasius, deservedly condemned, was kept in exile because of his crimes—sacrilegious toward God, profane toward the sacred mysteries, violent in demolishing a basilica, a dreadful persecutor in the destruction of bishops and innocent brethren—then the authority of the law, the canon of the Church, and the holy tradition of the apostles were upheld by all bishops in rejecting evils.

8. Athanasius’ return from exile. — But when Athanasius [Col. 0664C], after his condemnation, was arranging his return from exile, he arrived at Alexandria from Gaul after a very long time (in 338). Treating the past as nothing, he prevailed more fiercely in wickedness. For by comparison with what followed, the things he had first committed were slight. Indeed, throughout the whole route of his return he was overturning the Church.

> [Note: These accusations were occasioned by events occurring both at Athanasius’ first and at his second return to his church. Socrates, book I, chs. 3 and 15, relates that on both occasions various disturbances arose through the Arian faction. Some who refer all this to his first return suppose, because of the words that follow, that at that time he restored many exiles with him to their sees. Yet he may be accused here of restoring condemned bishops, because Paul, Asclepas, Marcellus, and Lucius went with him to Rome and recovered their churches through the same letters of Julius. But Socrates, book II, ch. 24, reports as occurring after the Council of Sardica that Athanasius, travelling to Alexandria by way of Pelusium, urged everyone in each city through which he passed to reject the Arians and receive those who professed the faith of consubstantiality. In some churches he also performed ordinations. This gave occasion for another accusation against him, because he had attempted to ordain in other men’s churches. That he had done this same thing, or something similar, before that synod is rather clearly suggested in the present material.]

He restored certain condemned bishops; to some he promised hope of return to episcopates; some he made bishops from among the unbelievers, while the legitimate priests remained safe and undisturbed. Through conflicts and killings of pagans, he disregarded all laws and surrendered everything to desperation. Thus by force, slaughter, and war he plundered the basilicas of Alexandria [Col. 0665A]. When a holy and upright priest had already been appointed in his place by judgment of the council—namely Gregory, at Antioch in 341—he, like a barbarian enemy and sacrilegious plague, brought in crowds of pagans, set God’s temple on fire, shattered the altar, and slipped out of the city and secretly fled.

9. Crimes attributed to other bishops returned from exile. The consecrated body of the Lord. The completed sacrifice. — Whoever hears what happened to Paul, formerly bishop of Constantinople, after his return from exile will shudder. For at Ancyra in the province of Galatia, after the return of the heretic Marcellus, there were burnings of houses and various kinds of warfare. Priests were dragged naked by him into the forum; and—what must be spoken with tears and mourning—the consecrated body of the Lord was publicly and openly profaned by being hung around priests’ necks [Col. 0665B]. The most holy virgins dedicated to God and Christ were publicly stripped of their garments in the forum, in the midst of the city, before crowds of people, and exposed in dreadful shame.

But at Gaza, a city in the province of Palestine, Asclepas, after his return, shattered the altar and caused many disturbances. Moreover, at Hadrianopolis, Lucius, after his return, ordered a sacrifice performed by holy and upright priests—if it is permitted to say so—to be thrown to dogs. Therefore, if these things are so, shall we still believe Christ’s sheep to be entrusted to wolves so great and such as these? Shall we make Christ’s members members of a prostitute? Far be it.

10. Athanasius’ crimes. He is received by Julius and the bishops of Italy. — Afterwards Athanasius travelled through various parts of the world, deceiving some by his fraud and pestilential flattery, misleading innocent bishops ignorant of his crimes, or Egyptians unaware of some of his actions. By begging written testimonials from individuals, he disturbed peaceful churches, or devised new ones for himself according to his own will.

> [Note: We supply the word “devised” (*fingebat*) from Sirmond’s various readings. What is said immediately before—that Athanasius, while travelling through various parts of the world, begged writings from individuals—indicates that he did this after the first or second return, rather than after the third. After the third, his presbyters Peter, Irenaeus, and others collected peaceable letters for him from every quarter, as Athanasius himself recalls in *To the Solitaries*, p. 826.]

Yet this could accomplish nothing against the judgment long before ratified by most holy and distinguished bishops. For the endorsement of persons who neither were judges in the council, nor ever accepted the council’s judgment, nor are known to have been present when the aforesaid Athanasius was heard, could neither avail him nor benefit him [Col. 0666A].

> [Note: Here they try to undermine the authority of the writings sent both by Alexandrians and by Mareotic presbyters and deacons, and by others, which Athanasius inserted in *Apology II*, pp. 791 ff. After examining these, Julius acquitted him in the Roman council of the charges brought against him.]

Finally, realizing that these measures had come to nothing, he went to Julius at Rome, and also to certain bishops of that region of Italy. By deceiving them through the falsity of letters, he was very easily received by them into communion. Then they began to labor not so much for him as for their own actions, because they had rashly believed and communicated with him. For even if those letters were from some persons, they were not from persons who had been judges or had sat in the council. And even if they had been from some persons, those who spoke in their own defense ought never rashly to have been believed.

> [Note: We restore this passage from Sirmond. It had previously been truncated in this form: “they put forward faith; they refused to believe.” They say that letters issued in Athanasius’ favor: first, are suspect of falsity; second, are not from those who judged him; third, since they are from persons inconsiderately joined in communion with Athanasius, and are speaking for themselves, they are not trustworthy. Finally the Italians are blamed because they refused to believe those who condemned Athanasius.]

Yet they refused to believe the judges who had sentenced him.

11. Those deposed by the Arians defend themselves. — For others also, who had been deposed in the past on account of their crimes, are now joined with Marcellus and Athanasius. Asclepas, however, was stripped of episcopal rank seventeen years earlier [Col. 0666B] (in 330); likewise Paul and Lucius, and all who are associated with such persons. Travelling together through foreign regions, they persuaded judges that those who had deservedly pronounced sentence against them were not to be believed, in order by this kind of traffic to secure for themselves some return to episcopates.

> [Note: We think the passage should be corrected thus: “and other persons, who were deposed in the past for their crimes, are now joined with Marcellus and Athanasius; we mean Asclepas, who earlier,” etc. Certainly those hypocrites, who everywhere displayed the utmost zeal for ecclesiastical discipline, were too prudent to boast that they were claiming the judgment of a civil court. Further, below, no. 15, the text can already be read without corruption: that those things should be heard which the Fathers had formerly judged against them.]

They did not defend themselves in the very places where they had sinned, nor nearby, nor where they had accusers; but among strangers, far from their own regions, ignorant of the evidence of the events, they tried to overturn a just sentence, referring their actions to men who knew nothing at all about them. They did this shrewdly. Knowing that many of the judges, accusers, and witnesses had died, after so many and such weighty judgments [Col. 0666C], they thought to institute another trial, wishing to plead their cause before us, who had neither acquitted nor judged them. For those who judged them had already gone to the Lord.

12. They are accused of subjecting Eastern bishops to Westerners. — They also wished to impose upon Eastern bishops [uncertain: “that they come as defenders in place of judges, and as defendants in place of defenders”], at a time when their defense had no force—especially since they could least of all be defended when their accusers were charging them face to face. They thought to introduce a new law: that Eastern bishops should be judged by Western bishops. And they wished the Church’s judgment to rest with men who pitied not so much those persons as their own actions [Col. 0667A].

> [Note: Faber, placing an asterisk, noted that something was lacking here. Yet the sense appears complete to us: the Westerners, who in no. 10 are said to have begun laboring not so much for Athanasius as for their own actions, are now said in the same sense to pity not so much him and his companions as themselves.]

Since ecclesiastical discipline has never accepted this impiety, we ask you, beloved brethren, also with us to condemn the criminal destruction and deadly schemes of the lost.

13. As though agreeing with those whom they had condemned. — While Athanasius was still a bishop, he himself condemned Asclepas, who had been deposed, by his own judgment. Likewise Marcellus never communicated with him. Paul, however, was present at Athanasius’ exposition and, writing the judgment in his own hand, himself condemned him with the others. And as long as each of them remained a bishop, he confirmed his own judgments. But when, for different reasons and at different times, each was deservedly expelled from the Church according to his deserts, they made a greater agreement by one conspiracy [Col. 0667B], each forgiving the others the offenses which, while bishops, they had condemned by divine authority.

> [Note: There is no trace of this condemnation either in Athanasius or in other writers of sacred history. Nor does it seem credible that Athanasius condemned Asclepas, whom he never reproaches and repeatedly extols with praise. The statements added concerning Marcellus and Paul should be judged of the same kind. Athanasius sufficiently indicates in *To the Solitaries*, p. 813, that he communicated with Paul before Paul was deposed from the episcopate. This strengthens our suspicion that perhaps the Arians, writing at Sirmium concerning the condemnation of Photinus, falsely inserted that Athanasius had withdrawn from communion with Marcellus; and that Hilary, somewhat too credulous, affirmed it on their testimony alone in fragment II, no. 21, as we noted there.]

14. Beginnings of the Council of Sardica. — Since Athanasius, travelling into Italy and Gaul, procured for himself a new trial after the death of some accusers, witnesses, and judges, and believed that he could be heard again after time had obscured the memory of his crimes, Julius bishop of Rome, Maximinus of Trier, Hosius, and many others of their party improperly assented to him. By the emperor’s favor they undertook to hold a council at Sardica. We came to Sardica, summoned by imperial letters. When we had arrived, we found Athanasius, Marcellus, and all the criminals expelled by the council’s sentence—each previously condemned as he deserved for his crimes—sitting and debating in the midst of the church with Hosius and Protogenes; and, what was worse, celebrating the divine mysteries [Col. 0667C].

Nor was Protogenes, bishop of Sardica, ashamed to communicate with the heretic Marcellus, whose sect and reprobate opinion he himself had condemned by his own voice, subscribing four times to the sentences of bishops in council. Therefore it is clear that he condemned himself by his own sentence when, by communicating with Marcellus, he made himself his associate.

> [Note: What “four times” means here is not easy to say, since Hilary, in the preceding fragment, no. 22, affirms that no synod was ever subsequently convened against Marcellus except that dissolved by the judgments of the Sardican bishops.]

15. The Easterners’ attempt to expel Athanasius and others from the synod. — But we, maintaining the discipline of ecclesiastical rule and wishing the wretched persons to remain apart for a little while, instructed those who were with Protogenes and Hosius [Col. 0668A] to exclude from their assembly persons already condemned and not communicate with sinners. Then, together with us, they were to hear the matters formerly judged against them by our Fathers; for Marcellus’ book did not await an accusation, since it was openly heretical in itself. They were not to believe false allegations, nor were any of them to conceal his utterly depraved mind because of the dignity of his episcopal office.

> [Note: Perhaps: “to remove them,” or “to live separated from them.”]

> [Note: The corrupt reading may be corrected thus: “For each of them concealed an utterly depraved mind”; or, “although each of them concealed an utterly depraved mind.”]

But they resisted this; for what reason, we do not know. They would not separate themselves from the communion of those persons, thereby confirming the sect of the heretic Marcellus; and they set the crimes of Athanasius and the wickedness of the others above ecclesiastical faith and peace.

16. When these things became known, we eighty bishops—who had come to Sardica from diverse and distant provinces, at great expense and hardship, to establish peace in the Church [Col. 0668B]—could not behold these matters without tears. For it was no light matter that they absolutely refused to dismiss from themselves those whom our Fathers had deservedly condemned earlier for their crimes. Therefore we considered it unlawful to communicate with them and would not mingle the holy sacraments of the Lord with profane persons, preserving and maintaining the rule of ecclesiastical discipline.

> [Note: Socrates, book II, ch. 20, on the authority of Sabinus, records only seventy-six; below there are only seventy-three subscriptions.]

For perhaps an evil conscience prevented them from dismissing the aforesaid Hosius and Protogenes—a conscience which each of them feared might be exposed by someone, and which they greatly dreaded being made public. Thus none of them dared pronounce judgment against those men, lest he condemn himself for communicating, contrary to prohibition, with persons with whom it was in no way proper to communicate [Col. 0668C].

> [Note: The manuscript reads “with knowledge.” The sentence would be fuller thus: perhaps, “they were prevented by an evil conscience, by which each feared that things which he owed to be exposed by someone might be made public.”]

17. But again and again we begged them not to shake what was firm and solid, not to overthrow the law or disturb divine ordinances, not to throw everything into confusion, and not to deprive the Church’s tradition even of a small portion of peace; nor to introduce a new sect, or in any respect place bishops and most holy councils of the East beneath men coming from the West. But they despised this and threatened us, promising that they would vindicate Athanasius and the other criminals. As though those who had received all criminals and lost persons into their fellowship could do or say anything else.

Moreover, they advanced this proposal in enormous arrogance—possessed rather by boldness and rashness than by lawful reason [Col. 0669A]. Seeing that those who receive condemned persons incur offense and guilt as violators of heavenly laws, they tried to establish a judicial authority such that they might call themselves judges of judges and, if it is permitted to say so, reopen the judgment of those who are already with God. For many days we begged them to reject the condemned persons from among themselves, join themselves to the holy Church, and agree with the Fathers who spoke the truth. But they absolutely denied that they would do so.

18. They propose sending delegates of both parties to Mareotis. — While we were disputing, five bishops from our side came forward, survivors of the group of six who had been sent to Mareotis [Col. 0669B]. They offered them the following choice: bishops from each council should be sent to the places where Athanasius committed his crimes and disgraceful acts, so that, under the witness of God, everything might be faithfully recorded. If the things we reported to the council were found false, we ourselves should be condemned and should not complain to emperors, council, or any bishop. But if what we said before were found true, we should bring before our body those among you whom you have appointed—that is, those who communicated with Athanasius after his condemnation, and those who are Athanasius’ and Marcellus’ supporters and defenders; and none of you should complain to emperors, council, or any bishop. Hosius, Protogenes, and all their companions feared to accept the option proposed by our party [Col. 0669C].

19. They defame those assembled at Sardica. — An immense multitude of all criminals and lost persons had gathered at Sardica: arrivals from Constantinople and Alexandria, guilty of murder, bloodshed, slaughter, robbery, plundering, spoliation, and every impious sacrilege and crime; men who broke altars, burned churches, and pillaged private homes; profaners of God’s mysteries and betrayers of Christ’s sacraments; men who, maintaining the impious and criminal doctrine of heretics against the faith of the Church, cruelly massacred God’s wisest presbyters, deacons, and priests. Hosius and Protogenes kept all these gathered with them in their own assembly [Col. 0669D]. Honoring them, they despised us all, the deacons and priests of God, because we too would never consent to join ourselves with such persons.

They spread among the people and all the nations—or, perhaps, among pagan people—the story of what had occurred between us, inventing falsehoods as truths. They said that the disagreement between us arose not from God’s cause but from human presumption. Mingling human matters with divine and private affairs with ecclesiastical concerns, they stirred up civic disorder and sedition against us, saying that we had inflicted upon the city a grievous injury through schism unless we communicated with them, which was unlawful. They repeatedly shouted these things. We, however, wholly refused communion with them unless they expelled those whom we had condemned and rendered due honor to the Council of the East.

20. They complain that those whom they call wicked have been granted communion. — You may learn from this what they themselves did and what sort of council they held. Protogenes, as we said above, anathematized Marcellus and Paul in the official proceedings, yet later received them into communion. They included in the council Dionysius of Helica in the province of Achaia, whom they themselves had expelled. Thus, those who expelled and those expelled, judges and defendants alike, joined in communion and handled the divine mysteries together.

> [Note: Thus the Pithoean manuscript, which is doubtless what Labbe said should be written. The Remigian manuscript seen by Sirmond reads “from Etica”; Faber printed “from Edica.” In the preceding Sardican letters two Dionysii subscribe: one “from Achaia, of Lignedon,” the other “from Arcadia, of Elis.” Further, Athanasius, *Apology*, p. 675, mentions Dionysius “of Leida,” ἐν Λήιδι.]

They ordained bishop Bassus, from the city of Diocletiana, who had been exposed in shameful acts and crimes and deservedly expelled from Syria. Though subsequently caught living still more wickedly among them and condemned by them, he now appears to be joined with them. And because [uncertain: Aethius of Thessalonica] repeatedly charged Protogenes with many reproaches and crimes, saying that he both had had and still had concubines, he would never communicate with him. Yet now, having been admitted into friendship, as though purified by association with worse persons, he is regarded among them as righteous [Col. 0670C].

> [Note: In Sirmond’s manuscript: “of Thessalonica, Protogenes.” If, instead of *Protogenis*, one reads *Protogenes*, with the change of *i* into *e* frequent in such texts, the sense will be that not the bishop of Thessalonica but Protogenes charged the bishop of Thessalonica with many crimes. Labbe has “John of Thessalonica,” and in the margin “of Thessalonica.” The name of this bishop of Thessalonica is uncertain. Alexander, bishop of that city, was prominent at the Council of Tyre; Athanasius, *Apology to Constantius*, p. 692, also mentions Eremius of Thessalonica, to whom violence was done at the Council of Milan until he promised to withdraw from Athanasius’ communion. But we know no John. One can scarcely doubt that the person intended is the same man who subscribes with the Westerners at the Sardican synod—not John, but Aethius of Macedonia, from Thessalonica. Perhaps the letters “io” are not the beginning but the end of the Thessalonican bishop’s name. Thus nothing prevents the reading: “Protogenes [was accused] by Aethius of Thessalonica,” etc.]

When Asclepas had come to Constantinople because of Paul, after the brutality and atrocity of the deeds committed in the middle of the church of Constantinople—after a thousand murders which defiled the very altars with human blood, after the killings of brethren and destruction of pagans—he still does not cease to communicate with Paul, for whose sake these things were done. So also those who, through Asclepas, communicate with Paul, receiving writings from him and sending writings to him. What kind of council, then, could be held out of this coagulation and gathering of lost persons—a council in which they did not so much punish their crimes as acknowledge them?

21. They refuse to mingle with these persons. — We, who preside over the most holy churches and are rulers of peoples, are not, according to their practice, people who forgive and remit what cannot ever be remitted or forgiven [Col. 0671A]. They forgave Marcellus, Athanasius, and the other criminals their disgraceful acts and blasphemies, which it was unlawful to forgive. For it is written: “If a man sins against a man, they shall pray for him to the Lord; but if a man sins against God, who shall pray for him?” (1 Sam. 2:25). “We have no such custom, nor does the Church of God” (1 Cor. 11:16). Nor do we permit anyone to teach such things or introduce new traditions, lest we be called betrayers of the faith and betrayers of the divine Scriptures—which would be wicked—and be condemned by the Lord and by men.

> [Note: Here “them” is missing; and afterwards the verb “are” should be repeated twice: “For we who preside over the most holy churches and rule peoples are not, according to them—that is, according to their custom—persons who forgive and remit what cannot be remitted,” etc.]

22. They cast the odium of schism upon the Westerners. — But the aforesaid persons also contrived these things against us [Col. 0671B]. Since they knew that we could not communicate with them by granting favor to criminals—

> [Note: That is, by granting criminals the benefit of communion and their former dignity.]

—they thought to frighten us with imperial documents, so as to drag us unwillingly into their communion. They looked to see the deep and everlasting peace of the Church throughout the whole world divided for Athanasius and Marcellus, because of whom the Lord’s name is blasphemed among the nations. If those men had any fear of God, they ought, lest this storm created through them should continue, even late to depart from their most perverse presumption, lest because of them the Church be torn against itself. Or if those who fight for them had fear of God, even if nothing condemnable were found in them, they still ought to abhor and shudder at them because the unity of the Church is torn apart on their account and profound peace is overthrown through their mad fury and lust for honors [Col. 0671C].

> [Note: Faber, placing an asterisk as though something were missing, read afterward: “they will look upon the deep division of the whole world,” etc. We have more readily written “deep” (*profundam*) instead of “depth” (*profundum*), because “profound peace” shortly recurs. For the manuscript archetype reads “they looked to see before them.” Thus the sense is complete: “They looked to see the deep and eternal peace of the Church throughout the world divided,” etc. Sirmond, from the Remigian manuscript, reads “through whom” rather than “because of whom.”]

23. They deny that the Church has authority to restore persons deposed long ago. — Seeing matters proceeding thus, each of us resolved to return to his own country. It pleased us to write from Sardica and report what had happened and declare our judgment. For we cannot again receive to episcopal honor Athanasius and Marcellus, impious blasphemers against the Lord who lived wickedly, formerly expelled and condemned. They crucify again the true Son of God and publicly expose him anew, piercing him with bitter blows (Heb. 6:6). One of them, by blaspheming against the Son of God and his kingdom, has once died an eternal death [Col. 0671D]. The other, by sinning terribly and profanely against the body of the Lord and his mysteries, and committing other monstrous crimes, was expelled and condemned by the bishops’ sentence.

Therefore, since we cannot depart from the tradition of the Fathers—for the Church has neither assumed such authority nor received such power from God—we ourselves do not receive the aforesaid persons to the honor and dignity of the Church, and we deservedly condemn those who do receive them [Col. 0672A]. Nor do we receive into the Church others who were deservedly condemned either formerly or later, adhering to God’s laws, paternal traditions, and ecclesiastical disciplines, and believing the prophet who says: “Do not transgress the ancient boundaries which your fathers established” (Prov. 22:28). Therefore we never shake what is fixed and firm, but rather preserve what has been established by the Fathers.

> [Note: They do not dare say “from Philippopolis.” But men who lie so shamelessly are rightly denied credence in other matters.]

24. Those to whom they judge communion should be denied. — After much else, beloved brethren, we expressly enjoin this upon you: let none of you ever, having been deceived by anyone, communicate with Hosius, Protogenes, Athanasius, Marcellus, Asclepas, Paul, or Julius [Col. 0672B]; nor with any of those condemned and rejected from the holy Church, nor with their associates, who communicate with them either personally or by writings. Therefore you must never write to them or receive writings from them.

For the rest, beloved brethren, we ask you to have regard for the unity of the Church and for lasting peace; choose holy bishops in whom both faith is sound and life holy. Abhor those who have been stripped of episcopal honor because of their crimes and seek to recover the position which they deservedly lost through their deeds. Abhor still more those whom you see committing worse things after their crime. They do not hear the Lord saying: “You have sinned; cease” [Col. 0672C] (Sir. 21:1).

> [Note: Sirmond reads, “for they grow young again.” The Pithoean manuscript has something like *inbere* or *jubere nesciunt*, from which Faber derived *inhibere*, “restrain,” etc. Their intended sense is sufficiently clear, although the precise word they used cannot be certainly discerned. “To cease,” “to restrain themselves,” or “to contain themselves” would equally suit their meaning.]

For they do not know how to restrain themselves and grow stronger in wickedness. The more deeply they sink into the abyss of vices, the more they overthrow the world. Devoting themselves to seditions, they inflict wars and most fierce persecutions upon the holy Churches and, in tyrannical fashion, strive to enslave the peoples of the Lord under their own dominion.

25.
