They wish so great a synod to have been assembled wrongly. — Recognize from these things the utterly evil designs of those men: they brought upon the world such a storm of tempest that they disturbed nearly the whole East and West; each of us left his ecclesiastical duties, deserted God’s people, and set aside the teaching of the Gospel, so that we—men advanced in years, weak in body, and infirm through illness—came from far away [Col. 0672D]. We were dragged through diverse places and left our sick behind upon the journeys because of a very few criminals, long ago deservedly condemned, who unlawfully sought primacy in the Church. The imperial government and religious emperors had to concern themselves with us, while tribunes and commanders were occupied with the most grievous public business of bishops’ lives and standing [Col. 0673A].

Nor were the people silent. All the brotherhood in every province waited in suspense and anxiety to see to what end this storm of evils would come; and the public postal service itself was worn out and reduced to nothing. Why say more? The east and west of the world are completely overturned and disturbed by a harsh and savage tempest because of one, two, or a few wicked persons who hold impious opinions and live shamefully—persons in whom no seeds of religion have taken root. Had they possessed them, they would imitate the prophet saying: “Take me and cast me into the sea, and the sea will be calm for you, for this tempest has come upon you because of me” (Jonah 1:12). But they do not imitate this because they do not follow the righteous; instead, as leaders of all criminals, they seek the Church’s primacy as though it were a kingdom of tyranny [Col. 0673B].

26. Judgments of synods are not to be reopened. — Nor do they seek this for the good of justice. Those who attempt to dissolve divine laws and ordinances and others’ decrees do not provide for the Churches. Therefore they sought to introduce this novelty, which the ancient custom of the Church abhors: whatever Eastern bishops might decide in council should be reopened by Western bishops, and likewise whatever bishops of the Western regions might decide should be annulled by Easterners. But they pursued this from their most perverse intention.

Yet the decrees of all councils duly and lawfully conducted must be upheld, as the acts of our forebears attest. In the city of Rome a council held under the heretics Novatus, Sabellius, and Valentinus was confirmed by the Easterners; and again, in the East, what was decreed concerning Paul of Samosata was subscribed by all [Col. 0673C].

> [Note: This is the same complaint they had already made in 341. Indignant because Julius had restored to their sees persons deposed by the Easterners, they assembled at Antioch and replied that he ought not to investigate persons whom they wished to expel from their own churches; for they had not objected when Novatus was expelled from the Church. At Antioch, however, as we have now learned from Socrates, book II, ch. 15, and as Sozomen, book III, ch. 8 confirms, they mention only what was done against Novatus; now they add Sabellius and Valentinus. But Novatus’ condemnation by the Roman council is established by Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VI, ch. 44. Whether Sabellius and Valentinus were likewise condemned in the same city by separate synods, we know with certainty from no other ancient record.]

> [Note: The printed editions and the Pithoean manuscript read “Asonus”; Sirmond better reads from the Remigian manuscript, “Samosata.”]

For this reason we exhort you, beloved brethren: considering the order of ecclesiastical discipline and providing for the peace of the whole world, rebuke those who communicate with criminals and cut evil persons off from the churches at the root, so that, while a storm rages because of them, the Lord Christ, floating upon the waters, may command every wind and storm of the sea to depart and grant the holy Church enduring and tranquil peace.

### 27. They condemn the principal men among the Westerners: why.

We, however, do injury to no one, but observe the precepts of the law [Col. 0673D]. For we have been grievously wronged and ill-treated [Col. 0674A] by those who wished, through their perversity, to disturb the rule of the Catholic Church. Yet, keeping before our eyes the fear of God and considering the true and just judgment of Christ, we have shown regard for no person and spared no one at the expense of maintaining ecclesiastical discipline.

Accordingly, the whole council condemned Julius of the city of Rome, Ossius, Protogenes, Gaudentius, and Maximinus of Trier, according to the most ancient law, as authors of communion with Marcellus, Athanasius, and the other wicked persons; and as those who also shared in the murders committed by Paul of Constantinople and in his bloody deeds.

For Protogenes was anathematized together with Marcellus, repeatedly subscribing to the judgment pronounced against him or against his book; and he was among those who passed judgment against Paul of Constantinople [Col. 0674B], and later communicated with him.

Gaudentius was condemned because, forgetful of his predecessor Cyriacus, who had subscribed to the sentences deservedly pronounced against wicked persons, he involved himself in Paul’s crimes, whom he even shamelessly defended.

Julius of the city of Rome was condemned as the leader and guide of evils: he was the first to open the door of communion to the wicked and condemned, and gave the rest access to annul the divine laws. He defended Athanasius presumptuously and boldly, a man whose witnesses and accusers he did not even know.

But Ossius was condemned for the aforesaid reason, and also on account of Mark of most blessed memory, upon whom he always inflicted grievous injuries; further, because he defended with all his strength all wicked persons justly condemned for their crimes, and because he lived in the East [Col. 0674C] with wicked and depraved men. For he was shamefully the inseparable friend of Paulinus, formerly bishop of Dacia: a man who was first accused of evil deeds and expelled from the Church, who remains in apostasy to the present day, publicly committing fornication with concubines and prostitutes, and whose books of evil practices Macedonius, bishop and confessor of Mopsuestia, burned.

Moreover, he adhered most disgracefully to Eustathius and Quimatius, and was dear to them; nothing need be said of the shameful infamy of their lives, for their end made them known to all.

> [Note: If Eustathius of Antioch is meant here, this passage strengthens the opinion of those who believe that he died both before the Council of Sardica and while in exile. Then, for *Quimatio*, read *Cimatio*. Athanasius, *To the Solitaries*, p. 812, mentions two Cimatios, one of Paltus and the other of Tarudus, driven into exile by the Arians. There is no doubt that a different person from Cimatius of Paltus is designated here, since Athanasius himself, *To the Antiochenes*, p. 575, makes it clear that he was still alive after the Alexandrian council of 362.]

Thus Ossius, joined from the beginning to such men and always favoring the wicked, came against the Church and continually brought aid to God’s enemies.

Maximinus of Trier was condemned because he refused to receive our fellow-bishop colleagues whom we had sent into Gaul [Col. 0674D], and because he himself was the first to communicate with Paul of Constantinople [Col. 0675A], an impious and depraved man; and because he was the cause of so great a disaster that Paul was recalled to the city of Constantinople, on account of which many murders occurred. He, therefore, was the cause of so many murders, because he recalled Paul, once condemned, to Constantinople.

> [Note: Namely Narcissus, Maris, Theodore, and Mark, whom Athanasius reports in *On the Synods*, p. 894, were sent by the Eusebians to Constans in Gaul some months after the Council of Antioch of 341.]

### 28.

For these reasons, therefore, the council judged it right to depose and condemn Julius of the city of Rome, Ossius, and the other persons mentioned above. Since this is so, most beloved brethren, you ought to guard yourselves against them and abstain from them; never admit them to your communion. Neither receive their letters nor send them letters of fellowship.

And since those who were with Ossius wished to undermine the Catholic and apostolic faith, introducing a new sect [Col. 0675B]—the sect of the Judaizing Marcellus, mingled with Sabellius and Paul—and its artifice, we have necessarily set forth the faith of the Catholic Church, which the aforesaid persons who are with Ossius denied, and the heretics introduced the heresy of Marcellus.

> [Note: In the Sirmond manuscript: *judeo croniti*. We suppose that Marcellus’s doctrine is here accused of agreeing with the Jews, and that he is said to have been imbued with Jewish error. Then, instead of *inde artem*, Sirmond found in the Remigius manuscript *Juda artem*. We therefore think the reading should be: “the sect of Marcellus, united with Judaism, Judaizing in accordance with Sabellius and Paul.” The sense may, however, be recovered from §2, where Marcellus is represented as mixing his assertions now with the falsehoods of Sabellius, now with the wickedness of Paul of Samosata, now with blasphemies, and as making one confusion out of these; or from §4, where he is said to restore both the arts and deceits of Paul of Samosata.]

It follows that, upon receiving our letters, each of you, giving assent to this judgment, should ratify our decrees by his own subscription. Our faith is as follows (see *On the Synods*, §34).

### 29.

We believe in one God, the Father almighty, founder and creator of all things, from whom every creature [or “fatherhood”] in heaven and on earth is named; and in his only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, who was begotten of the Father before the age [that is, before all ages], God from God, light from light [Col. 0675C], through whom all things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, were made; who is the Word, wisdom, power, life, and true light; who in the last times assumed humanity [was incarnate] for our sake, and was born of the holy Virgin Mary, was crucified, died, and was buried; who rose from the dead on the third day, ascended into heaven, sits at the right hand of the Father, and will come at the end of the world to judge the living and the dead and render to each according to his works. His kingdom endures unceasingly unto eternal ages. For he sits at the Father’s right hand not only in this age, but also in the age to come.

We believe in the Holy Spirit, that is, in the Paraclete, whom, after his ascension into heaven, he sent (or: promised) to the Apostles, teaching [Col. 0675D] and instructing them (or: “to teach and instruct them”) in all things; through whom the souls of those who faithfully believe in him are sanctified.

[We also believe in the holy Church, the forgiveness of sins, the resurrection of the flesh, and eternal life.]

> [Note: The material enclosed in brackets does not occur in the Sardican formula transcribed in *On the Synods*, §34, as we have already noted there.]

But those who say that the Son of God is from what did not exist [that the Son of God is from non-existent things], or from another substance and not from God; or who say that there was once a time or age when the Son did not exist—the holy and Catholic Church condemns them as heretics. Likewise, it condemns those who say that there are three gods; or that Christ is not God; or that before [read: “before the ages”] Christ and the Son of God did not exist; or that he himself is the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; or that the Son was not begotten; or that God the Father begot the Son neither by judgment [counsel] nor by will. All these [Col. 0676B] the holy and Catholic Church anathematizes and abhors.

I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.

Stephen, bishop of Antioch in the province of Coele Syria [or “Sprecila”]: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.  
Olympius, bishop of Doliche: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.  
Gerontius, bishop of Lamphania.  
Menophantus, bishop from Ephesus: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.  
Paul, bishop: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.  
Eulalius, bishop from Amantias: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.  
Macedonius, bishop from Amarquetias [Mopsuestia]: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.  
Thelaphius, bishop from Chalcedon: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.  
Acacius, bishop from Caesarea: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.  
Theodore, bishop from Heraclea: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.  
Quintianus, bishop from Taxe: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.

> [Note: Read: “from Gaza,” for he is the man who had usurped Asclepas’s see, mentioned in Fragment §8 above.]

Mark, bishop from Aretiis [Arethusa]: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.  
Cyrotus, bishop from Roeo: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.  
Eugeus, bishop from Lisicia: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.  
Antonius, bishop from Zeumate: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.  
Antonius, bishop from Docimium: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.  
Dion, bishop from Caesarea: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.

> [Note: This is, so far as may be conjectured, Dianius, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia. Sozomen, book III, chapter 5, records that he attended the Antiochene council of 341; Basil, *Letter* 86, testifies that, while bedridden in the illness from which he died, he declared that he had indeed assented with a sincere heart to the written Constantinopolitan creed of 360, but had not wished in any respect to invalidate the faith set forth at Nicaea.]

Vitalis, bishop from Tyre: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.  
Eudoxius, bishop from Germanicia: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.  
Dionysius, bishop from Alexandria in the province: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.  
Macedonius, bishop from Berytus: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.  
Eusebius, bishop from Dorlani: I pray [Col. 0676D] that you may fare well in the Lord.

> [Note: *Eufenius* was wrongly printed; the manuscripts have *Eusevius*. This bishop seems to have belonged to the city called Zorlanis on the Peutinger Table and Srolanis by the Anonymous Ravennate.]

Basilius, bishop from Ancyra: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.

> [Note: Here *Anquira* is read for *Ancyra*, just as above *Quimatio* was read for *Cimatio*, and below *Quirius* for *Scyrus*.]

Proheresius, bishop from Sinope: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.  
Eustacius, bishop from Epiphania: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.  
Pancratius, bishop from Pernasus: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.

> [Note: Perhaps Parnassus. Parnason, or Parnassus, was a maritime city which, according to the Antonine Itinerary, belonged to Galatia or Cappadocia. Earlier the Pithoean manuscript has *Pranriacius*, not *Pancratius*.]

Eusebius, bishop from Pergamum: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.  
Sabinianus, bishop from Cathimera: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.  
Bitinicus, bishop from Zelon: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.  
Dominius, bishop from Palladianum: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.  
Pison, bishop from Troas: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.  
Cartherius, bishop from Aspona: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.  
Filetus, bishop from Juliopolis: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.  
Quirius, bishop from Mareotis: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.

> [Note: Sozomen, book III, chapter 12, reports that Ischyrius of Mareotis was present at Philippopolis with the other Easterners; his name is corrupted here as *Quirius*.]

Filetus, bishop from Cratia: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.  
Thimasarcus, bishop: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.  
Eusebius, bishop from Mignenia [perhaps Magnienia]: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.  
Quirius, bishop from Philadelphia: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.  
Pison, bishop from Vanis: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.

> [Note: Perhaps “from Adana,” in which case he is Piso of the Adanites, who, according to Socrates, book III, chapter 25, subscribed at the Antiochene council; or perhaps “from Varnis,” since in the Antiochene list at the end of William of Tyre, Varnon is an episcopal see under the metropolitan see of Edessa.]

Timothy, bishop: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.  
Euthemon, bishop from Thaneos: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.

> [Note: In Athanasius’s list of Meletius, p. 789, appears “Eudaemon in Tanais” (*Εὐδαίμων ἐν Τάνει*). He is the same person whom Athanasius says, together with Callinicus and Ision, later subscribed below, concocted against him the accusation concerning a tax on linen garments: *Apology to Constantius*, p. 778.]

Callenicus, bishop from Pelusium: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.

> [Note: In the list of Meletius in Athanasius, p. 789: “Callinicus in Pelusium” (*Καλλίνικος ἐν Πελουσίῳ*).]

Eusebius, bishop from Pergamum: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.  
Leucadas, bishop from Ilium: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.

> [Note: In Athanasius’s list of Meletius, Ilium, or Heliopolis, is mentioned as a certain district in which some bishops adhered to Meletius. The immediately preceding subscription of Eusebius appears superfluous, since it has already occurred above.]

Noconius, bishop from Troas: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.

> [Note: In the Pithoean manuscript: “from Troades.” On the preceding page occurred Pison, bishop from Troas.]

Adamantius, bishop from Cius: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.  
Eddesius, bishop from Cos: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.  
Theodolus, bishop from Neocaesarea: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.

> [Note: The Pithoean manuscript has “from Neocaesarioso.” In Labbe: Theodulus, bishop from Neocaesarea.]

Sion, bishop: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.

> [Note: Is this Ision, listed as being at Athribis in the list of Meletius, and the companion of Callinicus and Eudaemon in fabricating the accusation against Athanasius?]

Theogenes, bishop from Lizia: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.  
Florentius, bishop from Ancyra: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.  
Isaac, bishop from Lueto: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.

> [Note: In the list of Meletius: “Isaac in Leto.”]

Eudemon, bishop … I have subscribed on his behalf; I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.  
Agapius, bishop from Theriacum [Remigius manuscript: Therincum]: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.  
Bassus, bishop from Car: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.  
Narcissus, bishop from Anapolis [Irenopolis, or Neronopolis]: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.  
Embracius, bishop from Miletus: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.

> [Note: The Pithoean codex has, in its first hand, “from Lecto,” and in its second, “from Nilecto”; whence the printed reading “from Nisilecto.”]

Lucius, bishop from Babtinum: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.  
Nonnius, bishop from Laodicea: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.  
Pantagatus, bishop from Gallias [perhaps Galatia]: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.  
Flaccus, bishop from Hieropolis: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.  
Sysimius, bishop from Perge: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.

> [Note: He may be the Sisinnius whom Athanasius, *To the Solitaries*, p. 858, lists among the old disciples of Arius condemned by Alexander.]

Diogenes, bishop: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.  
Cresconius, bishop: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.  
Nestorius, bishop: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.  
Emmonius, bishop: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.  
Eugenius, bishop: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.  
Antonius, bishop from Gusia: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.

> [Note: In the Pithoean manuscript: “from Gusra.”]

Demophilus, bishop from Beroea: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.

> [Note: The printed text had “from Cooe,” but the manuscript more nearly gives “from Beroe.”]

Euticius, bishop from Philippopolis: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.  
Severus, bishop from Cabula: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.  
Timothy, bishop from Anchialus: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.  
Valens, bishop from Mursa: I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.

> [Note: If they did not falsely attest in §16 that eighty bishops had assembled in one place, seven subscriptions are missing here.]

Here ends the decree of the Eastern bishops’ synod at Sardica, of the Arian party, which they sent to Africa.

## FRAGMENT IV  
*(Otherwise Part I)*

[Col. 0678C]

### HERE BEGINS A COPY OF A LETTER

> [Note: In the appendix to volume III, under the year 352, Baronius grants that this letter has the air of antiquity and was written in the age of Liberius; nevertheless, he wholly denies that it is Liberius’s. Most also reject it as fabricated and spurious.
>
> For, first, Athanasius never indicates by even the slightest word that Liberius, before his exile, withdrew from communion with Athanasius. On the contrary, at the end of the *Apology to Constantius*, p. 807, he adduces as a splendid testimony to his own innocence the fact that Liberius preferred to suffer everything rather than betray his cause.
>
> Secondly, when Athanasius, *To the Solitaries*, p. 837, states that “Liberius, after two years completed in exile, was bent and induced by threats of death to subscribe,” he immediately adds: “Yet that very fact sufficiently proves both their violence, and Liberius’s hatred of heresy, and his support for Athanasius while he possessed free inclination.” Certainly this would not help his cause at all if Liberius, at the beginning of his pontificate and under no compulsion, had excluded him from communion.
>
> Liberius himself openly declares that he had always recoiled from condemning Athanasius. When the eunuch Eusebius demanded his subscription against Athanasius, he courageously replied, according to Athanasius, *To the Solitaries*, p. 833, that he could by no means condemn one whom not one but now a second synod had declared entirely free from every charge, and whom the Roman Church had dismissed in peace; nor could he reject in his absence one whom, as he says there, “we loved and held in our communion” when present.
>
> Finally, when he had given these answers not only to the eunuch Eusebius at Rome but also to Constantius at Milan, in the presence of Epictetus and Eusebius, no one ever thought to object that Athanasius had already once been condemned by him.
>
> Some reply that Athanasius spared Liberius, who had now corrected himself and remained in his communion, out of modesty and friendship, prudently passing over what Liberius had done in hasty judgment. They hold that Liberius, moved by the Easterners’ letter, did write this letter, but was recalled from publishing it by the Egyptian letters, until, unable to bear exile and wishing to win the Easterners’ favor, he decided that it should be made public.
>
> But their defense rests upon mere conjectures and is refuted by Liberius’s own letter to the Easterners. So far from testifying that he had already long condemned Athanasius, he rather excuses the delay of that condemnation: “Because,” he says in Fragment VI, §5, “my predecessor, Julius, bishop of blessed memory, had received him, lest perhaps I should be judged by some as a transgressor. But when I learned, when it pleased God, that you had justly condemned him, I immediately gave my assent to your judgments,” and so forth.
>
> Therefore it was then for the first time that he gave his assent to the Easterners, when, overcome by weariness of exile, he departed from his former constancy. That he had never before condemned Athanasius is clear from the following Fragment V, §2, where he expressly declares that at the beginning of his pontificate he had received Eastern letters against Athanasius but had not given them either his credence or his judgment, because at the same time the opinion of eighty Egyptian bishops concerning Athanasius stood opposed. “Hence,” he says, “it appeared contrary to divine law, even when the number of bishops supporting Athanasius was greater, to give assent in any respect to Athanasius’s opponents, who were fewer in number.”
>
> Further, since it is clear from Fragment V, §§1 and 6, and from the following §4, that Liberius requested through envoys from Constantius not only at Milan in 354, but also at Arles in 353, that he order a council to be assembled at Aquileia, as he himself had long before approved, to consider Athanasius’s case [Col. 0680A], it follows correctly that Liberius had requested a council already in 352, that is, at the beginning of his pontificate, and that the request had pleased the Emperor. For “long before” can scarcely be restricted more narrowly than to the preceding year. Thus no period remains in which Athanasius could be judged to have been summoned by Liberius and separated from his communion.
>
> Therefore we agree all the more readily that this letter was fabricated by the Arians, since Athanasius himself demonstrates that the same men published many letters of this kind, under the names both of Athanasius and of the Emperor, at about the same time: *Apology to Constantius*, pp. 680 and 686. The Council of Sardica also confirms this, for letters forged by Theognis against Athanasius and Marcellus were read there, as we heard in Fragment II, §3.
>
> A further question arises here: whose are the materials appended to this letter as though an appendix? Those who consider the letter Arian fabrication judge the appendix likewise to have been forged by Arians; for praise of an act meriting everyone’s indignation is unworthy of Hilary but worthy of Arians. Yet who does not recognize in it the voice of a Catholic bishop, recounting the Arians’ unsuccessful endeavors and commending the Sardican Council, by which Athanasius was acquitted and the Arians condemned?
>
> Godefridus Hermant, note 3 on chapter 25 of book VI of the *Life of St Athanasius*, thinks this appendix belongs not to the immediately preceding letter inscribed to Liberius, but to the letter of the Sardican synod to Constantius, which Hilary had supplied at the end of Fragment II. Yet, if its words are considered more closely, they will appear to suit the preceding letter better than the lost letter of the Sardican synod. Indeed, although this entire work of Hilary is altogether confused and disordered, no appendix of this kind occurs torn away and separated from its proper place. We therefore judge neither that this piece has been displaced from its position nor that it is unworthy of Hilary; rather, what most take to be praise of the preceding letter is mere irony.
>
> We also suspect that Potamius and Epictetus are meant here as the architects of that letter, and that for *audire haec noluerunt* (“they refused to hear these things”) one should read *audere haec potuerunt* (“they were able to dare these things”). Thus Fortunatianus, deceived by them—who, according to Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 97, “is held detestable in this, that he was the first to solicit and break Liberius, bishop of the city of Rome, as he went into exile for the faith, and forced him to subscribe to heresy”—sent the same letter to various bishops to draw them away from communion with Athanasius. Yet he achieved nothing, because it was well known to everyone that Athanasius had never fallen from Liberius’s communion through the agency of the Egyptians.
>
> If this is so, the letter must have been fabricated not in 352 but in 355, when Liberius was driven into exile. Nevertheless, we assign it this place according to the time at which its authors pretended it had been published. See the notes on the following Fragment.]

## LIBERIUS, BISHOP OF THE CITY OF ROME, TO THE EASTERN BISHOPS

Liberius, bishop of the city of Rome, to all our most beloved brethren and fellow bishops established throughout the East: everlasting salvation.

### 1. Liberius grants his communion to the Easterners, but denies it to Athanasius.

Desiring the peace and concord of the Churches, after I had received letters from Your Charity concerning Athanasius and the others, addressed to Julius, bishop of blessed memory, I followed the tradition of the elders and sent from my side to Alexandria, to the aforesaid Athanasius, Lucius, Paul, and Helianus, presbyters of the city of Rome, so that he might come to the city of Rome. There, in his presence, that which ecclesiastical discipline had established might be determined concerning him.

> [Note: We restore the manuscript reading, in place of the printed reading *exigit*, “requires.”]

I also gave letters to the same man through the aforesaid presbyters, containing the warning that, if he did not come, he should know himself to be outside the communion of the Roman Church. The presbyters, having returned, reported that he had refused to come.

Therefore, following the letters of Your Charity which you gave us concerning the condemnation of the aforesaid Athanasius, know from these letters, which I have given to preserve our unanimity, that I have peace with all of you and with all bishops of the Catholic Church; but that the aforesaid Athanasius is outside my communion and that of the Roman Church, and outside the fellowship of ecclesiastical letters.

> [Note: Hilary himself interprets *de nomine* in Fragment VI, §4: that is, “concerning the condemnation.”]
>
> [Note: We supply *dedi* (“I gave”) from the Sirmond manuscript. Immediately above, *vestram* (“your”) would be preferable. Yet *ad unanimitatem nostram* may be understood as “for maintaining unanimity among us.”]

### 2. This letter is fabricated in vain: why.

“What is there in this letter that is not holy, what that does not arise from the fear of God? Yet Potamius and Epictetus, rejoicing to condemn the bishop of the city of Rome, as is contained in the Synod of Rimini, refused to hear these things [perhaps: “were able to dare these things”]. Indeed, Fortunatianus the bishop, sending the same letter again to different bishops, achieved nothing.

> [Note: Godefridus Hermant, book VII of the *Life of St Athanasius*, chapter 6, since he takes it as certain that some commendable act for the Catholic faith performed by Fortunatianus before his lapse is here recalled, thinks the letter of the Sardican synod sent to Constantius is meant. Yet it is not likely that Hilary would have said that the Sardican synod’s letter achieved nothing, when he immediately states that its authority prevailed with all. It is more probable, as we have said, that the pseudo-letter of Liberius is meant: Fortunatianus sent it after his lapse to various bishops, but accomplished nothing, because the Sardican synod, confirmed by Liberius after he had been informed by Egyptian letters concerning Athanasius’s case, carried great weight with all.]

But in denying communion to Athanasius they made themselves rather burdensome, and made the entire affair a danger to themselves, provided only that they might detract nothing from the Sardican Synod, by which Athanasius had been acquitted and the Arians condemned. Letters sent from all Egypt and Alexandria reminded them that, just as letters had formerly been written to Julius for restoring communion to the exiled Athanasius, so now, as will be clear from what follows, letters had been given to Liberius for preserving it.”

> [Note: The printed editions, following the Pithoean manuscript, read: “Letters from Egypt, and everything, warned that they had gone to Alexandria, just as letters had formerly been written to Julius concerning the restoration of communion to the rejoicing Athanasius; so now,” etc. The reading we now offer, assembled from substantially the same characters previously arranged incorrectly, is confirmed by the very truth of the history.
>
> At the beginning of the *Apology to Constantius*, p. 722, Athanasius preserves a letter of the Alexandrian synod, written by all Egypt, and, as Athanasius notes at its end, written to all and to Julius, bishop of Rome, in Athanasius’s favor. The Sardican Fathers praise it in Fragment II, §5, and in §10 testify that it was sent by eighty bishops. Liberius himself, in the following Fragment V, recalls another letter given to him by the same number of Egyptian bishops on Athanasius’s behalf at the very time when he received the Easterners’ letters against him.]
>
> [Note: The manuscript reading is *exsultante*, erroneously. Letters were written to Liberius just as they had been to Julius, because, like Julius, Liberius received letters from eighty Egyptian bishops in Athanasius’s favor, as will be understood from the following material—namely, from §2 of the following Fragment. Since that Fragment occupies a place in the first part of these Fragments in the archetypal manuscript, while the present material occurs only in the second part, it follows: first, that both parts belong to Hilary and that it is wrong for Blondel and certain others to deny him the part that is first in the manuscript; secondly, that the order of the Fragments in the manuscript is inverted, since the fifth is placed before that to which Hilary declares it should be attached; thirdly, that Nicholas Faber was entitled to publish in second place only the part of this work which he found first in the manuscript; and finally, that we are no less entitled to arrange the individual Fragments in a better order. No one will deny this unless he wishes perhaps to refer “as will be understood from the following material” not to the following letters of Liberius but to the Egyptian letter which has dropped out here.]

## FRAGMENT V  
*(Otherwise Part II)*

### HERE BEGINS THE LETTER OF THE LEGATES

> [Note: Namely, Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari; Pancratius the presbyter; and Hilary the deacon. Eusebius of Vercelli joined them, invited by Liberius’s letter, which Baronius transcribes under the year 354, §2. It is clear that this letter was sent after the defeat of Magnentius and the Council of Arles in 353.
>
> No one agrees with Valesius, in his notes on chapter 37 of Socrates, book II, in assigning it to 356; for through this embassy Liberius obtained the council held at Milan in 355. Scholars therefore agree that it was written in 354; and, as Antonius Pagi thinks after Baronius, while Constantius was still in Gaul. Ammianus, book XIV, chapter 4, testifies that at the end of that same year he withdrew to Italy for winter quarters. Baronius transcribed this letter under the year 354, §2, from the Paris edition of the *Library of the Fathers*, where it appears among the works of Lucifer.]

### SENT TO EMPEROR CONSTANTIUS [Col. 0682A] BY LIBERIUS, BISHOP OF THE CITY OF ROME, THROUGH BISHOP LUCIFER  
*(about 354)*

To the most glorious Constantius Augustus, Liberius, bishop.

### 1. Liberius requests a council. He is attacked by insulting reports circulated among the people by Constantius.

I beseech you, most tranquil Emperor, that your clemency may grant me a kindly hearing, so that the purpose of my mind may become evident to your gentleness. For from a Christian emperor and son of Constantine of sacred memory, I deserve to obtain this without hesitation.

> [Note: In Baronius: “so that I may be able,” and afterward “make known” instead of “become evident”; and above, “I pray” instead of “I beseech.”]

But I understand that I labor in vain, because, although I have repeatedly given satisfaction, I cannot bring back into favor toward me even your mind’s willingness to be appeased toward the accused. For a report of your piety, long since issued among the people [Col. 0682B], grievously wounds me, who must bear all things patiently. Yet it is astonishing to me that your mind, ever devoted to gentleness and never preserving anger until sunset, as Scripture says, should retain indignation against me.

For I, most religious Emperor, seek true peace with you: a peace not fashioned in words by an inward disposition of deceit, but reasonably confirmed by the precepts of the Gospels. It was not Athanasius’s affair alone; many other matters came forward, on account of which I had entreated your gentleness that a council might be held.

> [Note: In the preceding year, through Vincent of Capua, who at Arles consented with the Arians to Athanasius’s condemnation.]

Above all, I requested that the matter of faith—upon which rests our primary hope toward God, and which your mind’s sincere devotion toward God especially desires—should be carefully considered [Col. 0683A], so that the machinations of those who ought to admire our reverence toward God might be brought to an end.

> [Note: Baronius reads *nec eorum*. Perhaps *technae eorum* (“their artifices”); or *vel tunc aut dehinc eorum*, with *causae* (“cases”) understood afterward?] It would have been fitting for a worshipper of God, fitting for your rule, which is governed and enlarged by Christ’s piety, that your clemency should especially grant us this, for the reverence of the holy religion to which you wisely give attention.

2. He is falsely accused of having suppressed the letters of the Easterners. Why he did not believe them. — But many hasten to tear the members of the Church apart; they have fabricated the charge that I suppressed the letters, so that the accusations against him whom they said they had condemned might not become known to all. [Note: [Col. 0683C] Elsewhere, from the Pithoean manuscript: “as though those letters.” With Baronius we prefer: “What letters?”—supply, “did I suppress?” By these words the opinion of those who accept as genuine the preceding letter bearing the name of Liberius entirely collapses. For how could one be accused of suppressing the letters of the Easterners if, complying with them, he had summoned Athanasius to Rome and afterwards removed him from his communion?] What letters? Those of the Eastern and Egyptian bishops, in which the same accusations against Athanasius were contained throughout? Yet it is sufficiently clear to everyone, and no one denies, that we made known the letters of the Easterners, read them to the Church, read them to the council, and also replied to the Easterners concerning these matters; but we did not lend them our faith and judgment, because at that same time the judgment of eighty Egyptian bishops concerning Athanasius stood opposed to them, which we likewise recited and made known to the Italian bishops. [Note: [Col. 0683C] Pithoean manuscript: “knowledge.” With Baronius, “judgment” is preferable. Shortly, and also in Fragment VI, no. 3, we shall hear Liberius himself speak of “lending consent.”] [Note: [Col. 0683D] Faber printed “at that time,” although his manuscript read “at the same time,” as it also appears in Baronius. This again refutes what some devised in defence of the authenticity of the preceding letter: namely, that Liberius wrote it under the influence of the Easterners’ letters, but was dissuaded from issuing it by other letters from the Egyptians. For how could someone have received at the same time both Eastern and Egyptian letters, if, moved by the former, he first sent presbyters to Athanasius and awaited their return before hearing anything from Egypt?] [Note: [Col. 0683D] Baronius has “seventy-five.” Our manuscripts’ reading, “eighty,” is preferable. For the bishops said in Fragment II, no. 5, to have written from Egypt to Julius, are reported in no. 10 of the same Fragment to have numbered eighty [Col. 0684C]. Moreover, from the final words of the preceding Fragment we have heard that letters like those sent to Julius were sent to Liberius—that is, letters from the same men, written in Athanasius’s favour.] Hence it seemed contrary even to the divine law, when the number of bishops supporting Athanasius was greater, to lend assent in any respect. Eusebius, who had been sent, if he owes fidelity to God, left these writings with us in haste when departing for Africa; Vincentius, who had been sent with the others, subsequently carried all these writings to Arles, lest perhaps they be lacking when a council was sought. [Note: [Col. 0684C] Baronius reads “Theosebius”; and shortly thereafter, “all the writings … arrived at Arles.”]

3. He clears himself of accusations fabricated against him by Constantius. — Your prudence therefore sees that nothing entered my mind which it was not fitting for servants of God to consider. God is my witness; the whole Church with its members is witness: in faith and fear of my God I have trampled, and do trample, all worldly things, as evangelical and apostolic principle commands. Not in rash fury, but under established and observed divine law, and while living in another ecclesiastical ministry, I fulfilled nothing that pertained to the law through [673] boastfulness or desire for glory. I came unwillingly to this office—God is my witness—in which I do indeed desire, without offence to God, to remain as long as I shall be in this world. And I have carried out, not my own ordinances, but the apostolic ordinances, so that they might always be established and preserved. Following the custom and order of my predecessors, I allowed nothing to be added to, and nothing to be diminished from, the episcopate of the city of Rome; and preserving that faith which has run through the succession of so many bishops, of whom many were martyrs, I earnestly desire that it may always be kept inviolate.

4. Why he cannot communicate with the Easterners. — Finally, ecclesiastical concern and devotion itself persuade me now to disclose the matter to your piety. The Easterners declare that they wish to be joined to our peace. What sort of peace is this, most merciful Emperor, when there are among them four bishops—Demophilus, Macedonius, Eudoxius, and Martyrius—who, eight years ago, when at Milan, refused to condemn Arius’s heretical teaching and left the council in anger? [Note: [Col. 0684C] After Athanasius, *On the Synods*, p. 895, Socrates, book II, ch. 19, relates that, three years after the Council of Antioch of 341, the Easterners drew up an extended formula of faith and sent it through Eudoxius, Macedonius, and Martyrius to the bishops of Italy. Their arrival seems to have occasioned this council, [Col. 0684D] at which those four bishops refused to condemn the heresy of Arius. We note incidentally that it was customary among Westerners to propose in their councils that the Arian heresy be condemned together with the other heresies. For what was demanded of the aforesaid bishops in this year was likewise demanded of Valens and Ursacius in the same city in 347, as they themselves declare in Fragment II, no. 20. We shall shortly hear that the Council of Arles of 353 did the same. Athanasius, *On the Synods*, p. 876, also testifies that by this means the craftiness of Valens and Ursacius was exposed at Rimini. “For,” he says, “when the bishops proposed that the other heresies together with Arianism be condemned, and all the rest agreed, Valens and Ursacius with their companions refused.”] Your equity and clemency can judge whether it is lawful to lend assent to the judgments of such men, what that would be like, and what danger it would entail. What is now being attempted subtly, under cover of Athanasius’s name, is not new. There remain letters formerly sent by Bishop Alexander to Sylvester of holy memory, in which he reported that, before Athanasius’s ordination, he had expelled from the Church eleven presbyters and deacons alike because they followed Arius’s heresy. [Note: [Col. 0684D] Athanasius seems to provide a catalogue of these men in *To the Solitaries*, p. 858, where he complains that churches—taken from Catholics—are bestowed upon Arians, not novices but veterans, long ago condemned together with Arius by Bishop Alexander: thus, in Upper Libya, Secundus; in Alexandria, Euzoius the Chananite, Julius, Ammon, Marcus, Irenaeus, Zosimus, Serapion surnamed Pelecon; and in Libya, Sisinnius, together with young adherents of the same heresy, receive churches.] Some of these, now standing outside the Catholic Church, are said to have found conventicles for themselves, and George is even alleged to communicate by letter with them at Alexandria. [Note: [Col. 0685C] Valesius understood “George in Alexandria” as George, bishop of Alexandria, who is known to have invaded Athanasius’s see only in 356. He was therefore led to deny that this letter was written before that year. But another George is meant here—probably the bishop of Laodicea—who, as Athanasius testifies in *On the Synods*, pp. 886–887, had formerly been an Alexandrian presbyter and had been expelled by Alexander. Thus after “in Alexandria” one may suitably supply “formerly a presbyter.” More suitably still, one may understand him here to be charged with communicating by letter with the Alexandrian Arians.] What peace, then, can there be, most tranquil Emperor, if bishops are compelled—as has now happened throughout Italy—to obey the judgments of such persons when these judgments have been presented? [Note: [Col. 0685D] This is absent from the copies printed by Baronius. The Pithoean manuscript has, “if bishops are compelled to obey the judgments of such men when these judgments have been presented”; Faber seems not badly to have corrected it. The matter becomes clearer if the word order is altered thus: “If bishops are compelled to obey such judgments now presented.” What is repeatedly said concerning violence done to bishops is more plainly explained by Sulpicius Severus, book II, p. 246: “An edict was issued by the Emperor that those who would not subscribe to Athanasius’s condemnation should be driven into exile.”]

5. Hear another matter, since your serenity [674] patiently receives it. There remain letters of the envoys sent to your clemency, which arrived recently. They state that, because of the disturbance of all the churches, they had indeed wished at first to yield to the judgments of the Easterners; but they proposed the condition that, if those same men condemned Arius’s heresy, then, induced by this means, they would obey their judgments. [Note: [Col. 0685D] Namely Vincentius of Capua and Marcellus, as is made clear in the following Fragment, no. 3; the attempts of the former, or rather of the latter, are narrated here. For it should be believed that they first refused altogether to condemn Athanasius; then they agreed to his condemnation, provided that his opponents condemned Arius’s heresy; and finally Vincentius, compelled by force, carried out the Arians’ wishes.] They state that the agreement was confirmed with Scripture as witness; they proceed to the council and receive, after deliberation, the answer that they cannot condemn Arius’s doctrine, but that Athanasius—this alone being demanded—must be deprived of communion. Let your clemency therefore consider also whether, with the law of the Catholic religion rightly preserved, a man’s case ought to be carefully and thoroughly examined.

6. He earnestly requests a council. — Therefore again and again we beseech your mildness and your soul devoted to God, by the power of Him who, in defending you, showed to all mortals how great He is, [“against Magnentius, destroyed in 353”] that, keeping before your eyes the benefits of Him who governs your empire in all things, you cause these matters to be examined with every consideration in an assembly of bishops. [Col. 0685C] Thus, in peaceful times established through you, God favouring, and with your serenity’s consent, let all matters be discussed [Col. 0686A] so that whatever has been confirmed by the judgment of God’s priests—once it is established that all agreed upon the exposition of faith confirmed at Nicaea in the presence of your father of holy memory among so many bishops—may be preserved for the future as an example. May the Saviour Himself, who looks down from above upon the purpose of your mind, rejoice that, amid so great an expedition of affairs, you have not without reason placed the cause of faith and peace even before the necessities of the commonwealth. Therefore, to entreat your mildness to deign to hear our representations with a favourable mind, we have resolved to send my brother and fellow bishop, the holy man Lucifer, with Pancratius the presbyter and Hilary the deacon. We trust that, through your clemency, they will not find it difficult to obtain a council for the peace [675] of all the Catholic churches. May the mercy of almighty God preserve you for us, most merciful and most religious Augustus. [Note: [Col. 0686C] In Baronius: “most religious Emperor.”] End.

## FRAGMENT VI (otherwise Part I)

### LIBERIUS, BEFORE GOING INTO EXILE, WROTE THIS UNIFORM LETTER TO THE CONFESSORS—THAT IS, EUSEBIUS, DIONYSIUS, AND LUCIFER—WHO WERE IN EXILE (A.D. 355).

[Note: [Col. 0686C] Baronius, under the year 355, no. 32, prints the same letter. He testifies that in the acts of St. Eusebius it is addressed to Eusebius alone; in the Vatican codex, both to him and to the other exiles; and finally, in many other copies, it is inscribed as an encyclical to all confessors exiled in different places. This inscription is supported by Hilary’s calling it “uniform.” Hence, immediately after the words “to Dionysius and Lucifer,” “and the rest” seems to need to be supplied. Surely no one could believe that Liberius forgot Pancratius the presbyter and Hilary the deacon, who, sent together with Eusebius, Dionysius, and Lucifer, endured the same lot of exile? It is beyond doubt that the letter was directed especially to those who, at the Council of Milan in 355, deserved banishment because of their steadfast defence of the faith and of Athanasius. Nor is it less clear that it was written immediately after that council, in that same year, 355. Accordingly, if one considers chronology, the following letters, both to Caecilianus and to Hosius, ought to be placed not only before this letter but also before the preceding Fragment. But what Hilary himself had joined together ought not to be separated; for, as he himself warned, he sometimes follows the order of events rather than that of time. Nor is his design now hidden from discerning readers: namely, to gather in one place matters which would show from what height Liberius fell, and from how great a spirit he declined to so small a one.]

1. Liberius congratulates the exiles. — Although, under the appearance of peace, the enemy of the human race seems to have raged more violently against the members of the Church, yet your outstanding and singular faith, most beloved priests in the Lord, has shown you here to be approved by God and has already marked you out as martyrs destined for future glory. [Note: [Col. 0686D] The Pithoean manuscript reads “most acceptable”; Faber added “to God” to this word. Baronius’s reading seemed more genuine.] With what proclamation of praise, then, with what exultation of voice, can I set forth the merits of your courage? Placed between sorrow at your absence and joy at your glory, I find absolutely no way—except that I know from this [or: “here”] that I offer you more fitting consolation if you believe that I too have been driven into exile with you. Indeed, I am deeply grieved that, while I still hang in this very expectation, a harsher necessity meanwhile separates me from your fellowship. For I had wished, most devoted brothers, to be spent before all of you, so that your belovedness might follow an example of glory more fully through me. But let this be the crown of your merits: that you were the first, through perseverance in faith, to reach the illustrious glory of confession. I therefore beg your belovedness to believe that I am present with you, and not to think me absent [676] in affection; understand that I am greatly grieved because for the present I have been parted from your fellowship (or: “separated”). [Col. 0687B] You can know all the more what great glory you have gained from this: those crowned in persecution could experience only the bloody swords of the persecutor; but you, soldiers of God wholly devoted, having also experienced false brethren as enemies, have carried off victory over the faithless. [Note: [Col. 0687C] Baronius reads “persecution”; on that basis, and also on the basis of the Sirmondian manuscript, we restore later “bloody swords” in place of “the sword of fruits.”] [Note: [Col. 0687C] The Pithoean manuscripts read “however much,” then omit “holy”; we supply it from Baronius, preferring with him “the greater,” with the unexpressed comparative particle “the more.”] The more their violence could increase in the world, the greater rewards of praise are found to be bestowed upon holy priests. Therefore be secure in the heavenly promise.

2. He asks them to pray for him; he wishes to learn from them what happened at Milan. — And because you have become nearer to God, raise up to the Lord by your prayers me, your fellow priest and servant of God, so that I may be able to bear patiently the assaults which, being announced day by day, inflict more grievous wounds. [Note: [Col. 0687C] Pithoean manuscript: “when they announce, they inflict more grievous future things”; Baronius’s copy corrects it.] May the Lord deign to make me equal to you, with faith inviolate and the condition of the Catholic Church safe. [Note: [Col. 0687C] In Baronius: “may He deign to bring us rewards. And because,” etc.] And because I desire to know more faithfully what was done in the encounter itself, I beseech your holiness to deign to make everything known faithfully by letter, so that either my own mind, tormented by conflicting reports, or the strength of my body itself, now weakened, may receive greater reinforcement from your encouragement. Written in another hand: May God preserve you unharmed, brothers in the Lord.

### LIBERIUS, BEFORE GOING INTO EXILE, WROTE TO CAECILIANUS, BISHOP OF SPOLETO, CONCERNING VINCENTIUS OF CAPUA (ABOUT THE BEGINNING OF A.D. 354).

[Note: [Col. 0687C] In the Sirmondian manuscript: “to Aelianus.” Indeed, Aelianus subscribes to the Council of Sardica in Athanasius, p. 767.] [Note: [Col. 0687C] After Vincentius’s recent fall, lest he be deterred by Vincentius’s example from defending the truth; therefore either at the end of 353 or at the beginning of 354.]

3. He laments Vincentius’s fall. — Do not let what Vincentius did turn you away from the pursuit of a good work, dearest brother. And concerning Vincentius’s ruin he says thus to Hosius: “Among these matters, because I ought not to pass over your conscience in anything, many bishops from Italy assembled, who with me had entreated the most religious Emperor [677] Constantius to order, as they had long since decided, that a council be convened at Aquileia. [Note: [Col. 0687C] At the same time as to the bishop of Spoleto, [Col. 0687D] so that, transferring to another the intolerable weight of grief by which he was oppressed, he might himself bear it more lightly. Perhaps at that time, greatly anxious for the Church, its same governor wrote other letters to others. How much Vincentius’s fall lay upon his heart he indicates in another letter to Eusebius of Vercelli, cited by Baronius under the year 353, no. 20.] [Note: [Col. 0687D] We would prefer “among other things,” as Baronius seems to have read in the Vatican codex, from which he copied these same words of Liberius under the year 353, no. 19; then these two words are connected with the preceding “he says” and indicate that Hilary is not reproducing Liberius’s letter in full.] I inform your Holiness that Vincentius of Capua, together with Marcellus, likewise a bishop from Campania, undertook our embassy. I had hoped much of him, because he both understood the case excellently and had frequently sat as judge in the same case with your Holiness; I believed that through his embassy the whole Gospel of God could be preserved. [Note: [Col. 0687D] We emend thus from Baronius, since the text published from the Pithoean manuscript [Col. 0688C] read: “because he retained the case excellently, and, seeing in the same …, had sat.” Vincentius sat as judge with Hosius at the Council of Sardica, to which he subscribes above in Fragment II, and from which he was chosen as envoy to Constantius, as Athanasius relates in *To the Solitaries*, p. 882. Moreover, he is believed to have attended the Roman council of 341 and to be the Vincentius whom we read was a presbyter of the Roman Church and legate of Pope Sylvester at the Nicene council.] [Note: [Col. 0688C] The Pithoean and Sirmondian manuscripts read “the whole law of the Gospels”; then Pithoean alone reads “or the embassy,” while Sirmondian reads “his embassy.” We prefer Baronius’s reading.] He obtained not merely nothing, but was himself led into that pretence. [Note: [Col. 0688C] That is, yielding somewhat to their threats and insults—those whose initial attempts he had courageously resisted, as the preceding Fragment, no. 5, attests.] After his action, afflicted with a double grief, I resolved that I ought rather to die for God, lest I should appear the last betrayer or lend assent to judgments against the Gospel.” [Note: [Col. 0688C] Baronius has “appear as a betrayer,” for he seems to have lent assent to their judgments. If this reading is true, Liberius was not yet certain whether Vincentius had in fact lent consent. In Athanasius, *Apology to Constantius*, p. 692, we indeed find that Vincentius endured no slight violence and insults until he promised to abstain from Athanasius’s communion; but we do not find that he subscribed to anything either against the faith or against Athanasius. Whether Marcellus likewise went over to the same pretence, Liberius does not say. He laments Vincentius’s fall alone, as the more distinguished man from whom he had hoped much, and whose name had such weight that Damasus could later say, in Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, book II, ch. 21, that no prejudice against the faith should arise from the number of bishops assembled at Rimini, since the Roman bishop and Vincentius had not consented.]

4. Liberius condemns Athanasius. — “After all these things which Liberius had either done or promised, when sent into exile, [Col. 0689A] he reduced everything to nothing, writing to the treacherous Arian heretics who had passed an unjust sentence against the holy Athanasius, the orthodox bishop.” [Note: [Col. 0689B] “After two years had elapsed,” Athanasius says in *To the Solitaries*, p. 837, “he was bent in exile and induced by threats of death to subscribe.” Hence it follows that the three following letters were written late in 357, or certainly early in 358. We readily allow that some interval may have existed between them. For while Liberius, burning with desire for Rome, saw that he was receiving no help from those from whom he hoped for it, he repeatedly sought the aid of others. Thus the first probably belongs to 357 and the others to 358. Baronius copied the same letters under the year 357, no. 34, saying in no. 32 that he had found them in the Cresconian collection and in two codices.]

**To the most beloved brethren, the presbyters and fellow bishops of the East, Liberius (about the end of A.D. 357).**

5. Your holy faith, because of godly fear, is [678] known to God and to persons of good will. As the Law says, “Judge justly, sons of men” (Psalm 57:2), I do not defend Athanasius. [Note: [Col. 0689B] The Pithoean manuscript: “I did not defend.” With Baronius we prefer “I do not defend,” for it is well established that Liberius had formerly defended Athanasius.] But because Julius the bishop, my predecessor of good memory, had received him, I feared that I might perhaps be judged a betrayer by someone. [Note: [Col. 0689C] Elsewhere, from the Pithoean manuscript: “in some respect.” From Baronius we restore “by someone,” supported by the Sirmondian manuscript.] But when I learned—when it pleased God—that you had justly condemned him, I immediately lent assent to your judgments and sent letters concerning him—that is, concerning his condemnation—through our brother Fortunatianus, to be delivered to Emperor Constantius. [Note: [Col. 0689C] Faber was the first to print these words in a type distinct from the rest; Baronius nonetheless understood them as Liberius’s, and it is not certainly established whether they are not truly his.] Therefore, Athanasius having been removed from the communion of us all, whose letters I must not receive, I declare that I have peace and unanimity with all of you and with all the bishops of the East throughout every province.

6. He subscribes to the Sirmian creed. — For, that you may know more truly that I speak the true faith in this letter, my common lord and brother Demophilus, who in his goodwill has deigned to set forth your Catholic faith—the faith discussed, set forth, and received at Sirmium by many of our brethren and fellow bishops, and received by all who were present—[Note: [Col. 0689C] Baronius’s copies read: “that I proclaim the true faith through this my letter.” Afterwards, “which he set forth” seems to be missing.] [Note: [Col. 0689C] In the earlier printed copies “your” is missing; we supply it from the Pithoean manuscript. In its place the Sirmondian and Baronius manuscripts read “true.”] [Note: [Col. 0689C] Baronius, under the year 357, no. 34, omitted this note, from which a very great controversy has arisen among scholars. In an appendix, however, he later admitted that he found it in Cresconius’s collection. Since there are three Sirmian formulas—the first, written in 351 against Photinus; the second, published in 357 under the name of Hosius; and the last, issued in May 359—scholars dispute which Liberius here says he received. Valesius alone, in his notes on Sozomen, book IV, ch. 14, believes the third is meant, although nearly all agree that it had not yet been issued when Liberius wrote. Some indeed think that he was present at Sirmium when the aforesaid formula was issued and subscribed to it. But since he was summoned there only through the favour of the Easterners, and could obtain that favour from them only by this letter, he must here say that he received another faith than that which was issued when he reached Sirmium. Blondel and many others maintain that Liberius speaks of the second Sirmian formula: first, because Hilary alone labels it “treachery,” whereas in *On the Synods* he approves and excuses the first; and secondly, because Liberius says he received the faith “which was discussed, set forth, and received at Sirmium by many of our brethren and fellow bishops, and received by all who were present,” words which agree sufficiently with the preface of the second Sirmian formula. Petavius, in his notes on Epiphanius, p. 316, inclines to Blondel’s view, although he judges that Liberius could easily be cleared of heresy if he were said to have embraced, from the first part alone of the aforesaid formula—where they decree that *homoousion* and *homoiousion* should be passed over—in the interest of peace and quiet. But who would concede that he received only the first part, when he says: “I received this with a willing mind; I contradicted in nothing”? Yet Petavius’s certain assertion there—that Liberius did not subscribe to the first Sirmian formula—he proves by this one rather weak reason: namely, that this first exposition preceded not only Liberius’s restoration but also his exile. As though the man punished with exile because, adhering to Athanasius [Col. 0690C] and to the Nicene faith, he had refused to approve the Easterners’ new formulas, would not now do everything by which he might be recalled from exile, while testifying both that he abandoned Athanasius’s cause and that he subscribed to the Sirmian faith against Photinus, which, when he was banished, was the most recent among the Easterners. The opinion by which Baronius and others deny that Liberius subscribed to the second Sirmian exposition rests on weightier arguments. First, when this was composed, Theodorus was already dead; Cecropius, Eudoxius, and the rest were absent from Sirmium; finally, Basil, Macedonius, Silvanus, and others vigorously opposed it when it was brought to them. Yet below we find all of these men to be authors of the formula to which Liberius says he consented. Petavius objects that the appended addition was made not by Hilary but by a man ignorant of divisions within the Arian sect. Thus someone interprets the word *requirendum* (“to be investigated”), which appears at its end, in support of Petavius’s opinion—as though the author of this addition, being uncertain and doubtful, warned by this note that the whole matter should be examined more carefully. But the authority for the truth of this appendix comes not only from the Pithoean manuscript but also from the Cresconian collection. Nor does it occur to us by whom, or for what reason, so many bishops were invented—names which surely would not be known to an interpolator ignorant of Arian affairs, if he were defending the view that Liberius subscribed to the Sirmian faith of 351. As to the word *requirendum*, it is easy to suppose that, elsewhere dozing, a copyist inserted it in place of another word; especially since Baronius found “and others” in its place in his manuscripts. Salmasius explains this word otherwise, in his notes on Tertullian’s *On the Pallium*, p. 425. First, he observes that ancient scribes were accustomed to place the letter *r* in places where something was lacking for completeness of sense, something that had to be sought and investigated. An ancient and careful codex of the Greater Monastery of Tours, containing most of Hilary’s *Treatises on the Psalms*, presents examples of this on nearly every page. He then thinks that the aforesaid letter was written by some diligent reader in the margin of the book to indicate that one should investigate who those named there were and of what cities they were bishops. We, however, suspect that the note was appended because of the one name “Junior,” which seems more like an adjective than a proper name and does not occur in Baronius. Finally, he conjectures that the word *requirendum*, denoted by the marginal note, was transferred into the text by someone. Having noted these points about *requirendum*, let us return to the question at hand. If Liberius’s words are weighed, it will become plain that they refer in no way to the second Sirmian formula. He addresses his first letter to the Easterners; then he carefully reminds Ursacius and Valens, and afterward Vincentius and the Italian bishops, of letters sent to the Easterners. Whence had he such confidence in the Easterners unless he had subscribed to their faith? But at that time the faith of the Easterners was no other than the first Sirmian formula, together with the pseudo-Sardican and Antiochene formulas. Next, if he had subscribed to the second, he ought not to have said to the Easterners that he had received “your Catholic faith, which was discussed, set forth, and received at Sirmium by many of our brethren and fellow bishops.” For the second was set forth only by the Westerners Ursacius, Valens, Germinius, Potamius, and Hosius; and therefore “your” does not apply to it. Still less does “Catholic” suit it, for it scarcely left Sirmium before everyone rejected it. Nor should it have been called a faith “set forth by many brethren,” since one could scarcely devise even six authors of it. Moreover, if he received the faith set forth through the efforts of Valens and Ursacius, why did he not first strive to gain the favour of those men, who had great influence with the Emperor and were then in his court? Who also would deny that Demophilus had very often earlier attempted to bend Liberius to the Arian side? Yet earlier he could not have offered Liberius any confession of the Arian party more recent than the first Sirmian formula for subscription. We omit that the second could scarcely then have been brought to Beroea when Liberius fell. Finally, Sozomen, book IV, ch. 15, testifies that when Liberius reached Sirmium, he gave a confession in which he pronounced alien from the Church those who asserted that the Son was not like the Father in substance and in all things. [Col. 0691D] He would not have done this had he immediately before condemned the term “substance.” But, you will say, if Hilary understood Liberius to have agreed to the first Sirmian exposition, why does he now call “treachery” what he approves and excuses in *On the Synods*? We seem already to have shown in the books *On the Synods* and *Against Constantius* that Hilary never approved any Sirmian or other Eastern confession. Indeed, from his statement in *Against Constantius*, no. 24—“Whatever is besides the one faith is treachery, not faith”—it follows that even the first Sirmian formula, since it is besides the Nicene faith, is treachery. Nor should Hilary be charged with inconsistency because, having praised the same confession of faith elsewhere, he now sharply censures and reproves it. For just as those who depart from evil deserve praise, so those who fall away from good deservedly deserve blame. Indeed, when the Easterners formerly asserted that the Son came from nothing and came to be within time, but later confessed, in the Sirmian creed clarified by the decrees of Ancyra, that He was before the ages and from God’s substance, they progressed toward the true faith and in some manner became Catholic. In contrast, when Liberius, by confessing the Sirmian creed, suppressed [Col. 0692B] the holy faith of consubstantiality, he fell away from the true faith and became, in a certain sense, faithless and heretical. For by communicating with heretics and sharing the rule of belief which they maintained in a heretical sense—though he received it from them in a Catholic understanding—he shared in heresy. Catholic in faith and inner conscience, he was a heretic in communion and perhaps also in public reputation; concerning that report, Sozomen, book IV, ch. 15, should be read. In this sense Jerome, book I, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, must be understood to have said that Liberius was compelled by Fortunatianus to subscribe to heresy. This also is the point of Auxilius, book I, *On Ordinations*, ch. 25: “Who does not know that Liberius—alas, alas!—subscribed to the Arian heresy?”] “The Arian treachery is this; I have noted it, [Col. 0691A] not as an apostate.” Liberius continues: “I received it with a willing mind [679]; I contradicted in nothing; I lent assent; I follow it; it is held by me.” (“Anathema from me be pronounced upon you, Liberius, and your associates.”) (“Again anathema upon you, and a third time, Liberius the betrayer.”) [Note: [Col. 0692B] Baronius reads: “I received it, contradicting in nothing. I judged that your holiness should certainly be sought,” omitting the words inserted between them. Although in his latest edition he admits that he found those same additions in Cresconius’s collection, he entirely denies that they are Hilary’s. It will suffice for us to offer our conjectures on this point. Since in the Pithoean manuscript, after “I received,” there follows in one and the same context: “Saint Hilary pronounces anathema upon him: anathema upon you from me,” we think that the words “Saint Hilary pronounces anathema upon him” were written only in the margin of an older copy and afterwards entered the text through the work of some unskilled copyist. From this it follows: first, that interpolations of this kind are not recent; secondly, that from ancient times Hilary was believed to be the author of these additions, indeed of this entire collection. Moreover, we have already proved on apostolic authority that it was lawful for Christ’s most ardent Confessor to pronounce anathema upon a man who, though established in the highest dignity of the Church, had shamefully abandoned his Lord’s cause. But even if these additions were not unworthy of Hilary when he first learned of Liberius’s fall, it nevertheless seems foreign to him that, when he published this work after Liberius had already been corrected, he did not then erase and suppress them altogether.] I judged that your holiness should certainly be sought, because you now see clearly that in all things I agree with you. Deign, by common counsel and effort, to work so that I may now be released from exile and return to the see entrusted to me by God.

[Col. 0692A] 7. The authors of that creed. — “The perfidious creed composed at Sirmium, which Liberius calls catholic and says was explained to him by Demophilus, was drawn up by these men: Narcissus, Theodore, Basil, Eudoxius, Demophilus, Cecropius, Silvanus, Ursacius, Valens, Evagrius, [Note: In the Sirmond manuscript, as also in Baronius, Irenaeus. Evagrius, named earlier, is perhaps the same man as the bishop of the island of Mytilene, who stood on Acacius’s side at the Synod of Seleucia.] Irenaeus, Exuperantius, Terentianus, [Note: From his manuscripts Baronius printed Bustus. Among the subscriptions of the pseudo-Sardican synod one reads Bassus, bishop of Carthage.] Bassus, Gaudentius, Macedonius, [Note: The Remigian manuscript, with Sirmond, has Martius, Atticus, etc. Still more attractive is Baronius’s reading: Marcus, Aetius, Julius, Severinus; Severinus indeed subscribes, in Epiphanius, to the letter of the Synod of Ancyra, and below, Fragment XV, is numbered among those whom Germinius names at the beginning of his reply.] Marthus, Acticus, Julius, Surinus, Simplicius, and [Note: In the same manuscript: ‘and all the other juniors in whom he trusted, all heretics.’ In Baronius simply, ‘and others,’ with the rest omitted. In his appendix to the year 355, moreover, Junior appears again among those said to have subscribed against Athanasius at the Council of Milan. We have discussed sufficiently above the word *requirendum*.] Junior—(*requirendum*)—all heretics.”

[Col. 0693A] 681 Likewise Liberius [Note: Somewhat after the preceding letter to the Easterners, and thus about the beginning of 358. Baronius prints this as genuine under the year 357, no. 35. But, reconsidering his judgment in the Appendix, p. 25, he holds it spurious, fabricated by the persons who, as stated above, forged Fragment IV. Binius follows that latter opinion, nor does Labbe disagree; the grounds that moved them will shortly be examined. Yet meanwhile they must concede that our author neither suspected it to be false, nor found its style unlike the Pontiff’s other letters.] from exile, to Ursacius, Valens, and Germinius.

8. Liberius separates himself from Athanasius’s communion. — Since I know that you are sons of peace and that you also love the concord and unity of the Catholic Church, I therefore address you in this letter, most beloved lord brothers, not under compulsion of any necessity, God being witness, but for the good of peace and concord, which is to be preferred to martyrdom. [Note: Concinnius in Baronius: “my most beloved lords.”] Let your prudence therefore know that Athanasius, who was bishop of the Alexandrian church, [Note: From the Sirmond manuscript this passage is restored, though imperfectly. Earlier, from the Pithoean manuscript, it had been published as follows: “was bishop, before I came to the court of the holy emperor according to the letters of the Eastern bishops, and was separated from the communion of the Roman Church, as witness is,” etc. In Baronius, however: “was bishop before I came to the court of the holy emperor, [and I declare] according to the letters of the Eastern bishops that he has been separated from the communion of the Roman Church.” Baronius understands these words as though Liberius were saying that, before his own exile, before he arrived at the emperor’s court to which he had been summoned, he separated Athanasius from Roman communion in accordance with letters received from the Eastern bishops at the beginning of his pontificate. If this is correct, he rightly assigns this entire letter to those who fabricated the letter reported above in Fragment IV. But the reading supplied by Sirmond’s manuscript seems rather to mean that Liberius declares Athanasius to have been condemned by him before he sent to the emperor’s court either what he had written to the Easterners in his earlier letter or what they had replied concerning the same matters; and that he had already indicated this to the Roman Church. Indeed, even if Baronius’s reading is accepted, Liberius’s journey to the emperor, without prejudice to the genuineness of this letter, will mean not, as Baronius interprets it, his journey from Rome to Milan, whence he was exiled, but from Beroea, where he had been exiled, to Sirmium. For Sozomen, Book IV, chapter 15, makes it certain that Liberius, before receiving permission to return to Rome, was summoned to Sirmium, where the emperor was staying. He now testifies, therefore, that before completing this journey he condemned Athanasius in accordance with the Easterners’ letters: that is, either according to the form of judgment set down in those letters, or in compliance with the Easterners’ letters, since they had so insistently demanded this condemnation of Athanasius from him. In these matters there is no agreement with the pseudo-letter above.] was condemned by me before I sent letters of the Eastern bishops to the court of the holy emperor, and that he was separated from the communion of the Roman Church, as [Note: In Baronius, “as a witness is.” Did Liberius customarily use *testis* and *teste*, as we use *fidelis* and *fidele*? From this passage one may conjecture that Liberius wrote immediately after his defection to the Roman clergy a letter much like that which he sent to Vincentius; in it, as we have below, he earnestly asks Vincentius to inform the emperor as soon as possible of his peace with the Easterners.] all the presbyterate of the Roman Church bears witness.

[Col. 0693B] This alone was the reason why I seemed slow in sending letters concerning his name to our brothers and fellow bishops in the East: namely, that my envoys [Note: Elsewhere, with the Pithoean manuscript: “that the envoys and those whom.” Baronius’s copies are better: “that my envoys,” through whom, namely, he sent to Constantius the letter reported in the preceding fragment. Shortly afterward, “or bishops” has the same force as “and likewise the remaining bishops.”] whom I had sent from the city of Rome to the court, or the bishops who had been deported, might themselves, together with these men if possible, be recalled from exile.

[Col. 0694A] 9. He urgently asks to be sent back to Rome. — I also ask you to know that I requested brother Fortunatianus [Note: In Baronius, as in the Sirmond manuscript, the letter appears in a fuller form: “I requested him to carry my letters to the most clement emperor—letters which I wrote to the Eastern bishops, so that they might know that, together with them, I had separated myself from Athanasius’s communion. I believe that His Piety will gladly receive them for the good of peace; a copy of them I also delivered to Philagrius, the emperor’s eunuch” (or, as Sirmond has it, “I also sent [them] to Hilary, the emperor’s faithful servant. Let your charity see clearly that I have done these things with a kindly and innocent intention.
