Therefore by this letter I address and adjure you through God Almighty, and Christ Jesus his Son”—Sirmond adds “God”—“and our Lord”—Baronius alone adds “and the Holy Spirit”—“that you may deign to go to the most clement Emperor Constantius Augustus and ask that, for the good [Col. 0694D] of peace,” etc.). These words are not only confused but highly suspect as an interpolation. For what do they mean except that Liberius wrote first to the Easterners, then to the emperor, and afterward sent to the emperor through Fortunatianus the letters he had written to the Easterners? Yet above, no. 4, writing to the Easterners, he informs them that he had already given Fortunatianus letters to be carried to Emperor Constantius. By contrast, the reading which we retain from the Pithoean manuscript is clear and entirely consistent with the preceding letter.] to proceed with my letters to the most clement Emperor Constantius Augustus, to ask that, for the good of peace and concord—in which his piety always rejoices—he order me to return to the church divinely entrusted to me, so that in his time the Roman Church may endure no affliction.

You ought to know, most beloved brothers, from this letter of mine that I have peace with all of you bishops of the Catholic Church, in a fair and straightforward spirit. For you will obtain great [Note: Baronius: “You will also obtain great reward,” etc. The Sirmond manuscript: “For you will obtain great reward on the day of tribulation.”] consolation on the day of recompense if, through you, peace is restored to the Roman Church. I also wish you to let our brothers and fellow bishops Epictetus and Auxentius know that I have peace and ecclesiastical communion with them; I believe that they will gladly receive this. But whoever dissents from our peace and concord, which, God willing, has been established throughout the world, should know that he has been separated from our communion. [Note: Baronius’s copies also contain this note.] I have pronounced an anathema upon the betrayer, together with the Arians.

[Col. 0695A] Likewise Liberius from exile [Note: Immediately after the letters sent to the Easterners and, in our judgment, before he wrote to Ursacius, Valens, and Germinius. For here the order of Liberius’s letters can be established after he had fallen from his former constancy: first he informed the emperor, and at the same time the Roman clergy, through Fortunatianus, of his change of mind; then by letter he notified the Easterners that he was at peace with them and had withdrawn from Athanasius’s defense; next he informed Vincentius, and through him all the bishops of Campania, of the communion he had entered into with the Easterners; finally, while proceeding to the emperor’s court, he wrote to Valens, Ursacius, and Germinius, attempting to gain the favor both of these utterly depraved men and of Epictetus and Auxentius, men no less wicked than they. A striking example of human frailty, over which a precipice often hangs all the more perilously the higher one seems to have risen.] to Vincentius (A.D. 358).

10. He grieves that Urbicus has been taken from him. — I do not instruct but remind your holy heart, most beloved brother, that “evil conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Cor. 15:33). You know well the snares of evil men, through which I have come to this affliction; pray that the Lord may grant endurance. My most beloved son, the deacon Urbicus, whom I seemed to have as a consolation, has been taken away from me through Venerius, *agens in rebus*.

11. On what ground he asks for recall from exile. — I thought it right to inform your holiness [Note: In the Sirmond manuscript *vero* is added after *sanctitati*; in Baronius it is placed before it, followed by *et ideo*.] that I have withdrawn from that contention concerning Athanasius’s name, and have sent letters to our brothers and fellow bishops in the East concerning his name. Therefore, since, God willing, peace is [Col. 0695B] everywhere among you, may you deign to convene all the bishops of Campania, explain this to them, and, from their number and together with your letter concerning our unanimity and peace, write to the most clement emperor, so that I too may be delivered from great sorrow.

And in his own hand: “May God keep you safe, [Note: In Baronius: “most beloved lord brother.” Likewise: “written in his own hand on the same page.” Sirmond reads “on the page written through,” not “of the page written through.”] brother.” Likewise, in his own hand, written across the page: “We have peace with all the Eastern bishops, and I with you. I have been absolved before God; see to yourselves. If you wish me to perish in exile, God will be judge between me and you.”

## FRAGMENT VII (otherwise Part II)

### HERE BEGINS A COPY [Note: The authority of this letter is supported by Sozomen, Book IV, chapter 17, where he mentions the emperor’s letters to the bishops assembled at Ariminum and Seleucia, ordering them first to settle the controversies concerning the faith.] OF THE LETTER OF EMPEROR CONSTANTIUS TO THE ITALIAN BISHOPS WHO [Col. 0695C] [Note: In the editions: “assembled.” Yet “had assembled” in the manuscripts is not bad, since this is Hilary’s language, not that of the bishops writing the letter. Earlier we restored *Constantius* in place of *Constantine*, and later *Constantius* in place of *Constantine*, since the manuscript first had *Constantine* and *Constantinus*.] HAD ASSEMBLED AT THE COUNCIL OF ARIMINUM (given 27 May, A.D. 359)

Victor Constantius, greatest triumpher, ever Augustus, to the bishops.

1. Only the faith is to be discussed in the council. — Your earlier enactments, venerable fathers, maintain that the holiness of the law is upheld by ecclesiastical affairs. We have more than sufficiently perceived, from letters addressed to our prudence, that effort ought to be given to these matters; for this indeed accords with the office of bishops, and upon this foundation the salvation of all peoples far and wide is strengthened. But the matter has prompted the enactments to be set forth again. For no one will judge it superfluous to repeat what has been determined, since [Note: Elsewhere, “since by matters”; from the Sirmond manuscript this is restored as “since frequent.” Previously, in place of “to repeat,” “to examine” seemed preferable.] frequent admonition is accustomed to increase the measure of diligence.

Since this is so, let your sincerity recognize that the faith and unity must be discussed, and devote itself to ensuring that a fitting order be provided for ecclesiastical affairs. For the prosperity of all peoples everywhere will flourish, and steadfast concord will be preserved, when, with all questions of this kind wholly cut off, [Note: In the Pithoean manuscript: “lest all questions of this sort.” We would prefer “with questions concerning matters of this kind,” supplying afterward “matters,” namely, faith and unity. Thus the sense would be complete: “when, with all questions concerning such matters wholly cut off, it shall have admonished what ought to be followed.”] it shall have stirred up all to pursue such matters.

2. Not concerning the Easterners’ causes. — This matter ought not to extend the attention of the mind [Note: The word “farther” is added from the Sirmond manuscript.] too far. For reason does not permit anything concerning the Eastern bishops to be determined in your council. Therefore you must deliberate only about those matters which your gravity recognizes as belonging to you; and, when all is quickly completed, send ten men to my court by a unanimous agreement, as we informed your prudence in our previous letters (which are not extant).

For those designated will be able to answer all that the Easterners may propose to them, or to discuss the faith, so that every question may be settled with a suitable outcome and uncertainty put to rest. Since this is so, you must determine nothing against the Easterners; or, if you should wish to decide anything against them while the aforesaid persons are absent, whatever has been usurped will vanish without effect. For that decision cannot possess force to which our ordinances already now testify that strength [Col. 0696C] and authority (otherwise, “desire”) are denied.

Since this is so, in a manner befitting religious moderation you ought to accomplish what accords with the venerable bishops, so that what religion requires may be carried out, and no one may usurp what it forbids to be heard. [Note: Faber added here *ratio*, apparently led by the preceding words: “For reason does not permit anything concerning the Easterners to be determined.” But this word is absent from the manuscripts, whereas the noun *religio* is present, to which the verb *prohibet* may suitably refer. If anything were to be changed, we would gladly accept *audere* (“to dare”) in place of *audiri* (“to be heard”).] May the Divinity preserve you for many years, Fathers K. [Note: By this letter K one may suitably understand the term *carissimi*, “most beloved.”]

Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of June, in the consulship of Eusebius and Hypatius.

[Col. 0697A] Here begins [Note: The following fragment will confirm the authenticity of this document.] the Catholic definition adopted by all Catholic bishops before, terrified through worldly power, they were joined to the society of heretics, at the Council of Ariminum (A.D. 359).

3. Nothing is to be added to or taken away from the Nicene faith. — Thus we believe that all Catholics can approve: that we ought not to depart from the creed received, which in conference we have found intact among all; nor [ought we to depart] from the faith which we received through the prophets, from God the Father through Christ our Lord, with the Holy Spirit teaching, both in the Gospels and in all the apostles; so that, through the tradition of the Fathers in succession from the apostles, it has remained until now as set forth at the council held at Nicaea against the heresy which arose at that time.

We clearly believe that nothing ought to be added to all these things, nor can anything be diminished. Therefore it is resolved that nothing new be done; and that the term and reality of *substantia* (“substance”), impressed upon our minds by many holy Scriptures, should retain its firmness. The Catholic Church has always been accustomed to confess and profess this reality [Note: That is, the reality signified by the term *substantia*.] under its own name together with divine teaching. All Catholics, united in agreement upon this definition, subscribed to it.

4. In the same council, after it was determined that nothing should diminish the paternal tradition, those who opposed it were condemned by the spiritual voice of all united in agreement. This is a copy of the proceedings. [Note: Athanasius likewise inserted this copy in his work *On the Synods*, p. 879.]

Eusebius and Hypatius, consuls. [Note: Thus the Pithoean manuscript here, above, and in the following Fragment; not *coss.*] [Col. 0697C] On the twelfth day before the Kalends of August (21 July, A.D. 359).

When a synod of bishops had assembled at Ariminum, the faith had been discussed, and it had been resolved what ought to be done, Grecianus, bishop of Cagli, said:

“As was fitting [Note: In the editions, as in the manuscript, *dicunt* (“they say”). From Athanasius’s Greek version, ἔως προσῆκον ἦν (“as was fitting”), there is no doubt that *decuit* (“it was fitting”) should be read.], most beloved brothers, the Catholic synod has exercised patience, and has repeatedly shown itself a pious Church toward Ursacius and Valens, Germinius, and Gaius; [Note: Athanasius adds Auxentius to these. If he had been expressly condemned at the Synod of Ariminum, there would have been no reason for him later, while disputing against our Hilary at Milan, to boast so greatly of that council. Socrates is still less to be heard, Book II, chapter 37, where he includes not only Auxentius but Demophilus with the four named men. Demophilus’s case, as an Easterner’s, belonged to the Easterners under the emperor’s instruction quoted above. Moreover, in the following Fragment, no. 2, the council, informing the emperor of its proceedings, mentions only Valens, Ursacius, Germinius, and Gaius as condemned by it.] they have repeatedly changed what they believed, disturbed all the churches, and now try to instill their heretical mind into Christian minds. For they wish to overthrow the formulation established at Nicaea against the Arian heresy and the rest.

“They furthermore brought us a creed drawn up by themselves, which we were not permitted to receive. Indeed, they have already long been declared heretics by us, and this has been established for many days; we did not admit them to our communion, condemning them in our spoken judgment while present. Now again declare what pleases you, so that it may be confirmed by the subscription of each individual.”

All the bishops said: “It is resolved that the aforesaid [Note: In place of the doubled *SS.*, which may be interpreted as *supra scripti*, “above-written,” Athanasius’s Greek has the word προειρημένοι, “previously mentioned.”] heretics be condemned, so that the Church, unwavering in faith and truly Catholic, may remain in perpetual peace.”

686 APPENDIX [Note: What follows was first published by Nicholas Faber, not from the Pithoean codex from which he drew the preceding Fragments, but from the Dervensis codex, where it stands after the copy of the Nicene creed and immediately before the creed ascribed to St. Athanasius. As it could be published in no more suitable place, so it ought also to have been distinguished from the other Fragments bearing Hilary’s name. It is therefore now given the name of Appendix. Whether it adds nothing to the Nicene formulation, let each reader judge.]

### TO THE PRECEDING FRAGMENT

Condemnation of Arius’s blasphemy and exposition of the whole and Catholic faith which the Catholics confirmed and subscribed with their own hands in the proceedings at Ariminum.

[Col. 0698B] Although Arius’s blasphemies had previously been condemned, they lay concealed because it was not known that he had blasphemed. But God’s favor brought it about that, when we had assembled at Ariminum, his deadly heresy was brought forward again. Therefore, together with his blasphemies, we also condemn all heresies which have previously arisen against Catholic and apostolic tradition; and we anathematize them, just as they have long ago been condemned by earlier councils and in various places.

And we anathematize those who say that the Son of God is from things that do not exist, and from another [supply: substance], and is not born from God the Father as true God from true God. And if anyone says that the Father and the Son are two gods—that is, two principles [the reading *nota* is perhaps *nata*, “born”], and does not profess one Godhead of Father and Son—let him be anathema.

If anyone says that the Son of God is a creature or a made thing, let him be anathema. If anyone says that God the Father himself was born from the Virgin Mary, and calls the same one Father and Son, let him be anathema. If anyone says that the Son of God took his beginning from Mary, or that there was a time when the Son did not exist, let him be anathema. If anyone says that the Son of God was not truly and ineffably born from God the Father, but is an adopted son, let him be anathema. If anyone professes the Son of God to be either temporal or merely a human being, and not born from God the Father before all ages, let him be anathema.

If anyone says that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one person or three divided substances, and does not profess the one Godhead of the perfect Trinity, let him be anathema. If anyone says that the Son of God exists before all [Col. 0699A] ages, but not [probably *sed non*, “but not,” for *et non*] before absolutely every time, so as to assign time to him, let him be anathema. If anyone says that all created things were made not through the Word, but without him or before him, let him be anathema. And whatever other blasphemies of Arius or of anyone else may be found, we likewise anathematize them.

687 FRAGMENT VIII (otherwise Part II)

### THERE FOLLOWS THE LETTER [Note: This letter, according to Socrates, Book II, chapter 37, after Athanasius, *On the Synods*, p. 677, was first written in Latin and translated into Greek. It is found not only in Athanasius and Socrates, but also in Sozomen, Book IV, chapter 18, and Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book II, chapter 15, with notable variation—which Valesius, on the cited passage of Socrates, shows to be customary among Greek translators.] OF THE COUNCIL OF ARIMINUM TO EMPEROR CONSTANTIUS, [Note: That is, at whose court the bishops through whom this letter was sent, having been held for a long time, betrayed the true faith.] WHERE THE BISHOPS BETRAYED THE TRUE FAITH (written A.D. 359)

To the most blessed and glorious Augustus Constantius, the Synod of Ariminum.

1. The Synod of Ariminum decrees that nothing is to be innovated. — By God’s command, according to the ordinance of your Piety, we believe it was arranged [Col. 0699B] that bishops of the West should come to Ariminum from the various provinces, so that the faith might be made clear to all the Catholic Churches and heretics might be recognized. For when all of us who think rightly had assembled, it was indeed resolved that we should hold fast the faith that has endured from antiquity, which through prophets, Gospels, and apostles, through God himself and our Lord Jesus Christ—the Savior of your empire and bestower of your salvation—we have always maintained. [Note: From the preceding Fragment, no. 3, where the same thing is explained in a different order of words, one can easily supply “we received”; unless one prefers “we have always maintained the faith received,” in place of “we have always maintained.”]

For we judged it wicked to mutilate anything belonging to the holy men who sat in the Nicene council together with Constantine, of glorious memory, the father of your Piety. That formulation was made known and commended to the minds of the people, and was established against [Col. 0700A] the Arian heresy, [Note: We would prefer “thus established.” Shortly afterward the editions from the Pithoean manuscript have “cleansed.” More correctly Sirmond, from Remigius, has “conquered,” since the Greek reads καθεῃρέθησαν, not ἐκαθάρθησαν. This is illustrated by Hilary’s words, Fragment II, no. 27, where he entitles the Nicene formulation “against all heresies,” because, as the title of the Fragments themselves says, by that formulation all heresies had been suppressed and condemned.] so that heresies have thereby been defeated. If anything is taken from it, a way is opened for the poisons of heretics.

688. 2. It condemns those eager for innovation. — Therefore Ursacius and Valens at one time fell under suspicion of the same Arian heresy and were suspended from communion. They sought pardon, as their writings record, and at that time received it from the Council of Milan, at which legates of the Roman Church were also present. [Note: In A.D. 349, as was fully shown in Fragment II, although these matters are commonly referred to the Council of Milan in A.D. 347.]

[Note: Valesius considers that the following words, through “received the power of ruling the world,” have been transposed and should be placed at the beginning of this section before “Therefore Ursacius,” etc. Yet the Greek copies, though differing from this Latin in many respects, present them in no other place. Because the words “with Constantine present” were formerly joined with the preceding words, many understood them as saying that Constantine attended the Council of Milan. Since this is impossible, they indulged in various conjectures far from the truth; see Petavius’s separate dissertation on Photinus, much of which Labbe transferred into volume II of the *Councils*, p. 730. The synod deliberately emphasizes that Constantine, Constantius’s father, was witness and approver of the Nicene formulation, in order that Constantius might be ashamed to overturn what his own father had ratified—or rather, what he had received as ratified by the Fathers. Thus is refuted the opinion of those who suppose Constantine fell into heresy after his baptism. Hilary also opposes them no less, in his work *Against Constantius*, no. 27.]

With Constantine present, that formulation had been written after thorough examination; holding it, he was baptized and departed to God’s rest. We judge it wicked to mutilate anything in it, or to set aside in any respect so many holy men, confessors, and successors of martyrs who composed that formulation. [Note: From the Greek version, οἵ τινες κατὰ τὸν παλαιὸν τῆς καθολικῆς ἐκκλησίας θεσμὸν, ἅπαντα φρονοῦντες διαμεμενήκασιν· ὧν ὁ Θεὸς τὴν πίστιν etc., this passage may be restored: “since they themselves also preserved all things belonging to the earlier writers of the Catholic Church, whose faith remained until these times,” etc. That the Nicene Fathers adhered to their predecessors’ faith is clear even from Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book V, chapter 28.] For they themselves also preserved all things belonging to earlier Catholics according to all the Scriptures, and [their faith] has remained until these times, in which your Piety has received from God the Father, through God and our Lord Jesus Christ, [supply: the power] to rule the world.

[Note: From the Greek text Valesius here supplied: “But wretched men, endowed with an unhappy mind, again with rash daring proclaimed themselves heralds of impious doctrine, and now also,” etc.] Even then they were trying to overthrow what had been established by reason. For when your Piety’s letters ordered that the faith be discussed, those aforesaid disturbers of the Churches, joined by Germinius and Gaius, [Note: Greek copies expressly add Auxentius to these; he is not mentioned either in the judgment of the synod itself, described in the preceding Fragment, no. 4.] offered us some novel proposition for consideration, containing much perverse teaching. And since what they publicly offered in the council seemed unacceptable, they thought it should be written differently. It is evident that they changed these things frequently within a short time.

And lest the Churches be more frequently disturbed, it was resolved that the old, reasonable institutions be preserved. [Note: With the help of the Greek text Valesius restores this passage: “That they may be maintained ratified and inviolate. To instruct your Clemency, therefore, we sent our legates, who would announce the decision of the council through our letter. To them alone we entrusted this charge,” etc.] Therefore, to instruct your Clemency … we charged them solely that they should carry out the embassy on no other terms than that the former decrees remain most firmly established, so that your wisdom might know that if what the aforesaid Valens and Ursacius, Germinius and Gaius had promised [Note: Supply: “what had been decreed by the ancients.” Then the Greek renders “what they had promised” as ὥσπερ ἔφησαν, “as they said.”] were removed, peace could not be achieved. For greater disturbance has been introduced into every region and into the Roman Church.

3. It asks Constantius to receive its decrees and dismiss the bishops from Ariminum. — For this reason we ask your Clemency to receive and hear all our legates with gracious ears and a serene countenance; and that your Clemency permit nothing to be overthrown to the injury of the ancients, [Note: From the Sirmond manuscript we restore “permit anything,” which is absent in Pithoeus. Later Faber supplied “the ancient laws” to complete the sense, in place of “the injury of the ancients,” where the Greek has πρὸς ὕβριν τῶν τετελευτηκότων, “to the insult of the departed.”] but let those things remain which we received from our forefathers, whom we are confident were wise and did not act without the Holy Spirit of God. For by this novelty not only have believing peoples been disturbed, but unbelievers are also prevented from coming to faith.

We also pray that you order the many bishops detained at Ariminum—among whom very many are weakened by age and poverty—to return to their own provinces, lest the peoples of the Churches suffer through being deprived of their bishops. We further ask repeatedly that nothing be innovated, nothing diminished; but that the things which have remained uncorrupted in the time of your holy father Constantine and in your religious age may remain so. And may your holy prudence no longer permit us to be worn out or torn from our sees; but let the bishops, [add from the Greek: with their peoples,] always devote themselves in peace [Col. 0701C] to the prayers which they continually offer both for your safety and for your reign, and for the peace which the Divinity may grant you, in accordance with your merits, deep and everlasting.

Moreover, our legates will convey the subscriptions and names of the bishops or legates, [Note: In place of this conclusion, the Greek has: οἵ τινες καὶ ἐξ αὐτῶν τῶν θείων γραφῶν τὴν σὴν ἀναδιδάξουσι θειότητα, “who will also instruct your Divinity from the divine Scriptures themselves.”] as the same writing further informs your holy and religious prudence.

4. Proceedings concerning the legates. — “The Catholic bishops, subscribing to this letter of the whole faith, sent ten legates to the emperor. Nevertheless, the party of the heretics also sent ten legates from its own body. [Note: “But from our side,” says Sulpicius, “there were selected men who were young, poorly educated, and insufficiently cautious; whereas the Arians sent old men, shrewd and strong in talent, steeped in the lethargy of perfidy, who easily prevailed before the emperor.”] When they came to the emperor, they were received; but the Catholic legates were not received. Worn down by long delay and frightened by the emperor’s threats, [Col. 0702A] they condemned the whole faith which they had earlier defended and accepted the perfidy which they had previously condemned. You will find from the documents below that this was so.”

690 THE PROCEEDINGS IN WHICH THE BISHOPS, AS LEGATES, BETRAYED THE TRUE FAITH, BEGIN. (A.D. 359, 10 October.)

(In the consulship of Eusebius and Hypatius, on the sixth day before the Ides of October.)

5. The decrees of Ariminum are annulled. — When the bishops had taken their seats at the lodging at Nicaea—formerly called Ustodizus—in the province of Thrace: Restitutus, Gregory, Honoratus, [Note: In the Sirmond manuscript, Arthemius; in Pithoeus, Athenius. Since four bishops beyond the ten named above are listed here, the distinguished Godefridus Hermant conjectures that the first letter of the Ariminian synod was conveyed to Constantius by ten legates, and the second by four others, and that all of them met together at Nicaea, or Nicen as others call it.] Athenius, Hyginus, Justinus, Priscus, Primus, Taurinus, Lucius, Mustacius, Urbanus, Honoratus, Solutor—

Restitutus, bishop of Carthage, said: “Your prudence knows, most holy fellow priests, that when the faith was being discussed at Ariminum, contention produced such dissension that discord arose among the priests of God through the devil’s instigation. Consequently, I, Restitutus, and the party of bishops which followed [Col. 0702B] me, pronounced judgment upon our brothers Ursacius, Valens, Germinius, and Gaius, as though they were authors of wicked understanding: namely, that they should be separated from our communion.”

6. But because, being assembled face to face, we considered everything and examined everything, and found that nothing ought to displease anyone—namely, that in these matters their faith was catholic according to their own profession, to which we too all subscribed, and that they had never been heretics—and because concord in peace is of the greatest importance before God, it was resolved that, by our common consent, everything that had been transacted at Ariminum should be rendered void, and that their communion, by God’s favor, should be restored entire, and that no one should remain in dissension, which could or ought to stain them. And therefore, as I have said, since we are present, each person ought to say whether what I have set forth is correct, and to subscribe with his own hand. All the bishops said, “It is agreed,” and subscribed.

[Note: They least of all fulfilled in this matter the instructions of the synod, which, as Sulpicius testifies, had deliberately been given them: that they should in no way enter into communion with the Arians, and should reserve everything intact for the synod.]

7. “But what was the confession of faith to which they afterwards subscribed, and which Valens also carried with him to Ariminum, you will learn from what is written below. It ends.”

[Note: Hilary seems here to promise the creed proposed at Ariminum by Ursacius and Valens, immediately rejected with horror by the orthodox, and finally subscribed at Nicaea by the delegates. Unless perhaps only the following Fragment is meant, from which it appears how corrupt the confession of faith subscribed by the delegates was, since in it silence concerning substance and *homoousion* is prescribed and insisted upon in §§1–2.]

## Fragment IX (formerly Part II)

[Col. 0703A]

### Here begins a copy of the letter on faith sent to the Emperor Constantius by the faithless bishops.  
*(Written at the end of A.D. 359.)*

[Note: Again, the words “copy of the faith” seem rather to refer to the Ariminian *ecthesis* that has fallen out here than to the appended letter. Or, if this is the genuine title of the letter, this is not so much a new Fragment as a continuation of the preceding one, with which it is also joined in the Pithoean manuscript.]

[Note: We assign this letter to the end of the year 359. It was certainly not sent before the bishops detained at Ariminum had yielded to the Arians through weariness of exile. Nor did they yield until their own delegates, having fallen at Nicaea in Thrace, had returned to Ariminum. Indeed, even after their return they resisted for some time. For, according to Sulpicius, all at first recoiled from the cowardice of those delegates; and, though the delegates pleaded imperial coercion, communion was denied them, until gradually, as spirits relaxed, concession was made to the other side. Yet the delegates, as noted in the preceding Fragment, §5, accepted the formula proposed to them by the Arians on 10 October 359. From the subsequent Fragment it will be clear that these letters were conveyed by other delegates, chosen from the faction of Valens and Ursacius.]

To the lord Constantius, most deservedly glorious, most victorious Augustus: the synod of Ariminum, agreeing with the Easterners—that is, Migdonius, Megasius, Valens, Epictetus, and the rest who agreed with the heresy.

[Note: Hilary corrects the falsehood of this heading when he adds, “that is, Migdonius,” etc. For who does not see that it was written by those who adhered to the party of Valens and Ursacius? Certainly it does not suit those whose agreement had been extorted by force and threats either to profess that they had never believed otherwise, or to stigmatize as heretics those who believed otherwise than they themselves now professed under coercion, or so impiously to flatter the emperor whose violence they had experienced. But those who composed this letter inserted this in favor of those who agreed with them, so that they might now be permitted to return to their own churches; and they did so all the more willingly because their falsehood could more easily remain hidden. A second falsehood is contained in the words “agreeing with the Easterners,” since, according to Sozomen, *Hist.* IV.19, all the Easterners, with very few exceptions, clung tenaciously to retaining the term “substance.” Indeed, Hilary reports in *On Constantius* §12 that at the Synod of Seleucia 105 bishops advocated *homoiousion*, all the Egyptians except George advocated *homoousion*, and only nineteen advocated *anomoiousion*. Yet by this device Valens and Ursacius deceived the Westerners, affirming, in Sulpicius’s words, p. 259, that a present creed, framed on catholic principles and promulgated by the Easterners at the emperor’s instigation, was being rejected sacrilegiously; and adding: “What end would there be to discord, if what pleased the Easterners displeased the Westerners?” Hence the Council of Paris, below, §1, testifies that among the Easterners many of those present at Ariminum or Nicaea had been compelled, under the authority of their name, to keep silence concerning *ousia*.]

[Note: In the following Fragment “Magdonius” is written; shortly after, “Epictetus,” not “Epitectus,” should be read. Further, under the words “and the rest who agreed with the heresy” are meant either those who had always assisted the above-named supporters of heresy in advancing it, and had voluntarily agreed with the heresy which the Anomoeans defended in the East; or those who had been led astray by them through force and fraud. Hilary seems to have added these words only to exclude the latter interpretation. The following note confirms the former.]

1. **They reject the term “substance.”**—Enlightened by the writings of your Piety, we have rendered, and render, the greatest thanks to God because you have blessed us by informing us what, after the careful consideration of your Piety, we ought to do: namely, that no one should ever name in the Church of God the terms *ousia* or *homoousion*, unknown to it, since they are accustomed to cause scandal among the brethren. We rejoiced exceedingly because we recognized what we had held. O happy are we, to whom so great a good fortune has come: that, through knowledge of your Piety, the rest—who are accustomed to employ these terms concerning God and the Son of God—have been overcome and received a limit! We therefore, rendering obedience to your Clemency, because the state of truth has shone forth: since truth does not know how to be conquered, it has gained the victory, so that the name unworthy of God, which is nowhere written in the holy laws, may now be uttered by no one.

[Note: “The rest” must certainly be read. If one asks who these “rest” are, who are accustomed to employ the terms “substance” and *homoousion* concerning God and the Son of God, the whole Synod of Ariminum, except for a few Arians, must be included under that name. Thus only those now write who opposed the catholics at the beginning of the Synod of Ariminum, although they falsely claim for themselves the name of the whole synod.]

2. **They ask to be dismissed from Ariminum.**—Therefore we beseech your Piety, since we are still detained in the place where the synod was held, from which we gave our reply through our delegates, to command that we, who profess to retain the sound doctrine held among the Easterners, should now be dismissed to our peoples; so that lovers of truth may thereby be seen—those who do not change God’s name—and that we who hold catholic truth may not be detained any longer with those infected by perverse doctrine. Therefore, lord, we earnestly beseech your Piety before God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, God and Son of God: make us, who have subscribed to sound doctrine by withdrawing from the term *ousia* at your command, depart; and command that we be dismissed to our peoples, so that the Church may rejoice, which wholly refuses to change the names of God and his Son, through the authority of your power and glory. For divinity has bestowed so much upon you that it is evident that the sacrilegious terms *ousia* and *homoousion* now depart, since they are not found written in the divine Scriptures concerning God and the Son of God.

[Note: That is: we profess ourselves to retain the sound doctrine which is found among the Easterners.]

[Note: Perhaps: “so that, with the sacrilegious expressions abolished or banished.”]

3. Come to the aid, pious Emperor, of the worshippers of the Most High God; come to the aid of those who through Christ, the Son of God, pray to God the almighty Father; come to the aid of those who offer obedient ears to your judgment, who know no worship except that of God the Father through our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of his glory. And especially, lord Emperor, command us to return to our peoples, giving letters to Taurus, the most eminent prefect of the praetorium; for we too have rendered complete obedience, in the preaching of God’s name, to the Easterners and to your ordinance. In this matter, which we have always maintained, we ought now to return to our peoples. Concerning this matter, moreover, we have given letters to our Eastern bishops, so that they may know that we have always held this and remain with them in the catholic faith. May divine Piety make you always and everywhere in all things most glorious as an avenger—or perhaps, “victor”—lord most pious Emperor. It ends.

[Note: The Pithoean manuscript reads “herein,” for “in this matter,” and shortly after “to the archbishops,” not “to our fellow bishops”; these are corrected from the Sirmond manuscript.]

[Note: Thus in the Sirmond manuscript. In earlier editions, from the Pithoean manuscript: “to this accomplished praetorium.”]

[Note: The Pithoean manuscript reads “they offer all as devoted”; from this we conjectured that “they offer devoted minds” should be read, until the Sirmond manuscript supplied “they offer devoted ears.”]

## Fragment X (formerly Part I)

### Copy of the letter of the Eastern bishops, which they gave to the delegates returning from Ariminum.  
*(Written at the end of A.D. 359.)*

[Note: By whom, to whom, on what occasion, and when this letter was sent must now be briefly stated. That it was sent by the delegates of the Synod of Seleucia is evident both from its somewhat misleading opening and especially from Hilary’s appended words in §2: “Then the Eastern delegates of the synod, who were not in communion with the bishops, approach you.” Yet it may cause difficulty that it was written in the name of far more than ten persons, and that Basil, Eleusius, and Eustathius do not appear among them, although, together with Silvanus, they were, according to Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History* II.27, the chief delegates of the Synod of Seleucia. But nothing prevents us from thinking that some names have fallen out. It may also be that a letter written by the delegates, or at least by the greater part of them, was subscribed by other bishops of the same communion who had gathered from Seleucia to Constantinople, and dispatched in the name of all. Since it is addressed to the same persons whom Hilary identified as authors of the preceding letter, it is clear that the preceding letter was conveyed by those who had composed it; and that the delegates sent a second time from the Synod of Ariminum to Constantius were different from those who had conveyed to him the first letter of the same synod on the catholic side. When these later delegates arrived at Constantinople, Aetius had already been condemned; and because the Easterners insisted that those defending this heretic’s doctrine should be punished by the same sentence, they received that letter. It had been sent to them in order that they should not join Eudoxius and his associates, who had deservedly been condemned at Seleucia. It was therefore written somewhat after the preceding letter and before the delegates of the Synod of Seleucia were compelled to subscribe to the formula proposed by Eudoxius’s party—which, according to Sozomen, *Hist.* IV.23, happened on the night before the year 360.]

To the most beloved brethren Ursacius, Valens, Magdonius, Megasius, Gaius, Justinus, Optatus, Martialis, and the other delegates of the Synod of Ariminum: Silvanus, Sophronius, Neo, Herodianus, Patricius, Helpidius, Theophilus, Theodorus, Eumacius, Didymion, Ecdicius, Arsenius, Passinicus, Valentinus, Eucarpius, Leontius, Eortasius, and Macarius: greetings in the Lord.

[Note: The following Fragment, §4, adds Auxentius to these; while the title above adds Epictetus. With these additions the number of ten delegates is completed.]

[Note: The editions read “Patrinus,” but the manuscripts read “Patricius.”]

[Note: Alternatively, from the Pithoean manuscript, “Passumicus.” We prefer, with the Sirmond manuscript, “Passinicus.” In Socrates, *Hist.* III.25, Pasinicus of Zenorum is said to have acted in concert with Basil of Ancyra, Silvanus of Tarsus, Sophronius of Pompeiopolis, Leontius of Comana, and Theophilus of Castabala.]

1. **The delegates of the Synod of Seleucia instruct the Ariminian delegates how they stand toward Aetius’s supporters.**—Since we are devoted to unity and true peace, and resist heresy in accordance with the synod’s command, we thought it right to make known to you what is happening concerning the Church, lest ignorance make you partners in such great impiety. And although we suppose that you are not unaware that we, as delegates of the whole synod—numbering, that is, much more than a hundred bishops—have until now kept ourselves from entering this church, we wish you also to be informed of this, lest the heresy now ruling within the Church gain strength altogether: the heresy which has dared to deny that our Lord Jesus Christ, the true only-begotten Son of God, God from God, is like the Father. Thus you may know what blasphemous doctrines concerning the only-begotten God are both held and preached by them. We have demonstrated this very thing also to the most pious Emperor Constantius, and, moved by religious zeal, he desired that all these things should be anathematized. But a deceit is now being prepared, so that Aetius himself, the author of this heresy, rather than these impious sayings, may be condemned; and the sentence may appear to have been pronounced more against a man than against a doctrine. We therefore warn you, brethren, to reconsider these matters carefully and to make every effort that the catholic faith may remain. Besides, your Charity does not doubt that everything, as it occurs, ought to be reported to the Western churches. We pray that you, brethren, may fare well in the Lord.

[Note: Although this passage is corrupt, it is nevertheless clear that the Easterners mean that they represent the whole synod, since more than a hundred bishops stood on their side. Hilary in fact observed and recorded in *On Constantius* §12 that 120 bishops advocated *homoiousion*, but only nineteen *anomoiousion*. It could be restored thus: “And although we suppose that you are not unaware that we, being delegates of the whole synod, numbering bishops,” etc.]

[Note: Thus the Sirmond manuscript. But the editions, from the Pithoean manuscript, have: “thus what blasphemous doctrines concerning the only-begotten God are essentially preached by them.” Although the Easterners could speak of the only-begotten God “essentially” in the sense in which they say in *On Synods* §15: “And if anyone, hearing the only-begotten Son of the invisible God called like the Father, shall not say that the Son is like in essence,” etc. Moreover, that ruling heresy denied that the Son was like the Father not in public profession, but in the deeper meaning of its thought. For it had adopted the Acacian *ecthesis*, which professes that the Son is like the Father.]

2. **The recipient of these letters is badly received by his own party. The Ariminian delegates are guilty of faithlessness.**—“When these letters were received, to which the blasphemies mentioned above were also appended, an accusation is brought against the man who received them. Such was the rage of the hypocrites at their fraud being exposed that they determined upon the danger of deposition against him. What pain of convicted conscience it is to be deterred by the recognition of truth! If this book of Valens and Ursacius is not your faith, why do you not acquiesce in its condemnation? Is it not agreed by the public consent of the human race that poison is evil, the killing of an innocent person a crime, and impiety toward one’s lord a horror? But whoever does not condemn these matters when they are brought forward must necessarily profess himself a partner in their zeal; for there is no one who does not both denounce what he hates and approve what he does not denounce.

[Note: Here “to bring an accusation” has the same meaning for Hilary as “to bring a lawsuit,” just as when, in *On the Trinity* X.30, he says, “that I may not litigate concerning the rest,” meaning, “that I may not contend and bring a lawsuit concerning the rest.”]

[Note: Some refer this to the Synod of Constantinople, as though those who had previously met at Seleucia were here accused of joining the heretics at Constantinople. But from what has already been said, it is clear that this must be referred to the arrival in that city of the delegates of the Synod of Ariminum, who, coming to Constantinople after the Synod of Seleucia had concluded and condemned the heretics, nevertheless did not hesitate to join them despite being warned.]

“For after the Synod of Seleucia, when you came to Constantinople, why did you immediately join the condemned heretics? You did not defer approaching them even for a time, nor did you devote any delay to seeking advice concerning a prudent course of action. Then the Eastern delegates of the synod, not being in communion with the bishops, approach you; they inform you of all that had been done and show that the heresy too had been condemned. Ought you not at least even then to have withdrawn and reserved the course of all the disputes for judgment? But, through consciousness of some purpose of your own, I do not know what, you did not accept a sound judgment. For you immediately attach yourselves to your own party and enter into communion with your blasphemies. Nor do you even take this counsel: if shame had led some astray, that the Synod of Ariminum might be thought responsible. For you immediately betrayed your deceit in not anathematizing your own teachings.”

[Note: The Pithoean manuscript reads “ruling,” supported by §1: “lest the heresy now ruling within the Church gain strength altogether.” Yet Faber’s correction “condemned” seems not unsuitable, since immediately before it occurs: “Why did you immediately join the condemned heretics?”]

[Note: The editions, leaving a space for one or two words, read with the manuscript “to stand by.” By changing *d* to *b*, we restore the passage. Earlier, “then” might be preferable to “now”; for this is its meaning: “You should not rashly have joined the heretics when they had been condemned; but when the Easterners showed you their heresy, you ought at least then to have withdrawn from their fellowship.”]

[Note: In the Pithoean manuscript: “you diminish, nor do you at least take this counsel,” etc. Nicholas Faber’s correction should be retained. But though he thought something was missing here, the reading seems complete in this sense: even if some had at first been deceived and had continued in error somewhat from shame, they should at least have changed their counsel once they ought to have realized that their error would be imputed to the whole Synod of Ariminum. For in ancient books *extimari* frequently stands for *existimari* or *aestimari*, “to be thought” or “to be judged.”]

3. **Those who exposed their faithlessness; those who refuse to regard the Son as one of the other creatures; those who wish him to be from God; those who call him eternal; why they say that he is like according to the Scriptures.**—“For in a gathering of many persons accusing you, asking why you did not also say that the Son of God was not a creature, you replied that the holy bishops at Ariminum had not denied that Christ was a creature, but only that he was unlike the other creatures: because, when it was said that he was not created like the other works, this was not said because he was not a creation, but because he was excepted from the others; so that, though unlike the others, he nevertheless should not be something else. As though any creature were like another—an angel to a human being, a human being to a bird, a bird to a beast. If I lie in this, those who heard are witnesses. And if they too are silent, your book, most impiously defended by you, speaks with me; in it the Son is as alien to the Father, and Christ to God, as glass is to hyacinth.

[Note: Perhaps: “why you also did not say that the Son of God was not a creature,” as the appended reply seems to require.]

[Note: Supply: “this was said”; and afterwards remove the negative particle before “unlike.” Thus the sentence will be fuller and clearer: “This was not said because he is not a creation, but because he is excepted from the others; so that, although he is unlike the others, he should nevertheless be unlike in such a way that he is not something else.”]

“Then you deceived your hearers by saying that he was not from things that do not exist but from God. Was not the pretence evident even in your saying this? For according to your profession he is not from things that do not exist but from God because God’s will was the beginning of his coming into being. Surely I lie, do I not?—unless in assemblies, upon the presentation of their document, you condemned before the Easterners those who said that what he was born with was not from substance but from will. You also profess that he is eternal with the Father. You would indeed have spoken truly, had there not been an outcry against me because you had preached, before eternal times, the true God, the only-begotten God, born from God the true Father—so that his eternity with the Father might be that of angels and human souls, not in relation to things earlier, but to things future. You also said that he was like according to the Scriptures—as though not according to the Scriptures a human being were like God, and a grain of mustard, leaven, and a net like the kingdom of heaven. But it is idle to run through the falsehoods of your hypocrisy, for the works of your impiety cry out against you.”

[Note: Thus we emend it. The Pithoean manuscript had given the printed text: “because I had preached that the true only-begotten God was born true God from the true Father God.” It is plain that the formula is here refuted from which Auxentius later professed Christ to have been born before all times, true God, Son from God the true Father. Hilary exposes the poison concealed beneath these words in *Against Auxentius* §§5 and 7.]

[Note: A space had been left here to indicate that more words were missing. Yet the sentence may be regarded as complete: it warns us that the Arians attributed to Christ only that eternity proper to angels and our souls, as though he were eternal with respect not to things earlier but to things future. Thus among the Arians there was more than one way of understanding Christ’s eternity, adapted to their own heresy. Hilary had not yet fully exposed this one; but he had already set out another—by which they profess Christ to be before times—in *On the Trinity* XII.34: since times are usually reckoned from the creation of the sun and moon, “before ages and times” is understood no otherwise than in the case of angels and the devil himself. By this twofold interpretation, only those things which are proper either to angels or to ourselves are attributed to the Lord Christ, as Hilary says in *Against Auxentius* §6.]

[Note: That is, when at Sirmium, confronted by the delegates of the Synod of Ancyra, they were compelled to subscribe to the latter’s definitions, which condemn those who deny that the Son is truly and according to substance Son, or who affirm that he is Son merely according to efficacy and that the Father is Father of an essence unlike his own. See *On Synods* §§14 and 19. Further, Epiphanius, *Heresies* LXXIII, reproduces a document of the same Easterners, at the end of which, §22, is read: “If anyone says that the Son is not like the Father in all things, as a son is like a father, but like in will and unlike in substance, let him be anathema.” He testifies that Valens subscribed to this definition by name. Earlier, perhaps *conniventibus*, “with connivance,” should be read for *in conventibus*, “in assemblies.” For Hilary notes and approves, *On Synods* §63, that the Easterners used connivance in obtaining this subscription.]

4. **The nature of their crime.**—“A servant—not to say a good servant, but certainly a tolerable one—unwillingly hears an insult to his master and, if permitted, avenges it. A soldier drives away danger from his king even by exposing his own body and disregarding his life. Even dogs kept to guard a house, understanding by a kind of natural instinct, bark loudly; and whenever some breath of approaching persons touches them, they spring up wholly at the very suspicion. You heard the true Son of God and the only-begotten God denied, and you remain quiet. Why do I say that you remained quiet? You resist those who protest and join those who shout against them. Even that is too little. Weapons are also drawn from your library for the preaching of impiety, and war against God is begun with your support. Where, then, is your profession at Nicaea in Thrace, in which you said that all heresies had been condemned? But your falsehood has been brought into the light: the Sun of righteousness has disclosed to his preachers the night of your profession. For you approve these things, condemn them, and pass over to the heretics. Thus what formerly you deceived people about as a fraud, you have now exposed by a professed hatred of God in Christ.”

[Note: The words attributed to them by Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History* II.21, are: “Let all heresies, whether already condemned or recently arisen, which are contrary to this exposition of faith, be anathema.”]

[Note: Thus the Pithoean and Sirmond manuscripts. Faber nevertheless printed “to deny.” “God to be denied” would be acceptable: “you are thought to deny”; or even: “You heard … God denied; you do not resist, but remain quiet,” etc.]

[Note: Then at the Council of Milan in A.D. 349, shortly afterwards at Rome, and then at Sirmium immediately after the Synod of Ancyra in 357. At the end of this Fragment the manuscripts note: “Here ends the book of Saint Hilary from the Historical Work.”]

## Fragment XI (formerly Part II)

### Here begins the catholic faith set forth at the city of Paris by the Gallican bishops to the Eastern bishops

[Note: Nicholas Faber, without opposition to the present, observed that “the city of Paris” must be read. Blondel, *On the Primacy*, p. 127, places this council in A.D. 366; others commonly think that it was held in 362 and that Hilary attended it. Yet it is much more probable that it should be dated to 360. In this letter the Gallican bishops who had fallen at Ariminum acknowledge for the first time that they had been deceived under the false pretext of peace and unity; and they clearly indicate that up to this point they had been unaware of the proceedings of the Synods of Seleucia and Constantinople. Who could persuade himself that they began to learn these things only late in 360? Further, they state so plainly that they learned them not from Hilary’s spoken account but from letters sent by him that they imply both that he was absent from their gathering and had not yet returned from the East. Yet in 360, dismissed from Constantinople, Hilary returned to Gaul with such speed that Martin, hurrying to meet him after hearing the news, could catch up with him nowhere except at Poitiers. But to determine the date of this council more closely and establish it more persuasively, the sequence of events explained in this and the preceding Fragment must be considered. When the Easterners saw that they had achieved nothing with the delegates who had returned from Ariminum to Constantinople through the letters reported above, and indeed that they themselves, together with their adversaries’ faction, had been expelled from their sees, they immediately approached Hilary, still staying in the same city, by letter. Reporting to him what they had accomplished with the delegates of the Synod of Ariminum and how they had been scorned by them, and appending the letter containing the blasphemies of the heretics from whose fellowship they had tried to deter them, they asked him to inform the Westerners of all this as soon as possible. Hilary immediately sent to Gaul everything he had received from the Easterners, and reported what he himself thought of the proceedings of the Synod of Constantinople. Then the Gallican bishops, meeting at Paris, read Hilary’s letters and learned the Easterners’ constancy in retaining the word *ousia*. They sent them this letter, testifying that they had been deceived under the Easterners’ name into silence concerning *ousia*, and that they abhorred the faithlessness of the Ariminian delegates and others. This being so, no more time can necessarily have elapsed between the Councils of Paris and Constantinople than was needed for the Gallican bishops to be informed by Hilary of events in the East. Who would judge that this should be postponed beyond 360? Although Hilary may not have attended this council, he nevertheless presided over it in a sense, since nothing in it was accomplished except in accordance with his judgment.]

To the beloved and blessed fellow-priests, all the Eastern bishops abiding in Christ throughout the various provinces: greetings from the Gallican bishops.

[Note: Especially to those who at Seleucia and afterwards at Constantinople defended the term “substance.” Their delegates, in the preceding Fragment §1, speak in the name of the whole Synod of Seleucia; and it was on their behalf that Hilary had written to the Gauls.]

1. **The deceit of the heretics.**—With every disposition of our life and faith, we indeed give thanks to God the Father through our Lord Jesus Christ, because he has placed us in the light of the knowledge of his confession, amid prophetic and apostolic doctrines, lest, held in the darkness of worldly ignorance, we should be subject to the judgment of the world. For the one hope wholly sufficient for salvation is to confess God the almighty Father through his only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, in the Holy Spirit. Yet a no less great cause of daily thanksgiving is plainly added: that, freeing us from the error of the world, he now does not allow us to be joined to the inexpiable fellowship of heretics. For from your letters, which you sent to our beloved brother and fellow-priest Hilary, we have learned the devil’s deceit and the heretics’ schemes conspiring against the Lord’s Church, so that, divided into Eastern and Western parties, we might be deceived by mutually differing opinions. For many in number, who were present either at Ariminum or at Nicaea in Thrace, were compelled under the authority of your name into silence concerning *ousia*; a term devised long ago by you against the heresy of the Ariomaniacs, and always received by us devoutly and faithfully.

[Note: “And evangelical” must be added here, unless perhaps “prophetic doctrines” signifies the whole old Law and “apostolic” the new.]

[Note: No doubt while Hilary was still at Constantinople. For it is probable that the Easterners, when they saw themselves defeated by Eudoxius’s party and the Anomoean heresy ruling, set aside all hesitation and sought Western support. But since they had no hope of this service through the delegates of the Synod of Ariminum, whom they saw joined to their adversaries in fellowship and heretical perversity, they requested it from Hilary by letter. In those letters, as is quite clear from what follows, they primarily signified that they had been deposed by the enemies of the Son of God because they opposed their blasphemies and defended the term “substance” with the greatest constancy.]

[Note: Sozomen, *Hist.* IV.19, observes that the Westerners withdrew from the word “substance” not of their own accord but on account of the Easterners, as though all rejected it—although on the contrary all except a few asserted that the Son was like the Father in substance. For this reason they were held for a long time at Nicaea in Thrace, lest perhaps they discover the deceit.]

[Note: Namely, at the Council of Nicaea in 325, which consisted chiefly of Easterners. The Gallican bishops therefore attribute to them the invention of the word *homoousion* all the more readily in order to urge them more strongly to receive it. They then imply that they themselves have always accepted that term in a devout and catholic sense, in words adapted to Hilary’s thought; and, following his example, they do not reject likeness rightly understood. See *On Synods* §§68 and 88, and *On Constantius* §22.]

2. **The sense in which the synod embraces *homoousion*. It does not reject *homoiousion*.**—For we embraced the expression *homoousion* for the true and lawful birth from God the Father of the only-begotten God, rejecting the union itself according to Sabellius’s blasphemies and not understanding the Son to be any part of the Father. Rather, from the wholly perfect unbegotten God, the wholly perfect only-begotten God was born; and therefore we confess him to be of one *ousia*, or substance, with God the Father, lest he should seem rather to be a creature, adoption, or mere appellation. And because he is from him—as a son from a father, God from God, power from power, spirit from spirit, light from light—we do not reluctantly hear also of his likeness to God the Father, since he is the image of the invisible God (Col. 1:13). Yet we understand as worthy of the Father only that likeness which belongs to true God in relation to true God: so that not a union of divinity but unity may be understood. For union is singular, whereas unity is the fullness of the one born according to the truth of birth—especially since the Lord Jesus Christ himself professed to his disciples, saying: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). By this he signifies not only the love which is toward the Father but also the divinity which is God from God, according to: “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9); and, “If you are unwilling to believe me, at least believe my works, because the Father is in me and I am in the Father” (John 10:38).

3. **The Son before time; lesser than the Father in the form of a servant.**—Holding this faith always, therefore, we shall continue to hold it. We also reject those who say, “He was not before he was born,” not because we preach the only-begotten God as unbegotten, but because it is especially impious to place some time before the God of times, since “he was not before he was born” itself belongs to time. Yet we do not deny that the Son was obedient to the Father even unto death on the cross, according to the weakness of the human being he assumed; since he himself spoke of his ascent into heaven: “If you loved me, you would rejoice because I go to the Father; for the Father is greater than I” (John 14:28). By assuming flesh, he deigned to call us his brothers (John 20:17), although, remaining in the form of God, he willed to be in the form of a servant.

### 4. The Fallen Retract What They Did; the Authors of Error Are Condemned

Therefore, beloved, since from your letter our simplicity has learned that it was deceived by the silence concerning *ousia* [substance], and since our brother Hilary, the faithful preacher of the Lord’s name, has reported that those who returned from Ariminum to Constantinople were assembled, as the contents of your letter testify, yet that they could not be compelled to condemn such great blasphemies: we too retract all those things which, through ignorance, were wrongly done. We regard Auxentius, Ursacius, Valens, Gaius, Megasius, and Justinus as excommunicated, in accordance with your letters.

And certainly, as we have said, in accordance with the declaration of our brother Hilary, who denied that he would maintain peace with those who followed these men’s errors, we likewise condemn all the blasphemies which you appended to your letter. Above all, we reject their apostate priests, who have been introduced, through the ignorance or impiety of certain persons, into the positions of brethren most unworthily exiled. Before God we promise and confess this: whoever within Gaul thinks that he must oppose the things which we have decreed is to be removed from communion and from the episcopal see. For no one who, as formerly, either permits an opportunity for preaching by not condemning it, or resists concerning God and the majesty of Christ, the only-begotten God, otherwise than we hold concerning the meaning of *homoousion* [“of the same substance”], will be judged worthy of the sanctity of the priestly name.

Let Your Charity know that Saturninus also, who most impiously opposes salutary decrees, has already been excommunicated by all the Gallic bishops, according to the two letters of our brethren. Both his old crimes—though long concealed—and the irreligion of his new rashness, made known in his letters, have rendered him unworthy of the name of bishop.

> Here ends the Catholic faith set forth at the city of Farisea by the Gallic bishops to the Eastern bishops.

## HERE BEGINS THE LETTER OF EUSEBIUS TO GREGORY, BISHOP OF SPAIN  
*(Written about the year 360)*

To the most holy lord and brother Gregory, bishop: Eusebius, greeting in the Lord.

### 5. He Commends Gregory for Resisting Hosius and the Ariminian Defectors

I have received the letter of your sincerity, from which I have learned that, as befits a bishop and priest of God, you resisted Hosius in his transgression; and that, when many at Ariminum fell into communion with Valens, Ursacius, and the others—whom they themselves had formerly condemned after recognizing the crime of blasphemy—you withheld your assent, preserving, that is, the faith which the Nicene Fathers wrote.

We rejoice for you in this, and we rejoice for ourselves also, because you have deigned to remember us, possessing this purpose and this faith. If you continue in the same confession and retain no fellowship with hypocrites, I promise you our communion.

By whatever treatises you can, and with all the effort in your power, rebuke transgressors and reprove unbelievers, fearing nothing from secular power, as you have done; for he who is in us is greater than he who is in this world. We, your fellow priests, enduring a third exile, say what we thought should be made manifest: all the hope of the Ariomaniacs depends not upon their own strength or upon a united agreement [the manuscript reading is uncertain], but upon the protection of secular power. They do not know what is written: “Cursed are those who put their hope in man” (Jer. 17:5). But our help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth (Ps. 123:8).

We desire to persevere in sufferings, so that, according to what has been said, we may be glorified in the kingdom (Rom. 8:17). Deign to write to us what progress you have made in correcting the wicked; how many brethren you have found standing firm; and how many you yourself have corrected by exhortation. All who are with me, especially the deacon, greet you, and likewise ask that you would deign to greet, with our respect, all who faithfully adhere to your side.

702. Here ends the letter of Eusebius to Gregory, bishop of Spain.

## FRAGMENT XII  
*(Formerly Part I)*

> HERE BEGINS A COPY OF THE LETTER OF LIBERIUS, BISHOP OF THE CITY OF ROME, ADDRESSED TO THE CATHOLIC BISHOPS OF ITALY  
> *(A.D. 363, or even later)*

Liberius, to the Catholic bishops established throughout Italy: eternal greeting in the Lord.

### 1. Some Refuse Pardon to Those Who Fell at Ariminum; Liberius Judges Otherwise

Repentance effaces the fault of ignorance. This is what is to be observed from the Holy Scriptures. We read that godliness is profitable for all things, whereas bodily exercise yields to it, although it too retains fruits of usefulness. The circumstances of the present time require us to pursue godliness.

For if there are perhaps some who devote themselves to this endeavor, so as insolently to overthrow by a harsher judgment what has been wisely provided, and who judge that they may alter what has already been fortified by apostolic authority concerning godliness, when they say that no mercy should be shown to those who acted in ignorance at Ariminum—those for whom ignorance was unlawful, and who fell into the snare of error—must truth therefore be repaid?

But it seemed right to me, whose duty it is to weigh all matters with moderation, especially since all the Egyptians and Achaeans have accepted this united judgment amid many accusations, that pardon should indeed be granted to those of whom we have spoken above. But the authors must be condemned: those who, by crooked and malicious subtlety and obscurity, ensnared innocent minds, in order to draw a veil over truth, selling darkness as light and light as darkness.

### 2. The Manner in Which He Grants Forgiveness

Therefore, if anyone who had experienced within himself that pestilential, deceitful, and dark poison of the Arian doctrine should, restored by the most gentle exhortation of our discourse and recovering from the captivity of ignorance, drain it out and condemn it, and should rage more vehemently against its authors—whom he has found violent within himself—and should wholly commit himself afresh to the apostolic and Catholic faith, as far as the Council of Nicaea: through this confession, even if it seems mild and lenient to some, he shall recover what he had lost from uprightness through deceit.

But if anyone of so foolish a mind should be found—which I do not believe—who not only refuses to be converted and receive the antidote of healing, but believes that he can vindicate for himself the noxious venom and poison, he shall be overcome by reason and, having been assigned utterly to the authors of perfidy, shall be punished by the spiritual vigor of the Catholic Church.

## ANOTHER COPY OF THE LETTER OF THE BISHOPS OF ITALY

To the most beloved brethren throughout Illyricum who preserve the faith of the Fathers: the bishops of Italy, eternal greeting in the Lord.

### 3. The Italians Rescind the Decrees of Ariminum and Return to the Nicene Faith

By the grace of the divine gift, we have begun, according to the Apostle, all to think one thing and all to confess one thing. So far as Italy is concerned, it has returned to the faith of the Fathers—that is, the faith written at Nicaea—having recognized the deception which it suffered at Ariminum. We rejoice that God has also looked upon Illyricum with merciful favor, and that, having cast off the fellowship of unbelief by which it was burdened, it has begun to approve what belongs to sound judgment.

Therefore, most beloved brethren, receive our one and identical judgment, firmly established by subscription. We preserve the decrees of the Nicene deliberation against Arius and Sabellius, whose shared inheritance Photinus is condemned for holding. By the agreement of all the provinces, we rightly rescind the decrees of the Council of Ariminum, which were corrupted by the evasions of certain persons. We have also judged that copies of them should be sent, so that there might seem to be no disagreement either in maintaining the faith or in refuting the Council of Ariminum.

Whoever, therefore, desires to share in our unanimity, whoever desires to have undivided peace with us, should hasten to approve the points of our judgment and, without ambiguity, to send us his subscription to the aforementioned faith and his rescission of the Council of Ariminum. For we ask precisely what we ourselves offer by the consensus of many of these provinces.

Moreover, it is clear that the authors of the Arian or Aetian heresy—Valens, Ursacius, and their remaining associates—are not now being condemned because this has begun to be made manifest in Illyricum, but were condemned long ago.

Here ends.

## FRAGMENT XIII  
*(Formerly Part II)*

## HERE BEGINS THE LETTER OF BISHOP GERMINIUS AGAINST THE ARIANS WHO HAD ALREADY SUBSCRIBED AT THE COUNCIL OF ARIMINUM, KNOWING THAT THEY HAD DONE WRONG  
*(Published about A.D. 365)*

I, Germinius, bishop, believe and profess that there is one true God, the Father, eternal and omnipotent; and Christ, his only Son and our Lord God: the true Son of God from the true God the Father, begotten before all things; like the Father in divinity, love, majesty, power, glory, life, wisdom, and knowledge in every respect, as one perfect begotten from the Perfect.

I also profess the assumption of humanity from the Virgin Mary, as the prophets foretold would occur and as the words of the Gospels and Apostles teach to have been fulfilled. We accept, believe, and profess his sufferings, death, resurrection, and ascension into heaven; and that at the end of the world he will descend from heaven to judge the living and the dead and to render to each according to his works.

And we believe in the Holy Spirit, that is, the Paraclete, who has been given to us by God the Father through the Son.

Here ends.

## FRAGMENT XIV  
*(Formerly Part I)*

## HERE BEGINS A COPY OF THE LETTER OF VALENS, URSACIUS, AND OTHERS TO GERMINIUS  
*(Written in A.D. 366)*

To the most religious lord and brother Germinius: Valens, Ursacius, Gaius, and Paul, greeting.

### 1. Germinius Is Accused of Defending *Homoiousion*

Since concern for hope and salvation rests upon us, those who are concerned ought rather to be commended than to endure any rebuke. Now salvation and hope principally consist in the Catholic faith. Therefore, although, when Your Holiness was admonished at a meeting by our lords, brethren, and fellow bishops Valens and Paul, you were unwilling to answer concerning that which rumor asserts about you, most religious lord; nevertheless, because in your letter you testified that you persevere in the same love and are prepared to show that you preserve inviolate affection toward us, we, having assembled together at Singidunum, remind Your Holiness again by this letter to deign to write back to us once more, with every ground of ambiguity excluded.

It is openly asked that you state whether, as you have already professed, you will not depart from the Catholic faith which was expounded and confirmed by the holy Council at Ariminum and to which all the bishops of the East also consented. This is what was prescribed in it: “We say that the Son is like the Father according to the Scriptures”—not according to substance, nor “in every respect,” but simply. For if this exposition is altered, the formerly faithless assertion of Basil—on account of which a synod was held, and in which it was rightly condemned—will plainly be restored.

### 2. His Retraction Is Demanded

Therefore deign clearly to declare in your letter the point under inquiry: that you have not said, do not say, and will not say that the Son is like the Father in every respect except unbegottenness. Otherwise, what the bearers of the letter, Jovian the deacon and Martyrius the subdeacon, asserted in their verbal plea before my aforesaid lords, brethren, and fellow bishops Valens and Paul—namely, that you profess the Son to be like the Father in every respect—may appear more credible.

For if you make known in writing that you think thus, as we hope, the complaint made against our brethren and fellow bishops Palladius and Gaius by certain of your clerics, concerning an injury, will fall under your judgment, although you were unwilling to investigate it, as you were admonished at the first meeting; they, of course, must answer for their rashness. We have sent these matters to Your Charity through Secundianus the presbyter, Pullentius the reader, and Candidianus the exorcist, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of January [18 December], in the consulship of the most noble Gratian and Dagalaifus [A.D. 366], retaining a copy with ourselves.

## FRAGMENT XV  
*(Formerly Part I)*

## HERE BEGINS THE REPLY OF GERMINIUS TO RUFIANUS, PALLADIUS, AND THE OTHERS  
*(A.D. 367)*

To the most religious lords and brethren Rufianus, Palladius, Severinus, Nicha, Heliodorus, Romulus, Mucianus, and Stercorius: Germinius, greeting in the Lord.

### 1. That the Son Is Like the Father in Every Respect Is Taught Both by Tradition and by Scripture

From the report of Vitalis, *vir clarissimus* [man of senatorial rank], serving in the office of the exalted prefecture, we learned that Your Holinesses desire that it be plainly explained to you what it is in our faith that displeases Valens, Ursacius, Gaius, and Paul. I judged it necessary to disclose this to Your Holinesses by this letter, and to state that which I trust has been in you yourselves from the beginning.

What we received as handed down from the Fathers, what we learned once for all from the divine Scriptures, and what we teach daily, is this: that Christ, the Son of God and our Lord, is like the Father in every respect, except that he is not unbegotten; God from God, light from light, power from power, whole from whole, perfect from perfect; begotten before the ages and before all things that can be understood or spoken. No one knows his birth except the Father alone, as the Son himself declares: “No one knows the Son except the Father; nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son wills to reveal him” (Matt. 11:27).

Through him all things were made, and without him nothing was made, according to the divine words of our Savior himself, the Son, who says: “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John 5:18); and again: “Whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does” (ibid. 5:19); and again: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30); and again: “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9); and again: “As the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son also to have life in himself” (John 5:26); and again: “As the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he wills” (ibid. 5:21); and again: “Believe in God; believe also in me” (John 14:1); and again: “For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son, that all may honor the Son as they honor the Father” (John 5:22–23).

And again, when the Father said: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26), he did not say, “in your image,” or “in my image,” lest he demonstrate any unlikeness in the divinity of his Son. Rather, he joined the words, “in our image and likeness,” in order to show that his Son is God like himself in every respect.

Again, the Evangelist says: “We saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1:14). And the Apostle says to the Corinthians: “In whom the god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers, so that they should not shine with the illumination of the Gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God” (2 Cor. 4:4). Again the same Apostle: “And he transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love, in whom we have redemption and remission of sins, who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation” (Col. 1:13 ff.).

Again the same Apostle: “Have this mind in yourselves which was also in Christ Jesus, who, though he was in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as plunder, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, having become in the likeness of human beings” (Phil. 2:5 ff.).
