Who does not understand that, just as according to the form of a servant our flesh was real in Christ, so also in the form of God the Father’s divinity is real in the Son?

And again: “See that no one deceives you through philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elements of this world, and not according to Christ, because in him all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Col. 2:8). If, then, all the fullness of divinity dwells in Christ, he is no longer partly like and partly unlike, as those now assert who, in pursuit of their contentious desire, have turned backward and separated themselves from us.

### 2. How the Contrary Texts Are to Be Explained

For what they think they bring forward as something weighty from the divine Scriptures—when they call Christ a thing made and a creature—we, conversely, according to the Scriptures call him the way, the door, the stone of stumbling, the rock of offense, the foundation, the arm, the hand, wisdom, the Word, the lamb, the sheep, the shepherd, the priest, the vine, the day, and other such things. But we understand and say all these things in such a way as to understand them as powers and operations of the Son of God, not so as to compare his divine birth from the Father with names of this sort. For all things were made from nothing through the Son; but the Son was not made from nothing, but was begotten from God the Father.

### Editorial Notes and Apparatus

**[Col. 0712C.]** From comparison with the preceding Fragment we had emended this passage thus; and we found that Hermant and Sirmond agreed with us [Col. 0712D]. The former had previously preferred *impiety* to *piety*, and Sirmond’s manuscript supports this. Yet it is more fitting for bishops that, where it was said in plain speech that they had been convened, they should, out of honor and reverence for the priesthood, say that “their piety had been convened.” The passage will thus become clear: “since our brother Hilary also, the faithful preacher of the Lord’s name, has reported that the piety of those who returned from Ariminum to Constantinople had been convened (more plainly, that you had assembled), as the contents of your letter testify (reported in the following Fragment, and sent to us together with Hilary’s letter), yet that he could not compel them to condemn such great blasphemies (which, as Hilary observes above, were appended to the letters of the Easterners).”

**[Col. 0712D.]** Auxentius, Ursacius, Valens, Gaius, Megasius, and Justinus were delegates of the Synod of Ariminum, as is stated at the beginning of the preceding Fragment.

**[Col. 0712D.]** That is, by the Constantinopolitan synod of the year 360.

**[Col. 0712D.]** Perhaps: “permitting the preaching of *anomoios* [unlike] by not condemning it”?

**[Col. 0713C.]** Hilary writes in express terms, in *To Constantius*, no. 2, that Saturninus was excommunicated by the Gallican bishops after the Council of Milan of 355. They could have confirmed this again in other letters either after the Council of Béziers of 356, from which Hilary was driven into exile by Saturninus’ faction, or when the Gallic bishops condemned the Sirmian blasphemy, whose acceptance Saturninus was striving for with every effort. Hilary refers to this in *On the Synods*, no. 3: “You await the glorious triumph of holy and unchangeable perseverance, by not yielding to Saturninus’ threats, powers, and wars,” etc.

**[Col. 0713C.]** In the Pithoean manuscript, for brevity’s sake, *Span.* was written; from the index of that same codex we have restored the full word. Learned men understand Gregory here to be the man commonly called the Baetican and bishop of the city of Elibera, who later adhered to the Luciferian schism and deserved the highest praise from Faustinus and Marcellinus. It is clear that this letter was written after the Synod of Ariminum, but [Col. 0713D] while Eusebius was still in exile and, very probably, before he had learned either of Gregory’s schism or of Hosius’ death. If one adds the place which it occupies in the manuscript, immediately after the Parisian synod, according, unless we are mistaken, to Hilary’s arrangement, one will not deny that it was written at about the same time. At that time all lovers of fairness were exerting themselves with the greatest zeal to remedy the scandal of Ariminum.

**[Col. 0713D.]** In Sirmond’s manuscript, “anyone.” Perhaps “useful” or “pious.”

**[Col. 0713D.]** Thus Sirmond’s manuscript; elsewhere, from Pithoeus, “you will handle [it].”

**[Col. 0713D.]** Eusebius’ own letter to his Vercellian flock establishes that he was first banished to Scythopolis in Palestine. Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, under “Eusebius of Vercelli,” testifies that he was then sent from Scythopolis to Cappadocia. Finally, Rufinus, *Ecclesiastical History*, I.27, relates that he was deported with Lucifer to regions near Egypt; and certainly, according to the testimony both of Socrates, III.4, and of Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, III.5 [Col. 0714C], he was an exile in the Upper Thebaid adjoining Egypt when he returned from exile.

**[Col. 0714C.]** The printed editions have *limito*; the manuscripts have *linito*. Might it not be “not in sweet and united agreement”? Faber would prefer, “not in their own strength or united agreement.” Related is what Eusebius again writes of the Arians in Baronius, under the year 356, no. 100: “For this reason they have received human help, because they do not have divine help; if they had it, they would never subjugate to themselves by earthly power the souls of the innocent.”

**[Col. 0714C.]** Eusebius closes another letter in Baronius, under the year 356, no. 102, in this way: “Our brethren who are with me greet you—the presbyters and deacons, and also all our people—who together with me earnestly ask that, remembering us, you may deign to greet all yours with your courtesy.” Hence arises the suspicion that here too, in place of “especially the deacon,” one should read “the presbyters and deacons.”

**[Col. 0714C.]** Godfrey Hermant, *Life of St. Athanasius*, X.6, judges that this letter is mentioned by Pope Siricius when, replying to Himerius of Tarragona, who had written that some of the brethren were baptizing again those baptized by impious Arians who were hastening to the Catholic faith, he writes that this is not permitted, since the Apostle forbids it and the canons oppose it, and since general decrees sent to the provinces after the annulment of the Council of Ariminum by my predecessor Liberius of revered memory prohibit it. Yet this whole letter concerns not those baptized by Arians, but the reception of those who at Ariminum had defected to the Arian party. One might more plausibly maintain that the author of the *Life of Eusebius of Vercelli* referred to this same letter where he writes that the decrees of the Alexandrian synod were approved by Pope Liberius. Further, since Liberius here complains of certain persons who attempt to overthrow the decree of godliness, fortified by apostolic authority, there is no slight indication that he had already approved in other letters the decisions of the Alexandrian synod. We therefore think that this letter was written no earlier than 363. Certainly the sequence of events seems to have been this, in favor of those who had fallen at Ariminum [Col. 0715C]: first, synods held at Alexandria in 362 and then in Achaia; then the Roman pontiff’s confirmation of what they had decreed; and then the attempt by certain persons (who, unless Luciferians?) to annul as too mild and lax what he had confirmed. To prevent their schism and perverse opinion from spreading, Liberius wrote this letter in turn; it appears to have furnished the occasion for the following one.

**[Col. 0715C.]** Having long and attentively examined and reconsidered this passage, and compared it with the history of events, we perceived that, with a few changes, it could be restored as follows: “For if there are perhaps some who make it their endeavor (namely, the matter) insolently to destroy by a harsher judgment what has been provided by reason, they may suppose that they can invalidate what has already been fortified by apostolic authority concerning godliness, contending that no mercy should be shown to those who acted in ignorance (or, erred) at Ariminum. Was it unlawful for them not to know, so that they fell into the snare of error? Must severity of discipline therefore be rendered to them? But it seemed right to me, whose duty it is to weigh all things moderately, especially since all the Egyptians and Achaeans have accepted this united judgment, that pardon should indeed be granted to those of whom we have spoken above, who, as was said above, had fallen into the snare of error in such a way that, with the conscience of faith unharmed, they consented to heretics.”

**[Col. 0715D.]** We have already interpreted this as referring to the synod in Achaia held shortly after the Alexandrian one. Athanasius refers to it when, in volume II, p. 40, questioned by Rufinianus what should be thought of those who had indeed been compelled by necessity but had not been altogether ruined and had strayed from the faith, he answers that synods on this matter had been held, first at Alexandria and then by those who dwell in Greece, etc.

**[Col. 0715D.]** In the Pithoean manuscript, *benissima*, perhaps for *lenissima* [most gentle]. Shortly afterwards Sirmond’s manuscript has *latebrosum* [hidden, lurking], not *tenebrosum* [dark]. The sentence is again confused and disordered here, and could more clearly be constructed thus [Col. 0716C]: “Therefore, if anyone had experienced within himself that deceitful and lurking pestilential poison of Arian doctrine, let him, now restored by the most gentle exhortation of our discourse and recovering from the captivity of ignorance, drain it out and condemn it, and more vehemently,” etc.

**[Col. 0716C.]** Perhaps: “but rather believes that he can vindicate for himself the venom and poison; he shall both be overcome by reason and assigned to the authors of perfidy,” etc. The conclusion of the same letter of Liberius addressed to the Easterners in Socrates, IV.12, is not very dissimilar.

**[Col. 0716C.]** This letter is not to be separated from the preceding one. The particle *item* [likewise] indicates that Hilary joined and continued it to that letter. Some think it was written immediately after the Illyrian synod of 365. But all must agree that the Italians, through the efforts of our Hilary, Eusebius of Vercelli, and others, had annulled the decrees of the Council of Ariminum before 365 [Col. 0716D]. Nor did they long or greatly shrink from revoking what they had accepted unwillingly and under deception. Thus Liberius, in his reply in Socrates, IV.12, to the Easterners gathered at Lampsacus, before the Illyrian synod had been held, writes that all the blasphemies of the Council of Ariminum had been condemned with anathema by those very persons who then seemed to have been deceived through fraud, and that all had united in heart in the Nicene faith. Therefore, if the Italians here for the first time declare the decrees of the Council of Ariminum invalid, this must without doubt be referred to 363 or 364. Perhaps, immediately after the preceding letter of Liberius was delivered to them, they assembled and wrote this one with the fullest agreement.

**[Col. 0716D.]** A verb seems to be missing here, and shortly afterward the particle *cum* [when] seems superfluous before “the faith of the Fathers.”

**[Col. 0717C.]** A verb is supplied from Sirmond’s manuscript. Then the Pithoean manuscript has *condescensio* [condescension].

**[Col. 0717C.]** Elsewhere, from the manuscript, “consent.” It is clear from the preceding words, “we rightly rescind by the consensus of all the provinces,” that *consensu* [by consensus] should be read.

**[Col. 0717C.]** No other ancient records report Germinius’ repentance and his separation from Valens and Ursacius. Hilary himself, in the *Treatise against Auxentius*, written in 364, still joins him with the supporters of the Arian heresy. This profession of Germinius must therefore be assigned to the time when, as delegates of the Synod of Lampsacus were travelling through the West, the state of Arian affairs was entirely changed. This is confirmed by the following letter, dated in 366; there is no doubt that Valens and Ursacius wrote it as soon as they heard that their allies, formerly most closely bound to them, had changed, in order to recall him to their own side.

**[Col. 0717D.]** In the archetypal Pithoean manuscript a small space was left here, which Nicholas Faber filled with the relative pronoun *qui* [who]. We suspect that something else is required. For this letter is rather directed against those who then did not wish to revoke what they had wrongly subscribed at the Council of Ariminum. It may also be regarded as written against those who, at the Sirmian conference of 358, were compelled to retract what they had shortly before done wrongly in that same city [Col. 0718C]. Indeed, the appended confession of faith is opposed to the blasphemy which Hosius was compelled to ratify by his subscription, as we have already observed at p. 460 (col. 482 of our edition), note i.

**[Col. 0718C.]** Paul and Valens had scarcely learned through Jovian the deacon and Martyrius the subdeacon that the confession of faith issued by Germinius—the one contained in the preceding Fragment—had been published, when they confronted him concerning it. But, having received no answer on the matters about which they were most inquisitive [Col. 0718D], they gathered again at Singidunum with others and themselves wrote this letter.

**[Col. 0718D.]** The manuscript reads *contentione* [contention]. That *conventione* [meeting] should be read is clear from the final words, “as you were admonished at the first meeting.” The printed editions from Pithoeus read “to all our brethren and our fellow bishops”; they are corrected from Sirmond’s manuscript, from which we shortly afterward restore *jactitat* [rumor asserts] for *latitat* [lurks]. The sentence in fuller form would be: “when, at a meeting held by our lords . . . Valens and Paul, Your Holiness had been admonished, you were unwilling,” etc.

**[Col. 0718D.]** Nicholas Faber prefers, “or simply.”

**[Col. 0718D.]** Undoubtedly Basil of Ancyra, through whose chief agency it was first defined at Ancyra that the Son was like the Father in substance, and later at Sirmium that he was like him in every respect. This assertion was condemned by the Arians gathered at Constantinople in 360.

**[Col. 0719D.]** In Sirmond’s manuscript, “they do not belong to him, that is.”

**[Col. 0719D.]** This is not a reply to the preceding letter, which bears the names of Valens, Ursacius, Gaius, and Paul, not Rufianus, Palladius, etc., and which was delivered not through Vitalis but through Secundianus, Pullentius, and Candidianus. Nevertheless, it must be granted that the former supplied the occasion for this one: those who above testified that they retained a copy of their letter subsequently made it public. Upon obtaining it, Rufianus, Palladius [Col. 0720D], Severinus, and their associates wished to learn from Germinius himself what, in his faith, displeased Ursacius, Valens, Gaius, and Paul. He satisfies them by this reply. It must consequently have been sent somewhat after the aforesaid letter, that is, not long after the beginning of 367.

**[Col. 0720D.]** The editions from the Pithoean manuscript read *nunc* [now]; from Sirmond’s manuscript we restore *v. c.*, that is, *vir clarissimus* [man of senatorial rank]. A similar error from the same Sirmond manuscript was already corrected in Fragment IX, no. 3.

### 3. The Inconsistency of Valens, and the Occasion of the Creed Published by Mark of Arethusa

But I am astonished that the aforesaid Valens has either forgotten, or at least deceitfully conceals, what was formerly done and determined. For under the Emperor Constantius, of blessed memory, when disagreement concerning the faith had begun among certain persons, in the presence of that emperor himself, with George, bishop of the Church of Alexandria, Pancratius of Pelusium, Basil, then bishop of Ancyra, Valens himself and Ursacius also being present, together with my insignificance, after a disputation concerning the faith had been held until nightfall and brought to a definite rule, we all chose Mark to dictate the faith, in which faith it was thus written: “The Son is like the Father in all things, as the holy Scriptures say and teach.” We all agreed to this whole profession, 709 and subscribed it with our own hands. But if now some spirit of this world suggests anything else, we cannot yet know this openly. For as we have professed from the Scriptures that the Son is in all things like the Father, except in being unbegotten, let them too explain from the Scriptures in what respect he is like and in what respect unlike.

> [Note: At [Col. 0721A] we supply the word “Pancratius,” previously absent, from Socrates, book II, chapter 29.]
>
> [Note: We had judged that this was to be read thus, not as formerly, “and in that perversity,” when the Sirmond manuscript confirmed our judgment.]
>
> [Note: It is clear that the text must be emended thus, although previously the reading “expelled” prevailed. What this faith dictated by Mark was, where, when, and on what occasion it was published, must now be discussed briefly. It is readily gathered from the words of Socrates, book II, chapters 20 and 30, that it was published at Sirmium, although there, by confusing the three councils of Sirmium, he mixes much falsehood with truth. For although he correctly writes that a synod was held at Sirmium against Photinus in the year 351, it is false when he says that George, bishop of Alexandria, attended it; for George was appointed over that city only in the year 356. Further, although it is consistent with the truth that he mentions Basil of Ancyra having disputed most vigorously in that Sirmian gathering at which George of Alexandria was present, yet one must not concede to him that Basil then had any contest with Photinus, since Germinius had succeeded Photinus, who had long before been deposed.
>
> Socrates had also correctly heard that the formula of faith in the aforesaid gathering was dictated by Mark of Arethusa; but he incorrectly referred this to the creed written against Photinus, [Col. 0721C] in which that principal decree is nowhere found, namely, that the Son is like the Father in all things. Now everyone agrees that the assembly in question was held after the Synod of Ancyra in the year 358. Nor should it be less certain that nothing concerning Photinus was dealt with there, but that Basil’s entire disputation was directed against the authors and supporters of the Sirmian blasphemy.
>
> From the book *On the Synods* it is certain that Basil and the other Easterners, hastening from Ancyra to Sirmium in the year 358, compelled Valens and his associates there to subscribe to the faith set before them and to condemn what they had done shortly before. No one will deny that this occurred amid great contention between the parties. Nor will anyone deny that Basil and his companions, having assembled at Ancyra before Easter, could have reached Sirmium before Pentecost. Therefore, what is found in Epiphanius, *Heresies* LXXIII, §22, concerning Valens’s subscription on the night as Pentecost was beginning to dawn, may fittingly be referred to that forced subscription which the envoys of the Synod of Ancyra wrested from Valens and his companions at Sirmium.
>
> If this is so, Germinius here speaks of the formula issued in the year 358. For Epiphanius likewise reports that, on the night of dawning Pentecost, the creed was subscribed in which the Son is defined as like the Father in all things. Other considerations besides support this opinion. Yet more considerations favour the judgment of Nicholas Faber, who thinks that Germinius refers to the formula published at Sirmium, with the emperor present, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June, when Eusebius and Hypatius were consuls, and inserted by Athanasius, *On the Synods*, p. 875. First, the day noted by Epiphanius agrees with it. For in the consulship of Eusebius and Hypatius—that is, in the year 359—the night of Pentecost fell on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June. Further, when Epiphanius writes that Valens wished to possess a copy of the profession published there, [Col. 0722A] in order to bring it to the Synod of Rimini, he signifies that the Council of Rimini was then imminent. And this very formula, published in the consulship of Eusebius and Hypatius, was proposed by Valens and his companions to the Synod of Rimini. Finally, in it one reads that the Son is like the Father in all things, as the holy Scriptures say and teach.
>
> [Col. 0722B] But since in that same formula silence concerning substance is also decreed, it is difficult to understand how Basil could have consented to this definition. One could indeed reply that, since controversy had arisen between Valens and Basil on this point—Valens wishing silence concerning substance, Basil that the Son be like the Father in all things—Mark settled it in such a way that each found what he wished in one and the same exposition of faith. But in the passage cited from Epiphanius it is clear that Basil did not even then consent that the term “substance” should be omitted; as the proceedings of the Synod of Seleucia show, he afterwards steadfastly retained it. Moreover, who would believe that the term was suppressed by Mark of Arethusa, who, with the other Easterners, adhered to the first Antiochene formula, in which, as Sozomen notes, book IV, chapter 16, substance was affirmed?
>
> Although Sozomen is not sufficiently consistent with himself when, in book IV, chapter 16, he implies that the leaders of the Anomoeans alone were authors of the formula issued at Sirmium in 359; and yet in chapter 22 he expressly [Col. 0722C] testifies that those who at the Synod of Seleucia thought that the term “substance” should be removed pretended to follow the formula of faith which Mark had shortly before composed at Sirmium, and which had then been accepted both by the other bishops then at court and by Basil, bishop of Ancyra.
>
> Regarding the Sirmian formulas, it remains to ask which was suppressed by an edict of Constantius. Many, with Socrates, book II, chapter 30, and Sozomen, book IV, chapter 6, think this should be referred to the second formula. I should like to ask them when they think its authors laboured to snatch its copies from everyone’s hands. Was it immediately after it was published? But it was also afterwards sent into Gaul. Was it after Ursacius and Valens had been compelled to subscribe to the decrees of the Synod of Ancyra? Yet Hilary certainly would not have passed this over in silence in his book *On the Synods*, which he composed both after the publication of this formula and after that forced subscription of Ursacius and Valens. Nor will they say that this was done at the time of the Council of Rimini, when Valens and his companions were plainly intending to restore and [Col. 0722D] confirm the doctrine contained in it.
>
> More correctly, therefore, following Athanasius, *On the Synods*, p. 905, one will say that Valens and his associates, when the third formula was proposed to the Council of Rimini and all mocked it because of the consuls named in it, prevailed upon the emperor to allow them, by seizing the copies, to remove the source from which they had been overwhelmed by every disgrace and shame. Therefore, after the names of the consuls had been removed, as also the words “in all things,” which they had unwillingly and evasively accepted at Sirmium for the time being, though greatly inconvenient to them, they arranged for the same formula to be subscribed at Nike in Thrace, at Rimini, and at Seleucia. Sozomen, book IV, chapter 6, supports this view in that he does not say that the authors of the Sirmian formula sought to suppress it altogether, but that they accepted it for amendment. This applies to the third formula, not to the second.]

### 4.

And therefore, most beloved brothers, I have sent this profession boldly and without delay to the conscience of your love through Cyriacus, an official, the first opportunity that has presented itself after Carinius the deacon whom I sent to you: 710 so that through your most watchful devotion also it may be made known before God to the whole brotherhood, lest anyone, through ignorance, be entangled in the snares of the deceitful devil. It is now for your unanimity to write back to me what the Holy Spirit suggests to you. Moreover, I inform Your Charity that, because my hand was painful, I could not subscribe this letter; but I ordered our brothers and fellow presbyters Innocentius, Octavius, and Catulus to subscribe it.

[Col. 0723]

711 712 **FRAGMENTS FROM OTHER WORKS OF SAINT HILARY PRESERVED IN ANCIENT MONUMENTS.** (C, S)*

[Col. 0723B] From the treatises on Job.

> [Note: Augustine cites this fragment and, in a kind of preface, explains it thus in book II *Against Julian*, chapter 8, §27: “But in a certain homily on the book of holy Job, observe what he says: how he asserts that the devil’s unceasing warfare against us arises from this, that he stirs against us the evils which are in us. He wishes to teach that this occurs for our benefit, namely, through divine mercy turning the devil’s malice toward our cleansing. ‘For so great,’ etc.”]

#### I.

For God’s goodness toward us is so great and so wonderful in mercy that, through him by whom, in Adam’s offence, we lost the dignity of that first and blessed creation, we may again deserve to obtain what we lost. For then the devil did harm through envy; but now, while he strives to harm, he is conquered. Through the weakness of our flesh he deploys every missile of his power: when he inflames us to lust, entices us to drunkenness, provokes us to hatreds, summons us to greed, trains us for slaughter, and exasperates us to curses. But when, through firmness of mind, the creeping incitements of all these things are restrained, we are cleansed from sin by the glory of this victory. For it was thus said: “Or how shall one born of a woman be cleansed?” (Job 25:4). For if there is no enemy present, [Col. 0723C] there will be no war; and when war ceases, victory will be lacking. But unless victory over the vices colliding against us has been attained, there will be no cleansing at all from vices. For when the pirate of our body has been conquered by these ambushes, we are purified by the contest of the passions struggling against us. Therefore, remembering and recognizing that our very bodies are the material of all vices, through which, polluted and defiled, we possess nothing clean and nothing innocent within ourselves, let us rejoice that we have an enemy in whose struggle we fight, as it were, in the warfare of our own conflict.

Likewise.

> [Note: It is clear that this second fragment was excerpted from the same homilies on Job. Pelagius was the first to cite it under Hilary’s name without naming the work; Augustine afterwards mentioned and explained it in *On Nature and Grace*, chapter 62.]

#### II.

What writings of Job had he read, that he should keep himself from [Col. 0724B] every evil thing, because he worshipped God with the mind alone, unmingled with vices? But to worship God is the proper office of righteousness.

From the Preface to the Exposition of the Gospel according to Matthew.

> [Note: We owe this fragment and the following one to Cassian, who inserted them in book VII, chapter 24, of *On the Incarnation*—would that he had quoted them somewhat more fully.]

#### III.

For it was first necessary for us that the only-begotten God should be born as man for our sake—become that which he was not then.

Likewise, from the same work.

#### IV.

Then, thirdly, it was fitting that, because God born as man in the world, etc.

From the exposition of the Epistle to Timothy.

> [Note: Although this title identifies a hitherto unheard-of work of Hilary, the Council of Split, chapter 12, attributes the following words in this manner: “Therefore Saint Hilary, in the exposition of the Epistle to Timothy, speaks thus: ‘For when,’ etc.” That these words are our Hilary’s, I think no one who is not wholly unacquainted with his writings will doubt; nor anyone who compares them with his other words in book X of *On the Trinity*, §66. Whether, however, he expounded the whole Epistle to Timothy may reasonably be doubted.]

#### V.

For when Scripture says, “the man Christ” [Col. 0724C] (1 Tim. 2:5), and when it says, “Christ died” (Rom. 8:34), and when it says, “the Word became flesh” (John 1:14), the wording must not be stripped of its proper explanations through the reader’s deceit. For where there is “the man Christ,” “Mediator between God and men” comes first, so that one may subsist from both, God and man, and may stand as mediator between man and God by the confession in himself of both natures. But where there is “Christ died,” there follows, “who rose again, who is at the right hand of God.” In his death is the weakness of our flesh; in his resurrection, his power; in his session with God, his dignity.

713 From the book addressed to the Emperor Constantius.

> [Note: Arnobius, book II *On the Conflict with Serapion*, testifies that these words of Hilary were cited by Pope Celestine I in a council. There he also attributes them as follows: [Col. 0725B] “Hilary also, a man of keen intellect, writing to the Emperor Constantius concerning the incarnation of the Lord, says thus: ‘The Son of God, having become man, is God’; and, reversing the order, repeats, ‘God, the son of man,’ etc.” In the printed editions of Arnobius, the heading “To the Emperor Constantius” is by no means acceptable; moreover, some errors occur which we have corrected from an ancient Corbie manuscript. Of the many things in Arnobius’s said work which can be corrected from the same manuscript, we note only this one here: in book II, where Arnobius, after citing certain verses of Ambrose, adds in the manuscript, “Does he say, ‘Such a birth befits a man’?” But the word *say* is absent in the printed editions, though it is altogether necessary for understanding this passage. This fragment should be compared with the exposition of Psalm 143, §7.]

#### VI.

The Son of God, having become man, is God . . . God became son of man (for man became God, not God became man), and [probably: but] the son of man became the Son of God. For the Lord’s greatness surpassed the smallness of the servant-form, so that the very servant-form which he assumed ceased to be servantly through the Lord who assumed it. For if those who are not by nature sons of God are through him made sons of God, how much more did he himself, who is Son of God by nature, exalt into God that one with whom, by his own will, he was conceived and born in the virgin’s womb, so that at his name every knee should bend, of those in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father.

> [Note: It would be more pleasing to read, “The Son of God did not become the son of man” (for God became man, not man became God), but “the son of man became the Son of God.” Augustine notes such an opinion in Sermon 186, §2, in these words: “Therefore, let not the opinion of certain persons insufficiently attentive to the rule of faith and to the oracles of the divine Scriptures creep in upon you. For they say: ‘He who is son of man became Son of God; but he who is Son of God did not become son of man.’ In saying this, they attended to what is true, but could not express the truth. For what did they attend to, except that human nature could be changed for the better, while divine nature could not be changed for the worse?” This is true. Yet even thus—that is, with the divinity in no way changed for the worse—the Word nevertheless became flesh . . . and thereby he who was the Son of God became son of man, through the assumption of what is lower, not through conversion of what is higher.
>
> Hilary is indeed accustomed to conform his language precisely to the pronouncements of Scripture; for example, in book IX of *On the Trinity*, §5, he says of Christ: “In every respect he maintained the mode of evangelical language, teaching that he should be believed to be the Son of God and declaring that he should be preached as the Son of Man”; and in §3: “He himself, from natures united into one and the same thing, is the same reality of both natures, yet so that he lacked neither in either, lest perhaps, by being born, God should cease to be man, and, by remaining, man should in turn not be God.” Many more examples are readily available; but one for whom Hilary’s reading is already familiar needs no more.
>
> Therefore, a different and more hidden sense lies in the fragment cited. For since Hilary distinguishes a threefold state in Christ—the first before he assumed flesh, the second in mortal flesh, the last which followed his resurrection—he commonly professes him to be God and man in the second state, while in the third he says that man passed into God, in a sense often explained by us. Thus the passage cited appears wholly to concern the glorious state of Christ, to which the Apostle’s testimony appended below belongs. [Col. 0726C] Indeed, he who in Psalm 143, §4, says that in the Word assuming flesh the form of God was so emptied that he was wholly in the form of a servant, is far from declaring that the servant-form ceased to be servantly through the Word’s assumption of it. Those, therefore, who think that he is here giving a reason why there is one subsistence in Christ do not seem sufficiently to have grasped his meaning.]

From an uncertain work.

> [Note: This was excerpted either from the homilies on Job or from the lost treatises on the Psalms, and is recalled as follows by the Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 10: “Saint Hilary says: ‘Give us this day our daily bread,’ etc.” See Ambrose, book V *On the Sacraments*, §25.]

#### VII.

“Give us this day our daily bread” (Luke 11:3). [Col. 0725B] For what does God desire so much as that Christ should dwell in us daily—he who is the bread of life and bread from heaven? And because the prayer is daily, it is prayed that he also be given daily.

Likewise, another passage.

> [Note: Augustine celebrates these words, not without praise for Hilary, in book I *Against Julian*, chapter 3, §9: “Who does not know Hilary, the Gallic bishop, as a most vigorous defender of the Catholic Church against heretics? When he was treating of Christ’s flesh, observe what he said: ‘Therefore, when he was sent,’ etc.” He refers to the same matter again in the following book, chapter 4: “And therefore the venerable Hilary did not hesitate to say that all flesh is from sin; but did he therefore deny that it is from God?” Yet he did not state from where he excerpted it. For I do not think a book entitled *On the Flesh of Christ* is indicated here; rather, the reader is merely warned that Hilary is speaking in that passage of the prerogative of Christ’s flesh. A similar judgment occurs in book X of *On the Trinity*, §25.]

#### VIII.

Therefore, when Christ was sent in the likeness of sinful flesh, he did not possess sin as he possessed flesh. But because all flesh is from sin, being derived, that is, from Adam the sinful parent, he was sent in the likeness of sinful flesh: there being in him not sin, but the likeness of sinful flesh.

A doubtful fragment.

> [Note: The words below occur in the commentaries on the Pauline Epistles ascribed to Ambrose. Yet because Augustine cites them in book IV *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, chapter 4, thus: “So Saint Hilary understood ‘in whom all sinned,’” he seems to have wished to refute a heretical opinion by the authority of Saint Hilary of Poitiers. And it may rightly be supposed that he had never read those commentaries; for elsewhere they contain several statements opposed to Pelagius, yet he adduces nothing else from them against him. Accordingly, since we do not sufficiently recognize Hilary’s phrasing in this fragment, we present it as doubtful.]

“In whom all sinned.” “In whom,” that is, in Adam, all sinned . . . It is clear that all sinned in Adam, as though in a mass. For he himself, corrupted through sin, begot all who were born under sin.

A testimony concerning Hilary’s teaching on the procession of the Holy Spirit.

“Saint Hilary, in his exegetical writings on the Apostle, theologizing concerning the Father and the Son, says that no duality is to be understood in the Holy Spirit, because the Father and the Son supply existence to him; whence both are called one principle of the Holy Spirit.”

Hilary, in his explanations on the Apostle, speaking theologically concerning the Father and the Son, says that no duality is to be understood in the Holy Spirit, because the Father and the Son supply existence to him; whence both are one principle of the Holy Spirit. Behold the remarkable and clear teaching [Col. 0727B] of so great a Father against the Greek schismatics concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit and the Father and Son as one principle! Now the Second Council of Seville, canon 13, in Aguirre, vol. III, p. 353, affirmed that Saint Hilary wrote commentaries on Paul’s Epistles; and now, behold, from that lost work a splendid fragment preserved by the Greeks. (From *Spicilegium Romanum*, vol. VI, p. 73.)

## APPENDIX

### [LETTER OR SHORT TREATISE]

[Col. 0728]

# PREFACE BY JOHN CHRYSOSTOM TROMBELLI TO THE FOLLOWING LETTER OF HILARY

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0727B]

### In What Manuscript the Letter Now Published Was Found, and to Whom, in Our Judgment, It Should Be Attributed

1. If I have gained no slight profit from the diligence which I employed in examining the manuscripts of our library when I discovered the preceding short work, I gained a much richer reward when I found the distinguished letter which I now present to you, most courteous Reader, in a parchment manuscript containing Jerome’s letters and shorter works.

> [Note: This manuscript is listed as no. 21 in the old inventory. It is now on shelf IV, to the left, in the upper part of the shelf. It begins with the book which Jerome wrote against Jovinian. The letter which we publish is found on p. 118.]

I would not, however, have you attribute it to Jerome. Its style excludes Jerome as its author, and likewise Ambrose and Augustine, who, as is plain, followed a very different manner of writing. That this letter was originally written in Latin and was not translated from Greek is shown by its very diction, which contains nothing Greek in character. Its Latin authorship is also indicated by the version of Scripture which it follows; for it is either the Old Latin version itself often cited by the ancients, or another version akin to the Old Latin, likewise frequently used by the ancient Latin Fathers. But since, besides Jerome, Ambrose, and Augustine—whom, as we have said, the very writing forbids us to acknowledge as authors of this letter—there were many Latin Fathers who wrote letters, we must inquire to whom we should attribute it.

2. I think it entirely certain that it was composed before the Vulgate translation of the Bible was received by the churches. For the version cited in this letter differs greatly from the Vulgate. It thus precedes the seventh century, in which the Vulgate generally prevailed in almost all Western churches. But it sufficiently indicates a writer of the fourth century by the utmost diligence and earnest zeal with which it seeks to establish and impress the consubstantiality and eternity of the divine Word, and consequently to refute Arians and Semi-Arians. It passes over the heresies which subsequently arose, including even the Macedonian heresy, famous in the age of the Semi-Arians. Indeed, while speaking of the Holy Spirit, it uses expressions which, after that heresy had become established, could not have been used by a Catholic man such as our writer undoubtedly is. This letter was therefore written before Macedonius established a new heresy.

Among those whom we know to have written letters in that period and defended the divinity and eternity of the Word, Hilary of Poitiers and Eusebius of Vercelli stand out.

> [Note: Jerome teaches that Hilary composed several letters in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 10, with these words: “Several letters to different persons.” While discussing the letters of Hilary and Eusebius of Vercelli among writers of those times, he mentions only these; but Sulpicius Severus expressly teaches it in book II of his *History*, chapter 57: “Hosius,” he says, “being more than a hundred years old (as Saint Hilary relates in his letters), became delirious.”]
>
> [Note: See what Baronius teaches under the year of Christ 356, §§92 and following, and the preface to the Veronese edition of Hilary, p. 8, §24.]

But if anyone compares this letter with the letters of Eusebius published by Baronius, he will plainly see that it differs greatly from Eusebius’s style, but approaches the manner of expression which Hilary followed in his books. It differs from them only in this: those, being composed in an oratorical style, are loftier and more elevated; whereas this letter is written in a humble, though ornate and highly polished style. This is not surprising, since such a manner of expression suited a letter intended to be read in an ecclesiastical assembly for the instruction of many.

> [Note: Baronius reports that Hilary sometimes employed a humble style in his letters, saying of Hilary’s letter to his daughter under the year 355, §71: “In it you may see a most holy and equally eloquent man bending his naturally lofty style down to a girl, deliberately making it humble and easy for persuasion, and suited to the simple ears of a virgin.” Anyone who attends to letters of this kind—concerning which we shall say something shortly—will readily admit that letters written for the purpose of being publicly read in ecclesiastical assemblies were ornate and polished.]

Nor is it unworthy of that author concerning whom Jerome says:

> [Note: In the letter to Paulinus, formerly XIII, in the Veronese edition LVIII, §10.]

“Saint Hilary is raised on the Gallic buskin; and, though adorned with the flowers of Greece, he is sometimes entangled in long periods and is far removed from the reading of simpler brothers.”

Nor do we lack in it the abundance and polish which the same Jerome elsewhere testifies shine in the compositions of Gallic writers.

> [Note: In the letter to Rusticus, formerly IV, in the Veronese edition CXXV, §6: “the abundance,” he says, “and polish of Gallic speech,” etc.]

Finally, not to adduce many things, this letter certainly reveals one whose eloquence is shown by the equally explicit words of Jerome:

> [Note: In the letter to Pammachius and Oceanus, formerly LXV, in the Veronese edition LXXXIV, §7.]

“We are not more eloquent than Hilary”; for, as Jerome again testifies here:

> [Note: In the letter to Magnus, formerly LXXXIV, in the Veronese edition LXX, §5.]

“He both imitated the twelve books of Quintilian in style and number, and showed in the short work which he wrote against Dioscorus the physician what he could accomplish in literature.”

> [Note: There are, of course, twelve books *On the Trinity*, to which Jerome here refers.]

Certainly the beginning of this letter is very noble, and what follows is no less excellent, so that one may readily discern in it too the loftiness and eloquence which the ancients commend in Hilary.

3. Critics have also noted in Hilary that he inserts very unusual words into his writings.

> [Note: Erasmus, in the preface prefixed to the edition of the works of Saint Hilary.]

And this occurs in this very letter. For who would count words such as *initiat* (“initiates”), *splendificare* (“to make splendid”), *sacerdotare* (“to act as priest”), and *confuerit* among words which we use frequently? If Hilary uses Greek words in his books for purposes of explanation and of making the matter clearer, these too occur in this letter. If Hilary, as far as possible, avoids the term *homoousion* when explaining the consubstantiality of the Word, and substitutes other explanations for it in his books, lest he seem to contend concerning a word rather than concerning the consubstantiality, eternity, and excellence of the Word itself, he does the same here. He also observes in this letter what he devoutly observed in his other books while disputing against the Arians: he vigorously refutes their errors, yet calls no one by name and wholly abstains from the offensive names “Arians” and “Semi-Arians.” For this very reason he displeased Lucifer of Cagliari and appeared more lenient than was proper.

What more? Those somewhat freer expressions—especially when he discusses the Holy Spirit, the mystery of the Incarnation, and the creation of things—which occur in Hilary’s books *On the Trinity*, occur also in the letter which we publish; the same judgments are found, and, as we have said, the language is not unlike. Anyone who weighs the annotations which we shall append to the same letter will certainly acknowledge this. For no small part of them will have this purpose: by citing Hilary’s words, to show that the letter agrees with his other books not only in doctrine but sometimes even in expression itself, in the arrangement and construction of words.

[Col. 0730A] To this is added some resemblance between the names Hilary and Jerome; for both names begin with the same letters. Hence I suspect that Hilary’s name, indicated only by its first two letters (*Hi*), and placed before this letter, could easily have induced our copyist, perhaps not especially skilled, to attribute to Jerome this short work which should certainly have been attributed to Hilary.

4. Led by these conjectures, I attribute this letter to Hilary of Poitiers and therefore to a most distinguished and very ancient writer. Yet I do not wish to conceal the difficulties objected to me by a most illustrious man, who seemed to hold the first place in the republic of letters.

> [Note: Ludovico Muratori, in a letter written to me.]

First, this writer wishes those for whom this letter was to be read to be prepared for martyrdom. Therefore its author is older than Hilary, since he lived in the age of emperors who persecuted the Church. Second, the writer of this letter acknowledges that his faith had been called into doubt: “And let the enemies of my faith know that an account has been rendered, and recognize that it agrees with the Church.” But who would dare to say this of Hilary? To use Augustine’s words:

> [Note: Book I *Against Julian*, chapter 3; book II, chapter 7; and book VI *On the Trinity*, chapter 10.]

he was called “a most vigorous defender of the Catholic Church against heretics; a Catholic and distinguished doctor of the Catholic Church; and a man of no mean authority in the interpretation of the Scriptures and in the defence of the faith.”

I reply to these points as follows. Undoubted records show that in the time of Constantius many persons were not only sent into exile for defending the orthodox faith but also suffered martyrdom. Our excellent writer therefore rightly wished the faithful to be ready for martyrdom, so that they might testify with their blood to the truth of the orthodox confession. Could one not also rightly fear that, upon Constantius’s death, the empire might pass to a man devoted to the old superstition, and that under his rule the Church would again be harassed? Or, if you wish this letter to have been written during Julian’s reign, how rightly did Hilary wish those faithful to be ready to undergo martyrdom, since we know they were most severely vexed by the pagans, whom the emperor himself openly favoured?

5. Although it is unquestionable that Hilary deserved the praises with which Augustine, Jerome, Cassian, and other most celebrated men adorned him, yet some people, excessively strict and severe, doubted his faith.

> [Note: Volume II of Hilary’s works, p. 521.]

Anyone who attends to the book composed by Hilary in defence of his own faith against the accusations of Lucifer of Cagliari will readily admit this. Read it, I beg you, and you will plainly see that Hilary was compelled to defend his faith against the charges of that bishop.

## CHAPTER TWO

[Col. 0731A]

### To Whom the Same Letter Was Sent; What Its Subject Is; and at What Time It Was Written
1. But another question arises: namely, to whom this letter was sent. For this is absent from our manuscript. That it was sent to a bishop, who had shortly before undertaken the governance of a people, and who was likewise Catholic, and who had requested from Hilary an instruction to be read before the people, is indicated by the words occurring near the end of this letter:

> “I beg pardon before all [perhaps: in all things] from the most sincere holiness of your people, that your Holiness—whose way has been proved by God more experienced and more holy—may deign, in all matters in which my mediocrity has either passed something over or, having discovered it, has been unable to explain it better, to correct, revise, [Col. 0731B] and supply what is lacking; or, if you judge that this little work begun by us at your request and completed with God’s help lacks nothing, remember me in your holy prayers and in those of all the brethren.”

And indeed the words, “whose way has been proved by God more experienced and more holy,” suggest a worthy man, learned as well, or at least one who had had some practice in speaking and writing. Whether because he had little confidence in himself, or in order to secure authority for his faith and for himself, or also in order to possess a most complete instruction to hand down to his people, he requested from Hilary that letter in which both the doctrines of faith should be set forth in summary and morals directed toward piety. This is not surprising; for Hilary stood in high esteem among all.

[Note: [Col. 0731D] How highly Hilary was esteemed among the ancients is readily learned from the praises with which they adorned him. Please consult what the latest edition—namely, that which we have reprinted—of the works of St. Hilary offers on this subject at the beginning of its general preface; and again the selected testimonies of the ancients concerning St. Hilary, published by the most distinguished editor of the Congregation of St. Maurus (see vol. I of Hilary’s Works, col. 203, in our edition).]

[Col. 0731C] Outstanding integrity, miracles performed, uncommon learning, the exile he had endured, the labours he had borne for the Catholic faith, and his wonderful constancy against the enemies of the Catholic Church strongly commended him. Moreover, we know that more celebrated bishops were asked by newly elected bishops to send them letters by which their peoples might be instructed. An example is supplied by the letter which Ambrose, bishop of Milan, gave to Vigilius, a bishop newly elected.

[Note: [Col. 0731D] In the Benedictine Fathers’ edition this is letter XIX: “You requested from me the insignia of your instruction,” etc.]

In it he embraces nearly everything which a bishop ought either to pursue or to avoid. That letters of more distinguished bishops were read aloud in the sacred assemblies of the faithful is attested by much else; and it is clearly shown by the words in which Cyprian, writing to Pope Cornelius, teaches this:

[Note: [Col. 0731D] In Baluze’s edition, letter LV, p. 186, Venetian edition.]

> “Although I know, dearest brother, that because of the mutual love which we owe and show one another, you, presiding there with the most flourishing clergy and the most holy and numerous people, always read our letters to them, [Col. 0732A] nevertheless I now both remind and request you that, what you otherwise do freely and most kindly, you may also do at my request: namely, that when this letter of mine has been read, if any contagion of poisonous speech and deadly sowing had crept in there, it may be removed from the ears and hearts of the brethren, and the undiminished and sincere love of the good may be cleansed of every defilement of heretical disparagement.””

2. This letter is therefore to be held in greater esteem because letters of this kind are exceedingly rare even in the books of the ancients.

[Note: [Col. 0732D] Among Ambrose’s letters you will find only two belonging to this class: namely, the second to Constantius and the one just cited to Vigilius; none among Jerome’s letters and none among Augustine’s. The one directed by Ambrose to Constantius is indeed full of pious instruction, but contains very little concerning the Church’s firmness and Scripture, and scarcely mentions the remaining doctrines of our faith. The letter given to Vigilius concerns moral instruction alone and does not even touch upon the doctrines and mysteries of faith.]

Those which do survive contain encouragements toward piety and virtue, but either omit altogether or touch only very briefly upon the mysteries and doctrines of faith. This letter, on the contrary, embraces both: it carefully explains the mysteries of faith [Col. 0732B] and eloquently exhorts and stimulates its reader to attain the virtues.

3. Since the name of the bishop to whom this letter was sent is absent from our manuscript, we do not know the time at which it was composed by Hilary. That time would readily have become known if we possessed that bishop’s name; for we know the year in which at least the more eminent Latin bishops of that age—to one of whom this letter appears to have been sent—undertook the governance of their churches.

4. Yet I judge that the letter was composed in the final years of Hilary’s life. For the zeal and care which he devoted to illustrating and clearly expounding the Catholic doctrine by which the divinity of the Son is proposed to us as an object of faith, and to defending it [Col. 0732C] against the subtle explanations of the Arians and Semi-Arians, point to an age which had already uncovered all the schemes and evil artifices of Valens, Ursacius, and others akin to them. I am confirmed in this opinion when I attend to the expressions and explanations which seem drawn from the books *On the Trinity* and the *Commentaries on the Psalms*. From this we may reasonably infer that this letter was composed by Hilary after the books mentioned had been written and published.

The words placed near the end of the letter confirm this suspicion of mine: “And let the enemies of my faith know that an account has been rendered, and acknowledge that it agrees with the Church.” For they sufficiently indicate that a dispute had previously arisen between Hilary and Lucifer of Cagliari, [Col. 0732D] and that Hilary’s piety and religion had been called into question by him, so that Hilary was compelled to compose an explanation of his books, especially of the one entitled *On the Synods, or the Faith of the Easterners*. [Col. 0733A] Please see the work of which we speak, which the Maurist Fathers entitled *Apologetic Replies to the Critics of the Book on the Synods* (p. 521, vol. II, Verona edition).

5. With these points established, you plainly see how excellent is the letter which we publish: it contains many very distinguished instructions, composed by one who seems to have been called by the ancients “Teacher of the Churches” (see Cassian, *On the Incarnation*, book VII, ch. 24), because he not only opposed the Arians by his example and by writing many books, but also instructed bishops themselves—and consequently the peoples subject to them—by his letters, and thus grew through the advancement of others.

[Note: [Col. 0733D] “Hilary, a man of every virtue and ornament, distinguished alike in life and eloquence, who grew both as teacher of the Churches and as priest not only through his own merits but also through the advancement of others; and amid the storms of persecutions he stood so immovable that by the strength of his unconquered faith he also attained the dignity of Confessor.” Cassian, *On the Incarnation*, book VII, ch. 24.]

But we have already said enough by way of preface. Behold, then, the Letter itself.

[Col. 0733]

# THE LETTER, OR SHORT TREATISE, OF ST. HILARY

(The numbered annotations appended at the end of the letter are indicated by the numbers.)

[Note: [Col. 0733] Migne printed the notes to this *Epistola* as a separate document in columns 751–826. Each number in the text of the *Epistola* refers to the correspondingly numbered note in that separate document. To facilitate reference to the notes, they have been inserted into the *Epistola* in blocks at the head of each column. They may also be read as a complete document in columns 751–826.]

(C, G)*

[Col. 0733B]

[Note: [Col. 0733]

[Col. 0751A] 1. For a long time I doubted whether anything besides the name of the bishop to whom the letter was sent were missing here. But nothing prevents one from regarding it as complete; for a letter of this kind may quite suitably have such an opening.

2. Although the ancient Latins more often took the word *gloriosus* (“glorious”) in an unfavourable sense—

[Col. 0751D] Plautus’s comedy entitled *The Braggart Soldier* (*Miles gloriosus*) is famous. Pliny also, in the ninth letter of his third book: “He had also sent letters to Rome to a certain old woman, full of boastfulness and swaggering, in these words: ‘Hurrah, hurrah,’ etc.]

—ecclesiastical writers nevertheless generally use it in the sense of “excellent” and “outstanding.” In the very ancient canon of the Roman Mass, the Ascension is called “glorious.” In the book of Sacramentaries which the most distinguished Joseph Blanchini attributes to Leo—

[Col. 0751D] Vol. IV of the Roman edition of the *Anastasius Bibliothecarius*, 1735, p. XII ff.]

—I find the following: “Truly worthy . . . because you are glorious in your saints.” = “Because you are glorious in all your saints.”

[Col. 0751D] Pp. XIII, XIV, and XV: “because you are glorious in your saints.”]

Then follows (*Anastasius*, vol. IV, p. XIV): “May our offerings be pleasing to you, Lord, which have been instituted by your commands and which the glorious festival of the saints commends. Through [him], etc.” Again (ibid.):

[Col. 0751B] “Celebrating, Lord, glorious exchanges,” etc. And a little later (p. XV): “Truly worthy . . . who grant us unceasingly to celebrate the glorious victories of the holy martyrs.” “A glorious confession”; “a glorious resurrection”; “the glorious God, author of the solemnity”; and subsequently (pp. XVI and XVII), most expressly, “the glorious forerunner of the Only-begotten” (p. XX). In that codex of Sacramentaries which the excellent Cardinal Thomasius published (book XI, p. 142 of the old edition), the passion of the martyrs is called glorious. The following prayer is also prescribed for use on the feast of St. Felix: “Grant, we beseech you, almighty God, that as Blessed Felix was glorious through your gifts,” etc. In the same codex the Virgin Mary too is repeatedly called glorious.

[Col. 0751D] See the prayers to be said in the Mass of the Annunciation, pp. 148 and 149.]

Indeed, in subsequent times this epithet was so highly valued that it was bestowed upon men pre-eminent in rank and nobility as a kind of designation and mark of the highest honour. Please consult what Du Cange teaches on this matter.

[Col. 0751C]

[Col. 0751D] In the Lexicon under *Gloria*: “Glory, an honorific title,” etc.]

3. Through the copyist’s carelessness, unless I am wholly mistaken, the number held by this psalm in the sequence of Psalms is missing. Certainly our ancient teachers customarily cited psalms either by specifying the number which the psalm holds in the sequence, or by the words with which it begins, or in general terms such as: “in the Psalms,” or rather, “in the Book of Psalms.”

4. I long doubted whether the words “that is, the Gentiles” were a gloss on the word “Greeks,” transferred from the margin into the letter itself. Yet, since I saw that the word *Gentiles* was frequently used subsequently, I retained it, judging that Hilary, by substituting the word *Gentiles*, denoted those whom others called Greeks: namely, persons still devoted to the old Greek superstition.

[Col. 0752D] Acts 9:29; 11:20; 14:6; 18:4; Romans 1:16; 1 Corinthians 1:22, 24; Galatians 3:28.]

Hence Theodoret entitled the discourses which he published in defence of the Christian religion *On the Cure of Greek Affections*. See what Du Cange notes under *Gentiles*. I have corrected the manuscript reading *disseramus* (“let us discuss”) and substituted *edisseramus* (“let us explain fully”), as the syntax demands.

[Col. 0752A]

5. Everyone knows how stubbornly Jews converted to the faith opposed the admission of Gentiles to it.

[Col. 0752D] Acts 13:45: “But when the Jews saw the crowds, they were filled with jealousy,” etc.; and v. 50: “But the Jews stirred up the devout women,” etc.]

In his letter to the Romans, Paul chiefly aims to teach that Gentiles were called to the Christian religion no less than Jews. Hilary therefore requires Jews to acknowledge this before they receive baptism. Nearly all theologians discuss baptism administered in Christ’s name; above all I commend to the reader the distinguished John Joseph Orsi.

6. In bringing Gentiles to the faith there is a real and greater difficulty, both because they do not possess the Scriptures in which the true God, the new law, and Christ are set forth and promised, and because they are generally stained by graver vices, which the Apostle Paul describes.

[Col. 0752B]

[Col. 0752D] In 1 Corinthians 6:10; 1 Timothy 1:9–10; Titus 3:3.]

7. Before admitting catechumens to baptism, the Church consistently observed an order in instructing them, beginning with the unity and omnipotence of God, in order to teach them and turn them away from the vanity of idols. Consult the ancient formularies for instructing catechumens.

8. What Hilary here states briefly, Paul often and fully develops, especially in these words (Ephesians 4:17): “This therefore I say and testify in the Lord: that you no longer walk as the Gentiles walk,” etc.

9. What Hilary here teaches in the words, “that is, to believe in one God and fear him,” had already been taught by the Apostle Paul when writing to the Hebrews (Hebrews 11:6): “But without faith it is impossible to please God; for one who approaches God must believe that he exists and that he is a rewarder of those who seek him.” If he is a rewarder of those who seek him, will he not be an avenger upon those who, although they knew God, did not glorify him as God or give him thanks, but became vain in their reasonings (Romans 1:21)? “For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of those people who hold the truth of God in unrighteousness” (Romans 1:18). Who, then, could believe these things about God and not fear him? Please consult what Irenaeus teaches on this subject.

[Col. 0752C]

[Col. 0752D] Book I, formerly ch. 11, now 10, p. 48, vol. I of the Venetian edition of 1734.]

10. That God, the Creator of all things, was proposed for belief to catechumens before they were admitted to baptism is most plainly taught by all ancient formularies of the Creed. The Creed which we call Apostolic begins thus: “I believe in one God, the Father almighty, maker of heaven and earth.”

[Col. 0752D] See the Codex of Sacramentaries of the Roman Church, published by Cardinal Thomasius, book I, p. 56.]

Or, as Rufinus translates it: “I believe in God the Father almighty,” etc.

[Col. 0753A]

[Col. 0752D] *Commentary on the Apostles’ Creed*, no. 3, p. 55, vol. I, Verona edition of 1745.]

The Constitutions which we call Apostolic teach the same (book VII, ch. 41). The formula of the Council of Nicaea, translated into Latin by Hilary, likewise presses the same point:

[Col. 0753D] *On the Synods, or the Faith of the Easterners*, no. 83, p. 510, vol. II, Verona edition.]

“We believe in one God, the Father almighty, maker of all things visible and invisible.” Irenaeus says (*Against Heresies*, book I, ch. 10, no. 1): “The Church has received the faith which is in one God, the Father almighty, who made heaven and earth and sea and all things that are in them.” He continues to press the same point (*Against Heresies*, book II, ch. 1, no. 2 ff.). Hence Tertullian (*Against Marcion*, book I, ch. 21): “Faith, therefore, always stood in the Creator and his Christ,” etc.

A scribal error has crept into the printed text. It should read: “those things which either were made, or subsisted at his command, will, and agency.” For so the manuscript reads. The particle *vel* in “which *vel* were made,” etc., should here be understood as it is very often understood in ancient ecclesiastical books: that is, as *and* or *and also*, so that it is not disjunctive but conjunctive—“both those things which were made and those which subsisted at his command, will, and agency.” Or understand it in the manner in which Augustine understood it when he wrote:

[Col. 0753B]

[Col. 0753D] *On Genesis according to the Letter, unfinished book*, XXV, otherwise ch. 5.]

> “That God divided between light and darkness must be understood from the very fact that light was made: light is one thing, those privations of light another, which God ordered in the contrary darkness. For God is not said to have made darkness, because God made the forms themselves, not privations, which belong to nothingness . . . Yet we understand that these were ordered by him when it is said: ‘And God divided between light and darkness,’ lest even the privations themselves should not have their own order . . . Just as in singing the interposed silences, though they are privations of sounds, are nevertheless well arranged at fixed and measured intervals by those who know how to sing, and contribute something to the sweetness of the whole melody. Shadows also distinguish the more prominent features in paintings and please, not by form but by order. For God is not the author of our vices; yet he is their ordainer, when he places sinners in their proper place and compels them to suffer [Col. 0753C] what they deserve.”

If you desire an explanation of this article, consult Irenaeus—

[Col. 0753D] In the passages just cited, that is, *Against Heresies*, book I, ch. 10, etc.]

—Cyril of Jerusalem (*Catechesis* IX), Rufinus—

[Col. 0753D] *Commentary on the Creed*, no. 3, p. 55, vol. I, Verona edition, 1745.]

—Augustine—

[Col. 0753D] Vol. V, Sermon 213, otherwise 119, *On the Season*; Sermons 214 and 215; and vol. VI, Sermon on the Creed to Catechumens, p. 547.]

—and the authors to whom we owe the sermons published under Augustine’s name on this subject.

[Col. 0754D] Namely, Sermons 235, 236, 237, 238, 239, 240, and the following three in the appendix to the sermons. Again, the three sermons on the Creed, vol. VI of Augustine’s Works, p. 555.]

11. There are some errors in the manuscript which must be attributed to the copyist, though they are slight and readily corrected by conjecture. But I have not wished to alter the reading on my own initiative. I think the corrupt reading may be corrected in one of these two ways:

> “But why is it necessary to know what is called the Law and the Prophets, since it was indeed written through men, but not by men?”

Or:

> “That there is a body of Scripture: what is called the Law and the Prophets; what this indicates: namely . . .”

The first correction is not to be despised. The second is also highly probable and straightforward, for the words have this sense: Gentiles, when they seek admission to baptism, must be taught that there are Scriptures gathered into one body. [Col. 0753D] This body contains two parts, one of which is called the Law—for Hilary often uses the subjunctive in place of the indicative—and the other the Prophets. The person being baptized must know what is denoted by the titles “Law” and “Prophets.”

The very famous division of the whole Scripture of the Old Testament is into the Law—namely Moses, who comprehended the entire Law in five books written by himself—and the Prophets. Under the latter heading the historical books are included, especially under the title of the Prophets: either because so many things are foretold in the historical books that they too may conveniently be called prophetic books, or because here the name “prophet” is taken more broadly and denotes every sacred writer. In any case, the following Gospel sayings declare that whatever pertains to instruction in faith and direction of morals is found in Moses and the Prophets (Luke 16:29, 31): “They have Moses and the Prophets; let them hear them . . . If they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they believe though someone should rise from the dead.”

[Col. 0754A] Luke likewise affirms that Christ spoke to the same effect in these words (ch. 24:25): “And he himself, Christ, said to them: ‘O foolish and slow of heart to believe all that the Prophets have spoken! Was it not necessary for the Christ to suffer these things and so enter into his glory?’ And beginning from Moses and all the Prophets, [Col. 0754B] he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself.”

Later indeed (v. 44) he seems to separate the Psalms from the Prophets in these words: “the things written concerning me in the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms.” But these words appear to have the same sense as Christ’s other words (Mark 16:7): “Tell the disciples, and Peter”—that is, Peter especially. For Christ and his deeds, passion, and resurrection are foretold more frequently and, unless we are mistaken, more plainly in the Psalms than in any other sacred books.

[Col. 0754D] Acts 2:25: “For David says,” etc. Again Acts 6:11: “This is the stone,” etc.]

Moreover, we plainly learn from John’s Gospel that the Psalms are included under the name of the Law.

[Col. 0754D] John 10:34: “Is it not written in your Law?”—that is, Psalm 81:6: “I said, ‘You are gods,’” etc.]

12. “Why is this necessary?” Reconsider the preceding annotation.

13. “Namely.” Substitute: “the body of Scripture,” of which he is again speaking. When he calls it “written through men, not by men,” he doubtless refers to Paul’s words (2 Timothy 3:16): “All Scripture inspired by God is useful,” etc. Peter teaches this more expressly (2 Peter 1:20–21): “Understanding this first, that no prophecy of Scripture comes by one’s own interpretation; for prophecy was never brought at any time by human will, but holy men of God spoke, inspired by the Holy Spirit.”

[Col. 0754C]

14. He alludes either to one of the following testimonies, or rather to both. “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world, and that which contains all things has knowledge of speech; therefore one who speaks unrighteous things cannot remain hidden” (Wisdom 1:7). And Romans 8:26–27: “The Spirit himself, who searches hearts, knows what the Spirit desires.”

15. Reconsider what we said in annotation 13. Add these words drawn from Hilary, from which you will clearly perceive that the same meaning appears in both places:

[Col. 0754D] *On Psalm* 52, no. 5, p. 96, vol. I.]

“He appoints Moses as prophet and leader and establishes him as giver of the law; or he inspires the prophets throughout the whole time of the Law.”

16. What Hilary teaches here seems drawn [Col. 0754D] from these words of Jeremiah (ch. 1, vv. 9, 10):

> “The Lord said to me: ‘Behold, I have put my words in your mouth. Behold, today I have set you over nations and kingdoms, to pluck up and pull down, to destroy and overthrow, to build and to plant . . .’”

And below (v. 18):

> “For behold, today I have made you a fortified city, an iron pillar, and a bronze wall against all the land, against the kings of Judah, its princes, its priests, and the people of the land.”

Elsewhere (Jeremiah 6:27): “I have set you as a strong tester among my people, that you may know and test their way. All are rebellious princes, walking deceitfully; bronze and iron; all are corrupt.” Similar passages are very frequent in the books of the Prophets.

[Col. 0755A] We learn from many examples that prophets were sometimes charged to carry out the Lord’s promises and commands. I shall mention one drawn from chapter 9 of the Fourth Book of Kings: we see many things previously promised through prophets entrusted for execution to the ministry of prophets. The reader is asked to consult this passage.

17. All who set forth the articles of our faith place this one second: “And in one Jesus Christ, Son of God, [of God the Father almighty]”; for example, Irenaeus, the Apostles’ Creed, and others. All further teach that this article must be understood to mean that he is Son by nature, not by adoption and grace, as we are sons of God the Father.

[Col. 0755B] This is most rightly taught in the Apostles’ Creed when he is called the only Son:

[Col. 0755D] “And in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord.”]

For why is he the only Son unless he alone is Son by nature, whereas we are sons by adoption and grace, as we have said? I do not cite the Fathers who interpreted that Creed, since anyone may easily consult them for himself. I cite only Hilary, who treats this argument in no. 2 of book V *On the Trinity* (vol. II, p. 105: “But we [know] Wisdom,” etc.); in no. 43 of book VI, likewise *On the Trinity* (p. 166: “And since here [he is] the true Son of God,” etc.); and again in no. 41, the final section of book VII of the same work (p. 208: “Therefore it must be believed,” etc.). He most forcefully presses the same point in no. 36 and following sections of book VI *On the Trinity*.

I select only the following from no. 41:

> “He set forth no other purpose for writing the Gospel than that all might believe Jesus to be Christ, the Son of God. If it is sufficient for salvation to believe Christ, why did he add ‘Son of God’? But if believing Christ is faith only when one has believed not merely Christ but Christ the Son of God, then the name ‘Son’ in Christ, the only-begotten God, is not a customary term of adoption, when it is essential to salvation.”

[Col. 0755C] Hilary is therefore rashly adduced as favouring Elipandus and Felix of Urgell.

18. He undoubtedly refers to verse 3 of chapter 1 of John’s Gospel. The Fathers discuss this matter very fully and frequently. Tertullian, as is his custom, sets it forth obscurely and compactly, but nevertheless teaches matters from which one may draw the same meaning. Please consult what he teaches in chapter 18 of *Against Hermogenes*, and more plainly in chapter 19 of book V *Against Marcion*:

> “If Christ is not the firstborn of creation as the Word of the Creator, through whom all things were made and without whom nothing was made; if all things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers, were not created in him; if all things were not created through him and in him—for these things ought to displease Marcion—then certainly the Apostle would not have stated so unqualifiedly: ‘And he is before all.’ For how is he before all, if he is not before everything?”

And elsewhere, more plainly (*Apology*, ch. 21): “the *logos* of God . . . the same one who made and had made all things by his Word.” Cyril of Jerusalem teaches to the same effect:

[Col. 0755D] *Catechesis* X, no. 6, translated by the distinguished Antonio Agostino Touttée.]

> “Do you wish to learn that Christ the Lord exists with the Father even before the Incarnation, so that you may not only receive by faith what is said but also possess a demonstration from the Old Testament? Go to the first book, Genesis. God says, ‘Let us make man,’ not ‘in my image’ but ‘in our image.’ And after Adam had been made, Scripture says: ‘And God made man; in the image of God he made him.’ For it did not confine the dignity of divinity to the Father alone, but included the Son also, in order to make clear that man was the work not of God alone but also of our Lord Jesus Christ, who himself is true God. This same Lord, who works with the Father, also worked in the matter of Sodom, according to Scripture, which says: ‘And the Lord rained upon Sodom and Gomorrah fire and sulphur from the Lord out of heaven.’”

[Col. 0756A] Yet perhaps Hilary treats the matter more fully than the others in no. 15 and following sections of book II *On the Trinity*. I especially wish you, excellent reader, to consult what he teaches in no. 19: “For the Apostle taught,” etc. I also wish you to consult what he teaches on Psalm 91 (no. 3 ff.); again, no. 3 and 4 of the treatise on Psalm 148 [Col. 0756B] (p. 645, vol. I); no. 44 of book IX *On the Trinity*; and finally no. 43 of book XII *On the Trinity*. These Fathers appear to refer not only to John chapter 1 but also to verse 6 of Psalm 32: “By the Word of the Lord the heavens were established.”

19. This passage has some obscurity, and I think the copyist also erred here; for, in my judgment, words are missing which would indicate that these things were taught by John—for example, these or similar words: “as John teaches us,” or “as is evident from John the Evangelist.” Explain the words of this letter thus:

> “Through whom”—that is, John the Evangelist—“we have received [the teaching] that the *sermo*, that is, the *ratio* of the universe, was with God.”

For John taught: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God.” Nor should you be surprised that I take *Sermo* here as the divine Word. For although, as Petavius notes (*On the Trinity*, book VI, ch. 1, no. 5), the ancients—especially those who followed the Council of Nicaea—preferred to call the second person of the Trinity *Verbum* (“Word”) rather than *Sermo* (“Discourse” or “Word”), it cannot be denied that this same second person of the most holy Trinity was signified by the term *Sermo*, not only by those who preceded Nicaea—

[Col. 0756C]

[Col. 0755D] Tertullian, *Against Hermogenes*, ch. 20; *Against Praxeas*, ch. 15. Novatian, if he is the author of the book *On the Trinity*, ch. 31. Cyprian, book II of the *Testimonies*, ch. 3, and *On the Unity of the Church*. Lactantius, *Institutes*, book IV, ch. 4: for *logos* signifies both “discourse” and “reason,” because he is both the voice and the wisdom of God; and ch. 8, where he says: “rightly is he called the Discourse and Word of God.” Again ch. 9: “but the Greeks say *logos* more suitably than we say *verbum* or *sermo*.”]

—but also by those who followed it. Thus Paulinus of Nola (*Natalicia* VI for St. Felix, v. 25):

> Christ, God of Felix, be present; now give me the word—  
> God the Discourse, Wisdom, give me a clear mind.

Rusticus also says:

[Col. 0756D] At the beginning of the disputation against the Acephali; *Bibliotheca Patrum*, Paris edition, vol. IV, p. 798.]

> “If therefore the eternal Word is in every respect as [eternal] as the Father, and the Discourse of God is likewise impassible and unchangeable as the Father.”

Likewise Augustine:

[Col. 0756D] Book XII *Against Faustus*, ch. 35.]

> “The Discourse of God sent the Law through his servant, and it did not profit the human race dead in sins.”

Elsewhere (*Sermon 8 on the Words of the Apostle*, no. 1):

> “The human race would not be delivered unless the Discourse of God deigned to become human.”
