Indeed, Jerome, translating into Latin the first Paschal Letter of Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, represents Theophilus as writing thus:

[Col. 0756D] Letter 96 in the Verona edition, no. 7.]

> “But if the Discourse of God reigns, he is certainly God,” etc.

This use of the word was so pleasing to some that they introduced it into the Latin translation of Sacred Scripture itself. Augustine observes:

[Col. 0756D] Tractate, or Sermon, 108 on John, no. 3: “And in certain manuscripts it is written: ‘Your word is truth,’ just as in certain manuscripts it is also written there: ‘In the beginning was the Discourse.’”]

[Col. 0757C] In some manuscripts *Sermo* was read where we now read *Verbum*. Arnobius, called “the Younger” because he is believed to have lived after the time of Leo the Great, likewise says:

[Col. 0757A]

[Col. 0757C] Bellarmine, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, and *Bibliotheca Patrum*, Paris edition, vol. XV, pp. 352 and 355.]

> “Therefore the Discourse of the Father, proceeding from his mouth and full of power, makes all visible creatures.”

Hilary therefore rightly uses the word *Sermo* in the same sense not only in the little work we are elucidating but also in his other books. For example, in book II *On the Trinity* he says (no. 15, p. 36, vol. II):

> “Had you heard ‘in God’ and not ‘with God,’ so that you might take it as the discourse of a hidden thought? . . . Wait for the established reality of the Word and its name; for he says: ‘And the Word was God’ [John 1]. The sound of a voice and the expression of thought cease. This Word is a reality, not a sound; a nature, not discourse; God, not emptiness.”

[Col. 0757C]

[Col. 0757D] I have punctuated it thus in conformity with common usage and the example of others. Yet I acknowledge that it may be punctuated differently, provided that it denotes that this *Sermo* is something substantial and is true God.]

He presses the same point elsewhere, in the passages noted here:

[Col. 0757D] Book VII *On the Trinity*, no. 18, p. 181: “And where it is reported, ‘I said,’ *Sermo* belongs rather to the speaker”; and no. 19, “if the heavenly discourse,” etc. Again, no. 11, book X *On the Trinity*; and more expressly, no. 19, book XII *On the Trinity*, p. 430, “but the discourse of God,” etc. Also in *On the Synods, or the Faith of the Easterners*, no. 46, “The heretics, destroying,” etc.]

The Church herself likewise rightly uses the same word to denote the Word. Thus she addresses the divine Father:

[Col. 0757D] In the introit of the Sunday Mass within the octave of the Nativity, and in the antiphons for the *Magnificat* and *Benedictus* on the same day. We learn from the book entitled *Responsories and Antiphonaries of the Roman Church*, published by the excellent Cardinal Thomasius in 1686, that this antiphon has been used from the earliest times of the Church.]

> “While all things held deep silence, and night in its course had reached the middle of its way, your almighty Discourse, O Lord, came from heaven, from the royal [Col. 0757B] throne.”

It transfers and adapts to this feast what is stated in Wisdom 18:14–15.

Thus, then, Hilary commands us to believe by these words that the divine *Sermo* is not a mere sound but an existing person, and one who is with God and therefore a divine person. Nor did he begin to exist in time, but he was with God “in the beginning,” that is, before any times whatever, even imaginary and fictitious times, as the Fathers often say, and from eternity itself. Athanasius (*Orations* 3 and 5), Gregory of Nyssa (*Against Eunomius*, book II), and Augustine teach matters akin to those which Hilary himself most explicitly taught in books II (no. 13, “Look upon the world,” etc.) and XII (no. 43) *On the Trinity*. See what Petavius teaches on this subject (*On the Trinity*, book VI, ch. 1, no. 6 ff.).

20. The ancient Fathers called not only the Word or Logos the second person of the most holy Trinity, but also *ratio* (“reason”): a term which may be suitable for the divine Word on various grounds. Either because *sermo* (“discourse,” “word”) is a fuller, more forceful, and, if you will, more illustrious explanation of the term, as when synonyms are gathered together; or because the divine Word is that reason, or idea, to which the Father alone looked in creating the world—reason, I say, and idea unbegotten and consubstantial with God; or again because, as reason holds the first and chief place in an excellent work of craftsmanship, so the divine Word held the first and chief place in creating the world; or likewise because, as right reason appears and shines forth in an excellent work and is, as it were, present in each of its parts, so the power and wisdom of the divine [Col. 0758A] Word manifested itself and, as it were, shone forth in the creation of the world, and in some manner adhered to, and is present in, each of its parts. Again, because, just as reason put into practice expresses and reveals the craftsman, so the Word, both in its generation and in its operation, made the Father, his excellence, and his divinity known and manifest to the world. Finally—and here is the last explanation—some say that the divine Word is called *ratio* because it has relation, or reference and relationship, to the Father.

Tertullian seems to take this term in the first sense when he addresses the Gentiles thus (*Apology*, ch. 21): “We have already declared that God fashioned this whole universe by Word, Reason, and Power. Among your own philosophers also, it is agreed that *logos*, that is, Discourse and Reason, is regarded as the maker of the universe. . . . And we likewise assign a proper substance, namely Spirit, to the Discourse, Reason, and likewise Power, through all of which we have declared that God wrought.” [Col. 0758B] (Others read “we ascribe.”)

In the same sense he begins the book entitled *On Prayer* as follows: “The Spirit of God, the Word of God, and the Reason of God; the Word of Reason and the Reason of the Word; and the Spirit, both of them—Jesus Christ our Lord.” And indeed, that this term *ratio*, when used to denote the only-begotten Son of God, is as it were synonymous with the terms *Sermo* and *Verbum*, seems to be taught, to say nothing of others, by Lactantius, Ambrose—if he is the author of the book entitled *On the Divinity of the Son*, or *On the Orthodox Faith against the Arians*—and Augustine [Col. 0757D]:

Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, IV.9, says: “For *logos* signifies both discourse and reason, because he is both the voice and the wisdom of God.” Augustine—if indeed it is Augustine, for the Maurist Fathers deny the work to Augustine [Col. 0758C], and not without reason, as is clear from the warning prefixed to the work, p. 2 of the Appendix to vol. VIII—in the book *On Five Heresies*, ch. 6, says: “In the beginning was the Word. In Greek it is better said *logos*; for *logos* signifies both Word and Reason.” Finally Ambrose—if, as I said above, he is the author of that [Col. 0758D] book (see the warning prefixed to this treatise by the Maurist Fathers, p. 343 of the Appendix to Ambrose)—in the book entitled *On the Divinity of the Son*, ch. 6, says: “There is a certain *ratio*, which among the Greeks is called *logos*, which distinguishes the persons or appellations of Father and Son, because the Son himself is also called *ratio*.” These words are also found in the sermon formerly numbered 190 *On Time* among the works of Augustine, now numbered 113 among the rejected works in the Appendix, no. 2. There, after the preceding words have been quoted, the following is added:

> “Yet this *ratio* is called by many names: now Word, now Power, now Wisdom, now Right Hand, now Arm, now Pearl, now Treasure, now Nets, now Plough, now Fountain, now Rock, now Cornerstone, now Man, now Lamb, now Calf, now Eagle, now Lion, now Way, Truth, and Life; since he is God, all in all. Through these names the mysteries of the divine dispensations are made known, not in order that the majesty itself of the Son of God may be shown as properly defined.”

—or, if you prefer, by another writer lurking under Augustine’s name. But should we derive the reason for this usage from the fact that, to use Tertullian’s words (*Apology*, ch. 21), “he showed himself to be the *logos* of God—that is, that primordial, first-born Word—accompanied by power and reason, supported by the Spirit”? Or rather, because, as Petavius has already taught (*On the Trinity*, VI.1.6), *sermo* is the same as *ratio*, and hence he is called “the word of reason” and “the reason of the word” [Col. 0758C]? Certainly Hilary, in this very letter which we are elucidating, says (ch. 4, p. 40): “the Son of God, true wisdom, word, that is, reason, etc.”

The second meaning—namely, the one which derives this designation from the fact that the only-begotten Son of God is that reason, or idea, to which the Father alone looked in creating the world—is proposed by the author to whom we owe the book *On the Divine Names* (ch. 7), whether he be Dionysius the Areopagite or some other writer, certainly ancient and probable. For, in Petavius’s translation (*On the Trinity*, VI.1.3), he teaches as follows: “In the sacred Scriptures God is [Col. 0759A] celebrated as *Logos*, not only because he is the giver of reason and of higher wisdom, but also because he has simply comprehended beforehand within himself the causes of all things, and because he reaches and penetrates all things, as the sacred Scriptures testify.” [Col. 0759D]

As I have said, I have used Petavius’s translation, for others translate otherwise. Ambrosius Camaldulensis’s translation indeed differs somewhat from Petavius’s. Nevertheless, all the translations have the same sense.

Explaining this passage in his commentaries, Maximus says [in Petavius’s translation, *On the Trinity*, VI.1.3] that “the divine Word is called *logos* because the rational principles of the whole of nature are in him, as causes and as the principle of every creature; for through him all things exist. Indeed, the ideas and exemplary forms are in him; they are the eternal conceptions and operative reasons of all things, and thus nature itself. For nature itself is a *ratio* containing cause and nature, since the natures of existing things do not exist rashly or in vain.”

The third explanation, which we said consists in this: “as reason holds the first and chief place in an excellent work, so the divine Word held the first and chief place in creating the world”—this third explanation, I say, is proposed by those whose opinion Augustine describes when he testifies [*Eighty-Three Questions*, question 63] [Col. 0759B] that “the only-begotten Son of God is less properly called *ratio* than Word, in order to signify not only his relation to the Father, but also the operative power directed to those things which were made through the Word.” It is also proposed by those who, wishing the term *ratio* to be synonymous with *sermo* and *logos*, observe that the divine Discourse, even insofar as it is taken personally, held the chief place in creating the world. We have said something on this matter in the eighteenth annotation, and shall say more hereafter. Here I only cite Nazianzen, who says (*Oration* 36): “But if anyone should also wish to call him *logos* because he is present in all things, he will not depart from reason; for what is there that was not created by the Word?” [Col. 0759D]

I have used Petavius’s translation, from which Billio’s old translation scarcely differs. This passage may be found on p. 500 of vol. I of the Cologne edition of 1690. [Col. 0760D]

We stated that the fourth explanation consists in this: “as right reason appears and shines forth in an excellent work and is, as it were, present in each of its parts, so the power and wisdom of the divine Word manifested itself and, as it were, shone forth in the creation of the world, and in some manner adhered to, and is present in, each of its parts.” Nazianzen is said to support this by the earlier words just cited: “But if anyone should also wish to call him *logos* because he is present in all things, he will not depart from reason.” But certainly those support it who say that the term wisdom is synonymous with *ratio* [Col. 0759C], and who refer to the twenty-fourth verse of the seventh chapter and the first verse of the eighth chapter of the Book of Wisdom to the divine Word.

I heard someone cite to this end the following words of Lactantius; whether rightly or otherwise, let others judge: “For *logos* signifies both discourse and reason, because he is both the voice and the wisdom of God.” Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, IV.9. [Col. 0760D]

For in the cited passages we read: “Wisdom is more mobile than all things that move; and by reason of her purity she reaches everywhere. . . . Therefore she reaches mightily from one end to the other, and orders all things sweetly.”

We said that the fifth explanation is the one teaching that “as reason put into practice expresses and reveals the craftsman, so the Word, both in its generation and in its operation, signified and made known to the world the Father, his excellence, and his divinity.” Unless the authority of most eminent men deceives us, this is proposed by Nazianzen, who calls the Son of God *horos kai logos tou Patros* (ὄρος καὶ λόγος τοῦ Πατρός), that is, as Petavius translates [Col. 0759D] (*On the Trinity*, VI.1.3), “the definition and reason of the Father.” Why he calls him thus, Nazianzen subsequently explains in these words translated into Latin by Billio (vol. I, p. 590):

> “Moreover, he is called Word because he stands in relation to the Father as discourse does to the mind—not only because of a generation wholly free from passion, but also because of his union with the Father and his declarative power; perhaps also because he stands in the same relation to the Father as a definition does to the thing defined. For definition too is called *logos*. For he who has known the Son, Christ says—for that is the meaning of ‘he who has seen’ [John 14]—has also known the Father; and the Son is a brief, concise, and easy declaration of the paternal nature. For everything begotten defines its begetter by a certain silent voice.” [Col. 0760A]

The final explanation, however—namely, that “the divine Word was called *ratio* because it has reason, that is, reference and relation, to the Father”—is proposed by Nazianzen, whom I have just cited; also by Augustine, whose words I quoted a little above (*Eighty-Three Questions*, question 63); and finally, not to cite very many, by Ambrose, if you regard Ambrose as author of the book *On the Divinity of the Son* among Ambrose’s works: “There is a certain *ratio*,” he says (*On the Divinity of the Son*, ch. 6; Appendix to Ambrose’s Works, p. 346, etc.), “which among the Greeks is called *logos*, which distinguishes the persons or appellations of Father and Son, because the Son himself is also called *ratio*.”

These are the more celebrated explanations of the term *ratio* [Col. 0760B] when it is applied to the divine Word. Yet I suspect that Hilary, when he calls the Word “the reason of the universe,” also intended another explanation: that the only-begotten Son of God is the sole reason why the universe exists—sole, I say, because he created all things; and sole also because his incarnation was the reason for which all things were created. The theologians treat this matter most fully. Hence in Scripture he is called the beginning of the ways of the Lord; and Paul also calls him “the firstborn of every creature” (Col. 1:15), adding: “For in him were created all things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers: all things were created through him and in him; and he is before all things, and all things hold together in him.”

Jerome seems to have anticipated this conjecture of mine when he writes to Paulinus (*Epistle* formerly 103, in the Verona edition 53, no. 4): “*Logos* in Greek signifies many things: for it is both word, reason, [Col. 0760C] calculation, and the cause of each individual thing by which the several things that subsist exist; all of which we rightly understand in Christ.” This annotation, though somewhat lengthy, will nevertheless, I think, not be unwelcome to the reader.

21. This word *initiat*, insofar as it is used for *incipit* (“begins”) or *exorditur* (“commences”), is among those words which many have noted in Hilary as being very rarely used by others. Yet others employed it even before Hilary. Vitruvius, near the end of the preface to Book VII, calls *initiantes* those whom others customarily call *initiati* (“initiated”). Likewise Tertullian (*Against Valentinus*, ch. 15): “From these the rest were initiated”: that is, they derived their beginning or commencement. Julius Firmicus uses it in the same sense: “Spring is initiated,” he says, “when the sun has entered the first part of Aries.”

22. All who have argued on the subject teach that the first chapter of John’s Gospel is especially suited to refuting the utterly foolish persuasion of the Arians. [Col. 0760D] I mention here only Augustine (*Tractate* 1 on John, and often elsewhere) and Hilary (*On the Trinity*, II.13, pp. 34–35, and often elsewhere). And indeed, we learn from Jerome that John wrote the Gospel principally in order to oppose those who denied Christ’s divine origin:

> “Last of all he wrote a Gospel, at the request of the bishops of Asia, against Cerinthus and other heretics, and especially against the doctrine of the Ebionites then arising, who assert that Christ did not exist before Mary; and therefore he was compelled to declare his divine birth.” Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 9. [Col. 0761C]

I. Glorious David, in the Psalm (Ps. 18:5), says thus: “Their sound has gone forth into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.” From this, therefore, it may be understood that, once the sound has first been prepared—that is, the first principles of faith—one may advance to the innermost and more perfect matters of faith, lest, while the rudiments are wavering, the rebuking voice of the Lord be addressed to us: “If you have not been faithful in a little thing, who will give you that which is greater?” (Luke 16:10).

But since I see that there is a fixed pattern beyond which one may not proceed in setting out the difference between Jews and Greeks, that is, Gentiles, let us first explain the difference. (The manuscript reads: “let us discuss it.”) For I think that Jews need believe nothing else for the truth of faith than that Jesus Christ is the Son of God; that through him both the race of Israel is saved and the Gentiles are baptized in his name; for they know the rest [Col. 0733C] through the Law and the Prophets. But Gentiles, for whom the task is truly greater, must be admitted and instructed in the following order.

First, they must withdraw with their whole hearts from idols and from all human pleasures, so that, once evils have been cut off and uprooted, good and religious things may be sown in their hearts. That is: they must believe in one God and fear him. Then they must know that he made all things, and that all things in the world, whether created or established, stand fast by his command, will, and action. There is a body of Scripture; and what need is there to say that it is called the Law and the Prophets, though it was written through human beings, not by human beings? For the Spirit of God, who knows all things, inspired holy persons who spoke, whether to destroy perversity, [Col. 0733D] build up faith, raise hope, threaten judgment, or maintain promises. Then they must believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God, through whom God made all things and without whom nothing was made; and that in the beginning we received through him the Word—that is, the reason—of the universe, and that he was with God. For thus the glorious Evangelist John begins, saying (John 1): “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.” Then [Col. 0734B]

[Note: [Col. 0734]

23. All who professed the Christian religion were bound to confess the Holy Spirit as the third person of the most holy Trinity. This is certainly shown by the Apostles’ Creed, Irenaeus (*Against Heresies*, I.10), the Nicene Creed [Col. 0761A] (Hilary, *On the Synods*, no. 84), the creed also attributed to Athanasius, and the remaining formularies of Christian faith. This is not the place for me to vindicate the divinity of the Holy Spirit, which Catholic theologians most fully assert, and which was asserted not obscurely even by those Fathers who preceded the Council of Constantinople, and indeed the Nicene Council, in time.

See, not to enumerate all, Petavius, *On the Trinity*, II.12–14. [Col. 0761C]

Renatus Massuet collected the passages of Irenaeus testifying to the divinity of the Holy Spirit in Dissertation 3, nos. 51–53, pp. 116–117, vol. II of the Venetian edition of 1734. Although Tertullian is numbered among those who, having followed Montanus’s error, held unsound views concerning the Trinity and expressly concerning the Holy Spirit, nevertheless, before he allowed himself to be corrupted, he openly professed the divinity of the Holy Spirit in chapters 8, 9, and 13 of *Against Praxeas*. I wish the reader to consult these passages in such a way as not to pass over the remaining chapters of the same work. [Cols. 0761C–D]

To return to Hilary: some bolder critics censure him as though he hesitated to affirm the divinity of the Holy Spirit. He is censured wrongly, however. For he wrote the following concerning the Holy Spirit (*On the Trinity*, II.29, p. 43, vol. II):

> “Concerning the Holy Spirit, we ought neither to be silent nor are we compelled to speak; but, for the sake of those who do not know, we cannot be silent about him. Yet it is not necessary to speak concerning him, who must be confessed on the authority of the Father and the Son. And indeed, I think that whether he exists need not be discussed: for he exists, since he is given, received, and possessed; and he who is joined to the confession of the Father and the Son cannot be separated from the confession of the Father and the Son. [Col. 0761B] For the whole is incomplete for us if anything is lacking from the whole.”

Then he proceeds through those passages of Scripture by which the Spirit’s divinity is customarily affirmed and established. Elsewhere he speaks in this manner:

> “Although I remember that many have thought that the three measures of meal are to be referred to the sacrament of faith—that is, to the unity of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—and also to the calling of the three nations from Shem, Ham, and Japheth . . . yet in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, without the need for yeast mixed in from outside, all things are one in Christ.”

Hilary, *On Matthew* 13.6, p. 735, vol. I. [Col. 0761D]

I deliberately refrain from adducing other passages of Hilary to the same effect, lest I do what has already been done. That labour was anticipated by the distinguished Maurist monk who prepared and published the last Paris edition of St Hilary. Please see what he sets forth in no. 12 and the following sections of the preface to the books *On the Trinity*.

24. All the ancients make the Holy Spirit a participant in creation, and rightly so: for he is God, and the works which theologians call *ad extra* are common to the whole Trinity. I cite only Basil here, for in Book V *Against Eunomius* he says: “For the Spirit is joined to the living Word in creation, a living power and divine nature, which shone forth ineffably from the ineffable mouth,” etc.

In the latest Benedictine edition of the Fathers, p. 303, vol. I. [Col. 0761D]

Many Fathers attribute the perfection of things and the animation of living beings to the Holy Spirit. Why? Is it because the Holy Spirit is love, and the perfection of things is an eminent evidence of love? Or because, since he is as it were the completion and final term of the divine processions, it was fitting that the completion and final term of operations *ad extra* should also be attributed to him? You will learn these matters from theologians.

This is at least certain: many ancient and later interpreters referred to the Holy Spirit those words of Genesis 1:2, “The Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters”—namely, in order to make them fruitful and render them productive. [Col. 0762A]

Calmet cites several, though very distinguished, authorities. Add, if you wish, Prudentius (*Apotheosis*), Victor of Vita (*A Statement of Faith to Huneric*), whose words are: “The Spirit of God was borne over the waters, as Creator sustaining the creature by the power of his might, so that he himself, about to bring forth all living things from them, might furnish the unformed elements with the fostering heat of his own fire.” And, not to enumerate all, add our Steuco in the *Cosmopoeia*. Ausonius preceded Prudentius and Victor of Vita, for he says in the *Morning Prayer*:

> I acknowledge the Father of the Only-Begotten, and the Spirit mingled with the two,  
> who fluttered over the waves of the sea;

and in the poem *On the Lord’s Resurrection*:

> He, taught by your counsels, added this one thing:  
> [Col. 0762D] that the Spirit who swam over the waves of the sea  
> might quicken sluggish limbs with an immortal bath. [Cols. 0761D–0762C]

They likewise refer to the Holy Spirit the sixth verse of Psalm 32: “And by the spirit of his mouth”—that is, of the Word—“all their host,” namely that of the heavens. Tertullian sometimes mentions a created spirit, and therefore one distinct from the third person of the most holy Trinity (*Against Hermogenes*, ch. 32); elsewhere (*Against Marcion*, IV.26) he seems to teach the same things as Hilary here.

25. Paul had already taught the unity of baptism when writing to the Ephesians (ch. 4, v. 3): “One Lord,” he says, “one faith, one baptism.” Cyprian likewise teaches it—although he later erred in this, since from baptism’s unity he judged that it could be validly conferred only in the Catholic Church—and so do the other Fathers, both before the Council of Constantinople when explaining the Creed, and especially afterward, particularly when they elucidate Paul’s cited words in commentaries.

Cyprian, *Epistle to Januarius* 78: “Since baptism also is one,” etc. [Col. 0762D]

*Epistles* 73 and 74; *On the Unity of the Church*: “although there cannot be another baptism besides the one,” etc. [Col. 0762D]

To remain with Hilary, see what he says in nos. 1 and 2 of Book XI *On the Trinity*: “There is therefore one . . . But neither in the one baptism . . .” [Col. 0762D]

Our teachers explain the unity of baptism thus: it is one because, since it is the profession of faith instituted by Christ, the sure sign of that faith, and entry into it, we rashly seek another profession, another sure sign, and another entry. “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit,” etc. (Matt. 28:19). [Col. 0762D]

Cyril of Jerusalem explains it otherwise, saying (*Procatechesis*, no. 7): “It is not permitted to receive the washing two or three times; otherwise one might say, ‘What went badly once, I shall accomplish on a second occasion.’ But if it has gone badly even once, the matter admits no correction; for there is one Lord, one faith, and one baptism. For heretics alone are rebaptized, since that earlier rite was not baptism.” Please see what the most distinguished Toutée notes [Col. 0762C] on this passage.

26. Christ himself indicated that in baptism we are regenerated and reborn to God, when he addressed Nicodemus in these words (John 3:3): “Amen, amen, I say to you: unless anyone has been born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.” Peter teaches this most expressly in his First Epistle: “Born again, not from seed,” etc. (1 Pet. 1:23). Paul also teaches it in the third chapter of the Epistle to Titus.

See the interpreters on this passage and, to omit the rest, Jansenius of Ypres’s commentaries. [Col. 0762D]

Verses 4 and 5. Consult interpreters on this passage, not only Catholic ones but also non-Catholic writers, among whom Grotius earned no small praise. [Col. 0762D]

All who have elucidated the Apostles’ or Constantinopolitan Creed in their discourses, sermons, and writings likewise insist upon and explain it. [Col. 0763A] The Church also teaches this very frequently, as in the prayers recited at Mass on the Thursday after Easter:

In the Secret: “O God, who [the diversity of the nations] . . .” [Col. 0763C]

Also in those which she directs to be said on the Friday of the same week:

In the Secret: “Offerings . . .”; and in the Postcommunion: “Look upon us, we beseech thee . . .” [Col. 0763C]

The same occurs at Pentecost:

At the Vigil, at Mass: “Grant, we beseech thee, almighty God . . . those who have been reborn through thy grace.” [Col. 0763C]

If I were to add the Fathers, I should be almost endless. To avoid citing many, I indicate only passages from Zeno and Hilary. The reader may consult them for himself if he wishes.

Zeno, II.30 and following, p. 227 of the Verona edition prepared by the Ballerini brothers; Hilary, *On the Trinity*, I.22, p. 15, vol. II; *On Psalm* 63.11, p. 182, vol. I; and *On Matthew* 10.24, p. 719, likewise vol. I. [Cols. 0763C–D]

27. The resurrection of the dead is taught not only in the Apostles’ Creed but also in nearly all other ecclesiastical documents in which our faith is summarily set forth. You will cease to wonder at this when you know that this article is among those by which we most especially depart from the false opinions of the Gentiles and particularly of the Epicureans. The apostle Paul emphasized it when he proclaimed Christ to the Athenians in the Areopagus; on this account, and because he proclaimed Christ, he was held in contempt by the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers:

> “Now certain Epicurean and Stoic philosophers disputed with him; and some said, ‘What does this babbler wish to say?’ But others, ‘He seems to be a proclaimer of new gods,’ because he announced Jesus and the resurrection to them.” Acts 17:18. [Col. 0763D]

Yet he himself often proclaimed the same resurrection, so that no one might doubt it. I indicate several passages [Col. 0763B] at the foot of the page which the reader may consult for himself:

Acts 23:6; again, ch. 24, vv. 14 and 21; ch. 26, vv. 8 and 23; Rom. 6:5; 1 Cor. 15:12 and almost the whole chapter following; 2 Tim. 2:18; 1 Thess. 4:12, etc.; Heb. 6:2; 1 Pet. 4:5: “who is ready to judge the living and the dead.” [Col. 0763D]

It is also certain that the Jews were persuaded of this matter, indeed so persuaded that the Sadducees, who denied it, were counted among the heretics.

2 Macc. 12:44: “For unless Judas Maccabaeus had hoped that they would rise again, it would have seemed superfluous and vain to pray for the dead.” [Cols. 0763D–0764C]

Please see what Philastrius says in heresy V, and join to it what the excellent Canon Galeardus notes; for he adduces many passages of Scripture and other credible authors on the matter. Irenaeus also lists this same resurrection of the dead among the articles to be believed by catechumens: “and the resurrection of the dead . . . for the raising of all flesh of the human race.” [Col. 0764C]

All who comment upon either the Apostles’, Constantinopolitan, or even the so-called Athanasian Creed explain this article at length. Cyril of Jerusalem won much praise in this very matter (*Catechesis* XVIII, no. 1 and following). Augustine and other teachers of ours, both ancient and later, also discussed the subject. Nor will you regret reading [Col. 0763C] what Gregory the Great often teaches in support of the same resurrection. Here it is enough for me to indicate one passage, which I consider very convincing: namely Homily VIII on Ezekiel.

Nos. 6 and following: “But because [we speak] of the resurrection of the flesh,” etc. [Col. 0764C]

Hilary frequently treats of the resurrection, for example in no. 9 of his commentary on Psalm 63, etc.

28. This article is most closely connected with the preceding one. For why shall we all rise again, unless so that each person may receive from the Lord Jesus Christ, Judge of the living and the dead, according to what he has done in the body, whether good or evil (1 Cor. 5:10)? Paul indicates the connection we have mentioned between the two articles when, in the Epistle to the Hebrews, he joins the resurrection of the dead with eternal judgment: “and resurrection of the dead, and eternal judgment” (Heb. 6:2). Irenaeus states it most expressly [Col. 0764A] when he enumerates among the doctrines to be believed by those about to be baptized (*Against Heresies*, I.10):

> “the ascension in the flesh into heaven of beloved Jesus Christ our Lord, and his coming from heaven in the glory of the Father to recapitulate all things, and to raise up all flesh of the human race, so that to Christ Jesus our Lord and God and Saviour and King, according to the good pleasure of the invisible Father (Phil. 2:10, etc.), every knee may bow, of things heavenly, earthly, and infernal, and every tongue may confess to him, and he may execute just judgment in all things (Eph. 6:12): that he may send spiritual wickedness, the angels who transgressed and became apostates, and impious, unjust, iniquitous, and blasphemous human beings into eternal fire; but may bestow life upon the just and equitable, upon those who keep his commandments and persevere in his love—upon some from the beginning, upon others from repentance—grant incorruption as a gift, and surround them with eternal glory.” [Col. 0764D]

The new edition translates: “to renew all things.” Eph. 1:10. [Col. 0764D]

The same Irenaeus repeats this elsewhere, namely in Book III, ch. 4. [Col. 0764D]

The Apostles’ Creed, the Nicene Creed—“He will come to judge the living and the dead” (Hilary, *On the Synods*, no. 84)—and the other most ancient creeds likewise set forth this same article. [Cols. 0764D–0764B] This is unsurprising. Judicial authority seems especially to be a reward granted to Christ’s humanity because of the humility which he showed especially on the Cross. He loved his disciples, especially the Apostles, so greatly that he appointed them seats in that same judgment, in which they would judge angels also (1 Cor. 6:13). If anyone desires this article explained, let him consult those who expound the Apostles’ Creed, and especially Cyril of Jerusalem (*Catechesis* XV, no. 3 and following); and also interpreters on the passages of Scripture which I indicate here:

Matt. 24:29 and 25:31; Acts 24:25; Rom. 14:10; 1 Cor. 6:3; 2 Cor. 5:10; 1 Thess. 4:13 and following. [Col. 0764D]

29. Our manuscript actually reads: “So great is the difference between Jews converting and Gentiles believing.” If anyone wishes to read “those converting,” I have no objection. By these words, however they are read, Hilary concludes as with a kind of epiphonema what he had said before: namely, that Hebrews joining themselves to the Christian faith are to be instructed differently from those who come to the Church from idolatry. From the former, few things are required for belief, since they already know the rest; but from the latter a more explicit and fuller confession is required—namely, the confession which Hilary had briefly summarized and explained a little before, and which he is about to set out more fully.

Nor should you wonder that so few things were proposed to them for belief. For we learn the very same thing also from Irenaeus, who, when about to explain the faith which the Church, planted throughout the whole world to the ends of the earth, received from the Apostles and their disciples, comprises it in very few chapters.

*Against Heresies*, I.10. Again III.3, formerly ch. 2: “the tradition proclaiming one God,” etc. Also in ch. 4 of the same book he says that this tradition is to be preserved: “to believe in one God, maker of heaven and earth.” [Col. 0764D]

The Nicene Synod did the same, explaining itself at greater length concerning the divinity and dignity of the Son, which was particularly under dispute at that time, but summarily comprehending the remaining articles.

Hilary, *On the Synods*, no. 84: “We believe in one God,” etc. [Col. 0765D]

This is unsurprising, for these articles either contain or imply those articles which the Apostles’ Creed sets forth. Thus the Fathers whom I have cited do not at all oppose the conviction of those who affirm that the Apostles’ Creed was dictated by the Apostles themselves.

30. This letter may be divided, according to the diversity of its subjects, into three parts. The first part, with which we have so far been occupied, contains a summary of the articles of our faith; the second part, which we now approach, contains a more careful exposition of those same articles. Yet, to conceal nothing, I long suspected that one ought rather to read, *who he was* (or, if you prefer, *who he is*), and *what kind of Son of God [he was]*. I likewise suspected that the subsequent words, “for the three are one,” had been added. For these words seem to refer to that celebrated testimony of John [Col. 0765D], in the First Epistle, chapter V: “There are three who bear testimony in heaven,” etc.; a testimony to which Hilary does not appear to have referred elsewhere. Nevertheless, I judged that nothing should be changed, even in what follows. For the sense remains entirely sound if one reads, “who he was, and what kind of Son of God [he was].” Indeed, since the dispute between Arians and Catholics concerned not the present but, so to speak, the most ancient and eternal condition of the Son of God, Hilary could properly write, “who he was”—that is, from eternity and even before imaginary times—the Son of God.

Moreover, the words “for the three are one” could have been inserted by Hilary when writing not, as formerly when he composed the books *On the Trinity*, to Arians, but to Catholics, and hence to persons recognizing the force of that testimony, which had been cited even before Hilary by Cyprian. See what Catholics argue concerning this testimony against recent Arians. Certainly those words have been placed very properly for this reason: they give the reason why he joins the Son and the Holy Spirit with the Father, and afterwards explains more carefully what the Catholic religion commands us to believe concerning them. Thus, if he omitted that testimony in the books *On the Trinity* in order not to introduce an extraneous controversy concerning its authenticity [Col. 0765C]—if I may speak in that way—he rightly adduces it now when addressing Catholics who acknowledge it to be authentic, since it is especially well suited to establish the consubstantiality of the divine Persons.

31. If anyone wishes to draw from Hilary himself many points confirming the preceding statement—“Certainly it is fitting that your prudence should know this”—and to show, from a comparison of those passages with the one examined here, that both works have the same author, let him consult the passages which I shall immediately indicate: namely, section 19 of Book I *On the Trinity*: “And you indeed, whom the ardor of faith,” etc.; sections 19 and 26 of Book III *On the Trinity*; sections 14 and 38 of Book VII; likewise what he says in section 17 of Book VI *On the Trinity*; and finally what he teaches in sections 2 [Col. 0765D]—“And may one God alone dissolve for us the faith in God from God in the confession”—and 33 [Col. 0766D]—“For faith must not be undertaken according to our own discretion, but according to the force of the sayings”—of *On the Trinity*.

Hilary’s statement in this last passage is indeed most excellent: “No utterance concerning divine matters has been left to human speech other than God’s own Word; all else is narrow, confined, encumbered, and obscure.”

But what Hilary goes on to teach in these words—“Let man not seek Him on earth or arrange Him among fabricated things, lest he believe Him like to anyone”—is precisely what Scripture often inculcates concerning God. Thus in Deuteronomy, chapter IV, verse 15: “You saw no likeness on the day when the Lord spoke to you on Horeb out of the midst of the fire, lest perhaps, deceived, you make for yourselves a carved likeness, or an image of male or female,” etc. And in Isaiah, chapter XLVI, verse 5: “To whom have you likened me, equated me, compared me, and made me similar?” etc. Everything that theologians argue against the Anthropomorphites has a place here [Col. 0766A]. It will suffice for me to point to a few passages of Hilary by which the preceding statement may be confirmed.

Here first is Book I *On the Trinity*, section 19:

> “If, while treating of the nature and birth of God, we offer examples of comparisons, let no one suppose that they contain in themselves the perfection of an absolute rationale. For there is no comparison of earthly things with God. Rather, the weakness of our understanding compels us to seek certain forms from lower things as indications, as it were, of higher things, so that, prompted by familiarity with familiar realities, we may be led from the consciousness of our own perception to an apprehension of an unfamiliar perception. Every comparison, therefore, should be regarded as useful to man rather than suited to God, because it indicates understanding rather than fulfils it. Nor should it be considered an attempt to equate the natures of flesh and spirit, of invisible and tangible things; it declares itself necessary to the weakness of human understanding and free from the blame of offering an inadequate example. We therefore proceed to speak of God in God’s words, while nonetheless informing our own understanding by the appearance of our own things.”

Hilary teaches matters akin to these in section 2 of Book IV, section 9 of Book VI, and, not to enumerate every passage in which he teaches the same thing, section 18 of Book VII [Col. 0766B]. The author of the book entitled *On the Trinity*, or *On the Apostles’ Creed*, which is extant among Ambrose’s works, made so much of this article that he took it as his beginning [Col. 0766D]: “Therefore no one who is of sound mind should suppose that almighty God, who is Trinity and Spirit, is some visible or tangible body.”

32. I candidly set before the reader the emendation which I have made here. The manuscript reads: “Begotten: not made.” But I have written: “Not begotten, not made.” Either understand here God considered in essence—as I use the phrase of the Schoolmen—and precisely considered; or understand the Person of the Father. Take it as you please: one must certainly read “not begotten.” For when was the divine essence begotten? When was the Father begotten? But when Hilary here says that God is not begotten, he says that He is devoid of and unacquainted with every origin or principle, and much more with every cause. He teaches what all the Fathers and theologians teach when they say that the Father is unbegotten [*innascibilis*] [Col. 0766C], and what Hilary himself had stated most expressly in these words, Book IV *On the Trinity*, section 6: “He knows one unbegotten God; he knows also the one only-begotten Son of God. He confesses the Father eternal and free from origin,” etc.

Hilary pursues this point more fully, not only in the passages cited by Petavius, Book V *On the Trinity*, chapter 5, section 13, but also in section 58 of the book *On the Synods* [Col. 0766D]: “From an unbegotten substance, perfect birth,” etc.; and again in section 47 of Book XI *On the Trinity* (p. 404, vol. II), which you may consult if you wish. Add, if you please, the Fathers enumerated by Petavius in chapter 5 of Book V *On the Trinity*, sections 13, 14, and 15. Add Ausonius, whom I shall cite shortly.

33. The Fathers very often teach that God is incomprehensible, especially those who argued against the Arians and Anomoeans. Gregory Nazianzen devotes much of his fourth and thirtieth Orations to showing that we cannot grasp what God is, nor describe His excellence in speech. Chrysostom treats this same subject at greatest length. I select one passage to cite here, from the Third Oration against the Anomoeans [Col. 0766D], p. 463 of volume I of the Clermont-Montfaucon edition:

> “Let us therefore call Him,” Chrysostom says, “the ineffable, unintelligible God; invisible, incomprehensible, surpassing the capacity of human speech, exceeding the comprehension of the mortal mind; untraceable to angels, invisible to seraphim, unintelligible to cherubim, unseeable to principalities, powers, and virtues—in short, to every creature—and known by the Son and the Holy Spirit alone.”

Hilary insists on the same point in sections 5 and 6 of Book II *On the Trinity* [Col. 0767A] (p. 30, vol. II), and in section 62 of the book *On the Synods* (p. 497, vol. II). I would have you read the latter passage in its entirety. Novatian also—if he is the author of the book *On the Trinity* which was at one time published under his name and printed among Tertullian’s works—agrees with the same view, chapter 7:

> “For that which is, according to that which it is, can neither be uttered in human speech, received by human ears, nor comprehended by human faculties.”

The source of this incomprehensibility is, if we may so speak, infinity—that is, His infinite perfection and power. Since this is altogether unbounded and, as I have said, infinite, it makes Him wholly incapable of being comprehended. Scripture very frequently teaches this infinity. But, since I am not here acting the part of a theologian, it will suffice for me to adduce a single passage: the very well-known words of Job, chapter XI, verses 7, 8, and 9: “Can you perhaps comprehend the traces of God, and discover the Almighty unto perfection? He is higher than heaven: and what will you do? deeper than hell: and how will you know? [Col. 0767B] His measure is longer than the earth and broader than the sea.”

Here either the incomprehensibility of the extent of omnipotence is set forth, or the incomprehensibility of divine perfection itself and infinity; thus that incomprehensibility which indicates that God surpasses our knowledge because He possesses an eminent perfection, most excellent beyond every measure. Gregory the Great comments thus on these words of Job, Book X of the *Morals*, chapter 8, formerly section 13 and following:

> “He is therefore higher than heaven, because even the elect spirits themselves do not perfectly penetrate the vision of such sublimity . . . . He becomes higher than heaven when our contemplation itself fails in regard to Him.”

Augustine therefore rightly concludes concerning God, in his exposition of Psalm LXXXV, section 12, that “it is easier for us to say what He is not than what He is.” Indeed, he adds: “This only could I say: what He is not. Do you ask what He is? What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man. There is none like you among the gods, O Lord [Col. 0767C], and there are no works according to your works.” He teaches almost the same thing in section 9 of Tractate XXI on the Gospel of John. If here you adduce passages describing God as ineffable, you will do so rightly. For why is He ineffable? Certainly because He is incomprehensible. Very many passages of Scripture and of the Fathers accordingly tend to describe God as ineffable. I cite only Fulgentius, teaching this in the book *Against the Objections of the Arians*, Objection and Response II:

> “God is not unknowable because He is unutterable; rather, He is known by the faithful in order that He may be loved, although He cannot be narrated either by human tongues or angelic ones.”

34. “Inestimable” [*inextimabilem*] has been written for “inassessable” [*inaestimabilem*]. What we said in the preceding note readily shows that God is inassessable. For who can adequately assess Him who is incomprehensible? Yet if anyone desires that I produce some explicit testimonies of the holy Fathers to confirm this view, here at once is Tertullian, chapter 17 of the *Apology*:

> “He is invisible, even if He is seen; incomprehensible, even if through grace He is represented; inassessable, even if He is assessed by human senses: so true and so great is He. But what can commonly be seen, comprehended, and assessed is less than the eyes by which it is grasped and the hands by which it is found. But what is immeasurable is known to itself alone. This is what causes God to be assessed: that He does not admit of being assessed. Thus the force of His greatness has presented Him to men both known and unknown. And this is the height of the sin of those unwilling to recognize Him of whom they cannot be ignorant.”

Ambrose seems to have followed him—if Ambrose is indeed the person to whom you attribute the book *On the Divinity of the Son*, concerning whom see [Col. 0768A] what we said in the note on section 20—when he wrote the following concerning God, *On the Divinity of the Son*, chapter 6:

> “He is the one of whom, even when He is spoken of, He cannot be spoken; when He is assessed, He cannot be assessed; when He is compared, He cannot be compared; when He is defined, He grows by that very definition of Himself.”

35. “Invisible [God].” Theologians discuss this doctrine at length. We, whose purpose in these notes is to avoid disputations, consider that we have fulfilled our duty if we direct the reader to Petavius, who treats the subject very fully. Therefore see, I beg you, volume I, Book VII, chapter 1; for there he has collected the testimonies of the ancients. Add to them what Hilary teaches in his Commentary on Psalm CXVIII [Col. 0767D], letter VIII, section 7, on the words, “I have entreated your face with my whole heart,” etc. Add also what we shall cite from the commentary on Psalm CXXXV in note 38, since God is there called unseeable [*inconspicabilis*].

But since I earlier said that I would cite Ausonius, here he is; his authority readily confirms both the matter now under discussion and what was taught in section 32 and the following two sections [Col. 0768B]. Thus he prays to God the Father in the *Morning Prayer*:

> Almighty One, whom I worship in my mind, sole Father of all things,  
> Unknown to the wicked and unknown to none of the devout,  
> Lacking beginning and end, older than time  
> That has been or will be; whose form and measure  
> Neither mind can comprehend nor tongue declare;  
> Whom God, born of the unbegotten Begetter, alone has the right to behold and hear commanding face to face,  
> And to sit at the Father’s right hand.

36. “And impassible.” Does Hilary here exclude passions from God, or mutability, or both? Or does he rather refer these words to the Father, who did not assume the flesh in which the Son suffered? Let the reader judge. Certainly, in order to show that the Son of God, the Word, is God and consubstantial with the Father, he teaches that an impassible nature was communicated to Him by the Father. “To all creatures,” he says (*On the Synods*, section 58, p. 495), “the will of God gave substance; but perfect birth gave the Son a nature from an impassible and unbegotten substance” [Col. 0768C; cf. Col. 0767D, section 59].

He expressly removes passibility from the Father in the generation of the divine Son in the book *On the Synods* [Col. 0767D–0768D]: “And if the very name of Father signifies the impassible origin of the one being born,” etc., section 24. And elsewhere, Book IV *On the Trinity*, section 6: “He knows God, who is Spirit, in the Spirit—impassible and incapable of being cut apart.”

37. Whoever lacks these titles and attributes is an imaginary, not a true, God. Hilary expressly teaches this, I think, in order to oppose his confession to the confession of Arius. In order to deceive the unwary, Arius explicitly listed and expounded God’s perfections and attributes. “We know,” he said [Col. 0768D; in Hilary, Book IV *On the Trinity*, section 12, and Book VI, section 5], “one God: alone unmade, alone everlasting, alone without beginning, alone true, alone possessing immortality, alone good, alone powerful, creator of all things,” etc. By this means he intended to disparage Catholics, who, in his judgment, divided God into Persons and diminished the divine perfections. Hilary therefore, undertaking the defense of the orthodox cause, acknowledges that these things too are admitted by him; and hence acknowledges that in the Trinity of Persons God is unmade, incomprehensible, and so forth.

38. I once doubted whether the words “who has generated certain beings” might, in some more obscure manner, hint at the divine generation of the Word. Since the preceding words can readily be referred to the Father, I suspected, as I have said, that the divine generation was indicated by these terms. But I afterwards removed every suspicion. For who would think that the only-begotten Son of God, whom Hilary so frequently and clearly distinguishes from creatures, was designated by the common term “certain beings” [*quaedam*]? I therefore judge it much more advisable to refer the generation which Hilary mentions here to those creatures whom he wished to be endowed with intelligence. For intelligence makes them like God, grace makes them in some way partakers of the divine nature (2 Peter I.4), and it honors them with the title and dignity of sons of God.

Indeed, most people understand the words of Job, chapter XXXVIII, verse 7—“when . . . all the sons of God shouted for joy”—as referring to angels, on account of their outstanding intelligence and grace. Moreover, Hilary himself teaches this [Col. 0769D], in the exposition of Psalm CXXXV, section 8, on the words “who made the heavens in understanding”:

> “But when He who is infinite set a realm for the knowledge of Himself, He enclosed within the highest and first heaven, likewise situated in the sphere, a certain limit for the powers that were first to be generated to know Him. For the creations to be brought forth could not have borne the power of the unseeable God unless, through the interposition of a more tempered nature, they inhabited this abode, moderated for a habitation suited to weakness.”

Elsewhere, however, he warns that those same beings whom he admits may be called both sons and begotten are not so called with the signification of proper ownership. For, if we wish to speak properly, we become sons by grace; we are not born sons. We are therefore sons by adoption and election, not by generation, strictly and properly understood [Col. 0769B–0770D]:

> “Unless perhaps someone, from the fact that He says, ‘Israel is His firstborn Son,’ will understand the words ‘my firstborn’ as detracting from the Son’s proper generation; so that, because He also said ‘my’ of Israel, the adoption of made sons may be employed in place of the property of birth, and therefore what is said of the Son—‘This is my beloved Son’—may not be proper to God’s birth, since ‘my’ is also said to be proper to those whom it is manifest were not born. Yet that they are not born, though they are said to be born, is taught even by the words: ‘The people which shall be born, whom the Lord has made.’ Therefore the people Israel are born in order to be made; and because they are said to be born, they are not thereby understood not to be made. For he is a son by adoption, not by generation; and what he possesses is not propriety, but designation.”  
> —Hilary, Book XII *On the Trinity*, section 14.

Hilary could therefore call us begotten by God in the sense in which Paul teaches that we are called God’s offspring. For, preaching in the Areopagus, Paul said, Acts XVII.28: “For in Him we live, move, and are; as some of your poets also have said: ‘For we are also His offspring.’” What we shall say at length in Dissertation III may conveniently be brought forward to illuminate this passage.

39. This passage appears somewhat obscure. I once suspected that, by a copyist’s liberty, the reading had been arranged “has ordered, has adorned,” whereas perhaps the original exemplar read “has adorned, has ordered.” That is, “[true faith] has set forth that He has ordered the good and just Judge to command”: namely, has established that the good and just Judge commands—or rules—and exercises just judgment. But afterwards I observed that it can still be read as in our manuscript, namely, “has ordered, has adorned.” Recall what had been placed a little earlier: “True faith has always set forth God thus: not begotten,” etc. The cited words then have this sense: “True faith has always set forth [God] thus, so that we acknowledge [Him] as not begotten . . . and the good, just Judge, as one who commands.”

If you ask what God made, disposed, ordered, and adorned, I answer: all natures and their genera and species were made by God from the beginning: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth,” etc. Nor did God create corporeal things only, but spiritual things also. See what we stated in notes 10 and 18. He disposed the sun, moon, and stars, that they might divide day and night and be for signs, seasons, days, and years; that they might shine in the firmament of heaven and illuminate the earth (Genesis I.14; Psalm CXXXV.7–9). Thus He disposed all alternations and intervals of time. He also disposed things themselves: for you will find few things occurring everywhere; rather, He disposed and fitted nearly all things to their own places. The Book of Job has some material on this topic [Col. 0769D], chapter XXXVIII, verses 4, 5, etc., which I would have you consult; and the Book of Wisdom states it most clearly, chapter XI, verse 21: “You have disposed all things in measure, number, and weight.”

Among pagan authors, Virgil says: “Not every land bears every thing.” Why? Because, as we have said, God, disposing all things in measure, number, and weight [Col. 0770A], wished each part of the world to lack some things which it would seek from other regions, so that human beings might assist one another by mutual services.

But God also ordered privations and sins, in Augustine’s judgment. Recall what we said in note 10; add to it what Augustine teaches on Psalm LI, section 15: “Do not suppose that the wicked are without purpose in this world,” etc. All these things are supported by experience and by that ancient saying of Solomon, Proverbs XVI.4: “The Lord has made all things for Himself, even the wicked for the day of evil.” When I affirm that sinners and their errors are ordered by God, I likewise affirm that illnesses, diseases, and other things of this kind—penalties indeed for sin, but nevertheless occasions for our merit and incentives to patience—are ordered.

40. God has also adorned many things in this world, as experience and Scripture attest in these words, Genesis II.1: “Thus the heavens and the earth were completed, and all their adornment.” That the Creator of the heavens can readily be known from their adornment is manifest from Psalm XVIII.1: “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the works of His hands.” And as the stars are the ornaments of the heavens, so shrubs, trees, and herbs are the ornaments of the earth; their innumerable and varied kinds show almighty God to be their author (Wisdom XIII.5), so that those who, knowing God, did not glorify Him as God are without excuse (Romans I.19–20, etc.).

See what theologians argue on this subject, especially Petavius, volume I of *Dogmatic Theology*, chapter 1. Yet, while illustrating Hilary, it would be wrong not to adduce a longer passage from Hilary himself. For elsewhere he teaches the following, in the exposition of Psalm LXIII, section 6, p. 197 of volume I [Col. 0770B–0770C]:

> “We are also taught, by the following admonitions, to render obedient order, as the Prophet—or the Spirit through the Prophet—thus exhorts: ‘Say to God: How terrible are your works!’ For who would not tremble before His majesty—He who established the ages, founded the world, measured out time by its revolving alternation and course, adorned heaven with stars, filled earth with fruits, confined the sea by barriers, and chose man either to use or to rule these things? For through all these things the eternity of His power and might is known, as the Apostle says: ‘For His invisible things, understood through what has been made from the creation of the world, are clearly seen—His eternal power also and divinity.’ These things make the Creator’s name terrible, and the worthiness of His works displays the majesty of Him who made them. Therefore God, the maker of these works, must be proclaimed by us and confessed by others.”

He says similar things in his commentary on Psalm CXVIII [Col. 0770D], letter X, section 2, p. 334 of volume I: “Common judgment is,” etc.

41. Recall what I said earlier, namely in note 39. Yet if anyone wishes to think that something is lacking here, or has been badly written, I shall not oppose him. The ancient professions of our faith itself—the Apostles’ Creed, Irenaeus, and all others who speak of the principal articles of our faith—acknowledge that Christ has been established as our Judge.

42. These words must be referred to what he said a little earlier [Col. 0770D]: “has made certain things,” etc. Recall what I said in sections 39 and 40.

43. Hilary appears here to take “the time of recognition” either as the time during which a person lives and can then perceive what God has created, or as the time in which God more abundantly assists a person by His grace and strives [Col. 0771A] to lead him to Himself. Hilary seems to refer to two very celebrated passages of Scripture. The first is Luke XIX.42: “For if you too had known, even in this your day, the things that belong to your peace! But now they are hidden from your eyes . . . . They will not leave in you one stone upon another, because you did not know the time of your visitation.” The other is found in Paul’s Epistle to the Romans, chapter I, verse 18: “For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and injustice of those people who hold the truth of God in injustice; because what is known of God is manifest among them, for God has manifested it to them.”

44. The first part of this statement—“he will have after departure a just Judge”—is clear. It concerns the particular judgment immediately following each person’s death. Earlier, when enumerating the principal points of our faith, he mentioned the universal judgment. In this particular judgment each receives his own sentence according to his merits, whether good or evil. Paul seems clearly to indicate this when he says, Hebrews IX.27: “It is appointed to human beings once to die; but after this, judgment.” For the words “after this” indicate a judgment immediately following. The example of the rich man and Lazarus shows this as well: the rich man was at once cast down to hell, while Lazarus immediately attained Abraham’s bosom. Augustine indeed relies greatly upon this latter example, writing [Col. 0771D], *On the Soul and Its Origin*, Book II, chapter 4, formerly section 8:

> “It is most right and very salutary to believe that souls are judged when they have departed from their bodies, before they come to that judgment in which they must be judged once their bodies have been restored . . . . Who [can speak] against the Gospel,” etc.

Elsewhere he indicates the same thing [Col. 0771D], Book XX *On the City [of God]*, chapter 1, section 2: for he acknowledges “besides the final judgment, other judgments in which God judges even concerning the particular works of individuals; and human beings, often openly and always secretly, suffer divinely imposed penalties for their deeds, whether in this life or after death.” For if He punishes deeds after death by some judgment that is not final, a particular judgment must necessarily precede the final judgment [Col. 0771C]. And so much for the first part of this statement.

I come to the other part, which is much more difficult: namely, “who shall think himself converted not in his own time, but from the past.” Are the words “who shall think himself converted not in his own time” referred to the Judge, or rather to the one who, because he did not recognize his Maker in the time of recognition, will have Him after departure as a just Judge? Perhaps either explanation may be defended; but the course and continuity of the discourse seem to indicate that the words are referred to the Judge, who permits Himself to be entreated by a person while that person is still alive, but after death rejects every entreaty. I therefore interpret the words “but from the past” as meaning: “but now the suitable time has elapsed.”

Theologians treat this subject, especially Fr. Liberius, volume I of the *Controversies*, treatise III, *On the State of Souls*, part I, controversy 1. I, whose intended brevity prevents me from gathering much here, cite only Hilary, indicating two of his passages. Since they are somewhat longer, I ask the reader to read them independently. They are section 23 of the commentary on Psalm II, p. 92 of volume I—“Confession exists only in the age,” etc.—and section 4 of the commentary on Matthew, chapter XXVII, where he expounds the parable of the ten virgins: “The bridegroom and bride,” etc. [Col. 0771D].

45. That is, these things must be believed concerning God.

46. If you think that the conjunction “and” is missing in our manuscript after the word “believes”—and it may be absent through a copyist’s carelessness—so that you judge it should be read, “He who believes, and abstains himself . . . will have rest,” etc., then this statement of Hilary means the same as that of Gregory the Great explaining the celebrated Gospel passage, “He who believes and is baptized shall be saved; but he who does not believe shall be condemned.” “Perhaps,” Gregory says, *Homily 29 on the Gospels*, section 3 [Col. 0772A], “each person says within himself: ‘I already believe; I shall be saved.’ He speaks truly, if he holds faith together with works. For true faith is that which is not contradicted in conduct by what it says in words. Thus Paul says of certain false believers, Titus I.16: ‘They profess to know God, but deny Him by their deeds.’ Thus John says, 1 John II.4: ‘He who says that he knows God and does not keep His commandments is a liar.’”

Indeed, Hilary says the same thing in section 9 of his commentary on Psalm XIV, which passage of Hilary we shall cite in the following note.

But if you think that the conjunction “and” was absent from the original exemplar itself, and that the text should be read as in our manuscript, “He who believes abstains himself,” etc., explain it thus: one who truly believes abstains from all injustice, carrying out, that is, what our faith commands us to do. James the Apostle aptly says, chapter II, verse 17: “Faith, if it does not have works, is dead,” etc.

47. So abundant are the promises by which we are assured that eternal rest is to be granted us through upright works that it seems pointless to heap up many relevant testimonies. I shall offer one, but a clear saying of Christ. To the person asking Him, Matthew XIX.16, “What good shall I do in order that I may have eternal life?” He replied: “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments . . . . You shall not murder; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness; honor your father and mother; and love your neighbor as yourself.” By “life” here understand—as I have said elsewhere—that life which elsewhere is simply called “life” (Matthew VII.14; again XVIII.8), and elsewhere “the crown of life” (James I.12; Revelation II.10) [Col. 0772B].

“But what,” you ask, “is that rest which we shall have in life?” It is that of which Paul says, Hebrews IV.11: “Let us hasten to enter into that rest”; and of which Muratori treats in his book entitled *On Paradise against Burnet*, chapter 4, p. 38 and following. There he has collected passages of the ancient Fathers showing that by the name “rest” true and perfect blessedness is understood. Since I may speak only briefly in these notes, it is sufficient for me to cite one passage drawn from ecclesiastical prayers. Before Pius V, the following prayer was prescribed for recitation on the vigil of the Assumption of Mary:

> Grant, merciful God, assistance to our weakness, so that we who celebrate the rest of the holy Mother of God may, through the aid of her intercession, rise again from our iniquities. Through the same, etc.

If the most holy Pontiff altered these words, he did not alter them because he thought them less suitable, but lest those who delighted in attacking the Roman Church everywhere should have even the slightest occasion to criticize it, as though it spoke somewhat obscurely concerning heavenly blessedness [Col. 0772C].

But lest, while examining Hilary’s words and investigating his meaning, we should seem to neglect other passages of the holy Doctor tending to the same end, here are passages from which it is certainly manifest that he understands eternal blessedness by the name of eternal rest. Expounding the first verse of Psalm XIV, “Lord, who shall dwell,” etc., he says, p. 69 [Col. 0772D]:

> “It is the simple prayer of one entreating the Lord and desiring to learn from Him what character, zeal, and will belong to the person who is to dwell with God and rest in His high and heavenly places.”

And in section 9, p. 74, explaining these words of the same Psalm XIV, “who has not practised deceit with his tongue,” he writes:

> “That he may not falsify in words the truth which he thinks; that action may also follow the profession of Catholic doctrine and the judgment of thinking and preaching in this way. For according to the Apostle’s testimony, as one believes in the heart, so confession is made with the mouth unto salvation. Therefore, in order that ascent into God’s rest may be worthy, one must live in truth of speech and tongue, so that by the faithfulness of one’s actions the words of our thought may not be false.” [Col. 0773A]

Now compare, I beg you, the words already cited from this letter—“He will have eternal rest in life”—with what Hilary teaches in his exposition of Psalm LXII. From this very comparison of expressions, you will see why I may properly say that Hilary is the author of the letter under discussion. Here is what Hilary teaches concerning that Psalm, section 7, on Psalm LXII, p. 174: “There is also life after life, because one must live in Abraham’s bosom, in which the name of God is blessed by the rest of the poor.”

48. Something appears to be lacking here, by which a way may be opened for a fuller exposition of the words: “Next, it must be believed that Jesus Christ, the Son of God,” etc.

49. Here Hilary rejects those ridiculous and shameful begettings of gods invented by the pagans, who did not shrink, on occasion, from introducing the mingling of sexes [Col. 0773B]. Certain heretics seem to have imitated them; Irenaeus refutes these heretics, Book I, chapter 1, and again Book IV, chapter 1; add what Epiphanius has in *Heresy* 31. Petavius also lists them; see what Petavius says, Book X *On the Trinity*, sections 8, 9, and 12.

Hilary certainly appears elsewhere to refute the same error when he says, Book IV *On the Trinity*, section 6:

> “The Church knows God, who is Spirit, in the Spirit—impassible and incapable of division; for she has learned from the Lord that a spirit does not have flesh and bones, lest it should perhaps be believed that the injuries of bodily passions befall Him.”

He likewise rejects that generation of the Son which certain followers of Sabellius, as I suppose, devised with utter madness. Using Hilary’s words, Book IV *On the Trinity*, section 4, p. 73, volume II, they “employed and expressed this word *homoousios* [ὁμοούσιον, ‘of one substance’] in this sense: as though He who is Father were Himself also Son, stretched forth, that is, from His own infinity into the Virgin; and as though, assuming a body from her, He had added to Himself the name of Son in the body [Col. 0773C] which He assumed.”

50. He likewise rejects those who said that Christ was a mere man (see what Hilary sets forth in *On the Synods*, no. 38, canons VI and VII); and also those who could imagine him to be some spirit inferior to God which afterwards assumed flesh in the Virgin. For he maintains that he was unquestionably begotten from God, and is therefore the true Son of God, and consequently true God.

51. Some error has undoubtedly crept into these words: “his substance not divided, nor the substance of his majesty divided; and thus he may appear passible.” Either the latter words—“nor the substance of his majesty divided”—are a gloss on the preceding words, “his substance not divided,” which slipped from the margin into the text itself; or one must read, “nor the substance of his majesty diminished.” But, you will ask, how do the subsequent words agree with and connect to those above: “nor the substance of his majesty divided; and thus he may appear passible”? Does the Son, because he proceeds from the undivided substance of the Father, either appear passible or actually become so?

Therefore, either the manuscript must again be corrected and read: “lest by this he appear passible”; for the Father would be passible if his substance were cut apart. Or these words, “and thus he may appear passible,” must be understood as though he said: “We indeed confess that the Son is born from himself—that is, from God the Father—but in such a way that his [the Father’s] substance remains undivided. For if you make it divisible, he appears, or is shown, to be passible.” Here, plainly, the subjunctive is used in place of the indicative, as Hilary often does.

[Col. 0773D] I offer only one—but a very familiar—example, taken from the commentary on Matthew (Canon 27, otherwise chapter 27, on Matt. 24:48; this passage is used in the lessons of the third nocturn in the Common of a Confessor Bishop, second place): “Because he may have despaired of his coming, because he may not have obeyed the commands, because he may have devoted himself to present things, because he may have lived the life of the Gentiles, because through despair of judgment he may have afflicted with hunger, thirst, and slaughter the household entrusted to him”: in place of “he despaired,” “he did not obey,” “he devoted himself,” “he lived,” “he afflicted.” And, lest we depart from this very epistle, paragraph 3, p. 39, has: “so that even that which may have been fashioned for us”—that is, “was fashioned.”

Arius, indeed, and his followers accused Catholics of falling into the error of those who divided and cut up the divine substance, making it, as it were, subject to suffering in the Father and the Son, when they tried to explain the generation of the Son. Hence, in their professions of faith they chiefly exalted the fact that, acknowledging divinity in the one Father, they did not in the least cut or divide God, but preserved him whole, so to speak. Hear, I pray, what Arius himself babbles while writing to Alexander, bishop of Alexandria.

[Col. 0774D] Epiphanius gives this letter in Greek, *Heresy* 69, no. 5. But I use Hilary’s Latin translation, *On the Trinity*, book IV, no. 12, and book VI, no. 5.

> “We know one God alone, unbegotten . . . now God begot the only-begotten Son before all ages, through whom he made both the age and all things. He was born not merely in appearance, but truly, in obedience to his will: an unchangeable and unalterable perfect creature of God, yet not like one of the creatures; a work, yet not like the other works. Nor, as Valentinus imagined, is he an emanation born from the Father; nor, as Manichaeus explained, is he born as a part of the Father’s one substance; nor, as Sabellius, who divides the union, said that he is the Son who is also the Father; nor, as Hieracas, a lamp from a lamp, or a lamp divided into two parts; nor one who existed before and was afterwards born, or created anew as Son,” etc.

Nor did Arius alone teach this. Eusebius, bishop of Nicomedia, a man of great name among the Arians, did not shrink from attacking Catholics as though they maintained that “the one God was divided into two, or that there was something corporeal capable of suffering, and that the Son was from the Father himself or from him, as though a part of him, or from an outflow of substance.”

Likewise Eunomius (*in Gregory of Nyssa, Against Eunomius*, book III) “says that the substance of the Son was begotten from the Father, not brought forth by extension, nor perfected by increase, nor formed by change.” By these words, however, he is believed not only to set forth his own view, but also to accuse and criticize Catholics.

[Col. 0774C] Therefore Hilary, in order to evade their craftiness and defend Catholics against the charge, repeatedly impresses this very doctrine—not only in the little work we are explaining, but also in other books—the doctrine for whose sake the Arians said that they had departed from the Catholic party. In book II of *On the Trinity* (no. 8), he says:

> “But neither is the Son a part of the Father . . . nor can a portion be all things by nature. But he is perfect from the perfect, because he who has all things gave all things. Nor must he be thought not to have given because he possesses, or not to possess because he gave.”

In book III of *On the Trinity* (no. 4):

> “Therefore the perfect Son of the perfect Father, the only-begotten offspring of the unbegotten God, who received all things from him who has all things—God from God, Spirit from Spirit, Light from Light—confidently says: ‘The Father is in me, and I in the Father.’ For as the Father is Spirit, so also the Son is Spirit; as the Father is God, so also the Son is God; as the Father is Light, so also the Son is Light. Thus, from those things which are in the Father come those things in which the Son exists: that is, the whole Son was born from the whole Father [Col. 0774D]; not from elsewhere, because nothing existed before the Son; not from nothing, because the Son is from God; not in part, because the fullness of the Godhead is in the Son; nor in certain things, because it is in all things; but as he who could so willed, as he who begot so knows.”

Again, to the same effect (*On the Trinity*, book III, no. 17):

> “No one knows God unless he confesses both [Col. 0775A] the Father, the Father of the only-begotten Son, and the Son—not born from a portion, or an expansion, or an emission, but born from him ineffably and incomprehensibly, as Son from Father—possessing the fullness of the divinity from which and in which he was born: true, infinite, and perfect God. For this is God’s fullness. If anything of these things is lacking, it will no longer be the fullness which it pleased God to have dwell in him. This is proclaimed by the Son; this is made manifest to those who do not know; thus the Father is glorified through the Son, when the Father of the Son is acknowledged to be such.”

Thereafter, and especially in no. 9 and the following sections of book VI, he expressly and by name condemns every heretical explanation already mentioned. Let us select a few from many (*On the Trinity*, book VI, no. 10):

> “The devout faith of the Church condemns Manichaeus, according to the preachers of heretical madness.
