For it knows no portion in the Son, but knows whole God from whole God; knows one from one; not cut off but born; knows that the birth of God is neither a diminution of him who begets nor an infirmity of him who is born . . . For these things are thus known to it from God the only-begotten: that the Father and the Son are one, that the fullness of divinity is in the Son. Therefore it hates the notion of a portion of one substance applied to the Son, and through the truth of the birth reveres in the Son the proper reality of true Divinity.”

Thus, too, he introduces and refutes these impious disputants: both those who located the generation of the divine Word in some sort of emanation, and those who said that the Father would be corporeal and mutable if he had begotten the Son in the manner maintained by the orthodox (*On the Trinity*, book VI, no. 17):

> “If the Son is changeable because he is from God, then God is corporeal, who brought forth or extended from himself that which was his own into a Son. Why are you anxious lest God be changeable? We confess the birth; we proclaim the only-begotten, having been taught this by God. But you, lest the birth remain, lest the only-begotten God remain in the faith of the Church, oppose the nature of the unchangeable God, which cannot be extended or stretched out. I would offer you, unhappy error, examples even from certain natures in the world which beget, so that you might not suppose birth to be extension, nor believe that the natures of those born are losses to those begetting, and so that you might see that many living souls are begotten from living beings without bodily union. But it would be impious not to believe God concerning himself; and it would be judged the madness of ultimate frenzy to remove the authority for faith from him whose reverence you profess for life.”

Again, in no. 11 of book VII of *On the Trinity*:

> “For, as we have frequently said, we proclaim in the Son not the mystery of division but of birth.”

See what the Maurist Fathers note on this passage. Finally, not to cite everything, he discusses this subject very fully in nos. 22 and 23 of the book entitled *On the Synods*, or *On the Faith of the Easterners*. If you want much material on this question, consult Petavius.

[Col. 0775D] Book V of *On the Trinity*, chapter 6; and again chapter 8, no. 9 and following.

Here it pleases me only to cite Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, whom we have as a great defender of Catholic truth.

[Col. 0775D] In the letter to Alexander Constantine; the letter in Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, book I, chapter 4.

> “Concerning these”—he speaks of the Father and the Son—“we believe as the apostolic [Col. 0775D] Church believes: in one unbegotten Father . . . and in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, begotten not from nothing but from him who is Father; not after the manner of bodies, by cuts or the outflow of divisions, as Sabellius and Valentinus suppose, but in an inexplicable and ineffable manner, according to the words of the Prophet which we cited above: ‘Who shall declare his generation?’”

I pray you, consult what Gezo, Abbot of Derthon, published on this subject.

[Col. 0776D] *On the Body and Blood of Christ*, chapter 1 and following, p. 253 of volume III of Muratori’s *Anecdota*.

From this you will learn how great Hilary’s authority was among the ancients.

52. Recall what was said in no. 19. Here I cite only Athanasius’s admonitions [Col. 0776A] on this very subject.

[Col. 0776D] Oration V, translated, I think, by Petavius, in book VI of *On the Trinity*, chapter 2, no. 9.

> “The Word is not a dissoluble thing, nor merely a significant sound; rather, he is the substantial Word and substantial Wisdom, who is truly the Son of God. For unless he is substantial, God will be speaking into the air and into a body, having nothing more than human beings,” etc.

For the remaining Fathers who discuss this subject, consult Petavius in the very passage mentioned in note 19, namely chapter 2 of book VI of *On the Trinity*.

…that the Holy Spirit exists, 23 who gives life to and confirms all things which God made through the Word, 24. That there is one baptism 25 by which human beings are regenerated in God, 26. One must also believe in the resurrection of the dead in the same flesh, 27. There will be a judgment of God, in which, according to a person’s deeds, punishments will be rendered to the wicked (the manuscript has *repnentur*), or the appointed rewards of good works will be bestowed, 28. So great is the difference between Jews who convert and Gentiles who believe, 29: what God is, or what he is like, and how great; who and what the Son of God was, and who the Holy Spirit is. For the Three are one.

## II

It is certainly fitting that your prudence should know that we are able to speak and know these things concerning God—or, as the manuscript has it, “this”—which either he himself wished human beings to know concerning himself [Col. 0734C], or to which it has been permitted to a human being, by his permission, to attain.

Let no human being seek him on earth or compose him among fabricated things, lest he believe him to be like anyone else, 31. For true faith has always set forth God thus: unbegotten, unfashioned, 32 incomprehensible, 33 beyond estimation, 34 invisible, 35 and impassible, 36; and therefore the one true God, 37 who has begotten some things, 38 made some things, arranged and ordered them, 39 and adorned them, 40. That the excellent and just Judge commands what is just, 41. Therefore every human being is without excuse who has not recognized his Maker 42 at the time of recognition, 43 and after his departure will have a just Judge: he who has not judged that he should be converted in his own time, but from what is past, 44. These things it is lawful to believe concerning God, 45. Whoever has believed them keeps himself from every injustice, 46. Having done what is good and just, [Col. 0734D] he shall have eternal rest in life, 47.

## III

Having a Son: do not at once suppose that I say he was begotten in the manner in which human beings are procreated, 48, 49; but, as it is fitting to believe concerning God, that God has a Son, born indeed from himself, 50—not with his substance divided, nor the substance of his majesty divided, so that thereby he may appear passible, 51. Nor must the Word be thought to have been brought forth from the mouth as one like our own, so that he consists of letters and syllables; nor is the Son of God composite and therefore to be regarded as dissoluble, 52. Nor is he from nothing, as the remaining things were made, lest [Col. 0735A]

[Note: [Col. 0735]

53. Substitute “sons,” or, if you prefer, “words,” to whom you must beware of calling the Son of God equal or similar. Hilary is plainly attacking here the impious confession of Arius (*in Hilary, On the Trinity*, book IV, no. 12, and book VI, no. 5). Arius, having confessed that the Father, whom he alone acknowledged as God, “begot the only-begotten Son before all ages, through whom he made both the age and all things,” added: “a perfect creature of God, but not like one of the creatures; a work, but not like the other works,” etc.

I think that Hilary wishes here to teach that, if the Son is admitted to have been produced from nothing—which anyone must necessarily do who recognizes him as a creature, however supremely perfect—then the only-begotten of God will be similar, and therefore equal, to the remaining creatures in the chief and essential definition of creaturehood. For this alone separates creature from God: that the creature is from nothing, whereas God is from himself.

The Arian opinion, moreover, so displeased all those who were not outright Arians that it was condemned even by persons not regarded as wholly Catholic. These were the decrees of the Synod of Sardica (*Hilary, On the Synods*, nos. 34–35):

> “But those who say that the Son of God is from non-existent things, or from another substance and not from God . . . the holy and Catholic Church anathematizes.”

Indeed, in the second Synod of Sirmium, whose profession of faith Hilary gives, the same error is condemned in these words (*ibid.*, no. 38, anathema 1):

> “But those who say, ‘The Son is from no existent things,’ or ‘from another substance and not from God,’ or ‘there was a time or age when he was not,’ the holy and Catholic Church knows to be alien.”

To pass over the rest who refuted this blasphemy of Arius, Hilary often and splendidly rejects it. I choose one passage of Hilary, lest I seem excessive in a very well-known matter. In no. 2 of book XII of *On the Trinity* (p. 409, vol. II), he wrote:

> “For we know the Lord Jesus Christ not as a creature, because he himself is not one; nor as a work, because he is himself Lord of all works; but as God, the proper generation of God the Father,” etc.

54. This is an exceedingly explicit judgment of Hilary, from which it may easily become known that the author of both works is one and the same (*On the Trinity*, book II, no. 9, p. 32):

> “Both possess the secret of this birth. And if perhaps anyone blames his own understanding because he cannot attain the mystery of this generation—although both the Father and the Son are absolute understanding—he will hear from me with greater grief that it is unknown. I do not know; I do not inquire; yet I shall find consolation. The archangels do not know, angels have not heard, the ages do not contain it, the prophet did not perceive it, the apostle did not ask, [Col. 0776D] the Son himself did not disclose it.”

He also calls the birth of the divine only-begotten Son ineffable in no. 12 of book II and no. 16 of book VI of *On the Trinity*.

But lest I seem to cite Hilary alone, here is Athanasius (*Oration III*, p. 214), saying:

> “It is unfitting to ask how the Word exists from God, or how he is God’s radiance, or how God begets, and what is the manner of God’s generation. For one who would dare such things would be mad, attempting by his discourse to explain a matter inexplicable, proper to the divine nature, and known to God himself alone and to his Son. It is the same as if they inquired where God is, how God is, and of what sort the Father is. But just as it is impious to ask such questions, and characteristic of those who do not know God, so it is not lawful to adopt the same audacity in investigating the Son’s generation.”

Prudentius too, acting in his *Apotheosis* not as a poet but as a theologian, rebukes the Arians, most audacious investigators of the ineffable generation, in these verses:

> They press further, searching into what  
> Begetting itself may be—if it is lawful for human minds  
> To stretch as far as the secret which precedes  
> All ages and days of old, which rises  
> Above beginning itself and surpasses whatever humanity can seek.  
> Since the way to know the seeds of beginnings is difficult,  
> To what mortal will it be granted to discover what  
> God did beyond beginning, or in what manner  
> He brought forth the Word, who lacks every beginning?  
> This alone we know: that God is handed down to us as he  
> Whom the unbegotten begetter begot—one and one. Etc.

If you desire other Fathers, Petavius will provide them (*On the Trinity*, book V, chapter 6). I select one to cite here: Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, an outstanding critic of Arius and his heresy (*in Theodoret*, book I of the *History*, chapter 4):

> “The inexplicable subsistence of the only-begotten Son of God surpasses the most diligent comprehension of the Evangelists and even of the angels themselves. Therefore, in my judgment, he ought not to be counted among the pious,” etc.

55. Recall here the passages of Hilary and Alexander of Alexandria which we have just cited: “The angels do not know; angels have not heard,” etc. But you may conveniently cite here too, if you wish, the things we shall shortly bring forward. Moreover, the letter of Alexander of Alexandria which I mentioned treats this argument very fully.

56. Although Arius seemed to admit the eternity of the Son when he confessed that “God [the Father] begot the only-begotten Son before all ages, through whom he made both the age and all things,” he nevertheless in reality denied that he was eternal, acknowledging “God [the Father] alone as unbegotten, alone as everlasting, alone without beginning, possessing immortality” (*in Hilary, On the Trinity*, book IV, no. 12). That subsequent followers of Arius in impiety followed this error is learned from the documents abundantly collected by Petavius. I select some of them, which I note at the foot of the page.

[Col. 0777D] Petavius, *On the Trinity*, II.9.8; III.10.5–6; and book V, chapter 9.

I ask the reader to consult these for himself, praying that, in reading the letter of Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, of which I have spoken, he may clearly see how immediately those Catholics contending against Arius took it to heart to insist upon the eternity of the divine Word.

Although some Arians, either more moderate or perhaps more cunning, readily admitted that the Son was begotten before times, they nevertheless refused, when required to confess that he was coeternal with the Father, to do so. Rather, they introduced certain times which some called fictitious, fabricated, imaginary, or prior [Col. 0778A] times, preceding created things and therefore the heavens, sun, and stars, by whose motion and revolutions we measure times. They described the Father’s Word as begotten in those fictitious, fabricated, imaginary, prior times, and therefore as a genuine creature, though superior to and earlier than other creatures.

Catholics justly refuted the error of all these persons; theologians possess their arguments. Consult them, if you wish.

[Col. 0777D] See Petavius in the passage just cited, namely book II of *On the Trinity*, etc.

For one explaining Hilary’s little work, it is enough to confirm this doctrine from other passages in Hilary. He therefore says:

[Col. 0777D] *On the Trinity*, book IV, nos. 5–6, pp. 73–74, vol. II.

> “They also think that they can cleverly oppose prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic teaching by proclaiming the Son’s birth within time. For, because they falsely charge us with asserting that the Son always existed, it is necessary, by excluding his always having existed, that they confess his birth from time. For if he was not always, there will be a time when he was not. And if there is a time when he was not, there will be time before him; because he who is not always began to exist from time. But one who lacks time cannot lack that which always is. They assert that they reject the proposition that the Son always existed for this reason: lest, through his always having existed, he be believed to be without birth—as though, because he is said always to have existed, he is proclaimed unbegotten.”

After a few intervening words:

> “He confesses the Father as eternal and free from origin; he also confesses the origin of the Son from eternity—not himself from a beginning, but from the one without beginning; not from himself, but born from him who always exists from no one, born from eternity, namely a birth taking its origin from the Father’s eternity.”

If the reader wishes to consult other passages of Hilary, let him go to those which I note at the foot of the page.

[Col. 0777D] *On the Trinity*, book XII, no. 21, p. 420, “Therefore he would be,” etc.; *ibid.*, no. 27, p. 424, “But indeed when in matters of God,” etc.; *On the Synods*, no. 24, p. 475, “And if anyone [calls] the Word,” etc.; *Commentary on Psalm* 63, no. 10, p. 181, vol. I, “Now if the heretic destroys the faith,” etc.

It is not surprising that the orthodox so frequently insisted upon the eternity of the Word. Although the Arians evaded other points so thoroughly that they did not hesitate even to confess the only-begotten of God as God—

[Col. 0777D] That is, they warned that by this term *god* an inferior god, or one improperly called God, was meant. See Petavius, *On the Trinity*, II.9.4, “But that he is God,” etc. See also no. 69 and what we shall note there.

—yet, when they were asked to confess him eternal, they introduced evasive phrases. They said that he existed before the ages and that God the Father had used him, as it were, as a hand and instrument for creating the ages. Some less strict followers of Arius, such as the Fathers of Antioch, also confessed that he had always been in the beginning with God.

[Col. 0777D] The Synod of Antioch in 341, as the Maurist Fathers who edited Hilary’s works teach us, is rightly and deservedly suspect to many. See the Maurist Fathers’ note on the profession of faith issued at this Synod and rendered in Latin by Hilary in no. 29 of *On the Synods*. Yet the same Maurist Fathers observe that Athanasius and Socrates, when they report this formula of faith, omitted the word “always,” from which Hilary testifies that the Arians strongly recoiled in no. 5 of book IV of *On the Trinity*. But since Hilary teaches that it was actually expressed by the Antiochene Fathers, I do not doubt it in the least. See also what Hilary subsequently says, namely no. 33 of the same book, *On the Synods*.

Yet they refused to confess him truly and simply eternal, or everlasting, declaring that God the Father alone was everlasting and without beginning.

[Col. 0778D] See the profession of faith composed by Arius in Hilary, *On the Trinity*, IV.12, etc.

In addition to Arius’s ancient confession, we have other examples of this matter.

[Col. 0778D] Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, in Theodoret, book I, chapter 4, reporting the Arian view: “There was a time when the Son of God was not,” etc.

For there is no need to discuss this matter at length here, I offer one clear example. Palladius and Secundianus were condemned by the Council of Aquileia as unquestionably guilty of the Arian heresy because they refused to confess the only-begotten of God as everlasting. I pray you, read both the acts of the Council themselves, which, according to the highly probable opinion of many, Ambrose’s diligence preserved for us—

[Col. 0778D] Vol. II of the Maurist edition of Ambrose, pp. 790 and 792: “He specifically says that the Father alone is everlasting.” “Ambrose said: Does the Son of God possess immortality according to divinity, or does he not?”

—and the letter written by that Council to the emperors [Col. 0779A].

[Col. 0779D] Pp. 807–808, no. 5. See further what is said on this subject in the edition of the works of St. Ambrose prepared by the Maurist Fathers, after letter VIII, p. 786, vol. II: “Ambrose, having read Arius’s letter,” etc.

It contains these words: “They wished rather to follow Arius than to confess the Son of God as everlasting God . . .”

Hence, denial of eternity to the Word was a certain indication of an explicitly Arian profession. Therefore Eudoxius, though not entirely orthodox, nevertheless, in order to oppose Ursacius, Valens, and others associated in Arius’s impiety, and to establish the milder error of Aetius, took care that the eternity of the only-begotten of God should be expressed in three canons at the Synod of Ancyra—namely, X, XI, and XII (*Hilary, On the Synods*, no. 23). Hilary himself, in the short profession of faith which he issued against the Arians (*ibid.*, no. 64), required Catholics not only to confess that the Father is not within times, but also not to deny that the Son is cotemporal with the Father. For a fuller illumination of this passage, the material which we shall present in no. 76 will be useful.

57. Elsewhere I have said (*Preface*, chapter 1, no. 3) that Hilary, though writing in Latin, sometimes employs Greek words in order to explain himself more clearly. Whether he himself wrote this word in Latin characters—as Richard Simon maintains that the Latin Fathers consistently did—or in Greek characters, let the reader judge. In either event, this word, as anyone will readily recognize, denotes the only-begotten of God as denying or excluding time, that is, timeless, and therefore before times and eternal.

58. Lest it be objected that the orthodox said these things rashly, they often sought arguments by which to prove the eternity of the divine Word which they maintained. Among these, the chief seems to be the argument which Hilary briefly touches upon here, derived from the immutability of the Father—an immutability we must admit if we make him God. For he depicts as changed one who depicts the Father of the only-begotten Son as becoming a Father in time.

Other Fathers also use this proof, whom Petavius does not omit.

[Col. 0779D] Book V of *On the Trinity*, chapter 8, §§4, 5, and following, but especially §11.

Hilary certainly presses it often and fully, as in no. 5 of book IV of *On the Trinity*, and frequently elsewhere.

[Col. 0779D] Pp. 73–74, vol. II: “For because they falsely,” etc.

But it is preferable here to give one passage, from book XII of *On the Trinity* (no. 21, p. 420):

> “It is one thing to be always eternal without an author; another to be coeternal with the Father, that is, with the author. For where there is a father who is author, there is also birth; but where the author is eternal, there too is the eternity of the birth. For as birth is from the author, so from an eternal author is eternal birth. Everything which always is, moreover, is also eternal. Yet not everything eternal is also unbegotten. For what is born from eternity has an eternal existence as something born; but what is not born is, with eternity, unbegotten. But if what is born from eternity is not born eternal, then neither will the Father be an eternal author. If, therefore, anything is lacking from eternity to him who is born from the eternal Father, that same thing is without doubt lacking to the author; for what is infinite to him who begets is infinite also to him who is born. Reason and understanding admit no intermediate thing between the birth of God the Son and the generation of God the Father, because in generation there is birth, and in birth generation. Each exists without interval from the other, because without each neither exists.”

Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, pursues this same argument; I wish you would read him.

[Col. 0779D] In Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, book I, chapter 4: [Col. 0780D] “It must necessarily be said that the Father is always Father,” etc.

Augustine briefly touches on it in these words (*Letter* formerly 174, now 238, no. 24): “The Father always begets, and the Son is always born.” Add what Petavius says (*On the Trinity*, book II, chapter 5).

59. Scripture most explicitly testifies that God is free from every change and new state; the Fathers and reason suggest this as well. But it is not the purpose of the present undertaking to pursue these matters. Consult theologians, and above all Petavius (*Theology*, vol. I, book III, chapter 1).

This being established, Hilary proves that the generation of the divine Word is eternal from the fact that otherwise God the Father would change: he would begin in time to have a Son.

Hilary, however, anticipates what may readily be objected against God’s established immutability: namely, that God created the world in time, and yet the divine excellence and perfection are not thereby diminished. He anticipates it, I say, by warning that no change is introduced into God through the creation of things, because all things were established by an eternal and immutable decree, and all things were disposed in the most perfect divine idea; and thus they were carried into execution as they had been established and arranged.

[Col. 0780B] He had taught this elsewhere.

[Col. 0780D] “For he himself, God, is the head and beginning of all things, and all things were created in him, although afterwards, from the treasures stored up in himself, he brought forth each thing according to the decision of eternal power.” Hilary, *On Psalm* 91, no. 4.

Theologians have devised other explanations to exclude from God the change which might perhaps be feared from the temporal creation of things; Petavius recounts a great many of them (*Dogmatic Theology*, vol. I, book III, chapter 1). But Hilary chose—as I have said—to have recourse to the immutability of the divine decree, and therefore of God’s knowledge and idea.

I select the most explicit of several passages in Hilary: it occurs in no. 40 of book XII of *On the Trinity*:

> “For the preparation of things to be created is perpetual and eternal. The body of this universe was not brought into being through piecemeal thoughts, as though heaven had first been thought of, and then afterwards God had undertaken concern and deliberation for the earth; as though each matter had been separately considered: first, that it should be spread out in a plain; then, that by a better plan it should be raised into mountains; again, that it should be varied with hills; next, that it should be made habitable even on the very summits; that heaven should be prepared and set apart as God’s dwelling; that exhalations of wind should firmly hold clouds on high; then, that fixed springs should flow beneath heaven; and finally, that the earth should be secured by strong foundations. For Wisdom declares herself to be prior to each of these things. But since all things under heaven were made through God, and Christ was present when heaven was fashioned, and he precedes the eternity even of heaven prepared, this does not permit us to suppose that God had partial thoughts about trivial matters; for the entire preparation of these things is coeternal with God.”

60. Hilary also teaches elsewhere, not obscurely, that the world was created for human beings—“for us,” etc.—as when he says (*On Psalm* 65, no. 6, p. 197, vol. I):

> “For who would not tremble before the majesty of him who established the ages, created the world, measured times by their recurring succession and course, adorned heaven with stars, filled earth with fruits, enclosed the sea with barriers, and chose humanity either to use these things or to rule over them?”

He repeats the same point in commentaries on other psalms, which I strongly urge you to read.

[Col. 0780D] *Commentary on Psalm* 63, no. 9; *Commentary on Psalm* 134, no. 14; but especially *Commentary on Psalm* 118, letter X, nos. 1–2, p. 334, vol. I.

Let the reader judge whether that passage of Psalm 8, “You have subjected all things beneath his feet,” etc., indicates the same thing. I shall discuss this subject at length in a separate dissertation.

61. That is: although he had not yet created, he had nevertheless arranged and ordered them within himself. See no. 59.

[Col. 0781A] **62.** I certainly think that *simul* (“at once”) should be read, since our manuscript reads *semel* (“once”: “to make all things once”). For the contrast requires it: on the one hand, a simultaneous creation; on the other, the creation of all things distributed over several days. Hilary is less pleased with the former and embraces the latter—that is, creation apportioned among six days—although, in Ecclesiasticus, when speaking of creation, we read “at once”: “He who lives for ever created all things at once” [Ecclus. 18:1].

By what means this passage is reconciled with Genesis, interpreters of Sacred Scripture and theologians will explain to you. Once that point is established, I take the meaning of this passage to be as follows. It was not through God’s inability that the universe was not arranged in a single instant; rather, all things were arranged through the interval of six days so that, as though by stages, and according to the distinction of each thing’s rank and honor, everything might obey God as creator and disposer. If you desire a fuller interpretation of this passage, Ambrose’s words will provide it. I cite them all the more readily because I consider it highly probable that Ambrose, in setting them forth, had in mind the teaching of the earlier Fathers. Here, then, are Ambrose’s words [*On Cain and Abel*, II.6.22]:

> For the world itself is read to have been made distinctly, although beforehand a part of it was unformed; for the earth was invisible and unformed. Clearly light was first made, and God called the light; and God divided between light and darkness, and the darkness was called Night. And we read, in order, each of the things made: heaven, earth, fruit-bearing trees, diverse animals. The lighter things, air and fire, were distributed above; the heavier things below—namely, earth and water. God could certainly have commanded all things to be made at once; but he preferred to preserve distinction, which we should imitate in all our affairs, and especially in the reciprocal exchange of favors.

Interpreters further observe that created things emerged, as it were, gradually from that first matter: the less excellent first, and then the more excellent, the sequence being concluded by man, more excellent than all.

**63.** This passage seems somewhat obscure; you will make it utterly obscure if you read, as the manuscript does, *et nulla* (“and nothing”). But I certainly think *et nuda* (“and naked”) should be read—that is, without adornment or appearance. I take the sense to be this: God wished all things, ordered and progressively arranged, each according to its own rank and honor, to obey God, who brought forth creatures on successive days, lest those earlier unformed elements should be despised: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth; but the earth was empty and void” (others read “unformed”), “and darkness was upon the face of the deep” [Gen. 1:1 ff.].

For who would not despise them, and prefer to them things already beautiful and endowed with their own appearance and form? Yet while I offer this explanation, I fear that something may be missing in this period which would more aptly connect those earlier words, *passiva et nuda* (“passive and naked”), or, if you prefer, *nulla* (“nothing”), with the subsequent *inter se antiquiora* (“earlier than one another”). Whether my suspicion is plausible or not, let the reader judge.

**64.** By adding the word *magis* (“more”), I have somewhat corrected the defective reading of our manuscript. For it reads: *quanto illa, quae nulli*, etc. Who does not see that the word *magis* is demanded by the argument Hilary employs? This argument is of the kind which the Scholastics call from the lesser to the greater, or *a fortiori*.

If I undertook to adduce testimonies of the Fathers and Scholastics to confirm this argument, I should be almost endless. Certainly those Scholastics who maintain that the mystery of the Incarnation was wholly hidden and incomprehensible even to the angels themselves rely especially on the Fathers. It is enough for me to cite Leo and Hilary. The former repeatedly insists upon this, especially in the passages noted at the foot of the page [Sermon IX on the Nativity, no. 1, “It indeed surpasses …”; and Sermon X under the same title, or on the Nativity, no. 1, “But because of our Lord and Savior …”; and no. 4 of the same sermon, “But the Nativity of the Lord …”]. The latter develops it more fully in no. 12 of Book I of *On the Trinity* [vol. II, p. 9: “Therefore this doctrine of the divine sacrament …”], and in no. 19 of Book III of the same work, that is, *On the Trinity* [ibid., p. 60: “You ask how …”].

**65.** Hilary further presses the proof he had previously advanced. He first shows that Christ’s bodily birth is rightly called hidden, or ineffable, since Scripture itself calls it an overshadowing; then, having established this, he infers what he had just said: namely, that the eternal generation of the Word must, *a fortiori*, be called hidden or ineffable. If you wish, read Hilary discussing that overshadowing [*On the Trinity*, II.26, “But lest perhaps …”].

**66.** Recall what I said in nos. 54 and 55.

**67.** Recall what was said in nos. 31, 33, and 54. In the manuscript, *concussus* occurs in place of *concessos*; it is plainly an error, and I have therefore judged it should be corrected.

**68.** Hilary now undertakes a fuller explanation of the dignity and excellence of the divine Word, while at the same time setting forth a sufficiently extensive and accurate confession of his faith. Who could doubt that, when Hilary attributes these titles to Christ, he attributes them to him especially insofar as he is God? Yet many also belong to Christ insofar as he is man—or, to say it better and more truly, insofar as God is man—because of what theologians call the *communication of idioms*.

Hilary habitually repeats and recalls the same doctrines; anyone who has read through his books *On the Trinity* will acknowledge this. He himself gives the reason for this practice in these words [*On the Synods*, no. 62]: “For the infinite and immeasurable God could neither be understood nor displayed in the brief utterances of human speech; for brevity of speech often misleads both hearers and teachers.” Let us now elucidate the rest of his statements.

**69.** The word *initio* (“in the beginning”) may refer either to the Son’s eternal generation, concerning which enough has been said in no. 56, or to the remaining titles attributed to the same Son. Hilary explains elsewhere, with the greatest clarity, in what sense he calls the Son of God—and with this addition of the word *initio*—God:

> Therefore the Son of God is not a false God, nor an adopted God, nor a God merely so named, but true God … For he is God through whom all things were made.  
> [*On the Trinity*, V.5, vol. II, p. 107.]

And here, to note it in passing, not only the Arians but also those who abused Hilary’s authority in order to make Christ an adopted Son are refuted: for if he is God, how can he be adopted?

**70.** Before I proceed, the reader should know that these titles and other related ones, which are attributed to the only-begotten Son of God by ancient theologians, fall, as it were, into two classes. Some were attributed to the only-begotten God by the orthodox because Arians refused to attribute them to him, assigning them to the Father alone. Others were attributed because, while the Arians themselves—or at least the Semi-Arians—attributed them to the only-begotten Son and exalted them with great display and praise, the orthodox feared that, if they did not attribute them to the only-begotten Son, they would seem to speak less nobly of him than the Arians did.

Now when Hilary here calls the Word “true wisdom,” he means divine wisdom, without a cause. For Arius, in precisely this sense, acknowledged the one God—that is, the Father alone—as alone without beginning and alone true; while Hilary, whom we have just cited [no. 69], calls the only-begotten Son of God “true God.” Thus, although at the Council of Aquileia Palladius had confessed that “the only-begotten Son of God is wisdom” [“Palladius said: He is Wisdom,” p. 793, vol. II of the Maurists’ edition of Ambrose], because he refused to profess him as divine wisdom and wisdom without a cause—and hence as true wisdom in the sense now at issue—assigning that title to the Father alone, Ambrose did not hesitate to say of Palladius: “Palladius, as I see, has even attempted to deny that the Son of God is wise.”

Nor would I criticize those who say that Hilary teaches this in order to refute the impiety—indeed, rather the madness—of those who said that the Son of God is not wisdom itself but a work of wisdom. I judge it worthwhile here to quote the holy Doctor’s words, since they admirably confirm the point we are now explaining [*Commentary on Matthew*, XI.9, p. 724]:

> For many are accustomed to evade the apostolic saying [1 Cor. 1:24] that calls Christ the wisdom of God and the power of God in these ways: they say that, in creating him from the Virgin, God’s effective wisdom and power were displayed, and that in his birth there is to be understood a work of divine prudence and power; and thus that in him there is the efficacy of wisdom rather than its nature. Lest anything of this sort be understood, he called himself Wisdom, showing in himself Wisdom itself, not merely those things that belong to wisdom. For faith, hope, charity, chastity, fasting, self-control, humility, and kindness are works of wisdom; but these are works of the nature, not the nature itself; and the thing itself which brings things about does not consist in the things that are brought about.

Others may judge whether Hilary states the following in order to refute this madness [*On Psalm* 66.29, p. 235]: “But the Lord Jesus Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God.”

**71.** See nos. 19 and 20.

**72.** It has long been observed that Hilary understands God by the name “Spirit.” See, please, the preface [nos. 57 ff., especially nos. 62 and 63] to Volume I of St. Hilary, published by the Maurist monks. Add, if you wish, what is read in Book XII of *On the Trinity*, no. 8: “But because he declared to us a birth of Spirit from Spirit,” etc.

Hilary’s well-known passage is worth citing here [*On the Trinity*, IX.14]: “When he had emptied himself, so that Christ, remaining Spirit—that is, God—might nevertheless be the same Christ as man.” Nor is it surprising that God is understood under the name Spirit. For by antonomasia God is Spirit—that is, the most excellent Spirit. And God alone is Spirit if, by the term *spirit*, you understand that which by itself most perfectly comprehends all things; in this sense some of the ancients seem to have understood the word *spirit* [in the sense apparently intended by those who maintain that God alone is incorporeal and that all others—including angels themselves and our souls—are bodily; this is taught, to avoid citing many, by the author of *Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, believed to be Gennadius, chs. 11–13, and by others cited by Le Quien on ch. 3, Book II of John of Damascus’s *On the Faith*].

However that may be, besides those cited by the distinguished editor of St. Hilary’s works [Preface to vol. I, no. 58 ff.], here is a clear passage of Tertullian establishing that the ancient Fathers denoted God by the term Spirit. Thus he begins his book *On Prayer*: “The Spirit of God and the Word of God … both are Jesus Christ.” If you desire other passages of Tertullian, the most distinguished Muratori will indicate them to you [note 1 on this book of Tertullian, vol. III of the *Anecdota*].

Almost all the remaining titles subsequently listed—Way, Light, and so forth—are expressly found in that famous profession of faith,

> which was set forth at the Synod held for the dedication of the completed church of Antioch. Ninety-seven bishops who were present issued it when one of the bishops had come under suspicion of holding erroneous views.

Here is what those bishops declared [Hilary, *On the Synods*, nos. 28–29, vol. II, p. 478]:

> We believe … in one God, the Father … and in one Lord Jesus Christ, his only-begotten Son, God through whom are all things, who was begotten from the Father, God from God, whole from whole, one from one, perfect from perfect, King from King, Lord from Lord, Word, Wisdom, Life, true Light, true Way, Resurrection, Shepherd, Door, unchangeable and immutable, the unchangeable image of divinity, essence, power, and glory; the first-born of all creation, who always was in the beginning with God … the mediator of God and human beings, predestined for our faith and the guide of life.

If you say that Hilary had this profession in view, you will certainly say what has seemed probable to some. Indeed, Hilary criticizes this profession only in this respect [no. 31]: “that it seems perhaps not to have spoken explicitly enough of the undifferentiated likeness of the Father and Son, especially since it signifies that it understood the proper substance, order, and glory of each of the named Father, Son, and Holy Spirit to be indicated in their names, so that they are three in substance but one in harmony.”

That profession of faith which Hilary calls the second creed of the Eastern Synod [*On the Synods*, nos. 33–34] is less rich in titles; nevertheless, it too declares of the only-begotten Son of God: “who is Word, Wisdom, Power, Life, and true Light.”

But to return to Hilary: he teaches these things not only in the letter we are explaining, but also elsewhere. On Psalm 63 he says [no. 10, vol. I, p. 181]:

> If the heretic destroys faith, he will recognize that the Son of God has always existed, separated from the Father by no interval of time; that he himself is the Word, Power, and Wisdom of God; that he was the maker of the world and also the creator of man.

He includes more in his exposition of Psalm 118 [letter IX, likewise no. 9, p. 334]:

> God spoke the Law through Moses; he spoke through the prophets. But this is the law of God, not also the law of the mouth of God. Now the mouth of God is he who is also the power of God, the wisdom of God, the arm of God, the image of God—namely God and our Lord Jesus Christ.

Basil the Great teaches the same. I would gladly cite his words, were they not numerous, especially since he also gives the reason for these very titles. But the reader can easily consult the passages I mean in chapter 8—elsewhere nos. 17 and 19—of *On the Holy Spirit to Amphilochius*: namely, “Because of his manifold beneficence toward us,” etc.; and, “He does all things by the touch of power and by the operation of goodness of will: he feeds, enlightens, nourishes, leads, heals, raises up,” etc.

If you desire others who enumerate titles belonging to Christ, you will easily find them in the books of ancient writers. I indicate only two here. One is that writer to whom was formerly attributed Sermon 190 *On Time*, now rejected into the appendix as no. 113; I quoted his words in note 20 [p. 60]. The other is Ausonius, thus entreating Christ [*Morning Prayer*]:

> O Christ, graciously plead before the eternal Father,  
> Savior, God and Lord, my glory, Word,  
> Son—true from the True, Light from Light—  
> abiding with the eternal Father, reigning through the ages.

Why should anyone wonder at this, since Scripture either plainly attributes these very titles to Christ or allows them readily to be attributed to him, if one considers what Scripture declares concerning Christ? I noted some instances at the end of Hilary’s letter itself, lest I seem to have asserted this rashly.

I admit, indeed, that Christ is not expressly called “the strength of the Lord,” unless perhaps you think he is the same one who sometimes appeared in the form of an angel and called himself Gabriel, or, if you prefer, spoke in Gabriel. But if he is called the arm of the Lord, or of God, will he not be called strength? The Fathers, I think, do not hesitate for this reason to call Christ the arm of God or of the Lord. Moreover, does not the word *virtus* (“power”) seem synonymous with *fortitudo* (“strength”)? The Fathers very often confer this title on Christ. I cite only Rufinus, who says [*Exposition of the Creed*, p. 73, Vallarsi edition]: “And what is the power of the Most High except Christ himself, who is the power of God and the wisdom of God?” If you desire other passages of the Fathers, the distinguished editor of St. Hilary’s works will provide them [Preface to vol. I, no. 61 ff.].

When I indicated passages in which Christ is called wine, I noted two—Matthew 9:17 and John 15:1. In the former occur the words: “Nor do they put new wine into old wineskins.” The ancients understood the allegory and term “wine” to mean the evangelical law and hence its author, Christ. In the latter: “I am the true vine.” The vine, so to speak, is the parent of wine. Yet I admit that Hilary may also have had in mind Proverbs 9:2: “Wisdom … has mixed her wine”; and verse 5: “Come, eat my bread and drink the wine which I have mixed for you.” For reputable interpreters teach that these words foretell the most holy sacrament of the altar, in which Christ himself is present under the species of bread and wine. He may likewise have had in view Matthew 26:29: “But I tell you, I shall not henceforth drink of this fruit of the vine.” For the fruit of the vine mentioned there is Christ himself hidden under the species of wine.

**73.** Since the Incarnation itself is for humankind, Christ likewise is for humankind our Life, our Light, and our Shepherd.

**74.** He alludes to Paul’s celebrated statement [Acts 17:28]: “In him we live and move and are.” Perhaps he also alludes to those passages in which Christ is called our life, or the fountain of life, the fountain of water springing up into eternal life.

**75.** That is: from the reading of the Scriptures each person will learn the things we have said about Christ, and therefore those very titles we have listed.

might be joined as similar and equal to the other things that were made; but [it is known] as the begetter himself knows and as the begotten himself [knows], as the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “No one knows the Father except the Son, nor does anyone know the Son except the Father” [Matt. 11:27]. Likewise we read in the Scriptures: “My mystery is for me; my mystery is for me” [Isa. 24:16]. And indeed it is fitting that that generation should be hidden, in which no one was present—not even a moment of time. For before the ages, and before anyone dared to conceive it, the Son of God was born without times—what in Greek they call *achronos* (ἀχρόνως, “timelessly”). For the Son always exists because the Father always exists. It is impious to assign to God something which he did not formerly possess, since God is always perfect. Thus even what was afterward fashioned for our sake was already present with him, if not in substance, then in complete disposition. For he was no less able to make all things at once, but [created them thus] so that all things, ordered and arranged by degrees, might obey according to their own rank and honor, and so that passive and nonexistent things, earlier than one another, might not remain dishonorable.

For if the birth undertaken by the Son of God for our sake is incomprehensible, not disclosed to mortals, how much more is that birth known to no one except God the Father and himself alone? For the angel Gabriel speaks to Mary as the Evangelist relates: “The Spirit of the Lord shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you” [Luke 1:35]. What is overshadowed is hidden; it is not known to all. Therefore, if this birth, arranged for our sake [the text seems to require *disposita*, “arranged,” rather than *deposita*], is unknown to us, how much more that birth which is far removed from us? And why do I say “from us,” rather than “from every heavenly creature”? It is therefore enough that we have seen what divinity has wished us to know. Knowledge must not be extended further, lest anyone be judged sacrilegious who has passed beyond the permitted boundaries of knowledge.

**IV.** Therefore we have received Christ as the Son of God: in the beginning, true Wisdom [1 Cor. 1:24: “the power of God and the wisdom of God”]; the Word, that is, Reason; Spirit [John 4:24: “God is Spirit,” etc.]; Way [John 14:6]; Light [John 1:9, and again 3:19]; Arm [Isa. 53:1 and John 12:38: “And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?”—a passage which very many refer to Christ; see Calmet on this passage]; Strength [see Calmet on the preceding passage]; Power [1 Cor. 1:24]; Truth [John 14:6]; Bread [John 6:35, 48]; Wine [Matt. 9:17 and John 15:1, etc.: “I am the true vine”]; Life [John 1:4; 14:6; and often elsewhere]; Door [John 10:1, 2, 7, 9]; Shepherd [ibid., 11, etc.]; and very many other things, which are for humankind. And all live in him; and each person, as time goes on and as Scripture teaches, will learn them.

If, therefore, we confess that the Son of God has been made known, then through him we know that God the Father has made both visible and invisible ages. For it is not lawful to believe that God began to act from the time when the world began the beginning of its own birth—

[Col. 0736A] **76.** I think the sense contained in these words is this. If, then, with Scripture revealing it, we confess that the Son of God has been made known to us, we also know that God the Father made both visible and invisible ages through the same Son. Nor is it lawful to think that God began to work when the world was created, or ceased once it had been created; for the Lord himself testifies that he has not ceased, when he says: “My Father works until now,” etc.

If by “visible and invisible ages” he means visible and invisible creatures, he teaches here precisely what he had taught earlier. See number, or note, 18. He could certainly have meant those creatures by these terms, through the synecdoche by which what is contained is denoted by the name of its container.

But if he means the ages themselves, the passage becomes somewhat more obscure. We know the visible ages—namely, those which we measure through the revolutions of the sun, stars, and heavens. But it is difficult to explain what invisible ages are. Does he mean those ages which some have called imaginary, but Hilary himself calls times grasped by opinion [*On the Trinity*, XII.27, p. 42], or, more explicitly [ibid., no. 28], eternal times?

> But in matters concerning God, that is, in God’s birth, nothing is not before eternal time … He who must be confessed to exist before eternal times cannot be understood to have begun after something. Therefore, if for anything to be born before eternal times belongs neither to human natures nor to understanding, and yet God is believed, in his confessions concerning himself, to say this: how does the unbelief of our time declare, through the judgment of human understanding, that what apostolic faith has said has always been born—that is, existed before eternal times—was not before it was born? For what is born before time is always born, because that which is before eternal time is always.  
> [Hilary, *On the Trinity*, XII.27–28.]

Let this be another’s judgment.

We should here observe that we may suppose that, when Hilary says, “For it is not lawful to believe that God worked from the point at which the world took the beginning of its birth from the same birth,” he held the opinion that the creation of the angels preceded the creation of these visible and perceptible things. Since this opinion belonged to many ancient theologians and Fathers, especially Greek ones [see Petavius, *On the Angels*, I.15; see also the note on Novatian’s words, *On the Trinity*, I: “Although also in the higher things …”], it was undoubtedly Hilary’s. For he wrote [*Against Auxentius*, no. 6]: “Either all the regenerate are not truly sons of God, or all angels—certainly created through Christ—were created not before all times and before absolutely all ages?”

**77.** If you refer Hilary’s words to that class of operations which theologians call *ad intra*, you will explain them easily. For those actions which were eternal and are to endure eternally remain immutable; for this reason, as Augustine has already observed [*Against an Arian Sermon*, ch. 24, otherwise no. 20, p. 40, vol. VIII of the Maurists’ edition]:

> Nor should it trouble you that the future-tense word is “he will receive,” as though he did not yet possess it. For words of time are used indifferently, although eternity is understood to remain without time. For he received, because he proceeded from the Father; and he receives, because he proceeds from the Father; and he will receive, because he will never cease to proceed from the Father. So God both is, was, and will be; yet he neither has, had, nor will have a beginning or end of time.

They embrace all times. But if you refer them to that class of actions which we call external, or *ad extra*: if God created angels before the visible world—which Hilary certainly thought—then we believe God was at work before the world took the beginning of its birth. Nor does he cease to work, since at every moment he creates souls to be infused into human bodies, preserves all things, and governs them. See the passages noted at the bottom of the page [*On the Trinity*, VII.17; and *On Psalm* 91, nos. 3, 4, 5 ff., vol. I, p. 266].

What the rest of the eternal Father is, Hilary teaches in no. 8 of his commentary on Psalm 91 [vol. I, p. 269: “Therefore, because the works of God …”]. To understand clearly the words, “nothing has ever happened to him, but he always is,” recall what we said in no. 59.

But if you understand the words *semper sit* (“he always is”) to mean that Hilary teaches that this attribute, Being, is proper to God, and hence to the Father, you will certainly understand them in the sense rendered highly probable by other statements of Hilary. For he once wrote [*On the Trinity*, XII.23–24, vol. II, p. 421]:

> But if that which the Father always is is always proper to the Father, then that which the Son always is must necessarily be always proper to the Son. And how will it enter our speech and understanding that he was not before he was born, to whom it is proper always to be what he was born? Therefore the only-begotten God, containing in himself the form and image of the invisible God, is equal in all those things which are proper to God the Father, through the fullness of true divinity in himself. For, as we have taught in previous books, in power and in worship, just as the Father is worthy of honor and mighty, so, because the Father always is, it belongs also to the Son always to be in that which he is as Son. For according to the saying to Moses, “He who is has sent me to you,” an understanding that does not doubt sees that “that which is” is proper to God; because what is cannot be understood or said not to be. For being and not being are contraries, and these distinct meanings do not unite in one and the same thing: for while one remains, the other will not be. Therefore, where there is being, not-being cannot enter either thought or speech. For our understanding, drawn backward and always recalled to the understanding of him who is, finds that for him this alone—what he is—is always prior; because what is infinite in God always withdraws itself from the return of our finite understanding, so that backward-reaching attention cannot grasp anything before that which is proper to God, namely always to be, because, in advancing through eternity toward the understanding of God, nothing other than God’s always being is ever encountered.

If you desire other Fathers, Petavius, whom I urge you to consult, will supply many [vol. I, *Dogmatic Theology*, ch. 6]. That this attribute is also proper to the Son is perhaps shown by many of the testimonies adduced to prove the eternity of the divine Word, and hence by many of those cited by Petavius in Book V, chapter 9, of *On the Trinity*. I select one which I consider very apt to our purpose, taken from the letter of Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, to the bishop of Constantinople of the same name [Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, I.4]: “Let no one take this ‘always’ as suggesting unbegottenness, as those whose minds are blinded suppose; for ‘was,’ ‘always,’ and ‘before the ages’ are not the same as unbegotten.”

**78.** See nos. 57 and 72. With regard to the word ἀνάστιτεν (*anastiten*), is it derived from ἀνίστημι (*anistēmi*), “I raise, rouse, restore, renew,” etc., or from the unattested verb ἀναστάω (*anastaō*)? Or must the manuscript here be considered corrupt? Let the reader judge.

**79.** Perhaps the word *constat* (“it is established”) or another related word is lacking, so that the text should read: “It is therefore established that there are very many things which he has made through the Son.” Yet I would not have you understand the word *plurima* (“very many”) as though Hilary thought that very many things indeed, but not all things, were created by the divine Word. For he repeatedly and most expressly insists on the evangelical statement: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.” See no. 18. Here, therefore, he uses *plurima* for “all.” What these are he immediately enumerates, adding: “For how many thrones are there,” etc. Who does not know that there are very many creatures, both bodily and without bodies, whose names we scarcely know, indeed some whose very names we do not know? Hilary therefore rightly says: “of which either the names alone are known to us, or not even those.”

**80.** The words, “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man,” are taken from the Apostle Paul [1 Cor. 2:9]. But because it seems to me highly probable that these words were inserted into the letter itself by an unlearned copyist, having previously stood in the margin as a confirmation, as it were, of the statement “how great a splendor do we suppose is in invisible things, which we cannot even estimate,” I think they should be deleted—or, if you prefer, returned to the margin.

Moreover, the word *quanti* in this place—“for how many thrones, how many powers,” etc.—in my judgment means “how many”; Tertullian, Jerome, and other Fathers use it very frequently in that sense. Petavius treats at length of the number, rank, and offices of angels in a special work devoted to the subject [*On the Angels*, vol. III of *Dogmatic Theology*]. I too dealt with it, though much more briefly, in an Italian booklet written and published in 1747 [*Treatise on Guardian Angels*, part I, chs. 3, 4, etc.].

**81.** That is: if bodily things themselves are so beautiful, so splendid, so admirable, who could think himself able to comprehend the beauty and excellence of invisible things? It is the celebrated argument from the lesser to the greater, as they say. Our copyist consistently writes *extimare* for *aestimare*, or, if you prefer, *existimare*.

**82.** Hilary declares thousands of times that the world was made by the Son, or by God through the Son, as though through a consubstantial instrument. The passages of the holy Doctor are so numerous that, if I cited them, I might easily seem to be seeking a reputation for learning in a matter that is plain. You have some above, no. 18.

But does he, in the words “and indeed he commanded and made the light, through which the other things might become visible, and to which he gave the name Day,” criticize Tertullian, who understood the primordial light to mean the Word himself? Let this be another’s judgment. Here are Tertullian’s own words for the reader to weigh [*Against Praxeas*, ch. 12]:

> But what is written concerning the earlier works of the world? First, indeed, before the Son appeared: “And God said, Let there be light, and there was light” [Gen. 1]. At once the Word himself is light—the true light that enlightens every person coming into this world; and through him also the worldly light. Thereafter, with Christ the Word present and administering, God willed it to be made, and God made it.

The rest contained in this period of Hilary’s letter is readily clear in itself.

**83.** Either *ne terrena* should be read, or, if you read *neve terrena*, some words, though few, are missing at the end of the period to complete the sense. Here Hilary certainly takes the terms *firmament* and *heaven* to mean some solid and stable, though transparent, material that prevents us from seeing heavenly things. The very etymology of the word seems to favor this explanation. Everyone knows what more recent philosophers hold concerning the material of the heavens.

**84.** See the Scriptural passages I noted at the end of Hilary’s letter itself, and note 62. Refer the words, “And in a wonderful way he commanded that she first bring forth what had been made last,” to the earth. For heaven was created first [Gen. 1:1], but God willed the earth to bring forth green grass yielding seed, the first, as it were, offspring of created nature.

**85.** What we have just said also explains this passage. Moreover, the earth is not last among all things if, before the other things, it is given the power of producing green grass yielding seed.

**86.** Should these things be referred to evening (darkness) and morning (light), which made one day? Or to natural composites constituted from elements created at intervals? For fire was undoubtedly not formed with water, nor perhaps earth with air. Let the reader judge. See also nos. 62 and 63.

87. We have arrived at a passage which has seemed exceedingly difficult to many. First, the question is asked why the Son of God is called God the Craftsman. Next, why the Father is said to command (“at the Father’s command”). These points are easily explained if one remembers that omnipotence is assigned to the Father as a kind of proper attribute (“I believe in God the Father Almighty”), while wisdom is assigned to the Son—a matter treated at length by theologians. We conceive omnipotence as commanding, and wisdom as executing. Thus we confess that creation is the work of the whole Trinity; but since we assign to the Persons attributes as if proper to them, we also assign to them those dispositions which the narrowness of our minds tells us seem to proceed from those attributes.

Hilary himself indicates this when, arguing against the Arians, who maintained that the only-begotten Son of God was, as it were, a mere created instrument employed by the Father in creation [Col. 0788D] (see the doctrines of the Arians in Petavius, *On the Trinity*, book II, chapter 5, no. 16), he wrote as follows (*On the Trinity*, book IV, no. 20):

> “For you have said: all things are from the Father, but all things are through the Son. For by what was said, ‘Let us make man,’ the origin is from him from whom the utterance also began; but in the statement that God made after the image of God, he also through whom the operation is completed is signified. Then, lest you be permitted to lie about this, Wisdom—which you yourself have confessed to be Christ—will oppose you, saying: ‘When he set the springs beneath the heaven in their fixed places, when he made strong the foundations of the earth, I was with him, composing. I was she in whom he delighted. And daily I rejoiced before him at all times, when he rejoiced in the completed world, and rejoiced in the children of men.’ Every occasion has been closed off, and all error is constrained to confess the truth. Wisdom, begotten before the ages, is present with God. Nor is she merely present: she also composes. Therefore there is one composing with him. Understand the office of composition or arrangement. For the Father, in speaking, effects; the Son, in carrying out what has been said to be done, composes it. Yet the distinction of Persons has been made in such a way that the work is referred to both. For in the words ‘Let us make,’ both the command and the deed are made equal; while in what is written, ‘I was with him, composing,’ she signifies that she is not alone with herself in the operation.”

The same Hilary seems to me to have spoken in the same sense in no. 43 of book XII of *On the Trinity*, which I ask you to consult. Then you will understand why he also calls the Word a craftsman: namely, because, since the Son of God is Wisdom, the work is attributed to Wisdom herself as directing it, and therefore so too is the world—a pre-eminent work of craftsmanship. Nor is it only in this Epistle that he calls the divine Word a craftsman for that reason; he does so also in no. 4 of book XII of *On the Trinity*, where he treats at length of the Word of God creating the world:

> [Col. 0789C] “Peter bears witness, writing thus: ‘commending your souls as to a faithful Creator.’ Why do we impose the name of a work upon the maker? etc.”

Please consult this passage also.

[Col. 0789B] But why do we cite only the Fathers and pass over the hymn used by the Church? For the Church sings the following [Col. 0789C] in the hymn at Matins in Eastertide:

> When, as the world was being born, you its Maker,  
> Giving Adam the image of your countenance,  
> Joined a noble spirit  
> To the clay.
>
> When the devil’s envy and deceit  
> Had defiled the human race,  
> You, clothed in flesh, as Craftsman  
> Restore the ruined form.

This accords exactly with the hymn used by the Roman clergy before Urban VIII gave more elegant metres to ecclesiastical hymns:

> You who, at the beginning of the world,  
> Formed Adam the man,  
> . . . . . . . . . .
>
> That you might redeem the man  
> Whom you had already formed before, etc.

88. Those who think that the Fathers followed Plato himself, so far as possible, in interpreting the Scriptures, will not hesitate to ascribe to Platonists Hilary’s statement here: namely, that the soul had animated the very materials, so that they might furnish souls to living creatures subsequently born. But I would by no means assign him to their company. For I know that Platonic doctrines which put forward a soul of the world and kindred notions cannot meet with much approval among the orthodox.

I would therefore explain the statement in two ways. Either say that, in Hilary’s view, God imparted to the waters whatever it may be by which the souls of fishes, creeping things, and birds subsist. Although we do not know how this was done, it certainly was done: for fishes, creeping things, and birds, when they began to live, received souls from waters already made fruitful by the divine command. Or say that souls had already been imparted to those fishes, creeping things, and birds from which the fishes, birds, and creeping things yet to be born would receive their own souls. For the souls of fishes and creeping things are not created and infused into bodies already formed—for that happens only in the case of humankind—but are communicated and received through generation. Why, indeed, should it be impermissible to say of the souls of fishes what Basil taught concerning the souls of brute animals? His words provide us with a commendable parallel. See what Basil teaches on this subject [Col. 0790C] (*Hexaemeron*, Homily VIII, no. 2, p. 71, vol. I of the Maurist edition of the Fathers), clearly indicating the first explanation:

> “Let the earth bring forth a living soul. Why does the earth bring forth a living soul? So that you may learn the difference between the soul of a beast and the soul of a human being. How the human soul was formed you will learn a little later; now hear concerning the soul of brute animals. Since, according to what is written [Col. 0790A], the soul of every animal is its blood, and blood when coagulated is accustomed to be changed into flesh, while corrupted flesh is dissolved into earth, the souls of brute animals are rightly and deservedly something earthly. Let the earth, therefore, bring forth a living soul. Observe the affinity of soul with blood, of blood with flesh, and of flesh with earth; then return in reverse order by the same stages—from earth to flesh, from flesh to blood, and from blood to soul—and you will find that the soul of cattle is earthly. Take care not to suppose that the soul is older than the constitution of their bodies.”

The second explanation likewise rests upon Basil, whom it is worthwhile to hear teaching this (*Hexaemeron*, Homily IX, no. 2, p. 81):

> “Let the earth bring forth a living soul of cattle, beasts, and creeping things. Consider the voice of God passing through created things: it began then, remains effective even now, and will continue until the end, when the world shall be completed. For just as a ball, once set in motion by someone and then finding a downward slope, is carried downwards both by its own structure and by the advantage of the place, and does not come to rest until some level surface receives it, so the nature of things, impelled by a single command, penetrates created things equally in generation and corruption, and preserves the successions of kinds through likeness until it reaches its very end. For it makes horse the successor of horse, lion of lion, eagle of eagle; indeed, it transmits each animal, preserved through succeeding generations, until the consummation of the universe. No lapse of time destroys the distinctive properties of animals; rather, as though nature had only recently been established, it always runs fresh along with time. Let the earth bring forth a living soul. This command clung to the earth, and it does not cease to serve its Creator.”

Although, if someone were to say that the mode of generation called spontaneous by ancient philosophers, or generation from putrefaction, is mentioned here, he would say something by no means remote from probability. For the ancients believed that generations of this kind took place especially by the aid of water and rain. Hence Basil—for, since I have supported the foregoing by his authority, I am pleased to confirm this too by the same authority—immediately adds after the preceding words:

> “For some things are produced through succession from things which previously existed; but others are known even now to receive life from the earth itself. For it does not merely produce cicadas in rainy weather, or countless other kinds of creatures wandering in the air, most of which are unnamed because of their minuteness; it also produces from itself mice and frogs. For around Egyptian Thebes, when rain falls abundantly in hot weather, the country is immediately filled with field-mice. We have even seen eels formed and generated from mud in no other way; neither egg nor any other means produces their succession, but they themselves arise from the earth. Let the earth bring forth a soul, etc.”

By these explanations, in my judgment, the words of this Epistle which we have cited can readily be elucidated; nor are we compelled to say that the soul mentioned here is the Holy Spirit himself fertilizing the waters. Yet this opinion seems to have pleased our Steuchus, and it plainly pleased many ancient writers. Basil perhaps hints at it when he writes as follows [Col. 0790C] (*Against Eunomius*, book V, final chapter, p. 321, vol. I):

> “Not only may his surrounding body and the heat of the body be tranquil, but also everything that surrounds and encompasses him—namely heaven, earth, sea, and the rational beings in them. And let him understand that all things are fulfilled, and that the Spirit stands over them everywhere, as though descending upon them, poured into them, entering everywhere, and shining forth; for the Spirit of the Lord has filled the world, [Col. 0791A] and that which contains all things has knowledge of God.”

Recall what I said in no. 24.

89. Consult the passage of Genesis which I noted at the end of the Epistle. Here he teaches that animals did not receive a soul from outside, but along with the body itself, from matter already animated and living. Humankind, on the other hand, as we shall shortly see, did so otherwise.

90. He refers, I think, to those very familiar words of Psalm XXXII, verse 2: “He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created.” The very description of the creation and formation of things found in Genesis chapter I likewise declares the swiftness with which things were brought forth after the divine command: “And God said, Let there be light; and there was light,” etc. Hence every interval and delay is excluded. Please consult what Hilary teaches in his commentary on Psalm CXVIII (Letter X, *Iod*, no. 4: “In creation,” etc.).

“...has taken its beginning from the same birth, or must we believe that it ceased and came to an end after the fashioning of the world, when the Lord speaks and says: ‘My Father works until now’ (John 5:17)? 76 Whoever does not know him to be unwearied assigns rest to him either before or afterward; and does not know that nothing ever happens to him, but that he always is 77: which the Greek language calls ἀναστιτεν [uncertain reading]; and that in all things he is always perfect spirit 78.

V. There are, therefore, very many things which he has made through the Son 79: things of which either their names alone are known to us, or even those are unknown. For how many thrones are there? How many powers? How many dominions? How many principalities? How many spirits? How many angels? Things which neither eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor have ascended into the human heart [Col. 0736B] 80. How great, too, do we suppose the splendour in invisible things to be? We cannot estimate it, since among the things that are with us all are marvellous 81. For among all things even the world which we behold was fashioned through the Son 82.

Indeed, he commanded light to be and made it, so that other things might be visible; and he gave it the name Day (Gen. 1:3–4). To the darkness he added the name Night (Gen. 1:5). Then he displayed the firmament, which might drive apart the waters; and he willed it to be called Heaven (Gen. 1:6–7), so that earthly things 83 might not be mingled in sight with heavenly things, but that there might be something to distinguish human things from divine. For he had already created from nothing the very materials, the elements from which all things were to be made.

After this he commanded the waters to be gathered and assembled into one place, so that the Dry Land might appear (Gen. 1:9). Nor are the various things without names. For he called the gathered waters Sea (Gen. 1:10), and willed the separated dry land to possess the name Earth (Gen. 1:10). But these things seemed insufficiently furnished. He therefore added to them fruitful fertility and beauty (Gen. 1:11 ff.). And, in a wonderful manner, commanding that to generate first which had been made last 84, he did not disturb the order or show ignorance of his own creation; rather, he willed that what was last should possess something first, lest what was last should lie lowest in every respect 85, and he joined what was second to what was first, lest the first things despise the lower things 86.

Thus the Son of God, God the Craftsman, at the Father’s command, ordered matters 87 so that, by changing the sequence, he might arrange the ordering more fittingly. For he commanded the earth to bring forth every kind of pasture and trees with their life-renewing seeds (Gen. 1:11–12); and he adorned heaven with lights [Col. 0736D]—that is, sun, moon, and stars (Gen. 1:14)—by which he might mark the boundaries of day and night, or instruct farmers and sailors by signs (ibid., v. 16). He commanded all seas enclosed within the boundaries of the earth (Job 38:8 ff.) to bring forth their animals (Gen. 1:20–21): that is, the soul had animated the very materials, so that they might supply souls to living creatures subsequently born 88. But in order to make the earth more fruitful (*the manuscript has “had made”*) (Gen. 1:24–25), after pastures, after fruit-bearing trees, after every kind of seed, he commanded it to cast forth all living and animate things—the kinds of quadrupeds, wild beasts, and serpents (ibid.) 89. Nor was there any delay in all this 90: for when God the Father had commanded, the Son, being power itself, undertook the command without postponement. [Col. 0737A]

> [Note: [Col. 0737]

91. See the immediately preceding number, that is, no. 90, and Dissertation I. Where he wrote, “for when God,” etc., the copyist wrote in such a way that [Col. 0791B] we may also read, “for because God.”

92. He bestowed another fertility upon the earth when the human body was formed from it; for which reason humanity is sometimes called the offspring of earth, and by the Apostle Paul “earthly, from the earth” (1 Cor. 15:47 ff.). The very etymology of the name Adam also signifies this.

93. These statements have some difficulty. For what is signified by those words, “after divine things”? I suspect that some error has crept in here through the copyist’s carelessness. For in the original exemplar it could easily have read “after human things”—that is, earthly things—“divine things were lacking,” namely the creation of the human soul, which Hilary elsewhere calls divine (*On Psalm* CXVIII, Letter X, no. 7, p. 337, vol. I).

But if you prefer that no error slipped in here, say either that the human species and form, of which I shall speak more fully elsewhere [Col. 0791D] (see Dissertation I appended to this Epistle), is indicated here: for that species was divine, though representing humanity. Or say that the word “divine” perhaps denotes the Empyrean Heaven, which is sometimes called the Seat of God [Col. 0791D] (Psalm 10:4: “The Lord—his seat is in heaven”; Psalm 103:19: “The Lord has prepared his throne in heaven”; Psalm 113:3: “But our God is in heaven”; and ibid., v. 16: “The heaven of heavens belongs to the Lord, but he gave the earth to the children of men”); [Col. 0791C] or, more probably, the angels, who are called sons of God by Job and others, and indeed by Hilary himself (see annotation 38). Thus these words would mean: after he had already created the angels, pure spirits, he finally created man, who consists not only of spirit—on account of which he is said to draw his origin from heaven—but also of a body formed from earth.

94. Man can most properly be called born again. Leaving aside for the moment that Scripture mentions twice his formation—or, if we wish to call it so, his birth—and indicates in the second mention of that creation, birth, and formation the formation of Eve from Adam’s rib (Gen. 1:26–28; Gen. 2:7, 22–23), he may be called born again because the earth from which he was formed had previously existed. The creation of that earth was Adam’s first birth—in the cause, that is, or in the preceding matter, as the Schoolmen speak. But when he was made into a living soul (Gen. 2:7), he then seemed to be born again.

Hence elsewhere Hilary hints at a threefold perfection in the man made and prefigured [Col. 0792A]: one concerns the body, another the soul—and we are speaking here of these two—while the third concerns the image of God impressed upon humanity [Col. 0791D]. This will be discussed subsequently. The following teaching of Hilary in nos. 6 and 7 of his commentary on Psalm CXVIII, from which we recently transcribed some passages, will illuminate the present statement. He mentions only two origins of humanity and teaches precisely what he sets forth in this present little work. Here are the words of Hilary to which I referred:

> “The creation of all the other elements was both instituted and effected at the very time when they were commanded to subsist; no period separates their beginning from their completion, for the beginning received completion in the very fact that it was begun. But humankind, since it contains within itself an inward and an outward nature, each differing from the other, and has been constituted as a rational animal from two kinds into one, was established by a twofold beginning. For first it was said: ‘Let us make man after our image and likeness.’ Then, second: ‘And God took dust from the earth and fashioned man.’ The first work does not have within itself the origin of another nature assumed from elsewhere. But how greatly does the production of the second work differ from the first institution! God takes dust from the earth. Dust is taken, and earthly matter is fashioned or prepared into a human being; and, from one thing into another, it is refined by the work and skill of the craftsman. Therefore he did not take but made the first; the second he did not make as he made the first, but took it and then fashioned or prepared it.”

[Col. 0791D] Hilary teaches in no. 8 of his commentary on Psalm CXVIII:
