> “Either interpretation may rightly be understood, because we find both written: that he formed into that which is, namely the bodily form; or prepared into that which is said, ‘and he breathed into him the breath of life, and man became a living soul.’ He was therefore prepared or formed for this breathing, by which the nature of soul and body might be held together in the perfection of life by a kind of covenant of breathed-in spirit. Blessed Paul knows that he has a double nature within himself, when he delights in the law according to the inward man and sees another law in his members which leads him captive in the law of sin. Therefore what is made according to the image of God belongs to the dignity of the mind. But what is formed from earth is the beginning of bodily form and nature. And because God is understood either to speak to another when he says, ‘Let us make man,’ or because a threefold perfection of the man made and prefigured is recognized—since he is made after the image of God, formed from earth, and stirred into a living soul by the breathing of the Spirit—the Prophet testifies that he was made and formed by hands, not by one hand alone, because in his constitution the operation is shown to have been not of one alone, and also threefold.”

95. Does Hilary here approve the opinion of those who suppose Adam’s body was formed from a nobler portion—or, if one may so speak, as it were from the flower—of earth gathered from various and more excellent places? Or does he indicate something else here? Let the reader decide.

96. Hilary teaches the same thing elsewhere in different words, namely these (*On Psalm* LXVII, no. 22, p. 229, vol. I):

> “When he first bestowed upon us the soul for the breath and respiration of life, establishing humanity after the image and likeness [Col. 0792C] of himself, he poured it forth from the treasures of his power and divinity. For, according to the Apostle, we are his offspring; and according to the same Apostle, all things are from him, through him, and in him. Thus our dwelling and habitation are shown to be in him, while he embraces all things by the immeasurable power of his strength; through him, moreover, the work and accomplishment of our initiated origin are shown, because he has wrought in us the very thing that we are; while from him the beginnings of life bestowed for the origins of spirit are made known. It was therefore not foreign to the beneficence of divine goodness that he who, from himself, bestowed upon us—for we are his offspring—the elements of life and spirit…”

Elsewhere (*On Psalm* LXIII, no. 9) he had taught that the soul is not earthly, but arises from the breath of God and is mingled with the elements of the body.

97. See Dissertation I appended to these annotations.

98. He most expressly wishes the Father to be a partner in the creation of humankind and, if we may speak thus, a co-creator, whereas in recounting the creation of everything else he makes no mention at all of the Father. He teaches the same thing, but much more fully, in nos. 8, 9, and 10 of book V of *On the Trinity*, to which passages I refer the reader.

But why, I ask, does he invoke the Father here, when he seems to attribute the rest to the Son alone? If we wish, we may trace this back to the image impressed upon humanity; for Hilary expressly calls it the image of the Father [Col. 0793D]:

> “Let him nevertheless always remember that all things are through the Son, lest a heretical understanding appropriate to itself the operation of God the Father. Therefore, if humanity is created after the image of God the Father through God the Son, it is also created after the image of the Son; for no one denies that ‘after our image and likeness’ was spoken to the Son. The divine Word thus preserved in speech the principle of truth which the work fulfilled in deed: God might fashion humanity after the image of God, so as to signify God, and might not take truth away from God, since he who is understood to be God the Son in performing the work is true God also in the communion of the image.”

Yet it is not the image of the Father alone, but of the whole Trinity, as those words indicate: “Let us make man after our image and likeness.” Or should we also trace it to the fact that humankind is a distinctive and outstanding work of omnipotence, joining in itself whatever excellence and dignity body and spirit possess? For the work of omnipotence is especially referred to the Father. Let the reader decide.

This, at any rate, is certain: Theodoret, whom Petavius accordingly cites (*On the Works of Creation*, II, 2, 4), taught precisely what Hilary teaches here. He asserts that God the Father, foreseeing that his Son would one day assume the nature and substance of the man whom he was forming, fashioned Adam—the origin and foundation, as it were, of the human race—with his own hands [Col. 0793B]. Please consult Theodoret himself.

99. This expression, “so that earth might not prescribe for immortality,” is among those in which Hilary appears to imitate Tertullian. He gives here the reason why humanity, though consisting of a dissoluble body, was made immortal by God: namely, because immortal hands—that is, God’s hands—formed that human being. You will readily understand what God’s hands signify if you either have recourse to the human species and form, which we shall discuss at length in the earlier dissertation, or consult what Hilary teaches in his commentary on Psalm CXVIII; see nos. 3, 4, and 5 of Letter X, or *Iod*.

Hilary undoubtedly refers here to the two passages of Scripture: Job 10:8, “Your hands made me and fashioned me,” etc.; and Psalm 118:73, “Your hands made and fashioned me,” or, as Hilary reads it, “formed me, prepared me.” After the words “would establish man,” a gap occurs in the manuscript [Col. 0793C]; but it is so slight that I have disregarded it, and the sense in fact remains complete without any gap.

100. Hilary says much concerning the image impressed by God upon humanity, and the likeness which humanity will receive after death if it dies acceptable to God. Since these matters require no little effort, I shall defer them to a separate dissertation.

101. He refers to John’s passage (1 John 3:2): “Beloved, now we are children of God; and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is.” What Hilary here says briefly, he develops elsewhere at length, concluding book XI of *On the Trinity* thus (p. 406, vol. II):

> “Moreover, we shall advance into the conformed glory of our humanity, and, renewed in the knowledge of God, shall be re-formed after the image of the Creator, according to the Apostle’s saying: ‘Having put off the old man with his deeds and put on the new, who is renewed in the knowledge of God after [Col. 0793D] the image of him who created him.’ Thus humanity is completed as the image of God. For, made conformed to the glory of the body of God, it rises into the image of the Creator according to the ordained fashioning of the first human being. And after sin and the old man, the new man, made in the knowledge of God, attains the perfection of his constitution, knowing his God and thereby being his image; and, advancing through religion toward eternity, he will remain the image of his Creator through eternity.”

102. If anyone compares these matters with what Hilary wrote on Psalm CXVIII (Letter X, no. 8), and even more plainly on Psalm CXXIX (no. 3 and following), he will, I think, immediately admit that the author of this Epistle and of those commentaries is one and the same. I shall excerpt a few passages which, unless I am entirely mistaken, will plainly show what I assert. Here are the former words (*On Psalm* CXXIX, no. 3, p. 492):

> “First, we must understand that God is incorporeal and does not consist of certain parts and functions of limbs from which one body is made. For we read in the Gospel that God is spirit—an invisible, immeasurable, self-contained, and eternal nature. It is likewise written that a spirit does not have flesh and bones. Bodily limbs consist of these, and the substance of God has no need of them. But God, who is both everywhere and in all things, wholly hears, [Col. 0794B] wholly sees, wholly effects, wholly proceeds; and we are taught this from Scripture when it says, ‘I am God who is near and not far off,’ and again, ‘For in him we live and move and are.’ Therefore the power of God, which is equal and undivided, bears the names of functions and limbs: the power by which he sees is eyes; the power by which he hears is ears; the power by which he acts is hands; and the power by which he is present is feet—the distinctions of functions being performed by the power of this… God therefore is everywhere and is everywhere present; he hears, sees, and acts.”

Long before Hilary, Irenaeus had written (*Against Heresies*, book I, chapter 12, no. 2; formerly chapter 6):

> “The God of all things, who, at the same moment at which he thinks, accomplishes what he thinks; and, at the same moment at which he wills, thinks what he wills… since he is wholly thought, wholly sense, wholly eye, wholly hearing, and wholly the source of all good things.”

He repeats the same point in these words (*Against Heresies*, book II, chapter 13, no. 3; formerly chapter 16):

> “For the Father of all is very far removed from the affections and passions which occur among humans; he is simple, uncompounded, uniform in his members, wholly like and equal to himself. He is wholly sense, wholly spirit, wholly sentience, wholly *ennoia* [thought], wholly reason, wholly hearing, wholly eye, wholly light, and wholly the source of all good things, as it is fitting for devout and pious persons to speak of God.”

He teaches similar things shortly thereafter [Col. 0794D] (no. 9 of the same chapter 13, formerly chapter 16):

> “God is wholly *Nous* [Mind] and wholly *Logos* [Word], as we have said; and nothing is more ancient… As one does not err who calls him wholly sight and wholly hearing—for that by which he sees is also that by which he hears, and that by which he hears is also that by which he sees—so neither does one err who says that he is wholly sense and wholly Word.”

And again elsewhere (chapter 28, nos. 4 and 5; formerly chapters 47 and 48):

> “But God, being wholly mind, wholly reason, wholly working spirit, wholly light, and always the same… God, being wholly mind and wholly Logos, etc.”

He gives related teaching in book IV (chapter 11, no. 2; formerly chapter 24: “And God indeed,” etc.). Cyril of Jerusalem seems to copy Irenaeus when he says (*Catechesis* VI, no. 7):

> “For piety it suffices us to know only that we have one God: a God who exists, who exists from eternity, always like himself… who, adorned with many names, can do all things, and is of uniform substance… He does not see in part and lack sight in part; rather, he is wholly eye, wholly hearing, and wholly mind.”

Theodoret imitates these writers in his commentary on Psalm CXXIX, verse 2, “Let your ears be attentive,” etc.:

> “Although they used expressions in a human manner, they know that the divinity is incorporeal; they called the power of hearing ears [Col. 0795A], and the power of seeing eyes, because our eyes possess the power of seeing and the faculty of hearing has been entrusted to ears. But by the power through which God hears, he also sees; and by that through which he sees, he also hears.”

103. He anticipates an objection which could occur to the mind of some less educated person: namely, if humanity differs so greatly from God, in what part of humanity can the image of God be located? He anticipates it, I say, by teaching that humanity has two parts, either of which may by synecdoche be called “man”: the inward and the outward. The image of God of which we spoke is situated in the former.

104. See what we said in nos. 100 and 101.

105. “While” means “provided that.” Moreover, there is a manifest error in the words “without end.” But I do not know how to emend the passage. I suspect that a careless copyist omitted a few words contained within a single line, so that it should now read “and without … at the end”—that is, at the end of life, or at death—“he was proved” [Col. 0795B]. I also suspect that it formerly read *sine fictione*, “without pretence,” so that Hilary rightly requires inward piety to correspond to an outward profession of piety. I have likewise suspected that it originally read *sine infide* [without unfaithfulness]; for I do not doubt that this word was at some time in use, and that *infidus* [unfaithful] came from it, just as *infidelis* comes from *infidelitas*. But because these are mere conjectures, I have wished to alter nothing in Hilary’s text itself. Let the reader emend it as he pleases.

If anyone wishes to seek confirmation from Hilary himself of what is taught here, let him consult the passages which, for brevity’s sake, I note at the foot of the page [Col. 0795D]: *On Psalm* II, no. 15, pp. 38–39, vol. I; *On Psalm* CXVIII, Letter XX, nos. 9–10, p. 406 of the same volume; and *On the Trinity*, book I, no. 9, p. 7, vol. I. Moreover, this is often stressed in Scripture, as in Luke 9:62; Matthew 10:22; again 19:17 and 24:13; Hebrews 12:7; etc.

106. Here Hilary has in mind those words of Ecclesiasticus 15:14:

> “God established man from the beginning, and left him in the hand of his own counsel. He added his commandments and precepts. If you are willing to keep the commandments, they will preserve you, and to make pleasing faith for ever [Col. 0795C]. He has set before you water and fire; stretch out your hand to whichever you wish. Before man are life and death, good and evil; whichever pleases him shall be given to him,” etc.

If you wish to see these matters expounded by Hilary in a fuller and elegant style, go to no. 16 of his commentary on Psalm II (p. 39, vol. I: “But he who is perfect and good,” etc.).

107. When Hilary says, “lest, great and released from the law, he should be made equal to all animals,” I think he looked to the passage of Psalm XLVIII, verses 13–14: “Man, though he was in honour, did not understand; he was compared with senseless beasts and became like them.” Perhaps he also had in mind the words of Job 11:12: “The vain man is lifted up in pride and thinks himself born free like a colt of a wild ass.” What we noted in the immediately preceding annotation partly explains the following words: “after the law was added with a threat,” etc. But the holy Doctor undoubtedly alludes to Genesis 2:16:

> “And the Lord commanded him, saying: ‘From every tree of Paradise you may eat; but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat. For on whatever day you eat from it, you shall surely die.’”

108. Interpreters note here that the woman drawn from Adam’s rib was first called *Ishah*, a name common to all women; after sin, however, she was called Eve. This word indicates that God preserved her life after her sin; it also indicates Adam’s hope that through her human beings would be begotten and nourished, and the human race propagated. See Calmet. Yet Epiphanius teaches that this word is more fitting for the most holy Mary than for Eve—indeed, that it is fitting for Eve only because she was a type of Mary (*Heresies* 18, nos. 18–19).

109. That Eve was commanded not to eat the fruit of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil is plainly clear from Genesis, chapter III (vv. 1 ff.). It is likewise certain—and easily shown from what followed—that this same Eve would have shared in the reward promised to Adam, had she remained in innocence. For if she became liable to punishment because she committed sin, she would certainly have obtained the reward had she avoided the offense. The Fathers observe, however, that in almost all passages of Scripture where commandments imposed upon us are mentioned and rewards proposed, mention is made of man alone: either because both sexes are included under the name of man, or because, since the man is the head of the woman, he alone is named, although women too are affected by the commandments and the same rewards are offered to them. Cyprian aptly says, explaining in his treatise *On the Dress of Virgins* those words of Revelation [col. 0796B] (ch. XIV, 4), “These are they who have not defiled themselves”:

> “For the Lord does not promise the grace of continence only to males and pass over women. But because woman is a portion of man, and was taken and formed from him, in almost all the Scriptures God speaks to the first-created man; for the two are one flesh, and in the male the female too is signified.”

110. Consult the passages of Scripture which I have noted in the margin of the epistle itself. With regard to the word *Sermonem* (“the Word”), by which is meant the divine Word, the only-begotten Son of God the Father, see what we said in no. 20. Let the reader decide whether the words “that is, the Son” are a gloss of some copyist that slipped from the margin into the epistle itself, or whether they come from Hilary himself. The final part of this sentence, “for they too are free not to sin,” etc., is illustrated by what we set forth in no. 106, as also by what Petavius and other theologians and interpreters teach when discussing the work of the six days [col. 0796C].

111. To be more certain on this point, consult theologians who discuss in special treatises the Work—or creation—of the six days, together with commentators; and, among others, our Steuco of Gubbio, who illustrates this view by an elegant comparison in his *Cosmopoeia*.

For, with the command, the work was at hand. But since it greatly mattered that earthly things should be made fruitful, and, after divine things, human beings were lacking, he made man: so that man might not be wholly from heaven, nor yet be born again wholly from earth. For he formed the body from every kind of clay of the earth (Gen. II, 7), while intending to grant the spirit from heaven (ibid.). And although all things had been formed by the Father’s command, with the Word obeying, in the fashioning of man the Father himself also came forward as craftsman, so that earth might not prescribe mortality if immortal hands established man. He also granted that man should bear God’s image upon earth, intending afterward to bestow likeness, if that image were kept unharmed.

Do not suppose that this outward form of man was made according to the image. Far from it. For who could believe that God, in whose image man was made, has any part which does not hear, does not see, or does not accomplish all things? For man’s outward form does not see in every respect, does not hear in every respect, and is not all-powerful. But God is wholly light, wholly eye, wholly ear, wholly most powerful hand [col. 0737B]. Are the Scriptures, then, false? Far from it. Rather, the Apostle Paul teaches us that there is something inward in man which is itself called “man,” saying: “Even though our outward man is decaying, yet the inward is renewed day by day” (II Cor. IV, 16). This is what was made in God’s image: what we call the νοῦς, that is, the mind. It can be like God when it is impassible: when it has been proved steadfast, blessed, holy, and without end—“without end,” “unto the end,” or, if you prefer, “without unbelief,” or “in faith” [col. 0737C]. And he gave free choice and a mind capable of living, yet not without law, lest man, great and released from law, should be made equal to all living creatures; adding a threat after the law, so that, if he kept the law, he might come into eternity, but, if he did not keep it, he might bring death upon himself and lose salvation (Gen. II, 16). The name of the man who was made is Adam (Gen. II, 19).

## VI

But because in all animals both sexes had come forth for procreation (Gen. I, 22 ff.), provision was also made for man, that a woman too might be prepared for him for the sake of generation (Gen. I, 27; II, 20, 21 ff.). And she was made, as Scripture testifies, and received the name Eve (*Heva*) (Gen. III, 20); the prescription of an equal law did not separate her either from reward or from punishment [col. 0737D].

But after God had seen all things completed and adorned through his Word—that is, the Son—he handed over to man’s power everything that was with man (Gen. I, 28). When Lucifer saw that all things had been handed over to him, he begrudged man, to man’s misery (Gen. III, 1 ff.). “For they too are free not to sin, and are permitted to remain in blessedness if they keep the commands.” Through the woman he persuaded man to transgress God’s law and commandments (Gen. III, 1 ff.), so that man might become guilty of God’s commands and fall under the sentence (Gen. II, 17). He was therefore cast out into this world (Gen. III, 17 ff.); for, while he was without sin, he had dwelt in Paradise (Gen. III, 23).

[Note: [col. 0738]

112. Here Hilary gives the reason why we contract original sin: namely, because we derive from Adam, in whose will the Lord had established the wills of his descendants. We derive, I say, from Adam already disobedient and therefore guilty, who drew his descendants with himself into ruin. If I wished to treat this subject according to its importance, I should be almost endless; for that reason I refer the reader to theologians who discuss it at length. Whoever wishes to consult passages of Hilary relevant to the present matter should turn to those which I cite at the foot of the page: [col. 0795D] *On Psalm CXXXVIII*, no. 24, “For he will return,” etc.; [col. 0796D] (p. 573, vol. I); and *On Psalm CXLV*, no. 2, “For that life is not,” etc. (p. 630). See also the *Commentaries on Matthew*, chapter XVIII, no. 6, “One sheep,” etc. (p. 758 of the same volume).

113. Should anyone doubt this, let him consult, to omit other evidence, Genesis chapter IV. He will see God examining Cain, guilty of murder, and exhorting him to repentance. The following words are especially to be noted (ch. IV, 7): “If you do well, will you not be accepted? But if you do evil, sin”—that is, the punishment of sin—“will immediately be present at the door. But your desire shall be subject to you, and you shall rule over it.” Recall also what we said in no. 106. If you desire Hilary here too, pray read what he teaches in the *Commentaries on Psalm CXVIII* (Letter XXII, no. 3, and p. 412, vol. I), “But of equity,” etc.

114. Christ himself indicates this when he says (Matt. XXIII, 37): “Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those sent to you! How often I wished to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were unwilling.” Nor is it necessary here to understand by “Jerusalem” the inhabitants of Jerusalem; we may suitably refer the word to the human race and, specifically, to the race of Jacob. For unless the human race universally were denoted, Christ’s mention of Abel’s blood shed by Cain would not have been suitable:

> “That upon you may come all the righteous blood shed upon the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah, whom you killed between the temple and the altar” (Matt. XXIII, 35). [col. 0797D]

Hilary treats this subject very aptly in the passages indicated at the foot of the page: *On Psalm LII*, no. 5, p. 56, vol. I, “And lest God should be negligent toward men,” etc.; and on Matthew chapter XII, no. [col. 0798D] 22, p. 733; and more expressly on chapter XX, nos. 6 and 7.

But lest I seem to depend upon Hilary alone, I join Augustine to Hilary, teaching the same in these words (*Against Faustus*, XII.35):

> “The Word of God sent the law through his servant, but it did not profit the human race dead in sins; yet it was not sent without cause. For he who sent it knew that it had first to be sent. He himself came, conformed himself to us, became a sharer in our death, and we were made alive,” etc.

But above all others Gregory the Great treats this argument more fully and eloquently; I would not have the reader pass over his observations. For, in commenting upon Matthew chapter XX and explaining the parable in which the kingdom of heaven is said to be like a householder who hired laborers to cultivate his vineyard, he sets forth matters that wonderfully illuminate this view: *Homilies on the Gospels*, XIX.1, “Who indeed is signified by the likeness of the householder,” etc. See also commentators on Hebrews I, 1: “God, who in many portions and in many ways formerly spoke to the fathers in the prophets,” etc.

115. Hilary plainly alludes to Adam’s sin, which all contracted; and from it he takes occasion to show the necessity of the Lord’s incarnation and of proclaiming God’s mercy toward the human race, as he does elsewhere and often. For what human being could reconcile us to God if we all sinned in Adam and are born children of wrath, children of vengeance? It was therefore necessary that the only-begotten Son of God should take our flesh—holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners (Heb. VII, 26)—and in it make satisfaction to an angry God. Theologians discuss this subject, especially Petavius, who adduces very many Fathers on it [col. 0797C] (*On the Incarnation*, II, chs. 12, 13, and 14). I cite here Ambrose alone, who says:

> “He alone is the one who will redeem man, surpassing his brethren in loving-kindness, because he shed his own blood for others—a blood which no one can offer for his brother. . . . But why will he alone redeem? Because no one can equal him in loving-kindness, so as to lay down his life for servants; no one in integrity, for all are under sin, all are subject to that fall of Adam. The Redeemer alone is chosen, who could not be liable to the old sin.”

—on verse 8 of Psalm XLVIII, or the words: “A brother does not redeem; shall a man redeem? He shall not give God a propitiation.” [col. 0798D]

116. As to the first statement, “lest the devil should triumph altogether,” it denotes the earlier times preceding the incarnation, in which the demon indeed seemed to triumph, so completely were all things covered with vices and enveloped in the darkness of idolatry. Paul often indicates this, as when he says (Titus III, 3):

> “For we too were once foolish, unbelieving, led astray, serving diverse desires and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful and hating one another. But when the goodness and loving-kindness of God our Savior appeared, he saved us—not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy—through the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out upon us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Savior, so that, justified by his grace, we might become heirs according to the hope of eternal life.”

Paul teaches the same thing elsewhere, in verses 9 and 10 of chapter I of the Second Epistle to Timothy: “Who [God] delivered us,” etc.

As for the second part, “for this is his name,” everyone observes that the term *Diabolus* means “accuser,” or the author of sins [col. 0798A].

Finally, the third part, “after he begrudged man,” alludes to Wisdom II, 24: “But through the devil’s envy death entered the world”; it also alludes to Paul’s words (II Cor. XI, 3), “The serpent deceived Eve by his cunning,” and similar passages. Although some expressly state that Lucifer begrudged man from man’s very origin, those cited by Petavius teach that he certainly begrudged him once he had already been created (*On Angels*, III.2, 16, 17, etc.). Please consult them, and add Chrysostom in the passage cited below: *Homilies on Genesis*, XXII.2, p. 195, vol. II, Montfaucon edition.

117. The matters just cited from Paul’s Epistles may suitably be referred here.

118. Here Hilary briefly encompasses the reasons why the Word of God was incarnate. The first is that it was fitting for fallen man to be restored through the Son, through whom man had been created. Athanasius, Hilary, Cyril, Augustine, Fulgentius, Chrysologus, Pope Leo, Alcuin, and Ivo of Chartres press this same reason in the passages cited by Petavius (*On the Incarnation*, II.vi.16, and again ch. XV, nos. 2, 3, and 4). Lest I seem to pass over all of them, I give Leo’s words (*Sermon XII on the Passion*, ch. 2):

> “In this ineffable unity of the Trinity,” says Leo, “whose works and judgments are common in all things, the person of the Son properly undertook the restoration of the human race; so that, since he is the one through whom all things were made and without whom nothing was made, and since he gave life by the breath of rational life to man formed from the clay of the earth, the same one might restore our nature, cast down from the height of eternity, to its lost dignity; and he who was its creator might also be its re-creator. Thus he brought his purpose into effect, so as to employ, for the destruction of the devil’s dominion, the justice of reason more than the power of might.”

119. I fear an error has crept into the words “to bear man patiently,” and that the reading should be “to remove man by suffering from the power of the demon,” or something of that sort, signifying redemption accomplished through the Passion. Yet the words as they stand may have a commendable meaning. For Christ bore human weaknesses with the greatest patience; he both took human sins upon himself and bore them on the wood. He showed such mercy toward us that, while suffering every extremity from men, he cried to the Father: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke XXIII, 34). Unless, perhaps, you wish Hilary’s words to have the same meaning as the Church’s very familiar prayers: “O God, who chiefly revealest thy almighty power by sparing and showing mercy,” etc.

Whatever the case, the following matters concerning the defeat of the powers of this age, the conquest of death, and the rest of Hilary’s discussion are illustrated by the passages of the Fathers cited in note 115; and note 118 illustrates what follows: “he who had shared with the Father in the making of man.” See also what we cited in notes 100 and 101. To confirm Hilary’s words, “who could conceal himself in man and make man united with God perform and display mighty works,” hear Augustine expressing the same meaning (*On Psalm LVIII*, 7):

> “Man therefore came”—understand Christ, or the only-begotten Son of God made man—“to all those sufferings which would have had no power in him unless he were man. But if he were not man, man would not be liberated. Man came to the deep heart, that is, the hidden heart, presenting man to human sight while preserving God within; concealing the form of God, in which he is equal to the Father, and offering the form of a servant, in which he is less than the Father.” [col. 0798D–0799A]

Do not suppose, moreover, that the former words favor the Nestorians—“who could conceal himself in man”—or that the following words favor the Eutychians—“and make man united with God.” Remember, please, when Hilary wrote these words: long before the rise of the heresies of Nestorius and Eutyches, and thus at a time when it was safe to employ these freer forms of expression. It is therefore not surprising if he uses them: *On the Trinity*, II.16, “The Spirit—that is, the divine Word—mingled himself with the nature of human flesh,” etc. [col. 0799D]

The passages in which ancient Fathers call the human nature assumed by the Word “man” are so numerous that it would be wearisome to recount them. See, in order to bring these and related expressions to their correct meaning, what theologians teach; among many others, Petavius, *On the Incarnation*, VII.12–13. The passages in which they use the word *mixtus* (“mingled”) to denote the union of the Word with human nature indicate nothing other than the union of the divine Word with human nature. See again what theologians teach to understand these and related terms correctly. Among many others, I choose Petavius, *On the Incarnation*, I.15.7–8; IV.1–2, especially nos. 14–15; and ch. 10. See also note d on no. 26 of Hilary’s *On the Trinity*, II, at the words “The Spirit . . . mingled himself with the nature of human flesh,” etc. (this edition, vol. II, col. 67); for most approved Fathers who used these expressions are there cited.

To continue with Hilary: he undoubtedly understands “mingling” as “union” when he says (*Commentary on Psalm LXIII*, no. 9, p. 181, vol. I) that the soul is not earthly but arises from God’s breath and is joined to the elements of the body. Ausonius likewise, in order to denote that the Holy Spirit is one God with the Father and Son, calls him “mingled” with Father and Son (*Morning Prayer*):

> I acknowledge the Father of the Only-Begotten, and him mingled with the two,  
> The Spirit who hovered over the waters of the sea.

120. Consult the passages of Scripture indicated at the end of the epistle itself.

121. Nearly all the ancient Fathers say that Christ’s virginal birth was hidden from the demon, but for the most part they do not give the reason for this divine plan. Hilary gives here two very probable reasons. The first is that the demon might not fear to tempt Christ, whom he would not have tempted had he known him to be God; and that Christ’s victory over the demon might appear more clearly. For Christ would seem less decisively to have overthrown the devil if the devil were conquered without entering the contest and without temptations. Thus the words “and lest the devil should seem less overthrown by man” may be understood as though the particle *ne* (“lest”) were either added or necessarily understood. Yet the statement may also be taken as standing on its own.

122. The first part of this statement alludes to what Luke teaches concerning Christ’s conception from a virgin. The latter part gives the reason why Christ remained among men for a long time: namely, so that we might all, or nearly all, learn God—that all these things had been foretold beforehand in the Law and the Prophets—through his teachings and miracles, both those preceding his birth and those performed by him; while the angelic announcement and songs, the arrival of the Magi, the ancient prophecies, Simeon and the prophetess Anna, and also the testimony of John the Baptist all concurred in the same witness. Hilary touches on some of these in *On the Trinity*, II.26–27; I ask you to consult those passages.

To conceal nothing, I once suspected that the reading should be: “that all might finally learn these things,” etc.; or, “that all might learn to bear God,” that is, to submit to Christ’s law. Let the reader judge whether I am right.

123. I have corrected two corrupt readings found in the manuscript. For it reads *perterriti*, whereas undoubtedly one should read *praeteriti*, that is, those who preceded the Lord’s coming. It also reads: “To whom this [was given] to behold with these eyes,” etc., omitting the verb *videre* (“to see”) or *inspicere* (“to behold”). If anyone wishes to retain *his* (“these”), in order to contrast the eyes of the mind with bodily eyes, I have no objection, provided that the verb “to see” or “to behold” is added. See what Hilary teaches in his exposition of Psalm CXVIII, Letter 11, no. 3, p. 344, vol. I: “But these are now the eyes of the prophet,” etc. [col. 0800D]

Hilary here teaches two things: first, that the coming of the Lord Christ was foretold in the Law and the Prophets; second, why it was foretold. For the latter he gives two reasons, the first concerning those then present, the other those of former times. He wishes this coming to have been foretold long beforehand so that those present might not refuse to believe so marvelous a thing, since it had long been made known through predictions so certain and clear. But it was foretold to those who preceded the coming of the Lord Christ so that they might believe in the Messiah who was to come and hope that they would obtain salvation from him. Hence those frequent cries: “Oh that you would rend the heavens!” etc. (Isa. LXIV, 1); “Drop down, heavens, from above,” etc. (Isa. XLV, 8), and other similar words.

Indeed, Christ himself once testified (John VIII, 56, “that he might see my day”) that Abraham desired to see his day; that is, those times in which the only-begotten Son of God, having assumed a human body, lived among us, instructing the human race by his examples and teachings and saving it by his death. Moreover, that the coming of the Lord Christ had long before been foretold is shown by many, but especially by Cyril of Jerusalem, whose twelfth and thirteenth Catecheses I urge you to read. Yet who would omit Hilary, who elsewhere carries out splendidly what he here states briefly? I indicate a few of the many passages: no. 13 of the *Commentaries on Psalm LIV* (p. 123, vol. I); no. 1 of the *Commentaries on Psalm LXI* (p. 161, vol. I); no. 1 of the *Commentary on Psalm LXVI* (p. 208, vol. I); no. 20 of the *Commentary on Psalm LXVIII* (p. 253); no. 1 of the *Commentary on Psalm CXXXI* (p. 500); no. 38 of Book IV of *On the Trinity* (pp. 97–98, vol. II, and p. 123, vol. I). Finally, not to linger over individual passages, while explaining the Psalms he refers a great part of them to Christ; anyone who has read Hilary’s own treatises on the Psalms will acknowledge this. I have offered some observations on this subject in the notes to a sermon of St. Antipater found in the Vatican Library, which I published a few months ago, in vol. XLIII of the *Opuscula* collected by Father Calogera. See there note 18 and those following.

124. After the words “of his majesty and goodness,” I have added the word *speciem* (“appearance”), since this word or another akin to it is missing in the manuscript. Next, the manuscript reads *susceperant* (“had undertaken”); but I think one must certainly read *susceperat* (“had undertaken”), referring it to Christ, who came to take away the sins of the world. The syntax here seems somewhat obscure, but I did not wish to alter it, lest I seem excessively bold. Let one who considers the preceding periods judge whether anything is missing. The manuscript is written in such a way that it may also be read: “But if God . . . were to show [himself], perhaps,” etc.]

Because after the transgression he had begotten human beings, he led the whole human race with himself all the way to death. Nevertheless, the Good One, or the Just One, would not fail them, since those born later too were free not to sin, and God did not cease daily to admonish them. Then divine goodness and paternal mercy made ample provision in many ways: first through the righteous patriarchs, then through Moses and the prophets. But all these were dying in Adam.

In the last times, lest the devil should triumph altogether—for this is his name after he begrudged man—and lest man, after the allotted period of condemnation, should long be held in punishment contrary to God’s mercy, man received the salvation which he deserved by mercy alone. For God the almighty Father sent his Son, Jesus Christ, our God and Lord, through whom he had created all things; nor did he allow even this to be done without him.

Yet no one was fit either to bear man patiently—or perhaps the reading should be *tollere*, “to remove,” namely, from the demon’s power—or to know man; nor could anyone overcome the powers of this world and of this darkness, conquer death, open hell, utterly root out and destroy the force and power of sin, except the Son of God, who had shared with the Father in the making of man, who could both conceal himself in man and make man, united with God, perform and display mighty works. Through him, with the bonds recording our sins abolished (Col. II, 14), we might come in peace to God the Father and be made children of God (I John III, 1).

Therefore the Son of God was sent and secretly entered into man [col. 0738C] (Luke I): not because he, who was Lord of all, feared anyone, but lest the devil should fear to approach the man who was united with God; and lest the devil should seem less overthrown by man if he were conquered without encounter and contest. Therefore, when the Spirit of the Lord came upon the Virgin and the power of the Most High overshadowed her (Luke I, 35), Christ’s birth according to man was celebrated; and he passed through every age, so that all, or nearly all, might learn God: that all these things had been foretold beforehand in the Law and the Prophets, lest a marvelous matter should become unbelievable to all because of its suddenness; and so that those of former times, to whom it was not granted to behold this with their eyes, might, if they hoped without doubt in the coming of him who was foretold, escape the contagion of eternal death.

Thus God so great and such a Son of God was seen upon earth, as much as, or of such a kind as, humanity could behold. For he who, upon the mountain, granting an appearance of his majesty and goodness, manifested himself to the Apostles when his face shone brightly (Matt. XVII, 1; Luke IX, 29; II Pet. I, 17), so that the power of the sun seemed to have gone forth from it, while his garment appeared whiter than snow—for all that, disciples already instructed, already taught, already holy could not endure the brightness of Jesus, who had still undertaken to heal all the vices and sins of humankind (John I, 29). What if God so great had come as to display his brightness and power to human beings? Perhaps every creature, weak and liable to fall, would have yielded and collapsed. But the Son of God had come to save.

Thus, man having assumed a body, God in power (John [col. 0739A] I, 1 ff.).

[Note: [col. 0739]

125. By *parto corpore* understand “having assumed a body.” At the end of the epistle I have noted the passages of Scripture to which I believe Hilary turned his attention. If I undertook to cite the passages in which the Fathers pursue this same matter, I should be almost endless. Scriptural commentators and theologians—especially Petavius (*On the Incarnation*, II.6.1 ff.)—observe that the Lord Jesus assumed human flesh chiefly for two ends: first, to instruct us by his examples and teachings; second, by enduring death for us, to rescue the human race from the demon’s power.

126. At the end of the epistle I indicate the passages of Scripture to which I think he looked. As for the words “through the death of man,” we need not admit that they were corrupted by the copyist. Explain them either as “on account of the death of man”—the death which man underwent in Adam and which the Lord Christ endured the cross to conquer—or as “by the death of man”; for Christ died by the kind of death by which human beings ordinarily die. Refer the word “Immortal” to Christ, who, being God, was immortal in himself.

127. Let the reader consult the passages of Scripture which I indicate at the end of the epistle. Let him likewise consult the Fathers cited by Petavius on this subject (*On the Incarnation*, II.6). I wish to adduce only two here: Hilary—*On the Trinity*, I.13, p. 11, vol. I; *On Psalm LXVII*, no. 23, p. 230, vol. II, “And first, what in the sacrament of the Cross,” etc.; and *On Psalm LXVIII*, no. 14, p. 249—and Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catecheses* XIII and XIV, whose testimonies I indicate at the foot of the page. Recall what we said in nos. 115 and 118. Is there an error in the words “for the ruin and salvation of man,” etc.? Or do they signify that whatever man might have attempted in order to obtain salvation would have been useless? I desire the judgment of others.

128. Recall what we set forth in no. 119, in order to grasp the force of the expression “man triumphing with God.”

129. The words “because whoever has joined himself with God may seem to die, [yet] cannot perish” have seemed somewhat obscure to some. They become clear if you refer them to everlasting death, which those who remain joined to Christ will not undergo. If you wish to refer them to Christ himself, they have the same sense as Peter’s words (Acts II, 24): “Whom God raised up, having loosed the pains of hell, because it was impossible for him to be held by it. For David says concerning him . . . ‘For you will not abandon my soul in hell, nor allow your Holy One to see corruption.’” For I judge that the destruction (*interitus*) mentioned here by Hilary is the same as the corruption from which David and Peter declare Christ exempt.

For a more penetrating grasp of Hilary’s thought, it will help to consult what the most distinguished Maurist monk, editor of Hilary’s works, taught in §III of the preface (nos. 98 ff., p. 32, vol. I). Certainly, whoever hears Hilary’s words in *On Psalm LXIII*, no. 9, will acknowledge that by this word *interitus* he means annihilation: “But whoever will proclaim the death of the soul with the body will hear that the soul is not earthly, but arose from God’s breath and is joined to the elements of the body; and that death is not destruction but its departure from the body.”

130. After the words “life, once the enemy had been extinguished,” I have added “to man,” as required by the order and force of the argument. Hear, moreover, with what elegance and abundance of expression Hilary treats this very subject elsewhere (*On Psalm LXVIII*, no. 14):

> “When the nations were made coheirs, members of the same body, and fellow-partakers with Christ . . . when death, after it had raged in God, ceased; when the law of sin that is in our flesh was removed; when all creation, groaning, hoped for the revelation of the sons of God; when, in the Passion of the only-begotten Son of God, the effect of all causes and origins established before the foundation of the world was brought to completion: by judging the prince of this world, redeeming man from the law of sin, freeing creatures from the futility of corruption to which they had been enslaved, condemning spiritual wickedness by the Lord’s death, and praising God in all things and through all by the gift of eternity and the splendor of our immortality. All these things the power of the resurrection fulfilled, because, when death was driven from the human race through the firstfruits from the dead, the penalty of eternal death was decreed upon the authors of death.”

He had also set forth many excellent things on the same theme in nos. 6 and 19 of the exposition of Psalm LXVIII, at the words “who ascends above the setting.” [col. 0801D] In the third chapter of the *Commentaries on Matthew* (no. 2, p. 667), he teaches matters akin—indeed, identical—to those in our epistle:

> “By this arrangement of events he indicates”—Hilary means that the forty days in which Jesus fasted and afterward hungered signify this—“that after the forty days of his life in the world following the Passion, he would have hunger for human salvation. At that time he brought back to God the Father the gift awaited by him: the man whom he had assumed.” [col. 0802A]

But lest I seem to cite Hilary alone, I indicate, among many others, Cyril (*Catechesis* XIV), Gregory of Nyssa (in the oration entitled *On the Ascension*), Augustine—or some other author—of Sermon 176 *On Time*, and Leo the Great, in his two sermons on the Ascension, especially chapter 4 of Sermon I, “Above all creatures,” etc.

131. There have been some who would have preferred Hilary to have spoken more explicitly concerning the divinity of the Holy Spirit; and this we readily perceive from what the most learned Maurist monk, to whom we owe the edition of St. Hilary, collected in the preface to the books *On the Trinity* (no. 12). Yet Hilary undoubtedly asserted the equality and consubstantiality of that same Holy Spirit with the Father and the Son; this will be admitted by anyone who attends to what is set forth in that preface (no. 15). Nor is this conviction weakened by the phrase he uses in this letter: “He sent the Holy Spirit as his representative” [Col. 0802B].

For, as I have noted elsewhere, Hilary wrote at a time when the error of Macedonius—namely, the error which numbered the Holy Spirit among created things—had not yet arisen; and therefore he wrote somewhat more freely, imitating Tertullian, as he sometimes does elsewhere. Tertullian writes as follows (*On the Prescription against Heretics*, ch. 13): “The rule of faith is . . . that Jesus Christ . . . sat at the right hand of the Father, [and] sent the representative power of the Holy Spirit, to guide believers.” If Tertullian, then entirely orthodox, was permitted to write this, why was Hilary not permitted to do so, especially since the words can readily be understood in a Catholic and sound sense?

The Holy Spirit is called Christ’s representative in this sense: by his inward inspiration and internal breath he comforted the Apostles, helped and guided them, and, if one wishes to speak thus, moved them to those works to which Christ had invited them by warnings and examples. He is also called Christ’s representative because, through gifts poured into the Apostles, he made them workers of miracles, just as Christ’s authority and commands had made them workers of those same miracles. The Holy Spirit is said, for other reasons, to take Christ’s place: for example, because, by the abundance of gifts and their most complete conformity to the divine will, poured into them, he compensates for the bodily and visible absence of Christ the Lord; and for related reasons on account of which he was called by Christ himself “another Paraclete” (John 14:16–17).

We have so far dealt with the expression, “He sent the Holy Spirit as his representative.” But, to say something about the words “that he might be both a help and a sanctification to believing men,” I think that the kind of grace which theologians call actual is denoted by “help,” while that which they call habitual is denoted by the other word, “sanctification.” If, however, one should maintain that the kind of graces which the same theologians call *gratiae gratis datae*—gratuitously bestowed graces—is likewise denoted here, I certainly would not object. For this kind of grace too is both a help and a sanctification to the Church, insofar as it marks her as holy: God thus assists her and invites others to enter her [Col. 0802D] and become holy.

132. That is: up to this point we have set forth, in order, our doctrine concerning Christ.

133. After Hilary had sufficiently declared, in the preceding portions of this letter, his doctrine concerning the Father and the Son, he passes to the third person of the most holy Trinity, namely the Holy Spirit. He immediately states that the Holy Spirit likewise must be believed in; then he declares concerning the same Holy Spirit that he would both inspire and sanctify all things that were afterward to come about, by a communication of his substance . . . But what, you may ask, are these things that were afterward to come about? [Col. 0803A] Is it the Church, built in Christ as the cornerstone joining Jews and Gentiles? Is it the sacraments, and especially baptism, over whose waters the ancients said that the Holy Spirit moved?

> See the note appended to no. 24. You may add very many Fathers who, when treating of the waters of baptism and inviting catechumens to them, said that the Holy Spirit moved over those waters and sanctified them. Tertullian, *On Baptism*, book 4: “The Spirit immediately comes down from heaven and rests upon the waters, sanctifying them from himself; and thus, once sanctified, they absorb the power of sanctifying.”

Or is it the heart of the sinner, which is said to be created in conversion—“Create in me a clean heart, O God” (Ps. 50)—so that its renewal may be indicated? Either interpretation may suitably be admitted. What the period lacks may be supplied by *communication*, or *gift*, or some related word, since from what Petavius teaches we learn that, in justification, the Holy Spirit himself is communicated to us.

> See Petavius, *On the Trinity*, book VIII, ch. 4, no. 5 and following.

What I have just said concerning the two kinds of grace—actual and habitual—seems to me to be stated again here in the words: “and he might inspire and sanctify,” etc.

134. Let the reader remember that here Hilary revisits and explains more carefully what he had briefly set forth in the earlier portion of the letter. Nor do I think it appropriate to illustrate this passage more fully, since I have already taught what is very suitable for elucidating it. Recall, then, what I said in nos. 23, 24, and 30. Yet something seems to be missing here besides the word *communication*, which I said should be added. [Col. 0803B]

135. We dealt with the unity of baptism in no. 25. That sins are erased through baptism is beyond doubt and has been clearly demonstrated by theologians. Hilary, who here briefly comprises the articles of our faith, adduces a single testimony of Scripture, which in our Vulgate reads in full:

> “The like figure whereunto baptism now saves you also—not the putting away of the filth of the flesh, but the inquiry of a good conscience toward God—through the resurrection of Jesus Christ.”

136. Recall what I noted in no. 27.

“[Christ] taught as master” (John 13:13), “persuaded as brother” (Matt. 28:10), “accomplished as God” (John 13:13), “chose as one who foreknows” (John 6:71; 13:18; 15:16), “cared for as physician” (Matt. 8:16; 9:35; 11:8, etc.), and, as man, suffered with others (Heb. 4:15).125 And now, when all things had been accomplished and fulfilled which either the Law or the Prophets had foretold, or which human salvation required (John 19:28–30), at the end, through the death of the immortal man, he was dying (ibid., v. 30),126 so that, mortality having been removed, he might grant immortality to humankind.

Therefore, suspended upon the wood (Matt. 27:35), while the Jewish people cried out (Matt. 27:23)—among whom he had performed such great works—he hastened willingly to death (John 3:14, etc.; 8:28, etc.; 12:31–34, etc.), so that in him all the Devil’s envy might be overcome: “God reigned from the wood,” where the envious one had deceived man. He was to become the death of death. For, having opened the underworld and despised and trampled underfoot all things which then prevailed there for the ruin of man and against salvation, he enlightened all the righteous and those who hoped in him and recalled them to the realms above. He showed the Devil and the powers of this world and of this darkness that their malice had not prevailed, and that they themselves remained in punishments, while the man whom they envied had been set free. The manuscript reads *homini*, “for man.”127

Thus man, triumphing with God, death now conquered, escaped to the realms above, no longer mortal.128 Thus Christ Jesus our Lord suffered in order that he might rise; he rose because he had already suffered. He thereby taught that whoever has joined himself to God may appear to die [Col. 0739C], but cannot perish.129

Yet it seemed too little had been done for the punishment of the enemies if, after destroying the enemy, he had given life to man without adding glory. And so that a greater punishment might come upon the Devil and his angels, he brought into heaven in triumph the man who had flesh now incapable of dying, to display him to the holy angels and powers (Acts 1:9; Ps. 46:6), offering to God the Father the liberated man as a gift.130 Immediately he sent the Holy Spirit as his representative (Acts 2:1, etc.), whom, near to his passion, he had promised to the disciples (John 14:16–17), that he might be both a help and a sanctification to believing people.131 This is the order of our belief concerning Christ.132

## VII

But since we have now made mention of the Holy Spirit, we shall say that one must believe in the Holy Spirit [Col. 0739D], through whom he would both inspire and sanctify all things that were afterward to come about, by a communication of his substance (perhaps *communication* should be added) . . .133 Yet . . . the three are one: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.134 Then one must believe that baptism is one, through which people, purified and made children of God, are sealed in faith; through which every fault either of birth or of the old man’s error might be cleansed away: “in which the filth of the body is not put off, but there is the good inquiry of a pure conscience toward God through the resurrection of Jesus Christ” (1 Pet. 3:21).135

## VIII

After this, the order requires belief in the resurrection of the dead in the same flesh.136 For it is established—and it is not lawful to say otherwise—that the wise and foreknowing God [Col. 0740A] chose it better that man, once made, should be eternal than not exist. If you think it better not to exist, he had that option before he made him.137

[Note: [Col. 0740]

137. I once thought that something was missing here, for it is not immediately evident that what follows coheres with the earlier words—namely, “after this, the order requires belief in the resurrection of the dead in the same flesh.” Yet they do cohere, and I explain them thus: the resurrection of the dead must be believed; for by the departure of the soul from the body man does not perish or wholly pass away, but, according to the wise counsel of God who foresees all things, he remains after death, appointed to rise and be judged at a fixed time. If you think that it would have been better for man not to be eternal than to exist, know that God, before creating man, fully knew what would be better. Therefore, if he made man eternal, it must be said that this was better. What we shall bring forward next confirms this very explanation. I added the word “God”—“that God is foreknowing”—which is lacking in the manuscript, in order to complete the sentence.

138. *Homo qui fit*, “the man who is made,” means “it is established”; unless you prefer to read *qui sit*, “who is,” for Hilary often uses the subjunctive for the indicative, as I have said elsewhere. To come to the point itself: Hilary passes from theological reasoning to Scripture, adducing the Book of Wisdom, which he also attributes to Solomon—insofar, namely, as Solomon’s opinions are collected in it—and judges it suitable for proving his subject; he therefore judges it canonical. In the Vulgate, however, that passage reads: “God created man incorruptible.” Whether anything else, likewise drawn from Scripture, is missing here to confirm the matter under discussion, let the reader judge. Certainly the words “I shall set forth a few by way of example” seemed to require at least two passages to be adduced.

139. The suspicion I have just mentioned—that something is missing here—is increased by the very words cited from Genesis. For they seem to indicate other words of Hilary’s warning the reader that by sinning man deprived himself of the immortality of the body; hence God forbade man to eat from the tree [Col. 0804A] of life, by which death would be kept away. I remain uncertain whether the words “indeed, that he might remain immortal” were once a gloss on the words “God created man for immortality,” which passed from the margin into the text of the letter; or whether Hilary himself rather establishes by them that, although through sin man incurred the dissolution of the body and hence death in this sense, he nevertheless remains immortal in that part which is the inner man (see no. 103), and which had been established as immortal altogether—or, to use the language of the Scholastics, absolutely and independently of every condition. The latter pleases me more.

140. The manuscript reads *quid*, “what,” where I have substituted *quis*, “who”: “Who? Unless the man,” etc. If the reader wishes to retain the former reading, he may do so as far as I am concerned, provided that the word agrees with the rest. The words “the man who had been made immortal by God” denote the inner man, or soul (see no. 103); for this is immortal by nature, while the body was immortal by grace, from which it fell through sin.

141. After the words “for he was already in transgression,” the manuscript adds “he was possessed by sin.” I have deleted this because it is plainly a gloss on the preceding words, “for he was already in transgression,” which slipped from the margin into the letter itself. But I think the preceding words, which begin “But I believe,” etc., contain this meaning: if perhaps the reader is troubled that man was forbidden to take from the tree of life, let him know that this was done for man’s own good. He was already guilty of the crime he had committed. Therefore, had he approached the tree of life, by eating from which he would have prolonged his life, he would neither have known his fault nor directed his hope toward Christ who was to become incarnate; and thus he would not have erased that same fault by sorrow, chastisements, and repentance. It was therefore beneficially provided for him when he was forbidden to eat from the tree of life.

Before Hilary, Novatian had taught this, if he is the author of the book *On the Trinity* [Col. 0804C] attributed to him (ch. 1):

> “For what is sought does not arise from ignorance, but shows the hope of man’s future finding in Christ and of salvation; and the fact that he is barred lest he touch the tree of life does not proceed from the malign rancor of envy, but lest, living forever before Christ had forgiven sins, he should carry about with him, as his punishment, an ever-immortal sin.”

If you wish to see Hilary elsewhere raise and briefly refute the ancient complaint concerning man’s exclusion from eating the tree, consult the passage I indicate at the foot of the page (*On Psalm* 118, letter XVI, no. 9, p. 380, vol. I: “When Adam [was expelled] from paradise,” etc.).

142. I think the preceding sentence means this: it was therefore wisely and beneficially provided for man, who is the true work of God (see no. 97, etc.), that, being compelled to undergo temporary dissolution, he should, after evil has been driven out through Christ’s merits and grace, be raised to life—namely, through the resurrection of which he had spoken before (see no. 136).

143. I fear that something is missing here. Yet the sense still stands even if nothing is missing. We may interpret the sentence thus: man always remains, either because the inner man remains—that is, the soul, which is in no way dissolved—or because, although the body has lost immortality, the mind has not lost it.

144. Hilary meets the objection dictated by experience itself, for we all die. He denies that we truly or utterly perish; rather, he says, we are merely separated [Col. 0805A]. The individual soul remains; the body will rise at the time appointed by God and, reunited with the soul, will present itself before Christ the judge. You may understand the force of the words “man does not perish but is separated” from no. 129. Recall, I beg you, these words: “Whoever proclaims the destruction of the soul together with the body will hear that the soul is not earthly, but arose from God’s breath and is joined to the elements of the body; death, however, is not its destruction, but its departure from the body.”

145. In the manuscript this is read as follows: “but [he is] reserved, fearing, for the judgment of the resurrection of God”; in my judgment this is plainly erroneous. It should undoubtedly be read: “reserved for judgment on the day of resurrection.” I have deleted the word *timet*, “fears,” because all the ancients, whenever divine judgment is discussed, inculcated fear:

> “I feared your judgments,” etc.

Hence, I think, the note *time*, “fear,” or, if you prefer, *timet*, was added in the margin, and through a copyist’s ignorance slipped into the letter itself. Those accustomed to turn over ancient manuscripts encounter such things very frequently.

I now come to the sentence itself. These words are certainly obscure: “nor does man take up the materials from which the body was fashioned.” Does he reject here the opinion of those who thought that after death souls returned to their former bodies, and who invented the gods of the dead and the gods called lemures on that account? Or does he rather teach that, when man rises, he will not have a body of the sort from which he was originally constituted? For who will say that we shall have a clay body, when the human body was fashioned from clay, and the Apostle warns that those dear to God are to be changed at the resurrection:

> “We shall all indeed rise, but we shall not all be changed” (1 Cor. 15:51, etc.),

that is, they will have a body far more excellent?

146. He gives the reason why all, with absolutely no exception, shall be presented before the divine Judge: since the Lord Jesus both died for all and was chosen as Judge of all humans and angels, there will be no one who can escape his judgment, which for that reason will be universal and final.

147. Perhaps the little word *nam*, “for,” is here used in the manner in which it often is in Scripture:

> “For in Christ Jesus I have begotten you”;

that is, the particle *for* does not give a reason for the preceding statement, as frequently happens elsewhere, but takes the place of “and.” Understand the verb *expingi*, “to be displayed,” if no scribal error is present, thus: Hilary has taken Paul’s words, “For we must all be made manifest before the judgment seat of Christ, that each may receive the things proper to the body according to what he has done, whether good or evil” (2 Cor. 5:10), as though the word *referat*, “may receive,” meant the same as “may present” or “may exhibit,” so that all our works, whatever they may be, good or evil, will become known to all.

The words “according to his will” denote either predestination—

> “In whom [Christ] we also have perhaps been called, predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will” (Eph. 1:2)—

or they indicate that those who have done righteous works have done what God most desires. “For this is the will of God, your sanctification,” Paul says (1 Thess. 4:3). The same Apostle teaches related things in Rom. 12:2 and Eph. 5:17. Finally, the words at the end, “wherefore let us seek,” etc., are an exhortation following from the preceding statements and very suitable for stirring people to righteous works. Recall also, if you wish, what we set forth in nos. 8, 27, and 28.

[Col. 0805D] 148. Having passed through the more difficult matters, a long road still remains, though less rough. Having set forth and explained, in the preceding two parts of the letter, the doctrines of orthodox faith, Hilary turns to the proper formation of conduct—“Now let us treat of the person.” He divides his instruction into five parts. The first is directed to rich and poor. The second concerns men and women. In the third he explains what is fitting for every age. The fourth contains a general exhortation to all believers: he reviews their duties, urges them to undergo martyrdom if necessary, and to overthrow idolatry; then, in very brief counsels, he indicates how each should conduct himself rightly and commendably in the manner of life in which he lives. Finally, in the fifth he discusses the virtues.

Although henceforth I shall be much more sparing in appending notes—for what Hilary teaches is almost self-evidently clear—I shall nevertheless add some when I judge it appropriate. The reader himself should consult the passages of Scripture that I indicate at the foot of the page.

149. Here is how the Vulgate translator renders the preceding passage of Paul:

> “Command the rich of this world not to be high-minded, nor to hope in the uncertainty of their riches, but in the living God, who gives us all things abundantly to enjoy; to do good; to become rich in good works; to give readily; to share; to lay up for themselves a good foundation for the future, that they may obtain true life.”

What Hilary subsequently teaches briefly, he treats more brilliantly elsewhere. Here is how:

> “Prosperity makes certain rich persons insolent, and above all vain confidence in wealth drives away the fear of God. They are foolish and do not understand that they ought to be more devout because they are rich, since it is fitting to return thanks to the giver of the good things they desire; and that the charge of avarice is the more inexcusable because prosperity does not excuse the necessity of avarice. Indeed, what an unhappy confidence in an empty thing: to despise God because one possesses gold, as though gold were not among God’s creatures; or, in the judgment of a sound mind, to gain thereby an advance toward a blessed life because one has gold buried in the ground; or thereby to become not a man constituted of soul and body in general, but someone other than he was born; or, when he departs from life, to make use of his gold in death! He will indeed make use of it, if he has used it rightly in life: if he has fed the hungry with his bread, clothed the naked with his garment, relieved the sick at his expense, or restored the captive to freedom. These are indeed the splendid embassies of human treasures before God, the power of obtaining pardon for sins, and true patronage. Thus we shall be changed by gold: from earthly beings into heavenly, and from mortals into eternal beings.”  
> —*On Psalm* 51, no. 21, p. 90, vol. I.

God, being wise and foreknowing, chose it better that the man he made should be eternal than not exist. If you think nonexistence better, he had it readily available before making him.137 That man, who is constituted of body and soul, is eternal is taught to us in many passages of Scripture; but I shall set down a few by way of example. Solomon cries out, saying: “God created man for immortality” (Wis. 2:2).138 Nor without reason, after sin, is man forbidden in Genesis to approach the tree of life, lest he live forever (Gen. 3:22)—indeed, that he might remain immortal.139 Who? Unless the man who had been made immortal by God—and the body did not contain immortality.140

But I believe the reader may be troubled that man was forbidden by God from the tree of life, not realizing that in this too provision was made for man; for he was already [Col. 0740B] in transgression. Before, therefore, this death which God granted to humankind as a remedy, and by which, through the separation of body and soul, sin comes to an end and is uprooted, if he had approached the tree of life, then, because through sharing in life he necessarily would have become eternal, sin would necessarily have remained forever in an immortal man.141 Therefore this too was wisely—perhaps, deliberately—and beneficially provided for man: that, after the interruption of temporary dissolution had been cut away, the true work of God, evil excluded, might be raised to life.142 Therefore man is always [endures].143 But why do we die in this world? The explanation has been given above: man does not perish, but is separated.144 Nor does man take up the materials from which his body was fashioned, but is reserved for judgment on the day of resurrection.145

For it is not lawful [Col. 0740C] that anything should be lacking to God when he judges, since it is certain that God’s judgment has been appointed after the end of this age.146 For this too must be made clear: the whole human being must be displayed, because all will be found either in virtue or in guilt. And it is fitting that those who have done good should be rewarded according to his will, while the wicked should be destined for eternal punishments. Therefore let us seek lawful commands and avoid their opposites, so that, being obedient, we may obtain the rewards.147

## IX

Now, therefore,148 let us treat of the person. In the person two conditions must be addressed: the poor and the rich. To the rich of this world it must indeed be commanded (1 Tim. 6:17): “Do not be high-minded, nor hope in the uncertainty of their riches, but in the living God, who abundantly gives us all things for the fruit of good work; be rich, but be sharers in good deeds; lay up good for themselves for the future, that they may apprehend how good life is.” Then they ought to know that riches have not been received and are not to be possessed so that they may trust that they possess blessedness in these things alone, and misuse them; nor should they despise the poor, reckon riches a ministry of malice or an instrument of lust, consider them entrusted to themselves for their own sake, or suppose that they will never lose them.

Finally, let them know that they have been appointed by God as stewards of God’s grace, so that in their distribution their will may be known as either right or wrong;149 let them know that through abundance, unless they are wise, stronger temptations have rather come upon them. Let them learn to distribute their riches. But in comparison with immortality [Col. 0741A]

[Note: [Col. 0741]

150. Hilary perhaps alludes to that passage in the First Epistle of the Apostle Paul to Timothy (6:9): “For those who wish to become rich fall into temptation, into the snare of the devil, and into many useless desires,” etc. Hilary elsewhere speaks to the same effect:

> “But the chief root of iniquities is the love of money; whoever pursues it is submerged in the shipwreck of a most violent storm. For it follows: ‘Do not hope in iniquity, and do not desire robberies. If riches abound, do not set your heart upon them.’ For in them are great enticements of desire and love: they seize minds and capture wavering hearts. Therefore not only must the plunder of riches not be desired, but our will must be withdrawn from them even if they are offered and flow toward us, lest what has been desired and coveted should rule us. For such goods are not coeternal with our hopes, nor do they descend with us into hell or rise with us from hell. Faith, piety, self-control, kindness, and above all the knowledge of God must be sought. But these things are vain and, by their very nature, ensnaring toward every necessity of iniquity; they must be avoided.”  
> —*On Psalm* 61, no. 8, p. 169, vol. I.

Finally, unless I am mistaken, he indicates that passage of the Gospel: “Be merciful, as your Father [Col. 0807A] is merciful” (Luke 6:36); for by mercy we are made like God.

151. He says that restraint must first be observed in distributing money: it should indeed be distributed, but not squandered and scattered. Whether Hilary here silently indicates the well-known distribution of ecclesiastical money among ministers of the Church, sacred buildings, and the poor, let the reader decide. If he does indeed indicate it, he seems to give the poor precedence in that distribution, as the other Fathers also often do. Did not holy and most learned bishops often dispose even of Church property and sacred vessels in order to relieve the poor?

The words “let them not suppose that what is expended for the use of the poor in consideration of God’s commands can be exhausted,” allude both to the preceding statement of Paul—

> “Hope in the living God, who gives us all things abundantly to enjoy” (1 Tim. 6:17)—

and to God’s well-known promise:

> “Do good and lend, hoping for nothing in return, and your reward shall be great . . . Give, and it shall be given to you: a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and running over, shall be given into your bosom” (Luke 6:35, 38).

Elsewhere too, and often, the benefit of alms given to the poor is commended. [Col. 0807B] I select very few passages out of many and indicate them at the foot of the page:

> Tobit 4:7, 8, 12; Proverbs 28:27; 29:27; Sirach 29:13; Psalm 36:25; 2 Corinthians 9:9–10: “Now he who supplies seed to the sower,” etc.

Anyone who desires much material gathered both from Scripture and from the Fathers should consult Muratori’s discussion of this subject:

> *Della Carità Cristiana*, etc., ch. 7.

Hilary takes up the same matter again below: “Nor let there be lacking,” etc. (ch. 10, col. 742).

152. That is, “is expended” or “is laid out,” unless you wish to suppose a scribal error here and read *deperditur*, “is wasted.” For unbelievers think that what is given to the poor is wasted, though they do so rashly and wrongly.

153. He immediately proves by theological reasoning what he had proposed before—namely, that what is expended for the use of the poor in consideration of God’s commands cannot be exhausted. The word *confuerit* is among those which, although very rarely used by writers, are especially notable in Hilary. Yet the related word *confert*, which is still in use, shows that the same word was sometimes used among the ancients; it is, if one may speak thus, a part of the verb *consum*, which has the same force as *prosum*, “to be of use.”

Besides the passages I have just noted, what Hilary teaches here, which is self-evidently clear, has great force for proving the usefulness of almsgiving. Finally, he treats the danger arising from riches.

154. He at once states what the rich must observe. The passages of Scripture which I noted at the foot of the page in the immediately preceding number partly illustrate this proposition: “He will feel no want either in this age or in the age to come.” For other Scriptural passages to the same effect, see Matthew 5:5; 6:19–20; Luke 12:31–33; and Acts 20:33.

155. At the foot of the letter itself I noted the passage to which Hilary refers, namely Proverbs 19:17. Now let the reader receive what the excellent Calmet says concerning that passage:

> “He who has mercy on the poor lends to the Lord, and he will repay him in return. The Lord himself becomes his debtor and will repay with interest what he has given to the poor. Let him receive him as he himself has received his brother; he will have mercy upon him, etc. He does not simply say, ‘He gives to the Lord,’ but ‘He lends.’ He will not merely receive what he has given to the poor, but will receive it with interest. ‘Our avarice had to be attracted by promises of greater gain,’ says St. Basil on Psalm 28. This interest is permitted. Do you wish to become rich and make profit from silver? Give it freely to the poor; do not fear that the debt advanced will not be repaid. God is your surety; he himself owes you. When the poor man prays for himself, St. Augustine says on Psalm 36, he speaks as though to God: ‘Lord, I have borrowed; stand surety for me.’ Thus, even if you do not have the poor person as a debtor, you have a sufficient guarantor. Behold, God says to you from his own Scripture: ‘Give without anxiety; I repay.’”

Nor would I have you pass over Hilary himself, whose excellent counsels on this point occur in the place which I note at the foot of the page:

> *On Psalm* 131, no. 25, p. 515, vol. I: “Then he says: ‘The poor,’” etc.

156. Critics long ago observed that scribes sometimes, in order to appear learned, very frequently added biblical passages from their own invention. Hence older manuscripts are not infrequently shorter; while they usually give indications of passages of Scripture, they by no means cite them in full. I myself have found this in two manuscripts of Cyprian which we possess. The passage we are now illustrating also provides a clear example. In the manuscript it reads thus:

> “Let him know that mercy is set above sacrifices, the Lord saying: ‘Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.’” [Col. 0808B]

Do these words of Christ teach that mercy is set above sacrifices? Certainly not. The passage cited by Hilary must therefore be sought elsewhere, namely in Hosea, chapter 6, verse 6, where these most explicit words occur: “I desired mercy and not sacrifice.” You have similar words in Isaiah, chapter 1:

> Verses 11 and 17: “What is the multitude of your sacrifices to me? . . . Learn to do good,” etc.
