But if you do not wish to judge our scribe clever, but unskilled—or rather careless—you may suitably say that the words, “The Lord saying: ‘Blessed are the merciful,’” etc., were placed by someone in the margin to confirm Hilary’s statement, so that the person might be judged more blessed on this account. But the one who transferred them from the margin into the letter itself fitted them into a place where they did not belong. However that may be, they certainly had to be deleted here.

157. That is, glory before people, who praised him as generous, and eternal blessedness—for eternal blessedness is here denoted by the term “rest”; see no. 47. That blessedness was promised to those merciful toward the poor is shown by what I set forth in no. 151 and the following notes. See what Hilary writes on Matthew 27:

> No. 4, p. 794: “Those who sell are they,” etc.

158. He passes from the rich to the poor, whom he consoles with arguments carefully assembled. First, he says that God has beneficially provided for the poor, referring, I think, to the Apostle Paul’s words: “We know that all things work together for good to those who love God, to those who are called saints according to his purpose” (Rom. 8:28). Or, if you prefer, to Peter’s admonition: “He cares for you” (1 Pet. 5:7).
distribute their resources, that they may be like God.150 Let them be merciful, not judged lavish spendthrifts and destroyers of the Lord’s substance. Let them indeed do these things confidently and cheerfully. For the Apostle Paul says (2 Cor. 9:7): “God loves a cheerful giver.” Let them not suppose that what is spent for the uses of the poor, in view of God’s commandments, can come to an end.151 152 For these resources have been received from God, and are necessary; and it is fitting both to administer and to increase them profitably. For how can temporal things be lacking, when, on their account, if they are well bestowed, eternal things have been promised and made ready? Truth himself, who is Christ, speaks, saying (Matt. 19:29; Mark 10:29): “Whoever has left for my sake house, or estate, or parents, or the rest, shall receive a hundredfold in this age, and eternal life in the age to come.” And although some assign this to [Col. 0741B] a time of persecution, I nevertheless hear our Lord thus warning us: whenever, for his sake, his command has been fulfilled in any holy work, the appointed reward will not be lacking. Let us not be anxious. God takes care of us. The Prophet cries out, saying (Prov. 22:2, and more expressly Wis. 6:8): “I made both poor and rich; and I have equal care for all.” God takes care: and does anyone fear that the estate from which, at God’s command, he gives away will be diminished? Let us rather fear lest, if we are timid, barren, and faithless in good works, we be judged needy and destitute. Let us rather fear being filled with sorrow; for of such rich persons the Gospel, though in the case of one individual, nevertheless speaks inclusively, saying (Matt. [Col. 0741C] 19:22): “But when he heard it, he went away sorrowful, because he had many possessions.” Let him not fear that he will enter the kingdom of heaven with difficulty (ibid., vv. 23–24).153 Rather, let him be humble; let him be generous, that he may thereby be judged more blessed, if he feels no want either in this age or in the age to come.154 Let him give to the poor, that he may lend to God; let him reckon God his debtor (Prov. 19:17).155 Let him know that mercy is set before sacrifices.156 He will obtain glory and rest, if, from those riches by which others are judged corrupt and ruined, he receives the crown, the fruit of righteousness and mercy.157

## X. The Poor Person

But the poor person is to be consoled in such a way that he may know that, in poverty, he ought rather to consider the good things belonging to him. First, that God has beneficially provided for him: God, foreknowing, has considered his weakness and established that he could not bear the burden and anxiety of riches. Then let him perceive how many temptations and how many dangers he has passed beyond by reason of poverty.158 Abundance is lacking—which is often contrary [to bodily well-being?]; yet in poverty one proceeds most readily and without hindrance to riches of soul. Let him certainly consider from what evils he is free. He lacks envy, rivalry, snares, deceit, pride, contention, and those things which riches commonly generate for a person in the world; for through the flux of possessions and the abundance of resources the mind is loosened, its vigour [Col. 0742A]

> **Note [Col. 0742]**
>
> **159.** He anticipates and resolves an objection which poor people are accustomed to raise. Perhaps it should be understood: “which is often contrary to the body”; for abundance fosters luxury, drunkenness, and the remaining vices of this kind, which diminish bodily strength. Yet I was unwilling to trust my conjecture so far as to append the word *corpori* (“to the body”). The rest is clear and most elegant.
>
> **160.** The manuscript reads *vitam gerere* (“to conduct life”), plainly an error, but one which plainly shows that our manuscript sometimes needs emendation.
>
> **161.** By those words, “let mercy toward the needy not be lacking even on his part,” Hilary perhaps alludes, unless I am wholly mistaken, to that injunction of the elder Tobias, previously mentioned (no. 151): “According to what you are able, be merciful.” I do not, however, wish to conceal that I subsequently read thus in the manuscript: “because, just as a person is made righteous through frugality, if he gives to those below him and to those who have not. Let him not fear,” etc.—an undoubtedly corrupt reading, which I emended, as I could, by substituting very few words, namely these: “as the rich person [is made righteous] by generosity, so the poor person [is made righteous] by frugality.” These words are not found in the manuscript. As for the epithet “glorious” bestowed upon the Apostle Paul, see no. 2.

is broken, and bodily strength is enfeebled. But in poverty there are no wanton banquets, no shameful drinking bouts: all things are sober, all strict, all humble—not abject, since they are full of a pure conscience and virtue. He is not rich in external resources: he is righteous. A rich person does not readily attain to riches of soul, that is, to the virtues of this world. For he who says (Matt. 19:24) that it is harder for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven surely implies that it is easier for a poor man. Let him not suppose himself excluded from God’s care because of poverty: the Prophet bears witness, saying (Prov. 22:2, and more expressly Wis. 6:8): “I made both poor and rich, and I have equal care for all.” For God is not a respecter of persons (Acts 10:34; 1 Pet. **[reference uncertain: XVII]**).159 Nor does he declare that he cares only for the one who possesses the riches of this world; rather, he maintains care for all, including the poor, and will reward whomever he finds either humble amid riches or patient amid poverty.

There is required a distribution, as it were, and a service of each individual, like that of the whole human body. Let him consider that the human body is one body indeed, but has many members. Are all an eye, or a foot, or the remaining members? (1 Cor. 12:14). But, as Paul, teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth, says (1 Tim. 2:7): “We bestow greater honour upon those members which are inferior” (1 Cor. 12:23). And just as the strength of each member is displayed in its own rank and office, so Poverty and Riches are placed like members in the body of the whole human race, so that the poor person’s patience and the rich person’s humanity may be approved by God’s judgment.

The poor person ought to rejoice [Col. 0742C] and give thanks to God, because he has been freed from many bonds of property. On the day of testing he is not weighed down by the fetters of possessions; as a free disciple, entangled by no bonds, he follows the Lord more easily. Let righteous mercy toward the needy not be lacking even on his part, according to his ability (Tob. 4:8); for just as the rich person is made righteous by generosity, so the poor person is made righteous by frugality, if he gives to those beneath him and to those who have nothing. Let him not fear that he himself will lack, if in the practice of holy stewardship he has a most ready will: nothing will be lacking. The Spirit strengthens him through the Prophet (Prov. 10:3): “God does not slay the soul of the righteous by hunger.” And the Lord in the Gospel (Matt. 6:33): “Seek first the kingdom of God, and all these things shall be added to you.” Let him not desire to become rich in this world, lest he acquire very many evils for himself; for glorious Paul says and warns (1 Tim. 6:8): “Having therefore food and clothing, let us be content with these. But those who wish to become rich fall into temptation, a snare, and many desires, which plunge men into destruction.”161 Rather, if he has chosen to believe with true faith and for salvation, let him choose and acquire heavenly riches [Col. 0742D]

> **Note [Col. 0741D]**
>
> Perhaps he refers to Isaiah 33:6: “The riches of salvation are wisdom and knowledge; the fear of the Lord is his treasure.”

which every person acquires and takes up through righteousness, mercy, and other good deeds. Eternal things must be preferred to temporal, stable things to perishable, safer things to anxious, free things to dangerous, more illustrious things to dishonourable.

> **Note [Col. 0743]**
>
> **162.** I have already noted at the end of the Epistle itself that, by the words, “If he has chosen to believe with true faith and for salvation, let him choose and acquire heavenly riches,” etc., Hilary perhaps refers to Isaiah 33:6: “The riches of salvation are wisdom and knowledge; the fear of the Lord is his treasure.” I add that he perhaps also refers to that passage of Psalm 118: “In the way of your testimonies I have delighted, as in all riches.” Hilary indeed explains and illuminates these words thus in his commentary (*On Psalm* 113, letter 2, Beth, no. 9, p. 286, vol. I):
>
> “There are riches in gold, in silver, in money, in garments, in houses, in fields, and in their vines, olives, or crops. But the Lord’s prophet is made perfect by the fruit of doctrines and is rich in the resources of the Law and the prophetic teachings; and, although he belongs to an earlier time, he is nevertheless not ignorant of evangelical and apostolic precepts. For Paul too knows these riches, when he speaks to the Corinthians: ‘I give thanks to my God always for you, for the grace of God that was given you in Christ Jesus, because in every respect you have been enriched in him, in all speech and all knowledge.’ In these things, therefore, the prophet is rich, and in these he delights. But he must not be supposed to have delighted in the acquisition of worldly wealth, since he could not be rich in the Lord except through contempt for and poverty in this world.”
>
> **163.** Hilary now undertakes the second part of the moral instruction which he had set out to explain (see no. 148), and directs it to the education appropriate to the differing condition of the sexes. In the manuscript, moreover, there are some things requiring correction. These are: *omni gerere uni animo*; if you read them as written, they have no sense. You must therefore read them in the manner in which I emended them: that is, “to do all things in harmony, with one mind.” Or, if you prefer: “to be of one mind and concordant in every respect.” The first emendation, which I have accordingly printed, is easier and more probable.
>
> As for the lifting of hands in prayer, since many still practise it—especially those who expound that passage of Paul’s letter to Timothy, “I desire therefore that men pray in every place, lifting up pure hands without anger and dispute” (1 Tim. 2:8)—Tertullian certainly treats it in his treatise *On Prayer* [chap. XIV: “But we do not merely raise …”; chap. XVII: “But with modesty …”; see Muratori’s annotation on this chapter]. There, by “prayer” (as Hilary himself expressly says), he understands a whole and complete prayer, so to speak: namely public prayer, which includes the reception of the sacraments—that is, the reception of full penance and communion. He also then commands abstinence from conjugal intercourse. Please consult the interpreters on Paul’s words (1 Cor. 7:5): “Do not defraud one another, except perhaps by agreement for a time, that you may be free for prayer”—not only Orthodox interpreters, but also outsiders such as Hugo Grotius and other very learned members of the Protestant communion.
>
> **164.** We have come upon a passage which perhaps requires no slight explanation. For these words have acquired various meanings and denote many sacred rites; it would therefore be worthwhile to pause for a while in elucidating them, if the brevity of annotations which I have prescribed for myself allowed it. Yet I indicate the passages from which these matters may be understood most fully. All interpreters discuss the first verse of chapter 2 of the First Epistle to Timothy, concerning entreaties, prayers, petitions, and thanksgivings. Let the reader consult them; but above all, let him consult Augustine in the passage cited in the footnote [Letter to Paulinus, formerly no. 50, now no. 149, ch. 2, on questions concerning 1 Timothy, nos. 12–17]. There he will learn what *deprecatio* (“supplication”), *adoratio* (“adoration”), and *interpellatio* (“intercession”), of which Hilary speaks here, mean. I ask the reader not to pass over this passage of Augustine, for he discusses the matter most copiously and lucidly. From this same passage of Augustine he will also learn what is meant by *votum* (“vow”), when it is joined with *precatio* (“prayer”), *oratio* (“prayer”), *interpellatio* (“intercession”), or *postulatio* (“petition”).
>
> “For, Augustine says, all things that are offered to God are vowed, especially the offerings of the holy altar, by which sacrament is proclaimed that greatest vow of ours: that we have vowed to remain in Christ, namely in the unity of Christ’s body. The sacrament of this is that we, though many, are one body. Therefore, in the preparation for this sanctification, I think the Apostle commanded that *προσευχάς* be made properly—that is, prayers, or, as some less skilfully translated, adorations; for this corresponds to a vow, which in Scripture is more commonly called *εὐχή*.”
>
> In this sense the Church is thought to use the term when, very often in the prayers of the Mass, she mentions vows and votive offerings. There remains *exomologesis* (confession). Many treat of exomologesis; but I indicate here only one author whom we may consult—not urging the reader to embrace his opinion, but requesting that he consult and weigh the passages of the Fathers which he cites. This is Albaspinaeus, in Observations 26 and 27 of Book II of his *Observations*.
>
> **165.** Let the reader consult the scriptural passages which I note at the end of the Epistle itself, and he may perhaps grasp for himself what Hilary teaches. Yet I present here some points which seem to deserve special attention. The words, “For it befits every man to act as priest to God,” can readily be understood in two ways: either that all men professing the Christian faith ought to lead such a life that, even if married, they may be chosen for the priesthood (and indeed Hilary himself was elevated from married life to the episcopate); or that a man’s outward worship and dress ought to be such modest ones as befit a priest. Let the reader judge whether Hilary also indicates that a Christian husband should preside over his household by example and admonition, just as a priest presides over the Church by example and admonition. The words, “but also display the pattern of his life in other respects,” and likewise, “so that, if at the time he does not exercise a priestly ministry and office, he may nevertheless equal the priesthood by the likeness of his life,” seem to favour the latter two explanations.
>
> But before ending this note, I wish to warn the reader that I truly read the words “so that, if *tempor.* [at the time],” etc., in the manuscript precisely as I directed them to be printed. There is, moreover, some ambiguity in these words, though not such as to weaken the explanations above. Is some word lacking here to complete the sentence? Or should one read *tempore*, that is: “if for some time,” or “if at the time when he enters marriage, he does not exercise a priestly ministry and office,” though perhaps he will exercise it later—if, that is, his wife dies or, with her consent, he withdraws from conjugal life. We indeed have not a few examples of this in ancient ecclesiastical records.
>
> **166.** If you combine what is said in Leviticus 12:2 and 15:19, 20, and 24, you may perhaps understand why Hilary says these things: “or when, after childbirth,” etc. For he did not wish the ancient Hebrews to be more continent than Christians. The scriptural passages to which Hilary refers are noted at the end of the Epistle. He also sometimes applies to women the statements which were previously made to all persons.

and let the Rich Person be restrained and the Poor Person relieved.162

## XI. Now Let Us Speak of Sex

There are two sexes, male and female: that is, man and woman. After the matters above which we have set forth, a man, for the formation of a better life, must also observe this with everyone: that he love his wife as Christ loved the Church (Eph. 5:25), so that they may rightly be able to do all things harmoniously, with one mind, and together implore God concerning all things, “lifting up pure hands without anger and dispute” (1 Tim. 2:8); but let all things be done for divine edification. Then let him maintain the bond of union with modesty and mutual chastity; and let them come together when the intention is procreation, or when the time for prayer does not call them away (1 Cor. 7:5). By that prayer I mean the prayer celebrated with every ministry and participation in the sacraments.163 There are, moreover, supplication, adoration, *exomologesis* (confession), intercession (1 Tim. 2:1), and vow; all these have their own times.164

It is fitting for a man, therefore, to pray with head uncovered (1 Cor. 11:4, 7), and not with long hair (ibid., v. 14); his bearing should be simple, not ostentatious or artificially embellished, so that he may show not only by word that he has believed, but also display the pattern of his life in other respects. For it befits every man to act as priest to God (1 Tim. 2:8). And both in catechesis—that is, instruction—and in lay life he ought so to display a most pure conduct that, even if at the time (*tempor.* as the manuscript reads) he does not exercise priestly ministry and office, he may nevertheless equal the priesthood by the resemblance of his life. [Col. 0743C]

But a woman should learn to obey her husband (Eph. 5:22), calling him even “lord” (1 Pet. 3:6). Indeed, she should reverence all men, but serve her own husband, because “the man is the head of every woman” (Eph. 5:24). Let her also know how to live chastely with her husband (Titus 2:5), and let him do the same in every way, so that he knows no woman other than his wife (1 Cor. 7:1, 5, etc.). For he ought to know the proper times for intercourse and to abstain from union when it is a time for prayer,165 or when the woman is menstruating, or when she knows herself to be within the period of purification after childbirth. For God joined marriage not for indecency, but that it might serve procreation.

Let her learn to raise children piously (1 Tim. 5:10: “if she has brought up children”); to be modest, not quarrelsome, [Col. 0743D] not given to wine (Titus 1:7; Col. 3:18; Eph. 5:22; 1 Pet. 3:1), not proud toward her husband (Gen. 3:16; and Titus 2:3–5: “subject to their husbands”; and 1 Tim. 2:12, “nor to exercise authority over a man”), even though she seems greater in property.166 Let her also be modest in gait, not go forth with an artificially adorned appearance (1 Tim. 2:9–10; 1 Pet. 3:3), or arrayed with gold or costly clothing; nor should she cultivate elaborate curling of the hair. Rather, as befits Christian women who profess chastity, not merely in words but through good conduct (1 Pet. 2:12; 3:1–2), let her know that she ought to be silent in church, for it is not fitting for women to speak (1 Tim. 2:11–12; 1 Cor. 14:34). She ought to obey not only those older in age, [Col. 0744A]

> **Note [Col. 0744]**
>
> **167.** I think that some transposition of words has crept into the Epistle itself. For it seems it should be read in the manner in which I have emended it: “Let her also go forth modestly in gait, not with an artificially adorned appearance, or arrayed with gold or costly clothing; nor should she cultivate elaborate curling of the hair; but as befits Christian women,” etc. The manuscript reads: “Let her also go forth modestly in gait, not with an artificially adorned appearance; nor should she cultivate elaborate curling of the hair; or arrayed with gold or costly clothing; but as befits,” etc. Whoever considers the scriptural passages which I indicate at the end of the Epistle, and the passage of Cyprian which I shall cite below, will, I think, agree with me.
>
> **168.** What Peter indicates in the words noted at the end of the Epistle itself—“showing honour to the woman as to the weaker vessel,” etc.—perhaps explains what Hilary says in these words: “nor set herself before any man on account of her sex.” Namely, certain slight tokens of honour with which women were treated even in ancient times raised their light-minded spirits to pride. They were, of course, permitted to sit at the right hand of men, which was regarded as the highest mark of honour. Thus Solomon ordered a throne for his mother to be placed at his right hand [3 Kings 2:19: “And a throne was set for the king’s mother, and she sat at the king’s right hand”]. Indeed, the queen, his wife, is said to sit at the king’s right hand [Ps. 44:10: “The queen stood at your right hand”]. The right-hand place, moreover, was held more honourable among the Hebrews, as is learned from Genesis 48:13–14. Roman matrons were also permitted to use purple garments and golden ornaments [see what Ferrarius relates *On Dress*, part I, book III, ch. 22. Tertullian, however, in *On Idolatry*, ch. 17, affirms that purple and gold ornaments for the neck were insignia of rank. This can readily be confirmed from 1 Maccabees 8:14, together with 1 Maccabees 10:20 and 62]. They could also ride in carriages on feast days and ordinary days. Many others treat of this topic, but Titus Livy treats it copiously and lucidly (*Roman History*, book V, no. 25). Let the reader judge whether Hilary hints at other marks of honour conferred upon women, especially those who excelled the rest.
>
> **169.** Let the reader not suppose that Hilary here favours the opinion of those who thought that the bodies of holy women would be changed at the last judgment—a view of which Hilary himself is thought to have been an advocate [no. 10 of the Commentary on Matthew 5, p. 693, vol. I: “For he will raise the diversity of all bodies that have received life into one perfected and complete man,” etc.; and more clearly no. 4 of the Commentary on Matthew 23, p. 781: “Since therefore he [will make] them [like] angels,” etc. See also the very learned note appended by the Maurist Fathers to the latter passage]. Here “perfect man” plainly seems to mean a person wholly furnished with Christian virtues.
>
> **170.** It is clear that Hilary imitates Tertullian, who teaches as follows (*On Baptism*, ch. 18):
>
> “Moreover, those whose duty it is should know that baptism is not to be entrusted rashly. … Rather, this must be considered: ‘Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast your pearls before swine’; and, ‘Do not lay hands hastily upon anyone, lest you share in another’s sins.’ If Philip baptized the eunuch so readily, let us remember that an evident and explicit favour of the Lord intervened. The Spirit ordered Philip to proceed upon that road; the eunuch himself was found not idle, nor one who suddenly desired baptism, but one who had gone to the temple to pray, absorbed in divine Scripture. Thus he ought to have been found, for God himself had sent the Apostle to him; and again the Spirit commanded the Apostle to join the eunuch’s chariot. The Scripture of his faith presented itself; at the proper time he received exhortation; the Lord was revealed; faith did not delay; water did not wait; the Apostle, when the matter was completed, was taken away. Paul too was truly baptized quickly, for his host Simon had quickly recognized him as a vessel appointed for election. God’s favour sends forth its own prerogatives beforehand; every request can both deceive and be deceived. Therefore, according to each person’s condition and disposition, and also age, delaying baptism is more advantageous—especially in the case of little children. For what necessity is there that sponsors also be brought into danger? Since they themselves may fail their promises through death, and may be disappointed by the development of an evil disposition. The Lord indeed says, ‘Do not prevent them from coming to me.’ Let them come, then, when they are growing up; let them come when they are learning; when they are taught whither they are coming. Let them become Christians when they can know Christ. Why does innocent age hasten to remission of sins? Greater caution is used in worldly affairs: shall divine things be entrusted to one to whom earthly property is not entrusted? Let them know how to ask for salvation, so that you may appear to have given it to one who asks. For no lesser reason, the unmarried too should be deferred—those for whom temptation is prepared, both virgins because of maturity and widows because of their freedom—until they either marry or are strengthened in continence.”
>
> Tertullian and our Author wished, plainly, since persecution often afflicted the Church—and this, in my judgment, is what the words “by the condition of the time” signify—that Christians might resist the tyrants’ devices, whether gentle or harsh. They also wished that our mysteries should not be betrayed, and forbade holy things to be given to dogs. Children, however, generally yielded to blandishments, threats, or indeed tortures, and abandoned the Christian religion; they also disclosed whatever they knew. For this reason they did not wish children to be counted among Christians. Age itself is also commonly less suited to apprehending sublime mysteries, such as Christian mysteries undoubtedly are. For these reasons, as I have said, they generally forbade children to be taught the Christian religion.

I said “generally,” however, for if they knew children to be intelligent, very upright, and steadfast, they did not refuse to initiate these very children into our mysteries. Thus St. Babylas instructed the two boys who later shared his martyrdom. Agnes, who underwent martyrdom at thirteen years of age, undoubtedly shows that the Church sometimes received children into her bosom; yet, when the danger of persecution had been removed, the Church preferred baptism to be conferred upon them in childhood itself.
>
> **171.** I have judged that *aetatis defectu* (“through deficiency of age”) should be read. For although the word *defectu* is absent from the manuscript, it must be supplied, as the very sense of the words demands; otherwise the sense fails. Hilary then warns that children must be instructed by their own parents, because in public sermons precepts appropriate to their age and capacity cannot be set forth. The Church, however, will perform this when a more mature age makes them capable of receiving ecclesiastical instruction. Yet children must be taught gradually, not all at once, lest they either be overwhelmed by the multitude of instructions or, because of their obscurity, fail to learn what nevertheless must be learned.
>
> **172.** Whether *fidei donum* (“gift of faith”) should be read, with reference to that scriptural passage (Wis. 3:14), “there shall be given to him a chosen gift of faith,” or whether the manuscript’s own reading, *fidei bonum* (“the good of faith”), should be retained, let the reader decide. The manuscript reading can certainly be retained conveniently. By “divine gift” baptism can very properly be understood, as also confirmation to be received at the suitable time; although these words may be a fuller explanation of the preceding words, “the good of faith,” and may signify that the good of faith is a divine gift—a point which the Pelagians and Semi-Pelagians later attacked. I have emended the words “and not nature” by conjecture: the manuscript reads “and nature,” in which I perceived no sense; but the sense is clear and probable if you add the particle “not” and read “and not nature.” That is, by persevering in innocence and holiness, they should show that in them reigns not the old but the new Adam. What Paul teaches in chapters 5 and 6 of the Epistle to the Romans [especially verses 18 and following of chapter 5, and verses 2 and following of chapter 6] confirms this interpretation of mine.
>
> **173.** The manuscript reads *affirmandi* (“to be affirmed”) for *confirmandi* (“to be strengthened”). If you wish to retain that reading, I shall not oppose it, provided that you produce probable examples of this meaning. Children, moreover, are strengthened in the good of faith and the divine gift when, through instruction given in church, right precepts are instilled into them and they are told what a Christian must do in order to be pleasing to God and worthy of his calling.
>
> **174.** What we cited from Tertullian in no. 170 (“For no lesser reason, the unmarried too,” etc.) will, I think, sufficiently illuminate this passage. By “children” he certainly understands not only those who are still tender in age but also those who have reached youth. For he would by no means have said that children must beware of fornication if by “children” he had understood only those who were still tender in age. Although “fornication” sometimes denotes every impurity of the flesh.
>
> **175.** Let the reader not wonder that I retained the word *idolatriae* (“idolatry”), as it appears in our manuscript. For in almost all manuscripts, both of Cyprian and of the other ancient Fathers, *idolatria* is read where printed editions read *idololatria*. Baluzius and other critics noted this before me; nevertheless I thought it should not be omitted here. I now come to the meaning itself. Fornication is very frequently prohibited in Scripture. To confine myself to passages from the New Testament, I indicate in the footnote some that confirm what I say [Acts 15:20, 29; again 20:25; 1 Cor. 5:13; Gal. 5:19; 1 Thess. 4:3]. But it is more difficult to explain why fornication is said to have the beginning of idolatry. Except for what the excellent Calmet observes [Eph. 4:19; 5:5; Col. 3:5], that by *avaritia* (“covetousness”) fornication itself—or every form of lust—is understood, one may suitably answer that Hilary had regard to Paul’s words, in which this very point is emphasized. Paul, who, if he taught this, certainly did not teach it rashly, says most expressly [Col. 3:5: “Evil desire and covetousness, which is the service of idols”] that evil desire and covetousness—that is, unbridled lust desiring to be sated with impure pleasures—are idolatrous service. If you seek the deeper reason for this saying, and consequently seek why Hilary teaches: “And he who follows one must necessarily know both,” you will seek what I could not readily explain.
>
> Is it because, since there were no prostitutes among Christians, a man who was a fornicator was compelled to seek out the prostitutes of the Gentiles, who had devoted the commerce of their bodies to impure deities, especially Venus—so that fornication in those times was an interpretative acknowledgment and participation in idolatry? Or because these same women, having gained sway over the affections and mind of their lovers, surely led them to worship their deities? The people of Israel left us pitiable examples of this (Num. 25:1): while they remained at Shittim, they committed fornication with the daughters of Moab, who invited them to their sacrifices. “And they ate and worshipped their gods; and Israel was initiated to Baal-peor.” For this reason the Lord forbade the children of Israel (Exod. 34:16) to take as wives Amorite, Canaanite, Hittite, Perizzite, Hivite, and Jebusite women, adding: lest, after they have committed fornication with their gods, they cause your sons also to commit fornication with their gods. Solomon, neglecting this warning (3 Kings 11:2, 4, etc.), when he was now old, had his heart corrupted by women so that he followed foreign gods.
>
> Yet in order to corrupt minds and turn them away from the right faith, it was not necessary to seek out little women who worshipped false deities. Lust itself blinds the mind and, ensnaring it in bodily and sensible pleasures, draws it away from spiritual and incorporeal things, and therefore from the desire and pursuit of the rewards which the Christian faith sets before us. Hence it seeks to despise them and looks for seductive arguments by which it may persuade itself that it is foolishly despising present goods subject to the senses in order to pursue incorporeal goods reserved for another life. Do I say this rashly? Or do we not rather find these thoughts of the intemperate and lustful expressed in the Book of Wisdom (ch. 2, v. 5)?
>
> “For our time is the passing of a shadow, and there is no return from our end, because it is sealed and no one returns. Come, therefore, let us enjoy the good things that are, and quickly use creation as in youth. Let us fill ourselves with precious wine and ointments, and let not the flower of time pass us by. Let us crown ourselves with roses before they wither; let there be no meadow through which our luxury does not pass. Let none of us be without a share in our luxury; everywhere let us leave signs of joy, for this is our portion and this our lot.”
>
> Therefore, lest they fall into this supreme calamity, Paul warns the faithful to beware the example of Gentiles devoted to lust. It is fitting to quote his words here (Eph. 4:17): “This therefore I say and testify in the Lord: that you no longer walk as the Gentiles also walk, in the vanity of their mind, having their understanding darkened, alienated from the life of God through the ignorance—which, to speak with theologians, is deliberate and culpable—that is in them, because of the blindness of their bodies; who, having despaired, delivered themselves to impurity, to the working of every uncleanness in covetousness.” As to the word *initiated*, see what we said in no. 21.

but also all the brethren (1 Pet. 2:13).167 Nor should she set herself before any man on account of her sex (1 Pet. 3:7).168 For even when she has lawfully accomplished all things, she will be perfected into a perfect man (Eph. 4:13). Rather, let her seek virtue that will attain glory; let her not be hindered by the weakness of her sex, but through holiness, strength of mind, every continence, and devoted endurance, let her equal the most righteous men.

XII. Let instruction concerning the stages of life now be taken in hand. First, I think infancy must be deferred in teaching, because, whether owing to the condition of the time or to age, it cannot bear the teacher’s word. In the case of those to whom, through the deficiency of their age, precepts concerning evil and natural innocence cannot be given, parents must be bound to admonish them; although, as age advances, the Church will not fail, nor cease, to admonish. But this must first be impressed upon children: that they should never be absent when there is teaching, because not everything can be fully taught at one time. Next, they should join innocence to simplicity, lest they continue childhood in persistence in evil. Care must be taken and observed lest they be corrupted in the later stages of life. To their natural goodness they should also add the good and divine gift of faith, so that, always good, always holy, always innocent, always God’s work and not nature’s, they may persevere through the tradition of faith.

They must consider that, in order to remain chaste or modest, they ought to come to church more frequently, because they need to be strengthened more frequently, more frequently warned—those for whom, because of their still less stable age, the devil’s conflict will be more severe. They must observe all things with fear; and, before all else, they must beware of fornication, which has the beginning of idolatry: and whoever follows the one must know both. How, then, can someone be understood to believe and to have ceased to belong to the Gentiles, if he recalls the things by which Gentiles are marked? Let them indeed be obedient not only to their parents (Col. 3:20), but also to all who are older (1 Pet. 5:5), provided that their admonitions and requests bring no obstacle to what is lawful. Let them reckon that they have God as Father (Matt. 6:9); they ought to hope for his inheritance (ibid.; v. 10; Acts 20:32; Rom. 8:17; Col. 3:24), which consists not in temporal things but in eternal ones. Indeed, if God foresees it to be useful for them, he will also grant temporal things, especially when he sees each person seeking eternal things; for his Son, our Lord, says (Matt. 6:33): “Seek first the kingdom of God, and all these things shall be added to you.” Hence no one should doubt that an abundance of necessary things on earth will not be lacking to those for whom heavenly things are prepared (ibid., v. 34). Therefore, because these things are to be hoped for from God, one must obey no one—or rather, one must obey everyone because God wills it—not because some temporal reward should be hoped for from that person, but because in these matters too we strive to fulfil what is lawful before God (1 Pet. 2:13). Finally, they should be congratulated if, at the first beginning of free choice, they have approached God, associating their whole age with the good of faith: because, not having reached the completion of age, they came to attain not so much God’s forgiveness as his grace, while still children and innocent, rather than later becoming something over which they would grieve.

[Note: Col. 0745]

176. He passes from children and adolescents to young men, whose somewhat strengthened age he instructs with excellent counsels.

By the earlier words, “How, then,” etc., he alludes to that Gospel admonition (Matt. 7:16): “By their fruits you shall know them.” The words of James too are very well known (ch. 2, v. 18), and especially apt for confirming the point we are explaining: “But someone will say, ‘You have faith and I have works.’ Show me your faith without works, and I will show you my faith from works.” I interpret the words “the things by which Gentiles are marked” as meaning that Gentiles were recognized by an unchaste life, Christians by a chaste one. This interpretation is confirmed above all by the admonitions of the Apostle Peter (First Epistle, ch. 4, vv. 3–4): “For the time past suffices for fulfilling the will of the Gentiles, for those who walked in debaucheries, lusts, drunkennesses, revelries, drinking-bouts, and unlawful idolatries. In this they are astonished that you do not run with them into the same excess of debauchery, speaking evil of you.” The sayings of Paul likewise confirm it (Col. 3:5 ff.): “Therefore put to death your members,” etc. And elsewhere (Eph. 5:3 ff.): “But fornication and every uncleanness or avarice”—that is, as we said above, desire for pleasures—“must not even be named among you,” etc. He had taught something similar in the Epistle to the Romans [Col. 0814D, ch. 6, v. 19: “As you presented your members to serve uncleanness.”].

The following words, “provided that their admonitions and requests bring no obstacle to what is lawful,” I understand in the manner in which Gregory the Great understands Christ’s words (Homily 37 on the Gospels, no. 2; Luke 14:26): “If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father and mother and wife and children and brothers,” etc. “If we weigh the force of the command,” says Gregory, “we are able through discernment to do both: to love those who are joined to us by kinship of the flesh and whom we know as our neighbours, and not to fail to hate and avoid those whom we suffer as adversaries in the way of God.” These final words—“and the wife herself divinely procured”—undoubtedly indicate a marriage performed through the ministry of the Church. Whoever has understanding will judge this testimony of Hilary on the subject to be most distinguished.

177. He leaves each person free to take a wife if he pleases, and therefore rebukes the heretics who forbade Christians to marry. Then he reproves those who delayed baptism lest they be compelled to abstain from the uncleanness forbidden to Christians by Christian law. He says, of course, that they sin in this very delay. I would further warn the reader that I have substituted *amplectenda* (“to be embraced”), since the manuscript reads *consideranda*—“continence must be considered”—a corrupt reading, certainly, or one in which some intervening words are lacking. If the reader emends it better, he will do me a favour.

178. But he says that those are still more blameworthy who, after receiving baptism, give themselves over to uncleanness and works of the flesh; for, having been enlightened, they fall away (Heb. 6:4, 6). What I set forth in no. 175 may suitably be referred here. The rest will readily be understood by anyone who consults the passages of Scripture noted at the end of the epistle itself. I added, “among the old.” For I thought it should be read thus: “and, young in the inward person, they should, in God’s judgment, be placed among the old”; for the sense itself seems to demand this reading. The manuscript reads: “and, young in the inward person, they should be placed in God’s judgment.” This conjecture is confirmed by the words occurring not much later: “young in temptations; weighty old men in counsels and thoughts.”

179. After the word “vices” there was lacking some word denoting the devil as author of those very vices. I supplied it, since the sense likewise demands it. Who, indeed, would deny that the devil is the author of all vices? For he sins from the beginning (1 John 3:8), and through his cunning death entered the world (Wis. 2:24). Augustine (*On the Usefulness of Fasting*, no. 10, formerly ch. 8: “For the enemy, indeed,” etc.) and Leo the Great (Sermon VII on the Nativity, ch. 3: “For the enemy does not cease,” etc.) rightly describe the same devil as author of all errors and heresies, insofar as by his temptations and impulses he excites evil dispositions within us and urges us to commit every kind of wickedness.

180. I transferred certain words to this place from the preceding passage. In the manuscript itself, after the words “after they have believed, be found,” there follow words beginning thus: “And I think that all these should be admonished,” until one reaches words ending thus: “what we have believed, we have handed on.” Then follow other words: “Young men must consider,” etc. I transferred them here because I thought they concerned old men rather than young men. For unless these are referred to old men, you must say that instruction for old men was omitted, although Hilary had earlier promised to direct his discourse to every stage of life. “Let instruction concerning the stages of life now be taken in hand,” he says (paragraph 12). Whether some gap occurs after the words “weighty old men” I would not at all determine. Perhaps he thought that he sufficiently indicated that he was addressing old men when, after “weighty old men,” he immediately adds: “And I think that these”—that is, the weighty old men—“should be admonished,” etc.

But for clarity’s sake, it is pleasing here to set down the entire passage as it stands in the manuscript:

“Therefore, either a wife must be taken by them, or continence considered. Yet, lest frightened people delay faith, let them know that it is evil not to believe because of uncleanness; worse to be found unchaste after they have believed. And I think that all these should be admonished to obey everyone for God’s sake. Let them learn to govern their own household well. If they have children, let them treat them piously and instruct them in divine matters; for these are signs of our faith: if we have not merely believed, but have also handed on to others the things we have believed. Young men must consider that in all their deeds they should surpass their age: strong in spirit and virtue, and, young in the inward person, be placed in God’s judgment. They should also be congratulated that, not after the completion of every age but in the very heat of life and in adolescence itself, they have renounced the devil, author of vices, and unclean deeds; and that, renewed, they present themselves to God, pure in evil, young in temptations, weighty old men in counsels and thoughts. Let soldiers of Christ know,” etc.

181. In general he exhorts all Christians to answer their calling and to do what the holiness of our faith requires from them. He calls them soldiers of Christ, using a very common expression of that period [Col. 0815D, *In the Acts of St Cecilia*: “Come, soldiers of Christ,” etc.], not only because “the life of man upon earth is warfare” (Job 7:1), but also because canonical writers very often called the Christian life like military service—Paul above all, who frequently addresses and characterizes Christians by this allegory. I note at the foot of the page certain passages which the reader may consult for himself [Col. 0815D: 1 Tim. 1:18; 2 Tim. 2:3; 2 Cor. 10:3–4]. In mentioning gifts (*donativa*) and pay (*stipendia*), moreover, he both maintains the same allegory and alludes to what he elsewhere says about the unfading crown. Crowns were given not only to contestants in the arena, but also to soldiers; civic crowns, triumphal crowns, and others of that kind were bestowed upon them as rewards. He likewise alludes to Paul’s celebrated statement: “The wages of sin is death” (Rom. 6:23). For if death is the wages of sin, the wages of the Christian life will be eternal life (ibid.), which elsewhere is more explicitly called the crown of life. See no. 47.

182. He says most plainly that two kinds of persecutions threaten Christians: first, those from invisible enemies, concerning whom the Apostle Paul says (Eph. 6:11): “Put on the armour of faith, that you may be able to stand against the snares of the devil; for our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the world-rulers of this darkness, against spiritual forces of wickedness,” etc.; and second, those from visible enemies, whether tyrants or others who oppose the Christian faith—or, if one prefers, Catholic truth. See what we said in the preface (ch. 1, no. 4). I did not wish to substitute *contra* (“against”) for *circa* (“concerning/around”)—“concerning the devil”—which the manuscript has, because the latter reading can somehow be tolerated. Yet I myself would prefer to read “against the devil.”

183. You will find much eloquence on this subject, and material suited to persuasion, in the Acts of the Martyrs, in Tertullian’s book *To the Martyrs*, and in Cyprian’s letters and other short works.

184. Recall what was set out in the preceding number. Cyprian certainly teaches the same. I take the word *expugnatur* here to mean a most vehement struggle that ends most gloriously. Hilary’s zeal shines forth wonderfully in these final words: “Every discourse must be directed toward the destruction of idolatry and the praise of the martyr’s crown.”

XIII. Young men, however, must be admonished in this manner: if they have wives, they should be taught to live chastely with their wives. Let them know that it is wicked to touch another’s wife (1 Cor. 7:1). In this they will give proof and evidence that they have truly renounced their former life, if, after believing, their life is reformed for the better. For then a person ceases to be a Gentile and begins to be an initiated Christian, if, cautiously observing the whole law, he presents himself chaste and modest (1 Cor. 7). But if they have no wives, they must be bound either to have them or to abstain altogether, lest they think that the same things are permitted to them as they did before (Col. 3:5; Eph. 5:3). [Col. 0745B] They must know that they have renounced the devil, not in words but in deeds. Let them be admonished and know that fornication and adultery are forbidden. No woman may be touched except one’s wife, and she herself divinely procured. Therefore either a wife must be taken by them (1 Cor. 7:9: “Those who do not contain themselves, let them marry”), or continence must be embraced. Yet, lest frightened people delay faith, let them know that it is evil not to believe because of uncleanness; worse to be found unchaste after they have believed.

Young men must consider that in all their deeds they should surpass their age, strong in spirit and virtue; and that, young in the inward person (2 Cor. 4:16), they should, in God’s judgment, be placed among the old (1 Cor. 14:20). They should also be congratulated that, not after the completion of every age, but in the very heat of life and in adolescence itself, they have renounced the devil, author of vices, and unclean deeds; and that, renewed, they present themselves to God pure in evil (ibid.): young in temptations; weighty old men in counsels and thoughts. And I think that all these should be admonished to obey everyone for God’s sake (1 Pet. 2:13); let them learn to govern their own household well (1 Tim. 5:4); if they have children, let them treat them piously (ibid., v. 10; Titus 2:4) and instruct them in divine matters. For these are signs of our faith: if we have not merely believed, but have also handed on to others the things we have believed.

XIV. Let soldiers of Christ know that in peace they must be watchful, and in persecution most brave. Let them so understand that they have been given the name of military service, and so hope for the gifts or wages of eternal life, that, besides the daily conflicts of peace [Col. 0745D] which we wage concerning the devil whom we have renounced, they may consider the struggle and battles of persecution. Bodily punishments are not to be feared; rather, merits and promises must be considered. Captivity, servitude under an enemy, exile from the heavenly fatherland, God’s judgment, even the enemy’s mockery, eternal death, and eternal torments are what must be feared. Let us consider that we are all mortal and must die. How glorious and worthy of proclamation it is, if what must necessarily be suffered is conquered in glory. Every discourse must be directed toward the destruction of idolatry and the praise of the martyr’s crown, so that the soldier of Christ may go forth armed in every way to overcome the enemy and repel his darts. Let the one who is being evangelized be asked what he does.

[Note: Col. 0746]

[Col. 0816D] 185. I confess that I suspected the reading should be: “Let the one who evangelizes [or, the one evangelized] ask what he does”; or, if you prefer: “Let the one who is evangelized be asked what he does.” Yet I was unwilling to alter anything, for perhaps the word *evangelizat* here denotes one who wishes to receive the evangelical law. I think something is lacking here to complete the admonition appropriate to each condition of life. But who would dare to guess what it was? By *officialis* understand an official or attendant of a magistrate. It is certainly used in this manner in Facciolati’s Lexicon, under *Officialis*, where two examples are given: the first from Apuleius [Col. 0816D: “The aedile orders his official also to climb upon the fish and crush them all beneath his feet,” *Metamorphoses*, book 5], the other from an old inscription in Gruter [Col. 0817A: “The officials of the province of Aquitania belonging to that consul,” Gruter, *Inscriptions*, p. 422, no. 7]. The word *moderari* seems to be used in the sense of “to act with moderation.”

186. The passages of Scripture noted by me at the end of the epistle clearly indicate those to which Hilary looked. I think he also had others in view; but since he did not expressly cite them, let the reader seek them out for himself. I understand “full faith” (*fide plena*) not rashly to mean faith which has works. From James (ch. 1, vv. 17 and 26) we learn that faith without works is empty or dead.

187. Hilary refers to the explicit and solemn renunciation which we make against the devil when we receive baptism.

188. I suspect it should be read: “Hope for the things which are seen is not hope”; for above he says that hope concerns future things, and future things are not seen. Yet because the reading of our manuscript could somehow be tolerated, I left it. Let the reader amend it if he wishes. I have also deleted the word *quid* placed after *quis*—“what does anyone hope?”—because it plainly displayed a scribe’s error. Where the Vulgate reads in Psalm 18, as cited by Hilary, “holy fear,” another very ancient version reads “chaste fear.” Hilary follows the latter, and not without reason. The rest is clear in itself. After the word *judices* I deleted the word *putes*, found in the manuscript, because one readily understands that it was introduced into the epistle itself by an unskilled copyist. I fear that some word is missing in the definition of continence, such as “embracing,” or, if you prefer, “desire,” “love,” “longing,” or something similar. See the immediately following chapter 17: “In good things, eagerness must be required,” etc. Yet here too the reading of our manuscript can be tolerated.

If he is a soldier, or an official, or a judge, let him act with moderation. If a countryman, let him not grumble. If a townsman, let him not be crafty and calculating, nor exercise his ingenuity in evil affairs. If a merchant, let him not swear falsely. If a farmer, let him not hoard grain. If an artisan, let him not mock or deceive.

XV. Faith, as the Apostle Paul defines it (Heb. 11:1), is “the substance of things for which we hope, and the evidence of things we do not see.” A person ought to believe, and by faith, that God is able to fulfil what he has promised, and to transfer his hope to the future. Then, with full faith, he will be able most easily to attain the things that have been promised (Heb. 11:1). Faith places these invisible things before our eyes. Having entered into it, we abandon all things belonging to the devil, to the powers of this world, and to this darkness [Col. 0746B] (Eph. 6:11, etc.); we draw near to God with confidence. For we must believe and hope for the things God has commanded, when we renounce the things the devil had instilled.

XVI. Hope follows faith. Let us therefore speak of it. Hope, then, is the expectation of all future things which we possess in faith; through it we are saved, as the Apostle Paul writes (Rom. 8:24): “For by hope we were saved. But hope that is seen is not hope. For what a person sees, why does he hope for it? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it through patience.” This hope contains fear within itself—not the fear which anyone living in faith ought to forget and cast out, but that one of the spirits with which Jesus is filled, as Isaiah testifies (Isa. 11:1): “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root; and upon him shall rest the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him.” This is the spirit which David sings of when he says (Ps. 33:10): “Fear the Lord, you his righteous ones.” By it people are made blessed, as the same witness declares and says (Ps. 111:1): “Blessed is the man who fears the Lord.” He means that fear which is chaste and modest. For David says (Ps. 18:10): “The chaste fear of the Lord endures for ever and ever.” Thus fear too is twofold: one kind must be sought and the other avoided. The fear to be sought is the warning and safeguard of all that we believe or hope for. For we fear judgment because we hope; and we fear the Lord because we believe him to be a mighty judge.

XVII. But because the fear of God is chaste, and chastity is a kind of continence, we must now treat of continence and its virtues. Continence is the restraint of all evil things that are desired. I added “evil” lest judges think this definition applies alike to good and evil things. For someone who restrains himself from good things is not continent in a good sense; but one who restrains himself from evils is rightly so. Yet in all precepts there should certainly be a twofold consideration and teaching. And I think this should be retained and observed in other matters as well: when you have treated one side, you should recognize its contrary; and the nature of things themselves demands that, when you hold one side, you must abandon the other. We discover, indeed, that evil originally has no substance; for disobedience . . . beside good [Col. 0747A] evil is.

[Note: Col. 0747]

189. These words of Hilary are indeed most excellent: “We discover that evil originally has no substance; for disobedience . . . beside good evil is.” In the earlier part of this statement the impious doctrine of the Manichaeans, who derived the origin of evil from an evil principle, is at once indicated and refuted. When he adds, “for disobedience,” etc., he undoubtedly alludes to Adam’s disobedience, through which death, and consequently all evils, were introduced into the world. Would that the remainder of what Hilary taught in the manuscript about Adam’s same disobedience survived! We should then possess material by which not only the Manichaeans but all who have erred concerning the origin of sin might be refuted. But perhaps a not inconsiderable gap, together with the obscurity of what follows—arising, I think, from the incompetence of copyists—deprives us of this benefit.

Nevertheless, I think it worthwhile to note two matters: first, that the statement, “beside good evil is,” is precisely—unless we are altogether mistaken—the same as that found in Ecclesiasticus (ch. 23:15): “Against good is evil, and against death life; so also against the righteous man, the sinner.” Second, we do not know to what conclusion it is brought. Of the things which follow, we are wholly ignorant not merely of the aim but even of the sense; indeed, since their reading is undoubtedly corrupt, we do not know by what method they can be emended. For who could correctly emend words of this kind: “And which [or, and what; or, and how] if nowhere they are matched to themselves, the protection of good is preserved?” Yet we suspect that Hilary here taught that we are not compelled to evil, but that it lies in our power to embrace uprightness and persist in it, divine grace defending us from enticements and temptations; protected by that grace, we are preserved under good protection—or, if you prefer, we preserve the safeguard of good, that is, we do not abandon the good which we have already embraced.

XVIII. Continence, therefore, must be taught and maintained in evil things. In good things, eagerness must be required. David declares and teaches, saying (Ps. 111:1): “Blessed is the man who fears the Lord; he will greatly desire his commandments.” Again, in another psalm he warns that one ought to be continent in evils and eager for goods, saying (Ps. 33:14): “Restrain your tongue from evil, and let not your lips speak deceit. Avoid evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it.”

XIX. It is also pleasing to speak of those who are continent. For I see many who are continent only with respect to sexual union, and in every other part of continence are worse than Gentiles. [Col. 0747B] For, if you consider it, very many of them are irascible, drunken, insolent, proud, and, inflated all the more by the mere form, as it were, of continence, are assaulters, slanderers, greedy, puffed up, and greatly pleased with themselves. You would judge that the continence which they claim to possess has itself supplied rather the tinder, flame, and material of crimes. Yet these things ought to be cut away, for which we are daily rebuked; and then the virtue of continence must all the more be retained amid all other vices. For perfection, it is not sexual union that must be rejected, but chastity that must be preferred. For when the Apostle Paul admonished the churches, he did not command a uniform continence; rather, he instructed them concerning the matters in which it should be sought and found, saying: “That she may be,” he says (1 Cor. 7:34), “holy in body and spirit,” defining as not continent one who is not proved most continent in both respects.

Many—indeed, very many—are so inflamed with desire . . . as the outcome shows, that they are willing to undergo every kind of punishment or endure any sentence of the Church rather than withdraw from familiar companionship. They do not know that God, foreknowing, said of such persons (Matt. 5:28): “Whoever looks upon a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.” Such people cannot excuse their fault by saying that they have not directed their eyes toward lust, when they lie together under one roof or sleep in one bed. When reproved, they profess that they act spiritually, attaching to outsiders the names of affection or piety. Yet since we also understand the devil’s substance to be spiritual, it should be added: “of spiritual wickedness and malice” (Eph. 6:12)—from God, because of scandal to the Church and ruin. They cannot be torn away from this by their own persuasion, by the prohibition of elders, or by fear of a present sentence or future judgment, although a slight quarrel more often separates even those whom lawful marriages have joined.

“What evil is there in this? What evil is there in an inseparable love, that they cannot be separated from affection for one unrelated by blood?” It is shameful to say what they are not ashamed to do. Certainly they are not even free from kissing, which is the pledge and earnest-money of the serpent.

[Note: Col. 0748]

199. Hilary reports a second excuse advanced by those same cohabiting virgins. And this very excuse, whatever its value, was already being offered in Cyprian’s time. Cyprian rejects it with these truly excellent admonitions (in the same Letter LII, p. 220):

> “Let no woman suppose that she can be defended by this excuse, namely, that she may be inspected and tested to determine whether she is a virgin. For both the hands and the eyes of midwives are often deceived; and even if she is found incorrupt in that part of herself by which a woman may be such, she may nevertheless have sinned through another part of the body which can be corrupted but cannot be inspected. Surely cohabitation itself, embraces themselves, conversation itself, kissing, and the shameful and foul sleeping together of two persons—how much disgrace and guilt do these confess! If a husband, coming unexpectedly upon his bride lying with another, saw her so, would he not be indignant and rage, and perhaps in the anguish of jealousy take up a sword? What then will Christ—our Lord and Judge—do when he sees his virgin, consecrated to himself and devoted to his holiness, lying with another? How indignant he is, how angry, and what punishments he threatens against such incestuous unions! In order that each of the brethren may escape his spiritual sword and the coming day of judgment, we must provide and strive with every care.”

It is worth noting, however, that Cyprian and the others whom Baluze cites in his nineteenth note on the letter we have quoted did not reject the examination performed by midwives upon the bodies of virgins. Hilary certainly condemns it; Ambrose of Milan, a truly eminent man, followed his example.

> [Col. 0819D] See, I pray, what Tillemont draws from Ambrose’s own letters concerning this matter: vol. X of *Ecclesiastical History*, “On Ambrose,” chs. 85 and 86, p. 280 of the Venetian edition. Letters XLVI and XLVII cited by Tillemont are, in the Benedictine Fathers’ edition, V and VI of Class I, “To Syagrius”: “Care must be taken,” etc.; and, “The matters reviewed in our judgment,” etc.

200. What is said here is rather obscure; nevertheless, one understands that the virgins of whom he had spoken earlier were loved more ardently precisely because they professed themselves virgins, although they were virgins in name and profession only. Moreover, they rashly boasted of being virgins, seeking this praise from men when they ought to have expected it from the Lord alone, who would render to them the reward of chastity.

201. That the Apostle Paul commanded women to pray with covered heads [Col. 0820B] is beyond doubt. See the passage from the Epistle to the Corinthians which I indicate at the foot of the page.

> [Col. 0820D] 1 Cor. X, 5, etc.: “But every woman praying or prophesying with her head uncovered,” etc.

But the Virgins of whom Hilary speaks here prayed with uncovered heads—perhaps so that the ornamentation of their hair and head might be visible to all, with the approval of their seducers, whom he had earlier rebuked. He calls them corrupters of virgins because, if they did not corrupt their bodies, they certainly corrupted their minds and morals.

I hesitate whether the words “with their corrupters restraining [the Apostle]” are appropriately placed here. If, however, they stand in their proper place, I explain them thus: these men restrain—that is, restrict—the Apostle’s command, which had been extended to all women, to those alone who were joined in marriage. This was not new in Hilary’s age. For we read in Tertullian:

> [Col. 0820D] *On Prayer*, ch. 31, vol. III of Muratori’s *Anecdota*, p. 40:
>
> “But whether this is to be observed indiscriminately throughout the churches, as though uncertain, must be reconsidered: ought virgins to be veiled or not? For those who grant virgins exemption concerning the head seem to rely on this: that the Apostle did not expressly name virgins, but indicated that women ought to be veiled—not employing the term ‘females,’ denoting the sex, but ‘women,’ denoting a rank within the sex. For had he named the sex by saying ‘females,’ he would have made an absolute ruling concerning every woman. But when he names one rank within the sex, he separates another by silence. For, they say, he might either have named Virgins specifically, or, more concisely, females generally.
>
> “Those who make this concession should reflect on the meaning of the very word. What is *mulier* from the earliest writings of the sacred commentaries? They will find that it is the name of a sex, not of a rank within the sex. Indeed, God called Eve, who had not yet known a man, both *mulier* and *femina*: *femina*, as a general term for the sex; *mulier*, as a particular rank within the sex. Thus Eve, though still unmarried, bore the designation *mulier*; and the term became common to the virgin as well. Nor is it surprising that the Apostle, moved by the same Spirit by which all Scripture—and that account in Genesis—was divinely ordered, used the same word, calling her *mulier*, which by the example of unmarried Eve belongs also to a virgin.
>
> “Finally, the rest does not point otherwise. For by this very fact, that he did not name virgins—as he does elsewhere, where he teaches concerning marriage—he sufficiently declares that the statement concerns every woman and the whole sex, and makes no distinction between a virgin and another woman, since he does not name either separately. For he who remembers to distinguish elsewhere, where a difference calls for it—distinguishing the two kinds by their respective names—where he does not distinguish, and does not name each separately, intends that no difference be understood.”

Nor did Tertullian depart from this view after he had departed from the Church and adhered to Montanus. For he is said to have written his book *On the Veiling of Virgins* after joining Montanus; yet in chapter 4 of that work he teaches the same thing as here. Indeed, throughout chapter 22 of *On Prayer* he vigorously rebukes those who maintained that Virgins could pray in church with their heads entirely uncovered. I ask the reader to read that chapter in full.

Yet the term *mulier* is sometimes used to denote a woman subject to a husband, not a virgin, as is shown by examples from the ancient Latin writers collected by Baluze in note 12 on Cyprian’s Letter LXII to Pomponius (p. 223 of the Venetian edition). I likewise ask the reader to consult that note. The expression *initiantur intecto capite* (“they are initiated with uncovered head”) refers either to the offering by which they present themselves to God, vowing virginity to him in church, or, if one prefers, to public prayers. The remainder is self-evident, especially once that definition of continence which he had previously set forth has been established.

202. The definition of patience given here appears to have been drawn from various passages of Scripture, but chiefly from the first and second verses of chapter IV of the Epistle to the Ephesians. For that passage reads:

> “I therefore, a prisoner in the Lord, beseech you to walk worthily of the calling wherewith you have been called, with all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in charity.”

For it is especially attributed to patience that it bears with others (*supportantes invicem*). Hilary assigns it two parts: one is endurance of injuries and sufferings; the other, patient bearing of every expectation. As to the former, one readily agrees: for we are often admonished in Scripture to practice charity, patience, and gentleness (1 Tim. VI, 11), which require endurance of injuries and sufferings.

Nor can there be any doubt concerning the latter. To omit other passages, James’s admonitions point to this:

> [Col. 0821C] “Be patient, therefore, brethren, until the coming of the Lord. Behold, the husbandman waits for the precious fruit of the earth, patiently enduring until he receives the early and the latter rain. Be patient also, and strengthen your hearts, because the coming of the Lord draws near” (James V, 7).

If anyone possesses this kind of patience, will he not bear—carry—the hardships of life? Will he not also possess every good? Assuredly, he will possess these things who bears all expectations without rash haste.

203. He appears, I think, to allude to the Apostle’s words: “Knowing that tribulation works patience; and patience, proven character; and proven character, hope” (Rom. V, 3).

204. Hilary’s statements are clear if one recalls the definitions he set forth above. The words “I have comprehended above” have the same force here as that which I noted earlier.

205. Certainly *quando* must be read: for when nothing is hoped for, what is hoped for is borne impatiently. But our manuscript reads *quia*, through the incompetence, I think, of the last copyist.

“...to be proved; whereas integrity of mind is required of them before all else, although they cannot be completely examined even in body. For it is not permitted to human beings to know or uncover the hidden places of conscience, as Scripture says: ‘Man sees the face, but God sees the heart’ (1 Sam. XVI, 7). God alone beholds what is inward and secret. But the Lord’s warning is plain: ‘By their fruits you shall know them’ (Matt. VII, 20). Consider what their appearance is like: with what troubled brow, with what shamelessness they look about; how much boldness they display in their countenance, how much self-assurance they carry; in some, their dress is indecent and their gait affected by a profession of self-display. And the devotion, as it were, of such a profession advances to this end: that on account of the name of virginity alone which they bear, they may become desirable. Therefore they make themselves conspicuous when they ought to conceal themselves, rendering their service only to God, from whom chastity hopes for its reward.

“Thus, when they have crossed the threshold of God’s house, they enter upon prayers with heads uncovered, interpreting the Apostle—as their corrupters restrict him—as having legislated about married women, not virgins; unaware that everywhere he calls males of every age ‘men’ (*viri*) and designates all females by the appellation ‘woman’ (*mulier*). I know that I have strayed from the intended discussion of continence, but necessarily so: that henceforth all persons of either sex, instructed in complete continence, may know both from what they must abstain and what they must guard. Or, if one observes continence in one particular kind, yet refuses to receive admonition concerning other kinds, let that person not boast of belonging to the number of the continent; lest through obstinacy that person seem to lose even the part in which self-approval had been taken.

“Therefore, whoever is instructed in continence and wishes to attain it must not seek continence merely in the body or in one part of the body, but must recognize its observances in the entire movement of the soul. For the one who restrains anger is more continent than the one who merely withholds the tongue from abuse, slander, detraction, lying, perjury, and the other evil dispositions of the tongue. Finally, the one who restrains thought itself from all wickedness and refuses every iniquity is fully continent; I compare such a person not with human beings, but acknowledge that person as most like the holy angels.”

## XX. On Patience

Now we must speak of patience and all its goods [Col. 0748D]. Patience, then, is the endurance of all injuries and sufferings, and the bearing of every expectation without haste. Whoever understands and possesses it carries the grievous adversities of life and contains every good. It has hope as its sister. Although above I have stated that all good things are akin to one another. For one willingly suffers because one hopes, and endures what is hoped for; for what is not hoped for is borne impatiently, and when nothing is hoped for. By every virtue patience bears what is recognized when hope has perished. But if patience, which is the fruit of hope, follows hope, it rejoices in faith as its mother; hope has God as its protection; continence, its kind, has kinship with God. Hence the righteous, while they patiently perform all things (Rom. V, 3–4), become glorious witnesses of God, being found full of faith, solicitous in the fear of God, disciples of continence, and children of hope under the guidance of wisdom. Then they become fellow-heirs of Christ, when they imitate him unto death—“if indeed we suffer with him,” etc.; “let us follow his footsteps”—through the virtues, perhaps the struggles, of patience.

206. The words “by every virtue patience bears what is recognized when hope has perished” are indeed clear and plainly connected with what precedes. But what follows is more obscure: “But if patience, the fruit of hope, follows hope, it rejoices in faith as its mother; it has God as its steering-guide; continence as its kindred and kinship.” I explain them as follows. If patience, which is the fruit of hope, follows hope—for *spem* must be read, although the manuscript has *spes*—this patience, or, if one prefers, hope itself, rejoices in faith as its mother. Hope, moreover, has God’s particular protection: “Mercy shall surround those who hope in the Lord” (Ps. XXXI, 70). Continence, however—which is the kind, that is, embraces all these virtues; or, if one prefers this explanation, is their primary parent and, as it were, root—has kinship with God. For through continence we become, as it were, kin to God: either because through it we become partakers of the divine nature (2 Pet. I, 4), or because through it we draw near to God—if we draw near to him, he will draw near to us (James IV, 8)—or, if one prefers, because when we attain heavenly blessedness we shall be like God.

Hilary proves this both by the example of the martyrs, who, strengthened by faith and hope, endured every suffering and torment patiently and bravely, God assisting them by his protection and grace; and by the example of other Christians, who, by imitating Christ unto death through the virtues—or, if one prefers, struggles—of patience, become fellow-heirs of Christ.

> [Col. 0821D] The manuscript indeed reads *virtutibus* (“virtues”), but *certaminibus* (“struggles”) seems better suited to express the point under discussion.

If anyone offers a more probable explanation, he will certainly do me a great kindness. It is also worth observing that Hilary had regard to several passages of Scripture, though we can scarcely identify them with certainty, especially since he follows a version older than our Vulgate.

To conceal nothing: in our manuscript the words “hence the righteous, while they patiently perform all things” occur after the words “through the virtues—or rather the struggles—of patience.” After “kinship” it reads: “hence glorious witnesses of God,” etc. Yet the sense and arrangement of the sentence seem to require the period and the thought to be concluded thus: “then”—that is, finally—“they become fellow-heirs of Christ, when they imitate him unto death through the struggles of patience.” If, however, anyone wishes to retain the manuscript reading and thinks that Hilary took from it the occasion to discuss righteousness, I have no objection. As for the word *gloriosi* (“glorious”), recall no. 2.

## XXI. On Justice

But now let us discuss justice. Justice, then, is the most equitable distribution of individual things and persons. Whoever obtains it and adheres to it preserves life rightly ordered and free from disturbance; keeps fairness in all things; knows what is owed to God; what should be rendered to saints and equals; what must not be withheld from the authorities of this age; what should be retained for oneself; what belongs to one’s neighbor; and what should be granted or is fitting for strangers.

For it is just to worship and love God with the whole heart, the whole soul, and the whole strength; to honor saints and equals; to pay tribute to authorities (Rom. XIII, 7); not to be proud, but rather gentle and humble (1 Pet. II, 13–14); to love neighbors as oneself (2 Tim. III, 2); not to pursue strangers and enemies with hatred, but to love them; and to be subject to those prior in rank or older in age (1 Pet. V, 5). For the Lord too, though he was Lord of all, was baptized by John, because John was prior to him in the birth of human beings (Luke VII, 28), and thus declared that all righteousness was being fulfilled (Matt. III, 15). From this mercy is born; divine service is generated.

Whoever is found in all these things is not undeservedly said to remain in Christ (1 John II, 6), because Christ himself is all these things. The glorious Paul informs and instructs us concerning Christ, saying: “Who became for us from God righteousness and sanctification and redemption” (1 Cor. I, 30). Elsewhere also: “Who is mercy, peace, and love for us” (Jude II), love which the Greeks call *agapē* (ἀγάπη).
