Let us now turn to this, because among all the rest it is greatest; as the blessed Apostle confesses: “But these three remain: faith, hope, love” (1 Cor. XIII, 13).

207. The manuscript reads: “which if anyone obtaining, and to which anyone adhering, preserves his life disposed...” These words are plainly involved and lack clear sense. I have emended them as seemed more probable. Whoever wishes to emend them otherwise may do as he pleases. After the words “though he was Lord of all,” the manuscript adds, concerning John, “who was greater among those born of women”; but this is plainly a gloss referring to verse 43 of Matthew chapter V, and I have rightly removed it.

208. I think that Hilary has regard to the passage which I noted at the foot of his letter, namely verse 2 of the Epistle of Jude. Jude writes: “To those who are beloved in God the Father, preserved in Christ Jesus, and called: may mercy, peace, and love be multiplied to you.” There is no need to refer this passage to Paul; for these same words elsewhere suitably designate another passage of Scripture, and we are not compelled to think that another passage of Paul is meant. Christ can be called our mercy, peace, and charity—or love—both because he is their author and source, and because by his grace he produces them in us. I also suspect that some manuscripts formerly read differently, explicitly saying: “in Christ Jesus, who is for us mercy, peace, and charity, or love.” If you wish another passage to be intended by Hilary, I shall not oppose you, provided you identify a probable one.

209. Ecclesiastical writers call not only love itself *agapē*, but also its fruits, so to speak, and works proceeding from charity. Thus Augustine says: “Our agapes feed the poor, whether with produce or with meats.”

> [Col. 0822D] Book XX *Against Faustus*, ch. 20. See also ch. 4 of the same book.

Anyone wishing to know much on this subject should consult the writers cited by Du Cange.

> [Col. 0822D] In the *Glossary of Medieval and Late Latin*, under *agape*.

210. Here the Vulgate has *charitas* (“charity”). But Hilary, following an older version, reads *dilectio* (“love”), which he distinguishes shortly afterward from charity.

211. From the two preceding definitions it is clear that, in Hilary’s judgment, love is distinguished from charity. One who truly loves God possesses the remaining virtues and observes all the commandments: for who would not observe the commandments of one whom he truly loves? If I were to cite the Fathers, and indeed the very passages of Scripture confirming this, I should be almost endless; for both Scripture and the Fathers teach this very frequently, as does Hilary here. When he says, “Charity is the fulfillment of all commandments,” he seems to have regard to that passage in Paul’s Epistle to the Romans (Rom. XIII, 10), which in the Vulgate reads: “Love, therefore, is the fullness of the law.”

212. Very similar to Hilary’s admonitions are the teachings of Gregory the Great (*Homily XXVII on the Gospels*, no. 1), whose words it is fitting to cite here:

> “Since all sacred utterances are full of the Lord’s commandments, why does the Lord speak of love alone, as though it were a singular commandment, saying: ‘This is my commandment, that you love one another’? Is it not because every commandment consists in love alone, and all commandments are one commandment, because whatever is commanded is established in charity alone? For as many branches of a tree proceed from one root, so many virtues are generated from one charity. Nor has the branch of a good work any greenness if it does not remain in the root of charity.”

## XXII. On Love

Love is, therefore, the bond of souls: chaste, sincere, and without rivalry. Charity is the fulfillment of all commandments. This is the force of all precepts: whoever possesses it possesses all things; without it one remains evil and incomplete. And that your wisdom may know how great is the power of charity, let us read the Lord’s answer in the Gospel. When questioned, he said: “You shall love the Lord your God with your whole heart, with your whole soul, and with your whole strength; and you shall love your neighbor as yourself. On these two commandments hang the whole law and the Prophets” (Matt. XXII, 37). You see that all the chief points of the law hang upon this alone.

Truly, whoever possesses this may already be called God and son of God. Consider that by this alone you are made like God. Does one who loves God hope? Does one fear? Does one trust? No: one only loves.

213. Among the old complaints which Erasmus poured out against Hilary, not the least was that Hilary defended with great insistence that we too are one in nature with the Father and the Son. That stern critic would certainly have increased his complaints had he had this letter in his hands, in which whoever possesses charity is called, without any qualification, both God and the Son of God. Yet the hasty and unjust judgment of Erasmus against Hilary is excellently refuted by Father Constantius, to whom we owe Hilary’s edition; I ask the reader to consult him.

> [Col. 0823D] In the preface prefixed to Hilary’s works, no. 76 and following, p. 25 of vol. I.

This much is certain: any one of us adorned with supernatural charity may in some sense be called God. Did not Christ himself teach that this exalted title could be bestowed upon persons eminent in piety when, in refuting the Jews who disliked his calling himself God and the Son of God, he replied (John X, 34): “Is it not written in your law, ‘I said, you are gods’?” (These words are taken from verse 6 of Psalm LXXXI: “I said, ‘You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High.’”) It is as though he said: Why do you rebuke me for calling myself God and the Son of God, when this title has long since been made common to upright people? Did not Peter also say that people received into the adoption of God’s children through charity become partakers of the divine nature (2 Pet. I, 4)? This is why not only Hilary but other Fathers too call one imbued with charity God, or at least a son of God, or divine. Hear, I pray, what Ambrose teaches (*On Virgins*, I, ch. 3, otherwise no. 11): “The Word was made flesh, that flesh might become God.” Hear likewise what Augustine writes (*Tractates on the First Epistle of John*, II, no. 14, that is, the last):

> “Each is such as his love is. Do you love earth? You will be earth. Do you love God? What shall I say—will you be God? I do not dare say it on my own authority. Let us hear the Scriptures: ‘I said, You are gods, and all sons of the Most High.’ Therefore, if you wish to be gods and sons of the Most High, do not love the world or the things in the world.”

If anyone wishes to find similar statements in Bernard’s writings, let him consult the passages noted at the foot of the page.

> [Col. 0823D] Sermon 8 on the *Song of Songs*, no. 9: “May she, she herself, presume to be loved with a fatherly affection,” etc.; likewise Sermon 46 on the *Song of Songs*, no. 4: “For what our one says, and of our own,” etc.; and likewise Sermon 71 on the *Song of Songs*, no. 10.

214. There are six hundred passages of Scripture teaching that we are loved by God and therefore become like him if we love him—not moved by any fear, just as he loves us without being moved by any fear to love us. This likeness may also be explained in the manner set forth by Augustine, cited above. It may even be said by anticipation that we are like God insofar as we shall be like him in blessedness; grace is called by theologians the seed of that blessedness.

215. I fear that after the words “Does one trust? No,” some words are missing, by whose omission in our manuscript the objection previously proposed is resolved. Yet Hilary’s words may still stand without any break. For charity does not expressly hope or trust—although the Apostle Paul certainly teaches that it does in some sense hope and believe (1 Cor. XIII, 7): “Charity believes all things, hopes all things”—nor does it fear in any way, if the discourse concerns the fear which theologians call servile, although it fears with that fear which theologians call filial or reverential. Certainly in heaven charity remains and we love God, yet we neither believe nor hope. Theologians and interpreters of Scripture treat this subject extensively, especially in connection with Paul’s words (1 Cor. XIII, 8), “Charity never fails,” and with the others (1 Cor. XIII, 10), “That which is in part shall be done away,” etc. Consult them.

Paul says: “God, having loved the world, sent his only Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, so that through sin he might condemn sin in the flesh” (Rom. VIII, 3).

216. In the passage from the Epistle to the Romans which Hilary cites here, the words “having loved the world” are absent, as is the epithet “only,” which is given to the Son. What is absent here is taken from John’s Gospel: “For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son” (John III, 16). Should this be attributed to Hilary himself, who thought Paul taught what he cites? Or does he say that Paul teaches it because Paul teaches the greater part of it? Or should it be attributed to the manuscript which he used, in which the words he cites were written? Or to a copyist who combined two passages of Scripture cited by Hilary into one? Let the reader decide.

And Paul sets charity above all good things, saying:

> “Though I speak with the tongues of men and angels, but have not charity, I am nothing but sounding brass or a clanging cymbal. And though I have prophecy and know all mysteries and all knowledge; and though I have faith so as to move mountains; and though I distribute all that I have as food for the poor; and though I give up my body to be burned, but have not charity, I am nothing. Charity is magnanimous. Charity is kind. Charity does not envy, is not puffed up, does not act wrongly, is not provoked, is not confounded, does not seek its own, does not devise evil, does not rejoice over injustice, but rejoices in truth. It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things. Charity never fails” (1 Cor. XIII, 1 ff.).

Therefore, whoever wishes to discover this virtue, as it were, must have the whole Scripture opened; the whole Law disclosed; all the Prophets presented; all Christ’s virtues, deeds, and commandments made known; and the Apostles’ teaching thoroughly disclosed and taught. And although all the virtues which we have discussed above are incomprehensible to human beings when treated fully, much more so is that in which they are all consummated and upon which they depend—especially since John the Evangelist, in his Epistle, has forbidden us to dispute about it when he teaches that it is both the Son of God and God the Father, saying: “God is love” (1 John IV, 8). If anyone can speak of God in his entirety, that person can also speak of love, which is God.

Therefore, if it is sacrilege to dispute concerning God as much as is not permitted, it is religious to be silent; and the same must be thought concerning love.... For there is as much knowledge of love as of God, because God is love....

Let each person therefore know oneself. For if anyone has love within, that person is God’s dwelling-place, because God, who is love, remains in that person. It is fitting now to bring the discussion of the virtues to its end in the fullness of love and in the consummation of all good things, especially since all have been reconsidered; or, if anything has been omitted, let it be thought concluded in the fullness of the world.

Before all things—or perhaps, before everyone—I ask pardon from your people in the most sincere holiness, praying that your Holiness, whose way has been proved by God to be more skilled and holier, may deign to correct, restore, and supply in all matters in which my mediocrity has either omitted something or has not been able more fully to explain what it found. Or, if you approve that this little work—begun at your request and completed with God’s help—lacks nothing, remember me in your holy prayers and in those of all the brethren. And let the adversaries of my faith know that an account has been rendered, and acknowledge that it agrees with the Church; and let them receive the mystery more fully, so that we may rejoice not only that we have believed, but also that we have profited enemies and believers somewhat.

217. Where I have printed “Therefore, whoever wishes to discover this virtue, as it were,” the manuscript has “this hope, as it were.” But after *veluti* (“as it were”) there ought to be a word which, unless I am mistaken, denotes charity’s superiority to the other virtues. The word *veluti* suggests some hyperbole which Hilary employed in exalting the excellence of charity, but moderated by the preceding adverb *veluti*, which often has a diminishing force. Who could deny that he denotes a virtue by the term *species*, after knowing that he wrote: “although all the *species*—that is, virtues—which we have discussed above,” and below: “it is fitting now to bring the end of the *species*,” etc.? The words “God is love” plainly show that love is here taken for charity, but not in the sense in which Hilary had shortly before explained it. For who would say that God fulfills—that is, completes—all commandments? Can a commandment be imposed upon God for him to fulfill? That one must not dispute extensively about God, but receive in obedience what faith teaches concerning him, is taught by the very numerous and emphatic Scriptural and patristic admonitions which declare God ineffable and unsearchable. See no. 33 and following.

218. Something is certainly missing in this sentence, though only a little. If we trust conjectures, we may supply what is missing thus: “and the same must be thought concerning love; for there is as much knowledge of it—that is, of love—as of God, since God is love.” If you prefer to read *id ipsum* (“the same thing”) in place of “and alien,” I have no objection.

219. Does Hilary here allude to what the Apostle Paul once commanded in these words: “If we judged ourselves, we should certainly not be judged” (1 Cor. XI, 31)? Or rather to the most celebrated proverb of the ancient philosophers, “Know thyself,” often praised by the Fathers themselves? Let another’s judgment decide.

220. That is: it is fitting—or I deem it equitable—that the discussion of the virtues should end in the fullness of love and of all good things. He had previously said that this fullness of love, and indeed of all things, is in God.

221. The words “or, if anything has been omitted, let it be thought concluded in the fullness of the world” are, in my judgment, exceedingly obscure. Has some error entered the word *mundi* (“of the world”), so that something else should be substituted? But what should be substituted, I do not know. Or, retaining the word *mundi*, will you refer these words to the divine Word, creator of all things? Thus their sense would be: if perhaps we omitted anything in the enumeration of things by not expressly mentioning it, it has nevertheless not been omitted altogether; for when we have said that all things were created by God, the very things thought omitted by us have not in fact been omitted. But how far removed are these present remarks from what he had said earlier about God, the Word, and the creation of the world! Yet Hilary seems everywhere to preserve a continuous and connected sense. Or are words missing, omitted by the copyist, so that the sense appears interrupted? Amid such obscurity, let the reader choose what seems more probable. As to the account rendered concerning faith and the adversaries mentioned here, recall what we said in the final number of chapter 2 of the Preface.

222. The words “and let them receive the mystery more fully”—that is, the adversaries of my faith—are also obscure. Should one rather read *momentum* (“opportunity”)? Or something else akin to “opportunity”? If, however, you insist on retaining the word *mysterium*, we may explain it thus, in my opinion: let those adversaries of my faith also receive my confession and acknowledge that I fully agree with the Church, and at last understand why I expressed some matters rather obscurely in my books, veiling them so as not to offend the weaker. For now that an opportunity has presented itself to explain my views, I have explained them clearly. Or, if one prefers, understand *mysterium* to mean a formula of faith; then say that Hilary wishes the adversaries of his faith to receive the same formula of faith in which both he and they fully agree, a formula which most clearly declares Hilary’s orthodox belief. It will benefit enemies and believers alike, insofar as all will agree upon one and the same formula which most plainly declares the mysteries of our religion.

[Col. 0751]

# Notes on the Preceding Letter of Hilary

[Col. 0751A] 1. For a long time I doubted whether anything besides the name of the bishop to whom the letter was sent was lacking here. But nothing prevents one from considering it complete; for this type of letter can quite suitably have such an opening.

2. Although the older Latin writers more often took this word *gloriosus* in a bad sense [Note: [Col. 0751D] Plautus’ comedy entitled *The Braggart Soldier* (*Miles gloriosus*) is well known. Pliny too, in the ninth letter of his third book: “He had also sent letters to Rome, boasting to a certain old woman and full of self-glorification, in these words: Io, io,” etc.], nevertheless ecclesiastical writers generally use it for “excellent” and “distinguished.” In the very ancient canon of the Roman Mass, the Ascension is called “glorious.” In the book of Sacramentaries attributed to Leo by the most illustrious Joseph Blanchini [Note: [Col. 0751D] Vol. IV of the Roman edition of Anastasius Bibliothecarius, 1735, p. XII ff.], I find the following: “It is truly fitting. For thou art glorious in thy Saints.” = “For thou art glorious in all thy Saints” [Note: [Col. 0751D] Pp. XIII, XIV, and XV: “because thou art glorious in the Saints.”]. And later (vol. IV of Anastasius, p. XIV): “May our gifts be acceptable to thee, Lord, which have been instituted by thy commands, and which the glorious festival of the Saints commends. Through,” etc. Again (*ibid.*): [Col. 0751B] “Celebrating, O Lord, glorious exchanges,” etc. And after a few intervening words (p. XV): “It is truly fitting. Thou grantest us unceasingly to celebrate the glorious victories of the holy martyrs.” “Glorious confession”; “Glorious resurrection”; “Glorious God, author of the solemnity”; and subsequently there occurs (pp. XVI and XVII), and most expressly, “the glorious forerunner of the Only-begotten” (p. XX). In that codex of Sacramentaries which the excellent Cardinal Thomasius published (book XI, p. 142 of the old edition), the passion of the martyrs is called “glorious”; and this prayer is likewise prescribed to be said on the Nativity of St. Felix: “Grant, we beseech thee, almighty God, that, as blessed Felix was rendered glorious by thy gifts,” etc. In the same codex the Virgin Mary is likewise repeatedly called glorious [Note: [Col. 0751D] See the prayers to be said at the Mass of the Annunciation, pp. 148 and 149.]. Indeed, in later times this epithet came so much into esteem that it was bestowed upon men especially eminent in rank and nobility as a kind of token and mark of the highest honor. Consult, I pray, what Du Cange teaches on this matter [Col. 0751C] [Note: [Col. 0751D] In the Lexicon under *Gloria*: “*Gloria*, an honorary title,” etc.].

3. Through the copyist’s carelessness, unless I am wholly mistaken, the number which this Psalm holds in the sequence of Psalms is lacking. Our ancient teachers were accustomed to cite the Psalms either by identifying the Psalm through its number in the sequence, or by the words with which it begins; or generally in this fashion: “in the Psalms,” or rather “in the book of Psalms.”

4. I long doubted whether the words “that is, the Gentiles” were a gloss on the word “Greeks,” transferred from the margin into the letter itself. Yet, since I saw that the word *Gentiles* is frequently used afterward, I retained it; judging that Hilary, by substituting the word *Gentiles*, denoted those whom others called Greeks—that is, those still devoted to the ancient superstition of the Greeks [Note: [Col. 0752D] Acts 9:29; 11:20; 14:6; 18:4; Rom. 1:16; 1 Cor. 1:22 and 24; Gal. 3:28.]. Hence Theodoret entitled the discourses which he published in defense of the Christian religion *On Healing the Afflictions of the Greeks*. See what Du Cange has noted under the word *Gentiles*. I have corrected the word *disseramus* (“let us discuss”), found in the manuscript, and substituted *edisseramus* (“let us expound fully”), as the syntax requires.

5. Everyone knows how stubbornly the Jews converted to the faith resisted the admission of Gentiles to it [Note: [Col. 0752D] Acts 13:45: “But when the Jews saw the crowds, they were filled with zeal,” etc.; and v. 50: “But the Jews stirred up religious women,” etc.]. In his Epistle to the Romans Paul is chiefly concerned to teach that Jews no less than Gentiles have been called to the Christian religion. Hilary therefore requires the Jews to acknowledge this before they receive baptism. Almost all theologians discuss baptism conferred in Christ’s name; above all, the most distinguished John Joseph Orsi, to whom I refer the reader with affection.

6. To bring Gentiles to the faith is truly a greater labor, both because they do not possess the Scriptures, in which the true God is made known and the new law and Christ are promised [Col. 0752B]; and also because they are for the most part stained by greater vices, which the Apostle Paul describes [Note: [Col. 0752D] In 1 Cor. 6:10; 1 Tim. 1:9 and 10; Titus 3:3.].

7. The Church consistently observed an order in instructing catechumens before admitting them to baptism, beginning with the unity and omnipotence of God, so as to instruct them and turn them away from the vanity of idols. Consult the ancient formularies for instructing catechumens.

8. What Hilary here says briefly, Paul sets forth fully and often, especially in these words (Eph. 4:17): “This therefore I say and testify in the Lord: that you no longer walk as the Gentiles walk,” etc.

9. What Hilary here teaches in these words, “that is, to believe in one God and to fear him,” the Apostle Paul had already taught in writing to the Hebrews (Heb. 11:6): “But without faith it is impossible to please God; for one who approaches God must believe that he exists and that he is a rewarder of those who seek him.” But if he is a rewarder of those who seek him, will he not be a punisher of those who, though they knew God, did not glorify him as God or give him thanks, but became vain in their thoughts (Rom. 1:21)? “For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of those people who hold down the truth of God in unrighteousness” (Rom. 1:18). Who, then, can believe these things about God and not fear him? Consult, I pray, what Irenaeus teaches on this subject [Note: [Col. 0752D] Book I, chapter formerly 11, now 10, p. 48 of vol. I of the Venetian edition of 1734.].

10. All the ancient forms of the Creed most plainly teach that God, the maker of all things, was proposed for belief to catechumens before they were admitted to baptism. What we call the Apostles’ Creed begins thus: “I believe in one God, the Father almighty, maker of heaven and earth” [Note: [Col. 0752D] See the Codex of Sacramentaries of the Roman Church, published by Cardinal Thomasius, book I, p. 56.]; or, as Rufinus translates it [Note: [Col. 0752D] *Commentary on the Apostles’ Creed*, no. 3, p. 55, vol. I of the Verona edition of 1745.], “I believe in God the Father almighty,” etc. [Col. 0753A] The Constitutions which we call Apostolic likewise teach the same thing (book VII, chapter 41). The formula of the Council of Nicaea presses this point in these words translated into Latin by Hilary [Note: [Col. 0753D] *On the Synods, or on the Faith of the Easterners*, no. 83, p. 510, vol. II of the Verona edition.]: “We believe in one God, the Father almighty, maker of all things visible and invisible.” Irenaeus says (*Against Heresies*, book I, chapter 10, no. 1): “The Church has received this faith: in one God, the Father almighty, who made heaven and earth and sea and all things in them.” He presses the same point afterward (*ibid.*, book II, chapter 1, no. 2 and following). Hence Tertullian says (*Against Marcion*, book I, chapter 21): “Faith therefore always stood in the Creator and in his Christ,” etc.

A scribal error has slipped into the printed text; for it must be read: “the things which either were made, or subsist by his command, will, and action.” Thus the manuscript reads. Further, take the particle *vel* (“either”) in “the things which either were made,” etc., as it is very often taken in ancient ecclesiastical books, namely in the sense of *et* or *ac*, “and”; so that it is not a disjunctive but a conjunctive particle: that is, “and the things which were made, and which subsist by his command, will, and action” [Col. 0753B]. Or take it in the manner in which Augustine took it when he wrote [Note: [Col. 0753D] *The Literal Meaning of Genesis, Unfinished Book*, XXV, otherwise chapter 5.]:

> “God’s dividing between light and darkness must be understood as occurring in the very fact that light was made, since light is one thing and those privations of light are another, which God ordered in the contrary darkness. For it is not said that God made darkness, because God made the forms themselves, not privations, which pertain to nothingness. . . . Yet we understand that these privations too were ordered by him, when it is said, ‘And God divided between light and darkness,’ lest even the privations themselves should lack their proper order. . . . Thus, in singing, pauses of silence at fixed and measured intervals, although they are privations of sound, are nevertheless well ordered by those who know how to sing and contribute something to the overall sweetness of the melody. Shadows also in paintings distinguish what is more prominent and please, not by form but by order. For God is not the author of our vices; yet he is their disposer, when he assigns sinners their place and compels them to endure what they deserve.”

If you desire an explanation of this article, consult Irenaeus [Note: [Col. 0753D] In the places cited just now; that is, *Against Heresies*, book I, chapter 10, etc.], Cyril of Jerusalem (*Catechesis* IX), Rufinus [Note: [Col. 0753D] *Commentary on the Creed*, no. 3, p. 55, vol. I, Verona edition, 1745.], Augustine [Note: [Col. 0753D] Vol. V, Sermon 213, otherwise 119, *On Time*; Sermons 214 and 215; and vol. VI, Sermon on the Creed to Catechumens, p. 547.], and the authors to whom we owe sermons published on this topic under Augustine’s name [Note: [Col. 0754D] Namely Sermons 235, 236, 237, 238, 239, 240, and the following three in the appendix to the sermons; likewise three sermons on the Creed, vol. VI of Augustine’s Works, p. 555.].

11. There are certain errors in the manuscript that must be attributed to the scribe; they are slight, however, and easily corrected by conjecture. But I did not wish to alter the reading on my own initiative. I think the corrupt reading may be corrected in either of these ways:

“Now that the law and the prophets are called [such], what need is there for us to know this—that it was indeed written through men, but not by men?”

Or thus:

“That there is a body of Scripture; that it is called the law and the prophets; what this indicates: namely, that it was,” etc.

The former emendation is not to be despised. The latter also is highly probable and quite plain. For the sense of the words is this: Gentiles, when they seek admission to baptism, are to be taught that there are Scriptures gathered into one body [Col. 0753D]; and that body contains two parts, one of which is called the law—for Hilary often uses the subjunctive for the indicative—and the other the prophets. The person being baptized must know what is denoted by the terms “law” and “prophets.”

The division of the whole Scripture of the Old Testament into the law—or Moses, who comprehended the whole law in the five books written by himself—and the prophets, is very well known [Col. 0754A]. Under the latter member historical books are included, especially under the title “prophets”: either because so many things are foretold in the historical books that they too may suitably be called prophetic books, or because the term “prophet” is here taken more broadly and denotes any sacred writer. In any case, the following sayings of the Gospel declare that the things pertaining to instruction in faith and direction of morals are found in Moses and the prophets (Luke 16:29, 31): “They have Moses and the prophets; let them hear them. . . . If they do not hear Moses and the prophets, neither will they believe even if someone rises from the dead.” Luke likewise affirms that Christ spoke to the same effect in these words (chapter 24:25): “And he himself, Christ, said to them: ‘O foolish ones and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken. Was it not necessary for Christ to suffer these things and thus enter into his glory?’ And beginning with Moses and all the prophets, [Col. 0754B] he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself.”

He does indeed seem afterward (v. 44) to separate the Psalms from the prophets in these words: “the things written concerning me in the law of Moses and the prophets and the psalms.” But these seem to have the same sense as Christ’s other words (Mark 16:7): “Tell the disciples, and Peter”—that is, especially Peter. For in the Psalms Christ, his deeds, passion, and resurrection are foretold more frequently and, unless we are mistaken, more openly than in any other sacred books [Note: [Col. 0754D] Acts 2:25: “For David says,” etc. Again Acts 6:11: “This is the stone,” etc.]. Moreover, we learn clearly from John’s Gospel that the Psalms are included under the name of the law [Note: [Col. 0754D] John 10:34: “Is it not written in your law”—that is, Ps. 81:6—“I said, ‘You are gods,’” etc.].

12. “What need is there for this?” Recall the preceding annotation.

13. “Which indeed.” Substitute: “the body of Scripture,” of which he is again speaking. Moreover, when he calls it “written through men, not by men,” he undoubtedly has in view Paul’s words (2 Tim. 3:16): “All Scripture divinely inspired is useful,” [Col. 0754C] etc. Peter teaches this more expressly (2 Pet. 1:20–21): “Understanding this first, that no prophecy of Scripture comes by one’s own interpretation; for prophecy was never brought forth at any time by human will, but holy men of God, inspired by the Holy Spirit, spoke.”

14. He alludes either to one or the other of the following testimonies, or rather to both. “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the world, and that which holds all things together has knowledge of speech; therefore one who speaks unrighteous things cannot be hidden” (Wisdom 1:7). And: “The Spirit himself, who searches hearts, knows what the Spirit desires” (Rom. 8:26–27).

15. Recall what we said in Annotation 13. Add these words drawn from Hilary, from which you will clearly perceive that the same meaning appears in both places [Note: [Col. 0754D] On Psalm 52, no. 5, p. 96, vol. I.]: “Either he sets Moses over them as prophet and leader and appoints him lawgiver; or he inspires prophets throughout the whole time of the law.”

16. What Hilary here teaches seems to be drawn [Col. 0754D] from these words of Jeremiah (chapter 1, v. 9): “The Lord said to me: ‘Behold, I have put my words in your mouth. Behold, today I have appointed you over nations and kingdoms, to uproot and tear down, destroy and scatter, build and plant. . . .’” (*ibid.*, v. 18): “For behold, I have made you today a fortified city, an iron pillar, and a bronze wall [Col. 0755A] over all the land, against the kings of Judah, its princes, its priests, and the people of the land.” And elsewhere (Jer. 6:27): “I have made you a strong tester among my people, and you shall know and test their way. All are rebellious leaders, walking deceitfully; bronze and iron; all are corrupt”; and similar passages, very frequent in the books of the Prophets.

We learn from many examples that prophets were sometimes charged to carry out the Lord’s promises and commands. I shall mention one here, taken from chapter 9 of the Fourth Book of Kings: we see that very many things previously promised through the prophets were committed to execution through the ministry of prophets. I beg the reader to consult this passage.

17. All who set forth the articles of our faith place this second: “And in one Jesus Christ, the Son of God, [the Father almighty]”—as do Irenaeus, the Apostles’ Creed, and others. All further warn that this article must be understood to mean that he is Son by nature, not by adoption and grace, as we are sons of God the Father [Col. 0755B]. This is most correctly taught in the Apostles’ Creed when he is called the only Son [Note: [Col. 0755D] “And in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord.”]. For why is he the only Son, unless because he alone is Son by nature, whereas we are sons by adoption and grace, as stated? I do not cite the Fathers who interpret the same Creed, since anyone may easily consult them for himself. I cite only Hilary here, who treats this argument in no. 2 of book V *On the Trinity* (vol. II, p. 105: “But we [preach] wisdom,” etc.); and no. 43 of book VI, likewise *On the Trinity* (p. 166: “And since here [he is] the true Son of God,” etc.); again no. 41—that is, the final section—of book VII, likewise *On the Trinity* (p. 208: “Therefore it must be believed,” etc.). He presses the same point most strongly in no. 36 and following of book VI, also *On the Trinity*. From no. 41 I select only the following, which I shall set down here:

> “Accordingly, he set forth no other reason for writing the Gospel than that all should believe Jesus to be Christ, the Son of God. If it suffices for salvation to believe Christ, why did he add ‘the Son of God’? But if the faith of believing Christ is fulfilled only when one has believed not merely Christ but Christ the Son of God, the name of Son in Christ, the only-begotten God, is not derived from the customary adoption that is proper to salvation.”

Hilary is therefore rashly adduced as favoring Elipandus and Felix of Urgel.

18. He undoubtedly refers to verse 3 of chapter 1 of John’s Gospel. The Fathers discuss this matter very fully and frequently. Tertullian indeed does so obscurely, as is his way, and concisely; nevertheless, he teaches things from which you may draw the same meaning. Consult, I pray, what he teaches in chapter 18 of *Against Hermogenes*; and more clearly chapter 19 of book V *Against Marcion*:

> “If Christ is not the firstborn of creation as the Word of the Creator, through whom all things were made and without whom nothing was made; if all things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible—whether thrones, dominions, principalities, or powers—were not created in him; if all things were not created through him and in him (for these things had necessarily displeased Marcion), the Apostle surely would not have stated so bare a phrase: ‘And he is before all.’ For how is he before all, if not before everything?”

And elsewhere, more plainly (*Apology*, chapter 21): “the *logos* of God . . . the same one who makes and made all things by the Word.” Cyril of Jerusalem to the same effect [Note: [Col. 0755D] *Catechesis* X, no. 6, translated by the most distinguished Antonio Agostino Touttée.]:

> “Do you wish to learn that Christ the Lord existed with the Father even before the incarnation, so that you may not only receive by faith what is said but also have proof from the Old Testament? Come to the first book, Genesis. God says, ‘Let us make man,’ not ‘in my image,’ but ‘in our image.’ And after Adam had been made, he says, ‘And God made man; in the image of God he made him.’ For he did not restrict the dignity of divinity to the Father alone, but included the Son as well, so that it might be shown that man is not the work of God alone but also of our Lord Jesus Christ, who himself is true God. This same Lord, who works with the Father, also worked concerning Sodom, according to the Scripture which says: ‘And the Lord rained fire and brimstone upon Sodom and Gomorrah from the Lord out of heaven.’”

But perhaps Hilary treats the matter more fully than the others in no. 15 and following of book II *On the Trinity*. I especially desire, excellent reader, that you consult what he teaches in no. 19 (“For the Apostle taught,” etc.). I also wish you to consult what he teaches on Psalm 91 (no. 3 and following); again, what he teaches in nos. 3 and 4 of the tractate on Psalm 148 [Col. 0756B] (p. 645, vol. I), and no. 44 of book IX *On the Trinity*; finally no. 43 of book XII *On the Trinity*. These Fathers seem to refer not only to John chapter 1 but also to verse 6 of Psalm 32: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established.”

19. This passage contains some obscurity, and I think that the scribe also erred here. For words are lacking, in my opinion, indicating that these things were taught by John—for example, these or similar words: “as John teaches us” = “as is clear from John the Evangelist.” Then explain the words of this Epistle thus: “Through whom”—that is, John the Evangelist—“we have received [the teaching] that the Speech (*Sermo*), that is, the rational principle of the universe, was with God.” For John taught: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God.”

Do not be surprised that I take *Sermo* here for the divine Word. Although, as Petavius observes (book VI *On the Trinity*, chapter 1, no. 5), the ancients—especially those following the Council of Nicaea—preferred to call the second person of the Trinity *Verbum* (“Word”) rather than *Sermo* (“Speech” or “Word”) [Col. 0756C], it cannot at all be denied that this same second person of the most holy Trinity was denoted by the term *Sermo*, not only by those who preceded Nicaea [Note: [Col. 0755D] Tertullian, *Against Hermogenes*, chapter 20; *Against Praxeas*, chapter 15. Novatian, if he is the author of the book *On the Trinity*, chapter 31. Cyprian, *Testimonies*, book II, chapter 3, and *On the Unity of the Church*. Lactantius, *Institutions*, book IV, chapter 4: “For *logos* signifies both speech and reason, because he is both the voice and the wisdom of God”; and chapter 8, where he says: “rightly is he called the Speech and Word of God.” Again chapter 9: “But the Greeks say *logos* more aptly than we say *verbum* or *sermo*.”], but also by those who followed it.

Thus Paulinus of Nola (*Natalicia* VI for St. Felix, v. 25):

> Christ, O God, be present for Felix; grant me speech now—  
> O God the Word, Wisdom, grant a mind made clear.

Rusticus likewise [Note: [Col. 0756D] At the beginning of the disputation against the Acephali; *Bibliotheca Patrum*, Paris, vol. IV, p. 798.]: “If, therefore, the eternal Word is in every way such as the Father is, then the Speech of God is likewise impassible and unchangeable, as is the Father.” Augustine similarly [Note: [Col. 0756D] Book XII *Against Faustus*, chapter 35.]: “The Speech of God sent the law through his servant, but it did not profit the human race, dead in sins.” Elsewhere (*Sermon 8 on the Words of the Apostle*, no. 1): “The human race would not be delivered unless the Speech of God deigned to become human.”

Indeed Jerome, translating into Latin the first Paschal Epistle of Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, presents Theophilus writing thus [Col. 0756D] (*Epistle* no. 96 in the Verona edition, no. 7): “But if the Speech of God reigns, he is certainly God,” etc. This usage of the word was so pleasing to some that they introduced it into the Latin translation of Sacred Scripture itself. For, Augustine notes [Note: [Col. 0756D] Tractate or Sermon 108 on John, no. 3: “And in certain manuscripts it is written: ‘Thy Word is truth,’ just as in certain manuscripts it is also written there: ‘In the beginning was the Speech.’”], in certain manuscripts *Sermo* was read where we now read *Verbum* [Col. 0757C].

That Arnobius who is called the Younger, because he is believed to have lived after the time of Leo the Great, likewise says [Col. 0757A] [Note: [Col. 0757C] Bellarmine, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*; and *Bibliotheca Patrum*, Paris edition, vol. XV, pp. 352 and 355.]: “Therefore the Speech of the Father, proceeding from his mouth and full of power, makes all visible creatures.” Rightly, then, Hilary employs the word *Sermo* in this sense not only in the little work we are elucidating but also in his other books; for example, in book II *On the Trinity* he says (no. 15, p. 36, vol. II):

> “Had you heard ‘in God’ and not ‘with God,’ so that you might take it as the speech of a hidden thought? . . . Wait for the status and name of the Word; for he says: ‘And the Word was God’ [John 1]. The sound of voice and the utterance of thought cease. This Word is a thing, not a sound; a nature, not mere speech; God, not emptiness [Note: [Col. 0757C] I have punctuated it thus in conformity with common usage and the example of others. Yet I grant that it may be punctuated otherwise [Col. 0757D], provided it denotes that this *Sermo* is something substantial and the true God.].”

He presses the same point elsewhere, namely in the passages I note here [Note: [Col. 0757D] Book VII *On the Trinity*, no. 18, p. 181: “And where ‘I said’ is reported, it is rather the speech of one speaking”; and no. 19, “but the heavenly speech,” etc. Again no. 11, book X *On the Trinity*; and more expressly no. 19, book XII *On the Trinity*, p. 430, “but the speech of God,” etc. Also in *On the Synods, or on the Faith of the Easterners*, no. 46, “The heretics, destroying,” etc.]. The Church itself also rightly uses the same word to denote the Word. For it addresses the divine Father thus [Note: [Col. 0757D] In the Introit of the Sunday Mass within the octave of the Nativity, and in the antiphons for the *Magnificat* and *Benedictus* on the same day. We learn from the book entitled *Responsorials and Antiphonaries of the Roman Church*, published by the excellent Cardinal Thomasius in 1686, that this very antiphon has been used from the ancient times of the Church onward.]:

> “While all things kept profound silence, and night in its course had reached the middle of its way, thy almighty Word, O Lord, came down from the royal thrones of heaven.”

That is, it transfers to and adapts to this festival what is taught in Wisdom 18:14–15 [Col. 0757B].

Behold, then, what Hilary commands us to believe by these words: namely, that the divine *Sermo* is not a mere voice but an existing person, who is with God and therefore a divine person. Moreover, that person did not begin in time but was with God “in the beginning,” that is, before any even imaginary and fictive times, as the Fathers often say, and from eternity itself. The same Hilary teaches matters akin to those which he had stated most expressly in books II (no. 13, “Look upon the world,” etc.) and XII (no. 43) *On the Trinity*, as do Athanasius (*Orations* 3 and 5), Nyssenus (book II *Against Eunomius*), and Augustine. See what Petavius teaches on this question (book VI *On the Trinity*, chapter 1, no. 6 and following).

20. The ancient Fathers called the second person of the most holy Trinity not only *Sermo* or *Verbum*, “Speech” or “Word,” but also *ratio*, “reason”; and this term may suitably apply to the divine Word for various reasons. It may be used for the sake of a somewhat fuller, more effective, and, if you wish, more illustrious explanation of the word *sermo*, by collecting synonyms, as it were. Or it may be because the divine Word is that rational principle, or idea, upon which the Father looked exclusively in creating the world: a rational principle and idea unbegotten and consubstantial with God. Or again, because, as rational design holds the first and principal place in an excellent work, so the divine Word held the first and principal place in creating the world. Likewise, because as right reason is evident and conspicuous in an excellent work and is, as it were, present in each of its parts, so the power and wisdom of the divine [Col. 0758A] Word disclosed itself and, as it were, stood forth in creating the world, clinging in some manner to each of its parts and being present within them. Again, because as reason put into practice expresses and makes known the craftsman, so the Word, both its generation and its operation, made known to the world the Father, his excellence, and his divinity. Finally—and this is the last explanation—there are some who say that the divine Word is called *ratio* because it has relation, or reference, to the Father.

Tertullian seems to take this word in the first sense when he addresses the Gentiles thus (*Apology*, chapter 21):

> “We have already declared that God fashioned this whole universe of the world by Word, Reason, and Power. Among your own philosophers too, it is agreed that *logos*, that is, Speech and Reason, is regarded as the artificer of the universe. . . . We also ascribe to the Speech, Reason, and likewise Power through which, as we have declared, God fashioned all things, a proper substance, namely Spirit” [Col. 0758B] (others read “we inscribe”).

With the same meaning he began the book entitled *On Prayer* as follows:

> “The Spirit of God, the Speech of God, and the Reason of God; the Speech of Reason and the Reason of Speech; and the Spirit which is both—Jesus Christ our Lord.”

And indeed the term *ratio*, when employed to denote God’s Only-begotten, seems to be a synonym of the terms *Sermo* and *Verbum*, as Lactantius, Ambrose—if he is the author of the book entitled *On the Divinity of the Son, or On the Orthodox Faith against the Arians*—and Augustine teach, to pass over others [Note: [Col. 0757D] Lactantius says in book IV, chapter 9 of the *Institutions*: “For *logos* signifies both speech and reason, because he is both the voice and the wisdom of God.” Augustine, if that author is Augustine—for the Maurist Fathers deny that book to Augustine [Col. 0758C], and not without reason, as is clear from the prefatory admonition to the work, p. 2 of the Appendix to vol. VIII—in the book *On Five Heresies*, chapter 6, says: “In the beginning was the Word. In Greek it is better said *logos*; for *logos* signifies Word and reason.” Finally Ambrose—if, as I said above, he is the author of that book [Col. 0758D] (see the Maurist Fathers’ prefatory admonition to this treatise, p. 343 of the Appendix to Ambrose)—says in the book entitled *On the Divinity of the Son*, chapter 6: “There is a certain reason which among the Greeks is called *logos*, which distinguishes the persons or names between Father and Son, because the Son himself is also called reason.” These very words also occur in Sermon 190 *On Time* among the Augustinian sermons, now 113 among those rejected into the appendix, no. 2. After the foregoing words that sermon adds: “Yet this reason is called by many names: now Word, now Power, now Wisdom, now Right Hand, now Arm, now Pearl, now Treasure, now Nets, now Plough, now Fountain, now Rock, now Cornerstone, now Man, now Lamb, now Calf, now Eagle, now Lion, now Way, Truth, and Life—although he is God, all in all—so that through these names the mysteries of divine dispensations may be known, not so that the very majesty of the Son of God may be shown as properly defined.”], or, if you prefer, another writer concealing himself under Augustine’s name.

Should we trace the reason for this usage to the fact that, in Tertullian’s words (*Apology*, chapter 21), “he showed himself the *logos* of God, that is, that primal, firstborn Word, attended by power and reason, upheld by the Spirit”? Or rather, because, as Petavius has already taught (book VI *On the Trinity*, chapter 1, no. 6), *sermo* is the same as *ratio*, and hence he is called “the speech of reason and the reason of speech” [Col. 0758C]? Certainly Hilary himself, in the very Epistle we are elucidating, says (chapter 4, p. 40): “the Son of God, true wisdom, speech, that is, reason,” etc.

The second meaning—namely, that this designation is derived from the fact that God’s only-begotten is the rational principle or idea to which the Father alone looked in creating the world—is put forward by the author to whom we owe the book *On the Divine Names* (chapter 7), whether he is Dionysius the Areopagite or some other writer, certainly ancient and plausible. For, in Petavius’ translation, he says:

> “In the sacred writings the *Logos* is celebrated as God [Col. 0759A], not merely because he is the dispenser of reason and better wisdom, but also because he has beforehand comprehended in himself, simply, the causes of all things; and because he reaches and penetrates all things, as the sacred writings testify” [Note: [Col. 0759D] As I said, I have used Petavius’ translation, for others translate differently. Indeed, the translation of Ambrose Camaldulensis differs somewhat from Petavius’; nevertheless, all the translations have the same meaning.].

Maximus, elucidating this passage, says for that reason [Note: [Col. 0759D] In Petavius’ translation, book VI *On the Trinity*, chapter 1, no. 3.] that “the divine Word is called *logos* because the rational principles of the whole of nature are present in him, as causes and the principle of every creature; for through him all things exist. Indeed, the ideas and exemplary forms are in him; they are eternal conceptions and rational principles productive of all things; and therefore nature itself, since nature itself is a rational principle containing cause and nature, because the natures of existing things are not random and purposeless.”

The third explanation, which we said lies in this, “that as rational design holds the first and chief place in an excellent work, so the divine Word held the first and chief place in creating the world”—this third explanation, I say, is advanced by those whose opinion Augustine describes when he testifies [Note: [Col. 0759D] *Eighty-Three Questions*, chapter or question 63.] that [Col. 0759B] “the Only-begotten of God is less correctly called Reason than Word, so that there may be indicated not only his reference to the Father but also the operative power directed toward those things that were made through the Word.” It is also advanced by those who, wishing *ratio* to be synonymous with *sermo* and *logos*, observe that the divine Speech, insofar as it is also taken for a person, held the chief place in creating the world. We said something on this matter in Annotation 18 and shall say more below. Here I cite only Nazianzen, who says (*Oration* 36):

> “But if anyone also wishes to call him *logos*, because he is present in all things, he will not depart from reason; for what is there that has not been created by the Word?” [Note: [Col. 0759D] I have used Petavius’ translation, from which [Col. 0760D] the old translation of Billius scarcely differs. You will find this passage on p. 500, vol. I, Cologne edition of 1690.]

We affirmed that the fourth explanation lies in this: “just as, in an excellent work of craftsmanship, sound reason appears and stands out, and is, as it were, present in each of its parts; so the power and wisdom of the divine Word manifested itself in creating the world, and, as it were, stood forth, adhering in some manner to, and being present in, each of its parts.” Nazianzen is accordingly said to favor this view in the words cited above: “If anyone wishes, because it is present in all things, to call it *logos* (λόγος), he will not depart from reason.” But those certainly support it who say that the term *wisdom* is synonymous with *reason* [Note: [Col. 0760D] I have heard someone cite for this purpose the following words of Lactantius; whether rightly or otherwise, let others judge: “For *logos* signifies both speech and reason, because it is both the voice and the wisdom of God.” Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, book IV, ch. 9.], and who refer to the twenty-fourth verse of chapter VII and the first verse of chapter VIII of the Book of Wisdom as concerning the divine Word. For the following is read in the passages cited: “For wisdom is more mobile than all movable things; and because of her purity she reaches everywhere . . . Therefore she reaches mightily from one end to the other, and orders all things sweetly.”

We said that the fifth explanation is that which teaches “that, just as reason put into practice expresses and reveals the craftsman, so the Word—both its generation and its operation—signified and made known to the world the Father, his excellence, and his divinity.” Unless the authority of very eminent men misleads us, this is proposed by Nazianzen, who calls the Son of God the *horos* and *logos* of the Father (ὄρον καὶ λόγον τοῦ Πατρός), that is, as Petavius translates it [Col. 0759D] (*On the Trinity*, book VI, ch. 1, no. 3), “the definition and reason of the Father”; and he afterwards explains why he calls him so in the following words, rendered into Latin by Billius (vol. I, p. 590):

> “He is called Word because he stands related to the Father as speech to mind, not only because of a generation wholly free from passion, but also because of his union with the Father and his declarative power; perhaps, too, because he is related to the Father as a definition to the thing defined. For a definition too is called *logos* [Col. 0760A]. For he who has known the Son, Christ says—this is the meaning of ‘he who has seen’ [John XIV]—has also known the Father; and the Son is a brief, concise, and readily apprehended declaration of the paternal nature. For everything begotten defines its begetter by a certain silent voice.”

The final explanation, however—that which teaches “that the divine Word was called reason because it has a relation or reference to the Father”—is proposed by Nazianzen, whom I have just cited; also by Augustine, whose words I quoted a little earlier (*Eighty-Three Questions*, ch. 63); and finally, not to adduce very many, by Ambrose—if you consider Ambrose the author of the book *On the Divinity of the Son* among Ambrose’s works:

> “It is a certain reason,” he says (*On the Divinity of the Son*, ch. 6; in the appendix to Ambrose’s Works, p. 346, etc.), “which among the Greeks is called *logos* (λόγος), which distinguishes the persons or names of Father and Son; because the Son himself is also called reason.”

These are the more celebrated explanations of the word *reason* [Col. 0760B] when it is applied to the divine Word. Yet I suspect that Hilary, when he calls the Word “the reason of the universe,” also intended another explanation: namely, that the only-begotten Son of God is the one reason why the universe of things exists—one, I say, because he himself created all things; and one also because his incarnation was the reason for which all things were created. Theologians treat this matter at greatest length. Hence in Scripture he is called the beginning of the ways of the Lord; and Paul likewise calls him “the firstborn of every creature” (Col. I. 15), adding: “For in him were created all things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers: all things were created through him and in him; and he is before all things, and all things hold together in him.”

Jerome seems to have anticipated this conjecture of mine when he wrote the following to Paulinus (formerly Epistle 103; in the Verona edition, 53, no. 4):

> “*Logos* in Greek signifies many things: for it is word, reason, [Col. 0760C] calculation, and the cause of each individual thing, through which the particular things that subsist exist; and we rightly understand all these meanings in Christ.”

This note, although somewhat lengthy, will, I think, not be unwelcome to the reader.

**21.** This word *initiates*, insofar as it is used for *begins* or *commences*, is among the words which many have noted in Hilary as very rarely used by others. Yet others used it even before Hilary. Vitruvius, near the end of the preface to Book VII, calls *initiantes* those whom others customarily call *initiati*, “initiated persons.” Tertullian similarly writes (*Against Valentinus*, ch. 15): “From these the rest were initiated,” that is, they derived their beginning or commencement. Julius Firmicus likewise uses it in the same sense: “Spring is initiated,” he says, “when the sun has entered the first part of Aries.”

**22.** All who have disputed on this subject teach that the first chapter of John’s Gospel is most suitable for refuting the utterly foolish persuasion of the Arians. [Col. 0760D] I mention here only Augustine (*Tractate* 1 *on John*, and often elsewhere), and Hilary (*On the Trinity*, book II, no. 13, pp. 34–35, and often elsewhere). Indeed, from Jerome we learn that John wrote his Gospel chiefly in order to oppose those who denied Christ’s divine origin [Note: [Col. 0760D] “Last of all he wrote the Gospel, at the request of the bishops of Asia, against Cerinthus and other [Col. 0761C] heretics, and especially against the then-rising doctrine of the Ebionites, who maintain that Christ did not exist before Mary; whence he was compelled to declare his divine birth.” Jerome, in the book entitled *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 9.].

**23.** All who professed the Christian religion were bound to confess the Holy Spirit as the third person of the most holy Trinity. This is certainly shown by the Apostles’ Creed, Irenaeus (*Against Heresies*, book I, ch. 10), the Nicene [Col. 0761A] Creed (Hilary, *On the Synods*, no. 84), the creed attributed to Athanasius, and the remaining formulas of the Christian faith. This is not the place for me to defend the divinity of the Holy Spirit, which Catholic theologians assert most copiously [Note: [Col. 0761C] See, without enumerating them all, Petavius, *On the Trinity*, book II, chs. 12–14.], and which was asserted not obscurely even by those Fathers who preceded in time the Council of Constantinople—and therefore the Nicene Council as well [Note: [Col. 0761C] Dom Renatus Massuet collected passages from Irenaeus attesting the divinity of the Holy Spirit: Dissertation 3, nos. 51–53, pp. 116–117 of vol. II of the Venetian edition [Col. 0761D] of 1734. Tertullian, moreover, although numbered among those who, following Montanus’s error, held unsound views concerning the Trinity and explicitly concerning the Holy Spirit, nevertheless, before allowing himself to be corrupted, most openly professed the divinity of the Holy Spirit in chapters 8, 9, and 13 of *Against Praxeas*. I wish the reader to consult those passages in such a way as not to pass over the other chapters of the same book.].

To return to Hilary: he is criticized by some rather bold persons as though he hesitated to affirm the divinity of the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0761D] See the Preface to *On the Trinity*, no. 12, p. VIII of vol. II of the Verona edition.]. But he is criticized wrongly. For he wrote the following concerning the Holy Spirit (*On the Trinity*, book II, no. 29, p. 43 of vol. II):

> “Concerning the Holy Spirit, it is neither proper to be silent nor necessary to speak; yet we cannot be silent about him on account of those who do not know. Nor is it necessary to speak of him, since he must be confessed on the authority of the Father and the Son. And indeed I think that the question whether he exists ought not to be discussed: for he exists, since he is given, received, and possessed. And he who is joined to the confession of the Father and the Son cannot be separated from the confession of the Father and the Son; [Col. 0761B] for the whole is imperfect for us if anything is lacking from the whole.”

He then goes through those passages of Scripture by which the divinity of the Spirit is customarily asserted and established. Elsewhere too [Note: [Col. 0761D] *On Matthew*, ch. XIII, no. 6, p. 735 of vol. I.] he speaks thus:

> “Although I remember that many have understood the three measures of meal to be referred to the sacrament of faith—that is, to the unity of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—and also to the calling of the three races from Shem, Ham, and Japheth . . . yet in Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, without the need of yeast externally added, all things are one in Christ.”

I deliberately refrain from citing other passages of Hilary to the same effect, lest I do work already done; for that labor was anticipated by the most distinguished Benedictine monk of Saint-Maur who prepared and published the latest Paris edition of Saint Hilary. Please see what he sets forth in no. 12 and the following sections of the preface to the books *On the Trinity*.

**24.** All the ancients make the Holy Spirit a participant in creation, and rightly so: for he is God, and those works which theologians call *ad extra* are common to the whole Trinity. I mention only Basil here, since in Book V against Eunomius he says [Note: [Col. 0761D] In the latest Benedictine edition of the Fathers, vol. I, p. 303.]: “For the Spirit is joined to the living Word in creation, a living power and divine nature, which shone forth ineffably from the ineffable mouth,” etc. Many Fathers attribute the perfection of things and the animation of living things to the Holy Spirit. Why? Is it because the Holy Spirit is love, and the perfection of things is an outstanding proof of love? Or because [Col. 0762A] he is, as it were, the completion and final term of the divine processions, and it was fitting that the completion and final term of operations *ad extra* should likewise be attributed to him? You may learn these matters from theologians.

This at least is certain: very many ancient and more recent interpreters referred to the Holy Spirit those words of Genesis I.2, “The Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters”—that he might make them fruitful and impart productive power [Note: [Col. 0761D] Calmet cites some, though very distinguished, authorities. Add, if you wish, Prudentius (*Apotheosis*) and Victor of Vita (*A Statement of Faith to Huneric*), whose words are: “The Spirit of God was borne over the waters, as Creator holding the creature together by the power of his might, so that, about to bring forth all living things from them, he himself might furnish the unformed elements with the fostering warmth of his own fire.” And, not to enumerate all, add our Steuchus in the *Cosmopoeia*. Prudentius and Victor of Vita were preceded by Ausonius, who says in his *Morning Prayer*:

> I acknowledge the Father of the Only-Begotten, and the Spirit united with both,  
> Who hovered above the watery waves;

> and in the poem *On the Lord’s Resurrection*:

> Taught by your admonitions, he added this one thing:  
> [Col. 0762D] that the Spirit who swam above the watery waves  
> might quicken sluggish limbs by an immortal washing.], and also those words of verse 6 of Psalm XXXII: “And by the Spirit of his mouth”—that is, of the Word—“all their host,” namely, that of the heavens. Tertullian at times mentions a created spirit, and therefore one distinct from the third person of the most holy Trinity (*Against Hermogenes*, ch. 32); elsewhere (*Against Marcion*, book IV, ch. 26) he seems to teach the same things as Hilary here.

**25.** Paul had already taught the unity of baptism in writing to the Ephesians (ch. IV, v. 3): “One Lord,” he says, “one faith, one baptism.” Cyprian teaches it also [Note: [Col. 0762D] Epistle to Januarius 78: “Since baptism too is one,” etc.], although he himself later erred on this point [Note: [Col. 0762D] Epistles 73 and 74; *On the Unity of the Church*: “Although there cannot be another baptism besides the one,” etc.], in judging from the unity of baptism that it could be validly conferred only in the [Col. 0762B] Catholic Church. So too do the other Fathers, both those before the Council of Constantinople when explaining the Creed, and especially those afterward, particularly when they expound Paul’s cited words in commentaries. To remain with Hilary, see what he teaches in nos. 1 and 2 of Book XI *On the Trinity* [Note: [Col. 0762D] Vol. II, p. 373: “Therefore one . . . But neither in the one baptism,” etc.].

Our masters explain baptism’s unity in this way: it is one because, being the confession of faith instituted by Christ, a certain proof of that faith, and entry into it [Note: [Col. 0762D] “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit,” etc., Matthew XXVIII.19.], we wrongly seek another confession, proof, and entry. Cyril of Jerusalem also explains it differently, saying (*Protocatechesis*, no. 7):

> “It is not permitted to receive the washing twice or three times; otherwise one might say: ‘What failed the first time I shall accomplish at a second attempt.’ But if it has failed even once, the matter admits of no remedy: for there is one Lord, one faith, and one baptism. Heretics alone are rebaptized, because their former baptism was not baptism.”

Please see [Col. 0762C] what the eminent Toutée notes on this passage.

**26.** Christ himself indicated that in baptism we are regenerated and reborn to God when he addressed Nicodemus in these words (John III.3): “Amen, amen, I say to you: unless a man is born anew, he cannot see the kingdom of God” [Note: [Col. 0762D] See the interpreters on this passage and, omitting the rest, the commentaries of Jansenius of Ypres.]. Peter taught this most expressly in his first epistle [Note: [Col. 0762D] Ch. I, v. 23: “Born again not of seed,” etc.], and Paul in chapter III of his Epistle to Titus [Note: [Col. 0762D] Verses 4 and 5. Consult the interpreters on this passage, not only Catholic but also non-Catholic; among the latter Grotius earned no slight praise.]. All who have expounded the Apostles’ or Constantinopolitan Creed in sermons, homilies, and writings likewise emphasize and explain it. [Col. 0763A] The Church too frequently teaches it, as in the prayers recited at Mass on the Thursday after Easter [Note: [Col. 0763C] In the Secret: “O God, who [unites] the diversity of nations,” etc.], and those appointed for the Friday of the same week [Note: [Col. 0763C] In the Secret: “Offerings,” etc.; and in the Postcommunion: “Look upon, we beseech you,” etc.]. The same is found at Pentecost [Note: [Col. 0763C] At the Mass of the Vigil: “Grant, we beseech you, almighty God . . . who have been reborn through your grace.”]. If I added the Fathers, I would be almost endless. Not to cite many, I indicate only passages from Zeno and Hilary [Note: [Col. 0763C] Zeno, book II, tractates 30 and following, p. 227 [Col. 0763D] of the Verona edition prepared by the Ballerini brothers. Hilary, *On the Trinity*, book I, no. 22, p. 15 of vol. II; *On Psalm LXIII*, no. 11, p. 182 of vol. I; and *On Matthew*, ch. X, no. 24, p. 719 of the same first volume.]. Let the reader consult them if he wishes.

**27.** The resurrection of the dead is taught not only in the Apostles’ Creed, but also in nearly all other ecclesiastical documents in which our faith is stated in summary. You will cease to wonder at this when you know that this article is among those by which we most especially depart from the erroneous opinions of pagans, and above all of Epicureans. The Apostle Paul insisted on it when he proclaimed Christ to the Athenians in the Areopagus; and for this reason, as well as because he proclaimed Christ, he was despised by the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers [Note: [Col. 0763D] “Certain Epicurean and Stoic philosophers disputed with him; some said, ‘What does this babbler wish to say?’ Others, ‘He seems to be a proclaimer of new gods,’ because he proclaimed Jesus and the resurrection to them.” Acts XVII.18.]. Yet he himself often proclaimed the same resurrection, lest anyone doubt it. I indicate at the foot of the page certain [Col. 0763B] passages which the reader may consult [Note: [Col. 0763D] Acts XXIII.6; again ch. XXIV, vv. 14 and 21; ch. XXVI, vv. 8 and 23; Romans VI.5; I Corinthians XV.12 and nearly all the chapter following; II Timothy II.18; I Thessalonians IV.12, etc.; Hebrews VI.2; I Peter IV.4–5: “Who is ready to judge the living and the dead.”].

It is also certain that the Jews were convinced of this [Note: [Col. 0763D] II Maccabees XII.44: “For unless he [Judas Maccabaeus] had hoped that they would rise again, it would have seemed superfluous and vain to pray for the dead.”], so convinced that the Sadducees, who denied it, were counted among heretics. Please see what Philastrius teaches in Heresy V, and add to it what the excellent canon Galeardus notes; for he cites many passages of Scripture and other credible authors on this subject. Irenaeus also counts the resurrection of the dead among the articles which catechumens ought to believe [Note: [Col. 0764C] Book I, ch. 10: “And the resurrection of the dead . . . for raising again all the flesh of humankind,” etc.].

All who elucidate either the Apostles’ Creed, the Constantinopolitan Creed, or that very creed which we call Athanasian explain this article at length. Cyril of Jerusalem won great praise in this matter (*Catechesis* XVIII, no. 1 and following). Augustine and other teachers, both ancient and more recent, discussed this subject. Nor indeed will you regret reading [Col. 0763C] what Gregory the Great frequently teaches in affirming this same resurrection. It is enough for me to indicate one passage, which I regard as highly persuasive: Homily VIII on Ezekiel [Note: [Col. 0764C] Nos. 6 and following: “But because [the subject is] the resurrection of the flesh,” etc.]. Hilary often treats of the resurrection, as, for example, in no. 9 of his commentary on Psalm LXIII, etc.

**28.** This article is most closely joined to the preceding one. For why shall we all rise again, unless so that each may receive from the Lord Jesus Christ, Judge of the living and the dead, according to what he has done in the body, whether good or evil (I Cor. V.10)? Paul indicates the connection between these two articles when, in the Epistle to the Hebrews, he joins the resurrection of the dead with eternal judgment [Note: [Col. 0764D] Ch. VI.2: “And of the resurrection of the dead and of eternal judgment.”]. Irenaeus sets it forth most expressly when he lists, among doctrines to be believed by those about to be baptized (*Against Heresies*, book I, ch. 10):

> “The ascension in the flesh into heaven of our beloved Lord Jesus Christ, and his coming from heaven in glory to recapitulate all things [Note: [Col. 0764D] The new edition translates: “to restore all things.” Ephesians I.10.], and to raise again all flesh of humankind, so that to Christ Jesus our Lord and God and Savior and King, according to the will of the invisible Father (Philippians II.10, etc.), every knee may bow, of things in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess to him, and he may render just judgment upon all (Ephesians VI.12): sending spiritual wickedness, transgressing angels who became apostates, and ungodly, unjust, iniquitous, and blasphemous human beings into eternal fire; but granting life to the just and upright, to those who keep his commandments and persevere in his love—some from the beginning, others after repentance—bestowing incorruptibility upon them as a gift and surrounding them with eternal glory” [Note: [Col. 0764D] Irenaeus emphasizes this elsewhere too, namely in book III, ch. 4.].

The Apostles’ Creed, the Nicene Creed [Note: [Col. 0764D] Hilary, *On the Synods*, no. 84: “He shall come to judge the living and the dead.”], and the other most ancient [Col. 0764B] creeds set forth this same article. This is not surprising: judicial authority seems especially to be a reward conferred upon Christ’s humanity for the humility which he showed particularly on the Cross. Moreover, he loved his disciples, and especially the Apostles, so greatly that he appointed them seats in that same judgment, in which they would judge angels as well (I Cor. VI.3). If anyone wishes this article explained, let him consult those who expound the Apostles’ Creed, and above all Cyril of Jerusalem (*Catechesis* XV, no. 3 and following); also the interpreters on the Scriptural passages that I indicate here [Note: [Col. 0764D] Matthew XXIV.29 and XXV.31; Acts XXIV.25; Romans XIV.10; I Corinthians VI.3; II Corinthians V.10; I Thessalonians IV.13 and following.].

**29.** Our manuscript indeed reads: “So great is the difference between Jews converting and Gentiles believing.” If anyone wishes to read “Jews who are converting,” I have no objection. By these words, however one finally reads them, Hilary concludes, as it were with an epiphonema, what he had previously said: namely, that Hebrews joining themselves to the Christian faith must be instructed differently from those who come to the Church from idolatry. The former require that few things be proposed for belief, since they already know the rest; from the latter a more explicit and fuller confession must be required—namely, the one which Hilary had summarized in a few words and explained shortly before, and which he was thereafter going to set forth more fully.

Nor should you wonder that so few things were proposed to them for belief. For we learn the same thing also from Irenaeus, who, when about to explain the faith which the Church, sown throughout the entire world even to the ends of the earth, received from the Apostles and their disciples, comprehended it in very few chapters [Note: [Col. 0764D] Book I, ch. 10. Again, book III, ch. 3, formerly ch. 2: “They proclaim the tradition of one God,” etc. In ch. 4 of the same book he likewise says that this is the tradition to be preserved: “to believe in one God, maker of heaven and earth.”]. The Nicene Synod did likewise, explaining itself more fully concerning the divinity and dignity of the Son, [Col. 0765A] which was the subject chiefly disputed at that time, while summarily comprising the remaining articles [Note: [Col. 0765D] Hilary, *On the Synods*, no. 84: “We believe in one God,” etc.]. This is not surprising, for these very articles either include or imply those which the Apostles’ Creed states. Thus the Fathers I have cited in no way oppose the conviction of those who affirm that the Apostles’ Creed was dictated by the Apostles themselves.

**30.** We may divide this letter into three parts according to the diversity of its subjects. The first part, in which we have so far remained, contains the summary of the articles of our faith; the second part, which we now undertake, contains a more careful explanation of the same articles. Yet, to conceal nothing, I long suspected that one ought rather to read: “who he is—or, if you prefer, who is—and what kind of Son of God he is.” I likewise suspected that the following words, “for the three are one,” had been added later; for they appear to refer to that celebrated testimony of John [Note: [Col. 0765D] In the First Epistle, ch. V.]: “There are three who bear witness in heaven,” etc.; Hilary seems not to have referred to it in other places.

Nevertheless, I judged that nothing should be altered even in what follows. The sense remains entirely sound if one reads: “who he was, and what kind of Son of God he was.” Indeed, since Arians and Catholics disputed not concerning the present but concerning the most ancient—or rather eternal—state of the Son of God, Hilary could rightly write “who the Son of God was,” namely, from eternity and before even imagined times. The words “for the three are one” could have been written by Hilary, not against the Arians, as when he formerly composed the books *On the Trinity*, but while writing to Catholics, and hence to people who acknowledged the force of that testimony, which Cyprian had indicated even before Hilary. See what Catholics argue concerning this testimony against recent Arians. Certainly those words were most appropriately inserted, because they give the reason why he joins the Son and Holy Spirit to the Father, and afterwards declares more precisely what the Catholic religion commands concerning them. Therefore, if he omitted this testimony in the books *On the Trinity* in order not to introduce a controversy extraneous to his purpose concerning its authenticity [Col. 0765C]—if I may so speak—he rightly cites it now while addressing Catholics who acknowledge it to be authentic, since it is most suitable for affirming the consubstantiality of the divine Persons.

**31.** If anyone wishes to draw from Hilary himself much material confirming the foregoing conclusion—namely, “Certainly your prudence ought to know this”—and, by comparing those passages with the one examined here, to demonstrate that both works are by the same writer, let him consult the passages I shall immediately note: book I *On the Trinity*, no. 19, “And you indeed, whom the warmth of faith,” etc.; book III, nos. 19 and 26; book VII, nos. 14 and 38; likewise book VI, no. 17; and finally what he teaches in *On the Trinity*, nos. 2 [Note: [Col. 0765D] No. 2: “And may one God alone dissolve for us the faith of God from God in confession.”] and 33 [Note: [Col. 0766D] No. 33: “For faith must be undertaken not according to our own judgment, but according to the force of the sayings.”]. Hilary’s judgment in this last passage is especially excellent: “No other speaker concerning the things of God has been left to human utterances than the Word of God; all else is narrow, confined, impeded, and obscure.”

What Hilary next says in these words—“let man not seek him on earth, or construct him among fabricated things, lest he believe him like to anyone”—is precisely what Scripture often impresses concerning God. Thus Deuteronomy (ch. IV, v. 15): “You saw no likeness on the day when the Lord spoke to you in Horeb from the midst of fire, lest perhaps, deceived, you make for yourselves a carved likeness or an image of male or female,” etc. And Isaiah (ch. XLVI, v. 5): “To whom have you likened me, made me equal, compared me, and made me similar?” etc. All that theologians argue against the Anthropomorphites applies here. [Col. 0766A] It will be enough if I point to a few passages of Hilary by which the preceding proposition may be confirmed. Here first is Book I *On the Trinity*, no. 19:

> “If, when treating of the nature and birth of God, we offer examples of comparisons, let no one think that they contain in themselves the perfection of an absolute account. For there is no comparison of earthly things with God; but the weakness of our understanding compels us to seek certain forms from lower things as indications, so to speak, of higher things, that, prompted by familiarity with known things, we may be led from the awareness of our own perception to an apprehension of a perception unfamiliar to us. Every comparison, therefore, should be regarded as useful rather to man than fitting for God, because it indicates understanding rather than fulfills it; nor should it be thought an attempt to equate the natures of flesh and spirit, visible and tangible things, while it declares itself both necessary to the weakness of human understanding and free from blame for an inadequate example. We therefore proceed to speak of God with God’s words, while nevertheless instructing our understanding by the likeness of our own things.”
