Hilary teaches kindred matters in Book IV, no. 2, Book VI, no. 9, and finally—without enumerating every passage in which he teaches the same thing—in Book VII, no. 18. The author of the book entitled *On the Trinity*, or *On the Apostles’ Creed*, which appears among Ambrose’s works, considered this article so important that he began his discourse from it [Note: [Col. 0766D] “Therefore no one of sound mind should suppose that almighty God, who is Trinity and Spirit, is any visible or tangible body.”].

**32.** I candidly set before the reader the emendation I have made here. The manuscript reads: “Begotten: not made.” But I have written: “Not begotten, not made.” Here understand either God in essence, to use the phrase of the Scholastics, and considered precisely as such, or the person of the Father. Take it whichever way you please: it must certainly be read, “not begotten.” For when was the divine essence begotten? When was the Father begotten? When Hilary says here that God is not begotten, he says that God is without and ignorant of every origin or principle, and much more of every cause; and he teaches what all the Fathers and theologians teach when they state that the Father is unbegotten [Col. 0766C], and what Hilary himself had stated most explicitly in these words (*On the Trinity*, book IV, no. 6): “He knows one unbegotten God; he knows also one only-begotten Son of God. He confesses the Father eternal and free from origin,” etc.

Hilary treats the matter more fully not only in the passages cited by Petavius (*On the Trinity*, book V, ch. 5, no. 13), but also in no. 58 of *On the Synods* [Note: [Col. 0766D] “From the unbegotten substance, perfect birth,” etc.], and again in no. 47 of Book XI *On the Trinity* (vol. II, p. 404), which, if you wish, consult. Add, if you please, the Fathers cited by Petavius in Book V, ch. 5, nos. 13–15; and add Ausonius, whom I shall cite later.

**33.** The Fathers teach very frequently that God is incomprehensible, especially those who disputed against the Arians and Anomoeans. Nazianzen devotes a large portion of his fourth and thirtieth orations to showing that we can neither comprehend what God is nor describe his excellence in speech. Chrysostom pursues the same argument at great length. I select one passage to cite here (*Third Oration against the Anomoeans*, p. 463 of vol. I of Montfaucon’s splendid edition):

> “Let us therefore call God ineffable, unintelligible, invisible, incomprehensible, surpassing the power of human speech, exceeding the grasp of mortal mind, untraceable by angels, invisible to seraphim, unintelligible to cherubim, unviewable by principalities, powers, and virtues—in a word, by every creature—and known only by the Son and the Holy Spirit.”

Hilary likewise emphasizes this in Book II *On the Trinity*, nos. 5 and 6 [Col. 0767A] (vol. II, p. 30), and in no. 62 of *On the Synods* (vol. II, p. 497). I should like you to read the latter passage in full. Novatian also, if he is the author of the book *On the Trinity* once published under his name and included among Tertullian’s works, agrees with the same view (ch. 7):

> “For that which is, according to what it is, can neither be expressed by human speech, received by human ears, nor comprehended by human senses.”

The source, if we may speak thus, of this incomprehensibility is infinity—that is, God’s infinite perfection and power. Since this is wholly unlimited and, as I have already said, infinite, it makes him altogether incapable of comprehension. Scripture frequently teaches this infinity. But since I am not here undertaking the role of theologian, it will be enough for me to cite one passage, the very familiar passage of Job (ch. XI, vv. 7–9):

> “Can you perhaps comprehend the traces of God, and discover the Almighty unto perfection? He is higher than heaven—what will you do? deeper than hell—how will you know? [Col. 0767B] His measure is longer than the earth and broader than the sea.”

Here either the incomprehensibility of the extent of omnipotence is proposed, so to speak, or the incomprehensibility of God’s very perfection and infinity—and thus that incomprehensibility by which God is shown to surpass our knowledge because he possesses perfection outstanding and most excellent beyond every measure. Gregory the Great comments on these words of Job as follows (*Morals*, book X, ch. 8, formerly no. 13 and following):

> “He is higher than heaven because even the elect spirits themselves do not perfectly penetrate by vision the greatness of such loftiness . . . Thus he becomes higher than heaven when our contemplation itself fails in respect to him.”

Augustine therefore rightly concludes concerning God (*On Psalm* LXXXV, no. 12) that “it is easier for us to say what he is not than what he is.” He adds:

> “This alone could I say: what he is not. Do you ask what he is? ‘What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man.’ ‘There is none like you among the gods, O Lord, [Col. 0767C] nor are any works according to your works.’”

He teaches very similar things in no. 9 of Tractate XXI on John’s Gospel. If here you cite passages which describe God as ineffable, you will cite them rightly. For why is he ineffable? Certainly because he is incomprehensible. Very many passages of Scripture and the Fathers aim to describe God as ineffable. Here I cite Fulgentius alone, who teaches as follows (*Against the Objections of the Arians*, Objection and Response II):

> “God is not unknowable, though he is unutterable; rather, he is known by the faithful so that he may be loved, although he is not fully narrated either by human tongues or by angelic ones.”

34. *Inextimable* is used for *inestimable*. What we said in the preceding annotation readily shows that God is inestimable. For who can adequately estimate him who is incomprehensible? Yet if anyone wishes me to produce some explicit testimonies of the holy Fathers to confirm this proposition, here immediately is Tertullian (Apology, ch. 17):

> “He is invisible, though he is seen; [Col. 0767D] incomprehensible, though through grace he is manifested; inestimable, though he is estimated by human senses: so true and so great is he. But what can commonly be seen, comprehended, and estimated is inferior both to the eyes by which it is apprehended and to the hands by which it is grasped. But what is immeasurable is known to itself alone. This is what makes God estimable: that he does not admit of being estimated. Thus the power of his greatness has set him before human beings as both known and unknown. And this is the height of the fault of those unwilling to acknowledge him whom they cannot fail to know.”

Ambrose seems to have followed him—if Ambrose is indeed the person to whom you ascribe the book *On the Divinity of the Son*; on this see what we said [Col. 0768A] in the annotation on no. 20—when he wrote the following concerning God (*On the Divinity of the Son*, ch. 6):

> “This is he of whom, even when he is spoken of, he cannot be spoken; when he is estimated, he cannot be estimated; when he is compared, he cannot be compared; when he is defined, he grows by his very definition.”

35. Invisible [God]. Theologians discuss this doctrine at length. Since our purpose in these annotations is to avoid extended disputations, we consider that we have fulfilled our office if we refer the reader to Petavius, who treats this subject very fully. Please see volume I, book VII, chapter 1; for there he has assembled the testimonies of the ancients. Add to these what Hilary teaches in his *Commentaries on Psalm CXVIII* [Note: [Col. 0767D] Letter VIII, no. 7, on the words, “I have entreated thy face with my whole heart,” etc.]. Add also what we shall cite in annotation 38 from the commentary on Psalm CXXXV, since God is there called invisible-to-sight (*inconspicabilis*).

But since I previously said that I would cite Ausonius, here he is; his authority readily confirms both the point now under discussion and what was set forth in no. 32 and the following two sections. Thus he prays to God the Father (*Morning Prayer*):

> Almighty one, whom I worship in mind, sole Father of all things,  
> Unknown to the wicked, yet unknown to none of the godly,  
> Lacking beginning and end, older than time  
> That has been or shall come; whose form and measure  
> Neither mind can comprehend nor tongue declare—  
> Whom God, begotten of the unbegotten Father, alone has the right  
> To behold and hear commanding face to face, and to sit  
> At the Father’s right hand.

36. And impassible. Does Hilary here exclude passions from God, or mutability? Or both? Or does he rather refer these words to the Father, since the Father did not assume the flesh in which the Son suffered? Let the reader judge. Certainly, in order to show that the Son, the Word of God, is God and consubstantial with the Father, he teaches that an impassible nature was communicated to him by the Father:

> “To all creatures,” he says (*On the Synods*, no. 58, p. 495), “the will of God brought substance; but to the Son perfect birth gave a nature from an impassible and unbegotten substance.” [Note: [Col. 0767D] Besides the preceding passage, see what he says in no. 59.]

He expressly removes passibility from the Father in the generation of the divine Son in the book *On the Synods* [Note: [Col. 0767D] “And this is the very meaning of the paternal name, by which the impassible [Col. 0768D] origin of the one being born,” etc., no. 24.]. And elsewhere (*On the Trinity*, book IV, no. 6):

> “In the Spirit,” he says, “he knows God, Spirit, to be impassible and indivisible.”

37. He who lacks these titles and attributes is a fictitious, not a true, God. Hilary states this expressly, I think, in order to oppose his own confession to the confession of Arius. Arius, in order to deceive the unwary, expressly enumerated and explained the perfections and attributes of God:

> “We know,” he said [Note: [Col. 0768D] In Hilary, *On the Trinity*, book IV, no. 12, and book VI, no. 5.], “one God, alone unbegotten, alone everlasting, alone without beginning, alone true, alone possessing immortality, alone good, alone powerful, Creator of all things,” etc.

By this means he intended to disparage the Catholics, who, in his judgment, divided God into persons and so diminished the divine perfections. Hilary therefore, taking up the defense of the Orthodox, admits these things as well; and accordingly he admits that, even in the Trinity of persons, God is uncreated, incomprehensible, and so forth. [Col. 0768D]

38. I once doubted whether the words “who generated certain beings” (*qui quaedam generaverit*) might in some more obscure manner suggest the divine generation of the Word. Since the preceding words can readily be referred to the Father, I suspected that the divine generation might be indicated by these words, as I have just said. But afterward I removed all suspicion. For who would suppose that the only-begotten Son of God—whom Hilary so often and so plainly separates from creatures—was designated by the common expression “certain beings”? I therefore judge it much more advisable to refer the generation of which Hilary here speaks to those [Col. 0769A] creatures whom he wished also to be endowed with intelligence. For intelligence makes them like God; grace makes them in some fashion partakers of the divine nature (2 Peter 1:4), and honors them with the title and dignity of children of God.

Indeed, most interpreters understand the words of Job (38:7), “when . . . all the sons of God shouted for joy,” to refer to angels, because of their eminent intelligence and grace. Moreover, Hilary himself teaches this [Note: [Col. 0769D] In the treatise on Psalm CXXXV, no. 8, on the words, “who made the heavens in understanding.”]:

> “But when he who is infinite assigned a realm to his own knowledge, he enclosed within the highest and first heaven, situated in the same sphere, a certain limit for the powers which were first to be generated for the purpose of knowing him. For creations about to be generated could not have borne the power of the invisible God unless, through the interposition of a more tempered nature, they inhabited this dwelling-place, moderated to suit their weakness.”

Elsewhere, however, he warns that those very beings whom he allows may be called both sons and begotten must not be so called with the proper signification of the term. For if we speak properly, we become sons through grace; we are not born sons. Thus we are sons by adoption and election, not by generation, [Col. 0769B] generation being understood strictly and properly. [Note: [Col. 0769D] “Unless perhaps someone, because he says, ‘Israel is his firstborn son,’ will understand his saying ‘my firstborn’ as detracting from the Son’s proper generation; so that, because he also said ‘my’ of Israel, the adoption of made sons may have been used in place of the proper meaning of birth, and consequently what was said of him—‘This is my beloved Son’—may not be proper to the birth of God, since ‘my’ is also said properly of those whom it is manifest were not born. That they were not born, though they are said to be born, is taught also by the statement, ‘For the people that shall be born, whom the Lord made.’ Therefore the people of Israel is born in order to be made; and from its being said to be born, its being made is not excluded. For it is sonship by adoption, not by generation; nor is it a property, but a designation.” Hilary, *On the Trinity*, book XII, no. 14.]

Hilary could therefore say that we are begotten by God in the sense in which Paul teaches that we are called God’s offspring. For while preaching in the Areopagus, Paul said (Acts 17:28): “For in him we live and move and are; as some of your poets have also said, ‘For we too are his offspring.’” What we shall say at length in Dissertation III may suitably be brought forward to elucidate this passage.

39. This passage seems somewhat obscure. I once suspected that, through a copyist’s license, the text had been arranged to read “he has ordered, he has adorned,” whereas perhaps the earliest exemplar read “he has adorned, he has ordered”: “he has ordered,” I say, that he should command as the best and just Judge—that is, that he should command or rule and exercise just judgment. But afterward I observed that it can still be read as in our manuscript, that is, “he has ordered, he has adorned.”

Recall here what was placed a little earlier: “True faith has always thus expounded God: unbegotten,” etc. The words cited then have this sense: “True faith has always so expounded him that we acknowledge him to be unbegotten . . . and to command as the best and just Judge.”

If you ask what God made, arranged, ordered, or adorned, I answer: all natures, and their genera and species, were made by God from the beginning: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth,” etc. God created not merely bodily things but spiritual things as well. See what we set forth in annotations 10 and 18. He arranged the sun, moon, and stars, “that they may divide day and night, and may serve as signs, seasons, days, and years; that they may shine in the firmament of heaven and illumine the earth” (Genesis 1:14; Psalm CXXXV:7, 8, 9). He thus arranged all the alternations and intervals of time.

He also arranged things themselves. For you will find few things occurring everywhere; rather, he arranged and fitted nearly everything in its own place. The book of Job has some material on this subject ([Col. 0769D] 38:4, 5, etc.), which I urge you to consult; and the Book of Wisdom states it most clearly (11:21): “You have arranged all things in measure, number, and weight.” Among secular authors, Virgil says: “Not every land bears every thing.” Why? Because, as we have said, God, arranging all things in measure, number, and weight, [Col. 0770A] willed each part of the world to lack some things which it might obtain from other regions, so that human beings might help one another by mutual services.

Moreover, God has ordered—even in Augustine’s judgment—privations and sins. Recall what we said in annotation 10, and add what the same Augustine taught on Psalm LI (no. 15: “Do not suppose that the wicked are in this world for nothing,” etc.). All this rests on experience and on that ancient saying of Solomon (Proverbs 16:4): “The Lord has made all things for himself, even the wicked for the evil day.” When I affirm that sinners and their errors are ordered by God, I affirm likewise that illnesses, diseases, and other things of this kind—penalties indeed of sin, yet occasions of our merit and incentives to patience—are also ordered.

40. Moreover, God adorned no small number of things in this world, as experience and Scripture attest in these words (Genesis 2:1): “Thus the heavens and the earth and all their adornment were completed.” That their Creator can readily be known from the adornment of the heavens is manifestly clear from the words (Psalm 18:1): “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament announces the works of his hands.” As the stars are ornaments of heaven, so shrubs, trees, and herbs are ornaments of earth; the innumerable and diverse kinds of all these things show that almighty God is their author (Wisdom 13:5). Thus those who, knowing God, did not glorify him as God are without excuse (Romans 1:19, 20, etc.).

See what theologians discuss on this subject, especially Petavius, volume I of *Dogmatic Theology*, chapter 1. Yet, while elucidating Hilary, it would be improper not to cite a longer passage from Hilary himself. Elsewhere he teaches as follows (*On Psalm LXIII*, no. 6, p. 197, vol. I):

> “By the following admonitions we are also instructed in the order of obedience, the Prophet—or the Spirit through the Prophet—thus exhorting us: ‘Say to God: How terrible are thy works!’ For who would not tremble at his majesty, who instituted the ages, founded the world, measured out times by their recurrent succession and course, adorned heaven with stars, filled earth with fruits, enclosed the sea with boundaries, and chose humankind to use or rule these things? For through all these things the eternity of his power and might is known, as the Apostle says: ‘For his invisible things, understood from the creation of the world through the things made, are seen—his eternal power also and divinity.’ These things make the name of the Creator terrible; and the worthiness of his works displays the majesty of him who wrought them. Therefore God, the Creator of these works, must be proclaimed by us and confessed by all others.”

He says related things in his commentaries on Psalm CXVIII [Note: [Col. 0770D] Letter X, no. 2, p. 334, vol. I: “common judgment is,” etc.].

41. Recall what I said earlier, namely in annotation 39. Yet if anyone wishes to suppose that something is missing or badly written here, I shall not oppose him. The ancient professions of our faith themselves—the Apostles’ Creed, Irenaeus, and all others who speak of the chief articles of our faith—acknowledge that Christ has been appointed our judge.

42. These words must be referred to what he said a little earlier: “has made certain things,” etc. Recall what I said in nos. 39 and 40. [Col. 0770D]

43. Here Hilary seems to take “the time of recognition” either as the time during which a human being lives and may thereby discern what God has created; or as the time when God more abundantly assists by his grace and endeavors to lead the person [Col. 0771A] to himself. Hilary moreover seems to refer to two very notable passages of Scripture. The first is the one read in Luke 19:42: “For if you too had known, even on this your day, the things that belong to your peace! But now they are hidden from your eyes . . . They shall not leave in you one stone upon another, because you did not know the time of your visitation.” The other is found in Paul’s Epistle to the Romans (1:18):

> “For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and injustice of those human beings who hold the truth of God in injustice, because what may be known of God is manifest in them; for God has manifested it to them.”

44. The first part of this statement—namely, “he will have a just judge after departure”—is clear. It refers to the particular judgment immediately following the death of each individual; earlier, while enumerating the chief articles of our faith, he mentions the universal judgment. In this particular judgment each person receives sentence according to merits, whether good or evil. Paul seems certainly to indicate this when he says [Col. 0771B] (Hebrews 9:27): “It is appointed to human beings to die once; after this, however, judgment.” The words “after this, however,” indicate a judgment immediately ensuing. This is likewise shown by the example of the rich man and Lazarus: the rich man was immediately cast down into hell, while Lazarus immediately attained Abraham’s bosom.

Augustine relies greatly on this latter example, writing [Note: [Col. 0771D] *On the Soul and Its Origin*, book II, ch. 4, alternatively no. 8.]:

> “Most rightly and most salutarily it is believed that souls are judged when they have departed from their bodies, before they come to that judgment in which, their bodies now restored, they must be judged . . . Who is against the Gospel,” etc.

He indicates the same elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0771D] Book XX of *The City of God*, ch. 1, no. 2: “because he judges even now, and has judged from the beginning of the human race,” etc.]. He acknowledges “besides the final judgment, other judgments in which God judges even the individual works proper to each person; and human beings for the most part openly, and always secretly, suffer divinely imposed penalties for their deeds, whether in this life or after death.” If, then, he punishes after death by a judgment that is not the final judgment, a particular judgment must necessarily precede [Col. 0771C] the final judgment. So much for the first part of this statement.

I come to the second, which is far more difficult: namely, “who will consider himself converted not in his own time, but from the past.” Are the words “who will consider himself converted not in his own time” referred to the Judge, or rather to the person who, having failed to acknowledge his Maker in the time of recognition, will have him as a just judge after departure? Either explanation may perhaps be defended; but the sequence and continuity of the discourse seem to indicate that these words are to be referred to the Judge, who allows himself to be entreated by a person while that person is still alive, but rejects every supplication after death. Thus I interpret the words “but from the past” to mean: the fitting time has already elapsed.

Theologians treat this matter, especially Fr. Liberius (*Controversies*, vol. I, treatise III, *On the State of Souls*, part I, controversy 1). Since the brevity I have proposed for myself prevents me from assembling much here, I cite Hilary alone, indicating two of his passages. Because they are somewhat longer, I ask the reader to read them personally. They are no. 23 of the commentaries on Psalm II (p. 92, vol. I: “Confession only in this age,” etc.), and no. 4 of the commentary on Matthew 27, where the parable of the ten virgins is explained (“The bridegroom and bride,” etc.).

45. That is: these things must be believed concerning God.

46. If you think that the conjunction *and* is lacking in our manuscript after the word “will have believed”—and it may be lacking through a copyist’s negligence—so that you judge the reading should be: “whoever has believed, and abstains himself . . . will have rest,” etc., then this statement of Hilary means the same as Gregory the Great’s statement elucidating the celebrated Gospel passage, “Whoever has believed and has been baptized will be saved; but whoever has not believed will be condemned”:

> “Perhaps,” he says (*Homily 29 on the Gospels*, no. 3), “each person may say within himself: ‘I have now believed; I shall be saved.’ He speaks truly, if he holds faith together with works. For true faith is that which conduct does not contradict in what it declares by words. Hence Paul says concerning certain false believers (Titus 1:16): ‘They profess to know God, but deny him by their deeds.’ Hence John says (1 John 2:4): ‘Whoever says that he knows God and does not keep his commandments is a liar.’” [Col. 0772A]

Indeed, Hilary himself means the same in no. 9 of his commentary on Psalm XIV, which passage of Hilary we shall cite in the following annotation.

But if you suppose that the conjunction *and* was absent in the original exemplar itself, and that the text should be read as it stands in our manuscript—“whoever has believed abstains himself,” etc.—then explain it thus: whoever truly believes abstains from all injustice, performing precisely what our faith commands us to do. The Apostle James aptly says (2:17): “Faith, if it does not have works, is dead,” etc.

47. So numerous are the promises by which we are assured that eternal rest will be granted to us through upright works that it seems pointless to gather many testimonies relevant to this point. I shall cite one clear saying of Christ. When someone asked him (Matthew 19:16), “What good shall I do that I may have eternal life?” he answered:

> “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments . . . You shall not murder; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness; honor your father and mother; and you shall love your neighbor as yourself.”

By “life” here understand, as I have said elsewhere, that life which elsewhere is simply called “life” (Matthew 7:14; again 18:8), and elsewhere “the crown of life” (James 1:12; Revelation 2:10). [Col. 0772B]

“But,” you will say, “what is this rest which we shall have in life?” It is that of which Paul says (Hebrews 4:11), “Let us hasten to enter into that rest”; and of which Muratori treats in the book entitled *On Paradise against Burnet* (ch. 4, p. 38 and following). There he assembled passages from the ancient Fathers showing that by the name “rest” true and perfect blessedness is understood.

For me, who am permitted to discuss matters briefly in these annotations, it is sufficient to cite one passage taken from the prayers of the Church. Before Pius V, these prayers were prescribed for recitation on the vigil of the Assumption of Mary:

> “Grant, merciful God, protection to our frailty, that we who celebrate the rest of the holy Mother of God may, by the aid of her intercession, rise from our iniquities. Through the same,” etc.

If the most holy Pontiff altered them, he did not alter them because he considered them less fitting, but lest those intent on harassing the Roman Church everywhere should have even the slightest occasion for criticizing it, as though it spoke somewhat obscurely concerning heavenly blessedness.

But lest, while examining Hilary’s words and investigating his meaning, we appear to neglect other passages of the holy Doctor tending to the same purpose, here are passages from which it clearly appears that by “eternal rest” he understands eternal blessedness. Explaining the first verse of Psalm XIV, “Lord, who shall dwell,” etc., he says (p. 69):

> “It is the simple prayer of one entreating the Lord and desiring to know from him what character, zeal, and will the person who is to dwell with God and rest in his heights and heavenly places must possess.”

And in no. 9 (p. 74), explaining these words of the same Psalm XIV, “who has not practiced deceit with his tongue,” he writes:

> “That he may not falsify in speech the truth which he thinks; that the activity itself may follow the profession of Catholic doctrine and the judgment to think and preach in this way. For according to the testimony of the Apostle, as one believes in the heart, so confession is made with the mouth unto salvation. Therefore, if ascent worthy of God’s rest is to be attained, one must live in truthfulness of words and tongue, so that through faith expressed in deeds the words of our thoughts may not be false.” [Col. 0773A]

Now compare, I pray, the words already cited from the present epistle—“He shall have eternal rest in life”—with what Hilary teaches in his exposition of Psalm LXII. By this comparison of expressions, you will see why I may rightly say that the author of the Epistle under discussion is Hilary. Here, then, is what Hilary teaches on that Psalm (*On Psalm LXII*, no. 7, p. 174):

> “There is also life after life, because one must live in Abraham’s bosom, in which the name of God is blessed in the rest of the poor.”

48. Something seems to be missing here, by which a path might be prepared for a fuller explanation of the words: “Next, one must believe them, Jesus Christ the Son of God,” etc.

49. Here Hilary rejects those ridiculous and shameful begettings of gods invented by the pagans, who were not ashamed sometimes to introduce sexual intercourse; certain heretics seemed to imitate them. Irenaeus refutes these heretics (*Against Heresies*, book I, ch. 1; again book IV, ch. 1; add what Epiphanius has in heresy 31), and Petavius recounts them (see Petavius, *On the Trinity*, book X, chapters 8, 9, and 12).

Elsewhere Hilary seems to refute the same error when he says (*On the Trinity*, book IV, no. 6):

> “The Church knows in the Spirit God, Spirit, to be impassible and indivisible; for she has learned from the Lord that a spirit has neither flesh nor bones, lest perhaps it should be believed that the harms of bodily passions can befall him.”

He likewise rejects that generation of the Son which some, in the height of madness, imagined—followers of Sabellius, I think—who, to use Hilary’s own words (*On the Trinity*, book IV, no. 4, p. 73, vol. II),

> “employed and uttered this word *homoousion* [ὁμοούσιον, ‘of the same substance’] in the sense that he who is Father is himself also Son, having been extended, that is, from his infinity into the Virgin; and, assuming a body from her, added to himself, in the body which he had assumed, the name of Son.” [Col. 0773C]

50. He likewise rejects those who said that Christ was a mere human being (see what Hilary teaches in *On the Synods*, no. 38, canons VI and VII), and those who could imagine him to be some spirit inferior to God who afterward assumed flesh in the Virgin. For he intends him to be unquestionably begotten from God and therefore truly the Son of God, consequently true God.

51. Some error has undoubtedly crept into these words: “his substance not divided, nor the substance of his majesty divided, and through this he appears passible.” That is, either the latter words, “nor the substance of his majesty divided,” are a gloss upon the preceding words, “his substance not divided,” which entered the epistle itself from the margin; or the text should read, “nor the substance of his majesty diminished.”

“But,” you will ask, “how do the following words agree and connect with the preceding: ‘nor the substance of his majesty divided, and through this he appears passible’? Does the Son appear, or is he, passible because he proceeds from the undivided substance of the Father?” Therefore either the manuscript must again be corrected and read, “lest through this he appear passible”; for the Father would be passible if his substance were divided. Or the words “and through this he appears passible” must be understood as though he said: “We confess indeed that the Son was born from himself—that is, from God the Father—but in such a manner that the Father’s substance remains indivisible. For if you make it divisible, he appears, or is shown, to be passible.” The subjunctive is thus used for the indicative, which Hilary often does. [Note: [Col. 0773D] I cite only one, but a very well-known, example, taken from the commentary on Matthew (Canon 27, alternatively ch. 27, on Matthew 24:48; the passage is used in the readings of the third nocturn of the Common of a Confessor Pontiff, second place): “Because he may have despaired of the coming, because he may not have obeyed the commands, because he may have devoted himself to present things, because he may have lived the life of the Gentiles, because in despair of judgment he may have afflicted with hunger, thirst, and slaughter the household entrusted to him”: that is, “because he despaired, did not obey, devoted himself, lived, afflicted.” And, not to depart from this very epistle, paragraph 3, p. 39, it says: “that also which may have been fashioned on our account”: that is, “was fashioned.”]

Arius and his followers, to be sure, accused Catholics of falling into the error of those who divided and cut the divine substance, making the Father and Son, as it were, subjects of passion, when they endeavored to explain the Son’s generation. Hence in their confessions of faith they especially exalted the claim that, while acknowledging divinity in the one Father, they did not cut or divide God but preserved him whole, so to speak. Hear, I pray, what Arius himself babbles in writing to Alexander, Bishop of Alexandria. [Note: [Col. 0774D] Epiphanius has this letter in Greek, *Heresy* 69, no. 5. But I use Hilary’s Latin translation, *On the Trinity*, book IV, no. 12, and book VI, no. 5.]

> “We know one God, alone unbegotten . . . that God has now begotten an only-begotten Son before all ages, through whom he made both the age and all things. Begotten not merely in appearance but truly, obedient to his will; an unchangeable and unalterable perfect creature of God, yet not like one of the creatures; a thing made, but not like other things made. Nor, as Valentinus imagined, an emanation begotten from the Father; nor, as Manichaeus explained, a part of the one substance of the Father begotten; nor, as Sabellius, who divides the union, said that the one who is Father is himself Son; nor like Hieracas’s lamp from a lamp, or lamp divided into two parts; nor one who formerly existed and was afterward born or super-created into a son,” etc. [Col. 0774B]

Nor was Arius alone in teaching this. Eusebius, Bishop of Nicomedia, a great name among the Arians, did not hesitate to assail Catholics [Note: [Col. 0774D] In the letter to Paulinus, Bishop of Tyre, which Victorinus mentions in the preface to his work *Against the Arians*.] as though they “asserted one God divided into two, or some corporeal thing capable of suffering, and as though he had been from the Father himself or from the Father, like a part of him or from an outflow of substance.”

Likewise Eunomius (*Against Eunomius*, book III, in Nyssenus) “says that the substance of the Son was begotten from the Father, not brought forth by extension, nor perfected by increase, nor formed by change.” By these words he is believed not only to set forth his own opinion but also to accuse and reproach Catholics.

[Col. 0774C] Hilary therefore, in order to evade their cunning and defend Catholics from reproach, repeatedly inculcates, not only in the little book we are explaining but also in other books, the very doctrine on account of which the Arians said that they had departed from the Catholic party. In *On the Trinity*, book II, no. 8, he says:

> “But neither is the Son a part of the Father . . . nor does nature have all things when it is a portion. But he is perfect from the Perfect, because he who has all things gave all things. Nor must he be thought not to have given because he possesses, or not to possess because he has given.”

In *On the Trinity*, book III, no. 4:

> “Therefore the perfect Son of the perfect Father, and the only-begotten offspring of the unbegotten God—who received all things from him who has all things—God from God, Spirit from Spirit, Light from Light, confidently says: ‘The Father is in me and I in the Father.’ For as the Father is Spirit, so the Son is Spirit; as the Father is God, so the Son is God; as the Father is Light, so the Son is Light. Therefore, from the things which are in the Father are those things in which the Son is: that is, from the whole Father the whole Son was born; [Col. 0774D] not from elsewhere, because there was nothing before the Son; not from nothing, because the Son is from God; not in part, because the fullness of divinity is in the Son; nor in some things, because it is in all things; but as he who could willed, as he who begot knew.”

Again, to the same effect (*On the Trinity*, book III, no. 17):

> “No one knows God unless he confesses also the Father, Father of the only-begotten Son, and the Son—not born from a portion, expansion, or emission, but born from him ineffably and incomprehensibly as Son from Father—possessing the fullness of divinity from which and in which he was born: true, infinite, and perfect God. For this is the fullness of God. If anything of these is lacking, there will no longer be the fullness which it pleased him should dwell in him. This is proclaimed by the Son; this is manifested to the ignorant. Thus the Father is glorified through the Son when the Father of the Son is recognized as such.”

Thereafter, especially in no. 9 and the following sections of book VI, he expressly and by name condemns every heretical explanation already mentioned. Let us take a few passages from many (*On the Trinity*, book VI, no. 10):

> “The pious faith of the Church condemns Manichaeus, a follower of the preachers of heretical madness. For it knows no portion in the Son, but knows whole God from whole God; knows one from one; not cut off, but born; knows that the birth of God is neither a diminution of the begetter nor a weakness of the one born . . . For these things have become known to it from the only-begotten God: that the Father and Son are one, that the fullness of divinity is in the Son. Therefore it abhors applying to the Son a portion of one substance, and through the truth of the birth reveres in the Son the proper character of true divinity.” [Col. 0775B]

Thus he introduces and refutes as impious those who placed the generation of the divine Word in some emanation, as well as those who said that the Father would be corporeal and mutable if he begot a Son in the manner maintained by the Orthodox. Thus he says (*On the Trinity*, book VI, no. 17):

> “If the Son is changeable and corporeal from God, then God is changeable and corporeal, since he brought forth or extended from himself that which was his into a Son. Why are you anxious lest God be changeable? We confess the birth; taught by God, we proclaim the only-begotten as from God. You, lest birth remain and lest the only-begotten God belong to the faith of the Church, set against this the nature of the unchangeable God, which can neither be extended nor stretched forth. O unhappy error, I might offer you even examples from worldly things, from certain natures which are generated, lest you should consider birth an extension and believe the natures of those born to be losses to those begetting—so that even many living beings might be begotten from living beings without bodily union—were it not impious not to have believed God concerning himself, and the madness of ultimate frenzy to be judged to remove authority from the faith to which you profess veneration for life.” [Col. 0775C]

Again, in no. 11 of book VII of *On the Trinity*:

> “For, as we have often said, we proclaim in the Son the mystery not of division but of birth.”

See the annotations of the Benedictine Fathers of Saint Maur on this passage. Finally, not to cite everything, he treats this subject most fully in nos. 22 and 23 of the book entitled *On the Synods*, or *On the Faith of the Easterners*. If you desire much on this subject, consult Petavius. [Note: [Col. 0775D] *On the Trinity*, book V, ch. 6; and again ch. 8, no. 9 and following.]

Here I am pleased only to cite Alexander, Bishop of Alexandria, whom we regard as a great defender of Catholic truth. [Note: [Col. 0775D] In the letter to Alexander of Constantinople, quoted by Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, book I, ch. 4.]

> “Concerning whom”—he speaks of the Father and the Son—“we believe as the Apostolic Church thinks: in one unbegotten Father . . . and in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God; begotten not from nothing but from him who is Father; not in the manner of bodies, by cuttings or the outflow of divisions, as Sabellius and Valentinus imagine, but in an inexplicable and ineffable manner, according to the words of the Prophet which we have cited above: ‘Who shall declare his generation?’” [Col. 0775D]

Please consult what Gezo, Abbot of Derthon, published on this subject [Note: [Col. 0776D] *On the Body and Blood of Christ*, ch. 1 and following, p. 253, vol. III of Muratori’s *Anecdota*]; from it you will learn how highly Hilary’s authority was esteemed among the ancients.

52. Recall what was said in no. 19. Here I shall merely adduce Athanasius’s warnings on this very subject [Note: [Col. 0776D] Oration V, translated, I think, by Petavius, in Book VI *On the Trinity*, ch. 2, no. 9.]. “The Word is not, in a loose sense, or simply, a signifying utterance; rather, He is a substantial Word and substantial Wisdom, who is truly the Son of God. For unless He is substantial, God will be speaking into the air and will be a body having nothing more than human beings have, etc.” For the remaining Fathers who discuss this subject, consult Petavius in the very passage cited in annotation 19, namely chapter 2 of Book VI *On the Trinity*.

53. Substitute “sons,” or, if you prefer, “words”; do not say that the Son of God is equal or similar to them. Hilary is here attacking the impious confession of Arius (*On the Trinity*, Book IV, no. 12, and Book VI, no. 5), who, while confessing that the Father—whom alone he acknowledged as God—had “begotten the only-begotten Son before all ages, through whom He made both the age and all things,” added that He was “a perfect creature of God, but not like one of the creatures; a thing made, but not like the other things made, etc.” Hilary, I think, wishes here to teach that, if the Son is admitted to have been brought forth from nothing—which one must necessarily maintain if one acknowledges Him as a creature, however most perfect—then the only-begotten of God will be like, and therefore equal to, the other creatures in the chief and essential definition of a creature. For this alone distinguishes a creature from God: that a creature is from nothing, whereas God is from Himself.

Moreover, the Arian opinion so displeased all who were not outright Arians that it was condemned even by those who were not regarded as wholly Catholic. Thus it was decreed at the Council of Sardica (Hilary, *On the Synods*, nos. 34 and 35): “Those who say that the Son of God is from things non-existent, or from another substance and not from God . . . are anathematized by the Holy and Catholic Church.” Indeed, at the second Synod of Sirmium, whose profession of faith Hilary sets forth, the same error is condemned in these words (*ibid.*, no. 38, anathema 1): “Those who say, ‘The Son is from no existing things,’ or ‘from another substance and not from God,’ and that there was a time or age when He was not, the Holy and Catholic Church knows to be alien [from itself].”

To pass over the rest who refuted this blasphemy of Arius, Hilary frequently and forcefully rejects it. I select one passage of Hilary’s, lest I seem excessive in a matter so well known. In no. 2 of Book XII *On the Trinity* (p. 409, vol. II), he writes: “For we do not know the Lord Jesus Christ to be a creature, because He Himself is not one; nor a thing made, because He is Himself the Lord of all things made. Rather, we know Him as God, the proper offspring of God the Father’s generation, etc.”

54. This is Hilary’s most explicit opinion, from which it may readily be recognized that he is the author of both works (Book II *On the Trinity*, no. 9, p. 32): “Thus both [Father and Son] possess the secret of this birth. And if anyone perhaps blames his own understanding because he cannot attain the mystery of this generation, he will hear from me, with still greater sorrow, that it is unknown—even though both the Father and the Son are absolute intellect. I do not know; I do not inquire; yet I shall console myself. The archangels do not know; the angels have not heard; the ages do not contain it; the prophet did not perceive it; the apostle did not ask; the Son Himself did not disclose it.” He also calls the birth of the only-begotten divine Son ineffable, in no. 12 of Book II and no. 16 of Book VI *On the Trinity*.

But lest I seem to adduce Hilary alone, behold Athanasius saying this (*Oration* III, p. 214): “It is unfitting to inquire how the Word exists from God, or how He is God’s radiance, or how God begets, and what is the manner of God’s generation. For he would be mad who dared such things, attempting by his discourse to explain a reality that is inexplicable, proper to the divine nature, and known only to God Himself and to His Son. It is as though such persons were likewise to inquire where God is, how God is, and what sort the Father is. But just as it is impious to ask such questions, and characteristic of those who do not know God, so neither is it lawful to assume the same audacity in investigating the generation of the Son.”

Prudentius too, in the *Apotheosis*, speaking not in the person of a poet but of a theologian, rebukes the Arians, most audacious investigators of the ineffable generation, in these verses:

> They press on further, searching out what this very  
> Begetting is—if it be lawful for human minds to stretch  
> To that secret which precedes all times and ancient days,  
> Which rises above the very beginning itself  
> And surpasses whatever man can seek.  
> Since it is difficult to know the seeds of beginnings,  
> To what mortal will it be granted to discover what  
> God did beyond the beginning, or in what manner  
> He brought forth the Word who lacks every beginning?  
> This alone we know: God is declared to be He whom  
> The unbegotten Begetter begot—one and one. Etc.

[Col. 0777B] If you desire other Fathers, Petavius will provide them (*On the Trinity*, Book V, ch. 6). I select one for quotation here: Alexander, Bishop of Alexandria, the most eminent rebuker of Arius and his heresy (in Theodoret, Book I, *History*, ch. 4). “The inexplicable subsistence of the only-begotten Son of God,” he says, “surpasses the most diligent comprehension of the Evangelists and indeed of the angels themselves. Therefore, in my judgment, anyone is not to be counted among the pious, etc.”

55. Recall here those passages of Hilary and Alexander of Alexandria which we have just cited: “The angels do not know; the angels have not heard,” etc. But, if you wish, you may conveniently bring in here also the passages which we shall cite shortly. The letter of Alexander of Alexandria which I mentioned treats this argument very fully.

56. Although Arius seemed to have admitted the eternity of the Son when he confessed that “God [the Father] begot the only-begotten Son before all ages, through whom He made both the age and all things,” he nevertheless in fact denied that He was eternal, recognizing “God [the Father] alone as unbegotten, alone everlasting, alone without beginning, possessing immortality” (in Hilary, Book IV *On the Trinity*, no. 12). That Arius’s successors in impiety afterward followed this error may be learned from the documents abundantly assembled by Petavius. From them I select certain items, which I note at the foot of the page [Note: [Col. 0777D] Petavius, *On the Trinity*, II, 9, 8; III, 10, 5 and 6; and Book V, ch. 9.]. I ask the reader to consult these for himself, and entreat him, as he reads the aforesaid letter of Alexander, Bishop of Alexandria, to see clearly how greatly the defenders of Catholic doctrine against Arius immediately had at heart the inculcation of the eternity of the divine Word.

Although certain milder—or perhaps more cunning—Arians readily admitted that the Son had been begotten before times, yet, when required to confess Him coeternal with the Father, they refused. Instead, some introduced certain times, called by some fictitious, invented, imaginary, or prior [times], which preceded created things and therefore preceded the heavens, sun, and stars, by whose motion and revolution we measure time. In those fictitious, invented, imaginary, prior times they represented the Word of the Father as begotten and consequently as a true creature, although superior and earlier than the rest. The Catholics deservedly refuted the error of all these persons; theologians possess their arguments. Consult them, if you wish [Note: [Col. 0777D] See Petavius in the passage recently cited, namely Book II *On the Trinity*, etc.].

For one explaining Hilary’s little book, it is enough to confirm this doctrine from other passages of Hilary. Thus he says [Note: [Col. 0777D] Book IV *On the Trinity*, nos. 5 and 6, pp. 73–74, vol. II.]: “They think that they can cleverly oppose the teaching of the prophets, and also of the Gospels and the Apostles, by proclaiming the Son’s birth within time. For, since they perversely assert that we say the Son always existed, they must, by excluding what always was, confess that His birth was in time. For if He was not always, there will be a time when He was not. And if there is a time when He was not, there will be a time before Him; because one who is not always begins to be in time. But one who is without time cannot lack that which is always. They affirm that they reject the proposition that the Son always existed for this reason: lest, through His having always been, He be believed to exist without birth—as though, because He is said always to have existed, He were proclaimed unbegotten.”

And, after a few intervening words: “He confesses the Father eternal and free from origin; he also confesses the Son’s origin from eternity: not He Himself from a beginning, but from the One without beginning; born not through Himself, but from Him who always is from no one; born from eternity, receiving, that is, His birth from the Father’s eternity.”

If the reader wishes to consult other passages in Hilary, let him turn to those noted at the foot of the page [Note: [Col. 0777D] Book XII *On the Trinity*, no. 21, p. 420, vol. II: “Therefore He would be,” etc.; *ibid.*, no. 27, p. 424: “But when in matters concerning God,” etc.; Book *On the Synods*, no. 24, p. 475: “And if anyone [says] the Word,” etc.; *Commentary on Psalm* LXIII, no. 10, p. 181, vol. I: “Now if the heretic destroys the faith,” etc.].

It is no wonder that the orthodox so often emphasized the eternity of the Word. Though the Arians might evade the other points—even to the extent of not hesitating to confess the only-begotten of God to be God [Note: [Col. 0777D] They explained that by this word *god* was meant a god inferior to the true God, or one called God improperly. See Petavius, *On the Trinity*, II, 9, 4: “But that He is God,” etc. See also no. 69 and what we shall note there.]—nevertheless, when asked to confess Him eternal, they introduced deceitful expressions. They said that He existed before the ages and that God the Father had used Him, as it were, as a hand and instrument for creating the ages. Some less rigid followers of Arius, such as the Antiochene Fathers, even confessed that He had always been in the beginning with God [Note: [Col. 0777D] The Synod at Antioch in the year 341—at least, as the Maurist Fathers who edited Hilary’s works teach us—has with justice and reason been held suspect by very many. See the Maurist Fathers’ note on the profession of faith issued at this Synod and rendered in Latin by Hilary in no. 29 of Book *On the Synods*. Yet the same Maurist Fathers observe that Athanasius and Socrates, when setting out this formula of faith, omitted the word *always*, from which, as Hilary testifies in no. 5 of Book IV *On the Trinity*, the Arians especially recoiled. But because Hilary teaches that the Antiochene Fathers expressly used it, I have no doubt on the matter. See also what Hilary subsequently says, namely no. 33 of the same Book *On the Synods*.]. Yet they refused to confess that He was truly and simply eternal or everlasting, asserting that God the Father alone was everlasting and without beginning [Note: [Col. 0778D] See Arius’s profession of faith in Hilary, Book IV *On the Trinity*, no. 12, etc.].

Besides Arius’s ancient confession, we have other examples of this [Note: [Col. 0778D] Alexander, Bishop of Alexandria, in Theodoret, Book I, ch. 4, giving the Arian opinion: “There was a time when the Son of God was not,” etc.]. Since there is no need to discuss the matter at length here, I offer one clear example. Palladius and Secundianus were condemned at the Council of Aquileia as undoubtedly guilty of the Arian heresy because they refused to confess the only-begotten of God to be everlasting. Please read both the proceedings of the Council itself, which, as the highly probable opinion of many holds, Ambrose’s diligence has preserved for us [Note: [Col. 0778D] Vol. II of the Maurist edition of Ambrose, pp. 790 and 792: “He specifically says that the Father alone is everlasting.” = Ambrose said: “Does the Son of God possess immortality according to His divinity, or does He not?”], and the letter written by that Council to the Emperors [Note: [Col. 0778D] Pp. 807–808, no. 5. See also what is said on this subject in the edition of the Works of St. Ambrose prepared by the Maurist Fathers, after Letter VIII, p. 786, vol. II: “Ambrose, having read Arius’s letter,” etc.]. There occur these words: “They preferred to follow Arius rather than confess the Son of God, God, to be everlasting . . .”

Hence the denial of eternity to the Word was a certain mark of an expressly Arian profession. For this reason Eudoxius, though not wholly orthodox, nevertheless, in order to oppose Ursacius, Valens, and the other associates in Arius’s impiety, and to establish the milder error of Aetius, ensured that the eternity of the only-begotten of God was stated in three canons at the Synod of Ancyra—namely, the tenth, eleventh, and twelfth (Hilary, *On the Synods*, no. 23). Hilary himself, in that brief profession of faith which he issued against the Arians (*ibid.*, no. 64), required Catholics, if he required them to confess that the Father was not within times, also not to deny that the Son was contemporaneous with the Father. For a fuller illustration of this passage, the matters we shall adduce in no. 76 will be useful.

57. Elsewhere I have said (*Preface*, ch. 1, no. 3) that Hilary, writing in Latin, sometimes employs Greek words in order to explain himself more clearly. Whether he himself wrote this word in Latin letters—as Richard Simon maintains that the Latin Fathers consistently did—or in Greek letters, let the reader judge. However this may be, the word in question, as anyone can readily recognize, denotes the only-begotten of God as denying or excluding time, that is, as without time, and therefore before times and eternal.

58. Lest it be objected that the orthodox asserted these things rashly, they frequently sought arguments to establish the eternity of the divine Word which they maintained. Among these, the principal argument seems to be that which Hilary briefly touches upon here, drawn from the immutability of the Father, which we must admit if we acknowledge God to be God. For he describes as changed one who describes the Father of the only-begotten Son as becoming Father in time.

Other Fathers, whom Petavius does not omit [Note: [Col. 0779D] Book V *On the Trinity*, ch. 8, §§4, 5, and following, but especially §11.], employ this same proof. Hilary himself presses it both frequently and fully, as in no. 5 of Book IV *On the Trinity*, and often elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0779D] Pp. 73–74, vol. II: “For since they perversely,” etc.]. But it is better here to adduce one passage from Book XII *On the Trinity* (no. 21, p. 420), which runs thus:

> “It is one thing for that which is always eternal to be without an author; another for that which has a father—that is, an author—to be coeternal with him. For where there is a father who is an author, there is also birth; but where the author is eternal, there is also eternity of the birth. For as birth is from an author, so from an eternal author comes an eternal birth. Everything which always is is also eternal. Yet not everything which is eternal is also unbegotten. For that which is born from eternity has an eternal being as something born. But that which is not born is unbegotten with eternity. And that which is born from eternity—if it is not born eternal—then the Father too will no longer be an eternal author. Therefore, if anything of eternity has been lacking to Him who is born of the eternal Father, it is beyond doubt that the same has been lacking to the Author; because what is infinite for the begetter is infinite also for the one begotten. Neither reason nor understanding admits any intermediate thing between the birth of God the Son and the generation of God the Father, because in generation there is birth, and in birth there is generation. Each is without interval from the other, because without either, neither exists.”

Alexander, Bishop of Alexandria, pursues this same argument; I wish you would read him [Note: [Col. 0779D] In Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book I, ch. 4: [Col. 0780D] “It must necessarily be said that the Father is always Father,” etc.]. Augustine states it briefly in these words (Letter formerly 174, now 238, no. 24): [Col. 0780A] “The Father always begets, and the Son is always born.” Add what Petavius says (Book II *On the Trinity*, ch. 5).

59. Scripture most explicitly testifies that God is free from every change and from every new state; the Fathers and reason likewise indicate this. But it is not part of the present undertaking to pursue these matters. Consult theologians, and above all Petavius (vol. I, *Theology*, Book III, ch. 1). Once this is established, Hilary proves from it that the generation of the divine Word is eternal, because otherwise God the Father would be changed: He would begin in time to have a Son.

Hilary further anticipates an objection easily raised against God’s established immutability: namely, that God created the world in time, yet the divine excellence and perfection are not thereby diminished. He anticipates it, I say, by teaching that no change is introduced into God by the creation of things, because all things were established by an eternal and immutable decree and arranged in their utmost perfection within the divine idea; and they were thus brought into execution as they had been established and arranged. He had taught the same elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0780D] “For He Himself [God] is the head and source of all things, and in Him all things were created, although afterward, from the treasures stored in Himself, according to the decision of His eternal power, He brought forth each thing separately.” Hilary, *On Psalm* XCI, no. 4.].

Theologians have devised other means of excluding from God the change which might perhaps be feared from the temporal creation of things; Petavius recounts a great part of them (vol. I, *Dogmatic Theology*, Book III, ch. 1). But Hilary chose—as I have said—to appeal to the immutability of the divine decree, and hence of God’s knowledge and idea. From among several passages of Hilary, I select the most explicit, supplied by no. 40 of Book XII *On the Trinity*:

> “For the preparation of things to be created is perpetual and eternal; nor was the structure of this universe brought about by piecemeal thoughts, as though heaven were first conceived, and then God had afterward entered upon concern and deliberation about the earth, and had thought out each particular: first that it should be spread out into a plain, then afterward raised into mountains by a better plan, then diversified again by hills, and next made habitable even upon the very summits; as though heaven were prepared and set apart as God’s dwelling, while exhalations of winds might powerfully hold clouds high above; then as though certain springs might flow beneath heaven, and finally the earth might be strengthened with firm foundations. For Wisdom professes herself to be prior to each of these things. But since all things beneath heaven were made through God, and Christ was present in the fashioning of heaven, and precedes the eternity of the heaven thus prepared, this does not allow us to suppose that in God there were fragmentary thoughts about insignificant things, because the entire preparation of these things is coeternal with God.”

60. Elsewhere too Hilary teaches quite plainly that the world was created for human beings—that is, for our sake—as when he says (*On Psalm* LXV, no. 6, p. 197, vol. I): “For who would not tremble before the majesty of Him who established the ages, created the world, measured out times in their recurring succession and course, adorned heaven with stars, filled the earth with fruits, enclosed the sea within bounds, and chose man either to use these things or to rule them?” He emphasizes the same in commentaries on other Psalms, which I earnestly wish you would read [Note: [Col. 0780D] *Treatise on Psalm* LXIII, no. 9; *Treatise on Psalm* CXXXIV, no. 14; but especially *Treatise on Psalm* CXVIII, letter X, nos. 1 and 2, p. 334, vol. I.]. Whether that passage of Psalm VIII, “Thou hast subjected all things beneath his feet,” etc., indicates the same, let the reader judge. I shall discuss this subject at length in a separate dissertation.

61. That is: although He had not yet created them, He had nevertheless arranged and ordered them within Himself. See no. 59.

[Col. 0781A] 62. I certainly think that *simul* (“at once”) should be read, since our manuscript reads *semel* (“once”: “to make all things once”). This is required by the contrast between, on the one hand, the simultaneous creation of all things and, on the other, the creation of all things distributed over several days. Hilary prefers the latter, namely creation distributed over six days, although in the Book of Ecclesiasticus, treating creation, we read *simul* [Note: [Col. 0781D] Ch. XVIII, 1: “He who lives for ever created all things together.”]. Biblical interpreters and theologians will explain to you how this passage is reconciled with Genesis.

With this established, I judge the meaning of this passage to be as follows. It did not arise from any inability in God that all things were not arranged in a single instant; rather, all things were arranged throughout the interval of six days so that, as it were, by steps and according to the distinction of each thing’s rank and order, all might obey God creating and ordering. If you desire a fuller interpretation of this passage, Ambrose’s words will supply it. I cite them all the more willingly because I think it most probable that Ambrose, when he wrote them, had regard [Col. 0781B] to the teaching of earlier Fathers. Here, then, are Ambrose’s words [Note: [Col. 0781D] *On Cain and Abel*, Book II, ch. 6, no. 22.]:

> “For the world itself is read to have been made distinctly, although one part of it had previously been unformed; for the earth was invisible and unformed. Certainly light was first made, and God called the light; God separated light from darkness, and the darkness was called Night. And we read in sequence each thing that was made: heaven, earth, fruit-bearing trees, diverse animals. The lighter things, such as air and fire, were distributed above; the heavier below, namely earth and water. God could certainly have commanded that all things be made at once; but He preferred to preserve distinction, which we might imitate in all our undertakings, and especially in the reciprocal rendering of thanks.”

Interpreters further observe that creatures emerged, as it were, gradually from that primal matter: the less excellent first, then the more excellent, with man—the most excellent of all—bringing their sequence to a close.

63. This passage seems somewhat obscure; you will make it utterly obscure if you read, as the manuscript reads, *et nulla* (“and none”). But I certainly think that one should read *et nuda* (“and naked”), that is, without adornment and appearance. Its meaning, I think, is this: God willed ordered and gradually arranged things, each according to its own rank and dignity, to obey Him as He brought forth creatures day by day, lest those earlier unformed elements should be despised [Note: [Col. 0781D] “In the beginning God created heaven and earth. But the earth was empty and void” (others read “unformed”); “and darkness was over the face of the deep.” Gen. I:1, etc.]. For who would not despise them and prefer to them things already beautiful and endowed with their proper appearance and form?

Yet, while offering these observations, I fear that something may be missing in this period which would more suitably join the earlier words, “passive and naked” (or, if one prefers, “none”), with the later word “more ancient.” Let the reader decide whether my suspicion is probable or not.

64. By adding the word *magis* (“more”), I have somewhat corrected the defective reading of our manuscript; for it reads: “how much those things which [are] to none,” etc. Who does not see that the word *magis* is required by the argument Hilary employs? It is indeed an argument of that kind which the Scholastics call from the lesser to the greater, or *a fortiori* [from the stronger argument].

If I attempted to bring forward the testimonies of the Fathers and the Scholastics to confirm this argument, I should be almost endless. Indeed, those Scholastics who maintain that the mystery of the Incarnation was entirely hidden and incomprehensible even to the angels themselves rely especially upon the Fathers. It suffices for me to cite Leo and Hilary. The former repeatedly emphasizes this, especially in the passages noted at the foot of the page [Note: [Col. 0782D] Sermon IX *On the Nativity*, no. 1: “It indeed surpasses,” etc.; and Sermon X of the same title, or *On the Nativity*, no. 1: “But because [the birth] of our Lord and Savior,” etc.; and no. 4 of the same sermon: “But the Nativity of the Lord,” etc.]. The latter treats it more fully in no. 12 of Book I *On the Trinity* [Note: [Col. 0782D] P. 9, vol. II: “Therefore this teaching of the divine Sacrament,” etc.] and in no. 19 of Book III of the same work, that is, *On the Trinity* [Note: [Col. 0782D] P. 60 of the same volume: “You ask how,” etc.].

65. Hilary further presses the proof he had previously advanced. First, he shows that Christ’s bodily birth is rightly called hidden or ineffable, since Scripture itself calls it an overshadowing; then, once this is granted, he infers what he said recently: namely, that the eternal generation of the Word must, *a fortiori*, be called hidden or ineffable. If you wish, read Hilary’s discussion of this overshadowing (Book II *On the Trinity*, no. 26, “But lest perhaps,” etc.).

66. Recall what I said in nos. 54 and 55.

67. Recall what was said in nos. 31, 33, and 54. In the manuscript, *concussus* occurs in place of *concessos*, clearly an error; I therefore judged it should be corrected.

68. Hilary undertakes a fuller explanation of the dignity and excellence of the divine Word, and at the same time sets out a sufficiently extensive and precise confession of his faith. Who, indeed, could doubt that when Hilary attributes these titles to Christ, he attributes them especially to Him insofar as He is God? Yet many of them also belong to Christ insofar as He is man—or, to speak better and more truly, insofar as God is man—because of what theologians call the communication of properties.

Hilary is accustomed repeatedly to emphasize and recall the same doctrines; anyone who has read the books *On the Trinity* which he published will admit this. He himself gives the reason for this practice in these words (*On the Synods*, no. 62): “For the infinite and immeasurable God could neither be understood nor displayed in the brief utterances of human speech; for the brevity of discourse often misleads both hearers and teachers.” But let us elucidate the rest of his statements.

69. The word *in principio* (“in the beginning”) may refer either to the eternal generation of the Son, of which we have spoken sufficiently in no. 56, or to the other titles which he attributes to the same Son. Hilary explains elsewhere, and states most explicitly, in what sense he calls the Son of God and adds the phrase “in the beginning” [Col. 0782C]: “Therefore,” he says (Book V *On the Trinity*, no. 5, p. 107, vol. II), “the Son of God is not a false God, nor an adopted God, nor a God merely so called, but true God . . . For He is God through whom all things were made.”

Here, incidentally, not only the Arians but also those are refuted—“nor an adopted God”—who abused Hilary’s authority in order to make Christ an adopted Son. For if He is God, how can He be adopted?

70. Before I proceed, let the reader know that these titles, and other related ones attributed by the ancient theologians to the only-begotten of God, fall, as it were, into two classes. Some the orthodox attributed to the only-begotten because the Arians refused to attribute them to Him, assigning them to the Father alone. Others they attributed because the Arians themselves, or at least the Semi-Arians, attributed them to the only-begotten and exalted them with great display and praise; the orthodox feared that, if they did not attribute them to the only-begotten, they would seem to speak less splendidly of Him than the Arians did.

When Hilary here calls the Word true Wisdom, he understands divine Wisdom, without a cause. In this very sense Arius acknowledged one God—namely the Father—as alone without beginning and alone true; whereas Hilary, whom we have just cited in no. 69, calls the only-begotten of God true God. Hence, although Palladius had confessed at the Council of Aquileia that “the only-begotten of God is Wisdom” [Note: [Col. 0783D] “Palladius said: He is Wisdom,” p. 793, vol. II, Maurist edition of Ambrose.], he nevertheless refused to proclaim Him divine Wisdom and without a cause, and therefore true Wisdom in the sense under discussion, assigning that title to the Father alone. Ambrose did not hesitate to say of Palladius: “Palladius, as I see it, has even attempted to deny that the Son of God is wise.”

Nor would I blame those who say that Hilary says these things in order to refute the impiety—indeed, rather the madness—of those who said that the Son of God was not Wisdom itself, but a work of Wisdom. I think it worthwhile to quote the holy Doctor’s words here, since they remarkably confirm the point we are now clarifying (*Commentary on Matthew*, ch. XI, no. 9, p. 724):

> “For many commonly evade the Apostle’s saying (1 Cor. 1:24), in which he calls Christ the Wisdom of God and the Power of God, in these ways: they say that in His creation from a virgin the effective wisdom and power of God were present, and that in His birth a work of divine prudence and power is to be understood; thus there is in Him the efficiency rather than the nature of wisdom. To prevent any such understanding, He called Himself Wisdom, showing Wisdom in Himself, not the things that belong to Wisdom. For faith, hope, charity, chastity, fasting, self-control, humility, and kindness are works of wisdom; but these are works of a nature, not that nature itself; and the reality which produces them does not consist in the things which are produced.”

Whether Hilary says, in order to refute this madness, “But the Lord Jesus Christ is the Power of God and the Wisdom of God” (*On Psalm* LXVI, no. 29, p. 235), let others determine.

71. See nos. 19 and 20.

72. It has long been observed that Hilary understands God by the name “Spirit.” Please see the preface [Note: [Col. 0783D] Nos. 57 and following, especially nos. 62 and 63. Add, if you wish, what is read in no. 8 of Book XII *On the Trinity*: “But because Spirit from Spirit proclaimed to us the birth,” etc.] to volume I of St. Hilary, published by the Maurist monks. Hilary’s passage is very well known, and worth citing here (Book IX *On the Trinity*, no. 14): “When He had emptied Himself, so that Christ, remaining Spirit—that is, God—might be the same Christ, man.”

Nor is it surprising that God is understood by the name “Spirit.” For God is Spirit by antonomasia, that is, Spirit in the highest sense; and God alone is Spirit, if by *spirit* you understand that which comprehends all things most perfectly in itself. Some of the ancients seem to have taken the word *spirit* in this sense [Note: [Col. 0783D] They appear to take it in this sense when they teach that God alone is incorporeal, while all others, even the angels themselves and our souls, are corporeal. To avoid citing many, this is taught by the author of *Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, believed to be Gennadius, chs. 11, 12, and 13, and by others cited by Le Quien on ch. 3, Book II of John Damascene’s *On the Faith*.].

However that may be, besides those cited by the distinguished editor of Hilary’s works (in the preface to vol. I, no. 58 and following), here is a clear passage of Tertullian establishing that the ancient Fathers denoted God by the name “Spirit.” He begins his book *On Prayer* in this way: “The Spirit of God and the Word of God . . . both are Jesus Christ.” If you wish to cite other passages from Tertullian, the distinguished Muratori will indicate them [Note: [Col. 0784D] Note 1 on this book of Tertullian, vol. III, *Anecdota*.].

Nearly all the remaining titles subsequently listed—Way, Light, and so forth—are expressly contained in that very well-known profession of faith “which was set forth at the Synod held for the dedication of the completed church at Antioch. Ninety-seven bishops who were present set it forth when one bishop had come under suspicion of holding erroneous opinions.” Here is what those bishops declared [Note: [Col. 0784D] In Hilary, *On the Synods*, nos. 28 and 29, p. 478, vol. II.]:

> “We believe . . . in one God, the Father . . . and in one Lord Jesus Christ, His only-begotten Son, God through whom are all things, begotten from the Father, God from God, whole from whole, one from one, perfect from perfect, King from King, Lord from Lord, Word, Wisdom, Life, true Light, true Way, Resurrection, Shepherd, Door, unchangeable and immutable image of divinity, essence, power, and glory; firstborn of all creation, who was always in the beginning with God . . . Mediator of God and men, predestined for our faith and leader of life.”

If you say that Hilary had this profession in view, you will indeed say what has seemed probable to some. Hilary himself criticizes this profession only in this respect (no. 31): “that perhaps it seems to have spoken less expressly of the undifferentiated likeness of the Father and Son, especially since it held that the proper substance, order, and glory of each named one were denoted in the names Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, so that they are three in substance but one in concord.”

The profession which Hilary calls the second [profession] of the Eastern Synod (*On the Synods*, nos. 33 and 34) is less rich in titles; yet it too says of the only-begotten of God: “who is Word, Wisdom, Power, Life, and true Light.”

But to return to Hilary: he teaches these things not only in the letter we are elucidating, but also elsewhere. On Psalm LXIII he says (no. 10, p. 181, vol. I): “Now, if the heretic destroys the faith, he will know that the Son of God always existed, separated from the Father by no interval of time; that He Himself is the Word, Power, and Wisdom of God; that He was the maker of the world and also the creator of man.”

In his treatise on Psalm 118 (Letter IX, likewise §9, p. 334), he includes still more. For he says: “God spoke the Law through Moses; he spoke through the Prophets. But this is God’s law, not also the law of God’s mouth. Now the mouth of God is he who is also the power of God, who is also the wisdom of God, who is also the arm of God, who is also the image of God—namely God and our Lord Jesus Christ.”

The same is taught by Basil the Great, whose words I would gladly quote, were they not numerous—especially since he also explains the reason for these very titles. But the reader can readily consult for himself the passages to which I refer, in chapter 8—elsewhere §§17 and 19—of the book *On the Holy Spirit*, addressed to Amphilochius. Namely: “Because of his manifold beneficence toward us,” etc.; and: “He does all things by the touch of power and by the operation of goodness: he feeds, illumines, nourishes, guides, heals, raises up,” etc.

If you desire others who enumerate titles appropriate to Christ, you will easily find them in the books of ancient writers. I indicate only two here. The first is that writer to whom the sermon formerly numbered 190 *On Time* must be attributed, now rejected into the appendix as no. 113, whose words I cited in annotation 20 (p. 60). The other is Ausonius, thus praying to Christ (*Morning Prayer*):

> O Christ, graciously plead with the eternal Father:  
> Savior, God and Lord, my glory, Word,  
> Son—true from the True, Light from Light—  
> abiding with the eternal Father, reigning unto the ages.

Why indeed should anyone wonder at this, when Scripture itself plainly assigns these very titles to Christ, or at least they may readily be assigned to Christ if one considers what Scripture declares concerning him? I noted some matters at the end of the letter itself, lest I appear to have made this assertion rashly. I admit, indeed, that Christ is not very explicitly called “the strength of the Lord,” unless perhaps you think him to be the same one who sometimes appeared in the form of an angel and called himself Gabriel, or, if you prefer, spoke in Gabriel. But if he is called the arm of the Lord, or of God, will he not be called strength? The Fathers, surely, for this reason—as I think—do not hesitate to call Christ the arm of God or of the Lord. Moreover, the word *power* (*virtus*) appears synonymous with *strength* (*fortitudo*). The Fathers very frequently assign this title to Christ. I mention Rufinus alone, who writes as follows (*Explanation of the Creed*, p. 73, Vallarsi ed.): “And what is the power of the Most High, if not Christ himself, who is the power of God and the wisdom of God?” If you desire other passages from the Fathers, the distinguished editor of the works of St. Hilary will supply them (*Preface to vol. I*, §61 ff.).

When I indicated the passages in which Christ is called wine, I noted two: Matthew 9:17 and John 15:1. In the former occurs: “Neither do they put new wine into old wineskins.” Evidently, by the allegory and term “wine,” the ancient writers understood the evangelical law, and consequently Christ, its author. In the latter: “I am the true vine.” The vine, moreover, is, so to speak, the parent of wine. Yet I admit that Hilary could also have had in view the passages of Proverbs, chapter 9 (v. 2): “Wisdom … has mixed her wine”; and (v. 5): “Come, eat my bread and drink the wine which I have mixed for you.” Sound interpreters teach that by these words the most holy sacrament of the altar is foretold, in which Christ himself is present under the species of bread and wine.
