He could likewise have had in view that passage of Matthew (26:29): “But I say to you, I will not henceforth drink of this fruit of the vine.” For the fruit of the vine mentioned here is Christ himself, hidden under the species of wine.

73. Since the incarnation itself is for humankind, Christ likewise will be, for humankind, our life, our light, and our shepherd.

74. He refers to Paul’s celebrated statement (Acts 17:28): “In him we live and move and are.” Perhaps he also refers to those passages in which Christ is called our life, or the fountain of life, the fountain of water springing up into eternal life.

75. That is: from the reading of the Scriptures he will learn those things which we have said about Christ, and therefore the very titles which we have enumerated.

76. I think this is the sense contained in these words. If therefore, through the revelation of Scripture, we confess that the Son of God has been made known to us, we also know that God the Father created through that same Son the ages, both visible and invisible. For it is not permissible to suppose that God began to work when the world was created, or ceased after it was created; for the Lord himself testifies that he has not ceased, when he says: “My Father works until now,” etc.

If by “visible and invisible ages” he understands visible and invisible creatures, he teaches here the same thing that he had taught before. See number, or annotation, 18. He could indeed have understood creatures by those terms, by synecdoche—that is, by denoting the contained thing with the name of its container.

But if he understands the ages themselves, this passage then becomes somewhat more obscure. We know visible ages, namely those which we measure by the revolutions of the sun, stars, and heavens. But it is difficult to explain what invisible ages are. Does he indicate those ages which others have called imaginary, whereas Hilary himself calls them times which we apprehend by conception (*On the Trinity*, XII.27, p. 42), or, more expressly in the same place and §28, eternal times?

> [Note: Col. 0785D] “But since in the things of God—that is, in the birth of God—there is nothing which is not before eternal time … he who must be confessed to exist before eternal times cannot be understood to have begun after something. Therefore, if the birth of something before eternal times belongs neither to human natures nor to human understanding, and yet in this matter God is believed, on the basis of his own declarations, to have made such a profession concerning himself: how can the unbelief of our time declare, through the conception of human understanding, that what apostolic faith has said was always born—that is, existed before eternal times, born without the apprehension of eternal understanding—was not before it was born? For what was born before time was always born, because that which is before eternal time is always.” Hilary, cited passage, that is, *On the Trinity*, XII.27–28.

Let this be another’s judgment. Here, moreover, we must observe that, when Hilary says, “For it is not permissible to believe that God worked from the point at which the world received the same beginning of its birth,” we may suspect that he held the opinion which teaches that the creation of the angels preceded the creation of these visible and perceptible things. This opinion, indeed, was held by many ancient theologians and Fathers, especially Greeks.

> [Note: Col. 0786D] See Petavius, *On the Angels*, I.15. See also the note appended to those words of Novatian, chapter 1 of *On the Trinity*: “Although also in things above,” etc.

It was undoubtedly Hilary’s opinion, for he wrote (*Against Auxentius*, §6): “Either all the regenerate are not truly sons of God, or all the angels, certainly created through Christ, were created before all times and before absolutely all ages.”

77. If you refer these words of Hilary to that class of operations which theologians call *ad intra*, you will explain them easily; for those actions which were eternal and will endure eternally remain immutable. For this reason, as Augustine has already observed, they encompass all times.

> [Note: Col. 0786D] *Against an Arian Sermon*, ch. 24, otherwise §20, p. 40, vol. VIII of the Maurist edition of the Fathers: “Let no one be troubled that the word is in the future tense, ‘he will receive,’ as though he did not yet possess it; for terms of time are used indifferently, although eternity is understood to remain without time. For he received, because he proceeded from the Father; and he receives, because he proceeds from the Father; and he will receive, because he will never cease to proceed from the Father. Thus God both is, was, and will be, and nevertheless neither has, nor had, nor will have a beginning or an end of time.”

But if you refer them to that class of actions which we call external, or *ad extra*: if he created angels before the visible world—as Hilary certainly believed—we believe that God worked before the world received the beginning of its birth. Nor does he cease to work, since at every instant he creates souls to be infused into human bodies, and preserves and governs all things. See the passages which I note at the foot of the page.

> [Note: Col. 0786D] *On the Trinity*, VII.17; and *On Psalm 91*, §§3, 4, 5 ff., p. 266, vol. I.

What the rest of the eternal Father is, Hilary teaches in §8 of his commentary on Psalm 91 (p. 269, vol. I, “Since therefore the works of God,” etc.). To understand clearly the phrases, “nothing has ever happened to him, but he always is,” recall what we said in §59. But if you take the words “he always is” to mean that Hilary teaches that this attribute, *Being*, is proper to God, and therefore to the Father, you will certainly take them in the sense rendered highly probable by other statements of Hilary. For he once wrote (*On the Trinity*, XII.23–24, p. 421, vol. II):

> “Now if it is always proper to the Father that he is always Father, it must always be proper to the Son that he is always Son. And how can it enter our speech or understanding that he was not before he was born, when it is proper to him always to be what he was born? Thus the only-begotten God, possessing in himself the form and image of the invisible God, is equal in all those things which are proper to God the Father, through the fullness of true divinity in himself. For, as we have taught in the preceding books, he is to be honored and is powerful in power and worship, just as the Father is. Thus, as the Father always is, so it is also common to the Son always to be in that he is Son. For from the saying to Moses, ‘He who is has sent me to you,’ sound understanding does not doubt that what is belongs properly to God; because what is cannot be understood or said not to be. For being and non-being are contraries; nor do these different meanings meet in one and the same thing, because while one remains, the other will not be. Therefore, where there is being, non-being cannot enter either thought or speech. To our understanding, drawn backward and continually recalled to the understanding of him who is, only that which is is always prior concerning him; because what is infinite in God always withdraws itself from the backward movement of our finite understanding, so that the backward-reaching intention may not apprehend something else before that which is proper to God—his always being—because, in advancing through eternity toward an understanding of God, nothing other than God’s always being continually presents itself.”

If you desire other Fathers, Petavius will provide very many; I urge you to consult him (vol. I, *Dogmatic Theology*, ch. 6). That this attribute is also peculiar to the Son is perhaps shown by many of the testimonies brought forward to establish the eternity of the divine Word, and consequently by many of those which Petavius adduces in chapter 9 of book V of *On the Trinity*. I select one which I judge very suitable to our subject, taken from the letter of Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, to his namesake, bishop of Constantinople (*Theodoret, Ecclesiastical History*, I.4): “Let no one,” he says, “take this ‘always’ as grounds for suspecting that he is unbegotten, as those whose mental perception is blinded suppose; for ‘was,’ ‘always,’ and ‘before the ages’ are not the same as ‘unbegotten.’”

78. See §§57 and 72. As to the word ἀνάστιτεν, is it derived from ἀνίστημι, meaning “to raise up, awaken, restore, renew,” etc.? Or from the unused verb ἀναστάω? Or should the manuscript here be thought corrupt? Let the reader judge.

79. Perhaps the word *constat* (“it is established”) or another similar word is lacking, so that the text should read: “It is therefore established that there are very many things which he made through the Son.” But I would not have you take the word “very many” as though Hilary thought that many things indeed, but not all things, were created by the divine Word. For he frequently and most plainly presses that evangelical declaration: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.” See §18. “Very many,” then, here means “all.” What these are he immediately enumerates, adding: “For how many thrones there are,” etc. Who does not know that there are very many creatures, both bodily and without bodies, whose names we scarcely know—indeed, whose very names in some cases we do not know at all? He therefore rightly says: “whose names alone are known to us, or not even those.”

80. The words, “which no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man,” are taken from the Apostle Paul (1 Cor. 2:9). But since it seems highly probable to me that these words were inserted into the letter itself by an ignorant copyist, having first stood in the margin as a confirmation of that statement, “What great splendor, too, do we suppose there is in invisible things, which we cannot estimate,” etc., I think that they should be deleted or, if you prefer, returned to the margin.

Moreover, the word *quanti*—“for how many thrones there are, how many powers,” etc.—here, in my judgment, means “how many” (*quot*), as happens very often in Tertullian, Jerome, and other Fathers. Petavius treats copiously of the number, rank, and offices of angels in a special work devoted to that subject (*On the Angels*, vol. III of *Dogmatic Theology*). I too treated it, but much more briefly, in a booklet written in Italian and published in 1747 (*Treatise on Guardian Angels*, part I, chs. 3, 4, etc.).

81. That is: if bodily things themselves are so beautiful, so splendid, so marvelous, who could think himself able to comprehend the beauty and excellence of invisible things? It is the celebrated argument from the lesser to the greater, as they say. Our copyist consistently writes *extimare* for *aestimare*, or, if you prefer, *existimare*.

82. Hilary teaches a thousand times that the world was created by the Son, or by God through the Son, as through a consubstantial instrument. The passages of the holy Doctor are so frequent that, if I were to adduce them, I might easily seem to be seeking the reputation of learning in a matter that is evident. You have some above, in §18.

But does he, by the words, “And indeed he commanded light to exist, by which the other things might be made visible, and made it, giving it the name day,” criticize Tertullian, who understood the Word himself by the name of the primordial light? Let this be another’s judgment. Here are Tertullian’s very words, for the reader to weigh (*Against Praxeas*, ch. 12):

> “But how is it written concerning the preceding works of the world? First, indeed, before the Son appeared: ‘And God said, Let there be light; and there was light’ [Gen. 1]. The Word himself is immediately light—the true light which enlightens every human being coming into this world—and through him also the light of the world. Thereafter, with Christ the Word present and administering, God willed that it should be made, and God made it.”

The remaining matters contained in this section of Hilary’s letter are readily clear in themselves.

83. Either *ne terrena* should be read, or, if you read *neve terrena*, some words, though few, are lacking at the end of the period to complete the sense. Hilary here takes the words “firmament” and “heaven” to mean some solid and consistent, though transparent, matter which shuts off our sight of heavenly things. The very etymology of the word seems to favor this explanation. Everyone knows what more recent philosophers maintain concerning the material of the heavens.

84. See the passages of Scripture which I noted at the end of Hilary’s letter itself, and annotation 62. Refer these words—“And in a marvelous way, commanding that she should first bring forth that which had been fashioned last”—to the earth. For heaven was created first (Gen. 1:1); but God willed that the earth should put forth green herb bearing seed, as it were the first offspring of created nature.

85. What we have just said also elucidates this passage. Nor is the earth the last of all things if, before the other things, it is granted the power to germinate green herb bearing seed.

86. Are these matters to be referred to evening (darkness) and morning (light), which became one day? Or to natural compounds consisting of elements created at intervals? For fire was undoubtedly not formed together with water, nor perhaps earth together with air. Let the reader judge. See also §§62 and 63.

87. We have reached the passage which has seemed exceedingly difficult to many. First, it is asked why the Son of God is called God the craftsman. Next, why the Father is said to command: “at the Father’s command.” These matters are readily clarified if you remember that omnipotence is assigned to the Father as a kind of distinctive attribute—“I believe in God the Father Almighty”—whereas wisdom is assigned to the Son; theologians discuss this at length. We conceive omnipotence as commanding, as it were, and wisdom as executing. Thus we confess creation to be the work of the whole Trinity; yet, because we assign attributes as it were proper to the Persons, we also assign to them those dispositions which the limitations of our minds tell us seem to proceed from those attributes.

Hilary himself indicates this when, speaking against the Arians who asserted that the only-begotten Son of God was employed by the Father in creation as though a mere created instrument—see the views of the Arians in Petavius, *On the Trinity*, II.5.16—he wrote as follows (*On the Trinity*, IV.20):

> “For you have said: all things are from the Father, but all things are through the Son. For in that which is said, ‘Let us make man,’ the origin is from him from whom the speech began; while in that God made in the image of God, he also through whom the operation is completed is signified. Then, lest you be permitted to lie concerning this, Wisdom—whom you yourself have confessed to be Christ—will oppose you, saying: ‘When he set the fountains securely beneath the heaven, when he made strong the foundations of the earth, I was with him arranging them. I was she in whom he rejoiced. And I rejoiced daily before him at every time, when he rejoiced in the completed world and rejoiced in the children of men.’ Every pretext is shut off, and all error is constrained to confess the truth. Wisdom, begotten before the ages, is present with God. Nor is she merely present; she also arranges. Therefore she is arranging things with him. Understand the office of arranging or ordering. For the Father, in speaking, brings about; the Son, in working, arranges the things declared to be made. Yet the distinction made between the Persons is such that the work is referred to both. For in the words ‘Let us make,’ both the command and the deed are made equal; while in the statement, ‘I was with him arranging,’ Wisdom signifies that she is not alone with herself in the operation.”

Hilary seems to me to speak in the same sense in §43 of book XII of *On the Trinity*, which I ask you to consult. Then you will understand why he also calls the Word a craftsman: because, since the Son of God is wisdom, the work is assigned to wisdom as directing it, as it were; and thus the world too, which is certainly a most excellent work of craftsmanship. Nor does he call the divine Word a craftsman for this reason in our letter alone: he does so also in §4 of book XII of *On the Trinity*, where he treats at length of the Word of God creating the world.

> [Note: Col. 0789C] Peter is witness, writing thus: “Commending your souls as to a faithful Creator.” Why do we impose the name of a work upon the maker? etc.

I ask you to consult this passage also.

[Col. 0789B] But why do we cite only the Fathers and pass over the hymn used by the Church? The Church sings as follows:

> [Note: Col. 0789C] In the hymn at Matins in Paschal time:
>
> When, as the world was born, you as its Maker,  
> Giving Adam the image of your countenance,  
> Joined a noble spirit  
> To his clay.
>
> When the envy and deceit of the devil  
> Had defiled the human race,  
> You, clothed in flesh, as Craftsman  
> Reform its lost form.

This agrees exactly with the hymn used by the Roman clergy before Urban VIII gave more elegant meters to ecclesiastical hymns:

> You who, at the world’s beginning,  
> Fashioned Adam, the human being,  
> …  
> That you might redeem the human being  
> Whom you had already fashioned before, etc.

88. Those who maintain that the Fathers, in expounding Scripture, followed Plato himself insofar as this could be done will not hesitate to ascribe to Platonic ideas Hilary’s statement that “the soul had animated the very materials, so that they might furnish souls to living creatures subsequently born.” But I would by no means ascribe this to him. For I know that Platonic doctrines concerning the world-soul and similar matters cannot find much favor among the orthodox.

I would therefore explain the statement in two ways. Either say that, in Hilary’s view, God imparted to the waters whatever it is by which the souls of fish, creeping things, and birds subsist. Although we do not know how this was done, it certainly was done; for when fish, creeping things, and birds began to live, they received souls from waters already made fertile by the divine command. Or say that souls had already been implanted in the fish, creeping things, and birds, from which fish, birds, and creeping things yet to be born would also receive their souls. For the souls of fish and creeping things are not created and infused into bodies already formed; this happens only in the human being. Rather, they are communicated and received through generation. Why, then, should it not be permissible to say of the souls of fish what Basil taught concerning the souls of brute animals? His words furnish us with a commendable parallel. Here is what Basil teaches on this subject, clearly indicating the first explanation:

> [Note: Col. 0790C] *Hexaemeron*, Homily VIII, §2, p. 71, vol. I of the Maurist edition of the Fathers.
>
> “Let the earth bring forth a living soul. Why does the earth bring forth a living soul? So that you may learn the difference between the soul of a beast and the soul of a human being. You will shortly learn how the human soul was formed; but now hear concerning the soul of brute animals. Since, according to what is written, the soul of every animal is its blood, and blood when coagulated is accustomed to be transformed into flesh, while flesh when decayed is dissolved into earth, the souls of brute animals are rightly and properly something earthly. Let the earth, therefore, bring forth a living soul. Observe the affinity of soul with blood, of blood with flesh, and of flesh with earth; then return again in reverse order through the same sequence—from earth to flesh, from flesh to blood, from blood to soul—and you will find that the soul of cattle is earthly. Do not suppose that the soul is older than the constitution of their bodies.”

The second explanation likewise rests on Basil, whom it is better to hear teaching as follows (*Hexaemeron*, Homily IX, §2, p. 81):

> “Let the earth bring forth a living soul of cattle, beasts, and creeping things. Consider the voice of God passing through created things, which began then and remains effective even now, continuing until the world shall be consummated. For as a ball, when someone has set it in motion and it subsequently finds a slope, is borne downward through both its own construction and the suitability of the place, and does not rest before it reaches level ground; so the nature of things, stirred by one command, equally penetrates created things in generation and corruption and preserves, through likeness, the successions of kinds until it reaches its very end. For it makes horse succeed horse, lion lion, eagle eagle; indeed, it transmits every animal, preserved by succeeding generations, to the consummation of the universe. No duration of time destroys the characteristics of animals; but nature, as though only recently established, continually runs afresh together with time. ‘Let the earth bring forth a living soul.’ This command has adhered to the earth, nor does it cease to serve its Creator.”

Although, if someone should say that the kind of generation which ancient philosophers call spontaneous, or generation from putrefaction, is mentioned here, he will say something not at all remote from probability. For the ancients thought that such generations were chiefly accomplished by the aid of water and rains. Hence Basil—for, since I supported the foregoing by his authority, I gladly confirm this too by the authority of the same writer—hence, I say, Basil immediately adds after the preceding words:

> “For some things are produced from the succession of things which existed before; but others are known even now to receive life from the earth itself. For in rainy weather it produces not only cicadas and innumerable other kinds of flying creatures wandering in the air, most of which, because of their smallness, have no names; it also produces mice and frogs from itself. Around Egyptian Thebes, where there is abundant rain in hot weather, the region is immediately filled with field mice. We have even seen eels formed and generated from mud in no other way; neither an egg nor any other means produces their succession, but they themselves have their origin from the earth. ‘Let the earth bring forth a soul,’ etc.”

By these explanations, in my judgment, the words of this Letter which we have cited can readily be elucidated, and we are not compelled to say that the soul mentioned here is the Holy Spirit himself fertilizing the waters. Yet this opinion appears to have pleased our Steuchus and plainly pleased many ancient writers; and Basil perhaps hints at it when he writes:

> [Note: Col. 0790C] *Against Eunomius*, V, final chapter, p. 321, vol. I.
>
> “Let not only the body surrounding him [the human being] and the heat of his body be tranquil, but also whatever surrounds and encompasses him—namely heaven, earth, sea, and the rational beings in them. And let him understand that all things are fulfilled, and that the Spirit stands over them everywhere, as having descended upon, been poured into, entered everywhere, and shone upon them. For ‘the Spirit of the Lord has filled the world,’ and that which contains all things has knowledge of God.”

Recall what I said in §24.

89. Consult the passage of Genesis which I noted at the end of the letter. Here he teaches, moreover, that animals did not receive a soul from outside, but with the body itself and matter already animated and living. The human being, on the contrary, as we shall soon see.

90. He refers, I think, to the well-known words of Psalm 32, verse 9: “He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created.” The very account of the creation and formation of things which appears in Genesis 1 also declares the speed with which things were brought forth after the divine command: “And God said, Let there be light, and there was light,” etc. Hence every interval and delay is excluded. Please consult what Hilary teaches in his *Commentary on Psalm 118* (Letter X, *Iod*, §4, “In creation,” etc.).

91. See the immediately preceding number, namely 90, and Dissertation I. Where he wrote, *quippe quum Deus* (“since God”), the copyist wrote in such a way that we may also read *quippe quod Deus* (“since that God”).

92. He attributes another fertility to the earth when the human body was formed from it. For this reason the human being is sometimes called the offspring of the earth, and “earthly, from the earth” by the Apostle Paul (1 Cor. 15:47, etc.). The very etymology of the name Adam likewise indicates this.

93. These words involve some difficulty. What is signified by the expression “after divine things”? I suspect that some error has crept in here through the copyist’s carelessness. For in the original exemplar it could easily have read, “after human—that is, earthly—things, divine things were lacking,” that is, the creation of the human soul, which Hilary elsewhere calls divine (*Commentary on Psalm 118*, Letter X, §7, p. 337, vol. I).

If you prefer to hold that no error has entered here, say either that the human appearance and form of which I shall speak more fully elsewhere is indicated here—for it was a divine appearance, although representing a human being—or say that by the word “divine” the empyrean heaven is perhaps denoted, which is sometimes called the seat of God:

> [Note: Col. 0791D] Psalm 10:4: “The Lord—his seat is in heaven”; Psalm 103:19: “The Lord has prepared his throne in heaven”; Psalm 113:3: “But our God is in heaven”; and v. 16: “The heaven of heavens belongs to the Lord, but he has given the earth to the children of men.”

Or rather, say that angels are denoted, whom Job and others, and indeed Hilary himself, call sons of God—see annotation 38—so that these words have this sense: After he had already created the angels, pure spirits, he finally created the human being, who consists not only of spirit—on account of which he is said to derive his origin from heaven—but also of a body formed from earth.

94. He—that is, the human being—can most properly be said to have been born again. To omit for the moment that Scripture makes mention twice of his formation and, if we may so speak, birth, indicating in the second mention of his creation, birth, and formation the formation of Eve from Adam’s rib (Gen. 1:26–28; 2:7, 22–23): leaving this aside, he may be said to have been born again because the earth from which he was formed previously existed. The creation of that earth was Adam’s first birth, namely in the cause or preceding matter, as the Scholastics speak. But when he was made into a living soul (Gen. 2:7), he seemed to be born again.

Hence elsewhere Hilary intimates a threefold perfection of the human being, made and preformed: one concerns the body; another, the soul—of these two we speak here; the third concerns the image of God impressed upon the human being.

> [Note: Col. 0791D] Here is what he teaches in §8 of the commentary on Psalm 118: “Either may rightly be understood, because we find both written: that he formed into that which is, namely the bodily form; or prepared into that of which it is said, ‘And he breathed into him the breath of life, and man became a living soul.’ He was therefore prepared or formed for this breathing, by which the nature of soul and body might be held together in the perfection of life through a kind of covenant of breathed spirit. Blessed Paul knows that he has a twofold nature within himself, when he delights in the law according to the inward human being and sees another law in his members which makes him captive to the law of sin. Therefore what is made according to the image of God belongs to the dignity of the mind; but what is formed from earth is the beginning of bodily form and nature. And because God is understood either to speak to another when he says, ‘Let us make man,’ or because the human being’s threefold perfection, made and preformed, is recognized—being made in the image of God, formed from earth, and stirred into a living soul by the breathing of the Spirit—the Prophet testifies that he was made and formed by hands, not by one hand only; for in his constitution the operation is taught not to have been solitary alone, and likewise to have been threefold.”

The things which Hilary teaches in §§6 and 7 of his *Commentary on Psalm 118*, from which I have just quoted some passages, will elucidate his present view. For he mentions only two origins of the human being and teaches the same matters as in this present little work. Here are the words of Hilary to which I refer:

> “The creation of all the other elements was both begun and completed at the very time at which they were commanded to subsist. No span of time distinguishes their beginning from their perfection; for in that which had begun, the beginning received its completion. But the human being, because he contains within himself an inward and an outward nature, each unlike the other, and is a rational animal constituted as one from two kinds, was established by a twofold beginning. For first it was said: ‘Let us make man in our image and likeness.’ Then, secondly: ‘And God took dust from the earth and fashioned man.’ The first work does not have within itself the origin of another nature assumed from elsewhere. But how different is the accomplishment of the second work from the first establishment! God takes dust of the earth. The dust is taken, and earthly matter is shaped or prepared into a human being; and by the work and skill of the craftsman it is refined from one thing into another. Therefore he did not take the first, but made it; he did not make the second as he made the first, but took it and then shaped or prepared it.”

95. Does Hilary here approve the opinion of those who think that Adam’s body was formed from a nobler portion—if one may speak thus, as it were from the flower—of earth collected from various and more excellent places, or does he indicate something else? Let the reader judge.

96. Hilary teaches the same thing elsewhere in different words, namely these (*On Psalm 67*, §22, p. 229, vol. I):

> “When he established the human being according to the image and likeness of himself, he first poured out for us the soul, for the breath and respiration of life, from the treasures of his power and divinity. For according to the Apostle, we are his offspring; and according to the same Apostle, all things are from him, through him, and in him: so that in him our dwelling and habitation may be shown as a seat, since he embraces all things in the immeasurable power of his strength; through him, moreover, the work and result of our originated beginning may be shown, since he has worked in us that very thing which we are; and from him the beginnings of life granted at the origins of spirit may be recognized. It was therefore not foreign to the beneficence of divine goodness that he who bestowed from himself the elements of life and spirit upon us, who are his offspring…”

Elsewhere (*On Psalm 63*, §9), he had taught that the soul is not earthly, but arises from God’s breath and is mingled with the elements of the body.

97. See Dissertation I appended to these annotations.

98. He most expressly intends the Father to be a partner in the creation of man and, if we may so speak, a co-creator, although, when recounting the creation of all other things, he makes no mention whatever of the Father [Col. 0792D]. He teaches the same thing, but much more fully [Col. 0793A], in sections eight, nine, and ten of Book V *On the Trinity*, to which passages I refer the reader. But why, I ask, does he here call for the Father, when he seems to attribute everything else to the Son alone? If we wish, we may derive this from the image impressed upon man; for Hilary expressly calls it the image of the Father:

> [Note: [Col. 0793D] Book V *On the Trinity*, no. 9: “Yet let him always remember that all things are through the Son, lest a heretical interpretation appropriate to itself the operation of God the Father. If, therefore, man is made in the image of God the Father through God the Son, he is also made in the image of the Son; for no one denies that it was said to the Son: ‘according to our image and likeness.’ Thus the divine Word maintained in its sayings the rule of truth which the work fulfilled in its deeds: God formed man in the image of God, so as to signify God, and did not take truth away from God, since in the communion of the image there was true God, who was understood to be God the Son in accomplishing the work.”]

Although that image is not that of the Father alone, but of the whole Trinity, as those words indicate: “Let us make man according to our image and likeness.” Or shall we also derive it from the fact that man is the peculiar and outstanding work of omnipotence, uniting in himself whatever excellence and dignity body and spirit possess? (Moreover, the work of omnipotence is especially referred to the Father.) Let the reader judge. This at least is certain: Theodoret, whom Petavius therefore cites (*On the Works*, II.2.4), taught the very same thing as Hilary here. Namely, he maintains that God the Father, foreseeing that his Son would at some time assume the nature and substance of the man whom he was fashioning, made Adam, as it were the origin and foundation of the human race, with his very own hands [Col. 0793B]. Consult Theodoret himself, I beg you.

99. This expression, “that the earth might not prescribe limits to immortality,” is among those in which Hilary seems to imitate Tertullian. He here gives the reason why man, though consisting of a perishable body, was made immortal by God: namely, because immortal hands—that is, the hands of God—formed that same man. You may easily grasp what the hands of God denote if either you turn to that human appearance and form of which we shall speak at length in the earlier dissertation, or consult what Hilary teaches while expounding Psalm CXVIII. See nos. 3, 4, and 5 under letter X, or Iod. Hilary undoubtedly here has in view those two passages of Scripture: “Your hands made me and fashioned me,” etc. (Job X.8); and “Your hands made and fashioned me” (Psalm CXVIII.73), or, as Hilary reads it, “formed me, prepared me.” After the words “they established man,” there is a gap of some kind in the manuscript [Col. 0793C]; but it is so slight that I disregarded it, and indeed the sense remains complete without any gap.

100. Hilary offers many observations concerning the image impressed upon man by God, and concerning the likeness which man will receive after death if he dies acceptable to God. Since these require no small labor, I shall reserve them for a separate dissertation.

101. He has in view that passage of John (1 Epistle III.2): “Beloved, now we are children of God; and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that, when he shall appear, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is.” What Hilary here states briefly, he elsewhere develops fully and at length, concluding Book XI *On the Trinity* thus (p. 406, vol. II):

> “Moreover, we shall advance into the glory conformed to that of our man, and, renewed in the knowledge of God, we shall be re-formed into the image of the Creator, according to the Apostle’s saying: ‘Having put off the old man with his deeds and put on the new, who is renewed in the knowledge of God according to [Col. 0793D] the image of him who created him.’ Thus man is perfected as the image of God. For, made conformable to the glory of God’s body, he rises into the image of the Creator, according to the appointed formation of the first man. And after sin and the old man, being made a new man in the knowledge of God, he obtains the perfection of his constitution [Col. 0794A], recognizing his God and thereby being his image; and, advancing through religion unto eternity, he will remain through eternity the image of his Creator.”

102. If anyone compares these things with what Hilary wrote on Psalm CXVIII (letter X, no. 8), and even more plainly on Psalm CXXIX (no. 3 and following), he will immediately, I think, admit that one and the same man is the author both of this Epistle of ours and of those commentaries. I shall select a few passages which, unless I am wholly mistaken, will plainly demonstrate what I assert. Here is one (*On Psalm* CXXIX, no. 3, p. 492):

> “First, then, it must be understood that God is incorporeal, and does not consist of certain parts and functions of members from which one body is made. For we read in the Gospel that God is spirit—that is, an invisible, boundless, self-contained, and eternal nature. It is also written that a spirit has not flesh and bones. The members of a body consist of these, but the substance of God has no need of them. But God, who is both everywhere and in all things, wholly hears, [Col. 0794B] wholly sees, wholly acts, wholly moves; and this we are taught from the Scriptures, when it is said: ‘I am God near at hand and not far off’; and again: ‘In him we live and move and are.’ Therefore the power of God, which is equal and undivided, has the names of functions and members: thus the power by which he sees is eyes; the power by which he hears is ears; the power by which he acts is hands; the power by which he is present is feet—the diversity of functions being performed by the power of this virtue . . . . . God, therefore, is everywhere and is present everywhere; he hears, sees, and acts.”

Long before Hilary, Irenaeus had written this (*Book* I, ch. 12, no. 2; formerly ch. 6):

> “The God of all things, who, as soon as he has thought, accomplishes what he has thought; and, as soon as he has willed, thinks that which he has willed . . . since he is wholly thought, wholly perception, wholly eye, wholly hearing, and wholly the fountain of all good things.”

He insists upon the same thing in these words (*Against Heresies*, II.13.3; formerly ch. 16):

> “For the Father of all is very far removed from the affections and passions that arise among human beings [Col. 0794C]; he is simple and uncompounded, having like members, wholly like and equal to himself: being wholly perception, wholly spirit, wholly sensibility, wholly *Ennoea* [Thought], wholly reason, wholly hearing, wholly eye, wholly light, and wholly the fountain of all good things, as it is fitting for the devout and pious to speak concerning God.”

Shortly afterward he teaches similar things:

> [Note: [Col. 0794D] No. 9 of the same chapter 13, formerly chapter 16: “God is wholly *Nous* [Mind] and wholly *Logos* [Word], as we have said, and nothing else is more ancient . . . Just as one who says that he is wholly sight and wholly hearing—for by that by which he sees he also hears, and by that by which he hears he also sees—does not err, so too one who says that he is wholly perception and wholly Word.”]

And again elsewhere (ch. 28, nos. 4 and 5; formerly chs. 47 and 48):

> “But God, being wholly mind, wholly reason, wholly operative spirit, wholly light, and always the same . . . . . But God, being wholly mind and wholly Logos [Word], etc.”

He states related matters in Book IV (ch. 11, no. 2; formerly ch. 24: “And God indeed,” etc.). Cyril of Jerusalem seems to copy Irenaeus when he says this (*Catechesis* VI, no. 7):

> “For piety it is enough for us simply to know that we have one God—the God who exists, who exists from eternity, who is always like himself . . . who, distinguished by many names, can do all things, and is of uniform substance . . . He does not see in part and lack sight in part [Col. 0794D]; rather, he is wholly eye, wholly hearing, and wholly mind.”

Theodoret imitates these writers in his commentary on Psalm CXXIX (v. 2: “Let your ears be attentive,” etc.), saying:

> “Although they used words in a human manner, they knew that the Godhead is incorporeal; and they called the power of hearing ‘ears’ [Col. 0795A] and the capacity of seeing ‘eyes,’ since our eyes possess the capacity of seeing, and the capacity of hearing has been entrusted to ears. But by the same power by which God hears, he also sees; and by that by which he sees, he also hears.”

103. He anticipates an objection that might occur to the mind of some less instructed person. Namely: if man differs so greatly from God, in what part of man can the image of God be placed? He anticipates it, I say, by warning that man has two parts, each of which may by synecdoche be called “man”: the inner and the outer; and in the former is situated the image of God of which we have spoken.

104. See what we said in nos. 100 and 101.

105. “While” (*dum*), that is, “provided that” (*dummodo*). Moreover, there is a manifest error in the words “without end.” But I do not know how to emend the passage. I suspect that a few words enclosed by a single line were omitted by an inadvertent copyist, so that it should now be read, “and without . . . at the end” (that is, at the end of life, or in death) he was approved [Col. 0795B]. I also suspect that it was once read “without pretence” (*sine fictione*), so that Hilary rightly requires inward piety to correspond to the outward profession of piety. I likewise suspected that it was originally read “without faithlessness” (*sine infide*); for I do not doubt that this word was once in use, and that *infidus* [faithless] arose from it, as *infidelis* [unbelieving] arose from *infidelitas* [unbelief]. But because these are mere conjectures, I was unwilling to alter anything in Hilary’s text itself. Let the reader emend it as he pleases. If anyone wishes to seek from Hilary himself confirmation of what is taught here, let him consult the passages which, for brevity’s sake, I note at the foot of the page:

> [Note: [Col. 0795D] *On Psalm* II, no. 15, pp. 38–39, vol. I; *On Psalm* CXVIII, letter XX, nos. 9–10, p. 406 of the same volume; and Book I *On the Trinity*, no. 9, p. 7, vol. I.]

Besides, this is frequently inculcated in Scripture—for example, Luke IX.62; Matthew X.22; again XIX.17 and XXIV.13; Hebrews XII.7; etc.

106. Hilary here directs his mind to the words of Ecclesiasticus (XV.14):

> “God from the beginning established man, and left him in the hand of his own counsel. He added his commandments and precepts. If you are willing to keep the commandments, they will preserve you, and to act faithfully in a manner pleasing for ever [Col. 0795C]. He set before you water and fire: stretch out your hand to whichever you wish. Before man are life and death, good and evil: what pleases him shall be given him,” etc.

If you desire to see these matters expounded by Hilary in a fuller and elegant style, turn to no. 16 of the Commentaries on Psalm II (p. 39, vol. I: “But he who is perfect and good,” etc.).

107. When Hilary says: “lest, great and released from law, he should be made equal to all living creatures,” I think he had in view that passage of Psalm XLVIII (vv. 13–14): “Man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared to senseless beasts and became like them.” Perhaps he also had in view those words from Job (XI.12): “A vain man is lifted up in pride and thinks himself born free like the foal of a wild ass.” What we observed in the immediately preceding note partly elucidates the following words: “a threat having been added after the law,” etc. But the holy Doctor undoubtedly alludes to those words of Genesis (II.16): “And the Lord commanded him, saying: ‘Of every tree of paradise you may eat; but of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat: for on whatever day you eat of it, you shall die [Col. 0795D] the death.’”

108. The interpreters observe here that the woman drawn from Adam’s rib had previously been called *Ishah*, namely by the name common to all women; but after sin she was called Eve, by which term it is indicated that God preserved life for her after her sin. It also indicates Adam’s hope that through her human beings would be born and nourished, through whom the human race would be propagated. See Calmet. Epiphanius teaches, however, that this word is more properly applicable to the most holy Mary than to Eve—indeed, that it applies to Eve only because she was a type of Mary (*Heresies* 18, nos. 18–19) [Col. 0796A].

109. That Eve was commanded not to eat the fruit of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil is plainly learned from Genesis III (v. 1 and following). Moreover, it is certain, and is easily shown from the outcome, that this same Eve would have shared in the reward promised to Adam if she had remained in innocence. For if she was liable to punishment because she committed sin, she certainly would have obtained the reward if she had avoided the crime. The Fathers observe that in nearly all passages of Scripture where commandments imposed upon us are mentioned and rewards proposed, mention is made of man alone: either because both sexes are included under the genus of man, or because, since man is the head of woman, he alone is named, although the commandments also concern women and the same rewards are proposed to them. Cyprian elegantly says this (*On the Dress of Virgins*), while commenting on those words of Revelation (XIV.4): “These are those who have not defiled themselves”:

> “For the Lord does not promise the grace of continence only to males and pass women by; but because woman is a portion of man, taken and formed from him, in almost all Scriptures God speaks to the first-formed man, because the two are one flesh, and in the male the female too is signified” [Col. 0796B].

110. Consult the passages of Scripture which I have noted in the margin of the Epistle itself. As to the term “Word” (*Sermo*), by which the divine Word, the only-begotten Son of God the Father, is signified, see what we said in no. 20. Let the reader determine whether the words “that is, the Son” are some gloss of a copyist that slipped from the margin into the Epistle itself, or whether they proceed from Hilary himself. The final part of this sentence, “for it is also free for them not to sin,” etc., is elucidated by what we said in no. 106, and also by what Petavius and other theologians and interpreters teach when discussing the work of the six days [Col. 0796C].

111. To be more certain on this matter, consult theologians who treat specifically of the Work—or Creation—of the six days, and also interpreters; among them our Steuchus of Gubbio, who illustrates this opinion with an elegant comparison (*On the Creation of the World*).

112. Hilary here gives the reason why we contract original sin: namely, because we derive from Adam, in whose will the Lord had established the wills of his descendants. We derive, I say, from Adam already disobedient and therefore guilty, who drew his descendants down with himself into ruin. If I wished to treat this subject as it deserves, I should be almost endless; therefore I refer the reader to theologians who discuss it at length. If anyone wishes to consult Hilary’s passages relevant to the present subject, let him turn to those which I cite at the foot of the page:

> [Note: [Col. 0795D] *On Psalm* CXXXVIII, no. 24, “For he shall return,” etc. [Col. 0796D] (p. 573, vol. I); and *On Psalm* CXLV, no. 2, “For that life is not,” etc. (p. 630). See also the Commentary on Matthew XVIII, no. 6, “The one sheep,” etc. (p. 758 of the same volume).]

113. If anyone doubts this, let him consult, to say nothing of other passages, Genesis IV. He will see God seeking Cain, guilty of murder, and exhorting him to repentance [Col. 0796D]. Especially noteworthy are these words (IV.7): “If you do well, will you not receive? But if you do ill, sin—that is, the punishment of sin—will immediately be at the door. But your desire shall be subject to you, and you shall rule over it.” Recall also what we said in no. 106. And if here too you desire Hilary, read, I beg you, what he teaches in the Commentary on Psalm CXVIII (letter XXII, no. 3 and p. 412, vol. I: “But of equity,” etc.).

114. Christ himself indicates this when he says (Matthew XXIII.37): “Jerusalem, who kill the prophets and stone those sent to you! How often I wished to gather your children, as a hen gathers [Col. 0797A] her chicks under her wings, and you would not.” Nor is it necessary to understand by the name Jerusalem the inhabitants of Jerusalem; rather, we may suitably refer this term to the human race, and particularly to the race of Jacob. For unless the human race as a whole were denoted, Christ’s mention of Abel’s blood shed by Cain would not have been appropriate:

> [Note: [Col. 0797D] “That upon you may come all the righteous blood shed upon the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zachariah son of Barachiah, whom you killed between the temple and the altar” (Matthew XXIII.35).]

Hilary teaches most aptly on this subject in the passages indicated at the foot of the page:

> [Note: [Col. 0797D] *On Psalm* LII, no. 5, p. 56, vol. I, “and lest God be negligent toward men,” etc.; and Commentary on Matthew XII, no. [Col. 0798D] 22, p. 733; and more expressly on chapter XX, nos. 6 and 7.]

But lest I seem to rely on Hilary alone, I join Augustine with Hilary, teaching this (*Against Faustus*, XII.35):

> “The Word of God sent the law through his servant, and it did not profit the human race dead in sins; yet it was not sent without cause, for he sent it who knew that it had first to be sent. He himself came, conformed himself to us, became a partaker of our death, and we were made alive,” etc.

But above all these, Gregory the Great treats this argument more fully and eloquently. I should like the reader not to pass over his observations. For, in his commentary [Col. 0797B] on Matthew XX, explaining that parable in which the kingdom of heaven is said to be like a householder who hired workers to cultivate his vineyard, he sets forth matters which wonderfully elucidate this opinion:

> [Note: [Col. 0798D] Homily XIX on the Gospels, no. 1: “Who indeed [is represented by] the likeness of the householder,” etc.]

See also the interpreters on verse 1 of the Epistle to the Hebrews: “God, who at various times and in many ways formerly spoke to the Fathers through the prophets,” etc.

115. Hilary plainly alludes to Adam’s sin, which all contracted; and from it he takes occasion to demonstrate the necessity of the Lord’s incarnation and of proclaiming divine mercy toward the human race—a thing he does elsewhere and often. For what human being could reconcile us to God, if all sinned in Adam and are born children of wrath, children of vengeance? It was therefore necessary that the only-begotten Son of God, holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners (Hebrews VII.26), should take our flesh and in it make satisfaction to the God who was angry. Theologians discuss this subject, especially Petavius, who cites many Fathers to this purpose [Col. 0797C] (*On the Incarnation*, II, chs. 12–14). I shall cite here only Ambrose, who declares:

> [Note: [Col. 0798D] On verse 8 of Psalm XLVIII, or the words: “A brother does not redeem; shall a man redeem? He shall not give God propitiation.”]

> “He alone is the one who will redeem man, surpassing his brethren in loving-kindness, because he shed his own blood for others, which no one can offer for his brother . . . But why will he alone redeem? Because no one can equal him in loving-kindness, so as to lay down his life for servants; no one in integrity, for all are under sin, all are subject to the fall of that Adam. The Redeemer alone is chosen, who cannot be liable to the old sin.”

116. As regards the first statement, “lest the devil should triumph wholly,” it denotes those earlier times preceding the incarnation, when the demon certainly seemed to triumph: so wholly were all things covered with vices and enveloped in the darkness of idolatry. Paul often indicates this, as when he says (Titus III.3):

> “For we too were once foolish, unbelieving, wandering, serving various desires and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful and hating one another. But when the goodness and loving-kindness of God our Savior appeared [Col. 0797D], not by works of righteousness which we did, but according to his mercy he saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out upon us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Savior, that, justified by his grace, we might become heirs according to the hope of eternal life.”

The same Paul teaches related things in verses 9 and 10 of chapter I of the Second Epistle to Timothy: “Who [God] delivered us,” etc.

As for the second part, “for this is his name,” all observe that this word *Diabolus* means “accuser,” or author of crimes [Col. 0798A].

Finally, the third part, “after he envied man,” alludes to that passage from the Book of Wisdom (II.24): “Through the envy of the devil death entered into the world”; it also alludes to Paul’s words (II Corinthians XI.3): “The serpent deceived Eve by his craft,” and others like them. Some indeed state most expressly that Lucifer envied man from man’s very origin; but those cited by Petavius teach that he certainly envied man after he had already been created (*On Angels*, III.2, nos. 16–17, etc.). Consult them, I beg you, and add Chrysostom in the passage cited at the foot of the page (*Homily* XXII on Genesis, no. 2, p. 195, vol. II, Montfaucon edition).

117. What we have just brought forward from Paul’s Epistles may suitably be referred here.

118. Hilary here briefly summarizes the reasons why the Word of God was incarnate. The first is that it was fitting for fallen man to be restored through the Son, through whom man had been created. Athanasius, Hilary, Cyril, Augustine, Fulgentius, [Col. 0798B] Chrysologus, Pope Leo, Alcuin, and Ivo of Chartres insist upon the same reason in the passages cited by Petavius (*On the Incarnation*, II.VI.16, and again ch. XV, nos. 2–4). Lest I seem to pass over all of them, I adduce Leo’s words (*Sermon* XII on the Passion, ch. 2):

> “In this ineffable unity of the Trinity,” Leo says, “whose works and judgments are common in all things, the person of the Son properly undertook the restoration of the human race: so that, since he is the one through whom all things were made and without whom nothing was made, and who gave life by the breath of rational life to man formed from the mud of the earth, he might restore our nature, cast down from the height of eternity, to its lost dignity; and he who was its creator might also be its reformer. Thus he directed his counsel to its effect, so as to employ, for the destruction of the devil’s dominion, the justice of reason more than the force of power.”

119. I fear that an error has crept into the words “for man patiently to endure,” and that it should read “for man, by suffering, to be lifted from the power of the demon,” or something of that kind, so that redemption accomplished through the Passion may be signified [Col. 0798C]. Yet these very words may bear some praiseworthy meaning. For Christ endured human weaknesses most patiently; he both took human sins upon himself and bore them on the wood; and he had such compassion on us that, while suffering every extremity at human hands, he cried to the Father: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke XXIII.34). Unless perhaps you wish these words of Hilary to have the same sense as the very common prayers of the Church: “O God, who chiefly manifestest thy omnipotence by sparing and showing mercy,” etc. However this may be, the following statements concerning the powers of this world being overcome, death conquered, and the rest that Hilary pursues, are illustrated by the passages of the Fathers which I indicated in note 115; while note 118 illustrates the following words: “who had been a partner with the Father in the making of man.” See also what we cited in notes 100 and 101. To confirm Hilary’s words, “who could both conceal himself in man [Col. 0798D] and that man mingled with God might perform and display powers,” hear Augustine advance this same view (*On Psalm* LVIII.7):

> “Therefore man came”—understand, Christ, or the only-begotten one made man—“to all those sufferings, which would have had no force in him unless he were man. But if he had not been man, man would not have been delivered. Man came to the deep heart, that is, the hidden heart, presenting man to human sight while preserving God within: concealing the form of God, in which he is equal to the Father [Col. 0799A], and offering the form of a servant, in which he is less than the Father.”

Do not, however, suppose that the foregoing words favor either the Nestorians or the Eutychians: the words “who could conceal himself in man” favor the Nestorians, and the following words “man mingled with God” the Eutychians. Remember, I beg you, at what time Hilary wrote these things: long before the rise of the heresies of Nestorius and Eutyches, and thus at a time when it was safe to employ these freer expressions. Hence it is not surprising that he uses them:

> [Note: [Col. 0799D] Book II *On the Trinity*, ch. 16: “The Spirit,” that is, the divine Word, “mingled himself with the nature of human flesh,” etc.]

Indeed, passages in which the ancient Fathers call the human nature assumed by the Word “man” are so numerous that it would be tedious to enumerate them:

> [Note: [Col. 0799D] To bring these and similar expressions to their most correct sense, see what theologians teach. Among many, I indicate Petavius, *On the Incarnation*, Book VII, chs. 12–13.]

And passages in which they use the word “mingled” (*mixtus*) to denote the union of the Word with human nature signify nothing other than the union of the divine Word with human nature:

> [Note: [Col. 0799D] Here too see what theologians teach in order to bring these and similar expressions to their proper sense. Again, among many, I select Petavius, *On the Incarnation*, Book I, ch. 15, nos. 7–8, and Book IV, chs. 1–2—especially nos. 14–15—and also ch. 10. See likewise note d on no. 26 of Book II of Hilary’s *On the Trinity*, on the words “The Spirit . . . mingled himself with the nature of human flesh,” etc. (this edition, vol. II, col. 67); for very approved Fathers who used these expressions are cited there. To remain with Hilary, he undoubtedly understands by mixture the same thing as union when he says (Commentary on Psalm LXIII, no. 9, p. 181, vol. I) that “the soul is not earthly, but born from the breath of God and mingled with the elements of the body.” Ausonius also, in order to denote that the Holy Spirit is one God with the Father and the Son, calls him mingled (*mixtum*) with Father and Son (*Morning Prayer*):  
>
> “I acknowledge the Father of the Only-Begotten, and him mingled with the two,  
> the Spirit who hovered over the waves of the sea.”]

120. Consult the passages of Scripture which I indicated at the foot of the Epistle itself.

121. Almost all ancient Fathers say that the devil was ignorant of Christ’s virginal birth; but they generally do not give the reason for this divine plan [Col. 0799B]. Hilary here adduces two highly probable reasons. The first is that the devil might not hesitate to tempt Christ, whom he would not have tempted if he had known him to be God; and that Christ’s victory over the demon might appear the more clearly—a victory which would appear less complete if the devil were conquered without his own assault and temptations. Thus we may take the words “and less overthrown” to imply, or perhaps require, the addition of the particle “lest”: that is, “and lest he should be less overthrown,” etc. Yet the sentence may also be understood so as to stand by itself.

122. The first part of this statement alludes to what Luke teaches concerning Christ’s virginal conception. The second gives the reason why Christ remained long among human beings: namely, so that we might learn his divinity from his teaching and miracles, both those preceding his birth and those wrought by him; with the angelic announcement and hymns, the arrival of the Magi, ancient prophecies, the prophecies alike of Simeon and Anna, and the testimonies of John the Baptist concurring in the same witness [Col. 0799C]. Hilary touches upon part of these matters in nos. 26 and 27 of Book II *On the Trinity*, passages which I ask you to consult. To conceal nothing, I once suspected that it should read: “that at length they might learn all these things,” etc.; or: “that all might learn to bear God,” that is, to submit to Christ’s law. Let the reader judge whether I am right.

123. I have emended two things which I found corrupt in the manuscript. For it reads *perterriti* [terrified], whereas it undoubtedly should read *praeteriti* [those who went before], that is, those who preceded the coming of the Lord. It also reads: “To whom this with these eyes,” etc., omitting the verb “to see” or “to behold.” If anyone wishes, in order to contrast the eyes of the mind with the eyes of the body, to retain the word “these,” I have no objection, provided that he adds the verb “to see” or “to behold”:

> [Note: [Col. 0800D] See what Hilary teaches in his exposition of Psalm CXVIII, letter 11, no. 3, p. 344, vol. I: “But these are now the eyes of the prophet,” etc.]

Hilary here teaches two things: first, that the coming of Christ the Lord was foretold in the Law and the Prophets; second, why it was foretold. For the latter he gives two reasons, the first concerning those then present, the second those in the past [Col. 0799D]. He wishes this kind of advent to have been foretold long beforehand so that those then present might not refuse to believe something so [Col. 0800A] wonderful, since it had long been made known by such certain and clear predictions. But that advent was foretold to those who preceded the coming of Christ the Lord so that they might believe in the Messiah to come and hope to receive salvation from him. Hence those frequent cries: “O that you would rend the heavens,” etc. (Isaiah LXIV.1); “Drop down dew, you heavens, from above,” etc. (Isaiah XLV.8); and others like them. Indeed, Christ himself once testified (John VIII.56, “that he might see my day”) that Abraham desired to see his day: that is, those times in which the only-begotten Son of God, having assumed a human body, lived among us, instructing the human race by his examples and teachings, and saving it by his death. That the advent of Christ the Lord had long previously been foretold is shown by many writers, especially Cyril of Jerusalem, whose twelfth and thirteenth Catecheses, I beg you, to read. But who would omit Hilary, since he himself develops fully elsewhere what he here states briefly? I indicate a few among many: no. 13 [Col. 0800B] of the Commentary on Psalm LIV (p. 123, vol. I); no. 1 of the Commentary on Psalm LXI (p. 161, vol. I); no. 1 of the Commentary on Psalm LXVI (p. 208, vol. I); no. 20 of the Commentary on Psalm LXVIII (p. 253); no. 1 of the Commentary on Psalm CXXXI (p. 500); no. XXXVIII of Book IV *On the Trinity* (pp. 97–98, vol. II; and p. 123, vol. I). Finally, not to linger over individual instances, while expounding the Psalms he refers a great part of them to Christ; anyone who has read Hilary’s treatises on the Psalms will admit this. I brought forward some matters on this question in my notes on a sermon attributed to St. Antipater, found in the Vatican Library and published by me a few months ago (*Vol.* XLIII of the *Opuscula* collected by Father Calogera). See there note 18 and those following.

124. After the words “of his majesty and goodness,” I added the word “appearance” (*speciem*), since this or another related word is lacking in the manuscript. Next, the manuscript reads *susceperant* [they had assumed] [Col. 0800C]; but I think it absolutely must read *susceperat* [he had assumed], and I refer this to Christ, who came to take away the sins of the world. The syntax seems here somewhat obscure, but I was unwilling to alter it lest I appear more daring than is proper. Let anyone who considers the preceding periods judge whether anything is missing. The manuscript is so written that it can also be read: “if God . . . should show, perhaps,” etc.

125. By “body having been obtained” (*parto corpore*) understand “body having been assumed.” At the end of the Epistle I noted those passages of Scripture to which I think Hilary directed his attention. If I undertook to cite the passages in which the Fathers pursue the same subject, I should be almost endless. Interpreters of Scripture and theologians—especially Petavius (*On the Incarnation*, II.6.1, etc.)—observe that the Lord Jesus assumed human flesh chiefly for two ends: first, to instruct us by his examples and teachings; second, by enduring death for us, to rescue the human race from the power of the demon.

126. At the end of the Epistle I indicate the passages of Scripture to which I think Hilary had regard. As for the words “through the death of man” [Col. 0800D], since we are not compelled to confess that they were corrupted by the copyist, explain them either as “on account of the death of man” [Col. 0801A]—the death which man incurred in Adam, and which Christ the Lord bore the cross to conquer—or as “by the death of man”: for Christ died by the kind of death by which human beings ordinarily die. Refer the word “Immortal” to Christ, who, as God, was immortal in himself.

127. Let the reader consult the passages of Scripture which I indicate at the foot of the Epistle. Let him likewise consult those Fathers whom Petavius cites on this subject (*On the Incarnation*, II.6). I am pleased to bring forward only two here: Hilary:

> [Note: [Col. 0801D] Book I *On the Trinity*, no. 13, p. 11, vol. I; and *On Psalm* LXVII, no. 23, p. 230, vol. II, “And first, what is in the mystery of the Cross,” etc.; and *On Psalm* LXVIII, no. 14, p. 249.]

and Cyril of Jerusalem (*Catecheses* XIII and XIV), whose testimonies I indicate at the foot of the page. Recall what we said in nos. 115 and 118. Is there an error in the words: “For the ruin and salvation of man,” etc.? Or do they mean that whatever man might have attempted to obtain salvation would have been futile? I desire the judgment of others.

128. Recall what we said in no. 119, in order to grasp the force of the expression: “man triumphing with God.”

129. These words, “because whoever has joined himself with God may seem to die, [Col. 0801B] he cannot perish,” have appeared somewhat obscure to some. They become clear if you refer them to eternal death, which those who remain united to Christ will not undergo. If you prefer to refer them to Christ himself, they have the same sense as Peter’s words (Acts 2:24): “Whom God raised up, having loosed the pains of hell, since it was impossible that he should be held by it. For David says concerning him . . . ‘For thou wilt not leave my soul in hell, nor wilt thou give thy Holy One to see corruption.’” For the perishing (*interitus*) which Hilary mentions here, I judge to be the same as the corruption from which David and Peter declare Christ exempt.

Moreover, to follow Hilary’s thought more closely, it will help to consult what the illustrious Maurist monk, editor of St. Hilary’s Works, taught in § III of the Preface (no. 98 ff., p. 32, vol. I). Certainly, whoever hears the following will admit that by this word *interitus* Hilary means annihilation (*exterminium*) (On Psalm LXIII, no. 9): “But whoever shall preach the destruction of the soul together with the body shall hear that the soul is not earthly, but, sprung from the breath of God, is joined to the elements of the body; and that death is not annihilation, but its departure from the body.”

130. After the words “with the enemy extinguished, life,” I added “to man,” as required by the order and force of the argument itself. Hear, moreover, with what elegance and abundance of expression Hilary treats this same subject elsewhere (On Psalm LXVIII, no. 14):

> “When the nations became co-heirs, members of the same body, and fellow-partakers with Christ . . . when death, after it had raged in God, should cease; when the law of sin which is in our flesh should be removed; when every creature, groaning together, should hope for the revelation of the sons of God; when, in the Passion of the only-begotten God, the effect of all causes and origins before the foundation of the world should be consummated—when the prince of this world should be judged, man redeemed from the law of sin, creatures freed from the vanity of corruption to which they had been enslaved, spiritual wickednesses condemned by the Lord’s death, and God praised in all and through all by the gift of eternity and the brightness of our immortality [Col. 0801D]. All these things the power of the Resurrection accomplished: because, when death had been driven from the human race through the firstfruits from the dead, the punishment of death was decreed against the authors of eternal death.”

He had also set forth much that is excellent on the same subject in nos. 6 and 19 of the treatise on Psalm LXVIII. [Note: [Col. 0801D] On the words, “who ascends above the setting.”] Moreover, in chapter three of his Commentary on Matthew (no. 2, p. 667), he teaches matters akin—indeed, I might say identical—to those contained in our epistle. Here are his words:

> “By this arrangement of events he indicates” (Hilary is alluding to the forty days during which Jesus fasted and afterward was hungry) “that, after the forty days of dwelling in the world which he was to undergo after the Passion, he would experience hunger for human salvation. At that time he brought back to God the Father the awaited gift: the man whom he had assumed.” [Col. 0802A]

But lest I seem to cite Hilary alone, I point out among very many other Fathers whom you, reader, may consult: Cyril (Catechesis XIV), Gregory of Nyssa, [Note: [Col. 0802D] In the oration entitled “On the Ascension.”] Augustine—or some other author—of Sermon 176 *On Time*, and Leo the Great. [Note: [Col. 0802D] In the two sermons on the Ascension, especially chapter 4 of Sermon I, “Above all creatures,” etc.]

131. There have been some who would have liked Hilary to speak more expressly concerning the divinity of the Holy Spirit; and we readily see this from what the most learned Maurist monk—to whom we owe the edition of St. Hilary—collected in the Preface to the books *On the Trinity* (no. 12). Yet Hilary undoubtedly affirmed the equality and consubstantiality of this same Holy Spirit with the Father and the Son. Whoever attends to what is set forth in that Preface (no. 15) will acknowledge this.

Nor is this conviction weakened by the phrase which he uses in this epistle: “He sent the Holy Spirit as his vicar [or representative] in his place.” [Col. 0802B] For Hilary wrote at a time when Macedonius’s error had not yet arisen—that is, the error of reckoning the Holy Spirit among creatures. He therefore wrote rather more freely, imitating, as he sometimes does elsewhere, Tertullian, who wrote as follows (*On the Prescription against Heretics*, ch. 13):

> “But the rule of faith is . . . that Jesus Christ . . . sat at the right hand of the Father and sent the vicarious power of the Holy Spirit, who guides believers.”

If Tertullian, then wholly orthodox, was permitted to write this, why should Hilary not have been permitted to do so—especially since the words may readily be understood in a Catholic and sound sense? The Holy Spirit is called Christ’s vicar in this sense: that by his inward inspiration and internal breath he comforted the Apostles, aided and guided them, and, if one may so speak, moved them to those works to which Christ had invited them by admonitions and examples. He is also called Christ’s vicar because, by gifts poured into the Apostles, he made them workers of miracles, just as Christ’s authority and commands had made them workers of the same miracles.

For other reasons too the Holy Spirit is said to take Christ’s place: for instance, because, by the abundance of gifts and by the most complete conformity to the divine will infused into them, he compensates for the bodily and visible absence of Christ the Lord; and for related reasons, on account of which he was called by Christ himself “another Paraclete” (John 14:16–17).

Thus far we have dealt with the phrase: “He sent the Holy Spirit as his vicar in his place.” To say something now about the words, “that he might be both a help and a sanctification to believing human beings,” I judge that the kind of grace which theologians call actual is denoted by the word “help,” while that which they call habitual is denoted by the other word, “sanctification.” If you should also affirm that the kind of graces which these same theologians call *gratis datae*—graces freely given—is likewise denoted here, I would certainly not oppose you. For this kind of grace too is both an aid and a sanctification of the Church, insofar as it marks the Church as holy, which God thus assists and invites others to enter, that they may become holy. [Col. 0802D]

132. That is: thus far we have set forth in order our statement concerning Christ.

133. After Hilary had sufficiently declared, in the preceding parts of this epistle, his teaching concerning the Father and the Son, he turns to the third person of the most holy Trinity, namely the Holy Spirit. He immediately declares that we must likewise believe in him; then he states concerning the same Holy Spirit that he both inspires and sanctifies by his substance all things that would afterward come to be. . . . But what, you will ask, [Col. 0803A] are the things that would afterward come to be? Is it the Church, built in Christ as the cornerstone joining Jews and Gentiles? Is it the sacraments, and especially baptism, over whose waters the ancients said that the Holy Spirit moved? [Note: [Col. 0803D] See the annotation appended to no. 24. You may add very many Fathers who, when treating of the waters of baptism and inviting catechumens to them, said that the Holy Spirit moves over those same waters and sanctifies them. Tertullian, *On Baptism*, ch. 4: “Immediately,” he says, “the Spirit comes down from heaven and rests upon the waters, sanctifying them from himself; and thus, once sanctified, they imbibe the power of sanctifying.”] Or is it the heart of the sinner, which is said to be created in conversion, [Note: [Col. 0804D] “Create in me a clean heart, O God,” Psalm L.] so that its renewal may be indicated? Either may suitably be admitted.

What is lacking from the sentence may be supplied by “communication,” “gift,” or something similar; for from what Petavius teaches we learn that in justification the Holy Spirit himself is communicated to us. [Note: [Col. 0804D] See what Petavius teaches, *On the Trinity*, book VIII, ch. 4, no. 5 and following.] What I have just said about the twofold kind of grace—actual and habitual—seems to me to be taught again here in the words: “and might inspire and sanctify,” etc.

134. The reader should remember that Hilary is here taking up again and explaining more carefully what he had presented summarily in the earlier part of the epistle. Nor do I think it suitable to elucidate this passage more fully, since I have already taught matters very apt for its explanation. Recall, then, what I said in nos. 23, 24, and 30. [Col. 0803B] Yet something besides the word “communication,” which I said should be added, seems to be missing here.

135. We treated of the unity of baptism in no. 25. That sins are removed through baptism is beyond doubt and has been clearly demonstrated by theologians. Hilary, who here briefly embraces the chief articles of our faith, cites one testimony of Scripture only; in our Vulgate it is read in full as follows: “And baptism, corresponding to this, now saves you—not the removal of filth from the flesh, but the appeal of a good conscience to God—through the resurrection of Jesus Christ.”

136. Recall what I noted in no. 27.

137. I once thought that something was lacking here; for it is not immediately apparent how the following words cohere with the preceding ones—namely: “After these things, the order requires belief in the resurrection of the dead in the same flesh.” They do cohere, however, and I explain them thus: the resurrection of the dead must be believed, for by the departure of the soul from the body a human being does not perish or utterly cease to exist; rather, according to the wise counsel of God, who foresees all things, after death he remains for the appointed time, to rise again and be judged. But if you think it would have been better for a human being not to be eternal than to be, know that God, before he created man, knew well what would be better. Therefore, if he created him eternal, it must be said that this was better. What we shall cite next confirms this very explanation. I added the word “God” (“God foreknows”), which is lacking in the manuscript, in order that the sentence might stand.

138. “Man who becomes”: that is, “consists,” unless you prefer to read “who is,” that is, “who exists.” For Hilary often, as I have said elsewhere, uses the subjunctive for the indicative. To come to the argument itself: Hilary passes from theological reasoning to Scripture and cites the Book of Wisdom, which he also attributes to Solomon—inasmuch as Solomon’s opinions are gathered in it—and considers apt to establish the matter at issue; he therefore judges it canonical. In the Vulgate, however, the passage reads: “God created man incorruptible.” Whether something taken likewise from Scripture is lacking here in confirmation of our subject, let the reader decide. Certainly, the words, “I shall give a few examples,” seemed to require at least two passages to be adduced. [Col. 0803D]

139. That suspicion which I have just expressed—that something is lacking here—is strengthened by the words cited from Genesis themselves. For they seem to indicate other words of Hilary, warning the reader that through sin man had deprived himself of bodily immortality; and therefore God forbade man to eat from the tree [Col. 0804A] of life, by which death would have been prevented. I remain uncertain whether the words “indeed, that he might continue immortal” were formerly a gloss upon the words “God created man for immortality,” which passed from the margin into the text of the epistle itself; or whether Hilary himself rather establishes by them that, although by sinning man incurred the dissolution of the body, and hence death in that sense, he nevertheless continues immortal in that part which is the inner human being (see no. 103), and which had been made immortal altogether—or, to speak with the Scholastics, absolutely and independently of every condition. The latter seems more probable.

140. The manuscript reads *quid* (“what”), where I substituted *quis* (“who”): “What? Unless man,” etc. If the reader wishes to retain the former, he may do so, so far as I am concerned, provided that the word agrees with the rest. The words “man, who had been made immortal by God” denote the inner human being, or the soul (see no. 103); for this is immortal by nature, while the body is immortal by grace, from which it fell by sinning. [Col. 0804B]

141. After the words “for he was already in transgression,” the manuscript adds “he was possessed by sin.” I deleted these words because they are a manifest gloss on the preceding words, “for he was already in transgression,” having slipped from the margin into the epistle itself.
