But I think the preceding words, beginning “But I believe,” etc., contain this meaning: if perhaps the reader is troubled that man was forbidden to take from the tree of life, he should know that this was done for man’s own good. For he was already guilty of the crime he had committed. Therefore, if he had approached the tree of life, by eating of which he would have prolonged life, he would neither have known his fault nor directed his hope toward Christ, who was to be incarnate; and thus he would not have removed that same fault by sorrow, chastisements, and repentance. It was therefore for his good that he was forbidden to eat from the tree of life.

Before Hilary, Novatian had taught this, if he is the author of the book *On the Trinity* [Col. 0804C] attributed to him (ch. 1):

> “For what is sought does not arise from ignorance, but shows the hope of man’s future finding in Christ and of salvation; and the fact that he is barred lest he touch the tree of life does not proceed from the malignant spite of envy, but lest, living forever before Christ had remitted his sins, he should carry about with him, as his punishment, an ever-immortal sin.”

If you wish to see the old complaint concerning man’s being prevented from eating of the tree, brought forward and briefly refuted elsewhere by Hilary, consult the passage I indicate at the foot of the page (On Psalm CXVIII, letter XVI, no. 9, p. 380, vol. I: “When Adam [was expelled] from Paradise,” etc.).

142. I think the preceding statement has this sense: it was therefore providently and beneficially arranged for man, who is God’s true workmanship (see no. 97 ff.), that, although compelled to undergo temporary dissolution, when evil has been expelled through Christ’s merits and grace, he should be raised to life—namely, through the resurrection of which Hilary had spoken earlier (see no. 136).

143. I fear that something is lacking here. Yet the sense still stands, even if nothing is lacking. The sentence may be interpreted thus: man always remains, either because the inner man remains—that is, the soul, which is not dissolved—or, which comes to the same thing, because although the body has lost immortality, the mind has not lost it. [Col. 0804D]

144. Hilary meets the objection dictated by experience itself—for we all die—and denies that we truly or completely perish; he says rather that we are merely separated. [Col. 0805A] For the individual soul remains, while the body will rise at the time appointed by God and, reassumed by the soul, will present itself before Christ the judge. You will understand the force of the words “man does not perish but is separated” from no. 129. Recall, I pray, these words: “But whoever shall preach the destruction of the soul together with the body shall hear that the soul is not earthly, but, sprung from the breath of God, is joined to the elements of the body; and that death is not annihilation, but its departure from the body.”

145. The manuscript reads thus: “but to fear God’s judgment of the resurrection is to be reserved.” In my judgment this is an evident error, since it should undoubtedly be read: “to be reserved for judgment on the day of resurrection.” I deleted the word *timet* (“fears”), because all the ancients, when divine judgment is in question, inculcated fear. [Note: [Col. 0805D] “I was afraid of thy judgments,” etc.] Hence, I think, the marginal note “fear,” or, if you prefer, “he fears,” slipped through the copyist’s ignorance from the margin into the epistle itself. Those accustomed to peruse ancient manuscripts encounter this very frequently.

[Col. 0805B] I now come to the sentence itself. These words are indeed obscure: “nor does man take up the materials from which the body is fashioned.” Does Hilary here reject the opinion of those who supposed that souls recover their former bodies after death, and fabricated tales of the gods of the dead (*manes*) and the spirits of the dead (*lemures*) on that account? Or does he rather teach that, when man rises, he will not have a body of the kind from which he was originally constituted? For who would say that we shall have a body of clay, since the human body was fashioned from clay, when the Apostle warns that those beloved by God will be changed in the resurrection [Note: [Col. 0805D] “We shall all indeed rise, but we shall not all be changed,” 1 Corinthians 15:51, etc.]—that is, that they will have a body far more excellent?

146. He gives the reason why all, with no exception whatever, shall appear before the divine Judge: since the Lord Jesus both died for all and was appointed Judge of all, both human beings and angels, no one will be able to escape his judgment, which for that reason will be universal and final.

147. Perhaps the little word *nam* (“for”) is used here in the way in which it often is in Scripture [Note: [Col. 0805D] “For in Christ Jesus I begot you”: here the particle *nam* gives no reason for what precedes, as often occurs elsewhere.]: that is, not to give a reason for the preceding statements, but to serve as the equivalent of “and.” Understand the verb *expingi* (“to be stamped forth” or “made manifest”), if no scribal error is present here, in this sense: Hilary took Paul’s words, “For we must all be made manifest before the judgment-seat of Christ, that each may receive the things proper to the body, according to what he has done, whether good or evil” (2 Corinthians 5:10), as though that word meant “represent” or “display.” Thus our works, whatever they may be—good or evil—will become known to all.

The words “according to his will” denote either predestination [Note: [Col. 0806D] “In whom [Christ] we also have perhaps been called, being predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will,” Ephesians 1:2.] or indicate that those who have performed righteous works have done what God especially desires: “For this is the will of God, your sanctification,” says Paul. [Note: [Col. 0806D] 1 Thessalonians 4:3. The same Apostle teaches related things in Romans 12:2 and Ephesians 5:17.] Finally, the words at the end, “whence let us strive,” etc., are an exhortation consequent upon the foregoing statements and well suited to stir people to righteous works. Recall also, if you wish, what we said in nos. 8, 27, and 28.

[Col. 0805D]

148. Having passed through the more difficult matters, there still remains a long road, though a less rugged one. Having set forth and explained in the preceding two parts of the epistle the doctrines of orthodox faith, Hilary turns to the proper formation of the conduct of persons (“Now therefore let us treat of conduct”). He divides his instruction into five parts. The first is directed to rich and poor; the second to males and females. In the third he explains what is appropriate to every age. The fourth [Col. 0806A] contains a general exhortation to all believers: he reviews their duties, urges them to undergo martyrdom if necessary, and to overthrow idolatry; then, by very brief admonitions, he indicates how each person ought rightly and praiseworthily to conduct himself in the condition of life in which he lives. Finally, in the fifth he discusses virtues. Although from this point I shall be much more sparing in adding annotations—for what Hilary teaches is generally clear in itself—I shall nevertheless add some when I judge it appropriate. The reader should himself consult the passages of Scripture indicated at the foot of the page.

149. Here is how the Vulgate translator presents the foregoing passage of Paul: “Command the rich of this age not to be high-minded, nor to hope in the uncertainty of their riches, but in the living God, who abundantly provides us with all things for enjoyment: to do good, to become rich in good works, to give readily, to share, laying up for themselves a good foundation for the future, that they may lay hold of [Col. 0806B] true life.”

What Hilary next teaches briefly he sets forth elsewhere more fully. Here is how:

> “Certain rich persons are rendered arrogant by prosperity, and especially empty confidence in riches drives away the fear of God: fools, who do not understand that they ought to be the more devout because they are rich, since it is fitting that they return thanks to the giver of the desirable goods bestowed upon them; and that the guilt of avarice is the more inexcusable because wealth does not excuse avarice on grounds of necessity. Moreover, how unhappy is confidence in an empty thing: to despise God because one possesses gold, as though gold were not among God’s creatures; or as though, in the judgment of a sound mind, anyone could acquire progress toward a blessed life merely because he has gold buried away; or thereby become other than the human being, soul and body alike, that he was born to be; or, when he departs from life, make use of his gold in death! He will indeed use it, if he uses it rightly in life—if he has fed the hungry with his bread, clothed the naked with his garment, relieved the sick at his own expense, or restored the captive to freedom. These truly are splendid embassies of human treasures before God; this is the power for the remission of sins and true patronage. Thus we shall be transformed by gold: from earthly beings into heavenly, and from mortal into eternal.” (*On Psalm* LI, no. 21, p. 90, vol. I)

150. Hilary perhaps alludes to that passage in the First Epistle of the Apostle Paul to Timothy (6:9): “For those who wish to become rich fall into temptation and into the snare of the devil, and into many useless desires,” etc. Certainly, Hilary teaches elsewhere to the same effect:

> “But the chief root of evils is in the desire for money; whoever seeks it is sunk in the shipwreck of a most violent storm. There follows: ‘Do not hope in iniquity, and do not covet robbery. If riches increase, do not set your heart upon them.’ For they have great enticements to longing and love; they seize minds and take hold of wavering hearts. Therefore not only ought their acquisition by robbery not to be desired, but our will must be withdrawn from them even if they are offered and flow in abundance, lest what has been desired and coveted should become our master. For they are not goods coeternal with our hopes, nor do they descend with us into hell or rise with us from hell. Faith, devotion, self-restraint, kindness, and above all the knowledge of God must be sought. But these things are vain and, by their nature, seductive toward every necessity of wickedness; they must be avoided.” (*On Psalm* LXI, no. 8, p. 169, vol. I)

Finally, unless I am mistaken, he indicates the Gospel passage: “Be merciful, as your Father [Col. 0807A] is merciful” (Luke 6:36), for by mercy we are made like God.

151. He says that moderation must first be observed in distributing money: it should indeed be distributed, but not squandered and scattered. The reader may judge whether Hilary here tacitly indicates the well-known distribution of ecclesiastical money among ministers of the Church, sacred buildings, and the poor. If he does indicate it, he seems to give the poor precedence in this distribution, as the other Fathers often do. Did not most holy and most learned bishops often even dispose of ecclesiastical and sacred vessels to relieve the poor?

The words “let them not think that it can be exhausted,” etc., allude both to Paul’s preceding statement [Note: [Col. 0807D] 1 Timothy 6:17: “Hope in the living God, who abundantly provides us with all things for enjoyment.”] and to that celebrated promise of God: “Do good and lend, expecting nothing in return, and your reward shall be great . . . Give, and it shall be given to you: a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and overflowing, they shall give into your bosom” (Luke 6:35, 38). Elsewhere too, and often, the benefit of almsgiving to the poor is commended. [Col. 0807B] I select very few passages from among many and indicate them at the foot of the page. [Note: [Col. 0807D] Tobit 4:7, 8, and 12; Proverbs 28:27; 29:27; Ecclesiasticus 29:13; Psalm 36:25; 2 Corinthians 9:9–10: “Now he who supplies seed to the sower,” etc.] Whoever desires many materials gathered both from Scripture and from the Fathers should consult Muratori, who discusses this subject. [Note: [Col. 0808D] *On Christian Charity*, etc., ch. 7.] Hilary also takes up this same subject later: “Let it not be lacking even from himself,” etc. (ch. 10, col. 742).

152. That is, it is expended or spent—unless you prefer to suppose a scribal error here and read *deperditur* (“is wasted”); for to unbelievers what is given to the poor seems wasted, though wrongly and foolishly.

153. He immediately proves by a theological argument what he had previously proposed: namely, that what is paid out for the needs of the poor in consideration of God’s commands cannot be exhausted. The word *confuerit* is among those which are very rarely used by writers, but are especially noted in Hilary. Yet that the same word was sometimes used among the ancients is shown by the verb *confert*, still in use, which is, if one may so speak, a portion of the verb *consum*, having the same meaning as *prosum* (“to benefit”). Besides the points I have just noted, what Hilary teaches here, which is clear in itself, has great force in proving the benefit of almsgiving. Finally, he treats of the danger that threatens from riches. [Col. 0807C]

154. He immediately sets forth what the rich must observe. The passages of Scripture which I noted at the foot of the page in the immediately preceding number partly illuminate this statement: “He will experience want neither in this age nor in the age to come.” If you wish for other Scriptural passages to the same purpose, see Matthew chapter 5, verse 5; chapter 6, verses 19–20; Luke chapter 12, verses 31–33; and Acts chapter 20, verse 33.

155. At the foot of the epistle itself I noted the passage to which Hilary refers, namely Proverbs 19:17. Now let the reader receive what the excellent Calmet teaches on that passage:

> “He who has mercy on the poor lends to the Lord, and he will repay him his return. The Lord himself becomes his debtor and will repay with interest what he has bestowed upon the poor. He will receive him as he himself has received his brother; he will have mercy on him, etc. He does not simply say, ‘He gives to the Lord,’ but, ‘He lends at interest.’ He will not merely receive what he has given to the poor, but will receive it with interest. ‘Our avarice had to be attracted by promises of greater gain,’ says St. Basil on Psalm XXVIII. This interest is permitted. Do you wish to grow rich and make gain from silver? Bestow it liberally on the poor; do not fear that they will fail to repay the money lent. God is your security; he himself owes you. When the poor man prays for himself, St. Augustine says on Psalm XXXVI, he says, as it were, to God: ‘Lord, I have taken a loan; stand surety for me.’ Therefore, even if you do not have a poor debtor who can repay, you have a sufficient guarantor. Behold, God says to you in his Scripture: ‘Give securely; I repay.’”

Nor do I wish you to pass over Hilary himself, whose counsels on this point in the passage I note at the foot of the page are excellent. [Note: [Col. 0808D] On Psalm CXXXI, no. 25, p. 515, vol. I: “Then he says: ‘The poor,’” etc.]

156. Critics have long observed that copyists sometimes, in order to appear learned, inserted Scriptural passages very frequently from their own imagination. Hence the older manuscripts are often shorter, and, although they generally have indications of Scriptural passages, those passages are by no means quoted in full. I have found this in two manuscripts of Cyprian which we possess. But the very passage we are now elucidating provides a manifest example. The manuscript reads thus: “Let him know that mercy has been set before sacrifices, the Lord saying: ‘Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.’” [Col. 0808B] Do these words of Christ teach that mercy is set before sacrifices? Certainly not. Therefore the passage cited here by Hilary must be sought elsewhere—namely, in Hosea, chapter 6, verse 6, where these most explicit words occur: “I desired mercy and not sacrifice.” You have related words in Isaiah chapter 1. [Note: [Col. 0808D] Verses 11 and 17: “What is the multitude of your sacrifices to me? . . . Learn to do good,” etc.]

But if you do not wish to call our copyist clever but unskilled—or rather careless—you may suitably say that the words, “The Lord saying: ‘Blessed are the merciful,’ etc.,” were placed by someone in the margin to confirm Hilary’s statement, that a person may from this be judged more blessed. But the person who transferred them from the margin into the epistle itself adapted them to an inappropriate place. However this may be, they certainly had to be deleted here.

157. That is, glory among those people who praised him as generous, and eternal blessedness—for by the term “rest” eternal blessedness is denoted here; see no. 47. That blessedness was promised to those merciful to the poor is shown by what I said in no. 151 [Col. 0808C] and the following numbers. See what Hilary writes on Matthew chapter 27. [Note: [Col. 0808D] No. 4, p. 794: “Those who sell are those,” etc.]

158. He passes from the rich to the poor, whom he comforts with excellent arguments. First, he says that provision has been made by God for the poor person’s benefit, referring, I think, to the Apostle Paul’s words: “We know that all things work together for good to those who love God, to those who are called saints according to his purpose” (Romans 8:28). Or, if you prefer, to Peter’s admonition (1 Peter 5:7): “He cares for you.”

159. He anticipates and resolves an objection which the poor commonly make. Perhaps the meaning is: “which is often harmful to the body”; for abundance fosters luxury, drunkenness, and other vices of this sort, which diminish bodily strength. Yet I did not trust my conjecture so far as to add the word “body.” The rest is clear and highly elegant.

160. The manuscript reads “to lead life” (*vitam gerere*): an evident error, indeed, but one which plainly teaches that our manuscript sometimes needs emendation. [Col. 0808D]

161. By the words “let it not be lacking even from himself,” Hilary perhaps alludes to the admonition of the elder Tobit, which I mentioned above (no. 151): “According to what you are able, be merciful.” I do not wish, however, to conceal that the manuscript subsequently reads thus: “because just as he is made righteous by frugality, if he gives to those below him and to those who do not have. Let him not fear,” etc.—a reading undoubtedly corrupt, which I emended, as I think, by substituting very few words, namely: “the rich by liberality, so the poor [by frugality]”; [Col. 0809A] these words are not found in the manuscript. As regards the epithet “glorious” bestowed on the Apostle Paul, consult no. 2.

162. In the notes at the foot of the epistle itself, I observed that Hilary, in the words, “If he has chosen to believe with true faith and for salvation, let him choose and acquire heavenly riches,” etc., perhaps refers to Isaiah 33:6: “Riches of salvation are wisdom and knowledge; the fear of the Lord itself is his treasure.” I add that perhaps he also refers to Psalm 118: “I have delighted in the way of thy testimonies, as in all riches.”

Certainly, Hilary explains and comments upon these words as follows (On Psalm CXVIII, letter 2, *Beth*, no. 9, p. 286, vol. I):

> “There are riches in gold, in silver, in money, in clothing, in houses, and in fields, with their vines, olives, or crops. But the Lord’s prophet is made perfect by the fruit of doctrines, and is rich in the resources of the Law and prophetic teachings. And although he belongs to an earlier age, he is nevertheless not ignorant of evangelical and apostolic precepts. [Col. 0809B] For Paul too knows these riches, speaking to the Corinthians: ‘I give thanks to my God always for you because of the grace of God which has been given to you in Christ Jesus, because in him you have been enriched in everything, in all speech and in all knowledge.’ Therefore the prophet is rich in these things and delights in them. But one must not suppose that he delighted in the acquisition of worldly wealth, since he could not be rich in the Lord except through contempt for and poverty in relation to the world.”

163. Hilary now undertakes the second part of the moral instruction which he had set himself to explain (see no. 148), directing it toward instructing the different conditions of the sexes. The manuscript contains several things requiring emendation, namely: *omni gerere uni animo*. If you read these words as they are written, they have no meaning. You must therefore read them as I have emended them: “to do all things with one mind, in concord.” Or, if you prefer: “to be unanimous and concordant in every manner.” The first emendation is easier and more probable, and I have therefore adopted it. [Col. 0809C]

As many still treat of the raising of the hands in prayer, especially those who explain that passage of Paul’s Epistle to Timothy, “I desire therefore that men pray in every place, lifting up pure hands without anger and disputation” (1 Timothy 2:8), so Tertullian treats it in his treatise *On Prayer*. [Note: [Col. 0809D] Chapter XIV: “But we do not merely raise [our hands],” etc. Chapter XVII: “But with modesty,” etc. See Muratori’s annotation on that chapter.] There, by “prayer”—as Hilary himself expressly says—he understands, so to speak, complete and full prayer: namely, public prayer, including reception of the sacraments, that is, the reception of complete penitence and communion. He also commands abstention from marital intercourse. Please consult the interpreters on Paul’s words (1 Corinthians 7:5): “Do not defraud one another, except perhaps by agreement for a time, that you may give yourselves to prayer”—not only Orthodox interpreters, but also outsiders, such as Hugo Grotius and other highly learned men from the Protestant communion.

164. We have come upon a passage that perhaps requires no slight explanation. For these terms [Col. 0809D] have assumed various meanings and denote many sacred rites; it would be worthwhile to pause awhile in elucidating them, if that brevity of annotation which I have set before myself permitted it. I shall nevertheless point out the passages from which these matters may be most thoroughly understood. All interpreters discuss the first verse of the second chapter of the First Epistle to Timothy concerning supplications, prayers, petitions, and thanksgivings. Let the reader consult them. But above all, let him consult Augustine in the passage cited at the foot of the page [Note: [Col. 0809D] Letter to Paulinus, formerly 50, now 149, ch. [Col. 0810D] 2, on the questions concerning First Timothy, nos. 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, and 17.]; for then he will learn what are *deprecatio* [deprecatory prayer], [Col. 0810A] *adoratio* [adoration], and *interpellatio* [intercession], of which Hilary speaks here. I beg the reader not to pass over this passage of Augustine, for he discusses the matter most fully and lucidly. From this very passage of Augustine he will also learn what is meant by a *votum* [vow], when it is joined to *precatio* [prayer], *oratio* [prayer], *interpellatio* [intercession], or *postulatio* [petition].

“All things,” Augustine says, [Note: [Col. 0810D] Ibid., no. 16.] “that are offered to God are vowed, especially the offerings of the holy altar, by which Sacrament that great vow of ours is proclaimed: the vow by which we have vowed to remain in Christ, namely, in the unity of Christ’s body. The sacrament of this is that we, though many, are one body. Therefore, in the preparation for this sanctification, I think that the Apostle commanded *proseuchas* [προσευχάς], that is, prayers, to be made properly—or, as some have translated less skilfully, adorations. For this is related to the vow which is more commonly called in Scripture *euchē* [εὐχή].”

It is in this sense that the Church is thought to employ this word when, very frequently in the prayers of the Mass, it mentions vows and votive offerings. There remains *exomologesis* [confession]. Many have treated of exomologesis; but here I indicate only one whom we may consult. I do not urge the reader to embrace his opinion; I merely ask him to consult and weigh the passages from the Fathers which he adduces. This is Albaspinaeus, Observations, book II, observations 26 and 27.

165. Let the reader consult the passages of Scripture which I note at the foot of the epistle itself; perhaps he will then understand for himself what Hilary teaches. Yet I shall set forth here certain matters which seem to deserve special attention. Those words, “For it is fitting that every man perform priestly service to God,” can readily be understood in two ways: either that all men who profess the Christian faith ought to live such a life that, even if married, they may be chosen for the priesthood (and indeed Hilary himself was raised from marriage to the episcopate); or that a man’s outward worship and dress ought to be such as befit a priest. Whether Hilary also indicates here that a Christian man ought to preside over his family by example and admonition, just as a priest presides over the Church by example and admonition, let the reader judge. The words, “but let him also furnish others with an example of his manner of life,” and likewise, “so that, if at the time he is not exercising priestly ministry and office, he may nevertheless equal a priest by similarity of life,” seem to favour the latter two explanations.

But before ending this annotation, I wish to warn the reader that the words “so that, if at the time he is not exercising ministry,” etc., are in fact read in the manuscript as I have directed them to be printed. Yet there is some ambiguity in these words, though not such as to undermine the preceding explanations. Is some word missing by which the sentence is to be completed? Or should one read *tempore*: that is, “if for a certain time,” or “if at the time when he enters marriage, he is not exercising priestly ministry and office,” though perhaps he may exercise it later—if, that is, his wife dies, or if, with her consent, he withdraws himself from her cohabitation. We certainly have not a few examples of this in ancient ecclesiastical records.

[Col. 0810D] 166. If you compare what is stated in Leviticus 12:2 and 15:19, 20, and 24, you may perhaps understand why Hilary taught these things: “or after childbirth,” etc. For he did not wish the ancient Hebrews to be more continent than Christians. I have noted at the foot of the epistle the passages of Scripture to which Hilary refers. Sometimes, however, he applies to women what was said generally concerning all those set over others.

167. I believe that some transposition of words has crept into the epistle itself. For it seems that it should be read in the manner in which I have corrected it:

“But also, modest in her bearing, let her go forth not with a painted appearance, or [Col. 0811A] adorned with gold, or with costly apparel; let her not study the curling of her hair; but, as befits Christian women,” etc.

For the manuscript reads:

“But also, modest in her bearing, let her go forth not with a painted appearance; let her not study the curling of her hair; or adorned with gold, or with costly apparel; but, as befits,” etc.

If anyone considers the passages of Scripture to which I allude at the foot of the epistle, and the passage from Cyprian which I shall cite next, he will, I think, agree with me.

168. What Peter indicates in the words noted at the foot of the epistle itself—“giving honour to the woman as to the weaker vessel,” etc.—perhaps elucidates what Hilary says in these words: “Nor should she set herself before any man by consideration of her sex.” Certain slight marks of honour with which women were distinguished even in ancient times elevated their frivolous minds into pride. They were doubtless permitted to sit at the right hand of men, which was regarded as a mark of the highest honour. Thus Solomon ordered a throne for his mother to be placed at his right hand. [Note: [Col. 0811D] 3 Kings 2:19: “A throne was placed for the king’s mother, and she sat at the king’s right hand.”] Indeed, the queen, the king’s wife, is said to stand at the king’s right hand. [Note: [Col. 0811D] Psalm 44:10: “The Queen stood at your right hand.”] Among the Hebrews the right-hand place was considered the more distinguished, as we learn from verses 13 and 14 of Genesis 48.

Roman matrons too were permitted to use purple garments and golden ornaments. [Note: [Col. 0811D] See what Ferrarius relates concerning clothing, part I, book III, chapter 22. Tertullian, however, in *On Idolatry*, chapter 17, affirms that purple and gold ornaments for the neck were insignia of rank. This can readily be confirmed from what is related in 1 Maccabees 8:14; add to these what is found in chapter 10 of the same First Book of Maccabees, verses 20 and 62.] They could also ride in carriages on both festival and ordinary days. Although many others have treated this subject, Titus Livy treats it very fully and clearly (*Roman History*, book V, no. 25). Let the reader judge whether Hilary alludes to other marks of honour granted to women, particularly to those who excelled others.

169. Do not suppose that Hilary here favours the opinion of those who thought that the bodies of holy women would be changed at the last judgment—an opinion of which Hilary is considered to have been an advocate. [Note: [Col. 0812D] No. 10 of the Commentaries on Matthew chapter 5, p. 693 of vol. I: “For when he shall raise up the diversity of all bodies that have received life into one full and perfect man,” etc. And much more clearly, no. 4 of the Commentary on Matthew chapter 23, p. 781: “Since therefore he makes them equal to angels,” etc. See also the very learned annotation appended by the Maurist Fathers to this latter passage.] Here, plainly, “perfect man” seems to be taken for a person furnished in every respect with Christian virtues.

170. It is clear that Hilary imitates Tertullian, who says the following (*On Baptism*, chapter 18):

“But [Col. 0811C] let those whose office it is know that baptism is not to be entrusted rashly. … Rather, this must be considered: ‘Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast your pearls before swine’; and, ‘Do not lay hands hastily upon anyone, lest you share in another’s sins.’ If Philip baptized the eunuch so readily, let us remember that a manifest and explicit act of the Lord’s favour intervened. The Spirit commanded Philip to take that road; and the eunuch himself was found neither idle nor one who suddenly desired baptism. Rather, he had gone to the temple to pray and was absorbed in the divine Scripture. Thus he had to be found: God himself had of his own accord sent the Apostle to him; and again the Spirit commanded the Apostle to join the eunuch’s chariot. The Scripture concerning faith presented itself; he was exhorted at the proper time and admitted; the Lord was shown to him; faith did not delay; water was not awaited; and the Apostle, his task completed, was taken away.

“Paul too was truly baptized quickly. For Simon, his host, had quickly recognized that he was an appointed vessel of election. God’s favour puts forward its own special prerogatives. Every request may both deceive and be deceived. Therefore, according to each person’s condition and disposition, and even age, delay of baptism is more beneficial—especially in the case of little children. For why is it necessary that sponsors too be exposed to danger? They themselves may fail in their promises through death, and may be disappointed by the development of an evil disposition. Indeed, the Lord says: ‘Do not prevent them from coming to me.’ Let them come, then, when they are growing up; let them come when they are learning; let them come when they are taught why they come. Let them become Christians when they are able to know Christ. Why does innocent age hasten toward remission of sins? Greater caution is exercised in worldly affairs: shall one to whom earthly property is not entrusted be entrusted with divine things? Let them know how to ask for salvation, so that you may seem to have given it to one who asks. For no lesser reason the unmarried also ought to be delayed: temptation is prepared for virgins through maturity and for widows through freedom from marital bonds, until they either marry or are strengthened in continence.”

Tertullian and our author wished, then, because persecution often harassed the Church—and this, in my judgment, is what the words “the condition of the time” signify—that Christians should withstand the wiles of tyrants, whether alluring or harsh. They also wished our mysteries not to be betrayed, and forbade holy things to be given to dogs. Children, however, generally tended to yield to enticements, threats, or indeed tortures, and to abandon the Christian religion. [Col. 0812B] They also disclosed whatever they knew. For this reason they did not wish children to be enrolled among Christians.

Age itself is also usually less fitted to receive sublime mysteries, such as Christian mysteries undoubtedly are. For these reasons, as I said, they generally forbade children to be taught the Christian religion. I said “generally”: for if they knew children to be intelligent, very upright, and steadfast, they did not refuse to instruct these very children in our mysteries. Thus Saint Babylas instructed the two boys who afterwards shared his martyrdom. Agnes, who suffered martyrdom at thirteen years of age, undoubtedly indicates that the Church sometimes received children into her bosom; nevertheless, once the danger of persecution had been removed, she chose that baptism be conferred even in childhood.

171. I have determined that one should read “through deficiency of age.” Although the word *defectu* [through deficiency] is absent from the manuscript, it must nevertheless be supplied, as demanded by the very sense of the otherwise defective words. Hilary next warns that children are to be instructed by their parents themselves, since in public sermons precepts suited to their age and capacity cannot be set forth. The Church will carry this out when more mature age renders them fit to receive ecclesiastical instruction. Yet children must be taught gradually, not all at once, lest they be overwhelmed by the multitude of instructions or, because of their obscurity, fail to learn what nevertheless must be learned.

172. Let the reader decide whether one should read “the gift of faith,” in reference to that passage of Scripture, “there shall be given him a chosen gift of faith” (Wisdom 3:14), or whether the manuscript’s reading, “the good of faith,” should be retained. The manuscript reading can certainly be retained appropriately. By “deifying gift” baptism may most properly be understood, and confirmation, which ought to be received at the fitting time. Yet these words may be a fuller explanation of the preceding words, “the good of faith,” indicating that the good of faith is the deifying gift—which the Pelagians and Semi-Pelagians [Col. 0812D] later attacked.

I have corrected the words “and not of nature” by conjecture. The manuscript has “and of nature,” in which I saw no sense; but the meaning becomes clear and probable if you add *not* and read “and not of nature.” Those who persevere in innocence and holiness should show in themselves that not the old Adam but the new Adam reigns. What Paul teaches in chapters 5 and 6 of the Epistle [Col. 0813A] to the Romans confirms this interpretation. [Note: [Col. 0813D] Especially verses 18 and following of chapter 5, and verses 2 and following of chapter 6.]

173. The manuscript reads “affirming” instead of “strengthening.” If you wish to retain this reading, I shall not object, provided that you bring forward plausible examples of this meaning. Children are strengthened in the good of faith and in the deifying gift when, through instruction given in the Church, right precepts are instilled in them and they are taught what a Christian must do in order to be pleasing to God and worthy of his calling.

174. What we cited from Tertullian in no. 170 (“For no lesser reason the unmarried,” etc.) will, I think, sufficiently elucidate this passage. By “children” he plainly understands not only those who are still of tender age, but also those who have reached youth. For he would never have said that children must beware of fornication if by “children” he understood only those still of tender age. Though “fornication” sometimes denotes every form of fleshly impurity.

[Col. 0813B] 175. Let the reader not wonder that I retained the word *idolatriae* [of idolatry], as it stands in our manuscript. For in almost all manuscripts, both of Cyprian and of the other ancient Fathers, *idolatria* is read where printed editions read *idololatria*. Baluzius and other critics noted this before me; nevertheless, I thought it should not be omitted here.

I now come to the meaning itself. Fornication is very frequently forbidden in Scripture. To confine myself to passages taken from the New Testament, I indicate some at the foot of the page which confirm what I say. [Note: [Col. 0813D] Acts 15:20 and 29; again, chapter 20:25; 1 Corinthians 5:13; Galatians 5:19; and 1 Thessalonians 4:3.] But it is more difficult to explain why fornication is said to have the beginning of idolatry. Except for the observation of the excellent Calmet [Note: [Col. 0813D] Ephesians 4:19 and 5:5; Colossians 3:5.] that by “covetousness” fornication itself—or every kind of lust—is understood, one may conveniently answer that Hilary had regard to Paul’s words in which this very point is impressed. Paul, who certainly did not teach this rashly if he taught it, states most explicitly [Note: [Col. 0814D] Colossians 3:5: “Evil desire and covetousness, which is the service of idols.”] that evil desire and covetousness—that is, unbridled lust seeking to be glutted with unclean pleasures—are the service of idols.

If you inquire into the deeper reason for this saying, and thus also inquire why Hilary taught, “And it is necessary that whoever follows one should know both,” you will inquire into something I would not readily explain. Is it because, since there were no prostitutes among Christians, a fornicator who desired prostitutes was compelled to resort to those of the Gentiles, who had dedicated the commerce of their bodies to impure deities, and above all to Venus—so that fornication in those times was an interpretive approval and participation in idolatry? Or because those same women, having gained possession of their lovers’ affections and minds, surely led them to worship their deities?

The people of Israel left us a lamentable example of this matter (Numbers 25:1): while Israel stayed at Shittim, it committed fornication with the daughters of Moab, who invited them to their sacrifices. But they ate and worshipped their gods, and Israel was initiated into Baal-peor. For this reason the Lord forbade the children of Israel (Exodus 34:16) to take as wives Amorite, [Col. 0813D] Canaanite, Hittite, Perizzite, Hivite, and Jebusite women, adding: lest, after these women have prostituted themselves with their gods, they cause your sons also to prostitute themselves to their gods. Solomon, disregarding this warning (3 Kings 11:2, 4, etc.), when he was already old, had his heart corrupted by women so that he followed foreign gods.

Yet, in order to corrupt minds and alienate them from the true faith, there was no need to seek out women who worshipped false deities. Lust itself blinds the mind and draws it, entangled in bodily and sensible pleasures, away from spiritual and incorporeal things, [Col. 0814A] and therefore from the desire and pursuit of the rewards which Christian faith sets before us. It therefore seeks to despise those rewards and looks for plausible arguments by which it may persuade itself that it is foolish to disregard present, sensible things in pursuit of incorporeal goods reserved for another life. Do I say this rashly? Or rather, do we not find the sentiments of the intemperate and lustful expressed in the Book of Wisdom (chapter 2, verse 5)?

“For our time is the passing of a shadow, and there is no return from our end, because it is sealed and no one returns. Come, therefore, let us enjoy the good things that exist, and swiftly use creation as in youth. Let us fill ourselves with costly wine and ointments, and let not the flower of time pass us by. Let us crown ourselves with roses before they wither. Let there be no meadow through which our luxury does not pass. Let none of us be without a share in our luxury. Everywhere let us leave marks of joy, for this is our portion and this our lot.”

Therefore, lest they fall into this supreme calamity, Paul warns the faithful to beware of the examples of Gentiles devoted to lust. It is fitting to quote his words here (Ephesians 4:17): “This therefore I say and testify in the Lord: that you should no longer walk as the Gentiles also walk, in the vanity of their mind, having their understanding darkened, alienated from the life of God through the ignorance”—wilful and culpable, to speak with the theologians—“that is in them, because of the blindness of their body; who, having despaired, gave themselves over to licentiousness, to the working of all uncleanness in covetousness.” Regarding the word “initiated,” see what we said in no. 21.

176. From children and adolescents he passes to young men, whose somewhat more established age he instructs with excellent admonitions.

By those earlier words, “Therefore how,” etc., he alludes to the evangelical admonition, “By their fruits you shall know them” (Matthew 7:16). The words of James too are very well known (chapter 2, verse 18) and are most apt for confirming the point we are elucidating: “But someone will say: You have faith, and I have works. Show me your faith without works, and I will show you my faith from works.” I interpret the words which designate Gentiles thus: Gentiles are recognized from an impure life, Christians from a chaste one.

This interpretation is confirmed especially by the admonition of the Apostle Peter (First Epistle, chapter 4, verses 3 and 4): “For the time past suffices for fulfilling the will of the Gentiles, for those who have walked in luxuries, desires, drunkennesses, revellings, drinking-parties, and unlawful worship of idols. In this they are astonished that you do not run with them into the same flood of dissipation, and they speak evil of you.” It is likewise confirmed by Paul’s words (Colossians 3:5 and following): “Mortify therefore your members,” etc.; and elsewhere (Ephesians 5:3 and following): “But fornication and all uncleanness, or covetousness”—that is, as we said above, desire for pleasures—“let it not even be named among you,” etc. He had taught related things in the Epistle to the Romans. [Note: [Col. 0814D] Chapter 6, verse 19: “As you have yielded your members to serve uncleanness.”]

I understand the following words, “provided, however, that their warnings [Col. 0814D] and prayer bring no impediment to what is lawful,” in the manner in which Gregory the Great understands Christ’s words (Luke 14:26), “If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father, mother, wife, children, brothers,” etc. “If we weigh the force of the precept,” Gregory says, “we can, by discernment, do both: love those joined to us by kinship of the flesh and whom we know as neighbours, yet not fail to hate and avoid those whom we suffer as adversaries in the way of God.” The final words, “and his wife herself, prepared in a godly manner,” undoubtedly allude to marriage performed by the ministry [Col. 0815A] of the Church. Whoever has judgment will appreciate this most distinguished testimony of Hilary on this subject.

177. He leaves it to the freedom of each person to take a wife if he pleases, and accordingly rebukes those heretics who forbade Christians to marry. He then reproves those who delayed baptism in order not to be compelled to abstain from the impurity forbidden to Christians by Christian law. He says, namely, that they sin in this very delay.

I further wish to warn the reader that I have substituted the word “to be embraced,” since the manuscript reads “to be considered” (*consideranda continentia*, “continence to be considered”), a corrupt reading indeed, or one in which some intervening words are lacking. If the reader emends it better, he will do a welcome service.

178. But he says that those are more blameworthy who, after receiving baptism, give themselves to impurity and to works of the flesh; for, having been enlightened, they fall away (Hebrews 6:4, 6). What I stated in no. 175 may conveniently be referred here. The rest will readily be understood by anyone who consults the passages of Scripture noted at the foot of the epistle itself.

I added “among the old.” For I thought it should be read thus: “and, young men in the inner person, let them be placed among the old, with God as judge.” This reading seems demanded by the sense itself, for the manuscript reads: “and, young men in the inner person, let them be placed, with God as judge.” My conjecture is confirmed by the words occurring not far afterwards: “young in temptations; grave old men in counsels and thoughts.”

179. After the word “shameful deeds,” some term was lacking to denote the devil as the author of those same shameful deeds. I supplied it, as the sense also required. For who would deny that the devil is the author of all shameful deeds, since he sins from the beginning (1 John 3:8), and through his cunning death entered into the world (Wisdom 2:24)? Augustine (*On the Usefulness of Fasting*, no. 10, formerly [Col. 0815C] chapter 8: “For the enemy,” etc.) and Leo the Great (Sermon VII on the Nativity, chapter 3: “For the enemy does not cease,” etc.) rightly describe that same devil as the author of all errors and heresies, insofar as by his temptations and promptings he stirs up depraved affections in us and urges us to commit every kind of evil.

180. I have transferred certain words from the preceding passage to this one. In the manuscript itself, after the words “after they have believed, to be found,” there follow words beginning thus: “And I think all these should be admonished,” up to the words ending thus: “we have believed, we shall have handed on.” Then follow other words: “Young men must consider,” etc. I transferred them here because I thought they belonged rather to old men than to young men. For unless these words are referred to old men, one must say that the instruction of old men was omitted, even though Hilary had previously promised to direct his discourse to every age: “Now,” he says, “let the discourse concerning the ages be taken in hand” (paragraph 12).

Whether there is some gap after the words “grave old men,” I shall not determine. Perhaps he thought he had sufficiently indicated that he was addressing old men when, immediately after the words “grave old men,” he adds: “And I think these”—that is, grave old men—“should be admonished,” etc.

But, for clarity’s sake, I am pleased to set down this whole passage as it is read in the manuscript:

“Therefore, either he must take a wife, or continence must be embraced. Certainly, lest they delay faith through fear, let them know that it is evil, because of impurity, not to believe; but worse to be found unchaste after they have believed. And I think all these should be admonished to obey all persons for God’s sake. Let them learn to govern their household well. If they have children, let them treat them piously and instruct them in godly matters. For these are signs [Col. 0816A] of our faith: if we have not merely believed, but have also handed on to others the things which we have believed. Young men must consider how, in all their actions, they may surpass their age: strong in spirit and virtue; and, young in the inner person, let them be placed among the old, God being judge. They must also give thanks that, not when every stage of life has been completed, but in the very heat of life and in adolescence itself, they have renounced the devil of shameful deeds and unclean actions; and, renewed, let them present themselves to God, pure in malice; young in temptations; grave old men in counsels and thoughts. Let the soldiers of Christ know,” etc.

181. In general, he exhorts all Christians to answer to their calling and to do what the holiness of our faith requires of them. He calls them soldiers of Christ, employing a term common in those times, [Note: [Col. 0815D] In the Acts of Saint Cecilia: “Come, soldiers of Christ,” etc.] not only because “the life of man upon earth is warfare” (Job 7:1), but also because canonical writers very often called the Christian life like military service—Paul above all, who frequently addresses and portrays Christians through this allegory. [Col. 0816B] I note some passages at the foot of the page which the reader may consult. [Note: [Col. 0815D] 1 Timothy 1:18; 2 Timothy 2:3; and 2 Corinthians 10:3 and 4.]

In mentioning bonuses and pay, [Note: [Col. 0815D] On bonuses and pay, see what the Maurist Fathers note [Col. 0816D] on p. 742 of vol. I of the Works of Saint Ambrose, on the Exposition of Psalm 1.] he both retains the same allegory and alludes to what he says elsewhere about the unfading crown. For crowns were given not only to those contending in games, but also to soldiers: civic, triumphal, and other crowns of that sort were conferred upon them as rewards. He likewise alludes to Paul’s celebrated passage: “the wages of sin is death” (Romans 6:23). For if death is the wages of sin, the wages of Christian life will be eternal life (ibid.), which elsewhere is called more expressly the crown of life. See no. 47.

182. He says most plainly that two kinds of persecution threaten Christians: first, from invisible enemies, concerning whom the Apostle Paul says (Ephesians 6:11): “Put on the armour of faith, that you may be able to stand against the snares of the devil, because our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities [Col. 0816C] and powers, against the rulers of the world of this darkness, against spiritual forces of wickedness,” etc.; and second, from visible enemies—whether tyrants or others opposed to the Christian faith, or, if you prefer, to Catholic truth. See what we said in the preface (chapter 1, no. 4).

I did not wish to substitute *contra* [against] for *circa* [concerning/around] (*circa diabolum*, “concerning the devil”), which the manuscript has, because the latter reading can somehow be tolerated. Yet I myself would prefer to read *contra diabolum* [against the devil].

183. You will find very much eloquence on this subject, and arguments suited to persuasion, in the Acts of the Martyrs, in Tertullian’s book *To the Martyrs*, and in Cyprian’s letters and other minor works.

184. Recall what was said in the preceding number. Cyprian teaches the same things. Here I take the word “is overcome in battle” (*expugnatur*) to mean a most vehement struggle that ends most gloriously. Hilary’s zeal shines forth wonderfully in these final words: “every discourse must be adapted to the destruction of idolatry and the praise of the crown of martyrdom.”

[Col. 0816D] 185. I confess that I suspected one should read: “he who evangelizes [or: has been evangelized] should ask what he ought to do”; or, if you prefer, “he who is evangelized should be asked what he ought to do.” I nevertheless did not wish to alter anything. Perhaps the word *Evangelizat* here denotes one who desires to receive the evangelical law. I believe something is missing by which the admonition relating to each manner of life is concluded. But who would dare guess what it was?

By *officialis* understand an officer or attendant of a magistrate. It is certainly used in this way in Facciolati’s Lexicon, under *Officialis*, where two examples are cited: the first from Apuleius—[Note: [Col. 0816D] “The aedile orders his official to climb upon the fish and trample them completely beneath his feet.” *Metamorphoses*, book V.]—the other from an old inscription in Gruter: [Col. 0817A] [Note: [Col. 0817D] “Officials of that consul of the province of Aquitania.” Gruter, *Inscriptions*, p. 422, no. 7.] The word *moderari* seems to be taken in the sense “to be moderate.”

186. The passages of Scripture which I noted at the foot of the epistle clearly show those to which Hilary looked. I think he also had regard to others; but since he did not expressly cite them, let the reader seek them for himself. By “full faith” (*fide plena*) I understand, not without reason, faith that has works. From James (chapter 1, verses 17 and 26) we learn that faith without works is empty or dead.

187. Hilary refers to that explicit and solemn renunciation which we profess against the devil when we receive baptism.

188. I suspect one should read: “Hope of the things which are seen is not hope”; for earlier he says that hope concerns future things, and future things are not seen. Yet because our manuscript’s reading could somehow be tolerated, I retained it. Let the reader correct it if he wishes. I also deleted the word *quid* placed after *quis* (“who hopes what?”), because it plainly bore the marks of a scribal error. [Col. 0817B] Where the Vulgate, in Psalm 18 as cited by Hilary, reads “holy fear,” another very ancient version reads “chaste fear.” Hilary follows this latter reading, and not without reason. The rest is clear of itself.

After the word “judges,” I deleted *putes* [you might think], which appears in the manuscript; for one readily understands that an unskilled copyist introduced it into the epistle itself. I fear that some word is lacking in the definition of continence, such as “comprehension,” or, if you prefer, “desire,” “love,” “longing,” or something similar. See the immediately following chapter 17: “In good things, eagerness must be required,” etc. Yet here too our manuscript’s reading may be tolerated.

189. These words of Hilary are certainly most excellent: “We find that evil has no substance from the beginning; for in obedience … evil is alongside good.” In the first part of this statement the impious doctrine of the Manichaeans, who derived the origin of evil from an evil principle, is both indicated and refuted. When he adds, “for in disobedience,” etc., he undoubtedly alludes to Adam’s disobedience, through which death—and therefore all evils—were introduced into the world.

Would that the manuscript contained the remainder of what Hilary taught concerning this same disobedience of Adam! We would indeed possess material by which not only the Manichaeans but also all who have erred regarding the origin of sin might be refuted. But perhaps a considerable gap, together with the obscurity of what follows—which, I think, results from copyists’ incompetence—deprives us of this advantage.

Yet I think two things worth observing. First, the statement, “evil is alongside good,” is exactly, unless we are altogether mistaken, the same as what is read in Ecclesiasticus (chapter 23, verse 15): “Evil is against good, and life against death; so also the sinner against the righteous man.” Secondly, it is unknown to what end the statement is adduced. We are wholly ignorant not only of the aim but even of the sense of what follows; indeed, since its reading is undoubtedly corrupt, we do not know at all how it can be corrected. For who could correctly emend words of this kind: “And which [or: and what; or: and whom], if they are nowhere found to correspond to themselves, is the guardianship of good preserved?”

We nevertheless suspect that Hilary taught that we are not compelled to evil, but that it is in our power to embrace uprightness and persevere in it, divine grace doubtless protecting us from enticements and temptations; guarded by that grace, we are preserved in a good guardianship—or, if you prefer, we preserve the guardianship of good: that is, we do not abandon the good which we have already embraced.

190. Here Hilary takes continence in its broadest sense. By eagerness (*aviditas*) he means the most ardent desire to do good. He discusses continence at length shortly afterward.

191. After the word *conferre* [to confer/discuss], the word *sermonem* [discourse] may perhaps be missing. Hence in the Gospel: “What words are these that you confer [Col. 0818A] with one another?” Yet I suspect that Hilary actually wrote as our manuscript has it—that is, without any explicit mention of discourse. For Cassian simply called the pious discourses and mutual exhortations of monks *Collationes* [Conferences].

192. Immediately after this word, “only,” our manuscript has: “because God judges by contemplation: the conscience of each individual”—manifestly an error. Are these words perhaps a gloss formerly placed in the margin on the words, “continent with respect to marital union”? Or were they written in the autograph after the words which follow, “God has not commanded a uniform continence”? Or even after the words which also occur later, though at a greater interval, “God alone beholds inner and secret things”? Were they omitted from the epistle itself by some ancient copyist through accident, then cast into the margin with a mark indicating where they ought to be placed, and finally inserted here by a later copyist, whom we have often called incompetent? Let another’s judgment decide.

193. I interpret the words, “And, as it were, puffed up more by the appearance of continence,” as follows. From this semblance—and, as we commonly say, appearance and mask—of continence (for it is not true and solid continence, since continence, if we believe Hilary defining it a little earlier, is the restraint of all evil things that are to be desired), puffed up, I say, by this appearance of continence, they despise others to whom this gift has not been granted by God; they strike them and heap insults upon them, etc.

194. Where I have printed *continence*, the manuscript has *conscience*. But *continence* must undoubtedly be read: for he is speaking of those who put forward—that is, boast that they possess—continence. Yet the very continence which they possess is so far from making them truly continent that it rather makes them vicious; so that the continence they have seems to furnish fuel and material for crimes. I have added the word *crimes*: for the manuscript lacks an indication of that for which this mask and appearance of continence supplies material [Col. 0818C]. But the sense clearly establishes that it supplies material for vices and crimes.

195. Where I have printed, “although these things certainly ought to be cut away,” the manuscript reads, “although these things certainly ought to be persevered in.” But who could tolerate that? If the reader proposes a more plausible emendation, I shall certainly approve it.

196. In the earlier sentence, “we find many, or very many, to burn with desire in this way . . . as the outcome shows,” something is undoubtedly missing. But by what means I might restore it, I utterly do not know. Still, the sense of the omitted words seems to have been this: “We find many, or rather very many, to burn with desire in such a way that they cannot by any means be torn away from virgins with whom they live in the closest intimacy; and this the result indeed shows: for every kind of punishment,” etc. The manuscript reads, “or sleep beneath one roof.” If the word *and* has slipped into the printed text, let the reader correct it.

197. “The prohibition of the elders”: that is, of priests, whom we know from the sacred books themselves to have been honoured by the name *presbyters*, or “elders” [Col. 0818D]; or else of men elderly in age, whose authority in the Church, as persons distinguished by prudence and experience, was not slight. These men, to whom the licence described here by Hilary was rightly and deservedly displeasing, took every precaution they could that virgins consecrated to Christ should not live with men, and still more that they should not occupy one bed with them. The Church saw and condemned this serious evil even in the earliest times, and strove with all its strength to root it out. I indicate a few examples.

Consult, therefore, Cyprian’s sixty-second epistle, which in Baluze’s edition is entitled *On Virgins, to Pomponius* (p. 219 of the Venetian edition). In that letter I particularly wish you to observe the following:

> “First of all, therefore, dearest brother, both the overseers and the people must labour for nothing else than that we who fear God may keep the divine commands with every observance of discipline, and may not suffer our brethren to go astray . . . nor permit virgins to dwell with males—not merely, I say, to sleep together, but not even to live together—since both the weaker sex and an age still prone to slipping must in every respect be restrained and governed by us, lest opportunity be given to the devil, who lies in wait and desires to rage in order to harm, when the Apostle also says: ‘Give no place to the devil.’ The ship must be watchfully freed from dangerous places, lest it be wrecked among reefs and rocks.”

Likewise consult Jerome’s letter to Paul of Concordia (formerly no. CCXIII; in the Neronian edition, X); Chrysostom’s homily *Against Those Who Have Introduced Virgins into Their Homes*; and another homily by the same Doctor, usually entitled, *That Women under Religious Rule Ought Not to Cohabit with Men* [Note: The first of these is found on p. 227, the second on p. 248, of the Montfaucon edition volume. See also the prefatory notice placed before these homilies there.]. There is also a constitution of Theodosius the Younger on this matter, in Book XVI of the Theodosian Code, title II, law XLIV; I beg you to read it. Gothofredus has moreover annotated it extensively; I refer you to him.

[Col. 0819B] 198. “What evil is there in this?” etc. These are the words of those who excuse persons living familiarly beneath one roof with virgins to whom they are bound by no relationship—and indeed sleeping in one bed with them. Hilary rebukes them sharply, warning that they certainly do not refrain from kisses, although this was wholly intolerable: for it is no slight evidence of a mind already seized by the devil.

Cyprian declares that such persons are to be subjected by the Church to the rules of penance, when he says this (*Epistle* LII, p. 220):

> “And therefore you have acted wisely and vigorously, dearest brother, in suspending the deacon who often remained with a virgin, and also the others who had been accustomed to sleep with virgins. But if they do penance for this unlawful cohabitation and separate from one another . . . let them be admitted to the Church after receiving communion; yet with this warning: if afterward they return to the same males, or dwell together with them in one house and beneath the same roof, they shall be expelled under a graver censure, and such persons shall not afterward easily be received into the Church.”

[Col. 0819C] See also, I beg you, the letter which Jerome wrote to the deacon Sabinianus (no. 147 in the Veronese edition; formerly no. 48). Understand the serpent to mean the devil; for he is “the ancient serpent, who is called the devil” (*Apocalypse* 12:9, 14, and 15), and we know that Constantine the Great represented him in that form (*Eusebius, Life of Constantine*, III.3).

199. Hilary offers a second excuse from the opinion of those same persons cohabiting with virgins. And that excuse, whatever it may be worth, was advanced already in Cyprian’s time. Cyprian rejects it in these outstanding admonitions (in the same *Epistle* LII, p. 220):

> “Nor should anyone think that she can be defended by this excuse: that it may be inspected and tested whether she is a virgin. For both the hands and the eyes of midwives are often deceived; and, even if that virgin be found uncorrupted in that part of herself by which a woman may be such, she may nevertheless have sinned through another part of the body, which can be corrupted and yet cannot be inspected. Certainly the very cohabitation, the very embrace, [Col. 0819D] the very conversation and kissing, and the shameful and foul sleeping together of two persons lying together—how much disgrace and guilt do they confess! If a husband coming upon his bride were to see her lying with another, would he not be indignant and rage, and perhaps, in the pain of jealousy, take a sword in hand? What will Christ, our Lord and Judge, do when he sees his virgin, consecrated to himself and destined for his holiness, lying with another [Col. 0820A]? How indignant and angry he is, and what punishments he threatens for incestuous unions of this sort! Therefore each of the brethren must take every precaution and labour diligently, in order to escape his spiritual sword and the coming day of judgment.”

It is worth observing, however, that Cyprian and the others whom Baluze cites in his nineteenth note on the letter we have quoted did not reject an examination of virgins’ bodies conducted by midwives. Hilary certainly condemns it; Ambrose of Milan, a truly eminent man, followed his example [Note: See, I beg you, what Tillemont has drawn from Ambrose’s letters on this subject: vol. X of *Ecclesiastical History*, under Ambrose, chapters 85 and 86, p. 280 of the Venetian edition. Letters XLVI and XLVII cited by Tillemont are, in the Benedictine Fathers’ edition, V and VI of Class I, to Syagrius: “Care must be taken,” etc.; and “The matters which have been examined in our judgment,” etc.].

200. What is said here is rather obscure; yet you may understand that the virgins of whom he had spoken earlier were loved more passionately precisely because they professed themselves virgins, although they were virgins only in name and profession. Moreover, they rashly boasted that they were virgins, seeking this praise from human beings when they ought to have expected it from the Lord alone, who would render them the reward of chastity.

201. That the Apostle Paul commanded women to pray with covered heads [Col. 0820B] is beyond doubt. See the passage from the Epistle to the Corinthians indicated at the foot of the page [Note: 1 Corinthians X, 5, etc.: “But every woman praying or prophesying with her head uncovered,” etc.]. The virgins of whom Hilary speaks here prayed with uncovered heads, perhaps in order that the adornment of their hair and head might be visible to everyone, with the approval of their seducers, whom he had censured earlier. He calls them corrupters of virgins because, if not corrupters of their bodies, they were at least corrupters of their minds and morals.

I am uncertain whether the words “with their corrupters restricting [the command]” are properly situated. Yet if they stand in their proper place, I explain them thus: these men restrict—that is, confine—the Apostle’s command, which extended to all women, to those alone who were joined in marriage. This was not new in Hilary’s age, for we read the following in Tertullian [Note: *On Prayer*, ch. 31, vol. III of Muratori’s *Anecdota*, p. 40.]:

> “But what is observed indiscriminately throughout the Churches, as though it were uncertain, must be reconsidered: whether virgins ought to be veiled or not. For those who grant virgins exemption from covering the head appear to rely upon this: that the Apostle did not expressly name virgins, but designated women as those who should be veiled; and that in saying ‘women’ he named not the sex by saying ‘females,’ but a rank within the sex. For if he had named the sex by saying ‘females,’ he would have laid down an absolute rule regarding every woman. Or, when he names one rank of the sex, he excludes another by silence. For, they say, he could either have expressly named virgins too, or more briefly have spoken generally of females.

> “Those who make this concession ought to reflect on the status of the word itself: what is ‘woman’ from the first writings of the sacred commentaries? For they find that it is a name of the sex, not of a rank within the sex. Thus God called Eve, who had not yet known a man, both ‘woman’ and ‘female’: ‘female,’ as the general designation of the sex; ‘woman,’ as the specific designation of a rank within the sex. Thus, even then, Eve, though still unmarried, bore the name *woman*; and this designation became common also to the virgin. Nor is it surprising that the Apostle, undoubtedly moved by the same Spirit by whom all Scripture is divine and by whom Genesis too was composed, used the same term, saying ‘woman,’ a word which, following the example of unmarried Eve, applies also to the virgin. The remaining arguments, finally, do not hold. For precisely in not naming virgins, as he does elsewhere when he teaches about marriage, he sufficiently declares that the statement concerns every woman and the whole sex; and he makes no distinction between virgin and married woman, since he does not name the virgin at all. For he who remembers to distinguish elsewhere, where a difference is required—distinguishing both classes by their respective terms—when he does not distinguish, and does not name both, intends that no difference be understood.”

Nor did Tertullian abandon this view when he himself left the Church and adhered to Montanus. For he is said to have composed his book *On the Veiling of Virgins* after adhering to Montanus, yet in chapter 4 of that same book he teaches the same things as here. In the whole of chapter 22 of *On Prayer*, he sharply rebukes those who said that virgins could pray in church with heads entirely unveiled; I ask you to read that chapter in full.

Yet the term *woman* is sometimes used to denote one subject to a husband, rather than a virgin; this will be shown by the examples from ancient Latin writers which Baluze collected in note 12 to Cyprian’s Epistle LXII to Pomponius (p. 223 of the Venetian edition). I likewise ask the reader to consult it. The word *initiated*—“they are initiated with uncovered head”—refers either to that offering by which they present themselves to God, vowing their virginity to him in church, or, if you prefer, to public prayers. The rest is clear in itself, especially once the definition of continence [Col. 0821B] which he gave earlier has been established.

202. The definition of patience offered here seems to have been drawn from various Scriptural passages, but especially from verses 1 and 2 of chapter IV of the Epistle to the Ephesians. For that passage reads as follows: “I therefore beseech you, I who am a prisoner in the Lord, to walk worthily of the calling by which you have been called, with all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in charity.” For patience is especially assigned the task of bearing with others (*bearing with one another*).

Hilary assigns it two parts: one is endurance of injuries and sufferings; the other, the bearing of every kind of waiting. Regarding the first, you will readily agree: for we are often admonished in Scripture to practise charity, patience, and gentleness (1 Timothy VI, 11), which require endurance of injuries and sufferings. Nor can there be any doubt concerning the second: for, to omit the rest, that is the point of James’s admonitions [Col. 0821C] (ch. V, 7): “Be patient, therefore, brethren, until the coming of the Lord. Behold, the farmer awaits the precious fruit of the earth, patiently enduring until he receives the early and latter rain. Be patient therefore yourselves also, and strengthen your hearts, because the coming of the Lord draws near.”

If anyone possesses this kind of patience, will he not bear the adversities of life? Will he not also possess every good? Certainly he will have these things who endures every expectation without precipitation.

203. He alludes, I think, to the Apostle’s words (*Romans* V, 3): “Knowing that tribulation works patience; and patience, testing; and testing, hope.”

204. What Hilary teaches is clear if you recall the definitions which he set forth above. The words “was comprehended above” have the same meaning here as I indicated earlier.

205. *When* must certainly be read: for when nothing is hoped for, that which is hoped for is borne impatiently. But our manuscript reads *because*, through the ignorance, I think, of the last copyist.

[Col. 0821D] 206. These words, “but by every virtue patience bears through what is discerned when hope is perishing,” are indeed clear and are wholly connected with what precedes. But what follows is more obscure: “But if hope, the fruit of patience, follows, it rejoices in faith as mother; it has the guidance of God; continence, its kind, has nearness.” I interpret them thus.

If patience follows hope, which is the fruit of hope (for *hope* must be read, although the manuscript has *hopes*), it—or, if you prefer, hope—rejoices in faith as its mother; but hope has the special protection of God, for “mercy shall surround those who hope in the Lord” (*Psalm* XXXI, 70). Continence, however, which is the kind or genus of these virtues—that is, which embraces them all, or, if you wish the matter expressed thus, is their principal parent and, as it were, root—has nearness to God. For by continence we are made, as it were, near to God: either because through it we become partakers of the divine nature (2 Peter I.4); or because through it we draw near to God—“if we draw near to him, he will draw near to us” (James IV.8); or, if you prefer, because, once we attain heavenly blessedness, we shall be like God.

Hilary proves this by the example both of the martyrs, who, strengthened by faith and hope, endured whatever sufferings and torments patiently and courageously, God of course assisting them by his protection and grace; and of other Christians, who, by imitating Christ even unto death through the virtues—or, if you prefer, contests—of patience [Note: The manuscript indeed reads *virtues*, but *contests* seems better suited to indicate the point under discussion.], become fellow-heirs with Christ. If anyone proposes a more probable interpretation, he will certainly do me a great favour.

It is worth observing here that Hilary had regard to several passages of Scripture, though we can scarcely identify them with certainty, particularly since he follows a translation older than our Vulgate. To conceal nothing, the words “thence the righteous, while they do all things patiently,” in our manuscript occur after the words “they imitate [Christ] by the virtues of patience” (or rather, “contests”) [Col. 0822B]. And after the word “nearness” it reads there: “thence the glorious witnesses of God,” etc. Yet the sense and arrangement of the sentence seem to require that the period and sentence conclude thus: “then”—that is, in the final place—“fellow-heirs of Christ, while they imitate him unto death in the contests of patience.” Still, if anyone wishes to retain the manuscript reading and thinks that Hilary took from it an occasion to discuss righteousness, I have no objection. As to the word *glorious*, recall no. 2.

207. The manuscript reads thus: “which, if anyone obtaining, and to which anyone adhering, preserves his life duly ordered and without disturbance.” These words are plainly tangled and lack a clear sense. I have emended them as seemed more probable. If anyone wishes to emend them differently, let him do as he pleases.

After the words, “when, though he was Lord of all, [he was baptized] by John,” the manuscript adds, “who is greater among those born of women”; but this is an obvious gloss, referring to verse 43 of chapter V of Matthew, and I have rightly removed it [Col. 0822C].

208. I think that Hilary refers to the passage which I noted at the end of the epistle itself, namely verse 2 of the Epistle of Jude the Apostle. Jude writes: “To those who are beloved in God the Father, preserved in Christ Jesus, and called: mercy to you, and peace, and charity be fulfilled.” Nor need you refer this passage to Paul; for these words likewise indicate elsewhere another passage of Scripture, and we are not compelled to suppose that another passage of Paul is meant.

Moreover, Christ may be called our mercy, peace, and charity, or love, both because he is their author and source and because by his grace he produces them in us. I also suspect that some manuscripts formerly read differently and stated expressly: “in Christ Jesus, who is for us mercy, peace, and charity, or love” [Col. 0822D]. If you wish another passage to be indicated by Hilary, I shall not oppose you, provided you identify a plausible one.

209. Ecclesiastical writers call not only love itself *agapē*, but also its fruits, so to speak, and works proceeding from charity, *agapēs*. Hence Augustine says [Note: Book XX *Against Faustus*, ch. 20. See also ch. 4 of the same book.], “our *agapēs* feed the poor, whether with crops or with meat.” Whoever wishes to know much concerning this should consult the writers cited by Du Cange [Note: In the *Glossary of Medieval and Late Latin*, under *agape*.].

210. The Vulgate here has *charity*. But Hilary, following another, older translation, reads *love* (*dilectio*), which he distinguishes shortly afterward from charity.

211. From the two preceding definitions [Col. 0823A], it is clear that, in Hilary’s judgment, *love* (*dilectio*) is distinct from *charity* (*charitas*). He who truly loves God possesses the other virtues and keeps all the commandments. For who would not keep the commands of one whom he truly loves? If I were to cite the Fathers and indeed the passages of Scripture confirming this, I should be almost endless; for both Scripture and the Fathers teach this very point extremely often, as Hilary does here when he says, “Charity is the fulfilment of all commandments.” He seems to refer to the passage in Paul’s Epistle to the Romans (ch. XIII, 10), which in the Vulgate reads: “Love, therefore, is the fulfilment of the law.”

212. Very similar to Hilary’s admonitions is what Gregory the Great teaches (*Homily XXVII on the Gospels*, no. 1), whose words it is fitting to cite here:

> “Since all sacred utterances are full of the Lord’s commands, why does the Lord say concerning love alone, as though it were a singular command: ‘This is my commandment, that you love one another’? Unless it be because every commandment derives from love alone, and all commands are one command, since whatever is commanded is established in charity alone. For as many branches of a tree proceed from one root, so many virtues are generated from one charity. Nor does the branch of a good work possess any greenness unless it remains in the root of charity.”

213. Among the ancient complaints which Erasmus poured out against Hilary, this was not the least: that Hilary vigorously defended the proposition that we too are one in nature with the Father and the Son. That severe critic would surely have increased his complaints if he had had this epistle in his hands, in which, that is, whoever possesses charity is called God and God’s Son without any qualification. Yet the excellent Father Constantius, to whom we owe an edition of Hilary, admirably refutes Erasmus’s hasty and unjust censure of Hilary; I ask you to consult him [Note: In the preface to Hilary’s *Works*, no. 76 and following, p. 25 of volume I.].
