Certainly, any one of us adorned with supernatural charity may in some sense be called God. Did not Christ himself teach that this lofty title could be attributed to persons eminent in godliness, when, to refute the Jews who were displeased that he called himself God and Son of God, he answered (*John* X, 34): “Is it not written in your law, ‘I said: you are gods’?” Those words are taken from verse 6 of Psalm LXXXI: “I said: you are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High.” It is as if he said: “Why do you rebuke me because I call myself God and God’s Son, when this title has long been made common to righteous persons?”

Did not Peter likewise say that people assumed through charity into the adoption of the children of God are made partakers of the divine nature (2 Peter I, 4)? This is why not only Hilary but other Fathers too call divine, or certainly a son of God, one who is imbued with charity. Hear, I beg you, what Ambrose teaches (*On Virgins*, I.3; otherwise no. 11): “The Word became flesh, so that flesh might become God.” Hear likewise what Augustine writes (*Tractates on the First Epistle of John*, II.14, that is, the final section):

> “Each person is such as his love is. Do you love earth? You will be earth. Do you love God? What shall I say—will you be God? I do not dare say it on my own authority. Let us hear the Scriptures: ‘I said: You are gods, and all sons of the Most High.’ Therefore, if you wish to be gods and sons of the Most High, do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world.”

If anyone wishes to find similar things in Bernard’s writings, let him consult the passages noted at the foot of the page [Note: *Sermon 8 on the Song of Songs*, no. 9: “Let it—yes, let it presume that it is loved with a fatherly affection,” etc.; likewise *Sermon 46 on the Song*, no. 4: “For what our own and belonging to us says,” etc.; and likewise *Sermon 71 on the Song*, no. 10.].

214. There are countless passages of Scripture teaching that we are loved by God. We accordingly become like him if we love him, being moved by no fear, just as he loves us without being moved by any fear to love us. Yet this likeness may also be explained in the manner set forth by Augustine, just cited [Col. 0824A]. Indeed, by anticipation we may be said to be like God insofar as we shall be like him in blessedness; theologians call grace the seed of that blessedness.

215. I fear that after the words, “Does it trust? No,” some words are missing—words omitted, that is, in our manuscript—by which the objection previously proposed would be resolved. Yet Hilary’s words can still stand without any break. For charity does not expressly hope, does not expressly trust—for the Apostle Paul certainly teaches that it does in some sense hope and believe (1 Corinthians XIII, 7): “Charity believes all things, hopes all things”—and it does not fear in any way, if the discussion concerns the fear which theologians call servile, although it fears with that fear which theologians call filial or reverential fear.

Certainly charity endures in heaven, and we love God; yet we neither believe nor hope. Theologians and interpreters of Scripture discuss this matter extensively, especially in relation to Paul’s words (1 Corinthians XIII, 8), “Charity never fails,” and others (1 Corinthians XIII, 10), “That which is partial shall be done away,” etc. Consult them.

216. In the passage from the Epistle to the Romans cited here by Hilary, the words “when God loved the world” are lacking; likewise the epithet *only-begotten*, which is attributed to the Son. The omitted words are drawn from the Gospel of John (ch. III, v. 16): “For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son.” Should this be attributed to Hilary himself, who thought that Paul taught what he cites? Or rather, does he say that Paul taught these things because Paul teaches the greater part of them? Or should it be attributed to the manuscript which he used, in which the words he cites were written? Or to the copyist, who conflated two Scriptural passages cited by Hilary into one? Let the reader judge [Col. 0824B].

217. Where I have printed, “Therefore he who has this, as it were, appearance,” etc., the manuscript has, “therefore he who has this, as it were, hope,” etc. But after the word *as it were* some word ought to stand which, unless I am mistaken, denotes charity’s superiority to the remaining virtues [Col. 0824C]. The word *as it were* further suggests a certain hyperbole which Hilary employed in extolling the excellence of charity, and which he moderated by prefixing the adverb *as it were*, a word that often has a diminishing force.

Who could deny that he indicates a virtue by the name *appearance* (*species*), after knowing that he wrote: “And although all the appearances [that is, virtues] which we discussed above”; and below: “it is now fitting to conclude the appearances,” etc.? The words, “God is love,” clearly show that love is here taken to mean charity, though not in the sense in which Hilary had explained it a little earlier. For who would say that God fulfils—that is, completes—all commandments? Can a command be imposed upon God which he must fulfil?

That it is not permissible to dispute much concerning God, but that what faith teaches concerning him ought rather to be received with obedience, is taught by the very explicit and numerous admonitions of both Scripture and the Fathers which call God ineffable and incomprehensible. See no. 33 and following.

[Col. 0824D] 218. Something is certainly missing in this sentence, but only a little. If we trust conjectures, we may supply the omission thus: “and foreign to rashness.” The same must be thought concerning love: for there is as much knowledge of it—that is, of love—as there is of God, because God is love. If you prefer to read, in place of those words “and foreign,” “the same thing,” I shall not object.

219. Does Hilary here allude to what the Apostle Paul formerly commanded in these words (1 Corinthians XI, 31): “For if we judged ourselves, we should not indeed be judged”? Or rather, to that most celebrated saying of the ancient philosophers, “Know thyself,” so often praised by the Fathers themselves? Let the judgment remain open.

[Col. 0825A] 220. That is: it is fitting—or I consider it equitable—that the treatment of the virtues should end in the fullness of love and of every good thing. He had earlier said that this fullness of love, and indeed of all things, is in God.

221. The words, “or if anything has been omitted, let it seem to be concluded in the fullness of the world,” are, in my judgment, exceedingly obscure. Has some error crept into the word *world*, so that something else ought to be substituted? But what ought to be substituted I do not know. Or, retaining the word *world*, will you refer these words to the Divine Word, creator of all things, so that their sense is this: “If perhaps we have omitted anything in our enumeration of things, not mentioning it expressly, it has nevertheless not been omitted altogether; for when we have said that all things were created by God, those very things which seem to have been passed over by us have not been omitted”? But how far removed are the things he now says from what he had previously said concerning God, the Word, and the creation of the world? Yet Hilary seems everywhere to maintain an unbroken and connected sense [Col. 0825B]. Are some words missing, omitted by a copyist, so that the sense appears interrupted? Amid such great obscurity, let the reader choose what seems more probable [Col. 0826A]. Concerning the defence of the faith and the opponents whom he mentions here, recall what we said in the final number of chapter 2 of the preface.

222. The words “and may the opponents of my faith receive more mystery” are likewise obscure. Should one perhaps read *occasion* (*momentum*), that is, an opportunity, rather than *mystery*? Or something else akin to opportunity? But if you insist on retaining the word *mystery*, these words may, in my opinion, be explained thus: let those who oppose my faith also receive my confession and acknowledge that I agree completely with the Church; and let them at last know the reason why I have expressed certain matters more obscurely in my books, concealing them under a certain covering—namely, lest I offend the weaker persons. For now that an opportunity has presented itself to explain my views, I have explained them plainly.

Or, if you prefer, understand by *mystery* a formula of faith, and say that Hilary wishes the opponents of his faith to receive the same formula of faith in which both he and those opponents entirely agree. This formula of faith would make it wholly clear that Hilary believes orthodoxly; and it would benefit both his enemies and believers, insofar as all alike would agree upon one and the same formula that most plainly declares the mysteries of our religion [Col. 0826B].

[Col. 0825]

# DISSERTATIONS ON THE EPISTLE, OR LITTLE BOOK, OF SAINT HILARY

[Col. 0825C] FIRST DISSERTATION. On these words in Hilary’s epistle [Note: Ch. 3, p. 39.]: “SO THAT EVEN THAT WHICH WAS AFTERWARD MADE MAY HAVE BEEN MADE FOR OUR SAKE.” Whether all sensible things described by Moses were created for the sake of human beings.

1. To the annotations which I appended to Hilary’s Epistle I now at last add dissertations, in which certain topics of inquiry are treated that cannot be contained within the brief remarks required by annotations. In the first dissertation, then, I shall explain the words, “So that even that which was afterward made may have been made for our sake”; and I shall inquire whether, as these words indicate, all sensible things described by Moses were created for the sake of human beings.

[Col. 0825D] 2. This is a very ancient question, one debated even among Greek philosophers. The Stoics maintained that God made everything for our sake [Note: Lactantius, *On the Divine Reward*—which work is Book VII of the *Institutes*—ch. 7.], while the Epicureans and Academics opposed them: the former because they mocked God’s providence toward us, the latter because they considered the assertion less certain than the Stoics claimed.

Nevertheless, this opinion pleased other philosophers as well, such as Aristotle [Note: *Physics*, II.2; *Metaphysics*, I.2; and *Politics*, I.5.], who teaches that the human being is the end for whose sake all other things in nature were made. It also found favour with ancient Hebrew teachers and Fathers. Of the ancient Hebrew teachers I select Philo, for in his book entitled *On the Creation of the World* he says [Note: Translated by Gelenius, p. 15 of the Lyons edition of 1561.]:

> “Someone may ask here why the human being was the last of the works in the world’s creation. For, as the sacred writings teach, the Creator and Father made him after all things. Those who investigate the law more deeply and examine it with the greatest possible diligence say that, after God admitted the human being into kinship with himself by granting him reason, a gift surpassingly excellent, he did not begrudge him the other things either. Rather, he prepared all that the world contains for this creature most familiar and dear to him, desiring that, newly created, he should lack nothing contributing to life, and indeed to living well. The abundance and richness of things prepared for use provides the former; the contemplation of heavenly things provides the latter, by which contemplation the mind, struck with wonder, conceives love and desire for knowledge of such things.”

3. That the opinion in question was shared by all Christians is clear from the fact that Celsus ridicules and rebukes Christians on this account [Note: *Against Celsus*, IV.20, p. 523 of vol. I of Charles de la Rue’s edition.]. “Celsus adds,” says Origen, “that we say: ‘All things have been commanded to serve us.’” Yet Origen, in refuting Celsus, does not deny this; he merely says that perhaps it is not wholly true [Col. 0827A]—and indeed, if we speak strictly, angels and the heavens do not serve us, nor do stones, metals, or any inanimate things serve us, though we use them and they were created for our sake. He adds that the very point Celsus rebukes in Christians had been taught by Greeks, who nevertheless had not been reproached on that account. Celsus therefore wrongly condemns it in Christians.

But it is better to quote Origen’s own words, as rendered into Latin in the edition of the most learned Charles de la Rue:

> “Celsus adds that we say: ‘All things have been commanded to serve us.’ Perhaps he heard no one among our wise persons say such things . . . Then, when Greeks say [Euripides, *Phoenician Women*]:
>
> ‘The sun and night both serve mortals,’
>
> they praise the saying and elucidate it in commentaries. Whether we say the same thing or say it in other words, it is all one to Celsus, so that he may bring an accusation against us.”

It is noted in the margin that by “the Greeks” Origen meant Euripides, whose verse occurs in the *Phoenician Women*. At the foot of the page the entire Euripidean passage is supplied, both in Greek and in Latin translation; it reads as follows:

> “The dark eyelid of night and the light of the sun  
> he ordained to travel equally through the yearly circuit;  
> neither of the two begrudges the other its turn,  
> and thus sun and night serve human beings,” etc.

4. Let Augustine follow Origen. For, having proposed for himself the resolution of this question [Note: [Col. 0827D] *In the Book of Eighty-Three Diverse Questions*, question XXX.]: Whether all things were created for the benefit of human beings, he embraces the affirmative side and concludes the question in this manner: “Therefore all things that have been made were made for the use of man [Col. 0827C], because reason, which has been given to man, makes use of all things by judging them.”

5. Let us join Lactantius with Augustine; for he says this (*On the Anger of God*, ch. 13): “All the things of which the world consists, and which it generates from itself, are fitted for the use of man alone. Man uses fire for warming, for light, for cooking food, and for forging iron. He uses springs for drinking and bathing; rivers for irrigating fields and marking out regions. He uses the earth for obtaining a variety of crops, hills for planting vineyards, mountains for trees and timber, plains for grain. He uses the sea not only for commerce and for conveying supplies from distant regions, but also for the abundance of every kind of fish. But if [Col. 0827D] he uses these elements, which are nearest to him, there is no doubt that he also uses the heaven, since the functions of heavenly things are ordered toward the fertility of the earth, from which we live.”

Then, after describing the various uses both of heavenly and atmospheric phenomena, he finally adds: “Did God labor also for the sake of dumb animals? By no means, because they lack reason. But we understand that they too were made by God in the same way for the use of man: partly for food, partly for clothing, partly as aids to work; so that it may be clear that divine providence wished to furnish [Col. 0828A] and adorn human life with an abundance of things and resources, and for that reason filled the air with birds, the sea with fish, and the earth with quadrupeds.” And again (ch. 14): “It remains for me to show why God made man himself. As he fashioned the world for man, so he made man for himself, as the high priest of a divine temple, the spectator of the works and heavenly things.”

6. Nor should Gregory be omitted; for he states in the clearest terms the matter of which we are speaking (*Homily XXIX on the Gospels*, no. 2): “That person, indeed, is instructed for whose sake all things on earth were created” (he is speaking, moreover, of man). Add also, if you wish, Bernard (*Sermon I on Diverse Subjects*, no. 6), and the author of the little work entitled *Instruction of Priests*, which appears among Bernard’s works (it appears on p. 583, vol. III, Venice edition of Mabillon, 1727).

[Col. 0828B] 7. And indeed the teaching of these writers seems to us to be supported by a very probable argument. For man appears to be the most excellent of all creatures, and therefore all things rightly serve him, as I shall show with no little care in the following dissertation; nor can anyone point to anything among things made that is not in some way useful to man.

8. I know, indeed, that these claims are called into question by the Academics and ridiculed by the Epicureans. But anyone who weighs their arguments will admit that both reactions are undeserved; and therefore we ought to hear those arguments. They argue as follows: If all other things had been created for the sake of man, would nature have made man the most miserable of all living creatures? Yet it did make him most miserable—so much so that it is plainly evident that he was utterly despised by [Col. 0828C] God, or, as the ancients were accustomed to say, by nature. But it is better to set forth this argument, whatever its worth, in the very words in which the ancients presented it. Well known are those verses of Lucretius (*On the Nature of Things*, V.223 ff.), in which he teaches how cruel nature has been toward man:

> Then the child, like a sailor cast forth from savage waves,  
> lies naked on the ground, speechless, destitute of every  
> vital aid, when nature first has thrust him from his mother’s womb  
> with painful efforts into the breezes of light;  
> and he fills the place with mournful crying—as is fitting  
> for one to whom there remains to pass through so many evils in life.

9. Pliny likewise develops the point more fully, writing as follows (*Natural History*, VII, preface): “Nature seems to have generated all other things for man’s sake, in exchange for her great gifts exacting a great and cruel price; so that it is not easy to judge whether she has been a better parent to man or a harsher stepmother. Before all else, she alone of all animals clothes him with resources taken from others: she has given the rest various coverings—shells, bark, hides, spines, shaggy hair, bristles, hair, down, feathers, scales, fleeces. She has even protected trunks and trees by bark, sometimes double bark, against cold and heat. Man alone she casts out naked upon the ground on his birthday, immediately to cries and weeping; and no other among so many animals is subject to tears, and that from the very beginning of life. Yet, by Hercules, early and very swift laughter is granted to none before the fortieth day. From this first dawning of light, bonds receive him—bonds which not even beasts born among us endure—and the fastening of all his limbs; and the creature destined to rule the rest lies there, born unhappily, bound hand and foot, weeping; and he begins life with punishments, for the one fault of having been born. Alas for the madness of those who think themselves born from such beginnings for pride!” [Col. 0829A]

He proceeds with many other remarks, by which he shows quite plainly either that man is inferior to all other living creatures, or at least their equal, and consequently that the rest were not created for his sake.

10. And indeed Pliny himself, and other philosophers, openly demonstrate that other things do not serve man at all. To begin with the stars and heavens, and their motions and revolutions, Pliny declares of them (*Natural History*, II.8): “The heaven does not have so great a fellowship with us [Col. 0829B] that that radiance of the stars should also be mortal according to our fate.” Seneca likewise, to the same effect (*On Anger*, II.27): “None of those things which harm or benefit us is specifically directed toward us; for we are not the reason why the world brings back winter and summer. Those things have their own laws, by which divine matters are carried out. We think too highly of ourselves if we consider ourselves worthy for whose sake such great things are moved.”

And indeed, who could persuade himself that the immeasurable spaces of the heavens and the ether were created for man’s sake, when we are so far from using them that we do not even know them? For who, to say something about use—who, I say, uses the stars and those immense expanses of heaven of which we have spoken? To whom is Sirius, the Dog-star, or any other star useful? Those surely seem to be much wiser who judge that these things were created for some entirely different end, which we must admit we do not know, rather than for man’s sake. What then? Do not those appear entirely mistaken who deny that the heavenly spheres are empty of inhabitants, and assert that the same spheres were created for their sake? Do you laugh at these things and assign them to Fontenelle, who proposed them in jest? Read, I beg you, what the most distinguished Derham discusses on this subject not in jest but seriously, and you will plainly see that the opinion of those who maintain these points is highly probable [Note: [Col. 0829D] *Theological Astronomy*, preface, pp. 26 and 30 of the Italian edition.].

11. Or—to speak also of the second argument, namely that drawn from our ignorance—if the heavens and heavenly spheres had been created for our sake, would God have allowed us to suffer such ignorance of them that, as we have already said, we cannot know even their magnitude, [Col. 0829D] distance, or number? “Count the stars, if you can,” God once said while addressing Abraham (Gen. XV.5), setting before him, as it were, something altogether impossible. Moreover, Job and David indicate not obscurely that the use, knowledge, and indeed the very number of the stars have been entirely reserved to God, when they say these things of God: “Who makes Arcturus, Orion, the Hyades, and the inner chambers of the south; who does great and incomprehensible and wonderful things, without number” (Job IX.9). And: “Who counts the multitude of the stars and calls them all by names” (Ps. CXLVI.4–5). From this fact David draws the greatness of divine wisdom, adding: “Great is our Lord, and great is his power; and of his wisdom there is no number.” Indeed God himself addresses Job in these words (Job XXXVIII.18–19): “Tell me, if you know all things: in what way does light dwell, and where is the place of darkness . . . by what way is light scattered, and heat distributed over the earth?” (v. 24). “Do you know the order of heaven, and can you establish its ordinance on earth?” (v. 33).

12. But let us leave the heavens and, if you wish, come down to the things directly before us and often subject to our eyes. Shall we say that animals were created for our sake, when we usually experience them as harmful, or at least useless? Do we not experience wild beasts as harmful—indeed, even the tiniest creatures which, especially in summer, attack our bodies and cause us great [Col. 0830B] annoyance? Well known are these verses of Lucretius (*On the Nature of Things*, V.219):

> Moreover, why does nature nourish and increase  
> the dreadful race of wild beasts, hostile to humankind,  
> on land and sea?

And to the same effect we read in Cicero (*Academic Questions*, IV): “Why, if God made all things for our sake—for that is what you maintain—did he make so great a multitude of water-snakes and vipers? Why did he scatter so many deadly and destructive things over land and sea?” Lactantius seems to refer to this passage of Cicero when he writes (*On the Anger of God*, ch. 13): “The Academics, disputing against the Stoics, commonly ask why, if God made all things for the sake of human beings, so many things contrary, hostile, and deadly to us are found both in the sea and on land [Col. 0830C]. The Stoics, not considering the truth, answered this most foolishly. For they say that among things generated and among the number of animals there are many whose usefulness is still hidden, but will be discovered in the course of time, just as necessity and use have already discovered many things unknown to earlier ages.”

13. Theodoret presses the matter more strongly (*Question XX on Genesis*), explaining these words of Scripture: “And let him have dominion over the fish of the sea, the birds of heaven, cattle, the whole earth, and every creeping thing that creeps upon the earth.” “It should be observed,” he says, “that it has been passed over in silence that not all animals were created for man, but only those over which man is said to rule were created for him—namely the fish of the sea, birds of heaven, and cattle of the earth, perhaps also creeping things [Col. 0830D] of the earth, on account of the necessary use of medicines made from them. But those great sea-monsters and land beasts were not created for man; otherwise, when this power was granted to man, their names also would have been added. Yet we do not find the race of serpents placed among creeping things in Scripture, but among wild beasts. For it says: ‘The serpent was the most cunning of all the beasts.’ And in the Acts of the Apostles, etc. . . . Therefore man does not rule over those great sea-monsters or beasts, which perhaps were not created for him from the beginning. And something similar is said in the eighth [Col. 0831A] Psalm of those things here described as being under man’s dominion: ‘You have subjected all things under his feet,’ etc. . . . For there too sea-monsters and wild beasts are omitted.” Given these premises, it is not surprising if we are afraid and take flight at the sight of serpents and wild beasts. This shows, of course, that they prevail over us, not we over them.

14. Nor did Bernard conceal this argument; for he says (*Sermon I on Diverse Subjects*, no. 6): “But still, you say, many things gravely disturb us, many things more plainly oppose us; and I wonder how all things can be said to have been given to us, when scarcely any serve us as we wish. Some things seem to serve us, but only with our labor, and only if we have first served them. The very beasts of burden do not help us unless they have been fed, tamed, and sustained by fodder from us. The earth itself, which ought to have been more kindly toward us, does not choose to provide us bread without the sweat of our brow; indeed, even when we have cultivated it, it brings forth thorns and thistles for us. Finally, if we consider everything carefully, all other things demand service from us more than they render it to us—not to mention for the moment things ready to harm us, such as fire for burning, water for drowning, and wild beasts for tearing. And these things are indeed so.”

15. Yet perhaps things harmful to man are fewer in number than things useless to him. What benefit, I ask, does man derive from the innumerable host of gnats and other extremely small insects with which we see ourselves beset, especially in summer? This is indeed an old difficulty, but one not yet resolved, which the ancient [Col. 0831C] Academics hurled against the Stoics. “What great usefulness,” they said (as Lactantius reports in *On the Anger of God*, ch. 13), “can be found in mice, cockroaches, and serpents? . . . Is there some medicinal power hidden in these things, which, if it exists, would someday be discovered?”

16. But let us leave wild beasts and all animals. What benefit does man derive from steep, inaccessible, rocky mountains? What from plants which neither he himself eats nor beasts likewise consume? Thus far those who think otherwise.

17. These and other similar arguments, I admit, possess a great appearance of plausibility among the ancients; yet they have no truth. The first argument, drawn from Lucretius and Pliny, has exceedingly little force. And it should immediately be noted that Pliny himself was by no means displeased by the very opinion which we maintain, when he wrote (*Natural History*, VII, preface): “Indeed, since the human mind cannot encompass all things, first place is rightly assigned to man, for whose sake nature seems to have generated all other things.” But whatever he himself may have thought, it is beyond doubt that our position is not at all weakened by the points he adds and which were previously alleged (recall no. 9). For unless nature had made man unarmed and dependent upon another’s aid, it would have made him readier to inflict injury than to repel it; nor would that parental affection be exercised toward the little child—an affection through which, while the exceptional love of parents toward their children is shown by such sure [Col. 0832A] proofs, children are most closely bound to their parents by the bonds of gratitude, love, and obedience. From this, indeed, very many and most excellent advantages and benefits arise for humankind. Moreover, to drive away cold and the other inconveniences of this kind, man need not be born clothed in hides or protected by feathers—things which would certainly disfigure that most excellent form with which the supreme Craftsman willed man to be adorned—since he has endowed him with intellect and reason, by which he can surely easily ward off any inconveniences and procure for himself many advantages.” Lactantius states this well (*On the Workmanship of God*, ch. 7): “Where reason and hands are present, covering of hair is no more necessary than clothing; so fittingly do things agree in their own kind that nothing more unsightly could be imagined than a naked quadruped or a covered man.”

18. The crying with which man seems to begin life is a kind of expression of a natural discharge that is useless, indeed harmful, and which entails no inconvenience, even the slightest. But suppose it did. Is it not removed by a mother’s or nurse’s care? Moreover, in the judgment of many Fathers, that crying indicates that man has fallen from the state and height of innocence, and therefore of highest happiness; and it consequently admonishes man to give thanks to God for the restoration received, and to have recourse to him through prayer in order to obtain help and aid.

19. The bonds mentioned by Pliny do not hinder man but help him; and, to omit the other benefits [Col. 0832C] arising from this, they strengthen and reinforce his body and make it possible for him to retain and preserve the dignity God conferred upon him when he gave man an uplifted face to look upon heaven. For if, at the beginnings of childhood, the child’s upright and rigid little body were not bound by swaddling bands and wrappings, man himself would crawl on his feet, and that outstanding praise of Boethius would be taken from him (*Consolation of Philosophy*, V.5.8):

> The human race alone lifts its summit higher,  
> and, upright in its erect body, looks down  
> upon the earth.

20. But we must turn to the second objection, put forward in no. 10. Let anyone say what he pleases: I, for my part, will more readily and obediently believe [Col. 0832D] Scripture, in which God teaches us, than men—even men eminent in learning—who think otherwise. For we read this in Scripture (Gen. I.14–17): “And God said: Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven, and let them divide day and night; and let them be for signs, seasons, days, and years; that they may shine in the firmament of heaven and give light upon the earth,” etc. And elsewhere (Ps. CXXXV.7–9): “Who made the great lights . . . the sun to rule the day . . . the moon and stars to rule the night,” etc. And again (Deut. IV.19): “Lest perhaps, when you lift up your eyes to heaven, you see the sun and moon and all the stars of heaven, and, deceived by error, adore and worship those things which the Lord your God created for the service of all nations that are under heaven.” If he created them for the service of those [Col. 0833A] under heaven, he surely made them for our sake.

21. Pliny’s final words, “We are not the reason for the world,” etc., contain nothing that harms our position. For in that chapter he ridicules and rejects the opinion of the common people, who thought that stars were assigned to individual persons—bright ones to the rich, smaller ones to the poor, dark ones to the afflicted—and that they shone and were allotted to mortals according to each person’s lot. He immediately rejects this opinion, which is very far from the truth, by these words: because the stars neither are born nor die with the individual persons assigned to them, nor does their falling signify that anything is extinguished. Then he adds the remarks that have been objected: “The heaven does not have so great a fellowship with us that that radiance of the stars should also be mortal according to our fate.” These observations are as excellent for refuting the opinion he censures [Col. 0833B] as they are foolish if brought forward against the proposition now under discussion.

22. Seneca’s opinion, moreover, is not to be held in such esteem that it should be preferred to the teaching of Lactantius, Augustine, and indeed Scripture itself.

23. I readily admit that we do not know most of the things contained within the immense spaces of the heavens. But how many things benefit us—indeed, serve us—whose nature and number we wholly do not know? Do we know the nature or number of air, fire, and other things that we use every day? We believe God, from whose testimony we learn that all the stars of heaven were created by him for the service of all nations under heaven. I do not deny that they were made for other ends; but neither can we affirm that, because it is entirely hidden from us. Nor will they have been created for a contemptible end if they were created so that from their appearance we might rise to acknowledge and praise divine omnipotence—especially since he has willed such excellent, extraordinary, and, I might almost say, immense bodies to be in our service [Col. 0833C].

24. God did indeed create wild and savage beasts, poisonous creatures, and plants; yet it does not follow that he did not create them for man’s sake. If you consider man while he still possessed innocence, these and any other things you can imagine, however harmful, could not injure him [Note: [Col. 0833D] See, I beg you, what Augustine teaches on this subject, *On Genesis against the Manichaeans*, I.18, no. 29.]. If you consider him fallen from innocence, God placed them to frighten and admonish man, lest he depart from the commands [Col. 0833D] of him “who armed the creature for the vengeance of his enemies” (Wis. V.18). Consult those passages of Scripture which I note at the foot of the page (Lev. XXVI.22; Deut. XXXII.24; and 2 Kings [4 Kings] II.24). Moreover, has not the very fierceness of lions quite often displayed divine omnipotence in a marvelous way? What is more unusual, and therefore more suited to celebrating divine omnipotence, than the prodigy that occurred when God shut the lions’ mouths so that they might not devour Daniel [Col. 0834A] (Dan. VI.27 and 22): “and they did him no harm,” “and no injury was found in him, because he believed in his God”? And, to remain with Daniel, what is more wonderful, and therefore more fitting for demonstrating God’s providence toward good men, than what we learn of the same Daniel? I gladly recount it in Scripture’s own words (Dan. XIV.29 ff.): “Then the king saw that they [the Babylonians] rushed violently upon him, and, compelled by necessity, gave Daniel over to them. They cast him into the lions’ den, and he was there for six days. Now there were seven lions in the den, and two bodies and two sheep were given them daily; but then they were not given them, so that they might devour Daniel . . .” (v. 39). “Then the king came on the seventh day to mourn for Daniel; and he came to the den and looked in, and behold, Daniel [Col. 0834B] was sitting in the midst of the lions. And the king cried out in a loud voice, saying: ‘Great are you, O Lord, God of Daniel’” (v. 42) . . . “Let all inhabitants of the whole earth fear the God of Daniel, because he is the Savior, working signs and wonders upon earth, who delivered Daniel from the lions’ den.” Did not that lion also testify to divine omnipotence which killed by its bite the prophet who had not obeyed God’s commands, but did not touch his corpse (3 Kings XIII.24–25)?

25. What occurred then, we know to have happened not infrequently afterward as well, as ecclesiastical records testify. From these we learn that wild beasts were at times restrained from touching martyrs exposed to their bites [Note: [Col. 0833D] Ignatius Martyr, *Epistle to the Romans*, no. 4; Eusebius, *History*, VIII.7; *Acts of SS. Tarachus, Probus*, etc., no. 10, in Ruinart, p. 392 of the Verona edition.], or from devouring their corpses [Note: [Col. 0834D] Eusebius, *On the Martyrs of Palestine*, XI (in Ruinart, no. 42: “Their most sacred bodies,” etc.); *Acts of St Vincent*, X (in Ruinart, Verona edition, p. 328). The same event that is read in the *Acts* is also found in Prudentius’s hymn entitled *On the Martyrdom of St Vincent*, stanzas 99, 100, etc.].

[Col. 0834C] 26. But let us, if you wish, leave these matters and remain with examples that we see every day. Do we not use even poisonous animals, turning their flesh and their poison itself to medical use? Who does not know that we use the skins of bears and other wild beasts to ward off cold, and turn them to our own advantage? If we seriously consider these points, we shall readily admit what was established at the beginning: namely, that all bodies, however excellent, however at times harmful, were created for man’s sake.

27. That power of reason, intelligence, and deliberation with which God has endowed man—if it helps him turn even harmful animals to his own use—it helps him still more to avoid and evade their attacks and ferocity; or, if he cannot perhaps evade [Col. 0834D] and avoid them, it supplies him with remedies and medicines against their poisons and bites. Thus those whom we see killed by the bites of wild beasts and serpents are very few; and even among these you will find many who rashly provoked the beasts or serpents themselves to their own destruction. For who, to use Scripture’s words (Ecclus. XII.13), “will pity all who approach wild beasts”?

[Col. 0835A] 28. As for the objections derived from the multitude of wild beasts and serpents created by God, the following answer is common indeed, but not to be rejected; and, if you wish, you may suitably confirm it by what we shall afterward adduce from Theodoret’s eighteenth question on Genesis.

29. I now come to the words of Theodoret which they excerpted from *Question XX on Genesis* and pressed against us. I confess that when I read these in the old editions, I was somewhat troubled; for they oppose not only the Fathers whom I have cited, but also Theodoret himself. In his commentaries on the Second Epistle to the Corinthians, which I shall cite in Dissertation III, and in that very *Question XX on Genesis* which they quoted—if we follow the old edition of Picus—he teaches precisely what we have maintained, recording in writing: “If therefore the one who ought not to veil his head is the image of God, surely she who is veiled is not the image of God, although she shares the same soul. How then is man the image of God? According to rule and authority. This also seems to be attested by the divine voice which says: ‘Let us make man in our image and likeness.’ And, adding the manner, it says: ‘And let him rule over the fish of the sea, birds of heaven, beasts of the earth,’ and the rest. For just as God rules all things, so man rules the things upon earth. But why does woman not rule the aforementioned things, though she holds the rest under her authority, and instead has man as her head, while man is not subject to woman?” But I abandoned all doubt [Col. 0835C] when I learned from Sirmond, whose edition I later consulted, that the old edition is corrupt. For in his preface Sirmond warns that many things had entered from ancient catenae into the manuscript used by Picus to render these questions into Latin—especially into the Question XX with which we are concerned—and the authority of these catenae, as all know, is not very great. He adds that Picus’s edition had mixed together with Theodoret’s view the very opinions which Theodoret rejects—namely those of Origen, Diodore, and Theodore. He could have added other views as well, and consequently the view now under discussion, since, as I shall presently say, no trace of it appears in Sirmond’s edition. That edition of Sirmond was prepared from a most trustworthy royal manuscript. But when it prints Question XX itself, it says none of the things objected; hence they are certainly additions. Moreover, in Question XVIII on Genesis Theodoret had set forth things which marvelously confirm our position and plainly oppose the points objected. Do you suppose that Theodoret, a serious man and highly praised among the ancients, was here so frivolous as to put forward contradictory claims within a short interval? But I consider it worthwhile to place before the reader’s eyes the eighteenth question on Genesis just mentioned, so that from it he may clearly recognize that I have advanced the truth:

“Question XVIII. Why did God create wild beasts and creeping things? Children need both frightening objects and straps and rods. By the former we frighten them, by the latter we instruct them; and we do both, seeking every virtue for them. Since therefore the Lord God saw us to be inclined toward idleness, he first created wild beasts and creeping things as certain straps and frightening objects, so that by frightening us through them he might draw us to himself and make us implore his help. But just as those who have reached mature age despise such frightening objects and straps, so those trained in virtue do not fear the attacks of wild beasts. For before Adam had sinned, beasts stood by him, rendering obedience. Again, when Noah entered the Ark, the lion, leopard, and every most savage creeping thing followed like sheep. Lions were present with Daniel; although otherwise hungry, they did not dare approach him, because they saw in him a certain token displaying the divine image. Likewise the viper which had sunk its teeth into the Apostle’s hand, finding in him nothing tender or soft with respect to sin, immediately recoiled and threw itself into the fire, in some manner exacting punishment from itself for having attacked a body wholly unsuited to it. We fear wild beasts because we are not endowed with virtuous habits. And therefore God, taking thought even for indolent people, banished them to more remote places and granted them the nighttime for seeking food: for, it says, ‘In that very night all the beasts of the forest shall pass through.’ But to creeping things he gave the caverns of the earth, so that, lying hidden in them, they might not harm humankind. Yet lest we despise wild beasts as though we were entirely unharmed by them, as though they could not hurt us at all, he who wisely governs our affairs sometimes permits two or three out of many thousands to be stung by scorpions or bitten by serpents, so that, fearing lest we suffer something similar, we may invoke God the Creator for help, beseeching him to protect us by that providence which drives away all evils. Besides, wild beasts are not useless to us in other respects. For physicians compound from them not a few medicines for driving away diseases. Therefore let no one complain of the Creator on account of wild beasts considered in themselves, but let him investigate their usefulness. For the human body itself, although beautiful, well-proportioned, and endowed with the varied usefulness of its parts, is nevertheless not without mucus, spittle, and foul excrement which it discharges . . . In this manner [Col. 0836D] we examine each of the other things: not considering whether it is harmful or useful in itself, but whether it contributes some usefulness to the whole. For wild beasts also respect man on account of the authority over them granted to him from the beginning. Yet sometimes they despise him as a transgressor of the divine law, just as wicked slaves are accustomed to despise those whom they have been ordered by their masters to obey, if they see that they have lost their authority through crimes.”

And so much for Theodoret. Let us continue with the rest.

30. If wild beasts and serpents sometimes frighten us and we flee them, this neither happens everywhere nor constantly; nor, when it does happen, does it show that humans truly serve brute animals and wild beasts. For robbers too frighten us and we flee them; yet we are not therefore said to serve robbers. But it is better to explain the whole matter in Chrysostom’s most excellent words: “But here,” he says, “the Gentiles rise up against us and say: ‘It is evident that this is not true; for we do not rule over wild beasts as he promised, but they rather rule over us.’ But what they object is not true. For as soon as a man appears, wild beasts flee. If we sometimes suffer harm from them, either because hunger drives them or because we provoke them, this does not occur because they hold authority over us, but because of our own fault. For when robbers attack us, if we do not neglect matters but take up arms against them, this does not happen because they hold authority [Col. 0837B] over us, but because we provide for our own safety” (*Homily IX on Genesis*, no. 3). He repeats the same point elsewhere in almost exactly the same words (*Sermon III on Genesis*, no. 5, p. 66, vol. IV of Montfaucon’s edition).

31. Augustine resolves the same difficulty by admitting that we have in some measure lost the dignity in which we were made in God’s image when we lost innocence. Yet he admits that we have lost what we lost in such a way that he denies we have lost it entirely, maintaining that authority over wild beasts and animals still remains in man, insofar as we tame them but do not allow ourselves to be tamed by them. But it is better to hear Augustine’s own teaching (*On Genesis against the Manichaeans*, I.18, formerly no. 29): “They [the Manichaeans] also sometimes say: ‘How did man receive authority over the fish [Col. 0837C] of the sea, birds of heaven, all cattle, and wild beasts, when we see people killed by many wild beasts and harmed by many birds, which we wish either to avoid or capture, but often cannot? How, therefore, have we received authority over these things?’ To them one must first say here that those greatly err who consider man after sin, when he was condemned to the mortality of this life and lost that perfection in which he was made in God’s image. But his condemnation has only so much force: he rules over so many cattle; although, owing to the frailty of his body, he can be killed by many wild beasts, he can be tamed by none, while he himself tames many, indeed nearly all.”

32. But since they have disputed against us on Bernard’s authority, not only on that of Theodoret, let them hear, I beg, how Bernard himself resolves this difficulty, whatever it may be (*Sermon I on Diverse Subjects*, no. 6): “And these things are indeed so. Yet the Apostle does not lie, asserting even more plainly elsewhere that he knows ‘that all things work together for good to those who love God, to those who are called saints according to his purpose.’ Nevertheless, carefully observe that he says not that things serve at will, but that they cooperate for good. For they serve not according to our desire, but for our benefit; not for pleasure, but for salvation; not for our wish, but for our advantage. [Col. 0838A] Indeed, all things cooperate for our good in such a manner that among all these things are counted even things which are nothing: hardship, illness, even death itself, and sin.”

33. Thus far we have remained with those things believed harmful to man. As to things that are useless, the Stoics anticipated this difficulty and hoped they could entirely resolve it by observing that a great part of the things which ordinary people judge useless to man are in fact most useful, although their usefulness is not immediately apparent. For they say, to use their words as Lactantius reports them (*On the Anger of God*, ch. 13), “that among things generated and in the number of animals there are many whose usefulness is still hidden, but it will be discovered in the course of time; just as necessity [Col. 0838B] and use have already discovered many things unknown to earlier ages.”

34. Yet it is not necessary to resort to this solution, however very plausible it otherwise is. For we know that the things which they called useless are most useful; and, to pass over the fact that they are shown to be highly useful insofar as God sometimes employs them to display his omnipotence and mighty hand—a matter abundantly taught by the book of Exodus (Exod. 8:17 ff., 24 ff.)—to pass this over, I say: are not the tiniest insects most useful to humankind, since by their number, kind, and variety the divine craftsman reveals himself? Whoever attends to what the most illustrious Redi (*De' Viventi ne' viventi*), Vallisneri, and subsequently Réaumur, much more fully, taught about insects will plainly see that they are most useful to humankind—indeed for other reasons, but especially because one may readily recognize the divine hand, power, and goodness in their creation and diverse manner of life. Do not also those animals by which humankind especially takes delight and is clothed feed upon insects?

35. He who knows of the mines of metal and marble concealed in inaccessible and rocky mountains will teach that such mountains are most useful to humankind; so too will he who knows that reservoirs of snow and water, from which springs are drawn, especially in summer, are found in those same inaccessible and exceedingly rugged mountains. On this subject, not to summon them all, consult the most illustrious Vallisneri (*Origine delle Fontane*).

36. There are, I admit, some plants which humankind does not eat. Yet there are none which some bird does not eat. The crow certainly eats hemlock, a poisonous plant to us. But who does not know that birds serve human use? Moreover, humankind makes use even of those plants which it does not eat and which even birds eat only rarely. But if you judge them useless for other ends, they will nevertheless be useful because they set more plainly before our eyes that chain which Aristotle [Note: [Col. 0837D] *History of Animals*, book VIII, chapter 1: “But nature passes so gradually and imperceptibly from inanimate things to animate things that their boundary is hidden by the continuity itself, and the end of the one is the middle of the other.”], Cicero, and later Vallisneri repeatedly emphasized (in a separate work published on that subject); and anyone will readily discover this if he observes the works of nature more diligently and accurately.

## SECOND DISSERTATION

On those words of chapter V (col. 736, no. 87): **THE SON OF GOD, GOD THE CRAFTSMAN, ACTED AT THE FATHER’S COMMAND.** Likewise on those words of the same chapter (col. 737, no. 91): **GOD THE FATHER HAD COMMANDED; THE SON, POWER ITSELF, WITHOUT DELAY TOOK UP THE COMMAND: FOR WITH THE COMMAND THE WORK STOOD READY.** Finally, on these words (col. 737, no. 97): **AND SINCE ALL THINGS WERE FORMED BY THE FATHER’S COMMAND, WITH THE WORD OBEYING.**

1. Before Hilary many writers used this very expression, or elsewhere Hilary himself did, and after Hilary many likewise used either the very same or at least a similar expression. Therefore the author of our Epistle cannot possibly displease the reader for having used it. But lest I seem to have said this rashly, I here set down the passages of those who, as I said, used either precisely the same or at least a related expression. I classify these expressions under three heads. The first comprises those ancient Fathers who say most explicitly that the Father commanded; the second, that the Son obeyed; the third, that the Son rendered some sort of ministry to the Father. And all this before he assumed flesh. After recounting these passages, we shall then set forth what should be said concerning the meaning of these and similar expressions.

2. To the first head belong these words of Irenaeus (*Against Heresies*, book IV, formerly ch. 75, now 38, no. 3):

> “The human being, made and fashioned according to the image and likeness, is established by the uncreated God: the Father indeed thinking kindly and commanding; the Son ministering and forming; and the Spirit nourishing and increasing.”

3. Hippolytus also, a very ancient writer, in his book against Noetus, makes the most explicit mention of God commanding and God making.

4. Tertullian likewise says (*Against Praxeas*, ch. 12): “Although everywhere I maintain one substance in three cohering persons, nevertheless, by necessity of meaning, I must call distinct the one who commands and the one who makes.”

5. Origen teaches the same. For he not only mentions God commanding and God making (*Commentary on John*, tome II, p. 61, Huet edition), but expressly teaches this as well [Note: [Col. 0839D] *Against Celsus*, book II, no. 9, p. 393 of tome I, ed. Fr. Charles de la Rue.]:

> “For we maintain that in the creation described by Moses the Father, by commanding, said to him: ‘Let there be light,’ and ‘Let there be a firmament,’ and whatever else God commanded to be made; and that he said to that same one: ‘Let us make humankind according to our image and likeness.’ But the Word, as he had been commanded, made all that the Father commanded him to make. And we say this not as though it were a conjectural assertion, but rely upon the very testimonies of the prophets, accepted also among the Jews, in which these words are said concerning God and the things created by him: ‘He himself spoke, and they were made; he himself commanded, and they were created.’ For if God commanded and things were created, whom shall we suppose capable, in accordance with the mind of the prophetic Spirit, of carrying out such a command of the Father, except him who is the Word—if I may so speak, the living Word and the Truth?”

6. Moreover, the six bishops who wrote to Paul of Samosata before he was brought to order, among other arguments offered to refute him, say most explicitly [Note: [Col. 0839D] Tome I of Labbe’s Venetian edition of the Councils, p. 867.] that “the Son, in bringing the world forth, fulfilled the Father’s will, and that the Father commanded him to do it.”

7. Hilary also openly approves the distinction already mentioned between God commanding and God making—or executing—when he says (*On the Trinity*, book IV, no. 16): “But let us see to what result this distinction between God commanding and God making is carried.”

8. Novatian—if he is the author of the work *On the Trinity* appended to Tertullian’s works—likewise speaks to the same effect (*On the Trinity*, ch. 25):

> “Moses, introducing God as commanding that light first be made, the heaven established, the waters gathered, dry land revealed, fruits produced according to their seeds, animals brought forth, lights and stars placed in heaven, shows that no one else was then present with God to whom these works might be commanded to be made, except him through whom all things were made and without whom nothing was made. And if this is the Word of God—for ‘my heart has poured forth a good word’—he shows that in the beginning the Word was, and that this Word was with the Father, and further that the Word was God; that all things were made through him. But this Word was made flesh and dwelt among us, namely Christ, the Son of God, whom, while we subsequently recognize as human according to the flesh, we see before the foundation of the world as the Word of God and as God, etc.”

9. Cyril of Jerusalem, Hilary’s contemporary and perhaps even older, does not hesitate to describe “the Father as enjoining creation upon the Son and supplying him with the pattern of things to be made; but the Son as carrying it out and creating things according to the pattern received from the Father” (*Catechesis* XI, nos. 22–23).

10. Basil the Great, nearly Hilary’s contemporary, does not hesitate to acknowledge the Lord as commanding—or ordering—and **δημιουργὸν τὸν λόγον**, “the Word as creator/craftsman” (*On the Holy Spirit*, book I, ch. 16).

11. Marius Victorinus—or, as others call him, Fabius Marius Victor—was believed to have lived in the same age. I have seen the following verses of this writer cited for our purpose [Note: [Col. 0840D] *On the Creation of Things*. I searched long for this passage but did not find it. Yet Petavius, *On the Trinity*, book II, ch. 77, and others cite it. Who would think that they did so rashly?]:

> When, at God’s command and full of the Father’s mind,  
> the almighty Son was making.

12. Augustine too seems to favor the same expression when he says (*Sermon* 140, no. 6): “Not given from time, but commanded as begotten. For how is that which is the Father’s Word not the Father’s command?” Again he wrote [Note: [Col. 0841D] *Against the Sermon of the Arians*, ch. 3, formerly no. 4.]:

> “They fashion for themselves in the phantom of their own heart as it were two persons placed side by side, each in his own location: one commanding and the other obeying. They do not understand that the Father’s very command that all things should be made is nothing other than the Father’s Word, through whom all things were made.”

13. To these must be added those Fathers who expound the words of Psalm 148:5, “He commanded, and they were created,” as describing the Father as commanding the Son to create things. Preeminent among them is Irenaeus, whose words are indeed very well known but are nevertheless worth recalling here (*Against Heresies*, book III, ch. 8): “To whom, then, did he command? Clearly, to the Word through whom the heavens were established.”

14. Irenaeus is followed by the Fathers of the Council of Antioch held against Paul of Samosata (*Councils* of Labbe, tome I, p. 867), Athanasius (*On the Decrees*), Cyril of Alexandria (*Treasury*, book XXIX, p. 255), and Prosper (*Commentary on Psalm 148: ‘He commanded, and they were created’*). Since this last Father lived long after the Council of Nicaea and indeed after that of Constantinople, I gladly quote his very words: “For what God says, he says by the Word. And the Word, through whom all things were made, executes the command of the one speaking” (ibid.).

15. Under the second head—that is, passages of the Fathers in which the Son is said to have obeyed before he assumed human flesh—belong not a few of the passages just cited, and most explicitly Prosper’s last statement: “He executes the command of the speaker”; likewise the passages adduced from the Council of Antioch against Paul of Samosata. Add the following. Hilary observes (*On the Trinity*, book IV, no. 16) that in creating the world the Son was obedient to the words of God, that is, of the Father. In the same sense Gregory Nazianzen says (*Secret Poem* VIII, p. 171, l. 6): “There was a time when, in establishing the world, the great Word of the mind was obedient to the mind of the great Father.” Paulinus of Nola likewise says (*Poem* 32, v. 83):

> He—the only-begotten Son of God—willingly obeyed,  
> God in harmony with the Father in all things,  
> pursuing their common work with equal love.

16. The third head includes these matters. The *Apostolic Constitutions* (see Cotelerius’s preface to these Constitutions) teach most explicitly that the divine Word received a ministry from the Father and that this ministry may therefore rightly be referred to the same Father as its true author. Indeed, they sometimes employ an analogy that seemed very harsh to defenders of the consubstantiality of the Word. They teach, namely, that “the deacon ought to refer all things to the bishop, just as Christ refers all things to the Father.” And lest anyone interpret this as said of the power Christ possesses in his assumed human nature, they mention the power of creating and governing, which he unquestionably possesses from and in the divine nature, not at all from the human. Here is what they teach:

> “Whatever, however, the deacon is able to do, let him administer it himself, having received power from the bishop, just as Christ received from the Father the power of creating and providing.”

See, please, the whole of chapter 26 of book II of these same *Constitutions*. There one reads, among other things:

> “The deaconess represents the Holy Spirit, who ought to do or say nothing without the deacon, just as neither does the Paraclete speak or act anything from himself, but, glorifying Christ, awaits his will.”

17. Irenaeus (*Against Heresies*, book IV, ch. 17; in the new edition ch. 7, no. 4) denies that God the Father needed the service of angels in creating the world, since the Word, his excellent minister, is at hand:

> “For his offspring and his formation, that is, the Son and the Holy Spirit, the Word and Wisdom, minister to all his purposes; angels serve and are subject to them.”

Recall also the passage cited at no. 2: “the Son ministering,” etc.

18. This teaching is followed by the author to whom we owe the treatise *On the Incarnation*, found among Augustine’s works. For he says (*On the Incarnation*, book I, ch. 2) that “the Son ministered to the Father in every act of creation, because all things were made through him.” If he ministered to the Father in every act of creation, he ministered to the Father also long before he became incarnate.

19. I admit, however, that some of the passages we have cited may perhaps be evaded, whether by observing that the harsher expressions appended to the Fathers we have cited—such as *the Father commanding*—are absent from the most reliable manuscripts of Irenaeus used by Erasmus and other earlier editors of Irenaeus, as René Massuet, to whom we owe the latest edition of Irenaeus, shows (“and *commanding* are absent in Erasmus and the Gallican [edition],” p. 285, tome I of the Venetian edition); or by observing that the words concerning the power of creating and preserving, drawn from certain older editions, are absent from the Amsterdam edition of 1724 of the *Apostolic Constitutions*. Or one might observe that not all the Doctors whom we have cited should be held in the highest esteem, so that, moved by their authority, we should depart from ordinary and most approved forms of speech. For why may we not employ what Gennadius was permitted to state (*On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, ch. 4)? “Let us believe that there is nothing created or serving in the Trinity, as Dionysius, the source of Arius, wishes.” Basil too wrote concerning that Dionysius, though he was very ancient and otherwise a commendable man (*Letter* XLI, Maurist edition IX, no. 2):

> “We do not admire everything in that man; indeed, we reject some things altogether. For, so far as we know, he was almost the first to provide the human race with the seeds of the impiety now spread abroad, that of the Anomoeans.”

Although Basil immediately attempts somewhat to excuse him, adding: “I do not think that the cause was depravity of mind, but that he wished to struggle more vigorously against Sabellius.” Yet certainly not all the passages can be evaded. For who would dare say that all the passages from the Fathers previously set forth are corrupt, since they are not few and most of them are certainly uncorrupt? We must therefore resort to another solution.

20. Among reputable writers I have found two lines of solution. The first consists in observing that a milder meaning lies beneath these harsher expressions. The second receives the expressions strictly, but does not take them to concern the Word insofar as he is Word and uncreated. Let us consider both solutions.

21. Those who propose the first solution say, then, that both secular and sacred writers have this practice: they attach a milder sense and meaning to certain harsher words, intending less than appears on the surface, as the common proverb has it. I pass over foreign and secular writers, in whom examples of this sort are very frequent, in order to remain with sacred authors. Paul writes to the Colossians (Col. 4:10): “Aristarchus, my fellow prisoner, greets you, and Mark, the cousin, concerning whom you received commands.” Most interpreters hold that by this word no strict commands are meant. We also read in Joshua (Josh. 10:14): “The Lord obeying the voice of a man.” But who would take this strictly? Does God submit himself to a human voice and obey it? Elsewhere God himself says of himself (Isa. 43:24): “You have made me serve in your sins; you have given me labor.” Does God serve us when we sin, and do we impose labor upon him?

22. Hilary certainly follows this manner of speaking when he says (*On the Trinity*, book II, no. 24):

> “For the sake of the human race, the Son of God was born of the Virgin, with the Holy Spirit himself ministering to him in this operation, and with his own—that is, God’s—power overshadowing him; he sowed within himself the beginnings of a body.”

Does the divine Word—for here he understands the divine Word by the name of the Holy Spirit (see annotation g on this passage)—minister to himself?

23. Other similar expressions are not uncommon among the holy Fathers. But it is enough to have cited the foregoing.

24. Having established this, theologians observe that the expressions under discussion undoubtedly require some suitable explanation, although not everyone accepts the same explanation and it is very difficult to identify any certain one.

25. Most agree that these and similar phrases denote nothing other than that the Father is the principle of operations—not only of operations *ad intra*, concerning which no one disputes unless he is an Arian, but also of operations *ad extra*, insofar as all things proceed from him as from a fountain, for the Fathers themselves employ this comparison.

26. Augustine, cited at no. 12, seems to indicate this; but Basil certainly suggests this explanation in expounding Christ’s words, “I have received a command from the Father, what I should say,” etc. For he teaches the following [Note: [Col. 0843D] From the translation in the Maurist edition, *On the Holy Spirit to Amphilochius*, ch. 8, no. 19.]:

> “Yet lest perhaps, carried away by the greatness of the things done, we fall into the imagination that the Lord has no principle, what does he say who is life through himself? ‘I live because of the Father.’ And the power of God says: ‘The Son can do nothing from himself.’ Again, he who is perfect wisdom says: ‘I have received a command, what I should say and what I should speak.’ Through all these sayings he leads us to knowledge of the Father and refers to him the admiration due to the things he was doing, so that through him we may know the Father. For the Father is not perceived through a difference of works, as though he displayed an action peculiar to and separate from the Son—for whatever he sees the Father doing, the Son likewise does—but, through the glory rendered to him by the Only-Begotten, he receives the wonder of the works, while, beyond the greatness of the works, he is glorified also in their author and exalted by those who acknowledge him as the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ: ‘through whom are all things and for whom are all things.’ Therefore the Lord says: ‘All mine are yours,’ referring to him the origin of created things; and, ‘Yours are mine,’ receiving from him the principles of creating—not because he uses assistance in working, nor because the ministry of each individual work is entrusted through particular commands, for that would be slavish and infinitely remote from divine dignity; but because the Word, shining forth from the Father and full of paternal goods, does all things in likeness of him who begot him. For if he differs from the Father in nothing according to essence, he does not differ from the Father in power either. But where power is equal, operation too is altogether equal. Christ, indeed, is the power of God and the wisdom of God; thus all things were made through him, and all things were created through him and for him—not because he performs an instrumental and servile ministry, but because, as Creator, he fulfills the Father’s will.”

27. We may also, if we wish, give the verb *I command* an explanation akin to that which Gregory Nazianzen, according to Petavius, gives to the verb *I teach*: namely, that it denotes the communication of ideas. It seems worthwhile to cite here the words of the holy Doctor, which are also wonderfully helpful in explaining the third class of expressions:

> “For the Father, as it were, impresses upon him the forms of those same things; and the Word executes them, not ignorantly but knowingly, or, to speak more aptly, in a fatherly manner” (*Oration* 36).

Having quoted Nazianzen’s words, Petavius adds (*On the Trinity*, book II, ch. 4, no. 6):

> “In these words, **ἐνσημαίνει** does not mean simply ‘to designate,’ as the translator renders it, but ‘to imprint, as it were, in another’; from which it is clear that the Father’s indicating to the Son, or teaching him, what is to be done, and as it were going before by showing it, is nothing other than communicating to him in begetting, together with the nature and essence, the knowledge of things to be made and their forms and ideas.”

Thus far we have remained with the first solution, which rests upon the claim that a milder sense adheres to these harsher expressions.

28. We must now address the second solution, which takes these same expressions—or at least a large part of them, for Paulinus’s passage does not permit itself to be explained by this last interpretation—strictly, but denies that they can be taken of the Word insofar as he is Word and uncreated. They say, namely, that in creating the worldly things the Word assumed a certain bodily appearance, most like a human one—or rather, truly human—yet of remarkable form and beauty; and that in it he created all things, and hence created the human being, to whom in that same form he presented himself to be seen and spoke. Nor did he show himself in that form to Adam alone, but also to the other patriarchs, and often to the prophets themselves, so that he frequently appeared to them clothed in the same form which he had assumed in creation, or one at least very similar, and always human. Petavius adduces many Fathers in support of this view; consult, if you wish, the passage cited in the note below, where they are expressly listed [Note: [Col. 0845D] *On the Trinity*, book VIII, ch. 2, no. 5 and following, throughout the entire chapter.]. I shall select only a very few, referring the reader to Petavius himself.

29. Tertullian, arguing against Praxeas (ch. 7), says the following concerning the divine Discourse and Word carrying out the creation of things [Note: [Col. 0845D] That Tertullian speaks about the divine Word creating worldly things is made clear by his slightly preceding words: “As soon as God wished to bring forth into their substances and forms those things which he had arranged within himself through the Reason and Discourse of Wisdom” (ch. 6 of the same work).]:

> “Then, therefore, the Discourse himself also takes on his form and adornment, sound and voice, when God says: ‘Let there be light’ . . . But I say that nothing empty and void could have proceeded from God, as though it were brought forth from something empty and void; nor can that lack substance which proceeded from so great a substance and made so many substances, for he himself also made the things that were made through him. What sense is there in saying that he is nothing, without whom nothing was made? That what is empty should produce what is solid, what is void what is full, what is incorporeal corporeal things? For although something may at times be made different from that through which it is made, nevertheless nothing can be made through that which is empty and void. Is the Discourse of God an empty and void thing—the one called Son, who is himself also named God: ‘And the Discourse was with God, and the Discourse was God’? It is written: ‘You shall not take the name of God in vain.’ He, surely, is the one who, being in the form of God, did not deem equality with God a thing to be seized. In what form of God? Certainly in another form, yet not in no form at all . . . Whatever the substance of the Discourse was, that I call a person; and to it I assign the name of Son, and while I acknowledge the Son, I maintain that he is second from the Father.”

In Tertullian’s judgment, then, when the divine Word created things, he took on a form and adornment—that is, some outward and visible appearance, one of the greatest beauty and elegance. Tertullian indicates here—and often elsewhere—that this appearance was human: “In what form? Certainly in another [that is, of another kind, since he had not assumed flesh born], yet not in no form.” But he teaches it most openly while arguing against Marcion, for he says (*Against Marcion*, book II, ch. 27):

> “For we profess that Christ always acted in the name of God the Father: that he himself conversed from the beginning, that he himself met with the patriarchs and prophets—the Son of the Creator, his Discourse, whom he made Son by bringing him forth from himself . . . He was also disposed by the Father for those acts which you criticize as human, proclaiming from the very beginning the human being which he was to become at the end. He is the one who descended, who questioned, who asked, who swore, etc.”

If he conversed from the beginning, if from the very beginning he was human, as he was to be at the end, then in the very creation of the world—if one follows Tertullian—he was human. But he cannot be called human because he assumed human flesh from the beginning, for he assumed it at the end of the ages, when the most holy Mary supplied him with flesh. Therefore he can be called human because from the beginning he appeared in a human form or appearance, in which, if one follows Tertullian, he afterwards appeared to Abraham, Jacob, and the remaining patriarchs, and likewise to Moses and the other prophets.

30. In the same sense Prudentius teaches these things generally [Note: [Col. 0846D] In the *Apotheosis*, against the heresy that affirms that the Father suffered, poem I, v. 18 ff.]:

> Yet the image of the Father too, wherein he may lawfully be seen  
> to approach human eyes, was ready;  
> which dull sight, through its bluish mirror  
> and clouded, moisture-laden vision, could somehow approach.  
> Whoever among humankind is remembered to have seen God  
> saw the Son poured forth from him; for the Son is this:  
> he who, flashing forth from the Father, offered himself to be seen  
> through appearances which a human being could comprehend by sight.  
> For pure majesty is infinite and does not enter  
> the gaze unless it fashions itself through some moderation.

Then, again [Note: [Col. 0846D] Against the Unitarians, that is, the Sabellian heretics, poem II, v. 117.]:

> Rather search out the tokens of God in the very  
> fountainhead of antiquity; run through the records of the first  
> writer, whom no dull father or auguring grandfather,  
> no fable of old report, no chattering nurse,  
> no talkative diviner with clanging voice, nor shrill crow  
> taught about the matter of God; but God himself, openly revealed,  
> graciously instructed the trembling mortal with friendly speech,  
> and unfolded himself and his highest things.  
> Surely the most learned writer remembers that at that beginning  
> of the world the Father did not alone and without Christ  
> fashion the new material of creation.  
> “God,” he says, “made the human being and gave him  
> the face of God.” What else is that than to say that he was not alone?  
> God stood beside God at work,  
> when the Lord made the creature in the Lord’s image.  
> Christ is the Father’s form; we are Christ’s form and image;  
> by the Father’s goodness we are created in the countenance of the Lord,  
> Christ, who after ages was to come in our countenance.

31. Or does the Church have these matters in view when she orders this hymn to be sung [Note: [Col. 0846D] At Matins of the Lord, in Eastertide.]?

> Eternal King of heaven,  
> Creator of all things,  
> Son ever equal  
> to the Father before all ages.  
>
> When the world was being born, you, its Maker,  
> gave Adam the image  
> of your countenance and joined  
> a noble spirit to the clay.

Or, as it was formerly read more explicitly:

> Eternal King and Lord,  
> Creator of all things,  
> you who before all ages  
> were ever the Son with the Father.  
>
> You who at the world’s beginning  
> fashioned Adam, the human being,  
> and gave his face  
> likeness to your image.

32. But while discussing these matters, why do we pass over Leo the Great, who teaches generally that Christ appeared in human form to the most ancient Fathers, and therefore to Adam, the most ancient of the patriarchs, and who gives an elegant reason for this very fact?

> “The omnipotence of God could have appeared for the instruction and justification of humankind in the way it appeared to the patriarchs and prophets in the appearance of flesh, when it either entered into wrestling, engaged in conversation, did not refuse the duties of hospitality, or even ate food set before it. But those images were signs of that human being whose reality, to be taken from the stock of the preceding Fathers, mystical significations announced. And therefore no figures fulfilled the sacrament of our reconciliation, arranged before eternal times, because the Holy Spirit had not yet come upon the Virgin, nor had the power of the Most High overshadowed her, so that Wisdom, building a house for itself within her undefiled womb, the Word might become flesh; and so that the form of God and the form of a servant, converging into one person, the Creator of times might be born in time, and he through whom all things were made might himself be begotten among all things” (Letter XIII, in Quesnel’s edition XXVII, ch. 2).

33. Let us add Cassian, who teaches this (*On the Incarnation*, book IV, ch. 9):

> “This one, therefore, is he who spoke to the patriarchs, dwelt in the prophets, was conceived by the Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, seen in the world, conversed among human beings, fastening to the wood of the cross the bond-record of sins, triumphing in himself, killing by death the hostile and adversarial powers opposed to us, granting all the assurance of resurrection, and, by the glory of his body, destroying the corruption of human flesh.”

34. Our Eugubinus, Steuco, whom all know as a man of the highest distinction, appears to follow the traces of these Fathers, and especially of Prudentius, when he says (*Cosmopoeia*, Venetian edition of Nicoli, p. 159):

> “The Son and Word of God therefore came to the creation of the human being in human form, image, and appearance, bearing a most beautiful, most divine, and most pleasing form, surpassing the beauty of all human forms. Seeing and beholding it, the founder of our race must be thought to have gone mad with love and to have been almost consumed with desire for the Creator, more beautiful than all women. Assuming this appearance and divine beauty—most merciful and most beautiful—as he was, after many ages, to assume it even to flesh and bones, he created the human being, granting him this great appearance: he himself the first archetype, himself most beautiful, creator of a most beautiful offspring.
