How great and what kind of beauty do you think that first human being had? How great a grace of countenance, what charms must have dwelt in it?”

35. It is not for me now to determine what should be thought of the opinion of these writers. This at least is certain: by one or the other of these solutions, whatever is derived from those harsher expressions that I set forth in the title itself is resolved.

36. Nevertheless, while I make these observations, I do not wish anyone in our own times to use these expressions. For anyone who used them would give grounds for suspecting that he considered him who is commanded a servant, to use the warning of that ancient writer whom many call Gregory Thaumaturgus [Note: [Col. 0847D] In the *Exposition of the Faith*; yet Petavius, *On the Trinity*, book II, ch. 7, no. 8, Tillemont, *Ecclesiastical History*, tome IV, “Gregory Thaumaturgus,” art. 2, and others deny that it belongs to Thaumaturgus.]. Hence Gregory of Nyssa reproves Eunomius (*Against Eunomius*, book X) for saying “that the Son made the things made by the Father’s command, whereas he created them by his own power.”

37. Augustine also forbids the assertion (*Literal Commentary on Genesis*, book II, ch. 6) that “the Son is commanded by the Father, since he himself is the principal Word of the Father through whom all things were made. Moreover, it is unfitting that the Son should be understood to have made things as though commanded.” Elsewhere he says (*Against the Sermon of the Arians*, ch. 38): “I do not know why those men think that the Son obeyed a command before he received flesh.”

38. Likewise Idatius (*Against Varimundus*, book III), following Gregory of Nyssa, whom we have just mentioned, denies that the Son made the things made at the Father’s command, since he created by his own power.

## DISSERTATION III

On those words of chapter V (no. 100 ff.): **HE ALSO GRANTED THAT HUMANKIND SHOULD BEAR GOD’S IMAGE ON EARTH, INTENDING LATER TO GIVE THE LIKENESS, IF THE IMAGE WERE PRESERVED UNHARMED. DO NOT THINK THAT THIS OUTWARD FORM OF THE HUMAN BEING WAS MADE ACCORDING TO THE IMAGE**, etc.

1. The ancients discuss this subject very frequently—not only those who knew the divine Scriptures, but also those whom we know to have worshipped false deities.

Does not Ovid state this most explicitly (*Metamorphoses*, book I)?

> A holier creature, more capable of lofty mind,  
> was still lacking—one able to rule the rest.  
> Humankind was born, whether that maker of things,  
> the origin of a better world, made it from divine seed,  
> or whether the fresh earth, lately separated from the high  
> ether, still retained seeds of kindred heaven,  
> when the son of Iapetus, mixing it with flowing water,  
> shaped it in the likeness of the gods who govern all things.

2. Cicero too seems to have spoken in this sense when he introduces Paulus honoring humankind with the title of god:

> “Know, then,” says Paulus (*Dream of Scipio*), “that you are a god, if indeed a god is that which has vigor, perception, memory, foresight, and which rules, governs, and moves the body over which it has been set, just as that supreme God rules, governs, and moves this world.”

3. To proceed in order, we shall reduce the whole question to several principal headings. First, we shall inquire whether the image and likeness which God impressed upon us are two distinct things or only one. Second, we shall inquire wherein this image and likeness consist. Once these matters are established, the solution of a third question will follow as a corollary: in what part of the human being this image and likeness reside—whether in the body or in the soul. The solution of a fourth question will also follow: whether God impressed the image and likeness under discussion upon man alone—or, to speak more expressly, upon the male alone—or upon woman as well. Finally, the solution of a fifth question will follow: whether even an angel was made according to the likeness and image of God.

## FIRST QUESTION

Whether the image and likeness which God impressed upon us are two distinct things or only one.

4. Those who hold that only one thing, not two, is indicated here argue as follows. Let us, I pray, first recite the words on which the question rests. In Genesis 1, God, being about to create Adam, says this (vv. 26–27): “Let us make man in our image and likeness; and let him rule over the fish of the sea . . .” And God created man in his own image; in the image of God he created him; male and female he made them. Now, when this account is recalled, mention is made either of likeness alone or of image alone; thereafter the two are neither joined nor repeated. Why so? Unless because it was unnecessary for each to be expressly mentioned, since there is only one thing. Do you doubt the premise? We shall show it at once.

[Col. 0849C] Mention of likeness alone occurs in verse 1 of chapter 5, where what had been said in verses 27 and 28 of chapter 1 is recalled. Thus we read in the verse of chapter 5 just cited: “This is the book of the generation of Adam. On the day when God created man, he made him in the likeness of God; male and female he created them, and blessed them.” Conversely, in Genesis 9:6, Sirach 17, and elsewhere, image alone is mentioned. Thus the Scriptural passage first cited, namely verse 6 of Genesis 9, reads: “Whoever sheds human blood, his blood shall be shed; for man was made in the image of God.” And here are the words from Sirach to which I referred (17:1–2): “God created man from the earth, and made him according to [Col. 0849D] his own image. And again he turned him into it, and clothed him with power according to himself.” Likewise, in the First Epistle to the Corinthians (11:7): “A man indeed ought not to cover his head, because he is the image and glory of God.” Again, in the Epistle to the Colossians, chapter 3, verse 10: “And putting on the new man, who is renewed in knowledge according to the image of him who created him.”

5. Moreover, even where image and likeness are expressly joined in Scripture, those words denote nothing other than an outstanding likeness. Hear whether I speak truly. “Adam lived”—these are the words found in Genesis—“one hundred and thirty years, and begot in his image and likeness, and called his name Seth” (Gen. 5:3).

6. If you wish the Fathers to be added, we gladly add them. Let Augustine lead, teaching as follows (*Questions on Deuteronomy*, Question 4): “It is customary to ask what difference there is between likeness and image. But here I do not see what difference he intended, unless he signified one thing by these two terms,” etc.

Elsewhere, too, he uses “the image of God” for what is commonly attributed to likeness, as I shall say below. For he writes (*Exposition of Psalm* 57, no. 1): “All were made in the image of God, unless they wear down through earthly desires what he formed. . . .” And again (no. 3): “Why did you show Caesar’s image to your Creator, while you were blotting out his image in your hearts?”

7. Severian of Gabala is likewise of the same opinion: “What,” he asks, “[Note: [Col. 0849D] *Oration 5 on the Creation of the World*, no. 4, p. 284, vol. VI of Chrysostom’s works, Montfaucon edition.] does ‘according to the image’ mean? God is holy. If we are holy, we are according to the image of God. For he says: ‘Be holy, because I am holy.’ God is righteous. If we pursue righteousness, we are the image of God.”

8. Similarly, Ambrose places the image and likeness of God implanted in us in supernatural and moral virtues (*On Psalm* 118, octave 22), but in such a way that likeness differs not at all from image.

9. Peter Chrysologus likewise (*Sermon* 120): “Where,” he says, “the image itself of the Creator has been removed by the diseases of sins . . . [Col. 0850C] the Apostle Paul recalls us to Christ’s likeness and restores the whole form to the image of the Creator.” He proves this from the Apostle’s saying (Rom. 12:2): “Do not be conformed to this age,” etc. If you desire other Fathers of the same opinion, Petavius will furnish them (*On the Work of Creation*, II.2.10, 13); he indeed adduces Cyril of Alexandria to the same effect. [Note: [Col. 0849D] From the book *Against the Anthropomorphites* and from a manuscript catena.] He likewise adduces John Philoponus and Origen (*On the Work of the Six Days*, book II, ch. 2, no. 13). Having set these forth, he concludes that “it is more probable that Moses used both names for one and the same thing, and used them ἐκ παραλλήλου [in parallel], so that the latter is an explanation of the former.”

10. Philo had anticipated these observations (*On Creation*, p. 14, Lyons edition, 1561). For he says: “But since not every image resembles its archetypal model, and many are unlike it, after the words ‘according to the image’ there was added, more significantly, ‘and likeness,’ so that an exact impress, possessing a most evident form, may be understood.”

11. Others think otherwise and observe the following distinction between the image and likeness under discussion: either because image requires a more explicit and exact likeness—Augustine intimating this [Note: [Col. 0849D] “Where there is an image, likeness is immediately present. But where likeness is made, image is not immediately made,” etc., *Questions on Deuteronomy*, Question 4.] and Jerome of Arezzo stating it most expressly [Note: [Col. 0849D] In sermons not yet published, which I had copied from an ancient manuscript. He teaches this in a sermon for the twentieth Sunday after Pentecost: “Holy [Col. 0851D] Scripture likewise relates that God made man in his image and likeness. But image is more than likeness. For image is an expressed likeness of a thing, and is called imago [image], as though a true imitation. Likeness is some representation of things, as in the saying: ‘I saw men as trees walking.’ Therefore the Son of God is the image of the Father, because he is like the Father in every respect and unlike him in none. As Paul says: ‘Who is the image of the invisible God.’ For as is the Father, so is the Son: the Father almighty, the Son almighty; and so with the rest of those things predicated of the substance. Therefore the Son is truly image—that is, the express likeness of God the Father. Hence it was said: ‘Let us make man in our image.’ But man is made *to* the image, because Christ alone is the image; man, however, is made to the image, that is, that he may tend toward the image.” Lest you suppose Jerome of Arezzo unknown, consult what Ughelli reports, [Col. 0852D] *Italia Sacra*, vol. I, p. 467, and Cave after him, under the year 1144, p. 222, vol. II.]—or because image concerns the body and likeness the soul, as Irenaeus supposes (*Book V*, ch. 6); or because image indicates the natural gifts bestowed on Adam, while likeness indicates supernatural gifts. Hence, according to these writers, Adam retained the image after committing sin, but lost the likeness.

To remain among the ancient Fathers, Calmet cites Chrysostom, Severian of Gabala, Cyril of Alexandria, and finally Augustine, book VI of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 27 (*on this passage of Genesis*). He could have added many others, and certainly Origen and our own Writer, whom we shall subsequently cite; likewise Paulinus of Nola, Gregory of Nyssa, Maximus the Martyr, and quite a few others, whose passages Petavius lists (*On the Work of Creation*, book II, ch. 2, no. 13). Above all, this view is developed at greatest length by the author of the book *On Spirit and Soul*, [Col. 0851B] [Note: [Col. 0852D] Chapter 35. This book is found among Augustine’s works in the Maurist edition, pp. 35 ff. of the appendix to vol. IV.] which appears among Augustine’s works. Nor would I have you pass over Alcuin, who also treats the matter lucidly. [Note: [Col. 0852D] In the work entitled: “Sayings of Blessed Albinus the Levite on the passage from Genesis: ‘Let us make man,’ etc.,” p. 54 of Alcuin’s works. And, incidentally, though the Maurist Fathers had observed this before me, p. 611 of the appendix to vol. II of Ambrose, precisely the same material appears in chapter 3 of the book entitled *On the Dignity of the Human Condition*, formerly attributed to Ambrose.]

## SECOND QUESTION. In what does this image and likeness, of which we are speaking, consist?

12. How ancient this question is, and likewise how difficult to resolve, we readily learn from what Epiphanius relates. He treats of it both in the book in which he argues against heresies [Note: [Col. 0852D] Heresy 70, that of the Audians, nos. 2 and 3, and *Ancoratus*, no. 55.] and in the *Ancoratus*, summarizing the opinions of learned persons in this controversy. He concludes that “it must by no means be defined or affirmed in what part that image consists; but it must nevertheless be confessed to be in man, lest we remove the divine gift from the midst and distrust God’s authority” (*Heresy* 70, no. 2). Hence, in his judgment, the Audians, who place the image in question in the body, “being carried beyond due measure by contentious zeal in this matter, depart from ecclesiastical tradition and doctrine. For while it confesses that all human beings were created in God’s image, it defines no part in which the character of such an image should be thought to reside.”

He next rejects those “who hold that the image lies neither in soul nor body, but consists in virtue alone”; and also those “who say it is not virtue, but baptism and the grace bestowed in it.” Finally he determines as follows: “Thus one must believe that the image is found in man, especially in the whole, and does not reside simply [in one part]. But where it is chiefly found, and by what part the saying ‘according to the image’ is fulfilled, God knows—he who willed to endow the human race with this singular benefit of his image.”

13. Epiphanius’s view pleased few. They therefore investigated more carefully where it seemed preferable to place this image and likeness. In the preceding question we said that some Fathers located the image itself in the natural gifts bestowed upon us, but likeness in supernatural gifts. To these add not only the Writer whom we are illustrating—for he plainly teaches this in the words set before this dissertation: “He also granted that man should bear the image of God on earth, intending afterward [Col. 0852B] to give likeness, if the image were preserved uninjured,” etc.—but Origen also, whom our Writer seems plainly to follow. For Origen committed the following to writing: [Note: [Col. 0852D] Book III of *Peri Archōn*, or *On First Principles*, no. 1, p. 152, vol. I of the edition of Fr. Charles de la Rue.]

“For Moses indicates this before all others when, recounting the first creation of man, he says: ‘And God said: Let us make man in our image and likeness.’ Then he adds: ‘And God made man; in God’s image he made him; male and female he made them, and blessed them.’ Therefore, when he says that God made man according to the image of God but is silent concerning likeness, he indicates nothing else than that man received the dignity of the image in his first creation, whereas the perfection of likeness was reserved for consummation: namely, so that he himself might acquire it through the efforts of his own industry, by imitating God. Since the possibility of perfection was given him at the beginning through the dignity of the image, in the end he might himself, through the completion of works, bring perfect likeness to completion. But John the Apostle defines that these things are so more plainly and clearly when he declares thus: ‘Little children, we do not yet know what we shall be; but if it should be revealed to us concerning the Savior, you will doubtless say: we shall be like him.’ By this he most certainly indicates both the end of all things, which he says is still unknown to him, and the likeness of God to be hoped for, which will be bestowed through the perfection of merits. The Lord himself also indicates in the Gospel that these same things will come to pass, and indeed through his intercession, when he deigns to ask this of the Father for his disciples, saying: ‘Father, I will that where I [Col. 0853A] am, these also may be with me; and as I and you are one, so may they also be one in us.’ Here likeness itself seems already, if one may say so, to advance; and from being like, to become one—doubtless because at the consummation or end, God is all and in all.”

14. These two writers therefore hold that the likeness of which we speak is the blessedness to be obtained in heaven through the practice of virtues. Adam, if one considers strict right, deprived himself of it by sinning; nevertheless, stirred by divine mercy, he afterward recovered that very right.

15. Others, however—as I already said (Question I, no. 11)—place this likeness not in the attainment of blessedness after death, but in the virtues we possess in this very life. A stricter Scholastic, using the liberty of his own terminology, would readily express this as follows: “The likeness of God implanted in us does not consist in consummate blessedness and in the homeland, but in incipient blessedness and on the way; or, if you prefer, in the seed of heavenly blessedness”—for this is what they call the virtues—“not in blessedness itself, as in its fruit.”

But these writers do not entirely agree. Some, as we noted earlier from Epiphanius, place it in virtue—that is, in moral and natural virtue [Note: [Col. 0853D] Plato, *Laws*, after the middle, and *Theaetetus*, are commonly cited. See the passages in Petavius, *On the Work of Creation*, II.2.10.]—others in baptism and the grace bestowed in it, and therefore in supernatural virtue. [Note: [Col. 0853D] Paulinus of Nola, to omit the rest, places it in supernatural virtue, in the letter to Severus formerly numbered 2, now 24, no. 9: “for this reason,” etc.] Indeed, some seem to confine this likeness within narrower limits, restricting it to the class of virtues that the Scholastics call negative—that is, that whose object is the avoidance of evils—while assigning to image the class of virtues that pursue goods. They certainly interpret some words of Ambrose in this manner (*On the Good of Death*, ch. 5, no. 17): “Let us therefore flee these evils and transform our soul to that image and likeness of God. Flight from evils is likeness to God, and by virtues the image of God is acquired. Therefore he who painted us painted us, as the author, with the colors of virtues.”

16. Chrysostom likewise places this same likeness in supernatural virtues; I note his passage at the foot of the page. [Note: [Col. 0853D] No. 3 of the homily on “Lord, it is not in man,” vol. VI of the Montfaucon edition, p. 163.] So too Severian, [Note: [Col. 0854D] *Homily 5 on the Creation of the World*, no. 4, p. 484, vol. VI of Chrysostom.] and the author of the little work entitled *The Instruction of a Priest*, whether Bernard or another highly approved author. For he wrote: [Note: [Col. 0854D] Part I, ch. 1, p. 585, vol. III of the Venetian edition of St. Bernard’s works, 1727.]

“He created you when you did not exist; he recreated you when you had been lost. He created you that you might share in his blessedness; he recreated you lest, after your fall, you should remain deprived of the homeland and [Col. 0853D] deprived of eternal happiness. He created you in his image and likeness: in his image, by bestowing natural gifts upon you; in his likeness, by granting gratuitous gifts, so that you might excel in mind and overcome all irrational things by reason:

> While all other animals gaze downward toward the earth,  
> He gave man an exalted countenance and commanded him  
> To look upon heaven and lift his upright face toward the stars.

[Col. 0854A] “Thus, always looking upward, you might keep your Creator in mind and unceasingly recall your origin to your thoughts. For God made you, as has been said, in his image and likeness: in his image, that you might possess memory, understanding, discernment, and the other natural gifts; in his likeness, that you might possess innocence, righteousness, and other gratuitous gifts; in his image through knowledge of truth; in his likeness through love of virtue. Or certainly, you were made in God’s image through all these gifts bestowed upon you; you were made in his likeness, according to the essence of divinity, immortal and indivisible.”

17. From these final words you plainly perceive that he approves the opinion of those who place the image of God impressed upon humanity in natural gifts and [Col. 0854B] likeness in supernatural virtue; yet he does not disapprove the opinion of those who place it elsewhere. But Bernard most explicitly adopts the former opinion—if indeed you attribute the book of *Meditations* to Bernard—when he says: [Note: [Col. 0854D] *Meditations on the Knowledge of the Human Condition*, ch. 6, p. 371, vol. II of the Venetian edition, 1727.] “Therefore use yourself as God’s temple because of that in you which is like God. For the highest honor rendered to God is to venerate and imitate him. You imitate him if you are devout,” etc.

18. You will find several passages of Scripture cited for this opinion, such as that in Leviticus (11:44): “Be holy, because I am holy,” and others. But that passage in Matthew (5:44–45) seems better to me: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you; and pray for those who persecute and slander you, that you may be sons of your Father [Col. 0854C] who is in heaven”—that is, as Petavius rightly interprets it (*On the Work of Creation*, II.2.10), “that you may be like your Father who is in heaven.”

Almost all those who distinguish likeness from the image of God impressed upon us agree in this opinion.

19. Turning to the image of God implanted in us, I see six classes, as it were six principal divisions, of opinions on this question. Some have held that the image resides in something bodily. Others locate it in some spiritual attribute by which humanity agrees with God and is therefore in his image. In trying to identify and explain this, they have adopted various opinions, the chief of which I shall examine below. Others place it in a more explicit likeness that they posit between human beings and God, whether considered in his nature, or as triune, or as free from sin, or finally as blessed. Others locate it in the fact that, as God is the most perfect being, so man is the most perfect creature. Others seek this image in Christ and observe that Adam was said to be like God and in his image [Col. 0855A] because he was created like Christ; and consequently, like God not considered in his spiritual nature, but insofar as he assumed flesh—whether apparent, when he created man and afterward appeared to him, to the patriarchs, and to the prophets; or real and substantial, when he was incarnate in the most pure womb of the Virgin Mary. Finally, others indeed acknowledge that this image is in man, but profess ignorance as to wherein it resides.

20. To begin with the first class of opinions: the Audians, according to Epiphanius (*Heresy* 70, no. 2), “stubbornly considered the statement that Adam was created in God’s image to refer to the body. For, since it is written, ‘Let us make man in our image and likeness,’ it is immediately added that God fashioned man from dust taken from the earth. Since, therefore, Scripture says that man was formed from earth, you see that the whole thing fashioned from earth is most truly called man. It follows from this that it was said of that earthly thing that it would be created in God’s image.”

The Anthropomorphites followed the Audians in this matter, relying on the likeness which they imagined to exist between the divine and human body.

21. But who could endure this? Shall God impress his image upon a human body, when he is wholly spiritual and without any bodily mass? What theologians argue against the Anthropomorphites so thoroughly overthrows this opinion that there is no need to dwell on refuting it. I shall therefore cite Augustine alone, lest I seem to disregard the authority of the Excellent Doctor: “But you, brethren,” he says (*Exposition of Psalm* 48, no. 11), “consider yourselves to have been made in God’s image and likeness. God’s image is within; it is not in the body, not in these ears that you see, nor in eyes, nostrils, palate, hands, or feet. Yet it has been made: where understanding is, where mind is, where there is reason for investigating truth, where faith is, where your hope is, where your love is, there God has his image.”

And elsewhere (*Exposition of Psalm* 54, no. 3): “Moreover, beloved, we must remember that we were made in God’s image, and nowhere except in understanding itself. For in many respects we are surpassed by beasts; but where man knows himself to have been made in God’s image, there he recognizes in himself something more than was granted to cattle. When he considers all the things that man possesses, [Col. 0855D] he finds that he is properly distinguished from cattle by having understanding.” Epiphanius, arguing against the Audians, likewise shows this opinion to be utterly remote from plausibility (*Heresy* 70, no. 2). Theodoret does the same (*Questions on Genesis*, Question 20), and Zeno very briefly (book II, treatises 19–20, pp. 206–207, Verona edition of the Ballerini). Petavius nevertheless teaches that in some sense the human body also can be considered made in God’s image (*On the Work of Creation*, II.2.3), and adduces Augustine as guarantor, whose words I shall cite below [Col. 0856A] (no. 47), as well as Damascene (*Literary Eclogues*, A, no. 72).

22. Turning to those who hold that this image resides in some spiritual attribute by which man agrees with God and is thereby like him: many place it in virtue. To this opinion one may readily assign the Fathers whom Petavius cites in nos. 10 and 11 of chapter 2, book II of *On the Work of the Six Days*. They are Ambrose (*On the Good of Death*, ch. 5, no. 17), both in the passage already cited (no. 15) and elsewhere, where he writes (*On Luke*, book X, on chapter 12): “Christ alone is the full image of God, because of the expressed unity of the Father’s splendor in himself. But a righteous man is in God’s image if, in order to imitate the likeness of divine conduct, [Col. 0856B] he despises this world through knowledge of God and rejects earthly desires through reception of the Word, by which we are nourished unto life; whence we also eat Christ’s body, that we may be able to share in eternal life.” Also Chrysostom, Severian of Gabala (*Oration 5 on the Creation of the World*, no. 4, p. 484, vol. VI of the Montfaucon edition), the author of the homily entitled “That Man Cast Away God’s Image through Sin,” Cyril of Alexandria, and Gelasius, author of the history of the Council of Nicaea. [Note: [Col. 0855D] In the passages cited by Petavius, *On the Work of Creation*, book II, ch. 2, nos. 10–11.] Theodoret, whom I urge you to read (*Questions on Genesis*, Question 20), expounds and approves this opinion most carefully and copiously.

23. Add to these Jerome of Arezzo, whom I also cited earlier. Here is what this author teaches [Note: [Col. 0855D] In the sermon for the feast of All Saints.] in order to persuade us that God’s image consists in withdrawal [Col. 0856C] from sins and, to use the author’s own words, in purity. Explaining Christ’s words, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God,” he teaches concerning the image of God impressed on man:

“Purity of heart is placed sixth, because on the sixth day man was created in God’s image. For this purity is the image of God, by which, all disturbances being removed and every darkness of vices removed, we clearly see God. For those are called pure in heart who, having stripped off all *medullae* [uncertain; perhaps ‘defilements’] [Note: [Col. 0856D] The manuscript has *midull.*, a word whose meaning I entirely do not know; but perhaps it denotes defilements.] of worldly things, fix the gaze of their mind on contemplating God alone. This image had been darkened in man through fault, but now has been reformed through God’s grace. And now, on the sixth day—that is, in the sixth age—man has again been made in God’s image. This contemplation is the image of God, [Col. 0856D] because through it we imagine God for ourselves and, as it were, see God through an image, when by merit we follow him more than others; for unless a pure heart in man comes first, the image is not created.”

I do not wholly reject this opinion. In questions where there is much ambiguity in the word itself and its usage, we may assign very different meanings to the same word. Yet this explanation seems to have the disadvantage of attributing to image what distinguished men, including Jerome of Arezzo himself, attribute to likeness. [Col. 0857A] And you will find very few who affirm that the image of God impressed upon man from the beginning was abolished by sin.

Thus Augustine qualifies and, as it were, corrects what he had said in chapters 27 and 28 of book VI of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis* about the image of God being lost through sin (*Retractions*, book II, ch. 24): “What I said in the sixth book, that Adam lost by sin the image of God according to which he was made, should not be understood as though none remained in him, but as meaning that it had become so deformed as to require reformation.”

He gives the reason for this conviction when he observes that the image under discussion must be located in something perpetual and enduring forever (*On the Trinity*, book XIV, ch. 3, no. 4): “Far be it,” he says, [Col. 0857B] “that, since the nature of the soul is immortal and never afterward ceases to exist from the beginning in which it was created, that than which it has nothing better should not endure with its immortality. What, indeed, was created better in its nature than that it was made in the image of its Creator? Therefore the image of God which ought to be found is not in the retention, contemplation, or love of faith—which will not exist forever—but in that which will always exist.”

24. Others, however, place it not in such accidental qualities, as I may call them, but in essential ones. Yet they differ in trying to define and establish what these are. Many place this image in the spirit itself, or the human soul. But they do not at all agree whether the image should be placed in understanding, in will, or in both.

Philo teaches this, in Gelenius’s translation (*On Creation*, p. 13, Lyons edition, 1561): “The image is said to be according to the ruling mind of the soul; for in each person the mind is somehow fashioned after that unique archetype, and is the god, as it were, of the one who bears it about.” Clement of Alexandria seems to follow Philo (*Stromata*, book VI), teaching “that man was made in God’s image not on account of the form of his bodily structure, but because, just as God accomplishes all things by reason, so man, endowed with perfect thought, performs good and honorable actions by his rational faculty.” Zeno teaches related things (book II, treatises 19–20).

25. Augustine also approaches this opinion (*City of God*, book XII, ch. 23). After citing the words [Col. 0857D] “God therefore made man in his image and likeness,” he adds: “For he created in man such a soul that through reason and understanding he should excel all terrestrial, aquatic, and winged animals, which have no such mind.”

Elsewhere he is briefer, but no less explicit (*Tractate* III on John): “You differ from cattle only by understanding; do not glory in anything else. . . . How, then, are you better? By the image [Col. 0858A] of God. Where is God’s image? In the mind, in understanding.”

26. Prudentius, whom we shall cite below, may rightly be adduced for the same opinion; and so may Theodoret—or rather those cited by Theodoret—who located the image in question in the power of judgment bestowed on man. For, if you consider their thought thoroughly, that opinion may readily be reduced to understanding, or the capacity and power to understand and discern. If Theodoret declares that human understanding is not altogether like divine understanding, [Note: [Col. 0857D] “Again, after the likeness of God, Creator of all things, man rules and judges. But God, when he judges, has no need of accusers or witnesses. Thus he condemned Cain as an observer of his crime. [Col. 0858D] Man, however, needs witnesses and accusers in judging, because he does not know what has been done.”] who could doubt it? But it is one thing for man to be in some way like God in understanding itself, and another to be altogether like him. The latter, which Theodoret rightly rejects, we reject as well; the former we readily admit. [Col. 0858B] But whatever Theodoret may have thought, if anyone wishes to confirm and illuminate the opinion here proposed by the authority of another writer who is neither recent nor contemptible, let him, I pray, consult what the author of the book *On Spirit and Soul* teaches on this matter (ch. 36). I ask him, however, to consult the Maurist edition (*Appendix* to vol. VI of Augustine, p. 35), for in the margin of chapter 36, which I cite, he will find several passages from Bernard cited, from which this Writer seems to have copied what he teaches on this matter.

27. Those who place this same image in the will locate it in freedom. Tertullian favors them, teaching as follows (*Against Marcion*, book II, ch. 5): “I find that man was established by God free, possessed of choice and power over himself; observing no greater image and [Col. 0858C] likeness of God in him than the form of such a condition.” And afterward (ch. 6): “The image and likeness of God had to be constituted in free choice and self-power, in which the very image and likeness of God should be reckoned to consist—namely, freedom and power of choice.”

28. Jerome likewise writes: [Note: [Col. 0858D] In the letter formerly numbered 146; in the Verona edition, Letter 21 to Damasus, no. 40.] “God alone is one in whom sin cannot occur. All other beings, since they possess free choice—as does man, who was made in God’s image and likeness—can incline their will in either direction.”

Titus of Bostra similarly declares (*Against the Manichaeans*, book II): “God honored man by fashioning him in his image, so that, as he himself is good by the freedom of his nature, man might be an imitator of God through freedom of purpose—not abstaining from sin because power is lacking to nature itself, but honoring virtue through freedom of purpose.”

29. Does not Macarius indeed place the image of God of which we speak in freedom when he teaches this (*Homily* 15)? “You are in God’s image and likeness for this reason: just as God is his own master and has authority over himself and does what he wills . . . so you too have authority over yourself,” etc.

[Col. 0859A] 30. Marius Victor should be counted among these, for he represents God as speaking:

> “Now let us make man,” he says, “to rule the world,  
> And let him be God’s image. It is fitting that he be like his Creator,  
> Free in choice, enjoying with his mind the things created.”

31. Damascene and Bernard follow these. The former says (*On the Orthodox Faith*, book III, ch. 12): “Since man was made in the image of the blessed and supersubstantial divinity, and since the divine nature is in itself free, self-governing, and endowed with will, it follows that man, as its image, is free by his nature and endowed with will.” Bernard, moreover, observes that the image of God resides in freedom of choice (*On Grace and Free Choice*, ch. 9, no. 18).

[Col. 0859B] 32. Ambrose seems to locate this same image principally in understanding, but also in freedom, when he writes (*Hexaemeron*, ch. 8, otherwise no. 45):

“Therefore flesh cannot be in God’s image; rather, it is our soul, which is free and wanders here and there through expansive thoughts and counsels, surveying all things by contemplation. Behold, we are now in Italy, yet we think of matters which seem to concern eastern or western regions; we seem to be among those situated in Persia, and we see those living in Africa, if that land has received persons known to us. We follow those departing, remain with travelers, unite ourselves with those absent, speak with those separated from us, and even raise the dead again for conversation; we embrace and hold them as living, and render them the offices and services of life. That, therefore, is in God’s image which is measured not by bodily means but by the vigor of mind: which sees those absent, visits transmarine things by sight, traverses them by vision, searches hidden things, and in a single instant carries its senses here and there through the bounds of the whole world and the secrets of the universe; which is joined to God, clings to Christ, descends into hell, and ascends; which moves freely in heaven. Finally, hear the one who says: ‘But our commonwealth is in heaven.’”

The author of *The Instruction of a Priest*, whether Bernard or someone else, whom I cited in no. 16, may readily be assigned to the same opinion: “In the image, that you might possess memory,” etc.

33. The author of the book *On Spirit and Soul*, long attributed to Augustine, finds the same image in the remarkable manner in which the soul exists in the body, animates it, [Col. 0859D] and acts most excellently through it. It is pleasing to quote his ingenious observations, so that the reader may weigh them and compare them with the writers cited by the Maurist Fathers in the margin of this little work (ch. 35):

> “Not only because man was so excellently created by the Creator according to the counsel of the holy Trinity, but also because the Creator of all things created him in His own image and likeness—something granted to no other creature. This image must be considered more carefully in the dignity and nobility of the inward man. First, just as God, one and whole, is always everywhere, giving life to, moving, and governing all things—as the Apostle says (Acts 17:28), ‘in him we live and move and are’—so the soul is vigorous throughout its body, whole everywhere, giving it life, moving it, and governing it. For it is not greater in the larger members of its body and smaller in the smaller ones; rather, it is whole in the smallest and whole in the greatest. It is so infused into the body that it is not divided part by part according to the parts of the members. For wherever a part of the body is struck, the whole soul feels pain.
>
> “In a wonderful manner, presiding over the members by one and the same vivifying power, while it is itself not diverse by nature, it nevertheless performs diverse functions through the body. For it is that which sees through the eyes, hears through the ears, smells through the nostrils, tastes through the mouth, and touches through all the members; and by touching distinguishes smooth from rough. Though it is not diverse, it nevertheless performs diverse functions through the senses. From this it is understood that the soul is, according to its own manner, in its body as God is in His world. For it is inward and outward, above and below: above by governing, below by bearing; inward by filling, outward by surrounding. It is within so as to be without; it surrounds so as to penetrate; it presides so as to bear; it bears so as to preside. And just as God neither increases when creatures increase nor decreases when they decrease, so the soul is neither diminished when its members are reduced nor enlarged when they are increased. This is the image or likeness of almighty God which the soul possesses in itself.”

34. The author of the book *On the Dignity of the Human Condition*, long believed to be Ambrose, taught precisely the same thing when he wrote:

[Note: [Col. 0859D] In the book *On the Dignity of the Human Condition*, ch. 2. See, I beg you, what the Maurist Fathers teach concerning this writer, p. 612 of the appendix to vol. II of Ambrose. One point is certain: these words, and other passages of this little work tending to the same conclusion, occur in that work of Alcuin [Alchuvinus], [Col. 0860D] entitled *Sayings of Blessed Albinus the Levite on the Words of Genesis, “Let Us Make Man,” etc.* Thus it is clear that the work entitled *On the Dignity of Man* has been pieced together chiefly from Alcuin.]

> “Just as God, one and whole, is always everywhere, giving life to, moving, and governing all things, so the soul is vigorous throughout its body, whole everywhere, giving it life, moving it, and governing it.”

35. While enumerating other marks of the soul—either the very ones we have previously described or others wholly akin to them—in which he also places the image of which we speak, Prudentius mentions the soul’s eternity, writing as follows:

[Note: [Col. 0860D] In the *Apotheosis*, under the heading “On the Nature of the Soul,” v. 21.]

> It is like unto the ages, because it is consumed by none;  
> [Col. 0860D] because it is wise, capable of justice, and, as queen of things,  
> commands, foresees, weighs, provides against, and presses onward;  
> maker of words and manners, furnished with a thousand  
> arts, and taught to traverse heaven in thought:  
> by these qualities the Creator fashioned the soul in likeness to Himself.

Prudentius joined these features together with praise and good reason. For if you take any one of these attributes separately, it seems by no means adequate for establishing the image of God in the soul. Indeed, if you consider these things, you will declare an angel more like God than a human being, since they shine more clearly in an angel than in [Col. 0861A] man. Yet whether the image of God of which we speak is impressed upon an angel is rightly doubted.

Moreover, if we dispute about eternity, it is not of such a nature as by itself to make something like God. Do we not hold that the matter of which the empyrean consists will endure eternally? Yet who would call it like God, or place God’s image in it? The demons themselves, and souls tormented in hell, will endure perpetually. Are they therefore like God?

Apply these very considerations, if you wish, should anyone, fortified by the authority of Faustus of Riez and Maximus the martyr, place the image of God of which we speak in eternity.

[Note: [Col. 0861D] Read Petavius, *On the Works [of Creation]*, bk. II, 2, 14.]

36. Others have located it in the power to construct and establish buildings. I have seen their opinion set forth, described, and rejected in the following manner:

[Note: [Col. 0861D] Theodoret, *Questions on Genesis*, question XX, translated by Giovanni Pico.]

> “There are other respects in which man imitates God. For in imitation of God the Creator, man constructs houses, walls, cities, harbors, ships, shipyards, chariots, and countless other things, as well as images and figures of heaven, the sun, moon, and stars, likewise forms of human beings and of irrational animals. Yet there is an infinite difference in the manner of creating. For God creates all things from things which are and which are not, and does so without labor or time; because, as soon as He wills, He brings forth whatever pleases Him. Man, however, requires material; he needs instruments, deliberation, time, labor, and substantial arts for constructing a work. Thus an architect needs a smith, while a smith needs metals and coals; [Col. 0861C] likewise, all who cut timber depend upon those who cultivate plants or the land. In this manner each art borrows the use of other arts. Nevertheless, when man constructs something in this way, he somehow imitates the Creator, as an image imitates its archetype. For an image possesses the form of its archetype; but although it has the appearance of limbs, it does not have their actions. For it lacks the soul by which the body is moved.”

37. Others place it in a likeness to the Most Holy Trinity. But when they endeavor more carefully to identify this same likeness, they differ somewhat. Some who cite Damascene—

[Note: [Col. 0861D] From the book which he entitled *How We Were Made in the Image of God*. Vol. I of Le Quien’s edition, p. 573.]

—whether rightly, let others judge—adduce other grounds, but also this one: that Adam imitated the divine processions, in that he himself was not begotten, Abel was begotten, [Col. 0861D] and Eve proceeded. But the author of the book *On Spirit and Soul*, whom I also cited above, presents the matter somewhat differently, and teaches that two images of the Holy Trinity may be considered in the soul. The first is that, just as God is, lives, and knows, so the soul, according to its own mode, is, lives, and knows. (In this respect the author of the little book *On the Dignity of the Human Condition* agrees entirely, expressly teaching: “Just as God is, lives, and knows, so the soul, according to its own mode, is, lives, and knows.”) The second lies in the various correspondences [Col. 0862A] which the soul has with the Most Holy Trinity.

It is pleasing to expound this latter point, which that author treats more fully, in his own words (ch. 35):

> “It also possesses a certain image of the holy Trinity: first, in that, just as God is, lives, and knows, so the soul, according to its own mode, is, lives, and knows. There is also another Trinity in it, because it was created in the image of the perfect and supreme Trinity which is in Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Although the soul is of one nature, it nevertheless has three powers within itself: understanding, will, and memory. The same thing, though in other words, is indicated in the Gospel when it is said: ‘You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind’; that is, with all your understanding, [Col. 0862B] all your will, and all your memory.
>
> “For as the Son is begotten from the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, so will is begotten from understanding, and memory proceeds from both, as anyone wise can easily understand. For the soul cannot be perfect without these three, nor can any one of these three be complete, with respect to its proper condition, without the other two. And just as God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit are not three Gods but one God and three persons, so the soul’s understanding, the soul’s will, and the soul’s memory are not three souls in one body, but one soul and three powers.
>
> “In these three our inward man wonderfully bears the divine image in his own nature; and from these, as from the higher powers of the soul, we are commanded to love the Creator, so that He may be loved insofar as He is understood, and, insofar as He is loved, may always be held in memory. Nor is understanding concerning Him alone sufficient unless the will becomes love of Him. Indeed, these two are not sufficient unless memory is added, by which God may always remain in the mind of one who understands and loves. Thus, just as there can be no moment in which a human being does not use or enjoy God’s goodness and mercy, so there may be no moment in which he does not have Him present in memory. Therefore it seems to me rightly said that our inward man is the image of God.”

In this final description the author of the little work entitled *On the Dignity of Man*, formerly attributed to Ambrose, as we have said, agrees. Concerning the author of this work, see what we stated at no. [Col. 0862D] 34.

38. Augustine and Theodoret had pursued the same argument long before these writers. Augustine places the likeness between the soul, of which we speak, and the Most Holy Trinity in the correspondence of mind, love, and knowledge—or cognition—with the divine Persons; alternatively, memory, understanding, and will.

[Note: [Col. 0862D] *On the Trinity*, bk. IX, ch. 4 and following; again bk. XII, and the final chapter of bk. XIV.]

39. Jerome of Arezzo likewise explains the likeness of which we speak by the likeness that man has to the Most Holy Trinity, [Col. 0863A] and proposes nearly the same account as Augustine.

[Note: [Col. 0863D] See what we said concerning him at no. 11.]

Here is what he teaches (*Sermon for the Twentieth Sunday after Pentecost*):

> “When He said ‘likeness,’ He adds here ‘our,’ referring the likeness to the Trinity, since there is in man a certain likeness of the Trinity. For God created three things in man: memory, intellect, and will, by which he has a certain indivisible likeness with the Trinity. He is likened to the Father through memory; conformed to the Son through intellect; joined to the Holy Spirit through will. For just as the Father is from no one, but the Son is from Him, so memory, although it is a power of the soul, is from none of those powers, but intellect is from it. And just as the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, so will [Col. 0863B] proceeds from memory and intellect. For unless memory first apprehended a thing, intellect would not grasp it, nor would will subsequently seek it. Behold how man was made in the likeness of God.”

Theodoret’s opinion is not unlike this. He says (*Questions on Genesis*, question XX):

> “For the human soul has within itself rational and vital faculty; the mind produces discourse [*sermo*, λόγος], and spirit accompanies discourse—not begotten as discourse is, but perpetually following it and accompanying it as it is uttered.”

Damascene, however, finds another correspondence between the human soul and the Most Holy Trinity, as follows (*Third Oration on Images*, no. 20):

> “Just as the Father, who is mind, the Son, who is Word, and the Holy Spirit are one God, [Col. 0863C] so mind, word, and spirit are one human being.”

These observations, as I noted, taken from the third oration *On Images*, are almost repeated in the little work entitled *How the Image of God Is Impressed upon Man*.

40. Are we to take these matters strictly? Nothing could be further from the case. For if we submit the first explanation to examination, several matters arise which involve no slight difficulty. Whatever it may have been—image, likeness, or both—it would not have ceased in Adam but would have been transmitted to his descendants, had he remained innocent. It therefore cannot be placed in his not having been begotten.

But if we take the term “begotten” strictly, who would call Adam begotten of God? Strictly taken, that word indicates consubstantiality. Is Adam consubstantial with God? Moreover, if you consider the soul, Adam is said to have been created by God, not begotten; if the body, Adam is said not to have been begotten but formed. For he consists of a body, whereas God does not; and his soul itself is a spirit far inferior to God, inasmuch as it is created, mutable, and separated from the divine substance by an infinite interval. Does Adam, then, represent the generation of the divine Word?

Yet if you still insist on representing it at all, observe, I beg you, how aptly he represents it. Did Adam not have a son after Eve had been formed from his rib? Does the Father, however, have the Son after the Holy Spirit has proceeded? You wish the procession of the Spirit to be indicated by Eve’s being drawn from Adam’s rib; although, to omit other points, Eve was formed from Adam’s rib, whereas the Holy Spirit was not formed but proceeds in an ineffable and wholly divine manner.

III. Adam has a son by a woman, not from himself alone. Does this represent the generation of the divine Son? IV. Adam had many children, both male and female, both good and evil. Is this an image of the generation of God’s Only-Begotten Son? V. Adam had a son by Eve, who was formed from him; and her formation is said to suggest the procession of the Holy Spirit. Does the Father have a Son from the Holy Spirit? Thus far we have remained with the generation of the Son.

[Col. 0864B] 41. Nor is the procession of the Holy Spirit more successfully represented by the procession or production of Eve from Adam’s rib. For, leaving aside what I said above about that procession, the Holy Spirit proceeds by spiration; He proceeds not from the Father alone but also from the Son, and proceeds from the love of the Father and the Son. Do these things have any likeness or image in Eve’s procession—or rather formation—from Adam’s rib?

It remains, therefore, as I have already said, that the likeness and image of the Trinity which we described at no. 37 from another’s opinion must be understood in a very broad, not strict, sense. Nor do you find this expressly in Damascene, whom I have seen cited in support of this explanation. Whether this is because they cite manuscripts different from those possessed by Le Quien, whose edition [Col. 0864C] I use, I do not know. But these are the only words I find in him which I am pleased to quote here (*Third Oration on Images*, no. 20):

> “The third kind of images consists of things made by God through imitation: for example, man. … For just as the Father, who is mind, the Son likewise Word, and the Holy Spirit are one God, so mind, word, and spirit are one human being. Again, man imitates God by freedom of choice and authority to rule; for He says, ‘Let us make man in our image and likeness,’ and adds, ‘And rule over the fish of the sea,’ etc.”

But in the little work which he entitled *How Man Is in the Image of God*, he repeats much of what we have just cited, and then adds the following (p. 573, vol. I, Venetian edition):

> “When there is discourse concerning God, one God is celebrated [Col. 0864D] and worshipped in three hypostases: one Godhead, one nature, one force and power, one will; three persons and three hypostases, each with its own property. For the property of the Father is unbegottenness; the property of the Son, birth; and the property of the Spirit, procession. God is the Father, who lacks a beginning; God is the Son, who likewise has no beginning, although He is from the Father; God is the Holy Spirit, coeternal with both and likewise without beginning: proceeding from the Father, not after the manner of the Son, so as to be begotten like the Son, but by procession. The three are one in Godhead and in three hypostases.”

[Col. 0865A] 42. The other explanations offered by the author of *On Spirit and Soul*, the author of the little book *On the Dignity of the Human Condition*, Augustine, and Theodoret seem less broad and may suitably be admitted, provided that, first, you do not restrict them solely to human beings but make them common to angels; second, you acknowledge that these eminent doctors have sometimes not observed the order of the processions with exactness; and third, you recognize that, of the two likenesses we have explained from Augustine and Theodoret, the one placed in mind, knowledge, and love is less broad than that placed in understanding, will, and love, or in something akin to it.

Indeed, Theodoret himself passes this judgment on the opinion cited at no. 38:

> “These belong to man as to an image; for this reason neither discourse nor spirit subsists by itself. But in the Most Holy Trinity we understand three hypostases, united without confusion and subsisting in themselves. For before the ages God the Word was begotten from the Father, yet He is inseparable from His Begetter; and the Holy Spirit proceeds from God the Father and is understood in His proper hypostasis.”

The explanation drawn from Jerome of Arezzo also has the further disadvantage that, by making memory prior to the other two powers, it departs from the common conviction of all philosophers and theologians—for all hold intellect to be prior to memory—and approaches too closely the doctrines of the ancient Platonists and other pagan philosophers. They held, namely, that before being infused into the body the soul was endowed with memory and richly supplied with a clear knowledge of many things it had already learned. Would a Catholic propose these things?

43. Or will you say that the image of God is impressed upon man because, just as the Father, who is mind, the Son, who is Word, and the Holy Spirit are one God, so mind, word, and spirit are one human being? Are those things which we recognize in man—or, to speak more expressly, in the human soul—three hypostases and one substance or essence, as Father, Word, and Spirit are three hypostases and one God?

If such a correspondence sufficed to establish the image of God in man, you could easily place it in the human body. For the body belongs to the essence [Col. 0865D] of man, and man cannot be perceived without the body, just as the Most Holy Trinity cannot be conceived without the three divine persons. Yet who would place that image in the human body? It is therefore clear that likenesses of this sort—or, if you wish to call them so, images—are by no means strict but very broad. If this is sufficient for you, I shall indeed admit that the image of the Most Holy Trinity is impressed upon the soul, also for the reason you adduced from Damascene.

44. Those who place the image of which we speak in the blessedness which man will finally obtain when he sees God face to face in heaven cite these words of Ambrose (*Hexaemeron*, bk. VI, ch. 8, no. 45):

[Note: [Col. 0865D] They place this image in a more explicit likeness than that which they posit between man and God insofar as man is blessed. Recall no. 19.]

> “Is he not, then, in the image of God, in which God always is? But hear that he is in God’s image, for the Apostle says (2 Corinthians 3:18): ‘We all, therefore, beholding the glory of God with unveiled face, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord.’”

45. For my part, I do not hesitate to admit that a certain image may be located in blessedness, though Origen and the writer whom we are elucidating preferred to call it a likeness rather than an image. Recall no. 13. But most hold that, besides the image reserved by God for the life to come, another image was also impressed by God upon man in this life which we live.

Therefore, even if I grant that what they contend for is signified by Ambrose’s words—although they are somewhat obscure—I do not immediately concede that the image of which we speak must be extended to another life, the one which is to follow our death. Indeed, to remain with Ambrose himself: shortly before this I cited Ambrose’s opinion from that very no. 45 which they quoted, in which he teaches that the image of which we here speak is implanted in our soul, which is free and wanders here and there in its expansive thoughts and counsels.

46. Is there, then, anything else in which you might place this same image? There certainly is. If you ask what it is, I shall indicate it at once.

First, then, man may in some sense be called the image of God insofar as, just as God contains within Himself the perfections and excellences of all beings and causes, and is therefore called by philosophers the cause of causes, so man contains within himself the perfections and excellences of all creatures, and is therefore called the microcosm, or little world, and the most perfect of all creatures. What I have said of God is undoubtedly true. It remains, then, briefly to show what I have asserted concerning man.

Let us first consider man, so to speak, part by part. How excellent the human body is, and by what great interval it surpasses in appearance and form brute animals, has long ago been shown by very distinguished men; among them I name Lactantius, whom I urge you to read (*On the Workmanship*, bk. I). Long before Lactantius, Cicero wrote (*On Duties*, bk. I): “Nature herself has imposed upon us a character marked by excellence and superiority [Col. 0866D] over the other animals.” The very appearance and countenance of man plainly show how greatly he surpasses other animals in excellence and dignity. For, if you look upon those animals, in Boethius’s words (*Consolation of Philosophy*, bk. V, 5):

> You may see all things differing in diverse forms;  
> yet their downward-facing aspect can weigh down dull senses.  
> The human race alone raises its lofty head on high,  
> and, light of frame, stands with upright body and looks down upon the earth.

47. Augustine treats this argument (*On Genesis against the Manichees*, bk. I, ch. 17, no. 28), for he does not hesitate to suggest that even the human body may in some way be seen as made in God’s image, because it indicates that we are better than beasts:

> “For the bodies of all animals—whether they live in waters, on land, or fly in the air—bend toward the earth and are not upright as the human body is. By this it is signified that our mind also ought to be raised toward what is above it, that is, toward eternal spiritual things. Thus it is understood that man was made in the image and likeness of God chiefly through the mind, with the upright form of the body also bearing witness.”

Elsewhere he repeats this in the following words (*Eighty-Three Questions*, question 51, nos. 2–3):

> “How it is not incongruous to say that even the body was made in God’s likeness is easily understood by one who carefully considers the statement, ‘And God made all things very good’ (Genesis 1:31). For no one doubts that He Himself is supremely good. The human body also, because alone among the bodies of terrestrial animals it is not prone and cast down upon its belly, while still visible, but is upright for beholding heaven … and because it is such as to be more suited for contemplating heaven, may be seen in this respect as made more in the image and likeness of God than the other bodies of animals.”

48. Potho of Prüm likewise suggests this very point (*On the State of the House of God*, bk. I, near the end; vol. IX of the Paris edition of the *Library of the Fathers*, p. 569), insofar as he commends the beauty of the body in such a manner as to testify that the work of wisdom is displayed through the body’s diverse functions.

49. But why do we not cite Damascene? Drawing from an ancient writer whom Father Le Quien says was Methodius in the book *On the Resurrection*, he teaches the following:

[Note: [Col. 0867D] In the *Eclogae*, or *Parallels*, letter A, title VIII, Le Quien edition, vol. II, p. 310.]

> “Who joined together the hard substance of the bones? Who bound the limbs so that they might be stretched by sinews and relaxed by bending about the joints? Who, by suffusing it with blood, leavened the humors and soft flesh derived from earth? Surely God alone, the most excellent artificer, who fashioned man—that is, His rational and animated image, namely us—and from moist and very small seed in the mother’s womb shaped him as from wax. For who provides that the fetus, overwhelmed by an abundance of fluid and compression of the vessels, is not suffocated within? Or who, after it has been carried in the womb and finally brought forth into the light, makes it from weak and tiny into something great, beautiful, and strong, except that same most excellent Creator God of whom I have just spoken, who by the efficacy of His power, like a painter, changes forms in diverse ways? God is immortality, life, and incorruption; but the work of God is man. … Yet concerning man He did not likewise say, ‘Let [the earth] bring forth,’ but, ‘Let us make man in our image and likeness.’ And God took dust from the earth and fashioned him.”

He teaches related things in the *Parallels*, in the passage cited at the foot of the page.

[Note: [Col. 0868D] P. 760—erroneously numbered 748—of vol. II of Father Le Quien’s edition. I urge the reader to consult it.]

50. But if you consider the human mind, between man and beast “this is the chief difference,” to use Cicero’s words again (*On Duties*, bk. IV, 11): “The beast adapts itself only insofar as it is moved by sense, and only to that which is at hand and present, with exceedingly slight awareness of past or future. Man, however, being endowed with reason, by which he perceives consequences, sees causes of things and is not ignorant of their progressions and, as it were, antecedents, compares likenesses, joins and connects future things to present ones, readily sees the whole course of life, and prepares what is necessary for directing it. By the same power of reason, nature unites human being with human being for fellowship in speech and life; above all it implants a particular and preeminent love toward those whom people have begotten, and impels them to desire that gatherings and assemblies of human beings should exist and should be attended by themselves.”

51. To these add, lest I bring forward many witnesses, what Augustine teaches on this subject (*Eighty-Three Diverse Questions*, question 51, no. 3). I select a few words:

> “Not without reason,” he says, “is this man also said to share in the likeness of God, not only because he lives—which is also evident in beasts—but more especially because he turns to the mind that governs him, which wisdom illumines, something impossible for beasts, since they lack reason.”

Recall what we cited from Philo, Clement of Alexandria, and other Fathers at nos. 24 and 26, and again from Ambrose at no. 32.

52. The union itself of soul and body, although after man fell into sin—and thus fell from that most excellent state of innocence in which he was created—it has become somewhat disadvantageous to him, because the corruptible body weighs down the soul, though it would have been most beneficial had he remained in his former dignity and obedience to God, nevertheless is not even now without its benefits. It will finally make man a participant in the fullness of blessedness, which he will enjoy if he uses his body for the purpose for which man was created: namely, to obey and comply with the divine commands. Will not this body, which is sown in corruption, rise in incorruption? … And what is sown a natural body will rise a spiritual body (1 Corinthians 15:42, 44)?

A certain eminent and truly heavenly delight and sweetness will be poured into the body itself. Imbued and, as it were, absorbed by it, the body will suffer not merely no inconvenience from its mass and, if you permit the expression, its corporeity; rather, it will derive from it a most pleasant and altogether wonderful joy. Among many others who discuss this subject, the eminent Cardinal Bellarmine does so especially in the little work entitled *On the Happiness of the Saints*. Vindelinus, in the preface to his *Particular Physics*—an admittedly learned and ingenious philosopher, but the bitterest enemy of Bellarmine and indeed of all Catholics—declares that this little work contains more truth than those great books of controversies. By that judgment, while displaying his ill will toward Catholics, he nevertheless gives remarkable commendation to the little work in question.

[Col. 0869A] 53. Given these points, it is not surprising, first, that great and magnificent praises are attributed to man and that writers sometimes call him, as I said earlier, a little world; sometimes the most perfect of all creatures; sometimes the epitome of the whole creation; sometimes even every creature. They later explain this by saying either that he possesses formally the perfections of all creatures, or at least possesses them eminently.

[Note: [Col. 0869D] “If men can know it, within whom the world itself also exists, and each is an example of God in a small image.” Manilius, *Astronomics*, IV.]

He is called a little world because he seems alone to contain within himself whatever is dispersed among the other creatures; for this reason he is also called the epitome of all creation. They wish him to be called the most perfect of all creatures because he surpasses inanimate things by his excellence and by the spirit through which he is vivified; while he surpasses the angel by that very union of soul and body which we have just explained, on account of which he will attain a fuller blessedness in heaven.

54. They explain what I said concerning perfections possessed either formally or eminently as follows. Just as God possesses all perfections either formally—those, namely, which immediately display their excellence and involve no imperfection—or eminently—for He is said to possess eminently those perfections whose notion includes some imperfection, as does the perfection of creatures, since He possesses them all while setting aside every imperfection—so man possesses all the perfections which a creature can attain either actually and formally, such as a spiritual soul and an excellent and noble body; or eminently, that is, in such a way that he surpasses, or at least includes, the perfection which you admire in other creatures, or is at least equivalent to it.

Thus he has formally—that is, expressly and in itself—the goodness or perfection suited to himself, and eminently that of the other animals. For by the powers of his intellect and mind he is more perfect and excellent than animals, which, as we have said, he surpasses in intelligence and art, even if he is surpassed by them in strength. Hence it is much better to be a human being than a lion, bear, or any other brute animal. Likewise, he possesses a notable beauty suited to his kind, which, if you weigh it more carefully, surpasses that possessed by a field or by any other things endowed with striking appearance.

The ancient Fathers sometimes indicate what I have thus far pursued in the manner of the Scholastics: for example, Augustine (*On the Greatness of the Soul*, ch. 33, no. 70), Damascene (in the little work entitled *How Man Is in the Image of God*), and, more fully, Gregory the Great, whose words it is pleasing to quote here:

[Note: [Col. 0870D] Homily 29 on the Gospels, on the words, “Preach the Gospel to every creature,” Mark 16.]

> “Was the Holy Gospel, my brothers, to be preached to senseless things or brute animals, that it should be said to the disciples, ‘Preach to every creature’? But by the name of every creature, man is signified. For there are stones, but they neither live nor feel; there are herbs and shrubs, which live indeed but do not feel. … There are angels, [Col. 0870A] who live, feel, and discern. Yet man has something of every creature: he has being in common with stones, life with trees, sensation with animals, and understanding with angels. Therefore, if man shares something with every creature, in one respect man is every creature. Thus the Gospel is preached to every creature when it is preached to man alone, because he is taught for whose sake all things on earth were created, and from whom all things are not alien through a certain likeness.”

55. The ancient philosophers and poets had already discerned this same point before our doctors instructed in the Christian faith. I pass over Ovid, whose well-known verses (*Metamorphoses*, bk. XV),

> We too are a part of the world, since we are not bodies alone,  
> but winged souls,

are thought to confirm the point we have stated, insofar as they suggest that man—“we”—is the most excellent part of the world and contains its other parts. I pass over Ovid, I say, in order to cite more explicit passages from ancient writers. Does Cicero not seem to you to speak clearly when he says (*On the Universe*): “God made man, one visible living creature in whom all living creatures were contained”?

56. And what is clearer than these observations of Manilius (*Astronomics*, bk. IV)?

> … What wonder that human beings can know the world,  
> within whom the world itself exists,  
> and each is an example of God in a small image?

By these verses he indicates quite plainly that the image of God is rightly and deservedly located, reason being its guide and, as it were, teacher, in that excellence of man and comprehensive possession of all perfections of which we speak.

Could we not also, to turn our discourse to the most illustrious writers among the Hebrews, say that Philo himself teaches the same thing—Philo whom Jerome calls “the most eloquent of the Jews” (*On Illustrious Men*, ch. 2)—when he sets forth on this subject matters which, since I have reported them elsewhere, need not be repeated here? Yet let the reader recall them.

57. Once these points have been established, it is no wonder that God subjected all things to man, or at least commanded the remaining creatures to be obedient to him and to bring him assistance and help—one might almost say, household service—and willed man in this very respect to be like himself. Do you doubt it? [Col. 0870D] Hear the Lord himself declare it (*Gen.* 1:26): “Let us make man in our image and likeness, and let him have dominion over the fishes of the sea, the birds of heaven, the beasts, the whole earth, and every creeping thing that moves upon the earth.” On these words Chrysostom writes (*Homily* 8 on *Genesis*, no. 3):

> For when he says, “Let us make man according to our image and likeness,” he did not end his discourse there; rather, by what he adds, he makes clear to us in what sense he used the name “image.” For what does he say? “And let him rule over the fishes of the sea, the birds of heaven, [Col. 0871A] and all creeping things upon the earth.”” He therefore spoke of the image in relation to sovereignty and dominion, and not to anything else: because God made man ruler of all things upon the earth; nothing upon earth is greater than man, and all things are under his authority.

And again (*Homily* 10, no. 4):

> After he taught us by what preceded what it means that “he made him according to the image of God,” and in order to leave not even an impudent pretext of defense to those wishing to assail the doctrines of the Church, proceeding a little further he again teaches the same thing: that he used the word “image” because man was to rule and to have all creatures under himself.

And, after a few intervening words (no. 5):

> Have you seen the indescribable [Col. 0871B] power? Have you seen the greatness of this sovereignty? Have you seen all created things reduced beneath his authority? Henceforth imagine nothing mean concerning this rational creature; rather, consider the greatness of its honor and the Lord’s benevolence toward it, standing in awe of his boundless and indescribable goodness.

He repeats the same point elsewhere (*Book I to Stagirius*), warning that “God willed man to be on earth what he himself was in heaven.” See also what he teaches to this effect in Homily II on the Epistle to the Hebrews (no. 2).

58. Gregory of Nyssa had preceded Chrysostom in this explanation; Severian of Gabala and Theodoret follow him. Nyssenus, both elsewhere (*Dialogue* III, vol. I of the *Greek-Latin Library of the Fathers*, ch. 4) and in his book *On the Making of Man*, pursues at length [Col. 0871C] the point under discussion, especially urging this:

> As craftsmen in this life fashion an instrument in a form suited to its use, so the supreme craftsman made our nature as a kind of vessel fit for administering a kingdom; and by both the endowments of the soul and the very shape of the body he designed man such that he would be most fitted for kingship.

And the point he merely touches here he subsequently pursues, as we said, in a full and elegant argument. As to Severian of Gabala, consult the passage indicated by me at the foot of the page; there you will find the teaching under discussion.

> [Note: [Col. 0871D] *Oration* V, *On the Creation of the World*, no. 4, p. 484, vol. VI of Chrysostom’s works, Montfaucon edition. “Wherein consists the rationale of the image? In authority,” etc.]

59. Theodoret teaches the same view as follows (*On Chapter XI of the First Epistle to the Corinthians*):

> Man is the image of God, neither with respect to body nor with respect to soul, but only in regard to sovereignty and rule. Therefore, he to whom rule over all things on earth has been entrusted is called the image of God. But woman, since she is under the authority of man, is the glory of man and, as it were, the image of the image. For she too rules over others, but has been commanded to be subject to and obey her husband.

60. But lest we seem to cite Greeks alone, here is Ambrose teaching these things about man:

> [Note: [Col. 0872D] Book VI, Epistle XXXVIII—otherwise class I, Epistle XLIII—to Horontianus.]

> By this vigor of mind man subdues even external things; he sees things separated and distant; he subjects animals stronger than himself in bodily force; [Col. 0872A] and he instills in the rest such reverence for himself that, as though for a king, they vie in obedience and heed his voice. Though irrational, they recognize reason and adopt a discipline that nature did not confer upon them. In short, wild beasts, seeing his gentleness, are made gentle by his command. Often they have suspended their bites when recalled by the sound of a human voice. We see hares caught without a wound by the harmless teeth of dogs; indeed, lions themselves abandon their prey if a human voice rings out; leopards and bears are excited and recalled by voices; horses grow spirited at the applause of men and moderate their pace in silence; finally, they often pass by without the whip though they have been whipped: so much more forcefully does the scourge of speech spur them on.

61. Here likewise is Marius Victor, a Latin writer and ancient Father. In his work *On the Origin of the World*, he represents God as speaking thus at the creation of man:

> “Now let us make man,” he says, “that he may rule the world,  
> And be the image of God: it is fitting that he be like his Creator,” etc.

And later:

> Therefore he commanded this man, set over created things with his wife,  
> To increase through offspring and fill the empty lands.

Again:

> For man was first in merit, though last made in the whole order,  
> So that he might know himself to surpass the things created  
> And thereby render fitting praises to the Lord.

62. In the same sense Alcimus Avitus also makes God speak these words concerning man:

> Now let man be formed, whom the image of the highest  
> Deity touches, and who, endowed with our lofty honor,  
> May put on inwardly a beautiful form of mind.  
> Him it pleases us to walk erect upon raised feet,  
> That he may rule the world subjected beneath an eternal weight,  
> [Col. 0872C] Tame brute creatures, impose law and names upon all,  
> Mark the stars, know the paths of heaven and the constellations,  
> And learn, by examining their signs, to distinguish the seasons.  
> Let him subdue the savage sea and by steadfast intelligence  
> Possess whatsoever he sees; let the raging beast  
> Serve him, and, laying aside their fury, let beasts of burden learn  
> To endure rule; and, commanded to be bound,  
> Let frightened young bulls hasten into their accustomed chains.  
> And that the nature of man may appear more exalted,  
> Let him begin to raise his face upright toward heaven,  
> Seek his own Maker, and with faithful mind  
> Devote to him his life of service through enduring time.

63. But who would omit Augustine, who says (*Against the Manichees on Genesis*, Book I, ch. 17, no. 28):

> That man is said to have been made in the image of God is said with reference to the inner man, where reason and understanding reside. Hence he also has authority over the fishes of the sea, the birds of heaven, all cattle, [Col. 0872D] wild beasts, the whole earth, and every creeping thing upon earth.
