For when he had said, “Let us make man in our image and likeness,” he immediately added, “And let him have authority over the fishes of the sea, the birds of heaven,” and the rest; so that we might understand that man is said to be made in God’s image not because of the body, but because of that authority by which he surpasses all cattle. For all other animals are subject to man not because of the body, but because of the intelligence which we possess and they lack.

[Col. 0873A] 64. Here, if you wish, enumerate those Fathers who locate the devil’s sin in his envy of the supreme power and dominion over all things conferred upon man, which he had thought ought to be conferred upon himself. I would indeed enumerate them—neither contemptible nor few—had not the most illustrious Petavius anticipated my labor. I ask you to consult the passage cited by me at the foot of the page (*On Angels* III.2.8). Add, if you wish, the authority of Rabbi Saadia, who locates the image under discussion in rule and dominion (*reported from Aben Ezra by Petavius, On the Works* II.3.2).

65. Although there is no need to labor long here over the testimonies of the Fathers and Hebrews: the matter is so plain that it was known even to ancient writers themselves, placed amid the darkness of idolatry. In the opinion of many, this is indicated by Cicero’s words (*On Ends*, Book II): “The same reason in man contains something lofty and magnificent, fitted more for commanding than for obeying.” Ovid speaks more explicitly (*Metamorphoses* I):

> A holier creature, more capable of lofty mind,  
> Was still lacking—one that could rule the rest.  
> Man was born, etc.

66. Hence we see savage beasts tamed by man. While others describe this elegantly, Martial certainly described it in that famous epigram (usually found in Book I, no. 104), which begins:

> That the panther bears delicate yokes on its painted neck,  
> [Col. 0873C] And that fierce tigers submit patiently to the lash.

I would have you read the whole epigram; it is very elegant and charming, and wonderfully confirms the point at issue.

67. Before Martial, Philo had treated this argument at the greatest length. If I should cite his words, I fear I would be unduly prolix. Let the reader consult the place where they stand (*On the Creation*, trans. Gelenius, pp. 16–17, Gryphius edition of 1561).

68. What is more, fishes themselves, though most remote from human society, not infrequently

> Know their master and lick his hand  
> . . . . And, summoned by its master’s voice,  
> Each one comes at the call. [Col. 0873D]

I myself have often seen this when I visited the Reverend Fulgentius Musianus, of the Carthusian order, a man distinguished for piety and graciousness, who now presides over the community of the Bolognese religious, beloved by God and men. He had fish quite familiar with him; summoned by his voice, they immediately came running to take food from his hand.

69. Here, if you wish, recall what we established in Dissertation I: namely, that all sensible things were created for man’s sake. He too will admit that the angels themselves render service to man who agrees with St. Thomas and almost all the Scholastics in teaching that the course of the heavens and stars is directed and carried out by the angels. [Col. 0874A] For since this course serves man, those who direct and effect it certainly render service to man. Moreover, the same angels are our guardians and protectors, as the Apostle Paul says (*Heb.* 1:14), calling them “ministering spirits, sent for those who are to receive the inheritance of salvation.” I would say more here on this subject, had I not discussed it fully in a separate little work (*On Guardian Angels*). Consult, if you wish, Petavius (*On Angels* II.6.7 ff.).

70. For this reason many do not hesitate to place the image of God bestowed upon man in the fact that, just as God is the end of all things, or their final cause, so too is man—this one distinction only being made between God and man: God is the ultimate end of all things, whereas man ought to be directed to God himself [Col. 0874B] and strive toward him, in whom he may rest, and for whose glory he too was created. But since I have treated this subject more fully elsewhere (Dissertation I), let the reader recall that passage.

71. But we must now turn to the opinion of those who think that the image under discussion should be explained in this way: Adam was said to be in God’s image because man was endowed with that nature whose form God had assumed in order to create man, and in which form he appeared both to Adam himself and to the other patriarchs and prophets. But since we have sufficiently discussed this matter elsewhere, namely in the second Dissertation, I refer the reader to that passage.

72. But what is to be said of the opinion of those [Col. 0874C] who suppose Adam was called “in God’s image” because he received from God the nature and form which the Only-begotten Son of God would possess when he came to humankind as their head, Lord, and redeemer? Tertullian indeed proposed this both in his book *Against Praxeas*

> [Note: [Col. 0873D] Chapter XII: “But there was one according to whose image he was making [man]: namely, that of the Son, who was more certain and more truly to become man.”]

and in his book *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, writing as follows (ch. 6):

> Whatever shape was being given to the clay, Christ—the man to come—was being contemplated: for the Word was both clay and flesh, as he was then earth. For thus was the Father’s preface to the Son: “Let us make man in our image and likeness.” And God made man: what he had fashioned, therefore, he made in God’s image—namely, Christ’s. For the Word too is God, who, existing in the form of God, did not deem equality with God a thing to be grasped. Thus that clay, already then putting on the image of Christ to come in flesh, was not only God’s work but also a pledge.

73. Prudentius teaches the same, saying these things (*Apotheosis*):

> Christ is the Father’s form; we are Christ’s form and image.  
> By the Father’s goodness we are created in the face of the Lord,  
> Of Christ who, after ages, is to come in our form.

Add what we have said elsewhere on this subject (*Dissertation* II, no. 29 ff.).

74. But Petavius (*On the Works* II.2.4) rejects this opinion because, if it were true, God the Father, who is thought to have said, “Let us make man [Col. 0875A] in our image and likeness,” would not have said “our,” but “your,” O Son. Whether this observation sufficiently refutes that opinion, let others judge. I beg you, consult Petavius himself, Book II, chapter VII of *On the Trinity* (no. 4).

From what has been said thus far, let the reader judge what ought to be thought of the last opinion: namely, that of those who admit that the likeness and image under discussion exist in man, but maintain that it is altogether unclear wherein they consist. For if we have said anything plausible thus far—even if we cannot establish with certainty wherein it consists—the Fathers’ labors in this investigation have nevertheless enabled us to discover something probable in which to locate it. You will not doubt this if you weigh what we have set forth extensively from number thirteen [Col. 0875B] to this point.

## QUESTIONS III AND IV. In what part of man is the image and likeness under discussion located? And: Did God bestow the same image and likeness upon woman as well as upon man?

75. If we consider what we said in the preceding question, it will readily be clear that the image of God under discussion cannot be located in the body, unless perhaps this is said in the sense proposed under Augustine’s guidance at no. 47. That it can be located in the soul, however, I do not doubt. But whether you maintain that it resides in the substance of the soul, in its powers, or in some other manner, you will assert only when you adopt one of the opinions previously explained. For those who locate the image in the spirit locate it in the substance of the soul; those who locate it in the intellect, will, freedom, and similar things locate it in its powers. But those who hold that it consists in man’s exceptional perfection and excellence, in the dominion he exercises over creatures, and in related matters, must add something else, although these have their foundation in the soul—if we may so speak—and, as the Scholastics commonly say, their inherence and subject. Thus far concerning Question III.

76. As regards the fourth question, its solution follows from the solution of the first and second questions, especially the second. For if you locate this image in the soul and its powers and qualities, or, if you prefer, in virtues, who would exclude women from that dignity? Alcimus Avitus certainly makes women participants in this excellence, when he says (*To His Sister Fuscina*, Book I):

> See: the heavenly image lacks sex,  
> Which the inward human being retains in the mind,  
> And it admits no sex.

77. Marius Victor likewise seems to make women participants in the same excellence when he represents God as saying (*On Genesis*, Book I):

> “Now let us make man,” he says, “that he may rule the world,  
> And be the image of God: it is fitting that he be like his Creator,  
> Freely enjoying created things by the judgment of his mind.”

[Col. 0876A] 78. But if you locate that likeness in the exceptional perfection which man has above the other creatures, you must deny that woman was made in God’s image. For man is superior to woman and is her head. Chrysostom speaks most explicitly:

> [Note: [Col. 0875D] *Sermon* II on *Genesis*, no. 2, p. 653, vol. IV of the Montfaucon edition.]

> To know that the Godhead is not endowed with a human form, hear Paul saying: “A man indeed ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God; but woman is the glory of man, and therefore,” he says, “ought to have a covering upon her head.” Now, if in this passage he called “image” a likeness in every respect equal to the divine form, and man is therefore called God’s image because God is shaped in this manner, then according to them not man alone but woman also ought to be said to be made in the image; for the figure, form, and likeness of woman and man are one. Why then is man called the image of God, and woman not likewise? Because he makes no mention of the image situated in form, but of the image situated in dominion, which man alone has and woman does not. For he is subject to no one, whereas she is subject to him, as God says: “Your desire shall be toward your husband, and he shall rule over you.” Therefore man is God’s image because he has no one superior to him, just as God has no one superior to him, but rules over all. Woman, however, is the glory of man because she is subject to man.

79. Theodoret imitates Chrysostom and almost copies him entirely, teaching as follows:

> [Note: [Col. 0875D] In the Commentary on Paul’s First Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter [Col. 0876D] XI, on the words, “A man ought not to cover his head” (trans. Gentian Hervetus).]

> Man is the image of God, neither with respect to body nor with respect to soul, [Col. 0876C] but only in regard to sovereignty and rule. Thus he to whom rule over everything on earth has been entrusted is called the image of God. Woman, however, since she is under man’s authority, is the glory of man and as it were the image of the image. For she too rules over others, but has been commanded to be subject to and obey her husband.

He then adds another reason for excluding woman from this excellence:

> “For man,” he says, “is not from woman, but woman from man.” Therefore, even in the order of creation, man holds the first place. For man was not created for woman, but woman for man. This too is enough to show that man rightfully holds sovereignty: he was not brought forth for her use, but she herself was brought forth for his use.

He had taught the same in Question XX on *Genesis* [Col. 0876D] (in the old edition, translated by Giovanni Pico). Enough on these two questions.

## QUESTION V. Whether an angel was made in the likeness and image of God

80. The solution of this question likewise follows from the solution of Questions I and II, and especially the second. For if you locate likeness and image in the gifts of grace, who would deny that angels were made in God’s likeness and image, since in their very creation [Col. 0877A] they were enriched with exceedingly abundant and ample gifts of grace, and for this reason called sons of God?

> [Note: [Col. 0877B] “Now it happened that on a certain day the sons of God came and stood before the Lord” (*Job* 2:1). “When the morning stars sang together and all my sons of God praised me” (*Job* 38:7). Further, Paul writes (*1 Cor.* 8:5): “For although there are those who are called sons of God, whether in heaven or on earth”—a passage in which he appears to indicate angels. For who are the sons of God in heaven, if not angels? Yet, because the passages in Job are translated differently by some and Paul’s passage can be understood otherwise, it is not surprising that Chrysostom openly denies that angels are ever called sons of God. “Human beings,” he says, “have indeed been called sons of God, but angels never.” *Homily* XXII on *Genesis*, no. 2, p. 195, vol. IV of the Montfaucon edition.]

You will likewise say that they were made in God’s image if you locate the image in spirit, its powers, and lofty qualities. For these unquestionably exist not merely in angels, but exist in them preeminently and excellently. For this reason, I believe, Gregory the Great teaches not merely that the angel was made in God’s image, but that he was made in that image in some more excellent sense. It is fitting to cite his words here (*Morals*, Book XXXII, ch. 18). Referring to the devil what Ezekiel says of the king of Tyre, “You are the seal of the likeness of God,” he adds:

> For from the seal of a ring such a likeness is expressed representationally as exists essentially in the seal itself. And although man was created in God’s likeness, yet, attributing something greater to the angel, Scripture does not say that he was made in God’s likeness but calls him the very seal of God’s likeness, so that, the more subtle his nature, the more fully God’s likeness is believed to be expressed in him.

[Col. 0878A] 81. But if you locate it either in the perfection and excellence explained at no. 46 and following, or expressly in dominion over the other creatures, it must certainly be excluded from angels, and therefore so must the image of God of which we speak.

Theodoret, indeed, in Question XX on *Genesis*, devotes himself entirely to excluding that image from angels and placing it in man alone. To this end, besides adducing other reasons, he especially offers this: an angel exercises no authority over the remaining creatures, whereas man exercises the greatest authority. But it is better to cite Theodoret’s own words, from which the reader may perceive for himself what we have said:

> Some think that man was created in God’s image according to the invisible power of the soul, not understanding that the angel too is invisible, as is the demon. . . . But if man alone among all creatures is the image of God, there must be some special reason for this designation, etc.

And here let Dissertation III end.

## [SERMON ON THE DEDICATION.]

[Col. 0877]

## PREFACE BY JOANNES CHRYSOSTOMUS TROMBELLI TO THE FOLLOWING SERMON

[Col. 0877C] To the other offices of kindness and goodwill with which the Most Reverend Fathers and Lords Giovanni Gualberto Beccari and Filippo della Torre, eminent superiors of the Cassinese Congregation, heaped favor upon me while I was living among them at Florence, they wished to add this also. Knowing that I was searching out unpublished writings of the Fathers in order to publish them, they sent me a Sermon, attributed to Hilary of Poitiers, discovered in the celebrated library of their monastery in a manuscript containing the works of St. Hilary of Poitiers. It had been most carefully copied for me by the hand of the most learned Father Pietro Luigi Galletti, Lecturer in Philosophy, who has earned distinguished merit in the field of ancient literature, to which he also devotes the greatest study.

I immediately recognized that this sermon could not be ascribed to Hilary of Poitiers, since its very diction [Col. 0878C] protests against such an attribution, being far removed from the style which Hilary of Poitiers employs. But I did not know to whom I should ascribe it. Then, while turning over Combefis’s *Preachers’ Library* to discover whether this sermon had been published or not, I found that it had indeed been published and attributed to Bede,

> [Note: [Col. 0877D] You will find it among Bede’s summer sermons (p. 169, vol. VII of the Cologne edition of 1612). But many doubt whether all the sermons attributed to Bede in that edition were composed by Bede; some of them seem to have had another author.]

though with certain passages added and altered—either so that the sermon might be fitted to the Gospel passage prefixed to it in that edition,

> [Note: [Col. 0877D] In the old published books I consulted (see p. 718, vol. II of Martène, *On the Ancient Rites of the Church*, Antwerp—or rather Milan—edition of 1736), and likewise in the eleventh- and twelfth-century manuscripts preserved among us, the Gospel portion read at the dedication of a church, and still read, was taken from Luke chapter XIX: “Jesus entered and passed through Jericho.” But in Gaul at that period a passage appears to have been read from Matthew 7:17, “Every good tree,” etc.; Bede, if he is the author of this sermon, which we place second, likewise adapts himself to this reading. That yet another Gospel was sometimes read at a dedication is indicated by Bede in his homily *On the Dedication of a Church*: “At that time the Feast of Dedication took place at Jerusalem, and it was winter,” etc., p. 174, vol. VII of Bede’s works. In this he agrees exactly with Mabillon’s most ancient Gallican lectionary. See Book II of *On the Gallican Liturgy*, p. 168.]

or so that the analogy between the Jewish temple and the Christian Church might be explained more fully. This seems somewhat to have detracted from the purity and charm of the sermon itself.

> [Note: [Col. 0878D] In the already published sermon, the following above all occurs: “The columns stand before the door of the Temple, because the outstanding teachers preceded the coming of our Redeemer, who says, ‘I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he shall be saved’; of these the Apostle says, ‘James, [Col. 0879A] Cephas, and John, who seemed to be pillars,’ that they might bear witness to that same coming.” But did James, Cephas, and John, who did not foretell Christ but were his disciples, precede the Lord’s coming and therefore become “columns standing before the door of the temple”? Paul certainly calls them columns because they were steadfast in faith, like columns, and were as it were the chief supports of the Christian religion.]

I therefore judged that it should be published as it stands in the Florentine manuscript mentioned above. Yet, since I deny it to Hilary of Poitiers, if you wish to attribute it to another Hilary—which I permit—you may attribute it to Hilary of Arles. We know for certain that he erected sacred churches

> [Note: [Col. 0879A] In chapter 8 of the *Life of St. Hilary of Arles*, these words occur: “To persevere continually in the Mediator . . . to establish monasteries, build churches, strengthen monks by his instruction.”]

and therefore dedicated them, and that he delivered not a few sermons to the people.

> [Note: [Col. 0879B] In chapter 11 of the same *Life*, we read: “If a crowd of learned persons was absent, he nourished the hearts of country people with simple speech; but when he saw instructed persons had arrived, he was at once stirred in speech and countenance by a certain unusual grace; he appeared loftier than himself, so that Silvius, Eusebius, and Domnolus—men of his own time, deservedly celebrated for their writings—kindled with admiration, burst out in these words: ‘Not learning, not eloquence, but something, I know not what, attained beyond men . . . .’ And although his grace may be recognized without hesitation from those works which that same impetus of speech conceived, produced, adorned, and brought forth—namely, the life of Bishop Honoratus, homilies prepared for the feasts of the entire year, etc.” Perhaps moved by this conjecture, and also by the apparent similarity of style and phraseology to that found conspicuously in the *Life of St. Honoratus* written by Hilary of Arles, Combefis and others attribute no small part of the sermons customarily attributed to Eusebius of Emesa or Eucherius to Hilary of Arles. See Combefis’s *Preachers’ Library*, under “Resurrection of the Lord.”]

Moreover, the author of this sermon was accustomed to cite passages of Scripture [Col. 0880A] from the Vulgate translation, which Hilary of Arles certainly used.

> [Note: [Col. 0879C] In those sermons which Combefis judges Hilary to have delivered at the solemnity of the Lord’s resurrection—though certainly attributed to Eusebius of Emesa—the Vulgate translation of Scripture generally predominates. Moreover, in the *Life of Honoratus*, unquestionably composed by Hilary of Arles, Scripture passages are cited in this manner: no. 3, “Do not praise a man during his life”; and again, no. 8, “Before death, praise no one”; no. 10, “Set love in order within me”; no. 14, “In much patience, in vigils, in fasts, in chastity, in knowledge, in the word of truth, in the power of God”; no. 15, “Well done, good and faithful servant; enter into the joy of your Lord”; no. 20, “You shall walk upon the asp and basilisk, and trample the lion and dragon” = “Behold, I have given you authority to tread upon serpents and scorpions”; no. 26, “Sell all that you have and give to the poor, and come, [Col. 0880B] follow me”; no. 37, “Those who fear you shall see me and rejoice” = “For what have you that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?”
>
> These passages stand thus in the Vulgate: “Before death, praise no man whatsoever” (*Ecclus.* 11:30); “He set love in order within me” (*Song* 3:4); “In much patience, in tribulations, in necessities, in distresses . . ., in vigils, in fasts, in chastity, in knowledge, in long-suffering, in gentleness, in the Holy Spirit, in unfeigned love, in the word of truth, in the power of God” (*2 Cor.* 6:4–6); “Well done, good and faithful servant; enter into the joy of your Lord” (*Matt.* 25:21); “You shall walk upon the asp and basilisk, and shall trample the lion and dragon” (*Ps.* 90:13); “Behold, I have given you authority to tread upon serpents and scorpions” (*Luke* 10:19); “Sell what you have and give to the poor . . . and come, follow me” (*Matt.* 19:21); “Those who fear you shall see me and rejoice” (*Ps.* 118:74); “For what have you that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (*1 Cor.* 4:7). From this comparison of the passages you may clearly conclude either that Hilary of Arles used the very translation which we now follow, or at least one so closely akin to the Vulgate that it may be regarded as the Vulgate.]

This conjecture and suspicion of mine is greatly supported by the fact that Hilary of Arles’s own writing is by no means unlike the writing of this sermon. Yet, whoever may ultimately be assigned as the sermon’s author, it is surely praiseworthy and unquestionably ancient, and consequently deserves to recover its ancient form and pristine polish.

[Col. 0879]

## SERMON OF BLESSED HILARY ON THE DEDICATION OF A CHURCH, TAKEN [*cumptus*] AT POITIERS, IN THE CHURCH THERE CONSECRATED TO HIM. (C, G)*

> [Note: [Col. 0879D] The word *cumptus*, found in the manuscript, has no meaning. Perhaps *compositus* (“composed”) should be read.]

[Col. 0879D] Since, dearest brethren, by the favor of the Godhead we are celebrating the solemnities of the dedication of the Church, we ought to correspond to the solemnity which we observe. Thus, just as, by more diligently adorning the walls of that same church, lighting more lamps, increasing the number of readings, and adding the melody of psalms, we have customarily passed the night in joyful vigils, so too let us continually adorn the inner chambers of our hearts with the necessary ornaments of good works. Let the flame of divine devotion and brotherly love continually grow within us; let the holy remembrance of heavenly commandments and the sweet praise of angels continually resound in the sanctuary of our breast.

[Col. 0880D] For these are the fruits of a good tree, this the treasure of a good heart, these the foundations of the wise Architect, which today’s reading from the Holy Gospel commends to us: that we should possess not merely the form but rather the power of godliness. The mystical history of the Old Testament also carefully suggests this, when either Moses constructed the tabernacle or Solomon the temple for the Lord as a type of the Holy Church. For each house is reported to have been firmly founded: the tabernacle, indeed, because it had walls joined together from boards upon bases of silver; but the temple upon squared stones laid beneath as its foundation. The timbers also were incorruptible, from which the whole tabernacle was made, and with which the temple shone, adorned within and roofed above.

[Col. 0881A] They also brought forth the finest gold from the good treasury; with it the walls were overlaid within and without, and not only the walls of the Temple, but also the ceilings, beams, doors, doorposts, and pavements were covered. Moreover, almost all the vessels and implements of either house were of gold, nor was it permitted that these should be made except from the purest gold. The fruits of the trees offered in the house of the Lord were likewise commanded to be most pure and choice: namely, of the vine, olive, frankincense, myrrh, or stacte, and other such things. All these, clearly, understood spiritually, declare the true purity of our faith and conduct.

For both houses, as we have said, prefigure the Universal Church. Nor should anyone think it inappropriate that two houses of the Lord were made in mystery, although no believer doubts that the Church is the one house of Christ. For the two houses were established to signify the two peoples who were to come into the same faith: namely, the Jewish people and the Gentile. Accordingly, the tabernacle was properly built in the wilderness by the Jewish people alone. But the structure of the Temple was completed in devout faith by proselytes and Gentile foreigners, as many as could then be found among the people. The mighty king of Tyre, too, engaged by Solomon, most willingly assisted with hired workmen and timber, because before the Lord’s incarnation God was known only in Judaea.

[Col. 0881B] But after he, in that flesh in which he was born and suffered, had risen from the dead and, as God, was exalted above the heavens, the glory of his name immediately shone over all the earth; the whole world hastened to build his house and received from him the promise of heavenly gifts.

Scripture therefore relates that King Solomon commanded great stones to be taken up for the foundations of the Temple and squared. The great and precious stones, placed in the foundation and bearing upon themselves the whole burden of the Temple built above them, signify the outstanding teachers of the holy Church: great indeed in the excellence of their merits, precious in the brilliance of their miracles. Having heard the word from the Lord himself, they brought forth by their preaching the whole fabric of the growing Church. The king commanded these stones to be squared, thereby signifying that teachers of the Church ought to be well-ordered in character and immovable in mind.

[Col. 0881C] Just as a square, whichever way it is turned, will stand, so the life of the perfect—carefully directed according to the line of truth—knows how to be cast down from its stability by no assaults of temptation.

The Temple of God was built of Parian marble, that is, of white stone, to express the brightness of ecclesiastical chastity, concerning which the Lord says in the Song of Love: “As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among daughters.” It was sixty cubits in length, thirty cubits in breadth, and forty cubits in height. The length of the Temple therefore signifies the faith of the holy Church, through which she endures with long-suffering the adversities of the wicked amid her good works. Its breadth signifies love, by which she extends inwardly through the bowels of compassion. Its height signifies hope, through which, on account of good works wrought through love, she expects the rewards of heavenly life.

[Col. 0881D] And rightly is its length sixty cubits. For the perfection of good works is customarily signified by the number six, since God also made the adornment of the world in six days; and there are six ages of this world, during which the holy Church labors in godly actions for eternal rest. Rightly are there twenty cubits of breadth, because the commandment of love is twofold: for the Church is enlarged in tribulation, when every perfect person must love both the Creator with all the heart, all the soul, and all the strength, and the neighbor as oneself. Rightly are there thirty cubits in height, because all the hope of the elect hastens, by striving and purifying itself to the extent of its power, toward the vision of the Holy Trinity.

[Col. 0882A] It should certainly be noted that the thirty cubits of height extended not to the highest roof-ridge of the temple, but to the temple ceiling; then another thirty cubits of height rose to the ceiling of the middle sanctuary. Moreover, the upper chamber above it had sixty cubits in breadth, and thus the whole height of the house extended to one hundred and twenty cubits.

The first house therefore rises thirty cubits in height, because the present Church is wholly intent upon seeing the form of the Holy Trinity. The upper house likewise lifts itself thirty cubits high, because the souls of the perfect, released from their bodies, enjoy the immediate vision of that same blessed and undivided Trinity until the day of universal Judgment. The highest house is sixty cubits high, because all the elect, raised from the dead, will rejoice in the contemplation of their Creator—who is one God in three persons—with the eternal immortality alike of spirit and flesh.

[Col. 0882B] A middle wall was made in the temple from cedar boards, twenty cubits high, to divide the oracle into the Holy of Holies. On the front side of the temple it was twenty cubits in length, twenty cubits in breadth, and twenty cubits in height. The temple itself before the doors of the oracle was fifteen cubits [in extent], and there were tables and a golden lampstand there. There was also a golden altar near the door of the oracle, so that the rising vapor of incense burned upon it might cover the oracle, where was the Ark of the Covenant; above it were the Cherubim of glory overshadowing the mercy seat.

The first house, therefore, signifies the state of the present Church; the inner house, entrance into heavenly life. Thus tables and lampstands were rightly made in the former, because in this life we need the light of the holy Scriptures and the refreshment of heavenly sacraments. But in the future we shall not need such aids, where, according to the Psalmist’s word, all who appear with righteousness shall be satisfied with the manifest glory of the Lord.

[Col. 0882C] In this life, therefore, the hearts of the righteous, like a golden altar of incense, shine brightly through the purity of holiness. They are filled with the spices of spiritual desires; they burn with the fire of unceasing love; and, set as though at the entrance of heaven, they send forth amid the heavenly Holy of Holies the most sweet vapor of their prayer, where Christ sits at the right hand of God. He is most clearly signified by the Ark of the Covenant, which was within the veil; in it were the golden urn containing manna, Aaron’s rod that had budded, and the tablets of the covenant.

For the Ark itself signifies his human nature; the urn of manna, the fullness of his divinity; Aaron’s rod, the inviolable power of his priesthood; and the tablets of the covenant signify that he is the one who gave the law and who will also give blessing to those who keep the law.

[Col. 0883A] The Temple before the doors of the oracle was fittingly fifteen cubits in length, since in this life we must still be disciplined by fasts and self-restraint, if we are to seem to attain the fullness of inner sweetness. For everyone who wishes rightly to understand the forty-day fast of Moses, Elijah, or the Lord himself understands that this number signifies the discipline of the present life. The oracle itself, where the Ark was covered by the Cherubim of glory, fittingly had twenty cubits in length, breadth, and height. This number, as we have said, indicates the perfection of twofold love, because whatever is done for God in this pilgrimage is completed wholly in the breadth of love in that dwelling-place of the everlasting homeland, where his majesty is continually exalted by the praise of good spirits.

These few points, beloved, out of many concerning the construction of the Temple, we have wished to explain to your brotherhood for the joy of this present feast: so that the wonderful structure of the earthly house might delight its hearers, and that same structure, spiritually understood, might more ardently raise our minds toward love of the heavenly dwelling.

But after this dedication had thus been expounded and the celebration completed, Scripture concludes as follows (III Kings 8:66): “And Solomon dismissed the people, who went away blessing the king to their tents, rejoicing and glad of heart for all the good things which the Lord had done for David his servant and for Israel his people.”

[Col. 0883C] For, when the work of redemption has been accomplished, the Lord will dismiss his elect, rejoicing, into eternal dwellings. He will not, certainly, thereafter remove them from his presence; rather, bringing them from the ordeal of judgment—which, as the Apostle teaches, we know is to take place in the air (1 Thess. 4:16)—into the dwelling of the heavenly homeland, he will cause each to receive, according to his merits, the promised seat of the heavenly kingdom.

[Col. 0884A] It is rightly said that they went away blessing the king to their tents, because this is indeed the sole, most peaceful and most faithful occupation of the citizens above: to sing hymns of thanksgiving to their Creator. Hence it is written (Ps. 83:5): “Blessed are those who dwell in your house; for ever and ever they shall praise you,” rejoicing in due time and glad of heart for all the good things which the Lord had done for David his servant and for Israel his people.

For the righteous, rejoicing in the good things which they receive from the Lord, enter the dwellings of heavenly mansions, because however grievous and however long the labors of this age may have been, whatever ends in eternal blessedness is surely brief and light.

[Col. 0884B] Therefore, beloved, each of us ought, to the extent of his power, to labor in the building of God’s house—by exhorting, beseeching, reproving, and himself sweating in godly works—lest, if the heavenly King should now see anyone idle in the work of his temple, he render that person excluded at the time of the future dedication, from his great solemnity. Let us strive with the mutual help of love, so that Jesus Christ our Lord, finding you all glad of heart and untiring in the works which he himself commanded, may bring you all into the rewards which he promised: the perpetual vision of himself, he who lives and reigns with the Father as God in the unity of the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0883]

## EDITOR’S NOTICE

[Col. 0883C] In the Verona edition, a small work entitled *Metrum in Genesim, ad Leonem papam* (“A Poem on Genesis, addressed to Pope Leo”) is inserted at this point. Since no learned person denies that this poem does not belong to our Hilary, we have judged that it should be transferred to the works of the holy pope to whom it is dedicated.

[Col. 0883]

## ONE BOOK ON THE UNITY OF THE FATHER AND THE SON, AND AN INTERPRETATION OF CERTAIN PASSAGES OF HOLY SCRIPTURE. (C, G)\*

Those who arranged for this book to be printed by Froben in 1535 had scarcely taken it from the press when they discovered that it was not a new work by Hilary, but a compilation made by some industrious person—stitched together partly from the second book *On the Trinity*, but chiefly from the ninth—to which was appended from another source an addition concerning Christ’s various names. This addition, moreover, was copied from chapter 6 of the *Treatise on the Orthodox Faith*, published under the names of Ambrose and Gregory of Nazianzus, a work which very many suppose to be by Gregory of Baetica. From the same addition is composed Sermon 113, now found in the appendix to Augustine.

God, who is everywhere (from Hilary, *On the Trinity*, book II, §6), and is wholly everywhere, so transcends the governance of understanding—outside whom there is nothing, and to whom being always belongs—that he wills himself to be understood in the truth of the sacrament in this manner. This is the name of his inscrutable nature in the Father: invisible, ineffable, infinite God, concerning whom speech falls silent when it seeks to speak, sense grows dull when it seeks to investigate, and understanding is confined when it seeks to comprehend.

[Col. 0884C] Thus confession fails in naming him; and whatever language may be fitted to him will not speak of God as he is and as great as he is. Perfect knowledge is to know God in such a way that, though you know him not to be unknowable, you nevertheless know him to be inexpressible. He must be believed, understood, worshipped, and spoken of through these acts of devotion.

The Son, moreover, is the offspring of the Unbegotten (from §3): one from one, true from true, living from living, perfect from perfect, power from power, wisdom from wisdom, glory from glory, the image of the invisible God, the form of the unbegotten Father. This birth, then, certainly possesses its mystery (from §9). And if anyone perhaps charges his own understanding with being unable to attain the sacrament of this generation, though the Father is wholly understanding and the Son neither greater nor less than he, let him hear from me without resentment: “I do not know; I am ignorant; I do not inquire.”

[Col. 0885A] Yet I shall comfort myself: the archangels do not know, the angels have not heard, the prophet did not perceive, the apostle asked, the Son himself did not disclose it. Let the distress of complaints cease. Whoever you are who inquire into these matters, I do not call you back to the heights, I do not stretch you out into the expanse, I do not lead you down into the deep.

These things concerning the nature of divinity we have touched upon (from §§11 and 12), not comprehending the fullness of understanding, but understanding that what we say is incomprehensible. “Then,” you say, “faith has no office, if nothing can be comprehended.” On the contrary: let faith profess this as its office, namely, to know that that concerning which inquiry is made is incomprehensible to it.

There remains still something concerning the inexpressible generation of the Son; indeed, that “something” is still the whole. I burn, am carried away, grow dull, and do not know where to begin. For I do not know when the Son was born; and it is sinful for me to know when the Son was born. Whom should I call upon? Whom should I implore? From what books should I presume to draw words for an account of such great difficulties? Shall I unroll the whole school of Greece? But I have read: “Where is the wise man? Where is the scribe? Where is the inquirer of this age?” Thus in this world there are many sophists and wise men, but they have rejected the wisdom of God. Shall I consult the scribe of the law? But he does not know, and the cross of Christ is a stumbling-block. Perhaps I shall urge you to close your eyes and keep silence, because for reverence of him it is enough that the Gospels proclaim that he performed such great and astonishing miracles among human beings.

[Col. 0885B] From §13.—For in my defense amid these pondered difficulties stands a needy fisherman: unknown, unlearned, his hands occupied with linen, his garment wet, his feet stained with mud, wholly of the boat. Seek and discover whether it was more wondrous to raise the dead or to impart the knowledge of this doctrine to an unlearned man. For he says: “In the beginning was the Word.” Times are passed over, ages are sent beyond, eras are removed: my unlettered fisherman is free from time; he has conquered every beginning.

Beginning of book IX.—“A few days ago, while we were treating of the undifferentiated nature of God the Father and God the Son,” etc., as far as these words in §44: “And thus he taught perfect faith, since that which now is is the work of the same time, and that which the Father works the Son also works, and [the Son] is outside the union of the singular [nature].”

From chapter 6 of the *Treatise on the Orthodox Faith*.—Finally, according to our capacity, strength, and faith, let us consider what God is, and see whether anything can be compared with him. Certainly God is that which, even when named, cannot be spoken; when estimated, cannot be estimated; when compared, cannot be compared; when defined, increases by his very definition. He covers heaven with his hand, encloses the whole world in his fist; all things together do not know him, yet know him by fearing him; his name and power are served; and the world bears witness to him by the very momentary succession of its elements.

[Col. 0886A] There is a certain *ratio*, called among the Greeks *logos* (λόγος), which distinguishes the persons or names of Father and Son, because the Son himself is called *ratio*. Yet this *ratio* is called by many names: now Word, now Power, now Wisdom, now Right Hand, now Arm, now Pearl, now Treasure, now Net, now Plough, now Fountain, now Rock, now Cornerstone, now Lamb, now Man, now Calf, now Eagle, now Lion, now Way, now Truth, now Life—although he is God, all things and in all things. Through these names the mysteries of the divine dispensations are made known.

For this reason he is called Word: because he proceeded properly from the divine mouth, and because the Father neither commanded nor did anything without him. He is called Power because he is truly from God and always with God, and all the Father’s power abides in him. He is called Wisdom because, coming from the Father’s heart, he disclosed hidden things in heaven [in Ambrose: “heavenly things to believers”]. He is called the Right Hand because through him all divine works were completed. He is called the Arm because all things are upheld by him. He is called the Pearl because nothing more precious than he can be found. He is called Treasure so that all the riches of the heavenly kingdoms stored up in him may be recognized [Ambrose: “may be recognized as laid up”].

[Col. 0886B] He is called a Net because through him and in him the multitude of Gentiles, like fish, are gathered from the sea of this age into the Church, where the distinction between good and evil is recognized. He is called a Plough because the breasts of the Gentiles are broken up by the sign of his cross so that they may be prepared for the necessary seed. He is called the Fountain of Water because the hearts of the thirsty are watered from him by the grace of heavenly water. He is called the Rock because he provides strength to believers and hardness to unbelievers. He is called the Cornerstone because the one mediator, containing both walls of the Old and New Testament in himself, joined them together. He is called the Lamb in order that Christ’s innocence and passion may be shown. He is called Man because, according to the flesh, he deigned to be born for us human beings. He is called the Calf because he endured suffering for our salvation.

[Col. 0886C] He is called the Eagle because, after his venerable resurrection, he flew back to the Father as though on the oars of wings [variant: “the king of birds flies back to the Father’s seat”]. He is also called Lion because he is the King of kings, who crushed death and the devil by the power of his might. He is the Way because through him we have access [variant: “he is ascent”] to God the Father. He is the Truth because he knows no falsehood. He is the Life because he gives life to all things. You see, then, that through these names the meanings of divine arrangements and works have been prefigured; yet God himself is not properly defined by them.

From chapter 8 of the aforesaid *Treatise*.—Therefore God the Father is immeasurable, eternal, incomprehensible, beyond estimation. And his Son, our Lord, is as great as the Father is, but not from another source: he is from the Father. For he says, “I came forth from the Father,” that is, light from light.

[Col. 0886D] But if we acknowledge, as has already been said, that the Son of God was seen by the fathers, so that not the whole of what belongs to God was seen in him, but the dispositions of future things, which were to be accomplished at their respective times, were seen in him through an image: for who could see the Son before he assumed visible matter when he pleased, or deigned to clothe himself with humanity? For even if he was seen by Abraham, he was seen in the form of a human body, from the flesh of which he was to come [in Ambrose: “so that he might show that in the last times he would come in a human being”].

[Col. 0887]

## ONE BOOK ON THE ESSENCE OF THE FATHER AND THE SON AGAINST HERETICS. (C)

[Col. 0887A] Gillotius was the first to observe that this book also, published by Louis Miraeus from the Victorine library, was compiled from the books *On the Trinity*. Having marked the passages from which the several excerpts had been taken, he suppressed the rest. And indeed, who would seek muddy streams when a pure spring is at hand?

“The Gospel speaks: ‘He who does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him.’ All things are shut up against the devices of heretical frenzy,” etc.—from book VII of *On the Trinity*, from the middle of §21 to §31 of that same book: “And lest there should arise a calumny against the statement as though it were insolent, [that it might] demonstrate rather the consciousness [variant: power] of nature.”

To this the author joins these words from §33: “And let us hear him revealing all the knowledge of this faith to the Apostles; for he says, ‘I am the way, the truth, and the life,’” except that instead of “And let us hear,” he writes “hear.” He continues to the following words of §39: “that this saying of the Lord might follow: ‘Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father in me?’”

[Col. 0887B] From there he passes to book VIII, from which, after first introducing the words “My brethren,” he copies §14: “Let us read what has been written, and understand what we have read.” When he reaches the words of §20, “All that the Father has belongs to the Son, and all that belongs to the Son belongs to the Father. For he himself says, ‘All that is mine is yours, and all that is yours is mine,’” he omits what intervenes from there to the middle of §21. Then he again copies: “Therefore we are made alive because of the Spirit of Christ dwelling in us,” etc., as far as §26: “For Christ dwells in us; and when Christ dwells, God dwells.”

Finally, omitting the remaining words of this section, he takes up the beginning of §27. Having copied all of it and almost all of the following section, he concludes the book with these words: “But if by an adoptive name he is lord here, you are animated by a spirit of error, lacking the Holy Spirit; because no one can call Jesus Lord except by the Holy Spirit.” The author adds only: “because he himself works all things in all.”

[Col. 0887]

## EDITOR’S NOTICE

[Col. 0887C] Here in the Verona edition, which we have reprinted, after mention has been made of two letters ascribed to Hilary and addressed to Augustine, there follows a fragment bearing the prefixed title *The Faith of Alcuin*. We ought not to have reprinted either of these monuments at this point, since the aforementioned letters neither belong nor can belong to our author—as will be apparent to anyone who considers either their chronology or their text (see our edition of Augustine’s Works, vol. II, pp. 673 and 1007)—and since, without violating the rules of criticism, *The Faith of Alcuin* cannot be assigned to anyone other than the celebrated monk whose name it bears, nor suitably placed anywhere other than among his works.

[Col. 0887]

## PREFACE OF NICOLAS FABER TO THE FRAGMENTS OF SAINT HILARY

[Col. 0887D] To this work we have added only notes written at the foot of the page. Since Faber had been content to excerpt the words of authors and had not taken care to note from which book he had excerpted them, it seemed preferable to indicate the passages in the sacred historians according to Valesius’s editions, although later than Faber.

To the most distinguished man JACQUES-AUGUSTE DE THOU, counsellor of the sacred consistory and most learned and prudent president of the Parisian Senate, NICOLAS FABER, greetings.

### 1. The character of this work

Behold, most distinguished President, I restore to you the book of the blessed Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, which P. Pithou—a man preeminent in learning, prudence, and integrity of character—left by his last will; and which was entrusted to my good faith, so that it might come to you intact, that is, without any diminution, as was most fitting under the testator’s charge.

[Col. 0888D] If you count its leaves, the gift is not very large; but if you consider the dignity of the author, the fate of the book, and the importance of the matter with which it deals, it is of such a kind that it cannot fail to be most welcome. For to you, most richly furnished with every kind of learning, a most ardent lover of French welfare and renown, and a most devoted student of ancient piety and constancy, it cannot but be most pleasing that a book by an ancient Gallic writer should, under the auspices of your illustrious name, emerge into the light after so many years from darkness: a writer most celebrated and eloquent among the theologians who flourished in the West; “a lofty tree,” as Saint Jerome calls him (*Commentary on Isaiah*, ch. 60), “by which the Church of God was built”; and moreover a most courageous confessor, writing on the gravest controversy ever to have arisen in the Church.

[Col. 0889A] Although these considerations would sufficiently commend the gift, especially to you, who, in accordance with your devotion to letters and religion and your lofty, unbroken spirit against wealth and the vapors of courtly life—toward which alone people now run—have always preferred relics of this sort even to Attalic wealth: yet, if I know you rightly, you will assent to the judgment of Passienus and value still more highly in this matter the judgment of a most learned and judicious man, who while living uniquely loved and honored you for your distinguished learning, prudence, devotion, and piety in those public matters in which he agreed with you; and who, in dying, wished this public testimony of his favorable disposition toward you to remain for posterity.

### 2. That it is Hilary’s

As for the author of this book, no one will withhold belief from the manuscript codex which ascribes it to Saint Hilary; nor will anyone who has tasted something of the style or genius of so great a teacher dispute a powerful man’s title affixed to another’s possession. For one may perceive its long and involved periods and that character which Jerome himself, a writer of the most refined discernment, attributed to Hilary’s writings: like the Gallic Rhône, violent and very swift, yet carrying some mud along with it (Jerome, preface to the Epistle to the Galatians; Epistle 9 [13] to Paulinus).

[Col. 0889B] But what need is there of words in a matter so plain? If anyone should remain doubtful in this matter, let him compare this book with those writings which have by universal agreement been received as Hilarian; he will find neither water more like water nor milk more like milk.

Nor indeed was this historical work unknown to the ancients. For the inscription prefixed to this book establishes that it is the very work which Jerome reports Hilary to have written *Against Ursacius and Valens*, containing an account of the Council of Rimini.

### 3. Who Ursacius and Valens were

Ursacius and Valens themselves—one bishop of Singidunum in Upper Moesia, the other of Mursa in Pannonia (although Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, in more than one place calls them both Pannonians)—together with Caius, likewise a Pannonian, and Germinius, first bishop of Cyzicus and later of Sirmium, were the chorus-leaders of the entire tragedy of the Arian faction, and indeed hypocrites. Since the inheritance and succession of the Arian name had descended to them, as our Hilary says (*Against Auxentius*, §4), they did not dare, while Athanasius stood firm, to declare open war on the Nicene faith. They feared him as its courageous and powerful champion, and truly—as Gregory Nazianzen calls him (*Oration* XXI, §33)—“a pillar of the Church” (*stylos tēs ekklēsias*, στύλος τῆς ἐκκλησίας).

[Col. 0889C] They therefore resolved to pursue their purpose by underground devices, undertaking above all to remove and overthrow Athanasius himself. Hence came those calumnies concerning the murder of Arsenius and the breaking of the chalice intended for the sacred mysteries. When factionalists had deposed him under this pretext and he had been sent into exile by imperial decree, the entire world was shaken by the fall of so great a man.

Indeed, although Athanasius had demonstrated his innocence at the Alexandrian, Roman, and ecumenical Council of Sardica, while his accusers had not only been convicted and condemned by so many judgments but had also, by petitions presented to the same Sardican Synod and to Julius, Roman Pontiff, sought pardon for their offense and heresy, and had been restored to communion with the Church—

> [Note: Col. 0889D] What is related here confusedly leaves room for error. The petitions of Ursacius and Valens are well known; they did not present them to the Synod of Sardica, by which they were condemned together with the other obstinate heretics.

[Col. 0890A] —yet, like dogs returning to their vomit, they again stirred up those shameful dissensions, unworthy of the Church of God, which is the house of peace: the peregrinations of bishops to Milan, Sirmium, harsh Seleucia, Rimini, Constantinople, Nicaea in Thrace—and to what place in the world not?—as well as proscriptions, exiles, and slaughter. These afflicted Catholic bishops as long as Constantius lived.

At length, having cast off the mask and assailed the Nicene rule, they induced the emperor himself, upon whose power they relied, to compel the bishops assembled at Rimini to subscribe to a new formula of faith, framed in deceptive words. Contrary to the decree of the three hundred and eighteen fathers, it imposed silence upon the terms *ousia* and *homoousios* (οὐσίας καὶ ὁμοουσίου, “essence” and “of the same essence”), professed the Son to be like the Father according to the Scriptures, and pronounced an anathema upon those who called him a creature as other creatures are.

[Col. 0890B] Yet they did not think that they should stop there—for who has set himself a limit in sinning? Rather, made bolder by the success of their undertaking, they no longer represented the terms *ousia* and *homoousios* as the apple of discord over which controversy was being conducted. With head uncovered, they professed at the Council of Antioch the sheer—or rather impure and foul—doctrine of Arius: that the Son is altogether unlike the Father and a creature “from things that are not” (*kai ex ouk ontōn*, καὶ ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων).

> [Note: Col. 0890D] Or rather, they attempted to establish this; but, being unable to refute the objections, they recited the formula issued at Constantinople and departed. (Socrates, book II, ch. 45.)

Athanasius asserts that the emperor himself became the author and defender of this impiety.

### 4.

[Col. 0890C] Thus Ursacius and Valens are precisely those men “at whose insistence, under Emperor Constantius, the Council of Rimini was held against the formula of the Nicene treatise, in which all heresies had been comprehended”; and it is against them that this work was written.

Although, to state what I think, this book’s title promises much more on its front than it delivers within—

> [Note: Col. 0890D] The title of this book promises more than it delivers.

—except insofar as I judge that what is presented here is only the beginning and certain dismembered fragments, not a complete work or book, of a longer work perhaps comprising several books and containing an exact narrative of the proceedings at the Council of Rimini, or of what preceded it or followed after it.

[Col. 0890D] Indeed, at the very beginning of this book the author writes that he will begin his narrative from the Council of Arles, at which Paulinus, bishop of Trier and metropolitan of Gaul, as the Greeks call him, was deposed by the faction of Saturninus and the other Arians in the year of Christ 353 and driven into exile. Yet thereafter there is profound silence concerning him.

For whoever excerpted these things, “joining one summit of tales to another” (*koryphas heteras heterais prosaptōn mythōn*, Κορυφὰς ἑτέρας ἑτέραις προσάπτων μύθων), immediately appended to this proposal the synodical letters of the Council of Sardica, held six years earlier: one to all the Churches, the other to Julius, bishop of Rome, declaring and attesting Athanasius’s established innocence.

[Col. 0891A] I consider it superfluous to say more of these letters, since Cardinal Baronius—a man of most illustrious name and rank—inserted them into his learned and laborious *Ecclesiastical Annals,*

[Col. 0891B] omitting the names of the subscribing bishops, which his manuscript lacked; and since the latter letter appears in more than one place among ancient writers.

The same disorder may be perceived at the end of Fragment II. There, although Saint Hilary had said that he would shed light on his narrative by means of the speech which the same Council of Sardica delivered to Constantius at Antioch through Vincent, bishop of Capua, and Euphrates, bishop of Cologne—

> [Note: Col. 0891D] Euphrates, or Euphrata, according to Theodoret, book II, ch. 7. From this it is clear that, after returning from the Council of Sardica, those two bishops were chosen by Constans to convey his letters to Constantius. Whether they had first been sent by the council itself to the same emperor to perform that task is not so certain.

[Col. 0892D] —nevertheless, to the great loss of history, that speech does not appear here at all. In its place there are read certain letters of Liberius, bishop of Rome—

> [Note: Col. 0892D] Liberius’s first letter is doubtful (Fragment IV).

—and of others, heaped together, as it were, into a bundle, with no order of time or events preserved.

5. For the first document that occurs seems to have been written by Liberius around the beginning of his pontificate, which falls in the year of salvation 353. [Col. 0891C] It is likely that he did not long prolong the accusation begun before his predecessor Julius, but, as soon as he was proclaimed pope, immediately sent those envoys of his to Athanasius at Alexandria and condemned his refusal of judgment. Yet here lies a difficulty worthy of the divine avenger—that is, of that most distinguished and learned writer of the *Ecclesiastical Annals*. For since the writings of all authors establish that Athanasius had long before Liberius exposed the schemes and subtleties of his opponents and shown them up as manifest falsehood, what room was there for the accusation of men refuted by so many synods, or for the condemnation of one acquitted by so many judgments? Or how could Liberius exclude Athanasius from his communion, when he was unwilling to approve his condemnation—said to have been issued by certain Eastern bishops [Col. 0891D] and sent to him at the beginning of his pontificate—if he had considered it valid, as Liberius himself testifies in the letter to Constantius printed here (*Fragment* V, no. 2), after he had received at the same time the judgment of seventy-five Egyptian bishops attesting Athanasius’s innocence?

I pass over the fact that neither Athanasius himself, who dealt most carefully with his own affairs in more than one book, nor, so far as I know, any other ancient writer anywhere mentions this condemnation. Yet its style denies that it is false or forged; and besides, to what end would it have been forged? Thus the saying of the tragic poet is wholly true:

> All things does long and innumerable time  
> Bring forth from obscurity, and, once revealed, conceal again.

(Sophocles, *Ajax*, p. 39.)

6. The following letter, now *Fragment* XII, was written in the year 363. — Although the following letter of the same pope has no more suitable connection with the preceding documents, its historical setting is nevertheless more certain. So far as one can determine from its reading, everywhere most corrupt, it was written after the death of Emperor Constantius and the return from exile of Eusebius, bishop of Vercelli. Divine providence, which is never absent from its own in their time, had appointed, preserved, and nourished Eusebius, our Hilary, and Athanasius as a triumvirate for establishing and restoring the Christian commonwealth; that is, it was written about [Col. 0892B] the year of Christ 363.

At that time, alike in the West and earlier at the Synod of Alexandria in the East, in the year 362, peace and concord were sought and achieved by those three men—truly “men of God and the greatest stewards of souls”—through the Twelve Tables and the strong law called *siremps* [“the same”]. Those stained by communion with the Arians were received back into the Catholic Church, except for the authors of the heresy, if they renounced their perfidy. “The Catholic Church,” says Augustine, “received them into her maternal bosom, as Peter after he wept at his denial and was warned by the cock’s crow; or as the same Peter after his wrongful dissimulation was corrected by the voice of Paul” (Augustine, *On Christian Combat*, ch. 30).

Lucifer alone, bishop of Cagliari in Sardinia—otherwise to be counted among the lights of the Church for constancy in the faith and freedom in writing, if this stain be excepted—and a few others, whether from excessive holiness, I would say, or obstinacy: “Proudly receiving and impiously condemning this charity of their mother, because they did not rejoice over one rising after the cock’s crow, they deserved to fall with Lucifer, who rose in the morning” (Augustine, *ibid.*, ch. 30). So true it is that, in all matters, as moderation is best, so it is also most difficult to maintain.

7. The unwary disaster of the Council of Rimini. — For when Ursacius and Valens—for crimes cannot remain hidden long—found almost all the bishops exposing the ulcer of the faith of Rimini, which they had accepted and approved as orthodox, they explained the statement that the Son is like the Father not simply (*οὐχ ἁπλῶς*), but in a certain respect (*κατά τι*), that is, according to the Scriptures and insofar as that likeness accords with Holy Scripture. From this they inferred neither that the Son is equal to the Father [Col. 0892D] nor that He is one with Him—for likeness is always distinct from the reality—while they evaded calling Him a creature as other creatures are, conceding that He is more excellent, but still a creature.

“Then,” says Jerome, “the whole world groaned and was astonished to find itself Arian” (*Against the Luciferians*). And indeed, says that great Gregory, “the phrase ‘like according to the Scriptures’ was bait for impiety, covered with bronze: an image facing all passers-by, a winnowing-blast in every wind” (Nazianzen, *Oration* 21, no. 26).

Then bishops came together who, ensnared by such deceits, “had not fallen in understanding, but had been led astray by the written word and had partaken of the smoke, if not of the fire,” as Nazianzen says in the same discourse (*Oration* 21, no. 30). They were accused of heresy without conscious intent. Calling to witness the Body of the Lord—for that sacramental formula was used in the Church long before this period, as is shown by the oath which Cornelius reports in Eusebius that the impious Novatian, or Novatus, exacted from his followers [Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VI.43; Jerome, *Against the Luciferians*]—and whatever is holy in the Church, they declared that they had suspected no evil in their faith. “We thought,” they said, “that the sense agreed with the words; nor could we suppose that, in the Church of God, where simplicity and pure confession prevail, one thing should be uttered in the heart and another on the lips.”

And indeed, says the same Gregory, “simplicity is unguarded; together with what is unsound it admits the humane element, and, being free from malice, least of all suspects malice.” “I ask those excessively religious persons,” Jerome adds (*Against the Luciferians*), “what they thought ought to be done with the confessors?”—for thus that passage must be written. “Thus, by this gentleness and clemency, the Nicene faith was repaired and established, and the world was snatched from the jaws of Satan by three confessors.”

History also records that Liberius, bishop of Rome, remembering the Lord’s words, “And when you have turned, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22:23)—words spoken not only to Peter when he fell but also, in a sense, to Liberius himself, successor both to Peter’s seat and to his weakness—rendered distinguished service in this work.

[Col. 0893C] 8. Clearly, what Liberius here urges (*Fragment* XII)—that all the bishops of Italy, deceived by the perfidy of Rimini, should condemn that pestilential doctrine, rage more vigorously against its authors, whom they had found violent and deceitful toward themselves, and devote themselves afresh wholly to the Nicene faith—was fulfilled for him not long afterward. This we learn both from his letter to the Easterners preserved by Socrates (*History* IV.12), in which he reports that all the bishops of Italy had anathematized the formula of Rimini, subscribed to the Nicene faith, and were burning with the greatest zeal against Arius’s doctrine and disciples; and also from the letter which immediately follows here, in the same *Fragment*, sent by the bishops of Italy to the bishops of Illyricum.

This latter letter appears to have been written [Note: We have demonstrated that it was written earlier.] after the Illyrian synod held about the year of Christ 365, at which the Nicene faith in Illyricum, whence it had been violently expelled, was restored as if by a praetor’s edict. Our Hilary first, and afterward Eusebius, bishop of Vercelli, returning from exile, had laid substantial foundations for that restoration.

9. Germinius’s defection from Valens and Ursacius. — The letter of Ursacius, now *Fragment* XIV, bears in its consular dating Valens, Caius, and others assembled at Singidunum, and the consuls Gratian, *vir nobilissimus*, and Dagalaiphus, [Col. 0894A] whom the most diligent chronologists state held the consulship in the year of salvation 366. Those heretics were ill at ease as they experienced in themselves the old saying: “The deeds of the wicked quickly fall to destruction.” From the deception at Rimini nothing now remained to them except public hatred, odium, and infamy; while the Nicene faith everywhere recovered its former authority and dignity.

But they were especially distressed by the defection of Germinius, their old associate and inseparable comrade, without whom, as without Theseus, they had hitherto attempted nothing. For, adhering to the Semi-Arian confession, he said that the Son was like the Father in all things; nor did the faith accepted at Rimini under compulsion differ from this profession. Though, as stated above, it did not contain the words “in all things,” the clause “according to the Scriptures” was considered sufficient to convey and express them, because the Scriptures call the Son the image of the Father.

Ursacius, Valens, and the rest of that party, by contrast, say in this letter that the Son is indeed called like the Father, but not in substance or in all things—that is, absolutely; for this passage must be corrected thus. Otherwise, they add, the perfidious assertion of Basil, bishop of Ancyra, foremost among the Semi-Arians—whom the Arians had deposed at the Council of Constantinople in 360, and whose opinion [Note: Not indeed in itself, but by adopting its contrary; Athanasius, *On the Synods*, p. 906; Socrates, *History* II.45.] they afterward condemned at Antioch—will be restored.

Thus Germinius did not act so criminally or impiously when, provoked by this letter, he composed that profession of his faith, now first published among these fragments as *Fragment* XIII. It acknowledges Christ, the Son of God and [Col. 0894C] God, to be like the Father in all things: in divinity, love, majesty, power, glory, life, wisdom, and knowledge. He also published a fuller and richer exposition of it in the letter sent to Rufianus, Palladius, and Severinus (*Fragment* XV).

10. The formula dictated by Mark of Arethusa: what it was. — From that letter we further learn which is the creed for whose drafting Mark, bishop of Arethusa, was chosen—for that is the correct reading, not “expelled,” as Socrates proves (*History* II.30—and by whose authorship it was composed and under what auspices it was issued. For I fear Socrates is mistaken (*ibid.*) when he asserts that the rule of faith written by Mark of Arethusa was the creed promulgated against Photinus at the Synod of Sirmium. Rather, it was that formula which the same author says was suppressed, as soon as it had been published at that synod, like an ill-born offspring, from the Twelve Tables; [Note: It is more probable that it was suppressed after it had been read at Rimini, because its dated consuls provoked universal laughter.] and which Ursacius and Valens afterward offered to the fathers assembled at Rimini for subscription.

For this formula alone, not merely among the three creeds said to have been issued at that synod, but among the nine principal ones which Socrates—trying, as he calls it, to disentangle the labyrinth of creeds, though he actually entangles it further—lists as promulgated by the Arians during nineteen years (*History* II.41), namely from the year [Col. 0895A] of Christ 312—when at the Antiochene synod held at the Dedication they first dared, after the Nicene faith, to devise another new creed—to the consulship of Eusebius and Hypatius, when the perfidy of Rimini was stitched together: so manifold is falsehood (*τὸ ψεῦδος πολύμορφον*)—this formula alone, I say, contains the words: “The Son is like the Father in all things, as the holy Scriptures say and teach.”

Germinius’s letter attests that these words appeared in the creed dictated by Mark. Hence Epiphanius (*Heresies* LXXIII.22) calls it “the faith concerning the Son’s being like the Father in all things” (*πίστις περὶ τοῦ ὅμοιον εἶναι τὸν υἱὸν πατρὶ κατὰ πάντα*). This is the same creed which, as is clear from Athanasius’s letter *On the Synods*, had consuls appended contrary to ecclesiastical custom. For that reason it provoked among the fathers assembled at Rimini not more indignation at its impiety than laughter [Col. 0895B] at its novelty.

11. Which bishops comprised that assembly at Sirmium. — George, then, whom he calls bishop of Alexandria, was a Cilician by birth, if we trust Ammianus (Book XXII), or a Cappadocian according to Athanasius and others (*To the Solitaries*, p. 861; Titus 1:12). Indeed, if one considers his character, he was plainly Cretan: “always a liar, an evil beast, and a lazy belly,” so that he could not fail to be utterly bad, upon whom the three worst kappas (*τριὰ κάππα κάκιστα*) had converged.

Nazianzen depicts him in these colors (*Oration* XXI.19), portraying not a man but “some Cappadocian monster” (*τέρας τι Καππαδόκιον*): wicked in race, more wicked in mind, not wholly free but mixed, like mules; at first a slave of another’s table and purchasable for a cake of bread. From being a plunderer of the Constantinopolitan treasury, accused and fugitive for that crime, he had been installed by military force as an espionage-agent (*κατασκόπως*) in the Alexandrian church, in place of Gregory the robber and against Athanasius himself. [Col. 0895C]

We have said above that Basil did not win approval even from his own party. The bishop of Pelusium, whose name is here erased, is called Pancratius by Socrates (*History* II.29) and is counted among the Arians’ standard-bearers. But this Mark was bishop of Arethusa in Syria, not in Macedonia, as the Centuriators maintain. Earlier, with Narcissus of Neropolis (Athanasius, *On the Synods*, p. 894), Maris of Chalcedon, and Theodore, bishop of Heraclea in Thrace—men wholly devoted to every impiety—he had been sent by the Arians to Constans in Gaul after the Antiochene synod at the Dedication, against Athanasius. He was infamous both for professing the heresy and subscribing the forged Sardican decree, [Col. 0895D] but later, under Julian, illustrious and celebrated for the glory of confession, or even martyrdom—for the authorities differ on this point (Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History* III.7; Sozomen, *History* V.10).

12. At what time it was held. — But since, as someone says, “he who has once crossed the bounds of shame must be thoroughly and vigorously shameless,” what prevents us, just as we have tried to prove that ecclesiastical historians erred in identifying the rule of faith dictated by Mark of Arethusa, from inquiring whether they did not make the same mistake in assigning the time at which they report it to have been written and issued? “The Achaeans came seeking Troy,” says Theocritus.

[Col. 0896A] For I strongly approve their statement that it was issued at Sirmium; but I withhold judgment on their claim that it was issued by the Synod of Sirmium. They report (Socrates, *History* II.20; Sozomen, *History* IV.6) that three rules of faith were issued at that synod: the first, against Photinus; the second, which we say was written by Mark; and the third and last, which our Hilary calls the blasphemy of Hosius and Potamius.

Yet Hilary himself and Athanasius, who wrote expressly on synods, whose authority no sane person can avoid—and indeed must prefer to that of any other in a matter in which they took the leading part—mention only two creeds written by the Synod of Sirmium: the first and the last. Indeed, Athanasius expressly states here that, after that blasphemy of Hosius, there was composed the creed containing the consuls’ names, which we have shown was dictated by Mark.

For after inserting Hosius’s formula in his work *On the Synods*, Athanasius immediately adds: “When they had sent this out, changing their mind once more, they composed the creed which, because they had issued it with consuls’ names, brought them into great shame and disgrace. They took care, after changing their opinion as was their custom, that copies of it should be stolen from those who held them by the notary Martian; and, having persuaded Constantius to promulgate edicts against that creed, they again established another creed, adding, as usual, certain expressions. Thus they composed these things in Isauria, etc.” (*On the Synods*, p. 904).

From these words of Athanasius two conclusions follow. First, that the creed of Hosius, which declares the Son inferior to the Father and wholly unlike Him, was regarded as the final determination and judgment of the Sirmian council, and under that title was sent, according to custom, to the churches. Hilary also makes this clear at the beginning of his work *On the Synods* (no. 2): “I rejoiced in the Lord,” he says, “that you have remained unpolluted and unharmed by every contagion of detestable heresy, and that you have not only refused to receive the impiety of faithlessness recently sent to you from the town of Sirmium, but have condemned it when it was reported and made known.” Thus it appears to have been not merely sent, but publicly promulgated and prescribed to the people, so that they might swear to it.

Second, the creed bearing the consuls’ names was composed and published after the Synod of Sirmium, and not long before the Synod of Seleucia. But if the creed professing the Son to be like the Father in all things, written by Mark, bears the day and consuls under whom it was issued at Sirmium, from what surer source can the time of its promulgation be determined than from the consuls under whom it is said to have been issued?

Theodoret says of it—read here and below Sozomen, namely *History* IV.16 in the edition of Christophorson, or chapter 17 in Valesius’s edition—“They even considered it absurd that this formula should have such a heading prefixed to it as it had when it was issued at Sirmium, in the presence of Constantius, eternal, great Augustus, under the consulship of Eusebius and Hypatius; as Athanasius also writes.” So Theodoret. Nor does Socrates speak otherwise (*History* II.37; Athanasius, *On the Synods*, p. 874), though the error began with and was derived from him.

What does Athanasius himself say? “After the division had been made, and some had gone to Seleucia, surnamed the Rough, while others had gone to Rimini, where there were fifty bishops and more”—the number is erroneous, but that need not concern us now—“Germinius, Auxentius, Valens, Ursacius, Demophilus, and Caius also came to that place. There, while the other bishops framed their statements from the sacred writings, they produced a little document. Having read out the consuls under whom it was written, they demanded that it should be preferred to all synods. The question of heretics was to be omitted, and no inquiry made into their intention or opinion; rather, they should be satisfied solely with what was written in the document. Their text was as follows: ‘The Catholic faith was issued in the presence of our Lord, the most religious and illustrious victorious Emperor Constantius Augustus, [Col. 0897B] eternal, under the consulship of the most illustrious men Eusebius and Hypatius, at Sirmium’”—for this is the reading, as others before us have taught, from Socrates and Theodoret—or Sozomen—“on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June. We believe in one,” etc.
