If, when it was issued at Sirmium in Constantius’s presence on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June, it bore the names of Eusebius and Hypatius as consuls, how could it have been issued by the Synod of Sirmium, which those who assert it most cautiously place no less than three years before those consuls? Who, then, could fail to acknowledge from so many testimonies—unless he denied that the sun shines at noon—that the creed professing the Son like the Father in all things was composed at Sirmium indeed under the consulship of Eusebius and Hypatius, but long after the Synod of Sirmium; and that not long after it was written, it was presented to the fathers at Rimini?

13. Occasion of the meeting at Sirmium. — To set forth what has occurred to me on this question: it is certain that Emperor Constantius left no stone unturned to reconcile divergent opinions in religion. But by making himself too accommodating to heretics, Caesar himself dared to handle matters belonging to God. “In investigating simple and absolute religion,” says Ammianus (Book XXI), “he was more scrupulous in inquiry than effective in settlement; he himself fostered and increased the dissensions.”

To apply some remedy at last, he decided to convene an ecumenical synod (Sozomen, *History* IV.16). Accordingly, in letters sent to Basil, bishop of Ancyra, he ordered the Eastern bishops to examine what place would be suitable and convenient for holding the synod. But since they could not agree, some preferring one place and others another, Basil went to the emperor, who was then staying by chance at Sirmium. There he encountered several men held at court on private business, as well as Mark of Arethusa, George bishop of Alexandria, and Valens with his associates.

Then those ringleaders of the Arians, conferring among themselves how they might overthrow the Nicene faith, obtained from the emperor an order that the universal synod convened at Nicaea in Bithynia should, because of that city’s destruction by earthquake, be postponed and divided: Eastern bishops were summoned to Seleucia in Isauria, and Western bishops to Rimini. No one who has read Sozomen, the author of this account (*History* IV.15), will doubt that this meeting of the Arian bishops at court took place under the consulship of Eusebius and Hypatius—that is, in the very year in which those synods were held. Ammianus himself attests that in that year Constantius wintered at Sirmium and spent the greater part of it there; and numerous laws issued under those consuls prove the same by their subscriptions.

Many considerations lead me to conjecture that at this meeting the question concerning the creed recited by Germinius in this letter was debated before the emperor, and that the creed whose drafting was entrusted to Mark was composed. First, the persons: the same bishops among whom the question of faith was debated are listed in this letter as Sozomen remembers to have been at court. Next, the incidental character of the occasion in both accounts: Germinius does not say that these bishops were assembled to debate the faith, but that, when discussion arose before [Col. 0898B] the emperor and continued far into the night, they were finally brought to that formula. Finally, the place and time: we have shown that the creed calling the Son like the Father in all things was written at Sirmium under the consulship of Eusebius and Hypatius.

Nor do I think that the words in Epiphanius, *Heresies* LXXIII.22, concerning the faith “about the Son’s being like the Father in all things” (*περὶ τοῦ ὅμοιον εἶναι τὸν υἱὸν τῷ πατρὶ κατὰ πάντα*) can refer to another creed. Valens himself, subscribing it, repeated in his subscription that the Son was like the Father but omitted the two words “in all things”; he was compelled to add them by Emperor Constantius, before whom the affair was transacted. Valens himself testified that he had subscribed it “as the night of Pentecost was dawning” (*τῇ νυκτὶ ἐπιφωσκούσης τῆς πεντεκοστῆς*; Epiphanius, *Heresies* LXXIII.22). Epiphanius adds that, as soon as the creed had been subscribed, Valens seized it and took it with him to the synod at Rimini.

Therefore the creed declaring the Son like the Father in all things was written at the time of the Synod of Rimini, namely under the consulship of Eusebius and Hypatius, on the vigil of Pentecost—that is, the eleventh day before the Kalends of June. For in that consulship, the year of Christ 359, when the fourteenth moon fell on the fourth day before the Kalends of April, the venerable Sunday of the Lord’s resurrection was celebrated on the day before the Nones of that month, and the sending of the Holy Spirit on the tenth day before the Kalends of June, with the letter C—the mark of Sunday—if that notation was then in use.

14. Epilogue. — To conclude this entire discussion, then: the creed professing the Son like the Father in all things seems to have been written at Sirmium, not after an investigation held [Col. 0898D] in a formal assembly of bishops, but when a discussion arose during an incidental meeting of a few men before the emperor; not in a basilica or public place where synods were usually held, but in the emperor’s private chamber; not under the consulships of Sergius and Nigrinianus, or of Constantius for the ninth time and Julian for the eleventh, when the Synod of Sirmium is said to have been held, but on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June under the consulship of Eusebius and Hypatius. On the same day Emperor Constantius sent from Sirmium Laws XIV and XV of the title *On Praetorian Prefects and Quaestors* in the Theodosian Code to the Senate.

It is therefore no wonder that Athanasius (*On the Synods*, p. 873) censures the rashness of those who wrote such a creed: “Though they were only three or four,” he says—though in this he minimizes the matter, [Col. 0899A] for seven or eight were present [Note: Yet he does not refer to them, but to Ursacius, Valens, Germinius, Acacius, and Eudoxius, as is clear from p. 869.]—“they nevertheless dared to add consuls’ names to a rule of faith, something which the three hundred and eighteen fathers at Nicaea had not done.” But perhaps this is more fully discussed than the limits of a letter or preface permit; the remaining matters must be reviewed briefly.

15. The letters of Liberius, bishop of Rome, which now make up *Fragment* VI, placed after this letter of Germinius, are connected with the preceding material neither in subject nor in time. Yet if I refrain from saying to what part of Arian history they belong, because they have been inserted in those most exact *Ecclesiastical Annals*, I shall save time and paper. It will suffice to add this one point. From Hilary’s words appended to Liberius’s letter to the Eastern bishops (*Fragment* VI, no. 6, the formula to which Liberius subscribed), it appears that the rule of faith which we said above had been sent from the Synod of Sirmium to the churches was approved by Liberius himself through subscription, his resistance broken by weariness of exile and longing for his see, just as it was approved by the others who had yielded to Emperor Constantius’s violence. Thus the report was not wholly groundless which Sozomen (*History* IV.14) records that the Arians circulated: that the bishop of Rome had defected to the opinion of the Anomoeans.

For this reason our Hilary, carried away by zeal for the faith, pronounces anathema upon Liberius himself as an apostate and betrayer. And indeed, that creed could have been no other than the one dictated by Narcissus, Theodore, Eudoxius, Demophilus, and those other Arians conspicuous for rashness and perfidy, as we shall see below. From this we also learn who authored, and to what they belong, those names [Col. 0899C] of heretics which the most distinguished writer of the *Annals* noted in his manuscript to have been appended to this letter of Liberius to the Easterners (under the year 357, no. 34); as also to those words at the end of the following letter of the same pope to Ursacius, Valens, and Germinius: “I have pronounced anathema upon the betrayer together with the Arians.”

16. There remains the last letter in this collection [Note: Now *Fragment* X, against Aetius, or rather against the party of Acacius.] addressed to the delegates of the Council of Rimini. It is from Semi-Arian bishops, for the most part Palestinians, against Aetius, surnamed the Impious and the Godless. For although the Arians never agreed well among themselves—as is the habit of all heretics, except in opposing Christ’s Church—once the deception of Rimini had succeeded according to their desire, and they considered their business with the Catholics complete, [Col. 0899D] they began to fight one another more fiercely, divided much more openly in opinions, dispositions, and names.

Hence there arose a thousand names of factions and sects, a thousand artificers of harm. “Many names,” says Ambrose (*On the Faith* I.44), “but one perfidy: not differing in weakness, discordant in communion; not unlike in deceit, but distinct in thought.” These remarks concern the contents published here under the title of the book of Blessed Hilary on the Council of Rimini.

17. The second part of the collection. — The remaining documents, which seem to form, as it were, a second collection, are read in the manuscript from which these were transcribed before the documents we have explained. Yet one may infer even from this that they too were excerpted from the same work of Blessed Hilary: in several places the author’s words from which they were taken are intermingled with the acts themselves, displaying the phraseology of that most holy confessor; and almost all concern the Synod of Rimini, which was especially treated in that work. Yet in arranging them no more exact order of events or time was observed than in the preceding material.

18. The Parisian synod, now *Fragment* XI. — I judge that the creed said to have been set forth “at the city of Farisea” was written at Lutetia of the Parisians, and I conjecture that its heading should read, “at the city of Paris.” For by then the name Paris had almost displaced that of Lutetia. Zosimus, not much later in age, writes of Julian wintering there: “Julian, while staying at Paris—a small town in Gaul” (*Ἰουλιανοῦ δὲ ἐν τῷ Παρισίῳ, Γερμανίας δὲ αὕτη πολίχνη, διατρίβοντος*). [Note: Caesar is mentioned as spending the winter among the Parisians.]

Although the city then lacked the size and renown to which it was afterward raised by the residence of the Most Christian kings and the fame of learning—indeed, we find it called a “small town” (*πολίχνη*) and, by Ammianus (XV.11), merely a fortified place enclosed by the circuit of an island—it scarcely comprised half the area which later acquired the distinctive name of the city. The island, enclosed by the River Seine and joined to the mainland on both sides by bridges resting on piles, formed its whole extent. Yet its temperate climate, which even supported fig trees, and the beauty of its very calm and clear river seemed so pleasant and suitable to Julian while he was in Gaul that he most willingly spent his winters there (Ammianus XVII.7–8). When the army proclaimed him emperor there, he later called it his “dearest little town” (*φιλτάτην πολίχνην*) in his highly polished address to the Antiochenes, the *Misopogon*, and sought to display the elegance of his genius in describing it.

And indeed, much earlier, when Julius Caesar convened a council of the Gauls, that place had seemed suitable for holding it, and he transferred the assembly to Lutetia of the Parisians. Wherever this synod was held, it is beyond doubt that it was one [Note: We have shown that it was convened before Hilary’s return to Gaul.] of those which Hilary assembled in Gaul. Having been permitted by an edict of Emperor Constantius, shortly before that emperor’s death, to return to his episcopate, Hilary found, as Severus says (*Sacred History* II), nearly the whole world infected by the evil of perfidy. A man naturally gentle and mild, yet also fitted for persuasion—such is Rufinus’s characterization of him (*Ecclesiastical History* I.31)—he judged it best to summon all to repentance and convened numerous bishops in Gaul (Sulpicius, p. 262).

As a result, when all bishops confessed their error, they condemned what had occurred at Rimini and restored the ancient faith to the churches. It is also probable that Victurinus, bishop of Paris—whom Athanasius attests was present at the Synod of Sardica (*Apology to Constantius*, p. 767), and whom the acts of the Council of Cologne show was delegated to Cologne against Euphrates—if he survived to these times, contributed his confession to these synods. Jerome refers to these synods in the Eusebian *Chronicle* when, under the final year of Constantius’s life—for the years of Christ marked in that chronicle are neither Eusebius’s nor Jerome’s—he notes that Gaul, through Hilary, condemned the deception of Rimini, as the ancient manuscripts read. We see that this was accomplished by this creed as well. Although these synods were held only after Constantius’s death and Julian’s assumption of power, that is, about [Col. 0901B] the year of Christ 362.

19. When Hosius died. — The letter [Note: Second part of *Fragment* XI: when written.] of Eusebius, bishop of Vercelli, to Gregory, bishop of the Spanish city of Elvira, was written while Emperor Constantius was still alive. For it is he whom Eusebius means when he says that the hope of the Ariomaniacs depended not upon their own strength or united agreement—for the passage seems to require this correction—but upon the protection of a secular king. For they had, to use Athanasius’s words, “their hopes on earth and below, namely in Caesar and his eunuchs.”

Yet the letter was written after Hosius’s betrayal and also after the Synod of Rimini. It is worth observing that it speaks of Hosius as still alive, and as a man whom Gregory had not long before vigorously and fearlessly opposed when he was plotting something on behalf of the Arians. If so, Hosius must have lived to Constantius’s twenty-fourth year, the three hundred and sixtieth year after Christ; in that year this letter must have been sent, and Hosius himself must have died shortly afterward. For Athanasius, in his first oration against the Arians, delivered in the thirty-sixth year after the Nicene synod, that is, in the year of Christ 361, refers to Hosius as deceased.

Perhaps this gave Marcellinus and the other Luciferians the opportunity (Marcellinus and Faustinus, book addressed to the emperor)—as is the habit of heretics, who, because they lack truth, turn events occurring according to their own course into fabricated miracles by interpolating and exaggerating them in words—to invent that dreadful tragedy of his death, with its curses summoned from the same Gregory. This passage alone exposes its falsehood. For if Hosius had so miserably yielded up his soul in that conflict, Eusebius would not have passed so lightly over the astonishing and pitiable death of that great man and such immediate vengeance of the divine power.

20. It is clear from what we said above, when discussing the letter of Valens, Ursacius, and the others to Germinius which gave occasion to this document—or rather received occasion from it—that Germinius’s creed, now *Fragment* XIII, which immediately follows this letter, is much later than the letter. [Col. 0902A] Germinius’s formula is plainly conformed to the creed issued with the consuls’ names, which called the Son like the Father in all things, and is, as it were, diametrically opposed to the impiety of the faithlessness of the Synod of Sirmium, as our Hilary calls it (*On the Synods*, no. 2), which defined the Father as greater than the Son in honor, dignity, glory, and majesty.

21. The following letter of the Council of Sardica to Gregory, bishop of Alexandria, and to the others [Note: [Col. 0901D] The pseudo-Sardican letter, now Fragment III], is much earlier than those preceding it and wholly different in subject. For it contains a decree fabricated in the name of the Council of Sardica by the Arians—a decree mentioned by Socrates and incorporated by Sozomen into the outline of his History (Socrates, Book II, 20; Sozomen, Book III, 11)—certainly the final example of heretical rashness and audacity. For, since they lacked sufficient assurance to appear before the Fathers assembled at Sardica in A.D. 348, with Athanasius present, whom they had so shamelessly accused and slandered, they gathered at Philippopolis, a city of Thrace, and concocted the decree now before us under the name of the Fathers assembled at Sardica, whose renown had already spread among the peoples. By it they not only deposed Athanasius as though convicted of grave crimes, but also declared Julius, bishop of Rome, Hosius, Protogenes, Gaudentius, and Maximinus—the pillars of the Nicene faith—removed from rank and ecclesiastical communion. Nor were they content merely to have wronged such great men, unless also, to speak with the Prophet (Isa. 7:13), they should be burdensome to our God: they attempted to cast down Christ from [Col. 0902C] the Father’s right hand—that is, from the rank of *homoousia* and equal honour (*tēs homoousias kai homotimias*)—by drawing up a new formula of faith in which they omitted the terms *ousia* and *homoousios*.

22. Yet it is astonishing that even our Hilary inserted this very rule of faith into his work *On the Synods* as though it were a legitimate [Note: [Col. 0901D] If he had regarded it as legitimate, would he have entitled it [Col. 0902D] “Faith according to the Eastern Synod”? But it is one thing to excuse it, another to judge it Catholic.] Sardican synod, and expounded it as though Catholic; or that Athanasius himself, in his letter on the synods of Rimini and Seleucia, and after him Socrates, having enumerated nine Arian formulas differing both in wording and in sense, did not add this as a tenth. For Athanasius himself, in more than one place, is a most abundant witness (Letter to the Antiochenes, p. 576) that, when certain persons wished to add some things as though lacking to the Nicene formula, the Sardican Fathers replied that they were satisfied [Col. 0902D] with the Nicene faith and decreed that nothing further should be written: “lest those whose desire it was always to establish novelties should be given an opportunity of again and again defining new matters concerning the faith.”

Sozomen is certainly convicted of manifest error when he writes (Book III, ch. 12) that the Catholic Fathers at Sardica issued a formula of faith identical in meaning with the Nicene, though framed in more words, and that Hosius and Protogenes defended themselves before Julius, bishop of Rome, by appeal to it. It is clear that in that book *On the Synods* our Hilary was so little offended not only by the pseudo-Sardican formula [Col. 0903A] but also by the Antiochene formula at the Dedication, and the Sirmian formula against Photinus—three formulas especially approved by the Semi-Arians at the Synod of Ancyra—that he expounded them and attempted to excuse them in these words: “It ought not to seem surprising to you, dearest brethren,” he says (*On the Synods*, §63), “that formulas of faith have begun to be set forth so frequently; heretical madness imposes this necessity.” And shortly afterwards: “But necessity has introduced the custom of setting forth creeds and of subscribing to those set forth. For where the conviction of conscience is endangered, there a written statement is required; nor indeed is there any prohibition against writing what it is salutary to confess.”

Later, however, taught by experience that not only “Camarina must not be stirred,” as the proverb has it, but much less should what the Fathers had rightly established be overthrown under any pretext whatever; and recognizing how dangerous and lamentable it was “to have diverse faiths, which, while they become more numerous,” as he himself says (*To Constantius*, Book II, §4), “begin to result in there being no faith at all,” he condemned in one judgment, in his book to Constantius, every formula except the Nicene. “For even if,” he says (*To Constantius*, §24), “nothing defective is alleged to underlie them, nevertheless there is no ground of religious intent, because they are an evil contrivance.”

23. To what sort of bishops the letter of the Philippopolitan synod was addressed.—Further, no one can doubt that those illustrious architects of the new faith addressed this synodical letter especially to bishops whom they hoped could easily be deceived, or would find such an imposture agreeable. Among them Gregory the Cappadocian, plunderer of the Alexandrian Church, rightly takes the lead [Col. 0903C]. Long before, because of Arian heresy, he had been excluded from the communion of the Church; indeed, the Council of Sardica ordered that he should not even be regarded as a Christian. Not long afterwards he was killed by a popular uprising of the Alexandrians, receiving an end suited to his unrestrained violence (Fragment II, §8).

Nor was Donatus, who is called bishop of Carthage, much holier. This is the Donatus who succeeded Majorinus and long sustained and fostered in Africa that most destructive sect which set up altar against the altar of God at Carthage. He rose to such pride and madness that, just as the Pythagoreans are said to have customarily sworn by their teacher (Optatus, Book III, against Parmenianus), he permitted—and himself used—the practice of his followers’ swearing by him as by God, and calling themselves the party of Donatus, or Donatists, instead of Christians. [Col. 0903D] Jerome testifies that he also wrote a book consonant with the Arian opinion (*On Ecclesiastical Writers*).

Yet between these two notable heretics we recognize Amphion, an eminent confessor of Christ, venerable for his grey hair and holy life, as numbered with the wicked after the example of the Master. For this is Amphion, first bishop of Epiphania in Cilicia, who nearly forty years earlier had fearlessly confessed Christ under Maximian and was afterwards appointed in the place of Eusebius, bishop of Nicomedia, when that man had been deposed for heresy at the Nicene synod (Sozomen, Book I, chs. 10 and 21). It is due to his merits that we should restore, from the testimony to his apostolic holiness [Col. 0904A] and confession given by Athanasius in the First Oration against the Arians (p. 291), a reading corrupted in the learned translator’s version through a fault in the Greek manuscript he used. For where Athanasius, in that Oration, warns Catholics not to receive the formulas of faith of Ursacius, Valens, Demophilus, Germinius, and others of that sort, even though written in words drawn from Holy Scripture, any more than Christ received the devil speaking from those same Scriptures, because the words of the ungodly are deceitful; when he enumerates the lights of the Church in his age and the apostolic men in whose writings no evil may be suspected, the Latin translation gives: “or of Lupus and Appianus of Cilicia.” The Greek manuscript reads:

> ἢ Λούπου καὶ Ἀμφίωνος τοῦ ὁμολογητοῦ καὶ ἐπισκόπου τῆς Κιλικίας;

“or of Lupus and Amphion, the confessor and bishop of Cilicia?”

For he was called bishop both of Cilicia and of Nicomedia. Nor is there any reason for anyone to suspect that he afterwards departed from the right faith: the Church testifies that he persevered in Catholic peace, since it celebrates his feast on the day before the Ides of June. We must therefore conclude that he was mixed among those criminals in order that a man renowned and illustrious among all for the fame of his virtue might lend those skulking villains some appearance of holiness.

24. The Sardican decrees unknown to Augustine.—It is nevertheless remarkable that, when the blessed Augustine answers the Donatists, who sought to deceive by means of this decree and to prove that they had been recognized as Catholics by the Council of Sardica, he seems insufficiently aware of this fraud. More than once, in reply to Cresconius (Book III, ch. 34; Book IV, ch. 44), [Col. 0904C] he objects that the names of the cities of which the alleged bishops were bishops had not been added; therefore it could not be established that the Donatus whose name they displayed in this synodical letter was the one who had acted as bishop of Carthage. He adds further that it is not an ecclesiastical custom, when bishops write to bishops, to add the name of the city. Whence, then, did those city names enter here? Unless perhaps they were added by the Donatists; Augustine himself appears to suggest this suspicion when he writes: “I wonder whether this Donatus, whoever he may be, was made a Carthaginian, if not in your own letters” (*Against Cresconius*, Book IV, ch. 44).

25. It would be too long to investigate every one who subscribed this letter, nor perhaps would it be worth the effort. But Menophantus of Ephesus, Acacius of Caesarea, Theodore [Col. 0904D] of Heraclea, Mark of Arethusa—for it is a printer’s error that “of Arezzo” is read here—Eudoxius of Germanicia, Narcissus of Neropolis or Irenopolis, for he bore both names, Demophilus of Beroea, and Valens of Mursa, who closes the procession, “as it were the last of the Mysians,” furnish proof that it was written by heretics. These are famous standard-bearers and leaders of the Arians, according to the testimonies of Athanasius, Hilary, Epiphanius, and the writers of ecclesiastical history, and they are numbered among those who subscribed this decree. But perhaps enough—indeed more than enough—has been said of that forged decree.

26. We assign it to A.D. 354, Fragment V.—What remains, although nearly all of it belongs to the Synod of Rimini—except the letter of Liberius, bishop of Rome, to Constantius, sent in the year of salvation 351 through the Romans Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari, Pancratius the presbyter, and Hilary the deacon; for in Athanasius’s letter *To Those Leading the Solitary Life* Eutropius is named corruptly in place of Pancratius (p. 836)—nevertheless exists in confusion and without any order. Whoever wishes for more on Liberius’s letter should consult those never sufficiently praised *Annals* (Baronius, year 354, §1); there he will find in greatest abundance what may quench his thirst. Almost everything else is now published for the first time. In what order it should be arranged will become clear from the narrative of events.

[Col. 0905B] 27. Historical sequence of the Council of Rimini.—We said above that the faith composed at Sirmium in the presence of the Emperor, with the consuls appended, which declared the Son like the Father in all things, had been procured and drafted by Arian factions; that a universal synod convoked at Nicaea in Bithynia was divided; and that the Eastern bishops were directed to meet at Seleucia in Isauria, the Western bishops at Rimini. To what end, except to deceive and ensnare them? Certain of the strength of their party in the East, and fully confident that the Eastern bishops would readily approve that crafty and deceptive rule of faith, they believed that the Westerners, once assembled, would ultimately be compelled to subscribe to what the East had approved and what the Emperor—“a relentless vindicator of his authority,” as Ammianus describes him (Book XIV, ch. 5)—had ratified.

Indeed, our Hilary testifies (*On the Synods*, §63) that, except for Bishop Eleusius—he was bishop of Cyzicus—and a few with him, the ten Asiatic provinces within which he lived for the most part did not know the true God. “And would that,” he adds, “they did not know God; for their ignorance would be more readily pardoned than their hostility. Yet the grief of these bishops, unable to contain itself in silence, seeks the unity of that faith which it has long ago lost through others.”

Accordingly, once this faith had been written and the universal synod divided, the Arians obtained from the Emperor a rescript addressed to each synod, commanding the assembled Fathers first to consider the faith and then to investigate the cases of bishops and their mutual conflicts and accusations; after matters had been examined and decided, they were to appoint ten delegates to the imperial court [Col. 0905D] to report what had been done. [Note: [Col. 0905D] So Sozomen, Book IV, ch. 17. But Socrates, Book II, ch. 39, testifies that there was great dispute over this matter: some maintained that the faith, others that the cases of bishops, should first be investigated, because imperial letters were produced which at one time prescribed one course, at another another.] Another rescript was directed to the Fathers assembled at Rimini, prohibiting them from examining the cases of Eastern bishops and again instructing them to send ten delegates to the court. Sozomen mentions the former rescript; the latter—namely Fragment VII, §1—is recorded as sent on the sixth day before the Kalends of June, that is, on the fifth day after that formula of faith was drafted.

Then, furnished with these documents, Valens, Ursacius, and Germinius hurried by long journeys to Rimini, accompanied by Auxentius, a Cappadocian by race, “rather an informer than a Christian,” as Athanasius says (*Letter to the Solitaries*, p. 861). Though wholly ignorant of Latin, he had been forced by military power into the see of Milan by the Emperor after Dionysius had been exiled for piety. They were accompanied by Caius and others whom they found favourable to themselves in that synod, and they demanded, as we said above from Athanasius (*On the Synods*, p. 874), that all subscribe to their formula without any examination of the case and with eyes, as it were, blindfolded. But they were not only mocked because of the consuls appended to their rule; they were also denounced as heretics because of their impiety and the fox lurking beneath their feeble breast, and expelled from the synod itself.

Therefore, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of August, immediately following, the whole synod unanimously decreed that nothing could be added to or taken away from the Nicene rule (Fragment VII, §4). Ursacius, [Col. 0906B] Valens, Caius, and Germinius—to whom Athanasius adds Auxentius and Demophilus—were cast out from their rank and from communion with the faithful as disturbers of ecclesiastical peace and heretics. Ten delegates were sent to the Emperor, through whom this decision of the council might be made known. “And thus,” Athanasius writes, “the proceedings at Rimini had such an end.” This collection supplies the decision of the council more fully and completely than it exists in ancient writers, with two fragments of that same synod appended.

28. The devices of the condemned Arians. On the formula of Nicaea in Thrace.—Yet the Arians themselves, struck by this decision, neither lost heart nor abandoned their designs. They too sent ten of their own number to the Emperor, among whom were those who had been condemned. Outstripping the council’s delegates by speed, they so inflamed the Emperor against the synod [Col. 0906C] that he would not permit the delegates of the orthodox faith even to come into his presence. Instead, he held them at first in Hadrianopolis and then at Nicaea in Thrace, deceived by various delays, in the hope—as Theodoret says (*Ecclesiastical History*, Book II, ch. 19)—that the bishops waiting at Rimini for the return of their delegates, some burdened by old age, some by poverty, all wearied by their prolonged absence from their own sees, might through desire of returning be induced to subscribe to the proposed creed.

He even granted Ursacius authority to settle the matter of faith at his own discretion. Once he had received this authority, no one can fail immediately to suppose that this vigorous leader of the Plautine family did not sit idle with his hands folded. Then, supported by such great authority, the Arians, wishing to interpolate rather than amend their derided creed—as we mentioned above in another connection—had copies of it sought out and collected everywhere through Martianus the notary (Athanasius, *On the Synods*, p. 904). Removing the consuls, as thieves are accustomed to remove handles from another’s cups, and changing a few little words, they forced those good delegates, by violence and fraud alike, not merely to confirm the same perfidy—indeed a worse one—by their own subscription, but also, in the name of the council whose person they represented, to enter into communion with Ursacius, Valens, and the others who had been expressly condemned and deposed by the synod’s decision. [Col. 0907A] They called this interpolated creed “the Nicene faith,” in order to deceive the simpler sort by the likeness of the name.

And certainly anyone who compares the creed which the Fathers of Rimini were compelled to approve by their subscriptions, as it is found in Athanasius (*On the Synods*, p. 875) and Jerome (*Dialogue against the Luciferians*), with that which had the consuls appended, will find the former more perfidious in that the two words “in all things,” which Valens—as Epiphanius testifies (Heresy 71)—had unwillingly admitted, are omitted in it, while in every other respect it is entirely similar. Athanasius (*On the Synods*, p. 905) attributes this interpolation to the Council of Constantinople, which the Acacians convened after Seleucia. If that is so, I do not see how the dates can agree. For the fragment of the Nicene conventicle published here (Fragment VIII, §5) indicates that the conventicle was held on the sixth day before the Ides of October, under the same consuls Eusebius and Hypatius—unless perhaps [Note: [Col. 0907D] No error has crept in; but because the formula subscribed at Constantinople was the one published at Nicaea in Thrace, Athanasius rightly said that the Constantinopolitan synod did not adhere to the Sirmian faith, especially since he makes no mention of the Nicene conventicle.] an error has crept into the dating and “the sixth day before the Ides of November” ought to be read. Yet Athanasius and Sabinus, cited by Socrates (Book II, ch. 39), are most abundant witnesses that the Council of Seleucia began on the fifth day before the Kalends of October. The distance between the places and the circumstances of the affair do not permit men who were at Seleucia in Isauria on the fifth day before the Kalends of October to have held and completed a council at Constantinople by the sixth day before the Ides of the same month.

29. But who these delegates of the Council of Rimini were, and what rank or dignity they held in the Church, cannot easily be discovered from the histories, since we scarcely possess even their bare names. Only Restitutus, bishop of Carthage, is mentioned, though he too is unknown to the ancient writers. For, apart from Gratus, whom we have learned from the acts of the councils themselves and from Athanasius to have attended the Council of Sardica and to have convened the first council of Carthage, as Isidore Mercator calls it; and Genethlius, whom Aurelius succeeded about A.D. 390, no memory survives of any other bishop who occupied the see of Carthage about this time.

30. On the Council of Carthage under Genethlius.—Indeed, through the fault of copyists, the name of Genethlius himself has almost been erased from the second council of that city, although it was held under his leadership and auspices. Thus great men inquire, not without reason, when it was held and by whom. If, by resolving this question from ancient books and restoring the council to its proper author, we do not waste our effort on this introduction, it may be worthwhile. There are three reasons why this council is disputed. First, it is said to have been celebrated under the consulship of Valentinian IV and Theodosius, though Valentinian the Elder is nowhere recorded as having held the consulship with Theodosius, his colleague in imperial rule. Second, Genethlius’s name does not appear in it. Third and last, Aurelius, the bishop who succeeded Genethlius, seems to have presided over it.

But Isidore notes that this council was celebrated in Era 428. That era falls in A.D. 390, and the fasti assign to that year Valentinian IV and Neoterius—not Theodosius—as consuls. Therefore Neoterius must plainly be substituted for Theodosius. Moreover, the old manuscripts read Genethlius in all places where the printed editions give Genedius, through the fusion of the letter *t* with *l*. In Canon II of this council, where the text reads, “Aurelius the bishop said,” those same books read: “Epigonius, bishop of Bulla Regia, said.” Likewise, in Canons V and VI they write Genethlius instead of Aurelius. Once these corrections have been made, nothing remains from which controversy can arise. Fulgentius Ferrandus, deacon of Carthage, also confirms this. In chapter 194 of his *Summary of Canons* are these words: “that one entangled in certain crimes should not have the right to accuse: Council of Carthage under holy Genethlius, title VI.” This occurs in Canon VI of the council now under discussion. But enough on this matter.

31. On Musonius and Restitutus.—Thus, to return to the point from which we digressed, only Gratus and this Genethlius are mentioned by writers as bishops of Carthage around the time of the Council of Rimini. Athanasius, in his letter to the bishops of Africa, reveals that several bishops from their number attended the Council of Rimini, though he does not give their names. Jerome, in his work against the Luciferians, names Musonius, bishop of the province of Byzacena, and writes that all conceded him precedence in that synod because of his age. For “the province of Byzantium,” which [Col. 0908C] all editions read, is corrupt: the Latins never confuse these terms, as the Greeks do. Byzacena, however, is a province of that Africa assigned to the Western Empire, celebrated by Pliny and the geographers for extraordinary fertility, its fields returning a hundredfold profit to cultivators; it is also mentioned more than once in the African councils.

A Musonius is also mentioned as an old man and bishop of the principal see of the province of Byzacena in a Council of Carthage held on the Ides of August under the consuls Atticus and Caesarius, in A.D. 397. Yet I would deny that he is the same person as the man now under discussion, unless we had seen above that aged Hosius presided at the Nicene Council and, more than a hundred years old, attended the Council of Sirmium held thirty or more years later, surviving until A.D. 360.

As for Bishop Restitutus, all writers are equally silent. Unless perhaps the Basilica Restituta Perpetua at Carthage, in which more than one synod was held, derived its name from this Restitutus in question, having been built in honour of the martyr Perpetua. Likewise, we have learned from a notable, still unpublished fragment of a sermon of blessed Augustine—preached after the Conference at the dedication of that basilica—that a basilica built there by Bishop Aurelius, who was also called Florens, was named Florentia in his honour (see Augustine, Sermon 19, note a; Sermon 359, and note b, p. 1405). [Col. 0909A] Whoever that Restitutus may have been, or whoever the other delegates sent with him from the synod to the Emperor, they certainly showed themselves to be just such ill-taught and insufficiently cautious young men as Severus describes (*Sacred History*, Book II), when, exceeding the bounds of their commission—indeed acting contrary to the very mandate that they should in no way enter communion with Arians—they annulled the proceedings of the synod by admitting into communion the heretics whom it had rejected.

32. While these things were occurring in Thrace, the bishops who had assembled at Rimini—both those of the orthodox faith and those of Arian perfidy—were meanwhile ordered by Taurus, prefect of the praetorium, to await the return of their delegates. He had been instructed not to dismiss them before they agreed [Col. 0909B] upon one faith. There they were detained with the greatest discomfort and weariness. Therefore each party separately wrote to the Emperor, most earnestly begging and beseeching him, since winter was approaching, not to allow old men, far removed from their sees, to be postponed into the most difficult season, but to permit them to return to their cities as soon as possible. Socrates has the letter of the bishops of the orthodox faith (Book II, ch. 37). This collection presents that of the Arians, under the name of the Synod of Rimini agreeing with the East (Fragment IX).

33. History does not conceal the falls of eminent men. They sometimes turn out well for them. The example of Liberius (Augustine, *On the Agony of Christ*, ch. 30).—It would be superfluous to add here the rest of what was done in this affair and the outcome it eventually reached, since we have outlined it above and it has been treated at great length by Athanasius, Jerome against the Luciferians, and Sulpicius Severus. For our sole purpose was to address those matters which seemed pertinent to the connection and elucidation of these Fragments. Yet even here I fear that I may seem to have said too much and to have brought upon myself that tragic imprecation:

> ὄλοιο θνητῶν συλλέγων τὰς συμφοράς  
> “May you perish, gathering the misfortunes of mortals,”

by reopening and bruising, as though they were covered sores better left concealed, the reputation and good name of venerable Fathers, their controversies, disagreements, and defection.

But since history has this one purpose: that it may be, as Thucydides left in writing, a “possession for all time” (*ktēma es aei xynkeimenon*), from which people of every age may draw examples both of praise and of fortune and regulate themselves in relation to the varied and sudden events by which we are daily assailed, I do not see why their calamities, errors, and even crimes should bring us who merely read of them, rather than suffer them, less profit and benefit than their virtues and noble achievements. Especially since even for those very persons who, through human weakness, fall into such calamities, matters often turn out well.

I gladly pass over Croesus in Herodotus, who frankly acknowledged that his sufferings had become lessons (*pathēmata mathēmata*) to him, and Merops in the theatres, who confessed that misfortunes had made him wise, so that I may make room in an ecclesiastical discussion for an example drawn from sacred history, from which the Church derives her pattern. Blessed Ambrose writes admirably concerning the denial of Peter, chief of the Apostles: “Even the fall of the saints is useful. Peter’s denial did me no harm; his amendment benefited me. I learned to avoid the conversations of the faithless” (Ambrose, Book X on Luke, §89). Elsewhere the same author teaches that the adversary is sometimes compelled to tempt the saints to their hurt. “For while he tempts,” he adds, “he makes them better, so that the one who is tempted may be able to instruct others, though he had seemed weak in himself. Thus Peter is set over the Church after he has been tempted by the devil.”

Thus God’s immeasurable goodness ensures that sins turn out well, not only for others but also for those who commit them. For these are miracles of divine providence which the human mind cannot reach: that all things may turn out for good to the godly, and that “what has departed from the assigned order of things may nevertheless be brought back into another order, so that rashness may have no power in the kingdom of providence.” [Col. 0910B] Therefore no one should doubt that in Liberius, the pontiff and successor of Peter, there was renewed what Optatus of Milevis and Augustine observed: divine providence caused the very Apostle who was to receive the keys to deny, so that the Catholic Church, whose person he represented, might learn, as “a true mother, neither proudly to insult her sinful children nor to be slow in forgiving those who have been corrected” (ibid.). Liberius himself was permitted to fall for a time, so that from his fall he might rise against heresy more keenly and strongly, and might become more merciful and more ready to pardon those who repent and wish to return. The fact has also been preserved in writing and handed down to times like those former times: that those who stand may learn from it to fear for themselves, and may not show themselves harsh toward those returning to the Church.

34. The falls of Hosius and Lucifer.—No less worthy, certainly, either of contemplation or of instruction regarding human frailty and the inscrutable mystery of divine judgments, are the fates of Hosius and Lucifer, bravest defenders of the Catholic faith. The former, after most steadfastly confessing the Christian name under the fiercest persecutors, after immeasurable labours spent for the Catholic faith against heresy, and after most worthily discharging many embassies, so that he was regarded as the father of bishops, nevertheless, being excessively attached to his own grave (Hilary, *On the Synods*, §87)—for he had passed his hundredth year—would at the final close of life have utterly failed, had divine mercy not extended a hand to him as he yielded to Arian violence [Col. 0910D] and imperial threats and rushed headlong through approving the Anomoean perfidy of Sirmium.

The latter, superior even to the trials to which Hosius had yielded, after raising so many trophies over defeated perfidy—to use Jerome’s words (*Against the Luciferians*)—was conquered by the very author of dissensions in the very moment of triumph; he was separated from the Church and utterly overthrown. At this, who does not immediately cry out with the tragedian:

> Ὡς θνητὸν ἀνδρῶν καὶ ταλαίπωρον γένος,  
> Ὡς οὐδὲν ἐσμέν.  
> “How mortal and wretched is the race of men; how utterly nothing we are!”

And who does not cast off all confidence in himself and learn, according to the Apostle’s instruction, to work out his salvation with fear and trembling (Phil. 2:12)?

[Col. 0911A] 35. What the general defection of the Fathers at Rimini teaches us.—But the consideration of that general deception of the ecclesiastical order and that almost concerted apostasy is exceedingly useful and suited to our own age. From it we are plainly taught how cautious and circumspect we must be in dealing with heretics, and how dangerous it is to depart even a nail’s breadth from the boundaries fixed by the Fathers. For when those good Fathers allowed certain bare little terms—*ousia* and *homoousios*—to be omitted from their profession of faith, persuaded by the Arians that this was all they were doing, they eventually perceived, too late, that the confession of the most holy Trinity, who is God—that is, the sum of religion, for the preservation of which the Church, from Christ’s birth onward, had shed so much blood and given so many martyrs—had been wrested and torn away from them. [Col. 0911B] How much more firmly and wisely had those same men previously determined that nothing should be added to or subtracted from what had been established at the Synod of Nicaea, and that the name “substance” and the reality it denotes should retain their firmness (Fragment VII, §3, and Fragment VIII).

36. The purpose of councils.—Those are deceived, and seek to draw us with them into the same error, who wish to persuade us that, amid the storms of opinions in which we live, the Church needs councils to determine what she ought especially to follow. Although councils have perhaps never been more necessary than they are now, so that the Bride of Christ—whom he purchased for himself not with all the waves, but by the outpouring of all his most innocent blood—may be delivered from ambition, greed, trafficking, ignorance, and the filth and obscenity of morals; so that her genuine colour and splendour may be restored; so that that discipline which the Apostles and those nearest to them established in religion as a brazen wall against such plagues of charity and unity, whether collapsed through age or through the negligence of pastors, may be restored and revived; and so that its honour and authority may be restored to the sacred order—for the preservation of these things those earliest founders of religion ordained that provincial synods should be assembled twice every year—although, I say, we may perhaps need councils for recalling and restoring such things, I do not think that a council can establish something other than what has hitherto been believed and observed in the Church.

“For this always,” as that pilgrim of Lérins wrote (ch. 32), “and nothing beyond it, has the Church accomplished when stirred by heretical novelties: namely, that what she had received by tradition alone, she afterwards also committed to posterity in written record, comprehending a great mass of matter in a few letters”—that is, in the Creed—“and, usually for the sake of clearer understanding, recording not a new sense of faith but a new term with its proper precision.” No sound person should exclude such pious novelties—“new combinations of remedies against new poisons,” as our Hilary calls them (*To Constantius*, §16), “new wars against new enemies, recent councils against new snares” [Col. 0912A]—under the apostolic prohibition of profane novelties.

37. God does not fail his suffering Church. Julian raises her up while plotting her ruin.—Moreover, whoever sets before his eyes the condition of the Church after that defection—confused everywhere by tumults, quarrels, disputes, and schisms, torn and scattered; afflicted then by its own bishops no less than a little earlier by the conspiratorial enemies of the Christian name; in which neither bishops knew firmly what they ought to teach, nor peoples what they ought to follow; finally so desperate and ruined that it called forth in holy men a longing for the times of Nero, Decius, and Maximian (Hilary, *To Constantius*, §4)—and then turns the eye of his mind to that sudden and unexpected change of affairs which followed soon after the death of Constantius, when the bishops were recalled from exile to their own sees by the edict of the new prince, will certainly recognize that the Lord stood ready by the distressed little boat of the Apostles and stilled that shaking by the presence of his divine Majesty. “The beast dies,” says Jerome (*Against the Luciferians*), “and tranquillity returns.” And indeed:

> πολλὰς καὶ παραδόξους ἑδοὺς σωτηρίας οἶδε τὸ θεῖον καινοτομεῖν νεύων πρὸς φιλάνθρωπον.  
> “The divine power knows how to devise many strange paths of salvation, directing its innovations toward benevolence.”

For who would ever have believed, unless it had been attested to us by the writings of almost all the authors of that age, that that apostate dragon Julian—the “great Mind” of whom Isaiah speaks, and the Assyrian—who had desired nothing from imperial power so much as utterly to destroy the Christian religion, [Col. 0912C] and who had approached its overthrow soberly, as Julius Caesar of old approached the suppression of the Commonwealth, should have promoted the restoration of the Nicene faith and concord among the bishops? For, although he recalled from exile, on account of the Christian faith, all persons of every sect, only in order to nourish and perpetuate those disturbances by which the Church was then afflicted, and so that the leaders of the different sects—which at that time were almost innumerable—living within the same walls might, like most hostile enemies, pursue one another more fiercely at close quarters and more swiftly destroy each other: yet, by the unsearchable providence of God, which, as we read in *The Shepherd* of Hermas, “turns even the worst things to its own good end, so that through the Church His manifold wisdom may appear, according to the foreknowledge of the ages [Col. 0912D] which He accomplished in Christ,” we have seen above that, through the diligence, labour, and solicitude of those three confessors returned from exile, almost all who had subscribed to the crime of Rimini—whether deceived through simplicity, terrified by fear, or even infected with the Arian taint—acknowledged their fault and embraced the Nicene faith. Indeed, stirred by the common danger of an external persecution, they coalesced, as it were by a syncretism, into one faith; and not a few even of the heretics became martyrs. For who can resist the divine will? As Clement of Alexandria has excellently handed down in writing, “even the counsels and actions of those who have apostatized are steered toward a wholesome end. For it is the work of divine wisdom, virtue, and power [Col. 0913A] not only to do good, but especially to bring some good and beneficial end out of evils devised by certain persons, and profitably to make use of things which seem worthless.”

### 38. These Fragments discovered by the prompting of divine providence. Cassian’s books *On the Incarnation*.

I am persuaded that it is likewise a work of that same providence that these Fragments should especially now recover the light in these most turbulent times, in order that we, aroused by them to such a consideration of history, may conceive from the knowledge of it a sure hope: whenever we truly and wholeheartedly repent of our crimes, we shall find that the divine hand is neither maimed nor shortened, and that the same Lord will restore solid and firm tranquillity to the endangered bark of the Apostles. [Col. 0913B] For, in my judgment, anyone is grievously mistaken who thinks that the heresies which wander through and trouble almost the whole world derive more strength and force from the evil dispositions or cunning devices of their adherents than from our own vices and crimes.

Accordingly, just as we can never render, or even conceive in mind, thanks worthy of our deserts to the divine Majesty for this extraordinary kindness of His divinity toward us, so too we can scarcely—indeed, scarcely even at all—return equal gratitude to the pious shade of our excellent Pithou, who has so well deserved of humankind, and to whom that supreme Majesty willed that we should owe these Fragments. For he had so ordered his life that he everywhere put public advantage before his own affairs; and when the plague was raging at Paris, he withdrew to Troyes of the Tricassi, which had given us that luminary. [Col. 0913C] There he obtained from his brother François—a man most distinguished in his own right by virtue and learning, and altogether a true brother to so great a brother—an old copy of the Aesopic fables of Phaedrus, “the rogue,” as Martial calls him: a work than which the learned age of Tiberius produced nothing more charming or elegant. He resolved publicly to make known even the purpose of his retirement. Thus, having secured elegant typefaces suitable to a great and populous city indeed, but one wholly devoted and occupied with trade and commerce, and entirely removed from letters, and having hired workmen, he determined at his own expense to publish in print those fables and these Fragments.

While this plan was in progress—after the fables had been completed and these Fragments had almost been brought to the finishing-point—that man most worthy of immortality was taken up to a better life. [Col. 0913D] I would add here from what source he also drew forth these Fragments, were I not afraid of bringing a blush upon worthy men who profess knowledge of such matters: men who either, like that Aesopian cock, failed to recognize the worth of this treasure lying hidden in their libraries, or, having recognized it, retained it so long not without public loss. I shall say only what cannot be omitted: Pithou found at Paris the sole exemplar of these Fragments in the year of salvation CICICXC [the numeral is materially uncertain in the supplied text]. For he no more interrupted his chosen course of life—philosophizing and assisting the commonwealth—when the city was oppressed by sixteen tyrants, than Socrates did when the Thirty were afflicting his Athens.

I say, a single exemplar; nor was it very ancient, but was written only a hundred years before, on paper, in a French hand insufficiently acquainted with Latin, with words confused; and it further contained, in the same hand, an epitome of Cassian’s books *On the Incarnation of Christ*—perhaps that epitome which, according to Gennadius’s testimony, Eucherius, bishop of Lyons, composed. [Col. 0914A] From this he conceived the hope that the ancient copy from which this recent one had been transcribed might be recovered elsewhere; and this was why he had postponed their publication for so long. In this matter it most happily befell him that, snatched away by fate while publishing these two outstanding monuments of antiquity, he concluded the splendidly enacted drama of his life with a more illustrious ending, as with a swan-song.

Yet it was surely most difficult for a man adorned with every excellence of intellect and spirit—who, ever repeating to himself that saying of the ancient poet, “May we never cease from doing good to mortals,” had devoted and expended every day, every labour, every exertion, and all his thoughts upon public benefit—not to be overtaken by death in the midst of a noble work.

### 39. Eulogy of Pithou.

I say nothing of his literary studies, in which, by continually seeking out and examining libraries, by rescuing and publishing the writings of ancient authors either from errors or from destruction, and by exhorting, urging, and even helping others whom he judged capable of contributing something in that field, he never failed at any time to set something in motion and advance it. For although these pursuits were foremost in our Pithou, and he became especially known through the renown of his learning—since, from his earliest published specimens of divine genius, produced while still a young man, he was reckoned among the foremost men of letters, even with envy casting its vote, by those who then reigned in learning, because of his taste for abstruse and recondite scholarship—he increased the opinion formed of him until the very last day of his life, and it shall endure so long as letters endure. [Col. 0914C]

Yet how small a portion of the praise and glory of so great a man is this? For although no one knew any single author better than he knew all ancient writers in both languages—whom he had read one by one, compared with old exemplars, and thoroughly assimilated; although no one mastered private and domestic affairs more exactly than he did French and foreign history, the origins of peoples, chronological accounts, family successions, wars, treaties, agreements entered into by foreign peoples with one another or with us; and further, the laws, customs, and usages of individual provinces and cities—all of which he had acquired in perfect knowledge from his earliest years by tireless and truly Herculean labour, both from published books and from ancient libraries, the royal archives, those of the senate, financial officers, cities, and monasteries; and had copied a good part of the documents and records themselves in his own hand: [Col. 0914D] although, in Roman civil law, he attained such a degree that it might rightly be said of him and of his most celebrated teacher Cujas what was once said of great orators: that the former deprived his pupil of being the first jurisconsult, and the latter his teacher of being the only one; although, I say, all these qualities which severally would make any man great and worthy to be spoken of with care were amassed and accumulated in our Pithou, raising him to the highest praise and recommendation—how far short, nevertheless, are they of that wisdom which he had sought for himself, as though compounded from the discoveries of all the ancients who flourished in the repute of wisdom, acquired through the happy power of intellect and judgment, knowledge of affairs, constant reading, and experience?

How far short are they of that civic prudence with which he was endowed, like “a consummate craftsman,” if I may speak with Pindar, “and maker of good order and justice”; by which he knew not only how to give opinions and decisions on private and forensic matters with the greatest ease and equity, [Col. 0915B] but also how to deliberate wisely upon matters touching the highest concerns of the commonwealth, foresee the outcomes of counsels, and prudently meet doubtful and dangerous contingencies. For although, by a certain natural inclination strengthened by his hatred of the most sordid and polluted custom among us—that of attaining public office only through filthy means—he lived utterly removed from all ambition and from every splendour of life except that which virtue emits, so that he refused even offices and magistracies offered to him unbidden; yet, out of a desire to aid his country, with love for which he burned in an extraordinary degree, he stirred up, reminded, and suggested to those whom their lot had brought near to public affairs whatever either had been approved by the ancients in comparable circumstances or he himself, possessing a most keen and solid judgment, thought should be done. Throughout the whole course of his life, though a private man, he conducted public business and, without military cloak or bordered magistrate’s robe, exercised a perpetual magistracy. [Col. 0915C]

Finally, how far short are they of that integrity and innocence of character, and of that tireless constancy in uprightness throughout every part of life, by which virtues he attained the reputation not only of the most learned man in civil dress, but also of the wisest jurisconsult, the best citizen, and, plainly, a good man—the kind of man whom either Fimbria recognized or Socrates. And although these things are as well known to you as to me, I mention them all the more willingly because the memory of the virtues of a most beloved man can only be most pleasant, and especially because those who have come upon his final eulogy, published by friends among the deceased man’s papers, should, induced by your trustworthiness and authority—you who, because of the supreme friendship and long familiarity between you, joined by mutual admiration of each other’s virtues, knew him inwardly, “to the marrow,” as the saying is—be persuaded that it was written with the same modesty and truth with which that most modest man, utterly removed from every pretence and vanity, [Col. 0916B] and one who held truth to be “the beginning of great virtues,” conducted himself throughout his life in all other matters.

### 40. Adage.

But I fear that, as there is enough and more than enough of the oak, so there is also enough and more than enough of a preface—especially with you, most excellent sir. By the discerning judgment of our most merciful and most valiant king, on account of your singular prudence and your outstanding devotion, loyalty, and piety toward him and the commonwealth—a praise once distinctive of our nation, but now, to our great disgrace, exceedingly rare—you have long been assigned to compose and calm the restless minds of our great men; and I cannot, without wrongdoing, indeed even impiety, keep you longer away from public benefit. Therefore, having prayed to God, best and greatest, that He may long grant you safe and sound to your own people, to the senate, and to the suffering commonwealth, from whose destinies you are sprung, [Col. 0916C] here I make an end. I ask you again and again to love me, as you do, devoted and bound to you; farewell.

From the castle of Fossat, once called the fortress of the Bagaudae, a faction not unknown in the time of Diocletian.

According to the diversity of their ministries, they have diverse observances of commands, 293, which they keep perpetually, 293. Certain angels stand before God as though in a more particular office, 317. By the lot of their origin angels receive perpetual existence, I, 694. Beyond the reward of their own labor, glory has been granted them, 693, 694; illustrated by the analogy of sons, ibid. From what source angels praise Christ, II, 53. Division of the nations according to the number of angels, I, 49, 166. The multiplication of nations is not the angels’ work, II, 111. The power of multiplying nations exceeds an angel’s ministry, 88. Angels are divine ministers, I, 557. Angelic powers can be called members of God, 494. God does not need angelic intercession, but our weakness does, 494. Angels are in a sense God’s eyes, through which he mercifully looks upon us, 200; they are ministers of God’s will and of the blessedness communicated to us, 427. Through angels the law of Moses was ordained, 557. Angels are ministers of the law in the hand of the Mediator, 225, 226. The angel’s coming to strengthen Christ is absent from many manuscripts, II, 349. An angel was the first herald of the resurrection, I, 810. All the air is full of God’s angels, 278. Angels are witnesses of our will, 278. They both remain with us and stand before God, 278. Elisha’s prayer won their sight for his servant, 557. In heaven angels have both joy and concern for human salvation, 758. Angels are mountains, I, 427, 454. They surround the Church with a certain protection, 454; stand beside all believers everywhere, 557. Through our faith angels help us against spiritual wickedness, 200. Unless angels had been assigned for protection, our weakness could not withstand so many and such great spiritual wickednesses in the heavens, 533. Angels belong to the little ones, 758; they see God daily, 758. Angels preside over believers’ prayers, 758; with eager service they convey our desires to God, 758; they carried Lazarus’s soul into Abraham’s bosom, 445; lead the righteous into eternal rest, 142; into Abraham’s bosom, 143. To contemplate them within us is to contemplate their admonitions, ministries, and gifts, 427. Angels as lovers of women, I, 521, ibid., note. Transgressing angels are indicated by the name of kings, 723; they inhabit those abandoned to luxury, 723. Before Christ, nations were given to the dominion of angels, 49. Their authority over nations was perverse and unjust, 49. The number of angels is to be filled up from human beings, I, 758. The people of Israel remained in the wilderness in the life and manner of angels, I, 677. The soul is often signified by “spirit,” II, 364. God does not have a soul, II, 362. Those who suppose Christ’s soul to be of human nature and weakness: how far they err, I, 111, ibid., note. Christ’s soul proves itself God through signs and deeds, 602, ibid., note. The origins of souls are difficult to grasp, I, 491. The soul has an origin different from that of the flesh, 299. It is implanted in all of us, as it were, that our souls have a divine origin, 172. We should not lament the soul’s origin, but its bodily habitation, 423. Why the soul’s origin is divine and heavenly, 423. The soul’s nature is spiritual, I, 492; heavenly by nature, 493. To what end spiritual nature has been implanted in our souls, 97. The soul is incorporeal, 337. It does not have within itself an origin from another nature assumed from elsewhere, 337. It is wholly present in every member, 400 ff. The body may be cut away in decay while the soul remains unharmed, 401. The soul is Wisdom’s house, 481; it was made in God’s image, 337. By reason of the soul, the human being is in God’s image, 493. It is incorporeal, 493. It has nothing bodily in itself, 493. The conformation of souls is invisible, I, 424. The origins of souls proceed daily through the hidden operation of divine power, 266. A soul is never supplied by a human being, II, 334. Every soul is God’s work, 334. God is the parent of our soul, I, 185. Every human being is a progenitor of a soul, 90. Hilary said that the human soul was first poured forth from the treasures of divinity, 229. Nor does he agree with those who hold that souls are not created day by day, but were created at the beginning of things and are sent into bodies from some treasury, 229, note. The soul, not earthly but arising from God’s breath and mingled with the body’s elements, does not know death, I, 181. The soul’s nature is such that it remains eternal, 630. Hope of eternity is natural to every person’s mind, 171. The soul must become coeternal with God, whose Lord will rule forever, 627, 629. The first human being’s soul was formed before the body, I, 336, 493. The beginnings of souls, etc., show that Christ works daily, 267. The soul’s inborn radiance, 690. The soul is the superior nature, for whose effecting and operation the body is fitted, 492. The body is the soul’s garment, 723. The soul is corporeal, 400; in what sense, ibid., note. The forms of souls receive the corporeal substance of their own nature, 692. In its dwelling of flesh, the soul borrows a stain of corruption from association with it, 289, 290. The nobility of its heavenly nature is held captive in the body as in a contagious prison, 424. The companionship of earthly flesh is burdensome to it, 298. The human soul is weak through its nature and its association with flesh, 179. From this it has contracted some stain of sin, 299. The mind pours its own light or darkness into the body, I, 690.

[Col. 0920] How bodily pleasure overflows into the mind, and bodily sensation is imbued with the mind’s joys, I, 172. The soul’s subtlety is weighed down into bodily nature by sin, 717. The slavery of the sinful soul, 441. Divine discourse signifies defects of souls under bodily functions, 135. By the dissolution of the body, the soul is stripped of the burden and association of weak and perilous flesh, I, 422. Under the law, souls descend to the underworld after death, 572. Souls departing from the body are immediately received either by rest or by punishment, 92, 445. The righteous soul leaving the body rests in God’s reception, 112. See **Human being**. **The natural/psychic human being:** who this is, I, 73. **ANNIANUS,** I, 631. The year of God’s favor is eternal life, I, 192. Nineteen bishops defended the *anomoion* at Seleucia, II, 573. They asserted nothing but what was utterly profane, ibid.; in what sense they condemned unlikeness at Seleucia, 574. There they are condemned, and, condemned, hurry to Constantinople, 575. There again the Easterners resist their heresy, I, 693. Constantius wishes it anathematized, II, 694. Thus they condemn Aetius, its author, in such a way that the judgment seems directed more against the man than against the doctrine, 694. They claimed for themselves the saying, “But concerning that day no one knows,” etc., 512. At last the adversaries prevail, 574. The error of the Anthropomorphites is refuted, II, 492. **ANTICHRIST:** a human being, II, 275. The man of sin, son of the devil, I, 807; son of the devil, portion of sin, defender of the law, 811. Why he is called the abomination of desolation, 788 ff. Received by the Jews, he will stand in the place of sanctification, 789. He will sit in churches, II, 600. What terror he will instill in the Church, I, 742. The time of Antichrist, II, 595. The efforts of his ministers, I, 790. There are many antichrists, II, 593. An antichrist is one who does not confess the Son to be of one divinity with the Father, 599. Constantius is Antichrist, 564. Auxentius is Antichrist, 599. An Arian is Antichrist, 164. Scripture composed in Antichrist’s style, II, 597. **Antioch,** in the province of Coele Syria, II, 664. How many bishops were present at Antioch against the Samosatene, II, 513, ibid., note. They held what the Nicene Fathers held, 513. Proceedings drawn up at Antioch, II, 626. **The Council of Antioch at the Dedication,** II, 653. Against what heresy it was assembled, 480. How many bishops attended, 478. The creed set forth by them, 478. It ascribed to the Son an origin not begun but abiding, and from God’s substance, 483. It distinguishes Father and Son neither by time, nor name, nor essence, nor dignity, nor dominion, 482. Why this creed inconveniences the Arians, 579. **Antiochus’s victory,** I, 259. **ANTONIUS, of the Lord,** II, 665. **ANTONIUS of Gusra,** II, 668. **ANTONIUS of Zeumate,** II, 665. The author of the **Apocalypse** is the same John who wrote the Gospel, II, 165. **APOLLINARIUS** borrowed his errors from the Arians, I, 19–20, in the preface to vol. II. The distinction between an apostate and a sinner, I, 375. **THE APOSTLES:** those through whom Christ was to be carried abroad are prefigured in Joseph, I, 672. Prophecy of their election, 234. The apostles’ weakness, 221. Because they possessed an inclination of good will, what they attained, 221. The apostles’ favor toward the law, 765. For some time, held fast by love of the law, they were occupied by a kind of sleep of faith, 804. They still err in matters of the law when Christ satisfied the people by multiplying the loaves, 740. They had not yet been granted the ability to perfect and minister the heavenly bread, 740. Their favor in saving Israel, 746. The apostles were perfected by the sacrament—or sacraments—of water and fire, I, 682. Like salt, they are sowers of eternity, 682. They banish the world’s darkness, 682. They learned the rationale of Christ’s birth later than his mission and nature, II, 158 ff. The apostles’ faith immediately before Christ’s passion, I, 800: it was accepted by Christ, 800; whence it was shaken and whence confirmed, II, 348. Before Christ’s resurrection it wavered; afterward it was made firm, 604. Although the apostles’ faith affords less ground for wonder, it carries greater authority, II, 171. The apostles’ power, I, 506. They received the keys of heaven, 98, through the merit of faith, II, 157. The apostles go forth as it were from Christ’s body, I, 743. They are to be understood as having Christ’s powers in themselves, or even as themselves being those powers, 222; they receive the perfect image and likeness of Christ, 711; how they become heavenly, 711. Christ shares with the apostles that dwelling in heaven which is proper to himself, 186. The apostles are princes of the Churches, 234. Their primacy: the Churches take their beginnings from them, 580. The apostles are the Church’s eyes, I, 578; lamps of the Church, 362; foundations and pillars of the Churches, 221. In the apostles’ splendor lies all the Church’s adornment, 245. How the apostles are arrows, I, 474; how branches, 735; how prophets, sages, and scribes, 786. They are ministers of God’s grace, 740. Through the apostles’ ministry God’s mercy assists all, 727. The apostles’ constancy, I, 202. Against decrees of senates and edicts of kings, the apostles travelled through almost all nations, II, 594. The apostles’ preaching flourished amid emperors’ hatred of them, 594. Throughout the regions of the earth, the apostles prepared many dwellings for God, I, 70. Testimony to Christ’s resurrection belongs especially to the apostles, 750. They themselves will precede the rest in the glory and time of resurrection, 775. The apostles’ rule, II, 537. Unity of the apostolate, II, 162. Apostolic language signifies future things as already accomplished, II, 394. Nothing should be for sale in apostolic ministry, I, 711. Apostolic men, I, 779; II, 620, are called apostles, I, 474, ibid., note. The constant concern and business of apostolic men, II, 620. **Appeal:** Athanasius, fleeing from Tyre, appealed to the emperor, II, 652. Waters are called God by some because they flow without weariness, I, 197. By “waters” Scripture often means a human being, 451; the agitations of peoples and the persecutions of nations are signified, 243. We understand waters as peoples, 449. Waters: peoples destined to perish, 616. Which waters signify diverse kinds of people, 449. The purpose of waters above the heavens, 544. Waters consecrated by the Lord’s baptism, 199. **AQUAE of Dacia Ripensis,** II, 632. **AQUILA** translated the law for the Jews after the Lord’s passion, I, 153, writing according to the letter and remaining outside spiritual understanding, ibid. **Aquileia,** II, 638. The Italians request that a council be convened at Aquileia, 677. **The Aquitanian province,** II, 457. Noah’s ark, a figure of the Church, I, 638. What the Ark of the Covenant contained, I, 510; it is a figure of the body assumed by the Lord, 510. Church archive, II, 649. **ARCHYDAMUS,** II, 629. A bow signifies the preparation of punishment, I, 155. **Arles,** II, 672. What condition Liberius’s legates proposed at Arles, 674. **The Synod of Arles,** II, 540. What was done there against Paulinus, II, 621. **Aretiis,** II, 665. The method of testing silver, I, 203. Rams signify priests, I, 205. A synod to be convened at **Rimini**, II, 463. The division of the synods of Rimini and Seleucia was the devil’s fraud, 698. Constantius writes to the Council of Rimini, 683: he orders deliberation on faith and unity, 683, 688; but forbids any decision concerning the Easterners, 684; when everything is complete, he commands that ten legates be sent to him, 684. Valens and Ursacius, joined by Germinius and Gaius, throw the council into confusion, 688. The Synod of Rimini determines that nothing is to be added to or taken from the Nicene faith, II, 684, 687; it condemns heretics resisting it, 685; rejects Arius’s doctrine in many ways, 686. The crime of Epictetus and Potamius at the Synod of Rimini, 670. From Rimini ten legates from the Catholics and an equal number from the Arians were sent to the emperor, II, 689. The latter were immediately received; the former, wearied by long delay and frightened by threats, embraced perfidy, ibid., and rendered all the proceedings at Rimini void, 690. Bishops were detained at Rimini, many exhausted by age and poverty, 689. A confession of faith was brought to Rimini by Valens, II, 690, and signed by the legates, ibid. Violence was done to the Synod of Rimini, 566. There many were compelled, under the authority of the name of the Easterners, to silence concerning *ousia*, 698; a letter inscribed in the synod’s name was sent to Constantius, 691. Those detained at Rimini earnestly request leave to return to their own churches, 689, 691, 692. The legates of the Synod of Rimini returned to Constantinople after the Synod of Seleucia, II, 693, 695; summoned by the Easterners, they could not be induced to condemn the heresy, 700; though warned by the Easterners’ letters, they immediately joined the heretics condemned by the Synod of Seleucia, 695; they threaten deposition against whoever received those letters, 694; they answer that Christ was not denied to be a creature by the holy bishops of Rimini, 695. The character of the Council of Rimini’s faith, II, 706. Its impiety is exposed, 695. All the bishops of the East consented to it, 705. After its lapse, the Synod of Rimini sent a letter to the Easterners, 693. While many fell at Rimini, Gregory withheld his assent, 701. Eusebius urges him to rebuke those who fell, 701. At Rimini something very different from what had been supposed was done, 620. The effort and labor to secure agreement with the faith of Rimini reveal its injustice, [Col. 0922] II, 620. How great this effort was, ibid. Auxentius defends the proceedings of this synod, 602; he calls them the labors of six hundred men, 600. Italy and Illyricum annulled the proceedings at Rimini, II, 703. All Italy’s provinces reject them, 704, and request that their rejection be sent to them, 704. The Gauls likewise declare them void, 699. The Synod of Rimini was religiously dissolved by all, II, 598.
