All the Egyptians and Achaeans decreed that those who sinned at Rimini unknowingly should be pardoned, 702; apostolic authority confirmed this, 702. Some oppose this judgment, 702, 703. **Ariminiadenus,** II, 647. **ARIUS of Palestine,** II, 627, 632. **ARIUS the heretic,** II, 704. He maintains that the Son existed before Mary and the ages, 180. The conflict of Arius and Sabellius, 179 ff. Arius’s eleven disciples were expelled from the Church by Alexander, 673. Their conventicles, ibid. Arius’s letter to Alexander, 79, 134. Athanasius’s opponents refuse to condemn Arius’s doctrine at Arles in the year 353, 674. Four bishops likewise refuse this at Milan about the year 345, 673. Arius’s blasphemies are condemned by various anathemas, 686. Arius’s entire inheritance passed down to Ursacius, Valens, and others, 595. Arius’s spirit came from an angel of the devil transformed into an angel of light, 595. The Arian heresy, 176, spread from Alexandria through almost the whole world, 177. **Two Arii,** II, 642, ibid., note. Arii, that is, Arians, 642. Arius’s adherents, 636. Their creed, ibid. Authors of the Arian heresy, 704. **THE ARIANS** are nowhere identified by name in the books *On the Trinity*, 8, in the preface to vol. II; instead they are called “the present heretics,” II, 179. They preach that the Son is unlike God the Father, 179. “Those who are now [present],” 180, 181. Preachers of this present time, 27. Not preachers of the true God, 16. Preachers of a creature, ibid., 512. “You who now preach the only-begotten God to be a creature,” 243. Preachers of a new Christ, 376. Preachers of a novel apostolate, but one derived from Antichrist, 40. New reformers of apostolic faith, 410. An Arian is Antichrist, II, 164. The false priesthood of a novel apostolate, 161. A new maker of Christ from non-existent things, 164. To Hilary, the Arian is a devil, 600. The Arian heresy is called a new heresy, II, 176; “the new heresy now,” 179; the heresy of weakness, 471; it dared to profess that the Son of God is a creature, 471; the synagogue of Antichrist, 563. How subtly the Arians composed the rule of their faith, II, 103 ff., 133. Arian inventions recently devised, 537. A perfidy not issued long ago by many, 15. The novelty of Arian doctrine is clearly demonstrated, 145 ff. This doctrine is expounded, I, 224; II, 13, 23, 28, 72, 75, 194. By what art the Arians try to exclude the Son from divine properties, 75 ff. They say that they deny the Son always existed lest he be thought unbegotten, 73. They deny it in order that he may be subject to time, 74. Their sophistries against the Son’s eternity, 418. The Arians try to exclude the term “begetting/bringing forth” (*prolatio*), II, 137. Why they say they are moved to reject the *homoousion*, 73. Under the appearance of condemning Manichaeus, they reject one substance, 138. They are refuted when they deny the Son God’s substance in order not to wrong the Father, 75. Arians hold that between Father and Son there is only unity of will, not of nature, 217. They exalt the Father in order to cast down the Son, 376. How subtly they exclude the Son from deity, 126. Arians deny that the Son is God under the pretense of honoring God, 100, and thereby dishonor the Father, 100. They are profane toward the Father and blasphemous toward Christ, 642. So far as lies in them, they destroy the Father’s essence, 473. Pagan persecutors were enemies of Christ alone; the Arian heresy fights against God the Father, 568. The Arian hypocritically confesses Father and Son, 165, calling them Creator and creature, 165. Arian doctrine concerning Christ’s origin, passion, and Father, II, 375 ff. Concerning Christ’s passion and origin insofar as he is Spirit, I, 800, 801. They said that all things are from the Father, but all things through the Son, II, 86. They are refuted when they hold that Christ was created for the purpose of making works, 433. Arians confess that Christ is Wisdom, II, 86. Those who call Wisdom created have no ground on which to disguise their impious error, 438. They do not dare openly deny that Christ is God, 215, note. By what art they insinuate that Christ is not true God, 105; this is refuted from the law throughout Book V of *On the Trinity*. How Arians attempt to drive the simple from confessing Christ as God, II, 215. By what art they preach that the Son was born from non-existent things, 141. Their fraud in the phrase, “He was not before he was born,” 142. Their customary formula—and likewise these: “The Son is from non-existent things,” and, “There was when he was not”—are refuted throughout Book XII. Those who confess God the Father and Christ the Son of God, 472. Those who preach Christ as only-begotten Son and God, 145. Those who labored to make Christ believed neither God nor Son of God, [Col. 0923] II, 134, 175. They are ridiculous when they assert that nothing can be born from one, 216. Against Sabellius they demonstrate that the Son subsists before the ages, 16. They customarily reckon time from the creation of the sun and moon, 427. They are charged as worshippers of a creature, 233. Those who take away from the Lord communion in the Father’s substance, I, 731, yet worship him as God, 731, and do not dare take the name “God” from him, 731, are worse than those who are ignorant, 731. Arians are more unjust toward Christ than Jews, II, 170, 193. They deny what they cannot fail to know, 170. Everything is closed to them for salvation, ibid. Their blasphemy is without pardon, I, 731. Their salvation is more hopeless than that of the Jews, II, 170. They have no ground of excuse, 379. Incapable of the divine Spirit, they resist truth, 284. With every ingenuity of their impiety the Arians labor against the devout faith, II, 215. Their deceptive preaching, 214, 593, 595, 596. Serpentine movements, 135. Subtlety and frauds, 175. Cunning and ignorance, 537. They do not know how to know and confess the one true God, 126. They make Christ appear unable to speak consistently, 220, 312. The Arian contradiction is madness rather than ignorance, II, 196. Their folly, 218. The Arians’ faith is contrary to their knowledge, 192. It is not faith of knowledge but of guilt, 192. They bring darkness upon light, divide what cannot be divided, 29. They divide the evangelical and prophetic Spirit into disputes, 410. They have used our teachings against us, 175. They bark objections rather than argue, 538. The Arians’ calumny against defenders of the natural unity of Father and Son, 226. By ambiguity of words they deceive the simple, 71. By their interpretations they corrupt divine sayings, 71. How Arians abuse the Scriptures, II, 258, 259. By which Scriptures they deny Christ divine nature, 258. By which they deceive, 75. Their principal argument: “The Lord your God is one,” 82; refuted, 239. Another, no less customary, comes from the words, “The Lord created me,” 409, 428, note. They rely especially on the passage, “The Father is greater than I,” 179. Thereby they deceive the simple, assigning to Christ’s divinity what belongs to his humanity, 261, 269. They derive causes of impiety from the sacrament of our salvation, 376. They invade the sacrament of our salvation unto death, 302. Their objections are resolved by distinguishing Christ’s two natures, 378. Scriptural passages contrary to them, 19, 20, 40. They must be refuted from the very texts which they use, 218. Book XII of Hilary’s *On the Trinity* concerns the Arians, in the preface to vol. II, 17–18. Apollinarius borrowed his errors from the Arians, I, 777, note 20. Arians think wrongly about the Holy Spirit, II, 28. Most of them hold that Christ was not in the nature of the impassible God, 326. Some say that Christ was created from nothing in the likeness of God, 72. Arians conduct themselves not as bishops of Christ, but as priests of Antichrist, 593, 595. The Arians’ crimes were established at the Synod of Sardica, II, 623. They were found to be liars, 625; falsifiers of Scripture, 120, ibid., note; authors of forged letters, 625; persons using force against the faith of God’s people, 314. Their calumnies against Catholics, 324, 622. Intolerable persecutions, 535. Frequent cruelty against God’s servants, 622. Cruelty and violence, 536, 539 ff., 630. The slaughter caused by the Arian heresy is described, II, 461. How widely the devil spread the poison of Arian doctrine, 458. How powerful its preaching was, 323. The plague of the Arian heresy ranged through almost all the provinces of the Roman Empire, 131. Its cure was difficult, 132. How its supporters endeavored to spread the impious doctrine, 627. All the Arians’ confidence rests on the protection of secular power, 701. Hilary asks governors not to grant favor to Arians, 628. While writing their own doctrines rather than God’s, the Arians carried eternal error throughout the world, II, 544. Their frequent changes, ibid. ff. What they alleged as a pretext for perverting the Catholic faith, 547. By these changes they ensure that there is no one who is not guilty and impious, 582. At Sirmium they publicly professed what they had earlier whispered secretly, 505. They sought to publish in the emperor’s name what they themselves did not dare publish in their own, 506. At Rimini they deceitfully profess the Son to be like the Father according to the Scriptures, 577. They use expressions foreign to Scripture, 575, 577. Around the year 353 Italians were compelled to obey Arian judgments, 673. Those embracing Arian doctrine lacked no grounds for excusing themselves before people, 619. The Arians vainly boast of their peace, 593. Why they are unworthy of the Christian name, 628. **ARIOMANITES,** II, 180, ibid., note, 624, 698, 701. **ARSENIUS,** II, 693. **ARSENIUS, who was …** [The supplied source breaks off after *qui ab*.]

Said to have been killed by Athanasius, he is counted among the living, II, 625. Reed: whom it signifies, I, 722. Asapofebiis [name/reading uncertain], II, 632. Asclepas, II, 623, 631. Deposed, 624, 631. Condemned also by the judgment of Athanasius [col. 0924], II, 655. Marcellus never communicated with him, 655. Of what acts he is accused of having committed upon his return from exile, 653. Of what he did at Constantinople, 649. He proves himself irreproachable, 626. He is declared innocent, 627.

The ten Asian provinces, for the most part, do not know God, II, 498. By the name of asses the Gentiles are often signified, I, 757. Sprinkling. See *Adspersio* [Sprinkling]. Aspona, II, 666. Israel, taken captive, served the Assyrians, I, 458. Asterius of Arabia, II, 627, ibid., note. Star-bearing circles, II, 440. Asturus of Arabia, II, 632. Asturica, II, 631.

Athanasius: a deacon at the Council of Nicaea, II, 646. He was a vigorous advocate for making the Nicene faith known to all, ibid. By steadfast adherence to truth he overcame the Arian plague throughout all Egypt, 646. For this reason, false criminal charges were fabricated through testimony conspiratorially arranged against him, ibid. Proceedings at Tyre against him, 652. That Paul of Constantinople was present at and subscribed to Athanasius’s deposition, 652. Athanasius is said to have condemned Asclepas, 655. He was falsely accused of the murder of Arsenius, 625; and of the broken chalice, 625. He was condemned contrary to judicial procedure, 539, 620. They boast that they possess records of the proceedings against him, 625.

Athanasius’s journey to Julius, II, 654; his journey to Italy and Gaul, 655. The Easterners attempt to expel Athanasius from the Council of Sardica, 656. He is declared innocent by that council, 627, 631. How his innocence was demonstrated, 629, 633. What crimes they pretend that he committed before his first exile, 651; and upon his return from exile, 652. How the Arians seek to invalidate letters written by the Egyptians and others in Athanasius’s favour, 653 ff. Athanasius is portrayed as the disturber of the peace of the universal Church, 659, 661. Athanasius is accused of having solicited letters in different parts of the world, 654. He is condemned at Philippopolis, 660. The Council of Sardica demonstrates that every charge against Athanasius was fabricated, 641. Athanasius is acquitted by the Council of Sardica, 670. Which persons deserve greater credence: those who accused Athanasius, or those who defended him, 633; those who condemned him, or those who acquitted him, 684.

Athanasius separates Marcellus from his communion, II, 639; then Marcellus abstains from entering the church, 640. In 349 Athanasius is declared by the Easterners not to be guilty, 636. Thereafter Valens and Ursacius acknowledge as false what they had alleged concerning him, 636. They write him conciliatory letters, 638. Those Easterners who attempted in 349 to invalidate Athanasius’s acquittal, 633, 640. The letters written from all Egypt and Alexandria to Julius concerning the restoration of communion with Athanasius were of the same character as those written to Liberius concerning its preservation, 670. Why Liberius, at the beginning of his pontificate, did not condemn him, 672. Athanasius is alleged to have been summoned to Rome by Liberius, 669; to have refused to come, 669; and to have been declared excluded from communion with the Roman Church, ibid. The concern of holy men for Athanasius’s acquittal, 538.

The papal legates at Arles yield to those demanding Athanasius’s condemnation, provided only that they condemn Arius’s doctrine, II, 674. This error had seized the minds of nearly everyone: that bishops were being exiled because of Athanasius, and that this was not a cause worthy of the exile they had undertaken, 620. Under the pretext of Athanasius’s name, something else had long been subtly attempted, 673. Liberius mentions Athanasius’s affair before the Emperor, 671. He separates him from his communion, 681; denies that he is defending him, 678; excuses himself for having defended him, 678; and condemns him, 678. The excuses of those who consented to Athanasius’s condemnation are refuted, 634 ff. Athanasius is further mentioned at 622, 624, 625, and throughout the pseudo-Sardican letter, 647.

Athenius, II, 690. Athenodorus, II, 632. The impious are atheists, I, 20. They waver uncertainly in their opinions, I, 20. The difference between an atrium and a house, I, 523. The atrium: the inner and central part of a house, 527. Avarice is the root of all evils, I, 165. The slavery of the avaricious, I, 459. How solicitous birds are for their young, I, 134. Spiritual birds rest while flying, 369. The austerity of philosophers and heretics is vain and superstitious, I, 184. The value of gold arises from human error, I, 383. Authentic manuscripts of Scripture, I, 3, 185.

Auxentius, heir of Arius, II, 599. An angel of Satan, an enemy of Christ, a damned devastator, a denier of the faith, 600. He began as a presbyter in the Arian church at Alexandria, 598. Liberius bids Auxentius peace, 682. The Gauls regard Auxentius as excommunicated in accordance with the letters of the Easterners, 700.

The encounter of Auxentius with Hilary, II, 597. He denies knowing Arius, 598, 601. By Satan’s craft he deceived the king, the Counts, and the Church of God, 599. He wrote something different from what he professed [col. 0925], II, 598. He played with words by which he might deceive even the elect, 598. He calls himself bishop of the Catholic Church of Milan, 600. An example of his blasphemy, 600.

The help of God is necessary, I, 389; in tribulations, 560; so that temptation may not prevail, 389. The Lord must always be prayed to, 374. True faith is that help comes to us from the Lord, 427. How it does not fail those who hope in him, 560. See *Grace*.

## B

Babylon is interpreted as “confusion,” I, 549. The furnace of Babylon, 625. Victory of the Babylonians, I, 259. Judah was taken captive and enslaved to them, 458. Baptinus, II, 667. The respective power of the baptism of John and of Christ, I, 675. At the Lord’s baptism the waters were consecrated, I, 199. The effects of our baptism were foreshadowed in Christ’s baptism, 676. The unity and faith of baptism, II, 373, 375. What faith those to be baptized profess, I, 746; throughout the whole period of the fasts of the Lord’s Passion they remain, 746; when questioned, they answer that they renounce the devil, the world, and sins, 76. Faith sworn in baptism, II, 544. There is no baptism without faith in Christ, 546. A symbol of regeneration, 444. The confession of those being reborn, 298. Baptism in the Father and the Son, II, 126; in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, 15. Whether the apostles baptized in the name of Jesus, 512. Baptism is a ministry of the apostolic office, I, 237; it is required of a deacon, 237; it is the sacrament of divine generation, II, 15. In baptism remission of sins is given, I, 182. One reborn in Christ is God’s temple, 235. In what sense he is Israel, 106. By the sacrament of baptism souls receive splendor, 794. To the baptized are granted certain beginnings of the Holy Spirit, 192; possession of eternal bodies is begun, 199. The regeneration of baptism is the power of resurrection, II, 265. Through the washing of baptism, by the power of the word, we are renewed in soul and body, 719; the body passes into the nature of the soul, 719. The baptized are called little children, to whom belongs the kingdom of heaven, I, 182. The faith of those recently reborn is tender and not yet established, 180. Those reborn by baptism should remember that they possess not their own flesh but Christ’s, 270; in order that they may enter into fellowship in Christ’s flesh, they should afflict the flesh with its vices and desires, 270. By baptism the perfect purity of innocence is not restored, 290. After baptism in water, there remain the baptisms of the Holy Spirit, of fire, of suffering, or of death, 291. For those baptized in the Holy Spirit it remains to be perfected by the fire of judgment, 675.

BARABBAS, that is, “son of the father,” I, 807. BARBARIO, presbyter. See the preface to vol. II, notes 3 and 20. BARUCH is cited under Jeremiah’s name, II, 101, 130. BASAN signifies shame and confusion, I, 231, 534. BASIL of Ancyra, II, 665, 680, 708; condemned at the Synod of Sardica, 628. Basil’s faithless assertion, according to the Anomoeans, on account of which the synod was convened, 706. BASSUS, II, 680. BASSUS of Caralis, II, 667. BASSUS of Diocletianopolis, II, 632, formerly deported from Syria and afterwards ordained bishop, 658.

Blessedness is not of this world; what sort of blessedness is meanwhile granted to us, I, 481. The blessednesses of irreligious people are unhappy and difficult to attain, 491. Hope of eternal blessedness accords with reason, II, 7. Hope of blessedness belongs to all nations, I, 187. The desire to be blessed proceeds from the expectation of blessedness itself, 23. The blessed life is prepared for us through God’s mercy, I, 173, 174. Blessedness comes from God’s mercy, 608, without excluding the duty of meriting it, 608 ff. Whence we receive the merit of perfect blessedness, 92. Although the cause of blessedness is the merit of faith, God’s mercy is nevertheless supreme, 542. He created humankind to share in his own blessedness, 38. He willed that humankind should obtain it through the merit of love and obedience to him, 39. There are five degrees toward blessedness, 19. The character that those awaiting blessedness ought to have, 271. Blessedness must be sought through prayers and deeds, 187. The condition of a blessed and eternal life is secure if there is piety toward God, patience in adversity, and contempt for wealth, 165. The blessed man is like Christ, I, 24; and when he is so, 25. All created things await our blessedness, 644. Blessedness promised to the meek is the dwelling-place of the body which the Lord assumed, 680. The condition of the blessed life, 271 ff. The blessedness of the saints after death, 607. Lazarus exchanges the misery of his laborious life for the honor of blessed repose, 396.

The blessed are gods, I, 542. Their eternal realm is paradise, 26. The communion of the blessed with Christ, 618. Christ, the face of God, is present to each saint, 607. The blessedness of the saints after the resurrection, 163; their happiness and security, 641, 642. The glory and dwelling-places of the blessed are diverse, 186, 193. Not all will be chosen for cohabitation with God, 186; this is proper to Christ, though he also shares it with the apostles, I, 186. Yet all saints will receive the honor of heavenly glory, 186. The blessed are clothed with salvation, having been made conformed to Christ’s glory, 404. How the blessed, through Christ as mediator, are assumed into the unity of the Father’s majesty, 238 ff. The blessed lack nothing for the substance of body and soul, 641. Whatever comes to pass in them is eternal, together with the consciousness of blessedness, 26. Their joy is consummated, 516. They receive all glory and light from contemplation of God’s majesty, 326.

BEDA notes a passage of Hilary, I, 344, note. First and Second Belgica, II, 457. The war of Satan and the Lord prefigured in David and Goliath, I, 610. Beasts are carried toward something by a chance and uncertain movement, II, 305; how nature itself serves them, 2. The difference between blessing and praise, I, 622. We always owe both to God, 622. Praise excels blessing, 527. To bless God belongs only to God’s servant, not to the servant of sin, 523; nor to God’s servant who is wavering and inconstant, 523. The blessing given to Adam concerns not merely physical propagation, I, 208. Humanity fell from blessing through Adam’s sin, 521. A temporal blessing is not promised to the righteous, 479; it is customary for sinners, 479. The Church alone bestows blessings, I, 522. Constantius bows his head for the blessing, II, 569. Beneventum, II, 632. Goodwill: it is a greater sin to neglect the duty of goodwill than to omit tithing, I, 785. BERENICE, mother of Ptolemy, I, 384, note. Beroe, II, 668. Bethlehem is the same as Ephrathah, I, 508. In it is the beginning of the Church, 508. Bethsaida: “house of hunters,” I, 514. The number two has an unfavorable meaning, I, 595. Proceedings of the Synod of Béziers, II, 563. At it, Hilary denounces the advocates of introducing heresy, 460. A synod to be held in Bithynia, II, 462. BITINICUS, II, 666. Blasphemy of the Spirit, I, 730, 802. Blasphemy is rather the insult of a human being who reviles God than a reproach to God, 247. Blatea, II, 632.

What are the goods of this life, II, 1. Earthly goods, though goods, are nevertheless not perfectly good, nor promised to the righteous, I, 479. By sharing our goods with those in need, we shall become worthy of those goods for which we depend on God, 688. God, the giver of earthly goods, will grant eternity to those who use them rightly, 619. Many good things are not pleasant, and pleasant things are not good, I, 517. Fraternal unity is a pleasant good, 518. David merited the goods of the soul by the cry of mouth and heart and by purity of mind, 206. Whatever God does in us is good, 331. On what the hope of eternal goods is founded, 433. Good is not so much to be contemplated as carried out, I, 72. We cannot judge good things to be truly good unless we seek them, 421. How a person who knows the good is unable to accomplish it, 471. The dispensation of a gratuitous good should be gratuitous, 688. Perfect goodness is that which knows no change, I, 98; this belongs to God alone, ibid. Perfect goodness consists in the disposition of an upright heart, 456. Christ, as judge, refrains from the title “good,” 772. Whether no one is good—not Abel, not Seth, and so forth—97. A human being is good when he or she wills or does good, 99. God pardons lapses of weakness in a good will, I, 99, 221. The reproaches of one who deceives concerning him do not injure the integrity of one who obeys God’s law, 721. Desiring the goodwill of all toward us, let us be good to all, 697. The exercise of goodness benefits not one who offers it, but one who uses it, 39. Those who do not love goodness commonly feign it in speech, 84. Oxen are cattle of a stubborn nature, I, 205. What *Bresith* signifies, I, 32, ibid., note. Brevi in Macedonia, II, 633. Brevity of expression often misleads both hearers and teachers, II, 497. When Britain became open to the faith, and when to the Arians, II, 457. Its bishops are joined with those of Gaul, ibid. Brixa, II, 632. Some worshipped tombs as gods, I, 197. Valentinus’ Bythos, II, 137.

## C
Cabula. II, 668. CAECILIANUS of Spoleto. II, 676. No one who looks upon heaven will fail to perceive that God exists, I, 198, 440. Why heaven is God to some, 197; whence it is wondrous, 258. Wherein the preparation of heaven consists, II, 433. The unchangeable stability of heaven, I, 530. The arrangement of the heavens and of the world, 545. The heavens harmoniously ordered by God, 544. They are many, [Col. 0927] I, 544. The number of the heavens is uncertain, 544. Nor is it certain whether Paul knew it, 544. Hilary does not regard the heavens as animate, 543. The first heaven kindled by the power of the all-encompassing God, 544. The lower heaven, though manifold, is comprehended under the single name “firmament,” 544. Heaven bent down, 615. The visible heaven’s obedience to God’s word, 348. The visible heaven is not a dwelling worthy of God, 440. Yet the common opinion concerning God’s seat is not excluded: namely, that “the heaven of heavens” is His throne. 441. The heavens; the Angels, I, 220; the Saints, 350, ibid., note 710. The heavenly city restored to the Saints, I, 155, note. What heavenly hope is, 552. The heavenly Jerusalem is built before it is gathered together, 635; it is built in us through the work of faith and hope, ibid.; it is built by God’s mercy through the grace of justification, 635. The heavenly Jerusalem is also the Church militant, 454. What punishments the Prophet invokes upon the forgetfulness of heaven, 551. How great is the dignity of the heavenly dwelling, 69. Labour is needed to obtain it, 69. There are many ways to the land of promise, 546. Heaven will be bestowed not for miracles, but for good works, 698. Heaven stood open to Stephen as he entered it. 146. Why the heavenly Adam is second, I, 441; how He makes us heavenly. 441. Caesaraugusta. II, 631. CAESAREA in Cappadocia. II, 665. Caesarea in Palestine, II, 665; the Council was appointed to meet there, II, 652. CAIN made equal to the devil by a curse. I, 420. Caindo. II, 632. Who can comprehend by knowledge the afflictions of the Saints? I, 491. Amid afflictions, to rest in God’s goodness as in a most safe and familiar harbour. II, 3. A reed signifies weakness and emptiness. I, 807. CALEPODIUS. II, 632. The cup of wrath and the cup of life, I, 156. Christ prayed that the cup might pass, not from Himself, but from His own people. 802, 803. Calle. II, 685. CALLENICUS. II, 666. What calumny is, I, 389; every calumny is wicked, II, 379; domestic calumny is hard to guard against, I, 389. The Saints were attacked by it, 389. It commonly brings about the ruin of faith, 390. How it is to be avoided. 390. The nature of camels. I, 764. CALVUS. II, 632. CANDIDIANUS, exorcist. II, 706. By the name “dog” madness and shamelessness are denoted, I, 148. The characteristic of dogs. II, 696. What a song (*canticum*) properly is, I, 13, 195; what it is mystically. 13, 14. What “a song of a psalm” (*canticum psalmi*) properly is, I, 13; what it is mystically. 13, 195. The new song: because knowledge of God was granted to the Gentiles, I, 617; because of Christ’s wondrous resurrection, 617; because the Saints were given power to judge. 617. Some hold that the Songs of Ascents prophesy the Babylonian captivity and the people’s return, I, 416, 465; how modestly Hilary takes a different view, 417. In the Songs of Ascents one climbs from low things to lofty things. 439. Before Christ the whole world resounded with the profane chant of ceremonies, I, 189. The chant of God’s utterances is sweeter than the obscene tales of disgraceful spectacles, I, 311. The singing of Psalms in every place, 321. The day is begun in prayers to God and ended in hymns to God. 190. The songs of the Marsi and the songs of the Saints. I, 140. Canusium. II, 632. What hair signifies. I, 245. The captivity of Jerusalem which occurred in Jeremiah’s days: whether it was foretold in the Psalms, I, 465. Some hold that the Babylonian captivity and the people’s return from it are prophesied in the Songs of Ascents, 416. Hilary understands another captivity and liberation to be prophesied in these. 417, 423. The captivity of the Gentiles. I, 105. What captivity of the mind is, I, 548. Bodily captivity is grievous; but far more grievous is the captivity of the soul. 458. Capua. II, 632. The head is the seat of life, prudence, and all the senses, I, 597. All understanding is in the head, 689. Christ is the head of the Saints; the devil, of the wicked. 590. Census of heads. II, 569. Car. II, 667. One coal devastates, another purifies, I, 421. Coals of desolation. 421. CARINIUS. II, 709. The force and nature of charity, II, 619. The commandment of charity is bright, and by its light other hidden things are disclosed, I, 292. The rule of charity, 697. Perfect charity does not consist in being indulgent and obliging only at times, II, 277. Perfect charity fulfils every duty of every kind, 277. The affection of perfect charity, [Col. 0928] I, 409. Charity ought to be impatient for the things it loves, 422. In the calamity of sinners, charity considers itself driven down even below hell, 598; it is an eager advocate before God for our errors. 685. A song and a hymn do not differ. I, 117. “Flesh” frequently stands in Scripture for a human being, I, 129; for the entire human race, 185. Dead flesh, 290; flesh subject to the law of death and sin, 289; the dwelling-place of the soul, 290. Those who dwell within the bounds of the flesh pursue the things of the flesh, yet neither follow them completely nor abandon them; they must fear, 190. One must journey away from the flesh, 292. The Saints dwell with the flesh, not in the flesh. 424. Our flesh is the daughter of Babylon and confusion, I, 553. It must be subjected to the soul, whose rule it had usurped, 554. The vices of the flesh must be nailed to the cross, 376 ff. The incentives of the flesh are restrained by remembrance of God, 175. The torments of the flesh are the Lord’s arrows, 420; for the wicked they are punishment, but for those loved by God they serve innocence, 421. Those who rule the flesh are kings and lords, 543; they are worthy to have God as their Lord, 543; this they possess through God’s kindness. 543. Christ’s flesh is saving, I, 66; it is not from the common course of human origin. 61. The carnal man. I, 72. Carthage. II, 647. CARTHERIUS. II, 666. Cheese. I, 225. Castolona. II, 631. Castramartis. II, 632. CASTUS. II, 631. A chair signifies doctrine, I, 576; it is the seat of the priesthood. I, 773. The chair of pestilence. I, 21. Auxentius calls himself bishop of the Catholic Church of the Milanese. II, 600. CATULUS. II, 710. Caynopolis. II, 632. Cecropius. II, 679. Kedar is a people of the Ishmaelites, I, 423; in Hebrew it means, in Latin, “darkness.” 423. Census of heads. II, 569. A hundredfold reward promised to those who leave the world. I, 324. One should pray not that the cause for struggle be removed, but that help to conquer be granted. I, 346. The neck. I, 486. Chalcedon. II, 665. CHANAAN: “movement.” I, 535. Who the CANAANITES are. I, 744. Documents of the Churches, II, 597; they contain synodal proceedings. 629. Chatimera. II, 665. The perpetual voices of the CHERUBIM and SERAPHIM. I, 491. The name “Christian” is new, II, 122; it was not granted before Christ’s Passion. I, 799. The prerogatives of Christians, I, 642. All Christians are brothers, 784. A Christian made participant in heavenly teaching ought not to linger upon earth, 369. A customary utterance of harassed believers: “I am a Christian,” II, 536, ibid., note. The fasts, continence, and chastity of Christians are grounded in the hope of eternal life, I, 374. How this hope and these good works of theirs are mocked by the impious, 374. A sinful Christian becomes a servant of the world, a labourer of the devil, and so forth, 392 ff. Scripture of the law was understood and approved by Christians, 457. By God’s grace. 457.

CHRIST: by whom He is known and by whom unknown, II, 364. Any sort of confession of Christ is not the perfection of faith, 169. Christ’s various names, I, 80. Christ is God’s power and wisdom, 235. The only-begotten God, God’s Spirit, God’s Power, God’s Wisdom, God’s Son, 166; holy, 156, 227; He is the mouth, power, wisdom, arm, and image of God, 334; why and how He is God’s wisdom, power, and Word, II, 182 ff.; insofar as He is God, He is God’s hand, I, 616; He who is a worm, II, 383; Christ, David eternal, I, 159; from David’s womb, Lord of the eternal kingdom, 253; from Judah, the prince who is also the expectation of the Gentiles, 253; Christ as shepherd, king, righteous one, rising, and heir of the covenant of peace, 501; both rod and flower, 52; arrow, 421; mediator, 730; II, 224, 259, 388. Christ is remitter of sins, destroyer of death, conqueror of the devil, judge of the world, our God and Lord. I, 183. Christ is the mirror of the Father, II, 312; He makes the Father visible in Himself, 299. Knowledge of Christ according to the man does not provide knowledge of the Father, 203 ff. Christ displays the Father as His living image, 205; He is the living image and most complete form of the living God, 377. It is not a true image if the Father has anything that it lacks, 377. He is both the image of the Author and the truth, 258. As God’s image, He is not of another nature, 247; nor is He corporeal or finite, 248; when Christ is believed, God’s voice must be heard and His form seen. 274.

Those who maintain that Christ existed before Mary only by predestination are refuted, [Col. 0929] II, 489. The difference between Christ and the elements of the world in their existence, 252. Christ’s threefold state must be distinguished: before the man, in the man, and after the man, I, 571; II, 262. The middle state is that which began to be, namely, the man born; then alone was He both God and man, when He was in the man, I, 51. Before the man, He was God; in taking the man, He existed as man and God, II, 335. Some of His acts belong to Him not yet born, others to Him about to die, others to the eternal One. 262. Christ’s divinity before the ages is eternal, and effective in all God’s works and teachings, II, 428. Christ is the way of God, I, 322; the beginning of the way of God’s works, II, 435; His dispensation begun from eternity, 435. At every time He summoned all to heed the law, I, 766. Before assuming flesh He taught us remaining in the Spirit; afterwards, remaining in the body, 571, 572. Formerly He assumed various forms of angel, man, and fire, II, 436, so that you might learn to believe the created nature according to appearance rather than according to the substance of its nature, ibid. He caused those forms to disappear by the same power by which He assumed them. 437.

The different offices of Christ under the law and after the law, II, 102. Christ the mediator taught the composition of the ointment with which Aaron was anointed, I, 520; He spoke in the prophets, II, 122; He who was in the body was the same as He who remained in the Spirit in the prophets, 386; in the body He ran the path already trodden by Himself in the prophets. I, 567. Those who assert that Christ is not Wisdom itself but a work of Wisdom are refuted, I, 724 ff. Christ differs from the heavenly powers not merely in power, because some things are through them but all things through Him, II, 64. The Arians think they prove Him a creature from passages in which He calls Himself the way, the door, and so forth, 708. How those words are to be understood, 708. Those who hold that Christ was created for the sake of producing works are refuted, 433. Christ is not through a cause, but is Himself the cause of every cause, 387; He is not a creature, for the name of Creator is proper to Him, 410 ff.; nor can it apply to Him that He should hope, serve, need liberation, and so forth, 411. If He who is in the form of God is a creature, God will be a creature, 411. When Scripture was to call Christ the creator of the world, it confessed the Father as the world’s maker, 433. No Scripture has spoken of Christ as created from God, 438. In what sense it may be permissible to call Him created, 433, 438; how He is creation from eternity, 428. By saying that it is unknown whence He is, Christ teaches that He is not created, 154. So far is He from being from nothing that the impious do not know whence He is, 154. By teaching that He alone knows the Father because He is from Him, He signifies that He is not created. 153.

Christ is before times and ages, II, 427. Nothing can be conceived before His birth, 427. He did not begin in respect of origin, 252. In what sense heretics call Him firstborn of every creature, 643; in what sense Catholics do so, 249. By eternal birth Christ is firstborn of creation; by temporal birth, firstborn from the dead, I, 47; He precedes the eternity of the prepared heavens. II, 432. He who does not know Christ as God does not know God born, II, 381. In Christ, the principal point is that He has been born, 375. How aptly His eternal birth is signified by the word “coming forth,” 159; Christ is the Son of God, I, 44. This is chief among the teachings concerning Him, II, 148. It is known in many ways that He is truly God’s Son, 148. Where He is shown to be truly God’s Son, He is shown to be God by nature, 147. The attributes added to the name of Son indicate that He is the true Son, 151. Christ is asserted to be the true Son of God by name, birth, nature, power, and confession, 17. Christ’s birth is proved from the name God given to Him, 181; from His birth from God, 185. The Father testifies that Christ is not an adoptive but a proper Son, and why, 148, 149. Christ always declares God to be His own proper Father, and the Father always designates Him His proper Son, 414. Since Christ often proclaims lowly things of Himself, He is credible when He teaches that He is God’s Son, 150 ff.; with what clarity He could, He signified His birth, 192; how He explained His birth and nature to the Jews. 187.

Faith in Christ as Son of God is necessary for salvation, II, 164, 166. He Himself demands faith in His divine nature and birth, 208. He requires belief that He is God’s Son in advance, in order to obtain bodily healing, 168. He likewise demands it from the blind man now seeing, for the salvation of his soul, 168. Hope must be placed not in Christ alone, but in Christ the Son of God, 13. The merit of confessing Christ the Son of God. 162. The Jews knew that Christ would be the Son of God, though they did not know who Christ was, II, 170. Demons confess Him to be God’s Son, 169. If He is not believed to be God’s Son because of His body, let Him be believed through His works to be God’s Son, 197. How Arians prove Christ to be the Son of God against Sabellius, 179. He who denies that He is God’s Son is inexcusable, 167. He will receive Antichrist in place of Christ, 168. It was revealed to Peter that Christ is God’s Son, not by title but by nature, 160. The apostles believed Him Son by nature, not adoption, 156. How the devil strips from us the innate understanding of Christ as the natural Son, [Col. 0930] II, 168. What He did or taught surpasses all that belongs to those who are sons by mere designation, 148. To make Christ a degenerate son is an insult to the Father. 284.

Whether God’s anointing is to be ascribed to Christ’s eternal birth, II, 387, 388. How far Christ’s eternal birth may be explained through seals, 245 ff. How Arians preach Christ as Son, only-begotten, and God, 145. Even as God, Christ speaks of the Father reverently, I, 602. Out of reverence as Son He refers all that is His to the Father, 602. In this there is no confession of His own weakness, but a proclamation of the Father’s power, 602. Christ began to have God the Father as Lord when He became a servant, II, 382. Christ’s mission and nature became known to the apostles before the manner of His birth, 158 ff. The sum of the faith concerning Christ’s eternal birth. 428.

The Arians do not dare openly to deny that Christ is God, II, 215, note. By what sophistries they endeavour to drive simple people from this faith, 215. Auxentius and his associates concede that Christ, God from God, was born before every conceivable time, 595. Other opinions of the same men concerning Christ, 595 ff. Whence Sabellius proves Christ’s divinity, 179. In what ways we know Him to be God, 181. Christ’s divinity asserted in Psalm LXVII, 34, 237. Christ, God, obeyed God’s utterances in creating the world, 119. Christ was proclaimed as God by the law, the prophets, and the Apostle, 179 ff. By what artifice the Arians insinuate that Christ is not true God, II, 105. They are refuted from the law throughout Book V of *On the Trinity*. Christ is not denied to be God because the Father is called the only true God, 283; if He is God, He is true God, 111; He is not a God who began, but God born, 186; what He is as God neither began nor advanced, 186; as born, He possesses the Father’s very nature, 381; as truly born from God, so He is truly God, 120; He is true God if the Father is true God, 284; through true birth from God, true God and not another God, 216. Christ as true God is to be demonstrated throughout Book VII, 176, 181. Many arguments for Christ’s divinity, 283; another, 115. In the law, God’s power, God’s authority, God’s reality, and God’s name are attributed to Christ, 119. Christ the mediator gave the law of Moses through angels, 118. He who gave it is true God, ibid. Christ shows Himself Lord and God while seeming to deny it, 279; He performed things we cannot comprehend, that He might be understood as God able to do all things, 53. Whoever swears by Him swears by Him as true God, 176. All believers’ faith swears by Christ as true God, 123. Christ is proved God from the fact that He gives eternal life, 281, and that, no differently from the Father, He establishes the ministries of the Church, 237; He shows Himself God when He declares Himself exempt from the census, 755. Christ’s soul proved Him God by signs and deeds, 602, ibid., note. Christ so moderated His words that He revealed Himself both born and God, 381. An argument for Christ’s divinity is His resurrection, 120, 184. Another is that, although so humble, He did not refuse the name of God, 184. Performing what belonged to God, and among these things professing Himself God’s Son, He is not without reason believed to be God, 204, 205. The disciples understand Him to be true God from His divine powers. 280.

Christ is not God merely by designation, but God of creatures, He who is God over all, II, 240. By giving food of eternal life, because He is sealed by God, He indicates that He possesses the fullness of the form of Him who seals Him, 245; as in God’s form, He has wholly co-imaged in Himself everything that belongs to God, 246; as in God’s form and glory, He cannot be anything other than God, 246; His whole self is nothing other than God, 246. As our flesh is true in Him according to the form of a servant, so the Father’s divinity is true in the form of God, 708. If the fullness of divinity dwells in Him, He is not partly similar and partly dissimilar, 708. The mark by which Christ is recognized is the power of His works, I, 747. He does what is not unknown and is knowable, II, 362. His deity ought to have been understood by the Jews through the magnificence of His works, I, 112, 113. To deny Christ the divinity that He reveals by works is unforgivable blasphemy. 730, 731.

Christ has unity of substance with the Father, I, 783. He declared it as aptly as He could, II, 250. Since He and the Father are one God and Lord, 278. Everywhere He professes Himself neither the same as nor different from the Father, 271, 272. He is one from the one God the Father, I, 508. Nothing different could reside in One born from God as Spirit, II, 185. Christ is shown to be one with the Father by nature, when He so acts through Himself that He does not act from Himself, and so does not act from Himself that He acts through Himself, 295; He is inseparable from the Father, 240, 282. How He is in the Father and the Father in Him, 146. As He is not to be separated from the Father for faith, so neither is He for salvation, 282. He has the Father with Him in power and unity of nature, 280; He lives through the Father, 225. He possesses the Father’s nature, just as in the sacrament of the Eucharist we receive the nature of His flesh, 225. Son and Father have the same power, honour, work, nature, confession, form, and glory, 576 ff. Christ’s face is the glory of His divinity, I, 511. Christ’s whole glory is in God the one true Father alone, II, 291. He was glorified not with external glory but in the Father, 291. Christ and the Father have one glory, 291, and inseparable honour, 275. Christ [Col. 0931] made Himself equal to the Father in the honour of faith, II, 272; He made Himself equal to the Father in honour, power, and nature, 244; equality of nature is shown by equality of honour. 294. Christ’s substance, like the Father’s, is invisible, II, 377. By which authorities Christ’s equality with the Father is asserted, 146. Christ is not corporeal according to our manner, so that by being somewhere He is absent elsewhere, I, 455. His power is infinite, 708 ff. All power belongs to Him from the Father. 603.

What Christ’s power consists in regarding knowledge, and what this knowledge is, II, 188. The only-begotten God did not need instruction through ignorance of a demonstration, 189. Knowledge of the works which the Father willed to accomplish was innate in Him. 190. Christ is the end of the law, I, 509, the fullness of the law and prophets, 252. Every prophecy concerning Him is a lamp of Christ, 516. Christ is contained in the law, prophets, and Gospels, 735. He is compared to leaven, 735. His mysteries are safely explained when they are explained according to the Scriptures, II, 368. The law spoke of Christ’s bodily nature, Passion, and resurrection, I, 683; the law, prophecy, and so forth bore witness at every time that He is redeemer, 404. Some would have every word of the Psalms referred to Christ: what is to be thought of them, 178. Which Psalms are about Christ, 562; which of their prophecies are to be referred to Him, 17. Faith in Christ is the key to the Psalms, 5. David prophesied Christ by his own deeds. 600.

Christ’s coming is contained in all the commandments of the law, I, 410; it is foretold under the name David, 501 ff. The Psalmist hoped for Him throughout his whole life, 496. This was the expectation of the saints: that all flesh might be redeemed in Christ, 246. Christ’s coming is the work of the prophets, 5, 786. The mystery of Christ’s final dispensation. II, 435.

Christ left the couch of His eternal blessedness, I, 505; from God He became man, from mighty weak, and so forth, 505. Why God willed to be born, suffer, and die, II, 263. What Catholics and Arians think concerning Christ’s origin and Passion, 375 ff. Some say that Christ assumed Adam’s flesh and soul from the Virgin, 333. When He was born in the flesh, I, 767. The mysteries of Christ’s embodiment are ineffable to man, 684. Human reason fails at Christ’s temporal birth itself, II, 359. Christ’s eternal and temporal generation is expounded, 324 ff. The dignity of Christ commends the humility of His conception and birth, 41 ff. Christ was born under the law of men, but conceived not under the law of men, 354. Christ as man was born from Himself, 340, through the power of the origin proceeding from Himself, 339; made flesh through the Word, I, 675. Christ’s flesh took its origin from no other source than the Word, II, 332. He Himself is the origin of His own birth, 263; He Himself is the origin of His body, 332; He Himself is the source of His body and soul, 329; He did not live in the body through the principles of our body and soul, 330; through Himself He assumed for Himself a body from the Virgin and a soul from Himself, 334; He is not in the body of our defective weakness, since He is not in its origin, 345. Christ’s conception is spiritual, 352. From this it is proved that He is free from human vices. 352.

Christ is both from heaven, Son of Man, and in heaven, II, 331 ff. He is from earth as from the Virgin, from heaven as from the Word, 332 ff. Likewise, He is at once Son of Man and bread from heaven, 332. Christ’s body was prefigured by the ark of the covenant, I, 510 ff. Christ, placed in the body, is a tree, 731. Christ’s embodiment is not weakness in God but power, II, 114. Impiety does not understand this. 114. Christ assumed the body of our creation, I, 676, our earthly flesh, 166, the bodily nature of the first Adam, 255; He contains in Himself the nature of our whole race, II, 384; He is from Judah’s shoot, I, 234; from Judah’s shoot, Jesse’s root, and Mary according to the flesh, 512; in the law He is taught to be David’s son, 744; He is truly from David’s seed, 783; as man He is called David, 436, 511, taking the name of him from whose stock He also took His body, 501. Christ is David’s son according to the flesh and Lord according to the Spirit, II, 278; He received flesh from sinners, I, 158, from Judah and Moab, 158. Christ is the fruit of the womb, 472; at what price, 473; born from the Virgin’s flesh, which nevertheless was not diminished in what was hers, II, 61 ff.; He did not shrink from the shame of a human beginning, 40. In Christ, the shame of the human body, I, 232, to what extent, ibid., note. The Virgin so gave birth to Christ from herself that she gave birth from the Spirit of the Word, II, 330. Why Christ, truly born of the Virgin, is called by the Apostle both made and created, 437, 438. Why the order of Christ’s generation has consistency neither in number nor succession, I, 670. In Christ’s bodily procreation the signification of eternal birth is contained. 670.

Those who object that Catholics believe Christ not to be a man of our body and soul are refuted, II, 334. Christ was not seen in the guise of false flesh, I, 558; He did not assume a man of alien or simulated nature, 563; He is true and not simulated man, 600; His human affection is not simulated, 600; He was born a man of our body and soul. 112. Christ’s body was of its proper nature, II, 338; it had the reality, not the vices, of a human body, 339 ff. Christ, though Himself ignorant of sin, did not refuse to become a participant in our sin, [Col. 0932] I, 565; He assumed the body of our sin, II, 268, 354; born a man with our flesh, I, 242, He received sinful flesh: why, II, 11; He becomes participant in our flesh by assumption, not guilt, 11; He assumed our condition, I, 612. Christ has not the likeness of flesh, but the likeness of sinful flesh, II, 578. Having assumed the likeness of sinful flesh, He condemned sin through sin. I, 605.

Through assumption of flesh Christ was a child, I, 251; according to the flesh He is our kinsman, though He differs from us, 247; He has brothers only through assumption of flesh, II, 383, 388; having become a man of our body, I, 80, He made us His brothers, 80; by assuming the body of all of us, He became neighbour to all, 763. Through union with the flesh He assumed, we are in Him, 270. Christ’s flesh is a city whose citizens are human beings, 683. In Christ the body of the whole human race was sanctified. II, 40. The end of Christ’s embodiment, II, 41. Christ’s embodiment gains for man that he may be God, 261. He came for all. I, 707. Christ is Son of Man not in part, I, 111; in Him is the whole man, 675, note; He was born perfect man according to the condition of human conformity, II, 334; He was perfect man, consisting of soul and body, 330. We do not doubt that Christ is God the Word and that, as Son of Man, He consisted of soul and body. 362. Christ has in Himself all that is true of man and all that is true of God. II, 333. He who does not know Christ as both true God and true man does not know his life, 259. To deny that Christ is either God the Spirit or flesh of our body is equally perilous, 259. By what power God and man are united in Christ, I, 243. Various heretical inventions concerning the union of Word and man in Christ, II, 356; the true faith, 358. Some think that the Word dwelt in Christ merely as a prophetic spirit, 334, 356; others, that it passed into the soul of the body, 356; others, that it made the body alive in place of the soul, 356. Those who divide Christ into three parts or reduce Him to a single man of common kind are reproved. 364, 366.

Christ could not remain simultaneously in the form of God and the form of man; nor could God’s form be abolished so that there were only the form of a servant, I, 256, note; He emptied Himself from the form of God, II, 245; in emptying Himself, He lost, with the form of God, the unity of God’s nature according to the man assumed, 286. Christ’s emptying from the form of God was without destruction of the heavenly nature, I, 256. The emptying of form is not abolition of nature, II, 169. The emptying avails in order that the form of a servant may advance, 169. When Christ was emptied, the substance emptying itself was not absent from itself, not because it lacked itself, but because it was not seen to be present, I, 243. Christ emptied Himself not through loss of power and nature, but through a change of condition, II, 286. The emptying of God’s form does not know loss to its own detriment, I, 613. Power, although restraining itself into humility, did not fail from itself, 613. Christ’s emptying without change of the Word is excellently explained, II, 289, 295. In Christ, once born, one thing is seen by the eyes and another by the mind, 42. Christ, made man, did not cease to be God, I, 45; II, 114, 169, 310, 334; He did not lose what He was, but began to be what He was not, 59. God, having assumed flesh, was other than what He remained, yet He was not other than what He had remained, 260. Our assumption was no advancement for God, 261. The immutability of the only-begotten God after assumption of flesh. 51.

Christ’s two natures, I, 256, 678. Christ is at once true God and perfect man, II, 333, 367, 378, 384. Assumption of the servant’s form was not an inward property but an outward addition, I, 256, nor a nature belonging to a genuine origin and condition, ibid. Addition of the later nature brought no failure of the earlier nature, 117. Christ’s weaknesses belong to the nature brought forth, II, 114. Christ, proved as man, was known as God, I, 565 ff.; by words and deeds He always showed Himself Son of God and man, II, 261; He is shown to be of two natures when He says both that He is submerged and asks that He not be submerged. I, 250. Christ’s nature is indivisible, II, 345. True faith does not divide Christ, 358. The whole Word God is in Him; the whole man Christ is in Him, 358. Those who divide Christ are refuted, 334, 364, 366. Christ is the same God and man at once, I, 111; the same Spirit and man, II, 169; one and the same One who changes condition and assumes, 169; one and the same Son of God within and without, 507; not one in the form of God and another in the form of a servant, 333; not one Son of Man and another Son of God, 289; one subsists from both, God and man, 712; He is mediator between man and God through the confession in Himself of each nature, 712. He is mediator between God and men, since from the natures united into one and the same reality He is the reality of each nature, 259; I, 720; II, 388. From that union God both began to suffer and became able to die, I, 244. Christ’s indivisibility, II, 361, 365, 366. What happened in His body happened in Him, 363. The sufferings of our weaknesses are joined to God. 263.

Christ, God and man at once, sometimes speaks what belongs to God and sometimes what belongs to man, [Col. 0933] I, 117; He employs in both Gospels and Prophets sayings fitted to His twofold nature, 584. In Scripture concerning Him, one must discern what is to be assigned to His divinity and what to His humanity, 571. Understanding Christ’s mysteries consists in neither dividing nor confusing His natures, 563; II, 484, 485. If anything weak is spoken in His person, it must be referred to the man, I, 563. Christ’s latest things are those proper to the man assumed by Him; His ancient things are those which pertain to His eternity. 569. Christ is one thing by His own nature and another by our assumption, II, 264. In Him it is one thing to be nature and another to have assumed nature, I, 563. What He is as God belongs to His own nature; what He is as man is assumption of our nature, 584. Some of His names are natural, others assumed, II, 283. He assumed a body foreign to His own nature, I, 247. In the only-begotten God weakness was not natural but assumed, 246. He assumed the weaknesses of our nature, 563. Assumption of weakness did not make Him weak, 563. In what respect those err who consider Christ’s soul to be of human nature and weakness, 111. In Christ all things are contrary to nature. II, 114.

Christ’s two wills, II, 347: a free will, 297, yet not dissenting from the Father’s will, 297. Of His own will He fulfils the Father’s will. 54. Christ, while He remained in the world, did not enter into the vices and sins of the world, I, 700; He was free from sin, 145, 245; alone outside sin, 583; alone ignorant of guilt, 146; alone perfect and without sin, 364; He who was made sin, 355. Christ is not a sinner but one assuming sins, not weak but bearing weaknesses, I, 563; though He was not such, He was treated as debtor to sin and death, 245; He was afflicted as sinner and fool. 246. Christ, who had no need of circumcision, was presented in the temple to be circumcised. I, 274. Christ’s humility in baptism, I, 565. He did not need the washing for Himself, but for us, 676. Christ sanctified man both by assumption and by washing, 676; in baptism He was reborn to God as the perfect Son. 48. Christ’s temptation in the desert, I, 565: He offered His man to the devil for temptation, 677, that the devil might be conquered in man, 677. While abstaining from human food even unto temptation, He was nourished by God’s Spirit, 678. His fasting, hunger, and temptation are full of the effects of heavenly counsel, 676. How Christ’s fast was made a reproach to Him. 248.

Christ on the mountain was transfigured and displayed the condition of His kingdom. II, 398. Christ was sent to Judaea, but named the salvation of the Gentiles, I, 673. His work is testimony to His mission from the Father, II, 273. It is Christ’s proper work to save believers, I, 675. Born a man under the law for remission and condemnation of sin, 166, He does or suffers nothing for His own sake, 251. Christ’s activity in this world is the working of our salvation, 119. Christ’s cry, 244. Christ’s proper office was to bring knowledge of God, 782, to proclaim the Father and fulfil His will, 575. His greatest work was to make the Father known to us as Father, not as His creator, II, 63, 64, and to make man worthy as God’s dwelling, I, 504. He became man so that He might be for us, from among ourselves, a witness to divine things, II, 54; He presented in Himself the model of human wisdom, I, 364. How Christ is our guide on the path of the commandments, 308; He received in Himself only so much humility and materiality as there was power in us to understand Him, II, 51; under the ministry of the man assumed He carries out His whole work, 197. Whose hands of Christ were trained for battle. I, 611. Christ’s poverty. I, 263, 590. Christ has it by nature not to be humble, II, 394; He gave both command and example of humility, I, 364. The reward of His humility, 365 ff. Christ’s humility is our nobility, II, 41. In what respect Christ is less than John, I, 723, note; why He commands those healed to be silent about Him. 728. Christ’s splendour in the humility of flesh, II, 58. All glory accrued not to the Word but to the flesh, 288. Christ’s spittle and speech belong to the nature of the body, 354. Power goes out from Him as from the hem of a garment. I, 743. Whence Christ’s miracles came, II, 491. Whether His body itself had power to perform them, 337, ibid., note. It is not fitting that at the command and by the power of Christ’s soul a soul should be recalled into a body, 361. Christ’s body was assumed into service to the Spirit, that is, the Word, I, 675. Why He looked to heaven when about to multiply the loaves. 741.

Christ fulfilled in God’s works all the time He spent in man, II, 43; by forgiving sins He proves Himself God, I, 705. To Christ alone, by communion in the Father’s substance, belonged the authority to forgive sins, 706. Whatever Christ does, God does it. II, 268. God’s testimony concerning Christ is Christ’s own activity, II, 273. [Col. 0934] All Christ’s powers and works are to be praised as God’s. I, 704. Christ’s deeds are both truths and signs of things to come. I,
726 Heretics ascribe to Christ a dominant necessity of ignorance, II, 303. He does not fail to know the disturbances that will come upon minds still at rest, 304. As author of all things, he can be ignorant of nothing, 304. As one of an uncompounded nature, 305. Does he penetrate human things as the greater, while not penetrating paternal things as the lesser? 311. All treasures of knowledge are in him insofar as he is God; they are hidden insofar as he is a sacrament, 304. Christ’s ignorance is a dispensation rather than ignorance, II, 307, 309. He professed himself man, weak with the weakness of our nature, even to the knowledge of his unknown day, I, 605. His not knowing the day of judgment is a dispensation of silence, II, 316. It is an injury to the Father to suppose that he showed the Son the day of his suffering but concealed from him the day of his power, 305. What he does not know belongs to knowledge according to nature, 309. If he is ignorant of anything, his will is not one with the Father’s, 313. Christ, born a man with our body, spoke according to the manner of our nature, II, 262. His utterances are suited to the facts and true, 220. Whether he swore is uncertain, I, 502. He is said to have sworn because he fulfilled all things as though he had sworn them, 502. He swore that he would not return to heaven unless man had become a dwelling worthy of God, 505; for this reason he died, 505.

Christ’s subjection does not prove him inferior to the Father, II, 393; what it is, 397 ff. He always subjected himself to the Father, both in the honor of sonship and in the condition of manhood, 261. The subjection of Christ who is God is an act of piety, not a diminution of essence, 493. Christ, as God, is subject to the Father both in obedience and in name, 493. Christ is obedient to the Father and therefore lesser in the form of a servant, II, 699; willingly obeyed the Father’s will in all things, I, 110; obeying the Father, he is not without the function of will, 588. The nature of the merit of Christ’s obedience, 109.

Christ’s omnipotence is inferred from the weaknesses he assumed, II, 114. Christ entreats in the obedience of those whose weaknesses he bore and whose sins he took upon himself, I, 108. He prays for God’s remembrance of his own man, 502; he prays for salvation for the man whom he had assumed, 249. A request for glory, or reception of power, does not prove Christ weak, II, 281, 282. He seeks glory not for the divine nature but for the human, I, 136. What glorification he expects from the Father, II, 59. He demands back the glory of the assumed servile form, I, 109. This is the name of God, 109. Nor merely the honor of this designation, 109. But power and nature as well, 109. His prayer benefited us, not himself, II, 371. As man, Christ prays for salvation, which, even when about to die, he hopes for because of consciousness of his divinity, I, 243. He displays something beyond man when he prays for salvation for himself not for his own sake, 251. He who expects glory and resurrection from no other source is by no means weak, 120.

Christ proclaims the honor of the Father’s majesty through the confession of our humility, I, 612. He suffered all things according to manhood and spoke all things according to manhood, 108. He both suffers and speaks all things as man, 251. He accommodated himself to us in all things by which the weakness of our nature is held fast, II, 309. He underwent the lot of all human sufferings, I, 166, 242. He experienced the sufferings of all our flesh, II, 22. He passed through every humiliation of our nature, 40. He suffered what human beings can suffer, 368. Christ’s assumed flesh—that is, the whole man—was delivered over to the natures of suffering, 339.

Christ assumed the feelings customary to human life in order to prove himself true man, II, 365. In him remained the capacity to weep, thirst, and hunger, 338. Christ often gave himself over to sleep, weariness, thirst, and hunger, I, 245; in assuming our weaknesses and bearing sins, he spoke from the experience and practice of human exhaustion, 245. Through sleep, hunger, thirst, weariness, and tears he acted as man, II, 56. The devil attempted to mock the endurance of his hunger, I, 678. After recognizing in him, through the weakness of hunger, what belongs to man, 677. In order that Christ might hunger, he left his manhood to its nature; an operation did not secretly intervene to prevent hunger, 677. He left it so, because the devil had to be conquered by flesh, not by God, 677. In taking food or drink, he yielded to custom, not necessity, II, 339.

Christ’s soul is frequently sorrowful and distressed in the Gospels, I, 112. Why Christ wept when about to raise Lazarus, 248. Christ both wept and grieved, II, 362. He truly wept, 361. The Arians cannot account for the reason for his weeping, 360 ff. Christ sometimes weeps, groans, and is sorrowful; this too is attributed to the example of weakness, I, 248. He did not weep, thirst, or hunger for himself, II, 339. His tears were for us, I, 130. He was distressed through bodily weakness, 585. Christ’s hunger, thirst, death, and the like are not to be heard in isolation, II, 502. Bearing the natures of man and God, he had from human weakness the feeling of alarm, and from consciousness of divinity the confidence of security, I, 588. Both speech and the feelings of a weak man belong to him without dishonor to God, I, 128.

[Col. 0935] Christ’s entire life was harassed by the hatreds of the impious, I, 585, 586. He is compared to a mustard seed, 735. What he did and suffered the Father foreknew and ordained, 568. It was not possible that he should not suffer, 802. Dwelling and preaching in Abel and Zechariah, he had suffered, 786. Christ’s passion was shown already from the foundation of the world, 802. It was prefigured in Jacob’s struggle, II, 115. It is proclaimed in Psalm LXVII, I, 242; it is prophesied in the sufferings of David, 604.

Some attribute sorrow, fear, and the like to Christ’s divinity, I, 800. They are refuted, 800. The same persons assert that the Son of God began in time and was created from nothing, 801. Christ the Word could suffer, but could not be passible, II, 492. Christ did not fear the passion which he voluntarily undertook, I, 573, ibid., note. He intensely desired to fulfill it, 588 ff. For the confirmation of prophecy, 589. Because through the passion he provided for human salvation, 251. Why the passion was a delight to him, 574. At the time of the passion Christ wept and prayed, not from a natural fear, as it were, of suffering, but while displaying the feeling of the man whom he bore, 600. He had no cause to fear or grieve for himself, II, 327, 341. It is wrongly thought that he feared death, which he taught was not to be feared, 327, and which he voluntarily faced with power to live again, ibid. and 328.

Christ’s sadness was not according to human necessity, I, 250. It arose not from himself but from the disciples, 603, 801; II, 347. He was sorrowful unto death, not because of death, I, 802; II, 346. He feared blasphemy against the Spirit on their behalf, I, 802. As one mourning with others, he seeks not consolation but faith, 252. To fulfill every office of humility, Christ himself gave himself over to suffering and weakness, I, 107. He suffered in the midst of the earth, 534. What he suffered from the soldiers in the passion, 34. For the increase of glory he offered his shoulders to the scourges, 688. He was subjected to all insults customarily directed against the impious, 247. He became an object of reproach and a song to every race of men, 248. He suffered something beyond death, 505. Nothing concerning the sweat of blood and the coming of the angel occurs in most manuscripts, II, 349. To sweat blood is not weakness but power, 350. Christ was strengthened for our sake, just as he was sorrowful for our sake, 349.

Heretics deny that Christ was in the nature of the impassible God, II, 326. In what respect he was impassible, I, 506. Christ is defended against pain, II, 342. He underwent all that is weak while the dignity of his majesty remained unharmed, I, 120. All that belongs to our death and fear fell upon him rather than inhered in him, 120. He had a body for suffering, not a nature for feeling pain, II, 338. Whether Christ’s body possessed the nature of our pain, 337. Christ truly suffered, 337. How the onset of suffering was in him without the pain of suffering, 336. He grieves for us, yet does not grieve by a feeling of our pain, 354. Being born man introduced for us the impression that he experienced natural pain in his passion, 355. The nature of Christ’s sufferings corresponded to the nature of soul and body, 330. Christ was outside the fleshly nature of feeling pain, 343. By the power of his own body he took on the sufferings of our body, 354. Though he gave himself to suffering, Eternal Power nevertheless did not undergo the pain of suffering, I, 603. Christ so enacted the realities of our nature in passion and death that he bore them by the power of his own nature, II, 262. He assumed all our sufferings, but in suffering retained the nature of his omnipotence, 354. In the same Christ are both weakness for suffering and God’s power for life, 368.

Christ’s divinity did not yield beneath the nail of the wound, II, 355. Upon Christ fell all the terror of the storm raging against us, I, 243. This came solely from the assumption of flesh, because the terror of our weaknesses could not fall upon him as God, 243. Christ was not naturally weak, II, 342. The weaknesses in him were not natural but assumed, I, 252. This was known to God alone, 251. Christ grieves and speaks in the complaints of our sorrows, 242. Himself placed beyond the necessity both of fear and pain, he accommodates himself to what he assumed, ibid. The wicked had a right of suffering against his flesh, not against the eternal and impassible nature of divinity, 103. Once Christ’s natures have first been distinguished, 563, the divine alone is then exempted from pain, 564, 574, note. Christ is without pain as God, 564. He who does not feel pain cannot fail to remain God, 564. How Christ bears our sins and grieves for us, 803. In Christ is the pain of wounds and persecution, 254, 255. Because he grieves as man, it is wrongly inferred that he grieves as God, 255, note. In Christ the Son of God suffered, but did not suffer-with, II, 507. No weakness dominated Christ’s body, 342. Christ’s body was delivered over to suffering; but death, though permitted against it, did not become its master, I, 588. Christ’s passion is voluntary, not compelled, II, 355. It is not natural but assumed, I, 246. Christ’s power shone forth in the passion, II, 355. Christ’s passion is a triumph, 356. By his passion Christ swallowed up our weaknesses, I, 701. And even the pain of death itself, 803. According to man he suffered every weakness for us; according to God he triumphed in them all, II, 356.

[Col. 0936] Christ’s flesh was bound and pierced on the cross, II, 328. Prophecy of Christ’s death, I, 244. Jonah, an imitator of the Lord’s death and its duration, 244. On the cross Christ was doing greater works than if he had descended from it, 807. The cry of dying Christ testifies to a rupture caused by departing divinity, 807, ibid., note. The abandonment of Christ, which the Arians vainly object, II, 356 ff. Those who interpret it, 357. Christ’s security in death, I, 506. Christ endured death but did not know how to die, 115. Why he subjected himself to death—that is, to the departure, as it were, of soul and body, 115. When he wished, he gave up his spirit, 619. For Christ death was the departure of an immortal soul, 506. What was punishment for us was rest for him, 506.

Death must be proclaimed in the living God, although from this the impious argue that God died, II, 512. In Christ death belongs to the man, but the raising of the flesh to God, 267. Yet he who died is not other than he through whom he rises, 267. Hilary did not understand the Word to have departed from Christ’s dead flesh, for he says that he who lives died, 263; and that God was born man so that man might remain eternally in God, 263—and indeed does remain there, ibid.; and that God had placed himself within the law of death, 263. Christ who died is the same one who at the same time reigns in heaven, 365. When Christ died, his two natures were not divided, 364, 366. He who died is not other than he who was born, 336. He who died is not other than he who was buried, who descended into hell, or who ascended into heaven, 367. Christ is one: flesh stripped off and stripping himself of flesh, 266.

Christ’s glorification on the cross, II, 55. In his death the Son of God was manifested in various ways, I, 149. The triumph of dying Christ, 230: the cross was for him a confession to God and a return to the kingdom, II, 344. The effects of Christ’s death, 265. Christ died for all, I, 154. He destroyed the powers hostile to us together with their leader, ibid. He drank up every defect of human corruption, 809. Christ, immortal and unconquerable by death, died for the eternity of those who die, II, 11. He died to condemn in himself the impious assaults of the heavenly wickednesses, and to bring eternity to all, I, 166. All things were purchased at the price of Christ’s blood, 805.

Christ is our propitiation, I, 185. The redemption of all, 742. He is redeemer of soul and body, 715. Spiritual beings owe their continuance to him, II, 249. He would have wished the Jews to be saved, I, 708. Dying, he grieved that he did not bear the sins of all, 808. All flesh has been redeemed in Christ in order that it may rise, 130. He died for sinners unto the salvation of resurrection, 130. Christ’s death was unjust and justly avenged, 246 ff. Christ’s burial, I, 809 ff. Christ visited the infernal abodes, I, 115, 244, 58. For the completion of true manhood, he did not refuse descent into hell, 572. In going to hell, he was not absent from paradise, 602, I, 344. Christ’s preaching in hell, I, 344. Whether in descending there he delivered the righteous or sinners, 149, ibid., note. Christ’s body was owed to death but was not subject to corruption, I, 588.

Christ’s resurrection, and through him the flight of demons, are prayed for, I, 214. The end of Psalm LVIII aptly applies to him as risen, 151. Christ rose by his own power, 611. He is God to himself for his own resurrection, 131, II, 267. Christ’s departure from death is his own, I, 228. Christ and God who raises him from the dead have one operation, II, 266. Christ sits at God’s right hand in the body in which he was raised, I, 575; in that same body he was seen after the resurrection, 575. With the doors shut, he stands present by an entrance penetrable to himself alone, 575; II, 62. Christ’s body passed through solid things, 337. How this can be explained, 63. Christ has now assumed the nature of our flesh inseparably to himself, 222. He raised up with himself all who believe in him and seated them in heavenly places, I, 146, 379. In him the nations know that the flesh of their nature has been transformed into the substance of eternal salvation, 617. The Law and Prophets are witnesses of Christ’s divinity; the Apostles, of his resurrection, 749.

Why Christ was made terribly wondrous, I, 575. He always had the power of flying into heaven, 572, 573. Christ bore back to heaven the material of his assumed body joined to his Spirit, 683. He brought back as a gift to God the Father the man he had assumed and whom God awaited, 676. It was fitting that his return into heaven should be adorned by the eager meeting of heaven, 146. He ascended into heaven, with the heavenly powers and souls of the saints going before as the path for his journey, 233. Ascending on high, he received those taken captive by the devil, 227—namely, the nations as an inheritance, 227. For our man there is a session at God’s right hand in heaven, 167.

Christ’s reward for assuming our humility, I, 603, 613. Christ as man is advanced into God after the death of the cross, 50. The nature assumed from the Virgin’s flesh is transferred into his eternal glory, 200. To his body, glorified into God’s glory, are also given God’s name and kingdom, 200. To Christ as man God’s name and honor are given because of obedience, 565. Christ merited glory not because he created heaven, but because he was made in the form of a servant, 365. Matters concerning Christ’s glorious state, 572, II, 406. What his glory with the Father is, 287. The different degrees of Christ’s glory, 400. By the obedience through which the servile condition is assumed, it is granted also to that servile condition that it should be in the form of God, I, 613, 603. How the servile form advanced into God’s glory, 571. Him whom, by his own will, he conceived and bore in the Virgin’s womb, he exalted into God, II, 713. The greatness of the Lord overcame the littleness of the servile form, so that it ceased to be servile, 713. By the glory of the form of God, equality is restored to Christ, 300. Christ, according to the Spirit, is born into the form of God; according to the flesh, renewed into the form of God, 301. According to manhood he obtains unity of the divine nature through glory, 286, 298. In him flesh and Spirit are now both one, I, 793. He now lives wholly to God, II, 268. Formerly containing two in himself, he is now God only, 399. Man and God is now wholly God, ibid., 400, 401. No nature of the earthly body remains in any respect, 399. Yet the body has not been cast off, 399; rather, the nature of corruption has been swallowed up into the glory of divinity, I, 588. And human nature has been assumed into the glory of divine nature, II, 239. In Christ we have now been made full, 264. In Christ we behold ourselves through the assumption of our flesh, I, 453.

The gift of the Holy Spirit testifies that Christ has been exalted above the heavens, I, 136. Christ’s glory above the heavens and on earth, 137. Why angels praise him, II, 53. How he has now crushed the devil with his followers, I, 188 ff. All things are given to Christ as man, 612. Why Christ is our God, II, 97. He is God of those who will be saved, I, 228.
