Christ the King, I, 44. King of heaven, 45. The king is not hidden, 516. Marcellus assigns him a beginning and an end of reigning, II, 648. Christ does not lose the kingdom by handing it over to the Father, II, 393. He will reign until he places his enemies under his feet, I, 163. The time of this kingdom is comprehended from generation to generation, that is, until the resurrection of all, 163. Then he will hand over the kingdom to the Father, not so that he himself will then not be king, 163. But when he has handed it over, he himself will reign with those who are kings, 163. In Christ are the salvation, glory, and hope of the righteous man, whom Christ will raise with himself and make conformable to his heavenly glory, 168. As God, Christ is ruling always and will likewise rule always, 200. Although he always reigned, he did not always reign in the body, 200. Though he now reigns, he will not reign fully and perfectly until after the consummation of the ages, 200. Then control of the eternal kingdom will be given to him, 200. See **Kingdom**.

Christ, eternal king and priest, possesses the glory of both offices even in his fleshly birth, I, 668. The saving sacraments for the world of Christ’s dispensation, II, 111. The superiority of Christ’s offering over the offerings of the Law, I, 114. Christ’s inheritance and possession, I, 48 ff.—namely, the nations, 472. This is the reward of assumed flesh, 472, 473. Christ’s bride is the Church, I, 480. Christ is at once bridegroom and bride, 793. Christ is the Church, containing her wholly in himself through the sacrament of his body, 460. He is a body for us, II, 249. He is the body of all, 236. All now remain in Christ’s body, 264. Christ’s glorious body is signified by the name “mountain,” I, 71 ff. Christ’s body is Zion, 66. Christ is a stone from the mountain because of his flesh, and a mountain from the stone because of glory, 453. He can no longer be unknown: why, II, 376, 379. Christ in the flesh is treasure in a field, I, 735. To have found Christ is gratuitous, 735. But the power to possess him is not without a price, 735. Christ’s sleep and wakefulness in us, 702. Christ is the way to the Father, II, 203. Christ’s name is on the lips of nearly all heretics, 169. All kingdoms will understand Christ to be God, though late, I, 237. The Jews will know him as ruler of the ends of the earth, 150. Christ, at the place of his passion, will gather the saints for judgment, I, 789. Then he will present himself to all, 789. When and what Christ’s glorious advent will be, 790. On the day of judgment all will see Christ in that flesh in which he was transfigured, II, 59. In Christ now stand all things that are to be done through the fulfillment of the times, I, 284. Christ is our mediator, who will unite all to God, II, 399.

Food of the soul, I, 478.

**CICERO** confesses that the disagreement of the wise compels him to be ignorant of the Lord, I, 166, note. **Cio**, II, 666.

Contests of the circus games, I, 311.

Circuit against Christ, I, 590.

Christ was circumcised in the Temple, I, 274.

Spiritual circumcision, II, 10 ff. This is Christ’s circumcision, 265. Circumcision established only as a sign does not now benefit those who lack the author of spiritual circumcision, I, 356.

What constitutes a city, I, 438. The construction and completion of the City of God, 635, 641, 643. The city for God is the people of the faithful, 704. It consists of many coming together into one; and in each of us there is a city for God, 469. How the city of the Lord grows into the house of God, 438.

A cry of the mouth rather than of the heart is forbidden by the Lord in prayer, I, 397. Who cries with the whole heart, 397. The cry of the blood of martyrs, 592; of slain Abel, 397; of the Spirit, 397; of faithful prayer, 592; of faith in silence, 134, 397. To God, even the silent expectation of a faithful man is a cry, 601. The cry of Moses while silent, 397 ff.; of Christ, 244.

What is the brightness which Father and Son display to each other, II, 57.

The key of knowledge of the Scriptures, I, 5. Keys to each book, 15. The Apostles received the keys of the kingdom of heaven, II, 157. Faith dissenting from Peter’s faith did not obtain these, 162.

Clerical cases should not be heard by provincial governors, II, 535.

**Cocras**, II, 632.

The power of thought to present to the mind things that are absent, I, 426. Bodily and earthly thoughts will perish with the earthly body, 631. To know the thoughts of hearts belongs to God, II, 280.

The distinction between cognomina and pronomina, II, 148.

To know the future is proper to God, II, 306.

Knowledge of God is to be pursued above all, I, 169. It is to be sought from his own sayings, II, 14. It is to be sought in the Gospels, 192. No comparison of earthly things adequately reaches God, 14. It is a religious confession to know this alone concerning God: that God is, I, 491.

To worship God is the proper duty of justice, II, 712. The best worshiper of God, I, 283.

Collections were instituted by the Apostles only for the poor or those renouncing the world, I, 101.

The dove signifies the Holy Spirit, I, 773.

Neither the pillar of fire by night nor that of cloud by day went before when the people had to remain for a long time in the same camp, I, 305.

Three kinds of those who eat God’s people, I, 100.

Retinue, II, 681.

**COMITES**, II, 599, 651.

All things ought to be regarded as common to all, I, 680.

The sacrament of divine communion, I, 251. Judas was not worthy of communion in the eternal sacraments, 799. By communion in the holy body we are thereafter to be placed in communion in the holy body, 191. By that food we are saved in the present and prepared in the future for fellowship with God, ibid. Hilary distributes communion through his presbyters, II, 543.

By communion in sufferings one becomes a participant with those who fear God, I, 329.

Communion of dwelling, I, 713. One must not associate in their homes and familiarities with those who either persecute Christ or do not know him, 712. The mark of communion in letters mutually received and sent, II, 659, 660. Those who rashly enter into communion with persons condemned by anathema must suffer everlasting punishments, 538. The communion with heretics which Hilary permitted, 563.

Human comparison does not suffice for demonstrating divine realities, II, 71, 137, 199; its usefulness, 138, 200. There is no comparison of earthly things with God, 14; it aids our understanding, though it does not satisfy it, ibid.

God is free from composition, I, 492. Whatever is composite was not eternal, ibid.

If councils have judged contrary to one another, we must approve the better judgments, II, 513. A general council is sought to confirm the Nicene faith, 674. Those who took charge of the Council of Sardica, 661. The bishops undertook, through the Emperor’s favor, to hold a council at Sardica, 655. Liberius entreats Constantius that a council be held, 661, 674. The Italian bishops ask Constantius to order a council convened at Aquileia, 677. The Sardican council in the midst of the Church, 655. Likewise the Council of Milan in A.D. 355 was held in a church, 540, 542, until the bishops, fearing the people’s judgment, moved from the Lord’s house to the palace, 540. Delegates of the Roman Church attended the Council of Milan of the year 349, 688. Ursacius and Valens ask and obtain pardon there, 668. Councils of the East were customarily confirmed by those of the West, and conversely councils of the West by those of the East, 661.

The desire of flesh and spirit, I, 551. Vices ingrained in our nature, 385, do not allow human beings to be restrained within the laws of nature, 598. By the nature of our body we are carried into every course of crimes, 358. How this impulse is to be checked, 358. The stain of human flesh cannot be entirely abolished in this life, 608. Through bodily nature the Prophets possess innate material for vices, 345. The struggle of desire in the regenerate, 719. How it remains in the saints without harming them, 344. It is the desire of the heart, not bodily members, that must be cut off, 686. See **Desire**.

What confession is, I, 641; it must not always be referred to sins, 329. One kind is confession of sins; another, praise of God, 210, 541, 555. Both are fitting for our faith, 556. Confession of God must be public and constant, 202. Every undertaking and word of ours must be entered upon with confession of God, 184.

What confession of sin is, I, 541, 555. It includes a profession of ceasing, 541, 556. It is true in one who neither ceases to repent nor commits acts requiring repentance, I, 391. He loses the pardon of confession who persists in sins understood and confessed, 556. Confession and conversion must be complete, 556. This is to be sought from God, 556. Old offenses must be confessed without interruption, 391. Confession must not be interrupted even in the justified, 541 ff. This is the true confession of a righteous man: one which commends present righteousness through awareness and confession of past sins, 95.

The fruit of confession, I, 420. In confession lies every reward of our hope, 420. In confession of sins is the greatest remedy for the diseases of deadly vices, 555. Confession of sins brings it about that, although we deserve rebuke, we are not rebuked, 297. A crime must be confessed in order to obtain pardon, 297. After confession has been made, the Apostles loose those who are bound, 759. Shame at vices is called confession from its effect, 674. Where there is confession of sin, there is also justification from God, 462. To whom the pardon of confession is granted, 556. How confession obtains the pardon of sins, 760. Sins must be confessed in order that a person may be capable of God’s teaching, 300. Confession of sins has a place only in this age, 92. How one must confess to no one but God, I, 93, note.

To trust is more than to hope, I, 59.

The sacrament of confirmation. See I, 688, note; 711; 762, note.

Confusion arises from disgrace, I, 262. It arises from consciousness of sins, I, 342.

The marriage of Christ, now already complete, I, 778.

Teachers (or magi) abstain from the use of marriage, I, 184. The sole reason for ceasing from marriage, 686.

The consciousness of a good work is the light of souls, I, 795. It is to be purchased by the fruits of mercy, 794. Security of a right conscience before witnesses; trembling of an evil one, 286.

The sight of saints is grievous to the wicked and joyful to the righteous, I, 338.

**Preservation.** In order to be preserved, created things need God’s continuous operation, I, 269.

We now have some consolation, but not full consolation, I, 460. What ought to support and console the faithful amid afflictions, 391. Here, consolation for those who are despised comes from God alone, 445. Likewise consolation of the afflicted comes from God alone, 444. Who will grant them recompense after this life, 444 ff. The hope of the afflicted is eternal consolation, 320.

Many came from Constantinople to Sardica, II, 658.

Acts of the Constantinopolitan synod of A.D. 336, II, 649. Its judgment was false, 640.

The delegates from Rimini return to Constantinople, II, 693, 694.

Proceedings of the Constantinopolitan synod of A.D. 360, II, 575. This synod is called divided, 549. It disputes concerning the faith, 548. Hilary asks to be heard before it concerning the faith, ibid. Proceedings at Constantinople between the Anomoeans and the delegates of the Synod of Seleucia, 693 ff. There Constantius fosters Eastern dissensions, 566.

**CONSTANTINE** attended the Council of Nicaea, II, 688. His judgment against Athanasius, 652. Holding the Nicene Creed, he was baptized and departed to God’s rest, 688. The Nicene synod was his concern until death, 583, ibid., note. Constantine of holy memory, 671, 674.

**CONSTANTIUS**, rebellious heir of his father’s piety and enemy of divine religion, II, 583. By spreading insulting speeches among the populace, he had made Liberius [the construction is incomplete in the supplied text], 671. Liberius entreats Constantius through delegates to order a council convened at Aquileia, 677. Constantius honorably receives the delegation of the Synod of Ancyra, 506. He acknowledges that he had been deceived, 506. Engaged in wars and not yet regenerated, he was deceived by the Arians into imposing a formula of belief upon the churches, 506. He was circumvented in Hilary’s case, 543. His letters on that matter, 543. With Constantius present, Marcus dictated the creed, 708. Liberius’s letter to Constantius concerning the condemnation of Athanasius, 678. Liberius sends Fortunatianus to Constantius, 681.

Constantius’s letter to the Italian bishops assembled at Rimini, II, 683. Mention is made of it, 688. Other letters, no longer extant, are mentioned, 684. The perfidious bishops write to Constantius in the name of the Synod of Rimini, 691. They congratulate him that they have been enlightened by his writings, 691. Constantius wishes the blasphemies of the Anomoeans to be condemned, 694.

Constantius of blessed and religious will, II, 547. His disposition was also merciful toward the accused, 671. He seeks faith, 548. He desires to hear the faith from bishops, yet does not hear it, 444. He desires only the faith according to what is written, 547. He cries, “I do not wish words which are not written to be spoken,” 575. He is the teacher of profane men, 566.

Constantius’s instability in faith, II, 579 ff. His hypocrisy and persecution, 564 ff. Violence against the delegates of the Synod of Seleucia, 575. He threatens the people through the prefect and the bishops within the palace, 575. He surrendered to the devil the world for which Christ suffered, 575. By a novel triumph of ingenuity over the devil, Constantius accomplishes every cruelty without the odium of glorious deaths, 567. He goes before Antichrist, 566.

[Col. 0940] With what caution faith in consubstantiality is to be proclaimed, II, 181.

Custom has a great bond in itself, I, 283.

Consummation is manifold, I, 354. There is a consummation both of good and of evil, 347.

The power of continence, I, 551. By its cold, as by frost, the body burning with vices is frozen, 344. The danger to continence especially in the night season, 322. How it may be avoided, ibid. Encounters with wanton women are deceptive to the eyes of the continent, I, 327.

Contradiction and injustice are foremost among crimes, I, 123. Every human utterance is liable to contradiction, II, 301.

Controversies about words should be settled amicably, II, 518.

The obstinate are accused of a hard and lofty neck, I, 486.

Conversion of the sinner. See **Repentance**.

The banquets of ministers of the Church are costly under the pretext of religion, I, 101.

**Coo**, II, 666.

How the inmost heart lies open to God, I, 139. Purity of heart is vainly boasted of, 342. How it becomes unstained, 342. How the mouth of the heart ought to stand open to the Holy Spirit, 387.

The enlargement of the heart, I, 303. It is the office of an enlarged heart that divine words proceed from it, 317. The fruit and cause of a spacious heart, 317 ff. The cause and punishment of a constricted heart, 317. Nothing except Christ ought to enter our hearts, 810. Adultery conceived in the heart alone is already a crime, 139.

**Corbanan**, I, 806.

The crown of sanctified earth: the Lord glorious amid the choir of saints, I, 192.

**CORONATUS**, notary, I, 464.

**CORNELIUS**, firstfruits of the nations, I, 771.

A horn, the insignia of a kingdom, I, 516.

**Body.** The multiple meanings of this word, I, 692, note. The nature of bodies is impenetrable, II, 62. The power of sun and moon upon our bodies, I, 430. The body’s fellowship with the soul is burdensome, 298. It contaminates the soul, 299. How bodily vices infect the nature of the soul, 172. Bodies are compounded into material for vices, 172. They are material for every vice, II, 711. The body is both a dark and contagious prison of the soul, I, 424; the soul’s garment, 723. The Prophets spread out garments beneath themselves when they strip themselves of bodies, 772. Bodies dissolved by luxury are houses of demons, 723.

How the corrupt stain of our body is healed by the power of the Word, I, 699. A body chastised by continence is as a wineskin in frost, 344. Mortified through faith, it passes into the nature of the soul, 719. How, in obeying the soul, it passes into that nature, 717. The bodies of believers are houses of God, 187. Scripture calls human bodies instruments, I, 550. The body is the instrument of the soul, its affections, and its affairs, 196. God must be pleased by skillful works of the body, 197. It is sweet for the body to serve God, 528. Bodily ministry is incorporeal, although performed through a body, 478. How bodily sense is imbued with the joys of the mind, 172.

Eternal possession of bodies is promised to the faithful, I, 535. Bodily strength is to be hoped for by no one in this age, 431, but in eternity, 431 ff. It belongs to our body to die, become weak, and suffer need, 431. Bodies are buildings, either firm through faith or destined to fall through unbelief, 488. The brightness or darkness of bodies follows the brightness or darkness of souls, 690. What raised bodies will display to the pious and to the wicked, 142. What is fleshly to the body is swallowed up through glory into the nature of spirit, II, 406. Through glory the body is not abolished but changed, 399.

The body of Christ is the Church, I, 487. How Christ’s glorious body is true Zion, 260. The Lord’s body is thought to be called Zion throughout all Scripture, 640. Participation in Christ’s body and kingdom is open to all, unless someone is severed through unbelief or uselessness, 87 ff. The Lord’s body. See **Eucharist**.

There is nothing bodily in God, II, 141. Those who dwell with the face of God retain nothing bodily, I, 591, ibid., note. Nothing is not bodily in its substance and creation, 692. Kinds of souls receive the bodily substance of their own nature, 692.

He who wishes to correct others must first correct himself, I, 696.

It is prudent to wish to be corrected by a holy and faithful man, I, 597.

The method of fraternal correction, I, 75 ff.

Iniquity brings corruption; corruption deserves abomination, I, 95.

The raven is a figure of the sinner, I, 638, 639.

Grossness is either companion or cause of impiety and vices, I, 597.

**Cratia**, II, 666.

Creation and birth: how they differ,
II, 470. The creation of things [Col. 0941] from nothing and after time, 417. Things created from nothing have within themselves the necessity of not being, I, 792. The creation of heaven, earth, and the remaining elements is not distinguishable even by the slightest moment of operation, II, 432. Some created things have the administration of themselves, ibid. The sole cause of things to be made was God’s mercy, I, 544, 546. God founded created things not for His own benefit, but for that of creatures, 38. All efficacy in creating things resides in the Word, 691. The nature of things to be created did not come into existence through its own obedience to God’s Word, II, 83. All things were created through the Word, I, 336. What is peculiar to the creation of humankind, 336. For creatures other than humankind, some interval of time did not separate their beginning from their completion, 337. Creation belongs alike to the Father and the Son, II, 87. All things were created with the Father speaking and the Son acting, I, 645. God created all things in the Son, and afterward brought forth each one at will from the treasures laid up within Himself, 267. Which created things are always with God, II, 431. Which are begun and which unbegun, ibid., 432. They bear witness to the greatness of the Creator, I, 334. All the creations of the world bear witness to God’s magnificence through the unchanging ordinance of their respective functions, 351. There is nothing on earth besides humankind that perceives the fruit of its own kind, 335. All creatures rejoice in our salvation, for whose expectation they groaned together, 258. Why they await human blessedness, 644. How imperfect and weak created things are, II, 66. Religious worship of a creature is forbidden, 410. Creation was wine changed into water, II, 52. In what sense the only-begotten God may be understood as created, II, 461. **CRESCONIUS**, II, 667. The crime of impiety, II, 90. Christ’s cross set in the midst of the earth, I, 807. A Jew was unworthy to bear it, 807. What glory follows the crucified Christ, II, 55. The cross is His sitting together with God, 344. The scandal of the cross, I, 722. Its foolishness, 245. Its fruit, 246 ff., 720. The cross must be taken up at least in intention, 751. The vices of the flesh must be nailed to the cross, 376 ff., 720.

Repentance effaces the fault of ignorance, II, 702. **CUPAE**, II, 632. Desire for worldly things must be reproved by contempt for them, I, 688. The struggle of desire, 471. The slaughter of desires, 553. How desire spreads darkness, 606. Burning desire produces forgetfulness of God’s ordinances, 344. Strong desires are dangerous, I, 554. It is easier to tear them away when they break forth than to bend them back while pliant, ibid. The man of God who cuts off every desire, 384. How inward desires are frozen from without by self-restraint, 344. God’s utterances temper the fevers of unhealthy desires, 359. To break the desires of soul and body is the greatest gain of heavenly hope, 697. Let one who has attained perfection of his body not descend through desire, 789. See **Concupiscence**. All our concern ought to be not for present things but for future things, I, 688, 694. Let all concern be directed toward pleasing God, 690, 695. How curiosity does not fall upon one whose eyes are fixed upon God, I, 598. The chariot of God: the heavenly retinue obedient to God in harmonious concord, I, 226. The public post worn out, II, 661. The Jews had a spiritual guard, I, 123. A heavenly guard is sought for the Church, I, 123. The Lord’s keeping, by which believers departing from the body are preserved, I, 432. **CYPRIAN**, a man of holy memory, wrote on the Lord’s Prayer, I, 689. **CYRIACUS of Rimini**, II, 662, 649, note. **CYRIACUS the official**, II, 709. **CYROTUS of Roeo**, II, 665.

D
Demons: natures invisible to us and beyond comprehension, I, 189. They are called birds of the air, 702. They are signified by the name of foxes, 176. [They dwell] in the depth of the sea, 189. The means of life is generously granted to demons by God, 692. Demons flee the face of God in terror, but do not escape it, 215. They are tormented, torn, and burned by the words of believers, 189. At the mere laying on of our hands they groan aloud under their punishments, ibid. The torments and confessions of demons before the venerable bones of the martyrs, II, 567, ibid., note. The bellowing of punished demons, 376. They confess Christ to be the Son of God, 169. Demons rightly rule over us because of our vices, I, 548. Before the Law, the demon held the Israelites, 733. Driven out by the Law, it invaded the Gentiles, 733. When grace was granted to the Gentiles, it returned to the Jews, 733. Demons expelled from the Gentiles possess heretics, 704. Demons strive to weaken the most powerful works of our faith, 430. The power of demons is scattered by the splendor of God’s teaching, 615–616. The disgrace of demon-possession properly belongs to one alienated from God, 247. See Devil, Wickednesses, Powers. [Col. 0942]

**DANIEL**, II, 436. Aware of the times, 146.

**DARIUS**, I, 467, 635.

**DATHAN and ABIRON:** what benefit their punishment brought to their souls, I, 254, ibid., note.

**DAVID:** not without sin, I, 145. When he says that he is without iniquity, it is Christ’s utterance in him, 145. David is the name of Christ according to the flesh, 436, 510. What God promised David pertains to Christ, 506, 511. Christ’s coming is foretold under the name David, 501 ff. David, carrying out the judgments of the Law, does not understand them, I, 368. He almost fell away from faith, 346. His faith is not bounded by the ages, 316. David’s prerogatives according to lineage, grace, and mystery, 306. He performs more than the Law commands, 367. In keeping the Law, David reaches out toward those things prefigured in the Law, 316. His greatness in meditation on the beloved Law is as great as the whole day is in duration, 356. How he spiritually fulfills the Law, 291. He prays that he may behold the marvels of the Law, 292. He fulfills the Law through love, not fear, 406. Filled with the Holy Spirit, David neither thinks nor speaks common or earthly things, 289. David is in part the composer of the Psalms, 501. From the Latin titles it is uncertain whether he is author or merely occasion of a psalm, 611. David is indicated as author of a psalm that ought to be called Solomon’s, 472.

David’s life was always beset and full of dangers, I, 584. Though despised, he received the glory of king and prophet, 394. How he calls Christ’s glory or passion his own, 136. He prophesies through deeds in the Law, 727. By his actions he prophesies Christ, 600. By his sufferings he prophesies the Lord’s sufferings, 605, 128. He prophesied not so much by the Spirit as by his sufferings, 128. Not ignorant of the Lord’s Passion, he showed himself a prophet both by suffering and by speaking, 144. In the wilderness David was occupied solely with divine studies, 171. He is a prophet of Christ, who was to withdraw into the wilderness, 171. David was not ignorant of evangelical teaching, 107. An imitator of the Lord’s gentleness, 107. Through the likeness of his sufferings, a prophet of Christ’s Passion, 107–108. By his example as servant in faith and prophet he prefigured all the Lord’s words and deeds, 601.

David is at once in the Law and in the Gospels, I, 91. Whether consecrated under the Law or prepared for the glory of the Gospel, 407. As one conforming to God an evangelical and apostolic man, he was not ignorant of evangelical discourse, 407. [He was ignorant] neither of evangelical nor apostolic precepts, 287. [Nor] of manifold consummation, 354. He was a preacher of the Gospel, 341, and of the apostolic faith, 91. He himself was teacher, guardian, purifier, and judge both for himself and for all, 377. In himself he established for others a pattern of believing, acting, understanding, not knowing, hoping, and praying, 403. In Psalm 118 he brings the evangelical man to perfection through perfect observance of the Law, 403.

David shared evangelical hope and apostolic joy, I, 607. Certain that he was being prepared in conformity with God’s glory, 167. He hopes for eternal things, 91, 347, 374. His whole desire is directed toward heaven, 552. He longs to see God, 173, 325; and the Son of God, 173. He stretches his whole self toward the coming of Jesus, 412. His soul fails because of desire for Him, 343, 380. He seeks Him as his teacher, 330.

David does not become arrogant concerning his glory, I, 498. In what riches he rejoices, 286. His modesty, 326, 338, 342, 398, 399, 411. David was exceedingly humble although he had many grounds for pride, 366 ff. The modesty of humility kept him within evangelical discipline, 367. David does not attribute virtues peculiarly his own to merit, 378. Perfect in every work of goodness, he does not think this sufficient for salvation, 400. Though his body grows cold like a wineskin in frost, he does not yet trust in the firmness of his nature, 345. He prays that not glorious endowments but humility may be seen in him, 404. David bought the threshing-floor for the site of the Temple, I, 507. At midnight he rose to praise God, 328. He knew that thanksgiving must be given to God even in adversities, 331. His disposition toward sinners, 320. David asks not for vengeance on his enemies, but for their conversion, 341. He reserves vengeance for himself to God, 404. He gives no place to detraction, 167.

**Debt**, I, 431.

**DECIUS**, II, 564, 566, 567, 594.

**To turn aside:** what it means, I, 296, 456. The inclination to turn away from God follows vices; it does not precede them, 97.

**Failure of spirit:** whence it arises, I, 343. Failure of the soul is followed by failure of the eyes: what this means, 343.

**Bodily pleasure:** how it contaminates the soul, I, 172. How bodily sense ought to be imbued with the joys of the mind, 172.

**DEMOPHILUS**, II, 668, 680. He refused to condemn Arius’s heresy, 673. He explains the Sirmian creed to Liberius, 678.

**The teeth of sinners**, I, 140.

**To be assigned:** what it means, I, 613.

**Christ’s abandonment**, I, 808.

**Wilderness:** it must be understood as a place in which there is no dwelling of God, I, 722. The wilderness to which Christ withdrew after the resurrection, 121. Wastelands: the Gentiles, 220.

**To desire:** what should be desired most, I, 169. What we seem to desire for God, we desire for ourselves, 335. [Col. 0943]

**DESIDERIUS**, II, 647.

No place must be given to detraction, I, 367.

The duty of devotion must not fail amid temptations, I, 601.

The freedom of minds devoted to God, I, 780.

**GOD:** for what names He should be praised, I, 527. Through knowledge of God’s name we advance to knowledge of Him, 527. Names are fitted to divine things in accordance with an understanding of their nature, II, 64. Why knowledge of God ought to be desired, 3. To know God as not unknowable and yet inexpressible is perfect knowledge, 31. God is wholly an unfathomable depth, 404. A human being does not penetrate God’s secrets, I, 490. It is pious to investigate them, but one must confess them inscrutable, 491. The human mind fails in matters concerning God, II, 358. There is in God that which can be grasped, 359. Whoever wishes to see more in Him than he can see is blinded, 359. We can admire God according to what is in us, but cannot know Him according to what He Himself is, I, 621.

God is simple and must not be conceived in a human manner, II, 313. He must not be pursued by our understanding, but worshiped, 314. Hilary understands Him by veneration alone, 402. God’s power must not be measured by our mode of comprehension, 68. God’s deeds do not yield to the natural capacities of minds: why, 11. All His things are submerged in an incomprehensible depth, 403. How divine things ought to be considered after the Apostle’s example, 403. The form of a pious understanding in forming opinions about God, 403. How we understand God in natural things, 440. Human comparisons do not suffice for divine examples, 199. God is incomparable, I, 401. We are helped toward understanding Him by comparison with created things, 401. To what extent divine things are illuminated through bodily comparison, II, 200.

God is known only through Himself, II, 14. He cannot be understood except through God, 116–117. Knowledge of divine things must be drawn from divine teachings, 81; from God’s testimony concerning Himself, 200. Knowledge of God is in His works, I, 626. Those who appoint themselves judges of divine matters are reproved, II, 288. Diverse opinions of the ancients concerning God, 3; rejected, 4. Their various questions and opinions concerning God and divine matters, I, 165. How much more certain is the knowledge drawn from the sacred books, 166.

The infinite and immeasurable God cannot be understood or shown by the brief expressions of human speech, II, 497. It is impious to trust that one can set forth God’s nature in words, 402. Divine things are inexpressible, 71. One must speak of God only as He has spoken of Himself, 117. God’s matters must not be discussed according to human or worldly understanding, 198. Regarding them, no speech other than God’s has been left to us, 206. To what extent common speech may be used to express them, 72. For salvation it is sufficient to have believed what belongs to God; those who may not speak of Him as they please, 499.

God began to be manifested to the world through Moses, II, 127. How God’s name was unknown before Christ, 59. In former times God’s name was “God of Abraham, God of Isaac,” etc., I, 557; according to the Gospels, “Father of the only-begotten God,” 558. God has been manifested to us as Father; He was not manifested as Father in order that He might be shown to be God, II, 64.

What God is, I, 181. Those who would have God’s substance expand and contract are refuted, II, 490. Nothing is more fitting for God than that He should exceed whatever we can think, 5. We can render Him no greater or lesser service than to understand Him to be so great that He cannot be understood, though He can be believed, 7. God is most beautiful of all beauty, 6. His beauty can neither be explained in speech nor grasped by sense, 6.

Nothing is more proper to God than to be, II, 4. To Him alone belongs such being as is unmade, I, 577. Nothing is before Him, nothing from elsewhere, nothing outside Him, II, 405. The backward-reaching mind cannot grasp that, before what is proper to God—always to be—there is something else, 422. Whoever denies that God exists is judged foolish by common assent, I, 95. The pleasure of vices persuades one that God does not exist, while the necessity of truth compels one to confess that He does, 95. His splendid works testify that God exists, 533. God’s existence must be understood from what He accomplished under the Law, 198. No one fails to perceive God’s existence from contemplating the world, 95. Anyone looking upon heaven will perceive this, 198, 440.

God is not bodily according to our manner, I, 455. He is incorporeal, 492. Those who call Him corporeal because man was made in His image are refuted, 492. By the names of our bodily members is meant the power by which He effects what belongs to our members, 492. Another interpretation, II, 412. God’s members may be understood as angelic powers, I, 494. What God’s heart, hand, and eyes are, II, 413. God’s mouth, power, wisdom, arm, and image are Christ, I, 334.

God’s supreme simplicity, II, 141, 244. God is free from composition, I, 492; neither composed of composite things nor of inanimate things, II, 198; nor of obscure, weak, or unequal things, ibid. In God there are not parts but a whole; He is not made alive, but living, 306. The whole of what He is is one, 198. Everything in Him lives, 199. God distributes gifts in the Spirit, but is not divided in the gifts, I, 709. Whatever God is, God is wholly that, II, 141. In Him there is nothing but power, life, light, blessedness, and spirit, 141. The properties of the supremely simple God, 282. God teaches His whole self through His own things, 230. [Col. 0944]

God’s eternal immutability, I, 800 ff. God is not subject to change, I, 37; II, 314, 405. No sudden, novel undertaking can occur in God, I, 235. God, who knows no change, lost nothing of His substance when He became flesh, II, 491. When God’s Son was crucified, the Godhead did not undergo corruption, 491. God is such that, as He is, so He always is, I, 38. He is Himself; He is in Himself, with Himself, toward Himself, His own to Himself, and He Himself is all things to Himself, 38.

God’s simplicity and immensity, II, 230. God is everywhere, I, 455: wholly, always, and everywhere, 628; everywhere the same and whole, 400 ff., 493. How He is not in those who are corrupt, 401. Far from God are those far from knowledge of God, 198. God, being infinite, is diffused and infused throughout all things, II, 5. How He is diffused and transfused through all things, I, 545. God’s infinity exceeds all things, 623. There is no place without God and none not in God, II, 6. He is neither in some one thing nor absent from all things, 6. The error of those who confine God to a mountain or temple, 45. God is not enclosed by places, I, 468, 514. What are commonly called His houses, 467; what is the true one, 408. God’s dwelling is not visible heaven, 440, but the Son, 440, and, through the Son’s mediation, believers, 440. The common opinion about God’s seat is not excluded, namely, that the heaven of heavens is His throne, 441. God does not dwell in a habitation of a nature different from Himself, II, 100. All things are within God, and outside Him there is nothing capable of containing Him, 45. All things are in God; God is in Himself, 46. That God is all in all is our advancement, 406. What is infinite in God always withdraws itself from the repeated return of our finite understanding, 422.

God’s Wisdom teaches itself coeternal with the eternal things, II, 430.

God’s knowledge, II, 313. Why it is wonderful, I, 569. How it embraces all things, 235. Future things are to God as things already done, 436. To know future things is proper to Him, II, 306. Through knowledge of human nature, God foreknows human wills, I, 139. By foreknowing, He does not impose necessity, ibid. How awareness of our ignorance advances knowledge of God, II, 440. How God knows or does not know, I, 29 ff. God’s ignorance is not ignorance but mystery, II, 311. It is either a time for not speaking or an economy of not acting, 307. God’s knowing is not a change from ignorance, but the fullness of time, 307. God’s not knowing belongs rather to will than to nature, 309. God the Son is said not to know what He keeps silent, while the Father is said to know what He does not keep silent, 313. God questions either in order to grant pardon for sins or to render honor to faith, I, 419. Every seeing on God’s part belongs to the power of His nature, II, 188.

God’s power is signified by the right hand, I, 175. It belongs to God alone to command His own power, 234. God’s power and wisdom are Christ, in whom He can do all things and can do them wisely, II, 419. God’s hand is Christ as God, I, 616. To God alone belongs to do all that He wills, 530. God is not subject to the laws of nature, II, 314. He must be believed able to do all things, 53, 314. Human law cannot regulate God’s powers, 369. What is unintelligible to man is possible to God, 49, 60. Whatever is done wonderfully through human beings belongs to God, I, 543.

God’s power manifests itself surely in deeds whose reason remains hidden from us, II, 52. Works testify to God’s greatness, I, 560. The majesty of God is shown terrible through the dignity of His works, 197. We bear witness to God’s power and mercy by hope and fear, 639. God’s works are effected powerfully, 623. They bring us not merely wonder but benefit also, 623.

God lacks nothing, I, 38; II, 404. Nothing is lacking to Him, nothing is added to Him, 402. How nothing is added to Him when He is glorified by us, I, 263; II, 57. What we appear to desire for God, we desire for ourselves, I, 535. God must be worshiped for our cause rather than His own, II, 539. God’s holiness needs nothing except that another should avail himself of it, I, 624. It is full of sweet terror and terrible sweetness, 624 ff. God has no need of created things, 38. He created creatures not for His own benefit but for that of the creatures, 38. God’s mercy alone was the cause of creating things, 544, 546. In creating things, nothing is new or sudden to God, II, 431. God did not create the body of this universe through parts of thought, 431. Nothing has not always been with God, 431. Things that began to be created were not begun with respect either to God’s knowledge or to His power, 431. God made future things, I, 235: things which, in view of His knowledge and power, are done for Him, 581.

God’s providence, I, 636. Neglect of the things He created is unworthy of God, II, 4. God, author of all things, does not cease to work, I, 266, and does so without any labor, 266. God’s various miracles in governing the world, 530. Many deny that God cares for human actions, 622, lest they leave the Creator any judgment concerning life lived rightly or criminally, 20. They are refuted, 181. God’s perpetual providence toward the Church, 469.

God’s holiness does not withdraw itself from human aids, I, 627. God’s various regard for human beings, 96. How the incorporeal God turns or turns away His eyes toward us, I, 200. God looks in order to punish, 388; to terrify, ibid.; to pity, 388. This gaze must be earned by innocence, 388. As God looks toward punishment and mercy, so He inclines His face toward each, 390. [Col. 0945]

God knows nothing other than to be love, II, 305. In Him there is nothing but good and eternal things, I, 429. God can do nothing except according to His Word, and therefore nothing except good, 295. He cannot be charged with either injustice or malicious will, 113. He does not stir up evils out of malevolence, ibid. From our birth we learn that God is good, II, 147. The creation of the world shows Him wise, 147. God did not begin us for the origin of evil, 145. It is contrary to His goodness that He should have begotten us for injury or pain, I, 392. God’s kindness and benefits toward the Israelites, 536. God would have wished His people not to be judged, 536. God’s sweetness is always open to all on equal terms: why the wicked do not receive it, 624.

We need God’s kindness, I, 527. God is not an excessively harsh judge, but takes account of human weakness, 605. God’s goodness toward those who fall through weakness, 99. God should be praised especially for mercy, 626; why, 626. God’s mercy and patience, 330, 486, 626. God’s justice does not fail through mercy, 625. God’s goodness and severity must both be considered, 326. Justice regulates God’s goodness in the manner of using it, not of granting it, 624. God wills both our salvation and the condemnation, according to the established law, of those who sin, 717. According to the diversity of faith, He is nearer or farther from each person, 560. He is holy to the holy and turned away from the perverse, according to each person’s conduct, 429. God is a consuming fire to sinners and light to believers, 326. Though not considered by impious persons acting unjustly, He will turn evils back against them, 112.

By what words God’s severity is customarily expressed in Scripture, I, 232. Divine vengeance is expressed after the model of human vengeance, 232. What is meant by wrath, 40. It does not arise from a sudden movement, 40. How it is now restrained toward sinners, 41 ff. The words of an angry God, now tempered by kindness, invite repentance, 41 ff. How God, though angry, has mercy, 155. Faith confesses God just even when He punishes, 391. How God maintains justice and mercy in punishment, 626. He does not hand us over to vices, 428. When He abandons us as we abandon Him, He is said to hand us over, 428.

God has spoken of Himself according to the capacity of human nature, II, 84, 144, 244. God’s saying must be understood only as it has been spoken, 143. God’s language must be interpreted according to the usage of our speech, I, 262. What it means that God remembers His word, 319. God’s repentance, 650. Sleep, wakefulness, forgetfulness, and the like are attributed to God according to the difference in our merits, 615. God, who is free from sleep, wakes or sleeps in us according to our faith, 429.

God is invisible to bodily eyes, I, 325, and cannot be seen in this life, 325. Who is invisible, and who was seen upon earth, II, 101. David ardently desired the vision of God, I, 172. God could not become known to humankind except by assuming humanity, 614. He became human while the nature of His divinity remained intact, II, 325. In a human being He came to Jacob and Abraham, 94. In a human being He was understood and seen by Jacob, I, 150. Isaiah saw God and saw none other than the Son, II, 125. No one affirms that God the Father has been seen, 126. God the Father, seen or heard by no one, is seen or heard in the Son, 296. Formerly God was heard through prophecy; now He must be contemplated through the confidence of faith, I, 440. The unclean cannot endure God’s presence, 681. All who are pure in heart shall see God, 326. Those who see God receive all their glory from beholding His glory, 326. How we receive the light of the God who sees us, 390 ff. How God’s rest is in the saints, I, 514. How God inhabits the minds of the pious, 504.

To God alone belongs to have risen from the dead through Himself, II, 184.

There is only one God, II, 4. The Church recognizes no multitude of gods, I, 529. The God of the Law and of the Gospel is the same, 219, 558; likewise the God who gave the Law and of the universe, 636. How deceitfully the Arians profess one God, II, 103. One does not preach one God piously who preaches Him as solitary, 177. God is one for us, not alone, I, 442; not solitary, II, 484, 489; not unique, 241, 242, 246. God is one not in person but in nature, 501. One must confess neither union nor non-unity in God, 175. Moses and the Gospels testify to God and God, 105. The distinction between God commanding and God acting, 84, note; ibid., Equality, 87. Faith does not permit two true gods to be believed, 279. Why faith does not acknowledge the Father and the Son as two gods, 201 ff., 210.

God’s unity does not prejudice the Son’s deity, II, 82. With faith in the one God unimpaired, we confess the Son to be God, 128, 185. The Son and Father are one God, 95: not by union, but by property, 374. In our faith both are one, not one person, 13. How God’s unity remains with the Son’s generation, 278. God’s unity does not permit God’s Son to be unbegotten, 496. Because there is one unbegotten God, what belongs to the only-begotten God—that He is God—cannot be taken from Him, I, 443. Not because the one has been divided into two, 443. God is one because there are not two unbegotten beings nor two only-begotten beings, but one from one, and both one, 443. Father and Son are not each the same one, because the nature of begetting—not mere naming—made Father and Son, 443.

Only birth is believed equal to God, II, 197. He does not grasp the one true God who does not first confess Father and Son, 126. The true and one God exists in Father and Son subsisting, 106. God is one for us in the names and persons of Father and Son, 642. For no other reason has the hatred of Jews, Gentiles, and heretics been aroused against us, 642. The Arians at Sirmium determine that God the Father is greater than the Son, 464, and that He alone knows the Son’s birth, 465. God the Father is greater insofar as He is Father; but the Son, insofar as He is Son, is not lesser, 302, 499. God falls away from unity if He has something equal that is outside Him, 197. Those who deny that God was always Father are refuted, 427. God cannot be understood as a temporal Father, 475.

The Arians, so far as lies in them, destroy the essence of God the Father, 473. It was an advancement of dignity to have begotten power, not an alienation of nature, 197. The property of God the Father, II, 421; the property of God the Son, 421. Father is distinguished from Son solely by unbegottenness, 491. Apart from the cause of origin, birth differs in no respect from unbegottenness, 481. God is the principle for the Son, from whom all things receive their principle, 496. God is never without His Wisdom, Power, and Word, 439.

The unity of God the Father and God the Son must not be conceived in a human manner, II, 285. What it is like, 243. The essence of God the Father and God the Son is signified by the name life, I, 468; II, 472. Whence the one essence of both is demonstrated, 469. The nature of God the Father and Son is one, 226, 395; their Spirit one, 228; their power the same, 504. As the name of deity and nature is indivisible in Son and Father, so is power, I, 110. God the Father and Son have one work, II, 292; the same knowledge and will, 315. The will is the same with respect to nature, but is distinguished with respect to the signification of birth, 316. The Son differs from the Father neither in substance nor in time, 488. The substance of deity in Father and Son differs neither in kind nor in will, I, 513. As they are one in the name of essence, so also in kind, II, 484, 489, 493. The unity of Son and Father is in nature, I, 169; in power, 170. Both must be confessed as one, yet they must not be understood as one person, though both are one, 170. In the Son of God, power is either received or born, 170. The unity of God the Father and Son is proved from this: the Holy Spirit receives from both, II, 227. The Son is equal to the Father because the Holy Spirit receives from Him as from the Father, 315. Creation and our reconciliation belong to both, 249.

If the one God the Father does not permit Christ to be God, He is not permitted to be Lord, because Christ is the one Lord, II, 239, 242. God the Father and Christ the Lord are one Spirit, but not a singular Spirit, 235 ff., 239. They cannot be separated from one another in nature, Spirit, and power, 241. He who is in another cannot be dissolved from Him in whom He is, 129.

God the Father and Son mutually signify one another, II, 324. God the Word is known more as already being with God in the beginning than as being born, 475. How God is in God, 146. The Father’s and Son’s nature is mutual and mutually alike, 499. How they are mutually in one another, 201–202; how they are in themselves, 51, 207, 209, 298. The Son is the living image of the Father, in whom God’s form is naturally sealed, 324. Father and Son are each as a mirror of the other, 312. The Father will appear in the Son to one appearing to the Son or received by the Son, I, 173. By likeness of substance and property of nature, one is in the other, 621. Nothing can be like God unless it is from Him, II, 65. God the only-begotten is equal in all things to God the Father through the fullness of true divinity in Himself, 421. God the Father has His whole self in Him whose Father He is, 306.

After the final judgment, even the unwilling will understand the one God, I, 647. The Church’s faith concerning God the Father and His Son, II, 74. Hilary’s faith, 499. The Arians’ doctrine, 72. What is to be believed simply concerning the Son and the Holy Spirit, 444.

God must not be worshiped for His solitude, II, 146. God is Father only to those who honor the Son, 155. Equal veneration of God the Father and Son is imposed upon us, 412. The Son is praised in the Father, and the Father in the Son, I, 621. God must be praised by public and constant preaching, 202. Why He should be praised, 202. Every word and understanding ought to speak of God, II, 24. There is no limit to exalting God, I, 137. This is signified when He is said to be exalted above the heavens, ibid. When the Law has ceased, God must be honored with praises from a living and intelligent sacrifice, 174. God receives honor from us only through God, II, 116.

Many praise God from His works; few believe that He will be their king, I, 622. Dominion over the base and degenerate is unworthy of God, 542. The manner of intelligently seeking God, and the fewness of those who seek Him, 96. Rare is the person who dares call God his own, 353. Who would dare this, ibid.? To call God one’s own belongs to the saints, I, 387; it is also proper to the Son of God, 587. The God of Patriarchs and Prophets belongs to the Apostles as an inheritance of succession, 324. God is Father of all: in a proper and common sense, He is Christ’s Father, II, 384. God has no Father; He is Father to the Son, but to us Father and Son, II, 97.

Not all things now serve God, I, 351. God’s consolation for lost Israel is the faithful people, 536. God is preached among almost all nations, 237. God’s name is holy among all nations, 559. God cannot be exalted unless He has first descended, 135.

By nature God is only one; there are many gods by designation, II, 483. Human beings are gods by designation, I, 529; the blessed [are gods], 542. The name God is appointed to every saint through the gift of eternity, II, 596. Who the many gods in heaven and on earth are, I, 542. The gods in heaven are angels, 530. The heathen invented very many gods, I, 197. From the multitude of God’s powers, they falsely feigned the worship of names in false gods, 197. They are reduced to one, 198. God’s honor is transferred to elements which each person chooses for himself, 645. False gods arise from the elements of the world, from names of kings, and from the world’s error, 605. The names of heroes, the created elements, and materials of metals were thought to be gods, 201. The gods of the Gentiles are subjected to punishment by the power of believers, 189. Their temples fell silent after Christ was preached, 189. They had sounded somewhat before, 189. Servants of the Gentile gods, 442. How stubborn they are in error, 441.

By the name “right hand,” Scripture indicates the better part, I, 430. The right hand signifies power, 560. God’s right hand: God’s power, 175.

**Devil:** a pirate, II, 711. In a moment of time he traverses the whole world, I, 278. The Devil’s dwelling is the world, 85; his ministries and offices are in this world, 431. Pharaoh is a figure of the Devil, 534. The defeat of the Devil and his followers is prefigured in Pharaoh’s destruction, 223. How the Devil slanders, 380. How he now disturbs Christ’s kingdom together with his own followers, 200. He is author of all iniquities, 599. Every unbelief is the Devil’s work, 750. Our enemy, stationed on watch, always lies in ambush for us, 179. It is sweet to him that we sin, so that he may glory in the evidence of our sins, 278. The Devil supplies incentives to our vices, 278. He incites us to sin and accuses sinners, 279.

The Devil’s diverse temptations, I, 379. His arms and warfare, 730. His teeth are anger, cupidity, and the like, 450. The Devil and his angels continually spread snares for us, 368. The Devil’s temptations rage especially against saints, 677: why, ibid. His hatred and warfare against the righteous, 353. How a way is prepared for the Devil into us, 698. How he attempts to kindle the twofold desire, 345. What the Devil’s assaults effect in those filled with God and those empty of Him, 449. The Devil’s house is the sinner, 378. How a person is handed over to him, 378. The Devil binds us with cords of vices, 328. He especially sets traps through human beings, 585. He employs human agency to inflict injuries upon pious people, 484. While citing Scripture, he is silent about what is against himself, 678. He insinuates false interpretation into the imprudent, 382.

The Devil tries to test Christ’s deity and break His patience, I, 678. He suspected, but did not know, that Christ was God, 677. It was fitting for his wickedness that he should be conquered in a human being, 677. Through Judas and the Jews, the Devil persecuted Christ, 605. Christ suffered under that ruler, 590. In “Satan” the Devil hears the name of his crimes, 679. He was bound when Satan was named by the Lord, 730.

Diabolical powers, the strongest enemies, I, 614. Why and how they are mountains, 188, 614, 754, 774. These mountains have already been crushed by Christ, enveloped in the smoke of eternal fire, and thus prepared for the punishments of eternal judgment, 188. The Devil smokes; he is not yet wholly burned, 615. He is being prepared for vengeance, 615. The Devil’s power was shattered by the Lord’s coming, 615. The Devil is, however, subject to the faith of the saints, 615. Now, when he strives to harm, he is conquered, II, 711. Yet he still has very great strength, I, 615. God willed the Devil to be conquered not only through Christ but also through the disciples, 803. Whoever has crushed him and subjected his soul to faith is perfectly holy, 345. When the Devil has been conquered, the ministries of angels are not lacking to us, 679. The Devil possesses only those whom God abandons, 428; only those handed over to him when God has departed, 379. He is handed over to the Devil who is cut off from the Church, 379.

A deacon baptizing performs an apostolic office, I, 237.

**Diapsalma:** what it is, I, 14, ibid., note. By the intervention of a diapsalma, the person addressed changes, 112. The diapsalma changes the sense, 122. It indicates a change of sense and person, 201, 206. [Sometimes it occurs] without a change of person or sense, 134.

The rationale of what is said must be understood from the sense of the thing being said, II, 45.

**DIDIMION**, II, 693.

**Didrachma**, I, 756.

Difficulty arises from weakness, II, 314.

The dignity of a name lies in preserving the purpose of the will, I, 218.

Enlargement of the heart, I, 303.

Love is commended, I, 394. Why loving is more than doing, 383. Love is customarily preferred to love by comparison, 28. The proper duty of love, 476. Love’s activity is outside the necessity of fear, 406. It belongs to love to cut off both the use and the will of vices, 408. Love of God without Christ, or of Christ without God, cannot be useful, 782. Everything commanded in the Law is comprised in love of neighbor, 409. What perfect love is, 383.

The Son of God washed away the world’s first crimes in the flood, I, 182.

**Diocletianopolis**, II, 632.

Those who go barefoot were unknown to Hilary, I, 712.

Many examples and figures of the distinction between good and evil, I, 792, 794, 808.

With what fervor discipline should be embraced, I, 58.

Christ’s disciples were restrained by favor toward Israel, I, 761.

How destructive are the disputations of the impious, I, 167.

Heretics evade the point at issue in disputation, I, 20.

The guilt of crafty dissimulation, II, 461.

Division through faith or through the future judgment, I, 157.

In what things riches consist, I, 286. No one can be rich in the Lord except through contempt for and poverty in respect of the world, 287. Heavenly riches are possessed only at the cost of the world, 736. The allurements and vanity of riches, 169. Those who lack them ought not to covet them, and those who have them ought to withdraw their will from them, 169. One must beware lest riches, once desired, rule, ibid. Care for riches is dangerous, 764. The fault lies not in possessing but in the manner of possession, 763.

Wealth makes the rich insolent rather than vainly [so], I, 90. Trust in riches especially turns away the fear of God, 90. The rich ought to be more religious, 90. Their avarice is inexcusable, 90. How one may use riches after death, 90. Exchange between rich and poor, 794.

**Docimo**, II, 665.

David seeks for himself not an earthly teacher but Christ, I, 330. The Father teaches when the Son is heard, II, 296. Every age has been instructed by God’s teachings, I, 402. The manifold teaching of Scripture, 540. Teaching is indicated by the name of sitting and chair, I, 566. It is best to teach by example rather than words, 696. It is not enough to have taught what is right unless impious doctrines are refuted, II, 215. Apostolic and prophetic teachings are arrows, I, 473. Apostolic teaching and the teaching of the saints are signified by clouds, 532. How the teaching of God’s kingdom is a rod, 51. And
seq. To whom the understanding of heavenly doctrine is open, 387. Iniquity does not receive the truth of heavenly doctrine, 346. In order that a person may be capable of God’s teaching, sins must first be confessed to Him, 296. There will be no knowledge of God’s teaching unless faithful works have preceded it, 287. Teaching according to preference rather than reason, II, 321. Sound teaching goes into exile together with its preachers, II, 323. **DOEC**, a traitor, a figure of the Jews, I, 80. **DOLICEUS**, II, 664. Whence pain is felt, II, 329, 344. How it is warded off by the power of faith and by desire for glory, 353. Why the only-begotten God was not injured by the sensation of pain in the Passion, I, 114. Hilary perceived that pain befell Christ, 141, note. The pain of Christ’s wounds, 254, 255. **DOMINIANUS**, II, 631. He is lord who does not serve the flesh, I, 543. Sunday possesses the feast of the perfect Sabbath, I, 9. On Sunday one must neither fast nor worship prostrate with one’s body upon the ground, I, 8. **Dominicum**, meaning the Church, II, 540. **DOMINIUS**, II, 666. Houses of God are commonly called temples, I, 467 ff. God is not enclosed within houses made of buildings, ibid. The house of the Lord is spiritual, 433. The house of the Lord is the house of unanimity, 437. It is the house of one mind, faith, and charity, 437. No virtue exists for the house of God without peace, 438. Holiness, justice, and human self-restraint are a house and temple for God, I, 468. To be the house of God is greater than to be the city of the Lord, 438. The house of God, the Church, I, 186. It is one and yet many, 469. The stones of this house, 434. Its foundation, construction, and adornments, 468. The Apostles possess the keys of the house of God, 434. Those who preserve unity are joined to this same house, 434. Sinners have no share in this holy house, 434. The goods of God’s house are gifts given to it by Christ, 486. Some goods are complete and perfect, 186. The house of God: a human being assumed by the Son of God, I, 187. Its goods are virtue, glory, and eternity, 187. The house of God: the body of each believer, I, 187. The house of God: body and soul, I, 469. In its building human skill fails, 470. The one builder of that perfect edifice is Christ, 469. A spacious dwelling is required for the inconceivable God, I, 317. All things are difficult and constricted when we are unworthy of the indwelling of the divine Word, 317. How difficult it is to guard against domestic slanders, I, 389. They are accustomed to bring about the ruin of faith, 390. **DONATUS of Carthage**, II, 647. Precious gifts are those which commend charity, II, 163. God distributes gifts in the Spirit, but is not divided among the gifts, I, 709. The Apostle teaches that spiritual gifts must be used humbly, because he declares that they have been given for usefulness, 365. God’s gifts include even those things to which our own industry appears capable of attaining, 446. See **Gift** (*Munus*). **Dorlani**, II, 665. What is the difference between dozing and sleep? I, 301. God’s sleep within us, I, 429. **Dui**, II, 633. A guide is necessary for us on the way of God’s commandments, I, 308. **DUCES**, II, 651, 661.

## E

The wretchedness of drunkenness is vividly portrayed, I, 459. The relation between drunkenness and spiritual abundance is explained, 191, 192. By the name Zion the Church is signified, I, 184. By this name is understood either the Church that now exists or that of the saints which will be, 520. The Church, not carnal Israel, is to dwell in Zion, 260. The Church is the mountain of the Lord, 452, 454; the house of God, 186, 436; Christ’s mouth, 576; Christ’s body, 487; Christ’s bride, 480. Whoever hates her hates Christ, 487. The Church is prefigured in the daughter of the Canaanite woman, 744; in the Ninevites and the Queen of the South, 434. She is like a ship, 702, 705, 734, 747. How God has provided for her from the beginning of the age, 469. He has provided for her entire lifetime, 402. God’s care is set forth through the four watches, 742.

How the Church was formerly deserted but is now inhabited, I, 121 and following. Rachel bore the type of the Church, long barren and later fruitful, 672. In Ephraim and Manasseh the Church’s precedence over the synagogue is prefigured, 158. The Church, widow of the Law, is lawfully joined to Christ, 515. The Church is formed from an assembly of peoples, 260. She began with Christ, 508. The Church, that is, the Lord in the body, 454; that is, Christ’s body, 687. She is the city of the great King, ibid. The Church is Christ, containing her entire self within himself through the sacrament of his body, 460. The ark was a figure of the Church, I, 638. All are invited into it; few enter, 702. The inhabitants of the Church are spiritual, 450.

The unity of the Church, II, 162. How the body of the Church is one, I, 434. The Church, established by the Lord and confirmed by the Apostles, is one, II, 177. The Church alone bestows blessings, I, 522. Through the Church one ascends to the heavenly Jerusalem, 523. There is no road to heaven except through the Church, 71. Only the vows of ecclesiastical religion are useful, 184. Those outside the Church cannot understand the word of God, 734. Outside the Church there is no rest, 638. The peace and unity of the Church grants us strength and unity, 437. By the fact that she alone is one, the Church refutes all heresies, II, 178. Sabellius, Ebion, and Arius, in overcoming one another, overcome the Church, 16. The Church’s triumph over all heretics is their victory over one another, 178, 180. This is proper to the Church: that she conquers when she is injured, is understood when she is accused, and prevails when she is deserted, 177.

The Church’s teaching flowed from the beginnings of the Law, I, 233. The Church’s knowledge comes not from herself but from her Lord, II, 139. Mysteries formerly hidden were revealed to her by the Father, I, 576. The Church did not receive from God authority to depart from ancestral tradition, II, 660. One must use caution lest the Church which calls itself Catholic deceive, I, 713. Churches are shipwrecked in which the word of God does not keep watch, 703. That is not the Church which denies that Christ is the Son of God, II, 162.

The Church is one and many throughout the whole world, I, 70, 509. From the one Church of the Apostles there are many churches, 509. Churches deriving their origins from the Apostles are their sees of primacy, 580. The gathering of the Church is God’s inheritance, 222. The Church is founded throughout the world, 580; numerous throughout the world, 581. It was not founded by human votes, II, 594. Hilary [Col. 0950] groans that it must be sought out, II, 595. The Church’s growth in Hilary’s time, I, 228.

The Church would have everyone remain with and within herself, II, 177. What benefit heretics who depart from her bring her, 177. Sinners separate themselves from the body of the Church, I, 434. Those rejected by the Church are handed over to the devil’s dominion, 379. Those outside the Church become the dwelling-place of false prophets and demons, 702. The Church is comprehended in four orders, 538. The confusion of a Church embracing both clean and unclean, 810. Those who remain in the Church while not observing the Church’s discipline, 21. The avarice and luxury of Church ministers are censured, 101.

The Lord is governor of the churches, II, 622. Leaders are patriarchs, prophets, and apostles, I, 193. Towers are princes, 438, and likewise all who love God, 438. The three columns are Peter, James, and John, II, 149. The eyes are apostles and priests, I, 578. The Church is by nature dark in its remaining members, 578. The lowest members of the Church, 576. The Church’s distress in the time of Antichrist, I, 742; she is called by Christ, 742. The Church mourns not the slain Innocents but their slayers, 672. The Church’s hymns are public and victorious voices in the divine offices, praising God, 196. Charters of churches, II, 597.

What the heavenly Church is, I, 514. The Church is now the heavenly Jerusalem, 454. Churches which the enclosing walls of buildings contain for the secret—or sacred—religion of the sacraments are customarily called houses of God, I, 468. Constant dwelling in churches is the greatest step toward heavenly things, 70. Many attend church because they are ashamed to have their absence reproved, 356. The evil veneration of the Church of God in roofs and buildings, II, 600. To Hilary mountains, forests, lakes, and so forth are safer, ibid.

**ECCLESIASTICUS**, I, 21, ibid., note. Among Latins it is regarded as Solomon’s; among Greeks and Hebrews, as the Wisdom of Sirach, 594. It is called the Book of Solomon, 594, 700. Easterners regard it as the Lord’s utterance, II, 661.

**ECDICIUS**, II, 693.

**EDDESIUS**, II, 666.

Edicts of Constantius, II, 569, 570.

Good elevation of mind, I, 498; it must be tempered by humility of heart, 498.

The election of the faithful is set above the multitude of the unfaithful, 717. Abraham is the chief of the election, 528. Jacob is third in the election, 528.

The precept and merit of almsgiving, I, 688. The fruit of almsgiving, 794. Alms are plainly the embassies of human treasures, ambitious before God, 90.

The elements are greatest according to popular opinion, I, 684. Distinction between the elements of the world and of Christ, II, 252. **ELEUSIUS** is excepted from the company of heretics, II, 498.

Hilary greatly fears entrusting the blasphemies of the Arians to letters, II, 599.

Error among the many is difficult to cure, II, 132, especially error arising from a will toward impiety, 143. God will moderate the penalty for error committed in ignorance, 133.

What an uttered word is, I, 412.

Food incorruptible and eternal, I, 547.

To be is proper to God, II, 422.

What it means to empty power, II, 394. Christ’s emptying from the form of God was not the destruction of the divine nature, I, 256. Why, ibid.

**EVAGRIUS**, II, 632, 680.

All saints and prophets desired the evangelical age, I, 234. Its coming was foretold when the Law had been dissolved, 382. We are instructed in evangelical doctrine through men of the ancient Law, 402. The term “evangelical men under the Law,” 358. The evangelical man is shaped throughout Psalm CXVIII, 355. How prophetic sayings are explained by the Gospels, 387. The Gospels sometimes seem to conflict with one another to those who do not understand them, II, 512. They mutually supply one another’s fullness, 350. They are of one Spirit, 350. An inner meaning underlies the events of the Gospels, I, 738. The Law does not receive the Gospels, 705. Evangelical liberty, I, 367 and following. The immutability of evangelical teaching, I, 509. How greatly God’s power shone forth in the preaching of the Gospel, II, 594. To whom the power of receiving evangelical teaching is extended, I, 776. These are free from the guilt of unbelief because they could not obey it, 776. **Eucharist.** Christ, who was to shed the blood of his body for the remission of sins, consecrated it, I, 802. Christ gives thanks that he is transformed into evangelical food, 740. When the apostles had not yet been granted the power to make and minister the heavenly bread, 740. The same giver of heavenly bread to us had granted manna to the Jews, 220. The one bread which we taste on earth is that which we shall taste in heaven, [Col. 0952] 478, ibid., note. The sacrament of heavenly bread is received in faith in the resurrection, 707. From the altar the true blood of Christ is received, II, 571, ibid., note. We receive Christ’s flesh assumed from the Virgin, 332, note. We partake of food whose power is that, being itself alive, it gives life to others, I, 481. We truly receive the Word’s flesh as the Lord’s food, II, 222, 223. We truly receive under the mystery the flesh of Christ’s body, 223. Christ has mingled the nature of flesh with the nature of divinity in the sacrament of flesh to be communicated, 222. Through the mystery of the sacraments Christ remains naturally in us, 224. As he lives through the Father, so through his flesh we live, 225. We live naturally through him according to the flesh, 225. This is the reason for our life: that, though fleshly, we have Christ abiding in us through flesh, 225. Abiding bodily, 225. Christ’s flesh received and his blood drunk bring it about that we are in him and he in us, 223. What does God desire so much as that Christ should dwell in us daily? 714. The consecrated body of the Lord suspended around priests’ necks, 653. The sacraments of our salvation cast down, 634. Hands were violently laid upon Christ himself, 571, ibid., note. See **Communion**.

**EUDEMON**, II, 667. See 666. He refused to condemn the heresy of Arius, 674.

**EUDOXIUS**, II, 665, 680. His blasphemies publicly recited, 573 and following.

*Euge, euge* is the cry of mockers, I, 262.

**EUGEUS**, II, 665.

Two **Eusebii** among the principal Arians, II, 538.

**EUSEBIUS of Dorlani**, II, 665.

**EUSEBIUS of Mignenia**, II, 666.

**EUSEBIUS of Nicomedia**, II, 627.

**EUSEBIUS of Pergamum**, II, 665, 666.

**EUSTACIUS of Epiph[ania]**, II, 665.

**EUSTASIUS**, I, 663.

**EUTERIUS**, II, 632.

**EUTERIUS**, II, 632.

**EUTHEMON**, II, 666.

**EUTHITIUS**, II, 633, 647.

**EUTICIUS**, II, 668.

God examines in order to test and purify, not to know those who are his, I, 203.

Whether excommunication is effective against the dead, II, 582. See **Anathema** and **Communion**.

Excuses of the perverse heart, I, 594.

“To shake off” conveys a curse, I, 474.

An example is sought in difficult matters, I, 447. Teaching by example rather than words is best, 696. Examples drawn from bodily things are empty in comparison with God, II, 311.

Exercise, I, 119. The necessity of exercise, 287.

The self-emptying of God in Christ is very fully explained, I, 243; II, 405, 412.

What it means to go forth from God, II, 155, 156. How suitable the term “going forth” is for signifying the Word’s birth, 159, 280.

What Exodus means, I, 303.

## F
Face, image, form, and countenance do not differ, I, 257. The face of God is Christ, 607. Likewise, the judgment of God, 215. How demons flee the face of God and yet do not escape it, 215. How the face of God enlightens us, 390. The face of Christ: the glory of divinity, I, 511 [Col. 0953]. What Christ’s hunger was like, I, 677, ibid., note. How ruinous familiarity with the wicked is, I, 373. The Pharisaean city, II, 697, 700. The books on the Holy Spirit attributed to Paschasius, together with most of the homilies of Pseudo-Eusebius of Gaul, are ascribed to Faustus of Riez, II, 513, note. Description of earthly happiness, I, 619. Beastly happiness consists in leisure and wealth, II, 1. Very many have rejected this in themselves and reproved it in others, 2. Happiness awaited by the faithful, I, 433. The blessed harmony of eternal happiness, 431. Prefigured for the people Israel in the wilderness, 431. See *Blessedness*. Woman: the more beautiful form of the human body, as they suppose, I, 383. She is adorned with jewels, to the affront of nature, 383. The encounters of wanton women in the women’s quarters, snares for the eyes of the continent, 327. Garments do not fall over the face of women suspended by the feet, II, 567, ibid., note. In what form women will rise again, I, 781. Ardor in God’s service, I, 58. How the fig tree blossoms differently from the nature and condition of other trees, I, 774. The faithful are signified by willows, I, 550. How they are children, 757. The faithful’s natural unity through the nature of the one faith, II, 218. Their wise foolishness, 66 ff. Their right over the devil, I, 774. The faithful are of four orders, 538. The faithful people consoles God concerning lost Israel, 536. The faithful are exposed to persecution, I, 444. They grieve over the sins of persecutors, 444. God alone can then help them, 444. What consolation believers have when they cannot utter their faith as they wish, II, 499. The faithful in Christ are already filled with God, 263 ff. They dwell in Christ’s body as sharers in the Lord’s flesh, I, 86. If they lack the fruits of their faith, they will be uprooted, 87. Some stand midway between faithful and faithless, 28. These cannot be what they call themselves, 28. They will be judged, 28.

Faith, hope, and charity are commended, II, 617. Those three either will not be changed at all from without, or will acquire more abundantly than they possess, 617. The faith of the world is to believe only what it can comprehend, 251. The Arians entrust faith to human choice, 461. Faith must be entered upon not by our choice but by the force of what has been said, 203. It is not left to the uncertain pursuits of human intellect, 373. It is unchangeable, 373. One, 373. The same among the ancients and among us, 375. Abraham is the prince of our faith, I, 479. Each person is a son of Abraham by faith, 674, 675. Under the Law, the people were cleansed by faith through sprinkling with blood, 108. When faith of heart ceased, it performed all the sacraments of the Law through deceitfulness of mouth, 108. Sight did not prevent faith from remaining in Jacob, II, 115. David’s faith is not bounded by the ages, I, 316. The time of faith for Gentiles and Jews, I, 715. Christ awaited the first fruits of faith from Israel, 745; the rest were to be saved through the preaching of the Apostles, ibid. The one immovable foundation of faith, II, 40. Alas, earthly votes commend divine faith, 594.

The office of faith, II, 34. Faith is an office of soul and heart, I, 205. The necessity of faith in matters concerning God, II, 13, 14. Only that is rightly believed about God for which he himself is our author and witness, 68. Faith’s acceptance is not to be questioned but followed, I, 702. God must be believed in all things as they have been spoken by him, II, 61. Human reasoning must not be heard against God’s testimony, 144. Nothing is more just than faith, 369. The authority of the Lord’s word alone establishes the necessity of belief, 250. Yet the Lord has instructed our understanding as suitably as he could, 250. The holiness of works confirms faith in God’s words, I, 627. Faith should precede understanding, not follow it, II, 9. How faith precedes, rather than follows, understanding, 9. Faith, the harbour of our religion, II, 368. Simple faith is pre-eminent for salvation, 449. Faith is religious where there is also a natural lack of knowledge, 440. The greatest reward of faith is to hope for what one does not know, 219. How faith is not endangered by error arising from ignorance, 204. How awareness of our ignorance advances us, 440.

Faith may seek a demonstration of the thing believed, II, 204. Faith possesses rational knowledge, 15. Who supplies reasoning where faith lacks it, 419. From what source it draws its knowledge, 419. How dangerous philosophical sophistries are to simple faith, 418. Why an account of our faith must be rendered, 147. It is not enough to assert faith unless objections are also refuted, 18. The faith of the Arians is not knowledge but accusation, II, 192. Their fault: they do not believe what they understand, or they corrupt the understanding required for belief, 219. The merit of faith, II, 157, 168, 618. The gift of the Spirit is to be drawn through faith, 48. God, intending to render honour to faith, asks questions, 419. Faith is a prerequisite for gaining health, 168. The same is required for the salvation of the soul, 169. Faith is not to be expected from salvation, but salvation from faith, I, 709. What is sought must be merited by faith, 709. All salvation of the Gentiles is from faith, 700. Blessedness is reserved for the merits of faith, 370 [Col. 0954]. In faith is our first hope toward God, II, 671. Once the foundation of faith is uprooted, no hope remains, I, 553. Whoever is outside faith is outside the promises of the Gospel, II, 219. The needy in faith: the poor, I, 798. Salvation chiefly consists in the catholic faith, II, 705. Faith alone justifies, I, 705, 777. It perfects righteousness, 720. It perfects the righteous person, II, 369. It has the merit of obedience, not the confidence of known truth, I, 339. How it differs from knowledge, ibid. It would have no reward if the necessity of an attached will imposed it, II, 221.

The gift of faith, II, 234. To whom it is not given, 221, note. The Prophet began with his faith, I, 606. Faith should not be coerced, II, 538. Violence inflicted upon faith is disapproved, 594.
