Why a profession of coerced faith is not to be disapproved, 498. How great the darkness of those deprived of faith, and how great the light of those endowed with it, I, 165 ff. Impiety finds true faith difficult to understand, II, 114. Bonds that hinder faith, I, 456. Faith’s obedience advances us beyond natural opinion, II, 24. Religious faith is not confined by the capacities of human weakness, 369. It does not doubt divine works, 370. Faith takes up the understanding of the religion necessary to it, 7. It apprehends the mysteries of the kingdom, I, 734. It attains God’s power everywhere, 709. Our faith terrifies the wicked and refreshes the righteous, I, 182. The power of faith against magical tricks, 140; for warding off pain, II, 352, 353. Through faith the mind has that by which it is calmed, I, 166. Faith contains the power of a general remedy against every disease, II, 39. How great God’s grace is needed for holding faith, I, 281. The Spirit of faith is inseparably present with us, II, 409. The cry of faith, I, 134, 397.

Faith is hated by the rulers of this world, I, 297. It must be tested through suffering, thirst, hunger, and so forth, 172. In these, as it were, lie faith’s military service and victory, 173. Persecution is proof of faith, 346. Snares are always at hand against faith, 180. The attacks and devices of philosophers and heretics against it, 181; how empty they are, 181. Steadfast faith rejects the captious questions of philosophy, II, 10. Faith of heart, I, 108. Faith ought to be joined to mouth and heart, II, 370. Knowledge is in faith; reason is in God’s power, 370. Piety consists in not doubting, righteousness in believing, and salvation in confessing, 370. Faith is in simplicity, righteousness in faith, and piety in confession, 371. Perfect faith is bound by no religious obligation of secular office toward another, I, 703. The steadfastness of faith is taught by the example of idolaters and carnal people, I, 441, 443. The truth of faith must be professed in understanding and words, and likewise in works, 73. Good works are done in vain without faith, 73. Fear belonging to faith is proved by keeping God’s commandments, 330. Faith’s military service is to keep the commandments, 398. To add operation to faith is the doubling of money received, 796. Humility is the greatest work of our faith, 497. The person of perfect faith receives the anointing flowing down from Christ, 520 ff. Justification will especially be proved for us through faith, 281.

The truth of faith is shown from the futile efforts of heretics against it, II, 38 ff. The one faith of the Church conquers every heresy, 177, 180. The form of faith is certain; but, as regards heretics, every meaning is uncertain, 29. Our faith concerning the eternal generation of God, 188, 191 ff. Faith in the generation of the Word is proved by the marvellous teaching of the fisherman, 34, 38. Faith concerning the Son of God, 409. The perfect mystery of our faith concerning the Son, 128. The chief point of our faith, 497; the most fundamental, 471, 472. Faith in the one God the Father, without faith in Christ, does not avail for salvation, 238, 284, 291. The Church is constituted as both Jacob and Israel by the distinction of faith, I, 528. It is not enough to believe Christ unless we believe that he is the Son of God, II, 164, 169. Not to have believed Christ to be the Son of God is death, 149. Faith in Christ is the key of the Psalms, I, 5. The merit of perfect faith concerning the Son, II, 156. What faith concerning the Son and the Holy Spirit ought to be, 444. Apostolic men have always taken care to maintain faith in the Trinity, 641. The complete fulfilment of all faith lies in the sacrament of the regenerating Trinity, 23.

Unity of faith, II, 243, 373. The one seat of true faith, I, 224. Faith is not other than Peter’s faith, II, 162. Whatever is outside the one faith is outside faith, 375. Whatever is apart from the one faith is perfidy, not faith, 581. Many faiths began to exist so that none might exist, 545. Hypocrisy follows faith’s defection, II, 322. Division in faith arose from the fault of bad understanding, 178. Controversies concerning faith must be amicably settled, 518. Where opinions concerning faith vary, one must return to the faith confessed in baptism, 547. Apostolic and catholic faith, which remained until the Council of Nicaea, 703, note. Faith sworn in baptism, 544. The faith professed by those being baptized, I, 746. The faith which regenerated neophytes do not retain merely in writing, II, 499. Yet what is healthful to confess is not thereby prevented from being written, 499. It became necessary for faith to be drafted in various forms, 478. Westerners do not recognize written creeds, 499. Faith must be written, as though it were not in the heart, 546.

The Nicene faith is full and perfect, II, 643. It is described, 510, 643. Creeds issued at various times after the Council of Nicaea, II, 462 ff., 543 ff. On what occasion, 545. Yearly and monthly creeds, 546. A faith of times rather than of Gospels, I, 515. Believers are disturbed by novelty in faith, and unbelievers are prevented from approaching faith, II, 689. Though they put forward the apostolic faith sevenfold, they refuse to confess the evangelical faith, 547. Faith can be declared in a new expression, 509. The faith of the Westerners, II, 643. The creed published at Antioch at the Dedication Festival, II, 478. In what respect it is suspect, 480. The pseudo-Sardican creed, II, 482, 663. The fraudulent creed issued at Sirmium in A.D. 349, II, 641. The creed written at Sirmium against Photinus, II, 485. Whether Liberius accepted it, 678, ibid., note. The confession of faith written at Seleucia, II, 574. What creed was subscribed by the legates at Ariminum, II, 686. The catholic faith expounded at the Pharisaean city by Gallican bishops, II, 700. Auxentius is compelled to render an account of his faith before the Quaestor, the Master, and nearly ten bishops. How empty self-confidence is, I, 74. It is the height of folly and impiety to wish to rely upon one’s own power, 90. Our confidence is distrust of ourselves, 75. Everything must be in God, the guardian of confidence, 628. No one rules over the confidence we have in Christ, 455.

The difference between a potter’s vessel and a vessel belonging to a potter, I, 54. Philetus of Cratia, II, 666. Philetus of Julius, II, 666.

Who the Son truly is, II, 468. By the common agreement of humanity, a son is equal to the father’s nature, 293, 503. Many are called sons of God; one is the true Son, II, 409. Various heresies concerning the Son are condemned, 686. Some have called the Son of God an incorporeal sound of an unsubstantial word, 490. Valentinus called him an emanation, 79, 134; Manichaeus, a portion of one substance, 80, 134; Sabellius, the very same person as the Father, 80, 135; Hieracas, a lamp from a lamp, 80, 135. How absurdly Hieracas understands the Son as light from light, 140; how the Church understands it, 140. Some have called the Son of God an extension of God’s substance as far as the Holy Virgin, 490. The Arians deny that he is from God’s nature and in God’s nature, 136. They do not wish him always to have existed, 73. What reason they put forward for this opinion, ibid. The Church abominates the corrupt meanings they advance, 74.

The Arians deny that the Son is eternal from the past, I, 801. Those who imply that he is from non-existent things, II, 141. Those who understand him not to have been created like other created things, 695. What privilege they ascribe to him, 72. Their subtleties against the eternal birth of God’s Only-Begotten, 216, 418. The blasphemies of the Anomoeans against him, 573 ff. They affirm that the Father denies the Son knowledge of himself, 573. The Gospel of John declares that the Son is not inferior to the Father in time or nature, II, 9. He is as unknowable as the Father, II, 151; as inexpressible, II, 60; as invisible, II, 33, 377. Those who ask how, from where, and from what portion or loss of the Father he exists are rebuked, II, 60. What the Son must be believed to be, II, 74, 409, 439, 441. What he is and is not, II, 32, 33, 39. Why he is called Word, Wisdom, and Power, II, 182. The Son was born, not begun, II, 303. John calls him born, not created, II, 163. In the books, the Father has no other testimony concerning the Son than that he is his Son, II, 152. God the Only-Begotten neither was ever not Son, nor was anything before being Son, nor is himself anything but Son, II, 416. The Son of God is proper, not adoptive, II, 56; he is proper because he is Only-Begotten, II, 163. To the Son it is proper to be Only-Begotten, as to the Father it is proper to be unbegotten, II, 95. The title “Son” does not suit a work, II, 415. If he is a creature, the Father gave nothing great in giving him for the world, II, 163.

The deity of the Son is established by Hosea, II, 97; by Isaiah, II, 97. The agreement of Paul and Isaiah, II, 99. Baruch concurs with them, 101. What belongs to the Son cannot be taken away: that he is Judge, and consequently true God, II, 112. God the Only-Begotten is neither from nothing nor from time, II, 415; he was born—not from one who was not, but from God who was, II, 142. He is not bounded by time or subject to number, but is the source of all things that are or can be said to be, I, 43. This is in him: he himself is with him from whom he was before he was born, I, 801. What is to be thought of the phrase “before he was born,” I, 801, ibid., note. The statement “He was not before he was born” does not apply to the Son, II, 699. Marcellus did not assign the Word of God a beginning from Mary, nor did he assign an end to his kingdom, II, 626. Whoever confesses the Son of God before all ages, but not before absolutely all time, is anathema, II, 686.

The Son of God has always existed, I, 181. As the Father’s image, he is not younger than him, II, 475; as Son of him who always was, he always is, II, 475. The Son is neither unbegotten nor not eternal, since he is from the Father who always is, II, 420. Of him who is always Father, he is never not born, ibid. No interval is perceived between the Son’s birth from God and God’s generation as Father, II, 420. Though timeless, the Son is not unbegotten, II, 476, 484; he is not his own origin, II, 300; he is both eternal God and born, I, 748 ff. Through the mystery of birth he is the image of unbegottenness, II, 301. He is named after the Father himself by the title of his unbegotten power, II, 97. What the anointing of the Son of God was like, I, 519. His birth according to the Spirit, as opposed to birth according to humanity, II, 60.

Archangels do not know the generation of the Son of God, II, 32. The Father and Son possess its secret, II, 32. The birth of God’s Son remains within the knowledge of himself and the Father alone, 409. He is not unknowable because he is inexpressible, 507. How he may be investigated reverently, 33. By unutterable deeds he brought about faith in his unutterable birth, 60. The Church alone understands the generation of the Son, 251. What the birth of the Son of God is, II, 141. It is not from a portion, extension, or emission, but with fullness, 59. The Son of God is neither an emanation nor a part of the Father, 473. He is subsisting God, and the generation of an incorporeal nature is incorporeal, 285. What the Son received from the Father by being born, and how, II, 51. He was born as he who was able willed, as he who begot knows, 155, ibid., note. The birth of the Son was the will of him in whose power and authority it lay that he should be born, I, 748. In what sense he is said to be born from will, II, 484. He had his origin from God’s substance, not from will as creatures do, 495. Yet not against the Father’s will or through natural necessity, 495.

The Son’s generation is fittingly, though not perfectly, signified by the term *prolation* (“bringing forth”), II, 137. The name “going forth” of the Son is referred to an incorporeal birth, 155. Whoever believes and loves that the Son went forth from God has no need of intercession with the Father, 156. When the Son is said to be from the Father himself, he is neither the Father himself, nor from another, nor from no one, 143. He is said to be begotten from the womb in order to show that he was born from the Father’s substance, 143. There is no other reason to love the Son than that he is from God, 155. The Son is perfect from the perfect, I, 269. He subsists from no other source, but through the Father’s love and power, 269. He was begotten from living into living, II, 128. In being born, he has within himself all that belongs to God, 197. He subsists in the things that are the Father’s, 282. In what is proper to the Father, he subsists through the nature begotten within him, 468. The things belonging to the Son are within the Father’s goods, not merely subsisting outside them, 315. All power is innate in him, 281.

The Son possesses the advance of birth without novelty of nature, II, 198. Why he is not absent from the Father, is not referred to something else, and is not something new, 128. He is from the Father’s substance and within the Father’s substance, I, 684. Human understanding does not grasp the Son in the Father and, conversely, the Father in the Son, II, 49. The Son is from God and in God, 128. By what reasoning he is in the Father, 51. He has the Father with him in power and nature, I, 574. He is Son in power, substance, divinity, and generation, 578. He alone is worthy and sufficient for the Father to dwell in him, 440. He is not absent by nature from him from whom he was begotten, 440. The fullness of divinity makes the Son to be in the Father and the Father in the Son, II, 65. The Son differs from the Father in the property of designation, not in nature or substance, I, 570; not in power, 570. In the Son’s nature and name is the indication of the Father’s nature and name, 173. It is proper to the Son to know the Father’s infinity, 529. The Son, born from the Father with the mystery of his knowledge, cannot be anything other than living, II, 198. Knowledge and all things are mutual to Son and Father, I, 725 ff. The Only-Begotten God is the form and image of the invisible God, 257. As the Father’s image, he is not of a substance different from him, II, 468. He has all things that the Father has, 65.

The substance of Son and Father is the same, I, 725. The Gallic bishops explain how the Son is of one substance with the Father, II, 698. That he is one with the Father by nature is shown from the words of the Easterners, 504. The Son’s will is free and one with the Father’s, 296. The Son is one with the Father not merely in unity of will but also of power, I, 570. The Son’s power is shown equal to the Father’s because it brought efficacy to the Father’s command, II, 106. The Son is sometimes called God’s right hand, I, 560. The Son’s hand is the Father’s hand, because the power of both is one, II, 194. The Son’s work is God’s work, 191. His doing nothing except what he sees shows authority, not weakness, 293. The seat of Son and Father is one because their substance is one, I, 513. Praise of the Son is praise of the Father, II, 58.

The Son was begotten by the Father in likeness of nature, I, 513. The glory of the Father’s majesty is innate in the Only-Begotten, 513. That the Son is similar to the Father in essence is the most fundamental point of our faith, II, 471. Those who ascribe to him only likeness of power are refuted, 471, 472. The Gospels do not preach the Son as merely similar to the Father, 575. The Apostle calls the Son the image of God, but with an addition, 578. As image, the Son possesses all things that the Father possesses, 65. When it was determined that the Son is like the Father in all things, II, 708. Scripture and tradition teach that he is like the Father in all things except unbegottenness, 707. The equality of Son with Father is demonstrated from God’s omnipotence, goodness, and wisdom, II, 147. Though Christ did not call the Son equal to God, the Jews understood this against their will, I, 268. In the creation of the world the Son is made equal to God in name and work, II, 107. From likeness of glory he is shown to be one with the Father, I, 495. The reciprocal giving and receiving of glorification shows the unity of Son and Father, II, 56. They are one in divinity, worship, and injury, I, 36.

Those who do not worship the Son vainly call God their Father, II, 155. Paul never spoke of the Father without confessing the Son, 167. Honour paid to the Son takes nothing from the Father, 75. Those who deny the Son deny God under the appearance of honouring God, 100. In fact, they dishonour the Father, 100. Though not unequal to the Father in power, the Son refers all that is his to the Father in the honour of reverence, I, 575. By his words he bears witness to reverence for the Father, 602, ibid., note. In what respect he is not to be made equal to the Father, II, 493. He is equal to the Father not in unbegottenness but in generation, 324. The difference between the Son’s subjection and that of created things, 507.

What distinction may exist between Son and Father, II, 190. He is distinguished from the Father by subsistence, not by nature, 65; by person, not by kind, 99. Where the name of nature is one, the person is not one, 93. Birth from God into God permits him to be neither the same person nor another thing, 13. The begotten and the begetter can be neither one nor of different essences, 474. As begotten, the Son is neither the Father himself nor anything other than the Father, 473. He is other than the Father as one who receives life from him, 467. As image, he is other than the Father not in name alone, 467. As one with God, he is a lion; as subsisting from God, he is a lion’s cub, I, 506. As person distinct from the Father, he is called the angel of God; as God, he is the same in nature, II, 109 ff. He is the Angel of Great Counsel, 88, 90. The indivisibility and distinction of Son and Father are shown from the Psalm: “Once God spoke; these two things I heard,” etc., I, 169.

The Son stood beside the Father in creating the world, I, 645. In bringing created things into being—things formed within the providence of the Father’s thoughts through a certain predestination of future realities—he sees inwardly through mutual love and nature, 269. This is called the Son’s service, obedience, and ministry, 268. This is his doing nothing of himself, performing not his own will but the Father’s, and doing only what he sees, ibid. The Son of God, the Word, Power, and Wisdom of God, is maker of the world and creator of humankind, 182. He is mediator in the world’s creation, II, 83. The Son is one mediator both in giving the Law and in assuming flesh, II, 101. He is at once preacher of the Gospel and giver of the Law, I, 225, 226. He washed away the world’s first sins with the flood, 182. He is unchangeable, II, 405, 646. He appeared to the Fathers as he was born for us, without harm to his own nature, 113 ff. In human form he was worshipped by Abraham and wrestled with Jacob, confirming faith in the flesh he would assume, I, 253. He gave the Law to Moses, 182. He was in the prophets, and through them sang of the mysteries of his embodiment and passion, 182.

The Son, understood under the name of the Holy Spirit, II, 40. Without leaving heaven, he descended, I, 36. He himself sowed for himself the beginnings of his body, II, 40. By his own power and authority he assumed a body, 42. He undertook the shame of a human body, I, 232, ibid., note. He became flesh of our whole race, 121. He assumed in himself the nature of all flesh, 87. Assuming in himself the nature of the whole human race, 87, he took humanity from the womb of the holy Virgin, 563. The Son of God was born as man from the Virgin’s childbirth, 584. God, visible and tangible in a human being, II, 100. Made man, perfect in what is his and true in what is ours, II, 9. The Son was not changed, but concealed within himself he assumed the form of a servant, II, 405. When he emptied himself from the form of God, the form of a servant did not take away either God’s power or nature, I, 129. His being human benefited us and diminished nothing in him, 563. He brought glory to corruption rather than stain to eternity, II, 646. The Son of God became Son of Man so that man might become son of God, I, 87. The Son of God remained so even when made Son of Man, 36. In sharing our body, he exercised the power of his own strength, 129. He passed through the solid mass of the walls, II, 409.

The Son of God descended to the final sufferings of the age, I, 232. He was subjected to suffering voluntarily for human salvation, not by necessity of nature, 114. He hungered, thirsted, was sorrowful, and so forth, 111. The resurrection demonstrates that he was subject to our weaknesses not by nature but through assumption, 111. Every one of his complaints arises from the condition of our nature, 111. As an example of humility, the Son of God both prayed and suffered all that belongs to humanity, 111, so that it might be understood that he had taken up our birth together with the very offices of our weakness, 111. Those who say that he suffered sympathetically are refuted, II, 507. How the passion, cross, and death of the Son of God are wisdom and power to believers, I, 228. The Son, eternally begotten, is newly born through the glory of resurrection, I, 46 ff. The Son is our redemption, 497. He redeemed all, 497.

The distinction between created sons and the Only-Begotten, II, 415 ff. Who are adoptive sons, 166. People become sons of God not by birth of flesh but by faith, 9; not through necessity but power, ibid. This power comes to each person, 9. Who are the Lord’s sons; their hope and the condition of that hope, I, 513. Faith or unbelief makes people children of Abraham or of the devil, 674. Alien sons: the Jews, I, 616. Sons of those cast out, I, 474.

What an end is, I, 12, 78. It is not always abolition, II, 392. The end is all things and remains wholly itself, 392. It is the unmoving state of abiding toward which one tends, 392. It is the enduring perfection of an unchangeable condition, 393. The end of the ungodly is not abolition, 393. The end of faith, I, 346, ibid., note. The end of our perfection, 62 ff. How Psalms inscribed “for the end” are to be understood, 12, 128, 354. The title *in finem* (“for the end”) has a twofold interpretation, 65. What the ends of the earth are, I, 161. Things firm and immovable are called “weighty” in Scripture, I, 438. The firmament, I, 544, 545. It separates the upper and lower waters, 545. Fissia, II, 633. Flaccus, II, 667. Florentinus, II, 631. Florentius, I, 667. Rivers are works of the age and of the flesh, I, 550. The Gentiles are often denoted by the name “hay,” I, 694. The nature of leaves, I, 25.

Form, countenance, face, and image do not differ, I, 257. How “being formed” applies to Christ, I, 569. The form of God is the same as the nature of God, II, 411, 412. “Form of the Father’s majesty” means glory, 302. The form of God was not in Christ when he emptied himself, 298. The conjunction of the form of God and the form of a servant is not self-consistent, 268. While remaining in the form of God, he could not exist in the form of a human being; nor could the form of God be abolished so that there should be only the form of a servant, I, 256. The Word, emptying himself from the form of God into the form of a servant and of a human being, descended, 243. The Lord willed to be in the form of a servant, II, 699. The unity of the servant-form is not immediately to be resolved into the unity of the divine nature, 298. Fortunatianus of Aquileia, II, 632. Sent by Liberius to Constantius, 681. In Liberius’s name he vainly sends a letter to various bishops, 670. He conveys the letters of the fallen Liberius to the Emperor, 678. Fortunatus, II, 647. Those who maintain that all things came into existence by chance are refuted, I, 197. Those who teach that all things are driven by chance movements are refuted, I, 181. The laws of the forum are observed with difficulty alongside the laws of the Church, I, 21. All Christians are brothers, I, 784. Those who inflict the gravest injuries upon churches are called brothers, II, 535. Where fraternal unity is genuine, and how good and pleasant it is, I, 518 ff. Forehead. The sign on foreheads, I, 155. The proper fruit of the earth, I, 211. Lost through the first Adam, 211. Restored through the second, 211. Flight from persecution, I, 448. Lightnings are those who flash with knowledge, I, 532. Christ is the foundation of faith, I, 553. Cords of sinners, I, 328. A thief of one coin must be punished, but not as a thief of an immense treasure, I, 625. The thief: the devil, 793. Future things are to God as things done, I, 437. Through his knowledge and power, they are done for him, 581.

## G
GAIUS, II, 595, 693, 705, 707. At Ariminum he plots innovations with his associates, 688. He is condemned, 685, 690. The Gauls exclude him from their communion, 700.

GALAAD. What is denoted by the name, I, 157.

Galatia nurtured many impiously into the confession of one God, II, 176.

Galbanum, I, 593.

The sight of a *galbulus* cures jaundice, I, 339, note.

The Gauls, II, 655.

THE GAULS are suspected of sedition, II, 537.

THE GALLICAN BISHOPS separate themselves from the communion of Saturninus, Ursacius, and Valens, II, 562. When they began to confine the Lord’s communion to themselves alone, II, 461. Gauls and Easterners are held by mutual suspicions, 463. In the year 337 the Gauls write to Hilary, 459. While denying communion to Saturninus, they adhere to Hilary in faith and spirit, 459. They condemn the faithless creed sent from the town of Sirmium, 459. They do not yield to Saturninus’s threats, political powers, or wars, 460. They break all the insolence of the burgeoning heresy, II, 460. The renown of their faith moves the Easterners to repentance, 460. The Gauls ask Hilary what the Easterners are doing or have done in their confessions of faith, and what he himself thinks about these matters, 461. Hilary wishes the Gauls to distinguish themselves in synods, 463.

The Gauls, summoned to the coming synod in Bithynia, remain within Hilary’s communion, II, 462. They refrain from communion with those who keep defenders of the faith in exile, 461. They do not enter into deceitful dissimulation, 461. They refrain from association with the rest outside Gaul, 463.

The Gallican bishops assembled at Paris reply to the Easterners, II, 700. From the Easterners’ letter they acknowledge that they were deceived by silence concerning *ousia* [substance/essence], 699. They reject as apostates those who at Constantinople were unworthily substituted for brothers living in exile, 700. They determine that those who resisted the decrees of their synod must be removed from communion and from the priestly seat, 700.

The hen’s work, I, 787; and her concern for her chicks, 134.

GAUDENTIUS, II, 680.

GAUDENTIUS of Naissus, II, 632.

GAUDENTIUS is condemned by the pseudo-Sardican synod, II, 662. He defends Paul of Constantinople, 662.

Joys, when recognized as vices, sting the conscience, I, 156. It belongs to an impious and self-distrusting conscience to fear without joy; and to an insolent nature to rejoice without fear, 90.

Gaza, II, 632, 665, note.

The wretched commonly groan at the recollection of former blessings, I, 549.

Gems are prized among women, I, 384.

Generation consists in likeness of nature, not in the characteristic property of vices, II, 339. Heretics maintain that generation from the one and immutable God is impossible, 54, 215. We certainly know God’s generation, 32, 34, although we do not comprehend its rationale, 33 ff. This is not to be sought from the wise of the world or from the scribes of the Law, 34; it is expounded by a fisherman, 34. To what extent the generation of the Son may be explained by analogy with our own generations, 413. Whether “Today I have begotten you” is applicable to the generation of the Word, I, 43.

Two generations, whose proper task is to praise God, I, 623: the generation of the Law and the generation of faith, 633. The first began with Abraham, 623. The first is that of the Jews, the other that of Christians, 350, 536.

The nobility of the Father’s majesty is undifferentiated in the Son, I, 506.

The nations descended from Ham and Japheth, I, 770. They are signified by the names of waters, 122; deserts, 220; hay, 694; camels, 674, ibid., note, 764; donkeys, 757; and dogs, 696. They are especially situated beside Israel, 745. What vices rule among Gentile ignorance, 771. Although few from all nations are faithful, it does not follow from those few that not all nations are unbelieving, 149. The cause of the nations’ unbelief, 149.

It is fitting that all nations be subject to God, I, 159. The conversion of the nations is prefigured in Elijah’s nourishment by a raven, 639. The nations, who would supplant the earlier people by faith, are foreshadowed in Jacob, 105; but in Israel, insofar as they are to see God, 106. Christ, under the name “Saviour,” was promised especially to the nations, 66. The gathering of the nations that are to praise the Lord is announced in Psalm 64, 184. Before Christ, the nations were given over to the dominion of angels and divided according to their number, 49, 166; through Christ they were rescued from the perverse right claimed by their rulers, 49.

The nations seize the salvation prepared for the Jews, I, 708; those who seize the kingdom of heaven from the Jews, 723. The younger people of the nations buys the birthright of the elder, 394; it buys by the faith which the latter lost through unbelief, 395. How the nations are God’s people, and in what respect a people unknown to God, 612. How they are far from God, and how near, 198. The people of the nations, formerly captive: how they were freed by Christ, 105. The nations, transformed from the forests and lairs of the devil into God’s dwelling-places, 508. The nations brought, beyond expectation, to knowledge of God and fellowship, 227. The nations, not understanding after the manner of animals, 221; they became spiritual, 221.

The order of the nations’ salvation, I, 710. The salvation of the nations began in the period of the Law, 233; it was reserved for the preaching of the Apostles, 745. Christ is to be satisfied with the salvation of the nations together with the Apostles, 745. The whole salvation of the nations is from faith, 700; from faith in the deeds which the Jews beheld, 725. The nations live through the grace of the Spirit, 746.

The nations were given to Christ as an inheritance, I, 227. The baptized nations are Christ’s inheritance, 48. How they console God, 537. All nations were visited in the Son of God because he became flesh, 147; raised together and seated at God’s right hand in the heavenly places, 146. Nations that are visited yet do not obey will be rejected, 148.

*Genus*, nature, and substance are often the same as essence, II, 466.

GEORGE of Alexandria, heretic, II, 572, 708.

GEORGE of Laodicea, II, 627, 628, 631. After Alexander expelled Arius’s disciples, he communicated with them by letter, 673.

First and Second Germany, II, 457.

GERMINIUS, II, 508, 595. At Ariminum he plots innovations with his associates, 688, and there he is condemned, 685, 690. In a letter he maintains that the Son is like the Father in all respects, 704, 706. His associates try to turn him away from this faith, 705. He testifies that he is united in charity with those from whose faith he separates himself, 705.

GERONTIUS, II, 633, 664.

What the sword is and what it signifies, I, 718; it signifies authority, 651. “He who uses the sword shall perish by the sword,” 804.

Some glory is good and some bad, I, 81. We have no ground for boasting when we remember that all things are from God, 147, and that in all things there is need of God’s mercy, ibid. How vain it is to boast of knowledge or of the power to work miracles, 698. Jews who glory in themselves provoke the anger of him who alone can make them glorious, 201. Through desire for glory the mind does not feel pain, II, 353.

The glory of Father and Son is one, II, 287. The unity of Christ’s glory with the Father’s had, through the dispensation, gone beyond [the omitted referent is unclear], 288. The glory Christ requested for his flesh, I, 46 ff. The differing degrees of glory of the Son of Man, II, 400. The glory of Christ’s body, 397.

We who are subjected to Christ’s glory, II, 397. In Christ’s glorious body we contemplate the glory of our eternity, I, 260, 487. In Christ we are now filled; later we shall be filled in ourselves, II, 264. Faith in suffering-with and dying-with him glorifies us in Christ, I, 136.

Glory destined for humanity, II, 402. That heavenly glory should be given to earthly flesh surpasses the credibility of human hope, I, 227. This is the power of the flesh assumed by the Word: that it raises the corruption of our nature into heavenly glory, 229. The way to heavenly glory lies open to all, 270. Glory is prepared for us, through God’s providential goodness, without our anxiety, 695. The cause of heavenly glory is spiritual teaching and work, 596; its greatest cause is God’s mercy, 542. No one can attain it by personal merit unless advanced by God’s mercies, 340.

The endowments of eternal glory, I, 26; II, 406. All the glory and light of the blessed is drawn from beholding the glory of God, I, 390; how it is received from contemplation of God’s glory, 326. It will differ among the saints, 193. What will be granted to those whose faith was weaker, 193, ibid., note. How the perfection of heavenly glory will make us one with God, 239. How, through glory, God will be all in all, II, 399. The honor of glory will take all into the unity of paternal honor, 221; it was given for no other reason than that all might be one, 221. Hilary grasps the cause of this unity, but has not yet grasped its rationale, 221. Through glory, human nature is transformed into eternal substance, I, 613.

The body to be glorified into the nature of spirit, I, 289; it will be changed, not abolished, II, 399; but what is fleshly in it will be consumed into the nature of spirit, 406. The glorified body will have a solid and unchangeable nature, I, 431; its former matter, indeed the very matter of its origin, 54.

The ten steps in Hezekiah’s house, I, 414. The fifteen steps in the Temple, 415, 416.

A word-for-word rendering of Greek speech is obscure, I, 303. In the Greek word ἔρεις (*ereis*), pronunciation does not distinguish whether it means “you say” or “contention,” 582. The Greek translation from Hebrew, I, 303, 304; it is preferred to the Latin, I, 303; II, 386.

Whoever follows merely human grace loses divine grace, I, 102. See “To please.” Pardon through grace is necessary for all, 707. None but Christ gave salvation and freedom, 104. We are in God’s hand, for him to remake us as he wills, like a potter, 806. God bestows his gifts upon the righteous and the unrighteous alike, 330. God is present to all and does not withhold his aid from human beings, 627. The Word of God is like the sun, available to everyone so as to enlighten when it finds an entrance, 349. To whom the grace of receiving evangelical teaching was deferred, 776; to what extent those for whom it was deferred could not obey it, 776, 777. This delay imposed by necessity entails no fault of will, 777, and lies outside the guilt of unbelief, 776.

The necessity of grace, II, 48. The gifts of God’s grace and mercy are our light, I, 209; knowledge, 357; heavenly knowledge, 348; knowledge of God, II, 116, 117; knowledge of divine matters and heavenly commands, I, 338; and righteousness, 281. The reception of God’s teaching, 272; knowledge of the ordinances, 255; understanding of Scripture, 457. This is not denied to those who ask, 458. Knowledge is given to one who seeks it, 357; it is not given to one who does not desire it, 359. It belongs to God to grant both that we understand the Scriptures and that we explain what we understand in fitting words, II, 24. It is necessary to pray to God for the grace of understanding, I, 277. Grace is necessary for attaining the knowledge and true practice of a godly life, 273. Our conversion is from God, 461. By the gift of grace, the crimes of one’s former life are forgiven, 779. God has bestowed free grace upon all through justification by faith, 767.

We need God’s grace and mercy to attain eternal life, I, 340. Salvation must be expected from God’s mercy, 400. It is not our fear but faith that obtains God’s mercy, 180. By grace we are all saved, II, 98. Uprightness of conduct is a certain preparation for receiving light, I, 275. Knowledge of teaching will not be present unless faithful works have preceded it, 287. A human being needs God’s help to accomplish good, 381. It is solely the office of that nature that a person should both wish and begin to join himself to God’s household, 381. God’s house must be built by God—that is, by his teachings, 469. Our will cannot of itself accomplish the good that it knows, 470. We must always pray that he may favor us when we wish to keep his commandments, 282. Grace is necessary for keeping God’s ordinances, 280. Great grace is required to maintain the true faith, 281. What the Prophet meditated upon, although he began it through his own faith, he nevertheless shows not to be his own but a gift, 606. By God’s help the house of God must be built and guarded, 468, 469. Helped by God’s mercy, we persevere in faith, fear of God, and hope, 347.

The necessity of God’s grace for overcoming temptations, I, 179. We have great need of God’s aid in so great and continual a battle of this world, 372. Hope merits God’s help, 372. By God’s aid the devil’s snare is broken, 451. Human weakness, without God’s help, is unequal to enduring sufferings, 340. The Apostle knows himself unequal to tribulations unless aided by God, 560. God gave constancy and perseverance in confession to the Apostles and martyrs, 202. The respective part of God’s grace and merit in victory over temptations, 609.

How we ought to cooperate with God’s grace, I, 310. Grace is granted to our prayer, 310. As regards our beginning, it is God’s gift, 310. Many maintain that it is God’s own gift for someone to occupy himself with God’s concerns and works, 369. Many excuse their unbelief by saying that, because God’s will toward them has ceased, they remain unbelievers, 370. It is impious to suppose that one does not attain what is proper to believers because it was not granted by God, 309. In accordance with the diversity of merits, God is either absent from or present with each person by his help, 200. The Prophet referred everything to God’s gift, 309. To the objection, “If all things are from God, human ignorance is free from blame,” the answer is given, 309. The Prophet joined the duties of human devotion to God’s gifts, 310. First he set in the place of honor what is God’s, and then humbly subjected what is human, 310. All aids for bodily and spiritual life are from God, 628. No one should trust himself so much that he does not always fear falling and being dashed to pieces, 628. David is commended because he wants all things in himself to be begun by God’s goodness, 315. Without God’s help a human being is compared to dry land without water, 606. God alone is the faithful helper, 168; he must be entreated with tears, 168. Every affection must be poured out before him, so that we place no confidence in ourselves, 168. If anything is in us, it is from God, 90. Whatever is in us, we owe to God, 448. What we do must be understood to be God’s power, II, 234. No ground for boasting is left to humanity when it remembers that all things are from God and that in all things there is need of God’s mercy, I, 447.

The gifts of divine grace are to be rendered through the Apostles, I, 740. Through the Apostles mercy comes to the aid of all, 727. There is none of us who does not at times feel the gift of spiritual grace, 349. Through the vice of arrogance, God’s grace becomes useless and idle, 365; it is lost, 366. The dispensation of grace must be free, 788.

Thanks must be given to God for grace amid adversities, I, 331.

GRATIAN, consul, II, 706.

The administration of a free gift must itself be free, I, 711, 688.

Scripture is accustomed to call the weighty “firm,” I, 438.

GRECIANUS of Cale, II, 685.

GREGORY of Alexandria, II, 598, 647, perhaps also 690; he is called a holy and upright priest, 653; he is condemned in the Sardican synod, 628.

Eusebius of Vercelli replies to GREGORY of Spain, II, 700, congratulating him because he resisted Hosius and, while very many fell at Ariminum, stood firm, 701.

Gusia, II, 668.

Gymnosophists. See “Naked.”

## H
To possess is not a crime, but moderation in possessing must be maintained, I, 763. To possess and to be possessed are not the same, II, 46. Difference between a dwelling and a resting-place, I, 70. A dwelling worthy of God is not the visible heaven, 440, but the Son, 440; and, through the Son as mediator, the faithful, 440 ff. No created thing is worthy to be God’s dwelling, 504; to make man worthy of God’s habitation is Christ’s greatest work, 504. What God’s dwelling in devout minds is like, 504. The mutual indwelling of Father and Son, 440. To dwell and to be dwelt in are not identical, II, 100, 255, 257. The clothing of Christ, with whom the saints will reign, is white, I, 224. [Col. 0962] Hadrianople, II, 653.

The inheritance of God: what it is, I, 221. The Lord’s inheritance is not carnal Israel, but those born in Christ, 472; that is, the saints, 162. Although an inheritance is divided among several persons, it nevertheless belongs wholly to each heir under the name of inheritance, I, 369. Like heirs dividing an estate among themselves, we ought to choose the better portion, 324. What that portion is, ibid.

Heresy is like cheese, I, 224; it cuts itself off from the Church, II, 118; it arises from Scripture wrongly understood, 27; from the fault of evil interpretation, 178; it possesses nothing certain or fixed, I, 20; it displays its own folly, II, 219. Obstinate heresy is not so much prudent as audacious, 143; it is easily refuted, but not easily corrected, 143. Heresy arising from error is not without hope of correction, 143. Heretics are men of blood, I, 582; swine, 696. Heretics are possessed by demons driven out from the Gentiles, 704. The cause of the heretics’ error, II, 12. For them every perception is uncertain, 29; all things are uncertain and wandering, 131. Heretics are narrow-minded, incapable of understanding the divine Spirit and the Scriptures, 284. They lack the word of wisdom and knowledge, and faith, 238; they do not even grasp the causes of natural things, 344; not comprehending the rationale of heavenly wisdom, they adapt everything to the appearance of human wisdom, I, 224.

Heretics twist the Scriptures to their own side, II, 548. They hand down and teach everything otherwise than it is written, I, 419; by confused and intermingled words they evade the truth, II, 472; they avoid the point at issue in debate, I, 20. In their minds there is only a zeal for contention, 582. Heretics disparage faith either through an obtuse mind caused by impiety or through the domination of an opposing spirit, II, 418; having become reprobate in life, will, and judgment, they seek to please by novelty of doctrine, 642. They fashion God according to their own choice, I, 20—not with less impiety than those who deny Him, 20. It is incredible by what deceits they attempt to overthrow faith, 181; they deceive rather than conquer, II, 419. How one should answer heretics who rely upon human reasoning, 144. Divine authority must be opposed to their petty arguments, 143. All heretics come against the Church, 178; they oppose one another and gain victory not for themselves but for the Church, 178.

The fasts, continence, and so forth of heretics are vain, I, 73. Heretics have neither faith, hope, nor baptism, II, 243. They assemble churches for themselves in vain, I, 582. The Apostles are warned not to visit heretical churches, 711; heretics lack faith and integrity of life, and thus are incapable of receiving the Gospels, 801. Whether Hilary permitted communion with Arians, II, 563. How one should deal with leaders of heretics and with their associates, 562, ibid., note. Pardon is granted to notable heretics, so that heresy may be deprived of strength to the Church’s advantage, II, 635. Under association with heretics, most people falsely profess peace, I, 224. The effort of heretics is directed toward making excuses for excuses, 595.

The silence of the soothsayers, I, 559.

HEBION, that is, Photinus, II, 176, 180. Hebion’s doctrine, I, 224; II, 28. Which Scriptures contradict him, 40. How Hebion is refuted both by Sabellius and by Arius, 16. The Hebrew language consists of twenty-two letters, I, 272. The Hebrew language is ambiguous, 32. Paul used the Hebrew text of Scripture among the Hebrews, I, 33.

HELIANUS, II, 669.  
HELIODORUS, II, 706.  
Whether the presbyter Heliodorus deceived Hilary, I, 473, note, and 477, note.  
HELPIDIUS, II, 693.  
Heraclea, II, 665.  
HERACLIANEUS, II, 632.  
HERODIANUS, II, 693.

Hermon, a mountain of Phoenicia, I, 521; called Sanior by the Phoenicians, 521, note; it is worshipped in the profane religion of the Gentiles, 521. Hermon is interpreted “anathema,” 521. It is reported that angels who lusted after the daughters of men assembled upon this mountain, 521. The names of heroes were counted among the gods, I, 201.

HIERACAS said that the Son is a lamp from a lamp, II, 80, 135; with what absurd understanding, I, 140.

HIERONYMUS: whether, while disapproving Hilary’s opinion, he grasped its meaning, I, 473, note; 477, note. He criticizes another passage of Hilary and attributes the fault to Heliodorus, 477, note. Fragment from Jerome on Matthew, 811.

HILARY calls himself a disciple of truth, II, 572; he is called by a synod “a faithful preacher of the Lord’s name,” 700. He had a wife after attaining the episcopate, who was still alive, 528; and an only daughter, 525. Hilary extends the office of the priesthood laid upon him to the duty of public salvation, 12; as bishop, he considers that he possesses the ministry of evangelical preaching in the Church, 133. For the benefit of Catholics he sends a booklet to Constantius, 535; in the gravest danger to the faith he prudently issues a decree, 562, leaving its application to the judgment of Christ’s confessors, II, 565. He had never heard of the Nicene faith until he was about to go into exile, 518. The Gospels and Apostles made known to him the meaning of *homoousios* and *homoiousios*, 518. Having long before been regenerated, he remained in the episcopate for some time before going into exile, 518.

Hilary was given the power to enjoy worldly honours and conveniences, II, 619; these he despised, rejecting fellowship with unbelievers out of love for Christ, 619. Mountains and forests are safer for him than the churches of heretics, 600. Compelled to attend the synod of Béziers, Hilary’s conduct there, 563; there he denounces the advocates of introducing heresy, 460. By Saturninus, after he had deceived the Emperor, he was driven into exile, 459; he was exiled by faction, not for a crime, 543; after Constantius had been deceived and Julian mocked, 543. He remained in communion with all the Gallican churches, 543; he still distributed communion of the Church through his presbyters, 543. Once exiled, he resolves neither to depart from confession of Christ nor to reject an honourable condition of unity, 563. He does not regard it as criminal for anyone to converse with heretics, enter a house of prayer, or hope for a peace to be desired, 563.

Hilary rejoices in his exile, II, 323; resolves not to complain of the times, 322; writes nothing defamatory against the times or the Arians, 563, but acts with the disposition in which he cries: “Let us always be exiles, provided that the preaching of truth may begin,” 506. He ensures that truth is not exiled from the faithful, 323. As a bishop he wrote books on the Trinity, 533, and wrote them in exile, 325; the reasons which moved him to do so, 174. Very many of the ancients entitle those books *On the Faith*. See the Preface to vol. II, no. 2; several words of Hilary favour this title, ibid., no. 4. He rejoices in the hope of leading even Arians to truth through these books, 133.

Hilary informs the Gauls, through very many cities of the Roman provinces, of the faith and zeal of the Easterners, II, 457. He fears that the silence of the Gauls has been adopted from the pollution of their own conscience, 458; he resolves to send them no letters of ecclesiastical discourse, 458. In the third year of his exile he receives letters from them, 459; they excuse their delay in writing by the length and remoteness of his exile, 459. The Gauls send him the Lord’s communion, 462; they testify that they cling to him in faith and spirit, 459. Some ask him to inform them what the Easterners are doing or have done in their professions of faith, and what he himself thinks on these matters, 459.

While staying within Asia, Hilary writes the book *On the Synods*, II, 498. He renders to the Church the service due from his soldiery and the voice of his episcopate in Christ, 519; he judges it worthy to share with the Gauls certain counsels of pious faith, 463; above all he desires that they shine in synods, 463. He asks them to remember his exile in their holy prayers, 520; he does not know whether return to his own people is as pleasant as it is safe for him to die in exile, 520. He labours to lessen the mutual suspicions of Easterners and Gauls, 463. How he expounded the faith of the Easterners, 476. He leaves it to them to judge whether this faith is Catholic or heretical, 462. It is shown that Hilary never differed from Athanasius concerning the Eastern formulas in the book *On the Synods*, 453, note 13. What was criticized in that book, 521, 522.

In the apology he undertook for himself, Hilary explains why he praised the Easterners in the book *On the Synods*, II, 521; he shows that he did not call their faith true, ibid.; nor did he remove suspicion from them, 523; and that he mentioned *homoiousios* unwillingly, 522. He explains why and on what condition he did not condemn that word, 521, 522 ff. At that time he especially desires to gain a hearing from the Emperor against Valens and Ursacius, 521. He writes from exile to his daughter, 525, to dissuade her from vain ornaments and costly clothes, 527 ff.; and sends her a morning and evening hymn, 528.

Hilary is present at the synod of the Easterners at Seleucia, II, 572; how he conducts himself there, 572. There, being tested by one of the Anomoeans, he prudently investigates heretical impiety, 574. At Constantinople he personally presents a booklet to the Emperor, 543; he asks that the present agent of his exile be brought forward to confess the falsehoods he has committed, 544; he seeks a hearing concerning the faith while the synod is divided, 549. He leaves it to the Emperor’s decision how far and in what manner he should command him to speak, 544; he promises that he will say everything conducive to peace between East and West, with honour to the empire and the imperial faith, 549.

Hilary demonstrates that he wrote against Constantius not from any fault of human agitation, II, 563, 565; he longs for martyrdom, 561, 564. He attempts to publish a grave and multifaceted work, 620, from the place where the matter occurred, 620; with what purpose, 621. Letters from the Easterners were addressed to Hilary and sent by him into Gaul, II, 698. In their reply, the Gauls deny that they have peace with those with whom he had denied that he would have peace, 700.

Auxentius was accustomed to denounce Hilary as a heretic, II, 599; as one causing schisms everywhere, 602. Their meeting, 597. Once Auxentius’ fraud was exposed, Hilary is ordered to depart from Milan, II, 598; he despises the synods assembled against him by Auxentius, 600.

How modestly Hilary thinks of himself, II, 519. He calls himself the most unlearned of all, 461; testifies that he can explain the meaning of his own faith only with the greatest difficulty in words, 461; asks that no judgment be made of him before the end of the book, 461, 480, 500. Unwilling and trembling, he speaks about the Trinity, 29; he testifies that words, not understanding, fail him, 499; by humility and faith he supplies what is lacking in words, 50. Hilary’s faith concerning the holy Trinity, II, 439 ff. The character of his faith in the equality of Father and Son, 146, 147. Having attained the wisdom of God which is folly to the world, 105. He understands God by veneration alone, 402; why he is secure concerning his faith, 547, 550; how greatly he defers to the Word of God, 206. He believes God concerning all things just as they have been spoken by Him, 61; he speaks not from himself but as taught by God, 141; he always prays that he may be able to speak worthily, 499. For understanding the Scriptures and expressing them suitably, he asks for fellowship with the prophetic and apostolic Spirit, 24; he can receive no greater reward for the use of speech than to serve God, 24. Hilary’s prayer that he may always preserve the faith he professed at his regeneration, 444.

In interpreting the Scriptures, Hilary leaves each person to his own judgment, I, 426; he himself cannot adapt his discourse except to what he understands, 426. Leaving each to his own understanding, he treats what he has perceived according to the gift of spiritual grace, 581. He answers those who might suppose that by his interpretations he does violence to truth, 506 ff.; he shows that he does not pursue spiritual meanings in vain, 457; how modestly he departs from others’ opinions, 417; refutes what he does not approve, 466; judges others, II, 508; or states his own opinion, 508.

The course Hilary follows against heretics, II, 215. He speaks under the watch of all heretics seeking something to criticize, 176; secure because he ascends by apostolic, not his own, steps, 176. He resists heretics by the very statements with which they assail the faith, 279, 378, 391; he convicts them by the very statements through which they try to deceive, 107. How cautiously he refuted the Arians, 105; how cautiously he moderated the demonstration of the whole faith, 439. Hilary’s ardent charity, II, 145. He takes care to seek peace when lost, restore it when disturbed, and hold it when found, 593. In the book *On the Synods* he wishes to advance nothing except toward the benefit of unity, 510. At Constantinople he promises to say everything for the peace of East and West, 549.

Hilary will never desire peace except with those who maintain the Nicene faith, II, 600. Adhering to the Nicene faith, he has no need of other formulas, 580. He is afraid to commit Arian blasphemies to a letter, 599. Unwillingly he sets down the Sirmian blasphemy, 464. Whoever is an Arian is, for him, the devil, 600. Hilary’s indulgence toward Arians, II, 563. His reverence toward the Emperor, 506. His moderation toward them in the books *On the Trinity*. See Preface to vol. II, no. 9.

What Hilary ordinarily thinks and preaches concerning Christ’s passion, I, 113. He taught that suffering befell Christ, 142, note. He did not hold that the Word departed from Christ’s flesh when it died, II, 267, note. Whether all things were created by God simultaneously and at once, 417, ibid., note; 432, note.

HILARIUS, deacon and legate of Liberius, II, 674.

A certain appellative name for goats, I, 205 ff. Whether “today” is appropriate to the eternal generation of the Word, I, 43. What a holocaust is, I, 204.

Man is not vanity, but like vanity, I, 613. In the Scriptures he is often signified by the name “waters,” 451; likewise often by the name “flesh,” 129, 185. Nothing among God’s earthly works is more excellent than man, 334. Nothing is more lovable to God, 531, 532. The prerogatives of man, 531 ff. God is the author of human origin, II, 333. Man is the race of God, I, 229. God bestowed upon man from Himself the elements of life and spirit, 229. Man has his origin from nothing and after time, II, 417.

Human origin possesses this dignity: that it is proper for it first to be considered in itself, I, 336; next, that man was formed not by a hand but by the hands of God, 336, 561. He was made by “hands” because, from two kinds, he was established by a double beginning into one living being sharing in reason, 236; and because the formation of one who was not solitary involved a threefold operation, 338. The formation of man displays a threefold operation of God, 229, note; 338; 493 ff. In man’s creation are signified the maker, the thing made, and the exemplar, II, 85. Man is comprised of two natures, spiritual and earthly, I, 492; lowly and heavenly, ibid. He contains within himself an inner and an outer nature differing from one another, 337. The inner and outer man, 595. The inner man is the soul; the outer, the body, 493. The whole man is formed from soul and flesh, 111.

Man is the one rational, understanding, discerning, sentient animal on earth, I, 335. He was created first according to the soul, then according to the body, 337 ff., 493. According to the body he was fashioned from earth, 337; according to the soul he was made from no foreign substance, I, 337. Body and soul are held together by a covenant of a certain breathed Spirit of God, 337. Souls and bodies proceed daily for us by God’s hidden power, 266. Each person is a compound of soul and body, 90.

Man received at the beginning of creation God’s likeness according to his origin, I, 650. He is made according to the common image of Father and Son, II, 108 ff. What is made according to God’s image concerns the dignity of the mind, I, 337. Man is fashioned in the substance of his soul according to God’s image, 423; according to the soul he is made in God’s image, 493. He is not God’s image, but an exemplar of God’s image and likeness, 337. He is incorporeal and something divine, 337 ff.; he imitates the divine nature, 493. God’s image is consummated through glory, II, 406.

Man alone among living creatures shares in reason, I, 638. He was chosen either to use created things or to rule them, 197. Earthly things, both his own and others, are directed to man’s use; but man himself to nothing else, 335. He ought to use all things in order to know and venerate God, 335. Man was not begun by God for the origin of evil, II, 145. He was born to fly to heaven, I, 716. Those are impious who ascribe human birth and death to the necessity of nature, 20. Many deny man’s eternity in order to console their conscience for crimes, 622. Despair of eternal judgment overwhelms man—inclined and shaken toward vices, already falling, 167. Man is born for the knowledge of God, 541, 560. For this purpose he knows God: that he may become conformed to God, 614. To this extent he is accounted [such], ibid. He was brought forth into the knowledge of God in order that he might hope for progress from the knowledge of his Maker, 181.

Man’s eternity is shown from God’s goodness, I, 361. Reason itself suggests that it is not worthy of God, after granting man life and a share in counsel, to subject him to the failure of life, II, 7. Eternity was promised to man in God’s first word at his creation, I, 406. Men perceived themselves to have been born for spiritual and eternal goods, II, 3 ff. God perfected man, a rational animal, with life and consciousness for the purpose of bestowing His eternity, I, 38. He established his advancement toward that end by the merit of an innocent life, ibid. He created him free, ibid. He deterred him from evil by punishments and invited him to good by rewards, 39.

Man does not attain consummation by himself, I, 370; yet the merit of attaining it comes from the beginning of the will, 370. Man’s proper duty is to call upon God, 638; and to offer others faith, justice, and every affection of goodwill, 785. It was no more difficult for God to assume man than to form him in such an ordering of nature and life, 167. When man is something great, 335. Through vices he loses his own name, so that he is called serpent, horse, and so forth, 335.

The devil envied God’s benefits to man, I, 677; he must be conquered by the man whom he cast down, 677. Man’s body and soul were born to be one in heaven, and fall as one upon earth, 717. All human beings were begotten from the earth in the first parent Adam, 196. In the error of the one Adam, all went astray, 758. Man was expelled from paradise in the sin of the first man, 573; through the transgression of the first parent he was cast out from blessed rest, 635.

The wretchedness of human life began from Adam, not with Adam, I, 630. This is not his own [condition], but that which was first established in man, 630. What the nature of the first man was like, 608. The prophet desires to return to this, 608; yet he does not claim it as his own merit, 608. Nor is it granted in this life, 608. In Adam’s crime man became an exile from that Zion in which life exists without fear, sin, or pain, 549, 551. So long as he dwells here, he does not truly live, 389. So long as he lives here, he cannot be pure, 290. Bodily weakness and incentives to vice compel him to be imperfect, 291. Man is born and lives amid vices, 470. Man’s origin from God is holy; from bodily contagion it is defiled, 423. Man is driven toward vices by the instinct of nature, 21. Men are unskilled, fugitives, filthy, dead without hope, dark without law, II, 57. Man, subject to various impulses, cannot be equal [to himself], I, 98. Error is man’s due, 595. A cloud of darkness stands in the way of mortal eyes, 291. After Adam’s sin, human beings are held in ignorance of God and in the delight of every vice, 719.

How many things exceed human understanding, I, 491 ff. It cannot comprehend God, II, 314. It does not penetrate God’s secrets, I, 490. It cannot grasp that one thing can be simultaneously within and outside another, II, 49. How limited our understanding is, and how it fails in contemplating infinite things, 422. Man does not comprehend certain bodily acts of Christ, 52. He ought not to be the judge of God’s omnipotence and mysteries, 439. What is unintelligible to man is possible to God, 49. Human ignorance, I, 361; II, 33. Man does not know the cause, rationale, or end of his origin, I, 338, 361. The devout confession of human weakness is to know from God this alone: that God is, 491. Though he perceives the movement, life, or rationale of his own discerning mind, he does not understand it, II, 440. He is ignorant of many other things belonging to himself, II, 440. Ignorant in his own affairs with equanimity, he is ignorant in God’s affairs with insolence, 33. He perceives many things later through reason than through hearing, 390. Defects of human speech, I, 110. The human mind possesses of itself a nature capable of understanding God, but not the light of knowledge, II, 48.

Man cannot reach the knowledge of God by his own powers, II, 116. He is unworthy for God to make Himself knowable to him, I, 613. Our nature could not know the unknowable except through our nature, 614. Man needs God’s kindness, 527. He needs the light of God’s Word for every course of action, 361. The weakness of man in apprehending God’s things: how it is strengthened by faith, II, 66 ff. God instructed man by sacred writings in the knowledge of Himself, 145. How often the Lord has provided for human salvation, I, 95. The division of humankind into three, I, 704.

Man, pleasing to God in creation, displeasing through sin, found favour in Christ, I, 650. It was not alien to God’s goodness to restore to him life in Himself and eternity, 229. How He accomplished this, 230. By the Incarnation man acquired this: that he might be God, II, 286. Through the mystery of the Incarnation, man was born into God, 325. The one advanced into God by Christ, 261. To make man worthy of God’s habitation is Christ’s greatest work, I, 504. How much this was Christ’s concern, 505. The man consecrated as God’s eternal temple, 788. The man assumed by the Son of God is God’s house, 186. Christ took in every defect of human corruption, 809. As God has apprehended man, so God must be apprehended by man, 58. The man whom Christ had assumed He brought back as a gift awaited by God the Father, 677. How human beings suffered and were exalted in Christ, 186.

Man’s health is only begun here; after the resurrection it will be perfect, I, 635. Who is the carnal man, 72; who the natural man, ibid.; who the spiritual man, ibid. The garments of the new man, 494. Man, as man, ought to fear God; as a subject, to pray; as one affected by benefits, to love, 628. We ourselves must restrain ourselves by our own power from every evil way, so that henceforth we may keep God’s word, 358. A person passing through the night of ignorance, snares, weaknesses, desires, and vices must pray and work, 524.

God takes account of human weakness, I, 605. If faith remains in man, the defence of heavenly powers is present with him in every danger, 557. Man acts under the watch of angels, 557. He owes himself wholly to God, 781, and all that is his, 447. The end of human life and death is resurrection, II, 402. After the law of death, man will remain eternal through God’s sanctification, I, 423.

*Homoiousios* is nowhere written, II, 509. For Catholics it is irrelevant to faith; by Arians it is wickedly anathematized, 581. The bare word *homoiousios* is not without cause for offence, 515. What pious understanding of this word is, 505. There is also an impious one, ibid., note. Hilary mentioned *homoiousios* unwillingly, 522. On what condition it should be accepted, 521 ff. How many bishops proclaimed this term at Seleucia, 572. Some of them advanced certain things piously in words, 573. Those who defend *homoiousios* condemn the leaders of the Anomoeans, 574; but are afterwards defeated by them, 574. A letter on the exposition of *homoousios* and *homoiousios* was brought to Sirmium, 508.

The authors of the Sirmian formula are compelled to confess that they did not know the meaning of *homoousios* and *homoiousios*, II, 506. The Gospels and Apostles made known to Hilary the meaning of *homoousios* and *homoiousios*, 518. *Homoousios* was devised by the Easterners and received by the Westerners in holiness and faithfulness, 698. It was proclaimed by earlier bishops, 73. It is the faith of antiquity and the security of piety, 581. This word was employed for the greatest security of the faith, 75; in it lies the greatest and sole safeguard of religion, 576. Before the Council of Nicaea Arians attempted to evade *homoousios*, or “that of one substance,” 79, 81.

*Homoousios* contains both consciousness of faith and ready occasion for deceit, II, 500. When it is rightly proclaimed, 500. *Homoousios* is open to a threefold wrong understanding, 73, 500; it can be spoken piously and kept silent piously, 502. In what context it may be spoken piously and denied impiously, 501, 502. It ought not to be proclaimed bare, 501. The Arians pretend that they reject it because of its wrong meanings, 73. The Church condemns these meanings, 74. The Council of Nicaea approved *homoousios* in a sense free from suspicion, 510 ff. After the Nicene synod, the Fathers interpreted its proper force reverently, 518. *Homoousios* is not to be disapproved, even though it is commonly understood wrongly, 511.

*Homoousios* was condemned by an anathema at Ancyra, II, 517, note. On what pretext it was rejected by the Easterners, 509. Why it was rejected by the Fathers who condemned Paul of Samosata, 509. The Samosatene confessed *homoousios* wrongly, 512. Eighty bishops once rejected it, 513. In rejecting it, these established what the Nicene Fathers established by approving it, 513.

At Seleucia only the Egyptians steadfastly maintained *homoousios*, II, 572. What Hilary understands by *homoousios*, 510, 514. Objections against the term are removed, 514. The Gauls explain the meaning of this word, 698; and, under penalty of anathema, forbid any other view of God and the Lord than that expressed by this word, 700.

Honour is either the appearance or the dignity of a nature, II, 221. The honour of the same things is not different, 412. Equality of honour is something proper to equality of power and nature, 294. Only things of the same nature are equal in honour, 275. Worldly honour is the devil’s business, I, 679. Contempt for earthly honour is the kingdom of heaven, 362. One ought not presumptuously to claim any honour, but earn it by works of humility, 770. To receive honour from one another is characteristic of unbelievers, II, 274. Honour must be sought from God, II, 274. The honour of the servant belongs to the honour of the sender, 57. It must not be denied to anyone who fears God, I, 76 ff. God receives honour from us only through God, II, 116.

HONORATUS, II, 690, twice.

Exhortation has much force when a fall entices; it has more when reason leads, I, 216. What *Hosanna* means in Hebrew, I, 772. What humiliation signifies, I, 352. Offences precede humiliation, 332, 333; humiliation is their correction, 332, 333, 340.

Humility of heart, the greatest of all virtues, is the adornment of noble and royal birth, I, 365. In humility consists the head and sum of all commandments, 403. All the names and rewards of faith are contained in it, 403. Humility is the greatest work of our faith, 497. In preserving humility lies remembrance of the law, 404. The causes and reward of humility, 680. To consider God’s magnificence and mercy is conducive to humility, 404. Examples of humility, I, 445. David displays humility alone, 404. Christ provided both the command and the example of humility, 364. The reward of Christ’s humility, 365. Honour must be earned by works of humility, not presumptuously claimed, 770. Hidden mysteries are revealed by the Father to the humble, 576.

Humility ought not to lack constancy, I, 75. Let us be humble in heart but exalted in understanding and soul, 498. How one free from vice can profess himself vicious, 462.

HYMENIUS, II, 632. A hymn and a song are one and the same, I, 117. The celebrated sounds of hymns occur among divine offices, 196. Every profane hearer must be frightened by them, 196. With them we fight against the devil; by them our victory is shown, ibid. How the mind is distracted amid divine hymns, 551. Morning and evening hymns, 190. Morning hymn, II, 529. Fragment of another hymn, ibid.

Hypocrisy follows a falling away from faith, II, 322.

HYRENIUS, II, 680.

I
JACOB: supplanter, I, 105. He foreshadowed that the Gentiles would by faith supplant the earlier people, 106. He was a figure of the Church, 528 et seq. Jacob, the unexpected husband of an unknown wife, 479. Mourning the funeral of his living son because of the fratricidal lie of his brothers, ibid. God came to him in a man, II, 94. In the man he understood and saw God, I, 123, 150, 429; II, 115—not with bodily eyes, but with the eyes of faith, II, 115. With the eyes of faith he beheld God in a body, I, 106. The true Jacob: his prerogatives, 642.

Boasting is to be avoided by believers, I, 678.

Blessed is the loss of oneself, I, 751.

JANUARIUS, II, 632.

Jaundice is cured by looking upon a galbulus [a yellowish bird], I, 339; ibid., note.

The empty fear of idolaters, I, 102. Idolaters seek honor for the gods they have made for themselves by the price of metals, 537. They themselves should be left like their images, without the breath of life, 538. How far they are from the knowledge of the true God, 356.

The overthrow of idolatry, I, 559. Idolatry is abandoned daily, 228.

Christians rejoice in fasts, I, 461. Fasting during the time of the Lord’s Passion, 746. Whoever sees a Christian feasting on a fast day is angered with zeal for God, 392. Many fast because they fear rebuke from their pastors, 356. The faults of those fasting, 399. Let the conscience of one fasting be pure, and let good works accompany it, 689 et seq. The Apostles observed no fast during the days of Pentecost, 8. The same has been established for Sundays, ibid.

JEREMIAH: whether he is to precede Christ’s final coming, I, 769. The work of Baruch is attributed to Jeremiah, II, 130. By what authority Jeremiah’s name is prefixed to certain psalms, I, 3.

Jeropolis, II, 667.

Jerusalem, slayer of the prophets, I, 134. Jerusalem and Sion are the same place, 640. Only within Jerusalem were the priesthood, burnt offering, and the rest lawful, 155. Jerusalem did not confer sanctification upon its inhabitants, 452. Its destruction is foretold, I, 729. Jerusalem is not to exist when it has become worthy, 788. Jews were allowed by the Roman ruler to go around Jerusalem, but not to enter it, 151. They were accustomed to circle it as consolation for their present miseries, 147. The desolation of Jerusalem, 452. Jerusalem was captured and destroyed by the Babylonians, 511; later it was captured and burned by the Romans and now exists no more, 511. Jerusalem was built by Solomon, 466, and restored by Zerubbabel, 467. Today it offers only the ashes of its conflagration and the ugliness of hideous ruins, 467. Jerusalem, city of peace, I, 640. It was established as a prefiguration of the Church, that is, of Christ’s body, 687. Spiritual Jerusalem, 634, 635, 640. Earthly Jerusalem is an image of the heavenly, 434. Heavenly Jerusalem is the Church, 454: the harmonious assembly of the faithful and souls sanctified by the sacraments of the Church, 514. Every saint is, in one respect, Jerusalem, 553. Heavenly Jerusalem is built throughout the age of all generations, 434, until the time of the blessed and divine kingdom, 466. Eternal Jerusalem, the city of saints surrounding God, 159. Jerusalem, the assembly thronged by angels, 235.

JESUS son of Nun: a prophet of Christ’s name, II, 436.

JESUS: Savior, I, 209, 343, 409. Jesus is the name of our Lord derived from the body, 683. It is the designation of the man born of Mary, 200. How he was desired by the prophets, 409 et seq. Demons cannot bear the name of Jesus, 93. Men take it up for salvation, ibid.

IGINUS, II, 690.

The birth of the Son of God is illustrated by the example of fire, II, 199. Whether the fire of the Babylonian furnace possessed the nature of burning, 352. For the three boys it was dew, I, 625. Fire that burns away and removes sins, 159.

The unwearied fire must be undergone in judgment, I, 294. The saints will not feel that fire, ibid., note. The fire of judgment is a kind of baptism, 290. The fire of judgment, to which the wicked are assigned, 507, 694. It will remove the wicked so that they may not contemplate Christ, 141. Fire absorbs sinners with the sensation of punishment before they rise again, 141. In the wicked, the fuel of eternal fire will be eternal, 694.

Not knowing what one believes has not so much pardon as reward, II, 219. An example of ignorance without peril to faith, 204. Ignorance belongs to the nature of human frailty, I, 607. Error through ignorance is human, II, 508. Ignorance gives hope of pardon, 170. God has moderated the deserving of punishment for an error made in ignorance, 133. Human ignorance excuses Peter from guilt, 162. How dangerous ignorance of God’s commandments is, I, 296. Voluntary ignorance has no pardon: why, 405. Psalm CXVIII instructs human ignorance in morals, discipline, and the knowledge of God, 272. Ignorance of divine things must be confessed, or understanding of what is unknown must be sought by prayer, 338. Ignorance obtains knowledge of the truth solely through persistence in prayer, 697.

God forgives us without measure and wishes us likewise to forgive others without measure, I, 760.

Ilium, II, 666.

Illyricum rejects the proceedings at Ariminum, II, 703. In Illyricum, the founders of the Arian and Aetian heresies had long been known, 704.

Image, form, countenance, and face do not differ, I, 257. An image is a conceived and undivided likeness of one thing made equal to another, II, 467. It must have the species, nature, and essence of its author, 467. An image is not true unless it possesses everything possessed by that of which it is the image, 377. The Apostle calls the Son the image of God, but with an addition, II, 578. In what sense Christ is the image of God, 247 et seq. The Son is the living image of God, 205. The image of God, the firstborn of every creature, is not man, I, 337. There is a certain exemplar of God’s image in man, I, 337. In what sense the image of God is in man, 493; how it is brought to completion in man, II, 406. The Apostles obtain the perfect image of Christ, 711.

Ancient images of refined nobility, I, 751.

Human immortality is defended, I, 781 et seq. God created us for eternity, not for death, 412. Very many have perceived themselves to be immortal, II, 3, 7. Hope of immortality, 680; I, ibid., note. Having become immortal, they will need no food but will live from God, 239.

He who is impatient under afflictions insults God, I, 392.

The emperors convened the Synod of Sardica, II, 622. Imperial letters to terrify those unwilling to attend the council, 659.

What is imperfect, I, 577, 578. That is imperfect which subsists from its author in another, II, 65. Our bodies compel us now to be imperfect, I, 291.

The distinction between the ungodly and the sinner, I, 19. The ungodly cannot bear the presence of the righteous, as though it were a burden upon their conscience, 338. They are servants of spiritual wickedness for harassing the saints, 128. The labors of the ungodly are useless, 488. Their end, II, 391. The ungodly will not be judged, I, 29: why, 28.

Ungodliness has no wisdom or prudence in itself, II, 120. It understands true faith with difficulty: why, 114. It does not grasp understanding, 238. How it is mocked by God, I, 37. Professed ungodliness is beyond shame, II, 196. It is no lesser impiety to invent God than to deny him, I, 20.

An imprecation does not apply to a prophet, I, 489.

Incarnation. It was necessary for us that God should be born as man, II, 712. Otherwise our diseases could not be taken away, I, 66; nor would we bear fruit, II, 302. Neither we nor any before us have merited otherwise than through faith in Christ, incarnate or to be incarnate, I, 372. The Law foretold that the Word would become flesh, 123. The sayings of all the prophets agree concerning Christ’s coming, 253. Psalm CXXXI teaches the mystery of flesh assumed by the Son of God, 500. The prophets taught that the only-begotten God would come in a body; the Apostles, that he had come, 208.

The mystery of the Incarnation is not to be disbelieved because we do not understand it; rather, we shall be able to understand if we believe, II, 10. The Holy Spirit illumines our difficult faith concerning God’s Incarnation, 47. Was it harder for God to assume a man than to form him within so great an order of his nature and life? I, 167. God could not descend into man except by emptying himself from the form of God, II, 412. To have emptied the form of God is a power of divine might, ibid. Christ’s Incarnation is not weakness but mystery; not necessity but loving-kindness, II, 379, 380. Heaven is bent down when the power and honor of heavenly things are brought down to earth, I, 615.
