By the Incarnation glory was acquired not for the Word but for the man, II, 288. This was acquired for the man: that he might be God, 286. The Word became flesh so that flesh might advance into God, II, 9. The birth of human weakness was assumed by immortal nature, I, 473. God did not decline into man; rather, man advanced into God, II, 325. The immutability of the Word after assuming flesh is declared by the term “dwelling,” 9. The Son of God must also be believed to be the Son of Man, I, 749, 750. Neither without the other offers any hope of salvation, 749. The Father’s nature did not experience the assumption of flesh, II, 286, but remained outside the assumption of human sufferings, 298. The reward of the incarnate Word, I, 472, 473. The heritage and reward of the incarnate Word are the nations whom he begets as sons, 472. Through the Incarnation every human being is in the Lord, 66. In Christ we remain through faith in the body assumed by him, II, 302. We are unable to render anything worthy in return for the benefit of the Incarnation, 41.

The nature of incense, I, 592. It is composed of stacte, onycha, galbanum, and frankincense, ibid. It signifies the four kinds of prayers, 593; or that from the four elements a sacrifice of praise is offered to God, 593. Prayers are signified by incense, 205.

The indignation of devout love, I, 247.

The lower region has many inhabitants, I, 50—and they are alive, ibid. The abode of hell is signified by the deep of the sea, I, 250. The abode of infernal death is signified by a pit, 258. It seems due to man to go to the infernal abodes, 115. David had to endure hell before being saved, 374. It is a law of human necessity that, when bodies are buried, souls descend to the lower world, 572. Why Christ did not exempt himself from this, ibid. Hell: a prison, I, 603. To those set in that prison Christ preached resurrection, 603. An exhortation to the saints resting in hell, 344; ibid., note. When Christ descended to hell, he was not absent from paradise, II, 345. When Christ descended there, hell did not hold his saints, I, 149. Hell, the punitive lake, I, 607. Hell, chaos and torrents of flame, II, 344. The punishments of hell, I, 124. Avenging hell receives the wicked when they depart from the body, 59. Those dwelling on earth appear to them to be in the heights, 59; ibid., note.

An unbeliever is like one shipwrecked, I, 85. He is outside Christ’s body, 86, although by nature remaining in it, 87, because through the assumption of our nature he has been received as an inhabitant, 87. Unbelievers make war upon God’s words, II, 63. What would they dare against God’s works if permitted? 63. Unbelievers become children of the devil, I, 674.

All unbelief is folly, II, 66. It is altogether a work of the devil, I, 750. The cause of unbelief, II, 66. Unbelief was prefigured in Peter’s mother-in-law, I, 701. Unbelief, mother of our soul, 719; mother-in-law of our will, 719; wife of the Gentiles, 739. Pleasure, daughter of unbelief, 739. Unbelief concerning God’s promises is sin against the Holy Spirit, 696. God abandons those possessed by unbelief, 748. Christ has removed every occasion of unbelief concerning the resurrection, 694.

Who are the lowest members of the Church, I, 576.

The infinity of the eternal Father, II, 30. Whoever devoutly pursues infinite things, even if he never attains them, nevertheless advances by advancing, II, 33. What is infinite in God escapes the recurrent reach of our understanding, 422.

Human nature’s weakness was assumed by the immortal God, I, 473. Weakness in the only-begotten God is ours rather than natural to him, 120.

One must seek not the vengeance, but the conversion, of enemies, I, 341. Love of enemies is an evangelical command, 371. Christ taught us to love all enemies by not rejecting Judas’s kiss, 804. Through love of enemies we are called both to God’s inheritance and to his imitation, 688. We are commanded to love our enemies, not God’s enemies, I, 583. God’s enemies ought to be enemies to us, 393. Man’s spiritual enemies, 608. The strongest enemies are demonic powers, 614.

Who are workers of iniquity, I, 145. The difference under the Law between working iniquity and declining from it, 456. The distinction between iniquity and sin, 494. To pursue iniquity and one’s own desires is no different, 96. Whatever is outside the Law is iniquitous, 95. The devil is the author of every iniquity, 599. The chief root of iniquities is the love of money, 169. Iniquity brings corruption, 95. The working of iniquity renders prayers contemptible, 119. Iniquity is the less worthy of pardon in proportion as equity was not unknown, 786.

The wicked, while falsely claiming to possess the truth of doctrine, do not possess it, I, 345. They are vessels, servants, workers, and bearers of the devil’s wickedness, 485. They are prepared for the conflagration of judgment, 675. Immediately after death they pay the penalties of hell, 59. The punishment of the wicked in hell, 124. To what extent it is permitted to hate the wicked, 372.

The devil is the author of human injuries; human beings are his servants, I, 484. Believers are accustomed to suffer injuries, 444. Those who grieve over their own injuries and the sins of their persecutors, 444. God alone can help them, 444. When a saint is struck, he grieves not his own condition but that of the striker, 321. One who inflicts injury is worthy of compassion, not anger, 484. The greater the increase of injuries done to saints, the greater the departure from God’s Law, 400. The Gospels require that revenge for injuries be overlooked, 688. Evangelical law does not allow revenge for an injury to be demanded from anyone, 687. One mindful of injuries may not pass into the designation of God’s household, 681. Injuries and insults by which we are made equal to the Lord must be embraced as glory, 715.

Evils will not be lacking for the unjust, I, 113.

One who is unbegotten is not thereby at once timeless, II, 476. There are not two unbegotten beings, I, 529. The Church knows not two, II, 298. Unbegottenness is one power, 82. The Father alone is unbegotten, 442. Unbegottenness belongs to one, 496. “Unbegotten” is nowhere found written, 575. Unbegottenness and birth differ in word, not in nature, 303.

The innocents: martyrs, I, 672. The Church does not mourn them, but their killers, 672.

Innocence, the daughter of wisdom, produces blessedness, I, 482. How many things lie in wait for it, 605. Without God’s grace a human being cannot attain knowledge and true practice of an innocent and devout life, 273 et seq. Innocence according to the judgment of the world does not suffice for attaining eternity, 273.

The distinction between *inquirere* (“to inquire”) and *perscrutari* (“to investigate thoroughly”), I, 386.

Arrogance toward others is vain, I, 74. See Pride.

God inspires prophets throughout every period of the Law, I, 96. The author of the Psalms speaks as one inspired, 183.

The islands of Ocean have churches established by the Apostles, I, 70.

Understanding is the proper function of human reason, I, 97. It is hindered by carnal pleasures, 97. It is entirely in the head, 689. What may fall within human understanding, II, 403. Our understanding does not perceive eternal things, 404. It cannot attain invisible things except through visible things, I, 429. Understanding has no slight merit, 97. The gift of understanding must necessarily be sought from God by prayer, 227, 338. Understanding must be requested from God lest a false one be introduced by the devil, 382. Understanding of Scripture is God’s gift, 457. All understanding is from God, 357; II, 390. It is also from the Lord, 390. It is the chief gift of the Spirit, I, 396. It is given to those desirous of understanding, 357; II, 390, through the merit of faith, I, 390.

The proper manner of intelligently seeking God, I, 96. Commandments fulfilled in action make us understanding, 359. We must begin on our part in order that we may merit perfect understanding, 359. One who has received the spirit of understanding needs diligent searching, whose fruit is retention of what has been repeatedly considered, 306. The fruit of understanding is to practise what has been learned, 358. For one lacking understanding, it is prudence to ask wisely, 306.

Since no translators dared alter the order of the words, they explained the precise force of the words less clearly, I, 228. Why the translators of the Seventy are to be preferred to others, 31, 33. See Septuagint.

“I call upon”: those whom God hears when they call upon him, I, 628. Those who act wickedly do not call upon God, 101.

JOB: encomium, I, 244. Job, blameless, 97. Having passed through every warfare of temptations, 389. Glorious and blessed victor over human sufferings, 333. Free from the Law, he triumphs over the enemy of the Law, 308. Job worshipped God solely with a mind unmixed with vices, II, 712.

JOHN: he bore the form of the Law, I, 720, 739. To be strengthened for the preaching of the Gospel, II, 347. Still enclosed in his mother’s womb, he bursts forth into speech, 41. By the very character of his condition he prophesied, I, 720. He was a lamp to Jews and Gentiles, 362. What John’s place, preaching, clothing, and food signify, 572 et seq. John, preacher of repentance, points out Christ, I, 516. He did not fail to know Christ, 721, 723. Why he sent disciples to him, 720. The sublimity of his doctrine is a miracle no less than the sight of the blind, and so forth, II, 34. By the example of the injury done to him, John preceded the Lord’s Passion, I, 754. John’s glory, 723.

JOHN the Evangelist: pre-eminently a preacher of spiritual matters, II, 350. His prerogatives, 165. Whether he died, 162, note. He is the author of the Apocalypse, 165.

JONAM, II, 632.

JONAH, a figure of Christ, I, 747. An imitator of the Lord’s death, 244.

JOSEPH: Samaria was assigned to him by Jacob, I, 157.

JOSEPH, carpenter, I, 727; ibid., note. He and Mary were of one tribe, 669. That Joseph’s descent rather than Mary’s is recounted in Christ’s genealogy is of no consequence, 669. Joseph’s different visions of the angel, 673. He bears the image of the Apostles, to whom Christ was believed to be carried about, 16. Joseph’s sons by an earlier marriage, 671.

JOSEPH, disciple of the Lord: he bears the image of the Apostles, I, 809.

JOVIANUS, deacon, II, 706.

The stages and effects of anger, I, 145. There ought to be no time for anger in us, 760. One should not be angry with those from whom one suffers anything, but should pity their lot, 485. Anger without cause has in the Gospel the same penalty as homicide in the Law, 684.

The wrath of God is the punishment of one who endures it, I, 40, or the vengeance appointed for sinners, ibid. God’s wrath does not arise from a sudden emotion, 40. How restrained it presently is, 41 et seq. God’s wrath is not a movement of a mind inflamed toward the desire for vengeance, but the appointment of the punishment into which one worthy of punishment falls, 254. It is provoked by no crime more than pride, 295. How it may be escaped, 156. The merciful anger of fathers toward children, and of God toward human beings, 155.

Irenopolis, II, 631.

To mock and to deride do not differ, I, 37.

ISAAC prefigured Christ’s discipline in this world, I, 119.

ISAAC of Lueto, II, 667.

ISAIAH. See Esaias.

ISCHYRAS, II, 666, note. See Scyrus.

ISION, II, 666, note.

The boundaries of the ISHMAELITES, I, 423.

ISRAEL, carnal and spiritual, I, 435, 67. God’s benefits toward carnal Israel, 435. Its ungrateful disposition toward God, 435. Testimony against its crimes, 436. It will be judged by the Gentiles, 436. For forty years it lived in the manner and condition of angels, 733. It was captured by the Assyrians, 458. It will leave its name to God’s elect, II, 122. How deeply its salvation lay upon the Apostles’ hearts, I, 746. From Israel come two callings to the Gospel, 769, 771. Israel’s privilege of salvation is reserved, 745. The firstfruits of faith are expected from it, 745.

Israel: “seeing God,” I, 67. He foreshadowed that the Gentiles would see God, 106. He is worthy to be called Israel who beholds God by faith, 429; who contemplates God with the eyes of the mind, 447. Few are Israel, 538. The Savior was given to faithful, not carnal, Israel, 104. Entrance into heaven is difficult for proud Israel, 763.

The Italian bishops, about A.D. 353, are compelled to obey Arian opinions, II, 673. Liberius reads and communicates to the Italian bishops the letters he received, 672. Constantius addresses a letter to the Italian bishops assembled at Ariminum, 683. Italy, recognizing the deception suffered at Ariminum, returned to the Nicene faith, 703. Letter of the Italians to the bishops of Illyricum after the Synod of Ariminum, 703. Liberius writes to the Italian bishops concerning those who sinned at Ariminum, 702.

God’s journeys seen under the Law and after the Law, I, 233.

The jubilee year, I, 405.

What jubilation commonly means, I, 195. Jubilation and a cry of exultation differ, 196.

JUDAH was captured by the Babylonians, I, 458. The cities of Judaea, after the victory of Antiochus and the Babylonians, were destroyed in war by the Roman ruler, I, 259. Judaea was deserted by God’s dwelling, 673.

The JEWS are prefigured in Doeg the betrayer, I, 80. The beginning of the Jews’ origin according to sanctification is Abraham’s origin, 528. Before the Law the devil held the Jews, 733; but was expelled from them by the Law, 733. After grace had been granted to the Gentiles, he returned to them, 733, with vengeance for the grace they had rejected, 734. The Jews revered God only, not also the Father, II, 122. God was accustomed to protect the Jews against their enemies by heavenly warfare, I, 160. How he abandoned them, ibid. The Jews’ excessive iniquity surpassed the benefit of their spiritual guardianship, I, 123.

The Jews’ ungrateful disposition toward God, I, 537. Hereditary unbelief, 673. How the Jewish people was powerful, and how it was wicked in every age, 81 et seq. The destruction of the Jews’ kingdom and Jerusalem is foretold, 729. In Christ’s age, the Jews consisted of many peoples, 34. Therefore they were rightly deprived of the kingdom, and the chief priests were unworthy of that title, 35. Earthly and dry Jews are signified by sands, 581. The privilege of the Gospel was owed to the Jews, 711. The Gentiles take beforehand the salvation prepared for them, 708. The fewness of Jews who will believe, 709. One part of the Jews believed through the Apostles; another will believe through Elijah, 792.

The Jews’ attachment to the Law, I, 713. Their feigned profession of faith, 713. The Jews boast that they possess the keys of heaven and are teachers of the Law, 357. While boasting in the Law, they are convicted by the Law of having done nothing rightly, 762. Their malice toward an excellent good, 83. Captivated by pleasure, they lost the Law, 739. They are prefigured in Herod, 739. They lost the Law because of want of faith, 734.

How culpable the Jews’ unbelief is, I, 725. They are not free of guilt, since they knew the Father’s testimony concerning Christ, II, 273. The Law had foretold to them that the Word would become flesh, I, 123. Their insults against Christ are more blameworthy than those of the Gentiles, 123. The faith of the Gentiles leaves the Jews without excuse, 732.

The Jews whose tongue is a deceitful razor, I, 83. How the Jews are scattered in truth, 113. How they are ensnared by writings and weighed down under the burden of the Law, 253. The Jews’ guilt and the punishment to be rendered them for Christ’s death, 31. The Jews ceased to be God’s, 616. Their right hand is iniquitous, 616.

The Jews’ penal blindness, I, 757. Their hardening, 724. Their just rejection, 724. Their lamentable captivity, 549. Their dispersion, spiritual famine, empty food, and impenitence, 147, 148, 151. Envy, 148. Disaster and destruction, 86 et seq., 88, 126. Captured by the Romans, the Jews endured every kind of punishment and misery, 232. Today they are exiles, slaves, and dispersed throughout the whole world, 511. They are forbidden entry into Jerusalem, 147; ibid., note; 151. They were accustomed to circle it as consolation for their present miseries, 147.

Various epithets for Jews alienated from God, I, 111. How they are deceived, 37, and given over to reproach, 135. How they are now submerged and divided in tongues, 122. Excluded from God’s justice, 255. Blotted from the book of the living and not written in the book of the righteous, 255.

After the atonement of the Passion, repentance and pardon remained open to the Jews, I, 125. Had they believed the Apostles, they would have obtained forgiveness, 786, 787. The Church mourns their destruction, 672. Why entrance into heaven is difficult for them, 764. The Jews did not fail to know that Christ would be the Son of God, but did not know who this Christ was, II, 170. They provoke God’s wrath against themselves because they deny his mercy toward the Gentiles, I, 200 et seq. They avoid every utterance about Christ, or its hearing, lest it penetrate them; they stop their ears with their hands, 805.

Jews who deny Christ’s divinity are refuted, I, 731. The Jews vainly refer Psalm CXXXI to David and not to Christ, 500, 501. How they may be convicted concerning Christ’s existence before Mary, II, 428. Their literal interpretation is rejected, I, 507. The Jews’ reverence for sacred books, 500. Their superstition in oaths, 687. When Jews are to be placed in the Church, 715. For the sake of the fathers they are to be converted at the end of the ages, 150 et seq., 159. With Moses and Elijah Christ will judge Israel, 753. How Jewish observance is of no benefit, 356.

JUDAS: how he was of one mind with, guide to, and known by Christ, I, 124. He was the devil’s instrument, 484. He was Satan, because he was animated by him, 605. He was not worthy of communion in the eternal mysteries, 799. Judas’s flattering speech, 125. He sought an occasion for theft from the collection of money, 125. Judas’s wickedness graphically described, 590. The time of his death is considered closely, 805.

The distinction between judge and king, I, 57. Secular judges must not hear cases involving clerics, II, 535.

The judicial seat: what the chair of pestilence is, I, 21.

Those judgments alone are truly considered judgments which are just, I, 363. The form of judicial proceedings, II, 539, 620, 604 et seq. Whose judgment is right, I, 404. What it is to render judgment, 378. The Son’s judgment derives from the Father’s judgment, II, 190. It belongs to Christ alone to pray to be judged in power, I, 109. Authority to judge is given to the saints, 651.

One must not judge hastily concerning the opinions of authors whom one reads, II, 462. It is reverent to reserve to God what belongs to him, 508. It is not lawful to judge concerning God’s promises, I, 695. To have judged wrongly in other matters is sin; in these matters judgment is the beginning of guilt, 695, 696. Why, 695. Those who will judge should first remember that they will be judged by God with the judgment by which they judge, II, 634. Judgments of minds are to be indicated not by words but by deeds, I, 422.

The distinction between God’s judgments and the judgments of God’s mouth, I, 286. Some judgments of God are eternal, others belong to the present: the former are unsearchable; what we may know of the latter, I, 339. How all judgments of God’s mouth are pronounced, when God’s judgments are inexpressible, 286. God’s judgments must always be confessed to be righteous, 339, 392. Many accuse them amid adversities, 392. In those things which we complain of suffering unjustly, they are just, 363. They are pleasant to a pure conscience, 313.

God’s judgment on earth, by which life after death is assigned to the righteous and punishment to the ungodly, anticipates the final judgment, I, 143.

The Father is said to know the day of judgment because he reveals it to the Son, II, 313; and the Son to be ignorant because he keeps it silent, 314. Why the Father placed it in his own power, 317. Christ’s not knowing it is an administration of silence, 316. Christ, though not ignorant of the day of judgment, is said not to know it so that it may remain hidden, 310. Why it is hidden, I, 310. Christ does not fail to know the day of judgment, since its time is in him and the day is his through the mystery, II, 305.

Despair of eternal judgment plunges a person into vices, I, 167. The preaching of it offends the kings of the world, 444. Constantius incurs the terror of judgment, II, 582. The remembrance of God’s judgment must not depart, I, 320. It stirs one to repentance, 45.

The place of the last judgment, I, 790. The order of judgment and resurrection, 27. Moses and Elijah will precede Christ’s coming, 769. The opinion of some concerning Enoch and Jeremiah, 769. All flesh must stand before Christ’s tribunal, 130. The division of the future judgment, 157. Judgment will concern those who are intermediate between godly and ungodly persons, between sins and faith, 28, 143. Why it will not concern others, 28. What sort of judgment will befall those who are ignorant and those who sin knowingly, II, 133.

God’s judgment is signified by the countenance, I, 572. The severity of God’s judgment is signified by the bow, 141. How fearful God’s judgment is, 294. To desire its desire is to seek that innocence for which it will no longer be fearful, 294. Mary will come under the severity of judgment, 294. In judgment one must undergo unwearied fire and grievous punishments for the soul that is to be cleansed from sins, 294. Those who will judge the Gentiles and the Jews, 732. The judgment of the wicked will take place by comparison with the righteous, 57. In judgment the wicked will be confounded by shame at their disgrace and by comparison with another’s honor, 104. How all will see Christ in the flesh, II, 59. The wicked will not go forth to meet Christ, caught up with the saints in the clouds, I, 262. Confounded by resurrection, repelled from Christ’s meeting, they are recalled to hell, 262. In judgment fire will remove the wicked so that they may not contemplate Christ, 141. The fire of judgment, 675. The wicked are prepared for burning in the conflagration of judgment, 675. Judgment concerning the devil, 345.

The yoke of the Law and the yoke of evangelical sanctification, I, 35. Christ’s yoke, 487. Why it is heavy and how it is softened, 750. Why it is sweet, 726. It is profitable to have assumed it from youth, 283.

JULIAN Caesar, I, 543.

Juliopolis, II, 666.

JULIUS, II, 625, 634, 680. He is called fellow-priest, 622. Through his presbyters and by letter he summons the Easterners to Rome, 629, 623. Letters were written to him from all Egypt and Alexandria, 670. The Sardican letter was sent to him, 629. Why Julius did not attend the Synod of Sardica, 629. He is deposed, 660: why, 662. He grants pardon to Ursacius and Valens: why, 635, 638.

JULIUS Thebeept, II, 632.

JUNIOR, II, 680; ibid., note. The younger David is set above his elders, I, 394. The younger people purchases the birthright of the elder, I, 394 et seq.

The religious obligation of swearing is undertaken from knowledge of the truth, I, 363. It is a matter of confirmed knowledge, 363. Those living in the simplicity of faith have no need of the religious obligation of swearing, 687. Why the practice of swearing was permitted in the Law and forbidden in the Gospel, 686. One who swears by Christ as the true God is to be praised for the religious seriousness of that oath, 176. Christ, true God, is sworn by every mouth of believers, II, 123.

The distinction between ordinances (*justificationes*) and the way of ordinances, I, 300. An ordinance is the work of a righteous matter, 332. Nothing happens except by God’s ordinance, 333. Heavenly ordinances are prefigured in earthly ones, 330, 333. The efficacies of heavenly ordinances, 318. The ordinances of the Law contain within themselves the shadow of holy ordinances, 300. They contain a great meditation upon future hope, 288. God’s ordinances are overlaid with the shadow of the Law, 398. Why they must be known, 398. The law of ordinances is contained in the disciplines of a devout heart, 306.

Ordinances consist in observing every individual kind of duty, I, 280. They are many and diverse, 280. Whoever does not keep them all does not possess God’s ordinance, 280. We must be helped and directed by God’s grace to keep the ordinances, 280. Knowledge of the ordinances is God’s gift, to be sought from him in prayer, 285.

No living person can be justified in God’s sight, I, 603, 606. The grace of justification, 635. From one it has abounded to all, 155. Justification by faith, 155. Justification through true faith in God the Father and our Lord will especially be proven in us, 281. The thief is saved through justification by faith, 808. Faith alone justifies, 705. There is no justification from faith if that faith is ambiguous, 691. Justification of the Spirit, II, 379, 380.

JUSTINUS, II, 690, 693.

An encomium of justice, I, 378. Christ is justice, 84. Who tempers the sweetness of God’s justice, 624. God’s justice is merciful and his mercy just; not so human justice and mercy, 625. The distinctive office of justice is to worship God, II, 712. What thirst for justice means, I, 681.

Praise must be given to God for justice that has been known, I, 281. The fruit of justice known is observance of the ordinances, 281. The language of justice is common, not its pursuit, 139. To will justice here will be fruit, so that it may come to pass, 72. Works of justice, without God’s mercy, will not suffice to merit perfect blessedness, 92. God’s mercy grants to the will for justice allowance for the defects of human changeability, 92. Justice is completed by faith, 720. Earlier justice is lost in the time of injustice, 76.

No one is righteous by the Law, I, 707. The righteous have a threefold state, 8. The life of the righteous is commendable through the practice of justice, 92. The righteous person is never without fear, 559. Through God’s great care he is multiplied in strength of soul, 559. Evils are ready to inspire fear in the righteous, but are not mingled with them, 113.

Earthly blessing has not been promised to the righteous, I, 479, but spiritual blessing, 479 et seq. The righteous suffer manifold tribulation, 346, 456. He does not pray that it be absent from him, but that he may be helped to endure it, 346. What tribulation is dangerous to him, 419. Which righteous persons, set amid afflictions, withstand the reproaches of the ungodly, 333. Whence they have confidence amid calamities, 112, 175. The weapons of the righteous against the devil’s assaults, 353.

The years of youth are to be dedicated to God, I, 398. The prerogative of one consecrated to God in youth, 283.

## L
In what way deceitful lips differ from a deceitful tongue, I, 419 ff. What it means to eat the labours of one’s fruits, I, 478. Curdled milk, I, 333. Not to need milk is the greatest progress, I, 499. The function of tears belongs to the body, but sorrow of soul, as it were, sweats them out, II, 360–361. God must be entreated through tears, I, 168. The embassy of tears for obtaining what God has promised, 130. What a lake signifies, I, 607. Each person rejoices in that by which he is affected, I, 552. True joy is that whose cause is honourable, 215; and which is made perfect by the delight of the sight of God, 216. The alternation here of those rejoicing and those enduring, after this life, 446. LAMECH’s punishment, I, 760. Lamphania, II, 664. The distinction between snares and stumbling-blocks, I, 599. Snares for beasts, 450; snares for souls, 450. No one is caught in the devil’s snare who has not first sinned, 450. Snares lie in wait for us everywhere, 368, 587, 598. The Lord must be prayed to that we may escape them, 587. Larissa, II, 632. The Latin translation has not adequately expressed the Greek, I, 303, 304, 307, 376. It does not explain the proper force of the Greek word, 393. It has introduced great obscurity, 582. The thief-martyr immediately received the gift of martyrdom, I, 206. His confession and reward, II, 345. The thief is in Paradise, where Christ is, I, 24—that is, in possession of the kingdom of God, 24. Side. Liberius, following the tradition of the elders, sends presbyters from his side, II, 669. Eusebius greets all who adhere to Gregory’s side, II, 702. Laudocia, II, 667. All praise arises from the wonder of things, I, 258. It surpasses blessing, 527. The instability of human praise, 690. What reason has been set before rational creatures for praising God, I, 647. The first reason is His own infinity, 623; other reasons for praising Him, 623 ff. To praise the works of God is properly the task of the two generations, 623. Why all created things are invited to God’s praise, 258–259; by what means all celebrate it, 646, 647, 649. God’s praise, which began with Abraham, 623. The sacrifice of praise, I, 174. It should proceed from the holiness of works, 175. We praise God not so much in voice as in deed and acts of obedience, 634. How great a misery it is to be mute in God’s praises, 552. Let God’s praise be public and continual, 202. He is to be praised for the constancy of the Apostles and Martyrs, 202. Public praises of God and divine offices, 196. In the Son the Father is praised, and in the Father the Son; nor does it matter which of the two is considered to be praised, I, 621; II, 58. This reciprocity of glorification does not concern an increase in divinity; what it does concern, II, 58. See Blessing.

How greatly devout reading enlarges the heart, I, 317. The table of the Lord’s readings, 481. It will benefit nothing those who do not engage in good works, I, 481. Amid sacred readings, the habit of vices creeps in, 551, 540; hence arises contempt for them, 540. A reader ought not to judge authors too hastily, II, 462. The best reader expects understanding from what is said; he does not impose it: he does not bring it in, but reports it, 14. Meaning must be fitted to the words rather than words to one’s meaning, I, 571. Embassy of tears, I, 130. Legates of Julius to the Council of Sardica, II, 629, 631. Legates from the side: see Side. The privilege of the Gospel was owed to legislation, I, 711. The lion, terror of all beasts, I, 506; it sleeps without fear, I, 506. LEO, deacon, II, 629. LEONAS, count, II, 573. LEONTIUS, II, 698. LERENIUS, II, 632. LEUCADAS, II, 666.

What something like a natural law teaches, I, 375. The law set before the will of the first human being, 718. The laws of the world are one thing, those of God another, 364. There is the law of the Lord and the law of sin, 277. Law does not impose necessity upon the one who establishes it, 88. He from whom all nature derives law is not subject to the laws of nature, II, 314. God’s law must be meditated upon day and night, I, 22; how this can be done, 22. God is to be understood through the works of the law, 198. The law ought to be in mouth, mind, heart, and hands, continually and with a love not merely ordinary, 318 ff. Meditation upon and practice of the law together are preparation for eternal goods, 297. God’s law is to be obeyed not through fear but love, 22.

Many wrongly suppose that law, justification, commandment, testimony, and judgment are one and the same, I, 273. “Law” is used generically for commandment, judgment, justification, and testimony, 276. What is distinctive in these, and what properly bears the name of law, ibid. The Jews boast that they received the law from God the Father, though they received it through angels, from the hand of the Mediator, I, 225. In the giving of the law, the terror of fires, thunder, and the rest displays the ministry of angels, 226. The law was received from Christ the Mediator through angels, II, 118, 220, 557. The God who gave the law is none other than the Lord of the universe, I, 636. The Law and the Gospels belong to one and the same God, 737; to one Spirit, II, 279. The old and new Law have one giver and one faith, I, 225; one God, 219, 558; one Mediator, II, 101.

The law was written by Moses, I, 31. It needs the aid of tradition to be understood, 32. How that tradition originating from Moses was preserved, 31. The five books of the Law, 740. The Psalter is called among the books of the Law, 187. The Book of Judith, 460; ibid., note. The law of justifications is contained in certain disciplines of a devout heart, 305. It belongs to law to be obeyed from necessity, 367. How the sacrifices of the law are necessary and not voluntary, 114. The law of priesthood in the Law, 415. The work of the Law: the millstone, I, 799. Difficult is entry into heaven for one trusting in the law, 763. The law cannot bring help, 707, 710. The law’s sacrifices are weak for salvation, 707. No one is righteous from the law, 707. The law was not salvific, giving life by works but not justifying by faith, 104. Neglect of the law’s precepts incurred guilt, while their performance, under faith in future things, profited, 265. The law is holy through the shadow of future things and converts souls through knowledge of future things, 277. Through men of the ancient law we are instructed in evangelical doctrine, 402. How great was David’s love of the law, 356 ff. His faith was spiritual, though he performed the offices of the law bodily, 496. The Jews do not know the law, 357. Why, 357.

The law contained not efficacy but contemplated effects, I, 785. The law’s justification was the pedagogue of evangelical justification and faith, 352. The law’s commands signify more than they accomplish, 408. The sacraments of the law prefigure the evangelical age, II, 113 ff., 115. Something great lies hidden in the rites of the old law, I, 381. The deeds of the law are shadows of future things, 548. What the law foreshadowed through its various acts, 291. What the work of the law was, 721. The form of the law was in John, 721, 739. Because of the people’s unbelief, the law was held as though shut up in a prison, 721. How the law sends its own people on to the Gospels, 721.

The law is a shadow of truth, I, 765; a shadow and mirror of future things, 277 ff., 280, 291, 300, 782; a shadow of evangelical events, 220, 231; a counterpart of the true, II, 116. By its mysteries it prefigured the truth of apostolic doctrine, 116; it preformed eternal things, I, 405. The law is the pedagogue of those who will believe in the Gospels, I, 352. It is our pedagogue in Christ, 358. It contains the evangelical law, 359. It was set down for faith in those things which were to be revealed in Christ, 683. It was useful rather through faith than through effect, 264. It is not truth itself, but in it there is contemplation of truth, 264. It is a mirror of the things to be fulfilled in Christ, 264. Christ’s birth and the promise of Israel’s kingdom are from the law, 729.

The law nurtured its own people into evangelical faith, I, 768. He who nourished the people subject to Himself for Christ, I, 708. It pointed Christ out to them, 709. By its very acts it foretold that the Word would become flesh, 123. It always declared that Christ would come, 806. All the law’s commands bear witness to the coming of God’s only-begotten Son, 410. All testimonies of the law, 357; the whole law, 383, 782, 783. The law is, as it were, Christ’s seat and throne, 785. It was sanctified in Christ, 785. With Christ’s coming it is useless, 785. The adornment of altar and temple fashioned by its beauty an image of future things, 785. Law, Prophets, and Gospels are one and the same through God’s Spirit, 755. In the time of the law, the salvation of the Gentiles was begun, 223.

The law is the beginning of life, I, 352. From the beginnings of the Law the doctrine of the Church flowed forth, 223. The Gospels are supplements to the Law, 227. By whom the law’s weakness is supplied: Christ, 700. The burden of the law for those who have not attained knowledge of evangelical freedom, 253. The law’s difficulties and burdens, 724; they were relaxed through Christ, 724. The law could be fulfilled through Christ alone, 676. Meditation on the law is made perfect in Christ, 782. Christ surpassed the law by advancement, not abolition, 684. How the works of the law apply to all, 199. The law is a shadow: it vanishes where truth has arrived, I, 748. The time of the Gospel was foretold when the law had been dissolved, 382. The end of the Law is the beginning of the Church, 740. How the law has now become truth, 395. The Christian understands what the Jew, reading the law, does not know, 357. When the law has ceased, we are saved by God’s goodness, 727. The law’s work is now ineffective for salvation, 675, 699. How strongly the Apostles were held by love of the law, 765. What answer is to be made to Jews who reproach us for altering the precepts of the law, 225. The defender of the law is Antichrist, 791.

The law of God’s mouth is properly Christ’s law, I, 334. Christ’s law is good without qualification, I, 334. The bond of indebtedness of the law of sin, II, 265. Our flesh is subject to the law of death and sin, II, 289. The powers of the world exercised the law of sin against Christ, 245—that is, sin’s penalty, or the right of death, 246. Christ escaped the law of death, 217. Those subject to the laws of the Church are reproved because they wish to judge by the laws of the forum, I, 21. For the many names of laws, see below in the Index of Glosses.

The book of the living differs from the book of the righteous, I, 256. It is greater to be written in the book of the righteous than not to be erased from the book of the living, I, 256. God’s book: eternal remembrance, I, 579. It is preferable to be written in God’s book than in the book of the living, 579. For those written in God’s book, the day is full and without night, 579 ff. The number of those written in God’s book is fixed, 580. A person free from vices can declare himself captive in a twofold sense, I, 462. The Son’s free will, II, 297. What freedom of the will was like in Adam, I, 718; what it is like in his descendants, 719. Each person has been granted freedom to choose what he wishes, 412. God has granted every human being freedom of life and perception, 39. Freedom of will ceases after this life, 92. By freedom of will, the rich man could have been in Abraham’s bosom, 92. How freedom of will is subject to unbelief, 701. It is the office of kingship to watch over the freedom of subjects, II, 535. The Church’s freedom, I, 102. Our freedom must not be entangled in the bonds of worldly business, 456. God’s freedom is to be retained in that service which we owe to all, 75. Freedom of religion and faith is demanded, II, 536. The adversaries of the freedom of our faith are many; Christ is its protector, I, 455. The bonds by which it is impeded, 456.

Christ alone is Liberator, I, 105. LIBERIUS, a sincere lover of peace, II, 671. He steadfastly adheres to the footsteps of the elders, 673. Why he refuses peace to the Easterners who seek it from him, 673. Some invent that he suppressed letters, 672. He read the Easterners’ letters before the council, 672. He does not agree with them, since at the same time he had received contrary letters from eighty Egyptian bishops, II, 672. Letters were written to him from all Egypt and Alexandria, 670. Liberius’s letter to the Easterners, 668; shown to be false, ibid., note. Liberius’s letter to Constantius, sent through Lucifer, II, 670. Liberius cannot appease Constantius by repeated satisfaction, 671. He is grievously attacked by a speech of Constantius sent to the people, 671. He clears himself of the accusations brought against him, 672.

Liberius’s envoys to Constantius: Lucifer, Pancratius, and Hilary, II, 674. Liberius’s letter to confessors living in exile, 675. He congratulates them, 675. He grieves that he has been separated from their fellowship, 676. He asks them to pray for him, 676. He wishes to learn from them what occurred at Milan, 676. Liberius’s sorrow over the fall of Vincent of Capua, 676 ff. Liberius’s letter to the Easterners who pronounced an unjust sentence against holy Athanasius, II, 677. He denies that he is defending Athanasius, 678. He excuses himself for having defended him previously, 678. He removes him from his communion, 678, 681. He also gives letters concerning his condemnation to be conveyed to Constantius, 678. He subscribes to the Sirmian perfidy set before him by Demophilus, 678, ibid., note. Liberius’s letter to Ursacius, Valens, and Germinius, II, 681. Liberius is at peace with the Easterners, 682–683, and also with Auxentius and Epictetus, 682. In letters sent to Constantius through Fortunatianus, he asks to be restored to Rome, 681. He makes the same request of the Easterners, 682. Liberius’s letter to Vincent concerning exile, 682. He laments that Urbicus has been taken away from him, 682. He is afflicted with the greatest weariness of exile, 683. Liberius, an apostate, 678; a prevaricator, 682; anathema is pronounced against him, 679, 682. Banished from Rome, he was perhaps restored to it with no less impiety, 571. Liberius’s letter to the bishops of Italy, in which he maintains that pardon ought to be granted to those who erred at Rimini through mistake, II, 702.

The power of binding and loosing was given to Peter and the other Apostles, I, 238, 759. The tree of life: wisdom, I, 23. In what respect the tree of life is Christ, I, 24–25. How the lily blooms forth from itself, I, 694. It imitates the virtue of angelic substance, 694. The tongue’s dangerous and most ready slipping, I, 594. A door and bolt must be set upon the mouth, 594. The office of the tongue, 82. Who is said to devise injustice with the tongue, 82. Who is a razor working deceit, 83. The distinction between deceitful lips and a deceitful tongue, 419 ff. The swords and arrows of a murderous tongue, 180. The tongue of the foolish and the tongue of the wise, 82. The Gospel is preached chiefly in three languages, 11. Lisicia, II, 665. Lawsuits must be avoided even at a loss, I, 688. Hilary accommodates those who love the letter of Scripture, I, 128, 144. Those who abound in the Spirit do not need the letter, II, 449. The letter is required where the understanding of conscience is endangered, ibid. Ecclesiastical letters, II, 670. Letters of ecclesiastical discourse, I, 457. False letters forged by the Arians, II, 624. Lizia, II, 666. God is not contained by places, I, 468, 514. Perhaps He is in no way believed to exist who is nowhere, 468. Places derive some share of holiness from holy inhabitants, 713. Whom locusts signify, I, 674. Luca, II, 631. The proper offices of lamp and light, I, 363. A lamp for each individual: the word of God, 362; for the Church: the Apostles, 362; for Jews and Gentiles: John, 362. The lamp of commandments, 361.

LUCIFER, II, 440. Bishop of Sardinia, 540. Liberius’s envoy to Constantius, 671, 674. An exile, 562. He preached the Son’s likeness to the Father, 521–522. LUCIUS, II, 690. LUCIUS of Bap., II, 667. LUCIUS of Hadrianopolis, accused by the Arians there, II, 653. Perhaps the same person who subscribes as Lucius of Caynopolis, 632. LUCIUS of Verona, II, 632. LUCIUS, presbyter of the city of Rome, II, 669. The emotion of grief in weeping, I, 680. The consolation promised to that grief, 681. Lueto, II, 667. Lugdunum, II, 633. First and Second Lyons, II, 457. The unity of light’s nature, II, 141. Light from light is separable neither by division nor by kind of nature, 200. The Son as light from light according to the heretical sense, 140; according to the Catholic sense, 140. How we become participants in God’s light, I, 390. The sowing and harvest of honourable works are preparation for attaining light, 375. The Apostles and Prophets are lights, illuminated from the Light, 210. They pray to be enlightened, so that Christ may become known to the Gentiles, 209. They are unequal to this task unless enlightened, 210. What the moon can do to human bodies, I, 430. Our light is God’s gift, I, 209. The word of God, light to be set before each of our actions, 361. Let the light of God’s word not remain useless in us, 362; rather, let it always burn first for us and then also for others, 362. Those dissolved in luxury are the dwelling-place of demons, I, 723. The sands of Libya, I, 176. Lydia, II, 482.

## M
MACARIUS, a Semi-Arian. II, 693. MACARIUS, presbyter of Athanasius, II, 625. Charges brought against him, 634. Macedonius, bishop and confessor, from Mopsus, burned books of sorcery, II, 663. He appears to be the same person who signs himself Macedonius of Amarquetias, 665; who is also listed among the authors of the Sirmian formula, 680; and among those who refused to condemn the heresy of Arius, 673. [Col. 0978] The MACEDONIANS do not appear to have been considered by Hilary in the books *On the Trinity*, I, 816 ff. MACEDONIUS of Virito, II, 665. MACEDONIUS of Ulpiani, II, 632. Magari, II, 632. Magdalena: see Woman. MAGDONIUS, II, 693.  

The MAGI were rulers, II, 98; devoted to the magical art, II, 98; practitioners of a profession far removed from the knowledge of divine understanding, I, 672 and note. They worshipped the filth of the cradle, II, 42. Their adoration was foretold by Isaiah and the Psalmist, 97. When they came from the East, the prophecy foretold in the Psalms was fulfilled, I, 237. In gold they confessed the King, in incense God, and in myrrh man, 672. In the man is recognized death; in God, resurrection; in the King, judgment, 672, 184 note.  

Master, II, 597, 600. Official masters, II, 620. Masters abstain even from the use of marriage, I, 184.  

When we say, “May God be magnified,” it is either a prayer that a gift may be granted us by God, or a confession of a gift received, I, 263. Greatness has no limit, I, 624.  

“May I curse”: why Job and Jeremiah curse the day of their birth, I, 422. Things publicly established by conscience are not curses, II, 572.  

Savage malice, I, 140. A malicious disposition, pursuing ill will, does not abandon it merely because the opportunity for an evil deed is absent, II, 193. The presence of a malicious man greatly hinders one wishing to devote oneself to God, I, 373. The Prophet repels from himself wicked persons who oppose his faith, not those who are evil through the weakness of their nature, I, 373 note. Malice lies close to all through the common condition of their origin, I, 373. It is not absent even from the Apostles themselves, though already cleansed and sanctified in faith by the Word, 373. Malice preferred to goodness, 83.  

Evil is nothing in itself, but arises from human vice, I, 249. Nothing is evil to a human being except through his own fault, 789. Our weakness causes us to think evil that which we suffer, 363. Evils arise from human opinion, 431. The real evils from which God protects believers, 431. All evils return upon those who inflict them, 113. God does not stir up evils out of malevolence, ibid. God orders them both for the punishment of the wicked and for the merits of the just, 113. Evils are appointed for all; but, turned away from the just, they are redirected against the wicked, 113.  

Abstaining from evil has no praise unless the glory of good work follows it, I, 622. The wicked are instruments of demons, I, 686. It is not given to everyone to understand the wicked, 779. The wicked avoid the presence of the good, just as they avoid that of God, 97.  

What is signified by the name MANASSEH, I, 157.  

How perilous it is wholly to ignore the commandments of God, I, 296. What a commandment is, 277, 287. By its observance it gives light, 277. The commandment of love is bright; by its light other things that are hidden are disclosed, 292. The chief commandment to the Israelites: that they should believe in one God, II, 82, 183. Why God’s commandment was given, I, 354. The commandments were given so that they might be salutary to all and bring forth eternity, 413. How they avail heretics and Jews nothing, 356.  

The way of the commandments has been trodden from the foundation of the age, I, 308 ff. We cannot undertake the path of the commandments without a guide, 308. Christ is our guide upon it, 308. In God’s commandments each person abides more gloriously in proportion as the weakness of his nature has been almost subdued by its enemies, 347. None must be neglected, 281. The sentence of a curse encompasses even one who deviates from them slightly, 296. It is not enough to fulfil them unless devotion of mind is also present, 280. Their observance here is not perfect, 291. In heaven the commandments differ according to the differing ranks of angels, 293. They are kept by them perpetually, 293.  

MANICHAEUS, II, 548. As far as lies in him, he professed himself an advocate of the devil, 138. An unwitting worshipper of his own sun, 138. He rejects the Law and the Prophets, 138. What he thought concerning Christ’s birth, 138. He explained the Son as a part of one substance of the Father, 80, 134.  

The MANICHAEANS, II, 28. Their teaching concerning darkness coeternal with God is touched upon, II, 512. Their teaching concerning vice in created things, I, 249; concerning the nature and necessity of sin, 140. Vice cannot be referred back to an origin in an evil principle, 140. No necessity of sin is inherent in human natures, 246. Their assertion of one God of the Law and another of the Gospels is false, 224, 558. The sacrifices of the Old Law are not regarded as abominable, 175.  

What the “dwelling-places” are, I, 304 and note; 305 and note. A dwelling-place at Nicaea, II, 690. Angels ministered manna, I, 220. He who was the giver of manna on Sinai is also the giver to us of heavenly bread, 220.  

It belongs to the meek to be worthy before God in designation, number, and brightness, I, 636.  

By the name “hand,” Scripture frequently signifies the effect of an action, I, 430, 444, 448. The extension of the hands signifies the posture of prayer; their raising, [Col. 0979] the accomplishment of exalted work, I, 593. The raising of hands signifies not a posture of prayer, but an exalted work, 174. Wherein that raising of hands consists is explained, 524. By the laying on of hands demons are tormented, 189. By the laying on of hands and prayer, grace is to be given to the Gentiles, 760. To wash one’s hands in the blood of a sinner, 142. The hand of God is Christ as God, 616. The hands of the Father and of the Son, II, 193.  

MARCELLUS, II, 176 note, 622, 624, 631, 655, 656, 657, 659, 660. The doctrine attributed to him by his opponents, 648 ff., 650, 660. He was condemned at Constantinople, and the decision against him was deposited in the archive of the Church, 649. Marcellus was anathematized by Protogenes, 658. Though considered a heretic among his own people, he sought assistance during exile, 650. He concealed corrupt opinions, 650. What Ancyra suffered when Marcellus returned from exile, 653. Marcellus’s view concerning Christ’s subjection and kingdom, 389 note. His book is called openly heretical, 656. He is free from error, 626. Marcellus is declared innocent, 627.  

Marcellus was condemned by the Arians because of the book which he published on Christ’s subjection, II, 640. After this same book had been read, the Synod of Sardica restored him to the episcopate, 639. Hilary possesses this book, 639. No other synod was convened against him, 639. Athanasius separated Marcellus from his communion before Photinus was accused, 639 and note. Marcellus then himself abstained from entering the church, 640, 641. The Easterners, replying from Sirmium, cunningly mention him as though he were Photinus’s teacher, 639; and they write that Athanasius is guilty of denying him communion, 640. When Marcellus reads “the Word of God,” he does not understand it, 548.  

MARCELLUS, Liberius’s envoy to Constantius, II, 677. Marciarce, II, 632. MARCION, II, 548. The passage of Scripture by which he supports his heresy, 511. The MARCIONITES, II, 28.  

Why the sea is wonderful, I, 259. The inner and outer sea, 187. The inner is the Mediterranean and the outer the Ocean, ibid. note. The tides of the sea: movements of measured recurrence, II, 440. The sea, the world, I, 188. The depths of the sea, demons, 189. The deep of the sea, the abode of death, 244; the seat of hell, 258. In the Red Sea, salvation for the devout and punishment for the impious, 624 ff.  

Mareota, II, 666. There was no church at Mareota, 633, 634. Those sent to Mareota in the affair of Athanasius, with one exception, were present at Sardica, 657.  

MARCUS, of most blessed memory, whom Hosius always opposed, II, 663. MARCUS of Arethusa, II, 665, 680 note. Chosen by the assembly, he dictated the creed, 708. MARCUS of Fissia, II, 633.  

Several pearls, and the one precious pearl, I, 279. Useless pearls hinder the reception of the single most precious one, II, 527, 528.  

MARY, of Abraham’s race, I, 669. Mother of the Lord according to the flesh, 505. She did not give origin to Christ’s body, II, 331. From the Word himself she brought forth the Lord, I, 472 and note. She gave birth, without diminution of herself, to a perfect man from what was her own, II, 61; without the shame associated with our elements, 61. She did not receive what she brought forth, 61. She gave Christ’s body from herself only so much as women ordinarily give, 330, 331, 332. She gave birth to what she bore only from the Spirit of the Word, 330. Mary’s virginity is affirmed, I, 670. Those who deny her this glory after childbirth are sharply refuted, ibid. ff. Mary was not Joseph’s wife, 671. After childbirth she was recognized as his wife, ibid. Mary, the virgin capable of God, will come under the severity of judgment, 294.  

The women who anointed Christ: see I, 520. MARIUS, II, 622. The MARSI, I, 140. MARTHUS, II, 680. MARTIALIS, II, 693.  

Martyrs, as higher than the other saints, are denoted by hills, I, 193. The torments of martyrs are not to be feared, II, 564. The trials of martyrs come from parents, brothers, and so forth, I, 371. Their punishments and victories, 203. They leap into fire with the devoted haste of a bound, 203. When cast into the deep, they fall not into waters that kill but into the refreshment of eternal blessedness, 203. Martyrs dedicate themselves and their imitators to God, 204–205. They meet death with hymns and songs, II, 353. The people accompanied bishops to the confession of faith, 564. Those ignorant of the faith ran to martyrdom following the example of martyrs, I, 205. Christ is bathed in the blood of all the martyrs, 807.  

The suffering of martyrdom is a kind of baptism, I, 291. Martyrdom: the confession of believers throughout the whole world, 395; their afflictions, 395; the worthy voice of their constancy, 395. Exhortation to martyrdom, II, 561.  

MARTYRIUS refused to condemn the heresy of Arius, II, 671. [Col. 0980] MARTYRIUS of Neapolis, II, 632. MARTYRIUS, subdeacon, II, 706. Matthew’s calling, I, 707. Whether Methuselah’s years exceed the age of the Flood, II, 512 and note. Morning hymns, I, 190; II, 529. Morning mercy: the time of resurrection, I, 607. MAXIMIANUS, II, 566, 567. The cave of MAXIMILLA, II, 570.  

MAXIMINUS of Trier was responsible for Paul’s recall to Constantinople, II, 663. He restored communion to Athanasius, 634. Why he is condemned by the pseudo-Sardican synod, II, 662, 663. MAXIMUS, II, 647.  

Christ the Mediator in the creation of the world, II, 84; in the giving of the Law, I, 226. The Mediator is one and the same in the giving of the Law and in the assumption of flesh, II, 101. Christ, the Mediator of God and men, I, 226. How he fulfils that office, 720; II, 223, 259.  

Certain medicines are suitable for healing every disease, II, 39. Medicinal remedies prescribed by a wise man, I, 140. What the physician of the human race ought to be, I, 66.  

The Church of Milan confesses Christ consubstantial with the Father, II, 597. The people of Milan, most devout, 571. Their grief at the perfidy of the priests, 540. The council of Milan, A.D. 345 or thereabouts, II, 673. The Synod of Milan held in A.D. 347, II, 635, 637; another two years later, 635. After Photinus had been condemned there, letters were sent to the Easterners, 640. Proceedings of the Synod of Milan in A.D. 355, II, 540. Liberius wishes to learn of them after his legates had been driven into exile, 676. What occurred there seems to be alluded to, 506.  

MEDI, I, 423. Material for meditation, I, 606. The use and office of meditation, 288. Meditation on the Law, 784. It is not to be abandoned in temptations and afflictions, 352. It ought to be continuous, 22. How this may be possible, 22. It consists not only in reading words but also in the religious practice of deeds, ibid. Matters for meditation before dawn, 399. Meditation upon God by night and morning, 175. Everlasting meditation upon God’s just ordinances, 375.  

MEGASIUS, II, 691, 693. The Gauls removed him from their communion, 700. MELETIUS had neither church nor minister at Mareota, II, 626. The presbyters of Meletius were received by Alexander, 626.  

Remembrance of God, I, 319. One ought to share in the memorials of the saints, II, 583. Dead unbelievers are not to be joined to the memorials of the saints, I, 703. Adorned memorials, I, 786. Memorial, I, 536. MENOPHANTUS of Ephesus, II, 538, 627, 628, 631.  

The table of knowledge, I, 253 ff. The table of the Lord’s readings, I, 481. Those who do not engage in good works will make no progress at it, 481. The Lord’s table, from which we receive living bread, I, 481. For Hilary it is the same as the table of sacrifices, ibid. note.  

An officious lie, I, 74. Liars: those who are either deceived or deceive, I, 169. Liars upon the scales: those who perform unjust acts under the name of justice, 169.  

What the reward is: not of work, but of mercy, I, 496 and note. Merit, I, 39, 388; II, 157, 166, 168. One is not excluded from the duty of earning merit, although the pre-eminent honor is owed to God’s mercy, I, 608 ff. To whom it belongs to merit, II, 387. The merit of a will by which we delight in being good, I, 99. According to the difference of our merits, God is either wakeful or asleep, 615. Forgiveness is readily present through the merit of faith, 99. Blessed life is reserved, 370. David earned the goods of the soul both by the cry of mouth and heart and by purity of mind, 206. From what comes to us the merit of perfect blessedness, 92. The basis of merit lies in election, 780. Merit unto glory, 542. It is no merit not to act from oneself, II, 295. Blessed eternity must be earned by what is ours, I, 698, by the works of the present life, 680. The merit of attaining consummation comes from the beginning of the will, 370. On the merit of their past will, those departing from the body receive either rest or punishment, 92. Eternal glory is rendered for the merit of faith, though its greatest cause is God’s mercy, I, 542. One must not trust in one’s own merits but in God’s mercy, 399 ff. God’s mercy, not recompense, is to be requested by human beings, 289. By his own merit without God’s help a human being cannot attain eternal life, 340. Merit exists only through hope and faith in Christ, 372. Merit is anticipated by God, 315. No opportunity for meriting remains after this life, I, 92. No one is to be aided by another’s merits at Christ’s coming, 795. The merit of Christ’s obedience, I, 109; II, 287.  

Mesopotamia, I, 153; II, 482. The condemnation of bishops to the mines, written in the headings of ecclesiastical writers, II, 570. [Col. 0981] To measure something is an indication of proprietorship, I, 157. MIGDONIUS, II, 691. Mignenia, II, 666. Serving in the office of the exalted prefecture, II, 706. Mileto, II, 667. The Jews were protected by heavenly warfare, I, 160. The pay of our military service, II, 402.  

Christ’s least ones, I, 797. Who are the least of all, 721. Least of all: the Lord’s Passion and death on the cross, 684.  

How God alone performs wonders, I, 543. God’s various miracles in the governance of the world, I, 530. Whence Christ has the power of working miracles, I, 709, 704. It must not be attributed to Christ’s soul, II, 361. Christ’s miracles are wrought by no other nature than God’s, 179. Divine birth accomplishes all its work through the ministry of the assumed body, 197. There is a complaint that it has not been understood that God’s nature wrought miracles in the assumed man, 205. Let us rather do what God wills than glory in what he can do, I, 698. No less a miracle than the sight of the blind, and so on, is John’s sublime doctrine, II, 34. Frequent miracles are performed at the tombs of martyrs, 567.  

God’s compassions exceed the measure of human estimation, I, 305. All who are in the flesh need God’s mercy, I, 326, 707. It belongs to modest faith to regard it not apart from severity, 326. God’s mercy is the cause of our living, II, 145. Without God’s mercy we have no use of life, I, 160. God’s mercy began in us in the forgiveness of sin, 209. The Prophet is not uncertain of God’s mercy, 444. Divine discourse signifies the protection of God’s mercy by the covering of wings, 162. God’s mercy is spread over the whole earth, 330. It is ready for all, but stands by God’s servants, 609. It is God’s principal work, 626. Why, 626.  

God’s mercy must not be regarded as an irrational bestowal, I, 112. God delays it in order to test faith, 443. It is not our fear but faith that earns it, 180. It is to be hoped for by those who believe, 134. It must be earned by the pursuit of innocence, 388. One must trust in God’s mercy, not in one’s own merits, 399 ff. It, not recompense, must be sought from God, 289. Merciful is the anger of fathers toward children, and of God toward human beings, 155.  

Mercy has a measure, and justice must be applied in showing compassion, I, 596. To grant pardon for unlawful acts is not to show mercy, but to fail to preserve the justice of mercy, 596. Examples of unjust mercy, 625. The fruit of mercy is signified by oil, 689.  

The generation of MOAB was cursed by God in Genesis, I, 158. After ten generations it becomes worthy of a holy lineage, 158. The millstone: the work of the Law, I, 792. The work of the millstone, 757. The millstones of lions, I, 140.  

Certain diseases are cured by the sight alone of birds and certain plants, I, 339. Diseases of the human race, 65.  

A mountain: Christ’s glorious body, I, 71. Mountains: angels and saints, 454; patriarchs, prophets, apostles, and martyrs, 637; prophetic books, 427; angelic ministries, 427; the devil with his followers, 188, etc.; diabolical powers, 614. The mountain of the Lord: the Church, 452. Hilary complains that every lofty place of mountains is defiled by shrines, temples, and sacred rites, I, 71.  

Monsters arise from diversity of natures, II, 185. MONTANA, II, 570. MONTANUS, leader of all heretics, II, 649. Through frenzied women he maintained another Paraclete, II, 548. Montonis, II, 633. Morenis, II, 633. It is better to be imbued with good morals from childhood, I, 283.  

Death is customarily signified by sleep, I, 134, 223. The abode of death is denoted by the depths of the sea, 244, etc. Causes of death, II, 327. Death follows from the law of sin, I, 173. To what extent the law of death prevailed, 88. Death is not the destruction of the soul, but its departure from the body, 181. Prophecy of Christ’s death, I, 224. Its cause and rationale, 228, 230. Death is a penal transformation for us; for the only-begotten God, rest, 506. Death itself, in God dying, is confidence, 230. The elements of the world perceived their own destruction when Christ died, II, 55. Christ abolished the sentence of death through death, II, 11. How Christ cancelled the decree of our death, I, 506. Christ, dying, swallowed up the pain of death, 803. Death ceased after it had attacked God, 249. When death was expelled from the human race, the penalty of eternal death was decreed against the authors of death, 250. How justly the author of Christ’s death was condemned, 246 ff. What punishments the Jews suffered, 232. The Lord’s departure in death is unique to him, 229.  

For the saints death is sleep, I, 472. Faith removes the fear of death, II, 11. Death is desired by many, I, 422. Through death the soul is stripped of the burden and fellowship of weak and dangerous flesh, 422. The Prophet desires death, 607. It will not avail to have been heard unless, on departing from the body, one is to rest in blessed places, I, 607. Departing believers are kept in Abraham’s bosom until they attain the kingdom of heaven, 432. Death obtains fellowship with Christ for believers, 418 ff. The death of our own is a hastened progress toward our common hope, 418. Believers will experience only a slight libation of death, 752.  

The death of the living is to live for luxury, sleep, and the like, I, 448. The dead live to God, 88. The Arians declare war on the dead, II, 582. What the law against touching a dead body signifies, I, 290 ff.  

The sender and the one sent are not one, II, 474. The sender shows his authority over the one sent, 226. Sending distinguishes persons, not nature, 58, 100. Human emotions, I, 98.  

MOSES, prophet, leader and giver of the Law, I, 96; writer of the sacred books, II, 4. Author of certain Psalms, I, 3 and note. It does not conflict with this that he expressed Samuel’s name, 3. Moses avenged a Hebrew’s injury from a natural affection, II, 117. Even then he knew the God of the paternal blessings, 117. When he began to know God, I, 569. Through Moses God began to be made manifest to the world, II, 127. Moses, beholding with God all the hidden mysteries of heaven, 146. He set the Old Testament in writing, I, 31. He imparted the more secret mysteries of the Law to the Seventy Elders, 31. Under the veil of common words he concealed immense mysteries, 221.  

Moses confessed God and God throughout the entire body of his work, II, 88. Whether he died, I, 769 and note. Scripture is obscure concerning his tomb, II, 512. Moses was reserved by Christ as witness and participant in his eternal kingdom, I, 99. He was seen with Christ at the Transfiguration as evidence of resurrection, 753. Moses and Elijah will sit with Christ in the kingdom of heaven, 768. They will precede Christ’s final coming, 769. MOSES, fellow-presbyter, II, 638. MOYSIUS of Thebes, II, 632. MUCIANUS, II, 706.  

There was not only one woman who anointed the Lord, I, 520. Why women were first made aware of Christ’s resurrection, I, 810.  

The world (*κόσμος*, *kosmos*, “adornment”): some maintain that it was constituted by chance movements, I, 20. Those who suppose the world arose either from a chance concurrence or that it is God are refuted, 644 ff. Why some have called it God, 197. No part of the world is to be worshipped with divine honor, 645. The world does not exist from the blending and mixture of matter, II, 430; nor from a sudden thought of God, 430; nor from portions of thoughts, 431. All things are from nothing, 154. God is author and ruler of the world, I, 181. By contemplating the world we perceive that God exists, 95. The author of the world is made known by the multiplication of the five loaves, 741. A certain system of the world, 545 note. The duration of the present world, I, 752 and note, 767. The dwelling of this world is not the region of the living, 290. The whole world is full of snares, 598, 587. We cannot belong to the world while dwelling in this earthly and mortal body, I, 290.  

When receiving gifts is lawful and when forbidden, I, 77 ff. By gifts from things unjustly acquired, God’s holy person is burdened, II, 569. Mursa, II, 668. By walls, spiritual custody is signified, I, 123.  

The four kinds of musical art, I, 13. The Greek and Latin translations have not preserved the metrical music of the Psalms, 15. MUSTACIUS, II, 690. One must not deny to those wishing to borrow what we ourselves borrow from God, I, 688. Mysia, II, 482.  

Christ’s mysteries ought to be handled neither indiscriminately nor ignorantly and carelessly, I, 696. Mysteries are to be explained according to the Scriptures, II, 368. The divine solemn rites of the mysteries for the safety of the king, II, 536.  

## N

Nabla, I, 6. The death of NADAB and Abihu benefited the release of their souls, I, 253 note. NARCISSUS of Neroniade, II, 627, 628, 631, 667, 680. NATHAN, prophet of the coming Christ, I, 154.  

To be born and to have begun are not the same, II, 186. Those who are born have no form or power other than that of their origin, 645. Birth differs from creation, II, 470. It bears witness to an abiding author, 141. In birth there cannot fail to be the nature from which one is born, 192. It cannot bring another nature than that from which it subsists, 196, 128, 185. It exists in the power of the nature that begot it, 377. The name of the thing from which it is born encompasses its nature, power, and profession, 187. [Col. 0983] It does not possess a diversity at variance with its original substance, II, 472. Birth alone can provide equality of nature, 136. There will be no birth unless there is the property of nature, 185. Birth from differing natures does not introduce diversity, but receives it, I, 185. The birth of God the Son is illustrated by human birth, II, 199, and by comparison with fire, 199. It is aptly signified by the term “coming forth,” 280. The Son of God entered upon our birth, 111. The glory of Christ’s birth, 42. His temporal birth at baptism, I, 48; likewise through the glory of the resurrection, 46 ff. Human births receive their beginning both through time and through cause, II, 416.  

Some have worshipped nature, arising into being through chance motions and collisions, II, 3. The growth of things is according to nature; their diminution is contrary to nature, 260. He from whom all nature receives its law is not subject to the laws of nature, 314. Nature is enslaved to beasts, 2.  

Nature is not the same thing as a thing of nature, II, 229. A power is a thing of nature, 299. The power of nature establishes the truth of nature, 105. There is no diversity of nature where there is one name of nature, 116. Human nature, I, 630 note. Nature is twofold in the one Christ, I, 256 ff. To have assumed a nature is one thing; to be a nature is another, 563. See below, Index of Glosses.  

Shipwrecked churches, I, 703. The Church is like a ship, I, 702, 705, 734, 747. Neapolis, II, 632. Naiso, II, 632. The difference between mist and cloud, I, 331 note.  

The insincere gain of trade, a bond hindering faith, I, 456. How bodies—which are God’s houses—become houses of trade, I, 393. Neo, II, 693. Neocaesario, II, 666.  

Spiritual wickednesses, I, 345, 347. They are denoted by the beasts of the forest, 236. They are called hostile and opposing powers, 345; ministries of Satan, 346; gods of the Gentiles, 442. How they tempt us, 347. They choose the wicked as workers, as it were, of their own will, 484. NERO, II, 564, 566, 567, 570, 594. NESTORIUS, II, 667.  

Commendation of the NICENE council, II, 674. The holy Nicene Synod, 480, 509. At Nicaea 318 bishops assembled, II, 583, 643; three hundred or more, 643. The holy number of 318 Nicene bishops, II, 513. The aim of the Nicene synod in accepting *homoousion*, 510. The Nicene exposition, II, 510, 643. It is explained, 645 ff. It was written by saints, confessors, and successors of martyrs, 688; not without the aid of the Holy Spirit, 689. It was established against the Arian heresy and others, 685, 687; against Arius and Sabellius, 704. In few words it enclosed every contrivance of heretics, 645. The Nicene faith is full and perfect, 643. If anything is removed from it, an entrance is opened to the poisons of heretics, 687. This is the true faith, 579. Hilary, adhering to it, needs none other, 580. He had never heard it except when about to go into exile, 518. He will never desire peace except with defenders of the Nicene faith, 600.  

The Nicene faith was set forth publicly at Milan and rejected by Valens, II, 540. Those who wished to overthrow it at Rimini, 688. Those who had agreed to Rimini return to it, 703, 704. Nicaea in Thrace was formerly called Ustodizo, II, 690. There all heresies are said, falsely, to have been condemned, 697. By what authority those who agreed at Nicaea were compelled to be silent concerning *ousia*, 698. The acts of Nicaea in Thrace have now been annulled by all, 597. NICHAS, II, 706. NICOLAUS, deacon and false prophet, I, 788. Nicomedia, II, 647. Nicopolis, II, 632.  

Nothing. All things are from nothing, II, 154. “Too much” (*nimis*) means “very,” not that which uselessly exceeds the necessary measure, I, 580. Delicate ancestral portraits of nobility, 751. The dignity of origin consists in examples of deeds, I, 674. NOCONIUS, II, 666. The name is fitted to nature, not nature to the name, II, 91. God’s name is great everywhere, I, 558. The new name: the Christian name, II, 122. For the various kinds of names, see the Index of Glosses. NONNIUS, II, 667.  

The heresy of the NOVATIANS is contrary to the Law, the Prophets, and the Gospels, I, 558. NOVATUS, II, 662. Novempopulana province, II, 457. The temporal newness of Christ, II, 286. I prefer to have mentioned something new rather than impiously rejected it, II, 509.  

Night out of day, while Christ suffers, is a division of times, [Col. 0984] I, 808. One must rise at midnight to praise God, 328. The usefulness and necessity of nocturnal prayers, 321.  

Clouds are drawn up from the sea, I, 531. The various senses of “clouds,” 637. Clouds signify those whose life is in some manner aerial and heavenly, 238. Clouds: preachers, 239; apostolic doctrine, 532; the Lord, 137; saints caught up in clouds, 137; truth reaching unto the clouds, 137. To appear in clouds, caught up to meet Christ God, 137, 173.  

Certain philosophers are seen to shiver while naked, I, 184. The number two has an unfavorable sound, I, 595. How perfect the number eight is, 274; holy in the Law, 274. The mystery of the number fifteen, 416. The number forty, 677. Paul permitted second marriages without the charge of adultery, I, 218. He does not forbid them when he commends the continence of widowhood, 367. Marriage: the glorious resurrection, 794. The wedding garment, I, 780.

## O
Blindness. Knowledge is denied to those who would have despised it. I, 359.

Hardening. To Pharaoh was attached the obstinacy of an irreligious will. I, 380.

Voluntary obedience belongs to the Gospel, not spontaneous obedience to the law, I, 367. Obedience of the will will discover the path to the heavenly kingdom, 698. To obey the will entails an outward necessity, II, 297. The merit of Christ’s obedience, I, 109.

Obligations. I, 456.

The obscurity of the mind: whence it arises, I, 606; how it is driven away, 606.

Service rendered, under the appearance of religion, to an unworthy person is not cheated of its reward, 720 ff.

Faith of the Westerners, II, 643. The Easterners take care that their proceedings be reported to the Westerners, 694.

The tides of the Ocean, I, 530. Man does not comprehend the Ocean’s changes, 491. The islands of the Ocean have churches established by the apostles, I, 70.

Hidden things. I, 61.

OCTAVIUS. II, 710.

The number eight. I, 274.

To free one’s eye from a snare is rare, I, 587. The movement of a wandering eye is equated in the Gospels with adultery, 685. Eyes defiled by theatrical spectacles, 72. The eyes both of body and soul must be turned away from vanity, 311. How eyes fixed upon God are turned from vain things, 598. Eyes must be directed to God, but must not be raised from him to something else, 498. The weakness of bodily eyes for seeing God, an angel, and so forth, 325. How much the eyes of the mind surpass those of the flesh, 426. Failure of the eyes, 380. The eyes of Christ’s body are the apostles and priests, 577, 578.

It is not the mark of a saint to have given cause for hatreds, I, 408. The right use of hatred and love, 360. We are commanded to hate father, mother, and so forth when they draw us away from martyrdom or the service of God, 371. How hatred of the wicked does not conflict with the Gospel, 372. Our religious hatred is directed against him who hates God, 583.

Official. II, 709.

Imperial officials. II, 620.

The haste of officials against apostolic men. II, 620.

Divine office. Psalm 118 teaches how we ought to occupy ourselves in every kind of divine office. I, 331.

OG, that is, a wall or rampart. I, 534.

The perfection of the ogdoad, I, 9, 10.

Oil signifies the fruit of mercy. I, 689.

The oil of the sinner. I, 125.

OLIMPIUS. II, 664.

Olive tree. I, 91.

The pot in which Christ’s flesh was boiled, I, 159. A burning pot, consuming and removing sins, 159.

Whatever owes itself to another lacks omnipotence. I, 530.

Onyx. I, 593.

God does not cease from working, I, 266. The Father’s work lies in his will, 268. As an example of his own operation, the Son contemplates the Father’s will through their mutual love and nature, 268. The work of the Father and Son is one, 267. Moses related only God’s visible works to the untrained minds of human beings, 266; to what end, 267. How Paul leads us to an understanding of invisible things, 267.

The name “Son” does not suit a work, II, 415. Work is signified by the name “resurrection,” I, 566. By the name “hands,” the divine word signifies works, 442, 488. An exalted work is signified by the lifting up of hands, 174. The distinction between works and good will, 488 ff. Good works are food for the soul, I, 478. Here they are compared with labor; but their fruit will be in eternity, 478. Exhortation to work, 479. Work is to be preferred to prayer, 377. Those who are useless and unfruitful will be assigned not to glory but to fire, II, 302. Let our work shine forth for others while we ourselves do not parade it, [Col. 0985] I, 683. Let the works of our soul be praised even by the testimony of Gentiles, 167. External works of piety, although not to be omitted, are nevertheless to be ranked after inward virtues, 785. It is not enough for a work to be good in the integrity of the deed, unless it is also good in will, 456. Love may be absent from an act when one does what one would not have done except for fear or shame, 356. Works that are compelled rightly require the fullness of grace, 356.

Works of good will are children of wisdom, I, 481. From wisdom come works; from works comes recompense, 482. Good works are shared by Gentiles and heretics, 73. Without faith they are empty, ibid. Demons strive most forcefully to weaken works of faith, 430. Divine protection is promised so that they may remain unimpaired in us, 430. So long as these endure, we shall enjoy the eternal kingdom, 430. Good works that sanctify us, 524. One must work with a cheerful spirit and with God’s blessing, 524. One must work throughout one’s life in hope of the Lord, 496. One who has not spent every period of life in working must not despair, 496. The fruit of good work: ointment, 798. The reward of good works, 497.

Human works are empty, I, 467. How sinful they are, 399. The works of the world and of the flesh are rivers, 550; and hay in buildings, 488. Diabolical works, 442.

Workers of the devil. I, 484.

Reproach is the punishment of sin, I, 313. Sins deserve reproach, 296. Confession turns it away, 296.

OPTATUS. II, 693.

Restless wealth lacks the benefit of riches, II, 1. Contempt for riches is wealth, 364.
