Oracles ceased to be uttered after Christ. I, 189, and note there.

Prayer is a duty suited to our weakness. I, 310. Prayer is necessary for enduring passions, 340; for attaining knowledge of the heavenly commandments, 339; and against temptations, 179. God is not to be prayed to only when the things we fear have come upon us; rather, those things must be feared which, once they begin to be present, rule over us, 179. From this it is shown that one must pray without ceasing, ibid. We must always pray to God that, in restraining sins and extinguishing their incitements, he may strengthen the wavering endeavors of our will, 556. No human being knows how he ought to pray, 109. We do not know how to pray, 608. The Spirit compensates for our ignorance by a hidden movement of conscience, 608.

Work is to be preferred to prayer, I, 377. Whether our prayer anticipates God’s gifts, 310. God hears prayers everywhere, but innocence alone merits being heard favorably, 118. David’s prayer rests on God’s goodness, not on his own merits, 315. Those are rebuked who, when asking something of God, approach him as though demanding a debt of duty, 315. To ask that one’s own prayer be heard belongs to Christ alone, 100. The difference between God’s hearing and attending to prayer, 492. God must not be thought either neglectful of our prayer or to grant irrationally what is asked, 112. What prayers are contemptible, 118.

Prayer of the lips, I, 398. Prayer consists not so much in words as in affection, 171. Prayer is not in words: every work surpasses speech, 689. In prayer, the cry of the mouth, not that of the heart, is forbidden, 397. The cry of silent prayer, 592.

The qualities of good prayer, I, 161. That it may not be unpeaceful, 685. Pure prayer, 592. He prays with confidence who, while in the flesh, is a stranger to the flesh, 161 ff. Prayer with an outpouring of the heart, 168. The purity of the night just passed gives confidence for morning prayer, 175.

Various degrees of prayer, I, 411, 601. Three kinds of prayers, 118. Examples of each kind, 119. Four kinds of prayers signified in incense, 593. An example of praying, 605. The Lord’s Prayer, through the mirror of common words, reveals the pattern of a most hidden mystery, 110.

The power of prayer against ignorance, I, 697. God’s protection granted to the prayer of faith, 162. Prayer to God in temptations is the chief part and hope of salvation, 418. The teaching of our hope is that God, when prayed to, both has mercy and saves, 315.

We are taught to pray in every place, I, 689. The place of prayer is the heart, 689. Daily prayer, II, 714. The persistence of prayers: by what words it is signified, I, 198. Tribulations ought not to hinder us from persistence in prayer, 601. Who ought and can be without ceasing, 22. The whole life of every saint becomes prayer, 23.

Angels daily offer God the prayers of those being saved, I, 758. Hilary commends himself to the holy prayers of the Gauls, II, 520. Liberius asks to be supported by the prayers of confessors, 676.

The ranks of those standing in the synagogue. I, 415.

“Organs” in Scripture signify human bodies. I, 550.

Heresies of the East springing up in successive periods, II, 516. The regions of the East are desperate in faith, 620. All the bishops of the East assented to the Council of Rimini, 705. The peril of the Eastern Churches, 498, 500.

EASTERNERS assembled at Philippopolis pretend that they are writing from Sardica, II, 660. They cast upon the Westerners the odium of schism, 659. They complain that they are subjected to the judgment of the Westerners by a new law, 655, 657, 661. They wish honor to be accorded to Eastern councils, [Col. 0986] II, 658, and that these matters not be reopened by the Westerners, 661. The Easterners and Westerners, they say, have reciprocally confirmed what was decreed by one another, 662.

In the year 349 the Easterners declare Athanasius not guilty, II, 636. Their crafty and perverse reply to the Westerners who condemned Photinus in the year 349, 639. Letters of the Easterners to Julius, delivered to Liberius, 668 ff. Liberius’s letter to the same, in which peace with them is indicated, 668, 669. Letters of the Easterners to Liberius, 672. The Easterners seek peace from Liberius, 673. Why he denies it to them, 673. The condition proposed to the Easterners at Arles by Liberius’s legates, 674. Easterners and Gauls are held by mutual suspicions, 463. Hilary labors to relieve these, 463.

The decrees of the Easterners at Ancyra: by whom, when, and on what occasion they were issued, II, 477. The Easterners, having gathered a council among themselves, formulate definitions of faith, 476. They decree measures concerning doctrine already acquired long before, 476. They oppose the impiety of Sirmium, 460, 466, though not without some offense to the ears, 460. They were moved to shame by the reputation of the Gauls’ faith, which had been nurtured and increased, 460. Eastern delegates brought to Sirmium a letter concerning the exposition of *homoousios* and *homoiousios*, 508. On what pretext they rejected *homoousion*, 509. Their judgment and that of the Westerners concerning *homoiousion* is the same, 509.

Eastern delegates were honorably received by the emperor, II, 506. They recall him from error, 506. They compel those who had drafted or accepted heresy at Sirmium to subscribe to their decrees, 476, having confessed ignorance, 476, 506—as though they had not known the meaning of *homoousios* and *homoiousios*, 506. Commendation of the Easterners who opposed the Sirmian formula, 505. They brought hope that the true faith might be restored, 505; yet not the true faith itself, ibid., note. Hilary prudently observed this, 522. Why he nevertheless praised them, ibid. They hold something which cannot be heard except with offense, 521. They are not Arians, but are judged so because they deny *homoousion*, 515. Certain Easterners, confessing the Son’s likeness to the Father, wrongly deny equality, 503.

Liberius grants the Easterners his communion, II, 677 ff. Constantius forbids any determination at Rimini against the Easterners, 684. The Easterners are believed by those at Rimini to reject the terms *ousia* and *homoousios*, 692. Under the authority of their name, many at Rimini and Nicaea were compelled to silence concerning *ousia*, 698.

The Easterners write to the delegates returning from Rimini to Constantinople, II, 693. They resist the heresy of the Anomoeans, 693. They bring it about before Constantius that it is condemned, 694. They abstain from entering the church, 693, 695. They direct that these proceedings be reported to the Westerners, 694. The Easterners send letters to Hilary, which he dispatches to Gaul, 698. Gallican bishops reply to the Easterners, 697. Constantius nourishes Eastern dissensions, 566. The Easterners are subjected by force to the will of Constantius, 582.

The origin of all things is from nothing and after time, II, 417.

Worldly adornment is an insult to nature, I, 384.

Orphans: those who have renounced the devil as father, I, 217; or those who have been left desolate in the world, 218.

There is a mouth of the lips and a mouth of the heart, I, 387. With the mouth of the heart we receive spiritual foods for the life of the soul, 388. The mouth of the heart must be opened to the Holy Spirit through faith and desire, 387.

The mouth of Christ is the Church, I, 576.

By bones is signified hope of eternity, 103. The bones of martyrs are to be venerated, II, 567.

Constantius receives priests with a kiss, II, 569.

OSIUS. II, 631, 634, 655, 656, 658, 660, 662. The inseparable companion of Paulinus of Dacia, 663. He always inflicted grievous injuries on Marcus, 662. Liberius’s letter to Osius concerning the fall of Vincentius, 676. Commendation of Osius, 623. Osius was excessively fond of his own tomb, 513. Osius’s ravings, 580; his judgment at Sirmium, 461. A blasphemy drafted through him and Potamius, 464. Through Osius, forgetful of his own actions, the teaching of a new impiety breaks forth, 498. Osius was therefore preserved, so that it might not be unknown what manner of life he had previously lived, 498.

Leisure without wealth, and wealth without leisure, is material for evil rather than an occasion for good, II, 1. No day is without work for God, I, 269.

An idle word, that is, one foolish and useless, I, 732.

The wandering sheep: the human race, I, 758.

## P
Palestine, II, 482. PALLADIANUS, II, 666. PALLADIUS, II, 706. PALLADIUS of Dui, II, 633. Pamphylia, II, 482. PANCRATIUS, legate of Liberius, II, 674. PANCRATIUS of Pelusium, II, 708. PANCRATIUS of Pernas[o], II, 665. [Col. 0987] How the five loaves were multiplied, II, 53. The sacrament of the heavenly bread is received in faith in the resurrection, I, 707. See “Eucharist.” Pannonia, II, 177. The two Pannonias, 482. PANTAGATUS, II, 667. Pope Julius is called “fellow-priest” and “brother” by the bishops of the Sardican synod, II, 622. Liberius himself calls himself a fellow-priest and servant of God, II, 676. Paphlagonia, II, 482. The use of papyrus, II, 140, note. Paradise: the allotted portion and kingdom of Christ’s inheritance, I, 602. The delights of consummate blessedness, II, 345. The eternal region of the blessed, I, 26, whose inhabitants are blessed after the eternal transformation of their bodies, 375. Paradise contains within itself the tree of life, Christ, 24. Whoever possesses the kingdom of God is in it, ibid. The return to the paradise from which Adam departed is a figure, 706. Paul was in paradise before his martyrdom, II, 147. PARAGORIUS, II, 632. The healing of the paralytic on the Sabbath, I, 267 ff. Letter of the PARISIAN synod, II, 697. Partakers of Christ, I, 329. Particopolis, II, 632. Little children: either those reborn unto innocence or the ignorant, I, 387. All unbelievers are little children, 520. The Passover is celebrated, after the cup has been received and the bread broken, without Judas, I, 799. The books on the Holy Spirit by the deacon PASCHASIUS are to be ascribed to Faustus, II, 513, note. Sparrow, a domestic bird, I, 450. PASSINICUS, II, 693. Minds laid open, I, 505.

A father is not a father unless he acknowledges in the Son what substance he possesses in himself, II, 27. He cannot be called the father of a substance alien and unlike himself, 472. The Father’s nature is co-born in the Son’s birth, 111. Fathers are so called either by name or by kindred, I, 670. The conception of the eternal Father, II, 30, 50. A father has the name of his own nature in his son, 30. He does not have, in a human manner, from another that whereby he is Father, I, 30. All speech is inadequate to declare what belongs to him, II, 31. The proper designation “Father” differs from “Son,” but not in nature, I, 570. It is the mystery of fatherhood to be the author of a birth, II, 281. It is proper to the Father to be unbegotten, 77. He alone is unbegotten, 442. The Father’s name does not allow that he should be father in one respect and not father in another, 305. How he is wholly Father, ibid. ff. Why the Father is said to be in heaven, I, 37, note there. The Father, as Father, is greater than the Son by generation, not by kind, 570; he is greater by the authority of the giver, II, 301; yet the Son is not inferior, since unity of being is given to him, ibid. The Father’s name includes within itself the name of the Son, 201. The Father was not born of Mary, 686. The Father is glorified through the Son when he is recognized as the Father of such a Son, 58. This was the Son’s greatest work: that we should know him as Father, not merely as the maker of all things, 63–64.

How the Father dwells in the Son, I, 440–441. They are mutually in one another through the harmonious and non-dissimilar nature of the unbegotten and the only-begotten, 513. The Father is one with the Son both in power and in nature, 574. How he works alone and yet not without the Son, 545. He works in the Son, because the work of ministry is referred back to the work of its author, 269. The Father’s work consists in will, 268. The Father manifests his will to the Son through mutual love and nature, 269. See “God” and “Son.” A right over a faithful son is not retained by an unbelieving father, I, 703. Christ’s patrimony, I, 796. Each person deserved to suffer what he began to suffer, I, 332.

Suffering changes all flesh through sensation and pain, II, 491. The distinction between susceptibility to suffering and actual suffering, 492. Human weakness is unequal to enduring sufferings, I, 340. God promised help to those under tribulation, 340. It is impossible for a human being not to be overcome by the terror of suffering, II, 348. Nor can a person be known except through testing, ibid. David prays not that what he suffers may be absent, but that he may be able to bear it, I, 374. We cannot suffer except through Christ’s suffering, 803. When the heat of faith burns within us, all our pains die with Christ’s body and passion, 803. Through sufferings we are exercised for the proof of faith and for the reward of glorious endurance, 364. How God grants recompense after this life to those who suffer here and rejoice, 444 ff. The voice and work of those suffering for truth, 395. The consolation of sufferings is that through them we are made like the Lord, 715.

David was not ignorant of the Lord’s passion: by suffering he taught himself to be a prophet, and by speaking he taught others, I, 144. Christ’s passion is foretold throughout Psalm XXI, II, 384. Psalm XL declares the entire mystery of the Lord’s passion, I, 505. David was its prophet by his own sufferings, 107, 127, 128, 605. How devoutly Christ gave himself to his passion, 503. Why, 107. Why it was a delight to him, 574. He longed for it because through it he provided for human salvation, 251. [Col. 0988] The passion was voluntarily undertaken by the only-begotten God in order to discharge a penal obligation, not so as to injure the sufferer through the sensation of punishment: why this is so, I, 114. The unrighteous had a right of suffering against Christ’s flesh, not against his divinity, 104. The onset of suffering in him was without the pain of suffering, II, 336. Sufferings did not befall Christ insofar as he is God, but insofar as he is human, I, 243. Christ suffered in the midst of the earth, 807. Christ’s passion: a triumph, II, 356. See “Emotions.” Endurance is taught by Psalm CXXVIII, I, 483; how necessary it is for the devout, 483. The devil is the author of what they suffer; human beings are his agents, 484. Christ is both the example and the help of endurance, 168. God delights that the devil is conquered by the powers of our endurance, 392. Patras, II, 632.

The Lord was prophesied in the generations, names, and persecutions of the patriarchs, I, 772. Their visions: see “Visions.” PATRICIUS, II, 693. PAULINUS, bishop of Dacia, accused of wicked deeds and expelled from the Church, II, 663. His other crimes, ibid. Paulinus of Trier resisted the crimes of the Arians at Arles, II, 540. Why he was judged unworthy of the Church and worthy of exile, 621. How much he suffered at the hands of Constantius, 570. His exile, 562.

Paul’s election was foretold in the Psalms and Genesis, I, 234. Paul received knowledge of the faith from the Lord himself, II, 263; he says that everything came through Christ’s revelation, 125; he wrote in Greek, 167; he revealed only matters of which human nature was capable, 399; he sets forth the heavenly mysteries with as much clarity as he can, 389. The worldly person does not grasp Paul’s sayings, 265. Paul was in paradise before martyrdom, II, 147; he underwent every kind of temptation, I, 340; he was buffeted by Satan’s angel, so that the unwearied afflictions of every suffering might remove from him an occasion for pride, 295, 365. The devil strove against him with every device of his power, 295.

PAUL, bishop of Constantinople, is said to have been present at and to have subscribed Athanasius’s deposition, II, 655; to have been anathematized by Protogenes, 658; repeatedly, 662; and, after his return from exile, to have committed dreadful acts, 653, 659, 660, 663. He was deposed, 660. PAUL of Samosata, II, 509. He falsely confessed *homoousion*, 513. His invention, I, 724, note. His malice and artifices, II, 649–650. What was decreed under Paul of Samosata was signed by all, 662. PAUL, defender of the faith at Rimini, II, 705, 707; perhaps the one who subscribed to the pseudo-Sardican synod, 664. PAUL, Roman presbyter, II, 669.

Relations between poor and rich, I, 794. Christ satisfies the poor when he invites them to be satisfied, 515. Collections for the poor were instituted by the Apostles, 101. Care for the poor is the greatest work of ministry, 125. Voluntary poor, I, 515. Christ’s poverty, I, 263, 590. What true peace is, II, 593. Those making their way toward God’s house must learn the teaching of peace, I, 437. The enemies of peace attack the preacher of peace, 425. Very many falsely claim peace in fellowship with heretics, 224. Heretics boast of their “peace,” that is, of the unity of their impiety, II, 593. The peace of idle faith is dangerous, I, 346.

Brotherly peace must be set before the peace of God, I, 685; it must be made quickly, 685. How the peace of greeting is to be given cautiously, 713. For peace’s sake one must seek not what suits oneself, but what suits the whole body, 409. The cause of peace interrupted or not preserved must not originate with us, 518. Peace and strength are mutually connected in God’s house, 437. The fruits of peace, 437: they are now tasted beforehand in the Church’s unity, but will abound in eternity, 437. The Lord’s kingdom is in the peace and unanimity of the saints, 640. Love of peace will make us equal to the patriarchs, 425. God dwells among the peacemakers, I, 759. Pearata, II, 632.

Original sin, I, 370, 372, 718–719, 758; II, 11. Through Adam’s sin we lost the nobility of the first and blessed creation, I, 714. A human being is born under the origin of sin and under the law of sin, 413. The prophet understands himself to be placed in a body of sin, 605. Human bodily weakness and the condition of origin hold people in sins, 527. Christ alone is free from sin, 110, 312, 316.

The law of sin, I, 174, 245—that is, the punishment of sin and the claim of death, 246. From one person the sentence of death and the toil of punishment went forth to all, 155. The whole earth has long been rendered harmful by curses because of human vices, 7. The soul contracted some stain of sin through association with the flesh, I, 299. No one who lives is without sin, 326; no one can be, 312, note there, 316. The glory of those who boast that they are clean from sins is vain, 342. Both the origin and the law of sin remain in us, 146. This utterance is not suitable to human conscience: “Without iniquity I have run,” 146. It is a great thing to know that the practice of crimes is far from oneself, 289. When David prays that sins may be cut off from him, he confesses not a sin already committed but the weakness of the flesh, 313. Although the path to sin is in the prophet’s body, he is wholly free from committing sin, 301. There is no return to heaven unless forgiveness of sins has been granted, 706–707. The law of sin, resisting the law of the mind, dwells in our flesh, 166. Through it we were dying, 166. God was born human for its condemnation, 166. Once the law of sin was condemned, forgiveness of sins was bestowed, 166.

The distinction between sin and iniquity, I, 494. Sins of the heart, 139. The necessity of sin is not inherent in human natures, 246. No one is born for the necessity and nature of sin, 140. Every sin is inexcusable, 594. Whether any sin is necessary, and how it may be without guilt, 776–777, note there. Why the sins of the Apostles did not harm them: there was in them an inclination of good will, 221.

The rulers of the air are authors of sin for us, I, 231. Demons supply incentives to sin and accuse us of what we have done through them, 379. The practice of sin is taken up through the desire of the will and delight in vices, 247. No one perseveres in sins except because he delights in them, 597. Sins are cords, 328, 486. A thorn signifies the force and pain of sins, 141. By sins we lose things blessed, greatest, and nearest to God; through repentance we are not deprived of things second to such blessings, I, 558. The Lord’s face is turned away from everyone who remains in sins, 200. There are certain sins that remove from the mouth the word of truth, 315. Sins deserve reproach, 296, 313. Confession of sins removes reproach, 296.

How God overlooks our sins, I, 626. Forgiveness of sins, 556. The Law and the Gospel promise pardon for sins through repentance, 558. The Law could not remit sin, 705; no one can forgive except God, 705. It belonged to Christ alone to forgive sins, 706. God grants forgiveness of absolutely all sins through faith, 760, after returning to confession, 760, by his own gift rather than our merit, 760. Forgiveness of sins is gratuitous, 208. Sins are corrected by humiliation, 332. Consolation is prepared for those weeping over old sins, I, 681. One who has confessed sins must cease from them, 556. On those who wish to cease from sin but do not cease, 190. There may be grief for those whose crimes are grave, but there is no place for mercy, 696, note there. There is no place for confession of sins except in this age, 92. Sin against the Holy Spirit, II, 646. See “Blasphemy.”

All are sinners, I, 375. The distinction between a sinner and an impious person, 19. The distinction between sinners compelled by external force and those fallen by their own fault, 627. Sinners who persist by will, 627. Whoever, having become a partaker of spiritual grace, remains in sin is a sinner of heaven, 376. All believers have been raised together and seated in heavenly places in Christ; if they fall thence through sin, they become sinners of heaven, 376. A sinner is a worker of the devil, servant of the world, vessel of death, material for Gehenna, 392; one sins not because one does not love Christ, but because one prefers something else to him, 29.

How God is not in sinners, I, 401. It is a sinner’s fault that he is cast away from God, 285. A person is a sinner before falling into the devil’s snare, 450, note there, 599. One in whom the will to sin exists is empty of God, 378; he is handed over to the devil when abandoned by God, 378. The devil cannot gain possession of sinners unless God withdraws from them, 428. When God departs, we fall into every pit of sinners, 428. Our withdrawal from him is followed by his withdrawal from us, 428. God is said to hand us over to vices when we withdraw from him, 428. Paul also hands sinners over to the devil, 378.

God forbade the sinner to recount the holy sayings, I, 233. Living sinners are consumed by sin, 448. The sight of sinners causes grief to saints, 321. Charity laments the calamity of sinners as though it were its own, 598. How God calls sinners to repentance, I, 41 ff.; how Christ kills them in order to make them alive, 582. Fire and a coal of desolation cleanse sinners, 421. The order to be observed by one who wishes to call sinners back to a better life, 713. How difficult it is to reform those advanced in age, 283. The recollection of former crimes pollutes them too, 283. Who sin voluntarily, and whether they obtain forgiveness, 595, note. The Lord supports those who fall, not those already collapsed, 627. Whoever presently belongs to God, though dashed down, can be raised, 632. Repentance holds sinners upright, 627. The breaking and re-forming of the sinner, 52 ff. The shame of the sinner who ceases from sins, 341. We ought to cease from sins, not from repentance, 391. How much better the state of a changed life is than the state of sin, 461.

The lot of sinners after this life, I, 176. Christ died for sinners unto the salvation of resurrection, 130. Sinners will experience God as avenger, though amid their works of iniquity they did not think of him, 112; before the resurrection they are punished by fire, I, 142. Their crushing and emptiness after the resurrection, 110. Money signifies worldly honor, I, 811. Desire for money is especially the root of iniquities, 169. Labor to increase money is a bond that impedes faith, 456. Contempt for money frees one from earthly dominations, 378. Lack of money is preferable to lack of sin, 418. PELAGIUS vainly twists a passage of Hilary to support his own opinions, I, 681, note. Pelosio, II, 666. Penetration of walls, I, 129.

Wings signify the power of flying to heaven, I, 573. That Christ is emptied of wings means that he empties himself; that he takes wings means that he returns to his former glory, 121. What *πέρας* (*peras*, “end”) means, I, 354. A stroke from God is merciful, I, 254. Perfection: rare is the person in whom perfection of the fear of God grows together with advancing years, I, 283. One must always strive, and not cease striving toward perfection because it cannot be attained, 471. Pergamum, II, 665. Perge, II, 667. What it means to perish, I, 59. Nothing is more grievous to a person than consciousness of danger, II, 176. In all dangers, if faith remains in us, the protection of heavenly powers is present, I, 557. *Permaneo* (“I remain”) denotes eternity, I, 351. Pernaso, II, 665. PERSIANS, I, 423. Persian war, II, 570. What it means to search through, I, 386.

How the faithful are liable to persecution, I, 444. What the disposition of one suffering persecution ought to be, 408. The persecution of a righteous person must be unjust, 346. How useful and necessary it is, 346. The peace of idle faith is dangerous, and easy are the snares that beset those secure on watch, 346. Whether persecution of those struck by God is unjust, 254. Intolerable persecutions by brethren, II, 535. The persecution of false brethren confers greater merit, 676. How Arians surpass pagan persecutors in impiety, II, 567–568. Those who yielded when conquered by tortures have some excuse, 567. The necessity of perseverance, I, 76. God’s mercy is needed for perseverance, 381. God is the giver of the perseverance of martyrs and Apostles, 202.

Distinction of persons in God, I, 37; II, 87, 93. How it is signified in Scripture, 88. A personal union is not to be admitted, II, 475. The cause of obstinacy, II, 321. The obstinacy of the nations in false religions and of those enslaved to the body teaches the faithful steadfastness in faith, I, 441. Steadfastness in hope, 444. Emotions do not apply to God, I, 37. They belong to imperfect nature, 38. It is most difficult to restrain mental disturbances within oneself, 120. The foot signifies the movement of the mind, I, 428. The Lord’s feet: the Apostles, 509. The rock of Peter’s confession, II, 160. Peter’s confession: the blessed rock of faith, 40.

PETER, rock of the Church, I, 603. Martyr of blessed old age and faith, II, 160. First confessor of the Son of God, foundation of the Church, keeper of the heavenly kingdom’s gate, etc., I, 502, 749, note there. He is subject to the building-up of the Church, II, 147. Peter’s faith is the foundation of the Church, 160. He earned the glory of every blessedness, 162, 161. There is no other glory apart from it, 162. Peter earned surpassing glory, II, 161. He believed first and was chief of the apostles, I, 701. He preceded the rest in faith, 743. He first recognized the Son of God, 805. He first recognized what in Christ was of God, 749. When he first recognized the nature of divinity in Christ, II, 160. How he was taught this, 160.

Peter’s affection for Christ, I, 799. Peter’s ardor, fall, and repentance, 742. Peter’s apostleship, faith, blessedness, priesthood, and martyrdom, II, 161. Peter possessed no human property, I, 323. His resources, 324. The devil prompted Peter to call Christ away from suffering, I, 750. Which of the two was called Satan by Christ, 750, note there. The slight faith of Peter, who tried to deter Christ from his passion, II, 162. Why he is excused from blame, 162. He received a sentence of condemnation, 162. Peter was called Satan because of disbelief in the cross, I, 566, 503. He was Satan and not Satan, 503. Through love for Christ he detested the passion, II, 341.

Peter fell into grave danger to his faith, II, 346. Peter’s denial was an offence against the Son of Man, I, 802. Peter denied Christ as human almost without guilt, 805, note there. He wept because he had not been able to avoid this fault even after being warned, 805. Peter did not lack firm faith of will to confess even unto martyrdom, I, 100. Yet he could not maintain constancy, 100. Hilary does not clear him of blame, ibid., note. The time of the denial and of the weeping was the same, 100. Steadfast faith wept over the inconstancy of fear, 100. The keys of the kingdom of heaven were not taken from him, 100. Peter’s faith did not fail in that he repented, II, 348. Though frightened, it did not fail because repentance followed, 351. The prerogative of the see of the apostle Peter, II, 629. A lying phantom: heresy, II, 350. PHARAOH: the devil, I, 534. The PHARISEES, ignorant of the whole Law, I, 784. Their wickedness, 729. PHILAEMON brought Berenice a topaz as a gift, I, 384, note. PHILETUS. See FILETUS. Philippi, II, 632. Philippopolis, II, 668. Whom those assembled there consider should be denied communion, 660. They pretend to write from Sardica, 660. Deacons were with them, 658. The PHILIPPOPOLITAN decree, II, 647. This synod is called Sardican, 580–581. What displeased the Arians in its creed, 580.

Philosophy is incapable of heavenly mysteries, II, 263. By itself it is weak for forming human character, I, 273. Philosophy’s eloquence held the nations in error, 185. The philosophers’ art against faith is vain, I, 181. Steadfast faith rejects their deceptive and useless questions, II, 10. Philosophical questions that assail faith must be cast aside, 418, and refuted by Christ’s ministers, 419. The austere life of philosophers is vain and superstitious, I, 184. PHILOXENUS, II, 629. Phoenicia, II, 482.

Photinus, II, 176, 242. He is denoted by the name of Pannonia, 177. Instructed by Marcellus, he was for some time a deacon under him, 634, 642. He is an Ebionite, 176, 180. He is Sabellius’s partial inheritance, 704. He conquers Sabellius, yet is conquered by Sabellius and the Arians, 180. The Scriptural passage by which he is refuted with respect to the authority of his heresy, 511. The manifold deceit of the heresy renewed by Photinus, II, 488. What his heresy is, I, 224; II, 492, 497, 548. It was condemned by the Romans in the year 347, 637; at the synod of Milan, 635; and again there in 349, 635. From this the Western decree concerning Photinus was conveyed to the Eastern bishops, 639. But at that time he could not be removed because of popular faction, 639. Photinus’s various condemnations, 639, note. A creed was written against him, 485. The two Phrygias, II, 482. Piety is to be honored in anyone, I, 76. Its commendation, II, 702. Hope nourishes the profession of piety, 7. The devout have frequent struggle from their earliest years, I, 483. How many battles the life of the devout endures, 585. It is hateful to the wicked, to the devil, and to his ministers, 353. The sight of the devout is grievous to the impious and joyful to the righteous, 338. A person cannot attain knowledge and true practice of a devout life without God’s grace, 273. Pisidia, II, 482. PISON of Troas, II, 666. PISON of Vanis, II, 666.

One must please God also in the body, I, 196. One should please human beings insofar as possible, 197. To wish to please human beings alone is to displease God, 102. Human beings should be pleased from God’s standpoint rather than to God’s dishonor, 102. There is no greater bond of pleasing people than that no one should wish to please for his own sake, 103. God does not call the minds of the faithful away from human favor, 103. Whoever now wishes to please God must necessarily displease the impious, 400. The doctrine of Placitus, II, 321. What a street is, I, 303. PLOTARCHUS, II, 632. Rain: the word of God, I, 221. The separated rain: Paul, 220. Punishment prepared for the impious is signified by the bow, I, 155. The Lord’s punitive arrows, 421. The punishment of the rich man after this life, 444.

How easy it is for God to restore penitents, I, 54. The penitent has the consolation of pardon with God, 627; through grief for what has been lost, he declares the disposition of one unwilling to lose it, 627. It belongs to the penitent to serve more intensely those through whom he has fallen, II, 703. A blessing is prayed for penitents, I, 490. In all Scriptures forgiveness of sins through repentance is promised, I, 558. God loves our change, 521; by both threatening and delaying punishment, he seeks the sinner’s repentance, 41 ff. A time for repentance is granted to each person, 330, 792. How patiently he awaits even late repentance, 486. Reform, though late, is useful, 283. Even late, one must strive to go out to meet the bridegroom, 795.

The voice of repentance is prayer with tears, I, 391. This is forgiveness of sin, ibid. Repentance causes one to cease, 627–628. Repentance for sin ought not to cease, but sin should cease, 391. [Col. 0992] The power of repentance, I, 42. It keeps sinners upright, lest they fall utterly, 627. Repentance has the capacity to restore us to the fullness of grace that was lost, 728. Through repentance there is return from error, retreat from crime, and a declaration of ceasing, 673 ff. The rejoicing of a soul returning from captivity to vices into the freedom of knowledge of God, 458, 460. Our change is God’s gift: he gives the grace of repentance and restores the beginnings of new goods, 461—that is, he does not impute earlier sins and renews us into a new life, ibid. There is no time for repentance after Christ’s final coming, 795. God’s repentance, I, 54, 650. Repentance for deeds done is God’s measure for deeds to be done by a human being, 54. Lay repentance, II, 544.

The people of God: all human beings, II, 612. By privilege, the people Israel, ibid. In comparison with this people, the rest were regarded as virtually unknown, ibid. What is fitting for God’s people, I, 519. Three kinds of those who eat God’s people, 100. Swine: heretics, I, 696. PORPHYRIUS, II, 632. Royal gate, I, 475. How the righteous will bar their enemies from its entrance, 475. POTAMIUS’s opinion at Sirmium, II, 460. Potamius rejoices to condemn the bishop of the city of Rome, 670. Those in power who command unjust things are to be regarded as nothing, I, 75. Power is signified by the sword, I, 651. It belongs to perfect power to be able to do what one can say, II, 106. The power of binding and loosing, I, 238. The Church was founded despite the opposition of worldly powers, II, 594. Those are reproved who think their support necessary for its protection, I, 594. By God’s judgment the power of the wicked perishes as wax before fire, 215.

The powers of the air trample the crown of the head, without the awareness of those on whom they stand, I, 231. They penetrate even the bodies themselves as far as the seat of soul and mind, 231. They move throughout the whole world at every moment, 231. They are authors for each person of whatever he commits as an offence, 231. Those who bring about human death receive the whole punishment for human death when they become authors of God’s death, 230. Commandment, law, testimony, and so forth are not one and the same, I, 273. Gentile precepts, 185. Idol-worshippers do not possess even a moderate knowledge of God’s commandments, 356. David was not ignorant of evangelical and apostolic precepts, 287. Psalm XIV is full of the precepts of the Old and New Testaments, 69. Whatever God commands is just, attested, and true, 392.

God’s commandments must not only be performed but also loved, I, 394. They instruct those who fulfil them in deed, 359. The Lord’s more difficult commandments needed to be established by no slight authority, 752. The source of their confirmation, 753. God’s commandments are not difficult if the will is present, 354. All persons cannot fulfil all things to the utmost degree of pleasing God, 354. We cannot in any way worthily fulfil God’s commandments according to the purpose of the will, 464. Precipitation, I, 85. Predestination: God predestined those whom he foreknew, I, 220. Foreseeing their wills, he set apart the voluntary rain through foreknowledge, 221. He set apart the blessed rain of good will, 220.

Preaching is compared to a needle, I, 764. How it is a net, I, 736. The food and hunger of the prophets, 639. God gives the food of preaching, 632. It loosens chains and drives away the world’s blindness, 632. By the preaching of God’s word, as by arrows, the devil’s kingdom is overthrown, 616. A bishop owes the Church the ministry of preaching, II, 133. A sinner who remains in sin ought to abstain from the office of preaching, I, 316. God wishes his sayings to be handled by the chaste mouth of a chaste body, 316. How great an evil foolish preaching is for hearers, II, 214. Those preaching Christ must bar and instruct the simpler people against human doctrines, II, 419. How great their knowledge ought to be, 420. They must seek this from the omnipotent wisdom of God, 419. The powers for preaching the Gospel receive the word from the Holy Spirit, II, 222. The preacher of truth is an instrument of the Holy Spirit, 64. Help for him comes from God, 346. Iniquity must hate the preacher of truth, 346. The serpent’s prudence in overcoming the first parents is to be imitated by preachers in their dealings with sinners, I, 714. The highest prefecture, II, 706. Foreknowledge of sin does not entail necessity, I, 141. Prophetic foreknowledge, I, 583. We should not be concerned with present things but with future ones, I, 688.

Remembrance of God’s presence in one’s actions, I, 410. God is not worthy to be looked upon by one whose heart is unclean, 410. God’s presence requires us to be watchful and open toward him, 401. God is not in the vicious, ibid. [Col. 0993] The impious person cannot endure a saint’s presence, as though it were a burden on the conscience, I, 338. The book of things past, that is, Chronicles, I, 366, 507. PRAETEXTATUS, II, 637. Praetor, I, 35. Transgressors are commonly thought to be those who promise one thing and do another, I, 375. Transgressors are those who depart from the natural law, 375. All are such, 375. The book of Acts, I, 741. No one prays except for what he hopes, I, 243. Prayers bare of works are of no benefit, 524. Prayers for the emperor, II, 537: for the emperor’s safety, his rule, and peace, 689. Hilary’s presbyters, II, 543. Without a presbyter the sacrificial rite could not take place, 633. The presbyterate of the Roman Church, II, 681. Men deem nothing more precious than gold, women than jewels, I, 384.

Firstborn persons are regarded as fathers of those born after them, whether by name or by lineage, I, 670. PRIMUS, II, 690. A ruler contains in his name and office the cause of the whole body subject to him, I, 739. PRISCUS, II, 690. Procia, II, 632. The depths: it belongs to one ignorant, suffering, or secretly praying in the heart to cry out from the depths, I, 491. PROHERESIUS, II, 665. Knowledge follows testing, I, 565. Christ’s testing was his humility, 565. The term “bringing forth” (*prolatio*), which Arians attempt to exclude, II, 137. What Valentinus understands by it, and what the Church understands by it, 137. Greek always uses pronouns in an honorable and necessary sense, II, 386. The distinction between pronouns and surnames, 148.

The prophets are winepresses, I, 777. The prophets’ words are vegetables, 735. The prophets’ sayings are God’s words, 386. A prophet speaks through the office of the mouth, but with knowledge not his own, 529. Whether the prophets were granted understanding of what they preached, 412. Some spoke of future things from the standpoint of the past, 436. Prophetic knowledge rejoices in events yet to occur as though already accomplished, 134. Christ remained in them by the Spirit, II, 386. The prophets are spiritual, I, 98. Christ is the work of the prophets, I, 786; II, 64. Why they stirred up Jewish hatred against themselves, I, 786. They are prefigured by children, 724. It was the prophets’ office to call people back from sins; Christ’s distinctive work was to save, 675.

The whole labor and purpose of prophecy, I, 537. Prophecy is intended either for hearers’ knowledge or for innocence of will, 165. It is more worthy of prophetic grandeur to have proclaimed blessed, eternal, and heavenly things than earthly things, 466. The divine Spirit is the author of prophetic speech, 562. The Spirit of prophecy is always the same, 91; II, 129. Prophetic discourse is expressed by the word “belching forth,” I, 411. Prophecy recounts accomplished things for things yet to be accomplished, 173, 458. Why, 43, 471. Prophetic speech has common usage, but not common meaning, 417. The prophetic books are mountains, 427. They are not to be assessed by the judgment of the ears alone, 451. Every prophecy concerning Christ is his lamp, 516. The corrupt affection for relatives must be uprooted from us, I, 686. From what source the right and name of kinship are now to be derived, 734. The distinctiveness of the divine persons, II, 374. Equality of distinctiveness, 197. The multitude of proselytes among Israel, I, 744, 784. Prosperity: human nature is unaccustomed to favorable circumstances, I, 447. The Lord’s regard for human beings, I, 96. Faith in prayer deserves God’s protection, I, 161. PROTOGENES, II, 632, 656, 658. He is said in the records to have anathematized Marcellus and Paul, 662; and to have subscribed the judgment against Marcellus, 650. Repeatedly, 662. At the council he condemned Marcellus’s sect four times, 656. God’s providence, I, 636. It is denied by some, 622. All things praise the Creator’s providence, 647. Through God’s abundant care, the strength of the soul is increased, 559. Christ is our neighbor, I, 782. Human prudence fails in divine matters, II, 65. The first part of prudence is wisely to ask about what one does not understand, I, 306. That prudence alone is true which begins from the very first beginnings of childhood, 272.

To sing psalms signifies religious acts of the body, I, 631. Where “Sing psalms” is said, it refers to bodily works, 528. What a psalm properly is, I, 13; what it is mystically, 13–14. A psalm commonly signifies an office not so much of the voice as of bodily action, 634. What a “psalm of a song” properly is, I, 13, 195; what it is mystically, 14. [Col. 0994] The book of Psalms is one book, not five, I, 1. Why it is divided into three fifties, 632–633. The order and number of Psalms among the Hebrews are not the same as among the Septuagint, 652. Among the Hebrews the Psalms lack order and numbering, 7, 33. They were gathered into one volume by Ezra, 7, 6. The Septuagint reduced them to number and order, 7, 33. The order of subjects, not of times, was preserved, 7. The order and number of Psalms are mystical, 7.

The Psalms were first written in musical metre, I, 15. Their titles are varied, 12. The Psalms, although some are inscribed “Psalms of David,” I, 1, are not David’s alone, 3, but belong to those whose names they bear, ibid.; and those without a name belong to the person named as author in the preceding psalm, 3. Some are inscribed to Jeremiah, Haggai, and Zechariah without authority, 3. The titles of the Psalms direct us toward their understanding, I, 414. Psalm and title give one another authority, 414. Psalms simply inscribed “unto the end” are to be understood spiritually, 177. How those inscribed “understanding, unto the end” are to be understood, 95; and those inscribed *τῷ Δαυίδ* (“to David”) or *τοῦ Δαυίδ* (“of David”), 95. What the title “for those who shall be changed” means, 153.

The Spirit of God is the author of the Psalms, I, 562. The Psalms teach us perfect knowledge of God and obedience, 355. Some are easy, others difficult to grasp, 60. To understand them, it helps to know who is speaking and about whom, 16. The Psalms are prophecies of evangelical mysteries, 4. They are closed and sealed to learned and unlearned alike without the key of faith, 4–5; and each has its own keys, 15. The key of the Psalms is faith in Christ, 5. The Psalms do not announce only events of their own time, I, 415. In them there is nothing lowly or commonplace, 382; nothing except prophecy, 604. What lies hidden beneath familiar words, 382. When they are recognized as full of mysteries, 652. The book of Psalms is arranged beyond the merely literal understanding, according to the meaning of a higher interpretation, 652. The spiritual interpretation of the Psalms cannot be rejected, 457. A psalm may be understood spiritually even though its title sets forth a historical matter, 414. Some Psalms whose titles seem to present historical events signify effects of spiritual realities very different from those events, 177. The Psalms of the prophet contain true events, but those of Christ …
are prophecies, I, 128. Some think that in almost all the psalms nothing suits the person of Christ, 121. Hilary prefers, while preserving the truth of the events, to hold that very much applies to him, 121. Many believe that all the words of the psalms should be referred to Christ, 178. They are praised, but not approved, ibid. To what extent they ought to be referred to Christ, 178. Which psalms are all about him, 663. In them is contained every mystery of his bodily coming, 663. Every prophecy of the psalms is to be referred to Christ, 17. But where the speech of prophecy refers to him must be discerned by rational knowledge, ibid. What befits his person and dignity must be recognized, 17. The rule for understanding the psalms that concern Christ, 117. In psalms concerning Christ there is always something distinctive that does not fit another. 601

Psalm I: how many teachings it contains, I, 18. Psalm II: whether it is part of the first, or should be called the second, 31. Why it is called the first by Paul, 33. Psalm XIV: to be written upon the heart, marked in the memory, and stored in the inward parts, 77. Psalm XV: to be understood as spoken in the person of the Lord, 133. Psalm XVII: wholly spoken in the person of the Lord, 611. Psalm XXXVII likewise wholly spoken in the person of the Lord, suffering for us and bearing our sins, 261. Psalm XL, spoken in the person of the Lord, declares the entire mystery of the Passion, 505. Psalm LII is wholly about Christ, 95. Psalms LIII and LIV are to be referred to the same person, 107, 117. The exposition of Psalm LV is to be balanced between David and Christ as man, 128. Psalm LVI concerns Christ, 133. Psalm LVIII treats at once of David and of Christ, 144. Psalm LIX does not accord with the historical title prefixed to it, 152. It sets forth events, not because it was written on account of those events, but in order that the time at which it was written may be known, 153 ff.
