Profane knowledge yields to divine knowledge, I, 182. How uncertain and wavering is the knowledge of the Gentiles concerning divine matters, 165. Their most prudent men professed that they knew this one thing only: that man knows nothing of such matters, 166. Cicero’s saying, 166, note there. How splendid and varied a knowledge is gained from sacred books, 166 ff. Earthly knowledge must be refuted by heavenly knowledge, II, 419. Its power comes from him in whom God can do all things, 419. Heavenly knowledge is God’s gift, I, 348; the principal gift of the Spirit, 332. Only believers can attain knowledge, 332. Knowledge of the commandments must be sought from God in prayer, 338. The use of wisdom is perfected in the exercise of knowledge, 274. Those who shine with knowledge are flashes of lightning, 532. They become rain when they pour forth doctrine, 532.

The Scriptures are neglected by many as though they were fables of empty things, I, 312. They are cheapened by thoughtlessness, 540. Many boast that there is nothing rational or perfect in them, 314, because, owing to the impiety of their own intellect, they cannot comprehend them, 314. For those who understand the Scriptures, there is nothing in them except what is perfect, 314. In them there is neither confusion nor poverty of words, 273. The Scriptures do not consist in superfluities, 540. They contain nothing unworthy of their author, 540. Whatever is in them is lofty, [Col. 1001] divine, rational, and perfect, 540. Nothing is wiser or more eloquent than the Scriptures, 314, note.

The manifold teaching of the Scriptures, I, 540. Why their books are numerous and diverse, 540. The Word of God has provided for all who would come into life, 415. How much knowledge the Scriptures instill in us, 166 ff. Every Scripture calls us to hope for heavenly goods, 319. By the Scriptures God has instructed us in the knowledge of himself, II, 145. The Scriptures were committed to writing for no other reason than that they might flow into the knowledge of all, I, 405. How great a guilt it is not to seek knowledge of them, 405.

The spiritual senses of Scripture are not invented, I, 457; nor is violence done by Hilary to their truth, 506 ff. Those who think that everything must be understood according to the letter are refuted, 550, 553. They maintain that the prophets did not even speak earthly things rationally, 451. In the Scriptures, the order of statements conveys something deeper beyond the hearing of the ear, 231. Scriptural language is adapted so as to prefigure future things by present things, 762. Sometimes something is lacking to the rational account of present events, in order that we may be reminded that something else is thereby prefigured, 776.

Scripture is rich in meanings, I, 729. By bodily events it prefigures spiritual realities, 526, 531, 533; II, 249. The allegorical sense subtracts nothing from the truth of the letter, I, 531, 699. The truth of events is not corrupted when it is shown to be subject to an inner interpretation, 673. Faith in history is not endangered if we judge that an outwardly connected significance inheres in events that have occurred, 449.

From where the understanding of the Scriptures must be sought, II, 82. Scripture consists not in reading but in understanding; not in transgression but in charity, 548. Its secrets are hidden from the wise of the world, 512. Heretics draw the Scriptures to their own side, 548. A perverse interpretation must not be forced from the Scriptures, 223. How the Arians abuse them, 258, 259. The Scripture of the Law, published before Christ, was possessed by the Jews, received by the Gentiles, but understood and approved by Christians, I, 457. This understanding is God’s gift, 457. It is not denied to those who ask, 458.

Scripture, full of mysteries, requires an experienced and devout reader, I, 526. Moral uprightness is preparation for investigating God’s testimonies, 275. To understand the mysteries of the old Law, a heavenly teacher and very many merits of faith are required, 381. Knowledge of Scripture is acquired by frequent reading and the gift of spiritual grace, 526. Study of the Scriptures should be persistent, but their understanding must be expected from God, II, 24. Grace is necessary to understand them, I, 272. That he may understand Scripture and speak fittingly, Hilary asks for fellowship in the prophetic and apostolic Spirit, II, 24. Scriptural understanding must be sought from what precedes or follows, II, 259. The powers of words must be examined no less than the realities, I, 710. Individual matters must be distinguished according to persons, times, and powers, 526.

Scripture does not ordinarily repeat the same matters in two forms of expression, I, 488. It never changes its customary manner of speaking without cause, II, 121. When in Scripture a discourse begun by one person is attributed to several, unanimity among the several is taught, I, 202. The key of the Scriptures is knowledge of Christ, 5. In obscure passages of Scripture it helps to suggest a plurality of interpretations, 298. What should be provided for one who does not understand the Scriptures, II, 344.

The authority of Scripture, I, 781. In divine matters, sayings that are not more frequently uttered but are simply uttered suffice, II, 86. We must seek an account not of divine sayings, but of our own understanding, 86. How Scripture should be read, heard, and sung, I, 321. Jews reading sacred books do not dare to touch them with the hand, but place a cloth beneath them, 500. The soul refreshed by God’s utterances keeps within itself, as it were, some nourishment of eternal life, 320. The books that Hebrew religion handed down as written by Moses and the prophets, II, 4. Which Scriptures Hilary held canonical, I, 10, note. What is not contained in the book of the Law we ought not even to know, 521. Hilary combines two translations of Scripture at once, 642, note. An unknown passage of Scripture, 450.

“I know,” II, 633.

The fruit of searching is the preservation of what has been found, I, 306.

SCYRUS (also Ischyras), highly notorious, II, 625. He was not a presbyter of Meletius, 626. He is denied to have been a presbyter at all, 633, 634. As a reward for falsehood, he received the honor of the episcopate, 626. A bishop is alleged to have been ordained from a deacon, so that the liar’s authority might be greater, 625, 633.

Secoro, II, 632.

To reveal certain secrets of God is an inexpiable fault, I, 285. Those who presume to judge divine secrets are sharply rebuked, II, 60 ff.

SECUNDIANUS, presbyter, II, 706.

Our nature is incapable of secondary things. The dignity of God’s seat, I, 226. The seat of evangelical peace, I, 226.

Acts of the Synod of Seleucia, II, 572 ff. The Synod of Seleucia, with a number of bishops far exceeding one hundred, instructs its delegates to resist the heresy of the Anomoeans, 693. What those delegates did at Constantinople, 694 ff.

The interpretation of Selmon is “peace,” I, 223.

Hilary did not consider the Semi-Arians altogether orthodox, II, 451 ff. See Easterners.

What a path means, I, 308, 567.

The source of sensation in bodies, II, 329 ff., 352. On what the use of the senses depends, 48. Nothing falls within sensation unless it lies beneath the senses, 403. How sensation is altered through the purpose of the soul, 353.

The senses do not know the causes of many things whose effects they do know, II, 440. They attain certain things which speech does not explain, I, 741. The mind speaks to itself, understanding what it cannot express in speech, II, 6. Certain deeds of Christ surpass understanding, I, 741. Meaning must be subordinated to the words, not words to one’s own meaning, 571. One should not be ashamed sometimes to change one’s understanding, II, 390. Let human understanding become foolish to itself, so that it may be wise toward God, 103.

SEON, an unfruitful tree, I, 534.

North, II, 440.

The number seven is customary in Scripture, I, 409.

Seventy elders appointed by Moses to preserve the teaching of the Law, I, 7. Seventy teachers established by Moses throughout the whole Synagogue, 31. Made by him participants in the more secret mysteries of the Law, 32. They had successors in the same number and office, 32.

The SEVENTY translators, called by the title “Elders of the Hebrews,” I, 548. They were teachers and leaders of the synagogue, 33. Trained beyond the letter’s prescribed limits in knowledge of the Law and the prophets, 604. Aware of the tradition of Moses, 32. Endowed with spiritual and heavenly knowledge, 19. They translated the books of the Old Testament from Hebrew into Greek, 31. They translated the whole Law, 7. They translated the Psalms among the other books, 33. What they accomplished in their translation, 33. They reduced the Psalms to number and order, 7. They added a title where it is absent in other manuscripts, 610, 604.

The books of the Seventy translators are authoritative, I, 3. Among variant translations they are to be preferred, 514. Their translation is lawful and spiritual, received before the Lord’s Passion; in all the Psalms it makes their meaning and occasion plain, 153. Their authority is religious and ancient, 310. It is unsafe to depart from their translation, 301, 524. The basis of their authority, 33, note.

Tombs, the lifeless dwellings of bodies, I, 219. The tombs of the Apostles and Martyrs speak Christ, II, 376. Upon tombs are inscribed the life and death of brave men, I, 133.

Speech exists only when the voice is heard, not before or after, II, 35. Every human utterance is open to contradiction, 321. The mind cannot express in speech certain things it apprehends, 6.

The weakness of our speech in expressing the things of God, II, 31. What speech concerning God ought to be like, 117. A discourse on divine matters must be woven from God’s words, 14. To what extent it helps and is permissible to seek certain analogies from lower things, 14. Speech has no greater reward than to serve God, 24. It is God’s gift that we speak well concerning him, 24.

The distinction between prophetic and ordinary speech, I, 411. What the speech of a prophet ought to be like, 348.

The Word of God speaks to us, not to himself, and in speaking uses our language, I, 467. It is accommodated to our understanding, II, 84, 244. It must be evaluated from the words of our speech, I, 262, and from its own reasons, II, 82. How rich it is, I, 729. Examined in meaning, it contains more significance than when received by hearing, II, 5. How much deference is due to it, 206.

The serpent’s prudence, by which it withdraws its head from a blow, I, 714. The serpent’s prudence in the temptation of the first parents, 714. How preachers should imitate it, 714. The Arian heresy is compared to a serpent, II, 136.

One cannot serve God and the world, I, 690. Service to God must not be postponed until old age, 398. How advantageous it is to have been God’s servant from early youth, 283. No one denies himself to be God’s servant by word, but by deeds, 782. God’s servant is recognized not by words but by deeds, 697. How great the steadfastness of faith should be in those who serve God, 441. For one to remain God’s servant, one needs God’s mercy, 381.

Slaves of the flesh, I, 443. Slaves of sin, I, 442. Slaves of Gentile gods, 442, 443. The slavery of the greedy, I, 459; of the lustful, 459; of drunkards, 459.

Sitting signifies teaching, I, 566.

SEVERINUS, II, 680, note; 706.

The discipline of severity, I, 332.

SEVERUS of Cabula, II, 668.

SEVERUS of Ravenna, II, 632.

What is shown by the six days followed by the Lord’s glory, I, 752.

[Col. 1003] Certain heretics live on the dry food of bread, I, 184.

Shechem, also called Sichem, is Samaria, assigned by Jacob to Joseph, I, 157.

The nature of seals, II, 245, 246. The seals of the seven-sealed book, I, 5.

The sign on foreheads, I, 155.

Silence is suited to faith and youth, I, 284. The task of the silent person, 284. Why Christ commands those whom he heals to keep silence about him, 728.

SILVANUS, II, 693, 680.

SIMEON saw God by faith amid the filth of the cradle, I, 67.

Resemblance often deceives, II, 515. Nowhere will you find “likeness” concerning the Son, 578. Nowhere is the Son written to be like his begetter, 599. The Arians reject likeness according to substance, 706. The Son’s likeness according to the Scriptures is asserted deceitfully, 696. What likeness is holy to Hilary, 579. Why it must not be granted to heretics, 579. The Gauls do not reject the Son’s likeness to the Father when properly understood, 699.

True likeness is in the truth of nature, II, 515. Natural likeness makes the things themselves equal, 502 ff. Some confess likeness but vainly deny equality, 503. The Son’s likeness of nature is without any difference, I, 513. Birth is equal through likeness, II, 197.

Christ is the likeness of sinful flesh, not a likeness of flesh, II, 578, since in him there existed not sin but the likeness of sinful flesh, 714.

SIMON the Samaritan, I, 788.

Simplicity is commended, I, 737.

SIMPLICIUS, II, 680.

SINFERUNS, or Sympheron, II, 647.

Bishops gathered at Singidunum attempt to bring Germinius back to the Ariminian creed, II, 705.

Good singularity, I, 599.

Sinopa, II, 665.

Abraham’s bosom, in which the righteous are kept after this life until they enter the kingdom of heaven, I, 143, 174, 432. David hopes that he himself will live in Abraham’s bosoms, 91.

Zion is the mountain overlooking the city of Jerusalem, I, 184, 452, 487; a hill joined to the Temple of Jerusalem, 259. The true Zion, 513. In Latin Zion is called “contemplation,” 259, 453, 587, 640. By this name the Church is signified, 184, 487, 520; and the glorious body of Christ, 66, 487. In it we contemplate by faith our hope and life, 260, 640. Spiritual Zion, the seat of God’s kingdom, 632. Those who love the Lord will dwell in Zion, 260.

ZION, II, 666.

The Syracusan, II, 650.

The Synod of Sirmium in the year 349, II, 638, note. Its acts, 639 ff. Its fraudulent and heretical creed, 641, 643.

The Synod of Sirmium in 351 against Photinus, II, 380, 581. The creed of that synod, 485. What subsequently displeased the Arians in it, 580. Liberius subscribed to the Sirmian perfidy, 678. Its drafters, 680.

The Sirmian blasphemy drafted by Hosius and Potamius, II, 464. It emerged at Sirmium through Hosius, 498. What was attempted by it, 464. Hilary reluctantly transcribes it, 464. He calls its words Hosius’s ravings and the advances of Ursacius and Valens, 580. This formula is called “the faithless faith” and “the doctrine of impiety,” 498. The position of Hosius and Potamius, 460. Sent into Gaul, it was immediately condemned, 459, 463. The Easterners opposed it, 460, 463. They brought the definitions of Ancyra to Sirmium, 521. The authors and adherents of the Sirmian blasphemy compel subscription to them, 461, 476. Their excuse is deceptive, 506 ff.

The proceedings of the Sirmian assembly at which the creed was dictated by Mark, II, 708.

Bodily thirst admonishes the believer to thirst still more for God, I, 172. Thirst for righteousness, 167.

SOBAL, I, 153.

It contributed to Sodom and Gomorrah’s reconciliation to mercy that they were struck, I, 254.

At Christ’s Passion, the sun failed in the course of its activity, II, 55. The Manichaean worshipper of the sun, 138. The sun’s power upon human bodies, I, 430. The likeness of the sun extended everywhere, 401. By the example of the sun it is shown that God must not be scrutinized too inquisitively, II, 359.

The solidity of the world, I, 265, note.

How busy was David’s solitude, removed from every company of human beings, impiety, or ignorance, I, 171. It prefigured Christ’s dwelling in the wilderness, 171.

Do not be anxious, I, 126. The carelessness of relaxed anxiety is not negligence but faith, 695. Anxiety is aroused by the anguish of care, fear, or pain, 695. Our concern should be to cleanse sins and earn heavenly goods, 695.

God is not alone, II, 181.

SOLUTOR, II, 690.

[Col. 1004] Death is customarily signified by sleep, I, 223. God very frequently calls the death of saints sleep, 472.

SOPHRONIUS, II, 693.

The Spaniard, II, 700.

Spartum, II, 526.

The partisan contest of a theatrical spectacle, I, 598. Eyes defiled by theatrical spectacles, 72. Pious spectacles are more pleasing than shameful spectacles, 311.

Hope, the one solace of this life, I, 104. It consoles the afflicted, 320. No one prays except for what he hopes for, 243.

What is the hope of believers, I, 433; II, 618. How it is ridiculed by the impious, I, 374. It rests upon God’s promises, 319. Every Scripture calls us to hope for heavenly goods, 319. Our hope has no end, 399. Hope for eternal goods is contained in the life and deeds of the ancient Fathers, 402. What we hope for, we behold in Christ’s glorious body, 487. No hope without faith, II, 298. Hope of life is equally in the Father and the Son, 57. Hope fully directed toward salvation is in the confession of the Trinity, 698.

The merit of hope, II, 618. By hope and fear we attest God’s mercy and power, I, 639. Hope merits God’s help, 372. All our hope is in God, 90. It rests most firmly upon God’s mercy, 92. What hope is there for human sins if kindness is absent from God? 527.

Our hope is founded in Christ, I, 162. It is the surest defense against the devil, 162. It does not fear human hatreds, 129. Whether hope is presumption concerning uncertainties, or expectation of things known, 187. Hope must be shown in deeds, 319. Steadfast hope, 443. We ought to attend only to hope for what is to come, 688. In hope of the future, worldly things must be despised, 688. Hope is laid up for the saints, but is still delayed under the dispensation of times, 162. Every time is free for hope, 496. Even late hope should trust in Christ, 703.

Ears of grain are not food suitable for man, I, 727.

The force and pain of sinners is signified by a thorn, I, 142.

Breathing is more laborious through the mouth than through the nostrils, I, 387.

Spiritual things owe their continuance to Christ, II, 249.

The inhabitants of the Church are spiritual, I, 450.

Spiritual wickednesses use the ministries of the impious to harass the saints, I, 129. See “Wickednesses” or “Devil.”

The nature of spirit, II, 45. Whether “Spirit of God” denotes nature or a reality belonging to nature, 229. The Spirit of Christ and of God is one, 228, 231. By the word “Spirit” sometimes the Father is signified, sometimes the Son, 229, 230; at times the Holy Spirit, 231. Why Father and Son are called Spirit, 230.

The Holy Spirit is frequently understood in place of Father and Son, II, 44. Hence some doubt the Holy Spirit’s existence, 44. His existence is unquestioned, 43. Apostles and prophets speak only of the fact that he is, 44. The Holy Spirit is a reality of one nature with God and Christ, 231. He must not be separated from the confession of Father and Son, 43 ff. When the Holy Spirit is named together with Father and Son, it is fitting that unity should be proclaimed through likeness of substance as concord rather than essence, 481. Hilary asserted the divinity of the Holy Spirit: see Preface, vol. II, no. 15; 736, note. Why he did not add to him the name of God: see Preface, vol. II, no. 14. No one should dare to number the Holy Spirit among creatures, 140. Defective teachings concerning the Holy Spirit must be removed, II, 139.

The Holy Spirit is not unbegotten, since he is sent by the Son, II, 494. Why he is said to be sent by the Father when he is sent by the Son, 494. He is other than the Son, 494. He is not a part of the Father or the Son, 494. He was not created, 441; not begotten, 442. He did not take from creatures, 315, but from the things of the Father and Son, 315. He is through him through whom are all things and from whom are all things, 45. He receives from the Father and the Son, 645. The unity of the Holy Trinity is expressed, 645. He is God’s reality and not alien from him, 442. He is not a power of his own nature remaining from the Father through his Only-Begotten, 442. He measures the depth of God’s immeasurable majesty, 442. The Holy Spirit has no limit, 443. He is ineffable, 442. He speaks to God on our behalf things beyond speech, 442. His substance is not different from that of the Father and Son, 28.

The procession of the Holy Spirit, II, 226. Whether receiving from the Son is the same thing as proceeding from the Father, 227. The Lord did not leave uncertain from whom he is, 227. Freedom is left to the understanding whether he is from the Father or from the Son, 227. Although not by comprehension, yet by awareness we hold that the Spirit of God is from the Father through the Son, 442. The Son is giver and author of the Holy Spirit, 28. Giving through the Spirit and giving in the Spirit are not the same thing, 235. The Spirit is distinct both in office and in honor, 46, note. When God, who is Spirit, is said to be worshipped in Spirit, 46. This worship has the infinity proper to worship, 46.

The Holy Spirit is a gift in all, II, 26. He is the gift of believers, 44. A gift which we receive and return, 46, note. The most necessary gift, 48. In him are his cause, character, and power in their fullness, 48. How the manifestation of the Spirit occurs, 234.

[Col. 1005] Times do not introduce diversity of spirits, II, 386. The one Holy Spirit is everywhere, enlightening all patriarchs, prophets, and so forth, 47. The divine Spirit is the author of every prophetic utterance, I, 562. He speaks in the prophets, 427. In how many different ways he speaks, 60. The Spirit of prophecy is one and the same in many persons, II, 129. The Synagogue did not have the Holy Spirit, I, 773. Another Advocate besides the Lord is ours, 427. He has the affection of one who desires, 427. It must be reconciled that the Lord who is to send the Holy Spirit was born of the Holy Spirit, II, 512.

The Holy Spirit was sent in order to instruct, teach, and sanctify believers, II, 466: for consolation, sanctification, and consummation in believers, 479. His gift bears witness to the Lord’s glory, I, 136. The office of the Holy Spirit in us, II, 47. The Holy Spirit spoke through Paul’s soul, 629. The gift of the Holy Spirit illuminates our faith concerning God’s incarnation, 47. The Holy Spirit intercedes with God for those who make vows to God which the Church approves, I, 184. The first gifts of the Holy Spirit are granted to the baptized, 192.

Gifts of the Holy Spirit, II, 234. It is lawful neither to buy nor sell them, I, 773. The whole gift of the Holy Spirit is available as one gift to all, II, 48. It is absent nowhere, 48. It is given insofar as each person is willing to receive it, 48. The Holy Spirit does not force himself upon us, but must be sought and drawn, I, 388. Through faith there is salvation for the Gentiles, 746. When he fills us, he always becomes richer and fuller, 747. The Holy Spirit’s gift exceeds in itself the multitude of those who draw from it, 710. It is beneficial for there to be many through whom it is ministered, 710. It is poured out for us through prayer and petition, 711. By the power of this gift the devil is cast out and infirmities are healed, 711. The gift of the Holy Spirit is to be bestowed on the Gentiles through laying on of hands and prayer, 762.

The coming of the Holy Spirit is a certain baptism after the baptism of water, I, 291.

Blasphemy against the Spirit, I, 696, 730, 802.

Spirits burned without fires, II, 567.

By “spirit” the soul is frequently signified, II, 364.

One who pledges himself to Christ already stands in the form of eternity, I, 424.

Our Lord is bridegroom and bride in the body, God, I, 794.

What standing means, I, 509.

A stater, I, 756.

Stars: the elect, I, 635. Hilary does not seem to have believed stars to be animate, 645, note.

To whom astrology was entrusted, I, 128.

STEPHEN, the first martyr, I, 756. As though into the foremost regions of heaven, God the Father descended to meet him, 147.

STEPHEN of Antioch, II, 538, 627, 664.

STEPHEN of Arabia, II, 627, note.

STERCORIUS of Canusium, II, 632.

STERCORIUS, II, 706.

The style of Antichrist, II, 597. The style of Satan, 599.

Folly betrays itself when it opposes truth, II, 219. Unbelieving folly, 67. We must assume folly in order to take up wisdom, 68. The wise folly of believers, 66 ff.

103 et following. How Christ’s subjection is wrongly understood by some, II, 389, note. The distinction between the subjection of the Son of God and that of created things, 507. A certain subjection is a concession from nature to nature, 397. We shall be subjected to God when the weakness of our nature has been absorbed into the divine nature, I, 62. The sweat of blood is not weakness, but power, II, 351. To mock and to deride do not differ, I, 36. The name and reality of substance are indicated by many holy Scriptures, II, 685. Substance is the same as essence, 466, 646. It is that which subsists in itself, 467; which does not need external assistance to sustain itself, 646. The substance of Father and Son is one and the same, I, 725, 783. The generation which brings forth substance did not alter the nature of the substance, II, 286. Silence concerning substance is commanded by the Sirmian exposition of faith, 465; why, ibid. Constantius condemns the name “substance,” which he had professed, 581. *Sum*: the force of the word “to be,” II, 183. The sum of the dispensation, II, 286. The proud: the devil and his ministers, I, 379. How God is far removed from the proud, 560. The contempt of the proud at the judgment, 445. Pride despises human things and neglects divine things, I, 299. It renders good works vain, 295. By no fault is God’s wrath more provoked against us than by pride, 295. Through the vice of pride the grace of God becomes idle, 365. How greatly Paul feared pride for God’s ministers and the faithful, 295, 365; how he himself was delivered from it, 295, 366. The remedy for pride that trusts in itself and is insolent toward others, 74. The causes of pride are enumerated, and those which Christ removed, 364. Pious pride through confidence of faith, I, 445. [Col. 1006] Superstitions in austerity of life, I, 148. Good deafness and evil deafness, I, 140. SURINUS, II, 680. Received at the right hand of God, I, 175. SYLVESTER. Alexander’s letter to Sylvester, II, 673. Creed, II, 684. The creed of regeneration, 444, 550. The Synagogue, concealing the light beneath a bushel, I, 683. It did not have the Holy Spirit, 773. At Christ’s coming it was devoid of fruit, 683. Now it is like the fig tree which lacks fruit, not leaves, 773. It is compared to the same tree, 774. Weapons granted to the Church against the Synagogue, II, 428. Manasseh, set after Ephraim, a type of the rejected Synagogue, I, 158. What reverence is due to synods, II, 547. Hilary despises the synods which Auxentius was to assemble against him, 600. From the Nicene Synod, once the evangelical and apostolic doctrines have been unfolded, the light of Catholic unity shines forth, 643. The emperors convened the Synod of Sardica, 622. Chosen representatives from all the churches attended it: for what purpose, 624. Two presbyters and one deacon, delegates of Julius, were present there, 629. The Synod of Sardica asks those absent to confirm by letter what it decreed, 628. The custom of synods was that, after someone had been condemned, letters should be sent to all for their instruction, 640. The Easterners, on their way to Sardica, held synods in each locality, 627. See **Council**. A synod to be held in Bithynia, II, 462. The synods at Ancyra and Ariminum: to these two or one person from each Gallic province were to come, II, 463. Syria, I, 153. Coele-Syria, II, 482. SYSIMIUS, II, 667.

## T

Tabernacles established by various persons, I, 70. Leafy tabernacles customary in Hilary’s age, 70. To be silent: it is no less dangerous always to have kept silent than never [to have spoken], II, 562. Unequal distribution of talents is not to be attributed to the distributor, I, 795. TAURINUS, II, 690. TAURUS, praetorian prefect, II, 692. Taxis, for Gaza, II, 665. TELAPHIUS, II, 665. That the preaching of the new Gospel is called by the name of a weapon is an expression frequent among the prophets, I, 718. The temple and altar of the Synagogue were shadows of the incorruptible temple and sanctified altar, I, 415. In the temple there were fifteen steps: first the Levites, then Israelites, then proselytes, etc., stood upon them, 415. The temple is Christ himself, I, 727. The holy are a temple for God, 557. Holiness, righteousness, and human self-restraint are a temple for God, 468. Everyone reborn in Christ is God’s temple, 235. The eternal temple of God: what human being [is], 788. What time is, I, 43; II, 37. It is from the Word, II, 37. Times exist through Christ, 305. Arians commonly reckon them from the creation of sun and moon, 427. Angels precede times, 596. Eternal times, 427. The acceptable time, I, 249. How heretics purport to prove that darkness is coeternal with God, II, 512. Tenedos, II, 632. Christ’s temptation, I, 677. The order of Christ’s temptations is the same as Adam’s, 678. Whence our temptations arise, I, 455. Why God permits us to be tempted, 282. We must pray that he may not utterly abandon us in temptations, 282. Temptation is not to be rejected, but its domination [is], 389 ff. Many saints attained glory through temptations, 389 ff. David almost yielded to temptations, 346. His remaining in God’s commandments is the more glorious because the weakness of his nature was almost overcome, 347. The dangers of temptations, and how each person ought to prepare against them, 327 ff. The progress of temptations, 698. Various temptations from demons, I, 397. Spiritual wickednesses incite us to bodily vices by introducing the enticements of desires, 347. Whatever snares spiritual wickednesses spread are chiefly laid through human beings, 585. Various temptations from philosophers, heretics, and carnal Christians, 179. God alone can remedy these, 179. Against all these, sleepless care, nightly prayer, and perpetual confession to God will contend, 179. How many snares are spread before us, 455 ff. The snares of temptations are extended everywhere for us, 361, 368. Those who wholly entrust themselves to God fly free from them, 368 ff. Snares are spread before all: to fly free from them is glory, 450. The whole world is full of snares, 598, 587. The devil’s trials rage especially against saints, I, 677. Against the stronger, the battle of our enemy is both long and frequent, 485. Hence comes the unceasing character of our assault, [Col. 1007] not any overpowering strength in those who attack us, 485. He who has renounced the world complains vainly about the world’s temptations, 369. Temptations must not hinder prayer and devotion, 601. Those tried in prayer will find rest, 418.

Our nature is unequal to overcoming temptations, I, 418. It is also unequal to bearing them, 340. God promised help to those being tested, 340. He gives it through mercy, 340. That temptation should not dominate us is the Lord’s gift, 389. The snare of temptation is conquered with God’s help, 451. A soul subject to temptations will be preserved by meditation upon the law, 352. Hope is the safest defense against the devil’s snares, 162. All who were accustomed to kindle wars of vices against us have been extinguished by Christ, 153. Saints and angels are not lacking to those who wish to stand, 454. The Lord too is present, 454, when he is faithfully invoked, 455. Angels are a good defense, but the Lord’s is better, 454. When temptations have been overcome, angelic ministries are not lacking to us, 678. The devil’s temptations are an intolerable flood to those empty of God, but a torrent quickly passing over those full [of him], 449. Nothing must be ventured into God’s temptation, 678. TERENTIANUS, II, 680. A boundary differs from the thing bounded, I, 49.

The earth was established from nothing without any exertion on the part of one commanding it, I, 187. The earth’s position, 545. The earth is limited and subject, suspended over the abyss, 49. It is overlaid by the fluid nature of waters, 350. It was so founded that it might remain, 350. It does not remain except as long as this world remains, 351. Why it is wonderful, 258. How the earth’s fertility escapes our understanding, II, 440. The earth: the human body, I, 351. It remains insofar as heavenly glory is prepared for it, 351. The fruit of the earth lost through the first Adam and restored through the second, I, 211 ff. The land of the living, I, 88. Those passing beyond earthly things, I, 489. TERTULLIAN’s work *On the Lord’s Prayer*, I, 689. The subsequent error of the man detracted from the authority of his plausible writings, 689. Five testaments established for the human race, I, 767. Division of the Old Testament into twenty-two books, I, 10. The Old and New Testaments have the same doctrine, 201. It is characteristic of apostolic teaching to proclaim God in the Gospels from the Law and Prophets, 202. The New Testament: election, II, 88.

Those who sin fear witnesses, I, 278. No one can sin without a witness, 278. The presence of angels standing everywhere near us ought to deter us from sins, 278. Present testimonies and eternal testimonies, I, 353. Every age was instructed by God’s testimonies, 402. What God’s testimonies are, and how numerous, 277, 369. Why they are marvelous, 385. Why they are unknown, 386. Those cleaving to the testimonies are freed from confusion, 302. God’s testimonies are to be sought with the whole heart, 279. Certain testimonies that are not God’s, 278. Tetrarch, I, 34, 35. Thaneos, II, 666. Theatrical mimes, II, 206. Those devoted to theatrical games, I, 311. Eyes defiled by theatrical spectacles, II, 72. Thebes, II, 632. Thebaid, I, 384; II, 482. Tebeeptapyleos, II, 632. THEODOLUS, II, 666. THEODORE of Heraclea, II, 538, 622, 627, 665, 680. THEODORE, II, 693. THEODOLUS, II, 666. THEOGENES, II, 666. THEOGNITUS, author of forged letters, II, 623. The same man is called DIOGNITUS, 622. THEOPHILUS, II, 693. Therraco, II, 667. Thebaid, II, 482. Treasures of God’s power, I, 229, note, 267. Thessalonica, II, 632. Bishop of Thessalonica, II, 658. THIMASARCUS, II, 666.

THOMAS believed Christ to be true God, II, 184 ff. Thrace, II, 482. The Lord Jesus Christ rests in Thrones, Dominions, etc., I, 270. Whence fear arises, II, 344. Fear that does not fall upon one who is in Christ, 344. What natural fear is, I, 476. By what things it is aroused, ibid. It is not taught, ibid. It has no merit of faith in it, 476. Not our fear but faith obtains God’s mercy, 180. What fear of man is absent from saints, 131. To have lost God’s grace through fear of the world is beyond pardon, 408.

The fear of God must be learned, I, 476. The Scriptures, teaching it, place before or after it many things from which its rationale may be understood, 476. How God beneficially instills fear of himself, 43. The example of the Jews instills fear of God, 88. Fear restrains more people within the law; will restrains few, 22. More fear [Col. 1008] God from the condition of their nature, yet are disobedient to him, 330. The fear of faith lies in obedience alone, 330. The fear of God does not make happy those who fear God because he is terrible, 476. Blessed is the person in whose relation to God’s law there is not fear but will, 22. The fear of God is no slight duty of faith, I, 212. It must not arise from weakness but from reason, 212. Fear of God lies not in dread but in obedience, 477. It is wholly in love, 476. How far the duty of fear differs from the service of love, 355. To fear without joy belongs to an impious and self-distrusting conscience; to rejoice without fear belongs to an arrogant nature, 90. Why the righteous person passes no day without fear, 559. Fear founded upon knowledge fears prosperity no less than adversity, 212. What those who fear God desire and request in prayers, I, 628. Who becomes a participant with those who fear God, and who does not, 329. Fear is numbered last among the gifts of the Holy Spirit as the support of the rest, 312. Empty confidence in riches removes the fear of God, 90. To forget the fear of God is less impious than to prefer to it the fear of vain things, 102. Where fear of God is absent, it takes away with itself every beginning of prudence, II, 120.

TIMOTHY, instructed in sacred letters from infancy, II, 390. TIMOTHY of Anchilo, II, 668. Another TIMOTHY, II, 666. TITIUS, II, 633. The various titles of the Psalms, I, 12. They were added by the Seventy translators, 610, 640. The title is an indication of the matters to be treated, 61. It shows of what matters a psalm consists, 14. Psalm titles that direct us toward understanding, 414. The title and psalm confer authority upon one another, 414. A title indicating history does not exclude spiritual understanding, 414. What Toulouse suffered at the hands of the Arians, II, 571. The clergy and people of Toulouse dear to Hilary, II, 458, note. Topaz Island, I, 384. The topaz by itself contains the appearance of all other gems, I, 384. Its discovery, 384.

The Son possesses all that the Father is, and does not take from the Father all that he is, II, 251. The Word is wholly God; Christ wholly man, 357. See the Index of Glosses. To hand over to vices: in what sense God is said [to do so], I, 428. Hebrew tradition concerning the sacred books, II, 4. Traditions of the ancients concerning the books of the ancient law, I, 10. The more secret tradition of the law through the seventy elders, I, 31. Interpreters ignorant of this erred in many matters, 32. Ancient traditions concerning Ezra as compiler of the Psalms, 7. Tradition concerning the authors of the Psalms, 3. It is believed to have originated with Ezra, 4. Samaritan traditions, II, 45. The tradition of the fathers is commended, II, 684. Liberius defends the faith received by tradition, 669. The tradition of the parents is also used as a pretext by heretics, 648, 660. The Lord’s transfiguration, I, 752. What “to pass over” means, II, 350. The authority and antiquity of translations of Scripture are to be respected, I, 524. Trier, II, 570. **Τρίβος** (*tribos*) is a path worn and frequented by passage, I, 308, 567.

Tribulations are not to be feared by the Christian, I, 417. Which he must guard against, 418. What tribulation alone is dangerous to the righteous, 418. We must pray not that tribulation be removed, but that we may bear it bravely, 340. Offenses precede tribulation, 332. The usefulness of tribulation, 333, 340, 560. Our tribulations are brief, 455. They have the reward of victory, though they do not have the labor of a long battle, 455. Tribulation cannot be borne without God’s aid, 560. God does not fail those who hope in him, 560. Saints were proved by tribulations, 564. Tribunes, II, 661. TRIFON, II, 632.

The mystery of the Trinity was hidden from the Jews, II, 121. It is ineffable and incomprehensible, 29. It ought to be contained within the reverence of minds, 27. Whoever attempts to speak words concerning the Trinity does unlawful things and presumes what is not permitted, 27. Knowledge of the Trinity was sufficiently handed down in baptism, II, 25. The sacrament of the regenerating Trinity is defended, 23. Apostolic men were always concerned to explain and defend the mystery of the Trinity, 641. The Trinity, when pronounced among heretics, produces division, 645. The false naming of the Trinity among certain Easterners, 645. The persons of the Trinity are what they are called, II, 27, 28. Father, Son, and Holy Spirit truly are what they are named in baptism, 15. Father, Son, and Holy Spirit: one power from which all things come, one offspring through which all things come, one perfect gift of hope, 26. Without any external bond, all things are one, I, 736. The perfect Trinity has one divinity, not one person or three divided substances, II, 686. Those who devise diversities of substances in matters so common [Col. 1009] are condemned, 28. Discourse on the Trinity demonstrated, 15. Hilary’s fourth book *On the Trinity* is called the first, II, 134. Troada, II, 666. Troas, II, 666. TROGLODYTES, discoverers of the topaz, I, 384. Useful disturbance, by which the darkness of desire is driven away, II, 606. The towers of the Church: its leaders, I, 438. All who love God, 438. Tyre, II, 665. Proceedings at Tyre against Athanasius, 652.

## U

The Gospel law altogether suppresses the desire for revenge, I, 687. See Revenge. Ulpianis, II, 632. The character of unanimity, I, 518. The property of ointment, I, 519; it is Palestinian custom to anoint heads on feast days, 690, note. Christ the mediator taught the composition of the ointment with which Aaron was anointed, 520. Aaron’s anointing is a type of the anointing of God’s only-begotten Son, I, 519. The sweetness of Aaron’s anointing expresses the sweetness of unanimity, 520. Christ’s anointing, II, 386, 387; it flows down from him to a man of perfect faith, I, 520 ff. There are not two Only-begottens, I, 529. Union, II, 81. See more in the Index of Glosses.

The unity of God is shown, I, 529. God’s unity is for us, not union, 442; II, 191. The impiety of “union” is put forward in order that the religious unity of the Church’s faith may be removed, 139. Oneness through birth does not entail solitude, 192. The unity of Father and Son must not be conceived in a human way, 285; what it is, 243. The unity of Christ’s and the Father’s glory, 287. The unity of God’s nature, which Christ according to the flesh lost and recovered, 286, 298. The unity of Christ’s flesh and divinity through glory, I, 510, note. The unity of the Church: in what it consists, I, 434; it bears fruits displaying the form of eternal fruits, 437. All things are to be obtained by the merit of unity, 759. All believers are one in Christ, 477. Those who are one by the same thing are one by nature, II, 219. The natural unity of believers through the nature of one faith, 218; from the nature of the sacraments, 218. The unity of believers with Christ and God the Father through the sharing of glory, II, 221 ff.; through the mystery of the incarnate Word and the sacrament of the Eucharist, 222 ff. The wondrous unity of the blessed with the paternal majesty through Christ as mediator, I, 239 ff. The unity of soul and body, whether in glory or punishment, I, 717, note.

Unition. Things differing in nature must necessarily be joined by some more powerful force, I, 244. The Word fastened himself to flesh by the power of his own authority, 244. Universality is reckoned in the many, I, 148. URBANUS, II, 690. URBICUS, deacon, II, 683. URSACIUS of Brescia, II, 632. URSACIUS of Singidunum. See VALENS. Heretics contend that the terms *ousia* and *homoousios* are unknown to the Church, are nowhere said of God in the Scriptures, and cause scandal, II, 691, 692. The Synod of Rimini agrees to suppress them, 691, 692. In the silence concerning *ousia*, the Gauls acknowledge that they were deceived, 699. Ustodizo, II, 690. The injustice of usury, I, 76. “Usefulness” and “avarice” are denoted by the same Hebrew word, I, 311. How they are in fact the same thing, 311. The wife of the righteous: wisdom, I, 479.

## V

Cows worshiped in Samaria, I, 157, 236. VALENS Augustus, I, 600. VALENS of Mursa, II, 668. Having abandoned his church, he wished to invade another, 630. He stirred up sedition at Aquileia, 630. VALENS and URSACIUS, II, 622, 627, 680. Two wicked and unlearned young men, 538. Impious and unlearned young men, 630. Disturbers of the Church, 689. To them, with a few others, the whole inheritance of Arius flowed, 595. Their book is worthy of condemnation, 694, 695. They do not cease to scatter deadly seeds of adulterated doctrine, 630. They were deposed by the Synod of Sardica, 628. They presented a petition at Milan, 637. They asked and obtained pardon in writing at the Council of Milan, 688. In what year they asked to be received into the Church, 635, note. They confess as false everything that they insinuated concerning Athanasius before Julius, 636. Why Julius granted them pardon, 635. Their letters to Julius and Athanasius, 636, 638.

Valens, Ursacius, and Saturninus demand Athanasius’s condemnation, [Col. 1010] II, 634. Valens violently snatches the pen from Dionysius’s hands, 540. Valens and Ursacius are separated from communion with the Gallican bishops, 562. The developments of Valens and Ursacius in the Sirmian formula, 580. Their blasphemy condemned by African subscriptions, 582. At Sirmium in A.D. 358, Easterners compelled Valens and Ursacius to subscribe their decrees, 597. They demand that the letter concerning the exposition of *homoousios* and *homoiousios* be read to them, 508. There, while professing ignorance, they are suspected of falsehood, 508. Just as the Easterners were heard against them, so Hilary wished to be heard, 521. Liberius writes to Valens, Ursacius, and Germinius, 681.

Valens and Ursacius attended the Sirmian assembly of A.D. 359, at which a new formula was dictated by Marcus, II, 708. They and their associates promise Constantius that peace can be completed if the term “substance” is removed, 689. Which confession of faith Valens brought to Rimini, 690. Valens and Ursacius were condemned at Rimini, 685, 690. Many who had previously condemned them fell into communion with Valens and Ursacius at Rimini, 701. After the fall of the Synod of Rimini, Valens with his associates writes to Constantius, 691. Valens and Ursacius return from Rimini to Constantinople as envoys, 693. The Gauls hold both excommunicated, 700. Valens and Ursacius, authors of the Arian or Aetian heresy, were formerly condemned in Illyricum, 704. Valens and Ursacius take it badly that Germinius departs from the Riminian faith, 705, 706. Germinius accuses Valens of inconsistency and dissimulation, 708. VALENS of Chios, II, 633. VALENTINIAN Augustus, II, 600. By a severe edict he forbids disturbance of the church of Milan, 597. Moved by Hilary’s petition, he orders Hilary and Auxentius to be heard together, 597. He comes into communion with the latter because of the sincerity of his faith, 598. He orders Hilary to leave Milan, ibid. VALENTINUS, II, 662. He devised the notion that the Son was “brought forth” by the Father, 79, 34. Other inventions of his, 137. VALENTINUS the Semi-Arian, II, 693. The valley of this world producing salt, I, 154. Vanis, II, 666. Who vain people are, I, 169. The vanity of things from which the eyes must be turned away, I, 311. Everything transitory is vain, 613. The murmurs of prophets before Christ; silence afterward, I, 189. The snares of hunters, I, 450. And their arts, II, 577. Esau, a seller, I, 528. VENERIUS, II, 683. To grant pardon to unlawful acts is not to show mercy, but not to preserve the justice of mercy, I, 596. Pardon granted to those suspected of not having been corrected is praised, II, 508. Angels are signified by winds, I, 533.

Why the Son is called the Word, II, 183. Some call the eternal Word a discourse of an uttered voice, 334, and say that it was in Jesus as the Spirit of prophecy was in the prophets, 334. Our word is the product of our inward movement; God’s Word is otherwise, 440. The Word is free from time, 35, 39. It is not absent from its author, 35. It is not a vocal sound or an expression of thoughts, I, 442; II, 35. It is God, not emptiness, 36. He came to exist as God not after time, but by being born, 38. David recognizes the Word as God, I, 131. The generation of the Word is established from the marvelous teaching of the fisherman, II, 38. The Word created all things, II, 37. He did not create as one solitary, 37. Nor was he merely present with the one creating, but he himself created, 37. All things were created in him, 37. As heaven now obeys the Word of God, so after this age other creatures will obey him, I, 349. Hilary said that the Word dwelt in us and was mingled with us, neither favoring Nestorius nor Eutyches, 371, note. How the Word of God remains in the visible heaven, I, 348. The Word of God remains in the bodies of saints as in heaven, 351. The Word of God is available to each person, 349. Like the sun, it enters one open to it and refuses one not open to it, 349. Whom it inhabits, whom it abandons, whom it flees, 349.

The Word of God is often called a sword, I, 718. It is a mighty arrow, 420. Food of eternal life, 320. How it is at once lamp and light, 363. The light of God’s Word must be used for every action, 361, 363. The words of God are leaves, 25. God’s words are decrees, I, 64. They contain faith not so much of what will be as of what has been done, 792. Moses used words which God commanded him to use, 386. The words spoken by the prophets are God’s words, 386. They are ambiguous and obscure, 386. How they are made clear in the Gospels, 387. The holiness of works confirms their truth, 627. Those outside the Church cannot understand them, 734. God’s words are adapted to our understanding in such a way that they contain nothing unworthy of God’s majesty, II, 288. Nothing in them is empty; nothing is untrue, I, 394. With how great reverence they ought both to be proclaimed and heard, 64. They must be received with fear, 312. The swiftness of God’s Word in building God’s city, 641. [Col. 1011] There can be no keeping of God’s Word unless desires are first restrained, 358. What its true keeping is, 358. Words, even though unwritten, are rightly rejected if evil, II, 575. The calumny of a word need not be feared where the matter has no difficulty, II, 510. The Pleiades, II, 440. VERISSIMUS, II, 633. The nature of the worm, II, 383.

Truth: Christ, I, 113. Ministers of truth ought to utter true things, II, 565. The voice and work of those suffering for truth’s cause, I, 395. Truth was unknown to the world and the world’s sages, II, 13. Before the Gospel it remained among Israelites alone; now it remains among Christians alone, I, 350. Acquiring knowledge of truth lies only in persistent prayer, 697. Truth has nothing false, uncertain, or imperfect, 346. False things must not be joined to true things, II, 107. Truth stirs the movement of reason, II, 108. It cannot be understood unless the falsity of opposing things is exposed, II, 107. While attacked each day, it acquires the firmness of its nature, 177. The power of truth shines forth even through things opposing it, 177. Against truth, whether not understood or offensive, the error of a foolish or vicious will struggles, 321. The necessity of the true conquers the will, 172. People ought no more to be displeased at not having known truth than to hate having persisted in untruths, 391. God alone preserves truth in the world, I, 631. The truth of a thing is demonstrated from its own power, II, 106. No nature can lack truth, 111.

A literal translation produces obscurity, II, 464. A double translation was blended by Hilary into one, I, 596, note. VESPASIAN, II, 594. Evening is the beginning of the day according to the Law, I, 124. Evening hymns, I, 190. Modesty in dress is commended, II, 528 ff. Silk garments, dyed and gilded, are to be rejected, 527, 528. What a way is, II, 435. The law of public roads, I, 304 ff. The law of the way established by God for the people departing Egypt, 305. Its journey contains within itself great wonders of the heavenly journey, 305. The ways of God from the world’s beginning, II, 435. The way of God is the teaching of the religious life; and this is Christ, I, 209. The Lord’s way must not merely be entered but also pursued, 275 ff. Who walks in it, 276. There are many good ways, 279, 305, through which one comes to the one best way, 279 ff. The Lord’s ways are many and one, 477. The ways are the Law, Prophets, Gospels, and Apostles, 287, 559. From many, one converges into one, 559. Who walk in their own ways and who in God’s way, 299. Whoever is not in God’s way is in the way of sin, 299. The distinction between the ways of sin and the committing of sin, 301 ff. Confession of one’s ways is the penitent profession of one’s sins, 299.

Many love a way who do not love the way of truth, I, 302. The way of life is subject to heavy but passing troubles, 641 ff. It is narrow and afflicted, 302. By what stages one reaches the point of running in it, 302. No one can run in it who has not become a dwelling worthy and spacious for God, 303. The way of the commandments has been trodden since the foundation of the world, I, 308 ff. Before Moses, the way of the Law had no one walking in it, I, 308. The way to heaven is trodden by few, and contrariwise, I, 697. Christ is the guide of our way, 308. VIATOR, buried at Aquileia, II, 630. The alternation of those suffering and those rejoicing, I, 444; of those abounding and those in need, 445. Care concerning sustenance must be placed in God, I, 126.

God cannot be seen in this life or with the eyes of flesh, I, 325. The nature of flesh cannot endure God’s sight, 591. Human weakness cannot bear the vision of God, 572. What is immortal in God we shall not see unless made perfect in spirit and changed into immortality, 681. Those whom Christ has delivered the kingdom to God will see God, II, 398. Created things could not bear the power of the invisible God unless it were moderated by the interposition of a seat of more tempered nature, I, 544. The vision of the Son of God is desired in order to merit fellowship in eternity, I, 193. The Father is visible only to the Son, II, 101. The Son was seen among human beings, 101. Isaiah saw God, 225. No one declares that God the Father was seen, 126. Christ was seen by the Fathers in that in which he was born, 113. Abraham saw him as man, Lord, God, and judge, 91 ff. Why Christ was not seen by the Fathers under one single appearance, 436. Familiarity with the assumed appearance advances contemplation of the form, 113. The Father is seen in the Son through the wonder of works, not through contemplation of nature, I, 579. Certain birds and herbs merely seen cure certain diseases, I, 339. The widow who died to the Law, I, 218, 632. The dignity of widows, [Col. 1012] 514. How God is their judge, 218. Vigilance is necessary, I, 793, especially for those set over others, ibid. It is necessary against temptations, 179. God’s four watches over the Church, I, 742. Watches before dawn, I, 399. What they should occupy themselves with, 399.

VINCENT of Capua, II, 632. Sent to Arles, 672. Liberius’s envoy to Constantius, 677. He frequently sat as judge in Athanasius’s case, 677. Therefore Liberius hopes much of him, 677. He turns to wicked dissimulation, 677. Liberius laments his fall, 676. He writes to him concerning exile, 682. The bound, I, 258. Bonds hindering faith, I, 456. To be avenged belongs to an inferior nature, I, 591. Properly speaking, vengeance does not belong to Christ but to his servants, 591. Divine vengeance is expressed by the example of human vengeance, 232. Vengeance must be reserved for God, 561. Wine gladdening the human heart, and wine piercing the human heart, I, 156. The miracle of wine from water, II, 52. Those who do not obey the Gospel are a brood of vipers, I, 140. Men of blood, whose teaching is flattering or deceitful: heretics, I, 582. The rod is an emblem of power, I, 455. How God’s rod is doctrine, 51 ff. Christ is rod and flower, 52. Virginity is happy and blessed, I, 479. Virgins consecrated to God and Christ, II, 653. They ought to wear modest garments, 527. The bodies of virgins consecrated to God, 539. Their stripping is vividly depicted, 539, 624, 653. Perpetual vigor is indicated by greenness, I, 223. Virito, II, 665. Power is signified in the right hand, I, 560. Power is a matter of nature, II, 299. Likeness of power exists only through likeness of nature, 371. The word “power,” I, 238. Power and the work of power are not the same, I, 724. Why human beings have transferred themselves to the exercise of virtue, II, 3. Internal virtues must be preferred to external ones, I, 785. How many things lie in ambush against virtue, 327 ff. The nations visited in Christ, I, 147.

Life is all that God is, II, 245. Present life in the body—that is, in a lowly and humble condition—is not true life, I, 289, 541, 406, but a shadow of life, 291. It is full of pains and anxieties, 173. It is incapable of the promised goods, 482. Yet meanwhile it has their light, by which it beholds them as in a mirror, 482. It is a great gift of God, 173. Miserable life began from Adam, not with Adam, I, 630. This life is not ours, but that which was first instituted in the first human being, 630. The law of life was established in Adam under the condition of a decree, 88. We must not think that life was bestowed upon us by the immortal God for death, II, 3. Unless life is undertaken for the gain of eternity, it will be the source of miseries, not of life, I, 160. David desired the life to come, I, 347. His hope for it is shown by his aspiring toward a life he does not yet possess, 312. Knowing that he does not possess true life, David hopes for eternal life, 374. True life cannot exist unless the body has been glorified into the nature of spirit, 289. A human being cannot attain eternal life by personal merit without God’s help, I, 341. By what means the hope of eternal life is nurtured, 341. Faith does not bear life’s troubles reluctantly, but regards them as the beginnings of blessedness, II, 12. What life according to the dictate of reason is, II, 3. It is beyond bestial frenzy to follow custom rather than nature, 3. To live well is to act and understand well, 3. Life after this life in Abraham’s bosom, in which God’s name is blessed, I, 174. Another life, happier than these two, 174. Eternal life is dwelling with Christ, II, 297. The life of eternity is nourished and preserved not by anything else, but by itself, I, 239. Love of common life, I, 680.

VITALIS of Aquae, II, 632. VITALIS of Tyre, II, 665. VITALIS serving in the office of the exalted prefecture, II, 706. The vice of origin, I, 370, 373. The vices of nature grown together, 384. Vices of the tongue, 110. How many incentives of vices there are, 327 ff. They are supplied through the devil, 278. Our bodies are the material of all vices, II, 711. How we are cleansed from vices through temptation, 711. Instinct drives us toward the vices of our nature, I, 21. This instinct must not be yielded to, or its ways must quickly be abandoned, ibid. Bodily vices must not be allowed to grow together, but killed at their origin, I, 554. The destruction wrought by vices, 593. Vices produce the inclination to turn away from God, 97. He who obeys vices belongs to vices, 353. Demons rightly rule us because of vices, 548. To restrain vices, it helps to remember the presence of angels, 278. How the habit of vices opposes good will, 471. How the memory of vices draws away a mind rebounding from them, 551. Christ absorbed every vice of human corruption, 809. How one free from vices can confess oneself sinful, I, 462. Calling is public and general, I, 780; why it does not make people good, 779. We are gathered from every class of humankind, 185.

God’s will is full of goodness, I, 331. Christ fulfills the Father’s will in such a way that in him is the office of will, 588. Will is a movement of the mind, II, 221; it is moved by an alluring occurrence, but especially by the proposed reason for acting, I, 216; it is not given, II, 221; it must possess of itself the property of willing, I, 370. What willing is, II, 190. Whence obstinacy of will comes, 321. Will ought to follow reason, not go before it, 321. Those for whom knowing is not one cannot will one thing, II, 313. Will itself is no small ally of vices, I, 167. The weakness of our will in accomplishing the good it knows, 471. It does not obtain consummation by itself, 370; yet the merit of attaining it arises from its own beginning, 370. Mere willing without action does not obtain perfect blessedness, 22. To act from will is far better than to act from law, 538. Voluntary obedience belongs to the Gospel, not the Law, 367 ff. The distinction between good will and works, I, 488 ff. God beholds human wills at the very beginnings of human birth, 139. How greatly God regards the inclination of good will even in those who sin, 221. God pardons falls of weakness in one whose will is good, 99. How God does not impute vices to a will directed toward righteousness, 92. Envy is reckoned as a crime of will equivalent to a deed, 804. Freedom of will ceases after this life, 92. Pleasure is the cause of remaining in each thing, I, 597; it is the daughter of unbelief, 739. How swiftly carnal pleasure flees, 550. Our vows benefit not God but ourselves, I, 535. Only vows of ecclesiastical devotion are useful; they must be approved by zeal for the observance undertaken in the Church, ibid. Contempt for the body, the guarding of chastity, and endurance of fasting are to be vowed to God, 184. A vow of chastity, 760, note. The vows of martyrs for themselves and for those who would imitate them, 204, 206. We owe God the duty of a rejoicing voice, I, 196. It is permissible to declare faith in new words, II, 509. The Vulgate reading was unknown to Hilary, yet approved, I, 202, note. Foxes: what they signify, I, 702. Demons are signified by the name “foxes,” 176. Face, countenance, image, and form do not differ, I, 257.

## X

Xerophagies: see Dry.

## Y

YPATIUS, consul, II, 684, 685, 690.

## Z

Whether Hilary used the word *Zabulum* is uncertain, I, 674. By what authority the name ZECHARIAH is prefixed to certain psalms, I, 3. What a girdle signifies, I, 674. Zelon, II, 666. Zeal, I, 247. The disposition of zeal, 405; its cause, 392; examples, 392. Certain treatises of Hilary have been falsely ascribed to ZENO of Verona, I, 463. Zeuma, II, 665. What ZIPHAE are, I, 108.
