# INDEX OF GLOSSES

[Note: [Col. 1013] In this index, Roman numerals I and II refer to PL 9 and 10. Arabic numbers refer to column numbers printed in the text in bold type.]

## OBSERVATIONS
[Col. 1013] 1. Hilary, as is his habit, uses an abstract noun in place of a concrete one; e.g., *auctoritas* (“authority”) for *auctor* (“author”), II, 481; *habitatio* (“indwelling”) for *habitator* (“indweller”), I, 683. “The nativity of God” for “the Son of God,” II, 288.

2. He commonly uses the genitive of a substantive noun in place of an adjective: thus, “Lord of eternity,” meaning “eternal,” I, 331; “life of eternity,” 257; “nativity of divinity,” II, 437; “little ones of regeneration,” I, 773; “humility of will,” II, 41.

3. He sometimes reverses the natural order of nouns: thus, “will of creation” for “creation of will,” II, 145; “origin of his nature” for “nature of his origin,” 185.

**ABSISTERE** — “to stand apart from” power, II, 419.

**Absolvere** — that is, “to loosen,” I, 5, 35, 105; or to unravel what was entangled, II, 136; or to give an account of some matter, I, 115; II, 78, 259, 282. “Resolution of a statement,” 369, that is, the explanation of what is said, 370. “To resolve the tongue,” that is, to provide understanding of an unknown language, 234. “Obscurity fully resolved,” that is, obscurity untangled and explained, I, 748. *Absolutio*: explanation and demonstration, I, 128, 284; II, 23, 31, 87, 93, 127, 139. “Resolution of truth,” that is, what truth itself presents, 27. “To attain the resolution of truth,” that is, manifestly to attain the true nature of a thing, I, 17. *Absolutio* for perfection, 7. “The most complete majesty of the Son,” that is, the fullest, II, 77. “The completion of the perfect man,” as it were, integrity, 378. “The most complete and best use,” 2. “Clear and ready minds,” I, 714. “In Judah nothing is simple, nothing complete,” 590. *Absolutum* likewise means clear and manifest, 33, 38, 60, and frequently elsewhere. *Absolutio* for clarity, II, 192 and elsewhere. “In the clear,” 48, 52, that is, not in obscurity, 99. “In the clear” is opposed to a private matter, I, 736. An absolute name is opposed to a relative one, II, 88. In God things are absolute, not corporeal, 306.

**Abstentio** — abstinence, I, 22.

**Ad naturam** — as it were, “according to nature,” II, 316, 381.

**Admixtus** — as it were, added or joined, I, 125. “God joined to the world,” 401. “The soul joined to the limbs,” 401; to earthly nature, 299. Matter joined to us, 289; the habit of vices, 608. “To be joined now to dead flesh,” 290.

**Adoptare** — to assume, II, 42. *Adoptio*, assumption, I, 480; used of the Gentiles, 723.

“To worship cattle,” I, 733, note: where, in place of the fourth case, the third case should be read. See 762, note.

**Adspectatores** — spectators, I, 426.

**Adspiratus in prophetam** — inspired into a prophet, I, 498.

“The time of Christ’s advent,” for the time of his assumed flesh, II, 154, 156.

**Aenigmatum est** — “it belongs to riddles,” I, 133.

**Aeternitas** — eternity; God, I, 782. “The eternity of Christ” for Christ’s divinity, [Col. 1014] I, 144. “Eternity from eternity,” II, 422. “Eternity received a body of our nature,” I, 749. Eternity for the divine nature, 800; II, 222, 646. “Eternity” as substance, I, 696; nourishment, 678; ordinances, 679. “Eternity of dying,” II, 7. “The powers of eternities are numerous,” 137.

**Alius** — “another,” as though neuter *aliud*, to distinguish nature, II, 481.

“Other than yours,” II, 147.

**Allegoricorum lex** — the law of allegorical interpretations, I, 174.

**Allegorumena** — allegorical things, I, 277, 494, 504, 533, 537, 641.

**Ambitiosa** — as it were, encircled and surrounded, I, 371.

**Amittere manere** — “to lose being,” as it were, to cease to exist, II, 331, 341. “To lose existence,” 115, 384.

**Anima corporis** — the soul of the body, II, 357, 360, 364. “Intermixture of the soul,” II, 329; “its perpetual mobility,” I, 493. “The sea is animated, now by inhaling breath, now by giving it back,” 259.

**Anomoeusion** — “unlike in essence,” II, 573.

**Anquira** — Ancyra, II, 665. *Anquiritanus* — Ancyran, 708.

**Apprehendere** — conveys avidity, I, 52.

**Arii** — Arians, II, 510, 642.

**Ariomanitae** — Ariomaniacs, II, 180, 624, 698, 701.

“Awareness of the assisting Spirit,” II, 443. Mercy, which is ready for all, assists the servants of God, I, 609. Angels assisting human helps, 557. “To stand by an injury,” as it were, to be equipped to inflict injury, 613.

**Assumptivae appellationes** — assumptive designations, II, 182.

“Enlarged into sons of God,” II, 9.

“Let the distinction be increased,” II, 96.

“Nature as author,” II, 3.

“The Father, author of the Son,” I, 269. The unbegotten God is author, for generation, to the only-begotten God, II, 281. To be author of the nativity is the Father’s mystery, II, 281. “Unbegotten authority,” II, 325. “The authority of paternal nature,” of paternal operation, 293. The Father does not lose authority, 279. “Existing authority,” meaning that which is not from nothing, 142. *Auctoritates*: passages cited to establish authority, 105.

“Hearing of sound doctrine,” II, 323. “To ask for a hearing,” 547, 621. “To desire a hearing,” that is, to desire to be heard, I, 605.

## B

“The special blessedness of the Son’s powers,” II, 102. “Innumerable blessednesses,” I, 89. See II, 356, 377.

**Blandiloquus** — flattering in speech, I, 125.

**Blasphemiorum** — of blasphemies, II, 629.

**Bubus** — oxen, I, 205.

## C

“Judge of heaven,” I, 503. “Sinner of heaven,” 376.

**Coelestis natura** — heavenly nature, for divine nature, I, 243, 256, 493, 563, 568; II, 288; for spiritual nature, I, 26. “The heavenly nature of the soul,” II, 493. “Heavenly operations,” 55.

**Calumnia** — that which the zeal for quarrelling and contradiction suggests, II, 40, 369 and frequently elsewhere; or contradiction itself, 369. *Calumniari*: as it were, to contradict, I, 417; II, 170, 369; or to stir up disputes, 343, 369. “The calumny of opposition,” as it were, a reason for litigation, II, 19. “To do violence to the Scriptures,” 648, 649, note. “Scrupulous objections,” 368. “Arguments of our objection,” 288. “To bring an accusation,” as it were, to charge, 139. “To press an objection of inquiry,” 60. “The accusation of sin,” I, 146; of a garment, 561; of the trunk of the body, II, 342.

**Caput** — the chief point, or meaning, of Scripture, I, 685.

“The flesh of our whole race,” I, 189. “Assumed flesh,” that is, the whole human being, II, 339. “Flesh” and “man born” are synonymous, 288. By assuming one flesh inwardly, God dwelt in the whole of universal flesh, 41. Christ who was stripped of flesh and strips himself of flesh is the same, 266. Christ, made flesh, prayed that this flesh might begin to be to the Father what the Word is, 59.

“Most dear names,” I, 371. “The domestic affections of names,” 719.

**Caverna exiguissima** — a very small hollow, for the eye of a needle, I, 764.

Every cause is through Christ; Christ as God is not through a cause, II, 367. The cause of Christ’s eternal birth, 413, 381, 418.

Christ’s voice is referred by Hilary to the divine nature, II, 269, 366; it is distinguished from the terms “Son of Man,” 362; “man,” 340; “Jesus,” 358; and “David,” I, 510, note. “Christ our man,” 166; II, 406. “Christ Spirit” and “Christ Jesus,” that is, Christ God and Christ man, 246, 169. Christ is God by nature, man by dispensation; by nature in the form of God, by dispensation in the form of a servant, 335; 367. Christ’s going forth from God is by nature; his coming to us, by dispensation, 156. Christ remains both his own and ours, I, 117. The nature of God, remaining before all ages, was born into the nature of man from the Virgin’s childbirth, 117. Christ “before man,” that is, before he was man, II, 335; does not remain from non-existent things, nor did he begin in origin, but received an eternal origin from origin, 252. The fullness of divinity dwelling bodily in Christ is to be understood as nothing other than Christ, 255. Christ’s sanctification into Sonship, 195. Christ was formed by the Father as God, I, 569. It is doubtful whether he can be said to have been formed by the Father insofar as he is man, 569. He who is the form of God is distinguished from Jesus, 257.

Concerning Christ, the meanings of *totus* (“whole”) and *totum* (“the whole”) are explained, I, 46, note; likewise “the person of man,” 178, 564, 565; and “before man,” “in man,” and “after man,” 571. Christ was one thing as God before man, another as man and God, and another after man and God: wholly man and wholly God, II, 262. “Man from God,” that is, though he was God, he was made man, 334. God born in man, 261, 264. Mary did not give origin to Christ’s body, 331; every cause of his birth was supplied through the Spirit, 330. Christ’s flesh was not from the common kind of origin, I, 61; it was assumed in the Virgin, II, 331; initiated and created through itself, 331; from his own Holy Spirit, 330; it did not coalesce through the nature of human conception, 330, 333; nor through the defects of human conception, 339. In Christ the assumed body and the connatural body, 246. God’s power acquired for humanity, 325. Christ was emptied of the glory of paternal nature by dispensation, 291. In him there was not that substance which had received its own emptying, I, 243; there was the property of nature, but the form of God was not present, II, 298. Christ, born man, had introduced novelty of nature into himself, 286. Temporal novelty, together with the form of God, had lost the unity of the divine nature in respect of the assumed man, ibid. The novelty of the dispensation had brought upon Christ an offence against paternal unity, 287.

Christ, who was in the form of God, does not cease to be Christ when he receives the form of a servant, II, 169; he is the same both in changing his condition and in assuming it, 169. The change of condition is in the body, 169. Because Christ is one and the same speaker of all that he says, some maintain that he spoke all things concerning himself, 261. Nor do we deny that all of him who remains his is the utterance of his own nature, ibid. Since he did not possess weaknesses by the truth of his nature, he generated them for himself in respect of nature, 114. Everything in Christ is contrary to nature, 114. He who is life chose to die, and tireless power did not refuse to become weak, I, 505. “This [body] will not sleep in the sleep of death,” 506.

Christ is a body for us, II, 249; having become man, he was one thing from another, I, 47. In the restoration of flesh’s glory, that which had previously existed as another thing was reborn into the same thing, 48. Christ, rising, ascended beyond the setting of death, 216; he passed out of the law of death, 216; leaving the body within the tomb, he bestowed upon it fellowship in his divine nature, that is, glory, 131. What it means for Christ to be begotten into the perfect Son of God, 45, 47. Christ, man from God, died; from dead man he rose into God, I, 109; from Son of Man into Son of God—having also begun to be Son of Man—he was now reborn through the glory of resurrection, 115.

[Col. 1016] Christ’s bodily weakness is preserved in the name and nature of God, 109. To the Son of Man himself must be restored both the name and power of the Son of God, 109. The following mean the same: “the Lord Jesus in the glory of God the Father”; “the assumed man received into the nature of divinity”; “man assumed by the only-begotten God and placed in the life of his eternity”; or “received into the salvation of God’s countenance,” 257. Christ, man and God, now exists in the unity of the paternal nature, II, 286; now united both to the spirit of deity and to the origin of flesh, meaning, flesh glorified by divinity, I, 510; nor, after man, is he in God not wholly man and wholly God, II, 262; he is not God in part, but wholly God, 399; formerly containing two in himself, he is now God only, 399; while man and God, he is already God only, 400; since the dispensation in which he is man now remains wholly in God, 401. Spirit and flesh are now both one, I, 794.

**Ci** for *qui* (“who”) when it is altered. Thus *Anquira* is read for *Ancyra*, II, 665; *Quimatius* for *Cimatius*, 663; *Quirius* for *Scirus*, 666.

“The city of surroundings,” I, 159, is the heavenly Jerusalem; ibid.

**Clauso** — closed, I, 683.

**Cluditis** — “you shut,” I, 784, note.

**Coexcitatus** — raised together, I, 146, 156, 168, 176.

“The time of knowledge,” II, 35.

God’s cohabitation is distinguished from the reception of heavenly goods, I, 186.

**Coinnascibilis** — born together with, II, 303.

**Collatio verborum** — comparison of words, II, 464. Evangelical and prophetic comparison, 113. Contribution of money, I, 125.

**Comitatus diversitatum** — an accompaniment of diversities, II, 232.

**Comminister** — fellow-minister, II, 621.

**Communio** — for a thing that is common, II, 148, 379, 385. Communion of image, 108; of paternal substance, I, 731; of things obtained, II, 315. The mystery of divine communion, I, 251. “Dominical communion” for ecclesiastical communion, II, 461, 462.

**Compassio** — fellow-suffering, II, 507. “In sufferings to be suffered with,” I, 329.

“May the sight compensate for the father,” as it were, may it furnish the same thing as the father’s sight, II, 292.

“To mourn with those who mourn,” I, 329.

**Compresbyter** — fellow-presbyter, II, 638.

**Concaptus est** — he was conceived together, I, 462.

**Concorporales** — of one body, I, 136, 163, 255, 270. Incorporated with Christ, II, 571. Incorporation, I, 696.

God is not worthy to be seen by an impure heart, I, 410.

**Conditio et genus** — condition and kind, I, 114.

For Hilary, *confiteri* often means “to repent,” I, 92, 598, note. “Confession of repentance,” 40, 43; “of repenting,” 732.

“To receive no likeness of configured truth,” that is, to have nothing similar to oneself, I, 401.

All power was born together with the Son of God, II, 281. The Father begot in the Son knowledge of his own will, I, 268.

**Connuncupatus** — named together, II, 107, 170, 270.

“This faith rises again together in Christ,” II, 265.

“Conscious weakness,” for “one conscious of weakness,” II, 174. “Conscious nature,” 191, note. “Conscious power,” 192. “The confidence of salvation known to oneself,” I, 250.

**Conscientia** — consciousness, II, 294, 295. “Public awareness,” 136, 160, 563, 572.

“The consecration of God’s first priest,” I, 519; “consecrated judgment,” II, 654.

“To console threats with hope,” I, 319.

**Conss.** — consuls, II, 684, 685, 690.

“To consist of diverse things so as to remain,” II, 141.

**Consummatio** — completion, for an end, I, 2, 8. “It was being completed by being poured out,” II, 347. “Completion of remaining,” I, 375. “To complete the nature of God,” that is, to furnish the fullness of divine nature, II, 158. The Son completes the Father, 201. “To complete the living man,” 330. Man, the image of God, is completed, 406.

“To be contained of weak things,” II, 198; of inanimate things, 198. “Into dispute,” I, 444.

**Convallia** — valleys, I, 193.

“To cooperate” and “cooperation,” II, 87.

**Corpus** — body, for human nature, I, 250. “To become a body of one’s own consciousness and spirit,” II, 352. Body is opposed to image, I, 516; to shadow, 763; II, 113. “The body of the psalm,” I, 355; of the work, II, 87; of the resurrection, I, 137. “To be placed in the body of sin,” 605. Christ is a body for us, II, 236; he is the body of all, 249. The body passes into the substance of the soul, and the soul’s subtlety becomes dense into the nature of bodies, I, 707. See 719.

Christ’s corporeality, I, 683, 684. Incorporation, II, 303, 383. “Is embodied,” as it were, attains its own perfection, I, 492. The corporeal substance of souls, 692. “Corporeal Christ,” that is, man, 787. “Corporeal,” that is, while he was in mortal flesh, 46. *Corporalis* in the same sense, 591. “The commandment of bodily life,” that is, of the life which we live here in the body, 293. Nothing bodily exists among the blessed, 591. God is not bodily according to us, 455, note; 532, note. [Col. 1017] There are no corporeal things in God, but absolute things, II, 306. The bodily dwelling of the incorporeal God teaches the property of natural unity in the God who subsists from God, 257. The bodily dwelling of incorporeal divinity effects natural unity, 258. Divinity in Christ is bodily, not in part but wholly, 256. Divinity dwelling bodily in Christ signifies the truth of God’s nature in him, 252.

**Corruptivus** — corrupting, II, 118.

**Cruciarius** — one of the cross, I, 436.

**Cum** — as though *apud* (“with”), I, 85, 205; for *secundum* (“according to”), 380 and frequently elsewhere. *Cum* for *quando* (“when”), I, 14, 246, 266; II, 96, 110 and elsewhere.

**Curiosus** — one who has care, II, 302.

The Lord’s keeping, in which believers who have departed this life are reserved, I, 431.

## D

**Danielum** — Daniel, I, 387, note; 427, note. **Danielo**, 453.

“Eternal David,” I, 159.

“To be due,” as it were, to be fitting and proper, II, 374, 426. It is due to man to err, I, 595; it is due to enter the infernal abodes, 115. It was due to the Apostles to proclaim peace, 675.

**Dehonestas** — dishonour, II, 377.

“The descent of the only-begotten God,” II, 12.

**Deserere** — to dissent or be alien from, II, 184, 199. The God who was born did not abandon the property of his own nature, 284. See 128.

“To despair in God,” II, 401. “Despair of judgment,” as it were, hope that judgment will not occur, I, 167. *Desperata*: as it were, unexpected, 793.

**Despoliat** — he strips, I, 574.

“Constrained by love,” I, 518.

**Desum esse** — “to cease to be,” II, 375.

The nature of God is expressed by the terms “eternity,” I, 800; II, 222; “spirit,” I, 250; II, 225; and “power,” I, 709, 800.

“God from whom” and “God through whom,” II, 83, 84, 97, 240, 242. In the things of God there is nothing except what is born and eternal, 439. God from God and in God, by the mystery and power of nature, 129. God with God is not another in nature but one in the mystery of substance, 146. The Word, Wisdom, and Power are not lacking to God as his own, although they were born from him into God, 182. The immutable God, begetting immutable God, follows his own nature; such a birth does not abandon its own nature, I, 128. God the Father and the Son are both one, not one person, II, 13. We confess both as neither the same nor another, ibid. In God, three substances may rightly be spoken of among the Easterners, 480, 482. In divine matters three things were spoken of orthodoxly by the ancients, 480, note. God’s imputative or assumptive appellations, 182. The substance of the unbegotten Father, 483. The only-begotten essence of the Son, 483. The non-difference of the nature begotten and begetting, 484.

God the Father is to God the Son both the God of his birth and the Father of his nature, II, 381. God the Father is nature begetting; the Son, nature begotten, 298. In the generation of the Son, God follows his own nature, 128. He adds nothing alien to himself to the birth of the Only-Begotten, 207. Power and wisdom are not lacking to God the Father, although they were born from him into God, 182. Divinity begotten from God the Father and born in God the Son testifies that they are one, I, 622. The absolute perfection of God’s essence begotten from God’s essence, II, 484. The person of the begotten essence, 489. The birth of the only-begotten God is second from its author, yet not separable from its author, 439; I, 441. Faith embraces the only-begotten nature, begotten from the unbegotten, under the one name of the essence of the unbegotten God, II, 496. God the Son is born from a perfect and immutable cause in the property proper to himself, 413.

God the Father did not know the assumption of our flesh, II, 298. In begetting the Son he retains authority, 279. The Father is greater insofar as he is Father; but the Son, insofar as he is Son, is not lesser, 302. The Son of God is subject to the Father by the birth of his nature, 499. God obeying the sayings of God, 119. God the Word making himself man from the Virgin’s childbirth, 334. God born, 301. God dead, 301.

Perfect divinity, by birth, begotten into perfect God, II, 251. Only-begotten divinity, 325. We confess unity of divinity in the unbegotten God and in the only-begotten God according to property and nature, I, 442. The nature of paternal divinity brought into the nature of our assumed body, II, 399. The bodily dwelling of divinity in Christ, 252.

**Deifica doctrina** — deifying doctrine, II, 685.

**Diabolicum ingenium** — diabolical disposition, II, 576.

**Diapsalmi interjectio** — insertion of a *diapsalma*, I, 201, 209, 210. **Diapsalmae intercessio** — intervention of a *diapsalma*, 84, 88, 206. “With a *diapsalma* inserted,” 85, 125, 136, 147.

**Dignatio** — as it were, an abasement undertaken in kindness, II, 40, 41.

**Dignitas** — as it were, divinity, I, 571.

[Col. 1018] **Dimensio mortalium** — the measure of mortals, I, 157.

**Discretio personae** — distinction of person, II, 88, 96.

**Dispensatio** — for a secret plan, II, 309; for God’s secret plan to be effected in time, 397, 394; for nature, 384, 399. The dispensation of man is opposed to the nature of God, 266. “The saving mysteries of the dispensation for the world,” 111; the same as “the mysteries of heavenly mercy,” 113. “The mystery of the evangelical dispensation,” 113. “The dispensation of our body,” 249; of incorporation, 303; of assumed flesh, 286; of times, 431. The solidification of the firmament, the uncovering of dry land, and so forth, each has its own dispensation, 432. “The final dispensation,” 435. “The subjection of the mystery to be dispensed,” 394. The dispensation of silence, 316; of hidden knowledge, 313; of not acting, 307; of speaking, ibid.; of acting, protesting, or demonstrating, 311. “The dispensation of power,” as it were, its manifestation, 376.

**Disproficis** — [uncertain reading].

The number of diversity does not apply to God, II, 105.

God commanding and God making are distinguished, II, 84. “God from whom” and “God through whom,” 83. “He who is” and “he whose [it is],” 46. “He who is in” and “he in whom [he is],” 129. “Through whom” and “without whom,” 37. “To be in” and “to be present,” 36. “To have” and “to be had,” 31. Giver and gift, 31.

Teaching of the name rather than of the nature, II, 321. Teaching of the will, 321.

“To have the lordship of an inferior,” for serving an inferior, I, 443.

**Dominicum** — a church building, II, 540.

**Donec cum** — “until when,” I, 503, note; 728.

## E

The Church consists of the multitude of frequenting angels; but there is also the Church of the firstborn, and the Church of spirits founded in the Lord, I, 454.

“Bodily effects,” II, 143.

**Egredi sensum** — to go beyond understanding: to surpass, exceed, and escape, II, 6.

**Electio** — for the New Testament, II, 88; for the Jews, I, 528, 709.

“The elements of our origin,” II, 159; of earthly conception, 345, 352. The origins of our elements are shameful, I, 252. See II, 61. Christ’s body was not begun from earthly elements, II, 352. God gives us from himself the elements of life and spirit, I, 229.

**Epistola uniformis** — a uniform letter, II, 675.

**Epistolia** — letters, II, 631, 678.

**Essentia** — essence, II, 466, 646. God is from himself and for himself always unto that which he is, 288. He who is is cause to the Son for that which he is, 417. It is proper to the only-begotten God that being and being-in should differ in nothing, 209.

**Erans** — “you were,” II, 35, note.

“The emptying of the form of God,” I, 613. “Emptied from the form of God,” 227, 256. “To empty power,” II, 405.

**Evangelia** — Gospels, for the entire dispensation of our salvation, even before Christ’s birth, II, 180.

“Evangelizing powers,” I, 222.

“Mary is evangelized”: said of the Annunciation, 615.

**Ex** indicates a former state from which transition was made to another, e.g., “man from God,” I, 50, 441. “From flesh,” that is, when we were flesh, II, 41. “Dying from immortality,” that is, though he was immortal, 11. “From persecutor of the Church,” 99.

**Exaequabilis** — capable of equality, II, 259.

“To depart from the standard of evangelical charity,” as it were, to withdraw from evangelical charity, I, 341.

**Exceptio** — an excepting particle, II, 376. “Exception of comparison,” that is, exclusion of comparison, 337. “Exception of the solitary,” that is, an assertion of solitary existence which excludes another, 279. “Exception of the only-begotten,” in the same sense, 385. “Exception of paternal power,” that is, what is ascribed to the Father’s power alone, 317. See II, 15, 19.

“Emptied from the form of God,” I, 229.

**Exponere** — to lay aside, II, 648, 657, 658, 660; likewise *expositio*, 655. Cyprian also uses the term in this sense in Epistles 51 and 74, as does Firmilian in Cyprian’s Epistle 75.

Sabellius extended the Father into the Son, II, 28.

**Extrinsecus** — for that which extends outward, I, 9.

## F

“Familiar name,” for common or ordinary, II, 233.

“General familiarity,” as it were, a common designation, II, 148.

**Fastigium** — as it were, arrogance, I, 364, 366.

Faith of the heart, I, 108; of rational knowledge, II, 15. Faith not of knowledge but of accusation, 192. “Faiths,” in the plural, for confessions of faith, 462, 497, 499, 499. Faith for the Gospel, I, 684 [Col. 1019] and following. Evangelical faith for the baptismal words, II, 547, 547. Apostolic faith for the Creed, 547. Ecclesiastical faith, 239. Faith of fellow-suffering and faith of dying together, for the disposition of fellow-suffering and dying together for the faith, I, 136. “The mystery of faith,” that is, the unity of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, 735.

The Son is not [a product] of his origin, but a living nature subsisting from a living nature, I, 416; not from a beginning, but from one who is without beginning, 74. He subsists from the Father, II, 77; subsists by the birth of nature, 185. The Son is the birth of a living nature from the Living One, 159. The Son, a subsisting nature of true birth, 175. He has nothing except what is born, 78. He subsists in the substance in which he was begotten, 75; in that in which he remained, ibid. The Son was born from and in God’s nature, 136. The Son, from the one Lord, himself subsists as one into Lord, 279. Born into subsisting God, 183. God from God’s nature, 127. Named by the Father himself with the title of his unbegotten power, 97. The only-begotten Son subsists from the Father, undivided and inseparable not in person but in nature, 127.

The Son was born not without the power of his birth, II, 38. He subsists from his own things, 315. Those things which are in the Father complete the Son who subsists by birth, 183. The abiding nature of birth from God retains the Son in God, 146. The Son of God generated in himself, with respect to nature, things which were not formerly his in the truth of nature, 114. God’s being born was the will of him in whose power it was to be born, I, 748. He who is is cause to the Son for that which he is, II, 417. God is his Father, I, 587; II, 96, 97. The Son is second from God the Father, 441; after God in such a way as to be with God, ibid. He is called begotten, 51. “He whose [Son] he is,” 46; “that by which he is,” 65; “the one through whom,” 74.

The Son, rendering what is due to the Father, ascribes his obedience to the will of him who sent him, 300. By the example of paternal nature he gives life to the dead, 189. The Son’s obedience, compliance, subjection, 504; piety, 507. In the creation of the world, ministry, 431. In working, service, I, 268, 269. The Son, insofar as he is begotten, cannot be equal to the Father in that which begot him, 670. Through the honour of reverence he subjects his own things to the Father, 575, 602. The Father is superior to the Son, II, 56; and greater, ibid. and 570. The Son wholly [is], 286.

“The end of faith,” as it were, faith’s destruction, I, 346. “To dwell at the end of ceasing,” as it were, to be in a state of readiness to cease, 190.

**Floriet** — “he shall flourish,” I, 516, 523.

**Forma** is opposed to nature and substance, II, 248. Form for nature, I, 256; II, 411, 412; for glory, I, 256; II, 298. To be in the form of God has no other meaning than to remain in God’s nature, I, 411. The form of God is naturally sealed in God, II, 324. The form of God is the only-begotten God, I, 257. The form of God emptied itself from what it was into what it was not, 111. Whether the fact that Christ was formed in the form of a servant may be referred to the Father is uncertain, 569. By whom he was formed according to the form of divinity, ibid. God could not depart from God into man except by emptying himself from the form of God, II, 412. He who remained in the form of God could not receive the form of a servant except through his own emptying, since the concurrence of both forms was not fitting to him, 298. The emptying of the form of God is the dispensation of our salvation, 298. We do not immediately restore the unity of the servant-form into the nature of divine unity, 298. The form of God was not present because, through its emptying, the form of a servant had been assumed, 298. The condition of the servant-form is to be honoured into the form of God, 288. The Father begets the Son from himself into his own form, and again renews him from the form of a servant into the form of God, 301. Alienating the form of paternal majesty by assuming bodily humility, 302. The form was changed, and afterwards equality of form was restored, 300. The assumption of the servant-form is assumed into the form of God, 290. To have passed into the form of God is not to have lost the nature of God, 412.

**Frequentare** — as it were, to profess before a multitude, II, 283.

“The house of frequenting angels,” I, 402.

**Frequentabilis** — capable of being frequented, I, 510.

**Frequenter** — frequently, II, 597.

## G

**Genus** — nature, II, 20 and frequently elsewhere. “The powers of the individual kinds,” that is, the properties of the distinct natures that are in Christ, II, 20.

“General soul,” I, 90.

“To be generated into a living being,” II, 198.

“First and subsequent generation,” I, 572.

**Gignere** — to become, I, 38. “To generate into nature,” II, 114; “into a living being,” 128.

“Glorious in themselves,” as it were, glorying in themselves, I, 201.

“Man received into the nature of divinity,” that is, endowed with glory, 257.

Grace is opposed to law, I, 784.

## H

“Had to be begotten,” as it were, was to be begotten, II, 97.

[Col. 1020] “The heresy of weakness,” II, 349. “A heresy: a lying phantom,” 350.

“Man of persecutors,” II, 56.

Man consists of a common soul and body, 356. In man is an eternal form of heavenly origin, I, 423. “Whole man,” that is, the entirety of humankind in Christ, 675, note. “Our man,” II, 388.

**Homousios** — consubstantial, II, 75.

The same in office and merit, I, 782.

“The fire of judgment,” I, 754. The faithless will be left as material for heavenly fire, 792.

**Illex ad lasciviam vultus** — a countenance alluring to wantonness, I, 384.

“Natural image,” II, 324.

The Holy Spirit mingled himself with the nature of human flesh; that is, the Word assumed flesh, II, 42.

“Immoderate eternity,” that is, immeasurable, II, 5.

“Unpeaceable speech,” I, 685.

“The mystery of non-repentance,” that is, that which is not to be repented of, I, 650.

He who begot is impassible, II, 32, 51, 74, 326.

“Impious consciousness,” II, 458. “Was made impious,” 510.

**Imprecatus** — as it were, prayed, I, 429.

“Dwelling in us,” I, 448. “Remaining in us,” 448. “About to remain in God,” II, 401.

**Inaurire** — to put into the ears, I, 110, 118, 587.

**Incarnatio** — incarnation, II, 47, 64.

**Incognoscibilis** — unknowable, I, 613, 614.

**Incomposita natura** — an uncompleted nature, that is, one to whose perfection something is lacking, II, 305.

**Inconsummatum** — incomplete, II, 243.

“Unrestrained in creating a body,” II, 55.

**Incredibiles** — for unbelievers, II, 152.

The congregation of saints is unworthy of workers of malice, I, 373.

“The pain of indignity,” II, 294.

**Indigere aliquid** — to lack something, I, 263. See note 3 at the foot of the same page. “Needing to seek,” I, 712.

“The measure of indulgence,” as it were, the measure of the thing granted, II, 359.

**Inemendatus** — uncorrected, I, 779.

**Inexcessus** — not exceeded, II, 392.

“The uninvestigated justice of God,” I, 354.

**Inexscrutabilis** — unsearchable, II, 404.

**Inferi** — the lower regions, in a favorable sense, I, 374.

“The heresy of weakness,” II, 350.

“Weaknesses of flesh,” I, 422; “weaknesses of nature,” 98; II, 295. “Weak ones,” 160, 440. “By weak things,” I, 707; II, 54, 419.

“Forms of punishments,” I, 203, 395.

**Inhonorabilis** — dishonourable, I, 737.

**Inhonorificus** — not honouring, II, 190.

**Ininitiabilis** — incapable of being begun, I, 401, 578; II, 74, 303, 325, 326. The dominion of God in the created world, incapable of being begun, I, 179.

**Inintelligere** — not to understand, I, 306.

**Inintellecta** — things not understood, II, 204.

**Inintelligentia** — lack of understanding, II, 241, 343; I, 404.

“Unbegotten essence,” II, 476. The Son is the image of unbegottenness by the mystery of birth, 301.

**Innativitas** — unbornness, II, 706, 707, 709.

**Innumerosi** — innumerable, I, 442.

**Inobservans** — unobservant, I, 459.

**Inoperari** — to operate within, II, 235.

“The unworked [reality] of God,” I, 577.

**Inopinabilis** — unimaginable, II, 33.

**Inspirare** — to inspire, I, 96, 185.

**Insum** — for *intra sum*, “I am within,” II, 5. He who is in is not to be dissolved from him in whom he is, 129. “To be in” and “to be,” 146, 157.

**Integimentum** — covering, II, 361.

“Eternal understanding,” that is, understanding that proceeds eternally toward the act of understanding something, II, 424. God is neither within the judgment of understanding nor outside the understanding of perception, 7. “Let it be understood as one,” 127. “Understanding toward the Lord,” ibid.

**Intercessio** — the same as intervention, I, 278, 286.

“Envious of good things,” I, 39. “To be angry with God with the envy of one’s own tears,” as it were, to bear one’s misery unjustly and cast the reproach of one’s impatience upon God, 392.

“Useless for flight,” that is, incapable, I, 790. *Inutilis*, as it were, unworthy of approval, 97, 98. “Useless and irreligious pursuit,” 102. The useless desire of a miser who refuses alms that would be useful to a needy person is so called, 356.

**Ipse** — as it were, “the same,” I, 155; II, 235. “To be himself,” for possessing the same nature, 315.

“In immaturity,” I, 398, note.

**Insincerus** — insincere, I, 664.

**Instetur** — let insistence be made, I, 69.

**Insubstantiva vox** — unsubstantial word, II, 490.

**Iterscaplia** — [uncertain reading], I, 223.

**Ita quod** — “so that,” I, 746, 768; II, 136.

[Col. 1021] “To accomplish the strength of the journey,” I, 746.

“The right of compulsion,” for violence, II, 539.

“The right of necessary confession,” 303.

“Justification of spirit,” or “in spirit,” II, 379.

## L

“Clinging to the side,” II, 701. “From my side I directed,” 669.

“The law of allegorical interpretations,” I, 174.

The law did not contain efficacious power, but prefigured effects, I, 785. Laws of angels, 316; eternal laws, ibid. Law of the world, II, 260. Laws of God and laws of the age, I, 364. Laws of the Church and laws of the forum, 21. The law of Adam’s will established, 402; set before his will, 718. Law as it were natural, 375. Law of justice, 113; of sin, 166, 173, 245; of living, 113; of life, 88; of dying, 88; of death, 217, 290. The law of death imposed upon all, 242. The infernal law, 636. The law of death by which souls descend to the lower regions, 572. The law of descending to the lower regions, 572. The law of the soul released from the body, 316. The law of rising again, 88; of resurrection, 316. The nature of the earthly law, 98. The eternal body of the law, 316. Even the Gospel is simply called “law,” 368.

**Lucificat** — makes luminous, I, 361, 524, note.

## M

**Magis non** — “rather not,” for “rather than,” I, 260.

*Magis* placed after the particle *quam*, II, 278.

“More ready,” II, 260.

**Manere** — to remain, for to be, I, 111, 117, note. God born from God came forth from the One who remains, II, 159. God remaining from God, II, 201. Birth remaining from God, II, 146. “To remain from nature,” II, 197; “from non-existent things,” II, 252. “To remain in impiety,” I, 147. “To remain in flesh,” II, 328. Pain remained in the flesh, II, 328. “He remains for them,” I, 133, 151.

“Eternal manna,” I, 510, note. “They ministered manna,” 733.

“The inner and outer sea,” I, 187.

“Martyr of faith,” as it were, witness, II, 160.

“Martyrs of God’s promises,” I, 682.

**Meditari** — to foreshadow something future, I, 772, 782, 783, 785. “Meditation of the future,” as it were, an image of the future, I, 704. Meditation of the law was perfected in Christ, 782.

“The table of readings,” I, 481; of sacrifices, 253.

“Warfare of the body,” I, 445; of temptations, 389.

**Milia** — a word pertaining to travellers, I, 367.

The Son’s ministry in relation to the Father, I, 268, 269. The ministry of Wisdom in the creation of the world, II, 431.

**Ministeria poenae** — punishments’ ministries, for ministers of punishment, II, 355. “For ministries of vengeance,” as it were, for the punishment of evils, I, 113. “Ministries of Satan,” I, 346: the same as hostile and opposing powers, I, 345; or spiritual wickednesses in the heavens, 345, 347.

“It is remarkable how I understand,” II, 28.

God is of a mutable nature, II, 576.

“Moderated nature,” that is, finite, II, 314. *Moderatio*, for mode and measure, II, 359. “Defined moderation,” for a thing not infinite, II, 248.

“A delay unto the delay of war,” I, 89; and immediately afterward, from the Turin manuscript, “unto the delay of famine,” where the printed text has “unto death by famine.”

**Morosus** — slow, I, 21, 59. “Slow dissolution,” I, 422. “Slow explanations,” II, 282. “A not-slow account,” that is, one supplied without delay, II, 362.

**Mundipotentes** — powers of the world, I, 16, 483, note.

**Myrum confusionis** — myrrh of confusion, I, 519.

**Mysterium naturae** — mystery of nature, II, 128.

## N
For, meaning “indeed”: I, 229, 256, 418, 427; II, 52, 244, 434. The origin of those being born remains within the parts, II, 199; how, ibid. Wisdom, the Word, and Power were born from God into God, and, as Son, came to subsist in God with the substance of a true birth, 182. What is born from a living source has the progress of birth without novelty of nature, 198. “Christ to be born in man,” “to be born in a body,” and “to assume a body” are synonymous, I, 18, 109, 113. The Son of God born in man, II, 113. God born into man, 324. Man born into God, 325. Birth is the nature of being born, II, 142. The nature of birth, that is, the nature of that from which it is born, 258. Birth of divinity, 437. “Birth of God,” meaning the Son of God, 288. Birth of the human race, meaning human nature, I, 191; “our birth,” in the same sense, 111. Birth of nature, as natural birth, II, 185, 192, 194, 226. The birth of His own nature, that is, the Son of the Father, 287. The only-begotten birth of the unbegotten substance, 377. The only-begotten birth subsists in the only-begotten nature, 300. Birth did not follow so as to become co-born, 303. The birth of the Son ought to subsist from its author, 381. In being born into God, it subsists, ibid. If it had introduced any defect, that fault would rather be charged against the nature through which the birth subsisted, 284. He received what He was, and did not take away what He received, 140. Nor was the same God who was already there born; rather, God from God who was there was born, 141. God the Father is God of the Son’s birth and Father of His nature, 381. The subsisting birth did not make God to be of another nature, 285. The birth of God, which came forth from God into God, obtained what belonged and belongs to God, 142. It was not the God who remained who was born, but God was born from the abiding God, 142. Therefore, it was not what He was that was born; rather, God came forth born from and in those things which belonged to God, 142. Through the birth of the living nature from the Living One, God is in God, 207. Divine birth accomplishes its whole work under the ministry of the assumed body, 197.

The nature of begetting made Father and Son, I, 443. The nature through which birth subsists, II, 284. The nature of the author is co-born in the Son’s birth, 110. The begotten nature naturally had within itself the begetting nature, 298. The nature of God subsisted into the nature of God; that is, the Son was born from the Father, 188. A nature not alien from God subsisted, born into God, 382. It has in itself, and is not outside, that nature from which its birth remains, 196. The only-begotten nature is wholly from the Whole, 312. God’s nature from Himself, 207. God’s nature born into human nature, 117. A higher nature born into a lower one, 260. God’s nature, remaining itself, had taken our lowliness into itself, 299. It is one thing to be a nature, another to have assumed a nature, I, 563. The Father’s nature did not experience the assumption of flesh, II, 266. The slave-form is not Christ’s nature of genuine origin, 256. They worshipped a nature which might arise into something through accidental motions, II, 4. “Nature,” meaning a small quantity of loaves, 157. “Nature,” meaning natural quality, I, 717, 719. God’s nature is signified in glory, II, 246. The glory of nature is taken up into the glory of the nature that glorifies nature, 289. The nature of our assumed body was brought into the nature of the Father’s divinity, 399. To kindle in blind eyes the capacity of seeing, I, 129. The nature of the body is Christ’s word, II, 354. Natural God, II, 286. Natural necessities, that is, laws of nature, 412.

*Ne*, meaning “that not” or “in such a way that not”: I, 215; II, 16, 17, 24, 77, and frequently. *Ne non*, meaning “that not”: I, 307; II, 169, 276, 279. “It was necessary by admonition,” II, 398. “It is necessary by merits,” I, 382; by faith, 392. “It will be necessary by excision,” 401. “It is necessary: he will desire,” I, 251. “It is necessary: it must be believed,” 351. A necessity elicited, I, 599. Natural necessities, II, 412, 413. A doubled negation retaining negative force, I, 27, 110, and elsewhere. To neglect, meaning to leave behind, I, 759, 766. “No one [is] God,” as meaning “no other God,” II, 125. “I do not know whether,” I, 145. Ignorance, II, 310. Nests of rest, I, 701, 702; that is, places in which they may rest, 702. A natural name and a name arising from the will of the one naming, II, 182. An added and accidental name, 183. A title of honour, 184. “Name,” meaning cause and condemnation, 678, 681, 683. Household names, I, 599; names of kinship, 757; terms of endearment, 588. Kinships expressed by most affectionate names, 686, note. Names of human danger, II, 28; of truth, 136; of faith, I, 403; of boasting, 404. “It becomes known,” I, 237. Denominative terms, II, 258.

## O

Obedience of the will, as meaning obedience to the will, I, 505. “Obtained,” as meaning adventitious, II, 315. Dulling, II, 90, note. To preoccupy by an opinion of understanding, meaning to comprehend, II, 314. Change of offences, I, 514. To omit crimes, meaning to remit them, I, 779. “All flesh,” that is, persons from every class of humanity, I, 185. The fact that a few are faithful does not prevent all from being unbelievers, 149. “They ought,” I, 16, 562. “They ought to have,” II, 27. Opinion of productive powers, that is, the conception formed concerning created things, II, 441.

Origin, meaning that from which someone has arisen, II, 95, 220, 252; meaning principle, 145; meaning cause, I, 44. Origins of those who beget, II, 334. The cause of Gentile origins, 360. Origins of bodies brought forth, 330. To impart an origin, meaning to create, I, 38. The Son’s origin is from eternity; the Father is free from origin, II, 74. To receive an eternal origin from origin, 252. Mary did not give Christ’s body its origin, 331; for He Himself is the origin of His own body, 332. The body possessed an origin proper to itself, 339. The Holy Spirit introduced the origin of the Son of Man, 352. Begun, according to the power of the Spirit, for the origin of nature, ibid. The beginning of our origin was created in the image of unbounded eternity; that is, the soul was created in the image of the Word, I, 406. Conceived from the origin of our vices, II, 353. Original things, I, 487.

## P

The recompense of living bread, meaning eternal reward, I, 499. Living bread, used of the Eucharist and eternal blessedness, 478, note; 481, note. In the same papyrus, II, 140. Solomon’s Proverbs, I, 476. Division, II, 470. “The Passover which,” I, 589. The passion of condemnation, meaning the sentence by which Christ was condemned to suffer, I, 34.

The Father is called “He who is,” II, 64; “the One who is,” ibid.; “He Himself who is,” 46; “the One from whom [all is],” 74. He possesses the authority of unbegottenness, 74. The Father is author of Him whom He begot, 77, 78. He is Father to God the Son because the Son was born from Him into God, 96. The Father is greater, as unbegotten in relation to the begotten, I, 56; greater than the Son, 570. From those things which were unbegotten in Himself He begot the Only-Begotten, II, 51, imparting to His birth everything that is through love and power, ibid.; as He willed, He who had power, ibid. Parricide in the works of God, II, 63. The parricidal lie of Joseph’s brothers, I, 479. Paul is called from a persecutor of the Church, II, 99; from persecutor, apostle, 147, 166. “He impoverished Himself,” I, 257, 258. Sinner against heaven, I, 376. The body of sin, I, 174, 605. “To sin,” that is, attributing death to our body, II, 268. Christ’s enemies asserted the law of sin against Him, I, 245; that is, they asserted sin’s punishment, namely the law of death, ibid. Within the jurisdiction of conscience, II, 545. “Through this” or “through that,” as meaning “consequently,” II, 373, 375, and elsewhere. A foreign work, that is, one sent to persons absent, II, 620. To bring it about that one is God, II, 239. Of exhausted goodness, I, 680. Names of human danger, II, 28. A dangerous treasure, that is, one liable to perish, I, 690. “To remain” denotes remaining forever, I, 350; to remain denotes to inhere, 449. “He permits Himself into hearts,” as meaning “He admits Himself,” I, 499. Distinction of persons, II, 87, 88, 93, 95. The person of man in Christ, I, 118, 564. The person of the slave-form, 109, 564. Perseverance of hope, I, 443; of faith, 442. *Pharaoh*, even in oblique cases, I, 231, 232, 233; II, 181, note. The rock of Peter’s confession, II, 160. Weapons of punishments, I, 297; devices of punishments, II, 385. “They might repent,” I, 45, 54; “they might have repented,” 296; things to be repented of, 461, note. God’s repentance unto punishment, I, 54. Confession of repentance, 40, 43, 105. The former people, meaning that which belongs to the Law, I, 214. Power remaining within the body, that is, the Word, I, 708. “Rather not,” I, 160, 698; II, 19, 433. “Before your companions,” II, 385, note. Precept, meaning preconceived judgment, II, 391. God’s presence by His nature seems distinguished from His power present everywhere, I, 455. “About to grant,” II, 91. “Granted,” as meaning predetermined, I, 757. To pre-assume, meaning to assume, I, 480; II, 42. Transgressors of the Law, I, 372. The book of things past, I, 376. The presbyterium of the Roman Church, II, 681. God, ruler of His body and soul, II, 329; God, ruler of our origin, 333. Principal nature, that is, divine nature, I, 493. Principal commandment, II, 82, 183; what is principal in the Law, I, 558. The chief point is that the Father should be believed to be Father, II, 395. The Son’s chief property is to be born, 375. The most fundamental point of our faith, II, 471. The Father begot the Only-Begotten, II, 51. To advance toward a crime, II, 162; toward the spirit of Antichrist, 165; toward men of blood, as to reach the point of being men of blood, 145. This advances to the denial of faith, 133. By a fuller advance in doctrine, II, 88; toward which advance, 84. A confessed birth, II, 201. Confessed impiety, I, 407; II, 196. Confessed authority, 300. Inclined malice, I, 83. Inclined love of darkness, 28. Proper to Himself and solitary, II, 94. “More proper,” I, 317, 372. By the property of begetting, God remains unbegotten in Him whom He begot, II, 440; namely, in that which is from Himself and is His own, 441. In His own property—as Father and likewise as Son—He is one, II, 374. Providence, meaning the faculty of providing, I, 695. Public goodness, that is, goodness excluding no one, II, 688. “There is a struggle for the devil,” meaning that the devil strives, I, 353.

“I ask whether,” II, 111. “Who”: “He Himself who is, and whose He is,” II, 88. “Until,” I, 444, 553. “The same number,” I, 747, 767.

## S

A secular Sabbath, I, 270. Sacraments of the Church, I, 514. Sacrament of baptism, 237, 290, 550; of new birth, ibid., 270; of new generation, 495; of regeneration, II, 159, 167. Sacraments of baptism and the Spirit, I, 688. Sacrament of water and fire, 682. Sacrament of divine communion, 251. Sacrament of flesh and blood, II, 225. Sacraments of new grace, I, 708. Sacraments of human salvation, I, 348; II, 126. The sacraments of human salvation are brought to completion in the Father and Son through the power of regeneration, II, 126. # INDEX OF THE MATTERS CONTAINED IN THIS VOLUME

[Col. 1027] Preface to the books *On the Trinity*, 9–10. Summary of the following books from two manuscripts, 23–24.

# TWELVE BOOKS ON THE TRINITY

**BOOK I.**—Hilary, having set forth the philosophers’ opinions concerning blessedness and God, declares that a higher knowledge of God and a surer hope of immortality are supplied to us by the Scriptures, and especially by the Gospel of John. He then observes that heresies arose because men wished to confine God’s infinity within the limits of their own understanding. He proposes particularly to attack Arianism and Sabellianism. Finally, after warning the reader in what disposition sacred words, and his own statements about God, ought to be received, he sets forth the order and subjects of his books. 25.

**BOOK II.**—On the truth of the Trinity and the dignity and office of the individual persons; that the knowledge of so great a mystery handed down in baptism is sufficient; on the origin of heresies and heretics hostile to the faith of the Trinity. Hilary’s doctrine concerning God the Father. What the Son of God is and is not; and concerning heretics who wrongly complain that they cannot comprehend the mystery of that generation. An explanation of the divine generation of the Word. Faith founded upon the Scriptures is a medicine suited to cure every disease. Scriptural testimonies by which the opinions of Sabellius, Ebion, and Arius are refuted. That Christ, amid the very things which He is related to have endured for humanity’s sake, is truly shown to be God by certain indications of power and dignity. The Holy Spirit’s distinction from Father and Son, office, and divinity. 49.

**BOOK III.**—The eternal generation of the Word. Explanation of the words, “I am in the Father and the Father is in me.” That God can accomplish many incomprehensible things is shown from the miracles of water changed into wine and of the five loaves. Refutation of arguments by which heretics maintain that a birth from God is impossible. Commendation of simple and humble faith. 75.

**BOOK IV.**—That the Son of God is eternal and consubstantial with the Father; and that Moses’ words, “The Lord your God is one,” must be understood of unity of nature, not unity of person. Scriptural testimonies indicating that God is not solitary. That from the beginning of the world the Son of God made Himself visible to human beings in various ways, not through His own substance, since He is invisible and immutable, but through a creature subject to Him; and that God Himself truly spoke to Moses, Abraham, Hagar, and others who in the Old Testament are introduced as conversing with God. 95.

**BOOK V.**—Why this book is also called the second. The Arian heresy is woven so subtly that whoever agrees with it appears to deny the Son’s divinity, while whoever opposes it appears either to proclaim Father and Son as two Gods, or, in Sabellius’s manner, as one and the same. That the Son is true God; and in what respect Father and Son, distinct in person, are one God. 129.

**BOOK VI.**—The Arian plague, in Hilary’s time, had spread through nearly all the provinces of the Roman Empire and had acquired, as it were, public authority; it was therefore difficult to cure. The letter of the Arian party, already refuted from the Law and the Prophets in Book IV, is now more fully overthrown by the testimony of the Gospel and the Apostles; and the argument is refuted that, if anything is begotten from God, God must necessarily be corporeal. It is established from the words of God the Father, the Son, and the Apostles themselves that Christ is the true and natural—not adoptive—Son of God. 157.

**BOOK VII.**—The difficulty of combating the Arians. How Arius, Sabellius, and Photinus conquer or are conquered by one another to the Church’s advantage. He is God by nature who is by nature the Son of God. It is clear that Christ called Himself the Son of God—and consequently was so—from the fact that the Jews chiefly reproached Him for claiming God as His Father. Christ’s own words to the Jews prove both His birth from the Father and the unity of the Father’s nature. The anger aroused among the Jews by Christ’s words proves that they are indeed to be understood in the sense in which we understand them. 555.

**BOOK VIII.**—The natural unity of Father and Son. That knowledge and innocence are equally useful to a bishop. An exposition of the deceptive questions customarily used by Arians to mislead the simple. The slander of heretics, who boast that those who admit between Father and Son a unity distinct from harmony of will assert that They are discordant. Investigation of the passages of Scripture in which natural unity is affirmed. 234.

**BOOK IX.**—Confirmation of the arguments by which the unity of Father and Son in nature has been affirmed in the preceding books. Certain seeds of answers to objections borrowed by heretics from Scripture; and that the genuine sense of Scripture is to be sought not in the meaning of bare words detached from the rest, but from what precedes and follows and from the occasion of speaking. In Christ one must distinguish what He said or did before becoming man, what He said or did as man now about to die, and what He said or did as immortal. Refutation of the objection taken from Christ’s words: “Why do you call me good? No one is good but God.” How other passages of Scripture—“That they may know You, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom You sent …”; “The Father is greater than I”; and so forth—contribute nothing to the assertion of the Arian heresy. 278.

**BOOK X.**—Refutation of those who assert that in Christ there is no substance which did not suffer, hunger, thirst, and so forth. Exposition and refutation of the differing opinions into which those heretics divided. Christ’s wondrous conception is discussed in such a way that it is readily proved that our nature was assumed by the Word in its truth, without its destruction and without our vices. That Christ was sorrowful, prayed, and was strengthened by an angel, not for Himself but for the Apostles. The objection drawn from Christ’s cry that He had been abandoned by the Father is resolved. 343.

**BOOK XI.**—That there is no single faith among the Arians; and that, resisting unanswerable arguments, they seize upon the dispensation of the assumed body in order to insult divinity. Resolution of objections taken from words applying to Christ after the glory of His resurrection. Explanation of the Apostle’s words by which Arians think they prove that Christ, as servant, is to be subjected to the Father, is to surrender the power of His kingdom, and is to undergo abolition of nature. 398.

**BOOK XII.**—The assertion of Christ’s divine birth against the heretics’ customary statements: “He was not before He was born,” and “He was made from things that did not exist.” Explanation of the passage from Wisdom, “The Lord created me,” from the worship rendered to Christ, from the title Creator attributed to Him, from His being a form of God’s nature, and from His being begotten from the Father’s womb. The eternity of Christ’s birth. Answer to the objection, “If He was born, there was a time when He was not.” The difference between created and begotten. That Christ is called created in respect not of birth but of dispensation. An exposition of Hilary’s faith concerning Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. 433.

Preface to the book *On the Synods*, 471.

# BOOK ON THE SYNODS, OR THE FAITH OF THE EASTERNERS

He congratulates the bishops of Gaul on their refusal of communion with Saturninus. The occasion, difficulty, usefulness, arrangement, and aim of the work. 479–485. Mutual suspicions of Easterners and Gauls. The formula of Sirmium. An example of blasphemy written at Sirmium by Hosius and Potamius. 485–487. Definition of essence and substance. The Synod of Ancyra. The true distinction of the Son from the Father and Their consubstantiality. Explanation of difficulties. 487–497. Since the Son is born, He is neither the Father Himself nor anything other than the Father. How cautiously the two heresies are destroyed in opposition to the Son of God. The Son coeternal with the Father. Though timeless, the Son is not unbegotten. The rationale of these definitions. Exposition of the ecclesiastical faith set forth at the synod held upon the completion of the dedication of the church of Antioch. In what respect this faith is suspect. It is defended from the council’s purpose. In what sense three substances in the Trinity are rightly spoken of among Easterners. The distinction between birth and unbegottenness. 497–504.

Faith according to the Eastern synod. This faith establishes the Son’s eternal origin. God is only one: in what sense more than one may be spoken of. Faith, in proclaiming unity of substance in God, nevertheless does not teach that God is solitary. 504–509. Example of the faith written by Easterners at Sirmium against Photinus. Photinus’s manifold deception is refuted. The Son differs from the Father neither in substance nor in time. 509–514. Expansion and contraction do not apply to God, and consequently the Son is not an expansion of the divine substance. The sense in which heretics call the Son of God the Word. The Son, distinguished from the Father by birth alone, was not changed by assuming flesh. When the Son of God was crucified, divinity did not suffer corruption. What passibility and passion are. He is not a part of either Father or Son. “There is no God besides me” does not deny that the Son is God. The Son is from substance, not, like creatures, from will. 514–521.

The Son’s unbegottenness is incompatible with God’s unity. Faith in the East. Westerners do not know the written faith. Hilary’s faith concerning Father and Son. The author passes to the second part of the book: he is not to be judged before the end. When *homoousion* may rightly be proclaimed. Three erroneous senses of the same term. *Homoousion* may both be spoken and omitted piously. Those who confess likeness without equality are refuted. 521–530. Praise of the Easterners for restraining heresy. The deceit of the authors of the Sirmian formula. A letter brought from Sirmium concerning the exposition of *homoousion* and *homoiousion*. The purpose and authority of the Nicene Synod. The rejection of *homoousion* by eighty bishops is weak against its approval by three hundred. What Hilary understands by *homoousion*. The faith of Ancyra, with certain matters suppressed, brought to Sirmium. Exhortation to receive *homoousion*. 521–546.

# APOLOGETIC REPLIES TO THE CRITICS OF THE BOOK ON THE SYNODS

546. Notice concerning the following letter and hymn appended to it, 547. Saint Hilary’s letter to his daughter Abra, 549. A hymn sent to her by him, 551. Critical judgment on another hymn wrongly attributed to Hilary, 553. Notice concerning the following book, ibid.

# TWO BOOKS OF SAINT HILARY TO THE EMPEROR CONSTANTIUS AUGUSTUS
## BOOK ONE

That the Churches should not be oppressed by their brethren. That secular judges should not hear cases concerning clerics. The voice of oppressed Catholics. Prayers for the king. That pious priests should return to their sees. The cruelty of the Arians. Judicial procedure was not observed in the case of Athanasius. The unjust condemnation of Eusebius of Vercelli. 557

Notice introducing Book Two. 563

### BOOK TWO

Hilary in the presence of the emperor. He is in communion with the Churches of Gaul. Though exiled by a faction, he is assured of his innocence. He asks to be heard, with the author of his exile present. Constantius wishes to hear the faith from bishops, yet does not hear it. Why so many creeds are written. The Gospel faith is corrupted. One must return to the faith confessed at baptism. Hilary asks to be heard, intending to demonstrate the faith from the Scriptures. Heretics draw the Scriptures to support their own side. Pledge of the discourse to come. Ibid.

Preliminary dissertation on the book Against Constantius. 571

### BOOK AGAINST CONSTANATIUS [Col. 1030]

Exhortation to contend for the faith. How Hilary, in defending the faith, always devoted himself to peace and moderation. He speaks not from impatience, but from Christian freedom. He longs for the times of persecutors. What sort of persecution that of Constantius was. Hilary clears himself of the suspicion of reviling. Constantius is compared with Nero and Constantius. The relics of martyrs are to be venerated. The Lord’s name is in the words of Constantius, not in his deeds; he has the sheep’s clothing, but the deeds of a wolf. On the Synod of Seleucia. Blasphemies publicly recited. In what sense those who deny likeness condemn unlikeness. The Scriptures hand down that the Son is equal to the Father. The confession, “Like according to the Scriptures,” is deceitful. Nowhere is bare likeness preached concerning the Son. Once the Son’s equality has been set forth, likeness may be preached. Constantius’ inconstancy in faith. There is no faith where there is not one faith. Constantius’ violence against the Easterners and Africans. The Arians declare war on the dead. 577

Supplement from the books On the Trinity. 603

Notice introducing the book Against Auxentius. 605

### BOOK AGAINST THE ARIANS, OR AUXENTIUS

Hilary vainly attempts to establish true peace. Many antichrists. Violence imposed upon faith is condemned. The opinions of Auxentius, Valens, and others concerning Christ. Hilary’s proceedings with Auxentius at Milan. Auxentius evades in writing the faith which he had confessed. When Hilary exposes Auxentius’ fraud, he is ordered to depart. One should not have excessive attachment to church walls. An example of Auxentius’ blasphemy. Auxentius is called a heretic. He sets forth his faith. He adheres to the Creed of Rimini. 609

Preface to the fragments of Saint Hilary. 619

The old arrangement of the Fragments compared with the new. 625

### FRAGMENTS FROM A BOOK OF SAINT HILARY, IN WHICH ARE CONTAINED ALL THE MATTERS THAT SHOW HOW, FOR WHAT REASONS, AND AT WHOSE INSTIGATION, UNDER THE EMPEROR CONSTANATIUS, THE COUNCIL OF RIMINI WAS HELD AGAINST THE FORMULA OF THE NICENE TREATISE, IN WHICH ALL HERESIES HAD BEEN COMPREHENDED

627

### FRAGMENT I

The excellence of faith, hope, and charity. The merit of faith, the nature of hope, the affection of charity. Charity urges Hilary not to remain silent about the perversity of heretics. What kind of work he undertakes and what he omits from it. 627

### FRAGMENT II

Model letter of the Synod of Sardica to all the Churches.

“Causes of the Synod. The Eusebians fear to attend the Synod. How great their crimes are. Having entered Sardica, they dread the presence of their opponents. Athanasius’ innocence is established. Marcellus and Asclepas are blameless. The crimes, names, and devices of the Eusebians. The judgment of the Synod.”

Model letter sent by the Synod of Sardica to Pope Julius.

“Why Julius was not present at the Synod. The prerogative of Peter’s see. Julius’ legates. Three matters to be dealt with in the Synod. The perversity of Ursacius and Valens. The Synod’s decisions are to be made known through Julius to Sicily, Sardinia, and Italy. Names of heretics, and likewise of bishops who attended the Synod of Sardica.”

Athanasius’ innocence; the condemnation of Photinus; the repentance of Ursacius and Valens. Model letter of Valens and Ursacius to Pope Julius. Model of another letter of Valens and Ursacius to Athanasius.

“Athanasius separates Marcellus from his communion. Those Easterners who attempt to render the acts of Sardica void. The Sirmian rescript, full of deceit. The faith composed at Nicaea.” 632

### FRAGMENT III

Decree of the Eastern Synod.

“A feigned love for preserving unity and tradition. The doctrine of Marcellus. Marcellus, condemned by many bishops, is received into communion: communion must be denied to him. Crimes fabricated against Athanasius; his return from exile. Athanasius’ alleged misdeeds: he is received by Julius and the bishops of Italy. Those deposed by the Arians defend themselves. The beginnings of the Council of Sardica. The Easterners’ efforts to have Athanasius and others expelled from the Synod. They complain that those whom they proclaim criminal have been granted communion. They shift the odium of schism onto the Westerners. The judgments of synods are not to be reconsidered. Why they condemn the leading Westerners.” 638

### FRAGMENT IV

Model letter of Liberius to the Easterners.

“Liberius is in communion with the Easterners, but not with Athanasius.”

This letter was falsely fabricated. Why. 678

### FRAGMENT V

Letter sent to the Emperor Constantius by the legates of Liberius, bishop of the city of Rome, through Bishop Lucifer:

“Liberius demands a council. He is falsely accused of suppressing the Easterners’ letters. He clears himself of accusations fabricated against him by Constantius. Why he cannot communicate with the Easterners.”

### FRAGMENT VI

Letter of Liberius, before he went into exile, to confessors who were in exile.

“Liberius congratulates the exiles. He wishes to learn from them the proceedings at Milan.”

Another letter of Liberius concerning Vincent of Capua, to Caecilianus of Spoleto.

“He grieves over Vincent’s fall.”

Liberius [Col. 1031] condemns Athanasius, as is confirmed by three letters of his which are adduced. 686

### FRAGMENT VII

Model letter of Constantius to the Italian bishops who had assembled at the Council of Rimini.

“In the council only faith is to be discussed, not the cases of the Easterners.”

A Catholic definition adopted by all the Catholic bishops before, terrified by earthly power, they joined the fellowship of heretics. Condemnation of blasphemy and exposition of the whole and Catholic faith. 696

### FRAGMENT VIII

Letter of the Council of Rimini to Constantius, in which the bishops departed from the true faith.

“The Synod of Rimini decrees that nothing is to be innovated; it asks Constantius to receive its decrees.”

Proceedings of the legates. 699

### FRAGMENT IX

Letter sent to Constantius by faithless bishops.

“They reject the term *substance*. They ask to be dismissed from Rimini.” 703

### FRAGMENT X

Letter of the Eastern bishops, given to the legates after their return from Rimini. The legates of Rimini are charged with perfidy. Those who exposed the perfidy. Those who do not wish the Son to be like the other creatures; those who wish him to be from God; those who wish him to be eternal; why they say, “like according to the Scriptures.” What their crime is. 705

### FRAGMENT XI

The Catholic faith set forth at the city of Paris by the Gallican bishops to the Eastern bishops.

“The deceit of heretics. In what sense it embraces *homoousion* in synods. It does not reject *homoousion*. The Son before time. Inferior to the Father in the form of a servant. Those who fell retract what they had done and condemn the authors of error.”

Letter of Eusebius to Gregory, bishop of Spain. 710

### FRAGMENT XII

Letter of Liberius to the Catholic bishops of Italy.

“Some do not wish those who fell at Rimini to be forgiven. On what grounds he grants forgiveness.”

Model letter of the bishops of Italy.

“The Italians, having annulled the decisions of Rimini, return themselves to the Nicene faith.” 714

### FRAGMENT XIII

Letter of Bishop Germinius against the Arians. 717

### FRAGMENT XIV

Model letter of Valens, Ursacius, and others to Germinius.

“Germinius is accused because he defends *homoiousion*. His recantation is demanded.” 718

### FRAGMENT XV

Germinius’ reply to Rufinianus, Palladius, and the others.

“That the Son is like the Father in all things is taught by tradition and the Scriptures. Those who put forward contrary assertions must explain them. The inconstancy of Valens, and the occasion of the creed published by Marcus of Arethusa.” 719

### DISSERTATIONS ON HILARY’S LETTER, OR SHORT TREATISE

First Dissertation, on these words of Hilary’s Letter: “So that even that which was afterward fashioned on our account.” 825

Second Dissertation, on these words of chapter V: “The Son of God, God the artificer, governed [creation] at the Father’s command.” Likewise on the words of the same chapter: “God the Father had commanded; the Son, Power itself, had undertaken the command without delay; for together with the command the work stood ready.” Finally, on these words: “And since all things were formed by the Father’s command, with the Word obeying.” 839

Third Dissertation, on these words of chapter V: “He also granted that man should form the image of God on earth, intending later to give the likeness, if the image were kept unharmed. Do not suppose that this image is the outward form of man that was made,” etc. 848

Question II: In what this image and likeness consist. 851
